nodes.title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
nodes.summary: Ophthalmologic emergency — IOP 50-80 mmHg causes optic nerve damage within hours
nodes.body: Ophthalmologic emergency — rapid IOP elevation causes optic nerve damage within hours. Mechanism: Pupillary block → aqueous outflow obstruction → IOP 50-80 mmHg Classic Triad: 1. Severe unilateral eye pain 2. Fixed mid-dilated pupil 3. Rock-hard globe Risk Factors: - Age >50 (peak 55-65) - Female (2-4x higher) - Asian > Caucasian - Hyperopia (farsightedness) - Shallow anterior chamber - Precipitat

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Fixed mid-dilated pupil + rock-hard globe = AACG until proven otherwise
nodes.body: Does the patient have features suggestive of AACG? Symptoms: - Sudden severe unilateral eye pain - Headache (may mimic migraine) - Blurred vision / decreased acuity - Halos around lights (pathognomonic) - Nausea and vomiting (prominent — may mimic GI illness) Exam Findings: - Fixed mid-dilated pupil (4-6mm, non-reactive) - Red eye with ciliary flush - Corneal edema (hazy/cloudy) - "Rock hard" glob

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Distinguish AACG from mimics — fixed mid-dilated pupil and hard globe are key differentiators
nodes.body: AACG Mimics — Rule Out: | Condition | Key Distinguishing Features | |-----------|----------------------------| | Migraine | Mobile pain, normal pupils, normal IOP | | Cluster headache | Lacrimation, rhinorrhea, Horner syndrome | | Intracranial pathology | Other neuro findings, papilledema | | Iritis/Uveitis | Photophobia, cells/flare, CONSTRICTED pupil | | Conjunctivitis | Discharge, bilateral, no

nodes.title: IOP Assessment
nodes.summary: Rock hard globe + classic presentation — treat empirically even without tonometry
nodes.body: Intraocular Pressure Measurement: | Status | IOP (mmHg) | |--------|------------| | Normal | 10-21 | | Elevated | 22-30 | | AACG typical | 50-80 | | Treatment target | <35 | Measurement Methods: 1. Tonometry (Gold Standard): - Goldmann applanation - Tono-Pen - iCare rebound tonometer 2. Transpalpebral Palpation (No Equipment): - Patient looks down - Palpate through upper lid - Compare both eyes -

nodes.title: IOP Result
nodes.summary: IOP ≥40 or rock hard globe = begin treatment cascade immediately
nodes.body: What is the IOP (or clinical assessment)? If tonometry available, use measured value. If not, use clinical palpation assessment.

nodes.title: Subacute Angle Closure
nodes.summary: Subacute angle closure — start topical therapy, urgent (not emergent) ophthalmology within 24h
nodes.body: IOP 22-39 mmHg — May be subacute or intermittent angle closure: Characteristics: - Less severe symptoms - May have history of intermittent episodes - Symptoms resolve spontaneously then recur - Cornea may be clearer Management: - Start topical therapy (timolol, brimonidine) - Acetazolamide 250mg PO - Urgent (not emergent) ophthalmology consult - Monitor for progression If IOP rises or symptoms wor

nodes.title: Immediate Actions
nodes.summary: Position supine, bright lights, call ophthalmology STAT, antiemetics — do NOT delay meds
nodes.body: Phase 1 — First 5 Minutes: 1. Position Patient SUPINE: - Moves lens posteriorly - Relieves pupil block - Increases anterior chamber depth 2. Bright Lights: - Constricts pupil - May help open angle 3. Call Ophthalmology STAT: - Do NOT delay treatment while awaiting consult - Definitive treatment is laser iridotomy 4. IV Access + Labs: - BMP (for acetazolamide, mannitol) - Consider glucose if giving

nodes.title: Phase 2: Reduce Aqueous Production
nodes.summary: Give acetazolamide 500mg IV + timolol + brimonidine simultaneously — recheck IOP in 30-60 min
nodes.body: Give ALL of these simultaneously: | Drug | Class | Dose | Route | |------|-------|------|-------| | Acetazolamide | CAI | 500mg | IV preferred (PO if no IV/not vomiting) | | Timolol 0.5% | Beta-blocker | 1 drop | Topical q15-30min × 2-3 | | Brimonidine 0.15% | Alpha-2 agonist | 1 drop | Topical q15min × 2-3 | OR substitute Apraclonidine 0.5-1% for brimonidine Acetazolamide Contraindications: - Sul

nodes.title: Response Assessment
nodes.summary: IOP must drop below 40 before pilocarpine will work — assess response at 30-60 min
nodes.body: Recheck IOP 30-60 minutes after initial therapy. Target: IOP <40 mmHg (to enable pilocarpine) What is the IOP response?

nodes.title: Phase 3: Osmotic Agents
nodes.summary: Mannitol 1-2 g/kg IV for refractory IOP — avoid in CHF, renal failure, severe dehydration
nodes.body: IOP still elevated — add osmotic therapy: | Drug | Dose | Route | Onset | Cautions | |------|------|-------|-------|----------| | Mannitol 20% | 1-2 g/kg | IV over 20-30 min | 30-60 min | CHF, renal failure | | Glycerol | 1 mL/kg | PO (mix with cold juice) | 30-60 min | Diabetes (caloric) | | Isosorbide | 1.5 g/kg | PO | 30-60 min | Less common | Mannitol Preferred if IV access and no contraindica

nodes.title: Response to Osmotics
nodes.summary: Reassess IOP after osmotics — if still elevated, ophthalmology for paracentesis
nodes.body: Recheck IOP after osmotic therapy. Goal: IOP <40 mmHg for pilocarpine.

nodes.title: Phase 4: Pilocarpine
nodes.summary: Pilocarpine ONLY after IOP <40 — ischemic sphincter will not respond at higher pressures
nodes.body: ⚠️ TIMING CRITICAL — Wait until IOP <40 mmHg Why wait? - Ischemic iris sphincter muscle won't respond at high IOP - Giving early is ineffective and wastes time Pilocarpine 2% (or 4%): - 1 drop to affected eye - Repeat in 15 minutes × 2 doses total Mechanism: - Constricts pupil (miosis) - Pulls iris away from trabecular meshwork - Opens drainage angle Also treat FELLOW EYE: - Pilocarpine 2% 1 drop

nodes.title: Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Ongoing pain control, prednisolone, antiemetics — continue all IOP drops until laser iridotomy
nodes.body: Ongoing Management: Pain Control: - IV opioids as needed - Topical NSAID (ketorolac 0.5%) after cornea assessed Anti-inflammatory: - Prednisolone acetate 1% q1-4h - Reduces inflammation from IOP spike Antiemetics: - Ondansetron 4-8mg IV PRN Monitoring: - Recheck IOP every 30-60 minutes - Document pupil reactivity - Assess corneal clarity Maintenance Therapy (After IOP Controlled): - Continue timol

nodes.title: Refractory AACG
nodes.summary: Refractory AACG — do NOT discharge, ophthalmology must perform paracentesis or surgery
nodes.body: IOP remains elevated despite maximal medical therapy: Options (Ophthalmology Decision): 1. Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: - Immediate IOP reduction - Specialist procedure - Temporizing until laser available 2. Emergent Laser Peripheral Iridotomy: - If cornea clear enough - May need to wait for corneal edema to resolve 3. Surgical Iridectomy: - If laser not possible - OR availability required 4. Le

nodes.title: Bilateral AACG — Think Drugs
nodes.summary: Bilateral AACG = drug-induced (topiramate) — use cycloplegics, NOT pilocarpine; iridotomy ineffective
nodes.body: ⚠️ Bilateral angle closure is RARE naturally — suspect medication-induced: Topiramate (Most Common): - Causes ciliary body effusion (NOT pupillary block) - Bilateral presentation - Myopic shift (up to -17 diopters) - Occurs 1-2 weeks after starting Management of Topiramate-Induced: 1. STOP TOPIRAMATE (coordinate with prescriber) 2. Cycloplegics (atropine) — OPPOSITE of standard AACG! 3. Iridotomy

nodes.title: Medications That Precipitate AACG
nodes.summary: Common precipitants: anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, antihistamines, SSRIs, TCAs — ask about OTCs
nodes.body: Pupillary Block Mechanism (Cause Mydriasis): | Class | Examples | |-------|----------| | Anticholinergics | Atropine, scopolamine, ipratropium, glycopyrrolate | | Sympathomimetics | Phenylephrine, ephedrine, pseudoephedrine | | Antihistamines | Diphenhydramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine | | TCAs | Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine | | SSRIs/SNRIs | Fluoxetine, paroxetine, venlafaxine | | An

nodes.title: Definitive Treatment
nodes.summary: Laser iridotomy is definitive — treat BOTH eyes (fellow eye 40-80% risk of AACG)
nodes.body: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): Mechanism: - Creates hole in peripheral iris - Bypasses pupillary block - Equalizes pressure between anterior/posterior chambers Timing: - Once cornea clears (hours to 1-2 days after IOP controlled) - Outpatient procedure - Takes minutes Both Eyes: - Treat affected eye - Prophylactic LPI to fellow eye (40-80% will develop AACG) Alternatives: - Surgical iridectomy

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition based on IOP control and ophthalmology availability
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition:

nodes.title: Controlled — Admit/Urgent Follow-Up
nodes.summary: IOP controlled — admit if osmotics needed, discharge with 24h follow-up if drops-only
nodes.body: IOP controlled with medical therapy: Admission Indications: - IOP required osmotics to control - Significant comorbidities - Unreliable follow-up - Awaiting laser iridotomy Observation Unit / Discharge with 24h Follow-Up: - IOP well controlled on drops alone - Reliable patient - Ophthalmology available next day Discharge Medications: - Timolol 0.5% BID - Brimonidine TID - Prednisolone acetate 1% Q

nodes.title: Transfer Required
nodes.summary: Transfer if no ophthalmology — continue all IOP therapy, keep supine during transport
nodes.body: No ophthalmology or refractory IOP — arrange transfer: Before Transfer: - Continue all IOP-lowering therapy - Adequate IV access - Pain and nausea controlled - Clear documentation of treatments given and IOP trend Transfer Communication: - IOP at presentation and current - All medications given with times - Response to therapy - Suspected etiology (medication-induced?) Mode of Transport: - Ground

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge only if IOP <21, symptoms resolved, 24h ophthalmology follow-up confirmed
nodes.body: May discharge if ALL criteria met: Clinical: - IOP normalized (<21 mmHg) - Symptoms resolved - Subacute/intermittent presentation - Cornea clearing Logistics: - Ophthalmology follow-up confirmed within 24 hours - Reliable patient - Access to return if worsening - Can obtain/afford medications Discharge Medications: - Timolol 0.5% BID - Brimonidine 0.15% TID - Prednisolone 1% QID - ± Acetazolamide

nodes.title: Abdominal Pain — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Gestalt sick check + vitals trend + 4-question screen. If unstable: resuscitate in parallel with workup.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Ruptured AAA \u2014 age \u226550 + back/flank pain, pulsatile mass, syncope. 2. Mesenteric ischemia \u2014 pain out of proportion to exam, AF/vascular disease. 3. Ruptured ectopic \u2014 positive \u03B2-hCG + pain/shock. 4. Perforated viscus \u2014 rigid peritonitic abdomen, free air. 5. Inferior MI / aortic dissection presenting as epigastric pain \u2014 get an ECG.

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Differential
nodes.summary: Pick the most acute differential; walk its instrument to an explicit verdict. Excluded loops back.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous causes to an explicit verdict, one at a time. Each differential walks its instrument (score or imaging) to excluded, test further, or rule in + treat. Excluded loops back here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Aortic Catastrophe — Bedside US Gate
nodes.summary: Bedside aorta US: \u22653 cm + symptoms = rupture pathway; <3 cm normal = excluded.
nodes.body: In age \u226550 with new abdominal / back / flank pain, the aorta is the instrument. Point-of-care aorta US is ~98% sensitive for AAA presence and takes <5 min. A pulsatile mass has poor sensitivity (~50%) \u2014 its absence does NOT rule out AAA. - Aorta \u22653 cm + symptoms, or any instability / syncope with back pain \u2192 rupture pathway. - Aorta <3 cm and normal, low suspicion \u2192 AAA ef

nodes.title: Ruptured / Symptomatic AAA — Treat
nodes.body: Open Aortic Aneurysm. Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, type and CROSS 4-6 units (not just type-and-screen). - Permissive hypotension \u2014 target SBP 70-90 mmHg if active rupture; over-resuscitation worsens bleeding. - Activate massive transfusion protocol if unstable + rupture suspected. - Vascular surgery + IR (for EVAR) now \u2014 do NOT delay consult for confirmatory CT if unstable with
nodes.recommendation: Bedside US, type and cross, permissive hypotension, vascular + IR before imaging if unstable.

nodes.title: AAA — Excluded by Bedside US
nodes.body: A normal aorta on an adequate POCUS study makes AAA very unlikely. Document the diameter. Before leaving the aorta, make sure dissection is not the story \u2014 tearing pain, inter-arm BP differential, pulse deficit, or a widened mediastinum needs CTA regardless of aortic diameter. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: AAA excluded by POCUS; document diameter and reconsider dissection before moving on.

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia — Pretest Probability Gate
nodes.summary: Pretest probability + CTA. Normal lactate does not exclude. High suspicion = image now.
nodes.body: There is no validated exclusion score \u2014 this is a pretest-probability + CTA diagnosis. Suspect it with pain out of proportion to a benign exam plus an embolic source (AF, recent MI, valve disease) or vascular risk. A normal lactate does NOT rule it out early \u2014 lactate rises only after transmural infarction.

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia — Image + Treat
nodes.body: Open Mesenteric Ischemia. Next 5 minutes: - CTA mesenteric (arterial + venous phases) \u2014 do not delay for renal function unless eGFR <30; the diagnosis is more dangerous than the contrast. - Vascular surgery + IR early \u2014 endovascular or open intervention within hours. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics (transmural ischemia \u2192 bacterial translocation). - Fluid resuscitation, NPO, anticoagula
nodes.recommendation: CTA now, vascular + IR early, heparin per vascular. Normal lactate does not exclude \u2014 image anyway.

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia — Low Probability
nodes.body: With a benign exam, no vascular / embolic risk, and pain that fits the exam, mesenteric ischemia is unlikely and does not warrant immediate CTA. Do not anchor on "GI bug" or "ileus" in an AF patient with severe pain and minimal findings \u2014 if that picture emerges, come back and image. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Low probability; no immediate CTA. Re-image if out-of-proportion pain or vascular risk emerges.

nodes.title: Pelvic Emergency — \u03B2-hCG Gate
nodes.summary: \u03B2-hCG on every reproductive-age female. Positive = ectopic pathway; concerning = US now.
nodes.body: \u03B2-hCG (urine or serum) on EVERY reproductive-age female with abdominal/pelvic pain. The result forks the pathway.

nodes.title: Pelvic Emergency — Image + Treat
nodes.body: If \u03B2-hCG POSITIVE: open First Trimester Bleeding. Transvaginal US to locate IUP vs no IUP; OB consult with a low threshold \u2014 ruptured ectopic kills in minutes; type and cross for any hemodynamic concern; avoid pelvic exam before US if rupture suspected. If \u03B2-hCG NEGATIVE with concern: - Ovarian torsion \u2014 pelvic US with Doppler (sensitivity ~70-85%; clinical concern overrides a
nodes.recommendation: Positive \u03B2-hCG = ectopic pathway + OB. Negative + concern = pelvic US Doppler; clinical concern overrides negative US for torsion.

nodes.title: Pelvic Emergency — Excluded
nodes.body: Negative \u03B2-hCG with a benign pelvic exam and no torsion / TOA features makes an immediate pelvic surgical emergency unlikely. Do not discharge a reproductive-age female without a documented \u03B2-hCG and a pelvic exam (or documented reason it was deferred). Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Pelvic emergency excluded; document \u03B2-hCG and pelvic exam before discharge.

nodes.title: Perforated Viscus — Peritonitis Gate
nodes.summary: Peritonitis + sepsis or free air = perforation pathway; soft abdomen = unlikely.
nodes.body: Rigid / board-like abdomen + sepsis physiology + free air = perforation until proven otherwise. Etiology: peptic ulcer (most common), diverticular, malignancy, ischemic, iatrogenic, appendiceal.

nodes.title: Perforated Viscus — Surgical Emergency
nodes.body: Emergent surgical consult \u2014 do not delay for confirmatory CT if the patient is septic with peritoneal signs. The CT can run in parallel. Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, LR/NS 1-2 L bolus, type and CROSS 4 units. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV, OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV. - NPO, NG tube if obstructive features, Foley + UOP.
nodes.recommendation: Emergent surgical consult, broad-spectrum abx within 1 h, CT in parallel, reverse anticoagulation.

nodes.title: Perforated Viscus — Unlikely
nodes.body: A soft, non-peritonitic abdomen without free air makes perforation unlikely at this moment. Peritonitis can evolve \u2014 if the exam changes on reassessment, come back and treat as perforation. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Perforation unlikely now; re-examine and re-image if peritoneal signs evolve.

nodes.title: Above-the-Belt Mimic — ECG Gate
nodes.summary: ECG on every older epigastric-pain patient. Inferior STE / dissection / Boerhaave features = treat.
nodes.body: Get an ECG on every middle-aged-or-older patient with epigastric pain, especially with diaphoresis, dyspnea, or nausea. Inferior MI, aortic dissection, and Boerhaave all masquerade as "abdominal" pain.

nodes.title: Thoracic Catastrophe — Treat
nodes.body: Inferior STEMI: open STEMI. ST elevation II/III/aVF \u2014 get right-sided leads (V4R); RV infarction needs fluid loading and nitroglycerin is contraindicated. Aspirin 325 mg chewed, cath activation. Aortic dissection: CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis; rate before pressure \u2014 esmolol/labetalol to HR ~60 BEFORE a vasodilator; cardiothoracic surgery. Do NOT anticoagulate. Boerhaave (esophageal rupture):
nodes.recommendation: Inferior MI \u2192 STEMI pathway (V4R, no nitrate if RV). Dissection \u2192 rate before pressure + CTA. Boerhaave \u2192 water-soluble contrast CT + surgery.

nodes.title: Thoracic Mimic — Unlikely
nodes.body: A non-ischemic ECG with no dissection or Boerhaave features makes a thoracic catastrophe unlikely as the driver. Keep a single troponin + repeat ECG if the story is at all concerning. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Thoracic mimic unlikely; repeat ECG / troponin if the story is concerning.

nodes.title: Appendicitis — Alvarado Gate
nodes.summary: Alvarado score. \u22654 or high suspicion = image/surgery; \u22643 with benign exam = low probability.
nodes.body: Classic sequence: anorexia \u2192 periumbilical pain \u2192 migration to RLQ over 6-24 h \u2192 vomiting AFTER pain (reverse order favors gastroenteritis). Open Alvarado in the toolbar to risk-stratify (analgesia does NOT mask the exam \u2014 that dogma is dead).

nodes.title: Appendicitis — Image + Treat
nodes.body: Open Adult Appendicitis (pediatric \u2192 Pediatric Appendicitis). Next 5 minutes: - CBC, CMP, lipase, UA, \u03B2-hCG (always in reproductive-age female); IV access + analgesia. - Imaging by profile: US first (lean / young / female / pregnant); CT first (older / obese / equivocal); MRI (no gad) for pregnant if US non-diagnostic. - Surgical consult early in high pretest probability \u2014 do not wa
nodes.recommendation: Alvarado-driven imaging by patient profile; surgical consult early; preop antibiotics within 1 h.

nodes.title: Appendicitis — Low Probability
nodes.body: A low Alvarado with a reassuring exam makes appendicitis unlikely; consider a short period of observation with a serial exam rather than immediate CT in a young low-risk patient. US non-visualization of the appendix is NOT a negative study \u2014 escalate if suspicion persists. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Low probability; serial exam / observe rather than reflex CT. US non-visualization is not negative.

nodes.title: Biliary — RUQ Gate
nodes.summary: RUQ US + labs incl lipase. Cholangitis = abx + ERCP; cholecystitis = abx + surgery; colic = outpatient.
nodes.body: Recognize the spectrum: biliary colic (intermittent post-fatty-meal pain, afebrile, normal labs) \u2192 cholecystitis (Murphy + fever + leukocytosis, US wall thickening/pericholecystic fluid) \u2192 cholangitis (Charcot: fever + jaundice + RUQ pain; Reynolds adds shock + AMS). Get CBC, CMP, lipase (overlap with pancreatitis), and RUQ US.

nodes.title: Biliary Disease — Treat
nodes.body: Open Gallbladder Disease (biliary colic \u2192 cholecystitis \u2192 cholangitis with Tokyo grading). Cholangitis is a surgical/GI emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics (pip-tazo, or ceftriaxone + metronidazole), blood cultures \u00D7 2, GI consult for emergent ERCP within 24 h \u2014 source control is the priority. Acute cholecystitis: antibiotics + surgical consult for cholecystectomy; percutaneo
nodes.recommendation: Cholangitis \u2192 abx within 1 h + urgent ERCP. Cholecystitis \u2192 abx + surgery. Check lipase in all RUQ pain.

nodes.title: Biliary Colic — Outpatient
nodes.body: Uncomplicated biliary colic: afebrile, normal WBC, normal LFTs, normal or gallstones-only US. PO challenge, analgesia, antiemetic, and outpatient cholecystectomy referral with strict return precautions (fever, jaundice, persistent pain). Do not discharge RUQ pain without checking lipase (pancreatitis overlap) and at least a CBC + CMP if any fever, jaundice, or rebound. Return to the hub if another
nodes.recommendation: Biliary colic \u2192 PO challenge + outpatient surgery referral. Confirm lipase and LFTs are clean first.

nodes.title: Pancreatitis — Atlanta + BISAP Gate
nodes.summary: Atlanta 2-of-3 (lipase >3x ULN). BISAP for severity. Normal lipase + atypical pain = unlikely.
nodes.body: Atlanta diagnosis needs 2 of 3: (1) classic pain (epigastric, band-like, radiates to back, better leaning forward), (2) lipase >3\u00D7 ULN, (3) imaging consistent with pancreatitis. If diagnosed, open BISAP in the toolbar to triage severity (ICU vs floor).

nodes.title: Acute Pancreatitis — Treat
nodes.body: Open Acute Pancreatitis. Next 5 minutes: - Goal-directed fluids \u2014 LR preferred over NS (less SIRS); target UOP 0.5-1 mL/kg/h, HR <120, MAP >65. - Labs: lipase, CBC, CMP, triglycerides, ionized calcium, magnesium, ABG, lactate, type and screen. - RUQ US for a gallstone source (commonest etiology). - Analgesia (opioid PRN \u2014 the "morphine causes sphincter of Oddi spasm" concern is not clini
nodes.recommendation: LR resuscitation + early enteral nutrition + BISAP severity. Image for gallstone source; check ionized calcium.

nodes.title: Pancreatitis — Unlikely
nodes.body: A normal lipase with atypical pain makes acute pancreatitis unlikely (lipase >3\u00D7 ULN is one of the Atlanta pillars). If pain is classic but lipase is borderline, imaging can still satisfy the criteria. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Pancreatitis unlikely with normal lipase + atypical pain; image if the story is classic.

nodes.title: Diverticulitis / Colonic — LLQ Gate
nodes.summary: CT confirms + stratifies. Complicated = admit/IV abx/IR; uncomplicated = outpatient candidate.
nodes.body: Diverticulitis is the dominant LLQ diagnosis in age \u226540 ("left-sided appendicitis"): LLQ pain \u00B1 low-grade fever, altered bowel habits, localized tenderness, elevated WBC/CRP. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (oral not required) confirms and stratifies complicated (abscess, perforation, fistula) vs uncomplicated (Hinchey).

nodes.title: Complicated Diverticulitis / Colonic Emergency — Treat
nodes.body: Complicated diverticulitis, immunocompromise, or inability to tolerate PO: admit, IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole or pip-tazo), bowel rest, surgical consult. - Abscess \u22653-4 cm \u2192 IR drainage. - Hinchey III-IV / sepsis / free air \u2192 emergent surgery. Keep alive on the differential: sigmoid volvulus (elderly, distension, "coffee bean" sign \u2014 endoscopic decompression fir
nodes.recommendation: Complicated diverticulitis \u2192 admit + IV abx; abscess \u22653-4 cm \u2192 IR drain; Hinchey III-IV \u2192 surgery.

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Diverticulitis — Outpatient
nodes.body: Uncomplicated diverticulitis in a well-appearing patient tolerating PO: outpatient management \u2014 ciprofloxacin + metronidazole (or amoxicillin-clavulanate) \u00D7 7-10 d, or antibiotic-free management in selected uncomplicated cases (shared decision), clear liquids advancing as tolerated, follow-up. Colonoscopy 6 weeks after recovery for a first episode to exclude a malignancy mimic. Return to
nodes.recommendation: Uncomplicated \u2192 outpatient (antibiotics or selected antibiotic-free) + colonoscopy 6 wk post-recovery for first episode.

nodes.title: GI Bleed — Glasgow-Blatchford Gate
nodes.summary: Glasgow-Blatchford. GBS 0-1 = outpatient candidate; GBS \u22652 / unstable = resuscitate + endoscopy.
nodes.body: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Open Glasgow-Blatchford (GBS) in the toolbar for upper GI bleed \u2014 GBS 0-1 identifies very-low-risk patients who may be managed as outpatients. Use AIMS65 for mortality risk; Oakland for lower GI bleed discharge suitability.

nodes.title: GI Bleed — Resuscitate + Treat
nodes.body: Open GI Bleed. Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, monitor, type and cross; transfuse to a restrictive threshold (Hb ~7 g/dL, higher if active ischemia). - Upper GI bleed: IV PPI, and if cirrhotic add octreotide + ceftriaxone; GI for endoscopy within 24 h (urgently if unstable). - Reverse anticoagulation / correct coagulopathy per severity. - Massive transfusion protocol if exsanguinating; consi
nodes.recommendation: Two large-bore IVs, type and cross, restrictive transfusion (Hb ~7), PPI \u00B1 octreotide/ceftriaxone if cirrhotic, endoscopy.

nodes.title: GI Bleed — Very Low Risk
nodes.body: A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0-1 identifies patients at very low risk for intervention or death who may be considered for outpatient management with early endoscopy follow-up \u2014 provided vitals are normal, Hb is reassuring, and follow-up is reliable. Any melena with anemia, hemodynamic change, or anticoagulation raises the risk tier. Return to the hub if another differential remains open.
nodes.recommendation: GBS 0-1 + stable = outpatient candidate with early endoscopy follow-up.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Undifferentiated Abdominal Pain
nodes.summary: IV + fluids + ondansetron + analgesia (does NOT mask exam) + focused labs + \u03B2-hCG. NPO. Reassess 60-90 min.
nodes.body: No life-threat ruled in; pain fits a common workup. Standard ED bundle while labs/imaging cook: - IV access \u00D7 1-2, monitor (two large-bore if any surgical/hemorrhagic concern). - NS or LR 1-2 L bolus (LR if pancreatitis suspected). - Antiemetic: Ondansetron 4 mg IV (QT caution). - Analgesia: opioid PRN for moderate-severe pain \u2014 does NOT mask the exam. Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV or fentanyl 1

nodes.title: Reassess at 60-90 Minutes
nodes.summary: Improving = discharge; equivocal = image/observe; new red flag = STOP and return to triage.
nodes.body: Re-examine: pain trend, vitals trend, exam evolution, results back, ability to tolerate PO.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: CT with IV contrast (no oral) for most older/equivocal; US first for RUQ/pregnant/lean female; image only when indicated.
nodes.body: Do NOT image every abdominal pain. Choose by suspected pathology: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (oral not required): older (\u226550) / unexplained pain, equivocal appendicitis, diverticulitis, SBO/LBO, suspected perforation, sepsis with abdominal source, trauma, postoperative concern. CT angiography: Mesenteric Ischemia (arterial + venous), AAA rupture concern (if stable), dissection extendi

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit per deep-dive criteria; observe if equivocal; discharge if controlled + PO + no flags + reliable.
nodes.body: Defer to the deep-dive consult\u2019s admit criteria once a phenotype is committed. The framework below applies to undifferentiated patients.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for a specific diagnosis (severe/moderate pancreatitis, cholangitis, complicated appendicitis/diverticulitis, perforation, ischemia, sepsis, AAA), surgical need, uncontrolled pain, inability to tolerate PO, refractory vomiting with electrolyte derangement, elderly with vague pain, immunocompromise, pregnancy with concern, or active hemorrhage. Service: Surgery (appendicitis, complicated dive
nodes.recommendation: Admit per deep-dive criteria; match service to dominant diagnosis; ICU for instability; standard handoff.

nodes.title: Observe — Partial Response or Pending Workup
nodes.body: ED observation when: equivocal exam + intermediate concern, awaiting imaging or lab trends, pain partially controlled with social/safety barriers, reliable patient. Protocol: serial exam q2-4h (same provider when possible), documented each time; repeat WBC + CRP at 4-6 h if intermediate; repeat lactate at 2-4 h if any sepsis concern; continue fluids/analgesia/antiemetic; reassess HR + BP trend. Es
nodes.recommendation: Obs + q2-4h serial exams + repeat labs; escalate if worsening, discharge with 24 h recheck if improving.

nodes.title: Discharge — Universal Checklist
nodes.body: Before discharge: (1) pain reduced to acceptable/baseline, (2) tolerating PO (give a PO challenge), (3) vitals normal (orthostatics if any hypovolemia concern), (4) no new exam findings on recheck, (5) labs reviewed / trending favorably, (6) \u03B2-hCG documented in reproductive-age females, (7) written return precautions, (8) 24-48 h follow-up arranged (booked, not just recommended). Return preca
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after pain controlled, PO tolerated, no red flags, \u03B2-hCG documented, written precautions, 24-48 h recheck.

nodes.title: Acetaminophen Overdose — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: NAC is 100% effective within 8h — determine ingestion pattern to guide risk stratification
nodes.body: APAP Overdose Steps Summary Acetaminophen is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the US and UK. Found in >600 OTC and prescription products (Tylenol, Percocet, Vicodin, NyQuil, Excedrin, Fioricet). [1][3] Therapeutic dose: 10-15 mg/kg per dose (max 4g/day; 2g/day in chronic alcoholics) Toxic dose: >150 mg/kg (single ingestion) or >7.5g total in adults [1] Mechanism: Normal metabolism:

nodes.title: Acute Ingestion — History & Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Gather dose, timing, formulation, coingestants — CYP2E1 inducers and fasting lower toxicity threshold
nodes.body: Gather critical history elements: • Dose — Potentially toxic: >150 mg/kg or >7.5g total (>10g per IBCC). How many pills? What strength? • Timing — When did the ingestion occur? Single ingestion within <24h? • Formulation — Immediate-release or extended-release? • Coingestants — Opioids/anticholinergics delay absorption → delayed peak APAP level • Intent — Intentional vs unintentional (affects disp

nodes.title: Repeated Supratherapeutic Ingestion
nodes.summary: Nomogram does NOT apply to repeated ingestion — presents with hepatotoxicity without early symptoms
nodes.body: Chronic/Repeated Supratherapeutic Ingestion Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion = multiple ingestions spanning >24 hours (including acute-on-chronic use). More common than acute OD in clinical practice. [6][17] The Rumack-Matthew nomogram does NOT apply — there is no single "time of ingestion" to plot. Presents with hepatotoxicity without early Stage 1 symptoms (nausea/vomiting). Patients may pres

nodes.title: Unknown Ingestion Pattern
nodes.summary: Unreliable history — draw APAP + ALT now, start NAC empirically if either abnormal
nodes.body: Unreliable history — cannot apply nomogram. Criteria for unreliable history: [6] • Insufficient detail to establish dose and time • Conflicting statements • Symptoms, signs, or lab values inconsistent with stated history Immediate actions: • Draw APAP level + AST/ALT + INR + BMP + lactate NOW • Salicylate level (coingestion screening) • If APAP detectable OR ALT elevated → start NAC empirically •

nodes.title: Acute Ingestion — APAP Level & Timing
nodes.summary: Draw APAP level at 4h post-ingestion — plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 150 line
nodes.body: Draw serum APAP level at 4 hours post-ingestion (or immediately if >4 hours since ingestion). Plot on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. [4][6][18] Rumack-Matthew Nomogram Guide Treatment line: 150 mcg/mL at 4h (US uses this line; original Rumack line was 200) [4][18] High-risk line: 300 mcg/mL at 4h (indicates massive overdose) If level drawn <4h: An undetectable concentration after >2h typically exclu

nodes.title: Extended-Release / Coingestant Considerations
nodes.summary: ER or coingestant delays peak — redraw in 4-6h if below line but >10 mcg/mL
nodes.body: Extended-release tablets or opioid/anticholinergic coingestants may delay peak APAP absorption, making a single level unreliable. [6][13] If APAP level at 4-12h is above the treatment line → treatment is indicated regardless. If APAP level at 4-24h is <10 mcg/mL → no further levels needed, no treatment. If APAP level at 4-12h is below treatment line but >10 mcg/mL → redraw in 4-6 hours. If second

nodes.title: Chronic Ingestion — Lab Evaluation
nodes.summary: Nomogram does NOT apply — use (ALT)(APAP) product; treat if ALT elevated or APAP detectable
nodes.body: Rumack-Matthew nomogram does NOT apply to repeated supratherapeutic ingestion. [6] Order: APAP level, AST/ALT, INR, BMP, lactate. Use the (ALT)(APAP) product to assess hepatotoxicity risk: [17] • >10,000 mcg/mL × IU/L = strongly associated with hepatotoxicity • <1,500 mcg/mL × IU/L = hepatotoxicity very unlikely Treat if any of the following: • ALT elevated above normal • APAP level detectable • (

nodes.title: Chronic Ingestion — Start NAC
nodes.summary: Start IV NAC for chronic ingestion with hepatotoxicity — same stopping criteria as acute
nodes.body: Initiate IV NAC — chronic/repeated supratherapeutic ingestion with evidence of hepatotoxicity or ongoing APAP exposure. Use standard 3-bag IV protocol. Consult toxicology/poison control — these cases are complex. [6] Serial labs q6h: APAP level, AST/ALT, INR, BMP. Recalculate (ALT)(APAP) product with each set to track trajectory. Stopping criteria are the same as for acute ingestion: APAP <10 mcg/

nodes.title: Chronic Ingestion — Low Risk
nodes.summary: Low-risk chronic ingestion — normal ALT, undetectable APAP, (ALT)(APAP) <1500
nodes.body: Low risk of hepatotoxicity. ALT is normal, APAP is undetectable, and (ALT)(APAP) product <1,500. The <1,500 mcg/mL × IU/L cut-point derives from the paracetamol-aminotransferase product literature, not from the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. [6][17] • Counsel on safe acetaminophen use: max 4g/day (2g/day with chronic alcohol use) • Avoid combining multiple APAP-containing products • If risk factors pres
nodes.recommendation: Low-risk chronic ingestion — consider discharge after counseling on safe APAP use

nodes.title: Below Treatment Line
nodes.summary: Below treatment line — low risk if reliable history; if any doubt, give NAC anyway
nodes.body: APAP level is below the treatment line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. Low risk of hepatotoxicity if this is a reliable acute single ingestion. [4][6][18] However, consider: • Extended-release or coingestant → serial levels needed (see above) • Risk factors (CYP2E1 inducers, alcoholism, malnutrition) → lower threshold to treat • Any doubt about history reliability → empiric NAC If <4 hours since i

nodes.title: GI Decontamination — Activated Charcoal
nodes.summary: Activated charcoal 1 g/kg within 4h — do NOT delay NAC for charcoal; give concurrently
nodes.body: Activated Charcoal 1 g/kg PO (max 50g) Timing: Within 4 hours of ingestion (2023 US/Canada consensus extends traditional 1-2h window). [6] Massive ingestion (>30g): Consider activated charcoal even >4 hours post-ingestion — greatest benefit in massive poisoning where standard NAC may be inadequate. [9] Extended-release formulations: May benefit beyond 4h if evidence of ongoing absorption (rising A

nodes.title: NAC — Route Selection
nodes.summary: NAC is the definitive antidote — IV preferred (21h); pregnancy is NOT a contraindication
nodes.body: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) is the definitive antidote. [2][3] NAC Protocol Comparison Indications for NAC: • APAP level above treatment line on nomogram • Time of ingestion unknown and APAP level detectable • Elevated transaminases with history of APAP ingestion • Ingestion >150 mg/kg and level won't be available within 8 hours • Any doubt → give NAC (minimal side effects, potentially life-saving) [6]

nodes.title: IV NAC — 21-Hour Protocol (Preferred)
nodes.summary: 3-bag IV NAC: 150 mg/kg over 1h, 50 mg/kg over 4h, 100 mg/kg over 16h — cap at 100 kg
nodes.body: N-Acetylcysteine Standard 3-Bag IV Protocol: Bag 1 (Loading): 150 mg/kg IV in 200 mL D5W over 60 minutes Bag 2: 50 mg/kg IV in 500 mL D5W over 4 hours (12.5 mg/kg/hr) Bag 3: 100 mg/kg IV in 1000 mL D5W over 16 hours (6.25 mg/kg/hr) Total: 300 mg/kg over 21 hours [3][6][19] Cap dose at 100 kg for morbid obesity. [6] Anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, urticaria, bronchospasm) most common during Bag

nodes.title: Oral NAC — 72-Hour Protocol
nodes.summary: Oral NAC 72h protocol: 140 mg/kg load then 70 mg/kg q4h x17 — mix with cola for palatability
nodes.body: N-Acetylcysteine Oral NAC Protocol: [2] Loading: 140 mg/kg PO Maintenance: 70 mg/kg PO every 4 hours × 17 additional doses Total: 1,330 mg/kg over 72 hours Mix with cola or juice to improve palatability (oral NAC has a terrible smell and taste). If patient vomits within 1 hour of dose → repeat the dose. Consider Ondansetron 30 minutes prior to reduce vomiting. [6] Advantages: No IV access needed,

nodes.title: Two-Bag Modified Prescott Protocol
nodes.summary: 2-bag protocol: 200 mg/kg over 4h then 100 mg/kg over 16h — lower anaphylactoid rate
nodes.body: Simplified 2-bag regimen (used in Australia/New Zealand): [7][13][22] Bag 1: 200 mg/kg IV in D5W over 4 hours Bag 2: 100 mg/kg IV in D5W over 16 hours Total: 300 mg/kg over 20 hours Lower rate of anaphylactoid reactions compared to the standard 3-bag protocol — the slower initial infusion rate reduces histamine release. [7][22] Evidence base: Wong & Graudins found fewer adverse drug reactions afte

nodes.title: Anaphylactoid Reaction Management
nodes.summary: NEVER permanently stop NAC — anaphylactoid reactions are histamine-mediated, not true allergy
nodes.body: NAC Anaphylactoid Reaction Management NOT a true allergy — histamine-mediated, not IgE. Usually within first 2 hours, almost always within 6 hours. In a Canadian cohort of 6,455 NAC treatment courses, an anaphylactoid reaction was documented in 528 (8.2%), 75.4% were purely cutaneous, and 95.4% occurred within the first 5 hours; no deaths were attributed to anaphylactoid reactions. [11] Graded res

nodes.title: When to Stop NAC
nodes.summary: Stop NAC only when: APAP <10 + INR <2 + ALT improving + clinically well — all four required
nodes.body: Continue NAC until ALL stopping criteria are met: [6][13] ✅ 1. APAP level <10 mcg/mL (undetectable) ✅ 2. INR <2 ✅ 3. AST/ALT meets ONE of: • Normal • At patient's baseline • Decreased >25-50% from peak value ✅ 4. Clinically well Note: Small fluctuations in ALT (±20 IU/L or ±10%) are common and do not necessarily indicate ongoing injury, especially if the ALT level is low. [13] If criteria are NOT

nodes.title: Above Treatment Line — Start NAC
nodes.body: APAP level is above the treatment line (150 mcg/mL at 4h). Start NAC immediately. [4][6] NAC is nearly 100% effective when given within 8 hours of ingestion. Efficacy decreases with delay but still provides benefit even after hepatic failure is established. [2] Concurrent actions: • GI decontamination with Activated Charcoal if within 4 hours • Labs: APAP level q4-6h, AST/ALT, INR, BMP, lactate •

nodes.title: High-Risk (Massive) Overdose
nodes.body: High-Dose NAC & Massive Overdose Definition of massive overdose: [8][14] • >30 grams ingested (or >0.5 g/kg if <60 kg) • APAP level above the 300 line on the nomogram Clinical presentation: Early lactic acidosis + altered mental status within 12 hours — due to mitochondrial dysfunction, BEFORE liver damage occurs. Other symptoms during Stage 1 (within 24h) suggest massive ingestion or coingestant.

nodes.title: High-Dose NAC — Hendrickson Protocol
nodes.body: N-Acetylcysteine Hendrickson 2019: Keep Bag 1 + Bag 2 standard. INCREASE Bag 3 infusion rate based on severity: [8] • Above 300 line: 12.5 mg/kg/hr (2× standard) • Above 450 line: 18.75 mg/kg/hr (3× standard) • Above 600 line: 25 mg/kg/hr (4× standard) During hemodialysis: Double whatever rate you would otherwise use. HD removes ~50% of NAC. Minimum rate during HD: 12.5 mg/kg/hr. Maximum: 25 mg/kg

nodes.title: Fomepizole — CYP2E1 Inhibition
nodes.body: Fomepizole Mechanism: Inhibits CYP2E1 → prevents conversion of acetaminophen to toxic NAPQI. Complementary to NAC (which detoxifies NAPQI after it forms). [15] Dosing: 15 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes (loading) → 10 mg/kg IV q12h for 48 hours or until APAP level is undetectable. [6][15] ⚠️ Basis disclosure: Fomepizole is off-label for acetaminophen poisoning. There is no randomised outcome trial. The d

nodes.title: Hemodialysis — EXTRIP Guidelines
nodes.body: Hemodialysis removes both APAP and toxic NAPQI metabolites. May be beneficial in massive poisoning where NAC alone is inadequate. [9] EXTRIP indications for extracorporeal treatment: [9] • APAP level >900 mcg/mL • Altered mental status + lactate >3 + pH <7.1 • Clinical deterioration despite adequate NAC • Mitochondrial dysfunction (early lactic acidosis, altered consciousness) ⚠️ Hemodialysis is N

nodes.title: Established Hepatic Failure — Management
nodes.body: Four Stages of Acetaminophen Toxicity N-Acetylcysteine Continue IV NAC indefinitely — repeat Bag 3 (100 mg/kg over 16 hours) until the patient recovers or dies. [5][10] NAC provides benefit even in established hepatic failure — proven 28% mortality benefit in an RCT of patients with acetaminophen-induced fulminant hepatic failure (Keays 1991). [10] *Source detail:* Keays randomised 50 patients wit

nodes.title: King's College Criteria — Transplant Referral
nodes.body: APAP-induced acute liver failure — transplant referral criteria: [5] pH <7.30 after adequate fluid resuscitation (regardless of encephalopathy grade) — alone is sufficient OR all three: • INR >6.5 (PT >100 sec) • Creatinine >3.4 mg/dL • Grade III-IV hepatic encephalopathy Additional poor prognostic markers (not part of the original O'Grady criteria — later additions): [12] • Lactate >3.5 mmol/L af

nodes.title: Supportive Care — Complications
nodes.body: Manage complications of hepatic failure: [1][12][16] Coagulopathy: • FFP only if ACTIVE bleeding — FFP obscures INR trending, which is the single best prognostic marker • Vitamin K may be given but rarely helps in acute liver failure Cerebral edema (greatest risk of death in Stage 3): • Elevate HOB 30° • Hypertonic saline 23.4% for herniation • Mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg • Avoid stimulation, maintain nor

nodes.title: Empiric NAC — Unknown Ingestion
nodes.body: Start NAC empirically when: • History is unreliable AND APAP is detectable • History is unreliable AND ALT is elevated • Ingestion >150 mg/kg and level won't be available within 8 hours • Any clinical doubt When in doubt → give NAC. [2][6] Minimal side effects. Potentially life-saving. NAC has no absolute contraindications for acetaminophen toxicity. Draw labs now: APAP level, AST/ALT, INR, BMP, l

nodes.title: Admit — Ward Level Care
nodes.body: Admit to medical floor if: • NAC initiated (continue per protocol) • Elevated transaminases (AST/ALT monitoring q6-12h) • Altered mental status • Significant coingestant requiring monitoring • Unreliable history with ongoing concern Continue monitoring: • APAP level, AST/ALT, INR, BMP q6-12h • Reassess NAC stopping criteria at each lab check • Serial clinical assessments Escalate to ICU if evidenc
nodes.recommendation: Admit for NAC completion and serial lab monitoring. Escalate to ICU if signs of hepatic failure.

nodes.title: Admit — ICU Level Care
nodes.body: ICU admission for: • Evidence of hepatic failure: coagulopathy (INR >3), encephalopathy, acidosis (pH <7.3), renal failure • Massive ingestion with early lactic acidosis or altered mental status • King's College Criteria met — transfer to transplant center • Hemodialysis required • Hemodynamic instability ICU management: • Continue IV NAC indefinitely (repeat Bag 3) • Serial labs q6h: APAP, AST/AL
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for hepatic failure management. Continue NAC indefinitely. Contact transplant center early.

nodes.title: Observation & Monitoring
nodes.body: Observation period: 4-6 hours from time of ingestion with repeat labs before disposition. [1][6] Recheck at end of observation: • APAP level (should be trending down if detectable) • AST/ALT (any elevation warrants NAC regardless of APAP level) • INR • Creatinine Reassess for: • Delayed absorption (extended-release, coingestants) • Late-rising APAP levels • New symptoms If all labs remain normal a

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.body: Safe to discharge if ALL of the following are met: [1][6] ✅ APAP level below treatment line at ≥4 hours post-ingestion [18] ✅ Normal AST/ALT ✅ Normal INR ✅ Normal creatinine ✅ 4-6 hour observation complete ✅ Asymptomatic ⚠️ Psychiatric evaluation is MANDATORY for ALL intentional ingestions before discharge. [1] Discharge counseling: • Safe acetaminophen use: max 4g/day (2g/day with chronic alcohol
nodes.recommendation: Discharge after observation if all labs normal, asymptomatic, and psychiatric clearance obtained for intentional ingestions.

nodes.title: Acid-Base Assessment
nodes.summary: Order ABG/VBG + BMP + lactate + albumin, then choose Traditional or Stewart diagnostic pathway
nodes.body: Acid-Base Steps Summary — stepwise approach to both Traditional and Stewart methods. Order labs: ABG or VBG, BMP (Na, Cl, HCO3, BUN, Cr, Glucose), lactate, albumin, beta-hydroxybutyrate, serum osmolality. ABG vs VBG Evidence — VBG is sufficient for most ED acid-base assessments. Choose your diagnostic approach:

nodes.title: pH Assessment
nodes.summary: Classify pH as acidemia, alkalemia, or normal — normal pH does not exclude mixed disorders
nodes.body: What is the measured pH? 6 Rules for Expected Compensation — predict expected responses to primary disturbances.

nodes.title: Acidemia — pCO2 Assessment
nodes.summary: Determine if acidemia is respiratory (high pCO2) or metabolic (low/normal pCO2) in origin
nodes.body: Acidemia confirmed. Evaluate the pCO2 to determine the primary disturbance. Primary respiratory acidosis: pCO2 is elevated (the lungs are the problem). Primary metabolic acidosis: pCO2 is low or normal (kidneys/buffers are the problem, lungs are compensating).

nodes.title: Respiratory Acidosis — Acute vs Chronic
nodes.summary: Distinguish acute vs chronic respiratory acidosis using renal compensation rules (3-5 days for full effect)
nodes.body: pCO2 is elevated. The lungs are not adequately eliminating CO2. Acute vs Chronic: Renal compensation begins in hours but takes 3-5 days for full effect. Use the compensation rules to determine if HCO3 response is appropriate. 6 Rules for Expected Compensation

nodes.title: Acute Respiratory Acidosis
nodes.body: Use Rule 1 to calculate expected HCO3. If HCO3 is higher than expected → concurrent metabolic alkalosis. If HCO3 is lower than expected → concurrent metabolic acidosis. See Differential Diagnosis for common causes. Risk Pitfall: Intubating a patient with compensatory hyperventilation for metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA) can cause precipitous pH drop if minute ventilation is not matched post-intubati
nodes.recommendation: Treat the underlying cause. Support ventilation. If intubation required, match the patient's pre-intubation minute ventilation. Avoid O2 > 92% in COPD (oxygen-induced hypercapnia).

nodes.title: Chronic Respiratory Acidosis
nodes.body: Use Rule 2 to calculate expected HCO3. Full renal compensation may return pH near-normal despite significantly elevated pCO2. See Differential Diagnosis for common causes. Risk Pitfall: A pCO2 of 70 with appropriate renal compensation (HCO3 ~35, pH ~7.32) is NOT an intubation indication. Base decision on mental status, work of breathing, and clinical trajectory. pH ≤ 7.25 in COPD exacerbation → co
nodes.recommendation: Optimize bronchodilators and treat the acute exacerbation trigger. Consider NIV (BiPAP) before intubation. GOLD guidelines: admit for acute respiratory failure, severe symptoms, mental status changes, or failure of initial ED management.

nodes.title: Alkalemia — pCO2 Assessment
nodes.summary: Determine if alkalemia is respiratory (low pCO2) or metabolic (normal/high pCO2) in origin
nodes.body: Alkalemia confirmed (pH > 7.45). Evaluate pCO2. Primary respiratory alkalosis: pCO2 decreased (hyperventilation). Primary metabolic alkalosis: pCO2 normal or elevated (ventilatory compensation is limited).

nodes.title: Respiratory Alkalosis
nodes.body: Use Rules 3 & 4 to assess acute vs chronic compensation. See Differential Diagnosis for common causes. Risk Pitfall: Do NOT dismiss hyperventilation as a "panic attack" without ruling out PE, sepsis, and salicylate toxicity. Alkalemia may cause decreased coronary and cerebral perfusion via vasoconstriction, potentially causing ischemia and seizure. [4]
nodes.recommendation: Treat the underlying cause. Consider PE workup (D-dimer, CTPA). Check salicylate level if unexplained. In severe alkalemia: avoid aggressive correction — rebound acidosis is dangerous.

nodes.title: Calculate Anion Gap
nodes.summary: Calculate AG (Na-Cl-HCO3), correct for albumin — low albumin falsely narrows AG and masks HAGMA
nodes.body: Anion Gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) Normal AG: 8-12 mEq/L. Values as low as 6 ± 3 may be seen with modern analyzers. [7] Albumin-corrected AG (Figge correction for hypoalbuminemia): [8] Corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4.2 - measured albumin in g/dL) Critically ill, malnourished, and perioperative patients often have low albumin, which falsely narrows the AG and can mask an anion gap acidosis. Differential Dia

nodes.title: Anion Gap Result
nodes.summary: Classify metabolic acidosis as anion gap (>12) or non-anion gap (8-12) to guide differential
nodes.body: Interpret the anion gap (use albumin-corrected AG if albumin is low).

nodes.title: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis
nodes.summary: HAGMA confirmed — check lactate, BHB, tox screen, then proceed to Delta Gap for mixed disorders
nodes.body: Differential Diagnosis — MUDPILES mnemonic and full etiologies. Check: Lactate, beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), toxicology screen. Lactate & Ketone Pathophysiology Proceed to Delta Gap to assess for mixed metabolic disorders.

nodes.title: Delta Gap (Delta-Delta Ratio)
nodes.summary: Delta ratio (ΔAG/ΔHCO3) detects hidden second metabolic process — <1 concurrent NAGMA, >2 concurrent alkalosis
nodes.body: Delta Ratio = ΔAG / ΔHCO3 = (AG - 12) / (24 - HCO3) In a pure anion gap acidosis, every unmeasured anion that widens the gap should proportionally consume one bicarbonate. If this ratio is not 1:1, a second metabolic process is occurring.

nodes.title: Mixed: AG + Non-AG Acidosis
nodes.body: Delta ratio < 1 (or < 0.4 for significant hyperchloremic component). Bicarbonate has fallen MORE than the anion gap has risen, indicating a concurrent non-anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis alongside the AG acidosis. Common scenarios: • DKA with saline resuscitation (iatrogenic hyperchloremia) • Uremia + diarrhea • Renal tubular acidosis + lactic acidosis Evaluate: Urine anion gap (UNa + UK - UCl
nodes.recommendation: Treat each process. Consider balanced crystalloids (LR, PlasmaLyte) instead of NS for further resuscitation to avoid worsening hyperchloremia.

nodes.title: Mixed: AG Acidosis + Metabolic Alkalosis
nodes.body: Delta ratio > 2. The anion gap has risen MORE than bicarbonate has fallen, suggesting a baseline elevated HCO3 (metabolic alkalosis) that is partially offsetting the acidosis. Common scenarios: • DKA + vomiting (metabolic alkalosis from HCl loss) • Sepsis + NG suction • Lactic acidosis + diuretic use • Any AG acidosis in a patient with chronic respiratory acidosis (elevated baseline HCO3 from rena
nodes.recommendation: Identify and treat both processes. The metabolic alkalosis may mask the severity of the underlying AG acidosis.

nodes.title: Winter's Formula — Respiratory Compensation
nodes.summary: Apply Winter's Formula to predict expected pCO2 — detects concurrent respiratory disturbances
nodes.body: Apply Winter's Formula (Rule 5) to calculate the expected pCO2. Compare the patient's measured pCO2 to this expected range to detect concurrent respiratory disturbances.

nodes.title: Compensation Assessment
nodes.summary: Compare actual pCO2 to Winter's prediction — higher means concurrent respiratory acidosis, lower means respiratory alkalosis
nodes.body: Compare the patient's actual pCO2 to the Winter's formula predicted range.

nodes.title: Mixed: Metabolic + Respiratory Acidosis
nodes.body: The measured pCO2 exceeds the predicted range from Winter's formula. Both metabolic AND respiratory processes are contributing to acidemia. This is a particularly dangerous combination — the pH drops further than either process alone would cause. Common scenarios: • COPD exacerbation + sepsis • Sedation/opioid use + DKA • Neuromuscular disease + renal failure • Post-arrest (metabolic acidosis + hy
nodes.recommendation: Address both processes urgently. Maximize ventilatory support. Treat the metabolic cause. Consider sodium bicarbonate if pH ≤ 7.20 with AKI (BICAR-ICU criteria).

nodes.title: Non-Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) Acidosis
nodes.body: AG is normal (8-12). Acidosis is due to bicarbonate loss or impaired acid excretion without accumulation of unmeasured anions. Calculate Urine Anion Gap = UNa + UK - UCl Negative urine AG (< 0): GI bicarbonate loss (diarrhea most common). Positive urine AG (> 0): Renal tubular acidosis — differentiate by urine pH. Differential Diagnosis — full RTA types and NAGMA causes. Fluid Selection Guide — NS
nodes.recommendation: Treat the underlying cause. For diarrheal losses: isotonic bicarbonate replacement. For RTA: oral bicarbonate supplementation (Type I/II) or fludrocortisone (Type IV). Switch from NS to balanced crystalloid if iatrogenic.

nodes.title: Metabolic Alkalosis — Urine Chloride
nodes.summary: Urine chloride differentiates chloride-responsive (<20, give NS) from chloride-resistant (>20, won't respond to saline)
nodes.body: Metabolic alkalosis: elevated pH with elevated HCO3. Use Rule 6 to check pCO2 compensation. Urine chloride differentiates the two major categories:

nodes.title: Chloride-Responsive Metabolic Alkalosis
nodes.body: Urine Cl < 20 mEq/L. The kidneys are avidly retaining chloride, indicating volume depletion. See Differential Diagnosis for common causes (vomiting, diuretics, post-hypercapnia).
nodes.recommendation: Volume resuscitate with NS (replenishes chloride). Replace potassium (hypokalemia perpetuates alkalosis by increasing renal H+ secretion). Stop offending diuretic if applicable. This is the most common type of metabolic alkalosis in the ED.

nodes.title: Chloride-Resistant Metabolic Alkalosis
nodes.body: Urine Cl > 20 mEq/L. Volume repletion with saline will NOT correct this alkalosis. See Differential Diagnosis for common causes (hyperaldosteronism, Cushing, Bartter/Gitelman, severe hypokalemia).
nodes.recommendation: Treat the underlying cause. Aggressive potassium repletion. Consider acetazolamide 250-500 mg IV to promote bicarbonate excretion. Spironolactone for hyperaldosteronism. For refractory cases: dilute HCl infusion (0.1N) via central line — sp

nodes.title: Normal pH — Possible Mixed Disorder
nodes.body: A normal pH does NOT exclude acid-base disturbance. Opposing processes can cancel each other: • AG acidosis + metabolic alkalosis → near-normal pH • Respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis → near-normal pH • Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis Always check: • Anion gap (even with normal pH — elevated AG reveals hidden acidosis) • Base excess (abnormal BE with normal pH = compensated or mix
nodes.recommendation: Calculate the AG and assess base excess. An elevated AG with normal pH is a classic mixed disturbance (e.g., DKA + vomiting). Do not be falsely reassured by a normal pH — the underlying processes may be severe.

nodes.title: Mixed: Metabolic Acidosis + Respiratory Alkalosis
nodes.body: The measured pCO2 is LOWER than Winter's formula predicted range. The patient is hyperventilating beyond what metabolic compensation requires. Classic pattern of salicylate toxicity: direct central respiratory stimulation causes respiratory alkalosis PLUS metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. [2] Other common scenarios: • Early sepsis (hyperventilation + lactic acidosis) • H
nodes.recommendation: Check salicylate level. Consider PE workup. Evaluate for sepsis. This mixed pattern often indicates a serious underlying process.

nodes.title: Stewart: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Stewart Step 1-2: note pH and pCO2, then proceed to SID calculation using Na-Cl difference
nodes.body: Step 1: Note the pH — acidosis (< 7.35) or alkalosis (> 7.45). Step 2: Check pCO2 — respiratory component uses the same rules as the traditional approach. Stewart Approach Explained — SID concept, Gamblegram, weak acids, and clinical examples. Reference values: • Na: 140 mEq/L | Cl: 105 mEq/L | SID (Na-Cl): 35 mEq/L • Albumin: 4.2 g/dL | Lactate: 1 mmol/L | Base Excess: 0

nodes.title: Strong Ion Difference (Na − Cl)
nodes.summary: SID (Na-Cl) normal ~35 — low SID = acidosis from Cl excess or Na deficit, high SID = alkalosis
nodes.body: SID = Na − Cl (simplified). Normal ~35 mEq/L. The Na-Cl difference is the predominant determinant of metabolic acid-base status. A reduced SID suggests acidosis (strong anions "squeeze out" bicarbonate). An increased SID suggests alkalosis. [11] Na-Cl base-excess effect = (Na − Cl) − 35 For every 1 mEq/L change in the Na-Cl difference, the base excess changes by 1 mEq/L.

nodes.title: Low SID — Metabolic Acidosis
nodes.summary: Low SID acidosis — from NS resuscitation, RTA, or diarrhea; consider balanced crystalloids
nodes.body: Na-Cl effect = (Na − Cl) − 35 mEq/L → negative = acidosis contribution. In hyponatremic patients, a normal chloride concentration (relative hyperchloremia) will result in a decreased SID and metabolic acidosis. [11] Common causes: Fluid administration (NS, D5W, ½NS all have SID 0), RTA, diarrhea. Fluid Selection Guide — how NS causes acidosis. Differential Diagnosis — RTA types and NAGMA causes.

nodes.title: High SID — Metabolic Alkalosis
nodes.summary: High SID alkalosis — from chloride-rich GI losses, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, or contraction
nodes.body: Na-Cl effect = (Na − Cl) − 35 mEq/L → positive = alkalosis contribution. Hypernatremic patients will have an increased SID and metabolic alkalosis even with a chloride in the reference range. [11] Common causes of high SID alkalosis: • NG suction (chloride-rich gastric losses) • Diuretics (chloride wasting) • Hyperaldosteronism • Volume depletion / contraction alkalosis • Post-hypercapnia

nodes.title: Lactate Assessment
nodes.summary: Lactate effect = 1-measured lactate; >4 is critical — consider sepsis, shock, mesenteric ischemia
nodes.body: Lactate effect = 1 − measured lactate (mEq/L) Normal lactate ≈ 1 mmol/L → effect ≈ 0. As lactate rises, the effect becomes more negative (acidosis). Lactate & Ketone Pathophysiology — mechanisms, Type A vs B, mortality data.

nodes.title: Strong Ion Gap (Unmeasured Anions)
nodes.summary: SIG >2 = unmeasured anions (ketones, uremia, toxic alcohols) beyond Na-Cl, lactate, and albumin
nodes.body: SIG = Base Deficit + (SID − 35) + 2.5 × (4.2 − Albumin g/dL) − Lactate Alternative (Story simplified): Other Ions = BE − (Na-Cl−35) − (1−Lactate) − 2.5×(4.2−Albumin) If no base excess/deficit is available: use (24.2 − HCO3) as a substitute for base deficit. SIG > 2 indicates clinically important unmeasured anions are present beyond what Na-Cl, lactate, and albumin can explain. [11] See Stewart App

nodes.title: Elevated SIG — Unmeasured Anions
nodes.summary: Elevated SIG causes: uremia, DKA, AKA, toxic alcohols, salicylates — check osmolar gap if unclear
nodes.body: SIG > 2 indicates unmeasured anions contributing to acidosis. Causes: • Uremia (phosphate, sulfate, hippurate) • Diabetic ketoacidosis (BHB can be subtracted directly from SIG to quantify the ketone contribution) • Alcoholic ketoacidosis (starvation + depleted glycogen + hormonal cascade → ketogenesis) • Toxic alcohols: methanol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol → check osmolar gap • Salicylates

nodes.title: Osmolar Gap Assessment
nodes.body: Osmolar Gap = Measured Osm − Calculated Osm Calculated Osm = 2×Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 + EtOH/3.7 (Include EtOH term only if ethanol level is available — unmeasured ethanol falsely elevates the gap.) Interpretation: • Gap ≤ 10: Normal. Unmeasured anions are endogenous (uremia, ketoacids). • Gap 10-50: Elevated. Consider methanol, ethylene glycol, propylene glycol (lorazepam/diazepam/phenytoin in
nodes.recommendation: For suspected toxic alcohol: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading dose. Consult toxicology and nephrology. Dialysis indicated for methanol/ethylene glycol with end-organ damage, severe acidosis, or renal failure.

nodes.title: Treatment Considerations
nodes.summary: Bicarb for pH≤7.20 with AKI (RRT-sparing, no mortality benefit per BICARICU-2), TCA OD, salicylate tox, severe hyperK — NOT routine in DKA or lactic acidosis
nodes.body: Sodium Bicarbonate: Sodium Bicarbonate — indications, dosing, and evidence. Indications for bicarbonate: [12][17][19] • pH ≤ 7.20 with moderate-to-severe AKI — reasonable, but recent evidence tempers the benefit. BICAR-ICU (2018) suggested a mortality signal in the AKI subgroup; the confirmatory BICARICU-2 trial (JAMA 2025, n=627) found NO day-90 mortality difference (62.1% vs 61.7%). The consiste

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: ICU Admission: [18] • pH ≤ 7.25 (in-hospital mortality up to 25%) • Lactate > 4 mmol/L with hemodynamic instability or failure to clear with fluids • Toxic alcohol ingestion • Refractory acidosis requiring continuous bicarbonate infusion • Altered mental status, need for advanced ventilatory support, hemodynamic instability Floor Admission: • Correctable cause identified, responding to treatment •
nodes.recommendation: Emergency clinicians should have a low threshold for hospitalization in patients with acid-base disturbances associated with severe respiratory disease, ketoacidosis, sepsis, poisonings, or any acute condition not likely reversible within 3

nodes.title: Negative SIG — Unmeasured Cations
nodes.body: A negative SIG indicates unmeasured cations or laboratory artifact. Causes: • Hypercalcemia (unmeasured divalent cation) • Hypermagnesemia • Hyperkalemia (if K+ not included in SID calculation) • Immunoglobulins — multiple myeloma and plasma cell dyscrasias (paraproteins exist as cations at normal pH) [7] • Bromide intoxication (bromide displaces chloride in lab assays, falsely elevating measured
nodes.recommendation: Evaluate for myeloma (SPEP, free light chains) if unexplained. Check ionized calcium and magnesium. Consider bromide level if clinical suspicion.

nodes.title: Acute Agitation
nodes.summary: Assess immediate danger level to determine de-escalation vs rapid sedation pathway.
nodes.body: Steps Summary Is patient an IMMEDIATE DANGER to self, staff, or others? Assess: Combative? Threatening? Attempting to leave AMA? Unable to cooperate with any care?

nodes.title: Immediate Danger Protocol
nodes.summary: Activate security, prepare meds, attempt brief verbal de-escalation.
nodes.body: Parallel actions: 1. Activate security — multiple trained personnel 2. Prepare medications — draw up sedation agents 3. Clear the area — remove other patients/visitors 4. Brief verbal attempt (10-15 seconds max) If ANY verbal de-escalation possible: Use single calm staff member, offer choices, maintain distance. If patient actively attacking: Proceed directly to chemical restraint → do not delay.

nodes.title: Verbal De-escalation (BETA)
nodes.summary: BETA protocol: respect space, concise speech, identify feelings, offer choices. 5-10 min limit.
nodes.body: Project BETA — 10 Domains: 1. Respect personal space — 2+ arm lengths 2. Do not be provocative — no direct eye contact, hands visible 3. Establish verbal contact — calm, low voice, slow speech 4. Be concise — simple sentences, one instruction at a time 5. Identify wants and feelings — "I can see you're frustrated" 6. Listen actively — nod, reflect back 7. Agree or agree to disagree — find common g

nodes.title: De-escalation Response
nodes.summary: Assess response to de-escalation to determine next steps.
nodes.body: After 5-10 minutes of verbal de-escalation:

nodes.title: Rapid Organic Screening
nodes.summary: Check glucose, O2, temp, pupils before sedation. Cannot delay if immediate threat.
nodes.body: Check BEFORE sedation if possible: • Glucose — hypoglycemia mimics psych • O2 sat — hypoxia causes agitation • Temperature — fever = infection, hyperthermia = hyperactive delirium • Pupils — toxidrome clues • Diaphoresis — sympathomimetic, withdrawal CANNOT delay sedation if patient is immediate threat. Obtain these during/after sedation if needed.

nodes.title: Likely Etiology
nodes.summary: Etiology guides medication choice: delirium, intoxication, psychiatric, or undifferentiated.
nodes.body: What is the most likely cause? This guides medication selection.

nodes.title: Delirium Pathway
nodes.summary: Delirium — find and treat cause. Haloperidol preferred. Avoid benzos alone.
nodes.body: Delirium = medical emergency Find and treat the cause: • Infection (UTI, pneumonia, meningitis) • Metabolic (glucose, Na+, Ca2+, uremia) • Hypoxia • Medication toxicity • Withdrawal (alcohol, benzos) • Structural (stroke, bleed, mass) Sedation for delirium: • Haloperidol preferred in elderly — less sedating • Avoid benzodiazepines alone — worsen delirium (except in withdrawal) Labs: CBC, BMP, UA,

nodes.title: Intoxication / Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Substance type guides treatment approach.
nodes.body: Which substance?

nodes.title: Stimulant Intoxication
nodes.summary: Stimulant intoxication — cooling + benzodiazepines when feasible; ketamine for immediate high-threat or failed benzos.
nodes.body: High-threat situation — rapid control essential Physiology: Hyperdopaminergic + hyperthermia + rhabdomyolysis risk Treatment priorities: 1. Aggressive cooling if hyperthermic (>38.5°C) 2. Benzodiazepines when feasible — midazolam or lorazepam 3. Ketamine if immediate violent threat, severe hyperthermia preventing care, or failed benzodiazepines 4. Avoid antipsychotics alone — can worsen hypertherm

nodes.title: Withdrawal Agitation
nodes.summary: Withdrawal — benzos first-line. Avoid antipsychotics alone. See Alcohol Withdrawal consult.
nodes.body: → Alcohol Withdrawal Consult for detailed protocol Quick reference: • Benzodiazepines are first-line • Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV/IM q5-15 min PRN • Diazepam 10-20 mg IV q5-10 min PRN (if no liver disease) Do NOT use antipsychotics alone — lower seizure threshold. High-risk features: • Prior seizures or DTs • PAWSS ≥4 • Consider phenobarbital loading

nodes.title: Unknown Intoxication
nodes.summary: Unknown intoxication — lorazepam safest single agent.
nodes.body: When substance is unclear: Safest single agent: Lorazepam • Works for most toxidromes • Safe in withdrawal • Minimal cardiovascular effects Dosing: • Lorazepam 2 mg IV/IM, repeat q5-10 min as needed • Max: 10-20 mg for severe agitation Avoid: Antipsychotics if stimulant possible (worsen hyperthermia)

nodes.title: Hallucinogen Intoxication
nodes.summary: Hallucinogens — reassurance first, benzos if needed. Avoid antipsychotics.
nodes.body: Usually not violent — reassurance often works Management: • Quiet, dark environment • Calm verbal reassurance • Benzodiazepine if needed (lorazepam 1-2 mg) Avoid: Antipsychotics — can worsen "bad trip" Duration: LSD effects 8-12 hours; patient will return to baseline

nodes.title: Primary Psychiatric
nodes.summary: Primary psychiatric — droperidol + midazolam fastest. Olanzapine IM should not be paired with parenteral benzodiazepines.
nodes.body: Primary psychosis / mania: Preferred agents: • Droperidol + midazolam when rapid sedation is needed • Ziprasidone + midazolam as an atypical antipsychotic combo option • Haloperidol + lorazepam when local practice favors it • Olanzapine IM alone when antipsychotic monotherapy is appropriate Avoid: IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines (IM/IV). If both are needed, separate per local protoco

nodes.title: Undifferentiated Agitation
nodes.summary: Undifferentiated — droperidol + midazolam (ACEP Level B). Continue workup.
nodes.body: When etiology unclear: ACEP Level B recommendation: • Droperidol + midazolam — fastest, most effective • Alternative: Atypical antipsychotic + midazolam Continue workup in parallel: • Labs, glucose, toxicology • Imaging if indicated • Reassess once sedation achieved

nodes.title: Medication Selection
nodes.summary: Select medication protocol based on etiology and patient factors.
nodes.body: Choose sedation approach:

nodes.title: Droperidol Protocol
nodes.summary: Droperidol 5-10 mg IM/IV — fastest single agent. Add midazolam for faster control.
nodes.body: ACEP Level B — Fastest single-agent sedation Dosing: • Droperidol 5-10 mg IM/IV • IV onset: 3-5 min | IM onset: 10-15 min • Duration: 4-6 hours Add midazolam for faster control: • Midazolam 5 mg IM/IV Reassess at 15 min: • Adequate? → Monitor • Inadequate? → Repeat dose OR add benzo Side effects: QTc prolongation (rare at these doses), EPS, hypotension

nodes.title: Ketamine Protocol
nodes.summary: Ketamine 5 mg/kg IM — high-threat only. Requires airway monitoring.
nodes.body: ACEP Level C — High-threat situations only Indications: • Patient actively attacking staff • Stimulant intoxication with hyperthermia • Failed other agents Dosing: • Ketamine 5 mg/kg IM (max 400 mg) • OR 1-2 mg/kg IV • Onset: IM 3-5 min | IV 1-2 min • Duration: 15-30 min REQUIRES: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Pulse oximetry + capnography • Airway equipment at bedside Adverse effects: • Laryng

nodes.title: Benzodiazepine Protocol
nodes.summary: Lorazepam 2-4 mg or midazolam 5 mg. Midazolam = faster IM onset.
nodes.body: Best for withdrawal, unknown intox, liver disease Lorazepam (preferred if liver disease): • Lorazepam 2-4 mg IM/IV • IM onset: 15-30 min | IV onset: 1-3 min • Can repeat q5-10 min • Max: 10-20 mg for severe agitation Midazolam (faster IM onset): • Midazolam 5 mg IM/IV • IM onset: 12-15 min (fastest IM benzo) • Can repeat at 10 min Cautions: • Respiratory depression (especially + alcohol) • Elderly

nodes.title: Antipsychotic + Benzo Combo
nodes.summary: Droperidol + midazolam preferred. Avoid IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines.
nodes.body: For primary psychiatric agitation: Option 1 — Droperidol + Midazolam: • Droperidol 5 mg IM/IV + Midazolam 5 mg IM/IV • Fastest evidence-supported combination for severe agitation Option 2 — Ziprasidone + Midazolam: • Ziprasidone 20 mg IM + Midazolam 5 mg IM • Onset: 15-20 min Option 3 — Haloperidol + Lorazepam: • Haloperidol 5 mg IM + Lorazepam 2 mg IM • Onset: 30-45 min (slower) • Add diphenhydra

nodes.title: Elderly / Special Populations
nodes.summary: Elderly — reduce doses 30-50%. Haloperidol preferred. Avoid benzos alone.
nodes.body: Age >65 — Reduce ALL doses 30-50% Preferred: Haloperidol 2.5 mg IV/IM • Less sedating, safer in delirium • Avoid benzos if possible (worsen delirium) Lorazepam max: 1-2 mg (not 4 mg) Higher risk of: • Falls • Oversedation • Respiratory depression • Orthostatic hypotension ADEPT Framework: Assess baseline → Diagnose delirium → Evaluate triggers → Prevent complications → Treat medically Pregnancy: L

nodes.title: Reassess at 15-20 min
nodes.summary: Target RASS 0 to -1 (calm but arousable). Reassess response.
nodes.body: Goal: Calm but arousable (RASS 0 to -1) How is the patient responding?

nodes.title: Rescue Sedation
nodes.summary: Add complementary agent. If refractory (>40 mg lorazepam/4h), consider phenobarbital or ICU.
nodes.body: Inadequate response at 15-20 min: If gave antipsychotic alone: → Add benzodiazepine (midazolam 5 mg or lorazepam 2 mg) If gave benzodiazepine alone: → Consider antipsychotic (olanzapine 10 mg or ziprasidone 20 mg) If gave antipsychotic + benzo: → Reassess for organic cause → Consider ketamine if safety risk escalates Refractory agitation (>10 mg lorazepam/hr or >40 mg/4h): → Consider phenobarbital

nodes.title: Oversedation Management
nodes.summary: Airway management first. Flumazenil for benzo reversal (seizure risk if chronic use).
nodes.body: Airway first: 1. Head positioning — chin lift, jaw thrust 2. Suction if secretions 3. Supplemental O2 — nasal cannula or BVM 4. Capnography — monitor for hypoventilation Reversal agents: • Flumazenil — benzodiazepine reversal - 0.2 mg IV, repeat q1 min to max 1 mg - ⚠️ Seizure risk if chronic benzo use • Naloxone — if opioid co-ingestion suspected If airway compromise: → Intubation

nodes.title: Physical Restraint
nodes.summary: NEVER prone. Supine with head elevated. Bridge to chemical restraint only.
nodes.body: Use as BRIDGE to chemical restraint — not standalone treatment Indications: • Immediate danger while awaiting medication effect • Brief restraint during medication administration Safe technique: • NEVER prone position — highest mortality • Supine with head elevated 30° • 5-point restraint minimum (wrists, ankles, chest) • Minimum 5 trained personnel • Ensure no tight clothing around neck Monitorin

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis Risk
nodes.summary: Rhabdo risk with restraints + stimulants. Check CK, hydrate aggressively.
nodes.body: High risk in: • Prolonged struggling against restraints • Stimulant intoxication • Hyperthermia • Severe agitation Monitor for: • Dark (cola-colored) urine • Muscle tenderness • Weakness Labs: CK, BMP (K+), creatinine Treatment: • Aggressive IV hydration (target UOP 200-300 mL/hr) • Monitor K+ (hyperkalemia risk) • Avoid restraints if possible • Rapid sedation to stop struggling

nodes.title: Hyperactive Delirium
nodes.summary: Hyperactive delirium = high mortality. Aggressive cooling, rapid sedation, hydration, and close monitoring.
nodes.body: Hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia — HIGH MORTALITY Recognition: • Disoriented + combative + altered • Adrenergic overdrive (tachycardia, hypertension) • Hyperthermia (>40°C) • Often: stimulant use (cocaine, meth) Immediate management: 1. Aggressive cooling — ice packs, cold fluids, evaporative 2. Rapid sedation — benzodiazepines when feasible; ketamine 5 mg/kg IM if immediate safety threat or

nodes.title: Complete Evaluation
nodes.summary: Labs, imaging, ECG once sedated. Assess for underlying cause and safety risk.
nodes.body: Once sedation achieved: Labs: • CBC, BMP, glucose, lactate • Troponin (if tachycardia, hypertension) • UA, toxicology • CK if rhabdo concern Imaging: • CT head if: trauma, focal neuro findings, headache/seizure, anticoagulation/immunosuppression, delirium features, age >45 first psychiatric symptoms, or atypical presentation • CXR if: hypoxia, aspiration concern ECG: • QTc (if antipsychotics given

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition based on etiology, ongoing sedation needs, and safety assessment.
nodes.body: Where does this patient need to go?

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU for ongoing sedation, airway, rhabdo, arrhythmia, or refractory agitation.
nodes.body: ICU criteria: • Ongoing sedation requirements • Airway concern / intubated • Rhabdomyolysis with renal injury • Cardiac arrhythmias • Hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia • Refractory agitation (phenobarbital/propofol infusion)
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU for ongoing monitoring and management.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Admission
nodes.summary: Psychiatric admission for primary psych with ongoing safety risk.
nodes.body: Psychiatric admission if: • Primary psychiatric etiology confirmed • Ongoing safety risk (suicidal, homicidal) • Unable to care for self Requires medical stability assessment first: → Psych Medical Stability
nodes.recommendation: Admit to inpatient psychiatry after medical clearance.

nodes.title: Medical Admission
nodes.summary: Medical admission for underlying condition (sepsis, metabolic, withdrawal).
nodes.body: Medical admission if: • Underlying medical condition requiring treatment - Sepsis, DKA, stroke, etc. • Delirium requiring ongoing workup • Withdrawal requiring monitored taper
nodes.recommendation: Admit to medicine or appropriate specialty service.

nodes.title: ED Observation
nodes.summary: Observe until sober, then complete assessment and disposition.
nodes.body: Observation if: • Mild intoxication expected to resolve • Awaiting sobriety for complete assessment • Unclear etiology, low acuity Reassess when sober: • Complete psychiatric assessment • Safety evaluation • Disposition planning
nodes.recommendation: Observe in ED until sober, then reassess.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.summary: Discharge if benign etiology, safe, with follow-up arranged.
nodes.body: Discharge if: • Clear benign etiology (mild intoxication, resolved) • No safety concerns • Safe environment • Reliable follow-up available Provide: • Follow-up appointment • Crisis resources (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) • Return precautions
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with follow-up and crisis resources.

nodes.title: Management Complete
nodes.summary: Document interventions, debrief, review for QI.
nodes.body: Patient managed per protocol. Key reminders: • Document all interventions • Debrief with team • Review for quality improvement
nodes.recommendation: Document interventions and debrief with team.

nodes.title: Cyanosis / Hypoxaemia Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Central vs peripheral cyanosis; co-oximetry not just pulse ox; oxygen + POCUS while sorting the cause.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Tension pneumothorax \u2014 unilateral absent breath sounds + shock \u2192 decompress before imaging. 2. Massive / submassive PE \u2014 hypoxia, RV strain, clear lungs, VTE risk \u2192 echo + CTPA when stable. 3. Carbon monoxide \u2014 fire/smoke/generator, headache, confusion; pulse ox reads falsely normal. 4. Methemoglobinemia \u2014 saturation gap, chocolate-brown

nodes.title: Central or Peripheral Cyanosis?
nodes.summary: Central cyanosis = hypoxaemia/dyshaemoglobin emergency; peripheral = perfusion problem. Needs ~5 g/dL deoxyHb to be visible - anaemia hides it.
nodes.body: The pivot. Central cyanosis (blue tongue, lips, oral mucosa) reflects arterial desaturation or abnormal haemoglobin and is the emergency. Peripheral cyanosis (blue fingers/toes with pink mucosa) usually reflects low flow / cold / vasoconstriction, not hypoxaemia. Why cyanosis is an unreliable sign. Visible cyanosis requires roughly 5 g/dL of deoxygenated haemoglobin in capillary blood (Lundsgaard

nodes.title: Peripheral Cyanosis - Assess Perfusion
nodes.body: Isolated peripheral cyanosis with pink mucosa and a normal SaO2 is a perfusion problem, not central hypoxaemia.
