Consider: shock / low cardiac output, cold exposure or Raynaud phenomenon, arterial occlusion (acutely painful, pulseless, cold limb), or venous congestion. Do: re-warm, check bilateral pulses and cap refill, screen for shock (BP, lactate, POCUS IVC/heart). If a limb is acutely ischaemic
nodes.recommendation: Pink mucosa + normal SaO2 = perfusion problem; hunt shock or limb ischaemia, not lung disease.

nodes.title: Which Cause Are You Working Up?
nodes.summary: Choose a mechanism; the hub runs its pathway to a verdict. A saturation gap points to the toxic branch.
nodes.body: Pick the mechanism you want to rule in or rule out. Each path runs to a clear verdict and routes to the deep-dive consult. Work through more than one if the picture is mixed. Anchor on the co-oximetry / ABG: a saturation gap redirects you to the toxic branch.

nodes.title: Toxic Haemoglobin - Rule In (the Saturation Gap)
nodes.summary: Co-oximetry unmasks CO/MetHb when SpO2, cyanosis, and PaO2 disagree. SpO2 alone misses both. Draw co-oximetry before hydroxocobalamin.
nodes.body: Suspect when cyanosis, pulse-ox reading, and PaO2 do not agree, or with exposure history. Standard 2-wavelength pulse oximetry is unreliable in CO and methemoglobinemia \u2014 use co-oximetry (measures COHb and MetHb directly). Check ABG/VBG with lactate. - CO: COHb elevated; SpO2 falsely normal or high; fire/smoke/generator exposure, headache, confusion, multiple sick contacts. - Methemoglobinemi

nodes.title: Toxic Haemoglobin - Treat
nodes.body: Open CO Toxicity or Methemoglobinemia. - CO: high-flow 100% oxygen immediately (shortens COHb half-life); consider hyperbaric oxygen per criteria (syncope, ischaemia/ECG changes, focal neuro deficit, pregnancy with high COHb, persistent symptoms). - Half-lives that matter for the clinical decision: COHb ~4-5 h on room air, ~60-90 min on a tight non-rebreather, ~20-30 min at 2.5-3 ATA. A level draw
nodes.recommendation: 100% O2 (\u00B1 HBO) for CO; methylene blue for symptomatic methemoglobinemia; remove the agent. Watch for G6PD deficiency, serotonergic co-medication, and concurrent cyanide in fire victims.

nodes.title: Vascular - Rule In (PE / Tension Pneumothorax)
nodes.summary: Clear lungs + hypoxia -> PE (score it); unilateral silent chest + shock -> tension PTX, decompress clinically.
nodes.body: Sudden hypoxaemia/cyanosis with clear or unilateral lungs points vascular. - Massive/submassive PE: hypoxia, tachycardia, RV strain on ECG/echo, clear lung fields, VTE risk factors. Use Wells PE or Revised Geneva (toolbar) to anchor pretest probability. - Tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, distended neck veins, shock \u2014 this is a clinical diagnosis, decompre

nodes.title: Vascular - Treat
nodes.body: Open Pneumothorax for the pleural emergency. - Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle/finger decompression, then tube \u2014 do not wait for imaging. - Massive PE (SBP <90 / shock): resuscitate in place, bedside echo for RV strain, activate PERT; systemic thrombolysis or catheter therapy. Do not send a crashing unresuscitated patient to CT. Submassive PE \u2192 monitored bed + PERT discussion. Whe
nodes.recommendation: Tension PTX = clinical decompression before imaging; massive PE = resuscitate + lyse/intervene, echo first.

nodes.title: Parenchymal - Rule In (Pneumonia / ARDS)
nodes.summary: Confirm infiltrate; CURB-65/PSI for pneumonia, lung-protective support for ARDS. Screen sepsis with NEWS/MEWS/SIRS - SSC recommends against qSOFA as the sole screen.
nodes.body: Hypoxaemic respiratory failure with infiltrates. Confirm with CXR (or POCUS consolidation / B-lines). Grade severity and screen for sepsis. - Pneumonia: fever, cough, focal findings + infiltrate. Score disposition with CURB-65 or PSI (toolbar); screen sepsis with qSOFA + lactate. - Caveat on qSOFA: the Surviving Sepsis Campaign makes a strong recommendation AGAINST using qSOFA as the single screen

nodes.title: Parenchymal - Treat
nodes.body: Open Pneumonia; open Sepsis Management if septic. - Pneumonia disposition: CURB-65 0-1 / PSI I-II outpatient candidate; CURB-65 2 / PSI III observe; CURB-65 \u22653 / PSI IV-V admit, consider ICU by IDSA minor criteria. - Attribution note: these CURB-65 cut-offs are conventional practice rather than an ATS/IDSA recommendation. The 2019 ATS/IDSA CAP guideline conditionally recommends the PSI in pre
nodes.recommendation: Severity score sets site of care (ATS/IDSA prefers PSI over CURB-65); oxygen escalation + guideline antibiotics; lung-protective ventilation for ARDS.

nodes.title: Obstructive - Severity (COPD / Asthma Failure)
nodes.summary: Physiologic severity drives therapy; silent chest/AMS + cyanosis = impending ventilatory failure.
nodes.body: Cyanosis in obstructive disease signals severe, often hypercapnic, failure. Grade by physiology (speech, work of breathing, mental status, air movement), not one number. Silent chest, exhaustion, or altered mental status = impending ventilatory failure.

nodes.title: Obstructive - Treat
nodes.body: Open Asthma Exacerbation or COPD Exacerbation. Next 5 minutes: continuous albuterol for severe asthma, ipratropium, systemic steroid, magnesium for severe asthma; NIV early for COPD/hypercapnic failure when the patient is cooperative and protecting the airway. Titrate oxygen to 88-92% in the COPD retainer. Intubation warning: severe obstruction is a physiologically difficult airway \u2014 low rate
nodes.recommendation: Maximize bronchodilation + steroid; NIV early; controlled oxygen in retainers; avoid rushed intubation.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Oxygen + co-oximetry ABG + POCUS; treat the cause in parallel; reassess physiology frequently.
nodes.body: Default bundle while the cause clarifies: - High-flow oxygen (target 94-98%, or 88-92% in known CO2 retainers). In suspected CO, give 100% oxygen regardless of SpO2. - Monitor, IV, ECG. - ABG/VBG with co-oximetry early \u2014 the single test that unmasks CO and methemoglobin and quantifies ventilation. - CXR when stable; lung/cardiac POCUS when the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient is sick (B-

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Tiring patients need escalation; stable unclear patients need cause-directed imaging.
nodes.body: The hypoxaemic patient can improve or crash quickly. Reassess physiology, not just the diagnosis label.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: CXR + POCUS first; CTPA when stable and actionable; toxic Hb is a lab diagnosis, not imaging.
nodes.body: Imaging by likely cause: - CXR: pneumonia, pneumothorax, oedema, effusion, device/tube checks. - Lung POCUS: B-lines (oedema), absent sliding + lung point (pneumothorax), consolidation, effusion. - Cardiac POCUS: RV strain (PE), LV function, pericardial effusion/tamponade. - CTPA: suspected PE when pretest probability and testing support it and the patient is stable enough. - CT chest: unclear sev

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU/transfer for support or HBO, admit for oxygen or uncertainty, discharge only if stable on room air.
nodes.body: Disposition follows oxygen requirement, work of breathing, trajectory, and cause.

nodes.title: ICU / Resus / Transfer
nodes.body: ICU/resus for NIV or intubation, persistent severe hypoxaemia, shock, rising CO2/acidosis, massive PE, severe asthma/COPD with exhaustion, or ARDS. Arrange hyperbaric transfer for CO poisoning meeting HBO criteria (syncope, neuro deficit, ischaemia, pregnancy with high COHb) \u2014 in practice COHb >25%, or >15-20% in pregnancy, loss of consciousness, focal deficit, cardiac ischaemia, or persisten
nodes.recommendation: Escalate early. Hypoxaemic deterioration is abrupt; arrange HBO transfer for qualifying CO within 6 hours.

nodes.title: Admit / Observation
nodes.body: Admit or observe for a new oxygen requirement, persistent hypoxaemia, symptomatic CO not meeting HBO criteria (serial neuro checks), resolving methemoglobinemia after methylene blue, pneumonia with risk features, COPD/CHF needing repeated therapy, or PE workup/treatment. Use the cause-specific consult for the final destination and orders.
nodes.recommendation: Use the cause-specific consult for final destination and orders.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: stable room-air oxygenation at rest and with ambulation, cyanosis resolved, co-oximetry normalised (COHb/MetHb), clear diagnosis, durable treatment response, no high-risk alternate diagnosis, and return precautions given. Return precautions: worsening breathlessness, recurrent cyanosis, chest pain, syncope, confusion, headache (recurrent CO exposure at home \u2014 check the so
nodes.recommendation: Confirm co-oximetry normalised and the CO source is addressed before discharge.

nodes.title: Epigastric Pain / Dyspepsia — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Gestalt sick check + vitals + ECG-first mindset. If unstable: resuscitate in parallel with workup.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F "Just indigestion" is where killers hide. 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Inferior / atypical ACS \u2014 epigastric pain + diaphoresis / dyspnea / nausea. Get an ECG first. 2. Aortic catastrophe \u2014 dissection (tearing pain, BP differential) or ruptured AAA (age \u226550, back/flank, pulsatile mass, syncope). 3. Mesenteric ischemia \u2014 pain out of proportion to exam, AF / vascular disease; no

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Differential
nodes.summary: Pick the most acute differential; walk its instrument to an explicit verdict. Excluded loops back.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous causes to an explicit verdict, one at a time. Each differential walks its instrument (ECG, US, score, or imaging) to excluded, test further, or rule in + treat. Excluded loops back here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Cardiac Mimic — ECG Gate
nodes.summary: ECG in <10 min. Inferior STE / high-risk story = ACS pathway; non-ischemic + HEART-low = low probability.
nodes.body: Get a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes on every middle-aged-or-older patient with epigastric pain, especially with diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, or exertional onset. Inferior MI classically presents as "indigestion." A single normal ECG + troponin does NOT clear ACS \u2014 serial testing or a validated pathway (HEART) is required.

nodes.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome — Treat
nodes.body: Inferior STEMI: open STEMI. ST elevation II/III/aVF \u2014 get right-sided leads (V4R); RV infarction needs fluid loading and nitroglycerin is contraindicated if RV involved. Aspirin 325 mg chewed, activate cath lab. NSTEMI / unstable angina: open NSTEMI. Aspirin, anticoagulation, risk-stratify (HEART / GRACE), serial troponin, cardiology. Myocarditis mimic (younger, viral prodrome, diffuse change
nodes.recommendation: ECG-driven ACS pathway. Inferior MI \u2192 V4R, no nitrate if RV. ASA 325 chewed. Serial troponin if NSTEMI.

nodes.title: ACS — Low Probability
nodes.body: A non-ischemic ECG with a low-risk story (HEART low, normal/negative troponin per your accelerated pathway) makes ACS unlikely as the driver. Do not clear ACS on a single ECG in a diabetic, elderly, or female patient with a convincing story \u2014 use serial troponin + repeat ECG. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: ACS low probability by ECG + accelerated pathway; serial troponin if the story stays concerning.

nodes.title: Aortic Catastrophe — Dissection / AAA Gate
nodes.summary: Dissection features or aorta \u22653 cm + symptoms = treat. <3 cm + no dissection features = excluded.
nodes.body: Epigastric / back pain can be aortic. Dissection: abrupt tearing pain, inter-arm BP differential, pulse deficit, widened mediastinum. AAA: age \u226550 + back/flank pain \u2014 bedside aorta US is ~98% sensitive for AAA presence; a pulsatile mass has poor sensitivity (~50%), so its absence does not rule out AAA.

nodes.title: Aortic Emergency — Treat
nodes.body: Ruptured / symptomatic AAA: open Aortic Aneurysm. Two large-bore IVs, type and CROSS 4-6 units, permissive hypotension (SBP 70-90), vascular surgery + IR now; do NOT delay for CT if unstable with a bedside AAA. Aortic dissection: open Aortic Dissection. Rate before pressure \u2014 esmolol / labetalol to HR ~60 BEFORE a vasodilator; CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis; cardiothoracic surgery. Do NOT anticoagu
nodes.recommendation: AAA \u2192 type/cross, permissive hypotension, vascular+IR before CT if unstable. Dissection \u2192 rate before pressure + CTA, no anticoagulation.

nodes.title: Aortic Emergency — Excluded
nodes.body: No tearing pain / BP differential and a normal bedside aorta make an aortic catastrophe unlikely. Document aortic diameter and the absence of dissection features. If the pain is migratory or the mediastinum is wide on CXR, image with CTA regardless of aortic diameter. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Aortic emergency excluded; document diameter + absence of dissection features; CTA if features emerge.

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia — Pretest Probability Gate
nodes.summary: Pretest probability + CTA. Normal lactate does not exclude. High suspicion = image now.
nodes.body: There is no validated exclusion score \u2014 this is a pretest-probability + CTA diagnosis. Suspect it with pain out of proportion to a benign exam plus an embolic source (AF, recent MI, valve disease) or vascular risk / postprandial "food fear." A normal lactate does NOT rule it out early \u2014 lactate rises only after transmural infarction.

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia — Image + Treat
nodes.body: Open Mesenteric Ischemia. Next 5 minutes: - CTA mesenteric (arterial + venous phases) \u2014 do not delay for renal function unless eGFR <30; the diagnosis is more dangerous than the contrast. - Vascular surgery + IR early \u2014 endovascular or open intervention within hours. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics (transmural ischemia \u2192 bacterial translocation). - Fluid resuscitation, NPO, anticoagula
nodes.recommendation: CTA now, vascular + IR early, heparin per vascular. Normal lactate does not exclude \u2014 image anyway.

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia — Low Probability
nodes.body: With a benign exam, no vascular / embolic risk, and pain that fits the exam, mesenteric ischemia is unlikely and does not warrant immediate CTA. Do not anchor on "gastritis" in an AF patient with severe pain and minimal findings \u2014 if that picture emerges, come back and image. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Low probability; no immediate CTA. Re-image if out-of-proportion pain or vascular risk emerges.

nodes.title: Perforated Viscus — Peritonitis Gate
nodes.summary: Peritonitis + sepsis or free air = perforation pathway; soft abdomen = unlikely.
nodes.body: Rigid / board-like abdomen + sepsis physiology + free air = perforation until proven otherwise. Perforated peptic ulcer is the classic epigastric source (sudden severe pain, often on an NSAID). Free air on upright CXR is ~75% sensitive; CT with IV contrast is more sensitive and finds the source.

nodes.title: Perforated Viscus — Surgical Emergency
nodes.body: Emergent surgical consult \u2014 do not delay for confirmatory CT if the patient is septic with peritoneal signs. The CT can run in parallel. Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, LR/NS 1-2 L bolus, type and CROSS. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV, OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV. - IV PPI, NPO, NG tube if obstructive features, Foley + UOP.
nodes.recommendation: Emergent surgery, broad-spectrum abx within 1 h, IV PPI, CT in parallel, reverse anticoagulation.

nodes.title: Perforated Viscus — Unlikely
nodes.body: A soft, non-peritonitic abdomen without free air makes perforation unlikely at this moment. Peritonitis can evolve \u2014 if the exam changes on reassessment, come back and treat as perforation. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Perforation unlikely now; re-examine and re-image if peritoneal signs evolve.

nodes.title: Boerhaave / Esophageal Rupture — Mackler Gate
nodes.summary: Mackler triad (vomiting + pain + subcut emphysema). Water-soluble contrast CT confirms.
nodes.body: Mackler triad: forceful vomiting \u2192 severe lower-chest / epigastric pain \u2192 subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus in neck/chest). Often follows retching, alcohol, or an eating binge. High mortality if delayed \u2014 minutes count. Look for Hamman crunch, pleural effusion (often left), pneumomediastinum on CXR.

nodes.title: Boerhaave — Surgical Emergency
nodes.body: Time-critical \u2014 mortality climbs sharply after ~24 h. Next 5 minutes: - CT chest/abdomen with water-soluble oral contrast (Gastrografin) \u2014 avoid barium if perforation suspected. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics + antifungal within 1 h (mediastinitis): piperacillin-tazobactam \u00B1 fluconazole. - IV PPI, strict NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetic. - Emergent thoracic / surgical consult \u2
nodes.recommendation: Water-soluble contrast CT, broad-spectrum abx + antifungal within 1 h, NPO + PPI, emergent thoracic surgery, ICU.

nodes.title: Boerhaave — Unlikely
nodes.body: No forceful-vomiting history and no subcutaneous emphysema / mediastinal air make esophageal rupture unlikely. Keep it alive if there is a hard vomiting history with pain out of proportion \u2014 a normal plain CXR does not exclude an early contained perforation. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Boerhaave unlikely; image with water-soluble contrast if the vomiting-then-pain story is strong.

nodes.title: Pancreatitis — Atlanta + BISAP Gate
nodes.summary: Atlanta 2-of-3 (lipase >3x ULN). BISAP for severity. Normal lipase + atypical pain = unlikely.
nodes.body: Atlanta diagnosis needs 2 of 3: (1) classic pain (epigastric, band-like, radiates to back, better leaning forward), (2) lipase >3\u00D7 ULN, (3) imaging consistent with pancreatitis. If diagnosed, open BISAP in the toolbar to triage severity (ICU vs floor).

nodes.title: Acute Pancreatitis — Treat
nodes.body: Open Acute Pancreatitis. Next 5 minutes: - Goal-directed fluids \u2014 LR preferred over NS (less SIRS); target UOP 0.5-1 mL/kg/h. - Labs: lipase, CBC, CMP, triglycerides, ionized calcium, magnesium, lactate, type and screen. - RUQ US for a gallstone source (commonest etiology). - Analgesia (opioid PRN), antiemetic; early enteral nutrition as tolerated (the old "NPO for days" approach is obsolete)
nodes.recommendation: LR resuscitation + early enteral nutrition + BISAP severity. Image for gallstone source; check ionized calcium.

nodes.title: Pancreatitis — Unlikely
nodes.body: A normal lipase with atypical pain makes acute pancreatitis unlikely (lipase >3\u00D7 ULN is one of the Atlanta pillars). If pain is classic but lipase is borderline, imaging can still satisfy the criteria. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Pancreatitis unlikely with normal lipase + atypical pain; image if the story is classic.

nodes.title: Upper GI Bleed — Glasgow-Blatchford Gate
nodes.summary: Glasgow-Blatchford. GBS 0-1 = outpatient candidate; GBS \u22652 / unstable = resuscitate + endoscopy.
nodes.body: Dyspepsia can be the herald of a bleeding ulcer. Ask about melena, coffee-ground emesis, hematemesis, NSAID use, and anticoagulation; check for pallor / tachycardia / orthostasis and do a rectal exam. Open Glasgow-Blatchford (GBS) in the toolbar \u2014 GBS 0-1 identifies very-low-risk patients who may be managed as outpatients; use AIMS65 for mortality risk.

nodes.title: Upper GI Bleed — Resuscitate + Treat
nodes.body: Open GI Bleed Hub. Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, monitor, type and cross; transfuse to a restrictive threshold (Hb ~7 g/dL, higher if active ischemia). - IV PPI; if cirrhotic add octreotide + ceftriaxone; GI for endoscopy within 24 h (urgently if unstable). - Reverse anticoagulation / correct coagulopathy per severity. - Massive transfusion protocol if exsanguinating; consider IR / surgery
nodes.recommendation: Two large-bore IVs, type and cross, restrictive transfusion (Hb ~7), IV PPI \u00B1 octreotide/ceftriaxone if cirrhotic, endoscopy.

nodes.title: Upper GI Bleed — Very Low Risk
nodes.body: No melena / hematemesis, a normal rectal exam, and a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0-1 identify patients at very low risk who may be considered for outpatient management \u2014 provided vitals are normal, Hb is reassuring, and follow-up is reliable. Any melena with anemia, hemodynamic change, or anticoagulation raises the risk tier. Return to the hub if another differential remains open.
nodes.recommendation: GBS 0-1 + no bleeding signs = very low risk; document rectal exam / Hb before clearing.

nodes.title: Biliary — RUQ / Epigastric Overlap Gate
nodes.summary: RUQ US + labs incl lipase. Cholangitis = abx + ERCP; cholecystitis = abx + surgery; colic = outpatient.
nodes.body: Epigastric pain radiating to the right shoulder, worse after fatty meals, points biliary. Recognize the spectrum: biliary colic (intermittent, afebrile, normal labs) \u2192 cholecystitis (Murphy + fever + leukocytosis, US wall thickening) \u2192 cholangitis (Charcot: fever + jaundice + RUQ pain). Get CBC, CMP, lipase (overlap with pancreatitis), and RUQ US.

nodes.title: Biliary Disease — Treat
nodes.body: Cholangitis is a surgical/GI emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics (pip-tazo, or ceftriaxone + metronidazole), blood cultures \u00D7 2, GI consult for emergent ERCP within 24 h \u2014 source control is the priority. Acute cholecystitis: antibiotics + surgical consult for cholecystectomy; percutaneous cholecystostomy if a poor surgical candidate. Choledocholithiasis: elevated bili + dilated CBD \u2
nodes.recommendation: Cholangitis \u2192 abx within 1 h + urgent ERCP. Cholecystitis \u2192 abx + surgery. Check lipase in all epigastric/RUQ pain.

nodes.title: Biliary Colic — Outpatient
nodes.body: Uncomplicated biliary colic: afebrile, normal WBC, normal LFTs, normal or gallstones-only US. PO challenge, analgesia, antiemetic, and outpatient cholecystectomy referral with strict return precautions (fever, jaundice, persistent pain). Do not discharge epigastric pain without checking lipase (pancreatitis overlap) and LFTs if any jaundice. Return to the hub if another differential remains open.
nodes.recommendation: Biliary colic \u2192 PO challenge + outpatient surgery referral. Confirm lipase and LFTs are clean first.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Undifferentiated Dyspepsia
nodes.summary: ECG/troponin if any above-belt risk + antiemetic + PPI + focused labs incl lipase. GI cocktail is NOT a cardiac rule-out. Reassess 60-90 min.
nodes.body: No life-threat ruled in; the picture fits PUD / gastritis / GERD / functional dyspepsia. Standard ED bundle while labs / ECG cook: - ECG + single troponin if any above-the-belt features or age/risk (do this before committing to "dyspepsia"). - IV access, monitor if any concern; PO route fine if well. - Antiemetic: Ondansetron 4 mg IV (QT caution). - Empiric acid suppression: PPI (e.g., pantoprazol

nodes.title: Reassess at 60-90 Minutes
nodes.summary: Improving = discharge; equivocal = image/observe; new red flag = STOP and return to triage.
nodes.body: Re-examine: pain trend, vitals trend, exam evolution, ECG/troponin/lab results back, ability to tolerate PO.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: ECG first; CT-IV for perforation/older; CTA for vascular; water-soluble contrast CT for Boerhaave; US for biliary/aorta.
nodes.body: Do NOT image every case of dyspepsia. Choose by suspected pathology: ECG (not imaging, but first): every older / at-risk patient with epigastric pain \u2014 rules in the cardiac mimic. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (oral not required): suspected perforation, older/unexplained pain, sepsis with abdominal source, SBO. CT angiography: Mesenteric Ischemia (arterial + venous), dissection extending

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit per deep-dive criteria; observe if equivocal; discharge if benign + PO + no flags + reliable.
nodes.body: Defer to the deep-dive consult\u2019s admit criteria once a phenotype is committed. The framework below applies to undifferentiated / benign-appearing dyspepsia.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for a specific diagnosis (ACS, perforation, mesenteric ischemia, moderate/severe pancreatitis, upper GI bleed, cholangitis, Boerhaave), surgical need, uncontrolled pain, inability to tolerate PO, or hemodynamic concern. Service: Cardiology / Medicine (ACS); Surgery (perforation, Boerhaave, complicated biliary, mesenteric ischemia, ruptured AAA); GI (variceal / severe upper GI bleed, ERCP-nee
nodes.recommendation: Admit per deep-dive criteria; match service to dominant diagnosis; ICU for instability; standard handoff.

nodes.title: Observe — Partial Response or Pending Workup
nodes.body: ED observation when: equivocal exam + intermediate concern, awaiting serial troponin / imaging, pain partially controlled with social/safety barriers, reliable patient. Protocol: serial exam q2-4h (same provider when possible), documented each time; serial troponin + repeat ECG if any cardiac concern; repeat lactate at 2-4 h if any sepsis concern; continue PPI / analgesia / antiemetic. Escalate (i
nodes.recommendation: Obs + serial exams + serial troponin if cardiac concern; escalate if worsening, discharge with recheck if improving.

nodes.title: Discharge — Benign Dyspepsia Checklist
nodes.body: Before discharge: (1) pain reduced to acceptable/baseline, (2) ECG + troponin reassuring if there was any above-the-belt feature or cardiac risk, (3) tolerating PO (PO challenge), (4) vitals normal, (5) no new exam findings on recheck, (6) lipase / relevant labs reviewed, (7) written return precautions, (8) primary-care / GI follow-up for empiric therapy + alarm-feature workup. Empiric plan for li
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after cardiac features cleared, PO tolerated, no alarm features; empiric PPI + H. pylori test-and-treat + GI follow-up.

nodes.title: Acute Jaundice Hub — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Gestalt sick check + West Haven grade + 4-question screen (APAP, Charcot, encephalopathy, recent shock). Resus parallel if unstable, encephalopathic, or coagulopathic.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Acute cholangitis \u2014 Charcot/Reynolds; antibiotics within 1 hour + biliary drainage. 2. Acute liver failure \u2014 encephalopathy + INR \u22651.5 without prior cirrhosis; call transplant center. 3. Acetaminophen toxicity \u2014 acute or chronic supra-therapeutic; start NAC early. 4. Massive hemolysis \u2014 pallor + jaundice + falling H/H. 5. Ischemic hepatitis /

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the One That Fits
nodes.summary: Pick the most acute hit. Each branch links to its deep-dive or focused result + tells you the next 5-min action.
nodes.body: Ask history first, then anchor on the lab and exam pivot. Each branch routes to a deep-dive or focused result and tells you the next 5-min action while you transition. --- Basis: Branch triggers map to published criteria — Charcot/Reynolds and Tokyo Guidelines 2018 cholangitis criteria [4]; acute liver failure definition and King's College track from the ACG Acute Liver Failure Guidelines 2023 [7]

nodes.title: Ascending Cholangitis — Charcot / Reynolds
nodes.body: Open Gallbladder Disease for the full biliary pathway with Tokyo TG18 grading and ERCP triage. Recognize the spectrum: - Charcot triad (fever + jaundice + RUQ pain) — modern large cohorts (Kiriyama 2017, n>6000) show full triad present in only ~20-50% of cholangitis (sensitivity ~26%, specificity ~96%). Absence does NOT rule out — use Tokyo TG18 diagnostic criteria. - Reynolds pentad (Charcot + hy
nodes.recommendation: Tokyo TG18 grade. Blood cultures → antibiotics within 1 hour. Emergent GI for ERCP / PTBD in Grade III. ICU if any organ failure.

nodes.title: Acetaminophen Hepatotoxicity
nodes.body: Open Acetaminophen Toxicity for the full pathway — risk stratification, Rumack-Matthew plotting, NAC dosing (21-h IV or 72-h PO), King's College monitoring, hepatology / transplant escalation. Three exposure patterns that all hurt: [5] - Acute single ingestion with known time → 4-h-or-later level → plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram. - Repeated supra-therapeutic dosing (>4 g/d in healthy adults, >2 g
nodes.recommendation: Send APAP level + treat empirically with NAC if any clinical concern. Kings College from arrival. Transplant center early if INR climbing or acidotic.

nodes.title: Acute Liver Failure — Any Cause
nodes.body: Definition (ACG 2023): encephalopathy + coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) within 26 weeks of liver injury onset in a patient WITHOUT pre-existing cirrhosis. [7] Subtypes by time-to-encephalopathy: - Hyperacute (<7 d): APAP, ischemic, HSV — best transplant-free survival. APAP-ALF, the prototypical hyperacute presentation, runs ~65-75% spontaneous (transplant-free) survival in US ALFSG registry data. [26] - A
nodes.recommendation: Kings College from arrival - it rules IN, not OUT. NAC for ALL ALF. Glucose q1h. Vit K but NOT FFP. Transplant center within 1 hour of recognition.

nodes.title: Massive Hemolysis
nodes.body: Indirect hyperbilirubinemia + falling Hgb + ↑LDH + ↓haptoglobin + smear findings drives the workup. Etiology determines the next intervention. Recognize the pattern: - Indirect (unconjugated) hyperbili dominates — direct fraction <20% of total in pure hemolysis. - LDH >1000 with haptoglobin <10 mg/dL = ~90% specific for hemolysis. - Schistocytes on smear → microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC, malignan
nodes.recommendation: Type and cross. Coombs + smear + LDH/haptoglobin. Heme consult for TTP/AIHA. PEX for TTP, steroids for AIHA.

nodes.title: Ischemic Hepatitis ("Shock Liver")
nodes.body: Pattern recognition: AST and ALT in the thousands (often >25× ULN) within 24-72 hours of a hemodynamic insult — cardiac arrest, septic shock, hemorrhagic shock, severe heart failure exacerbation, post-arrest hypoperfusion, severe hypoxia. LDH is usually elevated proportionally (helpful: AST/LDH ratio <1.5 favors ischemic hepatitis over viral or APAP). [10] Key distinguishing features from ALF: - B
nodes.recommendation: Fix the upstream shock. Send APAP + viral panel. Repeat LFTs at 12-24 h — rapid fall confirms ischemic hepatitis.

nodes.title: Painless Obstructive Jaundice
nodes.body: Painless jaundice + weight loss + age ≥50 = malignant biliary obstruction until proven otherwise. [11] Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most common culprit; cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary tumors, and porta hepatis nodes also drive this presentation. Recognize the pattern: - Painless is the key differentiator from cholangitis or biliary colic. - Courvoisier sign — palpable, non-tender, distende
nodes.recommendation: RUQ US + CT pancreatic protocol. GI for ERCP with brushings. Admit for decompression workup. Outpatient discharge generally inappropriate.

nodes.title: Wilson Disease — De Novo Presentation
nodes.body: Young adult (typically <40) with acute liver failure pattern + Coombs-negative hemolysis + low alkaline phosphatase is Wilson disease until proven otherwise. [12] Pathognomonic lab pattern that should make you call it: - Alkaline phosphatase <40 IU/L (low — opposite of obstruction) - Alk phos to total bili ratio <4 (highly specific for Wilsonian ALF) - AST:ALT ratio >2.2 (mitochondrial injury patt
nodes.recommendation: Ceruloplasmin + 24-h urine copper + slit-lamp from ED. Hepatology + transplant center now. Chelation does not rescue fulminant Wilsonian ALF.

nodes.title: Budd-Chiari Syndrome
nodes.body: Triad: abdominal pain + ascites + hepatomegaly + jaundice in a patient with hypercoagulable risk factors (myeloproliferative neoplasm, OCP, pregnancy/postpartum, malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, Factor V Leiden, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, Behçet disease, hepatic vein web). [13] Recognize the pattern: - Subacute: weeks-to-months of worsening abdominal distension, RUQ pain, hepatomeg
nodes.recommendation: Hepatic vein Doppler US first. CT/MR venogram for planning. Heparin + hepatology + IR. TIPS / transplant per response.

nodes.title: Autoimmune Hepatitis Flare
nodes.body: Pattern: young or middle-aged female + jaundice + AST/ALT often >1000 (sometimes >2000) + elevated IgG + positive ANA / SMA / anti-LKM1. [14] Can present as acute liver failure or sub-fulminant pattern. Co-existing autoimmune disease (Hashimoto, celiac, T1DM, vitiligo) raises pretest probability. Recognize the pattern: - AST/ALT-dominant (>1000 not unusual) - Elevated IgG (>2× ULN highly suggestiv
nodes.recommendation: Send ANA/SMA/IgG/LKM/SLA + viral panel from ED. Hepatology drives steroid timing. Transplant center if ALF criteria met.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Undifferentiated Acute Jaundice
nodes.summary: IV + NPO + ondansetron + APAP-free analgesia + broad hepatic panel + APAP level (always) + viral / autoimmune / hemolysis workup. Reassess at 60-90 min.
nodes.body: No life-threat hit yet; pattern fits a more measured workup. The bundle below is BROADER than the typical abdominal-pain bundle because the lethal causes hide in serologies and special studies that take hours to result. [1,2] THE BUNDLE: - IV × 1-2, monitor - NS or LR 1-2 L bolus if any volume responsive feature; otherwise maintenance - NPO until disposition / dietitian / hepatology guidance - Ant

nodes.title: Reassess at 60-90 Minutes
nodes.summary: Pivot identified → exclusions branch. Equivocal → image/observe. New encephalopathy/INR climb → ALF pathway. Benign Gilbert pattern → discharge.
nodes.body: Re-examine: West Haven grade, vitals trend, lab returns, imaging findings, ability to tolerate PO. --- Basis: Serial reassessment and the lab-pivot framework are from the AFP adult-jaundice evaluation reviews [1,2,15]. The escalation trigger — new or worsening encephalopathy with a rising INR — is the acute liver failure threshold defined in the ACG Acute Liver Failure Guidelines 2023 [7].

nodes.title: Imaging Decision Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: RUQ US first for nearly everyone. MRCP for biliary tree mapping. CT/CTA for mass / vascular workup. ERCP is therapeutic. "Normal imaging" does not rule out hepatocellular causes.
nodes.body: Imaging strategy in jaundice is question-driven, NOT shotgun. The question is "obstruction vs hepatocellular vs vascular?" [11] RUQ US — first study in nearly every jaundice patient: - Cheap, fast, no radiation, no contrast - Detects biliary dilation (sensitivity ~85% for obstruction) - Detects gallstones, sludge, cholecystitis features (wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy)

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Transplant center if ALF / King's College met. ICU for cholangitic shock / shock liver / progressing ALF. Floor for stable workup. Discharge only for Gilbert / mild stable patterns.
nodes.body: Defer to deep-dive consult disposition criteria once a phenotype is committed. The framework below applies to undifferentiated jaundice or after the branch has been chosen. --- Basis: Transplant-center referral and ICU triage thresholds are from the ACG Acute Liver Failure Guidelines 2023 [7], the AASLD ALF Position Paper [16], and the King's College Criteria [8]. Tokyo Guidelines 2018 severity gr

nodes.title: Transplant Center Transfer — Criteria & Bundle
nodes.body: Indications for emergent transplant center transfer: [7,8] - Acute liver failure meeting King's College Criteria: - APAP track: arterial pH <7.3 after resuscitation OR (Cr >3.4 + INR >6.5 + Grade III-IV encephalopathy) - Non-APAP track: INR >6.5 OR any 3 of: age <10 or >40, non-A/non-B/DILI etiology, jaundice-to-encephalopathy >7 d, INR >3.5, bili >17.5 - Wilsonian ALF (poor prognosis without tran
nodes.recommendation: Confirm accepting attending + transport. Intubate before transport if Grade III-IV. Continue NAC. Vit K but NOT FFP unless bleeding. Complete handoff doc.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU level of care for jaundice patients meeting any of: [1,2,7] - Septic shock from cholangitis (Tokyo TG18 Grade III) - Ischemic hepatitis with ongoing hemodynamic instability - ALF not yet meeting transplant criteria but trending wrong (rising INR, climbing ammonia, hypoglycemia despite D10W, falling MAP, rising Cr) - Reynolds pentad without immediate ERCP availability — bridge with antibiotics
nodes.recommendation: ICU with hourly neuro/glucose, q2-4h coag, q6h ammonia. Vit K daily, NOT FFP. Low threshold for empiric antibiotics. Hepatology + transplant center daily contact.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor-level admission appropriate for: [1,2] - Stable obstructive jaundice awaiting ERCP (no cholangitis features, no shock, stable vitals) - Stable hepatitis workup in progress (viral, autoimmune, drug-induced) without encephalopathy or coagulopathy - Stable post-transfusion hemolysis without ongoing hemodynamic concern - Acute pancreatitis with mild jaundice (link to Acute Pancreatitis for sever
nodes.recommendation: Floor admit per dominant diagnosis. Service primary by diagnosis. Confirm stability criteria. Handoff covers serology ETAs and consult call-back times.

nodes.title: Discharge — Universal Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge is rare in acute jaundice and requires: [1,2] 1. Isolated indirect hyperbili pattern fitting Gilbert syndrome: - Indirect bili dominant (direct <20% of total) - Total bili usually <5 mg/dL, often <3 - Normal AST / ALT / alk phos / GGT / CBC / smear - Asymptomatic or only mild fatigue - Common triggers identified (fasting, illness, dehydration, exertion) - Confirm Gilbert with outpatient
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only for Gilbert / known stable baseline / very mild non-progressive pattern. INR <1.5, no encephalopathy, PO tolerated, written precautions, 48-72 h hepatology / PCP recheck.

nodes.title: Acute Monoarthritis Hub — Rule Out the Septic Joint
nodes.summary: The whole hub is built to exclude the SEPTIC joint. Arthrocentesis answers most patients. A prosthetic/instrumented joint is infected until proven otherwise \u2014 involve ortho, do not tap blindly.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Septic arthritis \u2014 a joint that is infected today can be destroyed in days. This is the diagnosis you must exclude in EVERY acute monoarthritis. 2. Disseminated gonococcal infection \u2014 young, sexually active; migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash. 3. Prosthetic joint infection \u2014 any hot prosthetic joint is infected until proven otherwise; do

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the One That Fits
nodes.summary: Infection first. Each branch links to its deep-dive + the next action. Crystals never exclude sepsis.
nodes.body: Infection first, always. Each branch routes to a deep-dive and the next action.

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis — Tap Then Treat
nodes.body: Open Septic Arthritis for the full diagnostic + antibiotic + drainage pathway, and Joint Arthrocentesis for the procedure. A native hot joint with fever is septic arthritis until synovial fluid says otherwise. No single feature rules it in or out \u2014 the joint aspirate is the test. Delay in drainage causes irreversible cartilage loss. [2] Next 5 minutes: - Arthrocentesis BEFORE antibiotics when
nodes.recommendation: Arthrocentesis first (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals), blood cultures, then empiric IV antibiotics (cover MRSA), and orthopedic consult for drainage. Crystals do not exclude infection.

nodes.title: Prosthetic Joint — Do Not Tap Blindly
nodes.body: A hot, painful prosthetic joint (or one recently operated/injected) is a prosthetic joint infection until proven otherwise \u2014 and the workup differs from a native joint. [3] Next steps: - Consult orthopedics BEFORE aspirating. ED aspiration of a prosthetic joint risks seeding the prosthesis and is often best done by orthopedics under sterile/image-guided conditions with their input on antibiot
nodes.recommendation: Orthopedics FIRST for a hot prosthetic joint \u2014 do not tap blindly. Send blood cultures + CRP/ESR + X-ray. Hold empiric antibiotics in the stable patient until cultures obtained; give them if septic.

nodes.title: Disseminated Gonococcal Infection
nodes.body: Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is a leading cause of acute arthritis in young, sexually active adults and presents two ways: (1) the classic triad of migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis (pustular/vesiculopustular lesions), or (2) a purulent monoarthritis. [4] Next steps: - Arthrocentesis if an effusion is present \u2014 send cell count, Gram stain (often negative in DG
nodes.recommendation: Suspect DGI in young sexually active patients with migratory arthritis + tenosynovitis + pustular rash. Tap the joint, NAAT all mucosal sites + blood cultures, empiric ceftriaxone, full STI workup. Joint Gram stain is often negative.

nodes.title: Crystal Arthropathy — Confirm, Never Assume
nodes.body: Gout and pseudogout (CPPD) are the most common causes of acute monoarthritis, but the ED trap is assuming crystal disease and missing an infected joint \u2014 the two coexist. [5] Open Gout for the acute-flare treatment and chronic pathway, and Approach to Arthritis for the broader differential and synovial-fluid interpretation. Recognize: - Gout \u2014 rapid-onset, exquisitely painful, often 1st
nodes.recommendation: Confirm crystals by aspiration but ALWAYS send cell count/Gram stain/culture too. Treat the flare with colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later, an NSAID, or a glucocorticoid - ACR 2020 does not prefer among them. If infection cannot be

nodes.title: Trauma / Hemarthrosis
nodes.body: A swollen joint after trauma \u2014 or a spontaneously swollen joint in an anticoagulated or bleeding-disorder patient \u2014 points to fracture, ligamentous injury, or hemarthrosis rather than infection or crystals. [1] Next steps: - X-ray the joint (fracture, effusion, lipohemarthrosis \u2014 a fat-fluid level indicates intra-articular fracture). CT/MRI for occult fracture or internal derangemen
nodes.recommendation: X-ray for fracture/effusion (lipohemarthrosis = intra-articular fracture). Reverse coagulopathy / replace factor for hemarthrosis. Immobilize + analgesia + ortho follow-up. Tap if infection cannot be excluded.

nodes.title: Lyme Arthritis
nodes.body: In endemic areas, Lyme disease is a cause of subacute/recurrent monoarthritis (classically a large joint, especially the knee) weeks to months after a tick bite \u2014 often with a large effusion but relatively modest pain. [6] Recognize: - Endemic exposure (Northeast/upper Midwest US, parts of Europe), prior erythema migrans or flu-like illness, recurrent knee swelling. - The effusion can be larg
nodes.recommendation: Consider Lyme for subacute recurrent knee monoarthritis in endemic areas; send two-tier serology. If acutely hot/febrile, tap to exclude septic arthritis first. Treat confirmed Lyme arthritis with 28 days of oral doxycycline 100 mg BID (or

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Undifferentiated Acute Monoarthritis
nodes.summary: Analgesia + arthrocentesis (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals) + CBC/CRP/ESR + blood cultures if febrile + X-ray + STI screen if fits. No intra-articular steroid until infection excluded.
nodes.body: No clear life-threat branch fits, but infection still must be excluded. Standard ED bundle centered on the joint aspirate: [1,2] THE BUNDLE: - IV access + monitor if febrile/systemically ill; analgesia (acetaminophen \u00b1 NSAID if no contraindication, or opioid for severe pain). - Arthrocentesis is the pivotal test \u2014 for any effusion where infection is on the differential (see Module 4 for

nodes.title: Reassess — What Did the Tap Show?
nodes.summary: High WBC/positive Gram stain \u2192 treat septic. Crystals + infection excluded \u2192 discharge with flare Rx. Inconclusive/dry tap \u2192 image + observe pending cultures.
nodes.body: Interpret the synovial fluid + clinical picture to choose the pathway.

nodes.title: Arthrocentesis & Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: Tap almost every acute monoarthritis unless cellulitis overlies the site, the joint is prosthetic, or uncorrected coagulopathy. X-ray first; ultrasound guides a dry tap; MRI for osteomyelitis or an un-aspiratable joint. No synovial WBC cuto
nodes.body: Arthrocentesis is the central decision in acute monoarthritis; imaging supports it. [2,7] Aspirate the joint when: - Any acute monoarthritis where septic arthritis cannot be confidently excluded (that is most of them) - Fever, systemic illness, or an atraumatic hot joint - Diagnostic uncertainty (is it crystal or infection?) - See Joint Arthrocentesis for landmarks and technique. Do NOT aspirate (

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if infection excluded and benign; observe if cultures pending/inconclusive; admit septic arthritis, PJI, or systemic illness for drainage + IV antibiotics.
nodes.body: Disposition follows whether infection is excluded and how the patient looks. Defer to the deep-dive consult once a diagnosis is committed.

nodes.title: Discharge — Infection Excluded, Benign Cause
nodes.body: Safe discharge criteria: [1,5] 1. Septic arthritis reasonably excluded \u2014 non-septic synovial fluid (low WBC, negative Gram stain) OR a confident non-infectious diagnosis, and the patient is systemically well. 2. Cause identified/plausible \u2014 crystal flare, osteoarthritis, minor trauma, resolving mechanical process. 3. Pain controlled and the patient can bear weight / use the limb adequate
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only when infection is reasonably excluded and the patient is well: treat the crystal/mechanical cause, arrange rheum/PCP follow-up and culture callback, give clear return precautions.

nodes.title: Observe — Cultures Pending / Inconclusive Tap
nodes.body: Short-stay/observation appropriate when: [2] - Synovial cell count is intermediate and Gram stain negative, but infection cannot be confidently excluded and cultures are pending - A dry or inconclusive tap requiring image-guided re-aspiration - Borderline systemic picture (low-grade fever, elevated inflammatory markers) without a clear diagnosis - Pain not yet controlled or unable to bear weight,
nodes.recommendation: Observe with serial joint/vital checks and pending cultures; re-aspirate under ultrasound if the tap was dry. Low threshold to start antibiotics and admit if the course trends septic.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit when: [2,3] - Septic arthritis (native joint) \u2014 IV antibiotics + orthopedic drainage; see Septic Arthritis. - Prosthetic joint infection \u2014 orthopedic admission; surgical planning (debridement vs exchange). - Disseminated gonococcal infection with purulent arthritis or systemic illness \u2014 IV ceftriaxone. - Systemic sepsis from a joint source \u2014 resuscitate, IV antibiotics, s
nodes.recommendation: Admit septic arthritis, PJI, DGI with systemic illness, or sepsis from a joint. Orthopedics for drainage; ID for antibiotics; ICU if shock. Give empiric IV antibiotics after cultures for a septic native joint.

nodes.title: Acute Pancreatitis
nodes.summary: Diagnose with 2 of 3: epigastric pain, lipase >3x ULN, imaging — most cases mild and self-limiting
nodes.body: Acute Pancreatitis Steps Summary — diagnosis, severity, resuscitation, complications. Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 criteria: [1][2] • Characteristic abdominal pain (epigastric, radiating to back, sudden onset) • Serum lipase (or amylase) >3× upper limit of normal • Imaging evidence on CT, MRI, or ultrasound Key Principles: • Most cases are mild and self-limiting • Early severity stratification guides

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Atlanta Classification: mild (no OF), moderate (transient OF <48h), severe (persistent OF >48h, 17-30% mortality)
nodes.body: Revised Atlanta Classification (2012): [3] Assess for organ failure using Modified Marshall Score: • Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio • Renal: Creatinine • Cardiovascular: SBP (fluid-responsive vs vasopressor-dependent) BISAP Score (within 24h of admission): [4] • BUN >25 mg/dL • Impaired mental status (GCS <15) • SIRS (≥2 criteria) • Age >60 years • Pleural effusion BISAP ≥3: 12-30% mortality risk

nodes.title: Mild AP — Initial Management
nodes.summary: LR 3-4L/24h (not aggressive), early PO feeding within 24-48h, opioids safe for pain — morphine OK
nodes.body: Fluid Resuscitation: [5][6] • Lactated Ringer's preferred over NS (reduced inflammation) • Moderate approach: 3-4 L in first 24 hours • Initial bolus: 10 mL/kg over 2 hours if hypovolemic • Maintenance: ~1.5 mL/kg/hr • Avoid net positive >3-4 L (overresuscitation harmful) Monitoring Goals: • Urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hr • Decreasing BUN • Improving hematocrit (Hct >44% is poor prognostic sign) Pain

nodes.title: Moderate AP — Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Enteral nutrition prevents infections, NG equivalent to NJ — start within 24-48h, avoid TPN
nodes.body: Aggressive Monitoring Required: [5][7] Fluids: • LR preferred; avoid NS (hyperchloremic acidosis) • Goal-directed: titrate to UOP, BUN, Hct • Consider early norepinephrine if fluid-refractory hypotension • Avoid excessive crystalloid (increases abdominal compartment pressure) Nutrition: • Enteral nutrition prevents infectious complications [8] • Nasogastric route equivalent to nasojejunal (easier)

nodes.title: Severe AP — Critical Care
nodes.summary: ICU required — NE if fluid-refractory, monitor for ACS (bladder pressure >20), enteral nutrition critical
nodes.body: ICU Admission Required [7][9] Hemodynamic Support: • Goal MAP ≥65 mmHg • Early norepinephrine if fluid-refractory • Avoid excessive crystalloid (worsens outcomes) • Consider POCUS for fluid responsiveness Respiratory Support: • High flow nasal cannula or BiPAP for hypoxemia • Low threshold for intubation if declining • Lung-protective ventilation if ARDS develops Abdominal Compartment Syndrome: •

nodes.title: Etiology Workup
nodes.summary: All patients need RUQ US + triglycerides + LFTs — gallstones 40-70%, alcohol 25-35%, HTG if TG>1000
nodes.body: Most Common Causes: [1][2] • Gallstones (40-70%) • Alcohol (25-35%) • Hypertriglyceridemia (TG >1,000 mg/dL) • Post-ERCP • Drugs, trauma, autoimmune All Patients Need: • RUQ ultrasound — evaluate for gallstones/CBD dilation • Serum triglycerides — etiology if >1,000 mg/dL • LFTs — ALT >3× ULN highly suggestive of biliary etiology Age >40 with Unknown Etiology: • Consider pancreatic tumor (EUS or M

nodes.title: Gallstone Pancreatitis
nodes.summary: Cholangitis = urgent ERCP <24h; no cholangitis = no routine ERCP; mild AP = same-admission cholecystectomy
nodes.body: Key Decision: Cholangitis Present? [10][11] Signs of Cholangitis (Charcot's Triad): • Fever • Jaundice • RUQ pain If Cholangitis Present: • Urgent ERCP within 24 hours • Antibiotics: Piperacillin-tazobactam or ampicillin-sulbactam • Do not delay for severity of pancreatitis If NO Cholangitis: • No routine ERCP • MRCP or EUS if CBD stone suspected but not confirmed • Avoid diagnostic ERCP (unnecess

nodes.title: Alcoholic Pancreatitis
nodes.summary: Give thiamine before glucose, watch for alcohol withdrawal 6-72h, cessation counseling critical
nodes.body: Management Considerations: [1] Acute Phase: • Same resuscitation principles as other etiologies • Watch for alcohol withdrawal syndrome • Thiamine 100mg IV before glucose-containing fluids • Consider CIWA protocol Alcohol Withdrawal Risk: • Onset 6-24 hours after last drink • Peak risk 24-72 hours • Benzodiazepines for prophylaxis/treatment Long-term: • Alcohol cessation counseling critical • Recu

nodes.title: Hypertriglyceridemic Pancreatitis
nodes.summary: Insulin infusion to activate lipoprotein lipase, target TG<500; apheresis if TG>2000 or refractory
nodes.body: Definition: TG >1,000 mg/dL as the etiology [13] Acute Management: • Insulin infusion: Activates lipoprotein lipase - Regular insulin 0.1-0.3 units/kg/hr - Dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia - Continue until TG <500 mg/dL • Apheresis/Plasmapheresis: - Consider if TG >2,000 mg/dL - Or if not responding to insulin - Rapidly reduces TG by 50-80% NPO Critical: • Dietary fat worsens hypertriglyceridemia

nodes.title: Other Etiologies
nodes.summary: Post-ERCP, drug-induced, autoimmune (responds to steroids), trauma — 10-25% remain idiopathic
nodes.body: Post-ERCP Pancreatitis: [14] • Most common complication of ERCP (3-5%) • Usually mild, self-limiting • NSAIDs and pancreatic duct stents reduce risk Drug-Induced: • Azathioprine, 6-MP, valproic acid, ACE inhibitors • GLP-1 agonists (controversial) • Discontinue offending agent Autoimmune Pancreatitis: [15] • Type 1: IgG4-related disease, older males • Type 2: Associated with IBD • Elevated IgG4, p

nodes.title: Complications Assessment
nodes.summary: Image only if no improvement at 48-72h — do NOT routinely image early in mild AP
nodes.body: Local Complications: [3][16] Early (<4 weeks): • Acute peripancreatic fluid collection (APFC) • Acute necrotic collection (ANC) Late (>4 weeks): • Pseudocyst (walled-off fluid) • Walled-off necrosis (WON) When to Image: • No improvement at 48-72 hours • Clinical deterioration • Suspected infected necrosis • Do NOT routinely image early in mild AP

nodes.title: Pseudocyst Management
nodes.summary: Most pseudocysts resolve spontaneously — size alone is NOT an indication for drainage
nodes.body: Definition: Encapsulated fluid collection with well-defined wall, NO solid debris, develops >4 weeks after onset [3] Observation (Most Cases): • Asymptomatic pseudocysts: serial imaging • Most acute fluid collections resolve spontaneously • Size alone is NOT an indication for drainage Intervention Indications: [17] • Symptomatic (pain, early satiety, nausea) • Gastric outlet obstruction • Biliary

nodes.title: Necrotizing Pancreatitis
nodes.summary: No prophylactic abx, no routine FNA — delay intervention until WON matures >4 weeks if stable
nodes.body: Definition: Necrosis of pancreatic parenchyma and/or peripancreatic tissue [3] Sterile Necrosis — Conservative Management: [18][19] • NO prophylactic antibiotics (ACG/AGA) • Supportive care: fluids, nutrition, pain control • Most sterile necrosis resolves without intervention • Allow walled-off necrosis (WON) to mature (>4 weeks) When to Suspect Infection: • Clinical deterioration after initial im

nodes.title: Necrotizing Pancreatitis — Management
nodes.summary: Assess for gas on CT, elevated PCT >3.5, clinical sepsis — determines sterile vs infected necrosis path
nodes.body: Is there evidence of infected necrosis? • Gas on CT imaging • Procalcitonin >3.5 ng/mL • Clinical sepsis syndrome • Failure to improve with supportive care

nodes.title: Sterile Necrosis — Conservative
nodes.summary: No prophylactic abx, enteral nutrition, serial imaging — ~30% will develop infected necrosis at weeks 2-4
nodes.body: Continue Supportive Care: [18] • Aggressive enteral nutrition • Pain management • Serial imaging (CT in 7-10 days or with clinical change) • NO prophylactic antibiotics Indications for Intervention in Sterile Necrosis: • Gastric outlet or biliary obstruction • Persistent symptoms >8 weeks despite conservative therapy • Disconnected pancreatic duct syndrome Timing: • Delay intervention until WON ma

nodes.title: Infected Necrosis — Overview
nodes.summary: Life-threatening emergency — pip-tazo or carbapenems with pancreatic penetration, delay intervention >4 weeks
nodes.body: Infected Pancreatic Necrosis is a Life-Threatening Emergency [18][19][20] Diagnosis: • Gas on CT (pathognomonic) • Clinical: fever, sepsis, rising WBC/PCT, failure to improve • FNA NOT routinely recommended Initial Management: • Antibiotics with pancreatic penetration: - Piperacillin-tazobactam (first-line) - Carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem) - Fluoroquinolone + metronidazole • Prolonged course: 2

nodes.title: Step-Up Approach
nodes.summary: PANTER step-up: delay+abx (35% resolve) → drain (35% resolve) → minimally invasive → open necrosectomy last
nodes.body: Step-Up Approach (PANTER Trial) — Superior to open necrosectomy [20][21] STEP 1: DELAY + ANTIBIOTICS • If patient stable: antibiotics alone, delay intervention • Goal: allow WON to mature (>4 weeks) • 35% of patients improve without drainage STEP 2: PERCUTANEOUS/ENDOSCOPIC DRAINAGE • Percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD) • OR endoscopic transluminal drainage (ETD) • 35% resolve with drainage alone

nodes.title: Intervention Decision
nodes.summary: Continue abx alone if improving; drainage if persistent sepsis >72h on abx or enlarging collections
nodes.body: Assess current clinical status and response to antibiotics: Continue Antibiotics Alone If: • Clinically improving • Inflammatory markers trending down • No expanding collections Proceed to Drainage If: • Clinical deterioration despite antibiotics • Enlarging collections • Persistent sepsis >72 hours on antibiotics • Gas persisting/increasing on imaging

nodes.title: Continuing Antibiotics
nodes.summary: Minimum 2-4 week abx course, may transition to oral cipro+metronidazole — no antifungal prophylaxis
nodes.body: Antibiotic Management: [19] Duration: • Minimum 2-4 weeks • Continue until clinical resolution • Serial imaging to monitor collections If Improving: • Continue current regimen • May transition to oral with good bioavailability - Ciprofloxacin + metronidazole - Amoxicillin-clavulanate Monitoring: • Daily clinical assessment • Trending WBC, procalcitonin, CRP • Repeat CT if clinical change No Antifu

nodes.title: Drainage Timing
nodes.summary: Delay drainage >4 weeks for WON maturation — PCD or ETD, consult GI and IR for multidisciplinary plan
nodes.body: Optimal Timing: >4 Weeks from Symptom Onset [20][21] Why Delay? • Necrosis becomes walled-off (organized collection) • Easier to drain/debride • Lower complication rate • Better demarcation of viable tissue Drainage Options: Percutaneous Catheter Drainage (PCD): • IR-placed drain into collection • May need upsizing or additional drains • Success: ~35% resolve with drainage alone Endoscopic Translu

nodes.title: Urgent Drainage
nodes.summary: PCD preferred even urgently over surgery; IR standby for pseudoaneurysm embolization; surgical consult essential
nodes.body: Indications for Urgent Intervention: [20][21] • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation • Multiorgan failure worsening • Abdominal compartment syndrome • Massive hemorrhage from pseudoaneurysm Approach: • PCD preferred even urgently (less morbid than surgery) • May need multiple drains • IR on standby for bleeding (angioembolization) If PCD Not Feasible or Fails: • Video-assisted retroperito

nodes.title: Disposition — Mild AP
nodes.summary: Discharge when PO tolerant, pain controlled — gallstone AP: same-admit or 2-week cholecystectomy
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: [1][2] • Pain controlled with oral medications • Tolerating oral diet • Hemodynamically stable • Trending labs improving Before Discharge: • Confirm etiology • Gallstone AP: Schedule cholecystectomy (same admission or within 2 weeks) • Alcohol AP: Cessation counseling, withdrawal precautions • HTG: Lipid clinic referral, fibrate prescription Follow-up: • PCP within 1-2 weeks •

nodes.title: Disposition — Complicated AP
nodes.summary: ICU for persistent organ failure or infected necrosis; multidisciplinary team: GI, IR, surgery, nutrition
nodes.body: ICU Admission Criteria: • Persistent organ failure (severe AP) • Infected necrosis requiring intervention • Hemodynamic instability • Respiratory failure Step-Down/Floor: • Moderate AP with transient organ failure resolved • Stable necrotizing pancreatitis on antibiotics • Pseudocyst not requiring urgent intervention Multidisciplinary Team: • GI (endoscopic drainage, nutrition) • IR (percutaneous

nodes.title: Acute Pancreatitis — Complete
nodes.body: Summary: • Diagnosed with 2 of 3 criteria (pain, lipase >3×, imaging) • Severity by Atlanta Classification guides management • Moderate fluid resuscitation (LR, ~3-4L/24h) • Early enteral nutrition • No prophylactic antibiotics • Gallstone → same-admission cholecystectomy (if mild) • Infected necrosis → step-up approach (delay + antibiotics → drain → debride) Key Resources: • BISAP Score • Atlanta
nodes.recommendation: Management pathway complete. Ensure appropriate disposition and follow-up.

nodes.title: Acute Psychosis Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess first-break vs known psychiatric patient. Red flags drive medical workup intensity.
nodes.body: First-break or new-onset psychosis? Key questions: * Age at onset? * Prior psychiatric history? * Onset timing (hours vs weeks)? * Substance use? Red flags for organic cause: * Age >45 with no prior psych history * Acute onset (hours-days) * Visual hallucinations predominant * Fluctuating mental status * Abnormal vital signs * New neurological deficits * Recent illness/prodrome

nodes.title: Age at Onset
nodes.summary: First psychosis age >=45 = organic cause likely. Full medical workup needed.
nodes.body: Age strongly predicts etiology: Typical age of onset for PRIMARY psychotic disorders: * Schizophrenia: 18-25 (men), 25-35 (women) * Bipolar with psychosis: 20-30 * Brief psychotic disorder: 30-50 Late-onset psychosis (>45) without prior history: * Medical/neurological cause in majority * Dementia, delirium, stroke * Parkinson's, Lewy body * Substance-induced * Brain tumor Very young onset (<13): *

nodes.title: Safety First
nodes.summary: Agitated patient - use Acute Agitation consult first, then return for workup.
nodes.body: Address agitation before diagnostic workup: -> Acute Agitation Consult Priorities: 1. Verbal de-escalation (BETA protocol) 2. Chemical restraint if de-escalation fails 3. Physical restraint only if immediately necessary Once patient is calm and cooperative: Return to this consult for psychosis workup. Consider during sedation: * POC glucose (rule out hypoglycemia) * Vital signs (fever, tachycardia

nodes.title: Known Psychiatric Patient
nodes.summary: Known psychiatric patient - check for triggers, ensure minimum workup.
nodes.body: Exacerbation of known psychotic disorder: Still consider organic causes if: * Presentation differs from baseline * Abnormal vital signs * New neurological symptoms * Medication changes or non-adherence * Recent substance use Common triggers for exacerbation: * Medication non-adherence (#1 cause) * Substance use * Psychosocial stressors * Sleep deprivation * Medication interactions Minimum workup:

nodes.title: First-Break Psychosis Workup
nodes.summary: First-break psychosis: vitals/glucose plus targeted labs; broaden with age, red flags, substance, or neurologic features.
nodes.body: Targeted first-break psychosis workup: Medical/neurologic causes are uncommon in low-risk young adults but high-impact when missed. Use red flags to decide how broad to go. Core ED assessment: * Full vitals, glucose, medication/substance history * CBC, CMP, glucose * TSH when thyroid symptoms, mood syndrome, or unclear cause * Urinalysis if urinary symptoms, pregnancy concern, elderly, or delirium

nodes.title: Late-Onset Psychosis Workup
nodes.summary: Late-onset psychosis: CT/MRI, LP if indicated, EEG, extensive labs, neurology consult.
nodes.body: Age >45 first psychosis = extensive workup: High-yield investigations: * CT head (stroke, tumor, hemorrhage) * MRI brain (if CT unrevealing) * LP (if meningitis/encephalitis suspected) * EEG (seizures, encephalopathy) Labs (in addition to standard): * Ammonia * Cortisol (Cushing's, Addison's) * Parathyroid hormone * Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies * Paraneoplastic panel * HIV, RPR Consider: * Neurol

nodes.title: Neuroimaging
nodes.summary: Image first-break psychosis based on risk factors: age >45, focal deficits, headache/seizure, trauma, delirium, atypical features.
nodes.body: When to image: CT head indicated in the ED if: * Age >45 with first psychiatric symptoms * Focal neurological deficits * Headache, seizure, or decreased consciousness * Recent head trauma * Papilledema * Anticoagulation or immunosuppression * Atypical presentation or delirium features MRI preferred if: * Concern for encephalitis * Demyelinating disease * Subacute neurologic symptoms * Small lesion

nodes.title: Organic Cause Identified
nodes.summary: Organic psychosis identified - treat underlying cause, low-dose antipsychotic PRN.
nodes.body: Treat the underlying cause: Common organic causes of psychosis: | Cause | Treatment | |-------|----------| | Stroke | Neurology, supportive | | Tumor | Neurosurgery, oncology | | Encephalitis | Acyclovir, immunotherapy | | Metabolic | Correct derangement | | Thyroid | Levothyroxine/PTU | | Substance | Supportive, time | | Medication | Discontinue | Antipsychotics for symptom control: * Low-dose, s

nodes.title: Delirium vs Primary Psychosis
nodes.summary: Delirium: fluctuating, inattention, visual hallucinations. Psychosis: stable, auditory.
nodes.body: Critical distinction - treatment differs: | Feature | Delirium | Primary Psychosis | |---------|----------|------------------| | Onset | Hours-days | Weeks-months | | Course | Fluctuating | Stable | | Attention | Impaired | Intact | | Hallucinations | Visual | Auditory | | Orientation | Disoriented | Oriented | | Sleep-wake | Disrupted | Variable | | Vital signs | Often abnormal | Usually normal |

nodes.title: Delirium Identified
nodes.summary: Delirium identified - NOT psych admission. Treat underlying cause.
nodes.body: Delirium is a medical emergency: -> Psych Medical Stability This is NOT a psychiatric admission. Search for cause: * Infection (UTI, pneumonia, meningitis) * Metabolic (glucose, sodium, calcium) * Drugs (anticholinergics, benzos, opioids, withdrawal) * Hypoxia, hypercapnia * Urinary retention, fecal impaction * Pain Avoid: * Antipsychotics as first-line (unless severe agitation) * Benzodiazepines

nodes.title: Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis Screen
nodes.summary: Anti-NMDA encephalitis: young woman, prodrome, psychosis -> movement disorder -> seizures.
nodes.body: Don't miss this treatable cause: High-risk features: * Young woman (80% of cases, but can occur in men/elderly) * Viral-like prodrome (fever, headache) * Psychiatric symptoms -> movement disorder progression * Seizures * Autonomic instability * Decreased consciousness Classic progression: 1. Psychiatric symptoms (psychosis, anxiety) 2. Movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetosis) 3.

nodes.title: Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis
nodes.summary: Anti-NMDA encephalitis: LP, tumor screen, steroids/IVIG/PLEX. 75% recover with treatment.
nodes.body: Urgent workup and treatment: Diagnosis: * LP: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, anti-NMDA receptor antibodies (CSF more sensitive than serum) * MRI: Often normal or nonspecific * EEG: Extreme delta brush pattern (specific but not sensitive) Tumor screen: * Pelvic ultrasound/CT (ovarian teratoma in 50%) * CT chest/abdomen (other teratomas) Treatment: * First-line: Steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis * Tumor remo

nodes.title: Antipsychotic Selection
nodes.summary: First-episode psychosis: second-gen antipsychotic, start low, monotherapy.
nodes.body: First-episode psychosis - antipsychotic principles: General approach: * Start low, go slow * Second-generation (atypical) preferred * Monotherapy * Allow 2-4 weeks for full effect Consider patient factors: * Metabolic risk (avoid olanzapine if diabetic/obese) * QTc prolongation risk (avoid ziprasidone, high-dose haloperidol) * EPS sensitivity (avoid high-potency FGAs) * Sedation needs (quetiapine,

nodes.title: Antipsychotic Dosing
nodes.summary: First-episode: start low (risperidone 1 mg, olanzapine 5 mg). Monitor metabolics.
nodes.body: First-episode dosing (lower than chronic patients): | Medication | Starting Dose | Target Range | |------------|--------------|---------------| | Risperidone | 0.5-1 mg BID | 2-4 mg/day | | Olanzapine | 5 mg daily | 10-15 mg/day | | Aripiprazole | 5-10 mg daily | 10-15 mg/day | | Quetiapine | 50 mg BID | 300-600 mg/day | | Ziprasidone | 40 mg BID | 80-160 mg/day | Baseline monitoring: * Weight, BM

nodes.title: Psychosis Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition: admit for safety/medical instability/grave disability; discharge only with low risk, support, and rapid follow-up.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on etiology, safety, function, and follow-up reliability: Psychiatric admission if: * Danger to self or others * Unable to care for self / grave disability * Severe disorganization, agitation, or command hallucinations * Needs medication initiation/titration with monitoring * Involuntary hold criteria met * First-break psychosis without reliable support or rapid follow-up Medic
nodes.recommendation: Psychiatric consultation and early intervention are recommended for first-break psychosis. Admit for safety, grave disability, severe symptoms, medical instability, or unreliable support/follow-up.

nodes.title: Adrenal Insufficiency — Presentation
nodes.summary: Adrenal crisis = hemodynamic deterioration resolving with IV hydrocortisone; 50% present as first diagnosis
nodes.body: Adrenal Insufficiency Steps Summary Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency. Defined as acute hemodynamic deterioration (SBP ≤100 mmHg or ≥20 mmHg below baseline) that resolves within 1-2 hours of parenteral hydrocortisone. Mortality rate: 0.5 per 100 patient-years in known AI patients. [2][4] Adrenal crisis can be the first presentation of previously undiagnosed AI in up to 50% of cases. Maintain h

nodes.title: Confirm Crisis Features
nodes.summary: Classic crisis: SBP ≤100, hyponatremia 84%, hypoglycemia, hyperK (PAI only) — infection is #1 trigger
nodes.body: Classic adrenal crisis presentation: • Hemodynamic collapse — SBP ≤100 mmHg or ≥20 mmHg below baseline • Hyponatremia (84% of cases) • Hypoglycemia • Hyperkalemia (PAI only — mineralocorticoid deficiency) • Unexplained fever, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting • Altered mental status, confusion, lethargy • Hypercalcemia (rare but described) Common precipitants: • Infection (#1 cause — viral in childr

nodes.title: Immediate Resuscitation
nodes.summary: NS bolus + draw cortisol/ACTH BEFORE steroids (but do NOT delay treatment) — cortisol <18 during stress = AI
nodes.body: Simultaneous actions — do NOT delay treatment for diagnostics. IV Access + Fluids: • Adults: 1L NS bolus, repeat PRN. Add D5 (or D50 bolus) if hypoglycemic. • Pediatrics: 20 mL/kg NS bolus, repeat PRN up to 60 mL/kg in first hour. D10 2-5 mL/kg for hypoglycemia. Draw crisis labs BEFORE steroids if possible — but do NOT delay treatment: • Random cortisol (most important single test) • ACTH level (d

nodes.title: Emergency Steroid Replacement
nodes.summary: Hydrocortisone 100mg IV stat, then 200mg/24h — at ≥50mg/day no fludrocortisone needed; dex if diagnosis uncertain
nodes.body: Hydrocortisone — first-line for adrenal crisis: Adults: • Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM bolus immediately • Then 200 mg/24h as continuous infusion (preferred) or 50 mg IV q6h • Taper to oral over 1-3 days as hemodynamics stabilize Pediatrics: • Hydrocortisone 50 mg/m² IV bolus (max 100 mg) • Then 50-100 mg/m²/day divided q6-8h • BSA required → use toolbar BSA calculator If hydrocortisone unavailable

nodes.title: Response Assessment (1-2 Hours)
nodes.summary: Hemodynamic improvement expected within 1-2h of IV hydrocortisone — no improvement suggests alternate diagnosis
nodes.body: Adrenal crisis should show hemodynamic improvement within 1-2 hours of parenteral hydrocortisone. [2] Expected response: • Blood pressure improves • Mental status clears • Vasopressor requirements decrease • Glucose stabilizes If no improvement: • Reassess diagnosis — is this truly adrenal crisis? • Ensure adequate volume resuscitation • Consider other shock etiologies (septic, cardiogenic, hypovo

nodes.title: Ongoing Crisis Management
nodes.summary: Continue 200mg/24h hydrocortisone, halve daily when stable — avoid aggressive K correction in PAI
nodes.body: Continue first 24-48 hours: • Hydrocortisone 200 mg/24h (continuous infusion preferred, or 50 mg IV q6h) [5] • Aggressive IV fluids — NS ± dextrose • Monitor glucose q1-2h (hypoglycemia common) • Treat precipitating cause aggressively Tapering (day 2-3): • Once hemodynamically stable, halve hydrocortisone dose daily • Transition to oral when tolerating PO • Resume maintenance dose + fludrocortison

nodes.title: Refractory Shock — Broaden Differential
nodes.body: If hemodynamics do not improve within 1-2 hours of hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + aggressive fluids: Reassess for alternative diagnoses: • Septic shock (most common crisis precipitant — may need independent treatment) • Hypovolemic shock (hemorrhage, GI losses) • Cardiogenic shock • Other endocrine emergency (thyroid storm, myxedema coma) Management: • Vasopressors — norepinephrine first-line • Broad-
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission mandatory. Continue stress-dose steroids while investigating alternative diagnoses. Endocrine consultation.

nodes.title: Identify & Treat Precipitant
nodes.summary: Infection is #1 trigger — also steroid withdrawal, CYP3A4 inducers, adrenal hemorrhage; ~10% no identifiable cause
nodes.body: Infection is the #1 trigger — viral in children, bacterial in adults. Precipitating Factors & Differential Diagnosis Common triggers: • Infection/sepsis (most common) • GI illness with vomiting (cannot take oral steroids) • Trauma or surgery without stress dosing • Abrupt steroid discontinuation • CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) • Adrenal hemorrhage (anticoagulation, meningoco

nodes.title: Infection-Precipitated Crisis
nodes.summary: Treat BOTH infection and crisis simultaneously — Waterhouse-Friderichsen = bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, permanent PAI
nodes.body: Treat BOTH the infection AND the crisis simultaneously. • Continue stress-dose Hydrocortisone throughout active infection • Broad-spectrum antibiotics per sepsis protocol • Blood and urine cultures, CXR, procalcitonin • Do NOT taper steroids until infection is controlled • Stress-dose steroids may mask fever — monitor WBC and procalcitonin trends instead Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: • Bilater

nodes.title: AI Type Classification
nodes.summary: PAI = adrenal destruction (high ACTH, hyperK); SAI = pituitary (low ACTH, no hyperK); TAI = exogenous steroids (most common)
nodes.body: Classification guides workup and long-term management. Lab Findings by AI Type Primary AI (PAI): Direct adrenal gland destruction — autoimmune (Addison disease, 80% in developed countries), infectious (TB #1 worldwide), hemorrhagic, infiltrative, bilateral adrenalectomy. Secondary AI (SAI): Pituitary ACTH deficiency — tumors, surgery, radiation, Sheehan syndrome, immune checkpoint inhibitors. Tert

nodes.title: Primary AI (Addison's Disease)
nodes.summary: Hyperpigmentation + hyperK = PAI; check 21-OH Ab, CT adrenals, TSH — treat cortisol BEFORE thyroxine
nodes.body: Hallmarks distinguishing PAI from other types: • Hyperpigmentation — ACTH-driven melanocyte stimulation. Look for palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars, areolae, sun-exposed areas. • Hyperkalemia — aldosterone deficiency (unique to PAI) • Salt craving, postural hypotension, weight loss • Low cortisol + elevated ACTH (>2× upper limit of normal) Etiologic workup: • 21-hydroxylase antibodies (positive

nodes.title: Secondary AI (Pituitary)
nodes.summary: No hyperpigmentation, no hyperK (RAAS intact) — MRI pituitary, full anterior pituitary panel; no fludrocortisone needed
nodes.body: Key differences from PAI: • No hyperpigmentation (ACTH is LOW, not high) • No hyperkalemia (aldosterone preserved — RAAS axis intact) • May have other pituitary hormone deficiencies (TSH, LH/FSH, GH, prolactin) Common causes: • Pituitary adenoma (most common structural cause) • Post-pituitary surgery or radiation • Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis — history of severe postpartum hemo

nodes.title: Tertiary AI (Steroid-Induced)
nodes.summary: Most common AI overall — risk with ≥pred 5mg/day for ≥3 weeks; HPA recovery takes 6-12 months after stopping
nodes.body: Most common form of adrenal insufficiency overall. Corticosteroid Equivalency & Alternatives Risk factors for HPA suppression: • ≥Prednisone 5 mg/day (or equivalent) for ≥3 weeks • Any dose for ≥3 weeks with Cushingoid features • Repeated high-potency inhaled, topical, or intra-articular steroids — Meta-analysis: 4.2% intranasal, 6.8% inhaled, 52.2% intra-articular [11] • Chronic opioid use — prev

nodes.title: Diagnostic Laboratory Evaluation
nodes.summary: AM cortisol <3 = confirmed AI, >15 = unlikely; ACTH high = PAI, low = SAI/TAI; check Na, K, renin, aldosterone
nodes.body: Lab Findings by AI Type Step 1 — Morning Cortisol + ACTH (draw at 8-9 AM): • AM cortisol <3 μg/dL → AI virtually confirmed • AM cortisol >15 μg/dL → AI unlikely (some guidelines use 18 μg/dL) • AM cortisol 3-15 μg/dL → indeterminate, needs cosyntropin stimulation test Step 2 — ACTH level distinguishes type: • ACTH >2× upper limit of normal → Primary AI • ACTH low or inappropriately normal → Second

nodes.title: Cosyntropin (ACTH) Stimulation Test
nodes.summary: Cosyntropin 250mcg IV/IM, peak cortisol ≥18 = normal — does NOT reliably detect SAI or recent-onset PAI
nodes.body: Gold standard for diagnosing PRIMARY AI. Protocol: 1. Draw baseline cortisol 2. Administer cosyntropin 250 μg IV or IM 3. Draw cortisol at 30 and 60 minutes Interpretation: • Peak cortisol ≥18 μg/dL → normal response, rules out PAI • Peak cortisol <18 μg/dL → confirms adrenal insufficiency Limitations: • Does NOT reliably detect SAI or recent-onset PAI (adrenals may still respond to supraphysiolog

nodes.title: Stimulation Test Result
nodes.summary: Peak ≥18 excludes PAI; <18 confirms AI — classify type with ACTH level
nodes.body: What was the peak cortisol after cosyntropin administration?

nodes.title: Normal Stimulation Test
nodes.body: A normal cosyntropin stimulation test excludes primary AI but does NOT exclude secondary AI (especially early or partial). If clinical suspicion for SAI remains high: • Endocrine referral for insulin tolerance test (ITT) or metyrapone test • ITT is the gold standard for SAI diagnosis but contraindicated in patients with seizure history, cardiovascular disease, or elderly If low clinical suspicion:
nodes.recommendation: Normal cosyntropin stimulation test excludes primary AI. If secondary AI still suspected, refer to endocrinology for insulin tolerance test.

nodes.title: Maintenance Replacement Therapy
nodes.summary: Hydrocortisone 15-25mg/day (2/3 AM, 1/3 PM); PAI also needs fludrocortisone 50-200mcg; SAI/TAI no fludro needed
nodes.body: Corticosteroid Equivalency & Alternatives Glucocorticoid replacement (ALL types): • Hydrocortisone 15-25 mg PO daily, divided BID or TID • Give 2/3 of dose AM upon waking, 1/3 early afternoon • Last dose >6 hours before bedtime to avoid insomnia • Typical regimen: 15 mg AM + 5 mg at 2 PM [1] • Alternatives: Prednisolone 3-5 mg PO daily, Dexamethasone 0.25-0.5 mg PO daily Pediatrics: • Hydrocortiso

nodes.title: Sick-Day Rules & Stress Dosing
nodes.summary: #1 crisis cause is failure to stress dose — double for fever >38C, triple for >39C, 100mg IM if vomiting then ED
nodes.body: The #1 cause of adrenal crisis is failure to increase steroids during physiologic stress. [3] Sick-Day Rules & Stress Dosing Guide Minor illness (cold, mild gastroenteritis): • Double oral hydrocortisone dose if fever >38°C (100.4°F) • Triple oral hydrocortisone dose if fever >39°C (102.2°F) • Continue increased dose until recovery, then resume baseline Moderate illness/injury: • Hydrocortisone 50

nodes.title: Medication-Related Crisis
nodes.summary: Steroid withdrawal, CYP3A4 inducers (double dose), checkpoint inhibitors (often irreversible), chronic opioids (~15%)
