nodes.body: Abrupt steroid withdrawal: • Most common cause of TAI crisis • Risk with ≥prednisone 5 mg/day for ≥3 weeks • Management: resume steroids at previous dose, then taper slowly CYP3A4 inducers (accelerate cortisol metabolism): • Rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St. John's wort • May need to double hydrocortisone maintenance dose while on CYP3A4 inducer [11] CYP3A4 inhibitors (can mas

nodes.title: Crisis Prevention & Patient Education
nodes.summary: Every AI patient needs: MedicAlert ID, IM hydrocortisone kit, steroid card, written sick-day plan, trained caregivers
nodes.body: Every AI patient must have ALL of the following: [16] 1. Medical Alert Identification • MedicAlert bracelet or necklace stating: "Adrenal Insufficiency — Requires Stress-Dose Steroids" 2. Emergency Injection Kit • Hydrocortisone 100 mg for IM self-injection (lateral thigh) • Patient AND family/caregivers trained in injection technique • Replace before expiration date • In a study, only 44% of pati

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for active crisis, floor for unable-to-take-PO or new diagnosis, discharge if stable on oral steroids
nodes.body: Disposition depends on clinical severity, treatment response, and ability to tolerate oral medications.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: • Active adrenal crisis requiring IV hydrocortisone and vasopressors • Persistent hemodynamic instability despite fluid resuscitation • Altered mental status • Precipitating illness requiring ICU-level care (sepsis, major surgery) ICU orders: • Hydrocortisone 200 mg/24h — continuous infusion preferred or 50 mg IV q6h • Aggressive IV fluids — NS ± D5 • Glucose monitoring q1-
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/24h continuous or 50 mg IV q6h. Treat precipitant. Endocrine consultation. Taper steroids as hemodynamics stabilize.

nodes.title: Admit to Floor
nodes.body: Floor admission criteria: • Known AI with acute illness preventing oral intake • New AI diagnosis requiring inpatient workup • Stress-dose steroids needed but hemodynamically stable Floor orders: • Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV/PO q8h, taper to maintenance over 2-3 days • IV fluids until tolerating PO • Treat precipitating illness • Endocrine consultation for all new diagnoses • Education before dischar
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor. Stress-dose hydrocortisone with taper to maintenance. Endocrine consultation if new diagnosis. Ensure patient education and crisis prevention kit before discharge.

nodes.title: Discharge with Follow-Up
nodes.body: ALL criteria must be met for discharge: • Hemodynamically stable • Tolerating oral medications and fluids • Precipitating illness resolved or stable • Adequate steroid supply at home • Emergency injection kit available (or prescribed) • Patient understands sick-day rules Discharge plan: • Resume Hydrocortisone at maintenance dose (or increase to stress dose if illness ongoing) • Fludrocortisone if
nodes.recommendation: Discharge on maintenance steroids with sick-day rules handout. Ensure emergency injection kit. Endocrine follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Adrenal Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage from DIC, HIT, anticoagulation — CT diagnostic, irreversible lifelong PAI
nodes.body: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: • Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, classically with meningococcal sepsis • Also seen with DIC, antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia • CT abdomen: enlarged adrenals with hemorrhage (high-density on non-contrast CT) • Irreversible PAI — lifelong glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid replacement Anticoagulation-associated adrenal hemorrhage: • Risk f

nodes.title: Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndromes
nodes.summary: Screen all PAI for thyroid/diabetes — CRITICAL: treat cortisol BEFORE thyroxine to avoid precipitating crisis
nodes.body: Screen all autoimmune PAI patients for associated conditions: Type 1 (APS-1 / APECED): • AI + hypoparathyroidism + chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis • AIRE gene mutation, childhood onset • Check: calcium, PTH, oral exam for candidiasis Type 2 (Schmidt syndrome — most common polyglandular syndrome): • AI + autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto or Graves — most common association) • ± Type 1 diabete

nodes.title: Adult Appendicitis — Recognition
nodes.summary: Anorexia + periumbilical → RLQ migration + vomiting AFTER pain + low-grade fever. Elderly/pregnant/immunocompromised present atypically.
nodes.body: Open first: - Steps Summary - Stop / Pitfalls Why it matters: [1,2,3] - Lifetime incidence ~7%; peak age 10-30 but presents at every age - Perforation rate climbs sharply with delay: ~20% at 36 h of symptoms, >65% at 48 h - Missed appendicitis is a leading driver of EM malpractice payouts Classic story (the one that should make you commit to imaging or surgical consult): [1,4] - Anorexia (more sen

nodes.title: Focused History & Exam
nodes.summary: Migration, anorexia, vomit-after-pain, low-grade fever, McBurney tenderness, Markle/cough sign, Rovsing/psoas/obturator by appendix location. Pelvic exam in females, testicular in males.
nodes.body: History elements (each maps to AAS or Alvarado scoring): [4,5,6] - Migration of pain (periumbilical → RLQ) - Anorexia (better question: "would you normally want to eat right now?") - Nausea/vomiting sequence — AFTER pain onset is classic; BEFORE pain favors gastroenteritis - Fever — typically low-grade (38.0-38.5°C); ≥39°C suggests perforation - Duration of symptoms (>48 h dramatically raises perf

nodes.title: Atypical Populations — Lower Threshold to Image
nodes.summary: Elderly: image early, mortality 5-10%. Pregnant: appendix migrates cephalad, MRI no-gad preferred. Immunocompromised: blunted exam, CT early. Kids <18 use peds-appendicitis tree.
nodes.body: Elderly (≥60 yo): [3] - Up to 50% lack classic migration - Fever and leukocytosis may be absent or mild - Mortality ~5-10% (vs <1% in young adults) — driven by delayed diagnosis and perforation - Image early — do not wait for the "classic" picture Pregnancy: [7] - Most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy (~1 in 1,500) - Appendix migrates cephalad and laterally as uterus enlarges —

nodes.title: Adult Appendicitis Score (AAS) — Sammalkorpi 2014
nodes.summary: AAS (Sammalkorpi 2014): <11 low, 11-15 intermediate, ≥16 high. Alvarado MANTRELS alternative.
nodes.body: AAS outperforms Alvarado for ED stratification in adults (better discrimination, sex-specific). Use AAS as primary; Alvarado is an acceptable alternative if your shop is anchored on it. [9,10] AAS — 16-point score: | Variable | Points | |----------|:------:| | Pain in RLQ | 2 | | Pain relocation (from periumbilical to RLQ) | 2 | | Pain intensity, mild-moderate | 1 | | Pain intensity, severe | 3 |

nodes.title: AAS Risk Stratification
nodes.body: Based on the score, pick the band:

nodes.title: High Probability — Surgical Consult Now
nodes.body: AAS ≥16 (or Alvarado 9-10 with classic picture) → surgical consult before imaging completes. Many centers will accept the case based on clinical pretest probability + AAS alone; some will request CT confirmation. Parallel orders (do not wait sequentially): - IV access × 2, NS 1-2 L bolus - CBC + CMP + lipase + lactate + UA (β-hCG if female) - Type and screen (preop) - Antibiotics — give within 1 h
nodes.recommendation: Surgical consult NOW + parallel orders. Antibiotics within 1 h of OR decision. Analgesia does NOT mask the exam.

nodes.title: Low Probability — Reassess and Decide
nodes.body: Reassess after: analgesia (don't skip — it doesn't mask findings), 1 L NS, antiemetic. Re-examine at 1-2 h: - Pain pattern stable, improving, or escalating? - Migration developing? - Any new peritoneal signs? - Trend the WBC + CRP if drawn Options: 1. Improving + benign exam + reliable patient → discharge with strict 12-24 h recheck + written return precautions (Discharge bundle) 2. Unchanged equi
nodes.recommendation: Reassess after analgesia + fluids. Discharge with 12-24h recheck if improving. Image + consult if worsening.

nodes.title: Workup — Labs and Adjuncts
nodes.summary: CBC + CRP + CMP + lipase + UA + β-hCG + lactate (if septic). Normal WBC does NOT rule out. Sterile pyuria is common in appendicitis.
nodes.body: Standard labs: [1,2,11] - CBC with diff — WBC ≥10k + PMN >75% is supportive but neither sens nor spec enough to rule in/out - CRP — kinetics matter; CRP rises slower than WBC. Combined elevation (WBC + CRP + PMN) has higher specificity than any single marker. A normal CRP + normal WBC + low AAS is the strongest single rule-out combination. - CMP — baseline for surgical clearance + look for dehydra

nodes.title: Imaging Strategy — Patient-Specific
nodes.body: Pick the patient profile. The modality matters more than the order:

nodes.title: Imaging in Pregnancy
nodes.body: Order of preference (ACR Appropriateness Criteria 2018): [13] 1. Graded compression US — first-line in all trimesters. Sensitivity ~70-85% when appendix visualized; specificity ~95%. Non-visualization rate climbs in 2nd-3rd trimester (~30-50%) — that's a non-diagnostic study, not a negative one. 2. MRI abdomen/pelvis WITHOUT gadolinium — if US non-diagnostic. Sensitivity ~94%, specificity ~97%. Sa
nodes.recommendation: US first → MRI no-gad next → CT only if both unavailable. Do NOT delay surgical consult while imaging completes.

nodes.title: Imaging — US First Pathway
nodes.body: Graded compression US is reasonable first-line in young, lean adults: [12,13] - Pros: no radiation, fast, can identify ovarian pathology + free fluid, repeatable - Cons: operator-dependent; non-visualization rate is high (~20-40% in adults); cannot reliably exclude appendicitis - Sensitivity: ~70-85% when appendix visualized; specificity ~95% A "non-diagnostic" US is NOT a negative US. If clinical
nodes.recommendation: US first in young/lean. Non-diagnostic US = escalate to CT, not "ruled out."

nodes.title: Imaging — CT Abdomen/Pelvis
nodes.body: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast is the gold standard in non-pregnant adults: [12,13] - Sensitivity ~95-98%, specificity ~95% - Oral contrast not required for diagnosis of appendicitis (saves 1-2 h and increases vomiting risk) - IV contrast preferred; non-contrast is acceptable in renal-insufficient patients CT findings supporting appendicitis: - Appendix diameter >6-7 mm - Wall thickening - Per
nodes.recommendation: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (no oral). Surgical consult for any positive CT. IR drain for abscess ≥3 cm.

nodes.title: Pediatric Pathway
nodes.body: Patients <18 yo use the dedicated pediatric pathway, which uses the Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS, Samuel 2002) rather than AAS, and US-first imaging is the standard. Open: Pediatric Appendicitis Key differences from adult pathway: - PAS uses tenderness + cough-pain as 2-point items (vs AAS's sex-stratified tenderness) - US is first-line in all kids — non-visualization rate is lower than in ad
nodes.recommendation: Open peds-appendicitis tree. Different scoring + imaging algorithm.

nodes.title: Antibiotics + Surgical Decision
nodes.summary: Cefoxitin OR ceftriaxone + flagyl uncomplicated. Pip-tazo for complicated/perforated. Antibiotics-alone option (CODA) for select uncomplicated without appendicolith — shared decision.
nodes.body: Preop antibiotic regimens (within 1 h of decision to operate): [1,2,15,17] Uncomplicated appendicitis (no perforation, no abscess): - Cefoxitin 2 g IV OR - Cefazolin 2 g IV + Metronidazole 500 mg IV OR - Ceftriaxone 2 g IV + Metronidazole 500 mg IV - Pip-tazo not required for uncomplicated disease Complicated appendicitis (perforated, gangrenous, or abscess on imaging): - Piperacillin-tazobactam 4

nodes.title: Surgical Consult — What to Communicate
nodes.summary: Call surgery early. Standard handoff: onset time, score, exam, imaging, preg status, anticoag, vitals trend. Analgesia + antibiotics while waiting. Reassess every 30-60 min.
nodes.body: Get surgery involved EARLY — pretest probability + AAS supports calling before CT in high-AAS cases. Many surgical services have an "appendicitis pathway" where the ED hands off based on clinical + score alone. Handoff content (one-pass call): 1. Time of symptom onset — drives perforation risk 2. AAS / Alvarado score + WBC + CRP 3. Exam: peritoneal signs present or absent? 4. Imaging status: US do

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Match disposition to imaging, surgical status, and reliability.

nodes.title: Disposition — Operative
nodes.body: Standard OR pathway: - Confirm NPO - Confirm antibiotics given within 1 h of decision (document time) - Type and screen sent - IV × 2, fluid resuscitation - Coags if anticoagulated - Reverse anticoagulation if indicated and surgical service requests (this depends on agent — DOACs may proceed without reversal in many centers; warfarin requires PCC or FFP if INR >1.5) - Surgical consent obtained by
nodes.recommendation: OR. Confirm NPO + antibiotics + T&S + reverse anticoag if needed. Lap appendectomy standard.

nodes.title: Disposition — Admit for Complicated Disease
nodes.body: Admit when: [1,2,15,17] - Abscess or phlegmon on imaging — planned IR drainage or non-operative management with interval appendectomy in 4-8 weeks - Diffuse peritonitis with stabilization needed before OR (rare — usually goes straight to OR) - Sepsis from perforation requiring resuscitation prior to OR - Antibiotic-alone trial elected (CODA pathway) — admit for IV antibiotics 24-48 h then transiti
nodes.recommendation: Admit. IV antibiotics. Surgical service primary. IR drain ≥3 cm abscess. Interval appendectomy 4-8 weeks.

nodes.title: Disposition — ED Observation / Serial Exams
nodes.body: ED observation unit appropriate when: [11] - Equivocal exam + intermediate AAS (11-15) - Non-diagnostic US, awaiting CT or repeat US - Pregnant with non-diagnostic US, awaiting MRI - Reliable patient with social support Observation protocol: - Serial exam every 2-4 h by same provider when possible - Repeat WBC + CRP at 4-6 h (trends matter — both rising = appendicitis until proven otherwise) - Con
nodes.recommendation: Obs unit + q2-4h serial exams + repeat labs at 4-6 h. Escalate if exam evolves; discharge with 24 h recheck if improving.

nodes.title: Disposition — Discharge with 12-24 h Recheck
nodes.body: Discharge appropriate ONLY if ALL of: [1,11] - Low AAS (<11) or Alvarado ≤4 - Improving exam after analgesia + fluids - Tolerating PO (gives confidence about gastritis / gastroenteritis) - No peritoneal signs, no hemodynamic concern - WBC trending down or normal + CRP normal - Reliable patient with transport + caregiver + ability to return - Shared decision-making documented Pre-discharge checklis
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only with: low AAS + improving + PO tolerated + reliable + 12-24 h recheck booked + written precautions.

nodes.title: Adult Pharyngitis Overview
nodes.summary: Most pharyngitis is viral; GAS 5-15% in adults. Triage first for airway/red flags, then Centor/McIsaac, test if ≥2, treat confirmed GAS. Hunt mimics every visit.
nodes.body: See Steps Summary for the rapid-action checklist. Why it matters: [1,2] - Pharyngitis is one of the top 20 reasons for adult ED visits - Most cases are viral (~75-80%) and self-limited - Group A Strep (GAS) causes ~5-15% of adult sore throats — antibiotics shorten symptoms by ~16h and prevent acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and suppurative complications - The high-stakes work is identifying airway-thr

nodes.title: Steps Summary
nodes.body: Rapid-action checklist for the adult sore throat: [1,3,5,22] 1. Airway scan — drooling, tripoding, stridor, voice change, trismus, severe neck swelling → STOP, manage airway first 2. Sepsis screen — vitals, mental status, perfusion 3. Calculate Centor/McIsaac → use Centor/McIsaac Calculator 4. Decision: - Score ≤1 → no test, no abx, symptomatic care - Score 2-3 → rapid GAS antigen; treat if positi

nodes.title: Red Flags / Airway Threat?
nodes.body: Look for any of these before doing a detailed exam: [11,13,17,18,19] - Airway: drooling, tripoding, stridor, severe trismus (can't open mouth >2 fingers), muffled/"hot-potato" voice - Neck: unilateral or bilateral swelling, asymmetry, tenderness over the IJ - Toxicity: sepsis vitals, AMS, severe odynophagia with inability to swallow secretions - Trismus + uvular deviation + hot-potato voice: perit

nodes.title: Airway-First Management
nodes.summary: Position of comfort, call ENT/anesthesia, surgical airway ready, broad-spectrum abx (amp-sulbactam or pip-tazo), imaging only when stable, never discharge airway-threatened pharyngitis.
nodes.body: Stop. Stabilize. Then evaluate. [17,18,19,20] Position: let the patient choose position of comfort — usually sitting upright, tripoding. Do NOT force supine for exam. Immediate actions: - Call for airway help early (anesthesia/ENT) - Have difficult airway cart at bedside - IV access, monitors, end-tidal CO₂ - Avoid sedation/paralytics until plan is set — these patients can lose their airway fast -

nodes.title: Centor / McIsaac Score
nodes.summary: McIsaac 5-point: fever, no cough, tender anterior cervical LAD, tonsillar exudate (each +1), age 3-14 +1, 15-44 0, ≥45 −1. 0-1 no test, 2-3 rapid antigen treat if +, ≥4 test, empiric per local protocol.
nodes.body: Centor (4-point) and McIsaac (modified, 5-point with age) stratify adult sore throat for GAS likelihood and guide testing. [3,5,6,22,23] | Criterion | Points | |-----------|:------:| | Fever >38°C (100.4°F) by history or measured | +1 | | Absence of cough | +1 | | Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy | +1 | | Tonsillar exudate or swelling | +1 | | Age 3-14 | +1 | | Age 15-44 | 0 | | Age ≥45 |

nodes.title: Centor/McIsaac Stratification
nodes.body: Select the patient's score band: [3,5,6,22,23] Basis: score bands and their GAS probabilities from McIsaac 2004 [3], Centor 1981 [6] and AAFP 2024 [22]; the score-driven testing strategy is the subject of the IDSA 2025 risk-assessment update [5,23].

nodes.title: Rapid GAS Testing
nodes.body: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT): [1,2,22] - Throat swab from tonsils + posterior pharynx (avoid cheeks, tongue) - Sensitivity 70-90%, specificity 95-99% - Result in 5-10 minutes - A positive RADT in a patient with compatible clinical findings is diagnostic for GAS — treat - A negative RADT in an adult with Centor/McIsaac ≥2: - IDSA 2012: does NOT require back-up culture (high specificity, low

nodes.title: First-Line Antibiotics for Confirmed GAS
nodes.summary: Pen V 500 mg PO BID-TID × 10 d (first-line); amoxicillin 1 g PO daily × 10 d; benzathine PCN G 1.2 MU IM × 1 if adherence issue. 10-day course required for ARF prevention. Avoid amoxicillin if mono.
nodes.body: IDSA 2012 + AHA: Penicillin remains first-line for ARF prevention. [1,4,7] Goals: [1,4] - Shorten symptom duration by ~16 hours - Reduce transmission to contacts (~24 h after first dose, patient no longer contagious) - Prevent acute rheumatic fever (ARF) — must be treated within 9 days of symptom onset - Prevent suppurative complications (peritonsillar abscess, otitis media, sinusitis) - Note: ant

nodes.title: Penicillin Allergy Alternatives
nodes.summary: Non-anaphylactic PCN allergy: cephalexin 500 mg PO BID × 10 d. Severe: clindamycin 300 mg PO TID × 10 d or azithromycin (check resistance). Avoid TMP-SMX, FQ, tetracyclines.
nodes.body: Clarify the allergy first. Most "PCN allergy" patients are not truly IgE-mediated. [1,8] Non-anaphylactic, non-severe PCN reaction (rash, GI upset, family history without confirmation): | Drug | Adult Dose | Duration | |------|------------|----------| | Cephalexin | 500 mg PO BID | 10 days | | Cefadroxil | 1000 mg PO daily | 10 days | Cross-reactivity between modern cephalosporins and penicillins

nodes.title: Symptomatic / Supportive Care
nodes.summary: NSAID + APAP combination is the workhorse. Single dose dex 10 mg PO/IM helps. Salt water gargle, lozenges. No empiric abx for low-score sore throat. Strong return precautions.
nodes.body: For viral pharyngitis or low Centor/McIsaac score. [1,9] Analgesia (combination beats either alone): - Ibuprofen 400-600 mg PO q6h (max 3.2 g/day) with food - Acetaminophen 1000 mg PO q6h (max 3-4 g/day) - Alternate ibuprofen + acetaminophen for sustained pain control Topical/local: - Salt-water gargle (1 tsp salt in 8 oz warm water q2-4h while awake) - Throat lozenges with benzocaine or menthol -

nodes.title: Complications / Mimics Screen
nodes.body: Actively scan for these on every visit — not just airway-threatened patients. [2,11,13,17,18,19] Basis: the screening findings listed here come from entity-specific sources — peritonsillar abscess [11], retropharyngeal abscess and the general deep neck space/airway differential [17], adult epiglottitis [18], Ludwig angina [19], Lemierre syndrome [13], and mononucleosis [2]. Each branch node below

nodes.title: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
nodes.summary: Trismus + uvular deviation + hot-potato voice = PTA. Drain (needle or I&D), amp-sulbactam or clinda IV, single-dose dex, ENT follow-up. Bedside US helpful; CT if non-diagnostic.
nodes.body: The most common deep neck space infection in adults. [11,12] Classic presentation: - Unilateral severe sore throat, often after several days of pharyngitis - Trismus (can't open mouth fully) - Uvular deviation away from the abscess - "Hot-potato" / muffled voice - Drooling, dysphagia - Tender unilateral cervical LAD - Bulging peritonsillar tissue with displacement of tonsil medially Workup: - Beds

nodes.title: Retropharyngeal Abscess / Lemierre Syndrome
nodes.summary: RPA: neck stiffness, posterior pharyngeal swelling. CT neck w/ contrast. Airway first, IV amp-sulbactam or pip-tazo, ENT drainage, admit ICU.
nodes.body: Retropharyngeal abscess (RPA): [13,17] - More common in children but occurs in adults (often after trauma, FB ingestion, dental infection) - Neck stiffness or extension preference ("won't flex"), torticollis - Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling/bulge - Drooling, dysphagia, dyspnea - Adult red flags: IVDU (posterior pharyngeal spread), recent dental work, immunocompromise Workup: - CT neck with IV

nodes.title: Lemierre Syndrome
nodes.summary: Lemierre = septic IJ thrombophlebitis, Fusobacterium, post-pharyngitis. CT neck/chest w/ contrast, blood cx, amp-sulbactam/pip-tazo/meropenem ± metronidazole, anticoag controversial, ICU + ID, 4-6 weeks abx.
nodes.body: "The forgotten disease" — septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum. [13] Clinical pattern: - Recent sore throat (often 4-12 days prior, sometimes improved transiently) - Persistent or recurrent fever - Unilateral neck pain/swelling/tenderness along the SCM (over the IJ) - Toxic appearance, rigors, sepsis physiology - Septic pulmonary emb

nodes.title: Epiglottitis & Ludwig Angina
nodes.summary: Adult epiglottitis: severe sore throat out of proportion to exam, drool/tripod. ENT fiberoptic, ceftriaxone + vanc. Ludwig: bilateral submandibular swelling + tongue elevation; awake intubation, amp-sulbactam/clinda, surgical drainage, ICU.
nodes.body: Both are airway emergencies — manage airway BEFORE detailed exam. [17,18,19,20] Adult epiglottitis: - Rare in Hib-vaccinated era but rising in adults (H. influenzae non-vaccine strains, S. pneumoniae, GAS, viruses) - Severe sore throat out of proportion to oropharyngeal exam - Drooling, tripoding, muffled voice ("hot-potato"), stridor (late) - Lateral neck X-ray: thumbprint sign at epiglottis (lim

nodes.title: Infectious Mononucleosis & Scarlet Fever
nodes.summary: Mono: posterior LAD + splenomegaly + atypical lymphs. AVOID amoxicillin (EBV rash). Supportive, dex for severe odynophagia, splenic precautions × 4-6 weeks. Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue, treat as GAS.
nodes.body: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV — Epstein-Barr virus): [2,14] - Teens and young adults - Exudative pharyngitis often clinically indistinguishable from GAS - Posterior cervical LAD (vs anterior in GAS), generalized LAD, fatigue - Splenomegaly in up to 50% — palpate the LUQ - Hepatomegaly, transient transaminitis, periorbital edema - Atypical lymphocytosis on CBC; monospot (heterophile antibodies) — f

nodes.title: Acute HIV & Gonococcal Pharyngitis
nodes.summary: Acute HIV: non-exudative pharyngitis + fever + rash + LAD; HIV RNA is the test (Ab can be negative). GC pharyngitis: NAAT; ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 + empiric doxy for chlamydia; partner notification.
nodes.body: Acute HIV (primary HIV infection): [15] - Non-exudative pharyngitis + fever + generalized LAD + maculopapular rash + myalgias + mucocutaneous ulcers - Mononucleosis-like illness 2-4 weeks after exposure - Standard HIV antibody tests can be NEGATIVE in acute phase (3-4 week window) - HIV-1 RNA (viral load) is the test of choice for suspected acute HIV — turn-around 24-48h, sensitivity >99% - Always

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Choose disposition based on diagnosis, severity, and airway status: [11,13,17] Basis: the admit-versus-discharge split is driven by the deep neck space / airway literature rather than by the GAS pharyngitis guidelines — peritonsillar abscess disposition from Galioto [11], retropharyngeal abscess and the general ENT-emergency disposition from Akhavan [17], and Lemierre syndrome from Riordan [13].

nodes.title: Home — Uncomplicated Pharyngitis
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: [1,4] - Stable airway, no drool/stridor/tripod - Tolerating PO fluids and analgesia - Adequate pain control on PO regimen - Reliable follow-up + transportation + phone - No red flags on exam (no trismus, no unilateral neck pain/swelling, no progressive symptoms) - Splenic precautions in place if mono Discharge plan: [1,4,9] - Antibiotics (if confirmed GAS or empiric per protoco
nodes.recommendation: Discharge home if airway is stable, PO tolerated, follow-up reliable, and return precautions reviewed. Prescribe 10-day GAS antibiotic course if indicated, NSAID + APAP, and consider single-dose dexamethasone for severe odynophagia.

nodes.title: Admit — Complicated Pharyngitis
nodes.body: Admission criteria: [11,13,17] - Peritonsillar abscess requiring observation post-drainage or failed drainage - Retropharyngeal abscess (essentially always) - Lemierre syndrome (ICU + ID + 4-6 weeks IV antibiotics) - Adult epiglottitis (ICU + ENT/anesthesia at bedside) - Ludwig angina (ICU + airway team + ENT/oral maxillofacial surgery) - Septic shock or toxic shock syndrome from GAS - Inability t
nodes.recommendation: Admit with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, airway monitoring, ENT/ID/ICU as indicated. Source control (drainage) for abscess. ICU for airway-threatened or septic patients.

nodes.title: Adult UTI Assessment
nodes.summary: UTI is over-diagnosed and over-treated — distinguish symptomatic from ASB, classify uncomplicated vs complicated
nodes.body: Urinary Tract Infection = infection involving bladder (cystitis), kidneys (pyelonephritis), or both. [1][2] UTI is one of the most common ED diagnoses, but also one of the most over-diagnosed and over-treated. Key Principles: • Distinguish symptomatic UTI from asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) • Classify as uncomplicated vs complicated • Use appropriate diagnostic criteria before treating • Choose an

nodes.body: Pyuria + Symptoms = UTI [1][2] Presence of pyuria supports the diagnosis of UTI when symptoms are present. Next Step: Classify the UTI Questions to determine classification: 1. Is the patient female AND non-pregnant? 2. Is there fever or flank pain (pyelonephritis)? 3. Are there complicating factors? Complicating Factors: • Male sex • Pregnancy • Structural abnormality (stones, stent, stricture) •

nodes.title: No Pyuria - Reconsider Diagnosis

nodes.body: Absence of pyuria makes UTI unlikely: [3][5] NPV of negative LE and negative nitrite: >95% Alternative Diagnoses to Consider: Gynecologic: • Vulvovaginitis (candida, BV, trich) • Cervicitis (gonorrhea, chlamydia) • Atrophic vaginitis (postmenopausal) Urologic: • Urethritis (STI) • Interstitial cystitis • Kidney stones • Bladder cancer (if hematuria) Other: • Prostatitis (men) • Epididymitis (men)

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Consider vaginitis, STI, stones, IC, prostatitis — confusion alone in elderly does NOT equal UTI

nodes.title: Urine Culture
nodes.summary: Send culture for complicated UTI, pyelo, men, pregnancy, catheter, treatment failure — not needed for simple cystitis
nodes.body: When to Send Urine Culture: [1][6] SEND CULTURE FOR: • Complicated UTI • Pyelonephritis • Men (all UTIs) • Pregnancy • Catheter-associated UTI • Recent UTI (<30 days) • Recent antibiotic use • Treatment failure DO NOT NEED CULTURE FOR: • Uncomplicated cystitis in young women • First UTI with classic symptoms • Reliable follow-up available Culture Thresholds: | Condition | Threshold | |-----------|

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Cystitis
nodes.summary: Nitrofurantoin 100mg BID x5d preferred, TMP-SMX x3d if resistance <20%, fosfomycin single dose, pivmecillinam 185mg TID x3-7d — avoid FQ for cystitis
nodes.body: Uncomplicated cystitis = lower UTI in non-pregnant premenopausal woman with no complicating factors. [1][2] Criteria (ALL must be met): • Female • Non-pregnant • No structural/functional urinary tract abnormalities • No recent instrumentation • Not immunocompromised • Lower urinary tract symptoms only (no fever/flank pain) First-Line Treatment Options: 1. Nitrofurantoin (PREFERRED) • 100mg BID x 5

nodes.title: Treatment Selection
nodes.summary: Select first-line agent: nitrofurantoin (lowest resistance), TMP-SMX (check local antibiogram), fosfomycin (single dose)

nodes.title: Complicated UTI
nodes.summary: All male UTIs are complicated; always culture; FQ or TMP-SMX x7-14d; consider prostatitis if recurrent
nodes.body: Complicated UTI = UTI with factors increasing treatment failure or recurrence risk. [6][7] ALWAYS Complicated: • Male sex (all UTI in men are complicated) • Pregnancy • Structural abnormality • Indwelling catheter • Recent urologic procedure • Renal transplant • Immunocompromised Other Complicating Factors: • Diabetes mellitus • Recent antibiotics • Hospital-acquired • Resistant organism history •

nodes.title: Pyelonephritis
nodes.summary: Fever + flank pain + CVA tenderness — always culture; CT only if no improvement at 48-72h, DM, or suspected abscess
nodes.body: Pyelonephritis = upper urinary tract infection involving kidney parenchyma. [8][9] Clinical Features: • Fever (≥38°C / 100.4°F) • Flank pain • CVA tenderness • Nausea/vomiting • ± Cystitis symptoms Labs: • UA with culture (always) • CBC (leukocytosis) • BMP (creatinine) • Blood cultures if septic Imaging: • NOT routine for uncomplicated pyelo • CT if: - No improvement in 48-72h - Suspected obstruc

nodes.title: Pyelonephritis Disposition
nodes.summary: Outpatient if tolerating PO, no sepsis, not pregnant, reliable follow-up — otherwise admit for IV antibiotics
nodes.body: Can this patient be treated as outpatient?

nodes.title: Outpatient Pyelonephritis
nodes.summary: FQ x7d or TMP-SMX x14d with IM ceftriaxone bridge — do NOT use nitrofurantoin (no renal tissue levels)
nodes.body: Outpatient treatment criteria (ALL required): [8][9] • Able to tolerate PO intake • No significant comorbidities • No sepsis • Not pregnant • Reliable follow-up • Home support First-Line Outpatient Regimens: 1. Fluoroquinolone (PREFERRED): • Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID x 7 days, OR • Levofloxacin 750mg daily x 5 days 2. TMP-SMX (if susceptible): • 1 DS tab BID x 14 days • Give single dose ceftriaxone

nodes.title: Inpatient Pyelonephritis
nodes.summary: Admit for IV FQ/ceftriaxone/gentamicin+ampicillin; step-down to PO when afebrile 24-48h and tolerating PO
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: [8][9] • Unable to tolerate PO (vomiting) • Sepsis or hemodynamic instability • Pregnancy • Complicated features (obstruction, abscess) • Significant comorbidity (diabetes, immunocompromised) • No reliable follow-up • Failed outpatient therapy IV Antibiotic Options: 1. Fluoroquinolone: • Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h, OR • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily 2. Cephalosporin: • Ceftriaxo

nodes.title: Nitrofurantoin
nodes.summary: Macrobid 100mg BID x5d — avoid if CrCl<30 or pyelonephritis; <5% E. coli resistance, minimal collateral damage

nodes.title: TMP-SMX

nodes.title: UTI in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: TREAT ASB in pregnancy (25-40% → pyelo) — nitrofurantoin/cephalexin x7d; ADMIT ALL pregnant pyelo for IV abx

nodes.title: UTI in Elderly
nodes.summary: Most over-diagnosed condition — foul/cloudy urine alone is NOT UTI; confusion alone is NOT UTI; do NOT treat ASB
nodes.body: UTI in Elderly - Most Over-Diagnosed Condition: [11] Key Principle: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is COMMON and should NOT be treated ASB Prevalence: • Community-dwelling elderly: 15-50% • Nursing home residents: 25-50% • Catheterized: up to 100% DO NOT TREAT ASB (IDSA Guidelines): • Positive UA/culture WITHOUT symptoms ≠ UTI • "Foul-smelling urine" alone is not a UTI • "Cloudy urine" alone is not a UT

nodes.title: Elderly - Assessment
nodes.summary: True symptoms = dysuria, new frequency, fever without other source — positive UA alone without symptoms = ASB
nodes.body: Does the elderly patient have true symptomatic UTI?

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria
nodes.body: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB): [11] Definition: Significant bacterial growth in urine WITHOUT urinary symptoms TREAT ASB ONLY IN: • Pregnancy (screen and treat at first prenatal visit) • Before urologic procedures that disrupt mucosa DO NOT TREAT ASB IN: • Elderly (regardless of living situation) • Diabetics • Catheterized patients • Spinal cord injury • Nursing home residents Evidence Against Tr
nodes.recommendation: Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in this patient. No reduction in outcomes, increases resistance and adverse effects.

nodes.title: Catheter-Associated UTI
nodes.summary: REMOVE or change catheter first, culture from new catheter — positive culture alone is NOT CAUTI
nodes.body: Catheter-Associated UTI (CAUTI): [12] Definition: Symptomatic UTI in patient with indwelling catheter or removed within 48h Symptoms of CAUTI (need ≥1): • Fever (no other source) • New flank/suprapubic pain • Costovertebral angle tenderness • Altered mental status (if no other cause) • New or worsening delirium ⚠️ NOT CAUTI: • Positive culture alone (always positive if catheterized) • Cloudy or fo

nodes.title: Male UTI
nodes.summary: All male UTIs complicated — FQ/TMP-SMX x7d minimum; prostatitis = 4-6 weeks; avoid nitrofurantoin (no prostate penetration)
nodes.body: All UTI in Men Are Complicated: [6][7] Reasons: • Anatomically longer urethra (UTI less common) • When UTI occurs, often underlying cause • Higher rate of treatment failure • Prostatitis common Workup: • UA with culture (always) • Consider prostate exam (tenderness = prostatitis) • Consider STI testing (young, sexually active) • Consider imaging if recurrent When to Consider Prostatitis: • Perinea

nodes.title: Discharge - Uncomplicated UTI
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions for Uncomplicated Cystitis: [1][2] Medications: • Nitrofurantoin 100mg BID x 5 days, OR • TMP-SMX DS BID x 3 days, OR • Fosfomycin 3g single dose Patient Instructions: • Take all antibiotics as prescribed • Increase fluid intake • Return if: - Fever develops - Flank pain develops - Symptoms worsen or don't improve in 48h - Vomiting (can't keep meds down) Follow-Up: • No rout
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with appropriate antibiotic (nitrofurantoin 5 days, TMP-SMX 3 days, or fosfomycin single dose). Return precautions for fever, flank pain, or worsening symptoms.

nodes.title: Disposition - Complicated UTI
nodes.summary: Outpatient if stable, tolerating PO, reliable follow-up — admit if septic, vomiting, unreliable, or failed outpatient therapy
nodes.body: Complicated UTI Disposition: [6][7] Outpatient Criteria (ALL required): • Stable vital signs • Able to tolerate PO • No sepsis • Reliable follow-up • Home support • Not high-risk Outpatient Management: • FQ or TMP-SMX x 7-14 days • Ensure culture sent • Close follow-up in 48-72h • Return precautions clearly explained Admission Criteria: • Sepsis or hemodynamic instability • Unable to tolerate PO •

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Discharge if stable with close follow-up for culture results; admit if septic or unable to tolerate PO
nodes.body: Based on clinical assessment, what is the disposition?

nodes.title: Discharge - Complicated UTI
nodes.body: Discharge with: • FQ (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) x 7 days, OR • TMP-SMX x 7-14 days (if culture susceptible) Instructions: • Take all antibiotics • Increase fluids • Follow-up in 48-72h for culture results • Return for: fever, worsening pain, vomiting, no improvement Culture Follow-Up: • Call patient with culture results • Adjust antibiotics if resistant organism • If not improving, may need a
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with oral fluoroquinolone x 7 days or TMP-SMX x 7-14 days. Ensure culture sent. Follow-up in 48-72h.

nodes.title: Admission
nodes.body: Admit for: • IV antibiotics • IV fluids • Monitoring Initial IV Options: • Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily • Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily Step-down to PO when: • Afebrile 24-48h • Tolerating PO • Clinically improved Complete total course: • 7-14 days depending on severity
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics. Start ceftriaxone 1g IV daily or fluoroquinolone IV. Step-down to PO when afebrile and tolerating oral intake.

nodes.title: Disposition - Pyelonephritis
nodes.body: Pyelonephritis Disposition: [8][9] Outpatient Criteria: • Uncomplicated pyelonephritis • Non-pregnant • Able to tolerate PO fluids and medications • No vomiting • No sepsis • Reliable follow-up within 24-48h • Home support available Outpatient Regimen: • FQ x 5-7 days (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin), OR • TMP-SMX x 14 days (if susceptible, give ceftriaxone 1g IM first) • Anti-emetic as needed • En
nodes.recommendation: If outpatient: FQ x 5-7 days, anti-emetic, culture, 24-48h follow-up. If admission criteria met: IV antibiotics until afebrile 24-48h, then PO step-down.

nodes.title: Disposition - Pregnant
nodes.body: Pregnant UTI Disposition: [10] Cystitis in Pregnancy: • Can treat outpatient if: - No fever - No vomiting - Able to tolerate PO - Reliable follow-up • Nitrofurantoin or cephalexin x 7 days • Follow-up culture recommended • OB follow-up in 1 week Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy: • ADMIT ALL CASES • IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) • Monitoring for preterm labor • Fetal monitoring as appropriate for gestati
nodes.recommendation: Cystitis: outpatient with nitrofurantoin or cephalexin x 7 days if stable. Pyelonephritis: ADMIT ALL pregnant patients for IV antibiotics and OB consultation.

nodes.title: ESBL-E Treatment

nodes.title: Resistant UTI Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition for Resistant UTI: ADMIT if: • Sepsis or hemodynamic instability • Unable to tolerate PO • Requires IV-only antibiotic (no oral option) • Significant comorbidities • Unreliable follow-up • Bacteremia suspected/confirmed OUTPATIENT if (all required): • Stable vital signs • Tolerating PO • Oral antibiotic option available (based on susceptibilities) • Reliable 48-72h follow-up • Culture
nodes.recommendation: Admit if septic, vomiting, IV-only antibiotic needed, or bacteremic. Outpatient with close follow-up if stable with oral options. Always send culture for resistant UTI.

nodes.title: Suspected Amniotic Fluid Embolism
nodes.summary: Peripartum sudden collapse + hypoxia + DIC — clinical dx of exclusion, ~30% have prodrome
nodes.body: AFE Steps Summary — first-2-minutes checklist. Amniotic Fluid Embolism is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Classic triad: hypoxia + hypotension + coagulopathy in labor or within 30 min postpartum. Mortality 20–60%; neurologically intact survival depends on minutes, not hours. [1][2][3] Prodrome in ~30%: agitation, "sense of doom," restlessness, shivering, paresthesias, metallic taste — precedes

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Rule out PE, anaphylaxis, sepsis, MI, eclampsia, hemorrhage, PPCM, air/LAST — treat empirically
nodes.body: Before committing to Amniotic Fluid Embolism, rule out treatable mimics: [1][6] • Pulmonary embolism — bedside echo: RV strain without the fibrinolytic DIC pattern • Anaphylaxis — urticaria, bronchospasm, clear trigger; responds to epinephrine alone • Septic shock — fever, leukocytosis, source; slower onset • Myocardial infarction — ECG changes, troponin; rare peripartum but possible • Eclampsia —

nodes.title: Call for Help — Activate Team
nodes.summary: Call OB, anesthesia, ICU, NICU, blood bank (MTP), ECMO — bring OR to patient
nodes.body: Announce the diagnosis out loud. Call every resource simultaneously: [2] • OB (senior) — bedside for perimortem C/S if arrest • Anesthesia — airway + hemodynamics + massive transfusion support • Critical care / ICU — ECMO eligibility, post-arrest care • NICU / Peds — neonatal resuscitation team to bedside NOW • Blood bank — activate Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) immediately • Perfusion / ECMO

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest?
nodes.summary: CPR if no pulse — standard hand position, standard joules, LUD, above-diaphragm IV
nodes.body: Check pulse (≤10 sec). If no pulse, begin high-quality CPR immediately. Pregnancy-Modified ACLS Key pregnancy modifications (AHA 2015): [9] • Hand position: standard — center of sternum (NOT higher; older teaching was wrong) • Manual left uterine displacement (LUD) — two-handed push-to-left preferred over tilt (see below) • Defibrillation: standard joules, standard pad placement — remove fetal mon

nodes.title: Manual Left Uterine Displacement (LUD)
nodes.summary: Two-handed push-to-left > tilt — continuous throughout CPR, do not delay compressions
nodes.body: Mandatory if fundus ≥ umbilicus (≈ ≥20 weeks). IVC compression by the gravid uterus can reduce venous return by up to 30% — CPR is ineffective without LUD. [9] Preferred: Two-handed push-to-left technique • Dedicated provider stands on patient's left • Both hands cup the uterus and push it up and to the patient's LEFT • Continuous throughout CPR — do not stop for rhythm checks Tilt is inferior — q

nodes.title: Airway & Oxygenation
nodes.summary: Intubate immediately, 100% FiO2, ETT 6.0-7.0, ETCO2 >20 = good CPR — expect difficult airway
nodes.body: Immediate intubation — all Amniotic Fluid Embolism patients need a definitive airway. [1][2] • 100% FiO₂ — maximize oxygenation • Smaller ETT (6.0–7.0) — airway mucosal edema in pregnancy • Rapid sequence — etomidate 0.3 mg/kg or ketamine 1–2 mg/kg; avoid propofol (hypotension) • PEEP 5–10 cm H₂O initially, titrate up for hypoxemia • Waveform capnography immediately after intubation — ETCO₂ >20 mm

nodes.title: Access & Monitoring
nodes.summary: 2x large-bore IV above diaphragm, A-line, central + IO backup — fibrinogen + TEG are critical labs
nodes.body: Establish rapidly (do not delay CPR): [2] • 2× large-bore peripheral IVs (16-18 g) — above the diaphragm • Arterial line — as soon as feasible (accurate MAP, serial labs) • Central line — IJ or subclavian once ROSC or for ECMO cannulation • IO access — tibial or humeral if no IV within 60 sec; above-diaphragm humeral preferred • Foley with urometer — trend urine output Labs (draw with first access

nodes.title: Perimortem C-Section Decision
nodes.summary: 4-min rule (AHA 2025): arrest + ≥20 wk = start hysterotomy, deliver by 5 min — at bedside; 4-min is a prompt, benefit extends beyond
nodes.body: Is the patient in cardiac arrest AND at ≥20 weeks gestation (or fundus ≥ umbilicus)? The 4-Minute Rule (AHA 2025): if ROSC not achieved by 4 minutes of arrest, start resuscitative hysterotomy at minute 4 — deliver by minute 5. The 4-minute mark is a *prompt to act*, not a rigid deadline — hysterotomy still benefits maternal resuscitation beyond that window, and earlier delivery-from-arrest = bette

nodes.title: Start Resuscitative Hysterotomy NOW
nodes.summary: Bedside midline vertical, no anesthesia, CPR continuous — maternal survival to 15 min, neonate to 30 min
nodes.body: Action — start immediately, do not wait for equipment beyond a scalpel: [7][8] 1. Continue CPR + LUD throughout the procedure 2. Midline vertical skin incision — xiphoid to pubis 3. Vertical uterine incision — avoid placenta if visible 4. Deliver fetus — clamp and cut cord, hand to neonatal team 5. Deliver placenta — manual extraction, uterine massage 6. Pack uterus — do not attempt definitive clo

nodes.title: Pharmacologic Adjuncts — A-O-K
nodes.summary: A-O-K NOT recommended (Pacheco 2025, case-reports only, harm risk) — mainstay is supportive: CPR, O2, BP, RV support, coagulopathy correction
nodes.body: A-O-K protocol (Rezai 2017) — proposed to block three pulmonary vasoconstriction/platelet pathways simultaneously. ⚠️ NOT recommended as of 2025. Pacheco et al. (Obstet Gynecol 2025;147:780-784) reviewed the evidence — case reports only — and cautions AGAINST A-O-K for suspected AFE, citing potential harms: worsening coagulopathy/bleeding (ketorolac antiplatelet effect in a DIC-prone patient), kid

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Support — RV-First Strategy
nodes.summary: RV failure physiology — pressors first (norepi + vaso), inotropes (milrinone no bolus), iNO — limit crystalloid
nodes.body: Amniotic Fluid Embolism shock = acute RV failure from pulmonary HTN. Fluid overload worsens RV distension and septal shift. [1][3] Vasopressors (first-line — start early, titrate aggressively): • Norepinephrine 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min — first choice (α > β) • Vasopressin 0.04 U/min — spares pulmonary vasculature, synergistic with norepi • Epinephrine 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min — if arrest or mixed shock Inot

nodes.title: DIC / Massive Transfusion
nodes.summary: MTP 1:1:1 + fibrinogen >150-200 — activate at dx, do not wait for labs
nodes.body: Activate MTP at diagnosis — do not wait for labs. Amniotic Fluid Embolism coagulopathy is often fibrinolytic PLUS consumptive. [10][12] MTP + DIC Targets — full transfusion table. Initial orders: • PRBC : FFP : Platelets = 1:1:1 (standard MTP pack) • Fibrinogen target ≥150–200 mg/dL (obstetric threshold higher than trauma) • Cryoprecipitate 10 units (or 2 pooled bags) — raises fibrinogen ~70–100 m

nodes.title: TXA + Antifibrinolytics
nodes.summary: TXA 1g IV over 10 min x 2 doses <3h — avoid rFVIIa (thrombotic death in Amniotic Fluid Embolism)
nodes.body: Tranexamic Acid (TXA) 1 g IV over 10 min → repeat 1 g IV over 10 min at 30 min if bleeding continues. [10] WOMAN trial (Lancet 2017): TXA within 3 h of postpartum hemorrhage onset reduces death from bleeding. NNT 267. No increase in thromboembolic events. Give early — effect diminishes after 3 h. Avoid rFVIIa — Leighton 2011 systematic review showed increased thrombotic death in Amniotic Fluid Emb

nodes.title: ECMO / Mechanical Circulatory Support
nodes.summary: ECMO survival 60-80% vs 30% — call team during resus, not after; Impella RP / RVAD alternatives
nodes.body: Consider VA-ECMO early — case series show survival 60–80% with ECMO vs ~30% without. [1][12] Indications — call ECMO team DURING the resuscitation, not after: • Prolonged CPR (>10 min) without ROSC • Refractory RV failure despite pressors + inotropes + pulmonary vasodilators • Refractory hypoxemia (PaO₂/FiO₂ <100) despite optimal ventilation • Patient is a reasonable candidate (not pre-existing ir

nodes.title: Refractory Arrest — Extended Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Extended CPR warranted in Amniotic Fluid Embolism — optimize every domain, consider ECMO, do not terminate early
nodes.body: Amniotic Fluid Embolism is one of the few arrest scenarios where extended CPR and "futile-appearing" resuscitation can still produce neurologically intact survivors. Do not terminate early without team consensus. [7][8][12] Optimize every domain: • CPR quality — rotate compressors q2 min, ETCO₂ >20 mmHg target, mechanical CPR device if available • LUD — confirm ongoing, two-handed push-to-left • H

nodes.title: Post-Resuscitation Care
nodes.summary: ICU + TTM 32-36 x 24h if comatose, trend fibrinogen/TEG, watch AKI/ARDS/Sheehan, report to AFE Registry
nodes.body: Transfer to ICU immediately after initial stabilization. [1][2][12] Neuroprotection: • Targeted temperature management 32–36°C × 24 h if comatose post-ROSC • Continuous EEG if persistent unresponsiveness — subclinical seizures common • Neuro exam formally at 72 h for prognosis (after rewarming, off sedation) Ongoing support: • Lung-protective ventilation (TV 6 mL/kg IBW, plateau <30, PEEP titrated

nodes.title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism Resuscitation Complete
nodes.summary: ICU transition with complete handoff, registry report, family/team debrief
nodes.body: Resuscitation goals achieved. Transition to ICU care. [1][2] Before handoff, confirm: ✓ Definitive airway secured, appropriate ventilator settings ✓ Hemodynamics stable on documented pressor regimen ✓ MTP products given — documented ratios, fibrinogen >150, platelets >50 ✓ TXA dosed ×1 (±repeat), hemostasis achieved ✓ Uterus firm or packed; Foley in place; bladder not distended ✓ Neonatal team has
nodes.recommendation: Transfer to ICU. TTM 32–36 °C × 24 h if comatose. Trend labs q1–2 h. Watch AKI/ARDS/Sheehan/delayed DIC. Maternal psychiatry consult before discharge. Report to AFE Registry.

nodes.title: A-Fib RVR: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Irregularly irregular rhythm 120-180bpm — always treat underlying precipitants alongside rate control
nodes.body: A-Fib RVR Management Steps \u2014 quick-reference for rate control, cardioversion, and anticoagulation. Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (RVR) is characterized by an irregularly irregular rhythm with a ventricular rate typically 120\u2013180 bpm. Confirm with 12-lead ECG. COMMON PRECIPITANTS \u2022 Electrolyte abnormalities (K\u207a, Mg\u00b2\u207a) \u2022 Sepsis / infection \u2

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Stability
nodes.summary: Stable vs unstable determines rate control agents vs immediate cardioversion pathway
nodes.body: Is the patient hemodynamically stable?

nodes.title: Ejection Fraction Assessment
nodes.summary: EF ≤40% = CCBs CONTRAINDICATED (Class 3: Harm) — must know EF before giving diltiazem/verapamil
nodes.body: Does the patient have reduced ejection fraction (EF ≤40%)? This is critical for rate control agent selection. Calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are contraindicated in HFrEF (Class 3: Harm). Check: • Prior echocardiogram • Known history of HFrEF or systolic heart failure • Bedside echo if available and EF unknown

nodes.title: Unknown EF — Proceed with Caution
nodes.summary: EF unknown — use metoprolol or esmolol safely; avoid CCBs until EF confirmed >40%; bedside echo to clarify
nodes.body: EF IS UNKNOWN — SAFE APPROACH When EF is unknown, avoid calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) until EF is confirmed >40%. Safe first-line options regardless of EF: • Metoprolol 2.5–5 mg IV q5min (use lower doses if concerned for HF) • Esmolol — ultra-short-acting, can rapidly titrate off if hemodynamics worsen • IV Magnesium Sulfate 2–4g — excellent safety profile If possible, obtain bed

nodes.title: Rate Control in HFrEF (EF ≤40%)
nodes.summary: CCBs CONTRAINDICATED in HFrEF — use metoprolol, digoxin (positive inotropy), or amiodarone; IV Mg as adjunct
nodes.body: RATE CONTROL IN HEART FAILURE WITH REDUCED EF ⚠️ CONTRAINDICATED in HFrEF: • Diltiazem — Class 3: Harm • Verapamil — Class 3: Harm • Non-dihydropyridine CCBs worsen HF outcomes and increase mortality FIRST-LINE — Beta-Blockers: • Metoprolol 2.5–5 mg IV q5min, up to 15 mg total • Use lower initial doses in decompensated HF • Esmolol if rapid titration needed or hemodynamic uncertainty • Beta-blocke

nodes.title: HFrEF Rate Control Assessment
nodes.summary: Target HR<110 in HFrEF — avoid aggressive rate control that worsens cardiac output
nodes.body: Is the ventricular rate now controlled? Target heart rate in HFrEF: • <110 bpm is reasonable initial target • Titrate to symptom control — some patients tolerate higher rates • Avoid aggressive rate control that worsens cardiac output • If hypotensive, prioritize digoxin + amiodarone over beta-blockers

nodes.title: HFrEF — Refractory Rate Control
nodes.summary: CCBs still contraindicated — escalate with digoxin, IV Mg, amiodarone, or cardioversion for decompensated HF
nodes.body: Select second-line intervention for refractory rate control in HFrEF. ⚠️ Remember: Calcium channel blockers remain contraindicated. Re-evaluate for underlying causes (volume overload, ischemia, infection). Ensure adequate trial of first-line agent.

nodes.title: Cardioversion in HFrEF
nodes.summary: Cardioversion beneficial in HFrEF — loss of atrial kick worsens CO; amiodarone post-cardioversion to maintain sinus
nodes.body: RHYTHM CONTROL IN HFrEF Cardioversion may be particularly beneficial in HFrEF: • Loss of atrial kick worsens cardiac output • Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy may be reversible • Rhythm control may improve HF symptoms Procedure: 1. Sedation with Midazolam or ketamine/midazolam 2. Synchronized cardioversion at 200J biphasic 3. Amiodarone infusion post-cardioversion to maintain sinus Anticoagulati

nodes.title: WPW / Pre-Excitation Screen
nodes.summary: WPW+AFib = life-threatening — AV nodal blockers ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED (may cause VF)
nodes.body: Is there evidence of WPW / pre-excitation syndrome? Look for: irregular wide-complex tachycardia, rate >200, variable QRS morphology, delta waves on prior ECG. WPW + A-Fib is a life-threatening emergency.

nodes.title: WPW + A-Fib Management
nodes.body: WPW with atrial fibrillation is a life-threatening emergency. AV nodal blocking agents are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED \u2014 including beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, and IV amiodarone. These agents may paradoxically accelerate ventricular response through the accessory pathway and precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
nodes.recommendation: Immediate synchronized cardioversion (200J biphasic). If cardioversion is not immediately available, Procainamide may be used as a temporizing measure.

nodes.title: Synchronized Cardioversion Protocol
nodes.summary: Synchronized 200J biphasic, sedate with midazolam, amiodarone post-conversion to maintain sinus rhythm
nodes.body: SYNCHRONIZED CARDIOVERSION PROTOCOL 1. PREPARATION \u2022 Confirm synchronization is enabled on defibrillator \u2022 Apply pads: anterior/lateral placement preferred (EPIC trial) \u2022 Hyperinflation may impair conduction \u2014 cardiovert at end-expiration if possible 2. SEDATION \u2022 Midazolam 3\u20135 mg IV bolus, additional 2 mg q2min PRN to adequate sedation \u2022 Alternative: MidaKet for

nodes.title: Post-Cardioversion Management
nodes.body: Patient has undergone or is undergoing cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable A-Fib RVR.
nodes.recommendation: Continue Amiodarone infusion to prevent recurrence. Monitor for reversion to A-Fib. Treat underlying precipitants (sepsis, PE, electrolyte abnormalities). Consider anticoagulation assessment once stabilized.

nodes.title: First-Line Rate Control Agents
nodes.summary: Diltiazem 0.25mg/kg IV (90% rate control) or metoprolol 2.5-5mg IV — do NOT combine BB with CCB
nodes.body: FIRST-LINE AGENTS FOR RATE CONTROL Beta-Blockers (Class 1 recommendation): \u2022 Metoprolol \u2014 2.5\u20135 mg IV q5min, up to 15 mg total \u2022 Esmolol \u2014 Ultra-short-acting, ideal when rapid titration needed \u2022 Safe in COPD (multiple studies confirm no adverse respiratory effects) \u2022 Preferred in CAD or compensated HFrEF \u2022 Use cautiously in decompensated heart failure Calciu

nodes.title: Rate Control Assessment
nodes.summary: Target HR<110 for stable outpatients (RACE II); ICU may tolerate <130; titrate to symptoms not strict targets
nodes.body: Is the ventricular rate now controlled? Target heart rate: \u2022 ICU / critically ill: <130 bpm may be reasonable \u2022 Outpatient / stable: <100\u2013110 bpm (RACE II trial) \u2022 Titrate primarily to control symptoms rather than strict targets \u2022 Some patients may benefit from mild compensatory tachycardia \u2014 do not aggressively normalize if rate is due to underlying process

nodes.title: Refractory Rate Control
nodes.summary: Re-evaluate underlying causes; add IV Mg, digoxin, amiodarone, or consider cardioversion — avoid BB+CCB combo
nodes.body: Select second-line intervention for refractory rate control. First-line agent was insufficient. Re-evaluate for underlying causes (sepsis, hypovolemia, pain, PE). Ensure adequate trial of first-line agent before escalating. \u26a0\ufe0f Avoid combining beta-blockers with calcium channel blockers.

nodes.title: Add IV Magnesium
nodes.summary: IV Mg 2-4g — blocks slow Ca channels with minimal toxicity; augments other antiarrhythmics; avoid if GFR<30
nodes.body: IV Magnesium Sulfate \u2022 2\u20134 grams IV bolus, may follow with continuous infusion \u2022 Blocks slow calcium channels in SA and AV nodes \u2022 Minimal toxicity \u2014 one meta-analysis detected no adverse events \u2022 Even if cardioversion doesn\u2019t occur, magnesium reduces heart rate and augments efficacy of other antiarrhythmics \u2022 Contraindicated if GFR <30 mL/min or oliguria \u

nodes.title: Add Digoxin
nodes.summary: Digoxin 0.25-0.5mg IV — slow onset ~3h, use as adjunct; useful when hypotension limits BB/CCB titration
nodes.body: Digoxin \u2022 Useful when hypotension limits further titration of beta-blockers or CCBs \u2022 Slow onset: ~3 hours to achieve rate control (vs 5 min for diltiazem) \u2022 Limited efficacy during exertion \u2014 slows primarily resting heart rate \u2022 \u26a0\ufe0f Post hoc analyses associate digoxin with increased mortality in A-Fib \u2022 Use at low doses, typically in combination with other A

nodes.title: Switch to Amiodarone
nodes.summary: Amiodarone 150mg IV bolus then 1mg/min — hemodynamically stable, may achieve cardioversion; re-bolus if needed
nodes.body: Amiodarone \u2022 Load with 150 mg IV bolus over 10 min, then 1 mg/min infusion \u2022 May need to re-bolus 150 mg x2\u20133 (total 150\u2013450 mg in boluses) \u2022 More hemodynamically stable than beta-blockers or CCBs \u2022 May achieve chemical cardioversion \u2014 beneficial if rhythm control desired \u2022 74% rate control achieved in clinical trials \u2022 \u26a0\ufe0f Do not conclude amio

nodes.title: Consider Rhythm Control
nodes.summary: Rhythm control stepwise: IV Mg → amiodarone → DC cardioversion; favored for NOAF, pulm HTN, HFrEF
nodes.body: RHYTHM CONTROL STRATEGY Consider when rate control strategy has failed or in new-onset AF where conversion is desirable. Stepwise approach: 1. IV Magnesium Sulfate infusion (front-line, excellent safety) 2. Amiodarone if magnesium alone insufficient 3. DC cardioversion (especially in intubated patients) Factors favoring rhythm control: \u2022 New-onset AF (NOAF) \u2014 likely to revert \u2022 Pulm

nodes.title: Post-Intervention Reassessment
nodes.summary: Reassess after second-line agent — if still refractory, combine agents or try rhythm control
nodes.body: Is the rate now controlled after second-line intervention?

nodes.title: AF Onset Assessment
nodes.summary: New-onset AF often reverts with illness resolution; chronic AF needs CHA2DS2-VASc anticoagulation assessment
nodes.body: Is this new-onset AF or known/chronic AF? Distinguishing onset is important for anticoagulation decisions and rhythm control candidacy. New-onset AF (NOAF): First episode, occurring during current hospitalization or acute illness. Often reverts spontaneously as underlying cause resolves. Known/Chronic AF: Pre-existing AF documented prior to current presentation, or AF duration >48 hours.

nodes.title: NOAF \u2014 Anticoagulation Considerations
nodes.summary: NOAF: anticoagulation generally NOT recommended — increases bleeding without reducing stroke; most revert to sinus
nodes.body: NEW-ONSET AF IN CRITICAL ILLNESS Anticoagulation is generally NOT recommended for NOAF: \u2022 Retrospective studies show anticoagulation increases bleeding risk without reducing stroke incidence \u2022 Most patients with NOAF will revert to sinus rhythm as critical illness resolves \u2022 Survey of UK intensivists: 64% do not routinely anticoagulate NOAF Exceptions \u2014 consider anticoagulation

nodes.title: CHA\u2082DS\u2082-VASc Assessment
nodes.summary: Score ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women) = anticoagulate; AF>48h without anticoagulation needs TEE or 3 weeks AC before cardioversion
nodes.body: ANTICOAGULATION FOR KNOWN/CHRONIC AF Assess stroke risk using CHA\u2082DS\u2082-VASc score: Anticoagulation Recommendations: \u2022 Score \u22652 (men) or \u22653 (women) \u2192 Anticoagulate (strong recommendation) \u2022 Score 1 (men) or 2 (women) \u2192 Consider anticoagulation \u2022 Score 0 (men) or 1 (women) \u2192 May omit anticoagulation Preferred agents: Apixaban, Rivaroxaban (DOACs prefe

nodes.title: A-Fib RVR \u2014 Disposition & Follow-Up
nodes.body: DISPOSITION CONSIDERATIONS \u2022 Continue rate control agent that achieved control \u2022 Target resting HR <100\u2013110 bpm for outpatient management \u2022 Assess heart rate response during exertion (ambulatory monitoring or brisk walk) \u2022 Ensure electrolytes are corrected (K\u207a, Mg\u00b2\u207a) \u2022 Address underlying precipitants \u2022 Cardiology follow-up for: new-onset AF, rhythm
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on clinical stability and rate control achieved. Ensure anticoagulation addressed per CHA\u2082DS\u2082-VASc. Arrange cardiology follow-up. Review Discharge Instructions with patient before discharge.

nodes.title: Alcohol Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Give thiamine IV BEFORE glucose, check glucose/electrolytes/LFTs — withdrawal from GABA downregulation + glutamate upregulation
nodes.body: Alcohol Withdrawal Steps Summary — quick reference. Alcohol withdrawal occurs when chronic alcohol use is abruptly reduced or stopped. Symptoms range from mild tremor to life-threatening delirium tremens (DT). Pathophysiology: • Chronic alcohol ↑ inhibitory GABA activity and ↓ excitatory glutamate activity • Brain adapts: down-regulates GABA receptors, up-regulates glutamate receptors • Cessation

nodes.title: Alcohol History & Timing
nodes.summary: Timeline: minor 6h, hallucinosis 8-12h, seizures 12-48h, DT 48-96h — BAL>200 = high risk
nodes.body: Key history elements: • How much does the patient drink? Pattern (daily vs binge)? • Does the patient withdraw when they stop drinking? • History of withdrawal seizures, DT, or intubation? • Verify EMR documentation — "alcoholism" may be years outdated [2] • Obtain collateral from family/friends if needed Admission blood alcohol level: • BAL >200 mg/dL = high risk for withdrawal [3] • Withdrawal c

nodes.title: Diagnostic Confidence
nodes.summary: Diagnosis of exclusion — exclude infection, trauma, metabolic; somnolence after low-dose benzo argues against withdrawal
nodes.body: Alcohol withdrawal is a diagnosis of exclusion. Consider alternative diagnoses: infection (meningitis), trauma (intracranial hemorrhage), metabolic derangements, drug overdose, hepatic failure. Clues the patient does NOT have withdrawal: • Becomes somnolent after moderate-low doses of benzodiazepine [2] • Remains agitated despite >15 mg/kg phenobarbital [1] • Delirium without other withdrawal feat

nodes.title: Diagnostic Uncertainty — Test Dose
nodes.summary: Midazolam 2-5mg IV test — if sedated, NOT true withdrawal (tolerance absent); if improved without oversedation, likely withdrawal
nodes.body: IV midazolam test dose can help clarify the diagnosis [2]. Midazolam 2-5 mg IV: • If patient becomes sedated → withdrawal is LESS likely (patients with true withdrawal exhibit benzodiazepine tolerance) • If favorable response (symptom improvement without oversedation) → withdrawal is likely, proceed with definitive treatment Midazolam has rapid onset and short duration — ideal for diagnostic asses

nodes.title: Hepatic Encephalopathy — Caution
nodes.body: ⚠️ Hepatic encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal are nearly opposite pathologies [1]: • Alcohol withdrawal: Inadequate GABA → hyperexcitability • Hepatic encephalopathy: Excess GABA → obtundation Giving GABAergic medications (benzodiazepines or barbiturates) to a patient with hepatic encephalopathy risks prolonged coma. Clues favoring hepatic encephalopathy over withdrawal: • Advanced cirrhosis (a
nodes.recommendation: Hepatic encephalopathy is a strong contraindication to phenobarbital. Use extreme caution with any GABAergic medication. Treat underlying liver disease.

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: PAWSS ≥4 predicts significant withdrawal; CIWA-Ar for monitoring severity; DT = hallucinations + disorientation + autonomic instability
nodes.body: Assess current clinical severity. PAWSS Calculator — Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale. Score ≥4 predicts clinically significant withdrawal [5]. CIWA-Ar Calculator — Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for monitoring. Minor symptoms: tremor, anxiety, insomnia, GI upset, headache, diaphoresis Moderate-severe: marked autonomic instability (hypertension, tachycardia, fever), halluc

nodes.title: Minor Withdrawal — Outpatient Management
nodes.body: Minor withdrawal symptoms typically resolve within 24-48 hours if they do not progress [3]. Outpatient options: • Chlordiazepoxide 25-50 mg PO q6-8h with taper over 3-5 days • Phenobarbital 130 mg PO q8h × 1-2 days (if preferred) Monitoring: • Close follow-up within 24-48 hours • Return precautions: seizure, hallucinations, worsening tremor, confusion • Avoid alcohol — discuss AUD treatment at fol
nodes.recommendation: Outpatient management with oral benzodiazepine or phenobarbital taper. Close follow-up within 24-48 hours. Return precautions for seizure, hallucinations, or worsening symptoms.

nodes.title: Prophylaxis — At-Risk Patient
nodes.body: Criteria for prophylactic phenobarbital [1]: • Definite history of heavy, steady alcohol intake until admission • Significant risk from withdrawal (history of seizures, DT, or comorbid medical conditions) • Normal mental status, no active neurologic problems • Not on benzodiazepines, high-dose opioids, or multiple respiratory depressants • No hepatic encephalopathy Phenobarbital prophylaxis protoc
nodes.recommendation: Prophylactic phenobarbital 10-15 mg/kg (divided doses) for at-risk asymptomatic patients. Alternative: oral chlordiazepoxide taper. Monitor closely for breakthrough symptoms.

nodes.title: Withdrawal Seizure Management
nodes.summary: Phenobarbital 15-20mg/kg IV for seizure — treats both seizure AND underlying withdrawal; phenytoin is NOT effective
nodes.body: ⚠️ Withdrawal seizures tend to recur — up to one-third progress to DT if untreated [3]. Characteristics: • Usually generalized tonic-clonic, brief, self-limiting • Peak risk 12-48 hours after last drink • Tend to cluster (2-6 seizures) • Recurrent or prolonged seizures → investigate structural/infectious causes Treatment: • Phenobarbital 15-20 mg/kg IV at 50-100 mg/min — excellent choice for withd

nodes.title: Post-Seizure Assessment
nodes.summary: Post-seizure: assess for ongoing withdrawal symptoms — high risk for DT, generally requires admission
nodes.body: After seizure is controlled and phenobarbital loaded (15-20 mg/kg), assess for ongoing withdrawal symptoms. Patients who have had a withdrawal seizure are at high risk for DT and should generally be admitted.

nodes.title: Post-Seizure — Stable
nodes.body: Seizure controlled with phenobarbital loading (15-20 mg/kg). The long half-life (~3-4 days) of phenobarbital provides ongoing seizure prophylaxis — gradual auto-taper protects against recurrence [1]. Disposition: Admit for observation (minimum 24 hours) • Monitor for recurrent seizures or progression to DT • Do NOT add benzodiazepines on top of large phenobarbital load — synergistic sedation risk
nodes.recommendation: Admit for observation after seizure controlled with phenobarbital. Long half-life provides ongoing prophylaxis. Avoid benzodiazepines on top of phenobarbital load.

nodes.title: Treatment Strategy
nodes.summary: Phenobarbital: dual GABA+glutamate mechanism, predictable levels, auto-taper; BZD: traditional, 5-10% refractory
nodes.body: Two evidence-based approaches exist. Select based on institutional practice, patient factors, and clinical comfort. Phenobarbital Dosing Guide — pharmacology and dosing reference. Phenobarbital monotherapy [1]: • Dual mechanism: ↑ GABA + ↓ glutamate (AMPA/kainate receptors) • No paradoxical agitation (unlike benzodiazepines) • Predictable pharmacokinetics — measurable levels • Long half-life provi

nodes.title: Phenobarbital — Contraindication Screen
nodes.summary: Screen for hepatic encephalopathy (strong contraindication), respiratory depression, porphyria, prior large BZD doses
nodes.body: Phenobarbital Contraindications Contraindications to phenobarbital: • Hepatic encephalopathy (strong contraindication) • Severe respiratory depression without ventilatory support • Porphyria • Already received large dose of benzodiazepines (synergistic sedation risk) Use caution in: • Older adults (>65) • Cardiovascular disease, COPD • Volume depletion • Advanced cirrhosis without encephalopathy

nodes.title: Phenobarbital Protocol
nodes.summary: Load 10mg/kg IV, then 130mg q30min to RASS 0 to -1; 20mg/kg=soft stop, 30mg/kg=hard stop; use ideal body weight
nodes.body: Step 1 — Loading dose (most patients): • Phenobarbital 10 mg/kg IV over 30 min • Achieves serum level ~15 μg/mL — well below toxic range • Use ideal body weight (phenobarbital is water-soluble) [11] • Omit loading if patient has received significant benzodiazepines Step 2 — Titration: • Phenobarbital 130 mg IV q30 min PRN • Target: RASS 0 to -1 (calm, cooperative) [10] • Each dose provides predict

nodes.title: Phenobarbital — Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Check level if uncertain; >20mg/kg without improvement = re-evaluate diagnosis; 30mg/kg = upper therapeutic limit
nodes.body: Assess response to cumulative phenobarbital dose. Expected response: Gradual, incremental improvement with each dose. Patient becomes calm, cooperative, awake (RASS 0 to -1). Pharmacokinetic reference: • 10 mg/kg → ~15 μg/mL (low therapeutic) • 20 mg/kg → ~30 μg/mL (mid-high therapeutic) • 30 mg/kg → ~40 μg/mL (upper therapeutic limit) • Toxic range: >50 μg/mL (ataxia, nystagmus) • Stupor/coma: >6

nodes.title: Phenobarbital — Controlled
nodes.summary: Auto-tapers over 3-4 days — do NOT add benzodiazepines; communicate total dose to all providers
nodes.body: Symptoms controlled with phenobarbital monotherapy. Key points for ongoing management: • Phenobarbital will auto-taper over ~3-4 days due to long half-life • Little additional GABAergic therapy should be needed • Do NOT add benzodiazepines — synergistic sedation risk, especially after large cumulative phenobarbital doses [1] • Communicate total phenobarbital dose to ALL providers caring for the pa

nodes.title: NARD — Non-Alcohol-Related Delirium
nodes.body: NARD Recognition Guide ⚠️ If symptoms persist despite adequate phenobarbital (>20 mg/kg), the diagnosis may NOT be alcohol withdrawal. Clues to NARD: • Agitation without other withdrawal signs (no tremor, normal BP, no tachycardia) • Symptoms persist >2-3 days into treatment • Cumulative phenobarbital >20 mg/kg without improvement This is a critical recognition point — continuing GABAergic medicat
nodes.recommendation: Stop escalating GABAergic medications. Evaluate for alternative causes of delirium. Use antipsychotics (haloperidol) for symptom control. Dexmedetomidine for overnight sedation if needed.

nodes.title: Benzodiazepine Selection
nodes.summary: Diazepam preferred (rapid onset, long-acting); lorazepam for cirrhosis (no active metabolites); avoid IM diazepam
nodes.body: Long-acting benzodiazepines are preferred — smoother clinical course, less chance of recurrent withdrawal or seizures [2]. Avoid intramuscular diazepam — variable absorption [2].

nodes.title: Benzodiazepine Dosing Strategy
nodes.summary: Symptom-triggered with CIWA-Ar q1-4h; diazepam 5-10mg IV q5-10min to RASS 0 to -1; some need >500mg total
nodes.body: Symptom-triggered therapy (recommended for most) [2][14]: • Assess with CIWA-Ar every 1-4 hours (severe: q10-15 min) • Medicate when CIWA-Ar ≥8 • Diazepam 5-10 mg IV q5-10 min, OR • Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q15-20 min (cirrhosis) • Reduces total medication and length of stay vs fixed-dose [14] Front-loading (high-risk patients): • Appropriate for patients at risk of dangerous complications (older, card

nodes.title: Benzodiazepine — Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Refractory if >50mg diazepam in 1h or >200mg in 3-4h — 5-10% will need phenobarbital rescue
nodes.body: Refractory DT is not clearly defined, but consider if [2]: • Symptoms not controlled after >50 mg diazepam (or 10 mg lorazepam) in the first hour • >200 mg diazepam (or 40 mg lorazepam) in the first 3-4 hours ~5-10% of patients will be benzodiazepine-refractory — they will subsequently respond to phenobarbital [1][9].

nodes.title: Refractory DT — Escalation
nodes.summary: Phenobarbital 130-260mg IV q15-20min + BZD is synergistic — intubation often needed; ketamine bridges while PB takes effect
nodes.body: Add phenobarbital to benzodiazepine regimen [1][2]: • Phenobarbital 130-260 mg IV q15-20 min until symptoms controlled • Do NOT exceed cumulative 15 mg/kg in 24 hours when given WITH benzodiazepines [2] • Intubation is frequently necessary due to synergistic respiratory depression ⚠️ Phenobarbital + benzodiazepines are synergistic — the combination is more dangerous than either alone. Use smaller

nodes.title: Refractory DT — ICU Management
nodes.body: ICU admission required. Intubation likely if using phenobarbital + benzodiazepine combination or propofol. Ongoing management: • Continue phenobarbital titration in ICU (avoid further benzodiazepines if possible) • Once controlled, do NOT simultaneously titrate both phenobarbital and benzodiazepines [1] • Maintenance: Phenobarbital 130-260 mg IV total per day ÷ 2-3 doses × 3-5 days [2] Consult med
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with likely intubation. Phenobarbital + benzodiazepine or propofol. Consult toxicology. Transition to phenobarbital monotherapy when possible.

nodes.title: Withdrawal Controlled — Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Thiamine 500mg IV q8h if AMS, 100mg daily if normal — aggressively replete Mg, K, phosphate; monitor for refeeding
nodes.body: Acute withdrawal symptoms are controlled. Address supportive care and plan disposition. Supportive Care Reference Thiamine (Wernicke prophylaxis): • If altered mental status: Thiamine 500 mg IV q8h × 2-3 days [2][3] • If normal mental status: Thiamine 100 mg IV daily [2] • Always give thiamine BEFORE or WITH glucose [2] Electrolyte repletion: • Magnesium Sulfate — alcoholics often severely deplete

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for DT/refractory/intubated; floor for controlled withdrawal needing taper; discharge if mild and resolved
nodes.body: ICU Admission Criteria ICU indications: • Delirium tremens • Refractory withdrawal requiring phenobarbital + benzodiazepine • Intubation/mechanical ventilation • Significant comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, sepsis) • Recurrent seizures • Cumulative phenobarbital >15 mg/kg with benzodiazepines Floor admission: • Controlled withdrawal requiring ongoing monitoring • Transition to oral phenobarb

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU management priorities: • Continuous monitoring: vitals, SpO2, neurologic status • Continue treatment pathway (phenobarbital or benzodiazepine) • Frequent reassessment using RASS (preferred over CIWA-Ar for intubated patients) [2][10] • Aggressive electrolyte repletion • Thiamine 500 mg IV q8h until alert Monitor for complications: • Aspiration pneumonia • Rhabdomyolysis (from prolonged agitati
nodes.recommendation: ICU with continuous monitoring. Target RASS 0 to -1. Aggressive supportive care. Plan early transition to floor when stable.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor management: • Transition to oral medications: — Phenobarbital 130 mg PO/IM PRN for breakthrough symptoms [1][12] — OR Chlordiazepoxide 25-50 mg PO q6h with taper • CIWA-Ar monitoring q4-6h [2] • Continue thiamine, electrolyte repletion Communicate to floor team [1]: • Total cumulative phenobarbital dose given • Avoid benzodiazepines if patient received large phenobarbital load • Phenobarbita
nodes.recommendation: Floor admission with oral medication transition. Monitor with CIWA-Ar q4-6h. Communicate total phenobarbital dose to receiving team. Plan AUD medication initiation before discharge.

nodes.title: AUD Medication Screening
nodes.summary: In-hospital MAUD initiation reduces ED visits and readmissions — patients are sober and receptive
nodes.body: AUD Medication Comparison Medication for Alcohol Use Disorder (MAUD) should be offered to patients with moderate-severe AUD or those who request medical therapy [15][16]. Benefits of in-hospital initiation: • Patients are sober and receptive • Can manage initial side effects (nausea, diarrhea) • Associated with reduced ED visits and readmissions [15] • Combination with psychosocial interventions i

nodes.title: AUD Medication Selection
nodes.summary: Naltrexone first-line (NNT 12, once daily); acamprosate if cirrhosis (safe, NNT 9-12); minimum 6 months duration
nodes.body: AUD Medication Comparison — detailed selection guide. First-line: Naltrexone [15][16][17] • NNT 12 (prevent return to heavy drinking) • Once daily dosing, reduces cravings • Supports both abstinence and reduced-consumption goals Second-line: Acamprosate [15][16] • NNT 9-12 (prevent return to any drinking) • Safe in cirrhosis (not hepatically metabolized) • Best for abstinence-focused patients If o

nodes.title: Naltrexone — First-Line AUD Treatment
nodes.body: Naltrexone Dosing: • Start 25 mg PO daily × 3-7 days (reduces side effects) • Maintenance: 50 mg PO daily • Take with food to reduce nausea • For persistent symptoms: may increase to 100 mg daily Contraindications: • Current opioid use (precipitates withdrawal) • Need for opioids in near term (stop 48-72h before surgery) • LFTs >5× normal or Child-Pugh C cirrhosis • GFR <45 mL/min Monitoring: • LF
nodes.recommendation: Naltrexone 25 mg daily × 3-7 days, then 50 mg daily. Monitor LFTs q6 months. Arrange outpatient follow-up for ongoing management.

nodes.title: Acamprosate — Cirrhosis-Safe Option
nodes.body: Acamprosate Dosing: • Start 333 mg PO TID (to minimize GI side effects) • Maintenance: 666 mg PO TID (1998 mg/day) • For weight <60 kg: consider lower starting dose • Take on empty stomach (food reduces absorption) Renal dosing: • GFR 30-50 mL/min: 333 mg TID • GFR <30 mL/min: Contraindicated Key advantage: Not metabolized by the liver — safe in advanced cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A-B) [15][16] Side ef
nodes.recommendation: Acamprosate 333 mg TID initially, titrate to 666 mg TID. No hepatic monitoring needed. Best for abstinence goal in patients with liver disease.

nodes.title: Other AUD Medications
nodes.body: AUD Medication Comparison Gabapentin [16][17]: • Least evidence among AUD medications • May help with residual withdrawal symptoms and neuropathy • Risk of misuse/abuse (~1% general population) • Renally cleared — contraindicated in renal failure • Avoid with concurrent opioid use Topiramate [16]: • Increased odds of maintaining abstinence (OR 1.88) • Requires slow dose titration to minimize side
nodes.recommendation: Third-line options for AUD when naltrexone and acamprosate have failed or are contraindicated. Arrange outpatient follow-up for titration and monitoring.

nodes.title: Discharge Planning
