nodes.body: Before discharge: • Ensure withdrawal symptoms have resolved • Patient tolerating oral medications • Electrolytes corrected • Thiamine — transition to PO (100 mg daily) • If on phenobarbital: auto-taper provides ongoing coverage for days [1] Discharge medications: • Thiamine 100 mg PO daily × 5 days • Folate 1 mg PO daily • Multivitamin daily • AUD medication if initiated (naltrexone, acamprosate)
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with thiamine, folate, multivitamin. AUD medication if appropriate. Follow-up within 1 week. Addiction medicine and psychosocial referrals.

nodes.title: Altered Mental Status Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Airway, breathing, glucose, vitals/temp, pupils/tox, trauma, quick neuro.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Hypoglycemia \u2014 fingerstick now; treat before anything else. 2. Hypoxia / hypercarbia \u2014 airway, oxygenation, ventilation. 3. CNS catastrophe (stroke, bleed, status epilepticus) \u2014 focal deficit, gaze, subtle seizure. 4. CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) \u2014 fever + altered; empiric coverage early. 5. Toxidrome / withdrawal (opioid, sedative, sal

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Glucose, opioid hypoventilation, stroke/bleed, seizure, sepsis/CNS infection, tox, DKA, metabolic, delirium.
nodes.body: Choose the first reversible killer or time-sensitive diagnosis. You can return after immediate treatment.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia
nodes.body: Treat immediately. Do not wait for the lab glucose if bedside glucose is low and the patient is altered. Next 5 minutes: IV dextrose if access; glucagon if no access but recognize vomiting/aspiration risk. Give thiamine when Wernicke risk exists, but do not delay dextrose for severe hypoglycemia. Recheck glucose and mental status, then identify cause: insulin/sulfonylurea, sepsis, renal failure, a
nodes.recommendation: Dextrose first, repeat glucose, then find the cause.

nodes.title: Opioid / Sedative Respiratory Depression
nodes.body: Consider Xylazine Toxicity if the patient remains deeply sedated after adequate ventilation improves. Next 5 minutes: support ventilation first. Naloxone titrated to adequate respirations, not full wakefulness, when opioid toxicity plausible. Prepare airway if persistent hypoventilation, aspiration, or mixed sedative toxicity. Pitfall: a patient may breathe better after naloxone but remain sedated
nodes.recommendation: Ventilation is the endpoint. Naloxone is a breathing drug, not a consciousness drug.

nodes.title: Stroke / ICH / SAH
nodes.body: Open Acute Ischemic Stroke, ICH, or SAH. Next 5 minutes: glucose already checked, stroke alert if within or near any treatment window, non-contrast CT head, CTA/perfusion as local protocol for LVO/window selection, BP management by diagnosis, reverse anticoagulation early if ICH suspected and patient is anticoagulated. Pitfall: severe hypoglycemia can mimic stroke. Treat glucose before locking in
nodes.recommendation: Stroke/bleed imaging and anticoag reversal decisions are time-critical.

nodes.title: Seizure / Nonconvulsive Status
nodes.body: Open Status Epilepticus. Next 5 minutes: time the seizure, benzodiazepine if ongoing >=5 min or recurrent without return to baseline, glucose and sodium, oxygen/suction/positioning, second-line antiseizure medication if benzodiazepine-refractory. If persistent unexplained AMS after convulsive seizure, suspect nonconvulsive status and get EEG pathway moving.
nodes.recommendation: Treat operational status at 5 minutes; persistent AMS after seizure needs EEG consideration.

nodes.title: Sepsis / CNS Infection
nodes.body: Open Sepsis Management or Meningitis / Encephalitis. Next 5 minutes: cultures if they do not delay therapy, lactate, broad antibiotics for sepsis physiology, empiric CNS antibiotics/acyclovir when meningitis/encephalitis is plausible. CT before LP when indicated, but empiric treatment should not wait for CT/LP. Pitfall: elderly septic patients may present as isolated AMS without fever.
nodes.recommendation: Treat sepsis/CNS infection early; do not delay antibiotics for LP logistics.

nodes.title: Toxicologic AMS
nodes.body: Open the matching tox consult when clues fit: TCA Toxidrome, Salicylate Toxicity, Toxic Alcohols, CO Toxicity, Alcohol Withdrawal, or Xylazine Toxicity. Next 5 minutes: ECG for QRS/QTc, glucose, VBG/ABG, lactate, BMP, osm gap/anion gap when relevant, acetaminophen/salicylate levels if ingestion possible, poison center early. Pitfall: urine drug screen rarely explains the immediate resuscitation pr
nodes.recommendation: ECG + acid-base + poison center are higher yield than UDS.

nodes.title: DKA / HHS
nodes.body: Open DKA. Next 5 minutes: fluids guided by perfusion, potassium before insulin decision, VBG/chemistry/ketones, ECG, identify trigger. Severe HHS can be profoundly altered from hyperosmolarity; avoid rapid osmotic shifts. Pitfall: insulin before knowing potassium can kill.
nodes.recommendation: Potassium gates insulin. Fluids and trigger search begin immediately.

nodes.title: Metabolic / Endocrine Encephalopathy
nodes.body: Open Sodium Disorders, Thyroid Emergencies, HD Emergencies, or electrolyte consults as indicated. Next 5 minutes: BMP including sodium/calcium, renal function, glucose, VBG, ammonia/LFTs if cirrhosis, TSH/free T4 if myxedema/thyroid storm clues, cortisol/hydrocortisone if adrenal crisis with shock/hypoglycemia/hyponatremia. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia: seizure/coma physiology needs hypertonic
nodes.recommendation: Correct life-threatening derangements first, then define cause.

nodes.title: Delirium / Dementia Worse Than Baseline
nodes.body: Open Delirium or Dementia & Agitation. Next 5 minutes: collateral baseline, medication list, infection/pain/urinary retention/constipation/hypoxia/glucose/electrolytes, avoid benzodiazepines unless withdrawal, use least-restrictive safety measures, document capacity for the decision at hand. Pitfall: "dementia" does not explain an acute change. Acute change is delirium until proven otherwise.
nodes.recommendation: Find the trigger; protect safety; document capacity specifically.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Airway, glucose, temp, ECG, targeted labs, CT head when indicated, collateral.
nodes.body: Default AMS bundle when no single cause declares itself: - Airway/ventilation: oxygen, ETCO2, suction, aspiration precautions. - Glucose now and repeat after treatment. - Vitals including core temperature if hypothermia/hyperthermia possible. - ECG. - CBC/CMP, VBG/ABG, lactate when ill, UA/CXR only when clinically pointed. - Tox labs when ingestion possible: acetaminophen, salicylate, ethanol, osm

nodes.title: Reassess After Immediate Fixes
nodes.summary: Persistent AMS stays medical until proven otherwise.
nodes.body: Recheck the patient after every reversible intervention.

nodes.title: Imaging / EEG / LP Decision
nodes.summary: CT/CTA/LP/EEG/MRI are selected by red flags and persistent unexplained AMS.
nodes.body: CT head now when: trauma, anticoagulation, focal deficit, severe headache, seizure with persistent AMS, immunocompromise, suspected bleed/mass, or unexplained persistent AMS. CTA/CTP: stroke alert, LVO concern, treatment-window question. LP: meningitis/encephalitis concern after empiric treatment; CT first only when indicated by AMS/focal deficit/papilledema/immunocompromise/recent seizure/age-ris

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge requires baseline mental status, clear cause, and reliable safety plan.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on return to baseline, cause certainty, and safety.

nodes.title: Admit / ICU
nodes.body: Admit/ICU for persistent AMS, airway risk, shock, sepsis/CNS infection, stroke/bleed, status/NCSE concern, severe toxidrome, severe electrolyte/endocrine derangement, DKA/HHS with AMS, unsafe environment, or inability to establish baseline.
nodes.recommendation: Persistent AMS is not a discharge diagnosis.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exams
nodes.body: Observation is appropriate when the patient is improving but not baseline, sedative/tox effect may recur, seizure/postictal state is prolonged, infection/metabolic workup is pending, or collateral is incomplete.
nodes.recommendation: Use serial neuro/mental status checks and reassess discharge eligibility.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: back to known baseline, reversible cause corrected, vitals stable, no focal neuro deficit, no concerning ingestion or recurrent hypoglycemia risk, safe supervision/transport, and return precautions are understood. Return precautions: recurrent confusion, seizure, fever, severe headache, weakness/numbness, vomiting, hypoglycemia symptoms, breathing trouble, fall/trauma, or inab
nodes.recommendation: Document baseline collateral and why discharge is safe.

nodes.title: Altitude Sickness — ED Evaluation
nodes.body: Steps Summary Altitude Illness Spectrum: • AMS — Acute Mountain Sickness (mild) • HACE — High Altitude Cerebral Edema (severe) • HAPE — High Altitude Pulmonary Edema (severe) Key History: • Current and recent altitude exposure • Rate of ascent • Time at altitude • Prior altitude illness • Acclimatization attempts Risk factors: Rapid ascent, sleeping at altitude, prior AMS/HACE/HAPE, exertion, dehy

nodes.title: AMS — Lake Louise Criteria
nodes.body: Lake Louise Acute Mountain Sickness Score: Recent gain in altitude PLUS headache AND ≥1 of: | Symptom | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | |---------|---|---|---|---| | Headache | None | Mild | Moderate | Severe | | GI symptoms | None | Poor appetite/nausea | Mod nausea/vomiting | Severe | | Fatigue/weakness | None | Mild | Moderate | Severe | | Dizziness | None | Mild | Moderate | Severe | Scoring: • 3-5 = Mild AMS

nodes.title: Mild AMS — Management
nodes.body: Mild AMS (Lake Louise 3-5): Treatment: • STOP ascent — do not go higher • Symptomatic treatment: - Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for headache - Ondansetron for nausea • Rest at current altitude • Hydration (avoid alcohol) Optional medications: • Acetazolamide 125-250mg PO BID (speeds acclimatization) • Dexamethasone 4mg PO q6h (if acetazolamide contraindicated) When to descend: • Symptoms worsen desp

nodes.title: Moderate-Severe AMS — Management
nodes.body: Moderate-Severe AMS (Lake Louise 6+): Treatment: • DESCEND — minimum 500-1000m (1500-3000 ft) • Dexamethasone 8mg PO/IM/IV x1, then 4mg q6h • Acetazolamide 250mg PO BID • Supplemental O2 if available • Symptomatic treatment (antiemetics, analgesics) If descent impossible: • Portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag) • Simulates descent of ~1500-2000m • Temporary measure only Monitor for progression t

nodes.title: Does Not Meet AMS Criteria
nodes.body: Consider alternative diagnoses: Common mimics: • Dehydration • Exhaustion/overexertion • Viral illness (coincidental) • Migraine • Carbon monoxide poisoning (stoves in tents) • Hypothermia • Hyponatremia (overhydration) Red flags requiring workup: • Focal neurologic signs • Fever • Neck stiffness • Rash • No altitude exposure history If symptoms persist or worsen: • Reassess for AMS/HACE/HAPE • Co

nodes.title: HACE — High Altitude Cerebral Edema
nodes.body: HACE is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY: AMS that has progressed to encephalopathy. Diagnostic criteria: • Recent altitude gain • Either: - Change in mental status AND/OR - Ataxia in person with AMS • OR: Both ataxia AND mental status change (even without AMS history) Clinical features: • Truncal ataxia (cannot walk heel-to-toe) • Confusion, disorientation • Drowsiness progressing to coma • Behavioral changes

nodes.title: HACE — Treatment
nodes.body: HACE Treatment — Life-Threatening Emergency: Immediate actions: 1. DESCEND IMMEDIATELY — minimum 1000m (3000 ft) - This is the definitive treatment - Do not wait for medications to work 2. Dexamethasone 8mg IV/IM/PO x1, then 4mg q6h 3. Supplemental O2 — maintain SpO2 >90% 4. Keep patient warm (hypothermia worsens outcome) If descent impossible (weather, terrain, nighttime): • Portable hyperbaric c

nodes.title: HACE — Monitoring & Prognosis
nodes.body: Monitoring: • Neurologic checks q1-2h • GCS tracking • Pulse oximetry • Watch for concurrent HAPE (common) Response to descent: • Should improve within hours of descent • Full recovery expected if treated promptly • Persistent symptoms: consider CT/MRI to rule out other pathology CT/MRI findings: • White matter edema (especially corpus callosum) • May be normal early • Not required for diagnosis i

nodes.title: HAPE — High Altitude Pulmonary Edema
nodes.body: HAPE is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema from hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Diagnostic criteria (≥2 symptoms + ≥2 signs): Symptoms: • Dyspnea at rest • Cough (dry → productive) • Decreased exercise tolerance • Chest tightness Signs: • Crackles or wheezing • Central cyanosis • Tachypnea • Tachycardia Typically occurs: • 2-4 days after arrival at altitude • More common >250

nodes.title: HAPE — Treatment
nodes.body: HAPE Treatment — Life-Threatening Emergency: Immediate actions: 1. DESCEND IMMEDIATELY — minimum 1000m (3000 ft) - Definitive treatment - Patient may need to be carried 2. Supplemental O2 — high flow, target SpO2 >90% - Most important intervention if descent delayed 3. Minimize exertion — even walking worsens hypoxia 4. Keep patient warm Medications (adjunctive, do not delay descent): • Nifedipine

nodes.title: HAPE — Monitoring & Prognosis
nodes.body: Monitoring: • Continuous pulse oximetry • Work of breathing • Mental status (HACE can develop) • Response to descent/O2 Response to treatment: • Dramatic improvement expected within hours of descent • Radiographic clearing may take days • Full recovery typical if treated promptly CXR findings: • Patchy infiltrates (often right > left, perihilar) • Kerley B lines • May mimic pneumonia Labs (if obta

nodes.title: Altitude Medications — Dosing
nodes.body: Acetazolamide (Diamox): • MOA: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, induces metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation • Prevention: 125 mg PO BID, start 1 day before ascent (RADICAL trial: 125mg superior to 62.5mg) • Treatment: 250mg PO BID • Pediatric: prevention 1.25 mg/kg q12h (max 125mg); treatment 2.5 mg/kg q12h (max 250mg) • Side effects: Paresthesias, dysgeusia, polyuria • CI: Absolute only with prior

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Admit to ICU: • HACE with altered mental status • Severe HAPE requiring intubation/high O2 • Concurrent HACE + HAPE • Hemodynamically unstable Admit to floor: • Moderate HAPE with O2 requirement • HACE responding to treatment • Need for observation after descent Discharge: • Mild AMS, improved with treatment • Patient has descended to safe altitude • No hypoxia, normal mental status • Can return t

nodes.title: Admit ICU
nodes.body: ICU Admission — HACE/HAPE: Orders: • Continuous pulse oximetry • Neuro checks q1-2h (HACE) • Supplemental O2 to maintain SpO2 >90% • Dexamethasone 4mg IV q6h (HACE) • Nifedipine 30mg SR q12h (HAPE) • IV access, labs (CBC, BMP, ABG) • CXR • CT head if focal neuro signs or not improving Avoid: • Excessive IV fluids • Sedatives (mask neuro changes) Consults: • Pulmonology (HAPE) • Neurology (HACE wit
nodes.recommendation: Admit ICU for HACE/HAPE. O2 >90%, dexamethasone if HACE, nifedipine if HAPE. Neuro checks. CT head if not improving.

nodes.title: Admit Floor — Observation
nodes.body: Floor Admission: Indications: • Moderate HAPE improving on O2 • HACE responding to dexamethasone • Severe AMS requiring monitoring • Need for rehydration Orders: • Pulse oximetry q4h • Neuro checks q4h • Continue medications (acetazolamide, dexamethasone) • PO intake as tolerated • Activity as tolerated Discharge criteria: • SpO2 >93% on room air • Normal mental status • Able to ambulate • Symptom
nodes.recommendation: Admit for observation. O2 PRN, continue acetazolamide/dexamethasone. Discharge when SpO2 >93% RA, asymptomatic.

nodes.title: Discharge — Mild AMS
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria (ALL must be met): • Mild AMS only (Lake Louise 3-5) • Improved with treatment/rest • SpO2 >93% on room air • Normal mental status, no ataxia • At low altitude or returning to low altitude • Reliable, can return if symptoms worsen Discharge Medications: • Acetazolamide 125-250mg PO BID x 2-3 days • Ibuprofen or acetaminophen PRN headache • Ondansetron PRN nausea Instructions: •
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with acetazolamide. Do not re-ascend until recovered. Written return precautions. PCP follow-up PRN.

nodes.title: Transient Monocular Vision Loss (TMVL)
nodes.summary: TMVL = eye TIA. 5-10% stroke risk at 1 year. Highest risk first 7 days.
nodes.body: Amaurosis fugax = "Eye TIA" Classic presentation: • Painless monocular vision loss • "Curtain" or "shade" descending over visual field • Duration seconds to minutes (usually <15 min) • Complete spontaneous recovery This is a stroke equivalent: • 5-10% stroke risk at 1 year • Highest risk in first 7 days • 20-30% have silent infarcts on MRI-DWI This consult covers: • Module 1: Recognition • Module

nodes.title: Vision Status
nodes.summary: Persistent vision loss = CRAO (eye stroke). Resolved = amaurosis fugax.
nodes.body: Assess current vision status: Is vision loss still present or has it resolved? Persistent vision loss (>1 hour) = possible CRAO (eye stroke) • Central Retinal Artery Occlusion • Time-critical treatment consideration • May qualify for IV tPA if <4.5 hours

nodes.title: ⚠️ Possible CRAO — Eye Stroke
nodes.summary: CRAO = eye stroke. <4.5h: consider IV tPA. Always consult ophthalmology and stroke.
nodes.body: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) If vision loss persistent >1 hour, this may be CRAO (completed "eye stroke"). Classic Fundoscopic Findings: • Pale, edematous retina • Cherry-red spot at macula • Box-car segmentation of retinal vessels • Retinal whitening Time-Critical Treatment: | Time Window | Action | |-------------|--------| | <4.5 hours | Consider IV tPA per stroke protocol | | <24 hou

nodes.title: Confirm Monocular vs Binocular
nodes.summary: Monocular = carotid territory. Binocular = posterior circulation. If uncertain, assume monocular.
nodes.body: Critical distinction: | Feature | Monocular (Eye) | Binocular (Brain) | |---------|-----------------|-------------------| | Cover test | Resolves when affected eye covered | Persists with either eye covered | | Anatomy | Retina, optic nerve, ophthalmic artery | Chiasm, optic tract, occipital cortex | | Implies | Carotid/ophthalmic artery disease | Vertebrobasilar or posterior circulation | Ask: "W

nodes.title: Binocular = Posterior Circulation
nodes.summary: Binocular TVL = posterior circulation. Full stroke workup needed.
nodes.body: Binocular transient vision loss suggests: • Vertebrobasilar TIA • Posterior circulation stroke • Occipital cortex ischemia Key features: • Homonymous hemianopia (same side of vision in both eyes) • May have associated symptoms: vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, dysarthria Workup: • MRI brain with DWI • MRA/CTA head AND neck (including vertebral arteries) • Echocardiogram • Telemetry for AF Proceed with s

nodes.title: 🚨 Giant Cell Arteritis Screen
nodes.summary: Screen ALL patients ≥50 for GCA. Order ESR + CRP STAT.
nodes.body: MANDATORY in ALL patients ≥50 years old GCA can cause permanent bilateral blindness within hours if untreated. GCA Red Flags: | Finding | Significance | |---------|-------------| | New headache | Classic, especially temporal | | Jaw claudication | Highly specific (LR+ 4.2) | | Scalp tenderness | Pain brushing hair | | Temporal artery abnormality | Tender, thickened, reduced pulse | | Constitutiona

nodes.title: GCA Laboratory Evaluation
nodes.summary: ESR ≥50 or CRP ≥10 = start steroids. 4% of GCA have normal labs.
nodes.body: Order STAT: • ESR (Westergren method) • CRP • CBC (look for thrombocytosis) Interpretation: | ESR/CRP | Action | |---------|--------| | ESR ≥50 mm/hr OR CRP ≥10 mg/L | High suspicion — start steroids | | Both elevated | Specificity 97% for GCA | | Both normal | NPV ~96%, but does NOT rule out GCA if clinical suspicion high | ~4% of GCA patients have normal ESR AND CRP

nodes.title: 🔴 Start GCA Treatment Immediately
nodes.summary: Start methylpred 1g IV x3 days. Biopsy within 2 weeks. Do NOT wait for biopsy.
nodes.body: Do NOT wait for biopsy — treat empirically! Vision-Threatening GCA (TMVL, diplopia, vision loss): | Severity | Treatment | |----------|----------| | High-dose IV | Methylprednisolone 1g IV daily x 3 days | | Alternative | Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 80mg) if IV unavailable | After IV pulse: • Transition to oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day • Arrange temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks • Rheumatology c

nodes.title: Normal Labs — Clinical Decision
nodes.summary: 4% of GCA have normal ESR/CRP. If high clinical suspicion, treat anyway.
nodes.body: ESR and CRP are normal, but... ~4% of biopsy-proven GCA patients have normal inflammatory markers. High Clinical Suspicion Features: • Classic temporal headache • Jaw claudication (highly specific) • Temporal artery abnormality on exam • PMR symptoms • Visual symptoms in BOTH eyes Decision: | Clinical Picture | Action | |-----------------|--------| | High suspicion | Start steroids anyway, pursue

nodes.title: Stroke/TIA Workup
nodes.summary: MRI-DWI preferred (20-30% have silent infarcts). CTA/MRA head and neck. ECG, echo, telemetry.
nodes.body: TMVL = Retinal TIA — requires full stroke workup Essential Studies: | Study | Rationale | |-------|-----------| | MRI Brain with DWI | 20-30% have silent infarcts; preferred over CT | | MRA or CTA Head/Neck | Carotid + intracranial vessel imaging | | Carotid Doppler | If CTA/MRA not available | | ECG | Screen for atrial fibrillation | | Echocardiogram | Cardiac source of emboli | | Telemetry | Det

nodes.title: Carotid Artery Evaluation
nodes.summary: Carotid stenosis most common cause. ≥70% stenosis = CEA indicated (NNT ~6).
nodes.body: Carotid stenosis is the most common cause of TMVL Imaging Findings: | Stenosis | Significance | |----------|-------------| | <50% | Medical management | | 50-69% | CEA beneficial if symptomatic (NNT ~22) | | 70-99% | CEA strongly indicated if symptomatic (NNT ~6) | | 100% | Occluded — no intervention, medical management | Symptomatic = ipsilateral TIA/stroke within 6 months Timing of CEA: • Best o

nodes.title: ✅ CEA Strongly Indicated
nodes.summary: CEA within 2 weeks. NNT ~6. Start antiplatelets + statin while awaiting surgery.
nodes.body: Symptomatic carotid stenosis ≥70% Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA): • NNT ~6 to prevent stroke • Should be performed within 2 weeks of event • Requires center with <3% perioperative complication rate Urgent Vascular Surgery Consult CEA vs CAS (Carotid Artery Stenting): • CEA is first-line for most patients • CAS may be considered if: - High surgical risk - Radiation-induced stenosis - Prior CEA with r

nodes.title: Consider CEA (50-69% Stenosis)
nodes.summary: CEA may benefit (NNT ~22). Discuss with vascular surgery. Aggressive medical management.
nodes.body: Symptomatic carotid stenosis 50-69% CEA may be beneficial: • NNT ~22 to prevent stroke (less benefit than ≥70%) • Consider patient factors: - Age (benefit greater in older patients) - Sex (men benefit more than women) - Comorbidities - Center's surgical complication rate Discuss with Vascular Surgery If NOT pursuing CEA: • Aggressive medical management • DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel x 21 days) • Hi

nodes.title: Other Etiologies of TMVL
nodes.summary: Consider: AF, PFO, valve disease, dissection, migraine. Complete cardiac workup.
nodes.body: If carotid stenosis <50%, consider other causes: Cardioembolic: • Atrial fibrillation • Patent foramen ovale • Valvular disease • LV thrombus • Recent MI Other Vascular: • Carotid dissection (trauma, neck manipulation) • Ophthalmic artery stenosis • Hyperviscosity syndromes Non-Ischemic TMVL: | Cause | Features | |-------|----------| | Ocular migraine | Positive symptoms (scintillations), headache

nodes.title: Antiplatelet Therapy
nodes.summary: DAPT x 21 days for high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥4). Load aspirin + clopidogrel Day 1.
nodes.body: DAPT for High-Risk TIA / Minor Stroke Based on CHANCE and POINT trials: Indications for DAPT: • ABCD² score ≥4 (high-risk TIA) • Minor ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) • Non-cardioembolic DAPT Protocol: | Day | Aspirin | Clopidogrel | |-----|---------|-------------| | Day 1 | 325 mg load | 300-600 mg load | | Days 2-21 | 81 mg daily | 75 mg daily | | Day 22+ | 81 mg daily | STOP | Duration: 21 days of D

nodes.title: Anticoagulation for Cardioembolic Source
nodes.summary: AF: start DOAC (timing depends on infarct size). Do not combine DOAC + DAPT.
nodes.body: If atrial fibrillation or other cardioembolic source identified: For Atrial Fibrillation: | Timing | Recommendation | |--------|----------------| | TIA (no infarct) | Start DOAC immediately | | Small infarct | Start DOAC in 1-3 days | | Moderate infarct | Start DOAC in 6-7 days | | Large infarct | Start DOAC in 12-14 days | DOAC Options: • Apixaban 5 mg BID (preferred) • Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily •

nodes.title: Secondary Prevention
nodes.summary: High-intensity statin. BP <130/80. LDL <70. Smoking cessation. Patient education.
nodes.body: Risk Factor Modification | Target | Goal | |--------|------| | Blood Pressure | <130/80 mmHg | | LDL Cholesterol | <70 mg/dL (high-intensity statin) | | HbA1c | <7% | | Smoking | Complete cessation | High-Intensity Statin: • Atorvastatin 40-80 mg daily • Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg daily • Start regardless of baseline LDL Lifestyle: • Mediterranean diet • Regular exercise • Limit alcohol • Weight manage

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Admit if ABCD² ≥3 or unable to complete workup in 24h. Low risk may discharge with follow-up.
nodes.body: AHA/ASA Recommendations: Admit if: • ABCD² score ≥3 AND presenting within 72 hours • Unable to complete workup within 24 hours as outpatient • High-grade carotid stenosis requiring CEA • Atrial fibrillation requiring anticoagulation initiation • Persistent symptoms or fluctuating deficits • Unable to ensure medication compliance • GCA requiring IV steroids May discharge with expedited outpatient w

nodes.title: Admission Orders
nodes.summary: Telemetry, MRI-DWI, CTA/MRA, echo. Consult neuro, vascular surgery PRN, ophthalmology PRN.
nodes.body: Inpatient Management: Monitoring: • Telemetry x 24-48 hours minimum • Neuro checks q4h • BP monitoring (goal <130/80) Studies (if not completed in ED): • MRI brain with DWI • MRA/CTA head and neck • Echocardiogram (TTE, consider TEE if high suspicion) • Extended cardiac monitoring if AF not found Consultations: • Neurology • Vascular surgery if high-grade stenosis • Ophthalmology if persistent vis

nodes.title: Discharge with Expedited Follow-up
nodes.summary: Carotid imaging within 24-48h. MRI within 24-48h. Neuro follow-up within 1 week. Clear return precautions.
nodes.body: Low-Risk Discharge Criteria: • ABCD² score 0-2 • Complete workup can be done within 24-48 hours • Patient reliable with good social support • Medications started in ED Prescriptions: • Aspirin 325 mg x1, then 81 mg daily • Clopidogrel 300 mg x1, then 75 mg daily x 21 days (if ABCD² ≥4) • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 mg) Expedited Outpatient Workup: • Carotid Doppler

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis Management
nodes.summary: Epinephrine is the ONLY first-line treatment — NO absolute contraindications; risk of NOT giving always exceeds risk of giving
nodes.body: Anaphylaxis Steps Summary Epinephrine is the ONLY first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. There are NO absolute contraindications to epinephrine in anaphylaxis — the risk of NOT giving it always exceeds the risk of giving it. Causes of anaphylaxis: • Medications — 34% • Food — 31% • Insect stings — 20% • Environmental — 7.5% • Exercise — 1.2% • Idiopathic — 11% [1][3]

nodes.title: Does This Meet Anaphylaxis Criteria?
nodes.summary: WAO criteria: skin+respiratory/CV/GI involvement, OR 2+ systems after known allergen exposure
nodes.body: WAO 2020 Diagnostic Criteria — either criterion: Criterion 1: Skin/mucosal involvement (urticaria, flushing, angioedema) PLUS at least one of: • Respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia) • Hypotension or end-organ dysfunction (syncope, incontinence, collapse) • Severe GI symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting) Criterion 2: After exposure to a known or likely allerg

nodes.title: Mild Allergic Reaction — Not Anaphylaxis
nodes.body: Isolated urticaria without respiratory compromise, hypotension, or multi-organ involvement. Treatment: • Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg PO/IV • Famotidine 20 mg PO/IV • Observe 2-4 hours LOW threshold to give epinephrine — if any concern for progression, treat as anaphylaxis. [1][3]
nodes.recommendation: Mild allergic reaction. Treat with antihistamines, observe 2-4 hours. Reclassify if symptoms progress.

nodes.title: Uncertain — Active Monitoring
nodes.summary: IV access, epi drawn up at bedside, reassess q5-10min — low threshold to treat as anaphylaxis
nodes.body: Aggressive monitoring with low threshold to treat: • Establish IV access immediately • Have Epinephrine drawn up at bedside (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) • Reassess every 5-10 minutes • Monitor for progression to multi-organ involvement • Low threshold to treat as anaphylaxis — early epinephrine improves outcomes [1][3]

nodes.title: Source Control & IM Epinephrine
nodes.summary: Stop trigger, epi 0.5mg IM anterolateral thigh — repeat q5min up to 3 doses; do NOT delay for IV/antihistamines/steroids
nodes.body: SIMULTANEOUS actions: Source control: • Stop all infusions/transfusions • Remove insect stinger (scrape, do not squeeze) • Sugammadex 16 mg/kg for rocuronium-induced IM Epinephrine — FIRST LINE: • Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) into anterolateral thigh • Pediatric: 0.01 mg/kg IM (max 0.5 mg) • Repeat every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses Do NOT delay for: • IV access • Antihistamines • Steroid

nodes.title: Response After IM Epinephrine?
nodes.summary: Assess 5min after each IM dose — up to 3 IM doses before escalating to IV epinephrine infusion
nodes.body: Assess 5 minutes after each dose. Good response: Improved blood pressure, reduced wheeze/stridor, improved skin perfusion. Poor response: Persistent hypotension, worsening respiratory distress, no clinical improvement. Up to 3 IM doses before escalating to IV epinephrine. [1][4]

nodes.title: Good Response to IM Epinephrine
nodes.summary: Good response to IM epi — continue monitoring, maintain IV access, proceed to adjunctive therapies
nodes.body: Continue monitoring — patient responding to IM epinephrine. • Continuous cardiac monitoring + SpO2 • Vitals every 5-15 minutes • Maintain IV access • Proceed to adjunctive therapies now that epinephrine has been given [1][3]

nodes.title: IV Access for Epinephrine Infusion
nodes.summary: NEVER give cardiac arrest dose (1mg IV push) to patient with pulse — 61-fold dosing error causing hypertensive crisis
nodes.body: IM epinephrine inadequate after 2-3 doses — escalate to IV epinephrine infusion. IV Epi PK Rationale Confirm IV access (large bore or central line, IO if needed). CRITICAL SAFETY: Do NOT give cardiac arrest dose (1 mg IV push) to a patient with a pulse — this represents a 61-fold dosing error compared to IM dosing. IV bolus epinephrine in non-arrest patients causes hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias

nodes.title: IV Epinephrine Infusion
nodes.summary: 1mg in 100mL NS (10mcg/mL): load 20mcg/min x2min, maintain 10mcg/min — aggressively wean after resolution
nodes.body: Epinephrine infusion protocol (PulmCrit approach): [4] Mixing: 1 mg epinephrine in 100 mL NS = 10 mcg/mL Protocol: 1. Loading: 20 mcg/min x 2 minutes (~40 mcg total) 2. Maintenance: 10 mcg/min (= 60 mL/hr) 3. Titrate up or down based on clinical response 4. AGGRESSIVELY WEAN after resolution Brown et al 2004: 19 patients treated with 5-15 mcg/min IV epinephrine — all responded within 5 minutes. [1

nodes.title: Peri-Arrest / Cardiovascular Collapse
nodes.summary: Push-dose epi 20-50mcg IV q1-2min; lay flat + elevate legs (35% plasma extravasates); prolonged resuscitation warranted
nodes.body: Epinephrine 20-50 mcg IV push, repeat every 1-2 minutes. If no IV access: IM 0.5 mg every 5 minutes + emergent IO access. Position: Lay flat, elevate legs — up to 35% of plasma volume extravasates within minutes during anaphylaxis. [1] If cardiac arrest: • Standard ACLS with epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes • Prolonged resuscitation — this is a reversible pathology • Consider VA-ECMO if avail

nodes.title: IV Fluid Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Up to 35% intravascular volume extravasates — aggressive NS/LR boluses, POCUS-guided; may need liters in first hour
nodes.body: Distributive shock — up to 35% of intravascular volume extravasates within minutes. [1] Adults: • 500-1000 mL NS/LR bolus, repeat aggressively • May need several liters in first hour [3] Pediatrics: • 20-30 mL/kg bolus, repeat to 60 mL/kg+ • IO access if no IV [2] POCUS-guided fluid management: • IVC collapse = volume responsive → more fluid • Hyperdynamic + empty chambers = more fluid • Adequate

nodes.title: Airway Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess for stridor, hoarseness, tongue swelling — angioedema without urticaria suggests ACEi or HAE (epi ineffective)
nodes.body: Airway edema can progress rapidly in anaphylaxis. Signs of upper airway involvement: • Stridor, hoarseness, voice change • Tongue/lip swelling • Drooling, difficulty swallowing • Accessory muscle use Angioedema WITHOUT urticaria → consider: • ACE-inhibitor angioedema (bradykinin-mediated — epinephrine ineffective) • Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency) [3]

nodes.title: Critical Airway — Intubation Preparation
nodes.summary: Difficult airway — video laryngoscopy, smaller ETT, surgical airway kit; nebulized epi temporizes; do NOT delay intubation
nodes.body: Prepare for difficult airway — call anesthesia/ENT early. Equipment: • Video laryngoscopy (first attempt) • Smaller ETT than usual (edema narrows the airway) • Surgical airway kit at bedside Temporizing: Nebulized epinephrine — racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% in 4.5 mL NS OR L-epinephrine 5 mL of 1:1000 (1 mg/mL). [1] Do NOT delay intubation if patient is deteriorating — airway edema worsens r

nodes.title: Refractory or Special Population?
nodes.summary: Identify refractory anaphylaxis (<0.5%), beta-blocked patients, or persistent bronchospasm requiring escalation
nodes.body: Before standard adjunctive therapies, identify refractory anaphylaxis or special populations requiring modified management. Refractory anaphylaxis: <0.5% of cases — persistent hemodynamic instability or respiratory compromise despite adequate epinephrine + IV fluids. [1]

nodes.title: Beta-Blocked Patient
nodes.summary: Methylene blue 1-2mg/kg IV blocks NO vasodilation; glucagon discouraged (weak evidence, causes emesis, only bypasses beta-1)
nodes.body: Blunted epinephrine response due to beta-adrenergic blockade. [1][3] Management: • Higher epinephrine doses (may need more frequent/larger IM doses) • Additional beta-2 agonism: Albuterol nebulizer + Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ • Methylene Blue 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5-10 min (guanylate cyclase inhibitor — blocks NO-mediated vasodilation) [1] Glucagon — DISCOURAGED by Farkas: • Weak evidence, only bypasses

nodes.title: Refractory Anaphylaxis
nodes.summary: Maximize epi + fluids → methylene blue → vasopressin → VA-ECMO; re-evaluate diagnosis if not responding
nodes.body: Persistent despite adequate epinephrine + IV fluids (<0.5% of cases). [1] Escalation ladder: 1. Maximize epinephrine infusion rate 2. Aggressive POCUS-guided volume resuscitation 3. Methylene Blue 1-2 mg/kg IV (blocks NO-mediated vasodilation — case reports only) [1][11] 4. Vasopressin infusion 5. VA-ECMO Re-evaluate the diagnosis: • Is this truly anaphylaxis? Differential Diagnosis • Missed ongoi

nodes.title: Bronchospasm Management
nodes.summary: Albuterol 2.5-5mg neb (continuous if severe) + terbutaline 0.25mg SQ for persistent wheezing despite adequate epi
nodes.body: Persistent wheezing despite adequate epinephrine — especially in patients with asthma overlap. [1] • Albuterol 2.5-5 mg nebulizer, continuous if severe • Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ (systemic beta-2 agonist) • Nebulized epinephrine for combined upper + lower airway symptoms • Ensure adequate epinephrine infusion (epinephrine is a bronchodilator via beta-2 receptors) [1][2]

nodes.title: Exercise-Induced Anaphylaxis
nodes.summary: Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis — neither food nor exercise alone triggers; avoid exercise 4-6h after trigger food
nodes.body: Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (FDEIA): • Triggered by exercise within 1-4 hours of eating specific foods (wheat, celery most common) • Neither food NOR exercise alone causes symptoms • Often misdiagnosed [3] ED management: Same as standard anaphylaxis protocol. Discharge counseling: • Avoid exercise 4-6 hours after eating trigger food • Carry EpiPen at all times during exercise • All

nodes.title: Antihistamines (H1 + H2)
nodes.summary: H1+H2 antihistamines are second-line ONLY — reduce urticaria/pruritus but do NOT treat hypotension or bronchospasm
nodes.body: Second-line only — NEVER delay epinephrine for antihistamines. [1][3] H1 blocker: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV every 6 hours H2 blocker: Famotidine 20 mg IV every 12 hours H1 + H2 combination is superior to H1 alone for cutaneous symptoms. [2][3] What antihistamines DO: • Reduce urticaria, flushing, pruritus • May reduce mucosal edema What antihistamines do NOT do: • Treat hypotension • Treat bronchos

nodes.title: Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: Controversial — no RCTs; does NOT prevent biphasic reactions; NOT needed for discharge; consider if refractory or asthma
nodes.body: Controversial — no randomized controlled trials. [1][2][3][6] If giving (pick one): • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV x1 • Methylprednisolone 60 mg IV x1 Consider if: • Refractory to 2+ IM epinephrine doses • Known asthma • History of biphasic reactions [1] Evidence: • Do NOT prevent biphasic reactions [2] • May reduce length of stay in hospitalized patients [2] • No benefit on acute symptoms (onset 4-6 ho

nodes.title: Tryptase & Diagnostics
nodes.summary: Tryptase peaks ~90min, draw within 3h — less useful for food-triggered; elevated baseline suggests mastocytosis
nodes.body: Serum tryptase: • Peak ~90 minutes after onset, draw within 3 hours • Less useful for food-triggered anaphylaxis (may be normal) [3] • Elevated level supports anaphylaxis diagnosis • Persistently elevated baseline → suspect mastocytosis Other labs: • CBC, BMP, lactate (shock assessment) • Troponin if hemodynamic compromise (Kounis syndrome — allergic coronary spasm) Tryptase is NOT required to dia

nodes.title: Monitoring & Weaning
nodes.summary: Aggressively wean epi infusion after resolution (~30min); vitals q15min x1h then q30min; watch for biphasic reaction
nodes.body: Epinephrine infusion weaning: • After symptom resolution, begin weaning over ~30 minutes • AGGRESSIVELY WEAN — reluctance to stop the infusion is the greatest weakness [4] • If symptoms recur during wean, uptitrate and try again in 1-2 hours Monitoring parameters: • Continuous cardiac monitoring + SpO2 • Vitals every 15 minutes for first hour, then every 30 minutes Biphasic Reaction Risk Factors [

nodes.title: Disposition Assessment
nodes.summary: Biphasic reactions 5-20%, mostly within 8-10h — risk factors: multiple epi doses, IV fluids needed, delayed initial epi
nodes.body: Biphasic Reaction Risk Factors Biphasic reactions: ~5-20% of cases, majority occur within 8-10 hours. No deaths have been reported from biphasic reactions. [1][2][3][5] Risk factors for biphasic reaction: • Multiple epinephrine doses required • IV fluid bolus needed • Delayed initial epinephrine • Inhaled beta-agonist required • Unknown trigger • Initial hypotension • Severe initial presentation [

nodes.title: Observe 4-6 Hours — Discharge
nodes.body: Standard observation: 4-6 hours from peak reaction. [1][2][3] Discharge Instructions Requirements before discharge: • Symptom-free for minimum 4 hours • Tolerating oral intake • Understands EpiPen use and return indications [8]
nodes.recommendation: Observe 4-6 hours post peak reaction. Discharge with EpiPen prescription, allergen avoidance education, and allergist referral.

nodes.title: Admit — Observation/Telemetry
nodes.body: Admit when biphasic risk factors present or delayed/incomplete response. [1] Admission criteria: • Required >1 dose epinephrine • Severe initial reaction • History of asthma • Late evening presentation • Unknown trigger Monitoring: • Telemetry • Vitals every 1-2 hours • Anaphylaxis kit at bedside Discharge Instructions at hospital discharge.
nodes.recommendation: Admit for extended observation (12-24h). Multiple risk factors for biphasic reaction.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU criteria: • IV epinephrine infusion required • Glucagon or methylene blue administered • Intubation or surgical airway • Stridor with ACE-inhibitor angioedema • Persistent hemodynamic instability • Refractory anaphylaxis (>4 hours) [1][3] ICU management: • Continue epinephrine infusion with aggressive weaning • POCUS-guided fluid resuscitation • Monitor for biphasic reaction • Serum tryptase •
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for ongoing vasopressor support, airway management, or refractory anaphylaxis.

nodes.title: Discharge Prescriptions & Education
nodes.summary: EpiPen x2 mandatory, allergist referral within 2-4 weeks — steroids NOT needed for discharge
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions Mandatory: • EpiPen x2 (prescribe — ensure patient demonstrates use) • Allergist referral within 2-4 weeks [2][3] • Allergen avoidance education • Medical ID bracelet recommended Optional short-course (symptomatic relief): • Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg PO every 6 hours PRN x 3-5 days • Famotidine 20 mg PO BID x 3-5 days Steroids NOT needed for discharge — no evidence supports o

nodes.title: Angioedema — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: ~110K ED visits/year, 44% HAE initially misdiagnosed - first run structured airway risk before classification
nodes.body: Angioedema Steps Summary ~110,000 ED visits/year in the US. Up to 44% of patients with hereditary angioedema (HAE) are initially misdiagnosed. The critical first step is a structured airway assessment before mechanism classification. [1][5][7] Use the airway-risk tool when the patient is not an obvious immediate airway. It combines hard airway triggers, Ishoo anatomic staging, and the 2023 AJEM ED

nodes.title: Objective Airway Risk
nodes.summary: Use hard airway triggers first, then AJEM score and Ishoo stage to decide intubate now vs monitored airway watch vs low-risk pathway
nodes.body: Angioedema Airway Risk Calculator Do not wait for a score if the airway is declaring itself. Intubate now for stridor, hypoxemia, inability to handle secretions, rapidly progressive tongue/floor-of-mouth swelling, altered mental status, exhaustion, or confirmed laryngeal edema. [5][9][27] AJEM 2023 ED intubation-risk score: • Hypertension: +2 • Anterior tongue swelling: +2 • Pharyngeal swelling: +

nodes.title: Secure the Airway
nodes.summary: Dual setup: intubation + cric ready; awake flexible/video approach preferred when oxygenation allows; avoid paralysis until anatomy and rescue plan are clear
nodes.body: DUAL SETUP: intubation + cricothyrotomy ready simultaneously. Call the most experienced airway operator early. Notify anesthesia/ENT/trauma airway when available. Keep the patient upright and spontaneously breathing if oxygenation allows. [9][27] High-risk features requiring definitive airway planning: stridor, hypoxemia, secretion intolerance/drooling, shortness of breath, voice change/hoarseness

nodes.title: Airway Monitoring
nodes.summary: Moderate-risk airway watch: q15 min reassessment, airway backup ready, scope if available, escalate for symptom progression or score >7
nodes.body: Supplemental O2, continuous monitoring, and q15 minute airway reassessment until clearly improving. Do NOT rely on NIPPV (CPAP/BiPAP) because it does not treat a supraglottic/anatomic obstruction and can delay definitive airway control. [5][27] Angioedema Airway Risk Calculator Moderate-risk watch group: AJEM score 5-7, stage 3 tongue/floor-of-mouth edema, progressive symptoms, pharyngeal edema, d

nodes.title: Classify the Angioedema
nodes.summary: Histamine (urticaria, responds to epi) vs bradykinin (no urticaria, epi/antihistamines/steroids INEFFECTIVE) — treatment entirely different
nodes.body: The most important distinction is histamine-mediated vs bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Treatment is entirely different for each. [3][5] Histamine vs Bradykinin Differentiation Histamine-mediated: Rapid onset (minutes-hours), urticaria/pruritus, responds to epinephrine/antihistamines. Accounts for 40-70% of ED presentations. [5] Bradykinin-mediated: Slow onset (hours-days), NO urticaria, does NOT

nodes.title: Bradykinin-Mediated — Identify Cause
nodes.summary: ACEi (30% of ED visits), HAE (family history, onset <20), post-tPA, acquired C1-INH deficiency, or abdominal presentation
nodes.body: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema is NOT an allergic reaction. Epinephrine, antihistamines, and corticosteroids are generally INEFFECTIVE. [3][5][20] Lab Interpretation Guide Key history: ACEi/ARB use, family history of angioedema, prior similar episodes, recent tPA administration, age of first episode, associated lymphoproliferative disorder.

nodes.title: Undifferentiated Angioedema
nodes.summary: Start empiric epi+antihistamine — if responds = histamine-mediated; if no response = likely bradykinin-mediated
nodes.body: When the etiology is unclear, assume histamine-mediated (the most common cause, 40-70%) and start empiric treatment. [3][5] Start: Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM + Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IV. Reassess in 30-60 minutes. A diagnostic/therapeutic challenge of epinephrine is reasonable — histamine-mediated angioedema will almost always respond rapidly. Failure to respond suggests bradykinin-mediated proce

nodes.title: Histamine-Mediated — Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess for multisystem involvement — anaphylaxis features (hypotension, wheeze) vs isolated localized swelling
nodes.body: Histamine-mediated angioedema exists along the spectrum of allergic reaction and anaphylaxis. Treatment is the same as for anaphylaxis. [3][5] Assess for multisystem involvement — this differentiates anaphylaxis from isolated angioedema.

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis Protocol
nodes.body: TREAT AS ANAPHYLAXIS — Epinephrine is first-line. [3][4] Epinephrine: • Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) into anterolateral thigh • Repeat every 5-20 minutes, up to 3 doses • Pediatric: 0.01 mg/kg IM (max 0.3 mg) • Refractory: IV epinephrine drip 1-4 mcg/min (0.01-0.02 mcg/kg/min) • "Dirty" drip: 1 mg epinephrine in 1 L NS = 1 mcg/mL, run wide open Adjuncts: • H1 blocker: Diphenhydramine 25-50
nodes.recommendation: Full anaphylaxis protocol. Observe minimum 4-6 hours. Biphasic reaction risk.

nodes.title: Isolated Histamine-Mediated Angioedema
nodes.body: No anaphylaxis features — localized, self-limited. • H1 blocker: Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IV/PO or Cetirizine 10 mg PO • Consider H2 blocker: Famotidine 20 mg IV — limited evidence but favorable safety profile [4] • Consider corticosteroid: Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV — not proven effective in RCTs for angioedema specifically, but commonly given [4] • Remove trigger if identified (food, insect st
nodes.recommendation: Observe 4-6 hours. Discharge with antihistamines and return precautions if stable.

nodes.title: ACEi-Induced Angioedema
nodes.summary: STOP ACEi immediately — not allergic, bradykinin-mediated; 5x risk in Black patients; can occur years after starting
nodes.body: STOP the ACEi immediately. This is NOT an allergic reaction — it is a side effect (class effect). [5][10][20] Key facts: • Up to 30% of all ED angioedema visits in the US [5] • ~0.7% of patients develop angioedema within 5 years of ACEi use [10] • NOT dose-dependent — can occur hours to 10+ years after starting [5] • 5-fold higher risk in Black patients (5% vs 0.5%) [20] • Can also occur with ARBs

nodes.title: ACEi-Induced — Treatment
nodes.body: Discontinue ACEi permanently. Observation is the cornerstone. [5][20][23] Targeted therapies (present both evidence perspectives): Antifibrinolytic approach (emerging evidence): • Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV load, then 1 g over 8 hours — blocks plasminogen→plasmin conversion, interrupting the kallikrein amplification spiral. Case series: all 31 non-intubated patients avoided intubation. A single dose m
nodes.recommendation: Stop ACEi permanently. Consider TXA or icatibant. Observe minimum 4-6 hours. PCP follow-up for medication change.

nodes.title: Hereditary Angioedema
nodes.summary: HAE types: Type 1 (85%, low C1-INH level), Type 2 (15%, low function), Type 3 (rare, normal C1-INH); 25% de novo mutations
nodes.body: HAE subtypes are caused by C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or dysfunction. Prevalence: 1:100,000 to 1:150,000. ~25% arise from de novo mutations (no family history). [2][5] HAE Classification & Triggers Lab Interpretation Guide Type 1 (85%): Deficient C1-INH level Type 2 (15%): Normal level but decreased C1-INH function Type 3 (rare): Normal C1-INH — linked to factor XII mutations

nodes.title: HAE — Acute Treatment
nodes.body: First-line: C1-INH replacement therapy. [11][12][13] C1-INH concentrates: • Berinert 20 units/kg IV push at 4 mL/min — preferred. FDA approved for acute HAE. Median symptom relief: 0.46 hours. 99% attack resolution with single dose. [11] • Ruconest 50 units/kg IV (<84 kg) or 4200 units (≥84 kg) — recombinant C1-INH from transgenic rabbits. Contraindicated if rabbit allergy. Median relief: 66 min.
nodes.recommendation: C1-INH concentrate is first-line for HAE Types 1 and 2. Icatibant or ecallantide as alternatives. TXA if targeted therapy unavailable.

nodes.title: First Presentation — Suspected HAE
nodes.summary: Send C4 (96% sensitive during attack) — low C4 + clinical suspicion warrants empiric treatment before confirmatory labs
nodes.body: Send C4 level — best screening test in the ED. [5] • C4 is 96% sensitive during an acute attack and 81% sensitive between attacks [20] • Low C4 + clinical suspicion warrants empiric treatment while awaiting confirmatory testing • Outpatient confirmatory workup: C1-INH level, C1-INH function, C1q If HAE is strongly suspected, do NOT delay treatment for lab confirmation. Start C1-INH concentrate if

nodes.title: Acquired Angioedema (AAE)
nodes.body: Very rare (~1.5 per million). Acquired C1-INH deficiency, typically presents after age 40. [5] Associated with: • Lymphoproliferative disorders (CLL, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Waldenstrom, MGUS) • Autoimmune disease (lupus — anti-C1-INH autoantibodies) Lab findings: • Low C4 (same as HAE) • Low C1-INH level or function (same as HAE) • LOW C1q — THIS distinguishes AAE from HAE (C1q is normal in HAE) [5
nodes.recommendation: Treat as HAE. Low C1q distinguishes AAE from HAE. Screen for lymphoproliferative disorder.

nodes.title: Post-tPA Angioedema
nodes.body: Incidence: 0.9-7.9% after alteplase administration. tPA increases kinins in plasma. [5] Management: • Consider stopping tPA infusion if airway is threatened — weigh stroke severity vs airway risk • Icatibant 30 mg SQ (case reports of benefit) • Berinert 20 units/kg IV (case reports) • Fresh Frozen Plasma 2 units if targeted therapy unavailable AVOID Tranexamic Acid — contraindicated in acute ische
nodes.recommendation: Consider stopping tPA. Icatibant or C1-INH if available. AVOID TXA in acute stroke.

nodes.title: Idiopathic Angioedema
nodes.summary: Trial high-dose antihistamine first — response = histaminergic; no response = try TXA, icatibant, or C1-INH
nodes.body: Idiopathic angioedema is defined as recurrent angioedema without urticaria, with no identified cause despite thorough evaluation. [4][25] Two subtypes (differentiated by treatment response): Idiopathic histaminergic: Responds to high-dose antihistamines (up to 4× standard dose), leukotriene antagonists, and/or steroids. Idiopathic non-histaminergic: Refractory to antihistamines → consider: • Trane

nodes.title: Pediatric HAE
nodes.body: 50-75% of HAE patients have first attack by age 12. Mean age of onset: 5-11 years. [5][24] Special considerations: • Smaller airway diameter → laryngeal edema leads to asphyxia faster than adults • Fiberoptic laryngoscopy more technically difficult (lower compliance) • 43.7% of pediatric HAE ED visits present with respiratory distress [24] Abdominal presentations common: • Colicky abdominal pain m
nodes.recommendation: Smaller airway = faster compromise. C1-INH concentrate preferred. US over CT for abdominal symptoms.

nodes.title: Pregnancy & Lactation
nodes.body: Physiologic changes in pregnancy can mitigate, aggravate, or have no effect on underlying HAE — variable and unpredictable. [5] Preferred acute treatment: • Berinert 20 units/kg IV — plasma-derived C1-INH, considered safest option [5] If Berinert unavailable: • Ruconest (recombinant C1-INH) — recommended if plasma-derived C1-INH not available and no rabbit allergy [5] • Icatibant — for life-threat
nodes.recommendation: Berinert 20 units/kg IV is preferred in pregnancy. Ruconest or Icatibant only if C1-INH unavailable.

nodes.title: Abdominal Angioedema
nodes.summary: GI angioedema in 73% of HAE — severe abdominal pain mimicking acute abdomen; CT shows ascites + bowel wall edema
nodes.body: GI involvement occurs in up to 73% of HAE patients. Abdominal pain is present in 95% of GI cases. [5] Presentation: • Severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, ascites • Can appear severe enough to mimic acute abdomen → unnecessary imaging and surgical exploration • Often recurrent — detailed history is critical Imaging findings: • CT: Ascites (most common), segmental bowel wall edema wit

nodes.title: Abdominal — Treatment
nodes.body: Treat the underlying angioedema — symptom improvement confirms the diagnosis. [5] For known/suspected HAE: • Berinert 20 units/kg IV — improvement in symptoms supports the diagnosis • Alternative: Icatibant 30 mg SQ or Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV In patients with known HAE and typical recurrent abdominal episodes: • Reasonable to defer imaging if clinical picture is consistent with prior episodes AND p
nodes.recommendation: Treat underlying angioedema. Symptom improvement confirms diagnosis. Avoid unnecessary surgery.

nodes.title: Disposition — Ishoo Staging
nodes.summary: Disposition: stage 1-2 and low score may discharge after observation; stage 3 or moderate score admit/observe closely; stage 4 or high score ICU/airway
nodes.body: Disposition should combine anatomic location, trajectory during observation, mechanism, and the objective airway-risk score. [4][7][8][26] Ishoo Staging & Disposition Guide Angioedema Airway Risk Calculator Modified Ishoo Staging: • Stage 1: Facial rash, facial edema, lip edema • Stage 2: Soft palate edema • Stage 3: Tongue edema, floor of mouth edema • Stage 4: Laryngeal edema (voice change, stri

nodes.title: Stage 1-2 — Observation / Discharge
nodes.body: ED observation 4-6 hours minimum. [5][7][8] Edema localized to the lips alone does NOT have increased intubation risk. [7][8] Stage 1: 85% treated and discharged from ED; 0.1% require airway intervention. [8] Discharge criteria: • No progression of symptoms during observation • No signs of airway compromise • Able to tolerate oral intake • Reliable patient with understanding of return precautions
nodes.recommendation: Observe 4-6 hours. Discharge with return precautions, PCP follow-up, and appropriate medication changes.

nodes.title: Stage 3 — Admit for Monitoring
nodes.body: Tongue and floor of mouth edema — admit for close airway monitoring. [7][8] • Continued medical therapy based on angioedema type • Serial airway assessments (including flexible laryngoscopy if available) • Dual setup at bedside (intubation equipment + cric tray) • Escalate to ICU if any progression of laryngeal symptoms Stage 3 has significantly higher risk of ICU admission and airway intervention
nodes.recommendation: Admit for close airway monitoring. Serial airway assessments. Low threshold for ICU escalation.

nodes.title: Stage 4 — ICU Admission
nodes.body: Laryngeal involvement — ICU admission required. [7][8] Stage 4 patients: 67% probability of airway intervention, 17% require ICU without airway intervention, 0% discharged from ED. [8] • Airway secured or continuous monitoring with dual setup at bedside • Ongoing targeted medical therapy • Serial laryngoscopy to assess for resolution • Extubation planning: Wait for visible improvement. Extubate ov
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. 67% require airway intervention. Refer HAE patients for long-term prophylaxis.

nodes.title: Anisocoria - First Decide if This Is a Sick Pupil
nodes.summary: Sick pupils first: CN III palsy, Horner/dissection, AACG, trauma/open globe.
nodes.body: Open quick tools first if needed: - Steps - Light/Dark Rule - Stop / Pitfalls Start with visual acuity, pupil sizes in bright and dim light, EOMs, ptosis, IOP if no open-globe concern, fluorescein/slit lamp when appropriate, and a focused neuro exam. Do not label this physiologic until the dangerous causes have been excluded. *Basis: the bright/dark localization framework and the dangerous-cause s

nodes.title: Emergency Screen Before Localization
nodes.summary: If neurologic, painful, red, or traumatic, do not reassure before excluding emergencies.
nodes.body: Immediate danger patterns: - New diplopia or ophthalmoplegia + ptosis + larger pupil: CN III palsy, PCom aneurysm until excluded - Small pupil + ptosis + acute neck/head/face pain: Horner syndrome from carotid dissection until excluded - Red painful eye + halos/vomiting/cloudy cornea: acute angle-closure glaucoma - Trauma + irregular pupil or poor view: open globe, hyphema, or orbital compartment

nodes.title: Red Painful Eye: Acute Angle-Closure Until Proven Otherwise
nodes.body: Pattern: painful red eye, halos, nausea/vomiting, headache, cloudy cornea, fixed or mid-dilated pupil, reduced vision, high IOP if measurable. Action: - Check IOP only if open globe is not suspected - Start acute angle-closure treatment immediately if high suspicion - Emergent ophthalmology - Use the Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma consult for medication sequence and disposition: Open AACG *Basis: AA
nodes.recommendation: Treat as acute angle-closure glaucoma if the eye is red/painful with compatible pupil and high IOP or classic exam.

nodes.title: Trauma or Irregular Pupil: Protect the Globe First
nodes.body: Pattern: blunt or penetrating eye trauma, teardrop or irregular pupil, hyphema, Seidel sign, peaked pupil, shallow anterior chamber, severe chemosis/proptosis, high IOP with vision loss, or restricted EOM. Action: - Shield the eye, avoid pressure, avoid tonometry if open globe possible - Antiemetic, analgesia, tetanus, NPO if surgical concern - CT orbits without contrast for globe/IOFB when indica
nodes.recommendation: Do not manipulate or measure IOP in possible open globe. Treat traumatic anisocoria as structural eye injury until cleared.

nodes.title: Measure in Bright and Dim Light
nodes.summary: Bright worse = big pupil abnormal. Dark worse = small pupil abnormal.
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Measure each pupil in bright room light. 2. Dim the room and wait several seconds. 3. Measure each pupil again. 4. Decide where the anisocoria gets larger. Interpretation: - Worse in bright light: the larger pupil is abnormal, usually parasympathetic problem - Worse in dark: the smaller pupil is abnormal, usually sympathetic problem - Same in bright/dark and <1 mm: physiologic anisoc

nodes.title: Large Pupil Abnormal: Parasympathetic Pathway
nodes.summary: Large abnormal pupil: do not miss CN III palsy or acute angle closure.
nodes.body: The larger pupil failed to constrict. Important causes are CN III palsy, acute angle closure, traumatic/iris abnormality, pharmacologic mydriasis, and Adie tonic pupil. Look hard for EOM abnormality, ptosis, headache/eye pain, red eye, IOP elevation, trauma, and drug exposure. *Basis: parasympathetic differential per Continuum pupil reviews [1,4]. Pupil involvement as a predictor of a compressive

nodes.title: CN III Palsy Pattern: Image for Aneurysm Now
nodes.body: Concerning pattern: larger poorly reactive pupil with ptosis, diplopia, impaired adduction/elevation/depression, eye down-and-out, headache, eye pain, or incomplete third nerve findings. ED action: - CTA head/neck or MRI/MRA head/neck per local pathway - If CTA/MRA negative but suspicion remains high, neurology/neurosurgery may still pursue catheter angiography - Ophthalmology plus neurology/neuro
nodes.recommendation: New painful or pupil-involving CN III palsy is an aneurysm rule-out emergency.

nodes.title: Large Irregular Pupil After Trauma or Surgery
nodes.body: Likely causes: traumatic mydriasis, iris sphincter tear, hyphema, lens injury, open globe, prior ocular surgery, or pharmacologic dilation after eye exam. ED action: - Visual acuity, slit lamp if safe, fluorescein if no obvious open globe - Avoid IOP measurement if open globe possible - CT orbits if open globe, IOFB, fracture, or retrobulbar hemorrhage concern - Ophthalmology based on injury sever
nodes.recommendation: Structural eye causes are diagnosed by eye exam, not by light/dark pattern alone.

nodes.title: Pharmacologic Mydriasis vs Adie Tonic Pupil
nodes.summary: Pharmacologic testing supports the diagnosis only after emergencies are excluded.
nodes.body: Open pharmacology quick card Ask about exposure: diagnostic/cycloplegic eye drops, scopolamine patch hand-to-eye transfer, leaking ipratropium neb or anticholinergic inhaler exposure, glycopyrrolate, anticholinergic plants, sympathomimetic/nasal decongestant sprays, cocaine/amphetamine exposure, botulinum toxin near the orbit, or accidental wrong-eye/wrong-drop exposure. Bedside pharmacologic clue

nodes.title: Likely Pharmacologic Mydriasis
nodes.body: Pattern: isolated large pupil, poor light response, normal EOMs, no ptosis, no neuro deficit, no red painful eye, compatible exposure, and no constriction with 1% pilocarpine if tested. Disposition: - Remove/stop exposure if possible - Explain expected gradual resolution based on agent - Ophthalmology follow-up if persistent, painful, vision change, irregular pupil, or uncertain exposure - Return
nodes.recommendation: Discharge is reasonable only when the exposure is clear and the neurologic/ocular danger screen is negative.

nodes.title: Adie Tonic Pupil Pattern
nodes.body: Pattern: young to middle-aged adult, larger pupil, poor light reaction, better near response, slow redilation, segmental iris sphincter palsy on slit lamp, usually unilateral and benign. Testing: dilute pilocarpine may show denervation hypersensitivity, but false positives occur and ED availability is variable. This is not a test to clear CN III palsy when EOM/ptosis/headache is present. Dispositi
nodes.recommendation: Adie is an outpatient diagnosis after CN III palsy, angle closure, trauma, and pharmacologic exposure are considered.

nodes.title: Small Pupil Abnormal: Sympathetic Pathway
nodes.summary: Small abnormal pupil: acute painful Horner means carotid dissection until proven otherwise.
nodes.body: The smaller pupil failed to dilate. Important causes are Horner syndrome, physiologic anisocoria, uveitis/iritis, miotic medications, and rare brainstem/cavernous sinus lesions. Look for mild ptosis, dilation lag in the dark, face/neck/head pain, anhidrosis, trauma, neuro symptoms, and carotid dissection risk. *Basis: sympathetic-pathway differential per Continuum pupil reviews [1,2]. Horner syndr

nodes.title: Likely Pharmacologic Miosis
nodes.body: Open pharmacology quick card Pattern: smaller pupil is abnormal, no painful red eye/photophobia, no ptosis or dilation lag suggesting Horner, no focal neurologic findings, and a compatible miotic/cholinergic exposure. Common exposures: pilocarpine or carbachol glaucoma drops, older cholinesterase-inhibitor miotics, apraclonidine/brimonidine or other topical glaucoma drops, organophosphate/carbamat
nodes.recommendation: Do not call a small pupil pharmacologic until painful Horner, uveitis, and neurologic causes have been considered.

nodes.title: Acute Painful Horner: Image Head and Neck Same Day
nodes.body: Concerning pattern: miosis + mild ptosis + dilation lag, especially with ipsilateral neck pain, face pain, headache, recent trauma/manipulation, TIA/stroke symptoms, or cluster-like pain. ED action: - CTA head and neck or MRI/MRA head and neck per local pathway - Include carotid dissection, cavernous sinus lesion, brainstem stroke, and apical lung/neck pathology in differential - Neurology/stroke
nodes.recommendation: Treat acute painful Horner syndrome as carotid dissection until excluded.

nodes.title: Horner Syndrome: Confirm and Localize
nodes.summary: Horner is a localization diagnosis. Acute painful Horner is a vascular emergency.
nodes.body: Classic triad: miosis, mild ptosis, and facial anhidrosis. The full triad is often incomplete. Dilation lag in dim light supports Horner. ED framing: - Acute, painful, traumatic, or neurologic Horner: same-day CTA/MRA head and neck - Chronic painless Horner with old photos confirming stability: outpatient neuro-ophthalmology may be appropriate - Pediatric Horner: needs specialist evaluation for ne

nodes.title: Small Painful Pupil: Consider Anterior Uveitis/Iritis
nodes.body: Pattern: photophobia, ciliary flush, consensual photophobia, cells/flare, small or irregular pupil from posterior synechiae, and pain out of proportion to simple conjunctivitis. ED action: - Visual acuity, slit lamp, fluorescein, IOP if no open-globe concern - Avoid starting topical steroid without ophthalmology direction - Cycloplegic and pain control per local ophthalmology guidance - Ophthalmol
nodes.recommendation: Photophobic red painful eye with small pupil is not physiologic anisocoria. Treat as inflammatory eye disease and involve ophthalmology.

nodes.title: Physiologic Anisocoria Likely
nodes.body: Reassuring pattern: - Difference usually <1 mm - Similar difference in bright and dim light - Normal visual acuity, EOMs, fields by confrontation, IOP if checked, and neuro exam - No ptosis, red eye, trauma, headache/neck pain, diplopia, or new neurologic symptom - Old photos or driver license show the same asymmetry Disposition: discharge with routine eye follow-up if needed and strict return pre
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after documenting normal eye/neuro exam and no dangerous features.

nodes.title: Uncertain Anisocoria: Do Not Force a Benign Label
nodes.body: Use this lane when: measurement is unreliable, exam is limited, old photos unavailable, the patient is intoxicated/altered, drop exposure is uncertain, or symptoms do not fit cleanly. Escalate if any of these remain: headache, neck/face pain, ptosis, diplopia, abnormal EOM, neuro deficit, red painful eye, trauma, irregular pupil, vision loss, or acute onset. Practical disposition: - If any neurolo
nodes.recommendation: When classification is uncertain, disposition follows the worst remaining red flag, not the most benign possibility.

nodes.title: Disposition and Documentation
nodes.summary: Document light/dark sizes, abnormal pupil, red flags, and exact reason for imaging or discharge.
nodes.body: Admit / transfer / emergent consult: - CN III palsy pattern or suspected aneurysm - Acute painful Horner or suspected carotid dissection - Stroke/TIA/brainstem signs - Acute angle closure not rapidly controlled - Open globe, orbital compartment syndrome, or serious ocular trauma Urgent ophthalmology or neuro-ophthalmology: - New unexplained anisocoria after ED danger screen - Adie tonic pupil conf

nodes.title: Ankle Injury — ED Evaluation
nodes.body: Steps Summary Ottawa Ankle Rules (OAR): Sensitivity 97.6% for excluding fracture. NPV >99%. X-ray indicated if ANY: • Bone tenderness at posterior edge of lateral malleolus (distal 6cm) • Bone tenderness at posterior edge of medial malleolus (distal 6cm) • Inability to bear weight (4 steps) immediately AND in ED Also check midfoot (separate Ottawa Foot Rules): • Base of 5th metatarsal tenderness •

nodes.title: Ankle Sprain — No Fracture
nodes.body: Ottawa Ankle Rules Negative: Fracture very unlikely (sensitivity 97.6%, NPV >99%). Management: • RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) • NSAIDs PRN • Ankle brace or stirrup splint for comfort • Early mobilization encouraged • Weight-bearing as tolerated Return Precautions: • Worsening pain despite rest • New inability to bear weight • Significant swelling increase Follow-up: PCP in 1-2
nodes.recommendation: Ankle sprain. RICE protocol, NSAIDs, ankle brace. Weight-bearing as tolerated. PCP follow-up if symptoms persist >2 weeks.

nodes.title: X-Ray Findings
nodes.body: Standard Views: AP, Mortise (15° internal rotation), Lateral Assess: 1. Fibula fracture location (Weber classification) 2. Medial malleolus — fracture or widened medial clear space 3. Posterior malleolus — lateral view 4. Mortise alignment — talar dome congruent? Weber Classification (based on fibula fracture level): • Weber A — Below syndesmosis (infrasyndesmotic) • Weber B — At syndesmosis level

nodes.title: Negative X-Ray — Consider Occult Injury
nodes.body: X-ray negative but high clinical suspicion: Consider: • Occult fracture (MRI sensitivity >CT for subtle injuries) • Syndesmotic injury without fracture (high ankle sprain) • Osteochondral lesion of talus • Stress fracture Syndesmotic Injury Exam: • Squeeze test — compress tibia/fibula at mid-calf, pain at ankle = positive • External rotation test — knee bent, externally rotate foot, pain = positiv

nodes.title: Weber A — Infrasyndesmotic
nodes.body: Weber A Fractures: Fibula fracture BELOW the syndesmosis. Characteristics: • Usually stable • Syndesmosis intact • Often avulsion fracture from lateral ligament • Low energy mechanism Stability Assessment: • Check medial clear space on mortise view • Normal: ≤4 mm (equal to superior clear space) • Widened: >4 mm = unstable Management: • Stable (isolated): Non-operative - Walking boot or short leg

nodes.title: Weber B — Transsyndesmotic
nodes.body: Weber B Fractures: Fibula fracture AT the level of the syndesmosis. Key Question: Is it STABLE or UNSTABLE? Stability Indicators: | Stable | Unstable | |--------|----------| | Mortise congruent | Mortise widened | | Medial clear space ≤4mm | Medial clear space >4mm | | No medial tenderness | Medial malleolus fracture or deltoid rupture | | Negative stress test | Positive stress test | Assess media

nodes.title: Stress Testing
nodes.body: Weight-Bearing or Stress Films: Used when stability uncertain on non-weight-bearing films. Options: 1. Weight-bearing mortise view — patient stands on injured leg 2. Gravity stress view — external rotation with leg hanging 3. Manual stress — external rotation under fluoro (usually ortho) Positive Test: • Medial clear space widens >4-5 mm under stress • Indicates deltoid ligament rupture • Fracture

nodes.title: Weber C — Suprasyndesmotic
nodes.body: Weber C Fractures: Fibula fracture ABOVE the syndesmosis. Characteristics: • Almost always UNSTABLE • Syndesmosis disrupted by definition • Higher energy mechanism • May have associated medial injury CRITICAL: Rule out Maisonneuve Fracture • Proximal fibula fracture + syndesmotic disruption • Palpate entire fibula to knee • If proximal tenderness: full leg films Management: • Virtually ALL require

nodes.title: Maisonneuve Fracture — Do Not Miss
nodes.body: Maisonneuve Fracture: Proximal fibula fracture + complete syndesmotic disruption + medial injury. Why Commonly Missed: • Ankle pain dominates — proximal fibula not examined • Proximal fracture not on ankle films • High index of suspicion required Red Flags — Get Full Leg Films: • Medial malleolus fracture without lateral malleolus fracture • Syndesmotic widening on ankle films • Tenderness over pr

nodes.title: Bimalleolar / Trimalleolar Fractures
nodes.body: Bimalleolar: Fractures of BOTH lateral AND medial malleoli. Trimalleolar: Lateral + medial + posterior malleolus (posterior tibial lip). Key Points: • ALL are inherently UNSTABLE • ALL require operative fixation • Higher complication rates than unimalleolar • Posterior malleolus involvement affects outcomes ED Management: • Assess neurovascular status • Reduce if grossly displaced/dislocated • Pos

nodes.title: Operative Fracture — Ortho Consult
nodes.body: Indications for Operative Fixation (ORIF): • Weber C (suprasyndesmotic) • Unstable Weber B • Bimalleolar or trimalleolar • Maisonneuve fracture • Ankle dislocation (after reduction) • Intra-articular displacement >2mm ED Management: 1. Neurovascular check — document pulse, sensation, motor 2. Reduction if dislocated (procedural sedation) 3. Posterior splint — ankle at 90°, well-padded 4. Non-weigh
nodes.recommendation: Operative ankle fracture. Reduce if displaced. Posterior splint, non-weight-bearing. Ortho consult today. Follow-up 24-48h for OR planning.

nodes.title: Non-Operative Fracture — Conservative Management
nodes.body: Non-Operative Management: Indications: • Stable Weber A • Stable Weber B (congruent mortise, no medial injury) • Isolated lateral malleolus avulsion Immobilization: • Walking boot (preferred) — allows early weight-bearing • Posterior splint — if significant swelling initially • Short leg cast — if non-compliance concern Weight-Bearing: • Modern approach: weight-bearing as tolerated from day 1 • Ev
nodes.recommendation: Stable ankle fracture. Walking boot, weight-bearing as tolerated. Ice, elevation, NSAIDs. Ortho follow-up within 5-7 days for repeat films.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: • Open fracture • Neurovascular compromise • Irreducible dislocation • Unable to manage at home • Pending OR (surgeon preference) Discharge Criteria: • Closed, stable or reduced fracture • Neurovascularly intact • Adequate pain control • Reliable follow-up arranged • Can manage non-weight-bearing at home Follow-up Timing: • Operative fractures: 24-48 hours (ortho) • Non-operati

nodes.title: Admit — Operative Management
nodes.body: Admission Orders: • NPO after midnight (anticipate OR) • Posterior splint, elevate on pillows • Ice 20 min q2h while awake • Strict non-weight-bearing • DVT prophylaxis if prolonged immobility expected • Pain management (consider regional block) • Ortho to determine OR timing Open Fracture Protocol: • Tetanus update • IV antibiotics (cefazolin ± gentamicin per Gustilo grade) • Irrigation in ED if
nodes.recommendation: Admit for operative ankle fracture. NPO, posterior splint, elevation, DVT prophylaxis. Ortho to schedule OR.

nodes.title: Discharge — Outpatient Management
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions: Immobilization: • Keep splint/boot on at all times except bathing • Do not get splint wet Activity: • Elevate above heart level as much as possible first 48-72h • Ice 20 min every 2-3 hours while awake • Weight-bearing per ortho instructions (usually WBAT in boot for stable fractures) Medications: • NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400-600mg q6h with food) or acetaminophen • Narcotic for
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with walking boot/splint. RICE protocol, NSAIDs. Ortho follow-up 5-7 days. Written return precautions.

nodes.title: Rectal Bleeding — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Gestalt sick check + vitals/orthostatics + quantify bleed + anticoagulation screen. If unstable: resuscitate in parallel.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 4 DO NOT MISS: 1. Brisk lower-GI hemorrhage / hemodynamic compromise \u2014 large-volume BRBPR or clots, tachycardia, hypotension, syncope. 2. Upper-GI source masquerading as maroon / BRBPR \u2014 a brisk UGIB can present per rectum; urea:creatinine ratio and NG/rectal exam help. 3. Anticoagulated / coagulopathic bleeder \u2014 warfarin, DOAC, antiplatelet, liver disease, or a bleedin

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Localize the Source
nodes.summary: Pick the most acute source; walk its gate to an explicit verdict. Excluded loops back.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous sources to an explicit verdict, one at a time. Each differential walks its gate (hemodynamics, instrument, or exam) to excluded, test further, or rule in + treat. Excluded loops back here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Brisk Lower-GI Hemorrhage — Hemodynamic Gate
nodes.summary: Hemodynamics drive it. Unstable/ongoing = resuscitate + urgent GI; stopped + stable = risk-stratify.
nodes.body: Large-volume hematochezia with hemodynamic instability is the emergency. ~10-15% of severe "lower" bleeds are actually a brisk upper source \u2014 keep UGIB on the list. Hemodynamics, not the color of the blood, drive the pathway.

nodes.title: Brisk Lower-GI Hemorrhage — Resuscitate + Treat
nodes.body: Open Lower GI Bleed (or the broader GI Bleed Hub). Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, monitor, type and CROSS; transfuse to a restrictive threshold (Hb ~7 g/dL, higher if active cardiac ischemia). - CBC, coags, fibrinogen, lactate; reverse anticoagulation / correct coagulopathy per severity. - Rule out an upper source in severe bleeds \u2014 an NG lavage or an urgent upper endoscopy; a markedly
nodes.recommendation: Two large-bore IVs, type and cross, restrictive transfusion (~7), reverse anticoagulation, exclude upper source, GI/CTA/IR.

nodes.title: Brisk LGIB — Excluded (Stable, Self-Limited)
nodes.body: Bleeding has stopped, vitals are stable, and volume was minor \u2014 this is not an active brisk hemorrhage right now. Risk-stratify with the Oakland score (toolbar): a score \u226410 identifies low-risk patients who may be considered for safe outpatient management. Any recurrence, hemodynamic change, or dropping Hb re-opens the emergency pathway. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Self-limited + stable; use Oakland score (\u226410 = low risk) to guide discharge vs admission. Re-escalate if it recurs.

nodes.title: Upper-GI Masquerade — Source-Localization Gate
nodes.summary: Melena/hematemesis/BUN:Cr >30/varices = treat as UGIB. Isolated BRBPR + normal ratio = unlikely.
nodes.body: A brisk upper-GI bleed can present as maroon stool or even BRBPR. Clues that the source is above the ligament of Treitz: hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis, melena, a BUN:creatinine ratio >30, known varices / peptic ulcer / NSAID use, or hemodynamic instability out of proportion to visible rectal blood.

nodes.title: Upper-GI Source — Resuscitate + Treat
nodes.body: Open Upper GI Bleed. Next 5 minutes: - Two large-bore IVs, monitor, type and cross; restrictive transfusion (Hb ~7). - IV PPI; if cirrhotic / suspected varices add octreotide + ceftriaxone (SBP prophylaxis). - Reverse anticoagulation / correct coagulopathy. - GI for upper endoscopy within 24 h (urgently if unstable / variceal). - A negative NG lavage does NOT rule out a post-pyloric source \u2014
nodes.recommendation: Type and cross, restrictive transfusion, IV PPI \u00B1 octreotide/ceftriaxone if cirrhotic, urgent upper endoscopy.

nodes.title: Upper-GI Source — Unlikely
nodes.body: Isolated bright-red blood per rectum with no melena, no hematemesis, a normal BUN:creatinine ratio, and stable vitals makes a brisk upper source unlikely as the driver. In any severe or unexplained bleed, keep the upper source in mind \u2014 the ratio is a clue, not a rule-out. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Upper source unlikely with isolated BRBPR + normal ratio; reconsider if the bleed is severe or unexplained.
