nodes.title: Anticoagulated / Coagulopathic Bleeder — Agent Gate
nodes.summary: Identify agent/disorder. Significant bleed on a thinner or a factor deficiency = reverse/replace; otherwise move on.
nodes.body: Identify the agent and the coagulopathy \u2014 it changes both the risk and the reversal. Warfarin (INR), DOAC (factor Xa or thrombin inhibitor), antiplatelet, liver disease (synthetic failure), or an inherited bleeding disorder (hemophilia, VWD) each has a specific correction.

nodes.title: Anticoagulated / Coagulopathic — Reverse + Treat
nodes.body: Open Anticoagulation Reversal (inherited factor deficiency \u2192 Hemophilia). Match reversal to the agent: - Warfarin \u2014 4-factor PCC (weight/INR-dosed) + IV vitamin K 10 mg; FFP only if PCC unavailable. - Dabigatran \u2014 idarucizumab. - Apixaban / rivaroxaban \u2014 andexanet alfa where available, otherwise 4-factor PCC. - Antiplatelet \u2014 platelet transfusion is generally NOT beneficia
nodes.recommendation: Agent-specific reversal: PCC+vit K (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet/PCC (Xa), factor replacement (hemophilia). Then treat the source.

nodes.title: Coagulopathy — Not the Driver
nodes.body: No anticoagulant, normal coags, and a minor bleed makes a coagulopathic driver unlikely. Still send a CBC and coags in any patient with meaningful bleeding \u2014 an unsuspected thrombocytopenia or liver disease can surface here. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Coagulopathy unlikely; still check CBC + coags in meaningful bleeding.

nodes.title: Malignancy / IBD — Alarm-Feature Gate
nodes.summary: Alarm features (age \u226550, weight loss, anemia, mass, systemic bloody diarrhea) = work up. None = unlikely.
nodes.body: Do not anchor on hemorrhoids when alarm features are present. Red flags: age \u226550 with new rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia, change in bowel caliber/habits, a palpable rectal mass, a family history of colorectal cancer, or bloody diarrhea with systemic features (IBD flare).

nodes.title: Malignancy / IBD — Work Up + Treat
nodes.body: IBD flare (known or new): open IBD Flare \u2014 CBC, CRP, stool studies to exclude infection, IV fluids; steroids per GI for a severe flare; screen for toxic megacolon (distension + systemic toxicity + colonic dilation on plain film \u2192 surgical emergency). Suspected colorectal malignancy (mass, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, age \u226550): do NOT clear as hemorrhoids \u2014 arrange colon
nodes.recommendation: IBD flare \u2192 IBD Flare consult + exclude infection/toxic megacolon. Alarm features \u2192 colonoscopy referral; never clear age \u226550 bleeding as hemorrhoids alone.

nodes.title: Malignancy / IBD — Low Probability
nodes.body: A young, well patient with no alarm features and clearly benign-appearing bleeding (bright red on tissue only) is low-risk for malignancy or IBD today. This does not remove the need for age-appropriate colorectal screening, and any new alarm feature (weight loss, anemia, altered habits) warrants a return and colonoscopy. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Low probability without alarm features; still ensure age-appropriate screening and return precautions for new alarm features.

nodes.title: Infectious / Ischemic Colitis — Pattern Gate
nodes.summary: Bloody diarrhea + pain = infectious vs ischemic colitis workup. Formed stool + BRB, no pain = unlikely.
nodes.body: Bloody diarrhea + abdominal pain points at colitis. Infectious (dysentery): Shigella, Campylobacter, EHEC (watch for HUS \u2014 avoid antibiotics if EHEC suspected), C. difficile, Entamoeba; travel/exposure history matters. Ischemic colitis: older / vascular / hypotensive event, sudden LLQ pain then bloody diarrhea, "thumbprinting" on imaging.

nodes.title: Colitis — Work Up + Treat
nodes.body: Open Diarrhea for the infectious pathway. Infectious colitis: stool culture + PCR panel, C. difficile toxin/PCR, ova & parasites if travel; rehydrate. Avoid empiric antibiotics if EHEC (Shiga-toxin) is suspected \u2014 they raise the HUS risk; check CBC/smear/renal function for HUS. Treat C. difficile per severity (oral vancomycin / fidaxomicin). Ischemic colitis: usually a clinical + CT diagnosis
nodes.recommendation: Infectious \u2192 stool studies + rehydration; avoid abx if EHEC (HUS risk). Ischemic \u2192 CT + supportive care; surgery for gangrene/perforation.

nodes.title: Colitis — Unlikely
nodes.body: Formed stool with bright-red blood and no diarrhea or abdominal pain makes an infectious or ischemic colitis unlikely as the driver. If diarrhea, fever, or pain develops, come back and work the colitis pathway. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Colitis unlikely without diarrhea/pain; reassess if diarrhea, fever, or pain develops.

nodes.title: Benign Anorectal — Exam Gate
nodes.summary: Inspect + DRE \u00B1 anoscopy. Prolapse = reduce/refer; hemorrhoids/fissure with benign exam + no alarms = conservative.
nodes.body: The commonest source of BRBPR is benign anorectal disease, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion in anyone with alarm features or age \u226550. Inspect and perform a digital rectal exam (\u00B1 anoscopy): hemorrhoids (painless bright-red blood coating stool / on tissue), anal fissure (severe pain with defecation + a posterior-midline tear), rectal prolapse (protruding mucosa).

nodes.title: Rectal Prolapse — Reduce + Refer
nodes.body: Open Rectal Prolapse Reduction. - Reduce the prolapse promptly (manual pressure \u00B1 topical sugar to reduce edema) to prevent incarceration / strangulation; analgesia and procedural sedation if needed. - Assess viability \u2014 a non-reducible, dusky, or strangulated prolapse is a surgical emergency. - Arrange colorectal surgery follow-up; screen for the underlying cause (chronic straining, pel
nodes.recommendation: Reduce early to prevent strangulation; surgical emergency if non-reducible/ischemic; colorectal referral + treat constipation.

nodes.title: Benign Anorectal — Conservative Management
nodes.body: Hemorrhoids or an anal fissure in a well patient with a benign exam and no alarm features: reassure and treat conservatively \u2014 high-fiber diet, adequate fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths, topical agents (and for a chronic fissure, topical nifedipine or nitroglycerin); manage the underlying constipation \u2192 Constipation. The safety net: benign anorectal disease is a diagnosis of exclusion
nodes.recommendation: Conservative care (fiber, softeners, sitz baths, topicals) + treat constipation; still arrange colonoscopy for age \u226550 or any alarm feature.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Rectal Bleeding
nodes.summary: IV + CBC/type-and-screen/coags/BUN:Cr + hold antithrombotics + DRE/anoscopy + Oakland score. Reassess Hb + hemodynamics.
nodes.body: No emergent source ruled in; stable minor bleeding. Standard ED bundle while labs cook: - IV access (two large-bore if any volume concern), monitor, orthostatic vitals. - Labs: CBC (baseline + trend Hb), type and screen (cross if significant), coags/INR, BUN + creatinine (BUN:Cr >30 hints upper source), CMP, lactate if any instability; consider stool studies if diarrhea. - Hold antithrombotics pen

nodes.title: Reassess — Bleeding + Hemodynamics
nodes.summary: Stopped + stable + low-risk = discharge; equivocal = image/scope; ongoing/dropping Hb = STOP and resuscitate.
nodes.body: Re-examine: is bleeding ongoing? Hb trend? Vitals / orthostatics? Oakland score? Source documented?

nodes.title: Imaging / Workup Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: Colonoscopy = primary tool; CTA/IR for brisk unstable bleeds; upper endoscopy if upper suspected; anoscopy for benign source. Never prep an unstable patient.
nodes.body: Match the study to the phenotype: Colonoscopy \u2014 the primary diagnostic + therapeutic tool for lower-GI bleeding; after resuscitation \u00B1 a rapid bowel purge. Also the mandatory follow-up study for new bleeding in age \u226550 or any alarm feature (malignancy exclusion). CT angiography (CTA) \u2014 for brisk, ongoing bleeding too unstable for prep or scope; localizes active extravasation (n

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit high-risk/ongoing/unstable; observe if equivocal; discharge low-risk self-limited with follow-up colonoscopy.
nodes.body: Defer to the deep-dive consult\u2019s admit criteria once a source is committed. The framework below applies to undifferentiated / benign-appearing bleeding.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for: ongoing or recurrent hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, a high Oakland score (>10), significant anemia or a dropping Hb, need for urgent endoscopy or IR embolization, anticoagulation with a significant bleed, or major comorbidity. Service: GI / Medicine for most managed bleeds; ICU for hemodynamic instability, massive transfusion, or ongoing brisk bleeding; Surgery / IR for uncontroll
nodes.recommendation: Admit per deep-dive criteria; ICU for instability/massive transfusion; IR/surgery for uncontrolled bleed; standard handoff.

nodes.title: Observe — Partial Response or Pending Workup
nodes.body: ED observation when: bleeding has slowed but not clearly stopped, awaiting a repeat Hb, awaiting prep/endoscopy, or an intermediate Oakland score with social/safety barriers. Protocol: serial vitals + orthostatics; repeat Hb at 4-6 h (and sooner if any instability); watch for recurrent bleeding; continue fluids; keep antithrombotics held pending the plan. Escalate (admit / IR / endoscopy) for recu
nodes.recommendation: Obs + serial vitals + repeat Hb at 4-6 h; escalate if recurrent bleed or falling Hb; discharge when stable + low-risk.

nodes.title: Discharge — Universal Checklist
nodes.body: Before discharge: (1) bleeding self-limited / clearly stopped, (2) vitals normal incl no orthostasis, (3) Hb stable / reassuring, (4) low-risk Oakland score (\u226410) for a lower-GI bleed, (5) a benign source documented (or a clear plan to find one), (6) reliable follow-up, (7) outpatient colonoscopy arranged for new bleeding in age \u226550 or any alarm feature, (8) written return precautions. R
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if self-limited, no orthostasis, Hb stable, Oakland \u226410, source documented, colonoscopy arranged for age \u226550/alarm features, written precautions.

nodes.title: Anticoagulant Reversal
nodes.summary: Before reversing: assess how coagulopathic, why anticoagulated, and how important is reversal — cirrhosis INR may mislead
nodes.body: Reversal Quick Reference — one-glance guide. Before reversing, consider: • How coagulopathic? Assess ALL meds affecting coagulation + labs. Critically ill patients often have multiple coagulopathies. • Why anticoagulated? AF or DVT = short interruption generally fine. Mechanical mitral valve = high thrombotic risk. • How important is reversal? Life-threatening bleeding → aggressive. Minor bleeding

nodes.title: What Is the Clinical Scenario?
nodes.summary: Triage by urgency: life-threatening = agent-specific reversal, minor = hold dose, supratherapeutic = tiered management
nodes.body: Determine urgency based on bleeding severity and clinical need.

nodes.title: Identify the Anticoagulant
nodes.summary: Act fast — for ICH on warfarin give PCC immediately without waiting for INR; identify agent and last dose timing
nodes.body: Act fast. For ICH on warfarin, give PCC immediately — do NOT wait for INR result. [1,15] ⚠️ Massive hemorrhage on unknown anticoagulant: activate MTP (1:1:1) [19] and give empiric 4-factor PCC 25–50 units/kg while you identify the specific agent and last dose. Do not delay PCC waiting for agent confirmation in life-threatening bleeding. [1,15] Review all medications affecting coagulation. Determin

nodes.title: Urgent Warfarin (Coumadin) Reversal
nodes.body: Two simultaneous therapies — BOTH required: [1] Vitamin K (Mephyton) 10 mg IV over 30 minutes • Takes 6-12h to work, but prevents INR rebound when PCC wears off (6-8h) • IV only — SC has erratic absorption, IM causes hematoma [2] 4-Factor PCC (Kcentra) — INR-based dosing: • INR 1.3-2: 15 units/kg (max 1,500 units) • INR 2-4: 25 units/kg (max 2,500 units) • INR 4-6: 35 units/kg (max 3,500 units) •

nodes.title: Dabigatran (Pradaxa) Reversal
nodes.body: [1] Idarucizumab (Praxbind) — specific reversal agent • 5 g IV total: two 2.5 g doses, no more than 15 min apart • Monoclonal antibody Fab fragment that binds and inactivates dabigatran • Onset: within minutes. Consider if last dose <12-24h (normal renal function) • For ICH: consider if dose within past 2-4 days [2] [2] If unavailable: 4-Factor PCC [6] [3] If ingested <2h: Activated Charcoal 50 g

nodes.title: Factor Xa Inhibitor Reversal
nodes.body: Apixaban (Eliquis), Rivaroxaban (Xarelto), Edoxaban (Savaysa), Fondaparinux (Arixtra) [1] 4-Factor PCC (Kcentra) — default first-line at most US centers • CNS bleeding: 50 units/kg (max 5,000 units) [5,6] • Non-CNS: 25 units/kg (max 2,500) or fixed 2,000 units (simplest, best evidence) [5] • ⚠️ PCC will NOT change the anti-Xa level (anti-Xa measures DOAC in the body, not clotting factor levels) [2

nodes.title: Heparin Type?
nodes.summary: Usually stopping infusion is sufficient (short half-life) — protamine for severe bleeding only; risks anaphylaxis/pulm HTN
nodes.body: In most cases, discontinuing the heparin infusion is sufficient — UFH has a very short half-life. Protamine is reserved for severe bleeding (e.g., ICH). ⚠️ Protamine may cause anaphylaxis or pulmonary hypertension. Excessive protamine causes paradoxical coagulopathy. [2,13]

nodes.title: UFH Reversal — Protamine
nodes.body: Protamine dosing by time since heparin: If given as bolus: • <30 min ago: 1 mg per 100 units heparin (max 50 mg) • 30-60 min: 0.5-0.75 mg per 100 units • 1-2h: 0.375-0.5 mg per 100 units • 2-6h: 0.25-0.375 mg per 100 units If given as infusion: • Calculate heparin given over last 2 hours (rate × 2) • Give 1 mg protamine per 100 units infused in last 2h Administration: • Give slowly over 15 minutes

nodes.title: LMWH Reversal — Protamine (Partial)
nodes.body: Protamine only neutralizes ~50% of enoxaparin (Lovenox) anti-Xa activity. Protamine dosing for enoxaparin (Lovenox): • <8h since dose: 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin (max 50 mg) • 8-12h since dose: 0.5 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin • >12h since dose: Protamine unlikely to help • May re-dose at 0.5 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin if bleeding persists (max 25 mg) Dalteparin (Fragmin) or tinzaparin (Innohep): •

nodes.title: tPA / Thrombolytic Reversal
nodes.body: Act immediately — don't wait for labs in an actively bleeding patient. Essential interventions: [1] Antifibrinolytic — choose whichever is faster to obtain: • Tranexamic acid (Cyklokapron) 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over next hour • Aminocaproic acid (Amicar) 4-5 g IV load, then 1 g/hour [2] Cryoprecipitate 10 units initially (two 5-unit pools) • Target fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL (>200 for ICH) [

nodes.title: Antiplatelet Agent Reversal
nodes.body: Rx #1 (front-line): DDAVP 0.3-0.4 mcg/kg IV over 20-30 min • Improves platelet function including P2Y12 inhibitors [10,11] • AHA 2022: level 2B recommendation for ICH on antiplatelets [1] • Usually single dose (tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing — depletes vWF stores) Rx #2: Consider higher fibrinogen target (>200 mg/dL) • Platelets cooperate with fibrinogen — increased fibrinogen may compensate [

nodes.title: Minor Bleeding Management
nodes.summary: Hold dose + local measures usually sufficient for minor bleeding — brief anticoagulation interruption generally safe for AF/DVT
nodes.body: For most agents, hold the dose + local measures is sufficient. • Drug elimination handles most minor bleeding • Consider the patient's overall coagulation status — ALL meds and coagulopathies • Brief anticoagulation interruption is generally safe for AF or DVT • Higher-risk indications (mechanical valve) → minimize interruption time Warfarin (Coumadin): Hold dose. Consider low-dose vitamin K if IN

nodes.title: Supratherapeutic — Which Agent?
nodes.summary: No active bleeding — warfarin uses INR-tiered vitamin K dosing; DOACs usually hold dose and let drug clear
nodes.body: No active bleeding, but anticoagulant levels are above therapeutic range.

nodes.title: Supratherapeutic INR — Warfarin
nodes.body: Elevated INR Quick Guide — detailed reference INR 3-5, no bleeding: • Hold warfarin • Resume at lower dose when INR is therapeutic INR 5-9, no bleeding: • Hold 1-2 doses of warfarin • Vitamin K 1-2.5 mg PO/IV if risk for bleeding • Resume at lower dose when INR is therapeutic INR >9, no bleeding: • Hold 1-2 doses of warfarin • Vitamin K 2.5-5 mg PO/IV • Repeat Vitamin K in 24h if INR remains eleva

nodes.title: Supratherapeutic DOAC
nodes.body: Hold dose(s) — drug elimination is usually sufficient. ⚠️ Beware: DOAC + new renal failure • Dabigatran (Pradaxa): 80% renally cleared → accumulates quickly in AKI • Can be severely supratherapeutic without obviously abnormal labs (unlike warfarin with INR of 9) • Rivaroxaban (Xarelto): 70% renal. Edoxaban (Savaysa): 50% renal. Apixaban (Eliquis): 25% renal. Crude screening (limited sensitivity):

nodes.title: Pre-Procedure Coagulation Management
nodes.summary: CVC/thoracentesis/paracentesis = low risk — technique matters more than INR; FFP cannot push INR below 1.7
nodes.body: Common pitfalls (IBCC): #1 We overestimate bleeding risk. Most bedside ICU procedures are LOW risk — SIR 2019 lists CVC, thoracentesis, and paracentesis all as "low risk." [9] #2 We fail to consider the big picture — all meds + all coagulopathies together. #3 We put excess faith in the INR. INR 2.5 in cirrhosis = rebalanced hemostasis. INR 2.5 on apixaban = high bleeding risk. Context matters. #4

nodes.title: Post-Reversal Monitoring
nodes.summary: Agent-specific monitoring intervals — watch for rebound (PCC wears off 6-8h, idarucizumab >12h adipose redistribution)
nodes.body: Warfarin (Coumadin): INR at 30 min post-PCC, then 6h and 24h. Watch for INR rebound when PCC wears off (6-8h). Vitamin K prevents this. Dabigatran (Pradaxa): PTT (or TT) at baseline, 2-4h post-idarucizumab (Praxbind), q12h. Watch for drug rebound >12h (adipose redistribution). [3] Xa inhibitors (Eliquis/Xarelto/Savaysa): INR after PCC (Kcentra), then q6h. Anti-Xa level if available. Rebounding INR

nodes.title: Resuming Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Most patients need anticoagulation restarted — the original indication still applies; failure to restart carries mortality risk
nodes.body: Most patients will need anticoagulation restarted — the original indication hasn't gone away. • Timing depends on: indication, bleeding site, severity, patient factors • ICH: Consider restarting in 4-8 weeks for high-risk indications (e.g., mechanical valve, recurrent DVT/PE) • GI bleed: May restart earlier (1-2 weeks) once hemostasis is secure • Mechanical valve: Shortest possible interruption —

nodes.title: Common Pitfalls
nodes.body: Mistakes to avoid: • PCC or FFP alone for warfarin → INR rebounds when they wear off (6-8h). Always give Vitamin K simultaneously. [2,16] • Vitamin K subcutaneously → erratic absorption. IM → hematoma risk. Always IV for emergent reversal. [16] • FFP to push INR below 1.7 → impossible (FFP contains factors at normal plasma concentration, not concentrated). Futile and dangerous (volume overload, TR

nodes.title: Aortic Emergency - Presentation
nodes.summary: Time-critical: ruptured AAA >80% mortality, untreated Type A dissection 1-2%/hour — misdiagnosis rate up to 30%
nodes.body: Aortic Emergencies Steps Summary Aortic emergencies are time-critical and often fatal. Ruptured AAA mortality: >80% overall, 41-50% even with surgical repair. Untreated Type A dissection mortality: 1-2% per hour, 50% at 48 hours. [1][2] Key principle: These conditions share overlapping presentations but require DIFFERENT management strategies. Misdiagnosis rate: up to 30% for both AAA and dissecti

nodes.title: Aortic Dissection - Initial Evaluation
nodes.summary: Type A (ascending) = surgical emergency; Type B (descending) = usually medical; pulse deficit/BP differential LR 5.7
nodes.body: Aortic dissection = intimal tear with blood tracking into the media, creating a false lumen. Stanford Classification: [1][2] - Type A: Involves ascending aorta (proximal to left subclavian). Surgical emergency. Mortality 1-2%/hour untreated. - Type B: Descending aorta only (distal to left subclavian). Usually medical management unless complicated. Acute Aortic Syndromes (all evaluated similarly):

nodes.title: ADD-RS Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: ADD-RS ≥2 = immediate CTA; ADD-RS 0-1 + D-dimer <500 = 99% sensitivity rule-out, can avoid ~50% of CTAs
nodes.body: Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) - use to guide diagnostic approach. [7][8] Score 1 point for EACH category present: High-risk conditions: - Marfan syndrome or other connective tissue disease - Family history of aortic disease - Known aortic valve disease - Known thoracic aortic aneurysm - Prior aortic manipulation/surgery High-risk pain features: - Chest, back, or abdominal pain wi

nodes.title: D-Dimer in Aortic Syndromes
nodes.summary: D-dimer to RULE OUT not diagnose — may be falsely negative in thrombosed/chronic dissections; do NOT delay CTA for high-risk
nodes.body: D-dimer cutoff: 500 ng/mL [7][8] Pooled performance (ADvISED study, n=1850): [8] - D-dimer sensitivity: 96.7% - ADD-RS = 0 + D-dimer negative: failure rate 0.3% (1 AAS in 294 patients) - ADD-RS <= 1 + D-dimer negative: failure rate 0.3% (3 AAS in 924 patients) Use D-dimer to RULE OUT, not to diagnose. An elevated D-dimer is nonspecific and requires imaging. Cautions: [7] - May be falsely negative

nodes.title: Imaging Strategy
nodes.summary: CTA is gold standard (~100% sensitivity); POCUS SPEED protocol for unstable patients (92% sens); type and cross 6-10 units
nodes.body: CT Angiography (CTA) is the diagnostic test of choice. [1][5] CTA protocol: - ECG-gated if available (reduces motion artifact at aortic root) - Arterial phase, thin-slice acquisition - From thoracic inlet to femoral arteries (full aorta) - Noncontrast series first (to distinguish IMH from other wall thickening) - Sensitivity/specificity: approaching 100% Alternative modalities: - TEE: 98% sensitiv

nodes.title: Classification of Aortic Pathology
nodes.summary: Classify CTA findings: dissection (intimal flap), IMH (crescent wall thickening >5mm), PAU (ulceration into media), or ruptured AAA
nodes.body: Based on CTA findings, classify the pathology: [1][2][5] Aortic Dissection: - Intimal flap with true and false lumen - Stanford A: ascending aorta involvement - Stanford B: descending aorta only Intramural Hematoma (IMH): - Crescent-shaped aortic wall thickening >5 mm - No intimal tear or false lumen visible - Type A IMH: surgical mortality similar to dissection - Type B IMH: medical management, ~

nodes.title: Acute Aortic Syndrome Ruled Out
nodes.body: ADD-RS 0-1 with negative D-dimer reliably excludes AAS. [7][8] Sensitivity of this combination: 98.9-99.9% Consider alternative diagnoses: - Acute coronary syndrome - Pulmonary embolism - Pericarditis - Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave) - Musculoskeletal pain - Biliary/GI pathology Disposition: - If another diagnosis identified, treat appropriately - If pain resolved and workup negative, may disc
nodes.recommendation: AAS ruled out with ADD-RS 0-1 + negative D-dimer. Pursue alternative diagnoses.

nodes.title: Anti-Impulse Therapy - Dissection
nodes.summary: Beta-blocker FIRST (HR 60-70, SBP 100-120) — esmolol preferred for unstable; vasodilators alone cause reflex tachycardia
nodes.body: Goal: Reduce aortic wall stress to prevent propagation and rupture. [1][9] Hemodynamic Targets: - SBP: 100-120 mmHg (measure in arm with highest pressure) - Heart rate: 60-70 bpm (higher acceptable with severe aortic regurgitation) - Adequate end-organ perfusion: intact mentation, adequate urine output - Pain control: persistent pain suggests ongoing dissection KEY: Beta-blocker FIRST before vasod

nodes.title: Vasodilator Therapy
nodes.summary: Add vasodilator AFTER beta-blocker if SBP>120 — nicardipine first choice, clevidipine if available (1-2min half-life)
nodes.body: Add vasodilator AFTER beta-blocker if SBP remains >120 mmHg. [1][9] Vasodilator options: Nicardipine - Excellent first choice - Start 5 mg/hr, titrate by 2.5 mg/hr q5-15 min - Max 15 mg/hr - No reflex tachycardia when beta-blocked Clevidipine - Preferred if available - Ultra-short half-life (1-2 min) - Start 1-2 mg/hr, titrate by doubling q90 sec - Max 32 mg/hr Sodium Nitroprusside - Historical ag

nodes.title: Hypotensive Dissection Management
nodes.summary: Check BP in all extremities; pseudohypotension from limb occlusion; tamponade = small-volume pericardiocentesis only as temporizing
nodes.body: Hypotension occurs in up to 25% of Type A dissections, <5% of Type B. [1] Causes of hypotension in dissection: - Severe aortic regurgitation - Hemopericardium with tamponade - Occluding MI (RCA or left main involvement) - Aortic rupture/hemorrhage - Pseudohypotension (limb artery occlusion) - Mesenteric ischemia Management: - Check BP in BOTH arms and legs - use highest pressure for management - I

nodes.title: Type A Dissection - Surgical Emergency
nodes.summary: ALL Type A = immediate surgery; mortality without surgery 50% at 48h, 1-2%/hour; CT surgery STAT consult
nodes.body: Type A dissection = IMMEDIATE SURGICAL INDICATION. [1][2][10] Mortality without surgery: 50% at 48 hours, 1-2% per hour. Mortality with surgery: 20% at 14 days (much improved from historical rates) Indications for emergent repair: - All Type A dissections (regardless of symptoms) - Tamponade, severe aortic regurgitation - Malperfusion syndromes (coronary, cerebral, visceral, limb) - Rupture or imp

nodes.title: Type B Dissection - Classify Complexity
nodes.summary: Uncomplicated Type B = medical management (<10% mortality); complicated = TEVAR (~30% mortality) — malperfusion defines complicated
nodes.body: Type B dissection is managed MEDICALLY unless complicated. [1][2][11] Uncomplicated Type B: 14-day mortality <10% Complicated Type B: 14-day mortality ~30% Definition of COMPLICATED Type B: [11] - Aortic rupture or hemothorax - Threatened rupture (rapid aortic expansion) - Major artery occlusion with malperfusion: - Mesenteric ischemia (elevated lactate, abdominal pain) - Limb ischemia (pulseless,

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Type B - Medical Management
nodes.summary: ICU for continuous BP monitoring, serial imaging at 24-48h; 5-year survival 60-80%; ~24% need late intervention
nodes.body: Uncomplicated Type B dissection responds well to aggressive medical therapy. [1][11] Anti-impulse therapy: - Target HR 60-70 bpm - Target SBP 100-120 mmHg - Pain control (adequate analgesia reduces sympathetic drive) ICU admission for: - Continuous BP monitoring - Serial imaging at 24-48 hours to assess for progression - Detection of complications Transition to oral therapy (once stable): - Metopr

nodes.title: Complicated Type B - TEVAR
nodes.summary: TEVAR preferred for complicated Type B — stent-graft seals entry tear; may need permissive hypertension if malperfusion
nodes.body: Complicated Type B dissection requires TEVAR (Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair) or open surgery. [1][11] TEVAR is preferred for complicated Type B: - Places stent-graft to seal entry tear - Excludes false lumen - Promotes thrombosis and remodeling - Less invasive than open repair Indications for urgent intervention: - Rupture or impending rupture - Malperfusion syndrome not responding to medica

nodes.title: Penetrating Atherosclerotic Ulcer
nodes.summary: PAU = ulcer through intima to media, mostly descending thoracic; up to 40% rupture risk; TEVAR if intervention needed
nodes.body: PAU = atherosclerotic plaque ulcerates through intima into media. [5][12] Characteristics: - Most common in descending thoracic aorta (62%) - Typically older patients (70s-80s) with severe atherosclerosis - May coexist with intramural hematoma - Risk of rupture reported up to 40% Management is individualized: [5][12] Indications for intervention: - Persistent or recurrent symptoms despite medical

nodes.title: AAA Rupture - Initial Evaluation
nodes.summary: Classic triad (hypotension, pain, pulsatile mass) present <50%; bedside US 100% sensitive for AAA but CANNOT detect rupture
nodes.body: Ruptured AAA is a surgical emergency with mortality >80% without intervention. [3][13] AAA defined as infrarenal aortic diameter >3 cm. [3] Classic triad (present in <50%): - Hypotension - Abdominal or back pain - Pulsable abdominal mass Risk factors: Age >65, male, smoking history, HTN, family history, connective tissue disease. Physical exam sensitivity for AAA by size: [3] - 3.0-3.9 cm: 29% - 4

nodes.title: AAA - Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: Unstable = bedside US + straight to OR (no CT); stable = CTA for anatomy; call vascular surgery on suspicion
nodes.body: Imaging choice depends on hemodynamic stability. [3][13] Hemodynamically UNSTABLE: - Bedside US confirms AAA - NO CT scan - delays definitive care - Straight to OR for surgical/endovascular repair - Call vascular surgery IMMEDIATELY upon suspicion Hemodynamically STABLE: - CT angiography (noncontrast + arterial phase) - Delineates anatomy for surgical planning - Identifies contained vs free ruptur

nodes.title: Ruptured AAA - Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Permissive hypotension SBP 70-90 — maintain tamponade, minimize crystalloid, 1:1:1 MTP; avoid intubation if possible
nodes.body: Permissive hypotension is the cornerstone of resuscitation. [13][14] Target SBP 70-90 mmHg while maintaining consciousness. Rationale: [14] - Maintains tamponade effect of contained hematoma - Prevents clot disruption from hypertensive surges - Avoids dilutional/hypothermic coagulopathy from crystalloid - Preserves platelets and clotting factors Resuscitation principles: - Two large-bore IVs or ce

nodes.title: Ruptured AAA - Surgical Options
nodes.summary: EVAR preferred when anatomy allows (local anesthesia); OSR for unsuitable anatomy; 30-min 3D analysis determines approach
nodes.body: EVAR (endovascular) vs Open Surgical Repair (OSR) [13] EVAR preferred when anatomy allows: - Can be performed under local anesthesia - Less physiologic stress - Anatomic requirements: - Aortic bifurcation diameter >=17 mm - Aneurysmal neck >=15 mm diameter - Suitable femoral/iliac arteries (not excessively tortuous/calcified) OSR indicated when: - EVAR anatomy unsuitable - Rupture with free intrap

nodes.title: Symptomatic Unruptured Aneurysm
nodes.summary: Symptomatic = impending rupture — admit for urgent surgery; repair threshold: men ≥5.5cm, women ≥5.0cm, or growth >0.5cm/6mo
nodes.body: Symptomatic aneurysm = impending rupture until proven otherwise. [3][15] Symptoms suggesting instability: - New or worsening abdominal/back pain - Tenderness over known aneurysm - Rapid growth on surveillance imaging - Peripheral embolization (blue toe syndrome) Management: - Admit for urgent surgical evaluation - CT angiography to assess for contained leak - Type and crossmatch - NPO for possible

nodes.title: Incidental Aortic Aneurysm
nodes.body: Asymptomatic aneurysm discovered on imaging performed for other reasons. AAA surveillance thresholds (ESVS 2024): [15] - <4.0 cm: Repeat US in 2 years - 4.0-4.9 cm: Repeat US annually - >=5.0 cm: Refer to vascular surgery Elective repair thresholds: [15] - Men: >=5.5 cm - Women: >=5.0 cm (lower threshold due to higher rupture risk) - OR growth rate >0.5 cm in 6 months Thoracic aortic aneurysm: - R
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with vascular surgery referral within 2-4 weeks for surveillance planning.

nodes.title: Disposition - Emergent Surgery
nodes.body: Patient requires emergent surgical intervention. [1][2][13] Before leaving ED: - Continuous hemodynamic monitoring - Two large-bore IVs or central access - Type and cross 6-10 units pRBCs - Coagulation labs, CBC, BMP, lactate - Foley catheter for UOP monitoring - NPO Ongoing ED management: - Anti-impulse therapy (dissection): HR 60-70, SBP 100-120 - Permissive hypotension (ruptured AAA): SBP 70-90
nodes.recommendation: Emergent surgical intervention. Maintain hemodynamic targets. Ensure adequate blood products available.

nodes.title: Disposition - ICU Admission
nodes.body: Patient requires ICU-level monitoring. [1][11] Indications: - Uncomplicated Type B dissection - Intramural hematoma - Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer - Post-operative monitoring ICU monitoring requirements: - Arterial line for continuous BP - Hourly neurologic checks (spinal cord ischemia) - Continuous cardiac monitoring - Urine output (renal perfusion) - Serial lactate (mesenteric ischemia) Med
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for continuous monitoring and IV anti-impulse therapy. Serial imaging and reassessment.

nodes.title: Disposition - Admit for Urgent Evaluation
nodes.body: Patient requires inpatient admission for urgent vascular surgery consultation. [3][15] Indications: - Symptomatic aneurysm (not actively ruptured) - Rapidly expanding aneurysm - Aneurysm at or above repair threshold - New peripheral embolization from aneurysm Admission orders: - Telemetry monitoring - NPO in case of emergent surgery - Type and screen - BP control (avoid hypertensive surges) - Pain
nodes.recommendation: Admit for urgent vascular surgery evaluation. NPO, telemetry, BP control.

nodes.title: Malperfusion Syndromes
nodes.summary: Branch vessel compromise: coronary (STEMI, not PCI), cerebral (stroke 5-10%), mesenteric (lactate, >50% mortality), spinal, renal, limb
nodes.body: Malperfusion = branch vessel compromise from dissection or thrombosis. [1][2] Coronary malperfusion: - RCA most commonly involved (right coronary ostium) - Presents as STEMI - check for dissection before cath lab - Treatment: emergent surgery, not PCI Cerebral malperfusion: - Carotid/vertebral involvement - Stroke in 5-10% of Type A dissections - Does NOT preclude surgery unless massive stroke Spi

nodes.title: Aortic Dissection Overview
nodes.summary: Intimal tear propagating into media — Stanford A (ascending, surgical) vs B (descending, medical), 1-2% mortality/hr untreated
nodes.body: Aortic dissection is a tear in the aortic intima with propagation of blood into the media. [1,2] Epidemiology: - Incidence: 2.6-3.5 per 100,000 person-years - Male predominance (65%) - Peak age: 60-70 years - Mortality: 1-2% per hour if untreated (Type A) Classifications: [1] Stanford (most commonly used): - Type A: Involves ascending aorta (regardless of origin) - Type B: Does NOT involve ascendi

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: HTN 75%, Marfan in young, bicuspid valve 5-10x risk, cocaine, pregnancy 3rd trimester, prior aortic surgery
nodes.body: High-risk conditions for aortic dissection: [1,2] Hypertension (most common - 75%): - Chronic shear stress on aortic wall - Often poorly controlled Connective tissue disorders: - Marfan syndrome (most important in young patients) - Ehlers-Danlos type IV - Loeys-Dietz syndrome - Turner syndrome Aortic pathology: - Bicuspid aortic valve (5-10x increased risk) - Prior aortic surgery or intervention -

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Sudden maximal-onset tearing chest/back pain, syncope 9-13%, pulse deficits 15-30%, BP differential >20mmHg
nodes.body: Classic presentation: sudden severe chest pain. [1,3] Pain characteristics (90% present with pain): - Sudden onset, maximal at onset (instantaneous) - Severe, "worst pain of life" - Tearing, ripping, or sharp quality (50%) - Anterior chest: Type A - Back/interscapular: Type B or extension - Migratory pain: suggests propagation Associated symptoms: - Syncope (9-13%) - poor prognostic sign - Dyspnea

nodes.title: Atypical Presentations
nodes.summary: Painless 6%, ACS mimic with coronary involvement — fatal to give thrombolytics, stroke, paraplegia, limb ischemia
nodes.body: Aortic dissection can mimic many conditions. [3,4] "Painless" dissection (6%): - More common in elderly, diabetics - May present with syncope, stroke, or heart failure only Stroke-like presentation: - Carotid artery involvement (Type A) - May delay diagnosis if only CT head obtained - Always consider dissection in young stroke Acute coronary syndrome mimic: - Coronary ostia involvement causes true

nodes.title: Clinical Assessment
nodes.summary: Route to risk stratification based on clinical suspicion level — high goes direct to imaging
nodes.body: What is the clinical scenario? [1]

nodes.title: ADD-RS Score
nodes.summary: ADD-RS 0-3 points across conditions/pain/exam — score 0 is 5% prevalence, score 2-3 is 30-50%
nodes.body: Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) stratifies pretest probability. [5,6] Category 1 - High-Risk Conditions (1 point): - Marfan syndrome (or other connective tissue disorder) - Family history of aortic disease - Known aortic valve disease - Known thoracic aortic aneurysm - Prior aortic manipulation (surgery, intervention) Category 2 - High-Risk Pain Features (1 point): - Chest, back, o

nodes.title: D-dimer in Aortic Dissection
nodes.summary: D-dimer <500 + ADD-RS 0-1 rules out with >99% NPV — NOT helpful if ADD-RS ≥2 or symptoms >24h
nodes.body: D-dimer can help rule OUT dissection in LOW-RISK patients. [5,6,7] Key evidence (ADvISED study 2018): [6] - D-dimer <500 ng/mL + ADD-RS 0-1 = very low miss rate - Sensitivity of D-dimer alone: ~97% - Negative predictive value in low-risk: >99% When D-dimer is helpful: - ADD-RS 0: D-dimer <500 essentially rules out - ADD-RS 1: D-dimer <500 may avoid CTA in appropriate patients When D-dimer is NOT h

nodes.title: Diagnostic Pathway
nodes.summary: Branch by ADD-RS score and D-dimer — determines imaging need vs rule-out vs immediate CTA
nodes.body: Based on ADD-RS score and clinical assessment: [5,6]

nodes.title: Dissection Ruled Out
nodes.body: Low-risk patient with negative D-dimer: [6] ADD-RS 0 + D-dimer <500 ng/mL: - False negative rate <1% - Consider alternative diagnoses for chest pain - Standard chest pain workup as indicated Alternative diagnoses to consider: - Acute coronary syndrome - Pulmonary embolism - Musculoskeletal pain - Pericarditis - Esophageal pathology - Pneumothorax Disposition: - If all other serious causes excluded
nodes.recommendation: Aortic dissection effectively ruled out with ADD-RS 0 and D-dimer <500. Evaluate for alternative diagnoses.

nodes.title: Imaging Modalities
nodes.summary: CTA first-line (95-100% sensitivity), TEE for unstable bedside, TTE does NOT rule out dissection
nodes.body: CTA is the first-line imaging test for aortic dissection. [1,8] CT Angiography (CTA): - Sensitivity: 95-100% - Specificity: 98-100% - Fast, widely available - Shows extent, branch involvement, complications - First choice in ED TEE (Transesophageal Echo): - Sensitivity: 98% - Specificity: 95% - Good for unstable patients (bedside) - Excellent for Type A, proximal extent - Limited view of distal as

nodes.title: CTA Findings
nodes.summary: Intimal flap, true vs false lumen, branch vessel involvement, IMH variant (no flap, >5mm wall thickening)
nodes.body: What to look for on CTA: [1,8] Primary findings: - Intimal flap separating true and false lumen - True lumen: often smaller, compressed - False lumen: often larger, may have slower flow - Entry tear location - Extent of dissection Branch vessel involvement: - Coronary arteries (Type A) - Brachiocephalic/carotid/subclavian - Celiac, SMA, renal arteries - Iliac arteries Complications to identify: -

nodes.title: Immediate Workup
nodes.summary: Crossmatch 6 units, troponin for coronary involvement, normal CXR does NOT rule out, bedside echo for tamponade
nodes.body: For high-suspicion patients, initiate workup and treatment simultaneously. [1] Do NOT delay imaging for labs. Labs to send: - Type and screen (crossmatch 6 units PRBCs) - CBC, BMP, coagulation studies - Troponin (coronary involvement vs MI) - Lactate (malperfusion) - BNP (heart failure, AR) ECG: - Often non-specific - May show LVH (chronic hypertension) - May show ischemia/STEMI (coronary involvem

nodes.title: Immediate Management Goals
nodes.summary: Anti-impulse therapy: HR <60 first (beta-blocker), then SBP 100-120 — beta-blocker BEFORE vasodilator
nodes.body: Goals of initial management: [1,9] 1. Pain control: - Reduces sympathetic drive - Reduces BP and heart rate - IV opioids (morphine, fentanyl) 2. Heart rate control (first priority): - Target HR <60 bpm - Reduces dP/dt (force of aortic wall stress) - Beta-blockers are first-line 3. Blood pressure control: - Target SBP 100-120 mmHg - AFTER heart rate controlled - Avoid reflex tachycardia from vasodi

nodes.title: Beta-Blocker Therapy
nodes.summary: Esmolol preferred (ultra-short, titratable), labetalol alternative — target HR <60 before adding vasodilator
nodes.body: Beta-blockers are the cornerstone of anti-impulse therapy. [1,9] Esmolol (preferred for titration): - Bolus: 500 mcg/kg IV over 1 minute - Infusion: 50-200 mcg/kg/min - Ultra-short acting (t½ 9 minutes) - Easy to titrate up/down - Stop if proceeding to OR Labetalol (alternative): - 20mg IV, then 20-80mg q10min - Max 300mg - Combined alpha/beta blockade - Longer duration (good for stable patients)

nodes.title: Vasodilator Therapy
nodes.summary: Vasodilator AFTER beta-blockade to prevent reflex tachycardia — nicardipine 5-15 mg/hr preferred
nodes.body: Add vasodilator AFTER beta-blockade to reach BP goal. [1,9] Why beta-blocker first: - Vasodilators cause reflex tachycardia - Tachycardia increases dP/dt and wall stress - Can worsen dissection propagation Nicardipine (preferred): - Start: 5 mg/hr IV - Titrate: 2.5 mg/hr every 5-15 min - Max: 15 mg/hr - Smooth, predictable control Nitroprusside (alternative): - Start: 0.3-0.5 mcg/kg/min - Titrate:

nodes.title: Hypotensive Dissection
nodes.summary: Hypotension = rupture/tamponade/severe AR — pericardiocentesis may precipitate complete rupture, do NOT delay OR
nodes.body: Hypotension in aortic dissection is a grave sign. [1,10] Causes of hypotension: - Aortic rupture (hemothorax, retroperitoneal) - Cardiac tamponade - Acute severe aortic regurgitation - Malperfusion (cardiogenic shock from coronary involvement) Management: - Fluid resuscitation (cautious) - Blood product transfusion if hemorrhage - Pericardiocentesis ONLY if tamponade and imminent arrest - Prefer s

nodes.title: Dissection Type
nodes.summary: Classify Type A (ascending, surgical emergency) vs Type B uncomplicated vs complicated based on imaging
nodes.body: Based on imaging, what type of aortic dissection is present? [1]

nodes.title: Type A Dissection
nodes.summary: Type A: 50% mortality at 1 week without surgery — emergent CT surgery, stroke is NOT a contraindication
nodes.body: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency. [1,10] Mortality without surgery: - 1-2% per hour in first 48 hours - 50% at 1 week - 90% at 1 year Mortality with surgery: - 15-25% overall - Higher if complicated (tamponade, malperfusion, shock) Immediate actions: - Emergent CT surgery consultation - Continue anti-impulse therapy - NPO - Blood products available (type and crossmatch) - Central line, ar

nodes.title: Type A Disposition
nodes.body: All Type A dissections require emergent surgical intervention. [1] ED management while awaiting OR: - ICU-level care in ED - Continuous arterial BP monitoring - Maintain HR <60, SBP 100-120 mmHg - Serial neuro exams - Serial lactate if concern for malperfusion - Blood products immediately available Transfer considerations: - If no CT surgery available, transfer emergently - Call accepting facility
nodes.recommendation: Emergent CT surgery consultation. Continue anti-impulse therapy. Prepare for OR or emergent transfer.

nodes.title: Type B Uncomplicated
nodes.summary: Uncomplicated Type B: medical management with IV anti-impulse therapy, ICU, serial imaging, lifelong beta-blocker
nodes.body: Uncomplicated Type B dissection is managed medically. [1,11] Definition of uncomplicated: - No malperfusion (visceral, renal, limb) - No rupture or impending rupture - No refractory pain despite medical therapy - No refractory hypertension - No rapid aortic expansion Medical management: - IV anti-impulse therapy (beta-blocker + vasodilator) - Admit to ICU - Serial imaging (CT or MRI) to monitor -

nodes.title: Type B Uncomplicated Disposition
nodes.body: Admit to ICU for medical management. [1,11] Initial ICU care: - Arterial line for continuous BP monitoring - IV beta-blocker (esmolol) + vasodilator (nicardipine) - Pain control - Serial abdominal exams (mesenteric ischemia) - Monitor urine output, lactate, lower extremity pulses Transition to oral therapy: - Once stable on IV meds x 24-48 hours - Metoprolol, atenolol, or labetalol - Add ACE inhib
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU for medical anti-impulse therapy. Vascular surgery consultation. Transition to oral agents, discharge with surveillance plan.

nodes.title: Type B Complicated
nodes.summary: Complicated Type B: malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/HTN — TEVAR first-line, open surgery 30-40% mortality
nodes.body: Complicated Type B requires intervention. [1,11] Features of complicated Type B: - Malperfusion syndromes: - Mesenteric ischemia (abdominal pain, bloody stool, lactate elevation) - Renal ischemia (oliguria, rising creatinine, hypertension) - Limb ischemia (pulseless, cool extremity) - Spinal cord ischemia (paraplegia) - Rupture (hemothorax, hemodynamic instability) - Rapid aortic expansion (>1 cm

nodes.title: Malperfusion Management
nodes.summary: Mesenteric ischemia is most lethal — emergent intervention; spinal cord: maintain MAP >80-90, CSF drain
nodes.body: Malperfusion is the major driver of mortality in Type B dissection. [10,11] Mechanism: - True lumen compression by false lumen - Branch vessel involvement (static or dynamic) - Static: dissection extends into branch - Dynamic: flap occludes branch ostium Management by territory: Mesenteric ischemia: - Most lethal malperfusion syndrome - Emergent intervention (TEVAR, fenestration, or surgery) - Mon

nodes.title: Complicated Type B Disposition
nodes.body: Complicated Type B requires urgent intervention. [1,11] Immediate actions: - Emergent vascular surgery consultation - Continue anti-impulse therapy - ICU admission - Prepare for TEVAR or surgery Pre-intervention management: - Arterial line, central line - Blood products available - For spinal cord protection: maintain MAP >80-90 - For mesenteric ischemia: antibiotics, NG decompression Post-interve
nodes.recommendation: Emergent vascular surgery consultation for TEVAR or operative intervention. ICU admission with aggressive medical management.

nodes.title: Approach to Arthritis
nodes.body: Arthritis = joint inflammation. The ED approach hinges on two critical questions: [1,2] 1. Is this septic arthritis? (orthopedic emergency) 2. What is the pattern? (guides differential) Joint count classification: - Monoarticular: 1 joint - Oligoarticular: 2-4 joints - Polyarticular: 5+ joints Acute vs chronic: - Acute: <6 weeks duration - Chronic: >6 weeks duration Key principle: Acute monoarticu

nodes.title: Joint Distribution Pattern
nodes.body: Count involved joints and characterize the pattern: [1,2] Monoarticular (1 joint): - Septic arthritis (most concerning) - Crystal arthropathy (gout, pseudogout) - Trauma/hemarthrosis - Early RA, reactive arthritis Oligoarticular (2-4 joints): - Reactive arthritis - Psoriatic arthritis - Gonococcal arthritis - Spondyloarthropathies Polyarticular (5+ joints): - Rheumatoid arthritis - SLE - Viral art

nodes.body: Oligoarticular (2-4 joints) differential: [1,2] Spondyloarthropathies: - Reactive arthritis (post-infectious: GI, GU) - Psoriatic arthritis - Ankylosing spondylitis with peripheral involvement - IBD-associated arthritis Infectious: - Gonococcal (migratory, then settles) - Lyme arthritis - Viral arthritis (early) - Endocarditis (rare) Crystal: - Polyarticular gout flare - CPPD (can be polyarticular

nodes.title: Polyarticular Arthritis
nodes.body: Polyarticular (5+ joints) differential: [1,2] Inflammatory (symmetric small joints): - Rheumatoid arthritis - SLE - Viral arthritis (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C, HIV) Inflammatory (asymmetric): - Psoriatic arthritis - Reactive arthritis - Polyarticular gout (chronic tophaceous) Crystalline: - Chronic tophaceous gout - CPPD/chondrocalcinosis Other: - Serum sickness - Drug reaction - Sarcoidosis -

nodes.title: Inflammatory vs Mechanical
nodes.body: Distinguishing inflammatory from mechanical arthritis is fundamental: [1,2] | Feature | Inflammatory | Mechanical | |---------|-------------|------------| | Morning stiffness | >60 min | <30 min | | Activity effect | Improves | Worsens | | Rest effect | Stiffens | Relieves | | Swelling | Soft tissue, effusion | Bony enlargement | | Warmth/erythema | Common | Rare | | Systemic symptoms | Common | A

nodes.title: Historical Clues
nodes.body: History guides the differential: [1,2,5] Timing: - Sudden onset (hours): crystal, septic, trauma - Gradual onset (days-weeks): inflammatory arthritis, infectious - Insidious (months): OA, chronic inflammatory Associated symptoms: - Skin: psoriasis (PsA), rash (SLE, gonococcal, Lyme) - Eyes: uveitis (spondyloarthropathy), conjunctivitis (reactive) - GI: diarrhea preceding (reactive), IBD - GU: uret

nodes.title: Physical Examination
nodes.body: Joint examination fundamentals: [1,6] Inspection: - Swelling (soft tissue vs bony) - Erythema (suggests crystal or septic) - Deformity (chronic disease) - Skin changes (psoriasis, tophi, nodules) Palpation: - Warmth (compare to contralateral) - Effusion (ballottement, bulge sign for knee) - Tenderness (joint line vs periarticular) - Crepitus (OA) Range of motion: - Active AND passive ROM - Painful

nodes.title: Initial Laboratory Workup
nodes.body: ED laboratory evaluation: [1,6,7] Basic labs (all acute arthritis): - CBC with differential - BMP - ESR, CRP - Uric acid (if gout suspected) Directed labs: - Blood cultures - if septic suspected (positive in up to 66%) - RF, anti-CCP - if RA suspected (not emergent) - ANA - if SLE suspected (not emergent) - HLA-B27 - spondyloarthropathy (not emergent) - Lyme serology - endemic areas - GC/Chlamydia

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis Suspicion
nodes.body: Red flags for septic arthritis: [3,8] High-risk features: - Fever >38.5C (>101.3F) - Joint erythema with warmth - Inability to bear weight or move joint - Rapidly progressive symptoms (hours) - Recent joint surgery or injection - Prosthetic joint - Immunocompromise (DM, RA, HIV, transplant) - IVDU - Overlying skin infection Critical point: Septic arthritis is an orthopedic EMERGENCY. nodes.body: Arthrocentesis is the gold standard for diagnosis. [3,8] Indications: - Any acute monoarthritis with uncertain etiology - Suspicion for septic arthritis - Therapeutic drainage - Prior to steroid injection (rule out infection) Contraindications (relative): - Overlying cellulitis (approach from uninvolved skin) - Coagulopathy (INR >1.5 or therapeutic anticoagulation - relative) - Prosthetic joint (d

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis: Empiric Treatment
nodes.body: If septic arthritis suspected, do not delay antibiotics. [3,8] Empiric regimen (non-gonococcal): - Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h - Covers MRSA (prevalence up to 50% regionally) Add gram-negative coverage if: [3] - IVDU (Pseudomonas risk) - Immunocompromised - Elderly - GNR on Gram stain - Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h OR - Cefepime 2g IV q8h (if Pseudomonas concern) Gonococcal suspected: - Ceftriaxone

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis: Drainage
nodes.body: Source control is essential - antibiotics alone are insufficient. [3,10] Drainage options: 1. Serial arthrocentesis: - Daily aspiration until effusion resolves - Effective for accessible joints (knee, ankle, elbow, wrist) - May be sufficient for gonococcal and some streptococcal infections 2. Arthroscopic I&D: - Breaks down loculations - Better visualization and debridement - 91% cure rate with sy

nodes.title: Prosthetic Joint Infection
nodes.body: PJI has different diagnostic thresholds and management. [11] Lower WBC threshold: Synovial WBC >3,000/uL (vs >50,000 for native) MSIS 2018 Criteria: [11] Major criteria (definitive): - Two positive cultures same organism, OR - Sinus tract communicating with joint Minor criteria (point-based): - Serum CRP >1 mg/dL (2 pts) - D-dimer >860 ng/mL (2 pts) - Synovial WBC >3,000/uL (3 pts) - Synovial PMN

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis: Disposition
nodes.body: All patients with suspected or confirmed septic arthritis require admission. [3] Admission orders: - Orthopedic surgery consult (all cases) - Infectious disease consult (recommended) - IV antibiotics per empiric regimen - Daily joint examination - Serial CRP (best trend marker) ICU admission criteria: - Sepsis/septic shock - Polyarticular with bacteremia - Suspected endocarditis (S. aureus bactere
nodes.recommendation: Admit all patients with suspected septic arthritis for IV antibiotics and surgical consultation. Consider ICU if septic.

nodes.title: Crystal Arthropathies
nodes.body: Crystal arthritis includes gout (MSU) and pseudogout (CPPD). [12,13] Gout: - Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals - Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent - Classic: 1st MTP (podagra), midfoot, ankle, knee - Risk factors: hyperuricemia, diuretics, alcohol, renal disease, metabolic syndrome Pseudogout (CPPD): - Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals - Rhomboid-shaped, positively (or weakly negative) b

nodes.title: Gout: Clinical Features
nodes.body: Classic gout presentation: [12] Acute gouty arthritis: - Rapid onset (peaks 12-24 hours) - Exquisitely tender joint - Erythema extending beyond joint (can mimic cellulitis) - May have low-grade fever - Self-limited (resolves 7-14 days untreated) Podagra: 1st MTP involvement (50% of first attacks, 90% lifetime) Triggers: - Dietary: alcohol (especially beer), red meat, shellfish, fructose - Medicati

nodes.title: Gout: Treatment
nodes.body: Acute gout treatment options: [12,14] First-line (choose based on patient factors): NSAIDs: - Indomethacin 50mg TID x 5-7 days, OR - Naproxen 500mg BID x 5-7 days - Avoid if: CKD, GI bleed risk, heart failure, anticoagulation Colchicine: - Colchicine 1.2mg then 0.6mg 1 hour later (day 1), then 0.6mg daily-BID - Most effective if started <36 hours - Avoid if: severe CKD (GFR <30), liver disease, dr

nodes.title: Pseudogout (CPPD)
nodes.body: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD): [13] Clinical presentations: - Acute CPP crystal arthritis ("pseudogout"): acute monoarthritis mimicking gout or septic - Chronic CPP arthropathy: OA-like, often wrists, MCPs, knees - Pseudo-RA: symmetric polyarthritis with morning stiffness Classic features: - Knee most common (50%), wrist, shoulder - Elderly patients (rare <50 years) - Chondrocalc

nodes.title: CPPD: Treatment
nodes.body: CPPD treatment parallels gout but with some differences: [13] Acute CPPD arthritis: - NSAIDs: Indomethacin 50mg TID or Naproxen 500mg BID x 7-10 days - Colchicine: 0.6mg BID (less effective than for gout, but can use) - Corticosteroids: Prednisone 30-40mg x 5-7 days OR intra-articular injection - Joint aspiration: therapeutic drainage can provide rapid relief Key differences from gout: - No urate-

nodes.title: Systemic Rheumatic Disease Features
nodes.body: Evaluate for systemic rheumatic disease if: [1,2] - Polyarticular involvement - Symmetric joint pattern - Morning stiffness >60 minutes - Extra-articular features present - Inflammatory markers elevated without infection Systemic features to assess: - Skin: rash, nodules, psoriasis - Eyes: dry eyes, uveitis, scleritis - Oral: ulcers, dry mouth - Pulmonary: dyspnea, pleuritis - Cardiac: pericarditi

nodes.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
nodes.body: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis. [15] Classic features: - Symmetric involvement of MCPs, PIPs, wrists - DIP-sparing (unlike OA and psoriatic) - Morning stiffness >1 hour (improves with activity) - Synovial thickening (boggy swelling) Extra-articular manifestations: - Rheumatoid nodules (20-30%) - Interstitial lung disease - Pericarditis, vasculitis - Fel

nodes.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
nodes.body: SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease affecting multiple organs. [16] Articular involvement: - 90% of SLE patients have arthralgia/arthritis - Symmetric polyarthritis (RA-like pattern) - Non-erosive (unlike RA) - Jaccoud arthropathy (reducible deformities) Key extra-articular features: - Skin: malar (butterfly) rash, discoid lesions, photosensitivity - Renal: nephritis (proteinuria, hematuria, c

nodes.title: SLE: ED Management
nodes.body: SLE flare management in the ED: [16] Mild flare (arthritis, rash, fatigue): - NSAIDs for arthritis/serositis - Topical steroids for rash - Continue hydroxychloroquine - Outpatient rheumatology follow-up Moderate flare: - Prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day - Close rheumatology follow-up Severe flare (nephritis, CNS, severe cytopenias): - Methylprednisolone 1g IV daily x 3 days (pulse steroids) - Admit for

nodes.title: Psoriatic Arthritis
nodes.body: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. [17] Clinical patterns (can overlap): 1. Asymmetric oligoarthritis: most common (70%) 2. Symmetric polyarthritis: RA-like 3. DIP predominant: classic, involves DIPs 4. Spondylitis: axial involvement 5. Arthritis mutilans: severe, destructive (rare) Key features: - Dactylitis: "sausage digits" (entire digit swollen) -

nodes.title: Reactive Arthritis
nodes.body: Reactive arthritis is sterile joint inflammation triggered by infection elsewhere. [18] Classic triad (complete in only 1/3): - Arthritis - Urethritis/cervicitis - Conjunctivitis "Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree" Triggering infections: - GI: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile - GU: Chlamydia trachomatis (most common), less often Ureaplasma - Onset: 1-4 weeks after

nodes.title: Other Infectious Arthritis
nodes.body: Non-septic infectious arthritis patterns: [19,20] Gonococcal Arthritis (DGI): [19] - Young, sexually active patients - Migratory polyarthralgia then localizes - Tenosynovitis (wrists, fingers, ankles) - Dermatitis (pustular/vesicular lesions) - Treatment: Ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM + Doxycycline for Chlamydia Lyme Arthritis: [20] - Endemic areas (Northeast, Upper Midwest US) - Large joint monoarthritis

nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on diagnosis and clinical status: [1] Admission criteria: - Septic arthritis (all cases) - Severe flare requiring IV therapy - Systemic disease with organ threat (lupus nephritis, vasculitis) - Cannot ambulate/function independently - Unreliable follow-up for high-risk condition Discharge criteria: - Crystal arthropathy with adequate pain control - Inflammat

nodes.title: Discharge: Rheumatology Referral
nodes.body: Discharge with urgent rheumatology referral when: [1,15] Indications: - New suspected inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, spondyloarthropathy) - SLE without acute organ threat - Reactive arthritis - Chronic crystal arthropathy needing disease management Discharge instructions: - Symptom management (NSAIDs, short steroid course if indicated) - Activity modification - Return precautions (fever, severe
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with rheumatology referral within 1-2 weeks. Provide symptom management and clear return precautions.

nodes.title: Discharge: PCP Follow-Up
nodes.body: Discharge with PCP follow-up for: [12,13] Indications: - Acute gout flare with good response to treatment - Acute CPPD with good response to treatment - OA flare - Resolved mechanical/traumatic arthritis Gout follow-up plan: - Complete treatment course (5-7 days) - Discuss dietary modifications - PCP to consider urate-lowering therapy if: - >2 flares/year - Tophaceous gout - CKD or uric acid nephr
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with PCP follow-up in 1-2 weeks. Complete treatment course. Educate on dietary modifications and return precautions.

nodes.title: Admission Required
nodes.body: Admission criteria for acute arthritis: [1,3] Definite admission: - Septic arthritis (confirmed or high suspicion) - Prosthetic joint infection - Severe inflammatory flare requiring IV steroids - Lupus with organ involvement (nephritis, CNS) - Vasculitis - Cannot ambulate or care for self Consider admission: - Polyarticular septic arthritis - Uncertain diagnosis requiring serial exams - Social fac
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics and/or IV steroids with appropriate specialty consultation.

nodes.title: Asthma Exacerbation
nodes.summary: Maximize medical therapy before intubation — most patients can avoid the tube with proper management
nodes.body: Asthma exacerbation = acute worsening of symptoms requiring escalation of therapy. [1][2] Key Principle: Maximize medical therapy aggressively before considering intubation. Most patients can avoid intubation with proper management. This consult covers: • Severity classification • Maximizing bronchodilator therapy • BiPAP with appropriate sedation • Intubation approach (when unavoidable) • Ventila

nodes.title: Severity Classification
nodes.summary: Classify severity by speech, RR, HR, SpO2, PEF — silent chest is a DIRE sign of critically severe obstruction
nodes.body: Classify severity to guide therapy intensity: [1][2] MILD-MODERATE: • Can speak in phrases/sentences • Prefers sitting to lying • Not agitated • RR <30, HR <120 • SpO2 90-95% • PEF >50% predicted SEVERE: • Speaks only in words • Sits hunched forward • Agitated • RR ≥30, HR ≥120 • SpO2 <90% • PEF ≤50% predicted LIFE-THREATENING: • Silent chest (no wheezing = no air movement) • Drowsy, confused, or

nodes.title: Mild-Moderate Management
nodes.summary: SABA q20min x3, ipratropium first hour only, steroids early (reduce admissions), reassess at 60-90 min by PEF
nodes.body: Standard initial treatment: [1][2][4] Immediate Actions: 1. SABA: Albuterol 2.5-5mg nebulized q20min x 3 doses 2. Ipratropium: 0.5mg nebulized with first 3 albuterol doses 3. Steroids: Prednisone 40-60mg PO or methylpred 125mg IV 4. Supplemental O2: Target SpO2 93-95% Response Assessment at 60-90 min: • Good response (PEF >70%) → Discharge pathway • Incomplete response (PEF 50-70%) → Continue trea

nodes.title: Treatment Response

nodes.body: Reassess at 60-90 minutes: Check: • Symptom improvement • Respiratory rate • SpO2 on room air or minimal O2 • Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) PEF Calculator What is the PEF response?

nodes.title: Severe - Immediate Actions

Continuous nebs: Start immediately (not intermittent) 3. IV steroids: Methylprednisolone 125mg IV 4. IV access: Large bore, draw labs 5. nodes.body: 🚨 CRITICAL STATUS - IMPENDING RESPIRATORY FAILURE: [3][6] Immediate Actions: 1. Call for help - anesthesia, ICU, RT 2. Prepare airway equipment - but don't intubate yet if possible 3. Aggressive medical therapy while preparing 4. BiPAP with ketamine sedation if patient can tolerate Signs of Impending Arrest: • Silent chest • Altered mental status • Bradycardia • Hypotension • Cyanosis If Patient

nodes.body: Ketamine has bronchodilatory properties: [9] Mechanism: • Direct smooth muscle relaxation • Catecholamine release (endogenous epinephrine) • Inhibits vagal-mediated bronchoconstriction Dosing for Bronchospasm (sub-dissociative): • 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV bolus (10-20mg for typical adult) • Can repeat q10-15 min as needed • Or 0.5 mg/kg/hr IV infusion Benefits in Asthma: • Does NOT cause respiratory depre

nodes.title: BiPAP - Indications

nodes.body: BiPAP can prevent intubation in severe asthma: [12] Indications for BiPAP: • Severe asthma failing maximal medical therapy • Fatigue/respiratory distress despite treatment • Rising pCO2 on VBG • Patient still alert and cooperative Contraindications: • Altered mental status (unless from hypercapnia) • Inability to protect airway • Facial trauma/burns • Uncooperative patient (consider sedation first

nodes.title: BiPAP Settings

nodes.title: Sedation for BiPAP

nodes.title: BiPAP Success - Weaning

nodes.body: Signs BiPAP is Working: • Decreased respiratory rate • Improved patient comfort • Decreased accessory muscle use • Improving pCO2 on VBG • SpO2 improving or stable Weaning BiPAP: 1. Continue for 1-2 hours minimum after improvement 2. Decrease IPAP by 2 cm q30-60 min as tolerated 3. Trial off BiPAP when: - IPAP ≤10, EPAP ≤5 - Comfortable - RR <25 - SpO2 >92% on low FiO2 After BiPAP: • Continue cont

nodes.title: Intubation Decision
nodes.summary: Intubation is HIGH RISK — paralysis removes compensation, air trapping causes hypotension; exhaust all options first
nodes.body: Intubation in asthma is HIGH RISK - avoid if possible: [3][6] Absolute Indications: • Respiratory arrest • Cardiac arrest • Severe hypoxemia despite maximal therapy • Obtunded/cannot protect airway Relative Indications: • Fatigue despite maximal therapy + BiPAP • Rapidly rising pCO2 with acidosis • Unable to tolerate BiPAP Why Is Intubation Dangerous? • Paralysis removes compensatory mechanisms •

Ketamine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV - dissociate the patient 2. Apply BiPAP or NRB for 3-5 minutes 3. When SpO2 optimal (ideally >95%), give: - Ketamine 1

Intubate immediately - use ketamine 1.5-2 mg/kg if IV available 3. Skip paralytic if truly agonal/apneic 4. Largest ETT possible If Already Intubated and Arrests: 1. Disconnect ETT from ventilator 2. Manual chest compression for 30-60 seconds 3. This allows air trapp

nodes.title: Ventilator Settings
nodes.summary: LOW rate 8-12, I:E 1:4-1:5, PEEP 0-5 — if hypotensive post-intubation, disconnect ETT and compress chest

nodes.title: Permissive Hypercapnia
nodes.summary: Accept pCO2 60-80+, pH >7.15 — do NOT increase rate to fix pCO2; Tuxen series: 0% mortality with permissive hypercapnia
nodes.body: Permissive hypercapnia is REQUIRED in severe asthma: [14][15] Concept: • Accept elevated pCO2 to avoid dangerous ventilator settings • Priority: prevent air trapping, not normalize pCO2 • "Lungs are obstructed, not dead - CO2 will normalize later" Acceptable Targets: • pH >7.15-7.20 (tolerate lower if stable) • pCO2: 60-80 mmHg OK (even higher if needed) • SpO2 >88-90% What NOT to Do: • ❌ Don't in

nodes.title: Vent Troubleshooting
nodes.summary: Hypotension = disconnect ETT test; high plateau = lower rate; breath stacking = deep sedation ± paralysis
nodes.body: Common Problems and Solutions: [3][14] HYPOTENSION Post-Intubation: Most common cause = air trapping 1. Disconnect ETT from vent for 30-60 sec 2. Compress chest to expel trapped air 3. Reconnect with LOWER rate, LONGER expiratory time 4. If persists → pneumothorax? → needle decompression HIGH PLATEAU PRESSURES (>30): • Auto-PEEP from air trapping • Decrease rate further • Increase expiratory time

nodes.title: Ongoing Vent Management

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: PEF-guided disposition decision: discharge, observation, floor, or ICU based on response to treatment

nodes.title: Discharge Planning
nodes.body: Discharge Medications: [1][2] MUST PRESCRIBE: 1. Rescue inhaler: Albuterol MDI 2 puffs q4-6h PRN 2. Oral steroids: - Prednisone 40-60mg daily x 5-7 days, OR - Dexamethasone 16mg single dose (better compliance) 3. Controller medication: ICS or ICS-formoterol if not already on Prescription Tips: • Verify inhaler technique before discharge • Spacer improves MDI delivery significantly • ICS-formoterol
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with rescue inhaler, oral steroids (prednisone 5-7 days or dexamethasone single dose), and controller medication. Verify inhaler technique. PCP follow-up in 2-7 days.

nodes.title: Observation Unit
nodes.summary: PEF 50-69% observation candidates — reassess PEF q4h, discharge if >70%, admit if not improving
nodes.body: Observation unit for borderline cases: Ideal Candidates: • PEF 50-69% predicted • Improving but not quite ready for discharge • Need additional nebulizer treatments • Social factors requiring observation Observation Protocol: • Continue nebs q2-4h • Reassess PEF q4h • Monitor for deterioration • Clear discharge criteria Discharge from Observation if: • PEF improves to ≥70% • Symptom resolution • S

nodes.summary: Floor admission for PEF 25-50%, supplemental O2 need, or high-risk features — expected LOS 1-3 days
nodes.body: Floor Admission Criteria: Admit to Medical Floor if: • PEF 25-50% predicted after ED treatment • Requiring supplemental O2 • Requiring nebs more frequently than q4h • High-risk features (prior intubation, multiple ED visits) • Unable to be safely discharged Floor Orders: • Continuous SpO2 monitoring • Scheduled albuterol q4h + PRN • IV or PO steroids • RT to titrate O2 to SpO2 ≥92% • Call MD if: R

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU Admission Criteria: [3][6] Mandatory ICU if: • Intubated • Requiring BiPAP • Hemodynamically unstable • Altered mental status • PEF <25% predicted • Requiring continuous nebulization • Rapid deterioration despite ED treatment ICU Goals: • Avoid intubation if possible • Aggressive bronchodilation • Permissive hypercapnia if intubated • Minimize ventilator-induced lung injury • Early mobilizatio
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU for close monitoring. If on BiPAP: continuous nebs, IV magnesium, IV steroids, ketamine infusion. If intubated: volume control with low rate, long I:E, permissive hypercapnia.

nodes.title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
nodes.summary: Acute AUB in nonpregnant reproductive-age women — PALM-COEIN classification, 20% have underlying coagulopathy
nodes.body: Emergency management of acute AUB in nonpregnant reproductive-aged women. Acute AUB refers to heavy bleeding requiring immediate intervention to prevent further blood loss. May occur spontaneously or within the context of chronic AUB (present >6 months). nodes.summary: Assess hemodynamic stability — tachycardia, hypotension, orthostasis route to emergent resuscitation
nodes.body: Assess vitals for signs of hemodynamic instability: • Tachycardia (HR >100) • Hypotension (SBP <90) • Orthostatic changes (SBP drop >20 or HR rise >20 on standing) • Altered mental status Signs of significant hemorrhage: pallor, diaphoresis, delayed capillary refill, cool extremities.

nodes.title: Unstable AUB — Resuscitate
nodes.summary: TXA 1g IV + conjugated estrogen 25mg IV, activate MTP if massive — Foley balloon tamponade 30mL if GYN unavailable

nodes.title: Pregnancy Excluded?
nodes.summary: Must rule out pregnancy before any hormonal therapy — all hormonal treatments contraindicated in pregnancy
nodes.body: Pregnancy MUST be ruled out before initiating any hormonal therapy. • Urine hCG (qualitative) — rapid screening • Serum beta-hCG (quantitative) — if clinical suspicion despite negative urine test All hormonal treatments for AUB (estrogen, progestins, OCPs) are contraindicated in pregnancy.

nodes.title: Pregnancy Confirmed — Consult Does Not Apply
nodes.body: This AUB consult covers nonpregnant reproductive-aged women only. For vaginal bleeding in pregnancy, evaluate per trimester: • 1st trimester: Ectopic pregnancy, threatened/missed abortion, molar pregnancy • 2nd/3rd trimester: Placenta previa, placental abruption, preterm labor See Pregnancy Bleeding consult (coming soon). Obtain OB consultation. Consider Rh status (RhoGAM if Rh-negative).
nodes.recommendation: Evaluate pregnancy-related vaginal bleeding per trimester-specific differential. OB consult.

nodes.title: Coagulopathy-Related AUB

nodes.body: Up to 20% of women with heavy menstrual bleeding have an underlying bleeding disorder. von Willebrand disease is most common (up to 13%). Testing: • vWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, Factor VIII • Consult hematology for interpretation Treatment of AUB with coagulopathy: • Tranexamic Acid — first-line adjunct, reduces bleeding 30-55% • Desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 mcg/kg IV — for known vWD res

nodes.title: Medical Management Selection

All hormonal therapies require pregnancy exclusion (already confirmed).

MUST follow with progestin — Medroxyprogesterone 10 mg PO daily × 10 days after bleeding controlled. Unopposed estrogen risks endometrial hyperplasia and rebound bleeding. nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit if unstable/Hgb <7/failed outpatient/suspected malignancy; discharge if stable with GYN follow-up in 1-2 weeks

nodes.title: Discharge with GYN Follow-up

nodes.title: Auricular Hematoma Drainage

nodes.title: Confirm Diagnosis & Timing
nodes.summary: Fluctuant tender pinna swelling; drain if <7d, no infection; >7d or infected = ENT

nodes.title: Perichondritis or Abscess — STOP
nodes.summary: Red hot pinna ± fever = perichondritis; cover Pseudomonas (cipro or pip-tazo); urgent ENT
nodes.body: Red, hot pinna with fever or systemic features = perichondritis until proven otherwise. This is a soft-tissue infection of the perichondrium, most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Insert 18-gauge needle on 5-10 mL syringe at the dependent (inferior) edge of the hematoma at an oblique angle 4. nodes.title: Awake Intubation: When RSI Is Too Risky
nodes.summary: Preserve spontaneous ventilation — confirm cords BEFORE paralyzing; requires 15-30 min prep, 85% overall success
nodes.body: Awake intubation preserves spontaneous ventilation and protective reflexes during airway instrumentation. The Core Principle: "Look before you leap" — Confirm vocal cord visualization BEFORE administering paralytic. National Registry Data (NEAR): - Used in 0.4-2% of ED intubations - Overall first-attempt success: 85% - Nasal fiberoptic: 92% success - Oral fiberoptic: 57% success - Video laryngosco

nodes.title: Primary Indication?
nodes.summary: Select primary indication — angioedema, epiglottitis, predicted difficult airway, neck trauma, or metabolic acidosis

nodes.title: Modified Approach: Bleeding / Aspiration Risk
nodes.summary: Awake VL 89% success — less dependent on topical anesthesia quality, can suction simultaneously
nodes.body: Fiberoptic may be difficult with blood/secretions. Video laryngoscopy may be better. For Airway Bleeding: - Consider awake video laryngoscopy instead of fiberoptic - Suction immediately available - Smaller scope if using fiberoptic (easier to clear) - Have multiple ETT sizes ready For High Aspiration Risk: - Position patient head-up 30-45 degrees - Have suction immediately available - Consider NG

nodes.title: Preparation Phase
nodes.summary: 15-30 min prep — equipment checklist, meds, backup surgical airway open and ready, timeline T-15 to T-0

nodes.title: Step 1: Antisialagogue
nodes.summary: Glycopyrrolate 0.2-0.3mg IV 15min before — dry mouth is CRITICAL, wet mucosa dilutes lidocaine → poor anesthesia
nodes.body: Drying the airway is CRITICAL for topical anesthesia to work. Glycopyrrolate (Preferred): - Dose: 0.2-0.3 mg IV - Give 15 minutes before topicalization - Minimal CNS effects (doesn't cross BBB) - Longer duration than atropine Alternative: Atropine - Dose: 0.5 mg IV - Crosses BBB (may cause confusion in elderly) - Faster onset but shorter duration Ondansetron (Adjunct): - 4 mg IV - Helps blunt gag

nodes.title: Nasal or Oral Route?

nodes.title: Ketamine Sedation Protocol
nodes.summary: Ketamine 20mg IV aliquots q2min to light sedation — NEVER paralyze until you see cords; watch for apnea at high doses

Dosing: - 20 mg IV aliquots every 2 minutes - Titrate to effect (drowsy but responsive) - Typical total: 40-60 mg over 5-10 minutes - Goal: Light sedation, follows simple commands What to Watch For: - Patient drowsy but breathing well ✓ - Can follow command "take a deep breath" ✓ - Eyes may be open with nystagmus ✓ Red Flags (too

nodes.title: Dexmedetomidine Protocol
nodes.summary: Dex 0.5-1 mcg/kg load over 10min → 0.6-0.7 mcg/kg/hr — cooperative sedation, no resp depression, antisialagogue bonus
nodes.body: Best patient comfort and fewest desaturation episodes. Loading Dose: - 0.5-1 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes - Use 1 mcg/kg for anxious patients - Use 0.5 mcg/kg for elderly (>65) Maintenance Infusion: - 0.6-0.7 mcg/kg/hour - Range: 0.2-1 mcg/kg/hour - Titrate to calm but arousable Characteristics: - Onset: 5-10 minutes - "Cooperative sedation" — patient calm, follows commands - Excellent antisialagogue

Excessive Secretions/Blood? - Suction carefully - Was antisialagogue given? - Consider VL instead of fiberoptic 3. nodes.title: Successful Awake Intubation

Post-Procedure Checklist: □ ETT position confirmed (capnography, auscultation) □ Tube secured appropriately □ Full sedation/paralysis given as appropriate □ Ventilator settings optimized □ CXR ordered to confirm position □ Document procedure in detail Documentation Should Include: - Indication for awake technique - Topicalization prot
