nodes.title: B12 Deficiency & Subacute Combined Degeneration
nodes.summary: B12 deficiency degenerates dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts (SCD). Neuro disease can precede/occur without anemia.
nodes.body: Subacute combined degeneration (SCD) is demyelination of the dorsal columns and the lateral corticospinal tracts from cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency. "Combined" = both tract systems at once, producing the signature mix of sensory loss + upper-motor-neuron signs. Why B12 matters: it is a cofactor for methionine synthase (myelin methylation) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency impairs myeli

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Paresthesias feet>hands, vibration/proprioception loss, sensory ataxia/Romberg, plus spastic UMN signs. Neuro disease can occur with NORMAL CBC/MCV.
nodes.body: Neurologic (the diagnostic core): - Symmetric distal paresthesias, feet > hands — often the earliest symptom - Loss of vibration & proprioception (dorsal column) → sensory ataxia, positive Romberg - Spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski (corticospinal) - The clue: UMN signs coexisting with dorsal-column sensory loss Cognitive/psychiatric: memory loss, dementia, depression, psychosis. Mucocutan

nodes.title: Etiology
nodes.summary: Pernicious anemia, dietary (vegan), malabsorption (ileal/bariatric), drugs (metformin/PPI), N2O abuse, age.
nodes.body: Find the cause — it sets the treatment route and duration: - Pernicious anemia — autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor (anti-IF / anti-parietal-cell antibodies); the classic malabsorptive cause. Lifelong replacement. - Dietary — strict vegan/vegetarian (B12 is animal-sourced). - Malabsorption — ileal resection / Crohn, gastrectomy / bariatric surgery, bacterial overgrowth. - Drugs — long-term metfor

nodes.title: Diagnosis — Mind the Gray Zone
nodes.summary: Low B12 confirms; 200-400 gray zone needs MMA + homocysteine (MMA most specific). CBC may be normal. MRI: inverted-V dorsal-column T2.
nodes.body: - Serum B12 — low confirms deficiency. BUT the 200-400 pg/mL gray zone does not exclude it: ~50% of subclinical deficiency has a "normal" B12. - Methylmalonic acid (MMA) — elevated; the most specific confirmatory test. Order it (with homocysteine) whenever B12 is borderline/low-normal or the clinical picture fits. - Homocysteine — elevated; sensitive but less specific (also raised by folate defici

nodes.title: Two Traps: Folate-Alone & Nitrous Oxide
nodes.summary: Never folate alone (masks anemia, neuro damage continues — replace B12 first). N2O causes SCD with NORMAL B12 — diagnose by MMA/homocysteine, stop exposure.
nodes.body: Trap 1 — Do NOT give folate alone (FLAGGED). Folate corrects the megaloblastic anemia (removing the hematologic warning sign) while neurologic degeneration continues unchecked. The masking effect is undisputed; some literature argues folate may even accelerate neuro damage. Practical rule: assess B12 status before or alongside any folate, and replace B12 first / together. Trap 2 — Nitrous oxide ca

nodes.title: Treatment — Replace Early
nodes.summary: Parenteral B12 1 mg (daily->weekly->monthly) for neuro disease; high-dose oral for mild/non-malabsorptive. Treat the cause. Recover best if treated EARLY.
nodes.body: Replace B12 — early treatment is the key prognostic lever. - Parenteral (IM/SC) cyanocobalamin or hydroxocobalamin 1000 mcg (1 mg): classic schedule daily ~1 week → weekly ~1 month → monthly thereafter (lifelong if the cause is irreversible, e.g., pernicious anemia). Hydroxocobalamin is retained somewhat better. - For significant neurologic disease (SCD): more intensive loading — 1 mg IM on ALTERN

nodes.title: Differential — Don't Miss Copper
nodes.summary: Copper deficiency is the near-identical mimic (check copper + ceruloplasmin, esp. bariatric/zinc or non-responders). Also GBS, MS/TM, tabes, HIV, compression.
nodes.body: Copper deficiency myelopathy ("human swayback") is clinically AND radiologically near-identical — same dorsal-column sensory ataxia + corticospinal signs and the same inverted-"V" MRI sign. - Causes: bariatric/gastric surgery (~47%), zinc excess (denture cream, supplements; ~16%), malabsorption. Often with cytopenias. - Check serum copper + ceruloplasmin — especially if the patient keeps deteriora

nodes.title: Disposition & Prognosis
nodes.summary: Mostly outpatient; admit for severe/progressive deficits or significant anemia. Recovery depends on early treatment. Lifelong replacement for irreversible causes.
nodes.body: Disposition: most patients are managed outpatient with hematology and/or neurology follow-up. Admit for severe or rapidly progressive neuro deficits, hemodynamically significant anemia, or inability to arrange timely treatment/follow-up. Prognosis: reversibility depends on duration before treatment — emphasize early initiation. Some deficits become permanent if treatment is delayed months to years
nodes.recommendation: Recognize subacute combined degeneration (dorsal-column sensory loss + corticospinal UMN signs), and remember neuro disease can occur without anemia. In the 200-400 pg/mL gray zone, send MMA + homocysteine. Never give folate alone. Consider

nodes.title: Back Pain Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Vitals, neuro/bowel/bladder, vascular/abdominal, infection, trauma, cancer risk first.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Ruptured / leaking AAA \u2014 age \u226550 + smoker, pulsatile mass, syncope; bedside US now. 2. Spinal epidural abscess \u2014 fever, IVDU/immunosuppression, point tenderness, deficit. 3. Cauda equina syndrome \u2014 saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral leg weakness. 4. Cord compression from malignancy \u2014 cancer history, night pain, progressive defici

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Cauda, spine infection, AAA/dissection, fracture/cancer, renal mimics, and radiculopathy are the main lanes.
nodes.body: Choose the first dangerous lane. Do not start with "sciatica" until these are screened.

nodes.title: Cauda Equina / Conus Medullaris
nodes.body: Open Cauda Equina Syndrome. Next 5 minutes: bladder scan/PVR, focused sacral exam when feasible, leg motor/reflex/sensation exam, urgent MRI lumbar spine, early spine/neurosurgery call if symptoms fit. Red flags: urinary retention or new overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, progressive bilateral leg weakness, fecal incontinence, severe neurologic deficit. Pitfall: pain may
nodes.recommendation: Suspected cauda equina needs emergency MRI and spine pathway.

nodes.title: Spinal Epidural Abscess / Vertebral Osteomyelitis
nodes.body: Open Low Back Pain Decision Support while using spine infection posture. Next 5 minutes: neuro exam, ESR/CRP, blood cultures when febrile/high suspicion, MRI spine with and without contrast; consider whole-spine MRI when symptoms do not localize or risk is high. Antibiotics after cultures when stable; do not delay antibiotics for sepsis or neurologic deficit. Pitfall: the classic triad is insensit
nodes.recommendation: MRI is the key diagnostic test when spine infection is plausible.

nodes.title: AAA / Aortic Dissection Back-Pain Variant
nodes.body: Open Aortic Aneurysm ED Management or Aortic Dissection. Next 5 minutes: two large-bore IVs, type/screen or MTP posture if unstable, bedside aorta ultrasound if rapid and available, CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis when stable, vascular/cardiothoracic surgery early. For dissection, impulse control before vasodilator when perfusing. Pitfall: do not anchor on musculoskeletal pain in an older vascular-risk p
nodes.recommendation: Vascular back pain is a resuscitation diagnosis. Image and consult early.

nodes.title: Fracture / Malignancy / Metastatic Cord Compression
nodes.body: Open Low Back Pain Decision Support. Next 5 minutes: neuro exam, pain control, CT or radiographs for trauma/fracture by risk, MRI when cancer with neurologic symptoms, severe progressive pain, suspected cord/cauda compression, or epidural disease. Consider steroids after specialist discussion when metastatic cord compression is suspected. Pitfall: new severe back pain in a cancer patient is malign
nodes.recommendation: Cancer, fracture risk, or neuro findings should trigger imaging beyond routine mechanical back pain care.

nodes.title: Renal / Urinary / Intra-Abdominal Mimic
nodes.body: Open Adult UTI or Urinary Retention when those fit. Next 5 minutes: UA, pregnancy test when applicable, renal function, bedside bladder scan if retention, CT/ultrasound strategy for stone/obstruction/pyelo complication by risk. Reconsider abdominal pathology when pain is not reproducible/mechanical or vitals are abnormal. Pitfall: flank/back pain plus fever, solitary kidney, AKI, pregnancy, uncont
nodes.recommendation: Treat renal/urinary mimics by obstruction, infection severity, pregnancy, and renal risk.

nodes.title: Radiculopathy / Mechanical Pattern
nodes.body: Open Low Back Pain Decision Support. Open L4/L5/S1 Radiculopathy Localization for the bedside dermatome/myotome/reflex map. Next 5 minutes: confirm no red flags, document motor/reflex/sensation, treat pain to enable mobility, avoid routine advanced imaging for uncomplicated acute low back pain/radiculopathy, encourage activity as tolerated. Pitfall: radicular pain does not equal cauda equina. Caud
nodes.recommendation: Mechanical/radicular pain can be outpatient only after red flags and function are reassessed.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Analgesia, repeat neuro/gait, PVR when indicated, ESR/CRP by infection risk, then reassess.
nodes.body: Default bundle when no killer has declared itself: - Analgesia: acetaminophen, NSAID if safe, topical/local measures, muscle relaxer selectively; avoid routine opioids when alternatives work. - Neuro exam before and after analgesia: gait, strength, reflexes, sensation. - Bladder scan/PVR when urinary symptoms, severe bilateral symptoms, or cauda concern. - ESR/CRP when infection risk exists; norma

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: New neuro/bladder/fever/vascular features reset the workup.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on function and the repeat neurologic exam.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: MRI for cauda/infection/cancer/neuro, CTA/US for aorta, CT/XR for fracture, no imaging for uncomplicated mechanical pain.
nodes.body: Image by suspected emergency: - MRI lumbar spine: cauda/conus, progressive neurologic deficit, suspected epidural abscess/vertebral osteomyelitis, malignancy with neuro signs, cord/cauda compression. - MRI with contrast / whole spine: infection, malignancy, nonlocalizing spinal infection symptoms. - CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis: aortic dissection or unstable vascular back-pain phenotype when stable en

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Danger signs admit; uncertainty observes; uncomplicated mechanical pain discharges after function and red flags are checked.
nodes.body: Disposition follows neurologic safety, infection/vascular risk, mobility, and pain control.

nodes.title: Admit / Transfer / Specialty Pathway
nodes.body: Admit/transfer for cauda/conus symptoms, progressive neurologic deficit, suspected or confirmed SEA/NVO, sepsis, AAA/dissection, unstable vitals, fracture needing intervention, malignancy/cord compression concern, inability to ambulate safely, urinary retention with neurologic concern, or pain requiring inpatient control.
nodes.recommendation: Admit or transfer when the diagnosis threatens neurologic function, vascular survival, infection control, or safe mobility.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exam
nodes.body: Observe when MRI/CTA/labs are pending, pain prevents a reliable exam or ambulation test, symptoms are evolving, infection risk is moderate with unclear labs, or social support/transport is unsafe after treatment.
nodes.recommendation: Observation is for serial neuro/gait/vitals and completion of targeted testing.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: no red flags, normal or baseline neuro exam, no bowel/bladder/saddle symptoms, ambulatory or baseline mobility restored, pain controlled enough for function, no infection/vascular/trauma/cancer concern, and follow-up is realistic. Return precautions: urinary retention/incontinence, saddle numbness, leg weakness, inability to walk, fever, worsening severe pain, abdominal pain/s
nodes.recommendation: Document red-flag screen, repeat neuro/gait exam, and explicit cauda/infection/vascular return precautions.

nodes.title: Acute Behavior Change — Sick Check First
nodes.body: "He's not acting right" is a medical complaint until proven psychiatric. Anchoring on "psych" is how patients die of hypoglycemia, meningitis, or sepsis in the waiting room. New behavior change — especially acute onset, at the extremes of age, with abnormal vitals or a focal exam — is organic until you have actively excluded medical causes. Medical clearance is a decision, not a checkbox. ⚠️ DO-NO

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Seven-branch triage: hypoglycemia / CNS infection / seizure / toxidrome / endocrine-metabolic / sepsis-delirium / primary psychiatric.
nodes.body: Screen the reversible medical killers first; only after they are addressed does a primary psychiatric cause become the working diagnosis. Each branch runs a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia — Glucose Gate
nodes.summary: Every behavior change gets a glucose; low + symptomatic = treat now and find the cause (esp. sulfonylurea/insulin).
nodes.body: Hypoglycemia mimics anything — agitation, psychosis, focal deficits, coma. Any new behavior change gets a point-of-care glucose immediately. A low glucose (typically <70 mg/dL, symptomatic) with behavior change is the diagnosis until the glucose is corrected and symptoms resolve. Consider the cause: insulin/sulfonylurea, alcohol, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, or a deliberate overdose.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia — Give Glucose, Find the Cause
nodes.body: Open Hypoglycemia for the full pathway. Next steps: - Treat immediately: oral glucose if able to swallow, otherwise IV dextrose (D50/D10); IM glucagon if no IV access. - Thiamine before glucose in malnourished/alcoholic patients (Wernicke prevention). - Recheck glucose and reassess mental status — behavior should normalize; persistent deficits mean another cause. - Sulfonylurea or long-acting insu
nodes.recommendation: IV dextrose (or glucagon) immediately, thiamine if malnourished, recheck glucose/mentation; observe/octreotide for sulfonylurea; find the cause.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia — Excluded
nodes.body: A normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia as the driver. (It is the fastest reversible cause to check — good that it is off the list.) Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia; continue the organic screen.

nodes.title: CNS Infection — Meningoencephalitis Gate
nodes.summary: Fever + behavior change → empiric antibiotics ± acyclovir NOW; do not wait for LP/CT.
nodes.body: Fever + new behavior change is meningitis/encephalitis until excluded. Look for headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, rash (meningococcemia), seizures, and focal deficits (encephalitis, esp. HSV — temporal/behavioral changes). The classic triad is often incomplete, especially in elders and the immunocompromised. Do NOT delay antibiotics for the LP or CT — treat empirically the moment you suspect

nodes.title: CNS Infection — Empiric Therapy Without Delay
nodes.body: Open Meningitis for the full pathway. Next steps: - Empiric antibiotics immediately (ceftriaxone + vancomycin; add ampicillin for Listeria in >50/immunocompromised) — do NOT wait for LP or CT results. - Add IV acyclovir if encephalitis is possible (behavior/personality change, focal temporal signs, seizures — HSV). - Dexamethasone before/with the first antibiotic dose for suspected bacterial menin
nodes.recommendation: Empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+ ampicillin if indicated) + dexamethasone + acyclovir for possible encephalitis, immediately; LP after CT when indicated.

nodes.title: CNS Infection — Unlikely
nodes.body: No fever, no meningismus, and no encephalopathic features make a CNS infection unlikely right now — but the elderly and immunocompromised can present atypically (afebrile). Keep a low threshold and reassess if fever, headache, or seizures develop. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: CNS infection unlikely without fever/meningismus; keep a low threshold in elders/immunocompromised and reassess.

nodes.title: Seizure — Nonconvulsive Status / Post-Ictal Gate
nodes.summary: Prolonged/fluctuating altered awareness → suspect NCSE; get EEG, treat status if confirmed, or watch a resolving post-ictal state.
nodes.body: Fluctuating awareness, staring, automatisms, aphasia, or unexplained prolonged confusion can be nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) — no obvious convulsion, but ongoing seizure. Also consider a post-ictal state after an unwitnessed seizure (gradual clearing, Todd paralysis, tongue-biting, incontinence). Known epilepsy, subtle rhythmic twitching, or prolonged post-ictal confusion (>30–60 min) s

nodes.title: NCSE / Post-Ictal — EEG + Treat Status
nodes.body: Open Status Epilepticus for the full pathway. Next steps: - If nonconvulsive status is suspected, get an urgent EEG and treat as status if confirmed — benzodiazepine first-line, then a second-line anticonvulsant (levetiracetam, valproate, or fosphenytoin). - Find the cause: glucose, electrolytes (Na, Ca, Mg), toxins, missed anticonvulsants, CNS infection/structural lesion; neuroimaging as indicate
nodes.recommendation: Urgent EEG for suspected NCSE; treat confirmed status (benzo → second-line agent); find/correct the cause; watch a resolving post-ictal state.

nodes.title: Seizure — Unlikely
nodes.body: No seizure features and a picture that clears or fits another process make NCSE/post-ictal state unlikely. If confusion is prolonged and unexplained, keep NCSE on the list and get an EEG. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Seizure unlikely without ictal/post-ictal features; reconsider NCSE (EEG) for unexplained prolonged confusion.

nodes.title: Toxidrome — Hyperthermia + Rigidity/Clonus Gate
nodes.summary: Hot + rigid/clonic + drug trigger → serotonin syndrome (clonus) vs NMS (lead-pipe) vs withdrawal; cool + benzos are common threads.
nodes.body: A hot, agitated, rigid, or autonomically unstable patient with a drug trigger has a life-threatening toxidrome. Separate the key ones by exam and history: - Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic drug + clonus (lower-limb > upper), hyperreflexia, agitation, hyperthermia; rapid onset. - NMS: antipsychotic (or dopamine-agonist withdrawal) + "lead-pipe" rigidity, hyporeflexia, hyperthermia, autonomic insta

nodes.title: Serotonin Syndrome — Stop Agent, Cool, Benzos
nodes.body: Open Serotonin Syndrome for the full pathway. Next steps: - Stop all serotonergic agents immediately. - Aggressive cooling and benzodiazepines for agitation and hyperthermia; avoid antipyretics (ineffective) and physical restraints alone (worsen hyperthermia/rhabdo). - Cyproheptadine (serotonin antagonist) for moderate-severe cases. - Severe hyperthermia (>41.1°C) → intubation, paralysis (non-depo
nodes.recommendation: Stop serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines + active cooling, cyproheptadine for moderate/severe; intubate + paralyze for severe hyperthermia.

nodes.title: NMS — Stop Antipsychotic, Cool, Supportive Care
nodes.body: Open NMS for the full pathway. Next steps: - Stop the offending antipsychotic (or restart dopaminergic therapy if NMS is from abrupt Parkinson-drug withdrawal). - Aggressive cooling, IV fluids, and benzodiazepines; supportive ICU care. - Dantrolene and/or bromocriptine for severe rigidity/hyperthermia (specialist-guided). - Monitor for rhabdomyolysis and AKI (elevated CK) — hydrate and protect the
nodes.recommendation: Stop antipsychotic, active cooling + IV fluids + benzodiazepines, dantrolene/bromocriptine for severe cases, watch CK/AKI.

nodes.title: Alcohol / Sedative Withdrawal — Benzodiazepines
nodes.body: Open Alcohol Withdrawal for the full pathway. Next steps: - Symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (CIWA-guided) are the cornerstone; escalate for severe withdrawal/delirium tremens. - Thiamine, fluids, and electrolyte correction (magnesium, potassium, phosphate); thiamine before glucose. - Phenobarbital or adjuncts for benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal; treat withdrawal seizures. - Monitor for DTs (
nodes.recommendation: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (CIWA), thiamine + fluids + electrolytes, phenobarbital for resistant cases; admit severe withdrawal/DTs.

nodes.title: Toxidrome — Unlikely
nodes.body: No hyperthermia, rigidity, clonus, autonomic instability, or drug trigger makes a life-threatening toxidrome unlikely. Reassess if new rigidity, clonus, fever, or autonomic signs appear. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Toxidrome unlikely without hyperthermia/rigidity/clonus/trigger; reassess if features evolve.

nodes.title: Endocrine / Metabolic — Crisis Gate
nodes.summary: Screen thyroid storm / adrenal crisis / DKA-HHS / sodium; BMP + glucose + TSH catch most metabolic mimics.
nodes.body: Endocrine and electrolyte crises are classic psychiatric mimics. Screen for: thyroid storm (hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmia, agitation/psychosis, goiter), adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, fatigue/confusion, steroid history), DKA/HHS (hyperglycemia, dehydration, acidosis, AMS), and sodium disorders (hypo-/hypernatremia cause confusion, seizures). A basic metabolic panel, gluco

nodes.title: Thyroid Storm — Treat the Storm
nodes.body: Open Thyroid Emergencies for the full pathway. Next steps: - Beta-blockade (propranolol) for adrenergic symptoms and to block T4→T3 conversion. - Thionamide (PTU or methimazole), then iodine (Lugol/SSKI) at least 1 hour after the thionamide (Wolff-Chaikoff), plus hydrocortisone. - Aggressive cooling and supportive care; treat the precipitant (infection, etc.). - Monitor for high-output heart failu
nodes.recommendation: Beta-blocker + thionamide + delayed iodine + hydrocortisone + cooling; treat the precipitant; ICU.

nodes.title: Adrenal Crisis — Steroids Now
nodes.body: Open Adrenal Insufficiency for the full pathway. Next steps: - Give hydrocortisone immediately (100 mg IV) — do NOT delay for confirmatory testing in a crisis; draw a cortisol first if it will not delay treatment. - Aggressive IV fluids (isotonic) for hypotension and hyponatremia; correct hypoglycemia. - Find and treat the precipitant (infection, missed steroids, stress). - Monitor electrolytes; e
nodes.recommendation: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately + aggressive fluids + correct glucose/Na; treat precipitant; admit.

nodes.title: DKA / HHS — Fluids, Insulin, Potassium
nodes.body: Open DKA for the full pathway. Next steps: - IV fluid resuscitation first (isotonic), then insulin infusion, with careful potassium repletion (do NOT start insulin if K⁺ <3.3 until replaced). - Find the precipitant (infection, missed insulin, MI, new-onset diabetes). - Monitor glucose, electrolytes, and the anion gap; watch for cerebral edema in children. - Behavior change/AMS in DKA/HHS resolves
nodes.recommendation: Fluids → insulin infusion → potassium repletion (hold insulin if K<3.3); treat the precipitant; monitor gap/electrolytes.

nodes.title: Endocrine / Metabolic — Excluded
nodes.body: A normal metabolic screen (glucose, electrolytes, and — where indicated — TSH) with no crisis features makes an endocrine/metabolic mimic unlikely. Revisit if labs return abnormal. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Metabolic mimic unlikely with a normal screen; revisit if labs return abnormal.

nodes.title: Sepsis / Delirium — Occult-Infection Gate
nodes.summary: Elderly acute confusion → hunt occult infection (UTI/pneumonia) + screen sepsis; delirium is a medical emergency with a reversible driver.
nodes.body: In older adults, acute confusion is often the ONLY sign of infection. New fluctuating confusion (delirium) with inattention should trigger a hunt for an occult source — especially UTI and pneumonia — plus a review of medications (anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines), pain, retention, and metabolic causes. Screen for sepsis (qSOFA in the toolbar); delirium is a medical emergency, not "just o

nodes.title: Sepsis — Source Control + Resuscitation
nodes.body: Open Sepsis for the full pathway; for a urinary source see Adult UTI. Next steps: - Sepsis bundle: blood cultures, lactate, early broad-spectrum antibiotics, and IV fluids for hypoperfusion; qSOFA/vitals in the toolbar. - Hunt the source: UA/culture (UTI), chest imaging (pneumonia), skin/soft tissue, abdomen, lines. - Reassess perfusion; vasopressors for fluid-refractory shock; admit to the approp
nodes.recommendation: Sepsis bundle (cultures, lactate, early abx, fluids) + source hunt (UTI/pneumonia) + admit; expect confusion to clear with source control.

nodes.title: Delirium — Find and Fix the Driver
nodes.body: Open Delirium for the full pathway. Next steps: - Delirium always has a medical cause — find it: infection, medications (deliriogenic drugs), metabolic derangement, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention/constipation, alcohol/drug effects, and environmental factors. - Non-pharmacologic management first (reorientation, sleep-wake, mobility, sensory aids, address pain/retention). - Reserve low-dose antips
nodes.recommendation: Find/fix the medical driver, non-pharmacologic measures first, low-dose antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation, avoid benzos (except withdrawal).

nodes.title: Sepsis / Delirium — Excluded
nodes.body: No delirium and no infection signs make an occult-infection/delirium picture unlikely. Keep it in mind for any elder whose behavior fluctuates, and recheck vitals if the picture changes. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Sepsis/delirium unlikely without infection signs/fluctuating confusion; keep a low threshold in elders.

nodes.title: Primary Psychiatric — Medical Clearance Gate
nodes.summary: Clear for psych ONLY with a negative organic screen + reassuring exam; any organic red flag = not cleared, keep working it up.
nodes.body: Only after the organic screen is negative does a primary psychiatric cause become the working diagnosis. Reassuring for a functional cause: normal vitals, normal glucose, a non-focal neuro exam, age <40 with a prior psychiatric history, gradual onset, and preserved orientation with auditory (not visual) hallucinations. Concerning for organic (do NOT clear): abnormal vitals, focal deficit, new symp

nodes.title: Primary Psychiatric — Cleared for Assessment
nodes.body: Medical clearance is appropriate once the reversible medical causes are addressed and the exam is reassuring. - Document the negative organic workup and the specific reasons the presentation is not organic — clearance is a reasoned decision, not a rubber stamp. - Manage acute agitation safely with verbal de-escalation first; use the Excited Delirium pathway for severe agitation threatening safety,
nodes.recommendation: Document a reasoned medical clearance, de-escalate agitation (excited-delirium pathway if severe), assess suicide/violence risk, refer to psychiatry.

nodes.title: Not Cleared — Keep Working It Up
nodes.body: Any residual organic red flag means the patient is NOT medically cleared. Abnormal vitals, a focal deficit, new symptoms after age 40, visual hallucinations, disorientation, or an acute fluctuating course all point back to a medical cause. - Return to the organic branches and complete the workup (labs, imaging, EEG as indicated). - Do not transfer to a psychiatric facility or anchor on "psych" unt
nodes.recommendation: Residual organic red flags = not cleared; complete the medical workup before any psychiatric disposition.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle
nodes.body: The behavior-change / medical-clearance bundle (scale to acuity): - Point-of-care glucose on everyone, first. - Full vitals + temperature (qSOFA), pupils, focal neuro screen; abnormal vitals or a focal exam = organic until proven otherwise. - Targeted labs: BMP (Na, glucose, renal), calcium/magnesium, CBC, LFTs, ammonia if liver disease, TSH, and — by risk — blood/urine cultures, UA, and a toxicol

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Organic emergency → treat + admit (imaging as needed); stable + cleared/treated → disposition.
nodes.body: After the glucose, vitals, focal screen, and initial labs — where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging / Diagnostics
nodes.body: Match the study to the suspected cause: - Non-contrast head CT — focal deficit, trauma, anticoagulation, depressed consciousness, or before LP with focal signs/immunocompromise (bleed, mass, hydrocephalus). - Lumbar puncture — suspected meningitis/encephalitis (after CT when indicated); do not delay antibiotics for it. - EEG — suspected nonconvulsive status or unexplained prolonged/fluctuating con

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit organic emergencies (ICU as needed); observe/admit delirium & evolving cases; psychiatric disposition once medically cleared + safe.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit the organic emergency to the appropriate level. - CNS infection, thyroid storm, adrenal crisis, severe toxidrome, status epilepticus, septic shock → ICU/step-down with definitive therapy and monitoring. - Continue the specific treatment started in the ED (antibiotics/acyclovir, steroids, cooling, antidotes, anticonvulsants). - Specialist involvement (neurology, endocrine, ID, toxicology, cri
nodes.recommendation: Admit organic emergencies to ICU/step-down with definitive therapy and specialist involvement.

nodes.title: Observe / Admit for Workup
nodes.body: Observation or admission for workup when the cause is not yet clear or the patient needs monitoring — e.g., delirium with a partially identified driver, a resolving post-ictal state, or a borderline metabolic derangement. - Serial exams and vitals; complete the diagnostic workup and treat the identified driver. - Non-pharmacologic delirium care; involve geriatrics/hospital medicine. - Do not disch
nodes.recommendation: Observe/admit unclear or evolving cases with serial exams, complete the workup, treat the driver; do not discharge unexplained behavior change.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Disposition
nodes.body: Once medically cleared and safe, proceed with the psychiatric plan. - Document the negative organic workup and the rationale for medical clearance. - Psychiatric evaluation / referral per your site's pathway; involuntary hold if the patient meets criteria for danger to self/others. - Ensure safety: suicide/violence risk assessment, a safe environment, and appropriate level of psychiatric care (inp
nodes.recommendation: Medically cleared + safe → psychiatric evaluation/hold as indicated, document clearance, safety assessment, medical return precautions.

nodes.title: Beta-Blocker Overdose — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Classic triad: bradycardia + hypotension + hypoglycemia — propranolol causes QRS widening, sotalol causes QT prolongation
nodes.body: Beta-Blocker OD Steps Summary — quick reference. Beta-blocker toxicity causes bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycemia (the classic triad). Hypoglycemia is especially common in children [1][2]. Agent characteristics matter: • Lipophilic (propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol) — cross BBB → CNS depression, seizures • Hydrophilic (atenolol, nadolol) — less CNS effects, dialyzable • Propranolol — sod

nodes.title: Mild Toxicity — Monitoring
nodes.summary: Mild toxicity still needs continuous monitoring — extended-release formulations cause delayed toxicity for 24-48h
nodes.body: Mild beta-blocker toxicity: • Sinus bradycardia (HR 50-60) • Normal blood pressure • Alert mental status • No hypoglycemia Still requires close monitoring: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • IV access • Baseline ECG — check for QRS widening (propranolol) or QT prolongation (sotalol) • Fingerstick glucose q1-2h (especially children) • Serial vitals q15-30 min Extended-release formulations can cause

nodes.title: Agent-Specific Considerations
nodes.summary: Propranolol: QRS widening → NaHCO3; Sotalol: QT/Torsades → Mg + pacing; Carvedilol: alpha block → worse hypotension
nodes.body: PROPRANOLOL — The Dangerous One: • Most lipophilic — crosses BBB easily • Sodium channel blockade → QRS widening (like TCA) • Seizures common • Treat QRS >100ms with Sodium Bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg [1][2] SOTALOL — The Arrhythmogenic One: • Class III antiarrhythmic effect (K+ channel blockade) • QT prolongation → Torsades de pointes risk • Monitor QTc closely • Have Magnesium Sulfate 2g IV ready [1]

nodes.title: Initial Stabilization
nodes.summary: ABCs, cardiac monitoring, ECG for QRS/QT, glucose, charcoal if <2h — atropine first but usually ineffective
nodes.body: Initiate immediately: • ABCs — airway management if CNS depression • Two large-bore IVs • Continuous cardiac monitoring • 12-lead ECG — look for QRS widening (propranolol) or QT prolongation (sotalol) • Fingerstick glucose — treat hypoglycemia (D50 if needed) • BMP, lactate, blood gas GI Decontamination: • Activated Charcoal 1 g/kg (max 50g) if ingestion within 1-2 hours and airway protected [1] •

nodes.title: Atropine Response
nodes.summary: Atropine 0.5-1mg IV — usually ineffective (acts on muscarinic, not beta receptors); escalate to glucagon + calcium
nodes.body: Atropine 0.5-1mg IV • May repeat q3-5 min to max 3mg total • Usually ineffective in beta-blocker toxicity because it acts on muscarinic receptors, NOT beta receptors [1][2] • Worth trying as first step — occasionally helps Did atropine improve heart rate and blood pressure?

nodes.title: Glucagon — First-Line Therapy
nodes.summary: Glucagon 3-5mg IV bolus (up to 10mg) then 2-10mg/hr infusion — bypasses blocked beta receptor via adenylate cyclase
nodes.body: Glucagon bypasses the blocked beta receptor and activates adenylate cyclase directly → increases cAMP → positive inotropic and chronotropic effects [1][2][4]. Dosing: • Bolus: 3-5 mg IV over 1-2 minutes • May repeat bolus up to 10 mg total if no response [1][2] • Infusion: 2-10 mg/hr once response achieved [1][4] Practical tips: • Onset: 1-3 minutes • Duration: ~15 minutes (hence need for infusion

nodes.title: Calcium — Inotropic Support
nodes.summary: Ca gluconate 3g or CaCl 1g IV — improves contractility; target iCa 2x normal, give simultaneously with glucagon
nodes.body: Calcium improves myocardial contractility by increasing intracellular calcium availability [1][4]. Dosing (choose one): • Calcium Gluconate 3g (30 mL of 10%) IV over 10-20 min • Calcium Chloride 1g (10 mL of 10%) IV over 10-20 min — 3x more elemental Ca²⁺ but caustic (central line preferred) May repeat q10-20 min as needed [4]. Infusion: 0.6-1.5 mEq Ca²⁺/kg/hr (gluconate or chloride) once response

nodes.title: Pacing Consideration
nodes.summary: Pacing may not capture in severe toxicity — bridge to other therapies, assess for HIET escalation or arrest
nodes.body: External (transcutaneous) pacing may be needed if bradycardia is refractory to atropine, glucagon, and calcium [1][2]. Key points: • May not achieve electrical capture in severe toxicity — myocardium is "poisoned" • Even with capture, mechanical response may be poor • Bridge to other therapies, NOT definitive treatment • Consider transvenous pacing if transcutaneous capture difficult Hemodynamic s

nodes.title: High-Dose Insulin Euglycemia Therapy (HIET)
nodes.summary: HIET cornerstone of BB/CCB toxicity — enhances cardiac glucose uptake → positive inotropy; onset 15-60min, be patient
nodes.body: HIET is a cornerstone of beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker toxicity management [1][4]. Mechanism: • In toxic/shock states, the heart switches from fatty acid to glucose metabolism • High-dose insulin enhances cardiac glucose uptake → positive inotropy • Also improves vascular resistance via NO-mediated effects [4] This is NOT DKA dosing — doses are much higher! Evidence: • Multiple case ser

nodes.title: HIET Dosing Protocol
nodes.summary: Insulin 1 unit/kg bolus → 1-10 units/kg/hr; MUST co-administer D10/D25 + aggressive K+ repletion (10-40 mEq/hr)
nodes.body: Regular Insulin Protocol: Bolus: 1 unit/kg IV push Infusion: Start at 1 unit/kg/hr • Titrate up to 10 units/kg/hr based on hemodynamic response [1][4] • Some cases have used even higher doses MUST co-administer: 1. Dextrose: • D25 or D50 bolus to achieve glucose 150-250 mg/dL • D10 or D25 infusion to maintain euglycemia • May need 25-50g dextrose/hr [4] 2. Potassium: • Target K+ 3.5-4.5 mEq/L • In

nodes.title: HIET Monitoring
nodes.summary: Glucose q15-30min (target 150-250), K+ q1h (target 3.5-4.5) — hypoglycemia is main risk, D50 at bedside
nodes.body: Monitoring during HIET: Glucose: • Check q15-30 min initially, then q1h once stable • Target: 150-250 mg/dL • Hypoglycemia is the main risk — have D50 at bedside Potassium: • Check q1h • Target: 3.5-4.5 mEq/L • Aggressive repletion often needed (10-40 mEq/hr IV) Hemodynamics: • Expect improvement in 15-60 minutes [4] • Can take longer — be patient before declaring failure • Arterial line recommend

nodes.title: HIET Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess HIET response at 30-60min — complementary with vasopressors, escalate to lipid emulsion if refractory
nodes.body: HIET can be used with vasopressors — they are complementary, not mutually exclusive [1][4]. Assess hemodynamic response after 30-60 minutes of HIET.

nodes.title: Vasopressor Therapy
nodes.summary: HIGH-DOSE norepi 0.1-3 mcg/kg/min needed — standard doses insufficient when beta receptors blocked; add epi for cardiogenic
nodes.body: Vasopressors are often needed as bridge therapy while waiting for HIET onset or as adjunct [1][2]. Key concept: Beta receptors are blocked → standard doses may be insufficient. HIGH DOSES often required [1][2]. First-line: Norepinephrine • Alpha > beta effects • Start at 0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP ≥65 • May need 0.5-3 mcg/kg/min — much higher than sepsis dosing [1][2] If cardiogenic component:

nodes.title: Adjunct Vasopressors
nodes.summary: Vasopressin 0.04 units/min bypasses adrenergic receptors — AVOID dobutamine (beta blocked) and dopamine (less effective)
nodes.body: Vasopressin • 0.04 units/min (fixed dose) • Bypasses adrenergic receptors entirely — V1 receptor agonist • Add to norepinephrine for refractory hypotension [1][2] Dopamine: • Less effective — beta-2 effects blocked • Not recommended as first-line [1] Dobutamine: • Pure beta agonist — ineffective when beta receptors are blocked • Avoid [1] Phenylephrine: • Pure alpha agonist • May worsen bradycardi

nodes.title: Vasopressor Response
nodes.summary: Assess vasopressor response — MAP ≥65 continue, refractory escalate to lipid emulsion therapy
nodes.body: Assess hemodynamic response to vasopressor therapy.

nodes.title: Lipid Emulsion Therapy (ILE/Intralipid)
nodes.summary: Intralipid 20% rescue for refractory toxicity — lipid sink for propranolol/metoprolol/carvedilol; less evidence for hydrophilic agents
nodes.body: Intralipid 20% — rescue therapy for refractory toxicity, especially with lipophilic agents (propranolol, metoprolol, carvedilol) [1][5]. Proposed mechanisms: • Lipid sink — sequesters lipophilic drug away from target tissues • Improved cardiac metabolism via fatty acid supply • Direct positive inotropic effect [5] Best evidence: Lipophilic beta-blockers (propranolol) and local anesthetic toxicity.

nodes.title: Lipid Emulsion Dosing
nodes.summary: Intralipid 1.5 mL/kg bolus (repeat x2), then 0.25-0.5 mL/kg/min x30-60min — max 10-12 mL/kg first hour
nodes.body: Intralipid 20% Protocol: Bolus: 1.5 mL/kg IV over 1 minute • May repeat bolus x2 if needed (q5 min) [1][5] Infusion: 0.25-0.5 mL/kg/min for 30-60 min Maximum dose: 10-12 mL/kg over the first hour [5] Practical tips: • Use 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid, Liposyn) • Standard bag is 500 mL • For 70kg adult: bolus ~105 mL, infusion ~1L+ over first hour • Can give through peripheral or central line Sid

nodes.title: Rescue Therapies
nodes.summary: Route to agent-specific rescue: propranolol QRS→NaHCO3, sotalol QT→Mg, ECMO, dialysis, or methylene blue for vasoplegia
nodes.body: Additional rescue options based on agent and clinical scenario [1][2][3]. Which clinical scenario applies?

nodes.title: Propranolol — Sodium Channel Blockade
nodes.summary: Propranolol QRS >100ms: NaHCO3 1-2 mEq/kg IV push → target pH 7.50-7.55; avoid phenytoin for seizures
nodes.body: Propranolol has unique sodium channel blocking properties (like TCAs) [1][2]. If QRS > 100 ms: • Sodium Bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV push • Repeat q3-5 min until QRS narrows • Target pH 7.50-7.55 • Same protocol as TCA toxicity Seizure management: • Propranolol is highly lipophilic — seizures common • Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) first-line • Avoid phenytoin (sodium channel blocker) See TCA Toxi

nodes.title: Sotalol — QT Prolongation & Torsades
nodes.summary: Sotalol: Mg 2g IV prophylactically if QTc prolonged + overdrive pacing for Torsades — AVOID amiodarone (further QT prolongation)
nodes.body: Sotalol has Class III antiarrhythmic effects (K+ channel blockade) [1]. Unique risks: • QT prolongation • Torsades de pointes • Delayed arrhythmias (may occur hours after ingestion) Management: • Magnesium Sulfate 2g IV over 2-5 min — give prophylactically if QTc prolonged • For Torsades: Mag 2g IV push, repeat 2g at 5-15 min if it persists, then a continuous infusion (a bolus alone wears off) + o

nodes.title: Hemodialysis — Hydrophilic Agents
nodes.summary: Atenolol/nadolol are dialyzable (small Vd, hydrophilic) — propranolol/metoprolol/carvedilol are NOT dialyzable
nodes.body: Hemodialysis is effective for hydrophilic beta-blockers with small volumes of distribution [1][3]: Dialyzable agents: • Atenolol — most dialyzable, Vd 1 L/kg • Nadolol — small Vd, renally cleared • Sotalol — dialyzable (but prolonged monitoring still needed for arrhythmias) • Acebutolol — partially dialyzable NOT dialyzable (lipophilic, large Vd): • Propranolol • Metoprolol • Carvedilol • Labetalo

nodes.title: Methylene Blue — Refractory Vasoplegia
nodes.summary: Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV for refractory vasoplegia — contraindicated with serotonergics (serotonin syndrome) and G6PD
nodes.body: Methylene Blue — experimental but used in refractory vasodilatory shock [2]. Mechanism: • Inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase • Counteracts pathological vasodilation • Improves vascular tone independent of adrenergic receptors Dosing: • 1-2 mg/kg IV over 15-30 min • May repeat or start infusion 0.5-1 mg/kg/hr Cautions: • Contraindicated with serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome

nodes.title: VA-ECMO — Rescue for Refractory Shock
nodes.summary: VA-ECMO last resort — BB toxicity is REVERSIBLE, aggressive bridge therapy can lead to full neurologic recovery
nodes.body: VA-ECMO is the last resort for refractory cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest [1][2]. Key principle: Beta-blocker toxicity is potentially REVERSIBLE — aggressive bridge therapy can lead to full neurologic recovery. When to consider: • Cardiac arrest refractory to all pharmacological therapies • Refractory shock despite maximum support (glucagon + calcium + HIET + high-dose pressors + lipid) • Youn

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest — Modified ACLS
nodes.summary: Cardiac arrest: give ALL — high-dose epi, glucagon 5-10mg, CaCl 1-3g, Intralipid; CPR 30-60+ min, consider ECMO
nodes.body: Cardiac arrest from beta-blocker toxicity requires modified ACLS [1][2]: During CPR give ALL of these: • Epinephrine — high-dose (standard 1mg may be inadequate when beta-blocked) • Glucagon 5-10mg IV bolus • Calcium Chloride 1-3g IV • Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus, may repeat Prolonged resuscitation: • Toxicological arrests are potentially reversible • Continue CPR longer than typical (30-60+ mi

nodes.title: Ongoing Monitoring
nodes.summary: Wean therapies gradually — extended-release toxicity may recur, continue monitoring 24-48h for sustained-release
nodes.body: Monitoring during treatment: • Continuous cardiac telemetry • Arterial line for continuous BP if on vasopressors • Fingerstick glucose q1h (HIET) or q2h (without HIET) • BMP q4-6h (K+, glucose, renal function) • Lactate q4-6h to assess perfusion • Serial ECGs for propranolol (QRS) or sotalol (QT) Wean therapies gradually: • Glucagon infusion: halve rate q2h while monitoring • HIET: halve rate q2-4

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Psych eval MANDATORY for intentional ingestion — extended-release requires 24-48h observation due to delayed effects
nodes.body: Psychiatric evaluation is MANDATORY for all intentional ingestions after medical clearance [1]. Extended-release formulations require prolonged observation (24-48h) due to delayed absorption and prolonged effects [1][3]. What is the patient's current clinical status?

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: • Any hemodynamic instability (bradycardia, hypotension) • Required glucagon, calcium, HIET, or vasopressors • Cardiac arrhythmias • QRS widening (propranolol) or QT prolongation (sotalol) • Altered mental status or seizures • Hypoglycemia requiring treatment In the ICU: • Continuous telemetry • Serial ECGs q4-6h • Monitor glucose and K+ frequently if on HIET • Extended-rel
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous cardiac monitoring. Continue glucagon/HIET/pressors as needed. Observe 24-48h for extended-release ingestions.

nodes.title: Monitored Bed — Observation
nodes.body: Monitored bed criteria: • Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic • Normal or near-normal vital signs • Normal ECG • Immediate-release formulation Monitoring protocol: • Continuous telemetry • Vitals q1h x4, then q2h • Fingerstick glucose q2-4h • Serial ECGs if concerning agent (propranolol, sotalol) • Minimum 6h observation for immediate-release [1] • Minimum 24h for extended-release [1][3] Poison Con
nodes.recommendation: Telemetry observation. Minimum 6h for immediate-release, 24h for extended-release. Escalate to ICU if any deterioration.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.body: Safe for discharge ONLY if ALL criteria met [1]: • Asymptomatic for ≥6 hours • Normal vital signs throughout observation • Normal ECG • Normal glucose • Immediate-release formulation only — extended-release requires longer observation • Psychiatric clearance obtained (MANDATORY for intentional ingestions) Before discharge: • Document lethal means counseling • Counsel family/caregivers to secure me
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with psychiatric clearance after 6+ hours of asymptomatic observation (immediate-release only).

nodes.title: Bleeding AV Fistula / Graft
nodes.summary: Start with focal pressure. Escalate early for brisk, spontaneous, aneurysmal, infected, or recurrent access bleeding.
nodes.body: Bleeding Access Steps Dialysis access bleeding can rapidly become fatal. Treat brisk bleeding from an AV fistula or graft as arterialized venous hemorrhage until controlled. Immediate priorities: - PPE; expose the access fully - Call vascular surgery/IR early for spontaneous, recurrent, aneurysmal, infected, or uncontrolled bleeding - Apply precise focal pressure directly over the bleeding point -

nodes.title: Active Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Focal pressure over the exact hole; resuscitate and call vascular/IR early.
nodes.body: Pressure Technique Control and resuscitation happen simultaneously. Hemorrhage control: 1. One gloved finger or thumb directly over the bleeding hole; use folded gauze, hemostatic gauze, or a hard focal pressure device if available. 2. Hold uninterrupted pressure for 10-20 min. Do not repeatedly peek. 3. Elevate arm if feasible. 4. Avoid bulky circumferential wraps that hide ongoing bleeding or oc

nodes.title: Response to Focal Pressure
nodes.summary: Controlled simple puncture bleeding can be observed; uncontrolled or high-risk lesion needs vascular control.
nodes.body: After uninterrupted focal pressure for 10-20 minutes, what is the status?

nodes.title: Needle-Site Oozing
nodes.summary: Needle-site oozing gets focused pressure, reassessment, and evaluation for recurrent/prolonged bleeding drivers.
nodes.body: For typical post-dialysis needle-site bleeding: - Direct focal pressure over the hole for 10-20 min - Confirm no expanding hematoma - Review dialysis heparin exposure and anticoagulants - Check platelet count/coags if prolonged, recurrent, or unexpected - After hemostasis: confirm thrill/bruit and distal perfusion Do not place a tight circumferential wrap and send the patient out without reassessm

nodes.title: Local Hemostatic Adjuncts
nodes.summary: Use topical/hemostatic adjuncts for localized puncture bleeding; high-risk structural lesions need vascular repair.
nodes.body: Drug / Hemostasis Adjuncts If focal pressure slows but does not stop a localized puncture-site bleed: - Add hemostatic dressing if available: chitosan, kaolin, oxidized cellulose, gelatin/thrombin, or equivalent local protocol product - Consider topical Tranexamic Acid: 500-1000 mg on gauze/pledget held with focal pressure for 10-20 min - If the source is a single superficial needle hole and vascu

nodes.title: Tourniquet / BP Cuff Bridge
nodes.summary: Tourniquet/BP cuff is a bridge for life-threatening uncontrolled access hemorrhage.
nodes.body: Tourniquet Criteria Tourniquet is not first-line for routine oozing. Use it when bleeding is life-threatening and focal pressure is failing or cannot be maintained. Indications: - Brisk hemorrhage with shock or impending shock - Spurting/pulsatile bleeding not immediately controlled by direct focal pressure - Bleeding cannot be controlled during transfer, procedure setup, or resuscitation - Need t

nodes.title: High-Risk Access Lesion
nodes.summary: Scab, ulcer, necrosis, infection, pseudoaneurysm, or spontaneous bleeding requires urgent access evaluation.
nodes.body: These findings are not simple puncture bleeding: - Spontaneous bleeding between dialysis sessions - Scab over the access, especially recurrent or enlarging - Ulcerated, necrotic, shiny, depigmented, or non-pinchable skin over aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm - Rapidly expanding aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm - Exposed graft material - Infection: erythema, warmth, drainage, fever, tunnel tenderness - Recurrent pro

nodes.title: Drug Adjuncts / Reversal
nodes.summary: TXA, DDAVP, protamine, and anticoagulant reversal are adjuncts after mechanical bleeding control starts.
nodes.body: Drugs are adjuncts after mechanical control is underway. Local / hemostatic: - Tranexamic Acid topical 500-1000 mg on gauze with pressure 10-20 min for localized bleeding - IV TXA 1 g over 10 min only for major hemorrhage after weighing thrombosis/seizure risk and renal failure dosing concerns Uremic platelet dysfunction / antiplatelets: - Desmopressin 0.3-0.4 mcg/kg IV over 20-30 min; one-time do

nodes.title: Definitive Access Plan
nodes.summary: Uncontrolled bleeding or high-risk access morphology needs urgent vascular/IR involvement.
nodes.body: Does this patient need urgent vascular surgery or interventional radiology?

nodes.title: Emergent Vascular Control
nodes.summary: Tourniquet, shock, transfusion, rupture, or exposed/infected graft requires emergent vascular control.
nodes.body: Indications: - Ongoing bleeding despite focal pressure/topical adjuncts - Tourniquet/BP cuff required - Hemodynamic instability, syncope, shock index elevation, transfusion/MTP - Expanding hematoma or compartment concern - Exposed graft, infected graft, pseudoaneurysm rupture Actions: - Continue focal pressure or tourniquet bridge - Activate MTP as needed - Reverse relevant anticoagulants without
nodes.recommendation: Emergent vascular/IR source control. Do not discharge after temporary hemostasis.

nodes.title: Urgent Access Evaluation
nodes.summary: High-risk access lesions need urgent access specialist follow-up or admission/transfer.
nodes.body: High-risk access lesions need urgent specialty evaluation even if bleeding stops. Examples: - Scab or ulcer over access - Necrotic/shiny/non-pinchable skin over aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm - Recurrent spontaneous bleeding - Recurrent prolonged bleeding after dialysis - Infection or drainage near access - Large, symptomatic, or rapidly expanding aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm Plan: - Vascular surgery/IR/nephr
nodes.recommendation: Temporary hemostasis is not enough; arrange urgent access evaluation and avoid cannulation over the lesion.

nodes.title: Controlled Bleeding: Risk Check
nodes.summary: Low-risk discharge requires controlled simple puncture bleeding, stable patient, intact access, and no lesion/infection/rebleed risk.
nodes.body: Before disposition, check: - Vitals stable without recurrent bleeding - Hemoglobin acceptable or stable for clinical context - Thrill/bruit present after hemostasis - Distal perfusion and neuro exam intact - No aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, ulcer, scab, skin necrosis, infection, exposed graft, or expanding hematoma - No supratherapeutic anticoagulation or recent high-dose heparin issue requiring monit

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition depends on access morphology, recurrence risk, anticoagulation, hemodynamics, and follow-up reliability.
nodes.body: Discharge may be reasonable only when all are true: - Simple needle-site bleeding, fully controlled after observation - Stable vitals and no recurrent bleeding - No high-risk access lesion or infection - Thrill/bruit and distal perfusion intact - No need for transfusion, tourniquet, reversal, or suture for structural lesion - Dialysis unit/nephrology follow-up arranged; access site restrictions co
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only truly low-risk simple puncture bleeds; high-risk lesions require urgent access evaluation.

nodes.title: Blood Culture Stewardship — Overview
nodes.summary: Order blood cultures when pre-test probability of bacteremia exceeds contamination rate (~3%); false positives cost $1-5K and add 2-4 hospital days
nodes.body: When to Order Blood Cultures The Problem: Blood cultures are often ordered reflexively. In the ED, 20-25% of all blood cultures are drawn, but many have low diagnostic yield and high contamination rates. [1][2] The Cost of False Positives: [2][3] • Unnecessary vancomycin and prolonged antibiotic courses • Longer hospital stays (mean 2-4 extra days) • Increased healthcare costs ($1,000-$5,000 per f

nodes.title: Sepsis / Septic Shock — High Yield
nodes.summary: 2 sets from 2 peripheral sites before antibiotics — septic shock has 69% bacteremia rate; do NOT draw through central lines
nodes.body: ALWAYS obtain blood cultures before antibiotics in sepsis/septic shock. [1][5] Pre-test probability for bacteremia: [4][6] • Severe sepsis: ~38% • Septic shock: ~69% Best Practice: [1][5] • 2 sets from 2 separate peripheral sites (not through indwelling lines — high false positive rate) • Draw 20-30 mL total (10-15 mL per set) • Before antibiotics when feasible — but do NOT delay antibiotics for c

nodes.title: Other High-Yield Indications
nodes.summary: High yield: endocarditis (3 sets), meningitis, osteomyelitis, HAP, CLABSI, complicated pyelonephritis, immunocompromised
nodes.body: Blood cultures ARE recommended for: [3][4][5] Suspected endocarditis: • 3 sets from 3 separate sites over 1-24 hours • Yield: ~95% with proper technique Meningitis/encephalitis: • Before or concurrent with LP • Critical for organism identification Osteomyelitis / septic arthritis: • Before antibiotics • Positive in 30-50% of cases Healthcare-associated infections: • Hospital-acquired pneumonia • C

nodes.title: Optimal Collection Technique
nodes.summary: 20-30mL total (volume matters most), chlorhexidine antisepsis, 2 peripheral sites, diversion device reduces contamination 64%
nodes.body: Volume matters most: [1][7] • 20-30 mL total (10-15 mL per bottle pair) • Each additional mL increases yield by 3% • Under-filling is the most common error Skin antisepsis: [1] • Chlorhexidine/alcohol preferred over povidone-iodine • Allow to dry before venipuncture • Reduces contamination by 30-50% Diversion devices: [1] • Initial ~0.5-1 mL of blood diverted away from culture bottle • Reduces con

nodes.title: Proceed with Blood Cultures
nodes.body: This is a HIGH-YIELD indication for blood cultures. Checklist: ✓ 2 sets from 2 separate peripheral venipunctures ✓ 20-30 mL total blood volume ✓ Chlorhexidine antisepsis, allow to dry ✓ Use diversion device if available ✓ Draw before antibiotics (but do not delay abx for culture) ✓ Document time of draw and sites used If positive: • Assess for true pathogen vs contaminant • Repeat cultures if unce
nodes.recommendation: Obtain blood cultures. Pre-test probability of bacteremia exceeds contamination risk. Follow optimal collection technique.

nodes.title: Infection Source — Assess Yield
nodes.summary: False-positive rate often exceeds true bacteremia rate in CAP, cellulitis, uncomplicated UTI — assess yield before ordering
nodes.body: Pre-test probability varies significantly by infection source. [3][4][8] The chance of a false-positive culture is greater than the prevalence of true positive cultures in many common ED presentations. [3] Yield by Infection Type Select the primary infection source:

nodes.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
nodes.summary: Routine CAP: 6-9% yield, antibiotics changed in <1% — skip unless ICU-level, immunocompromised, or risk factors
nodes.body: Blood cultures are generally NOT recommended for uncomplicated CAP. [3][4][8] Evidence: [4][8] • Overall yield: 0.5-14%, typically 6-9% for non-ICU CAP • Antibiotic selection rarely changes: only 0.5-1% of cases have antibiotics broadened based on blood cultures • False positive rate often exceeds true positive rate When to OBTAIN blood cultures in CAP: [4][5] • Severe CAP requiring ICU admission

nodes.title: Cellulitis / Skin & Soft Tissue
nodes.summary: Simple cellulitis: <2% bacteremia rate — contamination exceeds true positives; skip unless necrotizing, septic, or immunocompromised
nodes.body: Blood cultures are NOT recommended for uncomplicated cellulitis. [3][9] Evidence: [3][9] • Bacteremia rate in simple cellulitis: <2% • False positive rate (~3%) *exceeds* true positive rate • Cultures rarely change management When to CONSIDER blood cultures in SSTI: [3][9] • Suspected necrotizing fasciitis / deep space infection • Sepsis or septic shock physiology • Severe infections requiring sur

nodes.title: UTI / Pyelonephritis
nodes.summary: Pyelonephritis: 19-25% bacteremia but same organism in 97% as urine — blood culture changed management in only 2.3% of cases
nodes.body: Blood cultures add little value in most UTIs when a urine culture is available. [3][10] Evidence for pyelonephritis: [3][10] • Pre-test probability for bacteremia: 19-25% (moderate risk) • However: blood and urine cultures yield the *same organism* in >97% of cases • Blood cultures changed management in only 2.3% of cases When to SKIP blood cultures in UTI: [3][10] • Uncomplicated cystitis • Simpl

nodes.title: Febrile Patient — Risk Stratify
nodes.summary: Shapiro rule: >=2 points = 19% bacteremia risk (cultures indicated); <2 points = <1% risk (consider skipping)
nodes.body: Fever alone is NOT an indication for blood cultures. [4][6] The Shapiro Decision Rule helps predict true bacteremia: [6] Major criteria (3 points each): • Temperature >39.4°C (103°F) • Indwelling vascular catheter • Clinical suspicion of endocarditis Minor criteria (1 point each): • Temperature 38.3-39.3°C • Age >65 years • Rigors • Vomiting • Hypotension (SBP <90) • WBC >18,000 • Bands >5% • Plat

nodes.title: Bacteremia Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Rigors = LR 4.7 for bacteremia; high risk with indwelling devices, immunosuppression, liver disease, asplenia
nodes.body: Physical exam findings that increase bacteremia risk: [4][6] Most predictive: [6] • Rigors — likelihood ratio 4.7 for bacteremia • Shaking chills — highly specific • Fever + rigors in combination Other risk factors: [4] • Indwelling vascular device • Immunosuppression • Recent hospitalization • Injection drug use • Chronic liver disease • Asplenia • Prosthetic valves/joints Low-risk features: • Is

nodes.title: Blood Cultures NOT Recommended
nodes.body: This is a LOW-YIELD indication. Blood cultures are NOT recommended. [3] Reasons to skip: • Pre-test probability of bacteremia is low (<3-5%) • False positive rate may exceed true positive rate • Result unlikely to change management • Unnecessary vancomycin, prolonged stays, increased costs Document your reasoning: "Blood cultures not obtained given low pre-test probability of bacteremia, clear sou
nodes.recommendation: Do NOT obtain blood cultures. Pre-test probability is low and false-positive risk exceeds benefit. Use source-specific cultures instead.

nodes.title: Contamination — The Problem
nodes.summary: CoNS = most common contaminant (only 10-12% true infection); S. aureus, E. coli, Candida >90% true pathogens
nodes.body: Blood culture contamination rates in EDs often exceed 3% benchmark. [1][2] Most common contaminants: [2][11] • Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) — 45-60% of all isolates, only 10-12% represent true infection • *Corynebacterium* species • *Bacillus* species • *Propionibacterium acnes* Organisms that ALWAYS/NEARLY ALWAYS (>90%) represent true infection: [11] • *S. aureus* • *S. pneumoniae* • *

nodes.title: Interpreting Positive Cultures
nodes.summary: S. aureus/E. coli/Candida = true pathogen >90%; CoNS in single bottle with <3 SIRS = likely contaminant
nodes.body: When a blood culture comes back positive, assess likelihood of true bacteremia vs contamination. [11] Factors suggesting TRUE bacteremia: [11] • Organism: *S. aureus*, Enterobacteriaceae, *Candida* • Multiple positive bottles (≥2 of 4) • Positive culture from multiple separate draws • Clinical picture consistent with bacteremia • ≥3 SIRS criteria present (probability 72.3%) • Time to positivity <1

nodes.title: Likely True Bacteremia
nodes.body: This organism is highly likely to represent true bloodstream infection. [11] Next steps: • Continue/adjust antibiotics based on susceptibilities • Repeat cultures to document clearance (esp. *S. aureus*) • Search for source (POCUS, CT, echo) • Evaluate for endocarditis if *S. aureus* • ID consultation for persistent or complicated bacteremia Duration of therapy: • Varies by organism and source • *
nodes.recommendation: True bacteremia likely. Narrow antibiotics by susceptibilities, repeat cultures, source search, consider ID consultation.

nodes.title: Likely Contaminant
nodes.body: This organism is likely contamination, NOT true infection. [11] Clinical decision: • Assess patient clinical status — are they improving? • If stable/improving: contamination more likely • If deteriorating: consider repeat cultures and broader coverage For isolated CoNS in single bottle: [11] • If <3 SIRS criteria and no CVC: 77-85% likely contamination • Consider observation without vancomycin •
nodes.recommendation: Likely contamination. Do not reflexively treat with vancomycin. Reassess clinical status. Repeat cultures only if clinical concern.

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Neutropenic fever: always culture; ESRD/IVDU: low threshold; elderly may not mount SIRS; recent abx: draw at trough
nodes.body: Immunocompromised — Lower threshold for cultures: [5] • Febrile neutropenia (ANC <500): ALWAYS culture • Solid organ transplant within 1 year • Hematologic malignancy on chemotherapy • HIV with CD4 <200 • Chronic high-dose steroids ESRD/Hemodialysis: [3] • Higher bacteremia risk (intravascular devices) • Same initial fluid boluses recommended despite dialysis status • Culture if febrile or systemi

nodes.title: 2024 Shortage & Stewardship Response
nodes.summary: 2024 shortage showed 20-40% reduction in cultures caused no harm — overuse is the norm; stewardship improves care
nodes.body: The June 2024 blood culture bottle shortage accelerated stewardship adoption. [1][12] What happened: [12] • BD Diagnostics shortage forced conservation strategies • FDA added blood culture media bottles to shortage list • CDC issued Health Advisory urging mitigation plans What we learned: [1][12] • Stewardship protocols *reduced* blood culture use without increasing sepsis mortality • Many institu

nodes.title: Massive Transfusion Protocol
nodes.summary: MTP activation: ABC score ≥2 or SI ≥1.0; ongoing hemorrhagic shock despite resuscitation
nodes.body: When to Activate MTP ABC Score (Assessment of Blood Consumption): - 1 point each: - HR ≥120 bpm - SBP ≤90 mmHg - Penetrating torso injury - Positive FAST exam - Score ≥2: 75% sensitivity, 86% specificity for MT need Shock Index (SI = HR/SBP): - SI ≥1.0: Stronger predictor than ABC - AUROC 0.83, Sens 67.7%, Spec 81.3% Clinical Triggers: - Ongoing hemorrhagic shock despite 2L crystalloid - Persisten

nodes.title: MTP Protocol
nodes.summary: MTP: 1:1:1 ratio (PRBC:FFP:plt); O neg first; TXA + calcium; labs q30-60min; target fib >150, plt >50k
nodes.body: MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL Definition: ≥10 units PRBCs in 24h OR ≥4 units in 1 hour with ongoing bleeding 1:1:1 Ratio (Standard MTP): - 1 PRBC : 1 FFP : 1 platelet unit - Approximates whole blood composition - Evidence supports survival benefit Activation Steps: 1. Call blood bank: "Activate MTP" 2. Provide patient location, 2 identifiers 3. First cooler arrives in ~10 min 4. Send type & screen

nodes.title: MTP Cooler Contents
nodes.summary: MTP cooler: 4 O neg PRBCs, 2 FFP, 1 plt unit; FFP takes 20-30 min to thaw; warm all products
nodes.body: TYPICAL MTP COOLER CONTENTS First Cooler (Emergency Release): - 4 units O negative PRBCs (uncrossmatched) - 2 units FFP (thawed or liquid plasma) - 1 unit platelet concentrate (pooled) - TXA 1g preloaded (some institutions) Subsequent Coolers: - 4-6 units type-specific PRBCs - 4 units FFP - 1-2 units platelets - 10 units cryoprecipitate (if fibrinogen low) Whole Blood (If Available): - Approximate

nodes.title: MTP Deactivation
nodes.summary: Deactivate MTP when: hemorrhage controlled, hemodynamically stable, coagulopathy corrected, no further MT needed
nodes.body: WHEN TO DEACTIVATE MTP Deactivation Criteria: - Hemorrhage controlled (surgery, IR, direct pressure) - Hemodynamic stability achieved - No ongoing massive transfusion requirement - Coagulopathy corrected (INR normalized, fibrinogen adequate) - No further transfusions anticipated in next 4 hours Transition to Standard Transfusion: - Switch to type-specific blood - Continue monitoring labs - Maintai

nodes.title: Component Therapy
nodes.summary: Component therapy: PRBCs (Hgb <7 restrictive), FFP (PT >1.5x), platelets (<50k + bleed), cryo (fib <1.0)
nodes.body: Blood Component Selection PRBCs: - Restrictive threshold: Hgb <7 g/dL (stable) - Liberal threshold: Hgb <9-10 g/dL (shock, cardiac) - 1 unit = ↑Hgb ~1 g/dL FFP: - PT/aPTT >1.5x normal with bleeding - Fibrinogen <1.0 g/L with bleeding - Dose: 10-15 mL/kg Platelets: - Active bleed + plt <50k - Procedure: plt >50k needed - 1 transfusion = ↑plt 5-10k Cryoprecipitate: - Fibrinogen <1.0-1.5 g/L with ble

nodes.title: PRBCs (Packed Red Blood Cells)
nodes.summary: PRBCs: restrictive Hgb <7 (stable), liberal <9-10 (ACS/shock); 1 unit ↑Hgb 1 g/dL; peds 10-20 mL/kg
nodes.body: PACKED RED BLOOD CELLS Indications: - Acute hemorrhage requiring O2-carrying capacity - Symptomatic anemia Hemoglobin Thresholds: Restrictive (Stable Patients): - Transfuse if Hgb <7 g/dL - Outcomes equivalent or better than liberal - Use in most ICU, surgical, GI bleed patients Liberal (Specific Indications): - Hgb <9-10 g/dL - Active hemorrhagic shock - Acute coronary syndrome - Symptomatic card

nodes.title: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)
nodes.summary: FFP: PT/aPTT >1.5x with bleed; dose 10-15 mL/kg; takes 20-30 min to thaw; NOT for volume expansion
nodes.body: FRESH FROZEN PLASMA Indications: - PT >1.5x normal with active bleeding - aPTT >1.5x normal with active bleeding - Fibrinogen <1.0 g/L with bleeding - Warfarin reversal (when PCC unavailable) - Massive transfusion (MTP component) - TTP (therapeutic plasma exchange) Dosing: - Standard: 10-15 mL/kg (3-4 units adult) - Achieves ~30% factor replacement - Warfarin reversal: 5-8 mL/kg (10% factor replac

nodes.title: Platelet Transfusion
nodes.summary: Platelets: <50k + bleed → transfuse; microvascular/CNS bleed → maintain >100k; 1 transfusion ↑5-10k
nodes.body: PLATELET CONCENTRATE Transfusion Thresholds: Active Bleeding: - Platelet count <50k + bleeding → transfuse - Diffuse microvascular bleeding → maintain >100k - CNS hemorrhage → maintain >100k Prophylaxis (No Bleeding): - Bone marrow failure: <10k (no risk factors) - Bone marrow failure: <20k (with risk factors) - Before invasive procedure: >50k needed - Before neuraxial procedure: >80k - Before neu

nodes.title: Cryoprecipitate
nodes.summary: Cryo: fib <1.0 with bleed; 1 unit/10 kg (10 units adult); 10 units ↑fib ~75 mg/dL; target fib >150-200
nodes.body: CRYOPRECIPITATE Contents (per unit): - Fibrinogen ~250-366 mg - Factor VIII ~100 AHU - Factor XIII - von Willebrand Factor - Fibronectin Indications: - Fibrinogen <1.0 g/L with bleeding - Fibrinogen <1.5 g/L in massive transfusion - DIC with hypofibrinogenemia - Dysfibrinogenemia Dosing: - Generic: 1 unit per 10 kg body weight - Standard adult: 10 units (pooled) - 10 units increases fibrinogen ~75

nodes.title: Transfusion Complications
nodes.summary: Transfusion complications: TACO/TRALI (pulmonary), hemolytic, febrile, allergic, metabolic
nodes.body: TRANSFUSION REACTIONS Pulmonary (Both cause dyspnea + hypoxia during/after transfusion): - TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload): Volume overload → cardiogenic pulmonary edema - TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury): Immune reaction → non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema Immunologic: - Acute hemolytic: ABO incompatibility (emergency) - Febrile non-hemolytic: Most common reaction -

nodes.title: TACO vs TRALI
nodes.summary: TACO = volume overload (BNP high, diuretics work); TRALI = lung injury (BNP normal, supportive care only)
nodes.body: Both Present Similarly: Dyspnea, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates during or shortly after transfusion. The critical difference is the underlying mechanism. --- TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload) *Volume overload → heart can't handle the extra fluid* - Mechanism: Too much volume for the heart/kidneys to handle - Think: Flash pulmonary edema from CHF exacerbation - Timing: During trans

nodes.title: TACO (Circulatory Overload)
nodes.summary: TACO: volume overload → cardiogenic edema; BNP elevated; treat with diuretics, O2, upright positioning
nodes.body: TACO = Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload What is it? Volume overload causing cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Think of it like giving too much IV fluid to a CHF patient. Mechanism: - Patient has underlying cardiac or renal dysfunction - Transfusion adds volume the heart can't handle - Result: Elevated hydrostatic pressure → fluid leaks into lungs Diagnosis (3+ within 12h of transfusion): - D

nodes.title: TRALI (Acute Lung Injury)
nodes.summary: TRALI: immune lung injury → non-cardiogenic edema; BNP normal, no JVD; supportive care only; resolves 48-96h
nodes.body: TRALI = Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury What is it? An immune reaction that damages the lung capillaries, causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. The heart is fine, but the lungs are leaking. Mechanism: - Immune (80-85%): Donor plasma contains antibodies (anti-HLA or anti-HNA) that activate the recipient's neutrophils - Activated neutrophils sequester in pulmonary capillaries → release toxi

nodes.title: Acute Hemolytic Reaction
nodes.summary: Acute hemolytic: STOP transfusion, verify ID, aggressive fluids + bicarb for renal protection; Direct Coombs positive
nodes.body: ACUTE HEMOLYTIC TRANSFUSION REACTION Mechanism: - ABO incompatibility (most common cause) - Host antibodies bind donor RBCs → intravascular hemolysis - Can occur with just a few milliliters of blood Classic Triad (rarely all present): - Fever - Flank/back pain - Dark red/brown urine (hemoglobinuria) Other Signs: - Anxiety, chest pain, dyspnea - Hypotension (under anesthesia may be only sign) - Unc

nodes.title: Febrile Non-Hemolytic Reaction
nodes.summary: FNHTR: most common reaction; fever + Direct Coombs negative; treat with antipyretic; can resume if no other reaction
nodes.body: FEBRILE NON-HEMOLYTIC TRANSFUSION REACTION (FNHTR) Most common transfusion reaction Mechanism: - Cytokine accumulation during storage (especially platelets) - OR recipient HLA alloantibodies reacting against donor white blood cells Diagnosis (this is a diagnosis of exclusion): - Fever: ≥38°C OR rise ≥1°C from baseline within 4h - Moderate/severe: ≥39°C OR rise ≥1.5°C, chills/rigors - DAT (Direct A

nodes.title: Allergic Reactions
nodes.summary: Allergic: mild (antihistamine, resume), moderate (steroids), severe/anaphylaxis (epi, stop transfusion, airway)
nodes.body: ALLERGIC TRANSFUSION REACTIONS MILD ALLERGIC: - Itching, urticaria, localized swelling - Treatment: - Pause transfusion - Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IV - Can resume if symptoms resolve MODERATE ALLERGIC: - Pruritus, urticaria, flushing - Angioedema (non-airway) - Treatment: - Antihistamine - Consider corticosteroid - May resume if symptoms resolve SEVERE/ANAPHYLAXIS: - Airway edema, bronchospasm - H

nodes.title: Metabolic Complications
nodes.summary: Metabolic: hypocalcemia (citrate) → impairs clotting/cardiac; hyperkalemia (esp peds); hypothermia worsens coagulopathy
nodes.body: METABOLIC COMPLICATIONS OF TRANSFUSION HYPOCALCEMIA (Citrate Toxicity): - Citrate anticoagulant chelates ionized calcium - Risk factors: Massive transfusion, liver dysfunction - iCa <1.1 mmol/L associated with mortality Effects of hypocalcemia: - Impairs coagulation cascade (factors need Ca2+) - Impairs platelet function - Cardiac depression (QT prolongation, arrhythmias) Treatment: - See Calcium

nodes.summary: Special situations: emergency release O neg, AIHA, Jehovah's Witness alternatives, pediatric dosing
nodes.body: Special Transfusion Scenarios Emergency Release: - O negative (universal donor) - When type unknown, can't wait Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia: - All blood "incompatible" - Can still transfuse if life-threatening Jehovah's Witness: - Blood alternatives, cell salvage - Varies by individual preference Pediatric Considerations: - Weight-based dosing - Hyperkalemia risk higher Select topic:

nodes.title: Emergency Release (O Negative)
nodes.summary: Emergency release: O neg safest; O pos OK for males >16, females >50; ~0.1% hemolysis risk
nodes.body: EMERGENCY RELEASE BLOOD Indications: - Acute hemorrhage requiring immediate transfusion - Type unknown - Pretransfusion testing too slow Protocol: 1. Physician authorization required 2. Provide patient name/location, 2 identifiers 3. Blood available in ~10 minutes 4. Send type & screen (don't delay transfusion) Product Selection: O Negative: - Safest universal donor - Use for all females of childb

nodes.title: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
nodes.summary: AIHA: can transfuse "incompatible" blood in emergency; autoantibodies react with all RBCs; clinical status guides
nodes.body: AIHA TRANSFUSION MANAGEMENT Challenge: - Patient's autoantibodies react with ALL normal RBCs - All crossmatches will be "incompatible" - May mask underlying alloantibodies Key Principle: Most AIHA patients tolerate "incompatible" RBCs without significant increase in hemolysis Emergency Transfusion (Life-Threatening Anemia): - Use O negative blood if type unknown - Avoiding hemodynamic collapse > h

nodes.title: Jehovah's Witness
nodes.summary: Jehovah's Witness: preferences vary - ask; cell salvage, EPO, factors often OK; avoid stored bank products
nodes.body: JEHOVAH'S WITNESS TRANSFUSION ALTERNATIVES Preferences Vary by Individual - Always Discuss Generally Acceptable: - Cell salvage (blood in continuous circuit with body) - Recombinant erythropoietin (EPO) - Clotting factors, fibrinogen concentrate - Albumin, immunoglobulins - Cardiopulmonary bypass - IV iron preparations Generally NOT Acceptable: - Whole blood from blood bank - PRBCs, FFP, platelets

nodes.title: Pediatric Transfusion Dosing
nodes.summary: Pediatric dosing: PRBCs 10-20 mL/kg, FFP 10-15 mL/kg, plt 10 mL/kg; higher hyperkalemia risk
nodes.body: PEDIATRIC TRANSFUSION DOSING PRBCs: - Dose: 10-20 mL/kg - 5-10 mL/kg increases Hgb ~10 g/L - Max: 4 units per transfusion event FFP: - Dose: 10-15 mL/kg Platelets: - Dose: 10 mL/kg (pooled) Cryoprecipitate: - Dose: 0.1 unit/kg (or 1 unit per 5-10 kg) TXA: - Loading: 20 mg/kg over 10 min - Maintenance: 10 mg/kg/hr for 8 hours Calcium: - Calcium gluconate: 50 mg/kg - Calcium chloride: 10 mg/kg (cent

nodes.title: Transfusion Adjuncts
nodes.summary: Adjuncts: TXA (within 3h), calcium (q4 units), PCC (warfarin reversal), fibrinogen concentrate
nodes.body: Adjuncts to Blood Transfusion TXA (Tranexamic Acid): - Reduces blood loss by ~1/3 - Must give within 3 hours (best <1 hour) Calcium Replacement: - Citrate chelates calcium - Give 1g every 4 units PRBCs - Target iCa >1.1 mmol/L PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate): - Warfarin reversal (preferred over FFP) - Factors II, VII, IX, X Fibrinogen Concentrate: - Alternative to cryoprecipitate - More prec

nodes.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
nodes.summary: TXA: 1g bolus over 10 min, then 1g over 8h; MUST give <3h (best <1h); 32% mortality reduction
nodes.body: TRANEXAMIC ACID - ANTIFIBRINOLYTIC Mechanism: - Lysine analog blocks plasminogen binding sites - Inhibits fibrinolysis → prevents clot breakdown - Reduces blood loss by ~1/3 Adult Dosing: - Loading: 1 g IV bolus in 100 mL NS over 10 min - (Slow infusion prevents hypotension) - Maintenance: 1 g over next 8 hours - Maximum: 2 g total TIMING IS CRITICAL: - <1 hour from injury: 32% mortality reduction

nodes.title: Calcium Replacement Protocol
nodes.summary: Calcium: 1g gluconate (peripheral) or chloride (central) q4 units PRBCs; target iCa >1.1 mmol/L
nodes.body: CALCIUM REPLACEMENT IN MASSIVE TRANSFUSION Why Calcium Matters: - Citrate anticoagulant chelates ionized calcium - iCa <1.1 mmol/L associated with mortality - Calcium required for: - Coagulation cascade (factors II, VII, IX, X) - Platelet activation - Cardiac contractility Dosing (Joint Trauma System): Calcium Gluconate (Peripheral IV OK): - 1 g (30 mL of 10%) = 3 mmol Ca2+ - Give with first unit

nodes.title: PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate)
nodes.summary: PCC: 4-factor preferred; 25-50 IU/kg for warfarin reversal; faster than FFP, lower volume
nodes.body: PROTHROMBIN COMPLEX CONCENTRATE Contents: - 4-factor PCC (Kcentra): Factors II, VII, IX, X (preferred) - 3-factor PCC: Factors II, IX, X (± VII) FDA Indication: - Warfarin reversal with acute bleeding or urgent procedure Off-Label Uses: - DOAC reversal (if specific antidotes unavailable) - Bleeding in factor deficiency - Trauma coagulopathy (adjunct) Dosing (Warfarin Reversal): - Expressed in unit
