nodes.title: Botulism
nodes.summary: The 4 Ds: Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia, Descending paralysis — afebrile, clear sensorium, symmetric, dilated pupils
nodes.body: Botulism Summary - descending symmetric paralysis from Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin. Botulism is a rare but life-threatening neuroparalytic illness caused by botulinum toxin, the most potent biological toxin known. CLASSIC PRESENTATION - The "4 Ds": - Diplopia (double vision) - Dysarthria (slurred speech) - Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) - Descending paralysis (cranial nerves first, then de

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess for bulbar symptoms, descending motor weakness, autonomic dysfunction — sensory and mental status NORMAL
nodes.body: Assess for classic botulism features: Bulbar symptoms (earliest): - Diplopia, blurred vision, ptosis - Dysarthria, dysphonia - Dysphagia - Facial weakness (symmetric) Descending motor weakness: - Proximal > distal - Upper extremities before lower - Progresses to respiratory muscles Autonomic dysfunction: - Dilated, fixed or sluggish pupils - Dry mouth, decreased secretions - Constipation, ileus -

nodes.title: Determine Botulism Type
nodes.summary: Identify source: foodborne (preformed toxin, 12-36h onset), wound (IVDU, 4-14d), infant (spores, <1yr)
nodes.body: Botulism Types Comparison - foodborne vs wound vs infant. THREE MAIN TYPES - Identify the source: 1. FOODBORNE BOTULISM - Ingestion of PREFORMED toxin - Home-canned foods (low acid vegetables), fermented fish - Onset: 12-36 hours (range 6 hours to 10 days) - GI symptoms often precede neuro (nausea, vomiting, cramping) - Consider if >1 person affected from same meal 2. WOUND BOTULISM - Toxin produc

nodes.title: Foodborne Botulism
nodes.summary: Home-canned vegetables, fermented fish — GI prodrome before neuro; multiple cases from same meal is pathognomonic
nodes.body: Foodborne botulism results from ingestion of preformed botulinum toxin in contaminated food. High-risk foods: - Home-canned vegetables (especially low-acid: green beans, corn, beets) - Fermented fish (Alaska Native communities) - Improperly stored foods (garlic in oil, baked potatoes in foil) - Home-cured meats, sausages - Honey (spores, not preformed toxin - relevant for infants) Timeline: - Onse

nodes.title: Wound Botulism
nodes.summary: IVDU wound botulism: black tar heroin/skin-popping — NO GI symptoms, longer incubation 4-14d, wound may look benign
nodes.body: Wound Botulism in IVDU Checklist - high-risk assessment. Wound botulism occurs when C. botulinum spores germinate in a wound and produce toxin locally. KEY POPULATION: IV Drug Users - Black tar heroin (contaminated with spores from soil/tar) - Skin-popping (subcutaneous injection) - Muscling (intramuscular injection) - Sinusitis in cocaine users (intranasal route) Clinical differences from foodbor

nodes.title: Infant Botulism
nodes.summary: Infant <1yr: floppy baby, constipation first — BabyBIG (510-231-7600), do NOT give antibiotics (releases more toxin)
nodes.body: Infant Botulism & BabyBIG Guide - diagnosis and treatment specifics. Infant botulism is the most common form of botulism in the US. Mechanism: - Ingestion of C. botulinum SPORES (not preformed toxin) - Spores germinate in immature GI tract (lacks protective flora) - Toxin produced in vivo Age: <1 year (peak 2-4 months) Classic presentation - "Floppy Baby": - Constipation (often first symptom, may

nodes.summary: Botulism vs GBS vs MG: descending vs ascending, dilated pupils (unique), normal sensory, prominent autonomic, normal CSF
nodes.body: Descending Paralysis DDx - Botulism vs GBS vs MG vs Stroke. KEY DIFFERENTIATOR TABLE: | Feature | Botulism | GBS | MG | |---------|----------|-----|----| | Direction | DESCENDING | ASCENDING | Variable/fatigable | | Pupils | Dilated, fixed | Normal | Normal | | Reflexes | Normal->absent | Absent early | Normal | | Sensory | Normal | Abnormal | Normal | | Autonomic | Prominent | Variable | Minimal

nodes.title: Key Differentiating Features
nodes.summary: Red flags: fixed dilated pupils, clear sensorium, descending symmetric pattern, afebrile — treat empirically if uncertain
nodes.body: Botulism RED FLAGS (strongly suggests botulism over mimics): 1. Dilated, fixed or sluggish pupils - GBS and MG have normal pupils 2. Clear sensorium - Patient is alert despite profound weakness 3. Descending pattern - Starts cranial, moves caudally (GBS is ASCENDING) 4. Symmetric - Asymmetry suggests stroke 5. Normal sensory exam - Sensory abnormalities suggest GBS 6. Autonomic features - Constipa

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS — do NOT wait for labs to treat; mouse bioassay takes 1-4 days; normal CSF helps rule out GBS
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Botulism is a CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS. Do NOT wait for laboratory confirmation to treat - antitoxin is time-sensitive. Laboratory confirmation (takes days): Mouse bioassay - Gold standard - Inject patient serum into mice, observe for paralysis - Takes 1-4 days - Send: serum, stool, gastric contents, wound culture Samples to collect: - Serum (before antitoxin if possible, but do not delay trea

nodes.title: Imaging & Electrodiagnostics
nodes.summary: CT/MRI brain normal (rules out stroke), EMG incremental response at >50Hz (OPPOSITE of MG which is decremental)
nodes.body: Imaging: CT/MRI brain: - NORMAL in botulism - Rules out stroke, brainstem lesion - Important given bulbar symptoms MRI spine: - NORMAL in botulism - Rules out cord compression, transverse myelitis EMG/Nerve Conduction Studies: - May support diagnosis but do not delay treatment - Classic findings: - Low-amplitude compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) - Incremental response to rapid repetitive s

nodes.title: Antitoxin Treatment - Time Critical
nodes.summary: Call CDC 770-488-7100 NOW — HBAT 1 vial IV neutralizes circulating toxin only; earlier = better outcomes, 10% hypersensitivity
nodes.body: Antitoxin Dosing & CDC Contact - critical treatment information. ANTITOXIN IS TIME-SENSITIVE - DO NOT DELAY Mechanism: - Neutralizes CIRCULATING toxin only - Does NOT reverse toxin already bound to nerve terminals - Earlier administration = better outcomes, less ventilator time How to obtain (adults): - CDC Emergency Operations Center: 770-488-7100 (24/7) - State health department can also facilit

nodes.title: Antitoxin Administration
nodes.summary: Administer even if diagnosis uncertain — epinephrine at bedside for anaphylaxis; effective up to days after onset
nodes.body: Administration protocol: 1. Call CDC Emergency Operations: 770-488-7100 2. State health department facilitates release 3. Antitoxin shipped emergently from nearest depot 4. Pre-medicate with diphenhydramine + corticosteroid (optional) 5. Have epinephrine at bedside 6. Infuse HBAT per package insert (slow initial rate, increase as tolerated) Reactions (10% incidence): - Urticaria, pruritus (most co

nodes.summary: BabyBIG 50mg/kg IV for infants (510-231-7600) — human-derived, reduces hospital stay from 5.5 to 2.5 weeks; NO antibiotics

nodes.title: Supportive Care - Airway Management
nodes.summary: Airway is priority — intubate early if FVC <12-15 mL/kg; anticipate weeks of ventilation until nerve regeneration
nodes.body: AIRWAY IS THE PRIORITY Respiratory failure is the primary cause of death in botulism. Early intubation criteria: - Bulbar symptoms with aspiration risk - FVC declining or <12-15 mL/kg - Hypoxia, hypercapnia - Weak cough, inability to clear secretions - Progressive weakness despite antitoxin Anticipate prolonged ventilation: - Weeks to months until nerve terminals regenerate - Early tracheostomy co

nodes.body: Wound botulism requires additional interventions: 1. WOUND DEBRIDEMENT: - Surgical consultation - Thorough debridement of infected/necrotic tissue - May need multiple debridements - Send wound tissue for culture 2. ANTIBIOTICS: - Required for wound botulism (unlike foodborne/infant) - Targets C. botulinum and prevents further toxin production Antibiotic options: - Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h - Pre

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ALL suspected botulism = ICU admission — serial FVC q4h, rapid intubation access, do not delay antitoxin for transfer
nodes.body: ALL SUSPECTED BOTULISM: ICU ADMISSION There is no outpatient management of suspected botulism. ICU requirements: - Continuous pulse oximetry - Serial FVC monitoring (q4h minimum) - Cardiac monitoring (autonomic instability) - Rapid access to intubation - Antitoxin administration and monitoring Consultation: - Infectious disease - Pulmonology/Critical care - Neurology (confirm diagnosis, exclude mi

nodes.body: Respiratory monitoring: - FVC every 4 hours (more frequently if declining) - NIF (negative inspiratory force) - Single breath count - Cough strength assessment - Continuous pulse oximetry - ABG if clinical concern Intubation thresholds: - FVC <12-15 mL/kg - NIF weaker than -30 cmH2O - Any bulbar symptoms with aspiration risk - Rapid decline in respiratory parameters - Hypoxia or hypercapnia Neurol

nodes.title: Prognosis
nodes.body: PROGNOSIS IS GOOD WITH MODERN ICU CARE Mortality: - <5% with modern ICU care and antitoxin - Was 60% in pre-antitoxin era - Death usually from respiratory failure, aspiration, or delayed diagnosis Recovery: - Weeks to months - nerve terminals must regenerate - Full recovery expected in most cases - Earlier antitoxin = shorter ventilator course Recovery timeline: - Improvement begins when new nerve

nodes.title: Bradycardic Arrest: Recognition
nodes.summary: Confirm asystole in 2 leads — low gain and lead disconnect mimic flatline
nodes.body: Bradycardic Arrest Steps Summary Bradycardic arrest: extreme bradycardia (<20 bpm) or asystole causing pulselessness. Key steps: • Confirm rhythm in 2 leads — avoid misdiagnosing lead disconnect artifact as asystole • Check gain settings — low gain can mimic flat line • True asystole: no electrical activity in any lead • Extreme bradycardia: wide QRS escape rhythm, usually <20 bpm

nodes.title: Asystole Management
nodes.summary: Asystole is non-shockable — CPR + epi ASAP, TCP rarely captures
nodes.body: Asystole is a non-shockable rhythm — do NOT defibrillate. • CPR immediately — high-quality compressions • Epinephrine 1mg IV/IO ASAP, repeat q3-5 min • TCP rarely effective in true asystole — pacing spikes without capture • Search aggressively for reversible causes (H's and T's) Futility signal: • ETCO2 <10 mmHg after 20 min of CPR → consider termination of resuscitation

nodes.title: Transcutaneous Pacing

nodes.body: Transcutaneous pacing immediately — don't wait for medications. nodes.title: Atropine
nodes.summary: Atropine 1mg IV q3-5min max 3mg — ineffective for infranodal block
nodes.body: Atropine 1mg IV q3-5 min, max 3 doses (3mg total) Effective in: • Sinus bradycardia • AV nodal block (1° AVB, Mobitz I) Limited efficacy in: • Infranodal block (Mobitz II, 3° AVB) — block is below the vagal innervation • Transplanted hearts — denervated, no vagal tone to reverse • Wide-complex escape rhythms Do NOT delay pacing for atropine — atropine is an adjunct, not a substitute for pacing

nodes.title: Chronotropic Infusions
nodes.summary: Epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min bridge — titrate to HR >60 and adequate perfusion
nodes.body: First-line: • Epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min IV — titrate to HR >60 and adequate perfusion Alternative (if epi unavailable): • Dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion For denervated hearts (transplant): • Isoproterenol 2-10 mcg/min — direct beta-agonist, bypasses vagal pathway Key points: • These are bridges to definitive pacing — not endpoints • Titrate to clinical effect (HR, BP, mental status)

nodes.title: Reversible Causes of Bradycardic Arrest
nodes.summary: HyperK: calcium gluconate 1-3g IV stat — hypothermia: rewarm >30C before pacing
nodes.body: Treatable causes of bradycardic arrest: • Hyperkalemia (wide QRS, peaked T): Calcium Gluconate 1-3g IV + bicarb + insulin/dextrose • Hypothermia: active rewarming, defer pacing until >30°C (myocardium irritable below 30°C) • Drug toxicity: beta blocker → Glucagon 3-10mg IV; Ca channel blocker → calcium + high-dose insulin; Digoxin → DigiFab • AV block (complete): temporary pacing bridge → TVP → pe

nodes.title: Reversible Cause Identified?
nodes.summary: Reversible cause found? Treat cause while maintaining pacing and medications
nodes.body: Has a reversible cause been identified?

nodes.title: Treating Reversible Cause
nodes.summary: Treat empirically — calcium gluconate minimal downside even if hyperK unconfirmed
nodes.body: Continue treating identified cause while maintaining pacing/medications. • Reassess rhythm and hemodynamics after each intervention • If hyperkalemia suspected, treat empirically even before labs return — calcium gluconate has minimal downside • Monitor for response: narrowing QRS, improving rate, return of pulse • May need to treat multiple causes simultaneously

nodes.title: Transvenous Pacing
nodes.summary: Transvenous pacing via RIJ preferred — float without fluoro if unstable
nodes.body: Transvenous pacing (TVP) — definitive temporary pacing: Access: • Right internal jugular (RIJ) — preferred, direct line to RV • Femoral vein — alternative, easier access during CPR Placement: • RV apex or RVOT • Confirm capture on monitor AND by pulse/POCUS Emergency TVP: • Float without fluoroscopy if patient unstable • Use balloon-tipped catheter for flow-directed placement • Confirm position wi

nodes.title: Post-Capture Management
nodes.summary: Keep TCP pads as backup even after TVP — prepare for definitive pacing
nodes.body: TCP capture achieved — stabilize and plan: • Monitor closely — TCP can lose capture with patient movement • Prepare for transvenous pacing as definitive therapy • Continue medications as bridge (epi or dopamine infusion) • Identify and treat underlying cause • Cardiology consult for permanent pacing evaluation Do not remove TCP pads — keep as backup even after TVP placed

nodes.title: Patient Status
nodes.summary: ROSC vs deterioration vs TOR — determine next pathway at each pulse check
nodes.body: What is the current patient status?

nodes.title: ROSC Achieved
nodes.summary: Post-ROSC: 12-lead ECG, maintain pacing, TTM, cardiology for permanent pacer
nodes.body: ROSC → Post-Cardiac Arrest Care • Post-Cardiac Arrest Care • 12-lead ECG — identify cause (STEMI, hyperK pattern, drug toxicity) • Continue pacing — do not remove TCP until TVP or stable intrinsic rhythm • Cardiology consult for permanent pacing evaluation • Targeted temperature management per protocol • Serial labs: K, lactate, troponin, blood gas
nodes.recommendation: Post-ROSC care: maintain pacing, 12-lead ECG, identify cause, cardiology consult.

nodes.title: Re-arrest
nodes.summary: Re-arrest: resume CPR, check pacing capture, reassess reversible causes
nodes.body: Re-arrest — return to CPR immediately. • Reassess pacing capture — may have lost contact • Increase mA if electrical capture lost • Reassess reversible causes — something was missed or undertreated • Consider ECPR if available and criteria met • Continue epinephrine 1mg IV/IO q3-5 min

nodes.title: Termination of Resuscitation
nodes.summary: ETCO2 <10 after 20min = strong futility — exception: hypothermia, warm first
nodes.body: Asystole is the strongest futility signal in cardiac arrest. Consider TOR when: • ETCO2 <10 mmHg after 20 min of high-quality CPR • No reversible cause identified • No cardiac activity on POCUS (cardiac standstill) • No response to pacing, medications, or cause-directed therapy EXCEPTION — Hypothermia: • Rewarm to >30°C before declaring futility • "Not dead until warm and dead" • Active rewarming:

nodes.title: Code Called
nodes.summary: Document resuscitation timeline, pacing parameters, ETCO2, TOR rationale
nodes.body: Code called. Document all interventions, pacing attempts, and reasoning. Documentation checklist: • Resuscitation timeline (arrest → interventions → TOR) • Pacing parameters attempted (rate, mA, pad positions) • ETCO2 values throughout resuscitation • Medications given with times • Reversible causes evaluated • Termination rationale • Family communication
nodes.recommendation: Document resuscitation timeline, pacing parameters, ETCO2 values, and termination rationale.

nodes.title: Brain Herniation — Recognition
nodes.summary: Anisocoria + altered consciousness = assume herniation — treat before CT
nodes.body: Herniation = brain tissue displacement through rigid intracranial compartments. Immediately Concerning Signs: | Finding | Significance | |---------|-------------| | 👁️ Anisocoria | CN III compression (uncal herniation) | | 💪 Posturing | Brainstem involvement | | 📉 Declining GCS | Progressing herniation | | 🫀 Cushing triad | Imminent/active herniation | Cushing Triad (late, ominous): 1. Hyperte

nodes.title: 🚨 EMERGENCY — Treat Herniation NOW
nodes.summary: Parallel: intubate, osmolar therapy, HOB 30, hyperventilate, call neurosurgery
nodes.body: Immediate Actions (parallel, not sequential): 1. AIRWAY • Intubate if GCS ≤8 • Avoid hypoxia (SaO2 >95%) • Avoid hypotension during RSI 2. HYPEROSMOLAR THERAPY (choose one) • Mannitol 20% 1 g/kg IV over 15-20 min • Hypertonic saline 3% 250-500 mL IV bolus 3. POSITIONING • Head of bed 30 degrees • Head midline (no rotation) • Loosen cervical collar if present 4. HYPERVENTILATION (temporizing) • Tar

nodes.title: Herniation Syndromes — Types
nodes.summary: Five herniation types — uncal most common trauma, tonsillar most fatal
nodes.body: Five Major Types: | Type | Mechanism | Key Finding | |------|-----------|-------------| | Uncal | Temporal lobe → tentorial notch | Ipsilateral pupil dilation | | Central | Bilateral → diencephalon descent | Bilateral small pupils | | Subfalcine | Cingulate → under falx | Often precedes others | | Tonsillar | Cerebellum → foramen magnum | Cushing triad | | Upward | Posterior fossa → upward | Alter

nodes.title: Uncal Herniation
nodes.summary: Ipsilateral dilated pupil to bilateral — Kernohan notch false localizing
nodes.body: Most Common Herniation Type Mechanism: • Temporal lobe uncus herniates through tentorial notch • Compresses CN III and midbrain Classic Progression: Stage 1 — Early: • Ipsilateral pupil dilation (CN III compression) • May be subtle initially • Consciousness may be preserved Stage 2 — Progressive: • Pupil becomes fixed and dilated • "Down and out" eye position • Ptosis • Contralateral hemiparesis S

nodes.title: Central (Transtentorial) Herniation
nodes.summary: Bilateral small pupils then midposition fixed — Duret hemorrhage fatal
nodes.body: Bilateral Descent Through Tentorial Notch Mechanism: • Diffuse bilateral cerebral edema • Bilateral mass effect • Diencephalon/midbrain descends centrally Classic Progression: Early (Diencephalic): • Altered consciousness • Small, reactive pupils (bilateral) • Cheyne-Stokes respirations • Decorticate posturing Late (Midbrain/Pons): • Midposition, fixed pupils • Decerebrate posturing • Central neur

nodes.title: Tonsillar (Foramen Magnum) Herniation
nodes.summary: Cushing triad = imminent medullary compression — HTN + brady + irregular resp
nodes.body: Cerebellar Tonsils Through Foramen Magnum Mechanism: • Posterior fossa mass or edema • Cerebellar tonsils compress medulla • CSF outflow obstruction Clinical Features: Early: • Severe headache • Neck stiffness/pain • Head tilt • Vomiting Progressive: • Cushing Triad: - Hypertension (often severe, SBP >200) - Bradycardia - Irregular respirations • Altered consciousness • Lower cranial nerve palsies

nodes.title: CT Imaging — Critical Findings
nodes.summary: Midline shift >5mm CT = neurosurgery stat for emergent evacuation
nodes.body: Non-contrast CT Head is First-Line Midline Shift (MLS): | Shift | Significance | |-------|-------------| | 0-3 mm | Normal/minimal | | 3-5 mm | Concerning — close monitoring | | >5 mm | CRITICAL — emergent neurosurgery | | >11 mm (at IVF) | Strongest predictor of herniation (OR 10) | Other Critical CT Signs: | Finding | Implication | |---------|-------------| | Basal cistern effacement | ICP criti

nodes.title: CT Findings — Decision Point
nodes.summary: CT surgical vs medical — MLS >5mm or hematoma >60mL needs OR
nodes.body: Based on CT results: Emergent Surgical Indications: • Midline shift >5 mm • Epidural hematoma with mass effect • Subdural hematoma >10 mm thick or MLS >5 mm • Cerebellar hemorrhage >3 cm or with hydrocephalus • Obstructive hydrocephalus Medical Management + Monitoring: • Mass effect without surgical lesion • Diffuse edema • Small hematomas • Contusions without significant mass effect

nodes.title: Hyperosmolar Therapy — First-Line
nodes.summary: Mannitol 1g/kg or 3% HTS 250mL — HTS preferred if hypotensive
nodes.body: Choose ONE — Both Are Effective: Mannitol 20% • Dose: 0.5-1 g/kg IV over 15-20 min • Onset: 15-30 minutes • Duration: ~90 minutes • Max serum osmolarity: 320 mOsm/L • ⚠️ Diuretic effect — can drop BP Hypertonic Saline 3% • Dose: 250-500 mL (or 2-5 mL/kg) IV bolus • Onset: 10-20 minutes • Duration: 60+ minutes (more sustained than mannitol) • May be preferred if hypotensive • Less rebound edema Whi

nodes.title: Mannitol 20% Administration
nodes.summary: Mannitol 1g/kg IV 15-20min — hold if serum osm >320 or hypotensive
nodes.body: Dosing: • 1 g/kg IV over 15-20 minutes • Example: 70 kg patient → 350 mL of 20% mannitol • Can repeat 0.25-0.5 g/kg q6h as needed Monitoring: • Serum osmolarity (hold if >320 mOsm/L) • Urine output (expect diuresis) • Blood pressure (may drop) • Renal function Onset: 15-30 minutes Peak effect: 20-60 minutes Duration: ~90 minutes (variable) Cautions: • Avoid in hypovolemia — can worsen hypotension
nodes.recommendation: Mannitol 20% 1 g/kg IV over 15-20 min. Monitor osmolarity, BP, urine output. Reassess pupils/motor in 15-30 min. May repeat 0.25-0.5 g/kg q6h.

nodes.title: Hypertonic Saline 3% Administration
nodes.summary: 3% HTS 250-500mL bolus — target Na 145-155 for ICP control
nodes.body: Dosing Options: • 3% NaCl: 250-500 mL IV bolus (or 2-5 mL/kg) • 23.4% NaCl: 30 mL via central line (more concentrated) Monitoring: • Serum sodium (goal 145-155 mEq/L for ICP control) • Central line for concentrations >3% (peripheral OK for 3%) • Avoid rapid correction if chronic hyponatremia Onset: 10-20 minutes Duration: 60+ minutes (more sustained than mannitol) Advantages Over Mannitol: • No di
nodes.recommendation: Hypertonic saline 3% 250-500 mL IV bolus. Target Na 145-155 for ICP control. Reassess pupils/motor in 15-30 min. May repeat.

nodes.title: Positioning & Basic Measures
nodes.summary: HOB 30, head midline, loosen C-collar — simple interventions reduce ICP
nodes.body: Simple Interventions That Reduce ICP: Head Position: • Head of bed 30 degrees — improves venous drainage • Head midline — avoid neck rotation (compresses jugular) • Loosen cervical collar if present (impedes venous outflow) Oxygenation: • Maintain SaO2 >95% • Target PaO2 >80 mmHg • Hypoxia worsens cerebral edema Ventilation: • Normocapnia (PaCO2 35-45) when stable • Hyperventilation only for acute

nodes.title: ⚠️ Hyperventilation — Use With Caution
nodes.summary: PaCO2 32-35 BRIDGE ONLY max 2hrs — prolonged causes ischemia
nodes.body: TEMPORIZING MEASURE ONLY When to Use: • Acute herniation with clinical signs • Bridge to surgery or osmolar therapy • Impending herniation despite other interventions Target: • PaCO2 32-35 mmHg (mild hypocapnia) • Do NOT go below 25 mmHg Duration: • Maximum 2 hours • Shorter is better Why It's Dangerous Long-Term: • Causes cerebral vasoconstriction • Reduces cerebral blood flow • Leads to cerebral

nodes.title: Blood Pressure & CPP Targets
nodes.summary: Single SBP <90 doubles mortality — maintain MAP >80, CPP >60
nodes.body: Avoid Hypotension — It Kills Brain Cells Emergency Phase (ED) Targets: | Age | Minimum SBP | |-----|-------------| | 15-49 years | >110 mmHg | | 50-69 years | >100 mmHg | | >70 years | >110 mmHg | ICU Phase (with ICP monitoring): • Target CPP 60-70 mmHg • CPP = MAP - ICP • If ICP unknown, use MAP >80 mmHg Why BP Matters: • Single episode of SBP <90 = doubles mortality • Cerebral autoregulation imp

nodes.title: Neurosurgical Intervention
nodes.summary: MLS >5mm, EDH mass effect, SDH >10mm, cerebellar >3cm = OR
nodes.body: CALL NEUROSURGERY STAT For: Imaging Indications: • Midline shift >5 mm • Epidural hematoma with any mass effect • Subdural hematoma >10 mm or MLS >5 mm • Cerebellar hemorrhage >3 cm • Obstructive hydrocephalus (may need EVD) • Depressed skull fracture Clinical Indications: • Anisocoria + altered consciousness • Cushing triad • New/progressive posturing • Rapid neurological decline • GCS ≤8 with su
nodes.recommendation: Emergent neurosurgery consultation. Prep for OR. Continue ICP management while awaiting surgery. EVD if hydrocephalus.

nodes.title: ICP Monitoring Indications
nodes.summary: ICP monitor GCS <=8 + abnormal CT — treat >20-22, craniectomy >40
nodes.body: When to Place ICP Monitor/EVD: GCS ≤8 + Abnormal CT: • Hematoma, contusion, edema • Herniation signs • Basal cistern compression GCS ≤8 + Normal CT if ≥2 of: • Age >40 years • Motor posturing • SBP <90 mmHg Other Indications: • Hydrocephalus (EVD for drainage + monitoring) • SAH with poor grade • ICH with intraventricular extension • Post-craniotomy with swelling Treatment Thresholds: | ICP | Acti

nodes.title: Reassessment Protocol
nodes.summary: Pupils and motor q15-30min after each intervention — document trend
nodes.body: After Each Intervention, Reassess in 15-30 min: Pupillary Exam: • Size, reactivity • Anisocoria improving or worsening? • Document with pupillometer if available Motor Response: • GCS motor component • Posturing type (decorticate → decerebrate = worsening) • Laterality changes Vital Signs: • BP trend (Cushing response?) • Heart rate • Respiratory pattern ICP (if monitored): • Absolute value • Tren

nodes.title: Prognosis & Goals of Care
nodes.summary: Bilateral fixed + GCS 3 + lost brainstem reflexes = poor prognosis
nodes.body: Poor Prognostic Signs: • Bilateral fixed and dilated pupils • GCS 3 with loss of brainstem reflexes • Duret hemorrhage on CT • Age >65 with severe TBI • Refractory ICP despite maximal therapy When to Discuss Goals: • Persistent herniation despite treatment • Brainstem reflexes absent • Family present and stable Brain Death Evaluation: • Clinical exam for brainstem reflexes • Apnea test • Confirmat

nodes.title: Breech Delivery
nodes.summary: Breech = fetal buttocks/feet present first. 3-4% at term. C-section preferred; vaginal only if delivery imminent.
nodes.body: Breech Delivery Steps Summary — quick-reference checklist of maneuvers. Types of Breech — Frank, Complete, Footling (with images). Maneuvers Atlas — Pinard, Løvset, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit. Breech presentation = fetal buttocks or feet present first. Occurs in 3–4% of term pregnancies and up to 25% at 28 weeks — most convert spontaneously. [1][2] This is an obstetric emergency in the ED. Since the T

nodes.title: When to Suspect Breech
nodes.summary: HR above umbilicus, head palpable at fundus, soft presenting part — confirm with bedside US in <60 sec
nodes.body: CLINICAL SIGNS SUGGESTING BREECH • Fetal heart tones heard above the umbilicus (normal cephalic = below umbilicus) • Leopold maneuvers: hard, round head palpable at the fundus (top of uterus) • Irregular softer presenting part at the pelvic brim (buttocks feel softer than head) • Meconium passage without fetal distress — physiologic pressure on fetal abdomen • Vaginal exam: palpation of buttocks,

nodes.title: Is the Fetus Confirmed Breech?
nodes.summary: Breech confirmed → continue. Vertex → standard delivery. Transverse → C-section only.
nodes.body: After POCUS or vaginal exam: • If vertex confirmed → proceed with standard Precipitous Delivery • If breech confirmed → continue this consult • If transverse lie → C-section is the only safe option — vaginal delivery of transverse is not possible without internal version, which is beyond ED scope

nodes.title: Proceed with Vertex Delivery
nodes.body: POCUS or exam shows vertex presentation. Proceed with the Precipitous Delivery consult for standard ED vaginal delivery.
nodes.recommendation: Vertex presentation confirmed — use Precipitous Delivery consult for standard stepwise management.

nodes.title: Transverse Lie — C-Section
nodes.body: TRANSVERSE LIE In transverse lie the fetal long axis is perpendicular to the maternal spine (fetal back horizontal). Vaginal delivery is not possible and any attempt risks uterine rupture and fetal death. [2] MANAGEMENT: • Stat OB/Anesthesia page • Prepare for emergency C-section • Do NOT attempt internal podalic version — outside ED scope and carries high maternal morbidity • If delivery is immin
nodes.recommendation: Transverse lie — immediate C-section. Tocolysis with Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ if delivery imminent to buy OR time.

nodes.title: Call for Help — Now
nodes.summary: OB + Peds/NICU + Anesthesia STAT — OR must be available as backup even if delivering vaginally
nodes.body: CALL FOR HELP IMMEDIATELY • OB STAT — need OR capability within minutes • Pediatrics / NICU — neonate is at high risk for resuscitation • Anesthesia — for possible emergent C-section • Additional nursing — minimum 2 nurses (one for mom, one for baby) CONFIRM OR READINESS: • Anesthesia en route • OR suite being prepared • Blood bank notified (consider type and crossmatch) Even if you plan to delive

nodes.title: Classify the Breech Type
nodes.summary: Frank (50-70%, best) / Complete (5-10%) / Footling (10-40%, high cord prolapse risk — prefer C-section)
nodes.body: THREE MAIN TYPES OF BREECH 1. FRANK BREECH (50–70% of term breech) • Hips flexed, both knees extended • Fetal feet up near face ("pike position") • Buttocks present — feels like a smooth oval on exam • Most favorable type for vaginal delivery — buttocks dilate cervix like a wedge 2. COMPLETE BREECH (5–10%) • Hips AND knees flexed ("cannonball" or cross-legged) • Both buttocks and feet present at t

nodes.title: Is Delivery Imminent?
nodes.summary: Imminent = crowning/body delivering → manage vaginally. Not imminent → C-section preferred.
nodes.body: DELIVERY IS IMMINENT IF: • Breech is crowning (buttocks or feet visible at introitus) • Cervix fully dilated (10 cm) AND mother actively bearing down • Body has begun to deliver If NOT imminent → emergent C-section is preferred (better perinatal outcomes per Term Breech Trial). [3] If imminent → you must deliver vaginally. Stopping an active breech delivery is not safe; continue with maneuvers bel

nodes.title: Transfer for Emergent C-Section
nodes.body: TRANSFER FOR C-SECTION Per the Term Breech Trial (Hannah et al., Lancet 2000), planned Cesarean delivery for term breech reduces perinatal mortality and serious neonatal morbidity from 5.0% to 1.6% (RR 0.33, NNT ~30). [3] SUBSEQUENT COMMITTEE OPINIONS: • ACOG Committee Opinion 745 (2018): Cesarean is the preferred mode for most term breech fetuses, with planned vaginal breech delivery considered o
nodes.recommendation: C-section strongly preferred for term breech (Term Breech Trial, ACOG 745, RCOG 20b). Transfer to OR with OB. Continuous monitoring, left lateral tilt, IV access ×2, NPO, type and screen. Do not rupture membranes.

nodes.title: Immediate Cord Prolapse Check
nodes.summary: Check for cord prolapse on first exam. Footling = 15-20% risk. If prolapsed → Cord Emergencies consult.
nodes.body: Perform a sterile vaginal exam immediately to rule out cord prolapse. Cord prolapse risk by type: • Frank breech: ~0.5% • Complete breech: ~5% • Footling breech: ~15–20% If you palpate a pulsatile cord at or below the presenting part → cord prolapse. This is a separate emergency — see Cord Emergencies.

nodes.title: Cord Prolapse Management
nodes.body: CORD PROLAPSE WITH BREECH When the cord presents ahead of the fetus, compression during descent can cause rapid fetal hypoxia and death. This is a true emergency. IMMEDIATE STEPS: 1. Elevate the presenting part — insert a gloved hand into the vagina and manually push the fetal breech upward, off the cord 2. Knee-chest or Trendelenburg position — relieves cord pressure 3. Tocolysis: Terbutaline 0.2
nodes.recommendation: Cord prolapse + breech = emergency C-section. Elevate presenting part manually, knee-chest/Trendelenburg, Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ, cover cord with warm saline gauze.

nodes.title: Preparation for Vaginal Breech
nodes.summary: Dorsal lithotomy, buttocks at edge, empty bladder, IV ×2, type and screen, full NRP setup, minimum 4 personnel
nodes.body: EQUIPMENT • Sterile gloves × 2 pairs • Sterile towels, drapes • Sterile warm saline (for wrapping fetal body during delivery) • Cord clamps × 2 • Sterile scissors • Neonatal warmer — ON and prewarming • Full Neonatal Resuscitation setup • Suction, O2, bag-valve-mask (neonatal) PERSONNEL — minimum 4: • Delivering provider (you) • Assistant (OB or second ED provider) — for Løvset rotation and MSV if

nodes.title: Episiotomy Consideration
nodes.summary: Routine episiotomy NOT recommended. Selective if rigid perineum or needed room after umbilical delivery.
nodes.body: EPISIOTOMY IN VAGINAL BREECH Routine episiotomy is NOT recommended (same as for cephalic delivery). Selective episiotomy may be considered when: • Perineum is rigid and obstructing descent • After fetal body delivers to umbilicus and additional room is needed for arms or aftercoming head • Primigravida with tight introitus Timing: Perform after the buttocks are crowning but before the body deliver

nodes.title: HANDS OFF THE BREECH
nodes.summary: HANDS OFF until scapulae visible. Traction → head extension → entrapment. Let uterus and maternal pushing deliver.
nodes.body: THE MOST IMPORTANT RULE IN VAGINAL BREECH DELIVERY: HANDS OFF. Do NOT touch the fetus until the scapulae are visible at the introitus. WHY "HANDS OFF" MATTERS: • Traction on the body causes the fetal head to extend (go from flexed to extended) • An extended head cannot pass through the pelvis → head entrapment = catastrophic • Uterine contractions + maternal pushing alone deliver the body in the c

nodes.title: Spontaneous Delivery to Umbilicus
nodes.summary: Buttocks → body to umbilicus via maternal pushing only. Wrap body in warm moist towel. Keep back anterior.
nodes.body: STAGES OF SPONTANEOUS BREECH DESCENT 1. Buttocks crown and deliver — sacrum should be anterior (facing the mother's symphysis) 2. Body delivers to the umbilicus via maternal pushing 3. Legs deliver — may need Pinard maneuver for frank breech with extended legs (see next node) 4. Cord visible and pulsating — do NOT clamp yet; baby is still oxygenating WHAT TO WATCH FOR: • Back should rotate anterio

nodes.title: Keep Fetal Back Anterior
nodes.summary: Keep back anterior (sacrum to mom's symphysis). Grip fetal iliac crests with thumbs on sacrum — NEVER abdomen.
nodes.body: KEEP THE FETAL BACK ANTERIOR Sacro-anterior position (fetal sacrum facing mother's pubic symphysis) is the safest orientation for breech delivery. It allows: • Proper rotation of the shoulders under the pubic arch • Head to flex naturally as it delivers over the perineum If the back rotates posteriorly (sacrum facing maternal spine) → head is likely extended and delivery becomes dangerous. HOW TO

nodes.title: Are the Legs Extended? (Frank Breech)
nodes.summary: Flexed legs (complete) → deliver spontaneously. Extended legs (frank) → Pinard maneuver.
nodes.body: After buttocks deliver and you see the hips, are the legs extended (hips flexed, knees straight — frank breech) or flexed (knees up — complete breech)? • Complete breech — legs deliver spontaneously • Frank breech with extended legs — may need Pinard maneuver to flex each leg at the knee and deliver one foot at a time

nodes.title: Pinard Maneuver — Delivering Extended Legs
nodes.summary: Two fingers behind knee → reflex flexion → sweep foot laterally. Repeat other leg. Do not pull.
nodes.body: PINARD MANEUVER Used to deliver extended legs in frank breech presentation. STEPS: 1. Introduce two fingers into the vagina alongside one extended fetal leg 2. Press behind the knee (popliteal fossa) — this causes reflex knee flexion 3. Sweep the foot laterally (abduct) and deliver the foot 4. Repeat on the contralateral leg Once both feet are out, the body will continue descent with maternal push

nodes.title: At the Umbilicus — Check the Cord
nodes.summary: Loop cord down gently after umbilicus — do NOT clamp. 5-10 min window to deliver head after umbilicus.
nodes.body: ONCE THE UMBILICUS IS DELIVERED Bring a loop of cord down gently — this relieves traction on the cord as the thorax delivers. Do NOT clamp yet — baby is still receiving oxygenated blood. ASSESS CORD PULSATION: • Strongly pulsating → baby well-perfused, continue • Weakly pulsating or absent → delivery must proceed faster; proceed to arms and head NEXT: Shoulders. With further maternal pushing, the

nodes.title: Arms — Spontaneous or Nuchal?
nodes.summary: Arms flexed → spontaneous. Nuchal arm (elbow above neck) → Løvset maneuver.
nodes.body: After the scapulae appear at the introitus, assess the arms: • Arms flexed across chest — will deliver spontaneously with the next contraction (most common) • One or both arms trapped behind head ("nuchal arms") — must be freed with Løvset maneuver A nuchal arm is recognized by: • Elbow visible behind the fetal occiput on either side • Inability of body to descend further • Arm appears extended up

nodes.title: Løvset Maneuver — Delivering Nuchal Arms
nodes.summary: Grip iliac crests, thumbs on sacrum. Rotate 180° CW → sweep arm across chest. Reverse rotate → sweep 2nd arm.
nodes.body: LØVSET MANEUVER (pronounced "LOVE-set") Rotates the fetal body 180° in each direction to bring each nuchal arm under the pubic arch for delivery. GRIP: Two hands on fetal pelvis — thumbs on sacrum, fingers wrapped around the iliac crests. Never grip the abdomen. STEPS (for a nuchal anterior arm): 1. Apply gentle downward traction while rotating the body 180° clockwise (viewed from below). This bri

nodes.title: Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit Maneuver
nodes.summary: MSV: Body straddles arm, middle finger in mouth on MAXILLA (not mandible), other hand on shoulders. Downward traction → elevate.
nodes.body: MAURICEAU-SMELLIE-VEIT (MSV) MANEUVER The standard technique for delivery of the aftercoming head in vaginal breech. Keeps the head flexed — the key to avoiding entrapment. SETUP: • Let the fetal body "ride" on the operator's dominant forearm (face-down, straddling the arm) • The body provides natural weight to encourage head flexion HAND POSITIONING (this is critical): DOMINANT HAND (body-support

nodes.title: Burns-Marshall as Alternative
nodes.summary: MSV successful → postpartum. Failed → try Burns-Marshall. Still stuck → head entrapment emergency.
nodes.body: Was MSV successful in delivering the aftercoming head?

nodes.title: Burns-Marshall Technique
nodes.summary: Hold ankles, let body hang, wait 30-60 sec, arc body upward slowly over mom's abdomen. Slow arc avoids ICH.
nodes.body: BURNS-MARSHALL TECHNIQUE Alternative for delivery of the aftercoming head when MSV has not succeeded. STEPS: 1. Grasp the fetal ankles with one hand 2. Let the body hang vertically from the mother's perineum — the weight of the body encourages head flexion and descent 3. Wait 30–60 seconds for the occiput to appear under the symphysis — you will see the hairline emerge 4. Once the occiput is visib

nodes.title: Head Entrapment — Last-Resort Maneuvers
nodes.summary: Terbutaline tocolysis → emergent OR for C-section rescue. Dührssen and symphysiotomy are last-resort only.
nodes.body: HEAD ENTRAPMENT — TRUE EMERGENCY Head entrapment occurs when the fetal body has delivered but the head remains trapped above the cervix or at the pelvic outlet. Fetal death in 5–10 minutes without rescue. IMMEDIATE RESCUE OPTIONS — escalate rapidly: 1. TOCOLYSIS (buy time by relaxing uterus) • Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ OR Nitroglycerin 50–200 mcg IV • Works within 1–5 minutes 2. DÜHRSSEN INCISIONS (i

nodes.title: Delivery Complete — Neonatal Assessment
nodes.summary: Higher resus need than cephalic. Check for brachial plexus palsy, fractures, adrenal hemorrhage, ICH.
nodes.body: NEONATAL ASSESSMENT Breech neonates have a higher rate of resuscitation needs than cephalic — even in uncomplicated vaginal breech. Anticipate the need for bag-mask ventilation. IMMEDIATE NEONATAL CARE: 1. Clamp and cut cord (two clamps ~3 cm apart; delayed cord clamping 30–60 sec if vigorous) 2. Dry and stimulate the baby 3. APGAR at 1 and 5 minutes 4. Transfer to neonatal warmer 5. If HR <100 or

nodes.title: Maternal Postpartum Management
nodes.summary: Oxytocin 20u/L NS @ 250 mL/hr after placenta. Inspect cervix (high lac risk). Monitor q15min × 1hr. Admit to OB.
nodes.body: MATERNAL POSTPARTUM CARE PLACENTAL DELIVERY: Same as Precipitous Delivery — gentle cord traction with fundal counter-pressure until placenta delivers. UTEROTONIC: • Oxytocin 20 units in 1L NS at 250 mL/hr after placenta delivers • Breech deliveries have higher postpartum hemorrhage risk due to greater uterine manipulation LACERATION ASSESSMENT: • Inspect perineum, vagina, and cervix carefully — br

nodes.title: Breech Delivery — Complete
nodes.body: Delivery complete. POSTDELIVERY CHECKLIST ✓ Neonate assessed — APGAR at 1 and 5 min, brachial plexus exam, limb palpation ✓ Umbilical cord blood gas (if available) ✓ Placenta delivered and examined ✓ Maternal uterine tone firm ✓ Lacerations addressed ✓ Oxytocin infusing ✓ Mother and baby warm DISPOSITION • Admit mother to OB service for postpartum observation (minimum 24 h) • Admit neonate to nurs
nodes.recommendation: Breech delivery complete. Admit mom to OB × 24h minimum. Admit neonate to nursery/NICU. Document type of breech, maneuvers used, and timestamps. Screen neonate for brachial plexus palsy, fractures, and hip dysplasia.

nodes.title: Bronchiolitis — Clinical Recognition
nodes.summary: Age 28d-24mo, first wheeze, increased WOB — CXR and albuterol NOT indicated
nodes.body: Inclusion Criteria: \u2022 Age >28 days and <24 months \u2022 Clinical symptoms: increased work of breathing, persistent cough, feeding difficulty, \u00B1 fever \u2022 First episode of wheezing OR diagnosis of bronchiolitis If respiratory arrest is imminent, triage and initiate care in the resuscitation room. Use the BAS Calculator for objective severity scoring. See NOT Recommended Interventions

nodes.title: Exclusion Criteria
nodes.summary: Exclude CHD, chronic lung, immunodeficiency, recurrent wheeze from pathway
nodes.body: Does the patient have any of the following? \u2022 Chronic lung disease or cystic fibrosis \u2022 Congenital heart disease \u2022 Immunodeficiency \u2022 Toxic appearance or shock \u2022 Neuromuscular disease \u2022 Artificial or abnormal airway \u2022 Recurrent wheezing (>3 episodes) \u2022 Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation

nodes.title: Not Eligible for Standard Pathway
nodes.summary: Comorbidities need individualized management — not standard pathway
nodes.body: This pathway applies to previously healthy infants with first-episode bronchiolitis. Patients with significant comorbidities require individualized evaluation and management. Consider: \u2022 Subspecialty consultation \u2022 Alternative diagnoses (reactive airway disease, pertussis, foreign body) \u2022 Management guided by underlying condition
nodes.recommendation: Individualized management required. Consider subspecialty consult.

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: BAS calculator before and after every intervention for objective scoring
nodes.body: Classify severity using clinical findings. Use the BAS Calculator for objective scoring. Document BAS score before and after all interventions.

nodes.title: Mild Bronchiolitis — Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Gentle nasal suction + PO fluids + observe 1-2hrs — no meds needed
nodes.body: Interventions: \u2022 Nasal suction using nasal aspirator (gentle, superficial \u2014 NOT deep suction beyond nasopharynx) \u2022 Reposition for comfort \u2022 Assess hydration status and encourage PO fluids Document BAS score before and after interventions. Observe for 1\u20132 hours, then reassess. See NOT Recommended Interventions.

nodes.title: Moderate Bronchiolitis — Notify Provider
nodes.summary: Notify provider — suction, O2, IV if poor PO, target SpO2 >=90%
nodes.body: NOTIFY PROVIDER Interventions: \u2022 Nasal suction using nasal aspirator \u2022 Rehydration (IV if unable to tolerate PO) \u2022 Supplemental O\u2082 via nasal cannula or simple mask \u2022 Target SpO\u2082 \u226590% awake or \u226588% asleep Document BAS score before and after interventions. See NOT Recommended Interventions.

nodes.title: Severe Bronchiolitis — Escalate
nodes.summary: HFNC immediately — IV access, continuous monitoring, notify stat
nodes.body: NOTIFY PROVIDER IMMEDIATELY Interventions: \u2022 Nasal suction using nasal aspirator \u2022 Supplemental O\u2082 \u2014 prepare for HFNC initiation \u2022 Assess dehydration \u2014 IV fluid resuscitation if needed \u2022 Continuous monitoring \u2022 Place PIV if not already done Proceed directly to HFNC initiation.

nodes.title: Mild — Reassessment
nodes.summary: Reassess 1-2hrs — SpO2 >=90% RA and feeding well qualifies discharge
nodes.body: Reassess after 1\u20132 hours of supportive care. Check: SpO\u2082, RR, work of breathing, ability to feed, hydration status. Use BAS Calculator for objective scoring.

nodes.title: Response to Interventions
nodes.summary: After suction + O2 — discharge, NC admit, or escalate HFNC
nodes.body: Reassess after nasal suction and supplemental O\u2082. Are oxygen needs AND work of breathing adequately managed?

nodes.title: HFNC Initiation
nodes.summary: HFNC: <7kg 4 LPM, >=7kg 6 LPM — FiO2 21% titrate SpO2 >=90%
nodes.body: Starting Flow Rates: \u2022 <7 kg: 4 LPM \u2022 \u22657 kg: 6 LPM Start FiO\u2082 at 21%, titrate to maintain SpO\u2082 \u226590%. Patient must be watched for at least 30 minutes in the ED after starting HFNC. Continuous pulse oximetry required. Feeding: NPO for ~1 hour to assess response. See HFNC Protocol Reference for full details including contraindications and max flow rates.

nodes.title: HFNC Response (Q15min BAS)
nodes.summary: BAS q15min on HFNC — suction first if >=9 then reassess
nodes.body: Assess BAS every 15 minutes after HFNC initiation. If BAS \u22659: suction first, then reassess. If still \u22659 after suction, contact primary team. Use BAS Calculator for scoring.

nodes.title: HFNC Maintenance
nodes.summary: Stable HFNC: monitoring, BAS q4h, must be stable >=4hrs before wean
nodes.body: Monitoring: \u2022 Continuous pulse oximetry \u2022 BAS Q4h or per PEWS score \u2022 Document HR, RR, pulse ox \u2022 Suction PRN + BAS Q4h Feeding: \u2022 Mild BAS \u2192 May resume PO (first feed observed by staff) \u2022 Moderate to severe BAS \u2192 Consider NG feeds Must be stable for \u22654 hours on maintenance phase before weaning. See HFNC Weaning Protocol and Feeding Guidelines.

nodes.title: Escalation Decision
nodes.summary: Increase 2 LPM if not max — PICU if worsening >60min or apnea
nodes.body: Patient not improving on HFNC. If NOT at max flow: Increase by 2 LPM. \u2022 Max: 2 LPM/kg for \u22647 kg, 14 LPM for >7 kg \u2022 Monitor for signs of excess flow Critical care consult triggers: \u2022 Worsening after 60 minutes on HFNC \u2022 Severe respiratory distress on HFNC \u2022 FiO\u2082 >50% \u2022 Flow rates above recommended maximum \u2022 Apnea \u2022 Severe dehydration or shock

nodes.title: Ready to Wean?
nodes.summary: Stable >=4hrs HFNC maintenance required before wean attempt
nodes.body: Has the patient been stable on current HFNC settings for \u22654 hours? See HFNC Weaning & Holiday Protocol for detailed criteria and weaning steps.

nodes.title: ED Discharge
nodes.summary: Discharge: SpO2 >=90% RA, RR <60, feeding well, parents suction demo
nodes.body: ALL discharge criteria must be met: \u2022 SpO\u2082 \u226590% on room air \u2022 Respirations <60/min and/or minimal to no increased WOB \u2022 Tolerating oral feeding at a level to maintain hydration \u2022 Parents comfortable with providing home care \u2022 Parent/guardian education complete Parent Education: \u2022 Bronchiolitis: Home Care (English) \u2022 Bronquiolitis: Cuidados en el Hogar (
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with education. Parents should demonstrate nasal suction technique. Follow up with PCP in 1\u20132 days.

nodes.title: Admit \u2014 Acute Care Unit
nodes.summary: Admit ongoing O2/HFNC — BAS q4h, suction PRN, feeding assessment
nodes.body: Admission criteria: \u2022 Routine bronchiolitis management \u2022 FiO\u2082 <50% to maintain SaO\u2082 \u226590% \u2022 HFNC at standard flow rates \u2022 Continuation of care from higher acuity unit Orders: \u2022 BAS Q4h \u2022 Nasal suction PRN \u2022 Continuous or intermittent pulse oximetry \u2022 Assess hydration and feeding tolerance See Admission Criteria and HFNC Weaning Protocol. Inpati
nodes.recommendation: Admit to acute care unit. Continue supportive care. Wean HFNC when stable \u22654 hours.

nodes.title: Admit \u2014 High Acuity
nodes.summary: High acuity — worsening despite flow increases, lower PICU threshold
nodes.body: High acuity criteria: \u2022 Significant cardiac or pulmonary comorbidities \u2022 Moderate to severe symptoms (BAS 4\u201312) \u2022 Worsening clinical status despite increasing flow rates \u2022 Comorbidities requiring closer monitoring Continuous monitoring. Lower threshold for PICU transfer. See Admission Criteria.
nodes.recommendation: Admit to high acuity unit. Continuous monitoring. Reassess Q15min. Escalate to PICU if worsening.

nodes.title: PICU / Critical Care Consult
nodes.summary: PICU: worsening >60min, apnea, PPV, FiO2 >50%, severe dehydration
nodes.body: PICU admission indications: \u2022 Worsening clinical status after 60 minutes of HFNC \u2022 Requiring positive pressure ventilation \u2022 Witnessed episode of apnea \u2022 Flow rates above maximum recommended levels \u2022 FiO\u2082 >50% to maintain SpO\u2082 \u2022 Severe dehydration or shock NICU consideration: \u2022 <44 weeks corrected gestational age \u2022 Prematurity \u226432 weeks and <4
nodes.recommendation: PICU admission or transfer. Critical care consult immediately.

nodes.title: Inpatient Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Inpatient DC: SpO2 >=90% RA >=2 continuous hrs, RR <60, PO OK
nodes.body: ALL must be met: \u2022 SpO\u2082 \u226590% on room air for \u22652 continuous hours (not a single reading) \u2022 Respirations <60/min and age-appropriate \u2022 Minimal to no increased work of breathing \u2022 Tolerating PO feeding at a level to maintain hydration \u2022 Parents comfortable with home care \u2022 Parents demonstrate nasal suction technique \u2022 Return precautions reviewed and u
nodes.recommendation: Discharge when SpO\u2082 \u226590% on room air for \u22652 continuous hours, feeding adequately, and parents confident in home care.

nodes.title: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event (BRUE)
nodes.summary: BRUE = sudden, brief (<1 min), resolved episode of cyanosis/pallor, breathing change, tone change, or altered responsiveness in infant <1 year, unexplained after H&P.
nodes.body: BRUE replaced ALTE in 2016 — more precise definition, less alarming terminology. BRUE Definition (ALL criteria): Infant <1 year with a sudden, brief (<1 min), NOW RESOLVED episode of ≥1: | Feature | Description | |---------|-------------| | Cyanosis or pallor | Central (not acrocyanosis) | | Breathing change | Absent, decreased, or irregular | | Tone change | Hypertonia or hypotonia | | Responsive

nodes.title: Does This Meet BRUE Criteria?
nodes.summary: BRUE only if unexplained after H&P. Fever, infection, GER, choking, seizure = not BRUE.
nodes.body: Exclusion Criteria — NOT a BRUE if: ❌ Fever present (consider sepsis workup) ❌ Respiratory infection symptoms (bronchiolitis, URI) ❌ GER with witnessed vomiting/regurgitation ❌ Choking on feeding or foreign body ❌ Witnessed seizure activity ❌ Event NOT resolved (still symptomatic) ❌ Age ≥1 year If any exclusion present: Diagnose and treat the underlying cause instead. Does this infant meet BRUE cr

nodes.title: Not a BRUE — Explained Event
nodes.body: Cause identified — manage underlying condition: | Cause | Management | |-------|------------| | Fever | Peds Fever Pathway | | Bronchiolitis/URI | Bronchiolitis Pathway | | GER with event | Feeding modifications, positioning, consider GI referral | | Choking | Feeding evaluation, consider swallow study | | Seizure | Neurology referral, consider EEG | | Pertussis | Test + treat per guidelines | Doc
nodes.recommendation: This is NOT a BRUE. Manage the identified cause per appropriate pathway. BRUE terminology only applies when no cause is found after thorough H&P.

nodes.title: BRUE Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: Low-risk BRUE: >60 days, not very preterm, first event, <1 min, no CPR, normal exam. Any deviation = higher-risk.
nodes.body: Lower-Risk BRUE — ALL criteria must be met: | Criterion | Requirement | |-----------|-------------| | Age | >60 days old | | Prematurity | If preterm: GA >32 weeks AND corrected age >45 weeks | | Event count | First BRUE (no prior events, no cluster) | | Duration | <1 minute | | CPR | None required by trained medical provider | | Exam | Normal, no concerning findings | Higher-Risk BRUE — ANY of th

nodes.title: Risk Category
nodes.summary: All criteria met = lower-risk (minimal workup). Any criterion not met = higher-risk (extended evaluation).
nodes.body: Assess ALL lower-risk criteria: ☐ Age >60 days ☐ If preterm: GA >32 weeks AND corrected age >45 weeks ☐ First BRUE (no prior, no cluster) ☐ Event duration <1 minute ☐ No CPR by trained medical provider ☐ Normal physical exam ☐ No concerning history (FH of SIDS, social concerns) ALL boxes must be checked for lower-risk. Which risk category?

nodes.title: Lower-Risk BRUE — Management
nodes.summary: Low-risk BRUE: Avoid routine testing. May do ECG and pertussis test. Observe 1-4 hrs. Educate and reassure.
nodes.body: AAP Strong Recommendations AGAINST: ❌ Routine CBC, BMP, blood gas ❌ Chest X-ray ❌ Echocardiogram ❌ EEG ❌ Neuroimaging (CT/MRI) ❌ Upper GI series ❌ LP / CSF analysis ❌ Empiric acid suppression (PPI/H2) ❌ Admission solely for monitoring MAY Consider (weak recommendations): ✓ ECG — to screen for long QT, WPW ✓ Pertussis testing — if underimmunized or outbreak area ✓ Brief observation (1-4 hours) with

nodes.title: Low-Risk Workup
nodes.summary: Low-risk: ECG optional, pertussis if indicated, observe 1-4 hrs, parent education on CPR and safe sleep.
nodes.body: Consider these tests (not required): | Test | Rationale | |------|----------| | 12-lead ECG | Screen for long QT, WPW (channelopathies can cause apnea) | | Pertussis PCR | If underimmunized or pertussis exposure | Observation: • 1-4 hours with continuous pulse oximetry • Serial exams — watch for recurrence • Document normal VS and exam at discharge Parent Education: • Infant CPR training (offer be

nodes.title: Lower-Risk BRUE — Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: ✓ Normal observation period (1-4 hours) ✓ No recurrent events ✓ Normal vital signs and exam ✓ Parent education completed ✓ Follow-up arranged (PCP within 24-48 hours) Discharge Instructions: Return immediately if: • Another similar event • Color change (blue/pale) • Breathing difficulty • Feeding problems • Lethargy or decreased responsiveness • Fever Safe Sleep Reminders: • Ba
nodes.recommendation: DISCHARGE HOME with close PCP follow-up in 24-48 hours. Provide infant CPR resources. No routine testing needed.

nodes.title: Higher-Risk BRUE — Evaluation Framework
nodes.summary: Higher-risk BRUE: Tiered workup prioritizing time-sensitive conditions — NAT, feeding issues, arrhythmia, infection, congenital anomaly.
nodes.body: 2019 AAP Framework: Tiered, Hypothesis-Driven Approach Higher-risk infants need extended evaluation, but avoid indiscriminate testing — low yield, high false-positive rate. Prioritize TIME-SENSITIVE conditions: | Priority | Condition | Why Time-Sensitive | |----------|-----------|--------------------| | 1 | Child maltreatment | Ongoing harm, missed diagnosis | | 2 | Feeding/aspiration | Recurrent

nodes.title: Focused History — Higher-Risk BRUE
nodes.summary: Detailed event history, feeding history, PMH (prematurity), FH (SIDS, arrhythmia), social history (NAT red flags).
nodes.body: Event History: • Exactly what did the caregiver observe? • What was infant doing? (feeding, sleeping, awake) • Color change? (central cyanosis vs acrocyanosis vs pallor) • Tone? (limp vs stiff) • Eye deviation? Rhythmic movements? (seizure) • Duration? (usually overestimated) • What did caregiver do? (stimulation, CPR) • How quickly did infant return to baseline? Feeding History: • Breastfed or bo

nodes.title: Physical Exam — Higher-Risk BRUE
nodes.summary: Complete PE: fontanelle, retinal exam if NAT concern, cardiac (murmur), skin (bruising in non-mobile = NAT red flag).
nodes.body: Vital Signs: • Temperature (fever → infection pathway) • HR, RR, BP, SpO2 • Weight (FTT = feeding issues, NAT) General: • Well-appearing vs ill-appearing • Dysmorphic features (syndromes) • Interaction, tone, alertness HEENT: • Anterior fontanelle (bulging = ICP, sunken = dehydration) • Retinal hemorrhages (NAT — dilated fundoscopy if concern) • Oral lesions (HSV) • Stridor, noisy breathing (airwa

nodes.title: Higher-Risk BRUE — Testing
nodes.summary: Tier 1: Pulse ox, ECG, glucose, BMP/VBG, CBC, pertussis. Add head imaging + skeletal survey if NAT concern.
nodes.body: Initial Tier (feasible without admission): | Test | Indication | |------|------------| | Continuous pulse ox | All higher-risk — 4+ hours | | 12-lead ECG | All — screen long QT, WPW | | Pertussis PCR | Underimmunized, exposure, outbreak | | Respiratory viral panel | Respiratory symptoms | | Blood glucose | All — hypoglycemia | | VBG or BMP | Metabolic screen (acidosis, electrolytes) | | CBC | Infe

nodes.title: Higher-Risk BRUE — Admission
nodes.body: Admission Indications: ✓ Age ≤60 days ✓ Preterm <32 weeks or corrected age <45 weeks ✓ Multiple/cluster events ✓ Event duration ≥1 minute ✓ CPR required by trained provider ✓ Abnormal exam or vital signs ✓ Concern for NAT ✓ Abnormal testing ✓ Parental anxiety/unable to monitor at home Admission Orders: • Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring • Pulse oximetry • Apnea monitoring • Observed feeding
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT for continuous monitoring and hypothesis-driven workup. Social work consult if any NAT concern. Subspecialty consults based on clinical suspicion.

nodes.title: BRUE Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: DDx: GER/laryngospasm most common, then LRI, seizure. Serious underlying condition ~1-5%. Always consider NAT.
nodes.body: Common Causes (when identified, no longer a "BRUE"): | Category | Causes | |----------|--------| | GI | GER with laryngospasm, swallowing dysfunction, aspiration | | Respiratory | Pertussis, RSV, bronchiolitis, URI, laryngomalacia | | Neurologic | Seizure, breath-holding spell, apnea of infancy | | Cardiac | Long QT, WPW, SVT, structural heart disease | | Infection | UTI, meningitis, sepsis | | Me

nodes.title: Non-Accidental Trauma (NAT) Screening
nodes.summary: NAT red flags: recurrent events same caregiver, bruising in non-mobile infant, inconsistent history. TEN-4 FACES bruising rule.
nodes.body: NAT Red Flags in BRUE: ⚠️ High-Risk Features: • Recurrent events with same caregiver • Inconsistent or changing history • Delay in seeking care • Bruising in non-mobile infant (TEN-4 FACES) • Unexplained injuries • Prior CPS involvement • Domestic violence in home • Substance abuse • Young, isolated, or stressed caregivers TEN-4 FACES Bruising Rule: Bruising on Torso, Ear, Neck in any child <4 yea

nodes.title: Pertussis Consideration
nodes.summary: Pertussis in young infants: apnea, cyanosis without classic whoop. Test NP PCR if underimmunized or exposure. Admit <3 months.
nodes.body: Pertussis in Infants — The "Silent" Cause of BRUE: Infants <3 months may not have classic "whoop" — present with: • Apnea • Cyanosis • Paroxysmal cough • Post-tussive emesis • Poor feeding Test for Pertussis if: • Underimmunized (0-2 DTaP doses) • Pertussis exposure • Outbreak in community • Paroxysmal cough present • Any respiratory symptoms Testing: • Nasopharyngeal PCR (gold standard) • Results

nodes.title: Cardiac Causes of BRUE
nodes.summary: ECG for all higher-risk BRUE. Long QT (QTc >460), WPW, SVT can cause BRUE. Cardiology consult if abnormal.
nodes.body: Arrhythmias Presenting as BRUE: | Condition | ECG Finding | Risk | |-----------|-------------|------| | Long QT | QTc >460 ms (>480 concerning) | Sudden death, torsades | | WPW | Delta wave, short PR | SVT, sudden death | | SVT | Narrow complex, rate >220 | Shock if prolonged | | Heart block | AV dissociation | Syncope, bradycardia | ECG Screening: • Recommended for ALL higher-risk BRUE • "May con

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Low-risk + normal observation = discharge. Higher-risk or recurrent = admit. Transfer if needs subspecialty or PICU.
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria (Low-Risk BRUE): ✓ Meets ALL low-risk criteria ✓ 1-4 hour observation without events ✓ Normal vital signs and exam ✓ Parent education completed (CPR, safe sleep) ✓ Close follow-up arranged (24-48 hours) ✓ Parents comfortable with discharge Admission Criteria: ✓ Higher-risk BRUE (any criterion) ✓ Recurrent events during observation ✓ Abnormal testing ✓ NAT concern ✓ Unable to arr

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.body: Parent Education Checklist: ☐ Infant CPR — hands-on training or video demonstration ☐ Safe Sleep — supine, firm mattress, no bedding ☐ When to Return — written instructions provided Return Immediately If: • Another similar event • Color change (blue, gray, pale) • Breathing difficulty • Not feeding well • Hard to wake up • Fever • Stiff or floppy Follow-Up: • PCP visit within 24-48 hours • Documen
nodes.recommendation: DISCHARGE with close PCP follow-up in 24-48 hours. Provide infant CPR resources (AHA/Red Cross). Written return precautions.

nodes.title: Admission Orders — Higher-Risk BRUE
nodes.body: Admission Location: • General pediatrics (most cases) • PICU if: recurrent apnea, respiratory failure, hemodynamic instability Monitoring: • Continuous cardiorespiratory monitor • Pulse oximetry • Apnea alarm • Frequent VS checks Initial Orders: • Blood glucose (bedside) • CBC, BMP or VBG • 12-lead ECG • Continuous SpO2 Tier 2 Testing (based on suspicion): | Concern | Testing | |---------|--------
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT for continuous monitoring. Workup guided by clinical suspicion — avoid indiscriminate testing. Social work if any NAT concern.

nodes.title: Transfer Considerations
nodes.body: Transfer to Children's Hospital/PICU if: • Recurrent apnea requiring intervention • Respiratory failure • Hemodynamic instability • Suspected NAT requiring child abuse team • Complex cardiac, metabolic, or neurologic workup • Need for subspecialty expertise not available locally Stabilize Before Transfer: • Ensure airway patency • Adequate oxygenation (SpO2 >92%) • Glucose check and correct if low
nodes.recommendation: TRANSFER if recurrent apnea, instability, or need for subspecialty expertise. Stabilize and provide detailed documentation.

nodes.title: Brugada Syndrome
nodes.summary: Inherited channelopathy SCD risk — Type 1 coved ST >=2mm V1-V3 diagnostic
nodes.body: Brugada Summary — inherited channelopathy with SCD risk. Brugada syndrome (BrS) is an inherited sodium channelopathy causing distinctive ECG patterns and ventricular fibrillation risk. Key features: • Type 1 ECG pattern = diagnostic (coved ST elevation ≥2mm in V1-V3) • Male predominance (8:1) • Mean age of events: ~40 years • Often presents with syncope, VF, or sudden death • Risk is highest after

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Arrest, syncope rest/sleep, or incidental ECG — determine type
nodes.body: How did this patient present? High-risk presentations: • Cardiac arrest/VF • Syncope (especially nocturnal or at rest) • Nocturnal agonal breathing Incidental findings: • ECG obtained for other reason • Family screening • Pre-operative evaluation Consider Brugada if: • Young patient with unexplained syncope • Family history of sudden death <45 years • Syncope with fever

nodes.title: ECG Pattern Types
nodes.summary: Only Type 1 coved diagnostic — high precordial leads increase sensitivity
nodes.body: Brugada ECG Patterns: Type 1 (Coved) — DIAGNOSTIC • Coved ST elevation ≥2mm in ≥1 lead (V1-V3) • Followed by T-wave inversion • Concave or straight ST descent below baseline • This is the ONLY diagnostic pattern Type 2 (Saddleback) — SUGGESTIVE ONLY • Saddleback ST elevation ≥0.5mm • J-point elevation ≥1mm • Positive or biphasic T wave • Requires provocation test if clinical suspicion Type 3 — No

nodes.title: Rule Out Brugada Phenocopies
nodes.summary: Rule out hyperK, PE, hypothermia, MI — phenocopy resolves with treatment
nodes.body: Brugada phenocopies mimic BrS but are caused by reversible conditions. Check for: Metabolic: • Hyperkalemia (most common) • Hyponatremia, hypocalcemia • Hypothermia, acidosis Structural: • Pulmonary embolism • Anterior MI / RV infarct • Myocarditis, pericarditis Mechanical: • Tension pneumothorax • Mediastinal mass Technical: • Lead misplacement (V1/V2 too high) Phenocopy resolves with treatment o

nodes.title: Brugada Phenocopy
nodes.summary: Treat cause, repeat ECG — if resolves, no Brugada management needed
nodes.body: Brugada Phenocopy — Treat Underlying Cause Management: • Correct the underlying condition • ECG pattern should resolve • Repeat ECG after correction If phenocopy: • No long-term Brugada management needed • No ICD indication • No drug restrictions If pattern persists after correction: • May have true BrS unmasked by stressor • Proceed with Brugada evaluation • EP consultation recommended Document:

nodes.title: Phenocopy Workup
nodes.summary: BMP, Mg, ABG, troponin, CXR, echo — rule out mimics
nodes.body: Labs to rule out phenocopies: • BMP (K+, Na+, Ca++, glucose) • Magnesium • ABG/VBG (acidosis) • Troponin (MI) • D-dimer if PE suspected Imaging: • CXR (pneumothorax, mediastinal mass) • Echo (RV strain, pericardial effusion) Temperature: • Check for hypothermia or fever If all negative: • True Brugada syndrome likely • Proceed with Shanghai score assessment If positive: • Treat condition, repeat E

nodes.title: Shanghai Score Assessment
nodes.summary: Shanghai >=3.5 = probable/definite BrS — systematic scoring
nodes.body: Shanghai Diagnostic Score for Brugada Syndrome: | Component | Points | |-----------|--------| | ECG | | | Spontaneous Type 1 | 3.5 | | Fever-induced Type 1 | 3.0 | | Drug-induced Type 1 | 2.0 | | Clinical | | | Cardiac arrest / documented VF | 3.0 | | Nocturnal agonal breathing | 2.0 | | Suspected arrhythmic syncope | 2.0 | | Unclear syncope | 1.0 | | AF/flutter <30 years | 0.5 | | Family History

nodes.title: Syncope Evaluation
nodes.summary: Rest/sleep syncope without prodrome = high-risk arrhythmic syncope
nodes.body: Syncope in suspected Brugada: High-risk features (arrhythmic syncope): • Occurs at rest or during sleep • No prodrome (sudden loss of consciousness) • Associated with palpitations • Brief duration • Nocturnal occurrence Lower-risk features: • Clear vasovagal trigger • Typical prodrome (nausea, diaphoresis) • Prolonged standing • Situational (micturition, defecation) If Type 1 ECG + arrhythmic sync

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest / VF
nodes.summary: AVOID amiodarone Brugada VF — isoproterenol for refractory
nodes.body: Cardiac arrest with suspected Brugada: Immediate management: • Standard ACLS • Post-arrest care if ROSC ⚠️ AVOID in resuscitation: • Amiodarone (may worsen BrS) • Procainamide • Flecainide If VF refractory: • Consider isoproterenol (suppresses VF in BrS) Post-ROSC: • 12-lead ECG (Type 1 pattern?) • Continuous monitoring • Check temperature (fever-induced?) • EP consultation STAT ICD indication: •

nodes.title: Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: Prior arrest highest — Type 1 + arrhythmic syncope = ICD discussion
nodes.body: Risk factors for SCD in Brugada: High risk: • Prior cardiac arrest (highest) • Documented spontaneous sustained VT • Arrhythmic syncope + spontaneous Type 1 ECG Intermediate risk: • Spontaneous Type 1 ECG (vs drug-induced) • Family history of SCD • QRS fragmentation • Inducible VF on EPS (controversial) Lower risk: • Drug-induced only pattern • Asymptomatic • No family history Annual event rates:

nodes.title: ICD Indications
nodes.summary: ICD Class I VF/VT survivors — IIa Type 1 + arrhythmic syncope
nodes.body: ICD Recommendations (2022 ESC Guidelines): Class I (Definite): • Survivors of cardiac arrest from VF/sustained VT • Documented spontaneous sustained VT Class IIa (Reasonable): • Spontaneous Type 1 ECG + arrhythmic syncope • Spontaneous Type 1 ECG + ≥2 multiparametric risk factors Class III (Not Recommended): • Asymptomatic with drug-induced only pattern • Type 2/3 pattern alone Disposition: • Admi

nodes.title: Intermediate Risk Management
nodes.summary: ICD vs quinidine vs surveillance — Type 1 favors ICD
nodes.body: Intermediate risk Brugada — shared decision making: Options: 1. ICD implantation • Definitive protection against SCD • Complications: inappropriate shocks, infection, lead issues • Lifelong device management 2. Quinidine therapy • Class IIa indication • 88% effective at suppressing VF induction • Side effects: GI, thrombocytopenia • Availability issues in some regions 3. Close surveillance • Lifes

nodes.title: Low Risk / Asymptomatic
nodes.summary: Asymptomatic ~0.5%/yr — fever treatment and drug avoidance list
nodes.body: Asymptomatic Brugada — observation appropriate: Annual event rate: ~0.5% (vs 0.4% background mortality) Management: • Lifestyle modifications • Aggressive fever treatment (antipyretics immediately) • Drug avoidance list (provide to patient) • Avoid cocaine, cannabis, excessive alcohol • EP follow-up for ongoing risk assessment Patient education: • Symptoms to watch for (syncope, palpitations) • Fe

nodes.title: Known Brugada — Complication Type
nodes.summary: Known Brugada: fever, ICD shocks, storm, or drug exposure
nodes.body: Patient with known Brugada syndrome presenting with complication: What is the presenting issue?

nodes.title: Fever Management
nodes.summary: Fever unmasks Type 1 20x — antipyretics and cooling aggressively
nodes.body: Fever in Brugada Syndrome — TREAT AGGRESSIVELY Why fever is dangerous: • Temperature-sensitive sodium channels (SCN5A) • Fever unmasks Type 1 pattern 20× more frequently • 40% recurrence rate with subsequent fevers • Can trigger VF Management protocol: 1. Aggressive antipyresis: • Acetaminophen 1000 mg q6h (IV if available) • Ibuprofen 400-600 mg q6h (if no contraindications) • Do not wait for hig

nodes.title: ICD Shocks
nodes.summary: Device interrogation needed — appropriate vs inappropriate changes mgmt
nodes.body: ICD shocks in Brugada patient: Assess: • Number of shocks in past 24 hours • Circumstances (fever, medication, activity) • Symptoms before shocks Device interrogation needed to confirm: • Appropriate vs inappropriate shocks • VF/VT vs SVT vs artifact How many shocks in the past 24 hours?

nodes.title: Isolated ICD Shocks
nodes.summary: 1-2 shocks: telemetry, ECG, temp, meds review, await interrogation
nodes.body: 1-2 ICD shocks — evaluation: Immediate: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • 12-lead ECG • Check temperature (fever?) • Review medications • Magnet available at bedside Device interrogation (EP/cardiology): • Confirm appropriate vs inappropriate • Review stored episodes • Check lead integrity If appropriate shocks (VF terminated): • Assess for triggers (fever, drugs, ischemia) • May need medication a

nodes.title: Electrical Storm Protocol
nodes.summary: Isoproterenol for storm — NO beta-blockers or amiodarone
nodes.body: Electrical Storm (≥3 VF/VT episodes/day) — EMERGENCY First-line: ISOPROTERENOL Mechanism: Increases HR → decreases J-point → suppresses VF Protocol: • Bolus: 1-2 mcg IV • Infusion: 0.15-2.0 mcg/min • Target: 20% increase in heart rate • Duration: Continue until stable (mean 24±13 days) Add QUINIDINE when stable: • 200 mg PO TID → increase to 400 mg TID • Allows weaning of isoproterenol in 24-48h ❌

nodes.title: Drug Exposure Management
nodes.summary: Stop agent, continuous monitoring — duration per drug half-life
nodes.body: Exposed to contraindicated medication: Immediate actions: • Discontinue offending agent • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Serial 12-lead ECGs • Check for Type 1 pattern unmasking High-risk drugs (AVOID): • Class 1A/1C antiarrhythmics • Tricyclic antidepressants • Lithium • Cocaine • Flecainide, propafenone, procainamide Monitoring duration: • Depends on drug half-life • Ajmaline: minutes • Procain

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit: arrest, storm, febrile no ICD, Type 1+syncope, drug list
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: ADMIT to telemetry/ICU: • Cardiac arrest / VF survivor • Electrical storm • New Type 1 ECG with syncope or concerning symptoms • Febrile Brugada patient without ICD • Multiple ICD shocks • Drug exposure with ECG changes May discharge with close EP follow-up: • Asymptomatic incidental finding • Drug-induced only pattern (confirmed) • Known Brugada, routine visit, no acute issue

nodes.title: Burns: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Burns = trauma first — ABCDE before burn-specific assessment
nodes.body: Burns Steps Summary — stepwise approach to burn assessment and management. This consult covers the 7-module approach to burn management: initial assessment, TBSA calculation, fluid resuscitation, airway and inhalation injury, escharotomy, chemical burns, and wound care with disposition planning. Burns are trauma patients first. Complete a primary survey (ABCDE) before focusing on burn-specific ass

nodes.title: Burn Mechanism
nodes.summary: Mechanism determines protocols — thermal, chemical, electrical, radiation
nodes.body: Identify the mechanism of injury. Mechanism determines the initial management pathway and anticipates specific complications. Thermal burns are most common (>80%). Chemical and electrical burns require agent-specific and mechanism-specific protocols. Radiation burns are rare and require specialized consultation. Consider toxic inhalation in ALL burns — especially enclosed-space fires. CO and cyani

nodes.title: Electrical Burns
nodes.summary: Internal > visible — rhabdo, compartment syndrome, dysrhythmias
nodes.body: Electrical burns cause internal damage far exceeding external appearance. Current follows the path of least resistance: nerve > blood vessel > muscle > skin > tendon > fat > bone. High voltage (>1000V): • Entry/exit wounds — look for both • Deep tissue necrosis along current path • Rhabdomyolysis — aggressive IVF, target UOP 1-1.5 mL/kg/hr • Compartment syndrome risk (especially forearm, leg) • Ca

nodes.title: Radiation Burns
nodes.summary: REAC/TS 865-576-1005 — decontaminate before treating, remove clothing
nodes.body: Radiation burns are rare in the ED. Localized radiation injury typically presents with delayed onset (hours to days after exposure). Severity depends on dose, duration, and type of radiation. Immediate actions: • Contact REAC/TS (Radiation Emergency Assistance Center): 865-576-1005 — 24/7 consultation • Decontaminate BEFORE treating — external contamination is the priority • Remove all clothing (r
nodes.recommendation: Radiation burns are rare. Contact REAC/TS (865-576-1005). Decontaminate first — remove clothing (90% decontamination). Treat wound as thermal burn. Monitor for delayed effects.

nodes.title: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
nodes.summary: Early intubation ANY airway concern — edema peaks 12-24h
nodes.body: A — Airway: Facial burns, soot in nares/oropharynx, singed nasal/facial hair, hoarse voice, stridor → early intubation. Airway edema peaks at 12-24h. If you are considering intubation, do it now — the airway will only get worse. B — Breathing: Circumferential chest burns may restrict ventilation → escharotomy. Assess for inhalation injury. Auscultate for wheezing, stridor. C — Circulation: Establi

nodes.title: Inhalation Injury Screening
nodes.summary: Inhalation increases mortality 20-60% and fluid requirements 30-50%
nodes.body: High-risk signs for inhalation injury: • Enclosed space fire • Facial burns, singed facial/nasal hair • Soot in nares, mouth, or sputum • Carbonaceous sputum • Hoarse voice, stridor, dyspnea • Wheezing or rales • Hypoxia or altered mental status Inhalation injury significantly worsens prognosis — increases mortality by 20-60% and fluid requirements by 30-50%. It is the strongest predictor of morta

nodes.title: Burn Depth Assessment
nodes.summary: Capillary refill: brisk=superficial, sluggish=deep, absent=full
nodes.body: Burn Depth Classification Guide Five-tier burn depth classification: 1. Epidermal (Superficial): Red, painful, no blisters, blanches with pressure. Sunburn. Heals 3-5 days. NOT counted in TBSA. 2. Superficial Partial Thickness (2nd degree): Blisters, moist pink base, very painful, brisk capillary refill. Heals 7-14 days with minimal scarring. 3. Deep Partial Thickness (2nd degree): Blisters (may h

nodes.title: Patient Age for TBSA
nodes.summary: Only partial and full thickness count — superficial NOT included
nodes.body: Select the appropriate TBSA estimation method based on patient age. Only count partial thickness (2nd degree) and full thickness (3rd/4th degree) burns in TBSA. Epidermal/superficial burns (e.g., sunburn) are NOT included in TBSA calculations. Accurate TBSA estimation is critical — it drives fluid resuscitation volumes, burn center transfer decisions, and prognosis.

nodes.title: TBSA — Rule of 9's (Adult)
nodes.summary: Rule of 9s: head 9%, arm 9%, trunk 18%, leg 18%, palm 1%
nodes.body: Rule of 9's — Adult Body Surface Area: • Head & neck: 9% • Each upper extremity: 9% (entire arm) • Anterior trunk: 18% • Posterior trunk: 18% • Each lower extremity: 18% (entire leg) • Perineum/genitalia: 1% • Total: 100% Palm method: The patient's palm (fingers together) ≈ 1% TBSA. Useful for scattered or irregular burn patterns. For scattered burns, use the palm method to supplement the Rule of

nodes.title: TBSA — Lund-Browder (Pediatric)
nodes.summary: Lund-Browder for <=14yo — larger head, smaller legs
nodes.body: Children have proportionally larger heads and smaller legs than adults. The Rule of 9's is inaccurate for patients ≤14 years. Use the Lund-Browder chart for age-adjusted TBSA estimation. Age-adjusted percentages (Lund-Browder): | Region | 0-1 yr | 1-4 yr | 5-9 yr | 10-14 yr | |--------|--------|--------|--------|----------| | Head | 19% | 17% | 13% | 11% | | Neck | 2% | 2% | 2% | 2% | | Ant. trunk

nodes.title: TBSA-Based Triage
nodes.summary: Adults >=20% or peds >=10% TBSA need resuscitation formulas
nodes.body: Based on your TBSA calculation, select the appropriate fluid resuscitation pathway. Formal fluid resuscitation formulas are generally indicated for adults with ≥20% TBSA and children with ≥10% TBSA. Smaller burns can usually be managed with oral hydration and maintenance IV fluids.

nodes.title: Minor Burn Fluid Management
nodes.summary: Minor: PO fluids, IV maintenance if NPO — no formula needed
nodes.body: No formal resuscitation formula is needed for minor burns (adults <20% TBSA, children <10% TBSA). Fluid strategy: • Encourage oral fluid intake — patients with intact GI function and small burns can self-hydrate • IV maintenance fluids if NPO or unable to tolerate PO • Standard maintenance rate: 4-2-1 rule (4 mL/kg/hr first 10kg, 2 mL/kg/hr next 10kg, 1 mL/kg/hr thereafter) Monitoring: • Urine out
