nodes.title: Equipment Check
nodes.summary: CLUTCH drill auto-disengages inner table — critical safety
nodes.body: Essential Equipment: ✓ Drill (ONE of the following): • Hudson-Brace manual drill (hand-cranked) • Pneumatic/electric craniotome • In extremis: EZ-IO with 25mm needle (case reports) ✓ Drill Bits: • 14mm perforator with CLUTCH mechanism (critical) • Matchstick/cutting ball bit (backup) ✓ Instruments: • Scalpel (#10, #15 blade) • Self-retaining retractor (Weitlaner) • Penfield dissectors (#1-4) • Sha

nodes.title: The Clutch Mechanism — Critical Safety
nodes.summary: Do NOT stop/restart — continuous drill until spindle stops
nodes.body: The Clutch is the Most Important Safety Feature How It Works: • Drill bit automatically DISENGAGES when it penetrates the inner table • Detects the sudden drop in resistance • Prevents "plunging" into brain tissue This is What Allows Non-Neurosurgeons to Perform This Procedure Proper Clutch Drill Technique: 1. Position drill perpendicular to skull 2. Apply firm, STEADY downward pressure 3. Drill C

nodes.title: No Clutch Drill — Two-Bit Technique
nodes.summary: Two-bit: perforator outer, blunt burr inner table
nodes.body: ⚠️ Higher Risk — Only If Clutch Unavailable Two-Bit Technique: Step 1: Perforator Bit (Outer Table Only) • Use sharp perforator bit • Drill through OUTER table only • Stop when you feel decreased resistance • This is the diploe (spongy middle layer) Step 2: Switch to Blunt Burr • Remove perforator bit • Insert blunt/ball burr • Gently enlarge hole through inner table • Use irrigation to visualize

nodes.title: Austere/Field Equipment
nodes.summary: EZ-IO 25mm last resort — higher cortical injury risk
nodes.body: Minimal Equipment for Field Conditions: Absolute Minimum: • Cutting instrument (scalpel, knife) • Drill of ANY kind with bit • Something to retract scalp • Irrigation (saline, clean water) • Sterile (or cleanest available) dressing Improvised Equipment: • Drill: Cordless power drill with clean bit • Retractor: Bent spoon handles, improvised hooks • Hemostasis: Direct pressure, cautery if available

nodes.title: Pre-Procedure Preparation
nodes.summary: Intubate, osmotherapy, mark midline BEFORE draping, antibiotics
nodes.body: Preparation Checklist: □ Airway & Ventilation: • Intubate, sedate, paralyze • C-spine immobilization if trauma • Target EtCO₂ 35-40 mmHg • SpO₂ >94% □ Osmotherapy (Start Now): • Mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg IV OR • Hypertonic saline 23.4% 30mL □ Positioning: • Supine, head elevated above chest • Rotate head 30-40° off midline (operative side UP) • Generous shoulder bump • Mark midline and incision site BEF

nodes.title: Step 1: Incision
nodes.summary: 3-4cm vertical to bone — scalp bleeding not life-threatening
nodes.body: Scalp Incision: Incision Type: • 3-4 cm VERTICAL incision (linear) • Directly down to bone • Vertical orientation minimizes vascular injury For Temporal Approach: • 2 FB above and anterior to tragus • Stay above zygomatic arch • Avoid superficial temporal artery (runs anterior) Technique: 1. Incise skin and subcutaneous tissue 2. Continue through galea aponeurotica 3. Incise periosteum (pericraniu

nodes.title: Step 2: Expose Skull
nodes.summary: Clear periosteum, retractor, verify landmark before drilling
nodes.body: Skull Exposure: Clear the Periosteum: • Use scalpel handle or gauze to push periosteum from bone • Create 2-3 cm clear area around planned drill site • Periosteum is adherent — requires firm scraping Insert Retractor: • Place self-retaining retractor (Weitlaner) • Retract scalp edges • Should see clean, white bone Verify Landmark: • Confirm position relative to anatomical landmarks • If CT availab

nodes.title: Step 3: Drilling
nodes.summary: Perpendicular, steady, irrigate — clutch stops at inner table
nodes.body: Burr Hole Drilling Technique: ⚠️ CRITICAL: Use Clutch Bit If Available Clutch Drill Technique: 1. Position: Drill PERPENDICULAR to skull surface 2. Pressure: Apply firm, STEADY downward pressure • Assistant stabilizes head from opposite side 3. Irrigation: Apply saline during drilling • Prevents thermal injury • Clears bone dust • Improves visualization 4. Drill Continuously: Do NOT stop and resta

nodes.title: Step 4: Evacuate Hematoma
nodes.summary: Dark blood=EDH, bluish dura=SDH, normal=wrong site, brain=stop
nodes.body: What Do You See? After completing the burr hole, assess what is visible: A. Dark Blood Under Pressure (Epidural Hematoma) • Blood between skull and dura • Often clotted • May drain spontaneously when hole completed B. Dura with Bluish Discoloration (Subdural Hematoma) • Blood UNDER the dura • Requires opening dura to drain • Dura appears bluish/dark instead of normal gray C. Normal Dura (Gray, Pul

nodes.title: Epidural Hematoma Drainage
nodes.summary: Spontaneous drainage — NEVER suction brain tissue
nodes.body: Evacuating Epidural Hematoma: What to Expect: • Dark, clotted blood between skull and dura • May drain spontaneously under pressure • Often partially clotted — won't all drain through hole Technique: 1. Allow Spontaneous Drainage: • Blood under pressure will drain on its own • Do NOT suction aggressively 2. Gentle Irrigation: • Use saline to flush clot • Helps liquefy and evacuate 3. Gentle Suctio

nodes.title: Subdural Hematoma Drainage
nodes.summary: Tent dura, cruciate incision — do NOT explore subdural
nodes.body: Evacuating Subdural Hematoma: Subdural = Blood UNDER Dura Must open dura to drain. Technique: 1. Tent the Dura: • Use sharp hook to lift dura • Elevate a small tent of dura membrane • Do NOT plunge through 2. Incise Dura: • Use #15 scalpel blade • Make small CRUCIATE incision (+) • Careful — brain is immediately deep to dura 3. Drain Hematoma: • Subdural blood is often more liquid than EDH • Will

nodes.title: No Blood Found
nodes.summary: No blood: close and transport — max 2 holes, no hunting
nodes.body: No Hematoma at This Location Possible Explanations: • Wrong location (hematoma elsewhere) • Hematoma intraparenchymal (not extra-axial) • CT misinterpreted • False localizing signs Options: 1. Close and Transport (Recommended) • Do NOT explore with multiple random holes • Patient needs CT and neurosurgery • Transport immediately 2. Single Additional Burr Hole (Consider If): • Strong clinical suspi

nodes.title: Second Burr Hole
nodes.summary: Max 2 holes — both negative = close and transport
nodes.body: Placing a Second Burr Hole: When to Consider: • CT showed hematoma but first hole was misplaced • Clinical suspicion very high • Different anatomical location makes sense Maximum: 2 Burr Holes • More than 2 = unacceptable complication risk • If 2 holes negative, close and transport Location Options: 1. If first was temporal → try parietal • 4 FB posterior and superior to EAC 2. If first was fronta

nodes.title: Dural Tear / Brain Visible
nodes.summary: Brain visible = STOP — wet gauze, close, transport
nodes.body: Brain Tissue Visible = STOP This Means: • Dura was torn during drilling • Brain cortex is exposed • Risk of cortical injury with further manipulation Immediate Actions: 1. STOP all drilling/instrumentation 2. Do NOT explore further 3. Irrigate Gently: • Saline irrigation to clean debris • Remove bone fragments if visible 4. Cover with Saline-Soaked Gauze: • Keep brain moist • Prevent desiccation i

nodes.title: Step 5: Hemostasis
nodes.summary: Bone wax bone edge, bipolar MMA, Gelfoam dural ooze
nodes.body: Achieving Hemostasis: Identify Bleeding Source: Middle Meningeal Artery: • Arterial pumping from dura or bone • Most common cause of EDH • Runs in groove on inner skull Treatment: • Bipolar electrocautery if visible • Bone wax into foramen spinosum • May need to extend bone opening Bone Edge Bleeding: • Oozing from diploe (spongy bone) • Treatment: Bone wax • Pack firmly into bleeding bone edges V

nodes.title: Extend to Craniectomy?
nodes.summary: Extend only if drainage inadequate — increases risk
nodes.body: When to Extend Burr Hole to Craniectomy: Consider Extending If: • Inadequate drainage through single hole • Large clot not evacuating • Ongoing arterial bleeding requiring visualization • Brain herniating through defect (needs decompression) Technique to Extend: 1. Create Second Burr Hole: • 3-4 cm from first hole • Same technique 2. Connect Holes: • Leksell rongeur to nibble bone between holes •

nodes.title: Extending to Craniectomy
nodes.summary: Connect holes with rongeur — protect dura with Penfield
nodes.body: Craniectomy Technique: ⚠️ Significantly Higher Risk — Only If Necessary Step 1: Second Burr Hole • Place 3-4 cm from first hole • Ideally along planned craniotomy line • Same drilling technique Step 2: Connect Holes with Rongeur • Use Leksell or Kerrison rongeur • Nibble bone between holes • Protect dura with Penfield #4 as you go • Work slowly — do NOT tear dura Step 3: Remove Bone • Lift connect

nodes.title: Wound Closure
nodes.summary: LOOSE dressing only — tight packing INCREASES ICP
nodes.body: Closing the Wound: ⚠️ CRITICAL: DO NOT Tamponade Loose Dressing ONLY: • Tight packing INCREASES ICP • Can cause secondary brain injury • Gentle coverage is sufficient Closure Technique: 1. If Ongoing Hemorrhage: • Leave self-retaining retractor in place • Cover with saline-moistened gauze • Transport with wound open 2. If Hemostasis Achieved: • Irrigate wound thoroughly • Approximate scalp loosely

nodes.title: Complications
nodes.summary: Neurosurgical series: 11-20.5% any complication, ~3.9% mod-severe, ~2.1% ICH, 1.4-2.1% empyema, ~1.1% mortality. The old "~2.5%" figure was unsourced.
nodes.body: Intraoperative Complications: | Complication | Cause | Management | |--------------|-------|------------| | Cortical Injury | Drill plunge | Use clutch bit; stop if brain seen | | MMA Bleeding | Temporal drilling | Bipolar; bone wax in foramen | | Sagittal Sinus | Too medial | Stay ≥3 cm lateral; direct pressure | | Dural Tear | Aggressive instrumentation | Cover with dural substitute | | Scalp Bl

nodes.title: Post-Procedure Care
nodes.summary: BRIDGE not cure — needs definitive craniotomy
nodes.body: Immediate Post-Procedure: Remember: This is a BRIDGE, Not a Cure Patient still requires: • Definitive neurosurgical craniotomy • ICU-level care • Ongoing ICP management Immediate Actions: 1. Antibiotics: • Continue cefazolin 2g IV q8h or ceftriaxone 1g IV q24h • Meningitis prophylaxis 2. Arrange Immediate Transport: • Neurosurgical center • Air transport if available and faster • Pre-notify receiv

nodes.title: Transport Monitoring
nodes.summary: GCS pupils q15min — hyperventilate only acute pupil changes
nodes.body: Monitoring During Transport: Serial Neurologic Checks (q15 min): • GCS • Pupil size and reactivity • Motor response to commands Signs of Re-Expansion/Deterioration: • Declining GCS • New or worsening anisocoria • New seizure • Cushing's triad (late sign) If Patient Deteriorates: 1. Brief Hyperventilation: • EtCO₂ 30-35 mmHg • Maximum 5-10 minutes • Temporizing measure only 2. Additional Osmotherap

nodes.title: Documentation
nodes.summary: Document indication, herniation, procedure — medicolegal critical
nodes.body: Critical Documentation: Pre-Procedure: • Time of injury (if known) • GCS progression with times • Pupil changes with times • Herniation signs • CT findings (if available) • Time neurosurgery unavailable • Medical management provided Consent/Indication: • Emergency procedure performed under implied consent • Life-threatening emergency • No neurosurgical alternative available • Expected outcome with

nodes.title: Button Battery Ingestion — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Esophageal injury 15 MIN — STAT X-ray, NPO until located
nodes.body: Critical Time Window: - Esophageal tissue injury begins within 15 minutes - Esophageal batteries must be removed within 2 hours (ideally) - Aortoesophageal fistula can occur up to 28 days post-removal High-Risk Batteries: - Lithium coin cells (3V) — most dangerous - ≥20mm diameter — highest risk for esophageal impaction - ≥15mm in children <6 years — high risk Immediate Actions: 1. Obtain STAT X-r

nodes.title: Symptomatic Battery Ingestion
nodes.summary: Drooling, dysphagia, hematemesis = emergent, NO vomiting induction
nodes.body: Red Flag Symptoms: - Drooling, dysphagia, odynophagia - Chest pain, substernal discomfort - Vomiting (especially hematemesis) - Stridor, respiratory distress - Refusal to eat - Fever (suggests mediastinitis) If symptomatic + battery NOT visible on X-ray: - Consider CT with contrast - Battery may have passed but caused injury Immediate Management: - IV access, NPO - Emergent GI/ENT consultation - D

nodes.title: ESOPHAGEAL BATTERY — EMERGENT
nodes.summary: Remove within 2 HRS — honey delays but does not prevent injury
nodes.body: This is a TIME-CRITICAL emergency. Target: Remove within 2 hours (maximum 12 hours) Pre-Endoscopy Protection (if <12 hours from ingestion): Honey Protocol (age ≥12 months): - 10 mL orally every 10 minutes × 6 doses - Use commercial honey only - Delays tissue injury but does NOT prevent it Sucralfate Protocol (ED): - 1 g (10 mL suspension) PO every 10 minutes × 3 doses - Alternative to honey CONTRA

nodes.title: Emergent Endoscopic Removal
nodes.summary: OR preferred — do NOT delay for NPO status
nodes.body: Removal Considerations: Location: - Operating room preferred over endoscopy suite - Allows rapid conversion to open surgery if needed - Better imaging capability Team: - GI/ENT for endoscopy - Anesthesia - Cardiothoracic surgery on standby - Pediatric surgery available Technique: - Gentle removal to minimize additional trauma - Inspect for perforation after removal - Do NOT delay for NPO status Po

nodes.title: Gastric Battery — Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Risk: <6yo+>=15mm or >=20mm = high risk for endoscopy
nodes.body: Risk Stratification for Gastric Batteries: HIGH RISK (Consider early endoscopy): - Age <6 years AND battery ≥15mm - Battery ≥20mm (any age) - Symptomatic patient - Co-ingested magnet LOW RISK (Observation acceptable): - Age ≥12 years AND battery ≤12mm - Asymptomatic - No magnet co-ingestion - Reliable caregiver for follow-up Medium Risk: - Age 6-12 years OR battery 12-15mm - Requires closer monito

nodes.title: High-Risk Gastric Battery
nodes.summary: X-ray day 4 — still in stomach = endoscopic removal
nodes.body: Management: Age <6 years OR Battery ≥15mm Initial: - Asymptomatic: can observe initially - Symptomatic: consult GI for early removal Follow-Up Imaging: - Repeat X-ray at Day 4 - If still in stomach at Day 4: endoscopic removal recommended Discharge Instructions: - Normal diet/activity - Return for: vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody stool, fever - Inspect stools for battery passage - Follow-up arran

nodes.title: Low-Risk Gastric Battery
nodes.summary: Home, inspect stools — X-ray day 10-14 if unconfirmed
nodes.body: Management: Age ≥12 years AND Battery ≤12mm Home Observation: - Normal diet and activity - Inspect stools for battery passage - No need for inpatient observation Follow-Up Imaging: - If passage not confirmed by Day 10-14: repeat X-ray - Most batteries pass within 4-7 days Return Precautions: - Abdominal pain - Vomiting - Black or bloody stools - Fever - Decreased appetite No Intervention Needed If

nodes.title: Large Battery ≥20mm in Stomach
nodes.summary: >=20mm: GI consult, X-ray 48hrs — remove if past pylorus
nodes.body: Urgent Concern — Battery ≥20mm Initial Management: - GI consultation for endoscopy consideration - Higher risk of mucosal injury Follow-Up: - Repeat X-ray at 48 hours - If not progressing past pylorus: remove endoscopically - If progressed to duodenum: follow distal protocol Rationale: - Large batteries more likely to cause gastric injury - May not pass pylorus spontaneously - Earlier intervention

nodes.title: Battery Distal to Stomach
nodes.summary: Past stomach = low risk — most pass 4-7 days
nodes.body: LOW RISK — Beyond Pylorus Once past the stomach, serious complications are rare. Management: - Home observation - Normal diet and activity - Inspect stools for battery passage Follow-Up Imaging: - Repeat X-ray at Day 10-14 if passage not confirmed - No need for routine imaging if asymptomatic Surgical Removal Indications: - Symptoms develop (obstruction, perforation) - Battery fails to progress on

nodes.title: Battery Complications
nodes.summary: AEF up to 28 DAYS — sentinel bleed precedes catastrophe
nodes.body: Immediate Complications (First 24-48 hours): - Esophageal perforation → pneumomediastinum - Mediastinitis → fever, tachycardia, sepsis - Hemorrhage from vessel erosion Delayed Complications (Days 3-28+): - Aortoesophageal fistula (AEF) — most common fatal complication - Occurs up to 28 days post-removal - Mid-esophageal impaction highest risk - Tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) — up to 9 days post-r

nodes.title: Aortoesophageal Fistula (AEF)
nodes.summary: AEF catastrophic — CTA, CT surgery, MTP standby
nodes.body: CATASTROPHIC — HIGH MORTALITY Risk Factors: - Mid-esophageal impaction (aortic arch level) - Battery ≥20mm - Prolonged impaction (>2 hours) Presentation: - "Sentinel bleed" — minor hematemesis preceding massive hemorrhage - Chest/back pain - Sudden cardiovascular collapse Diagnosis: - CTA chest (preferred) - Do NOT delay imaging if suspected Management: - Immediate cardiothoracic surgery consultat

nodes.title: Perforation & Mediastinitis
nodes.summary: Pneumomediastinum + fever = mediastinitis — broad abx
nodes.body: Signs of Perforation: - Pneumomediastinum on X-ray/CT - Subcutaneous emphysema - Severe chest pain - Mediastinal widening Mediastinitis: - Fever, tachycardia - Chest pain, dyspnea - Sepsis syndrome - Odynophagia Management: - Broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover oral flora + GI flora) - NPO, TPN consideration - Surgical consultation - CT chest with contrast for extent of injury Antibiotic Options: -

nodes.title: Post-Removal Monitoring
nodes.summary: Admit esophageal 24-48hrs — CTA if mid-esophageal
nodes.body: Standard Post-Removal Care: Admission Criteria: - All esophageal battery removals - Any visible mucosal injury on endoscopy - Mid-esophageal impaction (AEF risk) - Symptomatic patients Monitoring: - Vitals q4h (watch for sepsis) - NPO initially - Advance diet when stable: clear liquids → soft diet - Serial exams for abdominal pain, chest pain Imaging: - CTA chest if mid-esophageal location (even i

nodes.title: Disposition Summary
nodes.summary: Admit esophageal, discharge asymptomatic gastric/distal
nodes.body: ADMIT: - All esophageal battery removals (24-48h minimum) - Post-endoscopic observation - High-risk patients without reliable follow-up - Symptomatic patients - Concern for perforation/mediastinitis DISCHARGE with Close Follow-Up: - Asymptomatic gastric/distal batteries meeting low-risk criteria - Reliable caregiver - Clear return precautions given - Follow-up imaging arranged Documentation: - Bat

nodes.title: Interventions to AVOID
nodes.summary: NO vomiting, charcoal, NPO delay, or blind balloon
nodes.body: DO NOT: - ❌ Induce vomiting (increases esophageal damage) - ❌ Give ipecac - ❌ Attempt blind balloon catheter removal - ❌ Give activated charcoal (no benefit) - ❌ Give laxatives or PEG solution - ❌ Check blood/urine metal levels - ❌ Attempt chelation - ❌ Delay endoscopy for NPO status (if esophageal) - ❌ Delay removal even if honey/sucralfate given Remember: - Honey/sucralfate DELAY injury — they d

nodes.title: Calcium Disorder
nodes.summary: Start with ionized calcium when available; route to hypoCa, hyperCa, or mixed Ca-phosphate workup.
nodes.body: Use ionized calcium when available. If using total calcium, correct for albumin and interpret with pH. Which pathway fits the patient?

nodes.title: Calcium Steps
nodes.summary: Confirm ionized Ca, check ECG and Mg/Phos/renal function, treat symptoms first, coordinate early in renal/TLS/rhabdo.
nodes.body: 1. Confirm: ionized Ca preferred; repeat if unexpected. 2. ECG: low Ca can prolong QT; high Ca can shorten QT and cause bradyarrhythmia. 3. Check Mg, phosphate, potassium, creatinine, albumin, pH, PTH when not obvious. 4. Treat symptoms first, then etiology. 5. In renal failure, TLS, rhabdomyolysis, or high phosphate, coordinate calcium/phosphate treatment with nephrology early.

nodes.title: Hypocalcemia Severity
nodes.summary: Severe symptoms or ECG changes need IV calcium; stable cases need Mg/Phos/PTH/Vit D workup and oral replacement.
nodes.body: Symptoms, ECG findings, and acuity determine urgency more than the total calcium alone. Severe features: seizure, tetany, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm/bronchospasm, hypotension, heart failure, arrhythmia, markedly prolonged QT, or acute fall after thyroid/parathyroid surgery, massive transfusion, pancreatitis, sepsis, rhabdo, or TLS.

nodes.title: Severe Hypocalcemia
nodes.summary: IV calcium now for severe symptoms or ECG instability; repeat based on symptoms, ECG, and ionized Ca.
nodes.body: Give IV calcium with cardiac monitoring. Peripheral access: Calcium Gluconate 1-2 g IV over 10-20 min; repeat until severe symptoms improve. Central access or peri-arrest: Calcium Chloride 500 mg-1 g IV over 10 min. Then recheck ionized calcium, Mg, phosphate, K, creatinine, and ECG. If calcium falls again, use repeated slow calcium gluconate doses or infusion while fixing the cause.

nodes.title: Hypocalcemia Workup
nodes.summary: Check Mg/Phos/PTH/Vit D/renal function; low Mg commonly makes hypocalcemia refractory.
nodes.body: Core labs: ionized Ca, Mg, phosphate, BMP/creatinine, albumin, pH/ABG or VBG if critically ill, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, and 1,25-OH vitamin D when renal/granulomatous disease is suspected. Treat concurrent hypomagnesemia before labeling hypocalcemia refractory. Review recent thyroid/parathyroid surgery, massive transfusion, pancreatitis, sepsis, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, denosumab/bisphosphonate

nodes.title: Stable Hypocalcemia
nodes.body: If stable and able to take PO, use oral calcium plus vitamin D strategy and arrange endocrine/nephrology follow-up based on etiology. Admit if symptomatic, acute post-op, severe ionized Ca depression, renal failure with phosphate problem, seizure, arrhythmia, prolonged QT, or need for IV infusion.
nodes.recommendation: Treat etiology, correct Mg, use oral calcium/vitamin D when safe, and admit high-risk or infusion-requiring patients.

nodes.title: Hypercalcemia Severity
nodes.summary: Severe hypercalcemia is Ca >14 or symptomatic; renal failure or volume overload changes the first move.
nodes.body: Classify by severity, symptoms, rate of rise, renal function, and volume status. Severe: corrected Ca >14 mg/dL, ionized Ca markedly high, altered mental status, dehydration/AKI, pancreatitis, arrhythmia, shortened QT/bradyarrhythmia, or inability to maintain oral hydration.

nodes.title: Severe Hypercalcemia
nodes.summary: Severe hypercalcemia: fluids if tolerated, calcitonin bridge, antiresorptive therapy, etiology-directed treatment.
nodes.body: 1. Stop calcium, vitamin D, thiazides, lithium, and immobilization drivers when possible. 2. Isotonic crystalloid for volume depletion; reassess lungs, urine output, and cardiac function. 3. Calcitonin 4 IU/kg SC/IM q12h as rapid bridge; limit to 48-72 hr. 4. Durable therapy: Denosumab or Zoledronic Acid, guided by renal function, malignancy context, and local protocol. 5. Glucocorticoids are most

nodes.title: Stable Hypercalcemia
nodes.summary: Stable hypercalcemia: PTH splits the differential; suppressed PTH should trigger malignancy/calcitriol/granulomatous/medication review.
nodes.body: Initial workup: repeat calcium/ionized calcium, albumin, creatinine, phosphate, Mg, ECG, PTH, and medication review. If PTH elevated or inappropriately normal: primary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism, lithium, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. If PTH suppressed: malignancy/PTHrP, vitamin D or calcitriol-mediated disease, granulomatous disease, thyrotoxicosis, adrenal insufficiency, milk-alkali, v

nodes.title: Renal / Phosphate Caveats
nodes.summary: In high phosphate states, calcium is for symptoms/electrical instability; severe hyperCa with renal failure may need dialysis.
nodes.body: High phosphate changes calcium management. In TLS, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, and severe hyperphosphatemia, IV calcium can increase Ca-phosphate precipitation risk. Give IV calcium when the patient is symptomatic or electrically unstable, but do not chase an asymptomatic low total calcium. Severe hypercalcemia with renal failure, anuria, volume overload, or neurologic/cardiac toxicity may requ

nodes.title: Disposition / Consults
nodes.body: Admit severe, symptomatic, acute post-op, AKI/renal failure, malignancy-associated, arrhythmic, or infusion/dialysis-requiring calcium disorders. Consult nephrology for dialysis patients, severe CKD-MBD, high Ca-phosphate product concern, renal failure limiting treatment, or dialysis consideration. Consult endocrine/oncology for severe unexplained hypercalcemia, suspected parathyroid disease, calc
nodes.recommendation: Disposition is driven by symptoms, ECG, renal function, trajectory, and need for IV therapy or dialysis.

nodes.title: STOP: Calcium Pitfalls
nodes.body: - Do not rely on corrected calcium when ionized Ca is available or pH is abnormal. - Do not give IV calcium repeatedly for asymptomatic hypocalcemia caused by severe hyperphosphatemia. - Do not delay IV calcium for seizure, tetany, laryngospasm, shock, or malignant ECG changes. - Do not use calcitonin alone for severe hypercalcemia; tachyphylaxis develops quickly. - Do not force hydration in sever
nodes.recommendation: Reassess ionized calcium, ECG, Mg, phosphate, renal function, and volume status before repeating calcium-directed therapy.

nodes.title: Capacity Assessment
nodes.summary: Capacity is decision-specific. Identify the specific decision being assessed.
nodes.body: Why is capacity being questioned? Common triggers: * Refusing recommended treatment * Leaving AMA * Consenting to high-risk procedure * Signing DNR/POLST * Psychotic, intoxicated, or delirious Key principle: Capacity is decision-specific - a patient may have capacity for one decision but not another. *Example: A patient with mild dementia may have capacity to refuse blood draw but not to refuse li

nodes.title: Capacity vs Competency
nodes.summary: Capacity = clinical (physician). Competency = legal (court). Presume capacity exists.
nodes.body: Important distinction: | Term | Definition | Who Determines | |------|------------|----------------| | Capacity | Clinical ability to make a specific decision | Physician | | Competency | Legal status to make decisions | Court | Key points: * Patients are presumed to have capacity until proven otherwise * Diagnosis alone does not determine capacity (dementia, psychosis, intoxication) * A patient w

nodes.title: Four-Abilities Framework
nodes.summary: Capacity uses four abilities: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and communication of a stable choice.
nodes.body: Four abilities required for capacity: 1. Understanding * Can the patient describe the condition, recommended treatment, risks/benefits, and alternatives in their own words? * *"Can you tell me what we are worried about and what treatment we recommend?"* 2. Appreciation * Can they apply the information to their own situation? * Do they believe the condition and consequences are personally relevant?

nodes.title: Assessment Questions
nodes.summary: Structured questions for understanding, appreciation, reasoning, communication.
nodes.body: Structured questions for each domain: Understanding: * *"Can you tell me in your own words what's wrong?"* * *"What treatment did we recommend?"* * *"What might happen without treatment?"* Appreciation: * *"Do you believe you have [condition]?"* * *"Why do you think we're recommending this?"* * *"What do you think will happen to YOU?"* Reasoning: * *"How did you arrive at your decision?"* * *"What

nodes.title: Capacity Determination
nodes.summary: All four abilities must be sufficiently intact; lack of capacity requires a significant decision-relevant deficit.
nodes.body: Assess each four-abilities domain: | Domain | Intact? | Notes | |--------|---------|-------| | Understanding of condition/options/risks | [ ] Yes [ ] No | | | Appreciation of personal relevance | [ ] Yes [ ] No | | | Reasoning about consequences/alternatives | [ ] Yes [ ] No | | | Communication of a stable choice | [ ] Yes [ ] No | | Capacity present if: All four abilities are sufficiently intact

nodes.title: Refusing Treatment
nodes.summary: Treatment refusal: higher stakes = higher bar. If has capacity, respect decision.
nodes.body: Patient refusing recommended treatment: Higher stakes = higher bar for capacity: * Refusing Tylenol -> low threshold * Refusing life-saving surgery -> thorough assessment If patient has capacity: * Respect the decision, even if you disagree * Document capacity assessment thoroughly * Ensure informed refusal (risks of declining) * Offer alternatives, follow-up If lacks capacity: * Cannot refuse - p

nodes.title: Leaving AMA
nodes.summary: AMA requires capacity assessment. If lacks capacity, patient cannot leave.
nodes.body: Patient leaving against medical advice: Capacity assessment is REQUIRED before AMA: * Intoxication raises concern but does not automatically remove capacity - assess clinically and reassess when the decision can safely wait * Delirious patients generally cannot leave AMA until delirium is addressed * Psychiatric patients may require hold if they lack capacity or meet danger/grave disability criter

nodes.title: Consenting to Procedure
nodes.summary: Valid consent: disclosure + capacity + voluntariness. Interpreter if needed.
nodes.body: Ensuring valid informed consent: Elements of informed consent: 1. Disclosure - nature, risks, benefits, alternatives 2. Capacity - patient can understand and decide 3. Voluntariness - no coercion Capacity for consent requires: * Understanding the procedure * Appreciating personal relevance * Weighing risks vs benefits * Communicating a choice Special situations: * Minors: parent/guardian consent (

nodes.title: End-of-Life Decisions
nodes.summary: End-of-life decisions: higher bar, check for depression, use surrogate if lacks capacity.
nodes.body: DNR, hospice, withdrawal of care: Higher bar for irreversible decisions: * Ensure patient fully understands implications * Consider if decision is consistent with values * Rule out depression affecting decision-making If patient HAS capacity: * Respect their autonomous decision * Document thoroughly * Involve palliative care if available * Ensure family is informed (with patient permission) If pat

nodes.title: Patient Has Capacity
nodes.summary: Patient has capacity - respect decision, document assessment.
nodes.body: Patient has decision-making capacity: Next steps: * Respect their autonomous choice * Ensure informed decision (risks, benefits, alternatives) * Document your assessment Documentation should include: * The specific decision being assessed * How you assessed understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and communication of a choice * Patient's responses demonstrating capacity * That you believe patient
nodes.recommendation: Patient has capacity. Respect autonomous decision. Document assessment thoroughly.

nodes.title: Patient Lacks Capacity
nodes.summary: Patient lacks capacity - use surrogate, substituted judgment or best interest.
nodes.body: Patient lacks decision-making capacity: Identify surrogate decision-maker: 1. Healthcare proxy / POA (if designated) 2. Spouse 3. Adult children (majority if multiple) 4. Parents 5. Siblings 6. Other relatives / close friends *(Hierarchy varies by state)* Surrogate uses: * Substituted judgment: What would patient want? * Best interest: If wishes unknown If emergency and no surrogate available: * T
nodes.recommendation: Patient lacks capacity. Identify surrogate decision-maker. Use substituted judgment.

nodes.title: Unclear / Borderline Capacity
nodes.summary: Unclear capacity: wait and reassess, psychiatry consult, ethics consult, or court.
nodes.body: When capacity is unclear: Options: 1. More time: * Repeat assessment when patient is sober, rested, less stressed * Intoxication clears, delirium may improve with treatment 2. Psychiatry consult: * Formal capacity evaluation * Especially if underlying psychiatric illness * May use MacCAT (MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool) 3. Ethics consult: * Mediate complex situations * Help when family disag

nodes.title: Documentation
nodes.summary: Document: specific decision, four-abilities assessment, conclusion with reasoning.
nodes.body: Document your capacity assessment: Include: 1. The specific decision being assessed 2. Clinical context (why capacity was questioned) 3. Mental status exam findings 4. Assessment of each ability: * Understanding: *"Patient stated [X] when asked about condition/treatment/risks"* * Appreciation: *"Patient expressed [Y] about personal impact"* * Reasoning: *"Patient weighed options by considering [Z]

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest — Scene Assessment
nodes.summary: Check obvious death — lividity, rigor, decomposition, DNAR
nodes.body: Cardiac Arrest Steps Summary Scene assessment: Are there obvious signs of death present that preclude resuscitation? • Decapitation • Hemicorporectomy • Dependent lividity • Rigor mortis • Decomposition • Valid DNAR • Obviously non-survivable traumatic injury

nodes.title: Do NOT Initiate CPR
nodes.summary: Document obvious death — do not initiate CPR
nodes.body: Do NOT initiate resuscitation when any of the following are present: • Decapitation • Hemicorporectomy (transection of the torso) • Dependent lividity (non-blanching discoloration in dependent areas) • Rigor mortis (stiffening of joints and muscles) • Decomposition • Valid DNAR/POLST — verify document, confirm identity • Obviously non-survivable traumatic injury (e.g., massive cranial destruction)
nodes.recommendation: Document signs of obvious death. Do not initiate CPR. Time of death = time of discovery.

nodes.title: Confirm Cardiac Arrest
nodes.summary: Confirm <=10sec — unsure = start CPR
nodes.body: Confirm arrest in ≤10 seconds: • No pulse (carotid) • No breathing or only agonal gasps Begin CPR immediately. Do not delay for equipment. Quick pulse check: ≤10 seconds. If unsure — start CPR. It is better to perform CPR on a patient with a pulse than to withhold it from a patient without one. Activate the team: • Call for defibrillator/AED • Assign roles: compressor, airway, timer, medications,

nodes.title: CPR — First 2 Minutes
nodes.summary: 100-120/min, 5-6cm, full recoil — ETCO2 >20 = good quality
nodes.body: High-quality CPR checklist: • Rate: 100-120 compressions/min • Depth: 2-2.4 inches (5-6 cm) in adults • Full recoil — allow complete chest recoil between compressions • Minimize interruptions — <10 sec for rhythm checks and shocks • Rotate compressor every 2 minutes (or sooner if fatigued) Monitoring: • Attach waveform ETCO2 immediately after airway secured • ETCO2 >20 mmHg = adequate CPR quality

nodes.title: Airway Strategy
nodes.summary: BVM first — defer intubation, continuous with advanced airway
nodes.body: Initial airway: • BVM first — adequate oxygenation without interrupting compressions • Defer intubation early in the resuscitation — CPR quality is the priority • OPA/NPA adjuncts as needed Advanced airway (when ready): • If intubated → attach waveform capnography immediately • Continuous compressions with advanced airway — no 30:2 cycles • Ventilate every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min) • Avoid hyperv

nodes.title: First Rhythm Check
nodes.summary: <10sec pause at 2min — shockable vs non-shockable
nodes.body: At 2 minutes: Pause compressions briefly (<10 sec) for rhythm analysis. Is the rhythm shockable or non-shockable? • Shockable: VF (chaotic, no organized QRS) or pulseless VT (wide, regular, fast) • Non-shockable: PEA (organized rhythm, no pulse) or asystole (flatline — confirm in 2 leads)

nodes.title: Shockable Rhythm — Which Pattern?
nodes.summary: VF vs pVT vs TdP — NO amiodarone for Torsades
nodes.body: Differentiate the shockable rhythm: • VF / Refractory VF: Chaotic, disorganized electrical activity. No discernible QRS complexes. • Pulseless VT: Wide-complex, regular, rapid rhythm without a pulse. • Polymorphic VT / Torsades: Twisting QRS axis, often with prolonged QTc. Do NOT give amiodarone.

nodes.title: VF Identified
nodes.summary: VF — VF/VT protocol for shock-first approach
nodes.body: VF identified → proceed to VF/VT Arrest Protocol for shock-first approach, antiarrhythmics, DSD, and ECPR. VF/VT Arrest Protocol

nodes.title: Pulseless VT Identified
nodes.summary: Pulseless VT — check polymorphic and QTc first
nodes.body: Pulseless VT → check for polymorphic features and QTc. Ventricular Tachycardia Protocol

nodes.title: Torsades de Pointes Identified
nodes.summary: Torsades: Mg 2g IV then infusion — amiodarone CONTRAINDICATED
nodes.body: Polymorphic VT with prolonged QTc = Torsades de Pointes. \u26a0\ufe0f Do NOT give amiodarone — it prolongs QT and will worsen TdP. Torsades de Pointes Protocol

nodes.title: Non-Shockable Rhythm — PEA or Asystole?
nodes.summary: PEA needs POCUS — asystole confirm 2 leads
nodes.body: Differentiate the non-shockable rhythm: • PEA: Organized electrical activity on the monitor, but no palpable pulse. May have narrow or wide QRS. POCUS at first pulse check is critical — look for cardiac activity and reversible causes. • Asystole / Extreme bradycardia: Flatline (confirm in 2 leads, check connections) or profoundly slow rate progressing to arrest.

nodes.title: PEA Identified
nodes.summary: PEA: POCUS — tamponade, RV dilation, absent sliding
nodes.body: PEA identified → POCUS at first pulse check is critical. Look for cardiac activity, tamponade, RV dilation, and other reversible causes. PEA Arrest Protocol

nodes.title: Bradycardic Arrest / Asystole
nodes.summary: Asystole: confirm 2 leads — consider pacing
nodes.body: Extreme bradycardia or asystole → pacing FIRST. Confirm asystole in 2 leads. Check lead connections. If any organized activity present, consider transcutaneous pacing. Bradycardic Arrest Protocol

nodes.title: Universal Resuscitation Principles
nodes.summary: ETCO2 >20=good, <10 20min=TOR, sudden jump=ROSC
nodes.body: ETCO2 targets (waveform capnography): • >20 mmHg = adequate CPR quality • <10 mmHg after 20 min = consider termination of resuscitation • Sudden jump >10 mmHg = likely ROSC — check pulse CPR quality optimization: • Use compression feedback device if available • Rotate compressor every 2 minutes • Minimize interruptions — all pauses <10 sec • Real-time ETCO2 as compression quality metric [1][5] ETC

nodes.title: Vascular Access
nodes.summary: IO 60sec if no IV — tibial preferred, equals IV
nodes.body: Access priority (do not delay CPR): 1. Large-bore peripheral IV — antecubital preferred, follow with 20 mL flush 2. External jugular (EJ) — if peripheral access fails 3. IO — if no IV within 60 seconds IO sites: • Proximal tibia (tibial plateau) — preferred in adults • Proximal humerus — alternative, faster drug delivery to central circulation • Distal tibia — pediatric alternative Key: IO drug de

nodes.title: Epinephrine Dosing
nodes.summary: 1mg q3-5min: non-shockable 1st cycle, shockable after 2nd
nodes.body: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes Timing by rhythm: | Rhythm | When to Give | |--------|-------------| | Non-shockable (PEA/asystole) | After 1st cycle — give ASAP | | Shockable (VF/pVT) | After 2nd shock | Key points: • Follow each dose with 20 mL NS flush • Do NOT use high-dose epinephrine (Class 3: No Benefit) [5][15] • Earlier epi in non-shockable rhythms associated with improved outcom

nodes.title: H's & T's — Reversible Causes
nodes.summary: Reversible causes EVERY check — hyperK and tension PTX priority
nodes.body: Search for reversible causes at EVERY pulse check. The 5 H's: • Hypoxia — POCUS: lung sliding, B-lines. Rx: secure airway, FiO2 100% • Hypovolemia — POCUS: flat IVC, no cardiac activity. Rx: volume, blood • H+ (Acidosis) — wide QRS, prolonged arrest. Rx: NaHCO3 1-2 mEq/kg • Hypo/HyperK — peaked T's, sine wave (hyperK); flat T's, U waves (hypoK). Rx: calcium, insulin/dextrose • Hypothermia — core t

nodes.title: POCUS in Cardiac Arrest
nodes.summary: POCUS checks ONLY <10sec — no activity = futility signal
nodes.body: POCUS during pulse checks ONLY — do NOT interrupt compressions. Timing: <10 seconds during scheduled pulse/rhythm checks. RUSH Exam targets: • Cardiac activity — any wall motion? (prognostic) • Tamponade — pericardial effusion + RV diastolic collapse • RV dilation — RV:LV >1:1 suggests massive PE • Absent lung sliding — tension pneumothorax • IVC — flat/empty suggests hypovolemia Prognostic value:

nodes.title: Situation-Specific Medications
nodes.summary: NaHCO3 wide QRS, Ca CCB, Mg TdP, Intralipid LAST
nodes.body: Beyond epinephrine — give when indicated: • Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV: Wide QRS / TCA toxicity, known hyperkalemia, prolonged arrest, pre-existing metabolic acidosis • Calcium (1-2g calcium gluconate or 1g calcium chloride IV): Hyperkalemia, calcium channel blocker OD, hypermagnesemia • Magnesium sulfate 2g IV over 1-2 min (torsades: repeat 2g at 5-15 min if it persists, then start a contin

nodes.title: ROSC Achieved
nodes.summary: 12-lead, SpO2 92-98%, SBP >90, TTM, electrolytes
nodes.body: ROSC achieved — immediate priorities: 1. 12-lead ECG immediately — STEMI? New arrhythmia? 2. Avoid hypoxia — titrate FiO2 to SpO2 92-98% (do not hyperoxgenate) 3. Avoid hypotension — target SBP >90, MAP >65. Vasopressors as needed. 4. Waveform capnography — confirm ETT placement, monitor ventilation 5. Targeted temperature management — initiate per protocol 6. Electrolytes — check and correct K+,
nodes.recommendation: Immediate 12-lead ECG, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, initiate TTM, emergent cath if STEMI. ICU admission.

nodes.title: Termination of Resuscitation Criteria
nodes.summary: ETCO2 <10 20min + no cause + no activity = near-zero
nodes.body: BLS Termination Rule (all must be present): • Arrest not witnessed by EMS • No bystander CPR • No AED shock delivered • No ROSC before transport ALS Termination Rule (BLS criteria PLUS): • No ROSC before transport • No shocks delivered by EMS ETCO2 Guidance: • ETCO2 <10 mmHg after 20 min of high-quality CPR → very low survival probability • Combined with no cardiac activity on POCUS = near-zero su

nodes.title: No Cardiac Activity on POCUS
nodes.summary: Adequate CPR confirmed, causes treated, no hypothermia
nodes.body: No cardiac activity on POCUS after adequate resuscitation = strong futility signal. Combined with ETCO2 <10 mmHg after 20 minutes = near-zero survival probability (EMCrit) [1][4][11]. Before termination, confirm: • Adequate CPR quality maintained (ETCO2 was >20 at some point) • All reversible causes considered and treated • No hypothermia (warm the patient before declaring death) • No toxin ingest

nodes.title: Code Called — Termination of Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Document time, interventions, ETCO2, TOR reasoning
nodes.body: Document the resuscitation thoroughly: • Time of arrest (witnessed or estimated) • Time CPR initiated • All interventions: shocks, medications (doses + times), airway management • ETCO2 values throughout resuscitation • POCUS findings at each pulse check • Reversible causes considered and treated • Reasoning for termination • Time of death Post-termination: • Family notification — in person, with
nodes.recommendation: Document all interventions, ETCO2 values, and reasoning for termination.

nodes.title: Cardiogenic Shock
nodes.summary: Shock spiral: hypotension worsens coronary perfusion
nodes.body: Definition: Inadequate tissue perfusion due to primary cardiac dysfunction. The SHOCK Spiral (EMCrit): > Hypotension → Coronary hypoperfusion → Worsening ischemia → Further pump failure → More hypotension Key Concept: Every minute in shock = myocardial damage. Time is myocardium. Mortality: 40-50% even with modern therapy. Early recognition and aggressive intervention are critical. [1][2]

nodes.title: Clinical Recognition
nodes.summary: SBP <90, cold, mottled, oliguria, lactate — SCAI staging
nodes.body: Classic Presentation: | Finding | Significance | |---------|-------------| | SBP <90 or MAP <65 | Despite adequate volume | | Cold extremities | Peripheral vasoconstriction | | Mottled skin | Poor perfusion | | Altered mental status | Cerebral hypoperfusion | | Oliguria | Renal hypoperfusion | | Elevated lactate | Tissue hypoxia | SCAI Shock Staging: • A - At risk (e.g., large STEMI, no hypotensio

nodes.title: SCAI D-E: Crashing Patient
nodes.summary: Push-dose epi while setting drips — avoid intubation
nodes.body: Immediate Actions (EMCrit "Stabilize First"): 1. Push-dose pressors while setting up infusions: • Epinephrine 10-20 mcg IV push (1 mL of 10 mcg/mL) • Phenylephrine 100-200 mcg if pure vasodilation 2. Airway: Avoid intubation if possible — sedation + PPV will crash them further • If must intubate: ketamine + push-dose epi ready 3. Call for help: Cardiology, CT surgery, ECMO team 4. Consider VA-ECMO

nodes.title: SCAI Stage A: At Risk
nodes.summary: SCAI A: large STEMI or EF <30% — anticipate decline
nodes.body: Patient at risk but not yet in shock: • Large anterior STEMI • Severe LV dysfunction (EF <30%) • Recent high-risk PCI • Acute myocarditis Proactive Management: • Serial lactates q2-4h • Continuous BP monitoring (arterial line preferred) • POCUS to track LV function • Low threshold for early pressors/inotropes • Do NOT wait for frank hypotension [1][2]

nodes.title: Identify the Etiology
nodes.summary: AMI=cath, ADHF=diuresis, RV=cautious fluids
nodes.body: The cause matters — treatment differs: | Etiology | Key Features | |----------|-------------| | AMI (most common) | Chest pain, ECG changes, troponin | | Acute decompensated HF | Chronic HF, volume overload, warm shock initially | | Myocarditis | Younger, viral prodrome, diffuse ST changes | | Takotsubo | Emotional stress, apical ballooning | | Valvular emergency | New murmur, acute MR/AR | | Arrh

nodes.title: AMI-Related Cardiogenic Shock
nodes.summary: STEMI+shock = emergent cath — PCI definitive
nodes.body: STEMI + Shock = Emergent cath lab Critical Path: 1. Stabilize hemodynamics (pressors/inotropes) 2. Activate cath lab immediately 3. PCI is definitive therapy — every minute of delay = worse outcomes 4. Consider MCS (Impella/IABP) before or during PCI Culprit-only PCI is standard (no multi-vessel in acute setting unless cardiogenic shock precludes identifying culprit) Avoid if possible: • Thromboly

nodes.title: Acute Decompensated HF with Shock
nodes.summary: Warm=vasodilated, cold=inotropes — find precipitant
nodes.body: Different phenotype than AMI-shock: Warm Shock (early ADHF): • May be vasodilated initially • Treat with diuresis + inotropes • Avoid vasopressors unless truly hypotensive Cold Shock (late/severe): • True cardiogenic shock • Needs inotropes ± vasopressors • May need MCS as bridge Key: Identify precipitant: • Medication non-compliance • Dietary indiscretion • New arrhythmia (A-fib with RVR common)

nodes.title: RV Failure
nodes.summary: NO aggressive fluids RV — norepinephrine, no nitrates RV MI
nodes.body: RV failure is a DIFFERENT animal: DO NOT give aggressive fluids — the RV is preload-dependent but can't handle excess volume. Management: • Small fluid boluses only if clearly hypovolemic (250 mL, reassess) • Norepinephrine to maintain coronary perfusion • Inotropes: Dobutamine or milrinone (careful with milrinone — vasodilation) • Reduce RV afterload: Treat PE if present, optimize ventilation • A

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Assessment
nodes.summary: POCUS: LV, RV, IVC, B-lines — CPO <0.6W = severe
nodes.body: EMCrit Approach — Phenotype Your Patient: Use POCUS to determine: • LV function (EPSS, visual EF) • RV size and function • IVC (preload status) • Pericardial effusion • B-lines (pulmonary edema) Cardiac Power Output (CPO): > CPO = (MAP × CO) / 451 CPO <0.6 W = severe cardiogenic shock Invasive Monitoring (PA catheter): • Consider in refractory shock • Helps guide therapy when clinical assessment u

nodes.title: Wet/Dry, Warm/Cold Assessment
nodes.summary: Cold+Wet = inotropes — Cold+Dry may need fluids
nodes.body: Forrester Classification: | | Dry (PCWP <18) | Wet (PCWP >18) | |---|---|---| | Warm (CI >2.2) | Normal | Pulmonary edema — diurese | | Cold (CI <2.2) | Hypovolemic — cautious fluids | Cardiogenic shock — inotropes | Most cardiogenic shock = Cold and Wet Bedside Assessment: • Cold = cool extremities, delayed cap refill, mottling • Wet = JVD, rales, edema, B-lines on US • Warm = normal extremity te

nodes.title: Cold and Dry
nodes.summary: Consider RV infarct — 250mL challenge then reassess
nodes.body: Uncommon in true cardiogenic shock — consider: • RV infarct (preload-dependent) • Hypovolemia + poor cardiac function • Post-diuresis overshoot Management: • Small fluid challenge (250 mL NS, reassess) • If no improvement with fluids → inotropes • Do NOT over-resuscitate — the heart can't handle it [1][2]

nodes.title: Warm and Wet
nodes.summary: Decompensated HF — diurese, vasodilators if BP OK
nodes.body: This is decompensated HF, not yet cardiogenic shock: Treatment: • Aggressive diuresis (IV furosemide) • Vasodilators if BP tolerates (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin) • Treat precipitant (A-fib, ischemia, etc.) Monitor closely — can progress to cold and wet (true shock). If SBP <90 or declining perfusion → transition to cardiogenic shock pathway. [1][2]

nodes.title: Initial Stabilization
nodes.summary: Art line, central, Foley, ECG + POCUS immediately
nodes.body: EMCrit "Big Picture": > Stabilize first, diagnose second, but don't forget the diagnosis. Immediate Actions: 1. Arterial line — cuff pressures are unreliable in shock 2. Central line — for pressors/inotropes 3. Foley — monitor UOP as perfusion marker 4. Labs: Lactate, troponin, BNP, CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags 5. ECG + POCUS — immediately Oxygenation: • High-flow nasal cannula preferred over intubation

nodes.title: Vasopressors and Inotropes
nodes.summary: Norepi first — dobutamine if CI low, avoid pure vasoconstrictors
nodes.body: EMCrit Pressor Selection: First-Line: Norepinephrine • Vasopressor + mild inotrope • Maintains coronary perfusion pressure • Start 5-10 mcg/min, titrate to MAP >65 Add Inotrope if CI remains low: • Dobutamine: 2.5-20 mcg/kg/min (may drop BP — watch for hypotension) • Milrinone: 0.375-0.75 mcg/kg/min (potent vasodilator — only if adequate BP) • Epinephrine: If need both pressor + inotrope (0.01-0.1

nodes.title: Pressor Selection by Phenotype
nodes.summary: Match drug to phenotype — escalating = consider MCS
nodes.body: Match the drug to the problem: | Phenotype | Recommendation | |-----------|---------------| | Hypotension + low CO | Norepinephrine + dobutamine or epinephrine | | Low CO, adequate BP | Dobutamine or milrinone | | Severe hypotension | Norepinephrine first, then add inotrope | | RV failure | Norepinephrine ± dobutamine (avoid milrinone) | | Post-cardiotomy | Epinephrine or milrinone | Warning Signs

nodes.title: Optimization on Medical Therapy
nodes.summary: Optimize preload, afterload, rhythm, acidosis, lytes
nodes.body: Once stabilized, optimize: Preload: • Avoid excess fluids in LV failure • Consider gentle diuresis if wet • Small boluses only if clearly dry Afterload: • Avoid excessive vasoconstriction • IABP reduces afterload (if placed) Rate/Rhythm: • Treat arrhythmias aggressively • A-fib with RVR → rate control • Bradycardia → pacing Metabolic: • Correct acidosis (improves catecholamine responsiveness) • Co

nodes.title: Mechanical Support Decision
nodes.summary: MCS early: escalating pressors, lactate, CPO <0.6W
nodes.body: When to consider MCS (EMCrit): Early MCS indicators: • Escalating pressor requirements • Lactate not clearing • SCAI Stage C-D despite medical therapy • CPO <0.6 W • Need for PCI but too unstable "Doors to Drugs to Devices" — don't wait for multi-organ failure to consider MCS. MCS Options: • IABP (intra-aortic balloon pump) • Impella (percutaneous LVAD) • VA-ECMO (venoarterial ECMO) • TandemHeart

nodes.title: Mechanical Circulatory Support
nodes.summary: IABP 0.5L, Impella 3-4L, ECMO full — match need
nodes.body: MCS Device Selection: | Device | Hemodynamic Support | Best For | |--------|--------------------|---------| | IABP | ~0.5 L/min | Afterload reduction, AMI | | Impella CP | 3-4 L/min | LV unloading, PCI support | | Impella 5.0/5.5 | 5+ L/min | Severe LV failure | | VA-ECMO | Full support | Biventricular failure, arrest | | TandemHeart | 4-5 L/min | Alternative to Impella | IABP (still has a role):

nodes.title: VA-ECMO Considerations
nodes.summary: VA-ECMO biventricular/refractory — bridge not destination
nodes.body: VA-ECMO = Full cardiopulmonary support Indications: • Refractory cardiogenic shock despite medical + MCS • Biventricular failure • Cardiac arrest with suspected reversible cause • Bridge to transplant/LVAD/recovery Contraindications: • Irreversible neurologic injury • Unwitnessed arrest with prolonged downtime • Terminal illness • Severe aortic regurgitation (relative) Complications: • Limb ischem

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: All cardiogenic shock = ICU — transfer if no MCS
nodes.body: All cardiogenic shock patients need ICU admission. Disposition Considerations: • CCU/CICU — standard for cardiogenic shock • Cath lab — if AMI requiring emergent PCI • Transfer — if need MCS not available at your facility Transfer Criteria: • Need for MCS not available locally • Need for cardiac surgery • ECMO candidacy • Transplant evaluation Communicate early with accepting facility — don't wait

nodes.title: Admit to CCU/CICU
nodes.summary: CCU art line, central, lactates — MAP >65, clearance
nodes.body: ICU Admission Orders: • Continuous arterial BP monitoring • Central venous access for pressors • Telemetry monitoring • Foley catheter with hourly I/O • Serial lactates (q4-6h until clearing) • Serial troponins • POCUS reassessment PRN • Cardiology consultation Goals: • MAP >65 mmHg • Lactate clearance • UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr • Improving mental status • Weaning pressors [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: Admit to CCU/CICU for continued resuscitation and monitoring. Cardiology consultation required.

nodes.title: Transfer to Higher Level of Care
nodes.summary: Stabilize, send data — do not delay for workup
nodes.body: Transfer Checklist: • Stabilize before transport (pressors running, airway secure) • Communicate directly with accepting physician • Send all data: ECG, labs, imaging, echo • Arrange appropriate transport (critical care transport if on pressors) Don't delay transfer for additional workup that won't change management. Information for receiving facility: • Current pressor doses • Hemodynamic status
nodes.recommendation: Transfer to facility with MCS/ECMO capability. Stabilize hemodynamics before transport.

nodes.title: Emergent Cardiac Catheterization
nodes.summary: AMI+shock = emergent PCI — ASA, heparin, pressors
nodes.body: AMI + Cardiogenic Shock = Emergent PCI Before cath lab: • Load aspirin 325 mg (if not contraindicated) • P2Y12 inhibitor per institutional protocol • Heparin per cath lab protocol • Continue pressors/inotropes • Consider MCS placement in cath lab In cath lab: • PCI to culprit lesion • Consider Impella placement if hemodynamically unstable • Avoid contrast nephropathy precautions (don't delay for t
nodes.recommendation: Emergent cardiac catheterization for revascularization. Continue hemodynamic support throughout.

nodes.title: Catatonia Suspected
nodes.summary: BFCSI >=2 = positive screen; DSM-5-TR diagnosis generally needs >=3 signs or strong clinical syndrome.
nodes.body: Is catatonia present? Screen with Bush-Francis Catatonia Screening Instrument (BFCSI) / BFCRS items: | Sign | Present? | |------|----------| | Immobility / stupor | [ ] | | Mutism | [ ] | | Staring / fixed gaze | [ ] | | Posturing | [ ] | | Negativism | [ ] | | Waxy flexibility | [ ] | | Echolalia / echopraxia | [ ] | | Stereotypy | [ ] | | Mannerisms | [ ] | | Verbigeration | [ ] | | Rigidity | [

nodes.title: Catatonia Unlikely
nodes.summary: Low BFCRS - consider depression, Parkinson's, locked-in syndrome, conversion.
nodes.body: Consider alternative diagnoses: * Severe depression - may mimic psychomotor retardation * Parkinson's disease - rigidity, bradykinesia * Locked-in syndrome - intact consciousness, vertical eye movements preserved * Akinetic mutism - frontal lobe lesions * Conversion disorder - inconsistent findings * Malingering - secondary gain If clinical suspicion remains high despite low BFCRS: Proceed with lo

nodes.title: Excited Catatonia
nodes.summary: Excited catatonia - medical emergency. High-dose lorazepam, avoid antipsychotics.
nodes.body: Excited catatonia is a medical emergency! Features: * Extreme motor agitation * Stereotyped, purposeless movements * Autonomic instability * Risk of exhaustion, hyperthermia, death Immediate management: * Lorazepam 2 mg IV - can repeat q5-10 min up to 8 mg * Supportive care: IV fluids, cooling if hyperthermic * Monitor vitals continuously * Consider ICU admission [!] Do NOT give antipsychotics - h

nodes.title: Lorazepam Challenge
nodes.summary: Lorazepam 2 mg IV challenge - response within 10-15 min strongly supports catatonia.
nodes.body: Diagnostic & therapeutic test: Lorazepam 2 mg IV push Score symptoms before and after if possible (BFCRS or focused sign count). Observe for 10-15 minutes. Positive response (strongly supports catatonia): * Increased speech * Decreased rigidity * Improved eye contact * Spontaneous movement * More interactive * Often defined as ~50% reduction in catatonia signs/severity Any meaningful improvement w

nodes.title: Positive Lorazepam Response
nodes.summary: Catatonia strongly supported. Lorazepam 2 mg q4-6h maintenance. Investigate etiology.
nodes.body: Catatonia strongly supported - continue benzodiazepines: Maintenance regimen: * Lorazepam 2 mg IV/PO q4-6h scheduled * Titrate to effect (some patients need 10-20+ mg/day) * Monitor for over-sedation, respiratory depression Duration: * Continue until underlying cause treated * Taper slowly over days-weeks once stable * Rapid taper -> relapse risk Next step: Investigate underlying etiology

nodes.title: No Lorazepam Response
nodes.summary: No lorazepam response - try higher dose or proceed to ECT.
nodes.body: Options after failed lorazepam challenge: 1. Repeat with higher dose: * Lorazepam 4 mg IV - some patients need more * If still no response after cumulative 6-8 mg -> ECT 2. Consider alternative diagnosis: * Locked-in syndrome * Akinetic mutism * Severe Parkinson's * Malignant catatonia (may need more aggressive treatment) 3. Proceed to ECT: * ECT is first-line for benzo-resistant catatonia * Respo

nodes.title: Partial Lorazepam Response
nodes.summary: Partial response - increase lorazepam dose, consider ECT if plateau.
nodes.body: Partial response - optimize benzodiazepines: Strategies: * Increase dose: Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q2h until response or sedation * Total daily doses of 20-30 mg may be needed * Add scheduled dosing: 2-4 mg q4-6h around the clock If plateau without full response after 48-72h: * ECT referral * Consider adjunctive memantine or amantadine Monitor for: * Respiratory depression * Aspiration risk (NPO if swa

nodes.title: Investigate Underlying Cause
nodes.summary: Investigate catatonia etiology: medical, psychiatric, or drug-induced.
nodes.body: Catatonia has many etiologies - identify & treat: Medical causes: * Encephalitis (anti-NMDA, viral) * Metabolic (hyponatremia, hepatic encephalopathy) * Autoimmune (lupus cerebritis) * Endocrine (thyroid, Addison's) * Drugs (withdrawal, intoxication) Psychiatric causes: * Mood disorders (depression, mania) * Schizophrenia * Brief psychotic disorder Workup: * CBC, CMP, TSH, UA * Urine drug screen *

nodes.title: Medical Cause
nodes.summary: Medical catatonia - treat underlying cause while continuing lorazepam.
nodes.body: Treat the underlying medical condition: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: * Urgent neurology consult * First-line: steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis * Tumor screen (ovarian teratoma) Metabolic: * Correct electrolytes, glucose * Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose, rifaximin Infectious: * Viral encephalitis: acyclovir * Bacterial: appropriate antibiotics Continue benzodiazepines while treating underlying

nodes.title: Psychiatric Catatonia
nodes.summary: Psychiatric catatonia - continue lorazepam, treat mood disorder once resolved.
nodes.body: Primary psychiatric catatonia: Most common associations: * Major depressive disorder (most common) * Bipolar disorder (manic or depressed phase) * Schizophrenia (less common than historically thought) Management: * Continue lorazepam * Treat underlying mood disorder once catatonia resolves * AVOID antipsychotics initially - see next When can antipsychotics be used? * Only AFTER catatonia fully res

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Catatonia
nodes.summary: Drug-induced catatonia - identify and address offending agent.
nodes.body: Common culprits: Medications: * Antipsychotic withdrawal (especially clozapine) * Benzodiazepine withdrawal * Corticosteroids * Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) Substances: * PCP/ketamine * Synthetic cannabinoids * Stimulant withdrawal Management: * Discontinue or reinstate offending agent as appropriate * Continue lorazepam * Supportive care Clozapine withdrawal catatonia: Restart cl

nodes.title: Avoid Antipsychotics
nodes.summary: AVOID antipsychotics in active catatonia - risk of NMS/malignant catatonia.
nodes.body: [!] CRITICAL: Avoid antipsychotics in active catatonia Risks: * Can worsen catatonia * Can precipitate malignant catatonia * Can trigger NMS (which shares features with catatonia) If patient on antipsychotic when catatonia developed: * Stop the antipsychotic * If clozapine - carefully weigh risks of stopping vs continuing * NMS Consult if fever + rigidity + autonomic instability When is it safe to

nodes.title: ECT for Catatonia
nodes.summary: ECT highly effective for benzo-resistant catatonia. Response >80%.
nodes.body: ECT is highly effective for catatonia: Indications: * Lorazepam-resistant catatonia * Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability) * Life-threatening complications (dehydration, DVT, PE) * Excited catatonia not responding to benzos Efficacy: * Response rate >80-90% * Often see improvement after 1-3 sessions * Bilateral placement typically used Course: * Usually 6-12 sessions * 3x/week initia

nodes.title: Catatonia Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit for lorazepam titration, etiology workup. ICU if malignant/excited.
nodes.body: Admission required for: * All catatonia patients (cannot safely discharge) * Benzodiazepine titration and monitoring * Etiology workup * Nutrition/hydration support * DVT prophylaxis ICU admission if: * Malignant catatonia (fever >38 degC, autonomic instability) * Excited catatonia with exhaustion * Respiratory compromise * Severe dehydration/rhabdomyolysis Psychiatry admission if: * Stable on lor
nodes.recommendation: Admit all catatonia patients. ICU if malignant features. Continue scheduled lorazepam, DVT prophylaxis, consider ECT if benzo-resistant.

nodes.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome — Recognition
nodes.summary: Ask EVERY back pain: bladder, bowel, saddle — easily missed
nodes.body: CES is compression of the cauda equina nerve roots causing a surgical emergency. Classic Triad (when present = high suspicion): 1. 🦵 Bilateral leg pain/weakness or sciatica 2. 🩲 Saddle anesthesia (S3-S5: perineum, genitals, inner thighs) 3. 🚽 Bladder/bowel dysfunction (retention, incontinence) ⚠️ No single symptom is pathognomonic — CES is a clinical constellation. nodes.summary: PVR >500 + bilateral = 48x CES odds — any pos = workup
nodes.body: Ask EVERY back pain patient these questions: Bladder: • "Any trouble starting or stopping urination?" • "Feeling like you can't fully empty?" • "Any loss of bladder control?" Bowel: • "Any loss of bowel control?" • "Can you feel when your rectum is full?" Sensation: • "Any numbness around your genitals or bottom?" • "Can you feel yourself wipe after using the bathroom?" nodes.body: Synthesize your clinical findings: HIGH SUSPICION (emergent MRI): • Bilateral neuro deficit + ANY red flag • Absent BCR • Reduced rectal tone + urinary symptoms • PVR >500 mL with bilateral sciatica INTERMEDIATE SUSPICION (urgent MRI): • Isolated perianal sensory loss • Borderline PVR (200-500 mL) • Unilateral symptoms with ANY bladder complaint LOW SUSPICION (outpatient): • Unilateral leg pain on

nodes.body: Bedside Bladder Ultrasound Protocol: 1. Have patient void (attempt to empty completely) 2. Scan bladder within 10 minutes 3. nodes.title: Imaging Strategy — MRI vs CT

nodes.body: MRI is the Gold Standard Timing per GIRFT Pathway: • Suspected CES → MRI within 4 hours • Do NOT defer to "next day" MRI Protocol: • T1/T2 sagittal and axial lumbar spine • Key findings: Central disc herniation, epidural mass, compression When CT is Acceptable (if MRI unavailable 24/7): • 2024 data: CT achieves 97% sensitivity/specificity for disc pathology • Use optimized lumbar protocol with thi
