nodes.title: Negative MRI with High Clinical Suspicion
nodes.summary: Neg MRI + bilateral + bladder = admit, repeat MRI
nodes.body: When imaging doesn't match clinical picture: Consider: 1. Repeat imaging — dynamic compression may need flexion/extension views 2. Spinal infarction — may not show on initial MRI; DWI sequences helpful 3. Conus medullaris syndrome — higher lesion, different imaging plane needed 4. Aortic dissection — can present with leg weakness; consider CT angio 5. Guillain-Barré — ascending weakness; CSF analy

nodes.title: CES Classification — I vs R
nodes.summary: CES-I TRUE emergency — surgery <24hrs prevents Retention
nodes.body: Two Types with Different Urgency: CES-Incomplete (CES-I) — TRUE EMERGENCY • Altered urinary sensation • Difficulty voiding, weak stream • But CAN still void (even if difficult) • ~40% of presentations • Better prognosis if treated urgently • Goal: Prevent progression to CES-R • Surgery timing: <24 hours strongly recommended CES-Retention (CES-R) — LESS TIME-SENSITIVE • Painless urinary retention •

nodes.title: Neurosurgical Management
nodes.summary: >48hrs: 9.6x mortality — Foley, sensation, steroids
nodes.body: Surgical Decompression is Definitive Treatment Timing Evidence: | Timing | Outcome Data | |--------|-------------| | <24 hours | Superior outcomes (NISC database) | | 24-48 hours | Acceptable but inferior to <24h | | >48 hours | 9.6x mortality, 2.4x non-routine discharge | Pre-Surgical Management: 1. Foley catheter — document PVR, sensation to insertion, catheter tug test 2. Steroids (if inflammat
nodes.recommendation: Emergent neurosurgery consultation. Surgery within 24 hours for CES-I, as soon as feasible for CES-R. Foley placement with documented sensation. Consider steroids for inflammatory causes.

nodes.title: Intermediate Suspicion — Approach
nodes.summary: Urgent MRI 4-6hrs, exams q2-4h — upgrade if worse
nodes.body: When findings are concerning but not classic: Examples: • Isolated perianal numbness, otherwise normal exam • Borderline PVR (200-400 mL) without bilateral symptoms • Unilateral sciatica with vague bladder symptoms • BCR equivocal or unable to assess Management: 1. Urgent MRI — within 4-6 hours (same day) 2. Serial exams — q2-4h while awaiting imaging 3. Neurology or neurosurgery consultation — lo

nodes.title: Low Suspicion — Outpatient Management
nodes.summary: Unilateral + intact + normal PVR = outpatient + written precautions
nodes.body: Low suspicion criteria (ALL must be present): • ✅ Unilateral leg pain only • ✅ Normal rectal tone • ✅ Intact BCR (if tested) • ✅ Normal PVR (<100-200 mL) • ✅ No saddle anesthesia • ✅ No bladder/bowel symptoms • ✅ Able to ambulate Outpatient Management: • NSAIDs / acetaminophen for pain • Activity as tolerated • Physical therapy referral • Spine clinic follow-up if symptoms persist >4-6 weeks MUST
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with strict return precautions. Written red flag instructions mandatory. Spine clinic follow-up if persistent symptoms.

nodes.title: Disposition Planning
nodes.summary: Confirmed=surgery, concerning=admit, low=written precautions
nodes.body: Disposition based on workup results:

nodes.title: Admission for Observation
nodes.summary: Neuro q4-6h, bladder scans, repeat MRI threshold low
nodes.body: Indications for observation despite negative imaging: • High clinical suspicion with negative MRI • Equivocal exam findings • Unable to obtain MRI (CT only available) • Patient unreliable for return precautions Observation Protocol: • Serial neuro exams q4-6h • Strict I/O with bladder scans • Low threshold for repeat imaging • Neurology consultation • Upgrade to emergent workup if ANY deterioratio
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored bed. Serial neuro exams q4-6h. Bladder scans. Low threshold for repeat MRI. Neurology consult.

nodes.title: Transfer to Neurosurgical Center
nodes.summary: Transfer no neurosurg — Foley, steroids, MD handoff
nodes.body: When to transfer: • CES confirmed or highly suspected • No neurosurgery at this facility • No MRI available and high clinical suspicion Pre-transfer: 1. Stabilize patient 2. Place Foley catheter (document sensation) 3. Start steroids if indicated 4. Pain control 5. NPO for potential surgery 6. Send all imaging with patient Communication: • Direct physician-to-physician handoff • Emphasize time-sen
nodes.recommendation: Emergent transfer to neurosurgical center. Foley placed, steroids given if indicated, imaging sent. Direct MD-to-MD handoff.

nodes.title: Common ED Pitfalls
nodes.summary: Not asking bladder/bowel = top spinal malpractice cause
nodes.body: How CES Gets Missed: | Pitfall | Solution | |---------|----------| | Don't ask about bladder/bowel | Mandatory screening ALL back pain | | Miss saddle anesthesia | Always test perineal sensation | | Rely on normal PVR | 50% of CES-I have PVR <200 mL | | "Just chronic back pain" | Escalate NEW symptoms in chronic patients | | Wait for MRI result to call surgery | Parallel process — call while imagi

nodes.title: Caustic Ingestion
nodes.summary: Establish 5 Ws — NEVER induce emesis, charcoal, neutralize, blind NG, or dilute
nodes.body: Caustic Ingestion Steps Summary - time-critical airway and GI pathway. Establish the 5 Ws: - Who: Patient demographics, age, weight - What: Substance, concentration, pH, form (liquid/solid/gel) - When: Time of ingestion - Where: Intentional vs accidental - Why: Suicide attempt vs unintentional exposure CRITICAL: Do NOT: - Induce emesis - Administer activated charcoal - Attempt pH neutralization -

nodes.title: Substance Type
nodes.summary: Alkali causes deep liquefactive necrosis; acid causes coagulative necrosis with eschar
nodes.body: Identify the caustic agent. Mechanism of injury differs between acids and alkalis. Alkalis (pH >11): Liquefactive necrosis - saponification of fats and proteins leads to deep penetrating injury. More esophageal injury, higher perforation risk. Acids (pH <3): Coagulative necrosis - eschar formation limits tissue penetration. More gastric injury, may cause "skip lesions." Common alkalis: Drain clean

nodes.title: Alkali Injury Pattern
nodes.summary: Alkali penetrates deeply — higher perforation and stricture risk than acid
nodes.body: Liquefactive necrosis - alkalis dissolve tissue proteins via saponification. Injury penetrates deeply without forming protective barrier. High-risk features: - Esophageal injury predominates (slower transit) - Transmural perforation more common - Delayed stricture formation (30% of grade 2b+ injuries) - Long-term esophageal cancer risk (1000x increased) Titrable Acid/Alkali Reserve (TAR): Amount o

nodes.title: Acid Injury Pattern
nodes.summary: Acid causes gastric injury with eschar — watch for HF causing systemic hypocalcemia
nodes.body: Coagulative necrosis - acids denature proteins to form protective eschar that limits tissue penetration. Injury characteristics: - Gastric injury more common (rapid esophageal transit, pyloric pooling) - May create "skip lesions" in esophagus - Gastric perforation and hemorrhage risks - Systemic absorption possible (especially HF, formic acid) Hydrofluoric acid (HF): Uniquely dangerous - penetrate

nodes.title: Airway Assessment
nodes.summary: Up to 50% need intubation — assess for edema, stridor, drooling, visible burns
nodes.body: Red flags requiring urgent airway evaluation: - Oropharyngeal edema - Stridor or voice changes - Hypersalivation/drooling with difficulty clearing - Respiratory distress - Visible posterior pharyngeal burns Up to 50% of adults with large caustic ingestions require intubation. [1] Do NOT use: - Blind intubation attempts - Laryngeal mask airways (LMA) - Bougies (perforation risk)

nodes.title: Secure Airway Immediately
nodes.summary: Fiberoptic/video laryngoscopy preferred — have surgical airway backup ready
nodes.body: Emergent airway management: - Fiberoptic or video laryngoscopy preferred - Consider awake fiberoptic intubation for suspected significant ingestion - Have surgical airway backup ready (cricothyrotomy kit at bedside) - Avoid blind attempts and bougie use Post-intubation: - Large-bore IV access x 2 - Initiate vasopressors if hypotensive - Continue to GI workup after stabilization If surgical airway
nodes.recommendation: Emergent airway control with fiberoptic/video laryngoscopy. Surgical backup mandatory. ICU admission.

nodes.title: Symptom Assessment
nodes.summary: Absence of oral burns does NOT exclude GI injury — 15% false negative rate
nodes.body: Evaluate for GI tract injury symptoms. Symptoms suggesting significant injury: - Odynophagia (painful swallowing) - Dysphagia - Retrosternal or abdominal pain - Vomiting (especially hematemesis) - Refusal to swallow - Hypersalivation Note: Absence of oropharyngeal burns does NOT exclude esophageal/gastric injury. Up to 15% of patients with significant GI injury have no visible oral burns.

nodes.title: Laboratory Workup
nodes.summary: Order CBC, BMP, coags, VBG with lactate, CRP — predict transmural necrosis
nodes.body: Order: - CBC with differential - BMP (renal function, electrolytes) - LFTs - Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen) - Type and screen - VBG or ABG with lactate - CRP (elevated suggests transmural injury) - Lipase (if abdominal pain) Predictive findings for transmural necrosis/perforation: - Leukocytosis - Thrombocytopenia - Elevated CRP - Metabolic acidosis - Renal dysfunction - Hepatic dys

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.summary: CXR for free air, CT for transmural necrosis — free air means surgical emergency
nodes.body: Chest/abdominal X-ray: - Evaluate for pneumomediastinum, pneumoperitoneum, pleural effusion - Free air suggests perforation - surgical emergency Contrasted CT chest/abdomen: - High specificity for transmural necrosis (~95%) - Lower sensitivity (~80%) - does NOT replace endoscopy - Useful for identifying perforation, mediastinitis - May guide surgical planning CT findings concerning for transmural

nodes.title: Perforation - Emergent Surgery
nodes.summary: Surgical emergency — bypass endoscopy, broad-spectrum abx, ICU, NPO
nodes.body: Surgical emergency - bypass endoscopy Patients with confirmed or strongly suspected perforation should proceed directly to OR without EGD. Indications for emergent surgery: - Pneumomediastinum or pneumoperitoneum - Peritoneal signs (rigidity, guarding) - Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation - Persistent lactic acidosis - CT evidence of transmural necrosis Surgical options: - Esophagectomy
nodes.recommendation: Emergent surgical consultation. NPO, broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU admission. Do NOT delay surgery for endoscopy.

nodes.title: Endoscopy Timing
nodes.summary: EGD within 12-24h — AVOID days 5-15 when tissue is most friable
nodes.body: Perform EGD within 12-24 hours for: - All intentional ingestions (regardless of symptoms) - Symptomatic patients - Large volume ingestions - High-concentration substances Endoscopy goals: - Grade injury severity (Zargar Classification) - Guide treatment and disposition - Predict stricture risk Timing considerations: - Optimal: 12-24 hours post-ingestion - Acceptable: Up to 48-96 hours with gentle

nodes.title: Zargar Classification
nodes.summary: Grade 2b+ has 70-100% stricture rate — drives treatment and disposition
nodes.body: Endoscopic grading of caustic injury: Zargar Classification Detail Grade 0: Normal mucosa Grade 1: Edema and hyperemia only Grade 2a: Friability, hemorrhages, superficial ulcers, blisters Grade 2b: Deep or circumferential ulceration Grade 3a: Focal areas of necrosis Grade 3b: Extensive necrosis Clinical significance: - Grade 0-2a: Excellent prognosis, no strictures - Grade 2b: 70-100% stricture ra

nodes.title: Grade 0-1 - Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Grade 0-1: excellent prognosis — clear liquid diet, PPI, discharge with GI follow-up
nodes.body: Excellent prognosis - no long-term sequelae expected Management: - Clear liquid diet trial after EGD - Advance diet as tolerated - PPI for symptom relief (Pantoprazole 40mg PO daily) - Pain control: Acetaminophen preferred - Avoid NSAIDs (GI irritation) No indication for: - Antibiotics - Corticosteroids - NG tube placement Follow-up: - Outpatient GI follow-up in 1-2 weeks - Psychiatric evaluation
nodes.recommendation: Clear liquid diet, advance as tolerated. PPI for symptoms. Discharge home with GI follow-up.

nodes.title: Grade 2a - Observation
nodes.summary: Grade 2a: low stricture risk — NPO 24-48h, observe, PPI, advance diet as tolerated
nodes.body: Superficial injury - low stricture risk (<1%) Management: - NPO for 24-48 hours, then clear liquid trial - Observation admission (floor) - IV fluids - PPI (Pantoprazole 40mg IV q12h) - Antiemetics (Ondansetron 4-8mg IV PRN) - Pain control Not routinely indicated: - Antibiotics (unless fever/infection signs) - Corticosteroids (no benefit for grade 2a) Discharge criteria: - Tolerating oral intake -
nodes.recommendation: Observation 24-48 hours. NPO then diet advancement. PPI, antiemetics, pain control. Discharge when tolerating PO.

nodes.title: Grade 2b - ICU Admission
nodes.summary: Grade 2b: ICU — 70-100% stricture rate, consider steroids per GI consult
nodes.body: Deep/circumferential injury - high stricture risk (70-100%) Management: - NPO - ICU admission - Central venous access - IV fluids/nutrition (consider TPN) - PPI (Pantoprazole 40mg IV q12h) - Serial abdominal exams Corticosteroids (CONTROVERSIAL): - May reduce stricture formation in grade 2b specifically - Consider Methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day IV x 3 weeks then taper - GI consult should guide d
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. NPO with nutrition support. Consider corticosteroids for stricture prevention per GI consult. Serial monitoring for perforation.

nodes.title: Grade 3a/3b - Surgical Consultation
nodes.summary: Grade 3: high mortality — emergent surgery likely, broad-spectrum abx, ICU
nodes.body: Necrotic injury - high mortality, surgery often required Immediate management: - ICU admission - NPO - Aggressive fluid resuscitation - Central line, arterial line - Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h) Surgical consultation: - Grade 3a: Consider conservative management with very close monitoring vs surgery - Grade 3b: Usually requires surgery (esophagectomy, gastrectom
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. Surgical consultation for grade 3a; emergent surgery likely for grade 3b. Broad-spectrum antibiotics.

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Observation
nodes.summary: Low-risk accidental ingestion — observe 4-6h, trial oral intake, watch for symptoms
nodes.body: Low-risk accidental ingestion: - Small volume (taste/sip) - Household concentration - Asymptomatic after ingestion - No oropharyngeal burns Observation period: - Monitor for 4-6 hours - Assess ability to swallow - Observe for delayed symptom development Trial of oral intake: - Offer clear liquids - If tolerated without pain, advance diet - If painful or refused, proceed to full workup

nodes.title: Discharge Assessment
nodes.summary: All criteria: asymptomatic, tolerating PO, no burns, accidental, reliable follow-up
nodes.body: Discharge criteria (all must be met): - Asymptomatic after 4-6 hour observation - Tolerates oral intake without pain - No oropharyngeal burns or edema - Accidental, low-concentration exposure - Reliable follow-up available If intentional ingestion: Psychiatric evaluation mandatory regardless of injury severity.

nodes.title: Discharge Home
nodes.summary: Soft diet 24-48h, return for dysphagia/vomiting/pain, PCP or GI within 1 week
nodes.body: Discharge instructions: Diet: - Soft diet for 24-48 hours - Avoid hot, spicy, or acidic foods - Small frequent meals Return precautions - seek care immediately if: - Difficulty or pain with swallowing - Vomiting (especially blood) - Chest or abdominal pain - Fever - Breathing difficulty Follow-up: - PCP or GI within 1 week - If any symptoms develop, return to ED If intentional ingestion: Do NOT di
nodes.recommendation: Safe for discharge with return precautions. PCP or GI follow-up within 1 week.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Evaluation
nodes.summary: Mandatory psych eval for ALL intentional ingestions — 1:1 if actively suicidal
nodes.body: Mandatory psychiatric evaluation for all intentional ingestions. Timing: - After medical stabilization - Before discharge from hospital - May require extended observation or admission Consult should address: - Suicide risk assessment - Intent and lethality of method - Protective factors - Safety planning - Disposition (outpatient vs inpatient psychiatric care) Documentation: - Medical clearance fo

nodes.title: Supportive Care Measures
nodes.summary: NPO initially, acetaminophen for pain, avoid NSAIDs, ondansetron for nausea
nodes.body: General supportive care: NPO status: - All symptomatic patients initially NPO - Advance diet based on EGD findings and tolerance Pain management: - Acetaminophen 1g IV q6h - Hydromorphone 0.2-0.5mg IV q2-4h PRN for severe pain - Avoid NSAIDs (GI irritation) Antiemetics: - Ondansetron 4-8mg IV q6-8h - Vomiting increases aspiration and re-exposure risk Nutrition: - Early TPN for grade 2b-3 injuries

nodes.title: Long-term Complications
nodes.summary: Grade 2b-3: near-universal strictures, 1000x esophageal cancer risk — lifelong surveillance
nodes.body: Stricture formation: - Grade 2b: 70-100% develop strictures - Grade 3: Near-universal stricture in survivors - Typically develops 3-8 weeks post-ingestion - May require serial dilations, stenting, or surgical reconstruction Upper GI hemorrhage: - Typically occurs 2-4 weeks post-ingestion - As necrotic tissue sloughs - May be massive Esophageal cancer: - 1000x increased risk (up to 6.5% lifetime) -

Two major classes: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine): • Primarily peripheral vasodilation • Reflex tachycardia common • LESS cardiac depression • Predominantly vasodilator

nodes.title: Dihydropyridine CCB Toxicity
nodes.summary: Dihydropyridines cause vasodilatory shock — amlodipine is most dangerous (30-50h half-life)
nodes.body: Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine, nicardipine): • Primarily block L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle • Relative cardiac sparing at therapeutic doses • In overdose: profound vasodilation with reflex tachycardia • Shock phenotype: VASODILATORY (warm extremities, low SVR, preserved or elevated CO initially) Amlodipine is particularly dangerous: • Longest half-life (

nodes.title: Non-Dihydropyridine CCB Toxicity

nodes.body: Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem): • Block L-type calcium channels in cardiac tissue • SA node suppression → bradycardia • AV node blockade → conduction delays • Myocardial depression → reduced contractility • Shock phenotype: CARDIOGENIC (cool extremities, poor CO, elevated lactate) [1][2] Verapamil is the most cardiotoxic: • Greatest negative inotropic effect • Most deaths occur with v

nodes.title: Unknown CCB — Treat by Phenotype
nodes.summary: Unknown agent — assess shock phenotype clinically and treat both components if mixed
nodes.body: When the specific CCB is unknown: Assess the shock phenotype clinically: Vasodilatory shock signs: • Warm extremities • Tachycardia (or normal HR) • Flash capillary refill • Wide pulse pressure initially Cardiogenic shock signs: • Cool, mottled extremities • Bradycardia • Narrow pulse pressure • Elevated lactate out of proportion to hypotension Mixed shock is common — treat both components [2]. Pr

nodes.title: Extended-Release Formulations
nodes.summary: Extended-release: delayed toxicity up to 24h — WBI mandatory, 24-48h ICU minimum
nodes.body: Extended-release CCBs are particularly dangerous: • Delayed onset of toxicity (up to 12-24 hours post-ingestion) • Prolonged and severe toxicity lasting 48-72+ hours • Bezoar formation in GI tract possible • May appear deceptively well initially [1][3] Common extended-release formulations: • Verapamil SR/ER, Diltiazem CD/XR/LA • Nifedipine XL, Amlodipine (inherently long-acting) GI decontamination

nodes.title: Shock Phenotype Assessment
nodes.summary: Treatment depends on phenotype — vasodilatory gets pressors, cardiogenic gets HIET

VASODILATORY SHOCK: • Warm extremities, flash cap refill • Normal or elevated cardiac output • Low systemic vascular resistance • More common with dihydropyridines • Treatment: VASOPRESSORS (norepinephrine, vasopressin) CARDIOGENIC SHOCK: • Cool, mottled extremities • Poor cardiac outpu

nodes.title: Glucagon

nodes.body: Glucagon 3-5 mg IV bolus [1][3]: • Bypasses the calcium channel via cAMP-mediated pathway • Less effective in CCB than in beta-blocker toxicity • May provide modest inotropic/chronotropic support • Still worth trying as a bridge while preparing other therapies Dosing: • Bolus: 3-5 mg IV • If response: infusion 2-5 mg/hr • Common side effect: nausea/vomiting — consider antiemetic Do not rely on glu

nodes.summary: HIET is first-line for cardiogenic shock — works via glucose metabolism, not calcium channels
nodes.body: HIET Protocol — dosing calculator. HIET is FIRST-LINE for cardiogenic shock phenotype [1][2][4]. Mechanism: • In shock, the heart switches from fatty acid to glucose metabolism • CCBs block insulin release from pancreas (hyperglycemia is diagnostic) • Exogenous insulin restores myocardial glucose uptake • Improves contractility independent of calcium channels • Some evidence of vasodilation revers

nodes.title: HIET Dosing Protocol
nodes.summary: Insulin 1 U/kg bolus then 1-10 U/kg/hr — maintain glucose 150-250, replete K+ to 4.0-4.5
nodes.body: Bolus: • Regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV push Infusion: • Start at 1 unit/kg/hr • Titrate up to 10 units/kg/hr as needed [1][2][4] • Some case reports use even higher doses Glucose management is CRITICAL: • If glucose <200 mg/dL: give D50W 25g (50 mL) with bolus • Start D10W infusion at 100-200 mL/hr • Titrate dextrose to maintain glucose 150-250 mg/dL • Check glucose q15-30 min initially, then q1h w

nodes.title: HIET — Onset and Monitoring
nodes.summary: Hemodynamic improvement in 15-60 min — do not stop early or underdose
nodes.body: Onset of effect: • Hemodynamic improvement typically within 15-60 minutes • May take longer — do not abandon therapy prematurely • Some patients require several hours to respond [4] Signs of response: • Improved blood pressure • Improved cardiac output (if monitored) • Decreased vasopressor requirements • Improved mental status • Lactate clearance Common pitfalls: • Stopping HIET too early • Inade

nodes.title: Vasopressor Selection
nodes.summary: NE 0.1-3 mcg/kg/min — HIGH doses needed in CCB toxicity due to receptor desensitization
nodes.body: High-Dose Vasopressor Guide — dosing reference. For VASODILATORY shock phenotype: Norepinephrine — first-line: • Start 0.1 mcg/kg/min • Titrate aggressively — up to 0.5-3 mcg/kg/min [1][2] • HIGH DOSES often needed in CCB toxicity Vasopressin — adjunct: • 0.04 units/min (fixed dose) • Bypasses the catecholamine pathway entirely • Add for refractory vasodilatory shock [1][2] Epinephrine: • Combined

nodes.title: High-Dose Vasopressor Rationale
nodes.summary: CCB toxicity requires much higher vasopressor doses than septic shock — escalate aggressively
nodes.body: Why such high doses? CCB toxicity causes profound receptor desensitization and catecholamine resistance [2]. Typical septic shock: NE 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min CCB toxicity: May need NE 1-3+ mcg/kg/min Multi-agent approach: • Norepinephrine (alpha + beta) • PLUS vasopressin (V1 receptor — independent of catecholamines) • PLUS epinephrine if cardiac output remains poor Phenylephrine (pure alpha): • Less p

nodes.title: Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid)
nodes.summary: Intralipid 1.5 mL/kg bolus for severe refractory cases — best evidence for verapamil
nodes.body: Intralipid Dosing — dosing calculator. Consider lipid emulsion for severe, refractory toxicity [1][5]. Best evidence: Verapamil (highly lipophilic) Dosing: • Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus • May repeat bolus x2 PRN (q5 min) • Infusion: 0.25-0.5 mL/kg/min • Maximum: 10-12 mL/kg in first hour Mechanism: • Creates a "lipid sink" to sequester lipophilic drugs • May have direct cardiac effects • Evi

nodes.title: Rescue Therapies

nodes.body: When standard therapy fails: Patient not responding to: • Calcium • HIET • High-dose vasopressors • Lipid emulsion What is the current status?

nodes.title: Methylene Blue
nodes.summary: Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg for refractory vasoplegia — avoid with serotonergic drugs
nodes.body: Methylene blue for refractory vasoplegia [1]: • Inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase • Blocks the NO-mediated vasodilation pathway • Mechanism independent of catecholamines Dosing: • 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5-15 minutes • May repeat q1h PRN • Some use continuous infusion 0.5 mg/kg/hr Cautions: • Contraindicated with serotonergic drugs (risk of serotonin syndrome) • G6PD deficiency — risk

nodes.title: Temporary Pacing
nodes.summary: Pacing improves rate but NOT contractility — continue HIET and other therapies
nodes.body: Temporary pacing for refractory bradycardia: Transcutaneous pacing: • Immediate temporizing measure • Often fails to capture or improve hemodynamics • Contractility is impaired — pacing improves rate but not inotropy Transvenous pacing: • More reliable capture • Consider if transcutaneous fails • Still will not address underlying contractile dysfunction Key point: Pacing addresses RATE but NOT the

nodes.title: VA-ECMO — Bridge to Recovery
nodes.summary: VA-ECMO bridges reversible CCB toxicity — contact ECMO team EARLY, full recovery possible
nodes.body: VA-ECMO is the ultimate rescue for refractory CCB toxicity [1][3]. Key principle: CCB toxicity is REVERSIBLE — patients can fully recover if bridged through the acute phase. When to consider: • Cardiac arrest despite all other measures • Refractory shock despite maximum medical therapy • Young, previously healthy patient with reversible cause • Lactate rising despite aggressive resuscitation Conta

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: All significant CCB ingestions require ICU — extended-release needs 24-48h monitoring minimum
nodes.body: All significant CCB ingestions require ICU admission [1][3]. Extended-release formulations: • Minimum 24-48 hour monitoring regardless of initial presentation • Watch for delayed deterioration — can occur 12-24 hours post-ingestion Psychiatric evaluation is mandatory for intentional ingestions after medical clearance. What is the current clinical status?

nodes.title: ICU Admission — Unstable
nodes.summary: ICU with arterial line — serial glucose q1h, K+ q2h, lactate q4h, wean slowly
nodes.body: ICU admission for active management: • Continuous telemetry and arterial line • Continue HIET, vasopressors, calcium as indicated • Serial labs: glucose q1h, K+ q2h, lactate q4h, iCa q4h • Wean therapies slowly as hemodynamics improve Duration of monitoring: • Until hemodynamically stable off vasopressors x12-24h • Extended-release: minimum 48-72h even after stabilization Watch for: • Late deterio
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous monitoring, ongoing HIET/vasopressors as indicated, and minimum 24-48h observation.

nodes.title: ICU Admission — High-Risk but Stable
nodes.summary: ICU even if stable — extended-release and verapamil can deteriorate 12-24h post-ingestion
nodes.body: ICU admission for monitoring: High-risk features requiring ICU even if currently stable: • Extended-release formulation (ANY) • Verapamil ingestion (ANY significant amount) • Large ingestion of any CCB • Co-ingestion with beta-blockers or other cardiotoxic drugs Monitoring plan: • Continuous telemetry — minimum 24-48 hours • Serial ECGs q4-6h • Serial labs q6h • NPO or clear liquids only (in case
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for 24-48h monitoring even if hemodynamically stable. Extended-release ingestions require prolonged observation.

nodes.title: Low-Risk Observation
nodes.summary: Low-risk only: small immediate-release DHP, asymptomatic x6h, normal vitals and ECG
nodes.body: Monitored observation may be appropriate for: • Small, unintentional immediate-release DHP ingestion • Completely asymptomatic • Normal vitals and ECG • Reliable history Observation criteria: • Continuous telemetry minimum 6 hours • Serial vitals q1h • Serial ECGs q2h • If any abnormality develops → escalate to ICU Discharge criteria: • Asymptomatic x6 hours • Normal vitals and ECG throughout • Ab
nodes.recommendation: Monitored observation x6h for low-risk immediate-release ingestions. Escalate immediately if any hemodynamic changes.

Key Context: Strangulation > Non-fatal strangulation is a MAJOR risk factor for cervical artery dissection. > Up to 50% of intimate partner violence victims experience strangulation. > Symptoms may be delayed 24-72 hours or more. nodes.title: Red Flags for Arterial Injury
nodes.summary: LOC during strangulation = high-risk for arterial injury — immediate CTA needed
nodes.body: HIGH-RISK features after strangulation: Immediate imaging needed: • Loss of consciousness during event • Incontinence during event • Voice changes/hoarseness • Difficulty swallowing • Neck pain or tenderness • Neurologic symptoms • Visible neck injury • Petechiae (face, eyes) Low-risk (still requires documentation and safety planning): • No LOC • No neurologic symptoms • No visible injury • Normal

nodes.title: Stroke from Dissection

nodes.body: Dissection-related stroke is an emergency: Presentation: • Unilateral headache → neurologic symptoms • May be hours to days after injury • Young patient with stroke = think dissection Immediate Actions: 1. Activate stroke protocol 2. CT head (rule out hemorrhage) 3. CTA head/neck (dissection + occlusion) 4. Consider thrombolysis if within window 5. Neurology consultation emergent NIHSS assessment

nodes.body: Trauma-related Dissection: Mechanisms: • Hyperextension/rotation injuries • Direct blow to neck • Seatbelt injuries • Sports (martial arts, football) Memphis Criteria for CTA screening: • Cervical spine fracture • Neurologic deficit not explained by imaging • Horner syndrome • LeFort II/III fracture • Skull base fracture involving carotid canal • DAI with GCS <6 Consider imaging liberally in neck

nodes.body: Spontaneous Dissection: Risk Factors: • Connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan) • Fibromuscular dysplasia • Hypertension • Recent infection • Migraine Classic Presentation: • Sudden severe unilateral headache/neck pain • Ipsilateral Horner syndrome • ± Stroke symptoms Minor Trauma Triggers: • Chiropractic manipulation • Vigorous coughing/sneezing • Yoga positions • Roller coasters • Ha

nodes.title: Low-Risk Strangulation
nodes.summary: Even low-risk strangulation needs documentation, safety assessment, and return precautions
nodes.body: Even "low-risk" strangulation requires: 1. Documentation: • Detailed history of event • Photograph any visible injuries • Document negative findings too 2. Safety Assessment: • IPV screening • Safety planning • Social work consultation • Domestic violence resources 3. Return Precautions: • Headache, vision changes, weakness • Voice changes, difficulty swallowing • Any neurologic symptoms • Return

nodes.title: Imaging Results

nodes.title: Negative Imaging
nodes.summary: Negative CTA with high suspicion — consider MRA or repeat imaging in 24-48h
nodes.body: CTA Negative — Next Steps: If high clinical suspicion: • Consider MRA (more sensitive for intramural hematoma) • Repeat imaging in 24-48h if symptoms persist • Observation with serial exams If low clinical suspicion: • Close follow-up • Strict return precautions • Primary care follow-up within 1 week Documentation: • Clinical decision-making • Return precautions given • Safety planning if strangul

nodes.title: Treatment of Cervical Artery Dissection
nodes.summary: CADISS trial: antiplatelet = anticoagulation — prefer aspirin for lower bleeding risk
nodes.body: Antithrombotic Therapy: Goal: Prevent stroke from thromboembolism Options (equivalent efficacy): Antiplatelet: • Aspirin 81-325 mg daily • Or dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) x 21 days, then aspirin alone Anticoagulation: • Heparin → Warfarin (INR 2-3) • Duration: 3-6 months CADISS Trial: No difference between antiplatelet and anticoagulation. Most centers: Antiplatelet therapy preferred

nodes.title: Endovascular and Surgical Options
nodes.summary: Most dissections heal spontaneously — stenting rarely needed acutely
nodes.body: Endovascular Therapy: Stenting: • Rarely needed acutely • Consider for: - Symptomatic pseudoaneurysm - Recurrent TIA despite antithrombotic therapy - Expanding dissection Surgical Repair: • Very rarely indicated • Consider for failed endovascular therapy • Pseudoaneurysm with mass effect Most dissections heal spontaneously with medical therapy alone. [1][4][6]

nodes.title: Stroke from Dissection
nodes.summary: tPA is NOT contraindicated in dissection-related stroke — standard criteria apply

nodes.title: Safety Assessment — Strangulation/IPV
nodes.summary: Screen ALL strangulation patients for IPV — social work, safety plan, DV hotline
nodes.body: Intimate Partner Violence Safety Assessment: Screen ALL strangulation patients: • "Are you safe at home?" • "Is the person who did this going to be there when you leave?" • "Do you have a safe place to go?" Resources: • Social work consultation • Domestic violence advocate • National DV Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 • Safety planning Documentation for legal purposes: • Detailed mechanism • Exam findings

nodes.title: Observation
nodes.summary: Serial neuro checks q2h, social work evaluation, safety planning, await imaging
nodes.body: Observation for High-Risk Strangulation: • Serial neurologic exams (q2h) • Await imaging results • Voice/swallowing assessment • Social work evaluation • Safety planning If imaging positive: Admit for treatment If imaging negative and symptoms resolve: May discharge with close follow-up Strict return precautions: • Any neurologic symptoms • Worsening voice changes • Difficulty swallowing • Headach
nodes.recommendation: Observation with serial neurologic exams. Social work evaluation for safety planning.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.summary: Return immediately for headache, weakness, vision or speech changes — follow-up in 1 week
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: • Negative imaging (or low clinical suspicion, imaging not indicated) • Stable neurologic exam • No voice changes or dysphagia • Safe discharge environment • Resources provided if IPV Discharge Instructions: • Return immediately for headache, weakness, vision changes, speech changes • Follow-up with PCP within 1 week • If IPV: DV resources, safety plan, hotline number Documenta
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with strict return precautions. Safety planning if IPV-related.

nodes.title: Radiculopathy — Conservative Management
nodes.summary: 80-90% resolve in 4-6 wk — NSAIDs, gaba, PT, no imaging if <6 wk no red flags
nodes.body: ~80-90% of cervical radiculopathy resolves with conservative care within 4-6 weeks. nodes.title: Myelopathy Screen — UMN Findings
nodes.summary: Hoffman + Lhermitte + hyperreflexia + gait = MRI emergent
nodes.body: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults >55. It is commonly missed because patients present with vague hand clumsiness or gait change attributed to aging. [13][14] Screen every patient with neck pain + any of: • Hand clumsiness ("dropping things, buttons hard") • Gait disturbance, falls • Bilateral arm or leg symptoms • Sphincter changes

nodes.summary: Assume c-spine injury until cleared — secondary injury from hypotension/hypoxemia may exceed primary
nodes.body: ATLS Principle: Assume cervical spine injury until cleared in ALL trauma patients. High-Risk Mechanisms: • Falls ≥3 ft or 5 stairs • Axial load (diving, falling object) • MVC >100 km/hr, rollover, ejection • Motorized recreation collision • Bicycle vs vehicle or ejection Red Flags: • Midline cervical tenderness • Neurologic deficit • Altered mental status • Intoxication • Painful distracting injur

nodes.title: Clinical Decision Rules
nodes.summary: CCR preferred over NEXUS — sensitivity 99-100% vs 94%, fewer missed injuries
nodes.body: Which Rule to Use? Canadian C-Spine Rule (CCR) • Sensitivity: 99-100% • Includes mechanism assessment • Works in intoxicated if alert • Age ≥65 mandates imaging NEXUS Criteria • Sensitivity: 94% • Simpler, 5 criteria • No age cutoffs • Less sensitive in elderly Bottom Line: ✅ CCR is preferred over NEXUS — higher sensitivity, fewer missed injuries [3][4]

nodes.body: C-Spine Cleared by Clinical Decision Rule ✅ No imaging required ✅ Remove cervical collar Document: • Which rule used (CCR preferred) • All criteria assessed • ROM if applicable Discharge Instructions: • Return if symptoms worsen • New numbness, tingling, weakness = return immediately • Ibuprofen/acetaminophen for pain • Activity as tolerated [3][4]

nodes.title: C-Spine Imaging Strategy
nodes.summary: CT c-spine is primary modality — if injury found, image full thoracolumbar spine
nodes.body: CT C-Spine is the Primary Modality CT Protocol: • Axial images from occiput to T1 • Sagittal and coronal reconstructions • ~98% sensitivity for fractures Plain films: No longer first-line for screening If injury identified: • Image full thoracolumbar spine (occult injuries in 20%) • Consider CTA for vertebral artery dissection MRI Indications: • Neurologic deficit with negative CT • Persistent sym

nodes.title: Persistent Pain — Negative CT
nodes.summary: Negative CT with persistent pain — MRI within 72h shows abnormalities in 25%
nodes.body: CT Negative with Persistent Pain Options: 1. Continue collar + repeat exam - Reassess in 24-48 hours - If resolves → clear 2. MRI within 72 hours - Most sensitive for ligamentous injury - Shows abnormalities in ~25% with negative CT - More useful after initial inflammation 3. Flexion-extension films - Only if cooperative and no neurologic symptoms - Can identify dynamic instability EAST Recommenda

nodes.title: Obtunded Patient — Clearance
nodes.summary: EAST 2022: high-quality negative CT alone sufficient for collar removal in obtunded patients
nodes.body: C-Spine Clearance in Obtunded Patient EAST 2022 Guidelines: ✅ High-quality negative CT alone is sufficient for collar removal Rationale: • CT has very high NPV for unstable injuries • MRI adds mostly low-significance findings • Transport risks for MRI often outweigh benefits • Collar complications increase 66% per day When to consider MRI: • Focal neurologic deficit present • Concerning mechanism

nodes.title: Upper C-Spine Injuries (C0-C2)
nodes.summary: 50% of cervical fractures at C1-C2 — always check both levels when one is injured
nodes.body: Upper Cervical Spine Injuries 50% of all cervical fractures occur at C1-C2. nodes.summary: Atlanto-occipital dislocation — often fatal, emergency surgical fusion if survived

Rigid immobilization 2. Avoid neck manipulation 3. EMERGENCY spine surgery consultation Treatment: Surgical occipitocervical fusion required Prognosis: Very poor — most fatal at scene. nodes.title: Spinal Cord Injury Syndromes
nodes.summary: Identify SCI pattern by motor/sensory distribution — determines prognosis and management
nodes.body: Identify the SCI Pattern: Exam findings determine syndrome and prognosis. Key Findings: • Motor weakness distribution • Sensory level and pattern • Rectal tone, priapism • Complete vs incomplete [12][13]

nodes.title: Complete Spinal Cord Injury
nodes.summary: Complete cord: total loss below level — <5% regain meaningful motor, focus on rehab
nodes.body: Complete Cord Transection Findings: • Total loss of motor function below level • Total loss of sensory function below level • Absent rectal tone • Flaccid paralysis initially (spinal shock) Spinal Shock: • Lasts hours to weeks • Areflexia below lesion • Resolution: Return of bulbocavernosus reflex • After shock resolves → spasticity develops Prognosis: • Poor for functional recovery • <5% regain m

nodes.title: Central Cord Syndrome
nodes.summary: Central cord: UE weakness > LE — BEST incomplete prognosis, 75% regain ambulation
nodes.body: Central Cord Syndrome — Most Common Incomplete SCI Classic Presentation: • Upper extremity weakness > lower extremity • Cape distribution sensory loss • Bladder dysfunction (retention > incontinence) • Variable motor/sensory patterns Mechanism: Hyperextension in elderly with pre-existing cervical stenosis or spondylosis Pathophysiology: Central cord (arm fibers) more affected than lateral (leg fib

nodes.title: Anterior Cord Syndrome
nodes.summary: Anterior cord: motor + pain/temp loss, preserved proprioception — WORST incomplete prognosis
nodes.body: Anterior Cord Syndrome — Worst Prognosis of Incomplete Findings: • Motor paralysis (corticospinal tracts) • Loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tracts) • Preserved proprioception and vibration (dorsal columns intact) Causes: • Anterior spinal artery occlusion • Burst fracture with anterior cord compression • Aortic surgery complication • Disc herniation Prognosis: ❌ Worst of incomplete inj

nodes.title: Brown-Séquard Syndrome
nodes.summary: Hemisection: ipsilateral motor, contralateral pain/temp — BEST overall prognosis, 75-90% ambulatory
nodes.body: Brown-Séquard Syndrome — Best Prognosis Cord hemisection. Findings: Ipsilateral (same side as lesion): • Motor paralysis • Loss of proprioception and vibration Contralateral (opposite side): • Loss of pain and temperature (1-2 levels below injury) Causes: • Penetrating trauma (knife, bullet) • Lateral mass fracture with cord compression • Tumor, epidural hematoma Prognosis: ✅ Best prognosis of all

nodes.title: Posterior Cord Syndrome
nodes.summary: Rare: proprioception/vibration loss only — sensory ataxia, Romberg positive
nodes.body: Posterior Cord Syndrome — Rare Findings: • Loss of proprioception and vibration (dorsal columns) • Motor preserved • Pain and temperature preserved • Sensory ataxia Causes: • Posterior spinal artery infarct • Tabes dorsalis (syphilis) • B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) • Multiple sclerosis Clinical: • Patients can't sense position in space • Romberg positive • Wide-based gait Rare a

nodes.title: SCI Resuscitation
nodes.summary: MAP 75-95 mmHg for 3-7 days (2024) — NE by consensus, AVOID phenylephrine alone

nodes.title: Steroids in SCI — NOT Recommended

Risks: • Increased infection • Wound complications • GI bleeding • Possible inc

nodes.title: Surgical Timing
nodes.summary: Early decompression <24h improves outcomes — DVT prophylaxis within 72h mandatory
nodes.body: Surgical Decompression Timing Early Surgery (<24 hours): • Associated with improved neurologic outcomes • Especially for incomplete injuries • STASCIS trial: 2-grade improvement more likely Indications for Urgent Surgery: • Progressive neurologic deterioration • Unstable fractures • Persistent cord compression • Incomplete injury with compression Consult Neurosurgery/Spine Immediately: • Any spina

nodes.title: Pediatric C-Spine Assessment
nodes.summary: PECARN 2024: GCS 3-8 = CT, altered mental status = x-ray, none = clinical clearance
nodes.body: PECARN 2024 — Pediatric C-Spine Rule High Risk (warrant CT): • GCS 3-8 or AVPU = U • Abnormal airway/breathing/circulation • Focal neurologic deficit → CSI rate: 12.1% Intermediate Risk (warrant X-ray): • Altered mental status (GCS 9-14) • Self-reported neck pain • Substantial torso or head injury • Posterior midline tenderness → CSI rate: 2.8% Low Risk (clinical clearance): • None of above → CSI

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: SCI/high cervical: ICU for MAP monitoring; stable fracture: floor; cleared: discharge with collar
nodes.body: Disposition Planning Consult Spine Surgery For: • Any unstable injury • Neurologic deficit • Progressive symptoms • Uncertain stability • Type II odontoid • Hangman's Type IIa/III • SLIC ≥5 Admit to ICU: • Spinal cord injury (MAP monitoring) • High cervical injury (C2-C4) • Neurogenic shock • Need for mechanical ventilation [1]

nodes.title: ICU Admission Checklist
nodes.summary: Arterial line, MAP 75-95, NE infusion, Foley, NG tube, DVT prophylaxis, q1h neuro checks
nodes.body: ICU Admission for C-Spine/SCI Orders: □ Continuous arterial line monitoring □ MAP goal 75-95 mmHg □ Norepinephrine infusion PRN □ Foley catheter (neurogenic bladder) □ NG tube if high cervical (ileus common) □ DVT prophylaxis within 72 hours □ Respiratory monitoring (PFTs if C2-C4) □ Q1h neuro checks Consults: □ Neurosurgery or Orthopedic Spine □ PM&R for rehab planning □ Respiratory therapy Avoid

nodes.title: Floor Admission Checklist
nodes.summary: Hard collar at all times, log-roll, neuro checks q4h, DVT prophylaxis, pain management
nodes.body: Floor Admission for Stable C-Spine Injury Orders: □ Hard cervical collar at all times □ Log-roll precautions for repositioning □ Neuro checks Q4h □ DVT prophylaxis □ Pain management □ Stool softener (avoid straining) Consults: □ Spine surgery for operative planning □ PT/OT evaluation Education: □ Do not remove collar □ Report any new weakness, numbness, or changes

nodes.title: Discharge with Collar
nodes.summary: Rigid collar at ALL times, no heavy lifting, return for new numbness/weakness/incontinence
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions — Stable C-Spine Fracture Collar: • Wear rigid collar at ALL times except brief showers • Keep collar on while sleeping • Follow-up in 1-2 weeks with spine surgery Activity: • No heavy lifting (>10 lbs) • No contact sports • Limit neck rotation • May work if sedentary job Return IMMEDIATELY if: • New numbness or tingling • New weakness in arms or legs • Loss of bladder/bowel

nodes.title: Cyanotic or Shocked Neonate
nodes.summary: CHD presents as blue baby (cyanotic) or shocked baby (obstructive); 1% of live births; critical CHD presents as ductus closes
nodes.body: Congenital Heart Disease (CHD) affects ~1% of live births. Critical CHD presents in the first weeks of life as the ductus arteriosus closes. KEY ASSESSMENT • Cyanosis that does NOT improve with supplemental O2 • Poor perfusion, weak pulses, shock • Murmur (may be absent in critical lesions) • Hepatomegaly, respiratory distress REFERENCES • Hyperoxia Test • 4-Extremity Vitals • PGE1 Dosing • THE MI

nodes.title: 4-Extremity Assessment
nodes.summary: Pre vs post-ductal sats: >3% difference suggests ductal shunt; arm > leg BP by >20 suggests coarctation; check femoral pulses
nodes.body: CRITICAL: 4-EXTREMITY BP AND PULSE OX Obtain simultaneous pre-ductal (right arm) and post-ductal (either foot) saturations. INTERPRETATION • Pre > Post by >3%: Suggests right-to-left shunt through PDA (ductal-dependent systemic lesions) • Post > Pre: Suggests TGA with coarctation (rare) • Both low (<90%): Cyanotic heart disease 4-EXTREMITY BLOOD PRESSURE • Arm BP > Leg BP by >20 mmHg: Coarctation

nodes.title: Hyperoxia Test
nodes.summary: Hyperoxia test: PaO2 <100 on 100% O2 = cardiac cause (fixed shunt); PaO2 >150 = pulmonary cause
nodes.body: HYPEROXIA TEST - Distinguishes cardiac from pulmonary cyanosis PROCEDURE 1. Obtain baseline ABG on room air (or current FiO2) 2. Place on 100% FiO2 for 10 minutes 3. Repeat ABG INTERPRETATION • PaO2 rises to >150 mmHg: PULMONARY cause (responds to O2) • PaO2 stays <100 mmHg: CARDIAC cause (fixed shunt, does not respond) • PaO2 100-150 mmHg: Indeterminate - may be cardiac CAUTION IN KNOWN CHD High

nodes.title: Consider Non-Cardiac Causes
nodes.body: Hyperoxia test suggests PULMONARY cause of cyanosis DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS • Persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn (PPHN) • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) • Meconium aspiration syndrome • Pneumonia/sepsis • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia • Airway obstruction STILL CONSIDER CHD IF: • Clinical suspicion high • Murmur present • Abnormal 4-extremity sats/BP • Echo shows structural abnorma
nodes.recommendation: Hyperoxia test suggests pulmonary cause. Consider PPHN, RDS, pneumonia. Still obtain echo if clinical suspicion for CHD remains.

nodes.title: Blue Baby - The 5 T's
nodes.summary: Blue babies = 5 T's: Tetralogy, Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, TAPVR, Truncus; most are ductal-dependent
nodes.body: CYANOTIC HEART DISEASE - The 5 T's All involve right-to-left shunting with deoxygenated blood entering systemic circulation. THE 5 T's: 1. Tetralogy of Fallot (most common cyanotic CHD) 2. Transposition of Great Arteries (most common cyanotic CHD in neonates) 3. Tricuspid Atresia 4. Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR) 5. Truncus Arteriosus DUCTAL DEPENDENCE Most cyanotic lesions are du

nodes.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
nodes.summary: TOF = VSD + pulmonary stenosis + overriding aorta + RVH; boot-shaped heart on CXR; tet spells are hypercyanotic emergencies
nodes.body: TETRALOGY OF FALLOT (TOF) Most common cyanotic CHD overall. Four features: 1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) 2. Pulmonary stenosis (RVOT obstruction) 3. Overriding aorta 4. Right ventricular hypertrophy CLASSIC CXR: Boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) TET SPELLS Hypercyanotic episodes due to RVOT spasm: • Triggered by crying, feeding, defecation • Infant becomes deeply cyanotic, limp • May progres

nodes.title: Tet Spell Management
nodes.body: TET SPELL - HYPERCYANOTIC EPISODE IMMEDIATE INTERVENTIONS (in order): 1. KNEE-CHEST POSITION Have parent hold infant with knees to chest. Increases SVR and reduces right-to-left shunt. 2. CALM THE INFANT • Minimize stimulation • Do NOT separate from parent if possible • Avoid painful procedures if possible 3. OXYGEN 100% FiO2 (helps somewhat, but cyanosis is from shunting) 4. MORPHINE Morphine 0.1
nodes.recommendation: TET SPELL: Knee-chest position first, then calm infant, O2, morphine 0.1-0.2 mg/kg. If refractory: phenylephrine, propranolol, ketamine.

nodes.title: Stable Tetralogy of Fallot
nodes.summary: Stable TOF: avoid dehydration/agitation, does NOT need PGE1, surgical repair at 3-6 months
nodes.body: STABLE TOF - Not in acute spell PRESENTATION • May be "pink tet" initially (mild cyanosis) • Cyanosis worsens with activity, crying • History of squatting in older infants (increases SVR) • Murmur: harsh systolic ejection murmur at LUSB WORKUP • CXR: Boot-shaped heart, decreased pulmonary vascular markings • ECG: Right axis deviation, RVH • Echo: Definitive diagnosis MANAGEMENT • Avoid dehydration

nodes.title: Transposition of Great Arteries
nodes.body: TRANSPOSITION OF GREAT ARTERIES (TGA) Most common cyanotic CHD presenting in the first week of life. ANATOMY Aorta arises from RV, pulmonary artery from LV. Two parallel circulations with no mixing = incompatible with life unless mixing exists. PRESENTATION • Severe cyanosis within hours of birth • May be well-appearing initially (ductus still open) • Rapid deterioration as ductus closes • Minimal
nodes.recommendation: TGA is DUCTAL-DEPENDENT. Start PGE1 immediately. Emergent cardiology for balloon atrial septostomy. Arterial switch surgery within 2 weeks.

nodes.title: Other Cyanotic Lesions
nodes.summary: Tricuspid atresia, TAPVR, Truncus, Pulmonary atresia - most are ductal-dependent; start PGE1
nodes.body: OTHER CYANOTIC HEART DEFECTS TRICUSPID ATRESIA • Absent tricuspid valve • All blood crosses ASD → LV → aorta and PDA • Requires PGE1 for pulmonary blood flow TOTAL ANOMALOUS PULMONARY VENOUS RETURN (TAPVR) • Pulmonary veins drain to systemic veins instead of LA • Obstructed TAPVR = surgical emergency • CXR: "Snowman" or "figure-8" heart (supracardiac type) TRUNCUS ARTERIOSUS • Single great vessel

nodes.title: Shocked Baby - Left-Sided Obstructive Lesions
nodes.summary: Shocked baby = left-sided obstruction; gray/pale not blue; check femoral pulses; coarctation, HLHS, critical AS
nodes.body: CARDIOGENIC SHOCK IN NEONATE Left-sided obstructive lesions present with shock as the ductus closes and systemic perfusion fails. CLINICAL FEATURES • Pale, gray, mottled (not blue) • Poor perfusion, weak pulses • Tachycardia, tachypnea • Hepatomegaly • Metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate • May appear septic KEY LESIONS: • Coarctation of the Aorta (most common) • Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (H

nodes.title: Coarctation of Aorta
nodes.body: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Narrowing of aorta, typically just distal to left subclavian artery (juxtaductal). PRESENTATION • May be asymptomatic initially with open ductus • Shock when ductus closes (typically days 1-14) • Weak or absent femoral pulses (PATHOGNOMONIC) • Upper extremity hypertension, lower extremity hypotension • BP gradient >20 mmHg arm > leg ASSOCIATED FINDINGS • Bicuspid aortic va
nodes.recommendation: Coarctation: Weak femorals + arm > leg BP gradient. Start PGE1 to reopen ductus. Surgical repair required.

nodes.title: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
nodes.body: HYPOPLASTIC LEFT HEART SYNDROME (HLHS) Underdeveloped left heart structures (LV, mitral valve, aortic valve, ascending aorta). Systemic circulation entirely dependent on PDA. PRESENTATION • May look well initially with open ductus • Rapid deterioration as ductus closes • Shock, acidosis, gray/mottled • Single S2 (no aortic component) • Hepatomegaly, poor pulses CRITICAL CONCEPT The RV pumps to bot
nodes.recommendation: HLHS is DUCTAL-DEPENDENT. PGE1 immediately. AVOID HIGH O2 - target SpO2 75-85%. Prepare for staged surgical palliation (Norwood).

nodes.title: Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1)
nodes.body: PROSTAGLANDIN E1 (Alprostadil) - THE DUCT DRUG Keeps ductus arteriosus patent. Life-saving in ductal-dependent lesions. INDICATIONS • Suspected ductal-dependent CHD • Cyanotic neonate failing hyperoxia test • Shocked neonate with suspected CHD • Do NOT wait for echo confirmation DOSING • Initial: 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min • Maintenance: 0.01-0.05 mcg/kg/min (can often wean) • Titrate to effect (improved
nodes.recommendation: PGE1 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min continuous infusion. Be ready for apnea (12% incidence). Do not wait for echo to start if clinical suspicion high.

nodes.title: PGE1 Side Effects
nodes.summary: PGE1 side effects: apnea (12%, have intubation ready), fever, hypotension, flushing, bradycardia, jitteriness
nodes.body: PGE1 SIDE EFFECTS AND MANAGEMENT APNEA (12%) • Most significant side effect • More common at higher doses • May require intubation - have equipment ready • Usually occurs within first hour FEVER • Common, typically low-grade • May confuse clinical picture (looks like sepsis) • Usually benign, monitor HYPOTENSION • Due to vasodilation • Support with fluids, consider inotropes • May need to decrease

nodes.title: Pitfalls to Avoid
nodes.summary: Avoid: high O2 in ductal-dependent lesions, excessive fluids, waiting for echo, missing coarctation, hyperventilation
nodes.body: CRITICAL PITFALLS IN NEONATAL CHD 1. HIGH FiO2 IN DUCTAL-DEPENDENT LESIONS • High O2 constricts ductus arteriosus • May worsen cyanosis paradoxically • Target SpO2 75-85% in HLHS and similar lesions • Room air or minimal O2 often better 2. EXCESSIVE FLUID RESUSCITATION • These are cardiogenic, not hypovolemic shock • Large fluid boluses may worsen pulmonary edema • Use small boluses (10 mL/kg) jud

nodes.title: Stabilization Priorities
nodes.summary: Stabilization: low intubation threshold on PGE1, ketamine for induction, accept SpO2 75-85% in HLHS, small fluid boluses
nodes.body: STABILIZATION OF NEONATE WITH SUSPECTED CHD A - AIRWAY • Low threshold to intubate if on PGE1 (apnea risk) • Ketamine preferred for induction (maintains SVR) • Avoid excessive positive pressure (affects preload) B - BREATHING • Target SpO2 based on lesion: - Cyanotic: accept 75-85% - HLHS: target 75-85% (NOT higher) - Shocked: monitor trend more than absolute • Avoid high FiO2 unless clear benefit

nodes.title: Airway Management in CHD
nodes.summary: Ketamine preferred for CHD intubation (maintains SVR); avoid propofol; avoid hyperventilation
nodes.body: INTUBATION IN CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE WHEN TO INTUBATE • Apnea (PGE1-induced or otherwise) • Severe respiratory distress • Need for transport • Hemodynamic instability requiring sedation PREFERRED AGENTS INDUCTION • Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV - Maintains SVR (good for CHD) - Maintains HR - Preserves respiratory drive longer • Fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg IV - Less hemodynamic effect - Use if ketamine contraind

nodes.title: Cardiology Consultation
nodes.summary: Call cardiology for any suspected CHD; provide vitals, 4-extremity sats, CXR/ECG, response to PGE1; most need surgical center
nodes.body: WHEN TO CALL CARDIOLOGY CALL IMMEDIATELY: • Any neonate with suspected CHD • Cyanosis not explained by pulmonary disease • Shock with suspected cardiac etiology • Abnormal echo findings • Started on PGE1 INFORMATION TO PROVIDE: • Age, weight, gestational age • Presenting symptoms and timeline • Current vitals including 4-extremity sats • Response to interventions (O2, PGE1) • CXR and ECG findings

nodes.title: Transfer Considerations
nodes.summary: Pre-transfer: secure airway if on PGE1, two IVs, backup PGE1 for transport, transport team with intubation capability
nodes.body: TRANSFER TO PEDIATRIC CARDIAC CENTER PRE-TRANSFER CHECKLIST: ☐ Airway secured (if on PGE1, low threshold to intubate) ☐ IV access (two if possible, one for PGE1) ☐ PGE1 running with adequate supply for transport ☐ Backup PGE1 infusion prepared ☐ Intubation equipment available ☐ Blood glucose checked and corrected ☐ Temperature maintained ☐ Parents informed and consented TRANSPORT TEAM • Neonatal o

nodes.title: ECMO Considerations
nodes.body: ECMO IN NEONATAL CHD INDICATIONS • Refractory cardiogenic shock despite maximal medical therapy • Bridge to surgery in unstable patient • Post-operative cardiac failure • Refractory arrhythmias with hemodynamic compromise CONSIDERATIONS • Requires ECMO-capable center (usually same as cardiac surgery) • Venoarterial (VA) ECMO for cardiac support • May be cannulated peripherally or centrally RELATIV
nodes.recommendation: ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock or bridge to surgery. Requires VA ECMO. Consider early transfer to ECMO-capable center.

nodes.title: The 5 T's of Cyanotic CHD
nodes.body: THE 5 T's - CYANOTIC CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE 1. TETRALOGY OF FALLOT • Most common cyanotic CHD overall • VSD + pulmonary stenosis + overriding aorta + RVH • "Tet spells" - hypercyanotic episodes • Boot-shaped heart on CXR 2. TRANSPOSITION OF GREAT ARTERIES • Most common cyanotic CHD in neonates • Parallel circulations - no mixing • Ductal-dependent • Egg-on-string CXR 3. TRICUSPID ATRESIA • Absen

nodes.title: Chemical Eye Burn
nodes.summary: Alkali reaches anterior chamber in <15 seconds — IRRIGATE BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE
nodes.body: True ocular emergency — IRRIGATE BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE. Mechanism: - Alkali: Lipophilic penetration, liquefactive necrosis — WORSE prognosis - Acid: Coagulative necrosis, protein barrier limits penetration Alkali can reach anterior chamber in <15 seconds. Time is cornea. Every minute without irrigation = worse outcome. Common Agents: | Alkali (More Severe) | Acid | |---------------------|------| |

nodes.title: Immediate Action
nodes.summary: Do NOT delay for history, VA, pH, or slit lamp — start irrigation NOW
nodes.body: DO NOT DELAY FOR: - History - Visual acuity - Slit lamp exam - pH testing - Ophthalmology consult START IRRIGATION NOW. At Scene: - Any non-caustic fluid (tap water, saline, water fountain) - Continue during transport In ED: 1. Topical anesthetic (proparacaine) 2. Sweep fornices for particulate matter 3. Begin continuous irrigation 4. Morgan lens if available Exception: Suspected globe rupture — d

nodes.title: Agent Type
nodes.summary: If unknown, treat as alkali — worst-case approach for deepest penetration
nodes.body: What type of chemical exposure? If unknown, treat as alkali (worst-case).

nodes.title: Irrigation Protocol
nodes.summary: Alkali: 30 min to 2+ hours irrigation; acid: 15-30 min — LR preferred over NS
nodes.body: Fluid Selection (in order of preference): 1. Diphoterine (amphoteric, if available) 2. Balanced salt solution (BSS) 3. Lactated Ringer's (LR) — preferred over NS 4. Normal saline (NS) — pH can be 4.5-7.0 5. Sterile water 6. Tap water (acceptable at scene) Avoid: Hypotonic solutions increase chemical penetration. Insert lens under upper lid 5. Have patient look up 6. Tuck lens under lower lid 7. Connect to IV tubing with fluid running Flow Rate: - Wide open initially - 250-500 mL over 15-20 min - Adjust based on tolerance Contraindic

nodes.body: CRITICAL for cement/lime/plite exposures: Particulate alkali continues releasing hydroxide until removed. Technique: 1. Apply topical anesthetic 2. Double-evert upper lid 3. Use moist cotton swab 4. Sweep upper fornix systematically 5. Repeat for lower fornix 6. Check lid margins and puncta Look for: - White calcium hydroxide particles (lime) - Cement fragments - Plaster debris - Any retained fore

nodes.title: pH Monitoring
nodes.summary: Target pH 7.0-7.4 — wait 5-10 min after stopping irrigation before checking (reservoir effect)
nodes.body: Target pH: 7.0-7.4 Testing Protocol: 1. Check pH of BOTH eyes before irrigation (baseline) 2. After irrigation, STOP flow 3. Wait 5-10 minutes (reservoir effect) 4. Touch litmus paper to inferior fornix (NOT cornea) 5. Read pH Use narrow-range pH paper (5.0-8.0) — more precise than universal strips. Interpretation: | pH | Action | |----|--------| | <7.0 | Continue irrigation | | 7.0-7.4 | Stop, re

nodes.title: pH Status
nodes.summary: pH must be stable on two readings 30 min apart before proceeding to exam
nodes.body: What is the pH after irrigation? (Must wait 5-10 minutes after stopping irrigation to allow chemical release from tissues.)

nodes.title: Continue Irrigation
nodes.summary: pH not normalized — continue irrigation, re-sweep fornices, may need 2+ hours for severe alkali
nodes.body: pH not normalized — continue irrigation: Steps: 1. Resume irrigation for additional 15-30 minutes 2. Re-sweep fornices for retained particles 3. Ensure adequate volume and flow rate 4. Recheck pH after 5-10 minute pause Refractory pH: - May indicate deep tissue penetration (severe alkali) - May indicate retained particulate - Consider ophthalmology consultation Do NOT stop irrigation prematurely.

External: - Lid burns, periorbital skin involvement - Forniceal shortening (early symblepharon) 3. Cornea: - Fluorescein — epithelial defect size - Stromal haze/opacity - Clarity (can you see iris details?) 4. Limbus: - Ischemia — perilimbal blanching (KEY prognostic) - Clock hours invol

nodes.title: Chest Pain Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: ECG in 10 min, monitor/IV, aspirin if ACS possible, POCUS if unstable.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI / OMI / NSTE-ACS) \u2014 serial ECG + troponin; watch posterior, RV, de Winter, Wellens, new LBBB. 2. Aortic dissection \u2014 tearing/migrating pain, pulse or BP differential, neuro deficit; do NOT anticoagulate until excluded. 3. Pulmonary embolism \u2014 pleuritic pain, dyspnea, hypoxia, RV strain, VTE risk. 4. Tension pneumothorax \

nodes.title: Which Diagnosis Are You Working Up?
nodes.summary: Choose a differential; the hub runs its validated rule-in/rule-out instrument to a verdict.
nodes.body: Chest pain triage is not "cardiac vs noncardiac." It is deciding which killer to rule in or rule out while serial ECG/troponin work continues. Pick a differential; each path runs its validated instrument (HEART, Wells/PERC, aortic ADD-RS in the toolbar) to a verdict. Work through more than one if the picture is mixed.

nodes.title: ACS - Step 1: ECG First
nodes.summary: ECG in 10 min drives everything; Sgarbossa for paced/LBBB; no-STEMI goes to HEART.
nodes.body: The ECG decides the lane before any score. 12-lead within 10 minutes, repeat during pain. If paced or LBBB, apply Sgarbossa (toolbar) to detect occlusion. Look for OMI-equivalents: posterior (posterior leads), de Winter T waves, hyperacute T waves, Wellens, aVR elevation.

nodes.title: ACS - Step 2: HEART Pathway (no STEMI)
nodes.summary: HEART <=3 + two negative troponins = safe discharge; positive troponin/ECG = ACS regardless.
nodes.body: For chest pain without STEMI, risk-stratify with a validated score, not gestalt (open HEART in the toolbar). The HEART Pathway pairs a HEART \u22643 with two negative troponins (0 and 3 h) for safe early discharge. - HEART 0-3: low risk (~1-2% 6-week MACE). - HEART 4-6: moderate (admit / observe / serial troponin). - HEART 7-10: high (early invasive / cardiology). A single elevated troponin or isc

nodes.title: STEMI / OMI - Activate + Treat
nodes.body: Open STEMI Management. Next 5 minutes: cath activation for STEMI or OMI-equivalent pattern; aspirin if not given; heparin and P2Y12 per local protocol; defib pads; treat ventricular dysrhythmia or cardiogenic shock in parallel. Do not miss: posterior MI (posterior leads), right-sided/RV MI (avoid nitrate-induced crash), de Winter, hyperacute T waves, new LBBB with a convincing ischemic story.
nodes.recommendation: Activate cath workflow when STEMI/OMI criteria are met or strongly suspected.

nodes.title: NSTE-ACS / High-Risk Ischemia - Treat
nodes.body: Open NSTEMI Management or Wellens Syndrome. Next 5 minutes: repeat ECG during pain, high-sensitivity troponin pathway, aspirin, anticoagulation if ACS remains likely and dissection is not suspected, pain control, cardiology for dynamic ECG or high-risk story. Consider TIMI (toolbar) to time the invasive strategy. Pitfall: Wellens with pain resolved is NOT reassuring. Do not stress test; it needs u
nodes.recommendation: Serial ECG/troponin + ACS therapy; early invasive for high-risk/dynamic features.

nodes.title: ACS - Observation / Serial Troponin
nodes.body: Intermediate risk or an incomplete troponin series is not a discharge. Complete the serial troponin pathway (institutional 0/1 h or 0/3 h high-sensitivity protocol), repeat the ECG, and reassess the story. - If the trend turns positive or the ECG evolves \u2192 NSTE-ACS pathway. - If it stays negative and HEART is low, the patient becomes a discharge candidate with follow-up / outpatient functiona
nodes.recommendation: Finish serial troponins before deciding; do not discharge on a single value.

nodes.title: ACS - Ruled Out by Pathway
nodes.body: ACS is low risk by a validated pathway (HEART \u22643 with two negative high-sensitivity troponins and a non-ischemic ECG). Document the pathway so the reasoning is independently reviewable. A negative ACS workup is not a diagnosis \u2014 return to the hub and rule in/out another cause if pain is unexplained.
nodes.recommendation: ACS excluded by HEART Pathway; document and pursue alternate cause.

nodes.title: Aortic Dissection - Risk Stratify
nodes.summary: ADD-RS 0-1 + D-dimer <500 rules out; ADD-RS >=2 or unstable goes straight to CTA.
nodes.body: Score before you scan. Open ADD-RS (Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score) in the toolbar: high-risk conditions, pain features, and exam findings across 3 categories. - ADD-RS 0-1 + D-dimer <500 ng/mL: dissection effectively ruled out (ADvISED pathway). - ADD-RS \u22652, or any instability / clear clinical suspicion: go straight to CTA \u2014 do not let D-dimer delay imaging.

nodes.title: Aortic Dissection - Confirm + Treat
nodes.body: Open Aortic Dissection. Next 5 minutes: bilateral arm BP, pulse/neuro check, CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis if stable enough, bedside echo if crashing, arterial line if available. Impulse control first: esmolol to target HR ~60 BEFORE a vasodilator, then SBP usually 100-120 if perfusing. Stop point: do NOT give heparin, thrombolytics, or routine ACS antithrombotics until dissection is excluded when the
nodes.recommendation: Anti-impulse (rate before pressure), CTA if stable, surgery for Type A / unstable.

nodes.title: Aortic Dissection - Ruled Out
nodes.body: Dissection is excluded by the validated ADvISED pathway (ADD-RS 0-1 + D-dimer <500). Document the score and D-dimer so the exclusion is reviewable. Return to the hub for the next differential if pain is unexplained.
nodes.recommendation: Dissection excluded by ADD-RS + D-dimer; document and pursue alternate cause.

nodes.title: PE - Step 1: Pretest Probability
nodes.summary: Score first (Wells). Unlikely -> PERC/D-dimer; likely -> CTPA.
nodes.body: Anchor the PE workup on pretest probability with a validated score, not gestalt alone (open Wells PE in the toolbar). The tier decides PERC vs D-dimer vs straight-to-CTPA. - Wells \u22644: PE unlikely \u2192 eligible for PERC or age-adjusted D-dimer. - Wells >4: PE likely \u2192 CTPA directly, do NOT D-dimer.

nodes.title: PE - Step 2 (LOW prob): PERC
nodes.summary: PERC-negative in low probability rules out PE with zero further testing.
nodes.body: Only in low pretest probability. Open PERC in the toolbar. All 8 criteria must be negative to rule out PE with no testing: age <50, HR <100, SpO2 \u226595%, no hemoptysis, no estrogen, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no recent surgery/trauma.

nodes.title: PE - Step 3: Age-Adjusted D-Dimer
nodes.summary: Age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 if >50). Below cutoff rules out; at/above -> CTPA.
nodes.body: For low probability not PERC-negative. Use an age-adjusted threshold in patients >50: cutoff = age \u00D7 10 ng/mL (FEU). Example: a 70-year-old uses 700, not 500 (ADJUST-PE). YEARS is an accepted alternative.

nodes.title: PE - Confirm / Image + Treat
nodes.body: Open PE Treatment. Next 5 minutes: oxygen, monitor, bedside echo for RV strain if unstable, anticoagulation if PE likely and bleeding risk acceptable, CTPA when stable, lower-extremity DVT ultrasound if CT delayed/contraindicated. Massive PE clues: hypotension, syncope, RV dilation/strain, obstructive shock \u2192 PERT, systemic thrombolysis, catheter therapy, or ECMO pathway. In high probability,
nodes.recommendation: Risk-stratify PE immediately; shock physiology changes the treatment lane.

nodes.title: PE - Ruled Out
nodes.body: PE is excluded by this validated pathway. Document the pathway (Wells tier + PERC or age-adjusted D-dimer) so the reasoning is independently reviewable. Return to the hub and rule in/out the next differential if chest pain is unexplained.
nodes.recommendation: PE excluded by validated pathway; document and pursue alternate cause.

nodes.title: Pneumothorax - Rule In
nodes.summary: Absent sliding + lung point rules in PTX; present sliding rules it out. Tension is clinical.
nodes.body: Lung POCUS beats supine CXR: absent lung sliding + absent B-lines + a lung point rules it in (lung point ~100% specific). Sudden pleuritic pain, unilateral hyperresonance, or a positive-pressure/procedure context raises suspicion.

nodes.title: Pneumothorax - Treat
nodes.body: Open Pneumothorax. - Tension physiology (hypotension, severe distress, tracheal shift): immediate needle/finger decompression, then tube \u2014 do not wait for imaging. - Stable: size and symptom-based management per BTS (observation, aspiration, or small-bore drain). Pitfall: a post-procedure or ventilated patient with sudden chest pain/hypotension is tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
nodes.recommendation: Tension is decompressed clinically before imaging; stable PTX is size-based.

nodes.title: Pericarditis / Myocarditis - Rule In + Screen for Danger
nodes.summary: Echo screens for tamponade and myocarditis; both change disposition from benign pericarditis.
nodes.body: Pericarditis is a clinical diagnosis (\u22652 of: pleuritic positional chest pain, friction rub, widespread STE / PR depression, new/worsening effusion). Bedside echo screens for the two things that change the lane: tamponade and LV dysfunction (myocarditis).

nodes.title: Pericarditis / Myocarditis - Treat
nodes.body: Open Pericarditis or Myocarditis. - Tamponade: resuscitate, cardiology, pericardiocentesis \u2014 do not delay for CT. - Myocarditis (troponin + LV dysfunction / arrhythmia / HF / syncope): admit, telemetry, cardiology. - Uncomplicated pericarditis: NSAID + colchicine, outpatient follow-up if no high-risk features (fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, trauma, anticoagulation, subacute course)
nodes.recommendation: Echo-driven: tamponade and myocarditis are admissions; uncomplicated pericarditis is outpatient.

nodes.title: Esophageal Rupture - Rule In
nodes.summary: Post-emesis severe pain + subcutaneous/mediastinal air rules in; do not await Mackler triad.
nodes.body: Suspect Boerhaave with severe chest/epigastric pain after forceful vomiting or retching, often with subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus), odynophagia, or sepsis. CXR may show pneumomediastinum, pleural effusion, or hydropneumothorax. Do not wait for the full Mackler triad.

nodes.title: Esophageal Rupture - Treat
nodes.body: Time-critical surgical disease. Next 5 minutes: NPO, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, antiemetics/analgesia, early thoracic or general surgery, CT chest with water-soluble contrast when stable. Do NOT: place a blind NG tube, discharge as reflux after severe post-emesis chest pain, or wait for the classic Mackler triad.
nodes.recommendation: NPO, antibiotics, water-soluble contrast CT, surgery early.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Repeat ECG/troponin pathway, CXR, POCUS when physiology demands, then reassess.
nodes.body: Default bundle while the diagnosis clarifies: - Repeat ECG if symptoms continue or change. - Serial high-sensitivity troponin pathway. - CXR for pneumothorax, pneumonia, widened mediastinum, edema. - POCUS if unstable, hypoxic, or suspected tamponade/RV strain/edema. - Aspirin if ACS possible and no contraindication. - Nitrates only if BP adequate and no RV infarct, PDE5 use, or severe AS. - Analg

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Deterioration returns to exclusions. Stable patients move to imaging or disposition by risk.
nodes.body: Reassessment should change the lane if the patient evolves.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: Imaging is diagnosis-directed: CTA aorta, CTPA, CXR/POCUS, echo, or coronary pathway.
nodes.body: Image the diagnosis you are willing to act on: - ACS: ECG + troponin first; coronary CTA or stress only for selected low/intermediate-risk patients after ACS exclusion per local protocol. - Dissection: CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis; echo if crashing or Type A/tamponade suspected. - PE: CTPA; DVT ultrasound if CT delayed/contraindicated; echo for unstable PE. - Pneumothorax: lung POCUS + CXR if stable;

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: High-risk admits; intermediate observes; low-risk discharge requires serial testing and follow-up.
nodes.body: Disposition follows risk and trajectory, not pain score alone.

nodes.title: Admit / ICU / Procedure Lane
nodes.body: Admit or transfer for STEMI/OMI, NSTEMI/high-risk ACS, dissection, massive/submassive PE needing intervention, myocarditis with HF/arrhythmia/syncope, tamponade, pneumothorax requiring drainage, esophageal rupture concern, persistent hypoxia, unstable vitals, or unsafe follow-up.
nodes.recommendation: Use the deep-dive consult and destination service early.

nodes.title: Observation Lane
nodes.body: Observation fits when the first pass is not diagnostic but risk is not low: persistent or recurrent pain, intermediate HEART, equivocal ECG/troponin, need for serial ECG/troponin, or pending targeted imaging.
nodes.recommendation: Serial ECG/troponin and diagnosis-directed imaging before discharge.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: serial ECG/troponin strategy is reassuring, symptoms controlled, vitals stable, no concerning alternate life-threat, patient understands return precautions, and follow-up is realistic. Return precautions: recurrent/worsening pain, dyspnea, syncope, weakness/numbness, fever, hemoptysis, persistent vomiting, or new severe back/tearing pain.
nodes.recommendation: Document the low-risk pathway used and specific return precautions.

nodes.title: Pneumothorax Management & Chest Tube
nodes.summary: Evidence shifting practice — conservative management safe for many previously automatic indications
nodes.body: This consult covers pneumothorax management and chest tube thoracostomy \u2014 from indications through insertion technique and post-procedure care. Chest tubes were once a bedrock procedure for EM, resuscitation, and critical care. They are becoming increasingly unnecessary as evidence supports conservative management in many scenarios previously considered automatic indications. KEY EVIDENCE SHI

nodes.title: Primary Indication
nodes.summary: Classify indication: pneumothorax, hemothorax, or empyema — determines management pathway
nodes.body: What is the primary indication?

nodes.title: Pneumothorax \u2014 Classification
nodes.summary: Classify PTX type — tension is clinical diagnosis, do NOT delay for imaging
nodes.body: Classify the pneumothorax. This determines the management pathway.

nodes.title: Tension Pneumothorax \u2014 Emergent Decompression
nodes.summary: Needle decompression 4th-5th ICS anterior axillary line — finger thoracostomy more reliable
nodes.body: Clinical diagnosis \u2014 do NOT delay for imaging. Signs: hypotension, tachycardia, JVD, tracheal deviation (late sign), absent breath sounds, decreased SpO2, obstructive shock. NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION (temporizing) \u2022 14-16 gauge angiocatheter \u2022 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (traditional) OR 4th-5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line (preferred \u2014 thinner chest wall,

nodes.title: Traumatic Pneumothorax \u2014 Assessment
nodes.summary: Small traumatic PTX <35mm on CT: observation safe in stable patients not on PPV
nodes.body: Evidence supports observation for small traumatic pneumothoraces in stable patients. Can observe <35 mm on CT scan in patients not requiring positive pressure ventilation [3]. For occult pneumothorax (visible on CT but not CXR) in mechanically ventilated patients, the OPTICC trial demonstrated that selective observation is safe, though close monitoring is required [4].

nodes.title: Traumatic PTX \u2014 Observation
nodes.summary: Admit for observation — repeat imaging at 6h and before discharge, convert if progresses
nodes.body: Small traumatic pneumothorax (<35 mm on CT) in a stable, non-ventilated patient. Observation is appropriate per current evidence.
nodes.recommendation: Admit for observation. Repeat imaging at 6 hours and prior to discharge. Supplemental O2 may accelerate reabsorption. Convert to chest tube if: progression on imaging, worsening symptoms, or new requirement for positive pressure ventilation

nodes.title: Pneumothorax on Mechanical Ventilation
nodes.summary: OPTICC trial: selective observation of occult PTX on ventilator is safe with close monitoring
nodes.body: Positive pressure ventilation increases risk of tension physiology. The OPTICC trial supports selective observation of small occult pneumothoraces even on ventilator, but close monitoring is essential. Consider: size of pneumothorax, ventilator settings (high PEEP increases risk), clinical trajectory, ability to monitor closely.

nodes.title: Occult PTX on Ventilator \u2014 Observation
nodes.summary: Close ICU monitoring — low threshold for chest tube if any progression, avoid PEEP increases
nodes.body: Selective observation of occult pneumothorax on ventilator, supported by OPTICC trial evidence.
nodes.recommendation: Close ICU monitoring. Serial imaging. Low threshold for chest tube if any progression. Communicate with respiratory therapy. Avoid increases in PEEP if possible. Immediate intervention if signs of tension.

nodes.title: Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax
nodes.summary: Brown NEJM 2020: conservative management non-inferior — 98.5% resolution at 8 weeks
nodes.body: Conservative management is increasingly favored for PSP.
