KEY EVIDENCE \u2022 Brown et al (NEJM 2020): Conservative management non-inferior to interventional treatment for moderate-sized first-episode PSP. At 8 weeks, 98.5% resolution without intervention [1]. \u2022 BTS/ERS guidelines support aspiration as first-line for symptomatic PSP before chest tube [20]. \u2022 Ambulatory management with Hei

nodes.title: PSP \u2014 Conservative Management
nodes.summary: PSP \u2014 Conservative Management — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Small primary spontaneous pneumothorax with minimal symptoms. Conservative approach supported by Brown et al (NEJM 2020).
nodes.recommendation: Observe 3-6 hours with repeat CXR. Supplemental O2 accelerates reabsorption (rate increases from ~1.25%/day to ~4%/day with high-flow O2). If stable or improving: discharge with outpatient follow-up in 2-4 weeks. No air travel or diving unt

nodes.title: Needle Aspiration
nodes.summary: Needle Aspiration — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: NEEDLE ASPIRATION \u2014 first-line for symptomatic PSP per BTS/ERS guidelines. PROCEDURE 1. Position: sitting upright or supine with head elevated 45\u00b0 2. Site: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (preferred) or safe triangle 3. Prep, drape, local anesthesia with 1% lidocaine 4. Insert 16-18 gauge IV catheter over superior rib edge 5. Connect to 3-way stopcock + 60 mL syringe 6. Aspirat

nodes.title: Aspiration Response
nodes.summary: Aspiration Response — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Did needle aspiration result in lung re-expansion on post-aspiration CXR?

nodes.title: Aspiration Successful
nodes.summary: Aspiration Successful — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Needle aspiration successful with lung re-expansion on CXR.
nodes.recommendation: Observe 4-6 hours post-aspiration. Repeat CXR before discharge. If stable: discharge with 2-4 week follow-up. No air travel or diving until confirmed resolution. Smoking cessation (strongest modifiable risk factor). Recurrence: ~30% at 1 ye

nodes.title: Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax
nodes.summary: Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: SSP in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, CF, ILD, malignancy, TB). Managed more aggressively than PSP due to limited pulmonary reserve. BTS: chest tube recommended for all SSP >1 cm or symptomatic. Even small SSP can be clinically significant with underlying disease.

nodes.title: SSP \u2014 Observation with Caution
nodes.summary: SSP \u2014 Observation with Caution — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Very small (<1 cm) SSP with minimal symptoms. Observation may be appropriate but requires close inpatient monitoring due to limited pulmonary reserve.
nodes.recommendation: Admit for observation with supplemental O2. Serial CXR at 6 and 24 hours. Low threshold for chest tube if any worsening. Pulmonology consult for underlying disease management. Consider pleurodesis discussion for recurrence prevention.

nodes.title: Hemothorax
nodes.summary: Hemothorax — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Chest tube indicated for hemothorax. The PCAT trial demonstrated pigtail catheters may be comparable to large-bore tubes in select cases, but large-bore (28-36 Fr) remains standard for traumatic hemothorax to ensure adequate drainage of blood and clot. Tube size: 28 Fr minimum for hemothorax. 28-36 Fr recommended.

nodes.title: Empyema / Pleural Infection
nodes.summary: Empyema / Pleural Infection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Chest tube indicated for empyema/parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage. Small-bore tubes (10-14 Fr) have similar clinical outcomes to large-bore for pleural infection drainage (Rahman et al). BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2010 supports image-guided small-bore catheter as first-line. If loculated: consider intrapleural fibrinolytics (tPA + DNase) or VATS.

nodes.title: Insertion Site \u2014 Triangle of Safety
nodes.summary: Insertion Site \u2014 Triangle of Safety — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: THE TRIANGLE OF SAFETY The safe zone for chest tube insertion is bounded by: \u2022 Anterior: lateral edge of pectoralis major \u2022 Posterior: anterior border of latissimus dorsi \u2022 Inferior: line of the 5th intercostal space (nipple level in males) \u2022 Superior: base of the axilla INSERTION SITE 4th or 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line (within the safe triangle). MID-ARM POINT (MA

nodes.title: Tube Size Selection
nodes.summary: Tube Size Selection — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Select tube size based on indication. PNEUMOTHORAX (air only): \u2022 Small-bore pigtail catheter: 10-14 Fr (Seldinger technique) \u2022 Standard: 20-24 Fr HEMOTHORAX / HEMOPNEUMOTHORAX: \u2022 Large-bore: 28-36 Fr (28 Fr minimum for blood drainage) EMPYEMA: \u2022 Small-bore (10-14 Fr) with image guidance \u2014 similar outcomes to large-bore [7] Small-bore pigtail catheters have equivalent outco

nodes.title: Pigtail Catheter \u2014 Seldinger Technique
nodes.summary: Pigtail Catheter \u2014 Seldinger Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Small-bore pigtail catheters (10-14 Fr) placed via modified Seldinger technique (e.g., Thal-Quik). ADVANTAGES \u2022 Less pain on insertion and while indwelling \u2022 Equivalent efficacy for simple pneumothorax \u2022 Faster insertion \u2022 Lower complication rate PROCEDURE 1. Position, prep, drape (same landmarks as standard) 2. Local anesthesia to skin, subcutaneous tissue, periosteum, parieta

nodes.title: Equipment
nodes.summary: Equipment — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: EQUIPMENT FOR TUBE THORACOSTOMY Set up on a large surface \u2014 not a mayo stand. STERILE SUPPLIES \u2022 Chest tube (selected size) \u2022 Scalpel (#10 blade) \u2022 Large curved Kelly clamp \u2022 Needle driver and pickups with teeth \u2022 Size 2 Ethibond suture or 0-silk \u2022 Sterile chlorhexidine prep and drapes \u2022 Sterile gloves + gown ANESTHESIA \u2022 30 mL bottle of 2% lidocaine wi

nodes.title: Patient Positioning
nodes.summary: Patient Positioning — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: POSITIONING \u2022 Bring patient to the edge of the bed (ipsilateral side) \u2022 Incision site near the level of the xiphoid process \u2022 Ipsilateral arm up: restrain or have patient place hand behind head (exposes axilla and triangle of safety) \u2022 Sit up to 45\u00b0 if possible (supine acceptable for unstable patients) PREP AND DRAPE \u2022 Wide prep with chlorhexidine \u2022 Drape to main

nodes.title: Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Anesthesia — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: LOCAL ANESTHESIA \u2014 FIELD BLOCK Inadequate anesthesia is the most common reason for procedural difficulty. TECHNIQUE 1. Skin wheal: 22-gauge needle, raise a wheal at the incision site with 2% lidocaine with epinephrine 2. Subcutaneous tissue: infiltrate generously along the planned dissection tract 3. Intercostal muscles: fan lidocaine through the muscle layers 4. Periosteum: anesthetize the r

nodes.title: PPE & Mental Preparation
nodes.summary: PPE & Mental Preparation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: PPE \u2022 Double glove \u2022 Face and eye protection \u2022 Hat and gown if available (always for non-emergent cases) MENTAL PREPARATION \u2022 Pause. Breathe. \u2022 Visualize each step before beginning. If you cannot visualize it, review the steps before proceeding. \u2022 This is a controlled procedure \u2014 deliberate technique prevents complications.

nodes.title: The Incision
nodes.summary: The Incision — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: SCALPEL TECHNIQUE \u2022 Hold scalpel like a pencil for control \u2022 Make a 3-4 cm transverse incision through the skin KEY POINTS \u2022 Make the skin incision ONE intercostal space BELOW the intended pleural entry point. This creates a subcutaneous tunnel that reduces air leak after tube removal. \u2022 In female patients, account for breast tissue \u2014 it may shift the apparent intercostal

nodes.title: Blunt Dissection
nodes.summary: Blunt Dissection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: TECHNIQUE: PUSH IN, SPREAD, CHECK Using the curved Kelly clamp: 1. Dissect through subcutaneous tissue toward the superior edge of the rib ONE space above the skin incision 2. Advance the CLOSED clamp through the intercostal muscles directly over the top of the rib 3. Stay ABOVE the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (though it runs variably) 4. Push through the parietal pleura with controlled

nodes.title: Finger Sweep & Safety Check
nodes.summary: Finger Sweep & Safety Check — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: FINGER SWEEP Insert a gloved finger through the tract into the pleural space. Sweep gently to confirm: 1. You are in the pleural space (not subcutaneous, not subdiaphragmatic) 2. No adhesions that would impede tube passage 3. No organs palpable (lung, diaphragm, liver/spleen) RIB FRACTURES = DANGER In trauma patients with rib fractures at the insertion site, fractured rib edges can lacerate the fi

nodes.title: Tube Insertion
nodes.summary: Tube Insertion — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: DO NOT USE TROCARS \u2014 EVER. Trocar insertion has an unacceptable rate of visceral injury. All chest tubes should be placed by blunt dissection. TUBE PREPARATION 1. Place two clamps on the tube 2. Cut the distal end at a slant (if not pre-cut) INSERTION \u2022 Clamp the tube tip with Kelly clamp OR guide with finger (with or without finger guidance \u2014 both are acceptable) \u2022 Direct the

nodes.title: Confirm Placement & Check for Kinking
nodes.summary: Confirm Placement & Check for Kinking — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: CHECK PLEURAL ENTRY \u2022 Re-insert finger alongside tube to confirm the tube is in the pleural space MAC SPIN TEST FOR KINKING Grasp the external portion of the tube and rotate clockwise 180\u00b0, then release [19]: \u2022 If the tube spins back to its previous position \u2192 the tube is kinked (reposition) \u2022 If it stays in the new position \u2192 the tube is NOT kinked (proceed) INITIAL

nodes.title: Securing & Connecting Drainage
nodes.summary: Securing & Connecting Drainage — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: SUTURE \u2022 Use a large horizontal mattress suture (size 2 Ethibond or 0-silk) through the skin adjacent to the tube \u2022 Tie securely, leaving long tails \u2022 Wrap the tails around the tube and tie again (Roman sandal / mesentery technique) \u2022 Place a separate drain stitch (stay suture) for wound closure after tube removal DRESSING \u2022 Petroleum gauze around the tube at the skin entr

nodes.title: Post-Insertion Chest Radiograph
nodes.summary: Post-Insertion Chest Radiograph — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Obtain a STAT portable CXR after chest tube placement to confirm: \u2022 Tube position (all holes intrathoracic, tip directed appropriately) \u2022 Lung re-expansion \u2022 No malposition, kinking, or new complication Tube resting location (anteroapical vs posterolateral) does NOT matter \u2014 function, not trajectory, dictates need for reintervention [11, 13]. AIS (injury severity) is the only s

nodes.title: Tube Malposition
nodes.summary: Tube Malposition — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Chest tube malposition on CXR. Common issues: \u2022 Tube advanced too far (tip in mediastinum or kinked) \u2022 Sentinel hole outside chest wall (subcutaneous air leak) \u2022 Tube in the fissure (may still function) \u2022 Too shallow insertion IMPORTANT: Never advance a tube that has already been placed \u2014 risk of introducing infection. A tube that is too deep can be pulled back under steri
nodes.recommendation: Options: (1) Pull back under sterile technique if too deep, (2) Place a second tube, (3) Consult thoracic surgery. Repeat CXR after any adjustment.

nodes.title: Massive Hemothorax \u2014 Surgical Indication
nodes.summary: Massive Hemothorax \u2014 Surgical Indication — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: MASSIVE HEMOTHORAX Criteria for emergent thoracotomy: \u2022 Initial drainage >1500 mL, OR \u2022 >200 mL/hr for 2-4 consecutive hours AUTOTRANSFUSION Blood from the chest cavity lacks clotting factors and has a slightly lower hematocrit than venous blood, but autotransfusion of hemothorax blood is safe and effective in trauma [14].
nodes.recommendation: Activate massive transfusion protocol. Emergent thoracic surgery consultation. Continue chest tube drainage. Autotransfuse via autotransfusion system if available. This is a surgical emergency.

nodes.title: Drainage System Management
nodes.summary: Drainage System Management — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: CHEST TUBE DRAINAGE SYSTEMS \u2014 3-BOTTLE CONCEPT All modern drainage units (Pleur-Evac, Atrium) are based on the classic 3-bottle system: 1. Collection chamber: measures fluid output 2. Water seal chamber: one-way valve \u2014 allows air out, prevents re-entry. Fluid level at 2 cm. 3. Suction regulation chamber: controls negative pressure (typically -20 cmH2O when used) RECOMMENDED SYSTEM Getin

nodes.title: Suction vs Water Seal
nodes.summary: Suction vs Water Seal — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: SUCTION IS NOT ROUTINELY NECESSARY \u2022 You do not need suction for initial management, CT transport, or patient transfer \u2022 Suction should be reserved for: failure of lung re-expansion on water seal, persistent large air leak, or specific clinical situations \u2022 When used: low-pressure suction, typically -20 cmH2O BY INDICATION \u2022 Primary spontaneous PTX: water seal or Heimlich valve

nodes.title: Air Leak Assessment & Troubleshooting
nodes.summary: Air Leak Assessment & Troubleshooting — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: AIR LEAK QUANTIFICATION The water seal chamber has graded markings to quantify the size of an air leak. CHECK FOR TIDALING Turn off suction and observe if the water column (or ball indicator) moves up and down with respiration. Tidaling = patent tube with communication to the pleural space. Absent tidaling = tube may be blocked, kinked, or lung fully expanded. TESTING FOR AIR LEAK 1. Clamp the suc

nodes.title: Antibiotics & Ongoing Care
nodes.summary: Antibiotics & Ongoing Care — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS Probably beneficial for trauma thoracostomies. The EAST 2022 practice management guideline conditionally recommends antibiotic prophylaxis for tube thoracostomy placed for trauma [17]. Not routinely indicated for non-traumatic chest tubes. ONGOING MANAGEMENT \u2022 Record output (volume, color, character) each nursing shift \u2022 Monitor for signs of infection at insertio

nodes.title: Removal Criteria
nodes.summary: Removal Criteria — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: CRITERIA FOR CHEST TUBE REMOVAL \u2014 all must be met: 1. Lung fully re-expanded on CXR 2. No air leak (no bubbling in water seal) 3. Fluid output <100 mL/day 4. Patient clinically stable WATER SEAL TRIAL \u2022 Place tube to water seal (disconnect suction) for a trial period \u2022 A normal CXR obtained 3 hours after placing on water seal effectively excludes development of a clinically signific

nodes.title: Removal Technique
nodes.summary: Removal Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: REMOVAL PROCEDURE 1. Pre-medicate with analgesia 2. Remove dressing and cut securing suture (leave stay suture intact) 3. Have petroleum gauze ready at bedside 4. Instruct patient: take a deep breath and bear down (Valsalva) \u2014 creates positive intrathoracic pressure, preventing air entry 5. Pull tube out in one smooth, swift motion 6. IMMEDIATELY apply petroleum gauze + occlusive dressing 7.

nodes.title: Disposition & Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Disposition & Follow-Up — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: AFTER SUCCESSFUL TUBE REMOVAL \u2022 Confirm lung remains expanded on post-removal CXR \u2022 If recurrent pneumothorax on post-removal film: small and asymptomatic may observe; large or symptomatic requires new tube DISCHARGE PLANNING \u2022 Wound care: keep dressing clean and dry, remove in 48 hours \u2022 Activity: avoid heavy lifting or straining for 1-2 weeks \u2022 No air travel until confir
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with follow-up CXR in 2-4 weeks. Smoking cessation and activity restrictions. Pulmonology referral if recurrent or SSP. Review Discharge Instructions with patient.

nodes.title: CHF Exacerbation: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Key question: SCAPE (flash pulmonary edema) vs FOPE (volume overload) — treatment differs completely
nodes.body: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure (ADHF) — rapid onset of signs/symptoms requiring urgent treatment. Key Question: Is this SCAPE (Sympathetic Crashing Acute Pulmonary Edema) or FOPE (Fluid Overload Pulmonary Edema)? | Feature | SCAPE | FOPE | |---------|-------|------| | Onset | Minutes to hours | Days to weeks | | SBP | Often >180 | Variable | | Volume status | Euvolemic or dry | True volume over

nodes.title: Is This SCAPE?
nodes.summary: SCAPE: acute onset, SBP >160, diaphoretic, minimal edema — NOT volume overload
nodes.body: SCAPE = Sympathetic Crashing Acute Pulmonary Edema NOT volume overload — it's a vicious sympathetic spiral: - Sympathetic surge → vasoconstriction → massive afterload - High afterload → LV can't eject → acute backward failure - Pulmonary edema → hypoxia → MORE sympathetic surge SCAPE Criteria (any 2+): - Acute onset (minutes to hours) - SBP >160 mmHg - Diaphoretic, restless, severe dyspnea - Minim

nodes.title: SCAPE: Immediate Treatment
nodes.summary: Simultaneous BiPAP + high-dose NTG — patient should be out of the water by 10 minutes
nodes.body: SCAPE is NOT volume overload. The problem is fluid redistribution into lungs from massive afterload. Treatment = break the sympathetic spiral. Simultaneous actions (do ALL at once): 1. BiPAP/CPAP — Immediate - Start CPAP 8-10 cm H₂O OR BiPAP 12/6 - Titrate UP aggressively: goal CPAP 15-20 or BiPAP 20-24/10-12 - Higher pressures = greater hemodynamic benefit - Reduces preload AND afterload 2. High-

nodes.title: SCAPE: What to AVOID
nodes.summary: No beta-blockers, no morphine (MIMO trial: increased arrest), no routine diuretics in SCAPE
nodes.body: Critical: These can HARM your SCAPE patient: | Agent | Why Harmful | |-------|-------------| | Beta-blockers | Impair pump function — absolutely contraindicated | | Morphine | MIMO RCT: significantly more cardiovascular serious adverse events (cardiac arrest, cardiogenic shock) vs midazolam | | Routine diuretics | Only if TRUE volume overload. Many SCAPE patients are intravascularly depleted | Whe

nodes.title: SCAPE Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess at 10-15 min — flash is fast both ways, rapid improvement expected with correct treatment
nodes.body: Assess at 10-15 minutes: Good response: - SBP dropping toward 140 - Respiratory effort improving - Less diaphoretic - SpO₂ improving on BiPAP - Patient less agitated Poor response: - SBP still >180 - No improvement in work of breathing - Worsening hypoxia despite BiPAP - Altered mental status Flash = fast both ways — rapid deterioration but also rapid improvement with correct treatment. What is th

nodes.title: SCAPE: Continue Treatment
nodes.summary: Patient responding — maintain NTG, wean BiPAP as tolerated, watch for BP crash when SCAPE breaks
nodes.body: Patient responding — continue current therapy: - Maintain NTG infusion at effective rate - Keep BiPAP at current settings - Monitor BP closely — when SCAPE breaks, BP can crash - Reduce NTG rate sharply as BP normalizes Transition plan: - Wean BiPAP as tolerated → high-flow NC → regular NC - Transition NTG drip to oral/patch as stabilizes - NOW can consider gentle diuresis if volume overloaded - A

nodes.title: SCAPE: Escalate Therapy
nodes.summary: Push NTG to 400-800 mcg/min, add second vasodilator — clevidipine or nicardipine
nodes.body: Partial response — escalate: 1. Increase NTG further: - Push to 400-800 mcg/min if BP allows - No ceiling dose in SCAPE 2. BiPAP settings: - Increase to BiPAP 24/20 if tolerated - Patient compliance key — may need sedation 3. Add second vasodilator: - Clevidipine — calcium channel blocker, very titratable - Nicardipine — alternative IV CCB - Enalaprilat — if normal renal function 4. Consider nitro

nodes.title: SCAPE: Refractory — Prepare for Intubation
nodes.summary: Refractory SCAPE: ketamine for RSI (not propofol), have vasopressor ready — now cardiogenic shock
nodes.body: Refractory SCAPE — patient failing BiPAP + high-dose NTG: Before intubation: - Push NTG to maximum (800+ mcg/min) - Ensure BiPAP settings maximized - Rule out pneumothorax, PE, tamponade If must intubate: - Ketamine preferred induction (less hypotension) - Avoid propofol (profound hypotension) - Have vasopressor ready (norepinephrine) - Post-intubation: continue aggressive vasodilation Consider: -

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Profile — Warm/Cold + Wet/Dry
nodes.summary: Warm/cold + wet/dry assessment — warm-wet is most common, cold-wet is cardiogenic shock
nodes.body: Assess perfusion (warm vs cold) and congestion (wet vs dry): | Profile | Perfusion | Congestion | Treatment | |---------|-----------|------------|------------| | Warm & Wet | Good | Yes | Diuretics first | | Cold & Wet | Poor | Yes | Inotropes + careful diuretics | | Cold & Dry | Poor | No | Fluids + inotropes | | Warm & Dry | Good | No | Not acute CHF | Signs of poor perfusion (COLD): - Cool extr

nodes.title: Warm & Dry — No Acute Decompensation
nodes.summary: Not acute CHF — outpatient optimization, address actual presenting complaint
nodes.body: Patient is euvolemic with adequate perfusion — this is NOT acute CHF exacerbation. Possible scenarios: - Chronic stable CHF presenting for other reason - Symptoms resolved prior to ED arrival - Alternative diagnosis (COPD, anxiety, anemia) Management: - Outpatient optimization of CHF medications - Cardiology follow-up if not recent - Address actual presenting complaint - Daily weight monitoring ed
nodes.recommendation: Outpatient management. Ensure CHF medications optimized. Cardiology follow-up.

nodes.title: Cold & Dry — Pure Cardiogenic Shock
nodes.summary: Rare pure cardiogenic shock — DO NOT give diuretics, cautious fluids then inotropes
nodes.body: Rare presentation: Poor perfusion WITHOUT congestion. Suggests: - Acute MI with cardiogenic shock - Fulminant myocarditis - Acute valve pathology - End-stage cardiomyopathy Management: - DO NOT give diuretics — patient is hypovolemic - Cautious IV fluids (250-500 mL boluses) - Inotropic support (dobutamine, milrinone) - Vasopressor if SBP <80 (norepinephrine) - Emergent cardiology + ICU - ECMO eva

nodes.title: Diuretic Strategy — Warm & Wet
nodes.summary: Furosemide 1-2.5x home dose IV — target urine output >100-150 mL/hr by 6 hours
nodes.body: Goal: Reduce intravascular volume, relieve congestion. IV Loop Diuretic (Furosemide): - Dose: 1-2.5x home oral dose IV - If no home diuretic: start 40-80 mg IV - If home dose >80 mg: give 1-2x as IV Monitoring targets: - Urine output: >100-150 mL/hr by 6 hours - Urine spot sodium: >50-70 mEq/L at 2 hours - Daily weight loss: 0.5-1 kg/day Bolus vs Infusion: - DOSE trial: no significant difference -

nodes.title: Diuretic Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Good response: UOP >150 mL/hr; diuretic resistance: UOP <50 mL/hr despite adequate dosing
nodes.body: Assess at 4-6 hours: Good response: - Urine output >150 mL/hr - Symptoms improving - Creatinine stable Partial response: - Urine output 50-150 mL/hr - Slow symptom improvement Poor response (Diuretic Resistance): - Urine output <50 mL/hr - Symptoms not improving - Rising creatinine What is the response?

nodes.title: Continue Diuretic Therapy
nodes.summary: Continue until euvolemic — transition to PO, discharge dose often higher than pre-admission
nodes.body: Patient responding — continue current regimen: - Continue IV loop diuretic until euvolemic - Monitor daily weights (goal -0.5 to -1 kg/day) - Check electrolytes q12-24h (K+, Mg++) - Track creatinine (transient rise acceptable) Transition to oral: - Once euvolemic, switch to PO - Discharge dose = dose that achieved euvolemia - Often higher than pre-admission dose Add guideline-directed medical ther

nodes.title: Escalate Diuretic Therapy
nodes.summary: Double dose or add metolazone 30 min before loop diuretic — sequential nephron blockade
nodes.body: Partial response — escalate: Option 1: Increase dose - Double the IV furosemide dose - Repeat q2-4h until response Option 2: Switch to infusion - Furosemide 5-10 mg/hr continuous - Better control, less peaks/troughs Option 3: Add thiazide (sequential nephron blockade) - Metolazone 2.5-5 mg PO - Give 30 min BEFORE loop diuretic - Synergistic effect on different nephron segments - Watch closely for

nodes.title: Diuretic Resistance
nodes.summary: May need furosemide 160-200mg IV, metolazone, albumin, or ultrafiltration — nephrology consult
nodes.body: Definition: Inadequate diuresis despite adequate loop diuretic dosing. Causes: - Cardiorenal syndrome (poor renal perfusion) - Hypoalbuminemia (drug binding) - NSAID use - Excessive sodium intake - True renal failure Management stepwise: 1. Verify dose adequate — may need very high doses (160-200 mg furosemide) 2. Add thiazide — metolazone 2.5-10 mg PO before loop diuretic 3. Optimize perfusion: -

nodes.title: Cardiogenic Shock Management
nodes.summary: Cold-wet: dobutamine for SBP 80-100, NE first for SBP <80 — milrinone for HFpEF or BB toxicity
nodes.body: Cold & Wet = cardiogenic shock + congestion Immediate actions: - IV access, cardiac monitor, labs (lactate, troponin, BNP) - Arterial line if available - Gentle or no diuretics (worsen hypotension) - Low-dose vasodilator only if SBP >90 Inotrope selection: | Agent | SBP | Mechanism | |-------|-----|------------| | Dobutamine | 80-100 | Beta-1 inotrope, mild vasodilation | | Milrinone | 80-100 | PD

nodes.title: Dobutamine for Cardiogenic Shock
nodes.summary: Dobutamine 2.5-20 mcg/kg/min — improves contractility, mild vasodilation, watch tachycardia
nodes.body: Dobutamine Dosing: 2.5-20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion Mechanism: - Beta-1: increased contractility, increased HR - Beta-2: mild vasodilation (reduces afterload) - Result: improved cardiac output Monitoring: - Target SBP >90 - Watch HR (tachycardia common) - Lactate trend (should improve) - Urine output (should increase) - ECG for arrhythmias Advantages: Improves contractility + reduces afterload Disadv

nodes.title: Milrinone for Cardiogenic Shock
nodes.summary: Milrinone 0.25-0.75 mcg/kg/min — NO loading dose in shock, long half-life 2-3h persists after stopping
nodes.body: Milrinone Dosing: 0.25-0.75 mcg/kg/min IV (no loading dose in shock) Mechanism: - PDE-3 inhibitor → increases cAMP - Positive inotropy + lusitropy (improved relaxation) - Systemic + pulmonary vasodilation Best for: - Diastolic dysfunction / HFpEF - Beta-blocker toxicity (works independent of beta receptors) - Pulmonary hypertension - Right heart failure Monitoring: - Hypotension common (vasodilati

nodes.title: Profound Shock — Vasopressor First
nodes.summary: SBP <80: NE first-line vasopressor, then add inotrope — consider ECMO if refractory to 2+ agents
nodes.body: SBP <80 — need BP support before inotrope can work Norepinephrine - Start 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min - Strong alpha (vasoconstriction) + beta-1 (mild inotropy) - First-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock Dopamine - 5-20 mcg/kg/min for combined inotrope + pressor - Higher doses = more alpha effect - More arrhythmias than norepinephrine Once SBP >80: - Add dobutamine or milrinone for inotropic support - G

nodes.title: Shock Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Improving: SBP >90, lactate declining, UOP increasing; not improving: escalate to mechanical support
nodes.body: Assess at 30-60 minutes: Improving: - SBP >90 - Urine output increasing - Lactate declining - Mental status improving - Extremities warming Not improving: - SBP still <90 despite inotrope - Lactate rising - Worsening end-organ function What is the response?

nodes.title: Mechanical Circulatory Support
nodes.summary: Refractory shock: VA-ECMO, IABP, Impella — activate cardiology and CT surgery early
nodes.body: Refractory cardiogenic shock — consider mechanical support: Options: - VA-ECMO: Full cardiac + pulmonary support. Rapid deployment. - IABP: Reduces afterload, improves coronary perfusion. Temporizing. - Impella: Percutaneous LVAD. Unloads LV. - Ultrafiltration: If volume overload refractory to diuretics. Indications: - Refractory to 2+ inotropes/vasopressors - Lactate rising >4 mmol/L - Multi-orga

nodes.title: Renal Function Assessment
nodes.summary: Transient Cr rise acceptable during diuresis — hold ACE-I/ARB during acute episode
nodes.body: Cardiorenal syndrome is common in ADHF. Check: - Baseline creatinine vs current - BUN/Cr ratio (>20 = prerenal) - Urine output trend - Potassium (diuretics cause hypokalemia, ACE-I cause hyperkalemia) AKI Staging: - Stage 1: Cr 1.5-1.9x baseline - Stage 2: Cr 2-2.9x baseline - Stage 3: Cr ≥3x baseline OR >4.0 Transient Cr rise is acceptable if diuresis effective and patient improving. Is there sig

nodes.title: Mild AKI — Cardiorenal Syndrome
nodes.summary: Continue diuretics if volume overloaded — permissive worsening renal function is acceptable
nodes.body: Cardiorenal syndrome: AKI from poor renal perfusion in CHF. Management: - Continue diuretics if patient still volume overloaded - Transient Cr rise is acceptable ("permissive worsening renal function") - Hold ACE-I/ARB during acute episode (restart once stable) - Avoid NSAIDs, contrast if possible - Optimize perfusion: maintain SBP >90, consider low-dose inotrope - Monitor K+ closely — supplement

nodes.title: Severe AKI — Consider RRT
nodes.summary: Stage 2-3 AKI: consider RRT if K+ >6.5, pH <7.15, or refractory volume overload
nodes.body: Stage 2-3 AKI with ADHF — high risk: Optimize first: - Hold diuretics temporarily if anuric - Optimize hemodynamics (inotropes if needed) - Stop all nephrotoxins - Check for obstruction (Foley, bladder scan) RRT Indications: - K+ >6.5 unresponsive to medical therapy - Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.15) - Volume overload refractory to diuretics - Uremic symptoms (encephalopathy, pericarditis) RRT

nodes.title: CHF Exacerbation — Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for shock/NTG drip; telemetry for diuresis; always address precipitant and optimize GDMT
nodes.body: ICU Admission: - Cardiogenic shock (inotropes/vasopressors) - SCAPE requiring NTG drip - Respiratory failure (BiPAP or intubation) - Severe AKI (Stage 3, RRT consideration) - ACS as precipitant Telemetry/Stepdown: - Warm & wet with good diuretic response - Stable hemodynamics - Mild AKI improving - No inotrope requirement Observation (if available): - Mild exacerbation, rapid response to IV diuret
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on hemodynamic stability, diuretic response, and risk stratification. ICU for shock or NTG drip. Address precipitant. GDMT optimization. Cardiology follow-up within 7 days.

nodes.title: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome
nodes.summary: CHS: cyclic vomiting in chronic cannabis users — ondansetron usually FAILS, use butyrophenones
nodes.body: CHS Steps Summary CHS is a clinical syndrome in chronic cannabis users characterized by cyclic nausea/vomiting and compulsive hot water bathing (~90% of patients). Traditional antiemetics (ondansetron) usually FAIL. GRACE-4 guidelines recommend butyrophenones as first-line therapy. Definitive treatment is cannabis cessation. *Basis:* Syndrome description derives from the original Allen 2004 case s

nodes.title: Clinical Phase
nodes.summary: Identify phase: prodromal (morning nausea), hyperemetic (profuse vomiting), or recovery (abstinent)
nodes.body: Which phase is the patient presenting in? Prodromal: Morning nausea, food aversion, vague abdominal discomfort Hyperemetic: Intense nausea/vomiting, compulsive hot bathing, significant dehydration Recovery: Resolving symptoms with cannabis abstinence *Basis:* The three-phase construct (prodromal / hyperemetic / recovery) is a descriptive framework from narrative and systematic reviews of case seri

nodes.title: Hyperemetic Phase
nodes.summary: Screen for complications: AKI, electrolyte abnormalities, Mallory-Weiss tear, Boerhaave
nodes.body: Profuse vomiting (often >7 episodes/day), diffuse abdominal pain, compulsive hot water bathing for relief, significant volume depletion. Complications to screen for: \u2022 AKI from dehydration \u2022 Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia) \u2022 Mallory-Weiss tear (hematemesis) \u2022 Boerhaave syndrome (rare but life-threatening \u2014 chest pain, subcutaneous emph

nodes.title: Diagnostic Criteria
nodes.summary: Clinical diagnosis of exclusion — daily cannabis >1 year, cyclic vomiting, hot water bathing relief
nodes.body: CHS is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. No standardized ED diagnostic criteria exist. Simonetto Criteria (2012): 1. Long-term cannabis use (usually daily, >1 year) 2. Cyclic nausea and vomiting 3. Symptom resolution with cannabis cessation 4. No alternative diagnosis Supportive features: \u2022 Compulsive hot water bathing (~90%) \u2022 Age <50 at onset \u2022 Morning predominance of nausea \u20

nodes.title: Red Flags Present?
nodes.summary: Screen for red flags: hematemesis, localized pain, peritoneal signs, fever, jaundice, age >50
nodes.body: Screen for features suggesting an alternative diagnosis: \u2022 Hematemesis or melena \u2022 Severe localized abdominal pain (RUQ, RLQ, epigastric) \u2022 Peritoneal signs (guarding, rigidity, rebound) \u2022 Bilious emesis \u2022 Fever >38.5\u00b0C \u2022 Jaundice \u2022 Age of first episode >50 \u2022 No cannabis use history Differential Diagnosis *Basis:* This is a consensus red-flag list, not

nodes.title: Alternative Diagnosis Workup
nodes.summary: Red flags: pursue targeted workup — biliary, pancreatitis, SBO, pregnancy, adrenal insufficiency
nodes.body: Red flags present \u2014 pursue targeted workup: Differential Diagnosis: \u2022 Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome \u2014 no cannabis association, may respond to triptans \u2022 Gastroparesis \u2014 worse postprandially, delayed gastric emptying study \u2022 Cannabis withdrawal \u2014 occurs AFTER cessation, not during use \u2022 Biliary disease \u2014 RUQ pain, Murphy sign, check LFTs/RUQ US \u2022 Pancrea

nodes.title: Alternative Diagnosis Found
nodes.summary: Alternative diagnosis found — treat underlying cause, reconsider CHS if no alternative identified
nodes.body: Workup reveals an alternative etiology for the patient's symptoms. *Basis:* "Diagnosis of exclusion" is the defining framing of CHS in the systematic review by Sorensen et al. [6] and in Richards' ED-focused review [7]; the same framing is carried in the 2025 Emergency Medicine Practice review [3]. There is no published rule for how much workup is enough before labelling a patient CHS, and no stud
nodes.recommendation: Treat the underlying cause. CHS remains a diagnosis of exclusion \u2014 if no alternative diagnosis is identified on repeat evaluation, reconsider CHS.

nodes.title: Lab Panel & ECG
nodes.summary: BMP, Mg, lipase, UDS, pregnancy test — get ECG BEFORE butyrophenones for baseline QTc
nodes.body: Order baseline labs: \u2022 BMP \u2014 Cr (AKI screening), electrolytes (hypokalemia, hyponatremia) \u2022 Magnesium \u2014 often depleted with prolonged vomiting \u2022 Lipase \u2014 rule out pancreatitis \u2022 Urine drug screen \u2014 confirms cannabis use \u2022 Pregnancy test \u2014 all women of reproductive age \u2022 Lactate \u2014 if severe dehydration/hypoperfusion ECG \u2014 obtain BEFOR

nodes.title: QTc Assessment
nodes.summary: QTc >500ms: avoid butyrophenones, use olanzapine instead — no significant QTc prolongation
nodes.body: Is the baseline QTc prolonged (>500ms)? Butyrophenones (haloperidol, droperidol) carry QTc prolongation risk. If QTc >500ms, avoid butyrophenones and use olanzapine instead. *Basis:* The 500 ms figure comes from the haloperidol injection FDA label, which states that a QTc exceeding 500 msec is associated with an increased risk of Torsades de Pointes [22]. It is a pharmacovigilance-derived threshol

nodes.title: Initial Resuscitation
nodes.summary: NS bolus 20 mL/kg — AVOID opioids and benzodiazepines (worsen gastroparesis, create dependence)
nodes.body: Immediate interventions: \u2022 IV access \u2014 2 large-bore IVs if severe dehydration \u2022 NS bolus 20 mL/kg for volume repletion \u2022 NPO (nothing by mouth until vomiting controlled) \u2022 Cardiac monitor GRACE-4 Good Practice Statement: \u26a0\ufe0f AVOID opioids and benzodiazepines \u2014 opioids worsen gastroparesis, benzodiazepines are ineffective for CHS nausea, and both create depend

nodes.title: First-Line Antiemetic \u2014 Butyrophenone Choice
nodes.summary: GRACE-4: butyrophenones over ondansetron — HaVOC trial showed haloperidol superior
nodes.body: GRACE-4 Recommendation 1: Suggest butyrophenones over 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron) for CHS (conditional, low certainty evidence). The HaVOC Trial (2021) demonstrated haloperidol 0.05 mg/kg IV achieved greater nausea VAS reduction at 2 hours compared to ondansetron 4mg IV. Choose butyrophenone: *Basis (read before applying):* The primary source is GRACE-4 recommendation 3a, whose published wordi

nodes.title: Haloperidol Protocol
nodes.summary: Haloperidol 0.05 mg/kg IV — LOWER dose than agitation dosing, may repeat once at 30 min
nodes.body: Haloperidol 0.05 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes (max 5 mg) HaVOC Trial Evidence: \u2022 Greater nausea VAS reduction at 2 hours vs ondansetron 4mg IV \u2022 More patients achieved adequate relief \u2022 Dose is LOWER than standard agitation dosing (0.1 mg/kg) May repeat once at 30 min if inadequate response Monitor: QTc (repeat ECG after dosing), EPS (treat dystonia with diphenhydramine 50mg IV/IM) *Basi

nodes.title: Droperidol Protocol
nodes.summary: Droperidol 0.625-2.5 mg IV — faster onset than haloperidol, more sedating
nodes.body: Droperidol 0.625-2.5 mg IV \u2022 Faster onset than haloperidol (3-10 min vs 10-20 min) \u2022 GRACE-4 recommends butyrophenones as a class for CHS \u2022 More sedating than haloperidol (greater H1/5-HT2A activity) May repeat once at 15-20 min if inadequate response Monitor: QTc (repeat ECG after dosing), blood pressure (alpha-1 blockade can cause hypotension) *Basis:* There is no randomised trial

nodes.title: QTc >500ms \u2014 Avoid Butyrophenones
nodes.summary: QTc >500ms: olanzapine 5-10 mg IM/PO — do NOT combine with parenteral benzodiazepines
nodes.body: QTc >500ms \u2014 haloperidol and droperidol are contraindicated. Use Olanzapine instead: \u2022 No significant QTc prolongation \u2014 major advantage \u2022 5-10 mg IM or PO \u2022 Do NOT combine with parenteral benzodiazepines Also apply topical capsaicin as adjunct.

nodes.title: Topical Capsaicin Protocol
nodes.summary: Capsaicin activates same TRPV1 pathway as hot water bathing — targeted relief without dehydration
nodes.body: GRACE-4 Recommendation 2: Suggest capsaicin in addition to standard antiemetics (conditional, very low certainty evidence). Capsaicin 0.075% Cream Mechanism: TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) receptor agonist \u2014 the same pathway activated by hot water bathing, which is why CHS patients instinctively seek hot showers. Capsaicin provides targeted activation without the dehydration

nodes.title: Capsaicin Application Technique
nodes.summary: Apply 0.075% cream to periumbilical area — wear gloves, initial burning is expected and temporary
nodes.body: Application: \u2022 Use 0.075% cream (e.g., Zostrix, Capzasin-HP) \u2022 Apply ~1 inch ribbon to periumbilical area (~15 cm diameter) \u2022 Wear gloves during application \u2022 Reapply every 6-8 hours as needed Patient counseling: \u2022 Initial burning sensation is expected and temporary \u2022 Avoid contact with eyes, nose, mouth \u2022 Do NOT apply heating pad over capsaicin \u2022 Wash hands

nodes.title: Response to Initial Treatment?
nodes.summary: Reassess 30-60 min after butyrophenone + capsaicin — ability to tolerate PO fluids is key
nodes.body: Reassess at 30-60 minutes after butyrophenone + capsaicin. Assess: \u2022 Nausea/vomiting frequency and severity \u2022 Ability to tolerate PO fluids \u2022 Vital sign improvement \u2022 Patient-reported symptom relief

nodes.title: Symptoms Improving
nodes.summary: Continue supportive care — trial PO fluids, recheck electrolytes, proceed to disposition
nodes.body: Continue supportive care: \u2022 Complete IV fluid resuscitation \u2022 Trial PO fluids \u2014 start with small sips of clear liquids \u2022 Recheck electrolytes if initially abnormal \u2022 Continue capsaicin application If tolerating PO, proceed to disposition planning.

nodes.title: Refractory \u2014 Escalation Options
nodes.summary: Repeat butyrophenone or add olanzapine — do NOT escalate to opioids or benzodiazepines
nodes.body: Persistent vomiting despite butyrophenone + capsaicin. Escalation options: 1. Repeat butyrophenone dose if first dose was subtherapeutic 2. Olanzapine 5-10 mg IM/PO as second-line agent 3. Reassess for alternative diagnoses if truly refractory 4. Consider admission for continued IV antiemetics \u26a0\ufe0f Do NOT escalate to opioids or benzodiazepines.

nodes.title: Olanzapine \u2014 Second-Line
nodes.summary: Olanzapine 5-10 mg IM/PO — no QTc risk, no dystonia — avoid with parenteral benzos
nodes.body: Olanzapine 5-10 mg IM or PO Advantages: \u2022 No significant QTc prolongation \u2022 No dystonia risk \u2022 Effective antiemetic with D2, 5-HT2A, 5-HT3, H1 receptor blockade \u26a0\ufe0f DO NOT combine with parenteral (IM/IV) benzodiazepines \u2014 risk of respiratory depression and death. Used when: \u2022 Butyrophenones contraindicated (QTc >500ms) \u2022 Refractory to butyrophenone therapy \u

nodes.title: Medications to AVOID
nodes.summary: Avoid opioids, benzos, ondansetron alone, and dronabinol — break the cycle of ineffective treatment
nodes.body: GRACE-4 Good Practice Statement: \u274c Opioids \u2014 worsen gastroparesis, promote dependence, do not treat underlying CHS nausea \u274c Benzodiazepines \u2014 ineffective for CHS nausea, cause sedation without antiemetic benefit \u274c Ondansetron as sole therapy \u2014 typically fails in CHS. The HaVOC trial showed butyrophenones are superior. May use as adjunct but should not be first-line. \

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if tolerating PO, adequate rehydration, electrolytes corrected; admit if refractory or AKI
nodes.body: Assess discharge readiness: Discharge criteria: \u2022 Vomiting controlled \u2022 Tolerating PO fluids \u2022 Adequate rehydration (normal Cr, improved UOP) \u2022 Electrolytes corrected or stable \u2022 Cannabis cessation counseling provided Admission criteria: \u2022 Persistent vomiting despite antiemetics \u2022 AKI (elevated creatinine) \u2022 Severe electrolyte derangements \u2022 Mallory-Wei

nodes.title: Admission
nodes.summary: Admit for IV hydration, scheduled butyrophenone + capsaicin, serial labs, GI consult if Boerhaave concern
nodes.body: Admit for: \u2022 Continued IV hydration and electrolyte repletion \u2022 Serial labs (BMP, Mg q6-8h) \u2022 IV antiemetic management (scheduled butyrophenone + capsaicin) \u2022 Nephrology consult if AKI does not improve with hydration \u2022 GI consult if concern for Boerhaave (CT chest/abdomen with PO contrast) \u2022 Social work/addiction medicine for cessation support
nodes.recommendation: Admit to medicine/observation for IV hydration, antiemetic management, and electrolyte monitoring.

nodes.title: Discharge with Counseling
nodes.summary: Discharge with OTC capsaicin cream, cessation counseling — cannabis cessation is the ONLY cure
nodes.body: CHS Discharge Instructions Prescriptions: \u2022 OTC capsaicin cream 0.075% (Zostrix) \u2014 apply to abdomen during episodes \u2022 Consider amitriptyline 25-50 mg qhs for prophylaxis (limited evidence) Counseling: \u2022 Cannabis Cessation Counseling \u2014 cannabis cessation is the ONLY definitive cure \u2022 Symptoms will recur with resumed cannabis use \u2022 Refer to primary care within 1 we
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with cannabis cessation counseling, OTC capsaicin cream, and close follow-up.

nodes.title: Cannabis Cessation Counseling
nodes.summary: Cannabis cessation: symptoms resolve within days to weeks — recurrence with ANY resumed use
nodes.body: Cannabis cessation is the ONLY definitive cure for CHS. Key counseling points: \u2022 Symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks of complete abstinence \u2022 Recurrence is expected with ANY resumed cannabis use \u2014 even reduced amounts \u2022 Synthetic cannabinoids (K2/Spice) can also cause CHS \u2022 CBD products may contain enough THC to trigger symptoms Support resources: \u2022 SAMHSA

nodes.title: Ciguatera Fish Poisoning
nodes.summary: Most common nonbacterial seafood poisoning — heat-stable toxin, no rapid test, clinical diagnosis
nodes.body: Ciguatera is the most common nonbacterial seafood poisoning worldwide, affecting 50,000-500,000 people annually. Caused by ciguatoxin from dinoflagellates that bioaccumulate in reef fish. KEY FEATURES \u2022 GI symptoms (early) + neurological symptoms (characteristic) \u2022 Pathognomonic: HOT-COLD REVERSAL (cold feels burning, hot feels cold) \u2022 Cardiovascular instability in 20-40% \u2022 No

nodes.title: Exposure History
nodes.summary: Confirm reef fish consumption within 72 hours — barracuda, grouper, snapper highest risk
nodes.body: Confirm fish consumption and timeline. Symptoms typically begin 15 minutes to 6 hours after ingestion, but can be delayed up to 72 hours.

nodes.title: High-Risk Fish Species
nodes.summary: Highest risk: barracuda, moray eel, amberjack — fish >5-6 lbs accumulate more toxin
nodes.body: If fish species unknown, assess risk based on geographic source and preparation. HIGHEST RISK (Avoid entirely) \u2022 Barracuda \u2014 most common culprit \u2022 Moray eel \u2022 Amberjack HIGH RISK \u2022 Grouper, Red snapper, Sea bass \u2022 Sturgeon, Parrotfish, Surgeonfish \u2022 Kingfish, Jack, Hogfish RISK FACTORS \u2022 Fish >5-6 lbs (larger = more toxin) \u2022 Fish head, liver, roe, intes

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Hot-cold reversal is essentially pathognomonic — distinguishes from scombroid, shellfish, GBS
nodes.body: Without fish exposure history, consider alternative diagnoses. OTHER MARINE TOXINS \u2022 Scombroid: histamine-like (flushing, urticaria, rapid onset) \u2022 Shellfish poisoning: paralytic, amnestic, neurotoxic \u2022 Tetrodotoxin: pufferfish (rapid paralysis) INFECTIOUS \u2022 Vibrio, Salmonella, Campylobacter \u2022 Norovirus (outbreak pattern) NEUROLOGICAL \u2022 Guillain-Barr\u00e9 (ascending

nodes.title: Symptom Pattern
nodes.summary: GI symptoms first (1-2h), neurological follow (6-24h), cardiovascular in 20-40%
nodes.body: Which symptom complex predominates? GI symptoms typically appear first (1-2 hours), neurological symptoms follow (6-24 hours), cardiovascular can occur early or late.

nodes.title: GI-Predominant Ciguatera
nodes.summary: Early GI presentation — IV fluids, antiemetics, monitor for neurological symptom development
nodes.body: Early presentation with primarily GI symptoms. Neurological symptoms often develop over the next 12-24 hours. TYPICAL GI SYMPTOMS \u2022 Nausea and vomiting (onset 1-2 hours) \u2022 Watery diarrhea (can be profuse) \u2022 Abdominal cramping \u2022 Duration: 1-4 days typically MANAGEMENT \u2022 IV fluids for dehydration \u2022 Antiemetics (ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO) \u2022 Monitor for neurological s

nodes.title: Neurological Severity
nodes.summary: Ask specifically about hot-cold reversal — patients may not volunteer this pathognomonic symptom
nodes.body: Neurological symptoms are the hallmark of ciguatera and can persist for weeks to months. ASK SPECIFICALLY about hot-cold reversal \u2014 patients may not volunteer this symptom.

nodes.title: Mild Neurological Symptoms
nodes.summary: Mild sensory only: perioral tingling, distal paresthesias — usually resolves in 1-2 weeks
nodes.body: Mild sensory symptoms without motor involvement. TYPICAL SYMPTOMS \u2022 Perioral paresthesias (tingling lips/tongue) \u2022 Distal extremity paresthesias \u2022 Mild headache \u2022 Metallic taste EXPECTED COURSE \u2022 May worsen over first 24-48 hours \u2022 Usually resolves within 1-2 weeks \u2022 Some patients develop chronic symptoms TREATMENT \u2022 Supportive care \u2022 Consider amitripty

nodes.title: Moderate Neurological Symptoms
nodes.summary: Hot-cold reversal in ~80% — consider IV mannitol within 72h, amitriptyline for neuropathy
nodes.body: Classic ciguatera presentation with hot-cold reversal and sensory symptoms. PATHOGNOMONIC: HOT-COLD REVERSAL \u2022 Cold objects feel burning hot \u2022 Hot objects feel cold \u2022 Present in ~80% if specifically asked \u2022 May persist for months OTHER SYMPTOMS \u2022 Diffuse paresthesias \u2022 Myalgias, arthralgias \u2022 Severe fatigue \u2022 Pruritus (itching) \u2022 Cold allodynia (burning

nodes.title: Severe Neurological Symptoms
nodes.summary: Ataxia, weakness, or AMS = ICU admission — airway assessment, continuous cardiac monitoring
nodes.body: Motor or CNS involvement indicates severe poisoning.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT TO ICU/MONITORED BED SEVERE NEUROLOGICAL FEATURES \u2022 Ataxia or incoordination \u2022 Motor weakness (may mimic GBS) \u2022 Altered mental status \u2022 Seizures (rare but reported) \u2022 Respiratory compromise IMMEDIATE MANAGEMEN

nodes.title: Cardiovascular Assessment
nodes.summary: Cardiovascular toxicity in 20-40% — bradycardia most common, usually responds to atropine
nodes.body: Cardiovascular toxicity occurs in 20-40% of cases. Bradycardia is most common; hypotension can be severe.

nodes.title: Ciguatera Bradycardia
nodes.summary: Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia — AVOID beta-blockers and CCBs
nodes.body: Bradycardia is the most common cardiovascular manifestation (67% of cardiac cases). Usually responds to atropine. MECHANISM \u2022 Ciguatoxin opens sodium channels \u2022 Vagal stimulation predominates \u2022 Direct cardiac ion channel effects MANAGEMENT ASYMPTOMATIC (HR 40-50) \u2022 Monitor on telemetry \u2022 IV access \u2022 Observe for progression SYMPTOMATIC (HR <40 or symptoms) \u2022 Atrop

nodes.title: Ciguatera Hypotension
nodes.summary: NS/LR 20 mL/kg bolus first — NE only if persistent shock after fluids
nodes.body: Hypotension occurs in up to 75% of patients with cardiovascular involvement. Usually responds to fluids. MANAGEMENT FIRST-LINE: IV Fluids \u2022 NS or LR 20 mL/kg bolus over 30 min \u2022 Repeat as needed \u2022 Monitor urine output REFRACTORY HYPOTENSION \u2022 Norepinephrine if persistent shock \u2022 Consider concurrent bradycardia (treat with atropine) \u2022 Rule out other causes (sepsis, ble

nodes.title: Cardiac Symptoms Without Instability
nodes.summary: ECG and troponin — ciguatoxin can cause direct myocardial injury and QT prolongation
nodes.body: Chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea can occur without hemodynamic compromise. WORKUP \u2022 12-lead ECG (assess rhythm, QT interval) \u2022 Troponin (ciguatoxin can cause myocardial injury) \u2022 Continuous monitoring ECG FINDINGS TO WATCH \u2022 Sinus bradycardia (most common) \u2022 AV blocks (rare) \u2022 QT prolongation \u2022 T-wave inversions MANAGEMENT \u2022 Observation with telemetry \

nodes.title: Severe Ciguatera Poisoning
nodes.summary: Multi-system: ICU for continuous monitoring — atropine for bradycardia, fluids for hypotension, consider mannitol
nodes.body: Multi-system involvement requires ICU-level care.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT TO ICU IMMEDIATE INTERVENTIONS \u2022 Continuous cardiac monitoring \u2022 Large-bore IV access \u2022 Airway assessment FOR BRADYCARDIA \u2022 Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV, repeat q3-5 min to max 3 mg \u2022 Transcutaneous pacing if refracto

nodes.title: ED Treatment Overview
nodes.summary: No antidote exists — supportive care with IV fluids, antiemetics, cardiac monitoring
nodes.body: Treatment is primarily supportive. No antidote exists. ALL PATIENTS \u2022 IV access and fluids for dehydration \u2022 Antiemetics: ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO q4-6h \u2022 Cardiac monitoring if any cardiovascular symptoms GI DECONTAMINATION \u2022 Activated charcoal: consider if within 3-4 hours (limited evidence) \u2022 AVOID ipecac and lavage PAIN/NEUROPATHY \u2022 Acetaminophen, NSAIDs for myalgi

nodes.title: IV Mannitol Consideration
nodes.summary: Mannitol evidence is mixed — best within 72h, monitor osmolality and renal function closely
nodes.body: IV mannitol has been used for neurological symptoms, though evidence is mixed. One RCT showed no benefit over saline, but case series report improvement. Best evidence is within 72 hours of ingestion.

nodes.title: Mannitol Protocol
nodes.summary: Mannitol 1 g/kg IV over 30-45 min — max 2 doses in 24h, keep osmolality <320, replace UOP
nodes.body: IV mannitol may reduce neurological symptoms if given early. DOSING \u2022 25% mannitol 1.0 g/kg IV over 30-45 minutes \u2022 May repeat in 3-4 hours if partial response \u2022 Maximum 2 doses in 24 hours MONITORING (REQUIRED) \u2022 Strict intake/output \u2022 Serum osmolality (keep <320 mOsm/kg) \u2022 Electrolytes q4-6 hours \u2022 Renal function CONTRAINDICATIONS \u2022 Oliguric or anuric rena

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Discharge if stable vitals, mild symptoms, tolerating PO; admit if cardiac or severe neuro; chronic path if symptoms persist >2 weeks
nodes.body: Assess for admission criteria.

nodes.title: Discharge Home
nodes.summary: Avoid ALL fish, alcohol, caffeine, nuts for 6+ months — amitriptyline for neuropathy, PCP follow-up
nodes.body: Mild ciguatera with stable vital signs.
nodes.recommendation: DISCHARGE CRITERIA MET \u2022 Normal vital signs \u2022 No severe neurological symptoms \u2022 No cardiovascular instability \u2022 Tolerating oral fluids \u2022 Safe discharge environment DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS \u2022 Antiemetic PRN (ondans

nodes.title: Observation
nodes.summary: Admit 23-hour observation — continuous cardiac monitoring, serial vitals, neuro checks
nodes.body: Moderate symptoms requiring observation.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT TO OBSERVATION (23-hour) INDICATIONS \u2022 Moderate neurological symptoms \u2022 Requiring IV hydration \u2022 Mannitol administered \u2022 Mild cardiovascular symptoms \u2022 Unreliable follow-up MONITORING \u2022 Continuous cardiac

nodes.title: Inpatient Admission
nodes.summary: Admit telemetry/ICU — continuous cardiac monitoring 24-48h, consult tox/neuro/cards as needed
nodes.body: Severe ciguatera requiring admission.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT TO TELEMETRY OR ICU ADMISSION CRITERIA \u2022 Bradycardia requiring atropine \u2022 Hypotension requiring IV fluids or vasopressors \u2022 Respiratory symptoms \u2022 Seizures or altered mental status \u2022 Severe dehydration \u2022

nodes.title: Chronic Ciguatera Syndrome
nodes.summary: Chronic ciguatera (3-20%): persistent fatigue, paresthesias, cognitive issues — sensitization for months to years
nodes.body: For patients with persistent symptoms >2 weeks. CHRONIC SYMPTOMS (3-20% of patients) \u2022 Fatigue (most common) \u2022 Persistent paresthesias \u2022 Myalgias, arthralgias \u2022 Cognitive difficulties \u2022 Depression, mood changes \u2022 Duration: months to years SENSITIZATION PHENOMENON \u2022 Symptoms recur with: \u2014 Any fish consumption (even safe species) \u2014 Alcohol (even years lat

nodes.title: Cluster Headache — ED Approach
nodes.summary: "Suicide HA" — unilateral, periorbital, 15-180 min, autonomic + restless. Start NRB O₂ ≥12 L/min while excluding red flags.
nodes.body: "Suicide headache." Strictly unilateral, periorbital/temporal, severe (10/10), 15–180 min, with prominent ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, ptosis, miosis, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, eyelid edema, forehead sweating) and psychomotor agitation — the patient paces and rocks, distinct from the migraine patient who lies still in the dark. Open first: - Cluster Step

nodes.title: Does this fit ICHD-3 §3.1 cluster?
nodes.summary: Confirm ICHD-3 §3.1 (≥5 attacks, severe unilateral periorbital, 15-180 min, autonomic OR restless, 1qod-8/d).
nodes.body: Required (all 5): - ≥5 lifetime attacks fitting B–D - Severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain - Duration 15–180 min (untreated) - ≥1 ipsilateral autonomic feature OR sense of restlessness/agitation - Frequency 1 every other day → 8/day during a bout Phenotype clues that ARE cluster, not migraine: - Patient paces, rocks, cannot sit still (migraine prefers dark/quiet) - Strict unil

nodes.title: Atypical Presentation — Reconsider Diagnosis
nodes.body: Atypical features make primary cluster unlikely. Imaging (CT → CTA → MRI / MRV depending on suspicion) is warranted before assuming a primary headache disorder. Return to the broader headache differential and re-screen for: - SAH — thunderclap onset, Ottawa SAH Rule - Cervical Artery Dissection — neck pain, Horner, recent trauma/manipulation - CVST — postpartum, hypercoagulable, papilledema - AACG
nodes.recommendation: Do not treat as primary cluster until red flags excluded and atypical features explained.

nodes.title: Red-Flag Exclusion — SNOOP10
nodes.summary: SNOOP10 + dedicated links to SAH, ICH, AACG, CAD, CVST, HTN-pregnancy. Exclude before treating cluster.
nodes.body: Cluster phenotype mimics several life-threats. Exclude these before any cluster-specific Rx. Each item below links directly to its standalone consult — do not skip. Systemic — fever, malignancy, immunocompromise → imaging + workup Secondary risk factors — pregnancy/postpartum, anticoagulation, recent trauma, recent procedure Neuro deficit — focal sign, AMS, seizure → SAH / ICH Onset thunderclap —

nodes.title: Any Red Flag Present?
nodes.body: If ANY red flag is positive, this is not "just cluster" — pursue the secondary workup on the relevant consult before returning here. *Basis: SNNOOP10 red/orange flags (Do, Neurology 2019) [35] and the ACEP 2019 clinical policy on adult ED acute headache [13].*

nodes.title: Red Flag Positive — Pursue Secondary Workup
nodes.body: Do not treat as primary cluster. The autonomic features can be present in carotid dissection (Horner), AACG (red eye, mid-dilated pupil), and CVST (with postpartum / hypercoag risk). Open the relevant consult: - SAH - ICH - Cervical Artery Dissection - CVST - AACG - HTN in Pregnancy - Meningitis / Encephalitis if fever / immunocompromise If the secondary workup is unrevealing AND phenotype remains
nodes.recommendation: Complete the secondary workup before initiating cluster-specific therapy.

nodes.title: Acute Rx — First-Line: 100% O₂
nodes.summary: 100% O₂ 12-15 L/min via NRB × 15 min. NOT nasal cannula. ~78% abort. Add triptan if not aborted by 7 min.
nodes.body: 100% O₂ at 12–15 L/min via non-rebreather (NRB) for 15 min, patient seated and leaning forward. - Onset ~5–10 min, full abort by 15 min in ~78% (Cohen JAMA 2009 RCT, AAN/AHS 2016). - DO NOT use nasal cannula — peak FiO₂ ~40%, inadequate for cluster. - Demand-valve mask delivers higher minute volume and may be more effective if available. - No relative contraindications in the ED setting (severe CO

nodes.title: Did O₂ Abort the Attack?
nodes.summary: Reassess at 7 and 15 min; partial response → add triptan.
nodes.body: Reassess at 7 and 15 min. *Basis: the 15-min oxygen endpoint is the primary endpoint of Cohen, JAMA 2009 [3]; sumatriptan 6 mg SQ has a 15-min response endpoint in the Sumatriptan Cluster Headache Study Group trial [4]; both are Level A acute options in the AHS 2016 guideline [1].*

nodes.title: Acute Rx — SQ Sumatriptan
nodes.summary: Sumatriptan 6 mg SQ — 74% abort ≤15 min. Alt: zolmitriptan 5 mg IN. Max 2 SQ/24h. Hold ergot 24 h before/after.
nodes.body: Sumatriptan 6 mg SQ × 1 — onset ≤15 min in ~74% (Ekbom NEJM 1991). Single attack only; max 2 SQ injections in 24 h with ≥1 h between. Alternative when SQ unavailable, refused, or contraindicated: - Zolmitriptan 5 mg intranasal — ~62% at 30 min (Cittadini Arch Neurol 2006). Slower than SQ. - PO triptan NOT preferred — onset too slow for typical 30–90 min cluster attack. Contraindications (absolute)

nodes.title: Refractory to O₂ + Triptan — What Next?
nodes.summary: Refractory: GON block (preferred — also bridges), repeat triptan w/in caps, or IN lidocaine 4%.
nodes.body: A small subset of cluster attacks survive both maximal O₂ and SQ sumatriptan. Options at this point: *Basis: greater occipital nerve block — Leroux, Lancet Neurol 2011, randomised double-blind placebo-controlled suboccipital steroid injection trial [7]; block technique per the Blumenfeld expert-consensus recommendations [2]. Intranasal lidocaine for cluster rests on small studies only: Kittrelle,

nodes.title: Perform Greater Occipital Nerve Block
nodes.body: Use the dedicated procedure consult — Greater Occipital Nerve Block — for landmarks, aspiration check, agent selection, and post-procedure care. Clinical bottom line for cluster: - Block the ipsilateral GON only (cluster is unilateral) - Bupivacaine 0.5% PLAIN 2–3 mL ± methylprednisolone 40 mg (steroid adjunct preferred for cluster bridge effect, per Leroux Lancet Neurol 2011) - Onset 5–15 min, LA
nodes.recommendation: GON block now; then move to bridge + maintenance plan.

nodes.title: Choose Bridge Therapy
nodes.summary: Prednisone 60 mg × 5 d taper OR GON block (preferred in pregnancy, diabetes, osteoporosis).
nodes.body: Why bridge: verapamil (maintenance prophylaxis, Module 5) takes 2–4 weeks to titrate to effective dose. The bridge suppresses attacks during this window. Two evidence-based options — pick based on patient factors: *Basis: oral prednisone as short-term transitional prevention in episodic cluster — Obermann, Lancet Neurol 2021, multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial [16]. The s

nodes.title: Prednisone Bridge
nodes.summary: Prednisone 60 mg × 5 d → taper 10 mg q2d × 10 d. Start verapamil day 1. Limit to 2-3 bridges/yr.
nodes.body: Prednisone 60 mg PO daily × 5 d, then taper 10 mg every 2 d (50 → 40 → 30 → 20 → 10 → 0). Total course ~15 d. Monitoring: glucose (esp. diabetic), BP, mood (rare steroid psychosis), insomnia. With repeated courses: avascular necrosis, cataract, osteoporosis. Cap: do not repeat the full bridge more than 2–3 times per year due to cumulative steroid toxicity. Concurrent action: START verapamil titrat

nodes.title: Occipital Nerve Block — Bridge Indication
nodes.summary: GON block + methylpred 40 mg: comparable to oral prednisone bridge, fewer systemic SE. Use procedure consult.
nodes.body: Greater occipital nerve block with bupivacaine 0.5% 2–3 mL PLAIN + methylprednisolone 40 mg on the symptomatic side. The steroid depot provides weeks of suppression — comparable to oral prednisone bridge (Leroux Lancet Neurol 2011) with substantially fewer systemic side effects. Use the dedicated procedure consult — Greater Occipital Nerve Block — for landmarks, aspiration check, contraindications

nodes.title: Maintenance — Verapamil (First-Line)
nodes.summary: Verapamil 80 mg TID → +80 mg q2wk → max 960 mg/d. Continue 2 wk past attack remission then taper.
nodes.body: Verapamil is the first-line prophylactic for episodic and chronic cluster. Dose required for cluster suppression is substantially higher than for any cardiac indication. Starting dose: 80 mg PO TID (240 mg/day total). Titration: increase by 80 mg every 2 weeks → 320 → 400 → 480 → 560 → 640 → 720 → 800 → 880 → 960 mg/day max, until attacks suppressed or ECG/side-effect limit reached. Bridge while t

nodes.title: Verapamil — ECG Protocol (CRITICAL)
nodes.summary: Baseline ECG + ECG BEFORE each +80 mg + 10 d after. HALT if PR >0.22 s, AVB, brady <50, sx hypotension.
nodes.body: 🛑 ECG IS MANDATORY BEFORE EVERY DOSE ESCALATION. Cohen Neurology 2007 documented PR prolongation in 19% and AV block in 4% across the cluster-dose titration range. Schedule: 1. Baseline 12-lead ECG before the first dose. 2. Repeat 12-lead ECG before EVERY dose escalation (i.e., before each +80 mg step). 3. Repeat 12-lead ECG ~10 days after each escalation (capture late conduction effects). HALT t

nodes.title: Verapamil Response After Adequate Titration
nodes.summary: Adequate trial = ≥480 mg/d × ≥2 wk. Failure → refractory ladder.
nodes.body: Adequate trial = titrated to 480–960 mg/day (or to ECG/side-effect limit) for ≥2 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose. *Basis: the 2-week-per-step escalation interval and the 960 mg/day ceiling are the protocol used in Cohen, Neurology 2007 [8]; verapamil efficacy per Leone, Neurology 2000 [17]; escalation and failure definitions per the EAN 2023 cluster guideline [20].*

nodes.title: Refractory Cluster — Ladder
nodes.summary: Refractory ladder: lithium (chronic), topiramate, CGRP mAb (galcanezumab), repeat ONB, neuro referral.
nodes.body: After verapamil failure or intolerance, options (typically initiated WITH neurology consult, not as ED monotherapy): 1. Lithium carbonate — best evidence for chronic cluster (>1 year without remission). Episodic cluster usually does not need lithium. 2. Topiramate — useful when verapamil contraindicated (heart block, severe hypotension) or as add-on. 3. CGRP monoclonal antibody (galcanezumab 300 m

nodes.title: Lithium Carbonate (Chronic Cluster)
nodes.summary: Lithium 300 BID → titrate to 0.6-0.8 mEq/L. Best for chronic. Beware NSAID/thiazide/ACEi/dehydration interactions.
nodes.body: Lithium carbonate 300 mg PO BID start; titrate to serum level 0.6–0.8 mEq/L (lower than bipolar target). Check level 5 days after each dose change. Best for: chronic cluster (no remission >12 months). Monitoring (every dose change + every 3 months on stable dose): - Serum lithium level - Renal function (Cr, eGFR) - Thyroid (TSH, free T4) — hypothyroidism in ~20–30% long-term - Calcium — hyperparat

nodes.title: Topiramate (Alternative / Add-on)
nodes.summary: Topiramate 25 mg qHS → 100 mg/d BID. Alternative when verapamil CI. Counsel cognitive SE, stones, contraception.
nodes.body: Topiramate 25 mg PO qHS × 1 week, increase by 25 mg/week to 100 mg/day divided BID (50 mg BID). May increase further to 200 mg/day if tolerated. Role: alternative when verapamil contraindicated (heart block, severe hypotension) or ineffective. May be combined with verapamil for refractory chronic cluster. Allow 2–4 weeks at target dose before declaring failure. Side effects to monitor: - Paresthes

nodes.title: Patient Education — Triggers, Bout Pattern, Take-Home Plan
nodes.summary: Avoid alcohol/nitrates during bout. Rx home O₂ + sumatriptan SQ + IN zolmitriptan + bridge + maintenance. Safety check.
nodes.body: During a bout, AVOID: - Alcohol (ANY amount — even one drink commonly triggers an attack during an active bout; outside the bout, alcohol does not trigger) - Nitroglycerin / nitrate-containing meds - High altitude / hypoxic environments - Strong solvent or paint fumes - Histamine-releasing meds where avoidable What to expect: - Episodic cluster (~80%): bouts of weeks to months, then remission of m

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if aborted + bridge + maintenance + neuro followup. Admit if refractory, SI, or no outpatient O₂.
nodes.body: Most cluster patients go home from the ED after attack abortion and a bridge plan. Admit only for the specific scenarios below. *Basis: no trial or guideline defines admission criteria for cluster headache. Outpatient management after acute abortive treatment plus transitional and preventive therapy is the pathway described in the AHS 2016 cluster guideline [1] and the EAN 2023 cluster guideline [

nodes.title: Discharge Plan
nodes.body: Confirm before discharge: - Attack aborted in ED (O₂ ± triptan ± ONB) - Bridge therapy initiated (prednisone taper started OR ONB performed today) - Maintenance started (verapamil 80 mg TID with written titration + ECG schedule) - Acute rescue prescriptions: SQ sumatriptan autoinjector ± IN zolmitriptan - Home O₂ ordered (E-cylinder + NRB; insurer-dependent, may require neurology letter) - Neurolo
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with full Rx bundle + neuro followup within 1 week.

nodes.title: Admit for Refractory Cluster / Safety
nodes.body: Admit when: - Attack does not abort despite O₂ + 2 SQ triptans + ONB + IN lidocaine - Active suicidal ideation (cluster carries the highest SI rate of any primary HA disorder) - Cannot arrange outpatient O₂ before next anticipated attack (esp. if attacks are circadian-overnight) - Initiating lithium without reliable outpatient monitoring - Concurrent medical issue (severe verapamil bradycardia, hy
nodes.recommendation: Admit to medicine/neurology service for inpatient titration + safety planning.

nodes.title: Carbon Monoxide Toxicity — Recognition
nodes.summary: Pulse ox is FALSELY NORMAL — must use co-oximetry; think CO for household cluster with flu symptoms
nodes.body: CO Toxicity Overview Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that binds hemoglobin with 240× greater affinity than oxygen. CO poisoning causes ~50,000 ED visits and ~400 deaths annually in the US. [1][2] Common sources: • Fires and smoke inhalation • Furnaces, water heaters, space heaters (especially in winter) • Portable generators (garage, enclosed space) • Car exhaust in enclosed spac

nodes.title: Clinical Recognition — Key Pitfalls
nodes.summary: Cherry red skin is RARE and usually postmortem — nonspecific symptoms mimic viral illness
nodes.body: Classic triad: Headache, nausea, dizziness — but these are nonspecific! CO poisoning is frequently missed because symptoms mimic viral illness, migraine, or food poisoning. [1] Cherry red skin: This finding is RARE and usually seen postmortem. Do NOT rely on this for diagnosis. [2] ⚠️ Pulse oximetry is FALSELY NORMAL — standard pulse ox cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) from oxyhemoglobi

nodes.title: Mild CO Toxicity (COHb 10-20%)
nodes.summary: COHb 10-20%: headache/nausea — level does NOT correlate with prognosis, LOC is more predictive
nodes.body: Typical symptoms: • Headache (most common complaint, often described as "throbbing") • Nausea and vomiting • Dizziness, lightheadedness • Fatigue, malaise • Difficulty concentrating Physical exam: Usually unremarkable. Patient is alert and oriented. Vital signs may be normal or show mild tachycardia. ⚠️ Important: COHb level does NOT correlate well with symptoms or prognosis. A patient with COHb o

nodes.title: Moderate CO Toxicity (COHb 20-40%)
nodes.summary: Any LOC (even transient) = HBO evaluation — troponin elevation correlates with worse outcomes
nodes.body: Symptoms: • Confusion, disorientation, impaired judgment • Syncope or near-syncope • Chest pain (myocardium is highly sensitive to hypoxia) • Dyspnea, tachypnea • Tachycardia, palpitations • Visual disturbances • Ataxia, weakness Physical exam: • Altered mental status (GCS may be decreased) • Tachycardia • Tachypnea • May have ECG changes (ischemia, arrhythmias) ⚠️ Any loss of consciousness — even

nodes.title: Severe CO Toxicity (COHb >40%)
nodes.summary: Seizures/coma/arrhythmias: immediate 100% O2, intubate if GCS ≤8, contact hyperbaric center NOW
nodes.body: ⚠️ CRITICAL — Immediate intervention required Symptoms: • Seizures • Coma (GCS ≤8) • Cardiac arrhythmias (VT, VF, heart block) • Myocardial infarction • Cardiovascular collapse • Respiratory failure • Death Immediate actions: 1. 100% O2 via NRB or BVM — do not wait for COHb confirmation 2. Intubate if GCS ≤8 or airway compromise 3. Cardiac monitoring — treat arrhythmias per ACLS 4. 12-lead ECG — l

nodes.title: Asymptomatic / Incidental Elevated COHb
nodes.summary: Incidental elevated COHb: confirm no subtle neuro symptoms, identify source, 100% O2 until <3%
nodes.body: Incidentally elevated COHb without symptoms: Normal COHb levels: • Non-smoker: <3% • Smoker: up to 10% (can be higher in heavy smokers) • Urban environment: may have slightly elevated baseline [1] If COHb is elevated but patient is asymptomatic: 1. Confirm no subtle neurologic symptoms (formal cognitive testing) 2. Identify and remove from CO source 3. Apply 100% O2 via NRB 4. Repeat COHb in 2-4 h

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Venous COHb (co-oximetry), ECG, troponin, BMP, lactate — pregnancy test in women of childbearing age
nodes.body: Essential labs: COHb level (co-oximetry): • Venous or arterial — both are accurate (venous is easier) • Standard ABG and pulse ox CANNOT detect CO — must use co-oximetry [1][3] • Normal non-smoker: <3% • Smoker: up to 10% • Symptomatic: usually >10% Cardiac: • ECG: Ischemia (ST changes, TWI), arrhythmias — myocardium is highly sensitive to hypoxia • Troponin: Elevated troponin = worse prognosis, c

nodes.title: Initial Treatment — 100% Oxygen
nodes.summary: Start 100% O2 immediately — half-life drops from 4-6h (room air) to 60-90min (NRB) to 20-30min (HBO)
nodes.body: Immediate treatment for ALL suspected CO poisoning: 100% O2 via non-rebreather mask (NRB) or BVM — start immediately, do not wait for lab confirmation. [1][3] COHb half-life: [1][2] • Room air (21% O2): 4-6 hours • 100% O2 via NRB: 60-90 minutes • HBO at 2.5-3 ATA: 20-30 minutes Continue 100% O2 until: • COHb <5% AND • Completely asymptomatic Intubation indications: • GCS ≤8 • Respiratory distress

nodes.title: Normobaric Oxygen (NBO) Protocol
nodes.summary: NRB 15 L/min until COHb <5% AND asymptomatic — reassess for HBO if symptoms persist at 4-6h
nodes.body: NBO therapy for mild CO poisoning without HBO indications: 100% O2 via non-rebreather mask (NRB) at 15 L/min to maintain reservoir bag inflation. Duration: Continue until: • COHb <5% (or <3% ideally) AND • Completely asymptomatic Monitoring: • Repeat COHb every 2-4 hours until normalized • Serial neuro checks • Cardiac monitoring (telemetry) • Repeat ECG if any cardiac symptoms Expected timeline:

nodes.title: Intubation — Airway Management
nodes.summary: Intubate for GCS ≤8 or respiratory failure — continue FiO2 100%, HBO is NOT contraindicated while intubated
nodes.body: Intubation indications: • GCS ≤8 • Respiratory failure (hypoxemia, hypercarbia, fatigue) • Airway compromise (secretions, vomiting, burns) • Unable to tolerate NRB mask • Need for transfer to HBO facility Post-intubation: • FiO2 100% — continue high-flow oxygen • Ventilator settings: target normal PaCO2 (avoid hyperventilation) • PEEP as needed for oxygenation If fire/smoke inhalation: • Assess fo

nodes.title: HBO Criteria — Does Patient Qualify?
nodes.summary: HBO if: LOC, COHb >25%, neuro symptoms, cardiac ischemia, pregnancy COHb >15%, persistent symptoms
nodes.body: HBO Criteria Overview HBO accelerates CO elimination (half-life ~20-30 min at 2.5-3 ATA) and may reduce delayed neurologic sequelae (DNS). [3][4] Indications for HBO (ANY ONE of the following): ✓ Loss of consciousness at any time (even transient) ✓ COHb >25% (some sources say >25-40%) ✓ Pregnancy with COHb >15% or any fetal distress ✓ Neurologic symptoms: confusion, ataxia, seizure, focal deficits

nodes.title: HBO Protocol & Transfer
nodes.summary: HBO at 2.5-3 ATA for 90-120 min — most effective within 6h, may help up to 24h
nodes.body: HBO mechanism: [3][4] • Accelerates CO elimination (half-life ~20-30 min) • Increases dissolved O2 in plasma • Reduces cerebral edema • May prevent/reduce delayed neurologic sequelae (DNS) Standard HBO protocol: • Pressure: 2.5-3 ATA • Duration: 90-120 minutes per session • Sessions: 1-3 treatments (controversial; some give single treatment, others repeat x3) Timing matters: • Most effective withi

nodes.title: Contacting Hyperbaric Center
nodes.summary: DAN hotline 1-919-684-9111 (24/7) — provide COHb, LOC history, neuro and cardiac status
nodes.body: Contact hyperbaric center EARLY — transfer arrangements take time. Information to provide: • Patient age, weight • Time and source of CO exposure • Peak COHb level and current level • Any loss of consciousness • Neurologic symptoms • Cardiac involvement (troponin, ECG) • Pregnancy status • Metabolic acidosis (pH, lactate) • Airway status (intubated?) • Time since exposure began Hyperbaric center l

nodes.title: CO Toxicity in Pregnancy
nodes.body: ⚠️ PREGNANCY = HIGH RISK Fetal vulnerability: [2][3] • Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) binds CO more tightly than adult Hb • Fetal COHb levels are 10-15% higher than maternal levels • Fetal COHb elimination takes ~5× longer than maternal • CO crosses placenta freely Risks: • Fetal hypoxia even with mild maternal symptoms • Fetal demise • Developmental abnormalities (with early exposure) • Neurologic injury

nodes.title: Fire / Smoke Inhalation — Cyanide Co-Exposure
nodes.summary: Suspect cyanide if smoke + AMS/hypotension/lactate >10 — hydroxocobalamin 5g IV empirically
nodes.body: ⚠️ Fire victims: Consider cyanide (CN) co-intoxication Cyanide is produced by combustion of synthetic materials (plastics, wool, silk, nylon). CN and CO are synergistically toxic. [1][2] Suspect cyanide if: • Enclosed space fire • Soot in airway/carbonaceous sputum • Altered mental status out of proportion to COHb • Hypotension • Severe lactic acidosis (lactate >10 mmol/L is highly suggestive) • C

nodes.title: Delayed Neurologic Sequelae (DNS)
nodes.summary: Delayed neurologic sequelae in 10-30% at 2-40 days — cognitive, personality, movement disorders
nodes.body: DNS occurs in 10-30% of patients with significant CO exposure. [2][3] Timeline: Symptoms appear 2-40 days after apparent recovery (most within 2-3 weeks). Manifestations: • Cognitive impairment (memory, concentration, executive function) • Personality changes (irritability, apathy, depression) • Movement disorders (parkinsonism, chorea) • Gait disturbances • Incontinence • Dementia-like syndrome R

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Discharge only if COHb <5%, asymptomatic, normal ECG/troponin, no LOC, source eliminated
nodes.body: Assess for safe discharge vs admission: Discharge criteria (ALL must be met): • Asymptomatic • COHb <5% • Normal ECG • Normal troponin • No history of LOC • No neurologic symptoms • CO source identified and eliminated • Safe environment to return to Admit if: • Persistent symptoms • Any cardiac involvement (troponin elevation, ECG changes) • Pregnancy • LOC at any time (even if now resolved) • Soc

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria Met
nodes.summary: Install CO detectors, do NOT return home until inspected — return for headache, confusion, memory changes
nodes.body: Safe to discharge if ALL criteria met: ✅ Asymptomatic (no headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion) ✅ COHb <5% (ideally <3%) ✅ Normal ECG ✅ Normal or negative troponin ✅ No history of LOC ✅ No neurologic symptoms ✅ CO source identified and eliminated Discharge instructions: 1. Do NOT return to the source until inspected by fire department or utility company and declared safe. 2. Install CO detectors
