nodes.recommendation: Discharge with CO detector counseling and return precautions for delayed neurologic symptoms.

nodes.title: Admission for Observation
nodes.summary: Admit for persistent symptoms, cardiac involvement, LOC history, or social concerns (intentional)
nodes.body: Admit for: • Persistent symptoms despite NBO • Cardiac involvement (elevated troponin, ECG changes) • Pregnancy (OB co-management) • History of LOC (monitor for DNS) • Social concerns (intentional exposure, unsafe home) • Inability to confirm CO source eliminated Admission orders: • Continue 100% O2 until COHb <5% and asymptomatic • Telemetry monitoring • Serial COHb q4-6h until normalized • Seria
nodes.recommendation: Admit for continued oxygen therapy, cardiac monitoring, and serial COHb levels.

nodes.title: CO Toxicity — Key Takeaways
nodes.summary: Critical: pulse ox falsely normal, start O2 immediately, HBO for LOC/COHb >25%/neuro/cardiac/pregnancy
nodes.body: Critical points to remember: 1. Pulse ox is FALSELY NORMAL — must use co-oximetry. 2. Classic symptoms are nonspecific — headache, nausea, dizziness mimic many conditions. 3. "Occult CO" — think CO when multiple household members have flu-like symptoms. 4. Start 100% O2 immediately — do not wait for labs. 5. COHb level does NOT correlate with prognosis — LOC and neuro symptoms are more predictive.

nodes.title: Coagulation Cascade — Pattern over Memorization
nodes.summary: Cell-based model: initiation → amplification → propagation; 5 labs (PT/PTT/plt/fibrinogen/D-dimer) answer 90% of questions
nodes.body: Coag Cascade Steps Summary The cell-based model has replaced the old "intrinsic vs extrinsic" cascade. [1] Hemostasis happens on platelet/endothelial surfaces in three overlapping phases: initiation (TF/VIIa), amplification (thrombin burst), propagation (fibrin formation). Five labs answer 90% of bleeding/clotting questions: [2] • PT / INR — extrinsic + common (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen) •

nodes.title: Bleeding vs Clotting?
nodes.summary: Branch 1: bleeding (mucosal/deep/surgical) vs thrombotic (unprovoked, unusual site, young) vs mixed (DIC/HIT/APS/TTP)
nodes.body: The first branch determines the entire workup. [2][3] Bleeding-dominant clues: • Mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gum, GI, GU, menorrhagia) • Deep tissue / joint bleeding (hemarthrosis, muscle hematoma) • Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising • Surgical / line oozing • Family history of bleeding disorder Thrombotic-dominant clues: [3] • Unprovoked DVT/PE, especially <50 years • Arterial events at young ag

nodes.title: Pattern Matrix — Five Labs, One Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Matrix: PT only = factor VII/VKA; PTT only = VIII/IX/XI/inhibitor; both = liver/DIC/severe VK def; mucosal vs deep splits bleeding
nodes.body: Lab Pattern Decoder Use the toolbar Pattern Decoder to map abnormal labs → likely disorder bucket. [2] Quick-reference matrix: [2][4] | Pattern | Likely bucket | |---------|---------------| | Isolated PT prolonged | Factor VII deficiency, early vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, mild liver dysfunction | | Isolated aPTT prolonged | Factor VIII/IX/XI deficiency (hemophilia, vWD), heparin, lupus anticoa

nodes.title: Simplified Cascade Map
nodes.summary: Cell-based: initiation (TF/VIIa) → amplification (thrombin burst) → propagation (fibrin); PT = extrinsic, PTT = intrinsic, both = common/severe
nodes.body: The cell-based model in plain language: [1] Initiation — endothelial damage exposes tissue factor (TF). TF + VIIa activates a small amount of X → IIa (thrombin). The PT measures this pathway. Amplification — that thrombin pulse activates platelets and factors V, VIII, XI on the platelet surface. Most thrombin is generated here. Propagation — large-scale fibrin generation; fibrinogen → fibrin → cro

nodes.title: Five Questions for Every Coag Consult
nodes.summary: 5 Qs: bleed/clot? which lab? mucosal/deep? anticoag on board? acquired/congenital? — most cases solved by Q4
nodes.body: Ask in order — most consults are answered before question 5: [2][3] 1. Is the patient bleeding or clotting? • Determines workup direction (Module 3 vs Module 5) 2. Which of the five labs is abnormal? • PT, aPTT, platelets, fibrinogen, D-dimer 3. Is the bleeding mucosal or deep tissue? • Mucosal/petechial → platelet or vWF problem • Deep tissue/joint → factor problem 4. Is there a known anticoagula

nodes.title: Baseline Coagulation Panel
nodes.summary: Panel: CBC/plt + PT + aPTT + fibrinogen + D-dimer + smear; add mixing study, anti-Xa, TT, factor assays, TEG as needed
nodes.body: The first-line panel for any bleeding or thrombotic workup: [2][4] | Lab | What it measures | Quick interpretation | |-----|------------------|----------------------| | CBC + platelet count | Number of platelets, anemia | <150 = thrombocytopenia; <50 = bleeding risk | | PT / INR | Extrinsic + common pathway (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen) | Sensitive to vitamin K, warfarin, liver | | aPTT | Intrinsic

nodes.title: Mixing Study Interpretation
nodes.summary: Mix 1:1 patient + normal plasma; corrects = factor deficiency, doesn't correct = inhibitor; incubation distinguishes lupus AC (immediate) vs factor inhibitor (time-dependent)
nodes.body: Mixing Study Calculator Mix 1:1 patient plasma + normal pooled plasma. Recheck the prolonged PT or aPTT. [4] Result interpretation: • Corrects (≤4 sec of normal range) → factor deficiency - Order specific factor assays based on PT vs PTT pattern • Does NOT correct → inhibitor present - Could be drug (heparin, DOAC), lupus anticoagulant, or specific factor inhibitor (e.g., acquired hemophilia) Incu

nodes.title: Factor Assays — Targeted Testing
nodes.summary: Targeted assays by pattern: PT only = VII; PTT only = VIII/IX/XI; both = V/X/II/fibrinogen; vWD needs vWF antigen + activity; XIII for normal coags + bleeding
nodes.body: Send specific factor levels based on the pattern: [2][4] Isolated PT prolonged (corrects with mixing): • Factor VII assay (most specific to extrinsic pathway) • Mild factor V or X deficiency can also present this way Isolated aPTT prolonged (corrects with mixing): • Factor VIII (hemophilia A, vWD type 2N or severe type 3) • Factor IX (hemophilia B / Christmas disease) • Factor XI (Rosenthal syndro

nodes.title: DOAC Detection & Monitoring
nodes.summary: TT very sensitive for dabigatran (normal TT rules out); anti-Xa is gold standard for FXa-DOACs; PT screens for rivaroxaban/edoxaban; warfarin = INR
nodes.body: DOACs (direct oral anticoagulants) cause confusing coag panels. Know what they affect: [5] | Drug | PT | aPTT | TT | Anti-Xa | Best test | |------|-----|------|-----|---------|-----------| | Apixaban | Variable | Variable | Normal | Elevated | Drug-specific anti-Xa | | Rivaroxaban | Often prolonged | Variable | Normal | Elevated | Drug-specific anti-Xa, PT can screen | | Edoxaban | Prolonged | Var

nodes.title: Viscoelastic Testing — TEG / ROTEM
nodes.summary: TEG/ROTEM: R = factors → FFP; K/α = fib/plt → cryo; MA = strength → plt; LY30 >3% = hyperfibrinolysis → TXA; not sensitive to DOACs
nodes.body: TEG and ROTEM measure global clot formation, strength, and lysis in real time. [6][10] Where it shines: [6][10] • Trauma resuscitation (goal-directed product replacement) • Cardiac surgery, liver transplant • Postpartum hemorrhage • Suspected hyperfibrinolysis (LY30 >3% on TEG → give TXA) • Distinguishing factor deficiency vs platelet dysfunction vs fibrinogen problem at the bedside Key parameters

nodes.title: Platelet Function Tests
nodes.summary: Plt dysfunction: ASA/NSAIDs, P2Y12 inhibitors, uremia (DDAVP/dialysis), liver, MPN, paraprotein; PFA-100 screens, LTA gold standard, bleeding time is obsolete
nodes.body: When platelet count is normal but the patient bleeds, suspect platelet dysfunction: [2] Acquired causes (much more common than congenital): [2] • Aspirin / NSAIDs — irreversible (ASA) or reversible (NSAID) COX inhibition • P2Y12 inhibitors — clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor • Uremia — most reversible cause; consider dialysis, DDAVP, conjugated estrogens, cryoprecipitate • Cardiopulmonary bypass

nodes.title: Isolated PT Prolonged
nodes.summary: Isolated PT: warfarin > early vitamin K def (FVII falls first) > mild liver > congenital FVII def > rivaroxaban/edoxaban
nodes.body: Differential — order from most to least common in adults: [2][4] 1. Warfarin or vitamin K antagonist — check med list and INR • Treat with vitamin K ± 4F-PCC per bleeding severity 2. Vitamin K deficiency (early) — factor VII has shortest half-life (~6 h), so it falls first • Common in malabsorption, prolonged antibiotic use, malnutrition, biliary obstruction • Treatment: Vitamin K Pathway 3. Mild

nodes.title: Isolated aPTT Prolonged
nodes.summary: Isolated PTT: corrects = hemophilia A/B, FXI def, vWD; doesn't correct = heparin contam, lupus AC (thrombotic!), acquired hem A (emergency), dabigatran
nodes.body: Differential — split by mixing study: [2][4] Mixing study CORRECTS (factor deficiency): • Hemophilia A (factor VIII) — X-linked, males; deep tissue/joint bleeds • Hemophilia B (factor IX) — X-linked, males; clinically indistinguishable from A • Factor XI deficiency — autosomal recessive, mild bleeding, common in Ashkenazi Jews • Factor XII deficiency — does NOT cause bleeding (lab finding only); o

nodes.title: Both PT + aPTT Prolonged
nodes.summary: Both prolonged: severe VK def, liver failure, DIC, supratherapeutic anticoag, common-pathway def, massive transfusion, hypofibrinogenemia; FVIII + fibrinogen + smear differentiate
nodes.body: Differential: [2][4] 1. Severe vitamin K deficiency — factors II, VII, IX, X all low • Treatment: vitamin K 10 mg IV; PCC if active bleeding 2. Liver failure — multifactorial deficiency including fibrinogen • Factor VIII normal or elevated (acute phase) — distinguishes from DIC • Treatment: target underlying cause; FFP/cryo if bleeding 3. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — see DIC tree

nodes.title: Thrombocytopenia with Bleeding
nodes.summary: Thrombocytopenia: production (marrow), destruction (ITP, DITP, DIC, TTP, HIT), sequestration (spleen), dilution; smear + 4Ts + ADAMTS13 differentiate
nodes.body: Platelet Disorder Quick-Jump Bleeding from low platelets is mucocutaneous: petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding, menorrhagia. [2] Differential by mechanism: [2][4][7][9] Decreased production (marrow): • Aplastic anemia, MDS, leukemia, marrow infiltration • Chemotherapy, radiation • B12/folate deficiency • Viral suppression (HIV, hepatitis, CMV, parvovirus) Increased destruction (immune): • ITP — i

nodes.title: Mucosal Bleeding Pattern
nodes.summary: Mucosal bleeding = platelet or vWF problem; vWD is most common inherited; DDAVP for type 1, factor concentrates for severe; TXA for mucosal/menorrhagia
nodes.body: Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gum, GI, GU, menorrhagia, petechiae) suggests platelet or vWF problem: [2] Most common: von Willebrand disease (vWD) [11] • Most common inherited bleeding disorder (1% population, ~1 in 1000 symptomatic) • Three types: - Type 1 (most common, 75%) — partial quantitative deficiency; mild-moderate bleeding - Type 2 (20%) — qualitative defect; subtypes 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N

nodes.title: Deep Tissue / Joint Bleeding
nodes.summary: Deep tissue bleed = factor problem; hemophilia A (VIII) > B (IX); acquired hem A is emergency in older adults; bypass agents (FEIBA, rFVIIa) + immunosuppression
nodes.body: Hemarthrosis, muscle hematoma, intracranial bleed, retroperitoneal bleed → factor deficiency. [2] Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) [2] • X-linked recessive — males almost exclusively; rare carrier symptoms • 80% of hemophilias • Severity by FVIII level: severe <1%, moderate 1-5%, mild >5-40% • Treatment: - Recombinant factor VIII concentrate — 50 IU/kg for major bleed (raises level by ~100%);

nodes.title: Reversible Treatments — Overview
nodes.summary: Match defect to treatment: vitK→vitK+PCC, heparin→protamine, dabig→idaru, FXa-DOAC→andexanet/PCC, low fib→cryo, low plt→plt, hem A→FVIII, vWD→DDAVP/concentrate
nodes.body: Match the treatment to the defect: [4][7] | Defect | First-line treatment | |--------|----------------------| | Vitamin K deficiency / warfarin | Vitamin K ± 4F-PCC if bleeding | | Heparin | Protamine sulfate | | Dabigatran | Idarucizumab | | Apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban | Andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC | | Fondaparinux / argatroban / bivalirudin | Supportive — no specific reversal; consider 4F-PCC

nodes.title: Vitamin K Pathway & Reversal
nodes.summary: VitK factors II/VII/IX/X; FVII falls first (6h); active bleed → vitK 10mg IV + 4F-PCC 25-50 u/kg; FFP if PCC unavailable
nodes.body: Vitamin K Pathway Overlay Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X (and protein C, S). [4] Half-lives (longest to shortest): • Factor II (prothrombin) — 60 h • Factor X — 40 h • Factor IX — 24 h • Factor VII — 6 h ← falls first in vitamin K deficiency Causes of vitamin K deficiency: [4] • Warfarin or vitamin K antagonist • Malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, IBD, biliary obstruction, pancreatic ins

nodes.title: PCC vs FFP — When to Choose
nodes.summary: 4F-PCC > FFP for warfarin reversal: faster onset (10-30 min), lower volume, more reliable INR correction; FFP if PCC unavailable or multifactorial
nodes.body: 4F-PCC (Kcentra) is preferred over FFP for warfarin reversal in major bleeding: [12] | Feature | 4F-PCC | FFP | |---------|--------|------| | Onset | 10-30 min | Hours | | Volume | 100-200 mL | 800-1200 mL (15 mL/kg × 70 kg) | | INR correction | Reliable | Often partial | | TRALI / TACO risk | Low | Higher | | Cost | High | Low | | Thrombosis risk | ~1.5% | Lower | | Vitamin K co-administration |

nodes.title: Cryoprecipitate & Fibrinogen Concentrate
nodes.summary: Cryo 10 units (or 0.06 u/kg) raises fibrinogen 0.5-1 g/L; fibrinogen concentrate 25-100 mg/kg is volume-sparing alternative; OB target ≥2 g/L
nodes.body: Fibrinogen replacement is essential when fibrinogen <1.5-2 g/L with bleeding. [10][12] Cryoprecipitate: [12] • Each unit (5-10 mL) contains ~150-250 mg fibrinogen, plus FVIII, vWF, FXIII, fibronectin • Standard dose: 10 units (1 pool ≈ 5 units) raises adult fibrinogen by 0.5-1 g/L • Or 0.06 units/kg • Recheck fibrinogen 30-60 min post-infusion Fibrinogen concentrate (RiaSTAP / Fibryga): [10][12] •

nodes.title: DOAC Reversal
nodes.summary: Dabig→idarucizumab 5g IV (RE-VERSE AD); FXa-DOAC→andexanet 400/800mg bolus (ANNEXA-I) or 4F-PCC 50 u/kg; LMWH→protamine partial; UFH→protamine 1mg per 100u
nodes.body: DOAC Reversal Selector Use the toolbar calculator to pick reversal agent based on drug + last dose timing + bleeding severity. [12][14][15] Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor): [12][15] • Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials) — full reversal in minutes, RE-VERSE AD trial confirmed efficacy • Hemodialysis can also remove dabigatran (dialyzable, ~60% protein-bound) • 4F-PCC is NOT effe

nodes.title: Platelet Transfusion Thresholds
nodes.summary: Plt transfusion: ≥50 if bleed, ≥100 if ICH/neurax, ≥20 ICU prophy, ≥10 stable; AVOID in TTP/HIT/ITP unless life-threatening; PATCH trial harm in ICH on antiplatelet
nodes.body: Threshold depends on the bleeding scenario: [12] | Setting | Platelet target | |---------|-----------------| | Active bleeding | ≥50 × 10⁹/L | | ICH / TBI / neuraxial procedure / neurosurgery | ≥100 × 10⁹/L | | Pre-procedure (LP, central line, surgery) | ≥50 × 10⁹/L | | Stable non-bleeding ICU | ≥20 × 10⁹/L (prophylaxis) | | Stable outpatient hem-onc | ≥10 × 10⁹/L | Dose: [12] • 1 apheresis unit (

nodes.title: Thrombotic Pattern Recognition
nodes.summary: Provoked → 3 mo anticoag, no testing; unprovoked + young/recurrent/unusual site/family hx → thrombophilia workup 4-6 wk after stopping anticoag
nodes.body: Hypercoag Workup Lookup Distinguish provoked vs unprovoked thrombosis: [3][13] Provoked (transient risk factor present): • Surgery / trauma / immobilization (within 3 months) • Pregnancy / postpartum / OCP / HRT • Active malignancy • Hospitalization with reduced mobility • Long-haul travel + risk → Treat 3 months anticoagulation, do NOT routinely test for thrombophilia Unprovoked or "high-risk" fe

nodes.title: Acquired Thrombophilias
nodes.summary: APS = clinical event + lab (lupus AC, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2GP-I) ×2 ≥12wk apart; triple-positive = highest risk; warfarin (NOT DOAC); also Trousseau, HIT, PNH, MPN, nephrotic
nodes.body: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is the most clinically important acquired thrombophilia. [13] Diagnosis (Sapporo criteria, revised 2006): [13] • Clinical: vascular thrombosis (any site) OR pregnancy morbidity (recurrent loss, late fetal death, severe preeclampsia/IUGR) • Lab (≥1 positive on 2 occasions ≥12 weeks apart): - Lupus anticoagulant (dRVVT, hexagonal phase, mixing study fails to correct)

nodes.title: Inherited Thrombophilias
nodes.summary: FV Leiden (most common, 3-8× risk), prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin def; test only if unprovoked + young/recurrent/unusual; not during acute event or on anticoag
nodes.body: Five major inherited thrombophilias — most patients with VTE do NOT need testing: [13] | Defect | Frequency (in VTE cohorts) | Risk increase | |--------|------------------------------|----------------| | Factor V Leiden (heterozygous) | 5-10% population, 20-50% of VTE patients | 3-8× | | Factor V Leiden (homozygous) | 1 in 5000 | 50-80× | | Prothrombin G20210A | 2-4% population | 2-3× | | Protein

nodes.title: When (and When NOT) to Test
nodes.summary: Test only when result changes management (duration of anticoag, family screening); time it 4-6 wk off anticoag; do NOT order routinely in ED
nodes.body: Thrombophilia testing rarely changes management. Consider these questions before ordering: [13] Will a positive result change duration of anticoagulation? • Most heterozygous defects → no change • Homozygous, compound heterozygotes, APS, antithrombin deficiency → may warrant longer/lifelong Will it identify family members at risk? • Yes for severe defects (homozygous, antithrombin deficiency) • Le

nodes.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
nodes.summary: 4Ts: thrombocytopenia + timing (5-10d) + thrombosis + other; ≥4 = stop ALL heparin, NO platelet transfusion, start argatroban/bivalirudin/fondaparinux; bridge to warfarin only after plt >150
nodes.body: HIT is a paradoxical prothrombotic disorder caused by anti-PF4/heparin antibodies. [7] 4Ts pre-test probability: [7] | Feature | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---------|---|---|---| | Thrombocytopenia | <30% drop | 30-50% or nadir 10-19 | >50% drop or nadir 20-100 | | Timing of plt fall | <4 days, no recent exposure | Consistent but unclear | 5-10 days from heparin start (or <1 day if recent exposure) | | Thrombos

nodes.title: Liver Disease — "Rebalanced" Hemostasis
nodes.summary: Cirrhosis = rebalanced hemostasis: PT/INR does NOT predict bleeding; FFP not for labs alone; thresholds: INR <2.5, plt ≥50, fibrinogen ≥1.5; TEG > PT in cirrhosis
nodes.body: Liver patients have a "rebalanced" coagulation system — abnormal labs do NOT reliably predict bleeding or clotting. [8] The paradox: [8] • Decreased pro-coagulant factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI) → bleeding tendency • Decreased anti-coagulant factors (protein C, S, antithrombin) → thrombotic tendency • Decreased fibrinogen synthesis but elevated FVIII (acute phase, endothelial origin) → unclear net

nodes.title: Pregnancy Coagulation Changes
nodes.summary: Pregnancy = hypercoag; fibrinogen baseline 4-6 g/L (treat <2 in OB); LMWH first-line, warfarin/DOAC contraindicated; APS = LMWH + ASA
nodes.body: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with shifted reference ranges. [3][12] Normal pregnancy changes: [3] • Fibrinogen rises to 4-6 g/L (vs 2-4 g/L non-pregnant) • Factors VII, VIII, X, XII, vWF rise • Protein S decreases (functional, due to estrogen) • PAI-1, PAI-2 rise (decreased fibrinolysis) • Net effect: 4-5× increased VTE risk vs non-pregnant Implications: [3][12] • A "normal" fibrinogen of

nodes.title: Pediatric Coagulation
nodes.summary: Peds: vitK-dependent factors low at birth (give 1mg IM); adult ranges by 6 mo; HSP, ITP, NAIT pediatric-specific; thrombosis usually line/cancer/CHD-related; LMWH first-line
nodes.body: Pediatric coag panels have age-specific reference ranges. [4] Newborns: [4] • Vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) start at ~50% adult level — give vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth • Protein C and S also low at birth • PT/aPTT prolonged compared to adult ranges Infants and young children: [4] • Factor levels reach adult range by 6 months • vWD often unmasked at first invasive procedure or menarc

nodes.title: Pitfalls & Pearls
nodes.body: Common pitfalls in coag interpretation: [2][4][7] 1. "Treating the labs" • Don't transfuse FFP for asymptomatic INR elevation in cirrhosis or non-bleeding patients • Don't transfuse platelets prophylactically in HIT, ITP, or TTP unless life-threatening bleeding 2. Forgetting drug effect • Most "abnormal coags" are drug effect — check med list first • Heparin contamination is the most common cause
nodes.recommendation: Pattern over memorization. The 5 labs (PT/PTT/plt/fibrinogen/D-dimer) plus a smear and a med list answer 90% of bleeding/clotting consults. Cross-link to dedicated trees (DIC, TTP, Anticoagulation Reversal, DVT, PE) for definitive managemen

nodes.title: Rapid Code Status Conversation
nodes.summary: Code status is a goals-of-care conversation — focus on values, make a recommendation
nodes.body: The "code status" conversation is really a goals-of-care conversation — not just a checklist of procedures to accept or refuse. Key Principles: • Focus on what the patient VALUES, not procedures • Make a recommendation when appropriate • Avoid asking patients to make medical decisions • Be honest about prognosis • A conversation, not a form to fill out Remember: This is hard. You're doing somethin

nodes.title: When is This Needed?
nodes.summary: Use Surprise Question: would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?
nodes.body: Situations requiring rapid code status discussion: | Situation | Urgency | |-----------|--------| | Active deterioration / impending arrest | Immediate | | ICU admission with poor prognosis | Within hours | | Terminal diagnosis, new to patient | Early in visit | | Chronic illness with acute decompensation | During ED stay | | Patient/family initiates discussion | When ready | The "Surprise Questio

nodes.title: Rapid/Emergent Conversation
nodes.summary: The 30-second conversation — make a recommendation, do not ask "do you want everything?"
nodes.body: When you have seconds to minutes: The 30-Second Conversation: "I'm Dr. [Name]. Your [mother/father/loved one] is very sick. I need to talk with you about what happens if [their] heart stops." "Based on what I'm seeing, if we do CPR, I don't think it will help [them] survive, and it may cause more suffering. What I'd recommend is that we focus on keeping [them] comfortable and let [them] die peacef

nodes.title: Goals-of-Care Framework
nodes.summary: REMAP framework: Reframe, Expect emotion, Map future, Align, Plan — takes 5-10 minutes
nodes.body: VitalTalk/REMAP Framework: R — Reframe: Set the stage > "I wish we were meeting under different circumstances..." E — Expect emotion, explore values > "What's most important to you right now?" > "What gives your life meaning?" M — Map the future > "Given what you've told me about what's important..." A — Align > "It sounds like what matters most is..." P — Plan > "Based on that, I'd recommend..."

nodes.title: Reframe — Setting the Stage
nodes.summary: Warning shot, assess understanding, share prognosis honestly — then PAUSE for processing
nodes.body: Opening the Conversation: Warning shot: > "I'm worried about what I'm seeing today..." > "I have some serious news to discuss..." Assess understanding: > "What have the doctors told you about your condition?" > "What's your understanding of where things are?" Share prognosis honestly: > "I wish I had better news. The cancer has spread despite treatment." > "I'm worried that [they] may not survive

nodes.title: Explore Values
nodes.summary: Ask what matters most — for surrogates: "what would THEY want?" to relieve decision burden
nodes.body: Understanding What Matters: Key Questions: > "What's most important to you as you think about the future?" > "What are you hoping for?" > "What abilities are so important that you can't imagine living without them?" > "What would be a fate worse than death for you?" For surrogates: > "If [they] could see [themselves] now, what would [they] say?" > "What did [they] tell you about what [they'd] want

nodes.title: Make a Recommendation
nodes.summary: Doctors SHOULD recommend — a recommendation is a gift, not an imposition on families
nodes.body: Doctors SHOULD make recommendations: Do NOT say: > "Do you want us to do everything?" > "We can keep trying or we can stop." This puts an impossible burden on families and implies false equivalence. DO say: > "Based on what you've told me about what's important to [them], I'd recommend..." > "Given the situation, I think the best thing we can do is..." > "In my medical opinion, CPR would not help

nodes.title: Key Phrases
nodes.summary: CPR is for sudden arrest in otherwise healthy patients — say "allow natural death" not "withdraw care"
nodes.body: Language That Works: On prognosis: > "I'm hoping for the best but preparing for the worst." > "I wish the situation were different." > "I'm worried this illness is very serious." On CPR: > "CPR is designed to restart a heart that stops suddenly in an otherwise healthy person. In [their] situation, it would not restore [them] to health." On ventilators: > "The breathing machine can buy time, but it

nodes.title: Phrases to Avoid
nodes.summary: Never ask "do you want everything?" or say "withdraw care" — use "shift focus to comfort"
nodes.body: Language That Harms: | Avoid | Why | Say Instead | |-------|-----|-------------| | "Do you want us to do everything?" | Implies CPR = "everything" | Make a recommendation | | "Withdraw care" | Implies abandonment | "Shift focus to comfort" | | "There's nothing more we can do" | Never true | "We'll keep you comfortable" | | "Fight" or "give up" | War metaphors create guilt | "Allow natural death" |

nodes.title: Common Scenarios
nodes.summary: Select scenario: patient with capacity, surrogate, family conflict, or wanting "everything"
nodes.body: Select the scenario you're facing:

nodes.title: Patient with Capacity
nodes.summary: Speaking directly with patient honors autonomy — always identify a surrogate even with capacity
nodes.body: Speaking directly with the patient: Advantages: • Honors autonomy directly • Avoids surrogate burden • Patient knows their own values Approach: 1. Assess understanding of illness 2. Share prognosis honestly 3. Explore values: "What matters most?" 4. Make a recommendation 5. Document carefully If patient doesn't want to discuss: > "I understand this is hard. I want to respect your wishes. Can you t

nodes.title: Surrogate Decision-Maker
nodes.summary: Substituted judgment: "what would THEY want?" — relieve burden: "you did not cause this illness"
nodes.body: When the patient can't speak for themselves: Key concept: Substituted judgment > "Our goal is to figure out what [they] would want, not what you want for them." Questions for surrogates: > "Did [they] ever tell you what [they] would want in a situation like this?" > "If [they] could see [themselves] right now, what would [they] say?" > "What did [they] value most in life?" Relieve the burden: > "Y

nodes.title: Family Conflict
nodes.summary: Refocus on the patient, identify legal decision-maker, consider time-limited trial — you cannot please everyone
nodes.body: When family members disagree: Strategies: 1. Refocus on the patient: > "Let's step back and think about what [patient] would want." 2. Identify the decision-maker: > "Who is the person legally authorized to make decisions?" 3. Hold a family meeting: • Private room • All stakeholders present (or on phone) • Chaplain/social work if available 4. Acknowledge the difficulty: > "This is one of the harde

nodes.title: "We Want Everything Done"
nodes.summary: Understand why — often means "dont give up" — reframe: "I will do everything that will HELP"
nodes.body: When family says "do everything": First, understand why: > "Tell me more about what 'everything' means to you." Often they mean: • Don't give up / keep fighting • Don't let them suffer • Make sure nothing is missed Reframe: > "I hear you — you want us to do everything that will help. So do I. What I'm worried about is doing things that would hurt [them] without helping." Be honest: > "CPR is desig

nodes.title: Uncertain Prognosis
nodes.summary: Time-limited trial with clear goals and endpoints — revisit early and often as prognosis clarifies
nodes.body: When you don't know the outcome: It's okay to say: > "I wish I could tell you exactly what will happen. I can't. But I can tell you what I'm seeing and what I'm worried about." Consider a time-limited trial: > "Let's try [intervention] for [48-72 hours]. If we see improvement, we'll continue. If not, we'll talk again about what makes sense." Document the plan: • Clear goals for the trial • Specifi

nodes.title: Documentation
nodes.summary: Document: who present, capacity, prognosis shared, values expressed, recommendation made, decision reached
nodes.body: Document thoroughly — this protects everyone: Include: • Who was present at the conversation • Patient's capacity (or why surrogate is speaking) • Prognosis communicated • Values and goals expressed • Specific recommendation made • Decision reached • Questions/concerns addressed Code Status Orders: • Full Code • DNR/DNI • DNR only (intubation acceptable) • Comfort measures only / Allow natural dea

nodes.title: POLST / MOLST Forms
nodes.summary: POLST is a portable medical order, not an advance directive — for serious illness with limited life expectancy
nodes.body: POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment): What it is: • A portable medical order (not an advance directive) • Follows patient across settings • Signed by physician/NP/PA AND patient/surrogate When to complete: • Serious illness with limited life expectancy • Clear goals have been established • Patient wants decisions documented as orders Not appropriate for: • Healthy patients • Pati

nodes.title: Transitions of Care
nodes.summary: Communicate code status at ALL handoffs — update EMR orders, arrange follow-up conversation
nodes.body: After the conversation: • Communicate code status at all handoffs • Update orders in EMR • Complete POLST if appropriate • Arrange follow-up conversation if goals are uncertain For palliative/hospice transitions: • Involve palliative care early if available • Hospice can be consulted from ED • Don't wait until "nothing more can be done"

nodes.title: Transition to Comfort
nodes.summary: Comfort care IS active treatment — aggressive symptom management, family presence, dignity
nodes.body: Comfort-focused care: This IS active treatment: • Symptom management (pain, dyspnea, nausea) • Emotional support • Family presence • Dignity and respect Do: • Continue medications for comfort • Allow family at bedside • Consider chaplain/spiritual care • Treat distressing symptoms aggressively Consider: • Inpatient hospice • Home hospice with rapid discharge • Inpatient palliative care "We will ne
nodes.recommendation: Transition to comfort-focused care. Continue aggressive symptom management. Support family presence.

nodes.title: DNR with Active Treatment
nodes.summary: DNR does NOT mean "do not treat" — clarify intubation, pressors, dialysis, feeding tube preferences
nodes.body: DNR does not mean "do not treat": Continue as appropriate: • Antibiotics • IV fluids • Vasopressors (if aligned with goals) • Dialysis • Surgery • ICU admission Clarify specific wishes: • Intubation preferences (DNI separate from DNR) • Vasopressor preferences • Dialysis preferences • Feeding tube preferences Re-evaluate as illness progresses. Goals may change. [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: DNR/DNI status does not preclude active treatment. Continue disease-directed therapy as appropriate.

nodes.title: Full Code — Goals Clarified
nodes.summary: Full code after discussion is a choice, not a default — document conversation and plan to revisit
nodes.body: Full code is appropriate when: • Patient/surrogate has clear understanding of prognosis • Values align with aggressive intervention • Reasonable chance of meaningful recovery • Patient prefers to "try everything" Document: • That conversation occurred • Understanding of prognosis was confirmed • Values support full intervention • Patient/surrogate voiced preference Plan to revisit if situation cha
nodes.recommendation: Full code status confirmed after goals-of-care discussion. Revisit if clinical status changes.

nodes.title: Combative Patient
nodes.summary: Combative Patient — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Combative Patient Steps Summary Scene Safety First • Remove sharps and potential weapons from reach • Ensure adequate staffing — minimum 5 people for physical restraint • Activate security — show of force avoids need for sedation in up to 27% of cases • Position yourself near the exit • One person communicates — everyone else listens • ABCs, vitals, fingerstick glucose when safe to obtain De-escal

nodes.title: Is the Patient Redirectable?
nodes.summary: Is the Patient Redirectable? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Assess agitation severity to guide treatment intensity. RASS +1 to +2 — Mild-moderate agitation. Patient may respond to verbal redirection and oral medications. RASS +3 to +4 — Severe agitation. Not redirectable. Immediate parenteral sedation needed.

nodes.title: Immediate Life Threat
nodes.summary: Immediate Life Threat — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Patient is an immediate danger — actively violent, weapon, or excited delirium features. Restrain + Sedate simultaneously: • Physical restraint per Restraint Protocol while administering IM sedation • Ketamine 4 mg/kg IM — fastest reliable sedation (onset 3–5 min) • OR Midazolam 5 mg IM + Haloperidol 10 mg IM • Prepare for intubation — have RSI equipment at bedside • Once controlled, proceed to as

nodes.title: Will Patient Accept Oral Medication?
nodes.summary: Will Patient Accept Oral Medication? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Verbal de-escalation is always first-line. If patient is cooperative enough for PO meds, oral route is preferred — faster to administer, less traumatic, promotes therapeutic alliance. Offer choice: "I can give you something to help you feel calmer." De-escalation Checklist

nodes.title: Special Population?
nodes.summary: Special Population? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Before selecting medications, identify any special population that changes the approach. Special Populations Guide

nodes.title: Elderly Patient (Age ≥65)
nodes.summary: Elderly Patient (Age ≥65) — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Half-dose ALL agents. Avoid benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation, fall risk, respiratory depression. First-line IM: • Haloperidol 0.5–2 mg IM/IV • Olanzapine 2.5–5 mg IM First-line PO (mild agitation): • Quetiapine 25–50 mg PO • Risperidone 0.5–1 mg PO All antipsychotics carry FDA black box for increased mortality in elderly with dementia-related psychosis (1.6–1.7×). Document risk-benefit disc

nodes.title: Pregnant Patient
nodes.summary: Pregnant Patient — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines preferred for acute agitation in pregnancy. • Lorazepam 1–2 mg IM/IV — most pregnancy safety data among benzos • Midazolam 2.5–5 mg IM If antipsychotic required: • Haloperidol has the most safety data in pregnancy (FDA category C) • Avoid Droperidol After sedation: • Fetal monitoring • OB consult • Left lateral tilt positioning to prevent aortocaval compression

nodes.title: Parkinson's / Lewy Body Dementia
nodes.summary: Likely Etiology? — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: AVOID typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol) — high D2 blockade worsens motor symptoms. Lewy body dementia: extreme neuroleptic sensitivity — even "safe" agents can trigger life-threatening reactions. First-line: • Quetiapine 12.5–25 mg PO (lowest D2 affinity) If IM needed: • Low-dose Midazolam 1–2 mg IM • Low-dose Olanzapine 2.5 mg IM (moderate D2 affinity, safer than typicals) Consult

nodes.title: Likely Etiology?
nodes.summary: Likely Etiology? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Etiology guides medication selection. Assess for: known psychiatric history, substance use, toxidrome features, vital sign pattern. Sedation Dosing Table Special Populations Guide

nodes.title: Psychiatric Disorder — Mild/Moderate
nodes.summary: Psychiatric Disorder — Mild/Moderate — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Antipsychotics preferred — treat the underlying psychosis. PO (if cooperative): • Olanzapine 5–10 mg PO (ODT available — dissolves on tongue) • Risperidone 1–2 mg PO • Haloperidol 5 mg PO IM (if refusing PO): • Olanzapine 10 mg IM • Ziprasidone 10–20 mg IM • Haloperidol 5 mg IM • Droperidol 2.5–5 mg IM ⚠️ DO NOT combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzos — risk of excess sedation and respiratory

nodes.title: Alcohol Intoxication — Mild/Moderate
nodes.summary: Alcohol Intoxication — Mild/Moderate — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Butyrophenones preferred for alcohol-related agitation. • Droperidol 2.5–5 mg IM — fastest onset (3–10 min), more sedating • Haloperidol 5 mg IM — slower onset (10–20 min) Avoid benzos in simple intoxication — potentiates CNS/respiratory depression with alcohol. PO option: Olanzapine 5–10 mg PO Key distinction: If patient is withdrawing (not just intoxicated), use the withdrawal pathway — benzos a

nodes.title: Alcohol / Sedative Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Alcohol / Sedative Withdrawal — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines first-line — treat the underlying GABA deficit. • Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV q15–20 min • Midazolam 2.5–5 mg IM if no IV access • Diazepam 5–10 mg IV q5–10 min For established withdrawal, phenobarbital protocol may be superior — see Alcohol Withdrawal consult. Antipsychotics alone are NOT adequate — they do not treat the GABA receptor dysfunction and lower seizure threshold. Give Thiamine

nodes.title: Drug Intoxication / Undifferentiated
nodes.summary: Drug Intoxication / Undifferentiated — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Assess for anticholinergic toxidrome — requires a different approach. Anticholinergic signs: Dry skin, flushed, mydriasis, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds, hyperthermia, delirium "Red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as a hare, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter"

nodes.title: Anticholinergic Delirium
nodes.summary: Anticholinergic Delirium — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Benzos or physostigmine. AVOID antipsychotics — additional anticholinergic burden. Sedation: • Midazolam 2.5–5 mg IM/IV • Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV Definitive antidote: • Physostigmine 0.5–2 mg IV slow push over 5 min • Reverses both central and peripheral anticholinergic effects Contraindications to physostigmine: • QRS >120 ms (risk of asystole — suspect TCA) • Known TCA ingestion • Reactive airway di

nodes.title: Sympathomimetic / Undifferentiated Agitation
nodes.summary: Sympathomimetic / Undifferentiated Agitation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines first-line when etiology is unclear or involves stimulant/polysubstance intoxication. • Midazolam 5 mg IM — fastest onset, reliable IM absorption • Lorazepam 2 mg IV (if access available) Benzos treat the widest range of etiologies safely: sympathomimetic toxicity, withdrawal states, undifferentiated agitation. Avoid antipsychotics in stimulant intoxication — lower seizure threshol

nodes.title: Response to Initial Treatment?
nodes.summary: Response to Initial Treatment? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Reassess 15–20 minutes after medication. Target: RASS 0 to −1 (calm, cooperative). Monitor SpO₂, BP, RR.

nodes.title: Redose or Add Second Agent
nodes.summary: Redose or Add Second Agent — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Redose same agent at equal or slightly higher dose after appropriate interval: • Antipsychotics: ≥20 min between doses • Benzodiazepines: ≥10 min between doses OR add a second class: • If antipsychotic alone failed → add a benzodiazepine • If benzo alone failed → add an antipsychotic ⚠️ Exception: If olanzapine IM was given, do NOT add parenteral benzo — switch to haloperidol first, then add benzo

nodes.title: Severe Agitation — Etiology
nodes.summary: Severe Agitation — Etiology — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: RASS +3 to +4 — requires rapid parenteral sedation. Combination therapy (antipsychotic + benzo) is recommended — more effective and faster than either alone. Sedation Dosing Table Special Populations Guide

nodes.title: Combination Therapy — Severe Agitation
nodes.summary: Combination Therapy — Severe Agitation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Droperidol + Midazolam (preferred): • Droperidol 5 mg IM + Midazolam 5 mg IM • Onset 3–10 min. Can draw in same syringe. Haloperidol + Midazolam ("B52"): • Haloperidol 5 mg IM + Midazolam 5 mg IM ± Diphenhydramine 50 mg IM • All 3 compatible in same syringe. Onset 10–15 min. If QTc concern (>500 ms): • Olanzapine 10 mg IM alone (no QTc effect) • Do NOT combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzos

nodes.title: Severe Agitation — Alcohol Intoxication
nodes.summary: Severe Agitation — Alcohol Intoxication — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Butyrophenones preferred: • Droperidol 5 mg IM — fastest onset • Haloperidol 10 mg IM For severe agitation, add Midazolam 5 mg IM. ⚠️ Monitor closely for respiratory depression — benzos potentiate CNS depression with alcohol. Avoid large benzo doses. If patient is withdrawing (not intoxicated), switch to withdrawal pathway — benzos are mandatory.

nodes.title: Severe Agitation — Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Severe Agitation — Withdrawal — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Benzos are mandatory — treat the underlying GABA deficit. • Midazolam 5 mg IM if no IV access • Lorazepam 2–4 mg IV • Diazepam 10–20 mg IV q5–10 min Withdrawal patients may need very large cumulative benzo doses. Phenobarbital is an excellent adjunct — longer duration, more reliable serum levels. See Alcohol Withdrawal consult. Antipsychotics are NOT adequate as monotherapy — they do not address t

nodes.title: Severe Anticholinergic Agitation
nodes.summary: Severe Anticholinergic Agitation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines only — NO antipsychotics (worsen anticholinergic toxicity). • Midazolam 5 mg IM, repeat q5–10 min PRN • May need large cumulative doses Definitive antidote: • Physostigmine 1–2 mg IV slow push over 5 min • Contraindicated if QRS >120 ms or TCA ingestion Monitor for seizures. Active cooling if hyperthermic.

nodes.title: Response to Treatment?
nodes.summary: Response to Treatment? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Reassess 15–20 minutes after parenteral sedation. Target: RASS 0 to −2. Monitor respiratory status closely — combination therapy increases respiratory depression risk. Pulse oximetry, capnography if available.

nodes.title: Refractory Agitation
nodes.summary: Refractory Agitation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Patient not responding to standard combination therapy. Reconsider diagnosis — is there an untreated medical cause? Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, sepsis? Escalation options: 1. Ketamine 4 mg/kg IM or 1–2 mg/kg IV • Fastest, most reliable. Onset 3–5 min IM. • Prepare for intubation. Avoid in elderly and known schizophrenia. • If given after other sedatives, reduce dose by 50%. 2. Dexmedetomid

nodes.title: Physical Restraints Needed?
nodes.summary: Physical Restraints Needed? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Physical restraints are a last resort but may be necessary for immediate safety while medications take effect. Restraints are NOT a substitute for chemical sedation — always administer medications concurrently. Restraint Protocol

nodes.title: Restraint Type Selection
nodes.summary: Restraint Type Selection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Select the least restrictive option that ensures safety: • Soft limb restraints (4-point) — Standard for acute agitation. Allows IV access, monitoring. • Mittens / hand covers — Supplement limb restraints when patient removing IVs/tubes. • Vest / torso restraints — Prevents sitting up. ⚠️ Asphyxiation risk — monitor closely. • Hard restraints (leather) — Extreme agitation. Increased injury risk. R

nodes.title: Restraint Application
nodes.summary: Restraint Application — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Team approach — minimum 5 people (1 per limb + 1 team leader). Team leader does NOT touch patient — directs and monitors. Application order: 1. Arms first (greatest threat) 2. Then legs 3. Each limb secured to bed frame (not side rails) Positioning: • Patient supine — NEVER prone (asphyxiation risk) • Diagonal pattern: R wrist → R upper rail, L wrist → L lower rail • Head of bed elevated NEVER: •

nodes.title: Restraint Monitoring & Documentation
nodes.summary: Restraint Monitoring & Documentation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Every 15 minutes: • Circulation checks — distal pulses, capillary refill • Sensation and skin integrity under restraints • Respiratory status • Offer food, water, toileting Every 1–2 hours: • Physician reassessment — document ongoing need • Attempt to release one limb at a time as patient calms Order time limits: • Adults (≥18): 4 hours maximum per order • Adolescents (9–17): 2 hours • Children (<

nodes.title: Restraint Documentation Checklist
nodes.summary: Restraint Documentation Checklist — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Required documentation (Joint Commission): 1. Behavior necessitating restraints 2. Less restrictive alternatives attempted (verbal de-escalation, PO meds) 3. Type of restraint applied 4. Time applied 5. Names of all staff involved 6. Neurovascular checks q15 min (documented) 7. Physician face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour 8. Physician reassessment q1–2h (documented) 9. Ongoing need assessment a

nodes.title: Post-Sedation Monitoring
nodes.summary: Post-Sedation Monitoring — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: ALL patients receiving pharmacological sedation require: Respiratory: • Continuous pulse oximetry • Capnography (ETCO₂) if available — detects hypoventilation before SpO₂ drops • BVM and suction at bedside • Head of bed elevated Cardiac: • Continuous telemetry if antipsychotic given • ECG — obtain after haloperidol or droperidol for QTc • QTc >500 ms or increase >60 ms → discontinue agent, correct

nodes.title: Medical Evaluation
nodes.summary: Medical Evaluation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Once safely sedated, complete the diagnostic workup. Do not attribute agitation to "psych" until medical causes are excluded. All patients: • Fingerstick glucose (recheck) • BMP, CBC, VBG with lactate • ECG • Urine drug screen (interpret cautiously) Consider based on presentation: • CT head — trauma, anticoagulation, focal deficits • CXR — aspiration, pneumonia • Blood cultures — if febrile • Ammo

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Disposition depends on etiology, treatment response, and ongoing safety. • Has the underlying cause been identified and treated? • Is the patient at baseline mental status? • Can the patient be safely monitored at the destination?

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Indications: • Intubation/RSI for airway protection • Refractory agitation requiring continuous sedation infusion • Hemodynamic instability • Rhabdomyolysis (CK >5000) • Excited delirium features — hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis • QTc >500 ms with arrhythmia risk Handoff: • Medications given (drug, dose, time, response) • Current drips • Restraint status and monitoring schedule • Pending workup

nodes.title: Floor / Observation Admission
nodes.summary: Floor / Observation Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Indications: • Ongoing alcohol withdrawal requiring serial benzo dosing • Active medical workup — imaging, labs pending • Need for continued restraints or q1–2h reassessment • Unclear etiology requiring monitoring Handoff: • Last sedation dose and time • Restraint status and next check time • Monitoring requirements (telemetry, pulse ox) • Pending studies

nodes.title: Psychiatric Evaluation
nodes.summary: Psychiatric Evaluation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Only after medical causes excluded. Required before psych eval: • Vitals normal • Labs unremarkable (or explained) • Patient at baseline mental status from medical standpoint Refer for: • Suicidal ideation • Psychotic decompensation • Grave disability If patient is medically cleared but still requires chemical restraint, they are NOT ready for psychiatric evaluation — continue medical management.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.summary: Discharge — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Criteria: • Agitation resolved, at baseline mental status • Vitals stable • No medical cause requiring admission • Safe disposition — not intoxicated, has support Minimum 1 hour observation after last sedation dose. Ensure patient can ambulate safely. Provide: • If EtOH-related: substance use resources, discuss AUD treatment • If psychiatric: safety plan, outpatient follow-up Document: medications

nodes.title: Adult Constipation Spectrum
nodes.summary: 15-20% prevalence. Spectrum: simple constipation → impaction → ileus → Ogilvie.
nodes.body: Constipation affects 15-20% of US adults, with higher prevalence in elderly and women. [1][2] This consult covers the ED approach to the constipation spectrum: • Simple constipation — infrequent, hard stools without impaction • Fecal impaction — hard mass in rectum that cannot be evacuated • Postoperative ileus (POI) — transient GI dysmotility after surgery • Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (ACPO

nodes.title: Key History Elements
nodes.summary: Assess last BM, alarm symptoms, post-surgical status, constipating medications.
nodes.body: Stool Pattern: • Last bowel movement (date, character) • Baseline frequency (normal varies: 3×/day to 3×/week) • Bristol Stool Scale type (1-2 = hard, 3-4 = normal, 5-7 = loose) • Straining, incomplete evacuation, digital maneuvers Alarm Symptoms: • Blood in stool (beyond hemorrhoid/fissure bleeding) • Unintentional weight loss • New-onset constipation age >50 without prior colonoscopy • Family hi

nodes.title: Red Flags Present?
nodes.summary: Red flags: obstruction, perforation, volvulus, ischemia, toxic megacolon.
nodes.body: Red flags requiring urgent evaluation: [2][3] 🚩 Bowel Obstruction: • Bilious vomiting • Complete obstipation (no gas or stool) • Severe cramping abdominal pain • High-pitched or absent bowel sounds • Distended, tympanic abdomen 🚩 Perforation/Peritonitis: • Rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness • Fever, tachycardia, hypotension • Severe localized pain 🚩 Volvulus: • Sudden severe pain with distention

nodes.title: Urgent Evaluation
nodes.summary: XR or CT. NPO, IV fluids, NG if vomiting. Surgical consult if obstruction/perforation.
nodes.body: Immediate workup for red flags: Labs: • CBC, BMP, lactate, lipase • Type & screen if surgical candidate • LFTs, coags if concern for ischemia Imaging: • Abdominal X-ray (upright + supine or decubitus) - Look for: dilated loops, air-fluid levels, free air, fecal loading • CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (preferred) - Identifies obstruction level, transition point - Evaluates for ischemia, perfor

nodes.title: Categorize the Problem
nodes.summary: Impaction = rectal mass. POI = post-op, diffuse dilation. ACPO = massive colonic dilation.
nodes.body: Distinguish the type — treatment differs significantly: Fecal Impaction: • Hard stool mass palpable in rectum or on abdominal exam • May have overflow "diarrhea" around impaction • Colon not significantly dilated on imaging Postoperative Ileus (POI): • Recent surgery (typically <5-7 days) • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention • Diffuse mild dilation on X-ray (small bowel + colon) • Hypoactive o

nodes.title: Fecal Impaction Assessment
nodes.summary: Risk: elderly, opioids, immobility. Paradoxical diarrhea common. Can cause delirium in elderly.
nodes.body: Fecal impaction = retained mass of hardened stool that cannot be evacuated voluntarily. [3][4] Risk factors: • Elderly, debilitated, immobile • Opioid use • Neurologic disease (stroke, Parkinson's, spinal cord injury) • Chronic constipation, dehydration • Psychiatric illness, cognitive impairment Presentation: • Abdominal discomfort, bloating, anorexia • Paradoxical "diarrhea" (liquid stool around

nodes.title: Prepare for Disimpaction
nodes.summary: Soften with mineral oil enema first. Pre-medicate for pain. Left lateral position.
nodes.body: Before manual disimpaction: Soften the stool first: • Mineral oil retention enema (120-150 mL) • Administer 30-60 minutes before disimpaction • Lubricates and softens impacted mass • Reduces trauma during extraction Provide analgesia/anxiolysis: • Acetaminophen 1 g PO/PR or • Ketorolac 15-30 mg IV • Consider low-dose benzodiazepine for anxious patients • Severe cases: procedural sedation or pudend

nodes.title: Manual Disimpaction Technique
nodes.summary: Scissoring + hook extraction. Stop if vagal symptoms. Follow with cleansing enema.
nodes.body: Manual Digital Disimpaction: [4] Technique: 1. Lubricate gloved index finger generously 2. Insert finger gently into rectum 3. Break up stool using scissoring motion 4. Hook and extract fragments with flexed finger 5. Move finger in circular motion to loosen stool 6. Remove fragments in small pieces 7. Stop if patient has significant pain or vagal symptoms 8. Repeat until rectum is empty Duration:

nodes.title: Post-Disimpaction Care
nodes.summary: Cleansing enema after manual disimpaction. Avoid phosphate enemas in elderly/renal disease.
nodes.body: Cleansing enemas after manual disimpaction: Tap Water Enema: • 500-1000 mL warm tap water • Safer than phosphate enemas • May repeat 2-3 times Normal Saline Enema: • 500-1000 mL warmed NS • Safest option, especially in elderly or renal impairment Sodium Phosphate (Fleet's) — use with caution: • Single dose only, 118 mL • Avoid in: elderly, renal impairment, heart failure, dehydration • Risk: fatal

nodes.title: Postoperative Ileus
nodes.summary: Expected 3-5 days post-colonic surgery. Opioids major contributor. Rule out mechanical SBO.
nodes.body: Postoperative ileus (POI) = transient impairment of GI motility after surgery. [5][6] Expected duration by surgery type: • Small bowel: 24-48 hours • Stomach: 24-48 hours • Colon: 3-5 days Prolonged POI = ileus beyond expected timeframe Risk factors: • Abdominal surgery (especially open, bowel manipulation) • Prolonged surgery, blood loss • Opioid use (major factor) • Electrolyte abnormalities (hy

nodes.title: Ileus Treatment
nodes.summary: NPO, NG if vomiting, correct K+/Mg2+, minimize opioids, early ambulation, gum chewing.
nodes.body: Conservative management (first-line): [5][6] • NPO until bowel function returns • NG tube if vomiting or significant distention • IV fluids — avoid hypovolemia • Correct electrolytes — especially K+, Mg2+ • Minimize opioids — use multimodal analgesia • Early ambulation — mobilize as soon as possible • Gum chewing — stimulates motility (evidence-based!) [6] Pharmacologic options: Alvimopan (Entereg

nodes.title: Refractory Ileus
nodes.summary: If >5-7 days: repeat CT, check for infection, consult GI/surgery. Consider ACPO if cecum >9 cm.
nodes.body: If ileus persists >5-7 days: Re-evaluate: • Repeat CT — rule out mechanical obstruction, abscess, leak • Check for infection (UTI, pneumonia, wound infection) • Review medications for contributing drugs • Check electrolytes again Consider: • Neostigmine (if features overlap with ACPO) • GI consult for colonoscopic evaluation • TPN if prolonged NPO expected Surgical consult if: • Concern for mechan

nodes.title: ACPO / Ogilvie Syndrome
nodes.summary: Massive colonic dilation without obstruction. Cecum >12 cm or >6 days = high perforation risk.
nodes.body: Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction (ACPO/Ogilvie Syndrome) [5][8] Massive colonic dilation WITHOUT mechanical obstruction. Named for Sir Heneage Ogilvie (1948). Pathophysiology: • Autonomic dysfunction — excess sympathetic, decreased parasympathetic tone • Results in functional obstruction at splenic flexure Risk factors: • Recent surgery (orthopedic, cardiac, obstetric, abdominal) • Critical illnes

nodes.title: ACPO Imaging
nodes.summary: Measure cecal diameter on XR. CT essential to rule out mechanical obstruction.
nodes.body: Imaging to confirm ACPO: Abdominal X-ray: • Massively dilated colon (cecum to splenic flexure) • Cecum often most dilated segment • Measure cecal diameter — critical for management - <9 cm: lower risk - 9-12 cm: moderate risk - >12 cm: HIGH perforation risk • Haustral markings preserved (unlike toxic megacolon) CT abdomen/pelvis WITH contrast: • Essential to rule out mechanical obstruction • Look

nodes.title: ACPO Initial Management
nodes.summary: Conservative Rx: NPO, NG, rectal tube, correct K+/Mg2+, stop offending meds. 80% respond.
nodes.body: Conservative management (24-72 hours): [5][8][9] • NPO — complete bowel rest • NG tube decompression if vomiting or upper GI distention • Rectal tube — may provide modest decompression • IV fluids — correct dehydration • Correct electrolytes — K+ >4.0, Mg2+ >2.0 • D/C offending medications — opioids, anticholinergics • Treat underlying illness — sepsis, infection, etc. • Mobilize patient — if poss

nodes.title: ACPO Monitoring
nodes.summary: Serial XR q12-24h, exam q4-6h, daily lytes. Expect improvement in 24-72h.
nodes.body: Monitoring during conservative management: Serial abdominal X-rays: • Every 12-24 hours • Track cecal diameter • Watch for pneumatosis or free air Clinical monitoring: • Abdominal exam Q4-6 hours • Watch for peritoneal signs, increasing tenderness • Vitals for fever, tachycardia Labs: • Daily BMP — monitor K+, Mg2+ • CBC — watch for leukocytosis (ischemia?) • Lactate if concern for ischemia Expect

nodes.title: Neostigmine for ACPO
nodes.summary: Neostigmine for refractory ACPO. 91% response rate. Need continuous monitoring + atropine ready.
nodes.body: Neostigmine — Pharmacologic Decompression [8][9][10] Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that enhances parasympathetic activity → colonic motility. Indications: • ACPO refractory to 24-72h conservative management • Cecum ≥12 cm • Duration >4-6 days • No contraindications Contraindications: • Mechanical bowel obstruction (must rule out first!) • Recent MI, severe cardiac disease • Active bronchospasm (a

nodes.title: Neostigmine Administration
nodes.summary: 2 mg IV over 5 min. Watch for bradycardia. Atropine 0.5 mg if symptomatic. Response in 10-30 min.
nodes.body: Neostigmine Dosing Protocol: [8][9][10] Dose: 2 mg IV over 5 FULL MINUTES (REAL five minutes on the clock) • Do NOT give as rapid IV push • Consider 1 mg increments if cautious (1 mg, wait, then another 1 mg) Monitoring during administration: • Continuous ECG — watch for bradycardia • BP every 2-3 minutes • Stop immediately if symptomatic bradycardia Give atropine 0.5 mg IV if: • HR <60 with sympt

nodes.title: ACPO: If Neostigmine Fails
nodes.summary: Colonoscopic decompression if neostigmine fails. Surgery mortality ~25%. PEG prevents recurrence.
nodes.body: If neostigmine fails (up to 3 doses): [5][8] Colonoscopic Decompression: • GI consult for urgent colonoscopy • Success rate ~70-80% • Can place decompression tube • Risk of perforation (~2-3%), especially with ischemic bowel • May need to repeat Percutaneous Cecostomy: • IR-guided tube placement into cecum • Reserved for high surgical risk patients • Bridge to surgery or long-term decompression Su

nodes.title: Simple Constipation Treatment
nodes.summary: PEG is first-line. Mag citrate for rapid effect. Avoid docusate alone — no better than placebo.
nodes.body: ED treatment for simple constipation (no impaction): [1][2] First-line (OTC): Osmotic Laxatives: • PEG 3350 (MiraLAX): 17 g daily in 8 oz liquid - Best evidence, AGA/ACG strongly recommended • Magnesium citrate: 150-300 mL PO × 1 - For rapid effect in ED - Avoid in renal impairment • Lactulose: 15-30 mL PO daily - Alternative if PEG not tolerated Stimulant Laxatives: • Bisacodyl: 5-10 mg PO or 10

nodes.title: Maintenance Therapy
nodes.summary: PEG 17 g daily long-term. Rx options: linaclotide, prucalopride if OTC fails. Fiber + fluids.
nodes.body: Maintenance regimen to prevent recurrence: [1][2] First-line: PEG 3350 (MiraLAX) • 17 g daily (1 capful in 8 oz liquid) • Titrate for 1 soft BM daily • Safe for long-term use Second-line options: • Lactulose: 15-45 mL daily • Magnesium oxide: 400-800 mg daily • Senna: 2-4 tablets at bedtime (for stimulant-dependent patients) Prescription options (if OTC fails): [1] • Linaclotide (Linzess): 145-290

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge: simple constipation treated. Admit: ACPO, ileus, refractory impaction, unstable.
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition: Discharge home if: • Simple constipation or mild impaction successfully treated • Tolerating oral intake • No red flags or complications • Reliable follow-up available Observation/admit if: • Moderate-severe impaction requiring repeated disimpaction • Dehydration requiring IV fluids • Elderly/frail with comorbidities • Unable to tolerate oral laxatives Admit (flo

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: PEG daily, fiber/fluids, PCP follow-up. Return if no BM × 3 days, severe pain, vomiting.
nodes.body: Discharge prescriptions: • PEG 3350 (MiraLAX): 17 g daily — 30-day supply • Consider bisacodyl 5 mg PRN if needed Patient education: 1. Take PEG daily — don't stop when stools normalize 2. Increase fiber (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) 3. Drink 1.5-2 L water daily 4. Stay active — daily walking helps motility 5. Don't ignore the urge — go when you feel it Follow-up: • PCP within 1-2 weeks • GI

nodes.title: Admission Orders
nodes.summary: NPO, NG, rectal tube, serial KUB, correct lytes, ambulate, GI/surgery consult as needed.
nodes.body: Admission orders for ACPO, ileus, or refractory impaction: Diet: NPO Activity: OOB to chair, ambulate TID if able IVF: LR or NS at maintenance rate Medications: • D/C opioids if possible — use multimodal analgesia • D/C anticholinergics, CCBs if able • PPI if NPO prolonged • DVT prophylaxis Tubes: • NG tube to low intermittent suction if vomiting/distention • Rectal tube for ACPO • Foley for stric

nodes.title: Continuous Bladder Irrigation — Clot Retention
nodes.summary: Manually evacuate clots FIRST (CBI can\u2019t); use a large-bore 3-way catheter.
nodes.body: For gross hematuria with clot retention. Two rules that prevent harm: (1) CBI does NOT break up clots — you must MANUALLY evacuate existing clots first; (2) use a large-bore 3-way catheter, not a standard Foley. Tools (open first): - Procedure Steps Summary - Catheter French-Size Selector - CBI Titration Card - Inflow-vs-Outflow Stop-Check - Urology Escalation + Hematuria Workup

nodes.title: Clot Retention vs Simple Retention?
nodes.summary: Confirm hematuria + clots before CBI; simple retention does not need CBI.
nodes.body: Distinguish clot retention (gross hematuria + clots obstructing outflow) from simple urinary retention (no blood). The pathway and catheter choice differ.

nodes.title: Not Clot Retention — Use Retention Pathway
nodes.summary: Simple retention → standard catheter + retention workup, not CBI.
nodes.body: Clear urine with painless retention is simple urinary retention. CBI is not indicated. Decompress with a standard catheter and work up the cause via Urinary Retention. If catheter placement is difficult, escalate per standard difficult-catheterization steps.
nodes.recommendation: Use the urinary-retention pathway; CBI is reserved for clot retention.

nodes.title: Identify + Address the Bleeding Source
nodes.summary: Correct coagulopathy, send CBC/coags/T&S, identify source while prepping.
nodes.body: While preparing the procedure, address reversible drivers: - Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets; correct supratherapeutic INR; consider reversal if bleeding is severe (cross-reference your institutional reversal pathway) - Check CBC, coags, type-and-screen if bleeding is brisk or hemoglobin is dropping - Note prior TURP/biopsy, known bladder/prostate tumor, recent instrumentation Reversal decisio

nodes.title: Step 1 — Place Large-Bore 3-Way Catheter
nodes.summary: Place a 22-24 Fr 3-way hematuria catheter; confirm placement before balloon inflation.
nodes.body: A standard 14-16 Fr Foley clogs with clots and has no irrigation channel. Use a large-bore 3-way (hematuria) catheter — typically 22-24 Fr — see Catheter French-Size Selector. 1. Sterile prep; insert the 3-way catheter; confirm intravesical placement (urine/blood return) before inflating the balloon. 2. Inflate the balloon to the manufacturer\u2019s volume. 3. The three lumens are: balloon inflati

nodes.title: Step 2 — MANUAL Clot Evacuation (Mandatory First)
nodes.summary: Toomey-syringe manual irrigation until clear BEFORE CBI; don\u2019t force; urology if can\u2019t clear.
nodes.body: This is the step clinicians skip — and CBI fails without it. CBI fluid flows around clots; it does not break them. 1. Using a catheter-tip (Toomey) syringe with ~60 mL sterile saline, instill and aspirate through the drainage port. 2. Repeat aspiration/instillation, evacuating clots, until the returns are clear or only lightly blood-tinged and no further clot is retrieved. 3. Be patient — this can

nodes.title: Step 3 — Start + Titrate CBI
nodes.summary: Titrate saline inflow to keep effluent light-pink/clear; track net balance.
nodes.body: Connect sterile normal saline to the irrigation (inflow) port and open the drainage (outflow) to a closed bag. - Titrate inflow rate to keep the effluent light pink to clear — faster for brisk bleeding, slower as it clears. See CBI Titration Card. - The goal is to keep clots from re-forming, NOT to break existing clots (those were removed manually). - Maintain a closed, sterile system; track net f

nodes.title: Inflow vs Outflow — Watch Closely
nodes.summary: Outflow must keep up with inflow; if not, STOP, troubleshoot, escalate.
nodes.body: The key safety check during CBI: outflow must roughly match or exceed inflow. If you keep running fluid in but little comes out, the bladder is overfilling. Review Inflow-vs-Outflow Stop-Check.

nodes.title: Outflow Lagging — STOP + Troubleshoot
nodes.summary: Outflow lag → STOP inflow, manual clear, urology if not resolved; don\u2019t overdistend.
nodes.body: Stop the irrigation inflow immediately. Continuing to instill fluid into a non-draining bladder risks overdistension and perforation. 1. Manually aspirate the catheter with a Toomey syringe to clear an obstructing clot. 2. Check the catheter is not kinked and the balloon is not displaced into the urethra. 3. If outflow does not promptly recover, or you suspect bladder injury (severe pain, low retu
nodes.recommendation: Outflow lagging inflow: STOP, manually clear, escalate to urology if not promptly resolved.

nodes.title: Disposition + Hematuria Workup
nodes.summary: Admit/observe; mandatory urology follow-up for all gross-hematuria clot retention.
nodes.body: CBI running well with clearing effluent: - Admit for ongoing CBI and monitoring in most clot-retention cases; brisk or persistent bleeding warrants urology involvement and possible intervention (cystoscopic fulguration, intravesical agents). - All gross hematuria with clot retention needs urologic follow-up even if it clears — to evaluate for malignancy and source. See Urology Escalation + Hematur
nodes.recommendation: Admit/observe with CBI; ensure urologic follow-up for all clot-retention hematuria.

nodes.title: COPD Exacerbation: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Target SpO2 88-92% NOT higher — hyperoxia worsens V/Q mismatch and CO2 retention
nodes.body: Acute Exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) - acute worsening of respiratory symptoms requiring additional therapy. Cardinal Symptoms (Anthonisen Criteria): - Increased dyspnea - Increased sputum volume - Increased sputum purulence Common Triggers: - Viral infection (50-70%) - Bacterial infection (30-50%) - Environmental pollutants - Medication non-adherence - Unknown (30%) Initial Actions: 1. IV access,

nodes.title: AECOPD Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Rome classification: mild (SpO2 >92%), moderate (88-92%, accessory muscles), severe (SpO2 <88%, AMS)

nodes.title: Mild AECOPD: Outpatient Management
nodes.summary: Mild: outpatient — prednisone 40mg PO x5 days (no taper), consider azithromycin or doxycycline
nodes.body: Mild exacerbation - often managed outpatient: Bronchodilators: - Increase SABA frequency (albuterol MDI 4-8 puffs q4h) - Add SAMA if not already using (ipratropium MDI 2 puffs q4h) Systemic Corticosteroids: - Prednisone 40 mg PO daily x 5 days - No taper needed for 5-day course Antibiotics: - Consider if 2+ cardinal symptoms WITH purulent sputum - Azithromycin 500 mg PO x 3 days OR - Doxycycline 1

nodes.title: Moderate AECOPD: ED Treatment
nodes.summary: Moderate: nebs q4-6h + methylpred 125mg IV + target SpO2 88-92% — reassess for BiPAP in 1-2h
nodes.body: Moderate exacerbation - requires ED treatment: Simultaneous interventions: 1. Oxygen Therapy: - Target SpO2 88-92% (not higher!) - Hyperoxia worsens V/Q mismatch and CO2 retention 2. Nebulized Bronchodilators: - Albuterol 2.5-5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized - Schedule q4-6h, PRN albuterol q2h - Can give through BiPAP without removing mask 3. Systemic Corticosteroids: - Methylprednisolone 125 m

nodes.title: Response to Initial Treatment
nodes.summary: Reassess at 1-2h: RR improving, less accessory muscle use = good; still distressed = start BiPAP
nodes.body: Reassess at 1-2 hours: Good Response: - RR improving (<24) - Less accessory muscle use - Patient more comfortable - SpO2 maintained 88-92% on low-flow O2 Partial/No Response: - RR still >24-28 - Persistent accessory muscle use - Worsening or unchanged dyspnea - Rising CO2 or respiratory acidosis What is the response?

nodes.title: Severe AECOPD: Immediate Interventions
nodes.summary: Severe: start BiPAP NOW 10/5 titrate to 18-20/8 — do NOT delay for ABG, give nebs through BiPAP
nodes.body: Severe exacerbation - imminent respiratory failure: Immediate simultaneous actions: 1. BiPAP - Start NOW: - Initial: 10 cm iPAP / 5 cm ePAP - Titrate to: 18-20 cm iPAP / 8 cm ePAP - FiO2 to target SpO2 88-92% 2. Nebulized bronchodilators: - Albuterol + Ipratropium through BiPAP - Continuous albuterol 10-15 mg/hr if severe 3. IV Methylprednisolone: - 125 mg IV push 4. IV Magnesium (if refractory):

nodes.title: Bronchodilator Therapy
nodes.summary: Albuterol + ipratropium nebulized q4-6h — combination superior to either alone, can give through BiPAP
nodes.body: SABA + SAMA Combination: Nebulized (preferred in acute setting): - Albuterol 2.5-5 mg + Ipratropium 0.5 mg - DuoNeb = combination product - Schedule: q4-6h, with albuterol q2h PRN MDI with spacer (equally effective): - Albuterol 4-8 puffs + Ipratropium 2-4 puffs - May be difficult in severe respiratory distress Key Points: - Combination SABA + SAMA superior to either alone [7] - Can deliver throug

nodes.title: Systemic Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: Prednisone 40mg PO daily x 5 days — no taper needed, longer courses offer no additional benefit
nodes.body: Systemic steroids improve outcomes in AECOPD: - Shorten recovery time - Improve FEV1 and oxygenation - Reduce treatment failure - Reduce hospitalization duration [8] GOLD 2024 Recommendation: - Prednisone 40 mg PO daily x 5 days - No taper needed - Longer courses offer no additional benefit Severe/ICU patients: - Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV initially - If critically ill: 125 mg IV daily x 1-2 day

nodes.title: Antibiotic Indications
nodes.summary: Antibiotics if purulent sputum + 1 other cardinal symptom OR on NIV — not routine for all exacerbations
nodes.body: When to use antibiotics in AECOPD: Anthonisen Criteria (GOLD 2024): - 3 cardinal symptoms (dyspnea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) OR - 2 cardinal symptoms IF one is purulent sputum OR - Requires mechanical ventilation (NIV or invasive) Point System: | Symptom | Points | |---------|--------| | Increased dyspnea | 1 | | Increased sputum volume | 1 | | Purulent sputum | 2 | Antibiotics indicated i

nodes.title: Antibiotic Selection - Standard
nodes.summary: Uncomplicated: azithromycin 500mg x 3d or doxycycline 100mg BID x 5d — narrow spectrum sufficient
nodes.body: Uncomplicated AECOPD: Age <65, no cardiac disease, <3 exacerbations/year, FEV1 >50% First-Line Options (5 days): - Azithromycin 500 mg PO daily x 3 days - Preferred if not recent use - Long half-life provides 7+ days coverage - Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 5 days - Excellent tolerability - Low C. difficile risk - Good H. influenzae coverage - Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID x 5 days - Goo

nodes.title: Antibiotic Selection - ICU/Complicated
nodes.summary: Complicated/ICU: levofloxacin 750mg daily; Pseudomonas risk: pip-tazo or cefepime
nodes.body: Complicated AECOPD (any of): - Age >65 - FEV1 <50% predicted - >=3 exacerbations/year - Cardiac comorbidity - Recent antibiotic use - Recent hospitalization Consider Pseudomonas coverage if: - Frequent antibiotic exposure - Recent hospitalization - Severe COPD (FEV1 <30%) - Prior Pseudomonas isolation Standard Complicated: - Levofloxacin 750 mg PO/IV daily x 5 days OR - Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875

nodes.title: NIV (BiPAP) Indications
nodes.summary: BiPAP reduces intubation (NNT 4) and mortality (NNT 10) — start if RR >30 or respiratory acidosis
nodes.body: BiPAP strongly recommended in AECOPD with: - Respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45) - Severe dyspnea with signs of increased work of breathing - Respiratory rate >30/min - Hypercapnic encephalopathy (somnolence from CO2) - Persistent hypoxemia despite supplemental O2 Evidence for BiPAP: - Reduces intubation (RR 0.41, NNT 4) - Reduces mortality (RR 0.52, NNT 10) - Reduces complications [10] Con

nodes.title: BiPAP Management
nodes.summary: Start 10/5, titrate to 18-20/8 — dexmedetomidine for intolerance (no respiratory depression)
nodes.body: Initial BiPAP Settings: - iPAP: 10 cm H2O - ePAP: 5 cm H2O - FiO2: Titrate to SpO2 88-92% Titration: - Increase iPAP by 2-3 cm every 5-10 min - Target: iPAP 18-20 cm / ePAP 8 cm - Max practical: ~20 cm iPAP / 8-10 cm ePAP Monitoring on BiPAP: - Tidal volume >300-400 mL - Minute ventilation >5-6 L/min - Respiratory rate trending down - Patient comfort and synchrony Sedation for BiPAP intolerance: -

nodes.title: BiPAP Response Assessment
nodes.summary: pH should improve within 2h on BiPAP — if no improvement, prepare for intubation
nodes.body: Assess at 1-2 hours: Improvement on BiPAP: - pH improving (should see change by 2 hours) - PaCO2 trending down - RR decreasing - Less accessory muscle use - Patient more alert/comfortable Failure of BiPAP: - pH <7.25 or worsening - Rising PaCO2 - Persistent tachypnea >30 - Worsening mental status - Hemodynamic instability - Unable to tolerate despite sedation Key principle: Improvement in pH and P

nodes.title: Continue BiPAP - Weaning Plan
nodes.summary: Improving on BiPAP — wean gradually over 24-48h, avoid continuous >48h (nasal ulceration)
nodes.body: Patient improving on BiPAP: Continue therapy: - Maintain current BiPAP settings - Continue scheduled bronchodilators through BiPAP - Complete steroid course - Antibiotics if indicated Weaning approach: - Avoid continuous BiPAP >48 hours (nasal ulceration) - Trial breaks as tolerated (meals, communication) - Gradually reduce support over 24-48 hours - Step down: BiPAP -> HFNC -> NC When to attempt

nodes.title: HFNC: Now Formally Endorsed (GOLD 2026)
nodes.summary: GOLD 2026 endorses HFNC for hypercapnic AECOPD failing/intolerant of NIV — flow 30-60 L/min, FiO2 to SpO2 88-92%
nodes.body: High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC): GOLD 2026 update: HFNC is now formally endorsed as a salvage or comfort option for hypercapnic AECOPD patients who fail or cannot tolerate NIV (BiPAP). Previously HFNC was off-label/adjunctive; GOLD 2026 elevates it into the official escalation pathway. [13] Use when: - BiPAP contraindicated (vomiting, facial issues) - BiPAP failed or not tolerated (GOLD 2026 Level

nodes.title: Intubation - Last Resort
nodes.summary: Ketamine preferred for induction (bronchodilation) — low RR to prevent auto-PEEP, have NE ready
nodes.body: Intubation in AECOPD - proceed if: - NIV contraindicated or failed - Respiratory arrest - Unable to protect airway - Multiorgan failure/shock - Deteriorating despite maximal NIV Pre-intubation considerations: Hemodynamics: - Optimize with fluids/vasopressors before intubation - These patients crash with induction Induction agents: - Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV (bronchodilation, BP preserved) - Propofol

nodes.title: Ventilator Management in COPD
nodes.summary: Low RR 12-14 for long expiratory time — permissive hypercapnia target pH 7.25-7.35, not normal CO2
