nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: ICU if on BiPAP/intubated; floor if stable on low-flow O2; discharge if returned to baseline
nodes.body: Determine appropriate level of care: ICU Admission: - Requiring NIV (BiPAP) - Intubated/mechanically ventilated - Hemodynamic instability - Altered mental status - Refractory hypoxemia Telemetry/Floor: - Moderate exacerbation responding to treatment - Stable on low-flow O2 (SpO2 88-92%) - No NIV requirement - Stable mental status Observation (if available): - Mild-moderate responding well - May be

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU for BiPAP or mechanical ventilation — ABG q4-6h, respiratory therapy q4-6h, wean as tolerated
nodes.body: ICU admission for severe AECOPD: Continue: - BiPAP or mechanical ventilation - Scheduled bronchodilators - Steroids (methylprednisolone 125 mg IV daily x 1-2 days, then PO) - Antibiotics if indicated Orders: - Continuous SpO2, cardiac monitoring - ABG/VBG q4-6h until stable - Respiratory therapy q4-6h - NPO if on BiPAP/intubated - DVT prophylaxis - Stress ulcer prophylaxis if intubated Consults: -
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for BiPAP or mechanical ventilation. Continue bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics. Goal: wean respiratory support, identify precipitant.

nodes.title: Telemetry/Floor Admission
nodes.summary: Nebs q4-6h, prednisone 5d, check eos — GOLD 2026: LABA/LAMA + triple if eos ≥300, RSV vax ≥50
nodes.body: Floor admission for moderate AECOPD: Orders: - Supplemental O2 to SpO2 88-92% - Albuterol + Ipratropium neb q4-6h scheduled, albuterol q2h PRN - Prednisone 40 mg PO daily (5-day total course) - Antibiotics if indicated - Continue home maintenance inhalers - Check blood eosinophil count on admission (GOLD 2026 — guides discharge maintenance therapy) Monitoring: - SpO2 checks q4h - RR assessment - E

nodes.title: ED Discharge - Mild AECOPD (GOLD 2026 Updated)
nodes.summary: GOLD 2026: LABA/LAMA after 1 exacerbation; eos ≥300 → triple therapy; dupi/mepo Level A; RSV vaccine ≥50
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: - Mild exacerbation - Returned to baseline or near-baseline - SpO2 >90% on room air (or baseline O2) - Able to take oral medications - Reliable follow-up - Adequate home support Discharge medications: - Prednisone 40 mg PO daily x 5 days - Increase SABA frequency as needed - Antibiotics if criteria met (azithromycin 500 mg x 3d OR doxycycline 100 mg BID x 5d) - Continue home ma
nodes.recommendation: ED discharge with 5-day prednisone, increased bronchodilators, antibiotics if indicated. GOLD 2026: initiate/escalate LABA/LAMA after this single exacerbation; if blood eos ≥300 → LABA/LAMA/ICS triple therapy and consider biologics referral

nodes.title: Cord Emergencies
nodes.summary: Four pathways: prolapse, nuchal cord, vasa previa, accident. Page OB/Anesthesia/NICU now.
nodes.body: Cord Emergencies Steps Summary — quick-reference overview of all four pathways. Cord emergencies are time-critical obstetric events — recognition → decompression/repositioning → emergent delivery determines neonatal outcome. This consult covers four ED scenarios: • Module 1: Triage — identify which cord emergency you face • Module 2: Umbilical Cord Prolapse — positioning, manual elevation, bladder

nodes.title: Which Cord Emergency?
nodes.body: Identify the presentation to choose the pathway. Palpable or visible cord after ROM → Umbilical cord prolapse (1 in 200–500 deliveries, 9× rise in perinatal mortality if untreated). [1] At delivery, cord around fetal neck after head delivers → Nuchal cord (~20–35% of deliveries — most benign, but tight/locked cords need careful management). [8][9] Painless vaginal bleeding + ROM + sinusoidal or br

nodes.title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse
nodes.summary: Overt vs occult prolapse — 50% iatrogenic. Examine vaginally within 5 min of any ROM with FHR changes.
nodes.body: Cord Prolapse Algorithm — full decision tree in one view. Definitions: • Overt prolapse — cord past presenting part with ROM; visible at introitus or palpable on vaginal exam • Occult prolapse — cord alongside presenting part; suspect with recurrent severe variable decelerations after ROM • Funic (cord) presentation — cord below presenting part with intact membranes; will become overt with ROM Epi

nodes.title: Call for Help — Mobilize OR
nodes.summary: Page OB, Anesthesia, NICU, OR team. DDI goal <30 min. Do not leave patient.
nodes.body: PAGE NOW: • OB — decision-to-delivery goal <30 min (RCOG); many centers target <15 min [1] • Anesthesia — STAT, for general or spinal • NICU / Neonatology — prepared for resuscitation at delivery • OR team — open the room, call the surgical tech Activate massive transfusion protocol if maternal bleeding (abruption or uterine rupture comorbidity). Do NOT leave the patient. One provider maintains ma

nodes.title: Maternal Positioning
nodes.summary: Knee-chest OR left-lat Trendelenburg. ALWAYS ≥15° left tilt. NEVER supine.
nodes.body: Knee-Chest & Positioning Guide — overlay with images. Position the patient to use gravity to decompress the cord. Three equivalent options: 1. Knee-chest (genupectoral) — most gravity assistance; face down with buttocks elevated. Best for stationary OR prep. 2. Trendelenburg with left lateral tilt — head-down, 15–30° tilt. Best for transport and maintaining IV access. 3. Exaggerated Sims — left la

nodes.title: Manual Elevation of Presenting Part
nodes.summary: Fingers in vagina, push presenting part cephalad continuously. Keep cord warm & moist. NEVER reduce cord.
nodes.body: Gloved hand in vagina — lift presenting part off the cord. Continuous pressure with fingers in the vagina, pushing the fetal presenting part (head, breech, shoulder) cephalad to keep it off the cord. Maintain continuously — do NOT remove your hand, including during transport to the OR, until the fetus is delivered. Cord handling rules: • Minimize handling — touching the cord causes vasospasm • If

nodes.title: Bladder Filling (Vago Procedure)
nodes.summary: Foley + 500-750 mL warm NS, clamp. Elevates presenting part, reduces contractions. Drain before skin incision.
nodes.body: The Vago technique (1970) frees the provider's hand, elevates the presenting part, and reduces uterine contractility — lifesaving adjunct when C-section is delayed (rural transfer, OR not ready). [5] Technique: 1. Insert 16F Foley catheter 2. Instill 500–750 mL warm normal saline via catheter 3. Clamp the catheter to retain 4. Elevates presenting part ~3–5 cm 5. Reduces contraction frequency (blad

nodes.title: Tocolysis for In-Utero Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Terbutaline 0.25 mg SC first-line. NTG 50-100 mcg IV fastest. Mag TOO SLOW for acute cord.
nodes.body: Tocolysis Dosing Guide — full comparative table. Indications: in-utero resuscitation during OR prep, transport, or when delivery is delayed. Relaxes uterus → improves placental perfusion and reduces cord compression. First-line — Terbutaline: Terbutaline 0.25 mg SC or IM × 1. Onset 1–5 min, duration 15–30 min. Watch maternal HR, glucose, K+. Avoid if maternal HR >120. [2] Fastest onset — Nitroglyc

nodes.title: Can the Patient Reach the OR Safely?
nodes.body: Disposition depends on dilation, fetal station, and available resources. OR within 30 minutes available? → emergent C-section remains standard of care. Fully dilated, vertex, presenting part at +2 or lower, skilled provider present, and delivery imminent (<5 min)? → operative vaginal delivery by experienced provider may be faster than C-section — but do NOT delay transfer to OR if delivery is not

nodes.title: Emergent Cesarean Section
nodes.body: Cord prolapse → Category 1 C-section. Target decision-to-delivery interval <30 minutes (RCOG); many centers achieve <15 min. [1][12] Anesthesia: • Spinal acceptable IF fetus stable on manual elevation and placement does not delay delivery • General anesthesia if fetus unstable or spinal attempts delaying delivery At delivery: • NICU team present — neonate often needs resuscitation (review NRP if n
nodes.recommendation: Category 1 C-section. DDI <30 min. NICU at delivery. Drain bladder before skin incision. Maintain manual elevation until delivery.

nodes.title: Assisted Vaginal Delivery
nodes.body: Only if ALL of the following: • Fully dilated (10 cm) and completely effaced • Vertex presentation, +2 station or lower • Experienced provider (operative delivery skilled) • Delivery genuinely imminent <5 min • Head engaged If any criterion missing → C-section. Do not "try" vaginal delivery as a temporizing measure. Proceed: • Vacuum or forceps assisted delivery to minimize cord compression time •
nodes.recommendation: Operative vaginal delivery ONLY if fully dilated, +2 vertex, experienced provider, imminent <5 min. Otherwise C-section.

nodes.title: Nuchal Cord — Palpate After Head Delivers
nodes.summary: Sweep finger around neck after head delivers. Type A unlocked (easy) vs Type B locked (risky).
nodes.body: Nuchal cord — umbilical cord looped around the fetal neck. Present in ~20–35% of all deliveries; most clinically insignificant. Tight nuchal cords (unable to slip over head) occur in ~6%. [8][9] After the head delivers (before shoulder delivery): • Sweep index finger around the neck to palpate for cord • Identify the number of loops (single vs multiple) • Assess tightness and whether it can be red

nodes.title: Loose, Tight but Reducible, or Too Tight?
nodes.body: Assess reducibility before proceeding with shoulder delivery. Loose → easily slipped over head with finger sweep Tight but reducible → can slip over shoulder with front-to-back maneuver (gently loop the cord over the shoulder that is about to deliver) Too tight to slip in either direction → perform somersault maneuver — do NOT cut first. Cutting a tight nuchal cord before delivery commits you to r

nodes.title: Somersault Maneuver
nodes.summary: Head flexed to thigh → deliver shoulders → body somersaults up → unwind AFTER delivery. Preserves placental transfusion.
nodes.body: Somersault Maneuver Step-by-Step — overlay with full technique and rationale. Schaefer (1987) / Mercer (2005) technique — for tight nuchal cord that cannot be slipped. Preferred over clamp-and-cut when possible. [6][7] Steps: 1. Keep fetal head flexed and close to mother's thigh / perineum — chin to chest 2. Deliver the anterior shoulder with gentle downward traction as usual 3. Deliver the poster

nodes.title: Clamp and Cut — Last Resort Only
nodes.summary: LAST RESORT. Double clamp + cut. Commits to immediate delivery. Prepare for neonatal volume resus.
nodes.body: WARNING: Only if somersault maneuver has failed and delivery cannot otherwise progress. Commits you to immediate, unobstructed delivery — if shoulder dystocia then develops, the fetus has no placental circulation → acute hypoxia and anemia. Technique (only if committed): 1. Double-clamp the cord with two Kelly clamps, close together 2. Cut between the clamps with sterile scissors 3. Deliver immedi

nodes.title: Proceed with Delivery
nodes.summary: Continue per Precip Delivery. Skin-to-skin, APGAR, delayed clamping if vigorous.
nodes.body: Cord managed — continue with delivery per standard steps. Cross-link: Precipitous Delivery consult — for shoulder delivery, cord clamping (delayed 30–60 sec if vigorous), neonatal assessment (APGAR), placenta delivery, oxytocin, and postpartum monitoring. After delivery of the baby: • Unwind any cord loops that remain • Skin-to-skin with mother unless resuscitation needed • Delayed cord clamping 3

nodes.title: Nuchal Cord — Managed
nodes.body: Nuchal cord managed with appropriate technique (slip, somersault, or last-resort clamp/cut). Post-delivery assessment: • Neonatal APGAR at 1 and 5 min; 10 min if <7 • Document: number of loops, tightness, maneuver used, any complications • Maternal: standard postpartum — uterine tone, lacerations, bleeding • Placental exam: cord length, vessel count (2 arteries + 1 vein), true knots Continue with:
nodes.recommendation: Document technique and complications. Continue Stage 3 per Precip Delivery consult. Placental exam for cord abnormalities.

nodes.title: Vasa Previa — Known Antenatal Diagnosis?
nodes.body: Disposition depends on whether diagnosis is known before presentation. Antenatal diagnosis: transvaginal US with color Doppler identifies fetal vessels crossing over or within 2 cm of the internal cervical os, typically 2nd trimester. Patients usually have scheduled C-section at 34–37 weeks. [3][4] Undiagnosed acute presentation: classic triad after ROM: 1. Painless vaginal bleeding (fetal blood —

nodes.title: Known Vasa Previa — Delivery Plan
nodes.summary: Planned C/S 34-37 wk. Steroids 28-32 wk. STAT C/S if ROM or labor.
nodes.body: Planned C-section at 34 0/7 – 37 0/7 weeks per SMFM Consult Series #37 (2015). [4] Antenatal management (outpatient or inpatient): • Antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity at 28–32 wks (betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2 doses, 24 hrs apart) • Some centers hospitalize at 30–34 wks for continuous monitoring and rapid C-section if ROM • Avoid digital cervical exam and amniotomy — rupturing membranes ov

nodes.title: Acute Vasa Previa — STAT C-Section
nodes.summary: STAT C/S. O-neg neonatal blood. NO digital exam. NO amniotomy. General anesthesia fastest.
nodes.body: Every minute matters. Fetal blood volume 80–100 mL/kg — exsanguination in minutes. [3] Immediate actions (simultaneous): • Page OB, Anesthesia, NICU — activate massive transfusion (neonatal side) • Prepare neonatal blood: O-negative, CMV-negative, irradiated, 10 mL/kg ready at delivery • Maternal large-bore IV × 2, type & crossmatch (maternal type), notify blood bank • High-flow O2 10 L/min NRB •

nodes.title: Apt Test — Fetal vs Maternal Blood
nodes.summary: Pink=fetal Hgb (vasa previa). Brown=maternal. Do NOT delay C/S for results.
nodes.body: Bedside test to differentiate fetal from maternal hemoglobin — faster than Kleihauer-Betke, doable in ED in ~2 minutes. Apt-Downey (1955). [14] Technique: 1. Mix the bloody fluid with a small amount of water in a test tube (hemolyzes RBCs) 2. Centrifuge briefly 3. Transfer 5 mL supernatant to a new tube 4. Add 1 mL of 1% KOH (potassium hydroxide) to the supernatant 5. Wait 1–2 minutes, observe col

nodes.title: Vasa Previa — Emergent Delivery
nodes.body: Vasa previa = STAT Category 1 C-section when acute, planned C-section at 34–37 wk when antenatally diagnosed. Outcomes: • Undiagnosed: fetal mortality ~56% [3] • Antenatally diagnosed and planned: fetal mortality <3% [3][4] At delivery: • Neonatal blood ready: 10 mL/kg O-negative, CMV-negative, irradiated • Cord blood gas and CBC • NICU admission — high risk for severe anemia, HIE, transfusion req
nodes.recommendation: Category 1 C-section. Neonatal O-neg blood 10 mL/kg at bedside. NICU admission. Cord blood gas + CBC.

nodes.title: Cord Accident / True Knot — Recognition
nodes.summary: Unexplained fetal brady ddx: cord compression, occult prolapse, abruption, rupture, maternal hypotension, tachysystole.
nodes.body: Unexplained sudden fetal bradycardia in active labor without visible cord, abruption, or uterine rupture → consider cord accident: true knot, nuchal/body entanglement, cord compression. [11] Differential for fetal bradycardia: • Cord compression — nuchal, body entanglement, true knot, cord around limb • Cord prolapse (occult) — re-examine vagina immediately • Placental abruption — painful bleeding

nodes.title: In-Utero Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Left tilt, O2, fluids, STOP oxytocin, vaginal exam for occult prolapse, tocolysis. No improvement in 5-10 min → deliver.
nodes.body: Goal: restore fetal perfusion and oxygenation while determining etiology and planning delivery. Many cases resolve with resuscitation if recognized early. Simultaneous actions: 1. Positioning — left lateral tilt ≥15°; trial right lateral or knee-chest if not improving. 2. Maternal oxygen — 10 L/min non-rebreather mask. 3. IV fluid bolus — 500 mL – 1 L crystalloid; corrects maternal hypotension fro

nodes.title: Monoamniotic Twin Cord Entanglement
nodes.summary: All mono-mono twins entangled. Planned C/S 32-34 wk. STAT C/S if fetal brady at any GA.
nodes.body: All monoamniotic-monochorionic (mono-mono) twins have cord entanglement. Historical stillbirth rate 30–70%; now 10–20% with intensive antenatal surveillance. [15] Standard management: • Inpatient admission with continuous FHR monitoring from 24–28 weeks • Antenatal corticosteroids at 28 weeks for lung maturity • Planned C-section at 32 0/7 – 34 0/7 weeks (ACOG/SMFM) [15] If mono-mono twin pregnanc

nodes.title: Cord Accident — Disposition
nodes.body: Path forward depends on response to in-utero resuscitation: Resuscitation successful (FHR normalizes): • Continue monitoring, investigate and treat reversible causes (tachysystole, hypotension) • Consider operative vs expectant management per cervical exam • OB consult — may need to proceed with delivery if recurrent Resuscitation fails OR recurrent events: • Category 1 or 2 C-section depending on
nodes.recommendation: Respond to resuscitation → continue monitoring with investigation. Fails/recurs → Category 1/2 C-section. Always inspect cord at delivery.

nodes.summary: Burr same-day OR defer 24-48h to ophthalmology; do not chase rust into stroma
nodes.body: Metallic FB (most often steel from grinding) oxidizes within hours and leaves a rust ring even after the FB itself is removed. The rust is corneal injury and must come out — but timing matters. Options: 1. Same-day removal with ophthalmic burr (Algerbrush) — preferred when available. nodes.title: Post-Removal Care

nodes.title: Disposition & Follow-up
nodes.summary: Discharge with abx drops, 24-48h follow-up for rust/contact lens/vegetative, return for vision change
nodes.body: Most patients discharge with primary care or optometry follow-up. Ophthalmology referral is for specific situations.
nodes.recommendation: Discharge criteria: • Successful FB removal • Symptoms improving (post-anesthesia pain expected for 24-48h as epithelium heals) • VA at baseline or better • Antibiotic drops/ointment prescribed • Patient understands return precautions Follo

nodes.title: Refer to Ophthalmology
nodes.summary: Central/vegetative/persistent rust/contact lens infiltrate/decreased VA = ophthalmology
nodes.body: Specific situations require ophthalmology referral rather than ED removal.
nodes.recommendation: Refer (urgent or emergent) for: • Central or visual-axis FB — scar risk • Penetrating or deep FB (any concern for partial-thickness perforation) • Multiple FBs or contaminated wound • Vegetative material (plant, wood) — fungal risk • Persis

nodes.title: CRAO: Stroke of the Eye
nodes.summary: CRAO is a CNS stroke — 30%+ have concurrent cerebral ischemia, stroke risk peaks days 1-7
nodes.body: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion = CNS Infarction (Stroke) Per AHA/ASA, CRAO is classified as a central nervous system stroke. Why This Matters: - 30%+ have concurrent cerebral ischemia - Risk of cerebral stroke peaks 1-7 days post-CRAO - Same embolic sources as stroke (carotid, cardiac) - Same time-critical treatment window Classic Presentation: - Painless (pain = think GCA) - Sudden (seconds to

nodes.title: Symptom Onset
nodes.summary: Document precise onset time — retinal damage irreversible at 90-100 min, tPA window 4.5h
nodes.body: When did vision loss begin? Precise timing is critical for treatment decisions. If patient woke with symptoms, use "last known well" time.

nodes.title: Key Examination
nodes.summary: APD present in 92-98% — if NO APD with complete vision loss, reconsider the diagnosis
nodes.body: 1. Visual Acuity: - Often counting fingers (CF) or hand motion (HM) - May be light perception (LP) or no light perception (NLP) - Document in affected and unaffected eye 2. nodes.summary: Cherry-red spot in 90% — pale retina from ischemic swelling, fovea visible through thin retinal layers

nodes.title: Confirm Diagnosis
nodes.summary: APD + cherry-red spot + sudden painless monocular loss = classic CRAO — proceed to GCA evaluation
nodes.body: Does exam support CRAO? Required: - APD present - Fundoscopic findings consistent - Painless, sudden, monocular

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: CRAO is painless — pain suggests GCA or optic neuritis; bilateral suggests cortical stroke

nodes.title: Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion
nodes.summary: Branch RAO: partial field loss, 80% recover to 20/40 — still requires stroke workup and admission
nodes.body: BRAO — Partial Vision Loss: Presentation: - Altitudinal or sectoral field defect - May be asymptomatic if small area - Less severe vision loss than CRAO Fundoscopy: - Whitening along distribution of occluded branch - May see embolus at bifurcation - Cherry-red spot usually absent Management: - Less emergent than CRAO - Still requires stroke workup - Same embolic sources - Same admission criteria P

nodes.title: GCA Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Must rule out GCA in ALL patients ≥50 — arteritic CRAO needs steroids, NOT tPA
nodes.body: Is the patient ≥50 years old? Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) can cause CRAO via arteritic mechanism. GCA-CRAO requires steroids, NOT tPA. Must rule out GCA in ALL patients ≥50.

nodes.title: GCA Symptom Evaluation
nodes.summary: Jaw claudication most specific (LR+ 4.2) — both ESR + CRP elevated = 99% sensitive for GCA
nodes.body: GCA Symptoms to Ask About: | Symptom | Sensitivity | |---------|-------------| | Headache (new) | 76% | | Scalp tenderness | 34% | | Jaw claudication | 50% | | Temporal artery abnormality | 65% | | Polymyalgia symptoms | 40% | | Constitutional (fever, weight loss, fatigue) | 40% | Jaw Claudication: - Pain/fatigue with chewing - Most specific symptom (LR+ = 4.2) Key Exam: - Palpate temporal arterie

nodes.title: GCA Suspicion
nodes.summary: If GCA suspected, start IV methylprednisolone 1000mg immediately — do NOT wait for biopsy
nodes.body: Is there clinical suspicion for GCA? High suspicion if: - Jaw claudication present - Temporal artery abnormality - PMR symptoms - Constitutional symptoms + headache - ESR/CRP markedly elevated

nodes.title: Arteritic CRAO (GCA)
nodes.summary: IV methylpred 1000mg daily x 3-5d — fellow eye at risk (25-50% bilateral within days-weeks)
nodes.body: ⚠️ GCA-CRAO: START STEROIDS IMMEDIATELY ⚠️ Do NOT give tPA for arteritic CRAO. High-Dose IV Methylprednisolone: - 1000 mg IV daily × 3-5 days - Then transition to oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day Why Immediate Treatment? - Fellow eye at risk (25-50% bilateral within days-weeks) - Steroids prevent fellow eye involvement - DO NOT wait for biopsy to start treatment Temporal Artery Biopsy: - Should be done

nodes.title: GCA Uncertain
nodes.summary: When uncertain: start steroids empirically — risk of fellow eye loss outweighs steroid risks
nodes.body: If uncertain about GCA: Labs to Send: - ESR (stat) - CRP (stat) - CBC with platelets Consider starting steroids if: - ESR significantly elevated (>50) - Clinical features suggestive - Risk of fellow eye involvement high Can give steroids AND tPA? - Controversial - If GCA ruled out, tPA is appropriate - If GCA confirmed, tPA not indicated (inflammatory, not embolic) When in doubt: - Start IV methyl

nodes.title: Activate Stroke Protocol
nodes.summary: Activate code stroke — CT head, labs, ECG; do NOT delay for ocular massage or eye drops
nodes.body: CRAO = Stroke Emergency Immediate Actions: 1. Stroke Alert — Activate code stroke 2. CT Head — Rule out hemorrhage before tPA 3. Labs: - CBC, BMP, coags, glucose - ESR, CRP, platelets (GCA screen if ≥50) 4. ECG — AFib screening 5. IV Access — For potential tPA Consults: - Neurology/Stroke team (primary) - Ophthalmology (diagnosis confirmation) Do NOT Delay for: - Ocular massage - Eye drops - Parac

nodes.title: tPA Decision
nodes.summary: tPA candidate if ≤4.5h, non-arteritic, no contraindications, CT negative — same as stroke protocol
nodes.body: Is patient a candidate for IV tPA? Requirements: - Symptom onset ≤4.5 hours - GCA ruled out (non-arteritic CRAO) - No contraindications to tPA - CT head negative for hemorrhage Note: Same contraindications as stroke tPA.

nodes.title: IV tPA for CRAO
nodes.summary: tPA 0.9 mg/kg (max 90mg) within 4.5h — 2026 AHA/ASA Class 2b/C-LD (uncertain benefit); THEIA + TenCRAOS RCTs negative; aspirin 300 mg PO is a reasonable alternative pending REVISION

nodes.title: Cricothyrotomy — CICO Decision
nodes.summary: CICO = cannot intubate + cannot oxygenate — do NOT delay; cognitive paralysis kills
nodes.body: Scalpel-Finger-Bougie Steps CICO = Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate This is a FAILED AIRWAY — the patient cannot be intubated AND cannot be oxygenated by any other means. [1][2] Incidence: 0.06-0.72% prehospital, 0.14-1.4% ED [1] Indications: [1][2] • Failed intubation with declining SpO₂ • Failed supraglottic airway (LMA/iGel) rescue • Massive facial trauma precluding oral/nasal approach • Complet

nodes.title: Contraindications
nodes.summary: Absolute: age <10-12 (use needle cric), laryngeal fracture (need trach); in true CICO, contraindications matter less than death
nodes.body: Absolute contraindications: [1][3][13][14] • Age <10-12 years — cricothyroid membrane too small; use needle cricothyrotomy + jet ventilation [13][14] • Laryngeal fracture or transected airway (need formal tracheostomy) Relative contraindications (proceed with caution): • Coagulopathy (expect more bleeding but proceed if CICO) • Anterior neck mass obscuring anatomy • Previous neck surgery/radiation

nodes.title: Cricothyroid Membrane Anatomy
nodes.summary: CTM = 9mm × 30mm between thyroid and cricoid; use laryngeal handshake from notch DOWN; ignore bleeding — this is tactile
nodes.body: Anatomy Diagram Cricothyroid membrane (CTM): [1][11][12] • Located between thyroid cartilage (above) and cricoid cartilage (below) • Average size: 9 mm height × 30 mm width [12] • Just large enough for a 6.0 ETT (outer diameter 8.2 mm) [12] • Covered by skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia — NO major vessels directly over CTM Source note (basis for the above): the 9 × 30 mm figure is the quoted adul

nodes.title: Equipment
nodes.summary: Essential: #10 scalpel, bougie, 6.0 ETT — that's it; have 5.5 backup for small patients
nodes.body: Equipment Checklist Minimal critical equipment: [1][2][5][9] Essential (the 3 items): 1. #10 or #20 blade scalpel — large blade for horizontal incision 2. Bougie (gum elastic bougie) — guides ETT placement 3. 6.0 cuffed ETT — smaller fits CTM; have 5.5 as backup Why 6.0 ETT? [1][5][9][12] • CTM height is ~9 mm [12] • 6.0 ETT outer diameter = 8.2 mm (fits through CTM) [12] • 5.0-5.5 may be needed i

nodes.title: Patient Positioning
nodes.summary: Neck extended (unless C-spine), operator at side, non-dominant hand stabilizes larynx throughout; US for difficult CTM (DAS 2025)
nodes.body: Optimal positioning: [1][2][15] Standard: • Supine with neck extended (unless C-spine precautions) • Shoulder roll to extend neck and elevate larynx • Operator standing at patient's side (not at head) C-spine precautions: • Maintain neutral alignment • Do NOT hyperextend • May need assistant for manual in-line stabilization • Collar should be opened or removed anteriorly Obese patients: • May need

nodes.title: Step 1: Vertical Skin Incision
nodes.summary: 4cm VERTICAL skin incision from thyroid notch to below cricoid — vertical is more forgiving; IGNORE bleeding
nodes.body: Technique Video SCALPEL-FINGER-BOUGIE technique: [1][2][5][9][15] Stabilize the larynx: • Non-dominant hand: thumb and middle finger grip lateral aspects of thyroid cartilage • Index finger identifies CTM from above (notch down method) • Maintain this grip throughout entire procedure Vertical skin incision: • Make a 4 cm VERTICAL incision through skin • Start above thyroid notch, extend below cric

nodes.title: Step 2: Blunt Dissection & CTM ID
nodes.summary: Blunt dissect with finger until CTM palpated — feels like soft trampoline between thyroid and cricoid cartilage
nodes.body: Identify the cricothyroid membrane: [1][2][5][9][15] After vertical skin incision: • Use finger to bluntly dissect through subcutaneous tissue • Push tissue aside until you palpate the CTM • Feel the firm thyroid cartilage above, cricoid below • CTM feels like a soft "trampoline" between the two Finger palpation is key: • Index finger of non-dominant hand identifies CTM • Maintain laryngeal stabil

nodes.title: Step 3: Horizontal CTM Incision
nodes.summary: HORIZONTAL stab through CTM → rotate blade 90° caudally → remove scalpel → keep finger in hole
nodes.body: Incise the cricothyroid membrane: [1][2][5][9][15] With index finger on CTM: • Make a HORIZONTAL stab incision through the membrane • Use the same #10 scalpel • Incise through the full width of CTM (~2-3 cm) • You will feel a "pop" as you enter the airway Scalpel technique: • Hold scalpel like a pencil • Blade facing down (toward feet) • Stab through membrane, then cut horizontally • Keep incision

nodes.title: Step 4: Bougie Insertion
nodes.summary: Bougie alongside finger into trachea — feel for "clicking" over tracheal rings; hold-up at 15-20cm confirms placement
nodes.body: Insert bougie into trachea: [1][2][5][9][15] Bougie placement: • Slide bougie alongside your finger through the CTM incision • Direct caudally (toward feet) into trachea • Advance approximately 10-15 cm Feel for tracheal rings: • "Clicking" sensation = bougie passing over tracheal cartilage rings • This confirms intratracheal placement • If no clicking, may be in esophagus or false tract Avoid fal

nodes.title: Step 5: ETT Over Bougie
nodes.summary: 6.0 ETT over bougie — advance only until cuff passes incision; right mainstem occurs in 46% if too deep
nodes.body: Railroad ETT over bougie: [1][2][5][9][15] Tube insertion: • Thread 6.0 cuffed ETT over the bougie • Advance until cuff is just past skin incision (not too deep) • ETT should pass 2-3 cm beyond CTM Depth: [1][5] • Do NOT advance far — risk of right mainstem intubation • Cuff should be at or just below CTM • ETT at teeth mark will be inaccurate (no teeth involved) • Final depth typically 2-4 cm pas

nodes.title: Confirm Placement
nodes.summary: Waveform capnography confirms tracheal placement; secure tube, CXR to confirm position and rule out complications
nodes.body: Confirm tracheal placement: [1][2][9][15] Gold standard: • Waveform capnography (ETCO₂) — sustained waveform = tracheal • Color-change CO₂ detector (less reliable in cardiac arrest) Clinical confirmation: • Bilateral breath sounds on auscultation • Chest rise with ventilation • Condensation in ETT • SpO₂ improvement (may be delayed) If NO ETCO₂ / no chest rise: • Deflate cuff, withdraw slightly, r

nodes.title: Post-Procedure Care
nodes.summary: Secure ETT, control bleeding with pressure, consult ENT/surgery for trach conversion within 24-72hr
nodes.body: Immediate post-procedure: [1][3][15] Secure the airway: • Tape or suture ETT to skin • Mark depth at skin level • Avoid excessive movement Control bleeding: • Now that airway is secure, address bleeding • Direct pressure with gauze • Rarely needs more than pressure Ventilation: • Start mechanical ventilation • Lower tidal volumes may be needed (smaller tube = higher resistance) • Monitor airway pr

nodes.title: Complications
nodes.summary: Bleeding 50% (use pressure), right mainstem 46% (don't advance too far), false tract (feel for rings)
nodes.body: Complications Guide Early complications: [1][3][15] Bleeding (most common): • Reported in up to 50% of cases [1] • Usually controlled with direct pressure • Rarely requires ligation or packing • Severe hemorrhage can cause aspiration or asphyxiation Right mainstem intubation: • Up to 46% with ETT (longer than trach tube) [1] • Prevention: advance only until cuff passes CTM • Treatment: withdraw un

nodes.title: Troubleshooting
nodes.summary: Can't find CTM: laryngeal handshake from notch down; bleeding: ignore during procedure; no ETT pass: try smaller tube or rotate
nodes.body: Common problems and solutions: [1][2][5][9][15] Cannot locate CTM: • Use laryngeal handshake from notch DOWN • Make vertical incision longer to expose more tissue • Palpate with finger in wound — feel for soft membrane • In obese patients, may need deeper dissection Too much bleeding: • IGNORE during procedure — tactile, not visual • Rely on palpation for landmarks • Control AFTER airway secured •

nodes.body: Airway secured. Immediate actions: ✓ Confirm ETCO₂ waveform ✓ Secure ETT to skin ✓ Document depth at skin level ✓ Control bleeding with pressure ✓ Obtain chest X-ray ✓ Start mechanical ventilation Consults: • ENT or trauma surgery for tracheostomy planning • Convert to formal trach within 24-72 hours Documentation: • CICO indication • Technique: scalpel-finger-bougie • Tube size: 6.0 ETT • Confirm

nodes.title: Croup — Clinical Recognition
nodes.summary: Parainfluenza causing subglottic inflammation — barking cough, stridor, hoarseness, age 6mo-3yr
nodes.body: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is a parainfluenza viral infection causing subglottic inflammation. Classic presentation: \u2022 Barking "seal-like" cough \u2022 Inspiratory stridor \u2022 Hoarseness \u2022 Low-grade fever \u2022 URI prodrome (1-3 days) Epidemiology: 3% of children aged 6 months to 3 years. nodes.title: Post-Dexamethasone Observation
nodes.summary: Observe 1-2h post-dex — most improve within 2-3h, dex half-life ~36h provides sustained benefit
nodes.body: Observe for 1-2 hours after dexamethasone administration. Most children start feeling better within 2-3 hours of steroid treatment. nodes.title: Fever / Toxic / Young Infant
nodes.body: Open Fever < 6 Months. High-risk signs: age <60 days with fever, hypothermia, ill appearance, lethargy, poor feeding, abnormal perfusion, respiratory distress, petechiae/purpura, bulging fontanelle, seizure, or caregiver report that the infant is not acting right. Follow age-based febrile infant pathway and local protocols. Do not let a transiently consolable exam override abnormal vitals or a hig
nodes.recommendation: Fever or toxic appearance in a young infant is an infectious workup lane, not a colic lane.

nodes.title: Respiratory / Cardiac Cause
nodes.body: Open Bronchiolitis, BRUE, or Neonatal Resuscitation when the phenotype fits. Look for: tachypnea, retractions, grunting, hypoxia, cyanosis, apnea, sweating or fatigue with feeds, hepatomegaly, poor pulses, murmur, shock, or differential saturation/pulses. Crying can be the presenting symptom of hypoxia, heart failure, congenital heart disease, respiratory infection, or metabolic stress.
nodes.recommendation: Respiratory effort, oxygenation, perfusion, pulses, and feeding fatigue decide this lane.

nodes.title: GI Emergency / Obstruction
nodes.body: Open Intussusception when episodic severe crying, leg drawing, vomiting, bloody stool, or lethargy between episodes fits. Do not miss: bilious emesis, volvulus/malrotation, incarcerated hernia, intussusception, constipation with fissure, anal fissure, or feeding intolerance. Actions: NPO for concerning obstruction, IV access if ill/dehydrated, glucose if lethargic, abdominal exam including groin,
nodes.recommendation: Bilious emesis or episodic severe crying with lethargy is an obstruction/intussusception pathway.

nodes.title: GU Emergency
nodes.body: Open Testicular Torsion when a male infant has scrotal swelling, testicular tenderness, high-riding/abnormal lie, discoloration, or unexplained severe distress. Also consider: incarcerated inguinal hernia, UTI/pyelonephritis, urinary retention, labial adhesions with retention, diaper dermatitis, balanitis/vulvovaginitis, and genital hair tourniquet. A diaper-area exam is mandatory in the inconsola
nodes.recommendation: Scrotal/groin/genital findings in a crying infant need immediate GU/hernia thinking.

nodes.title: Trauma / Non-Accidental Trauma
nodes.body: Look for bruising in non-mobile infants, oral frenulum injury, burns, scalp swelling, tenderness with limb movement, rib tenderness, abdominal tenderness, retinal/neuro symptoms, inconsistent or changing story, delay in care, or caregiver impairment. Actions: pain control, protect the child, follow local child-protection pathway, skeletal survey/head imaging/labs as indicated by age and findings,
nodes.recommendation: A crying infant with unexplained injury or unsafe story needs a safety workup, not reassurance.

nodes.title: Occult Pain Source on Full Exam
nodes.body: Completely undress and inspect: - Hair tourniquet: toes, fingers, penis, clitoris/labia. - Corneal abrasion/foreign body: fluorescein if eye redness, tearing, rubbing, photophobia, or unexplained crying. - Mouth: ulcers, thrush, trauma, teething only after dangerous causes excluded. - Ears: otitis media/externa when fever/URI/ear findings fit. - Skin: diaper dermatitis, cellulitis, burns, bites, p
nodes.recommendation: A full head-to-toe undressed exam is a diagnostic test in crying infants.

nodes.title: Neurologic / CNS Concern
nodes.body: Bulging fontanelle, seizure, abnormal tone, persistent lethargy, altered responsiveness, vomiting with neurologic signs, rapidly increasing head circumference, or inconsolability with abnormal exam should trigger CNS infection, intracranial hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, metabolic disease, or trauma thinking. Open VP Shunt Complications if a shunt is present. Use fever, trauma, seizure, and age-based
nodes.recommendation: Neurologic signs with crying should not be called colic.

nodes.title: Feeding / Dehydration / Reflux Mimics
nodes.body: Assess feeding volume/frequency, latch/formula preparation, vomiting, choking/coughing feeds, wet diapers, stooling, weight trend, jaundice, and caregiver technique. Escalate for dehydration, weight loss/failure to gain, bilious emesis, forceful/projectile vomiting, blood in stool, fever, lethargy, hypoglycemia, or unsafe feeding environment. Reflux and formula intolerance are diagnoses after dang
nodes.recommendation: Poor feeding plus crying is a physiology problem until hydration, glucose, and dangerous causes are addressed.

nodes.title: Colic / Benign Crying Pattern
nodes.body: Use this lane only when the infant is well appearing, afebrile, normally perfused, feeding and voiding adequately, gaining weight, has a normal full undressed exam, no trauma/safety concern, and caregivers can return if worse. Typical colic is recurrent crying in an otherwise healthy infant, often evening-predominant. It is a diagnosis of pattern plus normal exam, not a shortcut diagnosis.
nodes.recommendation: Colic is reasonable only after dangerous causes are screened and the caregiver plan is safe.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Rectal temp, vitals, glucose if risky, full undressed exam, feeding/hydration, analgesia, targeted testing, then reassess.
nodes.body: Default ED crying infant bundle: - Rectal temperature and full vitals. - Glucose if ill appearing, poor feeding, lethargic, young infant, or abnormal vitals. - Completely undress; inspect hair tourniquets, eyes, mouth, ears, abdomen/groin, diaper area, extremities, bruising/burns. - Feed observation when stable; assess hydration and caregiver technique. - Analgesia when a painful cause is suspecte

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Persistent inconsolability after a careful exam deserves another pass through dangerous causes.
nodes.body: Can the infant feed, console, maintain vitals, and remain well appearing after initial care?

nodes.title: Imaging / Targeted Workup
nodes.summary: Testing follows the lane: febrile infant, GI obstruction, GU torsion, trauma/NAT, eye, respiratory/cardiac.
nodes.body: Image/test by lane: - Fever/young infant: age-based urine, blood, CSF/inflammatory marker pathway per local protocol. - GI: ultrasound for intussusception; abdominal imaging/surgery for bilious emesis, obstruction, incarcerated hernia. - GU: scrotal ultrasound only if it will not delay surgical consultation for high-suspicion torsion. - Trauma/NAT: skeletal survey, head imaging, abdominal labs/ima

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge requires normal vitals, normal exam, feeding, consolability, and a safe caregiver plan.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on age, vitals, feeding, exam, diagnosis, caregiver reliability, and safety.

nodes.title: Admit / Consult / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit, transfer, or consult for fever/high-risk young infant pathway, ill/toxic appearance, abnormal vitals, poor feeding/dehydration, hypoglycemia, respiratory distress, suspected intussusception/obstruction, incarcerated hernia, torsion, neurologic signs, trauma/NAT concern, unsafe home, or persistent unexplained inconsolability.
nodes.recommendation: Persistent high-risk crying is not a discharge diagnosis.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exam
nodes.body: Observe when symptoms are improving but the infant is not clearly baseline, feeding/hydration needs demonstration, caregiver confidence is low, fever workup is pending, pain source treatment response is uncertain, or serial abdominal/neuro exams are needed.
nodes.recommendation: A period of observation can convert vague crying into a diagnosis or a safe discharge.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when infant is well appearing, afebrile or fever pathway completed, vitals normal, full undressed exam normal or benign source treated, feeding observed or reliable, urine output adequate, caregiver can soothe and return, and safety concerns are absent. Return now for: fever, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, lethargy, breathing trouble, blue color, bilious/green vomiting, blood in s
nodes.recommendation: Document full undressed exam, feeding/hydration, caregiver reliability, and return precautions.

nodes.title: CT Scan Decision Support
nodes.summary: Evidence-based decision support for CT imaging — reduce unnecessary radiation and contrast exposure
nodes.body: CT Decision Support Steps Summary CT imaging is used in 27 per 100 ED encounters — nearly matching ECG usage. An estimated 103,000 new cancers annually may be attributable to CT imaging in the U.S. [1,2] This tool applies validated clinical decision rules to guide CT ordering. Each rule has been prospectively validated in large multicenter studies. Radiation Dose Reference · Special Populations ·

nodes.title: Clinical Scenario
nodes.summary: Clinical Scenario — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Select the body region and clinical concern:

nodes.title: Patient Age
nodes.summary: Patient Age — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Age determines which decision rule applies:

nodes.title: Canadian CT Head Rule — Eligibility
nodes.summary: Canadian CT Head Rule — Eligibility — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: CCHR applies to: Adults ≥16 with minor head injury (GCS 13-15) AND witnessed LOC, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation, within 24 hours. Exclusions: Age <16, no clear trauma history, GCS <13, unstable vitals, obvious open skull fracture, bleeding disorder/anticoagulation, seizure prior to assessment. CCHR Calculator

nodes.title: CCHR — High-Risk Criteria
nodes.summary: CCHR — High-Risk Criteria — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Any HIGH-RISK feature mandates CT (for neurosurgical intervention): 1. GCS < 15 at 2 hours post-injury 2. Suspected open or depressed skull fracture 3. Any sign of basal skull fracture (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, CSF otorrhea/rhinorrhea, Battle sign) 4. Vomiting ≥ 2 episodes 5. Age ≥ 65 years

nodes.title: CCHR — Medium-Risk Criteria
nodes.summary: CCHR — Medium-Risk Criteria — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Any MEDIUM-RISK feature? (for brain injury on CT): 1. Retrograde amnesia ≥ 30 minutes before impact 2. Dangerous mechanism (pedestrian struck, ejected from vehicle, fall > 3 ft or > 5 stairs)

nodes.title: CT Head Indicated
nodes.summary: CT Head Indicated — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: CT head is indicated per Canadian CT Head Rule. Radiation context: Head CT ≈ 2 mSv (20 CXR equivalents, ~4 months background radiation). Cancer risk: ~0.23 per 1,000 patients. [15] Document: Clinical decision rule applied, specific criteria met, clinical indication.
nodes.recommendation: CT head indicated per CCHR. Document high-risk or medium-risk criteria met.

nodes.title: CT Head NOT Indicated
nodes.summary: CT Head NOT Indicated — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: No CT needed per Canadian CT Head Rule — no high-risk or medium-risk criteria met. Performance: High-risk criteria 100% sensitive for neurosurgical intervention. All 7 criteria 98.4% sensitive for clinically important brain injury. [3] Document: CCHR applied with result. Shared decision-making. Return precautions: • Worsening headache • Repeated vomiting • Confusion or difficulty waking • Weakness
nodes.recommendation: CT not indicated per CCHR. Provide return precautions.

nodes.title: CCHR Not Applicable — Clinical Judgment
nodes.summary: CCHR Not Applicable — Clinical Judgment — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: CCHR entry criteria not met. Use clinical judgment. Scenarios where CCHR does not apply: • GCS < 13 → CT indicated regardless • Anticoagulation or bleeding disorder → lower threshold for CT • Seizure prior to assessment → evaluate seizure etiology • Trivial mechanism without LOC/amnesia/disorientation → CT generally not needed • No clear trauma history → consider alternative diagnoses If on antico
nodes.recommendation: CCHR not applicable. Use clinical judgment based on risk factors.

nodes.title: PECARN ≥ 2 Years — High-Risk Features
nodes.summary: PECARN ≥ 2 Years — High-Risk Features — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Does the child have ANY of the following? (4.3% ciTBI risk if present) 1. GCS < 15 or altered mental status (agitation, somnolence, repetitive questioning, slow response) 2. Signs of basilar skull fracture (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, CSF otorrhea/rhinorrhea, Battle sign)

nodes.title: PECARN ≥ 2 Years — Intermediate Criteria
nodes.summary: PECARN ≥ 2 Years — Intermediate Criteria — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Any of the following? (~0.9% ciTBI risk if present) 1. Any loss of consciousness 2. History of vomiting 3. Severe mechanism (MVC with ejection/death of another passenger/rollover, pedestrian or unhelmeted cyclist struck by motorized vehicle, fall > 5 ft / 1.5 m, head struck by high-impact object) 4. Severe headache ⚠️ Fall threshold differs by age: > 5 ft for age ≥ 2 years, > 3 ft for age < 2 year

nodes.title: PECARN < 2 Years — High-Risk Features
nodes.summary: PECARN < 2 Years — High-Risk Features — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Does the infant have ANY of the following? (4.4% ciTBI risk if present) 1. GCS < 15 or altered mental status (agitation, somnolence, repetitive questioning, slow response) 2. Palpable skull fracture

nodes.title: PECARN < 2 Years — Intermediate Criteria
nodes.summary: PECARN < 2 Years — Intermediate Criteria — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Any of the following? (~0.9% ciTBI risk if present) 1. LOC ≥ 5 seconds 2. Non-frontal scalp hematoma (occipital, parietal, or temporal) 3. Severe mechanism (MVC with ejection/death of another passenger/rollover, pedestrian or unhelmeted cyclist struck by motorized vehicle, fall > 3 ft / 0.9 m, head struck by high-impact object) 4. Not acting normally per parent assessment ⚠️ Fall threshold differs

nodes.title: CT Head Recommended (PECARN ≥ 2y)
nodes.summary: CT Head Recommended (PECARN ≥ 2y) — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: CT head recommended. High-risk PECARN features present. 4.3% risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury. Radiation context: Head CT ≈ 2 mSv. Children are several times more radiosensitive than adults. [19] Image Gently: Child-size the dose, scan only indicated region, scan once. [19]
nodes.recommendation: CT head recommended per PECARN — high-risk features present.

nodes.title: CT Head Recommended (PECARN < 2y)
nodes.summary: CT Head Recommended (PECARN < 2y) — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: CT head recommended. High-risk PECARN features present. 4.4% risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury. Radiation context: Head CT ≈ 2 mSv. Infants are the most radiosensitive age group. [19] Image Gently: Child-size the dose, scan only indicated region, scan once. [19]
nodes.recommendation: CT head recommended per PECARN — high-risk features present.

nodes.title: Observation vs CT — Shared Decision-Making
nodes.summary: Observation vs CT — Shared Decision-Making — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Intermediate risk. Observation for 4-6 hours is a reasonable alternative to immediate CT. ~0.8-0.9% ciTBI risk. [7] Factors favoring CT: • Multiple intermediate criteria present • Worsening symptoms during observation • Physician experience and parental concern • Younger age (< 3 months) Factors favoring observation: • Single isolated criterion • Improving symptoms • Experienced observer available
nodes.recommendation: Intermediate risk — observation vs CT per shared decision-making.

nodes.title: CT Head NOT Indicated (PECARN Negative)
nodes.summary: CT Head NOT Indicated (PECARN Negative) — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: No high-risk or intermediate-risk features. CT not recommended. ciTBI risk < 0.02% (age < 2y) and < 0.05% (age ≥ 2y). 2009 validation sensitivity 100% (< 2y) and 96.8% (≥ 2y). [7] Reconfirmed 2024: prospective 6-ED validation (n=19,999) found sensitivity 100% (< 2y) and 98.8% (≥ 2y), NPV 100% for both. The two missed children needed no neurosurgical intervention. PECARN remains the operative stand
nodes.recommendation: CT not indicated per PECARN. Provide return precautions to caregivers.

nodes.title: Canadian C-Spine Rule — Step 1
nodes.summary: Canadian C-Spine Rule — Step 1 — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: For alert (GCS 15), stable trauma patients. In the only large head-to-head trial, CCR outperformed NEXUS — sensitivity 99.4% vs 90.7%, specificity 45.1% vs 36.8% (n=7,438 analyzable, 162 clinically important injuries). [6] *Caveat:* NEXUS's own 34,069-patient validation reported 99.6% sensitivity, and the CCR advantage lost significance (p=0.09) if all 845 indeterminate cases are counted as rule-n

nodes.title: Canadian C-Spine Rule — Step 2
nodes.summary: Canadian C-Spine Rule — Step 2 — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Step 2: Any LOW-RISK factor allowing safe ROM assessment? • Simple rear-end MVC (excludes: pushed into oncoming traffic, hit by bus/large truck, rollover, hit by high-speed vehicle) • Sitting position in ED • Ambulatory at any time post-injury • Delayed onset of neck pain (not immediate) • Absence of midline c-spine tenderness

nodes.title: Canadian C-Spine Rule — Step 3
nodes.summary: Canadian C-Spine Rule — Step 3 — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Step 3: Can the patient actively rotate their neck 45° left AND right?

nodes.title: C-Spine Imaging Indicated
nodes.summary: C-Spine Imaging Indicated — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Cervical spine imaging indicated per Canadian C-Spine Rule. Modality — ACR Appropriateness Criteria 2024 Update: when CCR or NEXUS indicates imaging in adult blunt trauma, non-contrast CT is the initial imaging study. Radiographs are deprioritized (sensitivity for fracture is substantially lower than CT). Routine MRI is not recommended for low-risk patients without neurologic deficit. [23] Radiati
nodes.recommendation: C-spine imaging indicated per Canadian C-Spine Rule. Non-contrast CT is the initial study per ACR 2024.

nodes.title: C-Spine Cleared Clinically
nodes.summary: C-Spine Cleared Clinically — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: No imaging needed per Canadian C-Spine Rule. No high-risk factors, at least one low-risk factor present, and full active ROM achieved. [5] Sensitivity: 100% (95% CI 98-100) in the derivation cohort [5]; 99.4% (95% CI 96-100) in the prospective head-to-head validation [6]. Pooled across both (n=16,363): 99.7%. Document: Canadian C-Spine Rule applied — all 3 steps cleared. No imaging indicated.
nodes.recommendation: C-spine cleared clinically per Canadian C-Spine Rule.

nodes.title: PE Workup — Pre-Test Probability
nodes.summary: PE Workup — Pre-Test Probability — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: What is your clinical gestalt for PE pre-test probability? Apply PERC only when pre-test probability is LOW (gestalt < 15%). [9] Wells PE Calculator · PERC Calculator

nodes.title: PERC Rule — Rule Out PE
nodes.summary: PERC rule: all 8 criteria must be met to rule out PE without further testing — age <50, HR <100, SpO2 ≥95%
nodes.body: ALL 8 criteria must be met to rule out PE without D-dimer: 1. Age < 50 years 2. Heart rate < 100 bpm 3. SpO₂ ≥ 95% on room air 4. No hemoptysis 5. No estrogen use (OCPs, HRT) 6. No prior DVT or PE 7. No unilateral leg swelling 8. No surgery or trauma within prior 4 weeks requiring treatment under general anesthesia ⚠️ PERC is valid only when gestalt pre-test probability is already < 15%. It is not

nodes.title: PE Ruled Out — PERC Negative
nodes.summary: PE Ruled Out — PERC Negative — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: PE ruled out. No further testing needed. Performance: sensitivity 97.4% (95% CI 95.8-98.5), specificity 21.9%, false-negative rate 1.0% — from the 8,138-patient prospective validation [26]. Note this figure applies to the combination of low gestalt AND PERC-negative, not PERC alone. RCT-level support: PROPER (JAMA 2018, 14 EDs, n=1,916) showed a PERC strategy was noninferior for 3-month thromboemb
nodes.recommendation: PE ruled out by PERC in low pre-test probability patient.

nodes.title: D-Dimer Testing
nodes.summary: D-Dimer Testing — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Obtain quantitative D-dimer. For low/moderate pre-test probability. Age-adjusted D-dimer (patients age ≥ 50): threshold = age × 10 µg/L FEU (= ng/mL FEU). ADJUST-PE failure rate 0.3%. 2026 AHA/ACC multisociety PE guideline: Class 2a, LOE B-R for low/intermediate probability. [8,24,25] ⚠️ UNIT TRAP — this is a 2× error waiting to happen. Age × 10 assumes your lab reports FEU (fibrinogen equivalent

nodes.title: Wells PE Score
nodes.summary: Wells PE Score — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Calculate Wells score to stratify risk: Score ≤ 4 = PE unlikely → proceed to D-dimer Score > 4 = PE likely → proceed to CTPA Wells PE Calculator

nodes.title: PE Excluded — Negative D-Dimer
nodes.summary: PE Excluded — Negative D-Dimer — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: PE excluded by negative D-dimer in low/moderate pre-test probability. [8,9] Document: Pre-test probability assessment, D-dimer result and threshold used (standard or age-adjusted). No CTPA indicated.
nodes.recommendation: PE excluded by negative D-dimer in appropriate pre-test probability.

nodes.title: CTPA Indicated
nodes.summary: CTPA Indicated — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: CT Pulmonary Angiography indicated. Radiation context: CTPA ≈ 10-15 mSv (~100-150 CXR equivalents). [15] Check eGFR and contrast allergy status before ordering. Pregnancy: CTPA fetal dose 0.01-0.66 mGy — well below 50 mGy threshold. Do NOT withhold medically indicated CT from pregnant patients. [16] Unstable patient: Bedside echo showing RV strain may support empiric treatment when the patient is
nodes.recommendation: CTPA indicated. Check eGFR and contrast allergy status.

nodes.title: High Pre-Test Probability — CTPA
nodes.summary: High Pre-Test Probability — CTPA — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: CTPA indicated. Do NOT use PERC or D-dimer in high pre-test probability — they are not validated for this population. [8,9] ~37.5% PE prevalence in high-risk patients. [8] If hemodynamically unstable, bedside echo showing RV strain may justify empiric treatment before CT transport — but echo cannot confirm or exclude PE (2026 AHA/ACC multisociety guideline). [24] Radiation context: CTPA ≈ 10-15 mS
nodes.recommendation: CTPA indicated for high pre-test probability. Do NOT use PERC or D-dimer.

nodes.title: Abdominal Scenario
nodes.summary: Abdominal Scenario — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Which abdominal concern?

nodes.title: Alvarado Score — Appendicitis
nodes.summary: Alvarado score ≥7: high likelihood appendicitis, consider surgical consult without CT
nodes.body: Calculate the Alvarado score (MANTRELS mnemonic, max 10 points). Alvarado Calculator

nodes.title: Appendicitis Unlikely
nodes.summary: Appendicitis Unlikely — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Alvarado 0-4. Appendicitis unlikely. Discharge with return precautions: • Worsening or migrating abdominal pain • Fever • Persistent vomiting • Inability to tolerate oral intake Document: Alvarado score and criteria, serial exam findings, return precautions provided.
nodes.recommendation: Appendicitis unlikely (Alvarado 0-4). Discharge with return precautions.

nodes.title: Appendicitis Possible — Observation / Imaging
nodes.summary: Appendicitis Possible — Observation / Imaging — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Alvarado 5-6. Compatible with appendicitis. Consider observation with serial exams and imaging. Imaging options: • POCUS: Sensitivity 91%. Negative POCUS does NOT rule out appendicitis. Good first-line in pediatrics and pregnancy. • CT abdomen/pelvis: ≈ 10 mSv (single phase). Most accurate. [15] • MRI: Preferred in pregnancy — comparable accuracy, no radiation. Pediatrics: Ultrasound first. [19] P
nodes.recommendation: Observation, serial exams, consider imaging (US first in peds/pregnancy, CT if equivocal).

nodes.title: Probable Appendicitis — Surgical Consult
nodes.summary: Probable Appendicitis — Surgical Consult — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Alvarado 7-8. Probable appendicitis. Surgical consult indicated. CT if diagnosis is equivocal or presentation is atypical. [14] CT abdomen/pelvis: ≈ 10 mSv (single phase). [15]
nodes.recommendation: Surgical consult. CT if diagnosis equivocal.

nodes.title: Very Probable Appendicitis
nodes.summary: Very Probable Appendicitis — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Alvarado 9-10. Very probable appendicitis. Surgical consult. CT may not be necessary with classic presentation and high clinical suspicion. [14]
nodes.recommendation: Surgical consult. CT may not be necessary with classic presentation.

nodes.title: Renal Colic — Imaging Guidance
nodes.summary: Renal Colic — Imaging Guidance — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Choosing Wisely: Avoid CT abdomen/pelvis in young (< 50), otherwise healthy patients with known stone history presenting with symptoms of uncomplicated renal colic. [20] When CT is appropriate: • First episode of flank pain / no prior stone history • Fever or concern for infection (pyonephrosis) • Concern for alternative diagnosis • Solitary kidney or transplant • AKI or rising creatinine • Persis
nodes.recommendation: CT if first episode, fever, alternative diagnosis concern, or AKI. POCUS for hydronephrosis as alternative.
