nodes.summary: Extremity Injury Type — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Select injury location:

nodes.title: Ottawa Ankle Rules
nodes.summary: Ottawa Ankle Rules — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Ankle X-ray indicated if pain in malleolar zone AND any of: 1. Bone tenderness along distal 6 cm posterior tibia or tip of medial malleolus 2. Bone tenderness along distal 6 cm posterior fibula or tip of lateral malleolus 3. Unable to bear weight 4 steps (immediately after injury AND in ED) Foot X-ray indicated if midfoot pain AND any of: 1. Tenderness at base of 5th metatarsal 2. Tenderness at na

nodes.title: Ankle/Foot X-Ray Indicated
nodes.summary: Ankle/Foot X-Ray Indicated — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Plain radiographs indicated per Ottawa Ankle Rules. CT is rarely needed for ankle/foot injuries. Consider CT only for: • Complex intra-articular fractures (pilon, calcaneus) • Lisfranc injury evaluation when plain films are equivocal • Pre-operative planning Document: Ottawa Ankle Rules applied, specific criteria met.
nodes.recommendation: X-ray indicated per Ottawa Ankle Rules. CT rarely needed.

nodes.title: No Imaging Needed (Ottawa Ankle)
nodes.summary: No Imaging Needed (Ottawa Ankle) — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Ottawa Ankle Rules negative. No imaging needed. Sensitivity: 97.6% for fractures. [11] Document: Ottawa Ankle Rules applied — no criteria met. No imaging indicated. Return precautions for persistent pain or inability to bear weight.
nodes.recommendation: No imaging needed per Ottawa Ankle Rules.

nodes.title: Ottawa Knee Rules
nodes.summary: Ottawa Knee Rules — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Knee X-ray indicated if ANY of: 1. Age ≥ 55 years 2. Isolated patellar tenderness (no other knee bone tenderness) 3. Tenderness at head of fibula 4. Unable to flex knee to 90° 5. Unable to bear weight 4 steps (immediately + in ED) Sensitivity: 98-100%. Can reduce knee radiographs ~28%. [12] Alternative: Pittsburgh Knee Rules (higher specificity 60% vs ~48%) X-ray if fall/blunt trauma AND either ag

nodes.title: Knee X-Ray Indicated
nodes.summary: Knee X-Ray Indicated — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Plain radiographs indicated per Ottawa/Pittsburgh Knee Rules. CT is rarely needed for acute knee injuries. Consider CT only for: • Tibial plateau fracture characterization • Complex intra-articular fractures • Pre-operative planning MRI preferred for suspected ligament, meniscal, or soft tissue injuries. Document: Knee rules applied, specific criteria met.
nodes.recommendation: X-ray indicated per knee rules. CT rarely needed for acute knee injury.

nodes.title: No Imaging Needed (Ottawa Knee)
nodes.summary: No Imaging Needed (Ottawa Knee) — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Knee rules negative. No imaging needed. Sensitivity: 98-100% for clinically significant fractures. [12] Document: Ottawa/Pittsburgh Knee Rules applied — no criteria met. No imaging indicated. Return precautions for persistent swelling, inability to bear weight, or mechanical symptoms.
nodes.recommendation: No imaging needed per knee rules.

nodes.title: Special Populations & Documentation
nodes.summary: Special Populations & Documentation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Reference Pages: Radiation Dose Reference Table Special Populations Guide (Pediatric, Pregnancy, Contrast Allergy) Documentation Template Choosing Wisely Quick Reference

nodes.title: Documentation Guidance
nodes.summary: Documentation Guidance — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: When ORDERING CT — Document: • Clinical indication and specific symptoms • Pre-test probability and decision rule result • Clinical question being answered • Risk-benefit discussion (especially peds, pregnancy, recent CTs) • Contrast decision and allergy status • Alternative imaging considered When NOT ORDERING CT — Document: • Decision rule applied and result • Shared decision-making discussion •
nodes.recommendation: Document the decision rule applied, not just the conclusion.

nodes.title: Positive Culture Callback — Source Triage
nodes.summary: Source determines pathway. Always ask: pathogen vs contaminant, symptomatic, on coverage, special host
nodes.body: Lab called with a positive culture on a patient previously seen in the ED. Determine source to drive the decision pathway. Universal first questions: [1][2] • What is the source? • Is the organism a likely pathogen or contaminant? • Is the patient symptomatic now? • Are they on adequate antibiotic coverage? • Special host factors (pregnant, immunocompromised, indwelling device)? Resistance Pattern

nodes.title: Blood Culture — Organism Identified
nodes.summary: S. aureus + Candida + GNB sepsis = always recall + admit. CoNS single bottle + stable = likely contaminant.
nodes.body: Almost always TRUE pathogen (>90%): [3][4] S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, GAS, E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Candida, Listeria, N. meningitidis, Salmonella Usually contaminant (<10% unless context): [3][5] CoNS, Corynebacterium, Bacillus, Cutibacterium (P. acnes), Micrococcus, single-bottle viridans strep Contaminant vs Pathogen Guide ID Consult Triggers Which organism?

nodes.title: S. aureus Bacteremia — Mandatory Workflow
nodes.summary: SAB = recall + admit + TTE + ID consult + cefazolin (MSSA) or vanco (MRSA). 14d uncomplicated, 4-6wk complicated.
nodes.body: S. aureus bacteremia is a NEVER-MISS diagnosis. Mortality 20-30% untreated. [6] Recall to ED immediately — do NOT defer to PCP. Admission mandatory. All SAB requires inpatient management. Workup: [6][7] • Repeat blood cultures q48h until clear (define duration of bacteremia) • TTE within 5-7 days; TEE if: persistent bacteremia, prosthetic valve, IVDU, suspicious lesions • ID consult is standard of

nodes.title: SAB — Disposition
nodes.body: Action plan: ✓ Call patient — return to ED now ✓ ED admission orders + ID consult on arrival ✓ Blood cultures (repeat set) drawn immediately ✓ Vanco load if pending speciation, cefazolin if MSSA ✓ TTE within 5-7 days ✓ Search for source (lines, skin, spine, joints)
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Empiric vanco or cefazolin per speciation. ID consult mandatory. TTE within 5-7d. Repeat blood cultures q48h until clear.

nodes.title: Candidemia — Mandatory Workflow
nodes.summary: Candidemia = recall + admit + echinocandin + ophtho + ID + line removal. 14d from first negative.
nodes.body: Candidemia mortality: 30-40%. Always recall, always admit. [8] Empiric: [8] • Echinocandin first-line: micafungin 100 mg IV qd, anidulafungin 200 mg load then 100 mg qd, or caspofungin 70 mg load then 50 mg qd • Fluconazole 800 mg load only if non-critical + no azole exposure + susceptible species likely Mandatory adjuncts: [8] • Ophthalmology consult — endophthalmitis screen within 1 week • ID co

nodes.title: Candidemia — Disposition
nodes.body: Action plan: ✓ Call patient — return to ED now ✓ Admit, ID + ophthalmology consults ✓ Empiric echinocandin (micafungin 100 mg IV qd) ✓ Remove central line if present ✓ Repeat cultures daily until negative
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Echinocandin. Ophtho + ID consults. Line removal. Treat 14d from first negative culture.

nodes.title: Gram-Negative Bacteremia — Coverage Assessment
nodes.summary: GNB pathway: recall if untreated, continue if improving on susceptible, escalate if ESBL or resistant
nodes.body: GNB workup: [9][10] Most common sources: UTI/pyelo (60%), intra-abdominal, biliary, line, pneumonia. Key question: is patient already on adequate empiric coverage AND clinically improving?

nodes.title: GNB Untreated — Recall and Admit
nodes.summary: Untreated GNB = recall + admit + ceftriaxone or pip-tazo. 7d non-inferior to 14d (Yahav 2019).
nodes.body: GNB without coverage = sepsis risk. Recall, admit. [9] Empiric: [9][10] • Community-acquired stable: ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h • Sepsis or healthcare exposure: pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h • ESBL risk or prior ESBL history: meropenem 1g IV q8h • Severe PCN allergy: aztreonam + vanco (if any gram-positive concern) Local antibiogram drives empiric choice. Duration: 7 days uncomplicated GNB (Yahav 2019 — non-in

nodes.title: GNB Untreated — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Recall patient to ED ✓ Admit ✓ Empiric ceftriaxone (CAB) or pip-tazo (HCAB/sepsis) ✓ Repeat blood culture ✓ Hunt source: UA, imaging if abdominal/biliary
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Empiric ceftriaxone or pip-tazo per context. Repeat cultures. Source-direct. 7d total duration if uncomplicated.

nodes.title: GNB on Coverage and Improving — Continue
nodes.body: Patient improving on susceptible PO therapy. Continue. [11] Action: ✓ Confirm susceptibility covers organism ✓ Confirm clinical improvement (call patient) ✓ Document plan, notify PCP ✓ Complete 7d total duration (Yahav 2019) ✓ Return precautions: worsening symptoms, fever
nodes.recommendation: Continue current oral therapy. 7d total. Document phone contact. Return if worsening.

nodes.title: ESBL Bacteremia — Carbapenem Required
nodes.summary: ESBL bacteremia = carbapenem + admit + ID. Avoid pip-tazo even if labeled susceptible (MERINO).
nodes.body: ESBL bacteremia: pip-tazo failed in MERINO trial — use carbapenem. [12] Recall and admit. Treatment: [12] • Meropenem 1g IV q8h is standard • Ertapenem 1g IV qd acceptable for non-critical, no Pseudomonas concern • Avoid pip-tazo even if "S" — MERINO trial showed inferior outcomes • ID consult Source hunt: ESBL more common in UTI/pyelo from healthcare exposure, prior antibiotic use, foreign travel

nodes.title: ESBL — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Recall + admit ✓ Meropenem 1g IV q8h ✓ ID consult ✓ Document foreign travel, prior antibiotics
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Meropenem. ID consult. Avoid pip-tazo regardless of in-vitro susceptibility (MERINO).

nodes.title: Resistant GNB — Recall and Change
nodes.body: Organism resistant to current Rx. Recall, switch therapy. Decision: • Stable, well-appearing, source-controlled → switch PO to susceptible agent + close follow-up • Sepsis criteria, fever, ill → admit, IV broad-spectrum per susceptibility • Uncertain → recall to ED for re-evaluation, blood cultures, decision
nodes.recommendation: Recall patient. Reassess in ED. Switch to susceptible agent. Admit if any sepsis criteria.

nodes.title: Streptococcal Bacteremia
nodes.summary: Strep blood: pneumo + GAS + GBS = recall, admit. Viridans single = consider contaminant unless endocarditis risk
nodes.body: Source-directed treatment. [13] S. pneumoniae bacteremia: [13] • Usually from CAP or meningitis source • Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h covers most strains • Add vanco if meningitis cannot be excluded • Recall + admit unless rapidly improving on PO amox for known CAP Group A strep (S. pyogenes): [13] • High virulence — recall + admit • Penicillin G IV + clindamycin (toxin suppression) • Hunt for necrotizi

nodes.title: Streptococcal Bacteremia — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Recall + admit (except clearly improving CAP with pneumococcal sensitivity) ✓ Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h covers most ✓ GAS: penicillin G + clindamycin, screen for necrotizing ✓ Viridans + multiple bottles or risk factors: TTE ✓ ID consult for endocarditis suspicion
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Ceftriaxone (or PCN G + clinda if GAS). TTE if endocarditis risk. ID consult if invasive.

nodes.title: Likely Blood Culture Contaminant
nodes.summary: Single-bottle CoNS in stable, non-device patient = contaminant. Do not treat. Document phone contact.
nodes.body: CoNS, single bottle, stable patient, no device, no immunocompromise = likely contaminant. [3][5] Cues for contamination: [5] • Single bottle out of 2-4 drawn • Time to positivity >14h • Patient now well, no fevers • No indwelling lines or prosthesis • Not immunocompromised • Organism: CoNS (NOT S. lugdunensis), Corynebacterium, Bacillus, P. acnes, Micrococcus Cues for TRUE BSI (treat as pathogen):

nodes.title: Contaminant — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Document phone contact and reassurance ✓ Notify PCP ✓ Return precautions: fever, rigors, new symptoms ✓ Do NOT start antibiotics
nodes.recommendation: No antibiotics. Document phone contact + return precautions. Notify PCP. Repeat only if symptomatic.

nodes.title: Other Blood Pathogens
nodes.summary: Pseudomonas/Listeria/anaerobes/Neisseria = recall + admit + organism-specific Rx. Listeria needs ampicillin (not ceftriaxone).
nodes.body: Pseudomonas: [9] • Recall + admit • Empiric pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h or cefepime 2g IV q8h • Hunt source: healthcare exposure, neutropenia, structural lung disease Listeria: [14] • Pregnant, >50, immunocompromised at highest risk • Recall + admit • Ampicillin 2g IV q4h (or TMP-SMX if PCN-allergic) • Cephalosporins do NOT cover Listeria Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium): • Indicates intra-abdominal

nodes.title: Other Pathogens — Disposition
nodes.body: Recall + admit. Empiric directed by organism. ID consult.
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Organism-specific empiric. ID consult. Public health notification for Neisseria.

nodes.title: Urine Culture — Symptomatic Status
nodes.summary: Symptoms → treat. Asymptomatic → DO NOT treat (exceptions: pregnancy, pre-urologic procedure).
nodes.body: The single most important question for urine culture interpretation. [15][16] CFU Thresholds Pregnancy Exception Patient status:

nodes.title: Symptomatic UTI — Syndrome
nodes.summary: Cystitis → 3-5d PO. Pyelo outpatient → 5-14d. Pyelo admit if sepsis, pregnancy, vomiting, obstruction.
nodes.body: Cystitis vs pyelonephritis drives both treatment and disposition. [15] Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic discomfort, urinary urgency. No flank pain, no fever. Pyelonephritis: flank pain, fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, costovertebral angle tenderness. Treatment Map

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Cystitis — Treatment
nodes.summary: Cystitis = nitrofurantoin 5d OR TMP-SMX 3d OR fosfo x1. Avoid FQ for cystitis. ESBL cystitis: nitro/fosfo still work.
nodes.body: First-line (any of): [15][17] • Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID x 5d (avoid CrCl <30, avoid in pyelonephritis) • TMP-SMX DS PO BID x 3d (only if local resistance <20%, no use in 3 months) • Fosfomycin 3g PO x 1 dose (single dose, lower efficacy, OK for ESBL cystitis only) Second-line: [17] • Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID x 5-7d • Cefpodoxime 100 mg PO BID x 5-7d • Augmentin 500/125 mg PO BID x 5-7d Avoid

nodes.title: Cystitis — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Confirm susceptibility on returned culture ✓ If current Rx susceptible + improving: continue, no change ✓ If resistant: call patient, switch to nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin ✓ Document phone contact + return precautions (flank pain, fever)
nodes.recommendation: Continue if susceptible + improving. Switch to nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin if resistant.

nodes.title: Pyelonephritis Outpatient — Treatment
nodes.summary: Pyelo outpatient: cipro/levo 5-7d if FQ resistance <10%, else ceftriaxone IV + PO. ESBL pyelo = ertapenem or admit.
nodes.body: Stable + PO tolerant + reliable follow-up only. [15][17] Regimen choice depends on local FQ resistance: [17] If local FQ resistance <10%: • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID x 7d • Levofloxacin 750 mg PO qd x 5d If local FQ resistance ≥10%: • Ceftriaxone 1g IV in ED, then FQ PO at home OR cefpodoxime 200 mg BID x 10d TMP-SMX: ONLY if susceptible, 14 days BID. Avoid for pyelo: [17] • Nitrofurantoin (poor

nodes.title: Pyelo Outpatient — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Confirm susceptibility on returned culture ✓ Continue if covered + improving ✓ Switch agent if resistant ✓ Return if worsening, vomiting, fever persists >72h ✓ ESBL → ertapenem or admit
nodes.recommendation: Continue if susceptible + improving. Otherwise switch per susceptibilities. ESBL → ertapenem outpatient or admit.

nodes.title: Pyelo Admit — Disposition
nodes.body: Admit if any of: sepsis criteria, pregnancy, intractable vomiting, obstruction, immunocompromised, failed outpatient therapy. [15] Empiric: [9][17] • Stable: ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h • Sepsis: pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h or cefepime 2g IV q8h • ESBL: meropenem 1g IV q8h
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Ceftriaxone or pip-tazo per severity. ESBL = meropenem. Source-direct.

nodes.title: Pregnant ASB — Must Treat
nodes.body: Treat ALL asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy (untreated → 25% pyelo, low birth weight, preterm). [16] Regimen (any of): [16] • Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID x 5-7d (acceptable 1st/2nd trimester; avoid at term ≥38wk — neonatal hemolysis) • Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID x 7d (safe all trimesters) • Fosfomycin 3g PO x 1 (safe all trimesters) • Amoxicillin/Augmentin if susceptible Avoid: TMP-SMX 1st/3rd
nodes.recommendation: Treat per local susceptibilities (cephalexin or fosfomycin safest all trimesters). Test of cure at 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Pre-Urologic Procedure ASB — Treat
nodes.body: Treat ASB before any urologic procedure with mucosal trauma (TURP, ureteroscopy, stone manipulation). [16] Short course (3-5d) timed to complete before procedure, per susceptibilities. Do NOT treat for non-mucosal procedures.
nodes.recommendation: Short course (3-5d) per susceptibilities timed to procedure. Coordinate with urology.

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria — DO NOT Treat
nodes.body: Per IDSA 2019 ASB guidelines, do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in: [16] • Elderly • Diabetics • Post-menopausal women • Indwelling catheter patients • Spinal cord injury • Neutropenic patients • ICU patients Why: treatment does NOT improve outcomes, drives C. difficile, drives resistance, causes adverse drug events. Action: document phone contact, no antibiotics, notify PCP, advise return if
nodes.recommendation: No antibiotics. Document phone contact + return precautions. Notify PCP.

nodes.title: Foley / Catheter Culture — Symptoms?
nodes.summary: CAUTI = symptoms + bacteriuria. Cloudy/smelly urine alone does NOT qualify. Candiduria usually do not treat.
nodes.body: CAUTI diagnosis requires SYMPTOMS plus ≥10³ CFU/mL. [18] Symptoms include: fever, suprapubic pain, costovertebral tenderness, acute hematuria, new altered mental status (in cognitively intact patients). Symptoms DO NOT include: [18] • Cloudy or foul-smelling urine alone • Pyuria alone (almost universal in catheterized patients) • Asymptomatic positive culture

nodes.title: Symptomatic CAUTI — Treatment
nodes.summary: CAUTI = replace catheter + ceftriaxone/cefepime + 7-14d. Treat from new catheter culture, not old.
nodes.body: Step 1: REPLACE the catheter before treatment if it has been in >2 weeks. [18] • Biofilm reservoir = treatment failure if old catheter kept • Send culture from NEW catheter, not old one • Consider catheter discontinuation altogether if possible — most effective intervention Step 2: Empiric therapy [18] • Acute community CAUTI: ceftriaxone 1-2g IV qd or cefepime if Pseudomonas concern • Chronic cat

nodes.title: CAUTI — Disposition
nodes.body: Action: ✓ Replace catheter (or remove if possible) before treatment ✓ Empiric per host: ceftriaxone (community) or pip-tazo (chronic) ✓ Tailor to susceptibilities ✓ 7-14d total ✓ Consider admission if sepsis, immunocompromised, frail
nodes.recommendation: Replace catheter. Empiric IV per setting. Tailor by susceptibilities. 7-14d duration.

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Catheter Bacteriuria — DO NOT Treat
nodes.body: Bacteriuria develops at 3-10% per catheter-day. By 30 days, 100% of catheterized patients are colonized. [18] Treating asymptomatic catheter bacteriuria does NOT reduce symptomatic CAUTI and drives C. difficile + resistance. Exceptions (rare): • Pre-urologic procedure with mucosal trauma • Pregnant (rare in catheterized population, but treat) • Confirmed CAUTI symptoms develop Action: ✓ No antibio
nodes.recommendation: No antibiotics. Remove catheter if not indicated. Educate patient/family on what does NOT need treatment.

nodes.title: Candiduria — Usually Do NOT Treat
nodes.summary: Candiduria usually do NOT treat. Exceptions: symptomatic, neutropenic, transplant, pre-urologic procedure.
nodes.body: Candida in catheter urine = colonization in most patients. [8] Do NOT treat: [8] • Asymptomatic catheterized patient • Asymptomatic non-catheterized patient with positive Candida urine TREAT only if any of: [8] • Symptomatic (fever, dysuria, CVA tenderness) • Neutropenic (high invasive candidiasis risk) • Renal/urologic transplant recipient • Pre-urologic procedure with mucosal trauma Regimen when

nodes.title: Candiduria — Disposition
nodes.body: Most: remove catheter, no antibiotics, document. Indicated: fluconazole 200-400 mg PO qd x 14d. Neutropenic/transplant: ID consult.
nodes.recommendation: Remove catheter if present. Treat only if symptomatic, neutropenic, transplant, or pre-urologic.

nodes.title: Wound Culture — Context
nodes.summary: Wound culture: surface swabs often misleading. Continue if improving. Change only if resistant or unusual organism.
nodes.body: Critical principle: surface wound swabs often show colonizers, not pathogens. [19] If patient is improving on empiric therapy + culture shows unexpected organism → continue current therapy. Recall and change ONLY if: not improving, clearly resistant organism (e.g., MRSA on PCN), unusual pathogen. SSTI Treatment Map Wound type?

nodes.title: Cellulitis Culture Result
nodes.summary: Cellulitis culture: continue cephalexin if improving. Recall + switch to TMP-SMX/doxy only if not improving + MRSA.
nodes.body: Non-purulent cellulitis is usually Strep, not Staph. [19][20] Empiric ED Rx: [19] • Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID x 5d (extend if not improved) • Add MRSA coverage (TMP-SMX, doxy, or clinda) only if: penetrating trauma, IVDU, purulent, prior MRSA, nasal MRSA colonization Culture growing MRSA: • If on cephalexin/dicloxacillin and improving — likely colonizer or co-infection; consider continue, follow cl

nodes.title: Cellulitis — Disposition
nodes.body: Continue if improving. Switch only if not improving + clearly resistant organism. Document phone contact + return precautions (spreading, fever, systemic).
nodes.recommendation: Continue current Rx if improving. Recall and switch only if not improving with resistant pathogen.

nodes.title: Abscess Culture Result
nodes.summary: Abscess: I&D primary. Antibiotics if systemic/large/face/etc. MRSA on cephalexin = switch. Decolonize if recurrent.
nodes.body: I&D is the primary treatment for abscesses, not antibiotics. [19][20] Antibiotics added to I&D indicated if: [20] • Systemic signs (fever, SIRS) • Large abscess (>2 cm) • Surrounding cellulitis • Immunocompromised • Face/hand/genital location • Failure of I&D alone Empiric (when indicated): • TMP-SMX DS BID x 5-7d (MRSA coverage) • Doxycycline 100 mg BID x 5-7d (alternative) • Clindamycin 300 mg Q

nodes.title: Abscess — Disposition
nodes.body: I&D primary. Continue antibiotic if susceptible + improving. Switch if on cephalexin and MRSA grew. Decolonize if recurrent.
nodes.recommendation: I&D primary. Continue covered antibiotic if improving. Switch if cephalexin + MRSA. Decolonization if recurrent.

nodes.title: Diabetic Foot Infection — Stage and Treat
nodes.summary: DFI: mild = PO cephalexin/augmentin; moderate = PO broad or admit; severe = admit IV. Probe-to-bone + osteo = 4-6wk + ID/surgery.
nodes.body: IWGDF/IDSA 2023 staging: [21] Mild DFI: cellulitis only, ≤2 cm beyond wound, no systemic signs. • PO cephalexin or augmentin x 1-2 weeks • Outpatient with close follow-up Moderate DFI: deeper involvement (joint, abscess, gangrene, bone), no SIRS. • PO augmentin OR levofloxacin + metronidazole OR moxifloxacin • Or admit for IV ampicillin-sulbactam, ertapenem • Consider MRI for osteomyelitis Severe

nodes.title: DFI — Disposition
nodes.body: Stage drives disposition. Mild: PO outpatient + close f/u. Moderate: PO broad or admit. Severe: admit IV. Osteo: 4-6 weeks + ID + surgery.
nodes.recommendation: Stage per IWGDF/IDSA. PO outpatient mild. Admit moderate-severe. ID + surgery for osteomyelitis.

nodes.title: Bite Wound — Always Cover Pasteurella + Anaerobes
nodes.summary: Bite wounds: augmentin first-line covers Pasteurella + anaerobes + Eikenella. Hand human bites → hand surgery.
nodes.body: Empiric: [22] • Augmentin 875/125 mg PO BID x 5d is the standard • PCN-allergic adults: doxycycline + metronidazole OR moxifloxacin • PCN-allergic kids: clindamycin + TMP-SMX Cat bites: prophylaxis recommended (deep puncture, Pasteurella aggressive). Human bites: always treat. Hand involvement → hand surgery consult. Dog bites: prophylaxis if deep, hand/face, immunocompromised, or signs of infecti

nodes.title: Bite Wound — Disposition
nodes.body: Augmentin most cases. Hand involvement = surgical consult. Capnocytophaga in immunocompromised = admit.
nodes.recommendation: Augmentin first-line. Switch only if resistant. Hand or face injury → surgery. Capnocytophaga → admit.

nodes.title: Sputum Culture — Context
nodes.summary: Sputum culture: continue if improving. Reassess if failing. Adjust for resistant organisms.
nodes.body: IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP Guideline: routine sputum cultures NOT recommended in outpatients. [23] Useful in: severe CAP, treatment failure, HCAP, structural lung disease (CF, bronchiectasis), suspected resistant organism. Interpretation criteria for "pathogen vs contaminant": [23] • Heavy growth of single organism + >25 PMN + <10 epithelial cells per LPF = likely pathogen • Mixed flora, few PMN, many epit

nodes.title: Sputum Culture + Improving
nodes.body: Continue current therapy. Most outpatient CAP improves on amoxicillin 1g TID or doxycycline regardless of sputum result. [23] Culture rarely changes management if patient is improving. Document phone contact + return precautions.
nodes.recommendation: Continue current Rx. Phone contact + return precautions. Complete 5d minimum or per guideline.

nodes.title: Sputum Culture + Not Improving
nodes.summary: Not improving + sputum result = recall, reassess severity, image, consider admit, broaden if atypical not covered
nodes.body: Recall and reassess. [23] Workup: • Repeat exam + vitals + chest imaging • Reassess severity (CURB-65, PSI) • Consider admission • Check culture susceptibilities Common reasons for failure: • Atypical pathogen not covered (mycoplasma, chlamydia, Legionella) — add macrolide or doxycycline • Resistant pneumococcus — switch to levofloxacin • Wrong diagnosis (PE, heart failure, malignancy) • Empyema —

nodes.title: Sputum Failing — Disposition
nodes.body: Recall to ED. Reassess severity. Image. Admit if any sepsis criteria. Broaden coverage per culture/susceptibilities.
nodes.recommendation: Recall + ED reassessment. Image. Admit if sepsis or moderate-severe. Broaden coverage as indicated.

nodes.title: Resistant Organism in Sputum
nodes.summary: Sputum Pseudomonas = cipro/levo + admit if sepsis. MRSA = treat if severe/post-influenza, watch for colonizer.
nodes.body: Pseudomonas: [23] • Chronic structural lung disease (CF, severe COPD, bronchiectasis), HCAP, immunocompromised • Treat if symptomatic + clinical fit: cipro 750 mg PO BID or levofloxacin 750 mg PO qd • Inhaled antibiotics (tobramycin) in chronic colonization (CF/bronchiectasis) • Admit if sepsis MRSA in sputum: [23] • Improving on standard CAP Rx + low colonization burden in COPD = likely colonizer

nodes.title: Resistant Sputum — Disposition
nodes.body: Pseudomonas = anti-pseudomonal PO + admit if sepsis. MRSA = add linezolid/vanco if severe or post-influenza.
nodes.recommendation: Anti-pseudomonal coverage if Pseudomonas. Vanco/linezolid if MRSA + severe disease. Admit if sepsis.

nodes.title: Stool Culture — Pathogen Type
nodes.summary: Stool pathogen: Salmo/Campy = treat only severe. Shigella = treat all. STEC = NEVER treat. CDI = severity-based.
nodes.body: Bacterial pathogen identification drives treatment decisions: [24] Stool Pathogen Treatment Map

nodes.title: Salmonella (Non-Typhi) — Usually Do NOT Treat
nodes.summary: Salmonella: most do NOT need Rx (prolongs shedding). Treat only <3mo, >65, immunocompromised, severe, bacteremia, prosthetic joints.
nodes.body: Most immunocompetent adults do NOT need antibiotics. [24] Antibiotics PROLONG fecal shedding without shortening illness. TREAT only if: [24] • Age <3 months or >65 years • Immunocompromised (HIV, transplant, sickle cell, chemo) • Severe disease (sepsis, hospitalized) • Bacteremia confirmed • Sickle cell disease • Vascular grafts or prosthetic joints (high seeding risk) Regimen (when indicated): [2

nodes.title: Salmonella — Disposition
nodes.body: Most: no antibiotics, supportive, return if worsening. If indicated: cipro or ceftriaxone per susceptibilities.
nodes.recommendation: No antibiotics for immunocompetent. Treat with cipro/ceftriaxone only if at-risk groups (age, immune, severe, prosthetic).

nodes.title: Shigella — Treat All
nodes.body: Treat all Shigella to reduce transmission and shorten illness. [24] First-line: [24] • Azithromycin 500 mg PO qd x 3d (preferred — rising FQ resistance) • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID x 3d (if susceptible) • Ceftriaxone 2g IV qd x 5d if severe Resistance: extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Shigella sonnei and S. flexneri increasing in MSM and travelers — check susceptibility, consider azithromycin or
nodes.recommendation: Treat all. Azithromycin x 3d first-line. Cipro if susceptible. Ceftriaxone IV if severe.

nodes.title: Campylobacter — Treat Severe Only
nodes.summary: Campylobacter: treat only severe/immunocompromised/pregnant/persistent. Azithromycin first-line (FQ resistance ~25%).
nodes.body: Most Campylobacter is self-limited. Treat only severe disease or immunocompromised. [24] Indications to treat: [24] • Severe illness (>8 stools/day, fever, blood, dehydration) • Immunocompromised • Pregnancy • Symptoms >1 week Regimen: [24] • Azithromycin 500 mg PO qd x 3d (first-line, FQ resistance ~25% in US) • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID x 3d if susceptible Guillain-Barré association: counsel p

nodes.title: Campylobacter — Disposition
nodes.body: Self-limited in most. Azithromycin x 3d if severe or at-risk. Counsel on GBS return precautions.
nodes.recommendation: Most no Rx. Azithromycin 500 mg qd x 3d if severe. Educate on GBS.

nodes.title: STEC / E. coli O157:H7 — DO NOT TREAT
nodes.summary: STEC: NO antibiotics, NO loperamide. Supportive + monitor HUS (CBC/BMP in 5-7d). Admit if HUS signs.
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Antibiotics INCREASE risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). [24] Action: [24] • NO antibiotics • NO loperamide or antimotility agents (also increase HUS risk) • Supportive care: hydration, monitor electrolytes • Monitor for HUS: CBC + BMP at 5-7 days post-infection • HUS signs: hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury — admit • Bloody diarrhea + child <10 = high suspicio

nodes.title: STEC — Disposition
nodes.body: NO antibiotics. NO antimotility. Supportive care. Monitor HUS labs in 5-7 days. Admit if HUS.
nodes.recommendation: No antibiotics. No antimotility agents. Hydration. CBC/BMP at 5-7 days. Admit if HUS signs.

nodes.title: Vibrio (Non-Cholera) — Treat Severe + High-Risk
nodes.summary: Vibrio: treat severe + cirrhotic + immunocompromised. Doxy + ceftriaxone. V. vulnificus mortality up to 50% in cirrhotics.
nodes.body: V. vulnificus and V. parahaemolyticus most common in US (Gulf Coast, raw oyster ingestion, salt water wound exposure). [24] TREAT severe disease and high-risk hosts: [24] • Sepsis, bacteremia • Cirrhosis or chronic liver disease (V. vulnificus mortality up to 50%) • Hemochromatosis • Immunocompromised • Necrotizing soft tissue from wound exposure to salt/brackish water Regimen: [24] • Doxycycline

nodes.title: Vibrio — Disposition
nodes.body: Admit for severe or high-risk. Doxycycline + ceftriaxone. Surgical consult if necrotizing.
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Doxycycline + ceftriaxone. Surgery if necrotizing wound. Public health notification.

nodes.title: C. difficile — Interpret Result
nodes.summary: CDI dx: NAAT + toxin both positive OR symptoms + NAAT. NAAT+/toxin-/asymptomatic = colonizer, no Rx.
nodes.body: Diagnostic interpretation: [25] • NAAT alone insufficient — can detect colonizers • NAAT + toxin EIA positive = true CDI • Symptomatic + both positive = treat • NAAT positive / toxin negative + asymptomatic = likely colonizer, do NOT treat • Patient with NO diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools/24h) — do NOT test or treat CDI Severity Calculator

nodes.title: CDI Initial Episode — Severity and Treatment
nodes.summary: CDI initial: fidaxomicin or vanco PO x 10d. Fulminant = vanco PO/NG + metronidazole IV + surgery consult.
nodes.body: Severity assessment: [25] • Non-severe: WBC <15k AND Cr <1.5 • Severe: WBC ≥15k OR Cr ≥1.5 • Fulminant: hypotension, ileus, megacolon Treatment (IDSA/SHEA 2021 update): [25] Non-severe AND severe (same regimen): • Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x 10d (preferred) OR • Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID x 10d • Metronidazole now SECOND-LINE / non-recommended for adults Fulminant: • Vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG QID + me

nodes.title: CDI Initial — Disposition
nodes.body: Non-severe/severe: outpatient if PO tolerant + reliable + no fulminant signs. Fidaxomicin or vanco PO x 10d. Fulminant: admit, ICU, vanco PO/NG + IV metronidazole, surgery consult. Stop offending antibiotics if possible. Hand hygiene with soap and water. Return precautions.
nodes.recommendation: Fidaxomicin OR vanco PO x 10d for non-severe/severe. Fulminant → admit, IV metronidazole + PO vanco, surgery.

nodes.title: CDI Recurrence — Strategy
nodes.summary: CDI recur: switch fidaxomicin↔vanco pulse-taper. Multiple recur = bezlotoxumab + FMT/ID consult.
nodes.body: First recurrence: [25] • If vanco used initially: fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x 10d • If fidaxomicin used initially: vanco pulse-taper (125 mg QID x 14d, then BID x 7d, then qd x 7d, then q2-3d x 2-8 weeks) Multiple recurrences (≥2): [25] • Bezlotoxumab 10 mg/kg IV (monoclonal antibody) as adjunct to standard Rx • Consider fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) consult • ID + GI consult SER-109 (live ora

nodes.title: CDI Recurrence — Disposition
nodes.body: First recurrence: switch agent (fidaxomicin↔vanco pulse-taper). Multiple recurrence: bezlotoxumab + FMT/ID consult.
nodes.recommendation: First recurrence: switch fidaxomicin or vanco pulse-taper. Multiple: bezlotoxumab adjunct + FMT/ID.

nodes.title: CDI NAAT+/Toxin-/Asymptomatic — Likely Colonizer
nodes.body: Do NOT treat colonizers. [25] NAAT positive without toxin and without diarrhea = colonization, not infection. Treating drives resistance and provides no benefit. Action: no antibiotics, document phone contact, return precautions for new diarrhea, hand hygiene with soap and water.
nodes.recommendation: No antibiotics. Document phone contact + return precautions.

nodes.title: CSF Culture Positive — Always Admit
nodes.summary: CSF positive = always admit. Vanco + ceftriaxone empiric. Add ampicillin if >50/preg/IC. Add dex if pneumo suspected.
nodes.body: No CSF positive is dischargeable. Always admit. [26] This pathway covers the rare case of LP done in ED for low-suspicion meningitis (e.g., headache, fever workup) with culture turning positive after discharge. Action: [26] • Call patient — return immediately • Admit • Neurology + ID consults • Neurosurgery if post-op or shunt Empiric (pending susceptibility): [26] • Adult community: vancomycin 15

nodes.title: CSF — Disposition
nodes.body: Recall + admit + neurology + ID. Empiric vanco + ceftriaxone ± ampicillin ± dexamethasone per context.
nodes.recommendation: Recall, admit. Vanco + ceftriaxone. Add ampicillin if >50/IC/preg. Dex if pneumococcal. Neuro + ID consults.

nodes.title: GAS Pharyngitis — Treat
nodes.summary: GAS positive = penicillin V or amox 10d. PCN allergy → cephalexin (non-anaphylactic) or azithro/clinda (anaphylactic).
nodes.body: Positive throat culture for Group A Strep = treat. [27] Primary goal: prevent rheumatic fever (especially <25 years) + reduce transmission + shorten illness. First-line: [27] • Penicillin V 500 mg PO BID or TID x 10d (gold standard, narrowest spectrum) • Amoxicillin 1g PO qd x 10d OR 500 mg PO BID x 10d • Single-dose benzathine PCN G IM 1.2 million units (for adherence concerns) Penicillin allergy

nodes.title: GAS — Disposition
nodes.body: Treat all positive culture (even if rapid was negative). Pen V or amoxicillin 10d. PCN allergy as above.
nodes.recommendation: Penicillin V or amoxicillin 10d. Cephalexin if non-anaphylactic PCN allergy. Azithro/clinda if anaphylactic.

nodes.title: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis
nodes.summary: CVST: 0.5-3% of all strokes — primarily young women, headache in >90%, seizures in 20-40%
nodes.body: CVST Steps Summary — diagnostic and treatment pathway. CVST accounts for 0.5-3% of all strokes, primarily affecting young adults and women of reproductive age (3:1 female predominance). Classic presentation: • Headache — >90% of cases, often severe, progressive • Seizures — 20-40% • Focal neurologic deficits — 20-50% • Altered consciousness — variable • Papilledema — suggests elevated ICP High-ris

nodes.title: Clinical Syndrome
nodes.summary: Identify dominant syndrome: isolated intracranial HTN, focal deficit, encephalopathy, or seizure
nodes.body: Identify the dominant clinical presentation: Isolated intracranial hypertension: • Severe headache, papilledema, visual changes • No focal deficits, no encephalopathy Focal syndrome: • Hemiparesis, aphasia, hemisensory loss • May mimic arterial stroke Encephalopathy: • Altered mental status, confusion, stupor, coma • Bilateral deficits, multifocal signs Seizure presentation: • New-onset seizures w

nodes.title: Seizure Management in CVST
nodes.summary: No seizure prophylaxis unless seizure already occurred — levetiracetam preferred after first seizure
nodes.body: Acute seizure treatment: • Standard seizure protocol — Lorazepam 4mg IV, then load AED • Levetiracetam 60mg/kg IV (max 4500mg) preferred Key points on seizure prophylaxis: [1,5] Primary prophylaxis (no prior seizures): NOT RECOMMENDED • Weak evidence, potential harm • Canadian Stroke Best Practices: strong recommendation against After first seizure: • Initiate anti-seizure medication • Continue fo

nodes.title: Diagnostic Approach
nodes.summary: D-dimer NPV 95-99.8% but 10% of CVST have normal D-dimer — MRI+MRV gold standard, CT+CTV acceptable
nodes.body: D-dimer role: [2,3] • Sensitivity: 83-97.8% • NPV: 95-99.8% • Measure BEFORE imaging UNLESS: — Isolated headache presentation — Symptoms >1 week (higher false-negative rate) Critical limitation: Up to 10% of CVST patients have normal D-dimer Imaging modalities (ranked): 1. MRI + MRV (Gold Standard) • Most sensitive for CVT diagnosis • TOF-MRV does not require contrast • GRE/SWI detects cortical ve

nodes.title: Imaging Findings by Phase
nodes.summary: Acute: T1 iso/T2 hypo; subacute: T1/T2 hyperintense — CT empty delta sign in SSS thrombosis

nodes.title: CVST Confirmed
nodes.summary: CVST confirmed — assess location, parenchymal involvement, and hemorrhage before starting treatment
nodes.body: Imaging confirms CVST. Before proceeding to treatment, assess: 1. Location of thrombosis: • Superior sagittal sinus (most common) • Transverse/sigmoid sinus • Deep venous system (worse prognosis) • Cortical veins 2. Parenchymal involvement: • Venous infarction present? • Hemorrhagic transformation? 3. Clinical severity: • Mental status (GCS) • Focal deficits Is there intracranial hemorrhage on ima

nodes.title: ICH Does NOT Contraindicate Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: ICH in CVST is NOT a contraindication to anticoagulation — hemorrhage is consequence of venous congestion
nodes.body: CRITICAL CONCEPT: [1,2,4] Intracranial hemorrhage secondary to CVST is NOT a contraindication to anticoagulation. Rationale: • ICH in CVST is a consequence of venous congestion, not the cause • Anticoagulation treats the underlying thrombosis • Hemorrhage extension risk is lower than risk of untreated CVST Evidence: • ISCVT study: No difference in hemorrhage extension with anticoagulation • Multip

nodes.title: Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: CVT-GS score: mild 0-2 (1.1% mortality), moderate 3-7 (19.6%), severe 8-13 (61.4%)
nodes.body: Use validated scoring systems to assess prognosis: CVT-GS (30-day mortality prediction): [4] Calculates based on: • Parenchymal lesion >6 cm (+3) • Bilateral Babinski signs (+3) • Coma (+3) • Male sex (+2) • Parenchymal hemorrhage (+2) • Stupor (+2) • Somnolence (+1) Score interpretation: • Mild (0-2): 1.1% mortality • Moderate (3-7): 19.6% mortality • Severe (8-13): 61.4% mortality ISCVT-RS (poor

nodes.title: Anticoagulation — First-Line
nodes.summary: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h immediately — do NOT delay, even with ICH present
nodes.body: Initiate anticoagulation IMMEDIATELY [1,2,3] Preferred: LMWH • Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h • More predictable anticoagulation • Lower HIT risk than UFH • No monitoring required Alternative: UFH • Weight-based IV infusion • aPTT goal: 1.5-2.5× control • Use if: — Renal impairment (CrCl <30) — Need for rapid reversal (surgery pending) — Concern for deterioration requiring intervention Key point: Star

nodes.title: Transition to Oral Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Transition to DOAC (rivaroxaban/apixaban) after 5-15 days — contraindicated in pregnancy and APS
nodes.body: Timing: After 5-15 days of parenteral therapy [1,3] Options: DOACs (increasingly favored): • Better safety profile than warfarin • No INR monitoring required • Rivaroxaban 20mg daily with food • Apixaban 5mg BID Warfarin: • INR target: 2-3 • Requires bridging with LMWH/UFH • Use when DOACs contraindicated DOAC Contraindications: • Pregnancy (teratogenic, crosses placenta) • Antiphospholipid syndro

nodes.title: Duration of Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Transient risk factor: 3 months; idiopathic: 6-12 months; severe thrombophilia: indefinite
nodes.body: Duration depends on etiology: [1,3] | Scenario | Duration | |----------|----------| | Transient/reversible risk factor | 3 months | | Idiopathic or mild thrombophilia | 6-12 months | | Severe thrombophilia | Indefinite | | Recurrent CVST | Indefinite | | Active malignancy | Duration of active disease | Transient risk factors: • OCP use (discontinue and reassess) • Pregnancy/puerperium • Recent sur

nodes.title: Assess for Escalation
nodes.summary: Monitor for deterioration despite anticoagulation — endovascular or craniectomy if declining
nodes.body: Monitor for deterioration despite anticoagulation: Signs requiring escalation: • Progressive neurologic decline • Worsening mental status • New or expanding hemorrhage • Signs of herniation Escalation options: • Endovascular therapy (thrombectomy/thrombolysis) • Decompressive craniectomy Is the patient deteriorating despite adequate anticoagulation?

nodes.title: Endovascular Therapy
nodes.summary: Reserved for neurologic deterioration despite adequate anticoagulation — very low quality evidence
nodes.body: Reserved for: [1,2] 1. Neurological deterioration despite adequate anticoagulation 2. Absolute contraindication to anticoagulation 3. Extensive thrombosis with severe deficit 4. Deep venous system involvement with altered mental status Modalities: • Catheter-directed thrombolysis • Mechanical thrombectomy • Combined approach Evidence: Very low quality — ESO states "cannot provide a recommendation"

nodes.title: Decompressive Craniectomy
nodes.summary: Decompressive craniectomy if herniation or midline shift ≥5mm — >50% favorable outcomes
nodes.body: Life-saving intervention for malignant CVST: [6] Indications: • Clinical signs of herniation (3rd nerve palsy, GCS decline) • CT showing: — Midline shift ≥5 mm — Effacement of basal cisterns — Significant mass effect from hemorrhagic venous infarction Outcomes: • >50% favorable outcomes • ~20% mortality • Better than medical management alone for malignant course Post-operative anticoagulation: • R

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Pregnancy: LMWH only (DOACs teratogenic); malignancy: LMWH preferred; OCP: discontinue estrogen
nodes.body: Does the patient belong to a special population requiring modified management? • Pregnancy/postpartum — LMWH throughout, DOAC contraindicated • Malignancy — prolonged anticoagulation, LMWH preferred • OCP user — discontinue estrogen-containing contraceptives

nodes.title: CVST in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: LMWH throughout pregnancy + ≥6 weeks postpartum — DOACs and warfarin contraindicated in pregnancy
nodes.body: Anticoagulation: [7] • LMWH throughout pregnancy (does not cross placenta) • Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h • Continue ≥6 weeks postpartum (minimum 3 months total) CONTRAINDICATED: • DOACs — teratogenic, excreted in breast milk • Warfarin — first trimester teratogenicity (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) Delivery considerations: • Vaginal delivery is safe if facilitated by responsive team • C-sec

nodes.title: CVST with Malignancy
nodes.summary: LMWH preferred for cancer-associated CVST — continue for duration of active malignancy
nodes.body: ~6% of CVST cases have coexisting malignancy [8] Treatment: • LMWH preferred for initial and long-term therapy • Used in 71-74% of cancer-associated CVST cases • DOACs: Insufficient evidence in malignancy-related CVST Duration: • Minimum 3 months • Duration of active malignancy • Consider indefinite if high recurrence risk Prognosis considerations: • Higher intracranial hemorrhage risk (13-fold in

nodes.title: OCP and Contraception
nodes.summary: Discontinue ALL estrogen-containing contraceptives — safe alternatives: progestin-only or copper IUD
nodes.body: OCP-associated CVST risk: [1,7] • OR 7.59 (95% CI 3.82-15.09) vs non-users • Third-generation pills (desogestrel, gestodene): Highest risk Post-CVST contraception: DISCONTINUE: • All estrogen-containing contraceptives • Combined OCPs • Estrogen patches/rings SAFE ALTERNATIVES: • Progestin-only methods: — Levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena) — Progestin-only pills (norethindrone) — Depo-Provera (medroxyprog

nodes.title: Admission and Follow-up
nodes.summary: All CVST patients require admission — ICU if AMS or high CVT-GS; neuro unit if stable
nodes.body: All CVST patients require admission: ICU admission if: • Altered mental status / encephalopathy • Deep venous system involvement • Large hemorrhagic infarction • High CVT-GS score (≥3) • Concerns for herniation Step-down/Neuro unit if: • Stable neurologic exam • Isolated intracranial hypertension • Low CVT-GS score (0-2) Monitoring: • Neuro checks q1-2h initially • Serial imaging if deterioration
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU or neuro unit based on severity. Continue anticoagulation. Plan transition to oral therapy and outpatient follow-up.

nodes.title: Super Glue (Cyanoacrylate) Removal \u2014 Eye / Eyelid / Skin
nodes.summary: Never acetone near eye, never force lids; most cyanoacrylate exposures self-resolve.
nodes.body: Cyanoacrylate exposure is alarming but usually benign. Two rules: NEVER use acetone near the eye, and NEVER force glued eyelids apart \u2014 both cause injury. Most exposures self-resolve without intervention \u2014 but tell the patient it takes days, not hours (typically 1\u20134 days for lids, longer in some series). Tools (open first): - Procedure Steps Summary - Eye vs Eyelid vs Skin Triage Ca

nodes.title: Where Is the Glue?
nodes.summary: Sort: eyelid-glued vs ocular-surface vs skin-only; eye involvement needs globe assessment.
nodes.body: Location determines the technique. Use the Eye vs Eyelid vs Skin Triage Card to sort it out.

nodes.title: Rule Out Globe Injury First
nodes.summary: Check acuity + rule out globe injury before manipulation; ophtho if trauma suspected.
nodes.body: Before any manipulation around the eye: - Assess visual acuity (each eye, best you can with lids involved) - Look for signs of globe injury or true corneal involvement; cyanoacrylate hardens fast and usually sits ON the surface rather than penetrating, but hardened fragments can cause corneal abrasion - If there is any suspicion of open-globe or significant ocular trauma, treat per Ocular Trauma /

nodes.title: Eyelid De-adhesion \u2014 Choose Approach
nodes.summary: Eyelids: antibiotic-ointment dwell (passive) or gentle hook technique; never force apart.
nodes.body: For glued lids, two safe, evidence-described approaches. Do not force the lids apart with traction. Apply topical anesthetic first (Topical Anesthetic Options).

nodes.title: Antibiotic-Ointment Dwell
nodes.summary: Ointment lubricates (does NOT dissolve glue); lids release over 1\u20134 d up to ~1 wk; trim, don\u2019t pull; no cotton on wet glue.
nodes.body: 1. Instill topical anesthetic for comfort. 2. Apply Bacitracin or erythromycin ophthalmic ointment generously along and into the glued lid margin/lashes. 3. Have the patient reapply every few hours. \u26a0\ufe0f Mechanism honesty: ointment does NOT dissolve cyanoacrylate. In vitro, bacitracin, K-Y jelly, baby shampoo, and water were all no better than control; only acetone dissolved the polymer, a

nodes.title: Gentle Hook Technique
nodes.summary: Gentle hook/swap through fissure gap, free lashes a few at a time; never force; trim stubborn lashes.
nodes.body: 1. Topical anesthetic first. 2. Identify any small gap in the lid fissure. 3. Gently introduce a smooth blunt instrument (muscle/Jameson hook or moistened swab) and roll/lift to free glued lashes a few at a time. Lubricate with ophthalmic ointment to ease release. 4. No forceful traction at any point \u2014 if it does not release easily, switch to the ointment-dwell approach and let time do the wo

nodes.title: Skin-Only De-adhesion
nodes.summary: Skin: warm soapy soak + petroleum, roll apart gently; acetone only far from eye/mucosa.
nodes.body: For glue on fingers, lips, or other non-ocular skin: 1. Soak in warm soapy water. 2. Apply a petroleum-based product (petrolatum, mineral oil, or a petroleum-based hand cleaner) and gently roll the skin apart \u2014 do not rip glued skin surfaces apart. 3. Acetone may be used for skin AWAY from the eye and mucous membranes, but petroleum is gentler and preferred; never use acetone near the eye, li

nodes.title: Recheck Cornea + Reassure
nodes.summary: Fluorescein-check for abrasion, treat if present; remove only loose fragments; reassure self-resolution.
nodes.body: Once the eye is accessible: - Perform a Fluorescein / Corneal-Abrasion Check; hardened glue fragments can cause corneal abrasion. - Treat any abrasion per standard care (topical antibiotic, analgesia, ophthalmology follow-up; do NOT patch if contact-lens-related risk or as per local practice). - Remove loose glue fragments from the conjunctival surface gently; do not chase well-adhered fragments \

nodes.title: Disposition + Note
nodes.summary: Discharge most w/ reassurance; ophtho for abrasion/retained glue/globe concern.
nodes.body: Disposition: - Discharge most patients once lids are open / skin freed and the cornea is intact or has a small abrasion managed routinely. - Ophthalmology referral for: corneal abrasion needing follow-up, retained adherent ocular-surface glue causing symptoms, or any concern for globe injury. - Return precautions: worsening pain, vision change, photophobia, discharge, or signs of infection. Note t
nodes.recommendation: Discharge once lids open + cornea intact; ophthalmology for abrasion/retained glue/globe concern.

nodes.title: Deep Neck Space Infections
nodes.summary: Deep neck infections can obstruct airway within hours — assess airway stability immediately
nodes.body: Deep neck infections (DNIs) are potentially life-threatening infections affecting the cervical fascial spaces. They can progress rapidly to airway obstruction, sepsis, mediastinitis, and death. [1,2] Mortality without treatment approaches 40-60% when complicated by descending necrotizing mediastinitis. With aggressive management, mortality has decreased to 8-16%. [2,3] Most common etiologies: - Od

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Clinical Presentation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Common presenting symptoms: [1,5] - Neck pain and swelling (unilateral or bilateral) - Odynophagia and dysphagia - Fever and malaise - Trismus (inability to open mouth) - Voice changes (hot potato voice) - Drooling RED FLAGS indicating severe disease: [2,5] - Stridor or respiratory distress - Tripod positioning - Crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema) - Bilateral neck swelling ("bull neck") - Floor of

nodes.title: Airway Assessment
nodes.summary: Airway Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Assess for signs of airway compromise IMMEDIATELY. [5,6] Stridor and cyanosis are late, ominous signs of impending respiratory failure. Earlier signs include: - Drooling or inability to handle secretions - Muffled "hot potato" voice - Tripod positioning - Difficulty lying flat - Floor of mouth elevation - Tongue protrusion

nodes.title: Neck Fascial Spaces
nodes.summary: Neck Fascial Spaces — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: The neck contains interconnected fascial compartments that facilitate infection spread. [1,7] Superficial space: - Between skin and investing fascia - Limited clinical significance Deep cervical spaces: - Submandibular (includes sublingual & submental) - Parapharyngeal (lateral to pharynx) - Retropharyngeal (posterior to pharynx, anterior to prevertebral fascia) - Danger space (between alar and pr

nodes.title: Clinical Syndrome
nodes.summary: Clinical Syndrome — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Based on presentation and suspected anatomic involvement, select the most likely clinical syndrome. [1,5,8]

nodes.title: Ludwig Angina
nodes.summary: Ludwig angina: bilateral submandibular cellulitis — tongue elevation can cause airway obstruction within hours
nodes.body: Ludwig angina is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening cellulitis of the floor of the mouth. [5,9] Classic triad: 1. Bilateral submandibular space involvement 2. Gangrenous cellulitis (not abscess formation) 3. No lymphatic involvement Clinical features: - "Bull neck" appearance with bilateral swelling - Firm, board-like induration of floor of mouth - Tongue elevation and posterior displacement

nodes.title: Ludwig Angina: Airway Priority
nodes.summary: Ludwig Angina: Airway Priority — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Airway management is the #1 priority in Ludwig angina. [5,6,9] Direct laryngoscopy will often fail due to: - Tongue elevation and posterior displacement - Board-like induration of floor of mouth - Trismus limiting mouth opening - Distorted anatomy Preferred approach: Awake fiberoptic intubation [6] - Maintain spontaneous respiration - Patient upright or semi-recumbent - Topical anesthesia (avoid n

nodes.title: Retropharyngeal Abscess
nodes.summary: Retropharyngeal abscess: posterior pharyngeal bulge — CT with contrast, ENT consultation for drainage
nodes.body: Retropharyngeal abscess is a potentially life-threatening infection between the pharynx and prevertebral fascia. [8,10] Pediatric (6 months - 6 years): - 50% of cases occur in children 6-12 months - Typically follows URI with suppurative lymphadenitis - Retropharyngeal lymph nodes drain nasopharynx, sinuses, middle ear - These nodes atrophy by age 5-6 Adult: - Usually from foreign body ingestion o

nodes.title: Retropharyngeal Abscess Management
nodes.summary: Retropharyngeal Abscess Management — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Imaging: [8,10,11] - CT neck with IV contrast is gold standard - Sensitivity ~100%, specificity ~45% (often overcalls abscess) - Ultrasound in peds: 89% sensitivity, 100% specificity Medical vs Surgical: [8] - Medical management successful in many children with small collections (<2 cm) - Surgical drainage required if: - Large abscess (>2 cm hypodense focus) - Failure to improve on IV antibiotics

nodes.title: Parapharyngeal Space Infection
nodes.summary: Parapharyngeal abscess can erode into carotid — CT with contrast mandatory, ENT for drainage
nodes.body: The parapharyngeal space is a critical lateral neck compartment. [1,7] Also called the "pharyngomaxillary" or "lateral pharyngeal" space. Anatomy: - Inverted pyramid from skull base to hyoid bone - Medial: pharyngeal constrictors - Lateral: mandible, parotid, pterygoid muscles - Contains carotid artery, IJV, CN IX-XII, sympathetic chain Clinical presentation: - High fever with toxic appearance - U

nodes.title: Lemierre Syndrome
nodes.summary: Lemierre Syndrome — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Lemierre syndrome: septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. [12,13] Also called "postanginal sepsis" or "the forgotten disease." Classic tetrad: 1. Recent oropharyngeal infection (pharyngitis/tonsillitis) 2. Bacteremia (typically *Fusobacterium necrophorum*) 3. Internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis 4. Septic emboli (lung most common) Clinical course: [12] - Pharyngitis 4-7 days befor

nodes.title: Lemierre Syndrome Treatment
nodes.summary: Lemierre Syndrome Treatment — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Antibiotic therapy is the cornerstone of treatment. [12,13] First-line: Beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor - Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV q6h, OR - Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h Alternative (penicillin allergy): - Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h (*F. necrophorum* almost always sensitive) - Plus coverage for other pharyngeal flora Duration: 4-6 weeks to penetrate fibrin clot. [12] Anticoagulation

nodes.title: Peritonsillar Abscess
nodes.summary: Peritonsillar abscess: unilateral swelling, uvula deviation, trismus — needle aspiration or I&D
nodes.body: Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) is the most common deep space infection of the head and neck. [14] Clinical presentation: - Severe sore throat (usually unilateral) - "Hot potato" muffled voice - Trismus - Uvular deviation away from affected side - Soft palate bulging - Cervical lymphadenopathy Diagnosis: Clinical. CT only if atypical presentation or concern for extension. Management: [14] - Needle asp

nodes.title: Emergent Airway Management
nodes.summary: Emergent Airway Management — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: AIRWAY IS THE ABSOLUTE PRIORITY. [5,6] Deep neck infections create a "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" scenario risk. General principles: 1. Maintain spontaneous ventilation as long as possible 2. Avoid sedation/paralysis (can cause complete collapse) 3. Have surgical airway immediately available 4. Expert help (ENT, Anesthesia) if time permits 5. Mark cricothyroid membrane BEFORE any attempt Pr

nodes.title: Airway Decision Algorithm
nodes.summary: Airway Decision Algorithm — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: STEP 1: Assess stability - Can patient maintain airway currently? - Rapidly progressive or stable? STEP 2: Prepare (regardless of stability) - Call ENT/Anesthesia early - Surgical airway tray at bedside - Mark cricothyroid membrane - Suction ready STEP 3: Choose approach [6] If time permits (stable but at risk): - Awake fiberoptic intubation in OR with ENT/Anesthesia - Double setup: FOI with trach

nodes.title: Imaging in Deep Neck Infections
nodes.summary: CT neck with IV contrast is imaging of choice — assess extent, identify drainable collections
nodes.body: CT neck with IV contrast is the gold standard. [1,7,11] Indications for emergent CT: - Clinical suspicion of deep neck infection - Delineate extent of disease - Identify drainable collections - Evaluate for complications (vascular, mediastinal) CT findings: [11] - Rim-enhancing hypodense collection (abscess) - Scalloping of abscess wall = purulence at surgery - Soft tissue swelling and fat strandi

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy
nodes.summary: Unasyn 3g IV q6h or clindamycin + ceftriaxone — cover oral flora including anaerobes
nodes.body: Deep neck infections are polymicrobial. [1,4] Common organisms: - Streptococci (Group A, viridans group) - Staphylococci (including MRSA in some populations) - Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) - Eikenella corrodens (oral flora) Empiric coverage must include: - Gram-positive organisms - Gram-negative organisms - Anaerobic coverage First-line regimens: [1,4,5] - Ampicillin-

nodes.title: Severe/Necrotizing Infections
nodes.summary: Severe/Necrotizing Infections — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Broadened coverage for severe infections or necrotizing fasciitis: [2,3] Regimen: - Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h, OR - Meropenem 1g IV q8h - PLUS Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h - PLUS Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h (toxin suppression) Clindamycin rationale: Suppresses bacterial toxin production in necrotizing infections. Duration: [1] - Uncomplicated: 2-3 weeks - Mediastinal involvement: 4-6 w

nodes.title: Surgical Management
nodes.summary: ENT consultation for all deep neck infections — I&D if drainable collection on CT
nodes.body: Surgery is required for most deep neck abscesses. [1,2,3] Indications for surgical drainage: - Frank abscess on imaging (rim-enhancing collection) - Clinical fluctuance - Failure to improve after 48-72 hours of IV antibiotics - Airway compromise - Necrotizing infection - Mediastinal extension Surgical approach: [1] - External transcervical incision and drainage most common - Wide debridement for n

nodes.title: Life-Threatening Complications
nodes.summary: Watch for mediastinitis, Lemierre syndrome, carotid erosion, airway compromise
nodes.body: Deep neck infections can rapidly progress to fatal complications. [2,3] Descending necrotizing mediastinitis: - Extension via danger space or carotid sheath - Mortality 40-60% even with aggressive treatment - Requires thoracic surgery consultation - CT chest to evaluate extent Airway obstruction: - Most common cause of death in Ludwig angina - Can occur rapidly with minimal warning Sepsis/Septic s

nodes.title: Descending Necrotizing Mediastinitis
nodes.summary: Descending Necrotizing Mediastinitis — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: The most feared complication of deep neck infection. [2,3] Infection spreads from cervical spaces into the mediastinum via: - Danger space (alar to prevertebral fascia) - Carotid sheath - Pretracheal space Clinical predictors of DNM: [3] - Age >=55 years - Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio >=13 - CRP >=30 mg/dL - Diabetes mellitus Clinical findings: - Chest pain and dyspnea - Subcutaneous emphysema e

nodes.title: Multidisciplinary Consultation
nodes.summary: Multidisciplinary Consultation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Deep neck infections require a multidisciplinary team. [1,2] Essential consultations: ENT (Otolaryngology): - All deep neck infections - Surgical drainage planning - Airway management assistance Anesthesia: - Difficult airway planning - Awake fiberoptic intubation Infectious Disease: - Complex antibiotic regimens - Prolonged therapy planning - Culture guidance Additional consultations as needed: -

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on clinical severity and airway status. [1,2]

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: ICU admission is required for: [2] - Any airway compromise or recent advanced airway - Post-operative monitoring after surgical drainage - Severe sepsis or septic shock - Necrotizing infection - Mediastinal involvement - Multi-organ dysfunction - Need for vasopressors ICU management: - Airway monitoring (may need days before extubation safe) - Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics - Repeat imaging to asse
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for airway monitoring, IV antibiotics, and close observation. ENT/surgical team involvement for source control.

nodes.title: Surgical Ward Admission
nodes.summary: Surgical Ward Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Floor admission criteria: - Stable airway without imminent compromise - Post-drainage with drains in place - IV antibiotic therapy - No signs of necrotizing infection or mediastinitis Ward management: - IV antibiotics per culture/sensitivity - Drain management and output monitoring - Serial clinical assessment for progression - Pain control - NPO or soft diet as tolerated - Dental extraction once
nodes.recommendation: Admit to surgical ward for IV antibiotics, drain management, and serial monitoring. Involve ENT/oral surgery for source control.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria (PTA only)

nodes.body: Discharge may be considered for SIMPLE peritonsillar abscess ONLY if: [14] - Abscess successfully drained (aspiration or I&D) - Pain controlled with oral medications - Tolerating oral intake (fluids/soft diet) - No signs of extension to deeper spaces - Reliable patient with follow-up access - No immunocompromise - Able to return immediately if worsening Discharge medications: - Amoxicillin-clavula
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with oral antibiotics and close ENT follow-up. Return precautions for any signs of progression or airway concerns.

nodes.title: Delayed Sequence Intubation (DSI)
nodes.summary: DSI = procedural sedation where the procedure is preoxygenation; ketamine preserves spontaneous breathing
nodes.body: DSI Quick Reference Core Concept: DSI is procedural sedation where the procedure is preoxygenation. [1] Rather than simultaneously giving sedative + paralytic (RSI), DSI uses a dissociative agent that preserves spontaneous breathing and airway reflexes, allowing adequate oxygen loading BEFORE paralysis. nodes.title: Delirium Management
nodes.summary: Delirium is a medical emergency — always identify and treat the underlying cause
nodes.body: Delirium Steps Summary — rapid assessment and management pathway. Delirium is acute brain dysfunction — DSM-5 defines as acute/fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition. 7-24% of elderly ED patients have delirium; up to 80% of ICU patients. Missed diagnosis rate 54-89%. Mortality comparable to sepsis and MI. Delirium is a SYMPTOM requiring urgent etiology search, not just behavioral manag

nodes.title: Scene Safety & Team Preparation
nodes.summary: Scene Safety & Team Preparation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Personal and team safety first. For agitated patients: remove sharps/equipment from reach, ensure adequate staffing (minimum 5 for physical restraint), activate security if needed. Approach calmly, non-threateningly. One person speaks. Verbal De-escalation: 10 Elements — AAEP Project BETA guidelines for engaging the agitated patient. Position yourself near the exit. Do not corner the patient. Show

nodes.title: Rapid Reversible Causes
nodes.summary: Rapid Reversible Causes — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Primary survey: ABCs, vital signs, fingerstick glucose. Check for immediately correctable causes before proceeding with delirium workup. Fingerstick glucose — hypoglycemia is common and immediately reversible. D50W 25g IV if <60 mg/dL. SpO2 — supplement O2 if hypoxic. Hypoxia causes direct brain insult. Temperature — fever suggests infection; >104°F (40°C) raises concern for excited delirium syndr

nodes.title: Correct Reversible Cause
nodes.summary: Correct Reversible Cause — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Treat the identified cause with standard emergency care: • Hypoglycemia: D50W 25g IV (adults) or D10W 2-5 mL/kg (peds). Recheck glucose in 15 min. • Hypoxia: Supplemental O2 to SpO2 >94%. Evaluate for pneumonia, PE, CHF. • Opioid toxicity: Naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV/IN. May repeat q2-3 min. Consider infusion if recurrent (2/3 of effective dose per hour). • Hypothermia: Active warming. Evaluate for under

nodes.summary: Delirium Screening & Subtype Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: RASS (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) — assess level of agitation or sedation to determine delirium subtype and guide management. CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) — gold standard ED screening tool. Delirium is present when ALL of: 1. Acute onset or fluctuating course (change from baseline) 2. Inattention (unable to recite months backward, spell WORLD backward, or count backward from 20) PLUS E

nodes.title: Hypoactive Delirium
nodes.summary: Hypoactive Delirium — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: RASS -1 to -3. The most commonly missed subtype — 32-67% undiagnosed in the ED. Higher mortality than hyperactive. Patients are often dismissed as "tired" or "baseline dementia." Verify with family/prior documentation before attributing to baseline. Common causes: Metabolic derangements, medication effects (opioids, sedatives, anticholinergics), infection (UTI/pneumonia in elderly), dehydration. A

nodes.title: Hyperactive / Mixed Delirium
nodes.summary: Hyperactive / Mixed Delirium — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: RASS +1 to +4. Agitation, combativeness, hyperactivity, hallucinations. Mixed delirium fluctuates between subtypes — most persistent course. Distinguish from primary psychiatric disorder: • Delirium: acute onset, fluctuating, inattention, altered consciousness • Primary psychosis: chronic/subacute, organized delusions, intact attention, stable vitals • New-onset "psychiatric" symptoms without psyc

nodes.title: Hyperactive Delirium With Hyperthermia
nodes.summary: Hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia — cooling, rapid sedation, IV fluids, and close monitoring.
nodes.body: Hyperactive Delirium With Hyperthermia — recognition, physiology, and emergency management. Medical emergency — severe agitation plus hyperthermia, acidosis, or prolonged physical struggle can rapidly progress to dysrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, or arrest. Temperature >104°F is a major danger sign. IMMEDIATE: Remove from prone position → aggressive cooling → IV access → rapid sedation and monitor

nodes.title: Etiology Assessment
nodes.summary: Etiology Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Multiple causes often coexist. In 13% of cases, no precipitant is identified. Precipitating Factors — comprehensive list by category. Vulnerability Factors — patient risk factors that lower the delirium threshold. Which category is most likely based on your clinical assessment?

nodes.title: Infection-Precipitated Delirium
nodes.summary: Infection-Precipitated Delirium — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Infection is the most common precipitant — cited in 16-67% of cases, particularly in the elderly. Most common sources: • Urinary tract infection — most common infectious cause in elderly. Delirium may be the ONLY presenting sign — fever is absent in up to 50% of elderly patients with UTI. • Pneumonia — second most common. Cough and dyspnea may be absent. Tachypnea or hypoxia may be the only clue.

nodes.title: Metabolic / Endocrine Causes
nodes.summary: Metabolic / Endocrine Causes — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Common metabolic precipitants: • Sodium disorders — hypo- and hypernatremia. Sodium Disorders consult for management. • Hypercalcemia — malignancy, hyperparathyroidism. "Stones, bones, groans, moans, psychiatric overtones." • Hepatic encephalopathy — check ammonia level. Lactulose, rifaximin. • Uremia — BUN/Cr ratio >18 associated with increased delirium risk. • Hypoglycemia / hyperglycemia — DKA,

nodes.title: Intracranial Pathology
nodes.summary: Intracranial Pathology — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Structural and neurologic causes of delirium: • Stroke — both ischemic and hemorrhagic. Delirium can be the presenting symptom, especially posterior circulation strokes. • Subdural hematoma — especially in elderly on anticoagulants. May present without clear trauma history. • Subarachnoid hemorrhage — "worst headache of life" may be absent in elderly; delirium may predominate. • Meningitis / encep

nodes.title: Toxic / Medication-Related Delirium
nodes.summary: Toxic / Medication-Related Delirium — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Medications are a particularly prevalent cause — especially in the elderly. Even without new prescriptions, dose changes and OTC interactions can precipitate delirium. Beers Criteria high-risk medications: • Anticholinergics — diphenhydramine, promethazine, scopolamine, oxybutynin, TCAs • Benzodiazepines — independent risk factor for delirium • Opioids — especially meperidine (highest risk) • Seda

nodes.title: Directed Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Directed Diagnostic Workup — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Directed by history, physical, and differential — not a shotgun approach. Clinical judgment and common sense are the consensus recommendation. For ALL patients with suspected delirium: • Fingerstick glucose (already done) • BMP: Na, K, Ca, Mg, glucose, BUN/Cr • CBC with differential • Urinalysis with culture • VBG or ABG with lactate • ECG — arrhythmia, MI (delirium is the ONLY symptom in up to 5%

nodes.title: Medication Review
nodes.summary: Medication Review — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Systematic medication reconciliation — one of the most easily correctable precipitants. Check for: • New medications within past 2 weeks • Recent dose changes • Drug-drug interactions (CYP inhibitors/inducers) • Polypharmacy (≥5 meds independently increases risk) • Anticholinergic burden — cumulative effect of multiple low-anticholinergic drugs • Recent discontinuation (withdrawal risk) See Precip

nodes.summary: Nonpharmacological Interventions — review key clinical information before proceeding

nodes.summary: Pharmacological Treatment Needed? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Pharmacological treatment is second-line — only when nonpharmacological interventions fail and safety is at risk. Indications: • Severe agitation threatening patient or staff safety • Unable to cooperate with essential workup or critical care • Physical restraints needed to facilitate evaluation Do NOT sedate hypoactive delirium — treat the underlying cause instead.

nodes.summary: Treatment Response — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Reassess 15-20 minutes after pharmacological intervention. Target RASS score: 0 to -1 (alert and calm to drowsy). Oversedation increases aspiration risk, delays evaluation, and masks clinical deterioration. Monitor: respiratory rate, SpO2, blood pressure, level of consciousness. Maintain head of bed elevated.

nodes.summary: Treatment Escalation — review key clinical information before proceeding

nodes.summary: Disposition — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Delirium is an independent risk factor for increased morbidity and mortality. Up to 37% of delirious ED patients are discharged home. Mortality for discharged delirium patients is 2-3× higher at 3-6 months compared to nondelirious patients. nodes.summary: Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: • Excited delirium syndrome • Intubated for airway protection • Hemodynamic instability • Cardiac arrhythmia (post-sedation or underlying) • Refractory agitation requiring continuous infusion • Rhabdomyolysis with renal failure Floor / observation admission criteria: • New-onset delirium without clear reversible cause • Persistent altered mental status • Elderly with infect
nodes.recommendation: Admit for further evaluation and management of delirium. Communicate baseline status, ED interventions, and suspected etiology to admitting team.

nodes.title: Discharge with Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Discharge with Follow-Up — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Discharge may be appropriate when ALL of the following are met: • Clear reversible cause identified AND corrected (e.g., hypoglycemia, UTI in young patient) • Patient has returned to documented baseline mental status • Vital signs stable and normalizing • Safe home environment with capable caregiver present • Reliable follow-up arranged within 24-48 hours • Patient and caregiver understand return
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with close follow-up. Ensure caregiver understands return precautions and follow-up plan.

nodes.title: Dementia & Agitation
nodes.summary: Start with safety, medical triggers, decision-specific capacity, and the correct Texas legal pathway.
nodes.body: Dementia Agitation Steps Agitation in dementia is a medical, neurologic, ethical, and legal problem. Do not default to a psychiatric hold before screening for delirium, pain, medication toxicity, infection, urinary retention, constipation, trauma, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, and caregiver/environmental triggers. nodes.title: Immediate Safety
nodes.summary: Safety first; de-escalate, correct immediate medical threats, and use restraint only for immediate safety.
nodes.body: Use a safety-first, least-restrictive approach. Immediate actions: 1. Call adequate staff/security; remove weapons, sharps, cords, and excess equipment. 2. One calm lead communicator; reduce stimulation; avoid crowding or arguing. 3. Check glucose, oxygenation, temperature, vitals, obvious trauma/pain, and medication exposure while de-escalating. 4. If danger prevents essential care: use targeted

nodes.title: Rescue Medication Route
nodes.summary: Use the lowest effective route/dose; avoid benzodiazepines unless a specific indication exists.
nodes.body: Medication Guide Choose the least sedating route that achieves safety. Medication is justified when the patient is dangerous, severely distressed, or agitation blocks urgent evaluation/treatment. Avoid routine benzodiazepines in older adults with dementia or delirium unless withdrawal, seizure, catatonia, severe stimulant toxicity, or a specific anxiety/panic indication is driving the agitation.

nodes.title: Oral Medication Options
nodes.summary: For PO rescue, use low-dose quetiapine, risperidone, or olanzapine based on EPS and sedation needs.
nodes.body: For a semi-cooperative patient who still requires medication: - Quetiapine: 12.5-25 mg PO for frail elderly or Parkinson/Lewy body concern; slower onset, less EPS. - Risperidone: 0.25-0.5 mg PO/ODT when mild antipsychotic effect is needed and no Parkinson/Lewy body concern. - Olanzapine: 2.5-5 mg PO/ODT when more sedation is needed; avoid parenteral benzodiazepines near IM olanzapine.
