nodes.title: IM/IV Rescue Medication
nodes.summary: IM/IV rescue is for danger or blocked essential care; dose low and reassess for complications.
nodes.body: Use the lowest effective dose and reassess frequently. Common ED options: - Haloperidol: 0.5-1 mg IM/IV; may repeat cautiously. Avoid or use extreme caution with Parkinson/Lewy body dementia, prolonged QTc, severe EPS history. - Olanzapine: 2.5-5 mg IM. Avoid parenteral benzodiazepines near IM olanzapine because of respiratory/hypotension risk. - Lorazepam: reserve for alcohol/benzodiazepine withd

nodes.title: Lewy Body / Parkinson Dementia
nodes.summary: Lewy body/Parkinson dementia has high neuroleptic sensitivity; prefer nonpharm and quetiapine when possible.
nodes.body: Suspect Lewy body/Parkinson dementia if visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, or known diagnosis. Avoid or use extreme caution: - Haloperidol, droperidol, risperidone, high-potency D2 blockade - Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine Preferred if medication is unavoidable: - Verbal/environmental control first - Quetiapine 12.5-25 mg PO if cooperative

nodes.title: Context Before Labeling Behavior
nodes.summary: Collateral defines baseline; acute or fluctuating change is delirium until proven otherwise.
nodes.body: Obtain collateral before calling this baseline dementia behavior. Ask family/caregiver/facility: - What is baseline cognition, function, speech, gait, sleep, and behavior? - When did this change start? Acute/fluctuating suggests delirium until proven otherwise. - Any pain, fall/head strike, fever, poor intake, missed dialysis, hypoxia, new meds, anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids

nodes.title: Pain, Retention, Constipation
nodes.summary: Occult pain, urinary retention, and constipation are common fixable drivers of agitation.
nodes.body: High-yield dementia agitation triggers: Pain: - Fracture/fall, pressure injury, dental pain, urinary infection, abdominal pathology, arthritis, wound infection - Treat pain directly; avoid undertreating because the patient cannot describe it Urinary retention: - Bladder scan early, especially after anticholinergics, opioids, constipation, BPH, immobility - Decompress if significant retention and c

nodes.title: Medical Workup
nodes.summary: Work up acute agitation as a medical change until reversible causes are reasonably excluded.
nodes.body: Tailor testing to the patient, but do not under-evaluate acute agitation off baseline. Minimum rapid checks: - Fingerstick glucose, SpO2, temperature, vitals, EKG/QTc if antipsychotic likely - Medication reconciliation and recent changes Common ED labs/tests when acute change or unclear baseline: - CBC, CMP including sodium/calcium/renal function, Mg, UA/culture when urinary symptoms or no source,

nodes.title: Medication / Toxic Review
nodes.summary: Medication toxicity and withdrawal are frequent, treatable contributors to agitation.
nodes.body: Look for medication causes before adding more sedating drugs. High-risk culprits: - Anticholinergics: diphenhydramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, oxybutynin, TCAs, scopolamine - Sedatives: benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, barbiturates - Opioids, especially dose escalation or renal accumulation - Steroids, fluoroquinolones, dopamine agonists, antiepileptics, polypharmacy - Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdr

nodes.title: Trauma / Neurologic Event
nodes.summary: Falls, anticoagulation, focal deficits, seizure, and headache should redirect toward neurologic evaluation.
nodes.body: Do not assume agitation is psychiatric or dementia progression when neurologic red flags exist. Consider head CT/neurology pathway for: - Fall/head strike, anticoagulation, new headache, vomiting, seizure, focal deficit, severe hypertension, new gait inability, or unexplained depressed consciousness - Subdural hematoma can present subtly in dementia - Nonconvulsive seizure can present as persisten

nodes.title: Capacity / Consent Decision
nodes.summary: Capacity is for this decision now; dementia diagnosis alone is not enough.
nodes.body: Capacity Tool Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate. Dementia diagnosis alone does not remove capacity; agitation alone does not prove incapacity. Identify the exact decision now: leaving, refusing test/treatment, accepting medication, transfer, discharge plan, or consent for procedure.

nodes.title: Has Capacity
nodes.summary: If capacity is intact, respect the decision and document informed refusal or consent.
nodes.body: If the patient has capacity for the specific decision: - Respect the decision, even if it is medically unwise - Provide informed refusal: risks, benefits, alternatives, return precautions - Offer a safer alternative plan: caregiver transport, follow-up, prescriptions, social work, crisis resources - Do not use dementia diagnosis alone to override refusal - Do not use a Texas mental-health hold unl
nodes.recommendation: Respect autonomous refusal/choice when decision-specific capacity is intact.

nodes.title: Lacks Capacity
nodes.summary: Medical incapacity uses emergency consent or surrogate consent; it is not automatically a psychiatric hold.
nodes.body: If the patient lacks capacity for the current medical decision: Immediate medical emergency: - Treat under implied emergency consent when delay risks serious harm - Use least restrictive means needed to prevent elopement or injury Non-emergent or ongoing care: - Look for medical power of attorney, guardian, advance directive, or surrogate - Texas Health & Safety Code Chapter 313 allows listed adul

nodes.title: Borderline / Fluctuating Capacity
nodes.summary: Treat reversible causes and reassess; high-stakes refusal requires higher confidence in capacity.
nodes.body: When capacity is unclear: - Treat reversible causes first when the decision can safely wait - Reassess after pain control, hydration, retention relief, glucose/oxygen correction, medication washout, or sleep - Use interpreters, hearing aids, glasses, family/caregiver support, and simple repeated explanations - Raise the rigor for high-stakes decisions such as refusal of admission, surgery, imaging

nodes.title: Texas Legal Pathway
nodes.summary: Texas Chapter 573 is for mental illness danger; dementia alone generally belongs on the medical incapacity pathway.
nodes.body: Texas Legal Tool Texas mental-health emergency detention requires a mental illness plus substantial risk of serious harm because of that mental illness and insufficient time for a warrant. Texas Health & Safety Code definition of mental illness excludes dementia. Therefore, dementia agitation alone is usually a medical incapacity/safety/surrogate problem, not a Chapter 573 psychiatric detention pr

nodes.title: Medical Incapacity Pathway
nodes.summary: Medical incapacity allows emergency stabilization and surrogate consent; it is separate from psychiatric detention.
nodes.body: Use this pathway when the problem is dementia, delirium, intoxication, brain injury, metabolic illness, or another medical/neurocognitive condition without separate Texas mental illness criteria. Actions: - Continue EMTALA medical screening/stabilizing evaluation - If lacks capacity and unsafe to leave: document medical incapacity for the specific decision and why leaving creates serious medical r

nodes.title: Texas Emergency Detention
nodes.summary: Chapter 573 requires qualifying mental illness plus danger because of that illness; dementia alone does not satisfy this definition.
nodes.body: Texas Chapter 573 emergency detention may apply only if: - The person has qualifying mental illness, and - Because of that mental illness, there is substantial risk of serious harm to self or others unless immediately restrained, and - There is insufficient time to obtain a warrant Examples that may qualify if danger criteria are met: - Dementia plus separate acute psychosis, mania, severe depress

nodes.title: Federal Overlay
nodes.summary: Federal law centers on MSE/stabilization, appropriate transfer, and strict restraint/seclusion requirements.
nodes.body: Federal rules do not create a generic dementia hold. They set ED duties and patient-rights boundaries. EMTALA: - Provide a medical screening exam for agitation/AMS - Stabilize emergency medical conditions within capability or arrange appropriate transfer - Do not transfer an unstabilized emergency condition unless EMTALA transfer requirements are met CMS restraints/seclusion: - Only for immediate

nodes.title: Behavioral Plan
nodes.summary: Use nonpharmacologic dementia care first; chronic FDA-approved agents are not ED rescue medications.
nodes.body: If no emergency medical trigger is found and agitation is likely dementia-related: Nonpharmacologic first: - Reduce noise/light/crowding; move to quieter area if feasible - Family/caregiver at bedside when safe - Hearing aids, glasses, interpreter, familiar objects - Food, fluids, toileting, warm blanket, sleep protection - Validate distress; avoid arguing with delusions when redirection works - M

nodes.title: Disposition / Safe Plan
nodes.summary: Disposition depends on medical trigger, capacity, safe caregiving, and the correct legal route.
nodes.body: Ethics / Disposition Tool Disposition should match medical risk, capacity, caregiver capability, and legal pathway. The safest plan may be medical admission even when psychiatry is not the right destination.

nodes.title: Medical Admission
nodes.summary: Medical admission is appropriate when the driver is medical, capacity is absent, or safe discharge is not achievable.
nodes.body: Admit medically when: - Delirium or reversible medical trigger is suspected or confirmed - Medication/restraint was needed and ongoing monitoring is required - Unsafe elopement risk with lack of capacity - No safe surrogate/caregiver plan - Need ongoing pain, infection, retention, metabolic, trauma, seizure, or medication-toxicity management - Facility refuses return due to behavior without medica
nodes.recommendation: Admit medically when agitation is driven by delirium/medical illness, incapacity, unsafe disposition, or need for monitoring.

nodes.title: APS / Ethics / Guardianship
nodes.summary: Unsafe caregiving or no decision-maker requires social work, APS/ethics, and possible guardianship pathway.
nodes.body: Escalate beyond ED medication when the environment is unsafe. Triggers: - Suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation, abandonment, medication theft, unsafe restraint at home/facility - Recurrent ED visits for agitation because care needs exceed home/facility capacity - No surrogate, family conflict, refusal of necessary placement, or high-risk discharge disagreement - Patient lacks capacity and no saf

nodes.title: Supported Discharge
nodes.summary: Safe discharge requires controlled symptoms, decision-making authority, and reliable caregiver/facility support.
nodes.body: Discharge may be reasonable only when: - No untreated emergency medical trigger is suspected - Agitation is controlled without unsafe sedation or unresolved restraint need - Capacity is intact for the discharge decision, or a valid surrogate accepts the plan - Responsible caregiver/facility can supervise, administer meds, remove hazards, and return if worse - Medication changes are conservative an
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only with controlled symptoms, no emergency trigger, valid decision-maker, and reliable supervision.

nodes.title: Documentation
nodes.summary: Documentation should make clear what was medical, what was capacity, what was legal, and what was safety.
nodes.body: Document the clinical and legal reasoning. Include: - Baseline mental status source and acute change timeline - Reversible trigger assessment and treatments given - Safety behaviors observed: objective threats, elopement attempts, violence, self-harm risk - Capacity assessment for the exact decision using understanding, appreciation, reasoning, communication - Legal pathway: medical incapacity/sur

nodes.title: Dementia - New Cognitive Concern
nodes.summary: Separate delirium from chronic cognitive decline, then prove functional impact and discharge safety.
nodes.body: Dementia steps | Differential | Diagnosis comfort Start by separating acute altered mental status from persistent acquired cognitive decline. ED framing: dementia is usually not diagnosed from a single ED visit. The ED role is to detect dangerous mimics, document the cognitive syndrome, obtain collateral, identify functional impairment, and route the patient to safe follow-up or protected disposit

nodes.title: Delirium First
nodes.summary: Acute cognitive change is delirium or medical illness until proven otherwise.
nodes.body: Do not call this dementia until acute causes are addressed. Delirium clues: acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, altered arousal, disorganized thinking, hallucinations, sleep-wake reversal, or sudden loss of baseline function. Dementia is a major delirium risk factor, but delirium is the actionable emergency. [2,3] Immediate ED checks: - POC glucose, oxygenation, temperature, vitals - Medication

nodes.title: Time-Sensitive Mimics
nodes.summary: Exclude delirium, stroke, metabolic, medication, psychiatric, sensory, and rapidly progressive mimics.
nodes.body: Do not miss these before labeling dementia progression: [2,3,6] Neurologic: stroke/TIA, ICH/subdural, seizure or nonconvulsive seizure, CNS infection, normal pressure hydrocephalus, rapidly progressive dementia/prion pattern, tumor. Metabolic/toxic: hypoglycemia, hyponatremia/hypernatremia, hypercalcemia, renal/hepatic failure, hypercarbia/hypoxia, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, medication toxic

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis Early
nodes.summary: Dementia is a syndrome; classify the likely pattern and reversible contributors early.
nodes.body: Differential guide Place the differential before the label. Dementia is a syndrome, not a single disease. Common patterns: [1,2,6] - Alzheimer disease: insidious episodic memory decline, word-finding difficulty, impaired learning - Vascular cognitive impairment: stepwise decline, stroke history, focal signs, executive dysfunction - Lewy body dementia: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations,

nodes.title: Collateral and Function
nodes.summary: Collateral and loss of ADL/IADL independence are essential to diagnosis and disposition.
nodes.body: Collateral is required. The patient may not recognize the deficit, and ED cognitive screening can be confounded by delirium, hearing, language, education, fatigue, pain, and stress. [1,2] Ask family/caregiver/facility: - Baseline cognition, language, gait, sleep, behavior, and independence - Time course: sudden, fluctuating, stepwise, or slowly progressive - ADLs: bathing, dressing, toileting, fee

nodes.title: Cognitive Screen
nodes.summary: Screens support documentation, but diagnosis needs time course, function, and collateral.
nodes.body: Use a screen to document, not to diagnose alone. [1,2,6] Useful ED/outpatient screens: - Mini-Cog: fast, includes recall and clock drawing - MoCA or SLUMS: broader cognitive domains when time allows - 4AT or CAM if delirium is possible - Clock drawing, 3-word recall, orientation, attention, naming, executive tasks Document conditions: hearing aids/glasses, interpreter, education/language mismatch,

nodes.title: How to Be Comfortable Diagnosing
nodes.summary: Diagnosis comfort requires persistent acquired decline, objective abnormality, functional impact, and collateral.
nodes.body: Diagnosis comfort guide You can be clinically comfortable saying suspected dementia / major neurocognitive disorder when all are present: [1,2] 1. Acquired decline from previous cognitive baseline. 2. Persistent or progressive course, not just hours to days. 3. Objective cognitive abnormality on history, exam, screen, or prior records. 4. Functional impact: IADL or ADL impairment from cognition. 5

nodes.title: Initial Workup
nodes.summary: Workup looks for reversible contributors and safety threats; biomarkers are specialty-directed.
nodes.body: ED testing is targeted to acuity and safety. Outpatient diagnostic evaluation is broader and longitudinal. [1,2] Usually reasonable baseline workup when new concern is credible: - CBC, CMP with calcium/renal/hepatic function, glucose - TSH, vitamin B12 - Depression screen, sleep, substance/alcohol screen when relevant - Medication review: anticholinergics, sedatives, opioids, steroids, dopamine bl

nodes.title: Imaging and Referral
nodes.summary: Image urgently for red flags; stable chronic decline can often be routed to outpatient MRI/referral.
nodes.body: Structural brain imaging is part of many diagnostic evaluations, but ED urgency depends on red flags. [1,2] ED CT/urgent imaging triggers: - Acute neurologic deficit, severe headache, seizure, head trauma/fall, anticoagulation, rapid decline, cancer/immunosuppression, fever/meningismus, papilledema - New gait disorder, urinary symptoms, or ventriculomegaly concern for NPH - Young onset, atypical s

nodes.title: Subtype Clues
nodes.summary: Subtype clues shape referral and medication safety, but follow-up confirms the diagnosis.
nodes.body: Do not overcall subtype from one visit, but document clues that guide follow-up. [1,2] - Alzheimer pattern: memory and learning predominant, gradual progression. - Vascular: stepwise decline, executive dysfunction, stroke/TIA history, focal signs. - Lewy body: fluctuations, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, antipsychotic sensitivity. - Frontotemporal: earl

nodes.title: Lewy Body / Parkinson Dementia Pattern
nodes.summary: Lewy body/Parkinson dementia increases neuroleptic sensitivity risk and changes agitation medication choice.
nodes.body: High-risk medication note: suspected Lewy body dementia or Parkinson disease dementia changes the agitation plan. [2,5,7] Clues: - Fluctuating cognition and alertness - Recurrent formed visual hallucinations - REM sleep behavior disorder - Parkinsonism - Marked sensitivity to antipsychotics Avoid or use extreme caution with high-potency dopamine blockers such as haloperidol and risperidone. If med

nodes.title: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus Pattern
nodes.summary: Gait-first cognitive decline with urinary symptoms should trigger NPH consideration and safety planning.
nodes.body: Consider NPH when gait impairment is early or dominant, especially with cognitive slowing and urinary urgency/incontinence. ED role: - Do not promise reversibility from the ED. - Look for unsafe gait, falls, subdural/trauma, infection, medication effects, and other mimics. - If CT shows ventriculomegaly or clinical suspicion is strong, route to neurology/neurosurgery or outpatient NPH evaluation d

nodes.title: Infection Edge Case
nodes.summary: Confusion alone is not a UTI diagnosis; treat infection when symptoms or systemic signs support it.
nodes.body: Infection guide Patients with dementia can present atypically, but confusion alone is not a UTI diagnosis. IDSA recommends observation and assessment for other causes rather than antibiotics for bacteriuria with delirium/confusion when there are no urinary symptoms or systemic infection signs. [4] Treat infection when supported by: fever, hypothermia, sepsis physiology, localizing symptoms/signs,

nodes.title: Infection With Dementia
nodes.summary: Treat true infection and delirium support together, then reassess cognitive baseline.
nodes.body: Management principles: - Treat the confirmed or strongly suspected source. - Correct dehydration, hypoxia, fever, pain, retention, and constipation. - Avoid deliriogenic medications when possible. - Reassess mental status after source control and supportive care. - Consider admission when infection causes delirium, poor intake, falls, inability to take antibiotics, sepsis risk, or unsafe supervisi

nodes.title: Agitation / Behavior Crisis
nodes.summary: Screen medical triggers first; use least-restrictive safety and the detailed agitation pathway when needed.
nodes.body: Agitation is usually a symptom, not the diagnosis. [3,5,7] First screen: - Immediate danger to patient/staff or essential care blocked? - Pain, urinary retention, constipation, hunger/thirst, sleep deprivation, hypoxia, hypoglycemia? - Infection with supportive signs? - Medication toxicity, withdrawal, intoxication? - Fall/head injury, subdural, seizure, stroke? - Caregiver/environmental trigger?

nodes.title: Open Dementia Agitation Consult
nodes.summary: Use the dedicated agitation consult for safety, meds, capacity, and legal/disposition details.
nodes.body: Use the dedicated agitation consult for medication choice, Lewy body/Parkinson cautions, Texas capacity/hold distinctions, restraint documentation, and protected disposition. Dementia & Agitation
nodes.recommendation: Open the Dementia & Agitation pathway when behavior creates immediate danger, blocks essential care, or raises legal/capacity questions.

nodes.title: Complications to Act On
nodes.summary: Dementia complications often decide ED disposition more than the cognitive score.
nodes.body: Safety guide Look beyond the memory complaint. Dementia complications often drive ED disposition. High-yield complications: - Falls, wandering, unsafe gait, getting lost - Medication errors, missed dialysis/appointments, inability to manage insulin/anticoagulants - Poor intake, dehydration, weight loss, dysphagia, aspiration - Driving, stove/firearms, financial exploitation, scams - Caregiver burn

nodes.title: Capacity and Safety
nodes.summary: Capacity is decision-specific; unsafe incapacity needs surrogate, social work, and protected disposition.
nodes.body: Capacity is decision-specific. Dementia diagnosis alone does not remove capacity. [2] Assess the exact decision: refusal of workup, discharge, transfer, medications, placement, or procedure. Capacity elements: - Understand relevant information - Appreciate personal consequences - Reason about options - Communicate a stable choice If lacks capacity and unsafe: identify surrogate/medical POA/guardia

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Disposition turns on medical stability, functional safety, supervision, capacity, and caregiver reliability.
nodes.body: Do not discharge the diagnosis. Discharge the actual safety situation. ED discharge can be reasonable when: - No delirium or dangerous mimic requiring treatment - Vitals/labs/exam do not suggest unstable medical illness - Patient can eat, ambulate/transfer safely, and take meds safely with support - Reliable caregiver/supervision and follow-up exist - No active wandering, elopement, abuse/neglect,

nodes.title: Safe Discharge Plan
nodes.summary: Safe discharge requires supervision, safety plan, medication review, and outpatient cognitive evaluation.
nodes.body: Discharge elements: - Name the working diagnosis: suspected dementia, mild cognitive impairment, delirium resolved, or cognitive concern needing evaluation - Give caregiver-facing safety plan: meds, meals, hydration, falls, wandering, stove/driving/firearms, sleep, follow-up - Arrange PCP/geriatrics/neurology/neuropsychology pathway - Request outpatient MRI or imaging review when indicated - Revie
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only with reliable supervision, safety plan, medication review, and arranged cognitive follow-up.

nodes.title: Observation, Admission, or Protected Placement
nodes.summary: Protected disposition is appropriate when function, supervision, or medical stability cannot support discharge.
nodes.body: Use observation/admission/protected disposition for: - Delirium or medical illness superimposed on dementia - Unsafe gait, recurrent falls, inability to transfer, unsafe ambulation - Medication mismanagement with high-risk drugs - Poor intake, dehydration, aspiration risk, failure to thrive - Wandering/elopement risk or unsafe behavior - No reliable caregiver/supervision - Suspected abuse, neglect
nodes.recommendation: Admit, observe, or arrange protected placement when medical stability, function, supervision, or capacity cannot support safe discharge.

nodes.title: Dental Avulsion
nodes.summary: Dental Avulsion — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Complete displacement of tooth from alveolar socket — a true dental emergency. TIME IS TOOTH: > Reimplantation success drops dramatically with extraoral dry time: > • <5 min: ~95% survival > • 15 min: ~80% survival > • 30 min: ~50% survival > • >60 min dry: Poor prognosis Key Question: Is this a PRIMARY (baby) or PERMANENT tooth? Primary teeth are NEVER reimplanted — risk of damaging permanent too

nodes.title: Primary or Permanent Tooth?
nodes.summary: Primary or Permanent Tooth? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: How to differentiate: | Feature | Primary (Baby) | Permanent | |---------|---------------|----------| | Age | <6 years typically | >6 years | | Size | Smaller, whiter | Larger, more yellow | | Root | Short, tapered | Long, blunted | | Crown shape | Bulbous, rounded | More angular | | Number | 20 total | 32 total | If uncertain: Assume permanent and proceed with reimplantation. A dental X-ray can c

nodes.title: Primary Tooth — Do NOT Reimplant
nodes.summary: Primary Tooth — Do NOT Reimplant — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Primary teeth should NEVER be reimplanted: Reasons: • Risk of damage to underlying permanent tooth bud • Risk of ankylosis affecting eruption • Risk of infection Management: • Reassure parents • Control bleeding with gauze pressure • Soft diet for 2-3 days • Dental follow-up within 1-2 weeks • Monitor for infection If tooth fragment present: X-ray to rule out embedded fragments. [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: Do NOT reimplant primary teeth. Control bleeding, reassure family, arrange dental follow-up.

nodes.title: Assess the Situation
nodes.summary: Assess the Situation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Critical Assessment: 1. Time since avulsion: • <60 min: Good prognosis • >60 min dry: Poor prognosis but still attempt 2. Storage medium: • HBSS (Hank's Balanced Salt Solution): Best, up to 24h • Milk: Good, up to 6h • Saliva (in mouth): Acceptable, up to 2h • Saline: Acceptable, up to 2h • Water: Poor (hypotonic, damages cells) • Dry: Worst 3. Tooth condition: • Clean root vs. contaminated • Root

nodes.title: Is the Tooth Present?
nodes.summary: Is the Tooth Present? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Locate the avulsed tooth: • Check the scene (ground, sports equipment) • Check patient's mouth (aspiration risk!) • Check clothing, hands If tooth not found: • CXR to rule out aspiration • Consider tooth embedded in soft tissue • X-ray of lips/face if swelling WARNING: If tooth cannot be located and patient has respiratory symptoms → CXR immediately. [1][2]

nodes.title: Missing Tooth
nodes.summary: Missing Tooth — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: If tooth cannot be located: 1. Rule out aspiration: • CXR (PA and lateral) • Tooth in bronchus requires urgent removal 2. Rule out embedded tooth: • Palpate lips, cheeks • X-ray soft tissue if suspicious • CT face if significant swelling 3. Rule out ingestion: • Usually benign, will pass • Inform patient 4. Document: • Tooth not found • Imaging obtained • Dental referral for prosthetic options [1]

nodes.title: Proper Tooth Handling
nodes.summary: Proper Tooth Handling — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Protect the periodontal ligament (PDL) cells DO: • Handle by CROWN only (white part) • Keep tooth moist at all times • Rinse gently with saline if contaminated • Place in storage medium immediately DO NOT: • Touch the root • Scrub or scrape the root • Let tooth dry out • Wrap in tissue/gauze (dries it out) • Use water (hypotonic, kills cells) Best Storage Media (in order): 1. HBSS (Save-

nodes.title: Reimplantation Decision
nodes.summary: Reimplantation Decision — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Who should reimplant? Reimplant in ED if: • Dentist not immediately available • Tooth has been extraoral >15-30 min • Every minute counts! Wait for dentist if: • Dentist available within 15-30 min • Tooth properly stored • Open apex (immature root) — needs specialist Contraindications to reimplantation: • Severe caries (decayed tooth) • Advanced periodontal disease • Uncooperative patient • Primar

nodes.title: Transport to Dentist
nodes.summary: Transport to Dentist — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: If dentist available quickly: 1. Store tooth properly: • HBSS (if available) • Cold whole milk (most accessible) • Patient's saliva (in cheek — if cooperative) 2. Call ahead to dentist/oral surgeon 3. Transport immediately — time is critical 4. Give patient: • Pain control • Gauze for socket bleeding • Written instructions If no dentist available within 1 hour → Reimplant in ED. [1][2]

nodes.title: ED Reimplantation Technique
nodes.summary: ED Reimplantation Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Step-by-Step Reimplantation: 1. Prepare the socket: • Gently irrigate with saline to remove clot • Do NOT curette the socket • Local anesthesia (lidocaine with epi — dental block or infiltration) 2. Prepare the tooth: • Handle by crown only • Rinse gently with saline if contaminated • Do NOT scrub the root • If dry >60 min: soak in HBSS or saline x 30 min 3. Insert the tooth: • Orient correctly (c

nodes.title: Poor Prognosis — Still Attempt
nodes.summary: Poor Prognosis — Still Attempt — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Even with prolonged extraoral time, attempt reimplantation: Rationale: • May maintain space for future implant • May allow bone preservation • Better than no tooth aesthetically • Root resorption likely but buys time Expected outcomes >60 min dry: • High risk of root resorption • May need extraction in 2-5 years • Serves as space maintainer Pre-soak protocol: • Soak tooth in HBSS or saline for 30

nodes.title: Already Reimplanted
nodes.summary: Already Reimplanted — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: If tooth was reimplanted at scene: This is ideal! Fastest reimplantation = best outcomes. ED management: 1. Do NOT remove and re-reimplant 2. Confirm proper positioning (X-ray) 3. Check occlusion 4. Splint if loose 5. Give medications (antibiotics, tetanus) 6. Arrange urgent dental follow-up Assess position: • Tooth should be at same level as adjacent teeth • Crown should face correct direction •

nodes.title: Splinting Technique
nodes.summary: Splinting Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Flexible splint is standard of care: Goal: Stabilize tooth while allowing physiologic movement. --- ED SPLINTING: STEP-BY-STEP Materials (pick one method): • 2-octyl cyanoacrylate (Dermabond) + N95 nasal bridge strip • COE-PAK periodontal dressing • Suture foil from suture pack + skin glue --- METHOD 1: Dermabond + N95 Strip (Preferred) Step 1 — Prepare: • Cut metal nasal bridge from N95 mask • Ro

nodes.title: Post-Reimplantation Imaging
nodes.summary: Post-Reimplantation Imaging — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Obtain X-ray after reimplantation: Confirm: • Tooth fully seated in socket • Correct orientation • No root fracture • No alveolar fracture • No foreign body Additional imaging if: • Multiple teeth involved • Alveolar fracture suspected • Mandible/maxilla fracture suspected → CT face • Tooth fragments missing → soft tissue X-ray Document tooth number and position. [1][2]

nodes.title: Medications
nodes.summary: Medications — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Standard medications after avulsion reimplantation: 1. Antibiotics (evidence-based): • Doxycycline 100 mg BID x 7 days (adults/children >12y) • Or Amoxicillin if <12y or doxycycline contraindicated • Penicillin allergy: Clindamycin 2. Tetanus prophylaxis: • Per standard wound guidelines • Td/Tdap if >5 years since last booster • TIG if unvaccinated/unknown 3. Pain control: • NSAIDs (ibuprofen) fir

nodes.title: Patient Instructions
nodes.summary: Patient Instructions — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions: Diet: • Soft diet x 2 weeks • Avoid biting on affected tooth • No hard, crunchy, or sticky foods Oral hygiene: • Gentle brushing with soft brush • Chlorhexidine rinse BID • No flossing around affected tooth x 2 weeks Activity: • No contact sports x 4 weeks • Mouthguard when cleared for sports Warning signs — return if: • Increasing pain • Swelling • Fever • Tooth becomes ve

nodes.title: Dental Follow-up
nodes.summary: Dental Follow-up — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: URGENT dental follow-up is essential: Timeline: • 24-48 hours: Dental evaluation, permanent splint if needed • 2 weeks: Splint removal, assess healing • 4 weeks: Clinical and radiographic evaluation • 3 months: Pulp vitality testing • 6 months: Repeat evaluation • Annually x 5 years: Monitor for resorption Expected Complications: • Root resorption (most common, especially if dry >30 min) • Pulp ne

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Most dental avulsions can be discharged: Admission considerations: • Associated maxillofacial fractures • Airway compromise • Severe bleeding not controlled • Multiple dental injuries requiring OR • Unable to tolerate PO (IV antibiotics needed) Before discharge: • Reimplantation complete (or tooth properly stored with patient) • Splint in place • Medications prescribed • Dental follow-up arranged

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.summary: Discharge — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Discharge Checklist: ✓ Tooth reimplanted or stored properly ✓ Splint applied if reimplanted ✓ Post-procedure X-ray obtained ✓ Antibiotics prescribed (doxycycline or amoxicillin) ✓ Tetanus updated if needed ✓ Pain control prescribed ✓ Chlorhexidine rinse prescribed ✓ Soft diet instructions ✓ Warning signs reviewed ✓ Dental follow-up in 24-48 hours Give written instructions — families are often in s
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with antibiotics, pain control, and urgent dental follow-up within 24-48 hours.

nodes.title: Admission
nodes.summary: Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Admit if: • Maxillofacial fractures requiring observation/surgery • Airway compromise • Uncontrolled bleeding • Multiple injuries requiring staged repair • Unable to tolerate PO (IV antibiotics) Consultations: • Oral and maxillofacial surgery • ENT if airway involvement • Trauma surgery if polytrauma Continue dental care: • Splinting if not already done • IV antibiotics if indicated • Pain control
nodes.recommendation: Admit for associated maxillofacial injuries or airway concerns. OMFS consultation.

nodes.title: Transfer
nodes.summary: Transfer — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Transfer if: • Complex maxillofacial fractures beyond local capability • Need for emergent oral surgery not available • Pediatric dental specialist needed Before transfer: • Stabilize airway • Control bleeding • Reimplant tooth if possible (or store properly) • Apply temporary splint • Start antibiotics • Document time of avulsion Communicate: • Time of injury • Storage medium used • Interventions
nodes.recommendation: Transfer to facility with OMFS coverage. Stabilize and reimplant before transport if possible.

nodes.title: Dental Extraction Complications - Sick Check
nodes.summary: Sort post-extraction complications into bleeding, dry socket, infection, sinus communication, or expected recovery.
nodes.body: First job: decide if this is bleeding, dry socket, infection, sinus communication, or expected recovery. Open quick tools: - Steps - Dental Box - TXA / Hemostasis - Photos - Tricks of the Trade Do not miss: 1. Airway-risk odontogenic infection. 2. Persistent socket hemorrhage in anticoagulated or coagulopathic patient. 3. Secondary hemorrhage from infection 5-10 days after extraction. 4. Dry socke

nodes.title: Primary Problem Right Now
nodes.summary: Bleeding, dry socket, infection, sinus communication, and expected course are the major branches.
nodes.body: Pick the lane that best matches the current risk. Treat the most dangerous branch first.

nodes.title: Post-Extraction Bleeding - Reset the Field
nodes.summary: Direct socket pressure with small damp gauze is the first intervention.
nodes.body: First steps: - Sit upright, suction, good light, remove loose clot only if it prevents seeing the socket. - Identify whether blood is from socket, gingival tear, laceration, or multiple sites. - Roll damp gauze small enough to sit directly in the socket. The gauze is a pressure plug, not a sponge. - Have patient bite continuously for 30-60 minutes. Do not keep checking every few minutes. - If avai

nodes.title: Bleeding After Direct Pressure
nodes.summary: Major bleeding gets resuscitation; most socket bleeding gets local escalation.
nodes.body: After sustained pressure, decide whether this is controlled, persistent local bleeding, or major hemorrhage.

nodes.title: Local Hemostatic Escalation
nodes.body: Local control sequence: 1. Anesthetize with lidocaine plus epinephrine if safe and available. 2. Irrigate lightly enough to see the site; avoid blasting out fresh clot. 3. Pack the socket with Gelfoam, Surgicel/oxidized cellulose, collagen sponge, or topical thrombin on gelatin sponge if available. 4. Add TXA-soaked gauze/dental roll held under firm bite pressure. 5. Figure-of-8 suture over the so
nodes.recommendation: Use staged local hemostasis before systemic reversal unless bleeding is life-threatening.

nodes.title: Anticoagulant / Antiplatelet / Bleeding Risk?
nodes.summary: Bleeding-risk medications increase monitoring needs but do not automatically require reversal.
nodes.body: Check anticoagulants, antiplatelets, liver disease, thrombocytopenia, uremia, hemophilia/vWD, and recent chemotherapy.

nodes.title: Anticoagulated / Antiplatelet Patient
nodes.body: Principle: most dental extraction bleeding is controlled locally. Stopping anticoagulation can create stroke/VTE/stent risk, so avoid casual reversal or medication interruption. ED approach: - If controlled: document hemostasis, reinforce pressure instructions, arrange dental follow-up. - Warfarin: check INR if bleeding is persistent, excessive, or INR status unknown. - DOAC: note last dose, renal
nodes.recommendation: Use local measures first; involve prescribing service/hematology for major, persistent, or high-risk bleeding.

nodes.title: Major Oral Bleeding / Resuscitation Pathway
nodes.body: Treat as a real hemorrhage until controlled. Immediate actions: - Suction and airway plan. Blood in the mouth can become an airway problem. - Two IVs, CBC, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen if severe, type/screen or crossmatch. - Direct socket pressure while preparing local control. - OMFS/dentistry consult. ENT/anesthesia if airway concern. - Consider reversal only for life-threatening bleeding or failed l
nodes.recommendation: Major uncontrolled oral bleeding needs resuscitation, airway awareness, local control, and specialty help.

nodes.title: Alveolar Osteitis / Dry Socket
nodes.body: Typical pattern: severe throbbing pain 2-5 days after extraction, radiating to ear/temple, bad taste/odor, empty socket or exposed bone, minimal swelling, usually afebrile. ED management: - Analgesia: NSAID plus acetaminophen when safe; dental block can help. - Gently irrigate loose debris with saline. Do not aggressively curette the socket. - Dental/OMFS follow-up for medicated dressing if availa
nodes.recommendation: Treat pain, gently irrigate if needed, and arrange dental dressing/source care. Avoid routine antibiotics for dry socket alone.

nodes.title: Post-Extraction Infection Pattern
nodes.summary: Deep-space infection is an airway problem; dry socket is pain without spread.
nodes.body: Separate localized socket/vestibular infection from deep-space infection.

nodes.title: Deep Odontogenic Infection / Airway Risk
nodes.body: Red flags: floor-of-mouth firmness/elevation, tongue elevation, drooling, muffled voice, dysphagia, odynophagia, stridor, severe trismus, submandibular swelling, toxic appearance, rapidly progressive swelling. Actions: - Sit upright, continuous reassessment, airway-capable team early. - ENT/OMFS/anesthesia depending on local workflow. - IV antibiotics with anaerobic and oral flora coverage per loc
nodes.recommendation: Airway plan comes before CT when post-extraction infection threatens the floor of mouth or neck.

nodes.title: Localized / Early Spreading Infection
nodes.body: Manage as a source-control problem. - Analgesia and oral intake assessment. - Look for fluctuance or retained debris; drainage/source control is definitive. - Antibiotics are appropriate when systemic involvement, fever/malaise, spreading cellulitis, immunocompromise, or lack of timely dental source care creates risk. - Common outpatient adult choices when indicated: amoxicillin or penicillin VK;
nodes.recommendation: Use antibiotics selectively and pair them with a dental source-control plan.

nodes.title: Oroantral Communication / Sinus Connection
nodes.body: Suspect after maxillary premolar/molar extraction when the patient reports fluid from mouth to nose, air/bubbling through socket, whistling, unilateral sinus symptoms, or visible opening into the sinus. ED handling: - Do not aggressively probe the socket. - Avoid forceful irrigation through the opening. - Sinus precautions: no nose blowing, no straw, sneeze with mouth open, avoid smoking, avoid vi
nodes.recommendation: Give sinus precautions and urgent dental/OMFS follow-up; avoid probing or aggressive irrigation.

nodes.title: Expected Post-Extraction Course
nodes.body: Reassuring pattern: mild oozing, soreness, swelling that is not rapidly progressive, no fever, no trismus/dysphagia, no deep-space signs, pain improving or controlled with nonopioid therapy. Supportive care: - Bite pressure for recurrent mild oozing. - Avoid smoking, straws, vigorous rinsing, spitting, and heavy exertion for the early clot-stabilization window. - Soft foods, hydration, head elevat
nodes.recommendation: Reinforce clot protection, nonopioid analgesia, and return precautions.

nodes.title: Medication Strategy
nodes.summary: NSAID/APAP first-line, antibiotics only for infection criteria, TXA as local bleeding adjunct.
nodes.body: Pain: NSAID alone or NSAID plus acetaminophen is first-line for acute dental pain after extraction when safe. Avoid NSAIDs when contraindicated: major renal disease, active GI bleed/high-risk anticoagulation, late pregnancy, severe allergy, or clinician-specific concern. Antibiotics: do not use for dry socket or pain alone. Use for systemic involvement, spreading cellulitis, immunocompromise, or s

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit airway, deep infection, uncontrolled bleeding, unstable, or intake failure.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on airway risk, bleeding control, systemic infection, pain control, oral intake, and follow-up reliability.

nodes.title: Admit / Transfer / Emergent Specialty
nodes.body: Escalate now for: airway concern, Ludwig/deep neck infection, sepsis, rapidly progressive facial/neck swelling, orbital involvement, uncontrolled hemorrhage, severe coagulopathy, inability to tolerate PO, failed outpatient therapy, or need for operative source control. Document: airway findings, bleeding control steps, anticoagulant status, infection extent, imaging/labs, and consultant plan.
nodes.recommendation: High-risk extraction complications require airway-aware specialty management and often admission or transfer.

nodes.title: Urgent Dental / OMFS Follow-Up
nodes.body: Use for: controlled bleeding with high rebleed risk, dry socket requiring dressing, localized infection needing source control, suspected oroantral communication, persistent pain beyond expected course, or unreliable access to dental care. Discharge language: - What was treated today. - Exact dental follow-up destination and timing. - Medication schedule and why antibiotics were or were not used.
nodes.recommendation: Urgent follow-up is part of the treatment, especially for dry socket dressing, sinus communication, or source control.

nodes.title: Routine Discharge / Expected Course
nodes.body: Discharge is reasonable when bleeding is controlled, no deep infection signs, no systemic toxicity, pain is controlled enough for oral intake, and the patient understands return precautions. Simple patient instructions: protect the clot, use scheduled nonopioid analgesia if safe, avoid smoking/straws/vigorous rinsing/spitting early, return for uncontrolled bleeding or spreading infection symptoms,
nodes.recommendation: Routine discharge requires controlled bleeding, controlled pain, no red flags, and clear follow-up.

nodes.title: Dental / Intraoral Nerve Blocks — ED Procedure
nodes.summary: Maxillary teeth (V2) = supraperiosteal/superior-alveolar (porous bone). Mandibular teeth (V3) = inferior alveolar block (dense bone).
nodes.body: Intraoral regional anesthesia controls odontogenic (toothache) pain, anesthetizes for dental fracture/avulsion management, and enables repair of intraoral and dentoalveolar lacerations — often more effective and humane than systemic analgesia alone. Key principle: the maxillary teeth (V2) are usually anesthetized by SUPRAPERIOSTEAL infiltration or superior-alveolar blocks because maxillary bone is

nodes.title: Which Tooth or Region Needs Anesthesia?
nodes.summary: Pick tooth/region → supraperiosteal, ASA, MSA, PSA, greater palatine, nasopalatine, IANB, mental, or long buccal.
nodes.body: Select the tooth or intraoral region. Maxillary = upper arch; mandibular = lower arch. Each routes to the block(s) that cover that territory. Confirm no overlying infection at the injection site and calculate the max LA dose first.

nodes.title: Contraindications + Pre-procedure Checks
nodes.summary: No infection at site, no LA allergy; topical first; verify max LA dose (1.8 mL/cartridge); aspirate (esp. IANB — vessels with nerve).
nodes.body: Absolute: - Active infection/cellulitis at the planned injection site (do not inject through infected tissue — risks spreading infection and the block often fails in acidic infected tissue) - Known true allergy to the local anesthetic class - Patient unable to cooperate / protect the airway with an anesthetized tongue and floor of mouth Relative — weigh risk/benefit: - Therapeutic anticoagulation

nodes.title: Shared Technique — All Intraoral Blocks
nodes.summary: Topical first; 25–27 ga (long needle for IANB); lidocaine 2% w/ epi standard; bevel to bone; aspirate (double for IANB); inject slowly; test.
nodes.body: Equipment: - 3 mL syringe (or dental aspirating syringe), 25–27 gauge needle (1 inch for infiltration; 1.5 inch/“long” for IANB) - Topical benzocaine 20% gel on a cotton applicator - 2x2 gauze to dry mucosa and retract - Good light + suction Agent (choose one): - Lidocaine 2% with epinephrine 1:100,000 — standard dental concentration; fast onset, ~60 min pulpal / 3–4 h soft-tissue; epinephrine pro

nodes.title: Supraperiosteal (Local) Infiltration — Maxillary
nodes.summary: Single maxillary tooth. Inject at mucobuccal fold to the root apex, bevel to bone, ~1–1.8 mL. Buccal only (palate not covered).
nodes.body: Indication: Anesthesia of a SINGLE maxillary tooth and its buccal soft tissue — the workhorse for one upper tooth (toothache, fracture, simple repair). Works because maxillary alveolar bone is thin and porous. Distribution of anesthesia: The targeted maxillary tooth (pulp) and the overlying buccal gingiva/mucosa. Does NOT anesthetize the palatal soft tissue (add a palatal injection if palatal work

nodes.title: Anterior Superior Alveolar / Infraorbital Block (V2)
nodes.summary: Maxillary incisors/canine + cheek/lip skin. Infraorbital foramen 1 cm below rim, mid-pupillary line. Intraoral via 1st-premolar sulcus, finger over foramen, 1.5–3 mL.
nodes.body: Indication: The maxillary central/lateral incisors and canine on one side (and their facial soft tissue) — useful for multiple anterior teeth or when local infiltration over an infected anterior tooth is undesirable. Distribution of anesthesia: Via the infraorbital nerve and its anterior superior alveolar branch: the maxillary incisors and canine (pulp), plus the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and up

nodes.title: Middle Superior Alveolar (MSA) Block (V2)
nodes.summary: Maxillary premolars + mesiobuccal root of 1st molar. Inject at mucobuccal fold above 2nd premolar apex, ~0.9–1.8 mL. MSA absent in ~30–50% (use ASA).
nodes.body: Indication: The maxillary premolars (and the mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar) when present — note the MSA nerve is absent in ~30–50% of people, in whom the ASA/infraorbital block covers the premolars. Distribution of anesthesia: The maxillary 1st and 2nd premolars (pulp) and overlying buccal gingiva; the mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar. Landmarks: - The mucobuccal fold above the maxillary 2nd

nodes.title: Posterior Superior Alveolar (PSA) Block (V2)
nodes.summary: Maxillary molars + buccal gingiva. Inject above 2nd molar, advance up/in/back ~16 mm along tuberosity, ~0.9–1.8 mL. Aspirate — pterygoid plexus = hematoma risk.
nodes.body: Indication: The maxillary molars (except the mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar, often MSA-supplied) and their buccal gingiva. Distribution of anesthesia: Maxillary 2nd and 3rd molars and the distobuccal/palatal roots of the 1st molar (pulp), plus the overlying buccal gingiva. Add a supraperiosteal infiltration over the 1st molar if its mesiobuccal root is not numb. Landmarks: - The mucobuccal fold

nodes.title: Greater (Anterior) Palatine Block (V2)
nodes.summary: Posterior hard palate soft tissue. Greater palatine foramen ~1 cm medial to 2nd/3rd molar gingiva. Pressure first, 0.3–0.5 mL only, slow.
nodes.body: Indication: Palatal soft-tissue anesthesia of the POSTERIOR hard palate — needed for palatal lacerations, palatal abscess drainage, or palatal manipulation of maxillary premolars/molars. Distribution of anesthesia: The palatal mucosa and bone from the distal of the canine back to the posterior hard palate, on the injected side (does NOT anesthetize teeth pulp — pair with a buccal/PSA block for too

nodes.title: Nasopalatine Block (V2)
nodes.summary: Anterior hard palate (canine to canine, bilateral). Incisive foramen under the incisive papilla behind central incisors. Approach lateral to papilla, 0.3–0.5 mL only.
nodes.body: Indication: Palatal soft-tissue anesthesia of the ANTERIOR hard palate behind the upper incisors — for anterior palatal lacerations or bilateral anterior palatal procedures. Distribution of anesthesia: The palatal mucosa and bone of the anterior hard palate from canine to canine (bilateral) — one injection covers both sides. Landmarks: - The incisive foramen, beneath the incisive papilla — the sma

nodes.title: Inferior Alveolar Nerve Block (IANB) (V3)
nodes.summary: All mandibular teeth + lower lip/chin + (lingual) tongue/floor. Coronoid notch, barrel over contralateral premolars, contact bone at ~20–25mm, withdraw 1mm, aspirate, 1.5mL + 0.5mL on withdrawal for lingual. No bone contact → CN VII palsy r
nodes.body: Indication: The single most useful ED dental block — anesthetizes ALL mandibular teeth of one quadrant, useful for any lower toothache, mandibular fracture/avulsion, or extensive lower-lip wounds. Mandibular teeth cannot be reliably infiltrated (dense cortical bone), so the IANB is required. Distribution of anesthesia: All ipsilateral mandibular teeth (pulp), the body of the mandible, the buccal m

nodes.title: (Long) Buccal Nerve Block (V3)
nodes.summary: Buccal gingiva of mandibular molars (adjunct to IANB). Inject submucosally distal/buccal to last molar at occlusal plane, ~0.3 mL.
nodes.body: Indication: Anesthesia of the BUCCAL soft tissue (gingiva/mucosa) of the mandibular MOLARS — an adjunct to the IANB when buccal soft-tissue work is needed (e.g., buccal laceration, rubber-dam clamp, surgical access to molars). The IANB alone does NOT numb the buccal gingiva of the molars. Distribution of anesthesia: The buccal soft tissue and gingiva lateral to the mandibular molars (does not anes

nodes.title: Mental (± Incisive) Nerve Block (V3)
nodes.summary: Mandibular premolars-to-midline + lower lip/chin. Mental foramen below 1st/2nd premolars, mid-pupillary line. ~1–1.8 mL; pressure over foramen = incisive (pulpal) block. Bilateral for midline lip.
nodes.body: Indication: The mandibular premolars to the midline (incisors, canine, premolars) and/or the lower lip and chin — when a full IANB is not needed (e.g., anterior lower-lip laceration, anterior lower tooth pain). Adding intraforaminal pressure converts it to an INCISIVE nerve block for pulpal anesthesia of the anterior teeth. Distribution of anesthesia: Mental block → lower lip, chin, and labial/buc

nodes.title: Test the Block Before Proceeding
nodes.summary: Wait 3–10 min, test pinprick/cold vs contralateral (lower-lip numb = IANB success). Full → proceed. Partial/none → supplement or re-block within max dose.
nodes.body: Wait for onset (3–5 min for infiltration/maxillary blocks; 5–10 min for the IANB). Test: - Soft tissue: pinprick the gingiva/lip vs the contralateral side. For the IANB, lower-lip numbness is the classic sign. - Tooth (pulp): cold test or gentle percussion is painless when anesthetized. Is the target anesthetized?

nodes.title: Rescue a Partial / Failed Block
nodes.summary: IANB fails most (too low/shallow or accessory mylohyoid) — re-confirm bone contact. Maxillary: tip-below-apex or absent MSA. Re-block / infiltrate / recheck max dose.
nodes.body: Common causes of failure: - IANB: too anterior/low, or not deep enough — the most commonly missed block. Re-confirm the coronoid notch and that you contacted bone ~20–25 mm in. Accessory innervation (mylohyoid nerve) can supply lower molars — add a buccal-floor infiltration. - Maxillary: tip below the apex (soft tissue only, no pulp), or absent MSA for premolars. - Insufficient wait (bupivacaine 8

nodes.title: Complications + Recognition
nodes.summary: Bite injury (warn!), hematoma (PSA pterygoid plexus, IANB vessels — aspirate), transient CN VII palsy (IANB too deep), intravascular injection, LAST → lipid emulsion.
nodes.body: Common / minor: - Failed/partial block (especially IANB) - Self-inflicted bite/burn injury of the numb lip, cheek, or tongue — WARN every patient, especially children - Transient pain on injection (palatal blocks worst) - Trismus / soreness at the IANB site Uncommon but important: - Hematoma — highest risk with the PSA block (pterygoid venous plexus → rapid facial swelling) and the IANB (inferior

nodes.title: Procedure Note Template
nodes.summary: Note must capture: block type, tooth/region, indication, consent w/ bite warning, agent/dose (cartridges→mg, under max), landmarks, aspiration, confirmed effect, dental f/u.
nodes.body: Procedure: [Supraperiosteal infiltration / ASA-infraorbital / MSA / PSA / greater palatine / nasopalatine / inferior alveolar / long buccal / mental] block, [tooth #/region], [right/left/bilateral]. Indication: [Odontogenic pain / dental fracture / dentoalveolar or intraoral laceration repair / abscess management] at [site]. Consent: Verbal informed consent obtained; risks of transient lip/tongue
nodes.recommendation: Document block type, tooth/region, indication, consent (incl. bite-injury warning), agent/dose (cartridges → mg, under max), landmarks with bone contact for IANB, aspiration, confirmed effect, and dental follow-up.

nodes.title: Dental Pain Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Airway, deep infection, trauma, pain control, and dental follow-up first.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Ludwig angina / deep space infection \u2014 floor-of-mouth swelling, drooling, airway threat. 2. Cavernous sinus thrombosis \u2014 spreading facial/orbital infection, cranial nerve signs. 3. Necrotizing fasciitis of the neck \u2014 pain out of proportion, crepitus, toxicity. 4. Cardiac referred pain (ACS) \u2014 jaw/tooth pain without dental source, risk factors. 5.

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Airway/deep space, systemic infection, trauma, abscess, pulpitis, pericoronitis, dry socket, and mimics are the first split.
nodes.body: Choose the first dangerous lane. You can return after the immediate action.

nodes.title: Airway-Threat / Deep-Space Odontogenic Infection
nodes.body: Open Deep Neck Infection. Next 5 minutes: sit upright, airway equipment and experienced help early, ENT/OMFS/anesthesia as local resources allow, IV access, broad IV antibiotics, CT neck/face with contrast only when stable enough and after airway risk is addressed. Ludwig angina and deep neck infection can deteriorate quickly. Danger signs: drooling, stridor, muffled voice, dysphagia, tongue eleva
nodes.recommendation: Airway plan comes before scanner plan when odontogenic infection threatens the floor of mouth or neck.

nodes.title: Spreading Infection / Systemic Involvement
nodes.body: Treat as infection with source-control needs. Find the source tooth, assess spread, give analgesia, start antibiotics when systemic involvement or spreading cellulitis is present, and arrange urgent dental/OMFS follow-up or admission. Immunocompromised, diabetic, toxic, trismus/dysphagia, or rapidly progressive swelling patients need lower threshold for imaging, IV antibiotics, and admission. ED p
nodes.recommendation: Systemic or spreading odontogenic infection gets antibiotics plus source-control planning.

nodes.title: Dental Trauma / Missing Tooth Fragment
nodes.body: Open Dental Trauma or Dental Avulsion. Next steps: account for all teeth/fragments, protect avulsed permanent tooth, do not reimplant primary teeth, assess alveolar fracture, tetanus when indicated, control bleeding, splint/refer per injury type. If a tooth or fragment is missing and aspiration is plausible, obtain chest imaging.
nodes.recommendation: Trauma follows time-sensitive tooth-preservation rules, especially permanent avulsion.

nodes.title: Localized Dental Abscess
nodes.body: Localized swelling without systemic toxicity or airway/deep-space signs. Priorities: analgesia, consider drainage if fluctuant and within ED skill/resources, dental source-control referral, and antibiotics only when guideline-supported: systemic involvement, spreading cellulitis, immunocompromise, or when definitive dental care is not immediately available for selected abscess scenarios. Common ad
nodes.recommendation: Drain/source control and dental follow-up matter more than reflex antibiotics.

nodes.title: Pulpitis / Uncomplicated Toothache
nodes.body: Typical pattern: severe tooth pain with hot/cold/sweet, caries or broken filling, no facial swelling, no fever, no trismus, no systemic signs. ADA guidance recommends against routine systemic antibiotics for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis or symptomatic apical periodontitis in immunocompetent adults when there is no systemic involvement. Treat pain and arrange definitive dental care. Open Denta
nodes.recommendation: Analgesia plus dental care, not automatic antibiotics, for uncomplicated pulpitis.

nodes.title: Pericoronitis / Periodontal Infection
nodes.body: Posterior molar pain with inflamed operculum, food trapping, bad taste, and local swelling often needs irrigation, analgesia, oral hygiene instructions, and dental follow-up. Antibiotics are reserved for systemic involvement, spreading cellulitis, immunocompromise, or significant trismus/deep-space concern. Escalate if trismus, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth findings, fever, or mandibular swelling sugg
nodes.recommendation: Local care and dental follow-up first; escalate for spread or systemic illness.

nodes.title: Alveolar Osteitis / Dry Socket
nodes.body: Severe pain 2-5 days after extraction, empty socket/exposed bone, foul taste, and minimal swelling usually suggests dry socket rather than spreading infection. ED care is analgesia, gentle irrigation if debris, avoid aggressive curettage, and dental/oral surgery follow-up for medicated dressing. Antibiotics are not routine unless cellulitis, fever, immunocompromise, or deep infection signs are pre
nodes.recommendation: Treat pain and arrange dental dressing/source care; do not use antibiotics for dry socket alone.

nodes.title: Dental Pain Mimics
nodes.summary: When dental exam does not fit, consider sinus/ear/TMJ/neuralgia/zoster/cardiac referred pain.
nodes.body: If the teeth do not explain the pain, widen the lens: - Maxillary sinusitis: upper tooth pain with sinus symptoms. - Otitis media/externa, mastoiditis. - TMJ dysfunction. - Trigeminal neuralgia: electric, brief, triggerable pain. - Herpes zoster before rash. - Cardiac ischemia can rarely refer to jaw/teeth, especially exertional symptoms, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, or risk factors. Open Chest P

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Exam, analgesia, block, selective antibiotics, and concrete dental follow-up.
nodes.body: Default ED dental pain bundle: - Visualize all quadrants, gingiva, floor of mouth, uvula, tonsils, neck, and facial symmetry. - Percuss culprit tooth, check mobility, look for vestibular fluctuance, draining sinus, caries/fracture. - Vitals and immune risk. - Analgesia: NSAID plus acetaminophen when safe; consider local dental block. - Avoid opioid-first strategy. - Antibiotics only when indicated

nodes.title: Analgesia / Dental Block Strategy
nodes.summary: NSAID/APAP first-line when safe; dental blocks are high-yield; opioids are rescue only.
nodes.body: For most adolescents/adults, ADA guidance supports NSAIDs, alone or with acetaminophen, as first-line acute dental pain therapy when there are no contraindications. Consider renal disease, GI bleed risk, anticoagulation, pregnancy, liver disease, heavy alcohol use, total acetaminophen dose, and age/frailty. ED tools: inferior alveolar, mental, infraorbital, posterior superior alveolar, or local in

nodes.title: Reassess After Analgesia / Initial Care
nodes.summary: Disposition depends on airway, infection spread, pain control, and dental follow-up.
nodes.body: Recheck airway, oral intake, swelling, fever, and pain control.

nodes.title: Imaging / Consult Strategy
nodes.summary: CT for deep infection/trauma extent, CXR for missing fragment aspiration, consult for source control.
nodes.body: Image selectively: - CT neck/face with contrast: deep-space infection, trismus/dysphagia, toxic/systemic patient, orbital involvement, rapidly progressive swelling, unclear extent. - Panorex/dental films: dental service dependent, fracture/root/periapical planning when available. - CT face: significant trauma, alveolar/maxillofacial fracture, embedded tooth fragment. - CXR: missing tooth/tooth fra

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit danger signs. Urgent dental follow-up for source control. Discharge only low-risk, controlled pain.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on airway, spread, systemic illness, immune risk, pain control, and dental access.

nodes.title: Admit / Transfer / Specialty
nodes.body: Admit, transfer, or emergently consult for airway-risk findings, Ludwig/deep neck infection, sepsis, orbital spread, rapidly progressive swelling, immunocompromise/diabetes with significant infection, inability to tolerate PO, failed outpatient therapy, or need for operative drainage/source control.
nodes.recommendation: Dangerous odontogenic infection needs airway-aware admission and source control.

nodes.title: Urgent Dental / OMFS Follow-Up
nodes.body: Use this lane for localized abscess/cellulitis without airway/systemic toxicity, fracture without emergent features, or pain requiring definitive dental procedure. Give specific follow-up timing, antibiotic rationale if prescribed, analgesic schedule, and return precautions for spread or airway symptoms.
nodes.recommendation: Every dental pain discharge needs a definitive dental-care destination, not just medication.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when no airway/deep-space/systemic red flags, pain is controlled enough for PO, diagnosis is low-risk, and dental follow-up is realistic. Return now for: fever, worse swelling, neck swelling, trouble swallowing, drooling, voice change, breathing difficulty, trismus, eye swelling/vision change, inability to drink, uncontrolled pain, or rapidly worsening symptoms.
nodes.recommendation: Document no deep-space signs, analgesia plan, antibiotic indication if used, and dental follow-up instructions.
