nodes.title: Type of Dental Injury?
nodes.summary: Type of Dental Injury? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Identify the primary injury pattern: [1][2] Examine for: • Crown damage (fracture line, exposed dentin/pulp) • Tooth mobility (compared to adjacent teeth) • Tooth position (displaced, intruded, extruded) • Gingival bleeding • Occlusion changes (bite feels "off") • Empty socket (avulsion)

nodes.title: Ellis Classification
nodes.summary: Ellis Classification — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Identify fracture depth: [1][4] Ellis I — Enamel only: • Smooth, whitish chip • No sensitivity to air/cold • Routine dental follow-up Ellis II — Enamel + Dentin: • Yellow/ivory dentin exposed • Sensitive to air, touch, temperature • May have slight bleeding Ellis III — Enamel + Dentin + PULP: • Pink pulp tissue visible or bleeding • Severe pain • DENTAL EMERGENCY

nodes.title: Ellis I — Enamel Fracture
nodes.summary: Ellis I: enamel only (white chip) — smooth sharp edges with emery board, dental follow-up 1-2 weeks
nodes.body: Enamel-only fracture — lowest urgency: [1][4] Exam findings: • White, chalky chip • Smooth or rough edges • No temperature sensitivity • No bleeding ED Management: • File/smooth rough edges if causing lip irritation • Can use emery board or fine file • Reassure patient No urgency for dental referral. Discharge instructions: • Routine dental follow-up (days to weeks) • Cosmetic repair if desired •
nodes.recommendation: Smooth rough edges if needed. Routine dental follow-up. No urgent intervention required.

nodes.title: Ellis II — Dentin Exposure
nodes.summary: Ellis II: dentin exposed (yellow layer) — cover with CaOH or GIC, dental follow-up within 24h
nodes.body: Dentin exposed — protect from sensitivity and infection: [1][4] Exam findings: • Yellow/ivory dentin visible • Sensitive to air, cold, touch • May have slight bleeding from dentinal tubules ED Management: 1. Irrigate with saline 2. Apply calcium hydroxide paste to exposed dentin 3. Cover with glass ionomer cement or dental wax 4. Alternative: Aluminum foil barrier Medications: • Ibuprofen 400-600
nodes.recommendation: Cover exposed dentin with calcium hydroxide + temporary seal. Dental follow-up within 24 hours.

nodes.title: Ellis III — PULP EXPOSURE
nodes.summary: Ellis III: pulp exposed (pink/bleeding center) — dental emergency, CaOH cover, urgent dental within hours
nodes.body: DENTAL EMERGENCY — Pulp viable only 3-6 hours: [1][4][5] Exam findings: • Pink pulp tissue visible • Active bleeding from tooth center • Severe pain ED Management — Time Critical: 1. Control bleeding: Gentle pressure with saline gauze × 3-5 min 2. Apply calcium hydroxide paste directly over exposed pulp 3. Cover/seal: Glass ionomer cement, zinc oxide, or foil 4. SAME-DAY dental referral — ideally
nodes.recommendation: EMERGENCY: Apply calcium hydroxide, seal, antibiotics. Same-day dental referral required.

nodes.title: Luxation Type
nodes.summary: Luxation Type — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Classify the luxation injury: [1][2][6] Concussion: Tender to percussion, no mobility, no displacement Subluxation: Loose but in normal position Extrusive: Tooth pushed partially OUT of socket (appears longer) Lateral: Tooth displaced forward/backward/sideways Intrusive: Tooth pushed INTO the bone (appears shorter)

nodes.title: Concussion — Minimal Injury
nodes.summary: Concussion — Minimal Injury — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Tooth tender but stable: [1][6] Exam findings: • Pain to percussion (tapping tooth) • NO mobility • NO displacement • Normal X-ray Management: • Observation only • Soft diet × 2 weeks • Monitor for color change (sign of necrosis) No splinting required. Follow-up: • Dental check if symptoms persist • Return if tooth darkens or pain worsens Prognosis: Excellent — pulp necrosis rare (~3%)
nodes.recommendation: Observation only. Soft diet. Follow up if pain persists or tooth discolors.

nodes.title: Subluxation — Loose Tooth
nodes.summary: Subluxation: tooth mobile but not displaced — soft diet, dental follow-up within 1 week
nodes.body: Tooth loose but not displaced: [1][6] Exam findings: • Increased mobility (wiggles) • Normal position • May have gingival bleeding • Tender to percussion Management: • Flexible splint × 2 weeks (if significantly mobile) • Soft diet • Chlorhexidine rinse 0.12% BID × 1 week Splinting technique: • Wire-composite or resin-bonded • Do NOT use rigid splints (causes ankylosis) Antibiotics: Not routinely
nodes.recommendation: Flexible splint if significantly loose. Soft diet. Dental follow-up within 1 week.

nodes.title: Extrusive Luxation
nodes.summary: Extrusive Luxation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Tooth pushed outward — reposition and splint: [1][6] Exam findings: • Tooth appears longer than adjacent teeth • Very loose • Elevated from socket ED Management: 1. Reposition: Gentle finger pressure back into socket 2. Verify occlusion: Should meet normally with bite 3. Flexible splint × 2 weeks Anesthesia: Local infiltration if needed for repositioning Medications: • Chlorhexidine rinse 0.12% BI
nodes.recommendation: Reposition gently into socket, flexible splint × 2 weeks. Dental follow-up 24-48h.

nodes.title: Lateral Luxation
nodes.summary: Lateral Luxation — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Tooth displaced forward or backward — reposition carefully: [1][6] Exam findings: • Tooth angled forward (labially) or backward (palatally/lingually) • Usually locked in position due to alveolar bone impaction • Occlusion disturbed • High-pitched percussion sound ED Management: 1. Reposition first (before bone reduction if fractured) 2. Firm digital pressure to unlock and guide back 3. May need to
nodes.recommendation: Reposition and flexible splint × 2 weeks. High necrosis risk. Dental follow-up within 24h.

nodes.title: Intrusive Luxation
nodes.summary: Intrusion: tooth pushed into socket — do NOT attempt to reposition, dental/OMFS referral promptly
nodes.body: Tooth pushed INTO bone — management depends on depth: [1][6][7] Exam findings: • Tooth appears shorter than neighbors • May be partially covered by gum • Minimal mobility (locked in bone) • High-pitched percussion sound Management by depth: | Depth | Permanent Teeth | Primary Teeth | |-------|-----------------|---------------| | <3 mm | Allow spontaneous eruption (4-6 weeks) | Allow eruption | | 3
nodes.recommendation: Management based on depth. >3mm needs surgical repositioning. Same-day referral.

nodes.title: Alveolar Fracture
nodes.summary: Alveolar Fracture — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Fracture of bone housing teeth — ORAL SURGERY REFERRAL: [1][8] Exam findings: • Multiple teeth move TOGETHER as a segment • Palpable bone step deformity • Malocclusion (bite feels "off") • Gingival bleeding Imaging: Periapical, occlusal, panorex, ± CBCT ED Management: 1. Closed reduction under local anesthesia (before swelling) 2. Reposition teeth FIRST if luxated (then reduce bone) 3. Splinting:
nodes.recommendation: Alveolar fracture = open fracture. Reduce, splint 3-4 weeks, antibiotics. Oral surgery referral.

nodes.title: Tooth Avulsion
nodes.summary: Tooth Avulsion — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Complete displacement from socket — TIME CRITICAL: [1][2][9] Reimplantation success drops rapidly: • <5 min dry: ~95% survival • 15 min dry: ~80% • 30 min dry: ~50% • >60 min dry: Poor prognosis First: Confirm primary vs. permanent tooth NEVER reimplant primary teeth — damages permanent bud

nodes.title: Primary Tooth Avulsion
nodes.summary: Primary Tooth Avulsion — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: DO NOT REIMPLANT primary teeth: [1][3] Risks of reimplanting primary teeth: • Damage to underlying permanent tooth bud • Ankylosis interfering with eruption • Infection Management: • Reassure parents — this is the correct approach • Control bleeding with gauze pressure • Soft diet × 2-3 days • Ice for swelling Assess for associated injuries: • Check for alveolar fracture • X-ray if fragment may be
nodes.recommendation: DO NOT reimplant. Control bleeding, reassure family, dental follow-up 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Permanent Tooth Avulsion — EMERGENCY
nodes.summary: Permanent Tooth Avulsion — EMERGENCY — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: TIME IS TOOTH — Act immediately: [1][2][9] Step 1: Locate the tooth If not found → CXR to rule out aspiration Step 2: Handle by CROWN only NEVER touch, scrub, or dry the root Step 3: If dirty, rinse briefly • <10 seconds under cold running water • Do NOT scrub or use chemicals Step 4: Optimal storage (if not reimplanting immediately) | Medium | Duration | Notes | |--------|----------|-------| | HB

nodes.title: Reimplantation Technique
nodes.summary: Reimplantation Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Reimplant in ED if dentist not available within 30 min: [1][9] Technique: 1. Rinse socket with saline (remove clot gently) 2. Rinse tooth root briefly (<10 sec cold water) 3. Insert tooth into socket with gentle pressure 4. Have patient bite on gauze to stabilize 5. Verify correct orientation (facial surface forward) 6. Check occlusion If resistance encountered: • Do not force • Clot may be blocki

nodes.title: Avulsion — Medications & Follow-up
nodes.summary: Avulsion: amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7d first-line (IADT 2020); doxycycline only if ≥12yo; tetanus; dental follow-up 24-48h
nodes.body: Post-reimplantation care: [1][2][9] Antibiotics (strongly recommended) — IADT 2020: • First-line (all ages): Amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7 days (peds: 25 mg/kg/day divided TID). Amoxicillin/penicillin are the IADT first choice — effective against oral flora, low side-effect profile. [1] • PCN allergy: Clindamycin 300 mg TID × 7 days (peds: 10 mg/kg/day divided TID) • Doxycycline (anti-resorptive opti
nodes.recommendation: Amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7 days first-line (IADT 2020); doxycycline only if age ≥12. Tetanus update, mandatory dental follow-up 24-48h.

nodes.title: Splinting Techniques
nodes.summary: Splinting Techniques — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Splinting principles: [1][6] FLEXIBLE splints preferred (allow physiologic motion) • Wire-composite • Resin-bonded • Soft wire + adhesive RIGID splints increase ankylosis risk — avoid if possible Duration by injury: | Injury | Splint Type | Duration | |--------|-------------|----------| | Subluxation | Flexible | 2 weeks | | Extrusive | Flexible | 2 weeks | | Lateral | Flexible | 2 weeks | | Intru

nodes.title: Dental Trauma — Disposition Summary
nodes.summary: Dental Trauma — Disposition Summary — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Follow-up timing by injury: [1][2] | Injury | Urgency | Follow-up | |--------|---------|----------| | Ellis I | Routine | Days to weeks | | Ellis II | Urgent | 24 hours | | Ellis III | EMERGENCY | Same day (<3h ideal) | | Concussion | Routine | PRN | | Subluxation | Urgent | 1 week | | Extrusive | Urgent | 24-48 hours | | Lateral | Urgent | 24 hours | | Intrusion >3mm | EMERGENCY | Same day | | Av
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on injury severity. All splinted teeth need dental follow-up. Ellis III/avulsion/alveolar fx = same-day.

nodes.title: Dexmedetomidine (Precedex) - Indications
nodes.summary: Selective α2 agonist — sedation without respiratory depression but watch for HOTN (30%) and brady (14%)
nodes.body: Dexmedetomidine Summary Class: Selective central α2-adrenergic agonist (8x more selective for α2 vs α1 than clonidine). Mechanism: Reduces presynaptic norepinephrine release in the locus coeruleus → sedation, anxiolysis, and analgesia WITHOUT respiratory depression. [1][2] Key advantages over propofol/midazolam: [1][3] - No respiratory depression — safe in non-intubated patients - Patient remains

nodes.title: ICU Sedation - Mechanically Ventilated
nodes.summary: PADIS 2018 + SPICE III: dex over benzos for ventilated adults, target RASS 0 to -2, reduces delirium and extubation time
nodes.body: Evidence: [3][4] - MIDEX/PRODEX (Jakob 2012, JAMA): Dexmedetomidine non-inferior to midazolam and propofol for light sedation, with shorter time to extubation and reduced delirium. - SPICE III (Shehabi 2019, NEJM): Early dexmedetomidine vs usual care showed NO mortality difference but reduced delirium and faster extubation in select subgroups. - PADIS 2018 (SCCM): Suggests dexmedetomidine OR propo

nodes.title: Alcohol Withdrawal - ADJUNCT Only
nodes.summary: ADJUNCT ONLY for EtOH withdrawal — never replaces benzos, reduces benzo req ~50%, start 0.2 mcg/kg/hr
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Dexmedetomidine is NEVER monotherapy for alcohol withdrawal. [5][6] Why: Dex suppresses sympathetic outflow (tremor, tachycardia, hypertension) but does NOT prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. Benzos remain first-line for seizure prophylaxis. [5] Evidence: - DahLIA trial (Reade 2018, JAMA): Dexmedetomidine reduced agitation and ICU LOS in severe alcohol withdrawal, but all p

nodes.title: Procedural Sedation - Cooperative Adult
nodes.summary: Awake fiberoptic = gold standard indication; SLOW for short ED procedures, NOT good analgesia alone
nodes.body: Best procedural indications: [7][8] - Awake fiberoptic intubation (gold standard — preserves airway reflexes and respiratory drive) - MRI in claustrophobic/anxious adults - Sedation for non-painful procedures in hemodynamically fragile patients - Bridge sedation in agitated patient awaiting CT/MRI clearance for definitive sedation Why dex for these: [7] - Patient remains arousable and cooperative

nodes.title: Pediatric Procedural Sedation
nodes.summary: IN 2-4 mcg/kg for kids = MRI/CT gold standard, 92% success, no resp depression — avoid in CHD with low CO
nodes.body: FDA-approved adult only — pediatric use is OFF-LABEL but widely supported by evidence. [9][10] Intranasal (IN) dexmedetomidine: [9] - Dose: 2-4 mcg/kg IN (divide between nostrils) - Onset: 15-25 minutes - Duration: 60-90 minutes - Best indications: MRI, CT, echo, EEG, non-painful procedures - Evidence: Mason et al, Pediatric Anesthesia 2011 — 92% success rate for MRI sedation - Bioavailability: 65

nodes.title: Ventilator Wean / Pre-Extubation
nodes.summary: Bridge from propofol/midazolam to extubation — preserves resp drive, continue 4-6h post-extub in fragile patients
nodes.body: Excellent indication for dex. [3][11] Why dex during wean: - Preserves respiratory drive (no resp depression) - Allows light sedation while patient breathes spontaneously on PSV/CPAP - Reduces delirium during the wean period - Faster extubation vs midazolam (MIDEX trial) Transition protocol from propofol or midazolam: [3][11] 1. Start dex at 0.4 mcg/kg/hr (no load) 2. Wait 30 minutes for steady-st

nodes.title: Loading Dose - To Load or Not to Load
nodes.summary: FDA says load 1 mcg/kg over 10min — ED reality: skip for ICU/EtOH, half-load for procedures, full only for awake fiberoptic
nodes.body: FDA label says load. ED reality often says skip. [1][2][12] FDA-labeled loading dose: - 1 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes - Reaches steady-state plasma concentration in ~15 minutes - Theoretical rationale: faster sedation onset The problem with loading: [1][12] - 30% incidence of hypotension during the load (vs 15% with maintenance-only) - 14% bradycardia, can be severe (HR <40) - Paradoxical hypertensi

nodes.title: Full Loading Dose Protocol
nodes.summary: Full load = 1 mcg/kg over 10 min, pre-treat with 500mL crystalloid, monitor BP q1-2min, atropine ready
nodes.body: Standard loading dose: [1][2] 1 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes Preparation: - Dexmedetomidine stock: 100 mcg/mL (200 mcg/2 mL vial) - Standard dilution: 200 mcg in 50 mL NS = 4 mcg/mL - For 70 kg patient: 70 mcg load = 17.5 mL of 4 mcg/mL over 10 min (105 mL/hr pump rate) During the load (continuous monitoring): - BP cycle q1-2 minutes - Continuous cardiac monitor - Continuous SpO2 - Have atropine 0.5

nodes.title: Reduced Loading Dose (0.5 mcg/kg)
nodes.summary: Reduced load 0.5 mcg/kg = half HOTN risk, still 10-15 min onset — best for elderly/fragile procedural patients
nodes.body: For procedural sedation in fragile patients or elderly. [7][12] Dose: 0.5 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes Rationale: - Half the hypotension risk of full load - Still achieves clinically useful 10-15 min onset - Particularly useful in elderly (>65), small adults, mild cardiac disease Preparation (70 kg patient): - 35 mcg load = 8.75 mL of 4 mcg/mL over 10 min (52.5 mL/hr pump rate) Monitoring during load

nodes.title: Maintenance Infusion - Starting Rate
nodes.summary: Start 0.2-0.4 mcg/kg/hr (no load), titrate q15-30min, max practical 1.5 mcg/kg/hr — add adjunct rather than push higher
nodes.body: Standard maintenance dose: [1][2] 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/hr IV continuous infusion Starting rate by scenario: [1][3][5] - Light ICU sedation (RASS 0 to -1): Start 0.2 mcg/kg/hr - Standard ICU sedation (RASS -1 to -2): Start 0.4 mcg/kg/hr - Deep sedation needs (RASS -2 to -3): Start 0.4 mcg/kg/hr (max effect at 0.7-1.5) - Alcohol withdrawal: Start 0.2 mcg/kg/hr - Pediatric: Start 0.2-0.3 mcg/kg/hr Pharmaco

nodes.title: Titration Strategy
nodes.summary: Titrate 0.1-0.2 mcg/kg/hr q15-30min — cap at 1.5 mcg/kg/hr, then add adjunct; tachyphylaxis after 5-7d
nodes.body: Titrate by 0.1-0.2 mcg/kg/hr every 15-30 minutes. [1][2] Titration rules: 1. Assess RASS q1h (more frequently during active titration) 2. Increase by 0.1 mcg/kg/hr if RASS above target by 1 3. Increase by 0.2 mcg/kg/hr if RASS above target by 2+ 4. Decrease by 0.1-0.2 mcg/kg/hr if RASS below target (over-sedated) 5. Wait 15-30 min between adjustments — earlier changes do not reflect steady state T

nodes.title: Duration of Therapy
nodes.summary: FDA <24h but routine 5-7d safe — tachyphylaxis emerges day 5-7, requires wean after >24h use
nodes.body: FDA label: Approved for sedation up to 24 hours. [1] Real-world practice: Routinely used 5-7 days, with growing evidence supporting longer durations. [3][13] Evidence for extended duration: [3][13] - MIDEX (2012): Used dex up to 14 days, no safety signal - SPICE III (2019): Early dex for up to 28 days in ventilated patients, no increase in mortality - Pediatric series: Up to 14 days with appropria

nodes.title: Hypotension Management (30% incidence)
nodes.summary: 30% HOTN — volume FIRST (most responds), then push-dose pressor, reduce dex LAST. STOP if needs NE drip
nodes.body: Hypotension is the MOST COMMON adverse event with dex. [1][2][12] Pathophysiology: Central sympatholysis (decreased norepinephrine release) → vasodilation and reduced cardiac output. Worsened by volume depletion. Definition + thresholds: - Mild: SBP 90-100 OR MAP 60-65 — observe, optimize volume - Moderate: SBP 80-89 OR MAP 55-59 — fluid bolus, reduce dex rate - Severe: SBP <80 OR MAP <55 — fluids

nodes.title: Bradycardia Management (14% incidence)
nodes.summary: HR <40 or symptomatic = HOLD dex + atropine 0.5mg IV, glycopyrrolate if recurrent — NOT phenylephrine (worsens via baroreflex)
nodes.body: Bradycardia is the second most common adverse event. [1][2][14] Pathophysiology: Reduced sympathetic outflow + increased baroreceptor reflex sensitivity → slower HR. Can be profound (HR <40) in vagally-toned patients (athletes, beta-blocked patients). Definition + thresholds: - Mild (asymptomatic): HR 50-59 OR HR drop 10-20% from baseline - Moderate (asymptomatic): HR 40-49 OR HR drop 20-30% from

nodes.title: Paradoxical Hypertension During Load
nodes.summary: Paradoxical HTN 10% during load (α1 at high concentrations) — slow load to 20min, or stop and resume as maintenance only
nodes.body: Paradoxical hypertension occurs in ~10% of patients receiving loading dose. [1][12] Pathophysiology: At high plasma concentrations (during loading), dex activates peripheral α1 receptors before central α2 sympatholysis predominates. Net effect = transient vasoconstriction. Clinical features: - SBP elevation 20-40 mmHg above baseline - Occurs during or immediately after loading dose - Self-limited

nodes.title: Dex vs Other Sedatives - Comparison
nodes.summary: Dex slow (15-30 min) but no resp depression + low delirium — propofol/midazolam for crashing patients, dex for ICU light sedation
nodes.body: Choosing between sedatives: [1][3][15] | Agent | Onset | Resp Depression | Hemodynamics | Delirium Risk | Cost | |-------|-------|-----------------|--------------|----------------|------| | Dexmedetomidine | 15-30 min | None | HOTN/brady | LOW | $$$$ | | Propofol | 30 sec | YES (severe) | HOTN | MEDIUM | $ | | Midazolam | 2-5 min | YES (severe) | Mild HOTN | HIGH | $ | | Ketamine | 30 sec | None (

nodes.title: Wean Protocol (after >24h continuous use)
nodes.summary: After >24h: 50% q12h wean, after >7d: 25% q12h — bridge with PO clonidine, NEVER abrupt stop after extended use
nodes.body: Abrupt discontinuation after >24h of dex causes withdrawal syndrome. [13][16] Withdrawal syndrome features: [13][16] - Rebound hypertension (sometimes severe) - Rebound tachycardia - Agitation, anxiety, restlessness - Diaphoresis - Insomnia - Onset: 6-24h after abrupt stop - Duration: 24-72h - Mechanism: Sympathetic rebound from chronic α2 receptor down-regulation Risk factors for severe withdrawa

nodes.title: Dexmedetomidine - Summary & "Reversal"
nodes.summary: No reversal — stop infusion, t1/2 = 2-3h, support hemodynamics with fluids + atropine + push-dose pressors
nodes.body: There is NO clinically available reversal agent for dexmedetomidine. [1][2] Atipamezole is a selective α2 antagonist that reverses dex effects rapidly, but it is veterinary-only in the US. Limited human data. Not available for clinical use. If patient is over-sedated or hemodynamically unstable: 1. STOP the infusion — elimination half-life is 2-3 hours, effects resolve within 4-6 hours 2. Support
nodes.recommendation: Dexmedetomidine is a uniquely useful α2 agonist for light sedation without respiratory depression. The dose-limiting toxicities (hypotension 30%, bradycardia 14%) are predictable and manageable with the right setup: volume optimization, atr

nodes.title: Drug-Facilitated Sexual Assault — ED Workup
nodes.summary: Drug-facilitated sexual assault: time-sensitive evidence collection — compassionate, trauma-informed approach
nodes.body: DFSA Steps Summary This consult is TIME-DRIVEN. Detection windows for DFSA agents are narrow — GHB is undetectable after 6 hours in blood and 12 hours in urine. Standard hospital drug screens miss most DFSA drugs. Forensic specimens must go to a state crime lab or forensic reference laboratory. Drug Detection Windows — full reference table Forensic Specimen Guide — tube types, volumes, chain of cu

nodes.title: Clinical Red Flags for DFSA
nodes.summary: Clinical Red Flags for DFSA — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Suspect drug facilitation when any of the following are present: • Amnesia disproportionate to reported alcohol intake • Unexplained injuries or soreness (especially genital/anal) • Intermittent consciousness or "blackout" periods • Waking undressed or in unfamiliar location • Uncertain whether sexual contact occurred • Witnesses describe sudden incapacitation • Residual sedation, confusion, or at

nodes.title: Medical Stability
nodes.summary: Medical Stability — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Assess vitals, GCS, and perform trauma assessment. Check for: • Strangulation signs (petechiae, voice changes, neck tenderness) • Genital/anal trauma • Bite marks • Defensive injuries (forearms, hands) • Residual drug effects (sedation, respiratory depression) Is the patient medically stable?

nodes.title: Medical Stabilization Required
nodes.summary: Medical Stabilization Required — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Address life threats before forensic workup. Preserve evidence while stabilizing: • Place clothing in paper bags (NOT plastic) • Minimize bathing, oral care, and voiding if safely possible • Delay urinary catheter and rectal exam if not emergently needed • If intubation required, save ET tube for toxicology • Document all injuries encountered during resuscitation Once stable, return to this consul
nodes.recommendation: Stabilize medically. Preserve clothing and minimize contamination. Forensic specimens can be collected after stabilization — but every hour of delay narrows detection windows.

nodes.title: Time Since Assault
nodes.summary: Time Since Assault — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Critical branch point. Detection windows are substance-specific but uniformly narrow. GHB has the shortest window (4-6h blood, 3-12h urine). When did the assault occur (or when was the patient last known to be well)?

nodes.title: Informed Consent Framework
nodes.summary: Informed Consent Framework — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: The patient has the right to consent to each element independently: • Forensic medical examination • Injury photography • Specimen collection (blood, urine, hair) • Law enforcement notification • Release of evidence to police The patient does NOT need to file a police report to receive a forensic exam or have specimens collected. Specimens can be held by the hospital or crime lab. VAWA Protections

nodes.title: Consent for Forensic Examination?
nodes.summary: Consent for Forensic Examination? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Explain the forensic exam process. Remind the patient they may decline any component at any time and can stop the exam at any point. Does the patient consent to a forensic examination?

nodes.title: Exam Declined — Still Offer Services
nodes.summary: Exam Declined — Still Offer Services — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Even without a forensic exam, offer all of the following: • STI prophylaxis (gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis) • Pregnancy prophylaxis (emergency contraception) • HIV PEP assessment — PEP Consult • Hepatitis B vaccination (if unvaccinated) • Safety assessment — is it safe to discharge? • Victim advocacy referral Consider offering urine collection for toxicology — the patient can hold the speci

nodes.title: Consent for Specimen Collection?
nodes.summary: Consent for Specimen Collection? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Forensic toxicology specimens include blood and urine (and potentially hair at follow-up). Important: Specimens can be held by the hospital or crime lab — the patient does NOT need to file a police report now. They can decide later. Does the patient consent to forensic specimen collection?

nodes.title: Consent for Injury Photography?
nodes.summary: Consent for Injury Photography? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Photo documentation of injuries significantly strengthens forensic evidence. Does the patient consent to photography of injuries?

nodes.title: Specimen Collection Declined
nodes.summary: Specimen Collection Declined — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Document the refusal in the medical record. Inform the patient: • Specimens can be collected up to 5 days post-assault (limited utility after 72h) • Hair collection is possible at 4-6 weeks post-assault — detects all major DFSA agents • They may change their mind at any time Proceed with forensic exam (if consented) and prophylaxis.

nodes.title: Specimen Collection Priority
nodes.summary: Specimen Collection Priority — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Confirm time since assault to guide specimen priority. Drug Detection Windows — full reference Forensic Specimen Guide — tube types and volumes What is the collection time window?

nodes.title: URGENT: < 6 Hour Collection
nodes.summary: URGENT: < 6 Hour Collection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: GHB IS STILL DETECTABLE — COLLECT IMMEDIATELY. Collect both blood and urine before any other forensic procedures: Blood: • Gray-top tube (NaF/KOx) — sodium fluoride preserves GHB, prevents in vitro production • Lavender-top (EDTA) — standard forensic toxicology • Additional red-top — clinical labs (BAL, hepatitis, HIV) Urine: • First-void specimen — do NOT discard • Minimum 50-100 mL in clean cont

nodes.title: 6-12 Hour Collection
nodes.summary: 6-12 Hour Collection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: GHB may still be detectable in urine (window up to 12h). Collect urine urgently. Urine (priority): • First-void specimen, 50-100 mL • GHB may still be present — time is critical Blood: • Gray-top (NaF) — GHB unlikely in blood but still collect • Lavender-top (EDTA) — benzodiazepines, ketamine, zolpidem, opioids still detectable Still detectable at 6-12h: • Flunitrazepam (Rohypnol) — blood 24-72h •

nodes.title: 12-72 Hour Collection
nodes.summary: 12-72 Hour Collection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Urine is the primary specimen. Blood is secondary but still valuable. GHB window is closed. Focus on: Urine (primary — longer windows): • Flunitrazepam metabolite (7-aminoflunitrazepam) — up to 72h • Ketamine/norketamine — up to 96h • Benzodiazepines — 24-72h depending on agent • Zolpidem — up to 24h • Opioids — 48-96h • Antihistamines — 48-72h • Alcohol metabolites (EtG/EtS) — up to 80h Blood (se

nodes.title: 72 Hours — 5 Day Collection
nodes.summary: 72 Hours — 5 Day Collection — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Urine only. Blood is unlikely to yield results at this interval. Still potentially detectable: • Cannabinoids — weeks in urine (chronic use) • EtG/EtS (alcohol metabolite) — up to 80h in urine • Some benzodiazepines (long-acting) — variable • Opioids — 48-96h (some agents) • Ketamine metabolite (norketamine) — up to 96h Collect first-void urine specimen. Plan for hair collection at 4-6 week follow

nodes.title: > 5 Days Post-Assault
nodes.summary: > 5 Days Post-Assault — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Standard blood and urine toxicology are unlikely to yield positive results at this interval. Hair collection is the primary option: • Collect at 4-6 weeks post-assault (allows drug to incorporate into hair shaft) • Pencil-thickness bundle from the posterior vertex • Cut at the scalp — do NOT pluck • Wrap in aluminum foil, label proximal end • Send to forensic reference laboratory (NMS Labs, Axiom

nodes.title: Forensic Drug Panel
nodes.summary: Forensic Drug Panel — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Hospital drug screens are INADEQUATE for DFSA. Standard hospital UDS/immunoassay: • Does NOT detect GHB • Does NOT detect flunitrazepam metabolites at relevant concentrations • Does NOT detect zolpidem, zaleplon, or zopiclone • Does NOT detect ketamine at low facilitative doses • Is NOT forensically admissible — lacks confirmation testing and chain of custody Specimens MUST go to a state crime lab

nodes.title: Hospital Tox Screen in Parallel?
nodes.summary: Hospital Tox Screen in Parallel? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: A hospital tox screen is useful for clinical management (e.g., identifying acute intoxication, guiding treatment) but does NOT replace the forensic panel. Order a hospital UDS/serum tox in addition to forensic specimens?

nodes.title: Lab Ordering & Specimen Handling
nodes.summary: Lab Ordering & Specimen Handling — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Clinical baseline labs: • CBC, CMP • Urinalysis • Urine pregnancy test • Blood alcohol level • HIV Ag/Ab combo (4th gen) • Hepatitis B panel (HBsAg, HBsAb, HBcAb) • Hepatitis C Ab • RPR/VDRL Forensic specimen handling: • Label each specimen with patient name, DOB, date/time, collector • Seal with tamper-evident tape • Complete chain of custody form — document every transfer • Store refrigerated (N

nodes.title: SANE Nurse Available?
nodes.summary: SANE Nurse Available? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Is a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) available at your facility or on-call? SANE-collected evidence is significantly more likely to be admissible and complete. SANE exams have higher prosecution rates than non-SANE exams.

nodes.title: SANE Nurse Handoff
nodes.summary: SANE Nurse Handoff — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Your role (ED physician): • Medical stabilization • Time-critical toxicology specimen collection (do NOT wait for SANE if <6h) • Prophylaxis initiation (STI, pregnancy, HIV PEP) • Clinical lab ordering • Medical documentation SANE role: • Forensic evidence collection kit (swabs, combings) • Detailed injury documentation and photography • Evidence packaging and chain of custody • Patient advocacy c

nodes.title: No SANE Available — Physician-Led Coordination
nodes.summary: No SANE Available — Physician-Led Coordination — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Contact RAINN National Sexual Assault Hotline: 1-800-656-4673 for guidance on evidence collection. Consider transfer to a SANE-equipped facility if: • Patient is medically stable • Patient consents to transfer • Transfer will not close critical specimen windows If performing evidence collection: • Use your facility's sexual assault evidence collection kit • Follow kit instructions exactly — each s

nodes.title: Clothing & Physical Evidence
nodes.summary: Clothing & Physical Evidence — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Clothing evidence handling: • Place each item in a separate PAPER bag — NOT plastic (plastic promotes bacterial growth and degrades DNA evidence) • If patient is wearing the same clothes as during assault, collect all items • If patient changed clothes, attempt to obtain original clothing from home/car • Place paper sheet under patient while undressing to catch trace evidence Additional evidence:

nodes.title: Documentation Requirements
nodes.summary: Documentation Requirements — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Document in the medical record: • Patient statements in direct quotes — use their exact words • Time of presentation and reported time of assault • All injuries: location, size, color, shape, age estimation • Specimens collected with date/time of each • Chain of custody transfers • Consents obtained and declined • All providers involved in care Critical: Document objective findings only. Do NOT: •

nodes.title: Prophylaxis Overview
nodes.summary: Prophylaxis Overview — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Three categories of prophylaxis to address independently: 1. STI Prophylaxis — gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis 2. Pregnancy Prophylaxis — emergency contraception 3. HIV PEP — based on exposure risk assessment Plus: Hepatitis B vaccination if unvaccinated. Each is offered independently — the patient may accept some and decline others. STI Prophylaxis Regimens — dosing reference

nodes.title: STI Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: STI Prophylaxis — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Empiric prophylaxis for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis: • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 — gonorrhea • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days — chlamydia • Metronidazole 2 g PO × 1 dose — trichomoniasis Cephalosporin allergy alternative: Gentamicin 240 mg IM × 1 + Azithromycin 2 g PO × 1 Accept STI prophylaxis?

nodes.title: STI Prophylaxis Ordered
nodes.summary: STI Prophylaxis Ordered — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Administer in ED: • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 • Metronidazole 2 g PO × 1 Prescribe: • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days Cephalosporin allergy: Gentamicin 240 mg IM × 1 + Azithromycin 2 g PO × 1 Pregnancy modifications: Substitute azithromycin 1 g PO × 1 for doxycycline. Metronidazole is safe in pregnancy (CDC category B).
nodes.recommendation: Follow-up STI testing: NAAT for GC/CT at 2 weeks. Repeat full STI panel (GC, CT, syphilis, HIV, Hep B/C) at 3 months. Test of cure not routinely needed unless symptoms persist.

nodes.title: Pregnancy Risk?
nodes.summary: Pregnancy Risk? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Is the patient at risk for pregnancy? Risk factors: • Reproductive-age female (typically 12-50) • Not on reliable contraception (IUD, implant, tubal ligation, hysterectomy) • Vaginal penetration occurred or suspected Urine pregnancy test should have been collected with baseline labs.

nodes.title: Emergency Contraception
nodes.summary: Emergency Contraception — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Ulipristal acetate (ella) is preferred — effective up to 5 days post-exposure with no decrease in efficacy over time. Levonorgestrel (Plan B) is an alternative — most effective within 72h, efficacy decreases with time and higher body weight. Copper IUD is the most effective EC option (>99%) if within 5 days — consider GYN consult for placement. Select emergency contraception:

nodes.title: Emergency Contraception Ordered
nodes.summary: Emergency Contraception Ordered — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Ulipristal acetate (ella): 30 mg PO × 1 dose • Effective up to 120h (5 days) post-exposure • Progesterone receptor modulator — delays ovulation • Do NOT take with levonorgestrel — they interfere • Hormonal contraception can resume 5 days after ulipristal Levonorgestrel (Plan B): 1.5 mg PO × 1 dose • Most effective within 72h • Efficacy may decrease if BMI > 25 • Can resume hormonal contraception i
nodes.recommendation: Follow-up pregnancy test at 2 weeks. If positive, early OB referral.

nodes.title: Hepatitis B Vaccination Status
nodes.summary: Hepatitis B Vaccination Status — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Is the patient vaccinated against Hepatitis B? Check HBsAb from baseline labs if available. If immune (HBsAb positive), no further Hep B intervention needed.

nodes.title: Initiate Hepatitis B Vaccine
nodes.summary: Initiate Hepatitis B Vaccine — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Hep B vaccine dose 1 today. Schedule doses 2 and 3: • Dose 2: 1 month • Dose 3: 6 months If source is known HBV-positive: • Add HBIG (Hepatitis B Immune Globulin) 0.06 mL/kg IM • Administer at different injection site from vaccine • HBIG most effective within 24h of exposure; for sexual exposure the effective interval is up to 14 days (7 days for percutaneous exposures)

nodes.title: HIV PEP Assessment
nodes.summary: HIV PEP Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Assess HIV transmission risk based on exposure type. Higher risk — PEP recommended: • Receptive anal intercourse • Source known HIV-positive with detectable viral load • Mucosal exposure to blood Lower risk — PEP case-by-case: • Receptive vaginal intercourse • Source HIV status unknown • Insertive anal/vaginal intercourse For full HIV PEP evaluation including regimen selection and follow-up: PEP C

nodes.title: HIV PEP — Initiate Now
nodes.summary: HIV PEP — Initiate Now — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: PEP must be started within 72 hours of exposure — ideally within 24 hours (CDC 2025). Earlier is better. For full PEP workup including regimen selection, baseline labs, and 28-day follow-up schedule: PEP Consult Key points: • Preferred regimen (CDC 2025): Biktarvy (BIC/TAF/FTC) × 28 days, or dolutegravir + (TAF or TDF)/(FTC or 3TC) • Start ASAP — do not delay for source testing • Baseline: HIV Ag/

nodes.title: Safe Discharge Assessment
nodes.summary: Safe Discharge Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Screen for ongoing safety concerns before discharge. Assess: • Is the assailant known to the patient? • Does the patient share housing with the assailant? • Does the patient have a safe place to go tonight? • Is there an ongoing threat? • Are there children at risk? • Does the patient have access to transportation?

nodes.title: Unsafe Discharge — Safety Resources
nodes.summary: Unsafe Discharge — Safety Resources — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Activate safety resources: • Social work consult — immediate • Victim advocacy — contact your facility's advocate or RAINN: 1-800-656-4673 • Domestic violence shelter referral — National DV Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 • Safety planning — develop specific plan with patient and advocate • Law enforcement notification — if patient consents and immediate threat exists If no safe discharge option: • Consid

nodes.title: Disposition & Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Disposition & Follow-Up — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Patient Handout — shareable follow-up guide with resources Follow-up schedule: • 2 weeks: STI testing (NAAT for GC/CT), pregnancy test • 4-6 weeks: Hair specimen collection if planned, HIV test (if PEP started) • 3 months: Repeat full STI panel (GC, CT, syphilis, HIV, Hep B/C) • 6 months: Final HIV test, Hep B vaccine dose 3 Resources: • RAINN: 1-800-656-4673 (24/7 hotline) • National DV Hotline:
nodes.recommendation: Ensure patient leaves with: written follow-up schedule, advocacy contact information, medication instructions, and patient handout. Arrange transportation. Coordinate warm handoff to victim advocacy before discharge.

nodes.title: Diabetes Management - Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Identify the acute diabetic emergency — DKA, HHS, or hypoglycemia require different management
nodes.body: Diabetes Management Steps Summary - quick reference. Approach to the diabetic patient: Immediate triage based on glucose level: - Glucose <70 mg/dL: Hypoglycemia pathway - Glucose 70-180 mg/dL: Assess for DKA/HHS risk factors - Glucose 180-300 mg/dL: Mild hyperglycemia, assess context - Glucose >300 mg/dL: Evaluate for DKA/HHS - Glucose >600 mg/dL: High suspicion for HHS Critical questions: 1. Typ

nodes.title: Current Glucose Level
nodes.summary: Current Glucose Level — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: What is the current point-of-care glucose? If glucose unknown, obtain fingerstick immediately. Clinical context matters: - Symptomatic hypoglycemia can occur at higher glucose in poorly controlled diabetics - Euglycemic DKA (glucose <250) occurs with SGLT2 inhibitors - Elderly/renal patients may have HHS at lower glucose levels

nodes.title: DKA/HHS Screening
nodes.summary: DKA/HHS Screening — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Check for diabetic emergencies before routine hyperglycemia management. DKA criteria — 2024 ADA/EASD consensus (all 3 required): [1][2] - D (hyperglycemia): glucose >=200 mg/dL OR known history of diabetes (history allows euglycemic DKA) - K (ketosis): beta-hydroxybutyrate >=3.0 mmol/L (or ketonuria >=2+) - A (acidosis): pH <7.3 AND/OR HCO3 <18 mmol/L *The 2024 consensus REMOVED the anion gap from

nodes.title: DKA Management
nodes.summary: DKA Management — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: DKA requires dedicated protocol management. Go to DKA Consult for comprehensive management including: - Fluid resuscitation strategy - Insulin drip protocol - Potassium management - Transition to subcutaneous insulin - Special populations (pregnancy, HD, SGLT2i) Key DKA pearls: - Never stop insulin just because glucose is low - add dextrose instead - Start basal insulin early (within 6-12h) to pre
nodes.recommendation: Navigate to DKA consult for detailed protocol management.

nodes.title: HHS Management
nodes.summary: HHS Management — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) [3] Characteristics: - Glucose often >600 mg/dL (can be >1000) - Serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg - Minimal ketosis (BOHB usually <3) - pH usually >7.3 - Profound dehydration (average 8-10L deficit) - Mortality 10-20% (higher than DKA) Key differences from DKA: - Slower onset (days to weeks) - More severe dehydration - Higher mortality - Often elderly with Type
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. Aggressive fluid resuscitation with NS. Slower glucose correction than DKA. Thromboprophylaxis. Search for precipitant.

nodes.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 Assessment
nodes.summary: Type 1 vs Type 2 Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Distinguishing diabetes type affects management decisions. Type 1 indicators: - Younger onset (though can occur at any age) - Normal or low BMI - Rapid onset of symptoms - History of DKA - On basal-bolus insulin - C-peptide low or undetectable - Autoantibodies positive (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) Type 2 indicators: - Older onset (though increasing in youth) - Overweight/obese BMI - Gradual symptom onset -

nodes.title: Insulin Pump Assessment
nodes.summary: Insulin Pump Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Is the patient on an insulin pump? Pump continuation criteria: [6] - Patient is alert and able to manage pump - Pump is functioning properly - Adequate supplies available - Patient is eating or will be eating - Not going to OR Disconnect pump if: - Altered mental status - Unable to self-manage - Going to surgery/procedure - DKA (need IV insulin) - Pump malfunction - MRI (must remove) When disconne

nodes.title: Continue Insulin Pump
nodes.summary: Continue Insulin Pump — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Insulin pump continuation protocol: [6] Document: - Pump type and model - Current basal rate(s) - Insulin-to-carb ratio (ICR) - Correction factor (sensitivity) - Target glucose range - Active insulin time Patient responsibilities: - Continue self-management - Count carbs and bolus for meals - Check glucose before meals and at bedtime - Alert staff to any pump alarms - Change infusion site if indic
nodes.recommendation: Continue patient-managed insulin pump with documented settings. Target glucose 140-180 mg/dL. Have backup insulin available.

nodes.title: Disconnect Insulin Pump
nodes.summary: Disconnect Insulin Pump — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Pump discontinuation with insulin transition: [6] CRITICAL: Must start alternative insulin within 30 minutes of pump removal. Pump users have no long-acting insulin depot - DKA can develop within 4-6 hours. Transition to IV insulin (preferred for DKA, NPO, surgery): - Start IV regular insulin drip at 0.5-1 U/hr - Adjust based on glucose monitoring - See DKA consult if acidosis present Transition t
nodes.recommendation: Disconnect pump and start IV insulin or SC basal-bolus within 30 minutes. Calculate TDD from pump history. Monitor closely.

nodes.title: New Diabetes Diagnosis
nodes.summary: New Diabetes Diagnosis — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Approach to new diabetes in the ED/hospital: Immediate assessment: 1. Check for DKA (glucose, VBG, BMP, ketones) 2. Assess symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue 3. HbA1c if not recently checked Classification clues: - Likely Type 1: young, thin, rapid onset, DKA at presentation, FH of autoimmune disease - Likely Type 2: older, obese, gradual onset, metabolic syndrome features - Unce

nodes.title: Inpatient vs Outpatient Management
nodes.summary: Inpatient vs Outpatient Management — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Is this patient being admitted or discharged? Admission criteria for diabetes-related issues: - DKA or HHS - Severe hypoglycemia with altered mental status - Recurrent hypoglycemia - New Type 1 diabetes - Significant comorbid illness - Unable to take oral medications - Social factors preventing safe discharge Outpatient management appropriate if: - Stable glucose - Eating/drinking normally - No ac

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Hypoglycemia Severity Assessment — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Classify hypoglycemia severity: [7] Level 1 (Alert, glucose 54-70 mg/dL): - Mild symptoms: tremor, palpitations, sweating, hunger - Patient can self-treat - Neurologically intact Level 2 (Alert, glucose <54 mg/dL): - More significant symptoms - Still able to self-treat - Clinically significant hypoglycemia Level 3 (Severe): - Altered mental status, confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness - Requi

nodes.title: Oral Hypoglycemia Treatment
nodes.summary: Oral Hypoglycemia Treatment — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Alert patient with hypoglycemia - oral treatment preferred: [7] First-line: Fast-acting carbohydrates (15-20g) - 4 glucose tablets (4g each) - 4 oz (120 mL) juice or regular soda - 1 tablespoon honey or sugar - 6-8 hard candies Rule of 15: 1. Give 15-20g fast-acting carbs 2. Recheck glucose in 15 minutes 3. Repeat if still <70 mg/dL 4. Once >70, give snack with protein/fat to sustain Avoid: - Choc
nodes.recommendation: Give 15-20g fast-acting carbohydrates. Recheck glucose in 15 minutes. Repeat if needed. Follow with protein-containing snack.

nodes.title: Severe Hypoglycemia - IV Access?
nodes.summary: Severe Hypoglycemia - IV Access? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Severe hypoglycemia requires immediate intervention. [7][8] IV access available: - Dextrose 50% (D50W) or Dextrose 10% (D10W) preferred - Faster and more reliable than IM glucagon No IV access: - Glucagon IM/SC/intranasal - Can use IM in outer thigh through clothing - Intranasal glucagon (Baqsimi) if available Special considerations: - Alcoholics: Give thiamine BEFORE or WITH dextrose (Wernicke pr

nodes.title: IV Dextrose for Severe Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: IV Dextrose for Severe Hypoglycemia — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: IV dextrose is first-line for severe hypoglycemia with IV access: [7][8] Adult dosing: - D50W: 25-50 mL (12.5-25g dextrose) IV push - D10W: 100-250 mL (10-25g dextrose) IV infusion Why D10W may be preferred: - Less osmotic/tissue injury if extravasation - Can run through peripheral IV safely - Easier to titrate - D50W is hyperosmolar and can cause phlebitis/tissue necrosis Expected response: - Men
nodes.recommendation: D50W 25-50 mL IV push or D10W 100-250 mL IV. Recheck glucose in 15 min. Give thiamine first in alcoholics/malnourished.

nodes.title: Glucagon for Severe Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: Glucagon for Severe Hypoglycemia — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Glucagon when IV access unavailable: [7][8] Intramuscular/Subcutaneous: - Glucagon 1 mg IM or SC - Can inject through clothing into lateral thigh - Onset: 10-15 minutes - May cause nausea/vomiting when patient wakes Intranasal (Baqsimi): - 3 mg intranasal (single-use device) - No reconstitution needed - Administer into one nostril - Patient does not need to inhale Limitations of glucagon: - Requir
nodes.recommendation: Glucagon 1 mg IM/SC or 3 mg intranasal. Position on side. Give oral carbs when alert. Obtain IV access.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia - Underlying Cause
nodes.summary: Hypoglycemia - Underlying Cause — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: After treating acute hypoglycemia, identify the cause: [7][9] Common causes in diabetics: - Missed or delayed meal - Excessive insulin dose - Increased physical activity - Alcohol (especially without food) - Medication error - Renal impairment (reduced insulin clearance) - New medication interaction Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia: - Glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride - Can cause prolonged hypoglycemia (

nodes.title: Sulfonylurea-Induced Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: Sulfonylurea-Induced Hypoglycemia — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia requires extended monitoring: [9] Why it is dangerous: - Long half-life (glipizide 2-5h, glyburide 10h, glimepiride 5-9h) - Continuous insulin secretion independent of glucose - Active metabolites in renal impairment - Hypoglycemia can recur for 12-72+ hours Management: 1. IV dextrose as above 2. D10W infusion to maintain glucose 100-150 mg/dL 3. Consider octreotide for r
nodes.recommendation: Admit for extended monitoring. D10W infusion to maintain glucose 100-150. Consider octreotide 50-100 mcg SC q6-8h for refractory cases.

nodes.title: Insulin-Induced Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: Insulin-Induced Hypoglycemia — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Insulin hypoglycemia - duration depends on insulin type: [7] Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine): - Peak: 1-2 hours - Duration: 3-5 hours - Observation: 2-4 hours usually sufficient Regular insulin: - Peak: 2-4 hours - Duration: 6-8 hours - Observation: 4-6 hours NPH/intermediate: - Peak: 4-10 hours - Duration: 10-16 hours - Observation: extended, consider admission Long-acting (glargine, det
nodes.recommendation: Duration of observation based on insulin type. Educate on cause. Adjust regimen if indicated. Consider endocrine follow-up.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia - Other Causes
nodes.summary: Hypoglycemia - Other Causes — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Investigate underlying cause for recurrent/unexplained hypoglycemia: Alcohol-induced: - Inhibits gluconeogenesis - Depletes glycogen stores - Glucagon may not work - Give thiamine with dextrose - May need D10W infusion Sepsis: - Increased glucose utilization - Impaired gluconeogenesis - Poor prognostic sign - Treat underlying infection Adrenal insufficiency: - Cortisol required for gluconeogenesis
nodes.recommendation: Investigate underlying cause. Treat accordingly. Ensure appropriate observation period before discharge.

nodes.title: Inpatient Glucose Targets
nodes.summary: Inpatient Glucose Targets — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Glycemic targets for hospitalized patients: [1][10] General inpatient (non-ICU): - Target: 140-180 mg/dL - Preprandial: <140 mg/dL - Random: <180 mg/dL - Avoid glucose <70 mg/dL (hypoglycemia) ICU patients: - Target: 140-180 mg/dL (same as general) - Previous target of 80-110 mg/dL abandoned due to increased hypoglycemia and mortality (NICE-SUGAR trial) Stricter targets (110-140 mg/dL) may be appr

nodes.title: Inpatient Insulin Regimen Selection
nodes.summary: Inpatient Insulin Regimen Selection — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Select insulin regimen based on clinical status: [1][10] Basal-bolus-correction (preferred): - Best for most hospitalized diabetics - Mimics physiologic insulin secretion - Better glycemic control than sliding scale alone - Requires patient to be eating IV insulin infusion: - Critical illness/ICU - NPO status expected >12-24 hours - DKA/HHS - Perioperative management - Refractory hyperglycemia Sli

nodes.title: Basal-Bolus-Correction Protocol
nodes.summary: Basal-Bolus-Correction Protocol — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Step 1: Estimate Total Daily Dose (TDD) [1][10] If insulin-naive or dose unknown: - General: 0.4-0.5 U/kg/day - Elderly/renal impairment: 0.2-0.3 U/kg/day - Insulin-resistant (obese, on steroids): 0.5-0.6 U/kg/day - High-dose steroids: may need 0.6-1.0 U/kg/day If on home insulin: - Use home TDD as starting point - May reduce by 20-25% for acute illness with poor intake Step 2: Distribute TDD - 50

nodes.title: Basal-Bolus Example & Orders
nodes.summary: Basal-Bolus Example & Orders — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Example: 80 kg patient, insulin-naive [10] Step 1: Calculate TDD - 0.4 U/kg x 80 kg = 32 U/day Step 2: Distribute - Basal: 16 U Glargine SC at bedtime - Bolus: 16 U divided = ~5 U Lispro with each meal Step 3: Correction Scale (CF = 1800/32 = 56, round to 50) | Glucose | Correction Dose | |---------|----------------| | 150-199 | +1 U | | 200-249 | +2 U | | 250-299 | +3 U | | 300-349 | +4 U | | >35
nodes.recommendation: Basal-bolus-correction: 50% TDD as glargine, 50% divided as meal-time lispro/aspart. Add correction scale. Adjust based on glucose trends.

nodes.title: IV Insulin Drip Protocol
nodes.summary: IV Insulin Drip Protocol — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: IV insulin for critical illness, NPO, or perioperative: [10][11] Standard preparation: - Regular Insulin 100 U in 100 mL NS = 1 U/mL Starting rate: - Glucose 150-200: start 1-2 U/hr - Glucose 200-300: start 2-4 U/hr - Glucose >300: start 4-6 U/hr - DKA: 0.1 U/kg/hr (see DKA consult) Titration (check glucose q1h): - Target: 140-180 mg/dL - Glucose dropping appropriately (50-70/hr): no change - Gluc
nodes.recommendation: Regular insulin drip 1 U/mL. Start 1-4 U/hr based on glucose. Target 140-180. Add dextrose when glucose <150-200.

nodes.title: NPO Diabetic Patient Management
nodes.summary: NPO Diabetic Patient Management — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Managing the NPO diabetic patient (non-critical): [10] Type 1 Diabetes (NPO): - MUST continue basal insulin (will develop DKA without it) - Hold meal-time bolus insulin - May reduce basal by 20-25% if prolonged NPO - Consider D5W maintenance to prevent hypoglycemia - Monitor glucose q4-6h Type 2 Diabetes (NPO): - Continue basal insulin at 75-100% of usual dose - Hold oral agents (especially metfor
nodes.recommendation: Type 1: Continue basal, hold bolus, monitor closely. Type 2: Continue basal at 75-100%, hold oral agents, correction scale PRN.

nodes.title: Steroid-Induced Hyperglycemia
nodes.summary: Steroid-Induced Hyperglycemia — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Corticosteroids cause significant hyperglycemia: [12] Mechanism: - Increase hepatic gluconeogenesis - Decrease peripheral glucose uptake - Increase insulin resistance Pattern with once-daily morning steroids: - Glucose peaks afternoon/evening (4-8 hours post-dose) - May be near-normal fasting - NPH at breakfast covers this pattern well Management approach: New hyperglycemia on steroids: - Start NP
nodes.recommendation: Add or increase insulin based on steroid dose. NPH covers afternoon peak from morning steroids. Reduce insulin as steroids taper.

nodes.title: Outpatient Diabetes Management
nodes.summary: Outpatient Diabetes Management — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Outpatient diabetes management decision points: [5] Is patient already on therapy? - If yes: assess current control, adjust regimen - If no: determine initial therapy HbA1c targets: - General: <7.0% - More strict (<6.5%): young, healthy, low hypoglycemia risk - Less strict (<8.0%): elderly, limited life expectancy, hypoglycemia risk When to initiate insulin: - HbA1c >10% - Glucose >300 mg/dL with

nodes.title: Oral Diabetes Agents
nodes.summary: Oral Diabetes Agents — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: First-line: Metformin [5][13] Metformin: - Start 500 mg daily with dinner, increase to 500 mg BID after 1 week - Target: 1000 mg BID (max 2550 mg/day) - GI side effects common initially (start low, titrate slow) - Contraindicated: eGFR <30, acute kidney injury, contrast within 48h - Hold if eGFR 30-45 (reassess) Second-line agents (add to metformin if not at goal): SGLT2 Inhibitors (empagliflozin,

nodes.title: Oral Agent Selection
nodes.summary: Oral Agent Selection — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Agent selection based on patient factors: [5][13] If HFrEF or CKD (eGFR 25-60): - SGLT2 inhibitor preferred (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) - Proven mortality benefit in heart failure - Renal protection independent of glucose If ASCVD: - GLP-1 agonist (semaglutide, liraglutide) or SGLT2i - Both have cardiovascular benefit If weight loss desired: - GLP-1 agonist (significant weight loss) - SGLT2 inh
nodes.recommendation: Metformin first-line. Add SGLT2i if HF/CKD, GLP-1 if weight loss/ASCVD. Avoid sulfonylureas if hypoglycemia risk.

nodes.title: Outpatient Insulin Initiation
nodes.summary: Outpatient Insulin Initiation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Starting insulin in the outpatient setting: [5] Basal insulin first (easiest for patients): - Glargine or degludec once daily - Start: 0.1-0.2 U/kg/day (or 10 U fixed dose) - Take at same time daily (bedtime or morning) - Titrate: increase by 2 U every 3 days until fasting glucose at target Calculator: TDD Estimator Example: 90 kg patient - Starting dose: 0.15 U/kg = ~14 U glargine at bedtime - Ta

nodes.title: Insulin Titration Protocol
nodes.summary: Insulin Titration Protocol — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Basal insulin titration (patient self-titration): [5] Fasting Glucose-Based Adjustment: | Fasting Glucose (mg/dL) | Adjustment | |------------------------|------------| | <70 (hypoglycemia) | Decrease by 2-4 U | | 70-130 (at goal) | No change | | 130-180 | Increase by 2 U | | >180 | Increase by 4 U | Titrate every 3 days until fasting glucose at goal. Adding mealtime insulin: - Start 4 U or 10% of
nodes.recommendation: Start basal 0.1-0.2 U/kg. Titrate by 2-4 U every 3 days based on fasting glucose. Add mealtime insulin when basal optimized but A1c still elevated.

nodes.title: Adjusting Existing Regimen
nodes.summary: Adjusting Existing Regimen — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Adjusting diabetes regimen for patients not at goal: [5] If on metformin alone (A1c 7-9%): - Add second agent: SGLT2i, GLP-1 agonist, or sulfonylurea - Choose based on comorbidities and patient factors If on dual oral therapy (A1c 8-10%): - Add third agent OR - Add basal insulin (often more effective) If on basal insulin + orals: - Optimize basal dose first (titrate to fasting goal) - If fasting a
nodes.recommendation: Intensify therapy stepwise. Optimize current regimen before adding agents. Basal insulin often more effective than third oral agent.

nodes.title: Special Situations
nodes.summary: Special Situations — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Select the clinical scenario:

nodes.title: IV to SC Insulin Transition
nodes.summary: IV to SC Insulin Transition — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Transitioning from IV insulin drip to subcutaneous: [10] Timing is critical: - Give SC basal insulin 2-4 hours BEFORE stopping IV drip - This allows SC insulin to reach therapeutic level - Stopping drip without basal = rapid hyperglycemia/DKA in Type 1 Calculating SC dose from IV drip: 1. Determine average hourly IV rate over last 6-12 hours 2. Calculate estimated daily dose: (hourly rate x 24) x

nodes.recommendation: Continue basal insulin, hold bolus/orals day of surgery. IV insulin for major surgery. Transition to SC when eating.

nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for severe sepsis, necrotizing infection, or hemodynamic instability. Emergent surgical consultation. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Sepsis bundle.

nodes.body: Empiric antibiotics indicated: • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID × 3 days (first-line for most regions) • Southeast Asia: Azithromycin 1000 mg PO × 1 dose or 500 mg PO daily × 3 days (fluoroquinolone-resistant Campylobacter >80%) • Children: TMP-SMX Adjunct therapy: • Loperamide with antibiotic — combination therapy reduces diarrhea duration by 1 additional day • IV rehydration if unable to tolerate o
nodes.recommendation: Empiric fluoroquinolone (or azithromycin for SE Asia) plus adjunct loperamide. Reassess for admission if not improving.

nodes.title: Treatment Approach
nodes.summary: Treatment Approach — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Rehydration is the cornerstone of diarrhea management. Antimotility Contraindications Oral rehydration is preferred when tolerated — it is effective, low-cost, and an indicator of discharge readiness. Solutions should contain sodium, potassium, and glucose. Commercial ORS (Pedialyte) preferred over sports drinks (inadequate sodium replacement). BRAT diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) has no p

nodes.title: Mild / Self-Limited Diarrhea
nodes.summary: Mild / Self-Limited Diarrhea — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Rehydration: • Oral rehydration solution (ORS) with sodium, potassium, glucose • Commercial options: Pedialyte, Lytren, Rehydrolyte • Resume normal diet at earliest opportunity — early refeeding improves recovery Symptomatic relief: • Loperamide 4 mg PO initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day) — preferred antimotility agent (no CNS effects, not habit-forming) • Bismuth Subsalicy
nodes.recommendation: Oral rehydration, symptomatic relief, discharge with return precautions.

nodes.title: Moderate Diarrhea Treatment
nodes.summary: Moderate Diarrhea Treatment — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: IV rehydration: • NS or LR bolus, reassess after each liter • Target: urine output, improved vitals, ability to tolerate oral fluids Antiemetics: • Ondansetron 4 mg IV q4-6h PRN for vomiting preventing oral intake Antimotility (if no contraindications): • Loperamide 4 mg PO then 2 mg PRN (max 16 mg/day) Assess for empiric antibiotic criteria: • Diarrhea >48 hours (higher probability non-viral) • F

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy
nodes.summary: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Empiric Antibiotic Criteria Adults (fever >38.5°C + positive fecal markers, dysentery, or >48h): • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID × 3-5 days Children: • TMP-SMX (dose by weight) × 3-5 days Persistent diarrhea (2-4 weeks) without systemic symptoms: • Metronidazole 250 mg PO TID × 7-10 days (covers Giardia) Elderly considerations: fluoroquinolones can increase theophylline and warfarin levels, and can
nodes.recommendation: Empiric fluoroquinolone for adults, TMP-SMX for children. Duration 3-5 days. Avoid antibiotics if STEC suspected.

nodes.title: Special Population Considerations
nodes.summary: Special Population Considerations — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Certain populations require modified workup, treatment, and disposition decisions.

nodes.title: Diarrhea in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Diarrhea in Pregnancy — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Dehydration is dangerous for both mother and fetus — aggressive rehydration is top priority. Safest antimotility: • Loperamide — acts peripherally (FDA Category B), safest option • AVOID diphenoxylate (CNS effects) and bismuth subsalicylate (contains salicylates) Antibiotics: • Metronidazole — Category B after first trimester, can be used if benefits outweigh risks • AVOID fluoroquinolones — carti
nodes.recommendation: Aggressive rehydration. Loperamide is safest antimotility. Metronidazole (Cat B) after first trimester if needed. Avoid fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX.

nodes.title: Pediatric Diarrhea
nodes.summary: Pediatric: oral rehydration is cornerstone — ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg facilitates oral rehydration success
nodes.body: Key differences from adults: • Rotavirus is the most common cause in children • ORS is preferred over IV — evidence-based and WHO-endorsed. Use commercial ORS (Pedialyte), NOT sports drinks or plain water • No antimotility agents — not recommended in children with acute gastroenteritis • No routine antiemetics in children with acute gastroenteritis, except: Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg IV/ODT (max 4 mg)
nodes.recommendation: ORS rehydration. No antimotility agents. Ondansetron to facilitate oral intake in vomiting children. Admit if severe dehydration or suspected HUS.

nodes.title: Diarrhea in the Elderly
nodes.summary: Diarrhea in the Elderly — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Higher risk of serious etiologies: • Ischemic colitis — consider in any elderly patient with diarrhea + abdominal pain • C. difficile — more common and more lethal in the elderly • Diverticulitis — can present with diarrhea • Colonic malignancy — occult in presentation • E. coli O157:H7 — more common in elderly Dehydration risks: age-related disordered thirst mechanism, medications (diuretics), di
nodes.recommendation: Higher suspicion for serious etiologies. Lower threshold for CT, admission, and surgical consult. Careful rehydration in those with cardiac/renal disease.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if tolerating ORT, no dehydration, reliable follow-up; admit if severe dehydration or bloody + toxic
nodes.body: Diarrhea Discharge Instructions Discharge if: • Hemodynamically stable • Benign abdominal examination • Tolerating oral fluids without vomiting • Adequate urine output • Low risk for complications • Reliable follow-up and understanding of return precautions Admit or observe if: • Failed ED rehydration or unable to tolerate oral fluids • Severe or persistent dehydration • Diagnostic dilemma (atypic
nodes.recommendation: Discharge stable patients who tolerate oral fluids with clear return precautions. Admit those failing ED treatment, immunocompromised, or with diagnostic uncertainty.

nodes.title: DIC — Recognition
nodes.summary: DIC is always secondary — find and treat the trigger; bleeding vs thrombotic phenotype determines therapy
nodes.body: DIC Steps Summary Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is an acquired syndrome of systemic intravascular coagulation activation that consumes platelets and clotting factors, simultaneously causing microvascular thrombosis and bleeding. [1][2] Always secondary — DIC is never a primary diagnosis. Find and treat the underlying trigger. [1][3] Mortality: 31-86% depending on etiology and severi

nodes.title: When to Suspect DIC
nodes.summary: Bleeding from multiple sites + microvascular thrombosis + known trigger = suspect DIC; send CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, smear
nodes.body: Suspect DIC in any critically ill patient with new coagulopathy and a known trigger. [1][2] Clinical clues: [1][2][3] • Bleeding from multiple uncontrolled sites (IV, line, mucosa, surgical wound) • Petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses without trauma • Microvascular thrombosis — purpura fulminans, digital ischemia, organ dysfunction (AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy) • Bleeding + thrombosis simultaneously is p

nodes.title: Etiology Quick-Jump
nodes.summary: Use toolbar Etiology Quick-Jump to navigate directly to sepsis, malignancy, obstetric, or trauma pathways
nodes.body: DIC Etiology Quick-Jump Use the toolbar overlay to jump directly to the etiology-specific pathway: • Sepsis-induced DIC → most common; SIC scoring useful • Malignancy-associated DIC → includes APL and solid tumor (Trousseau) • Obstetric DIC → placental abruption, Amniotic Fluid Embolism, retained products, severe preeclampsia/HELLP • Trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC) → overlaps with but distinct f

nodes.title: Overt vs Non-Overt DIC
nodes.summary: Overt DIC = decompensated with bleeding/thrombosis; non-overt = compensated trends — both need trigger control, only overt needs hemostatic resuscitation
nodes.body: Overt DIC = decompensated; consumption has outstripped synthesis. [4][5] • Falling platelets (often <100) • Prolonged PT/PTT • Falling fibrinogen • High D-dimer / FDPs • Clinically bleeding or thrombosing Non-overt (pre-DIC, "stressed") = compensated; abnormal trends without crossing thresholds. [4][5] • Mild thrombocytopenia or downward trend • Borderline coagulation studies • Elevated D-dimer •

nodes.title: DIC Mimics — Differential
nodes.summary: DDx: liver failure (FVIII low), vit K deficiency (PT only), HIT (stop heparin), TTP (normal coags), primary fibrinolysis (normal plt), MTP dilution
nodes.body: Conditions that mimic DIC but require different management: [2][6] Severe liver failure: • Prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia • Distinguishing: Factor VIII normal/elevated in DIC (acute phase), low in liver failure • D-dimer often modestly elevated in both Vitamin K deficiency / warfarin: • Prolonged PT > PTT, normal fibrinogen, normal platelets • Reverses with vitamin K / 4F-PCC H

nodes.title: Core Diagnostic Labs
nodes.summary: Plt + PT + fibrinogen + D-dimer + smear; repeat q6-12h — trends matter more than single values; obstetric fibrinogen threshold is <2 g/L
nodes.body: No single test is diagnostic — DIC is a clinical + lab gestalt. [1][2][4] Initial panel: [1][2] | Lab | Typical Pattern in Overt DIC | |-----|------------------------------| | Platelets | <100 or rapid decline | | PT / INR | Prolonged (often >1.5× ULN) | | aPTT | Prolonged | | Fibrinogen | <2 g/L (< 1.5 in non-pregnant; <2 g/L in obstetric) | | D-dimer / FDPs | Markedly elevated (often >5× ULN) |

nodes.title: ISTH Overt DIC Score
nodes.summary: ISTH ≥5 = overt DIC; sens 91% / spec 97%; less sensitive in early sepsis-DIC than JAAM
nodes.body: ISTH DIC Calculator ISTH 2001 criteria (validated and updated 2025): [4][5] | Parameter | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | |-----------|---|---|---|---| | Platelets (×10⁹/L) | >100 | 50-100 | <50 | — | | Fibrin marker (D-dimer/FDP) | No rise | — | Moderate | Strong | | PT prolongation | <3 s | 3-6 s | >6 s | — | | Fibrinogen (g/L) | ≥1 | <1 | — | — | Interpretation: [5] • ≥5 = compatible with overt DIC; repeat dai

nodes.title: JAAM DIC Score
nodes.summary: JAAM ≥4 = sepsis-DIC; more sensitive than ISTH in early sepsis-DIC; SIRS + platelets + PT ratio + FDP
