nodes.title: SIC (Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy) Score
nodes.summary: SIC ≥4 (with plt+INR ≥3) = sepsis-induced coagulopathy → predicts progression to overt DIC; candidate for anticoag trials
nodes.body: SIC Calculator Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy (SIC) score — Iba 2017: [8] | Parameter | 0 | 1 | 2 | |-----------|---|---|---| | Platelets (×10⁹/L) | ≥150 | 100-150 | <100 | | INR | ≤1.2 | 1.2-1.4 | >1.4 | | Total SOFA (resp + CV + hep + renal, max 12) | 0 | 1 | ≥2 | Interpretation: [8] • ≥4 (with platelet + INR subscore ≥3) = SIC • Identifies septic patients at risk for progression to overt DIC • Can

nodes.title: Serial Monitoring & Trends
nodes.summary: Monitor q4-6h while resuscitating; trend matters more than absolute value; fibrinogen is last to normalize
nodes.body: ISTH 2025: Trends in scores predict outcome better than single snapshots. [4] Recommended monitoring schedule: [2][4] | Phase | Frequency | |-------|-----------| | Resuscitation / active bleeding | CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen q4-6h | | Stabilization | q12h | | Recovery | q24h | Concerning trends: [4] • Platelet drop >30% in 24 hours • Rising D-dimer despite trigger control • Falling fibrinogen below a

nodes.title: Non-Overt (Compensated) DIC
nodes.summary: Non-overt DIC = treat trigger, monitor q12-24h, do NOT preemptively transfuse — most resolve with source control alone
nodes.body: Non-overt DIC is a window for upstream intervention. [4][6] Recognition: [4][5] • ISTH score 1-4 (not yet ≥5) • Platelets trending down but >100 • Coags borderline • D-dimer elevated • Clinically subtle — the patient looks "off" with abnormal labs but no overt bleeding/thrombosis Management priorities: [2][4][6] • Aggressive trigger control — antibiotics in sepsis, source control, definitive obste

nodes.title: Sepsis-Induced DIC
nodes.summary: Sepsis-DIC = source control + abx in 1h, goal-directed resus, SIC scoring, hemostatic support only if bleeding; anticoag controversial
nodes.body: Most common DIC etiology — both gram-negative and gram-positive. [1][3] Pathophysiology: [3][8] • Endotoxin/PAMP activation of tissue factor on monocytes/endothelium • Cytokine storm (TNF-α, IL-6) drives systemic coagulation activation • Endothelial glycocalyx disruption Phenotype: Predominantly thrombotic / microvascular, with bleeding only late in decompensation. [3] Treatment priorities: [3][9]

nodes.title: Malignancy-Associated DIC
nodes.summary: Malignancy-DIC = solid tumor (Trousseau, thrombotic, LMWH) vs hematologic (APL = emergency); treat cancer, LMWH > warfarin
nodes.body: Two phenotypes: [1][2][10] 1. Solid tumor (Trousseau syndrome) — chronic, thrombotic-dominant: • Pancreatic, gastric, lung, breast, ovarian adenocarcinomas • Migratory thrombophlebitis, marantic endocarditis, NBTE • Treatment: LMWH is first line (warfarin often fails) • Definitive therapy: treat the cancer 2. Hematologic — APL is the emergency: • See dedicated APL pathway: dic-apl • Other AML, ALL

nodes.title: APL-DIC — Bleeding Emergency
nodes.summary: APL = bleeding emergency, 5-10% early death from hemorrhage; ATRA 45mg/m²/day immediately, fibrinogen >150-200, NO heparin or TXA
nodes.body: APL-DIC ATRA Emergency Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, AML M3) DIC is a bleeding emergency. [11] 5-10% of APL patients die from hemorrhage in the first days — usually intracranial. [11] Recognition: [11] • Pancytopenia + circulating promyelocytes • Auer rods, faggot cells on smear • Severe bleeding diathesis at presentation • Markedly elevated D-dimer, low fibrinogen • PML-RARα fusion (t(15;17)

nodes.title: Obstetric DIC
nodes.summary: OB DIC = deliver/evacuate, MTP 1:1:1, cryo to keep fibrinogen ≥2 g/L (not <1), TXA 1g IV within 3h, no heparin
nodes.body: Obstetric DIC is rapid-onset, bleeding-dominant, and reverses with definitive obstetric management. [12] Triggers: [12] • Placental abruption (most common) • Amniotic Fluid Embolism — sudden cardiopulmonary collapse + DIC • Retained products of conception / fetal demise • Severe preeclampsia / HELLP • Placenta accreta spectrum / postpartum hemorrhage • Sepsis (chorioamnionitis, septic abortion) Ke

nodes.title: Trauma-Induced Coagulopathy (TIC)
nodes.summary: TIC = TXA 1g <3h, MTP 1:1:1, fibrinogen ≥1.5-2 g/L, calcium, normothermia; permissive hypotension OK except TBI
nodes.body: TIC overlaps with classic DIC but is mechanistically distinct. [13] Pathophysiology: [13] • Tissue injury + shock + acidosis + hypothermia + hemodilution • Activated protein C-mediated hyperfibrinolysis • Platelet dysfunction (not just thrombocytopenia) • Endothelial glycocalyx shedding Recognition: [13] • Major trauma (penetrating, blunt, TBI, burns) • Massive transfusion need • Lactate >4, base

nodes.title: Rare & Special Etiologies
nodes.summary: Rare triggers: pancreatitis, hepatic failure, snake bite (antivenom!), heat stroke, hemangiomas (Kasabach-Merritt), aneurysm, transfusion rxn
nodes.body: Less common DIC triggers requiring specific knowledge: [1][2] Acute pancreatitis: • Severe necrotizing disease activates coagulation via tissue factor and trypsin • Treatment: aggressive supportive care, source control of infected necrosis Fulminant hepatic failure: • Overlapping picture of DIC + liver failure • Factor VIII can help differentiate (normal/high in DIC, low in pure liver failure) • T

nodes.title: Bleeding vs Non-Bleeding Phenotype
nodes.summary: Bleeding-dominant = aggressive replacement to thresholds; thrombotic = minimize transfusion, consider anticoag — single most important decision
nodes.body: Blood Product Order Sheet The single most important branch in DIC management. [2][3][4] Bleeding-dominant DIC — replace what is consumed: [2][14] • Active hemorrhage from any site • Pre-procedure with abnormal coagulation • Obstetric, trauma, APL • Aggressive product transfusion to specific thresholds Thrombotic / non-bleeding-dominant DIC — minimize prophylactic transfusion: [2][4] • Microvascula

nodes.title: Platelet Transfusion
nodes.summary: Plt ≥50 if bleeding, ≥100 if ICH/neuraxial, ≥20 if non-bleeding ICU; 1 apheresis unit raises by 30-50; APL keep ≥30-50
nodes.body: Thresholds: [2][14] | Clinical scenario | Platelet target | |-------------------|-----------------| | Active bleeding | ≥50 × 10⁹/L | | Severe head bleed (ICH/TBI) or neuraxial procedure | ≥100 × 10⁹/L | | Pre-procedure (LP, central line, surgery) | ≥50 × 10⁹/L | | Non-bleeding, ICU | ≥20 × 10⁹/L prophylaxis | | Non-bleeding, stable | ≥10 × 10⁹/L (controversial in DIC) | Dosing: • 1 apheresis unit

nodes.title: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)
nodes.summary: FFP 15 mL/kg if PT/PTT >1.5x ULN AND bleeding; do NOT transfuse for labs alone; volume burden is real
nodes.body: Indication: [2][14] • PT or aPTT >1.5× ULN AND active bleeding (or pre-procedure) Do NOT transfuse FFP for abnormal labs alone in non-bleeding patient. [2] Dosing: [2][14] • 15 mL/kg IV (typically 4 units for 70 kg adult) • Each unit ≈ 250 mL • Recheck PT/PTT 30 minutes post-infusion • Repeat as needed for ongoing bleeding Volume considerations: [14] • Significant volume load — caution in CHF, ARD

nodes.title: Cryoprecipitate / Fibrinogen
nodes.summary: Cryo if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (<2 g/L if obstetric); 10 units or 0.06 u/kg raises by 0.5-1 g/L; fibrinogen concentrate is volume-sparing alternative
nodes.body: Cryoprecipitate is the fibrinogen-replacement product of choice in DIC. [2][12][14] Thresholds (etiology-dependent): [2][12] | Setting | Fibrinogen target | |---------|-------------------| | Non-pregnant DIC with bleeding | ≥1.5 g/L | | Obstetric DIC / PPH | ≥2 g/L (higher because pregnant baseline is 4-6 g/L) | | APL / leukemia DIC | ≥1.5-2 g/L (some experts say 2) | | Massive transfusion | ≥1.5-

nodes.title: 4-Factor PCC in DIC
nodes.summary: 4F-PCC 25-50 u/kg if volume-restricted or VKA reversal — controversial in pure DIC, theoretic thrombosis risk; discuss with heme
nodes.body: Use in DIC is selective and controversial. [2][14] Indications: [14] • Volume-restricted patient with severe coagulopathy and bleeding • Reversal of vitamin K antagonist on top of DIC • When FFP is not feasible (volume overload, time, immediate need) Dosing: [14] • 25-50 units/kg IV (Kcentra, Beriplex, Octaplex) • 25 units/kg if INR 2-4 • 35 units/kg if INR 4-6 • 50 units/kg if INR >6 or major ble

nodes.title: Blood Product Order Reference
nodes.summary: Quick ref: plt 1 apheresis (≥50 bleed), FFP 15 mL/kg (PT >1.5x), cryo 10u (fib <1.5/<2 OB), 4F-PCC 25-50 u/kg; MTP 1:1:1
nodes.body: Blood Product Order Sheet Access the full blood product order sheet via the toolbar overlay or the link above. Quick reference: [2][12][14] | Product | When | Dose | |---------|------|------| | Platelets | Bleeding + plt <50 (or <100 if ICH/neuraxial) | 1 apheresis unit | | FFP | PT/aPTT >1.5× ULN + bleeding | 15 mL/kg | | Cryoprecipitate | Fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (<2 g/L obstetric) + bleeding | 10 un

nodes.title: Heparin in DIC
nodes.summary: Heparin only if thrombotic-dominant + no bleeding; LMWH for Trousseau; AVOID in APL, obstetric bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia
nodes.body: Heparin in DIC is highly selective and never first-line. [4][9][14] Consider heparin (or LMWH) ONLY if: [4][9][14] • Thrombotic-dominant phenotype without active bleeding • Macrovascular thrombosis (DVT, PE, arterial occlusion) • Trousseau syndrome (cancer-associated thrombosis) — LMWH is first-line • Purpura fulminans / extensive microvascular thrombosis AVOID heparin in: [4][11][12] • Bleeding-d

nodes.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
nodes.summary: TXA 1g IV in trauma, PPH, TBI within 3h (CRASH-2/3, WOMAN); avoid in APL, snake bite, active thrombosis, gross hematuria
nodes.body: TXA is selective in DIC — etiology matters. [12][13] Use TXA in: [12][13] • Trauma (TIC) — CRASH-2: 1 g IV bolus + 1 g over 8 hours, given within 3 hours of injury • Postpartum hemorrhage / obstetric DIC — WOMAN trial: 1 g IV within 3 hours • TBI with intracranial hemorrhage — CRASH-3: 1 g IV within 3 hours • Surgical bleeding with hyperfibrinolysis on TEG/ROTEM AVOID TXA in: [11][12] • APL — cont

nodes.title: Antithrombin & Recombinant Thrombomodulin
nodes.summary: AT concentrate and rTM are specialty agents — not US standard; SCARLET (rTM) and KyberSept (AT) negative overall but signals in DIC subgroups
nodes.body: Specialty agents — not standard in US emergency care, but increasingly studied. [4][8][9] Antithrombin (AT) concentrate: [9] • Rationale: AT is consumed in DIC; replacement may restore endogenous anticoagulation • KyberSept trial (sepsis): no overall mortality benefit; subgroup with DIC and no concurrent heparin showed signal • Used in Japan and some European centers; not widely used in US • Dose:

nodes.title: Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Supportive: norepi for septic DIC, lung-protective vent, correct acidosis/Ca/Mg, normothermia; multidisciplinary team
nodes.body: Supportive measures that reduce DIC progression: [2][3] Hemodynamics: [3] • Adequate perfusion improves microcirculation and tissue oxygen delivery • Vasopressor of choice for septic DIC: norepinephrine • Avoid hypoperfusion (worsens microvascular thrombosis) Oxygenation & ventilation: [3] • Optimize oxygen delivery; avoid hypoxia • Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS Acid-base & electrolytes: [13

nodes.title: Reassessment Schedule
nodes.summary: Resuscitation: q4-6h labs; stabilization: q12h; recovery: daily — repeat ISTH each cycle, watch for phenotype switch
nodes.body: DIC is dynamic — repeat scoring is essential. [4] During active resuscitation (first 6-24 hours): [2][4] • CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer every 4-6 hours • Lactate, ABG q4-6h • Clinical bleeding survey q1-2h • ISTH score recomputed each cycle Stabilization phase (24-72 hours): [2][4] • Labs every 12 hours • Score recomputed daily • Reassess phenotype (bleeding ↔ thrombotic transitions can occur)

nodes.title: Defining Resolution
nodes.summary: Resolution: plt >100 & stable, PT/PTT <1.2x, fibrinogen ≥2 g/L, ISTH <5 x48h + trigger controlled; D-dimer lags weeks
nodes.body: No formal universal criteria, but practical signs of resolution: [4] Laboratory resolution: [4] • Platelets >100 × 10⁹/L and stable/rising • PT/aPTT within 1.2× ULN • Fibrinogen ≥2 g/L (≥4 g/L in postpartum recovery) • D-dimer trending down (may stay elevated for days-weeks) • ISTH score <5 sustained ≥48 hours Clinical resolution: [4] • No active bleeding • No new thrombotic events • Trigger contr

nodes.title: Disposition & Consults
nodes.body: Most DIC patients require ICU admission. [2][3] ICU criteria — virtually all DIC: [2] • Active bleeding • Hemodynamic instability • Need for blood product resuscitation • Multi-organ dysfunction • Need for invasive monitoring or vasopressor support • Severe trigger (sepsis, trauma, Amniotic Fluid Embolism, APL) Floor / step-down considerations: [2] • Mild non-overt DIC with controlled trigger • St
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for nearly all DIC patients. Emergent hematology + source-specific consults (OB, oncology, surgery, IR). Transfer to tertiary care if APL, severe trauma, or Amniotic Fluid Embolism.

nodes.title: Difficult Airway — Bougie-First Approach
nodes.summary: Difficult Airway — Bougie-First Approach — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Airway Steps Summary — rapid-reference stepwise pathway. Bougie-first intubation achieves 98% first-pass success vs 87% with stylet in difficult airways (BEAM trial, JAMA 2018). The benefit is strongest in poor laryngoscopic views (CL III–IV): RR 1.60 for first-pass success. Critical context: The BOUGIE trial (JAMA 2021) showed no benefit at sites with low bougie experience (median 10 prior uses)

nodes.summary: Standard RSI — Bougie Available as Rescue — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: RSI Drug Quick Reference Positioning: Ear-to-sternal-notch alignment (NOT just "sniffing position"). External auditory meatus at or above sternal notch. Obese patients need significant ramping. Preoxygenation: 3-5 min NRB or flush-rate O2. Apneic oxygenation with 15 L/min NC during laryngoscopy. Induction (choose one): • Ketamine 1.5-2 mg/kg IV — hemodynamically supportive, preferred in hypotensio

nodes.title: Bougie-First RSI Protocol
nodes.summary: Bougie-First RSI Protocol — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: RSI Drug Quick Reference Predicted difficult airway — plan bougie-first from the start. Positioning: Ear-to-sternal-notch alignment. Face plane parallel to ceiling. Equipment at bedside: • 15 Fr × 60 cm coude-tip bougie (Frova or SunMed) • Video laryngoscope (standard geometry preferred for bougie — C-MAC or standard GlideScope) • ETT: 7.0-7.5 mm (women), 7.5-8.0 mm (men), lubricated • Backup: sec

nodes.title: Awake Intubation — When to Consider
nodes.summary: Awake Intubation — When to Consider — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Awake intubation comprises <2-3% of all ED intubations. Consider when: • Predicted difficult intubation AND difficult mask ventilation • Predicted difficult intubation AND cannot tolerate brief apnea • Predicted difficult intubation AND difficult surgical airway • Known history of failed intubation • Upper airway obstruction with maintained spontaneous ventilation • Severe hemodynamic instability

nodes.title: Bougie Insertion — Step by Step
nodes.summary: Bougie Insertion — Step by Step — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: 1. Laryngoscopy — Obtain best possible view. Identify epiglottis or cords. 2. Insert bougie — Coude tip anterior, advance along midline under epiglottis into trachea. • CL III view: advance bougie behind epiglottis tip (blind pass beneath) 3. Confirm tracheal placement: • Tracheal clicks — felt at ~15-25 cm (unreliable — do not rely solely) • Hold-up sign — bougie meets resistance at ~30-35 cm (ca

nodes.title: Key Adjuncts & Common Errors
nodes.summary: Key Adjuncts & Common Errors — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Adjunct maneuvers: • Jaw thrust by assistant — lifts mandible, improves view • External Laryngeal Manipulation (ELM): Operator-directed movement of larynx to optimize view (superior to BURP) • BURP (Backward, Upward, Rightward Pressure): assistant applies to thyroid cartilage Common errors (EMCrit 388 — Weingart/Barnicle/Driver): • ❌ Preloading bougie through ETT • ❌ Not maintaining coude tip ante

nodes.title: ETT Passed Successfully?
nodes.summary: ETT Passed Successfully? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Was the endotracheal tube successfully advanced into the trachea? If uncertain, proceed to confirmation (Module 4) — waveform capnography is the gold standard.

nodes.title: Attempt Count — Escalation Decision
nodes.summary: Attempt Count — Escalation Decision — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Limit intubation attempts. Each attempt causes airway trauma, edema, and bleeding — making subsequent attempts harder. Between attempts: • Mask ventilate / apneic oxygenation • Reposition (optimize ear-to-sternal-notch) • Change device (DL → VL, or different blade) • Change operator (most experienced available) • Use bougie if not already attempted • Suction aggressively

nodes.title: Tube Confirmation — Algorithm
nodes.summary: Tube Confirmation — Algorithm — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Confirmation hierarchy (most to least reliable): 1. Waveform Capnography (GOLD STANDARD) • Sensitivity: 100% (non-arrest), 96.8% (cardiac arrest) • Specificity: 99-100% • Look for sustained 4-phase waveform × 5-6 breaths • Brief CO₂ from esophageal placement tapers after 2-3 breaths — must be sustained • False negatives: cardiac arrest (low pulmonary blood flow), massive PE • Mandatory per AHA/ACE

nodes.title: Sustained ETCO₂ Waveform?
nodes.summary: Sustained ETCO₂ Waveform? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Connect waveform capnography immediately after intubation. Look for sustained 4-phase waveform over at least 5-6 ventilations. If ANY doubt about tube placement — remove the tube.

nodes.title: Tube Confirmed — Post-Intubation Management
nodes.summary: Tube Confirmed — Post-Intubation Management — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Tube placement confirmed by waveform capnography. Immediate post-intubation: • Secure tube — commercial holder or tape • Depth check: 21 cm at teeth (women), 23 cm at teeth (men) • CXR — confirm position, rule out right mainstem, pneumothorax • Continuous waveform capnography monitoring Ventilator settings (initial): • Mode: AC/VC or AC/PC • TV: 6-8 mL/kg IBW (lung-protective) • RR: 14-18 • FiO₂:
nodes.recommendation: Tube confirmed. Secure, verify depth, obtain CXR, initiate sedation and lung-protective ventilation.

nodes.title: No ETCO₂ — Esophageal Intubation
nodes.summary: No ETCO₂ — Esophageal Intubation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: No sustained ETCO₂ waveform = esophageal placement until proven otherwise. Immediate actions: 1. Remove the tube — do not delay 2. Mask ventilate with BVM — two-person technique preferred 3. Apneic oxygenation — 15 L/min NC during prep for next attempt 4. Reassess: How many attempts? Can you oxygenate? If this was attempt #3 or patient is desaturating → proceed to Failed Airway Rescue.

nodes.title: Failed Airway — Vortex Approach
nodes.summary: Failed Airway — Vortex Approach — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Declare: "This is a failed airway." Communicate clearly to entire team. The Vortex Approach — three upper airway "lifelines": 1. Face mask (BVM) 2. Supraglottic airway (SGA / LMA) 3. Endotracheal tube (ETT) Green Zone = adequate oxygenation by ANY lifeline. Time to think, plan, call for help. CICO (Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate) = ALL three lifelines failed after best effort. → Immediate front-o

nodes.title: Can You Oxygenate?
nodes.summary: Can You Oxygenate? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Can the patient be oxygenated by ANY method — BVM, SGA, or apneic oxygenation? If SpO₂ is falling and you cannot ventilate by any method — this is CICO. Proceed immediately to surgical airway.

nodes.title: CI/CO — Green Zone Rescue
nodes.summary: CI/CO — Green Zone Rescue — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: You can oxygenate — you have time. Use it wisely. SGA Rescue: • i-gel preferred (no cuff inflation needed, faster placement) • LMA Supreme/ProSeal as alternative • Sizing: size 3 (30-60 kg), size 4 (50-90 kg), size 5 (>90 kg) • Success rate: >95% for ventilation rescue after failed intubation While oxygenating via SGA: • Call for help — anesthesiology, ENT • Consider awake technique if patient can

nodes.title: SGA Ventilation Successful?
nodes.summary: SGA Ventilation Successful? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Is the supraglottic airway providing adequate oxygenation and ventilation? Check: chest rise, ETCO₂ waveform through SGA, SpO₂ trend.

nodes.title: SGA Bridge — Plan Definitive Airway
nodes.summary: SGA Bridge — Plan Definitive Airway — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: SGA is maintaining oxygenation — stable for now. Next steps: • Maintain SGA and continuous monitoring • Consult anesthesiology and/or ENT urgently • Consider intubation through SGA via fiberoptic scope • If patient can be awakened — consider awake intubation • Prepare surgical airway kit at bedside • Document failed airway — notify all future providers Disposition: ICU admission with airway plan d
nodes.recommendation: SGA maintaining oxygenation. Consult anesthesiology/ENT for definitive airway plan. ICU admission.

nodes.title: CICO — Emergency Cricothyrotomy
nodes.summary: CICO — Emergency Cricothyrotomy — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Scalpel-Finger-Bougie Cric Steps Announce: "Can't intubate, can't oxygenate — performing cricothyrotomy." NAP4 Audit (Cook 2011): • Needle cricothyrotomy: 60% failure rate • Surgical cricothyrotomy: 100% success rate • DAS 2015 explicitly recommends scalpel-bougie technique over needle/cannula Equipment: | Item | Specification | |------|---------------| | Scalpel | #10 blade (broad — matches trach

nodes.title: Cricothyroid Membrane — Identification
nodes.summary: Cricothyroid Membrane — Identification — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Cricothyroid Membrane (CTM): • Located between thyroid cartilage (superior) and cricoid cartilage (inferior) • Dimensions: 9-19 mm horizontal × 9-20 mm vertical in adults Laryngeal Handshake (palpation technique): 1. Non-dominant hand stabilizes larynx 2. Thumb and 3rd finger grasp lateral thyroid cartilage 3. Index finger palpates downward to find CTM depression 4. Brace wrist against sternum for

nodes.title: Scalpel-Finger-Bougie Technique
nodes.summary: Scalpel-Finger-Bougie Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Step 1: Stabilize larynx with non-dominant hand (laryngeal handshake) Step 2: Vertical skin incision (~4 cm) over CTM — exposes landmarks even if anatomy is obscured. If anatomy is clear, single horizontal stab may suffice. Step 3: Palpate CTM with finger through incision — confirm depression between thyroid and cricoid Step 4: Horizontal stab through CTM (lower half to avoid superior vessels and

nodes.title: ETCO₂ Confirmed After Cric?
nodes.summary: ETCO₂ Confirmed After Cric? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Connect waveform capnography immediately. Look for sustained 4-phase waveform. If no ETCO₂: Recheck tube position — may need to advance further or re-examine incision site. The bougie may have tracked into a false passage.

nodes.title: Post-Cricothyrotomy Management
nodes.summary: Post-Cricothyrotomy Management — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Surgical airway confirmed by waveform capnography. Immediate: • Secure tube with ties (not tape — blood on skin prevents adhesion) • CXR — confirm position, rule out pneumothorax • Continuous waveform capnography monitoring • Monitor for: subcutaneous emphysema, bleeding, posterior wall perforation ICU management: • Convert to formal tracheostomy within 24-72 hours — consult ENT/surgery • Document
nodes.recommendation: Surgical airway successful. Secure with ties, CXR, continuous capnography. Consult ENT for conversion to tracheostomy within 24-72h. ICU admission.

nodes.title: Difficult Vascular Access: US-PIV + IO
nodes.summary: Escalate from failed blind IV to US-PIV or IO based on urgency.
nodes.body: Use this when peripheral access is delayed, repeated blind attempts are failing, or immediate resuscitation access is needed. Open first: - Access Steps - US-PIV Technique - IO Sites - Confirm / Use - Stop / Complications

nodes.title: How Urgent Is Access?
nodes.summary: Peri-arrest patients need IO; stable patients can get a controlled US-PIV attempt.
nodes.body: Access choice depends on whether the patient can tolerate more attempts.

nodes.title: US-PIV: Choose The Vessel
nodes.summary: Pick a straight, compressible, adequately sized vein that matches catheter length.
nodes.body: Scan before puncture. Target: - Compressible vein - Straight segment - Not directly adjacent to artery/nerve - Depth ideally within catheter length reserve - Diameter large enough for catheter and flow need Avoid tiny/deep/tortuous veins where most of the catheter will not sit inside the vessel.

nodes.title: US-PIV: Technique
nodes.summary: Dynamic needle tip tracking and catheter length in vein are the key steps.
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Sterile gel/cover per local practice. 2. Optimize probe, depth, gain, and needle visualization. 3. Use long-axis or short-axis with dynamic needle tip tracking. 4. Enter shallow enough to keep the catheter in vessel. 5. Confirm wire/catheter tip in lumen before flushing. 6. Secure well; deep US-PIVs fail from dislodgement. Video reference: US-guided long-axis antecubital IV cannulati

nodes.title: Did US-PIV Work?
nodes.summary: Failed US-PIV should not delay IO in unstable patients.
nodes.body: Confirm before relying on the line for resuscitation.

nodes.title: IO Access: Site Selection
nodes.summary: Choose tibial, humeral, or pediatric distal femur site and avoid fractured/infected bones.
nodes.body: Common ED sites: - Proximal tibia - Distal tibia - Proximal humerus - Distal femur in children when appropriate Avoid fractured bone, infected/burned insertion site, prior IO attempt in same bone, prosthetic limb/joint at target site, or inability to identify landmarks.

nodes.title: IO Insertion / First Use
nodes.summary: Correct IO use requires secure placement, forceful flush, and pressure-assisted infusion.
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Identify landmarks and stabilize limb. 2. Prep skin; use device per manufacturer/local protocol. 3. Confirm loss of resistance and stable needle hub. 4. Aspirate marrow if possible, but absence does not exclude correct placement. 5. Flush forcefully to open marrow space. 6. Use pressure bag/pump for flow. 7. For awake patients, consider Lidocaine before flush/infusion per local proto

nodes.title: Confirm / Use The Line
nodes.summary: Use only after confirming flush, stability, and no extravasation.
nodes.body: Confirm usability: - Flushes without extravasation - No rapidly increasing swelling or pain - Stable catheter/needle - Expected clinical response to medication/fluids IO and US-PIV are bridges. Replace with durable peripheral/central access when resuscitation stabilizes.

nodes.title: Any Access Complication?
nodes.summary: Monitor for extravasation, compartment syndrome, dislodgement, and inadequate flow.
nodes.body: Access complications become limb-threatening when missed during high-pressure infusion.

nodes.title: Access Achieved
nodes.summary: Secure, reassess, document, and replace with durable access when stable.
nodes.body: Secure the line, label access type/site/time, reassess frequently, and transition to durable IV/central access when feasible. Document number of attempts, ultrasound use, IO site, confirmation, complications, and patient response.
nodes.recommendation: Use the line for urgent therapy, but continue planning durable access.

nodes.title: Escalate Access
nodes.summary: Escalate to central/specialist/alternate route when access still fails.
nodes.body: Escalate when US-PIV/IO fails or does not meet resuscitation needs. Options: central venous catheter, external jugular access, surgical/trauma access pathway, vascular access team, or alternate medication route when clinically acceptable.
nodes.recommendation: Do not let access attempts delay airway, hemorrhage control, seizure control, or shock treatment.

nodes.title: Stop / Complication
nodes.summary: Stop infusion and reassess limb when extravasation or compartment syndrome is possible.
nodes.body: Stop infusion through suspected infiltrated IV or IO immediately. Actions: - Disconnect infusion - Leave catheter/needle in place briefly if antidote or aspiration is needed - Assess distal pulses, motor/sensory status, compartment firmness - Elevate limb when appropriate - Call surgery/orthopedics for compartment concern - Re-site access elsewhere
nodes.recommendation: Treat suspected IO/IV extravasation as a high-risk access complication until proven otherwise.

nodes.title: Stable Difficult Access
nodes.summary: Stable patients benefit from fewer attempts and better setup.
nodes.body: Limit blind attempts and improve the next attempt: ultrasound, warmed extremity, lower probe pressure, longer catheter, experienced operator, or vascular access team. If therapy is nonurgent, choose oral/IM/subcutaneous route when safe.
nodes.recommendation: Use the least harmful route that reliably delivers the needed therapy.

nodes.title: Digoxin Toxicity — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Digoxin toxicity: narrow therapeutic index — classic triad: GI symptoms, visual changes, arrhythmias
nodes.body: Digoxin Toxicity Steps Summary — quick reference. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index — toxicity can occur at therapeutic levels, especially in chronic use with predisposing factors [1][2]. Classic presentation triad: • GI: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia (often earliest symptoms) • Visual: Yellow-green halos (xanthopsia), blurred vision, photophobia • CNS: Confusion, fatigue, weakness, delirium Mec

nodes.title: Acute Digoxin Toxicity
nodes.summary: Acute Digoxin Toxicity — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Acute ingestion — intentional overdose, suicidal, or accidental (pediatric) [2][4]. Acute vs Chronic Comparison Characteristics: • High digoxin level (often >10 ng/mL in significant ingestions) • Normal or LOW potassium initially — Na+/K+-ATPase still functional extracardially • Minimal symptoms initially — may feel fine despite lethal levels • Hyperkalemia = DANGER — indicates Na+/K+-ATPase poiso

nodes.title: Chronic Digoxin Toxicity
nodes.summary: Chronic Digoxin Toxicity — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Chronic toxicity — insidious onset in patients on maintenance therapy [2][4]. Acute vs Chronic Comparison Risk factors: • Renal insufficiency (primary route of elimination) • Advanced age (decreased renal function, decreased Vd) • Hypokalemia (sensitizes myocardium to digoxin) • Hypomagnesemia • Hypercalcemia • Hypothyroidism (decreased clearance) • Drug interactions — amiodarone, verapamil, quini

nodes.title: Unknown or Mixed Presentation
nodes.summary: Unknown or Mixed Presentation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: When history is unclear: Treat as chronic toxicity if: • Patient is on maintenance digoxin therapy • Elderly with renal insufficiency • Any predisposing factors present Treat as acute toxicity if: • Evidence of intentional ingestion • Pediatric accidental ingestion • Very high digoxin level (>10 ng/mL) in previously non-digitalized patient General approach: • Labs: digoxin level, K+, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, B

nodes.title: ECG Assessment
nodes.summary: Classic ECG: scooped ST depression (Salvador Dali mustache) — ANY arrhythmia possible, bidirectional VT pathognomonic
nodes.body: ECG is critical — but remember: "dig can do anything" [1][2]. ECG Findings Reference Digoxin EFFECT (therapeutic) vs TOXICITY: • Effect: "Scooped" ST depression (Salvador Dali mustache), shortened QT — NOT toxicity • Toxicity: Arrhythmias — bradycardias AND tachycardias Classic arrhythmias of toxicity: • PAT with block — paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with AV block (PATHOGNOMONIC) [1][2] • Bidirect

nodes.title: Bradyarrhythmias in Digoxin Toxicity
nodes.summary: Bradyarrhythmias in Digoxin Toxicity — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Bradyarrhythmias — result from enhanced vagal tone and AV nodal suppression [2]. Arrhythmia Management Guide Common bradyarrhythmias: • Sinus bradycardia • Junctional bradycardia • 1st degree AV block (prolonged PR) • 2nd degree AV block — Mobitz I (Wenckebach) or Mobitz II • 3rd degree (complete) AV block Initial management: • Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV — temporizing measure, may not work in severe tox

nodes.title: Tachyarrhythmias in Digoxin Toxicity
nodes.summary: Tachyarrhythmias in Digoxin Toxicity — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Tachyarrhythmias — result from enhanced automaticity due to intracellular calcium overload [2]. Arrhythmia Management Guide Classic tachyarrhythmias: • PAT with block — pathognomonic. Atrial rate 150-250 with variable AV block. • Bidirectional VT — alternating RBBB/LBBB morphology. Highly specific. • Accelerated junctional rhythm — "regularized" AF in a dig patient • Ventricular ectopy — frequent

nodes.title: Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: Risk Stratification — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Key prognostic factors: Potassium level: • Hyperkalemia (K+ >5.5) = poor prognosis in both acute and chronic [3][4] • In acute: indicates severe Na+/K+-ATPase poisoning • In chronic: marker of end-organ toxicity • Hypokalemia sensitizes to digoxin — correct cautiously Digoxin level interpretation: • >2 ng/mL — concerning in chronic therapy • >10 ng/mL — severe acute ingestion • Chronic toxicity ca

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia in Digoxin Toxicity
nodes.summary: Hyperkalemia in Digoxin Toxicity — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: ⚠️ Hyperkalemia (K+ >5.5) in digoxin toxicity is a CRITICAL finding [3][4]. In acute toxicity: Indicates severe Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition — potassium cannot enter cells. Pre-DigiFab mortality with K+ >5.5 was >50%. DigiFab has dramatically improved survival [3]. Management: DO give: • DigiFab — definitive treatment, rapidly lowers K+ by restoring pump function • Sodium bicarbonate — shifts K+ intra

nodes.title: Treatment Overview
nodes.summary: Treatment Overview — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: General treatment approach: 1. GI Decontamination: • Activated Charcoal 1 g/kg (max 50g) if within 1-2 hours [2] • Digoxin has enterohepatic circulation — multidose charcoal may be beneficial in severe cases 2. Correct electrolyte abnormalities: • Hypokalemia — correct CAUTIOUSLY. Do not overshoot to normokalemia — risk of rebound hyperkalemia as digoxin redistributes [2] • Hypomagnesemia — correc

nodes.title: Supportive Care — Mild Toxicity
nodes.summary: Avoid all Class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics — no procainamide; activated charcoal within 1-2h if acute ingestion
nodes.body: For mild digoxin toxicity: GI decontamination: • Activated Charcoal 1 g/kg (max 50g) if within 1-2 hours of ingestion [2] Electrolyte management: • Correct hypokalemia cautiously — target low-normal range (3.5-4.0 mEq/L). Overcorrection can cause hyperkalemia as digoxin redistributes [2] • Correct hypomagnesemia — Mg²⁺ 2g IV, helps stabilize myocardium • Monitor calcium — hypercalcemia potentiates

nodes.title: Treatments to Avoid
nodes.summary: Treatments to Avoid — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: 🚫 Avoid or use with extreme caution: Cardioversion: • Can precipitate refractory ventricular fibrillation in digitalis-toxic heart [2] • If absolutely necessary (hemodynamically unstable VT/VF), use lowest effective energy • Have DigiFab ready before attempting Calcium (the "stone heart" myth): • Traditional teaching: avoid due to a "stone heart" (irreversible myocardial contraction). This rests

nodes.title: DigiFab — Indications
nodes.summary: DigiFab — Indications — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: DigiFab Dosing Calculator Indications for DigiFab (Digoxin Immune Fab): [2][3] Life-threatening criteria: • Life-threatening arrhythmia (VT, VF, high-grade AV block, symptomatic bradycardia unresponsive to atropine) • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock) • K+ >5.5 mEq/L (in setting of digoxin toxicity) Level-based criteria: • Acute ingestion: digoxin level >10 ng/mL [3] • Chronic toxicity:

nodes.title: DigiFab Dosing
nodes.body: Digoxin Immune Fab (DigiFab, Digibind) Dosing depends on known information: 1. If AMOUNT INGESTED is known (acute): Vials = (mg ingested x 0.8) / 0.5 • The 0.8 accounts for ~80% bioavailability • Each vial binds ~0.5 mg digoxin 2. If SERUM LEVEL is known: Vials = (level ng/mL x weight kg) / 100 3. EMPIRIC dosing (most common in practice): • Acute poisoning: 10-20 vials • Chronic toxicity: 3-6 vial

nodes.title: DigiFab Dosing — Known Ingestion
nodes.summary: DigiFab Dosing — Known Ingestion — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Formula: Vials = (mg ingested x 0.8) / 0.5 [3] Example: Patient ingested forty 0.25 mg tablets = 10 mg total Vials = (10 x 0.8) / 0.5 = 16 vials Administration: • Reconstitute each vial with 4 mL sterile water • Dilute in 100-250 mL NS • Infuse IV over 30 minutes • In cardiac arrest: may give as IV push [3] Post-DigiFab: • Response in 30-60 minutes (may take up to 4 hours) • May need repeat dosing

nodes.title: DigiFab Dosing — Known Serum Level
nodes.summary: DigiFab Dosing — Known Serum Level — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Formula: Vials = (level ng/mL x weight kg) / 100 [3] Example: 70 kg patient with level of 8 ng/mL Vials = (8 x 70) / 100 = 5.6 → 6 vials Important notes: • Level must be at steady state (≥6 hours post-ingestion) for accuracy • In acute ingestion, level may still be rising — use clinical judgment • In chronic toxicity, lower levels may cause significant toxicity Administration: • Reconstitute each

nodes.title: DigiFab Dosing — Empiric
nodes.summary: DigiFab Dosing — Empiric — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Empiric dosing when amount and level unknown: [3] Acute poisoning: • 10-20 vials initially • Use higher end (20 vials) for cardiac arrest or massive ingestion Chronic toxicity: • 3-6 vials initially • Start low — chronic patients often need less • Redose in 1-2 hours if inadequate response Rationale for lower chronic dosing: • Smaller total body load in chronic toxicity • Risk of rapid reversal ca

nodes.title: Post-DigiFab Management
nodes.summary: Post-DigiFab Management — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: After DigiFab administration: Response timeline: • Initial response: 30-60 minutes • Full effect: may take up to 4 hours • Duration: 15-20 hour half-life (renal elimination) [3] Repeat dosing: • May repeat in 1-2 hours if inadequate clinical response • Consider if: persistent arrhythmia, persistent hyperkalemia, recurrent symptoms Digoxin levels post-Fab: • MEANINGLESS — standard assays measure TO

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Disposition depends on severity: All patients need: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Serial potassium and renal function • ECG with any clinical change Dialysis is NOT effective — digoxin has a large volume of distribution (5-7 L/kg). Hemodialysis does not significantly remove digoxin. Fab fragments are renally cleared but not enhanced by dialysis [2]. Psychiatric evaluation is mandatory for all

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU Admission — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: • Any life-threatening arrhythmia (current or resolved) • DigiFab administered • Hemodynamic instability • K+ >5.5 mEq/L • High digoxin level (>10 acute, >6 chronic with symptoms) • Altered mental status • Requiring vasopressor support or pacing ICU monitoring: • Continuous telemetry — minimum 24 hours after last arrhythmia • Serial K+, Mg²⁺, BMP q6h initially • Serial ECGs
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous cardiac monitoring for minimum 24 hours. Serial electrolytes. Watch for rebinding toxicity in massive ingestions.

nodes.title: Telemetry / Monitored Bed
nodes.summary: Telemetry / Monitored Bed — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Telemetry admission criteria: • Mild symptoms (GI, visual changes) without significant arrhythmia • Stable vital signs • Normal or near-normal potassium • Elevated level but no end-organ toxicity Monitoring: • Continuous telemetry — minimum 12-24 hours • Serial K+, Mg²⁺, BMP q6-12h • Repeat ECG q6h and with any clinical change • Hold digoxin and other AV nodal blocking agents Escalation triggers →
nodes.recommendation: Telemetry admission with continuous monitoring for 12-24 hours. Serial electrolytes. Hold digoxin. Escalate to ICU for any arrhythmia or hemodynamic change.

nodes.title: Diplopia: Initial Approach
nodes.summary: First determine monocular vs binocular — cover each eye; monocular = ocular cause, binocular = neurological
nodes.body: Diplopia represents ~50,000 US ED visits annually. THE FIRST QUESTION: "Does the double vision go away when you cover EITHER eye?" | Type | Test Result | Significance | |------|-------------|-------------| | Monocular | Persists with one eye covered | Ocular pathology - generally non-emergent | | Binocular | Resolves when either eye covered | Ocular misalignment - needs neuro workup | Monocular Di

nodes.title: Diplopia Type
nodes.summary: Diplopia Type — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Does the double vision resolve when EITHER eye is covered? *Basis: the cover-one-eye discriminator between monocular and binocular diplopia is the standard first step in the cited reviews (PMID 16732215, 28722934).* [1][2][4]

nodes.title: Monocular Diplopia
nodes.summary: Monocular diplopia persists with one eye covered — refractive error, cataract, corneal issue; rarely emergent
nodes.body: Monocular diplopia = ocular pathology, NOT neurologic emergency. Common Causes: • Refractive error - improves with pinhole testing • Dry eye - improves with lubricating drops • Cataract - ghosting, halos • Corneal irregularity - keratoconus, scarring • Lens subluxation - trauma, Marfan syndrome • Macular pathology - distortion, metamorphopsia Bedside Test: • Pinhole test - if diplopia resolves = r

nodes.title: Diplopia Direction
nodes.summary: Diplopia Direction — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: What direction is the diplopia? Ask: "Are the two images side-by-side (horizontal) or stacked (vertical)?" *Basis: horizontal versus vertical localization follows the ocular motor palsy distribution in Rush and Younge 1981 (PMID 7458744) and the diplopia review (PMID 28722934).* [3][4]

nodes.title: Horizontal Diplopia
nodes.summary: Horizontal Diplopia — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Horizontal diplopia suggests CN III or CN VI involvement. Quick Localization: | Finding | Likely Nerve | |---------|-------------| | Cannot look OUTWARD (abduct) | CN VI | | Cannot look INWARD (adduct) + ptosis | CN III | | Cannot look INWARD only | INO (MLF lesion) | CN VI (Abducens): • Esotropia (eye turned in) • Face turn toward affected side • Diplopia worse at distance CN III (Oculomotor): •

nodes.summary: Vertical Diplopia — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Vertical diplopia suggests CN III or CN IV involvement. Quick Localization: | Finding | Likely Nerve | |---------|-------------| | Eye down and out + ptosis | CN III | | Head tilt, hypertropia worse with adduction | CN IV | | Thyroid history, proptosis | Thyroid eye disease | CN IV (Trochlear): • Superior oblique palsy • Compensatory head tilt to opposite shoulder • Hypertropia worse with: - Adduc

nodes.title: Diplopia Examination
nodes.summary: Diplopia Examination — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Systematic Diplopia Exam: 1. Pupil Assessment: • Size, reactivity, APD • Dilated pupil + CN III findings = EMERGENT 2. Extraocular Movements (H-pattern): • Test each direction of gaze • Note which direction worsens diplopia • Look for nystagmus 3. Eyelid Examination: • Ptosis (CN III, MG, Horner) • Lid lag (thyroid) • Fatigable ptosis (MG) 4. Cover-Uncover Test: • Patient fixates on target • Cover

nodes.title: Identify Affected Nerve
nodes.summary: Identify Affected Nerve — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Based on examination, which pattern fits best? *Basis: pattern-to-nerve assignment follows the localization scheme in Rush and Younge 1981 (PMID 7458744) and the diplopia review (PMID 28722934).* [3][4]

nodes.title: CN III Palsy Overview
nodes.summary: CN III Palsy Overview — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: CN III (Oculomotor) controls most eye movement + pupil. CN III Functions: • Superior rectus (upgaze) • Inferior rectus (downgaze) • Medial rectus (adduction) • Inferior oblique (upgaze in adduction) • Levator palpebrae (lid elevation) • Pupillary constriction Complete CN III Palsy: • "Down and out" eye position • Ptosis (complete) • Dilated pupil (if pupil-involving) • Loss of accommodation ⚠️ CRI

nodes.title: The Pupil in CN III Palsy
nodes.summary: The Pupil in CN III Palsy — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Why the Pupil Matters: Anatomy: • Pupillomotor fibers run on the dorsomedial surface of CN III • External compression (aneurysm) affects these fibers FIRST • Ischemia (diabetes) affects internal fibers, sparing peripheral pupillomotor fibers The "Rule of the Pupil" - And Its Limitations: ✅ Classical Teaching: • Pupil-involving = compressive (aneurysm) • Pupil-sparing = microvascular (safe) ⚠️ CRIT

nodes.title: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test
nodes.summary: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Parks-Bielschowsky 3-Step Test for CN IV Palsy: Purpose: Isolate the weak muscle in vertical diplopia Step 1: Which eye is higher (hypertropic)? • Right hypertropia = problem with RIGHT SO or LEFT IR • Left hypertropia = problem with LEFT SO or RIGHT IR Step 2: Does hypertropia worsen in R or L gaze? • Worse in LEFT gaze = SO of higher eye OR IR of lower eye • Worse in RIGHT gaze = SO of lower eye

nodes.title: CN VI Palsy Overview
nodes.summary: CN VI Palsy Overview — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: CN VI (Abducens) - Lateral Rectus Muscle Function: • Abduction ONLY (looking outward) Clinical Presentation: • Horizontal diplopia (worse at distance) • Esotropia - affected eye turned IN • Cannot abduct affected eye past midline • Face turn toward affected side (to minimize diplopia) Unique Feature - False Localizing Sign: • CN VI has the longest intracranial course • Tethered at Dorello's canal

nodes.title: Distal Radius Fracture Reduction
nodes.summary: Most common fracture in adults — assess for neurovascular compromise and need for reduction
nodes.body: Reduction Steps Summary — quick-reference TRAMP checklist to review before reduction. "Obtain & Maintain" — the two questions that guide every fracture decision: [1] 1. OBTAIN — Is the current position acceptable? If yes → immobilize and follow up. If no → reduce. 2. MAINTAIN — Will the fracture shift? If stable → fiberglass OK. If unstable → plaster cast with proper molding. This framework applie

nodes.title: Fracture Assessment — Is Reduction Needed?
nodes.summary: Fracture Assessment — Is Reduction Needed? — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Evaluate the fracture on AP and lateral radiographs. Acceptable position criteria: • Radial height maintained • Radial inclination >15° • Volar tilt neutral or positive • No significant dorsal angulation • No intra-articular step-off >2 mm Is the current position acceptable?

nodes.title: Stable Fracture — Immobilize Only
nodes.summary: Stable Fracture — Immobilize Only — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: Buckle (torus) fractures: • Removable wrist splint for 3–4 weeks • No follow-up x-ray needed — these do not displace Minimally displaced, stable: • Short arm splint or cast • Fiberglass is acceptable (no molding needed for stable fractures) • Ensure thumb, fingers, and elbow remain FREE Follow-up: • Ortho clinic in 5–7 days for repeat films • Return precautions: increasing pain, numbness/tingling,
nodes.recommendation: Stable fracture — immobilize with splint or cast. Ortho follow-up in 5–7 days.

nodes.title: Surgical Consult Required
nodes.summary: Surgical referral: unstable, intra-articular >2mm step-off, open fracture, bilateral, or failed reduction
nodes.body: Indications for operative management: • Open fracture (any grade) • Grossly unstable / comminuted distal radius • Intra-articular step-off >2 mm • Radiocarpal subluxation • Associated distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) instability • Failed closed reduction (2 attempts) ED management while awaiting consult: • Irrigate open wounds, apply sterile dressing • Reduce gross deformity if neurovascularly compr
nodes.recommendation: Surgical consult required. Irrigate, splint, antibiotics if open, and consult orthopedics.

nodes.title: Analgesia Selection
nodes.summary: Analgesia Selection — assess clinical status to guide next management decision
nodes.body: Choose your analgesia approach. Hematoma block is the preferred technique for most ED reductions — faster discharge (1.5 vs 4.6 hours), no NPO requirement, no monitoring team needed. [3][4][6] For complex reductions or patient anxiety, procedural sedation remains appropriate. Regional anesthesia offers superior and longer-lasting analgesia but requires more setup time.

nodes.title: Hematoma Block Technique
nodes.summary: Hematoma Block Technique — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Hematoma Block Evidence — comprehensive efficacy data, technique variations, and comparative studies. TECHNIQUE: 1. Identify the fracture site on dorsal aspect of wrist 2. Prep skin with chlorhexidine 3. Insert 20-gauge needle at dorsal fracture line 4. Aspirate — dark blood confirms placement in fracture hematoma 5. Inject 5–10 mL of 1% plain Lidocaine 6. For combined radius + ulna fractures: sec

nodes.title: Procedural Sedation
nodes.summary: Procedural Sedation — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Procedural sedation provides excellent analgesia and amnesia but requires more resources and time. COMMON AGENTS: • Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV — dissociative, maintains airway reflexes • Propofol 0.5–1 mg/kg IV — rapid onset/offset, no analgesia (add fentanyl) • Etomidate 0.1–0.15 mg/kg IV — hemodynamically stable REQUIREMENTS: • NPO assessment (ideally 2+ hours for clear liquids) • Dedicated monitorin

nodes.title: Regional Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Regional Anesthesia — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: BIER BLOCK (IV Regional) • Double-cuff tourniquet on affected arm • Exsanguinate, inflate proximal cuff to 100 mmHg above SBP • Inject 40–50 mL 0.5% lidocaine IV into dorsal hand vein • Switch to distal cuff after 5 min • Maintain tourniquet minimum 20 min to prevent systemic toxicity • Comparable efficacy to hematoma block with better patient satisfaction in some studies [10] US-GUIDED NERVE BLOC

nodes.title: T — Traction
nodes.summary: T — Traction — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: TRACTION — Disimpact the fracture first. [1] Before you can reduce the fracture, you must recreate length by separating the fragments. TECHNIQUE: • Patient seated, arm pronated on table • Apply longitudinal traction — waterski position (lean back, steady pull) • Make small circles to free the distal fragment • Goal: recreate the length that was lost from impaction • Do NOT try to reduce yet — just

nodes.title: R — Reduction
nodes.summary: R — Reduction — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: REDUCTION — Exaggerate, then correct. [1] The key insight: you must first increase the deformity to unlock the periosteum, then push the fragment back into place. TECHNIQUE: 1. With traction maintained, exaggerate the deformity (extend the wrist further dorsally) 2. This unlocks the dorsal periosteal hinge 3. Now push the distal fragment palmar (volar) with your thumbs 4. Simultaneously apply ulna

nodes.title: A — Apply Splint Materials
nodes.summary: A — Apply Splint Materials — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: APPLY — Plaster, not fiberglass, when molding matters. [1] Fiberglass sets too rigid too fast — you cannot mold it to maintain reduction. Save fiberglass for stable fractures that don't need molding. PLASTER TECHNIQUE: • 10 layers of plaster (standard thickness for adults) • 6-inch width for distal radius • Measure length on the uninjured side — wrist to proximal forearm • Cut a thumb hole before

nodes.title: M — Mold
nodes.summary: M — Mold — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: MOLD — Flat hands, oval shape, don't squeeze, don't move. [1][2] This is where most reductions are lost. Improper molding lets the fracture shift back. TECHNIQUE: • Use flat hands (thenar eminences) — never fingertips • Create an oval cross-section, NOT a circle - "Straight cast → crooked bone, crooked cast → straight bone" • Apply 3-point pressure: dorsal at fracture, volar proximal and distal •

nodes.title: P — Position
nodes.summary: P — Position — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: POSITION — 10° flexion, ulnar deviation, everything else FREE. [1] WRIST POSITION: • 10° flexion (slight volar tilt) — counteracts dorsal displacement • Ulnar deviation — restores radial inclination • Hold position with thumb + index finger + middle finger WHAT MUST BE FREE: • Elbow — cast stops below elbow (short arm) • MCP joints — cast stops at distal palmar crease • Thumb — full ROM through th

Crooked cast = straight bone." If the cast looks perfec

nodes.summary: Re-Attempt Reduction — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Assess what went wrong before trying again. [1] COMMON FAILURES: • Insufficient traction — fragments still impacted • Did not exaggerate deformity — periosteum still locked • Round cast (poor mold) — no mechanical block to re-displacement • Too much padding — mold doesn't transmit to bone • Moved hands during plaster setting — lost the mold BEFORE RE-ATTEMPT: • Remove the current cast/splint compl

nodes.title: Disposition & Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Disposition & Follow-Up — determine disposition and follow-up plan based on clinical findings
nodes.body: DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS: • Elevation — keep hand above heart for 48 hours to minimize swelling • Ice — 20 min on / 20 min off over cast padding • Finger exercises — wiggle fingers frequently to prevent stiffness • Neurovascular checks — ensure fingers remain pink, warm, with normal sensation RETURN IMMEDIATELY IF: • Increasing pain not relieved by elevation and medication • Numbness, tingling, or i
nodes.recommendation: Successful reduction. Discharge with elevation, ice, finger exercises, neurovascular check instructions, and ortho follow-up in 5\u20137 days. Review Discharge Instructions with patient.

nodes.title: Pediatric Considerations
nodes.summary: Pediatric Considerations — review key clinical information before proceeding
nodes.body: Remodeling potential changes what counts as "acceptable." [1] Children's fractures can remodel — but ONLY in the plane of joint motion. Rotation does NOT remodel. Any malrotation must be corrected. ACCEPTABLE ANGULATION BY AGE: • <10 years: up to 15–20° sagittal angulation may remodel • 10–16 years: less tolerance — aim for <10° angulation • Younger children tolerate more because more growth remai

nodes.title: Dizziness Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Glucose, ECG/vitals, gait, neuro, ocular motor exam, and meds/tox before labeling dizziness benign.
nodes.body: Hub Steps Summary | Hub Stop / Pitfalls This hub is for: dizziness, vertigo, lightheadedness, presyncope, imbalance, wooziness, "off," and unclear acute gait complaints. First 60 seconds: - Fingerstick glucose now. - Vitals including oxygen saturation and temperature. Orthostatics only when safe. - ECG early if lightheaded, presyncopal, weak, elderly, cardiac history, medication change, or unclear

nodes.title: Early Differential - Pick the Dangerous Bucket
nodes.summary: Neurovascular, vestibular, cardiac/perfusion, metabolic/endocrine, tox/medication, and other causes are screened up front.
nodes.body: Vascular / neuro: posterior circulation stroke/TIA, cerebellar hemorrhage, cervical artery dissection, vestibular migraine, seizure/postictal state. Vestibular: BPPV, vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis, Meniere disease, vestibular migraine, PPPD/residual dizziness after acute vestibular event. Cardiac / perfusion: dysrhythmia, ACS, PE, orthostatic hypotension, dehydration, occult bleeding/anemia, s

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Choose the First Positive Lane
nodes.summary: Neurovascular, cardiac/perfusion/bleeding, metabolic/sepsis/tox exclusions come before vestibular labeling.
nodes.body: If a dangerous lane is present, open the linked consult and treat that physiology first. You can return after stabilization.

nodes.title: Neurovascular Dizziness
nodes.body: Open Acute Ischemic Stroke, ICH, or Cervical Artery Dissection. Immediate actions: glucose confirmed/corrected, last-known-well, NIHSS-style focused exam, CT head, CTA head/neck when stroke/dissection/LVO concern exists, MRI when posterior stroke remains plausible after CT/CTA and the patient is not otherwise explained. High-risk objective findings: inability to walk unaided, severe truncal ataxia
nodes.recommendation: Treat as neurovascular until central signs, gait failure, and dissection/stroke features are resolved or explained.

nodes.title: Presyncope / Cardiac / Perfusion Dizziness
nodes.body: Open Syncope, Chest Pain Hub, A-Fib RVR, or GI Bleed Hub as clinically indicated. Immediate actions: ECG, monitor, IV access if unstable, glucose, CBC/CMP/troponin when indicated, pregnancy test when relevant, orthostatics only when safe, bedside echo/IVC/lung/aorta POCUS if shock or unclear perfusion. High-risk features: exertional syncope/presyncope, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, abnormal E
nodes.recommendation: Lightheaded dizziness with perfusion features follows the syncope/cardiac/bleeding pathway, not the vestibular pathway.

nodes.title: Metabolic / Sepsis / Toxicologic Dizziness
nodes.body: Open Hypoglycemia, Sepsis, CO Toxicity, Unknown Ingestion Hub, Potassium Disorders, Adrenal Insufficiency, or Thyroid Disorders. Immediate actions: correct glucose, oxygen if hypoxic or CO possible, ECG, medication reconciliation, temperature, VBG/chemistry when ill, lactate/cultures/antibiotics if sepsis physiology, co-oximetry if exposure cluster or headache/nausea/flu-like symptoms with normal
nodes.recommendation: Treat reversible physiology now, then determine recurrence risk before disposition.

nodes.title: Timing + Triggers - Sort the Syndrome
nodes.summary: Sort by AVS, triggered episodic, spontaneous episodic, presyncope, disequilibrium, or post-exposure syndrome.
nodes.body: Use timing/triggers and objective exam. Avoid relying on the patient word "vertigo" vs "dizzy" alone.

nodes.title: Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS)
nodes.body: Open Vertigo for the full HINTS+/BPPV/Mimics workflow. AVS definition: continuous dizziness/vertigo lasting hours to days, usually with nausea/vomiting, head-motion intolerance, gait unsteadiness, and spontaneous nystagmus. HINTS/HINTS+ is appropriate only when: - Continuous AVS is present. - Spontaneous nystagmus is present. - The examiner is trained and comfortable interpreting head impulse, nys
nodes.recommendation: Use the Vertigo consult for AVS. Do not use HINTS outside the correct AVS phenotype.

nodes.title: Triggered Positional Dizziness
nodes.body: Open Vertigo for Dix-Hallpike, supine roll, BPPV nuance, canalith repositioning, and discharge plan. Classic BPPV pattern: brief episodes, seconds to <1 minute, triggered by head position change, no spontaneous nystagmus at rest, no focal neurologic findings, able to ambulate at baseline between spells. Do not do Dix-Hallpike yet if: spontaneous nystagmus at rest, new focal neurologic sign, severe
nodes.recommendation: Classic BPPV is a bedside diagnosis and treatment pathway, not a reflex imaging pathway.

nodes.title: Spontaneous Episodic Dizziness
nodes.body: Common lanes: - Migraine or Vertigo for vestibular migraine phenotype. - Acute Ischemic Stroke for TIA/posterior circulation concern. - Syncope for dysrhythmia/perfusion symptoms. - Chest Pain Hub when ACS/PE physiology coexists. Key discriminators: duration, frequency, complete recovery between episodes, headache/photophobia/phonophobia, auditory symptoms, vascular risk, diplopia/dysarthria/ataxi
nodes.recommendation: Spontaneous episodic dizziness needs TIA, migraine, Meniere, dysrhythmia, medication, and panic differentiated by history plus objective risk.

nodes.title: Post-Exposure / Medication Dizziness
nodes.body: Open CO Toxicity, Unknown Ingestion Hub, or targeted tox/electrolyte consults. Ask specifically: new antihypertensive/diuretic, sedative, opioid, alcohol/cannabis, anticonvulsant, lithium, aminoglycoside, chemotherapy, salicylate, carbon monoxide source, multiple symptomatic people, recent dose change, renal failure, dehydration, missed meals. ED workup: ECG, glucose, orthostatics when safe, BMP/M
nodes.recommendation: Exposure-linked dizziness is managed by the tox/metabolic pathway and recurrence risk.

nodes.title: Lightheaded / Presyncopal Dizziness
nodes.body: Open Syncope for the full risk pathway. Core ED evaluation: history of position/exertion/palpitations/chest pain/dyspnea/bleeding, ECG, glucose, volume status, medication list, CBC/CMP/troponin when clinically indicated, pregnancy test when relevant. Orthostatic dizziness: confirm safely only after dangerous cardiac/bleeding features are screened. Treat volume depletion or medication effect, then
nodes.recommendation: Presyncope is a cardiovascular/perfusion presentation until proven otherwise.

nodes.title: Disequilibrium / Unsafe Gait
nodes.body: Open Acute Ischemic Stroke, Vertigo, Weakness Hub, or Cervical Artery Dissection based on the exam. High-risk gait findings: cannot sit upright, cannot stand, cannot walk unaided, severe veering/falling, new limb ataxia, new diplopia/dysarthria/dysphagia, new focal weakness/sensory loss. Lower-risk patterns: chronic stable neuropathy, baseline gait disorder, medication sedation that fully clears,
nodes.recommendation: Unsafe gait is an objective red flag. Reassess after treatment and document ambulation.

nodes.title: Imaging and Testing Strategy
nodes.summary: Image the dangerous diagnosis you are acting on, not the word dizziness.
nodes.body: Do not use CT as a dizziness screen. Test based on syndrome and objective risk. CT head: useful for hemorrhage/mass when severe headache, trauma, anticoagulation, altered mental status, or focal neuro signs exist. Poor early sensitivity for posterior fossa ischemia. CTA head/neck: use when posterior circulation stroke, dissection, LVO, neck pain/Horner, severe occipital headache, or high-risk neur

nodes.title: Reassess After Treatment / First Pass
nodes.summary: Repeat gait, ocular motor, neuro, vitals, glucose, and ECG/lab trajectory before disposition.
nodes.body: Repeat the exam after glucose correction, fluids, antiemetic, Epley, medication hold, or observation. The repeat gait and ocular motor exam often decides disposition.

nodes.title: Admit / ICU / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit, observe, or transfer for any of the following: - Stroke/ICH/dissection concern or central ocular motor signs. - Inability to walk at baseline, severe truncal ataxia, or unsafe gait after treatment. - Syncope high-risk features, abnormal ECG, persistent hypotension, ACS/PE concern. - Recurrent hypoglycemia, insulin/sulfonylurea risk, CO/tox exposure, dangerous electrolyte abnormality. - Seps
nodes.recommendation: Admit/observe when dizziness has objective risk, recurrence risk, or unsafe function.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exam
nodes.body: Observation is appropriate when symptoms improve but diagnosis remains uncertain, gait is not clearly baseline, AVS has uncertain central/peripheral findings, presyncope needs rhythm/orthostatic/lab trend, or metabolic/toxic dizziness could recur. Observation endpoints: stable vitals, reassuring ECG/rhythm, no evolving neurologic signs, safe ambulation, tolerating PO, glucose stable when relevant,
nodes.recommendation: Use observation to prove trajectory, not to delay a needed stroke/cardiac/tox pathway.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: - Vitals stable and glucose/ECG reassuring for the phenotype. - No focal neuro deficit, central ocular sign, severe headache/neck pain, or high-risk syncope feature. - Walking safely at baseline. - A low-risk diagnosis is documented: classic BPPV treated/referred, vestibular migraine with safe neuro exam, orthostasis/medication effect corrected, or benign/reversible cause with
nodes.recommendation: Document repeat neuro/ocular/gait exam and why central, cardiac, metabolic, and toxic causes are unlikely.

nodes.title: Suspected Diabetic Ketoacidosis — Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Confirm triad: hyperglycemia + ketonemia (BOHB >3) + acidosis (pH <7.3). Watch for euglycemic DKA with SGLT2i.
nodes.body: DKA is a life-threatening metabolic emergency. Defined by the 2024 consensus as: hyperglycemia (glucose >200 mg/dL, or known diabetes) + ketonemia (β-hydroxybutyrate >3 mmol/L or urine ketones 2+) + metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mEq/L). [1] Incidence: ~200,000 cases/year in the US. Mortality: 1-5% in young adults, up to 15% in elderly. Main precipitants: infection (30%), insul

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup — Laboratory Assessment
nodes.summary: Order VBG, BMP, BOHB, lactate, UA, cultures, ECG. BOHB >3 confirms DKA, >6 = severe.
nodes.body: Initial labs for suspected DKA: Acid-base & Electrolytes: • Arterial or venous blood gas — pH, HCO3 (reliable on VBG for pH and HCO3) • Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3). Normal ~10-12. AG >12-14 suggests metabolic acidosis. [2] • BMP: sodium, potassium, chloride, glucose, BUN, creatinine Ketone Assessment (most important for diagnosis): • β-hydroxybutyrate (most specific): >3 mmol/L = DKA confirmed, 1

nodes.title: β-Hydroxybutyrate Interpretation
nodes.summary: BOHB is the gold standard — urine dipstick misses DKA. >3 confirms, 1-3 investigate, <1 excludes.
nodes.body: β-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB) is the gold standard for ketone diagnosis. Unlike urine/serum acetoacetate or nitroprusside-based "ketones," BOHB: • Does not miss euglycemic DKA • Correlates with severity • Is the predominant ketone produced in DKA • Is NOT measured by urine dipstick (major cause of false-negative urine ketones in DKA) BOHB level interpretation: • >3 mmol/L: DKA confirmed — proceed to se

nodes.title: Moderate Ketosis (BOHB 1-3 mmol/L)
nodes.summary: Differentiate early DKA vs alcoholic/starvation ketoacidosis vs euglycemic DKA by glucose level.
nodes.body: BOHB in the 1-3 mmol/L range may represent: • Early/resolving DKA • Alcoholic ketoacidosis (history of heavy alcohol use, recent withdrawal, minimal hyperglycemia) • Starvation ketosis (minimal hyperglycemia, high AG acidosis without severe ketonemia) • Other AG metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis, methanol/ethylene glycol, uremia) Key discriminators: • Glucose level: >200 favors DKA; <150 favors

nodes.title: Alternative Ketosis Diagnosis
nodes.summary: NOT DKA — give dextrose + thiamine, hold insulin. Alcoholic ketoacidosis worsens with insulin.
nodes.body: If BOHB 1-3 mmol/L with glucose <150 and AG acidosis: Likely diagnoses: • Alcoholic ketoacidosis: Heavy alcohol use, recent cessation, minimal hyperglycemia, often hypoglycemic. Treatment: dextrose + fluids, NOT insulin. [5] • Starvation ketosis: Prolonged fasting, minimal hyperglycemia, normal lactate. Resolves with oral intake/dextrose. • Lactic acidosis: Check lactate level (>2-4 mmol/L). Eleva
nodes.recommendation: Do not initiate DKA insulin protocol. Give dextrose, IV fluids, thiamine. Hold insulin if hypoglycemic. Treat underlying cause. Lactate level determines lactic acidosis diagnosis.

nodes.title: DKA Excluded — Alternative Diagnosis
nodes.summary: DKA excluded — consider HHS (glucose >600, osm >320), lactic acidosis, or toxic ingestion.
nodes.body: If BOHB <1 mmol/L or absence of AG acidosis: Alternative diagnoses to consider: • Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS): Glucose >600, osmolality >320, minimal ketonemia. Risk factors: older age, renal impairment, medication-induced. [9] • Diabetic hyperglycemia without ketoacidosis: Mild hyperglycemia, stress hyperglycemia, or medication-related • Non-diabetic AG acidosis: Lactic acidosis, metha
nodes.recommendation: Exclude DKA confirmed. Identify alternative diagnosis. Adjust treatment accordingly.

nodes.title: DKA Severity Classification
nodes.summary: Classify by pH/HCO3/BOHB: mild (7.25-7.30), moderate (7.00-7.24), severe (<7.00). Severe = ICU.
nodes.body: DKA severity determines urgency, ICU admission, and management intensity. [1] 2024 Consensus Criteria (ADA/EASD/JBDS): | Severity | pH | HCO3 (mEq/L) | BOHB (mmol/L) | Altered Mental Status? | |----------|-----|-----|-----|-----| | Mild | 7.25-7.30 | 15-18 | 3-4 | No | | Moderate | 7.00-7.24 | 10-14 | 4-6 | Variable | | Severe | <7.00 | <10 | >6 | Often yes | Additional risk factors requiring ICU:

nodes.title: Special Populations & Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Screen for HD, pregnancy, SGLT2i, pump user, HF — each requires modified fluid/insulin protocol.
nodes.body: Certain populations have higher DKA mortality and require modified management: Higher-risk groups: • Hemodialysis patients: Euvolemic/hypervolemic, cannot tolerate aggressive fluids, avoid K supplementation • Insulin pump users: Rapid presentation, missed boluses cause rapid DKA • Pregnant patients: DKA can occur at lower glucose (<200), higher fetal mortality, requires ICU/L&D coordination, conti

nodes.title: Severe DKA — Immediate Management
nodes.summary: pH <7.0 = immediate parallel resuscitation: 2 IVs, NS bolus, check K+ before insulin, ICU.
nodes.body: Severe DKA (pH <7.0, HCO3 <10) requires aggressive, immediate intervention: Immediate actions (parallel, do NOT delay): • IV access: Two large-bore IVs, continuous cardiac monitor • Labs: VBG, CBC, BMP, lactate, BOHB, cultures, UA, EKG • Fluids: Normal saline 500-1000 mL IV bolus over 30-60 min. Reassess HR, BP, perfusion. • Insulin: Consider 10 U IV bolus IF: serum K <5.3 AND pH <6.9 AND delay to

nodes.title: Special Population Management Overview
nodes.summary: HD = restrict fluids/K+. SGLT2i = permanently discontinue. Pregnancy = fetal monitoring + OB/endo.
nodes.body: High-risk populations require protocol modifications to prevent harm: Hemodialysis patients: • Problem: Often euvolemic/hypervolemic; aggressive fluid resuscitation causes volume overload, pulmonary edema, hypertension • Solution: Target fluid resuscitation carefully; may only need insulin + modest fluids + dextrose • Insulin: Same 0.1 U/kg/hr drip protocol • Dialysis: Consider during severe DKA f

nodes.title: Mild DKA — Insulin Route Selection
nodes.summary: SC insulin is an option for mild DKA (pH ≥7.25, stable, alert). All criteria must be met.
nodes.body: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin is an evidence-based alternative to IV insulin for mild DKA. The 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS Consensus and SQuID II trial support SC insulin for uncomplicated mild DKA in appropriate patients. [1][6] SC insulin eligibility criteria (ALL must be met): • pH ≥7.25 AND HCO3 ≥15 mEq/L (mild DKA only) • BOHB ≤6 mmol/L • Alert and oriented, able to tolerate PO • Hemodynamically s

nodes.title: Subcutaneous Insulin Protocol for Mild DKA
nodes.summary: Lispro/aspart: 0.3 U/kg initial → 0.2 U/kg q2h (or 0.1 U/kg q1h). Same K+ rules as IV.
nodes.body: Rapid-acting SC insulin is safe and effective for mild DKA when eligibility criteria are met. [1][6] Initial Dose (Priming Bolus): • Insulin lispro (Humalog): 0.3 U/kg SC (max 30 units) — Calculate dose • Example: 70 kg patient → 21 units SC • Give immediately after confirming eligibility • Alternative: Insulin aspart (Novolog) same dosing Maintenance Dosing (choose one): Option A — Hourly SC dosi

nodes.title: Common Precipitating Causes — "Five Is"
nodes.summary: Use "Five Is": Infection (30%), Insulin noncompliance, Ischemia, Intoxication, Iatrogenic (SGLT2i/steroids).
nodes.body: Common triggers for DKA — "Five Is" framework: [1][2][3] • Infection (30-40%): Most common. Bacterial infection in adults (UTI, aspiration pneumonia, meningitis), viral in children. Fever, WBC >20-25k, bands elevated, CRP >70, lactate >2. • Ischemia/Infarction: Myocardial infarction, stroke, mesenteric ischemia. High mortality. • Insulin noncompliance (20-30%): Missed injections, running out of in

nodes.title: Red Flags for Infection?
nodes.summary: Any fever in DKA = infection until proven otherwise. Check WBC, lactate, NLR, cultures, UA, CXR.
nodes.body: DKA impairs immune function — infection may be underappreciated at presentation. Red flags for occult infection: • Fever (any temp >38°C is abnormal in DKA and suggests infection) • WBC >20-25k or <4k • Bands >10% (left shift) • Lactate >2 mmol/L (suggests tissue hypoperfusion/infection) • CRP >70 mg/L (sensitive for bacterial infection) • Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) >15 (strong infection

nodes.title: Infection Management in DKA
nodes.summary: Start empiric antibiotics immediately — do NOT wait for cultures. CTX + azithro; add vanc if HAP/immunocompromised.
nodes.body: Infection in DKA requires aggressive treatment — high mortality if missed. Empiric antibiotics: • Do NOT wait for culture results — start empiric coverage immediately • Community-acquired: Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV q12h + azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO q24h (covers S. pneumoniae, atypicals, H. influenzae) • Hospital-acquired or immunocompromised: Add vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (MRSA coverage) • Aspira

nodes.title: Other Precipitants
nodes.summary: Assess noncompliance (cost/access), SGLT2i/steroids, cardiac ischemia, new-onset DM, or substance use.
nodes.body: If infection excluded, assess for other triggers: Insulin noncompliance: • Missed injections? Patient reports or history? • Running out of insulin — cost, access, supply issues? • Intentional reduction? • Pump failure or disconnection? Medication-related (Iatrogenic): • Recent steroid initiation or high-dose (prednisone >20 mg/day)? Dexamethasone or IV methylprednisolone? • SGLT2 inhibitors (canag

nodes.title: Insulin Noncompliance — Management & Prevention
nodes.summary: High recurrence risk — ensure insulin supply, sick-day rules, and social work referral before discharge.
nodes.body: High recurrence risk in noncompliance-triggered DKA — requires intervention: During acute phase: • Provide insulin pen/vial supply before discharge • Refer to social work/case management for insulin access programs • If cost is barrier: Samples from clinic, 340B pharmacy programs, manufacturer copay assistance programs • If access/storage: Distribute to safe location, deliver to home Diabetes educ

nodes.title: Medication-Related DKA — Adjustments
nodes.summary: SGLT2i = permanently discontinue. Steroids = increase insulin significantly. Document as allergy.
nodes.body: Remove or modify offending agent if possible: Steroids: • If high-dose (prednisone >20 mg/day): Taper rapidly if clinically feasible • If essential (cancer, autoimmune): Continue, increase insulin doses significantly (may need 10-50% increase or more) • Educate on insulin adjustment with steroid taper SGLT2 Inhibitors: • PERMANENTLY discontinue — euglycemic DKA recurrence risk very high [10][11] •

nodes.title: Ischemic Complications — Evaluation
nodes.summary: DKA + ischemia = 30-50% mortality. Serial troponin, ECG, CT angio if mesenteric ischemia suspected.
nodes.body: DKA in setting of possible ischemia has very high mortality (~30-50%). Myocardial infarction: • Troponin I or T (high sensitivity preferred) — check at 0, 3, 6 hours • Serial EKG • Echocardiography if ejection fraction uncertain (affects fluid management) • Consider cardiology consultation • Management: Cautious fluid resuscitation (HFrEF risk with aggressive fluids), insulin therapy, possible IAB

nodes.title: Fluid Resuscitation Strategy
nodes.summary: Balanced crystalloid (LR/Plasmalyte) preferred per 2024 consensus; NS acceptable. 500-1000 mL bolus, then 150-200 mL/hr. 5-8L depleted.
nodes.body: Aggressive but careful IV fluid therapy is cornerstone of DKA management. [1][2][8] Overall strategy: • Correct dehydration: Most DKA patients are 5-8L depleted (sometimes >10L in severe DKA) • Target: Replace half deficit in first 8-12 hours, remainder over next 24 hours • Monitor: Reassess HR, BP, urine output, perfusion q1-2h • Adjust based on clinical response Fluid choice (UPDATED 2024 ADA/EA

nodes.title: Current Glucose Level?
nodes.summary: At glucose <=300: "Drop and Split" — cut NS in half, add D10W at equal rate. Never delay dextrose.
nodes.body: Fluid composition changes based on glucose level to prevent hypoglycemia once acidosis resolves. Glucose >300 mg/dL: • Continue normal saline at 150-200 mL/hr (or per urine output + insensible losses) • Goal: Replace remaining deficit gradually • NO dextrose yet Glucose ≤300 mg/dL (most commonly 200-300): • This is the critical transition point in DKA • "Drop and Split": Cut NS rate IN HALF + add

nodes.title: NS Protocol (Glucose >300)
nodes.summary: Continue NS at 150-200 mL/hr. Switch to Drop and Split the moment glucose hits 300 — common error point.
nodes.body: Continue normal saline at 150-200 mL/hr. Monitoring: • Recheck glucose q1-2h (expect 50-70 mg/dL/hr drop with insulin therapy running) • UOP goal: 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr • When glucose reaches ≤300 → IMMEDIATELY switch to "Drop and Split" (see next node) • Do NOT delay dextrose addition — hypoglycemia risk as pH normalizes and insulin continues Common error: Continuing NS after glucose drops below 300 → s

nodes.title: "Drop and Split" Protocol (Glucose ≤300)
nodes.summary: Cut NS in half, add D10W at equal rate. NEVER stop insulin for low glucose — increase dextrose instead.
