nodes.body: At glucose ≤300, implement the critical "Drop and Split" strategy: Action: • CUT normal saline rate IN HALF • ADD D10W at EQUAL rate to dropped NS rate • Example: 200 mL/hr NS → becomes 100 mL/hr NS + 100 mL/hr D10W Why this works: • Continues deficit replacement with dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia • Glucose typically drops 5-10 mg/dL/min once acidosis improving and glucose clearance increases •

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Patient — Fluid Protocol
nodes.summary: HD patient: minimal fluids (risk pulm edema), restrict K+, use BOHB not AG for resolution, consider dialysis.
nodes.body: Hemodialysis patients often euvolemic or hypervolemic — aggressive fluids cause harm: Assessment: • POCUS or clinical exam: JVD, edema, crackles? • Weight compared to dry weight • Recent dialysis: When was last session? Any fluid removal? Modified fluid strategy: • Very cautious initial bolus: 250-500 mL NS only if hypotensive • Maintenance: Minimal — often 50-100 mL/hr NS (smaller total than non-
nodes.recommendation: Minimal fluid resuscitation in HD patient. Insulin + dextrose protocol. Restricted K. Consider dialysis for severe DKA. Coordinate with nephrology.

nodes.title: Serum Potassium Level — Critical Gate
nodes.summary: HOLD insulin if K+ <3.3 — giving insulin with low K+ causes fatal arrhythmia. Replete K+ first.
nodes.body: Potassium is the MOST CRITICAL electrolyte in DKA — wrong management is fatal. Paradox of DKA potassium: • Presents with NORMAL or HIGH potassium despite total-body K depletion (often 1-2 L deficit) • Why? Acidosis shifts K OUT of cells — ECF K appears high, but ICF K is LOW • When insulin + bicarbonate given → K shifts BACK into cells → severe hypokalemia develops (risk of arrhythmia, cardiac arr

nodes.title: Hypokalemia Management (K <3.3)
nodes.summary: KCl 10 mEq/hr IV (10-20 mEq/hr only via central line) until K+ >3.3. Do NOT start insulin until repleted — fatal arrhythmia risk.
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Do NOT start insulin until K >3.3 — fatal arrhythmias if K falls further. Aggressive potassium repletion: • Potassium chloride (KCl) IV: 10 mEq/hr — this is a RATE, not a concentration in the bag [1] • Up to 10-20 mEq/hr ONLY with central venous access + continuous cardiac monitoring; peripheral ceiling is 10 mEq/hr at a maximum concentration of 40 mEq/L [1] • Potassium acetate may be su

nodes.title: K Repleted — Now Safe for Insulin
nodes.summary: K+ now >3.3 — safe to start insulin, but continue K+ repletion concurrently. Target K+ >5 during treatment.
nodes.body: Once K >3.3, insulin infusion can now be started safely. But REMEMBER: Insulin will lower K further. You must: • Continue potassium supplementation DURING insulin therapy • Target serum K 4-5 mEq/L during acute phase; withhold potassium once K >5.0 (normal renal function) [1] • Check K q1-2h × 4-6 hrs, then q4h • Adjust K supplementation based on trending Proceed to DKA insulin protocol (next node

nodes.title: Insulin Infusion Protocol
nodes.summary: Regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr IV. Goal glucose drop 50-70/hr. NEVER stop insulin — give dextrose instead.
nodes.body: Standard DKA insulin regimen: Dosing: • Regular insulin IV infusion: 0.1 U/kg/hr (starting dose, max 15 U/hr for safety) • Example: 70 kg patient → 7 U/hr. 100 kg patient → 10 U/hr. • Prepare: 100 units insulin in 100 mL normal saline = 1 U/mL solution. Use dedicated insulin drip IV (separate from fluid lines if possible to avoid delays in rate adjustment) Bolus insulin (optional, consider if): •

nodes.title: Early Basal Insulin (Glargine)
nodes.summary: Give glargine 0.25 U/kg SC within 6-12h of admission — prevents rebound DKA when IV drip stops.
nodes.body: Give basal insulin on admission — this is critical to prevent recurrent DKA. Timing: Administer insulin glargine within first 6-12 hours of DKA presentation. Do NOT wait until glucose normalized or acidosis resolved. Dosing: • Known diabetes on insulin: Use home insulin glargine dose if known (or home total daily insulin × 0.5 if not on glargine) • New diagnosis or dose unknown: 0.25 U/kg once dai

nodes.title: Electrolyte Management & Monitoring
nodes.summary: Target K+ >5 during treatment. Replace Mg/Phos if low. Give thiamine 100 mg IV on admission.
nodes.body: Aggressive potassium and phosphate/magnesium repletion is essential to prevent complications. Potassium Target: • Goal: Maintain K 4-5 mEq/L during acute DKA; withhold potassium once K >5.0 (normal renal function) [1] • Aggressive repletion: Potassium acetate IV (preferred over KCl to reduce chloride load and NAGMA risk) or potassium chloride • IV: add 20-30 mEq of potassium per LITRE of IV fluid

nodes.title: NAGMA (Hyperchloremic Acidosis) — Screen?
nodes.summary: Check for hyperchloremic acidosis (Cl >110) delaying recovery. Predicted final HCO3 = Na - Cl - 10.
nodes.body: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) complicates ~30% of DKA cases as AG closes. What is NAGMA? • Normal or low AG acidosis that develops as ketoacidosis improves • Caused by: aggressive normal saline (chloride load), urinary bicarb losses, impaired renal excretion • Delayed resolution — patient may seem "stuck" with persistent acidosis despite improving ketones Detection: • Calculate predi

nodes.title: NAGMA Treatment — IV Bicarbonate
nodes.summary: IV bicarb for NAGMA once AG <12: isotonic preferred, hypertonic if urgent. Watch for hypernatremia.
nodes.body: If NAGMA present (Cl >110 or predicted final HCO3 <20), consider IV bicarbonate to speed resolution. Timing: • Usually appears when initial acidosis improving (AG closing) and pH 7.15-7.30 range • Can start IV bicarb once AG <12 and HCO3 rising • Goal: Raise bicarb to >18-20 Bicarbonate Dosing Options: Option 1: Isotonic bicarbonate (preferred) • Sodium bicarbonate 250 mL of isotonic solution (150

nodes.title: DKA Resolution — Stopping Insulin Infusion
nodes.summary: Stop IV insulin when: AG <12, HCO3 >=18, glucose <250, tolerating PO, and basal given 2h+ prior.
nodes.body: ALL of the following criteria must be met to stop IV insulin and transition to SC insulin: Stopping criteria (per 2025 ADA Standards of Care §16 + 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS Consensus): [1] 1. Anion gap <12 (essentially normalized, or approaching normal for chronic renal disease) 2. Venous pH >7.30 AND serum bicarbonate ≥18 mEq/L (or ≥15-20 if NAGMA present) 3. Plasma/capillary β-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB) <0

nodes.title: Euglycemic DKA Management
nodes.summary: Euglycemic DKA: start D10W IMMEDIATELY (do not wait). SGLT2i = permanently discontinue. Easily missed.
nodes.body: Euglycemic DKA: glucose 150-250 + BOHB >3 + pH <7.3, often with SGLT2i use. Presentation: • Minimal hyperglycemia (may be euglycemic or only mildly elevated) — easily missed! • Nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, abdominal pain • Risk factors: SGLT2 inhibitors (primary), insulin pump with reduced basal dose, GLP-1 use, illness with reduced eating • Diagnosis: BOHB >3, pH <7.3, low-normal glucose Unique man
nodes.recommendation: Start D10W immediately. IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr. Aggressive K repletion. Discontinue SGLT2i permanently. Monitor closely for late hypoglycemia.

nodes.title: Intubation in DKA — Avoid if Possible
nodes.summary: Avoid intubation if possible — loss of hyperventilation worsens acidosis. Use ketamine if unavoidable.
nodes.body: Intubation in DKA is HIGH RISK and generally avoided unless absolutely necessary. [5] Why avoid intubation: • Removal of spontaneous hyperventilation → paradoxical CO2 retention and acidosis worsening • Positive pressure ventilation increases PEEP → worse acidosis • Risk of post-intubation hypotension despite fluids (loss of sympathetic tone) • Aspiration risk if altered MS or vomiting • Prolongs

nodes.title: Recurrent DKA (Prior Episode)
nodes.summary: Recurrent DKA = psychiatric/social crisis marker. Uptitrate glargine, mandate psych eval and social work.
nodes.body: Recurrent DKA (≥2 episodes in 12 months) is a marker of adherence, psychiatric, or social problems with very high mortality (~5-10% per episode). Management differs from first presentation: Acute phase: • Same insulin protocol (0.1 U/kg/hr drip or higher if needed) • Aggressive K repletion — maintain K >5 throughout • TREAT NAGMA aggressively with IV bicarbonate (more likely to develop in recurren
nodes.recommendation: ICU or monitored admission. Aggressive basal insulin uptitration. Psychiatry evaluation and referral. Social work intervention. Address adherence barriers. Endocrinology continuity.

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Patient — Detailed Protocol
nodes.summary: HD DKA: insulin + D10W, minimal NS, restrict K+, low-K dialysate, BOHB <1 for resolution (not AG).
nodes.body: HD patients with DKA have unique needs: euvolemia/hypervolemia, limited K tolerance, accelerated correction possible via dialysis. Pathophysiology: • Usually euvolemic or hypervolemic — aggressive fluids cause pulmonary edema, hypertensive crisis • K does NOT drain into dialysate if K concentration in bath = patient K (thus K may rise despite dialysis if not on low-K bath) • Acidosis can be correc
nodes.recommendation: Minimal fluid resuscitation. Insulin + dextrose protocol. Restrict K. Coordinate dialysis STAT for K/acid removal. Use BOHB <1 for resolution. Nephrology co-management.

nodes.title: Disposition Planning
nodes.summary: ICU if pH <7.1, altered MS, shock, ischemia, pregnancy, or ESRD. Most DKA = monitored floor minimum.
nodes.body: DKA severity, presence of complications, and social stability determine discharge vs admission level. ICU admission criteria: • pH <7.1 or HCO3 <10 (severe DKA) • Altered mental status (GCS <13) • Respiratory distress (RR >30, O2 requirement, considered for intubation) • Hemodynamic instability (SBP <90 despite fluids, need vasopressors) • Complications: myocardial infarction, stroke, mesenteric i

nodes.title: ICU Admission Orders
nodes.summary: ICU orders: insulin drip + glargine, aggressive K+, NS/D10W, thiamine, bicarb only if pH <7.0 (not routine). Labs q1-2h.
nodes.body: ICU-level DKA management: Monitoring: • Continuous cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, capnography if intubated • Arterial line if shock or severe acidosis (pH <6.9) • Hourly vitals, UOP q1h, neuro q1h • Labs: VBG/ABG q1-2h × 4h, then q2-4h. BMP q2h × 6h then q4h. Lactate q4h. BOHB q4-6h Medications: • Regular insulin IV drip: 0.1 U/kg/hr (adjust per protocol) • Insulin glargine 0.25-0.3 U/kg SC dail
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. Hourly reassessment. Insulin + aggressive electrolyte repletion. Endocrinology, and specialist consultations as indicated. Serial labs q1-4h.

nodes.title: Monitored Floor Admission Orders
nodes.summary: Floor orders: insulin drip, glargine, K+ repletion, D10W protocol, labs q2-4h. Discharge when all criteria met.
nodes.body: Moderate DKA on monitored medical floor: Monitoring: • Continuous cardiac monitor + continuous pulse oximetry • Vitals q2h, UOP q1h • Labs: VBG/ABG q2-4h initially, then q4-6h. BMP q2-4h × 6h then q6h. Lactate q4-6h initially. • Neuro checks q2-4h (watch for cerebral edema — rare but catastrophic) Medications: • Regular insulin IV drip: 0.1 U/kg/hr IV (adjust per glucose response) • Insulin glargi
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored floor. Insulin + electrolyte protocol. Endocrinology and case management consults. Discharge when stopping criteria met + patient stable on SC insulin.

nodes.title: Insulin Pump User — Troubleshooting & Management
nodes.summary: Pump DKA is rapid (4-8h to severe). Check site, reservoir, tubing, alarms. Suspend if any doubt.
nodes.body: Pump users develop DKA RAPIDLY — often 4-8 hours from pump failure to severe DKA. Why pump DKA is different: • No long-acting basal insulin depot — rely 100% on continuous delivery • Pump failure = complete insulin deficiency within hours • Often MORE severe at presentation (pH <7.0 common) • Rapid onset ketosis masks early symptoms STEP 1: Troubleshoot the pump system: Infusion site inspection: •

nodes.title: Pump Malfunction — Suspend vs Continue
nodes.summary: Suspend pump immediately if malfunction found. Document settings, remove set, start IV insulin drip.
nodes.body: When pump has clearly failed: SUSPEND THE PUMP immediately if: • Site infection/abscess at insertion site • Cannula completely dislodged or kinked • Device error/alarm showing delivery failure • Empty reservoir discovered • Significant air in tubing • Patient unable to manage pump during illness After suspending: • Remove infusion set and cap the reservoir • Document pump settings (basal rates, co

nodes.title: Pump Suspended — IV Insulin Protocol
nodes.summary: Pump off: IV insulin drip + glargine SC bridge. Document pump settings for outpatient endo follow-up.
nodes.body: Pump OFF — manage as standard severe DKA: Acute phase (IV insulin): • Regular insulin drip 0.1 U/kg/hr • Aggressive fluid resuscitation (pump DKA often MORE dehydrated) • Potassium repletion per protocol (goal K+ >5 during treatment) • Switch to D10W when glucose <300 Basal insulin bridge: • Insulin glargine 0.25-0.3 U/kg SC within 6-12 hours • This is CRITICAL — prevents rebound DKA when IV stopp
nodes.recommendation: Suspend pump. IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr. Glargine 0.25 U/kg SC within 6-12h. Transition to MDI or supervised pump restart. Endocrinology follow-up within 1 week.

nodes.title: Pump Restart Criteria — Before Discharge
nodes.summary: Restart pump inpatient ONLY if all criteria met, endo approves, and cause clearly fixed. Otherwise MDI.
nodes.body: Restarting pump in hospital is ONLY appropriate if ALL criteria met: Required criteria: • ✓ DKA fully resolved (AG <12, HCO3 >18, pH >7.30, glucose <250) • ✓ Patient alert, oriented, able to manage pump • ✓ Clear cause of failure identified AND corrected • ✓ Patient experienced pump user (>6 months on pump) • ✓ Endocrinology approves restart • ✓ New infusion set placed at DIFFERENT site • ✓ Fresh
nodes.recommendation: Only restart pump if ALL criteria met. Overlap with glargine x12-24h. Monitor q1-2h x6h. Ensure backup supplies and sick-day education. Endocrinology must approve.

nodes.title: Pump Functioning — Investigate Other Causes
nodes.summary: Pump working but DKA occurred — check for missed boluses, infection, or site absorption failure.
nodes.body: If pump appears to be working correctly, DKA was triggered by another cause: Common causes in pump users with functioning pumps: • Infection — UTI, pneumonia, skin/soft tissue (most common) • Missed boluses — meals without boluses (check pump history) • Illness-related insulin resistance — basal rate inadequate during acute illness • Site absorption issues — lipohypertrophy, scarring (pump "workin

nodes.title: Unknown Pump Status — Empiric Management
nodes.summary: When in doubt: suspend pump, start IV insulin immediately. Do NOT let troubleshooting delay treatment.
nodes.body: When pump status unclear or cannot be assessed: Default approach: Suspend pump and start IV insulin Rationale: IV insulin gives predictable delivery and tight control during critical illness. Pump can be reassessed when patient stable. Steps: 1. Suspend pump — remove infusion set, cap reservoir 2. Document pump settings if accessible (photo of settings screen helpful) 3. Start IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/
nodes.recommendation: Suspend pump if any uncertainty. Start IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr immediately. Give glargine 0.25 U/kg SC. Full pump assessment when patient stable.

nodes.title: Discharge Planning & Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Discharge only if all criteria met, insulin supply secured, sick-day rules taught, and follow-up within 1-2 weeks.
nodes.body: For very mild DKA (pH >7.25, HCO3 >15) in highly reliable patient with excellent support: Discharge checklist (ALL must be met): • ✓ DKA resolved per stopping criteria (AG <12, HCO3 >18, tolerating PO, glucose <250) • ✓ Stable on SC basal + bolus insulin ×2-4 doses • ✓ Electrolytes normal (K 3.5-5.5, Mg >1.5, Phos >1.5) • ✓ Understanding of sick-day rules • ✓ Adequate insulin supply (pens, vials,
nodes.recommendation: Discharge to home with strong outpatient support. Insulin supply + glucagon kit. Written sick-day rules & warning signs. PCP + endocrinology within 1-2 weeks. Case management follow-up call within 24h.

nodes.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
nodes.summary: DVT workup requires structured approach - Wells score guides need for D-dimer vs direct imaging
nodes.body: Clinical Overview: DVT affects ~1-2 per 1,000 adults annually. Up to 50% of untreated proximal DVT progresses to PE. Key Principles: • Clinical diagnosis alone is unreliable (50% of suspected DVT is ruled out) • Use validated clinical probability scores to guide testing • D-dimer is highly sensitive but nonspecific • Compression ultrasound is the diagnostic gold standard • Treatment should be risk

nodes.title: Wells Score for DVT
nodes.summary: Wells score ≤1 is "unlikely" (use D-dimer), ≥2 is "likely" (go to ultrasound)
nodes.body: Wells DVT Calculator Wells Criteria (modified): | Criterion | Points | |-----------|--------| | Active cancer (treatment within 6 months or palliative) | +1 | | Paralysis, paresis, or recent cast of lower extremity | +1 | | Bedridden >3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks | +1 | | Localized tenderness along deep venous system | +1 | | Entire leg swollen | +1 | | Calf swelling >3 cm compared to a

nodes.title: Clinical Probability Assessment
nodes.summary: DVT unlikely → D-dimer first; DVT likely → go directly to ultrasound
nodes.body: Based on Wells Score, classify pretest probability: DVT Unlikely (Wells ≤1): • Prevalence ~6% • Negative D-dimer safely excludes DVT • False negative rate <1% if D-dimer negative DVT Likely (Wells ≥2): • Prevalence ~28% • D-dimer NOT sufficient to exclude • Proceed directly to imaging • If imaging negative with high suspicion, repeat in 5-7 days Alternative scoring (three-tier): • Low (0): 5% prev

nodes.title: High-Risk DVT Features
nodes.summary: Phlegmasia = limb-threatening DVT - needs immediate anticoagulation and consider CDT
nodes.body: Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens (PCD): • Massive iliofemoral DVT with near-total venous obstruction • Triad: severe pain, cyanosis, massive edema • Risk of venous gangrene and limb loss • May progress to shock and death Phlegmasia Alba Dolens: • Less severe, "milk leg" (pale, swollen) • Can progress to PCD Management: • Immediate anticoagulation • Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) • Urgent v

nodes.title: D-dimer Interpretation
nodes.summary: Age-adjusted D-dimer = age × 10 µg/L for patients >50 - increases specificity
nodes.body: Standard D-dimer Cutoff: 500 µg/L (or 0.5 µg/mL FEU) Age-Adjusted D-dimer (patients >50 years): Cutoff = Age × 10 µg/L • Example: 75-year-old → cutoff 750 µg/L • Increases specificity without losing sensitivity • Reduces unnecessary imaging by 5-8% D-dimer Sensitivity: ~95-97% D-dimer Specificity: ~40-50% False Positives: • Pregnancy, postpartum • Active cancer • Recent surgery/trauma • Infection,

nodes.title: Age-Adjusted D-dimer
nodes.summary: Age-adjusted D-dimer reduces imaging by 30% in elderly with no increase in missed DVT
nodes.body: ADJUST-VTE Study (2014): Age-adjusted cutoff safely excludes VTE in older patients: | Age | Standard Cutoff | Age-Adjusted Cutoff | |-----|-----------------|---------------------| | 50 | 500 µg/L | 500 µg/L | | 60 | 500 µg/L | 600 µg/L | | 70 | 500 µg/L | 700 µg/L | | 80 | 500 µg/L | 800 µg/L | | 90 | 500 µg/L | 900 µg/L | Formula: Cutoff = Age × 10 µg/L (for age >50) Impact: • Increases proportio

nodes.title: Negative D-dimer: DVT Excluded
nodes.summary: Wells unlikely + negative D-dimer = <0.5% 3-month VTE risk - safe to discharge
nodes.body: DVT Safely Excluded: With DVT Unlikely (Wells ≤1) + Negative D-dimer: • 3-month VTE rate: <0.5% • No imaging required • No anticoagulation When to reconsider: • Symptoms persist >7 days • New or worsening symptoms • High clinical suspicion despite negative D-dimer Discharge instructions: • Return if leg swelling worsens • Return if shortness of breath develops • Return if chest pain occurs • Follo
nodes.recommendation: DVT excluded with Wells ≤1 + negative D-dimer. No imaging or treatment needed. Discharge with return precautions.

nodes.title: Compression Ultrasound
nodes.summary: Compression ultrasound is gold standard - non-compressible vein = DVT
nodes.body: Gold Standard: Compression Ultrasonography (CUS) Technique: • Compress vein with transducer • Normal: vein completely compresses • DVT: vein does not compress (thrombus visible) Types: • Proximal CUS: Popliteal fossa to common femoral - Sensitivity ~94%, Specificity ~94% • Whole-leg CUS: Includes calf veins - Higher sensitivity for isolated calf DVT - More false positives Interpretation: • Positiv

nodes.title: Ultrasound Results
nodes.summary: Proximal DVT requires treatment; isolated calf DVT can consider serial imaging
nodes.body: Based on compression ultrasound findings: Positive for DVT: • Proceed to treatment selection • Determine proximal vs distal location • Assess for iliofemoral involvement Negative: • If low/moderate probability: DVT excluded • If high probability: consider repeat US in 5-7 days Note on Calf DVT (isolated distal): • 15-25% propagate to proximal veins • Treatment controversial • Options: anticoagulat

nodes.title: Proximal DVT Confirmed
nodes.summary: All proximal DVT requires anticoagulation ≥3 months - assess for CDT in iliofemoral DVT
nodes.body: Definition: DVT involving popliteal vein or above (femoral, iliac) Risk of PE: 40-50% have subclinical PE on imaging Treatment Required: • All proximal DVTs require anticoagulation • Duration minimum 3 months • Assess for provoked vs unprovoked Iliofemoral DVT: • Involves iliac and/or common femoral vein • Higher risk of post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) • Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis if:

nodes.title: Isolated Calf DVT
nodes.summary: Isolated calf DVT: anticoagulation preferred but serial imaging acceptable if low risk
nodes.body: Definition: DVT limited to calf veins (tibial, peroneal, muscular) Prevalence: ~50% of all symptomatic DVTs Natural history: • 15-25% propagate to proximal veins (usually within 2 weeks) • Low risk of PE if remains isolated Management Options: 1. Anticoagulation (CHEST preferred): • Severe symptoms • High risk of extension (cancer, prior VTE, immobility) • D-dimer markedly elevated • Extensive cal

nodes.title: Calf DVT: Serial Imaging Protocol
nodes.summary: Repeat US at 1 and 2 weeks - anticoagulate if propagates to proximal veins
nodes.body: Serial Ultrasound Surveillance: • Repeat US at 1 week • If negative: repeat at 2 weeks • If propagation to proximal veins: anticoagulate Patient Instructions: • Avoid prolonged immobility • Stay hydrated • Leg elevation when resting • Return immediately if: - Increased swelling or pain - Shortness of breath - Chest pain Indications to switch to anticoagulation: • Extension to proximal veins • Wors
nodes.recommendation: Serial US at 1 week, then 2 weeks. Anticoagulate if proximal propagation. Return precautions for PE symptoms.

nodes.title: Negative Ultrasound
nodes.summary: Negative US with high probability → repeat in 5-7 days; low probability → DVT excluded
nodes.body: When to consider DVT still possible after negative US: High clinical probability (Wells ≥2) + negative US: • 5-7% still have DVT on repeat imaging • Recommend repeat US in 5-7 days • Consider D-dimer if not done • Alternative: whole-leg US or CT/MR venography Low/moderate probability + negative US: • DVT safely excluded • No repeat imaging needed • 3-month VTE rate <1% Iliac vein DVT: • May be mis

nodes.title: Repeat Ultrasound Protocol
nodes.summary: Repeat US in 5-7 days - consider interim anticoag if very high suspicion
nodes.body: High Clinical Probability + Negative Initial US: Options: 1. Repeat CUS in 5-7 days (preferred) - Detects propagating thrombus - 5-7% will have positive repeat 2. Whole-leg ultrasound - Includes calf veins - Single visit approach 3. D-dimer testing - If negative: lowers post-test probability - If positive: supports repeat imaging Before discharge: • Schedule repeat US appointment • Provide return
nodes.recommendation: Schedule repeat US in 5-7 days. Provide PE return precautions. Consider interim anticoagulation if very high suspicion.

nodes.title: Advanced Imaging
nodes.summary: CT/MR venography for suspected iliac DVT, May-Thurner, or pregnancy with high suspicion
nodes.body: When to consider CT or MR venography: CT Venography: • Can be added to CTPA (PE workup) • Good for iliac veins • Radiation exposure • Contrast required MR Venography: • Best for pelvic/iliac veins • No radiation (safe in pregnancy) • Limited availability • May-Thurner syndrome evaluation Indications: • Suspected iliac vein DVT • Pregnancy with high suspicion • Bilateral symptoms suggesting IVC inv

nodes.title: Anticoagulant Selection
nodes.summary: DOACs are first-line for most patients - select based on patient-specific factors
nodes.body: Anticoagulant Selection Tool First-Line: DOACs (Direct Oral Anticoagulants) • Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, dabigatran • CHEST 2021: DOACs preferred over warfarin for most patients • No bridging required (except edoxaban/dabigatran) Consider patient factors: • Renal function (CrCl) • Active cancer • Pregnancy/breastfeeding • Drug interactions • GI bleeding history • Antiphospholipid syndrome •

nodes.title: DOAC Options for DVT
nodes.summary: Rivaroxaban or apixaban preferred - single-drug approach, no bridging required
nodes.body: Preferred DOACs for DVT: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto): • 15 mg BID × 21 days, then 20 mg daily • Take with food • No bridging needed • Single-drug approach Apixaban (Eliquis): • 10 mg BID × 7 days, then 5 mg BID • With or without food • No bridging needed • Lowest GI bleeding risk • Preferred if GI bleed history Edoxaban (Savaysa): • 60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 15-50 or ≤60 kg) • Requires 5-10 days of ini

nodes.title: Cancer-Associated DVT
nodes.summary: Cancer DVT: apixaban preferred, LMWH if GI malignancy or drug interactions. Indefinite treatment.
nodes.body: CHEST 2021: DOACs or LMWH preferred over warfarin DOAC Options (preferred for most): • Apixaban - preferred, lowest GI bleeding - 10 mg BID × 7 days → 5 mg BID - Good option for GI malignancies (SELECT-D substudy) • Edoxaban - alternative - Avoid in GI malignancies (higher GI bleed) - 60 mg daily after 5+ days LMWH • Rivaroxaban - alternative - Caution in GI malignancies LMWH (if DOAC not suitable

nodes.title: DVT in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Pregnancy DVT = LMWH BID. Continue through pregnancy + 6 weeks postpartum. No DOACs.
nodes.body: ⚠️ DOACs and WARFARIN are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy Treatment: LMWH • Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BID (weight-based, use current weight) • Do NOT use once-daily dosing in pregnancy • Anti-Xa monitoring generally not needed (consider in extremes of weight) Duration: • Throughout pregnancy • Continue for at least 6 weeks postpartum • Minimum total duration: 3 months Delivery Planning: • Hold LMWH 24 hours

nodes.title: DVT with Renal Impairment
nodes.summary: CrCl 15-30: apixaban preferred. CrCl <15/dialysis: apixaban, warfarin, or UFH.
nodes.body: Anticoagulation in CKD: CrCl 30-50 mL/min: • DOACs okay with dose adjustments • Apixaban: 5 mg BID (or 2.5 mg BID if 2 of 3: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, Cr ≥1.5) • Rivaroxaban: standard dosing okay • Edoxaban: 30 mg daily • Dabigatran: use with caution CrCl 15-30 mL/min: • Apixaban: 5 mg BID (preferred DOAC in severe CKD) • Rivaroxaban: 15 mg daily (limited data) • Avoid dabigatran, edoxaban not studi

nodes.title: Other Special Populations
nodes.summary: APS = warfarin only. Obesity: standard DOAC dosing likely okay. High bleed risk: apixaban or LMWH.
nodes.body: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS): • ⚠️ DOACs are INFERIOR to warfarin • Use warfarin, target INR 2-3 • Triple-positive APS: higher target (INR 3-4) may be needed • TRAPS trial: higher thrombosis with rivaroxaban vs warfarin Extreme Body Weight: • >120 kg or BMI >40: - Standard DOAC dosing appears effective - Consider drug-specific anti-Xa levels if concern - Alternative: warfarin or LMWH with anti-

nodes.title: IVC Filter Indications
nodes.summary: IVC filter ONLY for true anticoag contraindication (active bleeding) - not for "high risk"
nodes.body: IVC Filter: Very Limited Indications Absolute Indication: • Acute proximal DVT/PE with true contraindication to anticoagulation - Active major bleeding - Recent major surgery with high bleeding risk - Hemorrhagic stroke - NOT "high bleeding risk" alone Relative Indications (controversial): • Recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation • Massive PE with hemodynamic instability (as bridge) • Po

nodes.title: Treatment Failure / Recurrent VTE
nodes.summary: Treatment failure: verify compliance → switch to LMWH or increase dose → consider IVC filter if recurs on therapeutic anticoag
nodes.body: Recurrent VTE on Anticoagulation: First: Confirm compliance and therapeutic levels • Missed doses? • Drug interactions? • Absorption issues? • Check anti-Xa level (for LMWH) or drug level (for DOACs) Management Options: On DOAC: • Switch to LMWH • Or increase DOAC dose (limited data) • Or switch to different DOAC On LMWH: • Increase dose by 25-33% • Check anti-Xa (target 0.6-1.0 IU/mL) • Consider

nodes.title: Duration of Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Provoked = 3 months. Unprovoked = extended/indefinite. Cancer = indefinite while active.
nodes.body: Minimum Duration: 3 months for all DVT Provoked DVT (transient risk factor): • Major surgery, trauma, immobilization, hospitalization • Duration: 3 months, then stop • Low recurrence risk (<3% per year after stopping) Minor Transient Risk Factor: • Long flight, oral contraceptives, minor surgery • Duration: 3 months, consider extended • Intermediate recurrence risk (5% per year) Unprovoked DVT (no

nodes.title: Extended Therapy Considerations
nodes.summary: Extended therapy for unprovoked DVT - can consider reduced-dose DOAC after 6 months
nodes.body: Factors Favoring Extended Therapy (>3 months): • Unprovoked DVT • Male sex (higher recurrence) • Positive D-dimer 1 month after stopping • Residual thrombus on imaging • Prior VTE • Active cancer • Antiphospholipid syndrome • Thrombophilia (moderate-strong) Factors Favoring Stopping at 3 Months: • Provoked DVT (major transient risk factor) • High bleeding risk • Patient preference • Falls risk • P

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Most DVT patients can be treated as outpatients if stable with reliable follow-up
nodes.body: Most DVT patients can be treated as outpatients Outpatient Treatment Criteria: ✓ Hemodynamically stable ✓ Low bleeding risk ✓ No severe symptoms (phlegmasia) ✓ No significant comorbidities requiring admission ✓ Adequate renal function for chosen anticoag ✓ Able to afford/obtain anticoagulation ✓ Reliable follow-up available ✓ Good social support ✓ No concurrent PE requiring admission Consider Admi

nodes.title: Outpatient DVT Treatment
nodes.summary: Discharge with DOAC, first dose in ED, follow-up in 1-2 weeks, PE precautions
nodes.body: Discharge Checklist: ✓ Anticoagulation prescribed - First dose given in ED (if appropriate) - Prescription sent to pharmacy - Patient can afford medication ✓ Patient education provided - Medication dosing instructions - Bleeding precautions - Drug/food interactions - Signs of PE (dyspnea, chest pain, syncope) ✓ Follow-up arranged - PCP or anticoagulation clinic in 1-2 weeks - Labs if on warfarin (
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with DOAC (first dose in ED). Follow-up in 1-2 weeks. Return for PE symptoms, bleeding, or worsening swelling.

nodes.title: Inpatient DVT Treatment
nodes.summary: Admit for phlegmasia, high-risk PE, or social concerns. Most ready for discharge in 24-48h.
nodes.body: Admission Indications: • Phlegmasia (limb-threatening DVT) • Concurrent high-risk PE • High bleeding risk requiring monitoring • Need for parenteral anticoagulation • Unable to obtain oral anticoagulation • Severe renal impairment • Social/compliance concerns Inpatient Management: • Start anticoagulation immediately (no delay for imaging) • If parenteral needed: LMWH or UFH • Monitor for bleeding
nodes.recommendation: Admit for high-risk features. Start anticoag immediately. Plan for transition to outpatient therapy within 24-48 hours if stable.

nodes.title: Shortness of Breath Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Work of breathing, mental status, and ventilation first; oxygen target depends on hypercapnia risk.
nodes.body: Hub Steps Summary | Hub Stop / Pitfalls \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Tension pneumothorax \u2014 unilateral absent breath sounds + shock \u2192 decompress before imaging. 2. Pulmonary embolism \u2014 hypoxia, RV strain, clear lungs, VTE risk factors. 3. Acute pulmonary edema / SCAPE \u2014 crackles, hypoxia, hypertension \u2192 NIV + nitrates early. 4. Anaphylaxis / airway angioedema \u2014 stri

nodes.title: Which Diagnosis Are You Working Up?
nodes.summary: Choose a differential; the hub runs its validated rule-in/rule-out instrument to a verdict.
nodes.body: Pick the differential you want to rule in or rule out. Each path runs its validated decision instrument (Wells, Geneva, PERC, CURB-65, and others in the bottom toolbar) to a clear verdict. Work through more than one if the picture is mixed. If no single diagnosis dominates yet, take the last option \u2014 it runs the default resuscitation bundle and the reassess / imaging / disposition arc while t

nodes.title: PE - Step 1: Establish Pretest Probability
nodes.summary: Score first (Wells or Geneva). Probability tier selects PERC vs D-dimer vs CTPA.
nodes.body: Anchor the entire PE workup on pretest probability. Use a validated score, not gestalt alone (open Wells PE or Revised Geneva in the toolbar). The result decides whether PERC, D-dimer, or straight-to-CTPA is correct. - Wells PE: \u22644 = PE unlikely; >4 = PE likely. - Revised Geneva: 0-3 low, 4-10 intermediate, \u226511 high (fully objective, no judgment call). 2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP multisociety

nodes.title: PE - Step 2 (LOW prob): Apply PERC
nodes.summary: PERC-negative in low probability rules out PE with zero further testing (sensitivity ~97.4%).
nodes.body: Only in low pretest probability (gestalt <15% or Wells \u22644). Open PERC in the toolbar. All 8 criteria must be negative to rule out PE without any testing. PERC: age <50, HR <100, SpO2 \u226595%, no hemoptysis, no estrogen, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no recent surgery/trauma. The eligibility gate is the whole rule. PERC is only valid when pretest probability is already <15% \u201

nodes.title: PE - Step 3: Age-Adjusted D-Dimer
nodes.summary: Age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 FEU if >50; age x 5 if the assay reports DDU). Below cutoff rules out; at/above -> CTPA.
nodes.body: For low/intermediate probability that is not PERC-negative. Use an age-adjusted threshold in patients >50: cutoff = age \u00D7 10 ng/mL (FEU). This safely raises the negative rate without missing PE (ADJUST-PE). Example: a 70-year-old uses 700 ng/mL, not 500. The YEARS algorithm is an accepted alternative (0 items + D-dimer <1000 rules out). \u26A0\uFE0F KNOW YOUR ASSAY UNITS BEFORE YOU TRUST THE

nodes.title: PE - HIGH Probability: CTPA Directly
nodes.summary: High probability -> CTPA. Never use D-dimer to rule out high-probability PE.
nodes.body: In high pretest probability, D-dimer cannot rule out PE and only delays diagnosis. Go straight to CTPA (or V/Q if contrast-contraindicated). - If unstable / suspected massive PE: bedside echo for RV strain while arranging definitive care; do not send an unresuscitated crashing patient to CT. - Consider empiric anticoagulation before imaging if the delay is meaningful and bleeding risk is acceptabl

nodes.title: PE - Confirmed / Imaging Positive: Risk-Stratify + Treat
nodes.body: PE confirmed on CTPA. Now risk-stratify severity to choose disposition and therapy (open PESI in the toolbar). - Unstable (SBP <90 / shock): massive PE \u2192 systemic thrombolysis or catheter therapy; activate PERT. Open PE Treatment. - Stable + RV strain (echo/CT) or elevated troponin: submassive \u2192 monitored bed, PERT discussion. - Low-risk (PESI I-II / sPESI 0): anticoagulation; consider o
nodes.recommendation: Confirmed PE: anticoagulate; stratify with PESI; lyse/intervene if massive.

nodes.title: PE - Ruled Out
nodes.body: PE is excluded by this validated pathway. Document the pathway (score tier + PERC or age-adjusted D-dimer result) so the reasoning is independently reviewable. Return to the hub and rule in/out the next differential if dyspnea is unexplained \u2014 a negative PE workup is not a diagnosis.
nodes.recommendation: PE excluded by validated pathway; document and pursue alternate cause.

nodes.title: Acute Pulmonary Edema - Rule In
nodes.summary: Diffuse B-lines + hypertension rule in SCAPE; A-line pattern argues against edema. NT-proBNP rule-in is age-stratified (450/900/1800); rule-out is <300 regardless of age.
nodes.body: Rule in cardiogenic pulmonary edema at the bedside. Diffuse bilateral B-lines on lung POCUS are ~94% sensitive / ~92% specific for cardiogenic edema and beat CXR early. BNP helps when the picture is mixed (<100 pg/mL argues against; >500 supports). If your lab runs NT-proBNP instead of BNP, the cutoffs are completely different and are age-stratified. The two assays are not interchangeable and an N

nodes.title: SCAPE / Pulmonary Edema - Treat
nodes.body: Open CHF Exacerbation and consider SCAPE High-Dose Nitroglycerin. Next 5 minutes: upright, NIV now, high-dose nitrates for the hypertensive SCAPE phenotype, ECG/troponin, POCUS for B-lines/LV function. Avoid reflex large fluid boluses. Pitfall: wheeze can be cardiac asthma. Diffuse B-lines + hypertension + acute distress push toward NIV/nitrates, not just nebulizers. Why NIV first \u2014 it is gui
nodes.recommendation: NIV + nitrates for the hypertensive pulmonary edema phenotype.

nodes.title: Pneumonia - Rule In + Severity
nodes.summary: Confirm infiltrate, then PSI (preferred over CURB-65 per ATS/IDSA) for site of care; severe-CAP criteria for ICU. qSOFA is a deterioration flag, not a sepsis screen.
nodes.body: Diagnosis needs a compatible syndrome (fever, cough, focal findings) plus an infiltrate (CXR, or POCUS consolidation/air-bronchograms when CXR lags). Once confirmed, decide disposition with a validated severity tool (open CURB-65 or PSI/PORT in the toolbar). These two tools are not equivalent \u2014 ATS/IDSA prefers PSI. The 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline recommends the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI/PORT

nodes.title: Pneumonia - Disposition + Treat
nodes.body: Open Pneumonia; open Sepsis Management if septic. Disposition (ATS/IDSA): - CURB-65 0-1 / PSI I-II: outpatient candidate. - CURB-65 2 / PSI III: observation vs short admission. - CURB-65 \u22653 / PSI IV-V: admit; consider ICU (use IDSA minor criteria / need for pressors or ventilation). Treat: oxygen, timely guideline-concordant antibiotics by severity and risk, lactate + blood cultures if septic
nodes.recommendation: Severity score sets site of care; antibiotics by ATS/IDSA severity tier.

nodes.title: Pneumothorax - Rule In
nodes.summary: Absent sliding + lung point rules in PTX; present sliding rules it out. Tension is clinical.
nodes.body: Lung POCUS beats supine CXR for pneumothorax: absent lung sliding + absent B-lines + a lung point rules it in (lung point ~100% specific). Sudden pleuritic pain, unilateral hyperresonance, or a positive-pressure/procedure context raises suspicion. \u26A0\uFE0F GUIDELINE UPDATE \u2014 stable pneumothorax is now managed by SYMPTOMS, not by size. The BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline and the 2024 ER

nodes.title: Pneumothorax - Treat
nodes.body: Open Pneumothorax. - Tension physiology (hypotension, severe distress): immediate needle/finger decompression, then tube \u2014 do not wait for imaging. - Stable: size and symptom-based management per BTS (observation, aspiration, or small-bore drain). Watch ventilated and severe COPD/asthma patients closely \u2014 positive pressure can convert a small PTX into tension. \u26A0\uFE0F CURRENT PARADI
nodes.recommendation: Tension is decompressed clinically before imaging; stable PTX is size-based.

nodes.title: COPD / Asthma - Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Physiologic severity drives therapy; silent chest/AMS signals impending failure.
nodes.body: Grade severity by physiology (speech, work of breathing, mental status, air movement), not by a single number. Silent chest, exhaustion, or altered mental status = impending ventilatory failure.

nodes.title: COPD / Asthma - Treat
nodes.body: Open Asthma Exacerbation or COPD Exacerbation. Next 5 minutes: continuous albuterol for severe asthma, ipratropium, systemic steroid, magnesium for severe asthma; NIV early for COPD/hypercapnic failure when cooperative and protecting the airway. Intubation warning: severe obstruction is a physiologically difficult airway. Use a low rate, long expiratory time, permissive hypercapnia, and disconnect
nodes.recommendation: Maximize bronchodilation and NIV early; avoid rushed intubation unless failing.

nodes.title: ACS as Dyspnea - ECG First
nodes.summary: ECG in 10 min; Sgarbossa for paced/LBBB; troponin for the rest.
nodes.body: Dyspnea can be an anginal equivalent, especially in older, diabetic, or female patients. 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes. If paced or LBBB, apply Sgarbossa (toolbar) to detect occlusion. Know which Sgarbossa you are using \u2014 the two populations are different. - The modified Sgarbossa criteria were derived and validated in left bundle branch block (Smith 2012): any concordant STE \u22651 mm, any

nodes.title: ACS - Treat
nodes.body: Open STEMI or NSTEMI. Next 5 minutes: ECG, monitor, troponin, POCUS for LV/RV/pericardium/lungs. Treat dysrhythmia instability immediately. Keep PE and aortic dissection in the differential when dyspnea and chest pain travel together. Use a high-sensitivity troponin pathway, not a single value. Both the 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP ACS guideline and the 2023 ESC guideline endorse validated 0/1-hour or 0/2-ho
nodes.recommendation: ECG + troponin (+ POCUS) guides the ACS-as-dyspnea patient.

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis - Clinical Criteria
nodes.summary: Meet NIAID/FAAN criteria -> IM epinephrine without delay.
nodes.body: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis (NIAID/FAAN). It is likely with acute onset of any ONE of: 1. Skin/mucosa + respiratory OR hypotension. 2. Two or more systems (skin, respiratory, GI, cardiovascular) after a likely allergen. 3. Hypotension after a known allergen for that patient. Current criteria \u2014 WAO 2020 simplified the 2006 NIAID/FAAN set from three to two, and the 2023 practice paramet

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis - Treat
nodes.body: Open Anaphylaxis Management. Next 5 minutes: IM epinephrine now for airway/breathing/circulation involvement; repeat q5-15 min as needed. Oxygen, fluids, albuterol for bronchospasm, early epinephrine infusion for refractory shock. Pitfall: antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts. They do not rescue airway, bronchospasm, or shock. Epinephrine dose \u2014 the drug and route referenced above: [28][2
nodes.recommendation: IM epinephrine first. Do not delay for adjuncts.

nodes.title: Toxic / Metabolic Dyspnea - Rule In
nodes.summary: Co-oximetry + ABG + gaps when saturation/cyanosis/PaO2 disagree or exposure is plausible.
nodes.body: Suspect when saturation, cyanosis, and PaO2 do not agree, or with exposure history. Standard pulse oximetry misleads in CO and methemoglobinemia \u2014 use co-oximetry. Check ABG/VBG with lactate and an anion gap.

nodes.title: Toxic / Metabolic - Treat
nodes.body: Open CO Toxicity or Methemoglobinemia. - CO: 100% oxygen immediately; consider hyperbaric per criteria (syncope, ischemia, neuro deficit, pregnancy, high COHb). - Methemoglobinemia: methylene blue for symptomatic levels; remove the offending agent. - Metabolic acidosis: treat the cause (DKA, salicylate, toxic alcohol); a tiring compensatory tachypnea is an intubation trap \u2014 match minute venti
nodes.recommendation: Use co-oximetry; treat the specific toxin; beware intubating compensated acidosis.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Position, oxygen target, ECG/CXR/POCUS, VBG when ventilation matters, treat the cause in parallel.
nodes.body: Default bundle while the diagnosis clarifies: - Upright positioning. - Oxygen target: 94-98% for most; 88-92% for hypercapnic risk. - Monitor, IV, ECG. - CXR when stable. - Lung/cardiac POCUS when the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient is sick. - VBG/ABG when ventilatory failure, severe COPD/asthma, tox, or altered mental status is possible. - Nebulizers if wheeze, NIV if COPD/CHF physiology an

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Tiring patients need escalation; stable unclear patients need diagnosis-directed imaging.
nodes.body: The dyspnea patient can improve quickly or crash quickly. Reassess physiology, not just the diagnosis label.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: CXR plus POCUS first for many; CT/CTPA only when stable enough and actionable.
nodes.body: Imaging by likely cause: - CXR: pneumonia, pneumothorax, edema, effusion, device/tube checks. - Lung POCUS: B-lines, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, consolidation. - Cardiac POCUS: LV function, RV strain, pericardial effusion/tamponade. - CTPA: suspected PE when pretest probability and testing support it and the patient is stable enough. - CT chest: unclear severe disease, complications, malignanc

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for support/escalation, admit for oxygen or uncertainty, discharge only if stable on room air with a clear plan.
nodes.body: Disposition follows oxygen requirement, work of breathing, trajectory, and cause.

nodes.title: ICU / Resus Admission
nodes.body: ICU/resus for NIV or intubation, persistent severe work of breathing, shock, rising CO2/acidosis, massive PE, severe asthma/COPD with exhaustion, SCAPE not rapidly improving, anaphylaxis needing infusion, or unclear diagnosis with unstable physiology.
nodes.recommendation: Escalate early. Dyspnea deterioration is often abrupt.

nodes.title: Admit / Observation
nodes.body: Admit or observe for a new oxygen requirement, persistent tachypnea, recurrent symptoms after treatment, pneumonia with risk features, COPD/CHF needing repeated therapy, PE workup/treatment, social inability to manage therapy, or diagnostic uncertainty that remains actionable.
nodes.recommendation: Use the cause-specific consult for final destination and orders.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: stable room-air oxygenation at rest and with ambulation as appropriate, work of breathing resolved or mild, clear diagnosis, durable treatment response, no high-risk alternate diagnosis, meds/equipment available, and return precautions given. Return precautions: worsening dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, fever/rigors, hemoptysis, new confusion, inability to speak full sentences,
nodes.recommendation: Document ambulation/room-air status when relevant.

nodes.title: Acute Dystonic Reaction
nodes.summary: Sudden focal painful spasm after dopamine blocker; screen airway first.
nodes.body: Core pattern: sudden painful sustained or intermittent muscle contraction after a dopamine-blocking medication. Most common timing: minutes to hours after an ED dose, or within the first 4-5 days after starting/increasing an antipsychotic or antiemetic. Typical clues: clear sensorium, anxiety/fear, normal temperature, focal craniocervical spasm, recent haloperidol/droperidol/metoclopramide/prochlo

nodes.title: Airway Screen: Laryngeal Dystonia
nodes.summary: Laryngeal dystonia: anticholinergic immediately, airway setup, do not dismiss as anxiety.
nodes.body: This is the dangerous phenotype. Laryngeal dystonia is rare but can obstruct the airway. Red flags: - Stridor - Dysphonia or aphonia - Dyspnea or throat tightness - Drooling or inability to swallow secretions - Cyanosis, hypoxia, severe agitation from air hunger Immediate actions: 1. Move to resus bay; airway equipment, suction, BVM, and RSI backup at bedside. 2. Stop the suspected culprit. 3. Giv

nodes.title: Does the Pattern Fit Drug-Induced Dystonia?
nodes.summary: Classic timing + dopamine blocker + focal spasm = treat now.
nodes.body: High-confidence diagnosis when ALL are true: - Sudden sustained/repetitive spasm or abnormal posture - Recent dopamine-blocking drug exposure or dose increase - Symptoms began within minutes-hours or within 4-5 days - Mental status is otherwise clear - No fever, clonus, meningismus, true loss of consciousness, or focal CNS deficit Treatment is both diagnostic and therapeutic. If the story fits, tr

nodes.title: First-Line ED Treatment
nodes.summary: Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV/IM or benztropine 1-2 mg IV/IM; peds diphen 1 mg/kg max 50.
nodes.body: Stop the offending drug and give an anticholinergic. Adult options - choose one: - Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV preferred for fastest onset; IM acceptable if no IV. - Benztropine 1-2 mg IV/IM; may repeat once after ~15-30 min if incomplete. Pediatric: - Diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg IV/IM, max 50 mg. Expected response: visible improvement usually within 5-30 min after parenteral anticholinergic. If severe d

nodes.title: Response After Anticholinergic
nodes.summary: Rapid improvement after anticholinergic confirms diagnosis; no response = rethink.
nodes.body: Reassess at 5-30 minutes: - Eye deviation resolved? - Neck/jaw/tongue/trunk spasm improved? - Swallowing and voice normal? - Respiratory symptoms gone? - Patient less distressed but not over-sedated? A rapid response strongly supports acute dystonia.

nodes.title: Partial Response
nodes.summary: Partial response: repeat anticholinergic, consider benzo, observe longer.
nodes.body: If improving but not resolved: 1. Recheck airway, voice, swallowing, and oxygenation. 2. Repeat the initial anticholinergic once if safe. 3. Add benzodiazepine if severe spasm, panic, or residual painful contraction. 4. Review medication list for long-acting/depot antipsychotic or repeated antiemetic dosing. 5. Observe longer because recurrence is more likely. Escalate if: airway symptoms persist,

nodes.title: No Response: Reset the Differential
nodes.summary: No anticholinergic response = reset diagnosis and look for dangerous mimics.
nodes.body: If adequate anticholinergic therapy does not help, acute dystonia is less likely. Re-check immediately for: - Seizure or nonconvulsive status - Tetanus or strychnine-like toxidrome - Hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia - Serotonin syndrome or NMS - CNS infection, stroke, intracranial mass, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy - True angioedema/anaphylaxis or mechanical airway obstruction - TMJ dislocation, dent

nodes.title: Culprit Meds + Incidence
nodes.summary: Highest risk: high-potency FGAs and antiemetic dopamine blockers; metoclopramide/prochlorperazine are common ED culprits.
nodes.body: Incidence varies by dose, route, age, prior reaction, and prophylaxis. Use the numbers as risk anchors, not precise prediction for a single patient. | Drug/class | Examples | Practical incidence/risk signal | |---|---|---| | High-potency first-generation antipsychotics | Haloperidol, fluphenazine, pimozide | Highest antipsychotic risk. Reported acute dystonia around 3-10%; ED agitation meta-analys

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Young, male, prior reaction, high-potency/parenteral D2 blocker, rapid escalation, cocaine = high risk.
nodes.body: Strong risk factors: - Prior acute dystonic reaction - Young age, especially <30-35 years - Male sex for antipsychotic-associated dystonia - High-potency D2 blockade - Parenteral administration (IM/IV) - Rapid dose escalation or repeated doses - Neuroleptic-naive patient - Recent cocaine use - Dehydration or acute medical illness - Family history of dystonia Medication clues: - First 5 days after

nodes.title: Clinical Presentations
nodes.summary: Oculogyric, torticollis, oromandibular/buccolingual, laryngeal, opisthotonos, limb/trunk dystonia.
nodes.body: Common phenotypes: | Presentation | What you see | |---|---| | Oculogyric crisis | Sustained upward/lateral eye deviation, eyelid spasm, anxiety, preserved awareness | | Cervical dystonia | Torticollis, retrocollis, neck pain, head pulled to one side/backward | | Oromandibular dystonia | Trismus, jaw opening/closing spasm, grimacing, tongue protrusion, dysarthria | | Buccolingual crisis | Tongue f

nodes.title: Bedside Exam
nodes.summary: Airway, vitals, mental status, focal neuro, true allergy signs, and 5-day med history.
nodes.body: Focused exam: - Airway: voice, stridor, secretions, swallow, work of breathing - Vitals: fever or major autonomic instability argues against simple dystonia - Mental status: clear sensorium supports dystonia; delirium/coma does not - Eyes: sustained gaze deviation without postictal state suggests oculogyric crisis - Jaw/tongue: trismus, tongue protrusion, dysarthria; distinguish from true edema -

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Danger mimics: NMS/SS, seizure, allergy, tetanus/electrolytes, CNS infection.
nodes.body: Pick the dangerous mimic if the presentation is not classic. Simple acute dystonia usually has normal temperature, preserved consciousness, focal patterned spasm, and rapid anticholinergic response.

nodes.title: Dystonia vs NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome
nodes.summary: Clear focal spasm = dystonia; fever/AMS/lead-pipe or clonus = alternate tox emergency.
nodes.body: | Feature | Acute dystonia | NMS | Serotonin syndrome | |---|---|---|---| | Onset | Minutes-hours; usually <5 days | Days-weeks | Hours | | Mental status | Usually clear | Altered | Agitated/delirious | | Temperature | Normal | High fever | Variable fever | | Tone | Focal patterned spasm | Generalized lead-pipe rigidity | Hyperreflexia/clonus | | Autonomic | Usually mild anxiety/tachy | Labile BP,

nodes.title: Seizure Mimic Check
nodes.summary: Preserved awareness favors oculogyric crisis; LOC/postictal/rhythmic clonus favors seizure.
nodes.body: Oculogyric crisis can look like seizure, but awareness is usually preserved. Seizure clues: - Loss of consciousness - Rhythmic clonic movements rather than sustained posture - Lateral tongue bite, incontinence, postictal state - Persistent gaze deviation with focal neuro deficit - No response to anticholinergic therapy Actions: glucose now, treat active seizure per status pathway, consider EEG/CT/

nodes.title: Allergy / Angioedema Mimic
nodes.summary: Tongue-feels-swollen can be dystonia; true swelling/wheeze/hypotension = allergy pathway.
nodes.body: Buccolingual dystonia often feels like tongue swelling but the tongue is not truly edematous. Allergy/angioedema clues: - Visible progressive swelling of lips/tongue/uvula - Urticaria, flushing, wheeze, hypotension - ACE inhibitor exposure or hereditary angioedema history - No jaw/tongue rhythmic posturing If anaphylaxis is possible: epinephrine first. Diphenhydramine does not treat shock or bronc

nodes.title: Tetanus / Electrolyte / Toxic Mimics
nodes.summary: Generalized triggerable spasms or no D2-blocker history: check tetanus, Ca/Mg, tox.
nodes.body: Consider when there is no dopamine-blocker story or the pattern is generalized. Tetanus: trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonos, autonomic instability, wound/immunization gap; spasms triggered by touch/noise. Hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia: perioral numbness, tetany, carpopedal spasm, QT prolongation, seizure risk. Strychnine-like tox: severe generalized painful spasms with preserved consciousness,

nodes.title: Prevent Recurrence
nodes.summary: Continue oral anticholinergic 24-72h after reversal because culprit drug outlasts antidote.
nodes.body: Why recurrence happens: the culprit dopamine blocker often lasts longer than IV/IM diphenhydramine or benztropine. After ED reversal: - Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg PO q6h for 24-72 h, OR - Benztropine 1-2 mg PO BID for 2-3 days when appropriate. Longer coverage may be needed after depot/long-acting antipsychotics or repeated antiemetic dosing. Coordinate with psychiatry/pharmacy if the antipsychotic

nodes.title: Avoid Rechallenge
nodes.summary: Record the exact drug and phenotype; avoid re-exposure when possible.
nodes.body: Document as a medication adverse reaction, not a vague allergy. ED documentation: - Offending drug, dose, route, and time - Phenotype: oculogyric/torticollis/jaw/tongue/laryngeal/etc. - Treatment response and time to response - Discharge anticholinergic plan Avoid: same medication and close dopamine-blocking relatives when reasonable. Safer substitutions: - Nausea/migraine: consider non-D2 options

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Peds: diphen 1 mg/kg max 50. Elderly: anticholinergic toxicity risk. Airway still wins.
nodes.body: Pediatrics: acute dystonia commonly follows antiemetics; children/adolescents can present with frightening oculogyric, jaw/tongue, or opisthotonic reactions. Use diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg IV/IM max 50 mg and observe until clearly back to baseline. Pregnancy: metoclopramide and prochlorperazine exposures occur in hyperemesis/migraine pathways. Treat maternal airway and distress first; diphenhydramine

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge only when resolved and airway safe; airway symptoms or atypical course need observation/admission.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on airway risk, diagnostic certainty, recurrence risk, and sedation.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge after complete resolution, airway safety, oral anticholinergic, and culprit avoidance.
nodes.body: Reasonable discharge when ALL are true: - Symptoms resolved or near-resolved after anticholinergic - Voice, swallowing, and breathing normal - Vitals stable, no fever/AMS/focal neuro deficit - No recurrent spasm during ED observation - Patient has oral anticholinergic plan and understands sedation precautions - Offending drug stopped/avoided or psychiatry/pharmacy plan documented - Return precauti
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after full airway-safe clinical resolution, recurrence prevention, and clear medication avoidance plan.

nodes.title: Observe / Admit
nodes.summary: Observe/admit if airway, recurrence, repeated dosing, long-acting culprit, or uncertain diagnosis.
nodes.body: Observe or admit for: - Laryngeal symptoms even if improved - Need for repeated IV/IM anticholinergic or benzodiazepine - Long-acting/depot antipsychotic exposure - Recurrent symptoms in ED - Persistent dysphagia, jaw/tongue spasm, aspiration concern - Significant sedation or anticholinergic toxicity - Diagnostic uncertainty requiring workup - Unsafe discharge or inability to obtain meds Observati
nodes.recommendation: Observation/admission for airway involvement, recurrence, repeated meds, long-acting culprit, persistent symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty.

nodes.title: ICU / Airway-Capable Setting
nodes.summary: ICU for persistent airway risk or dangerous mimic.
nodes.body: ICU or airway-capable monitored setting when: - Persistent stridor, hypoxia, or respiratory distress - Recurrent laryngeal dystonia - Need for airway intervention or continuous airway watch - Severe generalized spasms with hyperthermia/acidosis/rhabdo - Concern for NMS, serotonin syndrome, tetanus, strychnine-like tox, CNS infection, or status epilepticus Treatment priority: airway and oxygenation
nodes.recommendation: ICU/airway setting for persistent or recurrent laryngeal symptoms, hypoxia, or dangerous mimic concern.

nodes.title: When to Order Tests
nodes.summary: Clinical diagnosis; test only atypical features or mimics.
nodes.body: No routine test confirms acute dystonia. Diagnosis is clinical and often confirmed by rapid response to anticholinergic therapy. No labs needed for a classic, medication-linked, rapidly resolving reaction. Target tests when atypical: - Glucose for seizure/AMS - BMP plus calcium and magnesium for tetany/spasm - CK/creatinine/UA if prolonged severe spasms or restraint/agitation - Temperature and inf

nodes.title: Dysuria — Sick Check First
nodes.body: Dysuria is a high-frequency undifferentiated complaint — do NOT anchor on "just a UTI." The dangerous misses hide behind the same symptom: obstructive urosepsis, an untreated STI, acute bacterial prostatitis, and urinary retention. ⚠️ 5 DO-NOT-MISS diagnoses 1. Obstructive pyelonephritis / urosepsis — fever, flank pain, rigors, systemic toxicity, a stone or obstruction. A pus-under-pressure kidney

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Six-branch triage: urosepsis / STI / prostatitis / retention / priapism / uncomplicated cystitis.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous causes first, then the common ones. Each branch runs a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Urosepsis / Obstructive Pyelonephritis — Toxicity + Obstruction Gate
nodes.summary: Fever + flank + toxicity = pyelo; infection + obstruction = urosepsis emergency. qSOFA screens sepsis.
nodes.body: Fever + flank pain + systemic toxicity = upper-tract infection until proven otherwise. The lethal combination is infection PLUS obstruction (a stone, stricture, or tumor): the collecting system fills with pus under pressure and the patient decompensates fast. Screen sepsis with qSOFA (RR \u226522, SBP \u226490, altered mentation \u2014 open it in the toolbar) and ask what raises obstruction risk:

nodes.title: Urosepsis — Resuscitate + Decompress
nodes.body: This is a resuscitation, not a prescription. Run the Sepsis pathway. Next steps: - IV fluids, blood cultures \u00D7 2, lactate, and early broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone; anti-pseudomonal / broader coverage if healthcare-associated, recent instrumentation, or resistance risk; tailor to local antibiogram and prior cultures). - Imaging to find obstruction: CT abdomen/pelvis (non-contra
nodes.recommendation: Sepsis bundle + early broad-spectrum abx + CT to find obstruction + EMERGENT urology/IR decompression (stent or nephrostomy). Antibiotics alone will not save an obstructed kidney.

nodes.title: Upper-Tract Sepsis — Unlikely
nodes.body: An afebrile, well-appearing patient with no toxicity and no obstruction risk makes obstructive pyelonephritis / urosepsis unlikely right now. Pyelonephritis can still be present without frank sepsis \u2014 flank pain + CVA tenderness + fever/pyuria still warrants upper-tract-directed antibiotics and close follow-up (see Adult UTI). Reassess if fever, rigors, or hemodynamic change develop. Return t
nodes.recommendation: Urosepsis unlikely without toxicity/obstruction; treat pyelonephritis if present and reassess for decompensation.

nodes.title: STI / Urethritis / Cervicitis — Discharge + Risk Gate
nodes.summary: Normal UA does not reassure; discharge / sterile pyuria / risk = NAAT for GC/CT. Missed → PID / epididymo-orchitis.
nodes.body: A normal urinalysis does NOT rule out an STI. In a young, sexually active patient, dysuria with urethral/vaginal discharge, a new/multiple partners, or a partner with symptoms is gonorrhea / chlamydia (\u00B1 trichomonas, Mycoplasma genitalium) until NAAT for GC/CT proves otherwise. Sterile pyuria (pyuria without bacteriuria/positive culture) is a classic clue. In women, ascending infection \u2192

nodes.title: Urethritis / STI — Test + Empiric Treat
nodes.body: Open STI Comprehensive for the full workup and treatment; if PID features (lower abdominal/pelvic pain, cervical motion / adnexal tenderness in a woman), run PID. Next steps: - NAAT for gonorrhea + chlamydia (urine or urethral/vaginal/cervical swab); add trichomonas and consider Mycoplasma genitalium if persistent/recurrent. - Treat empirically at the visit (do not wait for NAAT if the picture fit
nodes.recommendation: NAAT GC/CT + empiric CDC-guideline treatment at the visit; screen HIV/syphilis; treat partners. Escalate to PID pathway if pelvic exam positive.

nodes.title: STI / Urethritis — Unlikely
nodes.body: No discharge, no risk factors, and a picture that fits lower-tract cystitis makes an STI less likely \u2014 but the threshold to test is low, because a missed STI drives PID and epididymo-orchitis. If pyuria is present without bacteriuria (sterile pyuria), keep the STI on the list and send NAAT. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: STI less likely without discharge/risk; keep a low threshold to send NAAT if sterile pyuria or any risk emerges.

nodes.title: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis — Male Perineal Pain Gate
nodes.summary: Febrile man + perineal pain + tender prostate = acute bacterial prostatitis; UA may be normal. Avoid vigorous massage.
nodes.body: A febrile man with dysuria + perineal / pelvic / low-back pain and an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate has acute bacterial prostatitis \u2014 often with obstructive urinary symptoms or acute retention. The UA can be normal or only mildly abnormal. Do a gentle DRE (avoid vigorous prostate massage \u2014 it can precipitate bacteremia). Send UA + culture (gram-negatives, especially E. coli, dominat

nodes.title: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis — Culture + Prolonged Antibiotics
nodes.body: Acute bacterial prostatitis confirmed or strongly suspected (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here; use Adult UTI for antibiotic selection reference): - Send UA + urine culture before antibiotics; blood cultures if febrile/toxic. - Antibiotics that penetrate prostate tissue for a prolonged course \u2014 a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for ~2\u20134 weeks (guided by culture
nodes.recommendation: Culture then prolonged prostate-penetrating antibiotics (2\u20134 wk FQ or TMP-SMX); admit + IV if toxic; manage retention; think abscess if not improving. (Consult gap.)

nodes.title: Prostatitis — Unlikely
nodes.body: No prostate tenderness and a picture that does not fit makes acute bacterial prostatitis unlikely. Keep it on the list for any febrile man with dysuria \u2014 the UA is unreliable here, so the exam drives the diagnosis. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Prostatitis unlikely without a tender prostate; reconsider in any febrile man with dysuria and a normal UA.

nodes.title: Acute Urinary Retention — Distended Bladder Gate
nodes.summary: Can\u2019t void + distended bladder + high PVR = retention; decompress. Screen cauda equina and the underlying cause.
nodes.body: Dysuria can be the cause OR the consequence of retention. A patient who cannot void, has suprapubic distension/pain, or has overflow incontinence needs the bladder assessed \u2014 palpate and confirm with a bladder scan / bedside ultrasound (a large post-void residual clinches it). Common drivers: BPH, obstructing stone/clot, prostatitis, medications (anticholinergics, opioids, sympathomimetics),

nodes.title: Acute Urinary Retention — Decompress + Find the Cause
nodes.body: Open Urinary Retention for the full management pathway. Next steps: - Immediate bladder decompression with a urethral catheter (suprapubic if urethral fails or is contraindicated). Document the drained volume. - Watch for post-obstructive diuresis after large-volume drainage \u2014 monitor urine output and replace fluids/electrolytes if brisk. - Check a BMP for obstructive (post-renal) acute kidne
nodes.recommendation: Decompress the bladder now, watch for post-obstructive diuresis, check renal function/K+, find the cause, and rule out cauda equina.

nodes.title: Retention — Excluded
nodes.body: The patient is voiding, the bladder is not distended, and the post-void residual is low \u2014 acute urinary retention is excluded as the driver of the dysuria. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Retention excluded with normal voiding and low PVR; reassess if the patient stops voiding.

nodes.title: Priapism — Persistent Erection Gate
nodes.summary: Painful erection >4 h = priapism; ischemic (low-flow) is time-critical. Corporal blood gas / Doppler distinguishes type.
nodes.body: A persistent (>4 h), often painful erection unrelated to stimulation is priapism \u2014 a GU emergency. It can present as "painful urination / penile pain." Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is the time-critical one \u2014 rigid, painful corpora, dark aspirate, and it threatens erectile function if not relieved quickly. Sickle cell disease, certain medications (erectile-dysfunction drugs, some psychiat

nodes.title: Priapism — Time-Critical Detumescence
nodes.body: Open Priapism for the full pathway \u2014 ischemic priapism is a time-dependent emergency. Next steps: - Confirm ischemic vs non-ischemic with corporal aspirate blood gas (\u00B1 penile Doppler): ischemic = hypoxic, acidotic, rigid, painful. - Ischemic: corporal aspiration \u00B1 irrigation, then intracavernosal phenylephrine (a diluted alpha-agonist, with cardiovascular monitoring); escalate to s
nodes.recommendation: Confirm ischemic type, then corporal aspiration + intracavernosal phenylephrine + urgent urology; treat sickle-cell trigger in parallel. Time-critical for erectile function.

nodes.title: Priapism — Excluded
nodes.body: No persistent erection \u2014 priapism is not the driver here. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Priapism excluded; reassess if a persistent painful erection develops.

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Cystitis — Simple-UTI Gate
nodes.summary: Dysuria + frequency, no discharge → >90% UTI. Confirm no complicating/upper-tract/STI features first.
nodes.body: Dysuria + urinary frequency + urgency WITHOUT vaginal discharge or irritation makes a UTI highly likely (the probability of cystitis exceeds ~90% when discharge is absent and internal dysuria is present). "Uncomplicated" means a non-pregnant, otherwise-healthy patient without fever, flank pain, or obstruction. Confirm there are no complicating / upper-tract features and no STI clues before treatin

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Cystitis — Short-Course Antibiotics + Discharge
nodes.body: Open Adult UTI for antibiotic selection and follow-up. Next steps: - First-line short-course antibiotics per guideline and local resistance \u2014 nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (where resistance is low), or fosfomycin; avoid fluoroquinolones for simple cystitis when alternatives exist. - Urine culture is not required for straightforward uncomplicated cystitis but send it if recurre
nodes.recommendation: Short-course guideline antibiotics (nitrofurantoin / TMP-SMX / fosfomycin), culture only if complicated/recurrent/pregnant, return precautions, discharge.

nodes.title: Pediatric UTI — Use the Peds Pathway
nodes.body: A child or infant with UTI features is a different workup (age-based catheterized specimen, higher stakes for pyelonephritis and underlying anomaly, fever-source evaluation in the young infant). Open Pediatric UTI for the age-appropriate pathway.
nodes.recommendation: Route children/infants to the pediatric UTI pathway for age-based sampling and workup.

nodes.title: Not Simple Cystitis — Re-Triage
nodes.body: A complicating feature has surfaced \u2014 fever, flank pain, systemic toxicity, pregnancy, a male patient, discharge/STI clues, or obstruction risk. This is no longer "uncomplicated cystitis." Return to the hub and run the matching dangerous branch (urosepsis, STI, prostatitis, or retention). Return to the hub for the correct differential.
nodes.recommendation: Any complicating feature means it is not simple cystitis \u2014 re-triage to the upper-tract / STI / prostatitis / retention branch.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle
nodes.body: The dysuria work-up bundle (scale to acuity): - Vitals + qSOFA if any toxicity; establish IV access and resuscitate the septic patient early. - Urinalysis + urine culture (culture when complicated, recurrent, male, pregnant, or upper-tract suspected). Remember: a normal UA does NOT exclude an STI or prostatitis. - NAAT for GC/CT in anyone with discharge, sterile pyuria, or STI risk. - Pregnancy te

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Toxic/obstructed → escalate to imaging + source control; stable + diagnosed → disposition.
nodes.body: After initial labs, cultures, and any decompression \u2014 where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.body: Match the study to the question: - Suspected obstruction / stone with infection \u2192 CT abdomen/pelvis (non-contrast for stone; contrast-enhanced if abscess or emphysematous pyelonephritis suspected). This is the study that finds the surgical emergency. - Pregnancy or radiation-sparing \u2192 renal/bladder ultrasound to assess for hydronephrosis and post-void residual. - Retention \u2192 bladder

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit urosepsis/obstruction; observe complicated-but-stable; discharge uncomplicated with clear follow-up.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit the septic / obstructed / toxic patient. - IV antibiotics, ongoing resuscitation, and source control (ureteral stent / percutaneous nephrostomy for obstructed infection; drainage for abscess). - ICU for persistent hypotension, rising lactate, or organ dysfunction. - Urology (\u00B1 IR) involved for decompression; medicine/hospitalist for sepsis management. - Serial reassessment of hemodynami
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics + source control; ICU if unstable; urology/IR for decompression.

nodes.title: Observe / Shared Decision
nodes.body: Observation / shared decision-making for the complicated-but-stable patient \u2014 e.g., pyelonephritis tolerating oral intake, a prostatitis patient started on IV who may transition to oral, or borderline vitals. - A dose of IV/IM antibiotics and a period of observation with a repeat assessment can decide admit vs discharge. - Ensure reliable follow-up and a clear plan before any discharge; treat
nodes.recommendation: Short observation \u00B1 IV antibiotics, reassess, then admit or discharge with tight follow-up.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge the uncomplicated patient with a clear plan. - Uncomplicated cystitis: short-course guideline antibiotics, hydration, symptomatic relief, and return precautions (fever, flank pain, vomiting, no improvement in 48\u201372 h). - STI: empiric treatment given, partner therapy counseled, HIV/syphilis screening, follow-up / test-of-cure per guideline. - Retention relieved: trial of void vs disc
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with guideline antibiotics, partner therapy if STI, catheter/void plan if retention, and explicit return precautions + follow-up.

nodes.title: Ear Foreign Body Removal
nodes.summary: First removal attempt has highest success (65-78%) — plan technique before starting
nodes.body: External auditory canal (EAC) foreign bodies are common ED presentations, especially in children. Success rates are highest on the first attempt — plan your technique carefully before starting. nodes.title: Emergent Findings?

nodes.body: Screen for emergencies before attempting removal.

nodes.title: Button Battery — EMERGENCY
nodes.summary: Button battery causes necrosis in 1-2h — do NOT irrigate, emergent ENT removal
nodes.body: Button batteries cause liquefaction necrosis within 1-2 hours. This is a time-critical emergency.

nodes.summary: Kill insect first with mineral oil, then irrigate or use forceps to extract

nodes.title: Organic Material Removal

nodes.body: Seeds, beans, food particles, and plant material require DRY extraction — they swell with moisture. CONTRAINDICATED: Irrigation • Organic material absorbs water • Swelling impairs removal • Can convert simple FB to impaction PRIMARY TECHNIQUE: Alligator Forceps • Grasp firmly but avoid crushing • Seeds may be slippery — may need multiple attempts • If object crushes, remove pieces ALTERNATIVE: Rig

nodes.title: Small Particle Removal
nodes.summary: Irrigate with body-temp water for small particles — contraindicated if TM perforation
nodes.body: Sand, dirt, small debris — irrigation is usually the best approach. PRIMARY TECHNIQUE: Irrigation • 20-50 mL syringe with 14-16 gauge plastic catheter • Body-temperature water or saline • Patient head tilted, affected ear up • Direct stream along superior canal wall • Catch effluent in basin TECHNIQUE TIPS: • Lukewarm water only (cold causes vertigo) • Low pressure — avoid Waterpik (too forceful)

nodes.title: Complex / Irregular Objects

nodes.summary: Mastoiditis workup: CT with contrast looking for coalescent mastoiditis, subperiosteal abscess, intracranial extension
nodes.body: Laboratory Studies: • CBC with differential • BMP, CRP • Blood cultures Imaging — CT with IV Contrast: [13] | Finding | Significance | |---------|-------------| | Mastoid opacification | Non-specific (also in AOM/OME) | | Loss of bony septae | Coalescent mastoiditis | | Cortical bone destruction | Advanced disease | | Subperiosteal abscess | Requires surgical drainage | | Tegmen defect | Intracran

nodes.title: Mastoiditis — Treatment
nodes.summary: Mastoiditis: ceftriaxone + clindamycin IV; add vancomycin if MRSA risk; ENT consult for surgical evaluation
nodes.body: Mastoiditis IV Antibiotics Common Pathogens: • Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common) • Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS) • Staphylococcus aureus • Haemophilus influenzae • Pseudomonas (if chronic OM, tubes, recent abx) First-Line Empiric Regimens: [13][14] | Scenario | Antibiotic | Pediatric Dose | Adult Dose | |----------|------------|----------------|------------| | Standard | Ceftriaxone | 50-100 m

nodes.body: Absolute Indications for Surgery: [13] • Subperiosteal abscess → Incision and drainage • Coalescent mastoiditis on CT → Myringotomy + mastoidectomy • Intracranial complication (abscess, thrombosis) • No improvement after 48 hours IV antibiotics Surgical Options: | Procedure | Indication | |-----------|------------| | Myringotomy ± tube | Drain middle ear, obtain culture | | Subperiosteal abscess I

nodes.title: Admit — Mastoiditis
nodes.summary: Admit mastoiditis: IV ceftriaxone + clindamycin, CT temporal bone, urgent ENT consult, neuro checks if CNS concern
