nodes.title: Eating Disorders - Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Screen all ED patients with unexplained electrolyte abnormalities or weight loss for eating disorders
nodes.body: Eating disorders are psychiatric conditions with the highest mortality rate of any mental illness. The ED is often the first medical contact for complications [1]. MARSIPAN Risk Assessment Three main types: - Anorexia Nervosa (AN): Restriction, fear of weight gain, distorted body image - Bulimia Nervosa (BN): Binge-purge cycles, often normal weight - ARFID: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorde

nodes.title: Eating Disorder Type Assessment
nodes.summary: Classify as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or ARFID — guides medical workup
nodes.body: Distinguish the primary eating disorder type: Anorexia Nervosa (Restrictive or Binge-Purge): - BMI <18.5 kg/m\u00b2 (or <5th percentile in peds) - Intense fear of gaining weight - Distorted body image - Restriction +/- purging behaviors Bulimia Nervosa: - Recurrent binge eating + compensatory behaviors - Often normal or slightly elevated BMI - Self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, excessive

nodes.title: Anorexia Nervosa - Vital Sign Red Flags
nodes.summary: AN vital sign red flags: HR <40, SBP <90, temp <35.5°C, BMI <13 — high mortality risk
nodes.body: Anorexia Nervosa causes adaptive physiological changes that can rapidly decompensate [1][2]. MARSIPAN Risk Assessment Vital Sign Red Flags (MEED 2022, RCPsych CR233): | Finding | High Risk Threshold | |---------|--------------------| | Heart Rate | <40 bpm (40-50 = high concern) | | QTc | >460ms (female) / >450ms (male) | | Blood Pressure | Systolic <90 mmHg | | Orthostatic Drop | SBP drop >20 mmH

nodes.title: Bulimia Nervosa - Assessment
nodes.summary: Bulimia: hypokalemia most common, metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, QTc risk from low K+
nodes.body: Bulimia Nervosa often presents with complications from purging behaviors rather than low weight [1][3]. Purging Methods & Complications: | Method | Complications | |--------|---------------| | Vomiting | Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, dental erosions, Mallory-Weiss tears, esophageal rupture | | Laxatives | Hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, dehydration, cathartic colon | | Diuretics | Hypokalemia

nodes.title: ARFID - Assessment
nodes.summary: ARFID: nutritional deficiency without body image distortion — same malnutrition complications as AN
nodes.body: ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder) is characterized by nutritional deficiency without body image disturbance [3]. Diagnostic Criteria: - Eating disturbance leading to: - Significant weight loss or failure to gain - Significant nutritional deficiency - Dependence on enteral feeding or supplements - Marked interference with psychosocial functioning - NOT explained by food scarcity or

nodes.title: Medical Complications Assessment
nodes.summary: Identify primary complication: cardiac instability, electrolytes, or refeeding syndrome risk
nodes.body: Eating disorders affect every organ system. Identify the primary complication requiring treatment [1][2]. Cardiovascular: - Bradycardia, hypotension, orthostatic changes - QTc prolongation, arrhythmias - Pericardial effusion, CHF (refeeding) Metabolic/Electrolyte: - Hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia - Hypoglycemia - Refeeding syndrome (phosphate, K+, Mg2+ drops) Hematologic: - Pancytop

nodes.title: Cardiac Complications
nodes.summary: Bradycardia <50 or QTc >500ms — admit to telemetry, correct electrolytes first
nodes.body: Cardiac complications are the leading cause of death in eating disorders [1][2]. QTc Calculator Bradycardia: - Adaptive response to starvation (reduced metabolic demand) - HR <40 bpm is HIGH RISK - may indicate decompensation - Asymptomatic bradycardia still warrants monitoring - Usually improves with nutritional rehabilitation QTc Prolongation: - QTc >450ms = high risk for arrhythmia - Caused by

nodes.title: Electrolyte Derangements
nodes.summary: Correct hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia before refeeding
nodes.body: Electrolyte abnormalities are common and potentially fatal [1][4]. Electrolyte Replacement Guide Hypokalemia (Most Common): - Causes: Vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, starvation - Symptoms: Weakness, constipation, arrhythmias - K+ <3.0 mEq/L: IV replacement required - K+ <2.5 mEq/L: HIGH RISK for arrhythmia - Target: K+ >3.5 mEq/L before refeeding Hypophosphatemia: - Often normal or high-normal on

nodes.title: Refeeding Syndrome
nodes.summary: Refeeding syndrome risk: start low-calorie feeds, monitor phosphate q12h for 72h
nodes.body: Refeeding syndrome is a potentially fatal metabolic response to nutritional rehabilitation after starvation [1][4]. Refeeding Risk Calculator Pathophysiology: - Starvation depletes intracellular phosphate, potassium, magnesium - Carbohydrate reintroduction triggers insulin release - Insulin drives electrolytes INTO cells - Rapid extracellular depletion: arrhythmias, respiratory failure, death High

nodes.title: Risk Stratification - MARSIPAN Criteria
nodes.summary: Risk stratify using MARSIPAN criteria: BMI, vitals, electrolytes, ECG — determines disposition
nodes.body: MARSIPAN (Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa) provides admission criteria [2]. MARSIPAN Risk Assessment HIGH RISK - Admit to Medical Unit: - BMI <13 kg/m\u00b2 (adults) or <70% median BMI (peds) - HR <40 bpm or QTc >450ms - SBP <90 mmHg or orthostatic drop >20 mmHg - Temperature <35.5\u00b0C - Hypoglycemia (glucose <60 mg/dL) - K+ <3.0, Phos <2.0, Mg2+ <1.5 mEq/L - Rapid weig

nodes.title: BMI Severity Classification
nodes.summary: BMI severity: <15 high risk, <13 extreme risk — correlates with medical instability
nodes.body: BMI is a key indicator of severity in Anorexia Nervosa (DSM-5 criteria) [1][3]. BMI Calculator Adult AN Severity by BMI: | Severity | BMI (kg/m\u00b2) | Risk Level | |----------|------------|------------| | Mild | 17.0-18.49 | Outpatient | | Moderate | 16.0-16.99 | Day program | | Severe | 15.0-15.99 | Inpatient | | Extreme | <15.0 | Medical admission | MARSIPAN Critical Thresholds: - BMI <13: Ext

nodes.title: Acute Management Principles
nodes.summary: Medical stabilization takes precedence over psychiatric disposition — correct lethal derangements first
nodes.body: ED management priorities for medically unstable eating disorder patients [1][2][4]. Initial Stabilization: 1. Cardiac monitoring: Continuous telemetry 2. IV access: Two large-bore IVs 3. Labs: BMP, Mg2+, Phos, CBC, LFTs, glucose, ECG 4. Fluids: Cautious - avoid rapid volume expansion (CHF risk) Specific Interventions: | Problem | Intervention | |---------|-------------| | Bradycardia <40 | Monitor

nodes.title: Electrolyte Replacement Protocol
nodes.summary: Replace K+ before refeeding, Mg2+ before K+ (Mg depletion causes K+ wasting), check phosphate
nodes.body: Systematic electrolyte correction before and during refeeding [4]. Electrolyte Replacement Guide Order of Correction: 1. Magnesium FIRST (enables K+ repletion) 2. Potassium SECOND (most common deficit) 3. Phosphate THIRD (often normal until refeeding) Potassium Replacement: - K+ 3.0-3.5: PO KCl 40-80 mEq/day in divided doses - K+ 2.5-3.0: IV KCl 10 mEq/hr (peripheral) + PO - K+ <2.5: IV KCl 20 mEq

nodes.title: Refeeding Protocol - Start Low, Go Slow
nodes.summary: Start 10-20 kcal/kg/day, advance slowly over 5-7 days, replace phosphate aggressively
nodes.body: Safe refeeding initiation prevents refeeding syndrome [1][4]. Refeeding Risk Calculator Before Starting: - Correct K+ >3.0, Mg2+ >1.8, Phos >2.0 - Give Thiamine 100-200 mg IV (prevents Wernicke) - Baseline ECG, electrolytes, glucose Initial Caloric Prescription: | Risk Level | Starting Calories | Advancement | |------------|------------------|-------------| | Extreme (BMI <13) | 5-10 kcal/kg/day |

nodes.title: Cardiac Monitoring Protocol
nodes.summary: Continuous telemetry if QTc >450ms, HR <40, or electrolyte derangement — arrhythmia risk
nodes.body: Cardiac complications require vigilant monitoring [1][2]. QTc Calculator Telemetry Indications: - HR <50 bpm or >100 bpm - QTc >450 ms - Electrolyte abnormalities (K+ <3.5, Mg2+ <2.0) - During refeeding initiation (first 72h minimum) - Any arrhythmia history QTc Monitoring: - QTc 450-480 ms: Moderate risk - daily ECG, correct electrolytes - QTc >480 ms: High risk - q12h ECG, aggressive electrolyte

nodes.title: Psychiatric Assessment
nodes.summary: Psychiatric assessment after medical stabilization — assess suicidality, capacity, and motivation
nodes.body: Eating disorders have high rates of psychiatric comorbidity [1][5]. Suicide Risk: - AN has the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder - ~20% due to suicide - All patients need suicide risk assessment - Document: ideation, plan, intent, means, protective factors Common Comorbidities: - Major Depression (50-75%) - Anxiety disorders (up to 60%) - OCD (25-40%) - Substance use disorders - Person

nodes.title: Suicide Risk Management
nodes.summary: Eating disorders carry high suicide risk — formal safety assessment on all presentations
nodes.body: Suicide risk assessment is critical in eating disorder patients [5]. Risk Factors Specific to Eating Disorders: - Prior suicide attempts (strongest predictor) - Purging behaviors (higher risk than restrictive AN) - Comorbid depression, substance use, personality disorder - Recent weight restoration (paradoxically increases risk) - Treatment dropout - Longer duration of illness Assessment Questions

nodes.title: Capacity Evaluation & Treatment Refusal
nodes.summary: Assess decision-making capacity — severe malnutrition can impair cognition and judgment
nodes.body: Capacity assessment is essential when patients refuse treatment [5]. Four Components of Capacity: 1. Understanding: Can explain the diagnosis and proposed treatment 2. Appreciation: Recognizes how illness applies to their situation 3. Reasoning: Can weigh risks/benefits, compare alternatives 4. Expression: Can communicate a stable choice Factors That Impair Capacity in AN: - Severe malnutrition af

nodes.title: Involuntary Treatment Considerations
nodes.summary: Involuntary treatment may be needed if life-threatening refusal of care and lacks capacity
nodes.body: Involuntary psychiatric hold may be necessary for life-saving treatment [5]. Criteria for Involuntary Hold (vary by state): 1. Mental illness present (eating disorder qualifies) 2. Imminent danger to self (medical instability or suicide risk) 3. Unable to provide for basic needs (nutrition) 4. Less restrictive alternatives insufficient Medical Criteria Supporting Involuntary Hold: - BMI <13 with r

nodes.title: Disposition Planning
nodes.summary: Admit if BMI <15, HR <50, K+ <3.0, QTc >500, orthostatic, or refeeding risk
nodes.body: Disposition depends on medical stability AND psychiatric safety [1][2]. Medical Admission Criteria (MARSIPAN): - BMI <13 kg/m\u00b2 (or rapid weight loss) - HR <40 or QTc >450ms - SBP <90 or significant orthostatic changes - Temperature <35.5\u00b0C - Electrolyte abnormalities requiring IV correction - Refeeding syndrome risk requiring monitoring - Unable to stop purging behaviors Psychiatric Admi

nodes.title: Medical Admission
nodes.summary: Medical admission: HR <50, QTc >450, K+ <3.0, BMI <15, orthostatic, refeeding risk
nodes.body: Medical admission for eating disorder requires specialized care [1][2]. Admission Orders: - Telemetry monitoring - Strict I/Os, daily weights (AM, gowned, post-void) - Electrolytes q6-12h initially, then daily - Glucose q6h (hypoglycemia risk) - Daily ECG until QTc normalizes - 1:1 or close observation during/after meals - Bathroom supervision (prevent purging) Nutrition Orders: - Registered dieti
nodes.recommendation: Medical admission with telemetry, refeeding protocol, and psychiatric consultation. Target HR >50, QTc <450ms, normal electrolytes before discharge. Arrange appropriate step-down level of care.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Admission
nodes.summary: Psychiatric admission if medically stable but high self-harm risk or unable to maintain nutrition
nodes.body: Psychiatric admission for eating disorders requires medical clearance [1][5]. Indications: - Acute suicidality with plan/intent - Severe self-harm behaviors - Treatment refusal with lack of capacity - Severe functional impairment - Failed outpatient/partial hospitalization - Need for intensive behavioral intervention Medical Clearance Requirements: - HR >50 bpm - QTc <450ms - Electrolytes stable (
nodes.recommendation: Psychiatric admission after medical clearance. Ensure HR >50, QTc <450ms, stable electrolytes. Document risk assessment and recommended treatment level. Coordinate medical monitoring post-discharge.

nodes.title: Outpatient Disposition
nodes.summary: Outpatient only if medically stable, eating disorder team in place, and reliable follow-up
nodes.body: Outpatient management is appropriate for medically and psychiatrically stable patients [1]. Prerequisites for Discharge: - HR >50 bpm - SBP >90 mmHg, no significant orthostatics - QTc <450ms - K+ >3.5, Phos >2.5, Mg2+ >2.0 - No active suicidal ideation - Supportive living environment - Commitment to follow-up and treatment Discharge Instructions: 1. Follow-up: PCP within 1 week, eating disorder sp
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with close outpatient follow-up. PCP within 1 week, eating disorder specialist within 2 weeks. Provide written nutrition plan, safety resources, and clear return precautions.

nodes.title: EPSS for Systolic Function
nodes.summary: EPSS >7mm suggests LVEF <50%, invalid in AR, MS, HCM, or non-sinus rhythms
nodes.body: E-point septal separation (EPSS) >7 mm is a validated threshold for detecting reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). [1][2][3] This measurement provides an objective, rapid assessment that complements visual estimation of cardiac function. WHAT IS EPSS? EPSS measures the shortest distance between the anterior mitral valve leaflet at its peak opening (E-point) and the interventricular s

nodes.title: Patient Positioning & PLAX View
nodes.summary: Probe at 3rd-4th ICS near sternum, marker toward left hip — visualize septum, MV, LV
nodes.body: PATIENT POSITIONING Position the patient supine or in left lateral decubitus. Left lateral decubitus brings the heart closer to the chest wall and often improves image quality. PROBE SELECTION Use a phased-array cardiac transducer (2–5 MHz). Its small footprint fits between rib spaces. OBTAIN PARASTERNAL LONG-AXIS (PLAX) VIEW • Place the transducer in the 3rd–4th intercostal space, right next to t

nodes.title: Activate M-Mode Through the Mitral Valve
nodes.summary: Place M-mode cursor through mitral valve leaflet tips perpendicular to septum
nodes.body: CURSOR PLACEMENT With a good PLAX view on screen, activate M-mode and position the cursor: • Place the M-mode cursor perpendicular to the interventricular septum • The cursor should pass through the tips of the mitral valve leaflets at the level where they open in early diastole • Ensure both the septum and anterior mitral leaflet are clearly visible on the M-mode tracing [3] OPTIMIZING THE TRACIN

nodes.title: Measure EPSS
nodes.summary: Measure shortest distance from E-point peak to septum during early diastole
nodes.body: Measure the shortest distance between the peak of the anterior mitral valve leaflet (E-point) and the interventricular septum during early diastole. [1][2] IDENTIFYING THE E-POINT On the M-mode tracing, the anterior mitral leaflet traces a characteristic pattern: • E-point — the tallest peak, representing maximal opening during early diastole • A-point — a smaller peak just before systole, from at

nodes.title: Interpret EPSS Results
nodes.summary: EPSS <7mm = normal, 7-10mm = grey zone (check B-lines/IVC), >10mm = reduced EF
nodes.body: What is the measured EPSS value? THRESHOLDS • < 7 mm → Normal systolic function likely • 7–10 mm → Grey zone — assess for signs of fluid overload • > 10 mm → Reduced systolic function (heart failure likely)

nodes.title: EPSS < 7 mm — Normal Systolic Function
nodes.summary: EPSS <7mm — normal systolic function likely, correlate clinically
nodes.body: EPSS < 7 mm suggests preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≥50%). The anterior mitral leaflet reaches close to the septum during early diastole, indicating adequate ventricular filling dynamics and normal LV cavity size. CLINICAL INTEGRATION • Combine with visual estimation of global cardiac function across multiple views • Consider alternative quantitative measures if clinical suspic
nodes.recommendation: EPSS < 7 mm — normal systolic function likely. Correlate with clinical presentation and other echo views. If suspicion for dysfunction persists, obtain formal echocardiography.

nodes.title: EPSS > 10 mm — Reduced Systolic Function
nodes.summary: EPSS >10mm — 100% sensitivity for LVEF ≤30%, initiate heart failure workup
nodes.body: EPSS > 10 mm indicates significant left ventricular systolic dysfunction. [2][4] EPSS has 100% sensitivity for detecting LVEF ≤30% when >7 mm. [2] A measurement >10 mm strongly suggests severe reduction in ejection fraction. The increased separation reflects poor ventricular contractility and/or significant LV dilation — the anterior mitral leaflet cannot reach the septum during early diastolic fi
nodes.recommendation: EPSS > 10 mm — high likelihood of severe systolic dysfunction (LVEF ≤30%). Consider formal echo, initiate heart failure workup, and manage per clinical presentation.

nodes.title: EPSS 7–10 mm — Grey Zone Assessment
nodes.summary: EPSS 7-10mm grey zone — scan for B-lines and assess IVC to clarify
nodes.body: EPSS is in the grey zone (7–10 mm). Look for additional signs of fluid overload to help determine if systolic function is truly reduced. ASSESS B-LINES (Lung Ultrasound) • Scan bilateral anterior chest with linear or curvilinear probe • B-lines are vertical hyperechoic artifacts extending from the pleural line to the bottom of the screen • ≥3 B-lines per intercostal space in ≥2 zones bilaterally =

nodes.title: Grey Zone + Fluid Overload — Likely Reduced EF
nodes.summary: Grey zone EPSS + B-lines or plethoric IVC — likely reduced EF, get formal echo
nodes.body: EPSS 7–10 mm with signs of fluid overload (B-lines and/or IVC plethora) supports the diagnosis of reduced left ventricular systolic function. The combination of borderline EPSS with pulmonary edema or elevated right-sided pressures increases the likelihood that LVEF is truly reduced. CLINICAL NEXT STEPS • Assess additional echo views (A4C, PSAX) for visual estimation of global function • Consider
nodes.recommendation: EPSS in grey zone with fluid overload signs — likely reduced systolic function. Recommend formal echocardiography and heart failure workup.

nodes.title: Grey Zone, No Overload — Indeterminate
nodes.summary: Grey zone EPSS without overload signs — indeterminate, consider MAPSE or formal echo
nodes.body: EPSS 7–10 mm without signs of fluid overload. The clinical significance is indeterminate. EPSS specificity is moderate (52%) at the >7 mm threshold [2] — false positives can occur, particularly in this borderline range. POSSIBLE EXPLANATIONS • Early / compensated systolic dysfunction without volume overload • False positive — normal LVEF with borderline EPSS • Conditions that affect EPSS accuracy
nodes.recommendation: EPSS in grey zone without fluid overload — indeterminate. Correlate clinically and consider formal echocardiography. MAPSE and fractional shortening may provide additional data points.

nodes.title: Basic Emergency Echo Views
nodes.summary: FoCUS provides rapid LV function, pericardial effusion, RV strain, and IVC assessment
nodes.body: Focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) provides rapid assessment of: • Global cardiac function (LV squeeze) • Pericardial effusion / tamponade • RV size and strain (PE evaluation) • Volume status (IVC assessment) The 5 essential views in emergency echo: 1. Parasternal Long Axis (PLAX) 2. Parasternal Short Axis (PSAX) 3. Apical 4-Chamber (A4C) 4. Subcostal 4-Chamber 5. IVC (from subcostal) Probe: Phase

nodes.title: Parasternal Long Axis (PLAX)
nodes.summary: PLAX: 3rd-4th ICS, marker toward left hip — remember the 3 L's rule
nodes.body: Position: Left sternal border, 3rd–4th intercostal space Indicator: Toward right shoulder (or left hip in some conventions) Structures visualized: • Left ventricle (LV) • Left atrium (LA) • Mitral valve (MV) • Aortic valve (AV) and root • Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) • Pericardium Remember the 3 L's: Parasternal Long axis should have the Left ventricle on the Left side of the screen.

nodes.title: PLAX Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess pericardial effusion, LV function, RV size, aortic root, wall motion
nodes.body: Key findings to assess: 1. Pericardial effusion • Anechoic stripe between epicardium and pericardium • Posterior effusion most common location • Size: small (<10mm), moderate (10–20mm), large (>20mm) 2. LV function • Visual estimation of global squeeze • EPSS measurement for quantitative assessment • Normal EF: walls move in >50% during systole 3. RV size • RVOT should be <2/3 of LV diameter • Enl

nodes.title: Parasternal Short Axis (PSAX)
nodes.summary: PSAX: rotate 90 degrees clockwise from PLAX, marker toward left shoulder
nodes.body: From PLAX: Rotate probe 90° clockwise Indicator: Toward left shoulder Multiple levels (fan through): 1. Base (aortic valve level) • "Mercedes-Benz sign" — aortic valve with 3 cusps • See LA, RA, RVOT, TV 2. Mitral valve level • "Fish mouth" appearance of MV opening 3. Papillary muscle level • Two papillary muscles visible • Best level for assessing LV function • LV should appear circular ("O" shap

nodes.title: PSAX Assessment
nodes.summary: D-sign = RV pressure overload (PE/pulm HTN), assess wall motion and LV squeeze
nodes.body: Key findings to assess: 1. D-sign (septal flattening) • Normal LV is circular ("O" shape) • Pressure overload → D-shape (RV pressure pushes septum) • Seen in massive PE, pulmonary hypertension • Flattening during systole = pressure overload • Flattening during diastole = volume overload 2. Wall motion • All walls should contract symmetrically • Regional hypokinesis/akinesis → coronary territory in

nodes.title: Apical 4-Chamber (A4C)
nodes.summary: A4C: cardiac apex 5th-6th ICS, probe nearly horizontal pointing toward right shoulder
nodes.body: Position: Cardiac apex (mid-clavicular line, 5th–6th ICS) Indicator: Toward patient's left flank (3 o'clock) Technique: Probe nearly horizontal, pointing toward right shoulder Structures visualized (all 4 chambers): • Left ventricle (LV) — apex at top of screen • Right ventricle (RV) — to the left of LV on screen • Left atrium (LA) • Right atrium (RA) • Mitral valve (MV) • Tricuspid valve (TV) • I

nodes.title: A4C Assessment
nodes.summary: RV:LV ratio >1 = massive PE, McConnell sign (apical sparing) highly specific for PE
nodes.body: Key findings to assess: 1. RV:LV ratio • Normal: RV < 0.6 × LV size • RV = LV suggests moderate RV dilation • RV > LV suggests severe RV dilation (massive PE) 2. McConnell sign • RV free wall akinesis WITH apical sparing • Highly specific for acute PE • The apex "winks" while the rest of RV doesn't move 3. TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion) • M-mode through lateral tricuspid annulu

nodes.title: Subcostal 4-Chamber
nodes.summary: Subcostal: best view for pericardial effusion, use when poor parasternal/apical windows
nodes.body: Position: Just below xiphoid process Technique: Probe nearly flat against abdomen, angled toward left shoulder Indicator: Toward patient's left When to use: • Poor parasternal/apical windows (COPD, obesity, ventilated patients) • Best view for pericardial effusion (liver provides acoustic window) • Required view for IVC assessment Structures visualized: • All 4 chambers (RV is closest to probe) •

nodes.title: Subcostal Assessment
nodes.summary: Tamponade: RA systolic collapse (sensitive), RV diastolic collapse (specific)
nodes.body: Key findings: 1. Pericardial effusion • Often the BEST view for posterior effusion • Look for anechoic stripe between heart and liver • Effusion will be between epicardium and bright pericardial line 2. Tamponade physiology • RA systolic collapse (very sensitive) • RV diastolic collapse (very specific) • Swinging heart in large effusion 3. Global cardiac function • Often easier to see in patients

nodes.title: IVC Assessment
nodes.summary: IVC >2.1cm with <50% collapse = elevated CVP; <2.1cm with >50% collapse = volume responsive
nodes.body: From subcostal view: Rotate probe to visualize IVC entering RA Orientation: Longitudinal view of IVC Measure: 1. IVC diameter (2–3 cm from RA junction) 2. Respiratory variation (sniff test or quiet breathing) Interpretation: | IVC Diameter | Collapse | Estimated CVP | |--------------|----------|---------------| | <2.1 cm | >50% | 0–5 mmHg (low) | | <2.1 cm | <50% | 5–10 mmHg | | >2.1 cm | >50% | 5

nodes.title: Emergency Echo Summary
nodes.summary: Complete 5-view FoCUS checklist: effusion, LV function, RV strain, volume status
nodes.body: FOCUSED CARDIAC ULTRASOUND CHECKLIST: ☐ Pericardial effusion — PLAX, subcostal (best) ☐ LV function — PLAX, PSAX, A4C (visual + EPSS) ☐ RV size/strain — A4C (RV:LV ratio, McConnell sign) ☐ Volume status — IVC (diameter + collapse) Red flags requiring immediate text: • Large pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology • Severely dilated RV with hypotension (massive PE) • Severely reduced LV func
nodes.recommendation: Complete 5-view focused cardiac ultrasound. Integrate findings with clinical presentation. Formal echocardiography recommended for complex cases or when findings significantly change management.

nodes.title: Eclampsia Overview
nodes.summary: Eclampsia = new tonic-clonic seizures in preeclampsia, can occur up to 4 weeks postpartum
nodes.body: Eclampsia = new-onset tonic-clonic seizures in a patient with preeclampsia. [1,2] Definition requirements: [1] - Pregnancy ≥20 weeks gestation OR postpartum - Generalized tonic-clonic seizure - Absence of other cause (epilepsy, intracranial pathology) Timing of eclampsia: [2] - Antepartum: 38-53% - Intrapartum: 18-36% - Postpartum: 11-44% (most within 48h, can occur up to 4 weeks) Key epidemiology

nodes.title: Preeclampsia Spectrum
nodes.summary: 20-38% of eclampsia occurs WITHOUT prior preeclampsia diagnosis or hypertension
nodes.body: Eclampsia exists on the spectrum of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. [1,3] Preeclampsia without severe features: - BP ≥140/90 on two occasions ≥4h apart after 20 weeks - Proteinuria (≥300mg/24h or protein/creatinine ≥0.3) - OR other end-organ dysfunction without severe features Preeclampsia with severe features (any of): [1] - SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 (two readings 4h apart) - Platelets <100,000 -

nodes.title: Warning Signs
nodes.summary: Headache 66-83%, visual changes 27-44% precede seizure — but 20% have NO warning signs
nodes.body: Prodromal symptoms often precede eclamptic seizure: [1,2] Headache (66-83%): - Severe, persistent, frontal or occipital - Unrelieved by acetaminophen - Different from patient's usual headaches Visual disturbances (27-44%): - Scotomata (blind spots) - Blurred vision - Photophobia - Cortical blindness (rare) Epigastric/RUQ pain (12-25%): - Suggests hepatic involvement/HELLP - May mimic GERD, cholecy

nodes.title: Current Status

nodes.title: Blood Pressure in Eclampsia

nodes.title: Nifedipine (Oral Option)

nodes.title: Maternal Stabilization

nodes.body: Priorities for maternal stabilization: [1,2,7] Airway/Breathing: - Maintain SpO2 >94% - Supplemental O2 as needed - Aspiration precautions (left lateral positioning) - Intubation if: persistent AMS, airway compromise, respiratory failure Circulation: - Two large-bore IVs - Fluid resuscitation cautiously (avoid pulmonary edema) - Avoid aggressive fluid boluses (1-2L max unless hemorrhage) Ongoing m

nodes.title: HELLP Syndrome
nodes.summary: HELLP in 10-20% of eclampsia: LDH >600, AST/ALT >2x, platelets <100K — delivery is treatment
nodes.body: HELLP syndrome occurs in 10-20% of eclampsia cases. [3,7] Diagnostic criteria: [3] - Hemolysis: LDH >600, schistocytes, indirect bili elevated - Elevated Liver enzymes: AST or ALT >2x upper normal - Low Platelets: <100,000/µL Clinical presentation: - Epigastric/RUQ pain (65%) - Nausea/vomiting (36%) - Headache (31%) - May occur without hypertension or proteinuria (15-20%) Complications: - DIC (20%

nodes.title: Fetal Assessment
nodes.summary: Allow fetal recovery 15-30 min after seizure — do not rush to cesarean during active seizure
nodes.body: Fetal status monitoring during eclampsia: [1,7] Expected findings during/after seizure: - Fetal bradycardia (common) - Late decelerations - Loss of variability - Usually recover within 10-20 minutes Management approach: [7] - Continuous electronic fetal monitoring - Allow fetal recovery after seizure (15-30 minutes) - Intrauterine resuscitation: - Maternal left lateral positioning - Oxygen supplem

nodes.title: Delivery Decision
nodes.summary: Delivery is definitive treatment — target within 12-24h, cesarean not mandatory for eclampsia
nodes.body: Delivery is the definitive treatment for eclampsia. [1,2] Timing of delivery: - Eclampsia at ≥34 weeks: delivery after stabilization - Eclampsia at <34 weeks: consider delay for steroids IF stable - Never delay delivery for steroids if maternal/fetal compromise Indications for immediate delivery: - Maternal hemodynamic instability - Non-reassuring fetal status (persistent Category III) - Placental

nodes.title: Anesthesia Considerations
nodes.summary: Neuraxial preferred if platelets >70K — magnesium prolongs succinylcholine effect
nodes.body: Anesthesia consultation is essential. [1,7] Regional anesthesia (preferred if eligible): [14] - Epidural or spinal - Contraindicated if: platelets <70,000, coagulopathy, patient refusal - Check platelet count before neuraxial General anesthesia risks in eclampsia: [7] - Difficult airway (edema, short neck) - Hypertensive response to intubation - Increased aspiration risk - Drug interactions with m

nodes.title: Postpartum Management
nodes.summary: Continue mag 24-48h postpartum — most maternal deaths from eclampsia occur postpartum
nodes.body: Most maternal deaths from eclampsia occur postpartum. [1,2] Magnesium continuation: - Continue 24-48 hours after delivery OR after last seizure - Minimum 24 hours - Some protocols extend to 48 hours for severe cases Postpartum monitoring: - Frequent vital signs (q1h initially) - Continued neurologic assessment - Strict I/O - Watch for pulmonary edema (fluid mobilization post-delivery) BP managemen

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for refractory seizures/BP, multi-organ dysfunction; L&D for stabilized patients

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU with arterial line, continuous mag, prepare for urgent delivery with multidisciplinary team
nodes.body: ICU/high-acuity admission criteria: [1,7] Indications: - Refractory seizures - Refractory hypertension requiring continuous infusion - Respiratory failure / need for intubation - HELLP with DIC - Multi-organ dysfunction - Pulmonary edema - Suspected hepatic hemorrhage - Altered mental status >30 minutes ICU management: - Arterial line for BP monitoring - Continuous magnesium infusion with close mo
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU with OB/MFM co-management. Continuous monitoring, prepare for urgent delivery.

nodes.title: L&D Admission
nodes.summary: L&D with continuous fetal monitoring, mag infusion, serial BP checks q15-30min
nodes.body: Criteria for L&D (vs ICU): [1] - Seizures controlled on magnesium - BP controlled with intermittent IV or oral agents - Stable maternal status - Reassuring fetal status - No multi-organ dysfunction L&D management: - Continuous fetal monitoring - Magnesium infusion 1-2g/hr - Frequent BP checks (q15-30 min initially) - Neurologic checks every 1-2 hours - Strict I/O - Foley catheter Preparation for d
nodes.recommendation: Admit to L&D with continuous monitoring. Prepare for delivery within 12-24 hours. Continue magnesium and BP management.

nodes.title: ECMO — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: VV-ECMO = oxygenation only (needs good heart), VA-ECMO = oxygenation + circulatory support
nodes.body: ECMO Steps Summary — quick reference. ECMO = Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation A form of prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass that provides temporary support for refractory respiratory and/or cardiac failure [1][2]. Two primary configurations: VV-ECMO (Veno-Venous): • Provides oxygenation and CO₂ removal ONLY • No hemodynamic support • Patient must have adequate cardiac function • Bridge to lung rec

nodes.title: VV vs VA ECMO Selection
nodes.summary: When in doubt between VV and VA, go VA — VA supports both heart and lungs
nodes.body: VV vs VA Decision Tool The fundamental question: Does the patient need circulatory support? Choose VV-ECMO if: • Isolated respiratory failure • Adequate cardiac output (CI >2.2 L/min/m²) • No significant vasopressor requirement • MAP maintained without high-dose pressors • Cardiac function adequate on echo Choose VA-ECMO if: • Cardiogenic shock (any cause) • Refractory arrest • Combined cardiopulm

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Assessment for ECMO Selection
nodes.summary: Echo: LVEF >35% + CI >2.2 + low pressors = VV candidate; LVEF <25% + high pressors = VA
nodes.body: Rapid bedside assessment to determine VV vs VA: ECHO findings favoring VV-ECMO: • LVEF >35-40% • No significant RV dilation/dysfunction • Normal or near-normal cardiac output • No significant valvular disease ECHO findings favoring VA-ECMO: • LVEF <25-30% • Severe RV dysfunction • Global hypokinesis • Severe MR/AR (relative contraindication) Hemodynamic parameters: | Parameter | VV Candidate | VA

nodes.title: VV-ECMO Indications
nodes.summary: VV-ECMO for P/F <80 on FiO2 100% despite prone/optimal vent — lungs must be recoverable
nodes.body: RESP Score Calculator — VV-ECMO survival prediction. VV-ECMO is indicated for severe, potentially REVERSIBLE respiratory failure [1][2][5]. Classic indications: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (EOLIA criteria): • P/F ratio <50 for >3 hours, OR • P/F ratio <80 for >6 hours • Despite optimal ventilation, prone positioning, and FiO₂ >80% Hypercapnic respiratory failure: • pH <7.20-7.25 with PaCO₂ >60 m

nodes.title: VV-ECMO — When to Call
nodes.summary: Call ECMO center EARLY — mortality doubles if MV >7 days before ECMO initiation
nodes.body: CALL THE ECMO CENTER EARLY — don't wait until the patient is moribund [2][6]. Dr. Augustin's guidance (CV-EMCrit): Call for referral when: • Young patient with single organ failure • Reversible cause of respiratory failure • Failing conventional management • Mechanical ventilation <7 days (ideally) EOLIA/CESAR trial thresholds: • P/F <80 despite optimization • pH <7.25 with rising PaCO₂ • Murray s

nodes.title: VV-ECMO — Circuit Basics
nodes.summary: VV circuit: femoral drain to IVC/RA, return via IJ — heart still does ALL the pumping
nodes.body: VV-ECMO Circuit Visualization How VV-ECMO works: Blood flow: 1. Deoxygenated blood drained from venous system (usually femoral vein → IVC) 2. Passes through membrane oxygenator (adds O₂, removes CO₂) 3. Returned to venous system (usually IJ → SVC/RA junction) 4. nodes.title: VV-ECMO — Initial Settings & Lung Rest

nodes.summary: Poor patient SpO2 despite good ECMO flows — check cannula separation and recirculation
nodes.body: Recirculation Troubleshooting Recirculation = oxygenated blood returns to the circuit before reaching the systemic circulation [1][7]. Problem: ECMO is oxygenating its own output, not the patient's blood. nodes.title: VA-ECMO — Circuit Basics
nodes.summary: VA circuit: femoral vein drain, femoral artery return — MUST place distal perfusion cannula
nodes.body: VA-ECMO Circuit Visualization How VA-ECMO works: Blood flow: 1. Deoxygenated blood drained from venous system (femoral vein → IVC/RA) 2. Passes through centrifugal pump (provides forward flow) 3. Passes through membrane oxygenator (gas exchange) 4. Returned to arterial system (femoral artery → aorta) 5. nodes.title: Harlequin Syndrome (North-South)
nodes.summary: Upper body cyanosis + lower body pink = Harlequin syndrome — coronary/cerebral hypoxia risk
nodes.body: Harlequin Syndrome Management Harlequin Syndrome = Differential Hypoxemia [7][9] Also called North-South Syndrome or dual-circulation syndrome. What happens: In peripheral (femoral) VA-ECMO, as the native heart recovers: • Heart ejects deoxygenated blood (if lungs still failing) → goes to upper body (coronaries, brain) • ECMO returns oxygenated blood retrograde → goes to lower body • Mixing zone i

nodes.title: LV Distension on VA-ECMO
nodes.summary: LV distension: aortic valve not opening on echo — may need Impella or surgical LV vent
nodes.body: LV distension is a serious VA-ECMO complication [1][3]. Mechanism: • VA-ECMO increases afterload (retrograde arterial flow) • Failing LV cannot eject against increased afterload • Blood accumulates in LV → distension → pulmonary edema • Aortic valve may not open → stasis → LV thrombus Signs of LV distension: • Pulmonary edema on CXR (worsening) • Aortic valve not opening on echo • Severe MR • Risi

nodes.title: ECPR — Extracorporeal CPR
nodes.summary: ECPR for witnessed arrest, shockable rhythm, <60min CPR, reversible cause — 31.5% good neuro outcomes
nodes.body: ECPR = VA-ECMO during cardiac arrest [3][4][8]. Rationale: Conventional CPR provides only 20-30% of normal cardiac output. ECMO provides full circulatory support, allowing time for treatment of reversible cause. Evidence: • Belohlavek RCT: 31.5% survived to 180 days with good neuro outcomes (ECPR) vs 22% (conventional CPR) [8] • Observational data: 15-50% survival with ECPR vs 10-20% with conventi

nodes.title: ECPR — Logistics
nodes.summary: Target cannulation within 60min of arrest — continue mechanical CPR during cannulation
nodes.body: ECPR requires preparation and rapid deployment [8]. Time is critical: • Every 10 min of CPR without ECMO = worse outcomes • Target: cannulation within 60 minutes of arrest • Have team pre-notified if considering ECPR Cannulation during CPR: • Continue chest compressions during cannulation • Mechanical CPR device (LUCAS) helpful • Femoral-femoral cannulation (percutaneous or cut-down) • Ultrasound-

nodes.title: ECMO Contraindications
nodes.summary: Absolute: irreversible disease, severe neuro injury. VA-specific: severe aortic regurgitation
nodes.body: Patient selection is critical — inappropriate candidacy is a leading cause of poor ECMO outcomes [1][2][6]. ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATIONS: • Irreversible underlying disease — no recovery possible, not a transplant candidate • Advanced malignancy with poor prognosis • Severe irreversible neurologic injury (massive stroke, anoxic brain injury) • Unwitnessed arrest with prolonged downtime and no signs o

nodes.title: Communicating with CV Surgery/ECMO Team
nodes.summary: Have P/F ratio, pressor doses, lactate trend, echo findings, and exit strategy ready for ECMO call
nodes.body: When calling for ECMO consultation, have this information ready: Patient basics: • Age, weight, height (for BSA) • Chief complaint, timeline of deterioration • Comorbidities (especially vascular disease, bleeding risk, frailty) Respiratory parameters (if VV): • P/F ratio, FiO₂, PEEP, Pplat • Vent settings and duration of mechanical ventilation • ABG: pH, PaCO₂, PaO₂ • Prone positioning attempted?

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ECMO patients require specialized ICU — arrange transfer if not available locally
nodes.body: ECMO patients require specialized ICU care with experienced teams. Disposition depends on ECMO availability and patient stability.

nodes.title: Initiate ECMO
nodes.summary: Pre-cannulation: consent, blood products ready, anticoagulation plan, goals of care discussed
nodes.body: ECMO initiation — ICU admission with ECMO support. Pre-cannulation checklist: • Consent obtained (if possible) or emergency consent • Blood products available (PRBCs, FFP, platelets, cryo) • Type and screen/crossmatch • Access assessed (ultrasound, pulses) • Anticoagulation plan • Goals of care discussed with family Immediate post-cannulation: • Confirm flows and pressures • CXR for cannula positi
nodes.recommendation: Proceed with ECMO cannulation per institutional protocol. ICU admission with ECMO team management.

nodes.title: Not an ECMO Candidate
nodes.summary: Document contraindications, ECMO team discussion, and goals of care — continue max conventional therapy
nodes.body: Patient does not meet ECMO criteria or has contraindications. Document clearly: • Specific contraindications (irreversible disease, prolonged arrest, etc.) • Discussion with ECMO team if consulted • Goals of care discussion with family Continue aggressive conventional care: • Optimize ventilation (lung-protective, prone positioning) • Maximize medical hemodynamic support • Consider other rescue th
nodes.recommendation: Not an ECMO candidate. Continue conventional management or transition to comfort care based on goals of care discussion.

nodes.title: Transfer for ECMO
nodes.summary: Contact ECMO center early — mobile ECMO teams can cannulate at referring hospital
nodes.body: Patient may be an ECMO candidate — arrange transfer to ECMO center. Contact ECMO center EARLY: • Don't wait until patient is crashing • Provide all relevant data (see Communication module) • They may send a mobile ECMO team Mobile ECMO (ECMO retrieval): • Some centers can cannulate at referring hospital • Patient travels on ECMO support • Discuss logistics: distance, weather, staffing Pre-transfer
nodes.recommendation: Transfer to ECMO center after discussion with receiving team. Optimize patient for transport. Consider mobile ECMO if available.

nodes.title: ED Extubation Protocol
nodes.summary: ED extubation starts only after the original indication has clearly improved.
nodes.body: Steps Summary | Readiness Checklist Use this for ED patients who are intubated but may no longer need invasive ventilation: short procedure recovery, resolved intoxication, reversed hypercapnic failure, post-seizure recovery, or prolonged ED boarding after ICU-level improvement. Default posture: extubation is elective. If the airway may be hard to regain, delay unless the team and backup plan are

nodes.title: Why Extubate Now?
nodes.summary: Proceed only when extubation has a clear benefit and the reason for intubation improved.
nodes.body: Choose the best indication. If there is no clear clinical benefit to extubating in the ED, continue ventilatory support and hand off to ICU.

nodes.title: Do Not Extubate Yet
nodes.summary: No clear benefit means no ED extubation.
nodes.body: Continue ventilator support, analgesia/sedation appropriate to the airway plan, and ICU handoff. Reassess when the indication for intubation has resolved.
nodes.recommendation: No ED extubation now.

nodes.title: Hard Stop Screen
nodes.summary: Screen first for reasons ED extubation is unsafe.
nodes.body: Do-NOT / Delay Criteria Any hard stop should push the plan toward continued ventilation, ICU handoff, or extubation only with specialty backup.

nodes.title: Delay Extubation
nodes.summary: Hard stop present. Delay extubation.
nodes.body: Keep the tube. Optimize ventilator, sedation, hemodynamics, and oxygenation. If extubation is still desired, do it with ICU/anesthesia/RT support and a reintubation plan.
nodes.recommendation: Delay extubation or transfer to a higher-support setting.

nodes.title: Can They Protect the Airway?
nodes.summary: Airway protection matters as much as ventilator mechanics.
nodes.body: Assess mental status, cough strength, secretion burden, gag/swallow when relevant, and ability to follow simple commands. A passed SBT does not compensate for poor airway protection.

nodes.title: Airway Protection Fails
nodes.summary: Poor airway protection is a failed extubation screen.
nodes.body: Do not extubate for ventilator numbers alone. Continue airway control and reassess after sedation clears, secretions improve, or neurologic status changes.
nodes.recommendation: Keep intubated.

nodes.title: Spontaneous Breathing Trial
nodes.summary: Run a short SBT unless the patient has already proven spontaneous ventilation.
nodes.body: SBT Setup Use a structured SBT when the patient has not already demonstrated spontaneous ventilation. Common approaches: T-piece, CPAP, or low pressure support for 30 minutes. Watch the patient, not just the ventilator. Failure signs: distress, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hypoxemia, rising CO2, arrhythmia, hypotension, or worsening mental status.

nodes.title: SBT Result
nodes.summary: Passed SBT moves to failure-risk assessment.
nodes.body: Did the patient pass a monitored SBT or equivalent spontaneous ventilation assessment?

nodes.title: SBT Failed
nodes.summary: Failed SBT means no extubation now.
nodes.body: Resume ventilator support. Treat the reversible cause: bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, pain/anxiety, metabolic acidosis, fluid overload, pneumonia, or oversedation.
nodes.recommendation: Do not extubate after a failed SBT.

nodes.title: Extubation Failure Risk
nodes.summary: Identify who needs NIV or HFNC immediately after tube removal.
nodes.body: Post-Extubation Support Guide High-risk features include COPD, CHF, obesity/OSA, age >65, weak cough, secretion burden, prolonged ventilation, failed prior extubation, hypercapnia during SBT, or high oxygen needs.

nodes.title: Post-Extubation Stridor Risk
nodes.summary: Use cuff leak testing selectively for stridor risk.
nodes.body: Cuff Leak / Stridor Guide Cuff leak testing is most useful when risk is high. Do not use it as a universal screen.

nodes.title: Cuff Leak Result
nodes.summary: Absent cuff leak increases stridor risk and should trigger prophylaxis or delay.
nodes.body: If a cuff leak test is used, interpret it as a risk tool. A failed leak test is not a diagnosis, but it should change the plan.

nodes.title: Delay for Airway Edema Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Failed cuff leak: delay and treat edema risk if feasible.
nodes.body: If extubation is not urgent, delay and give systemic corticosteroid prophylaxis. Existing airway-edema entry: Dexamethasone. If extubation cannot wait, bring airway-skilled help to bedside and prepare for stridor or reintubation.
nodes.recommendation: Delay extubation when feasible after failed cuff leak.

nodes.title: Choose Post-Extubation Support
nodes.summary: Prepare NIV, HFNC, or standard oxygen before tube removal.
nodes.body: Post-Extubation Support Guide Pick the support device before tube removal. Have it set up, fitted, and ready at bedside.

nodes.title: Prep: Extubate to NIV
nodes.summary: NIV should be ready before tube removal in hypercapnic or CHF risk patients.
nodes.body: Set up BiPAP before tube removal. Fit mask, confirm settings, and brief the patient if awake. Reasonable ED starting point: IPAP 10-12, EPAP 5, FiO2 titrated to target SpO2. Adjust for ventilation and comfort.

nodes.title: Prep: Extubate to HFNC
nodes.summary: HFNC is a strong default for high-risk hypoxemic extubation.
nodes.body: Set up HFNC before tube removal. Start high flow, then titrate FiO2 to oxygen target. Use this when oxygenation support and dead-space washout are desired but NIV is not clearly needed.

nodes.title: Prep: Standard Extubation
nodes.summary: Standard extubation still requires suction, oxygen, BVM, and reintubation readiness.
nodes.body: Position upright. Suction mouth and ETT. Stop tube feeds if present. Confirm cuff syringe, suction, BVM, oxygen device, airway cart, and reintubation drugs/equipment are immediately available.

nodes.title: Tube Removal
nodes.summary: Remove tube only after suction, cuff deflation, and support device readiness.
nodes.body: 1. Explain if awake and coach breathing. 2. Preoxygenate on planned support. 3. Suction oropharynx and ETT. 4. Deflate cuff completely. 5. Remove tube smoothly during inspiration or with gentle positive pressure. 6. Apply planned oxygen/NIV/HFNC immediately. 7. Reassess work of breathing, voice, stridor, SpO2, ETCO2 if available, and mental status.

nodes.title: First 30 Minutes After Extubation
nodes.summary: The first 30 minutes decides whether extubation is holding.
nodes.body: Failure Rescue Guide Watch continuously for stridor, fatigue, secretion failure, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, aspiration, or worsening mental status.

nodes.title: Extubation Holding
nodes.summary: Stable early course. Keep monitoring.
nodes.body: Continue close observation, oxygen titration, pulmonary toilet, aspiration precautions, and disposition planning. High-risk patients need ICU or step-down level monitoring even if the first minutes look good.
nodes.recommendation: Extubation successful so far. Continue monitored care.

nodes.title: Post-Extubation Stridor
nodes.summary: Stridor is airway obstruction until proven otherwise.
nodes.body: Sit upright, give humidified oxygen, call for airway help, and prepare to reintubate if severe or worsening. Temporizing meds: Racemic Epinephrine and Dexamethasone. Do not let transient improvement delay reintubation if obstruction is progressing.
nodes.recommendation: Treat immediately and prepare for airway failure.

nodes.title: Post-Extubation Respiratory Failure
nodes.summary: Do not let rescue NIV delay reintubation in severe failure.
nodes.body: Established post-extubation failure has high risk. NIV can be appropriate immediately after extubation for prevention, but rescue NIV should not delay reintubation in severe failure.

nodes.title: Short NIV Bridge
nodes.summary: NIV bridge is time-limited and requires a reintubation plan.
nodes.body: Use NIV only if the phenotype fits and improvement is immediate: lower respiratory rate, better mentation, improved SpO2/ETCO2, and less work of breathing. Prepare reintubation equipment while reassessing.
nodes.recommendation: NIV bridge with minutes-level reassessment. Reintubate if not clearly improving.

nodes.title: Reintubate Early
nodes.summary: Severe failure after extubation needs definitive airway control.
nodes.body: Call for help, prepare RSI or awake approach based on airway risk, and reintubate before crash physiology develops. Use the difficult-airway plan if the airway is predicted hard to regain.
nodes.recommendation: Reintubate. Do not persist with failing noninvasive support.

nodes.title: Goals-of-Care Extubation
nodes.summary: Align extubation and rescue limits with the patient-specific goals of care.
nodes.body: Clarify intent: comfort-focused extubation, trial of noninvasive support, or DNI with full medical therapy. Confirm symptom medications, family presence if desired, and what level of re-escalation is allowed.
nodes.recommendation: Follow the documented goals-of-care airway plan.

nodes.title: ED Methadone Management
nodes.summary: 72-hour rule allows any DEA provider to administer/dispense 3-day methadone for withdrawal
nodes.body: ED Methadone Steps Summary Methadone is a full mu-opioid agonist used for opioid use disorder (OUD) maintenance therapy. Unlike buprenorphine, methadone can only be dispensed for OUD maintenance through licensed Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs). [1] However, the 72-hour rule (21 CFR 1306.07(b)) allows any DEA-registered provider to administer or dispense up to a 3-day supply of methadone for emerg

nodes.title: Clinical Scenario
nodes.summary: Determine: established OTP patient, new initiation candidate, unclear dose, or inpatient bridging
nodes.body: What is the clinical scenario?

nodes.title: Initiation Eligibility
nodes.summary: Exclude AMS, respiratory depression, QTc >500, active sedative intoxication before initiation
nodes.body: Exclusion criteria for ED methadone initiation: - Altered mental status (intoxication, psychosis, delirium) - Respiratory depression or respiratory rate < 12 - Known prolonged QTc (> 500 ms) or Torsades history - Active sedative/alcohol intoxication - Concurrent benzodiazepine or sedative-hypnotic withdrawal Note: Screening ECG is not required for initial low-dose methadone. QTc prolongation risk

nodes.title: Methadone vs Buprenorphine
nodes.summary: Buprenorphine generally preferred — methadone when fentanyl use or prior bup induction failures
nodes.body: Buprenorphine is generally preferred for ED-initiated MOUD due to superior safety profile and lower regulatory burden. [6] Consider methadone when: - High-potency synthetic opioid (HPSO/fentanyl) use with high precipitated withdrawal risk - Prior buprenorphine induction failures - Patient preference for methadone - Very high opioid tolerance - Active fentanyl use with inability to abstain for bupr

nodes.title: Buprenorphine Preferred
nodes.summary: Buprenorphine is safer (partial agonist ceiling), no OTP required, better evidence for ED initiation
nodes.body: Buprenorphine advantages: - Partial agonist ceiling effect (safer in overdose) - No QTc prolongation - Any DEA-licensed provider can prescribe (no OTP required) - Bridge prescription can be written at discharge - Better evidence for ED-initiated treatment engagement [6] For buprenorphine protocols, see: Opioid Withdrawal Consult If buprenorphine precipitated withdrawal is a concern: - Consider mic
nodes.recommendation: Buprenorphine is first-line for most ED MOUD initiations. See Opioid Withdrawal consult for protocols.

nodes.title: OTP Dose Verification
nodes.summary: Always verify dose with OTP before guest dosing — patients may overstate dose
nodes.body: Guest dosing = administering methadone to a patient who is already enrolled in an OTP but cannot access their usual clinic. Verification is critical. Patients may: - Overstate their dose (risk of respiratory depression) - Have been discharged from their program - Have last-dosed more recently than reported To verify: 1. Call the OTP directly (patient should have clinic contact info) 2. Confirm: cu

nodes.title: Verification Outcome
nodes.summary: Determine if OTP verified the dose, clinic is closed, or patient is not enrolled
nodes.body: Were you able to verify the patient's methadone dose with their OTP?

nodes.title: Uncertain Methadone Dose
nodes.summary: When dose unverified, give conservative 20-30mg regardless of claimed dose — safety first
nodes.body: When a patient claims to be on methadone maintenance but dose cannot be verified: Do NOT administer the patient's claimed full dose. Risk of respiratory depression if dose is overstated. Safe approach: - Give conservative dose (20-30 mg) regardless of claimed dose - Explain rationale to patient - Document inability to verify - Arrange OTP follow-up for proper dosing Red flags for dose overstatemen

nodes.title: Not Currently Enrolled in OTP
nodes.summary: Not enrolled in OTP — treat as new initiation (max 30mg) or consider buprenorphine instead
nodes.body: Patient is not enrolled in claimed methadone program. This changes the clinical approach significantly. Options: 1. Treat as new initiation under 72-hour rule if withdrawal present (COWS >= 8) 2. Buprenorphine induction (preferred for most patients) 3. Symptomatic treatment only with non-opioid adjuncts Do NOT give high-dose methadone without verified tolerance. Risk of fatal respiratory depressio
nodes.recommendation: Patient not enrolled in OTP. Treat as new initiation (max 30 mg) or consider buprenorphine. Do not give high-dose methadone without verified tolerance.

nodes.title: Inpatient Methadone Continuation
nodes.summary: Continue verified methadone during hospitalization — abrupt discontinuation causes severe withdrawal
nodes.body: Hospitalized patients on methadone maintenance should continue their methadone to prevent withdrawal and facilitate treatment of their primary medical condition. Verification required: Confirm dose with OTP before administering. If verified: Continue home dose (QTc monitoring if >100 mg or other risk factors). If unverified: Use conservative dose (30-40 mg) and verify on next business day. Key poi
nodes.recommendation: Continue verified methadone dose during hospitalization. Coordinate discharge with OTP. Do not abruptly discontinue.

nodes.title: Verified Guest Dose
nodes.summary: Administer verified OTP dose, observe 30 min, may return daily for up to 72h
nodes.body: Methadone - Administer the verified daily dose. Protocol: 1. Give single daily dose as confirmed by OTP 2. Observe for at least 30 minutes post-administration 3. Patient may return tomorrow if clinic still closed (72-hour rule) 4. Document OTP verification, dose given, and plan If dose >100 mg: Consider ECG before administration if not recently checked. ED length of stay: Patients presenting for g
nodes.recommendation: Administer verified OTP dose. Observe 30 min. May return daily for up to 72 hours until OTP reopens.

nodes.title: Unverified/Conservative Dosing
nodes.summary: Give 30mg PO when unverified — may add 10mg after 2-4h if COWS still elevated (max 40mg Day 1)
nodes.body: Methadone 30 mg PO (conservative dose) When dose cannot be verified: - Give 30 mg regardless of claimed dose - Explain to patient: "We can't verify your dose, so we're giving a safe amount that will prevent severe withdrawal" - Most patients on maintenance will not experience significant intoxication from 30 mg - Arrange verification and proper dosing at next OTP visit If symptoms persist after 30
nodes.recommendation: Methadone 30 mg PO when dose unverified. May add 10 mg after 2-4h if needed (max 40 mg Day 1 unverified).

nodes.title: Methadone Initiation Dosing
nodes.summary: Standard starting dose 30mg PO — reduce to 20mg if recent opioid use or concurrent sedatives
nodes.body: 72-Hour Rule Initiation Protocol: Under 21 CFR 1306.07(b), ED physicians may administer or dispense up to 3 days of methadone for withdrawal management while arranging OTP linkage. [2][3] Standard starting dose: 30 mg PO [4] Reduce to 20 mg if: - Opioid use within prior 4 hours - Currently using sedatives (benzodiazepines, alcohol) - Significant drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitors) - Elderly or d

nodes.title: ED Methadone Initiation Protocol
nodes.summary: Day 1: 30mg (max 40mg), Days 2-3: 40mg — must link to OTP within 72 hours
nodes.body: Methadone 30 mg PO initial dose Day 1 Protocol: 1. Confirm COWS >= 8 before dosing 2. Give Methadone 30 mg PO 3. Observe 2-4 hours 4. If COWS remains >= 13: may give additional 10 mg (max 40 mg Day 1) 5. Observe 30 min after each dose Day 2-3 (if dispensing for take-home): - Day 2: 40 mg - Day 3: 40 mg - Dispense with clear instructions - OTP appointment must be within 72 hours If 72-hour linkage
nodes.recommendation: Methadone 30 mg PO Day 1 (max 40 mg). Days 2-3: 40 mg. Must link to OTP within 72 hours.

nodes.title: Rapid Titration (HPSO Era)
nodes.summary: Fentanyl-era rapid titration: 30mg start, 10mg increments — typical effective range 50-70mg
nodes.body: In the fentanyl era, patients with high-potency synthetic opioid (HPSO) dependence often require higher doses for adequate symptom control. [11][12] Rapid titration approach: - Start 30 mg - Assess COWS every 1-2 hours - Additional 10 mg increments as needed - Goal: COWS < 8 - Typical effective range: 50-70 mg by end of Day 1-2 [12] Bridge clinic data (2024-2025): - Mean starting dose: 51.6 mg - M

nodes.title: Alternative Approaches
nodes.summary: If methadone contraindicated: buprenorphine preferred, or clonidine + symptomatic management
nodes.body: When methadone is contraindicated or not appropriate: Option 1: Buprenorphine - First-line for most ED MOUD initiations - Safer (partial agonist ceiling) - No QTc prolongation - Can prescribe bridge without OTP linkage - Opioid Withdrawal Consult Option 2: Symptomatic management only - Clonidine 0.1-0.3 mg PO q1h PRN (max 0.8 mg/day) - Antiemetics (ondansetron) - Antidiarrheals (loperamide) - NSAI
nodes.recommendation: If methadone contraindicated: consider buprenorphine (preferred) or symptomatic treatment with non-opioid adjuncts.

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Pregnancy: methadone preferred, do NOT discontinue. Liver disease: reduce dose 50%
nodes.body: Pregnancy: - Methadone is preferred over buprenorphine in pregnancy (longer track record) - Do NOT discontinue methadone in pregnant patients (risk of fetal distress, preterm labor) - Continue home dose and coordinate with OB and OTP - Higher doses often needed in third trimester (increased metabolism) Hepatic impairment: - Reduce dose by 50% in severe liver disease - Monitor for accumulation (lon

nodes.title: Monitoring Protocol
nodes.summary: Monitor RR q15-30min x 2h, SpO2 continuous, COWS before and 2-4h after dosing
nodes.body: Post-dose monitoring: - Respiratory rate: q15-30 min x 2h, then q1h x 2h - SpO2: continuous or q30 min - Sedation: assess response to verbal/tactile stimuli - COWS score: before and 2-4 hours after dosing Observation duration: - First dose: minimum 2-4 hours - Subsequent doses: minimum 30-60 minutes if patient known tolerant - Guest dosing (verified): 30 minutes minimum Red flags requiring interve

nodes.title: QTc Prolongation Risk
nodes.summary: ECG if dose >100mg or QT-prolonging drugs — QTc ≥500ms: avoid methadone, cardiology consult
nodes.body: Methadone prolongs QTc in a dose-dependent manner. [13] When to obtain ECG: - Dose > 100 mg/day - Combining with other QT-prolonging drugs - History of cardiac disease, syncope, or arrhythmia - Family history of long QT syndrome - Electrolyte abnormalities (hypoK, hypoMg) When ECG NOT required: - Single dose <= 40 mg in otherwise healthy patient - Known stable maintenance dose without prior QTc is

nodes.title: QT-Prolonging Drug Interactions
nodes.summary: Common QTc interactions: ondansetron, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, CYP3A4 inhibitors
nodes.body: Common QT-prolonging medications in OUD patients: - Ondansetron (often used for withdrawal nausea) - Loperamide (especially at high/abused doses) - Antipsychotics: haloperidol, quetiapine, ziprasidone - Antidepressants: citalopram, escitalopram, amitriptyline - Antibiotics: fluoroquinolones, azithromycin - Antiemetics: prochlorperazine, promethazine CYP3A4 inhibitors (increase methadone levels): -

nodes.title: Respiratory Depression Management
nodes.summary: Methadone respiratory depression may be DELAYED (peak 3-4h) and PROLONGED (t1/2 8-59h)
nodes.body: Methadone respiratory depression: - May be delayed (peak effect 3-4h after PO dosing) - Prolonged (half-life 8-59 hours) - No ceiling effect (unlike buprenorphine) If respiratory depression occurs: 1. Stimulate patient, support airway 2. Naloxone - but be prepared for prolonged infusion 3. Initial: 0.04-0.4 mg IV (titrate to RR, not full reversal) 4. Infusion may be needed: 0.25-0.5 mg/hour 5. Mon

nodes.title: Methadone Toxicity/Overdose
nodes.summary: Titrate naloxone to RR not full reversal — continuous infusion often needed, observe 8-24h
nodes.body: Signs of methadone toxicity: - Miosis, sedation, slurred speech - Respiratory depression (RR < 12) - Hypotension - QTc prolongation, Torsades de Pointes Management: 1. Airway support (BVM, intubation if needed) 2. Naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV titrated to respiratory effort 3. Continuous naloxone infusion often needed: 0.25-0.5 mg/hr 4. Cardiac monitoring (QTc, arrhythmias) 5. Correct electrolytes (K+,
nodes.recommendation: Methadone toxicity requires prolonged observation (8-24h). Naloxone infusion often needed. Monitor for QTc prolongation and arrhythmias.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Assess stability for discharge with OTP plan vs observation/admission for high-risk features
nodes.body: Assess patient stability and disposition needs.

nodes.title: Discharge with OTP Linkage
nodes.summary: Discharge with OTP appointment within 72h, naloxone kit, and clear return precautions
nodes.body: Discharge checklist: 1. OTP appointment scheduled within 72 hours 2. Take-home doses (if dispensing under 72-hour rule): - Day 2: 40 mg - Day 3: 40 mg - Clear written instructions - Store safely away from children 3. Naloxone kit prescribed or provided 4. Return precautions: - Difficulty breathing - Excessive drowsiness - Chest pain or palpitations - Return of severe withdrawal symptoms 5. Documen
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with OTP appointment within 72 hours. May dispense up to 3-day supply. Provide naloxone and clear return precautions.

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.summary: Admit if respiratory concerns, QTc prolongation, polysubstance use, or social instability
nodes.body: Consider admission if: - First-dose observation with any respiratory depression - QTc > 500 ms or arrhythmia - Concurrent medical condition requiring inpatient care - Concurrent intoxication requiring monitoring - No safe discharge environment - Suicide risk - Unable to arrange 72-hour OTP linkage Inpatient management: - Continue methadone dosing (can be administered by hospital pharmacy) - Teleme
nodes.recommendation: Admit for respiratory depression, QTc >500 ms, or inability to safely discharge. Continue methadone, do not abruptly stop.

nodes.title: Linkage Barriers
nodes.summary: Common OTP linkage barriers: transportation, wait lists, hours, cost — buprenorphine if linkage impossible
nodes.body: Common barriers to OTP linkage: - Transportation: OTPs require daily in-person visits initially - Capacity: Wait lists at many programs - Hours: Most open early morning only - Cost: Insurance, Medicaid coverage varies - Distance: Rural areas may have limited OTP access Predictors of successful 72-hour linkage: [15] - OTP enrollment at time of ED visit (OR 2.63) - Higher methadone dose (OR 1.20 per

nodes.title: Documentation Requirements
nodes.summary: Document 72-hour rule use, COWS scores, doses given/dispensed, and OTP referral in chart
nodes.body: Required documentation for 72-hour rule use: 1. Clinical indication for methadone (opioid withdrawal, OUD) 2. COWS score before and after treatment 3. Doses administered (with times) 4. Doses dispensed for take-home (if any) 5. OTP referral made (program name, appointment date/time) 6. Patient counseling performed (overdose risk, safe storage, naloxone) 7. Statement that methadone was provided und

nodes.title: Harm Reduction & Education
nodes.summary: Prescribe naloxone, counsel on overdose risk and safe storage — methadone lethal to opioid-naive
nodes.body: Before discharge: 1. Naloxone - prescribe or provide 2. Overdose risk counseling: - Tolerance decreases rapidly during abstinence - Risk of overdose highest in first 2 weeks of treatment - Never use alone - Avoid mixing with benzodiazepines, alcohol 3. Fentanyl test strips if available 4. Safe storage: - Methadone is extremely dangerous to opioid-naive individuals - Keep locked away from children
nodes.recommendation: Provide naloxone, overdose risk counseling, safe storage education. SAMHSA helpline: 1-800-662-4357.

nodes.title: Emergency Contraception
nodes.summary: EC prevents ovulation; FDA-labeled non-abortifacient; no absolute contraindications; time-sensitive
nodes.body: Emergency contraception (EC) prevents pregnancy after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure. Key principles: • EC works by preventing ovulation — NOT by disrupting implantation • FDA-labeled as non-abortifacient (Dec 2022 label update) • Safe, effective, and legal in all 50 states • No absolute medical contraindications (ACOG/CDC) EC options by efficacy: 1. Copper IUD — >99% effective,

nodes.title: Pregnancy Testing
nodes.summary: Pregnancy test not required; EC will not harm existing pregnancy; safe if status unknown
nodes.body: Pregnancy test is NOT required before EC if timing is appropriate. When to test: • If last menstrual period (LMP) was >4 weeks ago • If patient has had multiple unprotected events • If considering IUD insertion If pregnancy test is positive: • EC will NOT work (already pregnant) • EC will NOT harm existing pregnancy • No teratogenic effects documented • Counsel on pregnancy options Safe to give EC

nodes.title: Time Since Intercourse
nodes.summary: Calculate from earliest unprotected intercourse; timing determines optimal method
nodes.body: Time since unprotected intercourse determines optimal EC method. If multiple events over several days, calculate from the earliest unprotected intercourse. Note: LMP and ovulation timing can extend window if intercourse occurred before ovulation.

nodes.title: Method Selection: 0-24 Hours
nodes.body: Best efficacy window — all methods highly effective. Decision factors: • Long-term contraception desired? → Cu-IUD • Weight >165 lbs or BMI >25? → Ulipristal or Cu-IUD • Need OTC access now? → Levonorgestrel • On enzyme-inducing meds? → Cu-IUD or double-dose LNG Efficacy at 0-24h: • Cu-IUD: >99% • Ulipristal: 94% (65% better than LNG) • Levonorgestrel: 91%

nodes.title: Method Selection: 24-72 Hours
nodes.body: Standard EC window — all oral methods still effective. At 24-72h, efficacy: • Cu-IUD: >99% • Ulipristal: 95% (42% better than LNG) • Levonorgestrel: 87-90% Consider ulipristal over levonorgestrel if: • Weight >165 lbs or BMI >25 • Approaching 72h mark • Want highest oral efficacy Levonorgestrel advantages: • OTC (no prescription wait) • Lower cost (~$40 vs ~$50)

nodes.title: Method Selection: 72-120 Hours
nodes.body: Extended window (3-5 days) — levonorgestrel efficacy significantly reduced. At 72-120h, efficacy: • Cu-IUD: >99% • Ulipristal: ~95% (maintains effectiveness) • Levonorgestrel: 72-87% (declining) Ulipristal is PREFERRED over levonorgestrel in this window — maintains efficacy while LNG drops significantly. [2,4] If ulipristal unavailable: • LNG is still better than nothing • Consider double dose (3

nodes.title: Method Selection: >120 Hours
nodes.summary: Only Cu-IUD may work beyond 5 days; oral EC not effective; counsel on pregnancy test timing
nodes.body: Beyond 5 days — limited options. Copper IUD may still work if: • Within 5 days of ovulation (not intercourse) • Can determine ovulation timing from LMP/cycle • Example: Intercourse day 7, ovulation day 14 → IUD on day 13 still effective If cycle timing uncertain: • Cu-IUD can still be placed if negative pregnancy test • Efficacy less certain but still reasonable option Oral EC NOT effective after

nodes.title: Levonorgestrel (Plan B)
nodes.summary: LNG 1.5 mg x1; OTC no age limit; efficacy drops after 72h and with higher weight; double dose if enzyme inducers
nodes.body: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg — single dose oral EC. Brands: Plan B One-Step, Take Action, My Way, AfterPill, others Dosing: • Standard: 1.5 mg x1 (or 2 × 0.75 mg tablets at once) • High-risk: 3 mg x1 if on enzyme inducers OR weight >165 lbs Timing: | Window | Pregnancy Rate | Efficacy | |--------|----------------|----------| | <24h | 0.5% | 91% | | <72h | 0.8% | 87-90% | | 72-96h | 1.2% | 75-80% | | 96-1

nodes.summary: WAIT 5 DAYS before hormonal contraception; barrier only for 5 days; contraindicated with enzyme inducers

nodes.summary: Backup option only; 100 mcg EE + 0.5 mg LNG x2 (12h apart); give antiemetic prophylaxis; 56-86% effective
nodes.body: Yuzpe regimen — combined estrogen-progestin EC. Use ONLY if LNG, UPA, and IUD unavailable.
