nodes.title: Copper IUD: Most Effective EC
nodes.summary: Cu-IUD >99% effective; unaffected by weight/timing/meds; up to 5 days; provides long-term contraception
nodes.body: Copper IUD (ParaGard) — gold standard for emergency contraception. Efficacy: >99% (pregnancy rate 0.1%) Timing: • Within 5 days of unprotected intercourse, OR • Within 5 days of ovulation (if determinable) • Can insert any time in cycle if pregnancy test negative Advantages: • Highest efficacy of any EC method • Unaffected by weight or body habitus • Unaffected by timing within window • Unaffected

nodes.title: Copper IUD Eligibility
nodes.body: Screen for IUD eligibility: Can insert in ED if: • Trained provider available • Equipment available • Patient desires IUD for EC + ongoing contraception Contraindications (CDC MEC Category 4): • Current pregnancy • Current purulent cervicitis or PID • Unexplained vaginal bleeding (until evaluated) • Cervical/endometrial cancer • Uterine cavity distortion (fibroids, anomaly) • Wilson disease (coppe

nodes.title: Copper IUD Insertion
nodes.summary: Standard insertion technique; NSAIDs for pain; string check 4-6 weeks; heavier periods first 3-6 months
nodes.body: ED IUD insertion for EC: Pre-procedure: • Pregnancy test (if not done) • Bimanual exam for uterine position • STI testing if high-risk (can insert before results) • NSAIDs for pain (ibuprofen 400-600 mg) Procedure: • Standard IUD insertion technique • Confirm string visibility and length • Document string length in chart Post-procedure: • Cramping and spotting expected • NSAIDs PRN for cramping •

nodes.title: IUD Referral
nodes.summary: Give oral EC as bridge; schedule IUD ASAP; UPA preferred if >72h; abstain/barrier until IUD placed
nodes.body: If unable to insert IUD in ED: Urgent referral options: • OB/GYN clinic (next day if possible) • Family planning clinic (Planned Parenthood) • Primary care if trained Bridge therapy: • Give oral EC NOW (ulipristal or levonorgestrel) • Oral EC can "bridge" until IUD placed • IUD can still be placed within 5 days of intercourse Important timing: • If >72h since intercourse, use ulipristal (not LNG)

nodes.title: Weight Considerations
nodes.body: Weight affects oral EC efficacy — levonorgestrel more than ulipristal. Evidence-based thresholds: • >165 lbs (~75 kg) or BMI >25: LNG efficacy reduced • >195 lbs (~89 kg) or BMI >30: Both LNG and UPA efficacy reduced • Cu-IUD unaffected by weight Recommendations by weight: | Weight | First Choice | Second Choice | |--------|--------------|---------------| | <165 lbs | Any method | — | | 165-195 lb

nodes.title: Drug Interactions
nodes.summary: Enzyme inducers reduce oral EC efficacy; UPA contraindicated; double LNG to 3 mg; Cu-IUD unaffected
nodes.body: CYP3A4 enzyme inducers significantly reduce oral EC efficacy. Medications that reduce EC efficacy: Anticonvulsants: • Phenytoin (Dilantin) • Carbamazepine (Tegretol) • Phenobarbital • Oxcarbazepine • Topiramate (>200 mg/day) Antibiotics: • Rifampin (most potent) • Rifabutin Antiretrovirals: • Efavirenz, nevirapine • Some protease inhibitors Other: • St. John's Wort • Griseofulvin Management: • Uli

nodes.title: EC Choice with Drug Interactions
nodes.body: Patient on enzyme-inducing medication: Choose the best option based on availability and patient preference.

nodes.title: High-Dose Levonorgestrel
nodes.summary: LNG 3 mg x1 for enzyme inducers or high weight; give 2 × 1.5 mg tablets; same counseling as standard dose
nodes.body: Levonorgestrel 3 mg — for enzyme inducers or weight >165 lbs. Dosing: 3 mg x1 (double the standard dose) How to give: • Two 1.5 mg tablets (Plan B) at once, OR • Four 0.75 mg tablets at once Evidence: • UK FSRH recommends doubling for enzyme inducers • Mixed evidence for weight-based doubling (2024 study showed no clear benefit) • Reasonable to offer when Cu-IUD or UPA unavailable Side effects: Sa

nodes.title: Contraindications & Safety
nodes.summary: No absolute contraindications to oral EC; IUD has standard IUD contraindications; safe in pregnancy (ineffective but not harmful)
nodes.body: ACOG/CDC: "No absolute medical contraindications to EC." NOT contraindications to oral EC: • Existing pregnancy (won't work, but won't harm) • History of ectopic pregnancy • Breastfeeding (safe for infant) • History of VTE/thromboembolism • Migraine with aura • Liver disease • Cardiovascular disease Ulipristal-specific: • Avoid if on enzyme-inducing medications • Avoid in severe hepatic impairment

nodes.title: Legal Status Overview
nodes.summary: EC legal in all states; FDA labeled non-abortifacient; Plan B OTC no age limit; ella Rx; Cu-IUD standard of care
nodes.body: Emergency contraception is LEGAL in all 50 states. FDA classification: • EC is a contraceptive, NOT an abortifacient • Dec 2022 label update: "does not terminate pregnancy" • Mechanism: prevents ovulation, does NOT disrupt implantation Access by method: | Method | Access | Age Limit | |--------|--------|----------| | Plan B | OTC | None | | ella | Rx | None | | Cu-IUD | Provider | None | Restricti

nodes.title: EC Disposition & Follow-up
nodes.body: Discharge instructions: Expected effects: • Nausea, headache, fatigue — usually mild • Menstrual changes — period may be early or late • Spotting or irregular bleeding Return precautions: • Period >7 days late → pregnancy test • Severe abdominal pain → evaluate for ectopic • Heavy bleeding → evaluate Ongoing contraception: • After LNG: Start hormonal method immediately + backup x7 days • After UPA
nodes.recommendation: Provide EC immediately. Counsel on expected effects and return precautions. Discuss ongoing contraception. Follow up with PCP/OB-GYN.

nodes.title: Sexual Assault Considerations
nodes.summary: Offer EC to all assault survivors; Catholic hospitals require LH testing; document offer and decision
nodes.body: EC in sexual assault cases: Standard of care: • Offer EC to ALL sexual assault survivors • Should be offered regardless of patient's stated desire for pregnancy • Patient may accept or decline Hospital requirements (most states): • Must provide information about EC • May be required to offer or dispense EC • Some states require direct dispensing Texas: • Must provide information about EC • NOT req

nodes.title: Epistaxis Assessment
nodes.summary: 90% anterior (Kiesselbach plexus) — assess hemodynamics, history, and anticoagulant use
nodes.body: Epistaxis Steps Summary - quick reference. Immediate assessment: \u2022 Hemodynamic stability (HR, BP, mental status) \u2022 Estimate blood loss (usually overestimated) \u2022 Establish IV access if significant bleeding \u2022 Type and screen if severe/recurrent History: \u2022 Duration and severity of current episode \u2022 Prior episodes and treatments \u2022 Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use \u202

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Status
nodes.summary: Assess hemodynamic stability — tachycardia, hypotension, or active hemorrhage = unstable
nodes.body: Assess hemodynamic stability before proceeding. Unstable indicators: \u2022 Tachycardia (HR >100) \u2022 Hypotension (SBP <90) \u2022 Altered mental status \u2022 Active hemorrhage with continuous swallowing/spitting blood \u2022 Signs of hypovolemia

nodes.title: Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Two large-bore IVs, type and crossmatch, compress nares while resuscitating — early ENT notification
nodes.body: Simultaneous resuscitation and hemorrhage control: \u2022 Large-bore IV access x 2 \u2022 NS bolus 500-1000 mL \u2022 Type and crossmatch \u2022 CBC, BMP, coagulation studies \u2022 Consider transfusion if Hgb <7 g/dL or ongoing hemorrhage While resuscitating: \u2022 Apply firm compression to bilateral nares (pinch fleshy part below nasal bones) \u2022 Patient upright with head slightly forward (r

nodes.title: Initial Hemostasis
nodes.summary: Firm compression of FLESHY part (not bony bridge) x 15-20min + oxymetazoline spray
nodes.body: Step 1: Compression Patient applies firm, sustained pressure over the fleshy part of nose (not bony bridge) for 15-20 minutes without releasing to check. Step 2: Topical vasoconstrictor + anesthetic \u2022 Oxymetazoline 0.05% spray 2-3 sprays per nostril \u2022 OR Phenylephrine / Epinephrine soaked pledget \u2022 Add Lidocaine 4% for anesthesia Step 3: Visualization After 10-15 min with vasoconstr

nodes.title: Bleeding Site Localization
nodes.summary: After vasoconstriction: visualize source — posterior if blood in oropharynx, no anterior source
nodes.body: After topical vasoconstriction and visualization: Anterior bleed indicators (90%): \u2022 Visible bleeding point on septum (Kiesselbach plexus) \u2022 Unilateral bleeding \u2022 Blood drips from anterior nares Posterior bleed indicators (10%): \u2022 Blood flows down posterior pharynx \u2022 Bilateral bleeding \u2022 No visible anterior source despite adequate visualization \u2022 Associated with:

nodes.title: Chemical Cautery
nodes.summary: Silver nitrate from periphery to center, 5-10 sec — NEVER cauterize both sides of septum
nodes.body: Silver nitrate cautery technique: 1. Ensure adequate anesthesia (topical lidocaine) 2. Dry the area with cotton-tipped applicator 3. Apply silver nitrate stick to bleeding point for 5-10 seconds 4. Work from periphery toward center 5. Apply to limited area only (excessive cautery causes necrosis) CAUTION: Never cauterize both sides of septum in same session - risk of septal perforation. Topical TX

nodes.title: Anterior Nasal Packing
nodes.summary: Inflatable balloon or expanding sponge preferred — apply topical TXA or oxymetazoline to packing
nodes.body: Packing options (in order of preference): 1. Inflatable balloon device (Rapid Rhino, Epistat): \u2022 Lubricate with water-soluble gel \u2022 Insert along floor of nose parallel to palate \u2022 Inflate with air (follow device instructions) \u2022 Secure with tape to prevent posterior displacement 2. Expanding sponge (Merocel, Rhino Rocket): \u2022 Coat with antibiotic ointment \u2022 Insert along
nodes.recommendation: Anterior nasal packing with balloon device or expanding sponge. Consider topical TXA-soaked packing for anticoagulated patients.

nodes.title: Packing Assessment
nodes.summary: Observe 15-30min post-packing — check posterior pharynx for ongoing bleeding
nodes.body: After anterior packing placement: Observe for 15-30 minutes to confirm hemostasis. Check posterior pharynx for ongoing bleeding (may indicate posterior source or failed anterior pack).

nodes.title: Posterior Epistaxis
nodes.summary: Posterior bleeds are more serious — 18% need surgery, call ENT early
nodes.body: Posterior bleeds are more serious - often require admission and ENT intervention. Risk factors: \u2022 Age >50 \u2022 Hypertension \u2022 Anticoagulation \u2022 Bleeding disorders \u2022 Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) Source: Usually sphenopalatine artery (branch of internal maxillary) Call ENT early - 18% of posterior epistaxis patients require surgical intervention. Options: 1. Dual

nodes.title: Posterior Packing
nodes.summary: Dual-balloon device or Foley catheter — inflate posterior balloon first, then anterior
nodes.body: Option 1: Dual-balloon device (preferred) Devices designed for posterior epistaxis (Epistat, Rapid Rhino Epistaxis): \u2022 Insert along nasal floor \u2022 Inflate posterior balloon first (5-10 mL air) \u2022 Then inflate anterior balloon (10-15 mL air) \u2022 Secure to prevent displacement Option 2: Foley catheter technique \u2022 10-14 French Foley catheter \u2022 Insert through nostril until ti
nodes.recommendation: Place posterior pack using dual-balloon device or Foley catheter. ENT consultation required. Admit to monitored bed.

nodes.title: Posterior Epistaxis Disposition
nodes.summary: ALL posterior packs require admission with continuous SpO2 and ENT consultation
nodes.body: All posterior packs require admission. Admission orders: \u2022 Continuous pulse oximetry \u2022 Cardiac monitoring (consider ICU/step-down) \u2022 Head of bed elevated \u2022 NPO if surgical intervention anticipated \u2022 IV access maintained \u2022 Serial H/H if significant blood loss Antibiotic prophylaxis (controversial): Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID or Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID E
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored bed. Continuous SpO2. ENT consultation for pack removal at 48-72h or surgical intervention if needed.

nodes.title: Anticoagulation Status
nodes.summary: Assess anticoagulant/antiplatelet status — 50-60% of ED epistaxis patients are on antithrombotics
nodes.body: Is the patient on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy? Agents to consider: \u2022 Warfarin \u2022 DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) \u2022 Heparin / LMWH \u2022 Aspirin \u2022 P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel) 50-60% of ED epistaxis patients are on antithrombotic therapy.

nodes.title: Warfarin Management
nodes.summary: Do NOT routinely reverse warfarin — local hemostasis first, Vitamin K only if supratherapeutic
nodes.body: Check INR immediately. Supratherapeutic INR (>3): \u2022 Vitamin K 2.5-5 mg PO (effect in 12-24h) \u2022 Hold warfarin until INR therapeutic Therapeutic INR but refractory bleeding: \u2022 Local hemostasis is still the priority \u2022 Consider holding 1-2 doses \u2022 Vitamin K 1-2.5 mg PO if persistent Life-threatening hemorrhage (rare): \u2022 4-factor PCC 25-50 units/kg + Vitamin K 10 mg IV \u2
nodes.recommendation: Check INR. Local hemostasis first. Consider holding 1-2 doses or low-dose Vitamin K only if supratherapeutic or refractory. Do not routinely reverse.

nodes.title: DOAC Management
nodes.summary: DOACs cause less severe epistaxis than warfarin — local hemostasis, hold 1-2 doses if severe
nodes.body: DOACs and epistaxis: \u2022 DOACs cause LESS severe epistaxis than warfarin \u2022 Most can be managed without reversal \u2022 Holding 1-2 doses is reasonable (12-24h effect similar to vitamin K for warfarin) Management approach: \u2022 Aggressive local hemostasis \u2022 Consider holding 1-2 doses if severe/recurrent \u2022 Do NOT hold if high CHADS-VASC (stroke risk > bleed risk) Life-threatening
nodes.recommendation: Local hemostasis is sufficient for most DOAC-associated epistaxis. Consider holding 1-2 doses for severe cases. Reversal rarely needed.

nodes.title: Antiplatelet Management
nodes.summary: Topical TXA especially helpful for antiplatelet patients — generally do NOT hold antiplatelets
nodes.body: Antiplatelet agents and epistaxis: \u2022 Aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors may prolong bleeding \u2022 Local hemostasis is still effective \u2022 Generally do NOT hold antiplatelet therapy for epistaxis Topical TXA particularly helpful: Tranexamic Acid 500 mg in 5 mL on pledget x 10-20 min Studies show faster hemostasis than packing in antiplatelet patients. Consider holding only if: \u2022 Severe/lif
nodes.recommendation: Local hemostasis. Topical TXA is helpful. Generally do not hold antiplatelets unless severe hemorrhage and no recent coronary intervention.

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Determine: no pack (discharge), anterior pack (ENT follow-up 24-48h), or admission
nodes.body: Bleeding is now controlled. Assess disposition based on: \u2022 Need for nasal packing \u2022 Anticoagulation status \u2022 Hemoglobin level \u2022 Ability to follow up \u2022 Risk of recurrence

nodes.title: Discharge - No Packing
nodes.summary: Saline spray, petroleum jelly BID, humidifier, avoid nose picking — return if not controlled in 20 min
nodes.body: Discharge instructions: Prevention: \u2022 Saline nasal spray 2-3x daily \u2022 Petroleum jelly to anterior septum BID \u2022 Humidifier at night \u2022 Avoid nose picking, forceful blowing \u2022 Avoid NSAIDs If bleeding recurs: \u2022 Pinch fleshy part of nose firmly x 15-20 min \u2022 Lean forward (not back) \u2022 Oxymetazoline spray if available \u2022 Return if not controlled in 20 min Follo
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with prevention instructions and return precautions. PCP follow-up in 1-2 weeks. ENT if recurrent.

nodes.title: Discharge - Anterior Pack
nodes.summary: Antibiotic prophylaxis while packed, mandatory ENT follow-up at 24-48h for pack removal
nodes.body: Patient is stable with anterior packing in place. Discharge instructions: \u2022 Keep pack in place - do not remove or adjust \u2022 Sleep with head elevated \u2022 Take soft diet \u2022 Avoid strenuous activity Antibiotic prophylaxis: Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID or Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID while pack in place. (Evidence limited but commonly prescribed to prevent toxic shock.) Follow
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with anterior pack. Antibiotic prophylaxis. Mandatory ENT follow-up at 24-48h for pack removal.

nodes.title: Admit - Anterior Epistaxis
nodes.summary: Admit if Hgb <8, unable to achieve hemostasis, high-risk anticoagulation, or coagulopathy
nodes.body: Admission indications for anterior epistaxis: \u2022 Significant anemia (Hgb <8 g/dL) requiring transfusion \u2022 Unable to achieve hemostasis in ED \u2022 High-risk anticoagulated patient \u2022 Coagulopathy requiring correction \u2022 Unreliable patient / unable to follow up \u2022 Multiple ED visits for recurrent epistaxis Admission orders: \u2022 Cardiac/SpO2 monitoring \u2022 Serial H/H if s
nodes.recommendation: Admit for monitoring, serial labs, ENT consultation, and definitive management.

nodes.title: ENT Consultation Triggers
nodes.summary: Emergent ENT for posterior or uncontrolled bleeding; urgent for bilateral packs or recurrent episodes
nodes.body: Emergent ENT consultation: \u2022 Posterior epistaxis (any) \u2022 Uncontrolled bleeding despite anterior packing \u2022 Hemodynamic instability \u2022 Need for surgical intervention (ligation, embolization) Urgent ENT consultation: \u2022 Bilateral anterior packs \u2022 Recurrent epistaxis (>2 episodes) \u2022 Suspected septal abnormality \u2022 Suspected HHT (hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasi

nodes.title: Hypertension and Epistaxis
nodes.summary: HTN rarely causes epistaxis — BP usually normalizes after bleeding controlled, treat bleeding first
nodes.body: Common misconception: Hypertension CAUSES epistaxis. Reality: \u2022 Epistaxis causes anxiety which raises BP \u2022 HTN may exacerbate but rarely initiates bleeding \u2022 BP usually normalizes after bleeding controlled Management: 1. Control the bleeding first - local hemostasis is the priority 2. Recheck BP after hemorrhage controlled and patient calm 3. If BP remains severely elevated (>180/12

nodes.title: Topical TXA in Epistaxis
nodes.summary: Topical TXA on pledget x 10-20min — faster hemostasis in antiplatelet patients than packing alone
nodes.body: Topical Tranexamic Acid: Tranexamic Acid 500 mg in 5 mL solution applied via pledget. Evidence: \u2022 RCT (124 patients on antiplatelets): TXA vs anterior packing - Faster hemostasis at 10 min - Less rebleeding at 24h and 1 week - Shorter ED stay - Higher patient satisfaction [5] \u2022 NoPAC trial: TXA vs placebo for epistaxis uncontrolled with first aid - No significant difference in this popul

nodes.title: Esophageal Food Bolus: Disimpaction
nodes.summary: Triage by secretions, exclude perforation and dangerous objects, bridge, then scope and biopsy.
nodes.body: Adult who suddenly cannot swallow during a meal ("steakhouse syndrome"). The bolus is almost always lodged at a pathologic narrowing. Priorities: triage by secretions, exclude perforation, exclude a hidden dangerous object, then relieve the obstruction and find the cause. Open first: - Disimpaction Steps - ASGE Timing Windows - Do NOT Core sequence: 1. Can the patient handle secretions? Drooling/c

nodes.title: Can the Patient Handle Secretions?
nodes.summary: Drooling / cannot swallow saliva = complete obstruction = emergent endoscopy.
nodes.body: The single most important triage question is whether the obstruction is complete. A patient who is drooling and cannot swallow their own saliva has a complete obstruction and is at risk of aspiration — this is an airway/emergent problem.

nodes.title: Any Sign of Perforation?
nodes.summary: Crepitus/severe pain/fever = suspected perforation: STOP, image, no push or pharmacology.
nodes.body: Before any reduction maneuver or pharmacology, screen for esophageal perforation — a feared complication that changes everything. Red flags: subcutaneous crepitus (neck/chest), severe or tearing chest/back pain, fever, tachycardia/sepsis, Hamman crunch, or a prolonged impaction (>24 h) with a sharp/bony bolus.

nodes.title: Suspected Perforation — STOP
nodes.summary: Suspected perforation: NPO, water-soluble CT, antibiotics, surgery/GI; no push or pharmacology.
nodes.body: Do not attempt pharmacologic disimpaction, blind passage, or effervescent agents. - Make the patient NPO; resuscitate; IV access, fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering oral/anaerobic flora. - Imaging: CT chest with water-soluble (not barium) oral contrast or a water-soluble contrast esophagram. Avoid barium when perforation is suspected. - Consult thoracic/GI surgery and gastroenterology eme
nodes.recommendation: NPO, resuscitate, water-soluble contrast CT/esophagram, antibiotics, emergent surgical + GI consult. No push, no pharmacology.

nodes.title: Is This Truly Just Soft Food?
nodes.summary: Confirm soft food only; a button battery or sharp object routes to GI Foreign Body.
nodes.body: Confirm the impaction is a soft food bolus and not a dangerous true foreign body that happens to be stuck with food. A button battery in the esophagus is a same-hour emergency; sharp bones, long/large objects, and magnets follow different rules.

nodes.title: Dangerous Object — Use GI Foreign Body Pathway
nodes.summary: Battery/sharp/magnet/true foreign body: switch to the GI Foreign Body consult.
nodes.body: This is not a simple food bolus. A button battery in the esophagus can cause liquefactive necrosis within hours and is a same-hour emergency; sharp/pointed objects, long (>5-6 cm) objects, and multiple magnets also need urgent endoscopy. Go to GI Foreign Body for object-specific timing, battery protocol, sharp-object handling, and magnet rules.
nodes.recommendation: Route to the GI Foreign Body pathway for object-specific, time-critical management.

nodes.title: Timing & ASGE/ESGE Windows
nodes.summary: Complete: scope <6 h. Partial: scope <24 h. Never leave a bolus impacted >24 h.
nodes.body: Timing drives urgency (ASGE/ESGE): - Complete obstruction (cannot manage secretions): endoscopy emergently, within ~6 hours — aspiration risk. - Partial obstruction / food bolus without complete obstruction: endoscopy urgently, within 24 hours. - A bolus should not be left impacted beyond 24 hours — prolonged contact causes pressure necrosis, ulceration, and perforation risk. Do not delay definiti

nodes.title: Pharmacologic Bridge (Optional, Low-Yield)
nodes.summary: Glucagon 1 mg IV (low-yield, may vomit). NO papain. No effervescent in complete obstruction.
nodes.body: Pharmacology is an adjunct, not a substitute for endoscopy. Success rates are low and it must never delay scope in complete obstruction. Glucagon (glucagon) relaxes lower esophageal sphincter smooth muscle: - 1 mg IV slow push; may repeat once after ~10-20 min if no response. - Common: nausea/vomiting (which can occasionally dislodge the bolus, but also raises aspiration/Boerhaave concern); warn t

nodes.title: Definitive Endoscopy
nodes.summary: Endoscopy is definitive: push to stomach or retrieve; protect the airway in complete obstruction.
nodes.body: Flexible endoscopy is the definitive treatment and is successful in the large majority of cases. Approaches: - Push technique: gently advance the bolus into the stomach once the distal lumen is confirmed patent — preferred when safe and quick. - Retrieval: extract piecemeal with a Roth net, snare, or forceps; an overtube protects the airway and allows repeated passes. - Airway protection (overtube

nodes.title: Find the Underlying Cause — Biopsy for EoE
nodes.summary: Impaction = narrowed esophagus until proven otherwise; biopsy for EoE (\u22656), start a PPI.
nodes.body: A food bolus impaction is a symptom of a narrowed esophagus until proven otherwise. Identify and address the cause. Common structural causes: Schatzki ring, peptic stricture, eosinophilic esophagitis, and (especially in older patients with weight loss/progressive dysphagia) malignancy. Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is the leading cause of food impaction in young adults, especially men, and recurr

nodes.title: Disposition & Follow-up
nodes.summary: Home on PPI with GI follow-up for EoE/biopsy/dilation; admit complications.
nodes.body: After the bolus is cleared and the cause addressed: Discharge an uncomplicated patient who is comfortable, tolerating secretions and oral intake, with no perforation concern. - Start/continue a PPI. - Arrange gastroenterology follow-up for biopsy results, EoE management, and dilation planning. - Counsel on recurrence prevention: chew thoroughly, avoid large meat boluses, treat reflux/EoE. Admit /
nodes.recommendation: Discharge uncomplicated, secretion-tolerant patients on a PPI with GI follow-up for EoE/biopsy and dilation; admit perforation, difficult extraction, or aspiration.

nodes.title: State of Extreme Agitation with Aggression: First Screen
nodes.summary: First decide whether this is a dangerous resuscitation syndrome or agitation that allows assessment first.
nodes.body: This consult is for severe hyperactive delirium with dangerous agitation, especially when paired with hyperthermia, acidosis, stimulant toxidrome, prolonged struggle, restraint, or physiologic collapse. Use the term "excited delirium" for searchability, not as a final diagnosis. Treat the physiology first, then find the cause. Terminology note: the AMA adopted policy in 2021 stating that current e

nodes.title: Danger Path: Control the Room and the Physiology
nodes.summary: Dangerous hyperactive delirium is a resuscitation syndrome: stop the struggle, sedate early, monitor, cool, and treat complications.
nodes.body: Treat as a resuscitation. Immediate actions: - Call security, nursing, respiratory therapy, and a physician team lead. - Assign roles before contact: medication, airway, monitor, IV/IO/labs, cooling, restraints. - Remove weapons and reduce noise/stimulation if this does not delay control. - Avoid prone, hog-tie, or compressive restraint. Move to supine or lateral as soon as safely possible. - Chem

nodes.title: Assessment-First Path: Keep It Short
nodes.summary: If safe, de-escalate while rapidly screening for glucose, oxygenation, temperature, toxidrome, trauma, and infection.
nodes.body: If the patient can be engaged safely, use verbal de-escalation while another clinician screens for reversible medical danger. Rapid screen: - Glucose. - Oxygen saturation and ETCO2 if available. - Temperature. - Pulse, BP, respiratory rate. - Trauma, toxidrome, meningismus, focal neuro deficit, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, sepsis, withdrawal, pregnancy, and medication causes. Escalate immediately to the

nodes.title: Which Phenotype Fits Best?
nodes.summary: Identify stimulant/hyperthermic physiology, undifferentiated severe delirium, older frailty, or a medical mimic.
nodes.body: Pick the dominant phenotype. You can return after the first sedation pass.

nodes.title: Core Syndrome: Hyperactive Delirium with Severe Agitation
nodes.summary: Severe hyperactive delirium is dangerous until physiology is controlled and medical causes are excluded.
nodes.body: This is not a psychiatric clearance problem. It is a high-risk physiologic state until proven otherwise. High-risk features: - Extreme agitation, panic, paranoia, or incoherent delirium. - Prolonged physical struggle or restraint. - Hyperthermia or hot, diaphoretic skin. - Tachycardia, hypertension, hypoxia, shock, or exhaustion. - Severe lactate/acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, hyperkalemia, dysrhy

nodes.title: Stimulant or Hyperthermic Phenotype
nodes.summary: Stimulant hyperthermia needs benzodiazepines, cooling, fluids, and complication surveillance; avoid antipsychotic-only therapy.
nodes.body: Think cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA, synthetic cathinones, PCP co-ingestion, serotonin syndrome, anticholinergic toxicity, or heat stroke. Treatment priorities: - Benzodiazepines are core therapy for stimulant agitation, sympathomimetic toxicity, and seizures. - Rapid external cooling for life-threatening hyperthermia. - IV crystalloid, electrolyte correction, and rhabdomyolysis surveillance. - A

nodes.title: Do Not Miss Medical Causes
nodes.summary: Treat the agitation while looking for tox, heat illness, infection, CNS, endocrine, withdrawal, pain, and medication causes.
nodes.body: Hyperactive delirium is a presentation, not the cause. Actively evaluate: - Hypoglycemia or hypoxia. - Sepsis, meningitis, encephalitis. - Intracranial hemorrhage, stroke, seizure/postictal state, head trauma. - Heat stroke, serotonin syndrome, NMS, anticholinergic toxicity, salicylate/toxic alcohols, CO, alcohol or sedative withdrawal. - Thyroid storm, adrenal crisis, hepatic/uremic encephalopath

nodes.title: Sedation Strategy: Pick the Patient in Front of You
nodes.summary: Choose sedation by immediate danger, stimulant/hyperthermia, undifferentiated agitation, frailty, QT risk, or acidosis.
nodes.body: The safest medication is the one that reliably stops dangerous muscle activity and lets the team monitor, cool, oxygenate, and diagnose. Do not delay sedation for ECG or labs if the patient is an immediate violent threat or physiologically crashing.

nodes.title: Immediate Threat: Ketamine Dissociation
nodes.summary: Ketamine 4-5 mg/kg IM is fastest for immediate violent threat, but requires airway-ready monitoring.
nodes.body: Use when the patient is an immediate danger and prolonged struggle is more dangerous than dissociation. Good fit: - Uncontrolled violent behavior preventing safe care. - Failed or impossible stepwise sedation. - Hyperthermic/exhausted patient who needs immediate control for cooling and monitoring. Cautions: - Prepare airway, suction, oxygen, monitor, and capnography. - Watch for hypersalivation, l
nodes.recommendation: Ketamine provides fastest reliable control when immediate threat makes prolonged struggle unsafe.

nodes.title: Stimulant, Withdrawal, or Hyperthermic Toxidrome: Benzodiazepines
nodes.summary: Midazolam 5 mg IM or 2-5 mg IV, repeat q5-10 min, is core therapy for stimulant and withdrawal physiology.
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines directly treat sympathomimetic surge, withdrawal physiology, seizures, and muscle activity. Use repeated titration when the patient remains dangerously agitated, hypertensive, tachycardic, hyperthermic, or seizing. Avoid underdosing the crashing stimulant patient, but plan respiratory support in older, intoxicated, hypoventilating, or multi-sedative patients.
nodes.recommendation: Use benzodiazepines as core therapy for stimulant/hyperthermic agitation, withdrawal, and seizure-risk agitation.

nodes.title: Undifferentiated Severe Agitation: Droperidol + Midazolam
nodes.summary: Droperidol 5-10 mg plus midazolam 5 mg is evidence-supported for undifferentiated severe agitation when QT/stimulant hyperthermia are not dominant.
nodes.body: For severe agitation without stimulant hyperthermia or high QT risk, ACEP supports droperidol plus midazolam, or an atypical antipsychotic plus midazolam, for more rapid and efficacious sedation than either class alone. Do not let the ECG requirement create a dangerous delay. If the patient is an immediate threat, sedate first and obtain ECG as soon as safe. Avoid this as antipsychotic-only therap
nodes.recommendation: Use combination sedation when undifferentiated severe agitation needs fast reliable control and stimulant hyperthermia/QT risk are not dominant.

nodes.title: Older, Frail, Dementia, or Respiratory-Risk Patient
nodes.summary: Older/frail patients usually need 25-50% lower doses, delirium trigger treatment, and more respiratory/QT monitoring.
nodes.body: Assume lower reserve, higher delirium burden, and higher harm from oversedation, aspiration, falls, QT prolongation, and anticholinergic load. Principles: - Treat pain, urinary retention, hypoxia, infection, dehydration, constipation, withdrawal, and medication toxicity. - Use verbal de-escalation, family/reorientation, hearing aids/glasses, light, warmth, and bladder/pain treatment when safe. - I

nodes.title: QT / ECG Decision
nodes.summary: Do not delay lifesaving sedation for ECG, but use ECG/electrolytes to guide QT-risk patients when practical.
nodes.body: Question: should ECG change medication timing? Bottom line: - Immediate threat: do not delay lifesaving sedation for ECG. - High QT risk but controllable patient: get ECG and correct electrolytes before butyrophenones when practical. - After haloperidol or droperidol: obtain ECG once safe if risk factors, higher doses, repeated dosing, electrolyte abnormality, or any concerning rhythm.

nodes.title: ECG Later: Sedation Cannot Wait
nodes.summary: For immediate threat, sedate first, then obtain ECG and correct electrolytes once safe.
nodes.body: When the patient is an immediate threat, prolonged struggle is the bigger danger. Action: - Sedate with the medication most likely to control the threat. - Place monitor as soon as possible. - Obtain ECG after chemical control. - Check K, Mg, Ca, pH, temperature, renal function, and co-ingestions. - Correct K to high-normal and Mg if QT prolonged or torsades risk. If QTc is > 500 ms after control,

nodes.title: High QT Risk: Medication Choices
nodes.summary: QTc > 500 ms or major QT risk should push away from repeated butyrophenones when alternatives are workable.
nodes.body: High-risk QT features: - Known long QT syndrome. - QTc > 500 ms or torsades history. - Multiple QT-prolonging medications. - Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia. - Bradycardia, structural heart disease, severe renal/hepatic dysfunction, or high-dose/repeated antipsychotic exposure. Prefer: - Benzodiazepines when tox/withdrawal/stimulant physiology or severe immediate safety need. - Ketamine

nodes.title: Standard QT Risk: Practical Monitoring
nodes.summary: Standard-risk patients can be sedated first with appropriate monitoring; escalate ECG concern with risk factors or repeated dosing.
nodes.body: For standard-dose droperidol or haloperidol in a patient without known QT risk: - Give needed sedation. - Monitor clinically and place ECG/cardiac monitor as soon as feasible. - Obtain ECG earlier if repeated dosing, older/frail patient, polypharmacy, electrolyte risk, renal failure, chest pain, syncope, stimulant intoxication, or dysrhythmia. Droperidol carries a boxed QT warning, but ED literatu

nodes.title: After Initial Sedation: Is Physiology Controlled?
nodes.summary: After sedation, immediately reassess control, oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, perfusion, and failure risk.
nodes.body: Reassess within minutes. Controlled means: - Patient can be monitored without prolonged struggle. - Oxygenation and ventilation are acceptable. - Temperature is measured and cooling is underway if elevated. - BP/perfusion are acceptable or being actively resuscitated. - Lactate/acidosis are expected to improve after control of struggle and heat. - Team can obtain labs, ECG, and trauma/tox/infectio

nodes.title: Refractory Agitation
nodes.summary: Failed sedation needs decisive second-class therapy, ketamine for immediate threat, and airway/ICU planning if repeated doses are needed.
nodes.body: If initial sedation fails: - Confirm dose, route, time since administration, and whether medication actually entered muscle/IV. - Add a second class rather than repeating tiny ineffective doses. - If benzodiazepines failed and immediate threat persists, use ketamine. - If antipsychotic failed and stimulant/withdrawal physiology is possible, add benzodiazepine. - If repeated sedation is required, m

nodes.title: Severe Acidosis, Exhaustion, or Shock
nodes.summary: Severe acidosis requires sedation, cooling, oxygenation, ventilation planning, shock treatment, and selective bicarbonate only for specific indications.
nodes.body: Severe acidosis in this syndrome is usually from muscle activity, hyperthermia, seizure, hypoxia, shock, stimulant toxicity, or rhabdomyolysis. It can improve quickly once movement and heat are controlled, but it can also signal impending arrest. Immediate actions: - Stop muscle activity with sedation. - Oxygenate and ventilate. Use ETCO2 and blood gas trends. - Cool if hyperthermic. - Treat shock

nodes.title: Need Airway or ICU Sedation Now?
nodes.summary: Intubate when airway, ventilation, exhaustion, shock, repeated sedation, or severe acidosis require controlled resuscitation.
nodes.body: Decide early. Intubation can be lifesaving, but it can also cause arrest if ventilation, acidemia, potassium, and shock are not anticipated.

nodes.title: Airway Plan for Acidotic Hyperactive Delirium
nodes.summary: For severe acidosis, preoxygenate, avoid succinylcholine if hyperK/rhabdo risk, and match minute ventilation immediately after intubation.
nodes.body: Before RSI: - Preoxygenate aggressively. - Treat hyperkalemia if suspected or confirmed. - Prepare vasopressor support for shock. - Choose induction that fits hemodynamics. - Avoid succinylcholine if hyperkalemia, severe rhabdomyolysis, crush, burn, neuromuscular disease, or prolonged immobilization is suspected. Use rocuronium. - Have post-intubation sedation ready before paralysis. After tube: -

nodes.title: Hyperthermia: Cool While Sedating
nodes.summary: Hyperthermic severe agitation needs immediate sedation plus active external cooling, not antipyretics.
nodes.body: Measure core temperature when feasible. Do not wait for labs. If temperature is elevated with severe agitation or stimulant/heat physiology: - Stop muscle activity with sedation. - Remove clothing and external heat sources. - Evaporative cooling: spray water plus fans. - Ice packs to neck, axillae, groin. - Cold IV crystalloid can help but is not enough alone. - Consider ice-water immersion or agg

nodes.title: Fluids and Perfusion
nodes.summary: Use fluids to restore perfusion and protect kidneys, then reassess urine output, CK, creatinine, K, Ca, and acid-base status.
nodes.body: Initial goals: - Restore perfusion. - Support renal flow in rhabdomyolysis. - Correct hypovolemia from exertion, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, poor intake, and stimulant physiology. Approach: - Use balanced crystalloid or normal saline based on local practice, electrolytes, and acid-base status. - Reassess after each bolus: BP, lung exam, urine output, lactate/pH, CK, creatinine, K, Ca. - Place Foley

nodes.title: Minimum Workup After Control
nodes.summary: After control, obtain ECG, core temp, acid-base/lactate, CK, renal/electrolytes, urine output, and targeted tox/infection/trauma testing.
nodes.body: Tailor to the patient, but severe hyperactive delirium commonly needs: - POC glucose. - Core temperature. - ECG and continuous monitoring. - VBG/ABG with lactate if severe, hyperthermic, hypoxic, shocked, or exhausted. - CMP, Mg, Phos, Ca. - CK now and repeat if rising. - UA for blood/myoglobin, urine output. - CBC, cultures, antibiotics if infection possible. - Troponin if stimulant, chest pain,

nodes.title: Complication Screen: What Is Most Dangerous Right Now?
nodes.summary: Screen for rhabdo/AKI, hyperkalemia, dysrhythmia/QT/ischemia, and hyperthermia organ injury.
nodes.body: Pick the dominant active complication. Multiple may be present.

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis / AKI
nodes.summary: Rhabdo needs fluids, urine output, CK/renal/electrolyte trends, hyperkalemia treatment, and full rhabdo pathway if severe.
nodes.body: Triggers in this syndrome: - Prolonged agitation, restraint struggle, stimulant/exertional hyperthermia, seizures, coma/immobility, trauma, or compartment syndrome. Actions: - IV crystalloid and urine output monitoring. - Repeat CK, creatinine, K, Ca, Phos, Mg, lactate/pH. - Treat hyperkalemia urgently. - Look for compartment syndrome and traumatic injury. - Avoid routine bicarbonate for CK alone.

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia / Electrolyte Threat
nodes.summary: Treat unstable hyperkalemia immediately and correct Mg/K/Ca strategically, especially when QT risk is present.
nodes.body: Hyperkalemia may come from rhabdomyolysis, acidosis, renal failure, crush/trauma, or succinylcholine exposure. Treat immediately if ECG changes, K severe, or patient unstable: - Calcium for membrane stabilization. - Insulin/dextrose, albuterol, and bicarbonate if severe acidemia or specific indication. - Fluids and renal elimination strategy. - Dialysis if refractory or renal failure severe. Also

nodes.title: Dysrhythmia, QT, Ischemia, or Stimulant Cardiotoxicity
nodes.summary: For dysrhythmia/QT/stimulant cardiotoxicity, correct physiology, electrolytes, temperature, acidosis, and use ECG-guided treatment.
nodes.body: Actions: - ECG now if not already obtained. - Correct hypoxia, hyperthermia, acidosis, K, Mg, Ca, and shock. - Treat stimulant chest pain/HTN primarily with benzodiazepines and supportive care. - Consider sodium bicarbonate for cocaine/sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening. - Avoid additional QT-prolonging sedatives if QTc > 500 ms or torsades risk. - Give magnesium for torsades or marked QT i

nodes.title: Hyperthermia Organ Injury
nodes.summary: Severe hyperthermia can drive rhabdo, AKI, DIC, liver injury, seizure, shock, dysrhythmia, and ICU-level illness.
nodes.body: Severe hyperthermia can cause: - Rhabdomyolysis and AKI. - DIC and bleeding. - Hepatic injury or failure. - Encephalopathy, seizure, coma. - ARDS. - Myocardial injury, dysrhythmia, shock. Actions: - Continue rapid active cooling. - ICU early. - Trend temperature, lactate/pH, CK, Cr, K, Ca, Mg, LFTs, INR/PTT, fibrinogen, platelets, troponin, urine output. - Treat seizures with benzodiazepines. - Tr

nodes.title: Restraint Safety After Medication
nodes.summary: Restraints are a bridge to medication and monitoring, not definitive treatment; avoid prone/compressive restraint.
nodes.body: Physical restraints should be brief and paired with chemical control and monitoring. Do: - Use trained team application with a leader. - Move to supine or lateral position as soon as safely possible. - Keep head/chest/abdomen free from compression. - Monitor airway, breathing, circulation, neurovascular status, and mental status. - Reassess restraints frequently and remove as soon as safe. - Docum

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for physiologic injury or repeated deep sedation; psych only after medical danger is excluded.
nodes.body: Disposition is driven by physiology, complication burden, repeated sedation, and ability to identify and reverse the cause.

nodes.title: ICU Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for hyperthermia, acidosis, organ injury, intubation, repeated sedation, dysrhythmia, shock, seizure, or unclear persistent delirium.
nodes.body: ICU is appropriate for: - Temperature >= 40 C or persistent hyperthermia. - pH < 7.20, rising lactate after sedation, or severe metabolic acidosis. - Intubation, respiratory failure, repeated deep sedation, or airway risk. - Shock, vasopressors, severe dehydration, or perfusion failure. - Rhabdomyolysis with AKI, severe CK trajectory, hyperkalemia, oliguria, or McMahon high risk. - Dysrhythmia, QT
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU or resuscitation-capable monitored setting when physiologic injury, repeated sedation, airway risk, or organ injury is present.

nodes.title: Medical Admission / Monitored Observation
nodes.summary: Use medical admission or observation for ongoing delirium, abnormal trends, older/frail patients, or continued monitoring needs.
nodes.body: Medical admission or monitored observation fits when: - Agitation is controlled, but delirium cause is not fully corrected. - Labs are abnormal but not ICU-level. - CK/Cr/K/lactate/temperature require trending. - Older/frail patient has new delirium. - Infection, withdrawal, intoxication, medication toxicity, or occult trauma remains possible. - Additional sedation, sitter, telemetry, or serial ex
nodes.recommendation: Admit or observe medically until delirium cause, complications, and sedation effects are stable.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Pathway After Medical Exclusion
nodes.summary: Psych pathway is appropriate only after dangerous medical causes and complications are resolved or excluded.
nodes.body: Psychiatric evaluation is appropriate only after the dangerous medical physiology is resolved or excluded. Reasonable criteria: - Normal or explained vital signs. - No hyperthermia, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, severe intoxication/withdrawal, sepsis, CNS emergency, or occult trauma requiring medical care. - No clinically important acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, electrolyte threat, dysrhythmia, or organ
nodes.recommendation: Move to psychiatric assessment only after medical danger and physiologic complications have been addressed.

nodes.title: Rare Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge is rare and requires baseline mentation, stable physiology, no complication signal, and safe observation.
nodes.body: Discharge is uncommon after true dangerous hyperactive delirium. Minimum criteria: - Clear reversible cause corrected. - Returned to baseline mental status. - Normal oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, perfusion, and gait as appropriate. - No significant acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, hyperkalemia, dysrhythmia, ischemia, DIC/liver injury, trauma, infection, or ongoing tox/withdrawal risk. - Sed
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after full recovery, stable physiology, no complication signal, and reliable follow-up/observation.

nodes.title: Extensor Tendon Repair
nodes.summary: ED-repairable zones: I, II, IV, V, VI. Refer zones III, VII, VIII to hand surgery
nodes.body: Extensor tendon injuries are common in the ED. Unlike flexor tendons, many extensor injuries can be definitively managed by emergency physicians with appropriate training. [1][2] Key Principles: - Extensor tendons lack true sheaths, making them prone to adhesions - Flat, thin distal tendons are more challenging than thick proximal tendons - Zone classification guides repair approach and referral d

nodes.title: Physical Examination
nodes.summary: Test extension against resistance at each joint — 90% laceration can still allow gravity extension
nodes.body: Preparation - Adequate lighting and analgesia (digital or regional block) - Hemostasis: Penrose drain wrap for digit; BP cuff at 260 mmHg for hand/forearm [4] - Examine through full ROM - position at time of injury may differ from presentation Key Assessment Steps: 1. Digital Cascade Assessment - Compare resting posture to contralateral hand - Loss of normal cascade = tendon injury 2. Active Exten

nodes.title: Examination Pearls
nodes.summary: Zone V over MCP = fight bite until proven otherwise. Always test against resistance, not just gravity
nodes.body: Critical Pitfalls: - Up to 90% tendon laceration can still allow gravity-dependent extension - always test against resistance [3] - Position of injury matters - examine with joint in the position it was when injured - Zone V over MCP - treat as human bite until proven otherwise ("fight bite") When to Suspect Partial Injury: - Pain with extension against resistance - Weak extension compared to cont

nodes.title: Zone Classification (Kleinert-Verdan)
nodes.summary: Odd zones overlie joints, even zones between joints — classification guides repair and referral
nodes.body: The dorsum of hand, wrist, and forearm are divided into 8 zones (I-VIII). Odd numbers overlie joints; even numbers are between joints. [1][3] Thumb has separate classification (TI-TV) - generally parallels finger zones. | Zone | Location | Key Structures | |------|----------|----------------| | I | DIP joint to fingertip | Terminal tendon | | II | Middle phalanx | Lateral bands | | III | PIP joint

nodes.title: Zone I - Mallet Finger
nodes.summary: Mallet finger: stack splint DIP in hyperextension x 8 weeks continuous — PIP must be free
nodes.body: Anatomy: DIP joint to fingertip. Terminal extensor tendon inserts on distal phalanx. Mechanism: - Closed: Forced flexion of extended DIP (ball striking fingertip) - Open: Laceration over dorsal DIP Presentation: - Flexion deformity at DIP (cannot actively extend) - "Dropped" fingertip Classification: - Type I: Closed, no fracture (most common) - Type II: Open laceration - Type III: Open with skin

nodes.title: Zone II - Middle Phalanx
nodes.summary: Zone II: figure-of-8 sutures for >50% laceration, splint DIP in extension x 6 weeks
nodes.body: Anatomy: Lateral bands merge with central slip contribution at middle phalanx level. ED Management: Partial Laceration (<50%): - Wound care - Splint in extension x 3-4 weeks - Hand surgery follow-up Complete or >50% Laceration: - May repair in ED - Figure-of-8 sutures with 4-0 or 5-0 non-absorbable braided suture - Avoid shortening - can cause extension lag - Splint DIP in slight extension Pearls:

nodes.title: Zone III - Boutonniere (Central Slip)
nodes.summary: Zone III (boutonniere): REFER to hand surgery — missed injuries cause PIP flexion + DIP hyperextension
nodes.body: Anatomy: Central slip inserts at base of middle phalanx. Lateral bands pass on either side. REFER TO HAND SURGERY - Complex anatomy beyond ED scope [4][5] Why Zone III is Complex: - Intricate interaction of central slip, lateral bands, and lumbrical insertion - Missed injuries lead to boutonniere deformity - Repair requires precise reconstruction to prevent deformity Boutonniere Deformity (if miss

nodes.title: Zone IV - Proximal Phalanx
nodes.summary: Zone IV: modified Kessler or Bunnell stitch — wrist 30-45 ext, MCP neutral splint x 6 weeks
nodes.body: Anatomy: Broad extensor expansion with contributions from intrinsic muscles. ED Management: May repair in ED - relatively straightforward anatomy [4][5] Partial (<50%): - Splint x 3-4 weeks - Hand therapy follow-up Complete or >50%: - Modified Kessler or Bunnell stitch with 4-0 or 5-0 non-absorbable - Can use 2 figure-of-8 sutures side-by-side for broad tendon - Volar splint with wrist 30-45 degre

nodes.title: Zone V - MCP Joint
nodes.summary: Zone V MCP: ANY laceration from punch = fight bite — irrigate, do NOT close, antibiotics, hand surgery
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Treat as human bite until proven otherwise [4][5] Anatomy: Sagittal bands stabilize extensor tendon over MCP. EDC, EIP, EDM present. Fight Bite Protocol (Any laceration over MCP from punch): 1. X-ray for tooth fragment, fracture, air in joint 2. Copious irrigation - at least 500 mL saline 3. Wound exploration - look for joint capsule violation 4. Do NOT close primarily - leave open 5. An

nodes.title: Zones VI, VII, VIII
nodes.summary: Zone VI: ED-repairable. Zones VII-VIII: REFER — retinaculum/muscle-tendon junction complexity
nodes.body: ZONE VI - Dorsum of Hand May repair in ED - often technically easy [4][5] - Juncturae tendinae connect adjacent tendons - Juncturae minimize tendon retraction after laceration - Multiple tendons may be involved Repair: - Modified Bunnell stitch with 4-0 non-absorbable - Excellent prognosis with primary repair Splint: Wrist 30 degrees, MCP neutral --- ZONE VII - Wrist/Retinaculum REFER TO HAND SURG

nodes.title: Repair Techniques Overview
nodes.summary: Use 4-0/5-0 braided non-absorbable suture — repair within 5 days for best outcomes (97.8% ROM)
nodes.body: General Principles [2][9] Suture Selection: - 3-0 for tendons at hand level (Zone VI) - 4-0 to 5-0 for finger tendons (Zones I-V) - Braided non-absorbable (Ethibond, Ticron) preferred - Tapered needle (avoid cutting needles) Surgical Field: - Good lighting, analgesia, tourniquet/hemostasis - Handle tendons delicately - avoid crushing with forceps - Minimize excessive punctures - adhesion risk - Ma

nodes.title: Modified Kessler Stitch
nodes.summary: Modified Kessler: locking loop core suture for zones IV-VI, knot buried between tendon ends
nodes.body: Indications: Zones IV, V, VI - thicker tendons that hold core sutures [2][9] Technique: 1. Single suture enters tendon 1/3 diameter deep, approximately 1 cm from cut end 2. Pass through lateral margin of tendon 3. Wrap around tendon 4. Re-enter perpendicular, 1-2 mm from cut end 5. Thread through tendon to exit at cut surface 6. Repeat on opposing half of tendon 7. Tie knot within repair (buried)

nodes.title: Modified Bunnell Stitch
nodes.summary: Modified Bunnell: crisscross pattern, good purchase in flat tendons — zones V-VI
nodes.body: Indications: Zones V, VI - alternative core suture technique [2][9] Technique: 1. Single suture enters tendon 1/3 diameter deep 2. Pass diagonally, exiting ulnar side 3. Wrap around tendon 4. Re-enter dorsally, pull through to exit radial side 5. Diagonally cross initial stitch to exit ulnar side (creates X pattern) 6. Repeat mirror image on opposite tendon end 7. Tie ends together Key Points: - C

nodes.title: Figure-of-8 Suture
nodes.summary: Figure-of-8: simplest technique, works for all zones especially thin distal tendons
nodes.body: Indications: All zones, especially thin distal tendons (I, II, III) [2][5][9] Technique: 1. Insert needle through one tendon end, approximately 3-4 mm from cut edge 2. Pass across to opposite tendon end 3. Insert through opposite tendon, same distance from edge 4. Cross back to first side, creating figure-of-8 pattern 5. Tie knot on dorsal surface or buried 6. May use 2-3 figure-of-8 sutures for b

nodes.title: Dermatotenodesis
nodes.summary: Dermatotenodesis: combined skin + tendon repair for Zone I open mallet injuries
nodes.body: Indications: Zone I (DIP) open mallet injuries [2] Concept: Incorporates skin closure with tendon repair - single suture anchors skin edges while passing through dorsal tendon. Technique: 1. Place 4-0 or 5-0 non-absorbable suture 2. Enter skin edge approximately 3 mm from wound 3. Pass through dorsal aspect of tendon stump 4. Continue through opposite tendon stump 5. Exit through opposite skin edg

nodes.summary: ALL extensor tendon injuries need hand surgery follow-up within 7 days

nodes.title: Facial Peripheral Nerve Block — ED Procedure
nodes.summary: Regional block of the face: no wound-margin distortion, less volume, less pain than infiltration.
nodes.body: Regional anesthesia of the face anesthetizes a whole sensory territory from ONE distant injection — superior to local infiltration for facial wounds because it: (1) avoids tissue distortion of wound margins (critical for accurate cosmetic approximation, especially the vermilion border), (2) needs far less anesthetic volume, and (3) is less painful than multiple infiltrations. Use for laceration re

nodes.title: Which Region Needs Anesthesia?
nodes.summary: Pick region → routes to supraorbital, infratrochlear, infraorbital, nasal, mental, inferior alveolar, auriculotemporal, or ear ring block.
nodes.body: Select the facial region of the wound or procedure. Each routes to the specific terminal trigeminal branch (or ear block) that covers it. Confirm the wound is suitable for delayed repair time (blocks add 5–10 min onset) and that there is no overlying infection at the planned injection site.

nodes.title: Contraindications + Pre-procedure Checks
nodes.summary: No infection at site, no LA allergy; verify max LA dose; aspirate before injecting (vascular face).
nodes.body: Absolute: - Overlying skin infection / cellulitis at the planned injection site (do not inject through infected tissue) - Known true allergy to the local anesthetic class (ester allergy more common than amide; if unsure, use a preservative-free amide or consult) - Patient refusal / inability to cooperate Relative — weigh risk/benefit: - Therapeutic anticoagulation (these are superficial blocks; bl

nodes.title: Shared Technique — All Facial Blocks
nodes.summary: 25–27 ga, lidocaine (fast) or bupivacaine (long), aspirate, inject slowly NEXT TO not into the foramen, wait 5–10 min.
nodes.body: Equipment: - 3 mL syringe, 25–27 gauge needle (1–1.5 inch) - Antiseptic prep (chlorhexidine or alcohol) - 2x2 gauze, bandage Agent (choose one): - Lidocaine 1–2% — fast onset (2–5 min), 1–2 h duration - Bupivacaine 0.25–0.5% — slower onset (5–10 min), 4–8 h duration; good for prolonged repairs - Epinephrine-containing LA is acceptable for most facial blocks and prolongs duration / reduces bleeding

nodes.title: Supraorbital + Supratrochlear Block (V1)
nodes.summary: Forehead/anterior scalp. Supraorbital foramen at mid-pupillary line on brow ridge; supratrochlear 1 cm medial. ~2–3 mL.
nodes.body: Indication: Lacerations/procedures of the forehead and anterior scalp to the vertex. Distribution of anesthesia: Ipsilateral forehead and anterior scalp (supraorbital covers the bulk; supratrochlear covers the medial forehead near the midline). Block both together for full hemi-forehead coverage. Landmarks: - The supraorbital foramen/notch sits on the superior orbital rim at the mid-pupillary line

nodes.title: Infratrochlear Block (V1)
nodes.summary: Medial canthus / nose bridge. Exits at superomedial orbital angle just above medial canthus. 1–2 mL, aim away from globe.
nodes.body: Indication: Lacerations of the medial canthal region, the bridge/upper-lateral side of the nose, and the medial lower eyelid. Distribution of anesthesia: Skin of the medial canthus, root and bridge of the nose, medial upper eyelid, and lacrimal sac region. Landmarks: - The infratrochlear nerve exits below the trochlea at the superomedial corner of the orbit, at the junction of the orbital roof and

nodes.title: Infraorbital Block (V2)
nodes.summary: Lower eyelid/cheek/upper lip/lateral nose. Foramen 1 cm below infraorbital rim at mid-pupillary line. Intraoral via gingivobuccal sulcus, finger over foramen, 2–3 mL.
nodes.body: Indication: The workhorse facial block — lacerations of the lower eyelid, medial cheek, lateral side of the nose, and the UPPER LIP (preserves the vermilion border without distortion). Distribution of anesthesia: Ipsilateral lower eyelid, medial cheek, lateral nose, and upper lip (and via anterior superior alveolar branches, the maxillary incisors/canine). Landmarks: - The infraorbital foramen lie

nodes.title: External Nasal / Nasal Tip Block (V1 + V2)
nodes.summary: Nasal tip/ala. External nasal branch at nasal bone–cartilage junction (0.5–1 mL each side) ± bilateral infraorbital. Small volumes.
nodes.body: Indication: Lacerations of the nasal tip, ala, and columella. Distribution of anesthesia: The nasal tip and dorsum are supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1); the ala and lateral nose by the infraorbital nerve (V2). Full tip anesthesia often needs BOTH. Landmarks: - The external nasal branch emerges at the junction of the nasal bone and the upper lateral cartila

nodes.title: Mental Nerve Block (V3)
nodes.summary: Lower lip/chin. Mental foramen below 2nd premolar at mid-pupillary line. Intraoral via sulcus, 1–2 mL beside foramen. Bilateral for midline.
nodes.body: Indication: Lacerations/procedures of the LOWER LIP and chin (preserves the vermilion border). Distribution of anesthesia: Ipsilateral lower lip and chin skin/mucosa (terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve). Landmarks: - The mental foramen lies below the 2nd mandibular premolar (apex), roughly midway between the upper and lower borders of the mandible, in the mid-pupillary line (vertically

nodes.title: Inferior Alveolar Nerve Block (V3)
nodes.summary: Hemi-mandible/teeth + lower lip. Mandibular foramen via coronoid notch, contact bone, withdraw 1mm, aspirate, 1.5–2 mL. Vascular.
nodes.body: Indication: Mandibular dental pain/procedures, and extensive lower-lip/chin wounds where a more proximal block than the mental nerve is needed (anesthetizes the entire hemi-mandible and ipsilateral lower lip). Distribution of anesthesia: All ipsilateral mandibular teeth, the body of the mandible, the ipsilateral lower lip and chin (via the mental branch), and the anterior 2/3 of the tongue + floor

nodes.title: Auriculotemporal Nerve Block (V3)

Distribution of anesthesia: Temple skin, anterior/superior external ear (tragus, anterior helix), anterior external auditory canal, and the TMJ region. nodes.title: External Ear Ring Block

nodes.body: Indication: Lacerations, hematoma I&D (auricular hematoma/cauliflower ear), and procedures of the external ear (auricle) — anesthetizes the whole auricle except the concha/EAC. nodes.title: Test the Block Before Proceeding
nodes.summary: Wait 5–10 min, test pinprick vs contralateral. Full → proceed. Partial/none → supplement or re-block within max dose.
nodes.body: Wait 5–10 minutes, then test pinprick/sharp sensation across the intended territory and compare to the contralateral side. Is the territory anesthetized?

nodes.title: Rescue a Partial / Failed Block
nodes.summary: Failure = wrong level / variation / short wait / low volume. Re-block, add local infiltration, recheck max dose.

nodes.body: Common / minor: - Local hematoma or ecchymosis (especially periorbital blocks and auriculotemporal near the temporal artery) — apply pressure - Transient pain on injection - Failed/partial block - Prolonged numbness beyond expected duration (self-limited) Uncommon but important: - Intravascular injection — facial vasculature is dense (angular, infraorbital, superficial temporal, inferior alveolar
