nodes.title: Febrile Seizure — Core Frame
nodes.summary: Job is NOT to rule out epilepsy — detect dangerous mimics (meningitis, HSV, status, NAT); AAP 2011/2025: no routine workup or prophylaxis for simple FS
nodes.body: Febrile Seizure Steps Summary · Disposition, Recurrence & Mimics Most febrile seizures are simple and benign. [1][2] Your job is NOT to "rule out epilepsy" — it is to detect dangerous mimics: [1][4][11] • Bacterial meningitis (especially under-vaccinated, ill-appearing, persistent AMS) • HSV encephalitis (focal features, prolonged AMS, focal seizure) • Febrile status epilepticus (≥30 min or recurr

nodes.title: Definition & Epidemiology
nodes.summary: FS = seizure + fever ≥38°C, age 6mo-5yr, NO CNS infection or other cause; 2-5% prevalence, 30% recur, 1-2% develop epilepsy
nodes.body: Febrile seizure (AAP definition): [1][2] • Seizure accompanied by fever (≥38°C / 100.4°F) without CNS infection or other identified cause • Age 6 months to 5 years • Outside this age window, the working diagnosis must be revisited Epidemiology: [4][6] • 2-5% of children in the US/Europe; 6-9% in Japan • Peak age 12-18 months • Family history positive in 25-40% • ~30% of children will have a recurr

nodes.title: Simple vs Complex
nodes.summary: Simple = generalized + <15 min + ONE in 24h + age 6mo-5yr; complex = any focal/long/recurrent feature; status = ≥30 min or recurrent without recovery
nodes.body: Simple vs Complex Classifier Simple febrile seizure (all four required): [1][2][4] • Generalized (no focal features) • <15 minutes duration • Single episode in 24 hours • Age 6 months to 5 years with previously normal development Complex febrile seizure (any one of): [1][2][4] • Focal features (focal motor, gaze deviation, post-ictal Todd's paralysis) • ≥15 minutes duration • ≥1 episode in 24 hour

nodes.title: Typical Simple FS Presentation
nodes.summary: Classic simple FS: toddler, rapid temp rise, brief generalized event, back to baseline; reassuring exam + benign source + vaccinated = home, no workup
nodes.body: Classic story (>90% of febrile seizures): [1][4][6] • Toddler 12-24 months, no prior history • Rapid temperature rise (often 39-40°C / 102-104°F) • Brief generalized tonic-clonic activity (1-3 minutes typical) • Brief post-ictal drowsiness, then back to baseline within 30-60 minutes • Returns to baseline behavior, feeding, interacting before discharge Reassuring exam findings: [1] • Alert and cons

nodes.title: Red Flags Demanding Workup
nodes.summary: Red flags = ill appearance, persistent AMS, meningeal signs, petechiae, focal deficit, under-vaccinated, recent abx, NAT concern → targeted workup
nodes.body: Any of the following pushes you toward LP, imaging, or admission: [1][4][11] Clinical red flags: • Ill / toxic appearance after the post-ictal period • Persistent altered mentation >1 hour • Meningeal signs (neck stiffness, Kernig, Brudzinski) — limited reliability under age 18 mo • Bulging fontanelle • Petechiae or purpura (purpura non-blanching = meningococcemia until proven otherwise) • Focal n

nodes.title: Workup Overview — What the Guidelines Actually Say
nodes.summary: Simple FS = no routine LP/labs/EEG/imaging (AAP 2011/2025); complex = TARGETED workup driven by features + exam; chase mimics not diagnoses
nodes.body: AAP 2011 (reaffirmed 2025) for SIMPLE febrile seizure: [1][2] • No routine LP — exception: meningeal signs, age <12 mo with concerning features, recent antibiotics • No routine labs (CBC, BMP, glucose) unless clinically indicated for fever workup • No routine EEG — does not predict recurrence or epilepsy in simple FS • No routine neuroimaging (CT or MRI) For COMPLEX febrile seizure: [1][4][11] • W

nodes.title: Meningitis Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Post-Hib/PCV era: bacterial meningitis as simple FS is <0.2%; LP only for meningeal signs, ill, AMS, petechiae, recent abx, or under-vaccinated <12mo
nodes.body: Meningitis Risk Decision Tool LP indication is the single highest-stakes decision in this consult. [1][11] LP indicated: [1][11] • Meningeal signs at any age • Persistent altered mentation >1 hour after seizure • Bulging fontanelle • Petechiae / purpura • Pretreatment with antibiotics within prior 5-7 days (could mask meningitis) • Toxic appearance LP "consider": [1][4] • Age <12 months with incom

nodes.title: When to Image
nodes.summary: No routine imaging; CT urgent if focal deficit, ↑ICP, NAT, or HSV concern; MRI for complex/recurrent or febrile status (FEBSTAT)
nodes.body: Imaging Decision Reference Routine imaging is NOT indicated for simple febrile seizure. [1][2] CT (urgent, before LP): [1][4][7] • Focal seizure with persistent neurologic deficit • Signs of increased ICP (papilledema, posturing, Cushing's response) • Suspected non-accidental trauma • Suspected HSV / abscess / intracranial hemorrhage • Concerning focal exam not explained by post-ictal state MRI (p

nodes.title: When to EEG
nodes.summary: No routine EEG; consider for non-convulsive status, prolonged AMS in febrile status, or recurrent complex events with abnormal exam
nodes.body: EEG is NOT routinely indicated in febrile seizures — even complex ones in many cases. [1][2] Why EEG is low-yield acutely: [1] • Does not predict recurrence of febrile seizures • Does not predict subsequent epilepsy • Often shows non-specific post-ictal slowing that resolves EEG is reasonable for: [4][7] • Suspected non-convulsive status epilepticus (persistent AMS without overt motor activity) •

nodes.title: Labs — When They Help
nodes.summary: No routine labs; check glucose + Na if any concern; broader metabolic if recurrent or persistent AMS; fever labs follow peds-fever algorithm
nodes.body: No routine labs in simple febrile seizure. [1][2] Labs as part of FEVER workup (not seizure workup): [1][4] • Determined by age, vaccination status, and source of fever • See Pediatric Fever consult for the full age-stratified algorithm Labs specifically for the SEIZURE itself: [1][4][11] • Glucose — quick bedside check; hypoglycemia mimics and exacerbates • Sodium — hyponatremic seizures (especia

nodes.title: LP — Cautions & Empiric Coverage
nodes.summary: Meningitis empiric: ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg + vanc 15 mg/kg; add ampicillin <1mo, acyclovir if HSV concern; do NOT delay abx for LP
nodes.body: Before LP: [4][11] • Stabilize airway / breathing / circulation first • Assess for contraindications (focal deficit, signs of ↑ICP, papilledema, coagulopathy, infected skin over puncture site) • If any concern for ↑ICP → CT first (do NOT delay if child is otherwise stable) • Do not delay empiric antibiotics for the LP — give meningitis-dose antibiotics first if seriously ill Empiric antibiotic cov

nodes.title: Active Seizure on Arrival?
nodes.summary: Most FS self-terminate in 1-3 min; if active on arrival → status pathway; benzo at 5 min; bedside glucose immediately
nodes.body: Most febrile seizures stop spontaneously within 1-3 minutes. Children rolling into the ED actively seizing are by definition outliers and are at risk for febrile status epilepticus. [5][7] Initial actions — first 60 seconds: [5][7] • Position (left lateral if possible), suction if needed • Oxygen by face mask, pulse oximetry • IV / IO access • Bedside glucose (treat hypoglycemia immediately) • Con

nodes.title: Time-to-Meds in Pediatric Status
nodes.summary: Status = ≥5 min or recurrent without recovery; benzo by 5-20 min, second-line by 20-40 min, anesthetic by 40+ min; #1 error is benzo underdosing
nodes.body: Status epilepticus is a time-critical diagnosis. Outcome correlates with time-to-first-benzodiazepine and time-to-second-line agent. [5][7] Operational status definition (treat now): [5] • Seizure ≥5 minutes OR • Recurrent seizure without return to baseline between events Treatment timeline (target): [5] • 0-5 minutes: stabilize, IV/IO, glucose, oxygen • 5-20 minutes: first-line benzodiazepine (gi

nodes.title: First-Line Benzodiazepine
nodes.summary: IV: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg or midaz 0.1-0.2 mg/kg; no IV: midaz 0.2 mg/kg IM/IN or diazepam 0.5 mg/kg PR; redose once at 5 min
nodes.body: Choose by access available — full weight-based dose at first attempt. [5][7] IV access available: • Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg/dose) — preferred for IV when available • Midazolam 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV (max 5-10 mg/dose) • Onset 1-3 minutes No IV access — get drug in fast: • Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM (max 10 mg/dose) — preferred IM agent • Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg intranasal (split between nares; max 10 m

nodes.title: Second-Line Agent (ESETT-Era)
nodes.summary: ESETT: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 PE/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg — equally effective; pick by safety profile (levetiracetam often first)
nodes.body: ESETT (NEJM 2019): levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate were equally effective in pediatric and adult benzo-refractory status — pick by availability and contraindications. [5] Levetiracetam: [5] • 60 mg/kg IV over 5-10 min (max 4500 mg) • Increasingly the first choice in many EDs (favorable safety profile, no cardiac monitoring requirement, no enzyme induction) • Watch for behavioral changes

nodes.title: Fever Control — What Antipyretics Do (and Do Not) Do
nodes.summary: Antipyretics do NOT prevent recurrence (AAP 2008/reaffirmed); acetaminophen 15 mg/kg or ibuprofen 10 mg/kg for COMFORT only; counsel parents accordingly
nodes.body: Antipyretics make the child more comfortable. They do NOT prevent recurrence of febrile seizure. [3] AAP 2008 (reaffirmed): [3] • Scheduled or symptomatic acetaminophen and ibuprofen do NOT reduce the risk of febrile seizure recurrence • Counseling parents that "more aggressive antipyretic use will prevent the next seizure" is incorrect and creates anxiety What antipyretics DO offer: [3] • Comfort

nodes.title: Disposition — Simple Febrile Seizure
nodes.body: Most simple febrile seizures go home from the ED with reassurance + return precautions. [1][2] Discharge criteria (all): [1][2] • Returned to neurologic and behavioral baseline • Tolerating PO • Reliable caregiver who understands return precautions • Identified benign source of fever (or appropriate fever workup completed) • No concerning exam findings • Outpatient follow-up arranged with PCP Retu
nodes.recommendation: Discharge home with reassurance, return precautions, antipyretic counseling for comfort, and PCP follow-up. No labs, LP, EEG, imaging, or antiepileptic prescription required.

nodes.title: Disposition — Complex Febrile Seizure
nodes.summary: Complex features alone do NOT mandate admission; admit for status, persistent AMS, recurrent in 24h, no fever source, social barriers, pending workup
nodes.body: Complex features alone do NOT mandate admission. [1][4] Discharge OK if (all): [1][4] • Back to neurologic baseline • Reassuring exam, identified benign fever source • Single complex feature only (e.g., short focal seizure, recovered fully) without other red flags • Reliable caregivers and follow-up • ED clinician judgment that no inpatient workup is needed Admit (or extended observation) if any o

nodes.title: Recurrence Risk
nodes.summary: Recurrence ~30% overall; <12mo at first = 50%; 0/1/2/3+ factors = 15-20%/25-30%/50%/75%; recurrence does NOT change long-term prognosis
nodes.body: Recurrence / Epilepsy Risk Calculator Overall recurrence risk after first febrile seizure: ~30%. [8] Risk factors that increase recurrence: [8] • Age at first event <12 months (single largest factor — recurrence ~50%) • Family history of febrile seizures • Lower peak fever at presentation (paradoxical — kids who seize at lower temps tend to do it again) • Short duration of fever before the seizure

nodes.title: Lifetime Epilepsy Risk
nodes.summary: Epilepsy lifetime risk: simple FS = 1-2%, with factors up to 10%; AED prophylaxis does NOT lower this risk; epilepsy reflects pre-existing susceptibility
nodes.body: Lifetime risk of epilepsy after a SIMPLE febrile seizure: ~1-2% (vs ~0.5-1% baseline). [9][10] Risk factors that increase epilepsy risk: [9][10] • Complex features at first event (focal, prolonged, or multiple in 24h) • Family history of epilepsy (not just febrile seizures) • Pre-existing neurodevelopmental concern or abnormal exam • Febrile status epilepticus (FEBSTAT — possible hippocampal scler

nodes.title: Prophylaxis — What Not to Prescribe
nodes.summary: No routine prophylaxis (AAP 2008); rescue diazepam ONLY after febrile status, neurology-coordinated; AEDs add side effects without changing epilepsy risk
nodes.body: No anticonvulsant prophylaxis is recommended for simple OR most complex febrile seizures. [3] AAP 2008 (reaffirmed): [3] • Continuous phenobarbital, valproate, or other anticonvulsants are NOT recommended • Side effects (cognitive blunting, behavior, hepatotoxicity) outweigh the modest reduction in recurrence • Intermittent oral diazepam at fever onset reduces recurrence but causes sedation, ataxi

nodes.title: Vaccination — Continue On Schedule
nodes.summary: Continue vaccines on schedule; vaccine-triggered FS is benign; MMRV gives ~1 extra FS per 2300 doses vs MMR+V — discuss for first dose at 12-15mo
nodes.body: Vaccine-Triggered Seizure Reference Do NOT delay routine immunizations after a febrile seizure. [12] Why: [1][12] • Vaccine-triggered febrile seizures are themselves benign (same prognosis as any febrile seizure) • The diseases prevented by routine vaccines (measles encephalitis, Hib meningitis, pneumococcal sepsis) are far worse • Prior febrile seizure is NOT a contraindication to any routine vac

nodes.title: Vaccine-Triggered Seizure in the ED
nodes.summary: MMR/MMRV peak 8-14d; DTaP peak 0-2d; classic timing + benign course = simple FS; do NOT skip subsequent vaccines
nodes.body: A child presenting with a febrile seizure 8-14 days after MMR/MMRV (or 0-2 days after DTaP) has a CLASSIC vaccine-triggered febrile seizure. [12] Recognition: [12] • Timing matches vaccine fever window • Otherwise classic simple febrile seizure presentation • Benign exam, identifiable post-vaccine fever Approach: [12] • Treat exactly like any other simple febrile seizure (no extra workup) • Reassu

nodes.title: Mimics — What Else Could This Be?
nodes.summary: Top mimics: bacterial meningitis, HSV encephalitis, NAT — anchoring on "febrile seizure" before excluding these is the #1 diagnostic error
nodes.body: Anchoring on "febrile seizure" before excluding mimics is the most common diagnostic error. [1][4][11] Which mimic is most concerning in this child?

nodes.title: Bacterial Meningitis Mimic
nodes.summary: Bacterial meningitis was 20% of pre-vaccine FS, now <0.2% in vaccinated; suspect with petechiae, AMS, ill appearance, recent abx → empiric abx + LP
nodes.body: The mimic that drives all the conservatism in this consult. [1][11] Why under-vaccinated children get LP: [1][11] • Pre-Hib/PCV era, ~20% of children presenting with first febrile seizure had bacterial meningitis • Post-Hib/PCV era, the rate is <0.2% in fully vaccinated, well-appearing children • The vaccine status drives the workup decision more than any single physical exam finding Suspect bacte

nodes.title: HSV Encephalitis Mimic
nodes.summary: HSV encephalitis: focal sz, persistent AMS, vesicular rash, neonate; start acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h empirically — do NOT wait for confirmation
nodes.body: HSV encephalitis is the time-critical viral mimic. [4][11] Why it matters: [4][11] • Mortality 70%+ untreated; ~25% with timely acyclovir • Survivors often have neurologic sequelae proportional to delay in treatment • Empiric acyclovir is cheap, low-risk, and lifesaving Clinical clues: [4][11] • Focal seizure or focal neurologic deficit • Persistent altered mentation • Vesicular rash (newborn or o

nodes.title: Non-Accidental Trauma Mimic
nodes.summary: NAT mimic: inconsistent history, injury pattern mismatch, retinal hemorrhages, non-mobile infant bruising; skeletal survey + head imaging + ophtho + CPS
nodes.body: NAT can present with seizure + fever and be misclassified as febrile seizure. [4] Red flags suggesting NAT: [4] • Inconsistent or changing history of mechanism • Injury pattern out of proportion to story (bruising in non-mobile infant, posterior rib fractures, classic metaphyseal lesions) • Retinal hemorrhages on dilated exam • Bulging fontanelle without meningitis • Apnea or unexplained altered m

nodes.title: Counseling — What to Tell Parents
nodes.body: Parents of a child after a first febrile seizure are scared. Anchor your counseling on three messages. [1][2][8] 1. "Your child had a febrile seizure. It is the most common type of seizure in childhood, and the prognosis is excellent." [1][8] • 1 in 25 children have a febrile seizure between ages 6 months and 5 years • The brain outgrows the susceptibility, usually by age 5 • Most kids never have
nodes.recommendation: Three-message counseling: prognosis is excellent, 1-in-3 recurrence does not change long-term outlook, here are the specific return precautions. Continue vaccines on schedule.

nodes.title: Fingertip Infection - Photo Triage
nodes.body: Steps Summary Photo Atlas - open to compare patient against side-by-side images. Quick visual cues: - Nail fold swelling/pus -> Paronychia - Tense, throbbing pulp -> Felon - Grouped clear vesicles -> Herpetic Whitlow (do NOT incise) - Dark blood under nail after trauma -> Subungual hematoma - Yellow/white pus under nail without trauma -> Subungual abscess Before branching, screen for Kanavel signs

nodes.title: Paronychia - Acute vs Chronic
nodes.body: See Photo Atlas - Paronychia for visual comparison. Acute (<6 weeks): bacterial, usually Staph aureus, occasionally anaerobes/oral flora after nail-biting. Tender, erythematous nail fold, may be fluctuant. Chronic (>=6 weeks): inflammatory, frequent water exposure, often Candida-colonized. Boggy, less tender, multiple digits possible. Cuticle absent. Which is this? [3,4]

nodes.title: Acute Paronychia - Bedside Drainage
nodes.body: Decision: Subungual extension changes the procedure. Simple lateral fold abscess (no pus tracking under nail): 1. Skin prep, no anesthesia for superficial; digital block if extensive. 2. Slide a #11 blade or 18g needle parallel to the nail, bevel up, between cuticle and nail plate at the point of maximal fluctuance. 3. Lift the eponychial fold off the nail to release pus. Do NOT incise the nail fo

nodes.title: Early Paronychia - No Drainage Yet
nodes.body: Conservative management for non-fluctuant cellulitis: - Warm soaks 15-20 min, 3-4x daily. - Elevation, keep dry between soaks. - Avoid manipulation, biting, picking. Antibiotics often unnecessary. Reserve for spreading erythema, immunocompromise, or failure at 48 h: - Cephalexin 500 mg QID x 5-7 days, OR - TMP-SMX DS BID if MRSA risk. Reassess at 48 h. If fluctuance develops -> drain (see acute pa
nodes.recommendation: Early paronychia without abscess. Warm soaks, no antibiotics unless cellulitis or risk factors. Recheck 48 h.

nodes.title: Chronic Paronychia
nodes.body: Pathophysiology: chronic irritant/inflammatory, with Candida as a colonizer rather than primary pathogen. Repeated wet work disrupts the cuticle barrier. ED management: 1. Stop wet exposure - cotton-lined gloves for housework/dishwashing. 2. Topical high-potency steroid (triamcinolone 0.1% or clobetasol BID x 3 weeks) - more effective than antifungals in head-to-head trials. 3. Topical antifungal
nodes.recommendation: Chronic paronychia is inflammatory. Topical steroid + dry + glove strategy. No oral antibiotics. Derm referral if refractory.

nodes.title: Felon - Pulp Space Abscess
nodes.body: See Photo Atlas - Felon. Anatomy: distal pulp is partitioned by 15-20 fibrous septa into closed compartments. Pus raises pressure rapidly -> ischemia, septic DIP arthritis, distal phalanx osteomyelitis. Classic exam: tense, glove-tight pulp; throbbing pain out of proportion; minor puncture/splinter often the trigger; Staph aureus most common. Is there a true abscess (fluctuance, point tenderness,

nodes.title: Felon - Bedside I&D Technique
nodes.body: Anesthesia: digital block with Lidocaine 1% plain (no epi), 1-2 mL each side at the base of the digit. Allow 5-10 min. Penrose tourniquet at the base for hemostasis. Choose the incision based on abscess location: 1. Volar longitudinal (preferred for superficial midline pus): - Single midline incision over the point of maximal fluctuance, NOT crossing the DIP flexion crease. - Spread with a small h

nodes.title: Early Felon - Conservative Trial
nodes.body: Without true abscess: - Cephalexin 500 mg QID x 7-10 days (Clindamycin 300-450 mg TID if penicillin-allergic). - Warm soaks 3-4x/day, elevate. - Recheck in 24 h - low threshold to drain if any progression. Early felons declare themselves quickly. [2,5]
nodes.recommendation: Early felon, no abscess: oral antibiotics + soaks, recheck 24 h, drain if any progression.

nodes.title: Herpetic Whitlow - Recognize, Do NOT Incise
nodes.body: See Photo Atlas - Whitlow. Recognition: - Grouped clear vesicles on an erythematous base, often coalescing. - Burning/throbbing pain typically out of proportion to exam early on. - Prodrome: tingling 24-48 h before vesicles appear. - High-risk groups: dental/respiratory therapy workers, kids who suck thumbs, healthcare workers; HSV-1 > HSV-2. - Self-limited 2-4 weeks. Recurrences possible. Why it

nodes.title: Subungual: Hematoma vs Abscess
nodes.body: See Photo Atlas - Subungual for side-by-side comparison. The trap: dark discoloration under the nail looks similar at first glance, but the management is opposite. | Feature | Hematoma | Abscess | |---|---|---| | Color | Dark red/blue/black | Yellow-white pus, may be pink-red | | History | Crush/blunt trauma | No trauma (or minor manicure/biting) | | Time course | Onset within hours of injury | Da

nodes.title: Subungual Hematoma - Trephination
nodes.body: Indication: painful subungual hematoma, regardless of size. Pain relief is dramatic and immediate. Old teaching to avoid: the "drain only if >50% of nail" rule has been abandoned. Trephinate based on pain, not percentage. [9] Tuft fracture is NOT a contraindication. Multiple studies and updated guidelines show trephination of a hematoma overlying a closed tuft fracture does not increase infection

nodes.title: Subungual Abscess - Drainage
nodes.body: Often an extension of paronychia that has tracked under the nail. Approach by extent: Lateral edge only: - Digital block with Lidocaine 1% plain. - Lift the lateral nail fold and slide a hemostat under the nail edge to release pus. - If pus persists, remove the lateral one-quarter of the nail with a small hemostat. Central or under most of the nail: - Trephinate the nail directly over the abscess

nodes.title: Suspected Flexor Tenosynovitis - Escalate
nodes.body: This is no longer a fingertip problem. Kanavel signs = flexor sheath infection until proven otherwise. Time to treatment determines outcome - delays >24 h drive tendon necrosis and amputation risk. Kanavel Signs Reference - any one positive raises concern; 3 of 4 is highly specific. Immediate ED steps: 1. Hand surgery consult NOW - do not wait for imaging if classic. 2. NPO; mark cellulitis border
nodes.recommendation: Suspected FTS: hand surgery consult now, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Vanc + pip-tazo), splint, elevate. Cross to Hand Infections consult for FTS pathway.

nodes.title: Disposition - Outpatient
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: - Source controlled (drained or not yet abscess). - No Kanavel signs, no deep space involvement. - Reliable patient, can return. - No systemic signs (fever, leukocytosis, lymphangitis). Discharge package: - Oral antibiotic if indicated (see specific module). - Warm soaks TID, elevation, dry between soaks. - Wound check / dressing change at 24-48 h. - Hand or PCP follow-up at 48
nodes.recommendation: Outpatient: drained or early infection, no FTS or deep involvement. Antibiotics per pathway, soaks, 48-72 h follow-up.

nodes.title: First Trimester Emergencies
nodes.summary: Pregnancy test ALL reproductive-age women with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding
nodes.body: First Trimester Emergency Steps — quick reference. ED approach to pregnancy-related emergencies in the first trimester (<14 weeks). Common presentations: • Vaginal bleeding — miscarriage (7-27%), ectopic pregnancy (2%) • Nausea/vomiting — NVP (85%), hyperemesis gravidarum (3%) • Dysuria/flank pain — UTI, asymptomatic bacteriuria, pyelonephritis • Abdominal pain — appendicitis, ovarian torsion, ect

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Assessment
nodes.summary: Paradoxical bradycardia may occur with hemoperitoneum — do not be reassured by normal HR
nodes.body: Assess for hemodynamic instability: • Hypotension (SBP <90) • Tachycardia (HR >100) • Altered mental status • Signs of peritonitis Paradoxical bradycardia may occur with hemoperitoneum due to vagal stimulation from peritoneal blood irritation. [3]

nodes.title: Unstable — Assume Ruptured Ectopic
nodes.summary: Unstable first trimester = ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise — emergent OB, do NOT delay
nodes.body: Unstable first trimester patient = ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise. [1] Immediate actions: • 2 large-bore IVs, aggressive fluid resuscitation • Type & crossmatch, activate MTP if needed • Bedside FAST exam — free intraperitoneal fluid? • Bedside pelvic ultrasound — IUP present? If free fluid + no IUP → ruptured ectopic: • O-negative blood transfusion • Emergent OB consult for surgical inte

nodes.title: Chief Complaint
nodes.summary: Determine chief complaint: vaginal bleeding/pain, nausea/vomiting, dysuria, or RLQ pain
nodes.body: Determine the primary presentation to guide workup. All stable patients need: • Urine pregnancy test (if not done) • Focused obstetric history — gravida/parity (TPAL), prior ectopic, assisted reproductive technology • Focused physical exam including pelvic if indicated

nodes.title: Ultrasound & Beta-hCG
nodes.summary: Bedside TVUS + quant hCG — EP has 99.96% NPV for ectopic when IUP identified on bedside US
nodes.body: Bedside or formal transvaginal ultrasound + quantitative beta-hCG. Emergency physicians have 99.96% negative predictive value for ectopic when IUP identified on bedside US. [5] Ectopic Pregnancy Sites & Risk Factors High-Risk Ultrasound Findings for Ectopic — diagnostic clues when no IUP seen. Risk factors: prior ectopic, PID/STI history, salpingitis, IUD in situ, smoking (>1 pack/day OR 4), assis

nodes.title: High-Risk US Findings for Ectopic
nodes.summary: Tubal ring, adnexal mass, echogenic free fluid, pseudosac — urgent OB consult even with low hCG
nodes.body: Ultrasound findings highly suggestive of ectopic pregnancy (even without definitive extrauterine embryo): Adnexal findings: • Tubal ring sign (88% specific) — hyperechoic ring around extrauterine gestational sac, separate from ovary [38] • Adnexal mass separate from ovary — especially if tender on transvaginal probe pressure ("probe tenderness") • Complex adnexal mass with cystic and solid compone

nodes.title: IUP Confirmed
nodes.summary: IUP confirmed rules out ectopic in general population — ART patients: 1 in 100 heterotopic risk
nodes.body: Intrauterine pregnancy confirmed on ultrasound. In the general population, this essentially rules out ectopic (heterotopic risk: 1 in 4,000-30,000). Exception — Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART): Heterotopic pregnancy risk is 1 in 100. Maintain suspicion if ART patient with IUP + concerning symptoms. [7] If the patient has vaginal bleeding with confirmed IUP, evaluate for miscarriage spectrum

nodes.title: Pregnancy of Unknown Location
nodes.summary: Pregnancy of unknown location — serial hCG q48h, but 1/3 of ectopics have normal hCG rise
nodes.body: No IUP visualized. Beta-hCG below the discriminatory zone. Discriminatory zone: ACOG recommends conservatively ≥3500 mIU/mL (transvaginal US). Below this, a normal IUP may simply be too early to visualize. [8] Serial beta-hCG monitoring: • Normal viable IUP: beta-hCG rises ≥53% in 48 hours [9] • Slower rise or plateau: concerning for ectopic or nonviable IUP • Declining levels: may indicate comple

nodes.title: No IUP Above Discriminatory Zone
nodes.summary: hCG ≥3500 with no IUP = nonviable pregnancy (ectopic or missed miscarriage) — OB consult
nodes.body: Beta-hCG ≥3500 mIU/mL with no IUP visualized. This strongly suggests a nonviable pregnancy — either: • Nonviable IUP (missed miscarriage, complete miscarriage) • Ectopic pregnancy Does not definitively diagnose ectopic. OB consultation recommended for further evaluation and management. Patient should have close follow-up with serial beta-hCG and ultrasound until diagnosis is established.

nodes.title: Ectopic Pregnancy — Management
nodes.summary: Confirmed ectopic — determine medical (methotrexate) vs surgical management with OB
nodes.body: Confirmed or highly suspected ectopic pregnancy. All management in consultation with OB. Determine if patient is a candidate for medical vs surgical management.

nodes.title: Methotrexate for Ectopic Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Methotrexate 50mg/m2 IM if stable, no fetal cardiac activity, hCG <5000, reliable follow-up
nodes.body: Methotrexate — single-dose IM regimen in consultation with OB. Candidates (all must apply): • Hemodynamically stable • No fetal cardiac activity (FCA has OR 9.1 for failure) [12] • Beta-hCG <5000 mIU/mL (>5000 has OR 5.45 for failure) [11] • Reliable for follow-up • No contraindications to methotrexate Absolute contraindications to methotrexate: • Immunodeficiency • Cytopenia (anemia, leukopenia,
nodes.recommendation: Medical management with IM methotrexate in consultation with OB. Requires reliable follow-up for serial beta-hCG monitoring.

nodes.title: Surgical Management — Ectopic
nodes.summary: Emergent salpingectomy for ruptured ectopic or unstable patient — do NOT delay for workup
nodes.body: Emergent OB consult for surgical intervention. Indications: • Hemodynamic instability / ruptured ectopic • Contraindications to methotrexate • Beta-hCG >5000 mIU/mL • Fetal cardiac activity present • Failed medical management • Unreliable for follow-up Procedures (OB to determine): • Salpingostomy — removes ectopic, preserves tube (consider if contralateral tube damaged) • Salpingectomy — removes
nodes.recommendation: Emergent OB surgical consultation. Salpingostomy or salpingectomy. Laparotomy for ruptured ectopic with hemoperitoneum.

nodes.title: Miscarriage Classification
nodes.summary: Classify by os status and US: threatened, complete, incomplete/missed, or septic abortion
nodes.body: Classify based on cervical os status and ultrasound findings. Miscarriage Types & Findings Miscarriage rates: 9-17% (age 20-30), 20% (age 35), 40% (age 40). Approximately half are due to fetal chromosomal abnormalities. [14] If fever + uterine tenderness → suspect septic abortion — emergent OB consult, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, surgical evacuation.

nodes.title: Threatened Miscarriage
nodes.summary: Viable IUP + closed os: only 3.4% progress to miscarriage if cardiac activity present
nodes.body: Vaginal bleeding with a viable IUP (closed cervical os, fetal cardiac activity detected). Prognosis: If fetal cardiac activity is present, only 3.4% progress to miscarriage. However, heavy bleeding may increase this to 11-18%. [15] Spotting alone has no significant increase in miscarriage risk (OR 1.1). Heavy bleeding + pain increases risk (OR 3.0). [15] Management: • Reassurance — most will have

nodes.title: Complete Miscarriage
nodes.summary: Empty uterus, closed os — confirm on US, serial hCG to zero, emotional support
nodes.body: All products of conception have passed. Uterus is empty on ultrasound. Cervical os is closed. Management: • Confirm with ultrasound — empty uterus, closed os • No further ED intervention needed • Serial beta-hCG should trend to zero • OB follow-up for confirmation of completed miscarriage • Emotional support and grief resources Managing Communication Around Pregnancy Loss

nodes.title: Nonviable Pregnancy — Management Options
nodes.summary: Expectant, medical, or surgical management — when available, mifepristone 200 mg followed 24h later by misoprostol 800 mcg is more effective than misoprostol alone
nodes.body: OB consultation for definitive management plan. Options for the stable patient should be individualized based on symptoms, diagnosis, preferences, access to follow-up, and local OB resources. [17, 18, 42] If visible products in cervix: Remove at bedside with ring forceps. Consider sending to pathology (especially in recurrent miscarriage). Surgical management is MANDATORY for patients with signifi

nodes.title: Expectant Management
nodes.summary: Expect cramping and heavy bleeding — 40% may ultimately need unplanned surgical management
nodes.body: Allow natural passage of products of conception. Success rate: 50-80% will have complete miscarriage within 7-10 days. Higher success in incomplete miscarriage (already-open os) vs missed miscarriage. Up to 40% of patients initially managed expectantly or medically may ultimately require unplanned surgical management. [19] Counsel patient: • Expect cramping and bleeding (may be heavy) • Return to

nodes.title: Medical Management — Mifepristone + Misoprostol
nodes.summary: Preferred: mifepristone 200 mg PO then misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally 24h later; misoprostol-only is an alternative
nodes.body: Preferred regimen when mifepristone is available: mifepristone 200 mg PO, followed 24 hours later by misoprostol 800 mcg intravaginally. This combination is more effective than misoprostol alone. [42] If mifepristone is unavailable: misoprostol 800 mcg intravaginally, with one repeat dose as needed, no earlier than 3 hours after the first dose and typically within 7 days if there is no response. nodes.title: Surgical Management — D&C
nodes.summary: D&C mandatory for hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability — lowest incomplete miscarriage rate
nodes.body: Dilation & Curettage (D&C) — most effective option. Indications: • Hemodynamic instability or significant hemorrhage (MANDATORY) • Patient preference • Failed medical or expectant management • Septic abortion Advantages: • Lowest rates of incomplete miscarriage, bleeding, and need for transfusion [17] • Definitive and rapid Arranged through OB consultation — typically same-day or next-day procedur

nodes.title: Septic Abortion
nodes.summary: Septic abortion: emergent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics AND surgical evacuation — do NOT delay
nodes.body: Intrauterine infection in the setting of miscarriage or therapeutic abortion. Presentation: fever, uterine tenderness, purulent cervical discharge. EMERGENT management: • Large-bore IV access, fluid resuscitation • Blood cultures • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (gentamicin + clindamycin + ampicillin) • Emergent OB consult for surgical evacuation • May progress rapidly to sepsis/septic shock Do not
nodes.recommendation: Emergent OB consult. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical evacuation. ICU admission if septic.

nodes.title: Rh Status & Anti-D Immune Globulin
nodes.summary: RhIg is not routine for pregnancy loss/abortion <12 weeks under ACOG 2024, but remains recommended at ≥12 weeks and relevant for ectopic/instrumentation or other higher-risk events
nodes.body: Rh(D)-negative and unsensitized patients: apply the clinical scenario and current local OB policy. Pregnancy loss or abortion <12 weeks: ACOG 2024 suggests that routine Rh testing and RhIg prophylaxis can be forgone; RhIg may still be offered after shared decision-making. SMFM remains more cautious and supports testing/RhIg when feasible. Do not use the <12-week pathway for: • Ectopic pregnancy •

nodes.title: NVP Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: NVP affects 85% — assess if tolerating PO. Hyperemesis gravidarum (3%) needs IV rehydration
nodes.body: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) affects 85% of pregnant women. Hyperemesis gravidarum (3%) is the most severe form. NVP is a diagnosis of exclusion — rule out other causes first. NVP is actually protective against pregnancy loss (nausea HR 0.44; nausea + vomiting HR 0.20). [21] NVP Stepwise Treatment Pathway Assess: Can the patient tolerate oral medications?

nodes.title: Oral NVP Therapy — Stepwise
nodes.summary: First-line: pyridoxine 10-25mg TID + doxylamine 12.5mg TID — superior to B6 alone
nodes.body: First-line (ACOG Level A): [22] • Pyridoxine (B6) 10-25 mg PO TID • OR Pyridoxine + Doxylamine 12.5 mg PO TID Non-pharmacologic adjuncts: • Ginger capsules 250 mg PO QID • P6 acupressure wristband (reduced nausea, vomiting, ketonuria in RCT) [23] • Convert prenatal vitamin to folic acid only (reduces nausea trigger) Pyridoxine + doxylamine is superior to pyridoxine alone. [22] Did first-line thera

nodes.title: Second-Line Oral Antiemetics
nodes.summary: Add dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine, prochlorperazine, or promethazine to first-line therapy
nodes.body: Add one of the following to pyridoxine ± doxylamine: • Dimenhydrinate 50 mg PO QID (max 200 mg/day if also taking doxylamine) • Diphenhydramine 50 mg PO QID • Prochlorperazine 25 mg PR q12h • Promethazine 12.5 mg PO or PR q6h No high-quality evidence supports one specific agent over another. [24] Did second-line therapy improve symptoms?

nodes.title: IV Therapy for NVP / Hyperemesis
nodes.summary: IV fluids with dextrose (check thiamine first), ondansetron 4mg IV, metoclopramide if refractory
nodes.body: IV fluid resuscitation: • D5NS preferred over NS (slightly decreased nausea at 8-16h) [25] • Consider adding Thiamine 100 mg IV if protracted vomiting (prevents Wernicke encephalopathy before glucose administration) [22] Lab workup: BMP (electrolytes, renal function), LFTs, urinalysis (ketonuria) IV antiemetics — choose one: • Metoclopramide 10 mg IV q8h — reasonable first choice, no fetal malform

nodes.title: Hyperemesis Gravidarum — Admit
nodes.summary: Admit hyperemesis gravidarum: unable to tolerate PO, ketonuria, electrolyte derangement, >5% weight loss
nodes.body: Hyperemesis gravidarum — loss of ≥5% prepregnancy body weight with persistent nausea, vomiting, and ketonuria. OB consultation and admission for: • Continued IV rehydration (D5NS at 125 mL/hr) • Electrolyte monitoring and repletion • Thiamine 100 mg IV daily (prevent Wernicke encephalopathy) • Parenteral antiemetic regimen • Nutritional assessment One quarter of women with severe NVP have consider
nodes.recommendation: OB consult. Admit for IV rehydration, [thiamine](#/drug/thiamine/NVP], parenteral antiemetics, and electrolyte monitoring.

nodes.title: Nonobstetric Evaluation
nodes.summary: Evaluate non-bleeding complaint: NVP, UTI, appendicitis, or other with known IUP
nodes.body: First trimester patients can present with nonobstetric conditions that require modified diagnostic and treatment approaches. Imaging Safety in Pregnancy Antibiotic Safety in Pregnancy

nodes.title: UTI & Asymptomatic Bacteriuria
nodes.summary: Treat ALL asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy — untreated leads to pyelo in 20-40%
nodes.body: In pregnancy, asymptomatic bacteriuria MUST be treated if discovered. Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria has a 2.4% risk of progression to pyelonephritis (vs 0.6% with treatment). [27] Send urine culture — negative urinalysis does not reliably exclude bacteriuria. First-line antibiotics (7-day course): • Amoxicillin 875 mg PO BID • Cephalexin 500 mg PO q6h • Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID — likely s

nodes.title: Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy — Admit
nodes.summary: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy: admit for IV antibiotics — high risk of preterm labor and sepsis
nodes.body: Admit ALL pregnant patients with pyelonephritis for initial IV antibiotics. Insufficient evidence for outpatient management. [29] Treatment: • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily • Continue IV until afebrile 48 hours • Transition to oral antibiotics (e.g., Cephalexin) guided by culture sensitivities Bilateral mild hydronephrosis is normal in pregnancy (from hormonal changes + uterine compression). Do not ove
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV ceftriaxone. Continue until afebrile 48h, then oral step-down guided by cultures.

nodes.title: Appendicitis in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: MRI preferred over CT for appendicitis in pregnancy — perforation rate higher due to delayed dx
nodes.body: Most common surgical problem in pregnancy, though pregnant women are actually less likely to have appendicitis than age-matched nonpregnant women. [30] Despite traditional teaching, RLQ pain is the most common location at all gestational ages. [31] Peritonitis is more common in pregnant patients with appendicitis (OR 1.3). Peritonitis → 4× higher rate of preterm birth. [32] Imaging algorithm: 1. U

nodes.title: Discharge — Pregnancy of Unknown Location
nodes.summary: PUL requires strict ectopic precautions and serial hCG q48h until definitive diagnosis
nodes.body: 48-hour follow-up for repeat beta-hCG and ultrasound. Discharge criteria: • Hemodynamically stable • Normal vital signs • No US evidence of ruptured ectopic • Reliable for follow-up Strict return precautions: • Severe or worsening abdominal pain • Heavy vaginal bleeding (soaking >1 pad/hour) • Lightheadedness, dizziness, or syncope • Fever • Shoulder pain (referred from diaphragmatic irritation) C
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with 48-hour beta-hCG recheck and ultrasound. Strict return precautions. Continue serial monitoring until definitive diagnosis.

nodes.title: Discharge — Miscarriage
nodes.summary: OB follow-up within 1-2 weeks, return for soaking >1 pad/hr, fever, or severe pain
nodes.body: Miscarriage Discharge Instructions — shareable patient handout Provide: • Clear explanation of diagnosis in compassionate, culturally sensitive manner [37] • Prescription for chosen management (misoprostol if medical, or expectant instructions) • Pain management: ibuprofen 600 mg PO q6h PRN • Grief counseling resources and pregnancy-loss support groups [37] OB follow-up within 1-2 weeks. Return pr
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with management plan, pain control, grief resources, and OB follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Discharge — NVP
nodes.summary: Discharge with B6 + doxylamine prescription, small frequent meals, ginger, return if unable to keep fluids down
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: • Tolerating oral intake • Normal vital signs • Electrolytes corrected (if checked) • Able to keep down oral medications Prescriptions: • Pyridoxine 25 mg PO TID ± Doxylamine 12.5 mg PO TID • Consider generic pyridoxine + doxylamine instead of brand combination (significantly cheaper) • Second-line agent if needed Counsel: • Small, frequent meals • Avoid triggers (strong smells
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with pyridoxine ± doxylamine. Generic prescriptions preferred for cost savings. OB follow-up in 1 week.

nodes.title: General Disposition Criteria
nodes.summary: Disposition based on diagnosis and stability — ensure OB follow-up for all first trimester emergencies
nodes.body: Admit if: • Hemodynamic instability • Ruptured ectopic (OR) • Pyelonephritis (IV antibiotics) • Appendicitis (surgical) • Hyperemesis gravidarum refractory to ED treatment • Septic abortion Discharge if: • Hemodynamically stable • Diagnosis established or safe plan for outpatient follow-up • Able to tolerate oral intake and medications • Reliable for follow-up (especially PUL patients — 48h rechec
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on diagnosis and clinical stability. Ensure OB follow-up for all pregnant patients.

nodes.title: Fishhook Removal — Overview
nodes.summary: Barb prevents simple removal; four techniques available; match technique to hook type and location
nodes.body: Fishhook injuries are common presentations. Most can be managed in the ED with proper technique selection. The barb is the key challenge — it prevents simple retrograde removal. HOOK ANATOMY: • Eye: Loop for line attachment • Shank: Straight portion from eye to bend • Bend: Curved portion • Point: Sharp penetrating tip • Barb: Angled projection preventing easy removal • Gap/Gape: Distance from poi

nodes.title: Eye Involvement — STOP
nodes.summary: Ocular fishhook = emergent ophthalmology; cover with rigid shield; do NOT attempt removal
nodes.body: Fishhook in the eye, eyelid, or orbit requires immediate ophthalmology consultation.

nodes.title: Select Removal Technique
nodes.summary: Retrograde for barbless; string-yank for small hooks on fixed parts; advance-cut for large hooks; needle-cover for sensitive areas
nodes.body: Choose technique based on hook characteristics and location. Start with least traumatic option.

nodes.title: Retrograde Technique
nodes.summary: Simplest technique; press shank down to disengage barb; back out along entry path; stop if resistance
nodes.body: The simplest technique but lowest success rate. Best for barbless or minimally embedded hooks. [1,4] INDICATIONS: • Barbless hooks • Very superficially embedded hooks • Barb not yet engaged in tissue TECHNIQUE: 1. Apply downward pressure on hook shank to disengage barb 2. nodes.body: Highly effective, minimally traumatic, often requires no anesthesia. [1,4,7] CONTRAINDICATION: • Free-floating body parts (earlobe, nose, lip) • Must have stable surface to press against EQUIPMENT: • 0-silk suture, fishing line, or umbilical tape (~18 inches) • Eye protection for all personnel TECHNIQUE: 1. Wrap string around bend of hook at midpoint 2. Wind string around index finger for secure g

nodes.body: Almost always successful, even for large hooks. Best when barb is near skin surface. [1,5,6] INDICATIONS: • Large hooks • Barb visible near skin surface • String-yank failed or contraindicated • Multiple-barbed hooks ANESTHESIA: Always required — local infiltration at exit point TECHNIQUE FOR SINGLE-BARBED HOOKS: 1.
