nodes.title: Lymphadenopathy/Splenomegaly Workup
nodes.summary: Adenopathy/splenomegaly: lymphoma, TB, Castleman, EBV/CMV, HIV, sarcoid, SLE; excisional lymph node biopsy is key diagnostic step
nodes.body: DIFFERENTIAL: • Lymphoma (Hodgkin, Non-Hodgkin) • Tuberculosis • Castleman disease • Kikuchi disease • Sarcoidosis • Infectious mononucleosis (EBV, CMV) • HIV • Systemic lupus erythematosus DIRECTED WORKUP: • Lymph node biopsy — excisional preferred over FNA • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast • EBV/CMV serologies • HIV serology • Quantiferon/PPD • LDH (lymphoma marker) • ACE level (sarcoidosi

nodes.title: Hepatic Abnormalities Workup
nodes.summary: Liver abnormalities: abscess, granulomatous hepatitis, HCC, viral hepatitis, Q fever, brucellosis; CT/MRI + serologies, consider biopsy
nodes.body: DIFFERENTIAL: • Hepatic abscess (pyogenic, amoebic) • Granulomatous hepatitis • Hepatocellular carcinoma • Metastatic disease • Drug-induced liver injury • Viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV, EBV, CMV) • Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) • Brucellosis DIRECTED WORKUP: • CT abdomen with contrast or MRI • Hepatitis panel (HAV IgM, HBV, HCV) • EBV/CMV serologies • Blood cultures (prolonged incubation for Bruce

nodes.title: Endocarditis Workup
nodes.summary: Endocarditis: blood cultures x3, TTE first then TEE if negative + high suspicion; culture-negative = HACEK, Bartonella, Coxiella
nodes.body: Infective endocarditis is a classic cause of FUO. CLINICAL FEATURES: • New or changing murmur • Splinter hemorrhages • Janeway lesions, Osler nodes • Petechiae • Splenomegaly • Embolic phenomena (stroke, renal infarcts) MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA: See Endocarditis Criteria WORKUP: • Blood cultures x 3 sets from separate sites • Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) — first line • Transesophageal echocard

nodes.title: Rash/Skin Findings Workup
nodes.summary: Rash guides diagnosis: maculopapular = drug/viral/Still; petechial = endocarditis/RMSF/vasculitis; nodules = sarcoid/TB/fungal; biopsy early
nodes.body: RASH PATTERNS AND DIFFERENTIALS: Maculopapular: • Drug reaction • Viral exanthem • Secondary syphilis • Adult Still disease (salmon-colored, evanescent) Petechial/Purpuric: • Endocarditis • Meningococcemia • Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever • Vasculitis Nodules/Erythema nodosum: • Sarcoidosis • Tuberculosis • Inflammatory bowel disease • Fungal infections (coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis) DIRECTED

nodes.title: Drug Fever Evaluation
nodes.summary: Drug fever: 3-7% of FUO; beta-lactams most common; patient appears well, relative bradycardia; fever resolves 48-72h after stopping
nodes.body: Drug fever accounts for 3-7% of FUO cases. COMMON CULPRITS: • Antibiotics: Beta-lactams (most common), sulfonamides, vancomycin, nitrofurantoin • Anticonvulsants: Phenytoin, carbamazepine • Cardiovascular: Procainamide, quinidine, hydralazine • Other: Allopurinol, heparin, interferon, biologics CHARACTERISTICS: • Onset: days to weeks after starting drug • Patient may appear paradoxically well desp

nodes.title: Drug Fever Management
nodes.summary: If drug fever suspected, discontinue culprit and observe for 48-72h defervescence; if not feasible, continue workup
nodes.body: Is there a suspected drug that can be safely discontinued?

nodes.title: Drug Fever — Observe After Discontinuation
nodes.body: Management: • Discontinue suspected medication • Observe for 48-72 hours • Fever typically resolves within 48-72h (may take up to 5-7 days for some drugs) IF FEVER PERSISTS >72 HOURS: • Unlikely to be drug fever • Resume FUO workup IF FEVER RESOLVES: • Diagnosis confirmed • Document drug allergy/intolerance • Substitute alternative medication if needed NOTE: Do not re-challenge patient to confirm
nodes.recommendation: Discontinue suspected drug. Observe 48-72h. If fever resolves, diagnosis confirmed. If persists, resume FUO workup.

nodes.title: Advanced Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Advanced FUO: FDG-PET/CT (50-70% yield), tissue biopsy (bone marrow, temporal artery, lymph node), TB/fungal/atypical serologies
nodes.body: When initial workup is non-diagnostic, consider: IMAGING: • FDG-PET/CT — 50-70% diagnostic yield in FUO - Best for occult infection, malignancy, vasculitis - Consider early if initial workup negative • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast (if not done) • MRI spine/pelvis (osteomyelitis, abscess) • Echocardiogram (TTE → TEE if negative) TISSUE DIAGNOSIS: • Bone marrow biopsy (granulomas, lymphoma,

nodes.title: Advanced Workup Results
nodes.summary: FUO etiologies: infection (~30%), malignancy (~20%), autoimmune (~20%), undiagnosed (~30%)
nodes.body: What category of disease was identified (or most likely)?

nodes.title: Infectious Etiology
nodes.body: COMMON INFECTIOUS CAUSES OF FUO: BACTERIAL: • Tuberculosis (most common infectious cause worldwide) • Endocarditis (especially culture-negative) • Intra-abdominal abscess • Osteomyelitis • Prostatitis (elderly men) • Dental abscess VIRAL: • EBV, CMV (prolonged mononucleosis) • HIV (acute seroconversion or advanced) FUNGAL: • Histoplasmosis, Coccidioidomycosis (endemic areas) • Disseminated candidi
nodes.recommendation: Treat based on specific pathogen identified. ID consultation recommended for complex infections. Source control as indicated.

nodes.title: Malignancy-Related FUO
nodes.body: MALIGNANCIES ASSOCIATED WITH FUO: HEMATOLOGIC (most common): • Lymphoma (Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin) • Leukemia (especially AML, CLL) • Castleman disease • Myelodysplastic syndrome SOLID TUMORS: • Renal cell carcinoma (classic FUO cause) • Hepatocellular carcinoma • Ovarian cancer • Atrial myxoma • Colon cancer (especially with liver metastases) FEVER MECHANISM: • Tumor necrosis • Cytokine production
nodes.recommendation: Oncology referral for definitive diagnosis and treatment. NSAIDs may help control neoplastic fever.

nodes.title: Autoimmune/Inflammatory FUO
nodes.body: AUTOIMMUNE/INFLAMMATORY CAUSES OF FUO: VASCULITIS: • Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) — age >50, headache, jaw claudication, visual changes - ESR often >100, temporal artery biopsy diagnostic - Start steroids immediately if vision threatened • Polyarteritis nodosa • ANCA-associated vasculitis CONNECTIVE TISSUE: • Adult Still Disease — quotidian fever, salmon rash, arthritis, ferritin >10,000 • Systemic
nodes.recommendation: Rheumatology consultation. Corticosteroids often indicated. Start immediately if GCA with visual symptoms.

nodes.title: Undiagnosed FUO
nodes.body: ~30% of FUO cases remain undiagnosed despite thorough workup. PROGNOSIS: • Generally favorable if patient remains stable • Many resolve spontaneously over weeks to months • ~50% eventually diagnosed on long-term follow-up MANAGEMENT OPTIONS: 1. Watchful Waiting (preferred if stable): • Close outpatient follow-up • Repeat evaluation if new symptoms develop • Serial inflammatory markers 2. Empiric T
nodes.recommendation: Watchful waiting is appropriate if stable. Close follow-up with repeat evaluation if symptoms change. Avoid empiric steroids until infection excluded.

nodes.title: Nosocomial FUO
nodes.summary: Nosocomial FUO: lines, surgical sites, C. diff, drug fever, UTI, pneumonia, DVT; culture all sites, consider line removal
nodes.body: Definition: Fever developing ≥3 days after hospital admission in a patient admitted without fever. COMMON CAUSES: • Line-related infection — central lines, peripheral IVs • Surgical site infection • Clostridium difficile colitis • Drug fever (antibiotics very common) • UTI — especially with Foley catheter • Pneumonia — HAP/VAP • DVT/PE — immobility • Sinusitis — NG tube, intubation • Decubitus ulc

nodes.title: Nosocomial FUO Disposition
nodes.body: Management approach: • Remove/replace all unnecessary lines and catheters • Culture all potential sources • Targeted antibiotics based on culture results • Discontinue unnecessary medications (drug fever) IF SOURCE IDENTIFIED: • Treat accordingly • Source control (line removal, abscess drainage) IF NO SOURCE FOUND: • Continue surveillance • Consider CT imaging for occult abscess • ID consultation
nodes.recommendation: Systematic evaluation of all devices and medications. Remove unnecessary hardware. Culture-directed therapy.

nodes.title: Neutropenic FUO
nodes.summary: Neutropenic FUO: empiric anti-pseudomonal therapy (cefepime/pip-tazo/meropenem); add vanco if MRSA risk; antifungal if fever persists 4-7d
nodes.body: Definition: ANC <500/µL (or expected to fall <500), fever ≥38.3°C single or ≥38°C sustained, fever ≥3 days despite appropriate antibiotics. HIGH-RISK FEATURES: • Profound neutropenia (ANC <100) • Prolonged neutropenia (>7 days) • Hemodynamic instability • Mucositis • Pneumonia • New abdominal pain COMMON PATHOGENS: • Gram-positive: Staph, Strep, Enterococcus • Gram-negative: Pseudomonas, E. coli,

nodes.title: Neutropenic FUO Disposition
nodes.body: ALL neutropenic fever patients require: • Hospital admission • Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics • Daily assessment ESCALATION: • Add vancomycin if clinical deterioration, MRSA risk, or catheter concern • Add antifungal (echinocandin or amphotericin) if fever persists 4-7 days • Consider CT chest for pulmonary aspergillosis • Consider G-CSF for prolonged neutropenia DURATION: • Continue antibioti
nodes.recommendation: Admit all patients. Empiric anti-pseudomonal antibiotics. Escalate if no response. Continue until ANC recovery.

nodes.title: HIV-Associated FUO
nodes.summary: HIV FUO: CD4 guides differential; <200 = PCP, MAC, fungal; workup includes mycobacterial cultures, fungal antigens, crypto antigen
nodes.body: Definition: Confirmed HIV, fever ≥38.3°C, duration ≥4 weeks outpatient or ≥3 days inpatient. DIFFERENTIAL DEPENDS ON CD4 COUNT: CD4 >200: • Similar to immunocompetent hosts • Bacterial infections, lymphoma CD4 <200: • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) • Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) — CD4 <50 • Disseminated histoplasmosis/coccidioidomycosis • CMV disease — CD4 <50 • Tuberculosis — any CD4

nodes.title: HIV-Associated FUO Disposition
nodes.body: Management approach: IF CD4 <200 OR SEVERELY ILL: • Admit for expedited workup • ID consultation mandatory • Empiric treatment based on clinical presentation COMMON EMPIRIC THERAPIES: • PCP suspected: TMP-SMX • MAC suspected: Azithromycin + ethambutol • TB suspected: RIPE therapy • Fungal suspected: Amphotericin B or itraconazole ALWAYS: • Optimize or initiate ART (with ID guidance to avoid IRIS)
nodes.recommendation: ID consultation essential. Empiric therapy guided by CD4 count and clinical presentation. Optimize ART.

nodes.title: Diagnosis Established
nodes.body: Diagnosis established from FUO workup. Treat based on the specific etiology identified: • Infection: Targeted antimicrobial therapy, source control • Malignancy: Oncology referral for staging and treatment • Autoimmune/Inflammatory: Rheumatology referral, immunomodulatory therapy • Drug fever: Discontinue offending agent FOLLOW-UP: • Ensure clinical response to treatment • Repeat labs to document
nodes.recommendation: Targeted treatment based on diagnosis. Appropriate subspecialty referral. Close follow-up to ensure response.

nodes.title: Biliary Pathology Assessment
nodes.summary: Biliary colic <6h, no fever; cholecystitis >6h + fever; cholangitis = fever + jaundice + RUQ pain
nodes.body: Gallbladder Overview Key Differentials: • Biliary colic: Transient cystic duct obstruction, pain <6h, no fever • Acute cholecystitis: Persistent obstruction + inflammation, pain >6h, fever • Cholangitis: CBD obstruction + infection (Charcot's triad) • Choledocholithiasis: CBD stone ± symptoms Initial Assessment: 1. History: pain duration, location, fever, jaundice 2. Physical exam: Murphy's sign 3

nodes.title: Physical Exam & Lab Patterns
nodes.summary: Murphy's sign 79-96% specific; Charcot's triad 95.9% specific for cholangitis; check LFT pattern
nodes.body: Murphy's Sign Murphy's Sign: • Technique: Hand on RUQ below costal margin, patient inspires • Positive: Inspiratory arrest when hand contacts gallbladder • Sensitivity: 75-86% • Specificity: 79-96% (excellent for ruling IN) • Negative Predictive Value: 90.5% Charcot's Triad (Cholangitis): • Fever + Jaundice + RUQ pain • Present in only 50-70% of cholangitis cases • Specificity: 95.9% (if all three

nodes.title: Imaging Selection
nodes.summary: US first-line; POCUS: stones + wall >5mm + sono-Murphy = cholecystitis; MRCP if CBD stone suspected
nodes.body: POCUS Gallbladder RUQ Ultrasound (First-Line): • Gallstones: Sensitivity >86%, Specificity >88% • Overall for cholecystitis: Sens 94%, Spec 84% POCUS Findings for Cholecystitis: • Gallstones (echogenic + shadowing) • Wall thickening >5mm (90% specific) • Pericholecystic fluid • Sonographic Murphy's sign When to Get Additional Imaging: CT: If complications suspected (emphysematous, gangrenous, perf

nodes.title: Biliary Colic
nodes.summary: Biliary colic: pain <6h, no fever, normal labs; ketorolac for pain; discharge with surgical referral
nodes.body: Diagnosis: Transient cystic duct obstruction without inflammation Clinical Features: • RUQ/epigastric pain <6 hours duration • Pain may radiate to back or right shoulder • Often triggered by fatty meal • No fever, normal WBC • Murphy's sign may be positive but no peritoneal signs Labs: Normal LFTs, WBC, lipase Management: Pain Control: • Ketorolac 15-30mg IV/IM (NSAIDs reduce recurrence) • Opioids
nodes.recommendation: Pain control (ketorolac preferred). Discharge with surgical referral for elective cholecystectomy.

nodes.title: Tokyo Guidelines — Cholecystitis Severity
nodes.summary: Tokyo grading: I = uncomplicated; II = local complications or WBC >18K or >72h; III = organ dysfunction
nodes.body: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 Grade I (Mild): • Acute cholecystitis without organ dysfunction • No severe local inflammation • <5% complication rate Grade II (Moderate) — ANY of: • WBC >18,000 • Palpable RUQ mass • Symptom duration >72 hours • Marked local inflammation: - Gangrenous changes - Pericholecystic abscess - Hepatic abscess - Biliary peritonitis - Emphysematous cholecystitis Grade III (Severe) —

nodes.title: Grade I Cholecystitis — Mild
nodes.summary: Grade I: antibiotics + early lap chole within 72h; pip-tazo or amp-sulb; 3-7 days antibiotics
nodes.body: Management: Antibiotics (Monotherapy): • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6-8h, OR • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV q6h, OR • Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h Duration: 3-7 days (can shorten if early cholecystectomy) Pain Management: • Ketorolac 15-30mg IV • Opioids PRN NPO + IV fluids Surgery: • Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours • Better outcomes than delayed surgery • Same-day surgery safe if av
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics (pip-tazo or amp-sulb) + early cholecystectomy within 72h. Pain control with ketorolac.

nodes.title: Grade II Cholecystitis — Moderate
nodes.summary: Grade II: broader antibiotics + early chole if feasible; perc drainage if high-risk; 7-10 days antibiotics
nodes.body: Management: Antibiotics (Broader Spectrum): • Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h, OR • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q12h + metronidazole 500mg IV q6-8h, OR • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6-8h Duration: 7-10 days Surgery: • Early cholecystectomy still preferred within 72h if feasible • May require experienced surgeon due to inflammation • Subtotal cholecystectomy option if anatomy obscured If High Surgical Risk: • Per
nodes.recommendation: Broader antibiotics + early chole if feasible. Percutaneous drainage if high-risk. Monitor for progression.

nodes.title: Grade III Cholecystitis — Severe
nodes.summary: Grade III: ICU, broad antibiotics (carbapenems), percutaneous drainage, delay surgery until stable
nodes.body: ⚠️ ORGAN DYSFUNCTION PRESENT — ICU LEVEL CARE Resuscitation: • IV fluids, vasopressors if needed • Respiratory support • Correct coagulopathy Antibiotics (Broad-Spectrum): • Meropenem 1g IV q8h OR imipenem 500mg IV q6h, OR • Ceftazidime 2g IV q8h + metronidazole, OR • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h + consider aminoglycoside Duration: 7-14 days Source Control: • Percutaneous cholecystostomy (P
nodes.recommendation: ICU + resuscitation + carbapenems. Percutaneous drainage first-line. Delay surgery until stable.

nodes.title: Cholangitis Assessment
nodes.summary: Cholangitis diagnosis: systemic inflammation + cholestasis + imaging; definite if all 3 present
nodes.body: Cholangitis Diagnosis Tokyo Guidelines 2018 — Diagnostic Criteria: A. Systemic Inflammation: • Fever (>38°C) and/or rigors • Elevated WBC (<4K or >10K) or CRP B. Cholestasis: • Jaundice (total bili >2) • Abnormal LFTs (ALP/GGT elevated) C. Imaging: • Biliary dilatation (CBD >6mm, or >10mm post-cholecystectomy) • Evidence of etiology (stone, stricture, stent occlusion) Diagnosis: • Definite: A + B

nodes.title: Cholangitis Severity Grading
nodes.summary: Cholangitis: I = responds to abx; II = ≥2 criteria (WBC, fever, age, bili, albumin); III = organ dysfunction
nodes.body: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 — Cholangitis Severity: Grade I (Mild): • Responds to antibiotics • No organ dysfunction • Does not meet Grade II/III criteria Grade II (Moderate) — ≥2 of: • WBC >12,000 or <4,000 • Temperature ≥39°C • Age ≥75 years • Total bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL • Albumin <0.7× lower limit of normal Grade III (Severe) — ANY organ dysfunction: • Cardiovascular: hypotension requiring vasopressor •

nodes.title: Grade I Cholangitis — Mild
nodes.summary: Grade I cholangitis: antibiotics + elective ERCP; cholecystectomy if stones; 5-7 days total
nodes.body: Management: Antibiotics: • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q12h + metronidazole 500mg IV q6-8h, OR • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV q6h, OR • Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV q12h + metronidazole (if beta-lactam allergy) Duration: 5-7 days after source control Biliary Drainage: • ERCP for stone extraction if choledocholithiasis confirmed • Can be performed electively (within 24-48h) for Grade I Monitoring: • Clinical respo
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics + elective ERCP within 24-48h. Cholecystectomy if gallstones. 5-7 days antibiotics.

nodes.title: Grade II Cholangitis — Moderate
nodes.summary: Grade II: broad antibiotics + ERCP WITHIN 24h; mortality 1.7% with timely drainage vs 3.4% delayed
nodes.body: ⚠️ REQUIRES URGENT DRAINAGE WITHIN 24 HOURS Antibiotics (Broader Spectrum): • Ceftazidime 2g IV q8h + metronidazole 500mg IV q6-8h, OR • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6-8h, OR • Cefepime 2g IV q12h + metronidazole Duration: 7-10 days Urgent Biliary Drainage (within 24h): • ERCP preferred — stone extraction + sphincterotomy • If ERCP fails → percutaneous transhepatic drainage (PTD) • If PTD not
nodes.recommendation: Broad antibiotics + ERCP within 24 hours. Mortality doubles if drainage delayed. 7-10 days antibiotics.

nodes.title: Grade III Cholangitis — Severe
nodes.summary: Grade III: ICU, sepsis bundle, carbapenems + vanc, EMERGENT ERCP within 2-4h; 50% mortality if delayed
nodes.body: ⚠️ SEPTIC SHOCK — IMMEDIATE INTERVENTION REQUIRED Resuscitation: • Large-bore IV access, aggressive fluid resuscitation • Vasopressors (norepinephrine) if hypotensive • ICU admission Antibiotics (Broadest Spectrum): • Meropenem 1g IV q8h + vancomycin 15-20mg/kg IV, OR • Carbapenem ± aminoglycoside (tobramycin 5-7mg/kg q24h) Duration: 10-14 days EMERGENT Biliary Drainage: • ERCP within 2-4 hours if
nodes.recommendation: ICU + resuscitation + carbapenems + vanc. EMERGENT ERCP within 2-4h. Mortality 50% without drainage.

nodes.title: Choledocholithiasis Assessment
nodes.summary: CBD stone probability: high (visible stone, cholangitis) → ERCP; intermediate → MRCP; low → surgery
nodes.body: CBD Stone Probability Probability Assessment: High Probability (>50%) — ERCP directly: • CBD stone visible on US/CT • Clinical cholangitis • Bilirubin >4 + dilated CBD (>6mm) Intermediate Probability (10-50%) — Get MRCP/EUS: • Dilated CBD (>6mm) without visible stone • Bilirubin 1.8-4 • Abnormal LFTs (elevated ALP, GGT) • Age >55 • Gallstone pancreatitis Low Probability (<10%) — Proceed to cholecy

nodes.title: MRCP Results
nodes.summary: MRCP: 85-100% sens, 90% spec for CBD stones; if positive → ERCP; if negative → proceed to chole
nodes.body: MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography): Performance: • Sensitivity: 85-100% • Specificity: 90% • NPV: Excellent (rules out CBD stone) Best for: • Intermediate probability patients • Confirms/excludes stone before ERCP • Avoids unnecessary ERCP (and its complications) Alternatives if MRCP unavailable: • EUS (endoscopic ultrasound) — similar accuracy • Intraoperative cholangiogram during

nodes.title: ERCP for Choledocholithiasis
nodes.summary: ERCP: sphincterotomy + extraction, >95% success; cholecystectomy after to prevent recurrence
nodes.body: ERCP Procedure Indications: • Confirmed CBD stone • Clinical cholangitis requiring drainage • High probability choledocholithiasis Procedure: • Sphincterotomy + balloon/basket extraction • >95% stone clearance rate Timing: • Cholangitis Grade II-III: within 24h (or emergent) • Non-emergent: within 48-72h of diagnosis Complications (5-10%): • Post-ERCP pancreatitis (3-5%) — rectal indomethacin redu
nodes.recommendation: ERCP for CBD stone extraction. >95% success. Cholecystectomy same admission or within 2 weeks.

nodes.title: Antibiotic Selection Summary
nodes.summary: Antibiotics by severity; cover gram-negatives + anaerobes; carbapenems for severe; de-escalate on cultures
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Cholecystitis: | Grade | First-Line | Alternative | Duration | |-------|-----------|-------------|----------| | I | Pip-tazo 4.5g q6-8h | Amp-sulb 3g q6h | 3-7 days | | II | Cefoxitin 2g q6h | CTX + metronidazole | 7-10 days | | III | Meropenem 1g q8h | Pip-tazo + aminoglycoside | 7-14 days | Cholangitis: | Grade | First-Line | Alternative | Duration | |-------|-----------|------

nodes.title: Cholecystectomy Timing
nodes.summary: Early chole (<72h) preferred; even up to 10 days safe; delayed >2 weeks has worse outcomes
nodes.body: Surgical Timing Evidence Early Cholecystectomy Evidence (WSES 2020): Within 72 hours ("Golden 72"): • Shorter total hospital stay • Lower complication rate • No increase in surgical difficulty • Cost-effective Within 24 hours: • Even better outcomes in some studies • Same-admission surgery safe if available Up to 10 days: • Still safe and feasible • No increased operative difficulty vs early • Bet

nodes.title: Disposition — Early Surgery
nodes.summary: Early lap chole: NPO, antibiotics until OR, typically discharge POD 0-1; follow-up 1-2 weeks
nodes.body: Admission for Early Cholecystectomy: Pre-Op: • NPO, IV fluids • Antibiotics (continue until surgery) • Surgical consult • Anesthesia clearance Surgery: • Laparoscopic cholecystectomy preferred • Subtotal cholecystectomy if anatomy unclear (equally safe) • Intraoperative cholangiogram if CBD stone concern Post-Op: • Advance diet as tolerated • Pain control • Antibiotics: can stop after surgery if u
nodes.recommendation: Admit for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (<72h). Stop antibiotics post-op if uncomplicated.

nodes.title: Disposition — Delayed Surgery
nodes.summary: Delayed: perc drain if needed, antibiotics, optimize, interval chole 6-8 weeks; low-fat diet
nodes.body: For high-risk patients requiring stabilization: Indications for Delayed Approach: • Grade III cholecystitis (stabilize first) • Severe comorbidities (ASA IV) • Anticoagulation requiring reversal/bridging • Acute MI or unstable cardiac disease • Pregnancy (prefer 2nd trimester) Bridge to Surgery: • Percutaneous cholecystostomy if needed • Complete antibiotic course • Optimize comorbidities Interval
nodes.recommendation: Percutaneous drainage if needed → stabilize → interval cholecystectomy 6-8 weeks.

nodes.title: Non-Surgical Management
nodes.summary: Non-surgical: antibiotics + perc drain, chronic tube option, 30-50% recurrence; close follow-up
nodes.body: For patients who are NOT surgical candidates: Indications: • Very high surgical risk (ASA V) • End-stage disease with limited life expectancy • Patient declines surgery Management: • Complete antibiotic course (7-14 days) • Percutaneous cholecystostomy for source control • Tube management and eventual removal Long-term Options: • Chronic cholecystostomy tube • Medical dissolution therapy (ursodiol
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics + percutaneous drainage. Long-term tube or monitor. 30-50% recurrence without surgery.

nodes.title: Generalized Itching — Sick Check First
nodes.body: Itching is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Most generalized pruritus is benign, but a handful of causes are time-critical: itching can be the *prodrome* of anaphylaxis, the herald of a life-threatening drug eruption, or the surface sign of biliary obstruction/cholangitis. Screen for those before you reach for an antihistamine. ⚠️ 4 DO-NOT-MISS diagnoses 1. Anaphylaxis prodrome — urticaria/flushing/itc

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Six-branch triage: anaphylaxis / DRESS-SJS-TEN / angioedema / cholestatic / urticaria / systemic-driver.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous causes first, then the systemic and benign ones. Each branch runs a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis — Systemic-Involvement Gate
nodes.summary: Skin + any second system = anaphylaxis; give IM epinephrine immediately, do not wait for shock.
nodes.body: Itching/urticaria with ANY second organ system involved is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise. Apply the criteria: acute onset of skin/mucosal signs PLUS at least one of — respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia), reduced BP/end-organ symptoms (collapse, syncope, incontinence), or severe GI symptoms after a likely allergen. Hypotension after a known allergen alone also qualifie

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis — IM Epinephrine Now
nodes.body: Open Anaphylaxis for the full pathway. Next steps (do not delay): - IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh immediately — repeat every 5–15 min as needed. This is the first and most important drug. - Position supine (or left lateral if pregnant/vomiting), high-flow O2, large-bore IV, IV fluids for hypotension. - Adjuncts (do NOT substitute for epinephrine): H1/H2 antihista
nodes.recommendation: IM epinephrine immediately + repeat PRN, O2, IV fluids; antihistamines/beta-agonist are adjuncts only; observe for biphasic and prescribe auto-injector.

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis — Excluded (for now)
nodes.body: Itching or hives with no airway, respiratory, GI, or hemodynamic involvement is not anaphylaxis right now. It can evolve fast — if any second organ system develops (throat tightness, wheeze, vomiting, lightheadedness), give IM epinephrine immediately. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Isolated hives/itch is not anaphylaxis; counsel and re-treat as anaphylaxis the moment a second system is involved.

nodes.title: Severe Drug Eruption — DRESS / Early SJS-TEN Gate
nodes.summary: New drug + fever + mucosal/skin pain/Nikolsky+ = DRESS/SJS-TEN; stop the drug, dermatology, supportive care.
nodes.body: A new drug + fever + a spreading eruption is a red-flag combination. DRESS: 2–8 weeks after a culprit drug (allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin) with fever, facial edema, diffuse rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and organ involvement (hepatitis, nephritis). SJS-TEN: skin pain/tenderness, dusky or target lesions, mucosal erosions (eyes, mouth, genitals), a positive N

nodes.title: DRESS / SJS-TEN — Stop the Drug + Emergent Dermatology
nodes.body: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction (no dedicated DRESS deep-dive yet — manage here). If the picture is frank SJS-TEN, open SJS-TEN for the full pathway. Next steps: - Immediately STOP the suspected culprit drug — this is the single most important intervention and improves survival. - Emergent dermatology consult; SCORTEN to prognosticate TEN. Involve ophthalmology, urology, and burn/ICU for extensi
nodes.recommendation: Stop the culprit drug now, emergent dermatology, SCORTEN + supportive burn-level care; steroids for DRESS organ involvement (specialist-guided).

nodes.title: Severe Drug Eruption — Unlikely
nodes.body: No fever, no mucosal involvement, no skin pain/Nikolsky sign, and no organ dysfunction makes DRESS/SJS-TEN unlikely right now. These can evolve over days — if a patient on a new high-risk drug develops fever, facial swelling, mucosal erosions, or skin pain, stop the drug and escalate immediately. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Severe drug eruption unlikely without systemic/mucosal signs; give strict return precautions to anyone on a new high-risk drug.

nodes.title: Angioedema — Airway + Mechanism Gate
nodes.summary: Angioedema = airway assessment first; separate histaminergic (treat allergic) from bradykinin (ACE-I/HAE) pathways.
nodes.body: Angioedema is deep dermal/subcutaneous swelling — lips, tongue, face, larynx — and threatens the airway. Distinguish the mechanisms: histaminergic/allergic (itchy, urticarial, responds to epinephrine/antihistamines/steroids) vs bradykinin-mediated (ACE-inhibitor–induced or hereditary/C1-inhibitor deficiency — NOT itchy, often no hives, poorly responsive to the allergic cocktail). The key ED questi

nodes.title: Angioedema — Airway First, Then Treat by Mechanism
nodes.body: Open Angioedema for the full pathway. Next steps: - Airway is priority one. Tongue/laryngeal involvement, voice change, or stridor → prepare for early, controlled intubation (awake/fiberoptic) with a double set-up and surgical airway backup. Do not wait for total obstruction. - Histaminergic/allergic angioedema (itchy, hives): treat like anaphylaxis — IM epinephrine, antihistamines, steroids. - AC
nodes.recommendation: Secure the airway early if involved; treat histaminergic angioedema like anaphylaxis; stop ACE-I for bradykinin type and use HAE-directed therapy when applicable.

nodes.title: Angioedema — Excluded
nodes.body: Only superficial itchy wheals without deep lip/tongue/facial/laryngeal swelling — this is urticaria, not angioedema. Reassess the airway if deep swelling develops. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: No deep swelling → angioedema excluded; work the urticaria branch and re-check the airway if deep swelling appears.

nodes.title: Cholestatic Pruritus — Obstruction + Infection Gate
nodes.summary: Cholestatic itch → find obstruction + rule out cholangitis (Charcot/Reynolds); pregnancy cholestasis carries fetal risk.
nodes.body: Itching with jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools points to cholestasis — bile acids deposited in the skin. The ED job is to find obstruction (stone, stricture, mass) and rule out ascending cholangitis: Charcot triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) ± Reynolds pentad (+ hypotension, confusion). Cholangitis is a septic emergency. Also consider cholestasis of pregnancy in a pregnant patient (fetal risk).

nodes.title: Cholestasis — Image the Biliary Tree + Treat Infection
nodes.body: Open Acute Jaundice for the full workup of the jaundiced patient. Next steps: - RUQ ultrasound first (ductal dilation, stones); CT/MRCP as indicated. - Cholangitis (Charcot/Reynolds): this is a septic emergency — resuscitate on the Sepsis pathway (IV fluids, blood cultures, lactate; qSOFA in the toolbar), broad-spectrum antibiotics, and urgent biliary decompression (ERCP). Consult GI/surgery early
nodes.recommendation: RUQ US + LFTs; cholangitis → sepsis resuscitation + broad-spectrum abx + urgent ERCP; cholestyramine for itch; OB involvement if pregnant.

nodes.title: Cholestatic Itch — Unlikely
nodes.body: No jaundice, normal LFTs, and no cholestatic features make biliary obstruction an unlikely driver of the itch. Keep it on the list if the picture changes (new jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain). Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Cholestasis unlikely with normal LFTs/no jaundice; revisit if jaundice or RUQ symptoms develop.

nodes.title: Acute Urticaria — Isolated vs Systemic Gate
nodes.summary: Simple urticaria = migratory itchy wheals <24 h, no systemic signs; fixed/painful lesions → reconsider vasculitis/drug eruption.
nodes.body: Acute urticaria = transient, migratory, intensely itchy wheals, each individual lesion lasting <24 h and blanching, with no scarring. Most is idiopathic or post-viral; triggers include foods, drugs, and infections. The essential safety check is that there is NO systemic involvement (no airway/GI/BP signs — that would be anaphylaxis) and no angioedema or drug-eruption red flags.

nodes.title: Acute Urticaria — Antihistamines + Trigger Avoidance
nodes.body: Simple acute urticaria (no dedicated consult — manage here): - Second-generation H1 antihistamines are first-line (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine), up-dosed as needed; add an H2 blocker for incomplete response. - A short steroid course for severe or refractory flares (limited evidence, use judiciously). - Identify and remove triggers (new drugs, foods, infections); most acute urticaria
nodes.recommendation: 2nd-gen H1 antihistamines first-line (± H2), short steroid for severe flares, remove triggers, anaphylaxis return precautions.

nodes.title: Not Simple Urticaria — Reassess
nodes.body: Fixed lesions lasting >24 h, painful or burning wheals, bruise-like/residual pigmentation, or any systemic feature argue against simple urticaria — consider urticarial vasculitis, a drug eruption, or an evolving systemic process. Re-run the DRESS/SJS-TEN and anaphylaxis gates and consider dermatology. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Fixed/painful/bruising lesions are not simple urticaria — reconsider vasculitis/drug eruption and re-screen the emergent branches.

nodes.title: Itch Without a Rash — Systemic-Driver Gate
nodes.summary: Itch without rash → screen renal/hepatic/heme-malignancy/endocrine drivers; aquagenic itch + B-sx are red flags.
nodes.body: Generalized itch with little or no primary rash points to a systemic driver. Key categories: renal (uremic pruritus in CKD/dialysis), hepatic/cholestatic (already screened), hematologic/malignancy (polycythemia vera — itch after a hot shower; Hodgkin lymphoma with B-symptoms — weight loss, night sweats, fever), endocrine (thyroid disease, diabetes), drug-induced (opioids), and pregnancy (cholestas

nodes.title: Systemic-Driver Itch — Targeted Workup + Referral
nodes.body: Systemic pruritus (no dedicated consult — manage here). If a hematologic malignancy is suspected, Oncological Emergencies covers acute complications. Screening labs when itch has no rash: CBC with differential (eosinophilia, polycythemia — high Hgb/Hct suggests PV), renal function (uremic itch), LFTs (cholestasis), TSH, glucose/HbA1c, and — if B-symptoms/lymphadenopathy — LDH and imaging for lymph
nodes.recommendation: No-rash itch → CBC/renal/LFT/TSH/glucose ± LDH+imaging for B-sx; treat the driver (renal, PV/lymphoma, endocrine) and refer.

nodes.title: Likely Dermatologic / Xerosis
nodes.body: No systemic clues and no primary lesions point to a dermatologic cause — most commonly xerosis (dry skin), especially in older adults and in dry/cold climates, or a low-grade dermatitis/scabies. Treat symptomatically and refer to dermatology if it persists. Proceed to disposition.
nodes.recommendation: Likely xerosis/dermatitis — emollients, gentle skin care, antihistamines for symptom relief, dermatology referral if persistent.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle
nodes.body: The generalized-pruritus work-up bundle (scale to acuity): - Screen for the emergencies first: airway/hemodynamic check (anaphylaxis), a full skin AND mucous-membrane exam (drug eruption, Nikolsky), and a medication reconciliation for new drugs in the last 2–8 weeks. - Vitals + qSOFA if febrile/toxic (DRESS, cholangitis, sepsis). - Targeted labs for itch without rash: CBC with differential, renal

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Anaphylaxis/severe drug eruption/airway angioedema/cholangitis → escalate + admit; stable + diagnosed → disposition.
nodes.body: After the emergency screen, skin/mucosal exam, and initial labs — where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging / Labs
nodes.body: Match the study to the question: - RUQ ultrasound / MRCP — cholestatic pruritus with jaundice (ductal dilation, stones, mass); the key study for suspected biliary obstruction/cholangitis. - CBC with differential — eosinophilia (DRESS), polycythemia (PV), cytopenias (lymphoma/hematologic disease). - Renal/hepatic panels, TSH, glucose — systemic-driver itch without a rash. - LDH + CT chest/abdomen/p

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit the emergencies (ICU/burn as needed); observe biphasic-risk/borderline; discharge benign with follow-up.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit the dangerous causes. - Refractory anaphylaxis → ICU (epinephrine infusion, airway). - DRESS / SJS-TEN → dermatology + burn unit/ICU for extensive disease; stop the culprit drug, supportive care, specialist co-management. - Airway angioedema → monitored/ICU setting until swelling resolves; HAE-directed therapy as needed. - Cholangitis → admit for antibiotics + urgent ERCP/biliary decompressi
nodes.recommendation: Admit anaphylaxis/DRESS-SJS-TEN/airway angioedema/cholangitis to the appropriate level (ICU/burn); stop culprit drugs, involve specialists.

nodes.title: Observe in the ED
nodes.body: Observation for the borderline patient — e.g., treated anaphylaxis watched for a biphasic reaction, resolving allergic angioedema, or an uncertain evolving eruption. - Serial airway/vital checks; repeat exam if the picture changes. - Ensure symptoms are controlled and the airway is stable before discharge; specialist input if uncertain. - Provide a prescription (auto-injector after anaphylaxis) an
nodes.recommendation: Short ED observation for biphasic/airway risk with serial checks, then discharge with an auto-injector + return precautions or admit.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge the well patient with a clear plan. - Simple urticaria: scheduled 2nd-gen antihistamines, trigger avoidance, allergy/derm referral if >6 weeks; anaphylaxis return precautions. - Xerosis/dermatitis: emollients, gentle skin care, dermatology follow-up if persistent. - Benign systemic itch: outpatient workup of the identified driver (renal, hepatic, endocrine, heme) with the appropriate spe
nodes.recommendation: Discharge benign/treated patients with symptom control, outpatient driver workup, specialist referral, and explicit airway/severe-eruption return precautions.

nodes.title: Weakness Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Glucose, ECG, vitals, airway/respiratory strength, meds/tox, and localization first.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Neuromuscular respiratory failure (GBS, myasthenic crisis, botulism) \u2014 single-breath count, NIF/FVC. 2. Hyperkalemia / severe electrolyte derangement \u2014 ECG now, but a normal ECG does not exclude life-threatening hyperkalemia. Send the potassium regardless. 3. Acute coronary syndrome / occult sepsis \u2014 weakness as an atypical presentation in elderly/diab

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Shock, stroke, neuromuscular respiratory risk, electrolytes, endocrine, cardiac/anemia, and tox are the first exclusions.
nodes.body: Pick the first dangerous lane. You can return after the immediate action.

nodes.title: Shock / Sepsis / Volume Problem
nodes.body: Open Sepsis Management when infection physiology is plausible. Next 5 minutes: monitor, IV/IO, glucose, ECG, lactate if ill, cultures if they do not delay antibiotics, crystalloid if hypoperfused, pressor early if persistent hypotension, POCUS heart/lungs/IVC when physiology is unclear. Pitfall: older adults may present with isolated weakness and no fever. Hypotension, tachypnea, confusion, or rig
nodes.recommendation: Treat physiology first. Weakness with shock is not a benign chief complaint.

nodes.title: Neurovascular Weakness
nodes.body: Open Acute Ischemic Stroke, ICH, Cervical Artery Dissection, or Altered Mental Status Hub as appropriate. Next 5 minutes: glucose corrected/confirmed, last-known-well, NIHSS-style focused exam, CT/CTA/perfusion per stroke workflow, BP strategy by diagnosis, anticoagulant/reversal history. Pitfall: generalized weakness can hide a focal deficit when the patient is tired, aphasic, neglectful, or unab
nodes.recommendation: If the exam localizes, activate the stroke/bleed workflow.

nodes.title: GBS / Myasthenia / Neuromuscular Respiratory Risk
nodes.body: Open Guillain-Barre Syndrome or Myasthenia Gravis. Next 5 minutes: assess bulbar symptoms, cough, secretion handling, neck flexion, single breath count or bedside respiratory mechanics if available, cardiac monitoring for dysautonomia, avoid premature discharge even if pulse ox is normal. Danger signs: rapidly progressive weakness, inability to walk, facial/bulbar weakness, autonomic instability,
nodes.recommendation: Normal SpO2 does not clear neuromuscular respiratory failure. Trend ventilation and bulbar safety.

nodes.title: Electrolyte Paralysis / Weakness
nodes.body: Open Potassium Disorders, Sodium Disorders, Calcium Disorders, Phosphorous Disorders, or Magnesium Disorders. Next 5 minutes: ECG first, BMP/Mg/Phos/Ca, renal function, CK if rhabdomyolysis concern. Treat unstable ECG hyperkalemia immediately with calcium. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia with seizure/coma follows hypertonic saline pathway. Severe hypoK/hypoPhos/hypoMg can present as profound weakn
nodes.recommendation: ECG-dangerous electrolyte disorders are treated before complete diagnostic certainty.

nodes.title: Endocrine / Metabolic Weakness
nodes.body: Open DKA, Adrenal Insufficiency, Thyroid Disorders, Hypoglycemia, Heat Stroke, or Hypothermia when the phenotype fits. Next 5 minutes: VBG/chemistry/ketones for DKA/HHS, potassium before insulin, temperature, TSH/free T4 if thyroid storm/myxedema clues, empiric hydrocortisone if adrenal crisis is plausible with shock/hypoglycemia/hyponatremia. Pitfall: fatigue plus hypotension/hypoglycemia/hyponat
nodes.recommendation: Correct the life-threatening physiology while the endocrine workup runs.

nodes.title: Cardiac / Dysrhythmia / Anemia / Bleeding
nodes.body: Open Chest Pain Hub, STEMI, NSTEMI, A-Fib RVR, or GI Bleed Hub when symptoms, ECG, or bleeding history point that way. Next 5 minutes: ECG, troponin if ischemia possible, orthostatics if safe, CBC, rectal/bleeding history when anemia/GI bleed plausible, POCUS when shock or dyspnea coexists. Pitfall: MI, dysrhythmia, GI bleed, and severe anemia often present as weakness in older adults, diabetics,
nodes.recommendation: Weakness with ECG change, syncope, dyspnea, pallor, or bleeding history needs cardiac/bleeding workup.

nodes.title: Toxicologic / Medication Weakness
nodes.body: Open TCA Toxidrome, Calcium Channel Blocker Overdose, Beta-Blocker Overdose, Digoxin Toxicity, Salicylate Toxicity, Toxic Alcohols, CO Toxicity, or the Unknown Ingestion Hub when clues fit. Next 5 minutes: ECG for QRS/QTc/bradycardia, glucose, VBG/anion gap/osm gap, acetaminophen/salicylate levels when ingestion possible, co-oximetry if exposure risk, medication reconciliation, poison center early
nodes.recommendation: Use ECG and acid-base physiology to find dangerous tox causes.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Glucose/ECG/labs, meds, focused neuro, orthostatics/ambulation, then reassess.
nodes.body: Default bundle when no killer has declared itself: - Glucose, ECG, monitor if ill. - CBC, CMP (potassium, sodium, calcium, renal function), Mg, Phos, CK when myopathy/rhabdo possible. - UA/CXR/cultures only when infection clues exist; do not shotgun without exam signal. - Orthostatic vitals and ambulation test when safe. - Medication reconciliation, recent illness, tick/travel, exertion, dialysis,

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Worsening or inability to walk is not benign weakness.
nodes.body: A repeat exam is the key test in vague weakness.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: CT/CTA for focal neuro, MRI for cord/progressive neuro, CXR/CT/US when physiology points there.
nodes.body: Image by localization and physiology: - CT/CTA head/neck: focal deficit, aphasia, gaze deviation, severe headache, anticoagulated fall, or stroke window question. - MRI brain/spine: progressive neurologic deficit, myelopathy, cord/root syndrome, suspected demyelination, or persistent unexplained neuro weakness after CT. - CXR: infection, CHF, hypoxia, dyspnea, or occult pneumonia in older adults.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge requires baseline function, clear cause, stable vitals, and safe ambulation/support.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on trajectory, ability to walk, cause certainty, and safety.

nodes.title: Admit / ICU / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit/ICU for shock, sepsis, stroke/bleed, ACS/dysrhythmia, dangerous electrolyte/endocrine derangement, progressive weakness, inability to ambulate, respiratory/bulbar weakness, suspected GBS/MG crisis, rhabdomyolysis with renal risk, unsafe environment, or persistent unexplained true weakness.
nodes.recommendation: Persistent true weakness is not a discharge diagnosis until dangerous localization is excluded.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exam
nodes.body: Observe when symptoms are improving but not baseline, orthostasis/dehydration needs treatment response, electrolytes require repeat checks, postictal/toxic/metabolic effect may recur, or gait/safety cannot be assessed immediately.
nodes.recommendation: Use repeat neuro exam, ambulation, vitals, ECG, and targeted labs before discharge.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: back to baseline strength/function, walking safely or baseline mobility restored, vitals stable, glucose/electrolytes/ECG reassuring or corrected, no focal/bulbar/respiratory signs, no concerning medication/tox recurrence, and reliable follow-up/support. Return precautions: worsening weakness, inability to walk, dyspnea, trouble swallowing/speaking, syncope, chest pain, fever,
nodes.recommendation: Document repeat exam, ambulation status, and why dangerous causes are unlikely.

nodes.title: GI Bleed Hub — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Look, count, feel — then commit. Shock index >1 = ongoing loss. Rectal exam now.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Hemorrhagic shock / massive bleed \u2014 shock index >1, ongoing hematemesis; activate MTP. 2. Variceal hemorrhage \u2014 cirrhosis stigmata; octreotide + antibiotics + early endoscopy. 3. Aortoenteric fistula \u2014 prior aortic graft + GI bleed = catastrophic until excluded. 4. Brisk upper bleed presenting as hematochezia \u2014 10\u201315%, more shocky; place an N

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the Source Pattern
nodes.body: Pick the branch that fits best. If two fit, pick the more dangerous one. None of these are mutually exclusive — patient can have variceal + coag + AAA simultaneously.

nodes.title: Upper GI Bleed Pathway
nodes.summary: Open Upper GI Bleed — Glasgow-Blatchford triage, PPI, octreotide + ceftriaxone if variceal, endoscopy timing.
nodes.body: Open Upper GI Bleed consult. Glasgow-Blatchford for triage, variceal vs non-variceal cascade, endoscopy timing. Recognize fast: [4] - Hematemesis (red blood = active variceal or arterial; coffee-grounds = older blood, less brisk) - Cirrhotic stigmata: jaundice, spider angiomata, caput, ascites, palmar erythema - Risk factors: NSAID, ASA, anticoag, prior PUD, prior varices, H. pylori, EtOH binge -

nodes.title: Melena — Upper Until Proven Otherwise
nodes.summary: Open Upper GI Bleed consult — melena is upper ~90% of the time. BUN/Cr >30 confirms.
nodes.body: Melena (black, tarry, malodorous stool) is upper GI bleed ~90% of the time. Treat as UGIB workup. Right-sided colonic bleed CAN cause melena if transit >14 h, but UGIB is the safer working diagnosis. Open Upper GI Bleed consult. BUN/Cr ratio >30 further supports upper source (urea from digested hemoglobin protein). Do NOT call it lower without negative upper endoscopy. Premature commitment to lowe

nodes.title: Lower GI Bleed Pathway
nodes.summary: Open Lower GI Bleed — Oakland score, but rule out brisk upper first if shocky.
nodes.body: Open Lower GI Bleed consult. Oakland score for triage, CTA vs colonoscopy timing, embolization decision. Red flag — brisk upper bleed presenting as hematochezia: 10-15% of hematochezia in shocky patients is upper source. Check the four-question screen before committing to lower pathway: 1. Hemodynamically unstable + hematochezia? → suspect brisk upper, place NG and/or send for urgent EGD before co

nodes.title: Anticoag/Antiplatelet + GI Bleed
nodes.summary: Open Anticoag Reversal — reverse the agent, then work the source. Reversal is independent.
nodes.body: Open Anticoagulation Reversal consult in parallel with source workup. Reversal is independent of source identification — bleeding patient + therapeutic anticoagulant = reverse. Identify the agent first — reversal differs by class: - Warfarin → 4-factor PCC (Kcentra) by INR/weight + vitamin K 10 mg IV - Dabigatran → idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV - Apixaban / rivaroxaban → andexanet alfa OR 4-facto

nodes.title: Massive GI Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Activate MTP. 1:1:1 ratio. TXA selectively (HALT-IT cautions in GI bleed). Permissive hypotension until source control.
nodes.body: Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol. Shock index >1.4, ongoing exsanguination, or anticipated need for >10 units in 24 h. Targets: [10] - 1:1:1 RBC:plasma:platelets ratio (start with the first balanced cooler) - TXA 1 g IV over 10 min (within 3 h of bleed onset) + 1 g over 8 h — strongest data in trauma. ⚠️ This does NOT extrapolate to GI bleeding, and TXA is not low-harm here. HALT-IT (n=12,009

nodes.title: Aorto-Enteric Fistula
nodes.summary: Prior aortic graft + GI bleed = aorto-enteric fistula. CTA + vascular surgery NOW. Herald bleed precedes exsanguination.
nodes.body: Don't miss this. History of AAA repair (open or endovascular) + GI bleed = aorto-enteric fistula until proven otherwise. The "herald bleed" precedes exsanguination by minutes-to-days. Suspect when: [12] - Prior aortic graft (any type, any era — even 20+ years old) - GI bleed of any volume, especially recurrent or intermittent - Back pain, abdominal pain, sepsis (graft infection co-exists) - Pulsat

nodes.title: Mesenteric Ischemia + GI Bleed
nodes.summary: Open Mesenteric Ischemia — CTA before colonoscopy. Pain out of proportion + bleed.
nodes.body: Open Mesenteric Ischemia consult. Pain out of proportion + AF / vasculopath / postprandial pain + GI bleed = mesenteric ischemia until proven otherwise. Why this matters: [14] - Colonoscopy in active mesenteric ischemia can perforate ischemic bowel - Resus alone delays the lethal diagnosis - Lactate may be normal early (5-15% have normal lactate at presentation in arterial mesenteric ischemia) — t

nodes.title: IBD Flare with Bleeding
nodes.summary: Open IBD Flare consult. Truelove-Witts for severity. Hold anti-motility. C. diff coinfection always.
nodes.body: Open IBD Flare consult. UC and Crohn flares can present with significant lower GI bleed; severe UC flare is its own emergency. Recognize severe flare (Truelove-Witts): [16] - ≥6 bloody stools/day - AND any of: temp >37.8°C, HR >90, Hgb <10.5 g/dL, ESR >30 Workup: - CBC, CMP, ESR, CRP, lactate, blood cultures if febrile - Stool studies: C. diff PCR + bacterial pathogens + ova/parasites (C. diff coi

nodes.title: Pediatric GI Bleed
nodes.summary: Peds GI bleed = different differential. Age-driven. Intussusception, Meckel, NEC, milk-protein, Peds STEC/HUS.
nodes.body: Pediatric GI bleed has its own differential. Adult deep-dives don't apply directly. Age-based differential: [18] - Neonate (0-30 d): swallowed maternal blood (NPO + Apt test), NEC (Neonatal Resus), milk-protein allergy, vitamin K deficiency, malrotation/volvulus - Infant (1-12 mo): intussusception, milk-protein colitis, Meckel diverticulum, anal fissure - Toddler (1-5 y): intussusception (rare bey

nodes.title: Initial Bundle (Stable, Undifferentiated)
nodes.summary: Bundle = IVs + NPO + T&C + PPI + octreotide if cirrhotic + risk score. Permissive hypotension until hemostasis.
nodes.body: Bundle for the stable, undifferentiated GI bleeder. Use while waiting for the source pattern to declare. Resus: - 2 large-bore IVs (16 g+), NPO - Type and cross 2-4 units - Transfusion threshold: restrictive, Hgb <7 g/dL; <8 g/dL is reasonable with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Villanueva (NEJM 2013, n=921) showed lower 45-day mortality and less rebleeding with the restrictive strategy, mos

nodes.title: Reassess at 30-60 Minutes
nodes.body: Reassess vitals, mental status, ongoing bleed activity (NG aspirate, repeat DRE, stool log), labs returning. Pattern changes the plan:

nodes.title: Imaging + Source Control Strategy
nodes.summary: Phenotype drives imaging. EGD for upper, colonoscopy for lower stable, CTA for unstable lower, CTA + vascular for AEF/mesenteric.
nodes.body: Match imaging to phenotype — don't shotgun. Upper source suspected: - Endoscopy (EGD) — within 24 h for stable, 12 h for cirrhotic, ASAP for shock or active bleed [4] - ⚠️ Do NOT chase a sub-12 h scope in NONvariceal UGIB. ACG 2021 deliberately deleted the 2012 "<12 h may be considered" language; Lau (NEJM 2020, n=516, GBS ≥12) found urgent (<6 h) endoscopy did not lower 30-day mortality (8.9% vs

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Match disposition to stability, source pattern, scope availability, and follow-up.

nodes.title: ICU Admit
nodes.summary: ICU for shock, ongoing bleed, MTP, variceal cirrhotic, AEF, mesenteric. Bundle includes PPI drip + octreotide + ceftriaxone if variceal.
nodes.body: ICU criteria: - Hemodynamic instability (SBP <90, shock index >1) - Ongoing active bleed - Massive transfusion activation - Cirrhotic with variceal bleed (high mortality) - Forrest Ia/Ib lesion post-endoscopy - Aorto-enteric fistula - Mesenteric ischemia ICU bundle: - Arterial line, central line if pressors needed - Continuous monitoring, serial Hgb q4-6h - Standing PPI drip + octreotide if varice

nodes.title: Floor Admit
nodes.summary: Floor: stable post-endoscopy with low-risk lesion. Telemetry, PPI BID, diet advance, anticoag restart per team.
nodes.body: Floor criteria: - Hemodynamically stable - Bleeding source identified and low-risk (Forrest IIc/III, post-banding, post-cautery) - Transfused 1-3 units, stable post-transfusion - Oakland >8 OR Glasgow-Blatchford >1 - Comorbidities requiring inpatient monitoring (CHF, CKD, severe anemia) Floor bundle: - Telemetry, serial Hgb q12h initially - PPI BID PO + step-down from drip if stable >24 h - Diet a

nodes.title: Observation / ED-Obs
nodes.summary: Obs: stable + low score + reliable patient. Serial Hgb. Discharge from obs with GI in 1 week.
nodes.body: Obs criteria: - Hemodynamically stable from arrival - No active bleeding - Glasgow-Blatchford ≤1 OR Oakland ≤8 in non-anticoagulated patient - Reliable patient + caregiver + follow-up - Concern for outpatient endoscopy compliance OR need for serial Hgb 12-24 h Obs bundle: - Serial vitals q4h, serial Hgb at 6-12 h - PPI PO BID - Discharge criteria: stable Hgb, tolerating PO, ambulating, no recurren

nodes.title: Discharge (Low-Risk)
nodes.summary: Discharge only for low Glasgow-Blatchford/Oakland + stable + GI follow-up arranged + WRITTEN return precautions.
nodes.body: Discharge criteria (rare in acute presentation; usually post-obs): - Hemodynamically stable throughout ED stay - Glasgow-Blatchford ≤1 (UGIB) OR Oakland ≤8 (LGIB) - No active bleeding, stable Hgb - Not on anticoagulant OR reversal completed + bleeding stopped - Reliable patient with phone access, caregiver, transportation - GI follow-up scheduled within 1 week with outpatient endoscopy - Toleratin

nodes.title: GI Foreign Body — Object Identification
nodes.summary: Object type determines urgency: button battery (emergent), sharp/magnets (urgent), blunt (often conservative)
nodes.body: GI Foreign Body Steps Summary Object type determines urgency and management. High-risk objects (emergent/urgent): • Button batteries — esophageal = emergent (<2h) • Magnets — multiple = urgent (can cause fistula) • Sharp objects — pins, bones, glass • Superabsorbent polymers — water beads Lower-risk objects: • Coins, small blunt objects • Small objects <2cm width, <5cm length History: • Time of in

nodes.title: Location Assessment
nodes.summary: X-ray neck-to-pelvis first; CT if perforation suspected; esophageal location = highest risk
nodes.body: Imaging to determine location: X-ray (AP + lateral): • First-line for radiopaque objects • Include neck through pelvis • Lateral view distinguishes esophageal from tracheal Button battery on X-ray: • "Double-ring" or "halo" sign on AP view • Step-off on lateral view CT if: • Suspected perforation • Object not visible on X-ray • Need precise localization Where is the object?

nodes.title: Esophageal Foreign Body
nodes.summary: Esophageal = emergency; button battery <2h, sharp <6h, food <6-24h depending on obstruction
nodes.body: Esophageal impaction is an emergency — risk of perforation, mediastinitis, aspiration. Common impaction sites: • Cricopharyngeus (C6) — most common in children • Aortic arch (T4) • GE junction (T10-11) Symptoms: • Dysphagia, drooling, inability to swallow • Chest/neck pain • Respiratory distress (if tracheal compression) • Stridor (concerning for airway compromise) Urgency by object: • Button batt

nodes.title: Esophageal Object Type
nodes.summary: Battery = emergent (<2h); sharp = urgent (<6h); food bolus = urgent (<6-24h); blunt = <24h
nodes.body: What type of object is lodged in the esophagus?

nodes.title: Button Battery — EMERGENT
nodes.summary: EMERGENT endoscopy <2h; give honey/sucralfate 10mL q10min while awaiting; severe injury in <2h
nodes.body: Esophageal button battery is a surgical emergency. Mechanism of injury: • Generates electric current → liquefactive necrosis • Severe mucosal injury in <2 hours • Perforation risk increases after 2-4 hours • Can cause fistula to trachea, aorta (fatal) IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: 1. NPO — no food or water 2. Give honey or sucralfate: • Honey 10 mL q10 min (up to 6 doses) — viscous coating delays injury • Su

nodes.title: Button Battery — Gastric Location
nodes.summary: Esophageal = emergent; gastric ≥20mm or symptomatic = urgent; gastric <20mm asymptomatic = may observe
nodes.body: If button battery has passed to stomach: Management depends on: • Battery size (≥20mm higher risk) • Patient age (<5 years higher risk) • Symptoms present • Time since ingestion ≥20mm battery or symptomatic → endoscopic removal <20mm, asymptomatic → may observe with serial X-rays

nodes.title: Button Battery — Observation
nodes.summary: Low-risk gastric battery: repeat X-ray 48h; remove if still in stomach; daily X-rays until passed
nodes.body: Low-risk gastric button battery may be observed: Criteria for observation: • Battery <20mm diameter • Patient asymptomatic • Age ≥5 years • No prior GI surgery or strictures Observation protocol: • Repeat X-ray in 48 hours • If still in stomach at 48h → endoscopic removal • If passed to small bowel → continue observation • Daily X-rays until passed Return precautions: • Abdominal pain, vomiting, b

nodes.title: Sharp Object
nodes.summary: Sharp objects: 15-35% perforation risk; esophageal <6h, gastric = urgent removal, distal = surgery consult
nodes.body: Sharp objects have 15-35% perforation risk if allowed to pass spontaneously. Examples: • Needles, pins, toothpicks • Fish/chicken bones • Glass fragments • Razor blades, dental hardware Management depends on location: • Esophageal → emergent/urgent endoscopy • Gastric → endoscopy recommended • Small bowel → surgical consultation, observation vs surgery

nodes.title: Esophageal Sharp Object
nodes.summary: Esophageal sharp: endoscopy <6h with overtube; watch for perforation (emphysema, pneumomediastinum)
nodes.body: Urgent endoscopy within 6 hours. Endoscopic removal considerations: • Use overtube or hood to protect mucosa during extraction • Grasp object so sharp end trails during removal • May require operative endoscopy or surgery if embedded Signs of perforation: • Severe chest/neck pain • Subcutaneous emphysema • Fever, tachycardia • Pneumomediastinum on imaging If perforation suspected → CT neck/chest/a

nodes.title: Gastric Sharp Object
nodes.summary: Gastric sharp: endoscopy recommended within 24h; 15-35% perforation risk if allowed to pass
nodes.body: Endoscopic removal recommended for gastric sharp objects. Rationale: • 15-35% perforation risk if allowed to pass • Gastric location allows safe endoscopic retrieval • Once past pylorus, intervention becomes more complex Observation may be considered if: • Object is small and has passed to small bowel • Patient asymptomatic • Daily X-rays show progression • Surgical backup available Urgent endosco

nodes.title: Distal Sharp Object
nodes.summary: Distal sharp: daily X-rays, surgery consult; 80-90% pass spontaneously; operate if no progress in 3 days or symptoms
nodes.body: Sharp object beyond reach of endoscopy — surgical consultation required. Management options: • Conservative observation with daily X-rays if asymptomatic • 80-90% will pass spontaneously without complication • Surgical intervention if fails to progress in 3 days or symptoms develop Surgical indications: • Signs of perforation (fever, peritonitis, free air) • Failure to progress on serial X-rays (s

nodes.title: Multiple Magnets / Magnet + Metal
nodes.summary: Multiple magnets = emergency; can cause fistula/necrosis; urgent endoscopy if gastric, surgery if distal
nodes.body: Multiple magnets or magnet + metal object = surgical emergency. Mechanism: • Magnets attract through bowel walls → pressure necrosis → fistula, perforation, obstruction • Single magnet without metal is low risk Management: If all objects in stomach: • Urgent endoscopic removal If beyond stomach or different locations: • Surgical consultation • Likely requires operative removal • High risk of bowel

nodes.title: Blunt Object
nodes.summary: Blunt <2cm width, <5cm length usually pass; esophageal remove <24h; gastric observe vs remove
nodes.body: Most blunt objects pass spontaneously. Objects that typically pass: • <2 cm width (adult pylorus ~2-2.5 cm) • <5-6 cm length (duodenal sweep) • Coins, small toys, marbles Objects at risk of retention: • >2 cm width or >5 cm length • Lodged in esophagus • Prior GI surgery or strictures Location determines management:

nodes.title: Esophageal Blunt Object
nodes.summary: Esophageal blunt: endoscopy within 24h; Foley technique option for coins <24h in cooperative patient
nodes.body: Blunt esophageal foreign body — removal within 24 hours. Coins: • Most common pediatric esophageal FB • Usually lodge at cricopharyngeus • Endoscopic or Foley catheter removal options Foley technique (for coins): • Fluoroscopy guidance • Airway protection equipment ready • Only for objects <24h, coin-like, cooperative patient Endoscopy preferred if: • Object irregular shape • Ingestion >24 hours •

nodes.title: Esophageal Food Bolus
nodes.summary: Complete obstruction (drooling) = <6h endoscopy; partial = <24h; glucagon has limited efficacy
nodes.body: Food bolus impaction — common in adults with underlying pathology. Assess for complete vs partial obstruction: • Complete: Cannot swallow secretions, drooling → endoscopy <6h • Partial: Can swallow liquids → endoscopy <24h Pharmacologic options (limited efficacy): • Glucagon 1 mg IV — relaxes LES; may help distal impactions • Effervescent agents — not recommended (aspiration risk) • Meat tenderize

nodes.title: Gastric Foreign Body
nodes.summary: Remove gastric objects if sharp, large (>2cm wide, >5cm long), battery, magnets; small blunt may observe
nodes.body: Gastric objects — management by type and size: Remove endoscopically if: • Sharp objects (any size) • Button batteries ≥20mm or symptomatic • Multiple magnets • Objects >2 cm width or >5 cm length • Fails to pass in 3-4 weeks May observe if: • Blunt object <2 cm width and <5 cm length • Single small magnet (no metal co-ingestion) • Asymptomatic patient Observation protocol: • Weekly X-rays • If in

nodes.title: Distal Foreign Body
nodes.summary: 95% of objects past stomach pass spontaneously; strain stools; surgery if no progress >3 days or symptoms
nodes.body: Object beyond stomach — expectant management for most. 95% of objects that reach small bowel will pass spontaneously. Observation protocol: • Regular diet (high fiber may help) • Strain stools to confirm passage • Weekly X-rays for concerning objects (sharp, large) • Most pass within 1 week Return/surgical intervention if: • Object fails to progress >3 days (same location) • Abdominal pain, vomiti

nodes.title: Object Not Visualized
nodes.summary: Not seen: consider CT if radiolucent object suspected (fish bone, plastic); may have passed already
nodes.body: If object not visible on X-ray: Possibilities: • Radiolucent object (plastic, wood, glass) • Already passed • Not actually ingested (false history) Management: • CT if high concern and radiolucent object suspected • Metal detector (for metallic objects) • Observation if low-risk history and asymptomatic • Endoscopy if symptomatic with negative imaging High-risk radiolucent objects: • Fish bones (m

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Emergent if battery/perforation; urgent if esophageal/sharp; discharge if low-risk distal object
nodes.body: Final disposition based on object type and intervention status.

nodes.title: Emergent Intervention
nodes.body: Emergent endoscopy/surgery required: Indications: • Esophageal button battery • Airway compromise • Signs of perforation • Complete esophageal obstruction with aspiration risk Actions: • NPO • IV access • GI and/or surgical consultation STAT • Transfer if endoscopy not available • For battery: honey/sucralfate while awaiting Target time to intervention: • Esophageal battery: <2 hours • Sharp esoph
nodes.recommendation: Emergent GI/surgical consultation. NPO. Endoscopy within 2-6 hours depending on object. Transfer if capability unavailable.

nodes.title: Urgent Intervention
nodes.body: Urgent endoscopy within 24 hours: Indications: • Esophageal blunt object • Esophageal food bolus (partial obstruction) • Gastric sharp object • Gastric button battery (high-risk features) • Multiple magnets in stomach Admission criteria: • Await endoscopy • Unable to tolerate PO • Anticoagulation requiring reversal • High-risk comorbidities May observe overnight and scope in AM if: • Stable, low-r
nodes.recommendation: GI consultation. Admit for endoscopy within 24 hours. NPO. IV fluids.

nodes.title: Discharge with Observation
nodes.body: Safe for outpatient observation: Criteria: • Object has passed to small bowel/colon • Blunt, small (<2cm wide, <5cm long) • Asymptomatic • No high-risk features Discharge instructions: • Strain all stools until object recovered • Normal diet (high fiber may help) • Return immediately for: abdominal pain, vomiting, bloody stools, fever Follow-up: • If not passed in 1 week → X-ray • If sharp object
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with stool straining instructions. Return precautions for obstruction/perforation signs. X-ray if not passed in 1 week.

nodes.title: Open Globe Injury
nodes.summary: Once suspected: PROTECT eye with rigid shield, do NOT manipulate, call ophthalmology immediately
nodes.body: Open Globe = Full-Thickness Injury to Cornea, Sclera, or Both This is an ophthalmic emergency requiring emergent surgical repair. Types of Open Globe: | Type | Definition | |------|------------| | Penetrating | Object enters eye, does NOT exit | | Perforating | Entrance AND exit wound | | Rupture | Blunt force causes wall to burst | | IOFB | Intraocular foreign body present | Key Principle: Once s

nodes.title: Mechanism of Injury
nodes.summary: High-risk mechanisms: metal-on-metal, high-velocity projectile, penetrating objects warrant high suspicion
nodes.body: What is the mechanism? High-risk mechanisms warrant high suspicion even if exam is equivocal.

nodes.title: Clinical Examination
nodes.summary: If obvious rupture (extruding contents, peaked pupil), STOP examining and shield immediately
nodes.body: Exam ONLY if Globe Not Obviously Ruptured If you see obvious rupture (extruding contents, peaked pupil), STOP examining and shield immediately. nodes.title: Teardrop Pupil Explained
nodes.summary: Teardrop pupil is pathognomonic — iris drawn toward wound site, stop exam and shield
nodes.body: The Teardrop Pupil: The iris is drawn toward the corneal/scleral defect, causing: - Pupil stretches toward the wound - Pupil "points" at the injury site - Creates characteristic teardrop shape Why This Happens: - Aqueous humor leaking out - Pressure gradient pulls iris toward defect - Iris may prolapse through the wound Clinical Pearl: In penetrating injury, the teardrop points toward the corneal

nodes.title: Seidel Test
nodes.summary: Seidel test: fluorescein streaming = aqueous leak — contraindicated if obvious rupture
nodes.body: Seidel Test — Detecting Aqueous Leak Technique: 1. Apply concentrated fluorescein strip to suspected wound 2. Examine under cobalt blue light (slit lamp or Wood's lamp) 3. Watch for streaming pattern Interpretation: | Result | Appearance | |--------|------------| | Positive | Dark orange dye turns bright green as aqueous dilutes it; streaming | | Negative | Dye remains orange, no streaming | ⚠️ IM

nodes.title: Confirm Open Globe
nodes.summary: If ANY doubt, treat as open globe until proven otherwise — CT orbits to confirm
nodes.body: Is open globe confirmed or highly suspected? Definitive signs: - Visible uveal tissue/vitreous prolapse - Teardrop/irregular pupil - Positive Seidel test - Obvious full-thickness wound High suspicion: - High-risk mechanism + any concerning finding - Significant VA loss with trauma

nodes.title: Closed Globe Injury
nodes.summary: Consider hyphema, corneal abrasion, retinal detachment, orbital fracture if low suspicion

nodes.title: Immediate Protection
nodes.summary: Rigid shield (Fox shield or cut cup), HOB 30 degrees, antiemetics to prevent IOP spikes
nodes.body: ⚠️ PROTECT THE GLOBE ⚠️ 1. Rigid Eye Shield: - Fox shield (commercial) - Cut Styrofoam cup works! - Tape to brow and cheek - NO PRESSURE on the globe 2. NO Pressure Patch: - Unlike corneal abrasion, no soft patch - Any pressure risks extrusion 3. Position: - Head of bed elevated 30° - Minimize eye movement - May patch BOTH eyes to limit consensual movement 4. Antiemetics (CRITICAL): - Ondansetron

nodes.title: Gout & Pseudogout: Overview
nodes.summary: Acute gout: rapid-onset monoarticular pain, MTP1 most common — rule out septic joint
nodes.body: Gout is the most common inflammatory arthritis in adults, caused by monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition. Pseudogout (CPPD) is caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition. Key ED considerations: - Both present as acute monoarthritis - Cannot reliably distinguish from septic arthritis clinically - Crystals do NOT rule out concurrent infection - Treatment overlaps significantly

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Classic podagra (MTP1) but any joint possible — rapid onset, erythema, exquisite tenderness
nodes.body: Classic gout presentation: - Rapid onset (peak severity in <24 hours) - Intense pain, swelling, erythema - Exquisite tenderness ("cannot tolerate bedsheet") - Self-limited (resolves in 7-14 days without treatment) Classic joint involvement: - 1st MTP (podagra): Most specific for gout (50% of first attacks) - Midfoot, ankle: Common - Knee: Frequent, especially in elderly - Upper extremity: Less com

nodes.title: Gout vs Pseudogout: Clinical Differences
nodes.summary: Gout: MTP1, younger men. Pseudogout: larger joints (knee/wrist), elderly, chondrocalcinosis on XR
nodes.body: Joint patterns differ: | Feature | Gout | Pseudogout (CPPD) | |---------|------|------------------| | Peak age | 40-60 years | >60 years | | Sex | Male predominant | Equal | | #1 joint | 1st MTP (podagra) | Knee | | Wrist | Less common | Common (TFCC) | | Polyarticular | Chronic/severe | Common ("pseudo-RA") | | Tophi | Yes | No | | Serum urate | Usually elevated | Normal | | Chondrocalcinosis | N

nodes.title: When to Aspirate vs Empiric Treatment
nodes.summary: Aspirate if first episode, fever, immunocompromised, or diagnostic uncertainty vs septic joint
nodes.body: Aspiration is the gold standard but not always required. ASPIRATE when: - First presentation or uncertain diagnosis - Suspected septic arthritis (fever, immunocompromised, bacteremia) - Atypical joint involvement - Treatment failure - Large effusion (therapeutic benefit) - Coexisting conditions (RA, prosthetic joint) Empiric treatment acceptable when: - Classic podagra presentation - Known crystal

nodes.title: Joint Aspiration Indications
nodes.summary: Joint aspiration indicated when septic joint cannot be excluded clinically
nodes.body: Joint aspiration provides: 1. Crystal identification (definitive diagnosis) 2. Gram stain and culture (rule out septic arthritis) 3. Cell count and differential 4. Therapeutic relief Send for: - Cell count with differential - Gram stain - Culture (aerobic, consider anaerobic if high risk) - Crystal analysis under polarized microscopy - Glucose (optional, compare to serum) - Lactate (if available)

nodes.title: Synovial Fluid Interpretation
nodes.summary: Negatively birefringent needle crystals = gout; positively birefringent rhomboid = pseudogout
nodes.body: WBC count classification: | Classification | WBC/mm3 | Interpretation | |----------------|---------|----------------| | Non-inflammatory | <2,000 | OA, trauma | | Inflammatory | 2,000-50,000 | Crystal, RA, reactive | | Septic | >50,000 | Bacterial infection | Crystal arthritis ranges: - Gout: 10,000-70,000/uL (can exceed 100,000) - CPPD: Similar range - PMN% usually >50% in both Key point: WBC cou

nodes.title: ACR/EULAR 2015 Gout Classification
nodes.summary: ACR/EULAR 2015 criteria: clinical scoring when aspiration not performed — sensitivity 92%, specificity 89%
nodes.body: Entry criterion (REQUIRED): At least 1 episode of peripheral joint or bursal swelling, pain, or tenderness. Sufficient criterion (diagnostic without scoring): Presence of MSU crystals in symptomatic joint/bursa or tophus = GOUT confirmed. If no crystal confirmation, use scoring system: Score >=8 = Gout classification (Sens 92%, Spec 89%) Clinical domain: - Joint pattern: 1st MTP (+2), ankle/midfoo

nodes.title: Serum Urate Interpretation
nodes.summary: Serum urate may be NORMAL during acute flare — does not rule out gout
nodes.body: Serum urate is supportive but not diagnostic. Important caveats: - Urate can be NORMAL during acute flare (up to 40% of cases) - Inflammatory cytokines promote urate excretion - Low urate (<4 mg/dL) makes gout UNLIKELY (-4 points) - High urate is not specific (asymptomatic hyperuricemia is common) Interpretation: | Level | Interpretation | Points | |-------|----------------|--------| | <4 mg/dL |

nodes.title: Imaging in Gout
nodes.summary: XR for baseline, US for double contour sign, DECT for tophi — rarely needed acutely in ED

nodes.title: Crystal Analysis Results
nodes.summary: Crystal analysis determines gout vs pseudogout and guides treatment approach
nodes.body: Crystal identification is definitive. Polarized microscopy findings: MSU (Gout): - Needle-shaped - Strong negative birefringence - Yellow when parallel to compensator axis - Blue when perpendicular CPP (CPPD/Pseudogout): - Rhomboid or rod-shaped - Weak positive birefringence - Blue when parallel to compensator axis - Yellow when perpendicular Mnemonic: "Positive Pseudogout" - CPP has Positive bire

nodes.title: Gout Confirmed: Key Points
nodes.summary: Gout confirmed: initiate anti-inflammatory therapy, do NOT start/stop allopurinol during flare
nodes.body: MSU crystal-proven gout. Acute flare management: 1. Initiate anti-inflammatory therapy immediately 2. Choice depends on contraindications (see next section) 3. Topical ice is helpful adjuvant 4. Continue any existing ULT (do not stop during flare) Long-term considerations (for outpatient): - ULT (allopurinol, febuxostat) reduces flare frequency - Can initiate ULT during acute flare (controversial

nodes.title: CPPD (Pseudogout) Confirmed
nodes.summary: CPPD (pseudogout) confirmed: treat same as gout (NSAIDs/steroids), investigate secondary causes
nodes.body: CPP crystal-proven pseudogout (CPPD). Key differences from gout: - No urate-lowering therapy - no medication dissolves CPP crystals - Often associated with underlying metabolic disease - Treatment is symptom-directed only Secondary causes to screen for: | Condition | Test | |-----------|------| | Hyperparathyroidism | Calcium, PTH | | Hemochromatosis | Ferritin, transferrin sat | | Hypomagnesemia

nodes.title: CPPD Treatment
nodes.summary: CPPD treatment: NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids — same agents as gout, similar dosing

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis Concern
nodes.summary: Septic joint is the critical mimicker — aspirate if febrile, immunocompromised, or prosthetic joint
nodes.body: High-risk features for septic arthritis: - Fever >38.5C - Immunocompromise (DM, steroids, HIV) - Synovial WBC >85,000/mm3 (even with crystals) - Recent joint surgery or injection - IV drug use - Skin infection overlying joint - Bacteremia or endocarditis - Prosthetic joint CRITICAL: Crystals do NOT exclude infection. Gout/CPPD joints are at INCREASED risk for septic arthritis. If uncertain: 1. Asp

nodes.title: Empiric Treatment Approach
nodes.summary: Empiric treatment reasonable for classic presentation with prior confirmed gout history
nodes.body: When empiric treatment is appropriate: - Classic podagra with known gout history - ACR/EULAR score >=8 (high probability) - Low suspicion for septic arthritis - Aspiration not feasible If treating empirically: - Choose agent based on contraindications - Reassess in 24-48 hours - If no improvement, reconsider diagnosis - Lower threshold for aspiration if treatment fails Document: - Clinical rationa

nodes.title: Acute Flare Treatment: Overview
nodes.summary: Acute flare treatment: NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids — choose based on comorbidities and contraindications
nodes.body: ACR 2020 treatment priority: 1. NSAIDs - First choice if no contraindications 2. Colchicine - Best if started within 36 hours of onset 3. Glucocorticoids - Oral, IA, or IM; first choice if NSAID/colchicine contraindicated 4. IL-1 inhibitors - Reserved for refractory cases Key principles: - Start treatment within 24 hours for best efficacy - Use FULL anti-inflammatory doses - Topical ice is helpful

nodes.title: Contraindication Screening
nodes.summary: Screen for NSAID (CKD, GI bleed, CHF), colchicine (CKD, liver), and steroid contraindications
nodes.body: Screen for contraindications to guide treatment selection. nodes.title: NSAID Treatment

nodes.body: NSAIDs are first-line for acute gout if no contraindications. nodes.body: Low-dose colchicine is preferred over high-dose. Acute flare (low-dose protocol): - 1.2 mg x1, then 0.6 mg 1 hour later - Total: 1.8 mg on day 1 - Optional: 0.6 mg daily or BID until flare resolves Critical timing: Most effective if started within 36 hours of symptom onset.
