nodes.title: Treatment Monitoring & Response
nodes.summary: Monitor pain response, reassess in 24-48h — if not improving, reconsider diagnosis (septic joint?)
nodes.body: Expected timeline: - Improvement within 24-48 hours - Pain significantly reduced by 72 hours - Resolution within 7-14 days If no improvement in 48-72 hours: 1. Reconsider diagnosis (septic arthritis?) 2. Verify adequate dosing 3. Consider aspiration if not done 4. May add second agent (combination therapy) Combination therapy options: - Colchicine + NSAID - Colchicine + steroid - IA steroid + syst

nodes.title: Disposition Assessment
nodes.summary: Most gout discharges home — admit if septic joint concern, severe renal failure, or unable to take PO
nodes.body: Most gout flares can be managed outpatient. Consider admission if: - Septic arthritis not excluded - Multiple joint involvement with systemic illness - Unable to take oral medications - Significant comorbidities affecting treatment - Unreliable follow-up - Refractory pain requiring IV/parenteral medications Outpatient management appropriate if: - Diagnosis confident (clinical or crystal-proven) -

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: Discharge with pain control, avoid alcohol and purine-rich foods during flare, rheumatology/PCP follow-up
nodes.body: Medications: - Complete prescribed anti-inflammatory course (do not stop early) - Take with food if stomach upset - If diabetic: monitor glucose closely (steroids cause hyperglycemia) Self-care: - Rest affected joint - Apply ice 20 minutes several times daily - Elevate limb if swollen - Stay well hydrated Return precautions (return to ED if): - Fever develops - Symptoms worsen despite treatment -
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with prescribed anti-inflammatory medication. Return precautions for fever, worsening symptoms, or no improvement in 48-72 hours. Follow up with PCP or rheumatology in 1-2 weeks to discuss long-term management.

nodes.title: Admission Orders
nodes.summary: Admit if septic joint suspected, severe comorbidities, or inability to control pain outpatient
nodes.body: Indications for admission: - Septic arthritis not excluded (pending cultures) - Polyarticular involvement with systemic symptoms - Unable to tolerate PO medications - Refractory pain - Significant comorbidities Admission orders: 1. NPO or diet as tolerated 2. IV access for medications/fluids 3. Anti-inflammatory therapy (IV methylprednisolone if PO not tolerated) 4. Pain management 5. Repeat arthr

nodes.summary: Rheumatology for recurrent flares, tophaceous gout, or ULT initiation guidance
nodes.body: Indications for rheumatology referral: Urgent (ED consultation): - Diagnostic uncertainty (gout vs septic vs other) - Polyarticular involvement with systemic symptoms - Refractory to standard therapy - Multiple contraindications requiring IL-1 inhibitor Outpatient referral: - Tophaceous gout - Frequent flares (>=2/year) despite ULT - Chronic kidney disease complicating management - Intolerance to

nodes.title: Urate-Lowering Therapy Counseling
nodes.summary: Do NOT start allopurinol in ED — ULT initiation triggers flares, needs outpatient titration
nodes.body: ULT is for long-term prevention, not acute treatment. Indications for ULT (outpatient decision): - Tophaceous gout - >=2 flares per year - CKD stage 3 or worse - Urolithiasis - First flare with serum urate >=9 mg/dL Starting ULT: - Can start during acute flare (ACR 2020 conditional recommendation) - If starting during flare, must provide anti-inflammatory prophylaxis - "Start low, go slow" (allopu

nodes.title: Gout & Pseudogout: Summary
nodes.summary: Gout ED summary: rule out septic joint, treat pain aggressively, do NOT start/stop ULT during flare
nodes.body: Diagnosis: - Crystal analysis is definitive (MSU = gout, CPP = pseudogout) - ACR/EULAR criteria if no crystals (score >=8 = gout) - Cannot reliably distinguish from septic arthritis clinically - Crystals do NOT exclude concurrent infection Treatment priority (ACR 2020): 1. NSAIDs (first choice if no contraindications) 2. Colchicine (best within 36h of onset) 3. Corticosteroids (if NSAID/colchicine
nodes.recommendation: Acute gout/CPPD: Treat with NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids based on contraindications. Discharge most cases with follow-up in 1-2 weeks. Consider rheumatology referral for tophaceous, refractory, or complex cases.

nodes.title: Guillain-Barre Syndrome
nodes.summary: Ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia — 3-5% mortality from respiratory failure or PE
nodes.body: GBS Summary - acute inflammatory polyneuropathy requiring early recognition and aggressive monitoring. Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy characterized by rapidly progressive, symmetric weakness and areflexia. Key features: - Ascending symmetric weakness (legs before arms) - Hyporeflexia or areflexia - Sensory symptoms (paresthesias, numbness) often pr

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, weak cough) or rapid progression = immediate respiratory assessment
nodes.body: Classic GBS presentation: - Symmetric ascending weakness starting in legs - Hyporeflexia or areflexia (early and key finding) - Sensory symptoms: paresthesias, numbness, pain - Cranial nerve involvement (facial weakness, bulbar symptoms) in 50% Temporal pattern: - Symptoms progress over days to 4 weeks - Nadir (worst point) typically reached by 2-4 weeks - If progression >8 weeks, consider CIDP (c

nodes.title: GBS Variant Syndromes
nodes.summary: AIDP most common (90%); AMAN post-Campylobacter; Miller Fisher = ataxia + areflexia + ophthalmoplegia
nodes.body: GBS Variant Guide - detailed comparison of GBS subtypes. AIDP (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy) - Most common variant in Western countries (90%) - Demyelinating pattern on EMG/NCS - Classic ascending weakness with areflexia AMAN (Acute Motor Axonal Neuropathy) - Strongly associated with Campylobacter jejuni infection - Pure motor involvement (no sensory symptoms) - Axonal p

nodes.title: Atypical GBS Variants
nodes.summary: Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant: high respiratory failure risk despite preserved leg strength
nodes.body: Miller Fisher Syndrome: - Triad: ataxia, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia - Anti-GQ1b antibodies highly specific (>90%) - Often follows respiratory infection - May progress to classic GBS (overlap syndrome) - Treatment: supportive, IVIG if progresses Pharyngeal-Cervical-Brachial variant: - Weakness of oropharyngeal, neck, and arm muscles - Leg strength preserved - High risk of respiratory failure despit

nodes.title: Respiratory Status Assessment
nodes.summary: Early elective intubation is safer than emergent — patients may appear comfortable with critically low reserve
nodes.body: Evaluate current respiratory status and trajectory. Indications for elective intubation: - FVC <20 mL/kg or <1L - NIF weaker than -30 cmH2O - Rapid decline (>30% in 24h) - Unable to protect airway (bulbar weakness) - Hypoxia or hypercapnia Early intubation is safer than emergent intubation. Patients may appear comfortable but have critically low reserve.

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup

nodes.body: LP Interpretation Guide - albuminocytologic dissociation analysis. nodes.title: Imaging & Additional Studies
nodes.summary: MRI spine to rule out compressive lesion — tick paralysis, botulism, MG are key mimics
nodes.body: MRI spine with contrast: - Primary role: rule out compressive lesion (cord compression, epidural abscess) - GBS findings: nerve root enhancement (especially cauda equina) - Enhancement may be absent early - Not required for diagnosis but helps exclude mimics GBS mimics to consider: - Transverse myelitis (sensory level, MRI cord signal) - Cord compression (back pain, sensory level) - Myasthenia gra

nodes.title: Treatment Principles
nodes.summary: Start IVIG or plasmapheresis within 2 weeks of onset — do NOT combine both, do NOT use steroids
nodes.body: IVIG vs PLEX Comparison - treatment selection guide. KEY PRINCIPLE: START TREATMENT EARLY - Most effective within 2 weeks of symptom onset - Benefit diminishes after 4 weeks - Do NOT wait for confirmatory testing Treatment is indicated for: - Unable to walk independently - Rapidly progressive weakness - Respiratory compromise - Significant bulbar dysfunction Two equivalent options: 1. IVIG (Intrav

nodes.title: Treatment Selection
nodes.summary: IVIG easier (peripheral IV, more available); PLEX may be faster in severe cases — equal efficacy
nodes.body: Select immunomodulatory therapy based on patient factors and resource availability. IVIG advantages: - Easier to administer (peripheral IV) - No central line required - More widely available - Can be given at smaller hospitals PLEX advantages: - May work faster in severe cases - No infusion reactions - May be preferred if IVIG contraindicated Neither is clearly superior - base decision on practica

nodes.title: IVIG Protocol
nodes.summary: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days — check IgA level first (anaphylaxis risk if IgA deficient)
nodes.body: IVIG Dosing: - 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days (total 2 g/kg) - Alternative: 1 g/kg/day x 2 days (same total dose) Administration: - Peripheral IV access adequate - Infuse slowly initially, increase rate as tolerated - Premedication with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine for infusion reactions Contraindications: - IgA deficiency (risk of anaphylaxis) - check IgA level if possible - Recent MI or stroke (risk

nodes.title: Plasmapheresis (PLEX) Protocol
nodes.summary: Plasmapheresis: 5 exchanges over 1-2 weeks — requires central line and specialized equipment
nodes.body: Plasmapheresis Dosing: - 5 exchanges over 1-2 weeks - Each exchange: 1-1.5 plasma volumes - Typically every other day Requirements: - Central venous access (dialysis catheter) - Specialized equipment and trained personnel - Usually requires transfer to tertiary center Advantages over IVIG: - May have faster onset of action - No infusion reaction risk - Some evidence suggests better outcomes in sev

nodes.title: Treatment Response & Relapse
nodes.summary: 10% have treatment-related fluctuation — may repeat same treatment, never use steroids
nodes.body: Expected response: - Clinical improvement typically begins within 1-2 weeks of completing treatment - Maximum improvement may take 6-12 months - 80% walk independently at 6 months Treatment-related fluctuation (TRF): - Worsening after initial improvement, occurring within 8 weeks - Occurs in ~10% of patients - May repeat same treatment (IVIG or PLEX) No response to initial treatment: - Consider sw

nodes.title: Supportive Care
nodes.summary: DVT prophylaxis is HIGH PRIORITY — immobile patients at major VTE risk. Gabapentin for pain
nodes.body: DVT Prophylaxis - HIGH PRIORITY: - GBS patients are immobile and high risk for VTE - Pharmacologic prophylaxis: enoxaparin or heparin - Mechanical: SCDs, graduated compression stockings - Continue until ambulatory Pain Management: - Neuropathic pain is common and often severe - Gabapentin 300-900 mg TID - Pregabalin 75-150 mg BID - NSAIDs and acetaminophen for musculoskeletal pain - Opioids may be

nodes.title: Nutrition & Psychological Support
nodes.summary: Assess swallowing before PO, psychological support critical — patients are fully aware of paralysis
nodes.body: Nutritional Support: - Assess swallowing before oral intake (bulbar involvement) - Speech therapy evaluation for dysphagia - NG tube if unable to swallow safely - Early consideration of PEG if prolonged intubation expected - Adequate calories for healing and rehabilitation Psychological Support - CRITICAL: - GBS causes sudden, profound paralysis in previously healthy individuals - Patients are oft

nodes.title: Autonomic Dysfunction Management
nodes.summary: Autonomic dysfunction in 70% — bradycardia can be fatal, use short-acting BP agents only
nodes.body: Autonomic involvement occurs in 70% of GBS patients. Cardiovascular: - Continuous telemetry monitoring - Sinus tachycardia (most common) - Bradycardia, asystole (may be fatal) - Blood pressure lability: alternating hypertension and hypotension - Avoid triggers: suctioning, turning, bladder distension Management principles: - Use short-acting agents for BP control - Avoid long-acting antihypertensi

nodes.title: Intubation Considerations
nodes.summary: AVOID succinylcholine (lethal hyperkalemia from denervated muscle) — use rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg
nodes.body: GBS Intubation Checklist - preparation and medication selection. CRITICAL: Avoid succinylcholine - Denervated muscle releases excessive potassium - Risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia - Use rocuronium for RSI Intubation timing: - Early elective intubation is safer than emergent - Do not wait until respiratory failure - Criteria: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than -30, bulbar compromise Anticipate co

nodes.title: Ventilator Management
nodes.summary: GBS is ventilatory failure (muscle weakness), not oxygenation failure — may need weeks on vent
nodes.body: Ventilator settings: - Lung-protective ventilation - Tidal volume 6-8 mL/kg IBW - PEEP as needed for oxygenation - GBS is primarily a ventilatory failure (muscle weakness), not oxygenation failure Weaning considerations: - May require weeks to months of ventilator support - Daily SBT when clinically improving - Track NIF and vital capacity recovery - Weaning success correlates with clinical neurol

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ALL suspected GBS patients require admission — most need ICU for respiratory and autonomic monitoring
nodes.body: ALL suspected GBS patients require admission. ICU admission criteria (most GBS patients): - Any respiratory compromise or declining FVC/NIF - Bulbar symptoms - Autonomic dysfunction - Rapidly progressive weakness - EGRIS score >=3 Step-down/floor admission: - Stable, mild weakness - Normal respiratory parameters after 24-48h observation - No bulbar or autonomic involvement - Still requires Q4-6h F

nodes.title: Prognosis
nodes.summary: 80% walk independently at 6 months — poor prognosis if age >60, rapid progression, axonal variant
nodes.body: Overall prognosis is favorable: - 80% walk independently at 6 months - Full recovery in 60-70% - 5-10% have persistent significant disability - 3-5% mortality Causes of death: - Respiratory failure - Autonomic dysfunction (arrhythmias, cardiac arrest) - Pulmonary embolism - Sepsis Poor prognostic factors: - Older age (>60 years) - Rapid progression to nadir (<7 days) - Need for mechanical ventilat
nodes.recommendation: Admit all suspected GBS patients. ICU for respiratory/bulbar/autonomic involvement. Start IVIG or PLEX within 2 weeks of symptom onset. Monitor FVC/NIF Q4-6h. Avoid succinylcholine if intubation needed. Most patients recover - communicate p

nodes.title: H. pylori — ED Decision Support
nodes.summary: First split: alarm features vs stable testing vs known positive vs failed treatment.
nodes.body: H. pylori Steps ED purpose: identify who needs urgent GI workup, who needs outpatient active-infection testing, and what current eradication regimen should be documented or started when treatment is appropriate. nodes.title: Alarm Features — Do Not Treat-and-Forget
nodes.summary: Alarm features require GI/EGD pathway; do not treat-and-forget.
nodes.body: This is not a simple outpatient H. pylori pathway. [1][2] Alarm / higher-risk features: - Hematemesis, melena, hemodynamic instability, or iron-deficiency anemia - Unintentional weight loss - Progressive dysphagia or odynophagia - Persistent vomiting - Palpable abdominal mass or lymphadenopathy - Family history of gastric cancer or high gastric cancer risk background - New dyspepsia at age >=60 -
nodes.recommendation: Treat the acute problem first. Alarm features require GI/EGD pathway, not routine ED dyspepsia discharge.

nodes.title: Who Should Be Tested?
nodes.summary: Test when dyspepsia/PUD risk fits, cancer-risk conditions exist, or test result will change care.
nodes.body: Testing Details Reasonable indications to test for active H. pylori: [1][2] - Current or prior peptic ulcer disease - Dyspepsia age <60 without alarm features - Dyspepsia age <50 with elevated gastric cancer risk - Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia after appropriate evaluation - Immune thrombocytopenic purpura - Gastric MALT lymphoma or post-endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer - Atrophic

nodes.title: Testing Route
nodes.summary: Use stool antigen or urea breath for active infection; biopsy if EGD is already indicated.
nodes.body: Choose the testing route by clinical setting. [1][3] Noninvasive active-infection tests: - Urea breath test - Stool antigen test Endoscopy-based tests: - Biopsy histology, rapid urease, culture, or molecular susceptibility testing when EGD is already indicated Avoid routine serology: antibodies may stay positive after past infection, so serology cannot prove active infection and cannot confirm era

nodes.title: Active-Infection Testing Rules
nodes.summary: Hold PPI/PCAB 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing.
nodes.body: Best practical tests: urea breath test or stool antigen test. [1][2] Avoid false negatives: - Hold PPI or PCAB for 2 weeks before testing. - Hold antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks before testing. - Bridge symptoms with H2 blocker or antacids if needed. nodes.summary: If EGD is already indicated, ask GI to test by biopsy and still plan eradication confirmation.
nodes.body: When EGD is already indicated, biopsy-based testing is appropriate. [1][3] Use this lane for: - Upper GI bleeding with suspected ulcer source - Gastric ulcer, complicated ulcer, or malignancy concern - Alarm-feature dyspepsia - Need for culture or molecular susceptibility after repeated treatment failure Practical ED note: the ED usually does not need to choose the biopsy method. nodes.title: Initial Eradication Regimen
nodes.summary: Default is 14-day optimized bismuth quadruple therapy; avoid empiric clarithro/levo regimens.
nodes.body: Regimen Table Current ACG North America default: optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days when susceptibility is unknown. [1][2] Important change: do not use clarithromycin triple therapy or levofloxacin regimens empirically unless susceptibility is documented. Resistance has made empiric macrolide/quinolone therapy unreliable. [1][2] Which situation fits?

nodes.title: Optimized Bismuth Quadruple Therapy
nodes.summary: BQT x14 days: PPI BID + bismuth QID + tetracycline QID + metronidazole TID/QID.
nodes.body: Preferred empiric regimen when susceptibility is unknown: [1][2] 14 days: - PPI standard dose BID - Bismuth subcitrate 120-300 mg QID OR bismuth subsalicylate 300-524 mg QID - Tetracycline 500 mg QID - Metronidazole 500 mg TID or QID Counseling: - High pill burden; adherence drives cure. - Bismuth can turn stool/tongue dark. - Avoid alcohol with metronidazole. - Tetracycline is contraindicated in
nodes.recommendation: Use optimized bismuth quadruple therapy x14 days when H. pylori is confirmed and susceptibility is unknown.

nodes.title: Penicillin Allergy Lane
nodes.summary: True PCN allergy usually points to BQT; consider allergy testing because amoxicillin matters for salvage.
nodes.body: If true penicillin allergy: optimized bismuth quadruple therapy is the main empiric option if tetracycline/metronidazole/bismuth are safe. [1][2] Do not reflexively use clarithromycin triple therapy just because the patient reports penicillin allergy. Use clarithromycin only when susceptibility is known. Consider penicillin allergy evaluation when feasible because amoxicillin resistance is uncommo

nodes.summary: Alternatives exist, but clarithro/levo require known susceptibility; complex salvage should be GI-directed.
nodes.body: Alternative regimens from the ACG guideline: [1][2] | Situation | Option | |---|---| | Treatment-naive, no PCN allergy, BQT impractical | Vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy x14 days may be used where available | | Treatment-naive or salvage option | Rifabutin-amoxicillin-PPI triple therapy x14 days | | Clarithromycin susceptible isolate | Clarithromycin-containing therapy may be used | | Levoflox

nodes.title: Test-of-Cure Is Mandatory
nodes.summary: Proof of eradication is required for every treated patient.
nodes.body: All treated patients need proof of eradication. [1][2] Acceptable tests: - Urea breath test - Stool antigen test - Biopsy-based testing if EGD is being done Timing: - At least 4 weeks after antibiotics are completed - Off PPI/PCAB for 2 weeks - Off bismuth and antibiotics for 4 weeks - H2 blocker or antacids may bridge symptoms Document before discharge: "H. pylori eradication requires test-of-cur
nodes.recommendation: Schedule urea breath or stool antigen test-of-cure at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and after 2 weeks off PPI/PCAB.

nodes.title: Persistent H. pylori After Treatment
nodes.summary: Confirm true persistence and do not reuse failed antibiotics blindly.
nodes.body: Failure Pathway First confirm this is true persistence: [1][2] - Was test-of-cure done at the correct time? - Was the patient off PPI/PCAB, antibiotics, and bismuth long enough? - Was the test stool antigen, urea breath, or biopsy-based, not serology? - What exact regimen and adherence? What was the prior regimen?

nodes.title: Failed Optimized BQT
nodes.summary: After BQT failure, move to different class/susceptibility-guided therapy; do not repeat failed antibiotics blindly.
nodes.body: After optimized BQT failure: avoid repeating the same regimen unless nonadherence was the clear cause and GI agrees. [1][2] Reasonable next steps: - Review prior macrolide, quinolone, metronidazole, tetracycline, and rifamycin exposure. - Consider rifabutin triple therapy or vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy if no true penicillin allergy. - If levofloxacin is considered, use only with documented
nodes.recommendation: Route for GI/susceptibility-guided salvage unless a clear guideline-supported alternative is available.

nodes.title: Multiple Failures or Unclear History
nodes.summary: Multiple failures need susceptibility-guided GI pathway.
nodes.body: High-risk for resistance or bad history. [1][3] Best next move: GI follow-up for susceptibility-guided therapy, preferably with culture or molecular testing if EGD is performed. Document the missing details: - Prior antibiotics and durations - Whether treatment was completed - Prior test-of-cure type and date - PPI/PCAB, bismuth, and antibiotic holds before testing - True drug allergies vs intoler
nodes.recommendation: Arrange GI-directed salvage with susceptibility testing when possible.

nodes.recommendation: Superficial fight bite. Leave open, amoxicillin-clavulanate x 10 days. Mandatory 24-48h follow-up. Written return precautions.

nodes.title: Herpetic Whitlow
nodes.body: Herpetic Whitlow (HSV-1 or HSV-2): Differentiation from Felon: • Vesicles (initially clear, may become turbid) • Pulp NOT tense (unlike felon) • Pain out of proportion • Often healthcare workers or autoinoculation Diagnosis: • Clinical appearance • Tzanck smear: multinucleated giant cells • Viral culture or PCR if uncertain Treatment: • Antivirals (if <48h): Valacyclovir 1g TID x 7 days or Acyclov
nodes.recommendation: Herpetic whitlow. DO NOT incise. Antivirals if <48h. Self-limited 2-4 weeks. Keep covered to prevent spread.

nodes.title: Deep Space Infections — Surgical Emergency
nodes.body: Deep Space Anatomy: | Space | Location | Presentation | |-------|----------|-------------| | Thenar | Thumb web | Loss of 1st web contour, thumb abducted | | Midpalmar | Central palm | Dorsal > palmar swelling, pain with finger extension | | Web space | Between fingers | "Collar button" — dual incision needed | Clinical Features: • Severe pain, swelling • Loss of normal hand contours • Finger held

nodes.title: Antibiotic Selection
nodes.body: Outpatient (Oral): | Indication | First Choice | MRSA Alternative | |------------|--------------|------------------| | Cellulitis | Cephalexin 500mg QID | TMP-SMX DS BID | | Felon/paronychia | Dicloxacillin 500mg QID | Doxycycline 100mg BID | | Fight bite | Amox-clav 875mg BID | Moxifloxacin + metronidazole | | Duration | 7-10 days | 7-10 days | Inpatient (IV): | Indication | First Choice | MRSA A

nodes.title: Discharge — Outpatient Management
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: • ✅ No deep space involvement • ✅ No flexor tenosynovitis • ✅ No systemic toxicity • ✅ Reliable follow-up available • ✅ Able to comply with elevation/wound care Discharge Instructions: Medications: • Complete full antibiotic course • NSAIDs for pain (avoid if diabetic/renal disease) Wound Care: • Warm soaks 3-4x daily for 15-20 min • Keep elevated as much as possible • Daily dr
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with oral antibiotics, warm soaks, elevation. Follow-up 24-48h. Written return precautions.

nodes.title: Admit — Inpatient Management
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: • Flexor tenosynovitis (ALL cases) • Deep space infection (ALL cases) • Fight bite with deep involvement • Severe cellulitis with systemic signs • Failed outpatient therapy • Immunocompromised with hand infection • Unable to comply with outpatient management Admission Orders: • IV antibiotics (see antibiotic selection) • Hand surgery consult • Splint in position of function • E
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics and hand surgery consult. Splint in position of function, elevation, NPO if OR anticipated.

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Emergencies
nodes.summary: Dialysis emergencies: hyperkalemia, access complications, infections, fluid overload, uremia
nodes.body: HD Emergency Summary — AEIOU framework for ESRD complications. AEIOU Mnemonic: • Access complications (bleeding, clotted, infected) • Electrolyte emergencies (hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia) • Infection (catheter sepsis, endocarditis) • Overload (pulmonary edema, HTN emergency) • Uremia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding) Key principles: • Many interventions work differently in ESRD • Diuretics o

nodes.title: Primary Complaint Category
nodes.summary: Triage by presentation: electrolyte emergency, access issue, infection, overload, or uremic syndrome
nodes.body: What is the primary presenting complaint? Quick assessment: • When was last dialysis? (missed sessions = higher risk) • What type of access? (fistula, graft, catheter) • Any fever? (infection until proven otherwise) • Breathing difficulty? (overload vs infection) Remember: HD patients may present atypically. • MI without chest pain • Infection without fever • Sepsis with hypothermia

nodes.title: Electrolyte Emergency
nodes.summary: Hyperkalemia is the most common lethal dialysis emergency — check ECG immediately
nodes.body: Hyperkalemia is the most common life-threatening emergency. Immediate actions: 1. 12-lead ECG — Look for: • Peaked T waves (earliest) • PR prolongation • QRS widening • Loss of P waves • Sine wave (pre-arrest) 2. STAT potassium level 3. Continuous cardiac monitoring ⚠️ ECG changes may precede lab result — treat empirically if high suspicion! Other electrolyte issues: • Hypocalcemia (tetany, seizur

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia — ECG Assessment
nodes.summary: ECG changes: peaked T-waves → wide QRS → sine wave → arrest — treat ECG, not just K+ level
nodes.body: Assess ECG for potassium toxicity: Progressive ECG changes: 1. Peaked T waves (K+ >5.5) 2. PR prolongation (K+ >6.5) 3. Loss of P waves (K+ >7.0) 4. QRS widening (K+ >7.5) 5. Sine wave → VF/Asystole (K+ >8.0) ⚠️ ECG may be normal with high K+ ⚠️ Severe changes may occur at lower K+ levels Are ECG changes present?

nodes.title: Severe Hyperkalemia Protocol
nodes.summary: Calcium gluconate 1g IV first, then insulin/dextrose, albuterol neb — emergent dialysis for definitive tx
nodes.body: 🚨 SEVERE HYPERKALEMIA — ECG changes present 1. CARDIAC MEMBRANE STABILIZATION (Immediate): • Calcium gluconate 1-2 g IV over 2-3 min • Onset: 1-3 minutes • Duration: 30-60 minutes • May repeat if ECG changes persist • Alternative: Calcium chloride 500-1000 mg (central line preferred) 2. SHIFT K+ INTRACELLULARLY: • Regular insulin IV — dose by hypoglycemia risk — Give WITH 25 g dextrose (D50 50 mL

nodes.title: Moderate Hyperkalemia
nodes.summary: Insulin 5 u (10 u if normal renal function) + 25 g dextrose, kayexalate controversial, arrange urgent dialysis within hours
nodes.body: K+ 5.5-6.5, no ECG changes: Management: 1. Continuous cardiac monitoring 2. Shift therapy: • Regular insulin IV + 25 g dextrose (D50 50 mL) — 5 units (or 0.1 units/kg, max 10) if dialysis-dependent, eGFR <60, pre-treatment glucose <150 mg/dL, weight <60 kg, or no diabetes; 10 units only with normal renal function AND adequate glucose. Dialysis patients → 5 units. • Albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized (ad

nodes.title: Mild Hyperkalemia
nodes.summary: Mild hyperK in dialysis patients often manageable with next scheduled session — verify timing
nodes.body: K+ <5.5, no symptoms, normal ECG: Management: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Repeat K+ in 2-4 hours • Diet review with patient • Schedule urgent dialysis if trending up • Contact nephrology for HD timing Patient education: • High-K foods to avoid (bananas, oranges, tomatoes, potatoes) • Importance of dialysis adherence • Salt substitutes often contain KCl Disposition: • May discharge if stable,

nodes.title: Electrolyte Emergency Disposition
nodes.summary: Emergent dialysis for severe hyperK, symptomatic hypo/hypernatremia, or refractory metabolic acidosis
nodes.body: Disposition based on severity: ADMIT: • Any ECG changes • K+ >6.5 mEq/L • Symptomatic (weakness, palpitations) • Multiple missed HD sessions • Unable to arrange urgent outpatient HD • Refractory to initial treatment May discharge if: • K+ <6.0, no symptoms, normal ECG • Dialysis scheduled within 24 hours • Reliable patient with good HD adherence history • Clear return precautions understood Always

nodes.title: Access Complication Type
nodes.summary: AV fistula/graft complications: bleeding, clotted access, steal syndrome, pseudoaneurysm
nodes.body: Access is the patient's lifeline — preserve at all costs. Access-arm precautions (KDOQI/ESVS): • No venipuncture or blood draws from the access extremity • No IV placement in the access extremity • No BP cuff on the access arm • No constricting bands, restraints, or tourniquets proximal to the access Access types: • AVF (arteriovenous fistula) — preferred, lowest complication rate • AVG (arteriove

nodes.title: Access Site Bleeding
nodes.summary: Direct pressure 10-20 min — if uncontrolled, consider thrombotic hemostatic agent, vascular surgery
nodes.body: Bleeding from HD access: Immediate management: • Direct pressure 15-20 minutes • Use two fingers, steady pressure • Elevate extremity • Do NOT tourniquet proximal to fistula (thrombosis risk) • Avoid excessive compression (also causes thrombosis) If hemodynamically unstable: • Large bore IV in contralateral arm • Crossmatch blood • Fluid resuscitation • Vascular surgery STAT After bleeding control

nodes.title: Thrombosed Access
nodes.summary: No thrill or bruit = clotted — interventional radiology for thrombectomy, temporary dialysis catheter
nodes.body: Thrombosed fistula/graft — TIME SENSITIVE Assessment: • No thrill or bruit = likely thrombosed • Document when access last worked • Assess for backup access options Best outcomes within 24-48 hours of thrombosis Management options: AVF/AVG: • Vascular surgery or IR consultation • Thrombectomy vs thrombolysis • May need temporary catheter for HD Catheter: • tPA lock (2 mg per lumen × 30-120 min) •

nodes.title: Steal Syndrome
nodes.summary: Steal syndrome: hand ischemia distal to access — pain, coolness, pallor, vascular surgery urgently
nodes.body: Dialysis-Associated Steal Syndrome (DASS): Signs: • Pale, cool hand distal to access • Pain, paresthesias, weakness • Symptoms worse DURING dialysis • Diminished pulses distally • May progress to tissue loss Severity grading: Mild: Cool hand, no rest pain → Monitor, conservative management Moderate: Rest pain present → Urgent vascular surgery referral Severe: Tissue loss, ulceration → Emergent vas

nodes.title: Access Emergency Disposition
nodes.summary: Vascular surgery or IR for access complications — temporary catheter if urgent dialysis needed
nodes.body: Disposition for access complications: ADMIT: • Hemodynamic instability from bleeding • Unable to control bleeding • Severe steal syndrome (tissue loss) • Need for emergent temp catheter and HD • Access infection (see infection pathway) Urgent outpatient management: • Clotted access (if HD can wait 24-48h) • Mild steal syndrome • Stable post-bleeding Key contacts: • Vascular surgery (clotted access

nodes.title: HD-Related Infection
nodes.summary: Blood cultures through catheter AND peripheral — start vancomycin + gram-negative coverage empirically
nodes.body: Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI): Risk hierarchy: • Non-tunneled catheter > Tunneled catheter > AVG > AVF Assessment: • Blood cultures × 2 (peripheral + through catheter) • Exit site exam (erythema, purulence) • Tunnel exam (track erythema) • Signs of metastatic infection Empiric antibiotics (IDSA guidelines): • Vancomycin 25 mg/kg (dose after HD) — Covers MRSA, coag-negative staph •

nodes.title: Endocarditis Workup
nodes.summary: Dialysis patients have 50x higher endocarditis risk — echo if blood cultures positive or new murmur
nodes.body: Consider endocarditis in HD patients with bacteremia: High-risk features: • S. aureus bacteremia (up to 25% have IE) • Prolonged bacteremia • New murmur • Embolic phenomena • Persistent fevers on antibiotics Workup: • TTE (initial screening) • TEE (if TTE negative and high suspicion) • Repeat blood cultures to document clearance Duration of antibiotics: • Uncomplicated CRBSI: 2-3 weeks • S. aureus

nodes.title: Volume Overload / Pulmonary Edema
nodes.summary: Fluid overload in missed dialysis: BiPAP, nitroglycerin, arrange emergent dialysis for ultrafiltration
nodes.body: Volume overload in ESRD: ⚠️ Diuretics often ineffective (no UOP) EMERGENT DIALYSIS is definitive treatment Temporizing measures: Oxygenation: • High-flow O₂ • NIPPV (BiPAP preferred) • Intubation if failing Reduce preload: • Nitrates (NTG 400 mcg SL → drip 50-200 mcg/min) • Positioning (upright) Diuretics? • Generally ineffective in ESRD • High-dose furosemide (160-200 mg IV) MAY work if residual

nodes.title: Overload Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit for emergent dialysis if severe pulmonary edema or not responding to medical management
nodes.body: Volume overload disposition: Emergent dialysis indications: • Severe pulmonary edema (hypoxic) • HTN emergency with encephalopathy • Refractory to medical management Admit for dialysis: • Moderate pulmonary edema • Significant O₂ requirement • Unable to arrange same-day outpatient HD • Missed multiple HD sessions May discharge if: • Mild symptoms resolving • Room air saturation • HD scheduled with

nodes.title: Uremic Emergency Type
nodes.summary: Uremic syndrome: encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding diathesis — all require emergent dialysis
nodes.body: Uremic manifestations: Neurologic: • Encephalopathy (AMS, asterixis, myoclonus) • Seizures • Peripheral neuropathy Cardiovascular: • Uremic pericarditis • Accelerated atherosclerosis Hematologic: • Platelet dysfunction → bleeding • Anemia of chronic disease GI: • Uremic gastritis • GI bleeding What is the primary uremic manifestation?

nodes.title: Uremic Encephalopathy
nodes.summary: Uremic encephalopathy: asterixis, confusion, seizures — dialysis is the treatment
nodes.body: Uremic Encephalopathy: Presentation: • Confusion, disorientation • Asterixis (metabolic flap) • Myoclonus • Seizures • Progresses to coma Differential (rule out): • Hypoglycemia • Electrolyte abnormalities • Sepsis • Stroke • Drug toxicity Management: • EMERGENT DIALYSIS is definitive • Treat seizures if present: — Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV — Levetiracetam 20-40 mg/kg IV ⚠️ Dialysis Disequilibrium Sy

nodes.title: Uremic Pericarditis
nodes.summary: Uremic pericarditis: NO anticoagulation during dialysis — hemorrhagic pericarditis risk
nodes.body: Uremic Pericarditis — DO NOT ANTICOAGULATE Presentation: • Pleuritic chest pain (worse supine, better sitting) • Pericardial friction rub (pathognomonic) • ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression • May progress to tamponade ⚠️ Critical distinction: • Uremic pericarditis → hemorrhagic effusion risk • Do NOT anticoagulate • Dialyze WITHOUT heparin Assessment: • Echocardiogram (effusion size, tampon

nodes.title: Uremic Bleeding
nodes.summary: Uremic bleeding: DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV for acute control, dialysis for definitive treatment
nodes.body: Uremic Platelet Dysfunction: Mechanism: • Uremic toxins impair platelet function • Normal platelet count, prolonged bleeding time Presentation: • Prolonged bleeding from venipuncture • GI bleeding • Epistaxis • Ecchymoses Management: Acute treatment: • DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 20-30 min — Onset: 1 hour, duration 4-8 hours — Releases vWF from endothelium — Tachyphylaxis with repeated doses For prol

nodes.title: Uremic Emergency Disposition
nodes.summary: All uremic emergencies require admission for dialysis and monitoring
nodes.body: Disposition for uremic emergencies: ADMIT ALL uremic emergencies: • Uremic encephalopathy → ICU • Uremic pericarditis → Telemetry/ICU • Significant uremic bleeding → Depends on severity Dialysis requirements: • Emergent for encephalopathy • Daily/intensive for pericarditis • WITHOUT heparin for pericarditis • Slow/gentle for first HD or DDS risk Consultations: • Nephrology (always) • Cardiology (p

nodes.title: Headache Hub — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Gestalt sick check + vitals trend + quick neuro + eye + skin. If unstable: resus first, hub later.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Subarachnoid hemorrhage \u2014 thunderclap, worst-ever, exertional onset. 2. Bacterial meningitis / encephalitis \u2014 fever + meningismus + altered; do not delay antibiotics. 3. CNS venous sinus thrombosis \u2014 progressive headache, hypercoag risk, papilledema, seizure. 4. Carbon monoxide poisoning \u2014 co-exposure, multiple sick contacts, headache + nausea. 5.

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread to Walk
nodes.summary: Walk each dangerous thread to a verdict. Excluded loops back here. All clear + benign pattern \u2192 Rescue.
nodes.body: Ask history-first. Each option opens a short chain that walks a validated rule or a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict. If a cause is EXCLUDED you loop back here to walk the next thread. When every dangerous thread is cleared and the pattern matches prior benign HA \u2192 Rescue.

nodes.title: SAH \u2014 Ottawa SAH Rule
nodes.summary: Ottawa SAH Rule (100% sens, ~13-15% spec \u2014 rule-OUT only): age \u226540, neck pain/stiffness, LOC, exertional onset, thunderclap, limited neck flexion.
nodes.body: The Ottawa SAH Rule applies to alert (GCS 15) patients older than 15 years with a new SEVERE non-traumatic headache reaching MAXIMUM intensity within 1 hour, presenting within 14 days of onset, with no head trauma in the preceding 7 days. \ud83d\uded1 Do NOT apply the rule to: new focal neurologic deficit \u00b7 papilledema on fundoscopy \u00b7 known aneurysm, prior SAH, or known brain tumor \u00b

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 SAH Workup Now
nodes.body: Ottawa SAH Rule positive \u2192 investigate. Open SAH for CT timing and LP-for-xanthochromia indications. Non-contrast CT head: 100% sensitive (95% CI 97-100) within 6 h of onset in the Perry prospective cohort using a third-generation scanner read by a qualified radiologist; pooled meta-analysis sensitivity 98.7% (LR- 0.01, ~1.5 misses per 1000). Sensitivity drops sharply after 6-12 h. ACEP 2019
nodes.recommendation: Open SAH consult. Non-contrast CT now (100% sens \u22646 h with modern scanner + expert read; pooled 98.7%). LP if CT negative + onset >6 h \u2014 mind the 6-12 h xanthochromia gap. BP 140-160. Neurosurgery on positive CT.

nodes.title: SAH \u2014 Ruled Out
nodes.body: Ottawa SAH Rule negative in an eligible patient rules out SAH (100% sensitivity, 95% CI 94.6-100, prospectively validated). No CT mandated by the rule alone. \u26A0\ufe0f The rule only applies to the eligible population (alert/GCS 15, older than 15 years, new severe headache peaking within 1 h, presenting within 14 days, no head trauma in the prior 7 days, no focal deficit, no papilledema, no know
nodes.recommendation: SAH excluded by negative Ottawa rule (eligible patients only). Continue triage.

nodes.title: Focal Deficit / AMS / Seizure \u2014 Confirm
nodes.summary: Objective focal deficit / AMS / seizure = image first. Fully reversible typical aura in a known migraineur = not this.
nodes.body: A true new focal neurologic deficit, depressed mental status, or a first/new seizure with headache is a rule-in for structural or infectious intracranial pathology until imaging says otherwise.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 Image First, Open the Deep-Dive
nodes.body: Non-contrast CT for hemorrhage / mass effect; add contrast or MRI if infection or tumor suspected. Open the consult that fits: - SAH if thunderclap onset is also present - ICH for any spontaneous intracranial bleed - Acute ischemic stroke pathway for the tPA / EVT decision and NIHSS - Meningitis / Encephalitis if fever + neuro signs OR isolated AMS in immunocompromised - Status Epilepticus if acti
nodes.recommendation: Image first. Open the deep-dive consult that fits. Reverse anticoagulation early if ICH suspected.

nodes.title: Focal / AMS / Seizure \u2014 Not This Thread
nodes.body: A fully reversible, typical aura (visual scintillations / march of sensory symptoms over 5-60 min, then resolution) in an established migraineur with NO new features does not require emergent imaging on its own. \u26A0\ufe0f First-ever aura, aura lasting >60 min, motor weakness (hemiplegic migraine mimics stroke), or any residual deficit \u2192 do NOT clear \u2014 image and treat as the rule-in br
nodes.recommendation: Reversible typical aura in a known migraineur \u2014 not a structural emergency. Continue triage.

nodes.title: Meningitis / Encephalitis \u2014 Confirm Suspicion
nodes.summary: Fever + HA + meningeal/CNS sign OR immunocompromise = treat empirically. Absent Kernig/Brudzinski does not exclude.
nodes.body: Fever + headache + ANY of: neck stiffness / meningismus, altered mental status, photophobia, petechial rash, seizure, or an immunocompromised host with new headache. Kernig/Brudzinski are insensitive \u2014 absence does NOT exclude.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 Antibiotics Within 60 Minutes
nodes.body: Open Meningitis / Encephalitis for empiric selection by age + immune status, CT-before-LP indications, CSF interpretation, and steroid adjunct timing. Empiric antibiotics target within 60 minutes of suspicion. Do NOT wait for imaging or LP. CT before LP IS indicated for AMS / focal deficit / papilledema / immunocompromise / new-onset seizure within 1 week / history of CNS disease / age \u226560 (I
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics within 60 min + dexamethasone with/before first dose. Open Meningitis consult. Do not delay for imaging/LP.

nodes.title: Meningitis \u2014 Unlikely
nodes.body: Afebrile, no meningeal or CNS signs, and immunocompetent makes acute bacterial meningitis unlikely on this visit. There is no validated ED rule that fully excludes it, so re-examine if fever or CNS signs emerge during the stay. Return to Rule In / Rule Out and walk the next thread.
nodes.recommendation: CNS infection unlikely with no fever/meningeal signs in an immunocompetent host. Re-check if picture changes.

nodes.title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma \u2014 Confirm
nodes.summary: Painful red eye + halos + mid-dilated fixed pupil + IOP >30-40 = AACG. Normal IOP + quiet eye = not this.
nodes.body: Painful red eye + halos around lights + nausea/vomiting + a mid-dilated, poorly reactive pupil, often a hazy/steamy cornea. Confirm with IOP measurement (tonometry).

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 AACG
nodes.body: Open AACG \u2014 emergent ophthalmology, IOP measurement now, medical IOP-lowering (timolol + brimonidine + dorzolamide + oral acetazolamide + IV mannitol if severe; pilocarpine once IOP begins to fall). \ud83d\uded1 Do NOT dim the room lights (pupillary dilation worsens angle closure). \ud83d\uded1 Do NOT use mydriatic drops. \ud83d\uded1 Do NOT discharge without ophthalmology disposition (defini
nodes.recommendation: Ophthalmology now. Medical IOP-lowering. No dim lights, no mydriatics, no discharge without ophtho.

nodes.title: AACG \u2014 Ruled Out
nodes.body: Normal IOP with a white, quiet eye and a normal pupil rules out acute angle closure as the cause. If the pain is more "behind/around" the eye with a NORMAL or miotic pupil + autonomic features (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, ptosis, rhinorrhea) + restlessness, think cluster instead \u2014 walk that thread from triage. Return to Rule In / Rule Out.
nodes.recommendation: Angle closure excluded by normal IOP/quiet eye. Consider cluster if autonomic. Continue triage.

nodes.title: Carbon Monoxide \u2014 Confirm with Co-oximetry
nodes.summary: SpO\u2082 is falsely normal \u2014 use co-oximetry. Elevated CO-Hgb or symptomatic exposure = CO toxicity. Normal co-ox = excluded.
nodes.body: \ud83d\uded1 Standard pulse oximetry reads CO-Hgb as oxyhemoglobin \u2014 FALSELY NORMAL. You cannot rule CO in or out with SpO\u2082. Use co-oximetry (arterial OR venous blood gas with co-ox, or a SpCO probe). While the level is pending, place the patient on 100% O\u2082 via non-rebreather \u2014 do not wait for the number.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 CO Toxicity
nodes.body: Open CO Toxicity for the full pathway (CO-Hgb thresholds, hyperbaric O\u2082 indications per UHMS 2019, pregnancy considerations). Next 5 minutes: keep the patient on 100% O\u2082 via NRB. CO-Hgb elimination half-life is ~4-5 h on room air \u2192 ~60-90 min on high-flow 100% O\u2082 \u2192 ~20-30 min on hyperbaric O\u2082 at 2.5-3 atm. Continue O\u2082 regardless of the measured level pending the
nodes.recommendation: 100% NRB now. Open CO Toxicity consult. HBO for pregnancy / LOC / neuro or cardiac ischemia / high CO-Hgb.

nodes.title: CO \u2014 Ruled Out
nodes.body: A true co-oximetry level in the normal range with no compelling exposure rules out CO poisoning as the cause of this headache. \u26A0\ufe0f Remember a level can normalize after the patient has been on oxygen or removed from the source for hours \u2014 correlate with exposure history and timing. Return to Rule In / Rule Out.
nodes.recommendation: CO excluded by normal co-oximetry. Mind timing/oxygen effect on the level. Continue triage.

nodes.title: Giant Cell Arteritis \u2014 Clinical Gate
nodes.summary: Age \u226550 + new HA + jaw claudication / scalp tenderness / vision change / PMR / \u2191ESR-CRP = treat empirically.
nodes.body: Age \u226550 is the entry criterion. Then look for the high-yield features that drive empiric treatment.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 GCA (Treat Before Biopsy)
nodes.body: Work up and treat IN PARALLEL \u2014 do NOT wait for biopsy to start steroid. 1. ESR + CRP stat (ESR usually >50; up to ~5% have normal ESR \u2014 CRP is more sensitive; check both). 2. Empiric high-dose corticosteroid NOW: - No visual symptoms: prednisone 60 mg PO daily. - Visual symptoms or jaw claudication: methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily \u00d7 3 days, then prednisone 60 mg PO. 3. Ophthalmolog
nodes.recommendation: ESR + CRP + empiric high-dose steroid NOW (IV pulse if visual/jaw). Biopsy within 1-2 weeks. Ophtho for visual symptoms.

nodes.title: GCA \u2014 Unlikely
nodes.body: Age <50, or no GCA features with normal ESR and CRP, makes giant cell arteritis unlikely. There is no perfect rule-out \u2014 if inflammatory markers were not checked and suspicion is more than trivial, send ESR + CRP before fully clearing. Return to Rule In / Rule Out.
nodes.recommendation: GCA unlikely by age/features/markers. Send ESR+CRP if any residual suspicion. Continue triage.

nodes.title: Cervical Artery Dissection \u2014 Clinical Gate
nodes.summary: HA/neck pain + Horner / focal deficit / compelling mechanism = CTA neck. Isolated neck ache without these = low-prob.
nodes.body: Headache and/or neck pain (often sudden, unilateral) PLUS any of: partial Horner syndrome (ptosis + miosis), pulsatile tinnitus, cranial nerve palsy, or posterior-circulation stroke symptoms. Ask about recent chiropractic manipulation, MVC (even minor), strenuous exertion, forceful cough/vomiting, or connective tissue disease.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 Dissection
nodes.body: Open Cervical Artery Dissection for risk stratification, imaging, and management. Imaging: CTA neck (carotid + vertebral) is the practical first study in most EDs; MRA + fat-suppressed neck MRI is the reference standard if available and the patient is stable. Vertebral dissection presents as posterior HA + neck pain \u00b1 posterior-circulation stroke \u2014 a different posture than carotid. Manag
nodes.recommendation: CTA neck. Open the dissection consult. Antithrombotic choice under stroke/neuro.

nodes.title: Dissection \u2014 Low Probability
nodes.body: Isolated neck ache without Horner, focal deficit, or a compelling mechanism is low-probability for cervical artery dissection. There is no ED decision rule that formally excludes it, so image if a Horner or deficit emerges, or if the mechanism story surfaces. Return to Rule In / Rule Out.
nodes.recommendation: Dissection low-probability without Horner/deficit/mechanism. Image if the picture evolves. Continue triage.

nodes.title: CVST \u2014 Clinical Gate
nodes.summary: Hypercoag context + papilledema/seizure/atypical deficit = MRV or CT venogram. Normal exam + no risk = low-prob.
nodes.body: Think CVST with a progressive or thunderclap headache PLUS a hypercoagulable context or raised-ICP picture: postpartum (peaks ~1-3 weeks out), OCP + smoking, thrombophilia, malignancy, dehydration; papilledema, seizure, or a focal deficit that does not fit an arterial territory; or an isolated raised-ICP picture without another cause.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 CVST
nodes.body: Open CVST. MRV is the workhorse; CT venogram is acceptable when MRV is unavailable (a plain non-contrast CT is insensitive \u2014 a dense-vein/cord sign is suggestive but its absence does not exclude). Treatment (refined in the CVST consult): therapeutic anticoagulation (UFH or LMWH) even when a hemorrhagic venous infarct is present on imaging; neurology + hematology consult; treat raised ICP and
nodes.recommendation: MRV (or CT venogram). Open CVST consult. Anticoagulate per the consult even with hemorrhagic infarct.

nodes.title: CVST \u2014 Low Probability
nodes.body: No hypercoagulable context, no papilledema or seizure, and a normal exam make CVST low-probability. A normal D-dimer lowers the probability further but does not fully exclude it in a high-suspicion patient \u2014 image if risk factors or ICP signs surface. \u26A0\ufe0f If papilledema IS present and venous imaging is negative, you are not done \u2014 think idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Clas
nodes.recommendation: CVST low-probability without hypercoag risk/ICP signs. Image if the picture evolves. Continue triage.

nodes.title: Pregnancy / Postpartum \u2014 Broaden the Net
nodes.summary: Check BP first. \u2265140/90 + proteinuria/end-organ = pre-eclampsia. Normotensive still needs CVST/RCVS/apoplexy workup.
nodes.body: Pregnancy and the postpartum period massively broaden the dangerous differential. Check the BP first \u2014 pre-eclampsia is the highest-yield, most treatable cause.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 Pregnancy/Postpartum Workup
nodes.body: Work these in parallel based on findings: - HTN in Pregnancy / Pre-eclampsia if BP \u2265140/90 + proteinuria or end-organ signs. Magnesium for seizure prophylaxis; treat severe-range BP; delivery is definitive. ACOG: severe-range BP is \u2265160 systolic OR \u2265110 diastolic persisting \u226515 min \u2014 treat within 30-60 min of confirmation (IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or PO immediate-rele
nodes.recommendation: Pre-eclampsia (Mg + BP + OB) / CVST / RCVS / apoplexy / dissection in parallel. MRI no-gad if feasible.

nodes.title: Post-Traumatic HA \u2014 Canadian CT Head Rule
nodes.summary: Canadian CT Head Rule (minor TBI, GCS 13-15, LOC/amnesia). ANY high/medium feature = CT. Anticoag/seizure/<16 excluded from rule.
nodes.body: The Canadian CT Head Rule applies to minor head injury (GCS 13-15, witnessed LOC / amnesia / disorientation) in patients \u226516 yo. It does NOT apply to anticoagulation/bleeding disorder, seizure after injury, or age <16 \u2014 those get imaged/assessed outside the rule. CT is required if ANY high- or medium-risk feature is present.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 CT for Post-Traumatic HA
nodes.body: Canadian CT Head Rule positive (or the rule does not apply because of anticoagulation / bleeding disorder / post-injury seizure / age <16) \u2192 non-contrast CT head. Open your shop\u2019s TBI / intracranial hemorrhage pathway. If anticoagulated + ICH suspected or confirmed: reverse early (4-factor PCC for warfarin/factor Xa inhibitors per protocol; idarucizumab for dabigatran; platelets rarely i
nodes.recommendation: Non-contrast CT. Reverse anticoagulation early if ICH. Neurosurgery for positive CT.

nodes.title: Post-Traumatic HA \u2014 CT Not Required
nodes.body: Canadian CT Head Rule negative in an applicable patient \u2014 CT is not required. In the derivation cohort the five high-risk factors were 100% sensitive (95% CI 92-100) for need for neurosurgical intervention, and all seven factors were 98.4% sensitive (95% CI 96-99) for clinically important brain injury (the 4 missed injuries were small contusions; none needed neurosurgery, none had sequelae).
nodes.recommendation: No CT by a negative Canadian CT Head Rule (applicable patients). Conservative for chronic without progression. Continue triage.

nodes.title: Cluster Headache \u2014 Phenotype Gate
nodes.summary: Strictly unilateral 15-180 min + ipsilateral autonomic + restless = cluster. First-ever/atypical = image first.
nodes.body: Severe, strictly unilateral, orbital/supraorbital/temporal pain lasting 15-180 min, with at least one IPSILATERAL autonomic feature (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion/rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, ptosis/miosis) and a sense of restlessness/agitation. First-ever cluster-type attacks warrant neuroimaging at least once to exclude a secondary mimic.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 Cluster
nodes.body: Open Cluster Headache for the full acute \u2192 bridge \u2192 maintenance pathway. Next 5 minutes while transitioning: place the patient on 100% O\u2082 via NRB at 12-15 L/min (NOT nasal cannula \u2014 peaks ~40% FiO\u2082, inadequate). O\u2082 is diagnostic and therapeutic \u2014 ~78% abort within 15 min. If not aborted by ~7 min, add SQ sumatriptan (screen contraindications in the cluster consul
nodes.recommendation: Start O\u2082 NRB 12-15 L/min. Open Cluster consult. SQ sumatriptan if not aborted; ONB if refractory.

nodes.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia \u2014 Confirm + Screen
nodes.summary: Paroxysmal shock-like V2/V3 pain triggered by touch/chewing, normal interictal exam = TN. Atypical features = MRI first.
nodes.body: Paroxysmal, electric-shock/stabbing pain in V2/V3 (occasionally V1), seconds to <2 min per paroxysm, triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, cold wind, or tooth-brushing, with a normal exam between attacks.

nodes.title: RULE IN \u2014 Trigeminal Neuralgia
nodes.body: Open Trigeminal Neuralgia for ICHD-3 confirmation \u2192 MRI triggers \u2192 carbamazepine ladder \u2192 surgical referral. \ud83d\uded1 Before the first carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine dose: screen HLA-B*1502 ancestry (Han Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese, Filipino, Malay, Indonesian). Positive = avoid both (SJS/TEN risk); bridge with gabapentin or baclofen while the test is pending or use those long-ter
nodes.recommendation: HLA-B*1502 screen by ancestry before CBZ. MRI for atypical features. Open TN consult.

nodes.title: Rescue Cocktail — Benign-Pattern HA
nodes.summary: Prochlorperazine 10 IV + diphenhydramine 25 IV + ketorolac 15-30 IV + Mg 1-2 g + 1 L NS. Metoclopramide if unavailable. ONB is first-tier. Avoid opioids/butalbital.
nodes.body: Every dangerous thread cleared, pattern matches prior benign HA (migraine, tension, undifferentiated). Standard parenteral cocktail (2025 AHS acute-migraine guideline, Robblee et al.): THE COCKTAIL: - Prochlorperazine 10 mg IV over ~15 min \u2014 workhorse antidopaminergic, the highest-evidence parenteral agent (2025 AHS Level A \u2014 "should be offered") - Diphenhydramine 25 mg IV \u2014 akathis

nodes.title: Reassess at 60-90 Minutes
nodes.summary: Reassess at 60-90 min. Discharge if \u226550% better + PO + no new neuro. Escalate or re-image if not.
nodes.body: Re-examine: pain-score trend, ability to tolerate PO, any NEW neurologic feature (red-flag emergence), orthostatic check before discharge.

nodes.title: Second Round / Observation
nodes.body: Options for partial response: - Repeat Prochlorperazine 10 mg IV (or switch to Metoclopramide 10 mg IV if akathisia despite diphenhydramine) - Add dexamethasone 10 mg IV \u2014 reduces 24-72 h recurrence (NNT ~9 pooled, Colman 2008). Note the evidence grade softened: Level B in the 2016 AHS assessment \u2192 Level C ("may be offered") in the 2025 AHS guideline. Still reasonable, no longer a strong
nodes.recommendation: Repeat antidopaminergic, add dexamethasone, consider obs-unit reassessment at 4-6 h.

nodes.title: Refractory — ONB or DHE
nodes.body: Greater occipital nerve block (ONB) \u2014 bedside, 5-15 min onset, works for status migrainosus + cluster + occipital neuralgia + cervicogenic + post-traumatic. Level A ("should be offered") in the 2025 AHS ED acute-migraine guideline \u2014 the only non-pharmacologic intervention to reach Level A. Open Greater Occipital Nerve Block for landmarks, aspiration check, agent selection, and post-proce
nodes.recommendation: ONB at bedside (first-tier); DHE if not contraindicated; admit if true status migrainosus.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: Image when ANY red flag. CT first; CTA/MRV/MRI/LP by suspicion. CT-before-LP if AMS/focal/papilledema/immunocomp/new seizure/age \u226560. IIH opening pressure \u226525 cm H\u2082O adults, \u226528 children.
nodes.body: You should NOT image every headache. Image when ANY of the following: Indications for non-contrast CT head: - First-or-worst / thunderclap onset - New HA in age \u226550 - Focal deficit, AMS, seizure - Post-traumatic with red flags (Canadian CT Head Rule) - HIV / immunocompromised with new HA - Anticoagulated with new HA - Papilledema - Pattern change in a known primary HA disorder (new quality, l

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if controlled + PO + no flags. Observe if partial/pending. Admit per deep-dive consult criteria.
nodes.body: Common framework across undifferentiated HA. The deep-dive consults carry phenotype-specific admit criteria \u2014 defer to those once you commit.

nodes.title: Discharge — Universal Checklist
nodes.body: Before discharge: 1. Pain reduced to an acceptable level (typically \u22643/10 or back to baseline) 2. Tolerating PO 3. Orthostatic vitals normal (prochlorperazine + diphenhydramine + ketorolac can drop BP) 4. No new neurologic findings on recheck 5. Suicide screen if cluster (highest SI of any primary HA), TN, chronic migraine, or mood-disorder features + chronic pain 6. Written return precaution
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after pain controlled, PO tolerated, no new neuro, written return precautions, follow-up arranged.

nodes.title: Observe — Partial Response or Pending Workup
nodes.body: ED observation unit appropriate when: - Partial response after the first cocktail round \u2014 second round + reassess at 4-6 h - Awaiting CSF or advanced imaging (MRI, MRV) - Status migrainosus on IV cocktail \u2014 assess at 4-6 h before escalating - Pain control insufficient for discharge but no admission criteria - Transportation / safety / social barriers to discharge Reassessment at 4-6 h: r
nodes.recommendation: Obs unit + 4-6 h reassessment. Re-examine for new neuro signs; escalate if no improvement.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit when: - Red-flag workup positive \u2014 SAH, ICH, meningitis, dissection, CVST, AACG with IOP not medically controlled, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, severe CO for hyperbaric - Refractory primary HA \u2014 status migrainosus failing IV cocktail + DHE; cluster failing O\u2082 + 2 SQ triptans + ONB; TN crisis with dehydration and weight loss - Active suicidal ideation - Severe medication adverse ev
nodes.recommendation: Admit per deep-dive consult criteria. Match the service to the dominant diagnosis.

nodes.title: Heat Stroke Management
nodes.summary: Heat stroke: core temp >40°C + AMS — COOL FIRST, then workup. Every minute of delay increases mortality
nodes.body: Heat stroke is a TRUE EMERGENCY — mortality 10-50% without rapid cooling. Every minute of delay increases mortality. Definition: Core temperature >40°C (104°F) + CNS dysfunction (altered mental status, seizures, coma). Two types: • Classic (non-exertional): Elderly, chronic illness, medications, heat waves • Exertional: Young healthy athletes, laborers, military [1][2][3][6]

nodes.title: Heat Illness Classification
nodes.summary: Distinguish heat stroke (temp >40°C + AMS) from heat exhaustion (temp <40°C, no AMS)
nodes.body: Heat stroke criteria (BOTH required): • Core temp >40°C (104°F) — use rectal or esophageal thermometry • CNS dysfunction (confusion, delirium, seizures, coma) Heat exhaustion: • Core temp <40°C • May have symptoms (headache, nausea, weakness) but normal mentation CRITICAL: Oral, axillary, and temporal thermometry are UNRELIABLE in heat illness — use rectal temp. [1][2][3]

nodes.title: Heat Exhaustion Management
nodes.summary: Heat exhaustion (temp <40°C, no AMS): oral rehydration, cool environment, observe for progression
nodes.body: Heat exhaustion is NOT heat stroke — but can progress rapidly. Treatment: • Move to cool environment • Remove excess clothing • Oral rehydration if tolerating PO • IV NS if unable to tolerate PO or severely symptomatic • External cooling (cool water misting, fans) Monitor closely: Any mental status change → reclassify as heat stroke. [2][3]
nodes.recommendation: Heat exhaustion — supportive care with cooling and rehydration. Close monitoring for progression.

nodes.title: Safe Discharge Criteria — Environmental Hyperthermia
nodes.summary: Heat exhaustion discharge: normal vitals, tolerating PO, AMS resolved, reliable environment
nodes.body: ALL of the following criteria must be met for safe ED discharge: [2][3][4] Clinical Criteria: • Core temperature <38°C (100.4°F) after cooling and observation • Normal mental status — alert, oriented, appropriate • Hemodynamically stable — HR <100, BP normal, orthostatics negative • Tolerating oral fluids — able to drink without nausea/vomiting • Symptoms resolved or improving — no weakness, dizzi

nodes.title: Immediate Cooling — TIME IS CRITICAL
nodes.summary: Start cooling IMMEDIATELY — every minute above 40°C increases organ damage and mortality
nodes.body: "Cool first, transport second" — begin cooling IMMEDIATELY. [1] Target: Core temp <39°C (102.2°F) within 30 minutes. • Mortality near-zero if cooled within 30 min • Mortality >50% if cooling delayed >2 hours [1][2] Remove all clothing and begin aggressive cooling while simultaneously establishing IV access and monitoring. Do NOT delay cooling for: • IV access • Labs • Imaging • Transport [1][3]

nodes.title: Cooling Method Selection
nodes.summary: Select cooling method: ice water immersion (gold standard) > evaporative > ice packs
nodes.body: Cold water immersion (CWI) is GOLD STANDARD — cooling rate 0.2°C/min (fastest). [1][2] Ice water immersion: Patient submerged in ice water bath up to neck. • Best for exertional heat stroke • May be difficult in elderly or obese Evaporative cooling: Continuous water misting + high-flow fans. • More practical in ED setting • Cooling rate 0.1°C/min What resources are available? [1][2][3]

nodes.title: Ice Water Immersion Protocol
nodes.summary: Ice water immersion: whole body in ice water bath — cooling rate 0.2°C/min, most effective method
nodes.body: GOLD STANDARD — cooling rate 0.2°C/min [1][2] Setup: • Large tub/tank filled with ice water (1-17°C / 34-63°F) • Submerge patient to neck level • Continuous agitation of water (prevents thermal boundary layer) • Assign staff to hold patient's head above water Monitoring during immersion: • Continuous rectal temperature probe • Stop immersion at 39°C (102.2°F) — temp will continue to drift down • C

nodes.title: Evaporative Cooling Protocol
nodes.summary: Evaporative cooling: undress, mist with tepid water, high-flow fans — if immersion not available
nodes.body: Second-line if immersion unavailable — cooling rate ~0.1°C/min [2][3] Setup: • Undress patient completely • Continuously spray lukewarm water (not ice cold) over entire body • High-flow fans directed at patient • Keep skin WET at all times Physics: Evaporation of water removes heat. Lukewarm water evaporates faster than ice-cold water. Adjuncts: • Ice packs to axillae, groin, neck (large vessels)

nodes.title: Ice Pack Cooling (Suboptimal)
nodes.summary: Ice packs to neck, axillae, groin as adjunct — least effective alone, use with other methods
nodes.body: LEAST effective method — cooling rate ~0.05°C/min [2] If this is all you have: • Place ice packs to axillae, groin, neck, and entire torso • Wet sheets over patient + fans • Cold IV fluids (4°C NS) • Rotate ice packs frequently (they warm up) Consider transfer to facility with immersion or evaporative capability if cooling is inadequate. Avoid: • Cooling blankets alone (too slow) • Antipyretics (A

nodes.title: Cooling Endpoint & Overshoot Prevention
nodes.summary: Stop cooling at 38.5-39°C to prevent overshoot hypothermia — continue core temp monitoring
nodes.body: Stop active cooling at core temp 39°C (102.2°F) [1][2] Why 39°C? • Temperature will continue to drift down after cooling stops (afterdrop) • Overcooling → shivering → heat generation → rebound hyperthermia • Hypothermia (<35°C) causes coagulopathy and arrhythmias After reaching 39°C: • Remove from ice bath / stop misting • Dry patient • Cover with light sheet • Continue rectal temp monitoring ever

nodes.title: Fluid Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Aggressive IV fluids for dehydration — avoid overcooled fluids through IV (peripheral vasoconstriction)
nodes.body: Heat stroke causes SIGNIFICANT volume depletion — hypovolemia, vasodilation, and third-spacing. [2][3] Initial resuscitation: • NS or LR 1-2 L bolus (adult) • Pediatric: 20 mL/kg bolus • Avoid dextrose-containing fluids initially Goal: MAP >65 mmHg, UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr Caution: • Pulmonary edema can occur with aggressive fluids + capillary leak • POCUS-guided resuscitation preferred • If hypotensive

nodes.title: Airway & Ventilation
nodes.summary: Assess airway in severe AMS — intubate for GCS <8 or inability to protect airway
nodes.body: Indications for intubation: • GCS ≤8 or unable to protect airway • Refractory seizures • Severe agitation requiring deep sedation • Respiratory failure Considerations: • RSI drugs: Avoid succinylcholine if rhabdomyolysis suspected (hyperkalemia risk) • Use rocuronium for paralysis • Cooling MUST continue during/after intubation [2]

nodes.title: Intubation Considerations
nodes.summary: Intubate for airway protection in severe AMS — continue cooling after intubation
nodes.body: RSI for heat stroke: Induction: Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV or Propofol 1-2 mg/kg IV Paralysis: Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV • AVOID succinylcholine — hyperkalemia risk with rhabdomyolysis Post-intubation: • Continue active cooling • Target normocapnia (avoid hyperventilation) • Sedation: propofol or midazolam + fentanyl [2]

nodes.title: Seizure Management
nodes.summary: Benzodiazepines first-line for heat stroke seizures — seizure activity generates more heat
nodes.body: Seizures are common in heat stroke — direct thermal brain injury + metabolic derangements. Seizures generate heat and worsen hyperthermia — must be controlled rapidly. [2][3]

nodes.title: Seizure Treatment
nodes.summary: Benzodiazepines first-line for heat stroke seizures — seizure activity generates more heat
nodes.body: First-line: Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IV or IM (max 10 mg) Alternative: Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) If refractory: • Propofol infusion or • Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV Avoid phenytoin/fosphenytoin — may worsen hyperthermia and is less effective for toxin-induced seizures. Continue aggressive cooling — seizures generate significant heat. [2][3]

nodes.title: Heat Stroke Complications
nodes.summary: Heat stroke complications: rhabdo, DIC, hepatic failure (peaks 48-72h), AKI, ARDS
nodes.body: Multi-organ dysfunction is common — heat stroke is a systemic inflammatory response. [1][2][3] Common complications: • Rhabdomyolysis — CK >5x normal, especially exertional • AKI — from hypovolemia, rhabdomyolysis, direct thermal injury • DIC — coagulopathy, bleeding • Hepatic failure — can be delayed 24-72 hours • ARDS — from capillary leak • Cardiac dysfunction — arrhythmias, myocardial injury L

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis Assessment
nodes.summary: CK >5000 = significant rhabdomyolysis — aggressive IV fluids targeting UOP 200-300 mL/hr
nodes.body: Rhabdomyolysis is common in EXERTIONAL heat stroke — less common in classic. Risk factors: • Exertional heat stroke (military, athletes) • Prolonged hyperthermia • Seizures • Agitation requiring restraint CK thresholds: • >5x ULN (>1000 U/L) = rhabdomyolysis • >10,000 U/L = high risk for AKI • >40,000 U/L = very high risk [2][3]

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis Treatment
nodes.summary: CK >5000: aggressive IV fluids targeting UOP 200-300 mL/hr — bicarb controversial
nodes.body: Goal: Prevent myoglobin-induced AKI [2][3] IV fluids: • Aggressive NS or LR — target UOP 200-300 mL/hr • May need 10-20 L/day in severe cases • POCUS-guided to avoid overload Urine alkalinization: • Controversial — consider if urine pH <6.5 • NaHCO3 150 mEq in 1L D5W at 200 mL/hr • Target urine pH >6.5 Monitor: • CK every 6-12 hours until trending down • Creatinine, potassium (hyperkalemia risk) •

nodes.title: Severe Rhabdomyolysis
nodes.summary: CK >40,000: continuous IV fluids, monitor for compartment syndrome and AKI
nodes.body: CK >40,000 — high risk for AKI and dialysis [2] Management: • Same as moderate rhabdo but more aggressive fluids • Early nephrology consult • Consider dialysis if: - Refractory hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5) - Severe metabolic acidosis - Volume overload despite diuresis - Anuria Monitor for compartment syndrome: • Pain out of proportion • Pain with passive stretch • Tense compartments • → Emergent fasciot

nodes.title: Coagulopathy & DIC
nodes.summary: DIC: transfuse products as needed — coagulopathy typically resolves with temperature correction
nodes.body: DIC is common in severe heat stroke — direct thermal injury to endothelium + systemic inflammation. [2][3] Labs: • PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer • Platelet count Treatment: • Supportive — treat underlying heat stroke • FFP if INR >2 AND bleeding • Platelets if <50,000 AND bleeding • Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <100 AND bleeding • TXA 1g IV if significant hemorrhage Do NOT give platelets or FF

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ALL heat stroke patients require admission — mild/stable to floor, unstable/organ dysfunction to ICU
nodes.body: ALL heat stroke patients require admission — multi-organ dysfunction can be delayed 24-72 hours. [2][3] Assess severity to determine level of care.

nodes.title: Admit — Monitored Bed
nodes.summary: Floor admission for mild heat stroke: resolved AMS, normal labs, observation for delayed complications
nodes.body: Telemetry/step-down admission criteria: • Cooled to <39°C within 30 minutes • Hemodynamically stable off vasopressors • GCS returned to baseline • No significant rhabdomyolysis (CK <10,000) • No active seizures Monitoring: • Continuous temp monitoring x 24h • Serial labs: CMP, LFTs, CK q12h • Neuro checks q4h • Watch for delayed hepatic failure (24-72h) [2][3]
nodes.recommendation: Admit to telemetry/step-down unit. Continue monitoring for delayed complications.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU for severe heat stroke: persistent AMS, rhabdo, DIC, organ failure, or cooling failure
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: • Intubated or requiring airway protection • Vasopressor requirement • Severe rhabdomyolysis (CK >40,000) • DIC with active bleeding • Persistent altered mental status • Refractory hyperthermia • Multi-organ failure ICU management: • Continue temp monitoring (may have rebound hyperthermia) • Aggressive fluid resuscitation • Serial labs q6h: CMP, LFTs, CK, coags, lactate • N
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for ongoing critical care. High risk for multi-organ dysfunction.

nodes.title: Hemophilia & Von Willebrand Disease
nodes.summary: Treat FIRST, test later — give factor replacement before imaging or definitive diagnosis
nodes.body: Hemophilia Steps Summary — quick reference. Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and B (factor IX deficiency) are X-linked bleeding disorders. Combined incidence: 1 per 5000 male births. Hemophilia A is 4× more common than B. [1] von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, affecting up to 1% of the population. Unlike hemophilia, vWD affects both sexes equally. [3]

nodes.title: Diagnosis Status
nodes.summary: Determine if known hemophilia or new suspected bleeding disorder — treatment first, diagnosis second
nodes.body: Does the patient have a known bleeding disorder diagnosis?

nodes.title: ED Workup for Suspected Bleeding Disorder
nodes.summary: CBC, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen — hemophilia: prolonged PTT with normal PT, correct with mixing study
nodes.body: Initial screening labs: • CBC with platelet count • PT (prothrombin time) • PTT (partial thromboplastin time) • Fibrinogen level Differential Diagnosis by Lab Pattern If isolated prolonged PTT → order factor VIII and IX levels If PTT normal + mucosal bleeding → consider vWD panel (vWF:Ag, vWF:RCo, factor VIII) Caution: vWF is an acute phase reactant — false negatives are common during acute illnes

nodes.title: Lab Results Pattern
nodes.summary: Isolated prolonged PTT: hemophilia A or B. PTT + PT prolonged: DIC, liver disease, or severe deficiency
nodes.body: What is the screening lab pattern?

nodes.title: Hemophilia Severity Classification
nodes.summary: Severity by factor level: severe <1%, moderate 1-5%, mild 5-40% — guides replacement dosing
nodes.body: Severity is defined by baseline clotting factor activity level: • Severe (<1%) — spontaneous bleeds, multiple per month, joints and soft tissue. 35% of hemophilia A, 60% of hemophilia B. [5] • Moderate (1–5%) — bleeds with mild trauma, 4–6 per year [5] • Mild (5–40%) — bleeds with surgery/significant trauma only. May not be diagnosed until adulthood. [10] If severity is unknown, assume severe for

nodes.title: Type of Bleeding
nodes.summary: Classify bleed severity: life-threatening (ICH, neck), major (hemarthrosis, muscle), or mucosal/minor
nodes.body: What is the presenting bleed type? Factor Products Reference

nodes.title: Type of Bleeding (continued)
nodes.summary: Additional bleed types: GI hemorrhage, hematuria, trauma — each requires specific factor targets
nodes.body: Additional bleed types:

nodes.title: Hemarthrosis Management
nodes.summary: Hemarthrosis: factor to 30-50%, ice, immobilize — do NOT aspirate unless ruling out septic joint
nodes.body: Target factor level: 40–60% [2][8] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 25–30 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 40–60 units/kg Supportive care: • Immobilize affected joint (crutches for weight-bearing joints) • Ice 15 min every 2–3 hours • Acetaminophen for pain — avoid NSAIDs (antiplatelet effects) • Compression bandage Single dose often sufficient. Repeat q12–24h if symptoms persist. [8]
nodes.recommendation: Factor replacement to 40–60%, RICE, acetaminophen. Single dose usually adequate. Outpatient if reliable family.

nodes.title: Muscle / Soft Tissue Bleed
nodes.summary: Classify muscle bleed: superficial vs deep (iliopsoas, forearm compartment) — deep = emergent
nodes.body: Is the muscle bleed in the iliopsoas?

nodes.title: Muscle / Soft Tissue Bleed Management
nodes.summary: Muscle bleed: factor to 40-60%, ice, rest — monitor for compartment syndrome if extremity
nodes.body: Target factor level: 40–60% [2] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 25–30 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 40–60 units/kg Repeat doses q12–24h × 2–3 days often required. Monitor for: • Compartment syndrome • Nerve compression • Significant blood loss (check hemoglobin) Physical therapy may be needed but can precipitate rebleeding — coordinate with hematology. [2]
nodes.recommendation: Factor replacement to 40–60%. Monitor for compartment syndrome. Often requires 2–3 days of repeat dosing.

nodes.title: Iliopsoas Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Iliopsoas hemorrhage: factor to 80-100%, CT confirmation, may need ICU — mimics appendicitis
nodes.body: Target factor level: 80% × 3 days, then >50% for remaining treatment [2] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 40–50 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 80–100 units/kg Classic presentation: • Hip, thigh, abdomen, and/or groin pain • Hip flexion contracture (present in 93% of cases) • Femoral nerve paresthesia (present in 57%) • Average 3.8 days of symptoms before presentation [10] Management:
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Factor replacement to 80%. Strict bed rest. MRI. Treatment 7–14 days. Life-threatening bleed potential.

nodes.title: Intracranial Hemorrhage — Inhibitor Status?
nodes.summary: ICH: FIRST determine inhibitor status — changes treatment completely
nodes.body: ⚠️ LIFE-THREATENING BLEED — ACT NOW FIRST: Does this patient have INHIBITORS? How to identify inhibitor patients: 1. ASK the patient/family: "Do you have inhibitors?" "Has factor replacement worked before?" 2. Check medications: On emicizumab (Hemlibra), FEIBA, or NovoSeven at home? → INHIBITORS 3. Check for ID card/treatment letter — most patients carry these 4. If unknown and crashing: Treat AS

nodes.title: ICH — Standard Factor Replacement
nodes.summary: ICH in hemophilia: factor to 100% BEFORE CT — intracranial hemorrhage until proven otherwise
nodes.body: Target factor level: 100% — ADMINISTER IMMEDIATELY [2][11] ⚠️ Factor replacement BEFORE imaging — do not delay for CT/MRI [2] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 50 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 100 units/kg Key facts: • ICH mortality: 20% overall (lower in pediatrics) [10] • ICH is 20–50× more frequent in males with hemophilia [10] • Factor administration within 6 hours of head trauma
nodes.recommendation: Factor to 100% STAT — before imaging. Admit ICU. Neurosurgery consult. 20% mortality.

nodes.title: ICH + Inhibitors — Bypassing Agents
nodes.summary: ICH + inhibitors: rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg q2-3h PREFERRED — FEIBA max 200 U/kg/day, avoid with emicizumab
nodes.body: ⚠️ FACTOR WILL NOT WORK — USE BYPASSING AGENTS [9][10] PREFERRED: rFVIIa (NovoSeven) — especially if on emicizumab • rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg IV q2-3h × 3 doses minimum • OR single high dose: 270 mcg/kg (subsequent doses q6h+) • No maximum daily dose • Safe with emicizumab [11] ALTERNATIVE: FEIBA • FEIBA 100 units/kg IV (life-threatening dose) • Repeat q8-12h as needed • ⚠️ MAX 200 units/kg/day (thromboti
nodes.recommendation: rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg q2-3h PREFERRED. FEIBA 100 U/kg alternative (max 200 U/kg/day). Avoid FEIBA if on emicizumab.
