nodes.title: Mucosal Bleeding Management
nodes.summary: Mucosal bleeding: factor to 30-50% + TXA — epistaxis, oral, GU bleeding often respond well
nodes.body: Factor replacement PLUS antifibrinolytic therapy [2][10] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 15–25 units/kg (target 30–50%) • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 30–50 units/kg (target 30–50%) Antifibrinolytics (particularly useful for oral bleeding — high fibrinolytic activity): • Aminocaproic Acid 50–60 mg/kg PO/IV q6h (max 5 g/dose) × 5–7 days • OR Tranexamic Acid 10–15 mg/kg PO/IV q8–12h [2] ⚠️ Che
nodes.recommendation: Factor replacement to 30–50% plus antifibrinolytics. Aminocaproic acid or TXA for 5–7 days.

nodes.title: GI Hemorrhage Management
nodes.summary: GI hemorrhage: factor to 80-100% + standard GI bleed workup — endoscopy after factor replacement
nodes.body: Target factor level: 80–100% × 1–6 days, then 50% × 7–14 days [2] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 40–50 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 80–100 units/kg Management: • Gastroenterology consultation to identify source • Type and crossmatch, CBC • Standard GI hemorrhage resuscitation • May represent comorbid GI disease Admit for factor level monitoring and GI workup. [2]
nodes.recommendation: Factor to 80–100%. GI consult for source identification. Admit for monitoring.

nodes.title: Hematuria Management
nodes.summary: Hematuria: factor to 50%, IV fluids, avoid TXA (risk of ureteral clot obstruction)
nodes.body: Target factor level: 50% × 3–5 days [2] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 25 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 50 units/kg Key management: • Vigorous hydration at 1.5× maintenance × 48 hours [2] • Urology consultation ⚠️ Antifibrinolytics (aminocaproic acid, TXA) are CONTRAINDICATED — can precipitate thrombi within the kidneys. [2]
nodes.recommendation: Factor to 50%. Vigorous hydration 1.5× maintenance. Antifibrinolytics CONTRAINDICATED. Urology consult.

nodes.title: Major Trauma — Inhibitor Status?
nodes.summary: Trauma: FIRST determine inhibitor status — changes treatment completely
nodes.body: ⚠️ LIFE-THREATENING BLEED — ACT NOW FIRST: Does this patient have INHIBITORS? How to identify inhibitor patients: 1. ASK the patient/family: "Do you have inhibitors?" "Has factor replacement worked before?" 2. Check medications: On emicizumab (Hemlibra), FEIBA, or NovoSeven at home? → INHIBITORS 3. Check for ID card/treatment letter — most patients carry these 4. If unknown and crashing: Treat AS

nodes.title: Major Trauma — Standard Factor Replacement
nodes.summary: Trauma in hemophilia: factor to 100% immediately — standard trauma workup, activate MTP if needed
nodes.body: Target factor level: 100% — ADMINISTER IMMEDIATELY [2] Factor dosing: • Hemophilia A: Factor VIII 50 units/kg • Hemophilia B: Factor IX 100 units/kg Key principles: • Do NOT delay factor for imaging [2] • Standard trauma resuscitation takes precedence • Any hemophilia patient with peritoneal signs → suspect bleeding regardless of trauma history [2] • Type and crossmatch, CBC, coagulation studies P
nodes.recommendation: Factor to 100% STAT. Do not delay for imaging. Standard trauma resuscitation. Admit.

nodes.title: Major Trauma + Inhibitors — Bypassing Agents
nodes.summary: Trauma + inhibitors: rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg q2-3h PREFERRED — FEIBA max 200 U/kg/day, avoid with emicizumab
nodes.body: ⚠️ FACTOR WILL NOT WORK — USE BYPASSING AGENTS [9][10] PREFERRED: rFVIIa (NovoSeven) — especially if on emicizumab • rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg IV q2-3h × 3 doses minimum • OR single high dose: 270 mcg/kg (subsequent doses q6h+) • No maximum daily dose • Safe with emicizumab [11] ALTERNATIVE: FEIBA • FEIBA 100 units/kg IV (life-threatening dose) • Repeat q8-12h as needed • ⚠️ MAX 200 units/kg/day (thromboti
nodes.recommendation: rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg q2-3h PREFERRED. FEIBA 100 U/kg alternative (max 200 U/kg/day). Avoid FEIBA if on emicizumab.

nodes.title: Factor Replacement Dosing Principles
nodes.summary: Factor VIII: dose = weight × desired rise × 0.5. Factor IX: weight × desired rise × 1.0
nodes.body: Factor Products Reference Two types of factor concentrates: [10] 1. Recombinant (manufactured in cell culture) — preferred 2. Plasma-derived (pooled human donor plasma) — acceptable alternative Both are highly effective: ≥90% hemostasis rate after 1–2 doses for typical bleeds. [10] Dosing formulas: • Factor VIII: 1 unit/kg → raises plasma level by 2% (0.02 IU/mL) • Factor IX: 1 unit/kg → raises pl

nodes.title: Factor Type
nodes.summary: Determine factor type: VIII (hemophilia A, 80%) vs IX (hemophilia B, 20%) — different dosing
nodes.body: Which hemophilia type?

nodes.title: Factor VIII Dosing
nodes.summary: Factor VIII: 1 IU/kg raises level ~2%. Half-life 8-12h. Dose = weight × target rise × 0.5
nodes.body: Formula: Dose (units) = (Target% − Baseline%) ÷ 2 × Weight (kg) 1 unit/kg raises factor VIII by ~2% [2] Examples at 70 kg (assuming baseline 0%): • Target 50% → 1,750 units • Target 80% → 2,800 units • Target 100% → 3,500 units Half-life: 8–12 hours — redose q8–12h for sustained coverage [2] Products: Factor VIII • Recombinant: Advate, Kogenate, Xyntha, Eloctate (extended half-life), Jivi, Adynova

nodes.title: Factor IX Dosing
nodes.summary: Factor IX: 1 IU/kg raises level ~1%. Half-life 18-24h. Dose = weight × target rise × 1.0
nodes.body: Formula: Dose (units) = (Target% − Baseline%) × Weight (kg) 1 unit/kg raises factor IX by ~1% [2] Examples at 70 kg (assuming baseline 0%): • Target 50% → 3,500 units • Target 80% → 5,600 units • Target 100% → 7,000 units Half-life: 18–24 hours — redose q18–24h [2] Products: Factor IX • Recombinant: BeneFIX, Alprolix (extended half-life), Rixubis, Rebinyn, Idelvion • Plasma-derived: AlphaNine SD,

nodes.title: Product Switching & Resource-Limited Settings
nodes.summary: Use recombinant products when available — plasma-derived as alternative, cryoprecipitate for FVIII only
nodes.body: Product switching: No clear evidence that switching factor brands increases inhibitor risk. In emergencies where the patient's specific brand is unavailable, use an alternative brand. Prefer recombinant over plasma-derived when switching. [10] Resource-limited settings (no factor concentrate available): [10] • Hemophilia A: Cryoprecipitate — 1 bag per 6 kg body weight (max 10 bags). Contains high

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Special populations: inhibitors, mild hemophilia A (DDAVP option), neonates, vWD
nodes.body: Select the applicable special consideration: Inhibitor Management Guide

nodes.title: Inhibitor Titer Assessment
nodes.summary: Poor response to factor replacement? Check for inhibitor antibody — changes management completely
nodes.body: Inhibitors are antibodies against infused factor that neutralize its activity. [10] • Low titer (<5 BU/mL): Can sometimes be overcome with higher-dose factor • High titer (≥5 BU/mL): Factor replacement is ineffective — requires bypassing agents Inhibitor titers are not useful acutely (results not available in ED). If suspected, check post-infusion factor levels at 30–60 min — little increase sugge

nodes.title: Low-Titer Inhibitor Management
nodes.summary: Low-titer inhibitor (<5 BU): can use high-dose factor to overwhelm antibody — monitor response
nodes.body: Patients with low-titer, low-responding inhibitors (<5 BU/mL) can still be treated with factor concentrates at higher doses. [10] Loading dose formula to neutralize inhibitor: [10] [Body weight (kg) × 80 × (1 − hematocrit) × antibody titer (BU/mL)] + additional 50 units/kg above the calculated loading dose Then: Check post-infusion factor level at 30–60 minutes to confirm adequate response. If fac
nodes.recommendation: Higher-dose factor with loading dose to neutralize inhibitor. Check post-infusion levels. Hematology consult.

nodes.title: High-Titer Inhibitor — Bypassing Agents
nodes.summary: High-titer inhibitor (≥5 BU): bypassing agents required — FEIBA 50-100 U/kg or rFVIIa 90 mcg/kg
nodes.body: Factor replacement will NOT work. Use a bypassing agent: [9][10] Option 1: FEIBA • Joint bleeds: 50–75 units/kg • Life-threatening bleeds: 100 units/kg • Repeat q12h as needed • ⚠️ Do NOT exceed 200 units/kg/day (thrombotic risk) [10] Option 2: Recombinant Factor VIIa (NovoSeven) • Standard: 90 mcg/kg q2–3h × 3 doses • OR single high dose: 270 mcg/kg • If 270 mcg/kg used, subsequent doses separate
nodes.recommendation: FEIBA or rFVIIa. Equally efficacious. Do not exceed FEIBA 200 u/kg/day. Hematology consult mandatory.

nodes.title: Mild Hemophilia A — Desmopressin Option
nodes.summary: DDAVP for mild hemophilia A: releases stored FVIII — test dose response. No effect in hemophilia B
nodes.body: For patients with mild hemophilia A (factor VIII 5–40%), Desmopressin (DDAVP) can be used in lieu of factor concentrate. [10] Dosing: • IV: 0.3 mcg/kg (dilute in 50 mL NS, infuse over 20–30 min) • Intranasal: 150 mcg (<50 kg) or 300 mcg (≥50 kg) • Use the HIGH-CONCENTRATION nasal spray (150 mcg/spray — NOT the lower dose used for enuresis) [10] Raises factor VIII 2- to 6-fold from baseline — gener
nodes.recommendation: DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV or intranasal. Requires prior documented response. Max 2–3 doses. Not for hemophilia B.

nodes.title: Neonatal Hemophilia
nodes.summary: Neonatal hemophilia: ICH from delivery, circumcision bleeding — factor replacement same principles
nodes.body: 30% of hemophilia is caused by de novo mutations — no family history. [10] Key considerations: • Maintain high index of suspicion for ICH in neonates with unusual intracranial hemorrhage • Consider screening imaging (ultrasound or CT) for all newborns with family history of hemophilia + instrument-assisted delivery [10] • Average age of diagnosis for severe hemophilia A: 1.2 years [10] • Average a
nodes.recommendation: High suspicion in neonates with unusual bleeding. 30% have no family history. Screen with CBC, PT/PTT, factor levels.

nodes.title: Von Willebrand Disease Overview
nodes.summary: Von Willebrand disease: most common inherited bleeding disorder — autosomal dominant, types 1-3
nodes.body: vWF Dosing Reference Most common inherited bleeding disorder — prevalence up to 1%, but only ~10% are symptomatic. [3] vWF functions: [10] 1. Platelet adhesion to injured vessel wall (GPIb/IX binding) 2. Platelet aggregation (GPIIb/IIIa interaction) 3. Stabilizes factor VIII in circulation (prevents degradation by protein C) Types: • Type 1 (80%) — quantitative deficiency, vWF:Ag <30–40% • Type 2A

nodes.title: vWD Bleeding Severity
nodes.summary: Classify vWD bleed severity: minor (mucosal) vs major (surgical, ICH) — guides treatment intensity
nodes.body: What is the bleeding severity?

nodes.title: Minor Bleed — DDAVP Responsiveness
nodes.summary: Minor vWD bleed: determine if DDAVP-responsive (Type 1 usually yes, Type 2B/3 contraindicated)
nodes.body: Does this patient have a documented prior response to desmopressin? [3] A desmopressin challenge test must have been performed previously showing adequate vWF rise. ⚠️ Do NOT rely on desmopressin without prior documented response. [4]

nodes.title: vWD Minor Bleed — Desmopressin
nodes.summary: DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV/SQ for vWD Type 1 minor bleeds — releases stored vWF and FVIII
nodes.body: Desmopressin (DDAVP): [4] • IV: 0.3 mcg/kg (dilute in 50 mL NS, infuse over 20–30 min) • Intranasal: one 150-mcg spray (<50 kg) or two 150-mcg sprays = 300 mcg (≥50 kg) • Use HIGH-CONCENTRATION spray (Stimate® 150 mcg/spray — NOT the lower dose for enuresis) [4] Precautions: • Restrict fluid intake to maintenance × 24 hours • If giving IV fluids → use normal saline only • Maximum 2–3 doses (tachyp
nodes.recommendation: DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV or 150/300 mcg intranasal. Max 2–3 doses. Restrict fluids. Contraindicated in Type 2B.

nodes.title: vWD Minor Bleed — vWF Concentrate
nodes.summary: vWF concentrate (Humate-P) for DDAVP-unresponsive minor bleeds — dose 40-60 IU/kg
nodes.body: vWF/FVIII Concentrate (Humate-P): [3][4] • Loading dose: 30–60 RCo units/kg • Maintenance: 20–40 RCo units/kg q12–48h • Maintain vWF:RCo and factor VIII >50 IU/dL × 3–5 days [3] Monitor daily trough vWF:RCo and factor VIII levels. Watch for excessive factor VIII accumulation over multiple days of treatment — can increase thrombotic risk. [4]
nodes.recommendation: vWF concentrate 30–60 RCo U/kg loading, then 20–40 U/kg maintenance. Maintain levels >50 IU/dL × 3–5 days.

nodes.title: vWD Major Bleed — vWF Concentrate
nodes.summary: Major vWD bleed: vWF concentrate 60-80 IU/kg, maintain through levels >50% for 7-14 days
nodes.body: vWF/FVIII Concentrate (Humate-P): [3][4] • Loading dose: 40–60 RCo units/kg • Maintenance: 20–40 RCo units/kg q8–24h • Maintain vWF:RCo and factor VIII >50 IU/dL × at least 7 days [3] Monitor daily trough levels. Avoid excessively high factor VIII levels — can accumulate over time with repeated dosing. [4] Admit for level monitoring and ongoing factor administration.
nodes.recommendation: vWF concentrate 40–60 RCo U/kg loading, then 20–40 U/kg maintenance. Maintain >50 IU/dL × 7+ days. Admit.

nodes.title: vWD Menorrhagia Management
nodes.summary: vWD menorrhagia: TXA + OCP first-line, DDAVP or vWF concentrate for severe cases
nodes.body: First-line: Hormonal contraceptives (oral contraceptive pills) [3] Adjunctive therapies: • Desmopressin (DDAVP) — if documented responder • Aminocaproic Acid 50–60 mg/kg q6h (max 5 g) × 5–7 days • OR Tranexamic Acid 10–15 mg/kg PO q8–12h ⚠️ Check urinalysis before starting antifibrinolytics — contraindicated with hematuria. [3] Menorrhagia definition: Bleeding >7 days OR >80 mL blood loss per cycl
nodes.recommendation: Hormonal contraceptives first-line. Add DDAVP and/or antifibrinolytics as adjuncts. Screen family members.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition based on bleed severity and factor response — discharge minor, admit major
nodes.body: Disposition depends on bleed type and severity. [2]

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge minor bleeds with factor access confirmed, hematology follow-up within 24-48h
nodes.body: Discharge is appropriate for: [2][10] • Hemarthrosis (after factor administration) • Minor mucosal bleeding (controlled) • Hematuria (responding to hydration) Requirements for safe discharge: • Bleeding controlled after factor administration • Reliable family comfortable with monitoring • Home factor infusion capability (if available) • Clear hematologist contact established — critical for safe di
nodes.recommendation: Discharge if bleeding controlled, reliable family, hematologist contact, follow-up in 24–48h.

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.summary: Admit life-threatening bleeds, inhibitor patients, and bleeds requiring serial factor dosing
nodes.body: Admit for: [2][10] • ICH → ICU + neurosurgery consult • Iliopsoas hemorrhage → floor with strict bed rest • GI hemorrhage → floor + GI consult • Major trauma → per trauma team • Muscle bleed with concern for compartment syndrome • Unreliable family or follow-up • New diagnosis requiring further workup • Patients with inhibitors and significant bleeding Hematology consult for ALL admitted patients.
nodes.recommendation: Admit for ICH (ICU), iliopsoas, GI bleed, major trauma, inhibitor patients, or unreliable follow-up. Hematology consult.

nodes.title: Rare Bleeding Disorder
nodes.summary: Rare bleeding disorders (factor XI, XIII, etc.): hematology consult, FFP or specific concentrate
nodes.body: Prolongation of both PT and PTT suggests: [10] • Factor V deficiency • Factor X deficiency • Fibrinogen deficiency • Prothrombin (factor II) deficiency • Combined factor deficiencies These rare bleeding disorders collectively represent only 3% of all inherited bleeding disorders, each occurring with a prevalence of ~1 in 500,000. [10] Management: • Hematology consultation urgently • Specific facto
nodes.recommendation: Rare bleeding disorder — hematology consult. FFP as empiric therapy. Specific factor assays.

nodes.title: Hemoptysis Hub — How Much Blood, How Fast?
nodes.summary: Triage by VOLUME and RATE first. Massive hemoptysis kills by asphyxiation, not blood loss \u2014 airway + isolate bleeding lung. Confirm it is truly pulmonary. Isolate for TB early.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 7 DO NOT MISS: 1. Massive hemoptysis \u2014 patients die of asphyxiation, not exsanguination. Airway + bleeding-lung-down are the priorities. 2. Is it really from the lungs? \u2014 exclude pseudohemoptysis (nasopharyngeal / GI source) before committing. 3. PE with hemoptysis / pulmonary infarction \u2014 pleuritic pain + risk factors. 4. Active TB / cavitary infection \u2014 airborne

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the One That Fits
nodes.summary: Rate first (massive?), then cause. Each branch links to its deep-dive + the next action.
nodes.body: Sort by rate first, then by cause. Each branch routes to a deep-dive and the next action.

nodes.title: Massive Hemoptysis — Asphyxiation Kills First
nodes.body: Open Massive Hemoptysis for the full airway-control, lung-isolation, and IR/bronchoscopy pathway. The core principle: patients drown, they do not exsanguinate. Priorities are (1) protect gas exchange, (2) localize and isolate the bleeding lung, (3) definitive control. [3] Next 5 minutes: - Position bleeding-lung-DOWN (lateral decubitus with the known/suspected bleeding side dependent) to protect t
nodes.recommendation: Bleeding-lung-down (upright if side unknown), secure the airway early with the largest ETT you can safely place, suction hard, reverse coagulopathy, TXA, and call IR (embolization) + bronchoscopy NOW. CTA to localize once stable. Expect a 1

nodes.title: Suspected TB — Isolate Before You Work It Up
nodes.body: Open Tuberculosis for the diagnostic + treatment + public-health pathway. Hemoptysis with fever, weight loss, night sweats, chronic cough, or TB risk factors (endemic-region origin, HIV/immunocompromise, incarceration, homelessness, known exposure) = active pulmonary TB until excluded. [4] Next 5 minutes: - Airborne isolation immediately \u2014 negative-pressure room, N95 for all staff, mask the p
nodes.recommendation: Airborne isolate NOW (N95, negative pressure, mask patient). CXR/CT, sputum AFB smear \u00d73 \u22658 h apart + NAAT + culture, HIV test (urine LAM if CD4 <200), notify public health. Do not de-isolate on a single negative test. Treat brisk

nodes.title: PE with Pulmonary Infarction
nodes.body: Open Pulmonary Embolism Treatment for risk stratification, anticoagulation, and thrombolysis pathway. Hemoptysis + pleuritic chest pain + VTE risk factors suggests pulmonary embolism with infarction. Hemoptysis is a recognized (if less common) PE presentation and creates a management tension: PE needs anticoagulation, but the patient is bleeding. [5] Next 5 minutes: - Risk-stratify (Wells / PERC a
nodes.recommendation: CTPA to confirm. Minor hemoptysis + confirmed PE \u2192 anticoagulate. Massive hemoptysis \u2192 anticoagulation relatively contraindicated; treat bleeding first, consider IVC filter, involve pulm/heme.

nodes.title: Coagulopathy / Anticoagulant Amplifier
nodes.body: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets, and coagulopathy do not usually CAUSE hemoptysis alone \u2014 but they turn a small lesion into a dangerous bleed. Find the underlying source AND correct the coagulopathy if bleeding is significant. [1] Next 5 minutes: - Send CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, type and screen; renal/hepatic function. - If bleeding is life-threatening, reverse: open Anticoagulation Revers
nodes.recommendation: Send coags + type/screen. Reverse (PCC/vitamin K, andexanet/idarucizumab, protamine, platelets) ONLY for life-threatening bleeding; TXA adjunct (neb 500-1000 mg q8h or IV 1 g). Weigh thrombotic risk \u2014 andexanet roughly doubles thrombot

nodes.title: Infectious Cause — Pneumonia / Bronchitis / Abscess
nodes.body: Acute bronchitis is the single most common cause of mild hemoptysis; pneumonia, lung abscess, and necrotizing infection cause larger volumes. [1,2] Open Pneumonia for the CURB-65/severity, antibiotic, and disposition pathway when consolidation is present. Recognize: - Acute bronchitis \u2014 blood-streaked sputum with a viral/post-viral cough, no consolidation, otherwise well. Usually self-limited
nodes.recommendation: Match to the syndrome: bronchitis (supportive), pneumonia (antibiotics per severity), abscess/cavity (CT + prolonged abx \u00b1 drainage). Screen TB. Image + follow up if smoker/weight loss/recurrent.

nodes.title: Cardiac Cause — Pulmonary Edema / Mitral Disease
nodes.body: Pink, frothy sputum with orthopnea, PND, and edema is usually cardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than true bronchial-artery hemoptysis; mitral stenosis and severe heart failure can cause frank hemoptysis from pulmonary venous hypertension. [1] Open CHF Exacerbation for the diuresis / afterload-reduction / disposition pathway when heart failure is the driver. Recognize: - Acute pulmonary edema \u20
nodes.recommendation: Treat the cardiac cause (CHF consult: oxygen/NIV, nitrates, diuresis). Get ECG, CXR, BNP, echo. Consider mitral stenosis with AF + diastolic murmur. Keep true hemoptysis on the differential if frank/recurrent.

nodes.title: Diffuse Alveolar Hemorrhage — The Bleed You Cannot See
nodes.body: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) is the hemoptysis diagnosis that hides. Bleeding is into the alveoli, not the airways, so up to one-third of patients have NO hemoptysis at all \u2014 the tell is hypoxemia + new bilateral infiltrates + an otherwise unexplained hemoglobin drop. Reported mortality is 20-50%, and it is driven by how fast immunosuppression starts. [13] The triad to pattern-match: 1.
nodes.recommendation: Hypoxemia + bilateral infiltrates + falling Hgb = DAH until proven otherwise, with or without hemoptysis. Send UA with micro, ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, complements now; CT chest; call pulm/neph/rheum. Sequential BAL confirms. Pulse steroids \u00

nodes.title: Pseudohemoptysis — Source Is Not the Lower Airway
nodes.body: Before committing to a pulmonary workup, confirm the blood actually comes from the lungs. Misattributed nasopharyngeal or gastrointestinal bleeding (pseudohemoptysis) sends patients down the wrong pathway. [1] Distinguish the source: - Pulmonary (true hemoptysis) \u2014 bright red, frothy, mixed with sputum, alkaline pH, preceded by coughing/gurgling, often a history of lung disease. - Upper airwa
nodes.recommendation: Confirm the blood is pulmonary (bright, frothy, alkaline, coughed) before working it up as hemoptysis. Examine nose/mouth for an ENT source; redirect to the GI-bleed pathway if hematemesis. Bleeding around a tracheostomy = tracheo-innominat

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Non-Massive Hemoptysis
nodes.summary: IV + O2 + quantify bleeding + CBC/coags/type-screen + CXR (CT chest if beyond bronchitis) + ECG. Isolate for TB on any risk. Escalate instantly if bleeding turns massive.
nodes.body: No life-threat hit, bleeding is small-volume and stable. Standard ED bundle while you work up the cause: [1,2] THE BUNDLE: - IV access, monitor, continuous SpO2, supplemental O2 to keep saturations up. - Quantify and track the volume/rate of bleeding \u2014 escalate immediately if it becomes massive (position bleeding-side-down, secure airway). - Focused labs: CBC (anemia, platelets), CMP, PT/INR

nodes.title: Reassess — Rate and Workup
nodes.summary: Stopped + benign + low-risk \u2192 discharge. Recurrent/abnormal \u2192 CT + admit/observe. Escalating \u2192 STOP, return to exclusions (airway + IR).
nodes.body: Re-examine: is the bleeding continuing, what does the imaging show, is a source identified?

nodes.title: Imaging & Workup Decision
nodes.summary: CXR for all; CT chest/CTA for anything beyond bronchitis, recurrent bleeding, smokers \u226540, or planned embolization. CTPA if PE. Bronchoscopy localizes/treats. Send ANCA/anti-GBM if pulmonary-renal picture.
nodes.body: The goal is to (1) localize the bleeding, (2) find the cause, (3) risk-stratify for recurrence. [1,2,6] Chest X-ray (everyone): cheap, fast; identifies mass, consolidation, cavity, edema. A normal CXR does NOT exclude a serious cause. Put a number on that: among patients with hemoptysis and a normal or non-localizing chest radiograph, roughly 9.6-10% still turn out to have a malignancy, and in tha

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge trivial/benign/low-risk; observe or admit moderate/recurrent; ICU for massive/ongoing bleeding or airway risk.
nodes.body: Disposition is driven by bleeding volume/rate, the cause, and recurrence risk. Defer to the deep-dive consult once a diagnosis is committed.

nodes.title: Discharge — Trivial Self-Limited Hemoptysis
nodes.body: Safe discharge criteria: [1,2] 1. Small volume, now stopped (blood-streaked sputum, not frank blood; no ongoing bleeding). 2. Benign, explained cause \u2014 e.g., acute bronchitis or an upper-airway source that has been controlled. 3. Normal or reassuring CXR, normal vitals, no hypoxia, no anemia on CBC. 4. Low malignancy/TB risk \u2014 non-smoker or smoker <40 without weight loss, no TB risk, no
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if bleeding trivial and stopped, cause benign and explained, CXR/CBC reassuring, low TB/cancer risk, follow-up arranged. Strong return precautions; complete outpatient CT if any risk feature. Cryptogenic hemoptysis needs ~3 y

nodes.title: Observe / Admit Ward — Moderate or Recurrent
nodes.body: Monitored inpatient bed appropriate when: [1,6] - Moderate-volume or recurrent hemoptysis that has settled but could recur - Abnormal imaging requiring CT chest and/or bronchoscopy - Pneumonia/abscess needing IV antibiotics - Anticoagulated patient with ongoing minor bleeding needing observation and possible reversal decisions - PE confirmed with hemoptysis requiring careful anticoagulation monito
nodes.recommendation: Monitored ward bed with suction/typed blood, serial hemoglobin, CT \u00b1 bronchoscopy, pulmonary consult, and cause-directed treatment. Escalate to ICU if bleeding turns massive.

nodes.title: Admit ICU — Massive or Ongoing Bleeding
nodes.body: ICU admission for: [3,6] - Massive / life-threatening hemoptysis (per Massive Hemoptysis) \u2014 actual or impending airway compromise, large volume, or hemodynamic instability - Ongoing active bleeding requiring airway protection, transfusion, or urgent IR embolization / bronchoscopy - Post-embolization or post-bronchoscopy monitoring after intervention - Respiratory failure from blood soiling th
nodes.recommendation: ICU with pulmonary + IR + thoracic surgery. Secure airway, isolate the bleeding lung, embolize (IR), correct coagulopathy, transfuse. Expect a 10-58% rebleed rate after BAE and document a post-procedure lower-extremity neuro exam (spinal co

nodes.title: Unfractionated Heparin Infusion Protocol
nodes.summary: UFH is preferred when titratability, reversibility, or renal/procedural flexibility matters.
nodes.body: Heparin Infusion Steps Use unfractionated heparin when rapid titration, short half-life, procedural flexibility, renal failure, or planned thrombolysis/procedure makes it preferable to LMWH or DOAC therapy. Before starting: confirm indication, bleeding risk, platelet count, baseline aPTT/anti-Xa availability, recent anticoagulants, and whether a bolus is appropriate.

nodes.title: Indication / Pathway
nodes.summary: Heparin dosing depends on indication and bolus safety.
nodes.body: Which heparin pathway is needed?

nodes.title: Contraindications / Stop
nodes.summary: Active bleeding or HIT concern should stop routine UFH infusion.
nodes.body: Do not start routine UFH infusion when any are present: - Active major bleeding - Suspected/confirmed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) - Severe uncontrolled hypertension with bleeding risk - Recent high-risk surgery/procedure where anticoagulation is not cleared - Intracranial hemorrhage or unsecured high-risk lesion unless specialist-directed - Platelets critically low or rapidly falling wi
nodes.recommendation: Hold UFH and escalate when bleeding, HIT, or high-risk contraindication is present.

nodes.title: VTE / PE Standard Dosing
nodes.summary: Standard VTE UFH is 80 U/kg bolus then 18 U/kg/hr, adjusted by protocol.
nodes.body: Common therapeutic VTE regimen: - Unfractionated heparin 80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/hr infusion - Use actual body weight unless local protocol specifies adjusted weight - Obtain baseline CBC, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, creatinine, and anti-Xa/aPTT monitoring plan - First anti-Xa/aPTT commonly 6 hr after start or dose change Massive PE with thrombolysis planned: coordinate timing with the

nodes.title: ACS / STEMI Adjunct
nodes.summary: ACS UFH uses lower bolus/infusion caps than VTE protocols.
nodes.body: ACS regimen depends on STEMI-with-fibrinolytic vs NSTEMI/UA: - STEMI + fibrinolytic: Unfractionated heparin 60 units/kg IV bolus, max 4,000 units; infusion 12 units/kg/hr, initial max 1,000 units/hr (per ACC/AHA STEMI guideline) - NSTEMI / unstable angina: 60-70 units/kg IV bolus, max 5,000 units; infusion 12-15 units/kg/hr; aPTT goal 50-70 sec (per AHA/ACC NSTE-ACS guideline) - Titrate by institu

nodes.title: No-Bolus / Modified Start
nodes.summary: No-bolus UFH is appropriate when therapeutic anticoagulation is needed but bolus risk is too high.
nodes.body: Use a no-bolus or reduced-intensity UFH start when full bolus bleeding risk is unacceptable but anticoagulation is still indicated. Examples: - Post-thrombolysis restart - Recent procedure/surgery after specialist clearance - Intracranial or spinal pathology after specialist clearance - Very high bleeding risk or frailty - Transition from another anticoagulant with residual effect Document the rea

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.summary: Use a protocolized anti-Xa or aPTT nomogram and monitor platelets/bleeding.
nodes.body: Monitoring essentials: - Baseline CBC/platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, creatinine, pregnancy status when relevant - Anti-Xa or aPTT per institutional nomogram - First level commonly 6 hr after start and 6 hr after dose changes - Platelets daily or per protocol to screen for HIT - Assess for bleeding every handoff Anti-Xa is often preferred when aPTT is unreliable: lupus anticoagulant, high factor VIII, li

nodes.title: Adjustment / Handoff
nodes.summary: Heparin changes should follow local nomogram and clear handoff.
nodes.body: Dose adjustment should follow the local nomogram, not ad hoc bedside changes. Handoff must include: - Indication and target range - Actual weight used for dosing - Bolus given or intentionally omitted - Current infusion rate in units/hr and units/kg/hr - Last level, next level due, and trend - Bleeding checks and platelet trend - Planned procedure, thrombolytic timing, or transition plan

nodes.title: Bleeding / Over-Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Major bleeding requires stopping UFH and considering protamine.
nodes.body: Is there major bleeding or urgent reversal need?

nodes.title: Protamine Reversal
nodes.summary: Protamine reverses recent UFH exposure; dose by recent heparin amount.
nodes.body: For major bleeding or urgent procedure: - Stop UFH - Use Protamine Calculator - Typical dose: 1 mg protamine per 100 units UFH received in the prior 2-3 hr, max 50 mg - Give slow IV over 10 min to reduce hypotension/anaphylactoid reaction risk - Recheck coagulation and clinical hemostasis after reversal Do not give excess protamine; it can worsen anticoagulation/bleeding.

nodes.title: High Level Without Bleeding
nodes.summary: Supratherapeutic UFH without bleeding is usually managed by holding/reducing per nomogram.
nodes.body: If aPTT/anti-Xa is supratherapeutic without bleeding: - Hold or reduce UFH per institutional nomogram - Recheck level at the protocol interval - Reassess renal/liver disease, lab interference, line draw contamination, and duplicate anticoagulants - Document bleeding exam and next level due Do not reverse with protamine solely for a high lab value without bleeding unless urgent procedure or local p

nodes.title: Disposition / Transition
nodes.summary: UFH requires a clear transition and monitoring plan.
nodes.body: Admit/ICU based on indication and instability. Transition planning: - VTE: transition to DOAC, LMWH, warfarin bridge, or procedural plan when safe - ACS/STEMI: coordinate with cardiology/cath lab and antiplatelets - PE thrombolysis: restart anticoagulation per protocol once safe - HIT concern: stop all heparin products and use non-heparin anticoagulant strategy Every handoff should state the targe
nodes.recommendation: Continue UFH only with clear indication, target range, monitoring, and transition plan.

nodes.title: Elevated Liver Enzymes — Start
nodes.summary: R-factor classifies pattern: >5 hepatocellular, 2–5 mixed, <2 cholestatic. Screen ALF up front.
nodes.body: Hepatitis Workup Summary Classify the injury pattern first, then chase the differential. Compute the R-factor = (ALT ÷ ALT-ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ALP-ULN): >5 hepatocellular · 2–5 mixed · <2 cholestatic. Before any leisurely workup, screen for acute liver failure — coagulopathy + encephalopathy in a patient without known cirrhosis is time-critical. *Basis: R-factor pattern classification per the ACG guidel

nodes.title: Acute Liver Failure Screen
nodes.summary: ALF = INR ≥1.5 + encephalopathy + <26 wks without cirrhosis → Module 7.
nodes.body: ALF = INR ≥1.5 + hepatic encephalopathy + illness <26 weeks, no prior cirrhosis. Check mental status, INR/coags, ammonia, glucose, lactate, and trend bilirubin. Any encephalopathy with coagulopathy = treat as ALF until proven otherwise. *Basis: ALF case definition per the AASLD position paper on acute liver failure [4] and the current ACG Acute Liver Failure Guidelines [9].*

nodes.title: Hepatocellular Injury (R >5)
nodes.summary: AST:ALT >2:1 → alcohol; ALT >1000 + shock → ischemic; consider viral, DILI, metabolic, inherited.
nodes.body: Use the AST:ALT ratio and the magnitude of transaminitis to narrow the cause. Massive transaminitis (ALT >1000) differential

nodes.title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Injury
nodes.summary: Alcohol: AST:ALT >2:1, transaminases usually <300, GGT high. Severity-stratify before steroids.
nodes.body: AST:ALT >2:1, both usually <300–400 IU/L (rarely >500). GGT elevated. History of heavy use. If jaundiced/sick, assess severity (Maddrey discriminant function ≥32 or MELD) before considering corticosteroids — see Management threads. *Basis: ACG Clinical Guideline on Alcoholic Liver Disease [5] and AASLD practice guidance on alcohol-associated liver diseases [16].*

nodes.title: Suspect Viral Hepatitis
nodes.summary: Send HAV IgM, HBsAg/anti-HBc/anti-HBs, HCV Ab+RNA, HEV IgM; HDV only with HBV.
nodes.body: Order the serologies, then interpret with the Viral Serology Interpreter. • Hep A — anti-HAV IgM (acute; fecal-oral, travel/outbreak) • Hep B — HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM vs total, anti-HBs • Hep C — HCV Ab + HCV RNA (confirms active) • Hep D — only co/super-infects with B • Hep E — anti-HEV IgM (travel, pork; severe in pregnancy) *Basis: hepatitis A testing per CDC/ACIP recommendations [13]; hepatitis B

nodes.title: Ischemic (Shock) Liver
nodes.summary: Shock liver: transaminases in thousands, rapid rise/fall after hypoperfusion. Fix the cause.
nodes.body: ALT/AST in the thousands, peaking fast and falling fast (~50%/day) after a hemodynamic insult (shock, arrest, severe hypoxia, RV failure). LDH high, early INR rise. Treatment is of the cause — restore perfusion/oxygenation. Liver typically recovers if the insult is corrected. *Basis: enzyme kinetics and clinical course of hypoxic (ischemic) hepatitis [20]; general evaluation framework [2].*
nodes.recommendation: Treat the hemodynamic cause; transaminases normalize as perfusion is restored.

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI)
nodes.summary: DILI: review meds/OTC/herbals/APAP. Hy's law flags high-risk. Stop agent; NAC for APAP.
nodes.body: Review all meds, OTCs, herbals/supplements, and acetaminophen dose/timeline. Apply Hy's law (hepatocellular DILI + bilirubin >2× ULN + no other cause → ~10% mortality risk). Stop the offending agent. For APAP toxicity, give N-acetylcysteine and use the dedicated APAP pathway. *Basis: Hy's law, causality assessment and withdrawal of the implicated agent per the ACG guideline on idiosyncratic drug-i

nodes.title: Metabolic / Autoimmune / Inherited
nodes.summary: MASLD (exclusion), AIH (↑IgG/ANA/ASMA), Wilson (<40, low ceruloplasmin), hemochromatosis (↑Fe sat).
nodes.body: • MASLD/MASH (formerly NAFLD) — most common chronic cause; mild ALT↑, metabolic syndrome; diagnosis of exclusion + imaging. • Autoimmune hepatitis — young/middle-aged, ↑IgG, ANA/ASMA positive; can flare to ALF → see Management. • Wilson disease — age <40, low ceruloplasmin, Coombs-negative hemolysis, low ALP-to-bilirubin ratio. • Hemochromatosis — high ferritin + transferrin saturation >45%. *Basi

nodes.title: Interpreting Viral Serology
nodes.summary: HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM = acute B; anti-HBs only = vaccinated; HCV Ab+/RNA+ = active C.
nodes.body: Feed the panel into the Viral Serology Interpreter to resolve acute vs chronic vs immune (vaccinated) vs resolved vs window period. Hep B quick map: • HBsAg+ / anti-HBc IgM+ → acute • HBsAg+ / anti-HBc IgG+ (>6 mo) → chronic • anti-HBs+ only → vaccinated/immune • anti-HBs+ and anti-HBc+ → resolved infection • anti-HBc+ alone → window period or occult Hep C: HCV Ab+ with HCV RNA+ = active; Ab+ / RN

nodes.title: Cholestatic Injury (R <2)
nodes.summary: Confirm hepatic ALP with GGT first. Then split extrahepatic (obstruction) vs intrahepatic.
nodes.body: First confirm the ALP is hepatobiliary, not bone/placental: check GGT (or ALP isoenzymes). GGT elevated → hepatobiliary; GGT normal → extrahepatic ALP source (bone, growth, pregnancy) — not liver disease.

nodes.title: Isolated ALP, Normal GGT
nodes.summary: High ALP + normal GGT = non-hepatic (bone, growth, placenta). No liver workup needed.
nodes.body: A high ALP with a normal GGT points away from the liver: bone (Paget, fracture, mets, vitamin D deficiency), growth in children/adolescents, or placenta in pregnancy. *Basis: use of GGT to confirm a hepatobiliary source for a raised ALP per ACG [1] and BSG [2].*
nodes.recommendation: Pursue non-hepatic ALP source (bone/placenta/growth); liver workup not indicated.

nodes.title: Extrahepatic / Obstructive Cholestasis
nodes.summary: RUQ US first → MRCP/ERCP if dilated. Stones/stricture/malignancy. Cholangitis = emergency.
nodes.body: Image the ducts: RUQ ultrasound first. If dilated ducts or stones, escalate to MRCP/ERCP. Causes: choledocholithiasis, benign/malignant stricture, pancreatic/cholangiocarcinoma. If ascending cholangitis (fever + jaundice + RUQ pain ± shock/AMS), this is an emergency — see the Gallbladder consult for biliary emergencies. *Basis: ultrasound-first imaging of a cholestatic pattern with escalation to M

nodes.title: Intrahepatic Cholestasis
nodes.summary: PBC (AMA), PSC (IBD, MRCP beading), drug cholestasis, infiltrative (sarcoid/lymphoma/amyloid).
nodes.body: • PBC — middle-aged women, anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA), pruritus. • PSC — associated with IBD; MRCP shows beading; ↑cholangiocarcinoma risk. • Drug-induced cholestasis — amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids, etc. → DILI. • Infiltrative — sarcoidosis, lymphoma, amyloid, granulomatous disease. *Basis: PBC diagnosis and AMA testing per AASLD practice guidance [17]; drug-induced cholestasi

nodes.title: Mixed Pattern (R 2–5)
nodes.summary: Mixed (R 2–5): usually DILI or evolving viral. Trend the labs; manage by dominant feature.
nodes.body: Both transaminases and ALP elevated. Most often DILI or an evolving/resolving viral hepatitis. Manage by the dominant clinical features and recheck the trend — the pattern often declares itself over time. *Basis: R-value definition of a mixed pattern per ACG [1]; mixed-pattern DILI per the ACG idiosyncratic DILI guideline [8].*
nodes.recommendation: Work up by dominant features (most often DILI or evolving viral); recheck LFT trend.

nodes.title: Targeted Management
nodes.summary: Cause-specific: NAC (APAP), steroids (AIH/severe alcohol), stop drug (DILI), ERCP (obstruction).
nodes.body: Match therapy to the cause: • Acetaminophen toxicity → N-acetylcysteine. • Autoimmune hepatitis → corticosteroids; GI/hepatology. • Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (Maddrey ≥32) → consider corticosteroids after sepsis/GI-bleed excluded. • DILI → stop the offending agent; supportive care. • Obstruction → biliary decompression (ERCP). If encephalopathy develops, treat with lactulose (titrate to

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit ALF/severe/obstruction; discharge mild stable cases with arranged recheck.
nodes.body: Admit: ALF features, severe symptomatic hepatitis, intractable vomiting/dehydration, cholangitis/obstruction needing intervention, or uncertain rapidly rising LFTs. Discharge with follow-up: mild stable transaminitis, reliable patient, clear outpatient plan and repeat labs arranged. *Basis: admission of patients meeting acute liver failure criteria per the ACG Acute Liver Failure Guidelines [9]; o
nodes.recommendation: Admit ALF/severe/obstructive cases; discharge mild stable transaminitis with timed recheck.

nodes.title: Acute Liver Failure — Management & Transfer
nodes.summary: ALF: NAC (APAP + early non-APAP), watch cerebral edema, ICU, transfer early to transplant center.
nodes.body: Apply the King's College Criteria to decide transplant-center transfer. Supportive care: • N-acetylcysteine — give for APAP-ALF and reasonable in non-APAP early ALF. • Watch for cerebral edema (grade III/IV HE) — elevate head, treat raised ICP. • Correct coagulopathy only for bleeding/procedures (don't mask the INR trend). • Glucose, electrolytes, renal support; low threshold for ICU. Transfer ear

nodes.title: King's College Criteria
nodes.summary: APAP: pH<7.3 OR (INR>6.5 + Cr>300 + grade III/IV HE). Non-APAP: INR>6.5 OR any 3 minors.
nodes.body: Acetaminophen ALF — list for transplant if arterial pH <7.3 OR all three: INR >6.5 + creatinine >300 µmol/L (>3.4 mg/dL) + grade III/IV encephalopathy. Non-acetaminophen ALF — INR >6.5 (PT >100 s) alone, OR any 3 of: unfavorable etiology (non-A/non-B, drug, halothane), age <10 or >40, jaundice-to-encephalopathy >7 days, INR >3.5 (PT >50 s), bilirubin >300 µmol/L (>17.5 mg/dL). *Basis: King's Colle
nodes.recommendation: Meeting criteria → emergency transplant evaluation. High specificity (~90%), modest sensitivity — transfer early even if not met.

nodes.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: HFNC for hypoxemic respiratory failure, post-extubation, pre-oxygenation — select indication
nodes.body: High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) delivers warmed, humidified gas at flow rates up to 60-70 L/min via nasal prongs. [1][2] Key Physiological Benefits: [1][3] - High FiO2 delivery: Near 100% at max settings (vs NRB ~60-70%) - PEEP effect: 3-5 cm H2O at 50-60 L/min (mouth closed) - Dead space washout: Reduces anatomic dead space, improves CO2 clearance - Reduced work of breathing: Even if SpO2 adequate

nodes.title: HFNC for Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure
nodes.summary: HFNC superior to conventional O2 for hypoxemic respiratory failure — FLORALI trial: reduced intubation
nodes.body: FLORALI Trial Evidence (Frat 2015): [5] - 310 patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 <300) - HFNC vs NIV vs standard O2 - No difference in intubation rate overall - Subgroup PaO2/FiO2 ≤200: HFNC significantly reduced intubation (38% vs 47% vs 50%) - 90-day mortality: HFNC 12% vs standard O2 23% vs NIV 28% Why HFNC > NRB for severe hypoxemia: [1][4] - NRB maxes at 10-15 L/min

nodes.title: HFNC for Post-Extubation Support
nodes.summary: HFNC non-inferior to NIV for post-extubation support in high-risk patients
nodes.body: Evidence for Post-Extubation HFNC: [6][7] Hernandez 2016 (High-Risk Patients): - HFNC vs NIV in high-risk extubation patients - Non-inferior for reintubation at 72h (22.8% vs 19.1%) - Better tolerated, fewer complications Maggiore 2014: - HFNC at 50 L/min vs standard O2 post-extubation - Better oxygenation at all time points - Lower reintubation rate (4% vs 21%) Current Practice: [1][7] - HFNC pre

nodes.title: HFNC for Pre-Oxygenation & Apneic Oxygenation
nodes.summary: HFNC during RSI provides apneic oxygenation — continue during laryngoscopy at 60 L/min
nodes.body: Pre-Oxygenation for RSI: [8][9] - Standard approach: NRB or BVM for 3-5 minutes - HFNC advantage: 60 L/min flow maintains high FiO2, washes out nitrogen - Can continue during laryngoscopy (apneic oxygenation) Apneic Oxygenation: [8] - Leave nasal cannula at 15-60 L/min during intubation attempt - Extends safe apnea time by 2-4 minutes - Particularly valuable in difficult airways Evidence is Mixed:

nodes.title: HFNC in CHF / Pulmonary Edema
nodes.summary: NIV (BiPAP) is first-line for CHF exacerbation — HFNC if NIV intolerance
nodes.body: HFNC vs CPAP/BiPAP in Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema: Key Consideration: CPAP/BiPAP provides higher PEEP (~10-15 cm H2O) vs HFNC (~3-5 cm H2O). For SCAPE (Sympathetic Crashing Acute Pulmonary Edema), BiPAP remains first-line. [10] When to Consider HFNC in CHF: - Mild-moderate pulmonary edema (not SCAPE) - BiPAP intolerance (claustrophobia, facial trauma) - Post-diuresis maintenance - Bridge while set

nodes.title: HFNC in Immunocompromised Patients
nodes.summary: HFNC reduces intubation rate in immunocompromised patients with respiratory failure
nodes.body: Meta-Analysis Evidence (Azoulay 2010, Frat 2015): [5][11] - Immunocompromised patients with ARF have high mortality - Intubation associated with increased mortality risk - Avoiding intubation improves outcomes HFNC Advantages: [11][12] - Reduced intubation rate vs standard O2 and NIV in meta-analyses - Better tolerated for prolonged periods - Allows oral intake and communication - Lower infection

nodes.title: HFNC Device Setup & Initial Settings
nodes.summary: Start flow 30-40 L/min, FiO2 to maintain SpO2 >92%, temp 37°C — titrate up to 60 L/min
nodes.body: Equipment Components: [1][2] - Air/oxygen blender (21-100% FiO2) - Heated humidifier (37C, 100% relative humidity) - Single heated-wire circuit - Large-bore nasal cannula (sized appropriately) Initial Settings: | Parameter | Starting Value | Titration | |-----------|---------------|------------| | Flow Rate | 30-40 L/min | Titrate to WOB (up to 60-70 L/min) | | FiO2 | 50-60% | Titrate to SpO2 92-9

nodes.title: HFNC Titration Strategy
nodes.summary: Titrate flow first for work of breathing, then FiO2 for oxygenation target
nodes.body: Flow Rate Titration: [1][2] Increasing Flow (20 -> 60 L/min): - Primary benefit: Dead space washout, reduced WOB - Secondary benefit: Modest PEEP increase (~1 cm H2O per 10 L/min) - Oxygenation benefit minimal above baseline matching inspiratory demand When to Increase Flow: - RR >25 despite adequate SpO2 - Accessory muscle use - Patient reports dyspnea - Speaking in short sentences FiO2 Titration

nodes.title: HFNC vs NRB vs NIV Comparison
nodes.summary: HFNC vs NIV vs conventional O2: HFNC provides 3-5 cmH2O PEEP at 60 L/min flow
nodes.body: Comparison of Oxygen Delivery Devices: [1][4] | Feature | Standard NC | NRB | HFNC | NIV | |---------|------------|-----|------|-----| | Max Flow | 6 L/min | 15 L/min | 60-70 L/min | N/A | | FiO2 | ~40% | ~60-70% | ~100% | ~100% | | PEEP | None | None | 3-5 cm H2O | 5-15 cm H2O | | Dead Space Washout | No | No | Yes | Variable | | Humidification | No | No | Yes (heated) | Yes | | Tolerability | Go

nodes.title: Monitoring on HFNC & ROX Index
nodes.summary: ROX index = (SpO2/FiO2)/RR — monitor at 2h, 6h, 12h to predict HFNC success vs failure
nodes.body: Continuous Monitoring Parameters: [1][13] - SpO2 (continuous pulse oximetry) - Respiratory rate - Heart rate - Work of breathing (accessory muscle use, nasal flaring) - Mental status - Ability to speak in sentences The ROX Index: [13][14] Developed to predict HFNC failure and need for intubation. Formula: `` ROX = (SpO2/FiO2) / Respiratory Rate `` Example: SpO2 95%, FiO2 60% (0.60), RR 24 - ROX =

nodes.title: ROX Index: Timing & Interpretation
nodes.summary: ROX ≥4.88 at 12h = low intubation risk. ROX <3.85 at any time = high failure risk, escalate
nodes.body: ROX Index Timing: [13][14] | Time Point | Failure Threshold | Success Threshold | |------------|-------------------|-------------------| | 2 hours | <2.85 | ≥4.88 | | 6 hours | <3.47 | ≥4.88 | | 12 hours | <3.85 | ≥4.88 | Key Findings from ROX Validation: [13] - Validated in FLORALI cohort - At 12-20 hours: PPV for success >80% if ROX ≥4.88 - Gray zone (3.85-4.88) at 12h: only 11% of patients, 33%

nodes.title: HFNC Success - Continue & Wean
nodes.summary: HFNC success: improved RR, reduced WOB, rising ROX index, stable SpO2 on lower FiO2
nodes.body: ROX ≥4.88 indicates low risk of HFNC failure [13][14] Continue Current Therapy: - Maintain HFNC at current settings - Reassess ROX every 4-6 hours - Monitor for improvement vs stability Signs of Improvement: - RR decreasing (<25) - Able to speak in full sentences - Reduced accessory muscle use - SpO2 maintained on lower FiO2 - Patient reports comfort Weaning Strategy: [1] 1. Wean FiO2 first - targ

nodes.title: ROX Gray Zone - Close Monitoring
nodes.summary: ROX 3.85-4.88: grey zone — reassess hourly, prepare for escalation if declining trend
nodes.body: ROX 3.85-4.88 = Indeterminate Risk [13] At 12 hours, only 11% of patients fall in this zone. Among them, 33% ultimately required intubation. Management: 1. Optimize HFNC settings: - Increase flow to 60 L/min if not already - Ensure FiO2 appropriate for target SpO2 - Check nasal cannula fit 2. Address reversible factors: - Secretion clearance - Positioning (head of bed elevation) - Treat underlying

nodes.title: HFNC Failure Criteria
nodes.summary: HFNC failure: ROX declining, RR >35, persistent accessory muscle use, worsening ABG — do NOT delay intubation
nodes.body: Clinical Signs of HFNC Failure: [1][13][14] ROX Index: - ROX <2.85 at 2 hours - ROX <3.47 at 6 hours - ROX <3.85 at 12 hours - Declining ROX despite optimization Clinical Indicators: - RR >35 despite maximal HFNC - SpO2 <88% on HFNC 60 L/min, FiO2 100% - Accessory muscle use - sternocleidomastoid recruitment - Paradoxical abdominal breathing - Altered mental status - confusion, agitation, somnolen

nodes.title: Escalation Options
nodes.summary: Escalation: NIV trial (if appropriate) or intubation — delayed intubation increases mortality
nodes.body: When HFNC Fails, Options Include: [1][2] 1. Non-Invasive Ventilation (NIV/BiPAP): - Higher PEEP (10-15 cm H2O vs 3-5 cm H2O) - Pressure support reduces WOB further - Best for: COPD, CHF, mild-moderate ARDS - Caution: May delay necessary intubation 2. Intubation & Mechanical Ventilation: - Definitive airway protection - Full ventilatory support - Required for: altered mental status, inability to pr

nodes.title: Transition to NIV
nodes.summary: NIV trial appropriate for COPD or CHF — if no improvement in 1-2h, proceed to intubation
nodes.body: NIV Settings After HFNC Failure: [1][2] Initial BiPAP Settings: - IPAP: 12-16 cm H2O - EPAP: 8-10 cm H2O - FiO2: 100% initially, titrate down - Rise time: 150-200 ms CPAP (for CHF): - Start 8-10 cm H2O - Titrate up to 15-20 cm H2O as needed - FiO2 to maintain SpO2 92-96% Monitoring on NIV: - Reassess within 1-2 hours - If no improvement, proceed to intubation - Do not delay intubation for prolonge

nodes.title: Intubation After HFNC Failure
nodes.summary: Continue HFNC at 60 L/min during intubation for apneic oxygenation — do not disconnect
nodes.body: Intubation Considerations: [1][8] Pre-Intubation Optimization: - Continue HFNC during preparation (apneic oxygenation benefit) - Head-up positioning 20-30 degrees - Preoxygenate 3-5 minutes at max HFNC settings - Have vasopressors ready (push-dose epinephrine or norepinephrine) Induction Agent Selection: - Ketamine: 1-2 mg/kg IV - preserves hemodynamics, bronchodilation - Etomidate: 0.3 mg/kg IV -

nodes.title: HFNC in COPD
nodes.summary: COPD: NIV (BiPAP) remains first-line — HFNC as alternative if NIV-intolerant
nodes.body: COPD Considerations: [2][17] Traditional Teaching: NIV is first-line for COPD exacerbation with hypercapnia. Emerging Role of HFNC in COPD: - May be effective for mild-moderate exacerbations - Better tolerated than NIV for prolonged use - Dead space washout improves CO2 clearance - Less effective than NIV for severe hypercapnia (pH <7.25) ROX Index in COPD: [17] - ROX index was developed in pneumo

nodes.title: HFNC in Obesity
nodes.summary: Obese patients may need higher flows (60 L/min) and elevated HOB for adequate PEEP effect
nodes.body: Obese Patients Present Unique Challenges: [1][2] Physiological Considerations: - Reduced FRC due to abdominal pressure on diaphragm - Increased atelectasis, especially when supine - Higher oxygen consumption - Difficult airway risk if intubation needed HFNC Benefits in Obesity: - PEEP effect helps recruit atelectatic lung - Better tolerated than NIV mask on obese face - Continuous O2 delivery duri

nodes.title: HFNC in Pediatric Patients
nodes.summary: Pediatric flows: 2 L/kg/min max — bronchiolitis has strongest evidence for pediatric HFNC
nodes.body: Pediatric HFNC Applications: [18] Bronchiolitis: - Most studied pediatric indication - HFNC reduces need for ICU admission - May prevent intubation in moderate-severe bronchiolitis Flow Rate by Age: | Age | Starting Flow | Max Flow | |-----|--------------|----------| | Infant | 2 L/kg/min | 2 L/kg/min (max ~8 L/min) | | 1-5 years | 1-2 L/kg/min | Up to 20-25 L/min | | >5 years | 1 L/kg/min | Up to

nodes.title: HFNC in DNR/Comfort Care
nodes.summary: HFNC appropriate for comfort care in DNR/DNI patients — reduces dyspnea without intubation
nodes.body: HFNC as Comfort Measure: [1] Advantages for Comfort Care: - Reduces dyspnea without invasive intervention - Allows communication with family - Permits oral intake - More comfortable than NRB mask - Maintains dignity Settings for Comfort: - Titrate to patient comfort, not SpO2 goals - Lower flow rates may be sufficient - Humidity provides comfort for dry airways Goals of Care Discussion: - HFNC is

nodes.title: HFNC Disposition Recommendations
nodes.summary: ICU admission for HFNC — requires continuous monitoring and rapid escalation capability
nodes.body: ICU Admission Criteria: [1][2] - HFNC flow >40 L/min + FiO2 >50% - ROX <4.88 at any time point - Concern for impending respiratory failure - Hemodynamic instability - Need for frequent reassessment - Post-intubation care Step-Down/Telemetry: - Stable on HFNC ≤40 L/min, FiO2 ≤50% - ROX >4.88 and stable/improving - No hemodynamic concerns - Underlying cause being treated Floor (if HFNC available): -
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on HFNC settings, ROX index, hemodynamic stability, and trajectory. ICU for high FiO2/flow requirements or ROX <4.88. Step-down for stable patients with improving trajectory. Ensure monitoring capability matches patient ac

nodes.title: HFNC Quick Reference
nodes.summary: HFNC: start 30-40 L/min, titrate to 60, monitor ROX index, escalate early if failing
nodes.body: HFNC Key Points Summary: Indications: - Hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 <300) - Post-extubation support - Pre-oxygenation/apneic oxygenation - Immunocompromised with ARF - NIV intolerance Initial Settings: - Flow: 30-60 L/min (titrate to WOB) - FiO2: 50-100% (titrate to SpO2 92-96%) - Temperature: 37C (decrease if uncomfortable) ROX Index: - Formula: (SpO2/FiO2) / RR - Success: ≥4.88 at 2

nodes.title: High Dose Insulin Protocol
nodes.summary: HDI/HIET treats BB/CCB poison-induced shock with insulin plus dextrose and close electrolyte monitoring.
nodes.body: High Dose Insulin Steps High-dose insulin euglycemia therapy (HDI/HIET) is used for poison-induced cardiogenic shock, especially calcium channel blocker and beta-blocker toxicity. Core indication: - Severe or persistent hypotension, bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, or mixed shock from calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker overdose - Use early when myocardial dysfunction is present; do not wait fo

nodes.title: Indication
nodes.summary: HDI is for hemodynamically significant BB/CCB toxicity, not routine asymptomatic observation.
nodes.body: What is the likely toxicologic syndrome?

nodes.title: CCB Toxicity
nodes.summary: CCB shock with myocardial dysfunction should trigger early HDI plus calcium and vasopressors.
nodes.body: HDI is a first-line therapy for CCB poisoning with myocardial dysfunction or shock, alongside IV calcium and vasopressors. Use HDI early when any are present: - Hypotension or shock - Bradycardia or high-grade AV block with poor perfusion - Cool extremities, low cardiac output, rising lactate - Severe hyperglycemia with shock phenotype - Failure to stabilize rapidly with fluids/calcium/vasopressor

nodes.title: Beta-Blocker Toxicity
nodes.summary: BB shock often needs HDI early; glucagon is a bridge, not a definitive endpoint.
nodes.body: Use HDI for beta-blocker overdose with persistent hypotension, bradycardia, or cardiogenic shock. Do not wait for glucagon to be definitive. Glucagon may be used as a bridge, but vomiting, tachyphylaxis, drug shortage, and transient response limit reliability. Use HDI early when any are present: - Persistent hypotension despite fluids/atropine/glucagon - Bradycardia with poor perfusion - Myocardia

nodes.title: Mixed / Unknown Cardiotoxic Shock
nodes.summary: Mixed cardiotoxic shock can justify HDI while parallel antidotes and tox consultation proceed.
nodes.body: If the patient has poison-induced cardiogenic or mixed shock and BB/CCB toxicity is plausible, start HDI while continuing diagnostic clarification. Parallel treatments may include: - IV calcium when CCB possible - Glucagon when BB possible - Norepinephrine and/or epinephrine for perfusion - Lipid emulsion for refractory lipophilic drug toxicity - Sodium bicarbonate if sodium-channel blockade/QRS w

nodes.title: HDI Not Yet Indicated
nodes.summary: Stable ingestion does not need HDI, but deterioration should trigger rapid escalation.
nodes.body: Do not start HDI for a stable, asymptomatic patient solely because a BB/CCB was ingested. Instead: - Call poison center for agent-specific observation time - Obtain ECG, glucose, electrolytes, lactate as indicated - Decontaminate if appropriate and safe - Observe extended-release products longer - Prepare HDI kit early if deterioration is plausible Start HDI immediately if shock, bradycardia with
nodes.recommendation: Observe and prepare, but reserve HDI for hemodynamically significant toxicity.

nodes.title: Before Starting HDI
nodes.summary: Set up insulin, dextrose, potassium, tox/pharmacy support, and close monitoring before bolus.
nodes.body: Do these in parallel; do not delay HDI in shock. Team/setup: - Call poison center/toxicology and pharmacy - Assign glucose, potassium, insulin pump, and hemodynamic monitoring roles - Obtain at least 2 reliable IVs; central access preferred for concentrated dextrose but do not delay insulin - Consider arterial line and bedside echo/POCUS Baseline labs: - Fingerstick/serum glucose - BMP with potass

nodes.title: Starting Glucose
nodes.summary: Dextrose bolus depends on starting glucose, but ongoing dextrose needs can rise later.
nodes.body: What is the initial glucose?

nodes.title: Initial Dextrose Bolus
nodes.summary: If glucose <200, give adult D50W 25 g before or with insulin.
nodes.body: If glucose is <200 mg/dL, give dextrose before or with insulin. Adult: - Dextrose 25 g IV (50 mL D50W) Pediatric: - D25W 2-4 mL/kg IV per poison center/pediatric pharmacy protocol Then start a dextrose infusion and titrate to maintain euglycemia. Concentrated dextrose may require central access depending on local policy, but insulin initiation should not be delayed in shock.

nodes.title: Starting Potassium
nodes.summary: Replace K if low, but do not delay life-saving HDI in crashing toxicologic shock.
nodes.body: What is the potassium before starting HDI?

nodes.title: Potassium Replacement
nodes.summary: Start K replacement for K <3.0; avoid excessive replacement because HDI causes redistribution.
nodes.body: HDI shifts potassium intracellularly; hypokalemia is expected and usually reflects redistribution rather than total body depletion. Approach: - If K <3.0 mEq/L, begin IV potassium replacement immediately - Continue HDI when shock is life-threatening, with frequent K/ECG monitoring - Target commonly used during HDI: K about 3.0-3.5 mEq/L; some older protocols targeted higher values - Avoid overcorr

nodes.title: Insulin Bolus
nodes.summary: Bolus regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV, with dextrose first/with bolus if glucose <200.
nodes.body: Use regular insulin. Initial bolus: - Regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus - Prepare in a clearly labeled syringe - Give after initial dextrose bolus if glucose <200 mg/dL If the patient is peri-arrest, do not delay insulin bolus while waiting for central access or perfect lab setup.

nodes.title: Insulin Infusion
nodes.summary: Start 1 unit/kg/hr, titrate q20-30 min by 1 unit/kg/hr up to 10 units/kg/hr with tox guidance.
nodes.body: Start infusion immediately after bolus. Initial infusion: - Regular insulin 1 unit/kg/hr IV - Use 1 unit/mL or concentrated preparation per pharmacy/local policy - Use smart pump and dedicated line when possible Titration: - If no hemodynamic improvement, increase by 1 unit/kg/hr every 20-30 minutes - Typical upper target: 10 units/kg/hr with poison center/toxicology guidance - Higher doses are re

nodes.title: Dextrose Infusion
nodes.summary: Use continuous dextrose to keep glucose in protocol target, with q15-20 min checks early.
nodes.body: Start dextrose early and titrate to glucose target. Adult starting option: - D10W 1/2NS at 100 mL/hr, then titrate - Use D20W/D25W/D50W through central access when fluid load becomes excessive Glucose target: - Maintain 100-200 mg/dL per Ontario Poison Centre protocol - Some US protocols use 150-250 mg/dL; follow local poison center guidance Monitoring: - Glucose q15-20 minutes for first hour and

nodes.title: Monitoring During HDI
nodes.summary: Glucose and potassium monitoring are mandatory; hemodynamic response may take 15-60 minutes.
nodes.body: Minimum monitoring: - Continuous telemetry and frequent BP; arterial line if available - Glucose q15-20 min for first hour and during titration, then q1h once stable - Potassium hourly during titration, then q2h if stable - Magnesium/phosphate q4-6h or per ICU protocol - Lactate, VBG/ABG, urine output, mental status, perfusion exam - Serial ECG for conduction/QRS/QT changes - Bedside echo or hemod

nodes.title: Response at 30-60 Minutes
nodes.summary: Assess response after 30-60 minutes; titrate insulin and escalate support if still unstable.
nodes.body: Assess hemodynamic response after initiation and titration. Expected onset is often 15-45 minutes but may be delayed. Do not abandon HDI too early if dose is still being escalated and perfusion is not worsening.

nodes.title: Continue Until Stable
nodes.summary: Continue until sustained stability; early withdrawal can cause recurrent hypotension.
nodes.body: Continue insulin and supportive therapies until sustained hemodynamic stability. Continue tracking: - Vasopressor requirement - MAP/SBP and HR - Lactate clearance - Urine output - POCUS/cardiac output if available - Glucose and potassium replacement needs Do not stop HDI abruptly just because the first BP improves. Sustained-release products and large ingestions can relapse.

nodes.title: Escalate If No Improvement
nodes.summary: Escalate insulin dose and parallel shock therapies; call ECMO early for refractory reversible shock.
nodes.body: If no hemodynamic improvement: - Confirm insulin is at an adequate dose and titrating q20-30 min - Increase insulin by 1 unit/kg/hr toward 10 units/kg/hr with toxicology guidance - Ensure glucose and potassium support are keeping pace - Continue vasopressors: norepinephrine and/or epinephrine are typical first-line choices - Give/repeat IV calcium for CCB toxicity per local protocol - Consider glu

nodes.title: Refractory Shock / Arrest
nodes.summary: Refractory BB/CCB shock should trigger toxicology and VA-ECMO discussion early.
nodes.body: For refractory shock or arrest: - Continue HDI if already started; escalate to toxicology-guided target - Use norepinephrine/epinephrine for perfusion - Use IV calcium for CCB toxicity - Consider lipid emulsion for lipophilic agents - Treat QRS widening with sodium bicarbonate when sodium-channel blockade suspected - Activate VA-ECMO/ECPR pathway early when available and patient is a candidate - C
nodes.recommendation: Escalate to maximal toxicologic shock support and early VA-ECMO/ECPR consultation for refractory reversible cardiogenic shock.

nodes.title: Weaning HDI
nodes.summary: Wean slowly after sustained stability; continue dextrose monitoring after insulin stops.
nodes.body: Wean only after sustained hemodynamic improvement. Suggested approach: - Wean vasopressors first when possible - Then decrease insulin by 1 unit/kg/hr at a time, or by local ICU/toxicology protocol - Continue glucose and potassium checks during every dose change - Watch for recurrent hypotension, bradycardia, or lactate rise - CCB patients may require increasing dextrose as toxicity improves - Con

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: HDI requires ICU care, poison center guidance, and detailed handoff.
nodes.body: Patients requiring HDI need ICU-level care. Handoff must include: - Agent, formulation, dose/time, and co-ingestions - Current insulin rate and highest rate used - Dextrose concentration/rate and recent glucose trend - Potassium/magnesium/phosphate replacement - Vasopressor doses and response - Calcium/glucagon/lipid/bicarbonate therapies given - ECG intervals/conduction issues - Poison center rec
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU with toxicology/poison center involvement and serial hemodynamic, glucose, electrolyte, and ECG monitoring.

nodes.title: STOP: HDI Safety Checks
nodes.summary: HDI requires deliberate safety checks because dosing is far above routine insulin protocols.
nodes.body: Stop and correct the process if any are present: - Insulin running without dextrose plan and glucose monitoring - No potassium monitoring/replacement plan - Infusion pump concentration unclear or unlabeled - Dose entered as DKA insulin rate instead of HDI rate - No poison center/toxicology/pharmacy involvement for severe toxicity - Persistent shock without escalation toward vasopressors, calcium,
nodes.recommendation: Verify insulin concentration, dose units, dextrose, potassium, monitoring, and escalation plan before and during HDI.

nodes.title: Atraumatic Hip Pain — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Sick check + vitals + weight-bearing + age anchor + 4-question screen. Fever + can\u2019t-weight-bear = septic hip until proven.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 4 DO NOT MISS: 1. Septic arthritis of the hip \u2014 fever + can\u2019t bear weight + resisted / painful ROM; arthrocentesis is the gold standard. A destroyed joint in <24 h. 2. Necrotizing soft-tissue infection / iliopsoas abscess \u2014 pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, skin changes, immunocompromise. 3. Occult / insufficiency hip fracture \u2014 elderly, groin pain, unable

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Differential
nodes.summary: Age-anchored; pick the most acute differential and walk its gate to a verdict. Excluded loops back.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous causes to an explicit verdict, one at a time. Age anchors the differential. Each branch walks its gate (score, exam, or imaging) to excluded, test further, or rule in + treat. Excluded loops back here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Septic Hip — Kocher / Arthrocentesis Gate
nodes.summary: Kocher risk-stratifies; synovial fluid is gold standard. High suspicion or infected fluid = treat as septic joint.
nodes.body: Fever + inability to bear weight + an ESR/CRP and WBC bump + a painful, guarded hip is septic arthritis until synovial fluid says otherwise. Kocher criteria (fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12k) risk-stratify a pediatric hip \u2014 open it in the toolbar. Synovial fluid analysis is the gold standard (WBC often >50k with PMN predominance, Gram stain, culture, crystals). A hip usually

nodes.title: Septic Hip — Aspirate + Treat
nodes.body: Open Septic Arthritis; for the aspiration technique use Joint Arthrocentesis. Next steps: - Arthrocentesis before antibiotics if achievable without delay (a hip usually needs US/fluoroscopic guidance) \u2014 but do NOT delay antibiotics in a septic-looking patient. - Blood cultures \u00D7 2, CBC, ESR, CRP, lactate. - Empiric IV antibiotics: vancomycin (MRSA coverage) + an antipseudomonal / gram-ne
nodes.recommendation: Image-guided arthrocentesis, blood cultures, empiric vancomycin + gram-negative coverage, EMERGENT ortho for washout. Do not delay abx in a septic-looking patient.

nodes.title: Septic Hip — Excluded / Low Probability
nodes.body: An afebrile, weight-bearing patient with a low Kocher score and benign synovial fluid (if sampled) makes a septic hip unlikely. Transient synovitis is the main mimic in children \u2014 but it is a diagnosis of exclusion; if the child cannot bear weight or has any inflammatory markers, do not clear the hip without imaging \u00B1 aspiration and orthopedic input. Return to the hub for the next differ
nodes.recommendation: Septic hip unlikely with benign markers / fluid; transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion \u2014 reassess and aspirate if any doubt.

nodes.title: Necrotizing Infection / Iliopsoas Abscess — Toxicity Gate
nodes.summary: Pain out of proportion + toxicity = nec-fasc / abscess; image + surgery. No toxicity = unlikely.
nodes.body: Pain out of proportion to exam + systemic toxicity is the alarm. Necrotizing soft-tissue infection (rapidly spreading, skin changes, crepitus, bullae) and iliopsoas / deep-space abscess (fever, flexed hip, positive psoas sign, back/flank pain) both masquerade as "hip pain." Immunocompromise, diabetes, IVDU, and recent instrumentation raise the risk.

nodes.title: Deep Infection — Resuscitate + Source Control
nodes.body: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection: open Necrotizing Fasciitis \u2014 this is a surgical emergency. Do NOT wait for imaging to consult surgery if the exam is convincing; broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin for toxin suppression), aggressive resuscitation, emergent operative debridement. Iliopsoas / deep abscess: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast; broad-spect
nodes.recommendation: Nec-fasc = emergent surgery + broad abx (do not wait for imaging). Abscess = CT + drainage. Consider pathologic fracture / mets.

nodes.title: Deep Infection — Unlikely
nodes.body: No systemic toxicity, benign overlying soft tissue, and localized joint-pattern pain makes a necrotizing infection or deep abscess unlikely right now. These evolve fast \u2014 if toxicity, spreading erythema, crepitus, or a psoas sign appears on reassessment, image and consult surgery immediately. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Deep infection unlikely; re-examine and image urgently if toxicity or spreading signs evolve.

nodes.title: SCFE — Adolescent Gate
nodes.summary: Obese teen + knee/thigh or hip pain + out-toeing; frog-leg lateral of both hips. Up to 25% present as knee pain.
nodes.body: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: the classic patient is an obese adolescent 8-15 (often around the growth spurt), with hip, groin, or referred knee/thigh pain and an externally rotated, out-toeing gait; the hip obligately externally rotates on passive flexion. Up to a quarter present with knee pain and no hip complaint \u2014 the great trap. Get AP pelvis + frog-leg (or cross-table) lateral of B

nodes.title: SCFE — Non-Weight-Bearing + Orthopedics
nodes.body: SCFE confirmed or strongly suspected (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - Make the patient strictly non-weight-bearing immediately (wheelchair, no crutches with weight-bearing) \u2014 continued weight-bearing can convert a stable slip to an unstable one, which carries a much higher risk of avascular necrosis. - Urgent orthopedic consult \u2014 the definitive treatment is operative in s
nodes.recommendation: Strict non-weight-bearing NOW + urgent ortho for in-situ pinning; do not reduce; image both hips. (Consult gap \u2014 managed in-hub.)

nodes.title: SCFE — Unlikely
nodes.body: Outside the SCFE demographic or with a normal frog-leg lateral, SCFE is unlikely. In an adolescent with persistent hip or knee pain and normal early films, keep SCFE on the list \u2014 a subtle slip can be missed; a low threshold to re-image or get orthopedic follow-up is appropriate. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: SCFE unlikely; maintain suspicion in any adolescent with persistent hip/knee pain \u2014 re-image or refer.

nodes.title: Avascular Necrosis of Femoral Head — Risk Gate
nodes.summary: Groin pain + steroids/alcohol/sickle cell; plain film often normal early, MRI most sensitive.
nodes.body: AVN (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head: insidious groin pain worse with weight-bearing, in a patient with a risk factor \u2014 corticosteroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, SLE, trauma, prior fracture, or idiopathic. Plain films are often normal early (before subchondral collapse / the "crescent sign"); MRI is the most sensitive test.

nodes.title: AVN Femoral Head — Image + Refer
nodes.body: AVN suspected (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - MRI is the gold standard and can detect AVN before plain-film changes; get AP + frog-leg films first, then arrange MRI (ED or urgent outpatient depending on severity). - Protected weight-bearing (crutches) and analgesia; early disease may respond to joint-preserving surgery (core decompression), advanced collapse needs arthroplasty \u2
nodes.recommendation: MRI (most sensitive), protected weight-bearing, orthopedic referral, treat the driver (e.g., sickle cell). (Consult gap \u2014 managed in-hub.)

nodes.title: AVN — Unlikely
nodes.body: Without a risk factor and with a mechanical pain pattern, AVN is unlikely. If risk factors are present but early films are normal, a normal X-ray does not exclude AVN \u2014 arrange MRI or orthopedic follow-up when suspicion persists. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: AVN unlikely without risk factors; if risk present, a normal X-ray does not exclude it \u2014 MRI / refer.

nodes.title: Occult / Insufficiency Fracture — Elderly Gate
nodes.summary: Elderly + can\u2019t-weight-bear + normal X-ray = occult fracture until CT/MRI says otherwise.
nodes.body: The classic miss: an elderly / osteoporotic patient with groin or hip pain and inability to bear weight after minimal or no trauma, whose plain X-ray is normal or subtle. Insufficiency fractures also occur with chronic steroid use, bisphosphonate-associated atypical femoral fractures, or metastatic bone disease. Do not clear a hip on plain films alone when the patient cannot walk.

nodes.title: Occult Hip Fracture — Advanced Imaging + Ortho
nodes.body: Occult / insufficiency fracture suspected (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - A normal X-ray does NOT rule out a hip fracture in a patient who cannot bear weight \u2014 obtain MRI (most sensitive, detects fracture within hours) or CT if MRI is unavailable. - Keep the patient non-weight-bearing and provide adequate analgesia (consider a fascia iliaca / femoral nerve block for a suspect
nodes.recommendation: Normal X-ray does NOT exclude \u2014 MRI (or CT); non-weight-bearing + analgesia (\u00B1 nerve block); ortho for fixation; screen for mets. (Consult gap \u2014 managed in-hub.)

nodes.title: Occult Fracture — Unlikely
nodes.body: A patient who bears weight well with a benign exam and negative films is unlikely to have a significant occult fracture. In the elderly with any inability to weight-bear, keep the threshold for MRI low \u2014 the consequences of a missed hip fracture (displacement, AVN, immobility) are severe. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Occult fracture unlikely if weight-bearing well; low threshold for MRI in the elderly who cannot walk.

nodes.title: Pediatric Limping Child — Age + Fever Gate
nodes.summary: Kocher + CRP separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis; keep osteomyelitis/Perthes/SCFE by age.
nodes.body: The limping child needs the septic hip / osteomyelitis excluded before "transient synovitis." Kocher criteria (fever >38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12k) plus CRP help separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis \u2014 open Kocher in the toolbar. Keep on the list by age: osteomyelitis (bone tenderness, fever), Legg-Calv\u00E9-Perthes (4-8 y, insidious), SCFE (older child), and non-

nodes.title: Pediatric Septic Joint / Osteomyelitis — Treat
nodes.body: Osteomyelitis: open Pediatric Osteomyelitis \u2014 focal bone tenderness + fever + elevated ESR/CRP; blood cultures, MRI, empiric antibiotics covering S. aureus (and Kingella in young children), orthopedic input. Septic hip in a child: high Kocher / infected synovial fluid \u2192 emergent orthopedic washout + IV antibiotics (see the Septic Arthritis pathway above); US-guided aspiration confirms. F
nodes.recommendation: Osteomyelitis \u2192 Peds Osteomyelitis consult (MRI + abx + ortho). Septic hip \u2192 aspirate + emergent washout + abx.

nodes.title: Transient Synovitis — Likely (Exclusion Diagnosis)
nodes.body: A well-appearing, afebrile, weight-bearing child with a low Kocher score and reassuring markers most likely has transient (toxic) synovitis \u2014 a self-limited post-viral inflammation. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion. Manage with NSAIDs, rest, and close follow-up in 24-48 h; give strict return precautions for fever, worsening pain, or inability to bear weight, which would mandate re-evaluati
nodes.recommendation: Transient synovitis (exclusion dx): NSAIDs + rest + 24-48 h recheck; return for fever / worsening / non-weight-bearing.

nodes.title: Mechanical Hip Pain — Pattern Gate
nodes.summary: OA / GTPS / bursitis once dangerous causes excluded; conservative care + referral.
nodes.body: Once the dangerous causes are excluded, chronic mechanical pain is common: osteoarthritis (deep groin pain, worse with activity, morning stiffness <30 min, reduced internal rotation), greater trochanteric pain syndrome / trochanteric bursitis (lateral hip pain, tender over the greater trochanter, worse lying on that side), and gluteal / iliotibial pathology.

nodes.title: Mechanical Hip Pain — Conservative Management
nodes.body: Open Approach to Arthritis for the degenerative / inflammatory work-up. - Osteoarthritis: analgesia (acetaminophen, topical or oral NSAIDs), activity modification, physical therapy, weight management; orthopedic referral for advanced disease / arthroplasty candidacy. - Greater trochanteric pain syndrome / bursitis: relative rest, NSAIDs, PT (hip abductor strengthening), and a corticosteroid inject
nodes.recommendation: OA/GTPS/bursitis \u2192 analgesia + activity modification + PT \u00B1 injection; ensure red flags are excluded first.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Atraumatic Hip Pain
nodes.summary: Analgesia (\u00B1 nerve block) + ESR/CRP/CBC if infection possible + AP/frog-leg films + advanced imaging for occult fx/AVN. Reassess weight-bearing.
nodes.body: No emergency ruled in; well-appearing patient.
