Standard ED bundle while the workup cooks: - Analgesia \u2014 acetaminophen / NSAID for mild-moderate; opioid PRN for severe; consider a fascia iliaca / femoral nerve block for a suspected fracture. - Labs when infection or systemic disease is possible: CBC, ESR, CRP (inflammatory / septic screen), CMP; blood cultures + lactate if febrile/toxic; consi

nodes.title: Reassess — Weight-Bearing + Labs + Imaging
nodes.summary: Weight-bearing + benign = discharge; normal film but can\u2019t-weight-bear = MRI/aspirate; fever/red flag = STOP.
nodes.body: Re-examine: can they bear weight now? Fever? Inflammatory markers? Imaging results back?

nodes.title: Imaging Decision Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: Plain films first (normal does not exclude occult fx/AVN/septic); MRI most sensitive; US to find effusion + guide aspiration; arthrocentesis is gold standard for septic.
nodes.body: Match the study to the suspected pathology: Plain radiographs (first-line): AP pelvis + frog-leg (or cross-table) lateral \u2014 fractures, OA, SCFE (both hips in adolescents), lytic lesions. A normal X-ray does NOT exclude occult fracture, early AVN, or septic arthritis. MRI (most sensitive): occult / insufficiency hip fracture (detects within hours), early AVN (before plain-film collapse), osteo

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit surgical/infectious/fracture diagnoses; observe if equivocal; discharge mechanical pain with follow-up.
nodes.body: Defer to the deep-dive consult\u2019s admit criteria once a diagnosis is committed. The framework below applies to undifferentiated / mechanical hip pain.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for: septic arthritis (emergent ortho washout), necrotizing infection / deep abscess (surgery + IV abx), hip fracture (occult or displaced \u2014 operative fixation), SCFE (non-weight-bearing + pinning), symptomatic AVN needing intervention, pediatric osteomyelitis, or systemic toxicity / sepsis. Service: Orthopedics (septic joint, fracture, SCFE, AVN); Surgery (necrotizing infection); Medic
nodes.recommendation: Admit per deep-dive criteria; match service to diagnosis; emergent ortho/surgery for septic joint or nec-fasc; standard handoff.

nodes.title: Observe — Pending Advanced Workup
nodes.body: ED observation when: normal plain films but persistent inability to bear weight (awaiting MRI / CT), awaiting synovial fluid or inflammatory-marker trends, or intermediate concern with social/safety barriers. Protocol: serial exams (weight-bearing, ROM, position); recheck temperature; repeat/trend inflammatory markers if intermediate; continue analgesia; keep non-weight-bearing if a fracture or SC
nodes.recommendation: Obs + serial weight-bearing/ROM + trend markers; escalate on fever/positive imaging; discharge when reassuring.

nodes.title: Discharge — Universal Checklist
nodes.body: Before discharge: (1) red flags excluded (afebrile, no septic-joint features, no toxicity), (2) able to bear weight or a clear plan if not (fracture/SCFE excluded by adequate imaging), (3) adequate imaging for the clinical picture (remember a normal X-ray does not exclude occult fracture / early AVN), (4) pain controlled, (5) reliable follow-up arranged (orthopedics / PCP), (6) written return prec
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if red flags excluded, weight-bearing (or fracture/SCFE excluded by imaging), pain controlled, follow-up arranged, written precautions.

nodes.title: HIV in the Emergency Department
nodes.summary: Assess HIV status and presentation: new diagnosis, well-controlled, immunocompromised, or prevention
nodes.body: HIV ED Management Steps Summary — quick reference. HIV is now a manageable chronic disease with HAART, but ~14% of HIV-infected persons remain unaware of their status, driving continued transmission. [1] Approximately 80% of new transmissions are from persons not yet diagnosed or not in regular care. The ED plays a critical role in: • Identifying undiagnosed HIV infection • Managing complications

nodes.title: Clinical Scenario
nodes.summary: Determine clinical scenario to guide evaluation and management approach
nodes.body: What brings this patient to the ED?

nodes.title: HIV Disease Status Assessment
nodes.summary: CD4 count and viral load guide risk stratification — CD4 <200 = AIDS, high OI risk
nodes.body: Ask the patient: • Most recent CD4 count and viral load (or at least if VL is "undetectable") • Current antiretroviral medications and compliance • Prior opportunistic infections • Recent travel or sick contacts Patients unaware of their CD4/VL or not engaged in care should be considered at higher risk for OIs and complications of untreated infection. [4] CD4 counts and viral load can be ordered f

nodes.title: HIV Screening & Testing
nodes.summary: ED HIV screening: opt-out testing recommended for all adults 15-65 — 4th gen Ag/Ab preferred
nodes.body: HIV Testing & Screening Guide — universal vs risk-based approach. CDC (2006): Routine opt-out HIV screening for ages 13-64 in healthcare settings where undiagnosed prevalence ≥0.1%. [3] USPSTF (Grade A): Routine screening ages 15-65. [7] ACEP: Endorsed ED HIV testing since 2007. [8] High-risk patients who should NOT be missed: • Sexually active MSM • Persons who inject drugs and their sex partners

nodes.title: Acute Retroviral Syndrome
nodes.summary: Acute seroconversion: fever + rash + lymphadenopathy WITHOUT respiratory symptoms — high viral load
nodes.body: Acute Seroconversion Features — clinical presentation guide. After HIV exposure, local viral replication occurs over several days before entering the bloodstream with high viremia. 75-90% of patients develop an acute illness during seroconversion. [1] Classic presentation: • Fever, headache, malaise • Sore throat (without exudate) • Lymphadenopathy (generalized) • GI symptoms (nausea, diarrhea) Mo

nodes.title: Diagnosing Acute HIV
nodes.summary: Standard antibody test may be negative early — order 4th gen Ag/Ab or viral load for acute infection
nodes.body: Diagnosis of acute seroconversion is challenging: • Third-generation (antibody-only) tests may miss early infection — no longer recommended as first-line • Fourth-generation tests (antibody + p24 antigen) can often identify infection as early as 2 weeks post-exposure — preferred initial test [9] • Early infection can still be missed within 2 weeks of exposure Critical rule: When acute infection is

nodes.title: New HIV Diagnosis — ED Management
nodes.summary: New HIV diagnosis in ED: baseline labs, PCP referral within 72h, consider same-day ART start
nodes.body: Confirmed or highly suspected new HIV infection: Immediate actions: • Baseline labs: CBC, BMP, hepatic function, CD4 count, viral load • Screen for co-infections: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis (RPR/VDRL), other STIs • Pregnancy test if applicable Rapid ART initiation: Current HHS and IAS-USA guidelines recommend same-day initiation of ART for newly diagnosed patients — reduces time to viral s
nodes.recommendation: Confirmed/suspected new HIV diagnosis. Draw baseline labs (CBC, BMP, LFTs, CD4, VL, HBV/HCV, syphilis, STI panel). Urgent referral to HIV specialist for same-day ART initiation. Counsel on transmission risk.

nodes.title: Well-Controlled HIV — Chief Complaint
nodes.summary: Well-controlled HIV patients have unique complications: CV, renal, neuro, metabolic — not just OIs
nodes.body: Patients with well-controlled HIV (CD4 >200, undetectable VL, treatment-adherent) are living longer and now present with typical diseases of aging, adverse medication effects, and chronic inflammatory state complications rather than OIs. [14] Treat these patients similarly to immunocompetent individuals, with attention to: • Higher baseline cardiovascular risk • Chronic inflammatory state → hyperc

nodes.title: Respiratory Complaints — Well-Controlled HIV
nodes.summary: Respiratory complaints: community-acquired pneumonia more common than PJP in controlled HIV
nodes.body: Well-controlled HIV patients develop traditional pulmonary infections of immunocompetent patients. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial pneumonia — treatment does not differ from non-HIV patients. [15, 16] Disposition can mirror practice for non-HIV patients, as well-controlled patients have similar pneumonia mortality. CURB-65 can be applied, though one small study found

nodes.title: Cardiovascular Disease in HIV
nodes.summary: HIV patients have 2x MI risk — PIs cause metabolic syndrome, consider ACS evaluation
nodes.body: HIV patients have increased cardiovascular risk from multiple factors: traditional risk factors, chronic inflammatory state, and medication effects (metabolic syndrome, abacavir MI association). [22, 23] Acute coronary syndromes: • HIV and some treatments are associated with CAD absent traditional risk factors • Abacavir has been associated with MI in retrospective studies (not yet confirmed prosp

nodes.title: Neurologic Complaints in HIV
nodes.summary: Neuro complaints: HAND (HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder), also stroke risk increased
nodes.body: Guide evaluation by CD4 count. Even well-controlled HIV carries slightly higher cerebrovascular risk. Stroke: • Risk ratio 2.56 (95% CI 1.43-4.61) compared to non-HIV [30] • Multifactorial: inflammatory state, atherosclerosis, smoking, metabolic medication effects • Follow standard evidence-based stroke algorithms HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND): • Most frequently identified neurolog

nodes.title: GI & Hepatobiliary Complaints
nodes.summary: GI issues common — consider medication side effects and opportunistic infections if CD4 low
nodes.body: Diarrhea is one of the most common HIV presentations in the ED. Up to 60% of patients on treatment report an episode in the prior month. [32] In well-controlled patients, OIs are rarely the cause. More common etiologies: • Medication side effect — leading diagnosis for isolated diarrhea [33] • HIV enteropathy • Same pathogens that affect non-HIV individuals Critical exception: C. difficile — more

nodes.title: Renal Disease in HIV
nodes.summary: HIV nephropathy and tenofovir nephrotoxicity — check creatinine and urinalysis
nodes.body: Renal disease can be caused by HIV infection itself AND nephrotoxic medications. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) nephrotoxicity: • Can cause Fanconi syndrome — polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration [37] • Labs: elevated creatinine, reduced GFR, acidemia, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia • UA: glucosuria, proteinuria • Higher risk in patients with pre-existing renal impairment • TAF (te

nodes.title: Other System Complications
nodes.summary: Endocrine, MSK, psych, derm complications common in long-term HIV — screen broadly
nodes.body: HIV System-Based Complications — comprehensive reference. Hematologic: • Cytopenias of all cell lines common — bone marrow suppression in uncontrolled HIV • Medication-induced anemia often macrocytic (diagnosis of exclusion) [28] • Higher VTE rates (2.6/1000 patient-years) • Evaluate for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) if hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia [41] Endocrine & Metabolic: •

nodes.title: Weakness in HIV — Broad Differential
nodes.summary: Weakness in HIV: GBS, myopathy (AZT), neuropathy, or deconditioning — workup based on pattern
nodes.body: Weakness is one of the most challenging presentations in HIV patients. Common causes of weakness in non-HIV patients are also common in HIV: • Sepsis — from any source • Metabolic: Hypoglycemia, electrolyte derangements (K+, Ca2+, Na+) • Carbon monoxide poisoning (in winter months) • Anemia — medication-induced or HIV-related HIV-specific considerations: • OIs (if CD4 <200 or unknown) — PJP, TB, d

nodes.title: Immunocompromised HIV — OI Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: CD4 <200: evaluate for PJP, toxo, crypto, CMV, MAC — OI risk by CD4 threshold guides workup
nodes.body: Patient has CD4 <200, detectable viral load, not in care, or unknown status. These patients are at risk for opportunistic infections AND chronic disease complications. AIDS is defined by CD4 <200 cells/mcL OR development of certain OIs or cancers. After acute illness, untreated HIV has ~8-10 years of clinical latency before AIDS develops. Many remain asymptomatic but have lymphadenopathy. Chronic

nodes.title: Pulmonary OIs — PJP, TB, Atypical Infections
nodes.summary: PJP: bilateral ground-glass opacities, LDH elevated, hypoxia with exertion — TMP-SMX + steroids if PaO2 <70
nodes.body: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP): • Classic: indolent, nonproductive cough + exertional dyspnea • CXR: perihilar or "batwing" infiltrate (see image below) • LDH typically elevated — a normal LDH helps rule OUT PJP [51] • LDH is not specific (elevated in lymphoma, TB, toxoplasmosis) • Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX when CD4 <200 Tuberculosis: • HIV patients at increased risk for both novel infection an

nodes.title: CNS Opportunistic Infections
nodes.summary: Toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions) vs CNS lymphoma (PET/thallium scan differentiates)
nodes.body: CNS OIs typically do not appear until CD4 <200. Rates have decreased significantly with treatment adherence. Toxoplasmosis: • Ring-enhancing mass lesion(s) on contrast CT or MRI • Fever, headache, focal neurologic deficits, seizures • Most common CNS mass lesion in AIDS Cryptococcal meningitis: • Subacute headache, fever, meningismus • May have only headache with subtle findings • LP with opening

nodes.title: GI Opportunistic Infections
nodes.summary: Cryptosporidium, CMV colitis, MAC — stool studies and colonoscopy based on CD4 and symptoms
nodes.body: As CD4 drops, GI OI risk increases significantly. C. difficile — more common in HIV vs non-HIV patients regardless of CD4 count. Careful history: recent antibiotics, hospitalizations. [34] With progressive immunosuppression (CD4 <100-200): • Cryptosporidium — watery diarrhea, can be chronic/severe • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) — bloody diarrhea, colitis, can cause perforation • Microsporidiosis — chroni

nodes.title: Other OIs & Complications of Advanced HIV
nodes.summary: CMV retinitis (CD4 <50), cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated MAC — systemic approach by CD4
nodes.body: Constitutional symptoms: • Fever, weight loss, night sweats → evaluate for disseminated MAC, TB, lymphoma • Pancytopenia from bone marrow suppression Dermatologic: • Kaposi sarcoma — purple-red nodular lesions (HHV-8 associated) • Disseminated VZV — can cross dermatomes, may be superinfected • Severe molluscum contagiosum, extensive seborrheic dermatitis • Oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV — cannot be s

nodes.title: Immunocompromised HIV — Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit for new OIs, severe presentations, or inability to take PO — avoid IRIS if starting ART
nodes.body: Low threshold for admission in immunocompromised HIV patients. Admit if: • Suspected or confirmed OI requiring inpatient treatment (PJP, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV) • Hemodynamic instability, sepsis • CNS symptoms with abnormal imaging or LP • Inability to tolerate oral medications or nutrition • Social barriers to outpatient follow-up If discharging: • Urgent follow-up with HIV s
nodes.recommendation: Low admission threshold for immunocompromised HIV patients. Consult ID for suspected OIs. Do NOT stop HAART without specialist guidance. Ensure linkage to HIV care on discharge.

nodes.title: Antiretroviral Drug Classes
nodes.summary: 5 ARV drug classes — ED-relevant adverse effects and drug interactions for each class
nodes.body: ARV Drug Classes & Side Effects — comprehensive reference table. Most current regimens use an INSTI + 2 NRTIs (e.g., Biktarvy). INSTI-based regimens are preferred for tolerability, reduced pill burden, and faster viral suppression. [12, 13] Which drug class or concern?

nodes.title: NRTI / NtRTI Adverse Effects
nodes.summary: NRTIs: lactic acidosis (rare but fatal), tenofovir renal toxicity, AZT myelosuppression
nodes.body: NRTIs/NtRTIs inhibit reverse transcription of HIV RNA into DNA. Current drugs are relatively well tolerated. [12] Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF): • Fanconi syndrome — polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, elevated creatinine [37] • Labs: acidemia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, glucosuria, proteinuria • Bone density loss and fractures • TAF (tenofovir alafenamide) has reduced renal and bone toxi

nodes.title: NNRTI Adverse Effects
nodes.summary: NNRTIs: hepatotoxicity (nevirapine), neuropsychiatric effects (efavirenz), rash
nodes.body: NNRTIs directly bind and inactivate HIV reverse transcriptase. Examples: efavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine, nevirapine, etravirine. Efavirenz — neuropsychiatric effects: • Vivid dreams, nightmares, insomnia, confusion (often resolve after first weeks) [55] • Severe cases: psychosis, suicidal ideation, attempted/completed suicide • Immediate discontinuation if severe psychosis or suicidality • Oft

nodes.title: Protease Inhibitor Adverse Effects
nodes.summary: PIs: atazanavir = radiolucent kidney stones (invisible on CT), CYP3A4 drug interactions
nodes.body: PIs prevent cleavage of essential polyproteins needed for mature HIV virion production. Most common today: atazanavir and darunavir, used with a booster (low-dose ritonavir or cobicistat). [13] Common side effects: Nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort. Metabolic effects: • Lipodystrophy (central fat accumulation, peripheral wasting) • Dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia • Type 2 diabetes (less co

nodes.title: INSTI & Entry Inhibitor Effects
nodes.summary: INSTIs: best tolerated class — insomnia, weight gain, rarely CPK elevation
nodes.body: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs): Block incorporation of viral DNA into host cell DNA. First-line for most patients. [12, 13] Examples: Biktarvy (bictegravir), Dolutegravir, elvitegravir/cobicistat, raltegravir. Generally very well tolerated — rare discontinuations in clinical trials. • ~90% of patients attain and maintain undetectable VL through 96 weeks [58] • Raltegravir has the lo

nodes.title: HBV Reactivation Risk — Stopping Therapy
nodes.summary: Stopping tenofovir/emtricitabine/lamivudine can cause fatal HBV reactivation — never abruptly stop
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Several NRTIs/NtRTIs have dual activity against HIV AND hepatitis B: • Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) • Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) • Emtricitabine (FTC) • Lamivudine (3TC) If a patient co-infected with HBV stops any of these medications, there is risk of acute hepatitis B flare — fatalities have been reported. [1, 36] ~10% of HIV patients are co-infected with HBV. [36] ED presentat
nodes.recommendation: HBV co-infection + ARV discontinuation → risk of fatal hepatitis flare. Provide supportive care, consult ID urgently for medication reinitiation. Never stop HAART for mild GI side effects.

nodes.title: Drug-Drug Interactions
nodes.summary: PIs inhibit CYP3A4 — dangerous interactions with benzodiazepines, statins, PDE5 inhibitors
nodes.body: PI-based regimens (especially boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat) carry the highest risk of drug interactions through CYP3A4 inhibition. [13] High-risk combinations in the ED: • Anticoagulants — warfarin, DOACs: altered metabolism • Statins — lovastatin and simvastatin contraindicated with PIs; use atorvastatin/rosuvastatin with dose adjustment • Corticosteroids — fluticasone + ritonavir → iatro

nodes.title: HIV Prevention — PEP & PrEP
nodes.summary: PEP within 72h of exposure, PrEP for ongoing risk — cross-link to PEP consult for protocols
nodes.body: The ED plays a vital role in preventing new HIV infections through PEP and PrEP awareness. [1, 60] Which prevention scenario?

nodes.title: Postexposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
nodes.summary: PEP: Biktarvy or TDF/FTC + dolutegravir x 28 days — start within 72h, ideally within 2h
nodes.body: PEP is most effective when given ASAP — ideally within 2 hours of exposure. NOT recommended when care is sought >72 hours after exposure. [60] Indications: Sexual exposure, needlestick/percutaneous, mucous membrane exposure, sexual assault. Preferred regimens (28 days): • Biktarvy 1 tablet daily — CDC 2025 preferred single-tablet regimen • TDF/FTC + Dolutegravir — equally effective, lower cost (of

nodes.title: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) Referral
nodes.summary: PrEP referral for ongoing risk: daily oral or long-acting injectable cabotegravir every 2 months
nodes.body: PrEP is highly effective: PROUD trial showed 86% relative risk reduction in HIV acquisition. IPREX and DISCOVER studies showed >90% reduction with daily adherence. [53, 54, 62] FDA-approved PrEP regimens: • TDF/FTC (Truvada®) — approved for all genders • TAF/FTC (Descovy®) — approved for MSM and transgender women only (women not studied) [54] PrEP follow-up protocol: • Daily medication, follow-up
nodes.recommendation: Refer appropriate patients to PrEP provider. Counsel on high effectiveness (>86% risk reduction) with daily adherence. Ensure baseline HIV test and renal function before starting.

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Determine: admission for acute illness vs discharge with close ID/PCP follow-up
nodes.body: Based on the clinical assessment, determine appropriate disposition.

nodes.title: Admission
nodes.summary: Admit for new OIs, severe dehydration, altered mental status, or inability to tolerate PO meds
nodes.body: Admission criteria: • Suspected or confirmed OI requiring inpatient treatment • Hemodynamic instability, sepsis, respiratory failure • CNS symptoms with concerning imaging or LP findings • New diagnosis with acute seroconversion illness and complications • Inability to tolerate oral medications • Social barriers to safe discharge and follow-up Orders: • Continue home HAART regimen (do NOT hold unl
nodes.recommendation: Admit for OI workup/treatment, acute illness, or inability to manage outpatient. Continue HAART, consult ID, check CD4/VL, screen HBV/HCV. Social work for linkage to care.

nodes.title: Discharge with Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Discharge with ID/PCP follow-up within 72h, medication reconciliation, and adherence counseling
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: • Stable vital signs, able to tolerate PO • No suspected OI requiring inpatient treatment • Well-controlled HIV with manageable complaint • Reliable follow-up available Discharge instructions: • Continue all HIV medications as prescribed — do NOT stop HAART • Follow up with HIV provider within 1-2 weeks (or sooner per complaint) • Return for worsening symptoms, new fever, inabi
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with continued HAART. Follow up with HIV provider. Link to care if not engaged. Offer HIV testing if untested. Refer for PEP/PrEP as indicated. Review Discharge Instructions with patient.

nodes.title: HOP Killers: Pre-Intubation Assessment
nodes.summary: Screen for 6 peri-intubation killers BEFORE RSI: hypotension, hypoxia, acidosis, RV failure, metabolic, ICP
nodes.body: Physiologically Difficult Airway: Standard RSI can kill patients with unstable physiology. The Original HOp Triad (Weingart): - Hypotension - Oxygenation failure (hypoxemia) - pH (severe acidosis) Expanded Killers: - Right Heart Failure (PE, pulmonary HTN) - Metabolic (hyperkalemia) - Elevated ICP Why Standard RSI Kills: 1. Sedatives drop SVR and sympathetic tone 2. PPV drops preload and cardiac o

nodes.title: Screen for Killers
nodes.summary: Systematic assessment: BP, SpO2, pH, RV function, K+/Ca2+, ICP signs — fix BEFORE paralysis
nodes.body: Before any high-risk intubation, screen systematically: | Question | Threshold | Killer | |----------|-----------|--------| | What is the SBP? | < 100 mmHg | Hypotension | | What is the SpO2? | < 93% on O2 | Hypoxemia | | What is the pH? | < 7.2 | Severe Acidosis | | Signs of RV failure? | JVD + hypotension | RV Failure | | What is the K+? | > 5.5 mEq/L | Metabolic | | Concern for elevated ICP? |

nodes.title: Multiple Simultaneous Killers
nodes.summary: Multiple killers present = highest risk — address each systematically before induction
nodes.body: Common Multi-Killer Scenarios: | Scenario | Killers | Key Approach | |----------|---------|-------------| | Septic shock + ARDS | Hypotension + Hypoxia | ROCKETamine + DSI + push pressors | | DKA + respiratory failure | Acidosis + Hypoxia | VAPOX + high RR vent settings | | Massive PE | Hypoxia + RV + Hypotension | Awake if possible, pressors, low PEEP | | TBI + hemorrhage | ICP + Hypotension | Ke

nodes.title: Killer #1: Hypotension
nodes.summary: Hypotension + induction agents = cardiac arrest risk — volume resuscitate and start pressors BEFORE RSI
nodes.body: Why RSI Kills the Hypotensive Patient: 1. Sedatives drop SVR - Even ketamine can cause hypotension in catecholamine-depleted patients 2. PPV drops preload - Positive pressure reduces venous return 3. Loss of sympathetic drive - Critically ill patients rely on endogenous catecholamines High-Risk Patients: - Septic shock (vasodilated, preload-dependent) - Hemorrhagic shock (hypovolemic) - Cardiogeni

nodes.title: Pre-Intubation Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Push-dose epinephrine ready, norepinephrine running, 500mL fluid bolus before blade touches lip
nodes.body: Optimize BEFORE Intubation: | Target | Goal | Why | |--------|------|-----| | MAP | > 65 mmHg (ideally > 75) | Buffer for post-induction drop | | SBP | > 140 mmHg | Provides hemodynamic reserve | | Volume | 1-2L crystalloid if hypovolemic | Optimize preload | | Access | 2 large-bore proximal IVs | Rapid fluid/pressor access | | Pressors | Running BEFORE induction | Already infusing, not scrambling

nodes.title: ROCKETamine Protocol
nodes.summary: Rocketamine (ketamine + rocuronium) preserves hemodynamics — avoid propofol in hypotension
nodes.body: Shock Dose RSI: Dose sedatives LOW, paralytics HIGH | Medication | Standard Dose | Shock Dose | Notes | |------------|---------------|------------|-------| | Ketamine | 1-2 mg/kg | 0.5 mg/kg | Add 0.5 mg/kg PRN until sedated | | Rocuronium | 1.0-1.2 mg/kg | 1.6 mg/kg | Higher dose = faster onset, longer safe apnea | Why Ketamine? - Least cardio-depressant induction agent - Maintains SVR via sympat

nodes.title: Push-Dose Pressors
nodes.summary: Push-dose epi 10-20 mcg q2-5min for post-induction hypotension — have vasopressor infusion ready
nodes.body: Epinephrine (Preferred): Preparation: 1. Draw 1 mL cardiac epinephrine (1:10,000 = 100 mcg/mL) 2. Add to 9 mL NS in 10 mL syringe 3. Mix thoroughly 4. Final concentration: 10 mcg/mL Dosing: - 0.5-2 mL (5-20 mcg) IV push q2-5 min PRN - Prophylactic: 5 mcg (0.5 mL) with induction meds - Onset: < 1 min | Duration: ~5 min Phenylephrine (if tachycardia a concern): - 1 mL (10 mg/mL) + 99 mL NS = 100 mcg

nodes.title: Post-Intubation Hypotension
nodes.summary: Post-intubation MAP target ≥65 — immediate vasopressor bolus if BP drops after induction
nodes.body: Immediate Actions: 1. Start norepinephrine infusion immediately - Can run peripherally via proximal IV up to 4 hours - Start 5-10 mcg/min, titrate to MAP > 65 2. Continue push-dose pressors as bridge while infusion takes effect 3. Expedite central line but do not delay vasopressors 4. Consider volume if truly hypovolemic (avoid in cardiogenic shock) Awake Intubation Alternative: - Consider for pro
nodes.recommendation: ROCKETamine (ketamine 0.5 mg/kg + rocuronium 1.6 mg/kg), push-dose epinephrine with induction, have vasopressor infusion primed.

nodes.title: Killer #2: Hypoxemia
nodes.summary: Desaturation during apneic period is the most common peri-intubation emergency
nodes.body: Why RSI Kills the Hypoxic Patient: 1. Cannot tolerate apnea - Shunt physiology (ARDS, pneumonia) = desaturation in seconds 2. Cannot preoxygenate adequately - Agitated hypoxic patients fight masks 3. Desaturation during laryngoscopy - Even brief attempts cause critical hypoxemia High-Risk Patients: - ARDS - Severe pneumonia - Pulmonary edema - Morbid obesity - Pulmonary embolism - Any SpO2 < 93% d

nodes.title: NODESAT Protocol
nodes.summary: Preoxygenate for 3-5 min: NRB 15L + NC 15L (dual oxygenation) — target SpO2 >95% before paralysis
nodes.body: N-O-D-E-S-A-T: | Letter | Intervention | Details | |--------|--------------|--------| | N | Nasal O2 | 15 lpm NC or HFNC 60 lpm | | O | Optimal positioning | Head elevated, ramped | | D | Delayed Sequence Intubation | If patient won't cooperate | | E | End-tidal CO2 | Baseline before paralysis | | S | Suction ready | At hand, tested | | A | Apneic oxygenation | NC stays on during laryngoscopy | |

nodes.title: Delayed Sequence Intubation (DSI)
nodes.summary: Delayed sequence intubation: ketamine dissociation first, then preoxygenate the compliant patient
nodes.body: Concept: Procedural sedation for preoxygenation. The "procedure" IS effective preoxygenation. Indications: - Agitated/delirious hypoxic patient unable to tolerate mask - SpO2 < 93% despite maximal preoxygenation attempts - Patient fighting NIV/mask DSI Protocol: 1. Push ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV (or dexmedetomidine 1 mcg/kg over 10 min) 2. Wait 30-60 seconds for dissociation 3. Apply preoxygenation (N

nodes.title: Apneic Oxygenation
nodes.summary: NC at 15 L/min during apnea — extends safe apnea time by 3-5 minutes
nodes.body: Keep NC in place during laryngoscopy - this is the key intervention. | Method | Flow Rate | Evidence | |--------|-----------|----------| | Standard NC | 15 lpm | Effective, widely available | | HFNC | 60 lpm | Longer safe apnea (11 vs 7 min), no superiority for preventing desaturation | HFNC Settings (if available): - Flow: 60 lpm - FiO2: 100% - Provides moderate PEEP + dead space washout Evidence

nodes.title: Hypoxic Intubation Summary
nodes.summary: If SpO2 <93% during attempt: BVM ventilate, reposition, reattempt — abort if cannot ventilate
nodes.body: NODESAT + DSI Summary: 1. Nasal cannula 15 lpm - Leave on throughout 2. Position head-up 20-30 degrees 3. DSI with ketamine if patient not cooperating 4. Preoxygenate 3+ minutes to SpO2 > 95% 5. Document ETCO2 before paralysis 6. Push paralytic only when adequately preoxygenated 7. Apneic oxygenation - NC stays on during attempt Post-Intubation: - Confirm with ETCO2 - Lung-protective ventilation (
nodes.recommendation: DSI with ketamine, NODESAT protocol, apneic oxygenation with NC 15 lpm during laryngoscopy.

nodes.title: Killer #3: Severe Acidosis
nodes.summary: Severe metabolic acidosis + apnea = lethal cardiac arrest — match pre-intubation minute ventilation
nodes.body: Why RSI Kills the Acidotic Patient: 1. Respiratory compensation lost during apnea - CO2 rises 3-6 mmHg/min, pH crashes 2. Even brief apnea is dangerous - Seconds can worsen pH enough to cause dysrhythmias 3. Post-intubation vent mismanagement - Standard settings (RR 12, TV 500) do not maintain needed minute ventilation High-Risk Patients: - DKA (especially pH < 7.1) - Sepsis with severe lactic aci

nodes.title: Winter's Formula & Target MV
nodes.summary: Calculate expected PaCO2 with Winter's formula — post-intubation ventilator must match this
nodes.body: Calculate Expected Compensatory PaCO2: Winter's Equation: `` Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 x HCO3) + 8 (+/- 2) `` Example: pH 6.9, HCO3 5 mEq/L - Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 x 5) + 8 = 15.5 mmHg - Patient must maintain PaCO2 of 13-18 to compensate - Standard vent settings (PaCO2 ~40) would be catastrophic Key Principle: Before intubating, know what PaCO2 the patient is maintaining and what minute ventilation yo

nodes.title: VAPOX Technique
nodes.summary: VAPOX: Vent to Avoid Peri-intubation Oxygen Desaturation and X-tra CO2 retention
nodes.body: Ventilator-Assisted Pre-Oxygenation: Equipment: - ICU ventilator at bedside (NOT a BiPAP machine) - NIV mask - Someone who can adjust vent in real time Pre-Intubation Settings (Pseudo-NIV Phase): | Parameter | Setting | Rationale | |-----------|---------|----------| | Mode | SIMV | Allows spontaneous breaths | | TV | 550 mL (8 mL/kg IBW) | Standard | | FiO2 | 100% | Maximize oxygenation | | Flow R

nodes.title: During RSI - Apneic Phase
nodes.summary: Ketamine preferred — avoid propofol (vasodilation worsens acidosis hemodynamics)
nodes.body: After pushing induction + paralytic: 1. Increase RR to 12 on ventilator 2. Perform jaw thrust to maintain airway 3. Wait 45 seconds for medication onset 4. The ventilator is breathing for the patient through the NIV mask during apneic window This is the key innovation: You're not truly apneic because the vent is providing breaths through the mask while you wait for paralytic onset. Once intubated,

nodes.title: Post-Intubation Vent Settings
nodes.summary: Set RR 20-30 to match pre-intubation compensatory minute ventilation — never start at RR 12
nodes.body: Immediately after tube placement: | Parameter | Setting | Notes | |-----------|---------|-------| | RR | 30 breaths/min | Match pre-intubation hyperventilation | | TV | 8 mL/kg IBW | Standard | | Flow Rate | 60 lpm | Standard intubated setting | | FiO2 | 100% initially | Wean as tolerated | Target: ETCO2 at least as low as it was before intubation GET ABG URGENTLY post-intubation - Do not wait! So
nodes.recommendation: VAPOX technique, post-intubation RR 30, match pre-intubation ETCO2, urgent ABG.

nodes.title: Killer #4: Right Heart Failure
nodes.summary: RV failure + positive pressure ventilation = cardiac arrest — minimize PEEP and intrathoracic pressure
nodes.body: Why RSI Kills the RV Failure Patient: 1. PPV increases RV afterload - Positive intrathoracic pressure transmitted to pulmonary vasculature 2. PPV drops RV preload - Reduced venous return to already struggling RV 3. Sedatives drop SVR - RV perfusion depends on systemic pressure The RV Death Spiral: ↑ RV afterload → RV dilation → Septal shift → ↓ LV filling → ↓ Cardiac output → ↓ Coronary perfusion

nodes.title: Avoid Intubation If Possible
nodes.summary: Avoid hyperinflation, high PEEP, hypoxia, and acidosis — all worsen PVR and crash the RV
nodes.body: AVOID INTUBATION IF AT ALL POSSIBLE Intubation is truly a last resort in RV failure patients. First, try: - NIV/CPAP - Basic airway maneuvers - Treat underlying cause (thrombolytics for PE, diuresis) Avoid These (Worsen RV Failure): | Avoid | Why | |-------|-----| | Hypoxia | Pulmonary vasoconstriction | | Hypercarbia | Pulmonary vasoconstriction | | Acidosis | Pulmonary vasoconstriction | | Propo

nodes.title: Pre-Intubation Stabilization
nodes.summary: Start vasopressors before intubation, have push-dose epi ready, gentle BVM ventilation
nodes.body: If intubation unavoidable, stabilize first: | Intervention | Details | Rationale | |--------------|---------|----------| | Vasopressors running | Norepinephrine or epinephrine infusion | Maintain systemic pressure > pulmonary | | Push-dose pressors ready | Epinephrine 10 mcg/mL syringes | Immediate hemodynamic support | | Avoid fluid boluses | Most RV failure patients are volume OVERLOADED | Fluid

nodes.title: Induction Strategy
nodes.summary: Ketamine for RV failure — maintain SVR, avoid myocardial depression
nodes.body: Awake Intubation Probably Preferred - Maintains spontaneous ventilation and endogenous catecholamines. If RSI Required: - Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg (maintains SVR) - Vasopressors infusing BEFORE induction - Push-dose epinephrine WITH induction meds Pulmonary Vasodilators (consider immediately post-intubation): | Agent | Route | Dose | Notes | |-------|-------|------|-------| | Inhaled nitric oxide | Via

nodes.title: Post-Intubation Ventilator Strategy
nodes.summary: Low PEEP (≤5), low Vt, avoid breath-stacking — permissive hypercapnia acceptable
nodes.body: RV-Protective Ventilator Settings: | Parameter | Target | Rationale | |-----------|--------|----------| | PEEP | Low (5-8 cmH2O) | Minimize RV afterload increase | | TV | 6-8 mL/kg | Avoid over-distension | | Pplat | < 30 cmH2O | Minimize transpulmonary pressure | | FiO2 | 100% initially | Oxygen is original pulmonary vasodilator | | RR | Adequate to avoid hypercarbia | CO2 is pulmonary vasoconstr
nodes.recommendation: Awake intubation if possible. If RSI: ketamine, vasopressors running, low PEEP post-intubation.

nodes.title: Killer #5: Metabolic (Hyperkalemia)
nodes.summary: Hyperkalemia + succinylcholine = lethal — always use rocuronium if K+ elevated
nodes.body: Why RSI Kills the Hyperkalemic Patient: Succinylcholine raises K+ ~0.5 mEq/L - In borderline patients, this can trigger fatal arrhythmias. Succinylcholine-Induced Cardiac Arrest: Well documented in patients with unrecognized hyperkalemia. AVOID SUCCINYLCHOLINE in: | Condition | Time Frame | Why | |-----------|------------|-----| | Hyperkalemia (K+ > 5.5) | Current | Additional K+ may be fatal | |

nodes.title: Pre-Intubation Hyperkalemia Treatment
nodes.summary: Calcium, insulin/dextrose, bicarb BEFORE induction if severe hyperkalemia — correct hypocalcemia too
nodes.body: Stabilize the membrane and shift K+ BEFORE intubation: | Intervention | Dose | Onset | Duration | Mechanism | |--------------|------|-------|----------|----------| | Calcium gluconate | 1-2 g IV over 5-10 min | 1-3 min | 30-60 min | Membrane stabilization | | Calcium chloride | 1 g IV (central line) | 1-3 min | 30-60 min | 3x more elemental Ca | | Regular insulin | 5 units IV (10 units if normal r

nodes.title: Paralytic Selection
nodes.summary: Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg — NEVER succinylcholine in hyperkalemia, burns, crush, or neuromuscular disease
nodes.body: Use Rocuronium, Not Succinylcholine: | Agent | Dose | Onset | Notes | |-------|------|-------|-------| | Rocuronium | 1.2 mg/kg | 60 seconds | No K+ release, safe in hyperkalemia | | Rocuronium | 1.6 mg/kg | 45 seconds | Higher dose for faster onset (shock) | Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg has equivalent onset to succinylcholine with longer duration. Key Points: - Rocuronium is the default paralytic for any
nodes.recommendation: Treat hyperkalemia first (calcium, insulin/glucose), use rocuronium 1.2-1.6 mg/kg instead of succinylcholine.

nodes.title: Killer #6: Elevated ICP
nodes.summary: Elevated ICP: prevent secondary brain injury during intubation — avoid hypotension and hypoxia
nodes.body: Why RSI Kills the Elevated ICP Patient: 1. Laryngoscopy raises ICP - Sympathetic response to airway manipulation 2. Hypotension drops CPP - CPP = MAP - ICP. If MAP drops while ICP elevated, brain suffers 3. Hypoxia worsens secondary injury - Injured brain is exquisitely sensitive 4. Hypercarbia increases ICP - CO2 is a cerebral vasodilator High-Risk Patients: - Traumatic brain injury (TBI) - Strok

nodes.title: Ketamine in Elevated ICP: Dogma Debunked
nodes.summary: Ketamine is safe in elevated ICP (debunked myth) — maintains hemodynamics and cerebral perfusion
nodes.body: Traditional Teaching: Ketamine raises ICP and is contraindicated in TBI. Current Evidence: This is NOT supported by modern studies. | Finding | Source | |---------|--------| | Ketamine does NOT increase ICP | Zeiler et al. systematic review | | Safe in intubated AND non-intubated TBI | Multiple studies | | May be neuroprotective | NMDA receptor antagonism | | Maintains hemodynamic stability | Crit

nodes.title: Induction Agent Selection
nodes.summary: Blunt sympathetic response: lidocaine 1.5mg/kg or fentanyl 3mcg/kg before laryngoscopy
nodes.body: Agent Options: | Agent | Dose | Considerations | |-------|------|----------------| | Etomidate | 0.3 mg/kg | Traditional choice, minimal hemodynamic effect | | Ketamine | 0.5-1 mg/kg | Safe in TBI, maintains hemodynamics | | Propofol | 1-2 mg/kg | Reduces ICP but causes hypotension | | Propofol/Ketamine | 75%/25% | Balanced approach | Pretreatment: - Fentanyl 3-5 mcg/kg IV 3-5 minutes before laryn

nodes.title: Post-Intubation ICP Management
nodes.summary: Post-intubation: HOB 30 degrees, midline head, target PaCO2 35-40, MAP >80
nodes.body: Post-Intubation Targets: | Parameter | Target | Notes | |-----------|--------|-------| | Head of bed | 30-45 degrees | Promotes venous drainage | | SpO2 | > 95% | Avoid hypoxia | | PEEP | Minimize (only as needed) | High PEEP can impair venous drainage | | ETCO2 | 35 mmHg | Then get ABG for PaCO2 | | PaCO2 | 35-40 mmHg | AVOID hyperventilation unless herniating | | Sedation | Propofol + fentanyl |
nodes.recommendation: Ketamine safe in TBI, maintain MAP > 80, avoid hyperventilation (target PaCO2 35-40), head of bed 30 degrees.

nodes.title: HOP Killers: Pre-Intubation Checklist
nodes.summary: Fix killers BEFORE paralysis — hypotension, hypoxia, acidosis, RV failure, metabolic, ICP
nodes.body: Before ANY high-risk intubation, systematically assess: | Killer | Screen | If Present | |--------|--------|------------| | Hypotension | SBP < 100? On pressors? | ROCKETamine + push pressors | | Hypoxemia | SpO2 < 93%? | DSI + apneic oxygenation | | Acidosis | pH < 7.2? | VAPOX + high RR vent settings | | RV Failure | JVD? PE? Pulm HTN? | Awake intubation, low PEEP | | Metabolic | K+ > 5.5? | Roc
nodes.recommendation: Identify all physiologic derangements before intubation. Address each killer with specific modifications to RSI technique.

nodes.title: Hypertension in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: 10% of pregnancies. Stroke (not seizure) is #1 preeclampsia death cause — treat severe BP <30–60 min. Active seizure → Eclampsia consult.
nodes.body: HTN in Pregnancy Steps Summary Hypertensive disorders complicate ~10% of pregnancies and are a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality in the US. [1,2] This consult covers the full spectrum: • Chronic hypertension (pre-pregnancy or <20 weeks) • Gestational hypertension (new HTN ≥20 weeks, no proteinuria/end-organ) • Preeclampsia — without and with severe features • Superimposed preeclamp

nodes.title: Definitions — ACOG 2020
nodes.summary: Severe-range = SBP≥160 or DBP≥110. Preeclampsia = HTN + proteinuria or end-organ. Superimposed = highest risk.
nodes.body: Hypertension thresholds: [1] | Category | BP / Timing | |----------|-------------| | Non-severe | SBP 140–159 OR DBP 90–109 on ≥2 occasions ≥4 h apart | | Severe-range | SBP ≥160 OR DBP ≥110 — confirm within minutes (not hours) if sustained | Chronic HTN: HTN diagnosed before pregnancy OR <20 weeks OR persists >12 weeks postpartum. Gestational HTN: New HTN ≥20 weeks, no proteinuria, no end-organ d

nodes.title: Severe Features of Preeclampsia
nodes.summary: Severe = SBP≥160/DBP≥110, plt<100K, LFTs >2×, Cr>1.1 or doubled, pulm edema, new HA/visual. IUGR/proteinuria no longer severity markers.
nodes.body: ANY one feature = preeclampsia with severe features → magnesium + expedited delivery planning. [1] Severe-range BP • SBP ≥160 OR DBP ≥110 on 2 readings ≥4 h apart (or sooner if antihypertensives started) Thrombocytopenia • Platelets <100,000/µL Hepatic • AST or ALT >2× upper limit of normal • Severe persistent RUQ/epigastric pain unresponsive to meds, not explained by other diagnosis Renal • Serum

nodes.title: Clinical Scenario
nodes.summary: Triage: active seizure → Eclampsia tree, severe BP → treat now, non-severe → workup, postpartum, or ASA prophylaxis.
nodes.body: What is the presenting scenario? [1,3]

nodes.title: Active Seizure — Go to Eclampsia Consult
nodes.summary: Eclampsia is in its own tree — navigate there. Start mag load and treat severe BP in parallel while en route.
nodes.body: Active eclamptic seizure management is covered in the dedicated Eclampsia consult. [6] Open: Eclampsia consult Immediate actions while you navigate there: [6] • Left lateral decubitus position, protect airway — do NOT put anything in the mouth • High-flow O₂ by NRB, pulse ox, continuous monitoring • 2 large-bore IVs, labs including CBC, CMP, LFTs, uric acid, coags, type and screen, Mg level • Star
nodes.recommendation: Navigate to the Eclampsia consult for full seizure management. Start magnesium load and treat severe BP in parallel.

nodes.title: Workup — Labs & Assessment
nodes.summary: CBC, Cr, LFTs, LDH, uric acid, UA + spot protein/Cr, T&S. Do NOT require proteinuria to diagnose severe preeclampsia.
nodes.body: Baseline preeclampsia labs (draw on every patient with new or worsening HTN ≥20 wk): [1] | Test | Why | |------|-----| | CBC with smear | Platelets <100K = severe feature. Schistocytes = HELLP/MAHA. Hemoconcentration = 3rd-spacing. | | Serum creatinine | >1.1 mg/dL or doubling = severe feature. Oliguria — AKI. | | AST, ALT, LDH | >2× ULN = severe feature. LDH >600 = HELLP hemolysis marker. | | Uri

nodes.title: Fetal Assessment
nodes.summary: Continuous EFM, growth + AFI + UA Doppler US. Betamethasone 23–34 wk if delivery within 7 d — do not delay delivery for steroids if deteriorating.
nodes.body: Every HTN-in-pregnancy evaluation includes fetal assessment. [1,7] Continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) when viable (≥23–24 weeks): • Baseline 20–30 min tracing • Watch for late decels, minimal variability, bradycardia Obstetric US — order when BP changes or clinical worsening: • Fetal growth (EFW, AC, HC) — IUGR/SGA raises preeclampsia suspicion • AFI / deepest vertical pocket — oligohydr

nodes.title: Classify the Disorder
nodes.summary: Classify: chronic, gestational, preeclampsia ± severe, superimposed, or HELLP. Severe features override everything.
nodes.body: Based on history + workup, which category fits best? [1] Tip: Severe features override everything — if any present, go to severe-features management regardless of subtype.

nodes.title: Severe-Range BP — Act Now
nodes.summary: Severe-range = ≥160/110. Treat within 30–60 min. Target 140–150/90–100. Stroke > seizure as cause of death. Don't drop MAP >25% in 1 h.
nodes.body: Severe-range BP = SBP ≥160 OR DBP ≥110. Persistent for ≥15 min = hypertensive emergency. [3,8] Why this is a true emergency: • Hemorrhagic stroke is the leading cause of maternal death from preeclampsia (SBP is the better predictor than DBP). [8] • Placental abruption, pulmonary edema, and cardiac failure risk climb sharply. Goals: • Target BP: 140–150 / 90–100 mmHg — do NOT chase "normal" BP. [3]

nodes.title: Choose First-Line Agent
nodes.summary: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or PO nifedipine IR — all first-line. Pick by access, contraindications, prior response.
nodes.body: All three are acceptable ACOG-endorsed first-line options. [3] Choose based on access, contraindications, and prior response.

nodes.title: Labetalol Protocol
nodes.summary: Labetalol 20/40/80/80 mg IV q10min, max 300 mg. Avoid in asthma, bradycardia, HF.
nodes.body: Labetalol IV — combined α₁ + β blocker (β:α ≈ 7:1). [3] Escalating ACOG protocol: | Step | Dose | Wait | If still ≥160/110 | |------|------|------|--------------------| | 1 | 20 mg IV over 2 min | 10 min | Step 2 | | 2 | 40 mg IV | 10 min | Step 3 | | 3 | 80 mg IV | 10 min | Step 4 | | 4 | 80 mg IV | 10 min | Switch to hydralazine | Maximum cumulative: 300 mg. If BP uncontrolled after protocol → s

nodes.title: Hydralazine Protocol
nodes.summary: Hydralazine 5–10 mg IV q20min, max 30 mg. Slower, reflex tachycardia — pre-load NS if volume-down.
nodes.body: Hydralazine IV — direct arteriolar vasodilator. [3] ACOG protocol: | Step | Dose | Wait | If still ≥160/110 | |------|------|------|--------------------| | 1 | 5–10 mg IV over 2 min | 20 min | Step 2 | | 2 | 10 mg IV | 20 min | Step 3 | | 3 | Switch to labetalol 20 mg IV | 10 min | Continue labetalol protocol | Maximum cumulative: 30 mg (some protocols up to 40 mg) before switching agents. Onset 1

nodes.title: Nifedipine IR Protocol
nodes.summary: Nifedipine IR 10 → 20 → 20 mg PO q20min. Safe with mag. NEVER sublingual.
nodes.body: Nifedipine IR PO — oral dihydropyridine CCB. [3] Use when: • IV access is delayed or unavailable • Patient tolerates PO, no active seizing, not NPO for delivery • Patient preference ACOG protocol: | Step | Dose | Wait | If still ≥160/110 | |------|------|------|--------------------| | 1 | 10 mg PO | 20 min | Step 2 | | 2 | 20 mg PO | 20 min | Step 3 | | 3 | 20 mg PO | 20 min | Switch to labetalol

nodes.title: BP Response
nodes.summary: Controlled → maintenance, uncontrolled → switch agent, refractory → infusion + delivery planning.
nodes.body: After escalating doses of first-line agent, what is the status?

nodes.title: After BP Controlled — Maintain
nodes.summary: Transition to PO: labetalol 200 mg q8–12h, nifedipine XL 30–60 mg daily. Avoid ACE-i/ARB/atenolol. Target <140/90 (CHAP).
nodes.body: BP controlled in the acute setting. Now consolidate. [3] Continue IV agent PRN for breakthrough severe-range BP — have next dose ready. Transition to scheduled oral agent for ongoing control: • Labetalol 200 mg PO q8–12 h (max 2400 mg/day) • Nifedipine XL 30–60 mg PO daily (extended release) • Methyldopa 250 mg PO q8 h (less commonly used acutely due to slow onset) Goal maintenance BP: <140/90 (pe

nodes.title: Switch First-Line Agent
nodes.summary: Labetalol ↔ hydralazine ↔ nifedipine in sequence. Don't stack. If BP drops: stop infusion, left lateral, 250–500 mL NS.
nodes.body: If one first-line agent at max dose fails, switch to another before jumping to an infusion. [3] From labetalol → hydralazine 10 mg IV (wait 20 min, then escalate). From hydralazine → labetalol 20 mg IV (wait 10 min, then escalate as before). From nifedipine → labetalol 20 mg IV (best-characterized IV data if PO failed). Do not stack full doses of two agents in parallel — risk of abrupt hypotension

nodes.title: Refractory Severe HTN
nodes.summary: Labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine infusion in ICU. Refractory BP = indication for delivery. Avoid nitroprusside >4 h.
nodes.body: Refractory = severe-range BP despite ≥2 first-line agents at max doses. [3] Continuous IV infusion options (ICU-level monitoring, arterial line preferred): Labetalol infusion • Start 1–2 mg/min IV, titrate to target • Typical: 20 mg bolus → 1–2 mg/min infusion Nicardipine infusion • Start 5 mg/hr IV, titrate by 2.5 mg/hr every 5–15 min • Max 15 mg/hr • Preferred if β-blocker contraindicated Clevid

nodes.title: Chronic Hypertension — Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Chronic HTN: treat to <140/90 (CHAP). Labetalol/nifedipine/methyldopa. ASA 81 mg 12–28 wk. Avoid ACE-i/ARB/atenolol/thiazides.
nodes.body: Chronic HTN in pregnancy = known HTN before pregnancy OR new HTN <20 wk OR persists >12 wk postpartum. [11] Risks (vs normotensive pregnancy): • 17–25% develop superimposed preeclampsia • 2–3× higher rates of placental abruption, preterm birth, IUGR, cesarean BP Treatment Threshold — updated by CHAP trial (NEJM 2022): [10] • Treat to <140/90 for ALL chronic HTN in pregnancy (not just severe) • CHA

nodes.title: Gestational Hypertension
nodes.summary: Gestational HTN: 15–25% progress to preeclampsia. Treat to <140/90. Deliver at 37 wk if stable.
nodes.body: Gestational HTN = new HTN ≥20 wk, no proteinuria, no end-organ dysfunction. [1] Natural history: • 15–25% progress to preeclampsia — follow closely with serial BPs + UA • Higher progression rate if diagnosed <32 wk • Should resolve by 12 weeks postpartum — otherwise reclassify as chronic HTN Outpatient management (if eligible): • BP check 2×/week (home cuff + office) • Weekly labs (CBC, CMP, LFTs,

nodes.title: Preeclampsia — No Severe Features
nodes.summary: PE w/o severe features: monitor, deliver at 37 wk. Mag NOT routine. BP meds only if persistently ≥140/90.
nodes.body: Preeclampsia without severe features = HTN ≥20 wk + proteinuria (≥300 mg/24 h or protein/Cr ≥0.3) OR end-organ findings below severe thresholds. [1] Confirm NO severe features present: Re-scan the list — BP <160/110, plt ≥100K, LFTs <2× ULN, Cr ≤1.1, no pulmonary edema, no new CNS symptoms. Management: • Admission for initial evaluation is usually prudent; select stable patients may be managed out

nodes.title: Preeclampsia with Severe Features
nodes.summary: Severe PE: control BP + mag + labs q6–12h + fetal monitoring + steroids (if <34 wk) + MFM. Deliver at 34 wk unless instability.
nodes.body: Any severe feature → preeclampsia with severe features → admit, magnesium, expedite delivery planning. [1] Immediate priorities: 1. Control severe-range BP (see Severe-Range BP module) — target 140–150/90–100 2. Start magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (next node) 3. Labs q6–12 h — CBC, CMP, LFTs, LDH, uric acid 4. Continuous fetal monitoring 5. Antenatal steroids if 23–34 wk and delivery e

nodes.title: Magnesium for Seizure Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Mag 4–6 g IV load, 1–2 g/hr ×24h postpartum. Monitor DTRs, RR, UOP, Mg q6h. Antidote: calcium gluconate 1 g IV.
nodes.body: Magnesium sulfate — seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features. [14] MAGPIE trial (Lancet 2002): 50% reduction in eclampsia risk (NNT ~100 severe preeclampsia, ~50 with features). Standard protocol: • Loading: 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min (typical: 4 g in 100 mL NS over 20 min) • Maintenance: 1–2 g/hr IV continuous infusion × 24 h after delivery OR after last seizure • IM alternative (lim

nodes.title: Superimposed Preeclampsia
nodes.summary: Chronic HTN + new proteinuria/severe feature/uncontrolled BP. Highest-risk. Same severe-features management; deliver 34–37 wk.
nodes.body: Superimposed preeclampsia = chronic HTN PLUS any of: [1,11] • New-onset proteinuria (≥300 mg/24 h or protein/Cr ≥0.3) after 20 weeks • Sudden worsening of BP requiring higher antihypertensive doses • Thrombocytopenia, elevated LFTs, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, new CNS symptoms (i.e., any severe feature) Highest-risk subgroup — higher rates of preterm delivery, abruption, IUGR, and severe

nodes.title: Delivery Timing Summary
nodes.summary: Deliver: chronic 38–39 wk, gestational/PE-no-severe 37 wk, PE-severe 34 wk, HELLP after stabilization. Vaginal OK — cesarean not mandatory.
nodes.body: Delivery is the definitive treatment for all HTN-in-pregnancy spectrum disorders. [1,13] | Diagnosis | Target GA for Delivery | |-----------|------------------------| | Chronic HTN, well-controlled, no complications | 38 0/7 – 39 6/7 weeks | | Chronic HTN on meds | 37 0/7 – 39 0/7 weeks | | Gestational HTN | 37 0/7 weeks | | Preeclampsia — no severe features | 37 0/7 weeks | | Preeclampsia — sever

nodes.title: HELLP Syndrome
nodes.summary: HELLP: LDH>600, AST/ALT>2×ULN, plt<100K. 10–20% of PE; 15–20% without HTN. Look for subcapsular hematoma if RUQ pain + ↓Hgb.
nodes.body: HELLP = Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets. Complicates 10–20% of preeclampsia cases; 15–20% present WITHOUT hypertension or proteinuria. [15] Diagnostic criteria (Tennessee classification): [15] • Hemolysis — LDH >600, schistocytes on smear, indirect bilirubin elevated • EL — AST or ALT >2× upper limit of normal • LP — Platelets <100,000/µL Mississippi classification (severity): | C

nodes.title: HELLP Management
nodes.summary: HELLP: mag + BP + platelets <20K or <50K if bleeding + deliver. Labs nadir 24–48h postpartum. 20–30% HELLP presents postpartum.
nodes.body: Management principles: [15] Maternal stabilization: • Same BP control as severe preeclampsia (labetalol/hydralazine/nifedipine → target 140–150/90–100) • Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis — load 4–6 g IV, maintenance 1–2 g/hr through 24 h postpartum • Serial labs q4–6 h in acute phase (CBC, LDH, AST/ALT, Cr, fibrinogen, coags) • Type and crossmatch, consider blood products: - Platelets <20K re

nodes.title: Postpartum Hypertension
nodes.summary: BP peaks 3–6 d postpartum. 55% postpartum PE had no antepartum PE. Up to 6 wk window. BP check 3–7 d post. ACE-i OK postpartum.
nodes.body: Most maternal deaths from preeclampsia occur postpartum. [4,16] Why it matters: • BP often peaks 3–6 days postpartum — autotransfusion + mobilization of extravascular fluid • Up to 55% of postpartum preeclampsia occurs in patients without antepartum preeclampsia • Risk window extends to 6 weeks postpartum — patients routinely present to ED with severe headache, vision changes, or seizure days/week

nodes.title: Aspirin Prophylaxis — Future Pregnancies
nodes.summary: ASA 81 mg daily 12–28 wk for ≥1 high-risk factor or ≥2 moderate-risk. Cuts PE ~15%. Counsel every prior-PE patient for next pregnancy.
nodes.body: Low-dose aspirin prevents preeclampsia in high-risk patients. [12,17] USPSTF + ACOG recommendation (2021): • 81 mg PO daily, started 12–28 weeks (ideally <16 weeks), continued until delivery • Reduces preeclampsia by ~15% and preterm birth by ~10% • Safety well established — no increase in abruption, PPH, or fetal bleeding High-risk (≥1 factor → prescribe aspirin): [12] • History of preeclampsia (

nodes.title: Discharge & Return Precautions
nodes.summary: Discharge: BP log, recheck 3–7 d, med rec, breastfeeding-compatible agents. Return for BP≥160/110, HA, visual, RUQ, dyspnea, seizure, ↓FM.
nodes.body: Before discharge, every HTN-in-pregnancy patient needs: [1,16] BP plan: • Written BP log (home cuff, properly sized) • BP recheck at 3–7 days post-discharge with OB • Target outpatient BP <140/90 (most protocols) Medication reconciliation: • Clear list of current antihypertensives with doses • Breastfeeding compatibility confirmed (labetalol, nifedipine XL, enalapril, captopril OK; avoid atenolol)

nodes.title: Disposition & Plan
nodes.summary: Disposition by severity. Stroke>seizure as killer. Mag only for severe features. Delivery is definitive. Eclampsia = separate tree.
nodes.body: Disposition summary: | Scenario | Disposition | |----------|-------------| | Chronic HTN, stable, <140/90 on meds, no severe features | Outpatient OB follow-up | | Gestational HTN, stable | Outpatient with 2×/wk BP + labs weekly; admit for severe features or fetal concern | | Preeclampsia — no severe features | Usually admit for initial evaluation; select patients to outpatient with close follow-u
nodes.recommendation: Match disposition to severity (see table). Admit L&D for any severe features; ICU for refractory BP, pulmonary edema, or multi-organ dysfunction. Delivery is definitive.

nodes.title: Human Trafficking Screening
nodes.summary: ED may be the only healthcare contact for trafficking victims — screen with universal protocol
nodes.body: Human trafficking occurs in every community — including yours. Definition: Use of force, fraud, or coercion to exploit a person for labor or commercial sex. For minors, ANY commercial sex is trafficking regardless of force/fraud/coercion. Two main types: • Sex trafficking — commercial sex acts induced by force, fraud, or coercion • Labor trafficking — forced labor through similar means ED relevanc

nodes.summary: Trafficking affects all demographics — children, immigrants, runaways, LGBTQ youth at highest risk
nodes.body: Trafficking affects all demographics: Vulnerable populations: • Runaway/homeless youth • LGBTQ+ youth (especially those rejected by family) • Foster care involvement • History of abuse/neglect • Undocumented immigrants • Substance use disorders • Intellectual/developmental disabilities • Economic vulnerability Traffickers can be: • Intimate partners • Family members • Employers • "Boyfriends" / Ro

nodes.summary: Red flags: controlling companion, inconsistent history, multiple STIs, branding/tattoos, fear of authority
nodes.body: Physical findings: • Multiple STIs, especially in young patients • Recurrent UTIs, pelvic pain • Signs of physical abuse (bruises, burns, scars) • Tattoos/brands (names, barcodes, "Daddy") • Poor dental health • Malnourishment despite appearing well-dressed • Untreated chronic conditions Pregnancy-related: • Multiple pregnancies, especially in teens • No prenatal care • Multiple abortions • Doesn'

nodes.summary: Behavioral clues: evasive answers, looking to companion for answers, fearful affect, inappropriate dress
nodes.body: Behavioral indicators: | Red Flag | What You See | |----------|-------------| | Controlling companion | Answers questions for patient, won't leave room | | Scripted responses | Rehearsed history, inconsistent details | | Fearful demeanor | Avoids eye contact, hypervigilant | | No control over ID/money | Someone else holds documents | | Doesn't know location | Can't say where they live/work | | Inc

nodes.title: Suspicion Assessment
nodes.summary: Determine if trafficking indicators are present to guide screening approach
nodes.body: How suspicious are you? Consider: • Number of red flags present • Patient demeanor • Controlling companion behavior • Inconsistencies in history • Your gut feeling Trust your instincts — if something feels wrong, it probably is. Remember: You don't need to be certain to screen. Screening is low-risk and may be life-saving. [6][7]

nodes.title: Separating from Companion
nodes.summary: MUST interview patient alone — separate from companion, use professional interpreter not companion
nodes.body: Safe separation is essential for screening: Strategies: • "It's hospital policy to examine patients privately" • "We need to take the patient to X-ray/CT" • "The patient needs to use the restroom" • Have security present but unobtrusive If companion resists: • Document the resistance • Involve security/social work • Do NOT confront the companion • Prioritize patient safety Never screen in front of

nodes.title: Universal Screening Approach
nodes.summary: Universal screening: frame as routine, non-judgmental, explain confidentiality, use validated tools
nodes.body: Consider routine screening for high-risk presentations: Normalize the questions: > "I ask everyone these questions to make sure they're safe..." High-yield presentations for screening: • Sexual assault • STI evaluation (especially adolescents) • Pregnancy in minors • Psychiatric complaints in young patients • Substance use in young patients • Injuries with inconsistent history Universal screening

nodes.title: Screening Questions
nodes.summary: Validated screening questions: "Has anyone ever made you do something you didn't want to do?"
nodes.body: Trauma-informed screening: Environment questions: > "Where do you sleep at night?" > "Is there anyone who controls where you go?" > "Do you feel safe at home?" Work questions: > "Can you leave your job if you want to?" > "Has anyone ever threatened you to make you work?" > "Do you owe your employer money?" Control questions: > "Does anyone hold your ID or documents?" > "Are you free to come and go

nodes.title: Screening Result
nodes.summary: Positive screen: assess safety, provide resources, do NOT force disclosure or pressure to report
nodes.body: Based on screening: Positive screen indicators: • Answers suggest exploitation • Patient discloses trafficking • Patient confirms red flag behaviors • Patient expresses fear of companion Uncertain: • Evasive answers • Inconsistent responses • Unable to adequately assess Negative screen: • No concerning responses • Patient denies exploitation • Plausible explanations for red flags [7]

nodes.title: Responding to Disclosure
nodes.summary: Trauma-informed response: believe the patient, validate experience, assess immediate safety needs
nodes.body: Trauma-informed response: DO: • Believe them • Stay calm and supportive • Emphasize it's not their fault • Respect their autonomy • Offer help but don't force it • Maintain confidentiality as much as possible SAY: > "Thank you for trusting me with this." > "This is not your fault." > "You deserve to be safe." > "There are people who can help if you want." DON'T: • Express shock or judgment • Promi

nodes.title: Does Patient Want Help?
nodes.summary: If patient wants help: social work, law enforcement (if consents), safe housing, National Hotline
nodes.body: Respect their autonomy: Leaving a trafficking situation is complex and dangerous. The patient may not be ready. If they want help: • Activate resources (social work, advocacy) • Safety planning • Consider admission for safety if appropriate If they don't want help: • Respect the decision • Provide resources for future use • Let them know they can return • Do NOT force intervention (except for mino

Activate resources: • Social work (immediately) • Hospital's trafficking response team (if exists) • Contact local anti-trafficking organization 3. nodes.body: When patient isn't ready to leave: This is normal and expected. Your role: • Plant seeds for the future • Provide resources they can hide • Treat their medical needs • Let them know the door is always open Provide discreetly: • Hotline number (on small card, band-aid wrapper, etc.) • Your contact information • Information about local resources Say: > "I understand you're not ready right now. You can come back anytime." > "Call this number day or night if you need help." Document: • Resources provided • Patient declined intervention • Safety discussion occurred Follow-up: • Conside

nodes.title: Organic Cause — Workup & Resuscitate
nodes.summary: Red flag = target the organic cause; functional syndromes stay diagnoses of exclusion
nodes.body: A red flag is present. Do not attribute to a functional syndrome. Resuscitate and target the suspected cause. [1][3] Directed workup: CT abdomen/pelvis for obstruction; CT head for headache + neuro signs; serum ketones + VBG + glucose for DKA; cortisol / empiric hydrocortisone for suspected adrenal crisis; Ca, BUN/Cr, Na for metabolic causes; ECG for MI presenting atypically. See the can't-miss mi
