nodes.title: Baseline ED Workup
nodes.summary: CBC/CMP/lipase/VBG/ketones/βhCG + ECG for QTc; resuscitate, thiamine before dextrose
nodes.body: Labs: CBC, CMP (glucose, Na, K, Ca, BUN/Cr), lipase, LFTs, VBG + serum ketones + lactate, urine βhCG (all reproductive-age women), UA. Add TSH/cortisol/ammonia when indicated. [1] ECG — electrolyte effects and a baseline QTc before QT-prolonging antiemetics (ondansetron, haloperidol, droperidol, promethazine). [1] Resuscitation: isotonic crystalloid; replace K/Mg; give thiamine before any dextrose

nodes.title: Pick the Pathway
nodes.summary: Pregnant → HG · cannabis → CHS · delayed emptying → gastroparesis · stereotypical → CVS
nodes.body: Organic causes excluded. Which pattern fits the recurrent vomiting? [4][8][9][10]

nodes.title: HG vs Normal NVP
nodes.summary: HG = NVP + >5% weight loss / ketonuria / electrolyte derangement; grade with PUQE
nodes.body: Hyperemesis gravidarum is a diagnosis of exclusion — persistent vomiting NOT attributable to another cause plus objective markers that separate it from ordinary nausea/vomiting of pregnancy (NVP): [4] • Weight loss >5% of prepregnancy weight • Large ketonuria (acute starvation) • Electrolyte / thyroid / liver derangement Use the PUQE score to grade severity (mild <6 · moderate 7–12 · severe ≥13).

nodes.title: HG Treatment Ladder
nodes.summary: Step 1 B6 ± doxylamine → Step 2 antiemetics → IV rehydration → steroids last
nodes.body: Where on the ladder is this patient? [4] Step 1 (first-line): Pyridoxine (B6) 10–25 mg PO q6–8h ± Doxylamine — the only FDA-approved NVP combination. Step 2 (antiemetics): Ondansetron, Promethazine, Metoclopramide, Prochlorperazine. [5][6] Antiemetic doses & QT flags.

nodes.title: HG — Outpatient
nodes.summary: B6 ± doxylamine + PRN antiemetic, hydration, OB follow-up; counsel ondansetron <10wk
nodes.body: Small frequent bland meals, ginger, avoid triggers. Pyridoxine ± Doxylamine first; add an oral antiemetic if needed. Counsel on the ondansetron first-trimester nuance — a small possible signal for cardiac septal/oral-cleft defects if used before 10 weeks — via shared decision-making. [4]
nodes.recommendation: Discharge on pyridoxine ± doxylamine, oral antiemetic PRN, hydration and dietary advice, obstetric follow-up. Return for inability to keep fluids down, weight loss, or dizziness. Keep pyridoxine at the NVP dose (10–25 mg q6–8h, ~30–75 mg/da

nodes.title: HG — IV Rehydration & Admission
nodes.summary: IV crystalloid to UOP, thiamine BEFORE dextrose, IV antiemetic, admit if PO intolerant
nodes.body: Isotonic crystalloid or LR, up to ~2 L over 2 h, then titrate to urine output ≥100 mL/h; replace K as needed. [4] Give thiamine 100 mg IV BEFORE any dextrose — glucose in a thiamine-deficient patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy. [2][14] IV antiemetic (ondansetron / metoclopramide / promethazine). Admit for persistent intolerance, electrolyte derangement, or weight loss.
nodes.recommendation: IV isotonic fluids titrated to UOP, thiamine before dextrose, IV antiemetic, electrolyte repletion. Admit if unable to tolerate PO after ED therapy. Watch for refeeding syndrome (K, Mg, phosphate) when nutrition resumes.

nodes.title: HG — Refractory
nodes.summary: Methylprednisolone last-resort (avoid <10wk), enteral before parenteral, MFM involvement
nodes.body: Corticosteroids are last-resort for HG refractory to fluids + antiemetics: Methylprednisolone 16 mg PO/IV q8h × 3 days, then taper over ~2 weeks; total course ≤6 weeks. [4] AVOID before 10 weeks gestation — association with orofacial clefts. Consider enteral (NJ) nutrition before parenteral for prolonged intolerance; monitor for refeeding syndrome. [4]
nodes.recommendation: Refractory HG: trial methylprednisolone 16 mg q8h ×3d then taper (avoid <10 weeks gestation), consider enteral nutrition before TPN, involve OB/MFM. Continue thiamine repletion; treat suspected Wernicke with thiamine 500 mg IV q8h ×3d.

nodes.title: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome
nodes.summary: Triad + hot-water bathing; standard antiemetics fail — route to the full CHS consult
nodes.body: Recognize the triad: stereotypical episodic vomiting + prolonged heavy cannabis use + relief with cessation. Compulsive hot-water bathing (>41°C) is near-pathognomonic (~92%). [11] Key differentiator: standard antiemetics and opioids typically fail — treatment is topical capsaicin, haloperidol/droperidol, benzodiazepines, and definitive cannabis cessation. [11][12] This has a dedicated consult wit
nodes.recommendation: CHS suspected — manage via the dedicated CHS consult: topical capsaicin, haloperidol (0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV, HaVOC RCT superior to ondansetron), benzodiazepine adjunct, avoid opioids, and cannabis cessation for cure. Always screen CVS patients

nodes.title: Gastroparesis — Recognition
nodes.summary: Delayed emptying, no obstruction; 4-hr scintigraphy gold standard; dm/idiopathic/med-induced
nodes.body: Delayed gastric emptying WITHOUT mechanical obstruction. Cardinal symptoms: nausea, vomiting, early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating. Symptom severity does not correlate with degree of delay. [13] Gold standard: 4-hour solid-phase gastric-emptying scintigraphy (>10% retention at 4 h) — outpatient; exclude obstruction (EGD/imaging) first. [13] Causes: diabetic, idiopathic (largest group), p

nodes.title: Gastroparesis — ED Flare & Management
nodes.summary: Glucose control + prokinetic (erythromycin/metoclopramide) + antiemetic; avoid opioids
nodes.body: ACG 2022: dietary modification (small, frequent, low-fat/low-insoluble-fiber), optimize glycemia (hyperglycemia acutely slows emptying), prokinetics + antiemetics. [13] Prokinetics: Metoclopramide 5 mg PO/IV TID before meals — BLACK-BOX tardive dyskinesia; ≤12 weeks. [7] Erythromycin IV 3 mg/kg q8h (acute flare) — tachyphylaxis limits chronic use. Domperidone (IND access). [13] AVOID opioids — the
nodes.recommendation: Acute flare: IV isotonic fluids + K/Mg repletion, glucose control, IV antiemetic (ondansetron/prochlorperazine), IV prokinetic (erythromycin 3 mg/kg or metoclopramide 10 mg IV), and AVOID opioids. Chronic: metoclopramide ≤12 weeks (tardive

nodes.title: CVS — Rome IV Criteria
nodes.summary: Stereotypical episodes, well in between, migraine link; screen for cannabis (→CHS)
nodes.body: Cyclic vomiting syndrome (Rome IV): stereotypical episodes of acute vomiting lasting <7 days; ≥3 episodes in the prior year (≥2 in last 6 months) separated by ≥1 week of baseline health; well between episodes. Supportive: personal/family history of migraine. [8][9] 4 phases: inter-episodic (well) → prodrome (window for abortive tx) → emetic → recovery. Always ask about cannabis — chronic use + hot

nodes.title: CVS — Abortive vs Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Emetic/prodrome → abortive; well phase → prophylaxis
nodes.body: Which phase is the patient in? [8]

nodes.title: CVS — Abortive (Emetic Phase)
nodes.summary: Sumatriptan + ondansetron + dextrose fluids + benzo sedation; aprepitant if refractory
nodes.body: Treat early in the prodrome. [8] • Sumatriptan 20 mg intranasal (or 6 mg SC) — take as early as possible. • Ondansetron 8 mg IV — aggressive antiemetic backbone. • IV fluids WITH dextrose (e.g., D10-containing crystalloid) + K repletion — aborts the catabolic/ketotic state. • Sedation with a benzodiazepine (± diphenhydramine) to break the cycle. • Aprepitant 125 mg day 1, then 80 mg days 2–3 (seco
nodes.recommendation: Abort early: sumatriptan (20 mg IN / 6 mg SC), ondansetron 8 mg IV, dextrose-containing IV fluids with K, benzodiazepine sedation ± diphenhydramine, and aprepitant for refractory. Avoid chronic opioids. Reassess for cannabis (CHS).

nodes.title: CVS — Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Amitriptyline first-line (ECG first); topiramate/propranolol alt; mito supplements adjunct
nodes.body: For ≥4 episodes/year or severe disease (ANMS/CVSA 2019): [8] • First-line: Amitriptyline — start 10–25 mg qHS, titrate to 75–100 mg/day (1–1.5 mg/kg); baseline ECG for QTc. • Alternatives: topiramate ~100 mg/day, propranolol 20–40 mg BID. • Mitochondrial supplements: CoQ10 ~100 mg TID, L-carnitine ~1000 mg BID, riboflavin ~400 mg/day.
nodes.recommendation: Start prophylaxis with amitriptyline (target 75–100 mg/day, ECG first); alternatives topiramate or propranolol; consider CoQ10/L-carnitine/riboflavin. Refer to neurogastroenterology. Confirm no cannabis use (would reclassify to CHS).

nodes.title: Antiemetic Safety & Disposition
nodes.summary: QTc before stacking; metoclopramide limits; avoid opioids; discharge on PO tolerance + follow-up
nodes.body: Cross-cutting safety before discharge: [1][4][7][13][14] • QTc check before stacking QT-prolongers (ondansetron, haloperidol, droperidol, promethazine, domperidone). • Metoclopramide — tardive dyskinesia; ≤12 weeks (gastroparesis), ~5 days (HG per EMA). • Avoid opioids in CHS and gastroparesis flares. • Thiamine before dextrose in any prolonged poor-intake patient. Antiemetic comparison & QT flags
nodes.recommendation: Discharge when tolerating oral intake with corrected electrolytes, appropriate antiemetic, and specialty follow-up (OB for HG, GI/neurogastro for gastroparesis/CVS, cessation support for CHS). Admit for refractory vomiting, persistent elect

nodes.title: Hyperthermia Hub - Core Temp First
nodes.summary: Get a CORE temp. True hyperthermia (normal set point, failed dissipation) needs active cooling, not antipyretics. >40C + AMS = cool now.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Heat stroke \u2014 core >40\u00B0C + altered mentation \u2192 immediate active cooling. 2. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome \u2014 rigidity + hyperthermia + dopamine-blocker exposure. 3. Serotonin syndrome \u2014 clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, serotonergic drugs. 4. Thyroid storm \u2014 fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation, goiter/Graves history. 5. Malignant hyperther

nodes.title: Pick the Dominant Clue
nodes.summary: Branch on the dominant clue: exertion->heat stroke, serotonergic+clonus->SS, antipsychotic+rigidity->NMS, hyperthyroid->storm, dry+mydriasis->anticholinergic, tinnitus/AG->salicylate, infection->sepsis.
nodes.body: Match the strongest feature to the most likely cause. You can return after starting cooling. Use the toolbar to jump directly to any pathway.

nodes.title: Heat Stroke / Heat Illness
nodes.body: Open Heat Stroke for the full pathway. Defining feature: core temp >40C with CNS dysfunction after exertional or environmental heat exposure. Skin may be sweating (exertional) or dry (classic/elderly). First minutes: active cooling immediately - cold-water immersion is fastest for exertional heat stroke; evaporative + ice packs to groin/axillae/neck for classic. Stop cooling at ~38.5-39C to avoid
nodes.recommendation: Suspected heat stroke: cool first, target ~38.5C, then manage end-organ injury. Cold-water immersion is the fastest cooling method for exertional cases.

nodes.title: Serotonin Syndrome
nodes.body: Open Serotonin Syndrome for Hunter Criteria and treatment. Defining features: serotonergic agent + clonus (spontaneous/inducible/ocular), hyperreflexia worse in the lower limbs, mydriasis, rapid onset (within 24h, often <6h). First minutes: stop the serotonergic agent, benzodiazepines for agitation/myoclonus, active cooling, cyproheptadine for moderate-severe. Distinguish from NMS (rigid + bradyre
nodes.recommendation: Serotonin syndrome: stop the agent, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine for moderate-severe. Clonus is the discriminator from NMS.

nodes.title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
nodes.body: Open NMS for the full pathway. Defining features: dopamine antagonist exposure (antipsychotic, antiemetic) or abrupt dopamine-agonist withdrawal + lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, AMS, very high CK. Onset over days. Bradyreflexia (opposite of serotonin syndrome). First minutes: stop the offending agent, aggressive cooling, IV fluids, benzodiazepines; dantrolene and/or bromo
nodes.recommendation: NMS: stop the dopamine antagonist, cool, fluids, benzodiazepines; dantrolene/bromocriptine for severe. Rigidity + slow onset distinguishes it from serotonin syndrome.

nodes.title: Thyroid Storm
nodes.body: Open Thyroid Disorders for the storm pathway. Defining features: known/undiagnosed hyperthyroidism + hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmia (often AF), agitation/delirium, GI/hepatic dysfunction, often a precipitant (infection, surgery, iodine load, DKA). Use the Burch-Wartofsky score. First minutes: beta-blockade (propranolol), thionamide (PTU/methimazole), then iodine at least 1h AFTER thionamide, hydroc
nodes.recommendation: Thyroid storm: beta-blocker, thionamide, iodine (>=1h after thionamide), steroids, cooling, treat precipitant. Score with Burch-Wartofsky.

nodes.title: Anticholinergic Toxidrome
nodes.body: "Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, blind as a bat." Defining features: hyperthermia with DRY/flushed skin, mydriasis, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds, delirium, tachycardia. Distinguishes from sympathomimetic (which sweats) and serotonin syndrome (clonus/hyperreflexia). First minutes: - Active cooling (evaporative); the skin cannot sweat, so passive cooling fails
nodes.recommendation: Anticholinergic toxidrome: evaporative cooling (dry skin defeats passive cooling), benzodiazepines, fluids. Physostigmine only for pure cases with normal ECG - consult toxicology.

nodes.title: Salicylate Toxicity
nodes.body: Open Salicylate Toxicity for the full pathway. Defining features: tinnitus, hyperpnea/tachypnea, nausea, AMS, and the classic mixed acid-base picture (primary respiratory alkalosis + primary anion-gap metabolic acidosis). Hyperthermia signals UNCOUPLED oxidative phosphorylation and is a marker of severe, life-threatening toxicity. First minutes: check salicylate level + VBG/ABG, serum alkalinizati
nodes.recommendation: Salicylate toxicity with hyperthermia = severe. Alkalinize, replete K, early dialysis. Hyperthermia indicates uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. Avoid hypoventilation around intubation.

nodes.title: Sepsis / Fever Physiology
nodes.body: Open Sepsis Management. When this is true fever, not hyperthermia: an infectious source, rigors, the set point is raised so antipyretics help, and skin can still sweat. But fever and true hyperthermia can coexist (e.g., infection precipitating thyroid storm or NMS). First minutes: lactate, cultures (do not delay antibiotics), early broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluids for hypoperfusion, source contr
nodes.recommendation: If infection physiology fits, run the sepsis pathway. Keep a hyperthermic toxidrome/NMS/storm on the differential if temp is disproportionate or neuromuscular signs appear.

nodes.title: Cooling Principles (All Causes)
nodes.summary: Active cooling (immersion for exertional, evaporative otherwise), cold fluids, benzodiazepines, target ~38.5C then stop. Antipyretics fail. Paralysis for intractable >41C - avoid succinylcholine with rhabdo.
nodes.body: These apply across every true-hyperthermia pathway while the cause-specific consult runs. Start now if core >40C with AMS - do not wait for the diagnosis. - Antipyretics do NOT work in true hyperthermia. The set point is normal; acetaminophen/NSAIDs are ineffective and NSAIDs add renal/GI/coagulopathy risk. - Active external cooling: - Exertional heat stroke: cold-water immersion is fastest. - Oth

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for >40C, AMS, rigidity, rhabdo/AKI, DIC, or instability. Admit/observe milder cases with serial monitoring.
nodes.body: Disposition follows the cause and the severity of end-organ injury.

nodes.title: ICU / Cause-Specific Pathway
nodes.body: ICU for core >40C, persistent AMS, rigidity requiring paralysis, rhabdomyolysis with renal risk, DIC, hepatic injury, or hemodynamic/respiratory instability. The cause-specific consult (Heat Stroke, Serotonin Syndrome, NMS, Thyroid Disorders, Salicylate, Sepsis) drives definitive therapy and monitoring.
nodes.recommendation: Severe undifferentiated or confirmed hyperthermia with end-organ injury is an ICU admission. Continue active cooling and run the cause-specific consult.

nodes.title: Admit / Observation
nodes.body: Admit or observe when hyperthermia is resolving with cooling, the cause is identified and reversible, and there is no end-organ injury. Serial core temperature, CK, renal function, and coagulation studies. Confirm the offending agent is stopped (toxidromes/SS/NMS) and arrange the relevant follow-up. Return/escalation precautions: rising temperature, new rigidity or clonus, falling urine output or
nodes.recommendation: Observe with serial temp and labs; escalate on rising temp, new rigidity/clonus, rhabdo signs, or instability. Confirm the offending agent is discontinued.

nodes.title: Hypertonic Saline Protocol
nodes.summary: HTS treats severe symptomatic hyponatremia and elevated ICP/herniation, not routine hypernatremia.
nodes.body: Hypertonic Saline Steps Hypertonic saline is used for two distinct emergencies: 1. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia with cerebral edema/seizure/coma 2. Elevated ICP or impending herniation from acute neurologic injury It is not a treatment for routine hypernatremia. If a hypernatremic patient is herniating, manage as a neurocritical emergency with specialist input; hyperosmolar rescue may still be

nodes.title: Which Emergency?
nodes.summary: The dose and endpoint differ for herniation versus hyponatremic encephalopathy.
nodes.body: Select the indication.

nodes.title: Herniation / Elevated ICP Rescue
nodes.summary: Herniation rescue uses hyperosmolar bolus therapy while definitive neurosurgical management is arranged.
nodes.body: Immediate actions: - Call neurosurgery/neurocritical care - Head of bed elevated, neck midline, avoid hypotension/hypoxia/fever - Treat seizures and reverse anticoagulation when indicated - Temporize ventilation only for acute herniation while definitive therapy is arranged Hyperosmolar options: - Hypertonic saline 3% NaCl 2-5 mL/kg IV bolus, often 150-250 mL over 10-20 min - 23.4% NaCl 30 mL IV o

nodes.title: Severe Symptomatic Hyponatremia
nodes.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia uses repeated 3% boluses to raise Na 4-6 mEq/L.
nodes.body: Indications: seizure, coma, severe encephalopathy, or signs of cerebral edema from hyponatremia. Bolus approach: - Hypertonic saline 100-150 mL of 3% NaCl IV over 10-20 min - Repeat up to 2 additional boluses for persistent severe symptoms - Initial target: raise serum sodium by 4-6 mEq/L to reverse severe symptoms - Do not aim to normalize sodium in the ED Check serum sodium q2h during active cor

nodes.title: Not Routine HTS
nodes.summary: Mild/chronic hyponatremia generally should not receive 3% saline boluses.
nodes.body: Do not use 3% saline for mild, chronic, or asymptomatic hyponatremia. Instead: - Identify cause and chronicity - Stop offending fluids/medications when appropriate - Use fluid restriction, salt/loop strategy, or other cause-specific therapy - Consider DDAVP clamp only when overcorrection risk or controlled correction strategy requires expert management Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symp
nodes.recommendation: Use non-emergent hyponatremia management unless severe neurologic symptoms are present.

nodes.title: Hypernatremia Safety Stop
nodes.summary: Hypernatremia is not an indication for HTS unless specialist-directed herniation rescue is needed.
nodes.body: Do not give hypertonic saline to correct hypernatremia. If hypernatremia plus herniation/elevated ICP is present: - Treat as competing life threats - Call neurocritical care/neurosurgery immediately - Avoid hypotonic fluid boluses in acute cerebral edema - Consider hyperosmolar rescue only if impending herniation benefit outweighs sodium/osmolality risk - Track serum sodium and osmolality closely
nodes.recommendation: Hold HTS for routine hypernatremia; use only specialist-directed ICP rescue if herniating.

nodes.title: Sodium Targets / ODS Prevention
nodes.summary: Treat symptoms first, then prevent overcorrection and ODS.
nodes.body: Hyponatremia correction limits: - Initial severe symptom target: +4 to +6 mEq/L - Avoid >8 mEq/L in 24 hr in high-risk patients - Avoid >10 mEq/L in 24 hr in most patients - High ODS risk: alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, hypokalemia, very low starting Na If overcorrection occurs or is likely, consider DDAVP and D5W relowering strategy with nephrology/ICU guidance.

nodes.title: Access / Monitoring
nodes.summary: 3% bolus may be peripheral, but concentrated/continuous therapy needs policy-driven access and monitoring.
nodes.body: Access: - 3% NaCl bolus can generally be given peripherally through a reliable IV - Continuous 3% infusion and 23.4% NaCl should follow local central-line policy - Use infusion pump and label line clearly Monitoring: - Neuro exam and vital signs during bolus - Serum sodium/osmolality q2h during active correction - Strict I/O and volume status - Avoid hypotension, hypoxia, fever, and hypoglycemia i

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: HTS patients need monitored disposition and sodium trajectory planning.
nodes.body: Disposition: - Herniation/elevated ICP: ICU/neurosurgery/neurocritical care - Severe symptomatic hyponatremia: ICU or closely monitored setting until sodium trajectory is controlled - Need for DDAVP clamp: ICU/stepdown per local capability - Overcorrection or high ODS risk: nephrology/ICU involvement Document indication, dose, sodium before/after, neurologic response, and next sodium check time.
nodes.recommendation: HTS use requires monitored disposition and explicit sodium follow-up plan.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia - Stabilize First
nodes.summary: Treat immediately when symptomatic or unsafe to swallow, then determine cause and recurrence risk.
nodes.body: Hypoglycemia steps | Treatment calculator Confirm the problem, but treat the patient. Definitions: [1] - Level 1: glucose <70 mg/dL and >=54 mg/dL - Level 2: glucose <54 mg/dL - Level 3: severe event with altered mental or physical function requiring assistance, regardless of exact glucose value Immediate actions: 1. Check POC glucose. 2. If symptomatic, altered, seizing, or unable to swallow, tre

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis Early
nodes.summary: Place the differential early so treatment does not hide a recurrent or dangerous cause.
nodes.body: Differential guide Do this before disposition. Most ED hypoglycemia is medication or nutrition-related, but recurrent or unexplained hypoglycemia should trigger a structured differential. Common ED buckets: [2,3] - Diabetes medication mismatch: insulin, sulfonylurea, meglitinide, dosing error, pump error - Poor intake or increased use: missed meal, vomiting, exercise, alcohol, frailty - Reduced cl

nodes.title: Severe Hypoglycemia Treatment
nodes.summary: Use IV dextrose when unsafe to swallow; glucagon is a bridge when access is unavailable.
nodes.body: Treatment calculator If altered, seizing, or unsafe to swallow: [1,4] IV access: - D50W 25 g IV push, usually 50 mL of D50W - Alternative: D10W 100-250 mL IV, titrated to mental status and glucose response - D10W is often smoother peripherally and avoids large osmotic bolus when time allows No IV access: - Glucagon 1 mg IM/SC, or intranasal glucagon 3 mg if available - Continue attempts at IV/IO a

nodes.title: Oral Treatment Route
nodes.summary: Use 15-20 g fast carbohydrate only if the patient is awake and can swallow safely.
nodes.body: If alert, cooperative, and able to swallow: [1] - Give 15-20 g fast-acting carbohydrate. - Recheck glucose in 15 minutes. - Repeat 15-20 g carbohydrate if still <70 mg/dL. - Once corrected and patient can eat, give a longer-acting carbohydrate or meal, especially if insulin or sulfonylurea remains active. Do not use oral treatment if: altered mental status, active seizure, aspiration risk, vomitin

nodes.title: Recheck and Durability
nodes.summary: Recheck at 15 minutes, repeat treatment if needed, and prove the correction is durable.
nodes.body: Rebound risk calculator After any treatment: - Recheck glucose in 15 minutes. - Repeat therapy until glucose is >70 mg/dL and symptoms improve. - Continue serial glucose checks based on cause and half-life. - Do not let one normal glucose drive discharge. If recurrent: start a dextrose infusion while identifying the cause. Typical infusion: D10W titrated to maintain glucose generally >100 mg/dL wh

nodes.title: Recurrent Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: Recurrent lows require infusion, medication review, and a cause-specific plan.
nodes.body: Recurrent hypoglycemia is not simple hypoglycemia. Stabilize: - Start D10W infusion and titrate. - Check glucose q15-30 min until stable, then q1h or per protocol. - Check potassium, magnesium, phosphate, renal function, liver panel, lactate, ethanol when clinically relevant. - Review EMS glucose, ED doses, timing of meals, insulin type, pump status, pill access, and renal function. Danger causes

nodes.title: Medication Cause and Rebound Risk
nodes.summary: Separate insulin effect from insulin secretagogue effect because sulfonylurea recurrence needs octreotide.
nodes.body: Rebound risk calculator Medication review: - Insulin: rapid, regular, NPH, basal, concentrated insulin, pump, accidental duplicate dose - Sulfonylureas: glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride - Meglitinides: repaglinide, nateglinide - Combination pills or medication access by household members - Renal dysfunction, older age, missed meals, alcohol, recent dose changes Key distinction: - Insulin overdose

nodes.title: Sulfonylurea or Meglitinide Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: Sulfonylurea recurrence is driven by persistent insulin secretion; octreotide prevents recurrent lows.
nodes.body: Suspect when: recurrent hypoglycemia after dextrose, older diabetic patient, renal dysfunction, glyburide/glipizide/glimepiride exposure, unknown pill ingestion, pediatric exploratory ingestion, or household medication access. [4,5] Management: 1. Correct initial hypoglycemia with oral carbohydrate or IV dextrose. 2. If recurrent or high-risk exposure, give octreotide. 3. Start D10W infusion only
nodes.recommendation: Treat with dextrose for immediate correction, add octreotide for recurrent or high-risk sulfonylurea/meglitinide exposure, and observe or admit.

nodes.title: Insulin Overdose or Pump Error
nodes.summary: Long-acting insulin or overdose can recur for many hours and needs monitored glucose support.
nodes.body: High-risk clues: large insulin dose, basal or long-acting insulin, concentrated insulin, pump malfunction, duplicate dose, intentional overdose, renal failure, or poor oral intake. [4] Management: - Oral carbohydrate if awake and able to eat. - D10W infusion titrated to glucose trend. - Consider higher concentration dextrose through central access if large ongoing requirements. - Monitor potassium
nodes.recommendation: Use titrated dextrose support, electrolyte monitoring, pump control if relevant, and prolonged observation or admission.

nodes.title: Critical Illness, Organ Failure, or Endocrine Cause
nodes.summary: Critical illness hypoglycemia is rarely dischargeable from the ED after one normal glucose.
nodes.body: Hypoglycemia can be a severity marker. [2,3] Look for: - Sepsis or shock - Liver failure or acute hepatic injury - Renal failure or missed dialysis - Starvation, malnutrition, alcohol-related fasting hypoglycemia - Adrenal crisis: hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, steroid withdrawal, adrenal disease - Hypopituitarism or adrenal suppression Management: - Treat hypoglycemia while treating the
nodes.recommendation: Treat glucose and underlying illness in parallel; admit most critical illness, organ failure, adrenal, and poor-intake patients.

nodes.title: Whipple Triad and Critical Sample
nodes.summary: Critical samples are most useful when drawn during the low glucose episode.
nodes.body: Critical sample guide Use this when hypoglycemia is unexplained, recurrent, non-diabetic, or discordant with the history. [2,3] Whipple triad: 1. Symptoms or signs compatible with hypoglycemia 2. Low plasma glucose documented during symptoms 3. Symptom improvement after glucose correction Critical sample during hypoglycemia, ideally before dextrose if no delay: - Plasma glucose - Insulin - C-pepti

nodes.title: Disposition Safety Check
nodes.summary: Disposition depends on durable correction, cause, medication half-life, oral intake, and safety.
nodes.body: Rebound risk calculator Discharge is reasonable only when all are true: - Clear reversible cause identified - Patient is eating reliably - Serial glucose checks remain stable after treatment - No sulfonylurea/meglitinide exposure - No long-acting insulin overdose or pump malfunction concern - No renal failure, liver failure, sepsis, adrenal crisis, hypothermia, frailty, or malnutrition driving the

nodes.title: Discharge Plan
nodes.summary: Safe discharge requires a corrected glucose plus a corrected reason for the low.
nodes.body: Discharge bundle: - Document cause and serial glucose stability. - Provide meal plan before leaving if insulin or diabetes medication remains active. - Reduce or hold culprit medication when appropriate. - Ensure access to glucose testing supplies and fast carbohydrate. - Prescribe or confirm glucagon for patients on insulin at risk for severe events. - Arrange timely PCP/endocrine follow-up. - Gi
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after durable correction, stable oral intake, medication adjustment, safe follow-up, and clear return precautions.

nodes.title: Observation or Admission
nodes.summary: Admission is for recurrence risk, high-risk medication exposure, illness severity, or unsafe outpatient correction.
nodes.body: Observation/admission triggers: - Recurrent glucose <70 mg/dL after treatment - Level 3 event, seizure, prolonged altered mental status, or aspiration risk - Sulfonylurea or meglitinide exposure - Long-acting insulin, concentrated insulin, pump malfunction, or intentional overdose - Need for dextrose infusion - Renal failure, hepatic failure, sepsis, adrenal crisis, hypothermia, pregnancy, frailty
nodes.recommendation: Observe or admit for recurrent, medication-driven, unclear, critical illness, unsafe, or infusion-requiring hypoglycemia.

nodes.title: Undifferentiated Hypotension — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: MAP <65 or SBP <90; shock index >1 = unstable; each hour at MAP <65 = 5% mortality increase
nodes.body: Shock Workup Summary Shock definitions: • Absolute hypotension: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg • Relative hypotension: SBP drop >40 mmHg from baseline • Shock Index (SI): HR/SBP — >1.0 suggests significant instability Each hour at MAP <65 increases mortality by ~5%. Immediate actions: 1. Two large-bore IVs (18G or larger) 2. Continuous monitoring 3. ECG immediately 4. Labs: CBC, CMP, lactate, VBG, t

nodes.title: RUSH Exam — Bedside POCUS
nodes.summary: RUSH = Heart (EF, effusion, RV), IVC (volume), FAST, Aorta, Pneumothorax; 2-5 min, improves dx accuracy to 85%
nodes.body: RUSH (Rapid Ultrasound in Shock) — HI-MAP: H — Heart: • EF (hyperdynamic vs depressed) • Pericardial effusion / tamponade • RV dilatation (D-sign) → PE • Wall motion abnormalities → MI I — IVC: • <2 cm + >50% collapse → hypovolemic • >2 cm + minimal collapse → cardiogenic/obstructive M — Morrison's / FAST: • Free fluid → hemorrhage, rupture A — Aorta: • AAA (>3 cm), dissection flap P — Pneumothora

nodes.title: POCUS Findings
nodes.summary: Match POCUS to shock type: distributive (hyperdynamic), cardiogenic (depressed LV), hypovolemic (collapsed), obstructive (RV/tamponade)
nodes.body: What does RUSH exam show? Match findings to shock type: • Hyperdynamic LV + collapsed IVC → Distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis) • Depressed LV + dilated IVC → Cardiogenic • Collapsed LV + collapsed IVC + free fluid → Hypovolemic • RV dilated + D-sign + dilated IVC → Obstructive (PE) • Pericardial effusion + collapsed RV → Tamponade • Absent lung slide → Tension pneumothorax

nodes.title: Distributive Shock
nodes.summary: Distributive = vasodilation; sepsis most common; anaphylaxis, neurogenic, adrenal are alternatives
nodes.body: Distributive shock = vasodilation with relative hypovolemia despite normal circulating volume. Subtypes: • Septic (most common) — infection source, fever, elevated lactate • Anaphylactic — allergen exposure, urticaria, angioedema • Neurogenic — spinal cord injury, warm skin, bradycardia • Adrenal crisis — refractory shock, chronic steroid use POCUS pattern: • Hyperdynamic LV (EF often >70%) • Smal

nodes.title: Septic Shock — Hour-1 Bundle
nodes.summary: Hour-1: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors for MAP ≥65
nodes.body: SSC 2021 Hour-1 Bundle Sepsis-3 definition: Suspected infection + qSOFA ≥2 or SOFA ≥2. Septic shock: Sepsis + vasopressors required for MAP ≥65 + lactate >2 despite fluids. Hour-1 Bundle (do ALL within 1 hour): 1. Measure lactate — repeat if >2 mmol/L 2. Blood cultures before antibiotics 3. Broad-spectrum antibiotics — each hour delay increases mortality 4. 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or

nodes.title: Anaphylactic Shock
nodes.summary: Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM FIRST; aggressive fluids; may need IV epi infusion; observe 4-6h for biphasic
nodes.body: Anaphylaxis requires IMMEDIATE epinephrine. Epinephrine IM: • Adults: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1:1000) anterolateral thigh • Repeat q5-15 min if needed Epinephrine IV (refractory/cardiac arrest): • 0.1-0.5 mg IV (1:10,000) • Epinephrine infusion: 1-10 mcg/min Additional treatments: • Aggressive IV fluids — 1-2 L crystalloid (may need 4-8 L) • Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV • Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV • Albuter

nodes.title: Neurogenic Shock
nodes.summary: Bradycardia + hypotension + warm skin; MAP target 85-90 for cord perfusion; norepinephrine + atropine
nodes.body: Neurogenic shock = loss of sympathetic tone from spinal cord injury (usually T6 and above). Classic triad: • Hypotension • Bradycardia (unlike other shock types) • Warm, dry skin (peripheral vasodilation) Management: 1. Volume resuscitation: • Cautious fluids — may worsen spinal cord edema • 1-2 L crystalloid, reassess 2. Vasopressors: • Norepinephrine preferred (alpha > beta) • Target MAP ≥85-90

nodes.title: Adrenal Crisis
nodes.summary: Refractory shock + steroids hx → hydrocortisone 100mg IV stat; expect improvement in 1-2h
nodes.body: Consider adrenal crisis if shock refractory to fluids and vasopressors. Risk factors: • Chronic steroid use (≥pred 5 mg/day × 3 weeks) • Known adrenal insufficiency • Recent steroid taper • Pituitary disease Classic features: • Hypotension refractory to pressors • Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia • Hypoglycemia Treatment: • Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately • Then 200 mg/24h (continuous or 50 mg q6h)

nodes.title: Cardiogenic Shock
nodes.summary: Pump failure; norepinephrine first-line; add dobutamine for low output; AVOID aggressive fluids; consider cath/MCS
nodes.body: Cardiogenic shock = pump failure with inadequate cardiac output. Causes: • Acute MI (most common) • Acute decompensated heart failure • Myocarditis, cardiomyopathy • Severe valvular disease • Arrhythmias POCUS findings: • Depressed LV function (EF <40%) • Dilated IVC with minimal respiratory variation • Possible pericardial effusion • Pulmonary B-lines (edema) Management: 1. Treat underlying cause

nodes.title: Hypovolemic Shock
nodes.summary: Collapsed IVC + hyperdynamic LV; hemorrhagic (blood products) vs non-hemorrhagic (crystalloid)
nodes.body: Hypovolemic shock = inadequate intravascular volume. Subtypes: • Hemorrhagic — trauma, GI bleed, ruptured AAA, ectopic • Non-hemorrhagic — dehydration, burns, third-spacing POCUS findings: • Hyperdynamic, small LV ("kissing ventricles") • Collapsed IVC with >50% respiratory variation • Free fluid (hemorrhage) or dry FAST What is the etiology?

nodes.title: Hemorrhagic Shock
nodes.summary: MTP 1:1:1 ratio; TXA 1g within 3h; permissive hypotension (SBP 80-90) until source control; TBI exception
nodes.body: Hemorrhagic shock requires source control + blood products. Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP): • Activate if shock index >1 + ongoing bleeding • Target 1:1:1 ratio (pRBC : FFP : platelets) Tranexamic Acid (TXA): • TXA 1 g IV over 10 min within 3 hours of injury • Then 1 g over 8 hours Source control: • Trauma → OR, IR, damage control surgery • GI bleed → endoscopy, IR embolization • Ruptured AAA

nodes.title: Non-Hemorrhagic Hypovolemic Shock
nodes.summary: Crystalloid (LR) 20-30 mL/kg bolus; reassess after each bolus; treat underlying cause (DKA, burns, etc.)
nodes.body: Non-hemorrhagic hypovolemia — treat underlying cause + volume resuscitation. Common causes: • Severe dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea) • DKA / HHS • Burns (third-spacing) • Pancreatitis Volume resuscitation: • Crystalloid: LR preferred (avoid hyperchloremic acidosis) • Initial bolus: 20-30 mL/kg over 1-3 hours • Reassess after each bolus — clinical exam, IVC, UOP DKA/HHS: • NS 1-2 L bolus, then 250

nodes.title: Obstructive Shock
nodes.summary: Obstructive = mechanical obstruction; tamponade, tension PTX, or massive PE — all require immediate intervention
nodes.body: Obstructive shock = mechanical obstruction to blood flow. Types: • Cardiac tamponade — Beck's triad, electrical alternans, dilated IVC • Tension pneumothorax — absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, absent lung slide • Massive PE — RV dilation, D-sign, elevated troponin What is the obstruction?

nodes.title: Cardiac Tamponade
nodes.summary: Echo-guided pericardiocentesis emergent; IV fluids to increase preload; avoid intubation; CT surgery for window
nodes.body: Cardiac tamponade = pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage. Diagnosis: • Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds • Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg • Electrical alternans on ECG • Echo: pericardial effusion + RV diastolic collapse Treatment: 1. Pericardiocentesis: • Emergent bedside under echo guidance • Subxiphoid approach • Even small drainage can dramatically improve hemodynamics 2. Temp

nodes.title: Tension Pneumothorax
nodes.summary: Clinical diagnosis — needle decompress 5th ICS anterior axillary line; follow with chest tube immediately
nodes.body: Tension pneumothorax = immediate needle decompression. Clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for imaging: • Hypotension + respiratory distress • Absent breath sounds (affected side) • Tracheal deviation (late sign) • JVD • Absent lung slide on POCUS Treatment: 1. Needle decompression: • 14-16G needle/angiocath • 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line (preferred) • OR 2nd intercostal space, midcl

nodes.title: Massive Pulmonary Embolism
nodes.summary: AVOID intubation + fluids; norepinephrine + high-flow O2; alteplase 100mg or 50mg if arrest; activate PERT
nodes.body: Massive PE = thrombolysis + anticoagulation. See full PE Treatment Consult for complete pathway. Key points for shock from PE: AVOID: • Intubation (positive pressure worsens RV) • Aggressive fluid loading (RV already dilated) DO: • High-flow O2 (pulmonary vasodilator) • Norepinephrine for BP support • Activate PERT (Class 1 recommendation) Thrombolysis: • Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h (standard) • 5

nodes.title: Fluid Responsiveness Assessment
nodes.summary: PLR best (>10-15% VTI increase = responder); IVC collapsibility limited accuracy; fluid responsiveness ≠ need
nodes.body: Fluid Responsiveness Guide Fluid responsiveness ≠ fluid need. Just because stroke volume will increase doesn't mean fluids are indicated. Passive Leg Raise (PLR) — Most Reliable: • 45° head-up → lower torso to flat + raise legs 45° • >10-15% increase in VTI/CO = fluid responder • Sensitivity 89%, Specificity 91% • Works in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmias IVC Assessment: • IVC <2 cm + >50% co

nodes.title: Vasopressor Selection
nodes.summary: Norepinephrine first-line; add vasopressin at high NE doses; can start peripherally; target MAP ≥65
nodes.body: Vasopressor Dosing Guide First-line: Norepinephrine • Start: 0.01-0.05 mcg/kg/min • Titrate: every 2-5 min to MAP ≥65 • Max: ~0.5-1 mcg/kg/min (consider adding second agent) • Can start peripherally — do NOT delay for central line Second-line options: Vasopressin: • Fixed dose: 0.03-0.04 U/min (no titration) • Add when NE >0.25-0.5 mcg/kg/min • "Decatecholaminization" strategy Epinephrine: • 0.01-

nodes.title: Source Control
nodes.summary: Source control within 6-12h; drainage, debridement, device removal, surgery; percutaneous preferred when possible
nodes.body: Source control within 6-12 hours is critical for septic shock. Source control priorities: • Drainage: abscess (percutaneous or surgical), empyema, biliary • Debridement: necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene • Device removal: infected lines, hardware, grafts • Definitive surgery: perforated viscus, bowel ischemia Percutaneous drainage preferred when feasible — lower morbidity than surgery. Imaging f

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Shock patients require ICU; OR for surgical emergencies; cath lab for STEMI/PE/hemorrhage
nodes.body: Final disposition based on shock etiology and treatment response.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: All patients with shock require ICU admission. ICU requirements: • Continuous hemodynamic monitoring • Central venous access (if not already) • Arterial line for continuous BP • Ventilator management if intubated • Vasopressor titration • Serial lactate monitoring • Source control coordination Targets: • MAP ≥65 mmHg (higher if chronic HTN) • UOP ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr • Lactate clearance ≥10% every 2-4h •
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU. Central line and arterial line. Vasopressor titration. Serial lactate. Source control within 6-12h.

nodes.title: Emergent Operating Room
nodes.body: Surgical emergencies in shock: • Hemorrhagic shock requiring damage control surgery • Perforated viscus with peritonitis • Necrotizing fasciitis • Bowel ischemia/necrosis • Ruptured AAA • Ruptured ectopic pregnancy Pre-operative optimization: • Massive transfusion protocol if hemorrhagic • Broad-spectrum antibiotics • Vasopressors to maintain perfusion • Permissive hypotension if hemorrhagic (unti
nodes.recommendation: Emergent OR. MTP if hemorrhagic. Maintain BP with pressors during transport. Direct handoff to surgical team.

nodes.title: Cath Lab or IR
nodes.body: Cath lab / IR for: Cardiology: • STEMI with cardiogenic shock → emergent PCI • Massive PE → catheter-directed therapy or thrombectomy Interventional Radiology: • GI hemorrhage for embolization • Pelvic hemorrhage • Ruptured hepatic adenoma • Abscess drainage Transport considerations: • Vasopressors must continue during transport • Resuscitation team accompanies patient • Blood products available •
nodes.recommendation: Emergent cath lab or IR. Continue vasopressors during transport. Resuscitation team accompanies. Blood products available.

nodes.title: Accidental Hypothermia
nodes.summary: Core temp measurement is essential — peripheral thermometers are unreliable in hypothermia
nodes.body: Definition: Core temperature <35°C (95°F) due to environmental exposure. "No one is dead until they are WARM and dead." Remarkable survivals documented: - Lowest survivor (accidental hypothermia): 11.8°C (53.2°F) — per ERC 2025 - Lowest survivor (induced hypothermia): 4.0°C - Longest CPR with intact neuro survival: 6 hours 52 minutes Key principle: Hypothermia is PROTECTIVE if it occurs BEFORE car

nodes.title: Temperature Measurement
nodes.summary: Esophageal or bladder probe for core temp — rectal temp lags behind core by 15-30 min
nodes.body: Accurate core temperature is ESSENTIAL — guides all decisions. Preferred (most accurate): - Esophageal probe — gold standard in intubated patients - Rectal probe — acceptable, but lags during rapid temp changes - Bladder probe — acceptable DO NOT USE: - Oral thermometry (unreliable) - Axillary (unreliable) - Temporal/forehead (grossly inaccurate) - Tympanic (may be falsely low if ear frozen) If no

nodes.title: Severity Classification
nodes.summary: Mild 32-35°C, moderate 28-32°C, severe <28°C — management escalates with severity
nodes.body: Temperature-based classification: | Severity | Temperature | Features | |----------|-------------|----------| | Mild | 32-35°C (90-95°F) | Conscious, shivering | | Moderate | 28-32°C (82-90°F) | Altered LOC, shivering stops | | Severe | 24-28°C (75-82°F) | Unconscious, VS present | | Profound | <24°C (<75°F) | No vital signs | Key sign: Shivering typically STOPS below 30-32°C. If patient is shiver

nodes.title: Hypothermic Cardiac Arrest
nodes.summary: Hypothermic arrest: do NOT declare dead until warm and dead (core temp >32°C) — prolonged CPR indicated
nodes.body: Check pulse for 30-45 seconds — pulse may be very slow and difficult to detect. Before starting CPR, check for HARD CONTRAINDICATIONS: DO NOT RESUSCITATE if: - ❌ Chest wall frozen solid (incompressible) - ❌ Obvious lethal injuries (decapitation, truncal transection) - ❌ Decomposition - ❌ Avalanche burial >35 min WITH airway packed with snow AND asystole - ❌ Potassium >12 mEq/L (no survivors) These

nodes.title: Resuscitation Decision
nodes.summary: Contraindications to resuscitation: obviously lethal injuries, frozen chest (incompressible), DNR, or K+ >12
nodes.body: Critical question: Did hypothermia occur BEFORE or AFTER cardiac arrest? - Hypothermia BEFORE arrest → PROTECTIVE → aggressive resuscitation indicated - Arrest BEFORE hypothermia → NOT protective → standard futility criteria apply Potassium thresholds: | K+ Level | Action | |----------|--------| | <10 mEq/L | Proceed with aggressive resuscitation | | 10-12 mEq/L | Poor prognosis, calculate HOPE sc

nodes.title: Resuscitation Not Indicated
nodes.summary: K+ >12 mmol/L is incompatible with life in hypothermia — reasonable to terminate resuscitation
nodes.body: Hard contraindication to resuscitation identified. Criteria met for termination/non-initiation: - Chest wall frozen and incompressible, OR - Obvious lethal injury, OR - Signs of prolonged death (decomposition), OR - Avalanche >35 min + snow-packed airway + asystole, OR - K+ >12 mEq/L (confirmed, non-hemolyzed) Documentation: Document specific contraindication and clinical reasoning. Family communi
nodes.recommendation: Resuscitation not indicated due to confirmed futility criteria.

nodes.title: CPR in Hypothermic Arrest
nodes.summary: Start CPR, withhold meds and defib until core >30°C — one shock attempt if VF, then rewarm first
nodes.body: Start CPR immediately if no hard contraindications. CPR modifications: - Standard compression rate and depth - Mechanical CPR strongly preferred for prolonged resuscitation/transport - Intermittent CPR acceptable if continuous not possible (unique to hypothermia) Gentle handling: - Physical manipulation can precipitate VF - Move patient horizontally - Avoid rough movements Rhythm check: - VF/VT →

nodes.title: Defibrillation in Hypothermia
nodes.summary: One defibrillation attempt for VF if temp >30°C — if unsuccessful, defer until core temp >30°C
nodes.body: VF/VT detected → Attempt defibrillation Temperature-based approach: | Core Temp | Defibrillation Strategy | |-----------|------------------------| | <30°C | Attempt 1-3 shocks max, then DEFER until rewarmed | | 30-35°C | Resume standard defibrillation attempts | | >35°C | Standard ACLS | Why limit shocks below 30°C: - Severely hypothermic myocardium is refractory to defibrillation - Repeated shock

nodes.title: Drug Therapy in Hypothermia
nodes.summary: Withhold ACLS drugs until core temp >30°C — drugs accumulate and may cause toxicity
nodes.body: Drugs accumulate in hypothermia — hepatic metabolism markedly reduced. | Core Temp | Drug Strategy | |-----------|---------------| | <30°C | WITHHOLD all vasopressors and antiarrhythmics | | 30-35°C | DOUBLE intervals — epinephrine q6-10 min (not q3-5 min) | | ≥35°C | Standard ACLS dosing | Why withhold below 30°C: - Effects that last seconds at 37°C can last 5+ minutes at low temps - Risk of drug

nodes.title: ECMO Decision
nodes.summary: ECMO for hypothermic arrest with no signs of life and K+ <12 — best outcomes for rewarming
nodes.body: ECMO/Extracorporeal rewarming is GOLD STANDARD for hypothermic cardiac arrest. Survival benefit: NNT = 2 (40-90% mortality reduction in appropriate patients) ECMO indicated if: - Core temp <30-32°C - No confirmed death BEFORE cooling - K+ <12 mEq/L - No unsurvivable injuries - HOPE score suggests reasonable survival Calculate HOPE score before transport decision. Is ECMO available? [1][2][4][5]

nodes.title: ECMO Transport Protocol
nodes.summary: Transport to ECMO center with continuous CPR — coordinate with receiving center early
nodes.body: Transport to ECMO center EVEN IF NOT CLOSEST HOSPITAL. Pre-transport: 1. Calculate HOPE score (≥10% survival → proceed) 2. Obtain K+ (must be <12 mEq/L) 3. Activate ECMO team at receiving center 4. Apply mechanical CPR device if available During transport: - Continuous CPR — do not stop for loading/unloading - Mechanical CPR preferred — consistent quality during movement - Horizontal positioning —

nodes.title: Transport Checklist
nodes.summary: Transport checklist: continuous CPR, warm IV fluids, core temp monitoring, receiving team notified
nodes.body: ECMO Transport Checklist: ☐ HOPE score calculated — document survival probability ☐ K+ confirmed <12 mEq/L — non-hemolyzed sample ☐ ECMO team notified — ETA and patient status ☐ Mechanical CPR applied — LUCAS, AutoPulse, or similar ☐ Core temp probe in place — continuous monitoring ☐ Warm IV fluids running — 40-43°C crystalloid ☐ Heated blankets to trunk — avoid extremities (afterdrop risk) ☐ Pati

nodes.title: During Transport
nodes.summary: Continue CPR during transport — mechanical CPR device (LUCAS) preferred for transport
nodes.body: Continuous CPR is critical — but intermittent is acceptable if continuous impossible. Monitor for: - VF conversion (pause briefly to check rhythm) - ROSC (check pulse q5 min during CPR pauses) - Core temp changes If ROSC during transport: - Continue rewarming - Standard post-arrest care - Still transport to ECMO center (may need ECMO for rewarming or cardiogenic shock) Arriving at ECMO center: - H

nodes.title: ECMO Rewarming
nodes.summary: ECMO is gold standard for hypothermic arrest — rewarms at 1-2°C per 3-5 min with circulatory support
nodes.body: VA-ECMO rewarming protocol: Rewarming rate: 6-10°C/hour (fastest available method) Target: Core temp 32-34°C initially, then slow to 36-37°C During ECMO rewarming: - Monitor K+ frequently (shifts out of cells during rewarming) - Watch for reperfusion injury - Anticipate coagulopathy correction as temp normalizes - Gradual weaning as cardiac function recovers Post-ECMO: - Targeted temperature manag

nodes.title: Invasive Rewarming (No ECMO)
nodes.summary: Invasive rewarming without ECMO: warm IV fluids 42°C, bladder lavage, thoracic lavage
nodes.body: When ECMO unavailable, use aggressive invasive techniques: Thoracic lavage (most effective non-ECMO method): - Rewarming rate: 3-6°C/hour - Bilateral chest tubes - Instill 300-500 mL warmed (42°C) crystalloid via anterior tube - Drain via posterolateral tube - Cycle q15 min or continuous flow Peritoneal lavage: - Rewarming rate: 3-4°C/hour - 40-42°C crystalloid - Continuous or intermittent drainag

nodes.title: Thoracic Lavage Technique
nodes.summary: Thoracic lavage: bilateral chest tubes, warm saline in one side, drain from other — 3°C/h rewarming
nodes.body: Procedure: 1. Bilateral chest tube insertion - Anterior tube (2nd-3rd ICS MCL) for INSTILLATION - Posterolateral tube (5th ICS MAL) for DRAINAGE 2. Fluid preparation - Warm crystalloid to 42°C (use fluid warmer or microwave) - LR or NS acceptable 3. Instillation - Infuse 300-500 mL via anterior tube - Clamp for 15 minutes - Unclamp and drain via posterior tube - Repeat cycle 4. Alternative: contin

nodes.title: Termination of Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Terminate resuscitation if K+ >12, incompressible chest, or obvious lethal injuries
nodes.body: When to stop resuscitation: Continue CPR until: - ROSC achieved, OR - Core temp ≥32°C with persistent asystole = can consider termination, OR - K+ confirmed >12 mEq/L during resuscitation, OR - Other contraindication identified "Warm and dead" = 32°C minimum Do NOT terminate based on: - Prolonged down time alone - Fixed/dilated pupils - Muscular rigidity - Multiple failed defibrillations (while st

nodes.title: Mild Hypothermia (32-35°C)
nodes.summary: Mild (32-35°C): passive external rewarming, warm blankets, warm environment, warm PO fluids
nodes.body: Swiss Stage HT-I: Alert, shivering Management: - Remove wet clothing - Warm, dry environment - Warm blankets (passive rewarming) - Warm oral fluids if alert and protecting airway - Active external warming if slow progress Rewarming rate: 0.5-2°C/hour with passive measures Monitoring: - Core temp q30-60 min - Cardiac monitor (watch for arrhythmias) - Mental status Disposition: May discharge if rewa

nodes.title: Mild Hypothermia Response
nodes.summary: Monitor during rewarming: serial core temp, ECG, glucose, electrolytes — watch for arrhythmias
nodes.body: Assess response to passive rewarming: Good response: - Shivering effective - Core temp rising 0.5-1°C/hour - Improving mental status Poor response: - Shivering ineffective or absent - Temp not rising - Deteriorating mental status - Developing arrhythmias [1][2][3]

nodes.title: Mild Hypothermia — Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge mild hypothermia if rewarmed >36°C, normal ECG, stable vitals, warm safe environment
nodes.body: May consider discharge if: - Core temp normalized (>36°C) - Mental status normal - Ambulating safely - No arrhythmias - Underlying cause identified and addressed - Safe environment to return to - Reliable follow-up Admit if: - Elderly or comorbid - Underlying illness (sepsis, intoxication, endocrine) - Social concerns (homelessness, abuse) - Unable to rewarm adequately
nodes.recommendation: Mild hypothermia with good response — may discharge if criteria met.

nodes.title: Moderate Hypothermia (28-32°C)
nodes.summary: Moderate (28-32°C): active external rewarming — Bair Hugger, warm IV fluids (42°C), continuous monitoring
nodes.body: Swiss Stage HT-II: Altered consciousness, shivering stopped HIGH ARRHYTHMIA RISK — handle gently! Management: - Remove wet clothing (cut off, avoid excessive movement) - Horizontal positioning - Cardiac monitoring (anticipate bradycardia, AF) - Active external rewarming (forced air warming preferred) - Warm IV fluids (40-43°C crystalloid) - Heated humidified O2 via HFNC or ventilator Rewarming rat

nodes.title: Complications to Anticipate
nodes.summary: Moderate hypothermia complications: afterdrop, rewarming arrhythmias, coagulopathy — handle gently
nodes.body: ECG changes: - Sinus bradycardia (universal) - Prolonged PR, QRS, QT - J waves (Osborn waves) — pathognomonic below 32°C - Atrial fibrillation (common) - VF risk increases as QRS widens Coagulopathy: - Platelet dysfunction + enzyme inhibition below 35°C - Lab PT/aPTT run at 37°C — won't detect hypothermic coagulopathy - Primary treatment: REWARM Electrolytes: - Cooling: Hypokalemia (intracellular

nodes.title: Moderate Hypothermia — Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit all moderate hypothermia for monitoring — ICU if arrhythmias or complications
nodes.body: All moderate hypothermia patients require admission. ICU admission if: - Arrhythmias - Hemodynamic instability - Requiring invasive rewarming - Significant comorbidities Telemetry admission if: - Stable hemodynamics - Responding to active external rewarming - No significant arrhythmias Workup for underlying cause: - Toxicology screen - TSH, cortisol - Blood glucose - Infection workup if indicated
nodes.recommendation: Admit all moderate hypothermia patients. ICU if unstable or arrhythmias.

nodes.title: Severe Hypothermia (<28°C)
nodes.summary: Severe (<28°C): active internal rewarming, handle extremely gently — rough movement triggers VF
nodes.body: Swiss Stage HT-III: Unconscious, vital signs present EXTREME VF RISK — handle as if "cardiac time bomb" Immediate management: - Minimize all movement - Horizontal positioning only - Continuous cardiac monitoring - Secure airway if GCS ≤8 (RSI acceptable, ketamine preferred) - Active internal rewarming required If hemodynamically stable: - Warm IV fluids + heated O2 + forced air warming - Prepare f

nodes.title: Severe Hypothermia — ECMO Decision
nodes.summary: ECMO for unstable severe hypothermia — invasive rewarming if ECMO unavailable
nodes.body: ECMO provides: - Fastest rewarming (6-10°C/hour) - Circulatory support - Ability to continue if arrest occurs Consider ECMO transfer if: - Core temp <28°C - Hemodynamically unstable - Not responding to standard rewarming - High risk of imminent arrest ECMO available and patient candidate? [1][2][4][5]

nodes.title: Post-Rewarming Care
nodes.summary: ICU for moderate-severe hypothermia. Discharge mild only if reliable follow-up and warm environment
nodes.body: After successful rewarming: ICU admission for: - Post-arrest care (TTM protocols) - Required ECMO/mechanical support - Significant organ dysfunction - Persistent arrhythmias Monitoring: - Delayed neuro-prognostication (≥72 hours post-arrest) - Serial K+ (rewarming hyperkalemia) - Coagulation parameters - Renal function (rhabdo risk) Workup underlying cause: - Intoxication (EtOH, drugs) - Infection
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for post-rewarming monitoring. Investigate underlying cause. Delayed neuro-prognostication.

Prepare for OR Imaging: • Upright CXR (free air under diaphragm) •

nodes.title: Small Bowel Obstruction
nodes.body: SBO in Crohn's Disease: Causes: • Stricture (most common) — fibrotic vs inflammatory • Adhesions from prior surgery • Phlegmon/abscess causing mass effect Inflammatory vs Fibrotic stricture: | Feature | Inflammatory | Fibrotic | |---------|--------------|----------| | Onset | During flare | Insidious | | CRP | Elevated | Normal | | Response to steroids | Yes | No | | Treatment | Medical | Surgical

nodes.title: Intra-abdominal Abscess
nodes.body: Abscess in Crohn's Disease: Common in fistulizing/penetrating Crohn's. Clinical features: • Fever, localized pain • Palpable mass • Elevated WBC, CRP • May have fistula drainage Imaging: • CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast • Look for fistula tracts Management: 1. IV antibiotics (cover GNR + anaerobes) - Ciprofloxacin + metronidazole OR - Piperacillin-tazobactam 2. IR drainage if >3cm and accessib

nodes.title: ED Workup
nodes.body: Standard IBD Flare Workup: Labs: • CBC — anemia, leukocytosis • CMP — dehydration, electrolytes • ESR, CRP — inflammatory markers • Albumin — nutritional status, severity marker • LFTs — if on immunomodulators Stool studies (CRITICAL): • C. difficile — test ALL IBD flares - High risk on immunosuppression - Can mimic or trigger flare • Stool culture • Consider CMV if steroid-refractory Imaging: • A

nodes.title: Mild IBD Flare — Treatment
nodes.body: Mild Flare — Usually Outpatient: Ulcerative Colitis: • Oral 5-ASA: mesalamine 4.8g/day • Topical therapy if distal: - Mesalamine suppository (proctitis) - Mesalamine enema (left-sided) • If not responding: oral prednisone 40mg/day Crohn's Disease: • Oral budesonide 9mg/day (ileal/right colon) • Or prednisone 40mg/day if more extensive • 5-ASA less effective in Crohn's For both: • Ensure adherence

nodes.title: Moderate IBD Flare — Treatment
nodes.body: Moderate Flare — May Need Admission: Treatment: • IV fluids for dehydration • Oral prednisone 40-60mg/day if tolerating PO • If not tolerating PO or more severe: - IV methylprednisolone 40-60mg/day OR - IV hydrocortisone 300mg/day divided • Electrolyte repletion • DVT prophylaxis (IBD = hypercoagulable) Rule out infection: • C. diff testing mandatory • Treat C. diff if positive (oral vancomycin pr

nodes.title: Severe UC Flare — Admit
nodes.body: Severe UC — Requires Admission: Initial management: 1. NPO initially, advance diet as tolerated 2. IV steroids: methylprednisolone 60mg/day or hydrocortisone 100mg q8h 3. IV fluids — monitor I/O 4. DVT prophylaxis — critical (hypercoagulable) 5. Check C. diff — treat if positive 6. Daily labs: CBC, CMP, CRP 7. Daily AXR — monitor for toxic megacolon Assess response at day 3: • Stool frequency, blo

nodes.title: Severe Crohn's Flare — Admit
nodes.body: Severe Crohn's — Requires Admission: Initial management: 1. Rule out surgical complications (abscess, obstruction, perforation) 2. IV steroids: methylprednisolone 40-60mg/day 3. IV fluids, electrolyte correction 4. Nutritional support — may need TPN if prolonged NPO 5. DVT prophylaxis 6. Infection workup: C. diff, CMV if steroid-refractory Imaging: • CT enterography or MR enterography to assess di

nodes.title: Biologics in IBD
nodes.body: Common Biologics — ED Considerations: Anti-TNF agents: • Infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab • ↑ Infection risk (TB, fungal, bacterial) • Check TB, Hep B before starting (usually outpatient) Anti-integrin: • Vedolizumab (gut-selective, lower infection risk) Anti-IL12/23: • Ustekinumab JAK inhibitors: • Tofacitinib, upadacitinib (UC) • FDA boxed warning: ↑ VTE/PE and death (10mg BID, OR

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Admit to ICU: • Toxic megacolon • Perforation/peritonitis • Sepsis/hemodynamic instability • Massive GI hemorrhage Admit to floor: • Severe UC or Crohn's flare • Unable to tolerate PO • Dehydration requiring IV fluids • Need for IV steroids • Anemia requiring transfusion • Obstruction or abscess Discharge: • Mild flare responding to treatment • Tolerating PO • Stable vital signs • Close GI follow-

nodes.title: Admit ICU
nodes.body: ICU Admission: Indications: • Toxic megacolon • Perforation or pending surgery • Sepsis/shock • Massive hemorrhage Orders: • NPO, NG tube if indicated • IV steroids (hold if septic and no clear benefit) • Broad-spectrum antibiotics • Aggressive IVF, pressors if needed • Serial abdominal exams • DVT prophylaxis (mechanical if surgery imminent) • Blood products PRN Consults: • GI (urgent) • Surgery
nodes.recommendation: Admit ICU. NPO, IV steroids if appropriate, broad antibiotics. Surgery and GI consults stat.

nodes.title: Admit Floor
nodes.body: Floor Admission: Orders: • Diet: NPO → clear liquids → low residue as tolerated • IV methylprednisolone 40-60mg/day (or hydrocortisone 100mg q8h) • IV fluids — correct dehydration • DVT prophylaxis (enoxaparin preferred) • Daily labs: CBC, CMP, CRP • Daily AXR if severe UC (toxic megacolon monitoring) • Stool C. diff if not already sent GI consult: • Timing of scope • Biologic escalation discussio
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV steroids, IVF. DVT prophylaxis mandatory. GI consult. Daily AXR if severe UC.

nodes.title: Discharge — Mild Flare
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: • Mild flare only • Tolerating PO • Hemodynamically stable • No signs of complications • C. diff negative (or treated) • Reliable with close follow-up Prescriptions: • Prednisone 40mg PO daily (if escalating therapy) - Taper per GI guidance (usually over 6-8 weeks) • Or optimize 5-ASA if not on maximal dose • Antidiarrheals PRN (if no toxic megacolon concern) Instructions: • St
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with oral steroids or optimized 5-ASA. GI follow-up 1-2 weeks. Written return precautions.

nodes.title: Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH)
nodes.summary: ICH: reverse anticoagulation AND lower BP simultaneously — time-critical interventions
nodes.body: ICH Steps Summary — time-critical hemorrhage management. Spontaneous ICH accounts for 10–15% of all strokes with ~40% 30-day mortality. Early hemostatic therapy, BP control, and neurosurgical consultation are the cornerstones of acute management. Immediate actions: • Non-contrast CT head — confirm diagnosis, estimate hematoma volume • Establish IV access ×2 • Activate stroke/neurosurgery team • NP

nodes.title: Evaluation & Imaging
nodes.summary: STAT: CBC, coags (PT/INR, PTT), BMP, type and screen — check antithrombotic medication list
nodes.body: Initial labs: • CBC, BMP, Mg, Phos • INR, PTT, fibrinogen • Anti-Xa level if on oral Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) • Toxicology screen (if clinically warranted) • Type & screen • ABG/VBG if intubated Hematoma volume (ABC/2): A × B × C ÷ 2 (cm) = volume in mL • A = largest diameter on axial CT • B = perpendicular diameter on same slice • C = number of slices with hemorrhage × slice thicknes

nodes.title: Anticoagulation Status
nodes.summary: Determine anticoagulant type: warfarin, dabigatran, Xa inhibitor, heparin, or antiplatelet
nodes.body: Determine anticoagulant/antiplatelet status immediately. Do NOT wait for lab results before initiating reversal — empiric reversal should begin as soon as the agent is identified. Causes of ICH — hypertensive, CAA, vascular malformation, coagulopathy

nodes.title: Warfarin Reversal
nodes.summary: 4-factor PCC 25-50 IU/kg + Vitamin K 10mg IV — target INR <1.4 within 4 hours
nodes.body: Goal: INR <1.4 as rapidly as possible. First-line: 4-Factor PCC • 25–50 IU/kg IV based on INR and weight • Onset: 10–15 minutes • Superior to FFP — faster correction, less volume PLUS Vitamin K • 10 mg IV slow push (over 15–30 min) • Prevents INR rebound after PCC wears off (6–8h) • IV route preferred — oral takes 12–24h FFP (15 mL/kg) only if PCC unavailable — slower, volume overload risk Monitor

nodes.title: Dabigatran Reversal
nodes.summary: Idarucizumab 5g IV for dabigatran reversal — immediate effect, one-time dose
nodes.body: First-line: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) • 5 g IV as two consecutive 2.5 g bolus doses • Onset: immediate — complete reversal within minutes • Specific monoclonal antibody fragment for dabigatran If idarucizumab unavailable: • 4-Factor PCC 50 IU/kg IV • OR activated PCC (FEIBA) 50 IU/kg IV Adjuncts: • Hemodialysis can remove dabigatran (60% reduction in 2–3h) — consider if idarucizumab unavailable and

nodes.title: Xa Inhibitor Reversal
nodes.summary: Andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC 50 IU/kg for Xa inhibitor reversal — PCC if andexanet unavailable
nodes.body: Applies to: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban Option 1: 4-Factor PCC • 50 IU/kg IV • Most widely available option • Onset: 15–30 minutes Option 2: Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) • Specific Xa inhibitor reversal agent • Dosing depends on agent and time since last dose • Note: recently withdrawn from US market due to thrombotic concerns — availability varies If last dose within 2h (intubated patient): • Act

nodes.title: Heparin / LMWH Reversal
nodes.summary: Protamine sulfate 1mg per 100U heparin given in last 2-3h — max 50mg, watch for anaphylaxis
nodes.body: Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): • Protamine 1 mg per 100 units UFH given in prior 2–3h • Max single dose: 50 mg • Onset: 5 minutes — complete reversal • Check PTT 15 min after administration LMWH (enoxaparin): • Protamine — partial reversal only (~60%) • If enoxaparin given within 8h: Protamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin • If 8–12h: Protamine 0.5 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin • If >12h: likely no benefit Thr

nodes.title: Hemostatic Adjuncts
nodes.summary: Platelets if <100K, cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <200 — TXA may reduce hematoma expansion
nodes.body: Not on anticoagulation — consider adjunct measures: Tranexamic acid (TXA): • TXA 1 g IV over 10 min (within 3h of onset) • Significant reduction in hematoma expansion (OR 0.82) • Did NOT improve mortality or functional outcomes in TICH-2 • May be considered — TICH-3 trial underway Antiplatelet agents: • Platelet transfusion is NOT recommended (PATCH trial — worse outcomes) • Desmopressin (DDAVP) 0

nodes.title: Blood Pressure Control
nodes.summary: Target SBP 130-150 in first 6h (INTERACT2) — nicardipine or clevidipine infusion preferred
nodes.body: Treat pain and anxiety FIRST — hypertension may be secondary. Proper analgesia/sedation (especially in intubated patients) can significantly improve BP. AHA/ASA 2022 BP Targets: • SBP 150–220 → target 130–150 mmHg (reasonable) • SBP >220 → target 140–180 mmHg (less evidence) • Avoid SBP <130 — potentially harmful • Avoid drops >70 mmHg in first hour Timing: Maximum benefit when started immediately

nodes.title: Hematoma Location
nodes.summary: Location guides neurosurgical consultation: supratentorial vs cerebellar vs intraventricular
nodes.body: Hematoma location determines surgical approach and prognosis. Supratentorial (most common): • Basal ganglia/external capsule (60–65%) • Thalamus (15–20%) • Lobar (cortical) Infratentorial: • Cerebellar (5–10%) — unique urgency • Pontine (5%) — poor prognosis regardless Intraventricular extension occurs in >40% and worsens prognosis.

nodes.title: Supratentorial Hematoma
nodes.summary: Supratentorial ICH: neurosurgery for large (>30mL), superficial, or deteriorating — deep basal ganglia usually conservative
nodes.body: Evidence for surgical evacuation is limited: STITCH-I Trial (1,033 patients): No benefit from early surgery overall. Possible trend toward benefit for hematomas within 1 cm of cortical surface and lobar hemorrhage with GCS 9–12. STITCH-II Trial (601 patients): Focused on predicted surgical benefit subgroup — still no significant difference vs conservative management. Possible indications for crani

nodes.title: Cerebellar Hematoma — Surgical Emergency
nodes.summary: Cerebellar ICH >3 cm (≈ >15 mL) or hydrocephalus/brainstem compression = emergent surgical evacuation — rapid herniation risk
nodes.body: The cerebellum is unique — patients may deteriorate rapidly (12–24h). Risks of cerebellar hemorrhage: • Direct brainstem compression → catastrophic damage • 4th ventricle compression → obstructive hydrocephalus • Upward transtentorial herniation Paradox: Cerebellar ICH patients tend to have better prognosis than other ICH types IF timely surgical intervention is performed. AHA/ASA 2022 — Immediate

nodes.title: Intraventricular Hemorrhage & EVD
nodes.summary: Intraventricular hemorrhage with hydrocephalus: emergent EVD placement by neurosurgery
nodes.body: IVH occurs in >40% of ICH patients and worsens prognosis. Complications: • Hydrocephalus and elevated ICP • Central (neurogenic) fever External Ventricular Drain (EVD): • Indicated for hydrocephalus contributing to reduced consciousness • Ideal candidate: initially well, then develops hydrocephalus with neuroworsening • Caveat: EVD increases survival but may not increase rate of good neurologic ou

nodes.title: Seizure Management
nodes.summary: Treat clinical seizures with levetiracetam — prophylactic AEDs controversial (AHA says consider)
nodes.body: Incidence: ~10% convulsive seizures; subclinical seizure rate is substantially higher. Risk factors: • Cortical involvement (lobar hemorrhages) • Coexisting subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage • Rebleeding Continuous EEG monitoring indications: • Impaired consciousness disproportionate to CT findings • Unexplained fluctuations in mental status • Any witnessed seizure or clinical signs of seizure T

nodes.title: ICP, Sodium & Fever
nodes.summary: Fever worsens ICH outcomes — target normothermia aggressively with acetaminophen and cooling
nodes.body: Intracranial Pressure: • ICP elevation from mass effect, perihematomal edema, and/or obstructive hydrocephalus • Edema peaks at ~5–6 days — anticipate delayed neurological deterioration • Boluses of hypertonic saline or hypertonic bicarbonate for acute ICP crisis (bridge to EVD or surgery) • Routine hypertonic saline not supported by evidence Sodium: • Avoid hyponatremia or rapid decreases in sodi

nodes.title: DVT Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Start DVT prophylaxis (pneumatic compression) immediately — pharmacologic prophylaxis after 48h if stable
nodes.body: AHA/ASA 2022 recommendations: Immediately: • Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) — start on admission After 24–48 hours: • If ICH has demonstrated stability on serial imaging: – Low-dose UFH 5000 units SQ q8–12h – OR Enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily – Starting chemical DVT prophylaxis is reasonable Caution: • Patients with underlying coagulopathy or imaging evidence of ongoing hemorrhage expansion m

nodes.title: Disposition & Prognosis
nodes.summary: ICU admission for all ICH — neuro checks q1h, repeat CT at 6h or with clinical change
nodes.body: All ICH patients → ICU admission for continuous neuro monitoring and BP management. Ongoing care: • Neuro checks q1h minimum (more frequent during acute phase) • Serial CT: 6h, 24h, and with any neuro decline • ICP monitoring if EVD placed • Transition IV antihypertensives to PO after >24h if stable • DVT prophylaxis per protocol • Early rehabilitation consultation • Goals of care discussion with
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU. Serial CT at 6h and 24h. IPC for DVT. Transition to PO antihypertensives when stable >24h. Early rehab and goals-of-care discussions.

nodes.title: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)
nodes.summary: IIH = elevated ICP without cause. Classic: obese woman with headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations. Vision loss is main morbidity.
nodes.body: Also known as: Pseudotumor Cerebri Definition: Elevated ICP (>25 cm H₂O) without identifiable cause, normal CSF composition, and normal neuroimaging. Classic Patient: • Obese woman of childbearing age (90%) • Incidence 20/100,000 in obese women vs 1/100,000 general population Cardinal Symptoms: | Symptom | Frequency | |---------|-----------| | Headache | 90% — often positional, worse AM | | Pulsat

nodes.title: Red Flags — Exclude Secondary Causes
nodes.summary: Exclude CVST, mass, meningitis. Check medications (vitamin A, tetracyclines, steroids). CVST risk: OCP, pregnancy, hypercoagulable.
nodes.body: Before diagnosing IIH, exclude secondary causes: 🚨 Emergent Etiologies: • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) • Intracranial mass/tumor • Meningitis/encephalitis • Hydrocephalus Risk Factors for CVST: • Pregnancy/postpartum • Oral contraceptives • Hypercoagulable state • Recent head trauma • Infection (otitis, mastoiditis) Medications Causing Elevated ICP: • Vitamin A / retinoids • Tetracycli

nodes.title: Secondary Cause Workup
nodes.body: Urgent Imaging Required: • CT Head without contrast — rule out mass, hydrocephalus, hemorrhage • MRV (or CTV) — rule out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis • MRI Brain with contrast — if mass suspected If CVST Confirmed: • Anticoagulation (even with hemorrhage in most cases) • Neurology/neurosurgery consult • ICU admission If Medication-Induced: • Stop offending agent • Still needs ophthalmology eva
nodes.recommendation: Order CT Head + MRV to rule out secondary causes. If CVST confirmed, anticoagulate and admit. Neurology consult.

nodes.title: Ocular Assessment — POCUS First
nodes.summary: Ocular POCUS is ACEP core competency. Measures ONSD (elevated ICP) and ODE (papilledema). Faster than fundoscopy, precedes papilledema.
nodes.body: ACEP Core Application: Ocular Ultrasound Ocular POCUS is a core emergency ultrasound competency per ACEP 2023 guidelines. Two Key Findings: 1. Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) • Measures elevated ICP non-invasively • Precedes papilledema by hours to days 2. Optic Disc Elevation (ODE) • Visualizes papilledema directly • ≥0.6 mm elevation = significant Advantages of POCUS: • Rapid (2-3 minutes) •

nodes.title: ONSD Measurement Technique
nodes.summary: ONSD technique: 3mm behind globe, measure inner to inner. <5mm normal, 5-6mm indeterminate, >6mm elevated ICP. Check both eyes.
nodes.body: Equipment: • High-frequency linear probe (7.5-12 MHz) • Tegaderm over closed eye (optional) • Generous ultrasound gel Technique — "Remember 3×5": 1. Patient supine, eyes closed, looking straight ahead 2. Place probe gently on closed eyelid (transverse) 3. Identify optic nerve as hypoechoic stripe behind globe 4. Measure 3 mm posterior to the globe 5. Measure inner edge to inner edge of sheath 6. R

nodes.title: ONSD Measurement Result
nodes.summary: ONSD >6mm = elevated ICP. 5-6mm indeterminate. <5mm normal. Always correlate with clinical picture.
nodes.body: Enter bilateral ONSD measurements: Interpretation: | Average ONSD | Significance | |--------------|--------------| | <5 mm | Normal — low probability of elevated ICP | | 5-6 mm | Indeterminate — clinical correlation needed | | >6 mm | Elevated — correlates with ICP >20 mmHg | Also assess for: • Optic disc elevation (ODE) ≥0.6 mm • Crescent sign — fluid around optic nerve Note: ONSD dilates before

nodes.title: Low Suspicion for Elevated ICP
nodes.summary: ONSD <5mm suggests normal ICP but not perfect. Consider fundoscopy if classic symptoms. Rule out other headache disorders.
nodes.body: ONSD <5 mm suggests normal ICP However, ONSD has limitations: • Sensitivity 88-100% (not perfect) • Prior optic nerve pathology may affect baseline • Chronic elevated ICP may have normal ONSD Still Consider IIH if: • Classic symptoms (positional headache, pulsatile tinnitus) • Transient visual obscurations • Typical demographics (obese woman of childbearing age) Next Steps: • Fundoscopic exam if s

nodes.title: Fundoscopic Examination
nodes.summary: Fundoscopy for papilledema grading. Frisén scale 0-5. Gold standard but requires expertise.
nodes.body: Fundoscopy remains gold standard for papilledema detection Perform if: • Symptoms concerning despite normal ONSD • Need to document baseline optic disc appearance • Cannot perform adequate POCUS Papilledema Grading (Frisén Scale): | Grade | Findings | |-------|----------| | 0 | Normal | | 1 | C-shaped halo, temporal blurring | | 2 | Circumferential halo | | 3 | Obscuration of vessels at disc | | 4

nodes.title: Fundoscopic Examination
nodes.summary: Papilledema: blurred margins, elevated disc, venous engorgement. Frisén scale 0-5. ONSD rises before papilledema develops.
nodes.body: ONSD elevated — now confirm with fundoscopy Papilledema Features: • Blurred disc margins (starts nasal, progresses circumferentially) • Elevated optic disc • Obscuration of blood vessels at disc margin • Venous engorgement • Loss of spontaneous venous pulsations • Peripapillary hemorrhages (later stage) Frisén Grading Scale: | Grade | Description | |-------|-------------| | 0 | Normal disc | | 1 |

nodes.title: Papilledema Status
nodes.summary: Papilledema confirms elevated ICP. Absence does not rule out IIH (IIHWOP exists). If ONSD elevated, proceed to diagnosis.
nodes.body: Fundoscopy findings: Papilledema is present if ANY of: • Blurred disc margins • Elevated optic disc • Obscured vessels at disc margin • Peripapillary hemorrhages Important: Absence of papilledema does NOT rule out IIH • "IIH without papilledema" (IIHWOP) is recognized • ONSD elevation may precede papilledema • ~5% of IIH patients lack papilledema Papilledema present?

nodes.title: Ophthalmology Consultation
nodes.summary: Ophthalmology for formal fundus exam, visual fields, OCT. Visual field PMD guides treatment. Urgent if severe vision loss.
nodes.body: Indications for Urgent Ophthalmology: • Cannot adequately visualize fundus • Uncertain papilledema findings • Need formal visual field testing • Severe papilledema (Frisén 4-5) • Rapid visual decline Ophthalmology Will Provide: • Dilated fundoscopic exam • Formal papilledema grading • Visual field testing (Humphrey perimetry) • Optic nerve photography for baseline • OCT if available Visual Fields

nodes.title: Alternative Diagnosis
nodes.body: Normal ONSD + Normal Fundoscopy = IIH Unlikely Consider Alternative Diagnoses: | Diagnosis | Features | |-----------|----------| | Migraine | Unilateral, throbbing, photo/phonophobia, nausea | | Tension headache | Bilateral, band-like, non-pulsatile | | Medication overuse | >15 days/month analgesic use | | Cervicogenic | Neck-related, unilateral, occipital | | Cluster headache | Unilateral, perior
