nodes.recommendation: IIH unlikely with normal ONSD and fundoscopy. Consider alternative headache diagnoses. Outpatient neurology follow-up if symptoms persist.

nodes.title: Diagnostic Criteria — Modified Dandy/Friedman
nodes.summary: Definite IIH: papilledema + normal exam + normal MRI/MRV + normal CSF + OP >25 cmH₂O. IIHWOP requires additional MRI findings.
nodes.body: IIH Diagnostic Criteria (Friedman 2013): DEFINITE IIH — All Required: 1. ✓ Papilledema present 2. ✓ Normal neurologic exam (except CN VI palsy) 3. ✓ Normal neuroimaging (MRI preferred, with MRV) 4. ✓ Normal CSF composition 5. ✓ Elevated opening pressure: • Adults: >25 cm H₂O • Children: >28 cm H₂O PROBABLE IIH: • Meets criteria 1-4 but OP 20-25 cm H₂O IIH WITHOUT PAPILLEDEMA (IIHWOP): • Meets crit

nodes.title: Neuroimaging
nodes.summary: MRI + MRV preferred. IIH findings: empty sella, ONSD on MRI, posterior globe flattening, transverse sinus stenosis. Rule out CVST.
nodes.body: Required Before LP: MRI Brain with MRV (preferred) or CT/CTV: Purpose: • Rule out mass, hydrocephalus • Rule out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) • Identify IIH-associated findings IIH Findings on MRI: | Finding | Sensitivity | |---------|-------------| | Empty sella | 70% | | Optic nerve sheath distension | 45% | | Flattening of posterior globe | 80% | | Transverse sinus stenosis | 90% | |

nodes.title: Lumbar Puncture
nodes.summary: LP confirms diagnosis: OP >25 cmH₂O with normal CSF composition. Therapeutic removal of 20-30mL for symptom relief.
nodes.body: LP is Required for Definitive Diagnosis Technique: • Patient in lateral decubitus position (most accurate OP) • Legs extended (flexion falsely elevates OP) • Measure opening pressure before removing fluid Opening Pressure Interpretation: | OP (cm H₂O) | Interpretation | |-------------|----------------| | <20 | Normal | | 20-25 | Borderline (probable IIH if symptomatic) | | >25 | Elevated (adult) |

nodes.title: LP Results
nodes.summary: OP >25 cmH₂O + normal CSF = definite IIH. OP 20-25 = probable IIH. Abnormal CSF = not IIH.
nodes.body: Opening Pressure and CSF Results: IIH Confirmed if: • OP >25 cm H₂O (adult) or >28 cm H₂O (child) • Normal CSF composition (protein, glucose, cells) Opening Pressure Result:

nodes.title: IIH Ruled Out
nodes.body: Diagnosis is NOT IIH If CSF Abnormal: • Elevated protein → inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic • Pleocytosis → meningitis, carcinomatosis • Low glucose → bacterial/fungal meningitis, carcinomatosis If OP Normal with Papilledema: • Consider pseudopapilledema (optic disc drusen) • Prior LP may have temporarily normalized pressure • Repeat LP after recovery period Alternative Diagnoses: • CVST (shou
nodes.recommendation: IIH ruled out. If CSF abnormal, evaluate for meningitis, carcinomatosis, or inflammatory process. Neurology consult for further workup.

nodes.title: Visual Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Visual severity guides treatment: mild = acetazolamide + weight loss, moderate = aggressive medical, severe/fulminant = urgent surgery.
nodes.body: Visual function determines treatment urgency Visual Field Testing (if available): • Perimetric Mean Deviation (PMD) from Humphrey VF Severity Classification: | Severity | PMD | Features | |----------|-----|----------| | Mild | -2 to -3.5 dB | Minimal visual field loss, low-grade papilledema | | Moderate | -3.5 to -7 dB | Moderate VF loss, papilledema grade 2-3 | | Severe | <-7 dB | Significant VF

nodes.title: Medical Management — Mild Visual Loss
nodes.summary: Mild IIH: Acetazolamide 500mg BID, titrate to 2-4g/day. Weight loss 5-10%. IIHTT showed benefit with mean dose 2.5g/day.
nodes.body: IIHTT Trial-Based Treatment: 1. Acetazolamide | Parameter | Recommendation | |-----------|----------------| | Starting dose | 500 mg PO BID (1 g/day) | | Target dose | 2-4 g/day as tolerated | | IIHTT mean dose | 2.5 g/day at 6 months | | Max dose | 4 g/day | Common Side Effects: • Paresthesias (tingling hands/feet) — expected • Fatigue • Dysgeusia (metallic taste, carbonation tastes flat) • GI up

nodes.title: Acetazolamide Dosing Protocol
nodes.summary: Start 500mg BID, titrate by 250-500mg/week to 2-4g/day. Check BMP in 2-4 weeks. 89% tolerate ≥1g/day per IIHTT.
nodes.body: Starting & Titration: Week 1: 500 mg PO BID (1 g/day) Week 2: Increase to 750 mg BID (1.5 g/day) if tolerated Week 3-4: Increase to 1 g BID (2 g/day) Beyond: Increase by 250-500 mg/week to max 4 g/day IIHTT Tolerability: • 89.5% tolerated ≥1 g/day • 44% tolerated max dose (4 g/day) • Mean tolerated dose: 2.5 g/day Contraindications: ❌ Sulfonamide allergy (cross-reactivity possible) ❌ Severe hepati

nodes.title: Medical Management — Moderate Visual Loss
nodes.summary: Moderate: Higher acetazolamide doses (2-4g/day), serial therapeutic LPs, close follow-up. Consider surgery if no improvement in 2-4 weeks.
nodes.body: More Aggressive Approach Required: 1. Acetazolamide — Higher Doses • Start 500 mg PO QID (2 g/day) or 1 g BID • Titrate rapidly to 3-4 g/day • Consider IV acetazolamide 500 mg if severe symptoms 2. Serial Therapeutic LPs • Remove 20-30 mL CSF per session • Temporary relief, buys time for medications to work • Can be done q1-3 days in acute setting 3. Weight Loss Counseling • Dietary consultation •

nodes.title: Severe/Fulminant IIH — Urgent Intervention
nodes.summary: Fulminant IIH: emergent ophthalmology + neurosurgery. IV acetazolamide, therapeutic LP, admit. Surgical options: ONSF, VP shunt, venous stenting.
nodes.body: Fulminant IIH is an Emergency Definition: • Rapid visual decline over days to weeks • Severe visual field loss (PMD <-7 dB) • Visual acuity loss • High-grade papilledema (Frisén 4-5) Immediate Actions: 1. Emergent Ophthalmology Consult 2. Emergent Neurosurgery Consult 3. IV Acetazolamide 500 mg 4. Therapeutic LP — remove 30-40 mL CSF 5. Admit to hospital Surgical Options: | Procedure | Indication

nodes.title: Admission — Severe/Fulminant IIH
nodes.body: Admission Required: Admission Criteria: • Severe or rapidly progressive visual loss • Visual acuity involvement • High-grade papilledema (Frisén 4-5) • Need for serial therapeutic LPs • Surgical intervention planned Admission Orders: • Neuro checks q4h (visual acuity, pupil exam) • Acetazolamide IV 500 mg q6h (or PO if tolerating) • Therapeutic LP if not recently done • Strict I/Os, daily weights
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT for severe/fulminant IIH. IV acetazolamide, therapeutic LP, urgent ophthalmology and neurosurgery consults. Consider emergent ONSF or shunting.

nodes.title: Discharge — Mild IIH
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: ✓ Mild visual loss only ✓ Stable symptoms ✓ Able to tolerate oral medications ✓ Close follow-up arranged ✓ Understands return precautions Discharge Medications: • Acetazolamide 500 mg PO BID (titrate to 2-4 g/day) • Potassium supplementation PRN (20-40 mEq/day) Follow-Up: • Ophthalmology: 1-2 weeks (visual fields, fundus exam) • Neurology: 2-4 weeks • PCP: 1-2 weeks (BMP check,
nodes.recommendation: DISCHARGE with acetazolamide 500mg BID. Close ophthalmology (1-2 weeks) and neurology (2-4 weeks) follow-up. Weight loss counseling. Return for vision changes.

nodes.title: Disposition — Moderate Visual Loss
nodes.summary: Moderate IIH: consider admit if rapid follow-up unavailable or needs serial LPs. Discharge if stable with 3-5 day ophthalmology follow-up.
nodes.body: Moderate IIH — Disposition Decision Consider Admission if: • Unable to arrange rapid follow-up • Needs serial therapeutic LPs • Not tolerating oral medications • Concern for progression • Social factors limiting compliance Discharge Possible if: • Stable symptoms after therapeutic LP • Tolerating medications • Ophthalmology follow-up within 3-5 days • Reliable patient with good social support • Cl

nodes.title: Admission — Moderate IIH
nodes.body: Admission for Observation and Treatment: Indication: • Moderate visual loss requiring close monitoring • Need for serial therapeutic LPs • Medication titration • Cannot arrange close outpatient follow-up Admission Orders: • Acetazolamide 500 mg PO QID (2 g/day) — titrate as tolerated • Daily visual acuity and pupil checks • Therapeutic LP q1-2 days PRN headache/symptoms • BMP daily (monitor potass
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT for moderate IIH. Acetazolamide 2 g/day, serial therapeutic LPs, daily visual checks. Ophthalmology and neurology consults. Discharge when stable.

nodes.title: Discharge — Moderate IIH (Close Follow-Up)
nodes.body: Discharge with Very Close Follow-Up: Discharge Medications: • Acetazolamide 500 mg PO TID-QID (1.5-2 g/day) • Potassium 20-40 mEq PO daily CRITICAL Follow-Up: • Ophthalmology: within 3-5 days (visual fields mandatory) • Neurology: within 1 week • PCP: within 1 week (BMP, weight) Patient Contract: • Patient verbally confirms understanding of severity • Clear return precautions documented • Emergenc
nodes.recommendation: DISCHARGE with acetazolamide 1.5-2 g/day. CRITICAL: Ophthalmology within 3-5 days. Low threshold for return. Document patient understanding of severity.

nodes.title: Infectious Endocarditis
nodes.summary: Suspect IE in bacteremia/sepsis with valve/device risk, murmur, emboli, stroke/ICH, or septic pulmonary emboli.
nodes.body: Core ED task: identify the patient who needs cultures, echo, early antibiotics, and early specialty escalation. Suspect IE in fever, bacteremia, sepsis without source, new murmur, embolic phenomena, back pain, stroke/ICH, renal/splenic infarct, septic pulmonary emboli, or glomerulonephritis plus a risk factor. [1-3] High-risk substrates: prosthetic valve, prior IE, transcatheter valve/valve repair

nodes.title: Immediate Stability
nodes.summary: Unstable/complicated IE needs simultaneous resuscitation, cultures, empiric therapy, echo, and early specialty activation.
nodes.body: Does the patient have a complicated or unstable presentation? Complicated features: shock, persistent hypotension, respiratory failure, acute pulmonary edema, severe valve regurgitation, new heart block/PR prolongation, focal neurologic deficit, ICH/SAH, septic emboli, prosthetic valve/device, immunocompromise, hemodialysis, or persistent positive blood cultures.

nodes.title: Unstable / Complicated IE
nodes.summary: Unstable IE: cultures if no delay, empiric vancomycin + cefepime, STAT echo/ECG, ID/cardiology/CT surgery.
nodes.body: Do these in parallel: - Sepsis resuscitation and ICU-level monitoring - 2-3 blood culture sets immediately if this does not delay antibiotics - Start empiric therapy: Vancomycin + Cefepime for unstable native-valve or healthcare-associated disease while cultures are pending; modify for local antibiogram, renal function, allergy, and ID input - STAT ECG: new AV block/PR prolongation suggests perian

nodes.title: Recognition Pattern
nodes.summary: Look for bacteremia plus valve/device risk, embolic disease, septic pulmonary emboli, back pain, renal/splenic infarct, or GN.
nodes.body: Clinical patterns that should trigger the IE pathway: - Persistent fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, malaise - New or changing murmur, heart failure, pulmonary edema - Stroke, TIA, ICH/SAH, confusion, seizure, headache with bacteremia - Back pain/discitis/vertebral osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, splenic/renal infarct - Septic pulmonary emboli: pleuritic pain, hypoxia, cavitary nodules, h

nodes.title: Blood Culture Strategy
nodes.summary: IE cultures: 2-3 sets before antibiotics if feasible; repeat q24-48h until clearance.
nodes.body: Before antibiotics if feasible: obtain at least 2 sets, preferably 3 sets when IE is suspected, from separate peripheral venipunctures if possible. Do not wait for fever spikes. [1,2] If unstable: draw cultures immediately, but do not delay antibiotics for ideal timing. Volume matters: underfilled bottles reduce yield. Use adult bottle volumes per local lab standard. After antibiotics start: repea

nodes.title: Duke-ISCVID Criteria
nodes.summary: Duke-ISCVID classifies probability; do not let criteria delay cultures, antibiotics, echo, or surgical escalation.
nodes.body: Use the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria to classify suspected IE as definite, possible, or rejected/insufficient evidence. [2] Definite clinical IE: - 2 major criteria, OR - 1 major + 3 minor criteria, OR - 5 minor criteria Possible IE: - 1 major + 1 minor, OR - 3 minor criteria Major buckets: typical microbiology and imaging/surgical evidence. 2023 criteria incorporate newer microbiology, prosthetic ma

nodes.title: Echo / Imaging Status
nodes.summary: TTE is a start; TEE is required for high suspicion, prosthetic/device concern, or suspected complications.
nodes.body: What is the current echo/imaging situation?

nodes.title: Echo Positive
nodes.summary: Positive echo: characterize valve, vegetation, regurgitation, abscess, device involvement, emboli, and surgical triggers.
nodes.body: Document what matters for management: - Valve involved; native vs prosthetic; left vs right sided - Vegetation size and mobility - New or severe regurgitation; ventricular function; pulmonary pressures - Abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, perforation, prosthetic dehiscence - CIED lead vegetation or pocket infection - Embolic complications and metastatic infection Escalate early for acute heart fail

nodes.title: Negative TTE, High Suspicion
nodes.summary: Negative TTE does not rule out high-risk IE; TEE and repeat imaging are often required.
nodes.body: A negative TTE does not exclude IE when suspicion remains high. [1,3] Obtain TEE when: - Prosthetic valve, transcatheter valve, valve repair, VAD, or CIED - S. aureus bacteremia or persistent bacteremia - Poor TTE windows or equivocal TTE - Aortic valve/root concern, new AV block/PR prolongation, abscess/pseudoaneurysm concern - Embolic disease, stroke/ICH, splenic/renal infarct, vertebral osteomy

nodes.title: U/S Identification
nodes.summary: POCUS can identify large vegetations or severe valve dysfunction, but it cannot rule out IE.
nodes.body: POCUS/TTE recognition goal: identify large, mobile valve-attached masses, new severe regurgitation, gross valve destruction, right-sided vegetations, RV strain from septic pulmonary emboli, pericardial effusion, or heart-failure physiology. Useful views: PLAX and PSAX for aortic/mitral valve, apical 4/5 chamber for mitral/tricuspid/aortic outflow, subxiphoid when needed, and color Doppler for regu

nodes.title: Valve / Hardware Context
nodes.summary: Native left-sided, prosthetic/device, and right-sided IE have different imaging, source-control, and surgery thresholds.
nodes.body: Which anatomic/device context best fits?

nodes.title: Native-Valve Empiric Therapy
nodes.summary: Stable IE: cultures first. Unstable IE: empiric vancomycin + cefepime while cultures pending, then narrow.
nodes.body: Stable patient: obtain cultures first and discuss timing of empiric antibiotics with ID if IE is strongly suspected but the patient is not septic. Culture yield matters. Unstable/septic or high-risk healthcare-associated disease: empiric Vancomycin + Cefepime is a common ED bridge while cultures are pending. Tailor to allergy, renal function, local antibiogram, and ID input. [1,3] Once organism id

nodes.title: Prosthetic Valve / CIED / VAD
nodes.summary: Prosthetic/device IE requires TEE/advanced imaging, early specialty teams, repeated cultures, and source-control planning.
nodes.body: Treat as complicated IE until proven otherwise. Actions: - ID + cardiology early; CT surgery or electrophysiology/device team depending on substrate - TEE is usually required; consider cardiac CT/PET/CT/WBC SPECT when echo is nondiagnostic and prosthetic/device infection remains likely [1] - Obtain cultures before antibiotics if feasible; repeat until clearance - Empiric therapy usually requires M

nodes.title: Right-Sided / IVDU / Dialysis
nodes.summary: Right-sided IE: think S. aureus, septic pulmonary emboli, catheter/source control, and TEE when TTE is insufficient.
nodes.body: Common pattern: tricuspid IE, S. aureus, injection drug use, hemodialysis catheter/access, septic pulmonary emboli. Look for: pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, hemoptysis, cavitary pulmonary nodules, persistent fever, vertebral osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, epidural abscess, or catheter infection. Imaging: TTE often sees tricuspid vegetations, but TEE may still be needed for pulmonary valve, devic

nodes.title: Culture / Organism Pathway
nodes.summary: Organism determines definitive regimen, duration, need for source control, and metastatic infection search.
nodes.body: What organism pattern is known or most likely?

nodes.title: S. aureus IE / SAB
nodes.summary: S. aureus bacteremia needs repeat cultures, echo/TEE threshold, source control, and metastatic infection search.
nodes.body: Any S. aureus bacteremia requires aggressive evaluation for source, IE, and metastatic infection. [3,5] Key actions: - Repeat blood cultures q24-48h until clear - Echo: TTE plus low threshold for TEE, especially prosthetic/device, hemodialysis, persistent bacteremia, unknown source, emboli, or poor TTE - Search for metastatic infection: spine/epidural abscess, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, sple

nodes.title: Strep / HACEK Pathway
nodes.summary: Strep/HACEK IE often uses ceftriaxone/penicillin-based therapy; duration depends on valve type and susceptibility.
nodes.body: Viridans streptococci / S. gallolyticus: therapy depends on penicillin susceptibility, native vs prosthetic valve, renal function, and duration plan. [1,3] Common definitive options include Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h or penicillin G-based regimens. Gentamicin-short-course synergy is increasingly avoided unless a specialist-directed scenario justifies toxicity risk. HACEK: ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h is c

nodes.title: Enterococcus Pathway
nodes.summary: Enterococcal IE often uses ampicillin + ceftriaxone for susceptible E. faecalis; avoid reflex gentamicin toxicity.
nodes.body: Think GU/GI source, older patient, healthcare exposure, prosthetic material, or persistent bacteremia. Preferred modern pattern for susceptible E. faecalis: Ampicillin + Ceftriaxone can provide synergy while reducing aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity. [1,3] Aminoglycoside caution: Gentamicin synergy requires strict renal dosing and levels; avoid reflex use in renal failure, older patients, or when dua

nodes.title: Culture-Negative IE
nodes.summary: Culture-negative IE needs exposure-driven testing and ID/microbiology coordination, not indefinite empiric broadening.
nodes.body: Common causes: prior antibiotics, fastidious organisms, intracellular pathogens, fungi, or noninfectious mimics. Do not simply broaden indefinitely. Reassess cultures, antibiotics received, exposure history, valve/device history, and imaging. Targeted testing to discuss with ID/microbiology: - Coxiella burnetii serology/PCR - Bartonella serology/PCR - Brucella testing when exposure risk - Trophery

nodes.title: Complication Screen
nodes.summary: Complications drive CT surgery, neuroimaging, transfer, and ICU decisions.
nodes.body: Which complication is present or most concerning?

nodes.title: Surgery / Source Control
nodes.summary: Surgical triggers: heart failure, abscess/heart block, persistent bacteremia, prosthetic complications, fungal/resistant infection, embolic vegetation.
nodes.body: Call CT surgery early for: [1,3] - Acute heart failure from valve regurgitation or obstruction - Periannular abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, prosthetic dehiscence, or new AV block - Persistent bacteremia/fever despite appropriate therapy and source control - Fungal IE, Candida IE, highly resistant organisms, or uncontrolled infection - Recurrent emboli or large mobile vegetation, especially afte

nodes.title: Neurologic Complications
nodes.summary: IE neuro event: image for hemorrhage/mycotic aneurysm; avoid lytics when IE suspected.
nodes.body: IE can cause ischemic stroke, ICH/SAH, meningitis/encephalitis-like presentations, seizure, brain abscess, and mycotic aneurysm. ED actions: - CT/CTA head/neck for focal deficit, severe headache, ICH/SAH concern, or before anticoagulation/surgery discussions when indicated - MRI brain when available for embolic burden or occult lesions - Avoid thrombolytics for presumed ischemic stroke if IE is su

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Suspected IE usually needs admission; complicated disease needs ICU/transfer/endocarditis-team capability.
nodes.body: Most suspected IE patients require admission. ICU / monitored setting: shock, respiratory failure, acute heart failure, high-grade AV block/new conduction disease, severe valve dysfunction, neurologic complication, persistent bacteremia, prosthetic/device infection, dialysis/IVDU with septic emboli, or need for urgent surgery. Transfer to endocarditis-capable center: complicated IE needing CT surg
nodes.recommendation: Admit suspected IE with ID/cardiology-directed plan; transfer early for surgical/device/prosthetic complications.

nodes.title: Ingrown Toenail — Avulsion + Phenol Matrixectomy
nodes.summary: Partial avulsion + phenol = definitive (recurrence ~1.4% vs ~10% avulsion-only).
nodes.body: Definitive bedside management of onychocryptosis. The high-yield point: partial nail avulsion ALONE recurs ~10%; adding phenol matrixectomy drops recurrence to ~1.4%. Do the matrix step unless contraindicated. Tools (open first): - Procedure Steps Summary - Digital Block Dosing - Phenol Contact-Time Checklist - Diabetic / PVD Stop-Check - Aftercare + Return Precautions

nodes.title: Stage + Vascular Screen
nodes.summary: Stage 1 → conservative trial; Stage 2-3 → partial avulsion + phenol.
nodes.body: Grade the ingrown nail and screen perfusion before committing to a procedure. Open the Diabetic / PVD Stop-Check if any vascular concern.

nodes.title: Stage 1 — Conservative Trial First
nodes.summary: Soaks + cotton/floss elevation + straight trimming; escalate if recurrent or granulating.
nodes.body: For a first, mild presentation without granulation or infection: - Warm soaks 10-20 min BID-TID - Lift the lateral nail edge with a wisp of cotton or a strip of dental floss under the corner; replace daily - Cut the nail STRAIGHT across, not rounded; do not dig into the corner - Wide toe-box footwear Reassess in 1-2 weeks. If no improvement, recurrent, or granulation/infection develops → partial n
nodes.recommendation: Conservative care for first mild presentation; escalate to avulsion if recurrent or worsening.

nodes.title: Perfusion + Phenol Safety
nodes.summary: Good perfusion → avulsion + phenol; diabetic/PVD → avulsion only, refer; infection → treat first.
nodes.body: Phenol is a chemical cautery that depends on local tissue healing. Poor arterial inflow + phenol = risk of delayed healing or necrosis. Review the Diabetic / PVD Stop-Check now.

nodes.title: Avulsion Only — Defer Phenol, Refer
nodes.summary: No phenol in diabetic/PVD foot; avulse for relief and refer for definitive care.
nodes.body: In diabetes or peripheral arterial disease, phenol risks delayed healing, ulceration, or necrosis. - Partial nail avulsion for symptom relief is acceptable for source control - Do NOT apply phenol - Refer to podiatry/foot-and-ankle surgery for definitive matrixectomy under controlled conditions - Optimize glycemic control and document pedal pulses / ABI if vascular disease suspected
nodes.recommendation: Diabetic/PVD: avulsion only, no phenol; refer for definitive matrixectomy.

nodes.title: Infected — Source Control First
nodes.summary: Drain abscess, avulse offending spicule, antibiotics if spreading; phenol deferred.
nodes.body: With active cellulitis or abscess: - Incise/drain any paronychial abscess - Avulse the offending lateral nail spicule (this is the source — removing it is often curative for the infection) - Oral antibiotics only if cellulitis extends beyond the nail fold (cover skin flora; consider MRSA per local patterns) - DEFER phenol until inflammation resolves; reassess for elective matrixectomy if recurrenc
nodes.recommendation: Drain + avulse offending spicule for source control; defer phenol until inflammation resolves.

nodes.title: Step 1 — Digital Block
nodes.summary: Two-point digital block, lidocaine plain, wait 5-10 min, test before cutting.
nodes.body: Achieve complete anesthesia before any cutting. Full dosing in Digital Block Dosing. Technique (traditional two-injection digital block): 1. Prep the toe with chlorhexidine. 2. Insert a 25-27 ga needle at the dorsolateral base of the proximal phalanx; raise a wheal, then advance toward the plantar surface, aspirate, and inject Lidocaine 1-2% PLAIN (no epinephrine in traditional teaching — see dosi

nodes.title: Step 2 — Tourniquet (Bloodless Field)
nodes.summary: Digital tourniquet for bloodless field (phenol needs it); timer on, remove <15-20 min.
nodes.body: Phenol is INACTIVATED by blood and tissue fluid — a bloodless field is mandatory for an effective matrixectomy. 1. After the block is fully set, apply a digital tourniquet at the base of the toe (a sterile Penrose drain, a cut surgical glove finger, or a commercial digital tourniquet). 2. Set a visible timer the moment the tourniquet goes on. Document the time. 3. Keep total tourniquet time well u

nodes.title: Anatomy — Lateral Nail Fold + Matrix
nodes.summary: Remove only the offending lateral strip; matrix (esp. lateral horn) is the phenol target.
nodes.body: Key structures for a partial avulsion: - Lateral nail fold — the soft-tissue groove where the offending nail edge digs in - Nail plate — the visible nail; you remove only the offending lateral 3-5 mm strip, NOT the whole nail - Germinal matrix — sits PROXIMAL, under the proximal nail fold (eponychium). This is the tissue phenol must ablate to prevent regrowth of the spicule. It extends ~5 mm proxi

nodes.title: Step 3 — Partial Nail Avulsion
nodes.summary: Free + cut a 3-5 mm lateral strip proximally to the matrix; remove whole strip incl. corner.
nodes.body: 1. With the field bloodless, slide a Freer elevator (or a small hemostat) under the offending lateral edge of the nail plate to free it from the nail bed and from the proximal nail fold. 2. Cut a longitudinal strip ~3-5 mm wide from the lateral nail using an English nail splitter or straight scissors, advancing PROXIMALLY all the way under the eponychium to the matrix. The cut must reach the proxi

nodes.title: Phenol Matrixectomy — Do It?
nodes.summary: Phenol if perfusion good + bloodless field; otherwise avulsion-only with recurrence counseling.
nodes.body: The avulsion relieves today's pain; phenol prevents the bounceback. With a clean bloodless field and good perfusion, ablate the matrix.

nodes.title: Step 4 — Phenol Matrixectomy
nodes.summary: Protect skin w/ petrolatum; phenol to matrix 3×30 s; neutralize w/ isopropyl alcohol.
nodes.body: Phenol (~88% liquified) chemically ablates the germinal matrix. Protect surrounding skin and respect contact time — full protocol in Phenol Contact-Time Checklist. 1. Ensure the field is dry and bloodless (phenol is neutralized by blood). 2. Protect the perionychium: apply petrolatum to the surrounding skin so phenol only contacts the matrix groove. 3. Using a tightly-wound cotton-tipped applicato

nodes.title: Avulsion Only — Counsel Recurrence
nodes.summary: Avulsion-only: ~10% recurrence; counsel and arrange definitive-care follow-up.
nodes.body: No phenol applied. The lateral strip is removed for symptom relief but the matrix is intact, so the spicule can regrow. - Recurrence ~10% (vs ~1.4% with phenol) - Counsel the patient explicitly that the nail may grow back ingrown - Arrange podiatry/surgery follow-up for definitive matrixectomy if it recurs - Proceed to dressing + aftercare

nodes.title: Step 5 — Tourniquet Off + Dressing
nodes.summary: Remove tourniquet + confirm reperfusion; non-adherent dressing; tetanus; give aftercare sheet.
nodes.body: 1. REMOVE THE DIGITAL TOURNIQUET NOW. Confirm brisk capillary refill returns to the toe before dressing. Document removal time. 2. Apply a non-adherent dressing (petrolatum gauze or bacitracin-impregnated gauze) over the nail fold. 3. Apply a bulky absorbent toe dressing; tube gauze or a loose wrap. Avoid circumferential tightness. 4. Tetanus prophylaxis per status. Hand off the Aftercare + Return

nodes.title: Procedure Note Template
nodes.summary: Note must capture stage, block, tourniquet on/off, strip completeness, phenol detail, dispo.
nodes.body: Procedure: Partial nail avulsion, [right/left] [great/—] toe, [lateral/medial] border [± phenol matrixectomy]. Indication: Stage [1/2/3] onychocryptosis [recurrent / with granulation / infected]. Consent: Risks of bleeding, infection, recurrence, delayed healing, and (if phenol) chemical burn discussed; patient agrees. Anesthesia: Digital block with lidocaine [1/2]% plain, [X] mL, full anesthesia
nodes.recommendation: Document stage, anesthesia, tourniquet on/off times, strip completeness, phenol details, dispo.

nodes.title: Lipid Emulsion Therapy
nodes.summary: Intralipid (ILE) for lipophilic drug toxicity with cardiovascular collapse — rescue therapy
nodes.body: ILE Steps Summary - quick reference. Intravenous Lipid Emulsion (ILE) is rescue therapy for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) and other lipophilic drug overdoses. [1][2] Key points: - Standard formulation: 20% Lipid Emulsion - Acts as a "lipid sink" absorbing lipophilic drugs from cardiac tissue - May have direct cardiotonic effects independent of drug sequestration [3] - ASRA recommended

nodes.title: Mechanism of Action
nodes.summary: ILE creates "lipid sink" absorbing lipophilic drugs + provides energy substrate to myocardium
nodes.body: Three proposed mechanisms: [3][5] 1. Lipid Sink (Partitioning) - Lipid emulsion creates an expanded lipid compartment in plasma - Lipophilic drugs redistribute from tissues (heart, brain) into this compartment - Most supported for highly lipophilic agents (log P > 2): bupivacaine, amitriptyline, verapamil 2. Metabolic/Energetic Effect - Provides fatty acids as alternative fuel source for myocardiu

nodes.title: Clinical Indication
nodes.summary: Strongest evidence: local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Consider for CCB, BB, TCA toxicity
nodes.body: Select the clinical scenario: ILE is indicated for LAST (primary indication) and considered for refractory lipophilic drug toxicity. [1][2][6] LAST is the ONLY well-established indication with high-quality evidence. Other uses are extrapolated from case reports and animal models.

nodes.title: LAST - Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity
nodes.summary: LAST (bupivacaine, lidocaine toxicity): ILE is first-line alongside standard ACLS — start immediately
nodes.body: ILE is the standard of care for LAST per ASRA and AHA guidelines. [1][4] Recognition: - CNS toxicity (early): Perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation, confusion, seizures - Cardiovascular toxicity: Hypotension, bradycardia, wide QRS, VT/VF, asystole - May progress rapidly from CNS to CV collapse - Bupivacaine is most cardiotoxic; lidocaine has higher CNS:CV toxicity ratio When to gi

nodes.title: Calcium Channel Blocker Overdose
nodes.summary: CCB overdose with shock: ILE as adjunct to HIET, vasopressors, and calcium — not first-line
nodes.body: ILE for refractory CCB toxicity - use AFTER standard therapies. [6][7] First-line treatments (do these first): 1. Aggressive IV fluids 2. IV calcium (calcium chloride 1-2 g or gluconate 3-6 g) 3. High-dose insulin-euglycemic therapy (HIET) - see CCB Overdose 4. Vasopressors (norepinephrine, epinephrine) 5. Glucagon if concurrent beta-blocker When to add ILE: - Shock refractory to fluids + calcium

nodes.title: Beta-Blocker Overdose
nodes.summary: Beta-blocker overdose: ILE for propranolol and other lipophilic BB — use after glucagon and HIET fail
nodes.body: ILE for refractory beta-blocker toxicity - use AFTER standard therapies. [6][9] First-line treatments (do these first): 1. IV fluids for preload optimization 2. Glucagon 3-10 mg IV bolus, then infusion 2-5 mg/hr 3. Calcium (calcium chloride or gluconate) 4. High-dose insulin-euglycemic therapy (HIET) 5. Vasopressors (epinephrine preferred for inotropy) 6. Transcutaneous pacing if bradycardia See B

nodes.title: TCA Overdose
nodes.summary: TCA overdose: sodium bicarbonate remains first-line — ILE as rescue for refractory cardiovascular collapse
nodes.body: ILE for refractory TCA toxicity - controversial, use after bicarbonate. [6][10] First-line treatment is sodium bicarbonate: - Target serum pH 7.50-7.55 - QRS narrowing is the treatment endpoint - Bolus 1-2 mEq/kg, then infusion - See TCA Overdose When to consider ILE: - Cardiac arrest refractory to bicarbonate - Hemodynamic collapse despite maximal therapy - Wide QRS with refractory hypotension Ev

nodes.title: Other Lipophilic Drug Toxicity
nodes.summary: Other lipophilic agents: consider ILE for diphenhydramine, bupropion, clomipramine toxicity as rescue
nodes.body: Case reports support ILE use for various lipophilic agents: [6][12] Reported successes: - Diphenhydramine (cardiac arrest) - Bupropion (refractory seizures, cardiac arrest) - Clomipramine - Quetiapine - Cocaine (with concurrent local anesthetic effects) - Flecainide - Lamotrigine General principle: Consider ILE when: 1. Agent is highly lipophilic (log P > 2) 2. Life-threatening toxicity present 3.

nodes.title: ILE Dosing Protocol
nodes.summary: Bolus 1.5 mL/kg 20% lipid over 2-3 min, then infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min — may repeat bolus x2
nodes.body: Standard ILE Protocol (ASRA 2020 checklist): [1] Use 20% Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid, Liposyn) BOLUS: - 1.5 mL/kg IV (lean body mass) over 2-3 minutes - For 70 kg patient: ~100 mL INFUSION: - 0.25 mL/kg/min continuous - May double to 0.5 mL/kg/min if circulatory stability not attained - Continue for at least 10-15 minutes after hemodynamic stability If cardiac arrest or recurrent instability: - Rep

nodes.title: Administration Details
nodes.summary: Use 20% lipid emulsion via large-bore IV — can give via peripheral or central line
nodes.body: Practical considerations: [1][2] IV Access: - Peripheral IV is acceptable (20% lipid emulsion is safe peripherally) - Central line preferred if available but DO NOT delay for access - Large bore (18G or larger) recommended for rapid bolus Administration: - Draw up in large syringes (60 mL) for bolus - Use IV tubing (not a pump) for initial bolus to ensure rapid delivery - Switch to pump for infusi

nodes.title: CPR Modifications for LAST
nodes.summary: During cardiac arrest: continue CPR, give ILE bolus, avoid vasopressin (impairs lipid distribution)
nodes.body: LAST-associated cardiac arrest has unique considerations: [1][4] Epinephrine dosing: - Use smaller doses than standard ACLS (<1 mcg/kg) - Start with 10-100 mcg IV, NOT 1 mg - High-dose epinephrine may worsen arrhythmias and reduce ILE efficacy - ASRA: "Avoid epinephrine doses >1 mcg/kg" Avoid: - Vasopressin - may worsen outcomes in LA toxicity - Calcium channel blockers - contraindicated - Beta-bl

nodes.title: Monitoring During ILE
nodes.summary: Monitor BP, HR, ECG, and mental status — expect improvement within 15-30 min of bolus
nodes.body: Real-time monitoring: [1][2] Hemodynamics: - Continuous cardiac monitoring (rhythm, rate) - Arterial line if available (BP, waveform) - Pulse oximetry - Capnography (ROSC detection, ventilation) Clinical response markers: - ROSC (in arrest) - Blood pressure improvement (MAP >65) - Heart rate normalization - QRS narrowing (if widened) - Resolution of seizures - Improved mentation When to repeat bol

nodes.title: Treatment Endpoints
nodes.summary: Stop infusion when hemodynamically stable — max total dose 10 mL/kg over first 30 minutes
nodes.body: When to stop ILE: [1][2] Clinical stability achieved: - Stable blood pressure (MAP >65) for 10+ minutes - Stable heart rate and rhythm - Resolution of neurologic symptoms - No recurrence of toxicity Maximum dose reached: - ~10 mL/kg in first 30 minutes - Continuing beyond this increases adverse effect risk - If still unstable: consider ECMO, other rescue therapies Weaning protocol: - Once stable 1

nodes.title: Laboratory Interference
nodes.summary: ILE causes lipemia interfering with BMP, LFTs, coags, troponin — send labs BEFORE or wait 2-4h
nodes.body: ILE causes significant lab interference: [2][13] Lipemia affects these assays: - Electrolytes (falsely elevated or decreased) - Troponin (may be falsely elevated) - Liver enzymes - Lipase - Drug levels (may be undetectable or falsely low) - Glucose (variable) - Magnesium Practical approach: - Draw labs BEFORE ILE if possible - Note on lab orders that patient received ILE - Use point-of-care testin

nodes.title: Complications & Adverse Effects
nodes.summary: Complications: lipemia, pancreatitis (rare), ARDS (very rare), lab interference — generally well-tolerated
nodes.body: ILE is generally safe in acute use, but complications can occur: [2][6][13] Reported adverse effects: Pulmonary: - ARDS (rare, typically with massive doses) - Fat embolism syndrome (very rare) - Impaired oxygenation Metabolic: - Hypertriglyceridemia (expected, usually transient) - Acute pancreatitis (rare, dose-related) - Hyperglycemia Hematologic: - Fat overload syndrome (hepatosplenomegaly, coag

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Pediatric dosing same mL/kg as adult. Pregnancy: ILE is safe. Soy allergy: theoretical risk, give anyway in arrest
nodes.body: Pediatrics: [1][14] - Same dosing: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion - Use pump for precise dosing in small children - Maximum dose ~10 mL/kg over first 30 min applies - LAST can occur in children receiving nerve blocks Pregnancy: [1] - ILE is indicated for maternal LAST - Treat mother first (fetal survival depends on maternal resuscitation) - No specific dose adjustments - Consider early c

nodes.title: Post-ILE Disposition
nodes.summary: Determine disposition based on clinical response and underlying toxicity
nodes.body: All patients receiving ILE require monitored observation: [1][2] Key considerations: - Risk of recrudescence (toxicity recurrence) as ILE metabolized - Lab interference resolves over 12-24 hours - Ongoing assessment for complications - Address underlying cause (needle placement, overdose, etc.) What is the clinical status?

nodes.title: Stable - ICU Admission
nodes.summary: Stable after ILE: ICU admission for observation, repeat labs in 4-6h when lipemia clears
nodes.body: Admit to ICU or monitored setting for minimum 4-6 hours observation. [1] Monitoring: - Continuous cardiac monitoring - Frequent vital signs - Neuro checks (if LAST from procedure) - Watch for recrudescence Labs: - Repeat BMP, troponin, LFTs in 12-24 hours - Triglycerides to confirm clearance - Drug levels if applicable Reporting: - Report all LAST cases to www.lipidrescue.org - Quality improvement
nodes.recommendation: ICU or monitored admission for minimum 4-6 hours. Watch for recrudescence as ILE is metabolized. Discharge once clinically stable and labs clearing.

nodes.title: Vasopressor-Dependent - ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU for ongoing vasopressor requirement or persistent toxicity — may need repeat ILE dosing
nodes.body: ICU admission required for ongoing hemodynamic support. [1][2] Management: - Continue vasopressors as needed - Wean as tolerated - May continue low-dose ILE infusion if recurrent instability - Optimize volume status - Serial labs (despite lipemia) Consider: - Toxicology consultation - Source control (remove depot LA if applicable) - Hemodialysis NOT helpful for lipophilic drugs - ECMO if refractor
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continued hemodynamic support. Continue vasopressors, consider ongoing ILE infusion. Toxicology consultation recommended.

nodes.title: Refractory - Consider ECMO
nodes.summary: Refractory cardiovascular collapse: consider ECMO if available — ILE buys time for definitive care
nodes.body: If ILE + standard measures have failed: [4][15] VA-ECMO/ECPR: - Consider early ECMO cannulation for refractory LAST arrest - May provide cardiac support while drug clears - Best outcomes when initiated early - Contact ECMO center immediately if not on-site Continued CPR: - LAST patients may have delayed ROSC (60+ minutes reported) - Continue high-quality CPR while arranging ECMO - Continue ILE dur
nodes.recommendation: Consider VA-ECMO/ECPR for refractory LAST arrest. Continue CPR and ILE while arranging ECMO. Early cannulation associated with better outcomes.

nodes.title: ILE Quick Reference
nodes.summary: ILE: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 2-3 min → 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion, max 10 mL/kg in 30 min — strongest for LAST
nodes.body: LIPID EMULSION 20% (Intralipid) PROTOCOL BOLUS: 1.5 mL/kg IV (lean body mass) over 2-3 minutes - 70 kg patient: ~100 mL - May repeat x2 at 5-minute intervals INFUSION: 0.25 mL/kg/min (15 mL/kg/hr) - 70 kg patient: ~17.5 mL/min or ~1050 mL/hr - Double rate to 0.5 mL/kg/min if unstable MAXIMUM: ~10 mL/kg in first 30 minutes (ASRA 2020 upper limit) - 70 kg patient: ~700 mL max DURATION: Continue infu

nodes.title: Pediatric Intussusception
nodes.summary: Intussusception peaks at 4-9 months - most common bowel obstruction in infants
nodes.body: Quick Reference: Red Flags Definition: Telescoping of proximal bowel (intussusceptum) into distal bowel (intussuscipiens). Most common is ileocolic (ileum into cecum/colon). Epidemiology: - Most common cause of bowel obstruction in children 6-36 months - Peak incidence: 4-9 months - 80-90% occur before age 2 years - Male:Female ratio 3:2 Pathophysiology: - Venous and lymphatic obstruction → bowel

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Classic triad present in <25% - lethargy may be only symptom in young infants
nodes.body: Classic Triad (present in <25%): 1. Intermittent, colicky abdominal pain with inconsolable crying 2. "Currant jelly" stool (blood + mucus) 3. Palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass (RUQ) More Common Presentation: - Episodes of severe, crampy pain (draws legs up, screaming) - Pain-free intervals between episodes - Vomiting (initially non-bilious, becomes bilious) - Lethargy between episodes (may be

nodes.title: Atypical Presentation
nodes.summary: Lethargy may be only symptom - episodic altered behavior in infants is a red flag
nodes.body: Lethargy as Presenting Symptom: In young infants, lethargy or altered mental status may be the ONLY presenting symptom. This is a diagnostic pitfall. Consider intussusception if: - Unexplained lethargy in infant 3-12 months - Episodes of "altered behavior" or "zoning out" - Inconsolable crying alternating with listlessness - Pallor or hypotonia without clear cause Why Lethargy Occurs: - Vagal resp

nodes.title: Concerning/Late Findings
nodes.summary: Bloody stool, bilious vomiting, distension = late findings suggesting ischemia
nodes.body: Signs of Advanced Disease: Bloody Stool / Currant Jelly: - Mix of blood, mucus, and sloughed mucosa - Indicates mucosal ischemia - Present in <50% of cases - LATE finding - absence does not rule out Bilious Vomiting: - Indicates complete small bowel obstruction - Urgent surgical concern Abdominal Distension: - Progressive obstruction - May indicate perforation if sudden Peritoneal Signs: - Rebound

nodes.title: Physical Examination
nodes.summary: Sausage mass in RUQ found in 60% - normal exam between episodes does not exclude
nodes.body: Vital Signs: - May be normal early - Tachycardia (pain, dehydration) - Fever (later - suggests necrosis/infection) General: - Well between episodes vs. lethargic - Pallor suggests significant illness - Note hydration status Abdominal Exam: - Sausage-shaped mass: RUQ, palpable in ~60% - Dance's sign: Empty RLQ (cecum displaced) - May be soft and non-tender between episodes - Distension suggests obs

nodes.title: Ultrasound Diagnosis
nodes.summary: US >97% sensitivity/specificity - look for target/donut sign (~3cm) in RUQ
nodes.body: Ultrasound Findings Guide Ultrasound is Gold Standard: - Sensitivity: >97% - Specificity: >97% - Negative predictive value: 99.7% Technique: - Linear high-frequency probe (children) - Curvilinear for larger children - Systematic scan of all quadrants - Focus on RUQ (most common location) Classic Findings: Transverse View - Target/Donut Sign: - Concentric rings of alternating echogenicity - Usually

nodes.title: Ultrasound Findings
nodes.summary: Ileocolic requires reduction; SB-SB usually transient and self-resolves
nodes.body: Based on ultrasound results: Positive for Intussusception: - Target/donut sign present - Pseudokidney sign - Typical ~3 cm diameter mass Concerning US Features: - Free peritoneal fluid - Absent blood flow on color Doppler - Large amount of trapped fluid within intussusceptum - Intussusception in left colon (advanced) Small Bowel-Small Bowel Intussusception: - Usually transient and self-resolving -

nodes.title: High-Risk Ultrasound Features
nodes.summary: Free fluid, absent Doppler flow, left-sided = higher risk - get early surgical consult
nodes.body: Features Associated with Failed Reduction / Surgical Need: Free Peritoneal Fluid: - Suggests prolonged/severe intussusception - May indicate bowel compromise - NOT an absolute contraindication to enema Absent Blood Flow on Doppler: - Indicates vascular compromise - Higher risk of necrosis - Consider surgical consultation before enema attempt Large Trapped Fluid: - Fluid trapped within the intussus

nodes.title: Small Bowel-Small Bowel Intussusception
nodes.summary: SB-SB intussusception usually transient - observe, repeat US if symptomatic
nodes.body: Transient Small Bowel Intussusception: Characteristics: - Usually <2.5 cm diameter - No lead point visible - Often found incidentally - Common in children with gastroenteritis Management: - Usually self-resolves within minutes to hours - Does NOT require enema reduction - Observation is appropriate When to Be Concerned: - Persistent on repeat imaging (>1 hour) - Associated with significant symptom
nodes.recommendation: Small bowel-small bowel intussusception usually self-resolves. Observe and repeat US if symptomatic. No enema reduction needed.

nodes.title: Negative Ultrasound
nodes.summary: Negative US has 99.7% NPV - consider alternate diagnoses
nodes.body: Ultrasound Negative for Intussusception: Negative Predictive Value: 99.7% If performed by experienced sonographer with adequate views, a negative ultrasound effectively rules out ileocolic intussusception. Consider Alternative Diagnoses: - Gastroenteritis - Constipation - Colic - Incarcerated hernia - Testicular torsion (in males) - Ovarian pathology (in females) - Malrotation with volvulus (more
nodes.recommendation: Negative US with adequate views has 99.7% NPV. Consider alternative diagnoses. Repeat imaging only if strong clinical suspicion persists.

nodes.title: Clinical Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Absolute contraindications: peritonitis, free air, shock → straight to surgery
nodes.body: Lead Point Risk by Age Assess for Contraindications to Enema Reduction: ABSOLUTE Contraindications: - Peritonitis (rebound, guarding, rigidity) - Pneumoperitoneum (free air on X-ray) - Hemodynamic instability / Shock Relative Concerns (higher failure risk): - Symptom duration >48 hours - Age <3 months or >5 years - Rectal bleeding / bloody stool - Lethargy or severely ill-appearing - Small bowel o

nodes.title: Surgical Intervention Required
nodes.summary: Surgery for peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed reduction, or pathologic lead point
nodes.body: Immediate Surgical Consultation Required: Indications for Surgery: - Peritonitis - Pneumoperitoneum (perforation) - Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation - Failed enema reduction (after 2-3 attempts) - Confirmed pathologic lead point - Recurrent intussusception (3+ episodes) Pre-Operative Management: - NPO - IV access x 2 - Fluid resuscitation (NS 20 mL/kg boluses as needed) - Type and scr
nodes.recommendation: Immediate surgical consultation. NPO, IV access x 2, fluid resuscitation, type and screen. Antibiotics if perforation suspected.

nodes.title: Higher Risk Features
nodes.summary: Age <3mo or >5yr = higher lead point risk. Get surgery consult early, still attempt enema.
nodes.body: Patients with Higher Failure Risk: Age Extremes: - <3 months: Higher risk of pathologic lead point; if intussusception confirmed, surgical consultation early - >5 years: Lead point present in ~30% (vs 3% in younger); consider CT to evaluate for lead point Prolonged Symptoms (>48 hours): - Lower success rate for reduction - Higher risk of bowel compromise - Still attempt enema if no contraindicatio

nodes.title: Enema Reduction
nodes.summary: Air enema 80-95% success; hydrostatic 73-86%. Max 3 attempts, 3 min each.
nodes.body: Reduction Contraindications Methods: Pneumatic (Air) Reduction: - Most widely used in North America - Success rate: 80-95% - Faster reduction time - Perforation detectable immediately (pneumoperitoneum) - Max pressure: 80-120 mmHg Hydrostatic (Saline) Reduction: - Under US guidance (no radiation) - Success rate: 73-86% - Preferred in some institutions - Lower perforation risk Pre-Reduction: - IV a

nodes.title: Reduction Outcome
nodes.summary: Success = air in terminal ileum. Failed reduction or perforation → surgery.
nodes.body: Assess reduction result: Successful Reduction: - Air/contrast flows freely into terminal ileum - No residual mass on imaging - Clinical improvement (less pain, more comfortable) Incomplete/Failed Reduction: - Unable to reduce after 2-3 attempts - Residual mass on imaging - Perforation during procedure Perforation During Reduction: - Immediate tension pneumoperitoneum (air enema) - Abdominal disten

nodes.title: Perforation During Reduction
nodes.summary: Perforation = surgical emergency. Decompress, resuscitate, emergent laparotomy.
nodes.body: Perforation - Surgical Emergency: Immediate Recognition: - Sudden abdominal distension - Tension pneumoperitoneum (if air enema) - Hemodynamic deterioration - Abdominal rigidity Immediate Management: 1. STOP the procedure 2. Call for surgical help immediately 3. Decompress if tension pneumoperitoneum: - Needle decompression (18G, LUQ or midline) - Relieves intra-abdominal pressure 4. Aggressive fl
nodes.recommendation: STOP procedure, decompress abdomen if needed, immediate surgical consultation, IV antibiotics, emergent OR.

nodes.title: Post-Reduction Management
nodes.summary: Observe 4+ hours, PO trial at 2 hours, watch for recurrence (8-10%)
nodes.body: After Successful Reduction: Observation Period: - Minimum 4 hours observation (CHOP guideline) - Some institutions observe 6-24 hours - Monitor for recurrence (8-10% overall) Oral Trial: - Begin clear liquids 2 hours post-reduction - Advance diet as tolerated - If tolerating PO, good sign for discharge Monitoring: - Vital signs q1-2 hours initially - Abdominal exams - Watch for return of symptoms

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: ED discharge safe if tolerating PO, asymptomatic, reliable follow-up
nodes.body: Consider Disposition Options: ED Discharge (after successful reduction): - Observation period completed (4+ hours) - Tolerating oral intake - Asymptomatic - Reliable caregivers with transportation - Close follow-up available Admission Considerations: - Age <36 months (some guidelines) - Unable to tolerate PO - Prolonged symptoms prior to reduction - High-risk features - Social concerns / poor foll

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: Clear return precautions - 10% recurrence, most within 24-48 hours
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria Met: - Successful reduction completed - Observation period (4+ hours) completed - Tolerating oral intake - Asymptomatic - Reliable caregivers Return Precautions (tell caregivers): Return IMMEDIATELY if: - Episodes of severe crying or drawing up legs - Vomiting (especially if green/bilious) - Bloody stool or "currant jelly" stool - Abdominal distension - Lethargy or decreased act
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with clear return precautions. PCP follow-up in 24-48 hours. Recurrence rate ~10%.

nodes.title: Admission for Observation
nodes.summary: Admit if not tolerating PO, very young, or social concerns
nodes.body: Admission Indicated: Reasons for Admission: - Age <36 months (per some guidelines) - Not tolerating oral intake - Persistent symptoms despite successful reduction - Multiple reduction attempts required - Concern for pathologic lead point - Social concerns or poor follow-up access - Caregiver discomfort with discharge Inpatient Monitoring: - Serial abdominal exams - Advance diet as tolerated - IV f
nodes.recommendation: Admit for serial exams, IV fluids, diet advancement. Discharge when tolerating PO and asymptomatic for 12-24 hours.

nodes.title: Iron Overdose — Recognition & Toxicity
nodes.summary: Iron OD: >60 mg/kg elemental iron is potentially lethal — toxicity peaks at 6-24 hours
nodes.body: Iron Overdose Steps Summary Iron is a common pediatric poisoning - prenatal vitamins and children's chewables look like candy. Toxicity depends on elemental iron content, not total pill weight. [1][2] Elemental iron content by formulation: - Ferrous sulfate: 20% elemental iron - Ferrous gluconate: 12% elemental iron - Ferrous fumarate: 33% elemental iron Toxicity thresholds (elemental iron): [1][2

nodes.title: Minimal Ingestion (<20 mg/kg)
nodes.summary: <20 mg/kg elemental iron: minimal toxicity expected — observe 6h, discharge if asymptomatic
nodes.body: Elemental iron <20 mg/kg is unlikely to cause significant toxicity. [1][4] Management: - No GI decontamination needed - No labs required if asymptomatic - Observe for 6 hours from time of ingestion - Discharge if remains asymptomatic with no GI symptoms Reasons to upgrade concern: - Development of any GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain) - Blood in stool - Altered mental status

nodes.title: Unknown Ingestion Amount
nodes.summary: Unknown ingestion amount: treat as potentially significant — 6h observation minimum, check serum iron
nodes.body: Unable to calculate elemental iron dose - treat based on clinical presentation and labs. [1][2] Immediate actions: - Draw serum iron level at 4-6 hours post-ingestion - Abdominal X-ray (iron tablets are radiopaque, but not all formulations visible) - Full labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags, lactate, type & screen - ABG/VBG if symptomatic Clinical indicators of significant ingestion: - Persistent vomiting

nodes.title: Classic Stages of Iron Poisoning
nodes.summary: Phase 1 (0-6h): GI. Phase 2 (6-24h): deceptive calm. Phase 3 (12-48h): shock and organ failure
nodes.body: Iron Poisoning Stages Five classic stages - timing is approximate: [2][3] Stage 1 (0-6 hours) - GI Phase: - Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain - GI hemorrhage (hematemesis, melena, hematochezia) - Direct corrosive injury to GI mucosa Stage 2 (6-24 hours) - Latent Phase: - Apparent clinical improvement - "Quiescent period" - DO NOT BE FOOLED - Patient may appear stable while cellular toxici

nodes.title: Moderate Ingestion (20-60 mg/kg) - Evaluation
nodes.summary: Moderate (20-60 mg/kg): obtain serum iron at 4-6h, abdominal XR, BMP, CBC, coags, LFTs
nodes.body: Elemental iron 20-60 mg/kg - potential for significant toxicity. [1][2] Immediate actions: - IV access - Draw serum iron level at 4-6 hours post-ingestion (peak level) - Abdominal X-ray - radiopaque tablets may be visible - Labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags, lactate, type & screen - ABG/VBG if any symptoms present Observe closely for Stage 1 symptoms: - Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea - Abdominal pain - GI b

nodes.title: Severe Ingestion (>60 mg/kg) - Evaluation
nodes.summary: Severe (>60 mg/kg): aggressive resuscitation, early deferoxamine, monitor for organ failure
nodes.body: Elemental iron >60 mg/kg - expect serious systemic toxicity. [1][2][3] Immediate actions: - Large bore IV access x2 - Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation - Type & screen (may need transfusion) - Draw serum iron level at 4-6 hours post-ingestion - Abdominal X-ray - Labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags, lactate, ABG Anticipate: - GI hemorrhage - prepare for blood products - Metabolic acidosis - may need bicarb

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: STAT labs: serum iron (4-6h peak), BMP, CBC, coags, LFTs, VBG — abdominal XR for radiopaque tablets
nodes.body: Serum iron level is the key diagnostic test. [1][2][3] Timing: Draw at 4-6 hours post-ingestion (peak absorption). Earlier levels may underestimate toxicity. Interpretation: [1][2] - <350 mcg/dL: Usually minimal symptoms - 350-500 mcg/dL: Moderate toxicity - >500 mcg/dL: Severe toxicity - deferoxamine indicated TIBC (Total Iron Binding Capacity): - NOT useful in acute poisoning - Falsely elevated

nodes.title: Iron Level <350 mcg/dL
nodes.summary: Serum iron <350: generally non-toxic — observe, supportive care, discharge if asymptomatic at 6h
nodes.body: Serum iron <350 mcg/dL at 4-6 hours post-ingestion suggests minimal toxicity. [1][2] Management: - Supportive care - IV fluids for hydration - Antiemetics PRN - Serial clinical reassessment No deferoxamine needed for levels <350 mcg/dL in absence of symptoms. Reasons to escalate treatment: - Persistent GI symptoms despite level <350 - GI hemorrhage - Metabolic acidosis - Altered mental status - Cl

nodes.title: Iron Level 350-500 mcg/dL
nodes.summary: Serum iron 350-500: moderate toxicity — IV fluids, monitor closely, consider WBI if tablets visible on XR
nodes.body: Serum iron 350-500 mcg/dL indicates moderate toxicity. [1][2] Management: - IV fluids - aggressive hydration - Antiemetics - Serial labs q4-6h (iron level, CBC, BMP, coags, lactate) - Close monitoring for progression Consider deferoxamine if ANY of the following: [1][2] - Symptomatic (persistent vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain) - Metabolic acidosis (even mild) - Signs of systemic toxicity (leth

nodes.title: Iron Level >500 mcg/dL - Severe Toxicity
nodes.summary: Serum iron >500: severe toxicity — start deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hr, ICU admission
nodes.body: Serum iron >500 mcg/dL = severe poisoning. Deferoxamine is indicated. [1][2][3] Immediate actions: - Start deferoxamine - Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation - ICU admission - Serial labs q4h - Prepare for cardiovascular collapse Clinical features to expect: - Hemorrhagic gastroenteritis - Metabolic acidosis (high anion gap) - Coagulopathy - Cardiovascular instability - Altered mental status Call Po

nodes.title: GI Decontamination
nodes.summary: Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron — WBI with GoLYTELY is the only effective GI decontamination
nodes.body: GI Decontamination in Iron Overdose Activated charcoal does NOT adsorb iron - it is NOT effective. [1][2] Whole Bowel Irrigation (WBI): [1][2][4] - Indication: Large ingestion, pill fragments visible on X-ray, sustained-release formulations - Solution: GoLYTELY (PEG-electrolyte solution) - Pediatric dose: 500 mL/hr via NG tube - Adult dose: 1-2 L/hr via NG tube - Endpoint: Clear rectal effluent AN

nodes.title: Whole Bowel Irrigation Protocol
nodes.summary: WBI: GoLYTELY 1-2 L/hr (adult) via NG until clear effluent and no tablets on repeat XR
nodes.body: GoLYTELY Protocol Whole bowel irrigation mechanically flushes iron tablets through the GI tract. [1][4] Indications: - Large ingestion (>60 mg/kg elemental iron) - Visible pills/fragments on abdominal X-ray - Sustained-release iron preparations - Ongoing GI absorption suspected Contraindications: - Unprotected airway (intubate first if needed) - Bowel obstruction or perforation - Ileus - Hemodynam

nodes.title: Endoscopic Removal
nodes.summary: Endoscopic removal for massive tablet load not clearing with WBI — rarely needed
nodes.body: Endoscopic removal may be needed for iron bezoars or large pill concretions. [1][2] Indications: - Large pill mass visible on X-ray - Failed whole bowel irrigation - Bezoar formation - Gastric concretion with ongoing absorption Considerations: - Iron tablets can coalesce into hard concretions - Mucosal injury may complicate endoscopy - Risk of perforation with friable GI mucosa - May require surgi

nodes.title: Deferoxamine Therapy
nodes.summary: Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hr IV continuous — start if serum iron >500 or shock/metabolic acidosis
nodes.body: Deferoxamine Protocol Mechanism: Deferoxamine chelates free (unbound) iron, forming ferrioxamine - a water-soluble complex excreted by the kidneys. [1][2][3] Indications for deferoxamine: [1][2] - Peak serum iron >500 mcg/dL - Severe symptoms regardless of level: - Shock or hypotension - Altered mental status - Metabolic acidosis - Significant GI bleeding - Lethargy or coma - Clinical deterioratio

nodes.title: Deferoxamine Dosing
nodes.summary: Deferoxamine: start 5 mg/kg/hr, titrate to 15 mg/kg/hr continuous IV — max 6 g/24h; do NOT use vin rosé urine to guide therapy (unreliable)
nodes.body: Deferoxamine IV Infusion (preferred route): [1][2][4] Starting dose: 5 mg/kg/hr IV Titrate up to: 15 mg/kg/hr as tolerated Maximum dose: 6 grams per 24 hours in adults [1] Rate titration: - Start at 5 mg/kg/hr to minimize hypotension - Increase by 5 mg/kg/hr every 30-60 minutes as BP tolerates - Target 15 mg/kg/hr in severe poisoning IM route (if no IV access): - 90 mg/kg IM (max 1 g per injection

nodes.title: Deferoxamine - Duration & Monitoring
nodes.summary: Stop deferoxamine when urine clears, patient improves, and iron <350 — limit to <24h if possible
nodes.body: Continue deferoxamine until ALL criteria are met: [1][2][3] ✅ Patient clinically improved ✅ Resolution of metabolic acidosis ✅ Serum iron normalized (<350 mcg/dL) ✅ Resolution of GI symptoms ✅ Hemodynamic stability Typical duration: 24-48 hours [2] DO NOT use "vin rose" urine color to stop therapy - it is unreliable. [2] Side effects: [1][2] - Hypotension - most common, infuse slowly - ARDS - asso

nodes.title: Rescue Therapies - Severe Cases
nodes.summary: Refractory iron toxicity: consider exchange transfusion or dialysis (removes deferoxamine-iron complex)
nodes.body: For severe, refractory iron poisoning, additional interventions may be needed. [2][3] Exchange transfusion: [2] - Consider in pediatric massive ingestion - Refractory shock despite aggressive resuscitation - Removes free iron from circulation Hemodialysis: [2][3] - Removes ferrioxamine complex (NOT free iron) - Consider if: - Renal failure (cannot excrete ferrioxamine) - ARDS developing from prolo

nodes.title: Exchange Transfusion
nodes.summary: Exchange transfusion for massive ingestions not responding to deferoxamine — rarely needed
nodes.body: Exchange transfusion removes iron-laden blood and replaces with fresh blood. [2] Indications: - Pediatric massive ingestion with refractory shock - Cardiovascular collapse not responding to deferoxamine + fluids + pressors - Profound metabolic acidosis not improving Logistics: - Requires large bore central venous access - Typically performed in ICU or PICU - Consult hematology/transfusion medicine

nodes.title: Hemodialysis in Iron Poisoning
nodes.summary: Hemodialysis removes deferoxamine-iron complex (ferrioxamine) — consider in renal failure
nodes.body: Hemodialysis has a LIMITED role in iron poisoning. [2][3] What dialysis does: - Removes ferrioxamine (deferoxamine-iron complex) - Does NOT remove free iron (protein-bound) - Corrects severe metabolic acidosis - Supports renal failure Indications: - Renal failure preventing ferrioxamine excretion - ARDS developing from prolonged deferoxamine (>24h) - Severe refractory metabolic acidosis - Volume o

nodes.title: Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Aggressive IV fluids for GI losses, correct coagulopathy, monitor for hepatic failure at 48-72h
nodes.body: Comprehensive supportive care is essential. [1][2] Fluid resuscitation: - Aggressive crystalloid for hypovolemia - GI losses can be massive - Target adequate urine output Blood products: - PRBCs for anemia from GI bleeding - FFP/platelets for coagulopathy - Type & screen early - may need multiple units Vasopressors: - Norepinephrine first-line for refractory shock - May need multiple agents Glucos

nodes.title: Disposition - 6-Hour Observation
nodes.summary: Observe 6h minimum for all >20 mg/kg ingestions — discharge if asymptomatic with normal labs
nodes.body: Low-risk ingestion - 6-hour observation period. [1][4] Criteria for observation only: - Elemental iron <20 mg/kg ingested - Asymptomatic at presentation - No pills visible on X-ray (if obtained) - Iron level <350 mcg/dL (if drawn) Safe to discharge after 6 hours if: ✅ Remains asymptomatic (no GI symptoms) ✅ No abdominal pain ✅ Normal mental status ✅ If labs obtained: normal or non-concerning Retur
nodes.recommendation: Discharge after 6-hour asymptomatic observation. Provide return precautions and safety counseling.

nodes.title: Disposition - Admit for Monitoring
nodes.summary: Admit moderate toxicity: persistent GI symptoms, elevated serum iron, or WBI in progress
nodes.body: Admit for monitoring and continued care. [1][2] Admission criteria: - Any symptomatic patient (GI symptoms, lethargy) - Iron level 350-500 mcg/dL - Elemental iron ingested 20-60 mg/kg - Ongoing GI decontamination (WBI) - Unreliable history with concerning features - Pediatric patient with significant ingestion Monitoring: - Serial iron levels q4-6h until trending down - CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags - Cli
nodes.recommendation: Admit for serial monitoring. Low threshold for ICU transfer if clinical deterioration.

nodes.title: Disposition - ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU for severe toxicity: deferoxamine infusion, shock, metabolic acidosis, or organ failure
nodes.body: ICU admission for severe iron poisoning. [1][2][3] ICU criteria: - Deferoxamine therapy required - Iron level >500 mcg/dL - Elemental iron ingested >60 mg/kg - Metabolic acidosis - Cardiovascular instability / shock - Altered mental status - Significant GI hemorrhage - Need for rescue therapies (exchange, dialysis) ICU management: - Continuous deferoxamine infusion - Aggressive fluid resuscitation
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for close monitoring and aggressive treatment. Continue deferoxamine until all stopping criteria met.

nodes.title: Acute Limb Ischemia — Recognize It Fast
nodes.summary: 6 P's of acute limb ischemia. ~6h muscle-viability window. Doppler + heparin + vascular consult early.
nodes.body: A sudden pale, painful, pulseless, cold limb is a true vascular emergency. Skeletal muscle tolerates only about 6 hours of ischemia before irreversible necrosis — the neuro signs (paresthesia, paralysis) are the early ominous markers. [4][5] The 6 P's (distal to the occlusion): - Pain — early, severe - Pallor — pale/marble-white skin - Pulselessness — absent distal pulses - Paresthesia — sensory l

nodes.title: Acute or Acute-on-Chronic?
nodes.body: How did this come on, and is there a background of peripheral arterial disease? - Acute = sudden, symptoms <2 weeks, often no collaterals. - Chronic PAD = gradual claudication history, collateral-supported, prior known disease. - Fixed mottling/skin staining that does NOT blanch = irreversible (Rutherford III). [1][4]

nodes.title: Embolic vs Thrombotic — It Changes the Plan
nodes.summary: Embolic = abrupt, no claudication, normal contralateral pulses, cardiac source. Thrombotic = on PAD.
nodes.body: Distinguishing the mechanism shapes both the source hunt and the revascularization strategy. [1][3] | Feature | Embolic | Thrombotic | |---|---|---| | Onset | Abrupt | More gradual | | Prior claudication | Usually none | Often present | | Contralateral pulses | Normal | Often diminished | | Source | AFib, recent MI/mural thrombus, valve | Pre-existing PAD plaque rupture | | Classic intervention |

nodes.title: Rutherford Category — The Central Triage Decision
nodes.body: Classify by the bedside exam — this single decision drives urgency. Use the Rutherford classifier. | Category | Sensory | Motor | Arterial Doppler | Venous Doppler | |---|---|---|---|---| | I — Viable | None | None | Audible | Audible | | IIa — Marginal | Minimal (toes) | None | Often inaudible | Audible | | IIb — Immediate | > toes + rest pain | Mild–moderate | Usually inaudible | Audible | | III

nodes.title: Rutherford I — Viable
nodes.summary: Viable limb: heparin + urgent (not emergent) revascularization after imaging.
nodes.body: Limb is not immediately threatened: no sensory or motor loss, audible arterial AND venous Doppler. - Start IV heparin anticoagulation now. - Urgent (not emergent) revascularization — often after CT angiography. - Admit, serial exams, vascular planning.
nodes.recommendation: Anticoagulate. Urgent — not emergent — revascularization, typically after imaging. Admit for serial vascular exams.

nodes.title: Rutherford IIa — Marginally Threatened
nodes.summary: Marginal limb: heparin + urgent revascularization; CDT suitable when no motor deficit.
nodes.body: Salvageable if promptly treated: minimal (toe) sensory loss, no motor deficit, often inaudible arterial Doppler but audible venous. - IV heparin immediately. - Urgent endovascular or open revascularization. - Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) is well-suited here — there is time and no motor threat. - Emergent vascular consult.
nodes.recommendation: Heparin now. Urgent endovascular or open revascularization; CDT well-suited when no motor threat. Vascular consult.

nodes.title: Rutherford IIb — Immediately Threatened
nodes.summary: Immediately threatened: heparin + EMERGENT surgical/mechanical revascularization. Lysis too slow.
nodes.body: Salvageable only with IMMEDIATE revascularization: sensory loss beyond the toes with rest pain, plus mild-to-moderate motor deficit, usually inaudible arterial Doppler. - IV heparin NOW. - EMERGENT surgical embolectomy/thrombectomy (Fogarty) or bypass; mechanical/aspiration thrombectomy. - Catheter-directed lysis alone is usually too slow for a motor-deficit limb. - Vascular surgery to the bedside
nodes.recommendation: EMERGENT revascularization (embolectomy/thrombectomy or bypass). Heparin now. Lysis alone too slow with motor deficit.

nodes.title: Rutherford III — Irreversible
nodes.summary: Irreversible limb: primary amputation. Do NOT reperfuse a dead limb.
nodes.body: Major tissue and nerve loss is inevitable: profound anesthesia and paralysis (rigor), inaudible arterial AND venous Doppler, fixed non-blanching skin staining. - → Primary amputation pathway. - 🛑 Do NOT reperfuse a dead limb — releases potassium, myoglobin and acid load and can be lethal. [5][12] - Supportive IV fluids; consider empiric antibiotics. - Vascular surgery for amputation planning; ICU
nodes.recommendation: Nonviable limb → primary amputation. Do NOT reperfuse (lethal reperfusion). Supportive care + vascular surgery.

nodes.title: Workup — Labs, Imaging, Source Hunt
nodes.summary: CTA first-line (extend to aorta/iliacs). Labs are baselines, not gatekeepers. Hunt the embolic source.
nodes.body: Labs (reperfusion/rhabdo baseline — NOT gatekeepers for revascularization): CK, myoglobin, potassium, creatinine, lactate, CBC, coags (PT/PTT before heparin), type & screen. Do not use CK/lactate to decide whether to revascularize. [2][5][12] Imaging: - CT angiography = first-line (ESVS 2020): fast, available, single acquisition of aorta + iliacs + runoff; finds the embolic source and relevant fin

nodes.title: Anticoagulation — The Cornerstone
nodes.summary: IV heparin immediately per local protocol (~80 U/kg bolus, ~18 U/kg/hr). DTI if HIT history.
nodes.body: Start IV unfractionated heparin immediately unless contraindicated — do NOT wait for imaging. It halts thrombus propagation and recurrent embolism. This is a Class 1 recommendation. [2][7] Dosing (FOLLOW YOUR INSTITUTIONAL HEPARIN PROTOCOL): - Bolus ~80 U/kg IV, then infusion ~18 U/kg/hr, titrated to aPTT 1.5–2.5× control. [19] - These figures trace to the Raschke weight-based heparin nomogram (An
nodes.recommendation: IV unfractionated heparin immediately per institutional protocol (~80 U/kg bolus, ~18 U/kg/hr). DTI if HIT. Do not wait for imaging.

nodes.title: Revascularization by Rutherford Category
nodes.summary: I = urgent revasc; IIa = urgent ± CDT; IIb = emergent surgical/mechanical; III = amputation.
nodes.body: Category I (viable): anticoagulate; urgent (not emergent) endo or open revascularization, often after imaging. Category IIa (marginal): urgent endovascular OR open; catheter-directed thrombolysis well-suited when there is time and no motor threat. Category IIb (immediately threatened): EMERGENT — surgical embolectomy/thrombectomy (Fogarty) or bypass; mechanical/aspiration thrombectomy. Lysis alone

nodes.title: Reperfusion Injury & Compartment Syndrome
nodes.summary: Reperfusion → hyperkalemia, rhabdo/AKI, compartment syndrome. Fasciotomy for delta-P <30 mmHg. Dialysis for refractory K+.
nodes.body: Reperfusion washes potassium, myoglobin and reactive oxygen species into the circulation → hyperkalemia (arrhythmia), metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuria/AKI, and DIC. [5][12] Compartment syndrome: - It is primarily a clinical diagnosis (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch). When pressures are measured, delta pressure (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) <30 mmHg is more reliable than a
nodes.recommendation: After revascularization: monitor for hyperkalemia, rhabdo/AKI, and compartment syndrome. Fasciotomy for clinical compartment syndrome / delta pressure <30 mmHg.

nodes.title: Chronic PAD Spectrum → CLTI
nodes.summary: Claudication → rest pain → tissue loss. CLTI = Rutherford 4–6 / Fontaine III–IV. ABI quantifies it.
nodes.body: Chronic disease runs: asymptomatic → intermittent claudication → ischemic rest pain → tissue loss (ulcer/gangrene). The end stage = Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia (CLTI), formerly "critical limb ischemia." [13][14] Staging: | Fontaine | Rutherford (chronic) | |---|---| | I asymptomatic | 0 asymptomatic | | IIa claudication >200 m | 1–3 mild→severe claudication | | IIb claudication <200 m | — |

nodes.title: PAD Medical Management (GDMT)
nodes.summary: GDMT: antiplatelet, statin, smoking cessation, supervised exercise (1A), cilostazol (avoid HFrEF).
nodes.body: Guideline-directed medical therapy (2024 ACC/AHA): [11][13] - Antiplatelet — aspirin or clopidogrel for all symptomatic PAD/CLTI. - Moderate-to-high-intensity statin — reduces all-cause and CV mortality (Class 1). - Smoking cessation — offered to every tobacco user. - BP to <140/90; metformin first-line for diabetic CLTI. - Cilostazol 100 mg BID — improves pain-free walking distance and ABI in cla
nodes.recommendation: Antiplatelet + high-intensity statin + smoking cessation + supervised exercise (Class 1A). Cilostazol for claudication (not HFrEF).

nodes.title: When to Refer to Vascular (Chronic)
nodes.summary: Refer for rest pain, tissue loss, or refractory claudication. CLTI = urgent referral + GDMT.
nodes.body: Refer to vascular surgery for: - Ischemic rest pain - Non-healing ulcer or gangrene (CLTI) - Lifestyle-limiting claudication failing medical therapy - Any ABI/TBI meeting CLTI criteria (ABI <0.40, ankle pressure <50 mmHg, or toe pressure <30 mmHg per GVG 2019) [17] CLTI without an acute threat → urgent (not emergent) vascular referral; start GDMT in parallel. [11][13]
nodes.recommendation: Refer for rest pain, non-healing ulcer/gangrene, or claudication failing therapy. CLTI = urgent vascular referral + GDMT.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Emergent vascular consult for threatened limb; ICU for reperfusion risk; transfer + heparin if no vascular.
nodes.body: - Emergent vascular surgery / endovascular consult NOW for any Rutherford IIa/IIb/III (and Category I urgently). [1][6][7] - ICU for hemodynamic instability, large muscle mass at risk, anticipated reperfusion syndrome, or post-revascularization monitoring. [5][12] - Floor/telemetry for stable Category I on heparin awaiting planned intervention. - No vascular service → transfer immediately to a vas
nodes.recommendation: Emergent vascular consult for any threatened limb. ICU for reperfusion risk. Transfer + heparin if no vascular service.

nodes.title: Mimics / Don't Miss
nodes.summary: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (warm, swollen), compartment syndrome, dissection-to-iliac, neuro mimics.
nodes.body: - Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (massive iliofemoral DVT): swollen, warm, cyanotic limb with initially audible arterial Doppler — the opposite of the pale/cold/pulseless arterial limb. Up to 40% mortality, ~50% amputation; can coexist with ALI. Confirm with venous duplex. Malignancy in 20–40%; left leg favored (May-Thurner). [16] - Acute compartment syndrome from another cause (trauma, crush, prolonge

nodes.title: Emergency Joint Arthrocentesis
nodes.summary: Tap suspected septic joint or unclear acute effusion; interpret fluid at bedside.
nodes.body: Use this for ED aspiration of an acutely painful/swollen joint when infection, crystal arthritis, hemarthrosis, or diagnostic uncertainty is clinically important. Open first: - Tap Steps - Contraindications - Knee Tap Technique - Fluid Interpretation - Stop / Escalate

nodes.title: Is Aspiration Indicated?
nodes.summary: Septic arthritis remains a clinical diagnosis until synovial fluid is evaluated.
nodes.body: Do not rely on fever, serum WBC, ESR, or CRP alone to exclude septic arthritis.

nodes.title: Contraindication Screen
nodes.summary: Screen route, infection over skin, prosthetic joint, anticoagulation, and anatomy.
nodes.body: Avoid passing through overlying cellulitis/abscess when an alternate route or specialist/image-guided approach is feasible. Relative cautions: anticoagulation/coagulopathy, prosthetic joint, small/deep joint, difficult anatomy, and inability to keep sterile field. Do not withhold a clinically urgent diagnostic tap solely for abnormal coagulation labs without weighing septic joint risk.

nodes.title: Which Joint / Approach?
nodes.summary: Large accessible joints can often be tapped in the ED; deep/prosthetic joints need help.
nodes.body: Use the safest route with the highest likelihood of obtaining fluid.

nodes.title: Knee Tap: Simple ED Technique
nodes.summary: Sterile large-joint tap: position, local anesthesia, safe trajectory, gentle aspiration.
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Position knee slightly flexed or extended with support. 2. Prep widely and maintain sterile field. 3. Use local Lidocaine without injecting into the joint if avoidable. 4. Common route: superolateral or lateral approach into suprapatellar recess. 5. Aspirate gently; redirect only after withdrawing to safe tissue plane. 6. Stop if patient has severe pain, paresthesia, or no safe traje

nodes.title: Image-Guided / Specialist Route
nodes.summary: Use ultrasound or specialist pathway for deep, prosthetic, small, or difficult joints.
nodes.body: Use ultrasound to confirm effusion and needle path when anatomy is unclear, effusion is small, or prior attempt failed. Escalate early for hip aspiration, prosthetic joint aspiration, small/deep joints, overlying infection blocking safe route, or anticipated need for operative washout.

nodes.title: Send The Fluid Correctly
nodes.summary: Culture, cell count/differential, and crystals are the core ED synovial tests.
nodes.body: Prioritize tests: 1. Gram stain and culture 2. Cell count with differential 3. Crystal analysis 4. Glucose/protein only if local practice uses them If fluid volume is limited, culture and cell count usually matter most. Blood cultures are recommended when septic arthritis is possible.

nodes.title: How Does The Fluid / Result Read?
nodes.summary: Interpret fluid by infection risk, appearance, WBC/PMN, Gram stain, culture, crystals, and blood.
nodes.body: Do not let crystals falsely reassure you; crystal arthritis and infection can coexist.

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis Pathway
nodes.summary: Culture, antibiotics, orthopedic consultation, admission, and source control planning.
