nodes.body: If septic arthritis is possible, obtain blood cultures when feasible, start empiric antibiotics after cultures/aspiration when this does not dangerously delay care, consult orthopedics, and admit. Needle aspiration is diagnostic; definitive management often requires serial aspiration or operative washout depending on joint and severity.
nodes.recommendation: Treat septic arthritis as time-sensitive joint-threatening infection.

nodes.title: Crystal Arthritis Result
nodes.summary: Crystals do not exclude infection.
nodes.body: Crystals support gout or CPPD, but infection is not excluded when fever, immunocompromise, bacteremia risk, prosthetic joint, severe pain, or highly inflammatory fluid is present. If the clinical story is low risk for infection, treat crystal arthritis and arrange follow-up.
nodes.recommendation: Treat crystals, but continue septic arthritis pathway if infection risk remains.

nodes.title: Bloody Fluid / Hemarthrosis
nodes.summary: Bloody fluid requires trauma/anticoagulation/fracture reassessment.
nodes.body: Bloody aspirate suggests hemarthrosis or traumatic tap. Reassess trauma, anticoagulation, fracture, ligament injury, and need for imaging or specialist input. Avoid repeated traumatic passes when diagnostic yield is low.
nodes.recommendation: Use history, imaging, anticoagulation status, and exam to determine disposition.

nodes.title: Low-Inflammation Fluid
nodes.summary: Low-inflammatory fluid should prompt a broader noninfectious differential.
nodes.body: Low-inflammatory fluid lowers concern for septic arthritis but does not replace clinical judgment. Reassess for osteoarthritis flare, trauma/internal derangement, bursitis, cellulitis, radiculopathy, or referred pain.
nodes.recommendation: Disposition depends on exam, culture plan, pain control, function, and follow-up reliability.

nodes.title: Stop / Escalate
nodes.summary: Unsafe route, deep/prosthetic joint, or failed attempt requires escalation.
nodes.body: Stop blind ED arthrocentesis and escalate when there is no safe route, overlying infection blocks all approaches, prosthetic/deep joint requires specialty pathway, patient cannot cooperate safely, or prior attempt caused severe pain/paresthesia. Do not delay antibiotics for a dangerous infection while waiting for an impossible tap.
nodes.recommendation: Escalate to ultrasound guidance, radiology, orthopedics, or empiric treatment when the tap is unsafe or not feasible.

nodes.title: Kratom Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Kratom = partial μ-opioid agonist; withdrawal milder but LONGER than opioids (peak day 3-4); ask about product type (7-OH products = worse)
nodes.body: Kratom Pharmacology — mechanism and why withdrawal occurs. Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) contains alkaloids that act as partial μ-opioid agonists. Chronic use causes dependence with opioid-like withdrawal on cessation. Key differences from opioid withdrawal: • Milder intensity but longer duration (1-3 weeks vs 5-7 days) • Peak symptoms day 3-4 (not day 1-2 like opioids) • More prominent neuropsychia

nodes.title: Withdrawal Timeline
nodes.summary: Onset 6-12h, peak day 3-4 (later than opioids), acute phase 4-7 days, PAWS up to 3 months
nodes.body: Timeline Comparison Chart Onset: 6-12 hours after last dose (earlier with high-potency products) Peak: Days 3-4 (median 96 hours) • Most intense phase: day 4-7 • This is LATER than opioid withdrawal (24-36h peak) Resolution: • Acute phase: 1-3 days, can extend 4-7 days • Post-acute withdrawal (PAWS): 2+ weeks of lingering symptoms • Full resolution: Up to 3 months (much longer than opioid ~1 week)

nodes.title: Symptom Profile
nodes.summary: Opioid-like symptoms PLUS prominent neuro (tremors, brain fog), severe fatigue (86%), potential cardiac complications
nodes.body: Similar to opioid withdrawal (78% of users report): • Fatigue, insomnia, anxiety, irritability • Myalgias, arthralgias, muscle cramps • Lacrimation, rhinorrhea, diaphoresis, mydriasis • GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramping • Tachycardia, restlessness, cravings Unique to kratom: • Prominent neurological symptoms: tremors, jerky movements, coordination issues • Protracted depression and cognitiv

nodes.title: Assessment
nodes.summary: COWS not validated for kratom but reasonable proxy; supplement with vitals, neuro exam, product type, timeline
nodes.body: COWS Score Calculator Use COWS to assess severity: • NOT formally validated for kratom, but reasonable proxy • May not capture kratom-unique features (tremors, coordination, brain fog) Supplement COWS with: • Vital signs (tachycardia, hypertension early; bradycardia late) • Neuro exam: mydriasis, hyperreflexia, tremor, orientation • Timeline of last use and daily dose • Product type (leaf vs extra

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: COWS guides treatment intensity: 0-4 observe, 5-12 symptomatic, 13-24 treat in ED, 25+ consider admission
nodes.body: What is the COWS score?

nodes.title: No Active Withdrawal
nodes.summary: COWS 0-4: observe, reassess in 2-4h, do NOT start buprenorphine yet
nodes.body: COWS 0-4 — no objective signs of withdrawal yet. Management: • Observe and reassess COWS in 2-4 hours • Withdrawal may evolve as kratom clears (onset 6-12h) • Do NOT start buprenorphine — risk of precipitated withdrawal Screen for: • Daily kratom dose and product type • Co-use with opioids or other substances • Readiness for treatment If patient reports recent kratom use, withdrawal will likely ev

nodes.title: Treatment Selection
nodes.summary: Two pathways: buprenorphine (best-supported, moderate-severe) vs non-opioid (clonidine/gabapentin, mild-moderate or opioid-naïve)
nodes.body: Treatment Comparison Two pathways: 1. Buprenorphine (best-supported) • First-line for moderate-severe withdrawal • Displaces kratom alkaloids from μ-opioid receptors • Case series show efficacy • Consider if: prior opioid use, severe symptoms, patient preference 2. Non-opioid (clonidine/gabapentin) • First-line for mild-moderate withdrawal • No risk of iatrogenic opioid dependence • Consider if: o

nodes.title: Buprenorphine Dosing
nodes.summary: Buprenorphine dosing by kratom use: <20g/d start 4-8mg, >40g/d start 12-16mg; wait for COWS ≥8; titrate q60-90min
nodes.body: Buprenorphine Dosing Tool Mechanism: High-affinity partial μ-opioid agonist displaces kratom alkaloids, suppresses withdrawal. Dosing based on daily kratom use: <20g kratom/day: • Start 4-8 mg SL buprenorphine or 4/1 - 8/2 mg buprenorphine-naloxone >40g kratom/day: • Start 12-16 mg SL or 12/3 - 16/4 mg buprenorphine-naloxone Titration protocol: 1. Confirm COWS ≥8 before first dose 2. Give initial

nodes.title: Buprenorphine Cautions
nodes.summary: Wait for COWS ≥8 to avoid precipitated WD; consider iatrogenic dependence risk in opioid-naïve; short-term taper vs ongoing MOUD
nodes.body: Precipitated withdrawal risk: • Wait for COWS ≥8 before initiating • Starting too early can precipitate withdrawal Iatrogenic dependence concern: • In opioid-naïve kratom users, buprenorphine may create new opioid dependence • Consider non-opioid pathway if patient has no prior opioid use history • Discuss with patient: short-term treatment vs ongoing MOUD Monitoring: • Reassess COWS at 60-90 minu

nodes.title: Clonidine
nodes.summary: Clonidine 0.1mg q4-6h PRN (max 0.8-1.2mg/d) — non-opioid, no cross-dependence; hold if SBP <90 or HR <50
nodes.body: Mechanism: α-2A adrenergic agonist reduces sympathetic outflow. Does NOT produce cross-dependence with kratom. Dosing: • 0.1 mg PO q4-6h PRN • Typical max 0.8-1.2 mg/day • Can give 0.1 mg IV for rapid effect Advantages: • Non-opioid — no risk of iatrogenic opioid dependence • Can be used as monotherapy in mild-moderate withdrawal • Effective for sympathomimetic symptoms • Good safety profile Cauti

nodes.title: Gabapentin & Adjuncts
nodes.summary: Gabapentin 300-600mg q6-8h (target 1600mg/d); adjuncts: loperamide (max 16mg/d), ondansetron, NSAIDs, trazodone
nodes.body: Gabapentin: • Reduces myalgias, chills, dysphoria, diarrhea, muscle tension • Dosing: 300-600 mg q6-8h, titrate to effect • Evidence: 1600 mg/day superior to 900 mg/day for opioid withdrawal • Good safety profile, no respiratory risk • Case report: successful kratom withdrawal in LVAD patient Other symptomatic adjuncts: • Loperamide 2mg initial, then 1mg after each loose stool (max 16mg/day) — CAU

nodes.title: Complications
nodes.summary: Watch for: bradycardia (peak day 3-4), seizures, delirium, severe dehydration, hepatotoxicity; continuous monitoring if admitted
nodes.body: Complications Reference Cardiac (monitor closely): • Bradycardia — documented at withdrawal peak (day 3-4), can progress to cardiac arrest • Tachycardia (early phase) • QTc prolongation (especially with 7-OH products) • Consider continuous monitoring if admitted Neurological: • Seizures (rare, high-dose chronic users) • Delirium with hallucinations • Tremors, jerky movements, hyperreflexia GI: • S

nodes.title: Cardiac Monitoring
nodes.summary: Cardiac arrest documented at peak (day 3-4); ECG for QTc; ICU if HR <50 with symptoms, arrhythmia, or instability
nodes.body: Documented cardiac complications: • Bradycardia progressing to cardiac arrest (day 4 of withdrawal in case report) • Tachycardia (early withdrawal) • QTc prolongation • Brugada syndrome exacerbation (chronic high-dose users) • Torsades de pointes (rare) When to monitor: • COWS ≥25 (severe) • Bradycardia (HR <50) or syncope • Known cardiac history • High-potency 7-OH product use • Concern for elect

nodes.title: Precipitated Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Naltrexone can precipitate kratom withdrawal — taper kratom before starting; wait for COWS ≥8 before buprenorphine
nodes.body: Naltrexone risk: • Naltrexone can precipitate kratom withdrawal similar to opioid withdrawal • Documented case report: severe withdrawal symptoms after naltrexone administration Management: • If patient on naltrexone and develops kratom withdrawal symptoms, supportive care only • If planning to start naltrexone for OUD, taper kratom first • Use buprenorphine bridge if transition needed Buprenorphi

nodes.title: Severe Cases — ICU
nodes.summary: Dexmedetomidine 0.5-1.4 μg/kg/h IV for severe agitation/delirium; ICU if COWS >24 + instability, seizures, arrhythmias, AMS
nodes.body: Dexmedetomidine for severe agitation/delirium: • Mechanism: Central α-2A agonist, sedating + analgesic • Preserves respiratory drive • Dosing: 0.5-1.4 μg/kg/h IV infusion Case report: Kratom withdrawal delirium (CIWA-AR 39, confusion, hallucinations) managed with dexmedetomidine + lorazepam; discharged after 48 hours. ICU admission criteria: • COWS >24 with vital instability • Acute agitation/deli

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition by severity: mild=discharge with meds, moderate=ED observation, severe=admit
nodes.body: Select disposition based on severity and response to treatment.

nodes.title: Discharge — Mild
nodes.body: Discharge criteria met: • COWS <13 or improving • Stable vital signs • Tolerating oral intake • No cardiac or neurological concerns Discharge with: • Clonidine 0.1mg PO q6h PRN x 5-7 days • Gabapentin 300mg TID x 5-7 days (if prescribed) • Loperamide PRN for diarrhea • Ondansetron PRN for nausea • Ibuprofen/acetaminophen PRN for myalgias Patient education: • Withdrawal peak is day 3-4 — symptoms m
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with clonidine 0.1mg q6h PRN, gabapentin 300mg TID, symptomatic meds. Warn: peak day 3-4. Return precautions for cardiac/neuro symptoms. Follow-up in 1 week.

nodes.title: ED Observation
nodes.body: ED observation indicated: • COWS 13-24 • Needs treatment titration (buprenorphine or clonidine) • Monitoring for complications Observation plan: • 6-12 hour observation period • Reassess COWS q2-4h • Titrate buprenorphine or clonidine as needed • IV fluids if dehydrated • ECG to assess QTc Discharge when: • COWS <13 and stable for 2+ hours • Tolerating PO • Stable vitals • Follow-up arranged Escal
nodes.recommendation: ED observation 6-12h. Titrate treatment, reassess COWS q2-4h. ECG for QTc. Discharge when COWS <13 and stable x2h. Escalate if worsening or complications.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admission indicated: • COWS >24 with vital instability • Cardiac concerns (bradycardia, arrhythmia, QTc prolongation) • Seizure or seizure risk • Severe agitation/delirium requiring IV medications • Intractable vomiting with dehydration • Altered mental status • Unable to tolerate PO • Inadequate social support for outpatient management Admission orders: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Buprenorp
nodes.recommendation: Admit with continuous cardiac monitoring. Buprenorphine or clonidine pathway. IV fluids. Dexmedetomidine if severe agitation. Serial COWS q4-6h. Addiction medicine consult.

nodes.title: Laceration Repair
nodes.body: > First-pass goal: rule out occult injury (nerve/tendon/vessel/joint/foreign body), then decide closure method and timing. Workflow: 1. Triage emergent findings 2. Neurovascular and tendon exam before anesthesia 3. Irrigation + foreign body sweep 4. Anesthesia 5. Closure decision (suture / staple / glue / leave open) 6. Technique + special-site rules 7. Aftercare + tetanus + follow-up Steps Summar

nodes.title: Emergent Findings?
nodes.summary: Screen arterial, open fx, tendon/nerve, and bite wounds before routine pathway
nodes.body: Screen for injuries that change the workup.

nodes.title: Arterial Bleeding — STOP
nodes.body: > Active arterial injury changes the algorithm. Do not blind-clamp; vessel ligation in ED risks nerve injury.
nodes.recommendation: Bleeding control ladder: 1. Direct pressure × 10 min uninterrupted 2. Elevate above heart if extremity 3. Pressure dressing 4. Tourniquet (note time) if life-threatening 5. Surgical consult for exploration Avoid: blind hemostat clamping nea

nodes.title: Open Fracture / Joint — STOP
nodes.body: > Bone visible, fat globules, or air in joint = open fracture or joint capsule violation.
nodes.recommendation: Actions: • Cover with saline-moist gauze • X-ray (consider Ottawa rules if applicable) • Tetanus prophylaxis • IV antibiotics: cefazolin within 1 hr of presentation • Orthopedics consult for OR washout (Gustilo I-IIIc) • Do NOT close in ED

nodes.title: Tendon or Nerve Injury Suspected
nodes.body: > Any motor weakness, sensory deficit, or tendon visible in wound base needs hand/plastic surgery.
nodes.recommendation: Document before block: • Two-point discrimination (<6 mm normal fingertip) • Motor: each FDS, FDP, EPL, EIP, etc. independently • Capillary refill Disposition: • Partial laceration <50%: can close skin, sling, hand clinic 3-5 d • Complete l

nodes.body: > Bites need separate rules. Hand bites do not close primarily. Irrigation: copious; consider extending wound to expose deep extent. Closure: • Face bite <24 hr, low-tension, clean: primary closure OK • Hand bite (human or animal): leave open, delayed primary closure at 72 hr if clean • Cat bite (deep puncture): leave open — high infection rate (~50%) • Dog bite trunk/extremity: case-by-case; prim

nodes.title: Wound Assessment
nodes.summary: Mechanism, time, FB risk, neurovascular exam documented before block
nodes.body: Document before anesthesia: • Location, length, depth • Mechanism (clean cut, crush, contamination) • Time since injury (golden period: face <24 hr, body <12 hr, hand <6 hr) • Foreign body suspected? (glass, wood, metal) • Motor and sensory exam distal to wound • Tendon function each compartment • Capillary refill + pulses X-ray indications: • Suspected radiopaque foreign body (glass >2 mm visible

nodes.title: Irrigation & Preparation
nodes.summary: Tap water = saline; 50-100 mL/cm at 5-8 psi; no antiseptics in wound
nodes.body: > Irrigation is the single most important infection-prevention step. Volume > antiseptic choice. Solution: tap water non-inferior to sterile saline (Moscati 2007). Use whichever is faster and adequate volume. Volume: 50-100 mL per cm of wound length. Pressure: 5-8 psi (19-gauge angiocath on 35-60 mL syringe, or commercial splash shield). Avoid in wound: povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, chlorhex

nodes.title: Foreign Body Concern?
nodes.summary: Sweep then image if any FB suspicion
nodes.body: After irrigation, sweep wound for residual debris.

nodes.title: Imaging for Foreign Body
nodes.summary: X-ray for glass/metal; US for wood/organic; mark with paperclip
nodes.body: Choose modality by FB type: | FB type | Best test | |--|--| | Glass >2 mm | Plain x-ray (99% sensitive) | | Metal | Plain x-ray | | Wood/plastic/thorn | Ultrasound (US) | | Deep, complex, near joint | CT | Tip: Mark wound entry with paperclip taped to skin to localize on film. If FB found and removable: extract, re-irrigate. If buried deep/migrated: ortho or surgery consult.

nodes.title: Anesthesia Selection
nodes.summary: Lido+epi safe in digits per Cochrane; max dose 7 mg/kg with epi; bicarb buffer reduces sting
nodes.body: > Lidocaine is workhorse. Epi is safe in digits (Prabhakar 2015 Cochrane review — no documented digital necrosis). Local infiltration: • Lidocaine 1%: max 4.5 mg/kg (300 mg adult) • Lidocaine 1% with epi 1:100,000: max 7 mg/kg (500 mg adult), longer duration, less bleeding • Bicarb buffer 1:10 (1 mL 8.4% NaHCO3 per 9 mL lido) reduces sting • Warm to body temp reduces sting • 30-gauge needle, injec

nodes.title: Pediatric Anesthesia
nodes.summary: LET first; add infiltration; intranasal midaz for anxiolysis; PSA if complex
nodes.body: Stepwise: 1. Topical LET gel × 20-30 min — sufficient for many small face/scalp lacs. 2. Add small-volume infiltration if needed — use 30-gauge through wound edge, inject slowly, buffered lido. 3. Consider intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg or PO midazolam 0.5 mg/kg for anxiolysis. 4. Procedural sedation (ketamine IM/IV) if needed — see Pediatric Procedural Sedation. Restraint: papoose or parent-hold

nodes.title: Regional Block
nodes.summary: Block for larger wounds; 1-5 mL per nerve; aspirate before inject
nodes.body: Why block over infiltration? • Higher total dose available without tissue distortion • Single injection covers large area • Better cosmesis (no tissue swelling at repair site) Most useful: • Digital block: 1 mL lido per side of digit, dorsal approach (Prabhakar — epi OK) • Supraorbital/infraorbital/mental: 1-2 mL each, onset 5-10 min • Wrist median/ulnar/radial: 3-5 mL each Always: aspirate before

nodes.title: Closure Method?
nodes.summary: Sutures default; glue for low-tension; staples for scalp; leave open if contaminated
nodes.body: Match closure to wound type, location, tension, contamination.

nodes.title: Tissue Adhesive (Cyanoacrylate)
nodes.summary: Low-tension, <5 cm; 3 thin layers; keep dry × 5 d; no ointment
nodes.body: > Equivalent cosmesis to sutures for low-tension, dry wounds (Quinn 1997). Indications: • Linear, <5 cm, low tension • Face, scalp, extremity (NOT joints, hands, feet bottom) • Dry, hemostatic wound bed Contraindications: • High-tension or joint-crossing wound • Mucosal surfaces • Hair-bearing scalp (consider hair apposition first) • Infected or contaminated • Bite wound Technique: • Approximate e

nodes.title: Staples
nodes.summary: Scalp/trunk/extremity; fast; remove 7-14 d
nodes.body: Best for: scalp, trunk, extremity (not face, hands, feet, joints). Pros: fast, lower infection rate than sutures, removable without anesthesia. Technique: • Approximate edges with forceps, evert • Staple every 0.5-1 cm, perpendicular to long axis • Confirm scalp galea closed first if deep Removal: 7-14 d depending on site (see aftercare table).

nodes.title: Steri-Strips / Hair Apposition
nodes.summary: Steri-Strips for superficial no-tension; HAT for scalp ≥3 cm hair
nodes.body: Steri-Strips: • Very superficial, no tension • Pre-treat skin with benzoin or Mastisol for adhesion • Cross-strips of perpendicular tape add strength • Avoid joint creases Hair apposition technique (HAT): • Scalp lacs with hair ≥3 cm long • Twist 4-5 strands from each side, cross over wound • Glue twist with cyanoacrylate • No suturing or shaving needed • Equivalent cosmesis to sutures

nodes.title: Leave Open / Delayed Primary Closure
nodes.summary: Contaminated, bite, late presentation → leave open, recheck 72-96 h
nodes.body: Indications: • Heavily contaminated • Hand bite (human or cat) • Presented late (>24 hr face, >12 hr body, >6 hr hand) • Crush with significant devitalized tissue • Abscess Management: • Irrigate thoroughly • Pack lightly with iodoform or wet-to-dry gauze • Daily wound check • Delayed primary closure at 72-96 hr if no infection Antibiotics: consider for high-risk wounds — see bite wound pathway or

nodes.title: Suture Selection
nodes.summary: Nylon 6-0 face / 4-0 trunk; absorbable OK for peds face (Karounis)
nodes.body: > Match suture to location and tension. Skin (non-absorbable): | Site | Size | Removal | |--|--|--| | Face | 6-0 nylon/prolene | 5 d | | Scalp | 4-0 to 5-0 nylon | 7-14 d | | Trunk/extremity | 4-0 to 5-0 | 7-10 d | | Hand/foot | 4-0 to 5-0 | 10-14 d | | Over joint | 3-0 to 4-0 | 10-14 d | Absorbable for skin: Karounis 2004 showed plain gut equivalent to nylon for pediatric face — avoids removal vi

nodes.title: Closure Technique
nodes.summary: Evert edges; match landmarks first; spacing 2-5 mm; technique by tension
nodes.body: Principles: • Evert edges (avoids inversion → depressed scar) • Equal bites either side • No tension across closure (use deep sutures if needed) • Match landmarks (vermillion border, eyebrow, hairline) FIRST • Knots 3 throws minimum (4 for monofilament) • Keep knots off the wound line Stitch types: • Simple interrupted: workhorse — most lacs • Vertical mattress: high tension, gaping wounds • Horiz

nodes.title: Facial Lacerations
nodes.summary: Vermillion = first stitch; never shave brow; cover ear cartilage; eyelid red flags → ophtho
nodes.body: Landmarks first — match before closure to avoid step-off. Vermillion border (lip): First stitch IS the vermillion line. Use 6-0 nylon, place suture exactly at white roll. A 1 mm step-off is visible at conversational distance. Eyebrow: Do NOT shave. Approximate hair direction. 5-0 or 6-0 nylon. nodes.title: Hand & Digit Lacerations

nodes.title: Scalp Lacerations
nodes.summary: Galea check + close if open; staples or HAT fast; rule out depressed skull/TBI
nodes.body: Galea check: palpate base of wound. Galea is fibrous layer — if disrupted, must close separately with absorbable (4-0 Vicryl) to prevent expanding hematoma. Hemostasis: scalp bleeds dramatically. Direct pressure × 10 min. Raney clips if available. Lido + epi infiltration helps both anesthesia and hemostasis. Closure options: • Hair apposition (HAT) — if hair ≥3 cm • Staples — fast, equivalent cosm

nodes.title: Aftercare, Tetanus, Disposition
nodes.summary: Petrolatum + sunblock; tetanus per CDC; antibiotics not routine; removal table by site
nodes.body: Wound care: • Keep clean and dry × 24 hr (48 hr if glue) • Then gentle wash with soap and water daily • Petrolatum or bacitracin (NOT on glue) — keeps scar moist, improves cosmesis • Avoid hydrogen peroxide and antiseptics after closure • Sunblock × 6 mo to prevent hyperpigmentation Tetanus (CDC): | Status | Clean wound | Dirty wound | |--|--|--| | Uncertain or <3 doses | Tdap | Tdap + TIG | | ≥3

nodes.body: > Document everything. Photo before and after if able (with consent).

nodes.title: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS)
nodes.summary: Presynaptic anti-VGCC NMJ disorder; improves with use (facilitation). ~50-60% paraneoplastic with SCLC, often preceding the cancer.
nodes.body: LEMS is a presynaptic autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction. Antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) on the motor nerve terminal reduce calcium influx and therefore reduce acetylcholine release. The postsynaptic receptor is normal — the defect is upstream. The mechanistic signature: one nerve impulse releases too little ACh (weakness, low resting CMAP), but ra

nodes.title: The LEMS Triad
nodes.summary: Triad: proximal (legs>arms) weakness + autonomic (dry mouth) + reflexes that augment with exercise. Facilitation = bedside hallmark.
nodes.body: (1) Proximal muscle weakness — the dominant complaint. Legs > arms, symmetric. Difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, waddling gait. Atrophy is mild relative to weakness. (2) Autonomic dysfunction — present in 80-96%. Dry mouth is the most common and often earliest symptom. Also constipation, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension, blurred vision, reduced sweating. (3) Hypo/arefle

nodes.title: LEMS vs Myasthenia Gravis
nodes.summary: LEMS: proximal, improves with use, autonomic, anti-VGCC, SCLC, RNS increment. MG: ocular/bulbar, fatigable, anti-AChR, thymoma, RNS decrement.
nodes.body: | Feature | LEMS | Myasthenia gravis | |---|---|---| | Weakness pattern | Proximal (legs > arms) | Ocular / bulbar onset | | Response to use | Improves (facilitation) | Worsens (fatigability) | | Reflexes | Hypo/areflexic; augment post-exercise | Normal | | Autonomic | Prominent (dry mouth, ED, orthostasis) | Absent | | Antibody | Anti-P/Q VGCC (~85-95%) | Anti-AChR / anti-MuSK | | Tumor | SCLC (~

nodes.title: Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Anti-P/Q VGCC (~85-95%); RNS shows high-frequency/post-exercise increment >60%. N-type antibody not useful alone; SOX1 flags SCLC.
nodes.body: Three pillars: clinical triad + serology + electrodiagnostics. Serology: - Anti-P/Q-type VGCC antibodies — positive in ~85-95% (titers >~30 pmol/L support the diagnosis in context). ~10-15% seronegative. - N-type VGCC antibodies are NOT useful in isolation (low sensitivity, nonspecific) — do not diagnose LEMS off an isolated N-type result. - SOX1 antibodies (~64% in SCLC-LEMS, ~95% specific) — a u

nodes.title: Hunt the Small Cell Lung Cancer
nodes.summary: CT chest -> PET; repeat surveillance for >=2 years if negative. DELTA-P (age>=50, smoking, weight loss, bulbar, ED, low Karnofsky) stratifies SCLC risk.
nodes.body: Every new LEMS diagnosis triggers a malignancy hunt — treating the SCLC often improves the neurologic syndrome, and LEMS may be the first sign of an otherwise-occult tumor. Imaging: - CT chest first-line; if negative, FDG-PET/CT. - If initial imaging is negative, repeat screening every 3-6 months for at least 2 years (high-risk: every 3 months). *FLAGGED: confirm the surveillance interval against

nodes.title: Drugs to AVOID — Highest ED-Safety Yield
nodes.summary: AVOID: NM blockers (prolonged paralysis), aminoglycosides/fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, CCBs (verapamil/diltiazem), IV contrast. These precipitate respiratory failure.
nodes.body: This is where the ED can harm a LEMS patient. Several common drugs worsen presynaptic NMJ transmission and can precipitate respiratory failure. Avoid / use with extreme caution: - Neuromuscular blockers (depolarizing AND non-depolarizing) — profound, prolonged paralysis. LEMS is frequently *first discovered* via unexpected prolonged blockade after anesthesia. If RSI is unavoidable, anticipate mark

nodes.title: Respiratory Monitoring
nodes.summary: Crisis less common than MG but occurs, often iatrogenic. Trend FVC/NIF + single-breath count; SpO2 is late. Thresholds mirror the MG consult.
nodes.body: Frank respiratory failure is less common than in MG but does occur — and is often iatrogenic (see drugs to avoid). It is the only truly emergent LEMS complication. Monitor: - FVC and NIF; bedside single-breath count (cannot reach 20 = concerning) - Bulbar safety: cough strength, secretion handling, swallow Pulse oximetry is a poor/late indicator of neuromuscular respiratory strength — do not be re

nodes.title: Treatment
nodes.summary: Amifampridine (3,4-DAP) 15-30 mg TID first-line; pyridostigmine adjunct. IVIG/steroids/PLEX for severe. Treat the SCLC. ED rarely initiates therapy.
nodes.body: Symptomatic: - First-line: amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine, 3,4-DAP) — blocks presynaptic K+ channels, prolonging the action potential and boosting calcium influx / ACh release. Start 15-30 mg/day PO in 3-4 divided doses; titrate by 5 mg every 3-4 days; single dose ≤20 mg. FDA max (Firdapse, US labeling updated May 2024): 100 mg/day for patients >45 kg (was 80 mg/day); for patients <45 kg start

nodes.title: Differential
nodes.summary: MG (fatigable/decrement), GBS (sensory/CSF/demyelinating), botulism (descending/pupils/exposure), myopathy (normal reflexes, high CK). Often misdiagnosed early.
nodes.body: - Myasthenia gravis — closest mimic; fatigability vs facilitation, ocular/bulbar vs proximal, autonomic features, antibody, RNS decrement vs increment. - Guillain-Barré — ascending weakness + areflexia, but with sensory involvement, CSF albuminocytologic dissociation, and a demyelinating EMG. - Botulism — also presynaptic with autonomic features (dry mouth, ileus), but descending, cranial-nerve-fi

nodes.title: Disposition & Prognosis
nodes.summary: Stable -> outpatient neuro+onc; admit for respiratory/bulbar compromise. Non-tumor: good prognosis. Paraneoplastic: tied to SCLC (paradoxically better SCLC survival).
nodes.body: Disposition: - Stable: outpatient neurology + oncology workup (antibody panel, EMG, CT/PET, DELTA-P). Therapy is rarely initiated in the ED. - Admit for respiratory compromise, rapidly progressive weakness, significant bulbar dysfunction, or decompensation after a precipitant drug. ICU + immunotherapy for crisis. Prognosis: - Non-tumor LEMS: near-normal life expectancy with treatment (~60% indepen
nodes.recommendation: Recognize the MG mirror-image (proximal weakness improving with use + dry mouth + augmenting reflexes), send anti-P/Q VGCC antibodies, and hunt SCLC with CT chest -> PET (DELTA-P to stratify). AVOID neuromuscular blockers, aminoglycosides/f

nodes.title: Laryngeal Trauma
nodes.summary: Laryngeal trauma: airway loss can be rapid and unpredictable — prepare for surgical airway immediately
nodes.body: Rare but lethal — second most common cause of death in head/neck trauma after intracranial injury [1] Incidence: 1:5,000 to 1:137,000 trauma patients CRITICAL WARNING: > RSI is CONTRAINDICATED in suspected laryngeal trauma. > Paralysis removes spontaneous ventilation. If intubation fails → CICO catastrophe. > Awake tracheostomy is preferred. [1][2]

nodes.title: Mechanism of Injury
nodes.summary: Blunt (clothesline, MVC, strangulation) vs penetrating — both can rapidly compromise airway
nodes.body: Blunt Trauma: • Motor vehicle accidents (historically most common, reduced with seatbelts/airbags) • Clothesline injuries — rider strikes horizontal object; high-velocity crush against C-spine; often cricotracheal separation + bilateral RLN injury • Direct blows — assault, sports, steering wheel impact • Strangulation/hanging — compression of all neck structures [1][3] Penetrating Trauma: • Knife

nodes.title: Clinical Signs Assessment
nodes.summary: Hoarseness, subcutaneous emphysema, stridor, dysphagia, anterior neck tenderness = laryngeal injury
nodes.body: HARD SIGNS (immediate concern): | Sign | Significance | |------|-------------| | Stridor | Active airway compromise | | Respiratory distress | Impending obstruction | | Subcutaneous emphysema | Mucosal disruption | | Loss of thyroid prominence | Cartilage fracture | | Hemoptysis | Mucosal laceration | | Expanding hematoma | Vascular injury | SOFT SIGNS: • Dysphonia/hoarseness (most common — 85%) •

nodes.title: Unstable Airway — Immediate Action
nodes.summary: Airway distress: prepare for surgical airway — intubation may worsen injury or create false passage
nodes.body: CRITICAL: DO NOT PARALYZE RSI is contraindicated: • Paralysis removes spontaneous ventilation • If intubation fails → no backup (can't mask, can't wake) • Laryngeal manipulation can create false passage or complete obstruction • Risk of "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" (CICO) [1][2] Preferred approach: 1. Awake tracheostomy (surgical airway of choice) 2. Call anesthesia, ENT, trauma surgery NOW 3

nodes.title: Airway Options
nodes.summary: Airway approach depends on stability: awake FOI, awake trach, or emergent surgical airway
nodes.body: | Option | When to Use | Cautions | |--------|-------------|----------| | Awake tracheostomy | PREFERRED for significant laryngeal trauma | Requires time, OR access | | Awake fiberoptic | Stable airway, need to assess before trach | Blood/secretions obscure; slow | | Cricothyrotomy | Emergent CICO, cannot wait | CONTRAINDICATED if laryngeal fracture or cricotracheal separation | | RSI/DL | AVOID i

nodes.title: Awake Tracheostomy
nodes.summary: Awake tracheostomy is gold standard for laryngeal trauma airway — avoids passing through injury site
nodes.body: Procedure: 1. Local anesthesia to anterior neck 2. Patient maintains spontaneous ventilation 3. Vertical incision, identify trachea below injury 4. Confirm placement with ETCO₂, breath sounds Double setup: Have both ENT and anesthesia present. Prepare simultaneously for: • Awake fiberoptic intubation • Awake tracheostomy Post-trach: Continue resuscitation, CT imaging when stable [1][2]

nodes.title: Cricothyrotomy Decision
nodes.summary: Cricothyrotomy risks further laryngeal damage — tracheostomy preferred if any time available
nodes.body: CRICOTHYROTOMY CONTRAINDICATIONS: • Laryngeal fracture • Laryngotracheal disruption • Tracheal transection In these cases → proceed directly to tracheostomy BELOW the injury [1][2] Is there suspected laryngeal fracture or tracheal disruption?

nodes.title: Emergent Tracheostomy
nodes.summary: Emergent tracheostomy by ENT/surgery when airway is failing — cricothyrotomy as absolute last resort
nodes.body: When cricothyrotomy is contraindicated: Proceed directly to tracheostomy below the level of injury. Technique (emergent): 1. Vertical midline incision from cricoid to sternal notch 2. Blunt dissection to trachea 3. Identify intact trachea below injury 4. Incision between tracheal rings 5. Insert trach tube, confirm with ETCO₂ If tracheal transection: May need to retrieve distal trachea from medias

nodes.title: Cricothyrotomy Technique
nodes.summary: Cricothyrotomy only if cannot ventilate and trach not immediately available — may worsen injury
nodes.body: Standard surgical cricothyrotomy: 1. Identify cricothyroid membrane 2. Vertical skin incision 3. Horizontal stab through membrane 4. Bougie insertion 5. 6.0 ETT or trach tube over bougie 6. Confirm with ETCO₂ Post-procedure: • Secure airway • Continue trauma evaluation • CT imaging when stable • ENT consult for definitive management [1]

nodes.title: Awake Fiberoptic Intubation
nodes.summary: Awake fiberoptic intubation: visualize injury, pass tube under direct vision — if anatomy allows
nodes.body: Indications: • Stable airway but concern for laryngeal injury • Need to assess before tracheostomy decision Technique: 1. Topicalize airway (lidocaine nebulizer, atomizer) 2. Maintain spontaneous ventilation 3. Advance fiberoptic scope through nose or mouth 4. Assess laryngeal injury 5. If passable → advance ETT 6. If not passable → proceed to tracheostomy Have surgical airway kit ready — prepared

nodes.title: Flexible Laryngoscopy
nodes.summary: Bedside flexible laryngoscopy by ENT to assess injury severity and guide airway management
nodes.body: Performed early in stable patients: • Assesses mucosal integrity, hematoma, vocal cord mobility • Can miss injuries masked by edema (repeat after swelling resolves) Findings that suggest significant injury: • Mucosal lacerations • Vocal cord immobility • Arytenoid dislocation • Epiglottic hematoma • Exposed cartilage If normal: Proceed to CT imaging [1][2]

nodes.title: Schaefer-Fuhrman Classification
nodes.summary: Schaefer-Fuhrman classification grades I-V guides management: observation vs OR vs emergent airway
nodes.body: | Grade | Findings | Airway | |-------|----------|--------| | I | Minor hematoma/laceration, no fracture | Stable | | II | Edema, hematoma, nondisplaced fracture, minor mucosal disruption | Variable | | III | Massive edema, displaced fractures, exposed cartilage, vocal cord immobility | Compromised | | IV | Severe disruption, unstable fractures, extensive mucosal injury, anterior commissure involv

nodes.title: Imaging Studies
nodes.summary: CT neck with contrast for stable patients — assess cartilage fractures, soft tissue injury, vascular
nodes.body: CT Neck with IV Contrast (Gold Standard): • Only perform if airway is stable or secured • Identifies: soft tissue edema, hematoma, cartilage fractures, cricoarytenoid dislocation • Low threshold for imaging — subtle CT findings may indicate significant injury [1] CT Angiography: • Add for penetrating trauma or suspected vascular injury • Assess carotid/vertebral dissection Direct Laryngoscopy + Es

nodes.title: Management by Grade
nodes.summary: Grade I-II: observation. Grade III-IV: OR repair within 24h. Grade V: emergent surgical airway
nodes.body: Key principle: Early repair (24-48h) yields better outcomes: • Early: 58% good voice, 87% good airway • Delayed (>48h): 22% good voice, 55% good airway [1][2] What is the injury grade?

nodes.title: Grade I — Conservative Management
nodes.summary: Grade I: minor edema, no fracture — observe 24h with humidified air, HOB elevated, voice rest
nodes.body: Treatment: • Humidified air • Voice rest • Head of bed elevation • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV + nebulized steroids • Anti-reflux medications (PPI or H2 blocker) • Antibiotics if mucosal disruption Monitoring: • ICU observation 24-48 hours • Serial flexible laryngoscopy • Watch for delayed edema/hematoma expansion [1]
nodes.recommendation: Conservative management with steroids, voice rest, humidified air. ICU observation 24-48h.

nodes.title: Grade II — Conservative or Surgical
nodes.summary: Grade II: edema with non-displaced fracture — admit, observe, ENT follow-up within 24h
nodes.body: Usually conservative (same as Grade I): • Humidified air, voice rest, HOB elevation • IV dexamethasone + nebulized steroids • Anti-reflux, antibiotics if mucosal disruption May require tracheostomy if: • Significant airway compromise develops • Edema progression despite steroids Close monitoring: • ICU observation • Serial exams for progression • Some may need surgical exploration [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: Conservative management. May require tracheostomy if airway compromises. ICU observation.

nodes.title: Grade III-IV — Surgical Management
nodes.summary: Grade III-IV: displaced fractures, exposed cartilage — OR exploration and repair within 24h
nodes.body: Surgical approach: 1. Secure airway (tracheostomy preferred) 2. CT imaging if not already done 3. Direct laryngoscopy + esophagoscopy in OR 4. Open repair: ORIF of displaced fractures, mucosal repair 5. Thyrotomy approach for endolaryngeal access 6. Laryngeal stent if anterior commissure involvement Timing: Ideally within 24-48 hours [1][2] Consults: • ENT (primary) • Trauma surgery • Anesthesia (
nodes.recommendation: Surgical management within 24-48 hours. Tracheostomy, ORIF of fractures, mucosal repair.

nodes.title: Grade V — Laryngotracheal Separation
nodes.summary: Grade V: complete laryngeal disruption — emergent surgical airway and OR reconstruction
nodes.body: EMERGENT SURGICAL MANAGEMENT: 1. Immediate tracheostomy below level of injury 2. Emergent surgical repair in OR 3. Primary anastomosis if possible 4. Highest mortality category Special considerations: • May need to retrieve distal trachea from mediastinum • Risk of bilateral RLN injury • Associated c-spine injury common [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: Emergent tracheostomy below injury, immediate surgical repair. Highest mortality category.

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Patient Observation
nodes.summary: Observation protocol: HOB 30 degrees, humidified air, voice rest, serial airway assessments
nodes.body: Delayed presentation warning: • Initially mild symptoms may accompany severe injury • Edema and hematoma can progress over hours to days For asymptomatic patients with mechanism: • Flexible laryngoscopy • CT neck if any suspicion • Observation 6-12 hours minimum Discharge only if: • Normal flexible laryngoscopy • No airway symptoms • Reliable patient with close follow-up [1][2]

nodes.title: Associated Injuries — Check For
nodes.summary: Check for associated injuries: C-spine, vascular (carotid/vertebral), esophageal, recurrent laryngeal nerve
nodes.body: | Injury | Incidence | Workup | |--------|-----------|--------| | Intracranial | 13-15% | CT head | | Skull base/facial fractures | 21% | CT face | | C-spine fractures | 8% | CT c-spine, maintain precautions | | Esophageal/pharyngeal | 3% | Esophagoscopy, contrast swallow | | Vascular | Variable | CT angiography | Maintain c-spine precautions until cleared — 8% have associated cervical spine injur

nodes.title: Consults & Disposition
nodes.summary: ENT and/or trauma surgery consultation for all confirmed laryngeal injuries — early involvement critical
nodes.body: | Specialty | When to Consult | |-----------|----------------| | ENT | ALL suspected laryngeal injuries | | Trauma Surgery | Penetrating trauma, polytrauma, vascular injury | | Anesthesia | Difficult airway, awake intubation planned | | Thoracic Surgery | Tracheal injury, mediastinal involvement | | IR | Vascular injury on CTA | Disposition: • Grade I-II: ICU observation 24-48h • Grade III-V: OR,
nodes.recommendation: ENT consult for all suspected laryngeal injuries. ICU admission for significant injuries.

nodes.title: Lateral Canthotomy & Cantholysis
nodes.summary: OCS = closed-box orbit + retrobulbar blood → optic nerve/retinal ischemia. Clinical diagnosis; cantholysis is the decompressing step.
nodes.body: > 🚨 Sight-saving, time-critical procedure for orbital compartment syndrome (OCS). The orbit is a closed bony box (~30 mL) sealed anteriorly only by the eyelids and orbital septum. A small added volume of blood (retrobulbar hemorrhage) spikes orbital and intraocular pressure, throttling the optic nerve and occluding the central retinal artery. Decompress before the retina dies. Indications · Proce

nodes.title: Recognize Orbital Compartment Syndrome
nodes.summary: Triad: relative proptosis + tense/tight lids + RAPD. Vision loss is LATE (<50%) — never wait for it.
nodes.body: Landmark anatomy — lateral canthal tendon, crura, Whitnall tubercle. The actionable early triad (Erickson 2020): 1. Relative proptosis — the globe bulges forward; compare to the other side 2. Tense, tight eyelids that resist opening; "rock-hard" globe with resistance to retropulsion 3. RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect / Marcus Gunn pupil) in the injured eye Supporting signs: severe eye pai

nodes.title: Decide to Decompress
nodes.summary: Decompress if clinically obvious OR IOP >40 (or >30 + symptoms). Ischemia irreversible ~90-120 min.
nodes.body: Combine the clinical picture with IOP if you can measure it quickly. Never delay decompression to obtain tonometry when the clinical picture is obvious, and never measure IOP if you suspect globe rupture. IOP threshold tool — enter IOP + symptoms for the action tier. Numbers to anchor on: - Normal IOP 10–21 mmHg - IOP >30 mmHg with symptoms → call ophthalmology, prepare to decompress - IOP >40 mmH

nodes.title: Equivocal — Temporize & Re-Examine
nodes.summary: Equivocal: serial exams q15-30min, HOB up, reverse anticoagulation, ophtho + CT. Decompress the moment OCS declares.
nodes.body: Not clearly OCS (soft orbit, normal acuity and IOP). Do not perform canthotomy on a globe that is not under threat, but keep a very low threshold to act — OCS can declare itself over minutes as a bleed expands.
nodes.recommendation: Plan: • Serial exams every 15–30 min: visual acuity, pupil/RAPD, IOP, degree of proptosis and lid tension • Elevate head of bed; reverse anticoagulation if present and feasible • Urgent ophthalmology consult and CT orbit to characterize the

nodes.title: Screen for Globe Rupture
nodes.summary: Rupture clues: enophthalmos, teardrop pupil, hyphema, IOP <5, Seidel+. Overlaps with OCS; weigh both.
nodes.body: Globe rupture is the main contraindication, because canthotomy + pressure on a ruptured globe extrudes intraocular contents. Screen quickly — but remember the signs overlap with OCS and a missed OCS also blinds. Rupture clues (the discriminators): - Enophthalmos (sunken globe) instead of proptosis - Teardrop / peaked or irregular pupil - Obvious corneal/scleral laceration, extruded uveal tissue -

nodes.title: Suspected Globe Rupture — Weigh Carefully
nodes.summary: Rupture + soft orbit = shield, no cut, ophtho. Rupture + tense vision-threatened orbit = decompress gently, no globe pressure.
nodes.body: Globe rupture is a relative, not absolute, contraindication in practice. Rupture and OCS signs overlap, and an untreated OCS blinds just as surely. The deciding question is whether the eye is under tension from a compartment (decompress) or open and decompressed by the rupture itself (protect, do not cut).
nodes.recommendation: If rupture is likely and the orbit is NOT tense (low IOP, enophthalmos): • Do not perform canthotomy. Protect the globe — rigid eye shield (no patch, no pressure), antiemetics, analgesia, tetanus, IV antibiotics, NPO • Emergent ophthalmolog

nodes.title: Equipment & Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Standard lac tray: lidocaine+epi (25G, away from globe), straight hemostat, iris scissors, toothed forceps, Tono-Pen.
nodes.body: Everything you need is in a standard laceration tray — do not hunt for a special kit. Procedure steps overview Equipment: - Antiseptic, sterile drape, gauze, saline - Topical ophthalmic anesthetic drops (proparacaine/tetracaine) - Lidocaine 1–2% with epinephrine on a 25-gauge needle (epi aids hemostasis) - Straight hemostat / Kelly clamp (for the crush step) - Iris / Stevens tenotomy scissors (pre

nodes.title: Step 1 — Crush & Canthotomy
nodes.summary: Crush canthus ~1 min, then cut horizontally ≤2 cm to the rim, skin lifted away from globe. Canthotomy alone ≠ decompression.
nodes.body: Landmark anatomy — orient yourself before you cut. a. Hemostat crush (optional but recommended). Lay a straight hemostat across the lateral canthus from the canthal angle to the orbital rim and crush for ~1 minute. This devascularizes the tissue (less bleeding) and marks your incision line. b. Canthotomy — the skin cut. With toothed forceps lifting the skin away from the globe, cut horizontally th

nodes.title: Step 2 — Inferior Cantholysis (the decompressing step)
nodes.summary: Pull lower lid up/out, point scissors toward nose (away from globe), strum & cut inferior crus until lid swings free. ~30 mmHg drop.
nodes.body: 📐 See where to cut — annotated anatomy This releases the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon and is what actually drops the pressure (~30 mmHg). This is the structure circled in blue in the teaching image: the inferior limb of the lateral canthal tendon. Technique: 1. Grasp the lower lid at the lateral "last lash" with toothed forceps and pull it up and out (toward the ceiling, away from

nodes.title: Reassess — Did It Decompress?
nodes.summary: Success = IOP <40 (ideally <30), soft globe, improving VA/RAPD, swinging lid. Still tense → superior crus.
nodes.body: Recheck immediately after the inferior cantholysis. Endpoints of success: - IOP reduced (target <40 mmHg, ideally <30) - Softening of the previously rock-hard globe; reduced proptosis - Improving visual acuity and resolving RAPD (can begin within minutes) - A freely swinging eyelid IOP target tool — recheck the action tier with the new IOP.

nodes.title: Step 3 — Superior Cantholysis (if still tense)
nodes.summary: Superior crus only if inferior fully released and still tense. Lacrimal artery/gland + levator superiorly → bleed/ptosis risk. Refractory → OR.
nodes.body: Only after you have confirmed the inferior crus is fully released and the orbit remains tense. Technique: Grasp the upper lid laterally with toothed forceps, distract it away and superiorly to tension the superior crus, then cut it — staying directed away from the globe. > ⚠️ The superior region carries the lacrimal gland, lacrimal artery, and levator aponeurosis — this is why the superior crus is

nodes.title: Disposition & Aftercare
nodes.summary: Ophtho parallel (not before), CT after, lid repair deferred, admit for serial exams. Adjuncts don't replace decompression.
nodes.body: The eye is decompressed. Now coordinate definitive care — but the ophthalmology consult runs parallel to, never before, the procedure.
nodes.recommendation: Disposition: • Emergent ophthalmology / oculoplastics consult (EM success rates are comparable to ophthalmology — do not wait for them to perform it) • CT orbit AFTER decompression to characterize fractures and associated injury — never a r

nodes.title: Le Fort Fracture — Overview
nodes.summary: Le Fort fractures: airway and hemorrhage are the immediate threats — secure airway first
nodes.body: Le Fort Steps Summary Definition: Midface fractures involving separation of maxilla from skull base. [1][2] Key Anatomical Rule: ⚠️ ALL Le Fort fractures require disruption of the pterygoid plates. If pterygoids are intact, it is NOT a Le Fort fracture. Mechanism: High-energy blunt trauma to midface: • Motor vehicle collisions (most common) • Assault/interpersonal violence • Falls from height • Sp

nodes.title: Physical Examination Technique
nodes.summary: Exam: midface mobility test — grasp anterior maxilla and check for movement at each level
nodes.body: Mobility Testing: [1][2] Place fingers on nasal bridge while mobilizing maxillary central incisors with other hand: | Finding | Fracture Type | |---------|---------------| | Only maxilla moves | Le Fort I | | Maxilla + nose move together | Le Fort II | | Entire midface + zygoma move | Le Fort III | Memory Aid: • Le Fort I = "Speak no evil" (involves mouth) • Le Fort II = "See no evil" (involves or

nodes.title: Le Fort Type
nodes.summary: Classify Le Fort level: I (floating palate), II (pyramidal), III (craniofacial disjunction)
nodes.body: Select the fracture pattern identified: IMAGE: Le Fort Types Comparison

nodes.title: Le Fort I — Horizontal Fracture
nodes.summary: Le Fort I: transverse maxillary fracture — floating palate, mobile alveolar ridge
nodes.body: Also called: Guerin Fracture, Floating Palate [1][2] Fracture Line: Transverse through maxilla above tooth roots, crossing: • Lateral nasal walls • Inferior maxillary sinus walls • Pterygoid plates Unique Identifier: Fracture of anterolateral margin of nasal fossa Clinical Signs: • Swollen upper lip • Anterior open bite malocclusion • Ecchymosis of maxillary buccal vestibule and palate • Mobile de

nodes.title: Le Fort II — Pyramidal Fracture
nodes.summary: Le Fort II: pyramidal fracture through nasal bridge and orbital floor — CSF leak risk
nodes.body: Also called: Pyramidal Fracture [1][2][3] Fracture Line: Pyramid-shaped with base at teeth, apex at nasofrontal suture: • Nasal bones • Medial orbital walls • Orbital floor • Infraorbital rims • Lateral maxillary walls • Pterygoid plates Unique Identifier: Fracture of inferior orbital rim Clinical Signs: • Significant facial deformity and swelling • Bilateral periorbital edema and ecchymosis ("rac

nodes.title: Le Fort III — Craniofacial Disjunction
nodes.summary: Le Fort III: craniofacial disjunction — entire face separates from skull, highest CSF leak risk
nodes.body: Also called: Floating Face [1][2][3] Fracture Line: Transverse through: • Nasofrontal suture • Medial and lateral orbital walls • Zygomaticofrontal suture • Zygomatic arches • Pterygoid plates Unique Identifier: Zygomatic arch fracture Clinical Signs: • Complete craniofacial disjunction • "Dish-face deformity" — facial elongation and flattening • Bilateral periorbital edema and severe ecchymosis •

nodes.title: Mixed Le Fort Patterns
nodes.summary: Mixed patterns common — different Le Fort levels on each side, complicating surgical planning
nodes.body: Mixed patterns occur in 56.5% of cases [1] Patients often have: • Different Le Fort levels on each side • Combinations of fracture types • Asymmetric involvement Management Principle: Treat to the HIGHEST level present. Example: Le Fort II on left + Le Fort III on right → Manage as Le Fort III CT with 3D reconstruction is essential for accurate classification and surgical planning.

nodes.title: Airway Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess airway: blood, edema, displaced fragments can rapidly obstruct — plan for difficult airway
nodes.body: Mechanisms of Airway Compromise: [4][5] • Posterior-inferior displacement of fractured midface into oropharynx • Hemorrhage flooding upper airway • Soft tissue edema (may be delayed) • Foreign bodies (teeth, bone fragments, blood, vomitus) Airway Statistics: [4] • 80% secured by oro/nasotracheal intubation • 8% require urgent cricothyrotomy • 6% require tracheostomy • Le Fort III: 43.5% eventually

nodes.title: Airway Management — Approach
nodes.summary: Oral intubation preferred — do NOT nasally intubate Le Fort II/III (cribriform plate disruption risk)
nodes.body: ⚠️ CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION: NEVER nasally intubate or place NG tube in suspected Le Fort II/III — risk of intracranial passage through fractured cribriform plate. [4][5] Preferred Approaches: [4] 1. Video laryngoscopy with copious suction — first-line in most cases 2. Awake intubation with ketamine — for anticipated difficult airway 3. Retromolar intubation — useful alternative when standard rou

nodes.title: Intubation Technique
nodes.summary: If oral intubation fails: surgical airway — avoid nasotracheal, avoid blind nasal passage in all Le Forts
nodes.body: Positioning: [4][5] • Maintain C-spine precautions (inline stabilization) • Slight reverse Trendelenburg if possible (reduces bleeding) • Suction IMMEDIATELY available Technique: 1. Preoxygenation — maximize before attempt 2. Video laryngoscopy with large-bore suction 3. Have assistant apply manual reduction of midface if needed 4. Limit to 1-2 attempts before surgical airway Double Setup: ✓ Crico

nodes.title: Hemorrhage Assessment
nodes.summary: Massive midface hemorrhage common — posterior nasal packing, Foley balloon, prepare for intervention
nodes.body: Bleeding Risk by Type: [3][6] Le Fort II and III have higher hemorrhage risk than other facial injuries. Common Sources: • Internal maxillary artery • Sphenopalatine artery branches • Can be life-threatening and obscure airway Is there significant hemorrhage?

nodes.title: Hemorrhage Control — Stepwise
nodes.summary: Anterior + posterior nasal packing — Foley catheter inflated in nasopharynx for posterior bleeding
nodes.body: Stepwise Approach: [6][7] 1. Direct Pressure & Hemostatic Sutures • Control lacerations • Pack oral cavity if needed 2. Anterior Nasal Packing • Gauze soaked in 1:10,000 epinephrine • Commercial devices (Rapid Rhino, Merocel) • Can leave up to 48 hours 3. Posterior Nasal Packing / Balloon Tamponade • Foley catheter: Insert through nose, inflate balloon (10-15 mL) in nasopharynx, apply anterior tra

nodes.title: Refractory Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Refractory hemorrhage: interventional radiology for embolization — call early, do not wait
nodes.body: If Packing Fails: [6][7] Interventional Radiology Embolization: • Superselective embolization of maxillary artery branches • ~90% success rate • Less invasive than open ligation • Complications: Monocular blindness, stroke (rare but serious ~2%) Surgical Ligation: • Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation: >85% success • Lower complication risk than embolization • Requires OR, general anesthesia

nodes.title: CSF Leak Assessment
nodes.summary: Test for CSF leak: halo sign on gauze, beta-2 transferrin — do NOT pack nose if CSF rhinorrhea
nodes.body: CSF Rhinorrhea/Otorrhea: [2][3] Indicates skull base/cribriform plate fracture. Detection: • Halo test: Clear fluid diffusing around blood drop on filter paper • ⚠️ Nonspecific — mucus and tears can also create halos • Confirmatory: Beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein in fluid Associated with: • 40.7% have concurrent skull fracture • Highest leak rate in Le Fort III Management if CSF Leak: •

nodes.title: C-Spine & Associated Injuries
nodes.summary: C-spine injury in 10% of midface fractures — immobilize until cleared
nodes.body: C-Spine Injury: [3] • Incidence: 1.4-5.4% have cervical spine injuries • C5-C7 commonly involved • Maintain inline stabilization until cleared • Le Fort III has highest association with C-spine injury Associated Injuries: [3] | Injury | Incidence | |--------|-----------|| | Skull fracture | 40.7% | | Traumatic brain injury | 5.4-10% | | Cervical spine injury | 1.4-5.4% | | Ocular injury | 24-28% |

nodes.title: Imaging Protocol
nodes.summary: CT face with 3D reconstruction — defines fracture pattern for surgical planning
nodes.body: CT Face (Gold Standard): [2][8] • Fine-cut CT (2-3mm slices) • Axial, coronal, and sagittal planes • Both bone and soft tissue windows Key Findings to Identify: • Pterygoid plate fractures (mandatory for diagnosis) • Anterolateral nasal fossa (Le Fort I) • Inferior orbital rim (Le Fort II) • Zygomatic arch (Le Fort III) 3D Reconstruction: • Best method for classifying Le Fort fractures • Essential

nodes.title: Ocular Assessment
nodes.summary: Ophthalmology consult for orbital floor involvement — check VA, pupil reactivity, EOM
nodes.body: Ocular Injury: [3] • Present in 24-28% of facial fractures • Higher risk with Le Fort II and III (orbital involvement) Examine For: • Pupil irregularity • Hyphema • Restricted extraocular movements • Proptosis vs enophthalmos • Visual acuity changes • Afferent pupillary defect Orbital Compartment Syndrome: ⚠️ EMERGENCY — Requires emergent lateral canthotomy if: • Tense globe with proptosis • Decre

nodes.title: Antibiotics
nodes.summary: Antibiotics if CSF leak or open fracture — avoid nasal instrumentation with CSF rhinorrhea
nodes.body: Indications: [9] • Fractures communicating with sinuses or oral cavity (most Le Fort fractures) • CSF leak • Open wounds Regimen: • No evidence supports continuation beyond 24 hours post-operatively • Consider patient risk factors (elderly, diabetic, immunocompromised, smoker) Typical Choices: Ampicillin-sulbactam (Unasyn) • 3g IV q6h OR if penicillin allergic: Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole • Ceftri

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit all Le Fort fractures — OR for reduction and fixation, monitor for complications
nodes.body: Most Le Fort fractures require admission. [3][9] ICU Admission Indications: • Airway compromise or high risk of deterioration • Intubated patient • Active hemorrhage requiring ongoing management • Significant TBI • Hemodynamic instability • CSF leak with skull base fracture Floor Admission: • Stable Le Fort I or II without airway concerns • No active bleeding • No significant associated injuries •

nodes.title: Specialty Consults
nodes.summary: OMFS or plastic surgery for fixation, ENT for nasal packing, ophthalmology for orbital involvement
nodes.body: Required Consults: | Specialty | When | |-----------|------| | OMFS / Facial Trauma Surgery | All Le Fort fractures | | Neurosurgery | CSF leak, skull base fracture, intracranial hemorrhage | | Ophthalmology | Orbital involvement, visual complaints, periocular injury | | Trauma Surgery | Polytrauma, associated injuries | | ENT | Complex nasal/sinus involvement | | Interventional Radiology | Refrac

nodes.title: Le Fort Fracture — Summary
nodes.summary: Priorities: secure airway (no nasal), control hemorrhage, check for CSF leak, admit for OR repair
nodes.body: Key Takeaways: ✓ All Le Fort fractures involve pterygoid plates ✓ NEVER nasally intubate Le Fort II/III ✓ Double setup: Cric kit OPEN when intubating ✓ C-spine injury until proven otherwise ✓ 40.7% have associated skull fractures ✓ Le Fort II has increased mortality ✓ OMFS consult for all Le Fort fractures ✓ Surgery typically 7-14 days post-injury Disposition: • Most require admission • ICU if air
nodes.recommendation: Admit for observation. OMFS consult. CT face with 3D reconstruction. CT head and C-spine. Ophthalmology if orbital involvement.

nodes.title: Lithium Toxicity
nodes.summary: Hold lithium, classify exposure type, check neuro/renal/ECG, and do not rely on one level.
nodes.body: Core ED problem: lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, no antidote, renal clearance, delayed CNS distribution, and poor correlation between a single serum number and clinical severity. First 60 seconds: - Airway/mental status/seizure check - ECG and monitor - Hold lithium immediately - Ask: acute ingestion, acute-on-chronic, or chronic accumulation? - Check renal function, sodium/volume status,

nodes.title: Sick Lithium Patient: Resus First
nodes.summary: Airway, benzos for seizures, stop lithium, fluids if hypovolemic, tox/nephrology, dialysis screen.
nodes.body: If coma, seizure, severe encephalopathy, unstable vitals, or dysrhythmia: 1. Airway and aspiration protection as needed. 2. Benzodiazepines for seizures/agitation; avoid antipsychotic reflex dosing when lithium neurotoxicity/NMS/serotonin syndrome is in the differential. 3. ECG/monitor, IV access, glucose, temperature. 4. Stop lithium and interacting meds. 5. Start isotonic crystalloid if hypovole

nodes.title: Classify the Exposure
nodes.summary: Acute number can overstate early severity; chronic/acute-on-chronic neurologic toxicity is more dangerous.
nodes.body: Exposure type changes risk interpretation. | Pattern | What it means | Practical risk | |---|---|---| | Acute lithium-naive overdose | Big ingestion but little tissue distribution early | GI symptoms early; initial levels may look scary before CNS toxicity appears | | Acute-on-chronic | Overdose in patient already taking lithium | Higher tissue burden; neurologic risk greater | | Chronic accumulat

nodes.title: Acute Lithium Ingestion
nodes.summary: Acute ingestion causes early GI symptoms; CNS toxicity and levels may be delayed, especially sustained-release.
nodes.body: Typical early phenotype: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, tremor. Neurologic toxicity can be delayed because lithium distributes into CNS/tissues over time. Immediate questions: - Immediate-release vs sustained/extended-release? - Number of tablets and mg per tablet? - Time since ingestion? - Co-ingestants, especially sedatives, antipsychotics, serotonergics, APAP/ASA? - Is the patient

nodes.title: Chronic / Acute-on-Chronic Toxicity
nodes.summary: Chronic toxicity is clearance failure: dehydration/AKI/interacting meds; neuro findings matter more than level.
nodes.body: This is the high-risk ED pattern. Chronic toxicity often occurs because lithium clearance falls, not because the patient took a huge dose. Common triggers: - Vomiting/diarrhea, febrile illness, poor PO intake, heat exposure - AKI/CKD, heart failure, older age - Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from lithium -> dehydration -> more lithium retention - New or increased NSAID, ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazid

nodes.title: Initial ED Workup
nodes.summary: Lithium level, renal/electrolytes, ECG, co-ingestants when intentional, serial q4-6h, monitor urine output.
nodes.body: Order immediately: - Serum lithium level now, then serial q4-6 h until clearly falling - BMP/CMP: Na, K, HCO3, BUN/Cr, glucose, calcium - Magnesium/phosphate if severe symptoms or renal disease - ECG and continuous monitor if symptomatic/high level - Pregnancy test when relevant - APAP, salicylate, ethanol, VBG/ABG/lactate/osmolality for deliberate self-harm or unclear ingestion - Urine output tra

nodes.title: Lithium Level Interpretation
nodes.summary: Levels guide risk but exposure pattern, renal function, neuro exam, and serial trend drive decisions.
nodes.body: Use levels as risk anchors, not stand-alone disposition. Approximate serum categories: | Level | Common label | Caveat | |---|---|---| | <=1.0-1.2 mEq/L | Therapeutic range | Toxicity still possible in sensitive/chronic patients | | 1.5-2.5 mEq/L | Mild toxicity | Nausea, vomiting, tremor, fatigue; chronic patients may be worse | | 2.5-3.5 mEq/L | Moderate toxicity | Confusion, ataxia, hyperreflex

nodes.title: Precipitants & Interacting Meds
nodes.summary: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, thiazides/diuretics, dehydration, low sodium, AKI/NDI are the usual setup.
nodes.body: Stop or hold contributors when safe: | Trigger | Why it matters | |---|---| | NSAIDs | Lower renal lithium clearance; ibuprofen/naproxen/indomethacin common | | ACE inhibitors / ARBs | Reduce GFR and lithium clearance; toxicity often after initiation/dose change | | Thiazides | Sodium loss -> proximal lithium reabsorption; classic high-risk interaction | | Loop diuretics / spironolactone | Volume/

nodes.title: Clinical Presentations
nodes.summary: GI early acute; neuro/renal/cardiac findings drive severity, especially chronic toxicity.
nodes.body: GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain; prominent early in acute overdose. Neurologic: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, fasciculations, confusion, delirium, seizures, coma. Renal/fluid: AKI, polyuria/polydipsia, nephrogenic DI, hypernatremia if free-water loss exceeds intake. Cardiac: T-wave flattening/inversion, QT prolongation, bradycardia, AV block

nodes.title: GI Decontamination Decision
nodes.summary: No charcoal for lithium; WBI only selected large acute/ER ingestions with safe airway.
nodes.body: There is no lithium antidote and charcoal does not bind lithium. Decontamination is only useful for selected acute ingestions before absorption is complete. Choose the best fit:

nodes.title: Whole-Bowel Irrigation
nodes.summary: WBI for selected large acute/ER ingestions only; avoid in airway risk, ileus, obstruction, shock.
nodes.body: Consider WBI when: - Large acute ingestion, especially sustained/extended-release lithium - Presentation early enough that tablets may still be in GI tract - Patient is alert/cooperative OR airway is protected - No ileus, obstruction, perforation, uncontrolled vomiting, shock, or hemodynamic instability Typical approach: polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution PO/NG at high-volume adult rates unt

nodes.title: Activated Charcoal Pitfall
nodes.summary: Charcoal is for co-ingestants only; it is not lithium therapy.
nodes.body: Activated charcoal does not meaningfully bind lithium. Use charcoal only if: - A clinically important co-ingestant is suspected - Timing is appropriate for that co-ingestant - Airway/mental status is safe or protected Do not let charcoal delay: serial lithium levels, IV fluids when volume depleted, poison center call, nephrology call, or dialysis evaluation.

nodes.title: IV Fluids: Sodium + Euvolemia
nodes.summary: Hold lithium, give isotonic fluids for volume/sodium depletion, avoid forced diuresis and diuretics.
nodes.body: Primary non-dialysis treatment: stop lithium and restore intravascular volume/sodium. Default: isotonic crystalloid for dehydration, vomiting/diarrhea, AKI from volume depletion, or chronic toxicity with sodium depletion. Goals: - Euvolemia and eunatremia - Adequate urine output without forced diuresis - Improve renal lithium clearance - Avoid iatrogenic volume overload Avoid: forced diuresis, rou

nodes.title: Electrolytes, NDI, and Urine Output
nodes.summary: Track sodium, renal function, and urine output; NDI/hypernatremia changes fluid strategy.
nodes.body: Lithium renal toxicity matters during the ED stay. Monitor: - Sodium: hypernatremia suggests water loss/NDI or inadequate free water access - Creatinine/eGFR and urine output - Potassium/magnesium/calcium if vomiting, WBI, arrhythmia, or renal disease - Volume status frequently Nephrogenic DI pattern: polyuria, polydipsia, hypernatremia, dehydration. If present, fluid choice and rate require close

nodes.title: Seizures, Agitation, Hyperthermia
nodes.summary: Benzodiazepines for seizures/agitation; cool hyperthermia and reassess for overlapping toxidromes.
nodes.body: Treat complications aggressively: - Seizures: benzodiazepines first-line; treat persistent seizures per status epilepticus pathway. - Severe agitation: benzodiazepine-forward approach while evaluating tox differential. - Hyperthermia: active cooling and search for serotonin syndrome/NMS/sepsis; lithium toxicity alone can coexist with these. - Rhabdomyolysis: CK/renal protection if prolonged seizur

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Screen
nodes.summary: Dialysis screen: severe neuro/cardiac, renal impairment + >4, >5, confusion, or delayed clearance.
nodes.body: Call toxicology/poison center + nephrology early if any dialysis trigger is possible. EXTRIP separates dialysis into recommended vs suggested indications. Clinical toxicity and kidney function matter as much as the number.

nodes.title: EXTRIP: Hemodialysis Recommended
nodes.summary: HD recommended: impaired kidney + Li >4, or decreased LOC/seizure/life-threatening dysrhythmia regardless of level.
nodes.body: Extracorporeal treatment is recommended when: 1. Kidney function is impaired AND lithium >4.0 mEq/L, OR 2. Decreased level of consciousness, seizure, or life-threatening dysrhythmia is present, regardless of lithium level. Actions: - Nephrology + toxicology now - Prepare for intermittent hemodialysis if available - Continue airway/ECG/electrolyte management - Continue serial levels; do not delay d

nodes.title: EXTRIP: Hemodialysis Suggested
nodes.summary: HD suggested: Li >5, confusion, or predicted time to <1 >36h; chronic neuro symptoms lower threshold.
nodes.body: Extracorporeal treatment is suggested when: - Lithium >5.0 mEq/L, OR - Confusion is present, OR - Expected time to lithium <1.0 mEq/L is >36 hours despite optimal management. Practical ED approach: - Discuss with toxicology/nephrology early rather than waiting for deterioration. - Chronic/acute-on-chronic patients with neurologic findings deserve lower threshold for dialysis discussion. - Very hig

nodes.title: Dialysis Modality + Rebound
nodes.summary: Intermittent HD preferred; monitor at least 12h after stopping for rebound and repeat HD if needed.
nodes.body: Preferred modality: intermittent hemodialysis for rapid lithium removal. CRRT is acceptable if intermittent HD is unavailable or not tolerated. Stopping target: continue until lithium <1.0 mEq/L OR clinical improvement is apparent. If lithium level cannot be rapidly measured, EXTRIP recommends at least 6 hours of ECTR. Rebound is expected: lithium redistributes from tissues back into serum after d

nodes.title: No Dialysis Trigger: Monitoring Plan
nodes.summary: Hold lithium, hydrate if needed, q4-6h levels/renal checks, frequent neuro exams, escalate if trend worsens.
nodes.body: If dialysis is not indicated now: - Hold lithium and interacting meds - Continue isotonic fluids if volume depleted - Repeat lithium q4-6 h until clearly falling - Repeat renal function/electrolytes with levels - Continue ECG/monitor if symptomatic, high level, renal disease, or ECG abnormality - Reassess neuro exam frequently: gait/ataxia, tremor, dysarthria, confusion, myoclonus, hyperreflexia E

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Mimics: stroke, sepsis, glucose/sodium, serotonin syndrome, NMS, sedatives, anticholinergic, withdrawal.
nodes.body: Lithium toxicity mimics and overlaps with common ED diagnoses. | Finding | Do not miss | |---|---| | Tremor/ataxia/dysarthria | Cerebellar stroke, alcohol/benzo intoxication or withdrawal, anticonvulsant toxicity | | Confusion/delirium | Sepsis, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia/hypernatremia, uremia, anticholinergic/sedative tox | | Hyperreflexia/myoclonus/hyperthermia | Serotonin syndrome, NMS, maligna

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: CKD/CHF/older adults, pregnancy, breastfeeding, NDI/hypernatremia, and intentional overdose need tailored disposition.
nodes.body: Older adults / CKD / CHF: lower renal reserve, higher risk from both toxicity and aggressive fluids. Involve nephrology early; avoid reflex large-volume fluids if overloaded. Pregnancy: maternal stabilization first. Lithium crosses placenta; coordinate OB, psychiatry, toxicology, and nephrology. Do not delay indicated dialysis for pregnancy alone. Breastfeeding: lithium is excreted in breast milk;

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition by symptoms, renal function, serial trend, HD criteria, and suicide risk.
nodes.body: Most symptomatic lithium toxicity is not an ED discharge. Disposition depends on symptoms, exposure pattern, renal function, serial level trend, dialysis need, and psychiatric safety.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge only if asymptomatic, falling level, renal stable, no delayed absorption or suicide concern, follow-up arranged.
nodes.body: Consider discharge only when ALL are true: - No symptoms and normal/reliable mental status/gait - No intentional self-harm or psychiatric hold need - Lithium level is falling on serial checks and generally <1.5 mEq/L - Renal function stable and patient can maintain hydration - No sustained-release delayed absorption concern - No interacting medication problem that cannot be fixed - Clear plan to h
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after asymptomatic status, falling level, stable renal function, and safe psych/medication follow-up.

nodes.title: Admit / Monitored Bed
nodes.summary: Admit if symptomatic, chronic, renal/electrolyte abnormality, rising levels, WBI, ECG issue, or intentional overdose.
nodes.body: Admit for: - Any neurologic symptoms, even with modest level - Chronic or acute-on-chronic toxicity - AKI/CKD, dehydration needing IV therapy, sodium abnormality/NDI - Rising/plateauing lithium levels or sustained-release ingestion - Need for WBI or prolonged serial levels - ECG abnormality, bradycardia, QT prolongation, AV block - Co-ingestants or intentional overdose - Unsafe outpatient medicati
nodes.recommendation: Admit symptomatic, chronic/acute-on-chronic, renal/electrolyte, rising-level, WBI, ECG, co-ingestant, or unsafe follow-up cases.

nodes.title: ICU / Dialysis-Capable Setting
nodes.summary: ICU for severe neuro/cardiac toxicity, HD criteria, unstable physiology, poor clearance, or airway risk.
nodes.body: ICU or dialysis-capable transfer for: - Seizure, coma, severe confusion, severe myoclonus/hyperreflexia - Life-threatening dysrhythmia, unstable bradycardia/AV block, shock - EXTRIP recommended or suggested dialysis criteria - Worsening renal failure or inability to clear lithium - Severe hypernatremia/NDI, pulmonary edema, or fluid strategy conflict - Need for airway protection, CRRT/HD, or repea
nodes.recommendation: ICU/dialysis setting for severe neuro/cardiac toxicity, dialysis criteria, unstable physiology, or poor clearance.

nodes.title: Restart & Prevention Plan
nodes.summary: Restart only after trigger fixed, renal/sodium stable, prescriber plan, and follow-up lithium level arranged.
nodes.body: Do not reflexively restart lithium from the ED. Coordinate with psychiatry/primary prescriber and nephrology when renal injury occurred. Before restart: - Toxicity resolved and lithium level safe/falling - Renal function and sodium stable - Trigger corrected: dehydration/illness, NSAID, ACEi/ARB, thiazide/diuretic, low sodium, dosing error - Follow-up level plan documented Patient instructions: -

nodes.title: Low Back Pain — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: 2.6M ED visits/yr; routine imaging increases costs without improving outcomes — screen for red flags first
nodes.body: Red Flag Checklist The Problem: Low back pain accounts for 2.6M ED visits/year in the US. Most cases are benign musculoskeletal strain. Imaging is often unnecessary and can lead to overtreatment. [1][2] High-Value Approach: Screen for red flags → targeted exam → image only when indicated → conservative treatment. [2][14] Key Concept: Routine imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI) for uncomplicated LBP increases

nodes.title: Traumatic LBP — Fracture Risk
nodes.summary: High-risk: fall >3ft, MVC, age >65, steroids, osteoporosis, midline tenderness
nodes.body: Assess fracture risk factors: [13][22][23] High-risk mechanisms: • Fall from height (>3 feet or >5 stairs) • Motor vehicle collision (ejection, rollover, >40 mph) • Direct blow to spine • Axial loading (diving, compression) Patient factors: • Age >65 (osteoporosis risk) • Known osteoporosis • Chronic steroid use (>3 months) • History of spinal cancer or metastases Physical exam findings: • Midline

nodes.title: Red Flag Screening
nodes.summary: CES: urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness; Infection: fever + IVDU/immunocompromised; Malignancy: cancer hx, weight loss
nodes.body: Red Flag Checklist Screen for emergent conditions: [13][14] CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME (CES): • Urinary retention or incontinence • Fecal incontinence • Saddle anesthesia • Bilateral leg weakness/numbness • Progressive neurologic deficit INFECTION (Epidural Abscess/Osteomyelitis): • Fever + back pain • IVDU • Recent spinal procedure (injection, surgery) • Immunosuppression (HIV, diabetes, steroids, che

nodes.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
nodes.summary: Urinary retention + saddle anesthesia + bilateral weakness — emergent MRI and neurosurgery consult within 48hr
nodes.body: EMERGENT — Time-critical diagnosis. [6][7] Classic Triad: 1. Urinary retention (most common — post-void residual >200 mL) 2. Saddle anesthesia (perineal numbness) 3. Bilateral leg weakness or numbness Other features: • Fecal incontinence or decreased anal tone • Sexual dysfunction • Progressive bilateral radiculopathy Exam: • Rectal tone — decreased or absent • Perianal sensation — test light touc

nodes.title: Spinal Infection
nodes.summary: IVDU + fever + back pain — ESR/CRP, blood cultures, MRI with contrast; vanc + CTX empirically
nodes.body: Epidural Abscess / Vertebral Osteomyelitis — High mortality if missed. [8][15] Risk Factors: • IVDU (most common risk factor) • Recent spinal injection or surgery • Immunosuppression (diabetes, HIV, steroids, chemo) • Bacteremia / endocarditis • Indwelling catheter / recent hospitalization Clinical Features: • Fever + localized back pain (may be subtle in immunocompromised) • Point tenderness over

nodes.title: Malignancy / Metastatic Disease
nodes.summary: Cancer history + weight loss + night pain — MRI with contrast, dexamethasone 10mg if cord compression
nodes.body: Spinal metastases or primary malignancy. [9][13] High-Risk Features: • History of cancer (especially breast, lung, prostate, kidney, thyroid, myeloma) • Unexplained weight loss >10 lbs / 4.5 kg • Age >50 with new, severe back pain • Pain worse at night or with rest • Failure to improve with conservative treatment Physical Exam: • Point tenderness over vertebral body • Neurologic deficit (suggests

nodes.title: Neurologic Examination
nodes.summary: SLR positive <60° = L5/S1 disc; test L4 (knee ext), L5 (great toe), S1 (ankle PF); reflexes patellar/Achilles
nodes.body: Dermatome Map Focused neuro exam for radiculopathy: [10][14] Motor (grade 0-5): • L4 — Knee extension (quadriceps) • L5 — Great toe dorsiflexion (EHL), ankle dorsiflexion • S1 — Ankle plantarflexion, toe walking Sensory: • L4 — Medial leg/ankle • L5 — Dorsum of foot, first web space • S1 — Lateral foot, small toe Reflexes: • L4 — Patellar reflex • S1 — Achilles reflex Provocative tests: • Straight

nodes.title: Lumbar Radiculopathy
nodes.summary: L5/S1 most common; 90% improve in 6-12 weeks — no imaging in first 6 weeks unless red flags or progressive deficit
nodes.body: Radicular pain from nerve root compression. [3][10][11] Most common levels: • L5 (45%) — weakness of great toe/ankle dorsiflexion, numbness dorsum of foot • S1 (45%) — weakness of plantarflexion/toe walking, numbness lateral foot, decreased Achilles reflex • L4 (5%) — weakness of knee extension, numbness medial leg, decreased patellar reflex Natural history: • 90% improve within 6-12 weeks with co

nodes.title: Mechanical / Musculoskeletal LBP
