nodes.summary: Benign, self-limited — no imaging needed; most resolve in 2-4 weeks; activity better than bed rest
nodes.body: Benign, self-limited condition. [2][3] Characteristics: • Worse with activity, better with rest • Paraspinal muscle tenderness • No neurologic deficit • No red flags • Often related to lifting, bending, poor posture Differential: • Muscular strain (most common) • Facet joint arthropathy • Degenerative disc disease • Lumbar spondylosis Key Message for Patients: • This is NOT a serious condition • I

nodes.title: Emergent Imaging
nodes.summary: Emergent MRI for CES, cord compression, abscess; add contrast for infection/malignancy; dex 10mg IV if cord compression
nodes.body: MRI is the gold standard for emergent spinal imaging. [4][7] Indications for EMERGENT MRI: • Cauda equina syndrome • Spinal cord compression • Epidural abscess (fever + IVDU + back pain) • Severe/progressive neurologic deficit MRI with contrast preferred for: • Suspected infection (abscess, osteomyelitis) • Suspected malignancy MRI without contrast acceptable for: • Disc herniation • Cauda equina

nodes.title: Fracture Imaging
nodes.summary: Plain films first for most fractures; CT for high-energy, neuro deficit, or polytrauma; MRI if cord concern
nodes.body: Plain films vs CT for suspected fracture. [22][23] Start with plain films (AP + lateral): • Adequate for most compression fractures • Quick, low radiation, low cost • Sensitivity ~85% for acute fractures CT spine indicated for: • High-energy mechanism (fall >10 ft, MVC, axial load) • Neurologic deficit • Plain films suspicious but inconclusive • Known malignancy (better for lytic lesions) • Polytr

nodes.title: When NOT to Image
nodes.summary: No imaging for uncomplicated LBP <6 weeks — radiation exposure, incidentals, no outcome benefit
nodes.body: ACEP Choosing Wisely / ACR Guidelines: [2][4] DO NOT image uncomplicated LBP: • No red flags • No neurologic deficit • Duration <6 weeks • Non-traumatic Why avoid unnecessary imaging? Harms: • Radiation exposure — lumbar CT = 6 mSv (equivalent to 3 years background radiation) • Incidental findings — lead to more tests, anxiety, unnecessary surgery • Overdiagnosis — "degenerative changes" on MRI ar

nodes.title: Conservative Treatment
nodes.summary: NSAIDs first-line (most effective); acetaminophen adjunct; avoid opioids; stay active — bed rest harmful
nodes.body: Medication Guide First-line medications: [3][11][12] NSAIDs (most effective) • Ibuprofen 400-600 mg PO q6-8h • Naproxen 500 mg PO BID • Ketorolac 10 mg PO q4-6h (short-term) • *Caution: GI bleed, renal impairment, cardiac disease* Acetaminophen (adjunct) • 650-1000 mg PO q6h (max 3g/day) • *Less effective than NSAIDs for LBP* Muscle relaxants (second-line) • Cyclobenzaprine 5-10 mg PO TID × 7-10 d

nodes.title: Discharge — Uncomplicated LBP
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions Discharge with: • NSAIDs ± acetaminophen • Muscle relaxant if significant spasm (short course) • Activity modification (avoid heavy lifting, not bed rest) • Return precautions reviewed Follow-up: • PCP in 2-4 weeks if not improving • Physical therapy referral if symptoms >2-4 weeks • No imaging needed unless red flags develop Return precautions — tell patient to return if: •
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with NSAIDs, return precautions for red flags. Follow-up PCP in 2-4 weeks if not improving. No imaging needed.

nodes.title: Admission — Emergent Pathology
nodes.body: Admission criteria: [7][15] ICU/close monitoring: • Hemodynamically unstable with spinal pathology • Sepsis from spinal infection Floor admission: • Cauda equina syndrome (awaiting surgery) • Epidural abscess (IV antibiotics, surgical planning) • Spinal cord compression from malignancy (steroids, XRT planning) • Unstable spine fracture Services to consult: • Neurosurgery — CES, epidural abscess, u
nodes.recommendation: Admit for emergent spinal pathology. Consult neurosurgery for CES (decompression within 48hr). IV antibiotics for infection.

nodes.title: Fracture Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition depends on fracture stability: [22][23] Stable compression fracture (most common): • May discharge with pain control • Spine surgery or orthopedic follow-up in 1-2 weeks • TLSO brace if prescribed • Osteoporosis workup (DXA, vitamin D, calcium) • Return if neurologic symptoms develop Unstable fracture or neurologic deficit: • Admit to spine service • Strict spinal precautions • Neurosu
nodes.recommendation: Stable compression fracture may discharge with spine follow-up. Unstable fracture or neurologic deficit requires admission.

nodes.title: Lower GI Bleed — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess hemodynamics first; shock index >1 = significant bleed; 15% of apparent LGIB is brisk UGIB
nodes.body: LGIB Steps Summary Lower GI bleeding originates distal to the ligament of Treitz. Presents as hematochezia (bright red blood per rectum), maroon stool, or melena (if slow transit). First priority: Assess hemodynamic status. • HR, BP, orthostatic vitals • Shock Index (HR/SBP) — >1.0 suggests significant bleeding • Mental status, skin perfusion • Signs of hypovolemic shock CRITICAL: Up to 15% of app

nodes.title: Hemodynamically Unstable LGIB
nodes.summary: Large-bore IV, type & cross, consider MTP if shock index >1; rule out UGIB with NGT if unstable
nodes.body: Immediate priorities: 1. Large-bore IV access — two 18G or larger 2. Type and crossmatch — anticipate transfusion 3. Activate massive transfusion protocol if: • Shock Index >1.0 with ongoing bleeding • Estimated blood loss >30% blood volume • Lactate >4 mmol/L 4. Rule out UGIB — NGT aspirate or early EGD if: • Hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis • BUN/Cr ratio >30 • Hemodynamically unstable with u

nodes.title: Risk Stratification — Oakland Score
nodes.summary: Oakland Score ≤8 = 95% safe discharge probability; >8 = admit for monitoring/intervention
nodes.body: Oakland Score Calculator Oakland Score predicts safe discharge in LGIB. Components: • Age (0-2 pts) • Sex (0-1 pts) • Previous LGIB admission (0-1 pts) • DRE findings (0-2 pts) • Heart rate (0-3 pts) • Systolic BP (0-5 pts) • Hemoglobin (0-22 pts) Interpretation: • Score ≤8: 95% probability of safe discharge — consider outpatient management • Score >8: Recommend admission for monitoring/interventi

nodes.title: Oakland Score Result
nodes.summary: ≤8 = low risk (outpatient); 9-16 = intermediate (individualize); >16 = high risk (admit)
nodes.body: What is the patient's Oakland Score?

nodes.title: Low-Risk LGIB (Oakland ≤8)
nodes.summary: Oakland ≤8 = outpatient colonoscopy within 7-14 days; ensure stable, no high-risk features
nodes.body: Safe for outpatient management in most cases. Criteria for discharge: • Hemodynamically stable throughout observation • No significant drop in hemoglobin • Bleeding has stopped or minimal • Able to tolerate oral intake • Reliable follow-up available • No high-risk features (anticoagulation, malignancy, cirrhosis) Discharge plan: • GI follow-up for outpatient colonoscopy within 7-14 days • Clear li

nodes.title: Intermediate-Risk LGIB
nodes.summary: Individualize Oakland 9-16: admit if ongoing bleeding, anticoagulation, comorbidities; discharge if stable + f/u
nodes.body: Oakland Score 9-16 — individualize disposition. Factors favoring admission: • Ongoing bleeding • Anticoagulation use • Comorbidities (cardiac, renal, hepatic) • Poor social support or unreliable follow-up • Anemia requiring transfusion Factors favoring observation/discharge: • Bleeding stopped • Hemoglobin stable • Young, otherwise healthy • Excellent follow-up

nodes.title: High-Risk LGIB
nodes.summary: Oakland >16: NPO, telemetry, serial Hgb, GI consult; reverse anticoagulation if present
nodes.body: Oakland Score >16 or high-risk features — admit for monitoring and intervention. Management: • NPO for potential colonoscopy/intervention • Continuous telemetry monitoring • Serial hemoglobin q6-8h • Type and screen (crossmatch if anticipated transfusion) • GI consultation for colonoscopy timing Assess for anticoagulation reversal if applicable: • Warfarin: Vitamin K + 4-factor PCC • Dabigatran: I

nodes.title: Resuscitation & Transfusion
nodes.summary: Transfuse Hgb <7 (stable) or <8 (cardiac); MTP if shock + ongoing bleeding; do NOT give TXA (ACG recommends against)
nodes.body: Transfusion Thresholds IV Fluid Resuscitation: • Balanced crystalloid (LR preferred over NS) • Avoid over-resuscitation — may worsen bleeding • Target MAP ≥65 mmHg Transfusion Thresholds: • Hgb <7 g/dL — transfuse in stable patients • Hgb <8 g/dL — transfuse if cardiovascular disease or symptomatic • Active hemorrhage — transfuse regardless of Hgb Massive Transfusion Protocol: • Activate if shock

nodes.title: Imaging & Localization
nodes.summary: CTA for unstable/significant; colonoscopy for stable (diagnostic + therapeutic); nuclear for intermittent
nodes.body: Goal: Identify bleeding source to guide intervention. Imaging options based on hemodynamic status: CTA (CT Angiography): • First-line for hemodynamically significant bleeding • Detects bleeding rates ≥0.3-0.5 mL/min • Can localize for embolization or surgery Colonoscopy: • First-line for stable patients • Diagnostic AND therapeutic • Timing (ACG 2023): NONURGENT colonoscopy for most — urgent colon

nodes.title: CT Angiography
nodes.summary: CTA detects ≥0.3-0.5 mL/min; positive → IR embolization; negative → colonoscopy or nuclear scan
nodes.body: CTA abdomen/pelvis with arterial and venous phases. Sensitivity: 85-90% for active bleeding ≥0.3-0.5 mL/min Findings indicating active bleeding: • Contrast extravasation into bowel lumen • "Spot sign" — focus of high attenuation If CTA positive: • Localization guides IR embolization or surgical planning • Proceed to angiography with embolization if IR available If CTA negative: • Bleeding may have

nodes.title: Colonoscopy
nodes.summary: NONURGENT colonoscopy for most (ACG 2023: 24h does not beat 14d); urgent only for ongoing significant bleeding; therapeutic options include clips, injection, coagulation
nodes.body: Timing (ACG 2023): • NONURGENT colonoscopy for most hospitalized patients — urgent colonoscopy within 24h does NOT improve rebleeding, mortality, transfusion, or LOS. In stable patients, within 14 days is as effective as within 24h. • Urgent only for ongoing hemodynamically significant bleeding not controlled by resuscitation (consider CTA ± embolization first in the unstable patient) • Elective/o

nodes.title: Nuclear Medicine Scan
nodes.summary: Tagged RBC scan detects 0.1-0.4 mL/min; useful for intermittent bleeding; guides angiography if positive
nodes.body: Tagged RBC Scintigraphy: • Detects bleeding rates as low as 0.1-0.4 mL/min • More sensitive than CTA for slow/intermittent bleeding • Can be imaged up to 24h after injection Limitations: • Less anatomically precise than CTA • May localize to region but not exact site • Requires 2-phase imaging (immediate + delayed) If positive: • Guides subsequent CTA or angiography for embolization • Guides surgi

nodes.title: Intervention Decision
nodes.summary: IR embolization if CTA+/unstable; colonoscopy if stable; surgery if failed other therapies or emergent indication
nodes.body: Based on imaging and clinical status, select intervention pathway: IR Embolization: • Source identified on CTA/angiography • Ongoing bleeding despite resuscitation • Hemodynamically unstable for colonoscopy Colonoscopic Therapy: • Source identified or suspected • Hemodynamically stable • Amenable to endoscopic treatment Surgical Consultation: • Failed endoscopic/IR therapy • Hemodynamic instabilit

nodes.title: IR Embolization
nodes.summary: IR embolization 70-90% success; 5-10% bowel ischemia risk; monitor for ischemia signs post-procedure
nodes.body: Angiography with selective embolization. Technique: • Selective catheterization of mesenteric vessels • Provocative angiography if no active bleeding seen • Embolization with microcoils, particles, or gelfoam Success rate: 70-90% for acute control Complications: • Bowel ischemia (5-10%) • Access site hematoma • Rebleeding (15-25%) Post-embolization care: • Monitor for abdominal pain, fever (ischem

nodes.title: Colonoscopic Therapy
nodes.summary: Clips for vascular lesions; epi injection + thermal for combined therapy; APC for angiodysplasia; bands for hemorrhoids
nodes.body: Endoscopic hemostasis options: Hemostatic clips: • First-line for most vascular lesions • Diverticular bleeding, post-polypectomy Injection therapy: • Epinephrine 1:10,000 dilution • Temporary hemostasis — combine with clips or thermal Thermal coagulation: • Argon plasma coagulation (APC) for angiodysplasia • Bipolar coagulation for point bleeding Band ligation: • Internal hemorrhoids • Rectal var

nodes.title: Surgical Intervention
nodes.summary: Surgery if failed other therapies, massive transfusion, or surgical pathology; localize source to avoid subtotal colectomy
nodes.body: Indications for surgery: • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation • Massive transfusion requirement (>6 units in 24h) • Failed endoscopic and IR therapy • Perforation or bowel ischemia • Known surgical pathology (cancer, diverticulitis with perforation) Surgical options: • Segmental colectomy if source localized • Subtotal colectomy if source not localized (higher morbidity) Pre-operative:

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU if unstable/ongoing bleed; floor if stable but needs monitoring; discharge if low-risk with f/u
nodes.body: Final disposition based on clinical course and intervention.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU criteria: • Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors • Massive transfusion protocol activated • Ongoing active bleeding • Post-intervention monitoring (embolization, surgery) ICU orders: • Continuous telemetry • Serial Hgb q4-6h • Serial lactate • Type and crossmatch 4+ units • NPO • GI and/or surgical consultation • Consider IR on standby
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU. Continue resuscitation. Serial hemoglobin monitoring. GI/Surgery/IR consultation as needed.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor admission criteria: • Hemodynamically stable • Oakland Score >8 or high-risk features • Requires monitoring or intervention • Anemia requiring transfusion but stable Floor orders: • Telemetry monitoring • Serial Hgb q6-8h × 24h • Type and screen • NPO until colonoscopy • GI consultation for colonoscopy timing • Hold anticoagulation per GI guidance
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor. GI consultation for nonurgent colonoscopy (ACG 2023: urgent <24h does not improve outcomes). Serial hemoglobin monitoring. Address anticoagulation.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: • Oakland Score ≤8 • Hemodynamically stable • Bleeding stopped • No high-risk features • Reliable follow-up available Discharge plan: • GI follow-up for outpatient colonoscopy within 7-14 days • Clear liquid diet × 24h → advance as tolerated • Hold anticoagulation per GI guidance (if applicable) • Iron supplementation if anemic Return precautions: • Recurrent bright red blood p
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with GI follow-up for outpatient colonoscopy in 7-14 days. Provide return precautions.

nodes.title: Lumbar Puncture — Indications
nodes.summary: LP indications: suspected meningitis, SAH workup, IIH diagnosis — do NOT delay abx for LP
nodes.body: LP Quick Procedure Guide | LP Do NOT — Contraindications Lumbar puncture is a bedside procedure to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for diagnosis or to measure/reduce intracranial pressure. DIAGNOSTIC Indications: • Infectious: Bacterial/viral/TB/fungal meningitis, encephalitis, neurosyphilis • Vascular: SAH (CT-negative but high clinical suspicion) • Inflammatory: MS (oligoclonal bands), GBS (alb

nodes.title: LP Indication
nodes.summary: Determine LP indication to guide urgency, CT need, and CSF testing priorities
nodes.body: What is the primary indication for LP? This determines urgency and whether imaging is needed first.

nodes.title: Meningitis — Time-Critical Management
nodes.summary: Suspected meningitis: give antibiotics FIRST, then CT if needed, then LP — never delay abx for LP
nodes.body: BACTERIAL MENINGITIS IS A TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY ⚠️ DO NOT delay antibiotics for CT or LP Order of operations: 1. Blood cultures × 2 2. Empiric antibiotics IMMEDIATELY (within 60 minutes of presentation) 3. CT head (if indicated — see criteria) 4. LP (when safe) 5. Adjust antibiotics based on CSF results Empiric Antibiotics (adults): • Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h • PLUS Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12

nodes.title: SAH Workup — CT-Negative
nodes.summary: SAH workup: LP only if CT negative and <6h from onset (CTA may replace LP in modern practice)
nodes.body: LP for SAH when CT head is NEGATIVE but clinical suspicion remains high When is LP indicated? • Thunderclap headache (peak intensity <1 minute) • "Worst headache of life" • CT head negative or non-diagnostic • Timing: LP most useful >12 hours after headache onset (allows xanthochromia to develop) CT Sensitivity for SAH: | Time from headache | CT sensitivity | |-------------------|----------------|

nodes.title: IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri
nodes.summary: IIH: measure opening pressure in lateral decubitus — elevated if >25 cmH2O in adults
nodes.body: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) LP is both DIAGNOSTIC and THERAPEUTIC in IIH. Diagnostic Criteria (Modified Dandy): 1. Signs/symptoms of elevated ICP (headache, papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, visual obscurations) 2. No localizing neurological signs (except VI nerve palsy) 3. Normal neuroimaging (MRI preferred; venous imaging to exclude CVST) 4. Opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O (adults), ≥2

nodes.title: CT Head BEFORE LP — Who Needs It?
nodes.summary: CT before LP if: immunocompromised, CNS disease, new seizure, papilledema, focal deficit, GCS <15
nodes.body: IDSA/ACEP Criteria — CT indicated if ANY of the following: [3][8] | Criterion | Rationale | |-----------|----------| | Age >60 years | Higher risk of mass lesion | | Immunocompromised | HIV, transplant, immunosuppressive Rx, malignancy | | History of CNS disease | Prior stroke, mass, focal infection, shunt | | New-onset seizure | Within past week | | Altered mental status | GCS <15 | | Focal neuro

nodes.title: CT Before LP?
nodes.summary: No CT criteria met: proceed directly to LP — do not delay for unnecessary imaging
nodes.body: Does the patient meet ANY criteria requiring CT head before LP? CT indicated if: • Age >60 • Immunocompromised • History of CNS disease • New seizure (past week) • Altered mental status (GCS <15) • Focal neurological deficit • Papilledema

nodes.title: CT Head — Proceed with Imaging
nodes.summary: Give antibiotics BEFORE CT — CT is to rule out mass effect/herniation risk, not to diagnose meningitis
nodes.body: Order CT Head WITHOUT Contrast Look for: • Mass lesion with midline shift • Obstructive hydrocephalus • Loss of basal cisterns • Posterior fossa mass • Cerebral edema • SAH (if indicated) Absolute contraindications to LP on CT: • Significant midline shift (>5mm) • Loss of suprachiasmatic or quadrigeminal cisterns • Posterior fossa mass • Obstructive hydrocephalus If CT shows any of the above: • DO

nodes.title: Coagulation Assessment
nodes.summary: Check INR and platelets — INR >1.5 or platelets <50K are relative contraindications
nodes.body: Coagulation Thresholds for LP [9][10] | Parameter | Traditional | Evidence-Based | |-----------|------------|----------------| | Platelets | >50,000/mm³ | >40,000 safe; >20,000 per 2025 AABB | | INR | <1.5 | <1.4 per ASRA | | PTT | <40 sec | <39 sec | Key evidence: • Study of 900 LPs: PLT <50,000 did NOT show higher adverse events • Pediatric study (199 children, PLT ~20,000): NO epidural hematoma

nodes.title: Coagulation Status
nodes.summary: Determine if coagulopathy needs correction before LP vs proceeding with caution
nodes.body: Is the patient's coagulation acceptable for LP? Safe thresholds: • Platelets >40,000/mm³ • INR <1.5 • No active anticoagulation (or appropriately held) Consider reversal or delay if: • Platelets <40,000 • INR ≥1.5 • DOAC within 72 hours

nodes.title: Mild Coagulopathy — Proceed with Caution
nodes.summary: Mild coagulopathy (INR 1.5-2, plt 20-40k): proceed with smallest needle, apply pressure after
nodes.body: PLT 20,000-40,000 or INR 1.5-2.0 Risk-benefit assessment: • Spinal hematoma is rare even in this range • Suspected bacterial meningitis: benefit likely outweighs risk • Elective LP: consider correction first Risk reduction strategies: • Use smallest gauge needle practical (22-25G) • Single attempt if possible (avoid multiple passes) • Atraumatic (pencil-point) needle preferred • Avoid antiplatelet

nodes.title: Severe Coagulopathy — High Risk
nodes.summary: Severe coagulopathy: correct before LP — vit K + PCC for warfarin, platelets for thrombocytopenia, hold/reverse anticoagulants
nodes.body: PLT <20,000, INR >2.0, or Active Anticoagulation Options: 1. Correct coagulopathy first (if time allows): • Platelet transfusion (target >50,000) • Vitamin K + PCC for warfarin (FFP slower) • Idarucizumab for dabigatran • Andexanet alfa for Factor Xa inhibitors • Wait for DOAC clearance (72h+) 2. Proceed despite risk (bacterial meningitis): • Discuss with attending • Document risk-benefit discussi

nodes.title: Consent & Preparation
nodes.summary: Consent, position, and prepare equipment — atraumatic needle reduces post-LP headache by 50%
nodes.body: Informed Consent — Discuss: • Indication for procedure • Alternative options • Risks: PDPH (10-30%), back pain (35%), bleeding, infection, nerve injury, herniation (rare) • Benefits: Diagnosis and/or treatment Equipment Checklist: ☐ LP tray (commercially prepared or assembled) ☐ Sterile gloves, drapes, prep solution ☐ Spinal needle (22-25G atraumatic preferred) ☐ Local anesthetic (1% lidocaine, 25

nodes.title: Patient Positioning
nodes.summary: Lateral decubitus for opening pressure measurement; sitting for easier access in obese patients
nodes.body: Choose patient position based on clinical needs: Lateral Decubitus: ✓ REQUIRED for accurate opening pressure measurement ✓ Standard for most diagnostic LPs ✓ Patient lies on side, knees to chest, neck flexed Sitting Position: ✓ Wider interspinous spaces — higher success rate ✓ Better for obese patients ✗ CANNOT accurately measure opening pressure ✗ Opening pressure falsely elevated in sitting Pron

nodes.title: Lateral Decubitus Positioning
nodes.summary: Lateral decubitus: fetal position, line up shoulders and hips — back at edge of bed, perpendicular
nodes.body: Lateral Decubitus Position — Setup: [1][2] 1. Patient lies on side (traditionally left lateral) 2. Spine parallel to bed edge, perpendicular to floor 3. Knees drawn toward chest (fetal position) 4. Neck flexed (chin toward chest) 5. Ensure spine is NOT rotated — shoulders and hips stacked 6. Place pillow between knees for comfort 7. Assistant holds position steady For Opening Pressure Measurement:

nodes.title: Sitting Position
nodes.summary: Sitting: patient hunched forward hugging pillow — easier landmark identification but no OP measurement
nodes.body: Sitting Position — Setup: [1][2] 1. Patient sits on bed edge, feet supported on stool 2. Leans forward over bedside table with pillow 3. "Cat stretch" — arches lower back outward 4. Head flexed, chin to chest 5. Arms resting on table or pillow Advantages: • Wider interspinous spaces (gravity-assisted) • Higher first-attempt success rate • Better for obese patients (landmarks more palpable) • Patie

nodes.title: Spinal Needle Selection
nodes.summary: Use atraumatic (Sprotte/Whitacre) needle 22G — reduces PDPH from 12% to 6% vs cutting needle
nodes.body: Needle Types: [1][11] | Type | Tip | PDPH Rate | Notes | |------|-----|-----------|-------| | Quincke | Cutting/beveled | 15-30% | Tactile "dura click"; easier insertion | | Whitacre | Pencil-point (blunt) | ~4% | Atraumatic; side port; spreads fibers | | Sprotte | Pencil-point | ~4% | Atraumatic; larger side port | ⚠️ USE ATRAUMATIC (pencil-point) NEEDLES when available • Dramatically reduces PDP

nodes.title: Landmark Identification
nodes.summary: Tuffier line (iliac crests) = L4 spinous process — enter at L3-4 or L4-5 interspace
nodes.body: Surface Landmarks: [1][2] Tuffier's Line (Intercristal Line): • Line connecting superior aspects of iliac crests • Crosses spine at L4 vertebral body or L4-L5 interspace • Palpate spinous processes to confirm level ⚠️ Landmark accuracy is poor in ~30% of patients • Consider ultrasound for difficult landmarks • Obese patients: landmarks palpable in only 32% Target Interspaces: • L3-L4 (preferred) o

nodes.title: LP Approach Selection
nodes.summary: Midline approach is standard; paramedian for elderly or difficult anatomy (calcified ligaments)
nodes.body: Choose your approach: [1][2][12] MIDLINE Approach: • Standard technique • Needle through interspinous ligaments • Requires good spine flexion PARAMEDIAN Approach: • 30-40% higher first-attempt success than midline • Avoids supraspinous/interspinous ligaments • Does NOT require full spine flexion • Better for: elderly (calcified ligaments), obese, kyphosis/scoliosis, failed midline • Lower PDPH inc

nodes.title: Midline Approach — Technique
nodes.summary: Midline: anesthetize skin and subcutaneous tissue, then advance needle with stylet
nodes.body: Midline LP Step-by-Step Guide Preparation: 1. Position patient (lateral decubitus or sitting) 2. Identify landmarks, mark insertion site 3. Sterile prep — wide area with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine 4. Drape with sterile fenestrated drape 5. Don sterile gloves Local Anesthesia: 1. Raise skin wheal with 1% lidocaine using 25G needle 2. Infiltrate deeper tissues along planned needle path 3. Use

nodes.title: Midline — Needle Insertion
nodes.summary: Advance toward umbilicus with slight cephalad angle — feel pop through ligamentum flavum and dura
nodes.body: Needle Insertion: [1][2] 1. Entry point: Midway between spinous processes, at superior aspect of inferior spinous process 2. Angle: Direct needle 15 degrees cephalad (toward umbilicus) 3. Bevel orientation: Parallel to longitudinal dural fibers (Quincke) 4. Advance slowly — feel for resistance changes Tactile Feedback: • Initial increased resistance: ligaments • "Pop" or "give": Ligamentum flavum

nodes.title: Paramedian Approach — Technique
nodes.summary: Paramedian: enter 1-1.5cm lateral to midline, angle medially toward spinous process
nodes.body: Why Paramedian? [2][12] • 30-40% higher first-attempt success than midline • Avoids supraspinous and interspinous ligaments (often calcified in elderly) • Does NOT require full spine flexion • Wider interlaminar space than interspinous space • Lower PDPH incidence (oblique track creates flap-valve closure) • Less back pain post-procedure Best for: • Age >50 (calcified ligaments) • Failed midline a

nodes.title: Paramedian LP — Step-by-Step Guide
nodes.summary: Paramedian 3-step: locate L5-S1 → mark 2cm lateral + 2cm caudal → angle 30-45° cephalad/medial

nodes.title: Paramedian — Needle Insertion
nodes.summary: Paramedian avoids supraspinous and interspinous ligaments — useful in elderly with calcification
nodes.body: Entry Point: [2][12] • 1-1.5 cm lateral to midline • At level of superior tip of lower spinous process • Can palpate spinous process, then move lateral Needle Trajectory: 1. Insert needle perpendicular to skin initially 2. Angle 10-30 degrees cephalad (sagittal plane) 3. Angle 10-20 degrees medially (toward midline) 4. Aim toward the interlaminar space Depth: Typically 3-7 cm (varies with patient

nodes.title: CSF Obtained
nodes.summary: CSF obtained: measure opening pressure first, then collect tubes in order (1-4)
nodes.body: CSF Flow: Once CSF flows: 1. Remove stylet 2. Observe CSF appearance (clear, cloudy, bloody) 3. Allow CSF to drip passively If no CSF flow: • Rotate needle 90° (bevel may be against nerve root) • Advance 1-2 mm • Replace stylet, advance, then remove • Aspirate gently (may cause nerve root injury) Opening Pressure Measurement: Do you need to measure opening pressure?

nodes.title: Opening Pressure Measurement
nodes.summary: Opening pressure: patient relaxed in lateral decubitus, legs extended after needle placed
nodes.body: How to Measure Opening Pressure Technique: [1][13] 1. BEFORE withdrawing any CSF 2. Attach 3-way stopcock to needle hub 3. Connect manometer column (marked in cm H₂O) 4. Open stopcock to allow CSF to rise in column Patient Requirements for Accurate OP: • Lateral decubitus position (NOT sitting) • Patient completely relaxed (no straining, no Valsalva) • Legs extended (not flexed to chest) — reduces

nodes.title: Opening Pressure — Interpretation
nodes.summary: Normal OP: 6-25 cmH2O in adults. >25 cmH2O elevated (IIH, meningitis). <6 cmH2O suggests CSF leak
nodes.body: Normal Opening Pressure: [1][13] | Population | Normal Range | |------------|-------------| | Adults | 6-25 cm H₂O | | Children | <28 cm H₂O | | Population mean | ~18 cm H₂O | Elevated OP (>25 cm H₂O): • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) • Meningitis (bacterial, fungal, TB) • SAH (elevated in ~60%) • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis • Mass lesion/tumor • Hydrocephalus • Hypertensive/hepat

nodes.title: CSF Collection
nodes.summary: Tube 1: cell count + diff. Tube 2: glucose + protein. Tube 3: special studies. Tube 4: repeat cell count
nodes.body: Standard Collection: | Tube | Contents | Volume | Tests | |------|----------|--------|-------| | 1 | First CSF | 1-2 mL | Cell count, differential | | 2 | | 1-2 mL | Protein, glucose | | 3 | | 2-3 mL | Gram stain, culture, PCR | | 4 | Last CSF | 1-2 mL | Cell count (compare to tube 1) | Additional tests as indicated: • Cryptococcal antigen (fungal meningitis) • Oligoclonal bands, IgG index (MS) •

nodes.title: CSF Analysis — Interpretation
nodes.summary: CSF interpretation: WBC count, protein, glucose, Gram stain — pattern differentiates bacterial vs viral
nodes.body: CSF Lab Interpreter Tool Normal CSF Values (Adults): | Parameter | Normal | |-----------|---------| | Appearance | Clear, colorless | | WBC | 0-5 cells/µL | | RBC | 0 cells/µL | | Protein | 15-45 mg/dL | | Glucose | 40-85 mg/dL | | CSF:Serum glucose | >0.6 | | Lactate | <25 mg/dL | Rapid Assessment: • Clear CSF: Likely viral or early bacterial • Cloudy/turbid: WBC >200/µL — bacterial until proven

nodes.title: CSF Patterns by Disease
nodes.summary: Bacterial: high WBC (PMNs), low glucose, high protein. Viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose, mild protein elevation

nodes.title: Traumatic Tap vs True SAH
nodes.summary: Traumatic tap: RBCs decrease tube 1 to 4. SAH: RBCs same all tubes + xanthochromia after 12h
nodes.body: Distinguishing Traumatic LP from SAH: [5][6] Classic Teaching (Tube 1 vs Tube 4): • Traumatic tap: RBC decreases tube 1 → tube 4 • True SAH: RBC count remains constant ⚠️ Reality: RBC clearing is UNRELIABLE • Clearing to zero/near-zero = strong evidence for traumatic tap • Partial clearing (25% reduction) occurs in BOTH traumatic tap AND SAH • Stable RBC count = concerning for SAH XANTHOCHROMIA is

nodes.title: Post-Procedure
nodes.summary: Post-LP complications: headache (most common), infection, bleeding, nerve injury, herniation (rare)
nodes.body: Post-LP Care: • Bed rest: NOT proven to prevent PDPH — patient may ambulate • Hydration: Encourage fluids (not proven but generally recommended) • Analgesia: PRN for back discomfort • Activity: Resume normal activity Return precautions — Seek care for: • Severe headache (especially positional) • Back pain with leg weakness • Numbness or tingling in legs • Urinary retention or incontinence • Fever

nodes.title: Post-Dural Puncture Headache (PDPH)
nodes.summary: Post-dural puncture headache: positional (worse upright), caffeine, analgesics — blood patch if refractory
nodes.body: PDPH Characteristics: [11][15] • Bilateral frontal or occipital headache • POSITIONAL: Worse upright, better supine • Onset: Usually within 5 days of LP • Associated: Nausea, neck stiffness, photophobia, tinnitus Incidence: • Cutting needles (Quincke): 15-30% • Atraumatic needles (Whitacre): ~4% • Risk factors: Female, young (18-40), low BMI, pregnancy, history of headaches Treatment: 1. Conservat

nodes.title: Failed LP — Next Steps
nodes.summary: Failed LP: reposition, try one level up/down, use ultrasound guidance, or paramedian approach
nodes.body: Failed LP — Options: 1. Reassess technique: • Confirm landmarks (consider US) • Try different interspace (L3-L4 vs L4-L5) • Optimize positioning (more flexion) • Try sitting position if in lateral 2. Try PARAMEDIAN approach: • 30-40% higher success than midline • Especially useful if calcified ligaments 3. Ultrasound guidance: • Mark midline and depth • First-attempt success: 87% (US) vs 50% (land

nodes.title: LP Complications
nodes.summary: Epidural hematoma, infection, nerve root injury — all rare but require awareness and documentation
nodes.body: Rare but Serious Complications: [1][9] Epidural/Spinal Hematoma: • Incidence: 0.20-0.23% (very rare) • Symptoms: Back pain, progressive weakness, sensory changes, urinary retention • Diagnosis: MRI spine URGENT • Treatment: Emergent neurosurgery consult, surgical decompression if deficit Brain Herniation: • Risk: Mass lesion, elevated ICP • Prevention: Follow CT criteria • Signs: Rapid deteriorati

nodes.title: LP Complete — Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition based on indication and CSF results — admit meningitis, discharge SAH rule-out if negative
nodes.body: Post-LP Disposition: Based on CSF Results: • Bacterial meningitis: ICU admission, IV antibiotics, dexamethasone • Viral meningitis: Usually supportive care, may discharge stable patients • SAH confirmed: Neurosurgery consult, angiography, ICU • IIH: Neurology follow-up, acetazolamide, weight loss counseling • MS/GBS workup: Neurology admission for further evaluation Discharge Instructions (Uncompl
nodes.recommendation: LP complete. Disposition based on clinical indication and CSF results. Educate patient on return precautions including positional headache, leg weakness, and urinary symptoms.

nodes.title: Acute Lymphadenopathy — Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Sick check: airway (deep-space infection), sepsis, malignancy red flags, acute HIV. Resuscitate/secure airway in parallel if unstable.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F Most swollen glands are benign reactive nodes. But screen for the dangerous ones: 1. Airway-threatening deep-space infection \u2014 suppurative node + trismus, drooling, stridor, "hot-potato" voice, neck swelling / torticollis. 2. Sepsis from a suppurative source \u2014 fever + toxic appearance + fluctuant node. 3. New hematologic malignancy \u2014 hard / fixed / matted / painless nod

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pattern & Danger First
nodes.summary: Characterize node pattern; walk the dangerous branch to a verdict. Excluded loops back.
nodes.body: Characterize the node pattern and hunt the dangerous causes to an explicit verdict, one at a time. Excluded loops back here for the next branch. Key discriminators: localized vs generalized \u00B7 tender/mobile vs hard/fixed/matted \u00B7 B-symptoms present? \u00B7 supraclavicular (concerning) \u00B7 duration (>2\u20134 wk persistent = workup) \u00B7 age (new persistent adenopathy in >40 raises ma

nodes.title: Suppurative Node — Airway / Deep-Space Gate
nodes.summary: Airway signs / trismus / toxicity = deep-space emergency; small fluctuant node no airway threat = simple.
nodes.body: A fluctuant, rapidly enlarging, or hot tender node with trismus, dysphagia, drooling, stridor, torticollis, or "hot-potato" voice is a deep-neck-space infection until proven otherwise (peritonsillar, retropharyngeal, submandibular / Ludwig angina).

nodes.title: Deep Neck Space Infection — Treat
nodes.body: Open Deep Neck Infection. Next 5 minutes: - Protect the airway first \u2014 anticipate a difficult airway; involve anesthesia / ENT early; have a surgical-airway plan. - Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering oral flora: ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV, or clindamycin; add MRSA coverage (vancomycin) if risk. - CT neck with IV contrast once the airway is safe \u2014 defines abscess vs phlegmon for surg
nodes.recommendation: Airway first, broad-spectrum IV abx, CT neck with contrast, urgent ENT/OMFS for drainage.

nodes.title: Simple Suppurative Adenitis
nodes.body: A small fluctuant node without airway threat or toxicity is a simple suppurative lymphadenitis. Incision and drainage if fluctuant; empiric antibiotics covering staph/strep (and MRSA per local rates); warm compresses; close follow-up. Reassess for airway progression \u2014 if trismus, voice change, or neck swelling develops, return to the deep-space pathway. Return to the hub if another pattern re
nodes.recommendation: I&D if fluctuant + staph/strep (\u00B1 MRSA) antibiotics; return precautions for airway progression.

nodes.title: Malignancy Phenotype — Red-Flag Gate
nodes.summary: SVC/tumor lysis = emergency; hard/fixed/supraclav + B-symptoms = malignancy workup + biopsy; soft mobile = unlikely.
nodes.body: Nodes that raise malignancy pretest probability: hard, fixed, matted, painless, >2 cm, persistently enlarging over weeks, supraclavicular location, or accompanied by B-symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss). A rapidly enlarging mediastinal/nodal mass with SVC syndrome (facial/neck swelling, distended veins, dyspnea) is an oncologic emergency.

nodes.title: Oncologic Emergency — Stabilize
nodes.body: A new hematologic malignancy can present in extremis. \u26A0\uFE0F No dedicated deep-dive consult yet \u2014 manage here and escalate. - SVC syndrome: elevate head of bed, oxygen, avoid upper-extremity IVs, urgent CT chest with contrast, emergent oncology / radiation-oncology consult. Airway and hemodynamic support as needed. - Tumor lysis (high-grade lymphoma / leukemia): check K+, phosphate, cal
nodes.recommendation: Treat SVC syndrome / tumor lysis / leukostasis; CBC+smear, LDH, uric acid; admit + urgent heme-onc.

nodes.title: Suspected Nodal Malignancy — Workup Pathway
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F No deep-dive consult yet \u2014 initiate the ED workup and arrange definitive diagnosis. - Labs: CBC with differential + peripheral smear, LDH, uric acid, LFTs, ESR/CRP, HIV, and (per exposure) EBV / CMV serologies. - Imaging: CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast (or CXR + node US in the ED) to map nodal burden and find a mediastinal mass. - Tissue is the answer: an excisional l
nodes.recommendation: CBC+smear, LDH, uric acid, HIV; CT staging; expedited EXCISIONAL biopsy + heme-onc. Avoid empiric steroids.

nodes.title: Malignancy — Lower Probability
nodes.body: Soft, mobile, tender nodes without B-symptoms, in a well patient, favor a reactive/infective cause. But persistence matters: any node that persists >2\u20134 weeks, keeps enlarging, is supraclavicular, or develops B-symptoms needs referral for biopsy regardless of initial reassurance. Return to the hub for the next pattern.
nodes.recommendation: Malignancy lower probability now; refer for biopsy if node persists >2-4 wk, enlarges, is supraclavicular, or B-symptoms appear.

nodes.title: Acute HIV — Retroviral Syndrome Gate
nodes.summary: Generalized adenopathy + fever + rash + pharyngitis + exposure. 4th-gen Ag/Ab AND HIV RNA (window).
nodes.body: Acute (primary) HIV presents as generalized tender lymphadenopathy + fever + maculopapular rash + pharyngitis + myalgias, typically 2\u20134 weeks after exposure. A 4th-generation Ag/Ab test can be negative in the earliest window \u2014 HIV RNA (viral load) is the test for suspected acute infection.

nodes.title: Suspected Acute HIV — Treat
nodes.body: Open HIV. Next steps: - 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab AND HIV-1 RNA (viral load) \u2014 RNA detects infection before antibody seroconversion. - Counsel + link to care urgently; early ART reduces transmission and reservoir. - Screen for co-infections (syphilis, gonorrhea/chlamydia, hepatitis B/C, TB). - If a source-exposure is <72 h and ongoing risk, consider PEP; discuss PrEP for future risk.
nodes.recommendation: 4th-gen Ag/Ab + HIV RNA (viral load); urgent linkage to care + co-infection screen.

nodes.title: Acute HIV — Unlikely
nodes.body: Without a compatible syndrome or risk exposure, acute HIV is unlikely. Still send an HIV test as part of any unexplained persistent lymphadenopathy workup \u2014 it is cheap, high-yield, and part of standard adenopathy evaluation. Return to the hub for the next pattern.
nodes.recommendation: Acute HIV unlikely; still include HIV testing in any unexplained persistent adenopathy workup.

nodes.title: TB / Subacute Constitutional — Gate
nodes.summary: Night sweats + weight loss + firm node + TB risk. CXR + IGRA/TST + isolate if pulmonary features.
nodes.body: Weeks of fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and cough \u2014 with a firm cervical/supraclavicular node (scrofula = TB lymphadenitis) \u2014 point to TB, especially with risk factors (endemic exposure, HIV, immunosuppression, incarceration, homelessness).

nodes.title: Suspected TB — Treat
nodes.body: Open Tuberculosis. Next steps: - Airborne isolation if any pulmonary features (cough, infiltrate) until active pulmonary TB is excluded. - CXR; sputum for AFB smear \u00D7 3 + culture + NAAT if pulmonary; IGRA or TST. - For isolated TB lymphadenitis (scrofula): node FNA/excisional biopsy with AFB stain, culture, and NAAT. - HIV testing (co-infection); notify public health; involve ID for treatment
nodes.recommendation: Airborne isolation if pulmonary features; CXR + sputum AFB/NAAT + IGRA/TST; node biopsy for scrofula; HIV test + ID/public health.

nodes.title: TB — Unlikely
nodes.body: Absence of constitutional symptoms and TB risk makes TB unlikely. Keep it on the differential for any persistent firm node with night sweats, especially in higher-risk patients \u2014 subacute presentations are easy to miss. Return to the hub for the next pattern.
nodes.recommendation: TB unlikely now; reconsider for persistent firm node + night sweats or new risk exposure.

nodes.title: Reactive Adenopathy — Local Source Gate
nodes.summary: Tender mobile node + local source = reactive; treat source. No source + persistence = workup bundle.
nodes.body: A tender, mobile, soft node with an obvious adjacent infection (pharyngitis, dental, skin/soft-tissue, conjunctivitis, scalp) is most often reactive. Treat the source and reassess. EBV mononucleosis (posterior cervical adenopathy + exudative pharyngitis + fatigue \u00B1 splenomegaly) and cat-scratch (regional node + cat exposure/papule) are common benign causes without dedicated consults yet.

nodes.title: Reactive Lymphadenopathy — Treat the Source
nodes.body: Treat the driving infection and let the node follow: - Streptococcal / bacterial pharyngitis with tender anterior cervical nodes \u2192 open Adult Pharyngitis. - EBV mononucleosis (no deep-dive yet): supportive care, avoid amoxicillin (rash), counsel splenic-precaution / no contact sports \u00D7 3\u20134 weeks for splenomegaly; monofocal heterophile / EBV serologies. - Cat-scratch (Bartonella) (no
nodes.recommendation: Treat the driving infection; EBV \u2192 splenic precautions + avoid amoxicillin; re-evaluate/biopsy if node persists >2-4 wk.

nodes.title: Pediatric — Adenitis vs Kawasaki Gate
nodes.summary: \u22655-day fever + Kawasaki features = urgent (echo, IVIG); unilateral tender node alone = bacterial adenitis.
nodes.body: In a child, distinguish acute bacterial cervical adenitis (unilateral, tender, warm, often staph/strep \u2014 may suppurate) from Kawasaki disease, where cervical lymphadenopathy (\u22651.5 cm, usually unilateral) is one of the principal criteria alongside \u22655 days of fever, conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, and extremity changes.

nodes.title: Kawasaki Disease Suspected — Urgent
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F No deep-dive consult yet \u2014 recognize and escalate; untreated Kawasaki risks coronary artery aneurysms. - Criteria: \u22655 days of fever PLUS \u22654 of \u2014 bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (edema/erythema, later periungual peeling), cervical lymphadenopathy \u22651.5 cm. Consid
nodes.recommendation: Apply Kawasaki criteria (incl. incomplete); labs + urgent echo; IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin within 10 days; admit + peds/cardiology.

nodes.title: Pediatric Bacterial Adenitis — Treat
nodes.body: Acute unilateral bacterial cervical adenitis (staph/strep) in a child: empiric antibiotics covering staph/strep (and MRSA per local rates) \u2014 e.g., clindamycin or cephalexin; warm compresses; ultrasound + I&D if fluctuant/abscessed; close follow-up. Return precautions: airway signs, spreading erythema, worsening fever/toxicity, or failure to improve in 48\u201372 h \u2192 re-image (US/CT), con
nodes.recommendation: Empiric staph/strep (\u00B1 MRSA) antibiotics; US + I&D if fluctuant; 48-72 h follow-up with airway/spread precautions.

nodes.title: Initial Workup Bundle — Undifferentiated Adenopathy
nodes.summary: History (B-symptoms, exposures, drugs) + exam (localized/generalized, consistency, supraclav) + targeted labs. 2-4 wk persistence = biopsy referral.
nodes.body: No emergency ruled in; the node is undifferentiated. Base the ED workup on pattern and duration: - History: duration, growth rate, B-symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), exposures (cats, TB contacts, travel, sexual history, tick), medications (phenytoin, allopurinol \u2192 drug-induced), constitutional symptoms. - Exam: localized vs generalized, size, consistency (soft/firm/hard), mobility

nodes.title: Reassess — Results & Trajectory
nodes.summary: Benign = discharge; red flags = malignancy pathway; airway/toxic = deep-space; undifferentiated well = image + outpatient.
nodes.body: Integrate history, exam, and available labs. Decide the next step.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision Cheat-Sheet
nodes.summary: US first for a discrete node; CT neck for deep-space; CT C/A/P for staging; CXR screen. Excisional biopsy is definitive for lymphoma.
nodes.body: Image by the question you are asking: Ultrasound (first-line for a discrete node): characterizes size, shape, hilum (benign reactive nodes keep a fatty hilum; loss of hilum + round shape favors malignancy), and guides FNA/biopsy. Good for pediatric and cervical nodes. CT neck with IV contrast: suspected deep-space infection / abscess (define drainable collection, airway). CT chest/abdomen/pelvis w

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit for infection/sepsis/oncologic emergency/systemic illness; discharge benign with structured follow-up.
nodes.body: Match disposition to the dominant pattern.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for: deep-neck-space infection / airway concern, sepsis from a suppurative source, oncologic emergency (SVC syndrome, tumor lysis, leukostasis, symptomatic cytopenias), Kawasaki disease, active TB needing isolation, or any systemically ill patient. Service: ENT / OMFS (deep-space infection); Heme-Onc + Medicine (new malignancy, cytopenias, tumor lysis); Pediatrics + Cardiology (Kawasaki); ID
nodes.recommendation: Admit per dominant pattern; match service; ICU for airway/shock; carry the biopsy + isolation plan in handoff.

nodes.title: Discharge — With a Biopsy Safety Net
nodes.body: Discharge when: well-appearing, no airway/sepsis/oncologic-emergency features, a plausible benign/reactive cause or a stable workup in progress, and reliable follow-up secured. Before discharge: (1) document node size / character / location, (2) send / plan the targeted labs (incl. HIV), (3) treat any local source, (4) written return precautions, (5) explicit follow-up with a hard 2\u20134 week re
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if well + reliable follow-up; document node, send HIV + targeted labs, mandatory 2-4 wk recheck + biopsy pathway.

nodes.title: Magnesium Disorder
nodes.summary: Route by low vs high Mg, but always interpret with renal function, ECG, reflexes, respiration, K, Ca, and phosphate.
nodes.body: Interpret magnesium with renal function, ECG, reflexes, respiratory status, potassium, calcium, phosphate, and recent magnesium exposure. Which pathway fits?

nodes.title: Magnesium Steps
nodes.summary: Assess ECG/reflexes/respiration/renal function; replace low Mg, antagonize toxic Mg with calcium, dialyze severe renal toxicity.
nodes.body: 1. Assess ECG, reflexes, respiratory rate, BP, renal function, and paired electrolytes. 2. Low Mg with torsades, seizure, severe arrhythmia, or severe symptoms: IV magnesium now. 3. Low Mg without instability: replace IV or PO based on severity, GI tolerance, and renal function. 4. High Mg/toxicity: stop sources, give IV calcium if symptomatic, support airway/hemodynamics, enhance elimination. 5.

nodes.title: Hypomagnesemia Severity
nodes.summary: Torsades/seizure/unstable rhythm gets IV magnesium immediately; stable mild cases can use oral/slow IV replacement.
nodes.body: Dangerous hypomagnesemia is clinical: torsades or prolonged QT, ventricular ectopy, seizures, tetany, severe weakness, refractory hypokalemia, refractory hypocalcemia, alcohol withdrawal, DKA, diarrhea, diuretics, amphotericin/cisplatin, or PPI-associated renal/GI wasting.

nodes.title: Torsades / Seizure Mg
nodes.summary: Torsades: Mg sulfate 2 g IV rapidly, correct K, stop QT drugs, manage bradycardia and defibrillate unstable rhythms.
nodes.body: Magnesium Sulfate 2 g IV over 5-15 min for torsades or unstable polymorphic VT (push over 1-2 min if pulseless/unstable); repeat 2 g at 5-15 min if it persists, then start a continuous infusion - a bolus alone wears off over hours and torsades recurs. Give even if serum magnesium is normal when torsades is present. Correct K to high-normal, stop QT-prolonging drugs, treat bradycardia with overdriv

nodes.title: Severe Hypomagnesemia
nodes.summary: Severe/symptomatic low Mg needs IV replacement and repeated dosing; reduce dose and monitor closely in renal impairment.
nodes.body: If symptomatic but stable: Magnesium Sulfate 1-2 g IV over about 1 hour; more aggressive repletion often requires scheduled 2-4 g doses or infusion when renal function is normal. For Mg <1.2 mg/dL or severe total-body depletion, plan repeated dosing because serum Mg rises quickly but intracellular repletion is slower. Reduce dose and increase monitoring in renal impairment.

nodes.title: Hypomagnesemia Workup
nodes.summary: Find GI, renal, drug, alcohol/nutrition, DKA/refeeding, and renal wasting causes; low Mg blocks K/Ca correction.
nodes.body: Check K, Ca, phosphate, creatinine, ECG/QTc, acid-base status, and urinary Mg wasting when persistent. Common drivers: diarrhea, malabsorption, alcohol use, malnutrition, DKA/insulin, refeeding, loop/thiazide diuretics, aminoglycosides, amphotericin, cisplatin, calcineurin inhibitors, EGFR inhibitors, PPIs, and inherited tubulopathies. Replete magnesium when potassium or calcium is refractory.

nodes.title: Stable Hypomagnesemia
nodes.body: Oral magnesium is reasonable when stable, mild-moderate, and able to tolerate GI effects. Use slower IV replacement when oral therapy is not tolerated, ongoing losses are high, or inpatient paired-electrolyte correction is needed. Discharge requires a cause addressed, no dangerous ECG/symptoms, renal-appropriate dose, and follow-up labs when ongoing losses or medications remain.
nodes.recommendation: Replace Mg, correct paired K/Ca problems, stop the cause when possible, and arrange lab follow-up for persistent-risk patients.

nodes.title: Hypermagnesemia Severity
nodes.summary: Hypermagnesemia toxicity is clinical: reflexes, respiration, BP, bradycardia, and conduction disease drive urgency.
nodes.body: Most clinically significant hypermagnesemia occurs with renal failure plus magnesium exposure: antacids/laxatives, supplements, obstetric MgSO4, missed dialysis, lithium/milk-alkali overlap, or massive tissue injury. Clinical toxicity matters more than the number: hyporeflexia, weakness, somnolence, hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, widened QRS, respiratory depression, or arrest.

nodes.title: Magnesium Toxicity
nodes.summary: Toxic Mg: stop source, support airway/hemodynamics, give IV calcium, diurese if renal function adequate, dialyze severe renal toxicity.
nodes.body: 1. Stop all magnesium sources. 2. Support airway, ventilation, circulation, and continuous ECG monitoring. 3. Give Calcium Gluconate 1-2 g IV over 5-10 min; repeat for recurrent cardiopulmonary toxicity. Use Calcium Chloride via central access if peri-arrest. 4. If renal function is adequate: isotonic fluids plus loop diuretic may enhance excretion. 5. If renal failure, severe level, persistent hy

nodes.title: Stable Hypermagnesemia
nodes.body: If mild, asymptomatic, and kidney function is adequate, remove exogenous magnesium and monitor. Recheck Mg, Ca, K, phosphate, creatinine, and ECG if level is meaningfully elevated or symptoms could evolve. Medication reconciliation should specifically look for magnesium-containing antacids, laxatives, supplements, bowel prep, and obstetric magnesium infusion.
nodes.recommendation: Stable mild hypermagnesemia is usually source control plus monitoring; escalate immediately if reflexes, respiration, BP, or conduction worsen.

nodes.title: Renal Failure Caveat
nodes.summary: Renal failure turns magnesium into a monitored drug; calcium buys time in toxicity, dialysis removes magnesium.
nodes.body: Renal impairment increases toxicity risk from both replacement and exposure. Avoid large empiric magnesium loads unless treating torsades, eclampsia, seizure, or clear severe deficiency. Use lower doses, longer intervals, and serial levels. For toxicity with renal failure, dialysis is definitive. Calcium antagonizes toxicity transiently but does not remove magnesium.

nodes.title: STOP: Magnesium Pitfalls
nodes.body: - Do not wait for the Mg level before treating torsades. - Do not keep chasing potassium or calcium without correcting magnesium. - Do not give large magnesium replacement doses to oliguric/anuric patients without a monitoring plan. - Do not miss magnesium-containing laxatives/antacids in renal failure. - Do not assume calcium fixes hypermagnesemia; it antagonizes toxicity temporarily while elimin
nodes.recommendation: Magnesium disorders are ECG, renal, and paired-electrolyte problems; reassess the whole physiology after each intervention.

nodes.title: Major Joint Dislocation — ED Evaluation
nodes.body: Steps Summary TIME-CRITICAL INJURIES: Hip, knee, and ankle dislocations are orthopedic emergencies with vascular compromise risk. Initial Assessment: 1. ABCs and trauma survey 2. Neurovascular status BEFORE anything else 3. Open vs closed injury 4. Associated fractures Document before reduction: • Pulses (palpable, Doppler, ABI) • Sensation (dermatomes) • Motor function • Skin integrity Which join

nodes.title: Vascular Assessment
nodes.body: Critical: Check pulses BEFORE and AFTER reduction Assessment: • Palpate distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial) • Compare to uninjured side • Check capillary refill (<2 seconds) • Note skin color and temperature If pulses absent or asymmetric: • Doppler assessment • Calculate ABI (abnormal <0.9) Red Flags: 🔴 Absent pulse 🔴 ABI <0.9 🔴 Expanding hematoma 🔴 Bruit 🔴 Cool/pale limb Vascul

If pulse returns — CTA, close monitoring 5. nodes.title: Knee Dislocation — Assessment
nodes.body: HIGHEST VASCULAR RISK: Popliteal artery injury in 20-40% of knee dislocations. Types (based on tibia position): • Anterior (most common) — hyperextension • Posterior — dashboard injury • Medial/Lateral — varus/valgus force • Rotatory — complex Warning: May spontaneously reduce: • High suspicion with multi-ligament injury • Gross instability in multiple planes • History consistent with dislocation

nodes.body: Popliteal Artery at Risk: • Tethered at adductor hiatus and soleal arch • Intimal tear, thrombosis, or transection • Ischemia time critical — 6-8 hour window Immediate Actions: 1. Reduce NOW — do not wait for OR 2. Reassess pulse after reduction 3. If pulse returns: CTA, close monitoring 4. If pulse absent: OR immediately CTA vs Immediate OR: • Hard signs (absent pulse, expanding hematoma): OR • S

nodes.body: Reduction Technique: Anterior Dislocation: 1. Inline traction on tibia 2. Lift distal femur anteriorly 3. Push tibia posteriorly 4. Knee should reduce with slight flexion Posterior Dislocation: 1. Inline traction 2. Lift tibia anteriorly 3. Push femur posteriorly 4. Reduce into extension Post-Reduction: • Immediate pulse check (CRITICAL) • ABI measurement • Posterior splint at 20° flexion • Repeat

nodes.title: Spontaneously Reduced Knee
nodes.body: High Suspicion — History + Instability: Signs of reduced knee dislocation: • Gross multi-planar instability • Effusion/hemarthrosis • Ligamentous laxity (ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL) • History consistent (hyperextension, dashboard) Still at vascular risk: • Intimal tears can be occult • Delayed thrombosis possible Management: • Serial ABI q4h x 24-48h • CTA recommended for all suspected knee dislocations •

nodes.body: Skin Tenting = Emergency: Risks if not reduced promptly: • Skin necrosis • Open fracture (skin breaks down) • Vascular compromise • Compartment syndrome Immediate Reduction: • Do NOT wait for X-ray • Do NOT wait for full sedation setup • Procedural sedation if immediately available • Otherwise: local hematoma block + reduce Technique: 1. Grasp heel and forefoot 2. Apply inline traction 3. Reverse

nodes.title: Ankle Dislocation Reduction
nodes.body: Reduction Technique: Posterior Dislocation (most common): 1. Patient supine, knee flexed (relaxes gastrocnemius) 2. Grasp heel with one hand 3. Apply inline traction 4. Dorsiflex foot while pushing talus anteriorly 5. Reduce should be felt/heard Anterior Dislocation: 1. Plantarflex the foot 2. Apply traction 3. Push talus posteriorly Lateral/Medial: 1. Inline traction 2. Reverse the lateral force

nodes.title: Open Ankle Dislocation
nodes.body: Open Fracture-Dislocation Protocol: Immediate: 1. Photograph wound (documentation) 2. Remove gross contamination 3. Sterile saline-moistened dressing 4. Reduce dislocation (reduces contamination risk) 5. Posterior splint Antibiotics — timing is the #1 driver of infection risk. nodes.title: Failed Reduction — OR Required

nodes.body: All major joint dislocations require admission or close follow-up. nodes.title: Discharge — Strict Precautions

nodes.title: Malaria — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Travel to endemic area + fever = malaria until proven otherwise — thick/thin smear STAT
nodes.body: Malaria Steps Summary Malaria is a life-threatening parasitic infection transmitted by *Anopheles* mosquitoes. Endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Any fever in a traveler returning from an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise. [1][2] Key Principle: Species identification drives all treatment decisions. *P. falciparum* can kill within 24-48 hours if untreated. [3][4] Critical ear

nodes.title: Symptom Timing & Presentation
nodes.summary: Symptoms typically 7-30 days after travel — P. vivax/ovale may present months to years later
nodes.body: Classic presentation: [1][2] • Fever (paroxysmal or continuous) — most common symptom • Rigors, chills, sweats — may occur in cycles • Headache, myalgias, malaise — nonspecific • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea — common Incubation period: [4] • *P. falciparum:* 7-14 days (most within 30 days) • *P. vivax/ovale:* 12-18 days (can be >6 months due to dormant liver stages) • *P. malariae:* 18-40 days • *P.

nodes.title: Low Probability of Malaria
nodes.summary: No travel history: consider airport malaria, transfusion-transmitted, or congenital malaria
nodes.body: Without recent travel to endemic areas, malaria is extremely unlikely (rare exceptions: airport malaria, congenital transmission, blood transfusion). [4] Consider alternative diagnoses: • Dengue, Zika, chikungunya • Typhoid fever • Rickettsial infections • Leptospirosis • Viral hemorrhagic fevers • Influenza, COVID-19 • Bacterial sepsis If high clinical suspicion persists despite negative travel h
nodes.recommendation: Malaria is unlikely without endemic area exposure. Pursue alternative febrile illness workup. If suspicion persists, obtain blood smears and consult infectious disease.

nodes.title: Diagnostic Testing — Blood Smears & RDT
nodes.summary: Thick smear (sensitive) and thin smear (speciation) — RDT as adjunct, not replacement
nodes.body: STAT thick and thin blood smears — gold standard for diagnosis. [1][2][4] Thick smear: • Concentrates parasites — higher sensitivity for detection • Used to confirm presence of infection • Estimates parasitemia density Thin smear: • Allows species identification and accurate parasitemia count • Essential for treatment decisions Parasitemia calculation: [5] • % infected RBCs = (infected RBCs / tota

nodes.title: Species Identification
nodes.summary: Species identification determines treatment: P. falciparum is most lethal, requires different therapy
nodes.body: Species identification is CRITICAL — determines treatment regimen, resistance patterns, and disposition. [1][3][4] Species Comparison Table Five species infect humans: • *P. falciparum* — most lethal, can progress to severe malaria in 24-48h, chloroquine-resistant in most regions • *P. vivax* — dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) require primaquine for radical cure, chloroquine-resistant in some re

nodes.title: Management While Awaiting Species ID
nodes.summary: If species unknown, treat as P. falciparum (most dangerous) until speciation available
nodes.body: If RDT positive or high clinical suspicion but species ID pending: [4][6] Do NOT delay treatment — initiate empiric therapy based on: 1. Geographic region of travel (resistance patterns) 2. Clinical severity 3. Most likely species Empiric approach: • Severe malaria (any species) → IV artesunate immediately [5][6] • Uncomplicated, travel to Africa or Papua New Guinea → assume *P. falciparum* → arte

nodes.title: Severity Classification
nodes.summary: Severe malaria criteria: AMS, seizures, severe anemia, parasitemia >5%, acidosis, renal/hepatic failure
nodes.body: Severe malaria is defined by WHO 2023 criteria as *Plasmodium* infection PLUS ≥1 of the following: [5] Severe Malaria WHO 2023 Criteria Clinical criteria: • Impaired consciousness (GCS <11) • Prostration (inability to sit/stand without assistance) • Multiple convulsions (≥2 in 24h) • Respiratory distress (acidotic breathing) • Circulatory collapse, shock (SBP <70 mmHg in children, <80 in adults) •

nodes.title: Severe Malaria — IV Artesunate

nodes.body: IV artesunate is the ONLY treatment for severe malaria. [5][6][8] STAT actions: 1. Call CDC Malaria Hotline immediately: 770-488-7788 (M-F 9am-5pm ET) or 770-488-7100 (24/7 after hours) [6] 2. Supportive care: fluids (avoid ov

nodes.summary: Cerebral malaria, ARDS, DIC, splenic rupture, severe anemia — ICU monitoring for all severe cases
nodes.body: Cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness, seizures): [5] • Supportive care — maintain airway, prevent aspiration • Treat seizures: benzodiazepines first-line • Avoid steroids (HARM, not help — increases mortality) [5] • Neurologic sequelae occur in ~10% (cognitive deficits, motor dysfunction) Hypoglycemia (glucose <40 mg/dL): [5] • Common in severe malaria and pregnancy • Monitor glucose q4-6h • D

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Malaria — Treatment by Species

nodes.body: Uncomplicated malaria = parasitemia without severe malaria criteria. nodes.title: P. malariae / P. knowlesi — Chloroquine
nodes.summary: P. malariae: chloroquine effective. P. knowlesi: can cause severe disease, treat as falciparum
nodes.body: *P. malariae:* [4][6] • Chronic low-grade parasitemia (can persist for decades if untreated) • Associated with nephrotic syndrome (immune complex deposition) • Chloroquine-sensitive worldwide • No liver stages — primaquine NOT required • Treatment: Chloroquine phosphate 1000 mg, then 500 mg at 6, 24, 48h (same as vivax) *P. knowlesi:* [4][6][14] • Zoonotic (macaque reservoir), Southeast Asia only

nodes.title: ICU Admission

nodes.body: ICU admission for severe malaria. nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.summary: Floor admission for moderate cases: oral ACT, serial parasitemia, can convert to outpatient
nodes.body: Floor admission for close monitoring. [4][6] Indications: • All *P. falciparum* cases (even if uncomplicated) • *P. knowlesi* • Pregnancy • Pediatric <5 years • Comorbidities Monitoring: • Vital signs q4-6h • Glucose q6-8h (or more frequently if symptomatic) • Repeat blood smears day 3 and day 7 (or until negative) • Daily CBC (monitor hemoglobin, platelets) • BMP daily (renal function) • Strict I

nodes.title: Outpatient Management (Rare)
nodes.summary: Outpatient only if uncomplicated, reliable follow-up, oral intake tolerated, parasitemia <2%

nodes.title: Bluebottle / Portuguese Man-of-War
nodes.summary: Bluebottle/Portuguese man-of-war: hot water immersion (not vinegar) — vinegar may worsen bluebottle stings
nodes.body: Important: Do NOT use vinegar (causes nematocyst discharge) First Aid: 1. Remove tentacles, rinse with seawater 2. Hot water immersion 43-45°C for up to 30 minutes 3. Ice if hot water unavailable ED Management: - Usually supportive care only - Oral/IV analgesia for pain - Antihistamines for itching - Rarely causes systemic symptoms Disposition: - Most patients can be discharged after pain control

nodes.title: Minor Jellyfish Stings
nodes.summary: Minor jellyfish stings: vinegar, remove tentacles, hot water immersion, NSAIDs for pain
nodes.body: Local Reaction Only: - Painful dermatitis, linear wheals - Usually self-limited Treatment: 1. Rinse with seawater (not freshwater) 2. Remove any visible tentacles 3. Hot water immersion 40-45°C for 20-30 min OR vinegar (regional preference) 4. Topical hydrocortisone for itching 5. Oral antihistamines Do NOT: - Apply pressure bandage - Rub with sand or towel - Apply freshwater (causes nematocyst di

nodes.title: Fish Envenomation — Overview
nodes.summary: Venomous fish spines: hot water immersion (45°C/113°F x 30-90 min) denatures heat-labile venom
nodes.body: Key Principle: All fish venoms are heat-labile Hot Water Immersion Protocol: - Temperature: 40-45°C (as hot as tolerated, non-scalding) - Duration: 30-90 minutes or until significant pain relief - Test water on unaffected limb first to prevent burns Common Venomous Fish: | Species | Potency | Distribution | |---------|---------|--------------| | Stonefish | Most potent | Indo-Pacific | | Stingray

nodes.title: Stingray Injury
nodes.summary: Stingray: hot water immersion, explore wound for retained barb, irrigate copiously, antibiotics
nodes.body: Presentation: - Painful puncture wound (usually foot/ankle) - Retroserrated barb may be retained - Local edema, erythema, necrosis possible Management: 1. Hot water immersion — most effective for pain 2. Imaging: X-ray (barbs are radioopaque) - MRI/US for radiolucent cartilage fragments 3. Wound exploration: Remove visible barb fragments 4. Irrigate thoroughly 5. Tetanus prophylaxis Antibiotics (R

nodes.title: Stonefish — Most Potent Fish Venom
nodes.summary: Stonefish: most venomous fish — hot water immersion, antivenom available for severe cases
nodes.body: Presentation: - Excruciating pain ("worst pain ever experienced") - Stepped on camouflaged fish on ocean floor - Rapid local edema - Systemic effects: hypotension, cardiac dysfunction (rare) Treatment: 1. Hot water immersion 40-42°C for 20+ minutes 2. Regional nerve block — may be more effective than HWI alone 3. IV opioids for uncontrolled pain Stonefish Antivenom (CSL): | Indication | Dose | |--

nodes.title: Lionfish / Scorpionfish
nodes.summary: Lionfish: hot water immersion effective, rarely systemic — wound care and pain management
nodes.body: Less potent than stonefish but still very painful Presentation: - Throbbing local pain, peaks 60-90 min, lasts up to 12 hours - Grade I: Local erythema/ecchymosis - Grade II: Vesicle/blister formation - Grade III: Local necrosis (days to weeks) Treatment: 1. Hot water immersion — 94% get complete or moderate relief 2. Remove visible spines 3. Local wound care 4. Tetanus prophylaxis 5. Antibiotics

nodes.title: Other Marine Envenomation
nodes.summary: Other marine organisms: sea urchins, octopus, cone snails, sea snakes — species-specific treatment
nodes.body: Select the creature type: | Creature | Toxin | Key Feature | |----------|-------|-------------| | Sea Urchin | Local toxins | Multiple spine punctures | | Blue-ringed Octopus | Tetrodotoxin | Paralysis, respiratory failure | | Cone Snail | Conotoxins | Paralysis, painless sting | | Sea Snake | Myotoxic + neurotoxic | Rhabdomyolysis, paralysis |

nodes.title: Sea Urchin Injuries
nodes.summary: Sea urchin spines: hot water soak, remove visible spines — deeply embedded spines may need surgical removal
nodes.body: Presentation: - Multiple spine punctures (usually feet/hands) - Intense local pain - Dark discoloration (may be dye — resolves in 48h) Treatment: 1. Hot water immersion 40-46°C for 30-90 minutes 2. Remove all visible spines carefully (avoid fragmentation) 3. Irrigate and debride wounds 4. Shaving cream + razor to remove pedicellariae 5. Imaging if retained spines suspected Complications (weeks to

nodes.title: Blue-Ringed Octopus — Tetrodotoxin
nodes.summary: Blue-ringed octopus: tetrodotoxin causes ascending paralysis — no antivenom, supportive care and intubation
nodes.body: Life-threatening — prepare for respiratory support Presentation: - Tiny, often painless bite - Symptom onset: 1-2 hours - Progressive ascending paralysis - Respiratory failure - Patient remains conscious despite paralysis First Aid: 1. Clean wound with freshwater 2. Pressure immobilization bandage (slows lymphatic spread) 3. Prepare for respiratory support ED Management: - No antivenom available -

nodes.title: Cone Snail — Conotoxin
nodes.summary: Cone snail: conotoxin causes neuromuscular paralysis — pressure immobilization, prepare for intubation
nodes.body: Similar presentation to blue-ringed octopus Presentation: - Sting may be painful or painless - Rapid onset paralysis - Paresthesias, hypotension - Respiratory failure First Aid: - Pressure immobilization bandage - Prepare for cardiovascular and respiratory support ED Management: - No antivenom available - Supportive care only - May require intubation for respiratory failure - Monitor for cardiovas

nodes.title: Sea Snake Envenomation
nodes.summary: Sea snake: delayed myotoxicity and neurotoxicity — observe 8h minimum, antivenom if symptomatic
nodes.body: Rare but serious Presentation: - Small puncture wounds (often painless initially) - Symptoms appear 30 min to 2 hours: - Ptosis, dysphagia - Non-rigid paralysis - Myotoxicity (rhabdomyolysis) - Respiratory failure in severe cases First Aid: - Pressure immobilization bandage (same as terrestrial snake) - Complete immobilization of limb and patient ED Management: - Contact Poison Control early (rare
