nodes.title: Anaphylaxis Management
nodes.summary: Anaphylaxis from marine envenomation: epinephrine 0.3-0.5mg IM, standard anaphylaxis protocol
nodes.body: If antivenom reaction occurs: 1. Stop infusion immediately 2. Maintain airway 3. Epinephrine 0.3-0.5mg IM (anterolateral thigh) 4. IV fluids NS bolus 5. H1 blocker: Diphenhydramine 50mg IV 6. H2 blocker: Famotidine 20mg IV 7. Methylprednisolone 125mg IV For envenomation-related anaphylaxis (rare): - Same protocol as above - Consider repeat epinephrine q5-15min if needed Note: True anaphylaxis from

nodes.title: Disposition Criteria
nodes.summary: Admit for systemic symptoms, cardiovascular instability, or need for antivenom — observe 4-6h minimum
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: - Pain controlled with oral analgesics - No systemic symptoms after 3-4 hour observation - Wound care instructions provided - Tetanus prophylaxis complete - Antibiotics prescribed if indicated Admit If: - Severe muscle cramping - Respiratory distress or paralysis - Hypotension or arrhythmias - Antivenom administration - Irukandji syndrome with ongoing symptoms - Blue-ringed oct

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: Discharge minor stings with wound care instructions, tetanus update, and return precautions
nodes.body: Wound Care: - Keep wound clean and dry - Watch for signs of infection (increasing redness, warmth, purulent drainage, fever) - Complete antibiotic course if prescribed - Follow up in 48-72 hours for deep punctures Return Precautions: Return immediately for: - Signs of infection - Worsening pain after initial improvement - New systemic symptoms (difficulty breathing, swallowing) - Fever Antibiotic
nodes.recommendation: Provide written wound care instructions and ensure patient understands return precautions.

nodes.title: Admission Indications
nodes.summary: Admit for antivenom, systemic envenomation, or wound complications — ICU for cardiovascular instability
nodes.body: ICU Admission: - Antivenom administration (anaphylaxis risk) - Respiratory failure or need for intubation - Cardiac arrhythmias or arrest - Blue-ringed octopus envenomation (even if currently stable) - Severe Irukandji syndrome Floor Admission: - Ongoing IV analgesia requirement - Observation for delayed systemic symptoms - IV antibiotics for severe wound infection - Penetrating trauma post-surger

nodes.title: Massive Hemoptysis
nodes.summary: Life-threatening hemoptysis: death is from drowning, not exsanguination — adult airway holds only 150-200 mL
nodes.body: Life-threatening hemoptysis = any volume causing: • Airway obstruction • Respiratory failure • Hemodynamic instability Volume thresholds (no consensus): • Classic: ≥600 mL/24h • Alternative: ≥200 mL/single episode OR ≥100 mL/hr • Best mortality predictor: ≥300 mL expectorated [1] Key insight: Adult tracheobronchial space is only 150-200 mL — even "small" volumes can cause asphyxiation. Death is fr

nodes.title: Etiology
nodes.summary: Bronchiectasis/lung CA most common in US, TB worldwide — 90% from bronchial arteries at systemic pressure
nodes.body: US/Developed Countries: | Cause | Frequency | |-------|----------| | Bronchiectasis | 20-30% | | Bronchogenic CA | 20-25% | | Chronic bronchitis | 15-20% | | Pneumonia | 10-15% | | Mycetoma/aspergilloma | 5-10% | Worldwide: TB is most common (7-85% by region) [1][2] Other causes: • Vascular: PE, pulmonary AVM, Rasmussen aneurysm (TB) • Iatrogenic: Post-biopsy, PA catheter perforation • Autoimmune:

nodes.title: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: O2, large-bore IVx2, T&C, STAT CXR to lateralize — route by stability: stable workup, unstable airway, or arrest
nodes.body: Simultaneous actions: 1. Supplemental O₂ (target SpO₂ >92%) 2. Large-bore IV x2 3. Type & crossmatch 4. STAT labs: CBC, BMP, coags (INR, PTT, fibrinogen), ABG 5. Review medications (anticoagulants, antiplatelets) STAT portable CXR — may lateralize bleeding (~50% sensitivity) What is the patient's hemodynamic and respiratory status?

nodes.title: Stable Patient Workup
nodes.summary: CTA bronchial artery protocol before bronchoscopy (75% vs 50% yield) — start TXA empirically, low threshold to escalate
nodes.body: CT Chest with IV Contrast (bronchial artery protocol preferred) • CT before bronchoscopy has superior yield (~75% vs ~50%) [2] • Identifies source, etiology, bronchial artery anatomy for IR While awaiting CT: • Continuous SpO₂ monitoring • Have airway equipment ready • Position patient if side known • Start TXA empirically Low threshold to escalate — edema/clot can compromise airway rapidly [1][2]

nodes.title: Positioning — Bleeding Side DOWN
nodes.summary: Bleeding side DOWN — uses gravity to protect good lung; up to 35% plasma volume can extravasate
nodes.body: Lateral decubitus with bleeding lung DOWN • Uses gravity to prevent spillage into unaffected lung • Apply as soon as bleeding is lateralized • Prioritize lung protection over V/Q matching [1] If side unknown: Patient upright or semi-recumbent to minimize aspiration. Up to 35% plasma volume can extravasate during severe hemoptysis — lay flat only after hemorrhage control or intubation.

nodes.title: Airway Decision
nodes.summary: Intubation for ineffective cough, SpO2 <90%, AMS, hemodynamic instability, or procedural airway control
nodes.body: Indications for intubation: • Ineffective cough with blood accumulation • Worsening hypoxemia (SpO₂ <90% despite O₂) • Altered mental status • Hemodynamic instability • Procedural airway control needed [1] Does the patient need intubation?

nodes.title: ETT Selection & Intubation
nodes.summary: Use LARGE ETT ≥8.5mm — facilitates bronchoscopy/blocker/suctioning; avoid double-lumen (clogs, narrow, difficult)
nodes.body: Use LARGE ETT: | Patient | Minimum ETT | |---------|-------------| | Average/tall men | 9.0 mm | | Average women | 8.0-8.5 mm | | General rule | ≥8.5 mm ID | Rationale: Facilitates bronchoscopy, endobronchial blocker placement, and suctioning [1][2] Why NOT double-lumen ETT: • Difficult emergent placement • Narrow lumens clog with blood • Cannot pass therapeutic bronchoscope • Only 7% of physician

nodes.title: Single-Lung Isolation
nodes.summary: Mainstem intubation or endobronchial blocker to isolate bleeding lung — confirm position with fiberoptic bronchoscopy
nodes.body: Option 1: Mainstem Intubation • Advance ETT into unaffected bronchus • Use bougie with 1/4 turn technique • Right mainstem easier to cannulate Option 2: Endobronchial Blocker (preferred) • Options: Arndt, Cohen, EZ-Blocker, Fuji Uniblocker • Can isolate lobar/segmental bronchus (vs whole lung) • Temporizing measure for 48-72 hours [1] Confirmation: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy through ETT to verify pos

nodes.title: Arrest / Peri-Arrest Management
nodes.summary: Arrest: intubate with large ETT → advance into contralateral mainstem if side known → aggressive suction → ACLS
nodes.body: Immediate actions: 1. Intubate with large ETT (≥8.5 mm) 2. If side known: advance ETT into contralateral mainstem bronchus 3. Suction aggressively 4. Standard ACLS resuscitation Consider: • Emergent rigid bronchoscopy if available • VA-ECMO if refractory arrest from reversible cause • Emergent thoracotomy (massive trauma with hemothorax source) Treat the underlying cause — this is a potentially re

nodes.title: Medical Management — "Cause a Clot"
nodes.summary: The 5 Cs: Compression, Cold, Coagulants (TXA), Causteries, Constriction (vasoconstrictors)
nodes.body: Hemostatic therapies: 1. Tranexamic Acid (TXA) — first-line 2. Cold saline lavage 3. Topical vasoconstrictors (bronchoscopic) 4. Coagulopathy reversal Pneumonic: The 5 C's [2] • Compression (wedge, balloon) • Cold (ice saline lavage) • Coagulants (TXA, thrombin) • Causteries (APC, electrocautery) • Constriction (vasoconstrictors)

nodes.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
nodes.summary: Nebulized TXA 1000mg load → 500mg q8h preferred; IV 500mg TID alternative; 96% resolution within 5 days in RCT
nodes.body: Nebulized TXA (preferred): | Regimen | Dose | |---------|------| | Loading | 1000 mg nebulized x1 | | Maintenance | 500 mg nebulized q8h | | Alternative | 250-500 mg q6-12h | IV TXA (if neb impairs expectoration): • 500 mg IV TID • Or standard trauma: 1g bolus → 1g over 8h Bronchoscopic instillation: • 500 mg diluted in 15 mL NS Evidence: RCT showed 96% bleeding resolution within 5 days (TXA) vs 5

nodes.title: Cold Saline Lavage
nodes.summary: Cold saline 50mL aliquots at 4°C via bronchoscope — topical epi 1:10,000 for vasoconstriction (arrhythmia risk)
nodes.body: Technique (bronchoscopic): • 50 mL aliquots of saline at 4°C • Average total: ~500 mL until bleeding stops • Mechanism: vasoconstriction Adverse effect: Transient sinus bradycardia [2] Topical Vasoconstrictors: | Agent | Dose | |-------|------| | Epinephrine | 2 mL of 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) | | Phenylephrine | 5 mL of 80-100 mcg/mL | Caution with epinephrine: Risk of fatal arrhythmia reported [2]

nodes.title: Coagulopathy Assessment
nodes.summary: Check for anticoagulant/antiplatelet use — route to agent-specific reversal or proceed to bronchoscopy
nodes.body: Check for anticoagulant/antiplatelet use: Is the patient on anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy?

nodes.title: Warfarin Reversal
nodes.body: | Agent | Dose | Onset | |-------|------|-------| | Vitamin K | 10 mg IV over 30 min | 6-12 hours | | 4-Factor PCC | 25-50 units/kg | Minutes | | FFP (if PCC unavailable) | 15 mL/kg | After thaw | CRITICAL: Give Vitamin K WITH PCC/FFP. PCC/FFP effect lasts ~8 hours; Vitamin K takes 6-12 hours to work [1]
nodes.recommendation: Reverse warfarin with 4F-PCC + Vitamin K. PCC provides immediate reversal; Vitamin K sustains it.

nodes.title: DOAC Reversal
nodes.body: Direct thrombin inhibitor (Dabigatran): • Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5g IV Factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban): • Andexanet alfa (if available) • OR 4-Factor PCC 50 units/kg [1]
nodes.recommendation: Reverse dabigatran with idarucizumab. For Xa inhibitors, use andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC.

nodes.title: Heparin Reversal
nodes.body: Unfractionated Heparin: • Protamine 1 mg per 100 units heparin (max 50 mg) • Dose based on heparin given in last 2-3 hours LMWH (enoxaparin): • Protamine reverses ~60% of effect • 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin (if within 8 hours) Note: Protamine can cause hypotension, bradycardia, anaphylaxis [1]
nodes.recommendation: Reverse UFH with protamine. LMWH only partially reversed.

nodes.title: Bronchoscopy
nodes.summary: Flexible bronchoscopy first for localization (93% success), rigid if therapeutic intervention needed for massive bleeding
nodes.body: Flexible bronchoscopy: • Localizes bleeding (93% success) • Can perform at bedside/ICU • Limited suction capacity, blood obscures view Rigid bronchoscopy: • Superior suction and visualization • Therapeutic: packing, APC, laser • Requires OR + general anesthesia Recommendation: Flexible first for localization; rigid if therapeutic intervention needed or massive bleeding [1][2]

nodes.title: Bronchial Artery Embolization (BAE)
nodes.summary: BAE first-line definitive therapy — 92-97% technical success; recurrence 10-58% (highest with aspergilloma/TB)
nodes.body: First-line definitive therapy for most patients [1][2] Success rates: • Technical success: 92-97% • Clinical success: 70-93% • Recurrence: 10-58% (varies by etiology) • Major complication rate: 0.1% Embolization materials: • PVA particles (355-500 µm) — CIRSE recommended • N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) — lowest recurrence • Coils, Gelfoam High recurrence risk: • Aspergilloma/mycetoma (highest) • Tu

nodes.title: Surgery Considerations
nodes.summary: Surgery if BAE fails or recurrent — lobectomy preferred over pneumonectomy (2x mortality); emergency surgery 10-40% mortality
nodes.body: Surgical indications: 1. BAE technical failure 2. Recurrent hemoptysis despite multiple BAEs 3. Life-threatening bleeding precluding safe BAE 4. Localized, resectable lesion with adequate pulmonary reserve Procedures: Lobectomy (preferred) > bi-lobectomy > pneumonectomy Mortality: • Emergency surgery: 10-40% • Pneumonectomy: 2x mortality vs lobectomy [1][2]

nodes.title: Surgical Intervention
nodes.body: Best surgical candidates: • Previously healthy patients • Localized disease (aspergilloma, broncholith, abscess) • Adequate FEV1 for resection Poor surgical candidates: • Diffuse lung disease (COPD, bronchiectasis) • Advanced malignancy • Bilateral disease Consult CT Surgery EARLY — even if BAE planned, surgery may be needed as backup [1]
nodes.recommendation: CT surgery consult for surgical evaluation. Lobectomy preferred over pneumonectomy.

nodes.title: Additional Therapies
nodes.summary: Vasopressin analogues (case reports only), bronchoscopic hemostatic agents: Surgicel, fibrin glue, APC, electrocautery
nodes.body: Vasopressin analogues (case reports only): • Terlipressin (Glypressin) — IV or endobronchial • Endobronchial has similar efficacy with 251x lower plasma concentration • Desmopressin — used in CF, leptospirosis Bronchoscopic hemostatic agents: • Oxidized regenerated cellulose (Surgicel) • Thrombin/fibrin glue • Argon plasma coagulation (APC) • Electrocautery, laser [2]

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: All massive/life-threatening hemoptysis requires ICU. ICU indications: • Any massive hemoptysis • Ongoing bleeding despite initial treatment • Respiratory failure or intubation • Hemodynamic instability • Post-BAE or bronchoscopy monitoring • Active coagulopathy reversal [1] Consults: • Interventional Radiology (BAE) • Interventional Pulmonology • CT Surgery (backup for BAE failure)
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for all massive hemoptysis. Continue monitoring, consult IR/IP/CT surgery.

nodes.title: Transfer Considerations
nodes.body: Transfer if your facility lacks: • Interventional radiology with BAE capability • Interventional pulmonology • Cardiothoracic surgery • ICU with ventilator capability Stabilize and transfer EARLY — do not delay for diagnostic workup. Transfer essentials: • Large-bore IV access (x2) • Intubated with large ETT if airway threatened • Bleeding side down positioning • TXA started • Type & screen/crossm
nodes.recommendation: Transfer early if lacking BAE, IP, or CT surgery. Stabilize before transfer.

nodes.title: Massive Transfusion Protocol
nodes.summary: Activate early — gestalt + ABC >=2, no wait for labs
nodes.body: MTP Steps Summary — quick reference. Definition: Transfusion of ≥10 units pRBCs in 24h, OR ≥4 units pRBCs in 1h with ongoing hemorrhage, OR replacement of >50% blood volume in 3h. [1,2] Key principle: Activate MTP early — waiting for lab confirmation of coagulopathy costs lives. Clinical gestalt + prediction scores guide activation. [1,3] Calculators: • ABC Score — MTP prediction • Shock Index — H

nodes.title: What Is the Etiology?
nodes.summary: Trauma, GI, PPH, AAA — ABC >=2 predicts MTP need
nodes.body: Common MTP indications: • Trauma (penetrating > blunt) • Massive GI hemorrhage • Postpartum hemorrhage • Ruptured AAA • Surgical bleeding ABC Score ≥2 predicts need for MTP with ~75% sensitivity. [4]

nodes.title: Trauma — MTP Activation Criteria
nodes.summary: ABC: penetrating+SBP<=90+HR>=120+FAST — >=2 activate
nodes.body: Activate MTP if ANY of the following: • ABC Score ≥2 • Shock Index >1.0 with evidence of hemorrhage • SBP <90 mmHg with suspected hemorrhage • Penetrating torso trauma with hypotension • Clinical gestalt: "this patient is bleeding out" ABC Score components: • Penetrating mechanism (+1) • SBP ≤90 mmHg on arrival (+1) • HR ≥120 bpm on arrival (+1) • Positive FAST exam (+1) Score ≥2: Sensitivity 75%,

nodes.title: GI Hemorrhage — MTP Considerations
nodes.summary: Unstable or >2 units/hr — GI early, endoscopy stops it
nodes.body: Activate MTP for GI bleed if: • Hemodynamic instability despite initial resuscitation • Ongoing transfusion requirement >2 units pRBCs/hour • Active hematemesis or hematochezia with shock • Shock Index >1.0 Key differences from trauma: • Often older patients with comorbidities • Anticoagulation is common — may need reversal • Endoscopy is definitive treatment • Call GI early — intervention stops b

nodes.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage — MTP
nodes.summary: TXA 1g within 3hrs + massage + uterotonics simultaneously
nodes.body: Definition: Blood loss ≥1000 mL OR signs of hypovolemia regardless of volume. [7] Activate MTP for PPH if: • EBL >1500 mL with ongoing bleeding • Hemodynamic instability • Coagulopathy developing (oozing from IV sites, mucosa) Critical actions in parallel: • Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV over 10 min (WOMAN trial — give within 3h of delivery) [8] • Uterine massage • Oxytocin (Pitocin) 40 units in 1L NS at

nodes.title: Ruptured AAA / Vascular Emergency
nodes.summary: AAA: permissive SBP 70-90 until aortic control
nodes.body: Immediate priorities: • Activate MTP immediately — these patients die from exsanguination • Permissive hypotension: target SBP 80-90 mmHg (conscious) • Avoid over-resuscitation — "popping the clot" • Call vascular surgery STAT Blood pressure targets: • Ruptured AAA: SBP 70-90 mmHg until aortic control [9] • Balance: too low = end-organ damage; too high = accelerated bleeding Blood products: • Star

nodes.title: Surgical Bleeding — MTP
nodes.summary: Damage control: stop bleeding, contamination, ICU, return OR
nodes.body: Intraoperative MTP activation criteria: • Estimated blood loss >50% of blood volume • Ongoing transfusion >4 units pRBCs in 1 hour • Unable to achieve surgical hemostasis • Developing coagulopathy (microvascular bleeding) Communication is critical: • Blood bank notification • Anesthesia — maintain normothermia • Nursing — prepare MTP cooler workflow • Consider cell saver if available Damage contro

nodes.title: Initial Resuscitation While Awaiting Blood
nodes.summary: Large IVx2/IO, max 1-2L crystalloid — TXA within 3hrs
nodes.body: Immediate actions (first 5 minutes): • Large-bore IV access: 2 × 16-18G peripheral or IO access • Type and crossmatch STAT (use rapid sample tube if available) • Activate MTP per hospital protocol • Crystalloid: 1-2 L LR or NS (avoid excessive crystalloid — dilutional coagulopathy) [10] • Consider permissive hypotension (SBP 80-90) in trauma, except TBI [9] Adjuncts: • Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV over

nodes.title: Blood Product Ratios — 1:1:1
nodes.summary: PROPPR: 1:1:1 (pRBC:FFP:plt) improved hemostasis
nodes.body: PROPPR Trial: 1:1:1 ratio (pRBC:FFP:platelets) improved hemostasis and reduced death from exsanguination compared to 1:1:2 at 24h (9.2% vs 14.6%). No difference in 24h or 30d mortality overall. [12] Practical 1:1:1: • 6 units pRBCs : 6 units FFP : 1 apheresis platelet (or 6-pack random donor) • MTP Component Calculator — calculates products needed Whole blood option: • Low-titer O whole blood incr

nodes.title: MTP Cooler Contents
nodes.summary: 6 pRBC + 6 FFP + 1 plt — switch type-specific ASAP
nodes.body: Initial MTP cooler (typical): • 6 units pRBCs (O-negative initially, then type-specific) • 6 units FFP (AB plasma is universal donor) • 1 apheresis platelet pack (or 6 random donor units) Subsequent coolers: • Released q15-30 min as long as MTP active • Switch to type-specific blood ASAP (preserves O-negative supply) • Communicate ongoing needs to blood bank Additional products to consider: • Cryo

nodes.title: Calcium Replacement
nodes.summary: CaCl 1g per 4 units — citrate chelation causes dysfunction
nodes.body: Why calcium matters: • Blood products contain citrate as anticoagulant • Citrate chelates ionized calcium → hypocalcemia • Low iCa → impaired coagulation + cardiac dysfunction + vasodilation [15] Dosing rule of thumb: • Calcium Chloride 1 g IV per 4 units blood products • OR Calcium Gluconate 3 g IV per 4 units • CaCl provides 3× more elemental calcium than Ca gluconate Target: iCa >1.0 mmol/L (id

nodes.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
nodes.summary: 1g IV 10min then 1g 8hrs — MUST within 3hrs, harmful after
nodes.body: Critical timing: Give within 3 hours of injury/onset! [11] CRASH-2 Trial: TXA given within 3h reduced death from bleeding (4.9% vs 5.7%). Given after 3h, TXA INCREASED mortality (4.4% vs 3.1%). [11] Dosing: • Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 hours (CRASH-2 protocol) • Alternative: 2 g IV/IO single bolus (no infusion required) — the optimal regimen remains unresolved; the 2025

nodes.title: Rh Considerations
nodes.summary: O-neg females <50 unknown Rh — O-pos males/postmenopausal OK
nodes.body: When to use O-negative vs O-positive pRBCs: O-negative (Rh-negative) — Use for: • Females of childbearing potential (age <50) with unknown Rh status • Pregnant patients • Known Rh-negative patients • Children with unknown type O-positive (Rh-positive) — Acceptable for: • Males of any age • Females >50 years (post-menopausal) • Known Rh-positive patients Why this matters: • O-negative blood is scar

nodes.title: RhoGAM Indications
nodes.summary: RhoGAM 300mcg/15mL Rh-pos — large = hematology consult
nodes.body: When to give RhoGAM (Rh Immune Globulin): Rh-negative female of childbearing age who receives Rh-positive blood products. Dosing: • RhoGAM 300 mcg IM covers ~15 mL of Rh-positive RBCs (~30 mL whole blood) • For larger exposures: 300 mcg per 15 mL RBCs transfused • Give within 72 hours of exposure (earlier is better) Calculating dose for massive transfusion: • If patient received 10 units Rh-positi

nodes.title: Goal-Directed Resuscitation
nodes.summary: TEG/ROTEM 10-15min real-time clot — guides components
nodes.body: TEG (thromboelastography) and ROTEM (rotational thromboelastometry) provide real-time assessment of clot formation and breakdown. Advantages over standard coags: • Results in 10-15 min (vs 45-60 min for PT/PTT) • Tests whole blood clotting (not just plasma) • Detects hyperfibrinolysis (TXA indication) • Guides specific component therapy [18]

nodes.title: TEG/ROTEM Normal Values
nodes.summary: R 5-10, MA 50-70, LY30 0-3% — know normals
nodes.body: TEG Parameters: • R-time (reaction time): 5-10 min — time to initial fibrin formation • K-time (kinetics): 1-3 min — time to achieve certain clot strength (20 mm) • Alpha angle: 53-72° — rate of clot strengthening • MA (maximum amplitude): 50-70 mm — clot strength (platelet + fibrin) • LY30 (lysis at 30 min): 0-3% — clot stability/fibrinolysis ROTEM Parameters (approximate equivalents): • CT (clot

nodes.title: TEG/ROTEM Interpretation Algorithm
nodes.summary: Long R=FFP, low MA=plt, high LY30=TXA — targeted
nodes.body: Prolonged R-time (or CT) → Factor deficiency → Give FFP • R >10 min or CT >79 sec • Indicates inadequate factor levels to initiate clot • Treatment: FFP 10-15 mL/kg or PCC Prolonged K-time (or CFT) / Low alpha angle → Fibrinogen deficiency → Give Cryo • K >3 min or low alpha angle • Indicates poor fibrin contribution to clot • Treatment: Cryoprecipitate 10 units (target fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL)

nodes.title: Goal-Directed Transfusion
nodes.summary: Start 1:1:1, adjust with TEG when available
nodes.body: TEG/ROTEM-guided vs empiric 1:1:1: Empiric 1:1:1 approach: • Simple, fast, no delay waiting for results • May over-transfuse some components • Standard of care when TEG/ROTEM unavailable Goal-directed approach: • Give specific products based on TEG/ROTEM results • May reduce total blood product usage • Requires trained interpretation and available testing [19] Hybrid approach (pragmatic): • Start

nodes.title: MTP Termination & Complications
nodes.summary: MTP termination, transition, complications
nodes.body: Select the topic for detailed guidance.

nodes.title: When to Terminate MTP
nodes.summary: Stop: controlled + stable + lactate trending down
nodes.body: Criteria for MTP deactivation: • Surgical/procedural bleeding control achieved • Hemodynamic stability without ongoing transfusion (MAP >65, HR <100) • Lactate trending down • Base deficit improving • No clinical evidence of ongoing hemorrhage • TEG/ROTEM normalizing (if available) Communication: • Notify blood bank that MTP is terminated • Cancel pending coolers • Return unused products to blood

nodes.title: Transition to Maintenance
nodes.summary: Hgb>7, INR<1.5, fib>150, plt>50k, rewarm>36C
nodes.body: Post-MTP management: Hemoglobin target: • Most patients: Hgb 7-8 g/dL • Active coronary disease: Hgb 8-9 g/dL • Ongoing bleeding: Higher threshold Coagulation targets: • INR <1.5 • Fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL • Platelets >50,000 (>100,000 for CNS injury) • iCa >1.0 mmol/L Rewarming: • Target core temp >36°C • Active warming: Bair Hugger, warm IV fluids, warm blankets • Hypothermia impairs coagulatio

nodes.title: MTP Complications
nodes.summary: Lethal triad: hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy
nodes.body: Lethal triad of trauma: Hypothermia + Acidosis + Coagulopathy [20] Hypothermia: • Core temp <36°C impairs clotting enzymes • Warm all products, active rewarming Hypocalcemia: • Citrate in blood products chelates calcium • Monitor iCa, give CaCl 1 g per 4 units • Symptoms: hypotension, arrhythmia, tetany Hyperkalemia: • Stored blood has elevated K+ (cell lysis) • Older units have more K+ • Monitor

nodes.title: Post-MTP Labs & Monitoring
nodes.summary: Labs q1h — watch rebleeding 6-24hrs
nodes.body: Immediate post-MTP labs: • CBC (Hgb, Hct, platelets) • Coagulation: PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen • Chemistry: BMP (K+, Ca++, renal function) • ABG: pH, lactate, base deficit, iCa • TEG/ROTEM if available Monitoring schedule: • q1h labs during active resuscitation • q4-6h once stable • Continuous: ECG, SpO2, BP, urine output Target values post-MTP: • Hgb >7 g/dL (>8 if cardiac disease) • Platelets >50,0

nodes.title: Permissive Hypotension
nodes.summary: SBP 80-90 except TBI >100-110 — minimize crystalloid
nodes.body: Concept: Accept lower-than-normal BP to avoid "popping the clot" with aggressive fluid resuscitation. [9] Target SBP: • Trauma without TBI: 80-90 mmHg • Ruptured AAA: 70-90 mmHg until aortic control • GI bleed: 90-100 mmHg EXCEPTIONS — Target higher BP: • Traumatic brain injury: SBP >100-110 mmHg (avoid secondary brain injury) • Spinal cord injury: MAP >85 mmHg • Elderly with chronic hypertension:

nodes.title: Damage Control Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Permissive + hemostatic + damage control surgery
nodes.body: Three pillars of damage control resuscitation: 1. Permissive hypotension • Target SBP 80-90 mmHg (except TBI) • Minimize crystalloid 2. Hemostatic resuscitation • 1:1:1 ratio blood products • TXA within 3 hours • Calcium replacement • Warm products 3. Damage control surgery • Abbreviated initial operation (stop bleeding, limit contamination) • Temporary abdominal closure • ICU resuscitation (corre

nodes.body: Select the special population for specific considerations.

nodes.title: Pediatric MTP
nodes.body: Weight-based dosing: [2,24] • pRBCs: 10-20 mL/kg • FFP: 10-15 mL/kg • Platelets: 5-10 mL/kg • Cryoprecipitate: 1-2 units/10 kg MTP activation criteria in peds: [24] • Estimated blood loss >40 mL/kg • Ongoing transfusion requirement • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation Special considerations: • Use appropriately sized blood tubing • Irradiated products for immunocompromised or neonates •

nodes.title: Anticoagulated Patient in MTP
nodes.body: Immediate reversal required for massive hemorrhage: [25] Warfarin: • 4-Factor PCC 25-50 units/kg IV • Vitamin K 10 mg IV over 30 min • Do NOT use FFP alone (volume-inefficient) Direct Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban): • Andexanet alfa if available OR • 4-Factor PCC 50 units/kg Dabigatran: • Idarucizumab 5 g IV OR • 4-Factor PCC 50 units/kg • Hemodialysis if idarucizumab unavailable Heparin/LM

nodes.title: Jehovah's Witness in MTP
nodes.body: Immediate priorities: • Establish patient's specific wishes (some accept certain fractions) • Document clearly in chart • Obtain ethics/legal consultation if unclear Acceptable to many Jehovah's Witnesses: • Albumin • Clotting factors (some accept PCC, fibrinogen concentrate) • Immunoglobulins • Cell saver (if circuit remains connected to patient) • EPO (erythropoietin) • Iron infusion Usually NOT

nodes.title: Measles - Clinical Recognition
nodes.summary: Fever + 3 Cs + rash — airborne isolation BEFORE workup
nodes.body: Suspect Measles When: - Fever (often >104F/40C) - Classic triad: Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis (the 3 Cs) - Maculopapular rash spreading cephalocaudally - Recent travel or exposure history - Unvaccinated or under-vaccinated patient Prodrome (2-4 days before rash): - High fever, malaise - 3 Cs develop progressively - Koplik spots (pathognomonic) may appear 1-2 days before rash Epidemiology: - R0 =

nodes.title: Airborne Isolation Protocol
nodes.summary: AIIR, N95, report health dept IMMEDIATELY
nodes.body: IMMEDIATE ISOLATION REQUIRED Room Requirements: - Negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room (AIIR) - Minimum 6 air changes per hour (12 preferred) - Direct exhaust to outside or HEPA filtration PPE for ALL Staff Entering: - N95 respirator (fit-tested) or PAPR - Gown and gloves - Eye protection if splash risk Patient Transport: - Patient wears surgical mask - Minimize transport; notify re

nodes.title: Assess Presumptive Immunity
nodes.summary: 2 MMR, pos IgG, prior disease, or born before 1957
nodes.body: Evidence of Immunity (any ONE): - Written documentation of 2 doses MMR vaccine (at least 28 days apart, first dose at age >= 12 months) - Laboratory evidence of immunity (positive IgG) - Laboratory confirmation of prior measles - Birth before 1957 in the US (considered immune due to natural exposure) Does the patient have evidence of presumptive immunity?

nodes.title: Consider Alternative Diagnoses
nodes.summary: 97% effective — DDx: drug rxn, roseola, rubella
nodes.body: Patient Has Evidence of Immunity Vaccine effectiveness is 93% (1 dose) to 97% (2 doses). Breakthrough measles is rare but possible. Alternative Diagnoses to Consider: - Drug hypersensitivity reaction (no prodrome, recent drug exposure) - Roseola infantum (usually <3 years, high fever resolves as rash appears) - Rubella (milder, lymphadenopathy prominent) - Parvovirus B19 (slapped cheek appearance)

nodes.title: Clinical Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Koplik spots pathognomonic — buccal mucosa before rash
nodes.body: Pathognomonic Finding: Koplik Spots - 1-3mm grayish-white papules on erythematous base - Location: buccal mucosa opposite upper 1st/2nd molars - "Salt grains on a red background" - Appear 1-2 days BEFORE rash, disappear 1-2 days AFTER rash - Present in 60-70% of cases Characteristic Rash: - Appears ~14 days post-exposure (3-7 days after prodrome) - Starts on face (hairline, behind ears) and neck -

nodes.title: Laboratory Confirmation
nodes.summary: PCR preferred early — NP + urine within 7d rash
nodes.body: Required for ALL Suspected Cases Serologic Testing: - Measles-specific IgM antibody - Sensitivity 83-89%, specificity 95-99% - May be negative first 72 hours after rash (false negative) - Obtain during rash or within 30 days RT-PCR Testing (Preferred): - Higher early sensitivity (94%), specificity 99% - Specimens: nasopharyngeal/throat swab AND urine - Urine + NP swab together improves sensitivity

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: High risk: <5yo, >20yo, pregnant, immunocompromised
nodes.body: Assess for Severe Measles: High-Risk Populations: - Age <5 years (especially <12 months) - Age >20 years - Pregnancy - Immunocompromised (HIV, chemotherapy, transplant) - Malnutrition or vitamin A deficiency Signs of Severe Disease: - Respiratory distress or hypoxia - Altered mental status - Severe dehydration (unable to drink, decreased UOP) - High fever refractory to antipyretics - Superimposed

nodes.title: Severe Measles Management
nodes.summary: Hospitalize — Vitamin A MANDATORY for all inpatients
nodes.body: Hospitalization Required Supportive Care: - IV fluids for dehydration - Supplemental oxygen PRN (target SpO2 >= 92%) - Antipyretics for fever control - Continuous monitoring Vitamin A - MANDATORY for Hospitalized Patients: - Reduces mortality and pneumonia-specific mortality - See Vitamin A Dosing Monitoring: - Watch for respiratory deterioration (pneumonia) - Neurologic status changes (encephalit

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Measles - Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Outpatient: hydration, antipyretics — NO abx or steroids
nodes.body: Outpatient Management: Supportive Measures: - Adequate oral hydration - Antipyretics (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for fever/discomfort - Rest - Dim lighting if photophobia present Vitamin A Supplementation: - Consider for all children with measles, even in US - Especially if: malnutrition risk, recent immigrant, vitamin A deficiency suspected - See Vitamin A Dosing What NOT to Give: - Antibiotics

nodes.title: Vitamin A Therapy
nodes.summary: 200,000 IU Day 1+2 — reduces mortality 64%
nodes.body: WHO/AAP Recommended Dosing: | Age | Dose | Schedule | |-----|------|----------| | <6 months | 50,000 IU PO | Day 1 and Day 2 | | 6-11 months | 100,000 IU PO | Day 1 and Day 2 | | >= 12 months | 200,000 IU PO | Day 1 and Day 2 | Administration: - Give immediately upon diagnosis - Repeat dose the following day (total 2 doses) - Give 3rd dose 2-4 weeks later if clinical signs of vitamin A deficiency

nodes.title: Complications Assessment
nodes.summary: Pneumonia #1 death — encephalitis 1/1000, 25% mortality
nodes.body: Common Complications: Respiratory (most common): - Otitis media (7-9% of cases) - Pneumonia (1 in 20 children) - leading cause of measles death - Primary viral (giant cell) pneumonia - Secondary bacterial pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, H. influenzae) Neurologic: - Acute encephalitis (1 in 1,000 cases) - Onset 3-10 days after rash - 25% mortality, 25% permanent neurologic sequelae - SSPE (sub

nodes.title: Measles Pneumonia
nodes.summary: Abx only documented bacterial superinfection
nodes.body: Pneumonia - Leading Cause of Measles Death Types: 1. Primary viral (giant cell) pneumonia - severe, may require ICU 2. Secondary bacterial pneumonia - more common, treatable Workup: - CXR (interstitial infiltrates vs lobar consolidation) - CBC, procalcitonin - Blood cultures - Sputum culture if productive - Consider respiratory viral panel (co-infection) Treatment: - Oxygen therapy (target SpO2 >=

nodes.title: Measles Encephalitis
nodes.summary: 3-10d: seizures, AMS — 25% mortality, 25% permanent
nodes.body: Acute Post-Measles Encephalitis Incidence: 1 in 1,000 cases Timing: 3-10 days after rash onset Presentation: - Fever recrudescence - Headache, altered mental status - Seizures (50%) - Focal neurologic deficits - Ataxia Workup: - CT head (rule out other causes) - LP (lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein) - MRI brain (periventricular demyelination) - EEG (diffuse slowing, epileptiform activity)

nodes.title: SSPE - Late Complication
nodes.summary: 7-10yrs fatal — vaccination only prevention
nodes.body: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE) A devastating late complication (7-10 years after infection) Incidence: - Historical estimate: 1 in 100,000 cases - More recent data: may be as high as 1 in 609 for infants <15 months - Higher risk: measles infection at age <2 years Pathophysiology: - Persistent measles virus infection in CNS - Progressive inflammatory and neurodegenerative process Clinic

nodes.title: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Identify exposed susceptible — virus airborne 2hrs
nodes.body: Identify Exposed Contacts Has anyone without evidence of immunity been exposed to this patient? Exposure = same airspace (room, enclosed area) as infectious patient: - 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset - Virus remains airborne for up to 2 hours Categories of Exposed Individuals: - Healthcare workers - Household contacts - Waiting room contacts - Other hospital patients/visitors Are there ex

nodes.title: PEP Timing Assessment
nodes.summary: MMR 72hrs or IG 6 days — timing determines PEP
nodes.body: Timing is Critical for PEP Efficacy Window for MMR Vaccine: Within 72 hours of exposure Window for Immune Globulin: Within 6 days of exposure How long since exposure occurred?

nodes.title: PEP with MMR Vaccine
nodes.summary: MMR >=6mo 72hrs — NOT pregnant, immunocomp, <6mo
nodes.body: MMR Vaccine PEP (within 72 hours of exposure) Eligible Patients: - Age >= 6 months (off-label 6-11 months during outbreak) - No contraindications to live vaccine - Not pregnant - Not severely immunocompromised Dosing: - Standard MMR dose subcutaneous - If age 6-11 months: dose does NOT count toward routine series (revaccinate at 12-15 months) - If age >= 12 months: counts as first dose NOT Eligibl

nodes.title: PEP with Immune Globulin
nodes.summary: IGIM infants, IVIG pregnant/immunocomp within 6 days
nodes.body: Immune Globulin PEP (within 6 days of exposure) Intramuscular IG (IGIM): - Dose: 0.5 mL/kg (max 15 mL) - Indicated for: - Infants <6 months of age - Infants 6-11 months if >72 hours post-exposure Intravenous IG (IVIG): - Dose: 400 mg/kg - Indicated for: - Pregnant women (any trimester) - Severely immunocompromised patients - When IGIM volume would be excessive Post-IG Vaccination: - Wait 6 months

nodes.title: Exposure >6 Days Ago
nodes.summary: Beyond 6d: neither effective — educate, self-isolate
nodes.body: Outside PEP Window Neither MMR nor IG will prevent infection if >6 days since exposure. Management: - Educate about symptoms to watch for - Instruct to self-isolate at first sign of illness - Provide clear return precautions - Coordinate with public health for monitoring Symptom Watch: - Fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes - Rash starting on face - Incubation: typically 10-14 days (rash ~14 days po

nodes.title: Public Health Reporting
nodes.summary: MANDATORY reporting — do NOT wait for lab confirm
nodes.body: MANDATORY IMMEDIATE REPORTING Measles is a nationally notifiable disease requiring IMMEDIATE reporting. Report to: - Local health department (same day) - State epidemiologist - CDC via state health department Information to Report: - Patient demographics - Vaccination history - Travel history (2-3 weeks before symptom onset) - Exposure history - Contact list for tracing - Laboratory results (when

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Admit respiratory, dehydrated, AMS, high-risk, no isolation
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: - Respiratory compromise or hypoxia - Severe dehydration (unable to maintain PO) - Altered mental status or neurologic concerns - High-risk patient (immunocompromised, pregnant, extremes of age) - Social concerns (cannot maintain isolation at home) - Suspected or confirmed complication Discharge Criteria: - Maintaining adequate hydration - No respiratory distress - No high-risk

nodes.title: Admit to AIIR
nodes.summary: AIIR, Vit A, ID consult, public health — N95 staff
nodes.body: Admission Orders: Isolation: - Airborne Infection Isolation Room (AIIR) - N95/PAPR for all staff entering - Maintain isolation 4 days after rash onset (longer if immunocompromised) Monitoring: - Continuous pulse oximetry - Neuro checks if encephalitis concern - Strict I/Os Treatment: - Vitamin A (age-based dosing) Day 1 and Day 2 - IV fluids PRN - Antipyretics - Antibiotics only for documented bac
nodes.recommendation: Admit to AIIR. Vitamin A, supportive care. ID and public health notification.

nodes.title: Discharge with Strict Isolation
nodes.summary: Home isolation 4d post-rash — no school/work/public
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions: Home Isolation - MANDATORY: - Strict isolation for 4 days after rash onset - Stay in separate room from other household members - No school, work, public places, or healthcare facilities - Other household members should be assessed for immunity Supportive Care: - Plenty of fluids - Antipyretics for fever - Rest Vitamin A: - Consider prescribing age-appropriate dose (2 doses
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with 4-day strict home isolation. Return precautions for respiratory distress, dehydration, or neurologic changes.

nodes.title: Psych Medical Stability
nodes.summary: Psych medical assessment: history, vitals, exam, mentation, and red flags drive testing; routine labs are not automatic.
nodes.body: Steps Summary Use "medical assessment/stability," not a blanket clearance mindset. Why this matters: • Medical mimics are uncommon in low-risk known psychiatric presentations, but high-impact when red flags are present • Missed medical diagnoses in psychiatric patients are reported across a wide range because risk depends heavily on age, vitals, exam, delirium, intoxication, and baseline history •

nodes.title: Vital Signs — Always Check
nodes.summary: Always check vitals + glucose. Abnormal vitals = organic cause more likely.
nodes.body: AAEP Recommendation: Check vitals on ALL patients Red flag vitals: • HR >120 or <50 • SBP >180 or <90 • RR >25 or <10 • Temp >38.5°C or <35°C • O2 sat <94% Also check: • Glucose (fingerstick) — hypoglycemia mimics psych • Pupils — toxidrome clues If ANY vital abnormal: → Organic cause more likely

nodes.title: Psychiatric History
nodes.summary: Known psych history with similar presentation = lower organic risk. Unknown = higher.
nodes.body: Does patient have KNOWN psychiatric history with SIMILAR presentation?

nodes.title: Known Psychiatric History
nodes.summary: Known history + normal vitals/exam = low organic risk. Any red flag = workup needed.
nodes.body: Patient has known psychiatric history. Are there ANY concerning features?

nodes.title: Red Flags for Organic Cause
nodes.summary: Age >40 first episode, visual hallucinations, fluctuating course, abnormal vitals = organic.
nodes.body: Organic cause until proven otherwise if ANY present: Historical: • Age >40 with first psychiatric symptoms • Acute onset (hours-days vs weeks-months) • No prior psychiatric history • Recent head trauma • Known medical illness (cancer, HIV, thyroid) • New medications or recent changes Clinical: • Visual hallucinations (vs auditory) • Fluctuating consciousness • Disorientation (time, place, person)

nodes.title: Red Flag Assessment
nodes.summary: Red flags present = organic workup. No red flags but first episode = moderate workup.
nodes.body: Are ANY red flags present?

nodes.title: Delirium vs Psychosis
nodes.summary: Delirium = inattention, fluctuating, visual. Psychosis = intact attention, auditory.
nodes.body: KEY DISTINCTION — guides entire workup: | Feature | Delirium | Psychosis | |---------|----------|----------| | Onset | Acute (hours-days) | Gradual (weeks-months) | | Course | Fluctuating | Stable | | Attention | IMPAIRED | Intact | | Orientation | Disoriented | Often oriented | | Hallucinations | Visual | Auditory | | Vitals | Often abnormal | Usually normal | | Sleep-wake | Disrupted | Variable

nodes.title: CAM Assessment
nodes.summary: CAM positive = delirium (organic). CAM negative = likely primary psychosis.
nodes.body: Confusion Assessment Method (CAM): Feature 1: Acute onset AND fluctuating course Feature 2: Inattention (cannot focus on interview) Feature 3: Disorganized thinking (rambling, illogical) Feature 4: Altered level of consciousness (not alert) DELIRIUM = Feature 1 + Feature 2 + (Feature 3 OR 4)

nodes.title: Delirium Workup
nodes.summary: Delirium = I WATCH DEATH mnemonic. Full workup for underlying cause.
nodes.body: DELIRIUM = medical emergency Find the cause (I WATCH DEATH): • Infection (UTI, pneumonia, meningitis) • Withdrawal (alcohol, benzos, opioids) • Acute metabolic (glucose, Na+, Ca2+, uremia) • Trauma (head injury, pain) • CNS pathology (stroke, bleed, mass, seizure) • Hypoxia • Deficiencies (thiamine, B12) • Endocrine (thyroid, adrenal) • Acute vascular (MI, PE) • Toxins/drugs • Heavy metals Workup:

nodes.title: Delirium Labs
nodes.summary: Delirium: CBC, BMP, UA, tox screen. CT head if focal/trauma. Consider ammonia, TSH.
nodes.body: Standard delirium panel: Always: • CBC with differential • BMP (Na+, K+, glucose, BUN, Cr) • Urinalysis • Toxicology screen Consider: • LFTs, ammonia (hepatic encephalopathy) • TSH (thyroid storm/myxedema) • Lactate (sepsis) • Troponin (cardiac cause) • B12, folate (deficiency) • Blood cultures (sepsis) • VBG/ABG (hypoxia, acidosis) Imaging: • CT head if: trauma, focal findings, anticoagulation, n

nodes.title: Psychosis Workup
nodes.summary: First psychotic break: targeted labs based on risk; known typical psychosis with normal assessment often needs no routine labs.
nodes.body: Primary psychosis (CAM negative): Still consider organic causes: • Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (young women, ovarian teratoma) • Stimulant intoxication (especially meth, cocaine) • Medication toxicity (steroids, anticholinergics) • Thyroid storm • Autoimmune encephalitis First psychotic break workup: • Vitals, glucose, CBC, BMP • TSH when thyroid symptoms, mood syndrome, or unclear cause • Tox

nodes.title: Labs for Psychosis
nodes.summary: First episode = full workup. Known + typical = minimal. Known + atypical = full.
nodes.body: Which scenario?

nodes.title: First Psychotic Episode
nodes.summary: First episode: targeted labs; image for neurologic/atypical features or age >40; MRI can be non-emergent if stable.
nodes.body: First episode requires targeted medical assessment: Labs: • CBC, BMP, glucose • TSH when clinically indicated • Toxicology screen when substance-induced symptoms are plausible • UA if urinary symptoms, pregnancy concern, elderly, or delirium concern • RPR/HIV/B12/folate based on risk factors, atypical features, or local protocol Imaging: • ED CT for focal deficits, headache/seizure, trauma, deliri

nodes.title: Minimal Workup
nodes.summary: Known psych + typical + normal = glucose + pregnancy only. Routine labs not required.
nodes.body: Known psychiatric history + typical presentation + normal vitals/exam: AAEP Recommendation: • Routine labs are NOT required • Check fingerstick glucose • Check pregnancy (if applicable) • Address specific concerns only This approach is evidence-based: • Studies show routine labs rarely change management • Reduces ED length of stay • Focus resources on high-yield assessments

nodes.title: Moderate Risk Workup
nodes.summary: Moderate risk: glucose, CBC, BMP, tox, UA, TSH. Clinical judgment for more.
nodes.body: No red flags but first episode or unknown history: Reasonable workup: • Fingerstick glucose • CBC, BMP • Toxicology screen • UA (especially elderly) • TSH Clinical judgment drives additional testing. This is an intermediate approach — not as extensive as delirium but more than minimal.

nodes.title: Full Medical Workup
nodes.summary: Full workup: CBC, BMP, LFTs, ammonia, TSH, tox, UA, lactate, imaging.
nodes.body: Atypical presentation or unclear etiology: Full panel: • CBC, BMP • LFTs, ammonia • TSH • Toxicology screen • UA with culture • Lactate • VBG/ABG Imaging: • CT head (or MRI if available) • CXR Consider: • LP if encephalitis/meningitis concern • EEG if seizure concern • HIV, RPR, B12

nodes.title: Low Risk — Known Stable
nodes.summary: Low risk: glucose + pregnancy only. Routine labs not indicated.
nodes.body: Known psychiatric history + similar presentation + normal assessment: Required: • Fingerstick glucose • Pregnancy test (if applicable) Not required: • Routine CBC, BMP • Toxicology screen (unless clinically indicated) • Imaging AAEP evidence: Routine testing in this population rarely changes management and prolongs ED boarding.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition: medical admission, psych evaluation, or discharge.
nodes.body: Where does patient need to go?

nodes.title: Medical Admission
nodes.summary: Medical admission for active medical problem. Psych eval when stable.
nodes.body: Active medical problem identified: • Delirium requiring treatment • Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis) • Metabolic derangement • Intoxication/withdrawal requiring monitoring • Acute organ dysfunction Continue psychiatric assessment in parallel if safe to do so. Psychiatry can evaluate once medically stabilized.
nodes.recommendation: Admit to medicine for treatment of underlying medical condition.

nodes.title: Medically Stable for Psychiatry
nodes.summary: Medically stable — document vitals, exam, labs if obtained, and stability for psych eval.
nodes.body: Medical stability documentation: ✓ Vital signs reviewed and stable ✓ Physical exam performed ✓ Mental status exam documented ✓ Labs reviewed (if obtained) ✓ No acute medical condition requiring admission ✓ Patient stable for psychiatric evaluation Communicate to psychiatry: • Pertinent medical findings • Medications given in ED • Labs and imaging results • Ongoing medical issues (stable)
nodes.recommendation: Patient is medically stable for psychiatric evaluation/admission.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.summary: Discharge if stable, safe, with follow-up and crisis resources.
nodes.body: Criteria for discharge: • No acute medical condition • No imminent safety risk • Stable psychiatric condition • Safe disposition (home, with family) • Follow-up arranged Provide: • Outpatient psychiatry follow-up • Crisis resources (988 Lifeline) • Return precautions
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with outpatient follow-up and crisis resources.

nodes.title: Meningitis & Encephalitis
nodes.summary: Untreated = 100% mortality — abx within 1 HOUR
nodes.body: Meningitis/Encephalitis Steps Summary — quick reference. Infectious meningitis and encephalitis are life-threatening conditions requiring time-critical empiric treatment. Untreated bacterial meningitis approaches 100% mortality; even with therapy, mortality is 14\u201325%. [1,3,4,5] Herpes simplex encephalitis mortality was 70% prior to antiviral therapy; now ~9% with treatment. [7,15] \u2022 Meni

nodes.title: Clinical Suspicion
nodes.summary: ALL 4 absent = 99% rules out meningitis
nodes.body: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is present in only 44\u201366% of bacterial meningitis cases. [3,5] However, when headache is added as a 4th symptom: \u2022 At least 2 of 4 symptoms are present in 95% of cases [5] \u2022 At least 1 of 4 is present in 99\u2013100% of cases [5] Stated differently: Absence of ALL 4 symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness, alter

nodes.title: Physical Examination
nodes.summary: Kernig/Brudzinski 2% sens — petechiae = meningococcus
nodes.body: Kernig and Brudzinski signs: \u2022 Sensitivity: only 2% (essentially useless for ruling out) [13] \u2022 Specificity: 97\u201398% (useful when positive, but rarely positive) [13] Jolt accentuation of headache: \u2022 Originally reported sensitivity 65\u201397%, but subsequent studies show only 21% sensitivity, 82% specificity [13] \u2022 Inadequate to confirm or refute diagnosis Key exam findings

nodes.title: Focal Neurological Deficits?
nodes.summary: Focal = encephalitis — acyclovir + CT before LP
nodes.body: Focal deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, personality changes, seizures) indicate brain parenchyma involvement and the presence of encephalitis rather than isolated meningitis. [8] This distinction guides both the diagnostic workup (MRI utility) and empiric treatment (acyclovir).

nodes.title: Encephalitis Suspected
nodes.summary: Acyclovir 10mg/kg q8h — HSV 70% vs 9% treated
nodes.body: Immediately start empiric treatment: \u2022 Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h (HSV-1 most common endemic cause) [7,29] \u2022 PLUS empiric bacterial meningitis coverage (see next steps) [1,27] CT is indicated in all patients with focal deficits (mass lesion must be excluded before LP). [12,18,27] MRI is superior to CT for detecting encephalitis and can distinguish subtypes (e.g., HSV \u2192 temporal lobe

nodes.title: CT Before Lumbar Puncture?
nodes.summary: CT before LP only GCS<=12, papilledema, focal, seizures
nodes.body: CT Before LP Criteria \u2014 international guideline comparison. CT is NOT needed before LP in most patients. CT is insensitive for meningitis/encephalitis. [12] Herniation after LP is rare: only 0.1% deteriorated within 1 hour, and 91% who deteriorated had a prior normal CT. [18] CT IS indicated before LP if ANY of the following: [12,18,27]

nodes.title: Start Antibiotics \u2192 CT \u2192 LP
nodes.summary: Abx + dexa BEFORE CT — never delay for diagnostics
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Start empiric antibiotics and Dexamethasone BEFORE CT imaging. Do NOT delay treatment for any diagnostic test. [1,19,20,27] Delayed antibiotics correlate with disease progression and increased mortality. [19,20] Diagnostic tradeoff (basis for treating first): antibiotics given before LP reduce CSF culture sensitivity, but CSF PCR remains reliable for days afterward \u2014 so the diagnosi

nodes.title: Proceed to Lumbar Puncture
nodes.summary: No CT needed — LP directly, abx within 1 hour
nodes.body: No indications for CT before LP \u2014 proceed directly. Start empiric antibiotics within 1 hour of suspicion, ideally immediately after LP. [1] If LP will be delayed for any reason, start antibiotics first \u2014 never wait. Antibiotics before LP reduce culture sensitivity but PCR remains reliable for days. [11,12] Blood cultures should be drawn before antibiotics (66% yield in ABM). [5]

nodes.body: Cryptococcal meningitis is the 2nd highest cause of mortality in HIV/AIDS patients. *C. neoformans* causes ~1 million cases/year in HIV/AIDS, with ~600,000 annual deaths. [17] Typically subacute: weeks of evolving headache, neck stiffness, malaise. Serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg): 99.7% sensitive, 94.1% specific \u2014 send immediately. [17] Empiric antifungal regimen (after ID consultation): \u

nodes.title: Adjunctive Blood & Serum Studies
nodes.body: No blood test can substitute for CSF analysis. Useful adjuncts: Blood cultures: Up to 66% yield in ABM \u2014 collect before antibiotics. [5] Serum procalcitonin (PCT): Most discriminating biomarker for bacterial vs viral meningitis. [10,16] \u2022 PCT >0.25\u20130.5 ng/mL: 90\u201395% sensitivity, 98\u2013100% specificity for ABM [16] \u2022 More sensitive than any CSF marker for this purpose \u2

nodes.title: CSF Results Pattern
nodes.body: CSF Interpretation Guide \u2014 detailed reference with normal values and patterns. Compare CSF results to expected patterns. Note: 6% of culture-proven ABM cases lack elevated WBC, and 10% have lymphocyte-predominant differentials. Early bacterial meningitis may mimic viral patterns. [1,14]

nodes.title: Bacterial Meningitis \u2014 Tailored Management
nodes.body: Continue empiric antibiotics. Await Gram stain, culture, and PCR for pathogen identification. CSF Gram stain: 60\u201399% sensitivity, 97\u2013100% specificity. Sensitivity reduced after antibiotics. Negative Gram stain does NOT exclude bacterial meningitis. [5,14] CSF culture: Definitive diagnosis + antibiotic sensitivities. Sensitivity reduced >30% if LP performed >4 hours after antibiotics. *N.

nodes.title: Viral CSF Pattern \u2014 Assess for Encephalitis
nodes.body: Viral meningitis is generally self-limited with lower morbidity than bacterial. However, viral encephalitis (especially HSV-1) has high mortality without treatment. [6,7] Most common causes: Non-polio enteroviruses (23\u201361%), HSV-2, arthropod-borne viruses. [6] Assess for encephalitis features:

nodes.title: Viral Encephalitis Treatment
nodes.body: HSV-1 is the most common endemic cause of viral encephalitis in the Western world. [7] Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h \u2014 continue for all suspected encephalitis. [7,29] \u2022 In the landmark RCT (208 patients): acyclovir reduced mortality from 70% to 28% [7] \u2022 Contemporary mortality with acyclovir + ICU care: ~9% [15] If HSV-1 PCR negative but high clinical suspicion: \u2022 Continue acyclovi

nodes.title: Viral Meningitis Management
nodes.body: Viral meningitis is generally self-limited with lower mortality and fewer long-term complications than bacterial causes. [6] Management: \u2022 Supportive care: IV fluids, antiemetics, analgesics \u2022 No directed antiviral therapy has proven to affect outcomes for most viral causes [6] Important caveats: \u2022 Early bacterial meningitis may mimic viral patterns \u2014 25% of *L. monocytogenes*

nodes.title: Fungal Meningitis Management
nodes.body: Fungal meningitis is primarily a disease of immunocompromised populations. Most cases present subacutely with weeks of evolving symptoms. [8] Most common cause: *Cryptococcus neoformans* (~1 million cases/year in HIV/AIDS). [17] Other causes: *Histoplasma*, *Coccidioides*, *Candida* species. Treatment (requires ID consultation): \u2022 Induction (1 week): Amphotericin B liposomal 3\u20134 mg/kg/da

nodes.title: Equivocal CSF Results
nodes.body: When in doubt, treat as bacterial meningitis. Key pitfalls with equivocal CSF: \u2022 6% of culture-proven ABM cases have NO elevated WBC count [1,14] \u2022 10% of ABM cases have lymphocyte-predominant (not neutrophil) differentials [1,14] \u2022 25% of *L. monocytogenes* cases have normal or near-normal CSF findings [1] \u2022 Early in disease course, bacterial patterns may be incomplete \u2022

nodes.summary: Dexa q6h 2-4d — STOP if Listeria or Crypto
nodes.body: Corticosteroid Guide \u2014 detailed evidence and dosing. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h \u00d7 2\u20134 days [1,21,27] Give WITH or up to 15\u201320 minutes BEFORE first antibiotic dose. [1,27] Evidence (Cochrane 2015, 25 studies, 4121 patients): \u2022 Overall ABM: nonsignificant mortality reduction (17.8% vs 19.9%) [21] \u2022 Pneumococcal meningitis in high-income countries: significant morta

nodes.body: Disposition Criteria \u2014 discharge vs ward vs ICU criteria. Most patients with meningitis and encephalitis will be admitted. Determine appropriate level of care: [1,23]

nodes.title: Discharge \u2014 Low-Risk Viral Meningitis
nodes.body: Discharge criteria (extrapolated from pediatric data, use clinical judgment): [23] \u2022 Nontoxic clinical appearance \u2022 Normal serum WBC count \u2022 Mild CSF pleocytosis only \u2022 Negative CSF Gram stain \u2022 Adequate symptom control (headache, nausea, vomiting) \u2022 Reliable support system and follow-up capability Return precautions \u2014 discuss thoroughly: \u2022 Worsening headach
nodes.recommendation: Outpatient management of low-risk viral meningitis with strict return precautions and 3-day follow-up. Review Discharge Instructions with patient.

nodes.body: Indications: \u2022 Alert enough to maintain airway \u2022 Stable vital signs \u2022 Not receiving titratable medications \u2022 Does not require close neurological monitoring Ward management: \u2022 Continue IV antibiotics pending CSF analysis results \u2022 Tailor antimicrobial therapy once causative agent identified \u2022 Continue dexamethasone if bacterial meningitis suspected (discontinue if

nodes.title: ICU Admission

nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for continuous neurological monitoring, possible advanced airway, and aggressive treatment with specialist involvement

nodes.title: Acute Mesenteric Ischemia
nodes.summary: AMI = inadequate gut blood flow. 14% mortality if treated <12h; 80-100% if >24h. Pain out of proportion is classic.
nodes.body: AMI Decision Summary Definition: Life-threatening abdominal emergency from inadequate intestinal blood flow. Mortality: • 14% if treated within 12 hours • 80-100% if delayed >24 hours The Classic Presentation: Severe abdominal pain OUT OF PROPORTION to physical exam Patient appears in extreme distress; abdomen is soft with minimal tenderness. ⚠️ WSES: "Severe pain out of proportion should be assum

nodes.title: The 4 Types of AMI
nodes.summary: AMAE (40-50%, embolism), AMAT (25-30%, thrombosis), MVT (10-15%, venous), NOMI (20%, ICU/vasopressors).
nodes.body: Type determines treatment: | Type | % | Mechanism | Classic Patient | |------|---|-----------|----------------| | AMAE (Arterial Embolism) | 40-50% | Cardiogenic embolus to SMA | AFib, recent MI, valvular disease | | AMAT (Arterial Thrombosis) | 25-30% | Atherosclerotic plaque rupture | Known PVD, chronic mesenteric angina | | MVT (Venous Thrombosis) | 10-15% | Venous occlusion | Younger, hypercoa

nodes.title: Risk Factor Assessment
nodes.summary: High-risk: AFib, age >60, PVD, vasopressors, hypercoagulable. Low threshold for CTA in these patients.
nodes.body: Which risk factors are present? High-risk for AMI: • AFib or recent MI • Age >60 + unexplained severe abdominal pain • Known vascular disease (PVD, CAD) • Hypercoagulable state • ICU patient on vasopressors • History of postprandial pain / "food fear"

nodes.title: Physical Exam Findings
nodes.summary: Pain out of proportion = soft abdomen + severe pain. Peritonitis = late/necrosis → emergent surgery.
nodes.body: Classic triad: 1. Severe abdominal pain 2. Minimal tenderness on exam 3. Rapid clinical deterioration Late findings (necrosis): • Peritonitis / rebound • Bloody diarrhea • Shock Is peritonitis present?

nodes.title: Peritonitis — Emergent Laparotomy
nodes.summary: Peritonitis = immediate laparotomy. Resect necrotic bowel, revascularize, plan second-look at 24-48h.
nodes.body: 🛑 Peritonitis = immediate laparotomy regardless of type Do not delay for CTA if: • Clear peritonitis • Free air on imaging • Hemodynamic instability with obvious acute abdomen Surgical goals: • Assess bowel viability • Resect necrotic segments • Revascularize if possible • Plan second-look laparotomy at 24-48h Call: • Vascular Surgery • General Surgery • OR / Anesthesia STAT

nodes.title: CTA — The Gold Standard
nodes.summary: CTA = gold standard (93-100% sens). Biphasic protocol. Do NOT wait for labs. Look for SMA occlusion, wall thickening.
nodes.body: CT Angiography: Sensitivity 93-100%, Specificity 94-100% 🛑 Do NOT wait for labs — go straight to CTA Protocol: Biphasic CTA (arterial + venous phase) • Arterial phase: SMA/celiac occlusion, emboli • Venous phase: MVT, bowel wall enhancement CT Findings — Ischemia: • Filling defect in SMA • Bowel wall thickening >3mm • Absent bowel wall enhancement • "Target sign" / halo appearance • Mesenteric fa

nodes.title: CT Findings — Necrosis
nodes.summary: Pneumatosis + portal venous gas = transmural necrosis (78-81%). Surgical emergency.
nodes.body: Late/severe findings indicating NECROSIS: | Finding | Specificity | |---------|-------------| | Pneumatosis intestinalis (bowel wall gas) | 97-100% | | Portal venous gas | 94-100% | | Free intraperitoneal air | Perforation | | Loss of bowel wall enhancement | Transmural | ⚠️ Pneumatosis + portal venous gas = transmural necrosis in 78-81% This is a surgical emergency — go directly to OR.

nodes.title: Laboratory Studies
nodes.summary: Lactate >2 suggests irreversibility; >3.8 predicts mortality. BUT normal lactate does NOT rule out AMI.
nodes.body: Order but do NOT delay imaging: | Test | Finding | Significance | |------|---------|-------------| | Lactate | >2 mmol/L | Irreversible ischemia (HR 4.1) | | Lactate | >3.8 mmol/L | Predicts mortality | | WBC | Leukocytosis | >90% but nonspecific | | D-dimer | >0.9 mg/L | 82% specificity, 60% sensitivity | | BMP | Metabolic acidosis | Late finding | | Amylase | Elevated ~50% | Risk of pancreatitis

nodes.title: CTA Result
nodes.summary: CTA determines type: AMAE (embolism), AMAT (thrombosis), MVT (venous), NOMI (non-occlusive), or necrosis → OR.

nodes.title: Resuscitation — The 11 As
nodes.summary: The 11 As: Aggressive fluids, Antibiotics, Anticoagulation, Analgesia, Avoid vasopressors, consults.
nodes.body: The 11 As Checklist Start immediately while awaiting definitive treatment: 1. Aggressive fluids — LR boluses, blood products PRN 2. Address metabolic derangements — correct acidosis, K+, Mg2+ 3. Antibiotics — Pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h 4. Anticoagulation — Heparin 100 U/kg bolus → 18 U/kg/hr (use local protocol for maximum and monitoring adjustments) 5. Analgesia — IV opioids (do NOT withhold) 6. Avoid

nodes.title: Anticoagulation — Start Early
nodes.summary: Heparin 100 U/kg bolus → 18 U/kg/hr, goal aPTT 40-60. Start immediately — can reverse with protamine if needed.
nodes.body: Unfractionated Heparin (preferred): • Bolus: Heparin 100 U/kg IV when AMI is suspected (use local protocol for maximum and adjustments) • Infusion: 18 U/kg/hr • Goal aPTT: 40-60 seconds Why heparin: • Can be rapidly reversed with protamine if surgery needed • Early anticoagulation improves survival • Prevents clot propagation 🛑 Do NOT delay anticoagulation waiting for surgery Start immediately; i

nodes.title: Antibiotics — Immediate
nodes.summary: Pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h (or meropenem 1g q8h). Covers gut flora. Start immediately for bacterial translocation.
nodes.body: First-line: Piperacillin-Tazobactam • Pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h • Consider extended infusion (3-4 hours) for better tissue penetration • Excellent gut flora coverage (aerobic + anaerobic) Alternative: Meropenem 1g IV q8h (if ESBL concern) Rationale: • Bacterial translocation occurs early in ischemia • Gut flora includes anaerobes, gram-negatives, enterococci • Delay worsens sepsis and mortality

nodes.title: Avoid Vasopressors
nodes.summary: Vasopressors worsen AMI. If required: norepi + dobutamine combo. Avoid vasopressin. Minimize dose.
nodes.body: 🛑 Vasopressors worsen mesenteric ischemia If absolutely required: • Norepinephrine + Dobutamine combination • Dobutamine provides inotropic support, may offset norepi vasoconstriction • Minimize dose and duration ❌ Avoid vasopressin — direct splanchnic vasoconstriction NOMI patients: • Already on vasopressors = the cause • Optimize cardiac output • Wean pressors as able • Consider papaverine infu

nodes.title: Type-Specific Treatment
nodes.summary: Treatment differs by type: AMAE/AMAT (revascularization), MVT (anticoagulation), NOMI (treat underlying cause).
nodes.body: Select the confirmed or suspected AMI type: (Based on CTA findings and clinical presentation)

nodes.title: AMAE — Arterial Embolism
nodes.summary: AMAE: Endovascular aspiration embolectomy (88% success) or surgical Fogarty embolectomy. 38% need laparotomy.
nodes.body: No peritonitis → Endovascular first (if expertise available) Aspiration embolectomy: • 88% technical success • 26% in-hospital mortality • 38% still require subsequent laparotomy Surgical option: • Fogarty catheter embolectomy via SMA arteriotomy • Observe bowel viability 10-15 min post-revascularization Post-procedure: • Anticoagulation (continue heparin) • Plan second-look laparotomy if any viab

nodes.title: AMAT — Arterial Thrombosis
nodes.summary: AMAT: Endovascular stenting (17% mortality) > open surgery (38%). Hybrid ROMS for complex cases.
nodes.body: No peritonitis → Endovascular preferred Angioplasty and stenting: • 30-day mortality 17% (vs 38% open surgery) • Lower morbidity than open approach Surgical options: • Antegrade aortomesenteric bypass (preferred) • Autogenous saphenous vein if bowel perforation present • Transaortic endarterectomy Hybrid approach (ROMS): • Retrograde open mesenteric stenting • Combines laparotomy with endovascular

nodes.title: MVT — Venous Thrombosis
nodes.summary: MVT: Anticoagulation is primary treatment. Surgery only if peritonitis. 6 months minimum, lifelong if hypercoagulable.
nodes.body: Primary treatment: Anticoagulation Unfractionated heparin: • Continuous infusion • Early heparin improves survival Surgery only if peritonitis develops Duration: • Minimum 6 months anticoagulation • Lifelong if underlying hypercoagulability identified Thrombolytics: • Rarely indicated • SMA thrombolysis ineffective with increased bleeding risk Workup: • Hypercoagulability panel • Malignancy screen

nodes.title: NOMI — Non-Occlusive
nodes.summary: NOMI: Treat underlying cause (reduce vasopressors, optimize CO). Papaverine 30-60 mg/hr into SMA. Mortality 70-90%.
nodes.body: Primary treatment: Correct the underlying cause The cause is usually: • Vasopressor use (norepi, vasopressin) • Cardiogenic shock • Severe sepsis • Post-cardiac surgery Management: • Optimize cardiac output • Aggressive fluid resuscitation • STOP or minimize vasopressors • Systemic heparin Papaverine infusion: • Papaverine 30-60 mg/hr into SMA catheter • Continue ≥24 hours • Associated with lower

nodes.title: Surgical Considerations
nodes.summary: Assess viability: visual, Doppler, fluorescein. Damage control if unstable. Hand-sewn anastomosis preferred.
nodes.body: Intraoperative bowel viability assessment: • Visual inspection: Pink/healthy vs red/edematous vs black/necrotic • Peristalsis assessment • Doppler flow • Fluorescein angiography: 1g IV, Wood lamp (viable bowel fluoresces) Damage control surgery if: • Severe physiologic compromise • Extensive intestinal resection • Severe abdominal sepsis Anastomosis: • Hand-sewn preferred (bowel edema increases st

nodes.title: Second-Look Laparotomy
nodes.summary: Second-look at 24-48h if viability uncertain. 53% require additional resection. Do not skip if any concern.
nodes.body: Timing: 24-48 hours after initial surgery Indications: • Questionable bowel viability at initial surgery • Extensive involvement • MVT with significant mesenteric involvement Purpose: • Reassess viability after revascularization • Resect additional necrotic segments (occurs in 53%) • Avoid unnecessary resection of potentially viable bowel ⚠️ Do NOT skip second-look if any viability concern at init

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: All AMI patients to ICU. Monitor lactate clearance, CVP. Continue heparin and antibiotics.
nodes.body: ALL patients with confirmed AMI → ICU admission Post-operative monitoring: • Serial lactate clearance • Central venous oxygen saturation • Hemodynamics Continue: • Heparin infusion (aPTT 40-60) • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (minimum 4 days) • Enteral nutrition when tolerated

nodes.title: Long-Term Management
nodes.summary: Long-term anticoag based on type. CTA/duplex follow-up. 30-day mortality 17-51%. Short bowel syndrome risk.
nodes.body: Anticoagulation duration: | Indication | Duration | |------------|----------| | Post-stent | Clopidogrel 6 months + lifelong ASA | | MVT | Minimum 6 months; lifelong if hypercoagulable | | AFib | Lifelong anticoagulation | Follow-up: • CTA or duplex within 6 months, then annually • Cardiac evaluation • Carotid duplex if diffuse atherosclerosis Prognosis: • 30-day mortality: 17-51% depending on app

nodes.title: AMI Management Complete
nodes.summary: AMI complete. Pain out of proportion, CTA now, heparin + abx, avoid pressors, type-specific treatment.
nodes.body: Key Takeaways: 1. Pain out of proportion = AMI until proven otherwise 2. CTA immediately — do NOT wait for labs 3. Normal lactate does NOT rule out AMI 4. Start heparin and antibiotics immediately 5. Avoid vasopressors — worsen ischemia 6. Peritonitis = OR immediately 7. Type determines treatment: AMAE/AMAT (revascularize), MVT (anticoag), NOMI (treat cause) AMI Stop Page

nodes.title: Methemoglobinemia - Recognition
nodes.summary: Cyanosis no O2 response + SpO2 82-86% — brown blood
nodes.body: MetHb Overview Methemoglobinemia occurs when hemoglobin iron is oxidized from ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+) state, rendering it unable to bind oxygen. Normal MetHb is <2%. [1][2] Classic presentation: - Cyanosis unresponsive to supplemental oxygen (pathognomonic) - SpO2 reads 82-86% despite high FiO2 (pulse ox plateau) - Chocolate brown blood that does not turn red on exposure to air [1][3] - Sy

nodes.title: Mild Methemoglobinemia (MetHb 10-20%)
nodes.summary: 10-20%: pulse ox falsely 82-86% regardless
nodes.body: Typical symptoms: - Cyanosis (may be subtle) - Headache - Fatigue, malaise - Mild dyspnea on exertion Key finding: Cyanosis that does NOT improve with supplemental O2. [1] Pulse oximetry: Reads falsely in the 80s because MetHb absorbs light at wavelengths similar to both oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin. SpO2 plateaus at ~82-86% regardless of true oxygenation. [1][3] Brown blood test: Place drop of blood

nodes.title: Moderate Methemoglobinemia (MetHb 20-40%)
nodes.summary: 20-40%: confusion, dyspnea — functional Hb = capacity
nodes.body: Symptoms: - Altered mental status / confusion - Dyspnea at rest - Tachycardia - Syncope or presyncope - Chest pain - Dizziness, weakness Physical exam: - Central cyanosis (lips, mucous membranes) - Tachycardia - Tachypnea - May appear anxious or confused Key principle: MetHb level does not always correlate with symptoms. Patients with baseline anemia or cardiopulmonary disease tolerate MetHb poorl

nodes.title: Severe Methemoglobinemia (MetHb >40%)
nodes.summary: >40%: seizures, coma — MB empirically, no wait
nodes.body: CRITICAL - Immediate intervention required Symptoms: - Seizures - Coma - Cardiac arrhythmias - Myocardial ischemia - Cardiovascular collapse - Death (usually >70%) Immediate actions: 1. High-flow O2 via NRB - increases dissolved plasma O2 2. IV access - prepare for methylene blue 3. Cardiac monitoring - treat arrhythmias per ACLS 4. Draw co-oximetry STAT (venous or arterial) 5. Give Methylene Blue

nodes.title: Asymptomatic / Incidental Elevated MetHb
nodes.summary: Remove cause, O2, co-oximetry q2-4h until declining
nodes.body: Incidental finding on co-oximetry: Normal MetHb levels: - Non-smoker: <2% - Smoker: up to 3-4% If MetHb elevated but patient is asymptomatic: 1. Confirm no subtle symptoms (formal neuro exam) 2. Identify and remove causative agent 3. High-flow O2 via NRB 4. Serial MetHb levels q2-4h to confirm declining 5. Monitor for symptom development Treatment threshold: [1][2] - Symptomatic: Treat regardless

nodes.summary: Benzocaine, dapsone, nitrates — identify and remove

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Co-oximetry gold standard — pulse ox CANNOT detect
nodes.body: Essential testing: 1. Co-oximetry (GOLD STANDARD): [1][2] - Directly measures MetHb percentage - Venous or arterial - both accurate - Standard pulse ox and ABG O2 sat CANNOT detect MetHb 2. ABG/VBG: - PaO2 is NORMAL (dissolved O2 unaffected) - Calculated O2 sat is NORMAL (falsely reassuring!) - Creates classic "saturation gap": Normal PaO2 + low SpO2 = MetHb [1] 3. Additional labs: - CBC (assess b

nodes.title: Treatment Decision
nodes.summary: Treat >30% or symptomatic — G6PD check but NO delay
nodes.body: Indications for Methylene Blue: [1][2][5] Definite indications: - MetHb >30% - Symptomatic at any level (dyspnea, confusion, chest pain, syncope) - Signs of tissue hypoxia (elevated lactate, ischemia) Consider treatment: - MetHb 20-30% even if minimal symptoms - Lower thresholds in patients with: - Anemia - Cardiopulmonary disease - Elderly Important: Check G6PD status before treatment if possible

nodes.title: Methylene Blue Protocol
nodes.summary: MB 1-2mg/kg IV 5min — max 7mg/kg, more = worse
nodes.body: Methylene Blue - First-line treatment [1][2][5] Dosing: - 1-2 mg/kg IV of 1% solution (10 mg/mL) - Infuse over 5 minutes (push too fast causes chest pain) - May repeat in 30-60 minutes if no response - Maximum total dose: 7 mg/kg (higher doses can paradoxically CAUSE MetHb) [2] Mechanism: - Acts as electron carrier in NADPH-dependent methemoglobin reductase pathway - Reduces ferric (Fe3+) back to

nodes.summary: No response 30-60min: G6PD, exposure, sulfhemoglobin
nodes.body: Assess response at 30-60 minutes: Good response: - MetHb decreased by >50% - Symptoms improving - Cyanosis resolving Poor response / Refractory: - MetHb not improving or worsening - Consider: 1. Unrecognized G6PD deficiency (most common cause) 2. Ongoing exposure to causative agent (dapsone has long half-life) 3. Inadequate dosing 4. Sulfhemoglobinemia (mimics MetHb but does not respond to MB) 5.

nodes.summary: Dapsone rebound — MB repeat + charcoal + cimetidine
nodes.body: Rebound occurs with agents that have prolonged text: [4] High-risk agents: - Dapsone (t1/2 ~24-30 hours, enterohepatic circulation) - Aniline dyes - Phenazopyridine Management: 1. Repeat methylene blue: - Give additional 1 mg/kg doses as needed - Monitor q2-4h for rebound 2. Activated charcoal: - Multiple-dose activated charcoal (MDAC) for dapsone - 25-50g q4-6h for 24-48 hours - Interrupts entero

nodes.title: G6PD Deficiency - Methylene Blue Contraindicated
nodes.summary: MB CONTRAINDICATED G6PD — oxidant causing hemolysis

nodes.summary: Unknown G6PD: MB if critical — African tolerate better
