nodes.title: Rescue Therapies for Severe/Refractory Cases
nodes.summary: Exchange transfusion >70% or refractory — any G6PD
nodes.body: Severe refractory methemoglobinemia: [5][8] Exchange transfusion is the definitive rescue therapy Indications: - MetHb >70% - MetHb >50% with hemodynamic instability - Failure of methylene blue (confirmed or G6PD-related) - Combined MetHb + severe hemolysis Exchange transfusion: - Removes dysfunctional RBCs containing MetHb - Replaces with normal donor RBCs - Works regardless of G6PD status or enz

nodes.title: Infant Methemoglobinemia
nodes.summary: <6mo high risk — lower enzymes, well water nitrates
nodes.body: Infants (<6 months) are HIGH RISK: [10][11] Why infants are vulnerable: - Lower NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase activity (50% of adult) - Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) oxidizes more easily - Higher gastric pH allows nitrate-to-nitrite conversion by bacteria - Higher fluid intake relative to body weight Common causes in infants: - Well water contaminated with nitrates (>10 mg/L) - Formula prepared with high-

nodes.title: Methemoglobinemia in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: MB IV if life-threatening — fetal Hb more susceptible
nodes.body: Pregnancy considerations: [2][5] Fetal vulnerability: - Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is more susceptible to oxidation - Fetal MetHb levels may be higher than maternal - Fetal hypoxia risk even with mild maternal MetHb Treatment: Methylene blue in pregnancy: - Category X via intra-amniotic injection (teratogenic) - IV administration: Risk less defined, likely safer than intra-amniotic - In life-threateni

nodes.title: Supportive Care (Mild Cases)
nodes.summary: Remove agent + O2 — natural reduction ~15%/hr
nodes.body: For mild methemoglobinemia not meeting treatment threshold: Supportive measures: 1. Remove offending agent - most important step 2. High-flow O2 via NRB (increases dissolved plasma O2) 3. IV fluids as needed 4. Cardiac monitoring Natural resolution: - Normal NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase reduces MetHb at ~15%/hour - Most mild cases resolve within 24-48 hours after removing cause Monitoring: - Seria

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: ICU: >30%, MB, dapsone, G6PD, or unstable
nodes.body: Assess for safe disposition: ICU admission criteria: - MetHb >30% at presentation - Required methylene blue treatment - Severe symptoms (AMS, seizure, arrhythmia) - Ongoing rebound risk (dapsone) - G6PD deficiency with MetHb - Hemodynamic instability - Need for exchange transfusion Observation criteria: - Mild MetHb responding to supportive care - MetHb trending down on serial labs - No severe sym

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: Co-ox q2-4h, hemolysis markers — 24-48h dapsone
nodes.body: ICU admission for: - MetHb >30% at presentation - Required methylene blue treatment - Dapsone or other rebound-risk agents - G6PD deficiency - Hemodynamic instability - Exchange transfusion ICU monitoring: - Continuous cardiac monitoring - Serial co-oximetry q2-4h initially, then q4-6h - H&H for hemolysis (especially if G6PD or high-dose MB) - Reticulocyte count - LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin (hemo
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous monitoring, serial co-oximetry, and observation for rebound or hemolysis.

nodes.title: Observation Unit / Monitored Bed
nodes.summary: Co-ox q4h until <5% — ICU if worsening
nodes.body: Observation for mild-moderate cases: Criteria: - Mild MetHb (10-20%) responding to supportive care - Minimal symptoms - MetHb trending down on serial labs - Low rebound risk agent Monitoring: - Serial co-oximetry q4h until <5% - Telemetry - Symptom checks Escalate to ICU if: - MetHb rises despite treatment - New symptoms develop - Hemolysis evident - Need for methylene blue or exchange Duration: -
nodes.recommendation: Observation with serial co-oximetry until MetHb <5% and asymptomatic. Escalate if worsening.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Asymptomatic, <5%, cause removed, no rebound = safe
nodes.body: Safe for discharge if ALL met: - Asymptomatic - MetHb <5% on most recent lab - Trending down on serial measurements - Offending agent identified and removed - No rebound-risk agent (avoid discharge after dapsone) - Reliable follow-up available Discharge instructions: 1. Avoid offending agent - provide list of cross-reactive drugs if applicable 2. Return precautions: - Shortness of breath - Blue di
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with avoidance of offending agent and return precautions. Follow-up in 3-5 days.

nodes.title: Methemoglobinemia - Key Points
nodes.summary: Co-ox Dx, MB first, no G6PD, dapsone rebounds
nodes.body: Critical takeaways: 1. Recognition: - Cyanosis unresponsive to O2 + SpO2 plateau at 82-86% - Chocolate brown blood that stays brown - PaO2-SpO2 "saturation gap" 2. Diagnosis: - Co-oximetry (venous or arterial) - standard pulse ox CANNOT detect MetHb - Identify causative agent (benzocaine, dapsone, nitrates most common) 3. Treatment: - Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 min (first-line) - Response

nodes.title: Migraine: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Secondary causes FIRST — SNNOOP10 red flags every headache
nodes.body: Primary headache — migraine, tension-type, cluster — accounts for most ED headache visits. But first, rule out secondary causes. Key Question: Does this patient have any red flags suggesting a dangerous secondary headache? SNNOOP10 Mnemonic — Red Flags: - Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, immunocompromise) - Neoplasm history - Neurologic deficit (decreased LOC, focal signs) - Onset sudden (th

nodes.title: Red Flag Assessment
nodes.summary: Thunderclap, worst, deficit, fever+stiff = workup first
nodes.body: Does the patient have ANY of the following? - Sudden onset "thunderclap" headache (peak intensity <1 min) - Worst headache of life - New neurologic deficit (weakness, numbness, vision loss, confusion) - Fever + neck stiffness (meningitis signs) - Papilledema on fundoscopy - New headache in patient >50 years old - Headache with immunocompromise or cancer history - Post-traumatic headache - Pregnanc

nodes.title: Secondary Headache Workup
nodes.summary: Thunderclap CT 6hrs 95% SAH — negative = LP xanthochromia
nodes.body: Red flag present — evaluate for dangerous secondary causes: Thunderclap headache: - CT head non-contrast (sens ~95% for SAH within 6h) - If CT negative + high suspicion → LP (xanthochromia) - Consider CTA for aneurysm, RCVS, CVT Fever + neck stiffness: - LP for meningitis (unless contraindicated) - Blood cultures, empiric antibiotics if delayed LP New neuro deficit: - CT head → MRI if CT negative

nodes.title: Does This Meet Migraine Criteria?
nodes.summary: ICHD-3: >=5 attacks, 4-72h, 2/4 features + N/V or phono
nodes.body: ICHD-3 Migraine Without Aura Criteria: A. ≥5 attacks meeting B-D B. Duration 4-72 hours (untreated) C. ≥2 of 4: - Unilateral location - Pulsating quality - Moderate-severe intensity - Aggravated by routine physical activity D. During headache, ≥1 of: - Nausea and/or vomiting - Photophobia AND phonophobia E. Not better explained by another diagnosis Migraine WITH Aura: Add fully reversible visual,

nodes.title: Other Primary Headaches
nodes.summary: Tension bilateral, cluster orbital autonomic
nodes.body: If not migraine, consider: Tension-Type Headache: - Bilateral, pressing/tightening (non-pulsating) - Mild-moderate intensity - NOT aggravated by routine activity - No nausea/vomiting - Treatment: NSAIDs, acetaminophen Cluster Headache (Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia): - Severe unilateral orbital/supraorbital pain - Duration 15-180 min, up to 8/day - Ipsilateral autonomic features (tearing, rhino

nodes.title: Assess Migraine Severity
nodes.summary: Mild oral, mod/severe IV cocktail, status >72hrs
nodes.body: Assess current attack severity: Mild: - Pain 1-3/10 - Able to function - No significant nausea/vomiting - May respond to oral meds Moderate: - Pain 4-6/10 - Functional impairment - Some nausea - May need parenteral therapy Severe / Status Migrainosus: - Pain 7-10/10 - Debilitated - Significant nausea/vomiting - May have been >72 hours (status migrainosus) - Requires IV therapy What is the severity

nodes.title: Mild Migraine — Oral Therapy
nodes.summary: NSAID + triptan best — triptan CI in CAD/stroke
nodes.body: Mild migraine may respond to oral medications: First-Line Options: - NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400-800 mg, Naproxen 500-550 mg, Ketorolac 10 mg PO - Acetaminophen: 1000 mg (if NSAIDs contraindicated) - Triptan: Sumatriptan 50-100 mg, Rizatriptan 10 mg, Eletriptan 40 mg Combination more effective than monotherapy: - Sumatriptan 50-100 mg + Naproxen 500 mg (or fixed-dose sumatriptan 85 mg/naproxen 500 mg ta

nodes.title: Moderate-Severe Migraine — IV Cocktail
nodes.summary: Diphenhydramine FIRST, prochlorperazine 15min + ketorolac
nodes.body: 2025 AHS Guidelines — ED First-Line: Standard "Migraine Cocktail": | Step | Medication | Dose | Notes | |------|------------|------|-------| | 1 | Diphenhydramine | 25-50 mg IV | Give FIRST (prevents akathisia) | | 2 | Prochlorperazine | 10 mg IV over 15 min | Level A — Must Offer (upgraded 2025) | | 3 | Ketorolac | 15-30 mg IV | 15 mg equally effective as 30 mg | | 4 | NS Bolus | 500-1000 mL | If

nodes.title: Status Migrainosus (>72 hours)
nodes.summary: Status >72h: hydration + cocktail + dexa + consider DHE
nodes.body: Status migrainosus = migraine lasting >72 hours Initial Management: - Aggressive IV hydration (1-2L NS) - Standard migraine cocktail (prochlorperazine + diphenhydramine + ketorolac) - Dexamethasone 10 mg IV (reduces recurrence) If standard cocktail fails: Dihydroergotamine (DHE) Protocol: - Metoclopramide 10 mg IV (give 30 min before DHE) - DHE 1 mg IV over 3 min - Can repeat DHE 0.5-1 mg q8h x 24

nodes.title: Treatment Response Assessment
nodes.summary: 30-60min: good=DC, none=rescue or nerve block
nodes.body: Reassess at 30-60 minutes: Good response: - Pain significantly improved (≥50% reduction) - Nausea resolved - Able to tolerate PO - Ready for discharge Partial response: - Some improvement but still significant pain - May need additional therapy No response: - Pain unchanged or worse - Consider rescue therapy or nerve block What is the response?

nodes.title: Rescue Therapy Options
nodes.summary: GON block Level A, SC triptan B — AVOID opioids
nodes.body: First-line failed — rescue options: Level A (Must Offer): - Greater Occipital Nerve Block — highly effective, no systemic side effects Level B (Should Offer): - Sumatriptan SC 6 mg — if no contraindications - Supraorbital Nerve Block — alternative to GON Level C (May Offer): - Valproate IV 500-1000 mg — third-line - Chlorpromazine IV 12.5 mg — alternative antiemetic - Magnesium sulfate 1-2 g IV —

nodes.title: Triptan Rescue
nodes.summary: Sumatriptan 6mg SC — CI CAD, stroke, HTN
nodes.body: Sumatriptan SC 6 mg: Dosing: 6 mg SC, may repeat x1 after 1 hour (max 12 mg/24h) Contraindications: - Coronary artery disease, prior MI - Stroke or TIA history - Uncontrolled hypertension - Hemiplegic or basilar migraine - MAO inhibitor within 14 days - Pregnancy (relative) Side Effects: - Chest tightness (usually benign "triptan sensation") - Tingling, flushing, dizziness - Injection site reactio

nodes.title: Valproate IV — Third-Line
nodes.body: Valproate sodium IV: Dosing: 500-1000 mg IV over 30-60 min Mechanism: Anticonvulsant with migraine prophylactic effect; may work acutely via GABA modulation. Evidence: Level C (may offer) — limited but some trials show benefit. Contraindications: - Hepatic disease - Pregnancy (teratogenic — neural tube defects) - Pancreatitis history - Urea cycle disorders Side Effects: - Nausea, sedation - Thromb

nodes.title: Greater Occipital Nerve Block
nodes.summary: 3mL bupivacaine 0.5% occipital — no systemic effects
nodes.body: GON Block — Level A Recommendation Indications: - Migraine with occipital component - Refractory to first-line therapy - Contraindication to other treatments Equipment: - 25-27 gauge, 1.5 inch needle - 3 mL syringe - 2% lidocaine OR 0.5% bupivacaine (2-3 mL per side) Technique: 1. Patient seated, head flexed forward 2. Locate occipital protuberance 3. GON is 1/3 distance from protuberance to masto

nodes.title: Sphenopalatine Ganglion Block
nodes.body: SPG Block — Non-Invasive Alternative Indications: - Migraine, cluster headache - Alternative when GON not appropriate Cotton Applicator Technique: 1. Soak 10 cm cotton-tipped applicator in 2% lidocaine 2. Patient supine, head in sniffing position 3. Insert along floor of nose / superior to middle turbinate 4. Advance until resistance at nasopharynx 5. Leave in place 10-20 minutes 6. Repeat on othe

nodes.title: Rescue Response Assessment
nodes.body: Reassess 30-60 minutes after rescue therapy: Improved: - Pain now tolerable - Ready for discharge planning Still refractory: - Multiple treatments failed - Consider admission for DHE protocol - Neurology consult What is the response?

nodes.title: Refractory Migraine — Consider Admission
nodes.body: Multiple treatments failed — options: Admission for DHE Protocol: - Metoclopramide 10 mg IV q8h (30 min before each DHE) - DHE 1 mg IV q8h x 24-72 hours - Requires telemetry monitoring - Contraindicated: CAD, uncontrolled HTN, recent triptan Neurology Consult indications: - Status migrainosus >72h refractory to ED treatment - Frequent ED visits for migraine - Need for prophylaxis evaluation - Atyp

nodes.title: Migraine — Disposition
nodes.summary: Dexa 10mg IV before DC — NNT=9 recurrence prevention
nodes.body: Before Discharge: 1. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV — prevents 48-72h recurrence (NNT=9) 2. Discharge Medications: - Triptan (sumatriptan, rizatriptan) — if no contraindications - NSAID (naproxen, ibuprofen) - Antiemetic PRN (ondansetron ODT, metoclopramide) 3. Return Precautions: - Sudden severe "worst headache of life" - New fever, neck stiffness - Confusion, weakness, vision changes - Seizure - Headach
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with dexamethasone (prevents recurrence), triptan + NSAID prescription, and neurology referral if frequent migraines. Return precautions for thunderclap headache, fever, or neuro changes.

nodes.title: The Sick Neonate (0-28 Days)
nodes.summary: THE MISFITS: Trauma, Heart, Endocrine, Metabolic, Inborn errors, Sepsis, Formula, Intestinal, Toxins, Seizures
nodes.body: THE MISFITS - Approach to the Critically Ill Neonate Neonates present nonspecifically. The same symptoms (lethargy, poor feeding, apnea) can represent dozens of diagnoses. THE MISFITS helps you systematically consider all life-threatening causes. THE MISFITS: • T - Trauma (NAT) / Temperature instability • H - Heart (CHD, arrhythmia, myocarditis) • E - Endocrine (CAH, hypoglycemia, thyroid) • M - M

nodes.title: Triage & Initial Stabilization
nodes.summary: ABCDE: secure airway, check SpO2 + femorals, IV access, CHECK GLUCOSE immediately, full exposure exam
nodes.body: IMMEDIATE ASSESSMENT - ABCDE A - AIRWAY • Position, suction • Intubate if apneic or severe distress • Low threshold to secure airway B - BREATHING • SpO2 (pre and post-ductal) • Respiratory rate, work of breathing • Provide O2 if needed (but consider CHD - see CHD consult) C - CIRCULATION • Heart rate, capillary refill, pulses (include femorals!) • IV/IO access immediately • NS bolus 10 mL/kg if s

nodes.title: Core Laboratory Workup
nodes.summary: Core labs: glucose, VBG, lactate, CBC, BMP, blood culture, cath UA; consider ammonia, LFTs, LP, HSV PCR
nodes.body: LABORATORY EVALUATION FOR SICK NEONATE ALWAYS ORDER: • Glucose (point-of-care immediately) • VBG or ABG with lactate • CBC with differential • BMP (Na, K, glucose, BUN, Cr, Ca) • Blood culture • Urinalysis + urine culture (catheterized) STRONGLY CONSIDER: • Ammonia (IEM screen) • LFTs (AST, ALT, bili, albumin) • PT/INR, PTT (liver function, DIC) • CSF studies (cell count, glucose, protein, culture

nodes.title: THE MISFITS Mnemonic
nodes.summary: THE MISFITS covers: Trauma/Temp, Heart, Endocrine, Metabolic, Inborn errors, Sepsis, Formula, Intestinal, Toxins, Seizures
nodes.body: THE MISFITS - Systematic Approach T - TRAUMA / TEMPERATURE • Non-accidental trauma (NAT/abuse) • Hypothermia, hyperthermia H - HEART • Congenital heart disease (see CHD consult) • Arrhythmias (SVT) • Myocarditis, cardiomyopathy E - ENDOCRINE • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) • Hypoglycemia • Thyroid disorders M - METABOLIC / I - INBORN ERRORS • Organic acidemias • Urea cycle defects • Fatty a

nodes.title: Jump to Specific Category
nodes.body: SELECT YOUR PRIMARY CONCERN:

nodes.title: THE - Trauma, Heart, Endocrine
nodes.body: T - TRAUMA / TEMPERATURE H - HEART E - ENDOCRINE These categories involve physical injury, cardiac pathology, and hormonal emergencies.

nodes.title: Trauma / Non-Accidental Trauma
nodes.summary: NAT red flags: inconsistent history, bruising in non-mobile infant, multiple healing injuries; skeletal survey, head CT, retinal exam
nodes.body: NON-ACCIDENTAL TRAUMA (NAT) / CHILD ABUSE Sick neonates may be victims of abuse. High index of suspicion required. RED FLAGS: • Inconsistent or changing history • Delay in seeking care • Injuries inconsistent with developmental stage • Multiple injuries in various stages of healing • Patterned bruising (belt, hand) • Bruising in non-mobile infant • Unexplained altered mental status INJURIES TO EVA

nodes.title: Heart - Congenital Heart Disease
nodes.body: CARDIAC CAUSES OF SICK NEONATE CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE See CHD Consult for comprehensive management KEY CLUES: • Cyanosis not improving with O2 (hyperoxia test fails) • Differential cyanosis (pre > post-ductal sats) • Weak/absent femoral pulses (coarctation) • Murmur (may be absent in critical lesions) • Hepatomegaly, respiratory distress CRITICAL ACTION: If ductal-dependent CHD suspected, start
nodes.recommendation: Suspected CHD: check 4-extremity sats, femoral pulses. Start PGE1 if ductal-dependent suspected. See full CHD consult for details.

nodes.title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)
nodes.body: CONGENITAL ADRENAL HYPERPLASIA - ADRENAL CRISIS 21-hydroxylase deficiency (most common). Cannot make cortisol or aldosterone. PRESENTATION • Typically presents at 1-2 weeks of life • Lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting • Dehydration, shock • Classic labs: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia • Hyperpigmentation (ACTH effect) • Ambiguous genitalia in females (virilization) CLASSIC TRIAD: 1. Hypona
nodes.recommendation: CAH crisis: NS boluses, D10 for hypoglycemia, Hydrocortisone 25 mg IV immediately. Check 17-OHP to confirm.

nodes.title: Neonatal Hypoglycemia
nodes.body: NEONATAL HYPOGLYCEMIA DEFINITION Glucose <50 mg/dL requires intervention Glucose <40 mg/dL is critical CAUSES IN SICK NEONATE: • Sepsis (increased metabolic demand) • Inborn errors of metabolism • Hyperinsulinism • Adrenal insufficiency (CAH) • Poor feeding, prematurity • Maternal diabetes (transient) SYMPTOMS • Jitteriness, tremor • Lethargy, poor feeding • Apnea, cyanosis • Seizures • Hypothermi
nodes.recommendation: Hypoglycemia <50: D10W 2 mL/kg IV push, then D10 maintenance infusion. Recheck in 30 min. Investigate cause. If a persistent hypoglycemia disorder is suspected, target >70 mg/dL per PES and draw the critical sample before correcting.

nodes.title: MIS - Metabolic, Inborn Errors, Sepsis
nodes.body: M - METABOLIC I - INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM S - SEPSIS These are the most common serious diagnoses in sick neonates.

nodes.title: Inborn Errors of Metabolism
nodes.body: INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM (IEM) Rare individually but collectively important. Typically present in first days to weeks of life. SUSPECT IEM IF: • Unexplained encephalopathy • Recurrent vomiting • Metabolic acidosis with increased anion gap • Hyperammonemia • Hypoglycemia refractory to treatment • Unusual odor (maple syrup, sweaty feet, musty) • Family history, consanguinity • Normal newborn then
nodes.recommendation: Suspect IEM if unexplained acidosis, hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia. Stop protein, give IV dextrose, treat hyperammonemia, consult genetics.

nodes.title: Neonatal Sepsis
nodes.body: NEONATAL SEPSIS Most common serious diagnosis in sick neonate. Must always be considered. RISK FACTORS: • Prolonged rupture of membranes (>18h) • Maternal GBS colonization • Chorioamnionitis • Prematurity • Indwelling catheters COMMON PATHOGENS: Early-onset (<7 days): GBS, E. coli, Listeria Late-onset (7-28 days): Coag-negative Staph, S. aureus, GBS, gram-negatives PRESENTATION: • Nonspecific: let
nodes.recommendation: Neonatal sepsis: Ampicillin + Gentamicin (verify dose/interval by postmenstrual age). Add Acyclovir 20 mg/kg if HSV risk. LP if stable. Ceftriaxone contraindicated ≤ 28 days with calcium-containing IV fluids.

nodes.title: HSV Encephalitis
nodes.body: NEONATAL HSV - CRITICAL DIAGNOSIS Herpes simplex virus can cause devastating encephalitis in neonates. Mortality approaches 80% if untreated. RISK FACTORS: • Maternal genital HSV (especially primary outbreak) • Vaginal delivery with active lesions • Prolonged rupture of membranes THREE PATTERNS: 1. SEM (Skin, Eye, Mouth): Vesicles, conjunctivitis - best prognosis 2. CNS disease: Seizures, lethargy
nodes.recommendation: HSV: Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h immediately if suspected. Do NOT wait for PCR. SEM 14d, CNS/disseminated 21d. Then oral acyclovir 300 mg/m2 TID x 6 months.

nodes.title: FITS - Formula, Intestinal, Toxins, Seizures
nodes.body: F - FORMULA MISHAPS I - INTESTINAL CATASTROPHES T - TOXINS S - SEIZURES These include GI emergencies, medication errors, and neurologic emergencies.

nodes.title: Formula Mishaps
nodes.summary: Formula errors: over-dilution causes water intoxication/hyponatremia; ask about mixing technique; correct electrolytes slowly
nodes.body: FORMULA ERRORS AND WATER INTOXICATION OVER-DILUTION: Parents may over-dilute formula (financial stress, misunderstanding). • Results in water intoxication • Hyponatremia, hypochloremia • Seizures, lethargy, irritability UNDER-DILUTION: • Hypernatremia • Dehydration • Can cause intracranial hemorrhage CONTAMINATED FORMULA: • Cronobacter (Enterobacter sakazakii) - powdered formula • Can cause mening

nodes.title: Intestinal Emergencies
nodes.body: INTESTINAL CATASTROPHES IN NEONATES Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and bloody stools are red flags. KEY DIAGNOSES: • Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) • Malrotation with midgut volvulus • Hirschsprung's disease with enterocolitis • Intestinal atresia/stenosis RED FLAGS: • Bilious (green) vomiting - volvulus until proven otherwise • Bloody stools • Abdominal distension • Absent bowel sounds

nodes.title: Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)
nodes.body: NECROTIZING ENTEROCOLITIS (NEC) Ischemic necrosis of intestinal mucosa. Most common GI emergency in premature infants. RISK FACTORS: • Prematurity (primary risk factor) • Formula feeding (breast milk protective) • Perinatal asphyxia • PDA, CHD • Polycythemia PRESENTATION: • Abdominal distension • Feeding intolerance, vomiting • Bloody stools (heme-positive) • Lethargy, temperature instability • Ap
nodes.recommendation: NEC: NPO, NGT, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (Amp/Gent/Flagyl). Surgical consult for pneumoperitoneum or deterioration.

nodes.title: Malrotation with Midgut Volvulus
nodes.body: MALROTATION WITH MIDGUT VOLVULUS - SURGICAL EMERGENCY BILIOUS VOMITING IN A NEONATE IS VOLVULUS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE Malrotation (abnormal intestinal rotation during development) allows midgut to twist on SMA pedicle, causing ischemia. PRESENTATION: • Bilious (green) vomiting - hallmark • Abdominal distension (may be minimal early) • Abdominal pain (infant draws up legs, irritable) • Bloody stoo
nodes.recommendation: BILIOUS VOMITING = VOLVULUS until proven otherwise. Emergent UGI series. Surgical consult immediately. NPO, NGT, fluids.

nodes.title: Toxins and Exposures
nodes.summary: Consider: breast milk drugs (opioids, benzos), environmental toxins, medication errors, neonatal abstinence syndrome
nodes.body: TOXINS AFFECTING NEONATES BREAST MILK DRUG TRANSFER: Many medications pass into breast milk: • Opioids: Sedation, respiratory depression • Benzodiazepines: Sedation, poor feeding • Antidepressants: Irritability or sedation • Methadone: Neonatal abstinence if discontinued • Alcohol: Sedation, poor feeding • Cocaine/amphetamines: Irritability, tachycardia ENVIRONMENTAL EXPOSURES: • Lead: Rare in neo

nodes.title: Neonatal Seizures
nodes.body: NEONATAL SEIZURES Seizures in neonates are often subtle and easily missed. TYPES: • Subtle: Eye deviation, lip smacking, cycling movements, apnea • Clonic: Rhythmic jerking (focal or multifocal) • Tonic: Sustained posturing • Myoclonic: Brief jerks (often benign, but can be pathologic) MIMICS (Jitteriness): • Stimulus-sensitive • No eye deviation or autonomic changes • Suppressible with passive fl
nodes.recommendation: Neonatal seizures: correct metabolic causes first (glucose, Ca, Mg). Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading dose - first-line per ILAE 2023, levetiracetam is NOT equivalent. EEG and MRI when stable.

nodes.title: Sick Neonate Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Resus: 3.0-3.5 ETT, 10 mL/kg fluid boluses, D10 for glucose, Amp+Gent+/-Acyclovir, maintain warmth
nodes.body: RESUSCITATION PRIORITIES AIRWAY • Position, suction, supplemental O2 • Intubate if: apnea, severe distress, protecting for transport • ETT size: 3.0-3.5 for term newborn • Use video laryngoscopy if available BREATHING • Target SpO2 >90% (accept lower if CHD suspected) • Avoid hyperoxia in preterm infants • PPV if needed (neonatal BVM, 20-25 cmH2O) CIRCULATION • IV access: peripheral IV, umbilical

nodes.title: Vascular Access
nodes.summary: Access: peripheral IV, UVC (first week), IO if unable; UVC: identify single thin-walled vein, insert 2-4 cm
nodes.body: VASCULAR ACCESS IN NEONATES PERIPHERAL IV: • First choice if obtainable • Hand, foot, scalp veins • 24g typically UMBILICAL VENOUS CATHETER (UVC): • Available in first week of life • Cut cord 1-2 cm from skin • Identify single large thin-walled vein • Insert 5F catheter until blood return (2-4 cm) • Confirm position (above diaphragm on XR) • Can give all medications and fluids INTRAOSSEOUS (IO): •

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics
nodes.body: EMPIRIC ANTIBIOTICS FOR SICK NEONATE STANDARD REGIMEN: • Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV q8h - Covers GBS, Listeria, Enterococcus • Gentamicin 4 mg/kg IV q24h - Covers gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella) - Synergy with Ampicillin for GBS ADD ACYCLOVIR IF HSV CONCERN: • Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h • HSV risk factors: maternal HSV, vesicles, seizures, CSF pleocytosis, LFT elevation MENINGITIS DOSING: • Ampici
nodes.recommendation: Empiric: Ampicillin + Gentamicin (verify dose/interval by postmenstrual age). Add Acyclovir 20 mg/kg if HSV risk. Add Vancomycin for late-onset or line infection. Avoid ceftriaxone at <= 28 days.

nodes.title: Admission Disposition
nodes.summary: All sick neonates admitted; NICU for prematurity, respiratory/CV support, TPN, seizures; PICU for older neonates with acute illness
nodes.body: DISPOSITION DECISIONS ALL SICK NEONATES ARE ADMITTED NICU ADMISSION: • Prematurity • Respiratory support beyond nasal cannula • TPN required (NEC, surgical abdomen) • Cardiovascular support (pressors, PGE1) • Active resuscitation needs • Complex congenital anomalies • Seizures requiring monitoring PICU ADMISSION: • Older neonates (>14-28 days) with acute illness • Respiratory failure requiring mec

nodes.title: Family Communication
nodes.summary: Acknowledge fear, use plain language, allow parents to stay, provide frequent updates, involve social work
nodes.body: COMMUNICATING WITH FAMILIES KEY PRINCIPLES: • Parents are terrified - acknowledge this • Explain what you're doing and why • Use plain language, not medical jargon • Allow parents to stay during procedures when safe • Provide frequent updates WHAT TO SAY: "Your baby is very sick. We are doing everything we can to find out what's wrong and treat it. I'm going to be honest with you about what we kno

nodes.title: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Confirm one eye, document onset, check VA/pupils/RAPD/fields/IOP when safe, then split vascular/GCA/eye emergency lanes.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Central retinal artery occlusion \u2014 sudden painless loss. Per the 2021 AHA/ASA scientific statement CRAO is an acute ischemic stroke of the eye, not merely a stroke "equivalent": it gets the stroke pathway, not an ophthalmology callback. 2. Giant cell arteritis \u2014 age >50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, high ESR/CRP \u2192 steroids now. 3. Retinal detach

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: CRAO/TMVL, GCA, glaucoma, trauma, retinal detachment, optic neuritis, and infection are first-pass exclusions.
nodes.body: Choose the first dangerous lane. You can return after the immediate action. Check this before you pick a lane: if the visual deficit is still there when the *unaffected* eye is covered, it is a homonymous hemifield defect from retrochiasmal or occipital ischemia, not monocular vision loss. That patient goes to Acute Ischemic Stroke and is not served by anything below.

nodes.title: CRAO / BRAO / Retinal Ischemic Stroke
nodes.body: Open Central Retinal Artery Occlusion and Acute Ischemic Stroke. Next 5 minutes: stroke-time history, visual acuity/RAPD, bedside fundus/photo if available, neuro exam, ECG, glucose, ophthalmology and stroke team. Per the 2021 AHA/ASA scientific statement, CRAO is an acute ischemic stroke and warrants the same emergent evaluation \u2014 stroke-center referral, not an outpatient eye clinic slot. If
nodes.recommendation: Treat sudden painless persistent monocular loss as retinal stroke until ophthalmology/stroke evaluation proves otherwise. Activate the stroke pathway, screen for GCA if age >=50, and do not substitute ocular massage or paracentesis for it.

nodes.title: Transient Monocular Vision Loss / Amaurosis Fugax
nodes.body: Open Amaurosis Fugax. Next steps: treat as retinal TIA. Confirm monocular history, screen GCA if age >=50, ECG/telemetry, vascular imaging of head/neck or carotids per local stroke pathway, brain MRI-DWI when available, secondary prevention after hemorrhage/contraindications considered. Pitfall: complete recovery does not make this benign. Retinal TIA can precede brain stroke, especially early aft
nodes.recommendation: TMVL gets urgent TIA/stroke workup, not routine outpatient eye follow-up only.

nodes.title: Giant Cell Arteritis Threat
nodes.body: Age >=50 plus compatible symptoms is vision-threatening disease. Order ESR, CRP, CBC/platelets, and ask specifically about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new temporal headache, PMR symptoms, diplopia, and fellow-eye symptoms. If clinical suspicion is high or vision symptoms are present, start high-dose corticosteroids immediately and involve ophthalmology/rheumatology. Do not wait for biopsy
nodes.recommendation: When GCA is plausible with visual symptoms, treat first and confirm after: pulse IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg/day x 3-5 days for vision loss, prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 80 mg) daily without it, biopsy within 2 weeks.

nodes.title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
nodes.body: Open Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Next 5 minutes: confirm IOP if open globe is not suspected, analgesia/antiemetic, start local protocol IOP-lowering therapy, ophthalmology emergently. Classic findings include painful red eye, halos, headache, nausea/vomiting, cloudy cornea, mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil. Numbers that matter: normal IOP is 10-21 mmHg; acute angle closure typically runs 50-80
nodes.recommendation: AACG is an eye-pressure emergency. Treat and call ophthalmology now.

nodes.title: Open Globe / Ocular Trauma / Compartment
nodes.body: Open Ocular Trauma or Globe Rupture. Next 5 minutes: rigid shield, NPO, antiemetic/analgesia, tetanus/antibiotics per open globe pathway, avoid pressure on the eye, avoid ultrasound/tonometry if open globe possible, CT orbit when stable. If proptosis, tight lids, RAPD, high IOP, and acute vision loss after trauma/surgery, consider orbital compartment syndrome and lateral canthotomy pathway. Orbita
nodes.recommendation: Protect the globe first. Do not perform pressure-based testing if rupture is possible.

nodes.title: Retinal Detachment / Vitreous Hemorrhage
nodes.body: Open Ocular POCUS when ultrasound is safe. Clues: flashes, floaters, curtain/shadow, peripheral field loss, high myopia, prior eye surgery, trauma, diabetic retinopathy or anticoagulation. Bedside ocular ultrasound can help when the view is limited, but do not ultrasound suspected open globe. Ophthalmology timing depends on macula status, detachment suspicion, and vision threat. What ED POCUS actu
nodes.recommendation: Use POCUS as an adjunct, not a rule-out test, and arrange urgent ophthalmology when the history fits. Preserved central acuity with a peripheral curtain suggests macula-on detachment and raises, not lowers, the urgency.

nodes.title: Optic Neuritis / Optic Neuropathy
nodes.body: Open Optic Neuritis for the full acute pathway, Optic Neuropathy Hub to sort the non-inflammatory optic neuropathies, or Multiple Sclerosis for the demyelinating context. Clues: subacute unilateral loss, pain with eye movement, reduced color saturation, RAPD, young adult, prior demyelinating symptoms. Consider atypical features: severe bilateral loss, older age, no pain, optic disc hemorrhage, sys
nodes.recommendation: Optic neuritis needs ophthalmology/neurology strategy and MRI planning, not empiric oral prednisone alone.

nodes.title: Orbital / Intraocular / Invasive Infection
nodes.body: Open Orbital vs Preseptal Cellulitis. Danger signs: ophthalmoplegia, pain with EOM, proptosis, decreased vision, RAPD, fever, immunocompromise, recent eye procedure/injection, contact lens ulcer, black eschar, diabetic ketoacidosis risk. Treat orbital/intraocular infection as sight-threatening and sometimes life-threatening. Next steps: ophthalmology, CT orbit/face with contrast when stable, IV an
nodes.recommendation: Vision change plus orbital signs is not simple conjunctivitis. Suspected endophthalmitis needs emergent ophthalmology for intravitreal antibiotics, not IV antibiotics alone.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Eye Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: VA, pupils/RAPD, fields, EOM, slit lamp/fluorescein, IOP when safe, fundus/photo, targeted vascular/GCA workup.
nodes.body: Default bundle when no killer has declared itself: - Visual acuity each eye. - Pupils/RAPD, EOM, confrontational fields. - External exam: red eye, cornea, hyphema, proptosis, lid swelling, vesicles. - Fluorescein/slit lamp when available. - IOP if open globe is not suspected. - Fundus/photo when available, but do not require it to activate vascular or ophthalmology pathways. - Glucose, ECG, neuro

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Persistent or unexplained monocular vision loss needs a specialist/stroke/eye emergency pathway.
nodes.body: Do not let the patient leave until vision-threatening diagnoses have a timeline and destination.

nodes.title: Imaging / Testing Strategy
nodes.summary: Stroke imaging for retinal ischemia, CT orbit for trauma/infection, POCUS for retina when safe, MRI orbits for optic neuritis.
nodes.body: Image/test by the threatened structure: - Stroke/retinal ischemia: brain MRI-DWI, CTA/MRA head/neck or carotid imaging, ECG/telemetry, echo per stroke pathway. - GCA: ESR/CRP/CBC now, temporal artery biopsy/ultrasound after treatment plan. - Retinal detachment/vitreous hemorrhage: ocular POCUS when globe intact; ophthalmology definitive exam. - Open globe/IOFB/orbital trauma: CT orbit/face, no ult

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: High-risk vascular, pressure, globe, infection, and severe persistent loss require emergent pathway.
nodes.body: Disposition is driven by diagnosis, visual acuity, progression, and follow-up reliability.

nodes.title: Admit / Transfer / Emergent Specialty
nodes.body: Admit/transfer/emergent consult for CRAO or retinal ischemia requiring stroke pathway, suspected GCA with vision symptoms, acute angle closure, open globe, orbital compartment syndrome, orbital cellulitis/endophthalmitis/invasive infection, severe persistent loss, or unreliable urgent follow-up.
nodes.recommendation: When the eye, retina, optic nerve, or brain is actively threatened, disposition is emergent specialty pathway.

nodes.title: Urgent Ophthalmology / Neuro Follow-Up
nodes.body: Urgent same-day or next-day ophthalmology is typical for retinal detachment/tear concern, vitreous hemorrhage with decreased view, optic neuritis, unexplained persistent visual symptoms, hyphema, significant corneal ulcer, or diagnostic uncertainty. Neurology/stroke follow-up is added for vascular or optic neuritis pathways.
nodes.recommendation: Give a specific specialist destination and timeframe, not vague "eye follow-up."

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when visual acuity is normal or baseline, pain controlled, diagnosis is low-risk and clear, IOP is safe when relevant, no RAPD/focal neuro/GCA/retinal detachment/open globe/orbital infection concern, and follow-up is reliable. Return now for: worse vision, recurrent curtain/shade, eye pain/redness, headache/jaw pain/scalp tenderness, diplopia, neuro symptoms, vomiting/halos, fever/s
nodes.recommendation: Document acuity each eye, pupil/RAPD, IOP when measured, and the specific follow-up plan.

nodes.title: Uncertain Crisis Type — Safe Approach
nodes.summary: If uncertain: STOP all anticholinesterase (safe for both), support airway, atropine for secretions, reassess in 30-60min
nodes.body: When you cannot distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis: Step 1: STOP all anticholinesterase medications • This is safe for both crisis types • If cholinergic: patient will improve as drug clears • If myasthenic: won't worsen acutely (pyridostigmine is symptomatic, not disease-modifying) Step 2: Support the airway • Low threshold for intubation • Suction secretions • Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV if

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Ice pack test 80% sensitive for ocular MG; AChR antibodies 85% in generalized; all need CT chest for thymoma (10-15%)
nodes.body: Bedside tests: Ice Pack Test — simple, non-invasive • Place ice on closed eyelid for 2 minutes • >2mm improvement in ptosis = positive • 80% sensitive for ocular MG • Works because cold improves neuromuscular transmission Antibody testing: • AChR antibodies: 85% sensitive in generalized MG, 50% in ocular MG • Anti-MuSK: 5-10% of "seronegative" MG • Anti-LRP4: Rare, newer marker • Seronegative MG e

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Exacerbation
nodes.summary: AVOID: aminoglycosides, FQs, beta-blockers, IV magnesium, NMBs at full dose — safe: PCNs, cephalosporins, carbapenems
nodes.body: Drugs to Avoid in MG — comprehensive contraindication list. MEDICATIONS THAT CAN PRECIPITATE CRISIS: Antibiotics: • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) • Fluoroquinolones (especially respiratory FQs — levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) • Macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin) Cardiovascular: • Beta-blockers (including ophthalmic — timolol drops!) • Calcium channel blockers

nodes.title: Acute Treatment Overview
nodes.summary: Two components: pyridostigmine (symptomatic) + immunotherapy (IVIG/PLEX rapid-acting, steroids slower); severity guides selection
nodes.body: Acute MG treatment has two components: 1. Symptomatic therapy: • Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) — improves transmission at NMJ • Does NOT modify disease course • May need to HOLD if concern for cholinergic crisis 2. Immunotherapy: • Rapid-acting: IVIG, plasmapheresis (PLEX) • Slower-acting: Corticosteroids, steroid-sparing agents Treatment selection depends on: • Severity (mild vs moderate-severe vs cr

nodes.title: Pyridostigmine (Mestinon)
nodes.summary: Pyridostigmine 30-60mg q4-6h — symptomatic only, does NOT modify disease; max 480-600mg/day, watch for cholinergic crisis
nodes.body: Pyridostigmine Dosing Guide — titration and monitoring. Mechanism: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — increases acetylcholine at NMJ. Dosing: • Start: 30 mg PO TID (with meals) • Titrate: Increase by 30 mg q3-5 days as tolerated • Typical maintenance: 60 mg PO q4-6h (while awake) • Maximum: 120 mg per dose, ~480-600 mg/day total Onset: 30-45 minutes; duration 3-6 hours Extended-release (Mestinon Tim

nodes.title: IVIG vs Plasmapheresis
nodes.summary: IVIG vs PLEX equally effective — IVIG easier logistics, PLEX faster onset; choice depends on availability/patient factors
nodes.body: IVIG vs PLEX Comparison — efficacy, logistics, and side effects. Both are equally effective for MG crisis and acute exacerbation. IVIG: • Dose: 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days OR 1 g/kg/day × 2 days • Onset: 2-5 days • Duration of effect: 3-6 weeks • Advantages: Easier logistics, peripheral IV access, no central line • Disadvantages: Risk of thrombosis, aseptic meningitis, renal toxicity • Contraindicated:

nodes.title: IVIG Dosing
nodes.summary: IVIG 2g/kg total (0.4g/kg/d x5 or 1g/kg/d x2) — onset 2-5d, check IgA first (anaphylaxis if deficient), thrombosis risk
nodes.body: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) for MG: Standard dosing: • Option 1: 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg) • Option 2: 1 g/kg/day × 2 days (total 2 g/kg) Practical example (80 kg patient): • Option 1: 32 g/day × 5 days = 160 g total • Option 2: 80 g/day × 2 days = 160 g total Administration: • Start slow: 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr for first 30 min • Titrate up to 4-8 mL/kg/hr as tolerated • Premedicate with

nodes.title: Plasmapheresis (PLEX)
nodes.summary: PLEX 5 exchanges over 10-14d — faster onset 1-2d; requires central venous access, watch for citrate toxicity/hypotension
nodes.body: Plasmapheresis for MG: Protocol: • 5 exchanges over 10-14 days • Typically every other day (Mon-Wed-Fri-Mon-Wed) • Each exchange removes 1-1.5 plasma volumes • Replacement fluid: 5% albumin (preferred) or FFP Mechanism: Physically removes circulating AChR antibodies. Advantages over IVIG: • Faster onset (1-2 days vs 2-5 days) • Can repeat without cumulative toxicity • No IgA deficiency concern Req

nodes.title: Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: Steroids cause INITIAL WORSENING in up to 50% — start in hospital with IVIG/PLEX cover for moderate-severe disease
nodes.body: Corticosteroids in MG: Dosing: • High-dose: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60-80 mg) • OR pulse: Methylprednisolone 1 g IV × 3-5 days, then oral taper ⚠️ CRITICAL WARNING: Steroids can cause INITIAL WORSENING in first 1-2 weeks. • Up to 50% of patients experience transient worsening • Can precipitate myasthenic crisis • Start in hospital if moderate-severe disease Safe steroid initiation strategies:

nodes.title: Airway Management
nodes.summary: Rocuronium 1/3 to 1/2 dose (0.3-0.5 mg/kg) — MG patients VERY sensitive; sugammadex available; avoid succinylcholine
nodes.body: Intubation indications (same thresholds as GBS): • FVC <15-20 mL/kg (or <1 L in average adult) • NIF weaker than -20 to -25 cmH2O • Declining trend despite treatment • Severe bulbar dysfunction (aspiration risk) • Respiratory distress, accessory muscle use ⚠️ NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKER CONSIDERATIONS: Succinylcholine: • Variable response — may be RESISTANT (need higher dose) or SENSITIVE • Resistance d

nodes.title: Thymectomy
nodes.summary: Thymectomy for thymoma (any stage) or generalized AChR+ MG age 18-65 — elective, stabilize first, do NOT operate in crisis
nodes.body: Indications for thymectomy: Definite indication: • Thymoma (any stage) — must resect for oncologic reasons • Present in 10-15% of MG patients Strong indication (MGTX trial): • Generalized MG, age 18-65, AChR antibody positive • Even WITHOUT thymoma • MGTX trial showed: thymectomy + prednisone > prednisone alone • Better clinical status, lower prednisone requirements at 3 years Less clear benefit:

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition by severity: ICU for crisis/intubated, monitored bed for worsening, outpatient for stable ocular/mild
nodes.body: Newer MG Maintenance Therapies (FcRn & Complement Inhibitors) — clinician reference: what to ask, complement-inhibitor meningococcal sepsis risk. Disposition depends on presentation severity and response to treatment. Consider: • Respiratory status (FVC, NIF) • Bulbar function (swallowing, secretion management) • Response to initial treatment • Ability to manage at home (medication compliance, fol

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: Myasthenic crisis requires ICU admission. ICU management: • Mechanical ventilation if intubated • Serial FVC/NIF q4-6h if not intubated • IVIG or plasmapheresis (begin immediately) • Hold pyridostigmine initially (risk of cholinergic crisis, secretions) • Steroids after IVIG/PLEX initiated (not before — worsening risk) • Identify and treat trigger (infection most common) • DVT prophylaxis • Nutrit
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for myasthenic crisis. Begin IVIG or PLEX immediately. Hold pyridostigmine initially. Identify trigger. Neurology consultation.

nodes.title: Hospital Admission
nodes.body: Admit to monitored bed (step-down or floor with telemetry). Indications for admission: • New diagnosis with bulbar or respiratory symptoms • Worsening symptoms despite outpatient treatment • Starting high-dose steroids (risk of initial worsening) • Need for IVIG or plasmapheresis • Unreliable follow-up or social situation Inpatient management: • Serial FVC/NIF q6-8h initially • Continue/adjust pyr
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored bed. Serial respiratory monitoring. Initiate appropriate immunotherapy. Neurology consultation. Educate on warning signs before discharge.

nodes.title: Outpatient Management
nodes.body: Outpatient management appropriate for: • Ocular MG only (Class I) • Mild, stable generalized symptoms • No respiratory or bulbar concerns • Reliable patient with good follow-up Outpatient plan: 1. Medications: • Start or adjust pyridostigmine (30-60 mg TID) • Consider low-dose prednisone (10-20 mg, slow escalation) if not responding to pyridostigmine alone 2. Patient education: • Warning signs req
nodes.recommendation: Outpatient management with pyridostigmine. Neurology follow-up within 1-2 weeks. Provide medication avoidance list. Educate on warning signs. Chest imaging to rule out thymoma.

nodes.title: Myocarditis — ED Recognition
nodes.summary: Suspect myocarditis with chest pain, arrhythmia, syncope, or HF after viral/immune/cardiotoxin exposure.
nodes.body: Myocarditis is a syndrome, not one disease. It can look like viral chest pain, STEMI/NSTEMI, heart failure, dysrhythmia, syncope, or cardiogenic shock. [1][2] High-yield ED triggers: • Recent viral syndrome, COVID/influenza-like illness, GI illness • Chest pain with troponin elevation and non-obstructive/atypical ACS pattern • New dyspnea, pulmonary edema, or cardiogenic shock without known CAD •

nodes.title: Do Not Miss Mimics
nodes.summary: Rule out ACS, dissection, PE, Takotsubo, sepsis, pericarditis, and demand injury before anchoring.
nodes.body: Myocarditis is a diagnosis of suspicion plus exclusion. Do not anchor. [1][2] Immediate mimics to actively rule out: • ACS/STEMI/NSTEMI — territorial ECG changes, coronary risk, dynamic troponin, wall-motion territory • Aortic dissection — tearing pain, pulse/BP difference, neuro deficit, widened mediastinum • PE — pleuritic pain, hypoxia, RV strain, DVT risk • Takotsubo — stress trigger, apical b

nodes.title: Initial ED Tests
nodes.summary: ECG + troponin + echo guide triage; normal early tests do not fully exclude high-suspicion myocarditis.
nodes.body: Minimum ED workup when myocarditis is on the table: [1][2][5][6] • 12-lead ECG + repeat ECG if symptoms evolve • High-sensitivity troponin, repeat if early or changing symptoms • BNP/NT-proBNP if dyspnea/HF features • CBC with differential: eosinophilia matters • CMP/Mg/Phos, lactate if ill, TSH when indicated • CRP/ESR: supportive inflammation markers • Viral testing when clinically useful: SARS-

nodes.title: POCUS / Echo Identification
nodes.summary: Echo detects danger: LV/RV dysfunction, effusion, low-output physiology, and mimics.
nodes.body: Echo cannot prove myocarditis, but it detects danger. [1][2][3] Look for: • New LV systolic dysfunction: global or regional • RV dysfunction or biventricular failure: higher-risk phenotype • Pericardial effusion / tamponade physiology • Wall thickening from edema in fulminant myocarditis • IVC plethora, pulmonary edema, low forward flow • Exclude mimics: tamponade, severe valvular lesion, RV strai

nodes.title: Risk Stratify: Stable vs Stage D
nodes.summary: Stage D = hemodynamic or electrical instability; stable abnormal tests still usually require monitored admission.
nodes.body: ACC staging maps well to ED disposition. [1] Stage C: symptomatic myocarditis • Chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, fatigue • Troponin/ECG/CMR/echo evidence • Hemodynamically stable, no sustained malignant rhythm Stage D: advanced / fulminant myocarditis • Hemodynamic instability needing inotropes, vasopressors, or temporary circulatory support • Electrical instability needing intervention: VT/VF,

nodes.title: Fulminant Myocarditis — First 15 Minutes
nodes.summary: Pads, telemetry, POCUS, norepi for MAP, avoid blind fluids, early advanced HF/ECMO-capable transfer.
nodes.body: Fulminant myocarditis is a time-to-center disease. Stabilize while arranging advanced HF/ECMO-capable care. [1][3][4] First 15 minutes: 1. Pads on, defib ready, continuous telemetry 2. Large-bore IV/IO, arterial line if available, lactate/VBG/ABG 3. POCUS: LV/RV function, effusion, IVC, lung edema 4. Norepinephrine for hypotension/MAP support; add inotrope if low-output with adequate MAP 5. Avoid

nodes.title: Shock Strategy
nodes.summary: Norepi for MAP, cautious inotrope if low-output, no blind large boluses, early MCS if hypoperfusion persists.
nodes.body: Goal: preserve coronary perfusion and forward flow while avoiding overload. [3][4] Vasoactive approach: • Norepinephrine if hypotensive: supports MAP/RV-LV coronary perfusion • Add dobutamine or milrinone only with close BP monitoring when low-output persists • Epinephrine may be used peri-arrest, but watch lactate/arrhythmias • Avoid pure afterload reduction in shock Fluids: • Small test bolus on

nodes.title: Electrical Instability
nodes.summary: VT/VF, high-grade AV block, or syncope with abnormal myocarditis workup = Stage D risk and monitored admission.
nodes.body: Electrical instability is Stage D until proven otherwise. [1][3] High-risk rhythms: • Sustained VT/VF • Recurrent nonsustained VT with symptoms or LV dysfunction • High-grade AV block or complete heart block • Syncope with abnormal ECG/troponin/echo • Wide-complex tachycardia in suspected myocarditis ED actions: • Pads on; defib/cardioversion per ACLS • Correct K/Mg; avoid QT-prolonging meds when

nodes.title: Transfer / Mechanical Support Triggers
nodes.body: Transfer early to an advanced HF / ECMO-capable center when any are present: [1][3] • Persistent hypotension or rising lactate despite pressor/inotrope support • Biventricular dysfunction or rapidly falling EF • VT/VF storm, recurrent malignant arrhythmias, high-grade AV block • Need for temporary circulatory support: IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO, VAD evaluation • Suspected giant-cell, eosinophilic, sar
nodes.recommendation: Stage D myocarditis: stabilize locally but arrange early transfer to an advanced HF/ECMO-capable center.

nodes.title: CMR vs Endomyocardial Biopsy
nodes.summary: CMR is key noninvasive test; biopsy is selective when it changes urgent therapy.
nodes.body: CMR is the key noninvasive test; biopsy is selective. [1][2][7] Cardiac MRI helps diagnose and risk-stratify: • Myocardial edema: T2-based abnormalities • Non-ischemic injury/fibrosis: T1 mapping, extracellular volume, LGE • Myocarditis pattern: often subepicardial or mid-wall; not a coronary territory • Pericardial inflammation / myopericarditis Endomyocardial biopsy is not routine for every susp

nodes.title: Etiology Framework
nodes.summary: Target the etiology workup: viral, ICI, giant-cell/eosinophilic/sarcoid, infectious, autoimmune, toxin.
nodes.body: Most ED cases are treated supportively first, but etiology changes consultation and therapy. [1][2] Ask and look for: • Viral/COVID/influenza-like illness • Recent vaccination with compatible timing • Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy • Autoimmune disease, sarcoid, lupus, vasculitis • Drug reaction, eosinophilia, DRESS • Tick/travel/infectious exposure: Lyme, Chagas, HIV, TB, diphtheria dependin

nodes.title: Likely Viral / Idiopathic Myocarditis
nodes.summary: Likely viral: supportive care, telemetry when abnormal tests, echo/CMR, no routine antivirals unless treatable infection suspected.
nodes.body: Common ED phenotype: chest pain after viral syndrome, elevated troponin, nonischemic ECG pattern, stable vitals. [1][2] Management: • Admit or observe with telemetry if troponin/ECG abnormal or myocarditis is likely • Echo for LV/RV function and effusion • Cardiology consult for CMR timing • Supportive care; avoid strenuous activity • HF guideline-directed therapy if LV dysfunction • Avoid routine

nodes.title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis
nodes.summary: ICI myocarditis is high-risk: hold ICI, cardiology/oncology, telemetry, early steroids by specialist protocol.
nodes.body: ICI myocarditis is uncommon but high mortality. Treat as high-risk until proven otherwise. [1][8] Clues: • On PD-1/PD-L1/CTLA-4 therapy: pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab, atezolizumab, etc. • Often early after starting therapy, but can occur later • Chest pain, dyspnea, weakness, myositis, myasthenia-like symptoms • Troponin elevation, conduction disease, VT, LV dysfunction ED actions: • Hold

nodes.title: Giant-Cell / Eosinophilic / Sarcoid Concern
nodes.summary: Giant-cell/eosinophilic/sarcoid patterns need cardiology and often biopsy-capable admission or transfer.
nodes.body: These are “do not miss” because urgent biopsy and immunosuppression may change outcome. [1][2][7] Giant-cell myocarditis clues: • New HF over days-weeks • VT or high-grade AV block • Failure to improve with usual care • Autoimmune history Eosinophilic myocarditis clues: • Eosinophilia, rash, fever, DRESS/drug exposure • Asthma/EGPA phenotype • Hypersensitivity or parasitic context Sarcoid myocardi

nodes.title: Infectious / Autoimmune Clues
nodes.summary: Target infectious/autoimmune testing to exposure, severity, immune status, and treatment-changing clues.
nodes.body: Target testing to exposure and phenotype. [1][2][5] Consider infectious workup when clinically indicated: • SARS-CoV-2, influenza, respiratory viruses • HIV if risk/unknown status • Lyme in endemic exposure with AV block/myocarditis pattern • Chagas in compatible geography/exposure • Blood cultures if febrile/toxic/endocarditis concern • TB/fungal/parasitic studies only when history supports it Co

nodes.title: Stable Myocarditis — Treatment
nodes.summary: Stable myocarditis: monitor, treat HF if present, restrict exercise, avoid cardiotoxins, cardiology/CMR follow-up.
nodes.body: No magic ED antidote for routine viral myocarditis. Treat the syndrome and prevent deterioration. [1][2] Core management: • Telemetry/observation or admission when abnormal ECG, elevated troponin, syncope, arrhythmia, or LV dysfunction • Treat HF with guideline-directed therapy when LV dysfunction exists • Avoid strenuous activity; give explicit exercise restriction • Avoid alcohol, cocaine/amphet

nodes.title: HF / LV Dysfunction Care
nodes.summary: LV dysfunction: diuretics/GDMT when stable; shock uses fulminant pathway; no discharge without monitored plan.
nodes.body: Treat myocarditis-associated HF like acute HF, with extra respect for rapid deterioration. [1][2][3] If congested but perfusing: • Diuretics for pulmonary edema/volume overload • Oxygen/NIV if needed, but watch hemodynamics • Start/continue guideline-directed HF therapy with cardiology input when stable If hypoperfused/shock: • This is no longer routine HF: use fulminant pathway • Pressor/inotrope

nodes.title: Pain Control: Myopericarditis vs Myocarditis
nodes.summary: NSAID/colchicine only for pericarditic phenotype without HF/LV dysfunction; avoid NSAIDs in symptomatic HF.
nodes.body: Pericarditic chest pain and myocarditis overlap. The treatment changes when HF/LV dysfunction is present. [1][2] Reasonable when pericarditic pain predominates AND no symptomatic HF/LV dysfunction: • NSAID such as ibuprofen per pericarditis protocol • Colchicine if myopericarditis/pericarditis phenotype • PPI if GI-risk NSAID use Avoid or discuss with cardiology when: • New LV dysfunction • Sympto

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Abnormal troponin/ECG/echo, arrhythmia, syncope, HF, or high-risk etiology usually means monitored care.
nodes.body: Most confirmed/suspected myocarditis with abnormal objective findings needs monitored care. [1][2] Admit/observe with telemetry if any: • Elevated troponin with suspected myocarditis • Abnormal ECG beyond nonspecific changes • Arrhythmia, palpitations with concerning ECG, syncope • New LV/RV dysfunction or HF symptoms • Pericardial effusion with concern • ICI therapy, eosinophilia, autoimmune/syst

nodes.title: Admit / Observe with Telemetry
nodes.body: Recommended for suspected myocarditis with objective abnormality or high-risk history. [1][2] Inpatient plan: • Telemetry • Troponin/ECG trends as clinically indicated • Formal echocardiogram if not done • Cardiology consultation • CMR planning when stable/available • HF therapy if LV dysfunction • Etiology-directed testing for atypical/severe/high-risk cases • Clear exercise restriction on discha
nodes.recommendation: Admit or observe on telemetry. Obtain formal echo/cardiology input, trend objective abnormalities, and plan CMR/follow-up.

nodes.title: Low Suspicion / Normal Objective Testing
nodes.body: Low suspicion is not “myocarditis ruled out forever.” It means no current objective evidence and no danger phenotype. [1][5] Possible discharge only if all are true: • Normal vitals and well appearing • No syncope, sustained palpitations, HF symptoms, or exertional chest pain • ECG reassuring • Troponin normal with appropriate timing/repeat strategy • No concerning echo/POCUS findings if performed
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if objective tests are reassuring, no danger features, and follow-up/return precautions are strong.

nodes.title: Return to Exercise / Sports
nodes.summary: No strenuous activity for 3-6 months in symptomatic myocarditis; return only after cardiology clearance/testing.
nodes.body: Do not let active myocarditis exercise. [1][9] ACC pathway: symptomatic Stage C/D myocarditis should avoid strenuous physical activity for 3-6 months. Before return, reassess with cardiology and objective testing. Typical clearance elements: • Symptom resolution • Normalizing troponin/inflammatory markers • LV function recovered on echo/CMR • No active inflammation/high-risk LGE pattern on CMR whe

nodes.title: Stop / Pitfalls
nodes.summary: Pitfalls: unsafe discharge, delayed transfer, blind fluids, NSAIDs in HF, missed ACS/PE/dissection, premature exercise clearance.
nodes.body: Do NOT: • Do not discharge suspected myocarditis with VT, high-grade AV block, syncope, new LV dysfunction, shock, or ICI therapy. • Do not wait for CMR before stabilizing/transfer in fulminant myocarditis. • Do not give large blind fluid boluses to pump-failure shock. • Do not treat new myocarditis as “just anxiety/viral pain” if troponin, ECG, echo, syncope, or rhythm is abnormal. • Do not use N

nodes.title: Nail Anatomy Overview
nodes.summary: Germinal matrix (proximal 1/3) produces 90% of nail; sterile matrix (distal 2/3) for adherence; regrowth 4-6 months
nodes.body: Understanding nail anatomy is essential for proper repair. [1,2] Key structures: Nail plate: The hard keratinized structure (the "nail" itself) - Grows ~3mm/month (fingernails), ~1mm/month (toenails) - Complete regrowth: 4-6 months (fingers), 12-18 months (toes) Nail bed: Soft tissue beneath the nail plate - Germinal matrix: Proximal 1/3, produces 90% of nail plate - Sterile matrix: Distal 2/3, ad

nodes.title: Clinical Anatomy Relevance
nodes.summary: Germinal matrix injury = nail growth abnormalities; 50% have distal phalanx fracture = open fracture; digital block safe
nodes.body: Why anatomy matters for repair: [1,2,3] Germinal matrix injuries (proximal): - Result in nail growth abnormalities - Split nail, ridged nail, absent nail - Require meticulous repair under magnification - Higher risk of permanent deformity Sterile matrix injuries (distal): - Result in non-adherence of nail to bed - Nail lifts off, catches on objects - Generally more forgiving with repair - Still ne

nodes.title: Injury Classification
nodes.summary: Injury patterns: simple/stellate laceration, subungual hematoma, avulsion, crush, amputation — each has distinct management
nodes.body: Common nail bed injury patterns: [1,3,4] Simple laceration: - Linear cut through nail bed - Often from sharp object or crush Stellate laceration: - Star-shaped pattern - Typical of crush injury - Multiple fragments to realign Subungual hematoma: - Blood under intact nail plate - May be >50% nail surface - Associated with occult laceration or fracture Avulsion: - Partial or complete nail plate avul

nodes.title: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Check vascular status (cap refill), sensory (two-point <5mm), motor (FDP/FDS/extensor), tendon assessment for mallet finger
nodes.body: Systematic evaluation of nail injuries: [1,4] History: - Mechanism (crush, laceration, avulsion) - Time of injury - Hand dominance - Occupation (musician, typist = higher cosmetic expectations) - Tetanus status Physical exam: - Vascular status: capillary refill, color, temperature - Sensory status: two-point discrimination (normal <5mm) - Motor status: FDP and FDS function - Tendon assessment: ext

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.summary: X-ray all nail bed injuries — 50% have fracture; Seymour fracture (pediatric) needs OR; nail bed + fracture = open fracture
nodes.body: X-ray is indicated for most nail bed injuries. [3,4] Obtain AP, lateral, and oblique views of affected digit. Evaluate for: - Distal phalanx fracture (present in ~50%) - Tuft fracture (crush mechanism) - Transverse shaft fracture - Joint involvement (DIP) - Foreign body Fracture implications: [4] - Nail bed laceration + fracture = OPEN fracture - Antibiotics indicated (see treatment) - Unstable fr

nodes.title: Injury Type
nodes.summary: Route by injury pattern: subungual hematoma, nail bed laceration, avulsion, or complex/amputation
nodes.body: What is the primary injury pattern? [1,4]

nodes.title: Subungual Hematoma
nodes.summary: Modern evidence: trephination alone sufficient for most hematomas (even >50%) if nail plate intact with adherent margins
nodes.body: Subungual hematoma is blood trapped between nail plate and nail bed. [1,5] Assessment: - Estimate hematoma size (% of nail surface) - Assess nail plate integrity (fractures, avulsion) - Check for associated fracture on X-ray Traditional teaching: - <25% nail surface → conservative management - 25-50% → consider trephination - >50% → nail removal and bed repair Modern evidence (2024): [5] - Trephin

nodes.title: Trephination Technique
nodes.summary: Electrocautery preferred (painless, fast); 18g needle alternative — no digital block needed for trephination alone
nodes.body: Trephination = creating hole in nail to drain hematoma. [1,5] Methods: 1. Electrocautery (preferred): - Battery-powered cautery device - Touch to nail surface, melts through - No pressure needed (painless) - Stop immediately when blood wells up - Fast, efficient, minimal equipment 2. 18-gauge needle: - Rotate needle between fingers while applying gentle pressure - Drill through nail plate - More t

nodes.title: Hematoma: When to Remove Nail
nodes.summary: Remove nail only if avulsed/disrupted or non-adherent margins — unnecessary removal may cause more harm than trephination alone
nodes.body: Nail removal rarely needed for isolated subungual hematoma. [5] Remove nail plate if: - Nail plate avulsed or significantly disrupted - Edges not adherent (suggests underlying laceration) - Unable to adequately decompress hematoma - Associated nail fold disruption - Obvious nail bed laceration visible at edges Do NOT remove nail if: - Nail plate intact with adherent margins - Adequate decompressio

nodes.title: Hematoma Aftercare
nodes.body: Post-trephination care: [1,5] Wound care: - Clean with saline - Apply antibiotic ointment (bacitracin) - Non-adherent dressing (Telfa) - Protective splint (aluminum finger splint) if fracture or significant injury Medications: - Tetanus prophylaxis if indicated - Antibiotics if fracture present - NSAIDs or acetaminophen for pain Follow-up: - Return in 48-72 hours for wound check - Soak in warm wat
nodes.recommendation: Trephination with protective dressing. Antibiotics if associated fracture. Follow up in 48-72 hours.

nodes.title: Nail Plate Removal
nodes.summary: Digital block before removal — elevate nail distal to proximal with hemostat/Freer; SAVE the nail plate for splinting
nodes.body: When nail plate removal is indicated for nail bed repair: [1,3] Indications: - Visible nail bed laceration requiring repair - Significantly disrupted/avulsed nail plate - Nail fold injury needing repair - Subungual hematoma with non-adherent nail margins Technique: 1. Digital block: - Perform digital nerve block (two injection sites at base of finger) - Wait 5-10 minutes for complete anesthesia -

nodes.title: Nail Bed Repair Principles
nodes.summary: Goals: anatomic alignment, prevent scarring, preserve germinal matrix, splint nail fold — use magnification for best outcomes
nodes.body: Goals of nail bed repair: [1,3,6] 1. Anatomic alignment of nail bed edges 2. Prevent scarring that causes nail deformity 3. Preserve germinal matrix function 4. Splint nail fold to prevent synechiae General principles: - Meticulous hemostasis (use tourniquet/finger tourniquet) - Magnification improves outcomes (loupes or operating microscope) - Fine absorbable sutures (6-0 or 7-0 chromic/Vicryl) -

nodes.title: Repair Technique
nodes.summary: 6-0/7-0 absorbable suture, digital tourniquet, irrigate → align edges → interrupted sutures → check for step-off
nodes.body: Step-by-step nail bed repair: [1,3,6] Setup: - Digital tourniquet (Penrose drain or commercial device) - Adequate lighting and magnification - 6-0 or 7-0 absorbable suture on small needle Repair steps: 1. Irrigate thoroughly (saline, remove debris) 2. Identify and align nail bed edges: - Match tissue edges anatomically - Germinal matrix especially important 3. Place interrupted sutures: - Simple i

nodes.title: Nail Fold Stenting
nodes.summary: MUST stent nail fold — without stent, synechiae form and nail cannot grow properly; original nail plate is best stent
nodes.body: Why stent the nail fold: [3,6] Without stent: - Eponychium adheres to nail bed (synechiae) - New nail cannot grow out properly - Results in split nail or no nail Options for nail fold stent: 1. Original nail plate (best): - Clean with saline/betadine - Trim sharp edges - Replace under nail fold - Secure with mattress suture through nail and eponychium - Holes can be drilled for drainage 2. Foil su

nodes.title: Associated Fracture Management
nodes.summary: Nail bed + fracture = OPEN fracture — cephalexin 500mg QID x5-7d; Seymour fracture (pediatric) usually needs OR I&D
nodes.body: Distal phalanx fractures with nail bed injury: [3,4] Key principle: Nail bed laceration + phalanx fracture = OPEN fracture Tuft fractures (most common): - Usually stable (comminuted but held by soft tissue) - Nail bed repair provides splinting - Replace nail plate for additional stability - Protective splint (aluminum) - Antibiotics for open fracture Transverse shaft fractures: - Assess stability

nodes.title: Nail Avulsion Injuries
nodes.summary: Always remove entire nail for bed inspection; replace original nail as stent; germinal matrix avulsion may need microsurgery

nodes.title: Complex Injuries
nodes.summary: Refer hand surgery for >50% tissue loss, germinal matrix loss, amputation, unstable fractures, vascular compromise
nodes.body: Complex nail bed injuries requiring specialist consultation: [3,4] Refer to hand surgery for: - Significant tissue loss (>50% nail bed) - Complete germinal matrix loss - Amputation through nail bed - Unstable fractures requiring fixation - Tendon involvement (FDP/extensor) - Vascular compromise - Multiple digit involvement Amputation considerations: [4] - Zone 1 (tip only): often heal by secondary

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition by complexity — simple repair can discharge, complex injury needs hand surgery consultation
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on injury complexity: [1,4]

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.body: Post-repair care: [1,3] Wound care: - Keep dressing clean and dry for 48 hours - After 48h: daily warm water soaks, reapply antibiotic ointment and non-adherent dressing - Leave nail plate stent in place until it falls off naturally Splinting: - Wear aluminum splint for comfort and protection x 2-3 weeks - OK to remove for gentle ROM exercises after 1 week Medications: - Complete antibiotic course
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with protective splint, wound care instructions, and follow-up in 7-10 days.

nodes.title: Hand Surgery Consultation
nodes.body: Indications for hand surgery involvement: [3,4] Urgent/emergent consultation: - Significant tissue loss requiring grafting - Complete germinal matrix injury - Unstable fractures needing fixation - Amputation with replantation potential - Vascular compromise - Open fracture needing OR I&D - Seymour fracture (pediatric) Consultation details to provide: - Mechanism and time of injury - Digit(s) invol
nodes.recommendation: Consult hand surgery for complex repair. Provide protective dressing, splint, antibiotics for open fracture, and analgesia.

nodes.summary: Airway/swallow, neuro, trauma, infection risk, and vascular clues first.

Epidural abscess / spinal infection \u2014 fever, IVDU/immunosuppression, midline tenderness, deficit. 4. Deep space neck infection (Ludwig, retropharyngeal) \u2014 airway threat: drooling, trismus, muffled voice. 5. Cervical

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Exclude trauma, meningitis, dissection, deep neck infection, SEA/NVO, myelopathy, and cardiac/aortic causes.
nodes.body: Choose the dangerous lane first. Mechanical neck pain is a diagnosis after exclusions.

nodes.title: Trauma / C-Spine Injury
nodes.body: Open Cervical Spine Injuries. Next 5 minutes: immobilize if unstable mechanism or neuro deficit, document neuro exam before analgesia/sedation if possible, CT C-spine by validated trauma criteria/local protocol, CTA neck if blunt cerebrovascular injury risk, spine consult for fracture/instability/neuro deficit. Pitfall: elderly ground-level falls, anticoagulation, intoxication, and distracting inj
nodes.recommendation: Treat traumatic neck pain with neurologic or high-risk mechanism features as C-spine injury until cleared.

nodes.title: Meningitis / Encephalitis
nodes.body: Open Meningitis / Encephalitis. Next 5 minutes: droplet precautions if meningococcal concern, blood cultures if they do not delay therapy, empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone when bacterial meningitis plausible, acyclovir when encephalitis plausible. CT-before-LP only when indicated, but treatment should not wait for CT/LP logistics. Pitfall: absence of classic triad does not exclude meningitis
nodes.recommendation: When CNS infection is plausible, empiric therapy is time-sensitive.

nodes.title: Cervical Artery Dissection
nodes.body: Open Cervical Artery Dissection and Acute Ischemic Stroke if focal deficits are present. Next 5 minutes: focused posterior circulation exam, Horner check, CTA head/neck if suspicion is meaningful, avoid neck manipulation, stroke alert if deficits/window. Ask about manipulation, minor trauma, coughing/vomiting, sports, and strangulation. Pitfall: young patient with posterior headache/neck pain and
nodes.recommendation: CTA head/neck when neck pain plus neuro/Horner/posterior circulation features fit.

nodes.title: Deep Neck Space Infection / Airway Risk
nodes.body: Open Deep Neck Space Infections. Next 5 minutes: airway assessment before supine CT, ENT/anesthesia early if voice change, drooling, floor-of-mouth elevation, stridor, or trismus; IV antibiotics covering oral flora; CT neck with IV contrast when stable enough. Pitfall: do not paralyze a difficult infected airway casually. Plan awake/controlled airway with help when airway signs are present.
nodes.recommendation: Airway plan comes before CT when deep neck infection has airway features.

nodes.title: Spinal Epidural Abscess / Vertebral Osteomyelitis
nodes.body: Open Cervical Spine Pain - Non-Traumatic. Next 5 minutes: neuro exam, ESR/CRP, blood cultures if febrile or high suspicion, MRI cervical spine with and without contrast; consider whole-spine MRI when symptoms do not localize or risk is high. Start antibiotics after cultures when sepsis/neuro deficit; do not delay treatment in unstable patients. Pitfall: fever is absent in many SEA cases. IVDU, bac
nodes.recommendation: MRI is the key test when spine infection or epidural abscess is plausible.

nodes.title: Myelopathy / Radiculopathy / Cord Compression
nodes.body: Open Cervical Spine Pain - Non-Traumatic. Next 5 minutes: document strength/reflexes/sensation/gait, check for Hoffman/clonus/hyperreflexia, look for urinary symptoms, avoid manipulation, MRI when myelopathy/progressive deficit/cord compression is suspected. Pitfall: bilateral hand clumsiness, gait instability, and hyperreflexia are not routine radiculopathy.
nodes.recommendation: Myelopathy signs need MRI and spine/neuro pathway, not routine discharge.

nodes.title: Cardiac / Aortic Neck Pain
nodes.body: Open Chest Pain Hub, STEMI, NSTEMI, or Aortic Dissection as indicated. Next 5 minutes: ECG within 10 minutes when ischemia is possible, bilateral arm BP/pulses when dissection fits, troponin pathway, CTA aorta for tearing pain/pulse deficit/neuro features. Pitfall: jaw/neck pain can be an anginal equivalent, especially in older adults, women, and diabetics.
nodes.recommendation: Neck pain with ischemic or aortic features belongs in the chest pain pathway.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Analgesia, repeat neuro/airway/swallow exam, infection screen by risk, then reassess.
nodes.body: Default bundle when no killer has declared itself: - Analgesia: acetaminophen/NSAID when safe; avoid masking evolving neuro deficits with heavy sedation. - Gentle range-of-motion only when trauma, infection, myelopathy, dissection, and airway infection are not suspected. - Focused repeat neuro exam: strength, sensation, reflexes, gait, cranial nerves when headache/dizziness. - Infection screen whe

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: New neuro, airway, swallow, fever, or cardiac features reset the workup.
nodes.body: Mechanical pain should improve and stay neurologically quiet.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: CT trauma, CTA dissection, CT neck contrast infection, MRI cord/spine infection/malignancy/progressive neuro.
nodes.body: Choose imaging by suspected threat: - CT C-spine: trauma/high-risk mechanism, elderly fall, midline tenderness, intoxication, neuro deficit per trauma criteria. - CTA head/neck: dissection suspicion, Horner, posterior circulation symptoms, strangulation/manipulation with neuro symptoms. - CT neck with IV contrast: deep neck infection, abscess, Lemierre concern, airway-safe patient. - MRI cervical

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Airway, neuro, infection, vascular, and trauma threats admit; benign mechanical pain can discharge with safeguards.
nodes.body: Disposition follows airway, neuro, infection, vascular risk, and function.

nodes.title: Admit / ICU / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit/ICU/transfer for deep neck infection with airway concern, meningitis/encephalitis, dissection/stroke, unstable C-spine injury, epidural abscess/vertebral osteomyelitis, myelopathy/progressive deficit, suspected malignancy cord compression, uncontrolled pain with red flags, or unsafe follow-up.
nodes.recommendation: Use the deep-dive consult and involve airway/ENT/neuro/spine early based on the threat.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exam
nodes.body: Observe when severe pain persists, red-flag labs/imaging are pending, swallowing/voice symptoms need serial exams, intoxication or unreliable exam limits clearance, or neuro symptoms are transient/equivocal.
nodes.recommendation: Observation is for serial airway/neuro exams and completion of targeted testing.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: benign mechanical pattern, vitals stable, pain improved, normal neuro exam, no airway/swallow concern, no infection/vascular/trauma red flags, and follow-up is realistic. Return precautions: fever, confusion, severe headache, weakness/numbness, gait trouble, vision/speech symptoms, syncope, chest pain, trouble swallowing, voice change, drooling, worsening pain, or new bowel/bl
nodes.recommendation: Document red-flag screen, repeat neuro exam, and specific return precautions.

nodes.body: Admit to ICU: • Operative repair needed • Endovascular intervention • Airway compromise (intubated) • Vascular injury on anticoagulation • Neurologic deficit Admit to floor: • Observation after negative workup • Minor injury managed non-operatively • Serial exams needed Discharge (rare): • Superficial wound only • Completely negative workup • No hard or soft signs • Reliable patient with follow-up
