nodes.summary: Pain out of proportion most sensitive (~90%); risk factors: DM, immunocompromise, IVDU, recent surgery; normal LRINEC does NOT rule out
nodes.body: Pain out of proportion is the most sensitive finding (~90%) but can be difficult to assess. [2] Findings that should increase suspicion: [2][3] • Rapid progression of erythema (mark borders with time) • Edema extending beyond visible erythema • Fever with focal pain and systemic toxicity • Skin changes not responding to antibiotics • Blistering or bullae (even if not hemorrhagic) • Wooden/indurate

nodes.title: Cellulitis vs NSTI — Red Flags
nodes.summary: NSTI red flags: failure to improve at 24-48h, rapid progression, new systemic symptoms, bullae, pain out of proportion
nodes.body: Cellulitis is far more common than NSTI, but missing NSTI is catastrophic. Features suggesting simple cellulitis: [2] • Slow progression (days, not hours) • Well-demarcated borders • Pain proportional to appearance • No systemic toxicity • Improvement with oral antibiotics Red flags that should prompt re-evaluation: [2][3] • Failure to improve after 24-48h of appropriate antibiotics • Worsening de

nodes.title: Simple Cellulitis — Close Follow-up
nodes.summary: Mark borders, treat cellulitis, mandatory return precautions for spread/pain/fever/bullae; 24-48h follow-up required
nodes.body: If low suspicion for NSTI: Mark wound borders — instruct patient to return immediately if erythema extends beyond marks. Standard cellulitis treatment: • Cephalexin 500 mg PO q6h OR • TMP-SMX DS 1-2 tabs PO BID (if MRSA risk) Discharge instructions: [2] • Return IMMEDIATELY if: - Erythema spreads beyond marked borders - Increasing pain - Fever develops - Bullae or skin color changes appear - Any s

nodes.title: Imaging — CT Is Preferred
nodes.summary: CT with contrast: 94% sensitive, 77% specific — look for gas, fascial thickening, non-enhancing fascia; normal CT does NOT rule out early NSTI
nodes.body: CT with IV contrast is the imaging modality of choice: [2][6] • Sensitivity ~94%, Specificity ~77% • Faster and more practical than MRI • Can assess extent of involvement CT findings suggestive of NSTI: [2][6] • Gas tracking along fascial planes (most specific) • Fascial thickening with enhancement • Non-enhancing fascia (indicates necrosis) • Fluid collections along fascial planes • Vessel thromb

nodes.title: LRINEC Score — Adjunct Only
nodes.summary: LRINEC >=6 increases suspicion BUT scores <6 do NOT rule out; Canadian guidelines recommend against using for decision-making; clinical suspicion trumps score
nodes.body: Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) [5] Calculate LRINEC Score | Parameter | Cutoff | Points | |-----------|--------|--------| | CRP | <150 mg/L | 0 | | | >=150 mg/L | 4 | | WBC | <15 | 0 | | | 15-25 | 1 | | | >25 | 2 | | Hemoglobin | >13.5 g/dL | 0 | | | 11-13.5 | 1 | | | <11 | 2 | | Sodium | >=135 | 0 | | | <135 | 2 | | Creatinine | <=1.6 mg/dL | 0 | | | >1.6 | 2 | | Glu

nodes.title: Resuscitation — Sepsis Protocol
nodes.summary: Sepsis protocol: 30 mL/kg LR, broad-spectrum abx within 1hr, norepinephrine if needed; do NOT delay surgery for resuscitation
nodes.body: NSTI patients are SEPTIC — apply sepsis bundle: [2][7] Immediate actions: 1. IV access — 2 large-bore IVs or central line 2. Fluid resuscitation — 30 mL/kg LR bolus within 3 hours 3. Broad-spectrum antibiotics — within 1 hour (see next step) 4. Labs — CBC, BMP, lactate, CRP, coags, blood cultures x2, wound cultures 5. Mark wound margins with time Vasopressors if needed: • Norepinephrine 0.05-0.5 m

nodes.title: Surgical Consultation — STAT
nodes.summary: Call surgery STAT; bedside finger test if surgery delayed; each hour of surgical delay increases mortality; multiple OR trips typical
nodes.body: Call surgery IMMEDIATELY — this is a surgical emergency. [2][3] Surgical consultation should be obtained for: • Any patient with suspected or confirmed NSTI • Cellulitis not improving on appropriate antibiotics • Any concerning skin findings (bullae, necrosis, crepitus) Bedside finger test: [2] • Under local anesthesia, make 2 cm incision to fascia • Insert finger and probe along fascial plane • P

nodes.title: Anatomic Location
nodes.summary: Location guides microbiology: extremity (Type 1/2), Fournier (polymicrobial + anaerobes), head/neck (odontogenic), trunk (post-surgical)
nodes.body: Location affects microbiology and additional considerations: Select primary location of infection:

nodes.title: Fournier Gangrene — Perineal NSTI
nodes.summary: Fournier gangrene: perineal NSTI, 40% mortality, polymicrobial; always include broad gram-negative + anaerobic + MRSA coverage; surgical debridement mandatory
nodes.body: Fournier gangrene is NSTI of the perineum, scrotum, and genital region. Mortality 40%. [4][8] Risk factors: [4] • Diabetes mellitus (most common) • Alcoholism / immunocompromise • Urinary tract infection / instrumentation • Perianal abscess / anal fissure • Recent surgery / trauma Key considerations: [8] • Polymicrobial — always include broad gram-negative AND anaerobic coverage • May require feca

nodes.title: Cervical / Head-Neck NSTI
nodes.summary: Head/neck NSTI: airway threat is primary concern; can spread to mediastinum; early intubation; consult ENT and CT surgery; often odontogenic origin
nodes.body: Cervical necrotizing fasciitis often originates from: [9] • Dental infection (most common) • Peritonsillar abscess • Ludwig angina • Penetrating trauma Key considerations: • Airway compromise is the primary threat • Can rapidly spread to mediastinum (descending necrotizing mediastinitis) • CT neck AND chest with contrast • Early intubation if airway concern • May require awake fiberoptic intubatio

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotic Therapy
nodes.summary: Triple therapy: pip-tazo + linezolid (or vanco) + clindamycin; clindamycin for toxin suppression is critical; 7-14 days total duration
nodes.body: Triple-drug therapy covering gram-positives (including MRSA), gram-negatives, and anaerobes: [2][3][10] NSTI Treatment Guide Recommended Empiric Regimen: 1. Broad-spectrum beta-lactam backbone: • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h (preferred) OR • Meropenem 1g IV q8h (if resistant organisms suspected) 2. MRSA Coverage: • Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h (PREFERRED) — superior toxin suppression, avoids ne

nodes.title: Special Organism Considerations
nodes.summary: Special exposures: saltwater = Vibrio vulnificus (high mortality), freshwater = Aeromonas; both require specific antibiotic coverage
nodes.body: Epidemiologic exposures may suggest specific pathogens: Select if any apply:

nodes.title: Vibrio vulnificus — Saltwater NSTI
nodes.summary: Vibrio vulnificus: saltwater/oysters, cirrhosis major risk, >50% mortality; add doxycycline + 3rd-gen cephalosporin to standard regimen
nodes.body: Vibrio vulnificus causes rapidly fatal NSTI with >50% mortality. [4][11] Risk factors: • Liver cirrhosis (100x increased risk) • Hemochromatosis • Immunocompromise • Raw oyster ingestion • Saltwater wound exposure (Gulf Coast, warm coastal waters) Clinical features: • Extremely rapid progression (hours) • Hemorrhagic bullae characteristic • Septic shock common at presentation • Often requires ampu

nodes.title: Aeromonas — Freshwater NSTI
nodes.summary: Aeromonas: freshwater exposure, leech therapy; add doxycycline + fluoroquinolone to standard regimen; resistant to ampicillin
nodes.body: Aeromonas hydrophila associated with freshwater exposure. [4] Risk factors: • Freshwater injury (lake, river, pond) • Immunocompromise • Liver disease • Leech therapy (medicinal leeches) Antibiotic regimen (ADD to empiric therapy): [4] • Doxycycline 100 mg IV q12h PLUS • Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h OR Levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h If already on pip-tazo or carbapenem: • Add doxycycline 100 mg IV q1

nodes.title: NSTI Classification by Microbiology
nodes.summary: Type I: polymicrobial 70-90% (DM, post-surgical); Type II: monomicrobial 10-30% (GAS, MRSA — extremities); Type III: Vibrio (saltwater)
nodes.body: NSTI Classification Type I — Polymicrobial (70-90%): [1][4] • Mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria • At least 2 organisms (often 4-5+) • Includes: Bacteroides, Clostridium, Peptostreptococcus, Enterobacteriaceae • More common in: diabetics, post-surgical, Fournier gangrene Type II — Monomicrobial (10-30%): [1][4] • Single organism, often more virulent • Group A Streptococcus (GAS) — most common, a

nodes.title: Toxin Suppression — Clindamycin
nodes.summary: Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h CRITICAL for toxin suppression; beta-lactams may increase toxin release (Eagle effect); consider dual suppression with linezolid in severe TSS
nodes.body: Clindamycin is CRITICAL for toxin-mediated disease: [2][3] Mechanism: [3] • Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis at 50S ribosome • Suppresses exotoxin production (superantigens, streptolysins) • Effect persists even as bacteria die • Beta-lactams may paradoxically INCREASE toxin release (Eagle effect) Dosing: [2] • Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h • Some experts recommend 1200 mg IV q6h for severe TSS [2

nodes.title: IVIG — Streptococcal TSS
nodes.summary: IVIG 1 g/kg day 1, then 0.5 g/kg days 2-3 for streptococcal TSS; evidence mixed but WSES recommends; neutralizes superantigens
nodes.body: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be considered for streptococcal NSTI with toxic shock syndrome. [2][12] Mechanism: • Neutralizes circulating superantigens • Contains antibodies against streptococcal exotoxins Evidence: [12] • Small RCTs suggest survival benefit • Canadian observational study: OR 8.1 for survival with IVIG • Larger US study showed no mortality benefit • Evidence remains limit

nodes.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO)
nodes.summary: HBO controversial, no RCTs; may be adjunctive after surgical debridement in stable patients; NEVER delay surgery for HBO
nodes.body: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is controversial for NSTI. [13] Theoretical benefits: • Increases tissue oxygen tension • May enhance neutrophil killing • Inhibits anaerobic bacterial growth • Reduces clostridial alpha-toxin production Evidence: [13] • Observational studies suggest possible benefit • No randomized controlled trials • Difficult to separate from selection bias (only stable patients can be

nodes.title: Monitoring & Serial Evaluation
nodes.summary: Serial wound exams q4-6h, mark borders, trend lactate/WBC/CRP; OR every 24-48h until clean; persistent shock = inadequate source control
nodes.body: Frequent reassessment is critical: [2][3] Clinical monitoring: • Serial wound exams (every 4-6 hours initially) • Mark wound borders with time at each exam • Monitor for progression despite therapy • Reassess for new areas of involvement Laboratory monitoring: • Lactate trending (should improve with debridement) • WBC and CRP (expect improvement by 48-72h) • Renal function (watch for AKI from seps

nodes.title: Complications
nodes.summary: Mortality 25-35% (Fournier 40%, Vibrio >50%); complications: septic shock, MODS, DIC, AKI, amputation; each hour surgical delay increases mortality 2-3%
nodes.body: Common complications of NSTI: [2][3] Acute: • Septic shock (most common cause of death) • Multi-organ dysfunction (MODS) • DIC and coagulopathy • Acute kidney injury • ARDS • Toxic shock syndrome Surgical: • Amputation (common for extremity NSTI) • Massive tissue loss requiring reconstruction • Skin grafting • Fecal diversion for Fournier gangrene • Permanent disfigurement Long-term: • Chronic pai

nodes.title: Antibiotic De-escalation
nodes.summary: De-escalate at 48-72h based on cultures; GAS: penicillin + clindamycin; MRSA: vanco/linezolid + clindamycin; 7-14 days total
nodes.body: De-escalate antibiotics based on culture results: [10] When cultures are final (typically 48-72 hours): If Group A Streptococcus (GAS): • Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h PLUS • Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h (continue for toxin suppression) If MRSA: • Vancomycin OR Linezolid PLUS • Clindamycin if toxin-producing If Clostridial: • Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h PLUS • Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h

nodes.title: Disposition — ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ALL NSTI patients require ICU; multidisciplinary care: surgery, ID, critical care, wound care, PT/OT, psych; notify family early of severity
nodes.body: ALL patients with confirmed or suspected NSTI require ICU admission. [2][3] ICU is mandatory for: • Hemodynamic instability / vasopressor requirement • Septic shock • Multi-organ dysfunction • Post-operative monitoring after debridement • Serial wound assessments • Potential return to OR Multidisciplinary team: • Surgery (general surgery, plastics, or subspecialty based on location) • Infectious d

nodes.title: Disposition — Low-Risk Cellulitis
nodes.summary: Cellulitis outpatient if: no systemic toxicity, reliable follow-up, understands return precautions; mark borders, 24-48h follow-up mandatory
nodes.body: If NSTI has been confidently ruled out and simple cellulitis is the diagnosis: Outpatient management appropriate if: • No systemic toxicity • Hemodynamically stable • Able to take oral antibiotics • Reliable follow-up within 24-48 hours • Understanding of return precautions Mandatory discharge instructions: • Mark wound borders before discharge • Return IMMEDIATELY if: - Erythema extends beyond ma

nodes.title: Neonatal Resuscitation (NRP)
nodes.summary: Stepwise NRP overview — 90% need no intervention, 10% need PPV/O2, <1% need CPR + meds; 6 modules from prep to post-resus
nodes.body: Algorithm — Quick Reference Setup and Tools — Quick Reference NRP Steps Summary — quick-reference checklist for neonatal resuscitation. Neonatal resuscitation follows a systematic, stepwise approach from initial assessment through advanced interventions. Key statistics: [1] • ~90% of newborns transition without intervention beyond warmth, drying, and stimulation • ~10% need early support (PPV, sup

nodes.title: Team & Equipment Preparation
nodes.summary: Assign team roles, prep radiant warmer, T-piece resuscitator, pulse ox (right hand), 3-lead ECG, suction, UVC kit, epinephrine
nodes.body: TEAM BRIEFING • Assign roles before delivery: team leader, airway manager, compressor, medication nurse, timekeeper/recorder • NRP pre-brief questions: gestational age, number of babies, risk factors (meconium, preeclampsia, prematurity), cord management plan • Communicate: "vigorous" vs "non-vigorous" dictates cord strategy EQUIPMENT CHECKLIST • Radiant warmer — turn ON now (prewarming) • T-piece

nodes.title: Cord Management (2025 Update)
nodes.summary: DCC 30-60 sec for vigorous term; intact cord milking if non-vigorous ≥35wk; NO milking <28wk (IVH risk); clamp immediately if resus needed
nodes.body: DELAYED CORD CLAMPING (DCC) — 2025 GUIDELINES [1][5] Vigorous term/late preterm: • DCC 30–60 seconds recommended • Improves placental transfusion, iron stores, and hemoglobin Non-vigorous ≥35 weeks: • Intact cord milking (ICM) may be reasonable (compared to immediate clamping) • Milk cord toward baby 3–4 times over 2 seconds Preterm 28–34 weeks: • ICM when DCC isn't possible <28 weeks: • ICM is NO

nodes.title: Preterm Considerations
nodes.summary: Plastic wrap <32wk, higher starting FiO2 for preterm, temperature is critical — both hypo/hyperthermia worsen outcomes
nodes.body: PRETERM ASSESSMENT [1][2] Viability assessment: • Dating most accurate in 1st trimester (±3–5 days) • Later dating accuracy: ±1–2 weeks • U/S: BPD + femur length for estimation Preterm-specific needs: • Plastic wrap <32 weeks — cover body (not face) to prevent heat loss • Higher starting FiO2 — 21–30% for ≥35 wk, 21–30% for <35 wk (titrate to SpO2 targets) • Temperature is critical — hypothermia w

nodes.title: Initial Evaluation
nodes.summary: Three questions at birth: term gestation? breathing/crying? good tone? — Yes to ALL = routine care, No to ANY = initial steps
nodes.body: INITIAL EVALUATION — The 3 Questions [1][2][3] Assess immediately at birth: 1. Term gestation? (≥37 weeks) 2. Breathing or crying? 3. Good muscle tone? (flexed, active)

nodes.title: Vigorous — Routine Care
nodes.body: VIGOROUS NEWBORN • Skin-to-skin contact with mother • Delayed cord clamping 30–60 seconds • Dry the baby with warm towels • Maintain normothermia (36.5–37.5°C) • APGAR scoring at 1 and 5 minutes Continue monitoring for transition. If at any point the baby develops apnea, labored breathing, or HR <100 → proceed to initial steps.
nodes.recommendation: Vigorous newborn — routine care. Skin-to-skin, delayed cord clamping, dry, maintain normothermia. APGAR at 1 and 5 minutes. Monitor for transition.

nodes.title: Initial Steps — Golden 30 Seconds
nodes.summary: Golden 30 seconds: Warm (radiant heater), Dry, Position (sniffing), Stimulate (flick soles/rub back), Clear airway PRN — mouth before nose
nodes.body: INITIAL STEPS — Complete within 30 seconds [1][2][3] W — WARM • Radiant heater ON — NO blankets on top (blocks radiant heat) • Plastic wrap for <32 weeks D — DRY • Vigorously dry with warm towels • Remove wet towels — replace with dry P — POSITION • Sniffing position — slight neck extension to open airway • Shoulder roll if needed for neutral alignment S — STIMULATE • Flick the soles of the feet •

nodes.title: Meconium-Stained Fluid
nodes.summary: Do NOT delay PPV for meconium suctioning (2025 change) — ventilation is priority; ET suction only if visible thick meconium blocks airway
nodes.body: MECONIUM MANAGEMENT (2025 Update) [1][6] Vigorous baby + meconium: • Proceed with normal initial steps • No special suctioning needed Non-vigorous baby + meconium: • Do NOT delay PPV for suctioning (2025 guideline change) • Begin PPV as indicated — ventilation is the priority • ET suctioning only if airway is obstructed (visible thick meconium blocking airway) Meconium aspirator is no longer routi

nodes.title: 30-Second Reassessment
nodes.summary: After initial steps assess breathing, HR, tone, color — breathing+HR≥100 = good, labored = CPAP, apnea/HR<100 = PPV now
nodes.body: 30-SECOND REASSESSMENT [1][2] After initial steps, evaluate: • Breathing — spontaneous, regular respirations? • Heart rate — auscultate or palpate umbilical stump (6 sec × 10) • Tone — flexed and active? • Color — improving?

nodes.title: Breathing Support
nodes.summary: SpO2 on RIGHT hand (preductal), CPAP 5-6 cmH2O for labored breathing, titrate O2 to targets — avoid hyperoxia
nodes.body: SUPPLEMENTAL O2 / CPAP [1][2] Pulse oximetry — apply to right hand/wrist (preductal) • Do NOT use left hand or feet (postductal — lower readings are normal) SpO2 targets by minute of life: [1] • 1 min: 60–65% • 2 min: 65–70% • 3 min: 70–75% • 4 min: 75–80% • 5 min: 80–85% • 10 min: 85–95% Labored breathing with adequate HR: • Start CPAP 5–6 cmH2O via mask • Supplement O2 to meet SpO2 targets • Avo

nodes.title: Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV)
nodes.summary: PPV is most important intervention — T-piece preferred, C-E grip, PIP 20-25, rate 40-60/min, FiO2 21% for ≥35wk, confirm chest rise
nodes.body: PPV — The Most Important Intervention in NRP [1][2][3] T-piece resuscitator preferred (2025) — provides consistent PIP and PEEP. Self-inflating bag acceptable if T-piece unavailable. [1] TECHNIQUE: • C-E grip — C fingers seal mask, E fingers lift jaw • Mask seal — covers mouth and nose, not eyes • Sniffing position — slight neck extension • PIP 20–25 cmH2O (avoid barotrauma) • Rate 40–60/min ("squ

nodes.title: SpO2 Targets & Monitoring
nodes.summary: Monitor SpO2 on RIGHT hand only (preductal) — targets: 1min 60-65%, 5min 80-85%, 10min 85-95%; cardiac monitor most accurate HR
nodes.body: PREDUCTAL SpO2 TARGETS [1][2] Monitor on right hand/wrist (preductal — above the ductus arteriosus). Target SpO2 by minute of life: • 1 min: 60–65% • 2 min: 65–70% • 3 min: 70–75% • 4 min: 75–80% • 5 min: 80–85% • 10 min: 85–95% Why preductal? The right hand receives blood from the aorta BEFORE the ductus arteriosus. Left hand and feet receive mixed blood — lower SpO2 is expected and doesn't indic

nodes.title: PPV Reassessment
nodes.summary: After 30 sec effective PPV check HR — ≥100 = improving, <100 = apply MR SOPA corrective steps
nodes.body: PPV REASSESSMENT — after 30 seconds of effective PPV [1][2] Check heart rate: • Auscultate, palpate umbilical stump, or cardiac monitor • 6-second count × 10 for quick assessment

nodes.title: Corrective Steps — MR SOPA
nodes.summary: MR SOPA: Mask adjust, Reposition, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure increase (by 5 cmH2O), Alternative airway (ETT/LMA)
nodes.body: MR SOPA — Corrective Steps for Ineffective Ventilation [1][2] If HR is not improving with PPV, systematically troubleshoot: M — Mask adjust • Reapply mask — ensure tight seal, no air leak • Reposition C-E grip R — Reposition • Sniffing position — slight neck extension • Shoulder roll for alignment S — Suction • Suction mouth then nose • Clear any secretions obstructing airway O — Open mouth • Open

nodes.title: Advanced Airway
nodes.summary: ETT or LMA for failed PPV — 30 sec attempt limit, LMA for ≥34wk >2kg (2025), intubate before CPR and for tracheal suctioning
nodes.body: ADVANCED AIRWAY — ETT or LMA [1][2] ETT Intubation: • Use cardiac monitor to confirm HR before and after • Attempt limit: 30 seconds per attempt — ventilate between attempts • Confirm placement: chest rise, bilateral breath sounds, CO2 detector • Secure tube — neonatal ETTs are extremely easy to dislodge LMA / Supraglottic Airway (2025 update): • May use as initial interface for ≥34 weeks, >2 kg [

nodes.title: ETT & Equipment Sizing
nodes.summary: ETT size = GA(wk)/10; depth at lip = 6 + weight(kg); Miller 0 for most neonates, Miller 00 for extreme preterm
nodes.body: NEONATAL ETT SIZING [1][2] ETT size = Gestational Age (weeks) / 10 Sizing table: • 23–24 weeks → ETT 2.5 • 25–28 weeks → ETT 3.0 • 29–34 weeks → ETT 3.5 • ≥35 weeks → ETT 3.5–4.0 Laryngoscope blade: • Miller 0 — most neonates • Miller 00 — extreme preterm (<28 weeks) ETT depth at lip: • 6 + weight (kg) = cm at lip • Example: 3 kg baby → 6 + 3 = 9 cm at lip Securing tips: • Hold tube to roof of mou

nodes.title: HR <60 After Effective Ventilation?
nodes.summary: HR <60 despite confirmed effective ventilation = initiate chest compressions — must secure airway first
nodes.body: CRITICAL DECISION POINT [1][2] After ensuring effective ventilation (confirmed chest rise, corrective steps applied): Is the heart rate still <60 bpm? HR <60 despite effective PPV indicates the need for chest compressions.

nodes.title: Chest Compressions
nodes.summary: 3:1 ratio (90 compressions + 30 breaths), 2-thumb encircling, lower third sternum, 100% FiO2, establish UVC, prepare epinephrine
nodes.body: NEONATAL CPR [1][2][3] MUST secure airway first — intubate or place LMA before starting compressions. Technique — 2-thumb encircling: • Both thumbs on lower third of sternum, just below the nipple line • Wrap fingers around the chest • Compress 1/3 of anteroposterior diameter Compression-to-ventilation ratio: 3:1 • "One—two—three—breathe" (120 events/min = 90 compressions + 30 breaths) • This is D

nodes.title: HR After 60 Seconds of CPR
nodes.summary: After 60 sec CPR reassess HR — ≥60 stop compressions and continue PPV, still <60 = epinephrine
nodes.body: CPR REASSESSMENT — after 60 seconds [1][2] Pause compressions briefly to assess heart rate. Is HR ≥60 bpm?

nodes.title: Epinephrine
nodes.summary: Epinephrine 0.01-0.03 mg/kg IV/IO of 1:10,000 q3-5min — IV/IO preferred over ET; flush with NS; continue CPR between doses
nodes.body: EPINEPHRINE — Neonatal Resuscitation [1][2][3] Epinephrine IV/IO (preferred): • 0.01–0.03 mg/kg of 1:10,000 (= 0.1–0.3 mL/kg) • Repeat every 3–5 minutes as needed ET (if no IV/IO access): • 0.05–0.1 mg/kg of 1:10,000 (= 0.5–1 mL/kg) • Higher dose needed via ET — absorption is unpredictable • Switch to IV/IO route as soon as access established IV/IO is ALWAYS preferred over ET. Establish UVC access

nodes.title: Umbilical Venous Catheter (UVC)
nodes.summary: UVC: catheterize the single large VEIN (not arteries), 5Fr term/3.5Fr preterm, insert only 2-4 cm until blood return, prime with NS
nodes.body: UVC PROCEDURE [1][2] Umbilical cord anatomy: • 2 arteries — thick-walled, small lumen (at top of cross-section) • 1 vein — thin-walled, large lumen (at bottom of cross-section) • Catheterize the VEIN — larger, easier to cannulate Catheter size: • 5 French — term • 3.5 French — preterm Procedure: 1. Tie umbilical tape at base of stump — gentle tie to control bleeding 2. Cut cord 1–2 cm above skin 3

nodes.title: Persistent Bradycardia
nodes.summary: Persistent HR <60 after epi — consider hypovolemia, pneumothorax, equipment failure; >20 min without response consider discontinuation
nodes.body: PERSISTENT HR <60 AFTER EPINEPHRINE [1][2] If the heart rate remains <60 after epinephrine and ongoing CPR, consider reversible causes: • Hypovolemia — maternal hemorrhage, placental abruption, cord avulsion • Pneumothorax — especially after vigorous PPV • Equipment failure — ETT displacement, monitor malfunction • Prolonged resuscitation — >20 minutes without response

nodes.title: Volume Resuscitation
nodes.summary: NS 10 mL/kg IV over 5-10 min for hypovolemia; O-neg pRBCs 10 mL/kg for blood loss; D10W 2 mL/kg for hypoglycemia; naloxone NOT recommended
nodes.body: VOLUME & GLUCOSE RESUSCITATION [1][2] Hypovolemia — clinical signs: • Pallor despite adequate oxygenation • Weak pulses • Poor response to resuscitation • Known maternal hemorrhage or placental abruption Normal saline: • 10 mL/kg IV/IO — infuse over 5–10 minutes • May repeat if needed O-negative pRBCs: • 10 mL/kg — for acute blood loss (abruption, cord avulsion) • Uncrossmatched O-negative D10W (1

nodes.title: Discontinuation of Resuscitation
nodes.body: WHEN TO CONSIDER STOPPING [1][4] No detectable heart rate after 20 minutes of comprehensive resuscitation (effective ventilation, chest compressions, epinephrine, volume) may be an appropriate time to discuss discontinuation. Factors to consider: • Gestational age and estimated viability • Duration of no detectable HR • Presence of any reversible causes • Parental wishes (if known) • Local institu
nodes.recommendation: After 20 minutes of comprehensive resuscitation without detectable HR, discuss discontinuation with the team and family. Document all interventions, timing, and personnel.

nodes.title: Post-Resuscitation Care
nodes.body: POST-RESUSCITATION MONITORING [1][2] APGAR scoring: • Assess at 1, 5, and 10 minutes after birth • Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration Normothermia: • Target 36.5–37.5°C — monitor continuously • Both hypothermia AND hyperthermia worsen outcomes • Therapeutic hypothermia criteria: ≥36 weeks, moderate-severe HIE, initiated within 6 hours under NICU conditions — NOT during active resusc
nodes.recommendation: Post-resuscitation: APGAR at 1/5/10 min, maintain normothermia (36.5-37.5°C), check glucose, NICU transfer for any neonate requiring PPV or more. Therapeutic hypothermia eligibility: ≥36 wk, mod-severe HIE, within 6 hours. Team debrief.

nodes.title: Neurogenic Shock vs Spinal Shock
nodes.summary: Differentiate neurogenic (hemodynamic: hypotension + bradycardia + hypothermia, T6+) from spinal shock (neurologic: areflexia)
nodes.body: These are DIFFERENT entities that can coexist: | Term | Type | Definition | |------|------|------------| | Neurogenic Shock | Hemodynamic | Distributive shock from loss of sympathetic tone | | Spinal Shock | Neurologic | Transient loss of all function below lesion | Neurogenic Shock Classic Triad: 1. ❤️ Hypotension — peripheral vasodilation, ↓SVR 2. 🫀 Bradycardia — unopposed vagal tone 3. 🌡️ Hyp

nodes.title: Neurogenic Shock Pathophysiology
nodes.summary: Loss of sympathetic T1-L2 tracts causes vasodilation, venous pooling, unopposed vagal bradycardia, and hypothermia
nodes.body: Sympathetic Nervous System Disruption Anatomy: • Preganglionic sympathetic neurons: T1-L2 • Cardiac sympathetic innervation: T1-T5 • Injuries at/above T6 cause neurogenic shock Mechanism: 1. Loss of descending sympathetic tracts 2. Peripheral vasodilation (↓SVR) 3. Venous pooling → ↓venous return → ↓cardiac output 4. Unopposed vagal tone → bradycardia 5. Loss of cutaneous vasoconstriction → hypoth

nodes.title: ⚠️ Rule Out Hemorrhage FIRST
nodes.summary: Neurogenic shock is diagnosis of EXCLUSION — complete E-FAST, pelvic XR, CXR, exam, and labs before attributing to neurogenic
nodes.body: NEUROGENIC SHOCK IS A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION 🔴 The most dangerous mistake: Missing hemorrhage masked by neurogenic shock. Why it's dangerous: • Trauma patients often have BOTH spinal injury AND hemorrhage • Neurogenic shock masks tachycardia — no "warning sign" of bleeding • Hypotension + bradycardia does NOT rule out hemorrhage Required workup BEFORE attributing to neurogenic shock: | Study | Lo

nodes.title: Fluid Resuscitation — Be Cautious
nodes.summary: Patients are vasodilated not volume-depleted — limit crystalloid to 1-2L then start vasopressors early
nodes.body: Patients are VASODILATED, not volume depleted Approach: • Small boluses: 250-500 mL NS with reassessment • Maximum initial: 1-2 L before vasopressors • UOP goal: >30 mL/hr Avoid: ❌ Hypotonic fluids (D5W, 0.45% NS) ❌ Aggressive crystalloid resuscitation Why not aggressive fluids? • Risk of pulmonary edema • Risk of worsening spinal cord edema • Dilutional anemia/coagulopathy in polytrauma • Does NO

nodes.title: Vasopressor Selection
nodes.summary: Norepinephrine first-line (alpha + beta for BP and HR) — start 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min, target MAP ≥85
nodes.body: FIRST LINE: NOREPINEPHRINE ✅ Why preferred: • Combined α₁ (vasoconstriction) + β₁ (chronotropic) • Addresses BOTH hypotension AND bradycardia • Best evidence for improved spinal cord perfusion Dosing: | Parameter | Value | |-----------|-------| | Start | 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min | | Titrate | Every 5-15 min | | Range | 0.05-2 mcg/kg/min | | Target | MAP ≥85 mmHg | SECOND LINE OPTIONS: Epinephrine — if

nodes.title: 🚫 AVOID Phenylephrine Monotherapy
nodes.summary: Phenylephrine pure alpha causes reflex bradycardia — WORSENS existing bradycardia in neurogenic shock
nodes.body: Phenylephrine is CONTRAINDICATED as sole agent Why: • Pure α₁ agonist — NO β activity • Causes reflex bradycardia (baroreceptor-mediated) • WORSENS the already-present bradycardia The problem: ↑ BP from α → baroreceptors sense hypertension → reflex ↓HR → patient more bradycardic When phenylephrine might be acceptable: • Lower thoracic injuries (below T6) where bradycardia is less prominent • MUST

nodes.title: Bradycardia Management
nodes.summary: Atropine 0.4-0.6mg IV first-line for bradycardia — aminophylline or isoproterenol if refractory, pacing for sustained
nodes.body: Target HR: >60 bpm with adequate perfusion FIRST LINE: Anticholinergics Atropine: • Dose: 0.4-0.6 mg IV q4h PRN • Max: 3 mg total • Often inadequate in neurogenic shock Glycopyrrolate: • Alternative to atropine • 0.1-0.2 mg IV • Less CNS penetration SECOND LINE (Refractory): Methylxanthines: • Aminophylline IV for acute management • Theophylline PO for ongoing • For atropine-refractory bradycardia

nodes.title: MAP Targets — Critical for Outcomes
nodes.summary: MAP target 85-90 mmHg for 3-7 days — 2-3 mmHg difference correlates with neurologic recovery, use arterial line
nodes.body: 2024 AO Spine / AANS / CNS Guideline (Kwon et al.) — Hemodynamic Targets: | Parameter | Target | Duration | |-----------|--------|----------| | MAP lower limit | 75-80 mmHg | 3-7 days | | MAP upper limit | 90-95 mmHg | 3-7 days | What changed: The old 2013 AANS/CNS target was a narrow 85-90 mmHg for 7 days. The 2024 GRADE update broadened the range (lower 75-80, upper 90-95) for 3-7 days because t

nodes.title: Ancillary Management
nodes.summary: VTE prophylaxis within 72h (40% DVT risk), active rewarming, NO steroids (strongly discouraged), spine immobilization
nodes.body: Temperature Management: • Poikilothermia common — cannot regulate temperature • Active rewarming for hypothermia • Temperature-sensing Foley for monitoring • Avoid hyperthermia (worsens secondary injury) VTE Prophylaxis: • Up to 40% DVT risk in SCI • LMWH or UFH within 72 hours (24h post-op if surgery) • SCDs/compression stockings • IVC filters NOT routinely recommended Steroids: 🚫 NOT RECOMMENDE

nodes.title: Spinal Shock — Neurologic Phenomenon
nodes.summary: Spinal shock is transient loss of ALL cord function below lesion — flaccid paralysis, areflexia, not circulatory shock
nodes.body: Definition: Transient loss of ALL spinal cord function below the level of injury: • Motor function → flaccid paralysis • Sensory function → anesthesia • Reflex activity → areflexia • Autonomic function → loss of bladder/bowel/vascular tone ⚠️ NOT a circulatory shock state — different from neurogenic shock Duration: Days to weeks (average 4-12 weeks) Clinical Features: • Flaccid (not spastic) paral

nodes.title: Four Phases of Spinal Shock
nodes.summary: Four phases over weeks-months — BCR returns 1-3 days marking end of spinal shock, NO prognostic value for recovery
nodes.body: Evolution of Spinal Shock: | Phase | Timing | Characteristics | |-------|--------|----------------| | 1 | 0-24 hours | Areflexia; motor neuron hyperpolarization | | 2 | 1-3 days | Initial reflex return; denervation supersensitivity | | 3 | 4 days - 1 month | DTRs return; Babinski may appear | | 4 | 1-12 months | Hyperreflexia, spasticity; autonomic dysreflexia | Pattern of Reflex Return: 1. Delaye

nodes.title: Spinal Shock & Prognosis
nodes.summary: Sacral sparing (perianal sensation, toe flexion, rectal tone) = incomplete injury = better prognosis; cannot assess during spinal shock
nodes.body: Why Spinal Shock Matters for Prognosis: During spinal shock: • Cannot reliably determine permanent vs temporary deficits • Must wait for resolution to assess true injury extent After spinal shock resolves: SACRAL SPARING = INCOMPLETE INJURY = Better Prognosis Look for: • Preserved perianal sensation • Voluntary toe flexion • Rectal tone present Complete Injury (no sacral sparing): • Poor prognosis

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: All neurogenic shock requires ICU — vasopressors, MAP protocol, high C-spine respiratory monitoring, emergent spine consult
nodes.body: All patients with neurogenic shock require ICU admission ICU Criteria: • Vasopressor requirement • MAP augmentation protocol • High cervical injury (C2-C4) — respiratory monitoring • Continuous cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia risk) • Potential for decompensation Consults: □ Neurosurgery or Orthopedic Spine — EMERGENT □ PM&R for rehab planning □ Respiratory therapy (C2-C4 injuries) [1]

nodes.title: ICU Admission Checklist
nodes.summary: ICU orders: arterial line MAP 85-90, NE infusion, atropine PRN, DVT prophylaxis, Foley, NG tube, avoid phenylephrine/steroids

nodes.title: Critical Pitfalls
nodes.summary: Five pitfalls: missing hemorrhage, fluid overload, phenylephrine monotherapy, inadequate MAP targets, assuming all hypotension is neurogenic
nodes.body: Pitfall #1: MISSING HEMORRHAGE • Neurogenic shock is diagnosis of EXCLUSION • Always complete FAST, pelvic XR, long bone assessment • Bradycardia masks usual tachycardic response to bleeding Pitfall #2: FLUID OVERLOADING • Patients are vasodilated, NOT hypovolemic • Max 1-2L crystalloid before vasopressors • Aggressive fluids → pulmonary edema, spinal cord edema Pitfall #3: PHENYLEPHRINE MONOTHERA

nodes.title: Neurosyphilis: When to Suspect
nodes.summary: Suspect neurosyphilis in any confirmed syphilis with neuro symptoms — visual, cognitive, cranial nerve, meningismus, stroke-like
nodes.body: Neurosyphilis should be considered in any patient with confirmed syphilis who has neurological symptoms or signs. The diagnosis requires a combination of clinical, serologic, and CSF findings. Key presentations: • Visual changes, hearing loss • Cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms • Cranial nerve deficits, meningismus • Stroke-like symptoms • Tabes dorsalis (late) • General paresis (late)

nodes.title: Neurological Symptoms Present?
nodes.summary: Triage by symptom type: neuro symptoms need LP, ocular/otic treat as neurosyphilis regardless of CSF, asymptomatic rarely needs LP
nodes.body: Does the patient have neurological, ocular, or otic symptoms?

nodes.title: Perform CSF Evaluation
nodes.summary: Order CSF-VDRL (highly specific), FTA-ABS (more sensitive), cell count, protein, glucose — reactive VDRL is diagnostic
nodes.body: CSF analysis is indicated for patients with syphilis and neurological symptoms. Order: • CSF-VDRL (highly specific, low sensitivity) • CSF FTA-ABS (more sensitive, less specific) • CSF cell count with differential • CSF protein • CSF glucose Interpretation aids: • CSF-VDRL reactive → diagnostic • CSF pleocytosis (>5 WBC/µL) → supportive • Elevated CSF protein → supportive • CSF FTA-ABS negative →

nodes.title: CSF-VDRL Result
nodes.summary: CSF-VDRL reactive = confirmed, abnormal CSF with neuro symptoms = treat even if VDRL negative, normal CSF = unlikely
nodes.body: What is the CSF-VDRL result?

nodes.title: Confirmed Neurosyphilis — Treat
nodes.body: A reactive CSF-VDRL is diagnostic of neurosyphilis. First-line treatment: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV • 3–4 million units IV q4h, OR • Continuous infusion • Duration: 10–14 days Alternative (if IV not feasible): Procaine penicillin 2.4 million units IM daily PLUS probenecid 500 mg PO QID × 10–14 days PCN allergy: Desensitization preferred. If not possible: Ceftriaxo
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV Penicillin G. ID consult recommended.

nodes.title: Probable Neurosyphilis — Treat
nodes.body: CSF-VDRL negative but CSF pleocytosis (>5 WBC/µL) or elevated protein with neurological symptoms → treat as neurosyphilis. Treatment (same as confirmed): Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV • 3–4 million units IV q4h × 10–14 days Follow-up: • Repeat CSF at 6 months • If CSF not improving, re-treat
nodes.recommendation: Treat as neurosyphilis. Repeat CSF at 6 months.

nodes.title: Neurosyphilis Unlikely
nodes.body: Normal CSF with non-reactive CSF-VDRL makes neurosyphilis unlikely. Consider alternative diagnoses for neurological symptoms. Treat underlying syphilis stage: • Early (primary/secondary/early latent): Benzathine PCN G 2.4M units IM × 1 • Late latent: Benzathine PCN G 2.4M units IM weekly × 3 weeks Re-evaluate if symptoms progress or new neuro symptoms develop.
nodes.recommendation: Treat syphilis per stage. Neuro follow-up if symptoms persist.

nodes.title: Ocular/Otosyphilis — Treat as Neurosyphilis
nodes.body: Ocular and otosyphilis can occur at any stage of syphilis and require treatment as neurosyphilis regardless of CSF findings. Ocular manifestations: • Uveitis (most common), optic neuritis • Retinitis, papillitis • Vision loss Otic manifestations: • Sensorineural hearing loss • Tinnitus, vertigo Treatment: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV • 3–4 million units IV q4h × 10–1
nodes.recommendation: Treat as neurosyphilis. Ophthalmology/ENT consult. ID consult.

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Late Latent Syphilis
nodes.summary: Routine LP NOT recommended for asymptomatic late latent — indicated only for treatment failure, HIV, developing neuro signs, or tertiary syphilis
nodes.body: Routine CSF examination is NOT recommended for asymptomatic late latent syphilis. Exceptions — CSF exam IS indicated if: • Treatment failure (titer not declining) • HIV co-infection with late latent syphilis • Neurological signs develop • Tertiary syphilis (aortitis, gumma)

nodes.title: Late Latent Syphilis Treatment
nodes.body: First-line: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly × 3 weeks (Total: 7.2 million units) PCN allergy: Desensitization preferred. Alternative: Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 28 days Follow-up: • Quantitative nontreponemal titers at 6, 12, and 24 months • 4-fold decline expected • If titers do not decline → evaluate for treatment failure, consider CSF exam
nodes.recommendation: Benzathine PCN G IM weekly × 3 weeks. Follow titers.

nodes.title: New Onset Psychosis Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Safety, vitals/glucose, delirium, neuro, tox, pregnancy/postpartum, and risk assessment first.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Delirium from a medical cause \u2014 fluctuating attention, abnormal vitals; psychosis is rarely "primary" in the ED. 2. CNS infection (encephalitis, incl. autoimmune/anti-NMDA) \u2014 fever, seizure, headache, movement disorder. 3. Toxidrome / withdrawal (stimulant, anticholinergic, serotonin, alcohol) \u2014 vitals, pupils, skin. 4. Hypoglycemia / hypoxia / metabol

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Safety, medical/delirium/tox, neuro/autoimmune, catatonia, mood/postpartum, and first-episode pathways.
nodes.body: Choose the first dangerous lane. You can return after the immediate action. Basis: lane structure follows the ACEP Adult Psychiatric Emergencies policy statement [1] and the AAEP Project BETA medical evaluation/triage consensus statement [11]; the autoimmune-encephalitis lane follows Graus et al. [4] and the Herken/Pruss psychiatric red-flag criteria [5].

nodes.title: Unsafe Agitation
nodes.body: Open Acute Agitation and Combative Patient. Immediate priorities: verbal de-escalation, reduce stimulation, staff safety, trauma-informed approach, least restrictive intervention, and medication chosen by likely etiology when medication is required. Even during agitation control, do glucose/vitals/temperature and look for delirium, tox, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, head injury, sepsis, withdrawal, antic
nodes.recommendation: Stabilize safety first, but do not let sedation replace the medical evaluation.

nodes.title: Medical / Delirium / Tox Red Flags
nodes.body: Open Psych Medical Stability, Delirium, Altered Mental Status Hub, or Organic vs Psych. Red flags: abnormal vitals, fever, hypoxia, hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia, fluctuating attention, disorientation, visual hallucinations, intoxication/withdrawal, anticholinergic signs, severe insomnia with autonomic findings, trauma, immunocompromise, age >45 without prior psychosis. ACEP policy supports targeted
nodes.recommendation: If attention, vitals, tox, glucose, or medical stability is abnormal, treat as medical/delirium until proven otherwise.

nodes.title: Neurologic / CNS Red Flags
nodes.summary: Neuro red flags split autoimmune encephalitis, CNS infection, and structural/stroke/bleed pathways.
nodes.body: Psychosis with neurologic or encephalitic features needs a different pathway. Basis: the autoimmune-encephalitis branch follows Graus et al. [4] and the Herken/Pruss psychiatric red-flag criteria [5]; the CNS-infection branch follows the IDSA encephalitis guideline [7] and the IDSA bacterial meningitis guideline [16].

nodes.title: Autoimmune Encephalitis Concern
nodes.body: Open Acute Psychosis / First Break. Red flags: rapid progression under 3 months, psychiatric symptoms plus seizures, movement disorder/dyskinesias, speech dysfunction/mutism, decreased consciousness, autonomic instability, central hypoventilation, catatonia, hyponatremia, headache, recent viral encephalitis, young woman with ovarian teratoma risk. Next steps: neurology early, MRI brain, EEG, LP wi
nodes.recommendation: Autoimmune encephalitis red flags should block routine psychiatric disposition.

nodes.title: CNS Infection / Encephalitis
nodes.body: Open Meningitis / Encephalitis. Next 5 minutes: cultures if they do not delay treatment, empiric antibiotics/acyclovir when CNS infection is plausible, CT before LP only when indicated, LP when safe. Psychosis can be an early encephalitis presentation. Pitfall: do not delay empiric therapy for CT/LP logistics when encephalitis/meningitis is plausible. Basis: empiric acyclovir for suspected encepha
nodes.recommendation: Treat CNS infection first when fever, meningismus, severe headache, immunocompromise, seizure, or AMS coexists.

nodes.title: Structural / Stroke / Bleed Concern
nodes.body: Open Acute Ischemic Stroke, ICH, or SAH when the phenotype fits. Image now when: focal neuro deficit, papilledema, seizure, head trauma, anticoagulation, severe headache, decreased consciousness, immunocompromise, or atypical late-onset first psychosis. Use CT for emergent bleed/trauma questions; MRI when CT is unrevealing and encephalitis, tumor, demyelination, or limbic process remains possible.
nodes.recommendation: Neuro signs or late/atypical first psychosis deserve brain imaging, not routine psych clearance.

nodes.title: Catatonia / Malignant Catatonia
nodes.body: Open Catatonia. Clues: stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia/echopraxia, rigidity, autonomic instability, fever, dehydration, rhabdo risk. Catatonia can coexist with mood disorder, psychosis, medical illness, autoimmune encephalitis, or NMS. Pitfall: avoid reflex antipsychotic escalation when catatonia is possible. Lorazepam challenge and medical evaluation are often t
nodes.recommendation: Catatonia is a medical-psychiatric emergency, not simple agitation.

nodes.title: Mood Psychosis / Postpartum Risk
nodes.body: High-risk phenotypes: postpartum psychosis, mania with psychosis, severe depression with psychotic guilt/nihilism, command hallucinations, insomnia with escalating disorganization, suicidal/homicidal risk, inability to care for infant/self. Pregnancy/postpartum psychosis requires urgent psychiatry and OB coordination, safety planning for parent and infant, and medical mimics considered: preeclamps
nodes.recommendation: Postpartum psychosis is high-risk and generally requires admission-level safety planning.

nodes.title: First-Episode Psychosis Pathway
nodes.body: Open Acute Psychosis / First Break and MSE Dictation Guide. Core ED work: safety assessment, vitals/glucose, targeted labs by history/exam, substance/medication review, pregnancy test when applicable, ECG before QT-prolonging medication or overdose concern, collateral, first-episode psychosis referral/admission planning. NICE and VA/DoD emphasize early-intervention services, full physical health a
nodes.recommendation: When no medical red flags exist, first-episode psychosis still needs safety, collateral, and early-intervention follow-up or admission.

nodes.title: Known Psychosis but Changed Presentation
nodes.body: A known psychiatric diagnosis does not clear a changed presentation. Search for: medication nonadherence, substance use, withdrawal, lithium/valproate toxicity, anticholinergic burden, infection, pain, sleep deprivation, steroids, dopaminergic drugs, pregnancy/postpartum, trauma, delirium, and neurologic red flags. Open Psych Medical Stability, Acute Agitation, or Delirium as appropriate. Basis: t
nodes.recommendation: Changed baseline gets a trigger search before psychiatric placement.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Vitals/glucose, targeted workup, collateral, neuro/tox/delirium, ECG when medication/overdose risk, safety assessment.
nodes.body: Default bundle when no single killer declares itself: - Vitals including temperature, glucose, oxygenation. - Full medication/substance/collateral timeline. - Focused neuro, trauma, toxidrome, withdrawal, delirium screen. - Pregnancy test when applicable. - CBC/CMP/TSH/UA/UDS/ethanol and other labs only when guided by history/exam, local psych transfer requirements, or first-episode context. - ECG

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Workup
nodes.summary: Persistent red flags stay medical. Stable first episode needs structured psych plan.
nodes.body: Psychosis disposition should follow reassessment, not first impression. Basis: serial reassessment before psychiatric disposition follows the AAEP Project BETA medical evaluation/triage consensus statement [11] and the ACEP Adult Psychiatric Emergencies policy statement [1].

nodes.title: Imaging / Labs / EEG / LP Strategy
nodes.summary: Use targeted testing. Image/LP/EEG/MRI for neuro, delirium, late-onset, encephalitis, seizure, or atypical features.
nodes.body: Do not order every test for every patient. Do not under-test red flags. Brain imaging: focal neuro deficit, seizure, severe headache, head trauma, papilledema, anticoagulation, immunocompromise, decreased consciousness, late-onset first psychosis, atypical course, or failure to clear. LP/EEG/MRI: fever/meningismus/encephalitis concern, seizure or persistent AMS, autoimmune encephalitis red flags,

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Medical red flags go medical. Safety/grave disability goes psych admission. Discharge requires strong supports and rapid follow-up.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on medical stability, safety, function, supports, and whether this is first episode. Basis: the medical-stability-before-psychiatric-placement principle follows the ACEP Adult Psychiatric Emergencies policy statement [1]; first-episode admission and referral planning follow the VA/DoD first-episode psychosis and schizophrenia guideline [9]; the capacity element follows Appelbau

nodes.title: Medical Admission / Transfer
nodes.body: Use medical admission/transfer for delirium, abnormal vitals, intoxication/withdrawal needing monitoring, seizure/NCSE concern, CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis concern, catatonia/malignant catatonia, severe metabolic/endocrine disease, pregnancy/eclampsia medical concerns, or inability to complete medical evaluation safely. Basis: each admission trigger rests on its own source. Delirium: In
nodes.recommendation: Medical red flags should not be routed to psychiatric placement as the primary disposition.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Admission / Hold Pathway
nodes.body: Psychiatric admission or involuntary pathway is appropriate when medically stable but dangerous to self/others, gravely disabled, severely disorganized, unable to care for basic needs, command hallucinations create risk, first episode has unreliable support, or medication initiation/monitoring requires inpatient care. Document risk assessment, collateral, capacity when refusal is an issue, and why
nodes.recommendation: Psych disposition still needs documented medical stability and risk rationale.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge after new psychosis is uncommon and requires: stable vitals, normal attention/level of consciousness, no neurologic/tox/medical red flags, no SI/HI/command-risk/grave disability, reliable collateral/support, safe environment, no weapons concern, rapid psychiatry or first-episode psychosis follow-up, medication plan if started, and clear return precautions. Return now for: confusion, feve
nodes.recommendation: If discharge is chosen, document why medical red flags and acute safety criteria are absent.

nodes.title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
nodes.summary: NMS = hyperthermia + lead-pipe rigidity + autonomic instability + AMS. Onset 4-14 days.
nodes.body: Steps Summary Definition: Life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics). Classic tetrad: * Hyperthermia (often >40 degC) * Lead-pipe rigidity (severe, generalized) * Autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis) * Mental status changes (confusion -> coma) Onset: Usually within 2 weeks of drug initiation/dose change (often 4-14 days)

nodes.title: Causative Agents
nodes.summary: Haloperidol, droperidol, olanzapine, metoclopramide. High potency = higher risk.
nodes.body: Dopamine antagonists: | Class | Examples | |-------|----------| | Typical antipsychotics | Haloperidol, droperidol, chlorpromazine | | Atypical antipsychotics | Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, clozapine | | Antiemetics | Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine | | Other | Lithium withdrawal, dopamine agonist withdrawal | Risk factors: * High-potency agents (haloperidol highest risk) *

nodes.title: Diagnostic Criteria
nodes.summary: Levenson: 3 major (fever, rigidity, elevated CK) + 2 minor. CK often >1000.
nodes.body: Levenson Criteria: Major (3 required if no other cause): * Fever (>38 degC) * Rigidity * Elevated CK (>1000 U/L typical) Minor (need 2 additional): * Tachycardia * Abnormal BP (hyper or hypotension) * Tachypnea * Altered consciousness * Diaphoresis * Leukocytosis Labs: * CK markedly elevated (often >1000, can be >100,000) * Leukocytosis (10,000-40,000) * Metabolic acidosis * Elevated LFTs, myoglob

nodes.title: Diagnostic Assessment
nodes.summary: Levenson criteria met = NMS diagnosis. Incomplete = early NMS or mimic.
nodes.body: Does patient meet Levenson criteria? Recent antipsychotic/dopamine blocker + rigidity + fever + elevated CK?

nodes.title: Physical Exam Findings
nodes.summary: Lead-pipe rigidity, normal/decreased reflexes, severe hyperthermia, autonomic instability.
nodes.body: Neuromuscular: * Lead-pipe rigidity (constant resistance through full ROM) * Normal or DECREASED reflexes (unlike SS) * Bradykinesia * Tremor * Dysphagia, dysarthria Autonomic: * Hyperthermia (often >40 degC, can reach 42 degC) * Tachycardia * Labile blood pressure * Diaphoresis * Tachypnea Mental status: * Confusion -> delirium -> coma * Mutism

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Mild (<39 degC), Moderate (39-40 degC), Severe (>40 degC, organ failure).
nodes.body: Assess severity:

nodes.title: Mild NMS Management
nodes.summary: Mild: stop agent, supportive care, benzos PRN. May last 5-10 days.
nodes.body: Management: 1. Stop causative agent(s) 2. Supportive care: * IV fluids * External cooling if febrile * Benzodiazepines PRN for rigidity/agitation 3. Monitoring: * Vitals q2-4h * Serial CK * Renal function 4. Consider bromocriptine if not improving Duration: Symptoms can persist 5-10 days after stopping oral agents; 2-3 weeks after depot.

nodes.title: Moderate NMS Management
nodes.summary: Moderate: stop agents, fluids, cooling, benzos, bromocriptine 2.5 mg q8h.
nodes.body: Management: 1. Stop ALL dopamine antagonists 2. Aggressive IV fluids - rhabdo prevention 3. External cooling 4. Benzodiazepines: * Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q5-10min PRN 5. Bromocriptine: * 2.5 mg PO/NG q8h * Increase to 5 mg q8h if no response * Max 45 mg/day 6. Admit to ICU or step-down for monitoring

nodes.title: Severe NMS Management
nodes.summary: Severe: intubate, dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q6h, bromocriptine, aggressive cooling/fluids.
nodes.body: LIFE-THREATENING - ICU mandatory 1. Airway: Intubate if severe rigidity/hyperthermia 2. Stop ALL dopamine antagonists 3. Dantrolene: * 1-2.5 mg/kg IV * Repeat q6h PRN (max 10 mg/kg/day) * Reduces muscle rigidity -> decreases heat production 4. Bromocriptine: * 2.5-5 mg PO/NG q8h (via NG if intubated) 5. Aggressive cooling: * Ice packs, cooling blankets, cold IV fluids 6. Aggressive IV fluids: * Ta

nodes.title: Stop Causative Agents
nodes.summary: Stop all antipsychotics/dopamine blockers. Symptoms persist 5-10 days (oral) or weeks (depot).
nodes.body: Discontinue ALL dopamine antagonists: * Typical and atypical antipsychotics * Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine * Droperidol Also consider: * Stopping lithium (can contribute) * Restarting recently discontinued dopamine agonists (if applicable) Duration of risk: * Oral agents: symptoms may persist 5-10 days * Depot/long-acting: may persist 2-3 weeks Rechallenge: If antipsychotic neede

nodes.title: Bromocriptine
nodes.summary: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg q8h, increase to 5 mg q8h. Continue 10 days after resolution.
nodes.body: Dopamine agonist - restores dopaminergic transmission Dosing: * Initial: 2.5 mg PO/NG q8h * Escalate: 5 mg q8h if no improvement in 24h * Max: 45 mg/day * Duration: Continue for 10 days minimum after NMS resolves Route: PO or NG tube Mechanism: D2 agonist - counteracts dopamine blockade Cautions: * Hypotension (start low) * Nausea/vomiting * Psychosis (rare at these doses) * Prothrombotic: bromocr

nodes.title: Dantrolene
nodes.summary: Dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q6h for severe hyperthermia. Max 10 mg/kg/day.
nodes.body: Muscle relaxant - for severe hyperthermia/rigidity Dosing: * 1-2.5 mg/kg IV * Repeat q6h PRN * Max: 10 mg/kg/day Mechanism: Blocks calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum -> reduces muscle contraction -> decreases heat production Indication: Severe hyperthermia (>40 degC) with marked rigidity Monitoring: * LFTs (hepatotoxicity risk) * Respiratory function (can cause weakness) NOT first-line fo

nodes.title: NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome
nodes.summary: NMS = slow onset, lead-pipe rigidity, normal reflexes. SS = fast onset, clonus, hyperreflexia.
nodes.body: Critical distinction: | Feature | NMS | Serotonin Syndrome | |---------|-----|-------------------| | Onset | Days (4-14) | Hours (<24h) | | Drug | Dopamine blocker | Serotonergic | | Rigidity | LEAD-PIPE (severe) | Mild, lower > upper | | Reflexes | Normal or ↓ | HYPERREFLEXIA | | Clonus | NO | YES (key finding) | | CK | Very elevated | Mildly elevated | | Bradykinesia | Yes | No | | Treatment | B

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: DDx: SS, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic, catatonia, infection, thyroid storm.
nodes.body: Other hyperthermic emergencies: * Serotonin syndrome - serotonergic drugs, clonus, hyperreflexia * Malignant hyperthermia - post-anesthesia, genetic, succinylcholine/inhalational agents * Anticholinergic toxicity - dry skin, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds * Lethal catatonia - psychiatric history, may precede NMS * Infections - meningitis, encephalitis, sepsis * Thyroid storm - thyroid hist

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for severe, step-down for moderate. All NMS requires admission.
