nodes.title: Approach to Acute Vision Loss
nodes.summary: Three main findings: RD (V-shaped, tethered to disc), PVD (undulating, floats freely), VH (diffuse echoes, swirling) — RD is surgical emergency
nodes.body: Ocular POCUS for Acute Vision Loss: Key Question: Is there something in the vitreous that should not be there? Three Main Findings: | Finding | Appearance | Movement | |---------|------------|----------| | Retinal Detachment | V-shaped or tent-shaped membrane | Minimal — tethered to disc | | Posterior Vitreous Detachment | Undulating membrane | Free — "seaweed in water" | | Vitreous Hemorrhage | D

nodes.title: Retinal Detachment Findings
nodes.summary: RD: V-shaped/tent-shaped, tethered at optic disc, restricted movement. Pooled sens 0.94 / spec 0.94, but as low as 75% with non-expert operators — a negative scan does NOT rule out RD
nodes.body: Retinal Detachment (RD) — SURGICAL EMERGENCY: Classic Appearance: • V-shaped or tent-shaped membrane in vitreous • Tethered at optic disc — does not float freely • Thick, hyperechoic compared to vitreous • May see undulating movement but anchored posteriorly Types: | Type | Description | |------|------------| | Partial RD | V-shape or fold, attached to disc | | Total RD | Complete "funnel" or "mor

nodes.title: Posterior Vitreous Detachment
nodes.summary: PVD: thin undulating membrane NOT tethered to disc, "seaweed in water" motion, continues moving after eye stops. ~14% have a retinal TEAR (not detachment); RRD only ~1-4%; RRD ~17% if VH present
nodes.body: Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD) — Usually Benign: What Is PVD? • Separation of vitreous gel from retina • Normal aging process — but the commonly quoted "50% by 50, 75% by 75" overstates it. Population autopsy/clinical data: essentially no PVD under age 40; by decade thereafter roughly 4% (5th decade), 24% (6th), 37% (7th), 59% (8th), 87% (9th). Foos found 27% in the 7th decade and 63% in the

nodes.title: RD vs PVD: Side-by-Side
nodes.summary: Key: RD tethered to disc (leashed), PVD floats freely (jellyfish); uncertain = treat as RD and consult ophthalmology
nodes.body: Key Differentiating Features: | Feature | Retinal Detachment | PVD | |---------|-------------------|-----| | Shape | V-shape / tent / funnel | Undulating membrane | | Attachment | Tethered to disc | Floats freely | | Movement | Restricted, "leashed" | Free, "seaweed" | | Thickness | Thicker, more echogenic | Thin, less echogenic | | After-movement | Stops with eye | Continues after eye stops | | U

nodes.title: Vitreous Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: VH: diffuse echogenic particles "snowstorm" pattern, swirling with eye movement — cannot see retina = cannot rule out RD, consult ophthalmology
nodes.body: Vitreous Hemorrhage — Blood in the Vitreous Cavity: Causes: • Diabetic retinopathy (most common) • Trauma • Retinal tear with vessel disruption • Posterior vitreous detachment • Age-related macular degeneration • Retinal vein occlusion Sonographic Appearance: • Diffuse echogenic particles throughout vitreous • "Snowstorm" or "starry sky" pattern • Swirling motion with eye movement ("washing machin

nodes.title: Other Ocular Pathology
nodes.summary: Additional findings: lens dislocation (Marfan, trauma), IOFB (hyperechoic with shadow, no MRI if metallic), choroidal detachment (dome-shaped, not to disc)
nodes.body: Additional Findings to Recognize: Lens Dislocation: • Lens not in normal biconvex position • May be posterior (in vitreous), anterior, or subluxed • Associated with Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria, trauma • Can cause acute glaucoma or visual axis obstruction Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB): • Hyperechoic structure with posterior shadowing (metal) • May see reverberation artifact (glass, metal) • D

nodes.title: ONSD for Elevated ICP
nodes.summary: ONSD is direct CNS extension — elevated ICP distends sheath within minutes, non-invasive bedside surrogate, repeatable for monitoring
nodes.body: Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) — Non-Invasive ICP Surrogate: Why It Works: • Optic nerve is a direct extension of the CNS • Optic nerve sheath is continuous with dura mater • Increased ICP → CSF distension of optic nerve sheath • Changes within minutes of ICP elevation Indications: • Suspected elevated ICP • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) • Trauma — cannot obtain CT immediately • P

nodes.title: ONSD Measurement Technique
nodes.summary: Measure 3mm behind globe, outer edge to outer edge, bilateral average — adult >5.0mm, child >4.5mm, infant >4.0mm = elevated ICP
nodes.body: Step-by-Step ONSD Measurement: 1. Position: • Patient supine, eyes closed, looking straight ahead • Ultrasound depth: 4 cm 2. Obtain View: • Longitudinal/sagittal plane (marker superior) • Identify optic nerve as hypoechoic band extending posteriorly from globe • Optic nerve sheath = hyperechoic borders surrounding nerve 3. Measure: • 3 mm posterior to the globe (this is critical) • Measure outer

nodes.title: ONSD Result
nodes.summary: Interpret ONSD: <5.0mm normal, 5.0-5.8mm borderline correlate clinically, >5.8mm strongly suggests ICP>20; age-specific thresholds for peds
nodes.body: What is the measured ONSD? Measure bilateral and use average or highest value.

nodes.title: ONSD Normal
nodes.summary: ONSD <5.0mm: elevated ICP unlikely (95%+ NPV) — if high clinical suspicion despite normal ONSD, continue workup with CT/LP
nodes.body: ONSD <5.0 mm — Elevated ICP Unlikely: Interpretation: • Normal optic nerve sheath diameter • Elevated ICP is unlikely but not excluded • High negative predictive value (95%+) Clinical Integration: • ONSD is a screening tool, not definitive • If high clinical suspicion despite normal ONSD: - Consider CT head, LP - Serial ONSD monitoring - Formal ophthalmology fundoscopy False Negatives Can Occur: •

nodes.title: ONSD Borderline
nodes.summary: ONSD 5.0-5.8mm grey zone — repeat measurement, bilateral assessment, clinical correlation; trends more informative than single value
nodes.body: ONSD 5.0-5.8 mm — Grey Zone: Interpretation: • Borderline elevation • May represent early or mild ICP elevation • Clinical correlation essential Consider: • Repeat measurement (ensure proper technique) • Bilateral assessment • Clinical context: symptoms, mechanism, timing High Suspicion Signs: • Headache worse supine • Pulsatile tinnitus • Visual obscurations • Papilledema on fundoscopy • Cushing'

nodes.title: ONSD Elevated — ICP Concern
nodes.summary: ONSD >5.8mm suggests ICP>20 but is a screening adjunct only (the "PPV 88-93%" figure is from n=100 vs CT, not invasive ICP) — HOB 30°, avoid hypoxia/hypercapnia, CT head, neurosurgery, osmotherapy if herniating
nodes.body: ⚠️ ONSD >5.8 mm — High Likelihood of Elevated ICP ⚠️ Interpretation — read the caveat before you quote a number: • Suggests ICP >20 mmHg and warrants urgent further evaluation • The frequently quoted "PPV 88-93%" comes from a single small study (n=100) that used CT findings, not invasive ICP, as its reference standard, in a population with ~49% disease prevalence. PPV is prevalence-dependent and d

nodes.title: Pediatric ONSD Thresholds
nodes.summary: Pediatric thresholds: infant <1yr ≥4.0mm, child 1-15yr ≥4.5mm, adult >15yr ≥5.0mm — open fontanelle may buffer ICP in infants
nodes.body: Age-Specific ONSD Thresholds: | Age Group | Normal ONSD | Elevated ICP | |-----------|-------------|-------------| | Infant (<1 year) | <4.0 mm | ≥4.0 mm | | Child (1-15 years) | <4.5 mm | ≥4.5 mm | | Adult (>15 years) | <5.0 mm | ≥5.0 mm | Pediatric Considerations: • Open fontanelle may buffer ICP — less reliable in infants • Consider fontanelle bulging, suture splaying on imaging • Clinical sign

nodes.title: Ocular Trauma Assessment
nodes.summary: FIRST rule out globe rupture before scanning — teardrop pupil, shallow AC, visible uveal tissue = rigid shield, NO pressure, emergent ophthalmology
nodes.body: POCUS in Ocular Trauma: ⚠️ FIRST: Rule Out Globe Rupture Before Any Scan ⚠️ Clinical Globe Rupture Signs: • Teardrop/peaked pupil • Severely shallow anterior chamber • Hyphema with hypotony • Visible scleral laceration • Extruding uveal tissue (dark tissue through wound) • Subconjunctival hemorrhage 360° • Severely reduced visual acuity If Rupture Suspected: • Do NOT scan — any pressure risks extr

nodes.title: Traumatic Findings
nodes.summary: Traumatic findings: hyphema (blood in AC), lens dislocation, IOFB (CT if metallic, no MRI), traumatic RD — globe rupture on US = already scanned too much
nodes.body: Post-Trauma Ocular Pathology: Hyphema: • Blood in anterior chamber • Layering red cells with fluid level • May completely fill AC (8-ball hyphema) • Risk: secondary hemorrhage, glaucoma Lens Dislocation: • Posterior dislocation — lens in vitreous • Anterior dislocation — lens in AC (can cause pupil block) • Subluxation — partial displacement • Associated with zonular damage Intraocular Foreign Bod

nodes.title: CRAO on Ultrasound
nodes.summary: CRAO diagnosis is clinical (painless sudden vision loss, cherry-red spot, APD) — POCUS primarily rules out other causes, rarely sees embolus
nodes.body: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion — POCUS Role: Primary Diagnosis is Clinical: • Painless, sudden monocular vision loss • Cherry-red spot on fundoscopy • APD (afferent pupillary defect) POCUS Utility: • Confirm diagnosis when fundoscopy limited • May see echogenic emboli in central retinal artery (rare) • Rule out other pathology (RD, VH, lens dislocation) • Assess for vitreous hemorrhage Sonograph

nodes.title: Ocular POCUS Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition based on primary finding: RD emergent, PVD outpatient, VH severity-dependent, elevated ONSD urgent workup
nodes.body: What were the primary findings?

nodes.title: Retinal Detachment Disposition
nodes.summary: RD surgical emergency — emergent ophthalmology, position detached area down, bilateral patching; macula-on within 24h, macula-off within 72h
nodes.body: ⚠️ RETINAL DETACHMENT = SURGICAL EMERGENCY ⚠️ Immediate Actions: 1. Emergent ophthalmology consultation 2. Position patient with detached area down (if known) 3. Bilateral eye patching (reduces eye movement) 4. Keep patient calm, minimal head movement Timing: • Macula-ON (central vision intact): EMERGENT surgery within 24 hours • Macula-OFF (central vision already lost): Urgent surgery within 72 h

nodes.title: PVD Disposition
nodes.summary: PVD usually benign — ophthalmology follow-up 24-48h, return precautions for sudden floaters/flashes/curtain/vision loss (~14% have a concurrent retinal TEAR; true RRD only ~1-4%)
nodes.body: Posterior Vitreous Detachment — Outpatient Follow-Up: PVD is Usually Benign: • Strongly age-related, but the classic "50% by 50, 75% by 75" overstates it. Prevalence is near zero under age 40, then roughly 4% (5th decade), 24% (6th), 37% (7th), 59% (8th), 87% (9th) [15][16] • Causes floaters and photopsia (flashes) • Does NOT require emergent treatment However — Concurrent Pathology (know which nu

nodes.title: Vitreous Hemorrhage Disposition
nodes.summary: VH: cannot see retina = cannot rule out RD; mild outpatient 24-48h, moderate same-day, dense emergent ophthalmology consult
nodes.body: Vitreous Hemorrhage — Needs Ophthalmology: Why Urgent: • Cannot visualize retina = cannot rule out retinal tear/detachment • VH may be from traction on retinal vessel during RD • Dense VH with acute vision loss = ophthalmology consult Disposition by Severity: | VH Severity | Retina Visible? | Disposition | |-------------|-----------------|-------------| | Mild | Yes, can see | Outpatient ophtho 24

nodes.title: Globe Rupture — Emergent
nodes.summary: Globe rupture: rigid shield (not patch), NPO, antiemetics, vancomycin + ceftazidime IV, tetanus, emergent ophthalmology — NO pressure/drops/IOP check
nodes.body: ⚠️ GLOBE RUPTURE = SURGICAL EMERGENCY ⚠️ Immediate Actions: 1. STOP any eye manipulation 2. Rigid eye shield — tape to forehead, do NOT press on orbit 3. NPO — patient will need OR 4. Antiemetics — prevent vomiting which increases IOP 5. Pain control — avoid crying/straining 6. Update tetanus 7. Broad-spectrum antibiotics — prevent endophthalmitis • Vancomycin 1g IV + Ceftazidime 2g IV • Or Levofl

nodes.title: Normal Ocular POCUS
nodes.summary: Normal POCUS does not exclude all pathology — small peripheral tears, subtle CRAO, corneal disease may be missed; persistent symptoms need ophthalmology
nodes.body: Normal Ocular Ultrasound: Findings: • Normal anterior chamber depth • Lens in normal position • Vitreous anechoic (no hemorrhage, no detachment) • Retina adherent to globe wall • ONSD within normal limits Clinical Correlation: • POCUS normal does NOT exclude all pathology • Small peripheral retinal tears may be missed • Subtle CRAO may appear normal on standard B-scan • Corneal pathology requires

nodes.title: Ocular Trauma — Triage & Red-Flag Screen
nodes.body: Ocular trauma ranges from corneal abrasion (annoying, benign) to open globe (vision-threatening, time-critical). The first 90 seconds of triage drive everything. Eight Never-Dos in ocular trauma (built into every branch of this consult): 1. ❌ NEVER perform tonometry (Tono-Pen, Goldmann) if open globe suspected 2. ❌ NEVER use succinylcholine in confirmed/suspected open globe (use rocuronium) 3. ❌ N

nodes.title: Visual Acuity — Document on Every Patient
nodes.summary: Always document VA — each eye, BCVA, pinhole. Snellen → CF → HM → LP → NLP. Required for OTS.
nodes.body: Visual acuity is the single most important documented finding in ocular trauma. It is the medicolegal anchor and the clinical baseline for every subsequent exam. Standard sequence: 1. Snellen at 20 ft (or app/handheld card at known distance) — each eye separately, with patient's glasses if available (best-corrected) 2. If unable to read top line at 20 ft → walk closer (e.g. "20/200 at 10 ft" → 10/
nodes.recommendation: Always document VA in standardized format (each eye, with/without correction, pinhole if abnormal). VA = OTS input + medicolegal anchor.

nodes.title: BETT — Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology
nodes.body: Standardized vocabulary (Kuhn 2002) used by ophthalmology and trauma: Open Globe Injury — full-thickness wound of eye wall (sclera + cornea) • Rupture — blunt mechanism, inside-out (eye wall fails at weakest point, often equator/posterior) • Laceration — sharp mechanism, outside-in - Penetrating — entry wound only, no exit - Perforating — entry + exit wounds - IOFB — laceration with retained intra

nodes.title: Ocular Trauma — Exam Rules
nodes.body: If open globe suspected (any of: peaked/teardrop pupil, full-thickness laceration, prolapsed uvea, hyphema with poor view, sudden severe pain + vision loss): • ❌ NO tonometry • ❌ NO lid retraction (use desmarres or just gentle lateral lift) • ❌ NO eye drops (cycloplegics, mydriatics, antibiotics — wait for OR) • ❌ NO seidel test (the dye costs nothing but pressure on globe does) • ❌ NO ultrasound

nodes.title: Pediatric Ocular Trauma — Special Rules
nodes.body: Children are not small adults in ocular trauma. Three patterns to know: 1. White-Eyed Blowout Fracture (WEBOF) — pediatric-specific • Trapdoor inferior orbital wall fracture with muscle entrapment • External eye looks normal (no bruise, no proptosis) → "white-eyed" • Triad: persistent N/V + bradycardia (oculocardiac reflex) + restricted up-gaze • Surgical emergency — 24-48 hr or muscle ischemia •

nodes.title: Open Globe Workup
nodes.body: Confirm or refute open globe before any maneuver that pressurizes the eye. Findings that strongly suggest open globe: • Peaked, teardrop, or eccentric pupil • Visible full-thickness corneal/scleral laceration • Prolapsed uvea (brown/black tissue at wound) • Subconjunctival hemorrhage 360° + chemosis (suggests posterior rupture) • Hyphema + poor view of fundus • Severe vision loss out of proportion

nodes.title: Open Globe — Management Bundle
nodes.summary: Open globe = shield + NPO + vanc/ceftaz + antiemetic + CT 1mm + OR <24h. No drops, no tono, no MRI, rocuronium.
nodes.body: Time-critical bundle (every minute matters): • ✅ Rigid Fox shield (NOT pressure patch — pressure extrudes contents) • ✅ NPO — assume OR within hours • ✅ NO eye drops of any kind (cycloplegics, abx, dilators) • ✅ IV antibiotics: vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftazidime 1-2 g (covers Bacillus cereus from soil/organic, gram-negatives) • ✅ Tetanus update if indicated • ✅ Antiemetic (ondansetron 4-8 mg IV)
nodes.recommendation: Open globe: shield, NPO, IV vanc + ceftaz, antiemetic, HOB 30°, CT 1 mm cuts, OR <24h. NO drops, NO tono, NO MRI until metal excluded. Rocuronium NOT sux.

nodes.title: Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB)
nodes.summary: IOFB: shield, vanc+ceftaz, CT 1mm. NO MRI till metal excluded. Organic = urgent OR (endophthalmitis).
nodes.body: IOFB present on CT — bridge to OR. Treat as open globe + IOFB-specific concerns. Material matters: • Metallic (most common — grinding, hammering) — high siderosis risk if iron-containing; requires removal • Magnetic vs non-magnetic — guides extraction technique • Glass / inert — may be left in place if posterior and visually quiet • Organic (wood, plant matter) — high endophthalmitis risk; urgent
nodes.recommendation: IOFB: shield + NPO + vanc/ceftaz + CT thin cuts + emergent OR. MRI contraindicated until metal excluded. Organic = highest endophthalmitis risk.

nodes.title: OTS — Ocular Trauma Score Overview
nodes.body: Kuhn 2002 prognostic tool for serious ocular trauma (open or closed). Predicts 6-month visual acuity by summing initial VA score + injury variables. Calculate at OTS calculator. Inputs: • Initial VA (NLP=60, LP-HM=70, 1/200-19/200=80, 20/200-20/50=90, ≥20/40=100) • Globe rupture (-23) • Endophthalmitis (-17) • Perforating injury (-14) • Retinal detachment (-11) • Afferent pupillary defect (-10) OT

nodes.title: Chemical Burn — IRRIGATE AT TRIAGE
nodes.summary: Chemical burn: IRRIGATE FIRST. 1-2 L until pH 7.0-7.4 sustained. Limbal ischemia = prognostic.
nodes.body: Irrigation comes FIRST. Before VA. Before history. Before exam. Time-to-irrigation is the most important predictor of outcome. Protocol: 1. Topical anesthetic (proparacaine) — single drop, allows tolerance of irrigation 2. Place Morgan lens (or wide-bore IV tubing) — both eyes if bilateral 3. Irrigate with 1-2 L LR or NS minimum (alkali burns may need 4-6 L+) 4. Sweep upper and lower fornices to r
nodes.recommendation: Chemical burn: irrigate AT TRIAGE before exam. 1-2 L minimum, pH 7.0-7.4 sustained x5min off. Alkali = worse. Stage with Roper-Hall/Dua.

nodes.title: Chemical Burn — Stage Severity
nodes.body: Use Roper-Hall or Dua classification calculator. Roper-Hall (classic): • Grade I: corneal epithelial damage, no limbal ischemia → excellent prognosis • Grade II: cornea hazy but iris details visible, <1/3 limbal ischemia → good • Grade III: cornea opaque, 1/3-1/2 limbal ischemia → guarded • Grade IV: cornea opaque, >1/2 limbal ischemia → poor Dua (newer, more granular): • Grade I: 0 clock hours li

nodes.title: Mild Chemical Burn — Treatment
nodes.summary: Mild burn: abx + cycloplegic + tears + ophtho 24-48h. No NSAID drops.
nodes.body: Roper-Hall I / Dua I-II: epithelial defect only, no/minimal limbal ischemia. • Topical antibiotic (erythromycin ointment QID or moxifloxacin drops QID) • Cycloplegic for comfort (cyclopentolate 1% TID — reduces ciliary spasm) • Preservative-free artificial tears q1-2h • Oral analgesic (ibuprofen + acetaminophen) • Ophthalmology follow-up in 24-48 hr • Return precautions: vision change, severe pain
nodes.recommendation: Mild burn: topical abx + cycloplegic + lubrication + oral analgesic + ophtho 24-48h. No NSAID drops.

nodes.title: Moderate Chemical Burn — Treatment
nodes.summary: Moderate burn: aggressive bundle (steroid+citrate+ascorbate+doxy+VitC). Same-day ophtho.
nodes.body: Roper-Hall II-III / Dua III-IV: corneal haze + 1/3-1/2 limbal ischemia. ED bundle: • Topical antibiotic (moxifloxacin or ciprofloxacin q2h) • Cycloplegic (cyclopentolate 1% TID, atropine 1% if severe inflammation) • Topical steroid (prednisolone acetate 1% q1-2h x 7-10 days) — anti-inflammatory; ophthalmology should ideally start, but if delayed access prednisolone is reasonable • Topical citrate
nodes.recommendation: Moderate burn: q2h abx + cycloplegic + topical steroid (with ophtho input) + citrate + ascorbate + doxy 100 BID + Vit C. Same-day ophtho.

nodes.title: Severe Chemical Burn — Treatment
nodes.summary: Severe burn: admit, AMG/PROKERA, multi-spec, plan reconstruction. Poor prognosis.
nodes.body: Roper-Hall III-IV / Dua V-VI: opaque cornea + >1/2 limbal ischemia. Vision-threatening — admit, ophthalmology + oculoplastics involved. • Continued irrigation if pH not stable • All moderate-burn meds intensified • Tenoplasty / amniotic membrane (PROKERA) at ophthalmology discretion • Anterior chamber paracentesis if alkali in AC and IOP refractory • Surgical tenoplasty / limbal stem cell transpla
nodes.recommendation: Severe burn: admit, multi-specialty (ophtho + oculoplastics), aggressive med bundle, AMG/PROKERA, prepare for limbal stem cell transplant. Counsel poor prognosis.

nodes.title: Closed-Globe Blunt Trauma — Sub-Triage
nodes.body: Open globe excluded. Now sort by dominant finding.

nodes.title: Hyphema — Management
nodes.summary: Hyphema: sickle screen, bedrest 30°, shield, atropine, pred, antifibrinolytic. NO CAI/mannitol if sickle. Re-bleed d2-5.
nodes.body: Grade with hyphema calculator: • Microhyphema: only RBCs in AC, no layered blood • Grade I: <1/3 AC layered • Grade II: 1/3-1/2 AC layered • Grade III: >1/2 but not full • Grade IV: full AC ("eight-ball" hyphema) — worst prognosis Hyphema 4-grade reference Critical: SICKLE SCREEN every Black, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Indian patient. • Sickled RBCs in AC are stiff → trabecular meshwork blocka
nodes.recommendation: Hyphema: sickle screen at-risk pts. Bedrest 30°, shield, atropine, pred, antifibrinolytic. NO ASA/NSAID. NO CAI/mannitol if sickle. Daily ophtho.

nodes.title: Hyphema in Sickle Cell — Special Rules
nodes.body: Sickle hyphema is its own emergency. Even sickle trait (HbAS) carriers can decompensate. Pathophysiology: AC has low pH and low pO2 → sickled RBCs → trabecular blockage → IOP spike → optic nerve ischemia. Sickle RBCs in AC are also resistant to clearance. Avoid: • ❌ Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, methazolamide PO; dorzolamide, brinzolamide topical) — acidify aqueous, worsen sickling

nodes.title: Orbital Compartment Syndrome — Lateral Canthotomy + Cantholysis NOW
nodes.summary: OCS: canthotomy + cantholysis NOW (90-120 min). Tendon cut = decompression. No waiting on CT/ophtho.
nodes.body: Vision-loss window: 90-120 minutes from onset of optic nerve ischemia. Do NOT wait for CT, ophthalmology, or transfer. This is a bedside ED procedure. Diagnosis (any 2 of): • Proptosis (most reliable physical finding) • IOP >40 mmHg • Vision loss / RAPD • Resistance to retropulsion • Severe orbital pain • Limited or absent EOM Common causes: retrobulbar hemorrhage post-trauma, orbital cellulitis w
nodes.recommendation: OCS: 4-step lateral canthotomy + INFERIOR CANTHOLYSIS at bedside NOW. Do NOT wait for CT, ophtho, or transfer. Tendon cut = actual decompression. 90-120 min window.

nodes.title: Orbital Wall Fracture
nodes.summary: Orbital fx: CT 1mm. Check entrapment+V2. Nasal precautions. Outpatient oculoplastics 7-10d. Peds entrapment = urgent.
nodes.body: CT orbits without contrast (1 mm coronal + axial cuts) is gold standard. Common patterns: • Inferior wall (orbital floor) — most common, "blowout" • Medial wall (lamina papyracea) — paper-thin • Combined floor + medial ED management: • Document VA, EOM, infraorbital sensation (V2 distribution) • Check for entrapment (restricted up-gaze + N/V + bradycardia = WEBOF in peds) • Check for retrobulbar h
nodes.recommendation: Orbital fx: CT 1mm coronal+axial. Check entrapment, V2, retrobulbar hemorrhage. Nasal precautions, ice, HOB 30°. Oculoplastics/ENT 7-10d. Peds entrapment = 24-48h.

nodes.title: Pediatric White-Eyed Blowout Fracture (WEBOF)
nodes.summary: Peds WEBOF: up-gaze restriction + N/V + brady = surgical EM. OR <24-48h or fibrosis.
nodes.body: Greenstick trapdoor fracture of pediatric orbital floor with muscle entrapment — the bone springs back, trapping the inferior rectus. Why it's dangerous: • Minimal external trauma signs ("white eye") → easy to miss • Entrapped muscle ischemia → fibrosis within 24-48 hr → permanent diplopia • Triggers oculocardiac reflex → bradycardia, syncope, arrest possible during exam Triad: 1. Restricted up-ga
nodes.recommendation: WEBOF: kids with up-gaze restriction + N/V/brady = surgical EM. CT 1mm coronal, oculoplastics same day, OR within 24-48h. Easy to miss.

nodes.title: Pediatric AHT — Eye Findings
nodes.summary: Peds AHT: multilayered retinal heme to ora serrata. Ophtho dilated exam + brain imaging + child protection.
nodes.body: Multilayered, multiquadrant retinal hemorrhages extending to ora serrata in a child without a credible accidental mechanism = abusive head trauma until proven otherwise. Classic findings: • Bilateral retinal hemorrhages (preretinal, intraretinal, subretinal — multilayered) • Extending to ora serrata (peripheral retina) — distinguishes AHT from accidental • Macular schisis (traumatic retinoschisis)
nodes.recommendation: Peds AHT eye: multilayered/multiquadrant retinal heme to ora serrata. Mandatory ophtho dilated exam, CT/MRI brain, skeletal survey, child protection.

nodes.title: Posterior Segment Injury
nodes.summary: Posterior segment: ophtho dilated exam. RD = OR. CR/commotio = ophtho follow. TON = CT.
nodes.body: Posterior segment findings after blunt trauma: • Vitreous hemorrhage — sudden vision loss, "floaters", red reflex dimmed/absent. B-scan US (only if globe confirmed closed) shows mobile echoes. Ophthalmology consult; usually self-clears in weeks. • Retinal detachment — flashing lights, "curtain across vision", peripheral visual field loss. RAPD if macula off. Urgent ophthalmology — surgical (vitrec
nodes.recommendation: Posterior segment: ophtho dilated exam (urgent if RAPD/severe loss). RD = surgical EM. CR/commotio = follow-up. TON = CT optic canal, steroids controversial.

nodes.title: Traumatic Iritis
nodes.summary: Traumatic iritis: cycloplegic + steroid + analgesic + ophtho 24-48h.
nodes.body: Anterior uveitis after blunt trauma — common, peaks 24-72 hr post-injury. Findings: • Photophobia (consensual photophobia = light in unaffected eye reproduces pain in affected — pathognomonic for iritis) • Cell + flare in AC on slit lamp • Ciliary flush (perilimbal injection) • Decreased VA (mild) • Small/sluggish pupil • Normal IOP usually (occasionally elevated from inflammation, occasionally lo
nodes.recommendation: Traumatic iritis: cycloplegic + topical steroid (with ophtho input) + oral analgesic + sunglasses + 24-48h ophtho.

nodes.title: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Isolated SCH: reassurance, tears. 360°+chemosis+pain = open globe r/o.
nodes.body: Bright red blood under conjunctiva — looks dramatic, usually benign in isolation. Reassuring features: • Painless • Normal VA • Sectorial (not 360°) • Sclera visible posteriorly • No history of high-velocity trauma Concerning features (rule out occult open globe): • 360° hemorrhage with chemosis • Bullous appearance • Pain out of proportion • Decreased VA • High-velocity mechanism (BB, grinding me
nodes.recommendation: Isolated SCH: reassurance + tears, resolves 1-2 wk. 360°/chemosis/painful = treat as open globe pathway.

nodes.title: Blunt Trauma — Normal Globe Discharge
nodes.summary: Normal blunt: discharge with compress, NSAID, return precautions.
nodes.body: Eye structurally normal after thorough exam: • Normal VA • Normal EOM • No RAPD • Normal AC (no cell, no hyphema) • Normal fundus exam (or ophtho-cleared) • No fracture on imaging (or no imaging needed) Discharge instructions: • Cool compresses x 24 hr, then warm compresses • Ibuprofen + acetaminophen for pain • HOB elevation while sleeping x 48 hr • Avoid ASA/anticoagulation if avoidable • Eye pr
nodes.recommendation: Normal blunt eye exam: discharge with cool→warm compress, NSAID, HOB 30°, return precautions, optional ophtho follow-up.

nodes.title: Lid / Cornea / Superficial FB
nodes.body: Sub-triage by injury type:

nodes.title: Lid Laceration — Repair Zones
nodes.summary: Lid lac: ED ok superficial lateral. Oculoplastics for margin/medial-1/3/levator/tarsus. Assess globe.
nodes.body: Repair zones determine who closes the lac: ED can repair (no consult needed): • Superficial, lateral to medial canthus • Parallel to lid margin, not involving margin • Not involving levator (no ptosis after injury) • Not involving canalicular system • Not involving tarsal plate full-thickness Oculoplastics required: • Lid margin involvement (must align gray line precisely — botched closure → perma
nodes.recommendation: Lid lac: ED can close superficial lateral. Oculoplastics for margin, medial 1/3 (canaliculus), levator, tarsus full-thickness, avulsion. Always assess globe.

nodes.title: Corneal Abrasion
nodes.summary: Abrasion: non-CL = abx+analgesic. CL = fluoroquinolone NO PATCH. NEVER tetracaine to-go.
nodes.body: Diagnosis: fluorescein uptake on cornea under cobalt blue. Look for vertical striations ("ice rink sign") = subtarsal FB; evert lid. Treatment by mechanism: Non-contact-lens (most cases): • Topical antibiotic (erythromycin ointment QID OR polymyxin/trimethoprim drops QID OR sulfacetamide) • Oral analgesic (ibuprofen 400 mg + acetaminophen 1 g) • Topical NSAID (ketorolac 0.5% QID) — Cochrane shows
nodes.recommendation: Corneal abrasion: non-CL = abx + analgesic + NSAID drop short-course. CL = fluoroquinolone, NO patch, 24h follow-up. NEVER tetracaine to-go.

nodes.title: Superficial / Corneal FB Removal
nodes.summary: FB: irrigation→swab→tangential needle on slit lamp. Refer central/penetrating/rust ring.
nodes.body: ED removal candidates: • Superficial corneal FB without full-thickness penetration • Conjunctival or subtarsal FB • Single-piece, visible, accessible Refer to ophthalmology if: • Penetrating / partial-thickness questionable → r/o open globe • Embedded in visual axis (central pupil zone) • Multiple FBs or buried • Iron rust ring in central cornea (refer if you can't remove cleanly) Technique: 1. To
nodes.recommendation: FB removal: irrigation → swab → tangential needle on slit lamp. Refer ophtho if penetrating, central, multiple, or rust ring you can't finish.

nodes.title: UV / Welder's Flash Keratitis
nodes.summary: UV keratitis: abx+cycloplegic+oral analgesic. Resolves 24-72h. NO tetracaine to-go.
nodes.body: Bilateral, painful, photophobic, 6-12 hr after UV exposure (welding without shield, snow blindness, tanning bed without goggles). Slit lamp: diffuse punctate epithelial keratitis, fluorescein uptake bilateral. Treatment: • Topical antibiotic (erythromycin ointment QID x 24-48h) • Cycloplegic (cyclopentolate 1% TID — ciliary spasm relief) • Oral analgesic (ibuprofen + acetaminophen, +/- short opioi
nodes.recommendation: UV keratitis: topical abx + cycloplegic + oral analgesic. Resolves 24-72h. Eye protection counseling. NO tetracaine to-go.

nodes.title: Disposition & Consult Tiers
nodes.body: Tier 1 — Immediate (in-hospital, page now): • Open globe / IOFB → ophthalmology to OR • Orbital compartment syndrome → cantholysis NOW (don't wait), then ophtho • Severe chemical burn (Roper-Hall III-IV / Dua V-VI) → ophthalmology bedside • Pediatric WEBOF (entrapment) → oculoplastics same day, OR within 24-48 hr • Retinal detachment with macula off-or-imminent • Endophthalmitis suspected • Severe

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: Discharge: dx, VA, meds, shield, activity, return precautions, follow-up, teach-back.
nodes.body: Document and verbalize: • Specific diagnosis and grade/severity • Current visual acuity (each eye) • Medications: name, dose, frequency, duration, technique (drops vs ointment) • Eye shield instructions (sleep with shield x 24h after blunt trauma even if minor) • HOB elevation 30° x 48 hr if hyphema or contusion • Activity restrictions (no contact sports, no heavy lifting if hyphema; no swimming w
nodes.recommendation: Discharge: dx + VA + meds + shield + activity + return precautions + specific follow-up + teach-back. Lower threshold to admit if anticoag or sickle.

nodes.title: Admit / OR / Transfer
nodes.summary: Admit/Transfer: open globe→OR, OCS, severe chem, sickle/large hyphema, peds. Stabilize first.
nodes.body: Admit indications: • Open globe → OR (can be admitted overnight if OR delayed) • OCS post-cantholysis monitoring + ophtho follow-up • Severe chemical burn for irrigation continuation, IOP monitoring, multi-spec involvement • Hyphema in sickle / large grade III-IV / non-compliant patient • Pediatric AHT (admit + child protection) • Endophthalmitis • Significant orbital fracture in peds with WEBOF T
nodes.recommendation: Admit: open globe, OCS, severe chem, sickle/large hyphema, peds AHT, endophthalmitis, peds WEBOF. Transfer: cantholyze + irrigate FIRST. Eye shield + antiemetic on transport.

nodes.title: OHSS Overview
nodes.summary: Iatrogenic IVF complication from VEGF-mediated capillary leak — early (3-7d post-hCG) or late (12-17d); can mimic acute abdomen, life-threatening if severe
nodes.body: Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) is an iatrogenic complication of ovarian stimulation - most commonly from IVF/ART. Key Concept: OHSS results from exaggerated ovarian response to gonadotropin stimulation, leading to VEGF-mediated capillary leak and third-spacing. Timing: [1,2] - Early OHSS: 3-7 days after hCG trigger (before embryo transfer) - Late OHSS: 12-17 days after hCG (due to endoge

nodes.title: Key History Questions
nodes.summary: Key history: hCG trigger date, oocyte retrieval date, embryo transfer status, pregnancy test; risk factors: young, low BMI, PCOS, prior OHSS
nodes.body: Essential history for suspected OHSS: [1,2] IVF/ART Timeline: - Date of last menstrual period - Date of hCG trigger injection - Date of oocyte retrieval (egg retrieval) - Did embryo transfer occur? (affects management) - Has she had a positive pregnancy test? Risk Factors for OHSS: [1,3] | Factor | Risk Increase | |--------|---------------| | Young age (<35) | High | | Low BMI | High | | PCOS | Ve

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Bloating, bilateral lower pain, N/V, weight gain >1kg/day, oliguria, hypotension, tachycardia — avoid aggressive pelvic exam (fragile ovaries)
nodes.body: Signs and Symptoms of OHSS: [1,2,3] Abdominal Symptoms (most common): - Bloating and abdominal distension - Abdominal pain (lower, bilateral) - Nausea and vomiting - Diarrhea Respiratory Symptoms: - Dyspnea (pleural effusion or ARDS) - Decreased breath sounds at bases - Tachypnea Systemic Signs: - Weight gain (>1 kg/day from third-spacing) - Decreased urine output (<500 mL/24h) - Hypotension (intr

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Exclude torsion (sudden unilateral pain, absent Doppler), ectopic pregnancy, ruptured cyst, PE — always get pelvic US and pregnancy test
nodes.body: Must rule out before diagnosing OHSS: [2,3] Critical to Exclude: Ovarian Torsion: [4] - Sudden, severe unilateral pain - Nausea/vomiting - Absent or decreased Doppler flow to ovary - OHSS increases torsion risk (enlarged, heavy ovaries) Ectopic Pregnancy: - Positive pregnancy test + pelvic pain - Ultrasound showing no intrauterine pregnancy - Can coexist with OHSS (heterotopic pregnancy) Ruptured

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Classify severity to determine disposition: mild (outpatient), moderate (may need admission), severe (Hct>45%, admit), critical (ICU)
nodes.body: Classify OHSS severity based on clinical and laboratory findings. [1,5] Severity determines disposition and management intensity. Select the severity category that best matches patient presentation:

nodes.title: Mild OHSS
nodes.summary: Mild: bloating, mild pain, ovaries <8cm, normal labs — self-limiting 7-10 days, outpatient supportive care
nodes.body: Mild OHSS Classification: [1,5] Clinical Features: - Abdominal bloating and discomfort - Mild abdominal pain - Ovarian size <8 cm on ultrasound Laboratory Findings: - Normal hematocrit (<45%) - Normal WBC (<15,000) - Normal creatinine - No electrolyte abnormalities Ultrasound: - Mildly enlarged ovaries - No or minimal free fluid Prognosis: - Self-limiting in 7-10 days - Can be managed outpatient -

nodes.title: Moderate OHSS
nodes.summary: Moderate: N/V, ovaries 8-12cm, US ascites, Hct may be elevated but <45% — may require brief hospitalization for IV fluids
nodes.body: Moderate OHSS Classification: [1,5] Clinical Features: - Moderate abdominal pain - Nausea and vomiting - Abdominal distension - Weight gain 2-5 kg Laboratory Findings: - Hematocrit may be elevated (but <45%) - WBC 10,000-15,000 - Normal or mildly elevated creatinine Ultrasound: - Ovarian size 8-12 cm - Ultrasound evidence of ascites Key Features Distinguishing from Severe: - No significant hemocon

nodes.title: Severe OHSS
nodes.summary: Severe: Hct >45%, oliguria, tense ascites, dyspnea, ovaries >12cm — MEDICAL EMERGENCY requiring hospitalization
nodes.body: Severe OHSS Classification: [1,5,6] Clinical Features: - Tense ascites - Severe abdominal pain - Persistent nausea/vomiting - Oliguria (<500 mL/24h or <30 mL/h) - Dyspnea (pleural effusion) - Weight gain >5 kg Laboratory Findings - KEY MARKERS: | Finding | Value | Significance | |---------|-------|---------------| | Hematocrit | >45% | Hemoconcentration | | WBC | >15,000 | Inflammation | | Creatin

nodes.title: Critical OHSS
nodes.summary: Critical: VTE (10-100x risk), ARDS, renal failure (Cr>1.6), anasarca, Hct>55% — requires ICU with multidisciplinary consults
nodes.body: Critical OHSS - Life-Threatening: [1,5,6] Defining Features: Thromboembolic Events: - DVT, PE (most common) - Arterial thrombosis (stroke, MI) - RARE but described - VTE risk 10-100x increased Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): - Severe hypoxia requiring high-flow O2 or intubation - Bilateral infiltrates on CXR Renal Failure: - Creatinine >1.6 mg/dL - Oliguria/anuria despite fluids - May

nodes.title: Pathophysiology
nodes.summary: VEGF-mediated capillary leak causes third-spacing with intravascular depletion — hemoconcentration drives VTE risk (both arterial and venous)
nodes.body: Understanding the mechanism guides treatment: [1,6,7] The VEGF Cascade: 1. hCG administration triggers massive ovarian VEGF release 2. VEGF increases vascular permeability 3. Capillary leak causes third-spacing of fluid 4. Intravascular depletion despite total body fluid overload Key Pathophysiologic Events: Third-Spacing: - Fluid shifts to peritoneal cavity (ascites) - Pleural effusions (usually

nodes.title: Why NOT Diuretics
nodes.summary: Do NOT give diuretics — patient appears fluid-overloaded but intravascular space is DEPLETED; diuretics worsen hemoconcentration and VTE risk
nodes.body: Critical Concept: Do NOT give diuretics for OHSS ascites! [1,2,6] The Paradox: - Patient appears fluid-overloaded (ascites, edema, weight gain) - BUT intravascular space is severely DEPLETED - Giving diuretics worsens hemoconcentration and VTE risk What happens with diuretics: 1. Further intravascular volume depletion 2. Worsening hemoconcentration (Hct rises) 3. Increased VTE risk 4. Worsening re

nodes.title: ED Management Principles
nodes.summary: ED goals: volume resuscitation (UOP>0.5-1 mL/kg/hr), pain control (no NSAIDs), VTE prophylaxis, contact REI clinic even after hours
nodes.body: ED Management Goals: [1,2,3] 1. Volume Resuscitation: - Replace intravascular volume - Target: UOP >0.5-1 mL/kg/hr - Monitor Hct (goal: normalize from elevated baseline) 2. Pain Control: - Acetaminophen (safe in pregnancy) - Opioids as needed (avoid NSAIDs - renal risk) 3. Prevent Complications: - VTE prophylaxis - Monitor for torsion, rupture, ARDS 4. Supportive Care: - Antiemetics - Electrolyte

nodes.title: Fluid Management
nodes.summary: NS/LR 1-2L bolus then reassess; albumin 25% 50-100g for severe hemoconcentration; target UOP>30-50 mL/hr, Hct<40-45%; avoid excessive fluids
nodes.body: IV Fluid Resuscitation for OHSS: [1,2,6] Crystalloid vs Colloid Debate: Crystalloids (NS or LR): - First-line for initial resuscitation - Start with 1-2 L bolus, then reassess - May require large volumes (2-3 L/day) - Risk: may worsen third-spacing Colloids (Albumin 25%): - Consider for severe OHSS with significant hemoconcentration - Dose: 50-100g (200-400 mL of 25% albumin) - Better intravascula

nodes.title: Pain Control & Antiemetics
nodes.summary: Avoid NSAIDs (renal risk); acetaminophen and opioids safe; ondansetron for nausea — use pregnancy-safe medications as patients may be pregnant
nodes.body: Symptom Management in OHSS: [1,2] Pain Control: AVOID NSAIDs: - NSAIDs can worsen renal function - Already at risk for prerenal AKI - Avoid ibuprofen, ketorolac, naproxen Safe Options: - Acetaminophen 650-1000 mg PO/IV q6h - Opioids for severe pain (hydromorphone, morphine) - Heating pad for comfort Antiemetics: - Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO q8h - Metoclopramide 10 mg IV/PO q6h (promotes gastric empt

nodes.title: Paracentesis
nodes.summary: US-guided paracentesis for respiratory compromise or tense ascites — avoid ovaries (10+ cm), slow removal 1-3L, albumin 6-8g/L if >2L removed
nodes.body: Therapeutic Paracentesis for Severe OHSS: [1,2,9] Indications: - Respiratory compromise from tense ascites - Severe abdominal pain/distension - Oliguria despite IV fluids - Concern for abdominal compartment syndrome Technique Considerations: - Ultrasound-guided (enlarged ovaries make blind approach dangerous) - Avoid ovaries - they can be 10+ cm - Use midline or lateral approach away from ovaries

nodes.title: Major Complications
nodes.summary: Life-threatening complications: VTE (10-100x risk), ovarian torsion (6-16%), ovarian rupture, AKI, ARDS, electrolyte disturbances
nodes.body: Life-Threatening Complications of OHSS: [1,5,8] 1. Venous Thromboembolism (VTE): - DVT, PE most common - Risk: 10-100x increased vs general population - Can occur weeks after OHSS onset 2. Arterial Thromboembolism: [8] - Less common but devastating - Stroke, MI, limb ischemia - Often in unusual sites (upper extremity, cerebral) 3. Ovarian Torsion: [4] - Enlarged, heavy ovaries prone to twist - Sud

nodes.title: VTE Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: All moderate-severe OHSS need VTE prophylaxis — enoxaparin 40mg SC daily, continue throughout illness, 3 months postpartum if pregnant
nodes.body: VTE Prevention is Critical in OHSS: [1,8,10] All moderate-to-severe OHSS patients need anticoagulation prophylaxis. LMWH (Preferred): - Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily - Or Dalteparin 5000 units SC daily - Continue throughout acute illness - Continue for 3 months if pregnant Duration of Prophylaxis: | Scenario | Duration | |----------|----------| | Severe OHSS, not pregnant | Until resolution of symptom

nodes.title: Ovarian Torsion
nodes.summary: Torsion risk 6-16% in severe OHSS — sudden unilateral pain, absent Doppler flow, surgical emergency; flow may be present despite torsion
nodes.body: Ovarian Torsion in OHSS Setting: [1,4] Why OHSS Increases Torsion Risk: - Enlarged, heavy ovaries (can be >10 cm) - Longer pedicle with more room to twist - Increased mobility - Risk: 6-16% in severe OHSS Clinical Presentation: - Sudden onset severe unilateral pain - Nausea and vomiting - May have intermittent pain (torsion-detorsion) - Fever (late sign, indicates necrosis) Diagnosis: - Pelvic ult

nodes.title: Renal Complications
nodes.summary: AKI from prerenal volume depletion — aggressive IV resuscitation, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs), paracentesis if compartment syndrome, nephrology if Cr>2.0
nodes.body: Acute Kidney Injury in OHSS: [1,5,6] Mechanism: - Prerenal AKI from intravascular volume depletion - Hemoconcentration reduces renal perfusion - Tense ascites can cause abdominal compartment syndrome Laboratory Findings: - Rising creatinine (>1.0-1.6 = severe OHSS) - BUN:Cr ratio >20:1 (prerenal pattern) - FENa <1% (prerenal) - Oliguria (<500 mL/24h) Management: - Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Admit if: Hct>45%, Cr>1.0, intractable N/V, oliguria, respiratory symptoms, torsion concern; discharge only if mild, tolerating PO, reliable REI f/u
nodes.body: Determine appropriate level of care based on OHSS severity: [1,2,5] Admission Criteria (any of): - Intractable nausea/vomiting - Unable to maintain PO intake - Hematocrit >45% - Creatinine >1.0 mg/dL - Severe abdominal pain - Respiratory symptoms - Oliguria - Concern for torsion or rupture Outpatient Criteria (ALL must be met): - Mild OHSS only - Tolerating PO - Adequate urine output - Normal labs

nodes.title: Discharge - Mild OHSS
nodes.body: Outpatient Management of Mild OHSS: [1,2] Discharge Instructions: Hydration: - Drink 1-1.5 L/day of electrolyte-containing fluids (Gatorade, Pedialyte) - Avoid excessive water (can worsen hyponatremia) Activity: - Pelvic rest (no intercourse, tampons) - Avoid strenuous activity, heavy lifting - Gentle walking OK Monitoring: - Daily weights (return if gain >2 lbs/day) - Track urine output (return i
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with strict return precautions. REI follow-up within 24-48 hours. Daily weights and hydration monitoring.

nodes.title: Admit - Floor/Telemetry
nodes.body: Inpatient Management of Moderate OHSS: [1,2,5] Admission Orders: Monitoring: - Strict I/O - Daily weights - Telemetry (for electrolyte abnormalities) Labs: - BMP q12-24h (Hct, creatinine, electrolytes) - CBC daily - LFTs if concerned for hepatic involvement Fluids: - NS or LR at 150-200 mL/hr initially - Titrate to UOP >0.5-1 mL/kg/hr - Consider albumin if Hct >45% Medications: - VTE prophylaxis:
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor/telemetry. IV fluids, VTE prophylaxis, close lab monitoring. Consult REI.

nodes.title: Admit - ICU
nodes.body: Critical Care for Severe/Critical OHSS: [1,5,6] ICU Admission Criteria: - Respiratory distress/ARDS - Renal failure (Cr >1.6 or oliguria) - VTE (PE, DVT, stroke) - Hemodynamic instability - Severe hemoconcentration (Hct >55%) - Multi-organ dysfunction ICU Management: Respiratory: - High-flow O2, BiPAP, or intubation as needed - Thoracentesis for large pleural effusions Cardiovascular: - Central li
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission required. Multidisciplinary care: REI, nephrology, pulmonary, hematology. Aggressive supportive care.

nodes.title: REI Communication
nodes.summary: Contact REI with timeline (hCG, retrieval, transfer, pregnancy status), severity, labs, management given, and disposition plan
nodes.body: Always Contact the REI (Fertility) Clinic: [1,2] Information to Communicate: Patient Identifiers: - Name and DOB - REI clinic and physician name Timeline: - Date of hCG trigger - Date of oocyte retrieval - Did embryo transfer occur? - Current pregnancy status Clinical Status: - OHSS severity classification - Current vital signs - Key lab values (Hct, Cr, electrolytes) - Ultrasound findings (ovaria

nodes.title: Prognosis & Recovery
nodes.summary: Not pregnant: resolves with menses (7-10d); pregnant: may worsen then improves by 8-10wk; fertility preserved, mortality rare with modern care
nodes.body: OHSS Prognosis: [1,2,5] Natural History: If NOT Pregnant: - OHSS resolves with next menstrual period - Usually 7-10 days after onset - Self-limiting once hCG clears If Pregnant: - OHSS may worsen initially (endogenous hCG rises) - Peak symptoms at 8-10 weeks gestation - Gradually improves as hCG plateaus - Can take weeks to fully resolve Long-term Outcomes: - Fertility is preserved - Future IVF cy

nodes.title: Oncological Emergencies — Triage
nodes.summary: Major onc emergencies: FN, TLS, hyperCa, MSCC, SVC, leukostasis, pericardial tamponade, CRS, ICANS, ICI irAEs

Major oncologic emergencies share a common trait: early recognition + rapid time-critical action prevents death or permanent disability. [1][2] Always ask: 1. What is the cancer type and stage? 2. nodes.title: Febrile Neutropenia — Definition
nodes.summary: FN = ANC <500 + Temp ≥38.3°C single OR ≥38.0°C × 1hr; antibiotics within 60 min, mortality drops 70% → <10%
