Bacteremia present in 10-25%. Mortality wit

nodes.title: MASCC Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: MASCC ≥21 = low risk (oral outpatient possible); always high risk: ANC<100 >7d, instability, GI sx, hypoxia
nodes.body: MASCC Score — predicts low-risk febrile neutropenia eligible for outpatient oral therapy. [5] | Variable | Points | |----------|--------| | Burden of illness: no/mild symptoms | 5 | | Burden of illness: moderate symptoms | 3 | | No hypotension (SBP >90) | 5 | | No COPD | 4 | | Solid tumor or no prior fungal infection | 4 | | No dehydration requiring IV fluids | 3 | | Outpatient at fever onset | 3

nodes.title: High-Risk FN — Inpatient IV Antibiotics
nodes.summary: High-risk FN: monotherapy (cefepime/pip-tazo/meropenem) within 60 min + vanc only if specific indication
nodes.body: Empiric Antibiotic Selection — within 60 minutes: [3][4] Monotherapy (preferred): * Cefepime 2 g IV q8h, OR * Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h, OR * Meropenem 1 g IV q8h (if ESBL or prior beta-lactam reaction) Add Vancomycin if: [3] * Hemodynamic instability / suspected sepsis * Suspected catheter-related infection * Skin/soft tissue infection * Pneumonia (until MRSA ruled out) * Severe mucosi
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Cefepime 2g IV q8h within 60 min. Add vanc if unstable/catheter/MRSA risk. Cultures × 2 + UA + CXR.

nodes.title: Low-Risk FN — Possible Outpatient Therapy
nodes.summary: Low-risk FN: cipro 750 BID + amox-clav 875 BID + ED obs 4-24h + close oncology f/u; admit if any doubt
nodes.body: Outpatient oral therapy may be appropriate IF ALL of the following: [3][5] * MASCC ≥21 * No high-risk features (see prior node) * Reliable patient with reliable transportation * Phone access + can return within 1 hour * No medical contraindication to PO antibiotics * Oncologist agrees with outpatient management * Close follow-up arranged within 24-48h Oral Regimen (combination required): [3] * Cip
nodes.recommendation: Low-risk FN: cipro + amox-clav PO; ED observation 4-24h; oncology follow-up within 24-48h. Default to admit if doubt.

nodes.title: Neutropenic — Afebrile but High Risk
nodes.summary: Afebrile neutropenia: still high risk; look for catheter, perirectal, mucositis, typhlitis, sinus mucor
nodes.body: Even without fever, neutropenic patients can have life-threatening infection — neutrophils are required to mount fever response. [3] Look hard for occult infection: * Catheter site (line tunnel pain, erythema) * Perirectal pain (perianal abscess can present without typical exam findings) * Oral mucositis with new pain * Subtle abdominal pain (typhlitis = neutropenic enterocolitis) * Sinus pain (co
nodes.recommendation: Afebrile neutropenia: hunt for occult source; treat empirically if any localizing sign; admit if ANC <100 or unstable.

nodes.title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome — Cairo-Bishop Criteria
nodes.summary: Cairo-Bishop: ≥2 lab abnormalities (urate↑, K↑, PO4↑, Ca↓); clinical TLS = lab + Cr/arrhythmia/seizure
nodes.body: Cairo-Bishop Laboratory TLS — ≥2 of the following within 3 days before to 7 days after cytotoxic therapy: [6][7] | Lab | Criterion | |-----|-----------| | Uric acid | ≥8 mg/dL or 25% increase | | Potassium | ≥6 mEq/L or 25% increase | | Phosphate | ≥4.5 mg/dL (adult) or 25% increase | | Calcium | ≤7 mg/dL or 25% decrease | Clinical TLS = Lab TLS + at least one of: * Creatinine ≥1.5× ULN * Cardiac

nodes.title: TLS Management — Aggressive IVF + Hypouricemic Agent
nodes.summary: TLS: NS 2-3 L/m²/d (UOP >100 mL/hr) + rasburicase if urate >8 (check G6PD!); no alkalinization; HD for refractory K/PO4
nodes.body: Step 1 — Aggressive IV Hydration (cornerstone): [6][7] * Normal saline 2-3 L/m²/day (200-250 mL/hr in adults if no CHF) * Goal urine output: >100 mL/hr (maintain even if oliguric — push fluids unless overload) * AVOID potassium-containing fluids (no LR) * AVOID alkalinization (urine alkalinization no longer recommended — promotes calcium phosphate precipitation) Step 2 — Hypouricemic Therapy: [6][

nodes.title: TLS — Admit ICU or Telemetry
nodes.summary: Clinical TLS → ICU; lab TLS → telemetry/ICU; q4-6h labs, strict I/O, continuous cardiac monitoring
nodes.body: Disposition: * Clinical TLS (renal/arrhythmia/seizure) → ICU * Lab TLS with high-risk tumor or rapidly worsening labs → ICU * Lab TLS, stable → Telemetry with q4-6h electrolytes * Continue IVF + rasburicase/allopurinol * Nephrology consult if Cr rising or RRT considered Monitoring (q4-6h initially): * BMP, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, uric acid * Strict I/O * Continuous cardiac monitoring
nodes.recommendation: ICU for clinical TLS or high-risk lab TLS. Continue NS 200-250 mL/hr, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg, q4-6h labs.

nodes.title: Hypercalcemia of Malignancy — Severity
nodes.summary: HCM: PTHrP 80% (squamous, breast, renal); severe = Ca >14 or symptomatic; check PTH, PTHrP, vit D
nodes.body: Most common metabolic complication of cancer — occurs in 20-30% of patients during disease course. Usually indicates advanced disease; median survival 30 days untreated. [9][10] Mechanisms: * PTHrP (humoral) — squamous (lung, H&N), renal, breast, ovarian (~80%) * Osteolytic mets — breast, multiple myeloma, lymphoma * 1,25-vit-D production — lymphomas, granulomatous * Ectopic PTH — extremely rare S

nodes.title: HCM Treatment — IVF + Calcitonin + Bisphosphonate
nodes.summary: HCM: NS 200-300 mL/hr + calcitonin 4 IU/kg q12h (rapid bridge) + denosumab 120 SC (Endo 2022 first-line) OR zoledronic acid 4 mg IV; avoid loop diuretics
nodes.body: Step 1 — Aggressive IV Hydration (cornerstone): [9][10] * Normal saline 200-300 mL/hr until euvolemic, then 100-150 mL/hr * Goal urine output >100 mL/hr * Most patients are profoundly volume depleted from hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic DI * Avoid LR (contains calcium) * AVOID loop diuretics in routine cases — only use if volume overload develops; prior dogma of forced calciuresis with furosemid

nodes.title: Mild HCM — Treat Underlying Cause
nodes.summary: Mild HCM: PO fluids, stop thiazides/Ca/vit-D, mobilize, treat underlying cancer, 1-wk f/u
nodes.body: Mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia (Ca 10.5-12): * Generous oral hydration (3-4 L/day) * Avoid thiazides, lithium, calcium/vit D supplements * Mobilization (immobility worsens calcium release) * Treat underlying malignancy — most effective long-term strategy * Outpatient endocrine + oncology follow-up within 1 week * Repeat Ca in 24-48h to confirm stable Admit if: * Rising despite hydration * New sym
nodes.recommendation: Mild HCM: oral hydration, avoid thiazides/Ca/vit-D, mobilize, oncology f/u 1 week. Admit if rising.

nodes.title: HCM — Admit
nodes.summary: HCM admit: ICU if severe/AMS, tele if moderate, q6-12h Ca, expect 1-2 mg/dL/day decline
nodes.body: Disposition: * Severe (Ca >14) or symptomatic → ICU or telemetry depending on AMS/arrhythmia * Moderate (12-14) → telemetry or stepdown * Repeat Ca q6-12h * Endocrinology + oncology consult * Ca usually drops 1-2 mg/dL/day with treatment * Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48-72h — bisphosphonate carries the long-term load
nodes.recommendation: Admit. ICU/telemetry. Continue NS + calcitonin + antiresorptive (denosumab 120 SC first-line per 2022 Endo Society, or zoledronic acid 4 mg IV). Recheck Ca q6-12h. Endo + onc consult.

nodes.title: MSCC — Red Flag Recognition
nodes.summary: MSCC: lung/breast/prostate top 3; thoracic 60%; ambulatory at presentation = ambulatory at 30d; act fast
nodes.body: MSCC affects 5-10% of cancer patients. First sign of cancer in 20%. Time-critical: ambulatory at presentation predicts ambulatory at 30 days; paraplegia is largely irreversible. [11][12] Most Common Primaries: * Lung, breast, prostate (50% of cases) * Multiple myeloma, lymphoma, renal, melanoma Location: * Thoracic 60-70% (most common) * Lumbosacral 20-30% * Cervical 10% * Multi-level in 30% Red f

nodes.title: MSCC — Steroids First, Then Image
nodes.summary: MSCC: dex 10 mg IV STAT (before imaging) → MRI whole spine → neurosurg + rad onc consult; surgery + RT > RT alone if ambulatory
nodes.body: Step 1 — Dexamethasone IMMEDIATELY (do not wait for imaging): [11][13] * Dexamethasone 10 mg IV bolus, then 4 mg IV/PO q6h * Some protocols use higher loading dose (96 mg) for severe deficit — efficacy similar, more side effects * Reduces vasogenic edema → preserves neurologic function * Start before imaging if high suspicion — every minute of cord compression risks permanent deficit Step 2 — Emer

nodes.title: Cancer + Back Pain — Image Liberally
nodes.summary: Cancer + new back pain: urgent MRI within 24h; pain often precedes deficit by weeks
nodes.body: Cancer patient with new back pain — even without neurologic findings — warrants urgent imaging. Pain precedes neurologic deficit by weeks in most cases. Recovery of function once neurologic deficit develops is dismal. Approach: * MRI whole spine with gadolinium within 24 hours * Plain films are inadequate to rule out MSCC * Consider dexamethasone empirically if delay anticipated and high pretest p

nodes.title: MSCC — Admit Neurosurgery / Onc
nodes.summary: MSCC admit: neurosurg if surgical, onc if RT; logroll precautions; ambulatory at presentation predicts outcome
nodes.body: Disposition: * Admit to Neurosurgery if surgical candidate, OR Oncology if RT-only plan * Telemetry if high thoracic/cervical lesion (autonomic risk) * Continue dexamethasone * Foley if retention * Strict bedrest with logroll until surgical/RT plan finalized for unstable spine * DVT prophylaxis (mechanical pre-op, then chemical post-op) Outcomes: * Ambulatory at presentation → 70-80% remain ambula
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Continue dex 4 mg IV q6h. Neurosurg vs RT-onc plan. Foley if retention. Logroll precautions until spine cleared.

nodes.title: SVC Syndrome — Recognition
nodes.summary: SVC: lung 50%, lymphoma 25%; Yale grade 4 = cerebral edema/airway/shock = emergent
nodes.body: SVC syndrome = obstruction of superior vena cava → impaired venous drainage from head, neck, upper extremities. Cancer is the cause in >60% of cases (lung cancer 50%, lymphoma 25%). Indwelling catheter thrombosis is the leading non-malignant cause and is increasing. [14][15] Classic presentation: * Facial swelling/plethora (worse on bending forward — Pemberton sign) * Distended neck and chest wall

nodes.title: SVC — Life-Threatening (Yale 4)
nodes.summary: SVC emergency: HOB up, LE IV access, dex 10 mg IV, urgent IR for stent; intubate carefully if airway compromise
nodes.body: EMERGENT INTERVENTION REQUIRED: [14][15] Immediate stabilization: * Head of bed elevated 30-45° * Supplemental oxygen * Avoid IV access in upper extremities (use lower extremity or femoral) * Consider intubation if airway compromise — anticipate difficult airway (edema, friable tissue) * Hemodynamic support if shock Empiric Steroids (if airway/CNS compromise — controversial in lymphoma without tis
nodes.recommendation: Yale 4 SVC: HOB up, lower extremity IV, dexamethasone 10 mg IV, urgent IR consult for stent, secure airway if needed.

nodes.title: SVC — Workup Before Empiric Treatment
nodes.summary: SVC workup: CT chest + tissue dx BEFORE empiric tx; stent first-line (95% relief in 72h); chemo if SCLC/lymphoma/germ cell
nodes.body: Workup priorities: [14][15] 1. CT chest with IV contrast — confirms SVC obstruction, identifies cause and extent (mass vs thrombus) 2. Tissue diagnosis — critical before therapy selection: * Bronchoscopy if endobronchial mass * Mediastinoscopy or CT-guided biopsy of mass * Excisional biopsy if peripheral lymphadenopathy * Bone marrow biopsy if hematologic malignancy suspected 3. Labs: CBC, CMP, LD

nodes.title: SVC — Admit
nodes.summary: SVC admit: ICU if Yale 4, tele if Yale 2-3, ward if Yale 0-1; HOB up, LE IV, multi-disciplinary consult
nodes.body: Disposition: * Yale 4 → ICU * Yale 2-3 → telemetry/stepdown * Yale 0-1 → admit oncology * HOB elevated, lower extremity IV access * IR + oncology + radiation oncology consults * Anticoagulation decision based on cause (thrombus vs mass)
nodes.recommendation: Admit. Severity-appropriate level. HOB up, LE IV, IR + onc + RT-onc consults. Anticoagulate if catheter thrombus.

nodes.title: Leukostasis vs Hyperviscosity — Recognition
nodes.summary: Leukostasis = cellular (AML, WBC >100k); hyperviscosity = protein (IgM Waldenström); both → AMS, vision, dyspnea
nodes.body: Two related but distinct emergencies: [16][17] Leukostasis (cellular hyperviscosity): * WBC >100,000/mm³ (usually with blast cells) — but symptoms can occur at lower WBC in AML * AML > ALL > CML in blast crisis * Symptoms: hypoxia, dyspnea, headache, dizziness, AMS, visual changes, retinal hemorrhage, priapism * Mortality 20-40% in first week if untreated Hyperviscosity Syndrome (protein): * Marke

nodes.title: Leukostasis Management
nodes.summary: Leukostasis: hydration + allopurinol + hydroxyurea 50-100 mg/kg or leukapheresis (NOT in APL) + induction chemo; HOLD pRBCs
nodes.body: Step 1 — Hydration + TLS Prophylaxis: [16][17] * IV fluids (NS, avoid LR) * Allopurinol 300 mg PO daily OR rasburicase if uric acid >8 (anticipate TLS as cells lyse) * Strict I/O Step 2 — Cytoreduction: Hydroxyurea (first-line if available): * Hydroxyurea 50-100 mg/kg/day PO divided BID-TID * Drops WBC by 50-80% within 24-48 hours * Continued until induction chemo started Leukapheresis: * Indicate

nodes.title: Hyperviscosity Syndrome — Plasmapheresis
nodes.summary: Hyperviscosity: plasmapheresis emergently; avoid pRBCs; underlying tx (rituximab if WM, chemo if MM)
nodes.body: Treatment: [17] Step 1 — Plasmapheresis (definitive symptom relief): * Hematology consult immediately * Removes paraprotein quickly — symptom relief within 24 hours * 1-1.5 plasma volume exchange * May need repeat sessions until induction therapy effective Step 2 — Underlying disease therapy: * Waldenström macroglobulinemia: rituximab + chemo (BTK inhibitors) * Multiple myeloma: chemo + steroids +
nodes.recommendation: Plasmapheresis emergently (heme consult). Avoid pRBC transfusion until viscosity reduced. Admit heme/ICU.

nodes.title: High WBC, Asymptomatic
nodes.summary: Asymptomatic high WBC: admit, IVF, allopurinol, q6h labs; cytoreduce AML >50-100k or rising fast
nodes.body: Asymptomatic patient with high WBC: * Admit hematology/oncology for monitoring + TLS prophylaxis * IV hydration * Allopurinol * Frequent labs (q6h initially) * Pre-emptive cytoreduction if WBC trajectory rising rapidly or AML * Watch for symptom development Threshold for empiric cytoreduction varies by lineage: * AML: WBC >50-100k → hydroxyurea even if asymptomatic * CML chronic phase: usually wel
nodes.recommendation: Admit heme/onc. IVF + allopurinol + frequent labs. Cytoreduce if AML >50k or rising rapidly.

nodes.title: Leukostasis — ICU Admit
nodes.summary: Leukostasis ICU: continue cytoreduction, watch for TLS; APL is the exception — no apheresis, ATRA immediately
nodes.body: Disposition: * Symptomatic leukostasis → ICU * Heme/onc + apheresis service consults from ED * Continue hydration, allopurinol/rasburicase, hydroxyurea * Plan for leukapheresis (unless APL) or immediate induction * Strict transfusion stewardship * Monitor for TLS (often worsens with cytoreduction) APL (suspected M3 AML): * DO NOT leukapheresis — high DIC risk [35] * Start ATRA 45 mg/m²/day immedia
nodes.recommendation: ICU. Continue hydration, allopurinol, hydroxyurea. Heme/apheresis consult. NO apheresis if APL — start ATRA immediately.

nodes.title: Malignant Pericardial Effusion / Tamponade — Recognition
nodes.summary: Malignant pericardial effusion: lung 33%, breast 25%; POCUS tamponade = RA systolic collapse + RV diastolic collapse + IVC plethora
nodes.body: Pericardial Effusion / Tamponade POCUS Reference Most common malignant causes: lung (~33%), breast (~25%), lymphoma, leukemia, melanoma, mesothelioma. Malignant effusions accumulate slowly and can reach >1 L before tamponade physiology develops. [20][21] Beck's Triad (full classic <30%): hypotension + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus: SBP drop >10 mmHg with inspiration

nodes.title: Tamponade — Pericardiocentesis (Bedside)
nodes.summary: Tamponade: avoid intubation/PEEP, vasopressors + cautious IVF, US-guided pericardiocentesis (apical/parasternal preferred); NOT in aortic dissection
nodes.body: Full pericardiocentesis reference Step 1 — Stabilize WITHOUT intubating if possible: • Positive pressure ventilation drops preload → can precipitate PEA arrest • If intubation unavoidable: ketamine induction, no PEEP initially, gentle hand-bagging • Norepinephrine or epinephrine for hemodynamic support • Cautious IV fluid bolus (250-500 mL) — temporizing only; do not over-resuscitate AVOID: beta-b

nodes.title: Stable Effusion — Workup + Plan
nodes.summary: Stable effusion: echo + workup + CT-surgery + onc consult; window for malignant; never drain in dissection
nodes.body: Workup: • Echo (formal echocardiogram) for size, location, hemodynamic effect • CXR, ECG (low voltage, electrical alternans) • CBC, BMP, coags, troponin, BNP • Identify underlying malignancy (CT chest/abd, primary cancer workup) Initial measures: • Telemetry, serial vitals • Avoid IV fluids beyond maintenance (don't worsen filling pressures) • HOB elevated 30-45° Definitive treatment by etiology:

nodes.title: Pericardial Effusion — Disposition
nodes.summary: Pericardial dispo: ICU post-tap or with tamponade; tele if stable; CT-surgery + onc; median survival 2-4 mo malignant
nodes.body: Disposition: • Tamponade or post-pericardiocentesis → ICU (post-drainage pulmonary edema, recurrent effusion, dysrhythmia) • Stable moderate-large effusion → telemetry/stepdown • Small asymptomatic → admit oncology for workup, consider expedited outpatient if stable + reliable Always: • CT-surgery + oncology consult • Repeat echo within 24h to assess re-accumulation • Goals of care discussion — ma
nodes.recommendation: Tamponade or post-tap → ICU. Stable → telemetry. CT-surgery + onc consult. Repeat echo 24h. GOC discussion.

nodes.title: CRS — ASTCT 2019 Recognition
nodes.summary: CRS: fever required; G1=fever only, G2=fluid-resp/low-flow O2, G3=pressor/high-flow, G4=multi-pressor/PPV
nodes.body: Full CRS / ICANS Protocol Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) is the dominant acute toxicity of CAR-T cells and bispecific T-cell engagers (blinatumomab, mosunetuzumab, teclistamab, talquetamab, glofitamab, epcoritamab). [23][24] Time course: • CAR-T: hours to 14 days post-infusion (peak day 1-7) • Bispecifics: most common with first dose / step-up dosing ASTCT 2019 grading requires fever ≥38.0°C plus

nodes.title: CRS Treatment Ladder
nodes.summary: CRS: pan-culture + empiric abx always; G2 toci 8 mg/kg; G3 add dex 10 mg q6h + ICU; G4 high-dose methylpred + anakinra
nodes.body: Universal: pan-culture + empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefepime 2g IV q8h ± vancomycin if catheter/MRSA risk) — CRS and sepsis indistinguishable. Grade 1: • Antipyretics: acetaminophen 650-1000 mg PO/IV q6h • IV fluids PRN • Telemetry • Consider tocilizumab if persistent fever >3 days Grade 2: • Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg), may repeat q8h up to 3 doses in 24h • IV fluids for hypotens

nodes.title: CRS — Disposition
nodes.summary: CRS dispo: G1 tele, G2+ ICU; loop in treating onc; cards/ID as needed; GOC
nodes.body: Disposition: • Grade 1: telemetry + heme/onc consult • Grade 2: step-down or ICU + heme/onc + cardiology if any dysfunction • Grade 3-4: ICU + heme/onc + cardiology + ID Always loop in: • Treating oncology team (have protocol-specific roadmap) • Cardiology if new hypotension/dyspnea/troponin • ID if suspected fungal or atypical infection • Document goals of care — many patients have advanced disea
nodes.recommendation: G1 tele, G2+ ICU. Pan-culture + empiric abx always. Treating onc team has the playbook — call them.

nodes.title: ICANS — ICE Score + ASTCT Grading
nodes.summary: ICANS: ICE 10-point score q4-8h; G1 ICE 7-9, G2 ICE 3-6, G3 ICE 0-2/sz, G4 unarousable/edema; tocilizumab does NOT treat ICANS
nodes.body: Full CRS / ICANS Protocol ICANS (Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity) typically follows CRS (median onset day 5, range 1-21 post-CAR-T). [23][24] ICE Score (10 points) — administered q4-8h during high-risk window: • Orientation: year, month, city, hospital (4 pts) • Naming: 3 objects (3 pts) • Following commands (1 pt) • Writing: standard sentence (1 pt) • Attention: count backward from

nodes.title: ICANS Treatment Ladder
nodes.summary: ICANS: G2 dex 10 mg q6h + Lev prophylaxis; G3 ICU; G4 methylpred 1g IV daily x3 + neurosurg if edema + anakinra refractory
nodes.body: Universal: Baseline EEG + MRI brain. Aspiration precautions, hold driving / sharp objects. Levetiracetam 750 mg IV BID for seizure prophylaxis once Grade 2+. Treat concurrent CRS with tocilizumab (does NOT treat ICANS itself). Grade 1: • Supportive: aspiration precautions, IV fluids • Baseline EEG + MRI brain • Hold driving / sharp objects • ICE q4h • Consider dexamethasone if no improvement in 24

nodes.title: ICANS — Disposition
nodes.summary: ICANS dispo: G1 step-down, G2+ ICU; coordinate with CAR-T center for follow-up
nodes.body: Disposition: • Grade 1: step-down with q4h ICE • Grade 2: ICU vs step-down (depends on trajectory and concurrent CRS) • Grade 3-4: ICU + neurology consult + neurosurgery if edema Long-term considerations: • Most ICANS resolves within 14 days; some neurocognitive deficits can persist months • BCMA-targeted CAR-T (ide-cel, cilta-cel) has higher rate of delayed neurotoxicity and parkinsonism (months
nodes.recommendation: G1 step-down, G2+ ICU. Steroids (NOT tocilizumab). Lev prophylaxis. Neurology + neurosurg if Grade 4.

nodes.title: ICI Toxicity (irAE) — Recognition
nodes.summary: ICI irAEs occur weeks-months post-dose; G1 cont, G2 hold + PO pred, G3 IV methylpred + infliximab if refractory, G4 d/c + ICU
nodes.body: Full ICI Toxicity Algorithm Drug class: PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab), CTLA-4 (ipilimumab, tremelimumab), LAG-3 (relatlimab). Combinations (ipi/nivo) carry 2-3× the irAE rate of monotherapy. [28][29] Critical: irAEs can occur weeks to MONTHS after the last dose. Always ask about ICI exposure in the past 6-12 months. Onset by or

nodes.title: ICI Pneumonitis
nodes.summary: ICI pneumonitis: CT + PJP PCR; G2 PO pred; G3-4 IV methylpred + pulm + add infliximab/MMF if refractory; permanent d/c G3-4
nodes.body: Most lethal pulmonary irAE. Presents with new dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxia. CT: ground-glass opacities, consolidation, NSIP/COP/AIP patterns. [28][29] Workup: • CT chest with contrast • Infectious workup: sputum, blood cultures, viral PCR, PJP PCR • Trend O2 sat, ABG if hypoxic • Rule out cardiac cause (BNP, troponin, echo) Management by grade: • Grade 1 (radiographic only, asymp): hold ICI, repeat
nodes.recommendation: G2 PO pred. G3-4 IV methylpred 1-2 mg/kg/day + ICU + pulm consult; add infliximab/MMF/IVIG if no response 48h.

nodes.title: ICI Colitis
nodes.summary: ICI colitis: r/o C. diff first; G2 PO pred ± infliximab; G3-4 IV methylpred + infliximab; perf = surgery
nodes.body: Presentation: ≥3 stools/day above baseline, abdominal pain, blood/mucus. [28][29] Workup: • Stool studies: C. diff PCR + cultures + ova/parasites • CBC, BMP, lactate, CRP • Sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy if Grade 2+ • CT abdomen if peritoneal signs (rule out perforation) Management by grade: • Grade 1: loperamide, hydration, hold ICI if persistent • Grade 2 (4-6 stools above baseline): hold ICI, predni
nodes.recommendation: Stool studies + C. diff PCR. G2 PO pred + infliximab if no response 48-72h. G3-4 IV methylpred + infliximab + GI consult. Perf = surgery.

nodes.title: ICI Hepatitis
nodes.summary: ICI hepatitis: r/o viral; G3 IV methylpred + hep consult; G4 ICU + MMF (avoid infliximab); transplant if fulminant
nodes.body: Presentation: asymptomatic LFT elevation → fulminant failure. [28][29] Workup: • AST/ALT/Alk Phos/T.bili/INR • Viral hepatitis panel (HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, EBV, CMV) • Autoimmune workup (ANA, ASMA, AMA) • RUQ US to exclude obstruction/mets Management by grade: • Grade 1 (AST/ALT ≤3× ULN): monitor, continue ICI cautiously • Grade 2 (3-5× ULN): hold ICI, prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day • Grade 3 (5-20× ULN
nodes.recommendation: Hep panel + autoimmune + RUQ US. G3 IV methylpred + heme. G4 ICU + MMF (NOT infliximab). Transplant eval if fulminant.

nodes.title: ICI Endocrinopathy
nodes.summary: ICI endo: cortisol BEFORE thyroid; adrenal crisis = hydrocortisone 100 IV; T1DM = DKA pathway; permanent hormone replacement common
nodes.body: Multiple distinct entities: [28][29] Hypophysitis (often ipi): headache, vision changes, fatigue, hypotension. MRI pituitary (enlarged stalk). Replace cortisol FIRST then thyroid (reverse order can precipitate adrenal crisis). Steroids only for mass effect. Adrenal insufficiency: treat as adrenal crisis — hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 50 mg q6h. See Adrenal Insufficiency consult. Thyroiditis
nodes.recommendation: Cortisol FIRST then thyroid (avoid adrenal crisis). Adrenal: hydrocortisone 100 IV. T1DM: ICU + insulin drip. Endo consult.

nodes.title: ICI Myocarditis — Critical
nodes.summary: ICI myocarditis: 25-50% mortality; trop + ECG + echo + MRI + biopsy; ICU + methylpred 500-1000 mg IV x3-5d (early!); abatacept if refractory; permanent d/c
nodes.body: Mortality 25-50%. Suspect with any new chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia, or troponin elevation in ICI-treated patient. [28][29][31] Workup: • Troponin (high-sensitivity) • BNP • ECG (any new conduction abnormality is concerning) • Echocardiogram • Cardiac MRI if hemodynamically stable • Endomyocardial biopsy = definitive diagnosis • ID workup to rule out viral myocarditis Management: • ICU admissio
nodes.recommendation: ICI myocarditis: ICU + methylpred 500-1000 mg IV daily x 3-5d (start within 24h) + cards consult; abatacept 10 mg/kg if steroid-refractory (avoid infliximab in CHF); permanent ICI d/c; check CK + AChR Ab for triple syndrome.

nodes.title: Other ICI irAEs
nodes.summary: Other irAEs: AIN, GBS, SJS/TEN, ITP, uveitis, pancreatitis; hold ICI G2+, steroids, specialty consult
nodes.body: Less common but important irAEs: [28][29] Renal (interstitial nephritis): rising Cr, sterile pyuria, eosinophiluria. Hold ICI, prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. Renal biopsy if Grade 3+. Neurologic (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia, encephalitis, transverse myelitis): ICU, IVIG, plasmapheresis, steroids. Neurology consult. Permanent ICI hold. Skin (toxic epidermal necrolysis, SJS, DRESS): burn unit, supportive ca
nodes.recommendation: Other irAEs: hold ICI for Grade 2+, steroids per algorithm, specialty consult (renal/neuro/derm/heme/ophtho as appropriate).

nodes.title: Chemotherapy Reference — Nadirs & Toxicities
nodes.summary: Chemo toxicities: cardiotox (anthracyclines), pulm (bleo), neuro (vinca), nadir d7-14; ICI = irAEs weeks-months later
nodes.body: Comprehensive Chemotherapy Regimens & Side Effects ED-Critical Toxicity Patterns: Cardiotoxicity: * Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin) — cumulative dose-dependent CHF * Trastuzumab — reversible LV dysfunction * 5-FU, capecitabine — coronary vasospasm * Immune checkpoint inhibitors — myocarditis (rare but lethal) Pulmonary: * Bleomycin — pulmonary fibrosis (avoid high FiO2) * Methotrexate —

nodes.title: Final Disposition Summary
nodes.summary: Disposition: always loop in oncology; document ECOG; goals of care; clear return precautions
nodes.body: Common ED Disposition Threads: * Always involve oncology — primary team knows the patient, prognosis, goals of care * Goals of care discussion — many patients have advance directives or prognostic limitations affecting decisions * Pain control — under-treated in cancer patients; standard opioid principles apply * Anti-emetics — ondansetron + dexamethasone preferred; avoid prochlorperazine in setti
nodes.recommendation: Always: oncology consult, goals-of-care discussion, performance status documented, clear return precautions.

nodes.title: Opioid Withdrawal
nodes.summary: OW rarely life-threatening but drives relapse and fatal overdose (5.5% die within 1yr) — ED-initiated MOUD improves treatment engagement and survival
nodes.body: Opioid Withdrawal Steps Summary Opioid withdrawal is rarely life-threatening on its own — but it is profoundly uncomfortable, drives patients back to opioid use, and the resulting loss of tolerance makes subsequent overdose frequently fatal. 5.5% of patients surviving an opioid overdose die within 1 year. [1][2] The ED may be the only healthcare touchpoint for patients with opioid use disorder (OU

nodes.title: Clinical Recognition
nodes.summary: Mydriasis, yawning, diaphoresis, piloerection, rhinorrhea, GI symptoms onset 4-12h post short-acting; use COWS score to quantify severity
nodes.body: History — symptoms begin 4–12 hours after last dose of short-acting opioids, 24–48 hours after methadone cessation: • Craving for opioids • Dysphoria and restlessness • Rhinorrhea and lacrimation • Myalgias and arthralgias • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea Physical Examination: • Mydriasis (pupillary dilation) • Yawning • Diaphoresis • Piloerection ("gooseflesh") • Increased bowel s

nodes.title: COWS Score Result
nodes.summary: COWS guides treatment: 0-4 observe, 5-12 consider MOUD or symptomatic, 13-24 initiate agonist therapy, 25+ aggressive treatment
nodes.body: What is the COWS score?

nodes.title: No Active Withdrawal
nodes.body: COWS 0–4 — no objective signs of withdrawal. • Observe and reassess in 1–2 hours if concern for evolving withdrawal • Do not initiate buprenorphine — risk of precipitated withdrawal if full agonist still active • Screen for OUD and assess readiness for MOUD • If patient reports recent opioid use, withdrawal may evolve as the drug clears
nodes.recommendation: Observe. Reassess COWS in 1–2 hours. Do not start buprenorphine until COWS ≥ 8.

nodes.title: Mild Withdrawal (COWS 5–12)
nodes.summary: Mild withdrawal — can initiate buprenorphine if COWS ≥8 and patient interested, otherwise symptomatic adjuncts
nodes.body: Mild withdrawal — symptomatic treatment may suffice, but opioid agonist therapy can be initiated if COWS ≥ 8 and patient is interested in MOUD.

nodes.title: Initial Workup
nodes.summary: Labs often unnecessary; BMP if significant vomiting/diarrhea (QT risk); UDS low utility (synthetics not detected); ECG if methadone or QT-prolonging meds
nodes.body: Laboratory Studies: • Most patients can be managed without labs • BMP if significant vomiting or diarrhea — check for hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia (QT risk with methadone/ondansetron) • Urine drug screen: low utility in acute management (many synthetic opioids not detected on standard 5-panel) [6] ECG: • If methadone use (current or planned) • If combining QT-prolonging medications • If electrol

nodes.title: Is This Opioid Withdrawal?
nodes.summary: Piloerection, yawning, lacrimation highly specific for OW; seizures and hyperthermia are NEVER seen — those suggest ethanol/sedative withdrawal
nodes.body: Key differentiators: piloerection, yawning, and lacrimation are highly specific for opioid withdrawal. Seizures and hyperthermia are never seen in uncomplicated opioid withdrawal. [4]

nodes.title: Consider Ethanol / Sedative Withdrawal
nodes.body: Ethanol and sedative-hypnotic withdrawal can be life-threatening — seizures, delirium tremens, and hyperthermia are possible. Opioid withdrawal does not cause seizures or hyperthermia. Key distinguishing features: • Significant hypertension AND tachycardia (both together) → ethanol/sedative WD • Seizures → ethanol/sedative WD (never opioid WD) • Hyperthermia → ethanol/sedative WD or sympathomimeti
nodes.recommendation: If ethanol/sedative withdrawal is suspected, prioritize its management — it carries higher immediate mortality risk than opioid withdrawal.

nodes.title: Other Toxidromes
nodes.body: Sympathomimetic Toxicity (cocaine, amphetamines): • Mydriasis, agitation, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension • Much more severe than opioid WD • Hyperthermia present • No yawning, piloerection, or lacrimation Cholinergic (Muscarinic) Toxicity (organophosphates, carbamates): • SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis • Miosis (not mydriasis), bradycardia, alte
nodes.recommendation: Differentiate by pupil size (mydriasis = OW/sympathomimetic, miosis = cholinergic), presence of yawning/piloerection (specific to OW), and vital sign severity.

nodes.title: Cause of Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Determine if withdrawal from interruption (standard treatment) or precipitated by antagonist (different management based on agent half-life)
nodes.body: What triggered the opioid withdrawal?

nodes.title: Treatment Pathway
nodes.summary: Buprenorphine is first-line for most patients — safe partial agonist, no QT risk; methadone for high tolerance or current methadone patients
nodes.body: Opioid agonist therapy is preferred over non-opioid adjuncts. Buprenorphine is the first-line choice for most patients. [3][7] Medications for Opioid Withdrawal

nodes.title: Buprenorphine Initiation
nodes.summary: Choose induction strategy: standard/high-dose when objective withdrawal is clear, low-dose overlap for fentanyl/methadone or prior PW risk, or wait if COWS is too low
nodes.body: Choose the induction strategy based on the clinical scenario. Fentanyl changes the first-dose decision. Do not dose by clock time alone. Use objective withdrawal signs or choose low-dose overlap if the patient has heavy fentanyl exposure, prior precipitated withdrawal, or cannot tolerate abstinence. Buprenorphine Initiation Guide Fentanyl-Specific Withdrawal Nuance

nodes.title: Fentanyl-Specific Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Fentanyl can persist in tissue; avoid clock-based buprenorphine starts, use objective withdrawal or low-dose overlap.
nodes.body: Clinical issue: chronic fentanyl exposure can make buprenorphine initiation less predictable. Time since last use alone is not a reliable marker of receptor-level readiness for buprenorphine. Pharmacokinetic considerations: • Fentanyl is highly lipophilic and redistributes into peripheral tissue with repeated exposure • Redistribution from tissue may prolong fentanyl/norfentanyl detection after la

nodes.title: Standard Buprenorphine Induction
nodes.body: Buprenorphine 8 mg SL initially when objective withdrawal is clear 1. Reassess COWS in 30–60 minutes 2. If symptoms persist: give additional 4–8 mg SL 3. Repeat until symptom control or COWS < 8 4. Maximum Day 1 total: 32 mg Fentanyl nuance: do not start by clock time alone. If the patient has heavy fentanyl exposure and is borderline, consider 2–4 mg SL first and reassess, or choose low-dose over
nodes.recommendation: Buprenorphine 8 mg SL → reassess 30–60 min → repeat 4–8 mg PRN → max 32 mg Day 1. Discharge with bridge Rx + MOUD referral.

nodes.title: Buprenorphine Microdosing
nodes.body: Buprenorphine 0.5–2 mg SL Can administer while patient is still on a full agonist (methadone, heroin, fentanyl). • Gradually increase buprenorphine dose over hours to days • Frequency guided by COWS score • Lowers precipitated-withdrawal risk by slowly replacing full agonist effect • Feasibility confirmed in ED setting [10] Best candidates: • Fentanyl-dependent (lipophilic, slow clearance makes tr
nodes.recommendation: Buprenorphine 0.5–2 mg SL while patient continues opioid use. Increase gradually to lower precipitated-withdrawal risk.

nodes.title: Wait for Adequate Withdrawal
nodes.summary: COWS <8 too early for standard induction — reassess q1-2h, many experts recommend COWS≥13 for fentanyl-dependent; consider microdosing as alternative
nodes.body: COWS < 8 - starting buprenorphine too early risks precipitated withdrawal, especially with fentanyl exposure. • Reassess COWS every 1–2 hours • SAMHSA recommends adequate withdrawal, generally COWS >12, and notes fentanyl may need a higher COWS score with lower initial dosing [19] • Many experts use COWS ≥ 13 plus objective signs for fentanyl-dependent patients [13] • Consider low-dose overlap/mic

nodes.title: Methadone
nodes.body: Methadone 20 mg PO or 10 mg IM (preferred if nauseated) Onset: 30–60 min PO, 10–20 min IM. Duration of symptom relief: ~24 hours. [14] Cautions: • Do NOT give full maintenance dose to unfamiliar patients — risk of respiratory depression • If patient reports missing a clinic dose, give only 20 mg unless clinic confirms the dose • QT prolongation — dose-dependent. ECG if > 40 mg or combining with ot
nodes.recommendation: Methadone 20 mg PO or 10 mg IM. Monitor for respiratory depression and QT prolongation. Arrange clinic follow-up.

nodes.title: Non-Opioid Adjunctive Therapy
nodes.summary: Non-opioid adjuncts for declining agonist therapy or as add-on — target autonomic, GI, anxiety symptoms; monitor QT if combining multiple agents
nodes.body: For patients who decline opioid agonist therapy or as add-on to buprenorphine/methadone for residual symptoms. Target specific symptom clusters with the agents below. Can combine multiple adjuncts safely, but monitor for QT prolongation if using ondansetron + loperamide + methadone together.

nodes.title: Symptom-Targeted Management
nodes.body: Autonomic Symptoms (tachycardia, diaphoresis, anxiety): • Clonidine 0.1–0.3 mg PO q1h, max 0.8 mg/day — check BP before each dose [16] • Lofexidine 0.54 mg PO q5–6h, max 2.88 mg/day — FDA-approved for OW [17] Anxiety / Insomnia / Muscle Cramping: • Diazepam 5–10 mg IV q5–10 min until sedation • Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV q10 min Nausea / Vomiting: • Ondansetron 4 mg IV/PO q6–8h PRN Diarrhea: • Loperamide
nodes.recommendation: Clonidine for autonomic symptoms, BZDs for anxiety, ondansetron for nausea, loperamide for diarrhea. Monitor QT if combining QT-prolonging agents.

nodes.title: Reassess After Treatment
nodes.summary: Combination opioid agonist + adjuncts is optimal — reassess COWS after treatment to gauge response and guide disposition
nodes.body: Combination approach is often optimal: Opioid agonist therapy (buprenorphine or methadone) addresses the core withdrawal, while adjuncts target residual GI, autonomic, and musculoskeletal symptoms. Reassess COWS after treatment to gauge therapeutic response and guide disposition.

nodes.title: Precipitating Agent
nodes.summary: Precipitated withdrawal can cause hemodynamic instability unlike natural OW — management depends on antagonist half-life (naloxone vs naltrexone)
nodes.body: Withdrawal was precipitated by an opioid antagonist. Management depends on the half-life of the precipitating agent. Iatrogenic (precipitated) withdrawal can produce sudden catecholamine surges and hemodynamic instability that may be life-threatening — unlike naturally occurring opioid withdrawal. [4]

nodes.title: Naloxone-Precipitated Withdrawal
nodes.body: Short-acting — naloxone half-life 30–90 min. Withdrawal typically resolves within 1–2 hours as naloxone clears. Preferred treatment: Buprenorphine 16–32 mg SL • Buprenorphine dose should match the naloxone dose that precipitated withdrawal • If naloxone 2–4 mg caused WD → give buprenorphine 16 mg • Escalate to 32 mg if symptoms persist [11] • This essentially functions as a rapid induction protoco
nodes.recommendation: Buprenorphine 16–32 mg SL for naloxone-precipitated withdrawal. Short-acting — resolves as naloxone clears. Monitor for re-narcotization.

nodes.title: Naltrexone-Precipitated Withdrawal
nodes.body: Long-acting, severe, and prolonged. Oral naltrexone: 24–72 hours. IM depot (Vivitrol): effects may last up to 30 days. Buprenorphine may be less effective — naltrexone blocks the mu receptor. However, buprenorphine's high receptor affinity may partially overcome naltrexone at high doses. Primary treatment — aggressive non-opioid adjuncts: • Clonidine 0.1–0.3 mg PO q1h — critical for hemodynamic co
nodes.recommendation: Aggressive non-opioid adjuncts: clonidine + benzodiazepines + IV fluids. Consider ICU for depot naltrexone. Buprenorphine may have limited efficacy due to receptor blockade.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Most OW patients dischargeable after symptom management — admit for hemodynamic instability, intractable GI, naltrexone-precipitated WD, or pregnancy
nodes.body: Most patients with opioid withdrawal can be discharged after symptoms are managed. Assess for ongoing treatment needs.

nodes.title: Discharge with MOUD Referral
nodes.body: Opioid Withdrawal Discharge Instructions MOUD Continuity: • Bridge prescription of buprenorphine/naloxone — 3–7 day supply minimum (longer if barriers to follow-up) • Arrange follow-up with addiction medicine / opioid treatment program within 72 hours • No X-waiver required since December 2022 — any clinician with DEA Schedule III authority can prescribe • SAMHSA Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 Harm Redu
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with buprenorphine bridge Rx (3–7 days), MOUD follow-up within 72h, naloxone kit, and overdose risk counseling.

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.body: Consider admission if: • Hemodynamic instability (especially from naltrexone-precipitated WD) • Intractable vomiting / diarrhea unresponsive to treatment • Significant dehydration with acute kidney injury • Naltrexone depot (Vivitrol)-precipitated withdrawal — may last days • Concurrent medical illness requiring inpatient care • Pregnancy with opioid withdrawal (risk of fetal distress) — obstetric
nodes.recommendation: Admit for hemodynamic instability, intractable GI losses, naltrexone depot WD, pregnancy, or concurrent illness. Continue MOUD + adjuncts.

nodes.title: Optic Neuritis - Confirm the Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Pain with eye movement + color desat + RAPD + central scotoma. Normal disc does NOT rule out ON.
nodes.body: Open first: - Steps Summary - Stop / Pitfalls Classic ON features: - Subacute monocular vision loss over hours to days (rarely bilateral simultaneous in adults) - Pain with eye movement (>90% of typical MS-ON) - the single most useful symptom - Color desaturation disproportionate to visual acuity (red looks washed-out, brown, or grey) - RAPD on the affected side (if bilateral and symmetric, RAPD m

nodes.title: Pick the Best Subtype Fit
nodes.summary: MS-ON / NMOSD / MOG-AD / neuroretinitis / atypical. AQP4 + MOG on every patient.
nodes.body: Subtype drives Rx (IV methylpred alone vs PLEX vs long-term immunosuppression) and prognosis. Send AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays in EVERY new optic neuritis. Basis for the above: Subtype definitions follow the 2015 international consensus diagnostic criteria for NMOSD [3] and the 2023 International MOGAD Panel proposed criteria [10], with MOG-IgG serostatus outcome data from [4]. The pref

nodes.title: MS-Associated Optic Neuritis
nodes.body: Demographics: Female:male ~3:1, age 20-50, peak 30s. ON is the presenting feature of MS in ~25% of cases; ~50% of isolated ON will develop MS within 15 years (ONTT 15-year follow-up). MRI risk stratification: - Brain MRI with >=1 demyelinating lesion: 72% MS at 15 years - Brain MRI with zero lesions: 25% MS at 15 years Acute Rx: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily x 3 days (ONTT regimen), optional ora
nodes.recommendation: IV methylpred 1 g x 3 days. Oral pred only AFTER IV, never alone. Neuro DMT discussion regardless of MRI.

nodes.title: NMOSD (Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder)
nodes.body: Red flags for NMOSD over MS-ON: severe loss (no light perception or hand motion only), bilateral or rapidly sequential, poor recovery, age >50 or non-white ethnicity, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis on cord MRI (>=3 vertebral segments), area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccup/vomit). Confirmatory test: AQP4-IgG by cell-based assay (NOT ELISA - older ELISAs are insensitive). Send be
nodes.recommendation: AQP4-IgG NOW. IV methylpred x 5 days. Add PLEX early for severe / refractory.

nodes.title: MOG-AD (MOG Antibody-Associated Disease)
nodes.body: Clinical clues: Often bilateral, prominent disc swelling (papillitis pattern), more common in children and young adults, may follow viral illness or vaccination, recovery often better than NMOSD but relapses common. Confirmatory test: MOG-IgG by cell-based assay (live cell-based preferred over fixed). Titer matters - low positive titers in adults may be nonspecific. Acute Rx: - IV methylprednisolo
nodes.recommendation: MOG-IgG cell-based assay. IV methylpred + SLOW taper over 4-6 weeks. PLEX for severe / refractory.

nodes.title: Neuroretinitis (Macular Star)
nodes.body: Distinguishing feature: Disc swelling PLUS a macular star (lipid exudate radiating from the fovea, visible 1-2 weeks after symptom onset). Not a true demyelinating ON - separate entity. Etiology: - Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) - most common identifiable cause; ask about cat/kitten exposure, scratches, regional lymphadenopathy - Syphilis - always rule out with RPR + treponemal test - L
nodes.recommendation: Bartonella + RPR + Lyme + TB. Doxy + rifampin if Bartonella confirmed. Penicillin if syphilis.

nodes.title: Atypical / Expanded Workup
nodes.body: Atypical features triggering expanded workup: bilateral simultaneous, no light perception at nadir, no recovery at 4-6 weeks, severe disc swelling with hemorrhages, age extremes, steroid-non-responsive, recurrent. Expanded panel: - AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG (cell-based) - ANA, ENA, anti-dsDNA (lupus / connective tissue) - ACE, lysozyme, chest CT (sarcoidosis) - RPR, treponemal, HIV - Bartonella, Lyme (esp
nodes.recommendation: Cast a wide net early. Steroid while workup pends; specific Rx is cause-directed.

nodes.title: MRI - Confirm + Stratify
nodes.summary: MRI brain + orbits fat-sat + gad. Cord MRI for NMOSD red flags. Do not delay steroid >24 h for imaging.
nodes.body: Order: MRI brain WITH and WITHOUT gadolinium, INCLUDING dedicated orbit sequences with fat-saturation. Sequences that matter: - T2/FLAIR brain - white matter demyelinating burden (MS risk stratification) - T1 + gad with fat-sat orbits - enhancing optic nerve segment confirms active ON; absence of enhancement does NOT rule out ON if clinical features fit - STIR orbits - bright signal in the affecte

nodes.title: Acute Rx - IV Methylprednisolone
nodes.summary: IV methylpred 1 g x 3-5 d. PLEX for severe NMOSD. NEVER oral pred alone. Rule out syphilis/TB first.
nodes.body: Standard regimen (ONTT - MS-ON): - Methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily x 3 days - Optional oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day x 11 days then 4-day taper - Outpatient infusion is acceptable if VA stable and patient reliable NMOSD or severe / atypical disease: - Methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily x 5 days - Add PLEX (5-7 sessions every other day) if severe, no improvement at 48-72 h, or NMOSD confirmed - IVIG (2

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit for severe / NMOSD / MOG-AD or no outpatient infusion access. Discharge for typical MS-ON if logistics confirmed.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on subtype, severity, social support, and infusion access. Basis for the above: No randomized trial addresses emergency department disposition in optic neuritis. The lanes below are derived from the Continuum optic neuritis review [6] and the proposed acute optic neuritis investigation protocol [13], combined with operational infusion-access and follow-up considerations. Clinic

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for: - NMOSD confirmed or strongly suspected (PLEX coordination, neuro-immunology) - Severe / no-light-perception ON - MOG-AD with severe disease or no outpatient taper access - First ON with severe VA loss requiring inpatient observation during pulse - Atypical features under expanded workup - Patients without reliable outpatient infusion or follow-up Inpatient orders: - IV methylprednisolo
nodes.recommendation: Admit for severe / NMOSD / MOG / atypical / social barriers. Pulse + PLEX coordination + specialty consult.

nodes.title: Discharge - Outpatient Infusion Path
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: - Typical MS-ON features, stable VA, mild-moderate severity - AQP4 / MOG sent (results pending acceptable if subtype clinically classic) - Patient understands the plan and red flags - Outpatient infusion appointment CONFIRMED before discharge (not just referred) - Neuro-ophthalmology follow-up within 1 week, neurology within 2-4 weeks - Pregnancy ruled out / discussed if female
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if outpatient infusion confirmed + neuro-ophtho booked + return precautions understood.

nodes.title: Observation / Short Admission
nodes.body: Observation appropriate for: - Equivocal subtype awaiting AQP4 / MOG result before disposition lane - Single IV methylpred dose given in ED, outpatient infusion arranged, awaiting ride/transport - Partial workup pending, follow-up not yet confirmed - Patient education / social work involvement needed before safe discharge Observation orders: - IV methylpred 1 g daily continued - Serial VA + neuro
nodes.recommendation: Observe for equivocal subtype, partial workup, or social barriers. Confirm follow-up before discharge.

nodes.title: Optic Neuropathy Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Vitals, neuro, both eyes: VA, RAPD, color, disc, pupil, IOP, lid, EOM. RAPD = optic nerve.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Arteritic AION (giant cell arteritis) \u2014 age >50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness \u2192 immediate high-dose steroids. 2. Methanol / toxic optic neuropathy \u2014 bilateral loss, high anion-gap acidosis, exposure. 3. Pituitary apoplexy / compressive lesion \u2014 sudden loss + headache + ophthalmoplegia. 4. Optic neuritis (MS/NMOSD) \u2014 pain on eye movement

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Worst Fit
nodes.summary: GCA, TON, pituitary apoplexy, methanol, ON, cortical, IIH, CRAO, CAD, orbital, nutritional, drug.
nodes.body: Pick the most time-critical diagnosis that fits. You can return after the immediate action.

nodes.title: GCA / Arteritic AION
nodes.body: Open GCA Deep-Dive when built (placeholder - EB Med Scout queued). Next 5 minutes: - Methylprednisolone 1 g IV NOW - do NOT wait for biopsy, do NOT wait for ESR/CRP if clinical suspicion is high - Send ESR, CRP, CBC (thrombocytosis common), platelets, BMP - Temporal artery biopsy scheduled within 1-2 weeks (steroid does NOT invalidate biopsy in the short window) - Ophthalmology + rheumatology stat
nodes.recommendation: Methylpred 1 g IV NOW. ESR/CRP/CBC/plt. Ophtho + rheum stat. Biopsy within 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Traumatic Optic Neuropathy
nodes.body: Open Traumatic Optic Neuropathy when built (placeholder). Next 5 minutes: - CT face + orbits thin cuts (1 mm bone algorithm) - thick cuts miss canal fractures - Ophthalmology + neurosurgery + oculoplastics stat - VA + RAPD + color desat documented at baseline; serial neuro exams - Pain control, head of bed up, avoid Valsalva - DO NOT give megadose steroid reflexively - CRASH and IOTS data shifted
nodes.recommendation: Thin-cut CT face/orbits. Ophtho + neurosurg + oculoplastics. Serial neuro/VA. Steroid decision is institutional.

nodes.title: Pituitary Apoplexy
nodes.body: Open Pituitary Apoplexy when built (placeholder). Next 5 minutes: - Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV BOLUS now (then 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg / 24 h continuous if unstable) - apoplexy = adrenal crisis until proven otherwise; steroid BEFORE imaging - Pituitary MRI with gadolinium - dedicated sella cuts (NOT just generic brain MRI) - Neurosurgery + endocrinology stat - Labs: cortisol, ACTH, TSH, free T4, prol
nodes.recommendation: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV NOW (BEFORE imaging). Pit MRI + endocrine panel. NSG + endo stat.

nodes.title: Methanol / Toxic Optic Neuropathy
nodes.body: Open Toxic Alcohols. Next 5 minutes: - Fomepizole load 15 mg/kg IV over 30 min, then 10 mg/kg q12h x 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h until methanol <20 mg/dL AND pH normal - Ethanol gtt alternative if fomepizole unavailable: load 0.6-0.8 g/kg IV/PO, maintain level 100-150 mg/dL - Bicarb drip for pH <7.30 - HD threshold: methanol level >50, severe acidosis (pH <7.15 unresponsive), end-organ damage (vis
nodes.recommendation: Fomepizole load NOW + bicarb + folinic. HD threshold = level >50, pH <7.15, vision loss. Poison Control stat.

nodes.title: Optic Neuritis (Demyelinating)
nodes.body: Open Optic Neuritis for full Rx algorithm (subtype work, NMOSD / MOG send-outs, IV methylpred dosing, PLEX criteria, disposition). Next 5 minutes: - MRI brain + orbits with fat-sat + gadolinium - Send AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays NOW (before steroid - assay is not affected, but send the bloods first) - IV methylprednisolone 1 g IV (1st dose - full course per deep-dive consult) - Neuro-op
nodes.recommendation: MRI + AQP4 + MOG + IV methylpred. Never oral pred alone. See Optic Neuritis.

nodes.title: PRES / Occipital Stroke
nodes.body: Open Acute Ischemic Stroke - this is cortical, NOT an optic nerve problem. Key distinguishing feature: RAPD is ABSENT in cortical / bilateral homonymous patterns (both pathways equally involved) - this is the cleanest bedside discriminator from true optic neuropathy. Next 5 minutes: - BP control to <160 systolic with labetalol or nicardipine drip (PRES) or per stroke protocol - MRI brain (DWI + FL
nodes.recommendation: RAPD absent -> cortical. BP control, MRI DWI+FLAIR+SWI, stroke pathway. Remove trigger.

nodes.title: IIH (Papilledema)
nodes.body: Open IIH. Next 5 minutes: - MRV first to rule out CVST (same demographic, way worse miss) - this is the most important step - MRI brain with gad (rule out mass / hydrocephalus) - LP with opening pressure measured supine (NOT seated) - >25 cm H2O confirms (>28 in obese patients per ICHD-3 / Friedman criteria) - Acetazolamide 500 mg PO BID start after CVST excluded; titrate up to 1-4 g/day per toler
nodes.recommendation: MRV FIRST (rule out CVST). MRI, LP with opening pressure supine. Acetazolamide. Ophtho + neuro.

nodes.title: CRAO (Cherry-Red Spot)
nodes.body: Open CRAO for full hyperacute pathway. This is a RETINAL artery occlusion, not technically optic neuropathy - included in the hub because it presents as sudden painless monocular vision loss and is the most common DDx trap. Next 5 minutes: - Treat as a stroke equivalent - stroke alert / activate stroke team if within tPA window (some centers now thrombolysing CRAO within 4.5 h) - Non-contrast CT h
nodes.recommendation: Stroke equivalent. Stroke alert, CTA, ESR/CRP for GCA, echo + tele. Tx as per CRAO.

nodes.title: Cervical Artery Dissection
nodes.body: Open Cervical Artery Dissection. Next 5 minutes: - CTA neck + head (or MRA with fat-sat T1 - shows the intramural hematoma) - Antiplatelet vs anticoagulation decision per stroke protocol and clot/hemorrhage status - Stroke + vascular neurology consult - Avoid manipulations of the neck (chiro / massage) and Valsalva activity Triad to recognize: - Horner syndrome (partial - ptosis + miosis, anhidros
nodes.recommendation: CTA neck/head. Antiplatelet/anticoag per stroke protocol. Stroke + vascular consult. Avoid neck manipulation.

nodes.title: Orbital Cellulitis (Compressive Mimicker)
nodes.body: Open Orbital Cellulitis. Next 5 minutes: - IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering MRSA + anaerobes (vancomycin + ceftriaxone +/- metronidazole; ampicillin-sulbactam if MRSA risk low) - do NOT wait for imaging - CT orbits with contrast (look for subperiosteal or orbital abscess, sinusitis source) - Ophthalmology + ENT consult; neurosurgery if cavernous sinus involvement suspected - VA + EOM + RAPD
nodes.recommendation: Vanc + ceftriaxone IV NOW. CT orbits w/ contrast. Ophtho + ENT. Watch for CST.

nodes.title: Nutritional or Hereditary Optic Neuropathy
nodes.body: No deep-dive consult yet (low ED urgency - workup-heavy, outpatient pathway). Next 5 minutes / ED workup: - B12, folate, RBC folate, thiamine (B1), copper, ceruloplasmin (Wilson) - HIV, RPR + treponemal - TSH - Heavy metal screen if exposure history (lead, mercury, arsenic) - ANA, ENA if autoimmune features - If Leber suspected (young male, sequential bilateral, family history): mtDNA testing for
nodes.recommendation: B12/folate/thiamine/copper/RPR/HIV/TSH. Empiric repletion. Leber genetics if pattern fits. Neuro-ophtho 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Optic Neuropathy
nodes.body: No deep-dive consult yet (outpatient pathway in most cases). Common culprits and clinical patterns: - Ethambutol - dose-dependent (esp >15-25 mg/kg/day), often irreversible past 6 months; bilateral central scotoma, decreased red-green color - Amiodarone - bilateral, slowly progressive, optic disc swelling; usually reversible if caught early - Isoniazid (INH) - similar to ethambutol but rarer - Sil
nodes.recommendation: ID the drug. Coordinate with prescriber - do NOT unilaterally stop. Neuro-ophtho 1-2 weeks. Reversibility varies.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Bedside: VA, RAPD, color, disc, IOP, fields, ONS US. Labs: ESR/CRP/CBC + targeted. Always ophtho. Empiric pulse if GCA.
nodes.body: Default bundle when no single cause declares itself: Bedside: - VA both eyes (CF / HM / LP / NLP is fine) - Confirm RAPD - Ishihara 1-2 plates (color desat documentation) - Disc photo via fundus camera if available; dilated exam by ophtho otherwise - IOP both eyes - rule out AACG mimicker (AACG hurts, IOP >40, mid-dilated fixed pupil; route to AACG) - Formal Humphrey field if available, otherwise

nodes.title: Reassess at 60 min
nodes.summary: Worsening -> exclusions. Stable + unsorted -> imaging. Stable + clear -> disposition.
nodes.body: Recheck VA, RAPD, neuro exam after the initial bundle.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: MRI brain+orbits w/gad+fat-sat default. CT trauma/sinus. MRV for IIH/CVST. CTA for Horner/CRAO. ONS US bedside.
nodes.body: MRI brain + orbits WITH gadolinium + fat-saturation orbit sequences - first-line for: - Demyelinating ON - Compressive lesions (tumor, mass, sellar / parasellar) - Pituitary apoplexy (add dedicated sella cuts) - CVST suspicion (add MRV) - PRES CT face + orbits thin-cut (1 mm bone algorithm) - first-line for: - Trauma -> TON - Sinusitis with compression - Orbital cellulitis -> Orbital Cellulitis MR

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit for life/sight-threat; observe for equivocal; discharge with confirmed 1-week ophtho follow-up.
nodes.body: Disposition is cause-specific. Defer to the deep-dive consult's admit criteria once the phenotype is committed.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for: - GCA on IV steroids pending biopsy (~24-72 h depending on pulse + bridge plan) - TON for serial neuro / VA checks (24-72 h minimum) - Pituitary apoplexy - ICU or neurosurg floor - Methanol on HD or fomepizole drip - ICU - Severe / NMOSD / MOG optic neuritis during pulse and PLEX coordination - PRES, malignant HTN, occipital stroke - admit per home consult - Orbital cellulitis on IV ant
nodes.recommendation: Admit for life- or sight-threat. Continue cause-specific Rx. Specialty consults + daily exams.

nodes.title: Observation
nodes.body: Observation appropriate for: - Equivocal GCA awaiting biopsy results with steroids on board, stable VA - Single-dose IV methylpred given, outpatient infusion arranged, awaiting ride / transport - IIH / papilledema awaiting LP opening pressure / MRV results - Partial workup pending; follow-up not yet confirmed by phone Observation orders: - Continue cause-specific therapy - Serial VA / neuro exams
nodes.recommendation: Observe for equivocal / pending workup / awaiting outpatient logistics. Confirm follow-up before discharge.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: - Stable subacute / chronic presentation with confirmed neuro-ophthalmology follow-up within 1 week - Drug-induced with offender stopped (or coordinated stop plan) + outpatient plan - Stable nutritional cause with B12 / folate / thiamine replacement started + follow-up - Typical MS-ON discharged after first IV methylpred dose with confirmed outpatient infusion Universal dischar
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only with confirmed 1-week ophtho follow-up, return precautions understood, suicide screen documented.

nodes.title: Chandler II: Orbital Cellulitis

nodes.body: Orbital Cellulitis (No Abscess): CT Findings: - Fat stranding posterior to orbital septum - Extraocular muscle edema/enhancement - Axial proptosis - ± Sinus opacification - NO discrete fluid collection Management: 1. Admit to hospital 2. IV antibiotics 3. Ophthalmology consult 4. ENT consult 5. Serial exams q4-6h Monitor for: - Vision deterioration - Worsening proptosis - New ophthalmoplegia - Abs

nodes.title: Chandler III: Subperiosteal Abscess
nodes.summary: SPA: may trial medical if <9yr, small medial abscess, no vision loss; surgery if vision deterioration, large abscess, non-medial, or no improvement 48h
nodes.body: Subperiosteal Abscess (SPA): CT Findings: - Lenticular rim-enhancing collection - Located along medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea) - May contain gas - Non-axial globe displacement Key Decision: Medical vs Surgical? May Trial Medical Management if ALL: - Age <9 years - Small abscess (<0.5-1.0 mL or <10mm) - Medial location - No vision compromise - No frontal sinusitis source - Not dental origin

nodes.title: Chandler IV: Orbital Abscess
nodes.summary: Chandler IV intraconal abscess = surgical emergency — emergent ophthalmology + ENT, IV abx, surgical drainage indicated
nodes.body: Orbital (Intraconal) Abscess — Surgical Emergency: CT Findings: - Ring-enhancing intraconal collection - Marked proptosis - May have air-fluid level - Severe mass effect Management: 1. Emergent ophthalmology + ENT consultation 2. IV antibiotics (broad-spectrum) 3. Surgical drainage indicated 4. Consider neurosurgery if intracranial extension Surgical Approach: - Medial abscess: Endoscopic drainage

nodes.title: Chandler V: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
nodes.summary: Chandler V: bilateral signs within 24-48h, CN VI palsy earliest, complete ophthalmoplegia, 20-30% mortality — MRI/MRV gold standard, ICU admission
nodes.body: ⚠️ LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY ⚠️ Pathognomonic Finding: - Unilateral signs → BILATERAL within 24-48 hours Clinical Red Flags: - Bilateral proptosis/chemosis - CN VI palsy (earliest, most common) — limited abduction - Complete ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI) - V1/V2 sensory loss (periorbital numbness) - Decreased corneal reflex - Severe retro-orbital/frontal headache - High fever, sepsis - Altered

nodes.title: CST Treatment
nodes.summary: CST treatment: vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole high-dose 4-6+ weeks IV; consider heparin anticoag and dexamethasone; drain primary sinus source
nodes.body: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis Management: Antibiotics (High-Dose, Broad-Spectrum): - Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h - Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h - Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h Consider: - Amphotericin B if fungal suspected (immunocompromised) - Higher doses for CNS penetration Anticoagulation: - Controversial - May reduce thrombus propagation - Consider heparin if no contraindication - Risk of hemorrhagi

nodes.title: IV Antibiotic Regimen
nodes.summary: Empiric IV: vancomycin + ceftriaxone ± metronidazole (if sinus/dental source); alternatives: ampicillin-sulbactam or pip-tazo monotherapy

nodes.summary: IV until afebrile 48h (typically 1-2 weeks), then PO step-down 2-3 weeks for total 3-4 weeks minimum; serial exams and imaging if not improving

nodes.summary: Adjuncts: nasal decongestant (oxymetazoline x3d), saline irrigation, head elevation 30-45, ENT consult for sinus source (>90% of cases)

nodes.title: Organic vs Psychiatric Emergency
nodes.summary: Medical causes underlie 19-80% of behavioral presentations - history is 94% sensitive
nodes.body: Quick Reference: Red Flags for Organic Cause The Challenge: 19-80% of presentations attributed to psychiatric illness have an underlying medical cause. Missed medical diagnosis rates: 8-48% in EDs, with highest rates in first presentations. Key Principle: The approach to behavioral complaints should be the same as general medical conditions: ABCs, thorough history (including collateral), physical

nodes.title: Vital Signs Assessment
nodes.summary: Abnormal vital signs suggest organic cause - all must be explained before psych disposition
nodes.body: Complete vital signs are mandatory - only 50% of psych patients have full VS documented. SMART Protocol thresholds: • Temp >100.4°F (38°C) or <96.8°F (36°C) • HR <50 or >100 • BP <100 systolic or >180/110 (x2, 15 min apart) • RR <8 or >22 • SpO2 <95% on room air Fingerstick glucose - the "6th vital sign." Hypoglycemia can mimic ANY psychiatric presentation from catatonia to mania. Any vital sign a

nodes.title: Abnormal Vital Signs
nodes.summary: Vital sign patterns guide differential - fever suggests infection/toxidrome, tachycardia suggests withdrawal/stimulants
nodes.body: Abnormal vitals strongly suggest organic etiology. Do NOT attribute to "anxiety" without investigation. Fever + behavioral change: • Infection (UTI most common in elderly, meningitis, encephalitis) • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) • Serotonin syndrome • Thyroid storm • Hyperactive delirium with severe agitation — hyperthermia + severe agitation + altered mental status + metabolic derangement

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia
nodes.summary: Hypoglycemia mimics any psych presentation - treat and recheck glucose in 15 minutes
nodes.body: Hypoglycemia can cause ANY psychiatric presentation: • Anxiety, agitation, combativeness • Confusion, altered consciousness • Bizarre behavior, psychosis • Catatonia, unresponsiveness • Seizures Treatment: • D50W 25g (50 mL) IV push (adults) • D10W 2-5 mL/kg (pediatrics) • Glucagon 1mg IM if no IV access Recheck glucose in 15 minutes. nodes.title: Critical History Elements
nodes.summary: Collateral history is critical - cannot diagnose delirium without knowing baseline
nodes.body: History is 94% sensitive for identifying organic causes. Essential collateral: Family, prior records, group home staff, EMS. What is BASELINE mental status? Key questions: • Psychiatric history? (prior diagnoses, hospitalizations, medications) • Substance use? (alcohol, drugs, new prescriptions) • Recent medication changes? (especially anticholinergics, steroids, opioids) • Recent illness, surgery

nodes.title: Red Flags for Organic Cause
nodes.summary: 63% of new-onset psych symptoms have organic cause - visual hallucinations, fluctuation, disorientation suggest delirium
nodes.body: Red Flags Quick Reference High-risk features suggesting organic etiology: • New-onset psychiatric symptoms without prior history • Age >45 with first psychiatric presentation • Age <12 with behavioral emergency • Altered level of consciousness (drowsy, obtunded) • Fluctuating course (waxes and wanes) • Visual hallucinations (rare in primary psych) • Disorientation (to person, place, time) • Memory

nodes.title: Low-Risk Presentation
nodes.summary: Low-risk: known psych history, similar presentation, normal VS/exam - routine labs not indicated
nodes.body: Low-risk criteria (all must be present): • Known psychiatric history • Similar to prior presentations • Alert, cooperative, oriented • Normal vital signs • Normal physical exam • Non-contributory history • Age <45 • No recent medication/substance changes ACEP 2017 recommendation: "Do not routinely order laboratory testing on patients with acute psychiatric symptoms" who meet low-risk criteria. nodes.title: Elderly Patient (≥65 years)
nodes.summary: Elderly + behavioral change = delirium until proven otherwise. UTI is #1 cause in elderly women.
nodes.body: Delirium is missed 76% of the time in ED elderly patients (Han 2009). Prevalence: 8-17% of older ED patients, with pooled meta-analytic estimates clustering ~15% and large recent cohorts at 14-16%. The full published range is 7-35% depending on screening method. Up to 40% in patients arriving from a nursing home. New psychiatric symptoms in the elderly = delirium until proven otherwise. Common pre

nodes.title: Targeted Medical Workup
nodes.summary: Selective testing based on presentation - not all patients need labs
nodes.body: Not all patients need labs. Routine testing of low-yield and not recommended by ACEP 2017. Selective testing based on clinical picture: All patients with red flags or concern for organic cause: • Fingerstick glucose (if not already done) • BMP (Na, glucose, renal function) • Consider CBC, UA If fever, infection suspected: • CBC, lactate, UA, CXR • Blood cultures if sepsis concern • LP if meningiti

nodes.title: Medical Condition Identified
nodes.summary: Classify as causal, contributory, or incidental - treat medical condition and reassess
nodes.body: Medical condition found - classify as: CAUSAL: Medical condition is directly causing the psychiatric symptoms • Treat the medical condition • Psychiatric symptoms should improve with treatment • Medical admission usually required CONTRIBUTORY: Medical condition is worsening or triggering underlying psychiatric illness • Treat both medical and psychiatric components • May need medical stabilization

Alcohol or sedative-hypnoti

nodes.title: Features Suggesting Primary Psychiatric Illness
nodes.summary: Auditory hallucinations, organized delusions, intact orientation favor psychiatric - visual hallucinations favor organic

Unable to care for self: • Gravely disabled? • Unable to meet basic needs? Document findings c

nodes.summary: Medical admission for organic cause, unstable vitals, or pending concerning workup

nodes.title: Disposition: Psychiatric Admission
nodes.summary: Ensure medically stable before transfer - document all medical evaluation performed
