Inattention (cannot spell WORLD backward, months backward, or count 20 to 1) 3. Altered level of consciousness (hyper- or hypoactive) 4. Disorganized thinking (illogical, rambling, unpredictable) Risk factors: • Age >65 • Cognitive i

nodes.title: Acute Ear Pain — Sick Check First
nodes.body: Most ear pain is benign otitis, but the ear is also a window onto dangerous local and referred disease. The two traps are (1) a destructive infection (necrotizing otitis externa, mastoiditis) mistaken for simple otitis, and (2) referred otalgia with a normal ear exam — where the real problem is cardiac, dental, throat, or nerve. ⚠️ DO-NOT-MISS diagnoses 1. Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa —

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Seven-branch triage: malignant OE / mastoiditis / Ramsay Hunt / referred / otitis externa / otitis media / trauma-FB.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous local infections and referred sources first, then the common benign causes. Each branch runs a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Malignant Otitis Externa — Skull-Base Gate
nodes.summary: Diabetic/immunocompromised + pain out of proportion + canal granulation ± CN palsy = necrotizing OE; imaging, IV anti-pseudomonal, ENT.
nodes.body: Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa is skull-base osteomyelitis, usually Pseudomonas, in older diabetics or the immunocompromised. The alarm is severe, deep, unrelenting ear pain out of proportion to exam (often worse at night), granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal floor, purulent discharge, and — in advanced disease — cranial-nerve palsies (VII first). It does NOT

nodes.title: Necrotizing Otitis Externa — Image + Anti-Pseudomonal + ENT
nodes.body: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa (no dedicated consult yet — manage here): - Urgent ENT consultation and admission — this is skull-base osteomyelitis, not simple otitis. - Imaging: CT temporal bones for bony erosion; MRI for soft-tissue/intracranial extent; nuclear studies help define osteomyelitis and monitor treatment. - Systemic anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., a fluoroquinolone such a
nodes.recommendation: Urgent ENT + admit, CT/MRI temporal bone, prolonged systemic anti-pseudomonal therapy, culture, glycemic control, follow cranial nerves.

nodes.title: Necrotizing OE — Unlikely
nodes.body: An immunocompetent host with an exam consistent with simple external otitis and no granulation tissue or pain out of proportion makes necrotizing OE unlikely. Reassess if a diabetic/immunocompromised patient fails to improve on topical therapy — that is the moment to image and consult ENT. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Necrotizing OE unlikely in an immunocompetent host with a benign exam; re-image/consult if a high-risk patient fails topical therapy.

nodes.title: Mastoiditis — Post-Auricular Gate
nodes.summary: Post-auricular swelling + protruding auricle + fever = mastoiditis; CT + IV antibiotics + ENT; watch for intracranial spread.
nodes.body: Mastoiditis is a suppurative complication of otitis media — infection of the mastoid air cells. Look for post-auricular swelling, erythema, and tenderness with a protruding/down-and-out auricle, fever, and a bulging or perforated TM. It can progress to a subperiosteal abscess or intracranial complications (meningitis, sinus thrombosis, brain abscess). New neurologic signs, severe headache, or toxi

nodes.title: Mastoiditis — CT + IV Antibiotics + ENT
nodes.body: Acute mastoiditis (no dedicated consult yet — manage here): - Urgent ENT consultation and admission. - CT temporal bones with contrast to confirm mastoid opacification/coalescence and detect a subperiosteal abscess or intracranial extension; add CT/MRI with venography if intracranial complications are suspected (meningitis, sinus thrombosis, abscess). - IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering typic
nodes.recommendation: Urgent ENT + admit, contrast CT temporal bones (± venography for intracranial), IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, surgical drainage as needed.

nodes.title: Mastoiditis — Unlikely
nodes.body: No post-auricular swelling/erythema, a normally positioned auricle, and no toxicity make mastoiditis unlikely. Reassess if post-auricular findings, a protruding auricle, or neurologic signs develop, especially in a patient with otitis media. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Mastoiditis unlikely without post-auricular findings; reassess if they develop in a patient with otitis media.

nodes.title: Ramsay Hunt — Vesicles + Facial-Nerve Gate
nodes.summary: Ear pain + vesicles + facial palsy = Ramsay Hunt; early antivirals + steroids, eye protection, ENT/neuro follow-up.
nodes.body: Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) is reactivation of varicella-zoster in the geniculate ganglion: severe ear pain, vesicles in the ear canal, auricle, or on the palate, and an ipsilateral facial (CN VII) palsy, often with hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo (CN VIII). It has worse facial-nerve recovery than Bell palsy, so early recognition and treatment matter. Vesicles may lag the pain,

nodes.title: Ramsay Hunt — Antivirals + Steroids + Eye Care
nodes.body: Herpes zoster oticus / Ramsay Hunt (no dedicated consult yet — manage here): - Start antivirals early (e.g., valacyclovir or acyclovir) — the sooner the better for facial-nerve outcome. - Add corticosteroids (commonly used in combination) unless contraindicated. - Protect the eye on the affected side — incomplete lid closure risks exposure keratopathy: lubrication, taping at night, ophthalmology i
nodes.recommendation: Early antivirals + steroids, meticulous eye protection, analgesia, document CN VII/VIII, ENT/neuro follow-up.

nodes.title: Ramsay Hunt — Unlikely
nodes.body: No vesicles and no facial-nerve palsy make Ramsay Hunt unlikely — but remember vesicles can lag the pain and the palsy may follow. Reassess if vesicles or a facial droop appear, and treat early if they do. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Ramsay Hunt unlikely without vesicles/palsy; reassess since vesicles/palsy can appear later, and treat early if so.

nodes.title: Referred Otalgia — Normal Ear, Find the Real Source
nodes.summary: Normal ear = referred pain: screen cardiac → chest-pain hub, throat/deep-neck → sore-throat hub, dental/facial → dental/facial-pain hubs.
nodes.body: Ear pain with a normal ear exam is referred pain until proven otherwise — the ear shares innervation (CN V, VII, IX, X, and cervical nerves) with the teeth, throat, TMJ, neck, and heart. Screen the dangerous sources: cardiac ischemia (jaw/ear can be an anginal equivalent, esp. with exertion/risk factors), deep-neck/throat infection, dental abscess, and — in a smoker/drinker with weight loss, dysph

nodes.title: Referred Otalgia — Rule Out Cardiac Ischemia
nodes.body: Open Chest Pain — jaw/ear pain can be an anginal equivalent, especially with exertion, diaphoresis, dyspnea, or cardiac risk factors. - Get an ECG and troponin and work the chest-pain pathway; do not let a "normal ear" falsely reassure you. - Treat as an acute coronary syndrome workup if the risk profile fits. - This is the single most dangerous cause of a normal-ear otalgia to miss.
nodes.recommendation: Exertional/high-risk referred otalgia → ECG + troponin + chest-pain pathway; treat as possible ACS.

nodes.title: Referred Otalgia — Throat / Deep-Neck Source
nodes.body: Open Sore Throat to work the pharyngeal/deep-neck source. - Screen for the dangerous throat causes referred to the ear: peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, epiglottitis, and deep-neck-space infection — look for odynophagia, trismus, drooling, muffled voice, neck swelling, and toxicity. - Assess the airway; image (CT neck) and consult ENT for suspected deep-neck infection or abscess. - Ear pain
nodes.recommendation: Throat-referred otalgia → sore-throat pathway; screen for deep-neck infection/epiglottitis, protect the airway, CT + ENT as indicated.

nodes.title: Referred Otalgia — Dental / Facial Source
nodes.body: Open Dental Pain or Unilateral Facial Pain to work a dental/jaw/facial source. - Dental abscess, pericoronitis, or a cracked/necrotic tooth commonly refer to the ear (CN V) — examine the teeth/gums and screen for a spreading odontogenic infection (facial swelling, trismus, floor-of-mouth involvement → dangerous). - TMJ dysfunction and trigeminal/facial neuralgias also refer to the ear — assess the
nodes.recommendation: Dental/facial-referred otalgia → dental-pain / facial-pain pathway; treat the source, escalate spreading odontogenic infection.

nodes.title: Benign Referred Otalgia
nodes.body: A low-risk patient with a benign referred source (e.g., mild TMJ dysfunction, cervical/musculoskeletal, minor pharyngitis) and a reassuring screen can be managed symptomatically. - Treat the identified source (TMJ measures/NSAIDs, cervical care). - Red-flag counseling: in a smoker/drinker with weight loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, or a neck mass, arrange ENT follow-up to exclude head-and-neck malign
nodes.recommendation: Benign referred otalgia → treat the source symptomatically; ENT follow-up to exclude malignancy if red flags/persistent.

nodes.title: Otitis Externa — Canal Gate
nodes.summary: Tragal tenderness + canal edema/discharge = otitis externa; topical drops ± wick; re-screen necrotizing OE in high-risk hosts.
nodes.body: Acute otitis externa ("swimmer's ear") is a diffuse infection of the ear canal: pain on tragal traction or auricle manipulation, canal edema/erythema, itch, and discharge. Confirm you are not missing a necrotizing picture (pain out of proportion, granulation, high-risk host) and check that the TM is intact if you plan certain topicals.

nodes.title: Otitis Externa — Topical Therapy
nodes.body: Acute otitis externa (no dedicated consult — manage here): - Topical antibiotic ± steroid drops are first-line (systemic antibiotics are usually unnecessary in uncomplicated disease). - Aural toilet (gentle cleaning) and, if the canal is very edematous, an ear wick to deliver drops. - Analgesia and keep the ear dry; treat any fungal (otomycosis) component appropriately. - Choose TM-safe drops if p
nodes.recommendation: Topical antibiotic ± steroid drops first-line + aural toilet/wick + keep dry; TM-safe drops if perforation possible; re-screen high-risk hosts.

nodes.title: Otitis Externa — Re-Screen Necrotizing
nodes.body: Pain out of proportion, granulation tissue, or a diabetic/immunocompromised host means this is not simple otitis externa — loop back to the necrotizing OE gate, image, and consult ENT. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Atypical/high-risk "otitis externa" → re-run the necrotizing OE gate (image + ENT), do not just re-dose drops.

nodes.title: Otitis Media — TM Gate
nodes.summary: Bulging TM + effusion = otitis media; analgesia ± antibiotics; re-screen mastoiditis/complications and nasopharyngeal cause in adults.
nodes.body: Acute otitis media is a middle-ear infection: a deep ache, a bulging, erythematous, or immobile TM with a middle-ear effusion, ± fever and conductive hearing loss. In adults it is less common than in children — consider a nasopharyngeal cause (obstruction/mass) for unilateral or recurrent adult OM. Watch for complications: mastoiditis, facial palsy, or intracranial spread.

nodes.title: Otitis Media — Analgesia ± Antibiotics
nodes.body: Acute otitis media (see Ear Infection for the full management pathway): - Analgesia is central; antibiotics (amoxicillin first-line; amoxicillin-clavulanate if risk factors) for adults with clear AOM, systemic symptoms, or failure of observation. - Treat contributing factors; decongestants/antihistamines have limited evidence. - Adults with unilateral or recurrent OM: consider nasopharyngeal patho
nodes.recommendation: Analgesia + antibiotics for clear/systemic adult AOM; consider nasopharyngeal cause for unilateral/recurrent disease; complication return precautions.

nodes.title: Otitis Media — Re-Screen Complication
nodes.body: Post-auricular swelling, a facial palsy, severe headache, neck stiffness, or toxicity means a complication of otitis media — loop back to the mastoiditis/intracranial gate, image, and consult ENT. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Complicated otitis media → re-run the mastoiditis/intracranial gate (CT + ENT), treat the complication.

nodes.title: Trauma / Foreign Body / Perforation — Mechanism Gate
nodes.summary: Button battery/insect FB and auricular hematoma are time-sensitive; simple TM perforation is usually conservative with follow-up.
nodes.body: Mechanical causes of ear pain: a foreign body in the canal (esp. a button battery or an insect — both time-sensitive), traumatic TM perforation (barotrauma, slap, Q-tip), auricular hematoma (needs drainage to prevent cauliflower ear), and canal laceration. A button battery in the canal is an emergency (liquefactive necrosis) and a live insect should be killed/immobilized before removal.

nodes.title: Time-Sensitive Ear Trauma — Act Now
nodes.body: Mechanical ear emergencies (manage here; procedural pathways available): - Button battery in the canal → emergent removal (liquefactive/alkaline injury); see Ear Foreign Body and consult ENT if not readily removable. - Live insect → immobilize/kill first (mineral oil or lidocaine) then remove; irrigation is contraindicated if the TM may be perforated or for organic material that swells. - Auricula
nodes.recommendation: Emergent removal of button battery/insect (ear-FB pathway/ENT), drain auricular hematoma, wound care for lacerations; document hearing/TM.

nodes.title: Simple TM Perforation / Minor Trauma
nodes.body: Most traumatic TM perforations heal spontaneously over weeks. - Keep the ear dry (no water/swimming), avoid drops unless prescribed, and provide analgesia. - ENT follow-up to confirm healing and document hearing; audiometry if hearing loss. - Return precautions for vertigo, worsening hearing, discharge/fever (superinfection), or facial weakness. - Avoid ototoxic drops with an open TM.
nodes.recommendation: Simple TM perforation → keep dry, analgesia, ENT follow-up + audiometry, avoid ototoxic drops, complication return precautions.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle
nodes.body: The otalgia work-up bundle (scale to acuity): - Full otologic exam: auricle and post-auricular area, canal and TM (otoscopy/pneumatic if available), and a check for granulation tissue, vesicles, or discharge. - Cranial-nerve exam — facial nerve first (Ramsay Hunt, necrotizing OE, mastoiditis); document any deficit. - Vitals + qSOFA for the toxic/febrile patient; screen for sepsis and intracranial

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Dangerous local/referred cause → image + consult + admit; benign/treated → disposition.
nodes.body: After the otologic and cranial-nerve exam and the referred-source screen — where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.body: Match the study to the question: - CT temporal bones (± contrast) — necrotizing otitis externa (bony erosion/skull base) and mastoiditis (coalescence, subperiosteal abscess). - MRI head/temporal bone + MR/CT venography — soft-tissue/intracranial extent, sinus thrombosis, or abscess when complications are suspected. - CT neck with contrast — deep-neck-space infection/abscess referred to the ear. -

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit the dangerous local/referred causes with the right specialist; observe the borderline; discharge benign/treated with follow-up.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: Admit + Specialist
nodes.body: Admit the dangerous cause with the appropriate service. - Necrotizing otitis externa → admit, IV anti-pseudomonal therapy, ENT, glycemic control. - Mastoiditis / intracranial complication → admit, IV antibiotics, ENT ± neurosurgery, surgical drainage as needed. - Referred cardiac (ACS) → cardiology/appropriate cardiac pathway and admission. - Deep-neck-space infection → ENT, airway management, IV
nodes.recommendation: Admit necrotizing OE / mastoiditis / intracranial / ACS / deep-neck with the right specialist, IV therapy, and drainage/definitive care as indicated.

nodes.title: Observe / Specialist in the ED
nodes.body: Observation or an in-ED specialist consult for the borderline patient — e.g., a high-risk host with severe otitis awaiting imaging to exclude necrotizing disease, or an uncertain referred source needing further workup. - Serial exams, complete the pending studies, and obtain specialist input before disposition. - Ensure adequate analgesia and reliable, timely follow-up.
nodes.recommendation: Short observation + specialist input, complete pending imaging/workup, then admit or discharge with tight follow-up.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge the well patient with a clear plan. - Otitis externa/media: topical/oral therapy as indicated, analgesia, keep the ear dry, and 48–72 h follow-up if not improving. - Treated referred source: manage the primary cause (dental, TMJ, minor throat) with the appropriate follow-up. - Ramsay Hunt: antivirals + steroids started, eye protection, ENT/neuro follow-up. - Simple TM perforation/minor t
nodes.recommendation: Discharge benign/treated patients with targeted therapy, analgesia, and explicit necrotizing/mastoiditis/complication return precautions + appropriate follow-up.

nodes.title: Failure to Sense (Undersensing)
nodes.summary: Undersensing: paces regardless of intrinsic rhythm — DANGER of R-on-T triggering VF; magnet converts to asynchronous but does NOT fix the problem
nodes.body: Pacing spikes occurring regardless of intrinsic rhythm. ECG Pattern: • Pacing spikes falling during or after native QRS • Pacing that ignores intrinsic beats • "Competition" between device and native rhythm ⚠️ DANGER: May pace on T wave → R-on-T → VF ⚠️ Causes: • Sensitivity programmed too low • Lead dislodgment • Lead fracture • Inadequate intrinsic signal amplitude • Fibrosis at lead-tissue inte

nodes.title: Oversensing
nodes.summary: Oversensing: device inhibited by non-cardiac signals (myopotentials, T-waves, EMI, lead fracture noise) — magnet bypasses sensing and restores pacing
nodes.body: Device is inhibited by signals it mistakes for cardiac activity. ECG Pattern: • Pauses without pacing when pacing should occur • Intermittent failure to pace • Often position-dependent or activity-related What Is Being Oversensed? • Myopotentials - skeletal muscle (pectoralis) • T-wave sensing - large T waves mistaken for QRS • EMI - electromagnetic interference • Lead fracture noise - random sign

nodes.title: Pacemaker-Mediated Tachycardia
nodes.summary: PMT in DDD pacemakers: retrograde conduction creates endless loop at upper tracking rate — magnet breaks loop immediately, also try adenosine
nodes.body: PMT (Endless Loop Tachycardia) - DDD pacemakers only. Mechanism: 1. PVC or loss of atrial capture 2. Retrograde conduction to atrium 3. Atrial lead senses retrograde P wave 4. Triggers ventricular pacing 5. Ventricular pace conducts retrograde to atrium 6. Cycle repeats → tachycardia at upper tracking rate ECG Pattern: • Regular tachycardia at or near upper tracking rate (usually 110-130 bpm) • Ve

nodes.title: Paced Rhythm ECG Basics
nodes.summary: Pacing spikes: vertical deflections; RV pacing = LBBB + LAD morphology; discordant ST-T normal; concordant ST changes = concerning for ischemia

A-sense, V-sense - no spikes, native rhythm 2. A-pace, V-sense - atrial spike

nodes.title: TCP Troubleshooting
nodes.summary: TCP troubleshooting: check pad contact/connections, increase to max mA, try A-P position; TCP is PAINFUL — sedate with fentanyl/midazolam/ketamine

Increase Output: • Go up to maximum (usually 140-200 mA) • If still no capture at max → TVP Check Connections: • Pads connected to pacer? • Pacer mode correct? Patient Factors: • Large body habitus (higher thresholds) • Pericardial effusion • Severe metabolic derangement Patient Comfort: • TCP

nodes.title: Painless Scrotal Swelling — Sick Check First
nodes.body: "Painless" is a trap — do NOT label a hydrocele until you have excluded the masqueraders. Torsion can be intermittent and only intermittently painful, malignancy is famously painless, and a constricting object or an incarcerated hernia can devastate the testis or bowel while the presenting complaint is just "swelling." ⚠️ 5 DO-NOT-MISS diagnoses 1. Missed / intermittent testicular torsion — a pain

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Seven-branch triage: torsion / Fournier / incarcerated hernia / constriction-priapism / epididymo-orchitis / benign / paediatric.
nodes.body: Work the dangerous causes first, then the benign ones. Each branch runs a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Testicular Torsion — Lie + Doppler Gate
nodes.summary: Painless/intermittent still needs torsion excluded. TWIST + abnormal lie; high probability = OR, do not wait for imaging.
nodes.body: A painless or intermittently painful scrotum does NOT exclude torsion. Intermittent torsion/detorsion presents with recurrent brief pain and swelling; a missed torsion may be subacute. Red flags: horizontal or high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn sign. TWIST score (hard testis, swelling, nausea/vomiting, absent cremasteric, high-riding) risk-stratifies. A high-probability

nodes.title: Torsion — Emergent Urology + Manual Detorsion
nodes.body: Open Testicular Torsion for the full pathway. Next steps: - Emergent urology consult for surgical exploration \u2014 salvage falls off sharply after ~6 hours of ischemia. Do NOT wait for imaging if the exam is convincing. - Attempt manual detorsion while arranging the OR (classically "open book" \u2014 medial-to-lateral rotation of the affected testis); relief of pain and normalization of lie sugg
nodes.recommendation: Emergent urology for exploration + attempt manual detorsion; do not delay surgery for imaging. Salvage is time-dependent.

nodes.title: Torsion — Unlikely
nodes.body: A normal testicular lie, an intact cremasteric reflex, and preserved Doppler flow make torsion unlikely right now. Intermittent torsion can still be the cause of recurrent painless swelling \u2014 counsel the patient about recurrence and arrange urology follow-up; recurrent episodes may warrant elective orchidopexy. ⚠️ A normal Doppler does NOT by itself exclude torsion. False-negative colour Dopp
nodes.recommendation: Torsion unlikely with normal lie/flow; consider intermittent torsion for recurrent swelling and refer to urology.

nodes.title: Fournier Gangrene — Toxicity Gate
nodes.summary: Pain out of proportion + toxicity + crepitus/dusky skin = Fournier; resuscitate + emergent debridement.
nodes.body: Fournier gangrene is a necrotizing soft-tissue infection of the perineum/scrotum \u2014 a surgical emergency. The alarm is pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity, with dusky/necrotic skin, crepitus, foul odor, or rapidly spreading erythema. Diabetes, immunocompromise, obesity, and alcohol use raise the risk. Do NOT wait for imaging to consult surgery if the exam is convincing. ⚠️ The hard sign

nodes.title: Fournier Gangrene — Resuscitate + Emergent Debridement
nodes.body: Open Necrotizing Fasciitis \u2014 Fournier is a necrotizing infection and follows the same pathway. Next steps: - Emergent surgical consult for operative debridement \u2014 do NOT wait for imaging. Source control is the definitive treatment; mortality rises with every hour of delay. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics: cover gram-positives, gram-negatives, and anaerobes (e.g., vancomycin + piperacillin-t
nodes.recommendation: Emergent operative debridement (do not wait for imaging) + broad-spectrum abx with clindamycin + aggressive sepsis resuscitation.

nodes.title: Fournier — Unlikely
nodes.body: No systemic toxicity, benign overlying skin, and localized non-tender swelling make Fournier gangrene unlikely right now. It evolves fast \u2014 if toxicity, crepitus, spreading erythema, or skin necrosis appears on reassessment, resuscitate and consult surgery immediately. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Fournier unlikely without toxicity/skin signs; re-examine and escalate immediately if necrotizing features evolve.

nodes.title: Incarcerated Inguinoscrotal Hernia — Reducibility Gate
nodes.summary: Non-reducible + tender + GI sx = incarcerated hernia, risk of strangulation; reducible = not an emergency.
nodes.body: A scrotal mass that is separate from the testis, extends up toward the inguinal canal, and is non-reducible \u2014 especially with GI symptoms (pain, vomiting, obstipation) \u2014 is an incarcerated hernia until proven otherwise. Incarceration risks strangulation and bowel ischemia. Reducible hernias are not emergencies; non-reducible + tender + systemic/GI symptoms = surgical emergency.

nodes.title: Incarcerated Hernia — Reduce / Surgery
nodes.body: Incarcerated inguinoscrotal hernia (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - A single gentle taxis (manual reduction) attempt is reasonable for an incarcerated hernia WITHOUT signs of strangulation (Trendelenburg, analgesia, gentle sustained pressure). Do NOT attempt reduction if there is any concern for strangulation (severe tenderness, skin changes, systemic toxicity) \u2014 reducing dead
nodes.recommendation: One gentle taxis only if NO strangulation signs; otherwise emergent surgery. Suspected ischemia → mesenteric-ischemia workup. NPO/IV/analgesia.

nodes.title: Incarcerated Hernia — Excluded
nodes.body: A reducible, non-tender inguinoscrotal bulge without GI symptoms is not incarcerated. Refer to general surgery for elective repair and counsel on incarceration warning signs (a non-reducible, painful, or discolored bulge with vomiting → return immediately). Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Reducible hernia is not an emergency; elective surgical referral + strict incarceration return precautions.

nodes.title: Constriction / Priapism — GU Emergency Gate
nodes.summary: Constricting object / paraphimosis / priapism = time-critical GU emergencies; release / reduce / detumesce.
nodes.body: A constricting object (hair tourniquet, ring, zipper), paraphimosis, or a persistent erection is a genital emergency masquerading as "swelling." Each threatens tissue via ischemia. Inspect carefully: is there a tourniquet, an entrapment, a retracted-and-swollen foreskin (paraphimosis), or a rigid painful erection >4 h (priapism)?

nodes.title: Constriction / Zipper / Paraphimosis — Relieve Now
nodes.body: Relieve the constriction immediately \u2014 tissue is ischemic while it is on. - Zipper entrapment: open Penile Zipper Release (mineral oil, cut the median bar, or unzip after lubrication). - Constricting ring / hair tourniquet: remove with lubrication, ring cutter, or careful incision of a hair tourniquet under magnification; check for a deep/embedded strand. - Paraphimosis: reduce it \u2014 comp
nodes.recommendation: Immediate release of the constricting object / reduction of paraphimosis; analgesia; urology if it fails or tissue is compromised.

nodes.title: Priapism — Time-Critical Detumescence
nodes.body: Open Priapism for the full pathway. Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is time-critical for erectile function. - Confirm ischemic vs non-ischemic with corporal aspirate blood gas \u00B1 Doppler. - Ischemic: corporal aspiration \u00B1 irrigation, then intracavernosal phenylephrine with cardiovascular monitoring; surgical shunt if refractory. Urgent urology. - Treat the trigger (sickle cell, drugs); analg
nodes.recommendation: Confirm ischemic type, then aspiration + intracavernosal phenylephrine + urgent urology; treat the underlying trigger.

nodes.title: Constriction / Priapism — Excluded
nodes.body: No constricting object, no paraphimosis, and no persistent erection \u2014 a genital-constriction emergency is not the driver here. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Constriction/priapism excluded; reassess if an entrapment or persistent erection develops.

nodes.title: Epididymo-Orchitis / STI — Risk Gate
nodes.summary: Epididymo-orchitis mimics torsion (Prehn +, cremasteric preserved). NAAT if young; enteric if older. Exclude torsion first.
nodes.body: Epididymo-orchitis is the main torsion mimic \u2014 gradual-onset swelling, epididymal tenderness, sometimes a positive Prehn sign (relief with elevation) and preserved cremasteric reflex, \u00B1 dysuria/discharge. In young sexually active men it is usually GC/CT (send NAAT); in older men or those with GU obstruction it is usually gram-negative/enteric. You must still be confident it is not torsio

nodes.title: Epididymo-Orchitis — Test + Empiric Antibiotics
nodes.body: Epididymo-orchitis (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here). If STI features, open STI Comprehensive for the full workup. - Send UA + culture and NAAT for GC/CT (and consider enteric coverage in older men or those with obstruction). - Empiric antibiotics per current CDC guidance: for likely STI \u2014 ceftriaxone + doxycycline; for enteric organisms (older men, insertive anal sex, or GU obstr
nodes.recommendation: NAAT + UA/culture; empiric CDC-guided abx (STI vs enteric by risk); scrotal support/NSAIDs; Doppler if torsion not confidently excluded. CDC 2021 regimens: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x10d (STI); + levofloxacin 500

nodes.title: Epididymo-Orchitis — Not the Picture
nodes.body: The exam and risk profile do not fit epididymo-orchitis \u2014 or torsion has not yet been confidently excluded. When in doubt between torsion and epididymo-orchitis, the safe move is Doppler ultrasound and urology input, because a missed torsion loses the testis. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: If epididymo-orchitis does not fit or torsion is not excluded, get Doppler + urology \u2014 do not under-triage.

nodes.title: Benign Scrotal Mass — Characterize the Lesion
nodes.summary: Characterize benign lesions by transillumination/location; a solid intratesticular mass is a tumor until proven otherwise. Transillumination does not exclude tumour; a non-decompressing varicocele needs abdominal imaging.
nodes.body: Once the emergencies are excluded, characterize the benign lesion \u2014 but remember a solid mass ON the testis is a tumor until proven otherwise. - Hydrocele: soft, cystic, transilluminates, surrounds the testis. New/tense hydrocele in an adult \u2192 ultrasound to exclude an underlying tumor. - Varicocele: "bag of worms," more prominent standing / with Valsalva, usually left-sided. A new right-

nodes.title: Benign Scrotal Mass — Reassure + Follow-Up
nodes.body: A soft, transilluminating mass separate from the testis (hydrocele, spermatocele, epididymal cyst, simple varicocele) in a well patient is benign. - Reassure; no emergent intervention needed. - Get a scrotal ultrasound as an outpatient for a new/tense adult hydrocele, a new right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele, or any diagnostic uncertainty \u2014 to exclude an underlying tumor or retroperi
nodes.recommendation: Reassure benign transilluminating lesions; outpatient ultrasound for new/atypical hydrocele or right-sided varicocele; urology follow-up. Scrotal US with duplex Doppler is ACR "Usually Appropriate" for any newly diagnosed palpable scrotal a

nodes.title: Possible Testicular Tumor — Ultrasound + Markers + Urology
nodes.body: A solid, firm intratesticular mass that does NOT transilluminate is a testicular tumor until proven otherwise \u2014 painless is the classic presentation, and germ-cell tumors are the most common solid malignancy in young men (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - Scrotal ultrasound (the key test to characterize an intratesticular mass). - Serum tumor markers: AFP, beta-hCG, LDH before a
nodes.recommendation: Solid intratesticular mass = tumor until proven otherwise: scrotal US + AFP/beta-hCG/LDH + urgent urology (radical inguinal orchiectomy; no transscrotal biopsy). Normal markers do NOT exclude a germ-cell tumour \u2014 ~52% of all GCT and ~7

nodes.title: Paediatric Scrotal Swelling — Different Differential
nodes.body: A prepubertal boy is not a small adult. Torsion still sits at the top of the list \u2014 use the Testicular Torsion consult, which carries the full paediatric and neonatal pathway \u2014 but four paediatric-specific entities dominate the "swollen but not very sore" presentation.[13] 1. nodes.body: The scrotal-swelling work-up bundle (scale to acuity): - Focused exam: testicular lie, cremasteric reflex, Prehn sign, transillumination, reducibility, skin changes/crepitus, and whether the mass is intratesticular or separate. - Color Doppler ultrasound is the workhorse \u2014 but do NOT let imaging delay the OR for a convincing torsion or Fournier. - Vitals + qSOFA if any toxicity; resuscitate a

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Torsion/Fournier/strangulation → escalate to OR + admit; stable + diagnosed → disposition.
nodes.body: After the focused exam \u00B1 Doppler and initial labs \u2014 where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.body: Match the study to the question: - Color Doppler scrotal ultrasound \u2014 the primary test: assesses testicular flow (torsion), characterizes masses (cystic vs solid, intra- vs extratesticular), and evaluates the epididymis. Do NOT delay definitive surgery for a convincing torsion or Fournier. - CT / MRI of the perineum and pelvis \u2014 to map necrotizing infection extent or an incarcerated/obst

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: OR/admit the surgical emergencies; observe the borderline; discharge benign/treated with urology follow-up.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: Admit / OR
nodes.body: To the OR / admit the surgical emergency. - Torsion \u2192 emergent scrotal exploration (detorsion + bilateral orchidopexy or orchiectomy). - Fournier \u2192 emergent debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU-level resuscitation as needed. - Strangulated hernia \u2192 emergent repair \u00B1 bowel resection. - Ongoing resuscitation, analgesia, and specialty (urology / general surgery) management
nodes.recommendation: OR for torsion / Fournier / strangulation; broad-spectrum abx + resuscitation; ICU if unstable.

nodes.title: Observe / Urology in the ED
nodes.body: Observation / ED urology consult for the borderline patient \u2014 e.g., torsion not fully excluded despite reassuring Doppler, a reduced hernia needing a period of observation, or a new solid mass needing expedited workup. - Serial exams, repeat Doppler if the picture changes, and specialist input before disposition. - Ensure reliable, timely follow-up before any discharge; treat pain.
nodes.recommendation: Short observation + specialist input, serial exams / repeat Doppler, then admit or discharge with tight follow-up.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge the well patient with a clear plan. - Benign lesion (hydrocele/varicocele/cyst): reassurance, outpatient scrotal ultrasound if new/atypical, urology follow-up. - Epididymo-orchitis: empiric antibiotics given, scrotal support/NSAIDs, partner therapy if STI, follow-up, and strict return precautions (worsening pain/swelling, fever, or new severe pain \u2014 reconsider torsion/abscess). - Co
nodes.recommendation: Discharge benign/treated patients with outpatient US as needed, antibiotics + partner therapy if STI, and explicit torsion/tumor return precautions.

nodes.title: Palpitations Hub — Get the ECG, Sort Stable vs Unstable
nodes.summary: Get a 12-lead ECG while symptomatic. Sort stable vs unstable first \u2014 unstable + tachyarrhythmia = synchronized cardioversion NOW. Wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Unstable tachyarrhythmia \u2014 hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea, altered mentation, shock = synchronized cardioversion NOW, do not wait. 2. Wide-complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise \u2014 do NOT treat as SVT with a nodal blocker. 3. The malignant substrates \u2014 WPW/pre-excited AF, Brugada, long-QT/Torsades, short QT, HCM, ARVC, CPVT, Wellens \u2014 a

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the One That Fits
nodes.summary: Instability first (cardiovert), then read the ECG: wide=VT, irregular=AF (pre-excited if wide+irregular), regular narrow=SVT, polymorphic=torsades, plus baseline red-flag substrates and secondary causes.
nodes.body: Instability first, then read the ECG. Each branch routes to a deep-dive and the next action.

nodes.title: Unstable Tachyarrhythmia — Cardiovert Now
nodes.body: An unstable patient (hypotension, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure, or altered mentation) whose picture is driven by a tachyarrhythmia needs immediate synchronized cardioversion \u2014 do not delay for a drug trial. [3] Next 5 minutes: - Confirm the instability is caused by the rhythm (not a fast sinus rate compensating for shock/sepsis/hemorrhage \u2014 cardioverting sinus tachycardia is
nodes.recommendation: Confirm the arrhythmia is causing the instability (not compensatory sinus tach), then immediate synchronized cardioversion (defibrillate if pulseless/polymorphic). IV access, correct K/Mg, treat reversible causes.

nodes.title: Wide-Complex Tachycardia — VT Until Proven Otherwise
nodes.body: Open Wide-Complex Tachycardia for the diagnostic approach and Ventricular Tachycardia for management. Any regular wide-complex tachycardia (QRS \u2265120 ms) is ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise \u2014 especially with structural heart disease or prior MI. Treating VT as \u201cSVT with aberrancy\u201d by giving an AV-nodal blocker (verapamil/diltiazem/adenosine as therapy) can precipit
nodes.recommendation: Treat regular WCT as VT: unstable \u2192 cardiovert; stable \u2192 procainamide 20-50 mg/min (stop if QRS widens >50%) or amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min + cardiology. Avoid AV-nodal blockers; adenosine only if regular AND monomorphic. Correc

nodes.title: Atrial Fibrillation / Flutter (incl. Pre-Excited AF)
nodes.body: Open Atrial Fibrillation with RVR for the rate/rhythm-control, anticoagulation, and disposition pathway. Irregularly irregular tachycardia = AF (or atrial flutter with variable block). Key ED tasks: control the rate/rhythm, decide on anticoagulation, and detect the dangerous variant. [5] Next 5 minutes: - Unstable \u2192 synchronized cardioversion. - Stable AF with RVR: rate control with a beta-bl
nodes.recommendation: Rate/rhythm control per LV function; anticoagulate at CHA2DS2-VASc \u22652 men / \u22653 women. The 48-h window is obsolete \u2014 unanticoagulated DCCV without TEE is Class 2b and only at CHA2DS2-VASc 0-1 with <12 h of symptoms. Pre-excite

nodes.title: Supraventricular Tachycardia
nodes.body: Open SVT for the vagal / adenosine / disposition pathway. A regular, narrow-complex tachycardia around 150-250 with abrupt onset and offset is paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT/AVRT). [6] Next 5 minutes: - Unstable \u2192 synchronized cardioversion. - Stable: vagal maneuvers first \u2014 the modified Valsalva (with leg raise) is more effective than the standard maneuver: 43% vs 17% conversion in the REVERT RC
nodes.recommendation: Vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva, 43% vs 17%) first, then adenosine 6 mg \u2192 12 mg rapid IV push. Reduce the first dose to 3 mg for central-line delivery, transplanted heart, or dipyridamole/carbamazepine; avoid in active bronchospasm

nodes.title: Torsades de Pointes / Long QT
nodes.body: Open Torsades de Pointes for the full pathway. Polymorphic VT in the setting of a prolonged QT is torsades de pointes. It is driven by QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte depletion (low K, low Mg, low Ca) and can degenerate into VF. [7] Put a number on the QT. The AHA/ACCF action thresholds are a QTc >500 ms, or a rise of \u226560 ms from the pre-drug baseline \u2014 either one demands prompt acti
nodes.recommendation: Act at a QTc >500 ms or a \u226560 ms rise from baseline. IV magnesium 2 g (even if level normal) followed by a continuous infusion, correct K to >4.5 mEq/L and Ca, stop QT-prolonging drugs, and raise the rate to 90-110 bpm (overdrive pacin

nodes.title: Dangerous Baseline Substrate — Read the Resting ECG
nodes.body: Even when the palpitations have resolved, the resting 12-lead can reveal a substrate that is dangerous and changes management. [1,2,10,11] Recognize and route: - WPW (short PR + delta wave): risk of pre-excited AF and sudden death; avoid AV-nodal blockers if they ever go into AF; EP referral for risk stratification/ablation. (Acute pre-excited AF \u2192 procainamide/cardioversion, see the AF branc
nodes.recommendation: Read the resting ECG for WPW (avoid nodal blockers in AF), Brugada, Wellens (admit, no stress test), long QT (>500 ms), short QT, HCM, and ARVC. Compare with old ECGs and get cardiology/EP input; counsel on substrate-specific trigger/drug a

nodes.title: Secondary Cause — Palpitations as a Symptom
nodes.body: Palpitations are often the visible tip of another problem. When the rhythm is sinus (or a rate-driven response), treat the driver rather than the heart rate. [1,2,8] Route to the cause: - ACS / ischemia \u2014 chest pain, diaphoresis, ischemic ECG: STEMI, NSTEMI/NSTE-ACS, or the Chest Pain hub; troponin, aspirin, cardiology. - Syncope with the palpitations \u2014 this is an arrhythmic-syncope stor
nodes.recommendation: When the rhythm is sinus/rate-driven, treat the cause: ACS, PE, thyroid, hypoglycemia, sepsis, anemia/hemorrhage, drugs, electrolytes. Palpitations plus syncope routes to the Syncope pathway (Canadian Syncope Risk Score), not to reassurance

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Palpitations, Currently Stable
nodes.summary: 12-lead ECG + continuous monitoring + focused labs (K/Mg/Ca, glucose, CBC, TSH, troponin if indicated). Risk-stratify by history; red flags = syncope (run the Syncope pathway + Canadian Syncope Risk Score), exertional palpitations, family h
nodes.body: No unstable arrhythmia and no dangerous ECG captured on arrival. Standard ED bundle while you characterize the episode and screen for a cause: [1,2,8] THE BUNDLE: - 12-lead ECG (and capture a rhythm strip during any recurrence) \u2014 the single highest-yield test; scrutinize for pre-excitation (delta wave), Brugada, prolonged QT, Wellens, ischemia, and prior MI. - Continuous cardiac monitoring wh

nodes.title: Reassess — Rhythm and Red Flags
nodes.summary: Resolved + normal ECG + no red flags \u2192 discharge. Red flags/abnormal ECG \u2192 monitor + cardiology. Recurrent/dangerous rhythm \u2192 STOP, return to exclusions.
nodes.body: Re-examine: the ECG/monitor, whether an arrhythmia recurred, and the red-flag history.

nodes.title: Workup & Monitoring Decision
nodes.summary: ECG + telemetry + labs (\u00b1 echo). Match ambulatory monitoring to episode frequency: Holter (~22% symptom-rhythm yield) for daily, event/patch or external loop recorder (~56%; 86% in palpitations) for weekly, implantable loop recorder fo
nodes.body: The goal is to capture the rhythm during symptoms and identify structural or ischemic substrate. [1,2,8] In the ED: - 12-lead ECG (repeat with any recurrence) + continuous telemetry while the patient is monitored. - Labs: electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca), glucose, CBC, TSH, troponin (if ischemia possible), \u03b2-hCG; PE/thyroid testing as indicated. - Echocardiography (structural heart disease, reduced E

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge benign/resolved/normal-ECG low-risk; observe recurrent-but-controlled or pending workup; admit dangerous rhythm/substrate, syncope, or structural/ischemic cause.
nodes.body: Disposition is driven by risk features and whether a dangerous rhythm/substrate is present. Defer to the deep-dive consult once a diagnosis is committed.

nodes.title: Discharge — Benign, Resolved Palpitations
nodes.body: Safe discharge criteria: [1,2,8] 1. Currently asymptomatic with a normal 12-lead ECG (no pre-excitation, Brugada, long QT, Wellens, ischemia, or prior MI). 2. No red flags \u2014 no syncope with the episode, not exertional, no family history of sudden cardiac death, no known structural heart disease. 3. No dangerous arrhythmia documented; normal or corrected electrolytes and glucose; no secondary
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if asymptomatic with a normal ECG, no red flags, stable, cause benign/corrected, with ambulatory monitoring matched to frequency, cardiology referral if indicated, trigger avoidance, and clear return precautions. Syncope with

nodes.title: Observe — Recurrent/Controlled or Pending Workup
nodes.body: ED observation / monitored bed appropriate when: [1,2,5,6] - Recurrent SVT or AF that has been controlled/converted but warrants a period of telemetry - Rate-controlled AF needing observation of response and anticoagulation decision-making - Borderline-risk history (some concerning features) while labs/echo/monitoring are completed - A secondary cause being treated (e.g., electrolyte correction, t
nodes.recommendation: Observe with telemetry for controlled recurrent SVT/AF or pending workup; complete labs/echo and get cardiology input. Escalate to admission for any dangerous rhythm, syncope, or high-risk substrate.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Monitored / ICU admission for: [1,2,4,7,10,11] - Documented dangerous arrhythmia \u2014 VT (Ventricular Tachycardia), pre-excited AF, torsades (Torsades de Pointes) \u2014 continuous monitoring, EP involvement. - Malignant substrate newly identified \u2014 Wellens Syndrome (urgent angiography), Brugada Syndrome, symptomatic long QT/WPW per cardiology. - Palpitations with syncope \u2014 high risk f
nodes.recommendation: Admit documented dangerous arrhythmia, malignant substrate, palpitations with syncope, structural/ischemic cause, or a secondary cause requiring inpatient care. Cardiology/EP for rhythm substrate; ICU for instability/torsades.

nodes.title: Diagnostic & Therapeutic Paracentesis
nodes.summary: Ascites tap: diagnostic SBP evaluation, therapeutic drainage, ultrasound-guided site, albumin when needed.
nodes.body: Use this for ED evaluation or drainage of ascites, especially when SBP, tense ascites, respiratory compromise, abdominal pain, fever, encephalopathy, AKI, or new/worsening decompensation is present. Open first: - Paracentesis Steps - Ultrasound Site - Fluid Labs - Albumin - Stop / Complications

nodes.title: Why Are You Tapping?
nodes.summary: Tap for SBP/decompensation evaluation or symptomatic tense ascites.
nodes.body: Diagnostic paracentesis is high-yield in hospitalized or ED patients with cirrhosis/ascites and possible infection or decompensation.

nodes.title: Contraindications / Cautions
nodes.summary: No safe pocket is the key stop point; routine INR/platelet correction is usually not needed.
nodes.body: Most coagulopathy in cirrhosis is not an absolute contraindication to paracentesis. Avoid or escalate for: no safe pocket, overlying cellulitis, severe bowel distension at target site, noncooperative patient without safe sedation plan, pregnancy/organomegaly at path, or suspected surgical abdomen where delay is harmful.

nodes.title: Ultrasound Site Selection
nodes.summary: Ultrasound confirms fluid pocket, depth, and bowel-free path.
nodes.body: Use ultrasound to identify: - Adequate fluid pocket - Bowel-free needle path - Abdominal wall vessels when possible - Distance from skin to fluid - Best patient position Common sites: left lower quadrant or right lower quadrant lateral to rectus; avoid scars, vessels, distended bowel, and infected skin.

nodes.title: Setup / Local Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Prep, mark, anesthetize to peritoneum, and have tubes/bottles ready.
nodes.body: Setup: - Consent/time-out when feasible - Sterile prep/drape - Mark site after ultrasound - Local Lidocaine down to peritoneum - Diagnostic kit or catheter-over-needle system - Tubes/bottles ready before puncture Use Z-track or oblique tract to reduce leak when feasible.

nodes.title: Needle / Catheter Technique
nodes.summary: Needle to fluid; diagnostic sample or catheter drainage; stop for pain/bowel/blood/instability.
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Enter at marked site with steady negative pressure. 2. Stop when fluid returns. 3. For diagnostic tap, collect labs and remove needle. 4. For therapeutic tap, advance catheter, remove needle, connect drainage. 5. Monitor pain, vitals, leak, bleeding, and flow. 6. Stop if severe pain, bowel contents, blood under pressure, hypotension, or unsafe catheter position.

nodes.title: Send Fluid Labs
nodes.summary: Cell count/differential, culture bottles, albumin, and protein are core tests.
nodes.body: Core diagnostic labs: - Cell count with differential - Culture inoculated into blood culture bottles at bedside when possible - Albumin and total protein Add selectively: glucose, LDH, cytology, triglycerides, amylase, AFB/fungal testing when clinically indicated.

nodes.title: How Do Results Interpret?
nodes.summary: PMN >=250 is SBP; large-volume taps need albumin planning; atypical fluid needs broader workup.
nodes.body: Use PMN count for SBP; culture can be negative early or after antibiotics.

nodes.title: SBP Treatment Pathway
nodes.summary: PMN >=250: antibiotics, admission, albumin when indicated, assess sepsis/AKI.
nodes.body: Treat PMN >=250 cells/mm3 as SBP. Typical ED actions: - Blood cultures if septic or not already obtained - Start empiric antibiotics such as Ceftriaxone per local resistance pattern - Give Albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 h of diagnosis, then 1.0 g/kg on day 3 (AASLD 2021) — strongest benefit when Cr >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL (Sort NEJM 1999: in-hospital mortality 10% vs 29%, AKI 10%
nodes.recommendation: SBP is time-sensitive infection; do not wait for culture positivity.

nodes.title: Large-Volume Paracentesis
nodes.summary: Large-volume drainage needs monitoring and albumin replacement planning.
nodes.body: For therapeutic drainage, reassess symptoms, vitals, and leak/bleeding during removal. Give Albumin 6-8 g per liter of ascites removed (20% or 25% solution) when >5 L is removed (AASLD 2021, Class IIa). Not required for taps <4-5 L. Example: 8 L removed → 48-64 g albumin IV. Prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.
nodes.recommendation: Albumin reduces post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction after large-volume drainage.

nodes.title: Atypical Fluid / Secondary Cause
nodes.summary: Low SAAG, hemorrhagic, chylous, malignant, pancreatic, or secondary peritonitis patterns need escalation.
nodes.body: Escalate evaluation for secondary peritonitis, malignancy, pancreatic ascites, chylous ascites, tuberculosis, traumatic bleeding, or low-SAAG nonportal hypertensive ascites when fluid pattern does not fit uncomplicated portal hypertensive ascites. Consider CT, surgery/IR/GI input, and targeted fluid studies.
nodes.recommendation: Atypical fluid should trigger broader diagnostic workup rather than routine discharge.

nodes.title: Routine / Negative Initial Result
nodes.summary: Routine fluid result still requires clinical disposition assessment.
nodes.body: If PMN <250 and no atypical pattern, manage the underlying ascites and clinical presentation. Disposition depends on vitals, renal function, pain, encephalopathy, GI bleed, sodium, follow-up, and whether this is new or worsening decompensation.
nodes.recommendation: A negative tap does not replace clinical disposition assessment.

nodes.title: Stop / Complications
nodes.summary: No safe pocket, severe pain, bowel/blood return, or instability requires stopping.
nodes.body: Stop and reassess for: no safe pocket, severe pain, suspected bowel puncture, persistent bleeding, hypotension, expanding abdominal wall hematoma, catheter malfunction, or unexpected bloody/bilious/feculent return. Escalate to ultrasound-guided proceduralist, IR, surgery, or GI when the procedure cannot be completed safely.
nodes.recommendation: No safe ultrasound pocket means no blind paracentesis.

nodes.title: Parkinson Disease in the ED
nodes.summary: PD is time-sensitive dopamine deficiency. Med rec, dysphagia screen, and flag PD-unsafe drugs immediately.
nodes.body: Parkinson disease (PD) patients in the ED have higher mortality, longer admissions, and 2-3x more complications than age-matched peers. The two biggest drivers are medication errors and dopamine-blocker exposure. The ED-critical rule: PD is a time-sensitive dopamine deficiency. Every missed or delayed levodopa dose risks: - Off-state with rigidity, akinesia, fall risk - Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia (

nodes.title: Medication Reconciliation — Get It Right
nodes.summary: Capture exact drug/dose/time/last dose. Levodopa is a stat medication on a strict schedule. Verify with pharmacy.
nodes.body: The single most important ED action in PD is matching the home regimen exactly. [1][2][3] What to capture (drug, dose, time, last dose taken): - Levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet, Rytary, Duopa, Inbrija, Vyalev/foscarbidopa-foslevodopa SC pump — FDA approved Oct 2024): immediate-release vs CR vs extended-release vs inhaled vs continuous SC infusion - Dopamine agonists: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotin

nodes.title: On-Time Medication Order Set
nodes.summary: Schedule levodopa as STAT + ongoing q-interval. Flag chart for PD-unsafe drugs. Verify formulation availability.
nodes.body: Build PD home meds into ED order set as STAT and SCHEDULED, not PRN. [2][3] Order set template: `` Levodopa/carbidopa [exact strength] PO STAT NOW Levodopa/carbidopa [exact strength] PO Q[home interval] starting at [next home dose time] Rotigotine patch [home dose] topical daily (if home med) Selegiline/rasagiline [home dose] PO QAM (if home med) Entacapone [home dose] PO with each levodopa (if ho

nodes.title: Off-State or Hyperpyrexic Crisis?
nodes.summary: Off-state = missed dose, treat with levodopa. PDH = NMS-like withdrawal syndrome, requires aggressive supportive care.
nodes.body: Two distinct PD emergencies share overlapping features. The distinction matters because management diverges. Off-state (common, expected, treatable): - Rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor return - May have dystonia (especially morning off) - Temperature normal - No autonomic instability - Mental status intact - Triggered by missed dose, wearing-off, dose failure (e.g., high-protein meal blocked absorpt

nodes.title: Off-State — Acute Rescue
nodes.summary: PO/inhaled levodopa first. NPO patients: apomorphine SC, rotigotine patch, or NG levodopa. Reassess in 30-60 min.
nodes.body: First-line rescue (if able to swallow): [4][6] - Inbrija (inhaled levodopa) 84 mg via inhaler — onset 10 minutes, ideal for ED rescue - OR levodopa/carbidopa ODT (Parcopa) 25/100 mg — dissolves on tongue, useful with mild dysphagia - OR standard levodopa/carbidopa 25/100 mg PO — onset 30-60 minutes If NPO or severe dysphagia: [6] - Apomorphine SC 2-6 mg (start low, titrate to effect, premedicate w

nodes.title: Parkinsonism-Hyperpyrexia (PDH) — NMS-Like Crisis
nodes.summary: PDH = NMS-like crisis from dopamine withdrawal. Restart levodopa NOW + dantrolene + bromocriptine + cooling + IVF + ICU.
nodes.body: PDH is a neuro-emergency. Mortality 4-25% without aggressive treatment. [4][5][7] Pathophysiology: Abrupt central dopamine deficit produces a syndrome clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). Diagnostic clues vs NMS: - PDH: PD patient with recent levodopa change/stop or DBS battery failure - NMS: typically antipsychotic exposure (haloperidol, risperidone, others) - O

nodes.title: Aspiration Risk — Screen Before PO
nodes.summary: Yale Swallow Protocol before PO. HOB 30-45° baseline, 90° for meals. NPO + NG/rotigotine if fail.
nodes.body: Aspiration pneumonia is the leading cause of death in PD. [1][8][9] Dysphagia prevalence: up to 80% of PD patients, often silent (no cough or choking visible). Quick ED dysphagia screen (Yale Swallow Protocol): [9] 1. Alert and able to follow commands? 2. No history of recent aspiration pneumonia? 3. Sit patient upright, give 3 oz water uninterrupted 4. PASS = no cough, throat clear, wet voice wit

nodes.title: NPO Patient — Bridge Therapy
nodes.summary: NPO bridge: rotigotine patch first-choice (LED conversion), apomorphine SC for rescue, NG levodopa IR if NG placed.
nodes.body: The "NPO PD patient" is at highest risk for off-state and PDH. Bridge therapy is mandatory. [4][6] Bridge options (ranked by ED ease): 1. Rotigotine patch (Neupro) — FIRST CHOICE for most ED NPO patients [6] - Dose: convert total daily levodopa equivalent (LED) — see LED calculator - Rough conversion: 1 mg rotigotine ≈ 30 mg levodopa - Patches: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 mg/24h - Onset: 4-6 hours to therape

nodes.title: DO NOT GIVE — PD-Unsafe Medications
nodes.summary: NEVER: haloperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine, risperidone, olanzapine. Flag chart with allergy/intolerance.
nodes.body: These medications cause acute parkinsonism, off-states, or PDH in PD patients. NEVER give without explicit neurology approval. [1][2][10] ABSOLUTELY AVOID: Antipsychotics (typical + most atypicals): - Haloperidol - Droperidol - Risperidone - Olanzapine - Ziprasidone - Aripiprazole (partial agonist but still risky) Antiemetics (dopamine blockers): - Metoclopramide (Reglan) - Prochlorperazine (Compa

nodes.title: PD-Safe Alternatives Cheat Sheet
nodes.summary: Antiemetic = ondansetron/granisetron/trimethobenzamide. Antipsychotic = quetiapine/clozapine. Migraine = no metoclopramide/prochlorperazine.
nodes.body: Common ED scenarios and PD-safe substitutes: [1][2][10] Nausea/vomiting: - Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV/PO q8h ✓ - Granisetron 1 mg IV/PO ✓ - Trimethobenzamide (Tigan) 300 mg PO or 200 mg IM q6-8h ✓ - Domperidone (if available, not US-licensed) ✓ - AVOID: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine Psychosis/agitation: - Quetiapine 12.5-25 mg PO q6h PRN (start low) ✓ - Clozapine (specialist-managed, A

nodes.title: Restarting Levodopa After NPO / Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Resume home dose immediately, no taper, no substitution. Sinemet IR vs CR vs Rytary are NOT bioequivalent.
nodes.body: Three restart scenarios: [4][6] Scenario A — Short NPO (<12 hours) without crisis: - Resume home schedule at next scheduled dose - If late: give the missed dose now AND continue schedule - No taper needed, no dose adjustment Scenario B — Prolonged NPO (>12-24 hours) or off-state: - Resume home dose immediately (do NOT under-dose) - Consider rotigotine 24h overlap to ensure steady state - Watch for

nodes.title: Protein-Levodopa Timing Pearl
nodes.summary: Levodopa 30 min before OR 60+ min after protein meal. Iron supplements separate by 2h. Tube feeds: pause around dose.
nodes.body: Large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) in dietary protein compete with levodopa for transport across the gut and blood-brain barrier. [6][11] Clinical consequence: Protein-rich meal within 30 minutes of levodopa can reduce effective brain dose by 30-50%, producing an unexpected off-state. Home dosing pattern most PD patients use: - Levodopa 30 minutes BEFORE meals - OR 60-90 minutes AFTER meals - Some

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Three buckets: home (off-state resolved), floor (aspiration/uncontrolled), ICU (PDH/respiratory/autonomic).
nodes.body: Most PD patients with off-state alone go home. Hyperpyrexic crisis, aspiration pneumonia, and uncontrolled symptoms admit. Choose the closest match:

nodes.title: Discharge Home — Checklist
nodes.summary: Discharge if baseline + PO tolerating + meds confirmed. Hand patient printed PD-unsafe drug list for future ED visits.
nodes.body: Safe discharge requires ALL of the following: [1][2] ☐ Returned to baseline motor function (patient/family confirms) ☐ Tolerating PO including home medications ☐ Yale Swallow Protocol passed (or not previously failed) ☐ Home medication list confirmed and unchanged ☐ Caregiver/family understands which medications to AVOID ☐ Follow-up with neurology within 1-2 weeks ☐ Return precautions reviewed: -

nodes.title: Admit — Floor or Step-Down
nodes.summary: Floor admit: exact home meds STAT+scheduled, allergy flags, ondansetron only, quetiapine only, swallow eval, neurology.
nodes.body: Admit for: [1][2] - Aspiration pneumonia - Moderate off-state not resolving with rescue - New dysphagia requiring formal swallow eval - Falls with injury - Functional decline at home with caregiver burnout Admission orders checklist: [2][3] ☐ Home med schedule reproduced EXACTLY (drug, dose, time) ☐ Mark levodopa as STAT and SCHEDULED, not PRN ☐ NPO status with rotigotine patch bridge if dysphagia

nodes.title: ICU Admission — PDH or Critical PD
nodes.summary: ICU: continuous monitoring, aggressive IVF/cooling, restart levodopa via NG + rotigotine, dantrolene + bromocriptine for severe, neurology immediately.
nodes.body: ICU criteria: [4][5][7] - PDH (parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome) - Severe autonomic instability - Hypoventilation, hypercapnia, intubation - Severe rhabdomyolysis (CK >10,000 or rising AKI) - Severe aspiration pneumonia with septic shock - Failure to oxygenate on the floor ICU-specific orders: [5][7] ☐ Continuous cardiac monitoring (autonomic instability) ☐ Foley for I/O monitoring (rhabdo, AKI)

nodes.title: PE in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: PE causes 10% maternal deaths; 5-10x VTE risk in pregnancy; symptoms overlap normal pregnancy; missing PE worse than radiation
nodes.body: PE is a leading cause of maternal mortality — responsible for ~10% of maternal deaths in developed countries. Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state: • 5-10x increased VTE risk vs. non-pregnant • Risk persists 6 weeks postpartum • Highest risk in 3rd trimester and postpartum Challenges: • Symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy (dyspnea, edema, tachycardia) • D-dimer normally elevated in pregnancy •

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Dyspnea 70-80%, pleuritic pain 50-70%; red flags: hypotension, syncope, severe hypoxia, RV dysfunction
nodes.body: Symptoms of PE in Pregnancy: | Symptom | Frequency | Notes | |---------|-----------|-------| | Dyspnea | 70-80% | Common in normal pregnancy too | | Pleuritic chest pain | 50-70% | More specific | | Cough | 20-40% | | | Hemoptysis | 5-15% | Highly specific | | Syncope | 5-10% | Suggests massive PE | | Unilateral leg swelling | 30-50% | Suggests concurrent DVT | Red Flags for Massive PE: • Hypotens

nodes.title: Initial Hemodynamic Assessment
nodes.summary: Classify massive (SBP <90, shock), submassive (stable + RV dysfunction), or low-risk to guide treatment
nodes.body: First: Is the patient hemodynamically unstable? Unstable (Massive PE): • SBP <90 mmHg or drop >40 from baseline • Requiring vasopressors • Signs of obstructive shock • Cardiac arrest Submassive (Intermediate Risk): • Hemodynamically stable • RV dysfunction on echo/CT • Elevated troponin or BNP Low Risk: • Stable hemodynamics • No RV dysfunction • Normal biomarkers [1][2]

nodes.title: Massive PE — Unstable Patient
nodes.summary: UFH bolus 80 U/kg, vasopressors, bedside POCUS for RV dilation; treat empirically if POCUS positive
nodes.body: Immediate Actions: 1. Resuscitation: • IV fluids (careful — RV preload-sensitive) • Vasopressors (norepinephrine preferred) • High-flow oxygen 2. Bedside POCUS: • RV dilation, D-sign, McConnell's sign • If positive → treat empirically 3. Anticoagulation: • UFH bolus 80 U/kg, then 18 U/kg/hr • UFH preferred over LMWH in massive PE (reversible) 4. Consider thrombolysis or embolectomy → Go to thrombo

nodes.title: Clinical Probability Assessment
nodes.summary: YEARS algorithm validated in pregnancy; 0 criteria + D-dimer <1000 excludes PE; fixed thresholds not trimester-adjusted
nodes.body: YEARS Algorithm (validated in pregnancy): YEARS Criteria: 1. Clinical signs of DVT 2. Hemoptysis 3. PE most likely diagnosis Interpretation: • 0 criteria + D-dimer <1000 → PE excluded • 1+ criteria + D-dimer <500 → PE excluded • Otherwise → Imaging required D-dimer in Pregnancy: • Normally rises throughout pregnancy • Trimester-adjusted cutoffs less useful • YEARS algorithm uses fixed thresholds •

nodes.title: Diagnostic Approach
nodes.summary: CTPA vs V/Q vs leg US; both far below teratogenic threshold (50-100 mGy); CTPA preferred for sensitivity
nodes.body: Which imaging study? CTPA (CT Pulmonary Angiography): • Higher sensitivity than V/Q • Radiation to breast tissue (~3-10 mGy) • Can visualize alternative diagnoses • Preferred in most centers V/Q Scan: • Lower breast radiation • Higher fetal radiation (though still minimal) • More non-diagnostic results • Consider if high breast cancer risk Radiation Perspective: • Fetal dose from CTPA: ~0.1 mGy •

nodes.title: CTPA Result
nodes.summary: Positive CTPA: treat immediately; negative: high NPV; inconclusive: consider V/Q or empiric treatment
nodes.body: CTPA Interpretation: Positive CTPA: • Filling defect in pulmonary arteries • Begin treatment immediately Negative CTPA: • High NPV in pregnancy • If clinical suspicion remains high, consider: - Repeat imaging in 24-48h - Leg ultrasound for DVT - Empiric anticoagulation Suboptimal/Inconclusive: • May need V/Q scan or repeat with better timing • Consider empiric treatment if high suspicion [1][2]

nodes.title: V/Q Scan
nodes.summary: High rate of non-diagnostic V/Q scans (25-50%); if non-diagnostic proceed to CTPA or empiric anticoagulation
nodes.body: V/Q Scan Interpretation: | Result | Interpretation | |--------|---------------| | Normal | PE excluded | | High probability | Treat as PE | | Non-diagnostic | Need additional testing | Limitations: • High rate of non-diagnostic scans (up to 25-50%) • Cannot evaluate other diagnoses • Ventilation phase can be omitted (perfusion-only) to reduce radiation If non-diagnostic: Proceed to CTPA or empiric

nodes.title: Leg Ultrasound First
nodes.summary: DVT found avoids chest radiation; 30-50% of PE patients have concurrent DVT; negative leg US does not exclude PE
nodes.body: Strategy: If DVT symptoms present, start with leg US Rationale: • If DVT found → treat as VTE (no need for chest imaging) • Avoids radiation entirely • Approximately 30-50% of PE patients have concurrent DVT If DVT found: • Begin anticoagulation • Treatment is same as for PE (LMWH in pregnancy) • May still need chest imaging if suspicious for massive PE If DVT negative but PE still suspected: • Pr

nodes.title: PE Excluded
nodes.body: Negative CTPA with low/moderate clinical probability: PE effectively ruled out. Consider alternative diagnoses: • Pulmonary edema • Pneumonia • Musculoskeletal pain • Anxiety/panic • Pericarditis • Aortic dissection Safety-netting: • Return precautions • Consider outpatient follow-up • If symptoms persist or worsen, reassess [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: PE excluded. Evaluate for alternative diagnoses. Provide return precautions.

nodes.title: Inconclusive Imaging
nodes.summary: If high clinical suspicion with inconclusive imaging, treat empirically; serial leg US or alternative imaging
nodes.body: Options for inconclusive results: 1. Serial leg ultrasounds (days 1, 3, 7) 2. Alternative imaging (V/Q if CTPA inconclusive, vice versa) 3. Empiric anticoagulation if clinical probability high 4. Repeat CTPA with optimized protocol High clinical suspicion → Treat empirically Better to anticoagulate a patient who may not have PE than to miss a PE in a pregnant patient. [1][2]

nodes.title: Anticoagulation in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: LMWH is treatment of choice; DOACs and warfarin contraindicated in pregnancy; UFH reserved for massive PE
nodes.body: LMWH is the treatment of choice in pregnancy Why LMWH over other options: • Does not cross placenta • No fetal teratogenicity • Predictable dosing • Can be self-administered at home DOACs are CONTRAINDICATED — cross placenta, teratogenic Warfarin CONTRAINDICATED in 1st trimester — teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy) UFH — reserved for massive PE or peripartum period [1][2][6]

nodes.title: LMWH Dosing
nodes.summary: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC BID; monitor anti-Xa monthly; hold 24h before delivery; 6 weeks postpartum minimum
nodes.body: Enoxaparin Dosing: • Therapeutic: 1 mg/kg SC BID (preferred in pregnancy) • Once-daily dosing less preferred due to pharmacokinetics Monitoring: • Anti-Xa levels (target 0.6-1.0 U/mL at 4h post-dose) • Check monthly or with significant weight changes • Adjust dose as pregnancy progresses (weight gain) Duration: • Throughout pregnancy • At least 6 weeks postpartum • Minimum 3 months total treatment

nodes.title: PE Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: RV dilation, elevated troponin/BNP indicate submassive; determines whether thrombolysis should be considered
nodes.body: Risk Stratification for Treatment Decisions: Submassive PE indicators: • RV dilation on CTPA or echo • Elevated troponin • Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP • Tachycardia, hypoxia Does patient have submassive or massive PE? This determines whether thrombolysis should be considered. [1][2][4]

nodes.title: Low-Risk PE Management
nodes.summary: Therapeutic LMWH; may manage outpatient if reliable patient can self-administer injections with close follow-up
nodes.body: Low-risk PE in pregnancy: • Hemodynamically stable • No RV dysfunction • Normal biomarkers Management: • Therapeutic LMWH • Can often be managed outpatient after initial stabilization • Close obstetric follow-up • Monitor for bleeding complications Outpatient criteria: • Reliable patient • Able to self-administer injections • No other high-risk features • Close follow-up arranged [1][2]

nodes.title: Submassive PE Management
nodes.summary: ICU monitoring; thrombolysis NOT routine for submassive; catheter-directed therapy as alternative if deteriorating
nodes.body: Submassive PE in pregnancy requires ICU monitoring: Management: • Therapeutic anticoagulation (UFH or LMWH) • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Serial echocardiography • Watch for deterioration Thrombolysis considerations: • NOT routine for submassive PE in pregnancy • Consider if clinical deterioration • Consider catheter-directed therapy as alternative Consult: • Pulmonology • Cardiology • MFM (Ma

nodes.title: Thrombolysis in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Thrombolysis NOT contraindicated in pregnancy for massive PE; maternal death 25-65% if untreated; tPA does not cross placenta
nodes.body: Thrombolysis is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy when indicated for massive PE. Indications: • Massive PE with hemodynamic instability • Cardiac arrest from PE • Impending cardiovascular collapse Risks: • Maternal hemorrhage (especially if near delivery) • Placental abruption • Fetal loss Risk-Benefit: • Maternal death from untreated massive PE: 25-65% • Maternal mortality justifies thrombolysis r

nodes.title: tPA Dosing for Massive PE
nodes.summary: Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h or 50 mg bolus in arrest; hold anticoagulation 2-4h post-tPA then restart UFH
nodes.body: Alteplase (tPA): Standard Dose: • 100 mg IV over 2 hours • Or 50 mg bolus if cardiac arrest Half-Dose Protocol (alternative): • 50 mg IV over 2 hours • May reduce bleeding risk • Efficacy data limited Post-tPA: • Hold anticoagulation 2-4h then restart UFH • Monitor for bleeding • Serial fibrinogen levels Alternative: Catheter-Directed Therapy • Lower systemic dose • May be preferred if available [

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition by severity: low-risk may discharge with LMWH; submassive/massive require ICU. Peripartum: LMWH→UFH ~36wk for neuraxial. Postpartum: ≥6wk, warfarin OK
nodes.body: Disposition depends on PE severity and patient stability: | Severity | Disposition | |----------|-------------| | Low-risk | May discharge with LMWH, close follow-up | | Submassive | ICU admission | | Massive | ICU, consider thrombolysis/embolectomy | Before discharge (if appropriate): • LMWH teaching and supplies • OB follow-up within 1 week • Hematology referral • Return precautions Peripartum a

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU Admission for Submassive/Massive PE: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Arterial line if on pressors • Serial echocardiography • Serial troponin/BNP • OB at bedside for fetal monitoring Consultations: • Pulmonology • Cardiology • MFM • Interventional radiology (for catheter-directed therapy) • CT surgery (for embolectomy backup) Delivery planning: • If near term, may need urgent delivery • Coor
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission required. Multidisciplinary team involvement. OB at bedside for fetal monitoring.

nodes.title: Admit to OB/Telemetry
nodes.body: Low-Risk PE Hospital Admission: • Telemetry monitoring • Initiate therapeutic LMWH • LMWH teaching • OB monitoring of fetus • Transition to outpatient when stable Before discharge: • Confirm ability to self-inject • Arrange LMWH supply • Follow-up appointments • Return precautions [1][2]
nodes.recommendation: Admit to OB floor with telemetry. Initiate LMWH, arrange outpatient follow-up.

nodes.title: Outpatient Management
nodes.body: Select patients with low-risk PE may be discharged: Requirements: • Hemodynamically stable • No RV dysfunction • Reliable patient • Support system at home • Ability to self-inject LMWH • Close follow-up arranged Discharge Instructions: • LMWH injection technique • Signs of bleeding to watch for • Signs of PE progression • OB follow-up within 1 week • Hematology follow-up Prescriptions: • LMWH supp
nodes.recommendation: Low-risk PE may be managed outpatient with therapeutic LMWH and close follow-up.

nodes.title: PE Risk Stratification (2026)
nodes.summary: 2026 AHA/ACC 5-category system (A-E); assess SBP, RV strain, troponin, lactate; bradycardia <40 = ominous
nodes.body: PE Treatment Summary Confirmed or high-probability acute PE. 2026 AHA/ACC categories replace old massive/submassive terminology. Assess hemodynamic status first: • SBP <90 or drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min? • Signs of shock (altered mental status, cool extremities, oliguria)? • Bradycardia (HR <40) = most ominous finding • Bedside echo for RV strain • Troponin, BNP, lactate (>2 mM = 10% absolute mortal

nodes.title: Crashing PE — Category D-E
nodes.summary: Category E = shock/arrest; Category D = pre-arrest (HR <40 = ominous); lactate >2 mM = 10% mortality increase
nodes.body: Category E: Cardiopulmonary failure — sustained SBP <90 or ≥40 mmHg drop for >15 min, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest. Category D: Pre-failure — transient/borderline hypotension, approaching deterioration, HR <40. Mortality >15% without immediate reperfusion. Red flags: • Bradycardia (HR <40) — most ominous, harbinger of brady-asystolic arrest • Lactate >2 mM — 10% absolute mortality increase, H

nodes.title: Immediate Resuscitation
nodes.summary: AVOID intubation + fluid loading; high-flow O2; norepinephrine early; activate PERT immediately
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Standard shock resuscitation worsens massive PE. 1. AVOID INTUBATION if possible • Positive pressure worsens RV performance • May precipitate cardiac arrest • Use high-flow O2 (100% O2 = pulmonary vasodilator) 2. AVOID FLUID LOADING • RV already dilated — fluids worsen failure • Diuresis may improve hemodynamics (Terlipressin 2013) • Cautious: <500 mL only if clearly hypovolemic 3. EARLY

nodes.title: Reperfusion Strategy
nodes.summary: UFH (no bolus) + alteplase 100 mg over 2h (or 50 mg reduced-dose); cardiac arrest = 50 mg bolus + CPR
nodes.body: Anticoagulation — start immediately: • UFH — no bolus if thrombolysis imminent; low-dose infusion ≤500 U/hr • UFH preferred (can be stopped if hemorrhage) Systemic thrombolysis — only intervention with mortality benefit data (foundational massive/submassive PE management). Dosing options: • Standard: Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2h (0.6 mg/kg up to 50 mg over first 15 min, remainder over next 1h45min)

nodes.title: Intermediate-Risk — Category C
nodes.summary: Category C = PESI >85, RV dysfunction, elevated troponin/BNP, lactate >2; stratify by combined risk factors
nodes.body: Normotensive but with evidence of elevated clinical severity. Category C criteria: • PESI >85 or sPESI ≥1 • RV dysfunction — echo (RV/LV >0.9, McConnell sign, TAPSE <16mm) or CT (RV/LV ≥0.9) • Elevated biomarkers — troponin AND/OR BNP/NT-proBNP • Lactate >2 mM Further stratify by combined risk factors:

nodes.title: High-Risk Category C
nodes.summary: UFH + ICU monitoring; PERT activation; mechanical thrombectomy OR CDT if intervention needed — both reasonable, individualize (PEERLESS: no mortality/bleeding difference)
nodes.body: Multiple risk factors: RV dysfunction + elevated biomarkers + lactate elevation. Management: • UFH preferred (allows rapid escalation) • ICU monitoring — watch for decompensation • Activate PERT for multidisciplinary planning 2026 update: For stable Category C patients, mechanical thrombectomy and CDT are both reasonable — the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline does not prefer one over the other (Class 2b). P

nodes.title: Low-Risk Category C
nodes.summary: Anticoagulation alone; telemetry monitoring; escalate to high-risk pathway if deterioration
nodes.body: Only 1-2 risk factors present (RV dysfunction OR elevated biomarkers, not all three). Anticoagulation alone — advanced therapy not routinely indicated. Per 2026 AHA/ACC, LMWH is preferred over UFH for initial parenteral therapy in stable patients: • Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h (preferred, Class I 2026) • UFH reserved for CrCl <30 or concern for rapid escalation Telemetry admission for monitoring (s

nodes.title: Advanced Interventions
nodes.summary: Mechanical thrombectomy and CDT both reasonable — guideline does not prefer either (PEERLESS: no mortality/bleeding difference); VA-ECMO for refractory shock; surgical embolectomy as backup
nodes.body: 2026 update: For patients stable enough for procedure, mechanical thrombectomy and catheter-directed lysis are both reasonable options — the 2026 AHA/ACC guideline does NOT prefer one over the other (Class 2b). Choose based on operator experience, clot location, urgency, and bleeding risk. PEERLESS trial results (N=550): • Mechanical thrombectomy vs CDT for intermediate-risk PE • Lower clinical de

nodes.title: Mechanical Thrombectomy
nodes.summary: Large-bore aspiration (FlowTriever); no systemic lytics; lower ICU admission; requires IR + patient stability
nodes.body: Large-bore aspiration devices (FlowTriever, Inari, etc.) remove clot without systemic thrombolytics. Advantages: • No systemic lytic exposure — lower bleeding risk • Faster clot removal than CDT • Lower ICU admission rates (PEERLESS) Requirements: • IR suite availability • Patient stable enough for transport • PERT coordination recommended Post-procedure: • Anticoagulation with UFH initially • Tra

nodes.title: Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis
nodes.summary: Alteplase 8-24 mg over 6-24h via catheter; peripheral slow infusion (20 mg over 6h, STRATIFY) may be equivalent
nodes.body: Low-dose alteplase delivered directly to clot via catheter. Typical protocol: • Alteplase 1-2 mg/hr per catheter (total 8-24 mg over 6-24h) • With or without ultrasound assistance (EKOS) Key insight (STRATIFY): • Peripheral slow infusion achieves equivalent outcomes to catheter-directed • Avoids procedural risk and cost • Option: 20 mg alteplase IV over 6h with fibrinogen monitoring Bleeding risk:

nodes.title: VA-ECMO
nodes.summary: Bridge to reperfusion for refractory shock/arrest; ~57% mortality with ECMO alone; requires ECMO center
nodes.body: Indications: • Refractory cardiogenic shock despite vasopressors/inotropes • Cardiac arrest from PE • Failed or contraindicated thrombolysis Role: Bridge to reperfusion (systemic lysis, surgical embolectomy, or catheter intervention).
