Outcomes: • Mortality ~57% with ECMO alone (no reperfusion) • Better outcomes when ECMO bridges to definitive clot removal Requirements: • ECMO center capability • M

nodes.title: Surgical Embolectomy
nodes.summary: Reserved for refractory cases; requires cardiopulmonary bypass; variable mortality 15-50%
nodes.body: Indications: • Refractory shock despite other therapies • Contraindications to thrombolysis AND catheter therapy • Cardiothoracic surgery available • Right heart thrombus in transit Requires: • Cardiopulmonary bypass • Experienced surgical team • PERT coordination Outcomes: Variable mortality (15-50%) depending on pre-operative status.

nodes.title: Low-Risk — Category A-B
nodes.summary: Category A = asymptomatic (may d/c); Category B = symptomatic low-risk (early d/c); sPESI 0, normal biomarkers
nodes.body: Category A: Asymptomatic/subclinical PE — may discharge from ED. Category B: Symptomatic, low clinical severity — early discharge possible. Criteria for low-risk: • No RV dysfunction on imaging • Normal cardiac biomarkers (troponin, BNP) • No hypotension • PESI Class I–II or sPESI = 0 Use PESI or sPESI to confirm.

nodes.title: Outpatient Treatment Eligible?
nodes.summary: Hestia-type criteria: stable, no O2 need, no bleeding risk, good support, able to take oral meds, not pregnant
nodes.body: Assess for outpatient management (Hestia criteria or institutional protocol): • Hemodynamically stable • No need for supplemental O₂ • No active bleeding or high bleeding risk • No severe renal impairment (CrCl >30) • No severe pain requiring IV analgesics • Good social support and reliable follow-up • Able to take oral medications • No pregnancy

nodes.title: Outpatient Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Apixaban 10 mg BID x7d then 5 mg BID, or rivaroxaban 15 mg BID x21d then 20 mg daily; no bridge needed
nodes.body: DOACs preferred (no parenteral bridge needed): • Apixaban 10 mg BID × 7 days → 5 mg BID • Rivaroxaban 15 mg BID × 21 days → 20 mg daily with food Follow-up: Within 3–7 days with primary care or hematology. Patient education: • Return for worsening dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, syncope • Adherence to anticoagulation is critical • Minimum 3 months of therapy; reassess for extended treatment

nodes.title: Brief Inpatient Stay
nodes.summary: Admit 24-48h observation; start oral DOAC; transition to outpatient when stable and tolerating PO
nodes.body: Admit for 24–48h observation with initiation of anticoagulation. Start oral DOAC therapy: • Apixaban 10 mg BID × 7 days → 5 mg BID, OR • Rivaroxaban 15 mg BID × 21 days → 20 mg daily Transition to outpatient when clinically stable and oral intake confirmed.

nodes.title: Anticoagulation Selection
nodes.summary: DOACs preferred; CrCl <30 use UFH; cancer VTE use DOAC or LMWH; pregnancy use LMWH only; HIT use argatroban/fondaparinux
nodes.body: Choice depends on renal function, bleeding risk, patient preference, and cost. 2026 AHA/ACC update: LMWH is recommended over UFH for initial parenteral anticoagulation in most patients with acute PE (Class I). Reserve UFH for patients with anticipated thrombolysis, severe renal impairment, or hemodynamic instability where rapid escalation may be needed. Key decision points: • CrCl <30 mL/min → UFH

nodes.title: DOAC Regimens (Preferred)
nodes.summary: Apixaban/rivaroxaban no bridge needed; edoxaban/dabigatran require 5-10d parenteral lead-in; minimum 3 months
nodes.body: Single-drug approach (no parenteral lead-in): • Apixaban 10 mg BID × 7 days → 5 mg BID • Rivaroxaban 15 mg BID × 21 days → 20 mg daily (with food) Parenteral lead-in required (5–10 days LMWH/UFH first): • Edoxaban 60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 15–50, weight ≤60 kg, or P-gp inhibitor) • Dabigatran 150 mg BID Duration: Minimum 3 months. Extended treatment for unprovoked PE, recurrent VTE, or persistent

nodes.title: LMWH Bridge to Warfarin
nodes.summary: Enoxaparin bridge to warfarin; overlap until INR 2-3 for 2 consecutive days; INR monitoring weekly then monthly
nodes.body: • Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h (or 1.5 mg/kg daily) • Start warfarin on day 1 — overlap until INR 2.0–3.0 for ≥24 hours • Discontinue LMWH after INR therapeutic × 2 consecutive days • Target INR: 2.0–3.0 Duration: Minimum 3 months. Extended for unprovoked or recurrent VTE. Monitoring: INR weekly until stable, then monthly.

nodes.title: Renal or Hepatic Impairment
nodes.summary: CrCl <30 use UFH; severe hepatic use UFH; HIT: stop ALL heparin, use fondaparinux or argatroban
nodes.body: CrCl <30 mL/min: • UFH preferred — renally independent clearance • Adjust LMWH dose for CrCl 15–30 (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC daily) • Apixaban may be used cautiously (least renal elimination of DOACs) Severe hepatic disease (Child-Pugh C): • UFH preferred • DOACs contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia): • Discontinue ALL heparin products immediately • Fonda

nodes.title: PEA Arrest: Recognition
nodes.summary: Organized rhythm with no pulse; begin CPR, attach ETCO2, POCUS at first pulse check, identify reversible causes
nodes.body: PEA Arrest Steps Summary Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA): organized rhythm on the monitor with NO palpable pulse. PEA is NOT a single diagnosis — it is a presentation with a treatable cause. Immediate actions: • Begin high-quality CPR • Attach ETCO₂ immediately — target >20 mmHg • POCUS at first pulse check • Obtain IV/IO access • Identify and treat reversible causes

nodes.title: RUSH Exam During Pulse Check
nodes.summary: RUSH exam at pulse check: pump (cardiac motion, RV dilation, effusion), lungs (sliding), tank (IVC), pipes (aorta)
nodes.body: RUSH Exam in Arrest Perform RUSH exam during pulse check (<10 sec): Pump (cardiac): • Cardiac activity present? • RV dilation (RV > LV)? • Pericardial effusion with RV diastolic collapse? Lungs: • Absent lung sliding → tension pneumothorax? Tank (volume): • IVC collapsed → hypovolemia? • IVC plethoric → obstructive cause? Pipes: • Abdominal aorta → AAA? POCUS findings direct specific treatment — d

nodes.title: Cardiac Activity on POCUS?
nodes.summary: PREM (motion present) = pseudo-PEA/profound shock; PRES (standstill) = true PEA with poor prognosis
nodes.body: POCUS pulse check at femoral or carotid artery (<5 sec) is more accurate than manual palpation for detecting a pulse. Simultaneously assess cardiac contractility on bedside echo. PREM = Pulseless Rhythm with Echocardiographic Motion (pseudo-PEA) PRES = Pulseless Rhythm with Echocardiographic Standstill (true PEA)

nodes.title: PREM: Pseudo-PEA Assessment
nodes.summary: Weingart chain: 4 tools to assess perfusion — POCUS pulse, arterial line, SpO2 waveform, ETCO2 >30-40
nodes.body: PREM (cardiac motion present) = pseudo-PEA = profound shock state, NOT cardiac arrest. Weingart Chain of Survival — where is this patient? 1. Rhythm capable of perfusion? ✓ (organized rhythm) 2. Rhythm causing cardiac contraction? ✓ (POCUS shows motion) 3. Contraction generating a pulse? → Assess now 4. Pulse generating sufficient BP to perfuse organs? 4 tools to assess for perfusion: • POCUS puls

nodes.title: Pseudo-PEA: Treat as Profound Shock
nodes.summary: Stop CPR if perfusion present; norepinephrine or push-dose epi 5-20 mcg; do NOT give full-dose 1mg epi in pseudo-PEA
nodes.body: Stop chest compressions — this patient has cardiac output. CPR during contractility may actually impair output. Vasopressor strategy (choose one): • Norepinephrine 10-50 mcg/min IV infusion — first choice if drip ready • Push-dose epinephrine: 5-20 mcg IV q1-5 min (10 mcg/mL dilution) — bridge while starting drip • Vasopressin 20 IU IV bolus — bridge to norepinephrine ⚠️ Do NOT give full-dose epi

nodes.title: PRES: True PEA — Cardiac Standstill
nodes.summary: No wall motion = very poor prognosis; check for fine VF; epi 1mg IV q3-5min; prolonged PRES is strongest futility signal
nodes.body: PRES (Pulseless Rhythm with Echocardiographic Standstill) = true PEA. No visible wall motion despite organized electrical activity — very poor prognosis. Check for fine VF: • Increase gain settings on monitor • Confirm lead placement • If fine VF identified → defibrillate Rule out agonal rhythm — wide, slow complexes with no mechanical activity is near-terminal. Prolonged PRES after adequate resus

nodes.title: QRS Width on Monitor?
nodes.summary: Wide QRS: think sodium channel blockade (hyperK, TCA); narrow QRS: think mechanical/RV problem (tamponade, tension PTX, PE)
nodes.body: QRS duration guides differential diagnosis and empiric treatment in PEA arrest. Caveat: Bergman 2016 challenged this approach in a small study (n=51). QRS width is an imperfect discriminator — use it as a memory aid and first-move guide, not a definitive diagnostic tool. Always integrate with POCUS findings and clinical context. Wide vs. Narrow PEA

nodes.title: Wide Complex PEA
nodes.summary: Empiric NaHCO3 1-2 mEq/kg IV push + calcium gluconate 1g IV immediately; lipid emulsion if TCA suspected
nodes.body: Wide complex PEA — think sodium channel blockade. Common causes: • Hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, sine wave) • TCA overdose • Sodium channel blocker toxicity (flecainide, procainamide) • Severe metabolic acidosis • Hypermagnesemia Empiric treatment — give immediately: • NaHCO₃ 1-2 mEq/kg IV push • Calcium Gluconate 1g IV (or calcium chloride via central line) • Lipid Emulsion if TCA or lipophilic d

nodes.title: Narrow Complex PEA
nodes.summary: Myocardium electrically intact; mechanical obstruction to RV; first-line: wide-open IV fluids; calcium/bicarb unlikely to help
nodes.body: Narrow complex PEA — think mechanical / RV problem (pseudo-PEA). Narrow QRS = myocardium is electrically intact. The problem is mechanical obstruction to RV inflow or outflow. Common causes: • Cardiac tamponade • Tension pneumothorax • Mechanical hyperinflation / auto-PEEP • Massive pulmonary embolism • Profound hypovolemia First-line treatment: wide-open IV fluids — narrow-complex PEA is frequent

nodes.title: Reversible Cause Identified?
nodes.summary: Identify hyperkalemia, TCA/Na channel blocker toxicity, or severe acidosis as reversible cause of wide complex PEA
nodes.body: Which reversible cause of wide complex PEA is most likely?

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia in Arrest
nodes.summary: Calcium for membrane stabilization, then insulin+D50 and albuterol for K shift, NaHCO3 if acidotic
nodes.body: Hyperkalemia — membrane stabilization + potassium shifting: 1. Calcium (membrane stabilizer): • Calcium Gluconate 1g IV over 2-3 min • Calcium Chloride 1g IV (central preferred — 3× more elemental Ca²⁺) 2. Insulin + Dextrose (shift K⁺ intracellular): • Regular insulin IV — dose by hypoglycemia risk - 5 units (or 0.1 units/kg, max 10) — eGFR <60, dialysis-dependent, pre-treatment glucose <150 mg/dL

nodes.title: TCA / Na Channel Blocker Toxicity
nodes.summary: NaHCO3 1-2 mEq/kg IV push, target pH 7.45-7.55; lipid emulsion 20% if refractory; prolonged resus may succeed in tox
nodes.body: TCA/Na channel blocker toxicity in arrest: 1. Sodium Bicarbonate: • Sodium Bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV push • Target pH 7.45-7.55 • Repeat q5 min if QRS still wide 2. Lipid Emulsion (if refractory): • Lipid Emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus • Follow with 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion Do NOT use: • Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics • Physostigmine in arrest Continue CPR — prolonged resuscitation may be successful

nodes.title: Severe Metabolic Acidosis
nodes.summary: NaHCO3 1 mEq/kg IV push; address underlying cause (DKA, sepsis, toxic alcohol); ensure adequate ventilation
nodes.body: Severe metabolic acidosis in arrest: Treatment: • NaHCO₃ 1 mEq/kg IV push • Address underlying cause (DKA, sepsis, toxic ingestion) • Ensure adequate ventilation — respiratory compensation is critical Common causes: • DKA / metabolic emergency • Lactic acidosis (sepsis, shock) • Toxic alcohol ingestion (methanol, ethylene glycol) • Salicylate toxicity Note: NaHCO₃ in arrest is most beneficial when

nodes.title: POCUS Finding?
nodes.summary: POCUS-guided: tamponade, tension PTX, massive PE, hypovolemia, or auto-PEEP — each has specific intervention
nodes.body: Which POCUS finding best matches the clinical picture?

nodes.title: Mechanical Hyperinflation / Auto-PEEP
nodes.summary: Disconnect ventilator for 10-15 sec to decompress; reduce RR and TV; bilateral needle decompression if no improvement
nodes.body: Mechanical hyperinflation (auto-PEEP) — RV inflow obstruction from air trapping. Clues: • Ventilated patient (especially asthma, COPD) • Hyperexpanded chest, bilateral air entry • Progressive hypotension preceding arrest • Absent lung sliding may be BILATERAL (distinguish from tension PTX) Immediate treatment: • Disconnect ventilator — allow passive exhalation for 10-15 seconds • Manually compress

nodes.title: Cardiac Tamponade
nodes.summary: Emergent pericardiocentesis subxiphoid; even 20-30 mL aspiration can restore cardiac output; do not delay for formal echo
nodes.body: Tamponade: pericardial effusion + RV diastolic collapse → emergent pericardiocentesis. Procedure: • Subxiphoid approach preferred in arrest • Ultrasound-guided if possible • Even small volume aspiration (20-30 mL) can restore cardiac output Technique: • 18g spinal needle or angiocath • Aim toward left shoulder • Aspirate while advancing under real-time POCUS guidance Post-procedure: • Leave cathet

nodes.title: Tension Pneumothorax
nodes.summary: Needle decompression 2nd ICS MCL or 4th-5th ICS AAL; do NOT wait for CXR; follow with finger thoracostomy or chest tube
nodes.body: Tension PTX: absent lung sliding on POCUS → immediate decompression. Needle decompression: • 2nd ICS midclavicular line (traditional) • 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line (newer guidance — higher success) • Use 14g angiocath, minimum 5 cm length DO NOT wait for CXR — this is a clinical/POCUS diagnosis in arrest. Follow with: • Finger thoracostomy or chest tube • Chest Tube Consult Bilateral tensio

nodes.title: Massive Pulmonary Embolism
nodes.summary: Alteplase 50 mg IV push; continue CPR 60-90 min after lytic; thrombolytics NOT contraindicated by CPR
nodes.body: Massive PE: RV dilation + McConnell sign → thrombolytics in arrest. Treatment: • Alteplase 50 mg IV push (half systemic dose) • Continue CPR for 60-90 minutes after lytic administration — do not stop early • Heparin bolus after alteplase if ROSC achieved Alternative: • Consider ECPR (extracorporeal CPR) if available and appropriate Key points: • McConnell sign = RV free wall akinesis with apical s

nodes.title: Hypovolemia
nodes.summary: Rapid 1-2L crystalloid; if hemorrhagic: MTP + TXA; if sepsis: broad-spectrum abx; if anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine
nodes.body: Hypovolemia: collapsed IVC → rapid volume resuscitation. Immediate actions: • Rapid 1-2L crystalloid IV bolus • IO access if IV access delayed • Identify and address bleeding source If hemorrhagic: • Activate massive transfusion protocol • Permissive hypotension target (SBP 80-90) once ROSC • TXA 1g IV if within 3 hours of injury If non-hemorrhagic: • Sepsis → broad-spectrum antibiotics • Anaphyla

nodes.title: CPR Quality & Monitoring
nodes.summary: Rate 100-120/min, depth 2-2.4in; ETCO2 >20 target; ETCO2 <10 after 20min predicts non-survival; sudden jump suggests ROSC
nodes.body: CPR quality metrics: • Rate 100-120/min, depth 2-2.4 inches • Full chest recoil between compressions • Minimize interruptions (<10 sec for pulse/rhythm checks) • Rotate compressor every 2 minutes ETCO₂ monitoring: • Target ETCO₂ >20 mmHg during CPR • ETCO₂ <10 mmHg after 20 min = strong predictor of non-survival → consider TOR • Sudden ETCO₂ jump >10 above baseline = possible ROSC — check pulse Rh

nodes.title: Epinephrine in PEA Arrest
nodes.summary: Epi 1mg IV/IO q3-5min in true PEA, give early (non-shockable); no formal dose cap but higher cumulative dose = worse neuro; pseudo-PEA use titratable vasopressors
nodes.body: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO: • Give as soon as feasible — PEA is non-shockable, so epi early (AHA 2025 Part 9, COR 2a) • Repeat every 3-5 minutes (operationally, every second CPR cycle after the first dose) • No formal cumulative-dose ceiling in AHA 2025 — but observational data associate higher cumulative doses (esp. in PEA/asystole) with worse neurologically-intact survival. Give early, avoid prolong

nodes.title: Rhythm/Pulse Check: ROSC?
nodes.summary: At 2-minute check: assess for ROSC (pulse, rising ETCO2), continue CPR, or consider termination criteria
nodes.body: At 2-minute rhythm check — is there return of spontaneous circulation?

nodes.title: ROSC Achieved
nodes.body: ROSC → immediate post-cardiac arrest care. Priorities: • 12-lead ECG immediately • Hemodynamic support — target MAP ≥65 mmHg • Avoid hyperoxia — titrate O₂ to SpO₂ 92-96% • Avoid hypotension and hyperthermia • Identify precipitating cause Post-Cardiac Arrest Care
nodes.recommendation: Immediate post-ROSC care: 12-lead ECG, hemodynamic support, identify cause.

nodes.title: Continue Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Re-evaluate reversible causes each cycle; repeat POCUS; check for rhythm change to VF/VT (defibrillate if so)
nodes.body: Continue CPR cycles. Each cycle — reassess: • Re-evaluate reversible causes (Hs and Ts) • Repeat POCUS — has anything changed? • Consider whether new information changes management • Reassess ETCO₂ trend Consider: • Has the rhythm changed? (PEA → VF/VT → defibrillate) • New information from labs, history, or imaging? • Any untreated reversible cause?

nodes.title: Termination of Resuscitation
nodes.summary: TOR when: no ROSC, no POCUS activity, ETCO2 <10 at 20min, no reversible cause; continue for tox, hypothermia, post-lytic
nodes.body: Consider TOR when ALL of the following are present: • No ROSC after adequate resuscitation • No cardiac activity on POCUS (multiple checks) • ETCO₂ <10 mmHg after 20 minutes of CPR • No reversible cause identified or all reversible causes treated • BLS/ALS TOR rules met Factors favoring continued resuscitation: • Toxicologic arrest (prolonged resus may succeed) • Hypothermia ("not dead until warm

nodes.title: Code Called
nodes.body: Document resuscitation details: • Total arrest time and CPR duration • All ETCO₂ values throughout resuscitation • POCUS findings (cardiac activity, IVC, lungs) • All medications administered with times • All interventions (decompression, pericardiocentesis, etc.) • Rhythm progression • Reason for termination Post-arrest: • Family notification and support • Debrief with resuscitation team • Consid
nodes.recommendation: Document all interventions and reasoning for termination decision.

nodes.title: Pediatric Arthritis: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Big 6 not to miss: septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, malignancy, SCFE, NAI, inflammatory arthritis; pain>swelling = infection/malignancy
nodes.body: Joint pain is common (5% of pediatric ED visits) but includes life- and limb-threatening diagnoses. The "Big 6" Not to Miss: 1. Septic arthritis - cartilage destruction within hours 2. Osteomyelitis - often presents as joint pain 3. Malignancy - leukemia presents with bone/joint pain in 25-43% 4. SCFE - orthopedic emergency if unstable 5. Non-accidental injury - always consider in young children 6

nodes.title: Is the Child Sick or Well?
nodes.summary: Sick vs well appearance drives urgency; ill + fever + refuses weight-bearing = septic arthritis until proven otherwise
nodes.body: Septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and malignancy present with systemically ill children. Signs of ill appearance: - High fever (>38.5C / 101.3F) - Toxic-appearing, listless - Refuses to bear weight - Severe pain with any movement - Tachycardia, poor perfusion Signs of well appearance: - Afebrile or low-grade fever - Active, playful between exams - Will bear weight (even with limp) - Pain with extre

nodes.title: Joint Involvement Pattern
nodes.summary: Mono = septic until proven otherwise; oligo (2-4) = JIA, reactive, HSP; poly (5+) = JIA, viral, ARF
nodes.body: Monoarticular vs polyarticular guides differential significantly. Monoarticular (single joint): - Septic arthritis (until proven otherwise) - Transient synovitis - Trauma - Osteomyelitis (near joint) - Lyme arthritis - Early JIA (oligoarticular) Oligoarticular (2-4 joints): - JIA (most common) - Reactive arthritis - HSP - Early polyarticular process Polyarticular (5+ joints): - JIA (RF+ or RF-) -

nodes.title: Duration of Symptoms
nodes.summary: Acute <2wk: focus on infection; chronic >6wk: JIA by definition; duration guides differential and urgency
nodes.body: Duration helps differentiate acute infectious from chronic inflammatory causes. Acute (<2 weeks): - Septic arthritis - Transient synovitis - Trauma - Reactive arthritis (post-viral/enteric) - Lyme arthritis - Osteomyelitis Subacute (2-6 weeks): - Evolving JIA - Reactive arthritis - Post-streptococcal - Chronic osteomyelitis Chronic (>6 weeks): - JIA (by definition) - Lyme arthritis (recurrent) - M

nodes.title: Acute Monoarticular Arthritis
nodes.body: Acute monoarticular arthritis = SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise. Key differentiating features: | Feature | Septic Arthritis | Transient Synovitis | |---------|-----------------|---------------------| | Appearance | Ill/toxic | Well | | Fever | High (>38.5C) | Absent or low-grade | | Weight bearing | Refuses | Usually preserved | | ESR | >40 mm/hr | <20 mm/hr | | CRP | >20 mg/L | <20 mg/L |

nodes.title: Hip Pain: The Classic Pediatric Dilemma
nodes.summary: Transient synovitis vs septic hip is defining ED challenge; FABER position of comfort; ultrasound effusion does not differentiate
nodes.body: Transient synovitis vs septic hip is the defining ED challenge. Both present with: - Atraumatic, acutely irritable hip - Limp or refusal to bear weight - Limited range of motion - Possible effusion on ultrasound Position of comfort: - Hip held in flexion, abduction, external rotation (FABER) - This position maximizes joint capsule volume Ultrasound findings: - Effusion present in BOTH conditions -

nodes.title: Kocher/Caird Criteria Assessment
nodes.summary: Kocher: 0=<0.2%, 1=3%, 2=40%, 3=93%, 4=99.6%; CRP >20 strongest predictor; CRP <20 + weight-bearing = <1% risk
nodes.body: Kocher Criteria (4 factors) - Probability of Septic Hip: | # Criteria | Probability | |------------|-------------| | 0 | <0.2% | | 1 | 3.0% | | 2 | 40.0% | | 3 | 93.1% | | 4 | 99.6% | The 4 Criteria: 1. Fever (history of temperature >38.5C) 2. Non-weight bearing 3. ESR >40 mm/hr 4. WBC >12,000/mm3 Caird Modification adds CRP >20 mg/L as 5th criterion. Critical Limitation: These criteria were devel

nodes.title: Low Risk Hip (0 Kocher Criteria)
nodes.body: With 0 criteria present, probability of septic arthritis is <0.2%. This is likely transient synovitis if: - Child appears well - Afebrile or low-grade fever only - Will bear weight (even with limp) - CRP <20 mg/L - Recent viral illness Management: 1. NSAIDs - Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6-8h or Naproxen 5-7 mg/kg q12h 2. Rest - limit activity until pain-free 3. Follow-up in 24-48 hours if not improving Re
nodes.recommendation: Likely transient synovitis. Trial of NSAIDs, rest, and close follow-up in 24-48 hours. Return if fever, unable to bear weight, or worsening. Expect resolution in 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Intermediate Risk Hip (1-2 Criteria)
nodes.body: With 1-2 Kocher criteria, probability ranges from 3-40%. This is the diagnostic gray zone. Additional stratification: - CRP <20 AND weight-bearing: Very low risk (<1%) - consider observation - CRP >20 OR non-weight-bearing: Higher risk - strongly consider arthrocentesis Decision factors: - Parent/family reliability for follow-up - Ability to return if worsening - Clinical gestalt (how sick does ch

nodes.title: Arthrocentesis Decision
nodes.body: Arthrocentesis is both diagnostic AND therapeutic. Strong indications for joint aspiration: - CRP >20 mg/L - Non-weight bearing - Clinical deterioration during observation - High parental anxiety / limited follow-up access - Provider clinical concern Ultrasound guidance: - Confirms effusion presence - Identifies optimal needle entry point - Reduces failed taps - Can be performed by EM or radiology

nodes.title: Synovial Fluid Interpretation
nodes.body: Synovial fluid analysis is the gold standard for distinguishing septic from non-septic arthritis. Interpretation: | Parameter | Septic | Inflammatory | Non-inflammatory | |-----------|--------|--------------|------------------| | WBC count | >50,000/uL | 2,000-50,000/uL | <2,000/uL | | PMN % | >90% | 50-80% | <25% | | Glucose | Decreased | Normal-low | Normal | | Gram stain | May be + | Negative |

nodes.title: Observation Protocol
nodes.body: For intermediate-risk patients choosing observation over immediate arthrocentesis. In-ED observation (4-6 hours): - Serial exams q2h - Trial of ibuprofen 10 mg/kg - Repeat CRP if initially elevated - Reassess weight-bearing Favorable signs (supporting transient synovitis): - Improved mobility after NSAID - Decreased pain with rest - Remains afebrile - CRP stable or decreasing Concerning signs (pro
nodes.recommendation: Observation with serial exams, NSAID trial, and mandatory 24-hour follow-up. Return immediately for fever >38.5C, inability to bear weight, or worsening symptoms.

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis Workup
nodes.summary: Cartilage destruction within 8h; ortho STAT for OR drainage; do NOT delay abx for aspiration if septic; age-based pathogens
nodes.body: Septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency. Time to treatment matters. Cartilage destruction begins within 8 hours of infection. Diagnostic workup: 1. Labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, blood culture, BMP 2. Imaging: Ultrasound (confirms effusion), X-ray (baseline, rule out fracture/tumor) 3. Arthrocentesis: Cell count, Gram stain, culture, PCR if available Consults: - Orthopedics: STAT for operative planning

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics for Septic Arthritis
nodes.summary: Low MRSA: cefazolin; high MRSA: vancomycin; <5yr add Kingella coverage; vancomycin does NOT cover Kingella
nodes.body: Empiric coverage based on age and local MRSA prevalence. Neonates (<3 months): | Regimen | Dose | Notes | |---------|------|-------| | Cefazolin + Gentamicin | 40 mg/kg q8h + 4 mg/kg q24h | Low MRSA settings | | Vancomycin + Cefotaxime | 15 mg/kg q6h + 50 mg/kg q8h | High MRSA or ill-appearing | Infants/Children (3 months - 5 years): | Setting | First-Line | Alternative | |---------|------------|-

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis Disposition
nodes.body: All confirmed or highly suspected septic arthritis requires admission. Disposition: - Admit for IV antibiotics and monitoring - OR for joint washout (hip always, other joints often) - Serial exams and CRP trending Surgical management: - Hip: Open or arthroscopic irrigation and debridement - Knee: May attempt serial aspirations vs arthroscopy - Other joints: Case-by-case basis Expected course: - IV
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics and operative joint drainage. Orthopedic surgery consultation is mandatory. Prognosis is excellent if treated within 24-48 hours.

nodes.title: Knee Pain: Differential Considerations
nodes.body: Knee is the most commonly affected joint in pediatric arthritis. Key differentials for acute knee monoarthritis: 1. Septic arthritis - ill, febrile, refuses weight-bearing 2. Transient synovitis - less common than hip, but occurs 3. Lyme arthritis - large, swollen knee with minimal pain 4. Reactive arthritis - post-infectious 5. Early JIA - oligoarticular subtype 6. Trauma - fracture, ligament inj

nodes.title: Lyme Endemic Area?
nodes.body: Lyme arthritis is the most common manifestation of late Lyme disease in children. Endemic areas (US): - Northeast: CT, DE, MD, MA, NH, NJ, NY, PA, RI, VT - Upper Midwest: MN, WI - Pacific Coast: Northern CA, OR, WA (less common) Lyme arthritis characteristics: - Weeks to months after tick bite (often no recalled bite) - Large joint swelling (knee most common) - Significant swelling with minimal pa

nodes.title: Other Joint Involvement
nodes.body: Approach to non-hip, non-knee monoarthritis is similar to knee. Common sites: - Ankle: Septic, reactive, JIA - Elbow: JIA, septic (less common) - Wrist: JIA, Lyme, reactive - Shoulder: Septic (uncommon), referred from neck/chest Same workup applies: 1. Assess systemic illness 2. Labs: CBC, ESR, CRP 3. X-ray of affected joint 4. Ultrasound if effusion suspected 5. Arthrocentesis if high concern for

nodes.title: Chronic Arthritis Evaluation
nodes.summary: JIA: arthritis >6wk, age <16, diagnosis of exclusion; swelling>pain, morning stiffness, no fever; do NOT start steroids without rheum
nodes.body: Arthritis lasting >6 weeks suggests inflammatory arthritis, most commonly JIA. Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA): - Most common chronic rheumatic disease in children - Arthritis of unknown etiology before age 16 - Persisting for at least 6 weeks - Diagnosis of exclusion (rule out infection, malignancy, other) When to suspect JIA in the ED: - Chronic symptoms (>6 weeks) - Morning stiffness that i

nodes.title: JIA Subtypes (ILAR Classification)
nodes.summary: 7 JIA subtypes; oligoarticular most common (ANA+ = uveitis risk); systemic JIA has quotidian fever + MAS risk
nodes.body: 7 JIA subtypes with distinct presentations and prognoses. 1. Oligoarticular JIA (50-80%) - <=4 joints in first 6 months - Peak 2-4 years, girls > boys - Knee most common, asymmetric - ANA+ in 70% --> high uveitis risk 2. Polyarticular RF-negative (15-25%) - >=5 joints, RF negative - Bimodal (2-4 yr, 10-14 yr) - Symmetric, large and small joints 3. Polyarticular RF-positive (5%) - >=5 joints, RF po

nodes.title: JIA: ED Management
nodes.body: ED goals: symptom relief, rule out mimics, facilitate rheumatology care. Workup to rule out mimics: - CBC with differential (leukemia screen) - ESR, CRP - BMP - Consider LDH, uric acid if malignancy concern - ANA (for uveitis risk, not diagnosis) - X-ray of affected joints (baseline) Symptom management: - NSAIDs are first-line: - Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg q6-8h (max 40 mg/kg/day or 2400 mg/day) - Naproxe

nodes.title: Suspected JIA Disposition
nodes.body: Most suspected JIA can be managed outpatient with timely rheumatology follow-up. Discharge criteria: - Infection ruled out (or very low probability) - Malignancy not suspected - Stable symptoms - Pain controlled with oral NSAIDs - Reliable follow-up Discharge plan: 1. NSAIDs - scheduled dosing (not PRN) 2. Activity: Gentle ROM, avoid high-impact until evaluated 3. Rheumatology referral - within 1-
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with NSAID therapy and urgent rheumatology referral within 1-2 weeks. Ophthalmology referral for uveitis screening in ANA-positive or symptomatic patients. Written return precautions for fever or worsening.

nodes.title: Oligoarticular Pattern Evaluation
nodes.body: 2-4 joint involvement: differential includes JIA, reactive arthritis, HSP. Oligoarticular JIA: - Most common JIA subtype - Asymmetric, large joints - Knee most common - ANA+ in 70% (uveitis risk) - Often young girls (peak 2-4 years) Reactive arthritis: - Post-viral, post-enteric, post-streptococcal - Asymmetric, lower extremity - Onset 1-4 weeks after infection - Self-limiting in most cases HSP (I

nodes.title: Polyarticular Pattern Evaluation
nodes.body: 5+ joints involved: JIA subtypes, viral arthritis, ARF, CTD. Polyarticular JIA: - RF-negative: Bimodal age, symmetric, large and small joints - RF-positive: Adolescent girls, aggressive erosive disease Viral arthritis: - Concurrent with or 2-4 weeks after viral infection - Rubella, parvovirus B19, EBV, hepatitis B - Self-limiting, resolves in ~6 weeks Acute rheumatic fever: - Migratory polyarthrit

nodes.title: Reactive & Post-Infectious Arthritis
nodes.summary: Post-infectious arthritis: viral (self-limiting), post-enteric, Lyme (abx needed), post-strep (differentiate PSRA vs ARF)
nodes.body: Arthritis occurring after infectious trigger - sterile joint inflammation. Post-Viral Reactive Arthritis: - Most common infectious cause in children - Concurrent with or 2-4 weeks post-infection - Common viruses: parvovirus B19, rubella, EBV, hepatitis B - Self-limiting, resolves in ~6 weeks - Treatment: NSAIDs, supportive care Post-Enteric Reactive Arthritis: - Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter

nodes.title: PSRA vs Acute Rheumatic Fever
nodes.summary: PSRA: non-migratory, slow NSAID response; ARF: migratory, dramatic NSAID response, risk of carditis; Jones criteria for ARF dx
nodes.body: This distinction is critical - management differs significantly. | Feature | PSRA | ARF | |---------|------|-----| | Latent period | <10 days | 2-3 weeks | | Arthritis pattern | Non-migratory, prolonged | Migratory, short-lived | | Arthritis duration | Weeks to months | Days (rarely >3 weeks) | | NSAID response | Slow/incomplete | Dramatic, rapid | | Age | Bimodal (8-14, 21-37) | Peak ~12 years |

nodes.title: ARF Workup & Management
nodes.body: If ARF is suspected, full workup is mandatory - carditis can be silent. Required workup: 1. Evidence of strep infection: - Throat culture (may be negative by time of ARF) - ASO titer (peaks 3-5 weeks post-infection) - Anti-DNase B (peaks 6-8 weeks) 2. Cardiac evaluation: - ECG: PR prolongation (minor criterion) - Echocardiogram: Valvulitis, regurgitation, pericarditis 3. Labs: - CBC, ESR, CRP (inf

nodes.title: ARF Disposition
nodes.body: ARF typically requires admission for cardiac monitoring and initiation of therapy. Admit if: - Any cardiac involvement (clinical or echo) - Moderate-severe arthritis requiring IV pain control - Diagnostic uncertainty - Need for high-dose aspirin initiation with monitoring May discharge if: - Mild arthritis only - Cardiology has evaluated and cleared - Reliable follow-up within 24-48 hours - Family
nodes.recommendation: Admit most ARF cases for cardiac monitoring and treatment initiation. Ensure strep eradication, anti-inflammatory therapy, and plan for secondary prophylaxis. Cardiology follow-up is mandatory.

nodes.title: Lyme Arthritis Management
nodes.body: Lyme arthritis is the most common late Lyme manifestation in children. Diagnosis: - Clinical presentation in endemic area - Two-tier serologic testing (ELISA then Western blot) - Rapid tests (Sofia IgG) now available with good sensitivity Treatment: Children <8 years: | Drug | Dose | Duration | |------|------|----------| | Amoxicillin | 50 mg/kg/day divided TID (max 500 mg TID) | 28 days | | Alt:

nodes.title: Lyme Arthritis Disposition
nodes.body: Most Lyme arthritis can be managed outpatient. Discharge with: 1. 28-day course of oral antibiotics (doxycycline or amoxicillin) 2. NSAIDs for symptom relief 3. Activity as tolerated 4. Follow-up with PCP or ID in 2-4 weeks Return precautions: - Fever develops - Symptoms significantly worsening despite antibiotics - Neurologic symptoms (facial palsy, meningitis symptoms) - Cardiac symptoms (syncop
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with 28-day oral antibiotic course and NSAIDs. Follow-up in 2-4 weeks. Symptoms may take 4-6 weeks to fully resolve. Serology NOT useful for monitoring.

nodes.title: Malignancy Red Flags
nodes.summary: Leukemia mimics arthritis in 25-43%; night pain, pain>swelling, thrombocytopenia, HSM/LAD are key red flags
nodes.body: Leukemia presents with bone/joint pain in 25-43% of cases. May be misdiagnosed as JIA, growing pains, or trauma. Pain Characteristics Suggesting Malignancy: - Severe pain out of proportion to exam - Night pain that wakes child from sleep - Pain localized to bone (not joint) - Progressive, unremitting - Limiting normal daily activities Systemic Features: - Unexplained fever - Fatigue, lethargy - We

nodes.title: Malignancy Workup
nodes.summary: HSM/LAD + MSK = immediate eval; CBC + peripheral smear + LDH/uric acid; do NOT start steroids (masks malignancy)
nodes.body: When to investigate for malignancy in child with MSK complaints. Hard stops requiring immediate evaluation: - Hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy + MSK complaints - Any unexplained cytopenia - Pancytopenia Consider heme/onc referral if >1 month MSK pain PLUS: - Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or LAD, OR - Fever + non-articular bone pain + systemic symptoms (fatigue, weight loss) + neutrophils <2 x 1

nodes.title: Orthopedic Mimics of Arthritis
nodes.summary: SCFE: obese adolescent, obligate external rotation; Perthes: age 4-8, AVN; growing pains: bilateral, evening/night only, normal exam
nodes.body: These orthopedic conditions present with joint/limb pain and are commonly missed. SCFE (Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis): - Age: 8-15 years (girls ~12, boys ~13) - Risk factors: Obesity, male, African American - Presents with hip, groin, thigh, or KNEE pain - Externally rotated leg, obligate external rotation with flexion - X-ray: AP and frog-leg lateral (if stable) - EMERGENCY if unstable - non

nodes.title: SCFE Screening
nodes.body: SCFE is commonly missed because of referred knee pain. ALWAYS consider SCFE in: - Adolescent (especially obese) with hip, thigh, or knee pain - Limp without clear cause - Hip stiffness or decreased ROM - "Growing pains" in obese adolescent Exam findings: - Antalgic gait - Leg held in external rotation - Obligate external rotation with hip flexion (pathognomonic) - Decreased internal rotation - Pos

nodes.title: SCFE Management
nodes.body: SCFE requires urgent orthopedic intervention. Immediate actions: 1. Strict non-weight bearing - use crutches or wheelchair 2. Do NOT attempt reduction - increases AVN risk 3. Orthopedic surgery consultation - STAT Classification determines urgency: | Type | Definition | Urgency | |------|------------|--------| | Stable | Can bear weight (with or without crutches) | Urgent surgery (within 24-48h) |
nodes.recommendation: Non-weight bearing immediately. Urgent orthopedic consultation. Do NOT attempt reduction. Surgical treatment required.

nodes.title: Growing Pains: Diagnosis of Exclusion
nodes.body: Growing pains are common but remain a diagnosis of exclusion. Diagnostic Criteria (ALL must be present): 1. Age 3-12 years 2. Pain in bilateral lower limbs (NOT joints) 3. Pain occurs in evening/night (never present upon waking) 4. Child does NOT limp 5. Normal physical examination 6. No systemic symptoms Typical characteristics: - Location: Calves, anterior thighs, shins, popliteal fossa - Timing

nodes.title: Growing Pains Disposition
nodes.body: If criteria met and exam normal, reassurance is the treatment. Parent education: - Growing pains are benign and self-limiting - Not actually related to growth - Common (10-30% of children) - Usually resolve by adolescence - NOT a sign of underlying disease when criteria met Symptomatic management: - Massage, stretching - Heat (warm bath, heating pad) - Acetaminophen or ibuprofen PRN for severe epi
nodes.recommendation: Reassurance and symptomatic management if classic criteria met and exam normal. No workup needed. Return if limp, morning symptoms, fever, or worsening.

nodes.title: HSP (IgA Vasculitis) Arthritis
nodes.body: HSP is the most common vasculitis in children - arthritis is a major feature. Classic Tetrad: 1. Palpable purpura (100%) - lower extremities, buttocks 2. Arthritis/arthralgia (50-80%) 3. Abdominal pain (50-75%) 4. Renal involvement (20-50%) Arthritis Characteristics: - Large joints: knees, ankles, elbows, wrists - Oligoarticular, periarticular swelling - Painful but often lacks warmth, erythema, e

nodes.title: Treatment Overview & NSAID Dosing
nodes.body: NSAIDs are the cornerstone of treatment for most non-septic pediatric arthritis. NSAID Dosing: | Drug | Dose | Frequency | Max Daily | |------|------|-----------|----------| | Ibuprofen | 10 mg/kg/dose | q6-8h | 40 mg/kg or 2400 mg | | Naproxen | 5-7 mg/kg/dose | q12h | 20 mg/kg or 1000 mg | NSAID Pearls: - Schedule doses (not PRN) for anti-inflammatory effect - May take 2-4 weeks for full effect

nodes.body: Timely referral improves outcomes in pediatric arthritis. nodes.title: Final Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition based on diagnosis and clinical stability. Admission criteria: - Septic arthritis (confirmed or high suspicion) - ARF with cardiac involvement - Systemic JIA with concerning features - Diagnostic uncertainty with malignancy concern - Unable to maintain hydration/pain control - Social concerns affecting safe discharge Discharge criteria: - Infection ruled out or very low probability - P

nodes.title: Admission Summary
nodes.body: Admission for pediatric arthritis. Admission orders: 1. IV access and fluids as needed 2. Antibiotics if septic arthritis (per protocol) 3. Pain management - NSAIDs or acetaminophen scheduled 4. Consults: Orthopedics, Rheumatology, ID as indicated 5. Labs: Daily CBC, CRP until trending down 6. Imaging: As needed for monitoring Nursing orders: - Vital signs q4h (q2h if septic) - Strict I/O - Pain a
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics, pain management, and subspecialty care as indicated. Daily labs until improving. Clear weight-bearing orders.

nodes.title: Discharge Summary
nodes.body: Discharge instructions for pediatric arthritis. Medications: - NSAID: [Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg OR Naproxen 5-7 mg/kg] scheduled, NOT PRN - Antibiotics if indicated (Lyme, etc.) Activity: - Rest as needed - Activity as tolerated unless otherwise specified - No contact sports until cleared (if JIA suspected) Follow-up: - PCP: Within 1-2 days if observation, 1 week otherwise - Rheumatology: Within 1-2 wee
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with scheduled NSAID therapy, clear follow-up plan, and written return precautions. Ensure family understands when to return.

nodes.title: Transfer Summary
nodes.body: Transfer for subspecialty care not available locally. Pre-transfer: 1. Stabilize patient (IV access, pain control, antibiotics if indicated) 2. Complete basic workup (labs, X-rays) to send with patient 3. Direct physician-to-physician communication with accepting facility 4. Document weight-bearing status and any restrictions Transfer documentation: - Chief complaint and HPI - Physical exam findin
nodes.recommendation: Stabilize and transfer with complete documentation. Direct MD-to-MD communication with receiving facility. Family receives clear instructions.

nodes.title: Pediatric Appendicitis Overview

nodes.body: Rapid-action checklist for suspected pediatric appendicitis: [1,2,5] 1. History + exam — migration, anorexia, vomiting after pain, fever, RLQ tenderness, pain with cough/hop 2. Calculate PAS — 10-point score (use the PAS Calculator) 3. Stratify: - PAS ≤3 → low risk; consider discharge with return precautions or short observation - PAS 4-6 → intermediate; imaging (US first) - PAS ≥7 → high risk; su

nodes.title: Focused History & Exam
nodes.summary: Migration, anorexia, vomiting-after-pain, fever, RLQ tenderness, pain with cough/hop; rectal exam not routine; <5yo presents atypically.
nodes.body: History elements (each maps to PAS): [5,6] - Anorexia — "would your kid normally eat their favorite food right now?" - Nausea/vomiting — sequence matters; vomit BEFORE pain → gastroenteritis more likely - Migration — periumbilical → RLQ over 12-24h - Fever — ≥38°C - Duration — >48h raises perforation risk Exam: [1,3] - General appearance: still/quiet vs writhing (peritoneal pain is positional) - R

nodes.title: Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS)
nodes.summary: PAS = 10-point score (Samuel 2002): tenderness/cough-pain 2 pts each, others 1 pt each; ≤3 low, 4-6 equivocal, ≥7 high; not validated in <5yo.
nodes.body: Samuel 2002 — 10-point validated score for kids 4-15. Sensitivity ~88%, specificity ~50%; used to stratify imaging and disposition. [5,6] | Criterion | Points | |-----------|:------:| | RLQ tenderness | 2 | | Pain with cough, percussion, or hopping | 2 | | Migration of pain to RLQ | 1 | | Anorexia | 1 | | Nausea or vomiting | 1 | | Fever ≥38°C (100.4°F) | 1 | | Leukocytosis (WBC ≥10,000/μL) | 1 |

nodes.title: Laboratory Workup
nodes.summary: CBC, CRP, UA, bHCG (post-menarchal); normal WBC does not rule out; pyuria does not rule out; CRP + WBC normal after 24h symptoms has strong NPV.
nodes.body: Send labs on every suspected case before final imaging/dispo decision. [1,2,7] Core labs: - CBC — WBC and PMN feed directly into PAS; WBC >18k or left shift suggests perforation - CRP — elevated CRP + leukocytosis has high specificity; normal CRP + normal WBC carries a strong negative predictive value, especially after 24h of symptoms [7,8] - Urinalysis — rule out UTI (pyuria mimicker); a few WBCs

nodes.title: Imaging Pathway — US First, CT Last
nodes.summary: US first (≥6-7 mm non-compressible appendix); MRI if equivocal; CT only as last resort; pregnant adolescent: US/MRI, avoid CT.

nodes.title: Admit for Observation
nodes.body: Admission criteria: [10,12] - Equivocal imaging + ongoing symptoms - Non-operative management trial (selected uncomplicated cases) - Perforated appendicitis with planned interval appendectomy - Abscess requiring drainage - Failed outpatient management/return visit Admission management: - IV abx (see Antibiotics) - NPO until surgical decision finalized - IVF maintenance - Surgical team or pediatric
nodes.recommendation: Admit to surgical service or pediatric hospitalist. IV antibiotics, NPO, IVF, q4h abdominal exams, repeat imaging in 12-24h if needed.

nodes.title: Discharge with Rapid Recheck
nodes.body: Discharge criteria (shared decision-making): [10,12] - PAS ≤3 with negative or non-diagnostic imaging, OR negative MRI/CT - Tolerating PO without vomiting - Adequate pain control with oral medications - Reliable family with transportation and phone - Live within 30-60 min of an ED capable of pediatric surgery - No language/communication barriers - Explicit return precautions verbalized back Discha
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if PAS ≤3, tolerating PO, reliable family, and explicit 12-24h recheck plan documented. Return precautions reviewed.

nodes.title: Admit to Pediatric Floor
nodes.body: Floor admission criteria: [3,4] - PRAM 4-7 after maximal ED therapy (continuous SABA + steroid ± MgSO4) - Ongoing supplemental O2 to maintain SpO2 ≥92% - Q2-4h albuterol still needed - High-risk features (prior intubation, ICU history, multiple recent ED visits) - Unable to safely discharge (social, geographic, late at night without f/u) Floor orders: - Continuous SpO2 monitoring - Albuterol nebul
nodes.recommendation: Admit to pediatric floor. Continuous SpO2, albuterol q2-4h, IV/PO steroid, O2 to SpO2 ≥92%. Escalation criteria to PICU well-defined.

nodes.title: Admit to PICU
nodes.body: PICU admission criteria: [3,4,11] - Intubated - On NIV/BiPAP - Receiving IV terbutaline infusion - Continuous nebulized SABA still required - PRAM ≥8 despite ED therapy - Cardiac arrhythmia from beta-agonist (SVT, sustained HR >200) - Elevated lactate from beta-agonist + clinical concern - Significant electrolyte derangement (K+ <2.5) - Prior intubation/ICU for asthma + current severe exacerbation
nodes.recommendation: Admit to PICU. If non-intubated: continuous SABA + IV methylpred + IV MgSO4 ± terbutaline ± NIV with ketamine. If intubated: volume control, low rate, long I:E, permissive hypercapnia, deep sedation + ketamine infusion.

nodes.title: Pediatric Constipation
nodes.summary: 3-5% of peds visits; 95% functional. Rome IV criteria for diagnosis.
nodes.body: Functional constipation affects 3-5% of all pediatric visits and up to 30% of children at some point. [1][2] Most cases are functional (95%)—related to withholding behavior, dietary factors, or toilet training issues. Only ~5% have an organic cause. Behavioral Clues: • Withholding postures—tiptoeing, leg crossing, hiding • Fecal soiling/encopresis (overflow incontinence) • Toilet avoidance Diet: • Fluid intake, fiber intake

nodes.title: Disimpaction: Oral vs Rectal

nodes.body: Rapid-action checklist for suspected pediatric DKA: [1,2,3] 1. Diagnose (ISPAD): glucose >200 mg/dL + venous pH <7.30 OR HCO3 <18 + ketonemia/ketonuria 2. Fluids (PECARN-updated): - Only 10 mL/kg 0.9% NS bolus over 20-30 min IF hemodyna

[1] Apply clinical gestalt over biochemistry alone — a child with pH 7.15 who is mentating well + perfusing well behaves differently than the same pH with AMS and shock.

nodes.title: Fluid Resuscitation — PECARN-Updated

nodes.title: Potassium Management
nodes.summary: K<3.3 = HOLD insulin + give K first; K 3.3-5.5 = 20-40 mEq/L in fluids w/ UOP; check q2h; phosphate repletion if available in severe DKA.
nodes.body: Total body K is depleted in every DKA patient despite normal/high serum K at presentation. Insulin + acidosis correction will drive K intracellular fast. [1,3] Initial K and what to do: [1] | Serum K | Action | |---------|--------| | <3.3 | HOLD INSULIN — give 0.5-1 mEq/kg KCl IV (max 40 mEq/hr) over 1h, recheck before starting insulin | | 3.3-5.5 | Add 20-40 mEq/L KCl to fluids once urine output

nodes.title: Insulin Therapy — Start AFTER 1 Hour of Fluids
nodes.summary: Insulin starts AFTER 1h fluids — 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr IV, NO bolus; target glucose drop 50-75 mg/dL/hr; faster = CE risk.
nodes.body: Key change from adult DKA: Start insulin AT or AFTER 1 hour of fluid resuscitation, NOT concurrently. UK national study showed greater cerebral edema risk when insulin given in the first hour. ISPAD 2022 reinforces this. [1,3] Insulin protocol: [1,3] - Insulin regular 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr IV continuous infusion - NO IV bolus (cerebral edema concern, no efficacy benefit in peds) - Start with 0.05 U/kg/

nodes.title: Adding Dextrose — Two-Bag System
nodes.summary: Add dextrose when glucose 250-300; two-bag system; do NOT stop insulin until anion gap closes — it's the ketones, not the glucose.
nodes.body: Once glucose reaches 250-300 mg/dL, add dextrose. Do NOT stop insulin — the anion gap, not the glucose, drives when you stop insulin. [1,3] Two-bag system (preferred in most peds protocols): [1,3] - Bag A: 0.45% NS + 20-40 mEq/L KCl (or per K plan), NO dextrose - Bag B: 0.45% NS + 20-40 mEq/L KCl + D10 (or D5) - Both run through same IV at the same total rate; vary the ratio to deliver D2.5 → D10

nodes.title: Cerebral Edema Recognition (Muir Criteria)
nodes.summary: CE = #1 killer; 4-12h into tx; Muir criteria 92/96 sens/spec; clinical dx (~40% initial CT normal); risk factors: <5yo, new-onset, severe acidosis, bicarb use.
nodes.body: Cerebral edema is the #1 killer in pediatric DKA. Mortality 20-25%, permanent neuro deficit in 10-25% of survivors. Most cases occur 4-12 hours into treatment — the child who is "looking better" then suddenly deteriorates. [4,5] Muir/Glaser bedside criteria (Diabetes Care 2004) — 92% sens, 96% spec: [4] DIAGNOSTIC (any 1 = diagnose): - Abnormal motor or verbal response to pain - Decorticate or dec

nodes.title: Cerebral Edema — Treat Now?
nodes.body: Use the Muir CE Criteria. If criteria met, treat IMMEDIATELY without waiting for imaging — overtreatment risk is much lower than delayed treatment risk. [4,5]

nodes.title: Cerebral Edema — Emergent Treatment
nodes.body: Act in this order. Do NOT wait for imaging — most initial CTs are normal in CE. [1,4,5] 1. Airway and head positioning (within seconds): - Elevate head of bed to 30° (or reverse Trendelenburg) - Avoid neck flexion / jugular compression - Intubate if GCS <8 or rapidly declining — RSI with hyperventilation to pCO2 30-35 transiently OK as bridge - Avoid hypoxia, hypotension, hypercapnia, hyperthermia
nodes.recommendation: HOB 30°, intubate if GCS <8. Mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 10-15 min OR 3% NaCl 5-10 mL/kg over 30 min. Reduce fluid rate 1/3. Head CT after stabilization. PICU + neurosurgery consult.

nodes.title: Resolution Criteria & SC Insulin Transition
nodes.summary: Resolution: pH >7.30 + HCO3 ≥18 + AG <12 + tolerating PO; give first SC long-acting 30-60 min BEFORE stopping IV insulin or DKA recurs.
nodes.body: Resolution criteria (ALL required) per ISPAD 2022: [1,3] - pH >7.30 - Serum HCO3 ≥18 mEq/L - Anion gap <12 mEq/L — the most important marker; pH/HCO3 can normalize from hyperchloremia while ketosis persists - Tolerating PO without nausea/vomiting - Clinically improved, eating, ambulating (age-appropriate) Transition to SC insulin (overlap is critical): [1,3] - Give the first SC long-acting dose (i

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition is driven by severity, monitoring needs, social factors, and whether new-onset vs established T1D. [1,3]

nodes.title: PICU Admission
nodes.body: PICU criteria: [1,3] - pH <7.10 (severe DKA) - Age <5 with moderate-severe DKA - Any cerebral edema (current or recent) - AMS / GCS <14 - Hemodynamic instability or refractory acidosis - Intubated or NIV - Comorbid sepsis, AKI, or other organ dysfunction PICU orders: [1,3] - Continuous cardiac + SpO2 + ETCO2 monitoring - Hourly glucose POC, q2h BMP/VBG, q4h Mg/Phos/iCa - Hourly strict I/O - Hourly
nodes.recommendation: PICU admit. Hourly glucose + neuro checks (Muir). q2h BMP/VBG. Two-bag dextrose system. Mannitol/3% NaCl drawn at bedside. Endocrine + neuro on board.

nodes.title: Pediatric Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor admission criteria: [1,3] - Mild-to-moderate DKA, pH ≥7.10 - Mentation intact, no Muir criteria - Stable hemodynamics - On standard insulin infusion with smooth glucose decline - No new-onset complications Floor orders: [1,3] - q1-2h vital signs and neuro checks (Muir documented) - Hourly POC glucose - q2-4h BMP/VBG until AG closing, then q4-6h - Strict I/O - Continue insulin regular infusio
nodes.recommendation: Pediatric floor admit. q1-2h vitals + neuro (Muir). Hourly glucose. q2-4h BMP. Endocrine + diabetes educator. Clear PICU escalation triggers.

nodes.title: ED Discharge (Mild DKA Protocol)
nodes.body: Emerging evidence (SQuID II trial 2023; ISPAD acknowledges): Carefully selected mild DKA in adolescents with established T1D can be managed with SC insulin protocols and discharged from the ED. [1,6] Eligibility (ALL required): [1,6] - Established T1D (NOT new-onset) - pH 7.20-7.29, mild DKA only - Mentation fully intact, no Muir criteria - Tolerating PO without vomiting - Anion gap closed (<12) i
nodes.recommendation: Mild DKA, established T1D, AG closed in ED, mentation intact, tolerating PO, reliable follow-up → discharge with SC protocol + endocrine f/u in 24-48h.

nodes.title: Mimics & Common Complications
nodes.summary: Mimics: HHS, AKA, salicylate tox, appendicitis, inborn errors, ingestion. Complications: CE, hypoK, hypoglycemia (don't stop insulin), hyperchloremic acidosis, recurrence from missed SC overlap.
nodes.body: Not every acidotic peds patient is DKA — and DKA has signature iatrogenic pitfalls. [1,3,7] Mimics to consider: [3,7] - Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS): Glucose >600, minimal/no ketosis, profound dehydration, calculated osmolality >320. Rare in peds (more in adolescents with T2D, obesity). Use lower insulin (0.05 U/kg/hr), more cautious fluid (~3 mL/kg/hr), watch for rhabdo and DIC. - Mixed

nodes.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
nodes.summary: Pearls: insulin at hour 1, PECARN settles fluid debate, bicarb almost never, dextrose (not stopping insulin) for low glucose, draw mannitol/3% NaCl up early, overlap SC before stopping IV.
nodes.body: High-yield teaching points: [1,2,3,4,5] 1. Insulin starts at HOUR 1, not zero. UK national data, ISPAD reinforces. The "old way" of starting insulin and fluids simultaneously is associated with higher CE risk. 2. PECARN means stop arguing about fluid rate/Na content. Neither matters for neurologic outcomes. Give adequate volume to perfuse, don't over-bolus, don't under-resuscitate from fear. 3. Th

nodes.title: Pediatric Electrolyte Emergencies Overview
nodes.summary: Peds = larger fluid shifts, immature cerebral autoregulation, smaller margin of error; check accucheck + BMP on every altered/seizing child.
nodes.body: See Steps Summary for the rapid-action checklist. Why kids are different: [1,2,3] - Higher total body water (75% in neonates vs 60% in adults) → larger fluid shifts with disturbance - Lower renal concentrating ability in infants → faster dehydration and electrolyte derangement - Cerebral autoregulation immature → faster brain edema with rapid Na shifts - Smaller margin of error in dosing — mg/kg m

nodes.title: Steps Summary
nodes.body: Rapid action checklist for suspected pediatric electrolyte emergency: [1,2,3,4] 1. ABCs + glucose — accucheck on every altered, seizing, or critically ill child 2. BMP + iCal + Mg + VBG — single-stick "electrolyte panel" early 3. Identify the disturbance — match clinical syndrome to lab 4. Symptomatic vs asymptomatic — drives speed of correction 5. Pick the right fluid: - Balanced crystalloid (LR,

nodes.title: Triage & Bedside Assessment
nodes.summary: Accucheck first; BMP + iCal + Mg + VBG single-stick; balanced crystalloid (LR/Plasmalyte) preferred over 0.9% NS for resuscitation.
nodes.body: Immediate bedside actions for any suspected electrolyte emergency: [1,4] Vitals + glucose + IV access: - HR, BP (correct cuff size), RR, SpO2, temp - Accucheck FIRST in any altered or seizing child — hypoglycemia mimics everything - Two IVs if unstable; consider IO if access difficult Focused exam: - Hydration: mucous membranes, cap refill, tears, fontanelle, skin turgor, UOP - Neuro: mental statu

nodes.title: Fluid Choice — Balanced > 0.9% NS
nodes.summary: Balanced crystalloid (LR/Plasmalyte) for resuscitation; isotonic IVF for maintenance per AAP 2018; avoid 0.45% NS maintenance (iatrogenic hyponatremia).
nodes.body: Default to balanced crystalloid for pediatric resuscitation. [5,6] Why NOT 0.9% NS (in large volumes): [5] - Cl 154 mEq/L (supraphysiologic) → hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis - Worsens AKI risk in critically ill kids - Strong ion difference of zero → acidifying - Older "isotonic" myth — sodium content sometimes drives iatrogenic hypernatremia Balanced options: [5,6] - Lactated Ringer (LR): Na 13

nodes.title: Identify the Disturbance
nodes.body: Based on labs and clinical picture, select the dominant electrolyte emergency: [1,2,3] *Multiple disturbances often coexist (e.g., DKA with K and Na changes). Treat the most life-threatening first — usually hyperkalemia with ECG changes or symptomatic hyponatremia.*

nodes.title: Hyponatremia — Workup & Severity
nodes.summary: Severity by number; symptomatic vs asymptomatic drives speed; most common cause is hypotonic fluid during gastroenteritis; check cortisol if no cause.
nodes.body: Hyponatremia (Na <135) is the most common pediatric electrolyte abnormality. [1,3,8] Severity: [3,8] - Mild: Na 130-134 - Moderate: Na 125-129 - Severe: Na <125 (high risk of cerebral edema, seizure, herniation) Symptomatic vs asymptomatic determines speed of correction, not the number alone. [8,9] - Symptomatic: seizure, AMS, vomiting, lethargy, herniation signs (Cushing triad, posturing) - Asymp

nodes.title: Symptomatic Hyponatremia — 3% Saline
nodes.summary: 3% NaCl 3-5 mL/kg over 10-15 min (max 100 mL); raise Na ~4-6 mEq/L acutely to reverse herniation; recheck Na at 1-2h.
nodes.body: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, AMS, herniation signs) → 3% saline IMMEDIATELY. [8,9,10] Dose: - 3% NaCl: 3-5 mL/kg IV over 10-15 min (max 100 mL per bolus) - May repeat ×2 if seizure persists or symptoms unchanged - Goal of bolus: raise Na by 4-6 mEq/L acutely — enough to reverse herniation, not enough to cause ODS Why 3% saline (not 0.9% NS): - 0.9% NS is hypertonic relative to plasma

nodes.title: The 8-10 Rule — Avoiding ODS
nodes.summary: ≤8-10 mEq/L per 24h (or ≤6-8 if chronic); over-shoot rescue = D5W 3 mL/kg + DDAVP; ODS is irreversible.
nodes.body: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) is irreversible and devastating. Respect the correction limit. [8,9,11] Rule: - Correct Na by ≤8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours - For chronic hyponatremia (>48h or unknown duration) → even slower, ≤6-8 mEq/L per 24h - Acute hyponatremia (<48h, clearly known) — can correct faster but still cap at 10-12 mEq/L per 24h Why slow: - Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatremia b

nodes.title: Hypernatremia — Slow Rehydration Over 48-72h
nodes.summary: Free water deficit replaced over 48-72h (not 24h); cap correction at 10-12 mEq/L per 24h; resuscitate shock with balanced crystalloid first.
nodes.body: Hypernatremia (Na >150) — the danger is cerebral edema from rapid correction. [3,12] Severity: [12] - Mild: 146-150 - Moderate: 151-160 - Severe: >160 (high risk of seizure, ICH, venous sinus thrombosis) Common pediatric causes: [1,3,12] - Hypertonic dehydration from gastroenteritis (most common — water loss > Na loss) - Breastfeeding failure neonates (insufficient intake, weight loss >10%) - Diab

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia — Confirm + ECG First
nodes.summary: ECG drives urgency more than number; peaked T → wide QRS → sine wave → arrest; always rule out hemolysis (poor draw) but never delay treatment if ECG abnormal.
nodes.body: Hyperkalemia (K >6.0) — the ECG drives urgency more than the number. [1,13,14] Severity by number AND ECG: [13] - Mild: K 5.5-6.0, normal ECG - Moderate: K 6.1-7.0, peaked T waves - Severe: K >7.0 OR any wide QRS, sine wave, arrhythmia, arrest ECG progression: [13,14] 1. Peaked, narrow T waves 2. PR prolongation, P wave flattening 3. QRS widening 4. Sine wave (T merges with QRS) 5. Asystole / VF /

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia Treatment Cocktail
nodes.summary: Calcium gluconate 60 mg/kg first if ECG changes; insulin 0.1 U/kg + D25 0.5 g/kg shifts K; albuterol synergistic; dialysis if refractory; kayexalate controversial in peds.
nodes.body: Treat in this order (ECG changes = treat empirically, in parallel): [13,14,15] 1. STABILIZE THE MEMBRANE (FIRST, if any ECG change): - Calcium gluconate 10% 60 mg/kg IV (= 0.6 mL/kg of 10%) over 5-10 min - Max single dose 3 g (30 mL of 10%) - Onset 1-3 min, duration 30-60 min — REDOSE if ECG still abnormal - Calcium chloride 10% 20 mg/kg IV (= 0.2 mL/kg) — 3× the elemental Ca of gluconate; central

nodes.title: Hypokalemia — Identify Cause + Replace
nodes.summary: U waves, prolonged QT, arrhythmias; always check Mg (refractory hypoK without Mg replacement); causes: GI losses, diuretics, DKA refeeding, alkalosis.
nodes.body: Hypokalemia (K <3.0) — replace, but slowly via peripheral IV. [1,16] Severity: [16] - Mild: K 3.0-3.4 - Moderate: K 2.5-2.9 - Severe: K <2.5 (arrhythmia risk) ECG findings: [14,16] - U waves (after T wave) - T wave flattening or inversion - Prolonged QT (proarrhythmic) - PVCs, torsades, atrial arrhythmias Common pediatric causes: [1,16] - GI losses: vomiting (pyloric stenosis classic), diarrhea, N

nodes.title: Hypokalemia Replacement
nodes.summary: Oral preferred; IV peripheral max 0.5 mEq/kg/hr; NEVER IV push; replace Mg concurrently; recheck K q1-2h.
nodes.body: Oral preferred when possible. IV peripheral has strict rate limits. [16,17] Oral KCl (preferred for mild-moderate, asymptomatic): - 1-2 mEq/kg/day divided BID-TID - Onset hours; safer than IV; no rate limit concerns - Hold if signs of obstruction, ileus, oliguria IV potassium chloride: [16,17] - Peripheral max: 0.5 mEq/kg/hr (max 10 mEq/hr) — burns the vein at higher concentrations - Central line:

nodes.title: Hypocalcemia — Tetany & QT Prolongation
nodes.summary: Use ionized Ca; symptomatic → calcium gluconate 50-100 mg/kg IV over 5-10 min; replace Mg concurrently; hold IV Ca if on digoxin.
nodes.body: Hypocalcemia (iCa <1.0 mmol/L or total Ca <8.0 mg/dL) — replace if symptomatic or severe. [1,18] Always check IONIZED calcium — total Ca is unreliable with low albumin or acid-base shifts. Use the Corrected Calcium Calculator only as a screening adjunct. [18] Symptoms: - Tetany: carpopedal spasm, perioral numbness, paresthesias - Chvostek sign: facial twitch with tap over facial nerve (CN VII) - T

nodes.title: Hypercalcemia — Hydrate First
nodes.summary: Hydrate first (0.9% NS 2-3× maintenance), then furosemide; calcitonin for acute; bisphosphonates for malignancy; dialysis if severe/AKI.
nodes.body: Hypercalcemia (Ca >12) — uncommon in kids; usually points to a serious underlying cause. [1,18,19] Severity: [19] - Mild: 10.5-12 mg/dL - Moderate: 12-14 mg/dL - Severe / crisis: >14 mg/dL or symptomatic (AMS, arrhythmia) Symptoms — "stones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones": - Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration - Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation - AMS, lethargy, weakness, hyporeflexia

nodes.title: Hypoglycemia — Age-Specific Dextrose
nodes.summary: Rule of 50s: D10 2-5 mL/kg neonate, D25 2 mL/kg child, D50 1 mL/kg adolescent; glucagon if no IV; send critical sample if IEM/hypopit suspected.
nodes.body: Hypoglycemia is reversible brain injury. Treat in minutes, not hours. [4,20] Thresholds: [4,20] - Neonate: <40 mg/dL (some references use <45-50) - Infant/child: <60 mg/dL - Symptomatic at any level → treat Symptoms by age: [4,20] - Neonate/infant: jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia, apnea, hypothermia, seizure - Older child: sweating, tremor, hunger, irritability, confusion, seizure,

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on severity, response to treatment, and underlying cause: [1,2,3]

nodes.title: PICU Admission
nodes.body: PICU criteria: [1,2,4] - Any symptomatic severe disturbance (seizure, AMS, herniation signs, arrhythmia) - Hypertonic saline infusion required for ongoing correction - Hyperkalemia with ECG changes after initial treatment - AKI requiring dialysis - Adrenal crisis / suspected CAH in neonate - Persistent hypoglycemia needing high-GIR drip (>10 mg/kg/min) - Refractory or recurrent seizures PICU manag
nodes.recommendation: Admit to PICU with continuous cardiac monitoring, hourly neuro checks, serial labs q2-4h, and subspecialty consult per cause.

nodes.title: Floor / Step-Down Admission
nodes.body: Floor criteria: [1,3,16] - Mild-moderate disturbance, asymptomatic or symptoms resolved after ED treatment - Stable on oral or low-rate IV electrolyte replacement - Telemetry indicated (post-hyperK, post-hypoK, QT prolongation) - Awaiting workup for underlying cause (endocrine, renal, GI) - Recurrent hypoglycemia in young child needing observation through feeds Floor management: - Telemetry if K/C
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor with telemetry (if K/Ca abnormality), serial labs q6-8h, and subspecialty consult per cause.

nodes.title: ED Observation / Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge criteria (highly selected): [1,3,16] - Mild, asymptomatic, single disturbance with clear reversible cause (e.g., mild hyponatremia from gastroenteritis corrected with ORT in ED) - Labs normalized or trending appropriately - Tolerating PO; adequate hydration - Reliable family with transportation and ability to return - Confirmed PCP follow-up within 24-48h - No drug toxicity or NAT concer
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only for mild, asymptomatic, reversible cases with reliable family and confirmed follow-up. Most pediatric electrolyte emergencies warrant admission.

nodes.title: Patient Age Group
nodes.summary: Age-stratified FWS pathway: rectal T >=38C in 0-6mo with no source; select age group to guide workup intensity
nodes.body: Fever Without a Source (FWS): T ≥38°C (100.4°F) rectally in an infant 0–6 months with no identifiable source on history and physical exam. REFERENCES \u2022 HSV Workup Criteria \u2022 UTI Risk Factors \u2022 Ceftriaxone Contraindications \u2022 Antimicrobial Dosing Select the patient\u2019s age:

nodes.title: Off-Pathway — Alternate Management
nodes.body: Patient meets one or more exclusion criteria for the FWS pathway. EXCLUSION CRITERIA • Preterm (<37 weeks gestational age) • Immunocompromised • Indwelling devices (VP shunt, central line) • Known immune deficiency • Recent hospitalization (within 7 days) • Current antibiotics or recent (<48h) OFF-PATHWAY TRIGGERS • Focal bacterial infection identified (cellulitis, abscess, pneumonia, osteomyeliti
nodes.recommendation: Manage per condition-specific guidelines. These patients require individualized assessment and may need broader workup than the FWS pathway provides.

nodes.title: Toxic / Ill-Appearing Infant
nodes.body: Ill-appearing infant requires full sepsis workup and empiric antibiotics regardless of age. FULL SEPSIS WORKUP \u2022 CBC with differential \u2022 Blood culture \u2022 CMP \u2022 UA + urine culture (catheterized) \u2022 Lumbar puncture: CSF cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel \u2022 Consider: CRP, Procalcitonin, stool culture (if diarrhea) \u2022 Co
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT to inpatient or PICU. Full sepsis workup with age-appropriate empiric antibiotics. Add Acyclovir if <21 days or HSV risk factors.

nodes.title: 0–21 Days: Pathway Screening
nodes.summary: Screen for focal infection, hypothermia, ill appearance, or viral syndrome before applying FWS pathway
nodes.body: Does the infant have any of the following? • Focal bacterial infection (cellulitis, abscess, pneumonia, osteomyelitis) • Hypothermia (<36°C / 96.8°F) • Clinically ill-appearing • Bronchiolitis or clear viral syndrome (RSV, influenza, etc.)

nodes.title: Order Full Sepsis Workup
nodes.summary: All 0-21d neonates: full sepsis workup with LP mandatory; CBC, blood culture, CMP, cath UA, CSF studies, hold tube 4
nodes.body: All 0\u201321 day neonates require full sepsis workup including LP. LABS TO ORDER \u2022 CBC with differential \u2022 Blood culture \u2022 CMP \u2022 UA (catheterized) \u2014 if positive, send urine culture \u2022 Lumbar puncture: \u2013 CSF cell count with differential \u2013 CSF glucose, protein \u2013 CSF Gram stain \u2013 CSF culture \u2013 Meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel \u2013 Hold tube #4

nodes.title: HSV Workup Indicated?
nodes.summary: HSV red flags: vesicles, seizures, lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, CSF pleocytosis
nodes.body: Does the infant have HSV risk factors or clinical features? \u2022 Skin vesicles (mouth, scalp, trunk) \u2022 Seizures \u2022 Lethargy, poor feeding \u2022 Hepatosplenomegaly \u2022 Thrombocytopenia or transaminitis \u2022 CSF pleocytosis \u2022 Maternal HSV history

nodes.title: Add HSV Coverage
nodes.summary: Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h; order HSV PCR blood + CSF, surface cultures; minimum 5 doses or until PCR negative
nodes.body: Add Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h HSV TESTING TO ORDER \u2022 HSV PCR \u2014 blood (plasma) \u2022 HSV PCR \u2014 CSF (from held tube #4) \u2022 Surface cultures: conjunctiva, throat, nasopharynx, rectum \u2022 Vesicle fluid: viral culture + PCR (if lesions present) \u2022 AST, ALT (hepatic involvement screen) DURATION \u2022 Minimum 5 doses or until HSV PCR results negative \u2022 If PCR not resulted

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics by Age
nodes.summary: Age-specific empiric abx: 0-7d ampicillin+gentamicin; 8-21d ceftriaxone (cefepime if contraindicated)
nodes.body: Select the neonate\u2019s age to determine the appropriate empiric regimen. See Antimicrobial Dosing Reference for complete dosing table.

nodes.title: CSF Pleocytosis?
nodes.summary: CSF abnormal if WBC >15 or positive Gram stain; traumatic taps common in neonates — treat as abnormal if uninterpretable
nodes.body: Review CSF results from the lumbar puncture. ABNORMAL CSF (0\u201328 days): \u2022 WBC >15 cells/mm\u00b3 \u2022 Positive Gram stain \u2022 Traumatic tap or uninterpretable Note: Traumatic taps are common in neonates. If bloody, use correction ratio or treat as if abnormal.

nodes.title: Meningitis Protocol
nodes.summary: Escalate to meningitic dosing; 0-7d: ampicillin 100 mg/kg + cefepime; 8-21d: ceftriaxone q12h + ampicillin q6h
nodes.body: Escalate to meningitic dosing based on age: 0\u20137 DAYS \u2022 Ampicillin 100 mg/kg IV q8h (meningitic dose) \u2022 Add Cefepime 50 mg/kg IV q12h \u2022 Discontinue Gentamicin \u2022 Consider Acyclovir if not already started 8\u201321 DAYS \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q12h (meningitic dose) \u2022 Add Ampicillin 75 mg/kg IV q6h (meningitic dose) \u2022 Consider Acyclovir if not already started

nodes.title: Admit — Await Cultures
nodes.body: ALL 0–21 day neonates are admitted regardless of clinical appearance or lab results. INPATIENT MANAGEMENT • Continue empiric antibiotics pending culture results • Blood cultures: finalized at 24–36 hours • CSF cultures: finalized at 48–72 hours IF PATHOGEN IDENTIFIED • Narrow antibiotics to targeted therapy • Duration based on organism and site IF NO PATHOGEN AT 24–36 HOURS + WELL-APPEARING • Disc
nodes.recommendation: Admit to inpatient. Continue age-appropriate empiric antibiotics. If cultures negative at 24–36h and infant is well-appearing, discontinue antibiotics.

nodes.title: Febrile Neonate with Viral Syndrome
nodes.summary: Febrile neonate <21d with RSV/bronchiolitis: IBI risk 1-2%, still need full sepsis workup including LP
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Age <21 days with bronchiolitis/RSV still requires full sepsis workup. ⚠️ IBI RISK IN RSV-POSITIVE NEONATES • Bacteremia: 1.1% • Meningitis: 0.8% • UTI: 5.2% This is NOT negligible risk. The viral syndrome does NOT exclude serious bacterial infection in this age group. FULL SEPSIS WORKUP REQUIRED • CBC with differential • Blood culture • CMP • Procalcitonin, CRP (optional but helpful) •

nodes.title: Neonatal Viral Syndrome — ADMIT
nodes.body: ALL 0–21 day neonates with fever + viral syndrome are ADMITTED. EMPIRIC ANTIBIOTICS • 0–7 days: Ampicillin + Gentamicin • 8–21 days: Ceftriaxone (or Cefepime if CI) + Ampicillin VIRAL SYNDROME MANAGEMENT • Supportive care: suctioning, hydration, oxygen PRN • Bronchiolitis: no role for bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics (for the viral illness itself) • Monitor for apnea — highest risk in inf
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT. Full sepsis workup + empiric antibiotics even with confirmed viral syndrome. Discontinue antibiotics if cultures negative at 24–36h and infant well-appearing.

nodes.title: 22–28 Days: Pathway Screening
nodes.summary: Screen for focal infection, hypothermia, ill appearance, or viral syndrome; viral syndrome has modified pathway
nodes.body: Does the infant have any of the following? • Focal bacterial infection identified • Hypothermia (<36°C / 96.8°F) • Clinically ill-appearing • Bronchiolitis or clear viral syndrome (RSV, influenza, etc.)

nodes.title: Order Labs + Inflammatory Markers
nodes.summary: CBC, blood culture, CMP, procalcitonin, cath UA; LP depends on inflammatory markers and shared decision-making
nodes.body: LABS TO ORDER \u2022 CBC with differential \u2022 Blood culture \u2022 CMP \u2022 Procalcitonin (PCT) \u2022 UA (catheterized) \u2014 if positive, send urine culture OPTIONAL \u2022 CRP \u2022 Stool culture (if diarrhea present) LP is not automatically required for this age group \u2014 it depends on inflammatory marker results and shared decision-making.

nodes.title: Inflammatory Markers
nodes.summary: Abnormal: T >38.5, PCT >0.5, CRP >2.0, ANC >4000; any single abnormal marker indicates higher risk
nodes.body: Are ANY of the following inflammatory markers abnormal? ABNORMAL CRITERIA: \u2022 Temperature >38.5°C (101.3°F) \u2022 Procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL \u2022 CRP >2.0 mg/dL \u2022 ANC >4,000 cells/mm\u00b3 Any single abnormal marker \u2192 higher risk. All normal \u2192 lower risk but still requires evaluation.

nodes.title: LP & CSF Results
nodes.summary: LP recommended if markers abnormal; shared decision if normal; CSF abnormal if WBC >15 or positive Gram stain
nodes.body: Lumbar puncture is recommended if inflammatory markers are abnormal. For normal markers, LP is a shared decision with the family. ABNORMAL CSF (22\u201328 days): \u2022 WBC >15 cells/mm\u00b3 \u2022 Positive Gram stain

nodes.title: Meningitis Protocol \u2014 ADMIT
nodes.body: MENINGITIS DOSING (22\u201328 DAYS) \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q12h (meningitic dose) \u2022 Add Ampicillin 75 mg/kg IV q6h (meningitic dose) \u2022 Consider Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h if HSV risk factors See Antimicrobial Dosing Reference for complete dosing.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT. Start meningitic-dose antibiotics immediately. Consider HSV coverage. Repeat LP in 24\u201348h if organism identified to document sterilization.

nodes.title: UA Results
nodes.body: Review the urinalysis results. Positive UA: Leukocyte esterase, nitrites, >5 WBC/hpf, or bacteria on Gram stain. If UA positive, ensure catheterized urine culture was sent.

nodes.title: UTI \u2014 Admit for IV Antibiotics
nodes.body: ANTIBIOTIC TREATMENT \u2022 Cefazolin 17 mg/kg IV q8h (without bacteremia) \u2022 Cefazolin 33 mg/kg IV q8h (with concurrent bacteremia) \u2022 Step-down to Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID when tolerating PO \u2022 Total duration: 10 days (IV + PO combined) ADMIT for IV antibiotics and monitoring.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT. Start IV Cefazolin. Step down to oral Cephalexin when tolerating PO and clinically improving. Total 10-day course.

nodes.title: Shared Decision: Disposition
nodes.body: Normal CSF and negative UA. Disposition depends on inflammatory marker status and shared decision-making with the family. IF ABNORMAL INFLAMMATORY MARKERS: Higher risk \u2014 admission preferred. If family elects home observation: \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV x1 before discharge \u2022 Mandatory follow-up in 24 hours IF NORMAL INFLAMMATORY MARKERS: Lower risk \u2014 home observation is reason

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: IF DISCHARGED HOME • Review Discharge Criteria — all must be met • Consider Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV x1 if inflammatory markers abnormal • Mandatory PCP or ED follow-up within 24 hours • Provide Return Precautions • Culture callback: blood culture results at 24–36h IF ADMITTED • Continue observation • If abnormal inflammatory markers: may give Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q24h • If normal inflammator
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on inflammatory marker status and shared decision-making. Ensure 24-hour follow-up regardless of disposition. Culture callback system in place.

nodes.title: 22–28 Day Febrile Infant with Viral Syndrome
nodes.summary: 22-28d with viral syndrome: lower IBI risk but UTI risk unchanged; need labs + UA, LP decision based on inflammatory markers
nodes.body: Modified workup for well-appearing 22–28 day infant with confirmed viral syndrome (bronchiolitis, RSV, influenza). KEY EVIDENCE • RSV-positive infants 22–28 days: bacteremia ~0.7%, meningitis <0.5% • When inflammatory markers ALL normal, meningitis risk approaches 0% • UTI risk remains 5–7% even with viral syndrome LABS TO ORDER • CBC with differential • Blood culture • Procalcitonin (critical for

nodes.title: Viral Syndrome: Inflammatory Markers
nodes.summary: Low risk if ALL normal: PCT <0.5, ANC <4000, T ≤38.5, CRP <2.0; any abnormal = LP recommended
nodes.body: Review inflammatory markers. All must be normal to defer LP. LOW-RISK CRITERIA (ALL must be met): • Procalcitonin <0.5 ng/mL • ANC <4,000 cells/mm³ • Temperature ≤38.5°C (101.3°F) • CRP <2.0 mg/dL (if obtained) If ANY marker abnormal → higher risk → LP recommended See Step-by-Step Criteria for details.

nodes.title: Viral Syndrome: UTI Screening
nodes.summary: UTI risk 5-7% even with viral syndrome; always screen with catheterized UA
nodes.body: UTI risk remains 5–7% even with confirmed viral syndrome. Review the urinalysis results. Positive UA: Leukocyte esterase, nitrites, >5 WBC/hpf, or bacteria on Gram stain. If UA positive, ensure catheterized urine culture was sent.

nodes.title: Viral Syndrome — Low Risk Disposition
nodes.body: 22–28 day infant with confirmed viral syndrome + ALL normal inflammatory markers + negative UA This infant is LOW RISK for serious bacterial infection. LP STATUS • LP NOT required if all criteria met • Document shared decision-making with family DISPOSITION OPTIONS ✓ Home observation (preferred if all criteria met): • Well-appearing, tolerating PO • Reliable caregiver • PCP/ED follow-up in 24 hour
nodes.recommendation: LOW RISK. Home observation with 24h follow-up. No LP or antibiotics needed if all low-risk criteria met. Document shared decision-making.

nodes.title: 29–60 Days: Pathway Screening
