nodes.summary: Screen for focal infection, hypothermia, ill appearance, or viral syndrome; viral syndrome has low IBI risk
nodes.body: Does the infant have any of the following? • Focal bacterial infection identified • Hypothermia (<36°C / 96.8°F) • Clinically ill-appearing • Bronchiolitis or clear viral syndrome (RSV, influenza, etc.)

nodes.title: Order Labs
nodes.summary: CBC, blood culture, CMP, procalcitonin, cath UA; LP determined by inflammatory marker results
nodes.body: LABS TO ORDER \u2022 CBC with differential \u2022 Blood culture \u2022 CMP \u2022 Procalcitonin (PCT) \u2022 UA (catheterized) \u2014 if positive, send urine culture OPTIONAL \u2022 CRP \u2022 Stool culture (if diarrhea present) LP is determined by inflammatory marker results.

nodes.title: Inflammatory Markers
nodes.summary: Same criteria: T >38.5, PCT >0.5, CRP >2.0, ANC >4000; abnormal = LP recommended; all normal = no LP needed
nodes.body: Are ANY of the following inflammatory markers abnormal? ABNORMAL CRITERIA: \u2022 Temperature >38.5°C (101.3°F) \u2022 Procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL \u2022 CRP >2.0 mg/dL \u2022 ANC >4,000 cells/mm\u00b3 Any single abnormal marker \u2192 higher risk \u2192 LP recommended. All normal \u2192 lower risk \u2192 no LP needed.

nodes.title: LP & CSF Results
nodes.summary: Lower CSF threshold for 29-60d: WBC >9 (vs >15 for 0-28d); positive Gram stain always abnormal
nodes.body: Lumbar puncture recommended for elevated inflammatory markers. ABNORMAL CSF (29\u201360 days): \u2022 WBC >9 cells/mm\u00b3 (lower threshold than 0\u201328 days) \u2022 Positive Gram stain

nodes.title: Meningitis \u2014 ADMIT
nodes.body: MENINGITIS DOSING (29\u201360 DAYS) \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q12h (meningitic dose) \u2022 Add Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q6h \u2022 Consider Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h if HSV risk factors Note: Vancomycin added (instead of Ampicillin) to cover MRSA and resistant GBS/pneumococcus in this age group. See Antimicrobial Dosing Reference for complete dosing.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT. Start meningitic-dose Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin. Consider HSV coverage. Obtain Vancomycin trough before 4th dose (goal 15\u201320 mcg/mL).

nodes.title: UA Results
nodes.body: Review the urinalysis results. Positive UA: Leukocyte esterase, nitrites, >5 WBC/hpf, or bacteria on Gram stain. If UA positive, ensure catheterized urine culture was sent.

nodes.title: UTI \u2014 Admit for IV Antibiotics
nodes.body: ANTIBIOTIC TREATMENT \u2022 Cefazolin 17 mg/kg IV q8h (without bacteremia) \u2022 Cefazolin 33 mg/kg IV q8h (with concurrent bacteremia) \u2022 Step-down to Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID when tolerating PO \u2022 Total duration: 10 days (IV + PO combined) ADMIT for IV antibiotics and monitoring.
nodes.recommendation: ADMIT. Start IV Cefazolin. Step down to oral Cephalexin when tolerating PO and clinically improving. Total 10-day course.

nodes.title: Shared Decision: Disposition
nodes.body: Abnormal inflammatory markers but normal CSF and negative UA. \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV x1 recommended \u2022 Home observation with mandatory 24-hour follow-up \u2022 OR admit for observation

nodes.title: Disposition \u2014 High Risk
nodes.body: IF DISCHARGED HOME \u2022 Review Discharge Criteria \u2014 all must be met \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV x1 before discharge \u2022 Mandatory PCP or ED follow-up within 24 hours \u2022 Provide Return Precautions \u2022 Culture callback: blood culture results at 24\u201336h IF ADMITTED \u2022 Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q24h \u2022 Monitor for clinical deterioration \u2022 Culture results at 24\u20
nodes.recommendation: Disposition based on shared decision-making. Give Ceftriaxone x1 if discharging. Ensure 24-hour follow-up and culture callback system.

nodes.title: Low Risk — Disposition
nodes.body: All inflammatory markers normal → low risk for serious bacterial infection. No LP needed. UA POSITIVE? • If UA positive: Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID x 10 days + home • Ensure catheterized urine culture was sent UA NEGATIVE? • No antibiotics needed • Home observation with follow-up DISCHARGE REQUIREMENTS • Review Discharge Criteria • PCP or ED follow-up within 24 hours • Provide Return Precautions •
nodes.recommendation: Low risk for SBI. If UTI: oral Cephalexin and home. If no UTI: no antibiotics, home observation with 24-hour follow-up.

nodes.title: 29–60 Day Febrile Infant with Viral Syndrome
nodes.summary: 29-60d with viral syndrome: IBI risk <0.5%, LP not needed; UTI risk 5-7% so always get UA
nodes.body: Well-appearing 29–60 day infant with confirmed viral syndrome (bronchiolitis, RSV, influenza) has VERY LOW IBI risk. KEY EVIDENCE • RSV-positive infants 29–60 days: bacteremia <0.5%, meningitis approaches 0% • AAP 2021: bronchiolitis is an exclusion criterion for the full FWS pathway • UTI risk remains 5–7% even with viral syndrome MINIMAL WORKUP • UA + urine culture (catheterized) — always requir

nodes.title: Viral Syndrome: UTI Screening
nodes.summary: UTI risk 5-7% even with viral syndrome; always get catheterized UA
nodes.body: UTI risk remains 5–7% even with confirmed viral syndrome. Obtain catheterized UA for all febrile infants, regardless of viral diagnosis. Positive UA: Leukocyte esterase, nitrites, >5 WBC/hpf, or bacteria on Gram stain.

nodes.title: Viral Syndrome — Supportive Care
nodes.body: 29–60 day infant with confirmed viral syndrome + negative UA This infant is VERY LOW RISK for serious bacterial infection. WORKUP COMPLETE • No LP required • No blood culture required (but reasonable if obtained) • No antibiotics needed VIRAL ILLNESS MANAGEMENT • Supportive care: hydration, suctioning PRN • Bronchiolitis: no bronchodilators, no steroids, no antibiotics • Influenza: consider oselta
nodes.recommendation: VERY LOW RISK. Supportive care for viral illness. No LP or antibiotics needed. Home with follow-up if well-appearing and tolerating PO.

nodes.title: 2\u20136 Months: Initial Assessment
nodes.body: Temperature threshold: \u226539°C (102.2°F) or <36°C Assess the infant for source of fever:

nodes.title: Focal Bacterial Infection
nodes.body: Identifiable bacterial source found on exam. Manage per condition-specific guidelines. COMMON FOCAL INFECTIONS \u2022 Urinary tract infection \u2192 UA + culture, antibiotics per UTI guidelines \u2022 Pneumonia \u2192 CXR, antibiotics per CAP guidelines \u2022 Cellulitis/abscess \u2192 I&D if fluctuant, antibiotics based on severity \u2022 Acute otitis media \u2192 antibiotics per AOM guidelines \
nodes.recommendation: Manage the identified focal infection per condition-specific guidelines. Consider additional workup if the infant appears ill out of proportion to the identified source.

nodes.title: Viral Syndrome \u2014 UTI Screen
nodes.body: Defined viral syndrome identified. Supportive care for the viral illness. However, still screen for UTI \u2014 UTI can coexist with viral infections in this age group. Obtain UA. See UTI Risk Factors for screening criteria.

nodes.title: FWAS: Labs & Risk Assessment
nodes.body: Fever Without an Apparent Source (FWAS) LABS TO ORDER \u2022 CBC with differential \u2022 Blood culture \u2022 UA (catheterized if risk factors present) \u2022 Procalcitonin OPTIONAL: CMP, CRP, stool culture (if diarrhea) Assess PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine) status and UTI risk:

nodes.title: Incomplete PCV \u2014 Additional Workup
nodes.body: Infant has <2 PCV doses \u2192 higher risk for invasive pneumococcal disease. ADDITIONAL ASSESSMENT \u2022 If WBC >15,000 or <5,000 cells/mm\u00b3: obtain blood culture + consider empiric Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV x1 \u2022 If WBC 5,000\u201315,000: lower risk, observe DISPOSITION \u2022 If given Ceftriaxone: mandatory 24-hour follow-up \u2022 Review Discharge Criteria \u2022 Provide Return Preca
nodes.recommendation: Assess WBC count. If abnormal, give empiric Ceftriaxone x1 and ensure 24-hour follow-up. Culture callback system in place.

nodes.title: UTI Management
nodes.body: TREATMENT OPTIONS BY CLINICAL STATUS WELL-APPEARING + TOLERATING PO \u2022 Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID x 10 days \u2022 OR Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM/IV x1, then oral step-down ILL-APPEARING OR NOT TOLERATING PO \u2022 Cefazolin 17 mg/kg IV q8h \u2022 Step-down to Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID when tolerating PO \u2022 If bacteremia: Cefazolin 33 mg/kg IV q8h Total duration: 10 days (IV + PO combined) EN
nodes.recommendation: Treat UTI based on clinical status. Well-appearing: oral Cephalexin or Ceftriaxone x1 + oral. Ill: IV Cefazolin. Total 10-day course. Follow up urine culture.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: ED DISCHARGE CRITERIA (all must be met) \u2022 Well-appearing on exam \u2022 Tolerating oral liquids \u2022 Reliable caregiver with transportation \u2022 PCP or ED follow-up within 24 hours confirmed \u2022 Caregiver comfortable with home observation \u2022 Review full Discharge Criteria IF CRITERIA NOT MET \u2192 ADMIT FOLLOW-UP \u2022 PCP or ED in 24 hours \u2022 Culture callback: blood culture
nodes.recommendation: Discharge home if all criteria met. Ensure 24-hour follow-up and culture callback system. Admit if discharge criteria not met.

nodes.title: Pediatric Foreign Body — Overview
nodes.summary: 6mo–5yr peak; classic triad only ~35% sensitive / 90% specific; normal CXR does NOT rule out; BB esophagus → OR <2h
nodes.body: Steps Summary · Esophageal Timing Table · BB Honey Protocol Highest risk: 6 months – 5 years. Peak around toddlers exploring orally. [7,8] Two pathways: - AIRWAY (tracheobronchial) — choking event, cough, wheeze, focal decreased breath sounds - ESOPHAGEAL — drooling, dysphagia, refusing PO, chest/throat pain, may be silent Classic aspiration triad (cough + wheeze + decreased breath sounds) is only

nodes.title: Initial Presentation
nodes.summary: Acute choking → BLS; stable aspiration → airway eval; ingestion → esophageal triage; occult → airway eval
nodes.body: Which scenario best fits the patient now?

nodes.title: BLS Choking Algorithm — by Age
nodes.summary: Effective cough = watch; <1yr back blows + chest thrusts; ≥1yr back blows ALTERNATING with abdominal thrusts (2025 AHA change); CPR if unconscious; no blind sweep
nodes.body: PALS Choking Algorithm STEP 1 — Assess cough effectiveness [12] - Effective cough (can cry/speak, color normal): WATCH, do not intervene. Encourage cough. Transport. - Ineffective cough (no sound, cyanotic, decreasing LOC): ACT NOW STEP 2 — Age-appropriate maneuver [12] Infant <1 year (conscious): - 5 back blows (heel of hand, between scapulae, head down) - 5 chest thrusts (2 fingers on sternum, s

nodes.title: Post-Stabilization Status
nodes.summary: All survivors of choking still need airway evaluation — retained particulate is common
nodes.body: After BLS maneuvers, what is the patient's status?

nodes.title: Failed BLS — Critical Airway
nodes.summary: Failed BLS = ENT/anesth/OR/PICU; Magill if visible; push FB distal as last bridge; rigid bronch is definitive
nodes.body: Cannot ventilate, cannot extract FB: Activate: - ENT, anesthesia, OR, PICU NOW - Pediatric advanced airway resources Bridge maneuvers: - Direct laryngoscopy + Magill forceps if FB supraglottic and visible - BVM ventilation between attempts (may push obstructing FB distal to one mainstem → restores ventilation through other lung) - Consider intentional right mainstem intubation to push FB into righ

nodes.title: Airway FB — Clinical Evaluation
nodes.summary: Witnessed event sens 76-92% but specificity population-dependent (23-95%); focal ↓ BS = most specific finding; 20-40% have normal exam; peanuts most common <3yr
nodes.body: History red flags [4,8,14] - Witnessed choking event — sensitive but NOT reliably specific. Sensitivity 76-92%; specificity varies enormously by population (reported as high as ~95% in selected bronchoscopy cohorts but as low as 23% when history alone is used in an unselected ED population). Treat a witnessed event as a trigger to evaluate, not as confirmation. [8,21] - Sudden cough or apnea while

nodes.title: Airway FB — Imaging Strategy
nodes.summary: CXR may be normal; insp/exp or decubitus to detect air trapping; CT only if rigid bronch unavailable; high suspicion → bronch
nodes.body: Standard: PA + lateral chest X-ray [4,7] Findings (any/none): - Radiopaque FB (rare — most are food/plastic) - Unilateral hyperinflation (ball-valve obstruction, expiratory air trapping) - Atelectasis distal to FB - Mediastinal shift - Consolidation (post-obstructive pneumonia) Specialized views to detect air trapping when standard CXR is normal but suspicion high: - Inspiratory + expiratory CXR (

nodes.title: Disposition by Suspicion + Imaging
nodes.summary: High suspicion → rigid bronch regardless of imaging; mod → obs + pulm; low + asx → home
nodes.body: Stratify based on clinical suspicion and imaging findings.

nodes.title: Rigid Bronchoscopy — Gold Standard
nodes.summary: Rigid bronch under GA = gold standard; dexamethasone + racemic epi prn post-op edema; 24h obs
nodes.body: Rigid bronchoscopy under GA — diagnostic AND therapeutic for tracheobronchial FB. [4,9] Indication threshold: Any one of: - Witnessed aspiration event with persistent symptoms - Radiologic findings (hyperinflation, atelectasis) - Recurrent same-lobe pneumonia - Persistent focal wheeze unresponsive to bronchodilator Pre-op: - NPO - IV access - Anesthesia + ENT/pediatric surgery - Discuss with famil

nodes.title: Observation — Moderate Suspicion
nodes.summary: Mod suspicion = inpatient obs + pulm/ENT; low threshold to escalate to bronch if persistent symptoms
nodes.body: Setting: Inpatient or extended ED observation, pulmonology / ENT consultation. [4] Monitor for: - Persistent or worsening cough/wheeze - New focal exam findings - Recurrent same-lobe pneumonia - Persistent hypoxemia Repeat imaging at 24-48h if symptoms persist. Threshold to escalate to bronchoscopy: Low. When in doubt, the diagnostic yield of rigid bronchoscopy in moderate-suspicion cases is accep

nodes.title: Esophageal FB — Object Triage
nodes.summary: AP+lateral first; BB = stat OR; multiple magnets = surgery; coin/sharp = symptom-based timing
nodes.body: Esophageal Timing Table Obtain STAT AP + lateral X-ray (neck, chest, abdomen) before triage. Lateral identifies "halo" sign of button battery vs single-density coin. [1,3] Select the most concerning object known or imaged:

nodes.title: Button Battery — Esophageal
nodes.summary: OR <2h regardless of sx; halo sign on AP; ENT+GI+anesth+OR + battery hotline; NPO; injury starts in 15min
nodes.body: TRUE EMERGENCY — OR within 2 hours regardless of symptoms. [2,3] For full button battery workflow (gastric, distal, complications) see → Button Battery consult. Immediate parallel actions: 1. Activate: ENT, GI, anesthesia, OR 2. Call: National Battery Hotline 1-800-498-8666 (24/7) 3. STAT XR AP + lateral confirms esophageal location (BB has "halo/double-ring" on AP, step-off on lateral) [3] 4. NPO

nodes.title: BB Pre-Removal Mitigation — Honey / Sucralfate
nodes.summary: Honey 10mL q10min ×6 doses if ≥12mo, awake, <12h; sucralfate alternative; NEVER delay OR; never honey <12mo
nodes.body: BB Honey Protocol Honey (pH-neutralizing, viscous coating) — first-line mitigation [5,6] Eligibility: - Age ≥12 months (infant botulism risk under 12mo — NEVER give honey <12mo) - Awake, able to swallow safely - <12 hours since ingestion - No mediastinitis or perforation signs - En route to or awaiting OR Dose: Honey 10 mL PO every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses total before OR. Sucralfate — alternativ

nodes.title: BB Post-Removal Surveillance
nodes.summary: ICU admit; esophagram at 4wk if circ injury; 28-day AEF vigilance; family education on Reese's Law
nodes.body: Immediate post-removal [3] - Document depth, orientation, duration, injury appearance at endoscopy - Esophagram or CT angio if any concern for vascular involvement - ICU/inpatient admission Surveillance for delayed complications [3] - Repeat esophagram at 4 weeks if significant circumferential injury → assess for stricture - Endoscopic dilation if stricture develops (≥4 weeks healing minimizes per

nodes.title: Magnet(s) — Single vs Multiple
nodes.summary: Single = observe/remove by symptoms; multiple OR magnet+metal = surgical consult; neodymium = worst; esoph BB ≠ magnet (different timing rules)
nodes.body: Critical question: Single magnet OR multiple magnets / magnet + metal? [1,13] Single magnet, esophageal: - Symptomatic → endoscopic removal <2h - Asymptomatic → ≤24h endoscopic removal Single magnet, beyond esophagus, asymptomatic: - Observation + serial X-rays q4-6h to confirm passage - Strict isolation from other magnets/metal Multiple magnets OR magnet + metallic co-ingestion (ANY location): -

nodes.title: Esophageal Coin
nodes.summary: Sx coin = <2h; asx = <24h or ~16h obs trial (25-30% pass, distal 56% vs proximal 27%); gastric coin = discharge; glucagon not useful for coins
nodes.body: Symptomatic (drooling, refusing PO, chest pain, respiratory): - Endoscopic removal <2 hours [1,10] Asymptomatic, esophageal coin: - Option A: Endoscopic removal <24 hours [1] - Option B (older child, distal esophagus): Observation trial with repeat X-ray at ~16 hours (Waltzman RCT protocol was an 8-16 hour window, not 24h) — 25-30% pass spontaneously. Passage is more likely with a distal coin (56%

nodes.title: Sharp / Long Object
nodes.summary: Sharp esoph = endoscopy regardless of sx (<2h sx, <24h asx); NASPGHAN: length >6cm OR diameter >25mm = endoscopy
nodes.body: Sharp objects (needles, pins, fish/chicken bones, broken glass, open safety pins): [1,4] Esophageal: - Endoscopic removal regardless of symptoms — risk of perforation - Symptomatic → <2 hours - Asymptomatic → <24 hours Gastric, sharp object: - Endoscopic removal if technically feasible (point-trailing technique) - Failed endoscopy + sharp object → close observation + serial imaging Long or wide ob

nodes.title: Food Bolus Impaction
nodes.summary: Peds food bolus rare without dz; sx + no secretions = <2h; glucagon no better than placebo in adult RCT — do not delay endoscopy; ALL peds food bolus → GI for EoE workup
nodes.body: Esophageal food bolus (uncommon in young children without underlying disease — eosinophilic esophagitis, stricture, web): [1,4] Symptomatic, unable to handle secretions: Endoscopic removal <2 hours Symptomatic, handling secretions: Endoscopic removal <24 hours Pharmacologic options (limited evidence in peds): - Glucagon 0.5 mg IV in child (1 mg in adolescent) — relaxes LES, in theory may allow pas

nodes.title: Disposition & Caregiver Education
nodes.summary: Admit any post-op + BB + multiple magnets; D/C with strict precautions; counsel on food age cutoffs + battery/magnet safety
nodes.body: Admit: - Any post-bronchoscopy / post-endoscopy patient × 24h - Button battery (regardless of clinical course) — ICU level - Multiple magnet ingestion, observation phase - Respiratory symptoms persisting post-extraction Discharge criteria: - Asymptomatic, normal exam, normal imaging - Object known to have passed OR very low-risk gastric position - Family understands return precautions - Follow-up

nodes.title: Pathway Complete
nodes.summary: Document everything — witness, object, time, mitigation, education
nodes.body: Pediatric foreign body pathway complete. Documentation reminders: - Witnessed event details (object, time, witness) - Imaging findings - Procedures performed - Mitigation given (honey/sucralfate timing for BB) - Family education provided and return precautions documented
nodes.recommendation: Discharge or admit per disposition criteria with appropriate follow-up.

nodes.title: Pediatric Hypertensive Emergency Overview
nodes.summary: Urgency = severe BP without end-organ damage; emergency = severe BP WITH damage; most peds severe HTN is secondary; reduce slowly.
nodes.body: See Steps Summary for the rapid-action checklist. Definitions (AAP 2017): [1] - Normal BP: SBP/DBP <90th %ile for age/sex/height - Elevated BP (formerly pre-HTN): 90th to <95th %ile, or 120/80 to <95th %ile in adolescents ≥13y - Stage 1 HTN: 95th %ile to <95th %ile + 12 mmHg, or 130/80 to 139/89 (≥13y) - Stage 2 HTN: ≥95th %ile + 12 mmHg, or ≥140/90 (≥13y) Urgency vs Emergency: [2,3] - Hypertensiv

nodes.title: Steps Summary
nodes.body: Rapid action checklist for severe pediatric HTN: [1,2,3] 1. Confirm BP — correct cuff size, manual recheck both arms 2. Symptoms? — HA, vomiting, vision change, AMS, seizure, focal deficit, dyspnea 3. End-organ workup — neuro exam, fundoscopy, UA, BMP, ECG; head imaging if neuro symptoms 4. Classify: - Urgency (asymptomatic, no end-organ damage) → oral agent - Emergency (end-organ damage) → IV age

nodes.title: Confirm the Blood Pressure
nodes.summary: Wrong cuff = wrong BP; bladder width 40% of arm circumference; manual auscultation preferred; check both arms and a leg for coarctation.
nodes.body: Most "abnormal" pediatric BPs in the ED are measurement errors. Always confirm before treating. [1,5] Cuff size (the #1 source of error): [1] - Bladder width: 40% of mid-arm circumference - Bladder length: 80-100% of arm circumference - Cuff too small → falsely HIGH reading - Cuff too large → falsely low reading Technique: [1] - Patient seated 3-5 min, feet flat, arm at heart level - Manual auscul

nodes.title: End-Organ Symptoms?
nodes.body: After BP confirmed in severe range, screen for symptoms of end-organ involvement: [2,3]

nodes.title: End-Organ Damage Workup
nodes.summary: Screen neuro (fundoscopy, head imaging if symptoms), cardiac (ECG for LVH), renal (UA, BMP); ANY end-organ damage = emergency.
nodes.body: Every child with severe HTN needs an end-organ damage screen. [2,3] Neuro: - Mental status, focal deficits, papilledema - Fundoscopy — flame hemorrhages, exudates, papilledema (hypertensive retinopathy) - Head CT (non-contrast) if AMS, seizure, focal deficit, severe HA - MRI preferred for PRES (parieto-occipital edema) Cardiac: - ECG — LVH (deep S V1 + tall R V5/V6), strain pattern - Listen for ga

nodes.title: PRES (Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy)
nodes.body: PRES is the most common neurologic presentation of pediatric hypertensive emergency. [3,6] Clinical features: - Headache, AMS, visual disturbance (cortical blindness), seizure - Often bilateral and posterior (parieto-occipital) - BP is usually severely elevated but PRES can occur at lower BPs if rapidly rising Imaging: - MRI: bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic edema (T2/FLAIR hyperintensity) -

nodes.title: Classify: Urgency vs Emergency
nodes.body: Based on workup, classify this presentation: [2,3]

nodes.title: Secondary Causes — Most Peds HTN Is Secondary
nodes.summary: Renal causes most common (60-80%); always check 4-extremity BPs for coarctation; screen for stimulants and endocrine causes.
nodes.body: Unlike adults, the majority of severe pediatric HTN is SECONDARY. Always screen. [1,4] Renal (most common, 60-80% of severe peds HTN): [4] - Renal artery stenosis (fibromuscular dysplasia, post-transplant) - Acute glomerulonephritis (post-strep, IgA, lupus) — hematuria, edema, low C3 - Chronic kidney disease, reflux nephropathy - Polycystic kidney disease - Hemolytic uremic syndrome (see STEC/HUS)

nodes.title: The 25% Rule for BP Reduction
nodes.summary: ≤25% drop in first 8h, next 25% over hours 8-16, target over 24-48h; avoid rapid drops (watershed infarct, PRES); NEVER use SL nifedipine.
nodes.body: The single most important treatment principle in pediatric hypertensive emergency. [3,6] Rule: - Reduce ≤25% of planned BP drop in the FIRST 8 hours - Reduce next 25% over hours 8-16 - Achieve target BP over 24-48 hours total Why slow: - Chronic HTN resets cerebral autoregulation to a higher range - Rapid normalization → cerebral hypoperfusion → watershed infarction, blindness, PRES - Pediatric br

nodes.title: Treatment: Hypertensive Emergency (IV)
nodes.summary: IV nicardipine first-line; labetalol if no contraindications; nitroprusside last-line (cyanide, raises ICP); never SL nifedipine.
nodes.body: End-organ damage present → IV titratable therapy in PICU. [2,3,6] First-line (titratable infusions): | Drug | Dose | Notes | |------|------|-------| | Nicardipine | 0.5-3 mcg/kg/min IV infusion (start 0.5, titrate by 0.5 q5min) | Arterial-selective; preferred first-line; no rebound; safe with most renal/cardiac comorbidities | | Labetalol | Bolus 0.2-1 mg/kg IV (max 40 mg/dose) → infusion 0.25-3 m

nodes.title: Treatment: Hypertensive Urgency (Oral)
nodes.summary: Oral isradipine, amlodipine, or labetalol; reduce gradually; recheck at 1-2h; consult nephrology/cardiology; follow up within 1 week.
nodes.body: Asymptomatic severe HTN without end-organ damage → oral agent, gradual reduction. [1,2,6] Goal: Reduce BP by ≤25% in 8 hours, then gradually normalize over 24-48 hours. Same 25% rule applies even though risk lower. Oral options: | Drug | Dose | Onset | |------|------|-------| | Isradipine | 0.05-0.1 mg/kg/dose PO q6-8h | 1-2h | | Amlodipine | 0.1-0.3 mg/kg/day PO (max 10 mg/day) | Slow (peak days)

nodes.title: Monitoring During Treatment
nodes.summary: Watch for over-shoot (AMS, oliguria) and under-shoot (persistent symptoms); art line BP if on drip; transition to oral with 4-6h overlap.
nodes.body: Watch for over-shoot and under-shoot during BP reduction. [3,6] Signs of TOO RAPID reduction (back off the drip): - New confusion, somnolence - Pallor, diaphoresis - New focal neuro deficit - Decreased UOP - Reflex tachycardia (especially with hydralazine, nifedipine) Signs of INADEQUATE reduction (escalate): - Persistent severe HTN at 1-2h - Worsening symptoms - New end-organ damage signs Monitor

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on severity and response: [2,3]

nodes.title: PICU Admission
nodes.body: PICU criteria: [2,3] - Hypertensive emergency (any end-organ damage) - IV antihypertensive infusion required - Encephalopathy, seizure, or PRES - AKI requiring close monitoring or dialysis - LV failure / pulmonary edema - Possible coarctation or pheochromocytoma PICU management: - Arterial line for continuous BP - IV antihypertensive drip (nicardipine, labetalol, clevidipine) - Hourly neuro checks
nodes.recommendation: Admit to PICU with arterial line, IV antihypertensive infusion, hourly neuro checks, and pediatric nephrology consult.

nodes.title: Floor / Step-Down Admission
nodes.body: Floor criteria: [2,6] - Hypertensive urgency requiring monitored oral therapy - Stable on oral regimen after ED initiation - Transitioning down from IV therapy - Awaiting completion of secondary cause workup - No active end-organ damage Floor management: - Telemetry - BP q1h × 4h, then q2-4h - Scheduled oral antihypertensive - Renal/cardiac labs daily - Pediatric nephrology consult Escalation crit
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor with telemetry, oral antihypertensive therapy, and pediatric nephrology consultation.

nodes.title: Discharge with Rapid Follow-up
nodes.body: Discharge criteria (rare in ED for severe HTN — most need admission): [1,6] - Asymptomatic, no end-organ damage - BP responsive to single oral agent in ED with sustained reduction - Reliable family with transportation and home BP cuff - Confirmed outpatient follow-up within 1 week - No suspected secondary cause requiring urgent workup - Already known to nephrology/cardiology with chronic HTN Disch
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if asymptomatic, BP controlled on oral agent, reliable family, and follow-up within 1 week. Most severe peds HTN warrants admission.

nodes.title: Pediatric Osteomyelitis - Clinical Recognition
nodes.summary: AHO peak at 12-24mo; empiric abx within 1h if ill-appearing; cultures before abx but do not delay treatment
nodes.body: Osteomyelitis Quick Reference - key clinical pearls. Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis (AHO) is the most common form of bone infection in children. Peak incidence occurs at ages 12-24 months. [1,2] Definitions: [1] - Acute: Symptoms <4 weeks in previously uninfected bone - Subacute: Symptoms 1-3 months, often insidious - Chronic: >3 months or relapse after treatment; often has sequestrum Key princi

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Infants: pseudoparalysis, irritability; toddlers: limp, Kingella predominates; school-age: localized bone pain, metaphyseal tenderness
nodes.body: Typical presentation varies by age: Infants (<12 months): - Pseudoparalysis (refusal to move limb) - Irritability when handled - May lack fever - Higher risk of joint involvement (transphyseal vessels) [2] Toddlers/Preschool (1-5 years): - Limp or refusal to bear weight - Localized pain, swelling, warmth - Fever (present in ~78% of AHO) [4] - *Kingella kingae* predominates in this age group [5] Sc

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis vs Osteomyelitis
nodes.summary: Kocher criteria: fever, NWB, ESR >40, WBC >12k; osteomyelitis and septic arthritis can coexist especially in infants
nodes.body: Kocher Criteria help distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis (originally validated for the hip): [6,7] 1. Fever (history of temp >38.5C) 2. Non-weight bearing 3. ESR >40 mm/hr 4. WBC >12,000/mcL Caird modification adds: CRP >20 mg/L [7] Probability of septic arthritis: - 0 criteria: <0.2% - 1 criterion: 3% - 2 criteria: 40% - 3 criteria: 93% - 4 criteria: 99.6% [6] Key clinical point

nodes.title: Concurrent Septic Arthritis
nodes.summary: Septic arthritis is ortho emergency; WBC >50k in synovial fluid; send Kingella PCR for age <5yr; emergent joint washout
nodes.body: Septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency requiring urgent drainage to prevent cartilage destruction and growth disturbance. [6,8] Joint aspiration findings suggesting septic arthritis: - WBC >50,000/mcL (often >100,000) - >90% PMNs - Low glucose - Positive Gram stain (40-70% sensitive) [8] Management: - Emergent orthopedic consultation - Joint washout/arthrotomy (especially hip) - Empiric antib

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.body: Certain populations have unique pathogen considerations that affect empiric antibiotic selection. [1,10,11]

nodes.title: Sickle Cell - Osteomyelitis Considerations
nodes.summary: Sickle cell: Salmonella + S. aureus; immunocompromised: broad spectrum + fungi; puncture wound: Pseudomonas
nodes.body: Salmonella is disproportionately common in sickle cell patients due to functional asplenia and bowel ischemia. [10,11] Pathogen distribution in SCD osteomyelitis: - *Salmonella* spp: 50-80% - *S. aureus*: 25-35% - Other gram-negatives: 10% [10] Diagnostic challenge: Bone infarction (vaso-occlusive crisis) mimics osteomyelitis. Key distinguishing features: - Fever >72 hours favors osteomyelitis - M

nodes.title: Immunocompromised Host
nodes.body: Broader pathogen spectrum in immunocompromised children: [1,12] - *S. aureus* (including MRSA) - Gram-negative bacilli (including *Pseudomonas*) - Fungi (*Aspergillus*, *Candida*) - Mycobacteria (especially in areas of high TB prevalence) Empiric regimen: - Broad-spectrum coverage including anti-pseudomonal agent - Consider antifungal coverage if neutropenic - ID consultation recommended Imaging:

nodes.title: Puncture Wound Osteomyelitis
nodes.body: Puncture wounds through footwear (especially rubber-soled shoes) carry specific risk for *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* osteomyelitis. [12] Typical presentation: - Puncture wound through shoe 1-3 weeks prior - Progressive pain, swelling of foot - Often involves small bones (metatarsals, calcaneus) Empiric coverage: - Must include anti-pseudomonal agent - Cefepime or Piperacillin-tazobactam - PLUS covera

nodes.title: Laboratory Workup
nodes.summary: CRP most useful for monitoring; blood cultures in ALL patients; WBC often normal; procalcitonin >2.0 specific for invasive infection
nodes.body: Recommended labs: [1,3,4] Inflammatory markers: - CRP: Most useful for monitoring response. May be normal early or in walled-off *S. aureus* infections. Peaks at 2-4 days, normalizes in 9-12 days with appropriate treatment. [3,4] - ESR: Less dynamic; remains elevated longer. Useful baseline. - Procalcitonin: >2.0 ng/mL highly specific for invasive bacterial infection. [3] WBC count: Often normal (

nodes.title: Imaging Strategy
nodes.summary: MRI gold standard (97% sensitive); X-ray changes take 10-14 days; bone scan for multifocal screening; US detects subperiosteal abscess
nodes.body: Imaging modalities: [1,8,13] Plain radiographs: - First-line, but insensitive early - Changes (periosteal reaction, lytic lesions) take 10-14 days - Rule out fracture, tumor MRI (gold standard): - 97% sensitive, 92% specific [13] - Detects bone marrow edema, abscess, subperiosteal collections - Best for defining extent and surgical planning Bone scan (Tc-99m): - Useful when MRI unavailable or for

nodes.title: MRI Findings in Osteomyelitis
nodes.body: Characteristic MRI findings: [1,8,13] T1-weighted: - Decreased signal in affected bone marrow - Loss of normal fatty marrow signal T2-weighted / STIR: - Increased signal (edema) - Best for detecting extent of involvement Contrast-enhanced: - Rim-enhancing abscess - Non-enhancing areas suggest necrosis - Subperiosteal collections Features requiring surgical intervention: - Subperiosteal abscess - I

nodes.title: Alternative Imaging Strategy
nodes.body: When MRI is unavailable or child is unstable: Plain radiographs: - Obtain AP and lateral views - Look for soft tissue swelling (earliest sign) - Periosteal elevation, lytic changes appear >10-14 days [1] Ultrasound: - Detects subperiosteal fluid collections - Can guide aspiration - Limited for intraosseous pathology [8] Bone scan (Tc-99m MDP): - Sensitive within 24-48 hours of symptom onset - Usef

nodes.title: Multifocal Osteomyelitis
nodes.body: Multifocal AHO occurs in ~7% of cases. [1] Associated with: - Virulent pathogens (MRSA, PVL+ strains) - Disseminated infection - Immune compromise Imaging approach: - Bone scan (Tc-99m MDP): Best for whole-body screening - Follow with MRI of affected regions for detail - Consider PET/CT if occult malignancy a concern Higher morbidity: - Longer antibiotic courses - More surgical interventions - Gre

nodes.title: Pathogens by Age
nodes.summary: <3mo: S. aureus, GBS, gram-neg; 3mo-4yr: Kingella kingae predominant; >4yr: S. aureus most common overall
nodes.body: Most common pathogens by age group: [1,2,5,9] <3 months (Neonates): - *Staphylococcus aureus* - Group B *Streptococcus* - Gram-negative bacilli (*E. coli*, *Klebsiella*) 3 months - 4 years: - Kingella kingae (predominant in many regions) [5,9] - *Staphylococcus aureus* - *Streptococcus pyogenes* (GAS) >4 years: - *Staphylococcus aureus* (most common overall) - MRSA in areas with high prevalence -

nodes.title: MRSA Risk Assessment
nodes.body: Empiric antibiotic selection depends on local MRSA prevalence and individual risk factors. [1,3] MRSA risk factors: - Prior MRSA infection or colonization - Local community MRSA prevalence >10-15% - Recent hospitalization - Recurrent skin/soft tissue infections - Household contact with MRSA [1] MRSA osteomyelitis features: - More severe illness - Higher rates of DVT, pulmonary emboli - More surgic

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics - MRSA Coverage
nodes.body: First-line MRSA regimen: [1,3] Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q6h (max 60 mg/kg/day) - Trough goal: 15-20 mcg/mL for serious MRSA infections - Excellent bone penetration - Monitor renal function Alternative: Clindamycin 10-13 mg/kg IV q8h (max 40 mg/kg/day) - Good oral bioavailability for step-down - Check local D-test resistance rates - Avoid if D-test positive (inducible resistance) Add gram-negative co

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics - MSSA Coverage
nodes.body: First-line MSSA regimen: [1,3] Cefazolin 40 mg/kg IV q8h (max 6g/day) - Excellent MSSA coverage - Good bone penetration - Low risk of resistance induction Alternative: Nafcillin 50 mg/kg IV q6h - More narrow spectrum - Higher rates of phlebitis Transition to oral: Cephalexin 25-30 mg/kg PO q8h - Excellent bioavailability - First-line for oral step-down If cultures return MRSA: Escalate to vancomyc

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics - Age <4 Years
nodes.body: ***Kingella kingae* considerations:** [5,9] *K. kingae* is the most common pathogen in children 6 months - 4 years in many regions. [5] Characteristics: - Fastidious organism - standard cultures often negative - Requires PCR or enriched culture techniques - Mild clinical presentation (low-grade fever, modest CRP) - Excellent prognosis with appropriate treatment [5,9] K. kingae antibiotic sensitivi

nodes.title: Surgical Consultation Criteria
nodes.body: Orthopedic consultation is recommended for all cases of AHO. [1,14] Indications for urgent surgical intervention: [1,14] - Subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess - Sequestrum (dead bone) - Concurrent septic arthritis - Failure to improve after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics - Need for pathogen identification (bone biopsy) Role of surgery: - Drainage of abscess/pus - Debridement of necrotic

nodes.title: Surgical Management
nodes.body: Surgical procedures: [1,14] Bone aspiration/biopsy: - Fluoroscopic or ultrasound-guided - Obtain tissue for culture and histology - Consider if blood cultures negative Debridement: - Removal of necrotic bone and tissue - Curettage of abscess cavity - May require multiple procedures Drainage: - Subperiosteal abscess drainage - Joint washout if concurrent septic arthritis Considerations: - Minimize

nodes.title: Monitoring Treatment Response
nodes.body: Markers of clinical improvement: [1,3,4] Clinical: - Resolution of fever (typically 24-72 hours) - Decreased pain and swelling - Return of limb function - Improved appetite and activity Laboratory: - CRP: Most useful marker. Should decrease by 50% within 2-4 days of effective treatment. Return to normal in 9-12 days. [3,4] - ESR: Slower to respond; may remain elevated for weeks. Less useful for ac

nodes.title: Transition to Oral Therapy
nodes.summary: PIDS/IDSA: early oral transition safe; criteria: afebrile 24-48h, tolerating PO, CRP decreasing; typical IV 2-7 days
nodes.body: PIDS/IDSA guidelines recommend early transition to oral therapy. [1] Criteria for oral transition: [1,3] - Significant clinical improvement - Afebrile for 24-48 hours - Tolerating oral intake - CRP decreasing (by 50% or to <20-30 mg/L) - Reliable oral option based on pathogen/sensitivities - Compliant family, reliable follow-up Typical IV duration: 2-7 days (median 3-4 days in recent studies) [1]

nodes.title: Oral Antibiotic Options
nodes.body: Oral step-down regimens: [1,3] For MSSA: - Cephalexin 25-30 mg/kg PO q8h - High bioavailability, well-tolerated For MRSA (if susceptible): - Clindamycin 10-13 mg/kg PO q8h - 90% oral bioavailability - Check D-test sensitivity For MRSA (clindamycin-resistant): - Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg TMP PO q12h - PLUS Rifampin 10 mg/kg PO q12h - Rifampin should NOT be used as monotherapy For Kingel

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Determine appropriate level of care based on clinical status and treatment needs. [1]

nodes.title: Discharge on Oral Antibiotics
nodes.body: Discharge criteria met: - Afebrile >24-48 hours - Clinical improvement (decreased pain, improved mobility) - CRP decreasing or normalized - Tolerating oral intake - Oral antibiotic with appropriate spectrum available - Family demonstrates medication administration understanding - Follow-up arranged Discharge instructions: - Complete full antibiotic course (typically 3-4 weeks total) - Take antibio
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with oral antibiotics. Ensure follow-up with orthopedics and primary care. Total antibiotic duration 3-4 weeks.

nodes.title: Continue Inpatient Therapy
nodes.body: Continue hospital admission for: - Ongoing IV antibiotic therapy - Clinical monitoring - Pending culture results - Pain management - Surgical intervention if needed Daily assessment: - Fever curve - Pain score and analgesic requirements - Limb examination (swelling, erythema, range of motion) - CRP trending (every 2-3 days) Criteria for reassessment of surgical need: - No improvement after 48-72 h
nodes.recommendation: Continue inpatient IV antibiotics. Daily clinical and laboratory monitoring. Orthopedics consultation.

nodes.title: Outpatient Parenteral Therapy (OPAT)
nodes.body: OPAT may be appropriate when: [1] - Clinically improved but oral option not available/suitable - Stable for discharge - Reliable family and home infusion support - PICC line can be placed Common OPAT regimens: - Ceftriaxone 50-100 mg/kg IV q24h (once daily dosing) - Vancomycin via home infusion (requires monitoring) OPAT considerations: - PICC line care and monitoring - Weekly labs (CBC, CMP, drug
nodes.recommendation: OPAT with home IV therapy and close monitoring. Consider early transition to oral antibiotics when criteria met.

nodes.title: Pediatric SSTI — Initial Classification
nodes.summary: Classify: purulent (I&D) vs non-purulent (cellulitis) vs severe (admit) vs necrotizing (OR); bedside US ~98% sensitive for abscess.
nodes.body: Skin and soft tissue infections are among the most common pediatric ED visits. Community-associated MRSA (CA-MRSA) is now the dominant organism in many US regions. [1,2,3] Step 1 — Assess for red flags requiring immediate resuscitation: - Hemodynamic instability, septic appearance - Pain out of proportion to exam - Crepitus, skin discoloration (dusky, purple, bullae) - Rapid spread (advancing bord

nodes.title: Bedside Ultrasound for SSTI
nodes.summary: POCUS sens ~98% for abscess; linear probe; cobblestoning = cellulitis; gas in soft tissue = NSTI suspicion (get surgery NOW).
nodes.body: Point-of-care US (POCUS) outperforms physical exam for abscess detection — sensitivity 96-98%, specificity 79-89% (Subramaniam 2016, Adams 2016). [4,5] Technique pearls: [4,5] - High-frequency linear probe (5-12 MHz) - Generous gel; scan in 2 orthogonal planes - Compare to contralateral side for baseline - Use a standoff pad or copious gel for small/superficial collections Findings: | Finding | Im

nodes.title: Purulent SSTI — I&D Mainstay
nodes.summary: I&D for fluctuant lesions; routinely add abx after I&D in kids (Talan/Daum trials); culture purulent material; loop drainage for large/recurrent.
nodes.body: Incision and drainage is the cornerstone of abscess management. Adjunctive antibiotics improve cure rates and reduce recurrence (Talan NEJM 2016, Daum NEJM 2017). [6,7] Indications for I&D: any fluctuant lesion ≥5 mm (smaller lesions may respond to warm soaks alone). Technique pearls: [1,2] - Adequate analgesia (topical LMX → field block with buffered lidocaine + bicarb; consider intranasal fentan

nodes.title: Purulent SSTI — Empiric Antibiotic Selection
nodes.summary: TMP-SMX 4-6 mg/kg/dose BID (8-12 mg/kg/day) OR clindamycin 10 mg/kg/dose TID; 5-7 days; 48-72h recheck mandatory.
nodes.body: Coverage goal: CA-MRSA + MSSA. [1,3,6] First-line (oral): [1,6,7] Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 4–6 mg/kg/dose TMP component PO BID (8–12 mg/kg/day total) (max 160 mg TMP/dose) - Best CA-MRSA coverage in most US regions - Talan NEJM 2016: TMP-SMX after I&D ↓ failure rate vs placebo (NNT ~14) [6] - Avoid in infants <2 months (kernicterus risk), G6PD deficiency, sulfa allergy Alternative (oral): [1,

nodes.title: Purulent SSTI — Discharge Plan
nodes.body: Discharge criteria after I&D: [1,2] - Adequate drainage achieved - Reasonable pain control - No systemic signs (afebrile, normal vitals) - Reliable caregivers, ability to do wound care - Follow-up arranged Discharge instructions: - Antibiotic course as above - Wound care (packing removal at 24-48h OR loop drain instructions) - Warm compresses 3-4×/day after first 48h - Return for: spreading rednes
nodes.recommendation: Discharge post-I&D on TMP-SMX or clindamycin × 5–7 days. Wound care + 48–72h recheck. Decolonization if recurrent.

nodes.title: MRSA Decolonization Protocol
nodes.summary: Recurrent SSTI: mupirocin BID + chlorhex daily × 5d + bleach baths 2×/wk × 3mo; treat household; avoid systemic abx prophylaxis.
nodes.body: For recurrent SSTI (≥2 episodes within 6 months) — household decolonization reduces recurrence rates. [9] Index patient + all household members: [9] 1. Nasal mupirocin 2% ointment — pea-sized amount in each nare BID × 5 days 2. Chlorhexidine 4% body wash — daily × 5 days, neck-down, leave on 1 minute before rinsing 3. Bleach baths — 1/4 cup household bleach (6%) in full bathtub of water (~40 gallo

nodes.title: Non-Purulent Cellulitis — Pathogen & Coverage
nodes.summary: Cellulitis = strep predominant; IDSA: empiric anti-strep coverage WITHOUT routine MRSA add; mark borders + elevate + warm compresses.
nodes.body: Non-purulent cellulitis = erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness without fluctuance or drainage. Beta-hemolytic streptococci (especially GAS) are the most common cause; *S. aureus* is far less common in pure cellulitis. [1,10] IDSA 2014 recommendation: for typical non-purulent cellulitis in immunocompetent patients, empiric anti-streptococcal therapy is appropriate — MRSA coverage is NOT routine.

nodes.title: Non-Purulent Cellulitis — Antibiotic Selection
nodes.summary: Cephalexin 25-50 mg/kg/day QID for mild; cefazolin 50 mg/kg q8h IV for inpatient; add MRSA cover only if risk factors; 5-day course typical.
nodes.body: Outpatient PO regimen (mild-moderate, well-appearing): [1,3] Cephalexin 25–50 mg/kg/day PO divided q6h (QID) (max 4 g/day) - First-line for streptococcal cellulitis - Excellent bioavailability Alternative (penicillin-allergic, non-anaphylaxis): Cefadroxil 30 mg/kg/day PO BID. Severe penicillin allergy: Clindamycin 10 mg/kg/dose PO TID (also covers MRSA). Inpatient / unable to tolerate PO: [1] Cefa

nodes.title: Non-Purulent Cellulitis — Discharge Plan
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: [1,2] - Well-appearing, afebrile, tolerating PO - Reliable caregivers and follow-up - Pain controlled - Border marked; baseline image (or marker outline) for comparison Return precautions: - Spreading erythema beyond marked border - New fever or worsening systemic symptoms - Severe pain out of proportion - Vomiting / unable to tolerate medication - Drainage of pus or new fluctu
nodes.recommendation: Discharge on cephalexin × 5 days. Mark borders, elevate, warm compresses. 48–72h recheck mandatory.

nodes.title: Erysipelas — A Specific Variant
nodes.summary: Erysipelas = sharply demarcated raised border, GAS predominant; penicillin V or amoxicillin first-line; NO MRSA add unless risk factors.
nodes.body: Erysipelas is a superficial dermal cellulitis with characteristic features that distinguish it from typical cellulitis. [1,10] Classic findings: - Sharply demarcated, raised border (vs cellulitis: poorly demarcated, flat) - Bright red ("flame-red") color - Often face (cheek, butterfly distribution) or lower extremity - Rapid onset over hours - Systemic symptoms common (fever, chills, malaise) - Ly

nodes.title: Severe SSTI — Admit + IV Antibiotics
nodes.summary: IV ceftriaxone + clindamycin baseline; add vanc for severe MRSA risk; linezolid for vanc-intolerant; source control urgent.
nodes.body: Criteria for admission: [1,2] - Toxic-appearing, hemodynamic instability - Failure of outpatient therapy - Inability to tolerate PO - Extensive area / rapid progression - Immunocompromised, neonate, or age <6 months - Concern for deep space involvement (orbit, neck, perineum) - Concurrent bacteremia or abscess requiring drainage Initial workup (severely ill): [1,2] - Blood cultures × 2 before anti

nodes.title: Severe SSTI — Admit / ICU Disposition
nodes.body: Admit: general pediatric ward for stable patients on IV antibiotics, source-controlled. ICU criteria: - Septic shock requiring pressors - Concern for necrotizing infection (see Module 5) - Multi-organ involvement - Need for emergent surgical intervention - Respiratory compromise (deep neck infection, orbital cellulitis with airway concerns) Consults: - Pediatric ID (severe, MRSA, immunocompromised
nodes.recommendation: Admit on IV ceftriaxone + clindamycin (add vancomycin if MRSA-severe). ICU if hemodynamic instability or nec fasc concern.

nodes.title: Necrotizing Fasciitis — Time-Critical
nodes.summary: PAIN out of proportion + rapid spread + systemic toxicity = NSTI; LRINEC POOR sensitivity in peds; vanc+pip-tazo+clinda within 1h; emergent OR.
nodes.body: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Mortality 20–40% even with treatment; doubles with each hour of delay to OR. [12,13] Suspect when: [12,13,14] - Pain out of proportion to visible skin findings (HALLMARK) - Rapid progression (advance of erythema over hours) - Skin findings disproportionately mild EARLY (vs systemic toxicity) - Crepitus, bullae (especially hemorrhagic), skin discolorat

nodes.title: Necrotizing Fasciitis — Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition: OR → PICU. Pre-op checklist (parallel, not sequential): - Surgery at bedside - Type & cross 2 units PRBC - Aggressive fluid resuscitation underway - Antibiotics given (vanc + pip-tazo + clinda) - IVIG dose prepared if STSS suspected - Family briefed on guarded prognosis - ICU bed arranged Post-op care: - Plan for 2nd-look at 24h - Hyperbaric oxygen therapy — controversial; consider if
nodes.recommendation: OR EMERGENTLY. Vanc + pip-tazo + clinda within 1 hour. ICU admission. Plan repeat OR at 24h. Consider IVIG for STSS.

nodes.title: Special Sites & Mimics
nodes.body: Anatomic location often dictates a different pathway: [1,18]

nodes.title: Periorbital vs Orbital Cellulitis
nodes.summary: Preseptal = no proptosis/EOM/vision change; orbital = proptosis/EOM restriction/vision change → CT + IV abx + ENT/ophtho. Most orbital from ethmoid sinusitis.
nodes.body: Critical distinction — orbital cellulitis is a sight- and life-threatening emergency. [18,19] Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis: anterior to orbital septum. - Lid swelling, erythema, tenderness - NO proptosis, NO EOM restriction, NO pain with eye movement, NO vision change - Often from local trauma, insect bite, sinusitis, conjunctivitis - Most common organisms: *S. aureus*, GAS, *S. pneumoniae*

nodes.title: Perianal / Perineal Infections
nodes.summary: Perianal abscess common in infants <2yr; I&D + abx in this group; recurrent abscess/fistula in older child → think Crohn disease.
nodes.body: Perianal abscess is most common in infants (<2 years), boys >> girls. [20] Workup: [20] - Examine in lateral or knee-chest position - Most are superficial (intersphincteric) and amenable to bedside I&D - Deep abscesses (ischiorectal, supralevator) require OR drainage — get surgery involved Antibiotics: [1,20] - Routine post-I&D abx in infants <2 years (high MRSA prevalence + immature immunity) - C

nodes.title: Lemierre Syndrome & Deep Neck Infections
nodes.summary: Lemierre = adolescent + sore throat → IJ thrombosis + septic pulmonary emboli (Fusobacterium); CT neck contrast; pip-tazo+metronidazole 4-6 wks.
nodes.body: Lemierre syndrome = septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically from *Fusobacterium necrophorum* oropharyngeal infection. Adolescents and young adults disproportionately affected. [21,22] Classic story: [21] - Adolescent with sore throat 4–7 days ago that "got better" - Now: neck pain (especially along SCM), fever, rigors, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain (septic pulmonary embol

nodes.title: SSTI Mimics — Don't Miss
nodes.body: Cellulitis is over-diagnosed. Common mimics: [10,23] Contact dermatitis — bilateral, pruritic > painful, well-demarcated to allergen exposure (poison ivy, jewelry, soap). NO fever, NO systemic signs. Stasis dermatitis — adolescents on prolonged sitting; bilateral lower legs; chronic; venous insufficiency in obesity. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) — unilateral leg swelling, warmth, tenderness; risk fac
nodes.recommendation: Reconsider diagnosis if bilateral, lacks fever/systemic signs, fails antibiotic therapy at 48–72h, or has features suggesting alternative dermatologic/vascular pathology.

nodes.title: STEC/HUS Overview
nodes.summary: STEC causes 5-15% HUS progression; peak age <5yr; HUS triad: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI; onset days 5-10
nodes.body: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) is a leading cause of acute kidney injury in children. [1] Key epidemiology: - Peak incidence: children <5 years old - Most common serotype: O157:H7 (but non-O157 increasing) - Seasonal peak: summer months (May-September) - 5-15% of STEC cases progress to HUS [1,2] HUS Triad: [2] 1. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) 2. Thrombocytopenia (<150,000/µL) 3. A

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Watery then bloody diarrhea; HUS: pallor, petechiae, oliguria; severe: anuria >24h, WBC >20k, CNS involvement
nodes.body: Prodromal phase (STEC colitis): [1,2] - Watery diarrhea → bloody diarrhea (60-90%) - Severe abdominal cramping - Nausea/vomiting - Low-grade or no fever (distinguishes from other bacterial causes) - Duration: 3-8 days HUS phase: [2,3] - Pallor, fatigue (anemia) - Petechiae, bruising (thrombocytopenia) - Decreased urine output (AKI) - Edema, hypertension - Irritability, lethargy Severe HUS features

nodes.title: Exposure Sources
nodes.summary: Ground beef, unpasteurized dairy, raw veggies; petting zoos; person-to-person (10-100 organisms); reportable disease
nodes.body: Common exposure sources: [1,4] Food-borne (most common): - Undercooked ground beef (hamburger disease) - Raw/unpasteurized milk and cheese - Raw vegetables (lettuce, spinach, sprouts) - Apple cider (unpasteurized) - Contaminated water Animal contact: - Petting zoos - Farm visits - Direct cattle/livestock exposure Person-to-person: - Daycare outbreaks - Household contacts - Fecal-oral transmission

nodes.title: STEC Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Shiga toxin EIA most important test; culture alone misses 50%; baseline CBC, BMP, LDH, retic, haptoglobin for HUS monitoring
nodes.body: Essential labs: [1,5] Stool studies: - Stool culture on sorbitol-MacConkey agar (O157) - Shiga toxin EIA (detects Stx1 and Stx2) - MOST IMPORTANT - Stool PCR for Shiga toxin genes (if available) Blood work (baseline for HUS monitoring): - CBC with smear (look for schistocytes) - BMP (creatinine, BUN, electrolytes) - LDH (elevated in hemolysis) - Reticulocyte count - Haptoglobin (decreased in hemol

nodes.title: HUS Monitoring Protocol
nodes.summary: Daily CBC/BMP/LDH days 5-10; early HUS signs: Hgb drop >2, platelets <150k, LDH rising, oliguria; admit if any lab abnormality
nodes.body: All confirmed/suspected STEC cases require close monitoring for HUS development. [2,3] High-risk monitoring schedule (days 5-10 post-diarrhea onset): | Day | Labs | Clinical Check | |-----|------|----------------| | Daily | CBC, BMP, LDH, retic | Urine output, weight, BP | Early HUS warning signs: [3] - Hemoglobin drop >2 g/dL - Platelet drop >50% or <150,000 - LDH rising (>2x normal) - Creatinine

nodes.title: Evolving HUS Workup
nodes.body: Patient with early/evolving HUS features requires aggressive workup. [2,3] Confirm HUS triad: 1. Anemia: Hgb <10, with schistocytes on smear, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin 2. Thrombocytopenia: Platelets <150,000 3. AKI: Creatinine elevated above baseline for age Additional workup: [5] - Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen) - usually normal in typical HUS - Complement studies (C3, C4, AH50

nodes.title: STEC Colitis Management
nodes.summary: Supportive care only; aggressive IV fluids (goal UOP 1-2 mL/kg/hr); acetaminophen for pain; avoid NSAIDs and opioids
nodes.body: Management goals: [1,2] - Supportive care - Avoid interventions that increase HUS risk - Close monitoring for HUS development Fluid management: - Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation - Maintain euvolemia (key to reducing HUS severity) - Goal: UOP 1-2 mL/kg/hr - D5NS or D5LR at 1.5x maintenance Diet: - NPO initially if severe vomiting - Advance to clear liquids → bland diet as tolerated - Avoid lactos

nodes.title: The Antibiotic Controversy
nodes.summary: Do NOT give antibiotics (may increase HUS risk); do NOT give antimotility agents (contraindicated in bloody diarrhea)
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Antibiotics for STEC are CONTROVERSIAL and generally NOT recommended. [1,2,6] Why avoid antibiotics: [6] - Meta-analyses show antibiotics may INCREASE HUS risk - Bacterial lysis releases more Shiga toxin - Quinolones and TMP-SMX most associated with risk - Even bactericidal antibiotics at sub-MIC can induce toxin 2024 AAP/IDSA position: [1] - Do NOT routinely give antibiotics for suspect

nodes.title: STEC Disposition
nodes.body: Based on clinical assessment, determine disposition for STEC colitis without current HUS features: [2]

nodes.title: Admission for STEC Monitoring
nodes.body: Admit for: - IV fluids and close monitoring - Daily CBC, BMP, LDH, reticulocyte count - Strict I/O with urine output tracking - Serial weights Nursing instructions: - Contact precautions - Notify MD immediately if: UOP <0.5 mL/kg/hr, new pallor, new petechiae/bruising, altered mental status, seizure Anticipated length of stay: - Minimum 5-7 days (through HUS risk window) - Longer if HUS develops C

nodes.title: Discharge with Follow-up
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: [2] - Tolerating adequate oral fluids - Normal or stable hemoglobin - Normal platelets - Normal creatinine - Normal urine output - Reliable family with transportation Discharge instructions: - Return precautions: decreased urination, blood in urine, increased pallor, confusion, seizure, worsening abdominal pain - Strict hand hygiene - No school/daycare until cleared by health d
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with strict return precautions and daily lab monitoring through HUS risk window (Day 10-14).

nodes.title: HUS Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Mild: plt >100k, Cr <2x normal; severe: plt <50k, anuria, HTN, CNS involvement; WBC >20k and anuria predict poor outcome
nodes.body: Assess HUS severity to guide management intensity. [3,7] Mild HUS: - Platelets 100,000-150,000 - Creatinine <2x upper normal for age - Preserved urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/hr) - No hypertension - No CNS symptoms Moderate HUS: - Platelets 50,000-100,000 - Creatinine 2-4x upper normal - Oliguria but responsive to fluids - Mild hypertension - No CNS symptoms Severe HUS: - Platelets <50,000 - Anuria or

nodes.title: HUS Fluid Management
nodes.summary: Early aggressive fluids before anuria may prevent dialysis; once anuric restrict to insensible losses only; manage hyperK
nodes.body: Fluid management is critical in HUS. [2,7] Early/oliguric phase: - Aggressive volume expansion may improve outcomes if given early (pre-anuric phase) - Goal: maintain euvolemia, support renal perfusion - 20 mL/kg NS boluses as needed for dehydration - Once euvolemic: maintenance + insensible losses Anuric phase: - Strict fluid restriction (insensible losses only: 300-400 mL/m²/day) - Daily weights

nodes.title: Transfusion Guidelines
nodes.summary: RBC transfuse for Hgb <7; generally AVOID platelet transfusion (worsens thrombosis); FFP not indicated in typical HUS
nodes.body: RBC transfusion: [2,7] - Transfuse for symptomatic anemia or Hgb <7 g/dL - Use irradiated, leukoreduced PRBCs - Transfuse slowly (2-4 hours) to avoid volume overload - Target Hgb 8-9 g/dL (avoid overtransfusion) Platelet transfusion: [7] - Generally AVOID in typical HUS - Platelets may worsen microvascular thrombosis - Consider ONLY if: - Active life-threatening bleeding - Planned invasive procedu

nodes.title: Hypertension Management
nodes.summary: Amlodipine first-line oral; nicardipine IV for emergency; avoid ACEi/ARBs acutely (hyperK risk in AKI)
nodes.body: Hypertension is common in HUS and requires treatment. [3,7] Causes: - Volume overload - Renal failure with RAAS activation - Microangiopathic damage to renal vasculature Treatment approach: First-line (volume-dependent): - Fluid restriction - Dialysis/ultrafiltration if fluid overloaded Antihypertensive agents: [7] | Agent | Dose | Notes | |-------|------|-------| | Amlodipine | 0.1-0.5 mg/kg/day

nodes.title: Dialysis Indications
nodes.summary: 50-70% need dialysis; indications: anuria >24h, K >6.5, pH <7.1, volume overload, uremic encephalopathy; PD often preferred
nodes.body: ~50-70% of children with STEC-HUS require dialysis. [3,7] Dialysis indications: [7] - Anuria >24 hours - Severe hyperkalemia (K >6.5 or ECG changes) - Severe acidosis (pH <7.1, HCO3 <10) - Volume overload with pulmonary edema - Uremic encephalopathy - Severe hypertension refractory to medications - BUN >80-100 mg/dL Modality: [7] - Peritoneal dialysis often preferred in young children - Gentler he

nodes.title: CNS Complications
nodes.summary: CNS involvement in 20-30% and is major mortality cause; seizures most common; urgent neuroimaging and aggressive BP control
nodes.body: CNS involvement occurs in 20-30% of HUS and is the major cause of mortality. [3,8] CNS manifestations: - Irritability, lethargy - Seizures (most common) - Altered mental status, coma - Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) - Cortical blindness - Hemiparesis Pathophysiology: - Microangiopathic thrombosis in cerebral vessels - Direct Shiga toxin neurotoxicity - Hypertensive encephalopathy - Uremic enceph

nodes.title: Eculizumab in HUS
nodes.body: Eculizumab is FDA-approved for atypical HUS, NOT typical STEC-HUS. [5,8] What is eculizumab: - Monoclonal antibody against complement C5 - Blocks terminal complement activation - Highly effective in atypical HUS (complement-mediated) Use in STEC-HUS: [8] - NOT standard of care - Shiga toxin activates complement, providing theoretical rationale - Case reports/series of benefit in severe STEC-HUS -

nodes.title: Other HUS Complications
nodes.body: Monitor for and treat additional complications: [3,7] Cardiac: - Myocardial dysfunction (Shiga toxin effect) - Pericardial effusion - Arrhythmias (electrolyte-related) - Consider echo if hemodynamically unstable GI: - Colonic necrosis/perforation (surgical emergency) - Intussusception - Rectal prolapse - Pancreatitis (check lipase) - Hepatitis Hematologic: - Severe bleeding (rare) - DIC (usually n

nodes.title: HUS Disposition
nodes.body: Determine appropriate level of care for HUS patient: [3,7]

nodes.title: PICU Admission
nodes.body: PICU admission criteria: [3,7] - Dialysis required or anticipated - Severe hypertension requiring IV antihypertensives - CNS involvement (seizures, altered mental status) - Respiratory distress/pulmonary edema - Hemodynamic instability - Need for frequent blood products - Severe anemia (Hgb <6) - Surgical complications (bowel necrosis) PICU management: - Continuous cardiac monitoring - Arterial li
nodes.recommendation: Admit to PICU with nephrology and hematology consultation. Monitor for multiorgan complications.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor admission criteria: [2,7] - Stable vital signs - No dialysis indication (yet) - Manageable hypertension with oral agents - No CNS symptoms - Maintaining some urine output Floor management: - Strict I/O with q1h urine output - Daily weights - Cardiac monitor - Labs q12-24h (CBC, BMP, LDH, retic) - Nephrology consultation Escalation criteria (call rapid/transfer to PICU): - Anuria >12 hours -
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor with nephrology consultation and strict monitoring. Low threshold for PICU escalation.

nodes.title: HUS Prognosis & Follow-up
nodes.body: Outcomes of STEC-HUS: [3,7,8] Short-term: - Mortality: 1-3% (higher with CNS involvement) - Dialysis required: 50-70% - RBC transfusion required: 80%+ Long-term renal outcomes: - Complete recovery: 70-85% - CKD: 10-25% - ESRD: 3-5% - Hypertension: 10-20% - Proteinuria: 15-30% Risk factors for poor renal outcome: - Anuria >2 weeks - Dialysis >4 weeks - Age <2 years - Severe CNS disease Long-term fo

nodes.title: Pediatric Submersion Injury
nodes.summary: Leading injury death ages 1-4; submersion duration is key prognostic factor; <5min good, >10min poor; no "dry drowning" entity
nodes.body: Submersion Summary — resuscitation and disposition pathway. Drowning is the leading cause of injury death in children ages 1-4 and second leading cause ages 5-14. Key prognostic factors: • Submersion duration — most important predictor • Scene CPR and time to ROSC • Water temperature (cold water may be protective) • Initial GCS and pupil reactivity Critical thresholds: • <5 min submersion: general

nodes.title: Scene Information
nodes.summary: Obtain submersion duration, water type/temp, scene CPR, time to first breath; stratify by current status
nodes.body: Critical history to obtain: Submersion details: • Estimated duration of submersion • Water type (fresh vs salt, pool vs natural) • Water temperature • Witnessed or unwitnessed Rescue details: • Time to rescue and extrication • CPR at scene (bystander or EMS) • Time to first breath/pulse Pre-event: • Trauma (diving, fall)? • Seizure prior to event? • Underlying conditions? Non-accidental trauma red

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest Management
nodes.summary: Airway first: 5 rescue breaths before compressions; do NOT Heimlich; if cold <30C limit shocks to 3 and hold meds
nodes.body: Drowning cardiac arrest priorities: Airway first! Drowning is a respiratory emergency: 1. Clear airway of water/debris 2. 5 rescue breaths before compressions 3. Then standard PALS CPR 15:2 Do NOT attempt Heimlich — aspirated water cannot be expelled Defibrillation: • Initial rhythm usually asystole or PEA (hypoxic) • VF/pVT rare but shockable if present Hypothermia considerations: • If core temp

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest — Hypothermia Status
nodes.body: Assess core temperature: Mild hypothermia (32-35°C / 90-95°F): • Standard PALS, active rewarming • Medications at standard intervals Moderate hypothermia (28-32°C / 82-90°F): • May have bradycardia, AF — often self-correcting • Space medication dosing (double intervals) Severe hypothermia (<28°C / <82°F): • VF may be refractory • Limit to 3 defibrillation attempts until >30°C • Withhold IV medicat

nodes.title: Mild Hypothermia Management
nodes.summary: Mild 32-35C: standard PALS, active rewarming 1-2C/hr; moderate 28-32C: space med dosing; severe <28C: limit defib, consider ECMO
nodes.body: Mild hypothermia (32-35°C): Rewarming methods: • Remove wet clothing • Warm blankets, forced-air warming (Bair Hugger) • Warm IV fluids (38-42°C) • Warm humidified oxygen Expected rate: 1-2°C/hour with external methods Resuscitation: • Standard PALS medications and dosing • Active CPR — do not withhold • Defibrillation for VF/pVT Monitor for: • "Afterdrop" — core temp may drop during rewarming • R

nodes.title: Severe Hypothermia Management
nodes.summary: Not dead until warm and dead; ECMO gold standard for severe hypothermic arrest; limit defib to 3 until >30C; withhold meds until >30C
nodes.body: Severe hypothermia (<28°C) — "Not dead until warm and dead": Modified resuscitation: • Limit defibrillation to 3 attempts until temp >30°C • Withhold IV medications until temp >30°C • Continue high-quality CPR Rewarming priority: ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass (if available): • Gold standard for severe hypothermic arrest • Can rewarm at 9-10°C/hour • Consider transfer to ECMO center If ECMO unavailab

nodes.title: Resuscitation Outcome
nodes.body: Assess resuscitation progress: Favorable signs: • Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) • Return of brainstem reflexes • Any purposeful movement Poor prognostic indicators: • Submersion >25 min in warm water • CPR >25 min without ROSC (normothermic) • Asystole as initial rhythm (not hypothermic) • No pupillary response after rewarming • Initial blood pH <6.75 ILCOR guidance: No single predictor

nodes.title: Termination Considerations
nodes.body: Consider termination when: Multiple poor prognostic factors present: • Warm water submersion >25 minutes • Normothermic CPR >25 minutes without ROSC • Asystole as initial rhythm (without hypothermia) • pH <6.75 on initial ABG • Serum K+ >10 mEq/L Do NOT terminate if: • Core temperature <30°C (continue until rewarmed) • ECMO available and transfer possible • Any signs of life during resuscitation F

nodes.title: Post-Arrest Care
nodes.summary: Target SpO2 94-98% (avoid hyperoxia); TTM 32-34C for comatose; treat seizures aggressively; avoid hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia
nodes.body: Post-ROSC management priorities: Airway & Ventilation: • Maintain intubation, lung-protective ventilation • Target SpO2 94-98% (avoid hyperoxia) • Avoid hyperventilation (worsens brain injury) Circulation: • Target MAP for age-appropriate cerebral perfusion • Avoid hypotension • Consider vasopressors if needed Temperature management: • Targeted Temperature Management (TTM): — 32-34°C for 24-72 hou

nodes.title: ICU Monitoring & Complications
nodes.body: Monitor for complications: Pulmonary: • ARDS — may develop 24-72 hours post-submersion • Aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia • Bronchospasm Neurologic: • Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy • Cerebral edema — may worsen at 24-48 hours • Seizures (up to 30%) Metabolic: • Electrolyte disturbances (usually mild) — Fresh water: hyponatremia (rare) — Salt water: hypernatremia (rare) • Acidosis • Rhabdomyolysi

nodes.title: Critical Patient Disposition
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: Mandatory ICU admission: • Post-cardiac arrest • Intubated/mechanically ventilated • GCS <13 • Hemodynamic instability • Significant respiratory failure • Hypothermia requiring active rewarming Transfer to higher level of care if: • ECMO capability needed • Pediatric intensivist not available • Neurosurgical intervention anticipated Prognosis communication: • MRI at 3-5 day

nodes.title: Altered Mental Status
nodes.body: Patient with altered mentation post-submersion: Immediate assessment: • Airway: Protected? Gag intact? • Breathing: Hypoxic? Work of breathing? • Circulation: Perfusion, heart rate, BP Consider intubation if: • GCS ≤8 • Unable to protect airway • Severe hypoxia despite supplemental O2 • Anticipated deterioration Workup: • Continuous SpO2, cardiac monitoring • ABG/VBG • Glucose (hypoglycemia as cau

nodes.title: AMS Management Pathway
nodes.body: Assess severity and trajectory: Improving mental status: • Serial neuro exams Q15-30 min • Continuous monitoring • Supportive care Static or worsening: • Intubation for airway protection • Consider head CT • ICU admission Key interventions: • High-flow O2 or intubation if needed • Treat seizures: Lorazepam + AED load [11] • Avoid hyperthermia • Correct glucose abnormalities What is the clinical tr

nodes.title: Seizure Management
nodes.body: Post-submersion seizures: First-line: Lorazepam • 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) • May repeat x1 in 5 minutes Second-line: Levetiracetam • 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg) • OR fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg Refractory status: • Intubate if not already • Midazolam or propofol infusion • Neurology consultation Important considerations: • Seizures may be due to hypoxic-ischemic injury • Also consider: hypoglycemia, hyp

nodes.title: Respiratory Symptoms
nodes.body: Patient with respiratory symptoms, normal mentation: Common symptoms: • Cough (most common) • Dyspnea/tachypnea • Wheezing/crackles • Chest discomfort Assessment: • Vital signs including SpO2 on room air • Work of breathing • Auscultation (often abnormal initially) Workup: • SpO2 on room air • Consider CXR (often normal initially) • ABG/VBG if significant hypoxia Pathophysiology: • Surfactant wash

nodes.title: Respiratory Treatment
nodes.body: Supplemental oxygen and monitoring: Mild symptoms (SpO2 >94% on room air): • Supplemental O2 PRN • Observation 4-6 hours • Serial exams Moderate symptoms (SpO2 90-94%, mild distress): • Supplemental O2 to maintain SpO2 >94% • Consider CPAP/BiPAP • Prolonged observation or admission Severe symptoms (SpO2 <90%, significant distress): • High-flow O2 or NIPPV • Consider intubation if failing • ARDS-pr

nodes.title: Asymptomatic Patient
nodes.summary: Asymptomatic with GCS 15 and SpO2 >=95%: no delayed deterioration if truly asymptomatic; complications within 4-8 hours
nodes.body: Asymptomatic after submersion event: Good prognostic signs: • Normal mental status (GCS 15) • Normal respiratory exam • SpO2 ≥95% on room air • Normal vital signs • Brief submersion (<5 min) "Secondary drowning" myth: • No evidence for delayed deterioration in truly asymptomatic patients • Complications manifest within 4-8 hours if they occur • Patient symptomatic at >8 hours extremely unlikely to

nodes.title: ED Observation Criteria
nodes.summary: Observe 4-8h; safe discharge if asymptomatic throughout, normal SpO2 RA, normal resp exam, reliable caregiver
nodes.body: ED observation for low-risk patients: Observe for 4-8 hours if: • GCS 15, normal mentation throughout • SpO2 ≥95% on room air at 4-6 hours • Normal vital signs • No respiratory symptoms or symptoms resolving • Adequate home observation possible Safe discharge criteria at 4-8 hours: • Asymptomatic throughout observation • Normal SpO2 on room air • Normal respiratory exam • Reliable caregiver for ho

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.body: Admit for observation if: Clinical indicators: • Any persistent respiratory symptoms • Oxygen requirement (even minimal) • Abnormal chest X-ray • GCS <15 at any point • Prolonged submersion (>5 min) • Required CPR at scene • Concerning trajectory during ED observation Disposition options: Floor/Observation unit: • Stable vitals, improving • Minimal O2 requirement • GCS 14-15 ICU: • GCS <14 • Signi

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.body: Safe for discharge if ALL present: Clinical criteria: • Normal mental status throughout • SpO2 ≥95% on room air at 4-6 hours • Normal respiratory exam • No persistent symptoms • Normal or unchanged chest X-ray (if obtained) Social criteria: • Reliable caregiver present • Able to return within 1 hour if needed • Understanding of return precautions • No child safety concerns Discharge instructions:

nodes.title: Pediatric Trauma: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Children NOT small adults; larger occiput, faster desaturation, BP drops late (>25-30% blood loss); use weight-based dosing for all meds
nodes.body: Pediatric Trauma Steps Summary - stepwise approach. Children are NOT small adults. Anatomic and physiologic differences affect injury patterns, clinical presentation, and management. Key pediatric differences: - Airway: Larger occiput causes neck flexion; smaller airway diameter; anterior/cephalad larynx - Breathing: Higher metabolic rate = faster desaturation; chest wall more compliant = pulmonar

nodes.title: Weight Estimation & Equipment Sizing
nodes.summary: Broselow tape gold standard; cuffed ETT = (age/4)+3.5; fluid bolus 20 mL/kg; blood products 10-20 mL/kg
nodes.body: Weight estimation is critical - all pediatric resuscitation is weight-based. Broselow Tape: Gold standard for weight estimation in resuscitation. Measures length and provides weight-based zone with drug doses, equipment sizes. Weight estimation formulas (if Broselow unavailable): - Infants (0-12 mo): (age in months + 9) / 2 kg - Children 1-5 yr: (age x 2) + 8 kg - Children 6-12 yr: (age x 3) + 7 k

nodes.title: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
nodes.summary: ABCDE with peds modifications; tachycardia is early, hypotension is LATE; intubate if GCS <=8; aggressive warming
nodes.body: A - Airway: Position (sniffing position or pad under shoulders in infants due to large occiput). Suction secretions/blood. Jaw thrust if c-spine concern. Consider early intubation if GCS <=8, inability to protect airway, or anticipated deterioration. B - Breathing: Higher RR baseline. Inspect for asymmetry, paradoxical movement. Auscultate. Chest wall is compliant - pulmonary contusion can occur W

nodes.title: Secondary Survey & Injury Pattern
nodes.body: Head-to-toe examination with full exposure. Head/Face: Palpate scalp for hematomas, lacerations, depressions. Check pupils, TM for hemotympanum. Facial stability. Neck: C-spine tenderness (if verbal). Tracheal deviation. JVD. Crepitus. Chest: Rib tenderness (high-energy if fractured). Breath sounds. Heart sounds. Abdomen: Distension, tenderness, guarding. Seatbelt sign (associated with hollow visc

nodes.title: Pediatric Hemorrhage Control
nodes.body: Pediatric blood volume: 70-80 mL/kg (higher in neonates ~85-90 mL/kg). A 10 kg child has only ~700-800 mL total blood volume - what appears to be "minor" bleeding can be catastrophic.
