nodes.title: Pediatric Transfusion Thresholds
nodes.summary: MTP 1:1:1 ratio; TXA 15 mg/kg within 3h; calcium replacement with transfusion; permissive hypotension NOT for TBI
nodes.body: Transfusion trigger in trauma: Hgb <7-8 g/dL (or ongoing hemorrhage regardless of Hgb). Blood product dosing (weight-based): - pRBCs: 10-15 mL/kg (expect ~1 g/dL Hgb rise per 3 mL/kg) - FFP: 10-15 mL/kg - Platelets: 5-10 mL/kg - Cryoprecipitate: 1-2 units/10 kg (for fibrinogen <150) Massive Transfusion Protocol (pediatric): - Ratio 1:1:1 (pRBC:FFP:Platelets by volume) - Consider TXA early: 15 mg/k

nodes.title: Pediatric Head Trauma: Overview
nodes.summary: TBI leading cause of pediatric trauma death; use PECARN for mild TBI imaging; high NAT suspicion in infants with SDH
nodes.body: TBI is the leading cause of death in pediatric trauma. Anatomic differences affect injury patterns: Pediatric-specific considerations: - Larger head-to-body ratio --> head more likely to be injured in falls/MVC - Thinner calvarium --> less protection, but skull fractures more common - Brain less myelinated --> more susceptible to diffuse axonal injury - Open fontanelles/sutures (infants) --> can a

nodes.title: Head Trauma Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Mild GCS 14-15: PECARN; moderate GCS 9-13: CT + observe; severe GCS <=8: intubate + CT + ICU + neurosurgery
nodes.body: Pediatric GCS modifications: Verbal response for preverbal children: - 5: Coos, babbles, appropriate crying - 4: Irritable, crying - 3: Cries to pain - 2: Moans to pain - 1: No response Classification: - Mild TBI: GCS 14-15 (use PECARN for imaging decision) - Moderate TBI: GCS 9-13 (CT indicated, observation vs admission) - Severe TBI: GCS 3-8 (intubate, CT, ICU, neurosurgery) Red flags requiring

nodes.title: PECARN Head CT Decision Rule
nodes.summary: PECARN: <2yr check skull fx, AMS, LOC >=5s, severe mechanism; >=2yr check basilar fx signs, AMS, LOC, vomiting, severe HA
nodes.body: PECARN criteria for children with GCS 14-15 after blunt head trauma. Age <2 years - CT indicated if ANY of: - GCS <15 - Palpable skull fracture - Altered mental status (agitation, somnolence, repetitive questioning, slow response) - Loss of consciousness >=5 seconds - Severe mechanism (MVC with ejection/death/rollover, pedestrian/cyclist vs vehicle, fall >3 feet, head struck by high-impact object)

nodes.title: Mild TBI Disposition
nodes.body: Mild TBI (GCS 14-15) with negative CT or low-risk by PECARN: Discharge criteria: - GCS returns to 15 and stable - No persistent vomiting - Reliable caregiver with return precautions - Can be observed at home Return precautions (give written instructions): - Worsening headache not relieved by acetaminophen/ibuprofen - Repeated vomiting (>2 episodes) - Increasing confusion or difficulty arousing - S
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with written head injury instructions. Return precautions for worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, seizure, clear fluid from nose/ears, weakness, unequal pupils. PCP follow-up in 1-2 weeks. No contact sports until medically cl

nodes.title: Moderate TBI Management (GCS 9-13)
nodes.summary: Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; HOB 30; CT head STAT; neurosurgery for EDH, SDH >5mm, depressed skull fx; admit 24h minimum
nodes.body: Moderate TBI requires CT imaging and close observation. Initial management: 1. ABCs with c-spine precautions 2. Avoid hypoxia (SpO2 >94%) and hypotension 3. Head of bed elevated 30 degrees (if no spinal injury) 4. CT head without contrast - STAT 5. Consider CT c-spine or MRI if clearing difficult CT findings requiring neurosurgical consultation: - Epidural hematoma (any size) - Subdural hematoma >

nodes.title: Severe TBI Management (GCS <=8)
nodes.summary: GCS <=8 = INTUBATE; 3% saline 3-5 mL/kg for herniation; normoventilation PaCO2 35-40; target CPP >40-50 mmHg
nodes.body: GCS <=8 = INTUBATE. Severe TBI is a neurosurgical emergency. Airway management: - RSI with c-spine inline stabilization - Video laryngoscopy preferred - Avoid hypoxia and hypotension during intubation - Target ETCO2 35-40 mmHg (avoid hyperventilation unless herniating) ICP management: - HOB 30 degrees, head midline - Normoventilation (PaCO2 35-40) - Avoid hyperthermia (target normothermia) - Hyper

nodes.summary: Compliant chest = contusion without rib fx; rib fx = HIGH energy; seatbelt sign = hollow viscus injury; FAST less sensitive in peds

nodes.body: Hemodynamically unstable abdominal trauma = surgical emergency. Immediate actions: 1. Massive transfusion protocol activation 2. Pediatric surgery/trauma surgery STAT 3. Prepare for emergent laparotomy 4. nodes.title: Pediatric Chest Trauma
nodes.summary: Rib fx in kids = high energy; tension PTX: needle decompression; hemothorax >15 mL/kg initial = consider thoracotomy
nodes.body: Chest trauma in children is less common but can be rapidly fatal. nodes.title: Pediatric Orthopedic Trauma
nodes.summary: Physis is weakest point; Salter-Harris fractures; greenstick/buckle unique to kids; always consider NAT in non-ambulatory children
nodes.body: Pediatric bones are different: - Physis (growth plate) is the weakest point --> Salter-Harris fractures - More porous, elastic bone --> greenstick, buckle (torus) fractures - Thicker periosteum --> remodeling potential is excellent - Growth disturbance can occur with physeal injuries Unique pediatric fracture patterns: - Greenstick: Incomplete fracture, one cortex intact - Torus (buckle): Compress

nodes.title: Salter-Harris Classification
nodes.summary: SALTR: I=Slipped, II=Above, III=Lower (intra-articular), IV=Through, V=cRush; III-V need ORIF and have growth arrest risk
nodes.body: SALTR mnemonic for physeal fractures: | Type | Description | Mnemonic | Prognosis | |------|-------------|----------|-----------| | I | Through physis only | Slipped | Good | | II | Through physis + metaphysis | Above | Good | | III | Through physis + epiphysis (intra-articular) | Lower | Guarded | | IV | Through metaphysis + physis + epiphysis | Through | Poor | | V | Crush injury to physis | cRu

nodes.title: Compartment Syndrome in Children
nodes.summary: Clinical diagnosis; pain out of proportion + passive stretch pain most reliable; 3 As in kids: anxiety, agitation, increasing analgesics
nodes.body: Compartment syndrome is a CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS. Do not wait for pressure measurement. Classic 6 Ps (late signs - do not wait for all): - Pain out of proportion (especially with passive stretch) - Pressure (tense compartment) - Paresthesias - Pulselessness (late) - Pallor (late) - Paralysis (late) Pediatric challenges: - Children may not articulate symptoms well - "3 As" in children: Anxiety, Agitati

nodes.title: Disposition Planning
nodes.body: Trauma center transfer criteria (pediatric-specific): Transfer to Pediatric Trauma Center if: - GCS <14 or declining GCS - Intubated or requiring airway intervention - Multisystem trauma - Solid organ injury grade III or higher - Pelvic fracture with hemodynamic instability - Spinal cord injury or unstable spine fracture - Penetrating trauma to head, neck, torso - Significant burns (>10% TBSA, fac

nodes.title: Trauma Center Transfer
nodes.body: Stabilize before transfer. Do not delay transfer for non-essential interventions. Pre-transfer checklist: - Airway secured if needed (intubate before transport if any concern) - Two large-bore IVs or IO access - Ongoing resuscitation as needed - C-spine immobilized - Chest tubes placed if indicated (do not clamp) - Foley catheter if abdominal/pelvic trauma - NG/OG tube if indicated - All imaging s
nodes.recommendation: Stabilize and transfer to Pediatric Trauma Center. Secure airway before transport if any concern. Ensure ongoing resuscitation during transport. Direct MD-to-MD report to receiving facility.

nodes.title: Admission to Local Hospital
nodes.body: Admission criteria and monitoring: Admit to ICU if: - GCS <14 - Hemodynamically unstable or required significant resuscitation - Solid organ injury grade III+ - Chest trauma requiring chest tube - Intubated - Multiple injuries Admit to floor if: - Stable with isolated injury - Low-grade solid organ injury for observation - Isolated fracture requiring pain management - Head injury requiring observa
nodes.recommendation: Admit to appropriate level of care based on injury severity. Serial exams and labs as indicated. Early subspecialty involvement. DVT prophylaxis if immobilized.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria & Instructions
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: - Hemodynamically stable - Pain controlled with oral medications - No concerning examination findings - Reliable caregiver who understands return precautions - Follow-up arranged Discharge instructions should include: - Specific injury diagnosed - Medications prescribed with weight-based dosing - Activity restrictions (time-specific when possible) - Signs/symptoms requiring imm
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with written injury-specific instructions, return precautions, and follow-up appointments. Ensure caregiver understanding before discharge.

nodes.title: Non-Accidental Trauma (NAT) Evaluation
nodes.summary: TEN-4-FACESp rule for concerning bruising; skeletal survey mandatory <2yr; CPS reporting is mandated — do not need certainty
nodes.body: High index of suspicion for NAT in pediatric trauma. TEN-4-FACESp rule - bruising concerning for abuse: - Torso bruising - Ear bruising - Neck bruising - In children <4 years or any age non-mobile - Frenulum injury - Angle of jaw - Cheeks - Eyelids - Subconjunctival hemorrhage - In pre-mobile infants (any bruising) Red flags: - Injury inconsistent with developmental stage - Changing or inconsisten

nodes.title: NAT Reporting & Documentation
nodes.body: Mandatory reporting requirements: Healthcare providers are mandated reporters. If you suspect abuse, you MUST report. You do not need certainty. Report to: - Child Protective Services (CPS) - state-specific hotline - Law enforcement if immediate danger - Hospital child protection team/social work Documentation (critical for legal proceedings): - Detailed history (use quotes when possible) - Who pr
nodes.recommendation: Mandatory reporting to CPS. Thorough documentation with quotes and photos. Do not discharge to suspected abuser. Hospital social work and child protection team involvement.

nodes.title: Pelvic Fracture Management
nodes.summary: Mortality 5-16% (50% if unstable); do NOT rock pelvis; activate MTP if unstable; mechanism predicts fracture pattern
nodes.body: Pelvic Fracture Steps Summary — quick reference for trauma resuscitation. High-energy pelvic fractures are potentially life-threatening injuries with mortality rates of 5-16% (up to 50% in hemodynamically unstable patients). [1][2] Immediate priorities: • Primary survey (ATLS) • Establish two large-bore IVs • Type and crossmatch • Activate massive transfusion protocol if unstable • Do NOT rock the

nodes.title: Physical Examination
nodes.summary: Assess stability ONCE (do not repeat); check for urethral injury BEFORE Foley; perineal laceration = open fracture
nodes.body: Pelvic instability assessment (perform ONCE — repeated exam disrupts clots): • Gentle AP compression at iliac crests • Gentle lateral compression • Leg length discrepancy • Rotational deformity Signs of urethral injury (evaluate BEFORE Foley placement): • Blood at urethral meatus • High-riding or boggy prostate on DRE • Scrotal or perineal hematoma/ecchymosis • Inability to void Other findings: •

nodes.title: Initial Imaging
nodes.summary: AP pelvis in trauma series; FAST for hemoperitoneum; CT with contrast is gold standard for stable patients; symphysis >2.5cm = unstable
nodes.body: AP Pelvis X-ray: • Part of trauma series (chest, pelvis, C-spine) • Identifies gross instability, pubic symphysis diastasis, sacral fractures • Pubic symphysis >2.5 cm = significant instability FAST Exam: • Evaluates for free fluid (hemoperitoneum) • Positive FAST in unstable patient → OR for laparotomy • Negative FAST does NOT rule out pelvic hemorrhage (retroperitoneal) CT Pelvis with IV Contras

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Status
nodes.summary: Classify stable, transient responder, or unstable; hemodynamic status drives entire management pathway
nodes.body: Assess hemodynamic stability to guide management pathway. Stable: SBP >90 mmHg, HR <100, responsive to initial crystalloid Transient responder: Initial response to fluids but recurrent hypotension Unstable: SBP <90 mmHg despite resuscitation, HR >120, signs of shock WSES Pelvic Trauma Grade Calculator

nodes.title: Unstable Patient — Immediate Actions
nodes.summary: Apply pelvic binder at greater trochanters immediately; TXA 1g IV if <3h from injury; activate MTP
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Apply pelvic binder immediately if not already done. Pelvic Binder Indications: • Hemodynamic instability with pelvic fracture • Clinical or radiographic evidence of pelvic instability • APC (open book) or VS injury patterns • Any unstable patient with high-energy mechanism Binder Placement: • Position at level of greater trochanters (NOT iliac crests) • Tighten until pelvis is reduced t

nodes.title: Identify Hemorrhage Source
nodes.summary: FAST positive = likely intra-abdominal source; FAST negative = retroperitoneal pelvic hemorrhage (90% venous, 10% arterial)
nodes.body: FAST exam result determines next step: Positive FAST (free intraperitoneal fluid): • Likely intra-abdominal hemorrhage source • May have concurrent pelvic bleeding Negative FAST: • Hemorrhage likely retroperitoneal (pelvic source) • 90% of pelvic hemorrhage is venous • 10% arterial — requires angioembolization Pelvic Hemorrhage Source Calculator

nodes.title: FAST Positive — Emergent Laparotomy
nodes.body: Unstable patient with FAST positive → OR for laparotomy. Intraoperatively: • Control intra-abdominal hemorrhage first • Damage control surgery principles • Consider preperitoneal pelvic packing if pelvic bleeding continues • External fixation can be applied in OR Sequence if concurrent pelvic and abdominal hemorrhage: 1. Laparotomy for abdominal hemorrhage control 2. Preperitoneal packing (extrape
nodes.recommendation: Emergent laparotomy. Consider preperitoneal packing and external fixation intraoperatively. Angioembolization post-op if arterial bleeding persists.

nodes.title: FAST Negative — Pelvic Hemorrhage
nodes.body: Hemorrhage source is likely pelvic (retroperitoneal). Management depends on injury pattern and available resources: Venous bleeding (90% of cases): • Responds to pelvic binder + resuscitation • Preperitoneal packing if refractory Arterial bleeding (10%): • Identified by contrast blush on CT (if obtained) • Requires angioembolization Decision point: Does patient respond to binder + resuscitation?

nodes.title: Responding to Resuscitation
nodes.body: Continue current management: • Maintain pelvic binder • Continue MTP until targets met • Obtain CT pelvis with IV contrast when stable CT findings guide next steps: • No contrast blush → continue supportive care • Contrast blush → angioembolization Resuscitation targets: • SBP >90 mmHg (permissive hypotension in trauma) • Hgb >7-8 g/dL • Platelets >50,000 • INR <1.5 • Fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL • L

nodes.title: Refractory Hemorrhage
nodes.body: Options for refractory pelvic hemorrhage: Preperitoneal Pelvic Packing (PPP): • Rapidly controls venous bleeding • Can be performed bedside or in OR • Effective within 20-30 minutes • Packs placed in space of Retzius Angioembolization: • Targets arterial bleeding (contrast blush on CT) • Requires angiography suite availability • May take 1-2 hours to complete • 80-100% success for arterial hemorrh

nodes.title: Preperitoneal Pelvic Packing
nodes.body: Procedure: • Midline or Pfannenstiel incision • Stay extraperitoneal (do NOT enter peritoneum) • Pack space of Retzius with laparotomy pads • 3 packs per side, directed toward SI joints • Apply external fixation if available • Close fascia loosely, leave skin open Expected outcomes: • 80-90% hemostasis for venous bleeding • Mean blood loss reduction: 50% • Pack removal in 24-48 hours If bleeding c
nodes.recommendation: Emergent preperitoneal packing. Consider external fixation. Proceed to angioembolization if arterial bleeding persists.

nodes.title: Angioembolization
nodes.body: Indications: • Contrast blush on CT angiography • Ongoing hemorrhage despite binder + resuscitation • Hemodynamically stable enough for transport Technique: • Selective internal iliac artery embolization • Bilateral embolization if diffuse bleeding • Coils or gelfoam depending on vessel size Success rate: 80-100% for arterial hemorrhage Complications: • Gluteal necrosis (rare with selective emboli
nodes.recommendation: Emergent angioembolization for arterial pelvic hemorrhage. Continue MTP during procedure.

nodes.title: REBOA Placement
nodes.body: Zone 3 REBOA for pelvic hemorrhage: Placement: • Common femoral artery access (7-12 Fr sheath) • Advance balloon to Zone 3 (infrarenal aorta, above bifurcation) • Confirm position with portable X-ray • Inflate balloon to occlude aorta Physiology: • Increases central perfusion pressure • Reduces distal hemorrhage • Buys time for definitive control Limitations: • Target inflation <30 min, max 60 min
nodes.recommendation: Zone 3 REBOA as bridge to definitive hemorrhage control. Target <30 min, max 60 min total occlusion (per 2025 AAOS hemorrhage control update). Proceed urgently to PPP or angioembolization.

nodes.title: Transient Responder
nodes.body: Initial response then recurrent hypotension suggests ongoing hemorrhage. Immediate actions: • Apply/tighten pelvic binder • Activate MTP if not already done • TXA if <3h from injury • Obtain CT if brief stability window allows Close monitoring required: • May convert to stable or unstable category • Serial reassessment q15-30 min • Low threshold for intervention If deteriorates → treat as hemodyna

nodes.title: Hemodynamically Stable — Complete Workup
nodes.body: Proceed with comprehensive imaging: • CT pelvis with IV contrast (arterial and delayed phases) • CT abdomen if indicated • CT cystogram if bladder injury suspected Assess for associated injuries: • Bladder injury: 5-10% of pelvic fractures • Urethral injury: 5-25% in males • Rectal injury: 1-5% • Lumbosacral plexus injury: variable Classification guides management: • Young-Burgess classification (

nodes.title: Fracture Classification
nodes.summary: Young-Burgess (mechanism-based) and Tile (stability-based) guide management; LC/APC/VS/CM each have distinct bleeding profiles
nodes.body: Choose classification system: Young-Burgess — mechanism-based, predicts bleeding risk: • LC (Lateral Compression) • APC (Anterior-Posterior Compression) • VS (Vertical Shear) • CM (Combined Mechanism) Tile — stability-based, guides surgical decision: • Type A: Stable • Type B: Rotationally unstable, vertically stable • Type C: Rotationally and vertically unstable Young-Burgess Calculator Tile Clas

nodes.title: Lateral Compression (LC) Injuries
nodes.summary: LC: side impact, lower bleeding risk; caution with binder (may worsen LC); LC-III windswept = highly unstable
nodes.body: Mechanism: Side impact (T-bone MVC, fall onto side) LC-I: • Transverse pubic rami fractures • Sacral compression (anterior) fracture • Stable — often non-operative LC-II: • LC-I + posterior iliac wing fracture (crescent fracture) • Rotationally unstable • May require fixation LC-III: • LC-I or LC-II ipsilateral • Contralateral APC (windswept pelvis) • Highly unstable — operative Bleeding risk: Low

nodes.title: Anterior-Posterior Compression (APC) Injuries
nodes.summary: APC: frontal impact, open book; HIGH bleeding risk; pelvic binder HIGHLY effective; APC-III = complete SI disruption
nodes.body: Mechanism: Frontal impact (head-on MVC, crush injury) APC-I: • Pubic symphysis diastasis <2.5 cm • Anterior SI ligaments intact • Stable — often non-operative APC-II: • Symphysis diastasis >2.5 cm • Anterior SI ligaments torn, posterior intact • "Open book" — rotationally unstable • Requires fixation APC-III: • Complete SI disruption (anterior + posterior) • Rotationally and vertically unstable •

nodes.title: Vertical Shear (VS) Injuries
nodes.summary: VS: axial load, highest bleeding risk, complete ligament disruption; always operative; may need traction plus binder
nodes.body: Mechanism: Axial load (fall from height, motorcycle ejection) Characteristics: • Vertical displacement of hemipelvis • Complete disruption of all pelvic ligaments • Highest bleeding risk of all patterns • Associated with L5 transverse process fractures Findings: • Leg length discrepancy (affected side shortened) • Hemipelvis displaced cranially • Often involves sacral fractures Management: • Alway

nodes.title: Combined Mechanism (CM) Injuries
nodes.body: Mixed patterns combining LC, APC, and/or VS elements. Common combinations: • LC + VS (lateral impact with axial load) • APC + VS (frontal with axial) • Bilateral injuries with different patterns Characteristics: • Complex, unpredictable bleeding patterns • Often require individualized surgical approach • High associated injury rate Management principles: • Treat as unstable • Early orthopedic cons

nodes.title: Management Based on Classification
nodes.body: Tile Classification guides operative decision: Type A (Stable): • LC-I, isolated rami fractures • Weight-bearing as tolerated • Rarely requires surgery Type B (Rotationally Unstable): • APC-II, LC-II • External fixation or ORIF • Internal rotation injuries may not need binder Type C (Completely Unstable): • APC-III, VS, LC-III • Definitive ORIF required • May need staged approach What is the injur

nodes.title: Stable Fracture Management
nodes.body: Tile A / Mechanically stable fractures: Treatment: • Weight-bearing as tolerated with assistive device • Pain control (multimodal analgesia) • DVT prophylaxis • Physical therapy Typical patterns: • Isolated pubic rami fractures • Avulsion fractures • Transverse sacral fractures without displacement Follow-up: • Orthopedic follow-up in 1-2 weeks • Repeat imaging only if symptoms worsen • Expected h
nodes.recommendation: Conservative management with weight-bearing as tolerated. Multimodal analgesia. DVT prophylaxis. Orthopedic follow-up.

nodes.title: Rotationally Unstable (Tile B)
nodes.body: Rotationally unstable, vertically stable fractures: Surgical options: • Symphyseal plating (APC-II with >2.5 cm diastasis) • Percutaneous SI screw fixation • External fixation (temporary or definitive) Indications for surgery: • Symphysis diastasis >2.5 cm • Sacral fracture with displacement • Associated acetabular fracture • Open fracture Timing: • Damage control: external fixation acutely • Defi
nodes.recommendation: Orthopedic consultation for surgical planning. External fixation if acute stabilization needed. Definitive ORIF when patient stable.

nodes.title: Completely Unstable (Tile C)
nodes.body: Rotationally AND vertically unstable — requires operative fixation. Acute management: • Pelvic binder (maintain) • Skeletal traction if vertical shear component • External fixation as bridge Definitive surgical options: • Anterior symphyseal plating • Posterior SI screw fixation • Posterior tension band plating • Spinopelvic fixation (for highly comminuted sacral fractures) Staged approach typical
nodes.recommendation: Emergent orthopedic consultation. Damage control stabilization acutely. Definitive ORIF when patient stable.

nodes.title: Urogenital Injury Assessment
nodes.summary: Evaluate BEFORE Foley: blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, scrotal/perineal hematoma, inability to void
nodes.body: Evaluate for urethral and bladder injury before Foley placement. Signs of urethral injury (evaluate BEFORE Foley): • Blood at urethral meatus • High-riding prostate on DRE (males) • Scrotal hematoma/ecchymosis • Perineal hematoma (butterfly pattern) • Inability to void • Pelvic fracture pattern (symphysis diastasis, pubic rami) Urethral Injury Risk Calculator Are signs of urethral injury present?

nodes.title: Foley Placement Safe
nodes.body: No signs of urethral injury — proceed with Foley catheterization. After Foley placement: • Note gross hematuria (bladder injury indicator) • Monitor urine output • If gross hematuria → CT cystogram Bladder injury evaluation: • Occurs in 5-10% of pelvic fractures • Higher risk with pubic rami fractures, symphysis diastasis • CT cystogram is gold standard

nodes.title: Urethral Injury Suspected
nodes.summary: Do NOT attempt blind Foley; RUG first if urethral signs present; complete disruption requires suprapubic catheter
nodes.body: DO NOT attempt blind Foley placement. Retrograde Urethrogram (RUG) Indications: • Blood at urethral meatus • High-riding prostate • Scrotal/perineal hematoma • Unable to void with full bladder RUG Procedure Guide RUG Interpretation: • Normal → proceed with gentle Foley attempt • Extravasation → suprapubic catheter • Partial tear → may attempt gentle single Foley attempt by experienced provider • C

nodes.title: RUG Result
nodes.body: What does the retrograde urethrogram show? Normal RUG findings: • Contrast fills entire urethra • No extravasation • Contrast enters bladder Abnormal findings: • Extravasation at bulbar urethra → anterior injury • Extravasation at membranous urethra → posterior injury (pelvic fracture-related) • Complete disruption — no contrast reaches bladder

nodes.title: Normal RUG — Proceed with Foley
nodes.body: RUG shows intact urethra. Proceed with gentle Foley placement: • Single attempt only • If resistance encountered → do not force • Use appropriate size catheter (16-18 Fr typical) • Consider coudé tip if prostatic enlargement After successful Foley: • Evaluate for bladder injury if gross hematuria • CT cystogram if hematuria present

nodes.title: Partial Urethral Tear
nodes.body: Extravasation with some contrast reaching bladder = partial tear. Options: Option 1 — Single gentle Foley attempt: • By experienced provider only • If passes easily → leave in place for 2-3 weeks • If any resistance → abort and place suprapubic Option 2 — Suprapubic catheter: • Safer option • Allows urethra to heal • Requires imaging guidance or surgical placement Urology consultation required. Lo
nodes.recommendation: Urology consultation. Consider single gentle Foley attempt by experienced provider OR suprapubic catheter. Follow-up imaging.

nodes.title: Complete Urethral Disruption
nodes.body: No contrast reaches bladder = complete urethral tear. DO NOT attempt Foley — place suprapubic catheter. Suprapubic catheter placement: • Ultrasound-guided percutaneous (if bladder distended) • Open surgical placement (if bladder not visible) • Place above pubic symphysis in midline Management: • Urology consultation (emergent) • Suprapubic catheter decompresses bladder • Definitive repair delayed
nodes.recommendation: Emergent suprapubic catheter. Do NOT attempt urethral catheterization. Urology consultation. Delayed urethroplasty in 3-6 months.

nodes.title: Bladder Injury Evaluation
nodes.body: Assess for bladder injury: Risk factors: • Pubic rami fractures (bone fragments can lacerate bladder) • Symphysis diastasis • Gross hematuria on Foley placement CT Cystogram technique: • Retrograde fill bladder with 300-350 mL dilute contrast • CT with filled bladder • Post-void images Is gross hematuria present?

nodes.title: CT Cystogram Results
nodes.body: CT cystogram findings: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture: • Contrast in paracolic gutters, around bowel loops • Usually at bladder dome (weakest point) • Requires surgical repair Extraperitoneal bladder rupture: • Contrast in perivesical space (flame-shaped) • Usually at bladder base/neck • Usually managed non-operatively What does the cystogram show?

nodes.title: Intraperitoneal Bladder Rupture
nodes.body: Contrast in peritoneal cavity — requires surgical repair. Mechanism: • Blunt trauma to distended bladder • Rupture at dome (weakest point) • Urine leaks into peritoneal cavity → chemical peritonitis Surgical repair: • Primary closure in 2-3 layers • Can often be done laparoscopically • Foley drainage for 7-14 days post-op Complications of delayed/missed diagnosis: • Peritonitis • Sepsis • Electrol
nodes.recommendation: Emergent surgical repair of intraperitoneal bladder rupture. Urology consultation. Foley drainage 7-14 days post-op.

nodes.title: Extraperitoneal Bladder Rupture
nodes.body: Contrast in perivesical space — usually managed non-operatively. Non-operative management: • Foley catheter drainage for 10-14 days • Antibiotics if concerned for infection • Repeat cystogram before catheter removal Indications for surgical repair: • Bladder neck injury • Bone fragments in bladder • Concomitant vaginal or rectal injury • Planned pelvic ORIF (repair at same time) • Failure of non-o
nodes.recommendation: Non-operative management with Foley drainage x 10-14 days. Surgical repair if bladder neck involved, bone fragments present, or at time of pelvic ORIF.

nodes.title: No Bladder Injury
nodes.body: No evidence of bladder injury. Continue standard pelvic fracture management: • Foley to gravity drainage • Monitor urine output • Pain control • DVT prophylaxis Proceed to definitive fracture management planning.

nodes.title: Definitive Management Summary
nodes.body: Management pathway determined by: • Hemodynamic status (WSES Grade) • Fracture stability (Tile classification) • Associated injuries (bladder, urethra, rectum) Key decision points: • OR vs conservative • Timing of definitive fixation • Need for additional interventions What is the primary management pathway?

nodes.title: Conservative Management
nodes.body: Stable pelvic fracture — non-operative treatment. Inpatient management: • Weight-bearing as tolerated with assistive device • Multimodal pain control • DVT prophylaxis (LMWH preferred, mechanical if bleeding) • Physical therapy evaluation • Bowel regimen (opioids + immobility = constipation) Discharge criteria: • Ambulatory with assistive device • Pain controlled with oral medications • Stable hem
nodes.recommendation: Weight-bearing as tolerated. Multimodal analgesia. DVT prophylaxis. Orthopedic follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Operative Management
nodes.body: Unstable pelvic fracture requiring surgical fixation. Timing considerations: • Damage control (acute): External fixation, traction • Definitive ORIF: When patient optimized (typically day 5-14) Surgical approaches: • Anterior: Pfannenstiel, ilioinguinal, Stoppa • Posterior: Prone positioning, percutaneous SI screws • Combined: For complex injuries Fixation options: • Symphyseal plating (APC injuri
nodes.recommendation: Orthopedic surgical fixation. Timing based on patient stability. Post-op DVT prophylaxis and early mobilization.

nodes.title: Post-Damage Control — Staged ORIF
nodes.body: Damage control completed — planning staged definitive fixation. Current interventions in place: • Pelvic binder or external fixation • ± Preperitoneal packing (remove in 24-48h) • ± Post-angioembolization Optimization goals before ORIF: • Lactate normalizing • Temperature >36°C • pH >7.2 • INR <1.5 • Platelets >50,000 • No active hemorrhage Typical ORIF timing: Day 5-14 If preperitoneal packs in p
nodes.recommendation: ICU optimization. Remove preperitoneal packs at 24-48h. Definitive ORIF when physiology normalized (typically day 5-14).

nodes.title: Pelvic Pain, Female Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Vitals, pregnancy test, hemorrhage risk, torsion/PID/TOA, surgical abdomen, and urinary causes first.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy \u2014 positive \u03B2-hCG + pain/shock; pregnancy test on everyone. 2. Ovarian torsion \u2014 sudden severe unilateral pain, nausea, adnexal mass. 3. Tubo-ovarian abscess / severe PID \u2014 fever, CMT, sepsis. 4. Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst with hemoperitoneum \u2014 sudden pain, free fluid, falling H/H. 5. Non-gyn surgical abdomen (appendic

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Pregnancy/ectopic, torsion, PID/TOA, ruptured cyst, surgical abdomen, urinary disease, postpartum/procedure, OHSS/ART, assault/trauma, non-pregnant bleeding, and postmenopausal lanes are first exclusions.
nodes.body: Choose the most dangerous lane first. You can return after the immediate action.

nodes.title: Pregnant Until Ectopic Is Excluded
nodes.body: Open First Trimester Emergencies when early pregnancy is possible. Immediate actions: IV access, type and screen/cross if unstable, CBC, quantitative beta-hCG, Rh status, bedside pelvic US when available, formal transvaginal US, OB/GYN early when unstable or ectopic suspected. Key ED rule: an indeterminate ultrasound does not exclude ectopic pregnancy. Do not use beta-hCG below a discriminatory zo
nodes.recommendation: Pain plus positive pregnancy test is ectopic until safely explained.

nodes.title: Ovarian / Adnexal Torsion
nodes.body: Classic pattern: sudden unilateral pelvic pain, nausea/vomiting, adnexal tenderness or mass, intermittent episodes, pregnancy, cyst, fertility treatment, or adolescent patient. Fever and leukocytosis may be absent. Torsion is not a reproductive-age-only diagnosis. Roughly 15% of cases are pediatric/premenarchal and roughly 15% are postmenopausal; 10-25% of all torsion occurs in pregnancy (81% of t
nodes.recommendation: High-suspicion torsion gets OB/GYN consultation even with Doppler flow present.

nodes.title: PID / Tubo-Ovarian Abscess
nodes.body: Open Pelvic Inflammatory Disease. PID minimum threshold: pelvic/lower abdominal pain with no better cause plus cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness. Treat empirically when the clinical threshold is met. CDC 2021 minimum criteria, verbatim intent: presumptive treatment is indicated for a patient with pelvic or lower abdominal pain, no cause other than PID can be identified, and at least
nodes.recommendation: Do not wait for NAAT results to treat clinically suspected PID when minimum criteria are met.

nodes.title: Ruptured Hemorrhagic Cyst / Hemoperitoneum
nodes.body: Sudden unilateral pain, pain after exertion/intercourse, peritoneal irritation, free pelvic fluid, anticoagulation, or falling hemoglobin suggests hemorrhagic cyst rupture or another bleeding source. Actions: pregnancy test to exclude ectopic, IV access, CBC trend, type and screen if significant pain/free fluid/instability, analgesia, pelvic ultrasound, OB/GYN if unstable, persistent peritoneal si
nodes.recommendation: Rule out ectopic and trend physiology before calling this benign cyst pain.

nodes.title: Appendicitis / Surgical Abdomen / GI Mimics
nodes.body: Open Appendicitis - Adult or the broader Abdominal Pain Hub when the pattern is not gynecologic. Appendicitis, diverticulitis, bowel obstruction, perforation, and inflammatory bowel complications can present as pelvic pain. Migration, anorexia, peritoneal signs, persistent vomiting, focal RLQ/LLQ tenderness, or systemic illness should pull the workup beyond gynecology. Imaging: choose US first whe
nodes.recommendation: A pelvic exam diagnosis should not override peritoneal signs or surgical-abdomen physiology.

nodes.title: Urinary / Renal Lane
nodes.body: Open UTI-Adult when infection fits. Consider: pyelonephritis, infected stone, renal colic, urinary retention, urethritis/cervicitis overlap. Fever with obstruction, solitary kidney, pregnancy, AKI, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, or sepsis physiology needs escalation. UA can be contaminated by vaginal bleeding/discharge. Interpret with symptoms, microscopy, culture, and imaging when stone/obstruction
nodes.recommendation: Do not miss infected obstructing stone or pyelonephritis masquerading as pelvic pain.

nodes.title: Postpartum / Post-Procedure Pain
nodes.body: Recent delivery, miscarriage management, abortion, IUD procedure, hysteroscopy, laparoscopy, or pelvic surgery changes the differential. Danger lanes: hemorrhage, retained products, endometritis, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, uterine perforation, bowel/bladder injury, ovarian vein thrombosis, wound/abscess, and PE/vascular disease. Use vitals, bleeding amount, fever, peritoneal signs, lactate if
nodes.recommendation: Postpartum or procedural pelvic pain deserves a lower threshold for OB/GYN involvement and imaging.

nodes.title: Assisted Reproduction / OHSS Lane
nodes.body: Open Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome for the full pathway. Ovulation induction, IVF, or recent oocyte retrieval changes three things at once: 1. Torsion risk climbs - roughly 6-16% in severe OHSS. Enlarged, cyst-laden ovaries torse. Keep the torsion lane open even if the pain sounds like "expected" post-retrieval discomfort. 2. Thrombosis risk climbs - VTE risk is 10-100x baseline in OHSS, inclu
nodes.recommendation: In an ART patient, pelvic pain means torsion, VTE, and heterotopic pregnancy are all live until excluded.

nodes.title: Assault / Trauma / Forensic Lane
nodes.body: Open Drug-Facilitated Sexual Assault Workup for the forensic and prophylaxis pathway, Human Trafficking when exploitation is suspected, and Pregnancy Trauma when the patient is pregnant. Medical stabilization comes before evidence collection. Blunt or penetrating pelvic trauma can produce pelvic fracture with retroperitoneal hemorrhage, bladder/urethral injury, vaginal laceration, or uterine injur
nodes.recommendation: Stabilize first, then run the forensic, prophylaxis, reporting, and safety-planning package.

nodes.title: Non-Pregnant Bleeding / AUB Lane
nodes.body: Open Abnormal Uterine Bleeding or the Vaginal Bleeding Hub. First confirm the pregnancy test is truly negative before you commit to a non-pregnant framework. A point-of-care urine test can be falsely negative in very early pregnancy or with dilute urine. Hemodynamics drive urgency: tachycardia, orthostasis, syncope, or a falling hemoglobin with heavy bleeding is a resuscitation problem regardless
nodes.recommendation: Treat heavy non-pregnant bleeding by physiology first, then sort the gynecologic cause.

nodes.title: Postmenopausal Pelvic Pain
nodes.body: Torsion still happens here. Roughly 15% of adnexal torsion occurs in postmenopausal patients. Do not treat menopause as a rule-out for torsion, and do not treat a normal Doppler as a rule-out either. Any postmenopausal bleeding is malignancy-until-proven-otherwise and requires endometrial evaluation, not ED reassurance. Arrange gynecologic follow-up explicitly and document it. Adnexal mass in a po
nodes.recommendation: Postmenopausal pelvic pain widens the differential toward malignancy and vascular disease without closing the torsion lane.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Pregnancy test, analgesia, targeted labs, pelvic exam when useful, ultrasound/CT by lane, then repeat exam.
nodes.body: Default ED bundle: - Pregnancy test, vitals trend, IV access if moderate/severe pain or any bleeding/instability. - Analgesia and antiemetic early. Pain response does not rule out torsion, ectopic, or surgical disease. - CBC, CMP as indicated; UA/culture by urinary symptoms; GC/CT testing and wet prep when PID/cervicitis possible. - Pelvic exam when it changes care and patient consents. - Bedside

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Persistent or worsening pain after initial care should widen the differential, not narrow it.
nodes.body: Repeat vitals and abdominal/pelvic exam after analgesia, fluids, antiemetics, and first imaging/labs.

nodes.title: Imaging Strategy
nodes.summary: US first for pregnancy/gynecologic suspicion, CT for non-gynecologic surgical disease, MRI selectively.
nodes.body: Pregnancy positive or pregnancy possible: pelvic US first for IUP/ectopic/free fluid; OB involvement for indeterminate but concerning cases. Gynecologic source likely, beta-hCG negative: transabdominal plus transvaginal pelvic US with Doppler is usually first-line. Do not use normal Doppler flow to exclude torsion when suspicion is high. Non-gynecologic source likely: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV con

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit dangerous physiology or surgical/OB/GYN concerns. Discharge only with diagnosis, improvement, and return precautions.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on physiology, pregnancy status, diagnostic certainty, pain control, and follow-up reliability.

nodes.title: Admit / Consult / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit, transfer, or consult urgently for suspected ectopic pregnancy, torsion, TOA/severe PID, sepsis, surgical abdomen, large hemoperitoneum, unstable vitals, pregnancy complication, immunocompromise with infection, failed outpatient therapy, inability to tolerate PO, uncontrolled pain, or persistent diagnostic uncertainty with concerning exam. Named CDC hospitalization criteria for PID: a surgic
nodes.recommendation: Do not discharge unresolved high-risk pelvic pain just because initial imaging is equivocal.

nodes.title: Observation / Serial Exam
nodes.body: Observe when pain is improving but diagnosis remains uncertain, ultrasound is pending/equivocal, hemoglobin or vitals require trend, pregnancy of unknown location needs a plan, or serial abdominal exams will determine CT/surgical consultation.
nodes.recommendation: Observation is appropriate when the initial snapshot does not safely explain the pain.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when vitals are stable, pregnancy/ectopic risk has an explicit plan, pain is controlled, PO tolerated, abdominal/pelvic exam is non-peritoneal, dangerous causes have been addressed, and follow-up is realistic. Return now for: worsening pain, syncope, shoulder pain, heavy bleeding, fever, vomiting, new discharge, positive pregnancy test without follow-up, dizziness, or inability to t
nodes.recommendation: Document pregnancy status, repeat exam, diagnostic lane, follow-up timing, and return precautions.

nodes.title: Penile Zipper Entrapment — Overview
nodes.summary: Zipper anatomy: slider, median bar, teeth, faceplates — each technique targets one of these
nodes.body: Steps Summary Foreskin or penile shaft skin caught in a zipper slider. Common in uncircumcised boys (commando, rushed dressing) and intoxicated adults. Disproportionately distressing — calm + analgesia first, then technique selection. Goal: release skin with the least trauma. Most cases are managed at bedside without urology consult. [1,2,3] Zipper anatomy (every technique exploits one of these):

nodes.title: Red Flags Before You Touch the Zipper
nodes.summary: Urethral bleeding, skin avulsion, or vascular compromise → urology BEFORE manipulation
nodes.body: Screen for findings that require urology / plastics BEFORE any release attempt.

nodes.title: Stop — Urology / Plastics Now
nodes.summary: Urethral bleeding, skin avulsion, or vascular compromise → no manipulation, urology now
nodes.body: Findings suggest urethral injury, significant skin loss, or vascular compromise. ED bedside release is contraindicated.
nodes.recommendation: IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: • Do NOT attempt zipper release • Cover wound with saline-moistened gauze • Pain control + IV access • Urinalysis, consider retrograde urethrogram if urethral injury suspected • Urology consult (plastics if large skin avu

nodes.title: Bedside Assessment
nodes.summary: Age, slider position, skin viability, swelling, time elapsed drive technique + analgesia choice
nodes.body: Verify before pain control: [1,2,3] • Age + cooperation (pediatric vs adult) • Exact location of entrapped skin (foreskin most common) • Position of the slider along the teeth (proximal/distal to skin) • Skin viability — pink and intact vs dusky • Swelling around the entrapment site • Time since entrapment (>2 hr → more edema, harder to release) Document a brief NV exam of the glans and shaft. Com

nodes.title: Pain Control Strategy
nodes.summary: Adults → topical/local; anxious or swollen → penile block; uncooperative peds → sedation
nodes.body: Choose the lowest-acuity option that will let you work without forcing patient movement.

nodes.title: Topical / Local Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Topical 2% lidocaine x10 min, then small subdermal wheals of plain 1% lidocaine if needed
nodes.body: Sequence: [1,2,3] 1. Apply topical 2% lidocaine gel or LET / LAT for ~10 min if skin is intact (avoid open mucosa). 2. If still tender, infiltrate skin around the entrapment with 1% lidocaine WITHOUT epinephrine. 3. Stay subdermal — do NOT inject into the shaft proper. Volume: small wheals, usually <3 mL total. Track cumulative dose; the penis is an end-artery territory and the foreskin is thin. S

nodes.title: Dorsal Penile Nerve Block
nodes.summary: 10 mL plain 1% lidocaine at 10 and 2 o\u2019clock, deep to Buck\u2019s fascia, NO epinephrine
nodes.body: Use plain lidocaine 1% — NO epinephrine. The dorsal penile arteries are end-arteries. Technique: [1,2] 1. Sterile prep at the base of the penis. 2. 25-27G needle, insert at 10 and 2 o\u2019clock positions just below the symphysis pubis. 3. Aspirate, then inject 2-5 mL plain 1% lidocaine on each side, deep to Buck\u2019s fascia. 4. Total typical volume 10 mL plain 1% lidocaine (100 mg). 5. Wait 5-1

nodes.title: Pediatric Procedural Sedation
nodes.summary: Sedate before manipulation; IN midazolam for brief tries, full sedation if destruction needed
nodes.body: A struggling child + a zipper near genitalia is a setup for iatrogenic injury. Sedate before you touch. [1,3] Approach: • Anxiolysis first: intranasal midazolam 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg) for a brief release attempt with mineral oil • Full sedation if destruction technique needed or if first attempt fails — see Procedural Sedation consult • Common agents: intranasal/IV ketamine or IV propofol per insti

nodes.title: Select Release Technique
nodes.summary: Mineral oil first → median-bar cut if jammed → lateral teeth or slider-side cut as alternates
nodes.body: Start with the least destructive option that fits the situation. Escalate if it fails — do NOT force a stuck slider.

nodes.title: Mineral-Oil Lubrication + Retrograde Unzip
nodes.summary: Soak 10-15 min in mineral oil, gentle retrograde unzip; stop and escalate if it does not budge
nodes.body: First-line for intact skin. Reduces friction and frequently allows the slider to back off without any cutting. [1,2,3] Technique: 1. Soak the entrapped skin in mineral oil (or any liquid paraffin / lubricant) for 10-15 minutes. 2. Apply gentle traction to the skin away from the slider. 3. With other hand, slowly slide the zipper in the opposite (retrograde) direction of the entrapment. 4. Use stea

nodes.title: Median-Bar Cut (Preferred Destruction Technique)
nodes.summary: Cut the median bar inside the slider with bone/wire cutters — faceplates fall off, skin frees
nodes.body: Most reliable rescue when oil fails or slider is jammed. Cutting the median bar inside the slider releases both faceplates and the zipper falls apart. [1,2,3,4] Equipment: • Bone cutter, wire cutter, or trauma shears strong enough to bite through the slider bridge • Hemostat to stabilize the slider • Drape and protect surrounding skin (a tongue depressor between slider and skin is gold) Technique:

nodes.title: Lateral Teeth Separation
nodes.summary: Pry teeth apart distal to slider with screwdriver/hemostat — only if slider is NOT jammed
nodes.body: Useful when no bone cutter is available and the slider is intact (not jammed inside the entrapped skin). [2,5] Technique: 1. Adequate analgesia first. 2. Insert a small flat-head screwdriver (or hemostat tip) between the front and back rows of teeth at a point distal to the slider. 3. Twist gently to pry the teeth apart along their entire distal length. 4. Once teeth distal to the slider have sepa

nodes.title: Slider Destruction (Side Cuts)
nodes.summary: Cut along both slider faceplate seams to peel housing apart — slower than median-bar cut
nodes.body: Alternate destruction technique when the median bar is inaccessible or shears cannot reach it. [1,2,3] Technique: 1. Adequate analgesia. 2. Protect skin with a tongue depressor. 3. Using bone / wire cutters, cut along each side (the faceplate seam) of the slider, top and bottom. 4. The slider housing peels apart, releasing the median bar mechanism and freeing the teeth. 5. Inspect skin, irrigate,

nodes.title: Post-Release Assessment
nodes.summary: Inspect skin after release — minor injury → ED wound care; full-thickness loss → urology
nodes.body: Skin is free. Inspect the entrapment site now.

nodes.title: Wound Care
nodes.summary: Saline irrigation, ointment, loose dressing, heal by secondary intention; primary closure rare
nodes.body: Genital skin heals well by secondary intention. [1,3,6] Immediate: 1. Irrigate gently with sterile saline (low-pressure, just enough to clear debris). 2. Pat dry, apply petrolatum or bacitracin ointment. 3. Loose, non-adherent dressing — change daily. 4. Leave most superficial wounds open — primary closure is rarely needed. Patient counseling: • Twice-daily gentle soap-and-water cleansing in the s

nodes.title: Tetanus Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Tetanus-prone wound; give Tdap if last booster >5 years and skin is broken
nodes.body: Zipper-entrapment skin tears are tetanus-prone (contaminated, devitalized edge). [7] Quick rule (CDC/ACIP): • Wound breaks skin AND last Td/Tdap >5 years → give Tdap (or Td) • Unknown or <3 lifetime doses → give vaccine and consider TIG • Skin fully intact → no tetanus action needed Use the calculator for edge cases (immunocompromised, unknown history): Tetanus Prophylaxis.

nodes.title: Antibiotic Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: No routine antibiotics; cover only if immunocompromised, deep contamination, or cellulitis
nodes.body: Routine prophylactic antibiotics are NOT indicated for clean, superficial zipper-related skin tears. [1,3,6] Consider antibiotics ONLY for: • Immunocompromised host (diabetes, HIV with CD4 <200, neutropenia, chemo, chronic steroids) • Full-thickness laceration with contamination • Signs of cellulitis at presentation or delayed presentation (>24 h) If indicated (skin coverage): • Cephalexin 500 mg

nodes.title: Return Precautions
nodes.summary: Return for swelling, redness, discharge, fever, urinary symptoms, skin color change
nodes.body: Return to ED immediately for: [1,3] • Worsening swelling, redness, or pain after 24-48 h • Purulent discharge or foul odor • Fever >100.4\u00B0F (38\u00B0C) • New blood in urine or trouble urinating • Skin color change (dusky, black, or pale) • Recurrent erection without stimulation (concern for vascular injury) Routine follow-up: PCP or urology in 3-5 days for wound check. Sooner if any concerns

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge after release if pain controlled, wound stable, tetanus addressed; PCP/urology 3-5 days
nodes.body: Most patients discharge home after a successful bedside release.
nodes.recommendation: DISCHARGE CRITERIA: • Zipper released, skin viable • Pain controlled with oral analgesics • Tetanus status addressed • Patient (or caregiver) understands wound care and return precautions DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS: • Wound care as in the wound

nodes.title: When to Call Urology
nodes.summary: Urology for urethral injury, significant skin loss, failed bedside release, or vascular compromise
nodes.body: Consult urology (or plastics) for any of the following: [1,3,6] • Suspected urethral injury — blood at meatus, hematuria, inability to void • Significant skin loss — full-thickness laceration, devascularized flap, or skin avulsion • Failure of bedside release after one destruction technique AND adequate analgesia • Recurrent or strangulating injury with vascular compromise • Complex pediatric case

nodes.title: Exposure Type
nodes.summary: Classify exposure as occupational or nonoccupational to guide PEP evaluation pathway
nodes.body: Patient Info Sheet: PEP \u2014 printable summary of transmission risk, treatment effectiveness, and side effects. What type of HIV exposure occurred?

nodes.title: Substantial Risk Fluid?
nodes.summary: Substantial-risk fluids (blood, semen, vaginal/rectal secretions) warrant PEP evaluation
nodes.body: Was the exposure to a substantial-risk body fluid? SUBSTANTIAL RISK \u2022 Blood \u2022 Semen / vaginal secretions \u2022 Rectal secretions \u2022 Breast milk \u2022 Any visibly bloody body fluid NEGLIGIBLE RISK \u2022 Urine, saliva, sweat, tears (without visible blood)

nodes.title: PEP Not Indicated
nodes.body: Exposure involved only negligible-risk body fluids. No documented cases of HIV transmission from these fluids.
nodes.recommendation: PEP is not recommended. Provide reassurance and risk reduction counseling. BASELINE LABS STILL RECOMMENDED \u2022 HIV Ag/Ab combo (4th gen) \u2022 Hepatitis B surface Ag, surface Ab, core Ab \u2022 Hepatitis C Ab

nodes.title: Time Since Exposure
nodes.summary: PEP must start within 72 hours — efficacy decreases with delay, not recommended after window
nodes.body: Has it been \u226472 hours since the exposure? PEP must be initiated as soon as possible. Efficacy decreases with delay and is not recommended after 72 hours.

nodes.title: PEP Not Indicated
nodes.body: Exposure occurred >72 hours ago. PEP is not recommended beyond this window due to lack of efficacy data.
nodes.recommendation: PEP is not recommended. Provide risk reduction counseling. Discuss PrEP for ongoing risk. BASELINE LABS STILL RECOMMENDED \u2022 HIV Ag/Ab combo (4th gen) — repeat at 4\u20136 weeks and 3 months \u2022 Hepatitis B surface Ag, surface Ab, co

nodes.title: Patient HIV Status
nodes.summary: Confirm exposed patient is HIV-negative or unknown — PEP only for HIV-negative individuals
nodes.body: What is the exposed patient\u2019s HIV status?

nodes.title: Not a PEP Candidate
nodes.body: Patient is already HIV-positive. PEP is prophylaxis for HIV-negative individuals only.
nodes.recommendation: Refer to HIV specialist for ART management. Verify viral load and treatment adherence. PEP is not applicable.

nodes.title: Source HIV Status
nodes.summary: Assess source HIV status — U=U if undetectable, but PEP still offered per patient preference
nodes.body: What is the source person\u2019s HIV status? If source is known HIV+ on ART with sustained undetectable viral load (<200 copies/mL), transmission risk is negligible (U=U). PEP may still be offered per patient preference.

nodes.title: PEP Not Indicated
nodes.body: Source is confirmed HIV-negative. No HIV transmission risk from this exposure.
nodes.recommendation: PEP is not recommended. If source HIV test was a rapid test, confirm with lab-based assay. Consider window period if source has recent high-risk behavior. BASELINE LABS STILL RECOMMENDED \u2022 HIV Ag/Ab combo (4th gen) \u2022 Hepatitis B s

nodes.title: Start PEP Immediately
nodes.summary: Do not delay PEP for labs — start meds now, draw baseline HIV/HBV/HCV/BMP/CBC/pregnancy/STI
nodes.body: Do not delay PEP for test results. Start medications now; adjust later based on labs. BASELINE LABS \u2022 HIV Ag/Ab combo (4th gen) \u2022 Hepatitis B surface Ag, surface Ab, core Ab \u2022 Hepatitis C Ab \u2022 BMP (creatinine for renal dosing) \u2022 CBC \u2022 Pregnancy test (if applicable) \u2022 STI screening (GC/CT, syphilis RPR) For occupational exposures, also test the source patient for

nodes.title: Special Population?
nodes.summary: Screen for pregnancy or renal impairment — affects regimen selection and dosing
nodes.body: Does the patient have any of the following?

nodes.title: Pregnancy Considerations
nodes.summary: Biktarvy safe in pregnancy — avoid efavirenz, OB/HIV specialist follow-up recommended
nodes.body: PEP is safe and recommended in pregnancy. Use the same preferred regimen. \u2022 Biktarvy (BIC/FTC/TAF) \u2014 preferred single-tablet regimen, extensive safety data in pregnancy \u2022 Alternative: TDF/FTC + Dolutegravir \u2022 Avoid efavirenz-based regimens \u2022 OB/HIV specialist consultation recommended

nodes.title: Renal Impairment
nodes.summary: Use TAF-based regimen for CrCl <50, avoid Biktarvy if CrCl <30 — consult ID/pharmacy
nodes.body: Dose adjustment required for CrCl <50 mL/min. \u2022 Use TAF-based regimen (TAF is preferred over TDF in renal impairment) \u2022 Biktarvy \u2014 do not use if CrCl <30 \u2022 If CrCl <30: consult ID/pharmacy for alternative regimen \u2022 Avoid TDF if CrCl <60 (nephrotoxic)

nodes.title: 28-Day Regimen
nodes.summary: Biktarvy 1 tab daily x28d preferred — prescribe full course from ED, not starter packs
nodes.body: PREFERRED REGIMEN Biktarvy (bictegravir/emtricitabine/TAF) \u2014 1 tablet PO daily x 28 days ALTERNATIVE REGIMEN TDF/FTC (Truvada) 1 tablet PO daily + Dolutegravir (Tivicay) 50 mg PO daily x 28 days SECOND ALTERNATIVE TDF/FTC + Darunavir 800 mg PO daily + Ritonavir 100 mg PO daily x 28 days Prescribe full 28-day course from the ED. Do not dispense starter packs \u2014 patients may not follow up f

nodes.title: Follow-Up & Disposition
nodes.body: HIV TESTING SCHEDULE \u2022 Baseline: HIV Ag/Ab (4th gen) at initial visit \u2022 4\u20136 weeks: Repeat HIV test \u2022 3 months: Repeat HIV test (final if 4th gen used) MEDICATION FOLLOW-UP \u2022 2-week visit: Assess adherence, side effects, renal function \u2022 Complete full 28 days \u2014 early discontinuation reduces efficacy HEPATITIS B & C FOLLOW-UP \u2022 Review baseline Hepatitis B surf
nodes.recommendation: Prescribe full 28-day course. Schedule follow-up at 2 weeks. Arrange HIV testing at 4\u20136 weeks and 3 months. Review HBV serology and vaccinate if susceptible. Discuss PrEP for ongoing risk. For occupational exposures, report to employee

nodes.title: Pericarditis — Diagnostic Criteria
nodes.summary: Diagnosis: ≥2 of 4 criteria — chest pain, friction rub, ECG changes, pericardial effusion
nodes.body: Pericarditis Steps Summary Diagnosis requires ≥2 of 4 criteria: [1][2] | Criterion | Sensitivity | |-----------|-------------| | Chest pain — sharp, pleuritic, positional (better sitting forward) | ~85-90% | | Pericardial friction rub — scratchy, 3-component (best at LLSB, leaning forward) | ~30% | | ECG changes — diffuse ST elevation with PR depression | ~60% | | Pericardial effusion — new or wor

nodes.title: ECG in Pericarditis
nodes.summary: Stage I: diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression; PR depression in II most sensitive; Spodick sign = downsloping TP
nodes.body: Classic 4-stage ECG evolution: [1][4] | Stage | Timing | Findings | |-------|--------|----------| | I | Hours-days | Diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression (reciprocal ST depression + PR elevation in aVR) | | II | Days | ST/PR normalization | | III | Days-weeks | Diffuse T-wave inversions | | IV | Weeks-months | T-wave normalization | Key distinguishing features from STEMI: • Diffuse ST elev

nodes.title: Laboratory Evaluation
nodes.summary: CRP most useful for monitoring; troponin elevated in 30-50% (myopericarditis); check renal function for colchicine dosing
nodes.body: Recommended labs for all patients: [1][2] • CRP — elevated in >75%; useful for monitoring response and guiding taper • ESR — less specific but supports inflammation • Troponin — elevated in 30-50% (myopericarditis) • BMP — renal function (colchicine dosing), uremia • CBC — leukocytosis supports inflammation Consider based on clinical suspicion: • TSH — hypothyroidism can cause pericardial effusion

nodes.title: Echocardiography
nodes.summary: Echo for all — effusion in ~60%; large >20mm = high risk; RV diastolic collapse = early tamponade sign
nodes.body: Echo is indicated for ALL suspected pericarditis: [1][2] Findings: • Pericardial effusion — present in ~60% • Pericardial thickening (>3mm) • Fibrinous strands • Wall motion abnormalities (suggests myopericarditis) Effusion size classification: | Size | End-diastolic depth | |------|--------------------| | Small | <10 mm | | Moderate | 10-20 mm | | Large | >20 mm | Tamponade physiology: • RV diast

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Consider ACS (territorial ECG), PE (hypoxia), dissection (tearing, BP differential), MSK (reproducible)
nodes.body: If only 1 criterion present, consider: Cardiac: • ACS — territorial ECG changes, troponin, risk factors • Myocarditis — heart failure symptoms, arrhythmias • Aortic dissection — tearing pain, BP differential, wide mediastinum Pulmonary: • PE — pleuritic pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, risk factors • Pneumonia — fever, cough, consolidation • Pleuritis — unilateral, friction rub with respiration Other:

nodes.title: High-Risk Features
nodes.summary: Major high-risk: fever >38°C, large effusion >20mm, subacute onset, tamponade, NSAID failure
nodes.body: Assess for predictors of complicated course: [1][2][7] Major criteria (any = high risk → admit): • Fever >38°C (100.4°F) • Subacute onset (symptoms over days-weeks) • Large pericardial effusion (>20mm) • Cardiac tamponade • Failure to respond to NSAIDs after 1 week Minor criteria (consider admission if present): • Myopericarditis (elevated troponin) • Immunosuppression • Trauma • Oral anticoagulan

nodes.title: Myopericarditis
nodes.summary: Myopericarditis = troponin+ with normal LV function; same treatment but stricter activity restriction (6 mo for athletes)
nodes.body: Myopericarditis = pericarditis + troponin elevation with preserved LV function [1][5][8] Classification: • Myopericarditis — predominant pericarditis features + elevated troponin + normal LV function • Perimyocarditis — predominant myocarditis features + LV dysfunction → treat as myocarditis Management differences: • Treatment: same as pericarditis (NSAIDs + colchicine) • Stricter activity restric

nodes.title: Large Pericardial Effusion
nodes.summary: Large effusion without tamponade: admit, serial echo, avoid anticoagulation; pericardiocentesis if diagnostic need or worsening
nodes.body: Large effusion (>20mm) without tamponade: [1][6] Immediate management: • Admit for monitoring • Serial echos (daily until stable) • Avoid anticoagulation if possible • Treat underlying cause aggressively Indications for pericardiocentesis (non-emergent): • Diagnostic — suspected bacterial/TB/malignant etiology • Therapeutic — symptomatic large effusion • Hemodynamic compromise developing Pericardi

nodes.title: Cardiac Tamponade
nodes.summary: Clinical diagnosis — Beck's triad in ~30%; IV fluids to temporize; emergent pericardiocentesis is definitive
nodes.body: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for echo confirmation if unstable [1][6] Beck's triad (present in ~30%): • Hypotension • Elevated JVP • Muffled heart sounds Other findings: • Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg drop in SBP with inspiration) • Tachycardia • Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration — actually more common in constrictive) • Electrical alternans on ECG Immediate management: 1.

nodes.title: Admit for Monitoring
nodes.body: Admission criteria: [1][2][7] • Fever >38°C (100.4°F) • Large pericardial effusion (>20mm) • Cardiac tamponade • Suspected bacterial or tuberculous pericarditis • Immunocompromised patient • Traumatic pericarditis • Failure to respond to outpatient therapy • Significant myocarditis features (LV dysfunction, arrhythmias) • On anticoagulation with large effusion Inpatient management: • Telemetry mon
nodes.recommendation: Admit to telemetry. Serial echos. Anti-inflammatory therapy + treat underlying cause. Cardiology consult.

nodes.title: Etiology Assessment
nodes.summary: 80-90% idiopathic/viral — extensive workup only for high-risk, recurrent, or specific clinical suspicion
nodes.body: Most acute pericarditis is idiopathic/viral (80-90%) [1][2] Extensive workup not needed for uncomplicated first episode. When to pursue specific etiology: • High-risk features present • Recurrent pericarditis • Large effusion requiring drainage • Suspected secondary cause Major etiologic categories: | Category | Examples | |----------|----------| | Idiopathic/Viral | Coxsackie, EBV, CMV, HIV, COVI

nodes.title: Dressler Syndrome (Post-MI Pericarditis)
nodes.summary: Post-MI: aspirin preferred (650-1000mg TID), avoid ibuprofen; colchicine adjunct; careful with anticoagulation
nodes.body: Post-cardiac injury syndrome — occurs 1-8 weeks after MI, surgery, or trauma [1][9] Two types of post-MI pericarditis: Early (within 1 week): • Direct inflammation from infarct • More common with transmural MI • Usually self-limited Late (Dressler syndrome, 1-8 weeks): • Autoimmune mechanism • Associated with fever, pleuritis, elevated ESR • Less common in reperfusion era Treatment considerations:

nodes.title: Autoimmune Pericarditis
nodes.summary: SLE most common CTD; treat underlying disease; lower threshold for steroids; higher recurrence risk
nodes.body: Pericarditis associated with connective tissue diseases: [1][2] Common associations: • SLE — most common CTD causing pericarditis (25-50%) • RA — pericardial involvement in up to 30% • Systemic sclerosis — often with myocardial involvement • Sjogren syndrome • Mixed connective tissue disease Management differences: • Treat underlying disease (rheumatology involvement) • NSAIDs + colchicine still f

nodes.title: Bacterial / Tuberculous Pericarditis
nodes.summary: Purulent = emergency — drainage + IV abx; TB common in endemic/HIV — ADA >40 suggests TB; high constriction risk
nodes.body: Purulent/bacterial pericarditis is a medical emergency [1][10] Bacterial pericarditis: • Usually contiguous spread (pneumonia, empyema, post-surgical) • Organisms: Staph, Strep, Gram-negatives • High mortality (20-30%) even with treatment • Requires drainage + IV antibiotics • Often progresses to constrictive pericarditis Tuberculous pericarditis: • Common in endemic areas and HIV patients • Subac

nodes.title: Uremic Pericarditis
nodes.summary: Uremic (BUN >60): intensified daily dialysis, heparin-free; NSAIDs ineffective; dialysis-associated may respond to anti-inflammatory
nodes.body: Pericarditis in ESRD patients — usually BUN >60 mg/dL [1][11] Two types: Uremic pericarditis (pre-dialysis or underdialyzed): • BUN typically >60 mg/dL • Treatment: Intensified dialysis (daily for 1-2 weeks) • NSAIDs generally ineffective • Steroids not helpful Dialysis-associated pericarditis: • Occurs in patients on adequate dialysis • Different mechanism — may respond to anti-inflammatory thera

nodes.title: First-Line Treatment
nodes.summary: NSAID + colchicine first-line; ibuprofen 600mg TID or aspirin (post-MI); high-dose 1-2 weeks then taper 3-4 weeks
nodes.body: NSAID + Colchicine for ALL acute pericarditis [1][2][3] This combination reduces recurrence from ~30% to ~15% (COPE, ICAP trials) Step 1: Choose NSAID: | Drug | Dose | Notes | |------|------|-------| | Ibuprofen | 600mg TID | Most commonly used | | Indomethacin | 25-50mg TID | May be more effective | | Naproxen | 500mg BID | Fewer GI effects | | Aspirin | 750-1000mg TID | Preferred post-MI | Durat

nodes.title: Colchicine Therapy
nodes.summary: Colchicine 0.5mg BID (≥70kg) or daily (<70kg); 3 months first episode, 6 months recurrence; no loading dose
nodes.body: Colchicine reduces recurrence by ~50% [1][3][12] Dosing: | Weight | Dose | Duration (first episode) | Duration (recurrence) | |--------|------|--------------------------|----------------------| | ≥70 kg | Colchicine 0.5mg BID | 3 months | 6 months | | <70 kg | Colchicine 0.5mg daily | 3 months | 6 months | No loading dose needed (unlike gout) Key considerations: • Start with NSAID (not as monother

nodes.title: Activity Restriction
nodes.summary: No strenuous activity until symptom-free + normal CRP + no effusion; athletes: 3 mo (pericarditis), 6 mo (myopericarditis)
nodes.body: Activity restriction is critical — especially for athletes [1][2][8] General population: • Avoid strenuous activity until: - Symptom-free - CRP normalized - No pericardial effusion • Typically 1-2 weeks for uncomplicated cases Athletes (competitive sports): | Condition | Minimum restriction | |-----------|--------------------| | Uncomplicated pericarditis | 3 months | | Myopericarditis (troponin+,

nodes.title: Corticosteroid Therapy
nodes.summary: Avoid first-line (2-4x recurrence risk); if needed: low dose 0.25-0.5 mg/kg (max 25mg); very slow taper over months; 2025 ACC: IL-1 preferred over steroids for recurrent inflammatory phenotype
nodes.body: Avoid steroids first-line — increase recurrence risk 2-4x [1][2][3] Note (2025 ACC): for recurrent/refractory inflammatory-phenotype pericarditis, IL-1 inhibitors are now preferred over escalating corticosteroids — see Refractory Pericarditis. [15] Indications for steroids: • Contraindication to NSAIDs (renal failure, active GI bleeding) • Contraindication to colchicine • NSAID failure after 1-2 w

nodes.title: Recurrent Pericarditis
nodes.summary: 15-30% recurrence; risk factors: no colchicine, rapid taper, steroids, female; escalation: NSAIDs → steroids → IL-1 blockers
nodes.body: Recurrence occurs in 15-30% despite optimal therapy [1][13] Definitions: • Recurrent: symptom-free interval ≥4-6 weeks between episodes • Incessant: symptoms persist >4-6 weeks OR recurrence within 6 weeks of stopping therapy Risk factors for recurrence: • Incomplete initial treatment • Premature NSAID taper • Not using colchicine • Steroid use (especially high-dose or rapid taper) • Female sex •

nodes.title: First Recurrence
nodes.summary: First recurrence: same treatment but colchicine for 6 months; confirm CRP normal before taper; address compliance
nodes.body: Same therapy as initial episode but longer duration [1][3][13] Treatment: • NSAIDs at full dose until symptom-free + CRP normal • Colchicine for 6 months (vs 3 months for first episode) • Slow NSAID taper (over 4-6 weeks) • Address modifiable risk factors (activity, compliance) Key points: • Confirm CRP normalization before tapering • May need longer NSAID course (2-4 weeks vs 1-2 weeks) • Conside

nodes.title: Refractory / Steroid-Dependent Pericarditis
nodes.summary: Refractory: IL-1 antagonists preferred (rilonacept FDA-approved, anakinra); RHAPSODY showed 96% recurrence reduction
nodes.body: IL-1 antagonists are now preferred over corticosteroids as second-line for the inflammatory phenotype (2025 ACC Expert Consensus) [1][13][14][15] Indications for IL-1 therapy: • Recurrent/incessant pericarditis after failing colchicine (typically by 2nd recurrence) • Steroid-dependent (unable to taper below physiologic dose) • Contraindication to steroids • Inflammatory phenotype (elevated CRP, fe

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Low-risk: discharge with close follow-up; high-risk: admit; uncertain: observe with serial echo
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on risk stratification and clinical status.

nodes.title: Discharge with Follow-Up
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: [1][2][7] • No high-risk features • Hemodynamically stable • Tolerating oral medications • Reliable follow-up available • Understands activity restrictions Discharge medications: • Ibuprofen 600mg TID (or alternative NSAID) + Colchicine 0.5mg BID • PPI for GI protection Patient instructions: • Take medications as prescribed — do NOT stop early • Activity restriction until sympt
nodes.recommendation: Discharge on NSAID + colchicine + PPI. Activity restriction. Follow-up in 1-2 weeks with CRP. Continue colchicine 3 months.

nodes.title: Observation Unit
nodes.body: Consider observation for borderline cases: • Moderate effusion without tamponade • Myopericarditis awaiting echo/cardiac MRI • NSAID intolerance needing alternative therapy • First-time pericarditis with equivocal high-risk features • Social concerns affecting follow-up reliability Observation plan: • Serial echos (6-12 hours apart) • Telemetry monitoring • Initiate anti-inflammatory therapy • Car
nodes.recommendation: Observation with serial echo, telemetry, cardiology consult. Reassess in 12-24 hours for discharge vs admission.

nodes.title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
nodes.summary: HF with EF <45% in late pregnancy to 5mo postpartum — 6-10% mortality, 50-70% recover with treatment
nodes.body: PPCM Quick Reference Definition: Heart failure secondary to LV systolic dysfunction (EF <45%) developing towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, where no other cause of HF is found. [1][2] Timing: - Classic: Last month of pregnancy to 5 months postpartum - ~80% present within first month postpartum - Can present earlier in pregnancy (rare) or up to 6 months postpartum Inc

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: African American, age >=30, multiparity, preeclampsia, obesity — AA women have worse outcomes
nodes.body: Established risk factors: - African American race (1 in 1,421 vs 1 in 9,861 in Hispanics) - Age >=30 years - Multiparity - Multiple gestation (twins/triplets) - Preeclampsia/eclampsia (OR 3.28) - Gestational hypertension - Obesity - Diabetes Additional associations: - Prolonged tocolytic use - Anemia - Family history of cardiomyopathy - Prior PPCM (recurrence risk 30-50%) African American women ha

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Red flags: new dyspnea at rest, PND, unable to lie flat, persistent tachycardia >100 — believe her
nodes.body: Classic HF symptoms (easily attributed to "normal pregnancy"): - Dyspnea on exertion / orthopnea / PND - Fatigue - Peripheral edema - Cough (especially nocturnal) - Palpitations Red flags suggesting PPCM over normal pregnancy: - New onset dyspnea at rest - PND (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea) - Unable to lie flat - New or worsening edema - Persistent tachycardia (>100 bpm at rest) - JVD, S3 gallop,

nodes.title: Low Suspicion - Monitor Closely
nodes.summary: Low suspicion — outpatient echo within 1-2 weeks, BNP, clear return precautions for orthopnea/PND
nodes.body: If symptoms are mild and more consistent with normal pregnancy: Consider outpatient workup: - Schedule outpatient echo within 1-2 weeks - Consider BNP/NT-proBNP (normal values unchanged in pregnancy; marked elevation suggests pathology) Clear return precautions: - Orthopnea (cannot lie flat) - Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea - Worsening dyspnea at rest - New or worsening edema - Palpitations or synco

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Echo diagnostic (EF <45%), BNP markedly elevated, troponin often mildly elevated — get echo STAT
nodes.body: Essential: 1. Echocardiogram - DIAGNOSTIC - LVEF <45% (often <35% at presentation) - May show LV dilation (LVEDD >2.7 cm/m2) - RV dysfunction, functional MR/TR - Look for LV thrombus 2. BNP/NT-proBNP - Markedly elevated in PPCM - Normal pregnancy: minimally elevated - BNP >1860 pg/mL predicts persistent LV dysfunction 3. Troponin - Often mildly elevated - High troponin T (>0.4 ng/mL) predicts wors

nodes.title: Assess Severity
nodes.summary: Stratify by EF and hemodynamics — EF <35% needs aggressive treatment, <25% consider ICU/MCS
nodes.body: Severity stratification based on LVEF and hemodynamics: Mild-Moderate (LVEF 35-45%): - Ambulatory symptoms - Hemodynamically stable - No respiratory distress at rest Severe (LVEF <35%): - Symptoms at rest - Tachycardia, hypotension - Hypoxemia - High-risk for LV thrombus Critical/Cardiogenic Shock: - SBP <90 mmHg or requiring vasopressors - Signs of end-organ hypoperfusion - Acute pulmonary edema

nodes.title: Cardiogenic Shock - Critical PPCM
nodes.summary: Cardiogenic shock — NIPPV/intubation, vasopressors, left lateral tilt if pregnant, activate team
nodes.body: Immediate actions: 1. Airway/Breathing: - High-flow O2, NIPPV if tolerating - Early intubation if failing (ketamine preferred for induction) - Avoid hypotension during intubation 2. Circulation: - 2 large-bore IVs - Arterial line for continuous BP monitoring - Central line for vasopressors 3. Positioning: - If pregnant: left lateral tilt to prevent IVC compression - Elevate head of bed if pulmonar

nodes.title: Inotropes & Vasopressors
nodes.summary: Dobutamine first-line inotrope, add norepinephrine if MAP <65 — avoid epi infusion post-ROSC
nodes.body: For cardiogenic shock: First-line inotrope: - Dobutamine 2.5-20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion - Increases contractility and cardiac output - May cause hypotension (beta-2 vasodilation) If hypotensive (MAP <65): - Norepinephrine 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min - Preferred over dopamine (fewer arrhythmias) - Add to dobutamine if needed Alternative: - Milrinone 0.375-0.75 mcg/kg/min - PDE inhibitor - more vasodilation -

nodes.title: Mechanical Circulatory Support
nodes.summary: IABP, VA-ECMO, or LVAD for refractory shock — PPCM has HIGH recovery potential, do not give up early
nodes.body: Indications: Refractory cardiogenic shock despite inotropes/vasopressors Options (escalating support): 1. IABP (Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump) - Bridge to recovery or LVAD - Less invasive, widely available - Afterload reduction + coronary perfusion 2. VA-ECMO - For severe biventricular failure - Bridge to recovery or decision - PPCM patients often young, good ECMO candidates - ELSO Registry: acceptabl

nodes.title: Pregnancy Status
nodes.summary: Pregnancy status determines medication safety — ACEi/ARB contraindicated before delivery
nodes.body: Is the patient still pregnant or postpartum? This affects medication selection (ACE inhibitors contraindicated in pregnancy) and may require urgent delivery considerations.

nodes.title: Stable PPCM - Initial Management
nodes.summary: Reduce preload/afterload, maintain CO — O2, IV access, monitoring, fluid/salt restriction
nodes.body: Goals of acute ED management: 1. Reduce preload (diuresis) 2. Reduce afterload (vasodilators) 3. Maintain cardiac output 4. Prevent thromboembolism Immediate measures: - Oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94% - IV access - Cardiac monitoring - Foley catheter (monitor UOP) - Strict I/O Fluid restriction: 1.5-2 L/day Salt restriction: <2 g sodium/day Position: Semi-upright (head elevated); if pregnant, left l

nodes.title: Severe PPCM - Aggressive Management
nodes.summary: EF <35% — urgent echo, cardiology STAT, IV diuretics, low threshold for ICU, start anticoagulation
nodes.body: LVEF <35% with symptoms at rest requires aggressive treatment: Immediate: - Oxygen, cardiac monitoring, IV access - Urgent echo if not done - Cardiology consult STAT Treatment priorities: 1. IV diuretics for decongestion 2. Afterload reduction (carefully if hypotensive) 3. Consider IV vasodilators if SBP >110 4. Low threshold for ICU admission High-risk features requiring ICU: - EF <25% - RV dysfu

nodes.title: Diuretics
nodes.summary: Furosemide 20-40mg IV, titrate to UOP 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr — safe in pregnancy at lowest effective dose
nodes.body: Loop diuretics - cornerstone of decongestive therapy: Furosemide (Lasix) - Initial dose: 20-40 mg IV bolus - Titrate based on urine output (target 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr) - May need higher doses (80-200 mg) in severe congestion - Continuous infusion: 5-20 mg/hr if boluses ineffective Pregnancy considerations: - Generally safe in pregnancy - May reduce placental perfusion - use lowest effective dose - Moni

nodes.title: Vasodilator Selection
nodes.summary: ACEi/ARB contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic) — use hydralazine + nitrates until delivery
nodes.body: Key question: Is the patient still pregnant? ACE inhibitors/ARBs: - CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogenic) - FIRST-LINE postpartum - Cornerstone of long-term HFrEF therapy Pregnancy-safe afterload reduction: - Hydralazine + Nitrates Postpartum: - Switch to ACE inhibitor/ARB immediately after delivery - Safe during breastfeeding: enalapril, captopril, benazepril [1][2][8][9]

nodes.title: Hydralazine + Nitrates (Pregnancy-Safe)
nodes.summary: Hydralazine + ISDN for pregnancy-safe afterload/preload reduction — avoid nitroprusside (cyanide risk)
