nodes.body: Hydralazine: - Hydralazine 25-50 mg PO TID-QID - Alternative: 10-20 mg IV every 4-6 hours (acute) - Direct arterial vasodilator (afterload reduction) Isosorbide dinitrate: - Isosorbide dinitrate 20-40 mg PO TID - Venodilator (preload reduction) IV Nitroglycerin (acute decompensation): - Nitroglycerin 10-20 mcg/min, titrate up to 200 mcg/min - Use if SBP >110 mmHg - Excellent for acute pulmonary ed

nodes.title: ACE Inhibitors (Postpartum)
nodes.summary: Start ACEi immediately postpartum — enalapril/captopril safe for breastfeeding, titrate to target dose
nodes.body: First-line postpartum - start immediately after delivery: Lisinopril 2.5-5 mg daily, titrate to 20-40 mg daily OR Enalapril 2.5 mg BID, titrate to 10-20 mg BID Safe for breastfeeding: Enalapril, captopril, benazepril (minimal breast milk transfer) If ACE-intolerant (cough): - ARB: Losartan 25-50 mg daily (titrate to 100 mg) ARNI (Sacubitril/Valsartan): - May consider if persistently low EF on max

nodes.title: Beta-Blockers
nodes.summary: Start when euvolemic and stable — metoprolol in pregnancy, carvedilol postpartum, avoid in shock
nodes.body: Start once patient is euvolemic and hemodynamically stable: Pregnancy: - Metoprolol tartrate 12.5-25 mg BID, titrate to 100 mg BID - Beta-1 selective preferred - AVOID atenolol (IUGR risk) Postpartum: - Carvedilol 3.125 mg BID, titrate to 25 mg BID - Superior LV recovery vs metoprolol in some studies - Note: excreted in breast milk Titration: - Start low, go slow - Double dose every 2-4 weeks as t

nodes.title: Bromocriptine - Disease-Specific Therapy
nodes.summary: Blocks toxic 16-kDa prolactin — MUST anticoagulate while on bromocriptine, suppresses lactation
nodes.body: Mechanism: Blocks prolactin release, prevents formation of toxic 16-kDa prolactin fragment that damages cardiomyocytes ESC Guideline: Class IIb recommendation (may be considered) Dosing (ESC BOARD regimen): Uncomplicated PPCM (EF 35-45%): - Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO daily x 7 days Severe PPCM (EF <25% or cardiogenic shock): - Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO BID x 2 weeks - Then 2.5 mg PO daily x 6 weeks CRI

nodes.title: Anticoagulation Assessment
nodes.summary: PPCM has HIGH thromboembolic risk — LV thrombus in 17%, anticoagulate if EF <30-35% or LV thrombus
nodes.body: PPCM carries HIGH thromboembolic risk: - LV dysfunction + pregnancy hypercoagulability - LV thrombus incidence ~17% (higher than DCM) - Stasis from dilated, poorly contracting LV AHA recommends anticoagulation if EF <30% ESC recommends anticoagulation if EF <35% Absolute indications for therapeutic anticoagulation: - LV thrombus visualized on echo - Prior systemic embolism - Atrial fibrillation Co

nodes.title: Therapeutic Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Enoxaparin 1mg/kg q12h in pregnancy, warfarin postpartum — do NOT use warfarin during pregnancy
nodes.body: Indications: - LV thrombus on echo - Atrial fibrillation - Prior systemic embolism Pregnancy: - Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SQ every 12 hours - Monitor anti-Xa levels (target 0.6-1.0 IU/mL, 4h post-dose) - Dose adjustments needed as pregnancy progresses Near delivery: - Switch to UFH 24-36 hours before planned delivery - Allows reversal with protamine if needed - Hold LMWH 24 hours before epidural/spinal P

nodes.title: Prophylactic Anticoagulation
nodes.summary: Prophylactic enoxaparin 40mg SQ daily — required if on bromocriptine, minimum 8 weeks postpartum
nodes.body: Pregnancy: - Enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily (prophylactic dose) - OR weight-based: 0.5 mg/kg SQ daily - UFH if delivery imminent (shorter half-life) Postpartum: - Continue LMWH until EF recovers - Can transition to warfarin (safe for breastfeeding) - DOACs: limited data in breastfeeding, generally avoid Duration: - Until EF >=35-40% on repeat echo - Minimum 8 weeks postpartum (highest risk period) On b

nodes.title: No Anticoagulation Indicated
nodes.summary: EF >=35% without thrombus/AF — standard VTE prophylaxis only, reassess if EF declines or AF develops
nodes.body: If EF >=35%, no thrombus, no AF: - Routine anticoagulation not required - VTE prophylaxis per standard obstetric guidelines Continue close monitoring: - Repeat echo at 2-4 weeks - Watch for deterioration Re-assess anticoagulation if: - EF declines <35% - New AF - New symptoms suggesting embolism - Starting bromocriptine [1][2][7]

nodes.title: Delivery Considerations
nodes.summary: Vaginal delivery preferred if stable — epidural reduces catecholamine surge, C-section for OB indications only
nodes.body: If patient is still pregnant, coordinate with OB/MFM and cardiology. Timing of delivery: - Hemodynamically stable: attempt to stabilize mother, optimize gestational age - Hemodynamically unstable: urgent/emergent delivery after maternal stabilization - Inotrope-dependent or mechanical support: urgent delivery indicated Mode of delivery: - Vaginal delivery preferred if hemodynamically stable - C-se

nodes.title: Vaginal Delivery Recommendations
nodes.summary: Early epidural, continuous cardiac monitoring, shorten second stage, hold LMWH 24h before epidural
nodes.body: Preferred for hemodynamically stable patients: Labor management: - Early epidural (reduces pain/catecholamine surge) - Continuous cardiac monitoring - Arterial line if severe LV dysfunction - Central line if on vasopressors Second stage: - Shorten with assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum/forceps) - Avoid prolonged Valsalva (decreases preload) - Consider passive descent Fluid management: - Avoid over

nodes.title: Urgent Delivery - Hemodynamically Unstable
nodes.summary: C-section if inotrope-dependent or decompensating — perimortem C-section within 4-5 min if cardiac arrest
nodes.body: Planned delivery timing (antepartum PPCM): - Stable on therapy: continue pregnancy with close MFM/cardiology co-management; aim for term delivery - Severe LV dysfunction (LVEF <30%): plan early delivery around 37 weeks — advanced PPCM carries a high risk of decompensation in late pregnancy and peripartum, and earlier planned delivery limits ongoing hemodynamic load - Mode: vaginal delivery with ea

nodes.title: Postpartum Management
nodes.summary: Auto-transfusion post-delivery may cause pulmonary edema — start ACEi, optimize GDMT, contraception essential
nodes.body: Immediate postpartum period (highest risk for decompensation): - Auto-transfusion of ~500 mL blood volume after delivery - May precipitate pulmonary edema - Close monitoring x 24-48 hours minimum Medication transition: - Start ACE inhibitor/ARB immediately - Continue/optimize beta-blocker - Continue diuretics as needed - Continue anticoagulation until EF improves Breastfeeding: - Generally safe wi

nodes.title: Disposition Assessment
nodes.summary: 50-70% recover EF by 6 months — worse prognosis: EF <30%, LV dilation, AA race, high BNP/troponin
nodes.body: Recovery rates: - ~50-70% recover LV function (EF >50%) by 6 months - Most recovery occurs within first 2-3 months - IPAC Study: 71% recovered EF >50% at 12 months Predictors of WORSE prognosis: - LVEF <30% at presentation - LV dilation (LVEDD >60 mm) - African American race - BNP >1860 pg/mL - High troponin (>0.4 ng/mL) - QRS >120 ms - RV dysfunction Predictors of BETTER prognosis: - Higher initi

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: - Cardiogenic shock - Requiring inotropes/vasopressors - Mechanical circulatory support (IABP, ECMO, Impella) - Respiratory failure / intubated - Unstable arrhythmias - Acute decompensation with end-organ dysfunction ICU management: - Continuous hemodynamic monitoring - Optimize GDMT as tolerated - Cardiology + OB/MFM co-management - Early discussion re: advanced therapies
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for hemodynamic monitoring and advanced therapies. High recovery potential - aggressive support warranted.

nodes.title: Telemetry/Stepdown Admission
nodes.body: Admission to telemetry/stepdown for: - LVEF <35% but hemodynamically stable - Symptomatic at rest requiring IV diuretics - New diagnosis requiring medication initiation - Need for close monitoring during GDMT uptitration Inpatient goals: - Achieve euvolemia - Initiate/uptitrate GDMT (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker) - Start anticoagulation if indicated - Consider bromocriptine - Cardiology consult mandator
nodes.recommendation: Admit to telemetry for HF management and GDMT optimization. Cardiology consult mandatory. Arrange close outpatient follow-up.

nodes.title: Admission - General Floor
nodes.body: Admission criteria (general floor acceptable): - New diagnosis PPCM with LVEF 35-45% - Symptomatic HF requiring IV diuretics - Hemodynamically stable - Need for medication optimization Inpatient goals: - Achieve euvolemia - Initiate/uptitrate GDMT - Echo to assess LV function, thrombus - Start anticoagulation if indicated - Cardiology consult Discharge criteria: - Euvolemic (no orthopnea, minimal
nodes.recommendation: Admit for HF management, medication optimization, and monitoring. Arrange close cardiology and OB follow-up.

nodes.title: Peripheral Neuropathy — ED Evaluation
nodes.body: Steps Summary ED Role in Peripheral Neuropathy: 1. Identify emergencies (GBS, cord compression, vasculitis) 2. Rule out dangerous mimics 3. Determine workup urgency 4. Initiate symptomatic treatment Presentation Patterns: • Symmetric distal — most common, "stocking-glove" • Asymmetric/multifocal — vasculitis, mononeuritis multiplex • Proximal weakness — GBS, CIDP, myopathy First Question: Are RED

nodes.title: Red Flags — Emergent Workup Required
nodes.body: RED FLAGS requiring emergent evaluation: | Red Flag | Concern | |----------|----------| | Acute onset (<4 weeks) | GBS, cord compression, vasculitis | | Rapid progression | GBS, malignancy, toxic | | Motor > sensory | GBS, motor neuron disease | | Asymmetric pattern | Vasculitis, radiculopathy, mononeuritis multiplex | | Autonomic symptoms | GBS, diabetic autonomic, porphyria | | Respiratory sympt

nodes.title: Classification — Pattern Recognition
nodes.body: Classify the neuropathy by: 1. Anatomic Distribution: • Focal — single nerve (carpal tunnel, peroneal) • Multifocal — multiple nerves, asymmetric (vasculitis, DM) • Symmetric distal — stocking-glove (most common) • Symmetric proximal — GBS, CIDP, myopathy 2. Fiber Type: • Large fiber — weakness, vibration/proprioception loss, areflexia • Small fiber — pain, temperature loss, autonomic dysfunction

nodes.title: Asymmetric / Multifocal Neuropathy
nodes.body: Asymmetric patterns suggest specific etiologies: Mononeuropathy (single nerve): • Carpal tunnel (median) • Ulnar neuropathy (elbow) • Peroneal palsy (fibular head) • Radiculopathy (dermatomal) Mononeuritis Multiplex (multiple nerves, asymmetric): • Vasculitis — PAN, RA, granulomatosis with polyangiitis • Diabetes — diabetic amyotrophy • Infections — Lyme, leprosy, HIV, HCV • Sarcoidosis • Malignan

nodes.title: Small Fiber Neuropathy
nodes.body: Small Fiber Neuropathy (SFN): Affects Aδ and C fibers — pain/temperature sensation and autonomic function. Clinical Features: • Burning pain, allodynia, "pins and needles" • Length-dependent (feet → hands) • Normal strength and reflexes • Normal EMG/NCS (tests large fibers only) • Autonomic: sweating abnormalities, orthostatic intolerance, GI dysmotility Common Causes: • Diabetes/prediabetes (most

nodes.title: Standard ED Workup
nodes.body: Initial Laboratory Evaluation: Tier 1 — Order on ALL patients: • CBC with differential • Comprehensive metabolic panel • Fasting glucose or HbA1c • TSH • Vitamin B12 Tier 2 — If Tier 1 unrevealing: • SPEP with immunofixation (paraproteinemia) • HIV • Hepatitis B and C • ESR/CRP • RPR/VDRL Tier 3 — Specialist-guided: • Anti-ganglioside antibodies (GBS variants) • Paraneoplastic panel • Genetic test

nodes.title: EMG/NCS — When to Order?
nodes.body: Electrodiagnostic Studies (EMG/NCS): Not routinely needed in ED, but consider urgent referral if: Indications for URGENT EMG/NCS: • Acute/rapidly progressive weakness • Motor-predominant symptoms • Suspicion for GBS or CIDP • Asymmetric presentation • Normal initial workup with persistent symptoms What EMG/NCS Tells You: • Axonal vs demyelinating — helps narrow differential • Severity and distribu

nodes.title: Emergent Workup — Acute Neuropathy
nodes.body: Emergent Evaluation for Acute Neuropathy: Bedside Respiratory Assessment: • FVC (Forced Vital Capacity) — most useful - <20 mL/kg or <1 L = high intubation risk - Decline >30% from baseline = concerning • NIF (Negative Inspiratory Force) - Worse than −30 cmH2O = impending failure • Check q4h if GBS suspected Lumbar Puncture: • Classic GBS finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation - Elevated protein

nodes.title: GBS vs Mimics — Critical Differentiation
nodes.body: Guillain-Barré Syndrome Features: • Acute ascending weakness (<4 weeks to nadir) • Areflexia or hyporeflexia • Symmetric involvement • Recent infection (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV) • Autonomic instability (HR, BP fluctuations) Key GBS Mimics to Exclude: | Mimic | Distinguishing Features | |-------|-------------------------| | Transverse myelitis | Sensory level, sphincter early | | Cord compression |

nodes.title: GBS Mimic Workup
nodes.body: Targeted Workup by Suspected Mimic: Spinal Cord Lesion: • MRI spine with contrast • Look for sensory level on exam • Cord compression = surgical emergency Botulism: • Descending paralysis (cranial → limbs) • Dilated, poorly reactive pupils • Dry mouth, constipation • Stool for botulinum toxin • Contact public health Tick Paralysis: • Ascending paralysis mimics GBS • Look for tick — scalp, hairline

nodes.title: GBS — ED Management
nodes.body: Suspected GBS — Immediate Actions: 1. Airway/Respiratory Monitoring: • Serial FVC and NIF q4h minimum • Intubation thresholds: - FVC <20 mL/kg or <1 L - NIF worse than −30 cmH2O - Rapid decline (>30% in hours) - Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk • Early intubation preferred — RSI okay 2. Autonomic Monitoring: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Watch for HR/BP lability • Avoid medications that
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU. Serial respiratory monitoring (FVC/NIF q4h). Neurology consult for IVIG or plasmapheresis. Continuous cardiac monitoring for autonomic instability.

nodes.title: Symptomatic Treatment — Neuropathic Pain
nodes.body: First-Line Agents (all have similar efficacy): Gabapentinoids: • Gabapentin 300 mg TID, titrate to 900-3600 mg/day • Pregabalin 75 mg BID, titrate to 150-600 mg/day • Onset: 1-2 weeks for full effect • Adjust for renal function SNRIs: • Duloxetine 30-60 mg daily • Venlafaxine ER 75-225 mg daily • Also treats comorbid depression/anxiety TCAs: • Amitriptyline 10-25 mg qHS, titrate to 75-150 mg • Nor

nodes.title: Treat Underlying Cause
nodes.body: Reversible Causes — Treat in ED if Identified: B12 Deficiency: • Cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM × 1, then daily × 1 week • Or high-dose oral (1000-2000 mcg daily) • Recovery may take months Thiamine Deficiency: • Thiamine 100-500 mg IV/IM • Especially if alcohol use disorder • Can mimic GBS (dry beriberi) Hypothyroidism: • Start levothyroxine (outpatient usually) • Neuropathy improves slowly with trea

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: ICU Admission: • Respiratory compromise (FVC <20, declining) • Autonomic instability • GBS or suspected GBS • Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk Floor Admission: • Unable to ambulate safely • Rapid symptom progression • Needs IV treatment • Unreliable follow-up Observation: • Diagnostic uncertainty • Pending LP results • Serial neuro exams needed Discharge: • Chronic/stabl

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU Admission Protocol: Monitoring: • Serial FVC/NIF q4h (or more frequently if declining) • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Frequent neuro checks • Swallow evaluation before PO intake Treatments: • DVT prophylaxis (mechanical + pharmacologic) • PPI for stress ulcer prophylaxis • Pain management • Early PT/OT consult Intubation Preparation: • Have equipment ready • RSI is safe in GBS • Avoid succi
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU with continuous monitoring. Serial respiratory assessments q4h. Neurology consult for IVIG or PLEX. DVT prophylaxis. Intubation equipment at bedside.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor Admission Protocol: Workup to Complete: • Tier 1 and Tier 2 labs if not done • Consider LP if inflammatory cause suspected • EMG/NCS during admission • MRI if structural lesion suspected Monitoring: • Neuro checks q4-6h • Fall precautions • PT/OT evaluation Symptomatic Treatment: • Initiate neuropathic pain medication • Treat identified deficiencies (B12, thiamine) Consults: • Neurology (rou
nodes.recommendation: Admit to floor with fall precautions. Complete workup (labs, consider LP/EMG). Neurology consult. Initiate symptomatic treatment. Clear escalation criteria to nursing.

nodes.title: Discharge — Outpatient Management
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria (ALL must be met): • ✅ No red flags (acute, progressive, motor, autonomic) • ✅ Able to ambulate safely • ✅ Chronic/stable symptoms • ✅ Follow-up arranged Discharge Instructions: Medications to Start: • Gabapentin 300 mg TID (titrate weekly) • OR pregabalin 75 mg BID • Prescribe short course only — needs follow-up Labs to Order (outpatient): • Fasting glucose or HbA1c • TSH, B12
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with gabapentin or pregabalin. Order outpatient labs (glucose, TSH, B12, SPEP). PCP follow-up 1-2 weeks. Neurology referral. Written return precautions.

nodes.title: Peritoneal Dialysis — Complication
nodes.summary: Always drain a fresh exchange on arrival — the effluent is the diagnostic specimen.
nodes.body: Peritoneal Dialysis Steps Summary PD patients arrive sick from one of six problem domains. Identify the dominant complaint first — the workup branches early. Always drain a fresh exchange on arrival; the effluent is your single most useful diagnostic specimen. Ask: When was the last exchange? CAPD or APD? Recent catheter trauma? Last cloudy bag?

nodes.title: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
nodes.body: The PD catheter is already in place — your job is to use it correctly, sterilely, and capture the right specimens. Quick steps: 1. Mask + cap on you AND the patient. Sterile gloves. 2. Wipe transfer-set connection with chlorhexidine ×30 s. 3. Connect an empty drain bag to the outflow port. Bag below abdomen. 4. Open clamp → drain by gravity (200–300 mL/min, total 1.5–2.5 L over 10–20 min). 5. Samp

nodes.title: Diagnose PD-Associated Peritonitis
nodes.summary: Need 2 of 3: clinical features + WBC >100 with >50% PMN + positive culture. Inoculate effluent into blood culture bottles.
nodes.body: ISPD diagnostic criteria — need 2 of 3: 1. Clinical features (abdominal pain ± fever) 2. Cloudy effluent with WBC >100/µL after ≥2 h dwell, >50% PMN 3. Positive effluent culture Specimen handling matters. Inoculate 5–10 mL of effluent directly into two blood culture bottles at the bedside — this raises culture yield from <50% to >80%. Send a separate sample for cell count + Gram stain. [1][2] Clou

nodes.title: Empiric IP Antibiotic Therapy
nodes.body: Start within 6 h of diagnosis — do not wait for culture. Cover gram-positive + gram-negative organisms. ISPD recommends center-specific regimens. [1] Gram-positive (pick one): • Cefazolin IP 15–20 mg/kg once daily (preferred in low-MRSA centers) • Vancomycin IP 15–30 mg/kg every 5–7 days (if high MRSA prevalence) Gram-negative (pick one): • Ceftazidime IP 1000–1500 mg once daily • Gentamicin IP 0.

nodes.title: Day 3–5 Reassessment
nodes.summary: Clinical response expected by 72 h. No improvement at day 3 = treatment failure.
nodes.body: Effluent should clear and pain should improve within 72 h of effective therapy. Persistent cloudy effluent at day 3 = treatment failure. [1]

nodes.title: Targeted Therapy by Organism
nodes.body: Coag-negative Staph (most common): continue cefazolin × 2 weeks. S. aureus (MSSA): cefazolin × 3 weeks. MRSA → vancomycin × 3 weeks + consider rifampin. Streptococcus / Enterococcus: ampicillin or vancomycin × 3 weeks. Pseudomonas: dual therapy (ceftazidime + gentamicin or oral ciprofloxacin) × 3 weeks. High catheter-loss rate — strongly consider removal. Polymicrobial / enteric: consider surgical

nodes.title: Refractory or Recurrent Peritonitis
nodes.summary: Refractory at day 5 = pull catheter. Fungal = pull immediately.
nodes.body: Definitions matter for catheter decisions: [1] • Refractory: failure to clear by day 5 of appropriate antibiotics. • Relapsing: new episode within 4 weeks of completion, same organism. • Recurrent: new episode within 4 weeks, different organism. • Repeat: new episode >4 weeks later, same organism.

nodes.title: Fungal Peritonitis — Catheter Out
nodes.body: Mortality >25%, catheter loss rate ~40%. Suspect when effluent stays cloudy at day 5 despite appropriate antibiotics, especially in patients with recent antibiotic exposure, immunosuppression, or prior bacterial peritonitis. [1][3] Immediate actions: 1. Remove the PD catheter within 24–48 h of diagnosis. Do not attempt salvage. 2. Start fluconazole 200 mg PO/IV daily (Candida albicans coverage). 3

nodes.title: Non-Infectious Cloudy Effluent
nodes.body: Cloudy + WBC <100 + no PMN predominance: infection is unlikely. Consider: • Eosinophilic peritonitis — eosinophils >10% on differential. Self-limited. Usually triggered by new dialysate, icodextrin, or air. No antibiotics. • Chemical peritonitis — exposure to disinfectant or hypertonic dialysate. Resolves with rinsing. • Chyle — milky effluent that does not clear; triglycerides >100 mg/dL. Look fo

nodes.title: Exit-Site vs Tunnel Infection
nodes.summary: Tunnel infection has highest peritonitis risk — image with ultrasound.
nodes.body: Exit-site infection: purulent drainage at the exit site ± erythema. Crust alone does not equal infection. [2] Tunnel infection: erythema, edema, or tenderness along the subcutaneous catheter tract — frequently occult. Ultrasound shows fluid around the cuff. Highest peritonitis risk. Obtain exit-site swab for culture before starting antibiotics. Pseudomonas + S. aureus are the most aggressive organ

nodes.title: Exit-Site Treatment
nodes.body: Empiric oral therapy (start before culture if mild): • S. aureus suspected: dicloxacillin 500 mg PO QID or cephalexin 500 mg PO QID. MRSA → trimethoprim-sulfa or doxycycline. • Pseudomonas suspected (green drainage, biofilm): oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID × 3 weeks. Add second agent (gentamicin IP or oral) if severe. • Duration: 2 weeks minimum, 3 weeks for Pseudomonas or S. aureus. Local care: in

nodes.title: Tunnel Infection — High Risk
nodes.body: Concurrent peritonitis develops in ~40% of tunnel infections. Catheter salvage fails frequently. [2] Workup: • Ultrasound the tunnel — fluid >1 mm around the deep cuff predicts catheter loss. • Exit-site culture + blood cultures if febrile. • Send PD effluent for cell count even if not visibly cloudy. Treatment: • Broad IP coverage: vancomycin + ceftazidime until culture returns. • Plan catheter r

nodes.title: Mechanical Complication
nodes.summary: Outflow failure is most common; hydrothorax is the most dangerous.
nodes.body: Mechanical PD problems do not need antibiotics but can derail dialysis fast. Localize first.

nodes.title: Outflow Failure
nodes.body: Stepwise workup — start with the cheapest fix: [5] 1. Constipation (most common cause). KUB abdominal radiograph — look for stool burden + catheter tip position. Polyethylene glycol or lactulose. Avoid milk of magnesia in ESRD. 2. Catheter kink or external clamp — visual check, reposition external segment. 3. Fibrin plug — flush with heparinized saline 5000 U in 10 mL. Adding heparin 500 U/L to al

nodes.title: Dialysate Leak
nodes.body: Early leak (<30 days post-insertion): pericatheter wetness, scrotal/labial edema. Stop PD for 1–2 weeks → switch to temporary HD while the tract heals. Resume with low-volume supine exchanges. [5] Late leak: usually a hernia or abdominal wall defect. CT with intraperitoneal contrast (mixed with dialysate) localizes the tract. Genital edema: patent processus vaginalis or inguinal hernia tracking di

nodes.title: Abdominal Wall Hernia
nodes.body: Incidence 10–25% of PD patients. Highest risk: prior surgery, polycystic kidney disease, older age, high intra-abdominal pressure from large fill volumes. [5] ED priorities: • Examine for incarceration / strangulation — tender, irreducible, skin changes, peritonitis. Surgical emergency. • If reducible: low fill volumes + supine exchanges + elective repair. PD usually can resume 2 weeks post-repair

nodes.title: PD-Related Hydrothorax
nodes.body: Sudden right-sided pleural effusion in a PD patient = pleuro-peritoneal communication. ~90% right-sided. Dyspnea may be the only symptom; fever is absent. [5][6] Confirm: • Thoracentesis: pleural fluid glucose higher than serum (dialysate has dextrose) confirms diagnosis. Cell count is bland. • Alternative: peritoneal scintigraphy with Tc-99m injected into dialysate. Treatment: • Stop PD immediate

nodes.title: Metabolic Emergency in a PD Patient
nodes.summary: PD clears solutes slowly — severe metabolic emergencies need HD bridge.
nodes.body: PD removes solutes slowly compared to HD. Severe metabolic derangements often need temporary HD rather than aggressive PD. Volume overload is the most common cause of hospitalization in PD patients.

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia in PD Patient
nodes.body: Treat the membrane first, then move K+ around. Standard ED algorithm applies — HyperK Consult. [4] PD-specific points: • PD clearance of K+ is ~10–15 mEq/h (CAPD with hourly exchanges of 1.5% dextrose). HD clears K+ at 50–80 mEq/h. For K >6.5 with ECG changes, arrange HD — not aggressive PD. • Avoid kayexalate — does not work fast enough; sodium load worsens overload. • Patiromer or sodium zirconi

nodes.title: Volume Overload / UF Failure
nodes.body: Causes: peritoneal membrane dysfunction (high transporter status), missed exchanges, dietary indiscretion, residual renal function decline. [4][7] Acute management: • 4.25% dextrose dialysate (most hypertonic available) — short 2-h dwells maximize ultrafiltration. • Icodextrin for one long dwell (8–12 h) — sustained UF without glucose absorption rebound. • Furosemide IV 80–240 mg — useful if resid

nodes.title: Hyperglycemia from Dialysate
nodes.body: PD dialysate absorbs ~60–100 g glucose per day (more with 4.25%). Diabetic PD patients may need 25–50% higher insulin doses than during pre-dialysis CKD. [4] ED management: • Standard IV insulin + fluids for DKA / HHS — see DKA Consult. • Avoid additional dextrose-containing dialysate during treatment. • Icodextrin is glucose-sparing — switch to it if hyperglycemia is dialysate-driven. • Maltose i

nodes.title: Severe or Late Complication
nodes.body: These complications can be life-threatening or end PD as a modality.

nodes.title: Hemoperitoneum
nodes.body: Benign causes (most): menstrual retrograde flow (premenopausal women — recurs cyclically), ruptured ovarian cyst, recent exercise, recent colonoscopy. [4][7] Serious causes: ruptured viscus, splenic/renal cyst rupture (polycystic kidney disease), abdominal trauma, intra-abdominal malignancy, anticoagulation. ED workup: • Check hemoglobin + coagulation panel. • CT abdomen/pelvis if hemodynamically

nodes.title: Encapsulating Peritoneal Sclerosis
nodes.body: Rare (~1–4% incidence after >5 y PD) but catastrophic — mortality 25–50% at 1 year. Fibrotic cocoon encases small bowel. [3][8] Suspect when long-duration PD patient develops: • Recurrent bowel obstruction symptoms • Weight loss, anorexia, abdominal pain • Bloody or turbid ascites • UF failure with high transporter status Workup: • CT abdomen — characteristic findings: peritoneal calcifications, b

nodes.title: PD Failure → HD Bridge
nodes.body: Indications to abandon PD acutely: • Refractory peritonitis (no improvement at day 5) • Fungal peritonitis • Relapsing or recurrent peritonitis (≥2 episodes) • Tunnel infection with deep-cuff involvement • Hydrothorax (not amenable to pleurodesis) • EPS • Persistent UF failure Bridge plan: 1. Temporary HD catheter (internal jugular preferred; avoid subclavian — preserves future fistula sites). 2.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: PD patients have higher admission rates than HD patients for infectious complications. Threshold to admit is low.

nodes.title: Admit — Renal / Medicine
nodes.body: Continue IP antibiotics under nephrology guidance. Daily effluent cell counts + cultures until clear. Plan for catheter decisions if no improvement by day 3.
nodes.recommendation: Admit to medicine with nephrology consult.

nodes.title: Admit — ICU
nodes.body: Hemodynamic monitoring, vasopressors if needed, urgent HD access planning. Surgical consult for perforation or strangulated hernia.
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with nephrology + surgery as indicated.

nodes.title: Home with PD Nurse Follow-Up
nodes.body: Requires: reliable patient, same- or next-day home PD nurse visit, ability to perform additional exchanges, clear return precautions (fever, worsening pain, no clearing by 72 h).
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with 24-h nephrology and PD nurse follow-up.

nodes.title: Phosphate Disorder
nodes.summary: Route to hypoPhos, hyperPhos, or dynamic shift context; always interpret with Ca/Mg/K/renal function.
nodes.body: Serum phosphorus reflects phosphate concentration. Interpret with calcium, magnesium, potassium, renal function, acid-base status, insulin/nutrition exposure, and cell-lysis risk. Which pathway fits?

nodes.title: Phosphate Steps
nodes.summary: Confirm severity, check paired electrolytes and renal/cell-lysis context, replace or eliminate with close rechecks.
nodes.body: 1. Confirm severity and symptoms. 2. Check Ca, Mg, K, creatinine, glucose/insulin exposure, acid-base status, CK, uric acid, and nutrition/refeeding risk. 3. Low phosphate: replace orally unless severe, symptomatic, unable to take PO, or critical illness requires IV. 4. High phosphate: stop phosphate load, treat cell lysis/renal failure, avoid unnecessary calcium, and consider binders or dialysis.

nodes.title: Hypophosphatemia Severity
nodes.summary: Severe or symptomatic hypophosphatemia needs monitored IV replacement; stable patients usually get oral replacement.
nodes.body: Symptoms usually emerge when phosphate is <1 mg/dL, but ICU, DKA, alcoholism, malnutrition, refeeding, sepsis, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, or myocardial dysfunction lowers the treatment threshold.

nodes.title: Severe Hypophosphatemia
nodes.summary: IV phosphate for phos <1 or symptomatic; choose NaPhos vs KPhos by potassium and renal function.
nodes.body: Use IV phosphate when phos <1 mg/dL, severe symptoms, inability to take PO, respiratory failure, myocardial dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, or critical illness. Typical adult IV strategy — dose is elemental phosphorus and is the same for either salt, infused over about 6 hours: - Phos 1.7-2.2 mg/dL: 0.2 mmol/kg - Phos 1.0-1.7 mg/dL: 0.4 mmol/kg - Phos <1.0 mg/dL: 0.6 mmol/kg Reduce dose by

nodes.title: Stable Hypophosphatemia
nodes.body: Use oral phosphate replacement when stable, asymptomatic/mildly symptomatic, and able to take PO. Treat the cause: refeeding, DKA/insulin shift, respiratory alkalosis, alcohol use, poor intake, antacids/binders, vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, renal wasting/Fanconi, or iron infusion-related FGF23 effect. Recheck phosphate and paired electrolytes within the clinical timeframe of the trig
nodes.recommendation: Oral replacement is preferred for stable mild-moderate hypophosphatemia; admit when severe, symptomatic, recurrent, renal-risk, or shift-state physiology is active.

nodes.title: IV Phosphate Monitoring
nodes.summary: IV phosphate requires Ca/Mg/K/Cr monitoring and attention to hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, precipitation, and AKI.
nodes.body: Monitor during and after IV replacement: - Phosphate, calcium/ionized calcium, magnesium, potassium, creatinine - ECG/telemetry for severe deficiency, K-containing replacement, or cardiac disease - Symptoms: weakness, respiratory failure, paresthesias/tetany, arrhythmia, rhabdo Complications of aggressive IV phosphate: hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia with KPhos, soft-

nodes.title: Hyperphosphatemia Context
nodes.summary: Hyperphosphatemia management depends on acute cell lysis/load versus chronic CKD-MBD.
nodes.body: High phosphate is usually renal failure, cell lysis, phosphate load, or pseudohyperphosphatemia. Severity depends on trajectory, calcium symptoms, renal function, and TLS/rhabdo context.

nodes.title: Acute Hyperphosphatemia
nodes.summary: Stop phosphate load, treat cell lysis/AKI, use binder if enteral, and dialyze severe renal or symptomatic cases.
nodes.body: Immediate actions: 1. Stop phosphate intake/load and offending bowel prep/enemas/supplements. 2. Treat the driver: TLS, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, phosphate ingestion, vitamin D excess. 3. Hydrate and promote renal excretion if kidney function and volume status permit. 4. Use non-calcium phosphate binder such as Sevelamer when enteral therapy is appropriate. 5. Call nephrology early for severe AKI, anur

nodes.title: CKD-MBD Hyperphosphatemia
nodes.body: In CKD, do not manage phosphate as an isolated number. Review serial phosphate, calcium, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, diet, binder adherence, vitamin D/calcimimetic therapy, and dialysis adequacy. KDIGO recommends lowering persistently elevated phosphate toward normal, avoiding hypercalcemia, limiting calcium-based binders in adults receiving phosphate-lowering therapy, and using serial trends rathe
nodes.recommendation: Coordinate chronic CKD-MBD changes with nephrology; ED management focuses on severe symptoms, acute loads, missed dialysis, and dangerous Ca-phosphate physiology.

nodes.title: Refeeding / DKA / Shift States
nodes.summary: Refeeding/DKA states can rapidly shift phosphate intracellularly; monitor and replace phos/K/Mg together.
nodes.body: High-risk settings: malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, eating disorder, bariatric surgery, prolonged poor intake, DKA after insulin, respiratory alkalosis, sepsis, major burns, and post-operative critical illness. Monitor phosphate with potassium and magnesium. Replace before and during nutrition/insulin escalation when severe or falling rapidly. Consider thiamine and controlled calorie advanceme

nodes.title: STOP: Phosphate Pitfalls
nodes.body: - Do not give IV phosphate without checking potassium and renal function. - Do not use potassium phosphate when hyperkalemic, anuric, or high-risk for potassium accumulation — it delivers a fixed 1.47 mEq of potassium per mmol of phosphorus (30 mmol P = 44 mEq K), and the FDA label restricts it to serum K below 4 mEq/L. - Do not run phosphate through a line carrying calcium (lactated Ringer, calci
nodes.recommendation: Phosphate therapy is paired-electrolyte therapy: recheck Ca/Mg/K/Cr and treat the driver.

nodes.title: PID — Clinical Diagnosis
nodes.summary: CDC minimum: sexually active + pelvic pain + CMT/uterine/adnexal tenderness; low threshold to treat
nodes.body: PID Steps Summary Pelvic inflammatory disease is infection of the upper genital tract (uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, peritoneum). CDC 2021 Minimum Criteria — treat if ALL present: • Sexually active female • Pelvic or lower abdominal pain • Cervical motion tenderness, OR • Uterine tenderness, OR • Adnexal tenderness (unilateral or bilateral) Low threshold to treat — missed PID leads to serious

nodes.title: Additional Diagnostic Criteria
nodes.summary: Additional: fever >101F, mucopurulent discharge, elevated WBC on wet prep, positive GC/CT NAAT, US findings
nodes.body: Additional criteria increase diagnostic specificity: Clinical: • Oral temp >101°F (38.3°C) • Mucopurulent cervical discharge • Friable cervix Laboratory: • Elevated WBC on wet prep (>1 WBC per epithelial cell) • Elevated ESR or CRP • Positive NAAT for GC and/or CT • Positive cervical culture Imaging/Definitive: • Thickened, fluid-filled tubes on US (tubo-ovarian complex) • Tubo-ovarian abscess (TO

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Rule out ectopic pregnancy; consider appendicitis, ovarian torsion, UTI — imaging if diagnosis unclear
nodes.body: Consider alternative diagnoses if PID criteria not met: Gynecologic: • Ectopic pregnancy — always check pregnancy test • Ovarian cyst rupture/torsion • Endometriosis • Ovarian tumor GI: • Appendicitis (RLQ pain, migration, anorexia) • Inflammatory bowel disease • Diverticulitis Urologic: • UTI/pyelonephritis • Nephrolithiasis Other: • Mesenteric lymphadenitis • Muscle strain KEY: If ectopic pregna

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Pregnancy test mandatory; GC/CT NAAT; wet prep; US if mass, TOA suspected, or severe illness
nodes.body: Standard workup: • Pregnancy test — mandatory (ectopic must be excluded) • GC/CT NAAT — cervical or urine • Wet prep — WBCs, clue cells, trichomonads, yeast • CBC, CMP, CRP — if systemic illness suspected • HIV testing — offer to all Imaging: • Pelvic ultrasound if: - Pelvic mass palpated - TOA suspected - Diagnosis uncertain - Pregnancy test positive - Moderate-severe illness Does the patient req

nodes.title: Pelvic Ultrasound Findings
nodes.summary: US for TOA: complex multiloculated mass; TOA requires IV antibiotics ± drainage
nodes.body: Ultrasound findings in PID: Suggestive of PID: • Thickened, fluid-filled fallopian tubes • Free pelvic fluid • Tubo-ovarian complex (inflamed tube/ovary) Tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA): • Complex multiloculated pelvic mass • May involve tube, ovary, bowel • Requires IV antibiotics and possible drainage Alternative findings: • Simple ovarian cyst • Ectopic pregnancy • Appendicitis What are the ultrasou

nodes.title: Risk Assessment — Inpatient vs Outpatient
nodes.summary: Admit if: TOA, pregnancy, severe illness, cannot tolerate PO, surgical emergency not excluded
nodes.body: PID Admission Criteria CDC criteria for hospitalization: • Surgical emergency cannot be excluded (ectopic, appendicitis) • Tubo-ovarian abscess present • Pregnancy • Severe illness (high fever, nausea/vomiting, severe pain) • Unable to tolerate or follow outpatient regimen • No clinical response to oral antibiotics within 72 hours Additional considerations: • Immunocompromised (HIV with low CD4) •

nodes.title: Outpatient Treatment — CDC 2021
nodes.summary: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM × 1 + doxycycline 100mg BID × 14d + metronidazole 500mg BID × 14d
nodes.body: CDC PID Treatment Regimens Recommended regimen: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 dose (If weight ≥150 kg: 1 g IM) PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 14 days PLUS Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 14 days --- Metronidazole rationale: • Covers anaerobes and BV organisms • CDC recommends adding for all PID (previously optional) • Essential if BV on wet prep or TOA concern

nodes.title: Outpatient Follow-Up
nodes.summary: F/U in 48-72h mandatory; admit if no improvement; retest GC/CT in 3 months; IUD may remain during treatment
nodes.body: Follow-up in 48-72 hours is mandatory. Expected improvement: • Decreased pain • Resolution of fever • Improved tenderness on exam If no improvement in 72 hours: • Admit for IV antibiotics • Consider imaging for TOA • Reassess diagnosis Additional counseling: • Complete all antibiotics even if feeling better • No intercourse until treatment complete AND symptoms resolved AND partners treated • Retu

nodes.title: Partner Treatment
nodes.summary: Treat all partners from past 60 days; EPT is legal option; partners get ceftriaxone 500mg IM + doxy 7 days
nodes.body: Partner Treatment Card All sexual partners within past 60 days must be treated. Partner regimen (for GC/CT): • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days Expedited partner therapy (EPT): • Legal in most states • Provide prescription or medication for partner(s) • Alternative when partner unlikely to seek care Counseling: • Partners should be treated even if asymptomatic • Absta

nodes.title: Inpatient Treatment — CDC 2021
nodes.summary: IV: cefoxitin 2g q6h + doxy 100mg q12h; or clinda 900mg q8h + gent; transition to PO after 24-48h improvement
nodes.body: IV regimen options: OPTION A (preferred): • Cefotetan 2 g IV q12h OR Cefoxitin 2 g IV q6h • PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg PO/IV q12h OPTION B: • Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h • PLUS Gentamicin 2 mg/kg IV load, then 1.5 mg/kg IV q8h (or 5 mg/kg daily) --- Transition to oral: • After clinical improvement (24-48h afebrile, decreased pain) • Complete 14-day total course • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID + metronidazo

nodes.title: Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA)
nodes.summary: TOA: IV antibiotics + metro; drainage if >3-5cm or no improvement 48-72h; ruptured TOA = surgical emergency
nodes.body: TOA requires IV antibiotics and possible drainage. Initial management: • IV antibiotics (same regimens as severe PID) • Add metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h for enhanced anaerobic coverage • Serial imaging to monitor response Drainage indications: • Abscess >3-5 cm (varies by institution) • Failure to improve on antibiotics after 48-72h • Ruptured TOA (surgical emergency) Drainage options: • Interventi

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if mild-moderate; admit if severe/TOA/pregnant; surgery if ruptured TOA or peritonitis
nodes.body: Final disposition based on severity and treatment response.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge with outpatient treatment: Prescriptions: • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 14 days • Metronidazole 500 mg PO BID × 14 days • IM ceftriaxone given in ED Follow-up: • 48-72 hours for clinical reassessment (MANDATORY) • GC/CT retest in 3 months Patient instructions: • Complete all antibiotics • Partners must be treated • No intercourse until treatment complete + partners treated • Return for:
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline + metronidazole. Mandatory 48-72h follow-up. Treat partners. Retest GC/CT in 3 months.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit for IV antibiotics: Orders: • IV antibiotics per CDC regimen • IV fluids • Pain management • NPO if surgery possible • OB/GYN consultation Monitoring: • Vitals q4h • Daily abdominal/pelvic exam • WBC, temp trending Transition to oral: • After 24-48h afebrile with clinical improvement • Complete 14-day total course as outpatient If TOA: • IR or surgical consultation for drainage • Serial imag
nodes.recommendation: Admit. IV cefoxitin + doxycycline (or clinda + gent). OB/GYN consult. Transition to PO after 24-48h improvement.

nodes.title: Surgical Consultation
nodes.body: Urgent/emergent surgical consultation: Indications: • Ruptured TOA with peritonitis • Failed medical management of TOA • Septic shock • Diagnostic uncertainty (cannot exclude surgical emergency) Surgical options: • Laparoscopy for drainage and washout • Laparotomy for ruptured TOA • Possible salpingectomy or oophorectomy if necrotic tissue Pre-operative: • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics • Aggressiv
nodes.recommendation: Urgent OB/GYN surgical consultation. IV antibiotics. NPO. Consider OR for drainage or exploration.

nodes.title: Functional Seizures (PNES)
nodes.summary: 5-10% of epilepsy patients. 7-year diagnostic delay. Real seizures — not faking.
nodes.body: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES), now preferably called functional seizures or dissociative seizures, are paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are NOT caused by abnormal electrical brain activity. [1][2] Epidemiology: • 5-10% of epilepsy outpatients, 20-40% of epilepsy inpatients • 11-27% of ED "seizure" presentations • 70% female, peak age 20-40 years • Mean diagnostic

nodes.title: Rule Out Dangerous Mimics First
nodes.summary: Rule out status epilepticus, syncope, hypoglycemia, toxic/metabolic, CNS pathology first.
nodes.body: Before considering PNES, exclude life-threatening conditions: 🚩 True Status Epilepticus: • Continuous seizure >5 min or recurrent without recovery • Tongue bite (lateral, not tip) • Incontinence + prolonged postictal confusion • If ANY doubt → treat as epileptic seizure 🚩 Syncope / Cardiac: • Convulsive syncope can mimic seizure • Check ECG if concern for arrhythmia 🚩 Hypoglycemia: • Always che

nodes.title: Treat as Epileptic Seizure
nodes.summary: If uncertain, treat as epileptic seizure first. PNES and epilepsy can coexist (10-30%).
nodes.body: If red flags present or diagnostic uncertainty, treat as epileptic seizure. See Status Epilepticus consult for management. Key points: • Benzodiazepines are first-line for status epilepticus • Airway protection if prolonged seizure • Monitor for complications After stabilization: • If seizure features were atypical, reconsider PNES • Video-EEG monitoring may be needed to differentiate • Neurology

nodes.title: Avoid Iatrogenic Harm
nodes.summary: No benzos (26% adverse effects). No intubation (deaths reported). No ASM escalation.
nodes.body: Misdiagnosis of PNES as status epilepticus causes significant harm. [3][4] DO NOT give benzodiazepines for suspected PNES: • 26% adverse effect rate in RAMPART/ESETT trials when given to PNES patients [3] • Respiratory depression requiring intervention • 1 in 5 PNES patients given benzos were admitted to ICU • Cumulative dosing worsens outcomes DO NOT intubate: • Associated with prolonged hospital

nodes.title: Safe Observation Approach
nodes.summary: Safety measures, verbal reassurance, document semiology, video record if possible.
nodes.body: During the event — supportive observation: Safety measures: • Side rails up, remove nearby hazards • Do NOT restrain — may worsen event • Protect head from injury (pillow, cushion) • Do NOT put anything in mouth Verbal reassurance: • Speak calmly: "You are safe. I am Dr. [name]. You are in the emergency room." • Avoid alarming language • Do NOT suggest the patient is faking Document semiology (see

nodes.title: Semiologic Signs Overview
nodes.summary: Eye closure PLR 40.5, asynchronous movements PLR 10.2, ictal weeping PLR 8.2.
nodes.body: No single sign is pathognomonic. However, certain features strongly favor PNES over epileptic seizures. [5][6] High specificity for PNES (PLR >5): | Sign | Positive Likelihood Ratio | |------|---------------------------| | Ictal eye closure | 40.5 | | Asynchronous movements | 10.2 | | Ictal weeping/crying | 8.2 | | Fluctuating course | High | | Side-to-side head shaking | High | | Hip thrusting |

nodes.title: Ictal Eye Closure — Key Sign
nodes.summary: Eye closure during seizure: PLR 40.5 for PNES. Epileptic seizures usually have eyes OPEN.
nodes.body: Ictal eye closure is the MOST predictive sign of PNES. [5][6] Positive Likelihood Ratio: 40.5 What to observe: • Eyes forcibly closed during the event • Resistance to passive eye opening • May have flutter or rapid blinking Why it matters: • Epileptic seizures typically cause eye opening at onset • Tonic/clonic seizures: eyes deviated upward or to one side, open • Temporal lobe seizures: staring w

nodes.title: Movement Patterns
nodes.summary: Asynchronous movements PLR 10.2. PNES longer (>2 min), fluctuating. Epileptic: synchronous, brief.
nodes.body: Asynchronous limb movements strongly favor PNES. [5][6] PNES movement patterns: • Asynchronous — limbs move out of phase with each other (PLR 10.2) • Side-to-side head shaking — "no-no" pattern • Pelvic thrusting — though can occur in frontal lobe epilepsy • Opisthotonus (back arching) — "arc de cercle" • Trembling/shaking — non-rhythmic • Fluctuating intensity — waxing and waning Epileptic seizur

nodes.title: Awareness & Responsiveness
nodes.summary: Preserved awareness + bilateral motor = PNES. Epileptic: impaired awareness, postictal confusion.
nodes.body: Preserved awareness during bilateral motor activity strongly suggests PNES. [5][6] Testing during event (if safe): • Call patient's name — do they respond? • Give a simple command: "Squeeze my hand" • Present a word or object — can they recall it postictally? PNES features: • Preserved awareness during bilateral limb movements • Can follow commands during event • Postictal recall of information pr

nodes.title: Other Distinguishing Features
nodes.summary: Ictal crying PLR 8.2. Incontinence/tongue bite do NOT distinguish. PNES not from true sleep.
nodes.body: Additional features to assess: [5][6] Ictal crying/weeping (PLR 8.2): • Emotional vocalization during or after event • Very rare in epileptic seizures Stuttering/stammering: • Suggests PNES • True aphasic speech arrest is different Gradual onset: • PNES often build up slowly • Epileptic seizures usually have abrupt onset Modulation by bystanders: • Seizure intensity changes when attention is given

nodes.title: Historical Features
nodes.summary: Female, 20-40yo, psychiatric comorbidity, refractory to ASMs, stress-triggered, no nocturnal events.
nodes.body: History features suggestive of PNES: [1][2][7] Demographic: • Female (70%) • Young adult (peak 20-40 years) • History of other functional symptoms (chronic pain, fibromyalgia, IBS) Psychiatric history: • Depression, anxiety, PTSD (very common) • History of trauma (30-40%) — but do NOT ask directly in ED • Borderline personality disorder • Somatization • Prior conversion symptoms Seizure history: •

nodes.title: PNES + Epilepsy Comorbidity
nodes.summary: 10-30% have both PNES and epilepsy. Cannot assume all seizures are functional.
nodes.body: 10-30% of PNES patients ALSO have epilepsy. [1][5] Clinical implications: • Cannot assume ALL seizures in a PNES patient are functional • Must distinguish which events are epileptic vs functional • ASMs may still be needed for comorbid epilepsy How to approach: • Ask: "Do all your seizures look the same?" • Compare current event to prior documented events • Review prior video-EEG reports if availa

nodes.title: Diagnostic Certainty
nodes.summary: Gold standard = video-EEG. ED can achieve "possible" or "probable" PNES diagnosis.
nodes.body: Determine your level of diagnostic certainty: [1][8] Gold standard: Video-EEG capturing typical event with no epileptiform activity and history/semiology consistent with PNES. In the ED, you can achieve: • Possible PNES — suggestive history and semiologic features, no video-EEG • Probable PNES — witnessed event with multiple positive semiologic signs (eye closure, asynchronous movements, preserved

nodes.title: Established PNES Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Verify diagnosis, confirm typical semiology, supportive care, assess why they came in today.
nodes.body: For patients with established PNES diagnosis: [4] Verify the diagnosis: • Review EMR for prior video-EEG report • Confirm current event matches their typical semiology • Ask patient: "Does this feel like your usual seizures?" Management: • Supportive observation — no benzos, no intubation • Verbal reassurance during event • Brief period of observation post-event If event is DIFFERENT from usual: •

nodes.title: Communicating the Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Real seizures, recognized condition, treatable with therapy. Avoid minimizing language.
nodes.body: How you communicate the diagnosis significantly impacts outcomes. [7][8] Key messages: 1. "Your seizures are REAL" • "I can see these events are distressing and real." • "You are not making this up or faking." 2. "This is a recognized medical condition" • "This is called functional seizures (or psychogenic nonepileptic seizures)." • "It's related to how your brain processes stress and emotions." •

nodes.title: Sample Communication Script
nodes.summary: Real, recognized, treatable. Hardware vs software analogy. CBT is effective.
nodes.body: Example script for explaining PNES to patient/family: [7][8] --- *"I've had a chance to observe your seizure and review your records. I want to share what I've found.* *First, I want you to know that your seizures are real. You're not making them up, and you're not crazy. What you're experiencing is a recognized medical condition called functional seizures.* *The best way to explain it: your brain

nodes.title: Safety Assessment
nodes.summary: Screen for suicidal ideation, depression, anxiety. Do NOT probe trauma in ED.
nodes.body: PNES patients have high rates of psychiatric comorbidity. Screen for safety. [1][2] Psychiatric comorbidities (screen in ED): • Depression — very common • Anxiety disorders — very common • PTSD — common (but do NOT probe for trauma details in ED) • Suicidal ideation — actively screen • Self-harm history Ask directly: • "Are you having any thoughts of hurting yourself?" • "Have you ever tried to hu

nodes.title: Injury Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess for injuries. Severe injuries (fractures) more common with epileptic seizures.
nodes.body: Evaluate for injuries sustained during event: Common PNES-related injuries: • Head trauma from falls • Soft tissue injuries • Burns (if event near heat source) • MVA if driving Less common but possible: • Fractures from falls • Shoulder dislocation (posterior — consider epileptic seizure) • Vertebral compression fractures Physical exam: • Head: lacerations, hematomas • Oral: tongue bite (lateral =

nodes.title: ED Workup
nodes.summary: Fingerstick glucose always. CT/labs only if clinically indicated. Minimize unnecessary testing.
nodes.body: Limited workup needed for suspected PNES with typical presentation: [1][4] Routinely obtain: • Fingerstick glucose — always • Basic vitals — including SpO2 Consider based on presentation: • BMP — if concern for metabolic cause • Serum prolactin — elevated 10-20 min post-event suggests epileptic seizure (limited utility) • Drug screen — if intoxication suspected • ECG — if syncope considered Usuall

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Discharge if resolved, safe, and follow-up arranged. Admit if uncertain, recurrent, or unsafe.
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition: Discharge home if: • Event resolved, returned to baseline • No injuries requiring admission • No active suicidal ideation • Safe environment, reliable support system • Follow-up can be arranged Observation / Admit if: • Diagnostic uncertainty (? epileptic seizure) • Recurrent events not resolving • Significant injuries • Suicidal ideation or psychiatric crisis •

nodes.title: Discharge Planning
nodes.summary: Neurology (2-4 wk) for video-EEG, mental health (1-2 wk) for CBT, PCP. Proper diagnosis reduces ED visits.
nodes.body: Essential components of PNES discharge: [1][7][8] Education: • Explain diagnosis using empathetic, clear language • Provide PNES Patient Handout • Reassure that condition is treatable Follow-up — CRITICAL: 1. Neurology (within 2-4 weeks) • For video-EEG if not yet done • Confirm diagnosis • Manage any comorbid epilepsy • Coordinate care 2. Mental health (within 1-2 weeks) • CBT is first-line treat

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: Return if >5 min seizure, different event, SI, or injury. No driving until neuro eval.
nodes.body: Provide clear written instructions: What the patient should know: • You had a functional seizure (also called PNES) • This is a real medical condition, not "faking" • Treatment with therapy (CBT) is effective • Epilepsy medications will not help Return to ED if: • Seizure lasting >5 minutes without recovery • Injury during seizure • Seizure looks different from your usual events • Thoughts of hurt

nodes.title: Admission Considerations
nodes.summary: Admit for diagnostic uncertainty, recurrent events, injuries, or psychiatric crisis. Avoid ICU/intubation.
nodes.body: Indications for admission: Medical/Neurological: • Diagnostic uncertainty — need inpatient video-EEG • Recurrent events not resolving • Significant injuries requiring monitoring • First presentation needing workup • Concern for comorbid epilepsy with breakthrough seizures Psychiatric: • Active suicidal ideation • Psychiatric crisis requiring stabilization • Medication adjustment under supervision

nodes.title: Pneumonia Type
nodes.summary: Triage by acquisition setting: CAP vs HAP/VAP vs complicated vs aspiration vs influenza
nodes.body: Pneumonia Overview Clinical definition: Acute respiratory infection with pulmonary infiltrate on imaging + compatible symptoms (cough, dyspnea, fever, sputum production). Key initial questions: • Where was pneumonia acquired? • Is the patient immunocompromised? • Are there risk factors for resistant organisms? This pathway covers: • Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) • Hospital-acquired pneumonia

nodes.title: CAP Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: PSI preferred over CURB-65 per IDSA 2019; PSI I-II = outpatient, III = observation, IV-V = admit/ICU
nodes.body: PSI/PORT Calculator | CURB-65 Calculator | SMART-COP Calculator IDSA 2019 recommends PSI over CURB-65 for disposition decisions. PSI/PORT Score (5 classes): • Class I-II (<50 pts): Outpatient • Class III (51-70 pts): Observation/short admission • Class IV (71-130 pts): Hospitalization • Class V (>130 pts): ICU-level care CURB-65 (simpler, 5 variables): • 0: 0.9% mortality → outpatient • 1-2: 9.2%

nodes.title: Severity Score Result
nodes.summary: Route to outpatient, inpatient, or ICU based on severity scoring
nodes.body: Based on PSI or CURB-65: Low severity (PSI I-II or CURB-65 0-1): • Outpatient treatment appropriate • Ensure no severe CAP criteria Moderate severity (PSI III or CURB-65 2): • Consider observation or short hospitalization • Patient factors may tip decision High severity (PSI IV-V or CURB-65 ≥3): • Hospitalization required • Assess for ICU need Always check for severe CAP criteria regardless of sco

nodes.title: Severe CAP Criteria
nodes.summary: Severe CAP: 1 major (shock/vent) or 3+ minor criteria → direct ICU admission
nodes.body: Severe CAP Criteria Major criteria (any 1 = ICU): • Septic shock requiring vasopressors • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Minor criteria (3+ = severe CAP): • RR ≥30 • PaO2/FiO2 ≤250 • Multilobar infiltrates • Confusion/disorientation • Uremia (BUN ≥20) • Leukopenia (WBC <4,000) • Thrombocytopenia (<100,000) • Hypothermia (<36°C) • Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resusci

nodes.title: Outpatient Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Comorbidities (COPD, CHF, DM, CKD, liver disease, asplenia) → broader coverage needed
nodes.body: Does the patient have comorbidities? Comorbidities that affect treatment: • Chronic heart disease • Chronic lung disease (COPD, asthma) • Chronic liver disease • Chronic kidney disease • Diabetes mellitus • Alcoholism • Malignancy • Asplenia • Recent antibiotic use (<90 days) These patients need broader coverage due to higher risk of resistant organisms.

nodes.title: Outpatient CAP — Healthy Patient
nodes.summary: Healthy outpatient: amoxicillin 1g TID or doxycycline 100mg BID × 5 days; NO macrolide monotherapy
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference IDSA 2019 First-Line (choose one): 1. Amoxicillin (preferred) • 1g PO TID × 5 days 2. Doxycycline • 100mg PO BID × 5 days 3. Respiratory Fluoroquinolone (if allergies) • Levofloxacin 750mg daily × 5 days • Moxifloxacin 400mg daily × 5 days ⚠️ Macrolide monotherapy (azithromycin) NO LONGER recommended • S. pneumoniae resistance >30% in US • Only use if local resistance <
nodes.recommendation: Amoxicillin 1g PO TID or doxycycline 100mg BID × 5 days. NO macrolide monotherapy. Return if worsening.

nodes.title: Outpatient CAP — With Comorbidities
nodes.summary: Comorbid outpatient: FQ monotherapy OR beta-lactam + macrolide/doxy × 5 days
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference IDSA 2019 — Choose ONE regimen: Option 1: Respiratory Fluoroquinolone (preferred) • Levofloxacin 750mg PO daily × 5 days, OR • Moxifloxacin 400mg PO daily × 5 days Option 2: Beta-lactam + Macrolide/Doxycycline • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg TID × 5 days, PLUS • Azithromycin 500mg day 1, then 250mg daily × 4 days, OR • Doxycycline 100mg BID × 5 days Option 3: 3rd-Ge
nodes.recommendation: FQ monotherapy OR beta-lactam + macrolide/doxy × 5 days. Close follow-up in 48-72h.

nodes.title: MRSA Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: MRSA coverage if: prior isolation, recent hospitalization/abx, ESRD, IVDU, abscess/empyema, recent flu
nodes.body: MRSA Risk Factors Add empiric MRSA coverage if ANY of: • Prior MRSA isolation (respiratory or other site) • IV antibiotics within past 90 days • Hospitalization within past 90 days • Nursing home/long-term care resident • End-stage renal disease (ESRD) • Injection drug use • Lung abscess or empyema • Recent influenza Local epidemiology matters: • If MRSA prevalence >10-20% in your facility, lower

nodes.title: Pseudomonas Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Pseudomonas coverage if: prior isolation, bronchiectasis, severe COPD, tracheostomy; NOT routine COPD
nodes.body: Pseudomonas Risk Factors Add empiric Pseudomonas coverage if ANY of: • Prior Pseudomonas respiratory isolation (strongest predictor) • Bronchiectasis • Severe COPD (FEV1 <25% predicted) • Tracheostomy history • Lung abscess or empyema • Recurrent pneumonia requiring hospitalization Note: Isolated COPD without additional factors has same Pseudomonas risk as general population (~1-2.5%). Do NOT add

nodes.title: Inpatient CAP — Non-Severe
nodes.summary: Non-severe inpatient: CTX + azithro OR FQ; add vanc/linezolid if MRSA risk; 5 days total
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference IDSA 2019 — Choose ONE regimen: Option 1: Beta-lactam + Macrolide (preferred) • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV daily + azithromycin 500mg IV/PO daily, OR • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV Q6h + azithromycin 500mg daily Option 2: Respiratory Fluoroquinolone Monotherapy • Levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO daily, OR • Moxifloxacin 400mg IV/PO daily If MRSA risk flagged, add: • Vancomycin 15-20 mg/
nodes.recommendation: CTX + azithro OR FQ monotherapy. Add vanc/linezolid if MRSA risk. 5 days total. De-escalate at 48h.

nodes.title: Inpatient CAP — MRSA/Pseudomonas Risk
nodes.summary: MRSA/Pseudomonas risk: cefepime/pip-tazo + azithro/levo + vanc; de-escalate at 48h based on cultures
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference Empiric Regimen (cover all gaps): Anti-pseudomonal Beta-lactam (choose one): • Cefepime 2g IV Q8h, OR • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h, OR • Meropenem 1g IV Q8h (if ESBL concern) PLUS Atypical Coverage: • Azithromycin 500mg IV daily, OR • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily (also covers Pseudomonas) PLUS MRSA Coverage (if flagged): • Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV Q8-12h (troug
nodes.recommendation: Cefepime/pip-tazo + azithro/levo + vanc. Aggressive de-escalation at 48h based on cultures.

nodes.title: Severe CAP — ICU Admission
nodes.summary: Severe/ICU CAP: CTX 2g + azithro/levo; add anti-pseudomonal + vanc if risk factors; consider steroids if shock
nodes.body: Severe CAP Criteria | Antibiotic Dosing Reference Standard Severe CAP Regimen: Beta-lactam + Macrolide or FQ: • Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily + azithromycin 500mg IV daily, OR • Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily + levofloxacin 750mg IV daily If Pseudomonas risk: • Cefepime 2g IV Q8h OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h • PLUS levofloxacin 750mg IV daily (dual Pseudomonas coverage) If MRSA risk: • ADD vancomycin
nodes.recommendation: CTX 2g + azithro/levo. Add anti-pseudomonal + vanc if risk factors. Consider steroids if shock. 7+ days.

nodes.title: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia
nodes.summary: HAP = ≥48h post-admission; VAP = 48-72h post-intubation; must cover MRSA + Pseudomonas + GNB
nodes.body: Definitions: • HAP: Pneumonia ≥48h after hospital admission (non-intubated) • VAP: Pneumonia 48-72h after endotracheal intubation Key pathogens (different from CAP): • Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) • Pseudomonas aeruginosa • Enterobacteriaceae (Klebsiella, E. coli) • Acinetobacter (ICU-associated) All HAP/VAP requires coverage for: 1. S. aureus (MRSA if local rate >10-20%) 2. Pseudomonas

nodes.title: MDR Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: High MDR risk: recent abx, shock, ARDS, prolonged hospitalization, high local resistance
nodes.body: Assess risk for multidrug-resistant organisms: High MDR Risk if ANY of: • IV antibiotics within 90 days • Septic shock at time of VAP/HAP • ARDS preceding VAP • ≥5 days hospitalization prior to VAP • Acute renal replacement therapy prior to VAP • High local MRSA prevalence (>10-20%) • High local gram-negative resistance rates Local antibiogram is critical — adjust based on your facility's resistan

nodes.title: HAP/VAP — Low MDR Risk
nodes.summary: Low MDR HAP/VAP: pip-tazo or cefepime ± vanc; 7 days; de-escalate at 48h if cultures negative
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference Empiric Regimen: Anti-pseudomonal Beta-lactam (choose one): • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h, OR • Cefepime 2g IV Q8h, OR • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily (if beta-lactam allergy) MRSA Coverage (if local rate >10-20%): • Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV Q8-12h, OR • Linezolid 600mg IV BID Duration: 7 days total De-escalation: • Stop MRSA coverage at 48h if cultures negative
nodes.recommendation: Pip-tazo or cefepime ± vanc. 7 days. De-escalate at 48h if cultures negative. Never aminoglycoside monotherapy.

nodes.title: HAP/VAP — High MDR Risk
nodes.summary: High MDR HAP/VAP: dual anti-pseudomonal (different classes) + vanc/linezolid; 7 days; aggressive de-escalation
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference Empiric Regimen (broad coverage): TWO anti-pseudomonal agents from different classes: Agent 1 — Beta-lactam: • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h, OR • Cefepime 2g IV Q8h, OR • Meropenem 1g IV Q8h (if ESBL concern), OR • Imipenem 500mg IV Q6h Agent 2 — Non-beta-lactam: • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily, OR • Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV Q8h, OR • Amikacin 15-20 mg/kg IV daily, O
nodes.recommendation: Dual anti-pseudomonal (different classes) + vanc/linezolid. 7 days. Aggressive de-escalation at 48-72h.

nodes.title: Complicated Pneumonia
nodes.summary: Complicated PNA: effusion vs empyema vs abscess; CT preferred; thoracentesis for effusions
nodes.body: Effusion Assessment Complicated pneumonia includes: • Parapneumonic effusion • Empyema • Lung abscess • Necrotizing pneumonia Initial assessment: • Chest imaging (CT preferred if complicated PNA suspected) • If effusion present → diagnostic thoracentesis • Send fluid for: pH, glucose, LDH, protein, cell count, gram stain, culture What does the patient have?

nodes.title: Parapneumonic Effusion Assessment
nodes.summary: ACCP staging: Stage 1-2 = no drainage; Stage 3 (pH <7.2, loculated, positive culture) = drain; Stage 4 (pus) = drain
nodes.body: RAPID Score Step 1: Confirm exudate (Light's Criteria — ANY 1): • Pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5 • Pleural/serum LDH ratio >0.6 • Pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit of serum normal Step 2: ACCP Staging (determines drainage need): | Stage | Pleural Findings | Risk | Drainage? | |-------|-----------------|------|----------| | 1 | Minimal (<10mm), free-flowing | Very low | No | | 2 | >10mm, free-flowing,

nodes.title: Simple Parapneumonic Effusion (Stage 1-2)
nodes.summary: Simple effusion: antibiotics alone; 95% resolve; re-tap if enlarging, fever >72h, or deteriorating
nodes.body: Management — Antibiotics alone: • Standard CAP regimen based on severity • Duration: 5-7 days • Drainage NOT required Monitoring: • Repeat imaging at 48-72h • 95% resolve with antibiotics alone ⚠️ Indications to Reclassify → Drain: • Enlarging effusion despite antibiotics • Persistent fever >72h • Clinical deterioration • New loculations on follow-up imaging Re-tap if any of above — check pH, gluc
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics alone. Repeat imaging 48-72h. Re-tap if enlarging, persistent fever, or deteriorating.

nodes.title: Complicated Effusion — Drainage Method
nodes.summary: Free-flowing = tube; loculated = tPA/DNase or VATS; large/organizing = consider early surgery
nodes.body: Drainage is REQUIRED for Stage 3 effusions. Assess effusion characteristics: Free-flowing (no loculations): • Chest tube (≥14 Fr) or pigtail catheter • Success rate ~90% Loculated/Septated: • tPA + DNase (MIST2 protocol) with chest tube • Success rate ~90% vs 16% for tube alone • Alternative: early VATS Large/Organizing (>50% hemithorax or pleural thickening >2mm): • Consider early VATS • Higher t

nodes.title: Chest Tube Drainage
nodes.summary: Small-bore (10-14 Fr) image-guided; -20 cmH2O suction; assess response at 24-48h
nodes.body: Chest Tube Placement: Size: ≥14 Fr (larger not proven better) • Small-bore (10-14 Fr) catheter equally effective • Image-guided placement preferred Placement: • Under ultrasound or CT guidance • Avoid "safe triangle" blind insertion if loculated Management: • -20 cm H2O suction • Daily drainage volume tracking • Flush Q6-8h with 20-30mL saline Success criteria at 24-48h: • Clinical improvement (fe

nodes.title: Intrapleural Fibrinolytics (MIST2)
nodes.summary: MIST2: tPA 10mg + DNase 5mg BID × 3 days; 90% success vs 16% placebo; contraindicated if fistula/bleeding
nodes.body: tPA + DNase Protocol (MIST2 Trial): Indication: Loculated/septated parapneumonic effusion or empyema Regimen: • tPA 10mg + DNase 5mg in 30mL saline • Instill via chest tube, clamp 1 hour • BID × 3 days (6 total doses) Evidence (MIST2 NEJM 2011): • Combination: 90% success, 4% surgery rate • tPA alone: 55% success • DNase alone: 22% success • Placebo: 16% success Contraindications: • Bronchopleural

nodes.title: Successful Tube Drainage
nodes.summary: Remove tube when <100-150mL/day + lung re-expanded; antibiotics 2-4 weeks; follow-up CXR 4-6 weeks
nodes.body: Tube Management: Continue drainage until: • Output <100-150 mL/day (some use <50mL) • CXR shows lung re-expansion • No air leak Tube Removal: • When output low AND imaging clear • Consider water seal trial before removal • CXR 2-4h post-removal to rule out pneumothorax Antibiotics: • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV Q6h, OR • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h • Add MRSA coverage if risk factors • Dura
nodes.recommendation: Remove tube when <100-150mL/day + lung re-expanded. Antibiotics 2-4 weeks total. CXR at 4-6 weeks.

nodes.title: Failed Tube Drainage — Escalation
nodes.summary: Failed drainage: try tPA/DNase if not done; otherwise VATS; thoracotomy reserved for VATS failure
nodes.body: Signs of Drainage Failure (at 24-48h): • Persistent fever • No clinical improvement • Persistent/enlarging effusion on imaging • Loculations developing • Tube output <50mL with significant residual fluid Options: 1. Intrapleural Fibrinolytics (if not yet tried): • tPA + DNase protocol • Success ~90% for loculated effusions 2. VATS (Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery): • Break up loculations • De

nodes.title: Surgical Indications — VATS vs Thoracotomy
nodes.summary: VATS: failed tube, loculated, organizing; Thoracotomy: VATS failure, trapped lung, fistula. Early surgery (7-10d) better.
nodes.body: VATS Indications (preferred first-line surgical approach): • Failed chest tube ± fibrinolytics (48-72h no improvement) • Multiloculated empyema • Empyema with thick fibrinous peel • Large effusion (>50% hemithorax) • Organizing effusion (>2mm pleural thickening) • Early Stage 3 empyema (some centers prefer early VATS) VATS Procedure: • Debridement of loculations/peel • Complete evacuation of infec
nodes.recommendation: VATS first if tube/fibrinolytics fail. Thoracotomy for VATS failure, trapped lung, or fistula. Early surgery (7-10d) preferred.

nodes.title: Empyema (Stage 4) — Frank Pus
nodes.summary: Frank pus = immediate drainage; choose method by loculation status; antibiotics 2-4 weeks with anaerobic coverage
nodes.body: RAPID Score | Antibiotic Dosing Reference Definition: Frank pus in the pleural space IMMEDIATE DRAINAGE REQUIRED Antibiotics (anaerobic coverage critical): • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV Q6h, OR • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h, OR • Ceftriaxone 2g IV + metronidazole 500mg IV Q8h If MRSA risk: Add vancomycin or linezolid Duration: 2-4 weeks total (IV → PO) Common Organisms: • Streptococcus (esp

nodes.title: Lung Abscess Management
nodes.summary: Lung abscess: antibiotics first (amp-sulb) × 3-4 weeks; drain if >6cm, refractory, or resistant organisms
nodes.body: Antibiotic Dosing Reference First-Line Treatment (antibiotics alone): • Success rate 63-95% Preferred Regimen (anaerobic coverage): • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3g IV Q6h, OR • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125mg PO TID Alternative: • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IV daily + clindamycin 600mg IV Q6h, OR • Ceftriaxone + metronidazole 500mg IV Q8h Duration: 3-4 weeks total (minimum) • IV until clinical improvement (7-14
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics first (amp-sulb) × 3-4 weeks. Drain if >6cm, refractory, or resistant organisms.

nodes.title: Aspiration Pneumonia
nodes.summary: Aspiration PNA: treat as standard CAP; add anaerobic coverage ONLY if empyema, abscess, or necrotizing
nodes.body: Modern Approach: DO NOT routinely cover anaerobes Standard treatment = Standard CAP regimen: • Beta-lactam + macrolide OR respiratory fluoroquinolone • Anaerobic coverage NOT needed for simple aspiration PNA ADD Anaerobic Coverage ONLY IF: • Evidence of empyema • Necrotizing pneumonia • Lung abscess (diagnosed on CT) • Severe periodontal disease + putrid sputum When Anaerobic Coverage Needed: • Pi
nodes.recommendation: Treat as standard CAP. Add anaerobic coverage ONLY if empyema, abscess, or necrotizing. 5-7 days.

nodes.title: Influenza Pneumonia
nodes.summary: Influenza PNA: oseltamivir 75mg BID × 5d; add CAP abx if severe or deteriorating; MRSA coverage not routine
nodes.body: Antiviral Therapy (start within 48h, but benefit even if later): • Oseltamivir 75mg PO BID × 5 days, OR • Peramivir 600mg IV × 1 (if unable to take PO) Bacterial Superinfection Risk: 26-77% of hospitalized influenza patients When to Add Bacterial Coverage: • Severe disease at presentation (extensive infiltrates, respiratory failure, hypotension) • Deterioration after initial improvement • Persiste
nodes.recommendation: Oseltamivir 75mg BID × 5d. Add CAP abx if severe or deteriorating. MRSA coverage not routine.

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Discharge if: afebrile 24h, HR <100, RR <24, SBP ≥90, O2 sat ≥90%, tolerating PO, normal mentation
nodes.body: Criteria for Discharge (all must be met): • Temperature <37.8°C for ≥24h • Heart rate <100 bpm • Respiratory rate <24 • Systolic BP ≥90 mmHg • O2 sat ≥90% on room air (or baseline) • Tolerating oral intake • Normal mentation (or baseline) • Able to take oral antibiotics Red flags requiring extended observation: • Persistent hypoxia • Hemodynamic instability • Altered mentation • Inability to toler

nodes.title: Discharge Instructions
nodes.summary: Discharge: complete 5-day abx course PO; PCP follow-up 1 week; repeat CXR 6-8 weeks if smoker or >50yo
nodes.body: Oral Antibiotic Transition: • Complete total 5-day course (IV + PO) • Respiratory fluoroquinolone if monotherapy appropriate • Amoxicillin-clavulanate + azithromycin if combination needed Follow-up: • PCP follow-up within 1 week • Repeat chest X-ray at 6-8 weeks (especially if smoker, age >50, or persistent symptoms) • Pneumococcal and influenza vaccination if not up to date Return Precautions: •
nodes.recommendation: Complete 5-day abx course PO. PCP follow-up 1 week. Repeat CXR 6-8 weeks if smoker or >50yo.

nodes.title: Inpatient Monitoring
nodes.summary: Reassess 48-72h; if not improving: re-culture, CT chest, broaden coverage; consider PE, malignancy, CHF
nodes.body: Reassess at 48-72h: Signs of Clinical Response: • Defervescence • Improving oxygenation • Decreasing WBC • Declining procalcitonin • Hemodynamic stability If NOT Improving: • Re-culture (blood, sputum, consider BAL) • CT chest to evaluate for complications (abscess, empyema) • Broaden antibiotic coverage • Consider resistant organisms or alternate diagnosis Alternate Diagnoses to Consider: • PE wi

nodes.title: POCUS for Pneumothorax
nodes.summary: POCUS detects 20-50 mL air — indicated for chest trauma, sudden dyspnea, decreased breath sounds
nodes.body: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is highly sensitive and specific for pneumothorax detection, especially in supine trauma patients. Can detect as little as 20-50 mL of air. Indications: • Chest trauma • Sudden dyspnea • Pleuritic chest pain • Decreased breath sounds • Subcutaneous emphysema • Post-procedure evaluation

nodes.title: POCUS Technique
nodes.summary: Linear probe at 2nd-4th ICS MCL, M-mode confirmation, part of eFAST in trauma
nodes.body: Probe: High-frequency linear probe Position: Scan anterior chest at 2nd-4th intercostal spaces, mid-clavicular line Steps: 1. Compare bilateral lung sliding 2. Use M-mode to confirm findings 3. Look for lung point if no sliding Tip: In trauma, this is part of the eFAST exam. Supine position — air rises anteriorly.

nodes.title: Lung Sliding Present?
nodes.summary: Lung sliding + B-lines = no PTX; absent sliding + barcode sign = possible PTX, find lung point
nodes.body: Assess for lung sliding — the shimmering movement of the visceral pleura against the parietal pleura during respiration. Also look for: • Comet tail artifacts (B-lines) • Seashore sign on M-mode (normal) • Barcode/stratosphere sign on M-mode (abnormal)

nodes.title: Normal: Pneumothorax Excluded
nodes.body: Lung sliding, comet tails, and B-lines exclude pneumothorax at the scanned locations. Negative predictive value >99% If clinical suspicion persists despite normal POCUS: • Scan additional rib spaces • Consider CT chest • Repeat imaging if symptoms change

nodes.title: Abnormal: Stratosphere Sign
nodes.summary: Absent sliding alone is not diagnostic — rule out mainstem intubation, adhesions, apnea, ARDS
nodes.body: Absent lung sliding with stratosphere sign on M-mode (barcode sign) suggests pneumothorax. Important: Absent sliding alone is not diagnostic — can also be seen in: • Mainstem intubation • Pleural adhesions • Apnea • Severe ARDS Check multiple rib spaces and look for the lung point.

nodes.title: Lung Point Identified?
nodes.summary: Lung point is pathognomonic for PTX (100% specificity) — slide probe laterally to find border
nodes.body: The lung point is pathognomonic for pneumothorax — where lung sliding appears and disappears with respiration at the border of the collapsed lung. Specificity: 100% Slide the probe laterally from the area of absent sliding until you see intermittent sliding.

nodes.title: Pneumothorax Confirmed
nodes.summary: PTX confirmed — estimate size by lung point location: anterior=small, mid-axillary=moderate, posterior=large
nodes.body: POCUS confirmed pneumothorax (lung point = 100% specificity). Size estimation by lung point location: • Anterior chest only → Small • Extends to mid-axillary line → Moderate • Extends posteriorly → Large

nodes.title: No Lung Point — Massive PTX?
nodes.summary: No lung point = suspect massive PTX with complete collapse — if unstable, treat as tension
nodes.body: If absent lung sliding throughout the entire hemithorax without a lung point, suspect massive pneumothorax with complete lung collapse. Confirm with CXR — assess for mediastinal shift. If hemodynamically unstable → treat as tension pneumothorax.

nodes.title: Signs of Tension?
nodes.summary: Hypotension + JVD + tracheal deviation = tension — do NOT wait for imaging, decompress now
nodes.body: Assess for tension pneumothorax: • Hypotension • Tracheal deviation • Distended neck veins • Severe respiratory distress DO NOT wait for imaging if tension suspected.

nodes.title: Immediate Needle Decompression
nodes.body: Needle decompression STAT: • 14-gauge angiocath • 2nd ICS, mid-clavicular line • OR 4th-5th ICS, anterior axillary line Follow with chest tube placement. See Chest Tube / Pneumothorax Management for tube thoracostomy procedure.

nodes.title: Stable Patient — Size Assessment
nodes.summary: 2024 ERS/EACTS/ESTS + BTS 2023 — symptom-based, not size-based; conservative for asymptomatic PSP, needle aspiration before chest tube for symptomatic
nodes.body: Obtain CXR or CT to assess pneumothorax size, but 2024 ERS/EACTS/ESTS + BTS 2023 emphasize symptom-based, not size-based, decisions.
