[6] POCUS lung point location provides initial size estimate. Updated paradigm (2024): • Asymptomatic / minimally symptomatic PSP → conservative management regardless of size (Brown et al NEJM 2020 conservative-non-inferior trial) • Symptomatic → needle aspiration pr

nodes.title: Asymptomatic / Minimally Symptomatic PSP — Conservative Management
nodes.body: 2024 ERS/EACTS/ESTS + BTS 2023: Conservative (watch-and-wait) management is first-line for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP), regardless of size. [6] Evidence: Brown et al (NEJM 2020 PSP-CMT trial): conservative care non-inferior to chest drain for 8-week radiologic resolution, with fewer adverse events and lower 1-year recurrence. Pooled meta-analysis (1

nodes.title: Symptomatic PSP — Intervention
nodes.body: 2024 ERS/EACTS/ESTS strong recommendation: Needle aspiration is preferred over chest tube as the first invasive intervention for symptomatic PSP. [6] Step 1 — Needle Aspiration: • 16-18G angiocath or aspiration kit, 2nd ICS MCL • Aspirate up to 2.5 L; stop if resistance, cough, or 2.5 L reached • Reassess with CXR — if lung re-expanded: observe, then discharge with close follow-up • Success rate ~

nodes.title: Trauma — eFAST Protocol
nodes.summary: Supine trauma — air rises anteriorly, 50% of PTX occult on CXR; chest tube if positive pressure ventilation planned
nodes.body: In trauma, pneumothorax evaluation is part of the eFAST exam. Key points: • Supine position — air rises anteriorly • Up to 50% of pneumothoraces are occult on initial CXR but visible on CT • POCUS detects occult PTX missed on supine CXR Occult PTX management: • Observation appropriate for small, stable occult PTX • Consider chest tube if positive pressure ventilation planned or PTX enlarging

nodes.title: ROSC Confirmed — Immediate Priorities
nodes.summary: Secure airway, 12-lead ECG immediately, target ETCO2 35-45, arterial line, labs/CXR
nodes.body: Post-ROSC Steps Summary ROSC confirmed. Immediate priorities: Airway & Ventilation: • Secure airway if not already — intubate if GCS ≤8 • Waveform capnography to confirm ETT placement • Target ETCO₂ 35-45 mmHg — guides ventilation Immediate Workup: • 12-lead ECG — STEMI identification is the #1 priority • Avoid hypoxemia (SpO₂ <90%) and hypotension (MAP <65) • Arterial line for continuous BP monit

nodes.title: STEMI on 12-Lead ECG?
nodes.summary: STEMI identification is #1 priority post-ROSC — emergent PCI if found, do not delay
nodes.body: STEMI or STEMI-equivalent on 12-lead ECG?

nodes.title: STEMI + ROSC → Emergent PCI
nodes.summary: STEMI + ROSC = emergent PCI — do not delay for CT head, TTM can start in cath lab
nodes.body: STEMI + ROSC → emergent PCI. Do not delay for CT head or other workup. • Activate cath lab immediately • TTM can be initiated in cath lab • Transfer to PCI-capable center if not available • Dual antiplatelet therapy per ACS protocol • Heparin bolus per cath lab protocol STEMI Management

nodes.title: No STEMI — Stabilize First
nodes.summary: COACT trial: no STEMI = no benefit from immediate angiography — stabilize hemodynamics first
nodes.body: No STEMI: stabilize hemodynamics first. Consider coronary angiography if: • Witnessed arrest with shockable rhythm • High suspicion for cardiac cause • Hemodynamic instability suggesting cardiogenic shock COACT Trial (2019): Immediate angiography in OHCA without STEMI did NOT improve survival vs delayed/selective strategy. Timing is less urgent — can wait for clinical stabilization.

nodes.title: Indeterminate ECG — Cardiology Consult
nodes.summary: Indeterminate ECG or new LBBB — cardiology consult, early angiography if shockable rhythm
nodes.body: Indeterminate ECG or new LBBB: cardiology consult. Consider early angiography within 2h if: • Shockable rhythm arrest • Hemodynamically unstable • High suspicion for ACS Non-shockable rhythm with stable hemodynamics → angiography can be deferred pending further workup and clinical trajectory.

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Targets
nodes.summary: MAP >=65, SpO2 90-98% or PaO2 60-105, PaCO2 35-45 — titrate FiO2 down once reliable oxygenation is measured
nodes.body: Hemodynamic and gas-exchange targets: • MAP ≥65 mmHg — avoid hypotension; use fluids and vasopressor/inotrope support as clinically indicated • SpO₂ 90-98% or PaO₂ 60-105 mmHg — avoid hypoxemia and severe hyperoxemia (PaO₂ >250 mmHg has been associated with worse outcomes) • PaCO₂ 35-45 mmHg — avoid hypocapnia (cerebral vasoconstriction) • ETCO₂ 35-45 mmHg — use as a ventilation trend, confirmed w

nodes.title: Vasopressor Support
nodes.summary: No single post-ROSC vasopressor is preferred by AHA; tailor fluids, vasopressor, and inotrope support to shock phenotype
nodes.body: Vasopressor and inotrope support: AHA 2025: There is insufficient evidence to recommend one specific vasopressor for undifferentiated post-ROSC hypotension. Choose support based on the shock phenotype, bedside echo, rhythm, and perfusion. • For vasodilatory shock, Norepinephrine is a reasonable commonly used option: 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min • Refractory vasodilatory shock: consider Vasopressin 0.04 unit

nodes.title: Patient Following Commands?
nodes.summary: Comatose patients need aggressive fever prevention; following commands = good neuro sign
nodes.body: Is the patient following commands after ROSC?

nodes.title: Comatose — Prevent Fever Aggressively
nodes.summary: TTM2: no benefit of routine 33C cooling — control temperature at 32-37.5C for at least 36h and prevent fever
nodes.body: Patient not following commands after ROSC: initiate deliberate temperature control. TTM2 Trial (2021): 33°C vs 37.5°C showed no difference in mortality or neurological outcome. AHA 2025: • Maintain a controlled temperature between 32°C and 37.5°C • Maintain temperature control for at least 36 hours • If using a normothermia strategy, actively prevent fever and keep temperature below 37.5°C • Routi

nodes.title: Following Commands — Standard Care
nodes.summary: Awake post-ROSC — standard care, treat fever, echo for arrest cause, neuro consult if seizure concern
nodes.body: Following commands = good neurological sign. Standard care: • Monitor temperature and treat clinically significant fever per ICU protocol • No post-arrest temperature-control pathway is required solely because the patient is awake and following commands • Continue hemodynamic optimization • Workup for arrest cause (echo, labs, serial ECGs) • Neurology consult if any concern for seizure activity

nodes.title: Neuroprognostication — Wait 72h Minimum
nodes.summary: Delay prognostic impressions until >=72h from ROSC or normothermia and after confounders clear; use multimodal evidence
nodes.body: ⚠️ Do NOT make a prognostic impression before at least 72 hours from ROSC or achievement of normothermia, and only after sedation, hypothermia, neuromuscular blockade, and other confounders have cleared. Premature withdrawal of care can cause an avoidable death. Multimodal approach: • Clinical exam: interpret brainstem reflexes and motor response in context, after confounders clear • EEG: backgrou

nodes.title: Post-Arrest Seizures
nodes.summary: 20-30% have post-arrest seizures — continuous EEG, levetiracetam first-line, myoclonus is not always seizure
nodes.body: Post-arrest seizures occur in 20-30% of comatose survivors. • Obtain continuous or repeated EEG in patients who do not follow commands and when seizures are suspected • Clinical seizures may be subtle (eye twitching, nystagmus) or masked by paralysis • Do not give routine antiseizure prophylaxis when there is no seizure or ictal-interictal EEG pattern • Treatment when indicated: Levetiracetam 60 m

nodes.title: ICU Bundle
nodes.summary: Glucose 140-180, EEG x24-48h, echo, TV 6 mL/kg IBW, labs q4-6h, DVT prophylaxis
nodes.body: ICU bundle: • Glucose 140-180 mg/dL — avoid hypoglycemia (<70), treat hyperglycemia with insulin infusion • Seizure surveillance: continuous EEG × 24-48h minimum • Echo: assess LV function, wall motion abnormalities, post-arrest stunning • Ventilator: TV 6 mL/kg IBW, PEEP 5-8, target PaCO₂ 35-45 • Labs q4-6h: lactate (trending down = good), troponin, electrolytes, ABG • Foley: strict I/O monitorin

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: Admit to ICU. Document: code duration, initial rhythm, ETCO₂ values during resuscitation, number of shocks, medications given, total epi doses, neurological exam at ROSC, cooling plan. Communicate to ICU: • Arrest circumstances (witnessed/unwitnessed, bystander CPR, initial rhythm) • Total downtime • Interventions and response • Current hemodynamics and vasopressor support • TTM plan and current t
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous monitoring. Document full resuscitation details. TTM plan. Neuroprognostication after 72h minimum.

nodes.title: Post-Tonsillectomy Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: PTH: primary <24h (0.1-1%), secondary days 5-10 (1.5-4.3%); main risk is ASPIRATION not exsanguination
nodes.body: PTH Overview Definition: Bleeding from tonsillar fossa following tonsillectomy Incidence: • Overall: 0.1-7.5% (average ~4.2%) • Primary (<24h): 0.1-1% • Secondary (days 5-10): 1.5-4.3% — more common • Lethal hemorrhage: 7 per 100,000 ⚠️ CRITICAL CONCEPT: Primary risk is ASPIRATION, not exsanguination • Most deaths from airway compromise, not blood loss • Children compensate until 40% blood loss, t

nodes.title: Initial Stabilization
nodes.summary: Upright positioning, suction ready, IV access, labs; primary <24h vs secondary days 5-10
nodes.body: Immediate Actions: Positioning: • Sit patient upright (reduces aspiration risk) • Suction at bedside • Avoid manipulation, coughing, straining (destabilizes clots) Access: • Large-bore IV • Labs: CBC, type & screen, consider PT/PTT • Estimate blood loss Assess Timing: Primary Hemorrhage (<24h): • Usually surgical technique related • Often requires OR return Secondary Hemorrhage (days 5-10): • Slou

nodes.title: Hemorrhage Timing
nodes.summary: Secondary more common (66%); peak day 6-7; risk factors: age >6, recurrent tonsillitis, ADHD
nodes.body: Primary Hemorrhage (<24 hours): • Usually surgical technique related • More likely to require OR return • Associated with: coblation technique, surgeon inexperience Secondary Hemorrhage (days 5-10): • Most common type (66% of all bleeds) • Caused by sloughing of fibrin eschar • Peak incidence: day 6-7 • May respond to conservative management Risk Factors for Any Bleeding: • Age >6 years (11+ years

nodes.title: Primary Hemorrhage (<24h)
nodes.summary: Primary (<24h): usually surgical, lower threshold for OR return, immediate ENT consult
nodes.body: Primary hemorrhage is often surgical in nature. Characteristics: • Within 24 hours of surgery • Usually from inadequate intraoperative hemostasis • Often requires surgical re-exploration • Higher volume bleeds more common Management: • Same initial stabilization • Lower threshold for OR return • ENT consultation immediately • These patients are still recovering from anesthesia — watch airway close

nodes.title: Secondary Hemorrhage (Days 5-10)
nodes.summary: Secondary (days 5-10): fibrin eschar sloughs; ~50% manageable conservatively; peak day 6-7
nodes.body: Most common type — often manageable conservatively. Pathophysiology: • Fibrin eschar sloughs as healing progresses • Exposes underlying vessels • Peak at day 6-7 post-op Characteristics: • May present with minor blood-tinged sputum • Or active bleeding • ~50% can be managed without surgery Favorable Features for Conservative Management: • Blood-tinged sputum only (not active bleeding) • No fresh c

nodes.title: Late Hemorrhage (>14 days)
nodes.summary: Late (>14d): unusual, consider infection, coagulopathy, underlying pathology; ENT consult
nodes.body: Unusual presentation — consider other etiologies. Possible Causes: • Delayed eschar separation (rare) • Infection at surgical site • Foreign body • Coagulopathy (undiagnosed) • Malignancy (very rare) Workup: • Careful examination of tonsillar fossa • Coagulation studies if not already done • Consider CT if concerning features Management: • Same principles as secondary hemorrhage • ENT consultation

nodes.title: Bleeding Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Grade 1: blood-tinged; Grade 2: oozing, stable; Grade 3: brisk, unstable; clot = 17.3% rebleed
nodes.body: Severity Classification Grade-Based Classification: Grade 0 (Non-hemorrhagic): 80.8% of cases • Concern for bleeding but none visualized Grade 1 (Minor): 11.9% • Blood-tinged sputum • Small amount of blood in mouth • No active oozing Grade 2 (Moderate): 6.0% • Active oozing from tonsillar fossa • Frank blood in mouth • Hemodynamically stable Grade 3 (Severe): 1.3% • Brisk, active hemorrhage • Fres

nodes.title: Grade 1 — Minor Bleeding
nodes.summary: Grade 1: 10.2% rebleed; observe 4-6h; discharge if stable with reliable follow-up
nodes.body: Blood-tinged sputum, no active bleeding visible. Risk Assessment: • Rebleed risk: 10.2% • Most can be observed Initial Management: • Keep NPO • IV access, labs • Notify ENT • Ice chips may be soothing Observation Acceptable If: • No active bleeding on exam • Hemodynamically stable • Older child who can cooperate • Can follow instructions (no straining, coughing) Consider Discharge If: • Observed 4

nodes.title: Grade 2 — Moderate Bleeding
nodes.summary: Grade 2: oozing but stable; ENT notification; hemostatic measures; observe 12-24h; ~50% avoid OR
nodes.body: Active oozing, hemodynamically stable. Initial Management: • NPO, IV access • Labs: CBC, type & screen • ENT notification (not emergent but urgent) • Begin hemostatic measures Hemostatic Options: • Ice/cold fluids • Suction gently (avoid dislodging clot) • Consider silver nitrate if appropriate (see next) • TXA (emerging evidence) Observation Required: • Minimum 12-24 hours • Watch for recurrence

nodes.title: Grade 3 — Severe Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Grade 3: brisk bleeding → OR; 2 large-bore IVs, type & cross, ENT STAT; prepare for difficult airway
nodes.body: ⚠️ ACTIVE BRISK BLEEDING — PREPARE FOR OR Immediate Actions: • Maintain upright position if conscious • Suction ready • Large-bore IV × 2 • Type & crossmatch • ENT to bedside STAT Signs of Shock (may be late in children): • Tachycardia • Delayed capillary refill • Pallor • Altered mental status • Hypotension (LATE sign in peds) Blood Product Preparation: • Type & crossmatch immediately • Consider

nodes.title: Minor Bleeding — Conservative Measures
nodes.summary: Cold therapy, positioning, avoid straining; H2O2 gargle NOT proven effective; observe 4-6h
nodes.body: For blood-tinged sputum without active bleeding: Cold Therapy: • Ice chips • Cold fluids (if alert and able to swallow) • Ice pack to neck (external) Positioning: • Upright or side-lying • Avoid supine (aspiration risk) Avoid: • Coughing, straining • Hot foods/drinks • NSAIDs Hydrogen Peroxide Gargle: • 3% H2O2 diluted 1:6 with water • 20mL gargle (do NOT swallow) • Evidence: NO proven benefit (10

nodes.title: Hemostatic Intervention
nodes.summary: Silver nitrate: 81% initial control but 19% rebleed; TXA emerging; direct pressure temporizes
nodes.body: Hemostatic Options Available Interventions: 1. Silver Nitrate Cautery: • 81.4% initial control • But 19.3% rebleed → still need OR • Best for: older cooperative children, non-brisk bleeding • NOT for active hemorrhage or fresh clot 2. Tranexamic Acid (TXA): • Emerging evidence — increasingly used • IV or nebulized • May reduce need for operative management • See TXA protocol 3. Direct Pressure: •

nodes.title: Silver Nitrate Cautery
nodes.summary: Silver nitrate: 81% initial control, 19% rebleed; only for cooperative child, non-brisk bleeding
nodes.body: Bedside Silver Nitrate Application: Indications: • Older cooperative child/teenager • Non-brisk bleeding with visible source • NO active hemorrhage or fresh clot Technique: • Apply silver nitrate stick directly to bleeding site • Hold for 10-15 seconds • May need multiple applications Success Rate: • 81.4% achieve initial hemostasis • BUT 19.3% still require operative control • No statistical diff
nodes.recommendation: Silver nitrate for cooperative child with non-brisk bleeding. 81% initial success but 19% rebleed.

nodes.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA) Protocol
nodes.summary: TXA: 10-15 mg/kg IV (max 1g) or 500mg nebulized; emerging evidence; may reduce OR need
nodes.body: TXA Dosing ⚡ EMERGING EVIDENCE — Increasingly Used Mechanism: Antifibrinolytic — stabilizes clot Dosing (Weight-Based): IV Administration: • 10-15 mg/kg IV bolus (max 1000mg) • Can repeat q8h (max 30 mg/kg/day or 3000mg/day) Nebulized (for active hemorrhage): • 500mg in 5mL NS • Nebulize over 15-20 minutes • Case reports show effectiveness Evidence: • Perioperative TXA reduces intraoperative blood
nodes.recommendation: TXA 10-15 mg/kg IV (max 1g) or 500mg nebulized. Emerging evidence supports use. May reduce OR need.

nodes.title: Airway Considerations
nodes.summary: Main risk = aspiration; 2.7% difficult intubation; senior provider; have VL/bougie/suction ready
nodes.body: PTH Airway ⚠️ MOST DEATHS FROM ASPIRATION, NOT EXSANGUINATION Fatality analysis: aspiration contributed to ~50% of deaths. Pre-Intubation: • Keep upright if conscious (reduces aspiration) • Suction immediately available • Avoid manipulation that dislodges clots • Senior provider should intubate Difficult Intubation Risk: • 2.7% in surgical cohort • Usually due to blood in upper airway, not anatomi

nodes.title: ENT/OR Decision
nodes.summary: OR: brisk bleed, clot + active hemorrhage, airway threat, shock; observe if stable, non-brisk
nodes.body: When to call ENT IMMEDIATELY: • ALL post-tonsillectomy bleeding within 3 weeks • Fresh blood from operative site • Any active hemorrhage GO TO OR IMMEDIATELY IF: • Active, brisk hemorrhage • Fresh clot in tonsillar fossa with active bleeding • Failed bedside hemostatic measures • Airway compromise • Signs of shock OBSERVATION ACCEPTABLE IF: • Non-brisk ooze, stable vitals • No active bleeding on e

nodes.title: Proceeding to OR
nodes.summary: OR: senior anesthesia, RSI + VL, suction ready; post-op ICU if significant; reop rate 0.92%
nodes.body: Preparation for OR: Notify: • ENT surgeon • Anesthesia • OR staff Pre-Op: • Large-bore IV × 2 • Type & crossmatch (if not already) • Blood products available • NPO (already in effect) Airway Plan: • Senior anesthesiologist • RSI with cricoid pressure OR controlled RSI • Video laryngoscope available • Suction ready • Deep plane of anesthesia before laryngoscopy In OR: • Suction/cautery of bleeding
nodes.recommendation: OR for active bleeding. Senior anesthesia, RSI, VL ready. Post-op ICU if significant hemorrhage.

nodes.title: Observation Protocol
nodes.summary: Observe 4-6h (minor) to 12-24h (active stopped); NPO then clear liquids; transfuse if Hgb <7
nodes.body: Observation for Stable Patient: Duration: • Minimum 4-6 hours for minor bleeding • 12-24 hours for any active bleeding that stopped Monitoring: • Frequent vitals • Repeat Hgb if significant blood loss • Watch for recurrence NPO Initially, Then: • Ice chips • Clear cold liquids if stable • Advance as tolerated Activity: • Bed rest • Avoid straining, coughing • HOB elevated Blood Products: • Transfu

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria & Instructions
nodes.summary: Discharge: no bleeding 4-24h, stable, PO tolerated; avoid NSAIDs; return for any new bleeding; ENT f/u 1-2d
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: • No bleeding for minimum 4-6 hours (minor) or 12-24 hours (moderate) • Hemodynamically stable • Tolerating oral fluids • Reliable caregivers • Close follow-up available • Access to emergency care Discharge Instructions: Activity: • Rest for 24-48 hours • No strenuous activity for 1 week • No contact sports until cleared by ENT Diet: • Cold, soft foods • Avoid hot, spicy, acidi
nodes.recommendation: Discharge if no bleeding 4-24h, stable, tolerating PO. Avoid NSAIDs. Return for any new bleeding.

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.summary: Admit if: active bleed, Hgb <10, transfusion, young child, unreliable f/u; 7.1% rebleed; avg stay 1.6d
nodes.body: Admit for Observation If: • Any active bleeding (even if stopped) • Hemoglobin <10 g/dL • Required blood transfusion • Hemostatic intervention performed • Young child (higher aspiration risk) • Unreliable follow-up or distant from hospital • Coagulopathy • Parental/caregiver anxiety Admission Orders: • NPO initially • IV fluids (maintenance) • Frequent vitals (q1-2h initially) • Strict intake/outp
nodes.recommendation: Admit for active bleeding, Hgb <10, transfusion, young child, unreliable follow-up. Average stay 1.6 days.

nodes.title: Blood Product Considerations
nodes.summary: Transfuse if Hgb <7 (stable) or <10 (bleeding); 10-15 mL/kg pRBCs; most PTH do NOT need transfusion
nodes.body: Pediatric Transfusion Transfusion Thresholds (Pediatric): Standard (Stable, Not Actively Bleeding): • Hemoglobin <7 g/dL • Post-transfusion goal: 7.0-9.5 g/dL Active Bleeding/Shock: • Hemoglobin <10 g/dL • More liberal threshold justified Special Populations: • Cyanotic heart disease: maintain >10 g/dL • Sickle cell: pre-op transfuse to 9-11.5 g/dL Volume: • 10-15 mL/kg pRBCs • Should raise Hgb ~2

nodes.title: Potassium Infusion Protocol
nodes.summary: IV potassium is high-alert therapy for severe or clinically significant hypokalemia.
nodes.body: Potassium Infusion Steps Use IV potassium when hypokalemia is severe, symptomatic, associated with ECG changes/arrhythmia, ongoing losses are significant, or the patient cannot take oral replacement. Core safety rule: IV potassium is a high-alert medication. Confirm indication, renal function/urine output, infusion concentration, access, pump programming, and monitoring before administration.

nodes.title: Clinical Scenario
nodes.summary: Route and rate depend on severity, ECG risk, renal function, and DKA status.
nodes.body: Which potassium replacement scenario fits best?

nodes.title: Contraindication / Do Not Reflexively Infuse
nodes.summary: Renal failure, anuria, or hyperkalemia risk should stop automatic potassium infusion.
nodes.body: Do not give routine IV potassium when any are present: - Hyperkalemia or rapidly rising K - Anuria or severe renal failure without specialist-directed replacement - Unknown current potassium in an unstable renal patient - Potassium-containing IV fluid running without a clear indication - Concern for pseudohypokalemia or hemolyzed/invalid lab driving treatment If life-threatening hypokalemia coexis
nodes.recommendation: Hold routine potassium infusion and reassess indication, renal function, urine output, and current K.

nodes.title: Severe / Symptomatic Hypokalemia
nodes.summary: Severe symptomatic hypokalemia needs monitored IV K, magnesium correction, and frequent reassessment.
nodes.body: Severe hypokalemia with arrhythmia, ECG changes, paralysis, respiratory weakness, or K <=2.5 requires monitored IV replacement. Initial approach: - Continuous ECG monitoring - Replace magnesium concurrently if low or unknown and torsades/arrhythmia risk is present - Prefer central access for rates >10 mEq/hr - Typical severe replacement: Potassium chloride IV 20 mEq/hr via central line with contin

nodes.title: DKA / HHS Potassium Rules
nodes.summary: In DKA/HHS, hold insulin when K <3.3 and replace before insulin.
nodes.body: Potassium determines whether insulin can safely start. DKA/HHS rules: - K <3.3 mEq/L: hold insulin; give Potassium chloride IV 10 mEq/hr until K >=3.3 (10-20 mEq/hr only with central access + continuous cardiac monitoring) - K 3.3-5.2 mEq/L: give 20-30 mEq potassium per LITRE of IV fluid while insulin runs — a concentration in the bag, not an hourly rate - K >5.2 mEq/L: do not give potassium initi

nodes.title: Access / Monitoring
nodes.summary: Access and monitoring determine safe potassium infusion rate.
nodes.body: What access and monitoring are available?

nodes.title: Peripheral Infusion
nodes.summary: Peripheral KCl is generally limited to 10 mEq/hr per line with a pump.
nodes.body: Peripheral route: - Typical maximum: 10 mEq/hr per peripheral line - Common concentration: 10 mEq in 100 mL, infused over 1 hr - Use infusion pump; never IV push - Burning/phlebitis is common; slow rate, dilute, or use a second line when needed - If larger hourly replacement is required, use multiple peripheral lines or central access per local policy For moderate hypokalemia, oral replacement is

nodes.title: Central Monitored Infusion
nodes.summary: Central monitored potassium allows higher rates but still needs strict safeguards.
nodes.body: Central line + continuous ECG monitoring: - Common severe replacement: 20 mEq/hr - Higher rates require institutional protocol, pharmacist/senior clinician involvement, and frequent serum K checks - Avoid routine concentrated potassium through peripheral lines - Verify pump channel, bag concentration, and line tracing before starting If arrhythmia or paralysis is present, treat as a resuscitation

nodes.title: Magnesium Co-Repletion
nodes.summary: Correct magnesium to make potassium repletion effective and reduce arrhythmia risk.
nodes.body: Hypomagnesemia causes renal potassium wasting and makes hypokalemia difficult to correct. Actions: - Check magnesium early - Replete magnesium when low, unknown with arrhythmia, torsades risk, alcoholism/malnutrition, diuretic use, or refractory hypokalemia - Treat torsades or marked QT prolongation with IV magnesium while correcting potassium Failure to correct magnesium is a common reason potass

nodes.title: Monitoring / Endpoints
nodes.summary: Monitor ECG, serial K, renal function, magnesium, and total administered potassium.
nodes.body: Monitoring: - Continuous ECG for severe hypokalemia, rates >10 mEq/hr, arrhythmia, digoxin use, or high-risk cardiac disease - Recheck K q2-4 hr during aggressive IV replacement - Check Mg, phosphate, creatinine, glucose/acid-base when relevant - Track total potassium administered from all sources Endpoints: - Resolve symptoms/ECG changes - K generally >3.0 for immediate safety, then target 3.5-4.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Severe or high-rate potassium replacement generally needs admission and monitoring.
nodes.body: Admit/ICU when: - Severe symptoms, arrhythmia, ECG changes, paralysis, respiratory weakness - Need for central/high-rate replacement - DKA/HHS requiring insulin infusion - Ongoing GI/renal losses or unclear cause - Renal failure or high overshoot risk Discharge only when the cause is addressed, patient is asymptomatic, ECG is safe, potassium has stabilized, oral replacement/follow-up is arranged,
nodes.recommendation: Disposition depends on arrhythmia risk, replacement rate, renal function, and cause control.

nodes.title: Stop / Safety Check
nodes.summary: Potassium IV push or unverified infusion setup is unsafe.
nodes.body: Stop before potassium infusion if: - No infusion pump - Dose/rate/concentration cannot be verified - No current potassium or renal function in a high-risk patient - Hyperkalemia, anuria, or rapidly worsening renal failure - The line cannot be traced to the patient Potassium must never be given IV push.
nodes.recommendation: Do not start IV potassium until indication, rate, access, pump, and monitoring are verified.

nodes.title: Potassium Level
nodes.summary: Route to hyperkalemia or hypokalemia pathway — repeat if unexpected, consider pseudohyperkalemia
nodes.body: Potassium Disorders Steps Summary — stepwise management of hyperkalemia and hypokalemia. What is the serum potassium level? Confirm result with clinical context. Consider repeating if unexpected.

nodes.title: Pseudohyperkalemia & Lab Verification
nodes.summary: Rule out hemolysis, polycythemia, prolonged tourniquet — POC testing if severe polycythemia
nodes.body: Rule out pseudohyperkalemia before treating: \u2022 In vitro hemolysis (most common artifact) \u2014 repeat lab \u2022 Severe polycythemia (platelets >1M or WBC >50K) \u2014 use heparinized tube or POC \u2022 Prolonged tourniquet application or fist clenching \u2022 Delayed sample processing Point-of-care testing is generally accurate but cannot detect hemolysis. If lab reports severe hyperkalemia

nodes.title: Check ECG Immediately
nodes.summary: First response: check ECG — features confirm diagnosis; normal ECG with severe lab = consider pseudohyperkalemia
nodes.body: The first response to a lab report of hyperkalemia should be to look at telemetry and obtain an ECG. Hyperkalemia ECG Findings \u2014 progression by K+ level If ECG shows hyperkalemia features \u2192 confirms diagnosis, treat as severe. If severe lab value but normal ECG \u2192 consider pseudohyperkalemia, repeat lab. Most patients with hyperkalemia are asymptomatic, even with severe elevations.

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia Severity
nodes.summary: Severe: K+ >=6.5 + ECG changes or rapid rise; bradycardia and QRS widening most dangerous findings
nodes.body: Classify severity based on potassium level, ECG changes, chronicity, and ongoing K+ release. Severe hyperkalemia (KDIGO): \u2022 K+ \u2265 6.5 mEq/L with ECG changes \u2022 K+ \u2265 6.0 mEq/L with rapid rise or ongoing release (TLS, rhabdo) Chronic hyperkalemia (e.g., dialysis patients) is better tolerated than acute. Most dangerous ECG findings: Bradycardia (RR 12.3), QRS widening (RR 4.7), junc

nodes.title: Moderate Hyperkalemia Management
nodes.summary: Gentle kaliuresis with furosemide 40-80mg IV, replace urine volume with LR to maintain euvolemia
nodes.body: [1] Treat definable causes: \u2022 Discontinue offending medications and nephrotoxins \u2022 Establish euvolemia with adequate perfusion \u2022 Consider renal diet with limited K+ intake [2] Gentle kaliuresis: \u2022 Furosemide 40-80 mg IV \u2014 may be sufficient as sole diuretic \u2022 Replace urine volume with Lactated Ringers to maintain even fluid balance If single diuretic fails \u2192 escal

nodes.title: Step 1: Temporizing Measures
nodes.summary: Start ALL three temporizing measures simultaneously — calcium, insulin/dextrose, beta-2 agonist
nodes.body: Start ALL temporizing measures simultaneously. These shift K+ into cells and stabilize the myocardium. They are temporizing only \u2014 K+ will return to baseline in 2-4 hours without definitive elimination therapy. Three interventions: 1. IV Calcium \u2192 membrane stabilization 2. Insulin + Dextrose \u2192 intracellular K+ shift 3. Beta-2 agonist \u2192 intracellular K+ shift Do NOT provide temp

nodes.title: IV Calcium \u2014 Membrane Stabilization
nodes.summary: Calcium gluconate 3g IV over 10 min (peripheral) or CaCl 1g (central) — 30-60 min effect, may repeat
nodes.body: Indications: ECG changes (especially bradycardia, QRS widening, conduction delays). Controversial for isolated peaked T-waves. Dosing: \u2022 Peripheral access: Calcium Gluconate 3 grams IV over 10 minutes \u2022 Central access: Calcium Chloride 1 gram IV over 10 minutes Duration: 30-60 minutes only \u2014 may need to repeat 1-2 times. Rapid IV calcium may cause flushing, nausea, abdominal discomf

nodes.title: Insulin + Dextrose \u2014 K+ Shift
nodes.summary: Insulin 5 units IV (10 units if normal renal function AND adequate glucose) + 25 g dextrose — glucose at 30/60/120/240 min, K+ drops 0.5-1.2
nodes.body: Regular Insulin IV \u2014 dose by hypoglycemia risk (must be IV, NOT subcutaneous). Give WITH 25 g dextrose (D50W 50 mL) unless glucose >250 mg/dL. \u2022 5 units (or 0.1 units/kg, max 10) \u2014 eGFR <60, dialysis-dependent, pre-treatment glucose <150 mg/dL, weight <60 kg, or no diabetes \u2022 10 units \u2014 normal renal function AND adequate glucose Check glucose at 30, 60, 120 and 240 minutes

nodes.title: Beta-2 Agonist \u2014 K+ Shift
nodes.summary: Terbutaline 0.5mg SQ preferred over nebulized albuterol — single injection vs 4-8 nebs, similar efficacy
nodes.body: Preferred: Terbutaline 0.5 mg SQ \u2014 single injection, logistically superior. Alternative: Albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized (4-8 standard nebs back-to-back). Nearly always underdosed in practice \u2014 a single 2.5 mg neb is inadequate. If hypotensive/bradycardic: Epinephrine infusion \u2014 treats both hyperkalemia AND hemodynamic instability simultaneously. Effect: Onset 5-30 min. K+ reduction: 0

nodes.title: Step 2: Volume Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Do NOT use normal saline — high chloride worsens hyperK; isotonic bicarb preferred if acidotic
nodes.body: Assess volume status and serum bicarbonate to guide fluid choice. Do NOT use normal saline \u2014 high chloride content worsens hyperkalemia. Isotonic bicarbonate is the preferred resuscitative fluid for hyperkalemic patients with metabolic acidosis.

nodes.title: Isotonic Bicarbonate Resuscitation
nodes.summary: 3 amps NaHCO3 in 1L D5W AS the resuscitative fluid — hypertonic bicarb ampules alone are ineffective
nodes.body: Preparation: 3 ampules NaHCO\u2083 in 1 liter D5W = 150 mM isotonic bicarbonate solution. Dosing: 500-1000 mL/hour if severely hypovolemic. Target serum bicarb 24-28 mEq/L. Isotonic bicarb lowers K+ three ways: 1. Dilution 2. Shifting K+ into muscle cells 3. Alkalosis promotes renal K+ excretion Common mistake: Giving isotonic bicarb at 100-150 mL/hr alongside another crystalloid. This prevents ac

nodes.title: Step 3: Kaliuresis (Diuretic Strategy)
nodes.summary: Scale diuretic to renal function — "nephron bomb" for moderate-severe CKD, replace urine losses with crystalloid
nodes.body: Scale diuretic intensity to severity of hyperkalemia and renal function. Normal renal function: \u2022 Furosemide 40-80 mg IV alone may suffice Moderate-severe renal dysfunction ("nephron bomb"): \u2022 Furosemide 160-250 mg IV (or Bumetanide 4-5 mg IV) \u2022 + Chlorothiazide 500-1000 mg IV (or Metolazone 5-10 mg PO) \u2022 +/- Acetazolamide 250-1000 mg IV/PO \u2022 +/- Fludrocortisone 0.2 mg PO

nodes.title: Assess Diuretic Response
nodes.summary: Monitor urine output and K+ — add fludrocortisone if making urine but K+ not falling
nodes.body: Monitor urine output. If the patient produces urine, check potassium content. If making urine but K+ not falling \u2192 consider adding Fludrocortisone 0.2 mg PO. Check electrolytes (including Mg) frequently and replete as needed.

nodes.title: Step 4: Potassium Binders
nodes.summary: SZC 10g PO q8h mildly effective — avoid Kayexalate (colonic necrosis risk), do not rely as sole treatment
nodes.body: Lokelma (SZC) 10 grams PO q8h Only mildly effective (~0.2 mM reduction at 4 hours, ~0.4 mM at 24 hours). Should NOT be relied upon as sole treatment. May help avoid or delay dialysis in borderline cases. Avoid Kayexalate \u2014 antiquated, probably ineffective for acute hyperK, and can cause colonic necrosis. Patiromer is less effective than SZC (~0.23 mM at 7 hours). Only use if SZC unavailable.

nodes.title: Step 5: Dialysis
nodes.summary: Dialysis for chronic HD patients or anuric despite diuretic bomb — do not delay for binders
nodes.body: Indications for emergent dialysis: 1. Chronic hemodialysis patient (kaliuresis is futile) 2. Failure of all other measures (anuric despite diuretic bomb, not a candidate for large-volume isotonic bicarb) Do NOT delay dialysis while hoping potassium binders will work. For chronic HD patients, 5 grams of SZC daily on non-dialysis days may help reduce intradialytic hyperkalemia.

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia Monitoring & Reassessment
nodes.body: Ongoing monitoring during acute hyperkalemia treatment. Recheck K+ every 1-2 hours. Repeat ECG with any clinical change. Insulin K+ shift lasts ~4 hours \u2014 plan for redosing or definitive elimination. Monitor glucose q1h for 4-6 hours post-insulin. Check Mg, Ca, phosphorus frequently. Replace urine losses with appropriate crystalloid. Address underlying cause simultaneously.
nodes.recommendation: Recheck K+ every 1-2 hours during acute treatment. Repeat ECG with any clinical change. Insulin K+ shift lasts ~4 hours \u2014 plan for redosing or definitive elimination. Monitor glucose q1h for 4-6 hours post-insulin. Check Mg, Ca, phosph

nodes.title: Hypokalemia Assessment
nodes.summary: Check ECG for arrhythmia, assess for life-threatening features — arrhythmia, paralysis, respiratory failure
nodes.body: Check ECG for arrhythmia risk. Hypokalemia ECG Findings Assess for life-threatening features: \u2022 Arrhythmia (VT, TdP, new AF) \u2022 Respiratory failure \u2022 Paralysis or severe weakness

nodes.title: Severe Hypokalemia \u2014 IV Replacement
nodes.summary: KCl 5-10 mEq over 15-30 min IV with cardiac monitoring — always correct concurrent hypoMg (50% coexist)
nodes.body: Potassium Chloride IV 5-10 mEq over 15-30 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring. Repeat until hemodynamically stable, ECG changes resolve, and K+ > 3 mEq/L. Then: \u2022 20-40 mEq IV at up to 10 mEq/hr (peripheral) \u2022 Up to 20 mEq/hr (central line + cardiac monitoring) Use glucose-free fluids \u2014 glucose stimulates insulin and worsens intracellular K+ shift. Always check and correct ma

nodes.title: Mild-Moderate Hypokalemia \u2014 Oral Replacement
nodes.summary: KCl 20-40 mEq PO (each 20 mEq raises K+ ~0.2) — dietary potassium alone is insufficient
nodes.body: Potassium Chloride Oral 20-40 mEq PO Each 20 mEq raises serum K+ ~0.2 mEq/L. KCl is the preferred salt (most causes of hypoK involve concurrent chloride losses). Recheck K+ in 2-4 hours. Target K+ \u2265 4.0 mEq/L \u2014 especially in heart failure and arrhythmia-prone patients. Dietary potassium alone is INSUFFICIENT \u2014 food K+ is coupled with phosphate, not chloride, and ineffective for repl

nodes.title: Hypokalemia Etiology
nodes.summary: Check urine K+ to differentiate renal vs extrarenal losses — diuretics, GI losses, DKA treatment common
nodes.body: Common causes: \u2022 Diuretics (thiazides > loops \u2014 0.6 vs 0.3 mEq/L decrease) \u2022 GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea, NG suction) \u2022 Refeeding syndrome \u2022 DKA treatment (insulin shifts K+ intracellularly) \u2022 Alkalosis Workup: \u2022 BMP, Mg, Phos \u2022 Urine K+ and Cl- \u2022 If urine K+ > 30 mEq/day \u2192 renal losses \u2022 If urine K+ < 25 mEq/day \u2192 extrarenal losses Key

nodes.title: Long-Term Hypokalemia Management
nodes.body: Chronic K+ replacement and prevention strategy. Oral KCl 50-75 mEq/day for chronic replacement. For diuretic-induced hypokalemia: low-salt diet, consider K-sparing diuretic, ACEi/ARB, or beta-blocker addition. Loop diuretics cause less hypoK than thiazides. Correct hypomagnesemia. Target K+ \u2265 4.0 mEq/L in heart failure patients.
nodes.recommendation: Oral KCl 50-75 mEq/day for chronic replacement (raises K+ ~0.14 mEq/L, enhanced with ACEi/ARB). For diuretic-induced: low-salt diet, consider K-sparing diuretic, ACEi/ARB, or beta-blocker addition. Loop diuretics cause less hypoK than thiaz

nodes.title: Periodic Paralysis Assessment
nodes.summary: Episodic flaccid paralysis with triggers — transcellular redistribution, NOT true depletion
nodes.body: Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis (HypoPP) Episodic flaccid paralysis, proximal > distal, with normal-to-decreased reflexes. Lasting minutes to days with spontaneous recovery. Triggers: Rest after strenuous exercise, carbohydrate-rich evening meals (morning attacks), stress, cold, high sodium intake, corticosteroids, alcohol KEY DISTINCTION: Hypokalemia in HypoPP is transcellular redistribution, NOT

nodes.title: HypoPP: Acute Attack Management
nodes.summary: Oral KCl 1 mEq/kg immediate-release ONLY — avoid aggressive IV (rebound hyperK), avoid glucose/steroids
nodes.body: CRITICAL: This is NOT true K+ depletion \u2014 aggressive replacement causes dangerous rebound hyperkalemia. Potassium Chloride Oral 1 mEq/kg oral (~60 mEq for 60 kg patient) \u2022 Use immediate-release or liquid formulation ONLY \u2022 AVOID slow-release KCl \u2014 too slow and unpredictable \u2022 If no improvement in 30 min \u2192 0.3 mEq/kg additional dose \u2022 Monitor K+ every 30 minutes F

nodes.title: HypoPP: Prevention & Long-Term
nodes.body: Long-term prevention of hypokalemic periodic paralysis attacks. Trigger avoidance: low sodium, low carbohydrate diet, avoid steroids/cold/stress/alcohol. Daily oral KCl 10-20 mEq TID (especially nocturnal dose for morning attacks). Acetazolamide is first-line pharmacologic prevention. If intolerant: K-sparing diuretics (triamterene, spironolactone, eplerenone). Genetic counseling: CACNA1S or SCN4A

nodes.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Leading cause of maternal mortality — call for help early. 6-module approach starts here.
nodes.body: PPH Steps Summary — quick-reference checklist to review before and during resuscitation. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide and remains a top cause of preventable maternal death in the US. [1][2] Call for help early. Mortality triples when diagnosis or escalation is delayed. This consult walks through ED management of PPH in 6 modules: • Module 1: Reco

nodes.title: PPH Definition (ACOG 2017)
nodes.summary: ≥1000 mL OR signs of hypovolemia within 24h post-delivery — EBL is underestimated 30-50%.
nodes.body: ACOG / reVITALize consensus definition (2017): [1] Cumulative blood loss ≥1000 mL OR blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours following the birth process — regardless of delivery route. Timing: • Primary (early) PPH — within 24 hours of delivery — ~99% of cases • Secondary (late) PPH — 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum — think retained products, endometritis, subinv

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Assessment
nodes.summary: Shock Index >0.9 abnormal in pregnancy; >1.0 = shock. Pregnancy masks early hypotension.
nodes.body: Assess the patient before fixating on blood estimation: • Vital signs — HR, SBP, SpO₂, mental status • Shock Index — HR/SBP ratio (>0.9 abnormal in pregnancy; >1.0 = hemorrhagic shock) [3] • Skin: pallor, cold, clammy, mottling • Urine output if catheterized Pregnancy physiology obscures early shock. Healthy peripartum patients compensate well — tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure appear befor

nodes.title: Unstable — Activate Protocol
nodes.summary: Trendelenburg + 2 large-bore IVs + O-neg blood + activate MTP if SI >1.0. Keep patient warm.
nodes.body: HEMORRHAGE EMERGENCY — EXECUTE IN PARALLEL Call STAT: OB attending, anesthesia, charge nurse, blood bank ("MTP on standby for OB hemorrhage"), OR if not already aware. Position: Trendelenburg, 2–3 assistants at bedside. Airway/Breathing: High-flow O₂ via NRB, prepare for intubation if obtunded. Circulation: • 2 large-bore IVs (16-18g) or IO if access fails • Warmed crystalloid bolus (LR or NS) — 1

nodes.title: Team Assembly
nodes.summary: OB primary; if unavailable: IR (UAE 84-96% success, fertility impact), Vascular (IIA ligation, no fertility impact), Surgery (hysterectomy last resort), Hematology (DIC).
nodes.body: CALL FOR HELP — assign roles: • OB attending — definitive management, surgical decisions • OB anesthesia — airway, access, hemodynamic support, arterial line • Blood bank — activate MTP, confirm sample available, send emergency-release cooler • Charge nurse — runner, documentation, recorder • Second RN — dedicated to medications and blood products • Pharmacy — mix uterotonics, prepare TXA --- IF O

nodes.title: Access, Labs & Blood
nodes.summary: 2 IVs, CBC/fibrinogen/coags/T&C 4-6u. Fibrinogen <200 = severe PPH. Early blood products.
nodes.body: VASCULAR ACCESS • 2 large-bore IVs (16-18g) minimum — IO if peripheral access fails • Arterial line if ongoing resuscitation LABS (send STAT) • CBC with platelets, fibrinogen, PT/PTT, INR • Type & crossmatch 4-6 units pRBC (if not already typed, draw and send) • Basic metabolic panel, LFTs, lactate • Ionized calcium (hypocalcemia from citrated blood worsens coagulopathy) • ABG if unstable FIBRINOG

nodes.title: Fundal Massage — Do This NOW
nodes.summary: Cup fundus + circular massage + empty bladder — fastest intervention for atony.
nodes.body: External fundal massage is the first mechanical intervention. Do not wait for uterotonics to mix. TECHNIQUE 1. Place one hand flat on the lower abdomen, palm over the uterine fundus 2. Massage firmly in a circular motion — "cup" the fundus and knead 3. Apply downward compression toward the pelvis 4. Continue until the uterus feels firm, globular, and well-contracted 5. Keep massaging intermittentl

nodes.title: Tranexamic Acid (TXA) — Within 3 Hours
nodes.summary: TXA 1g IV within 3h of delivery (WOMAN trial) — faster is better, repeat at 30 min if ongoing.
nodes.body: Give Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as PPH is diagnosed. EVIDENCE — WOMAN TRIAL (Lancet 2017) [7] • 20,060 women with PPH, 21 countries • TXA vs placebo within 3 hours of delivery • Death from bleeding: 1.5% vs 1.9% (RR 0.81, p=0.045) • Best effect when given within 1 hour (RR 0.69 for death from bleeding) • NO BENEFIT if given >3 hours post-delivery — do not give late DOSE • 1 g I

nodes.title: Bimanual Uterine Compression
nodes.summary: Vaginal fist + abdominal hand compress uterus between both — 5-10 min or until bleeding controlled.
nodes.body: If bleeding continues despite massage and uterotonics are mixing — perform bimanual uterine compression. This is the single most effective mechanical maneuver for uterine atony. TECHNIQUE (see diagram) 1. Gloved, dominant hand — insert into vagina, form a fist, and press against the anterior vaginal fornix 2. Non-dominant hand — place flat on the abdomen and cup the posterior uterine wall from abo

nodes.title: The 4 T's of PPH
nodes.summary: Tone (70%) → Trauma (20%) → Tissue (10%) → Thrombin (<1%). Check tone first.
nodes.body: 4 T's Differential Reference — full differential with clinical clues. The 4 T's is the universal PPH differential. Commit it to memory — you will use it in every hemorrhage. [1][5][8] | T | Cause | Frequency | Clinical clue | |---|---|---|---| | Tone | Uterine atony | ~70-80% | Boggy, soft uterus; fundus above umbilicus | | Trauma | Lacerations, hematoma, inversion, uterine rupture | ~20% | Firm u

nodes.title: Primary Cause?
nodes.summary: 4-way branch: Tone (boggy) / Trauma (firm + bleeding) / Tissue (retained) / Thrombin (oozing).
nodes.body: Based on the exam, what is the most likely primary cause of bleeding? Tone = boggy/soft uterus Trauma = firm uterus, active bleeding from canal, or signs of inversion/rupture Tissue = incomplete placenta or persistent bleeding despite firm uterus and no lacerations Thrombin = generalized oozing (IV sites, mucosa) or known coagulopathy/Amniotic Fluid Embolism If unclear, default to Tone — it is the

nodes.title: Trauma — Which Injury?
nodes.summary: Speculum every quadrant — cervix, vagina, perineum. Check fundus for inversion.
nodes.body: Firm uterus + active bleeding = trauma. Speculum exam under adequate light and analgesia. Inspect systematically: • Cervix — grasp with ring forceps, walk around every quadrant • Vagina — sidewalls and posterior fornix • Perineum — 1st–4th degree laceration grading • Vulvar/paravaginal mass — hematoma • Fundus — appears indented or absent abdominally = uterine inversion Uterine rupture (prior C-se

nodes.title: Laceration Repair
nodes.summary: 1st/2nd OK for EM; 3rd/4th/cervical → OB. Optimize exposure before repair.
nodes.body: GENITAL TRACT LACERATIONS Classification (perineal): • 1st degree — skin/mucosa only • 2nd degree — extends to perineal muscles • 3rd degree — involves anal sphincter • 4th degree — extends through rectal mucosa Cervical lacerations — common at 3 and 9 o'clock; bleed briskly. Use ring forceps to walk around the entire cervix. MANAGEMENT • Optimize exposure — adequate lighting, retractors, assistan

nodes.title: Uterine Inversion — Emergency
nodes.summary: STOP uterotonics → Johnson maneuver (push fundus up) → tocolyze if needed → resume uterotonics.
nodes.body: UTERINE INVERSION — TRUE OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY Incidence: 1 in 2,000–20,000 deliveries. Mortality reaches 15% with delayed recognition. [10] CLINICAL CLUES • Sudden, profuse hemorrhage after placental delivery • Absent or dimpled fundus on abdominal palpation • Bluish-gray fleshy mass visible at introitus (complete inversion) or palpable in the vagina • Neurogenic shock out of proportion to blood lo

nodes.title: Vulvar / Paravaginal Hematoma
nodes.summary: Expanding mass + disproportionate pain → OR for evacuation. IR if supralevator.
nodes.body: VULVAR AND PARAVAGINAL HEMATOMAS Unlike laceration bleeding, hematomas occur from injured vessels under intact mucosa. Blood accumulates rapidly in the pelvic soft tissue and can hide significant volume loss. CLINICAL CLUES • Severe, disproportionate perineal or rectal pain • Expanding firm mass at the vulva or vaginal sidewall • Hemodynamic decline without visible blood loss • Inability to void (

nodes.title: Uterine Rupture
nodes.summary: Prior C-section + severe pain + loss of fetal station → OR for laparotomy. Activate MTP.
nodes.body: UTERINE RUPTURE Catastrophic disruption of the uterine wall. Incidence 0.3-0.7% in VBAC (trial of labor after cesarean), ~0.02% in unscarred uterus. [12] RISK FACTORS • Prior C-section or uterine surgery (including myomectomy) • Trauma (MVC, penetrating, blunt abdominal) • Oxytocin augmentation, induction with prostaglandins • Grand multiparity, obstructed labor CLINICAL CLUES • Severe abdominal p

nodes.title: Tissue — Retained Products
nodes.summary: Explore uterus manually — stop if resistance (accreta). Ultrasound-guided D&C if needed.
nodes.body: RETAINED PLACENTA / PRODUCTS OF CONCEPTION CLINICAL CLUES • Placenta appears incomplete on inspection (missing cotyledon, torn edge, ragged membranes) • Firm uterus but persistent bleeding • Placenta not delivered within 30 minutes postpartum (retained placenta by definition) • Bedside ultrasound: echogenic material in the uterine cavity MANAGEMENT 1. MANUAL EXTRACTION / EXPLORATION • Adequate ana

nodes.title: Thrombin — Coagulopathy
nodes.summary: Oozing + labs (fibrinogen <200) → 1:1:1 MTP + cryo + Ca + keep warm. Treat lethal triad.
nodes.body: COAGULOPATHY IN PPH Less than 1% of PPH as primary cause, but common as a secondary complication after massive transfusion or prolonged severe hemorrhage. Early recognition changes management. CAUSES • Dilutional coagulopathy — after large crystalloid or unbalanced blood product resuscitation • DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) — severe PPH, sepsis, abruption, intrauterine fetal demise

nodes.title: Uterine Atony — Start the Ladder
nodes.summary: 4-drug ladder: Oxytocin → Methergine (avoid HTN) → Hemabate (avoid asthma) → Miso. Use in parallel with mechanical measures.
nodes.body: Uterotonic Ladder Reference — full comparison with contraindications. Boggy uterus = atony = #1 cause of PPH (70-80%). MECHANICAL MEASURES (continue while starting meds) • Fundal massage (ongoing) • Bimanual compression • Empty bladder (Foley) UTEROTONIC LADDER — escalate every 5-10 minutes if bleeding uncontrolled: 1. Oxytocin — first-line (already running for prevention) 2. Methylergonovine (Met

nodes.title: Oxytocin (Pitocin) — First Line
nodes.summary: 20u in 1L NS at 250 mL/hr (or 10u IM). NEVER IV push. Reassess in 5-10 min.
nodes.body: Oxytocin (Pitocin) — first-line uterotonic in every PPH. DOSE • 20 units in 1 L NS or LR — infuse at 250 mL/hr (≈83 mU/min) • Alternative if no IV access: 10 units IM • NEVER give IV push — causes profound hypotension and can trigger cardiac arrest MAX 40 units / 500 mL (higher concentrations trigger hypotension) CAUTIONS • Water intoxication with prolonged high-dose infusion (antidiuretic effect)

nodes.title: Second-Line — HTN / Preeclampsia?
nodes.summary: Methergine CI: HTN, preeclampsia, CAD, Raynaud. If any present → skip to Hemabate/Miso.
nodes.body: Before giving methylergonovine, screen for the key contraindication: METHYLERGONOVINE CONTRAINDICATIONS • Hypertension (any SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90) • Preeclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP • Coronary artery disease (vasoconstriction risk) • Raynaud's phenomenon Methylergonovine causes significant vasoconstriction and has triggered MI, CVA, and severe hypertensive emergencies when misused in these patients. B

nodes.title: Methylergonovine (Methergine)
nodes.summary: 0.2 mg IM, may repeat q2-4h (max 5 doses). NEVER IV. Reassess in 5-10 min.
nodes.body: Methylergonovine (Methergine) — ergot alkaloid uterotonic. DOSE • 0.2 mg IM — onset 2-5 minutes, duration 3 hours • May repeat every 2-4 hours as needed, maximum 5 doses (1 mg total) • NEVER give IV — severe hypertensive reactions, MI, CVA reported CONTRAINDICATIONS (re-verify) [1][25] • Hypertension / preeclampsia / eclampsia • CAD, recent MI, CVA • Raynaud's • Sepsis (risk of vasospasm, gangrene

nodes.title: Third-Line — Asthma / Pulmonary HTN?
nodes.summary: Hemabate CI: asthma (absolute), pulmonary HTN, severe cardiac/hepatic disease.
nodes.body: Before giving carboprost (Hemabate), screen for the key contraindication: CARBOPROST CONTRAINDICATIONS • Asthma (active or history) — absolute CI (causes bronchospasm, can trigger fatal attack) • Pulmonary hypertension • Significant cardiac, renal, or hepatic disease • Active pelvic inflammatory disease Carboprost is a PGF2α analog. Bronchoconstriction is the most dangerous adverse effect. BASIS F

nodes.title: Carboprost (Hemabate)
nodes.summary: 0.25 mg IM q15-90 min (max 8 doses = 2 mg). ABSOLUTE CI: asthma. Causes GI side effects.
nodes.body: Carboprost (Hemabate) — 15-methyl PGF2α analog. DOSE • 0.25 mg (250 mcg) IM — into the deltoid or vastus lateralis • May repeat every 15-90 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses (2 mg total) • Onset: 3-5 minutes; duration ~2 hours • Intramyometrial dosing (by OB during laparotomy) also effective — 0.25 mg directly into the myometrium CONTRAINDICATIONS (re-verify) [1][26] • Asthma (any history) — absolut

nodes.title: Misoprostol (Cytotec)
nodes.summary: 800-1000 mcg PR or SL. Few CIs — useful when HTN + asthma block other agents. Fever/shivering common.
nodes.body: Misoprostol (Cytotec) — synthetic PGE1 analog. Useful when other uterotonics are contraindicated (HTN + asthma). DOSE • 800-1000 mcg PR (rectal) or SL (sublingual) — single dose • Onset: 10-15 minutes rectally, faster SL • Cheap, shelf-stable, does not require refrigeration — widely used globally CONTRAINDICATIONS • Known hypersensitivity to prostaglandins — essentially none other than this • No c

nodes.title: Reassess — Bleeding Controlled?
nodes.summary: Controlled = firm uterus, <100 mL/15 min. Ongoing → advanced interventions.
nodes.body: After mechanical measures + TXA + targeted 4T's treatment, reassess: CONTROLLED • Uterus firm • Bleeding <100 mL in last 15 minutes • Vital signs stabilizing or normalized • No expanding hematoma UNCONTROLLED / ONGOING • Any of: persistent heavy bleeding, worsening shock, cumulative EBL ≥1500 mL, ongoing transfusion need, falling fibrinogen • Escalate to advanced interventions. [1][5][9]

nodes.title: Bakri Balloon — Intrauterine Tamponade
nodes.summary: Bakri 300-500 mL saline under US — 75-86% success. >100 mL/hr drainage = failure.
nodes.body: Bakri Balloon Placement Guide — detailed step-by-step. Bakri balloon is the first-line advanced intervention when uterotonics fail. Success rate 75-86% for atony, reducing the need for hysterectomy. [16] INDICATIONS • Persistent uterine atony despite maximal medical therapy • Bleeding from lower uterine segment (placental site after previa) • Temporizing measure during transport to OR or IR CONTRA

nodes.title: Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol
nodes.summary: 1:1:1 pRBC:FFP:plts; cryo if fib <200; Ca per 4u blood; TXA + warm + correct pH. Treat lethal triad.
nodes.body: When to activate Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP): • Ongoing hemorrhage after 2 units pRBC without control • Shock Index >1.0 with active bleeding • Cumulative EBL ≥1500 mL with ongoing transfusion need • Hemodynamic collapse (SBP <90 or lactate >4) • Cardiac arrest from hemorrhage (cPR with ongoing transfusion) RATIO • 1:1:1 pRBC : FFP : platelets (or closest institutional equivalent) • Cryopre

nodes.title: Surgical & Interventional Options
nodes.summary: IR (UAE) for stable; B-Lynch, O'Leary, hypogastric ligation; hysterectomy for refractory/accreta.
nodes.body: If bleeding persists despite uterotonics + Bakri + MTP → definitive intervention. INTERVENTIONAL RADIOLOGY • Uterine artery embolization (UAE) — fertility-preserving; ideal for stable-enough-to-transport patient • Success rate ~80-90% • Requires rapid access to IR suite — not a solution for the crashing patient SURGICAL (in OR with OB) • B-Lynch compression suture — vertical suture compresses uter

nodes.title: Definitive Control?
nodes.summary: Controlled → ICU. Refractory despite everything → hysterectomy is the final step.
nodes.body: After escalation to surgical or interventional management, reassess: CONTROLLED • Bleeding stopped • Hemodynamics improving • Transfusion requirements decreasing REFRACTORY • Ongoing bleeding despite uterotonics + Bakri + MTP + IR/OR • Proceed to hysterectomy — this is the final life-saving step [1][5][22]

nodes.title: Peripartum Hysterectomy
nodes.summary: Final step when all else fails. Supracervical faster; total needed for lower-segment bleeding.
nodes.body: Peripartum hysterectomy — the final life-saving step. Incidence: ~1 in 1000 deliveries; the most common indication is placenta accreta spectrum, followed by refractory atony, rupture, and lacerations. [22] INDICATIONS (any one triggers operative discussion) • Refractory hemorrhage despite all conservative and fertility-preserving measures • Placenta accreta / increta / percreta • Uterine rupture w

nodes.title: Post-PPH Monitoring
nodes.summary: VS q15min ×1h → q30 ×2h → hourly ×24h. Oxytocin infusion 4-24h. Repeat CBC/fibrinogen 2-4h.
nodes.body: After bleeding is controlled, intensive monitoring for 4-24 hours. Late decompensation and re-bleeding are common. MONITORING • Vital signs every 15 minutes × 1 hour, then q30 min × 2 hours, then hourly × 24 hours • Uterine tone checks every 15 min × 1 hour, then hourly — recurrent atony triggers re-bleeding • Foley catheter strict I/O — urine output goal >30 mL/hr • CBC, fibrinogen, coags at 2-4

nodes.title: Rh Status & Other Postpartum Care
nodes.summary: RhoGAM if Rh-neg mom w/in 72h; abx after instrumentation; mechanical VTE prophylaxis immediately.
nodes.body: RH IMMUNE GLOBULIN (RhoGAM) • All Rh-negative mothers with Rh-positive or unknown newborn should receive Rh Immune Globulin 300 mcg IM within 72 hours of delivery [23] • Even if mother was previously sensitized, standard of care is to give — consult OB • Larger doses if large fetomaternal hemorrhage suspected (Kleihauer-Betke test guides dosing) [23] ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS • Following manual place

nodes.title: PPH Controlled — Disposition
nodes.body: Postpartum hemorrhage controlled with appropriate measures. PPH Discharge Instructions — shareable return precautions for once the patient is ready for discharge or transfer to the postpartum unit. DISPOSITION • ICU admission if: ≥4 units transfused, hysterectomy, hemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, Amniotic Fluid Embolism, or requiring vasopressors • Step-down / OB unit if: controlled bleeding
nodes.recommendation: PPH controlled. Admit to ICU if ≥4 units transfused, hysterectomy, or instability; otherwise step-down / L&D. Continue oxytocin infusion 4-24h. Repeat labs at 2-4h. VTE prophylaxis (mechanical immediate, pharmacologic once hemostasis confir

nodes.title: Refractory PPH — OR / Hysterectomy
nodes.body: Refractory postpartum hemorrhage despite full medical, mechanical, and initial surgical measures. DEFINITIVE SURGICAL MANAGEMENT — OR NOW PROCEED WITH: • Peripartum hysterectomy (supracervical if crashing; total for lower-segment or cervical bleeding) • Anticipated blood product requirements: ≥10 units pRBC, matching FFP and platelets, cryoprecipitate • Continued TXA, calcium replacement, warming
nodes.recommendation: Refractory PPH → OR for peripartum hysterectomy. Continue MTP, TXA, calcium, warming. Post-op ICU with ventilator support, vasopressors, q4-6h labs. Multidisciplinary debrief within 24 hours.

nodes.title: Possible Rupture of Membranes
nodes.summary: Triage immediate maternal/fetal threats, then sterile speculum exam, targeted fluid testing, and OB disposition.
nodes.body: Prelabor rupture of membranes (PROM) means rupture of the fetal membranes before the onset of labor. Preterm PROM (PPROM) means PROM before 37+0 weeks. In the ED, first decide whether the mother or fetus needs immediate action. If stable, use the history and a sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of fluid, then use targeted testing when the exam is equivocal. PROM Steps | Ferning Photo

nodes.title: Immediate Maternal or Fetal Threat?
nodes.summary: Threats to mother, fetus, or cord take priority over confirming membrane status.
nodes.body: Look for maternal instability, heavy bleeding or suspected abruption, umbilical cord prolapse, nonreassuring fetal status, suspected intra-amniotic infection, active labor, or imminent delivery. Do not delay an emergency response to complete a ROM test.

nodes.title: Emergency OB Response
nodes.summary: Call OB/L&D, monitor and resuscitate, and do not delay definitive care for ROM testing.
nodes.body: Activate OB/L&D now and add neonatal/MFM support based on gestational age and local capability. Start continuous fetal monitoring when feasible, obtain IV access, and resuscitate the mother. Do not delay delivery, cord-prolapse treatment, hemorrhage control, or transfer for AmniSure, ferning, nitrazine, or ultrasound. Avoid a digital cervical examination. If cord prolapse is present, relieve press
nodes.recommendation: Treat the time-critical obstetric problem first. Confirm ROM only if it will not delay definitive care.

nodes.title: Focused History
nodes.summary: Characterize the leak, assess infection/bleeding/labor, and capture gestational age and pregnancy risk factors.
nodes.body: Ask: • Gestational age, due date, gravida/para, and prenatal complications • Gush versus intermittent trickle; exact onset and continued leakage • Fluid color, odor, and amount; clear versus green/brown or blood-tinged • Contractions, pelvic pressure, back pain, or urge to push • Vaginal bleeding, fever/chills, uterine tenderness, or feeling unwell • Fetal movement and any prior nonreassuring feta

nodes.title: Sterile Speculum Examination
nodes.summary: Sterile speculum: look for pooling, cord, blood, and infection; avoid digital examination.
nodes.body: Avoid a digital cervical examination when ROM is suspected unless delivery is imminent or OB specifically directs it. Digital examination increases ascending-infection exposure and can shorten latency in PPROM. [1][3] Use a sterile speculum and adequate lighting: 1. Inspect the vagina and cervix for blood, purulence, meconium, lesions, cervicitis, and a visible cord. 2. Look for clear fluid poolin

nodes.title: What Did the Speculum Examination Show?
nodes.summary: Pooling establishes the clinical diagnosis; no pooling requires context-sensitive testing or reassessment.
nodes.body: Choose the finding that best matches the examination. If the exam is incomplete or unsafe, choose the equivocal pathway and involve OB.

nodes.title: ROM Confirmed Clinically
nodes.summary: Frank pooling is a clinical diagnosis; proceed to gestational-age routing and OB disposition.
nodes.body: Visible pooling of amniotic fluid or fluid passing through the cervical os supports a clinical diagnosis of ROM. When pooling is clearly observed, NICE recommends no additional diagnostic test before initiating care consistent with PPROM. [3] Do not add a digital examination simply to document dilation. Continue maternal and fetal assessment, record the time and character of leakage, and move to g
nodes.recommendation: Treat as ruptured membranes and obtain an OB/L&D plan. No additional ROM test is required when frank pooling is clearly seen.

nodes.title: Equivocal Examination: Order the Right Test
nodes.summary: At Dell Seton, use Rupture of Fetal Membranes for AmniSure/PAMG-1 when pooling is absent or equivocal.
nodes.body: Dell Seton workflow: order Rupture of Fetal Membranes for the AmniSure/PAMG-1 test when the sterile speculum examination does not establish ROM. Use the test as an adjunct to the history and examination. A positive PAMG-1 result supports ROM, but it does not assess fetal status, infection, abruption, or labor. A negative result lowers the likelihood but does not overrule persistent high suspicion

nodes.title: Fluid Test Result and Clinical Fit
nodes.summary: A test result must fit the clinical picture; discordance is a reason to reassess, not to anchor.
nodes.body: Interpret the result alongside the speculum examination, history, gestational age, and maternal/fetal status.

nodes.title: ROM Supported by Fluid Testing
nodes.summary: Positive AmniSure or convincing ferning supports ROM; continue full maternal/fetal assessment.
nodes.body: A positive AmniSure/PAMG-1 or convincing arborization supports the presence of amniotic fluid in the vaginal sample. PAMG-1 has generally performed better than nitrazine or ferning in diagnostic studies, but reported accuracy varies by population and reference standard. [2][4] Correlate the result with the examination and do not treat a positive result as a diagnosis of infection or fetal compromi
nodes.recommendation: Treat ROM as supported and obtain an OB/L&D plan. The test confirms membrane status, not the absence of other obstetric emergencies.

nodes.title: High Suspicion Despite a Negative or Discordant Test
nodes.summary: Persistent high suspicion overrides false reassurance from a single negative or poorly collected test.
nodes.body: Do not close the case on a negative test when the history remains convincing or the sample may have been scant or contaminated. • Recheck the timeline and ongoing leakage. • Review how and where the specimen was collected; a dry or poorly sampled swab can be falsely negative. • Repeat targeted testing or obtain OB/MFM input according to local protocol. • Use ultrasound as supportive information, n

nodes.title: ROM Not Established at This Encounter
nodes.summary: A negative evaluation lowers likelihood but does not excuse follow-up when symptoms or gestational risk persist.
nodes.body: No pooling and negative or low-concern testing do not establish ROM at this encounter. Consider urinary leakage, physiologic leukorrhea, cervical mucus, semen, vaginitis/cervicitis, or other vaginal discharge. See Differential and Test Pitfalls. If leakage continues, the history remains convincing, or gestational age is preterm, obtain an OB plan for observation, repeat examination/testing, or fol
nodes.recommendation: ROM is not confirmed, but follow-up must match the residual clinical suspicion and gestational age.

nodes.title: Gestational-Age Routing
nodes.summary: Term, preterm, and previable/periviable ROM follow different OB pathways; gestational age drives disposition.
nodes.body: Use the best documented gestational age and the patient's maternal/fetal condition. If gestational age is uncertain, treat the uncertainty as clinically important and involve OB/MFM.

nodes.title: Term PROM: OB/L&D Plan
nodes.summary: Term PROM needs an OB/L&D delivery plan with GBS, infection, contractions, bleeding, and fetal-status review.
nodes.body: Confirmed ROM at or beyond 37+0 weeks requires an OB/L&D plan, including timing and mode of delivery, GBS status, fetal status, and infection assessment. Coordinate directly with the receiving OB team; do not treat a stable ED appearance or a positive test as a reason to bypass L&D planning. Reassess for fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, purulent fluid, bleeding, contractions, or nonre
nodes.recommendation: Contact OB/L&D for term PROM management and disposition. Continue maternal and fetal monitoring while the plan is made.

nodes.title: PPROM: OB/MFM and Appropriate Capability
nodes.summary: PPROM requires OB/MFM disposition; gestational age and maternal/fetal condition determine the management lane.
nodes.body: Confirmed PPROM before 37+0 weeks requires OB/MFM involvement and admission or transfer to a facility with the needed maternal and neonatal capability. Gestational age, fetal status, maternal status, infection, labor, and local protocol determine antibiotics, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate, latency versus delivery, and monitoring. Suspected intra-amniotic infection, abruption, nonrea
nodes.recommendation: OB/MFM disposition is required. Transfer to appropriate obstetric and neonatal capability if the current facility cannot provide it.

nodes.title: Previable or Periviable PPROM
nodes.summary: Previable/periviable PPROM requires urgent specialist counseling and maternal-safety surveillance, not a one-size-fits-all algorithm.
nodes.body: Call OB/MFM and neonatal specialists urgently. Do not apply a later-gestation PPROM algorithm without individualized counseling. Current SMFM guidance, endorsed by ACOG, recommends counseling about maternal and fetal risks and benefits; both immediate delivery/abortion care and expectant management may be offered when no contraindication requires immediate delivery. [5][6] Discuss maternal risks i
nodes.recommendation: Urgent OB/MFM-led shared decision-making and disposition. Escalate immediately for infection, hemorrhage, instability, or fetal compromise.

nodes.title: OB Handoff Checklist
nodes.summary: Handoff gestational age, leak history, maternal/fetal status, speculum findings, tests, treatments, and destination.
nodes.body: Give OB/L&D the following in one concise handoff: • Gestational age, gravida/para, prenatal complications, and GBS status • Time and character of leakage; contractions, bleeding, fever, fetal movement • Maternal vitals, uterine tenderness, and infection/abruption concern • Fetal heart-rate pattern and monitoring status • Sterile speculum findings: pooling, cervix, cord, blood, purulence • Testing:

nodes.title: Precipitous Delivery
nodes.summary: Rapid labor and delivery in the ED — page OB/Peds immediately, 5-module stepwise approach
nodes.body: Delivery Steps Summary — quick-reference checklist to review immediately before delivery. Precipitous delivery occurs when labor and delivery happen rapidly — often before planned arrival at a delivery unit. ~3% of all US deliveries. [4] Page OB and Pediatrics immediately. Do not delay — even if delivery seems far off. This consult provides a stepwise approach to assessing and managing an ED preci

nodes.title: Rapid OB History
nodes.summary: G/P, gestational age, complications, contraction timing, signs of imminent delivery — never trust a multip
nodes.body: OB HISTORY — RAPID ASSESSMENT • Gestational age / due date • Gravida / Para (G_P_) • Singleton vs multiples • Pregnancy complications (preeclampsia, GDM, placenta previa) • Contraction timing — onset, frequency, duration • Fluid leakage or bleeding (ROM, bloody show) SIGNS OF IMMINENT DELIVERY • Crowning — fetal head visible at introitus • Perineal bulging — stretching of perineum from descending

nodes.title: Cervical Exam
nodes.summary: Effacement (0-100%), dilation (0-10cm), station (-5 to +5) — station +3-5 with full dilation = imminent
nodes.body: CERVICAL EXAM Effacement — thinning of the cervix, measured 0–100%. At 100% effacement the cervix is paper-thin. Dilation — opening of the cervical os, measured 0–10 cm. At 10 cm the cervix is fully dilated and ready for delivery. Station — position of the fetal presenting part relative to the ischial spines: • -5 to -1 — presenting part is above the ischial spines (floating to engaged) • 0 — pres

nodes.title: Is Delivery Imminent?
nodes.summary: Crowning, fully dilated, or active pushing = deliver in ED — transfer only if safe to do so
nodes.body: Is delivery imminent? Delivery is imminent if: • Crowning or fully dilated (10 cm) • Active pushing with visible presenting part • No time for safe transfer If the patient can be safely transferred to L&D or a facility with OB capabilities, transfer is preferred. [7]

nodes.title: Transfer to OB Facility
nodes.body: EMTALA CONSIDERATIONS Active labor may constitute an emergency medical condition under EMTALA when safe transfer is not possible. [7] Assess and provide necessary stabilizing treatment before transfer. If an emergency medical condition remains unstable, transfer only when EMTALA's appropriate-transfer requirements are met. If delivery is imminent, the hospital must deliver the baby regardless of O
nodes.recommendation: Transfer to facility with OB capabilities. Antenatal transfer preferred over neonatal transfer. Ensure EMTALA compliance — active labor may constitute an emergency medical condition when safe transfer is not possible.

nodes.title: Call for Help
nodes.summary: Minimum 4 people: delivery provider, mom nurse, baby nurse, baby provider — turn on neonatal warmer NOW
nodes.body: CALL FOR HELP Page OB and Pediatrics STAT — even if you've already called, confirm they are en route. TEAM ASSIGNMENTS Minimum 4 people: • You — delivering provider (at the perineum) • Nurse 1 — assigned to mom (vitals, meds, documentation) • Nurse 2 — assigned to baby (warming, stimulation, APGAR) • Provider 2 — assigned to baby (Neonatal Resuscitation if needed) EQUIPMENT — NEONATAL • Neonatal w

nodes.title: Equipment & Positioning
nodes.summary: Sterile gloves, cord clamps x2, scissors, bulb suction, confirm vertex with US if time permits
nodes.body: DELIVERY EQUIPMENT • Sterile gloves (two pairs) • Sterile scissors or scalpel (for cord cutting) • Umbilical cord clamps x2 (Kelly clamps work if cord clamps unavailable) • Bulb suction • Clean towels and warm blankets for baby • Chux pads / absorbent pads under the patient CONFIRM VERTEX PRESENTATION If time permits, perform a bedside ultrasound to confirm vertex (head-down) presentation. If NOT

nodes.title: Ready to Deliver
nodes.summary: Pre-delivery checklist confirmed — OB paged, team assigned, warmer on, equipment ready, patient positioned
nodes.body: PRE-DELIVERY CHECKLIST ✓ OB and Peds paged ✓ Team assigned (mom nurse, baby nurse, baby provider) ✓ Neonatal warmer ON and prewarming ✓ Delivery equipment at bedside ✓ Patient positioned and draped ✓ Vertex presentation confirmed (if time for U/S) You are ready to deliver. The next modules walk through each stage of labor and delivery step by step. [1][2][3]

nodes.title: Three Stages of Labor
nodes.summary: Stage 1 = dilation, Stage 2 = delivery, Stage 3 = placenta — multips progress much faster than expected
nodes.body: THREE STAGES OF LABOR Stage 1 — Cervical Dilation • Latent phase: irregular contractions, 0–5 cm dilation • Active phase: strong regular contractions, nulliparous ~1.2 cm/hr, multiparous ~1.5 cm/hr • Transition: 8–10 cm, intense contractions, nausea/shaking common Stage 2 — Delivery of the Baby From full dilation to delivery. Active pushing: 1–2 hours (nulliparous), often shorter for multiparous.

nodes.title: Coaching the Patient
nodes.summary: Push 10 sec x3 per contraction — when crowning, STOP pushing and breathe to reduce tearing
nodes.body: COACHING THE PATIENT During contractions: • Take a deep breath at the start of each contraction • Bear down and push for 10 seconds x 3 per contraction • Rest between contractions — use this time for encouragement When the head is crowning: • Tell the patient to STOP pushing • Breathe through contractions — pant or blow • This allows controlled, slow delivery of the head and reduces perineal teari

nodes.title: Delivering the Head
nodes.summary: Perineal support: upward pressure on chin + counter-pressure on occiput for slow controlled delivery
nodes.body: DELIVERING THE HEAD Perineal support technique: • Place one hand on the perineum with a towel — apply gentle upward pressure on the fetal chin through the perineum • Other hand on the fetal occiput — apply gentle counter-pressure to control the speed of delivery • Goal: slow, controlled delivery of the head to minimize perineal tearing Key points: • Let the uterus do the work — do NOT pull on the

nodes.title: Nuchal Cord Check
nodes.summary: Sweep finger around neck immediately after head delivers — nuchal cord in 20-30%, usually manageable
nodes.body: NUCHAL CORD CHECK Immediately after the head delivers, sweep your finger around the baby's neck feeling for the umbilical cord. Nuchal cord occurs in 20–30% of deliveries and is usually manageable. [1][2]

nodes.title: Tight Nuchal Cord — Clamp and Cut
nodes.summary: Double-clamp and cut between clamps — baby must be delivered promptly after cord is cut
nodes.body: TIGHT NUCHAL CORD — CLAMP AND CUT If the cord is too tight to slip over the baby's head: 1. Apply two clamps on the cord close together 2. Cut between the clamps with sterile scissors 3. Unwrap the cord from the neck 4. Deliver the baby promptly — the cord is now cut and the baby has no placental circulation This is time-sensitive. Once the cord is cut, the baby must be delivered and assessed quic

nodes.title: Shoulder Delivery
nodes.summary: Gentle downward traction for anterior shoulder, then upward — turtle sign = shoulder dystocia emergency
nodes.body: SHOULDER DELIVERY Anterior shoulder (top): • Apply gentle DOWNWARD traction on the head (toward the floor) • Guide the anterior shoulder under the pubic symphysis • The shoulder should slip out — do NOT force Posterior shoulder (bottom): • Then apply gentle UPWARD traction (toward the ceiling) • Deliver the posterior shoulder CRITICAL SAFETY POINTS: • Apply traction in the long axis of the fetal n

nodes.title: Cord Clamping & Cutting
nodes.summary: Do NOT drop the baby — skin-to-skin, deferred cord clamping at least 60 sec unless resuscitation needed
nodes.body: CORD CLAMPING AND CUTTING DO NOT DROP THE BABY. The baby is wet and slippery. 1. Place the baby directly on mom's abdomen — skin-to-skin contact 2. Dry the baby vigorously with a warm towel 3. Clamp the cord in two places, approximately 3 cm apart, with the first clamp ~3 cm from the baby's abdomen 4. Cut between the two clamps with sterile scissors DELAYED CORD CLAMPING Current NRP 9th edition (O

nodes.title: Neonatal Assessment
nodes.summary: Dry/stimulate/warm — 90% need no intervention, 10% need PPV, <1% need compressions, NRP if HR <100
nodes.body: IMMEDIATE NEONATAL ASSESSMENT Dry and stimulate the baby with warm towels. Most babies will cry and become pink within the first minute. APGAR SCORING Assess at 1 minute and 5 minutes after delivery: • Appearance (color) • Pulse (heart rate) • Grimace (reflex irritability) • Activity (muscle tone) • Respiration (breathing effort) NEONATAL TRANSITION STATISTICS [5] • ~90% of newborns transition wit

nodes.title: Placental Delivery
nodes.summary: Gentle cord traction + fundal counter-pressure — NEVER force, aggressive traction risks uterine inversion
nodes.body: STAGE 3 — PLACENTAL DELIVERY The placenta typically delivers 5–15 minutes after the baby. Up to 30 minutes is normal. SIGNS OF PLACENTAL SEPARATION • Cord lengthening — the cord appears to get longer as the placenta detaches • Gush of blood — normal separation bleeding • Uterine fundus rises — becomes firm and globular DELIVERY TECHNIQUE • Apply gentle, steady traction on the cord with one hand •

nodes.title: Placental Examination
nodes.summary: Check all cotyledons present (jigsaw pattern), count cord vessels (normal = 3), save for pathology
