nodes.body: PLACENTAL EXAMINATION After delivery, inspect the placenta carefully: COMPLETENESS • All cotyledons (lobes) present — the maternal surface should look like a complete jigsaw puzzle • Check edges for torn vessels (suggests retained succenturiate lobe) • Retained placental fragments → postpartum hemorrhage risk [8] CORD VESSELS • Normal: 2 arteries + 1 vein (3-vessel cord) • Single umbilical artery

nodes.title: Oxytocin & Uterine Massage
nodes.summary: Oxytocin 20 units in 1L NS IV at 250 mL/hr (or 10 units IM if no IV access) — do NOT IV push, bimanual massage until firm uterine tone
nodes.body: OXYTOCIN — POSTPARTUM UTEROTONIC Preferred (IV access established): Oxytocin 20 units in 1L NS (or LR) at 250 mL/hr. No IV access: Oxytocin 10 units IM into the anterolateral thigh — this is the WHO-preferred prophylactic route in low-resource or pre-IV settings. [8] Do NOT give IV push — can cause profound hypotension. [8] Timing: Start after the placenta is delivered. Do not wait to assess bleed

nodes.title: Laceration Assessment
nodes.summary: 1st/2nd degree tears — repair in ED; 3rd/4th degree — defer to OB; PPH = >1000 mL blood loss
nodes.body: LACERATION ASSESSMENT Examine the vaginal canal and perineum for tears: CLASSIFICATION • 1st degree — perineal skin/vaginal mucosa only • 2nd degree — extends into perineal muscles • 3rd degree — involves the anal sphincter • 4th degree — extends through the rectal mucosa MANAGEMENT • If you are comfortable → repair 1st and 2nd degree tears in the ED • 3rd and 4th degree tears → defer to OB (speci

nodes.title: Delivery Complete
nodes.body: Delivery complete. Congratulate the mother. POSTDELIVERY CHECKLIST ✓ Uterus firm (not boggy) ✓ Bleeding controlled ✓ Vaginal/perineal lacerations assessed and addressed ✓ Baby assessed — APGAR at 1 and 5 minutes documented ✓ Placenta examined and saved for pathology ✓ Oxytocin infusing ✓ Skin-to-skin contact maintained MONITORING • Monitor mom for 1 hour post-placenta delivery: uterine tone, vagin
nodes.recommendation: Delivery complete. Monitor mom x1 hour (uterine tone, bleeding, vitals q15 min). Monitor baby (temp, respiratory, feeding). Admit to OB service. APGAR and all times documented.

nodes.title: Pregnancy in Trauma
nodes.summary: Mother first — fetal survival depends on maternal survival. Blood volume ↑50%, can lose 30% before shock.
nodes.body: Pregnancy Trauma Tools — resuscitative hysterotomy, RhIg calculator, monitoring guide. Trauma is the leading non-obstetric cause of maternal death — affects 6-7% of pregnancies. [1][2] GOLDEN RULE: Mother First > The best fetal resuscitation is maternal resuscitation. > Fetal survival depends on maternal survival. Key physiologic changes: • Blood volume ↑ 50% — can lose 30% before shock signs • Ca

nodes.title: Gestational Age Assessment
nodes.summary: Fundus at umbilicus = 20 weeks. Above umbilicus = left tilt required + continuous monitoring.
nodes.body: Fundal height landmarks: • Symphysis pubis: 12 weeks • Umbilicus: 20 weeks • Xiphoid: 36 weeks Why GA matters: • <20 weeks: Standard trauma care, no aortocaval compression • 20-24 weeks: Left tilt required, viability borderline • >24 weeks: Viable fetus, continuous fetal monitoring required If unsure: Fundus at or above umbilicus = treat as ≥20 weeks. [1][2]

nodes.title: Early Pregnancy (<20 weeks)
nodes.summary: Standard trauma care. No left tilt required. RhIg if Rh-negative. OB follow-up.
nodes.body: Management is essentially standard trauma care: • No aortocaval compression concerns • Fetus not yet viable • Left tilt NOT required but not harmful Still required: • Rh status and RhIg if Rh-negative • OB consultation • Pelvic ultrasound to confirm pregnancy status • Consider ectopic if <12 weeks with abdominal trauma Radiation: • Risk of teratogenicity highest in first trimester • But: still per

nodes.title: Maternal Resuscitation Priorities
nodes.summary: Smaller ETT, chest tubes 1-2 spaces higher, LEFT UTERINE DISPLACEMENT >20 weeks, target SBP >90.
nodes.body: ABCs with pregnancy modifications: A — Airway: • Airway edema is common — use smaller ETT (6.0-7.0) • Increased aspiration risk — RSI preferred • Preoxygenation critical — FRC ↓, O2 consumption ↑ B — Breathing: • Chest tube placement 1-2 intercostal spaces higher (elevated diaphragm) • SpO2 target >95% (fetal oxygenation) C — Circulation: • LEFT UTERINE DISPLACEMENT if >20 weeks • Aggressive fluid

nodes.title: Left Uterine Displacement
nodes.summary: Manual displacement: push uterus LEFT from patient's right side. Or tilt 15-30° left.
nodes.body: CRITICAL after 20 weeks gestation: Why? • Gravid uterus compresses IVC and aorta when supine • Can reduce cardiac output by 25-30% • Causes supine hypotension syndrome --- METHODS: 1. Manual displacement (preferred during CPR): • Stand at patient's right side • Place hands on right side of uterus • Push uterus to the LEFT and upward • Maintain throughout resuscitation 2. Left lateral tilt (if not

nodes.title: Laboratory Studies
nodes.summary: KB test on all trauma. Fibrinogen <200 = DIC/abruption. Normal pregnancy Hgb 10-11 g/dL.
nodes.body: Standard trauma labs PLUS: Pregnancy-specific: • Type and screen — Rh status critical • Kleihauer-Betke test — quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage • Fibrinogen — <200 mg/dL suggests DIC/abruption (normal pregnancy 400-600) • PT/PTT/INR — DIC screening ⚠️ Normal pregnancy lab changes: • Hgb 10-11 g/dL (hemodilution) • WBC 10-15k (normal) • Platelets may ↓ slightly • Fibrinogen elevated (400-600 norm

nodes.title: Imaging in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: CT is safe — fetal dose is well below harm threshold. Do NOT withhold necessary imaging.
nodes.body: DO NOT WITHHOLD NECESSARY IMAGING Risk perspective: • Fetal radiation threshold for harm: >100 mGy (10 rad) • CT abdomen/pelvis: ~25 mGy • CT chest: ~0.06 mGy to fetus • Plain films: <0.01 mGy Multiple CT scans are still below harm threshold. --- IMAGING APPROACH: Safe — no restrictions: • Ultrasound (preferred for fetal evaluation) • MRI (no gadolinium in 1st trimester if possible) • Plain radiog

nodes.title: Fetal Assessment
nodes.summary: FHR 110-160 normal. Minimum 4-6h monitoring. 24h if high-risk features.
nodes.body: Components of fetal evaluation: 1. Fetal heart tones: • Normal: 110-160 bpm • Bradycardia (<110): Fetal distress — may need emergent delivery • Tachycardia (>160): Maternal fever, hypovolemia, fetal distress 2. Ultrasound: • Confirm fetal heart activity • Assess placental location • Look for retroplacental hematoma (abruption) • Estimate amniotic fluid volume • Gestational age if unknown 3. Contin

nodes.title: Monitoring Duration
nodes.summary: Low-risk: 4-6h monitoring. High-risk: 24h. Non-reassuring FHR: urgent OB consultation.
nodes.body: Continuous cardiotocographic (CTG) monitoring is standard for viable pregnancies (>24 weeks). Minimum 4-6 hours for: • Minor trauma • Normal FHR pattern • No contractions • No vaginal bleeding • Negative or low KB Extend to 24 hours if ANY: • ≥6 contractions/hour • Vaginal bleeding • Significant abdominal tenderness • Non-reassuring FHR • Positive Kleihauer-Betke • High-energy mechanism • Seatbelt

nodes.title: Non-Reassuring Fetal Status
nodes.summary: Bradycardia, late decels, loss of variability = fetal distress. Optimize mother, STAT OB, prepare for cesarean.
nodes.body: Signs of fetal distress: • Persistent bradycardia (<110 bpm) • Recurrent late decelerations • Loss of beat-to-beat variability • Prolonged deceleration (>2 min) • Sinusoidal pattern --- IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: 1. Optimize maternal status: • Left uterine displacement • Oxygen supplementation • IV fluid bolus • Correct hypotension • Stop any oxytocin if running 2. STAT OB consultation 3. Prepare for emer
nodes.recommendation: Optimize maternal status, left displacement, O2, fluids. STAT OB. Prepare for emergent cesarean.

nodes.title: Pregnancy-Specific Injuries
nodes.summary: Abruption most common cause of fetal death. Rupture rare but catastrophic. KB test for all.
nodes.body: Injuries unique to or modified by pregnancy: • Placental abruption — most common cause of fetal death after trauma • Uterine rupture — rare but catastrophic • Preterm labor — may occur after any trauma • Fetomaternal hemorrhage — mixing of fetal/maternal blood • Direct fetal injury — rare, usually late pregnancy Pregnancy Trauma Differential — complete differential diagnosis. Which condition are y

nodes.title: Placental Abruption
nodes.summary: US sensitivity only 25% — clinical diagnosis. Fibrinogen <200 = DIC/severe. Monitor 24h.
nodes.body: Separation of placenta from uterine wall before delivery. #1 cause of fetal death after trauma. Occurs in 1-5% of minor trauma, 40-50% of major trauma. [1][2] --- CLINICAL FEATURES: • Vaginal bleeding (may be absent in concealed abruption) • Uterine tenderness • Increased uterine tone/tetanic contractions • Back pain • Non-reassuring FHR • Maternal instability out of proportion to visible blood lo
nodes.recommendation: Clinical diagnosis — US sensitivity only 25%. Fibrinogen <200 = significant. Emergent cesarean if unstable.

nodes.title: Uterine Rupture
nodes.summary: Loss of fetal station + palpable parts = RUPTURE. Immediate laparotomy. 10-35 min to prevent fetal death.
nodes.body: Complete disruption of all uterine layers — OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY Rare (0.6% of all uterine ruptures are trauma-related) but nearly 100% fetal mortality if not rapidly recognized. [1][8] --- CLINICAL FEATURES: • Sudden, severe abdominal pain • Loss of fetal station on vaginal exam (cardinal sign) • Easily palpable fetal parts through abdomen • Fetal bradycardia → absent FHT • Maternal shock • Should
nodes.recommendation: IMMEDIATE LAPAROTOMY. Loss of fetal station + palpable parts = rupture until proven otherwise.

nodes.title: Preterm Labor
nodes.summary: ≥6 contractions/hr significant. Tocolytics NOT recommended in trauma. Steroids if 24-34 weeks.
nodes.body: Regular uterine contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks. After trauma: • Common — uterine irritability expected • Most contractions resolve with observation • True preterm labor requires cervical change --- EVALUATION: • Tocodynamometry — ≥6 contractions/hour is significant • Cervical exam (if no vaginal bleeding and not previa) • Fetal fibronectin (if 22-34 weeks, membranes intact) • Ce

nodes.title: Fetomaternal Hemorrhage & Rh Considerations
nodes.summary: RhIg 300 mcg to ALL Rh-negative patients within 72h. KB % × 50 ÷ 30 = vials needed.
nodes.body: Fetomaternal hemorrhage (FMH): Fetal blood enters maternal circulation. Occurs in 8-30% of minor trauma, 40% of major trauma. [1][5] --- RH-NEGATIVE PATIENTS: Risk: If mother is Rh-negative and fetus is Rh-positive, exposure causes isoimmunization → affects future pregnancies (hydrops fetalis, fetal anemia). Only 0.01-0.03 mL needed to isoimmunize. --- KLEIHAUER-BETKE TEST: • Quantifies fetal RBCs

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Manual LUD, same defib doses. No ROSC by 4 min + ≥20 weeks = begin resuscitative hysterotomy.
nodes.body: Modified ACLS with pregnancy-specific considerations: KEY MODIFICATIONS: 1. Manual left uterine displacement — assign team member 2. Defibrillation — same doses, remove fetal monitors 3. Chest compressions — may need slightly higher on sternum 4. IV access — above diaphragm preferred (IVC compression) 5. Intubation — smaller ETT (6.0-7.0), increased aspiration risk 6. No modification to medication

nodes.title: Resuscitative Hysterotomy Technique
nodes.summary: Vertical midline skin + vertical uterus. Begin at 4 min, deliver by 5 min. Primary benefit is maternal.
nodes.body: Formerly "perimortem cesarean section" INDICATION: Maternal cardiac arrest with uterus ≥20 weeks (fundus at/above umbilicus) and no ROSC within 4 minutes. GOAL: Relieve aortocaval compression. Primary benefit is MATERNAL. --- EQUIPMENT: • Scalpel (#10 blade) • Mayo scissors • Hemostats/clamps (for cord) • Bulb suction • Towels for packing • Neonatal resuscitation ready --- STEP-BY-STEP: 1. Vertica

nodes.title: Post-Resuscitative Hysterotomy
nodes.summary: Continue CPR after delivery. Pack uterus. Neonatal resuscitation. Survival possible even if delayed.
nodes.body: After delivery: MATERNAL: • Continue CPR • Cardiac output should improve once aortocaval compression relieved • If ROSC achieved: definitive surgical management • Pack uterus with towels for hemorrhage control • May need definitive uterine repair or hysterectomy NEONATAL: • Immediate neonatal resuscitation • Prepare for profound asphyxia • May need full NRP including intubation, compressions • NIC

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Low-risk: discharge after 4-6h. High-risk: 24h admission. Fetal distress: emergent cesarean.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on: • Gestational age • Severity of trauma • Maternal stability • Fetal status • Monitoring findings [1][2]

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Reassuring FHR, <6 contractions/hr, no bleeding, RhIg given. Return for bleeding, decreased movement, pain.
nodes.body: Safe to discharge if ALL: ✓ Minimum 4-6 hours monitoring completed ✓ Reassuring fetal heart rate pattern throughout ✓ <6 contractions per hour ✓ No vaginal bleeding ✓ No significant abdominal tenderness ✓ Maternal vitals stable ✓ Negative or trivial Kleihauer-Betke ✓ RhIg given if Rh-negative --- DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS: Return immediately for: • Vaginal bleeding • Decreased fetal movement • Regula
nodes.recommendation: Discharge if reassuring monitoring, no bleeding, stable vitals, RhIg given. OB follow-up in 24-48h.

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.summary: L&D admission. Continuous fetal monitoring. Serial exams. Steroids if 24-34 weeks.
nodes.body: Admit for 24-hour monitoring if ANY: • ≥6 contractions per hour • Vaginal bleeding • Abdominal tenderness • Non-reassuring FHR (even if now normalized) • Positive Kleihauer-Betke (>5 fetal cells/500) • High-energy mechanism • Seatbelt sign • Significant maternal injuries requiring admission • Concern for abruption • Preterm labor (<37 weeks) --- ADMISSION PLAN: • L&D if OB unit available • Continu
nodes.recommendation: Admit to L&D. Continuous monitoring 24h. Serial exams. OB management.

nodes.title: Emergent Cesarean Delivery
nodes.summary: Bradycardia, abruption, rupture = emergent cesarean. Decision-to-incision <30 min.
nodes.body: INDICATIONS FOR EMERGENT CESAREAN: Fetal: • Persistent fetal bradycardia (<110 bpm) • Prolonged deceleration unresponsive to resuscitation • Sinusoidal pattern • Evidence of severe abruption Maternal: • Uterine rupture • Severe hemorrhage with maternal instability • Maternal cardiac arrest (resuscitative hysterotomy) --- PREPARATION: • Activate OR (or perform at bedside if arrest) • Blood products
nodes.recommendation: Immediate OR activation. Blood ready. NICU team. Decision-to-incision <30 min (cardiac arrest: 5 min).

nodes.title: RhIg Administration
nodes.summary: Give 300 mcg immediately to all Rh-neg patients. Add more if KB shows large FMH.
nodes.body: Rh Immune Globulin (RhoGAM): WHO: All Rh-negative pregnant patients after trauma. WHEN: Within 72 hours of trauma (ideally within 12h). STANDARD DOSE: 300 mcg IM • Covers up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood • Adequate for most minor-moderate trauma LARGE FMH (KB >30 mL fetal blood): Vials = (KB % × 50) ÷ 30, round up + 1 Example: KB = 2.5% fetal cells (2.5 × 50) ÷ 30 = 4.2 → round to 4, add 1 = 5 via

nodes.title: Kleihauer-Betke Testing
nodes.summary: Fetal blood (mL) = KB % × 50. Does NOT rule out abruption. Give RhIg empirically.
nodes.body: Kleihauer-Betke Test: Purpose: Detects and quantifies fetal RBCs in maternal circulation. Principle: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) resists acid elution; adult Hgb does not. Fetal cells stain pink; adult cells appear as ghosts. --- INDICATIONS: • All Rh-negative pregnant patients with trauma • Quantifying fetomaternal hemorrhage • Can be done on Rh-positive if risk stratification desired --- INTERPRETING

nodes.title: Priapism: Overview
nodes.summary: Erection >4h unrelated to stimulation — classify ischemic vs non-ischemic, assess SCD/medication history
nodes.body: Priapism = prolonged erection lasting > 4 hours, unrelated to sexual stimulation. Two types: \u2022 Ischemic (low-flow) \u2014 EMERGENCY. Most common. Veno-occlusive. \u2022 Non-ischemic (high-flow) \u2014 NOT an emergency. Arterial. Usually post-trauma. History to obtain: \u2022 Duration of erection \u2022 Pain level \u2022 Trauma history (straddle injury, perineal blunt trauma) \u2022 PDE5 inhib

nodes.title: Ischemic vs Non-Ischemic: Key Differences
nodes.summary: Ischemic: painful, rigid, dark blood, emergency; Non-ischemic: painless, partial, post-trauma, not emergency
nodes.body: ISCHEMIC (Low-Flow) \u2022 Painful, fully rigid \u2022 No trauma history \u2022 Dark blood on aspiration \u2022 Compartment syndrome of the penis \u2022 UROLOGIC EMERGENCY NON-ISCHEMIC (High-Flow) \u2022 Painless or mild discomfort \u2022 Partially erect (not fully rigid) \u2022 Trauma history (straddle injury, kick, fall) \u2022 Bright red blood on aspiration \u2022 Arterial fistula \u2192 unregu

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.summary: Classify ischemic vs non-ischemic based on pain, rigidity, trauma history, blood color
nodes.body: Based on history and exam, which type of priapism is this?

nodes.title: Corporal Blood Gas Analysis
nodes.summary: Ischemic: pO2 <30, pCO2 >60, pH <7.25, dark blood; Non-ischemic: pO2 >90, pH normal, bright red
nodes.body: Aspirate blood from corpus cavernosum and send for blood gas. BLOOD COLOR \u2022 Dark, deoxygenated = ischemic \u2022 Bright red, oxygenated = non-ischemic ISCHEMIC PATTERN \u2022 pO\u2082 < 30 mmHg \u2022 pCO\u2082 > 60 mmHg \u2022 pH < 7.25 NON-ISCHEMIC PATTERN \u2022 pO\u2082 > 90 mmHg \u2022 pCO\u2082 < 40 mmHg \u2022 pH 7.35\u20137.45 Note: Exact cutoffs are not standardized across studies, b

nodes.title: Blood Gas Result
nodes.summary: Interpret corporal blood gas pattern to definitively classify ischemic vs non-ischemic
nodes.body: What does the corporal blood gas show?

nodes.title: Non-Ischemic Priapism
nodes.summary: Not an emergency — 62% resolve spontaneously, no aspiration or phenylephrine needed
nodes.body: NOT a urologic emergency. \u2022 Usually from perineal trauma \u2192 arterial fistula \u2022 Partially tumescent, painless \u2022 62% resolve spontaneously \u2022 No aspiration or phenylephrine needed \u2022 ED risk much lower than ischemic type

nodes.title: Non-Ischemic Priapism \u2014 Observation
nodes.body: Non-ischemic priapism is not an emergency. \u2022 Most cases resolve on their own \u2022 If persistent: selective arterial embolization (85\u2013100% success) \u2022 Requires interventional radiology referral \u2022 Erectile function preserved in 80\u2013100% of cases
nodes.recommendation: Observation is first-line. If persistent or patient prefers intervention, refer to interventional radiology for selective arterial embolization. Urology follow-up within 1\u20132 weeks.

nodes.title: Ischemic Priapism \u2014 Emergency
nodes.summary: Compartment syndrome of the penis — smooth muscle necrosis begins at 4-6h, ED at 30-70% if >24h
nodes.body: UROLOGIC EMERGENCY. \u2022 Ischemic priapism = compartment syndrome of the penis \u2022 Smooth muscle necrosis begins at 4\u20136 hours \u2022 Delayed treatment > 24 hours \u2192 30\u201370% erectile dysfunction \u2022 Time-sensitive: proceed to assess duration and etiology now

nodes.title: Sickle Cell Disease?
nodes.summary: 40% of males with SCD experience priapism — SCD has specific initial management steps
nodes.body: Does this patient have sickle cell disease (SCD)? \u2022 ~40% of males with SCD experience priapism \u2022 SCD priapism has specific initial management steps

nodes.title: SCD Priapism \u2014 Duration
nodes.summary: SCD <4h: try supportive measures first; >=4h: emergent procedural intervention required
nodes.body: How long has the erection been present? \u2022 < 4 hours: supportive measures may help \u2022 \u2265 4 hours: requires emergent procedural intervention

nodes.title: SCD Priapism < 4hr \u2014 Supportive Care
nodes.summary: IV hydration, analgesia, warm packs, O2 — do NOT use RBC transfusion to treat priapism in SCD
nodes.body: Try supportive measures first: \u2022 IV hydration (NS bolus) \u2022 Analgesia (ketorolac, opioids PRN) \u2022 Warm shower or warm packs \u2022 Supplemental O\u2082 \u26A0\uFE0F Do NOT use RBC transfusion to treat priapism in SCD patients. Monitor for resolution. If no improvement, proceed to aspiration.

nodes.title: SCD Supportive Care Response
nodes.summary: Assess if supportive measures produced complete detumescence — if persistent, proceed to aspiration
nodes.body: Did supportive measures produce detumescence (complete resolution of rigidity)?

nodes.title: SCD Priapism \u2014 Resolved
nodes.body: Priapism resolved with supportive care. \u2022 Hematology follow-up for recurrence prevention \u2022 Options: hydroxyurea, GnRH agonists, PDE5i prophylaxis Return Precautions
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with hematology follow-up. Discuss recurrence prevention. Return immediately for any erection lasting > 4 hours.

nodes.title: SCD Priapism \u2265 4hr \u2014 Emergent
nodes.summary: SCD >=4h: same treatment as non-SCD ischemic — continue hydration, hematology consult, proceed to block
nodes.body: SCD priapism \u2265 4 hours requires the same procedural treatment as non-SCD ischemic priapism. \u2022 Continue IV hydration and analgesia \u2022 Hematology consult for crisis management \u2022 Do NOT use RBC transfusion to treat priapism \u2022 Proceed to penile block for anesthesia

nodes.title: Ischemic Priapism \u2014 Duration
nodes.summary: Duration drives urgency — post-ICI may try conservative, 4-36h = penile block, >36h = surgical likely
nodes.body: How long has the erection been present? Duration drives treatment urgency and prognosis.

nodes.title: Post-ICI Prolonged Erection (< 4hr)
nodes.summary: Try ice packs, ejaculation, exercise briefly (<30-60 min) — do not delay if fully rigid and painful
nodes.body: Post-intracavernosal injection priapism. Conservative measures (try briefly, < 30\u201360 min): \u2022 Ice packs \u2022 Attempt ejaculation \u2022 Exercise (walking, climbing stairs) \u26A0\uFE0F Do NOT let conservative measures delay treatment. If fully rigid and painful, proceed directly to phenylephrine.

nodes.title: Post-ICI Response
nodes.summary: Assess if conservative measures produced detumescence — if not, proceed to phenylephrine
nodes.body: Did conservative measures produce detumescence?

nodes.title: Post-ICI Priapism \u2014 Resolved
nodes.body: Prolonged erection resolved with conservative measures. \u2022 Observe 30\u201360 min to confirm sustained resolution \u2022 Adjust ICI dose on follow-up with urology Return Precautions
nodes.recommendation: Observe 30\u201360 minutes. Discharge with urology follow-up to adjust ICI dose. Return immediately for any erection > 4 hours.

nodes.title: Prolonged Ischemic Priapism (> 36\u201348hr)
nodes.summary: >36-48h: smooth muscle necrosis advanced — still attempt aspiration/phenylephrine, early prosthesis if failed
nodes.body: Duration > 36\u201348 hours: \u2022 Smooth muscle necrosis likely advanced \u2022 Aspiration + phenylephrine less likely to succeed \u2022 Still attempt aspiration + phenylephrine first \u2022 If unsuccessful: immediate surgical consultation \u2022 AUA/SMSNA recommends early penile prosthesis over delayed placement Proceed to penile block.

nodes.title: Dorsal Penile Nerve Block \u2014 Overview
nodes.summary: 10 mL total 1% lidocaine WITHOUT epinephrine — end-artery territory, NEVER use epi
nodes.body: Adequate anesthesia is essential before aspiration. Dorsal penile nerve block provides excellent analgesia for corporal aspiration and irrigation. Agent: 1% lidocaine WITHOUT epinephrine \u2022 The penis is supplied by end-arteries \u2022 NEVER use epinephrine \u2014 risk of ischemic necrosis Dose: ~10 mL total (5 mL per side)

nodes.title: Dorsal Penile Nerve Block \u2014 Technique
nodes.summary: Inject at 10 and 2 o'clock positions under Buck's fascia — avoid 12 o'clock (dorsal vein) and 6 o'clock (urethra)
nodes.body: PROCEDURE 1. Clean the base of the penis with antiseptic 2. Identify the 10 o'clock and 2 o'clock positions at the penile base 3. Insert a 27-gauge needle at the 10 o'clock position 4. Advance under Buck's fascia (feel a slight pop) 5. Aspirate to ensure you're not in a vessel 6. Inject 5 mL of 1% lidocaine (no epi) 7. Repeat at the 2 o'clock position with 5 mL You must pop through Buck's fascia t

nodes.title: Penile Block \u2014 Confirm Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Wait 5-10 min for full effect, test with pinprick — supplement if inadequate
nodes.body: \u2022 Wait 5\u201310 minutes for full anesthetic effect \u2022 Test with pinprick on penile shaft \u2022 If inadequate, supplement with additional local at injection sites When adequate anesthesia confirmed, proceed to corporal aspiration.

nodes.title: Corporal Aspiration \u2014 Setup
nodes.summary: 18-21g butterfly at 2 or 10 o'clock — avoid 12 (dorsal NV bundle) and 6 (urethra), single side sufficient
nodes.body: EQUIPMENT \u2022 18\u201321 gauge butterfly needle or angiocath \u2022 Three-way stopcock \u2022 20\u201360 mL syringe (for aspiration) \u2022 10\u201320 mL syringe with normal saline (for irrigation) \u2022 Sterile prep and drape INJECTION SITE \u2022 Lateral aspect of proximal penile shaft \u2022 2 o'clock or 10 o'clock position \u2022 AVOID 12 o'clock (dorsal neurovascular bundle) \u2022 AVOID

nodes.title: Corporal Aspiration \u2014 Procedure
nodes.summary: Aspirate until blood turns bright red, irrigate with NS 20-30 mL, repeat cycles to clear stagnant blood
nodes.body: PROCEDURE 1. Insert needle at 2 or 10 o'clock into corpus cavernosum 2. Aspirate dark, deoxygenated blood 3. Continue aspirating until blood turns bright red (bright red = fresh arterial inflow restored) 4. Typically 20\u201330 mL per aspiration cycle TIP: Can send initial aspirate for blood gas if type not yet confirmed. IRRIGATION 5. After aspiration, irrigate with 20\u201330 mL normal saline 6.

nodes.title: Aspiration Response
nodes.summary: Aspiration alone only 36% success — if still rigid, proceed to intracavernosal phenylephrine
nodes.body: Did aspiration and irrigation produce detumescence? \u2022 Aspiration + irrigation alone: ~36% success rate \u2022 If not resolved, proceed to phenylephrine injection

nodes.title: Aspiration Successful
nodes.body: Priapism resolved with aspiration and irrigation. \u2022 Observe 30\u201360 min to confirm sustained resolution \u2022 Urology follow-up in 1\u20132 days Return Precautions
nodes.recommendation: Observe 30\u201360 minutes to confirm sustained detumescence. Discharge with urology follow-up in 1\u20132 days. Return immediately for recurrence > 4 hours.

nodes.title: Intracavernosal Phenylephrine
nodes.summary: Pure alpha-1 agonist — 74% success rate, combined with aspiration 70-100%, onset 1 min
nodes.body: Phenylephrine = first-line sympathomimetic (AUA/SMSNA 2022). Why phenylephrine? \u2022 Pure alpha-1 agonist \u2192 no intrinsic inotropy, no increase in heart rate \u2022 Causes smooth muscle contraction \u2192 venous outflow \u2022 74% success rate (vs 25% terbutaline) \u2022 Combined with aspiration: 70\u2013100% success Onset: 1 minute | Duration: 10\u201320 minutes Tap for mixing instructions:

nodes.title: Phenylephrine \u2014 Dosing Protocol
nodes.summary: 200 mcg q5 min x5 doses max (1mg total) — hold if SBP >160 or HR >110, monitor BP/HR between doses
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F The corpora cavernosa communicate freely \u2014 only ONE side needs to be injected. PHENYLEPHRINE (first-line) \u2022 200 mcg (2 mL of 100 mcg/mL solution) per dose \u2022 Inject into corpus cavernosum \u2022 Every 5 minutes \u2022 Up to 5 doses TOTAL (= 1 mg max) EPINEPHRINE (alternative \u2014 if phenylephrine unavailable) \u2022 20 mcg (2 mL of 10 mcg/mL solution) per dose \u2022 I

nodes.title: Phenylephrine \u2014 Injection Technique
nodes.summary: Inject through aspiration needle, wait 5 min, re-aspirate, assess — 5 doses TOTAL not per side
nodes.body: TECHNIQUE 1. Inject 2 mL phenylephrine (200 mcg) through the same needle used for aspiration 2. Wait 5 minutes 3. Re-aspirate to remove additional stagnant blood 4. Assess for detumescence 5. If still rigid, repeat injection (up to 5 doses total) Remember: Corpora cavernosa communicate freely. Only one side needs injection. 5 doses = 5 doses TOTAL, not per side. Alternating approach: \u2022 Aspira

nodes.title: Phenylephrine Response
nodes.summary: Assess after up to 5 doses — refractory after 1 hour requires surgical intervention
nodes.body: After phenylephrine injection(s), has detumescence occurred? \u2022 May require up to 5 doses (every 5 min) \u2022 Combined aspiration + phenylephrine: 70\u2013100% success

nodes.title: Phenylephrine Successful
nodes.body: Priapism resolved with aspiration + phenylephrine. Return Precautions
nodes.recommendation: Observe 60 minutes. Monitor BP/HR. Discharge with urology follow-up in 1\u20132 days. Return immediately for recurrence > 4 hours.

nodes.title: Refractory Ischemic Priapism
nodes.summary: Failed medical management after 1 hour — requires surgical shunting or prosthesis based on duration
nodes.body: Failed aspiration, irrigation, and phenylephrine (1 hour max). \u2022 This is refractory ischemic priapism \u2022 Requires surgical intervention \u2022 Duration of priapism determines surgical approach \u2022 Urgent urology consultation required

nodes.title: Refractory \u2014 Total Duration
nodes.summary: Total duration determines surgical approach — <36h shunting, >=36-48h consider immediate prosthesis
nodes.body: How long has the priapism been present in total? This determines the surgical strategy.

nodes.title: Surgical Shunting
nodes.summary: Distal shunts first (less invasive), proximal if distal fails — urology consultation required
nodes.body: Shunting creates a pathway for blood to drain from the corpora cavernosa. Two categories: \u2022 DISTAL shunts \u2014 preferred first (less invasive, lower morbidity) \u2022 PROXIMAL shunts \u2014 if distal fails (more invasive, higher complication rate) Distal shunts connect corpus cavernosum to glans penis. Proximal shunts connect to corpus spongiosum or saphenous vein. Urology consultation requ

nodes.title: Shunt Selection
nodes.summary: Select shunt type — distal (corporoglanular) attempted first, proximal only if distal fails
nodes.body: Which shunt is being performed? Distal shunts are attempted first.

nodes.title: Distal Shunt Procedures
nodes.summary: Winter (Tru-Cut), Ebbehoj (#11 blade), Al-Ghorab (open), T-shunt — fistula for drainage through glans
nodes.body: WINTER (percutaneous) \u2022 Tru-Cut biopsy needle through glans into distal corpora EBBEHOJ (percutaneous) \u2022 No. 11 scalpel blade through glans into corpora AL-GHORAB (open) \u2022 Open excision of distal tunica albuginea through glans incision T-SHUNT (variation) \u2022 No. 10 blade with 90-degree rotation All create a fistula at the glans for blood to drain into the corpus spongiosum.

nodes.title: Proximal Shunt Procedures
nodes.summary: Quackels or Grayhack — more invasive, higher complications, only when distal shunts fail
nodes.body: QUACKELS \u2022 Corporospongiosal shunt at penoscrotal junction GRAYHACK \u2022 Saphenous vein-to-corpus cavernosum anastomosis \u26A0\uFE0F More invasive, higher complication rate. Used only when distal shunts fail.

nodes.title: Post-Shunt Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess detumescence after surgical shunting — if persistent, consider proximal shunt or prosthesis
nodes.body: Did surgical shunting produce detumescence?

nodes.title: Shunt Successful
nodes.body: Priapism resolved with surgical shunting. \u2022 Post-op monitoring per urology \u2022 ED risk depends on duration of priapism before resolution \u2022 Consider PDE5i trial at 4\u20136 weeks for erectile rehabilitation Return Precautions
nodes.recommendation: Post-op monitoring per urology. Follow-up within 48 hours. Counsel on erectile dysfunction risk (depends on duration). PDE5i trial at 4\u20136 weeks for rehabilitation.

nodes.title: Shunting Failed
nodes.body: Shunting has failed to produce detumescence. Options: \u2022 If distal shunt attempted \u2192 may try proximal shunt \u2022 If both failed, or duration > 48hr with necrotic tissue: \u2192 Immediate penile prosthesis recommended (AUA/SMSNA 2022) Early prosthesis (within days) has better outcomes than delayed placement: \u2022 Easier implantation \u2022 Less penile fibrosis \u2022 Better length pres
nodes.recommendation: Urgent urology consultation for penile prosthesis implantation. Early implantation preferred over delayed. If proximal shunt not yet attempted, consider before prosthesis.

nodes.title: Prolonged Priapism (> 36\u201348hr) \u2014 Prosthesis
nodes.summary: >36-48h with failed medical management — early prosthesis preferred (better outcomes, less fibrosis)
nodes.body: Duration > 36\u201348 hours with failed medical management: \u2022 Smooth muscle necrosis likely advanced \u2022 AUA/SMSNA 2022: consider immediate penile prosthesis \u2022 Still attempt aspiration + phenylephrine first if not yet done \u2022 If unsuccessful, do not delay surgical consultation Early prosthesis placement (within days) has better outcomes: \u2022 Easier implantation before fibrosis

nodes.title: Treatment Approach \u2014 Prolonged Priapism
nodes.summary: After attempting aspiration/phenylephrine — decide: resolved, shunt, or immediate prosthesis
nodes.body: After attempting aspiration + phenylephrine, what is the plan?

nodes.title: Prolonged Priapism \u2014 Resolved
nodes.body: Detumescence achieved despite prolonged duration. \u2022 High risk of erectile dysfunction (30\u201370% at > 24hr duration) \u2022 Urology follow-up within 48 hours \u2022 Early erectile rehabilitation counseling \u2022 PDE5i trial at 4\u20136 weeks Return Precautions
nodes.recommendation: Observe. Urology follow-up within 48 hours. High probability of ED given prolonged duration. Early erectile rehabilitation counseling. PDE5i trial at 4\u20136 weeks.

nodes.title: Immediate Penile Prosthesis
nodes.body: Immediate prosthesis implantation for refractory prolonged ischemic priapism. AUA/SMSNA 2022: early placement preferred over delayed. Benefits: \u2022 Prevents penile shortening from fibrosis \u2022 Restores erectile function \u2022 Avoids difficult delayed implantation in scarred tissue \u2022 Patient satisfaction 60\u2013100%
nodes.recommendation: Urology proceeding with penile prosthesis implantation. Post-op care per urology team. This is the definitive treatment for refractory prolonged ischemic priapism.

nodes.title: ED Procedural Sedation
nodes.summary: Short ED sedation workflow: risk, setup, agent, monitor, rescue, recover.
nodes.body: Use this for short ED procedures when analgesia, anxiolysis, amnesia, or dissociation is needed and the team can immediately rescue airway/ventilation. Open first: - Sedation Steps - Airway Rescue Setup - Agent Selection - Monitoring - Stop / Escalate

nodes.title: Is ED Sedation Appropriate?
nodes.summary: Confirm the procedure fits ED sedation and not anesthesia/OR escalation.
nodes.body: Confirm the procedure is urgent/beneficial and can be completed safely with ED airway rescue capability.

nodes.title: Risk Screen
nodes.summary: Risk screen before drug choice: airway, aspiration, cardiopulmonary reserve, age/frailty.
nodes.body: Screen for: difficult airway features, severe OSA/obesity hypoventilation, active vomiting/aspiration risk, severe cardiopulmonary disease, pregnancy, intoxication, elderly/frail physiology, and prior sedation complication. Do not delay urgent sedation solely for fasting status, but adjust plan and risk discussion when aspiration risk is high.

nodes.title: Setup Before Medication
nodes.summary: Monitoring and rescue setup must be complete before medication.
nodes.body: Minimum setup: - Preoxygenate when feasible - Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring, BP cycling - Capnography when available, especially moderate/deep sedation - Suction ready - BVM, oxygen, oral/nasal airways, and intubation backup immediately available - Dedicated monitor separate from procedure operator - Resuscitation meds and reversal agents accessible

nodes.title: Choose Sedation Strategy
nodes.summary: Pick dissociation, brief deep sedation, or analgesia/anxiolysis plan.
nodes.body: Match the agent to procedure pain, desired immobility, hemodynamics, airway risk, and clinician familiarity.

nodes.title: Dissociative Ketamine Plan
nodes.summary: Ketamine: dissociative option with airway vigilance and emesis/laryngospasm planning.
nodes.body: Use Ketamine when dissociation is the desired endpoint. Practical reminders: - Dose intentionally; avoid repeated small under-doses that prolong agitation - Monitor for vomiting, hypersalivation, emergence reaction, and rare laryngospasm - Avoid when severe uncontrolled hypertension, active psychosis, or concerning airway secretions make another strategy safer

nodes.title: Brief Deep Sedation Plan
nodes.summary: Short-acting deep sedation needs titration, oxygenation, and rescue readiness.
nodes.body: Common ED options include Propofol, Etomidate, or ketofol per local protocol. Practical reminders: - Titrate to effect with immediate airway rescue readiness - Expect apnea/hypotension risk with propofol - Etomidate has no analgesia; pair with analgesia when needed - Avoid casual redosing after procedure completion

nodes.title: Analgesia + Anxiolysis Plan
nodes.summary: Opioid/benzodiazepine plans require slow titration and ventilation reassessment.
nodes.body: Use lower-depth sedation when full dissociation/deep sedation is not needed. Common pairings include Fentanyl plus cautious Midazolam titration. Avoid stacking respiratory depressants without reassessing ventilation after each dose.

nodes.title: During Sedation
nodes.summary: Ventilation trend and clinical exam drive rescue decisions.
nodes.body: Monitor the patient, not only the procedure. Track: - Airway patency and chest rise - SpO2 and capnography trend - BP and perfusion - Sedation depth - Pain response and procedure progress Call out deterioration early: falling ETCO2 waveform, apnea, obstruction, desaturation, hypotension, or vomiting.

nodes.title: Any Sedation Complication?
nodes.summary: Complications trigger immediate rescue, not watchful waiting.
nodes.body: Interrupt the procedure if oxygenation, ventilation, perfusion, or airway protection becomes unsafe.

nodes.title: Airway Rescue Sequence
nodes.summary: Rescue airway/ventilation immediately and escalate if BVM fails.
nodes.body: Stop procedure stimulation and restore ventilation. Immediate sequence: 1. Reposition airway; jaw thrust 2. Suction if needed 3. Supplemental oxygen / BVM ventilation 4. Oral or nasal airway if tolerated 5. Treat laryngospasm with airway maneuvers, positive pressure, and escalation per local protocol 6. Intubate or call airway help if ventilation cannot be restored
nodes.recommendation: Ventilation is the endpoint. Escalate early if BVM ventilation is ineffective.

nodes.title: Recovery / Disposition
nodes.summary: Recovery requires airway, perfusion, mentation, pain control, and safe disposition.
nodes.body: Recover until the patient has stable airway/ventilation, stable hemodynamics, improving mental status near baseline, controlled pain/nausea, and a safe escort/disposition plan. Document: indication, consent/emergency exception, risk screen, ASA/airway assessment, time-out, meds/doses/times, monitoring, complications, recovery status, and discharge instructions.
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after return to safe baseline and procedure-specific disposition criteria are met.

nodes.title: Stop / Escalate
nodes.summary: Escalate when procedure, physiology, or airway risk exceeds ED sedation capacity.
nodes.body: Do not proceed with routine ED sedation when risk exceeds ED rescue resources. Escalate for: anticipated impossible ventilation, severe unstable cardiopulmonary disease, inability to monitor, no recovery space, procedure too long/complex, or complication requiring advanced airway/ICU/OR.
nodes.recommendation: Use anesthesia, OR, ICU, or specialist pathway when the sedation risk is not matched by ED resources.

nodes.title: Acute Proximal Weakness — Sick Check First
nodes.body: True acute neuromuscular weakness is an airway/breathing emergency until proven otherwise. The muscles that fail to lift an arm are the same ones (diaphragm, intercostals, bulbar muscles) that fail to breathe and protect the airway. Do not anchor on "just weak" — a patient can talk, look comfortable, and be minutes from respiratory arrest. ⚠️ 5 DO-NOT-MISS diagnoses 1. Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Seven-branch triage: GBS / myasthenic crisis / botulism / tick paralysis / periodic paralysis-dyskalemia / Lambert-Eaton / myopathic mimic.
nodes.body: Pattern is the key: ascending vs descending, reflexes, pupils, fatigability, exposure history, and potassium. Each branch runs a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential. Two pattern traps worth naming up front: - Dry mouth is not specific to botulism. LEMS also produces autonomic dryness. The separator is *direction and facilitation*: bot

nodes.title: Guillain-Barré — Ascending Areflexia Gate
nodes.summary: Ascending symmetric areflexia + progression = GBS; watch VC/NIF, autonomics; do not trust SpO2.
nodes.body: GBS is progressive, relatively symmetric weakness with hyporeflexia/areflexia, often ascending from the legs, frequently after a preceding infection (Campylobacter, viral, recent vaccination). Watch for respiratory failure and autonomic instability (labile BP/HR, arrhythmias). Bedside markers of impending respiratory failure: falling vital capacity (<20 mL/kg), NIF worse than −30 cmH₂O, MEP <40, a

nodes.title: GBS — Airway Watch + Immunotherapy
nodes.body: Open Guillain-Barré Syndrome for the full pathway. Next steps: - Serial respiratory mechanics (VC + NIF) and continuous monitoring — intubate early for a falling VC (<15–20 mL/kg), NIF worse than −30, bulbar failure, or rapid progression. Do not wait for hypoxia/hypercapnia. - Monitor for autonomic instability (arrhythmias, labile BP) — telemetry, cautious with vasoactive drugs. - Immunotherapy: I
nodes.recommendation: Serial VC/NIF with early intubation, telemetry for autonomics, IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x5 OR plasma exchange (not both, no steroids), neuro/ICU admission; rocuronium not succinylcholine; do not temporize with BiPAP.

nodes.title: GBS — Unlikely
nodes.body: Intact reflexes, a non-ascending pattern, and no progression make GBS unlikely right now. GBS evolves over hours to days — preserved reflexes early do not fully exclude it, so if weakness ascends or respiratory mechanics decline, re-escalate and get neurology. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: GBS unlikely with intact reflexes/no progression; re-check reflexes + VC/NIF serially and escalate if it ascends.

nodes.title: Myasthenia Gravis — Fatigability + Bulbar Gate
nodes.summary: Fatigable ptosis/diplopia/bulbar weakness + trigger = myasthenic crisis; secure airway, avoid unsafe drugs, IVIG/PLEX.
nodes.body: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness that worsens with use and late in the day, classically with ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech). Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure from weakness, often triggered by infection, surgery, or drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers — including timolol eye drops — and IV magnesium, whi

nodes.title: Myasthenic Crisis — Airway + Immunotherapy
nodes.body: Open Myasthenia Gravis for the full crisis pathway. Next steps: - Serial VC/NIF; intubate early for bulbar failure or declining mechanics — avoid depolarizing/prolonged neuromuscular blockade pitfalls (MG patients are resistant to succinylcholine, sensitive to non-depolarizers). - Identify and remove the trigger — treat infection, stop precipitating drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta-b
nodes.recommendation: Serial VC/NIF + early intubation (mind NMBA pitfalls), remove triggers/unsafe drugs, IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 d or plasma exchange, neuro/ICU; steroids only with airway backup; BiPAP trial reasonable if PaCO2 <45 and no bulbar weakness.

nodes.title: Myasthenia — Unlikely
nodes.body: No fatigability and no ocular/bulbar involvement make myasthenia an unlikely driver. If fatigable ptosis/diplopia or bulbar symptoms appear, re-run this gate and involve neurology. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: MG unlikely without fatigable/ocular/bulbar signs; reassess if fatigability or bulbar symptoms emerge.

nodes.title: Botulism — Descending Paralysis Gate
nodes.summary: Descending bulbar-first paralysis + dilated pupils + dry mouth + afebrile = botulism; antitoxin early, airway watch, call public health.
nodes.body: Botulism is a symmetric, DESCENDING flaccid paralysis that starts with the bulbar muscles — the classic "4 Ds": diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia — plus dilated/fixed pupils, dry mouth, and ptosis, with a clear sensorium and no fever or sensory loss. Sources: home-canned/improperly preserved food, wounds (including injection drug use), and infant botulism. Descending paralysis + normal me

nodes.title: Botulism — Antitoxin + Airway Support
nodes.body: Open Botulism for the full pathway. Next steps: - Give botulinum antitoxin as early as possible — do NOT wait for confirmatory testing; antitoxin only halts *further* paralysis and cannot reverse what has already bound, so every hour of delay is fixed deficit. - ☎️ The phone call IS the treatment. Antitoxin is not stocked in your pharmacy. - Non-infant (≥1 yr) — BAT / HBAT (heptavalent, equine, ty
nodes.recommendation: Early antitoxin via public health — BAT/HBAT 1 vial IV (CDC EOC 770-488-7100) for age >=1 yr, BabyBIG 50 mg/kg for infants (CA IBTPP 510-231-7600) — plus aggressive airway support (rocuronium, not succinylcholine) and mandatory reporting; w

nodes.title: Botulism — Unlikely
nodes.body: An ascending pattern, sensory involvement, or fever argues against botulism (which is descending, purely motor, and afebrile with a clear sensorium). Reconsider GBS/tick paralysis or an infectious cause. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Botulism unlikely if ascending/sensory/febrile; pivot back to GBS/tick/infectious causes.

nodes.title: Tick Paralysis — Exposure + Search Gate
nodes.summary: Ascending flaccid paralysis + outdoor exposure → hunt for and remove the tick; recovery follows removal.
nodes.body: Tick paralysis is an ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia that mimics GBS but reverses when the attached tick is removed. It follows outdoor/wooded exposure, is toxin-mediated (no fever, normal sensation, normal CSF), and progresses over hours to days. The diagnosis is made by finding and removing the tick — search the entire scalp/hairline, ears, axillae, groin, and skin folds meticulously.

nodes.title: Tick Paralysis — Remove the Tick
nodes.body: Open Tick Paralysis for the full pathway. Next steps: - Find and completely remove the attached tick (fine forceps, steady traction at the skin surface, remove mouthparts) — this is diagnostic and therapeutic; improvement usually begins within hours to a day. - Support respiration — serial VC/NIF; intubate if mechanics decline before improvement occurs. - Search thoroughly — there may be more than
nodes.recommendation: Remove the tick completely (diagnostic + therapeutic), support respiration until recovery, recheck for additional ticks; expect up to ~2 days of continued progression (North American) and worsening after removal (Australian Ixodes holocyclu

nodes.title: Tick Paralysis — Unlikely
nodes.body: No exposure history and no tick found after a thorough head-to-toe search make tick paralysis unlikely. If ascending weakness continues, treat down the GBS pathway and involve neurology. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Tick paralysis unlikely with no tick after full search; default to GBS workup for ongoing ascending weakness.

nodes.title: Periodic Paralysis / Dyskalemia — K⁺ + ECG Gate
nodes.summary: Acute weakness → stat K+ and ECG; correct hypo/hyperkalemia cautiously (rebound overshoot), treat thyrotoxicosis if present.
nodes.body: Sudden flaccid weakness with an abnormal potassium is immediately treatable and immediately dangerous. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis (often after carbohydrate load, rest after exercise, or thyrotoxicosis — especially Asian men) and hyperkalemic periodic paralysis both present with episodic weakness sparing the respiratory muscles until severe. Any acute weakness gets a stat potassium and ECG — th

nodes.title: Dyskalemic Paralysis — Correct Potassium Carefully
nodes.body: Periodic paralysis / severe dyskalemia (no dedicated consult yet — manage here). Use the electrolyte pathways: Potassium Disorders. Next steps: - Continuous ECG monitoring — the arrhythmia is the lethal threat. - Hypokalemic: replace potassium cautiously — total-body potassium is often normal (it has shifted intracellularly), so aggressive replacement risks rebound hyperkalemia as the shift revers
nodes.recommendation: ECG monitoring + cautious K+ correction (avoid rebound); thyrotoxic PP → beta-blocker + treat thyroid; hyperkalemic → stabilize/shift/eliminate. Never give K+ in dextrose. Send a TSH on any young adult with hypokalemic flaccid paralysis.

nodes.title: Dyskalemia — Excluded
nodes.body: A normal potassium and a normal ECG exclude dyskalemic paralysis as the current driver. Keep it in mind for episodic recurrent weakness and recheck electrolytes if the picture changes. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Normal K+/ECG excludes dyskalemic paralysis now; recheck for episodic/recurrent weakness.

nodes.title: Lambert-Eaton (LEMS) — Facilitation Gate
nodes.summary: Proximal legs>arms weakness + dry mouth + post-exercise facilitation = LEMS; ~50-60% paraneoplastic (SCLC); avoid NMBAs, Mg, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, CCBs, iodinated contrast.
nodes.body: **LEMS is the presynaptic mirror image of myasthenia gravis, and it is the single most on-topic diagnosis for a *proximal* weakness complaint. Antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels cut acetylcholine release, so the presentation is proximal weakness, legs > arms, symmetric — exactly "can't rise from a chair, can't lift overhead." The triad: 1. Proximal weakness (legs > arms) wi

nodes.title: LEMS — Avoid the Wrong Drugs, Hunt the Cancer
nodes.body: Open Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome for the full pathway. ⚠️ Highest ED-safety yield: drugs that can tip a LEMS patient into respiratory failure. - Neuromuscular blockers — BOTH depolarizing and non-depolarizing. LEMS patients are exquisitely sensitive; prolonged paralysis is the rule. If you must intubate, plan for it and have sugammadex/prolonged ventilation available. - IV magnesium — compet
nodes.recommendation: Suspect LEMS: avoid NMBAs, IV magnesium, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, calcium-channel blockers and iodinated contrast; send anti-P/Q VGCC, get CT chest to hunt small cell lung cancer; admit for respiratory/bulbar compromise, otherwise

nodes.title: Lambert-Eaton — Unlikely
nodes.body: No post-exercise facilitation and no autonomic dryness make LEMS unlikely as the driver. Keep it on the list for subacute, smoking-associated proximal weakness that has been building over weeks to months rather than hours — LEMS is usually a slower burn than the other branches on this hub, and it is frequently mislabelled as deconditioning, statin myopathy, or functional weakness before anyone che
nodes.recommendation: LEMS unlikely without facilitation or autonomic features; reconsider for subacute smoking-associated proximal weakness building over weeks to months.

nodes.title: Myopathic / Systemic Mimic — Muscle + Systemic Gate
nodes.summary: Myalgia/dark urine/high CK → myopathy-rhabdo workup; focal/UMN/sensory-level → CNS or cord pathway.
nodes.body: Proximal weakness with muscle pain, tenderness, or dark urine points to a myopathic or systemic cause rather than a neuromuscular-junction/nerve emergency. Consider rhabdomyolysis (myalgia, dark urine, high CK — renal and electrolyte risk), inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis/dermatomyositis), steroid or statin myopathy, thyroid myopathy, and severe electrolyte disturbance. Also remember an acute

nodes.title: Myopathy / Rhabdomyolysis — Workup + Protect the Kidneys
nodes.body: Myopathic proximal weakness (manage here; use the deep-dive when rhabdo is confirmed): - Check CK, potassium, calcium, phosphate, renal function, and urinalysis. A markedly elevated CK with pigmenturia → Rhabdomyolysis — aggressive IV fluids and monitor for hyperkalemia and AKI. - Correct electrolyte disturbances driving the weakness (potassium, calcium, phosphate, magnesium). - Medication review:
nodes.recommendation: CK + electrolytes + renal/UA; rhabdo → LR to UOP 1-3 mL/kg/h + watch K+/AKI (alkalinization not routine); stop myotoxic drugs; refer inflammatory/endocrine myopathy. If CK stays high or weakness progresses after stopping a statin, send anti

nodes.title: CNS / Cord Mimic — Do Not Miss a Central Lesion
nodes.body: Focal weakness, upper-motor-neuron signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski), or a sensory level is NOT a myopathy — it is central. - Acute focal deficit → stroke pathway: Stroke — time-critical, get neuro imaging and consider reperfusion. - Sensory level / bilateral leg weakness / bladder-bowel involvement → cord compression/myelopathy: emergent MRI of the spine; steroids and neurosurgery if co
nodes.recommendation: Focal/UMN/sensory-level weakness = central lesion: stroke pathway for acute focal deficit, emergent spine MRI for a cord syndrome; do not delay. Tailor steroids to the lesion — dexamethasone for malignant epidural compression, but abscess n

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Respiratory-Failure Watch
nodes.body: The acute-neuromuscular-weakness bundle centers on breathing (scale to acuity): - Bedside respiratory mechanics up front and serially: single-breath count, forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF/MIP). Warning thresholds: FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF worse than −30 cmH₂O, MEP <40 cmH₂O ("20/30/40 rule"), rapid decline, or weak cough/poor swallow. - Intubate on trending mechanics and

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Declining VC/NIF, bulbar failure, or lethal dyskalemia → intubate + ICU; stable + diagnosed → disposition.
nodes.body: After bedside mechanics, the pattern exam, and initial labs/ECG — where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging / Diagnostics
nodes.body: Match the test to the suspected level of the lesion: - Lumbar puncture — GBS (albuminocytologic dissociation: high protein, normal cell count; may be normal in the first days). - Nerve conduction studies / EMG — confirm GBS (demyelinating), botulism (incremental response), MG (decremental response/jitter); usually inpatient/specialist. - MRI brain/spine — when a CNS or cord lesion is possible (foc

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU/admit crises and intubated/lethal-K patients; monitored bed for evolving processes; discharge corrected reversible causes.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: ICU / Admit
nodes.body: ICU / admit the neuromuscular emergency. - GBS / myasthenic crisis / botulism → ICU or step-down with continuous respiratory monitoring, immunotherapy/antitoxin, and airway management. - Any intubated patient → ICU; anticipate prolonged ventilation in botulism. - Lethal dyskalemia → monitored bed with continuous ECG until corrected and stable. - Neurology (and public health for botulism) involved;
nodes.recommendation: ICU/step-down for GBS/MG crisis/botulism/intubated/lethal-K; continuous respiratory + cardiac monitoring, immunotherapy/antitoxin, specialist involvement.

nodes.title: Admit to a Monitored Bed
nodes.body: Admission to a monitored bed for the evolving or uncertain neuromuscular process — e.g., early GBS with stable mechanics, borderline myasthenia needing serial VC/NIF, or tick paralysis after removal awaiting improvement. - Serial respiratory mechanics and neuro exams; low threshold to escalate to the ICU. - Complete the diagnostic workup (LP/NCS/MRI) and involve neurology before disposition. - Do
nodes.recommendation: Monitored-bed admission with serial mechanics/neuro exams and a low escalation threshold; complete workup with neurology.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge only when the cause is reversible and corrected and respiratory function is normal. - Corrected dyskalemia with a clear trigger, normal repeat ECG, and resolved weakness → discharge with electrolyte/endocrine follow-up and trigger counseling. - Benign/stable myopathy (e.g., statin myopathy after stopping the drug, mild self-limited myositis) → discharge with the appropriate outpatient wo
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only reversible, corrected causes with normal breathing; outpatient workup + strict neuromuscular/respiratory return precautions. Statin myopathy needs a repeat CK and named follow-up (anti-HMGCR IMNM progresses off the drug); sen

nodes.title: Psychiatric Assessment — Overview
nodes.summary: 10-component MSE: appearance through insight/judgment — CPT 90792 requires full MSE + treatment plan
nodes.body: A comprehensive psychiatric assessment follows a structured format including both historical information and a systematic Mental Status Examination (MSE). The MSE is a structured way to assess and document a patient's current cognitive, behavioral, and emotional functioning. Unlike the MMSE (cognitive screening), the MSE offers a broader view of the patient's psychological state during a specific

nodes.title: History Taking
nodes.summary: Chief complaint, psych/med/substance history, collateral sources — document who provided information
nodes.body: Presenting Complaint: • Chief complaint in patient's own words • Onset, duration, and course of current symptoms • Precipitating events or stressors Psychiatric History: • Previous psychiatric diagnoses • Prior hospitalizations (voluntary vs. involuntary) • Previous treatments and response • History of self-harm or suicide attempts Medication History: • Current psychotropic medications (dose, dura

nodes.title: 1. Appearance
nodes.summary: Assess hygiene, dress, posture, facial expression, apparent age — insights into functioning and mood
nodes.body: Appearance refers to how the patient presents physically. These observations offer insight into level of functioning, mood, and potential psychiatric symptoms. Hygiene & Grooming: • Clean, neat, shaven • Body odor, disheveled, unkempt, malodorous Dress: • Appropriate, casual, neat, business, fashionable • Bizarre, inappropriate, dirty, stained, ragged, layered Posture: • Relaxed, rigid, slumped, t

nodes.title: 2. Behavior & Motor
nodes.summary: Eye contact, cooperation, psychomotor activity, movement disorders (tardive dyskinesia), level of arousal
nodes.body: Behavior refers to how the patient moves, responds, and engages during the encounter. Eye Contact: • Good, fleeting, intense, avoidant, staring, none Cooperativeness / Attitude: • Friendly, cooperative, open, relaxed, candid • Guarded, evasive, hostile, withdrawn, suspicious • Passive, sullen, manipulative, demanding, overly friendly Psychomotor Activity: • Normal, restless, tense, agitated • Decr

nodes.title: 3. Speech & Language
nodes.summary: Rate, rhythm, volume, content, latency — pressured speech suggests mania, poverty suggests depression
nodes.body: Speech patterns offer insight into cognitive and emotional state. Disruptions may indicate mood disorders, anxiety, thought disorganization, or neurocognitive impairment. Rate: • Normal (~100-150 words/minute) • Rapid / pressured (→ mania, anxiety) • Slow / hesitant (→ depression, sedation) • Delayed onset Rhythm: • Normal prosody, articulate • Monotone, stuttering, dysarthric, slurred Volume: • N

nodes.title: 4. Mood (Subjective)
nodes.summary: Document in patient's own words — mood is SUBJECTIVE (what they tell you), sustained emotional state
nodes.body: Mood is the patient's self-reported emotional state — what they TELL you they feel. It represents a sustained emotion present over a prolonged period that can alter their perception of the world. Ask the patient: • "How is your mood today?" • "How have you been feeling over the past few days?" • "Would you say your emotions have been steady or up and down?" • "Have you felt sad or discouraged?" •

nodes.title: 5. Affect (Objective)
nodes.summary: Affect is OBJECTIVE — your observation of intensity, quality, range, congruence with stated mood
nodes.body: Affect is the clinician's objective observation of the patient's emotional expression — what you SEE. It is an observable emotion expressed in the moment, fluctuating during the encounter. Intensity: • Normal • Flat (no emotional expression → schizophrenia, severe depression) • Blunted (minimal expression) • Exaggerated Quality: • Sad, agitated, euphoric, anxious, angry, fearful, indifferent Fluct

nodes.title: 6. Thought Process
nodes.summary: HOW they think — goal-directed, tangential, loose associations, flight of ideas, thought blocking
nodes.body: Thought process describes the *form and flow* of thinking — HOW the patient thinks. Assess the amount, speed, and the way thoughts are linked together. Stream of Thought (amount and speed): • Goal-directed / linear — thoughts connect logically (normal) • Rapid — increased speed but still coherent • Impoverished — slow thinking, few spontaneous ideas • Thought blocking — abrupt interruption mid-sen

nodes.title: 7. Thought Content & Perception
nodes.summary: WHAT they think — delusions, obsessions, hallucinations, command hallucinations (ask specifically)
nodes.body: THOUGHT CONTENT — WHAT the patient is thinking about. Content of Thought: • Delusions (fixed false beliefs): — Paranoid / persecutory — being watched, followed, harmed — Grandiose — inflated self-importance or abilities — Somatic — false beliefs about body — Referential — events/media directed at them — Erotomanic — belief someone is in love with them — Nihilistic — belief that self/world doesn't

nodes.title: 9. Cognition
nodes.summary: Orientation, attention (serial 7s), memory (3-word recall), abstract reasoning, clock drawing test
nodes.body: Cognitive assessment determines how well the patient processes information, recalls memories, and maintains awareness. Alertness: • Alert, lethargic, obtunded, stuporous, comatose Orientation (document as A&Ox3 or A&Ox4): • Person — "What is your name?" • Place — "Where are you right now?" • Time — "What year/month/day is it?" • Situation — "Why are you here today?" Clouding of Consciousness: • Dr

nodes.title: 8. Safety — SI/HI Screening
nodes.summary: Ask directly about SI/HI — previous attempts strongest predictor, ask specifically about firearms access
nodes.body: Joint Commission NPSG.15.01.01 (renumbered NPSG.08.01.01 in 2026): Requires screening all patients age 12+ evaluated/treated for a primary behavioral health condition using a validated tool (C-SSRS, PHQ-2, Patient Safety Screener, ASQ). Positive screen → full risk assessment using an evidence-based process. Suicidal Ideation — ask directly: • "Do you feel that life is not worth living?" • "Have yo

nodes.title: Passive Suicidal Ideation
nodes.summary: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown), means restriction counseling, 988 Lifeline, outpatient follow-up 48-72h
nodes.body: Passive SI — patient expresses desire to be dead or not alive but denies active plan or intent. Further Assessment: • Frequency and duration of thoughts • Any preparatory behaviors (giving away possessions, writing notes) • Access to means — ask specifically about firearms • Substance use (acutely increases risk) • Recent changes in behavior or functioning Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Interventio

nodes.title: Active Suicidal Ideation — Psych Emergency
nodes.body: Active SI with plan or intent requires immediate intervention. Immediate Actions: • 1:1 sitter / continuous observation • Remove all potential means (sharps, cords, medications) • Place patient in safe environment (ligature-resistant room) • Voluntary vs. involuntary hold based on jurisdiction Consult Psychiatry for: • Risk assessment and safety planning • Medication evaluation • Inpatient admissi
nodes.recommendation: Psychiatric consultation. 1:1 observation. Means restriction. Consider voluntary vs. involuntary hold. Inpatient admission likely indicated.

nodes.title: Homicidal Ideation — Safety Protocol
nodes.body: Homicidal ideation requires immediate safety measures and may trigger duty to warn/protect obligations. Immediate Actions: • Ensure staff safety — do not interview alone • Security at bedside if agitated or threatening • Search for weapons per hospital protocol • 1:1 observation Assessment: • Specificity of target (identified vs. generalized) • Specificity of plan • Access to weapons • History of
nodes.recommendation: Psychiatric consultation. 1:1 observation. Assess Tarasoff duty. Notify security. Document all threats and actions taken.

nodes.title: 10. Insight & Judgment
nodes.summary: Insight: good/fair/poor/absent; Judgment: decision-making capacity (4 criteria); synthesize overall risk
nodes.body: Insight — the extent to which the patient recognizes and appraises their experiences. Levels of Insight: • Good / Complete — acknowledges illness, understands need for treatment, willing to engage • Fair / Partial — acknowledges some symptoms but minimizes severity or attributes to wrong cause • Poor / Limited — denies illness, blames external factors, resistant to treatment • Absent / None — no r

nodes.title: Laboratory Considerations
nodes.summary: Labs are targeted by risk; low-risk known psych with normal vitals/exam often does not need routine testing.
nodes.body: Consider labs to rule out medical contributors to psychiatric symptoms: ACEP Clinical Policy + AAEM Position (consistent in 2024): Routine laboratory testing — including urine drug screens (Level C) — is NOT indicated for the alert, cooperative, asymptomatic adult psychiatric patient. Testing should be driven by history, vital signs, and physical exam findings. Low-risk known psychiatric presentat

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Document all 10 MSE components, diagnosis, capacity assessment, treatment plan — use objective language
nodes.body: Determine appropriate level of care based on the complete assessment. Your documentation must include: 1. Complete medical and psychiatric history 2. Mental status examination findings (all 10 components) 3. Initial diagnosis 4. Evaluation of capacity to respond to treatment 5. Initial treatment plan Use objective and descriptive language. Avoid vague terms like "seems sad." Instead: "Patient avoi

nodes.title: Discharge — Outpatient Follow-Up
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria Met: • No active suicidal or homicidal ideation • Patient is not acutely intoxicated • Adequate support system identified • Patient agrees to safety plan • Outpatient follow-up arranged Discharge Plan: • Safety plan completed and reviewed with patient • Means restriction counseling documented • Crisis resources provided (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) • Outpatient psychiatry app
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with safety plan, means restriction counseling, crisis resources, and outpatient psychiatry follow-up within 48-72 hours.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Admission
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: • Active suicidal or homicidal ideation with plan/intent • Acute psychosis requiring stabilization • Inability to care for self (gravely disabled) • Failed outpatient management • Need for medication adjustment requiring monitoring • Substance withdrawal requiring medical management Voluntary Admission: • Patient consents to treatment • Document capacity to consent • Patient re
nodes.recommendation: Psychiatric admission — voluntary or involuntary per clinical assessment. Document specific safety concerns, legal criteria met, and disposition reasoning.

nodes.title: Psych Triage
nodes.summary: Route to appropriate psychiatric pathway based on primary presenting concern.
nodes.body: What is the PRIMARY presenting concern? Select the most urgent/dominant feature. Many psychiatric presentations overlap — this routes to the most appropriate starting point.

nodes.title: Agitation Pathway
nodes.summary: Agitated patient — route to Acute Agitation consult for BETA protocol and chemical restraint.
nodes.body: → Acute Agitation Consult Immediate priorities: • Verbal de-escalation (BETA protocol) • Chemical restraint if de-escalation fails • Rule out organic causes (hypoglycemia, hypoxia, intoxication) Key decision: Is this delirium/medical OR primary psychiatric?

nodes.title: Suicidal Patient Pathway
nodes.summary: Suicidal patient — route to Suicidal Patient consult for C-SSRS and risk stratification.
nodes.body: → Suicidal Patient Consult Immediate priorities: • 1:1 constant visual observation • Remove ligatures, sharps, medications from room • Environmental safety checklist • ASQ or C-SSRS screening Key decision: Risk stratification → disposition (discharge vs voluntary vs involuntary)

nodes.title: Altered Mental Status Pathway
nodes.summary: Altered mental status — route to Psych Medical Stability for organic workup.
nodes.body: → Psych Medical Stability Critical question: Is this DELIRIUM or PRIMARY PSYCHOSIS? Delirium red flags: • Acute onset (hours-days) • Fluctuating course • Inattention (cannot focus on interview) • Visual hallucinations • Abnormal vital signs • Age >45 with first psychiatric symptoms Use history, vitals, exam, mentation, and red flags to decide the medical workup intensity.

nodes.title: Psychosis Pathway
nodes.summary: Psychosis — start with medical stability assessment, then use Acute Psychosis / First Break for workup and disposition.
nodes.body: Start with: Psych Medical Stability Then continue: Acute Psychosis / First Break Rule out organic causes FIRST when red flags are present: • Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis • Stimulant intoxication • Medication toxicity • Encephalitis/meningitis • Metabolic derangement New-onset psychosis in patient >45: Medical cause until proven otherwise. If agitated: Acute Agitation for chemical restraint opti

nodes.title: Anxiety / Panic Pathway
nodes.summary: Anxiety/panic — rule out PE, ACS, arrhythmia before diagnosing panic disorder.
nodes.body: Panic attack vs medical emergency: Before diagnosing panic, rule out: • Pulmonary embolism (consider PERC, Wells) • Acute coronary syndrome (especially if risk factors) • Arrhythmia (check ECG) • Hyperthyroidism • Pheochromocytoma • Stimulant intoxication If true panic attack: • Reassurance, calm environment • Breathing exercises • Benzodiazepine if severe (lorazepam 0.5-1 mg PO/SL) • Outpatient p

nodes.title: Withdrawal Pathway
nodes.summary: Withdrawal — route to Alcohol Withdrawal consult for CIWA-Ar and benzo protocols.
nodes.body: → Alcohol Withdrawal Consult Early treatment prevents: • Withdrawal seizures (peak 12-48h) • Delirium tremens (peak 48-96h) DT mortality — say the number correctly: untreated DTs historically carried 15-37% mortality. With modern ICU care, aggressive benzodiazepine/phenobarbital treatment, and correction of electrolytes, mortality is roughly 1-4%. Quote the low number only for the patient who is a

nodes.title: Catatonia Pathway
nodes.summary: Catatonia — lorazepam challenge 2 mg IV. Avoid antipsychotics initially.
nodes.body: → Catatonia Consult Recognize catatonia early — it is treatable. Bush-Francis catatonia signs: • Immobility / stupor • Mutism • Staring / fixed gaze • Posturing / waxy flexibility • Negativism (resistance to movement) Treatment: • Lorazepam challenge: 2 mg IV — improvement within 10-15 min strongly supports diagnosis • If response: Continue lorazepam 2 mg q4-6h • If no response: Consider ECT ⚠️ AV

nodes.title: Eating Disorder Pathway
nodes.summary: Eating disorder — check electrolytes, ECG, vitals. MEED CR233 risk matrix (any red or 2+ amber = admit). Refeeding syndrome risk.
nodes.body: Eating disorder emergency — focus on medical stability: Check immediately: • Electrolytes: K+, PO4, Mg2+ (refeeding risk) • ECG: QTc prolongation, bradycardia • Glucose • Vitals: Bradycardia, orthostatic hypotension High-risk features that should trigger admission (legacy MARSIPAN 2014 thresholds): • BMI <13 or rapid weight loss >1 kg/week • K+ <3.0 or PO4 <0.5 • HR <40 or BP <90 systolic • QTc >4

nodes.title: Routed to Consult
nodes.summary: Continue with specialty consult for detailed management.
nodes.body: Continue with the linked specialty consult for detailed management. Return to Psych Triage if the clinical picture changes or a different pathway is needed.
nodes.recommendation: Follow the linked consult pathway for detailed management.

nodes.title: Mental Status Exam
nodes.summary: Reference Mode (read-only descriptors) or Build Dictation (interactive checklist → EMR summary).
nodes.body: Choose how you want to use this consult. Reference Mode — read-only walkthrough of standardized MSE descriptors for each component. Appearance & Behavior 2. Speech & Mood/Affect 3. Thought Process &

nodes.title: Peritonsillar Abscess — Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Pus between tonsillar capsule and pharyngeal muscles — hot potato voice, trismus, uvular deviation
nodes.body: PTA Drainage Steps Summary Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) is a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and pharyngeal muscles. [1][2] Classic presentation: • Severe sore throat (odynophagia) • "Hot potato" voice (muffled, wet) • Trismus (difficulty opening mouth) — 30-60% • Uvular deviation (pushed to opposite side) • Unilateral tonsillar swelling and exudate • Fever • Drooling Symptom durati

nodes.title: Clinical Examination
nodes.summary: Exam alone 75% sensitive — assess asymmetric swelling, uvular deviation, fluctuance, then US to confirm
nodes.body: Physical exam findings: [1][2] Inspect oropharynx: • Asymmetric tonsillar swelling • Soft palate bulging • Uvula deviated AWAY from affected side • Tonsillar exudate Assess trismus: • Limited mouth opening (<3 cm) • May limit examination and procedure access Palpate (if tolerated): • Fluctuance over anterior tonsillar pillar • Tenderness Clinical exam alone has sensitivity ~75%, specificity ~50% [

nodes.title: Managing Severe Trismus
nodes.summary: Dexamethasone 10mg first to reduce trismus, then topical anesthesia, analgesics, sedation if needed
nodes.body: Severe trismus limits examination and procedure access: [1][2] Strategies: 1. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV/IM — give first • Reduces edema and trismus within 30-60 min • Improves mouth opening significantly 2. Topical anesthesia spray • Benzocaine 20% or lidocaine 10% • Reduces reflex guarding 3. Analgesics • Morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV or hydromorphone 1-2 mg IV • Reduces pain-induced guarding 4. Procedural

nodes.title: Intraoral Ultrasound for PTA
nodes.summary: Intraoral US sensitivity 91% — confirms abscess vs cellulitis, identifies carotid, guides aspiration
nodes.body: Intraoral POCUS is gold standard for ED diagnosis: [3][4] Test characteristics: • Sensitivity: 91% • Specificity: 75% • Eliminates need for CT in most cases Advantages: • Confirms abscess vs cellulitis • Measures abscess size and depth • Identifies carotid artery location • Guides needle aspiration in real-time Indications for CT instead: • Deep space infection concern (parapharyngeal, retropharyn

nodes.title: POCUS Technique
nodes.summary: Endocavitary probe, scan superior pole first (70% of abscesses), use Color Doppler to locate carotid
nodes.body: Equipment: [3][4][5] • Endocavitary probe (preferred) with sterile sheath • Alternative: Linear hockey-stick probe • Sterile gel Patient preparation: • Upright position, head extended • Topical anesthetic spray to oropharynx • Wait 1-2 minutes for effect Scanning technique: 1. Insert sheathed probe intraorally 2. Direct toward suspected abscess 3. Scan systematically: superior pole (70%), mid-tons

nodes.title: Ultrasound Findings
nodes.summary: Hypoechoic collection with defined borders = abscess (drain); diffuse edema without pocket = cellulitis
nodes.body: Interpret the ultrasound: [3][4] Abscess (drainable): • Hypoechoic or anechoic fluid collection • Well-defined borders • May have debris/loculations Cellulitis (no drainage): • Diffuse edema, no discrete collection • Hyperechoic "dirty" appearance • No anechoic pocket What did ultrasound show?

nodes.title: Peritonsillar Cellulitis — No Drainage
nodes.body: No drainable abscess identified — treat with antibiotics alone: [1][2] Management: • IV antibiotics if unable to tolerate PO • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV/IM single dose • Observation 4-6 hours for improvement • IV fluids if dehydrated Antibiotics: • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID × 10 days • Or Clindamycin 300-450 mg PO Q8h × 10 days Consider admission if: • Unable to tolerate oral intake •
nodes.recommendation: Peritonsillar cellulitis — antibiotics + steroids, no drainage. Close follow-up.

nodes.title: Equivocal Ultrasound
nodes.summary: Equivocal US — diagnostic aspiration reasonable, CT if deep space concern, or trial antibiotics + follow-up
nodes.body: If ultrasound findings are unclear: [1][4] Options: 1. Diagnostic needle aspiration • Even if US equivocal, aspiration attempt is reasonable • No pus obtained = cellulitis (treat medically) • Pus obtained = abscess (continue drainage) 2. CT scan with contrast • More definitive if diagnosis uncertain • Especially if concern for deep space extension • Consider if: atypical presentation, failed aspir

nodes.title: Choose Drainage Method
nodes.summary: Needle aspiration first-line (85-95% success); I&D for large >2cm, recurrent, or failed aspiration
nodes.body: Needle aspiration vs Incision & Drainage: [1][2][6] Needle Aspiration: • First-line for most patients • Less painful, faster • Success rate 85-95% • Can be US-guided Incision & Drainage: • For large abscesses (>2 cm) • Recurrent drainage needed • Failed needle aspiration (2 attempts) • Multiple loculations • Patient preference Which approach?

nodes.title: Aspiration — Preparation
nodes.summary: 18g needle with depth limiter at 10mm, headlamp, Yankauer suction — patient upright with head extended
nodes.body: Equipment: [1][5][6] • 18-gauge needle on 10 mL syringe • Needle guard or depth limiter (CRITICAL) • Headlamp for visualization • Yankauer suction • Topical anesthetic spray (benzocaine 20% or lidocaine 10%) • Local anesthetic: Lidocaine 1% with epinephrine (optional) Set up depth limiter: • Mark syringe at 10 mm from needle tip • Or use commercial needle guard • Maximum insertion depth: 8-10 mm P

nodes.title: Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Topical benzocaine/lidocaine spray first, optional local infiltration — dexamethasone 10mg at procedure time
nodes.body: Topical anesthesia (always): [1][6] • Spray benzocaine 20% (Cetacaine) or lidocaine 10% generously • Cover tonsil, soft palate, base of tongue • Wait 1-2 minutes for effect • Reduces gag reflex and provides mucosal anesthesia Local infiltration (optional, for I&D or difficult aspiration): • Lidocaine 1% with epinephrine • 27-gauge needle, 6-10 mL total • Inject around fluctuant area • Inject at ba
