nodes.title: Needle Aspiration Technique
nodes.summary: DEPTH LIMIT 8-10mm maximum — target superior pole at 45 degrees, max 2-3 passes, US-guided preferred
nodes.body: CRITICAL SAFETY: Limit needle depth to 8-10 mm [1][5][6] Carotid artery is 2.5-4 cm posterior/lateral to tonsil. Target: Superior pole of tonsil (70% of abscesses) Technique: 1. Visualize with headlamp and tongue depressor 2. Insert 18g needle at 45° angle toward tonsillar fossa 3. Advance MAXIMUM 8-10 mm (use depth limiter!) 4. Aspirate while slowly withdrawing 5. If no pus, redirect slightly and

nodes.title: Aspiration Result
nodes.summary: Pus = successful drainage; no pus despite correct position = likely cellulitis; failed = proceed to I&D
nodes.body: Assess what was aspirated: [1][6] Successful aspiration: • Purulent material obtained • Patient often feels immediate relief • Swelling/bulge may decrease Unsuccessful: • No pus despite 2-3 attempts in correct location • Only blood obtained

nodes.title: No Pus Obtained — Likely Cellulitis
nodes.body: If needle position confirmed but no pus: [1][2] This is likely peritonsillar cellulitis, not abscess. Management: • Treat as cellulitis (antibiotics alone) • Dexamethasone 10 mg if not already given • Observe 4-6 hours for improvement Antibiotics: • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID × 10 days • PCN allergy: Clindamycin 300-450 mg Q8h × 10 days Consider CT if: • Clinical suspicion very high
nodes.recommendation: Likely cellulitis. Treat with antibiotics + steroids. Close follow-up mandatory.

nodes.title: Post-Aspiration Care
nodes.summary: Assess pain relief, swelling decrease, voice improvement — ice water gargles, observe 30-45 min
nodes.body: After successful needle aspiration: [1][6] Immediate care: • Withdraw needle slowly while observing for bleeding • Have patient spit (not swallow) any blood/drainage • Ice water gargles × 2-3 minutes — reduces bleeding, promotes drainage • Observe 30-45 minutes Assess adequacy: • Patient reports pain relief • Swelling decreased • Voice improved • Trismus improved If significant residual collection

nodes.title: Incision & Drainage — Preparation
nodes.summary: #11 or #15 blade, curved hemostat, local anesthesia 6-10mL — for large >2cm, recurrent, or failed aspiration
nodes.body: Indications for I&D over aspiration: [1][6][7] • Large abscess (>2 cm diameter) • Recurrent abscess or prior failed aspiration • Multiple loculations suspected • Uncooperative patient (with sedation) • Patient or provider preference Equipment: • #11 or #15 scalpel blade • Curved hemostat (Kelly or Mosquito) • Headlamp • Yankauer suction • Local anesthetic (1% lidocaine with epi, 27g needle) • Topi

nodes.title: I&D Technique
nodes.summary: Incise anterior pillar 1-1.5cm, depth 5-8mm, blunt dissect with hemostat — stay anterior, do NOT suture
nodes.body: Incision & Drainage technique: [1][6][7] Incision location: • Anterior tonsillar pillar (mucosa only) • Curvilinear or vertical incision • From base of uvula toward last mandibular molar • Length: 1.0-1.5 cm • Stay on ANTERIOR pillar — avoid lateral (carotid) direction Depth: • Superficial incision through mucosa only • Penetrate just enough to enter abscess cavity • Limit depth to 5-8 mm • Scalpe

nodes.title: Post-I&D Care
nodes.summary: Suction remaining pus, ice water gargles, observe 30-45 min — direct pressure for brisk bleeding
nodes.body: After incision and drainage: [1][6] Immediate: • Suction any remaining pus/blood • Have patient spit (not swallow) • Ice water gargles × 2-3 minutes • Observe for 30-45 minutes Complications to watch for: • Bleeding (usually minor, self-limited) • Aspiration of pus • Inadequate drainage (may need revision) If brisk bleeding: • Direct pressure with gauze • Consider topical epinephrine (1:1000) • Us

nodes.title: Antibiotic Selection
nodes.summary: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg BID x10-14d first-line; clindamycin for PCN allergy — polymicrobial coverage
nodes.body: PTA is polymicrobial — need anaerobic + aerobic coverage: [1][2][8] First-line oral: • Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID × 10-14 days Penicillin allergy: • Clindamycin 300-450 mg PO Q6-8h × 10-14 days IV options (if admission): • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV Q6h • OR Clindamycin 600-900 mg IV Q6-8h Severe/immunocompromised: • Clindamycin 600 mg IV Q6h + Ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV Q12h • Add Vanco

nodes.title: Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: Dexamethasone 10mg single dose — reduces pain, trismus, edema, speeds recovery, safe with no infection risk
nodes.body: Single-dose steroids improve outcomes: [1][2][9] Adult dose: • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV/IM/PO × 1 • OR Methylprednisolone 2-3 mg/kg IV/IM Pediatric dose: • Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO × 1 (max 10 mg) Benefits: • Reduces pain and trismus • Decreases edema • Shortens hospital stay • Speeds recovery Timing: Give at or before drainage for maximum benefit Safety: Single dose is safe — no increased infecti

nodes.title: Pain Management
nodes.summary: Alternate acetaminophen/ibuprofen q3h, viscous lidocaine for throat — opioids limited 3-5 days if severe
nodes.body: Adequate analgesia improves oral intake: [1] Oral options: • Acetaminophen 650-1000 mg Q6h • Ibuprofen 400-600 mg Q6h • Combination: Alternate acetaminophen/ibuprofen Q3h Topical: • Benzocaine spray Q2-3h PRN for throat comfort • Viscous lidocaine 2% swish and spit Opioids (for severe pain): • Hydrocodone/acetaminophen 5/325 mg Q4-6h PRN • Limited course (3-5 days) Other comfort measures: • Ice ch

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Discharge if tolerates PO, pain controlled, minimal bleeding; admit if airway concern or septic
nodes.body: Assess for safe discharge: [1][2][10] Discharge criteria: • Post-drainage observation 30-45 min without complication • Patient tolerates oral fluids • Pain controlled • Minimal bleeding • Reliable follow-up • Able to take oral antibiotics Admission criteria: • Unable to tolerate oral intake/medications • Severe dehydration • Airway compromise (stridor, drooling) • Deep neck space infection concern

nodes.title: PTA — Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge planning: [1][2][10] Prescriptions: • Antibiotics × 10-14 days (see antibiotic section) • Dexamethasone 10 mg PO × 1 if not given IV • Analgesics PRN Follow-up: • ENT or PCP within 24-36 hours — MANDATORY • Check for reaccumulation, assess healing • Earlier if symptoms worsen Return precautions: • Difficulty breathing or swallowing • Worsening pain or swelling • Fever >24h after drainage
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with antibiotics 10-14 days. ENT follow-up within 24-36 hours mandatory.

nodes.title: PTA — Admission
nodes.body: Admission orders: [1][2] Nursing: • NPO if surgical intervention anticipated • IV fluids (NS or LR) • Head of bed elevated 30° • Strict I&Os Medications: • IV antibiotics: Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g Q6h OR Clindamycin 600-900 mg Q6-8h • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV × 1 if not given • IV analgesics PRN • IV fluids for hydration Consultations: • ENT (all admissions) • Anesthesia consult if airway concern Mo
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics, hydration, ENT consultation. Monitor airway closely.

nodes.title: Complications & Prevention
nodes.summary: Carotid injury (most feared) — depth limit prevents it; recurrence 2-15%, tonsillectomy if >1 episode/12mo
nodes.body: Procedure complications: [1][6][11] Carotid artery injury (most feared) • Prevention: Depth limit 8-10mm, Color Doppler, medial needle direction • If hemorrhage: Direct pressure ± topical epi • Uncontrolled: ENT/vascular surgery emergently Post-aspiration hemorrhage • Usually minor, self-limited • Ice water gargles, direct pressure • Delayed hemorrhage (>24h) → rule out pseudoaneurysm Aspiration •

nodes.title: PTSD Screening — ED Approach
nodes.summary: DSM-5-TR Criterion A: direct/witness/learn-of/repeated exposure; time-window drives pathway: <3d ASR, 3d-1mo ASD, >1mo PTSD
nodes.body: Universal screening at trauma centers is now ACS best-practice standard (Zatzick stepped care). [1][2] DSM-5-TR Criterion A — qualifying trauma: • A1: Directly experiencing the event • A2: Witnessing in person, the event happening to others • A3: Learning event happened to a close family/friend (must be violent/accidental) • A4: Repeated/extreme exposure to aversive details (first responders, ED s

nodes.title: Triage by Presentation
nodes.summary: Triage: recent <1mo→ASD pathway; >1mo+sx→PCL-5; SA<120h→SANE; IPV→private screen; high-risk→PC-PTSD-5
nodes.body: Select the chief presentation. Each pathway carries specific time-sensitive actions.

nodes.title: Time Since Trauma
nodes.summary: Time gates Dx: 0-3d=ASR (no Dx), 3d-1mo=ASD (≥9/14 sx), >1mo=PTSD; ASD misses majority of eventual PTSD
nodes.body: Time window determines diagnosis pathway — never diagnose PTSD before 1 month. [3][5] 0-3 days: Acute Stress Reaction (ASR) — ICD term, NOT a DSM-5-TR diagnosis. PFA + reassurance only. 3 days - 1 month: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD). Requires ≥9 of 14 symptoms across 5 categories (intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, arousal). Total symptom count, NOT cluster-by-cluster. >1 month: PTS

nodes.title: PC-PTSD-5 Screen (5-item)
nodes.summary: PC-PTSD-5: 5 items, JCAHO/VA endorsed; cutoff ≥3 sens, ≥4 balanced; stem question gates symptom items
nodes.body: JCAHO/Joint Commission and VA/DoD endorsed primary screen. [7] Performance characteristics (Prins 2016): • AUC > 0.92, kappa ≥ 0.75 • Cutoff ≥3 = optimally sensitive (94.8%) — best for ED screening • Cutoff ≥4 = optimally balanced (men/overall sample) • Women may need cutoff ≥3 to avoid false negatives Stem question first: Has the patient ever experienced a Criterion A trauma? If NO — do not score

nodes.title: PC-PTSD-5 Result
nodes.summary: PC-PTSD-5: ≥3 → PCL-5; 0-2 → document, education, follow-up if sx emerge
nodes.body: Use the PC-PTSD-5 calculator and select the result band.

nodes.title: PCL-5 Full DSM-5-TR Screen
nodes.summary: PCL-5: 20 items, DSM-5-TR aligned; cutoff 31-33; cluster rule needs B≥1, C≥1, D≥2, E≥2 (items rated ≥2)
nodes.body: 20-item self-report, fully aligned with DSM-5-TR. [8] Scoring: Each item 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Extremely); total range 0-80. Probable PTSD cutoff: 31-33 (Bovin 2016, National Center for PTSD). Population-specific variation 23-49 across studies. [9] Two scoring methods: • Total severity ≥31-33 → probable PTSD (most reliable single metric) • DSM-5-TR cluster rule: items rated ≥2 ("Moderately") count

nodes.title: PCL-5 Result
nodes.summary: PCL-5: ≥33 probable PTSD; 23-32 subthreshold; <23 below; ALL pathways → C-SSRS suicide screen
nodes.body: Use the PCL-5 calculator and select the result band.

nodes.title: Acute Stress Disorder Screen (DSM-5-TR)
nodes.summary: ASD (DSM-5-TR): ≥9/14 sx across 5 categories + impairment; ASR (ICD, 0-3d) is NOT a DSM Dx
nodes.body: ASD (3 days - 1 month post-trauma): Requires ≥9 of 14 symptoms across 5 categories. [3] Categories (any combination, total ≥9): • Intrusion (5): recurrent memories, dreams, dissociative reactions/flashbacks, distress at cues, physiological reactivity • Negative mood (1): persistent inability to experience positive emotions • Dissociative (2): altered sense of reality, inability to remember key tra

nodes.title: C-SSRS Suicide Screen — MANDATORY
nodes.summary: C-SSRS mandatory for every PTSD pt; severity 4-5 OR recent behavior = HIGH risk = psych consult
nodes.body: Every PTSD/ASD patient gets a suicide screen. [10][11] Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (Screen Version): FDA-recommended, validated in ED including PTSD/veteran populations. • Severity 1-3 (ideation without method/intent/plan) = low/moderate risk • Severity 4-5 (active method/intent/plan) = HIGH risk → psychiatric admission consideration • Any "yes" to behavior section in past 3 months = HI

nodes.title: Acute Stress Reaction (0-3 days)
nodes.summary: ASR (0-3d): PFA + reassurance + 2-4wk FU; AVOID benzos + CISD; pediatric → caregiver anticipatory guidance
nodes.body: Normal acute response — NOT a DSM-5-TR diagnosis. [3][12] Management: • Psychological First Aid (PFA) — 5 elements (see PFA protocol) • Reassurance: stress reactions in first month are EXPECTED (sleep disturbance, intrusions, avoidance, irritability) • Written discharge materials (PTSD Coach app: free, NCPTSD) • Avoid pharmacotherapy unless medical stabilization required • Specifically AVOID: benz
nodes.recommendation: ASR management: PFA + reassurance + written materials + 2-4 week follow-up; AVOID benzos + CISD; anticipatory guidance for caregivers.

nodes.title: Acute Stress Disorder Management
nodes.summary: ASD: PFA + early TF-CBT referral + hydroxyzine/trazodone for sleep + C-SSRS + warm handoff 1-2wk
nodes.body: ASD (3d-1mo, ≥9/14 symptoms + impairment). [3][12] Management: • Psychological First Aid — see PFA protocol • Trauma-focused CBT referral — early TF-CBT can reduce PTSD progression • Sleep support if needed (non-benzo): hydroxyzine 25-100 mg qhs OR trazodone 25-100 mg qhs (counsel re priapism) • C-SSRS suicide screen (mandatory) • Safety plan if any IPV/SI/unsafe living • Warm-handoff referral to
nodes.recommendation: ASD: PFA + early TF-CBT referral + non-benzo sleep support + C-SSRS + safety plan + warm-handoff in 1-2wk.

nodes.title: Psychological First Aid (PFA) — ED Protocol
nodes.summary: PFA 5 elements: listen, info, practical, connect, refer; AVOID CISD (Cochrane OR 2.51); Stepped Care = ACS std
nodes.body: WHO/IASC/NICE-recommended early intervention. [12][13][14] Hobfoll 5 elements: safety, calming, self/community efficacy, connectedness, hope. ED PFA in 5 minutes (5 actions): 1. Listen and validate — NO forced disclosure of trauma details 2. Provide accurate information — about the event and normal stress reactions 3. Practical assistance — transportation, food, contacts, shelter 4. Connect to soc

nodes.title: Trauma-Focused CBT — Gold Standard Referral
nodes.summary: TF-CBT first-line: CPT, PE, EMDR (VA/DoD 2023); warm handoff > paper referral; PTSD Coach app + 988
nodes.body: 2023 VA/DoD CPG (published Annals 2024): Three trauma-focused psychotherapies are first-line OVERALL for PTSD (preferred over pharmacotherapy). [17] 1. Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) — addresses stuck points and trauma-related cognitions 2. Prolonged Exposure (PE) — graded exposure to trauma memories and avoided situations 3. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) — bilateral sti

nodes.title: Pharmacology Decision
nodes.summary: Pharm decision: SSRI for chronic, prazosin for nightmares, non-benzo for sleep; AVOID benzos/CISD
nodes.body: Most ED clinicians do NOT initiate chronic PTSD pharmacotherapy — defer to psychiatry/PCP follow-up. However, ED-relevant scenarios do exist.

nodes.title: First-Line PTSD Pharmacotherapy
nodes.summary: First-line: sertraline 25→50-200, paroxetine 10→20-50, venlafaxine XR 37.5→75-300; fluoxetine removed 2023 CPG
nodes.body: 2023 VA/DoD CPG Recommendation 15 — three agents recommended: [17] Sertraline (Zoloft) — FDA-approved for PTSD • Start: 25 mg PO daily × 1 week • Target: 50-200 mg/day Paroxetine (Paxil) — FDA-approved for PTSD • Start: 10 mg PO daily • Target: 20-50 mg/day Venlafaxine XR (Effexor) — off-label, recommended • Start: 37.5 mg PO daily • Target: 75-300 mg/day Notable change: Fluoxetine was REMOVED fro
nodes.recommendation: First-line: sertraline 25mg→50-200mg, paroxetine 10mg→20-50mg, OR venlafaxine XR 37.5mg→75-300mg. Counsel onset 4-6wk, transient activation. Coordinate with outpatient.

nodes.title: Prazosin for PTSD Nightmares
nodes.summary: Prazosin nightmares: 1mg qhs → titrate weekly; Raskind max total 20mg men, 12mg women; VA/DoD weak FOR nightmares, AGAINST overall PTSD
nodes.body: Indication: trauma-related nightmares + sleep disruption. [18][19] Evidence picture: • PACT trial (Raskind NEJM 2018): negative in 26-week, 12-VA-site RCT in clinically stable veterans (likely underpowered, over-selected) • 2025 meta-analysis (Mendes, 10 RCTs, n=648): improves insomnia (SMD -0.654) and nightmares (SMD -0.641); does NOT improve overall PTSD symptoms • 2023 VA/DoD CPG: weak FOR praz
nodes.recommendation: Prazosin nightmares: start 1mg qhs × 2d → 2mg qhs × 5d → titrate weekly. Max total daily 20mg men, 12mg women (Raskind); practical bedtime caps 15mg men, 10mg women. Counsel orthostasis.

nodes.title: Non-Benzo Sleep Bridges
nodes.summary: Sleep bridges: hydroxyzine 25-100, trazodone 25-150 (priapism warn), mirtazapine 7.5-30; AVOID Z-drugs + benzos
nodes.body: Off-label, reasonable bridge therapy when sleep is dominant complaint. [20] Hydroxyzine 25-100 mg qhs • First-line PTSD sleep-onset agent (Harvard South Shore algorithm) • Non-habit-forming • Anticholinergic — caution in elderly Trazodone 25-200 mg qhs (most patients 50-150 mg) • PTSD-specific data: 72% reduction in nightmares, 92% sleep onset improvement (Palo Alto VA survey) • WARN: 12% priapism
nodes.recommendation: Non-benzo sleep: hydroxyzine 25-100mg qhs OR trazodone 25-150mg qhs (warn priapism) OR mirtazapine 7.5-30mg qhs. AVOID Z-drugs + benzos.

nodes.title: What to AVOID — Critical Safety Teaching
nodes.summary: AVOID: benzos (worsen PTSD), propranolol prophylaxis, CISD; MDMA-AT FDA rejected 8/2024; cannabis insufficient
nodes.body: STRONG: AVOID Benzodiazepines [21][22] Guina 2015 meta-analysis (18 trials, 5236 participants) + 2023 VA/DoD CPG: • BZDs are ineffective for PTSD treatment AND prevention • Associated with WORSE overall PTSD severity, INCREASED risk of developing PTSD when given after trauma, worse psychotherapy outcomes, aggression, depression, substance use • Mechanism: interfere with extinction learning, reduce
nodes.recommendation: NEVER: benzos for trauma/PTSD (Guina 2015), routine propranolol prophylaxis, CISD/single-session debriefing (Cochrane OR 2.51).

nodes.title: Sexual Assault — Acute (<120h)
nodes.summary: SA acute: SANE + kit (≤120h) + HIV PEP + EC + STI ppx + hep B + tetanus + RAINN warm handoff + C-SSRS
nodes.body: Time-sensitive multi-track response. [23][24] Forensic & medical: • SANE (Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner) — activate immediately • Forensic kit consent + chain of custody (kit valid up to 120h, ideally <72h) • Gentle but thorough exam; minimize re-traumatization • Photo documentation per institution protocol Pharmacology: • HIV PEP within 72h: tenofovir-emtricitabine + raltegravir (or per local pro
nodes.recommendation: SA <120h: SANE + forensic kit + HIV PEP + EC + STI ppx + hep B + RAINN 1-800-656-HOPE warm handoff + C-SSRS + 1-2wk FU.

nodes.title: IPV / Domestic Violence
nodes.summary: IPV: PRIVATE screen, HARK/HITS, NDV 1-800-799-SAFE, lethality assess, shelter if high, never share plan w/partner
nodes.body: USPSTF 2024 recommends screening reproductive-age women for IPV and providing intervention services. [25] CRITICAL: Screen in PRIVATE. Separate the patient from accompanying partner BEFORE any IPV question is asked. Use a clinical reason ("I need to do a confidential exam") if needed. Validated tools: • HARK (4 items): Humiliation, Afraid, Rape, Kick • HITS (4 items): Hurt, Insulted, Threatened, S
nodes.recommendation: IPV: PRIVATE screen with HARK/HITS, document, NDV 1-800-799-SAFE warm handoff, safety plan (NEVER shared with partner), shelter if high lethality, C-SSRS.

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Disposition: high SI/severe ASD→admit; moderate+support→OP warm handoff; crisis svc; IPV→shelter coord
nodes.body: Combine PCL-5/PC-PTSD-5/ASD result + C-SSRS + social context to choose disposition.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Admission Pathway
nodes.summary: Psych admit: C-SSRS 4-5, recent behavior, severe ASD; voluntary > involuntary; TX = APOWW/OPC/MHW; 1:1 obs + means restriction
nodes.body: Indications for emergent psychiatric consult/admission: [26] • C-SSRS severity 4-5 (active method/intent/plan) • Recent suicidal behavior (any "yes" to behavior section past 3 months) • Homicidal ideation with means • Acute psychosis or severe dissociation impairing safety • Inability to maintain safety post-discharge (e.g., severe IPV with no safe place) • Severe ASD with functional collapse Volu
nodes.recommendation: Psych admit: 1:1 obs + lethal means restriction + voluntary preferred; involuntary if danger to self/others or grave disability. TX: APOWW/OPC/MHW. Document.

nodes.title: Outpatient Disposition with Warm Handoff
nodes.summary: OP disposition: low C-SSRS + safe + appt ≤2wk; warm handoff std; 988 + PTSD Coach + RAINN/NDV/Vet hotlines
nodes.body: Most ED PTSD/ASD presentations are appropriate for outpatient referral if criteria met. [17][27] Discharge criteria (ALL must be met): • C-SSRS low risk (severity 1-3, no recent behavior) • Adequate social support • Safe living environment (no active IPV without shelter plan) • No active substance intoxication impairing decision-making • Patient willing/able to engage in outpatient care • Appointm
nodes.recommendation: OP discharge if: C-SSRS low + safe + supported + appt scheduled. Warm handoff > paper. Provide 988 + PTSD Coach + population-specific hotlines. Document fully.

nodes.title: Crisis Services / Mobile Crisis
nodes.summary: Crisis svc: warm 988 transfer, mobile crisis, CSU, 24-48h FU; appropriate for moderate SI w/ engagement
nodes.body: Indications: • Moderate distress with insufficient outpatient access • Active SI without plan/intent who can engage with crisis support • IPV survivors needing immediate shelter coordination • Patient prefers crisis services over admission and risk allows Resources: • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline — connects to local mobile crisis where available • Local mobile crisis team (varies by community) •
nodes.recommendation: Crisis svc: warm 988 transfer + mobile crisis dispatch + CSU if available + 24-48h FU + lethal means counseling.

nodes.title: IPV Shelter Coordination
nodes.summary: IPV shelter: NDV 1-800-799-SAFE, Campbell DA, SW, safety plan never shared, peds CPS, AVOID benzos
nodes.body: Active IPV + no safe place to go = shelter coordination before discharge. [25] Steps: • Confirm patient consent and willingness • Lethality assessment (Campbell DA): firearm in home, choking history, threats with weapon, escalation • Call NDV Hotline 1-800-799-SAFE — they coordinate local shelter availability • Social work consult for transportation, paperwork, child custody concerns • Document co
nodes.recommendation: IPV shelter coord: consent + Campbell DA lethality + NDV 1-800-799-SAFE + SW + safety plan (NOT shared) + peds CPS if applicable. AVOID benzos. 24-72h advocate FU.

nodes.title: Push-Dose Pressors - Indications
nodes.summary: Push-dose pressors bridge immediate hemodynamic support — epinephrine preferred over phenylephrine, NEVER give 1mg arrest dose to patient with pulse
nodes.body: Push-Dose Pressors Summary Definition: Vasopressors administered as IV bolus doses for immediate blood pressure support, bridging to continuous infusion. Key principle: Push-dose pressors provide immediate hemodynamic support when continuous infusions cannot be established within 5-8 minutes. [1][2] Epinephrine has won: Dr. Weingart now recommends push-dose epinephrine over phenylephrine for most

nodes.title: Peri-Intubation Hypotension
nodes.summary: Peri-intubation hypotension in ~40% of critically ill — optimize preload, have push-dose pressor drawn up before induction, epinephrine preferred
nodes.body: Hypotension affects ~40% of critically ill patients undergoing emergency intubation and is independently associated with increased mortality. [4][7] Mechanism: Multifactorial - loss of sympathetic drive, induction agent vasodilation, apnea worsening acidosis, reduced venous return after positive pressure ventilation. [4][7] Prevention strategy: [7] 1. Optimize preload with IV fluids BEFORE inducti

nodes.title: Septic Shock - Bridge to Infusion
nodes.summary: Bridge to infusion while awaiting pharmacy drip — peripheral NE safe <6h per SSC 2021, diastolic <40 suggests severe vasoplegia
nodes.body: The problem: Pharmacy-mixed vasopressor drips take 10-15 minutes minimum. Untreated hypotension kills. [1][2] Bridge indication: Push-dose pressors bridge the gap while waiting for continuous infusion or central line placement. [2][3] Key points: - Start peripheral vasopressors immediately (SSC 2021: peripheral NE is safe for <6 hours) [9] - Push-dose pressors provide temporary support, NOT defini

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis - Refractory to IM Epinephrine
nodes.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis: IV epi 10-20mcg/min NOT cardiac arrest dose — 61-fold dosing error giving 1mg to patient with pulse
nodes.body: Refractory anaphylaxis: Persistent symptoms despite 2-3 doses of IM epinephrine. Occurs in <1% of cases. [5][10] CRITICAL: Do NOT give cardiac arrest dose (1 mg IV) to patient with a pulse. This is a 61-fold dosing error compared to IM dosing. [5] IV Epinephrine Protocol (PulmCrit approach): [5][10] 1. Mix 1 mg epinephrine in 100 mL NS = 10 mcg/mL 2. Loading: 20 mcg/min x 2 minutes (~40 mcg total)

nodes.title: Bradycardia with Hypotension
nodes.summary: Push-dose epi for symptomatic bradycardia — beta-1 provides chronotropy + inotropy, phenylephrine is NOT appropriate (worsens bradycardia)
nodes.body: Push-dose epinephrine for symptomatic bradycardia provides immediate chronotropic and inotropic support. [1][2] Indications: - Symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension - Bradycardia not responsive to atropine - Bridge to transcutaneous or transvenous pacing - Beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity Why epinephrine? Beta-1 agonism provides chronotropy (increased heart rate) AND inotropy (i

nodes.title: Procedural Hypotension
nodes.summary: Procedural hypotension often manageable with single push-dose — pre-hydrate, have pressor drawn up, use hemodynamically stable induction agent
nodes.body: Common scenarios: - Post-propofol hypotension (propofol causes vasodilation + negative inotropy) - Post-cardioversion transient hypotension - Sedation for procedures in hemodynamically fragile patients Key principle: Anticipated transient hypotension can often be managed with a single push-dose, avoiding the need for continuous infusion. [2][3] Agent selection: - Epinephrine: Preferred for most si

nodes.title: Agent Selection
nodes.summary: Epi preferred (inopressor for most), phenylephrine for tachycardia + pure vasodilation, NE emerging but primarily anesthesia
nodes.body: Choose the appropriate agent based on clinical scenario: Epinephrine (PREFERRED for most situations): [1][6] - Combined alpha + beta agonist (inopressor) - Increases cardiac output AND vasoconstriction - Works in all circumstances - Safer to mix than phenylephrine (cardiac amp is 1:10,000) Phenylephrine: [1][3] - Pure alpha-1 agonist (pure vasoconstrictor) - NO cardiac output increase (may decreas

nodes.title: Push-Dose Epinephrine - Preparation
nodes.summary: 1mL cardiac epi (1:10,000) + 9mL NS = 10mcg/mL — same concentration as lido with epi, safe peripherally, LABEL syringe clearly
nodes.body: EXACT DILUTION (EMCrit Method): [1][2] Step 1: Take a 10 mL syringe filled with 9 mL of normal saline Step 2: Draw up 1 mL from the cardiac epinephrine amp (NOT the anaphylaxis amp) - Cardiac amp = 1:10,000 = 100 mcg/mL (0.1 mg/mL) - Contains 10 mL at 100 mcg/mL Step 3: Mix well (shake syringe) Result: 10 mL of epinephrine at 10 mcg/mL (1:100,000) Memory aid: This is the same concentration as lido

nodes.title: Push-Dose Epinephrine - Dosing
nodes.summary: 5-20mcg (0.5-2mL) IV push q1-5min, onset <1min, duration 5-10min — bridge to continuous infusion, reassess MAP after each push
nodes.body: Dosing (from 10 mcg/mL syringe): [1][2][3] Standard dose: 0.5-2 mL (5-20 mcg) IV push every 1-5 minutes Typical starting dose: 10-20 mcg (1-2 mL) Pharmacokinetics: - Onset: <1 minute - Duration: 5-10 minutes (usually effects gone within 5 min) - Redose as needed every 2-5 minutes Titration: - Start with 10 mcg if not in extremis - May increase to 20 mcg per push if inadequate response - Can give e

nodes.title: Push-Dose Epinephrine - Safety
nodes.summary: Full cardiac amp (1mg=1000mcg) to patient with pulse causes malignant HTN, VT/VF, ICH, death — ALWAYS dilute, ALWAYS label
nodes.body: CRITICAL SAFETY - The 1 mg Error: [1][2][5] Giving a full cardiac amp (1 mg = 1000 mcg) to a patient with a pulse can cause: - Malignant hypertension - Tachyarrhythmias (VT, VF) - Myocardial ischemia - Intracranial hemorrhage - Death Prevention: 1. ALWAYS dilute the cardiac amp 2. ALWAYS label the syringe clearly 3. ALWAYS double-check concentration before each dose 4. Use pre-mixed syringes when

nodes.title: Push-Dose Epinephrine - Efficacy
nodes.summary: 71.8% achieve >25% SBP increase — CHF patients respond better (inotropic effect), advantages over phenylephrine: alpha + beta effects
nodes.body: Evidence for push-dose epinephrine: [3][6][11] Response rates: - 71.8% of patients achieved >25% SBP increase with push-dose epinephrine [11] - Mean SBP increase 41.3%, DBP 44.3%, MAP 35.1% in peri-intubation case series [4] Predictors of response: [11] - History of CHF associated with better response (OR 11.889) - Likely due to inotropic effects beneficial in low-output states Advantages over phe

nodes.title: Push-Dose Phenylephrine - Preparation
nodes.summary: 1mL phenylephrine (10mg/mL) in 100mL NS = 100mcg/mL — higher error potential than epi, use pre-mixed syringes when available
nodes.body: EXACT DILUTION (EMCrit Method): [1][2] Step 1: Draw up 1 mL of phenylephrine from the vial - Vial concentration: 10 mg/mL - This equals 10 mg (10,000 mcg) Step 2: Inject into a 100 mL bag of normal saline Step 3: Mix well by inverting bag several times Result: 100 mL of phenylephrine at 100 mcg/mL Step 4: Draw up into syringe for administration - Each 1 mL = 100 mcg CAUTION: Phenylephrine mixing r

nodes.title: Push-Dose Phenylephrine - Dosing
nodes.summary: 50-200mcg (0.5-2mL) IV push q3-5min — pure alpha agonist, no inotropy, may cause reflex bradycardia, 55.9% response rate
nodes.body: Dosing (from 100 mcg/mL syringe): [1][2][3] Standard dose: 0.5-2 mL (50-200 mcg) IV push every 3-5 minutes Typical starting dose: 100-200 mcg (1-2 mL) Pharmacokinetics: - Onset: <1 minute - Duration: 5-20 minutes (usually effects gone within 5 min) - Longer duration than epinephrine in some cases Titration: - Start with 100 mcg - May increase to 200 mcg if inadequate response - Redose every 3-5 mi

nodes.title: Push-Dose Phenylephrine - Safety
nodes.summary: Avoid phenylephrine in bradycardia, low CO, or impaired contractility — case report of 1000x overdose (50mg vs 50mcg), use pre-mixed
nodes.body: Peripheral IV safety: [1][2] Phenylephrine is approved for IM and subcutaneous use, so extravasation from a peripheral IV is NOT a major concern. Potential adverse effects: - Reflex bradycardia - pure alpha agonism triggers baroreceptor-mediated parasympathetic response - Decreased cardiac output - increased afterload without inotropy can reduce stroke volume - Hypertension - overcorrection possib

nodes.title: Push-Dose Phenylephrine - Best Indications
nodes.summary: Best for: tachyarrhythmia with hypotension, pure vasodilation with preserved CO, patient on beta-blockers — Weingart now prefers epi for almost all
nodes.body: Best indications for phenylephrine over epinephrine: [1][3] 1. Hypotension with tachyarrhythmia: - Rapid atrial fibrillation with hypotension - SVT with hypotension - Sinus tachycardia >130 where additional chronotropy is undesirable 2. Pure vasodilatory state with preserved cardiac function: - Post-spinal anesthesia hypotension - Drug-induced vasodilation (propofol, sedatives) - Distributive shoc

nodes.title: Push-Dose Norepinephrine - Overview
nodes.summary: Push-dose NE emerging but less common — less bradycardia than phenylephrine, maintains CO better, peripheral NE safe <6h per SSC 2021
nodes.body: Push-dose norepinephrine is LESS COMMON than push-dose epinephrine or phenylephrine, but emerging evidence supports its safety and efficacy. [8][12] Why less common? - Norepinephrine is primarily alpha-1 (like phenylephrine) with some beta-1 - Epinephrine provides more robust beta effects - Mixing is similar complexity to phenylephrine - Historical concerns about extravasation (though peripheral u

nodes.title: Push-Dose Norepinephrine - Preparation & Dosing
nodes.summary: 4-8mcg IV push q1-2min, use diluted concentration (10-16mcg/mL) — primarily anesthesia settings, epi simpler for most ED scenarios
nodes.body: Preparation (if using push-dose NE): Norepinephrine stock: typically 4 mg/4 mL (1 mg/mL) or 4 mg/250 mL (16 mcg/mL premix) For push-dose use: 1. Use a pre-diluted concentration of 16 mcg/mL or similar 2. Alternatively: Draw 1 mL of 1 mg/mL NE + 99 mL NS = 10 mcg/mL Dosing: - Typical push-dose: 4-8 mcg IV push - Cesarean section studies used 4-8 mcg boluses [8][12] - May repeat every 1-2 minutes as

nodes.title: Peripheral Norepinephrine - Safety Evidence
nodes.summary: Peripheral NE safe up to 48h per 2024-25 data — 51.6% never needed central line, use large-bore proximal IV, have phentolamine ready
nodes.body: 2024-2025 Evidence supports peripheral norepinephrine: [8][9][12] Cleveland Clinic Prospective Study (CHEST 2024): - Implementing peripheral NE protocol avoided 1 CVC day per patient - 51.6% of patients never required central line insertion - Safe, feasible, and associated with decreased CVC utilization 2025 Follow-up data: - Multiple cohorts now support peripheral NE for 24-48 hours (mean time to

nodes.title: Troubleshooting - Poor Response
nodes.summary: Systematic troubleshooting: hypovolemia (empty tank), wrong agent (phenyl failing = try epi), acidosis, obstructive causes
nodes.body: If push-dose pressors are not achieving adequate MAP: Reassess the situation systematically. Common issues: 1. Hypovolemia - pressors work poorly in empty tank 2. Inadequate dose - may need more frequent or larger doses 3. Wrong agent - switch from phenyl to epi if cardiac output low 4. Ongoing hemorrhage - source control + transfusion 5. Acidosis - severe acidosis impairs pressor response 6. Tens

nodes.title: Hypovolemia - Volume First
nodes.summary: Pressors work poorly in empty tank — POCUS IVC, give 500-1000mL crystalloid, >30mL/kg initial sepsis resuscitation then restrict
nodes.body: Pressors work poorly in an empty tank. [9] POCUS assessment: - IVC collapse on inspiration suggests volume responsiveness - Hyperdynamic, empty-appearing LV - Passive leg raise increases stroke volume Volume resuscitation: - Crystalloid: 500-1000 mL bolus, reassess - Blood products if hemorrhagic shock - LR preferred for large-volume resuscitation Evidence from PRESSURE study: [4] Patients who rec

nodes.title: Switch Agents - Phenylephrine to Epinephrine
nodes.summary: Phenylephrine failing: likely low CO — epi has 71.8% vs 55.9% response rate, consider vasopressin or methylene blue if refractory
nodes.body: When phenylephrine fails, consider switching to epinephrine. [1][11] Reasons phenylephrine may fail: 1. Low cardiac output - phenylephrine increases afterload without inotropy, can worsen CO 2. Bradycardia - phenylephrine may cause reflex bradycardia 3. Septic cardiomyopathy - needs inotropic support 4. Beta-blocker toxicity - may benefit from combined approach Epinephrine advantages: [1][6] - Pro

nodes.title: Refractory Shock
nodes.summary: Refractory shock: escalation ladder — maximize pressor, add vasopressin, stress-dose hydrocortisone, methylene blue, consider VA-ECMO
nodes.body: If shock persists despite adequate push-dose pressors + fluids: [9] Reassess diagnosis: - Is this truly distributive shock? - Rule out obstructive causes (PE, tamponade, tension PTX) - Consider cardiogenic component - Sepsis mimics (adrenal crisis, thyroid storm) Escalation ladder: 1. Maximize push-dose pressor (more frequent dosing) 2. Start continuous norepinephrine infusion (can be peripheral)

nodes.title: Transition to Continuous Infusion
nodes.summary: Push-dose is 5-15min bridge — prepare continuous infusion simultaneously, start low rate, wait 5-10min, wean push-dose as infusion takes effect
nodes.body: Bridge to infusion - the goal of push-dose pressors. [1][2] Timing: - Push-dose is temporary (5-15 minutes max duration as primary therapy) - Continuous infusion should be prepared SIMULTANEOUSLY with push-dose administration - Once infusion available, transition promptly Norepinephrine infusion (first-line for most shock): [9] - Start 0.05 mcg/kg/min (4-6 mcg/min) - Titrate by 0.02-0.05 mcg/kg/mi

nodes.title: Push-Dose Pressors - Summary
nodes.body: Key takeaways: Agent Selection: - Epinephrine - preferred for most situations (inopressor) - Phenylephrine - reserved for tachycardia with pure vasodilation - Norepinephrine - emerging push-dose use, primarily anesthesia settings Preparation: - Epi: 1 mL cardiac amp + 9 mL NS = 10 mcg/mL - Phenyl: 1 mL (10 mg) + 100 mL NS = 100 mcg/mL - LABEL SYRINGES CLEARLY Dosing: - Epi: 5-20 mcg IV push q1-5 m
nodes.recommendation: Push-dose pressors bridge the critical gap while continuous infusions are prepared. Epinephrine is preferred for most situations. ALWAYS dilute properly and label syringes. Transition to continuous infusion as soon as practical.

nodes.title: Rabies — Clinical Concern or Exposure?
nodes.summary: Rabies is 100% fatal once symptomatic — PEP is highly effective if given promptly, no confirmed PEP failures when administered correctly
nodes.body: Rabies Steps Summary — quick-reference for both clinical rabies workup and post-exposure prophylaxis. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptomatic. Post-exposure prophylaxis is highly effective if given promptly — no confirmed PEP failures when administered correctly. Select your clinical scenario below.

nodes.title: Clinical Scenario
nodes.summary: Two clinical scenarios: suspected active rabies infection (neuropsychiatric symptoms) vs animal exposure requiring PEP evaluation
nodes.body: Is this a patient with suspected rabies infection (neuropsychiatric symptoms + possible exposure history) or a patient with a recent animal exposure requiring PEP evaluation?

nodes.title: Suspected Clinical Rabies
nodes.summary: Frequently missed initially — pain/paresthesia at prior bite site is relatively specific, incubation weeks to months, nationally notifiable
nodes.body: Rabies is frequently missed at initial presentation. The diagnosis requires high clinical suspicion. Key clues: • Acute neuropsychiatric illness + travel to rabies-endemic area • Pain, paresthesia, or pruritus at a prior bite site — relatively specific for rabies • History of animal exposure weeks to months prior (incubation typically several weeks to months) • Patients may not recall or report an

nodes.title: Clinical Form
nodes.summary: Two clinical forms: furious (80%) with hydrophobia/aerophobia/agitation, or paralytic (20%) mimicking GBS with preserved consciousness
nodes.body: Approximately 80% develop furious (encephalitic) rabies and 20% develop paralytic rabies. These forms are clinically distinct. Bat rabies variants can present atypically.

nodes.title: Furious (Encephalitic) Rabies
nodes.summary: Furious: hydrophobia + aerophobia + fluctuating consciousness + hypersalivation — survival 5-6 days, distinguishes from HSV/tetanus/anti-NMDAR
nodes.body: Characteristic features: • Hydrophobia — pharyngeal/laryngeal spasms triggered by attempts to swallow water or even the sight/sound of water • Aerophobia — similar spasms triggered by air blown on the face • Fluctuating consciousness with periods of agitation alternating with lucidity • Inspiratory spasms involving contraction of inspiratory muscles • Hypersalivation with difficulty swallowing • A

nodes.title: Paralytic (Dumb) Rabies
nodes.summary: Paralytic: ascending flaccid paralysis mimicking GBS but with preserved consciousness — pain at bite site, fever, survival ~11 days
nodes.body: Characteristic features: • Ascending flaccid paralysis beginning in the bitten extremity — closely mimics Guillain-Barré syndrome • Preserved consciousness until preterminal phase (key distinguishing feature from GBS) • Lower motor neuron weakness without hyperexcitability of furious rabies • Progression to coma, myoedema, bladder incontinence Average survival: ~11 days (longer than furious form).

nodes.title: Atypical Rabies Presentations
nodes.summary: Bat rabies variants present atypically — focal brainstem signs, myoclonus, hemichorea, always consider rabies in unexplained acute encephalitis
nodes.body: Bat rabies variants can present with atypical features: • Focal brainstem signs • Myoclonus • Hemichorea • Horner's syndrome Rare presentations mimicking: • Transverse myelitis • Neuromyelitis optica • Tetanus with locked jaw Diagnostic challenge: These presentations may not trigger clinical suspicion for rabies. Always consider rabies in the differential of acute, unexplained neuropsychiatric ill

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: No single test sufficient — collect saliva (RT-PCR), nuchal biopsy (DFA), CSF and serum antibodies, contact CDC/public health lab immediately
nodes.body: Immediately consult local public health laboratory or CDC — rabies diagnostic testing is not available at most hospital or reference laboratories. Diagnostic Specimens & Interpretation — complete 4-specimen protocol with sensitivities and timing. No single test is sufficient for antemortem diagnosis. Four specimen types should be collected: 1. Saliva — RT-PCR for viral RNA (≥3 serial samples for >

nodes.title: Management of Clinical Rabies
nodes.summary: Once symptomatic, no effective therapy exists — nearly uniformly fatal, palliative care vs aggressive ICU approach decision
nodes.body: Once clinical symptoms develop, no effective therapy exists and rabies is nearly uniformly fatal. Of ~10 documented rabies survivors, most had received partial PEP before symptom onset, and nearly all had permanent neurological deficits.

nodes.title: Palliative Care Approach
nodes.body: Recommended for most patients with clinical rabies. • Liberal use of sedatives and analgesics for comfort • Symptom management: antispasmodics for pharyngeal spasms, anxiolytics for agitation • Family counseling regarding prognosis • Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures Infection control: • Standard + contact precautions throughout • Careful handling of all secretions (saliva, respiratory, CSF) •
nodes.recommendation: Palliative care with liberal sedation/analgesia. Standard + contact precautions. Report to public health. Counsel family on prognosis.

nodes.title: Aggressive / ICU Approach
nodes.body: The Milwaukee Protocol has failed in at least 26 subsequent cases and is now considered ineffective. The original protocol included therapeutic coma with burst suppression, but this is no longer recommended. Modified approach (current): • Ketamine and midazolam for sedation and dysautonomia • Nimodipine (with caution — hypotension risk) • ICU supportive care • Standard + contact infection control
nodes.recommendation: Modified Milwaukee Protocol: ketamine + midazolam + nimodipine + ICU support. Outcomes remain extremely poor. ID and neuro consults. Standard + contact precautions. Report to public health.

nodes.title: Type of Animal Contact
nodes.summary: WHO exposure categories: I (intact skin/no PEP), II (minor scratch/vaccine only), III (bite/mucous membrane/bat/RIG + vaccine)
nodes.body: Classify the exposure using WHO categories. Category I — No exposure: Touching, feeding, licks on intact skin Category II — Minor: Nibbling uncovered skin, minor scratches/abrasions without bleeding Category III — Severe: Transdermal bites/scratches, mucous membrane contamination, broken skin + saliva, any direct bat contact

nodes.title: No PEP Indicated — Category I
nodes.body: Skin was not broken and no mucous membrane contamination occurred. This is not a rabies exposure. Wound care: Wash affected area with soap and water as a general hygiene measure. Update tetanus prophylaxis if not current.
nodes.recommendation: PEP is not recommended. Provide reassurance and wound care. If patient reports a bite or broken skin on re-evaluation, reassess as Category II or III.

nodes.title: Animal Species — Category II
nodes.summary: Category II animal species: dogs/cats/ferrets (10-day observation), bats (treat as Cat III), raccoon/skunk/fox (high-risk wildlife)
nodes.body: What animal was involved? Species determines risk level and whether observation is an option. Rabies Risk by Animal Type — detailed reference table.

nodes.title: Animal Species — Category III
nodes.summary: Category III requires RIG + vaccine regardless of species — dogs/cats/ferrets can be observed but START PEP immediately
nodes.body: What animal caused the severe exposure? Category III exposures require RIG + vaccine unless the animal can be confirmed rabies-negative. Rabies Risk by Animal Type — detailed reference.

nodes.title: 10-Day Observation — Category II (Vaccine Only)
nodes.summary: Category II: healthy dog/cat/ferret can be observed 10 days — hold PEP if available and healthy, start if unavailable/stray/wild-acting
nodes.body: Healthy dogs, cats, and ferrets can be observed for 10 days. If animal is: • Available and healthy — begin wound care, hold PEP pending observation. If animal develops signs of rabies or dies → begin PEP immediately. • Unavailable, stray, or wild-acting — begin PEP now (vaccine only for Category II) • Dead or euthanized — send head for testing. Begin PEP pending results; discontinue if negative. O

nodes.title: 10-Day Observation — Category III (RIG + Vaccine)
nodes.summary: Category III: start RIG + vaccine immediately even if animal available — may discontinue if healthy at day 10, RIG cannot be given after day 7
nodes.body: Healthy dogs, cats, and ferrets can be observed for 10 days. For Category III exposures: • Animal available and healthy — Start RIG + vaccine immediately. If animal remains healthy at day 10, may discontinue vaccine series. • Animal unavailable, stray, or wild-acting — complete full RIG + vaccine series • Dead or euthanized — send head for testing. Start PEP pending results; discontinue if negativ

nodes.title: Bat Exposure — Special Rules
nodes.summary: Bat bites can be invisible — PEP for sleeping person, unattended child, intoxicated, or anyone who cannot exclude bite/scratch
nodes.body: Bats require a lower threshold for PEP due to small, unnoticed bites. PEP IS indicated if bat was found in room with: • Sleeping person • Unattended child • Intoxicated or cognitively impaired person • Person who cannot reliably exclude bite/scratch PEP is NOT indicated ONLY if patient can definitively confirm no bite, scratch, or mucous membrane exposure occurred. Bat bites can be virtually invis

nodes.title: High-Risk Wildlife — Category II
nodes.summary: Raccoons, skunks, foxes, coyotes are high-risk reservoirs — Category II gets vaccine, friendly diurnal raccoon/skunk raises rabies suspicion
nodes.body: Raccoons, skunks, foxes, and coyotes are high-risk rabies reservoir species in the US. • If animal captured/killed → send for testing. Start vaccine pending results. • If animal escaped → assume rabid, begin vaccine series (no RIG for Category II). Wild animal behavior note: A "friendly" or diurnal raccoon/skunk should raise suspicion for rabies.

nodes.title: High-Risk Wildlife — Category III
nodes.summary: All Category III wildlife exposures get immediate RIG + vaccine — start full PEP pending testing, discontinue only if confirmed negative
nodes.body: Raccoons, skunks, foxes, and coyotes are high-risk rabies reservoir species in the US. Immediate PEP (RIG + vaccine) is indicated for all Category III wildlife exposures. • If captured/killed → send for testing. Start full PEP pending results; discontinue only if testing confirms negative. • If escaped → complete full PEP course. Consult local public health for animal disposition and testing.

nodes.title: PEP Generally Not Indicated — Small Rodent/Rabbit
nodes.body: Small rodents (mice, rats, squirrels, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chipmunks) and rabbits are almost never found to be infected with rabies and have not been known to transmit rabies to humans. Exceptions requiring public health consultation: • Woodchucks (groundhogs) — higher risk among rodents • Unusual behavior in the animal • Local public health advisory Wound care: Wash with soap and water
nodes.recommendation: PEP is not routinely recommended. Provide wound care. Contact local public health if any concern. For woodchuck/groundhog bites, consult public health — PEP may be indicated.

nodes.title: Wound Management
nodes.summary: Wound care reduces risk by 90% — soap and water >=15min, povidone-iodine, delay primary closure if possible, infiltrate RIG before suturing
nodes.body: Wound care is the single most effective rabies prevention measure — reduces risk by up to 90% in animal studies. Immediate wound care: 1. Wash wound with soap and water for at least 15 minutes — vigorous flushing 2. Irrigate with povidone-iodine (Betadine) or virucidal agent if available 3. Do NOT apply caustic agents (bleach, acid) Suturing guidance: • Delay primary closure if possible — leaving

nodes.title: Previous Rabies Vaccination?
nodes.summary: Previously vaccinated patients need only 2 doses and no RIG (unless immunocompromised) — determines PEP protocol complexity
nodes.body: Has the patient previously completed a full rabies vaccine series (pre-exposure or post-exposure)? Previously vaccinated patients need a shorter protocol (2 doses, no RIG) unless immunocompromised.

nodes.title: Immunocompromised?
nodes.summary: Check for immunocompromising conditions — HIV, chemo, chronic steroids, transplant, anti-CD20 therapy modifies PEP protocol
nodes.body: Is the patient immunocompromised? Immunocompromising conditions include: • HIV/AIDS • Active chemotherapy or radiation • Chronic corticosteroid use (>2 mg/kg or >20 mg/day prednisone for >14 days) • Solid organ or stem cell transplant • Primary immunodeficiency • Anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab) within 6 months

nodes.title: Previously Vaccinated — Immune Status
nodes.summary: Previously vaccinated immunocompetent patients have anamnestic response — 2 doses only (days 0, 3), no RIG needed
nodes.body: Previously vaccinated patients have an anamnestic immune response — they need only 2 vaccine doses and no RIG. However, immunocompromised patients may not mount an adequate anamnestic response.

nodes.title: Full PEP — RIG + 4-Dose Vaccine
nodes.summary: RIG 20 IU/kg infiltrate wound (remainder IM distant from vaccine) + 4-dose vaccine days 0/3/7/14 — RIG only with first dose, never after day 7
nodes.body: RABIES IMMUNE GLOBULIN (RIG) • Rabies Immune Globulin (HRIG) 20 IU/kg • Infiltrate as much as anatomically feasible into and around the wound(s) • Inject remainder IM at a site distant from the vaccine injection site • Give with the first vaccine dose ONLY — do NOT give RIG after day 7 of the vaccine series • Do NOT exceed 20 IU/kg (may interfere with active antibody production) RABIES VACCINE • R

nodes.title: Immunocompromised PEP — RIG + 5-Dose Vaccine
nodes.summary: Immunocompromised: RIG even if previously vaccinated + 5-dose series (add day 28) + post-vaccination serology (RVNA >=0.5 IU/mL)
nodes.body: Immunocompromised patients require a modified protocol: RIG — Give even if previously vaccinated: • Rabies Immune Globulin (HRIG) 20 IU/kg — infiltrate wound, remainder IM distant from vaccine VACCINE — 5-dose series: • Rabies Vaccine (HDCV or PCECV) 1.0 mL IM • Days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 (additional day 28 dose) POST-VACCINATION SEROLOGY: • Check rabies virus neutralizing antibody (RVNA) titer 7-14

nodes.title: Previously Vaccinated — 2-Dose Booster
nodes.summary: Previously vaccinated immunocompetent: 2-dose booster only (days 0 and 3), NO RIG needed — memory B cells provide rapid anamnestic response
nodes.body: No RIG needed — previously vaccinated, immunocompetent patients already have memory B cells. VACCINE — 2-dose series: • Rabies Vaccine (HDCV or PCECV) 1.0 mL IM deltoid (adults) or anterolateral thigh (children) • Days 0 and 3 only Applies to patients who have received: • Prior complete PEP series • Pre-exposure prophylaxis (2- or 3-dose series) • Prior series with documented adequate antibody tit

nodes.title: Vaccination Schedule
nodes.summary: Three schedules by status: unvaccinated (4-dose + RIG), immunocompromised (5-dose + RIG + serology), previously vaccinated (2-dose only)
nodes.body: UNVACCINATED, IMMUNOCOMPETENT — 4 doses: Day 0 (today) | Day 3 | Day 7 | Day 14 + RIG on Day 0 only UNVACCINATED, IMMUNOCOMPROMISED — 5 doses: Day 0 (today) | Day 3 | Day 7 | Day 14 | Day 28 + RIG on Day 0 (even if previously vaccinated) + Post-series serology PREVIOUSLY VACCINATED, IMMUNOCOMPETENT — 2 doses: Day 0 (today) | Day 3 No RIG needed Administration site: • Adults: deltoid muscle (NEVER

nodes.title: Follow-Up and Disposition
nodes.body: FOLLOW-UP VACCINATION VISITS: • Schedule vaccine doses per protocol above • Doses can be given at PCP, urgent care, public health department, or ED • Do not restart the series if a dose is delayed — resume where left off ANIMAL OBSERVATION (dogs/cats/ferrets only): • If 10-day observation in progress → contact animal control/public health for updates • Animal develops rabies signs or dies → ensure
nodes.recommendation: Administer Day 0 vaccine (+ RIG if indicated) before discharge. Schedule remaining vaccine doses. Report bite to animal control. Provide wound care instructions. Return for signs of wound infection or if observation animal becomes ill.

nodes.title: Rectal Prolapse Reduction: Bedside Review
nodes.summary: Confirm reducible prolapse, relieve edema with sugar, reduce gently, then refer.
nodes.body: Use this for the patient with rectal tissue protruding through the anus. Most acute prolapse can be reduced at the bedside; the job is to confirm it is reducible, relieve edema, and reduce gently before tissue becomes nonviable. Open first: - Reduction Steps - Prolapse vs Hemorrhoid - Do NOT Core sequence: 1. Confirm it is prolapse (concentric rings) and full-thickness vs mucosal. 2. Screen viabil

nodes.title: What Is Protruding?
nodes.summary: Concentric rings + sulcus = full-thickness; radial folds = mucosal/hemorrhoid.
nodes.body: Inspect the protruding tissue. Full-thickness rectal prolapse shows concentric (circular) mucosal rings and a palpable sulcus between the prolapse and the anal verge. Mucosal prolapse / prolapsing internal hemorrhoids show radial folds and no sulcus. In a child, a circumferential protrusion is usually mucosal prolapse, but a finger that passes alongside the mass into a sulcus suggests intussuscept

nodes.title: Mucosal Prolapse / Prolapsing Hemorrhoids
nodes.summary: Mucosal/hemorrhoidal prolapse: gentle reduction, treat constipation, refer if strangulated.
nodes.body: Mucosal prolapse and prolapsing internal hemorrhoids are usually reducible with gentle pressure and rarely strangulate, but the same edema-reduction principles apply. - Reduce gently after analgesia; the granulated-sugar technique works here too if the tissue is edematous. - A thrombosed or strangulated hemorrhoid that will not reduce, or one with necrosis, warrants surgical/colorectal evaluation
nodes.recommendation: Reduce gently, treat constipation, and refer non-reducible or strangulated hemorrhoids for surgical evaluation.

nodes.title: Is the Tissue Viable / Reducible?
nodes.summary: Necrosis, strangulation, peritonitis, or rupture = do NOT reduce; call surgery.
nodes.body: Before reducing, assess for tissue compromise. Reducing dead bowel or a perforation back into the abdomen is harmful. Red flags against bedside reduction: frank necrosis or black/gangrenous mucosa, deep ulceration, peritonitis, hemodynamic instability, evisceration of small bowel through a rupture, or an irreducible incarcerated prolapse despite adequate edema reduction and analgesia.

nodes.title: Do NOT Reduce — Surgical Emergency
nodes.summary: Nonviable/ruptured/strangulated prolapse goes to surgery, not bedside reduction.
nodes.body: Stop. Do not attempt bedside reduction. - Nonviable (necrotic/gangrenous) prolapse, strangulation, peritonitis, instability, or a ruptured prolapse with eviscerated bowel needs emergent colorectal/general surgery consultation. - Resuscitate: IV access, fluids, analgesia, blood work, and broad-spectrum antibiotics if perforation/peritonitis is suspected. - Keep eviscerated bowel moist with saline-s
nodes.recommendation: Emergent surgical consultation; resuscitate, do not reduce nonviable or ruptured prolapse.

nodes.title: Analgesia, Positioning, Sedation
nodes.summary: Knee-chest/lateral position, perianal block + analgesia/sedation to relax the sphincter.
nodes.body: Make the patient comfortable and relaxed — a tense patient and a painful prolapse defeat reduction. Positioning: knee-chest (prone jackknife) or left lateral decubitus with hips flexed; Trendelenburg can help gravity assist a large prolapse. Analgesia / relaxation (titrate; see drug references): - Local perianal field block with lidocaine (or bupivacaine for longer duration) to relax the sphincter

nodes.title: Granulated Sugar (Sucrose) Technique
nodes.summary: Liberal granulated sugar, 10-15 min dwell, osmotically shrinks edema; reapply as needed.
nodes.body: Edema is what blocks reduction. Granulated table sugar is hyperosmotic and osmotically draws fluid out of the prolapsed mucosa, shrinking it. Steps: 1. Liberally pour/pack ordinary granulated table sugar over the entire exposed mucosal surface. 2. Let it dwell 10-15 minutes (a cold compress or wrapping the mass can add osmotic/contraction effect). 3. As the prolapse shrinks, it often begins to red

nodes.title: Manual Reduction
nodes.summary: Gentle steady circumferential pressure, invaginate the apex first, roll it inward.
nodes.body: Once edema is reduced and the patient is comfortable: Technique: 1. Apply gentle, steady, circumferential pressure with the thumbs/palms over the apex of the prolapse. 2. Invaginate the leading edge (apex) first, rolling it inward through the anal canal like reversing a sock. 3. Maintain firm, patient pressure for 1-2 minutes rather than short forceful pushes. 4. Once the apex passes the sphincter

nodes.title: Did It Reduce?
nodes.summary: Confirm reduction by DRE; persistent incarceration becomes a surgical problem.
nodes.body: After the attempt, confirm with a digital rectal exam that the rectum is fully reduced and the tone/canal are normal.

nodes.title: Pediatric Rectal Prolapse
nodes.summary: Peds prolapse: usually benign/mucosal; reduce gently and hunt the cause (constipation, CF).
nodes.body: Pediatric rectal prolapse is usually mucosal, benign, and self-limited, often reducing spontaneously or with gentle pressure. Reduce gently with steady pressure (the sugar technique can help if edematous); sedation is rarely needed. Always look for the underlying cause: - Constipation/straining is the most common driver — treat aggressively. - Cystic fibrosis — prolapse can be the presenting sign;
nodes.recommendation: Reduce gently, treat constipation, and screen for cystic fibrosis and other underlying causes.

nodes.title: After Reduction: Disposition & Follow-up
nodes.summary: Home with bowel regimen + colorectal referral; colonoscopy if new/>50; admit difficult cases.
nodes.body: Most patients with a successfully reduced prolapse go home. Bowel regimen (prevent recurrence and straining): - Stool softener / osmotic laxative (polyethylene glycol or equivalent) and dietary fiber. - Avoid straining and prolonged toileting; treat constipation or diarrhea. Referral: - Refer all full-thickness prolapse to colorectal surgery — definitive treatment is operative (e.g., rectopexy or
nodes.recommendation: Discharge reduced viable prolapse with a bowel regimen and colorectal referral; colonoscopy for new-onset/age >50; admit difficult or borderline cases.

nodes.title: Refractory VF/VT
nodes.summary: VF/pVT persisting after 3+ shocks and ACLS — 10-25% of OHCA, only 2-12% survival with standard care
nodes.body: Definition: VF or pulseless VT persisting after: • 3+ defibrillation attempts with 2-minute CPR cycles • Standard ACLS interventions (epi, antiarrhythmic) 2025 AHA terminology: "Persisting VF/pVT" (preferred when mechanism unclear) [1][2] Subtypes: | Type | Definition | |------|------------| | True shock-refractory | VF never terminates | | Recurrent VF | VF terminates but refibrillates <5 sec | |

nodes.title: Optimize Basics (Before Escalation)
nodes.summary: Switch pads to AP position after 3 failed shocks, ensure CPR quality 100-120/min and full recoil
nodes.body: Pad Placement Check: • Standard: Anterolateral (AL) — right infraclavicular + left lateral chest • Vector change: Anterior-Posterior (AP) — left parasternal + left infrascapular • After 3 failed shocks → switch to AP position [1][3] CPR Quality: • Rate: 100-120/min • Depth: ≥2 inches (5 cm) • Full chest recoil • Minimize interruptions (<10 sec for shocks) • Consider mechanical CPR (LUCAS, AutoPuls

nodes.title: Epinephrine Timing (2025 AHA)
nodes.summary: Epi 1mg IV/IO q3-5min — give after 2nd shock in VF/pVT, ASAP in asystole/PEA, no high-dose
nodes.body: | Rhythm | When to Give | |--------|-------------| | VF/pVT | After 2nd shock (not immediately) | | Asystole/PEA | ASAP | | Maintenance | 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 min | KEY: Do NOT use high-dose epinephrine routinely (Class 3: No Benefit) [2] Standard dosing: • Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO push every 3-5 minutes • Continue throughout resuscitation

nodes.title: Reversible Causes — H's and T's
nodes.summary: Systematically search Hs and Ts — hyperK, toxins, PE are treatable causes of refractory VF
nodes.body: Search for and treat reversible causes: The H's: • Hypoxia • Hypovolemia • Hydrogen ion (acidosis) • Hypo/Hyperkalemia • Hypothermia • Hypoglycemia The T's: • Tension pneumothorax • Tamponade (cardiac) • Toxins • Thrombosis — Coronary (MI) • Thrombosis — Pulmonary (PE) Any reversible cause identified?

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia Treatment Stack
nodes.summary: Calcium chloride 1g IV for membrane stabilization, then insulin/D50 and albuterol for K shift
nodes.body: During cardiac arrest: 1. Calcium chloride 1g IV (or Calcium gluconate 3g IV) — membrane stabilization 2. Regular insulin + D50 50 mL (25 g dextrose) IV unless glucose >250 mg/dL — intracellular shift - 5 units (or 0.1 units/kg, max 10) — eGFR <60, dialysis-dependent, pre-treatment glucose <150 mg/dL, weight <60 kg, or no diabetes - 10 units — normal renal function AND adequate glucose - Check glu

nodes.title: Toxin-Induced VF/VT
nodes.summary: Match antidote to toxin — NaHCO3 for TCA, glucagon for BB, calcium for CCB, Intralipid for LAST
nodes.body: Key antidotes during arrest: | Toxin | Treatment | |-------|----------| | TCA | NaHCO₃ 1-2 mEq/kg IV, target pH 7.5 | | Beta-blocker | Glucagon 5-10 mg IV, high-dose insulin | | CCB | Calcium chloride 1-3g IV, high-dose insulin | | Digoxin | DigiFab | | Local anesthetic (LAST) | Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus | | Cocaine | Benzodiazepines, avoid beta-blockers | Continue ACLS while administering an

nodes.title: PE-Induced Cardiac Arrest
nodes.summary: tPA 50mg IV bolus for PE arrest — continue CPR 60-90min post-lytic, consider ECPR
nodes.body: Massive PE with arrest: • tPA 50 mg IV bolus (half the systemic lysis dose) • Continue CPR for 60-90 minutes after thrombolytic • Consider ECPR if available Relative contraindications may be overridden in arrest setting — PE is a reversible cause [2] Alternative: Mechanical thrombectomy if ECMO available

nodes.title: Vector Change Defibrillation
nodes.summary: Move pads to AP position after 3 failed shocks — DOSE-VF showed 21.7% vs 13.3% survival
nodes.body: After 3 failed standard shocks → change vector: Move pads to AP position: • Anterior: left parasternal • Posterior: left infrascapular DOSE-VF Trial evidence: • Vector change alone: 21.7% survival (vs 13.3% standard) [3] Perform vector change BEFORE adding second defibrillator — it's faster and may be sufficient

nodes.title: Double Sequential Defibrillation (DSD)
nodes.summary: DSD showed 30.4% survival — requires two defibrillators, four pads, two operators
nodes.body: DOSE-VF Trial: DSD showed 30.4% survival to discharge (vs 13.3% standard) [3] Setup requires: • Two defibrillators • Four defibrillation pads • Two operators (for near-simultaneous shock) Is a second defibrillator available?

nodes.title: DSD Setup & Technique
nodes.summary: Defib 1 in AL position, Defib 2 in AP — max energy, shocks <1 second apart with countdown
nodes.body: Pad Placement: `` Defib 1: Right infraclavicular + Left lateral (standard AL) Defib 2: Left parasternal + Left posterior (AP) `` Technique: 1. Charge both defibrillators 2. Shocks delivered <1 second apart (near-simultaneous) 3. One operator per defibrillator 4. Verbal countdown coordination Energy: Use maximum energy on both devices [3]

nodes.title: Antiarrhythmic Selection
nodes.summary: Choose amiodarone 300mg or lidocaine 1-1.5mg/kg — both acceptable per AHA, lidocaine may have higher prehospital ROSC
nodes.body: First-line antiarrhythmics (either is acceptable per AHA): Amiodarone: • First bolus: 300 mg IV/IO • Second bolus: 150 mg IV/IO Lidocaine: • First bolus: 1-1.5 mg/kg IV/IO • Second bolus: 0.5-0.75 mg/kg 2025 update: Target trial emulation suggests lidocaine may have higher prehospital ROSC rates [2] Which antiarrhythmic has been given?

nodes.title: Antiarrhythmic Dosing
nodes.summary: Amiodarone 300mg then 150mg, or lidocaine 1-1.5mg/kg then 0.5-0.75mg/kg — post-ROSC infusion details
nodes.body: Amiodarone: | Dose | Amount | |------|--------| | First bolus | 300 mg IV/IO | | Second bolus | 150 mg IV/IO | | Post-ROSC infusion | 1 mg/min x 6h, then 0.5 mg/min | | Max 24h | ~2.2 g | Lidocaine: | Dose | Amount | |------|--------| | First bolus | 1-1.5 mg/kg IV/IO | | Second bolus | 0.5-0.75 mg/kg | | Infusion | 1-4 mg/min | | Max | 3 mg/kg total |

nodes.title: Esmolol — Sympatholytic Strategy
nodes.summary: Consider esmolol 500mcg/kg bolus if still VF after 3 shocks + epi + amiodarone — counters catecholamine excess
nodes.body: Consider esmolol if: • Still in VF after 3 shocks + 3 mg epi + 300 mg amiodarone [4] Rationale: Excessive catecholamines impair defibrillation; esmolol increases fibrillation threshold. DOSING: | Parameter | Dose | |-----------|------| | Bolus | 500 mcg/kg IV (or fixed 40 mg) | | Infusion | 50-100 mcg/kg/min | Has standard therapy failed?

nodes.title: Esmolol Protocol
nodes.summary: Esmolol 500mcg/kg bolus (~40mg fixed), infuse 50-100mcg/kg/min — short t1/2 ~9min, continue CPR
nodes.body: Esmolol dosing: Bolus: 500 mcg/kg IV (~40 mg for 80 kg patient) Infusion: Start 50 mcg/kg/min, titrate to 100 mcg/kg/min Practical tips: • Can give as fixed 40 mg bolus if weight unknown • Very short half-life (~9 min) — effect wears off quickly if ROSC • Continue CPR during administration Evidence: Observational data suggests improved ROSC rates [4]

nodes.title: Other Pharmacologic Options
nodes.summary: MgSO4 only for torsades, NaHCO3 only for acidosis/hyperK/TCA — neither for routine refractory VF
nodes.body: Magnesium Sulfate: • Torsades de Pointes: Magnesium 2g IV over 2 min, repeat 2g at 5-15 min if it persists, then a continuous infusion • Routine refractory VF: NOT recommended [2] Sodium Bicarbonate: • Severe acidosis (pH <7.2): 1 mEq/kg IV • Hyperkalemia: 50-100 mEq IV • TCA overdose: 1-2 mEq/kg IV • Routine use: NOT recommended [2] Procainamide: • 20 mg/min up to 17 mg/kg • Used for stable VT, u

nodes.title: ECPR Assessment
nodes.summary: ELSO criteria: witnessed, shockable, bystander CPR, age <70, reversible cause, collapse-to-flow <60min
nodes.body: ELSO Criteria for ECPR: ✓ Witnessed arrest ✓ Initial shockable rhythm ✓ Bystander CPR initiated ✓ Age <70 years ✓ Presumed reversible cause (MI, PE, hypothermia, toxin) ✓ Refractory to standard ACLS 10-20 min Time targets: • Decision to cannulate: by 10-15 min of refractory arrest • Collapse to ECMO flow: <60 minutes • No-flow time: <5 minutes [5]

nodes.title: ECPR Activation
nodes.summary: ECPR contraindications: no-flow >5min, >60min low-flow, terminal illness — ELSO 29% survival to discharge
nodes.body: ECPR Contraindications: • Known severe neurologic impairment pre-arrest • Metastatic malignancy or terminal illness • No-flow >5 minutes (no bystander CPR) • Prolonged low-flow (>60 min in non-hypothermic) • Irreversible primary disease • Severe sepsis or hemorrhagic shock [5] If proceeding: 1. Continue high-quality CPR 2. ECMO team cannulates (typically femoral VA) 3. Target ECMO flow: 3-4 L/min

nodes.title: Emerging Therapies
nodes.summary: Stellate ganglion block, overdrive pacing, or catheter ablation — last-resort options for truly refractory VF
nodes.body: Advanced options for truly refractory VF: 1. Stellate ganglion block — interrupts sympathetic outflow to heart 2. Overdrive pacing — suppresses PVCs, shortens vulnerable period 3. Emergency catheter ablation — if on ECMO with ongoing storm Are any of these available?

nodes.title: Stellate Ganglion Block (SGB)
nodes.summary: US-guided left C6 block with 10mL 1% lidocaine — STAR study: 92% arrhythmia suppression, 1% complications
nodes.body: Mechanism: Interrupts sympathetic outflow to myocardium STAR Study (2024): 131 patients, 19 centers [6] • 92% arrhythmia suppression • Complication rate: 1% • Periprocedural mortality: <1% Technique: 1. Ultrasound-guided at C6 (Chassaignac's tubercle) 2. Left-sided block preferred (more cardiac autonomic regulation) 3. Inject 10 mL of 1% lidocaine 4. Success marker: Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (

nodes.title: Overdrive Pacing
nodes.summary: Pace 40% above baseline rate to suppress PVCs — transvenous at 110-120bpm for 24-48h bridge
nodes.body: Mechanism: Pacing 40% above baseline rate suppresses PVCs and shortens vulnerable period Indications: • Brady-dependent R-on-T phenomenon • Pause-dependent polymorphic VT • Drug-refractory electrical storm Protocol: 1. Temporary transvenous pacing 2. Start at 110-120 bpm 3. Continue 24-48 hours as bridge to definitive therapy 4. Titrate rate until PVCs/VT disappear Evidence: French multicenter stu

nodes.title: Resuscitation Termination Considerations
nodes.body: No universal criteria — consider termination when: • Prolonged arrest (>60 min in non-hypothermic) • No ROSC despite all interventions • No reversible cause identified • ECPR not available or contraindicated • Irreversible comorbidities Continue resuscitation if: • Reversible cause still being treated • ECPR in progress or available • Hypothermic cardiac arrest (warm and dead) • Drug overdose (may
nodes.recommendation: Consider termination after prolonged arrest with no reversible cause and no ECPR. Continue if reversible cause, hypothermia, or toxin.

nodes.title: Post-ROSC Management
nodes.body: Immediate post-ROSC: 1. Antiarrhythmic infusion: Continue amiodarone or lidocaine drip 2. Target hemodynamics: SBP >90, MAP >65 3. Sedation: Propofol or dexmedetomidine (sympatholytic) 4. Temperature control: Actively prevent fever — continuous core temp monitoring, treat any temp >37.5°C. Target 32-36°C is acceptable if active TTM employed; maintain control for ~36h (2025 AHA) 5. Cardiology consu
nodes.recommendation: Antiarrhythmic infusion, targeted temperature management, emergent cath if indicated, ICU admission.

nodes.title: Resuscitative Hysterotomy
nodes.summary: Emergent delivery during maternal arrest — goal is maternal resuscitation via aortocaval decompression
nodes.body: Resuscitative Hysterotomy Steps Summary — quick-reference checklist. Resuscitative hysterotomy (RH) — formerly perimortem cesarean delivery (PMCD) — is emergent delivery of the fetus in the setting of maternal cardiac arrest. The primary goal is maternal resuscitation, not fetal rescue. [1][2] Why the name change? "Perimortem" implied certain maternal death. "Resuscitative" reframes the procedure

nodes.title: Indications — When to Perform
nodes.summary: Indication: maternal arrest + fundus at/above umbilicus + no ROSC by 4 min — EM physician decides at bedside
nodes.body: RESUSCITATIVE HYSTEROTOMY IS INDICATED WHEN ALL OF THE FOLLOWING: 1. Maternal cardiac arrest (pulselessness requiring CPR) 2. Estimated gestational age ≥20 weeks OR fundus palpable at or above the umbilicus 3. No ROSC within ~4 minutes of high-quality CPR with LUD KEY POINT: This is a procedure done *during* CPR, not after it fails. You are not trying to save the fetus first — you are trying to sa

nodes.title: Fundal Height Assessment
nodes.summary: Fundus at/above umbilicus = ≥20 wk = RH indicated. If unsure, assume ≥20 wk and proceed.
nodes.body: Palpate the uterine fundus. Where is it? Fundal height is a rapid bedside surrogate for gestational age when dates are unknown: • Below umbilicus → <20 weeks → fetus not viable, uterus not causing aortocaval compression → standard ACLS applies • At umbilicus → ~20 weeks → threshold for RH • Above umbilicus → >20 weeks → RH strongly indicated if arrest occurs • Fundus at xiphoid → ~36-38 weeks (ter

nodes.title: Standard ACLS — Fetus Pre-Viable
nodes.body: Gestational age <20 weeks — resuscitative hysterotomy is NOT indicated. The uterus is not large enough to cause significant aortocaval compression, and the fetus is not viable. MANAGEMENT: • Proceed with standard ACLS — Cardiac Arrest • Treat reversible causes (H's and T's) • Still apply LUD — even at <20 weeks, some physiologic benefit; it is low cost • If early pregnancy complication suspected (
nodes.recommendation: Standard ACLS — resuscitative hysterotomy not indicated at <20 weeks. Still apply LUD for marginal benefit.

nodes.title: Why Pregnancy Physiology Matters
nodes.summary: Gravid uterus compresses IVC → ↓preload by 30% → CPR ineffective. Delivery = aortocaval decompression = ROSC.
nodes.body: AORTOCAVAL COMPRESSION SYNDROME: In the supine position after ~20 weeks, the gravid uterus compresses: • Inferior vena cava (IVC) → reduced venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ cardiac output by up to 30% • Abdominal aorta → reduced uterine + lower extremity perfusion During CPR, this physiology makes chest compressions functionally ineffective — you can compress the heart, but there is nothing to pump.

nodes.title: Left Lateral Uterine Displacement (LUD)
nodes.summary: Manual LUD > tilt during arrest. Two-handed pull up-and-left, continuous, dedicated provider.
nodes.body: LUD IS MANDATORY for every pregnant patient ≥20 weeks with hemodynamic compromise or arrest. [1][10] TECHNIQUE — MANUAL LUD (preferred during arrest): One provider stands on the patient's left side: 1. Two-handed grip on the uterus from the patient's left 2. Pull the uterus up and to the left (toward the patient's left shoulder) 3. Maintain continuously — this is a dedicated role, not a periodic m

nodes.title: IV Access & Airway Considerations
nodes.summary: IV above diaphragm (IVC compression!). Pregnant airway: rapid desat, edema, aspiration risk — VL + small ETT.
nodes.body: IV ACCESS — ABOVE THE DIAPHRAGM: • Place IV/IO in upper extremities or neck (external jugular, subclavian), NOT femoral or below-diaphragm sites • Reason: drugs given below the uterine compression point may not reach central circulation. IVC compression blocks return. [1][4] • IO humerus is excellent if no IV AIRWAY — ANTICIPATE DIFFICULT: Pregnancy is a physiologically and anatomically difficult

nodes.title: Pre-Arrest Optimization (if still perfusing)
nodes.summary: Peri-arrest: LUD, O2, fluids, find cause, call help, scalpel ready — prepare before arrest begins.
nodes.body: IF THE PATIENT IS DECOMPENSATING BUT NOT YET IN ARREST: Aggressive optimization may prevent arrest entirely: • LUD — always • High-flow O2 — maternal SpO2 <95% causes fetal hypoxemia • IV fluids — 1-2 L crystalloid bolus unless pulmonary edema • Treat reversible causes — hemorrhage, hypoxia, eclampsia, sepsis, PE, LAST, amniotic fluid embolism • Call for help — OB, anesthesia, neonatology, blood b

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest Confirmed — Start the Code
nodes.summary: Call code, start CPR, manual LUD, start timer, page OB/Neo, scalpel to bedside, assign roles, find cause.
nodes.body: CARDIAC ARREST IN PREGNANCY — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: All at once (parallel processing, not sequential): 1. Call the code — announce "maternal cardiac arrest" 2. Start high-quality CPR — see ACLS Modifications in Pregnancy 3. Establish continuous manual LUD — dedicated provider 4. Start the timer — designate timekeeper, call out minutes 5. Page overhead: OB, neonatology, anesthesia, blood bank, OR 6. H

nodes.title: Start the Clock
nodes.summary: Timekeeper calls out q30sec. 4-min = decision point. Without a timer, RH slips past unnoticed.
nodes.body: DESIGNATE A TIMEKEEPER IMMEDIATELY. The timer starts at the moment of arrest (or loss of pulse), not when you remember to start it. TIMEKEEPER CALLS OUT: • Every 30 seconds — "30 seconds into arrest" • At 2 minutes — rhythm check, pulse check • At 3 minutes — "3 minutes — consider hysterotomy preparation" • At 4 minutes — "4 MINUTES — DECISION POINT" — loud, clear • At 5 minutes — "5 minutes — if

nodes.title: ACLS Modifications in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Same drugs, energies, pad placement. Different: LUD, IV above diaphragm, difficult airway, 4-min RH clock.
nodes.body: Full ACLS Pregnancy Modifications HIGH-YIELD DIFFERENCES FROM STANDARD ACLS: Hand position for compressions: • Standard position (center of chest) — AHA 2015/2023 no longer recommends higher hand position. [4][12] • Compression depth and rate identical: 5-6 cm, 100-120/min Defibrillation: • Same energies as non-pregnant (200J biphasic) • Standard pad placement (anterolateral) • Fetal monitors MUST

nodes.title: BEAU-CHOPS — Reversible Causes in Pregnant Arrest
nodes.summary: BEAU-CHOPS: Bleeding, Embolism, Anesthetic, Uterine atony, Cardiac, HTN, Other, Placenta, Sepsis.
nodes.body: Pregnancy-specific reversible causes of cardiac arrest. See full BEAU-CHOPS B — Bleeding / DIC Hemorrhage (placenta, uterine rupture, abruption, Amniotic Fluid Embolism-DIC) — activate MTP. Massive Transfusion. E — Embolism PE, amniotic fluid embolism, air, fat. Amniotic Fluid Embolism is uniquely pregnancy-related and often fatal. A — Anesthetic complications High spinal, local anesthetic systemi

nodes.title: The 4-Minute Decision Point
nodes.summary: 4 min + no ROSC = incision. 5 min = delivery. Past 4 min? Start NOW anyway — later still beats never.
nodes.body: FOUR MINUTES OF HIGH-QUALITY CPR HAVE ELAPSED. Assess: Has ROSC been achieved? THE RULE (Katz 1986, refined by SOAP 2014, AHA 2023): • If NO ROSC at ~4 minutes → begin incision • Goal: fetus delivered by 5 minutes after arrest • This is the 4-minute decision / 5-minute delivery rule [1][2][15] CURRENT EVIDENCE (2015+): The rigid 4-minute threshold has been re-examined: • Rose 2015 — "Challenging t

nodes.title: ROSC Achieved — Continue Resuscitation
nodes.body: ROSC ACHIEVED — RESUSCITATIVE HYSTEROTOMY AVERTED (for now). IMMEDIATE POST-ROSC PRIORITIES: • Continue LUD — aortocaval compression persists, may cause re-arrest • Aggressive hemodynamic support — vasopressors (Norepinephrine if needed) • Airway — intubate if not already; anticipate difficult airway • Fetal monitoring — continuous CTG; fetal distress may persist after maternal ROSC • Identify and
nodes.recommendation: ROSC achieved — continue LUD, aggressive hemodynamic support, identify cause, ICU admission with MFM/ICU co-management. Keep RH available if re-arrest occurs.

nodes.title: Proceed with Resuscitative Hysterotomy
nodes.summary: Bedside now. No OR move, no prep, no consent needed, no anesthesia, continue CPR. No absolute contraindications.
nodes.body: DECISION MADE. PROCEEDING WITH RH.
