DO NOT: • ❌ Move the patient to the OR • ❌ Wait for obstetrics to arrive • ❌ Prep with betadine, drapes, or formal sterile technique • ❌ Give anesthesia — the patient is in arrest • ❌ Stop CPR DO: • ✅ Perform the procedure at the bedside, right now • ✅ Continue CPR throughout the procedure • ✅ Continue LUD until the moment you open the uterus • ✅ Have the neonata

nodes.title: Equipment — Scalpel is All You Need
nodes.summary: Scalpel is the only essential tool. Everything else is optional. Don't wait for an OB tray.
nodes.body: MINIMUM EQUIPMENT: • #10 or #20 scalpel — the ONLY essential tool • Everything else is optional NICE TO HAVE (if immediately available — do not wait for them): • Sterile or clean gloves • Suction (Yankauer) • Sterile towels (can substitute clean towels) • Cord clamps x2 (Kelly clamps or hemostats work) • Umbilical cord scissors (scalpel also works) • Warmed saline • Bovie (for later hemostasis, no

nodes.title: Patient Positioning
nodes.summary: Flat supine, LUD continues, CPR continues, quick splash antisepsis if instant. <60 sec to skin incision.
nodes.body: POSITIONING: • Patient supine, flat (no tilt — manual LUD continues) • You stand on the patient's right (if right-handed) • CPR continues at the head — chest compressor and airway provider • LUD provider on patient's left — pulls uterus up and to the left; releases only when you are about to incise the uterus • Neonatal team at the warmer — ready to receive BRIEF ANTISEPSIS (only if instant): • Sp

nodes.title: Step 1 — Skin Incision
nodes.summary: One firm vertical midline stroke: xiphoid → symphysis. Skin → fat → fascia → muscle → peritoneum.
nodes.body: VERTICAL MIDLINE INCISION. LANDMARKS: • From: just below the xiphoid • To: symphysis pubis • Length: 15-20 cm — full length of the uterus TECHNIQUE: • One deliberate, firm, deep stroke with the scalpel • Go through: skin → subcutaneous fat → fascia (linea alba) → muscle (rectus abdominis — often already separated by pregnancy) → peritoneum • Do NOT make repeated small strokes — one confident pass

nodes.title: Step 2 — Uterine Incision
nodes.summary: Classical vertical uterine incision. Shallow 1-2cm entry to avoid fetal injury, then extend with fingers.
nodes.body: VERTICAL (CLASSICAL) UTERINE INCISION. LUD provider releases the uterus now. LANDMARKS: • Start: mid-fundus • Direction: vertical, midline • Length: 10-15 cm — enough to deliver the fetus TECHNIQUE: • Shallow initial cut — 1-2 cm deep only — to avoid lacerating the fetus • Feel for fetal parts or amniotic sac through the initial incision • Once in the uterine cavity: enlarge the incision with scis

nodes.title: Step 3 — Deliver the Fetus
nodes.summary: Cup fetal head, deliver head first (or presenting part). Target <5 min from arrest. Hand to neo team.
nodes.body: DELIVER THE FETUS: 1. Reach into the uterus with your dominant hand 2. Cup the fetal head — identify vertex, breech, or transverse lie 3. Deliver the head first (if vertex) or the presenting part (if breech) 4. Apply gentle fundal pressure from above (second provider) if needed 5. Follow with the body and limbs IF BREECH PRESENTATION: • Grasp feet or hips • Deliver feet → legs → body → shoulders →

nodes.title: Step 4 — Clamp and Cut the Cord
nodes.summary: Two clamps 2-3cm apart, cut between. No delayed clamping — fetus needs the warmer now.
nodes.body: CLAMP AND CUT THE UMBILICAL CORD: 1. Two clamps (or hemostats) on the cord, 2-3 cm apart 2. First clamp ~3-5 cm from the fetal abdomen 3. Cut between the two clamps with scissors or scalpel 4. Hand the fetus to the neonatal team DO NOT DELAY CLAMPING. This is not the time for 30-60 seconds of delayed clamping — the maternal circulation is non-functional. The fetus needs immediate resuscitation on

nodes.title: Step 5 — Deliver the Placenta
nodes.summary: Gentle cord traction + fundal counter-pressure. Manual extraction if stuck. ROSC often happens here.
nodes.body: DELIVER THE PLACENTA: • Gentle cord traction — one hand on the cord, steady pull • Other hand on the fundus — apply counter-pressure to guard against uterine inversion • Placenta should separate and deliver within 30-60 seconds IF PLACENTA DOES NOT DELIVER WITHIN 1-2 MINUTES: • Manual extraction — reach into the uterus, sweep the placental edge off the uterine wall with the side of your hand, deli

nodes.title: Step 6 — Continue CPR
nodes.summary: Delivery = inflection point, not endpoint. Keep CPR going. Pack abdomen, don't close until ROSC.
nodes.body: CONTINUE CPR AND RESUSCITATION. KEY POINT: Delivery of the fetus is not the end of the resuscitation — it is the inflection point that *makes* the resuscitation possible. IMMEDIATELY AFTER DELIVERY: • Continue chest compressions at 100-120/min • Continue ACLS medications per protocol • Reassess rhythm at the next scheduled 2-min pulse check • Watch for ROSC — now that preload is restored, it is mu

nodes.title: Neonatal Status
nodes.summary: Assess term, tone, breathing. Vigorous → routine care. Any concern → NRP. APGAR at 1 and 5 min.
nodes.body: THE NEONATAL TEAM ASSESSES THE NEWBORN ON THE WARMER. Initial assessment (first 30 seconds): • Term? (appearance, vernix) • Tone? (good flexion vs. flaccid) • Breathing or crying? If breathing, good tone, term → routine care (warm, dry, stimulate, skin-to-skin if mother ROSC). If any concerns → initiate NRP (Neonatal Resuscitation Program) — Neonatal Resuscitation. APGAR score at 1 and 5 minutes —

nodes.title: Vigorous Newborn — Routine Care
nodes.body: NEONATE IS VIGOROUS. Despite maternal arrest, this neonate is breathing, crying, and has good tone — excellent outcome. ROUTINE NEWBORN CARE: • Warm, dry, stimulate • APGAR at 1 and 5 minutes — APGAR Calculator • Pulse oximetry (right hand, preductal) • Monitor temperature closely — hypothermia is the #1 risk in ED deliveries • Skin-to-skin with mother if mother has ROSC and is stable DISPOSITION:
nodes.recommendation: Routine newborn care: warm, dry, stimulate. APGAR at 1/5 min. NICU evaluation regardless of appearance. Monitor temperature.

nodes.title: Neonatal Resuscitation Required
nodes.body: INITIATE NEONATAL RESUSCITATION (NRP). Full NRP Protocol. INITIAL STEPS (30 seconds): • Warm, dry, stimulate (but do NOT delay PPV if HR <100) • Position airway — sniffing position, gentle suction only if obstructed • Reassess HR, respirations, tone IF HR <100 OR APNEIC: • Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV) — 40-60 breaths/min, room air initially for term, 30% O2 for preterm • Continue for 30 sec
nodes.recommendation: Initiate NRP: PPV if HR <100, compressions if HR <60, epinephrine if HR <60 despite PPV + compressions. APGAR q5min until >7. Transfer to NICU.

nodes.title: Maternal Status After Delivery
nodes.summary: Delivery relieves compression — ROSC often happens now. Reassess pulse, ETCO2, rhythm, BP.
nodes.body: RE-ASSESS THE MOTHER AT THE NEXT PULSE CHECK. Delivery has restored preload. This is the moment ROSC most commonly occurs. REASSESS: • Pulse — palpate carotid or femoral • End-tidal CO2 — sudden rise suggests ROSC • Rhythm — organized rhythm with pulse • Blood pressure — arterial line if not yet placed WHAT IS THE MATERNAL STATUS?

nodes.title: Maternal ROSC — Post-Arrest Care
nodes.summary: ROSC post-RH: hemostasis, MTP, airway, pressors, find cause, OR for closure, ICU with MFM/ICU.
nodes.body: ROSC ACHIEVED AFTER RESUSCITATIVE HYSTEROTOMY. IMMEDIATE PRIORITIES (the next 15 minutes): 1. Hemostasis — uterine atony is near-universal after RH. Proceed to Uterine Atony Management. 2. Massive transfusion — activate MTP if not already. Expected blood loss 1-2+ L. Massive Transfusion. 3. Airway secured — intubate if not already 4. Hemodynamic support — Norepinephrine infusion, arterial line, ce

nodes.title: Uterine Atony Management
nodes.summary: Oxytocin drip + TXA 1g IV + bimanual massage first-line. Misoprostol, methergine (not in HTN), carboprost (not asthma) 2nd-line.
nodes.body: UTERINE ATONY IS NEAR-UNIVERSAL AFTER RH. The uterus has been cut, the patient was in arrest with no myometrial tone, and postpartum hemorrhage is nearly certain. FIRST-LINE — UTEROTONICS (start all that apply): • Oxytocin — 20 units in 1L NS IV at 250 mL/hr (do NOT give IV push — profound hypotension) • Tranexamic Acid (TXA) — 1 g IV over 10 minutes, repeat once at 30 min if bleeding continues (W

nodes.title: Continued Arrest After Hysterotomy
nodes.body: NO ROSC AFTER RESUSCITATIVE HYSTEROTOMY. The aortocaval decompression maneuver did not achieve ROSC. Continue aggressive resuscitation. CONTINUE FOR AT LEAST 10 MORE MINUTES (post-delivery): • Standard ACLS — epinephrine q3-5 min, rhythm-appropriate shocks • Reassess and treat reversible causes • Consider Intralipid if LAST possible • Ultrasound — rule out tamponade, tension PTX, massive hemorrhag
nodes.recommendation: Continue full resuscitation for at least 10 more min post-delivery. Consider ECMO, open chest if indicated. Pregnant patients tolerate prolonged arrest — err toward longer resuscitation.

nodes.title: Disposition & Transfer
nodes.body: FINAL DISPOSITION AFTER MATERNAL ROSC + RESUSCITATIVE HYSTEROTOMY: IMMEDIATE (next 30 minutes): • Transfer to OR — formal surgical closure, uterine repair, hemostasis verification • Blood products continuing — MTP until hemostasis, goal fibrinogen >200, platelets >50 • Arterial line, central line placed • OB + trauma surgery + anesthesia at bedside in OR NEONATE: • Level III NICU for post-arrest n
nodes.recommendation: OR for formal closure. ICU with MFM/ICU co-management, post-arrest care bundle, TTM. Level III NICU for neonate. Cause workup. Team debrief and family support.

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis - Recognition
nodes.summary: Skeletal muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin, CK, K, phosphate — CK >1000 diagnostic, AKI in 15-55%, classic triad present in <10%
nodes.body: Rhabdomyolysis is skeletal muscle breakdown releasing intracellular contents (myoglobin, CK, potassium, phosphate) into circulation. Classic triad (present in <10%): • Myalgia • Muscle weakness • Dark/tea-colored urine (myoglobinuria) Diagnostic criteria: • CK >5x upper limit of normal (~1,000 U/L) • Many clinicians use CK >1,000 U/L as threshold [1] AKI incidence: 15-55% of cases, higher with: •

nodes.title: Severity Stratification by CK Level
nodes.summary: CK guides treatment intensity: 1-5K (mild, 2% dialysis), 5-15K (moderate, 3-8%), >15K (severe, 5-14%), >50K (ICU, 9-21%)
nodes.body: CK level guides treatment intensity and disposition: | CK Level | Severity | Fluid Target | AKI Risk | |----------|----------|--------------|----------| | 1,000-5,000 | Mild | 2-3 L/day | ~2% dialysis | | 5,000-15,000 | Moderate | 3-6 L/day | ~3-8% dialysis | | >15,000 | Severe | >6 L/day | ~5-14% dialysis | | >50,000 | Very Severe | Aggressive + ICU | ~9-21% dialysis | 2025 cohort study (n=73,036

nodes.title: Etiology Assessment
nodes.summary: Identify underlying cause — traumatic/crush (compartment risk), exertional (better prognosis), drug-induced, or metabolic/infectious
nodes.body: Identify the underlying cause - guides management and prognosis. Traumatic/Physical: • Crush injury, prolonged immobilization • Compartment syndrome • Excessive exercise (exertional rhabdo) • Seizures, electrical injury, burns Non-traumatic: • Drugs/Toxins: Statins (especially + fibrates/cyclosporine), alcohol, cocaine, amphetamines, heroin, NMS, serotonin syndrome • Metabolic: Hypokalemia, hypoph

nodes.title: Drug/Toxin-Induced Rhabdomyolysis
nodes.summary: Statin-induced: stop immediately (rechallenge later OK), cocaine: treat hyperthermia/avoid beta-blockers, NMS/SS: see specific consults
nodes.body: Statin-induced: • Risk ~0.1% overall, higher with: - High-intensity statins (rosuvastatin, atorvastatin high-dose) - Fibrate combination (avoid gemfibrozil) - CYP3A4 inhibitors (cyclosporine, macrolides, azoles) • Management: STOP statin immediately. Can rechallenge with different statin after recovery if needed. Cocaine/Amphetamines: • Sympathomimetic excess + hyperthermia + vasoconstriction • Tr

nodes.title: Compartment Syndrome Evaluation
nodes.summary: Compartment syndrome: pain with passive stretch, pressure >30mmHg or delta <30mmHg — fasciotomy within 6h, do NOT elevate limb
nodes.body: Compartment syndrome requires urgent evaluation in crush/trauma patients. Early signs (6 Ps - unreliable order): • Pain - disproportionate, worse with passive stretch • Paresthesias - nerve ischemia • Pressure - tense compartment on exam • Pallor - late sign • Paralysis - late sign (muscle death) • Pulselessness - very late sign Diagnosis: • Clinical suspicion is paramount • Compartment pressure m

nodes.title: Laboratory Workup
nodes.summary: CK, BMP, Ca/Phos/Mg, UA (dipstick + blood but no RBCs = myoglobinuria), ECG for hyperK, LDH/AST from muscle not just liver
nodes.body: Initial labs: Muscle injury markers: • CK - most sensitive marker, peaks 24-72h • Myoglobin - cleared faster than CK, may be negative with high CK • LDH, AST (also from muscle, not just liver) Renal function: • BUN, Creatinine, GFR • Urinalysis: + blood on dipstick but no RBCs = myoglobinuria • Urine myoglobin (if available, not necessary for diagnosis) Electrolytes (critical): • Potassium - life-

nodes.title: Critical Electrolyte Abnormalities?
nodes.summary: Check for hyperK (>6 or ECG changes), symptomatic hypocalcemia, and severe acidosis — treat immediately before fluid resuscitation
nodes.body: Check for life-threatening abnormalities requiring immediate intervention: Hyperkalemia: • K >6.0 mEq/L or ECG changes • Treat immediately: calcium, insulin/glucose, albuterol, bicarbonate • See Potassium Disorders Hypocalcemia: • Corrected Ca <7.0 mg/dL with symptoms • Caution: Only treat symptomatic hypocalcemia • Aggressive Ca replacement may worsen muscle calcium deposition Metabolic acidosis:

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia Management
nodes.body: Life-threatening hyperkalemia requires immediate treatment: Cardiac membrane stabilization: • Calcium gluconate 1-2 g IV over 2-3 min (preferred) OR • Calcium chloride 500-1000 mg IV (central line preferred) Potassium shifting: • Regular insulin IV — dose by hypoglycemia risk. Give WITH 25 g dextrose (D50W 50 mL) unless glucose >250 mg/dL — 5 units (or 0.1 units/kg, max 10) — eGFR <60, dialysis-de
nodes.recommendation: Treat hyperkalemia immediately with calcium, insulin/glucose, albuterol. Consider dialysis if refractory or anuric.

nodes.title: Symptomatic Hypocalcemia
nodes.body: Only treat symptomatic hypocalcemia: Symptoms requiring treatment: • Tetany, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek/Trousseau signs • Seizures • QT prolongation with arrhythmia Treatment: • Calcium gluconate 1-2 g IV over 10-20 min • May need continuous infusion: 1-2 g/hr CAUTION - Asymptomatic hypocalcemia: • Common in early rhabdomyolysis (Ca deposits in damaged muscle) • Do NOT aggressively replace if asym
nodes.recommendation: Only treat symptomatic hypocalcemia. Avoid aggressive calcium replacement in asymptomatic patients - calcium often normalizes spontaneously.

nodes.title: Fluid Resuscitation - Cornerstone of Treatment
nodes.summary: Aggressive IV fluids are the mainstay — target UOP 1-3mL/kg/hr, early resuscitation <6h reduces AKI, LR may have pH advantages over NS
nodes.body: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the mainstay of treatment. [1][7] Goals: • Maintain urine output 1-3 mL/kg/hr (some recommend up to 200-300 mL/hr) • Early resuscitation (<6 hours) reduces AKI risk • Replace volume deficit AND ongoing losses Fluid choice - NS vs LR: [7] • Both are acceptable per AAST consensus • LR may have advantages: - Better maintenance of alkaline urine pH - Less hyperchlo

nodes.title: Fluid Selection
nodes.summary: LR preferred (better pH, less NAGMA with large volumes), K content 4mEq/L is clinically insignificant — NS acceptable alternative
nodes.body: Choose crystalloid based on clinical context: Lactated Ringers (preferred by many): • Maintains alkaline urine pH better than NS • Avoids hyperchloremic acidosis with large volumes • K content (4 mEq/L) does NOT worsen hyperkalemia - this is a myth [7] • LR actually may LOWER K by avoiding acidosis-induced K shift Normal Saline: • Acceptable alternative • May require bicarbonate supplementation fo

nodes.title: LR Fluid Protocol
nodes.body: Lactated Ringers Protocol: Initial bolus: • 1-2 L IV bolus (20 mL/kg if pediatric) Maintenance: • 200-500 mL/hr (adjust based on UOP) • Goal UOP: 1-3 mL/kg/hr (or 200-300 mL/hr) Monitoring: • Urine output q1-2h (Foley catheter recommended) • Reassess volume status frequently • BMP, CK q6-12h Duration: • Continue until CK trending down AND <5,000 U/L • OR until clear urine (myoglobinuria resolved)
nodes.recommendation: Aggressive LR resuscitation targeting UOP 1-3 mL/kg/hr. Continue until CK <5,000 and trending down.

nodes.title: NS Fluid Protocol
nodes.body: Normal Saline Protocol: Initial bolus: • 1-2 L IV bolus Maintenance: • 200-500 mL/hr (adjust based on UOP) • Goal UOP: 1-3 mL/kg/hr Considerations: • Monitor for hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) • If severe acidosis develops, may need to: - Switch to LR - Add bicarbonate supplementation • Check urine pH - if goal is alkalinization, may need bicarbonate Same duration and monitoring as LR p
nodes.recommendation: NS is acceptable. Monitor for hyperchloremic acidosis with large volumes. Goal UOP 1-3 mL/kg/hr.

nodes.title: Special Populations - Modified Fluid Strategy
nodes.body: Heart Failure: • Cautious fluid resuscitation • Smaller boluses (250-500 mL), reassess frequently • Lower maintenance rates • Continuous pulse oximetry, consider POCUS for volume assessment • May need loop diuretics if volume overloaded • Nephrology consult for early dialysis consideration ESRD / Dialysis Patients: • Minimal to no IV fluids needed • Focus on dialysis for volume/toxin removal • Urg
nodes.recommendation: Modify fluid strategy for CHF and ESRD. Early nephrology consultation recommended.

nodes.title: Urine Alkalinization (Bicarbonate) - Evidence
nodes.summary: Bicarbonate for urine alkalinization is NOT proven effective (2025 meta-analysis) — fluids alone sufficient, consider only for pH <7.1
nodes.body: The role of bicarbonate for urine alkalinization is CONTROVERSIAL. [9] Theory: • Myoglobin is more soluble at alkaline pH • Alkaline urine may prevent myoglobin precipitation in tubules • Target urine pH >6.5 Evidence (2025 meta-analysis): [9] • 5 studies analyzed • Urine alkalinization NOT significantly effective in: - Preventing AKI (OR 2.11, p=0.3) - Preventing acute renal failure (OR 1.26, p=0

nodes.title: Adjunctive Therapy Decisions
nodes.summary: Adjunctive therapy decisions: bicarbonate for severe acidosis, diuretics/dialysis for oliguria, or continue fluids alone
nodes.body: Based on clinical scenario, select appropriate adjunctive measures:

nodes.title: Bicarbonate Protocol (If Used)
nodes.body: If bicarbonate therapy chosen: Indications (weak evidence): • Severe acidosis (pH <7.1) • Very high CK (>30,000) WITHOUT oliguria/AKI • Adequate volume status Protocol: • Sodium bicarbonate 150 mEq in 1L D5W • Run at 150-200 mL/hr • Target urine pH >6.5 Monitoring: • Urine pH q2-4h • Serum pH, bicarb, K, ionized calcium q4-6h Contraindications: • Hypocalcemia (bicarb worsens it) • Pulmonary edema/
nodes.recommendation: Bicarbonate not routinely recommended. If used, target urine pH >6.5. Monitor for hypocalcemia.

nodes.title: Oliguria Management
nodes.body: Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) despite adequate fluid resuscitation: Step 1 - Ensure adequate volume: • Reassess volume status (POCUS, CVP if available) • If hypovolemic, continue aggressive fluids Step 2 - Consider loop diuretics: • Furosemide 40-80 mg IV • May help maintain urine output and aid K excretion • No evidence diuretics prevent AKI - use for volume management Step 3 - Nephrology consultation
nodes.recommendation: Ensure adequate volume first. Loop diuretics for volume management. Early nephrology consult if oliguria persists. Dialysis for standard indications.

nodes.title: Monitoring Protocol
nodes.summary: Serial CK q6-12h (peak 24-72h, should decline 50% q48-72h), BMP, UOP q1-2h with Foley, ECG if K abnormal — persistent CK = ongoing injury
nodes.body: Serial monitoring is essential: Labs: • CK: q6-12h until clearly trending down • BMP (K, Cr, bicarb): q6-12h initially • Calcium, phosphorus, magnesium: q12-24h • Urine output: q1-2h (Foley catheter) CK trending: • Peak typically 24-72 hours • Should decline by 50% every 48-72 hours • Persistent or rising CK suggests ongoing injury Volume status: • Daily weights • Lung exam, JVD assessment • I/O b

nodes.title: Complications to Monitor
nodes.summary: AKI 15-55%, hyperK life-threatening, early hypoCa (do NOT treat unless symptomatic), late hyperCa in recovery, DIC rare but monitor
nodes.body: Acute Kidney Injury (15-55%): • Peak incidence with CK >15,000 • Most common cause: myoglobin-induced ATN • Usually reversible with supportive care • 5-8% require dialysis (higher with severe CK elevation) Hyperkalemia: • Can be life-threatening • Monitor ECG for peaked T-waves, widened QRS • Treat aggressively (see hyperkalemia node) Hypocalcemia (early): • Usually asymptomatic, self-limited • On

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: McMahon Score >=6 predicts RRT need — disposition by severity, electrolytes, response to treatment, and comorbidities
nodes.body: Disposition based on severity, response to treatment, and comorbidities: McMahon Score ≥6: Predicts need for RRT - consider ICU admission [3] Score components: • Age >70: 2 points • Female: 1 point • Initial CK >40,000: 2 points • Initial phosphate >4.0: 2 points • Initial calcium <7.5: 2 points • Initial creatinine elevated: 2 points • Initial bicarbonate <19: 2 points • Cause NOT exercise, seizu

nodes.title: ICU Admission Criteria
nodes.body: ICU admission recommended for: • CK >50,000 U/L (some use >100,000) • AKI with oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr despite fluids) • Life-threatening hyperkalemia (K >6.5, arrhythmias) • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1) • Compartment syndrome (post-fasciotomy care) • Need for dialysis or high likelihood • McMahon Score ≥6 • Multiorgan dysfunction • Hemodynamic instability ICU goals: • Close electrolyte mon
nodes.recommendation: ICU for severe rhabdomyolysis with AKI, severe hyperkalemia, acidosis, or need for dialysis.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor admission appropriate for: • Moderate CK (5,000-15,000) OR • Mild CK (1,000-5,000) with risk factors • Stable electrolytes (K <5.5, normal creatinine) • Adequate urine output on fluids • No compartment syndrome concern • McMahon Score <6 Floor management: • IV fluids to maintain UOP 1-3 mL/kg/hr • BMP, CK q12h • Telemetry if K abnormal • Serial exams for compartment syndrome (if applicable)
nodes.recommendation: Floor admission for moderate rhabdomyolysis with stable electrolytes and adequate urine output.

nodes.title: Observation or Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge may be considered if ALL criteria met: [11] Safe discharge criteria: • CK <5,000 U/L (conservative: <10,000) • CK is trending DOWN after hydration • Normal creatinine (or baseline if CKD) • Normal potassium • Able to tolerate oral fluids • Underlying cause identified and addressed • Reliable follow-up available Observation (6-12 hour) with discharge: • CK 5,000-10,000 with normal renal f
nodes.recommendation: Discharge if CK <5,000 and trending down, normal creatinine, and cause addressed. Aggressive oral hydration and close follow-up.

nodes.title: Early Pregnancy RhoGAM Guidelines
nodes.summary: 2024 ACOG: RhoGAM NO LONGER routinely recommended before 12 weeks — major practice change, exceptions exist for high-risk scenarios
nodes.body: 2024 ACOG Practice Advisory: Major Practice Change Anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) is NO LONGER routinely recommended before 12 weeks gestation for threatened miscarriage, spontaneous abortion, or ectopic pregnancy. [1] This represents a significant departure from prior practice based on updated evidence. 2024 vs Prior Practice Comparison Key Points: - Risk of alloimmunization from first-trimester

nodes.title: Rh(D) Status
nodes.summary: Determine Rh(D) status: positive (no RhoGAM), negative unsensitized (candidate), negative sensitized (consult MFM), weak D (genotype)
nodes.body: Determine the patient's Rh(D) blood type status. Type & Screen includes: - ABO blood group - Rh(D) status (positive or negative) - Antibody screen (indirect Coombs) If antibody screen positive: Patient may already be sensitized. Consult blood bank/MFM. Rh Typing Interpretation

nodes.title: Rh(D) Positive - No RhoGAM Needed
nodes.body: Patient is Rh(D) positive. RhoGAM is NOT indicated for Rh-positive patients regardless of clinical scenario. RhoGAM is only given to prevent Rh-negative mothers from developing antibodies against Rh-positive fetal red blood cells.
nodes.recommendation: No RhoGAM indicated. Document Rh-positive status in chart.

nodes.title: Already Sensitized
nodes.body: Antibody screen positive indicates prior sensitization to Rh(D) antigen. RhoGAM is NOT effective once alloimmunization has occurred. It can only prevent sensitization, not reverse it. Next steps: - Identify specific antibody (anti-D vs other) - Quantify antibody titer - MFM consultation for ongoing pregnancy management - Serial middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler to monitor for fetal anemia if co
nodes.recommendation: Consult MFM/blood bank. RhoGAM not indicated once sensitization has occurred. Serial MCA Doppler monitoring for ongoing pregnancy.

nodes.title: Weak D / D Variant
nodes.summary: Weak D: RHD genotyping recommended — types 1/2/3 safe (no RhoGAM), partial D treat as Rh-negative, if genotyping unavailable give RhoGAM
nodes.body: Weak D phenotype occurs in ~0.2-1% of Caucasians. Serologic typing may show: - Weak positive reaction - Discordant results between testing methods - "Du" (historical term) AABB/ACOG Recommendation: RHD genotyping to determine if patient needs RhoGAM [5] Genotype Interpretation: - RHD gene present (types 1, 2, 3): Typically safe, no RhoGAM needed - RHD gene absent or partial: Treat as Rh-negative,

nodes.title: Gestational Age Assessment
nodes.summary: Critical threshold 12 weeks — below 12wk most events do NOT require RhoGAM per 2024 ACOG, above 12wk standard indications apply
nodes.body: Patient is Rh(D) negative and unsensitized. Determine gestational age to guide RhoGAM decision. Gestational Age Reference Critical threshold: 12 weeks gestation 2024 ACOG guidance varies significantly based on whether the event occurs before or after 12 weeks.

nodes.title: First Trimester Event (<12 weeks)
nodes.summary: First trimester <12wk: RhoGAM NOT routinely recommended — alloimmunization risk <0.1%, fetal RBCs express Rh(D) starting ~7-8wk GA
nodes.body: 2024 ACOG Practice Change: RhoGAM is NOT routinely recommended before 12 weeks for most indications. [1] Rationale: - Fetal RBCs express Rh(D) antigen starting ~38 days post-conception (~7-8 weeks GA) - Volume of fetal-maternal hemorrhage in early pregnancy is negligible (<0.1 mL) - Risk of alloimmunization from first-trimester events is extremely low - Studies show no significant reduction in sen

nodes.title: Threatened Miscarriage <12 Weeks
nodes.body: 2024 ACOG: RhoGAM is NOT recommended. [1] Threatened miscarriage at <12 weeks with: - Vaginal bleeding (light to moderate) - Closed cervical os - Viable intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound Evidence: - Risk of alloimmunization is negligible (<0.1%) - No RCTs demonstrate benefit of RhoGAM in this setting - Prior recommendations were based on expert opinion, not evidence [2] Note: If heavy bleeding
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM NOT indicated for routine threatened miscarriage <12 weeks. Reassess if progresses to heavier bleeding.

nodes.title: Spontaneous Abortion <12 Weeks
nodes.body: 2024 ACOG: RhoGAM is NOT recommended. [1] Spontaneous abortion at <12 weeks includes: - Complete miscarriage - Incomplete miscarriage - Missed abortion - Medical management with misoprostol - Surgical management (D&C/MVA) Evidence: - Cochrane review: No difference in alloimmunization rates with vs without RhoGAM before 12 weeks [2] - Volume of fetal blood exposure is insufficient to trigger matern
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM NOT indicated for spontaneous abortion <12 weeks (including surgical management). Document Rh status for future pregnancies.

nodes.title: Ectopic Pregnancy <12 Weeks
nodes.body: 2024 ACOG: RhoGAM is NOT recommended. [1] Ectopic pregnancy at <12 weeks managed by: - Medical therapy (methotrexate) - Surgical management (salpingectomy, salpingostomy) - Expectant management Rationale: - Tubal/extrauterine pregnancies rarely develop adequate placentation for significant fetal-maternal hemorrhage - Even ruptured ectopic at <12 weeks typically involves minimal fetal blood Note: L
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM NOT indicated for routine ectopic pregnancy <12 weeks. Use clinical judgment for ruptured ectopic with large hemoperitoneum.

nodes.title: First Trimester Exceptions
nodes.summary: First trimester exceptions requiring RhoGAM: molar pregnancy, invasive procedures (CVS/amnio), abdominal trauma, significant bleeding
nodes.body: RhoGAM IS indicated in first trimester for specific high-risk scenarios regardless of gestational age. [1] These exceptions involve: - Higher volume fetal-maternal hemorrhage - Invasive procedures - Conditions with theoretical increased risk

nodes.title: Molar Pregnancy
nodes.body: RhoGAM IS indicated for molar pregnancy at ANY gestational age. [1] Rationale: - Molar tissue can express Rh(D) antigen - Evacuation of molar pregnancy disrupts abnormal trophoblastic tissue - Risk of fetal-maternal hemorrhage is higher than typical miscarriage Applies to: - Complete hydatidiform mole - Partial hydatidiform mole - Gestational trophoblastic disease Dosing: Standard 300 mcg IM dose
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM indicated for molar pregnancy at any gestational age. Give within 72 hours of evacuation.

nodes.title: Invasive Procedures
nodes.body: RhoGAM IS indicated for invasive procedures at any gestational age. [1, 3] Procedures requiring RhoGAM: - Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) - Amniocentesis - Cordocentesis (PUBS) - Fetal surgery/intervention - External cephalic version (later GA) Rationale: These procedures involve direct placental/fetal manipulation with significant risk of fetal-maternal hemorrhage. Timing: Give RhoGAM within 72 h
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM indicated for invasive fetal procedures at any gestational age. Administer within 72 hours.

nodes.title: Abdominal Trauma
nodes.body: RhoGAM IS indicated for abdominal trauma at any gestational age. [1, 3] Includes: - Motor vehicle collision - Falls with abdominal impact - Assault/intimate partner violence - Penetrating abdominal trauma Rationale: Trauma can cause placental separation and significant fetal-maternal hemorrhage even in early pregnancy. Second/Third Trimester Trauma: Consider Kleihauer-Betke testing to quantify fet
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM indicated for abdominal trauma at any gestational age. Consider KB testing if >20 weeks.

nodes.title: Significant Vaginal Bleeding
nodes.body: Consider RhoGAM for heavy vaginal bleeding even in first trimester. [1] Definition of significant bleeding: - Soaking >1 pad per hour for 2+ hours - Hemodynamic changes (tachycardia, hypotension) - Symptomatic anemia - Visible clots or tissue Clinical judgment applies: The 2024 ACOG guidance acknowledges uncertainty in heavy bleeding scenarios. When in doubt, giving RhoGAM is reasonable as the ris
nodes.recommendation: Consider RhoGAM 300 mcg IM for heavy first-trimester bleeding with clinical judgment. When uncertain, giving RhoGAM is reasonable.

nodes.title: Second/Third Trimester (≥12 weeks)
nodes.summary: After 12 weeks: standard RhoGAM recommendations apply — 2024 ACOG changes only affect events before 12 weeks gestation
nodes.body: Standard RhoGAM recommendations apply for events at or after 12 weeks gestation. [3] 2024 ACOG changes apply ONLY to events <12 weeks. After 12 weeks, follow established guidelines. Select the clinical scenario:

nodes.title: Routine 28-Week Prophylaxis
nodes.body: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM at 28 weeks gestation - unchanged by 2024 guidance. [3] Standard protocol: - Given at 28-week prenatal visit - Protects through delivery (12-week window) - Required even if no sensitizing events Evidence: - Reduces third-trimester sensitization from 2% to 0.1% - Combined with postpartum dose, reduces overall sensitization to 0.1-0.2% Repeat antibody screen not required before 28-
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM at 28 weeks for all Rh-negative, unsensitized pregnant patients. Standard of care - unchanged by 2024 ACOG.

nodes.title: Sensitizing Event ≥12 Weeks
nodes.body: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM within 72 hours for sensitizing events at ≥12 weeks. [3] Sensitizing events: - Vaginal bleeding (any amount) - Placental abruption - Placenta previa with bleeding - Abdominal trauma - External cephalic version - Amniocentesis/CVS - Second-trimester loss/IUFD - Preterm labor If >20 weeks: Order Kleihauer-Betke to assess for large fetal-maternal hemorrhage requiring additional dose
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM within 72 hours. Order KB if >20 weeks to quantify hemorrhage.

nodes.title: Postpartum RhoGAM
nodes.body: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM within 72 hours of delivery if newborn is Rh-positive. [3] Postpartum protocol: 1. Cord blood: ABO/Rh typing of newborn 2. If newborn Rh-positive: Give RhoGAM 300 mcg IM 3. If newborn Rh-negative: No RhoGAM needed 4. Order KB (rosette if available) to screen for large FMH Even if 28-week dose given, postpartum dose is still required. Missed 72-hour window: Give up to 28 days post
nodes.recommendation: RhoGAM 300 mcg IM within 72 hours of delivery if newborn Rh-positive. Confirm cord blood Rh. Screen for large FMH.

nodes.title: RhoGAM Dosing & Administration
nodes.summary: Standard 300mcg covers 30mL fetal blood, MICRhoGAM 50mcg for first trimester only — give IM within 72h, deltoid or gluteal
nodes.body: Standard Dosing: | Product | Dose | Coverage | Use | |---------|------|----------|-----| | RhoGAM | 300 mcg (1500 IU) | 30 mL fetal blood | Standard - any GA | | MICRhoGAM | 50 mcg (250 IU) | 2.5 mL fetal blood | First trimester only | 300 mcg standard dose covers: - Up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood - Up to 15 mL of fetal packed RBCs Administration: - Route: IM (deltoid or gluteal) - Timing: Withi

nodes.title: Special Scenarios
nodes.summary: Special scenarios: massive FMH requiring additional doses, KB interpretation for dose calculation, weak D genotyping guidance
nodes.body: Select if any of these special clinical situations apply:

nodes.title: Massive Fetomaternal Hemorrhage
nodes.body: Large FMH (>30 mL fetal blood) requires additional RhoGAM doses. [8] Causes of massive FMH: - Placental abruption - Abdominal trauma - Manual placenta removal - Intrauterine fetal demise - Multifetal gestation reduction Detection: - Rosette screen: Qualitative (positive/negative for large FMH) - Kleihauer-Betke: Quantitative (% fetal cells) - Flow cytometry: Most accurate Dosing Calculation: `` Fe
nodes.recommendation: For massive FMH: Calculate fetal blood volume from KB, divide by 30, round up, add 1 extra vial. Give within 72 hours.

nodes.title: Kleihauer-Betke Interpretation
nodes.body: Kleihauer-Betke (KB) Test quantifies fetal RBCs in maternal circulation. [8] Indications for KB: - Trauma at >20 weeks - Abruption - Postpartum (some institutions) - Any suspected large FMH Calculation: 1. % fetal cells = fetal cells counted / total cells counted x 100 2. Fetal blood volume = % fetal cells x maternal blood volume / 100 - Maternal blood volume ≈ 5000 mL (adjust for patient size) 3.

nodes.title: Weak D Genotyping Details
nodes.body: When to order RHD genotyping: [5, 6] - Serologic Rh typing shows weak or discordant result - Patient reports conflicting Rh results from prior testing - Planning future pregnancies and want definitive answer Genotype Results: | Type | Gene | RhoGAM Needed? | |------|------|----------------| | Weak D types 1, 2, 3 | RHD present | NO | | Weak D type 4.0, 4.1 | Partial RHD | YES | | Partial D (any) |

nodes.title: RhoGAM Guidelines Summary
nodes.body: 2024 ACOG Early Pregnancy RhoGAM Summary: <12 weeks - NO RhoGAM needed for: - Threatened miscarriage - Spontaneous abortion (complete/incomplete) - Ectopic pregnancy - Medical or surgical management of above <12 weeks - RhoGAM IS needed for: - Molar pregnancy (any GA) - Invasive procedures (CVS, amnio) - Abdominal trauma - Heavy bleeding (clinical judgment) ≥12 weeks - Standard indications: - 28-w
nodes.recommendation: Follow 2024 ACOG guidance: No routine RhoGAM <12 weeks for SAB, threatened SAB, or ectopic. Standard indications apply ≥12 weeks.

nodes.title: Right Heart Failure — Phenotype Recognition
nodes.body: Right heart failure (RHF) is high-mortality and easy to miss. Classic phenotype: • Clear lungs + elevated JVP + cool extremities (vs LHF: wet lungs + JVP + cool) • Hypotension out of proportion to exam • Hypoxia without obvious LV dysfunction • Refractory to fluids — or gets worse with fluids • Common ED triggers: massive/submassive PE, RV MI, acute-on-chronic PAH crisis, sepsis-induced RV failure

nodes.title: Unstable RHF — Initial Resuscitation
nodes.summary: Unstable RHF: norepi + POCUS + V4R + restrained fluids + early PERT/ICU. Peri-arrest PE = 50 mg alteplase push.
nodes.body: Simultaneous priorities (90 seconds): 1. Bedside POCUS — RV/LV ratio, D-sign, McConnell, TAPSE, IVC, aorta, lung sliding 2. Norepinephrine start 0.1 mcg/kg/min — TARGET MAP ≥65 (preserves RV coronary perfusion) 3. NO large-volume bolus — give 250 mL crystalloid only if IVC <2 cm AND collapsing 4. 12-lead ECG + V4R — look for inferior STEMI (RV MI mimics PE) 5. Activate PERT / cards / pulm consults
nodes.recommendation: Norepi first (NOT phenyl), POCUS in 90 sec, NO big bolus, V4R always, alteplase 50 mg push if peri-arrest PE.

nodes.title: POCUS — Right Heart Failure Criteria
nodes.body: See full overlay: POCUS RV Failure Reference for views + values + image plates. Top 6 findings (any one is significant; ≥2 = high specificity): • RV/LV end-diastolic ratio ≥1.0 (apical 4-chamber) — normal <0.6 [6] • D-sign on PSAX — septal flattening = RV pressure overload (acute = systolic D; chronic = diastolic D) • McConnell sign — RV free-wall hypokinesis with apical sparing — >94% specific fo

nodes.title: NOT Right Heart Failure — Common Mimics
nodes.summary: Mimics: tamponade, tension PTX, LHF, hypovolemia, constriction — different management.
nodes.body: Before you commit to RHF management, exclude: • Cardiac tamponade — diastolic RV/RA collapse, swinging heart → pericardiocentesis. Different physiology entirely. • Tension pneumothorax — absent lung sliding + lung point + obstructive shock • Severe LV failure with RV dysfunction — wet lungs, B-lines, dilated LV → afterload reduction OK • Hypovolemic shock — small/collapsing IVC, hyperdynamic LV —
nodes.recommendation: Mimics: tamponade (drain), pneumo (decompress), LHF (treat differently), hypovolemia (fluids OK), constriction (cards). Do NOT apply RHF playbook.

nodes.title: What is driving the RV failure?
nodes.body: Etiology dictates therapy. Use POCUS + ECG + history to pick the dominant trigger:

nodes.title: Acute PE — Severity Stratification
nodes.body: Risk-stratify before choosing therapy. Use sPESI + BOVA + RV imaging + biomarkers (troponin, BNP). Massive (high-risk): sustained SBP <90 ≥15 min, vasopressors required, or arrest Submassive intermediate-high: RV strain on imaging + positive biomarkers + normotensive Submassive intermediate-low: RV strain OR positive biomarker (not both) Low-risk: sPESI 0, no RV strain, normal biomarkers

nodes.title: Massive PE — Reperfusion NOW
nodes.summary: Massive PE = lyse: 100 mg alteplase/2hr or 50 mg push periarrest. CDT/Inari if contraindicated. ECMO bridge.
nodes.body: Systemic thrombolysis (first-line if no absolute contraindications): • Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours (standard FDA dose) • Peri-arrest / arrest: alteplase 50 mg IV push, repeat 50 mg in 15 min if no ROSC; continue CPR ≥60 min after lytic • Hold heparin during infusion, restart aPTT <80 post-lysis Catheter-directed alternatives (call PERT): • CDT/EKOS — local tPA 1 mg/hr × 12-24 hr (lower bleed
nodes.recommendation: Massive PE: alteplase 100 mg/2hr OR 50 mg push if peri-arrest. CDT/thrombectomy if lytic contraindicated. ECMO bridge if available.

nodes.title: Submassive PE Intermediate-High — Catheter > Systemic Lytic
nodes.summary: Submassive int-high: heparin + PERT + CDT/Inari preferred. MOPETT half-dose 50 mg is option. Full lyse if decompensating.
nodes.body: PEITHO showed full-dose lytic in submassive PE reduced decompensation but doubled major bleed (11.5%) and tripled stroke (2.4%) — net negative outside the most ill subset. [11] Modern approach: • Heparin anticoagulation immediately (UFH preferred — titratable) • Activate PERT — multi-D decision • Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT/EKOS) — local tPA 1 mg/hr × 12-24 hr; SEATTLE II showed RV/LV rati
nodes.recommendation: Heparin + PERT activation. CDT/thrombectomy preferred. Half-dose lytic (50 mg) reasonable. Full-dose only if decompensating.

nodes.title: Submassive PE Intermediate-Low — Anticoagulate + Monitor
nodes.summary: Int-low: anticoag + monitor + DOAC bridge + 3-mo CTEPH screen.
nodes.body: Heparin (UFH or LMWH) + admit to monitored bed. • Repeat troponin q6h × 2 to confirm trajectory • Repeat echo if hemodynamics worsen • If stable at 24-48 hr → transition to DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban) per ESC 2019 [4] • Outpatient follow-up at 3 mo for repeat echo + chronic thromboembolic disease screen
nodes.recommendation: Heparin/LMWH + monitor. Transition to DOAC at 24-48h if stable. 3-mo CTEPH screen.

nodes.title: Low-Risk PE — Outpatient Eligible
nodes.summary: Low-risk + HESTIA: discharge on DOAC, follow-up 72h.
nodes.body: HESTIA criteria all met → outpatient candidate with apixaban or rivaroxaban. Apixaban: 10 mg PO BID × 7 days, then 5 mg BID Rivaroxaban: 15 mg PO BID × 21 days, then 20 mg daily Must have: • Hemodynamically stable, sPESI 0, no RV strain on imaging or biomarkers • No active bleed, no severe pain, reliable follow-up <72 hr • Adequate renal function, no pregnancy • Patient understands return precauti
nodes.recommendation: HESTIA-eligible PE: apixaban 10 mg BID×7d→5 mg BID OR rivaroxaban 15 mg BID×21d→20 mg daily. Follow-up <72h.

nodes.title: RV MI — Preload-Dependent Resuscitation
nodes.summary: RV MI: NO nitrates/morphine/diuretics. YES volume + dobutamine + cath lab. Preload-dependent.
nodes.body: Confirm with V4R lead — ST elevation ≥1 mm = RV infarction (40% of inferior MIs). [13] STRONG WARN — DO NOT GIVE: • ❌ Nitrates (nitroglycerin, ISDN) — preload drop = profound hypotension • ❌ Morphine — venodilation • ❌ Diuretics — preload drop • ❌ Beta-blockers acutely — bradycardia + ↓ contractility • ❌ ACE inhibitors acutely DO: • ✅ Volume: 500 mL crystalloid bolus, repeat to JVP/POCUS endpoint
nodes.recommendation: RV MI: NO nitrates/morphine/diuretics/BB. YES volume 500 mL → dobutamine → norepi. Cath lab now. Preserve sinus + AV synchrony.

nodes.title: Acute-on-Chronic PAH Crisis
nodes.summary: PAH crisis: keep home meds, iNO/epo, norepi+vaso, dobutamine, NO bolus, NO phenyl, call PH ctr.
nodes.body: Highest-mortality phenotype — these patients live on the edge of RV failure. Triggers: missed home meds, infection, surgery, dehydration, arrhythmia, anemia. STRONG WARN: • ❌ DO NOT abruptly stop home prostacyclin (epoprostenol/Flolan, treprostinil) — rebound PH crisis can be fatal within hours • ❌ DO NOT give large fluid bolus (>500 mL) — RV dilation worsens ischemia • ❌ DO NOT intubate without p
nodes.recommendation: PAH crisis: never stop home prostacyclin, no big bolus, iNO/inhaled epo, norepi+vaso, dobutamine. Call PH center.

nodes.title: Sepsis-Induced RV Failure
nodes.summary: Sepsis + RHF: small fluids, norepi+vaso, dobutamine, lung-protective, source control.
nodes.body: Sepsis can cause RV failure via: • Acute pulmonary hypertension (cytokines, hypoxic vasoconstriction, microthrombi) • Septic cardiomyopathy involving RV • ARDS-related cor pulmonale Modified resuscitation: • Restrained fluid strategy — POCUS-guided, 250 mL aliquots, stop when IVC plethoric or RV dilates further • Norepinephrine first + vasopressin 0.03 U/min (pulmonary-sparing) • Source control +
nodes.recommendation: Septic RHF: POCUS-guided 250 mL aliquots, norepi+vaso, dobutamine prn, lung-protective vent, source control.

nodes.title: Post-LVAD or Post-Cardiac-Surgery RV Failure
nodes.summary: Post-LVAD: call coordinator, iNO/epo, milrinone, MCS. Never touch LVAD speed alone.
nodes.body: Post-LVAD RV failure occurs in 10-40% of LVAD recipients. Mechanism: increased venous return from improved CO unmasks marginal RV. Critical: contact LVAD coordinator IMMEDIATELY — they have institution-specific protocols. • Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (iNO, inhaled epo) — first-line • Inotropes: milrinone 0.25-0.75 mcg/kg/min preferred (afterload reduction PLUS inotropy) • Avoid systemic vasodi
nodes.recommendation: Post-LVAD RHF: call coordinator NOW. iNO/inhaled epo, milrinone, RV MCS. NEVER adjust LVAD speed unsupervised.

nodes.title: ARDS-Related Cor Pulmonale
nodes.summary: ARDS cor pulmonale: lung+RV-protective vent, prone, iNO, ECMO escalation.
nodes.body: Acute cor pulmonale occurs in 20-25% of ARDS patients and doubles mortality. [19] Lung-protective + RV-protective ventilation: • TV 4-6 mL/kg PBW (already standard) • Plateau pressure ≤27 cm H2O (lower than ARDSNet 30) — protects RV • Driving pressure ≤14 cm H2O • PEEP titrated to RV — NOT lung compliance alone • pH ≥7.20-7.25 (avoid permissive hypercapnia <7.15 — raises PVR) • Prone position if P
nodes.recommendation: ARDS+RHF: plateau ≤27, DP ≤14, PEEP for RV, pH ≥7.20, prone <150, iNO/iEpo, ECMO for refractory.

nodes.title: Fluid Strategy in RHF — POCUS-Guided
nodes.summary: RHF fluid = POCUS-guided 250-500 mL aliquots. Plethoric IVC = stop. RV MI = exception, give volume.
nodes.body: The biggest mistake in RHF is reflexive fluid loading. A dilated RV pushes the septum into the LV, drops LV filling, raises wall stress, and worsens RV ischemia. Decision rule: • IVC small/collapsing + small RV → 250-500 mL bolus, reassess • IVC plethoric OR RV already dilated → NO fluid, go straight to vasopressors/inotropes • Each bolus reassessed at the bedside — no "give 30 mL/kg" reflex Excep
nodes.recommendation: RHF fluid: POCUS first, 250-500 mL aliquots only if IVC small. Plethoric IVC = stop, escalate. RV MI is the exception — volume-dependent.

nodes.title: Pressors + Inotropes in RHF
nodes.summary: Pressor ladder: norepi → +vaso → dobutamine/milrinone → iNO/iEpo. Avoid phenyl alone.
nodes.body: See Pressor/Inotrope Reference Card for full doses. Pressors: • Norepinephrine 0.05-1.0 mcg/kg/min — FIRST-LINE (preserves RV coronary perfusion, modest pulm-vasoconstrictor) • Vasopressin 0.03 U/min — add-on (V1 receptors don't constrict pulmonary vasculature — pulmonary-sparing) • Phenylephrine — AVOID alone (raises PVR > SVR, worsens RV) • Epinephrine — reserve for refractory cardiogenic shock
nodes.recommendation: Norepi first → add vasopressin 0.03 → dobutamine OR milrinone for inotropy → inhaled iNO/epo for pulm afterload. AVOID phenyl alone.

nodes.title: RV-Protective Intubation (Farkas Protocol)
nodes.summary: Farkas RSI: norepi pre-induct, ketamine+etomidate (NO propofol), low TV, low PEEP, pH≥7.25.
nodes.body: Intubation is the leading cause of death in severe RHF/PAH — induction agents drop SVR + preload, positive-pressure ventilation drops RV preload AND raises PVR, hypoxia + hypercapnia at any point arrests these patients. See full bundle: Farkas RV-Protective RSI Pre-induction (mandatory): • Norepinephrine running at MAP ≥75 BEFORE induction (push-dose phenyl is NOT enough) • If known PAH: inhaled N
nodes.recommendation: Farkas bundle: norepi MAP 75 + iNO/iEpo if PAH, ketamine+low-dose etomidate, NO propofol bolus, TV 4-6, PEEP ≤5, pH ≥7.25, FiO2 to 92%.

nodes.title: Disposition — When to Call PERT / PH Team / Transfer
nodes.summary: ICU + PERT + PH ctr + ECMO + GOC.
nodes.body: See full overlay: Disposition + PERT Activation ICU criteria (any one): • Massive or submassive intermediate-high PE • Vasopressor or inotrope requirement • Mechanical ventilation • Lactate >4 or worsening • Active arrhythmia • Post-thrombolysis monitoring Activate PERT (Pulmonary Embolism Response Team) for: • Any massive or submassive PE • Bleeding contraindication to lytic • Decompensation desp
nodes.recommendation: ICU for vasopressors/lytic/intubated. PERT for any massive or escalation. PH ctr for prostacyclin patients. ECMO if refractory. GOC early.

nodes.title: Ring Removal
nodes.body: > First decision: is the finger viable? Vascular compromise = immediate cut, skip the gentle methods. Workflow: 1. Triage neurovascular status 2. Identify ring material (metal grade matters) 3. Choose technique: • Manual reduction with lube • String / Penrose wrap • Ring cutter (standard or heavy-duty) • Diamond bur / rotary (tungsten, ceramic) 4. Post-removal NV recheck + injury workup Steps Summ

nodes.title: Neurovascular Status?
nodes.summary: White/cool = cut now; blue = quick attempt then cut; pink/warm = gentle methods
nodes.body: Examine the digit distal to the ring.

nodes.title: Vascular Compromise — CUT NOW
nodes.body: > Ischemic finger = ring becomes a tourniquet. Every minute matters. Skip lube and string — proceed directly to cutting.
nodes.recommendation: Immediate actions: 1. Elevate hand above heart 2. Ice pack on dorsum (NOT under ring) 3. Digital block with lidocaine plain (epi OK per Prabhakar 2015 but unnecessary) 4. Choose cutter by material 5. Standard ring cutter for gold/silver/alu

nodes.title: Venous Congestion — Limited Time
nodes.summary: Quick attempt OK; escalate to cut if no progress 5 min
nodes.body: Quick attempt allowed, but bias toward cutting if any doubt. Try (max ~3-5 min): • Elevate × 5 min • Ice pack on dorsum + circumferential compression with Coban or Penrose • Lube (surgilube, soap, oil) • ONE attempt at manual reduction Escalate to cut if: • No progress after 5 min • Skin abrasion forming • Color worsening to white • Pain escalating Proceed to material check for cutter selection.

nodes.title: Ring Material?
nodes.summary: Soft metal = standard cutter; tungsten/ceramic = diamond bur or vise
nodes.body: Material dictates cutter — wrong tool wastes time.

nodes.title: Unknown Material
nodes.summary: Ask patient; assume hard if cutter binds in 30-60 s
nodes.body: Ask: "Do you remember what your ring is made of?" — patients often know if it is tungsten or ceramic (popular wedding band materials, marketed as "scratch-proof"). Visual clues: • Tungsten: heavy, very shiny, scratch-resistant, brushed or polished • Ceramic: very light, often black or white, perfectly smooth • Titanium: very light, dull grey-silver • Stainless: silver, magnetic (use magnet) If sti

nodes.title: Manual Reduction Attempt
nodes.summary: Elevate, wrap, lube; pull + rotate; stop after 2-3 failed attempts
nodes.body: > First-line for comfortable finger with intact NV exam. Quick, painless, ring preserved. Setup: 1. Elevate hand × 5 min, ice pack dorsum 2. Wrap circumferentially with elastic bandage (Coban) distal-to-proximal × 5 min to squeeze edema out 3. Generous lubricant: surgilube, soap + water, lidocaine jelly, hand sanitizer, mineral oil 4. Patient elevates arm during attempt Technique: • Grip ring firm

nodes.title: Manual Reduction Result?
nodes.body: Choose next step.

nodes.title: String-Wrap Technique
nodes.summary: Tape under ring → wrap distally tight → pull proximal end → ring walks off
nodes.body: > Inoue method (1995). Compresses edema distal to ring, then unwinds to ratchet ring distally. Contraindications: • Underlying PIP/DIP fracture or laceration • Skin tear under or distal to ring • Already ischemic — cut instead • Failed manual + significant swelling — cut faster Materials: • Umbilical tape, dental floss, 2-0 silk, or thin Penrose drain • Lubricant • Mosquito hemostat Technique: 1.

nodes.title: String-Wrap Result?
nodes.body: Did the ring come off?

nodes.title: Cutter Selection
nodes.summary: Confirm material before picking cutter
nodes.body: Match cutter to material — confirm material before starting.

nodes.title: Standard Ring Cutter
nodes.summary: Guard under ring; cut thinnest section; saline coolant; spread with hemostats
nodes.body: Setup: 1. Digital block with lidocaine plain 1% — 1 mL each side of digit, dorsal approach 2. Slide cutter guard between ring and finger (the small curved hook) 3. Position blade over thinnest part of ring (NOT over a stone setting) Technique: • Engage blade slowly while squeezing handles • Rotate the wheel a few turns each pass • Keep guard between blade and skin throughout • Cool with saline dro

nodes.title: Heavy-Duty / Electric Cutter
nodes.summary: Cool with saline; pause for heat; abort if no bite in 60 s (means tungsten/ceramic)
nodes.body: Indications: thick steel, thick titanium, hardened wedding bands too thick for the standard wheel. Tips: • Same digital block + guard setup • Use saline drip or wet gauze to cool — these blades generate heat • Slow steady pressure; let the tool work • Pause every 15-30 s to check ring and skin temperature • If blade glazes the surface without biting after 60 s → STOP, switch to diamond bur (materi

nodes.title: Tungsten / Ceramic Ring
nodes.summary: Tungsten: vise crack first (brittle); else diamond bur; ceramic: vise almost always works
nodes.body: > Standard cutters fail on these materials. Tungsten is harder than steel; ceramic shatters but is dense. Three working methods: 1. Vise-grip crack (tungsten only — best, fastest): • Wrap finger with thick gauze for protection • Clamp ring with locking pliers / vise-grips at 12 o'clock • Squeeze firmly — tungsten is brittle, will fracture into 2-3 pieces with a CRACK • Repeat at 6 o'clock if neede

nodes.title: Tungsten/Ceramic Result?
nodes.body: Did the ring come off?

nodes.title: Surgical Consult
nodes.body: > Rare scenario — usually only if tungsten ring with severe ischemia and no diamond bur or vise available, or significant underlying soft tissue trauma needs OR exploration.
nodes.recommendation: Actions: • Maintain elevation, monitor NV every 5 min • Call hand surgery / plastic surgery for OR removal • Transfer to ED with equipment if local ED lacks tools • Avoid further manual attempts — wastes ischemic time • Document NV exam, ti

nodes.title: Post-Removal Exam
nodes.summary: Recheck NV, screen for occult fx, x-ray if any concern, elevate ×24 h
nodes.body: > Do not stop at "ring is off." Document NV recovery and screen for underlying injury that caused the swelling. Recheck: • Color, warmth, cap refill (compare contralateral finger) • 2-point discrimination (radial + ulnar digital nerve territories) • Active flexion (FDS, FDP) and extension (EDC, EPL) • Range of motion each joint Imaging: • X-ray if any deformity, point tenderness, joint instability

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: > Document method, NV before and after, and follow-up plan.
nodes.recommendation: Discharge instructions: • Elevate hand above heart × 24 hr • Ice 15 min/hr while awake × 24 hr • Resume normal activity as tolerated • Bacitracin or petrolatum on any abrasion • Avoid rings on the affected finger until swelling resolves ful

nodes.title: Pre-Intubation RV Assessment
nodes.summary: RV dysfunction patients at extreme risk of peri-intubation arrest — PPV increases RV afterload, sedation drops preload, triggers death spiral
nodes.body: Why Assess RV Before Intubation? Patients with RV dysfunction are at extreme risk of cardiovascular collapse during intubation. The Problem: • Sedation causes vasodilation → drops preload • Positive pressure ventilation (PPV) → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return • PPV → ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance → ↑ RV afterload • Hypoxia/hypercapnia during intubation → pulmonary vasoconstriction The

nodes.title: The RV Death Spiral
nodes.summary: RV death spiral: PPV increases afterload, RV dilates, septum shifts into LV (D-sign), CO falls, SBP drops below PASP, RV ischemia, PEA arrest
nodes.body: The Mechanism of Peri-Intubation Arrest in RV Failure: Step 1: PPV increases RV afterload • ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance • When airway pressure > PA pressure, pulmonary vessels collapse Step 2: RV dilates • Thin-walled RV cannot generate enough pressure • Volume backs up → RV enlarges Step 3: Septal shift (D-sign) • Dilated RV pushes septum into LV • LV becomes "D-sha

nodes.title: Clinical Signs of RV Dysfunction
nodes.summary: Clinical signs: JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, hypotension — delirium appears EARLIER in RV than LV failure, ECG shows RAD/RBBB/S1Q3T3
nodes.body: Physical Exam — Signs of Right Heart Failure: | Sign | Significance | |------|-------------| | JVD | Elevated RA pressure | | Peripheral edema | Systemic venous congestion | | Hepatomegaly / RUQ tenderness | Congestive hepatopathy | | Ascites | Advanced RV failure | | Cool extremities | Poor cardiac output | | Hypotension | Cardiogenic shock | | Oliguria | Congestive nephropathy | Early Warning Si

nodes.title: POCUS Assessment — Overview
nodes.summary: 60-90 second POCUS: subcostal (wall thickness/IVC), A4C (RV:LV ratio/TAPSE), PSAX (D-sign) — red flags: RV>LV, TAPSE <10, severe D-sign
nodes.body: Rapid RV Assessment by POCUS Bedside echo takes 60-90 seconds and can identify patients at extreme risk. 3-View Protocol: 1. Subcostal — RV:LV ratio, wall thickness, IVC 2. nodes.title: Normal RV — Standard Approach

nodes.title: Pre-Intubation Optimization
nodes.summary: Optimization checklist: SBP 120-130 (>PASP), vasopressors running, BiPAP preoxygenation, pulmonary vasodilator ready, arterial line, small volume only
nodes.body: The Goal: Optimize BEFORE Induction Every minute spent optimizing reduces peri-intubation risk. Optimization Checklist: □ Hemodynamics • Target SBP 120-130 mmHg (anticipate drop) • Target MAP ~80 mmHg • SBP must exceed PASP (prevents RV ischemia) □ Vasopressors • Norepinephrine infusion running, OR • Push-dose epi + vasopressin at bedside □ Oxygenation • BiPAP with 100% FiO₂ for preoxygenation • G

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Targets

nodes.title: Vasopressor Selection

nodes.body: Preoxygenation for RV Failure: Why BiPAP Is Preferred: • Allows gradual transition to positive pressure • Can monitor hemodynamic response as you increase settings • REVERSIBLE if patient decompensates • PREOXI trial: BiPAP reduced hypoxemia (9.1% vs 18.5%) and cardiac arrest (0.2% vs 1.1%) Technique: 1. nodes.title: Intubation Approach
nodes.summary: Choose optimized RSI (full pre-optimization, fast) vs awake intubation (preserves spontaneous breathing, less hemodynamic perturbation)
nodes.body: Choose Your Approach: Option 1: Optimized RSI • Standard RSI with full optimization • Ketamine or etomidate • Vasopressor support • Rapid sequence Option 2: Awake/Spontaneously Breathing • Preserves spontaneous breathing • Less hemodynamic perturbation • Ketamine sedation + topicalization • Strongly consider for severe PAH Decision Factors: | Factor | Favors RSI | Favors Awake | |--------|--------

nodes.title: RSI Drug Selection
nodes.summary: Ketamine or etomidate both reasonable — reduce dose in shock, rocuronium 1.2-1.6mg/kg, optimization matters more than drug choice
nodes.body: Induction Agent Selection: | Agent | Dose | Advantages | Disadvantages | |-------|------|------------|---------------| | Ketamine | 1-2 mg/kg | Sympathomimetic, bronchodilator | RSI trial: 22% cardiovascular collapse vs 17% etomidate; catecholamine-depleted patients may not respond | | Etomidate | 0.2-0.3 mg/kg | Hemodynamically stable | Adrenal suppression (likely not significant for single dose)

nodes.title: RSI Technique
nodes.summary: RSI sequence: BiPAP preox, confirm optimization, pre-treat with push-dose epi + vasopressin, induce, intubate rapidly, start inhaled vasodilator
nodes.body: RSI Sequence for RV Failure: 1. Pre-oxygenate with BiPAP (minimum 3 minutes, FiO₂ 100%) 2. Confirm optimization: • SBP >120, MAP ~80 • Vasopressors running or push-dose ready • Inhaled pulmonary vasodilator at bedside 3. Pre-treat: Push-dose epi (10-20 mcg) + vasopressin (1-2 units) 4. Induce: • Ketamine 1-1.5 mg/kg OR etomidate 0.2-0.3 mg/kg • Rocuronium 1.2-1.6 mg/kg 5. Maintain oxygenation: • B

nodes.title: Awake Intubation Option
nodes.summary: Awake intubation: ketamine 0.5-1mg/kg dissociative dose + topical lidocaine, preserves spontaneous ventilation and negative intrathoracic pressure
nodes.body: Awake/Spontaneously Breathing Intubation: When to Consider: • Severe RV dysfunction (RV > LV, TAPSE <10mm) • Known severe pulmonary hypertension • Previous peri-intubation arrest or near-arrest • Cooperative patient with reasonable airway Advantages: • Preserves spontaneous ventilation • Maintains negative intrathoracic pressure longer • Less hemodynamic perturbation • Gradual transition to PPV Te

nodes.body: The Critical 15-30 Minutes This is when patients "insidiously slip into an RV death spiral." Monitor intensively. Immediate Actions: 1. Connect to ventilator immediately - Do NOT bag aggressively - Each squeeze increases intrathoracic pressure 2. Start inhaled pulmonary vasodilator at maximal dose 3. nodes.title: Salicylate Toxicity — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Order salicylate level, ABG, BMP, APAP level — classify as acute, chronic, or unknown exposure type
nodes.body: Salicylate Toxicity Steps Summary — quick-reference pathway. Order labs: Salicylate level, ABG/VBG, BMP (Na, Cl, HCO3, K, Cr, glucose), lactate, acetaminophen level (common co-ingestant). Clinical suspicion triggers: Unexplained tachypnea/hyperpnea, tinnitus, altered mental status, unexplained anion gap metabolic acidosis, mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis. nodes.summary: Estimate mg/kg dose — oil of wintergreen is 1400mg/mL; enteric-coated delays peak 12-24hr
nodes.body: Estimate the ingested dose (mg/kg) from history. If uncertain, assume worst case. Oil of wintergreen warning: 1 mL of methyl salicylate = ~1,400 mg aspirin. A single teaspoon (~5 mL) = ~7,000 mg — potentially lethal in a child. [1][3][15][22] Enteric-coated tablets: Peak absorption may be delayed 12-24 hours. Extended observation required. nodes.title: Chronic Salicylate Toxicity
nodes.summary: Chronic toxicity is underrecognized and more lethal at same levels — Done nomogram does NOT apply
nodes.body: Chronic toxicity is underrecognized and more lethal than acute toxicity at the same serum levels. [2][4] Commonly elderly patients on chronic aspirin or salicylate-containing products (Pepto-Bismol, topical products, combination cold medicines). Often misdiagnosed as sepsis, CHF exacerbation, dementia, or delirium. Chronic Toxicity Recognition Key point: The Done nomogram does NOT apply to chronic

nodes.title: Chronic Toxicity — Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Clinical status matters more than level in chronic toxicity — assess for AMS, acidemia, pulmonary edema
nodes.body: Clinical status is more important than serum level in chronic toxicity. [9][15][21] Assess for signs of severe toxicity:

nodes.title: Low-Risk Acute Ingestion (< 150 mg/kg)
nodes.summary: Observe 6hr minimum (12hr enteric-coated), repeat levels at 2hr and 4hr — reassess if rising
nodes.body: Minimal symptoms expected at this dose. [1][18] • Observe minimum 6 hours (children and adults) [18] • Repeat salicylate level at 2 and 4 hours [18] • Enteric-coated tablets: Observe minimum 12 hours (delayed absorption) [18][22] • If levels declining and patient remains asymptomatic → observation pathway • If levels rising → reassess risk category

nodes.title: Moderate Risk (150-300 mg/kg)
nodes.summary: Start alkalinization early, GI decon, NEVER use normal saline — serial levels q2h
nodes.body: Expect symptomatic toxicity: tachypnea, tinnitus, nausea/vomiting. [1][18] • Start alkalinization early [6][15] • GI decontamination if within window [7] • Check acetaminophen level (common co-ingestant in intentional OD) [15] • Serial salicylate levels q2h [15][18] • Volume resuscitate — NEVER with normal saline (acidifying). Use D5W or LR. [2][15]

nodes.title: Severe/Massive Ingestion (> 300 mg/kg)
nodes.summary: Life-threatening >300mg/kg — consult nephrology EARLY for HD, anticipate rapid deterioration
nodes.body: Life-threatening ingestion. > 500 mg/kg is potentially lethal. [1][3][18] • EARLY nephrology consult for hemodialysis — do not wait for clinical deterioration [5][12][15] • Anticipate rapid deterioration: metabolic acidosis, altered mental status, seizures [15] • Start alkalinization immediately [6][15] • Activated charcoal if within window and airway protected [7] • Volume resuscitate with D5W or

nodes.title: Unknown Timing — Worst-Case Approach
nodes.summary: Treat as moderate-severe until proven otherwise — serial levels q2h to determine trajectory
nodes.body: Treat as moderate-severe until proven otherwise. [2][15] • Serial salicylate levels q2h — determine if rising (acute with delayed absorption) or plateauing (chronic) [15][18] • If level rising: may indicate enteric-coated, bezoar, or recent large ingestion [18][22] • If level elevated with acidemia out of proportion: consider chronic toxicity [9][21] • Start alkalinization if symptomatic or level

nodes.title: Resuscitation Assessment
nodes.summary: Volume resuscitate with isotonic bicarb or LR — NEVER normal saline; give D50W for any AMS even with normal glucose
nodes.body: Volume resuscitate — patients are often 4-6L depleted (diaphoresis, tachypnea, vomiting, diarrhea). [2] • Use isotonic bicarbonate (if pH < 7.5) or LR/Plasmalyte (if at target pH). NEVER normal saline. [2] • Check fingerstick glucose — give Dextrose D50W empirically for any AMS, even with normal serum glucose (neuroglycopenia). [2][4][17] Assess for immediate threats:

nodes.title: Seizures / Severe Altered Mental Status
nodes.summary: BZD for seizures, empiric D50W even with normal glucose (neuroglycopenia) — seizures = severe, needs HD
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines first-line for seizures: • Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) • Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM (max 10 mg) if no IV access Empiric dextrose: Dextrose D50W 50 mL IV — even with NORMAL serum glucose. Salicylate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, causing massive CNS glucose consumption (neuroglycopenia). CSF glucose drops before serum glucose. [2][4][17] Seizures in salicylate toxicity = sev

nodes.title: THE DANGEROUS AIRWAY
nodes.summary: Intubation causes cardiac arrest by eliminating compensatory hyperventilation — HFNC preferred, avoid RSI if possible
nodes.body: CRITICAL WARNING: Intubation in salicylate toxicity is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS and frequently causes cardiac arrest. [2][3][4][15][16] The Dangerous Airway — Death Spiral The patient's compensatory hyperventilation (often RR 30-40) is the ONLY thing maintaining their pH. If you eliminate this compensation during intubation, pH crashes precipitously → more non-ionized salicylate crosses the BBB → brain

nodes.title: Intubation Protocol — Call for EMERGENT Hemodialysis
nodes.body: If intubation is unavoidable: [2][3][4][15][16] • Pre-intubation: Bolus Sodium Bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV. Give >5-10 minutes before paralysis to allow CO2 blow-off from infused bicarb. • Intubation: Most experienced operator. Rapid sequence. Consider ketamine (maintains respiratory drive longest). • Post-intubation ventilator settings: TV 8 mL/kg, RR 30-35 (match pre-intubation minute ventilation)
nodes.recommendation: EMERGENT: Call nephrology STAT for hemodialysis. Continue NaHCO3 infusion. Vent settings: TV 8 mL/kg, RR 30-35, target pH not pCO2. ABG q15min initially.

nodes.title: Non-Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
nodes.summary: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema from capillary leak — BiPAP to temporize, this is HD indication
nodes.body: Occurs in severe toxicity from direct capillary leak injury. NOT volume overload. [1][2][3][13][22] • BiPAP/CPAP may temporize — avoid intubation if possible [15][16] • Volume-restrict (despite general hypovolemia) [2][15] • This is an indication for EMERGENT hemodialysis [5][15] • If progressing to respiratory failure requiring intubation, see airway warning

nodes.title: GI Decontamination
nodes.summary: Charcoal effective for salicylates with extended window (2-4hr) due to delayed gastric emptying
nodes.body: Activated charcoal effectively adsorbs salicylate. Salicylate's delayed gastric emptying may extend the window of efficacy. [1][3][7] Do NOT induce emesis. Gastric lavage is rarely indicated. [7][15][18] Time since ingestion and formulation:

nodes.title: Single-Dose Activated Charcoal
nodes.summary: Activated charcoal 1g/kg (max 50g) — extended window for salicylates, may repeat in 4hr if levels rising
nodes.body: Activated Charcoal 1 g/kg PO (max 50g). [7] Most effective within 1 hour, but consider up to 2-4 hours for salicylates (delayed gastric emptying in overdose, bezoar formation). [1][18][22] Contraindications: Unprotected airway, bowel obstruction/perforation, caustic co-ingestion. [7] A second dose of charcoal may be given 4 hours later if salicylate levels continue to rise. [1][15][19]

nodes.title: Multi-Dose Charcoal / Whole Bowel Irrigation
nodes.summary: MDAC 25g q2-4h or whole bowel irrigation for enteric-coated/bezoar — monitor for obstipation
nodes.body: For enteric-coated formulations or massive ingestions with suspected bezoar: [1][3] Multi-dose activated charcoal (MDAC): Activated Charcoal 25g q2-4h for 3-4 additional doses. Monitor for obstipation. [19] Whole bowel irrigation (WBI): PEG-electrolyte solution (GoLYTELY) via NG at 1.5-2 L/hr (adults). Consider for confirmed bezoar on imaging or persistently rising levels despite charcoal. May req

nodes.title: Alkalinization — Cornerstone of Treatment
nodes.summary: Urinary alkalinization is cornerstone — urine pH 8.0 increases clearance 10-fold vs pH 6.0
nodes.body: Urinary alkalinization is the CORNERSTONE of salicylate management. [1][2][3][4][15][22] Alkalinization Protocol Detail Mechanism: Alkaline urine ionizes salicylic acid → trapped in renal tubules → cannot be reabsorbed. Urine pH 8.0 increases renal clearance 10-fold vs pH 6.0. [2][6][8] Even if the patient is already alkalemic from respiratory alkalosis (pH up to 7.55), bicarbonate is still benefi

nodes.title: NaHCO3 — Bolus + Infusion
nodes.summary: NaHCO3 bolus 1-2 mEq/kg then infusion in D5W — target urine pH 7.5-8.0; NEVER use NS carrier; acetazolamide CONTRAINDICATED
nodes.body: Sodium Bicarbonate Bolus: 1-2 mEq/kg IV (typically 2-3 amps of 8.4% NaHCO3). [2][3][6][15] Infusion: 150 mEq (3 amps 8.4%) in 1L D5W at 150-200 mL/hr. [2][6][15][22] • D5W carrier provides CNS glucose support • NEVER use normal saline as carrier — acidifying (SID = 0) [2] Targets: [2][6][15] • Serum pH: 7.45-7.55 (check q2h) • Urine pH: 7.5-8.0 (check hourly via Foley) • Do NOT exceed serum pH > 7

nodes.title: CRITICAL — Potassium Repletion
nodes.summary: Hypokalemia BLOCKS urinary alkalinization — replete K+ to 4.0-4.5 mEq/L; add 20-40 mEq KCl per liter of bicarb
nodes.body: Hypokalemia BLOCKS urinary alkalinization. You CANNOT achieve alkaline urine without adequate K+. [1][2][3][6] When K+ is low, the distal tubule reabsorbs K+ and excretes H+ instead — producing acidic urine despite systemic alkalosis. No amount of bicarbonate will overcome this. [6][22] KCl IV 20-40 mEq/hr IV (with cardiac monitoring for rates > 20 mEq/hr). [2] Add 20-40 mEq KCl per liter of bicar

nodes.title: Dextrose for Neuroglycopenia
nodes.summary: D50W empirically for any AMS even with normal serum glucose — CSF glucose drops before serum from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation
nodes.body: Dextrose D50W 50 mL IV for any AMS or declining mental status — even with NORMAL serum glucose. [2][4][15] Salicylate uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in CNS mitochondria → massive local glucose consumption → CSF glucose drops critically low while serum glucose remains normal. This neuroglycopenia causes altered mental status and seizures that may respond to dextrose. [4][17] • Add D5W to all m

nodes.title: Alkalinization Monitoring
nodes.summary: Monitor urine pH hourly, ABG q1-2h — declining tachypnea or persistent acidic urine are warning signs
nodes.body: Monitor q1-2h: ABG/VBG, BMP (K+, HCO3, glucose), salicylate level, urine pH. [1][2][3][6][15] Level Interpretation & Monitoring Warning signs during monitoring: • Declining tachypnea (losing compensation — death spiral risk) [15] • Persistent acidic urine despite bicarb (check K+) [6] • Rising salicylate levels (ongoing absorption, bezoar) [18] • Worsening mental status (tissue redistribution) [15

nodes.title: Alkalinization Working — Continue
nodes.summary: Continue infusion until level <30 declining x2 — do NOT stop on single level, taper slowly to avoid rebound acidosis
nodes.body: Continue infusion until: [1][2][15][18] • Salicylate level < 30 mg/dL AND trending down on serial levels • Patient clinically improving (resolving tachypnea, normal mental status) • Acid-base normalizing Do NOT stop based on a single level — redistribution from tissue stores can cause rebound. [2][15] Taper bicarb slowly — sudden discontinuation can cause rebound acidosis. Continue K+ repletion th

nodes.title: Alkalinization Not Working
nodes.summary: Check K+ first (most common cause), then renal function and volume — alkalinization failure itself indicates HD
nodes.body: If urine pH remains < 7.0 despite adequate bicarbonate infusion: [1][2][3][6] #1 — Check K+. Hypokalemia is the most common cause of alkalinization failure. Replete aggressively. [6][15] #2 — Assess renal function. AKI prevents renal excretion of both acid and salicylate. [5][15] #3 — Volume status. Hypovolemia → increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption. nodes.title: Hemodialysis Indications (EXTRIP)
nodes.summary: EXTRIP criteria: level >100 acute, pH <7.20, AMS/seizures, pulm edema, renal failure — consult nephrology early
nodes.body: Hemodialysis is extremely effective for salicylate toxicity — removes salicylate AND corrects acidosis simultaneously. [2][5][12][15] EXTRIP Hemodialysis Indications Consult nephrology early. HD takes time to arrange (access, setup). Patients who need emergent HD often deteriorate faster than logistics allow. [2][12][15] EXTRIP Recommended — regardless of level: [5] • Altered mental status • ARDS

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Protocol
nodes.summary: Standard intermittent HD preferred over CRRT — continue NaHCO3 during and after HD; expect tissue rebound
nodes.body: Standard intermittent HD preferred over CRRT — much higher clearance rate. Even in hypotension (since fluid isn't being removed, HD doesn't worsen hemodynamics). [2][5][15] • Continue Sodium Bicarbonate infusion DURING and AFTER HD [5][15] • HD removes salicylate from blood but tissue stores redistribute after HD [5][15] • Typical duration: 4-6 hours • Continue K+ repletion • Continue glucose moni

nodes.title: Post-HD Rebound Monitoring
nodes.summary: Recheck level 2hr post-HD — if rebounds >30 or symptoms recur, repeat HD; some need 2-3 sessions
nodes.body: Rebound is expected. Salicylate redistributes from tissue stores to blood after HD. [2][5][15] • Recheck salicylate level 2 hours post-HD [5][15] • If level rebounds > 30 mg/dL or symptoms recur → repeat HD [5][15] • Continue alkalinization between and after HD sessions [15] • Some patients with massive ingestions need 2-3 HD sessions • Follow salicylate levels and clinical status after each sessi

nodes.title: Early Nephrology Consult
nodes.summary: Consult nephrology early — HD setup takes 1-2hr; better to have them at bedside and cancel if unneeded
nodes.body: Consult nephrology EARLY — before the patient meets strict indications. [2][12][15] HD takes time to arrange: • Vascular access (dialysis catheter placement) • Dialysis nursing and equipment setup • May take 1-2+ hours from consult to running It is better to have nephrology at bedside and cancel if not needed than to need emergent HD without access. Hemodialysis is documented to be underutilized a
