nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: All symptomatic patients require admission; intentional ingestion needs psych eval when medically cleared
nodes.body: All symptomatic patients require admission. [1][18] Intentional ingestion requires psychiatric evaluation when medically cleared. Chronic toxicity: lower threshold for ICU admission (higher mortality, more insidious course). [2][9][21] Clinical course:

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission for: [1][2][15] • Any patient who received hemodialysis [5] • Required intubation [16] • Seizures [15] • Pulmonary edema [13][15] • Persistent acidemia (pH < 7.30) [15] • Ongoing alkalinization infusion [6] • Altered mental status [15] Continue serial labs q2-4h. Watch for rebound after HD. [5][15] Psychiatric evaluation when medically stable if intentional ingestion. Poison Control:
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. Continue serial salicylate levels, ABG, BMP. Watch for post-HD rebound. Psychiatric evaluation when medically cleared for intentional ingestions.

nodes.title: Floor / Monitored Bed Admission
nodes.body: Symptomatic with improving trajectory. [1][2][15][18] • Continue serial salicylate levels q4h [18] • May need continued alkalinization — transfer to ICU if worsening [6][15] • Transition to KCl PO for ongoing K+ repletion [6] • Continue D5W-based IV fluids [15][17] Psychiatric evaluation if intentional ingestion. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored bed. Serial salicylate levels q4h. Continue alkalinization if needed. Psychiatric evaluation for intentional ingestions.

nodes.title: Observation / Discharge Criteria
nodes.body: Low-risk ingestion with two consecutive declining levels below 25 mg/dL and asymptomatic. [1][3][18] Minimum observation periods: • Standard tablets: 6 hours [18] • Enteric-coated tablets: 12 hours minimum (delayed absorption) [18][22] • Accidental pediatric ingestion < 150 mg/kg: 6 hours with serial levels [1][18] Discharge criteria: [18][22] • Asymptomatic • Two consecutive declining levels in t
nodes.recommendation: Discharge if asymptomatic with two declining levels < 25 mg/dL and normal acid-base. Psychiatric evaluation mandatory for intentional ingestions. Return for tinnitus, rapid breathing, confusion.

nodes.title: SCAPE High-Dose Nitroglycerin
nodes.summary: SCAPE requires immediate NIV plus high-dose nitroglycerin to rapidly reduce afterload/preload.
nodes.body: SCAPE Steps SCAPE is sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pulmonary edema, and high catecholamine tone. ED first-line therapy is noninvasive ventilation plus rapidly titrated high-dose Nitroglycerin. Nitroprusside is not the usual ED first-line pathway; see the Nitroprusside? tool for cautions.

nodes.title: SCAPE Pattern?
nodes.summary: High-dose nitrates are for hypertensive flash pulmonary edema, not hypotensive shock.
nodes.body: Does the patient fit SCAPE physiology?

nodes.title: Not SCAPE: Shock Pathway
nodes.summary: Hypotensive pulmonary edema is not a high-dose nitrate indication.
nodes.body: If pulmonary edema is accompanied by hypotension, cold shock, RV infarct, or cardiogenic shock, do not use high-dose nitrate strategy. Actions: - Oxygenation/ventilation support - Bedside echo and ECG - Vasopressors/inotropes as indicated - Treat MI, dysrhythmia, mechanical valve/papillary muscle rupture, PE, tamponade, or sepsis as appropriate - Early ICU/cardiology involvement
nodes.recommendation: Use cardiogenic shock pathway rather than high-dose nitrate SCAPE protocol.

nodes.title: Alternative Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Use high-dose SCAPE dosing only for the appropriate hypertensive phenotype.
nodes.body: If SCAPE physiology is not present, target the likely cause: - COPD/asthma: bronchodilators, steroids, ventilation strategy - Pneumonia/ARDS: antibiotics, sepsis/ARDS care - PE: PE risk stratification - ACS without severe HTN: ACS pathway Nitrates may still be appropriate for ACS/HTN/pulmonary edema, but not high-dose SCAPE dosing unless the hypertensive crashing phenotype is present.
nodes.recommendation: Treat the primary respiratory/cardiac diagnosis rather than applying high-dose SCAPE dosing.

nodes.title: Contraindication Check
nodes.summary: Contraindications must be checked before high-dose nitrate escalation.
nodes.body: Any high-risk nitrate contraindication?

nodes.title: Nitrate Safety Stop
nodes.summary: Contraindications should stop high-dose nitrate use.
nodes.body: Avoid high-dose nitroglycerin when: - SBP is low or rapidly falling - RV infarct/preload-dependent state is likely - Recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure: sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 hr, tadalafil within 48 hr - Severe aortic stenosis or obstructive HCM with instability - Marked anemia/raised ICP concern where nitrate is unsafe Use NIV/oxygenation, bedside echo/ECG, and shock/ACS-specific managemen
nodes.recommendation: Hold high-dose nitrate protocol and manage with alternative pathway.

nodes.title: NIV First Minutes
nodes.summary: NIV plus nitrate should start immediately and concurrently.
nodes.body: Immediate actions: - Sit upright - Apply noninvasive ventilation immediately, typically CPAP/BiPAP with high EPAP/PEEP - Start high-dose Nitroglycerin concurrently; do not wait for diuretics - Obtain ECG, CXR/POCUS, troponin/BNP/BMP as stabilization allows NIV and nitroglycerin should improve work of breathing and BP within minutes when SCAPE is the correct physiology.

nodes.title: High-Dose Nitroglycerin
nodes.summary: SCAPE often needs rapid high-dose nitroglycerin titration rather than slow standard CHF dosing.
nodes.body: Common ED approach for severe hypertensive SCAPE: - While preparing infusion: SL nitroglycerin 0.4 mg q5 min if able - Loading-dose strategy (current EMCrit/IBCC): a front-loaded IV bolus of ~600-2000 mcg over ~2 min (titrated to initial SBP), OR a brief high-rate infusion of 400-800 mcg/min for ~2.5 min, to rapidly break the crisis. Higher end for SBP >200. - IV push strategy by protocol: nitrogl

nodes.title: Monitoring / Response
nodes.summary: Response should be rapid; failure should trigger reassessment and escalation.
nodes.body: Expected response: - Reduced dyspnea and diaphoresis - Falling BP without hypotension - Improved oxygenation and ventilator synchrony - Decreased rales/work of breathing If not improving: - Reconfirm diagnosis - Check mask seal/NIV settings - Escalate nitrate if BP remains very high and no contraindication - Evaluate ACS, valve catastrophe, dysrhythmia, renal failure, PE, aortic syndrome, sepsis -

nodes.title: Diuretics / After Stabilization
nodes.summary: Diuretics may be needed, but NIV/high-dose nitrate are the immediate SCAPE priorities.
nodes.body: Furosemide is not the first-minute treatment for SCAPE physiology. Use diuretics after initial stabilization when volume overload is likely: - Chronic CHF with congestion - Renal failure/volume overload - Clear volume excess after BP/WOB improve Avoid delaying NIV and nitrates while waiting for diuretic effect. In SCAPE, the immediate problem is often afterload/sympathetic redistribution rather th

nodes.title: Nitroprusside?
nodes.summary: Nitroprusside is an ICU hypertensive emergency tool, not routine first-line ED SCAPE care.
nodes.body: Nitroprusside is not the usual ED first-line SCAPE medication. Why nitroglycerin is preferred in the ED: - Familiar ACS/pulmonary edema medication - Rapid titration - Venous and arterial dilation at high dose - No cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity concern - Easier transition as patient stabilizes Nitroprusside may be considered in ICU-level hypertensive emergency with invasive monitoring and expert ove

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: SCAPE patients need monitored disposition and cause-directed therapy after rescue.
nodes.body: Disposition: - ICU/stepdown while on high-dose nitrate infusion or NIV - Cardiology/ICU if ACS, valve emergency, persistent respiratory failure, renal failure, or recurrent SCAPE - Wean nitrate only after sustained work-of-breathing and BP improvement - Transition to oral antihypertensives/diuresis after cause is clarified Document peak nitroglycerin dose, response time, BP nadir, NIV settings, EC
nodes.recommendation: Continue monitored care until BP, oxygenation, and precipitating cause are controlled.

nodes.title: Sedation Options
nodes.summary: Side-by-side sedative comparison for ED procedures, agitation, ICU sedation, withdrawal, frailty, acidosis, and QT risk.
nodes.body: Use this as a pharmacy-side comparison of ED sedatives. Open first: - Visual Sedative Comparison - Use-Case Selector - Do NOT / Pitfalls Core rule: choose the drug by the clinical target, not by habit. Analgesia, anxiolysis, amnesia, dissociation, deep hypnosis, cooperative sedation, withdrawal control, and chemical control are different goals.

nodes.title: What Is the Sedation Goal?
nodes.summary: Choose by target: procedure, agitation, ICU, withdrawal, fragile physiology, or drug comparison.
nodes.body: Pick the clinical target first. The fastest drug is not always the safest drug.

nodes.title: Procedural Sedation Strategy
nodes.summary: Procedural sedation starts with rescue setup, then agent choice by pain, depth, hemodynamics, and airway risk.
nodes.body: Before medication: - Dedicated monitor, not the procedure operator. - Suction, oxygen, BVM, airway adjuncts, and rescue meds ready. - Continuous SpO2, BP cycling, ECG for deeper sedation or risk, and capnography when available. - Painful procedures need analgesia unless using dissociative ketamine. Choose the procedure profile.

nodes.title: Propofol
nodes.summary: Propofol: onset seconds, duration 3-10 min, clean fast off, no analgesia, apnea/hypotension are the big risks.
nodes.body: Fast hypnotic. No analgesia. Onset/duration: - IV onset: 15-60 sec. - Clinical duration: 3-10 min after bolus. Best use: - Brief deep procedural sedation. - Cardioversion or reduction when airway-ready team is present. - Post-intubation deep sedation when BP tolerates it. - Status epilepticus ICU infusion after airway control. Major risks: - Apnea and airway obstruction can occur quickly. - Dose-d
nodes.recommendation: Use propofol when rapid titratable hypnosis and rapid recovery are the priority and airway/BP rescue are ready.

nodes.title: Ketamine
nodes.summary: Ketamine: dissociation plus analgesia, IV onset <1 min, IM 3-5 min, watch saliva/emesis/laryngospasm and post-dose airway risk.
nodes.body: Dissociative sedative with analgesia and amnesia. Onset/duration: - IV onset: 30-60 sec. - IM onset: 3-5 min. - IV duration: 10-20 min. - IM duration: 15-30 min, recovery longer. Best use: - Painful procedure where dissociation is desired. - Immediate dangerous agitation when prolonged struggle is more dangerous. - Asthma/bronchospasm or need to avoid hypotension. - Analgesic adjunct at subdissoci
nodes.recommendation: Use ketamine for dissociation, analgesia, severe agitation, or bronchospasm, but reassess airway and physiology after control.

nodes.title: Etomidate
nodes.summary: Etomidate: fast brief hypnosis, less BP effect than propofol, no analgesia, myoclonus and adrenal suppression signal.
nodes.body: Short hypnotic. No analgesia. Onset/duration: - IV onset: 30-60 sec. - Clinical duration: 3-10 min. Best use: - RSI induction when hemodynamic neutrality is useful. - Very brief procedures when propofol hypotension is a major concern. - Cardioversion or reduction when analgesia is handled separately. Major risks: - Myoclonus is common and can interfere with reductions or imaging. - Nausea/vomiting
nodes.recommendation: Use etomidate when a very short hypnotic with less immediate BP depression is useful, but plan analgesia and myoclonus management.

nodes.title: Benzodiazepine / Opioid Strategy
nodes.summary: Benzos provide anxiolysis/amnesia but no analgesia; opioids provide analgesia but no amnesia; together they depress ventilation.
nodes.body: Midazolam provides anxiolysis, amnesia, and sedation. Fentanyl provides analgesia. Together they can cause synergistic respiratory depression. Midazolam: - IV onset: 1-5 min; IM 5-15 min; IN 5-10 min. - Duration: usually 30-60 min IV, longer in older/frail, hepatic disease, or repeated dosing. - No analgesia. Lorazepam: - Slower onset and longer duration. - Best for withdrawal and seizures, not qu

nodes.title: Nitrous Oxide
nodes.summary: Nitrous: onset 2-5 min, offset 3-5 min, great for brief cooperative procedures, avoid closed gas spaces.
nodes.body: Rapid inhaled anxiolysis with mild analgesia. Onset/duration: - Onset: 2-5 min. - Offset: usually 3-5 min after stopping and oxygen washout. Best use: - Short pediatric or adult procedure. - Laceration repair, IV start, abscess setup, minor orthopedic manipulation. - Patient needs to leave quickly and can cooperate with mask. Major risks: - Nausea/vomiting, dizziness, dysphoria, diffusion into clo

nodes.title: Agitation / Aggression Strategy
nodes.summary: Agitation sedation depends on immediate danger and physiology, not just psychiatric diagnosis.
nodes.body: First decide whether the patient is an immediate danger or whether evaluation can happen first. Do not let the label drive the drug. Match the physiology: - Immediate threat: fastest reliable control. - Stimulant/hyperthermia/withdrawal/seizure: benzodiazepine physiology. - Psychosis/undifferentiated severe agitation: antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine often works faster than either alone. - Frail,

nodes.title: Droperidol
nodes.summary: Droperidol: fast ED agitation drug, 2-4 h duration, QT/EPS cautions, often paired with midazolam.
nodes.body: Butyrophenone antipsychotic and antiemetic. Onset/duration: - IV onset: 3-10 min. - IM onset: 5-15 min. - Duration: often 2-4 h, sometimes longer. Best use: - Undifferentiated severe agitation. - Nausea, migraine, cannabinoid hyperemesis per local practice. - Combination with midazolam for faster agitation control when QT/stimulant hyperthermia are not dominant. Major risks: - QT prolongation in s
nodes.recommendation: Droperidol is a strong ED agitation option, but check QT risk when practical and avoid repeated dosing in high-risk QT patients.

nodes.title: Haloperidol / Olanzapine
nodes.summary: Haloperidol is slower but familiar; olanzapine lasts longer; both need QT/EPS/frailty/Parkinson caution.
nodes.body: Haloperidol: - IM onset: 15-30 min; IV onset faster but QT/EPS monitoring matters. - Duration: 4-8 h or longer. - Best for psychosis, delirium agitation when slower onset acceptable, and when respiratory depression from benzos is undesirable. - Major risks: QT prolongation, EPS, dystonia, akathisia, NMS, Parkinson/Lewy worsening. Olanzapine: - IM onset: 15-30 min; PO/ODT often 30-60 min. - Duratio

nodes.title: ICU / Post-Intubation Sedation
nodes.summary: ICU sedation should be analgesia-first, RASS-targeted, and usually propofol/dex over benzodiazepine infusions when feasible.
nodes.body: PADIS-style approach: - Treat pain first. - Target light sedation when feasible. - Use RASS or another scale. - Propofol or dexmedetomidine are generally preferred over benzodiazepine infusions for mechanically ventilated adults when feasible. Pick the ICU target.

nodes.title: Dexmedetomidine
nodes.summary: Dex: cooperative light sedation with preserved respirations, slow onset, brady/hypotension are limiting.
nodes.body: Alpha-2 agonist. Cooperative sedation without meaningful respiratory depression. Onset/duration: - No-load onset: 15-30 min. - Loading onset: 5-10 min, but loading can cause bradycardia/hypotension. - Context-sensitive offset: often 30-120 min after stopping. Best use: - Light ICU sedation, extubation bridge, NIV tolerance, awake airway cooperation, anxious but cooperative patient. - Delirium-pron
nodes.recommendation: Use dexmedetomidine for cooperative light sedation when respiratory drive preservation is important and brady/hypotension risk is acceptable.

nodes.title: Withdrawal / Seizure-Risk Sedation
nodes.summary: Withdrawal requires seizure-preventing GABAergic treatment; dex is adjunct only.
nodes.body: Withdrawal sedation is physiology treatment, not just calming. Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal need GABAergic therapy that prevents seizures and delirium tremens. Dexmedetomidine may control tachycardia/agitation but does not treat seizure risk.

nodes.title: Phenobarbital
nodes.summary: Phenobarbital: good withdrawal physiology drug, IV onset minutes, very long tail, respiratory depression with co-sedatives.
nodes.body: Long-acting barbiturate with GABAergic and anti-glutamate effects. Onset/duration: - IV onset: about 5-30 min depending on rate and endpoint. - IM onset: slower and less titratable. - Clinical duration: many hours; half-life about 3-4 days. Best use: - Alcohol withdrawal, especially escalating benzodiazepine needs or protocolized phenobarbital pathway. - Refractory withdrawal adjunct or alternativ
nodes.recommendation: Use phenobarbital for withdrawal physiology when a protocol and monitoring plan exist; respect the long tail and co-sedative stacking.

nodes.title: Special Population / High-Risk Physiology
nodes.summary: Special populations change the drug choice more than the procedure sometimes.
nodes.body: Pick the constraint that should dominate drug choice.

nodes.title: Older / Frail Patient
nodes.summary: Older/frail patients need lower starts, slower redosing, less stacking, and more respiratory/QT/delirium caution.
nodes.body: Principles: - Start 25-50% lower for most sedatives. - Redose slowly after observed effect, not by clock alone. - Avoid benzodiazepines for routine delirium when possible. - Avoid dopamine-blocking antipsychotics in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia. - Avoid stacking opioids, benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, alcohol, and sleep meds. - Consider etomidate or carefully reduced ketamine/propofol

nodes.title: Severe Acidosis / Shock
nodes.summary: Severe acidosis needs ventilation planning, reduced dosing, and immediate post-airway minute ventilation matching.
nodes.body: The danger is not just the sedative. It is loss of compensatory ventilation and collapse after apnea, paralysis, or hypotension. Principles: - Preoxygenate and resuscitate before sedation when feasible. - Avoid post-intubation hypoventilation in metabolic acidosis; match minute ventilation immediately. - Reduce induction/sedative doses in shock. - Propofol can abruptly drop BP and stop breathing.

nodes.title: QT / ECG Risk
nodes.summary: QT risk should guide antipsychotic choice when practical, but immediate danger still gets controlled first.
nodes.body: Do not delay lifesaving chemical control for ECG when the patient is an immediate threat. Get ECG first when practical if: - Known long QT syndrome. - QTc >500 ms. - Torsades history. - Multiple QT-prolonging medications. - Severe hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia. - Syncope, chest pain, stimulant toxicity, renal failure, older/frail, repeated antipsychotic doses. Drug implications: - Drop

nodes.title: OSA / COPD / Hypoventilation / Intoxication
nodes.summary: Respiratory-risk patients need capnography, lower dose, less stacking, and airway rescue before the first dose.
nodes.body: High-risk pattern: - OSA, obesity hypoventilation, COPD, neuromuscular weakness, intoxication, opioid exposure, alcohol, sedative co-ingestion, pregnancy, older/frail. Principles: - Use the lowest effective depth. - Avoid rapid stacking. - Use ETCO2 when available. - Prefer agents that preserve ventilation when they fit the goal: ketamine for dissociation, dexmedetomidine for cooperative light sed

nodes.title: Pediatric / Pregnancy Notes
nodes.summary: Peds and pregnancy need weight/airway discipline, aspiration planning, and the lowest depth that safely accomplishes the goal.
nodes.body: Pediatrics: - Ketamine is a common ED dissociative agent with strong pediatric experience. - Nitrous is useful for brief cooperative procedures. - Intranasal midazolam can help anxiolysis but has no analgesia. - Dose by weight and monitor with the same airway rescue discipline. Pregnancy: - Maternal oxygenation and perfusion are fetal resuscitation. - Avoid unnecessary deep sedation. - Anticipate

nodes.title: Drug-by-Drug Pearls
nodes.summary: Jump directly to a sedative family.
nodes.body: Open the focused drug family.

nodes.title: Side-Effect Pattern Recognition
nodes.summary: Know each drug signature: apnea, hypotension, QT/EPS, bradycardia, myoclonus, saliva/emesis, and long-tail stacking.
nodes.body: Pattern map: - Apnea/obstruction: propofol, benzo/opioid stacking, intoxication, OSA/COPD. - Hypotension: propofol, dex loading, high sedative burden, shock physiology. - Hypertension/tachycardia: ketamine, stimulant physiology, pain under-treatment. - Bradycardia: dexmedetomidine, high vagal tone, beta-blockers, conduction disease. - QT/EPS: droperidol, haloperidol, other dopamine blockers. - Myo
nodes.recommendation: Recognize the adverse-effect pattern early and rescue the physiology, not just the number on the monitor.

nodes.title: Seizure Hub — Is This Still Seizing?
nodes.summary: Still seizing = status, go now. Glucose on everyone. Pregnant = eclampsia. Airway-position the postictal patient; do not reflexively intubate a self-resolving seizure.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Status epilepticus \u2014 seizing \u22655 min OR back-to-back without recovery. Treat NOW, do not wait. 2. Hypoglycemia \u2014 check a glucose on EVERY seizing patient before anything else. 3. Eclampsia \u2014 pregnant or postpartum (up to 6 weeks) + seizure = magnesium, not just benzos. 4. Intracranial catastrophe \u2014 SAH, ICH, CVST, herpes encephalitis, mass pre

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the One That Fits
nodes.summary: Pick the most acute hit. Each branch links to its deep-dive + the next action.
nodes.body: Each branch routes to a deep-dive and tells you the next action while you transition.

nodes.title: Status Epilepticus — Treat the Clock
nodes.body: Open Status Epilepticus for the full timed algorithm (benzo \u2192 second-line AED \u2192 anesthetic infusion \u2192 refractory pathway). Definition: \u22655 min of continuous convulsive activity OR \u22652 seizures without return to baseline between them. Do NOT wait for a "classic" 30-minute definition \u2014 neuronal injury and pharmacoresistance start early. [3] Next 5 minutes: - Benzodiazepin
nodes.recommendation: Full-dose benzo NOW, second-line AED immediately after (do not wait). Glucose + thiamine. If refractory: intubate, anesthetic infusion, continuous EEG.

nodes.title: Hypoglycemic Seizure — Fastest Reversible Cause
nodes.body: Open Hypoglycemia for the full workup (etiology, sulfonylurea/octreotide pathway, refractory management). Every seizing patient gets a fingerstick. A hypoglycemic seizure stops when the sugar is corrected \u2014 do not keep escalating anti-seizure meds against a glucose of 30. [4] Next 5 minutes: - IV access + D10 or D50: adults 25 g dextrose IV (50 mL D50 or 250 mL D10); repeat glucose in 15 min.
nodes.recommendation: Dextrose IV now, recheck at 15 min. Thiamine if alcoholic/malnourished. Hunt the cause; sulfonylurea/long-acting insulin needs infusion + admission.

nodes.title: Eclampsia — Magnesium, Not Just a Benzo
nodes.body: Open Eclampsia for the full obstetric pathway (magnesium dosing, BP control, delivery planning, HELLP). Any seizure in pregnancy or up to 6 weeks postpartum is eclampsia until proven otherwise \u2014 even without a documented history of preeclampsia and even with a normal-appearing BP. [5] Next 5 minutes: - Magnesium sulfate 4-6 g IV over 15-20 min, then 1-2 g/h infusion. This is the anticonvulsan
nodes.recommendation: Magnesium sulfate is the drug (4-6 g load, then 1-2 g/h). Control severe BP. Emergent OB consult \u2014 delivery is definitive. Calcium gluconate for Mg toxicity.

nodes.title: Structural Catastrophe — Image the Brain
nodes.body: Seizure with thunderclap headache, focal deficit, persistent altered mentation, or trauma = structural cause until imaged. The candidates and their consults: - Subarachnoid Hemorrhage \u2014 worst-headache-of-life before the seizure; non-contrast CT, LP if CT negative and within window. - Intracerebral Hemorrhage \u2014 focal deficit + hypertension; reverse anticoagulation, BP control. - Cerebral
nodes.recommendation: Emergent non-contrast CT head; add CTV/MRV for CVST, CTA for SAH/dissection. Diagnosis-specific BP control. Reverse anticoag if bleed. Early neuro/neurosurgery consult.

nodes.title: CNS Infection — Do Not Delay Acyclovir
nodes.body: Fever + seizure + headache/neck stiffness/altered mentation = CNS infection until excluded. Open Meningitis for the antibiotic + steroid + LP pathway. Next 5 minutes: [7] - Empiric antibiotics WITHIN 1 HOUR \u2014 do not wait for the LP or CT: ceftriaxone 2 g IV + vancomycin; add ampicillin if age >50, immunocompromised, or pregnant (Listeria). - Add IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg if any concern for HSV en
nodes.recommendation: Antibiotics within 1 h + acyclovir if any HSV concern \u2014 BEFORE CT/LP. Dexamethasone if bacterial. LP when safe. Do not delay drugs for imaging.

nodes.title: Toxic Seizure — Targeted Antidote
nodes.body: Drug-induced seizures often do not respond to standard AEDs \u2014 they need the antidote and are frequently refractory to phenytoin (avoid phenytoin in tox seizures; it can worsen sodium-channel toxicity). Recognize the pattern and open the consult: - TCA / sodium-channel blocker \u2014 wide QRS + seizure + hypotension: TCA Toxidrome. Give sodium bicarbonate boluses; benzos for seizure. - Isoniaz
nodes.recommendation: Benzos first-line + specific antidote (bicarb for TCA/wide-QRS, pyridoxine for INH, cyproheptadine + cooling for serotonin syndrome). Avoid phenytoin. Call Poison Control.

nodes.title: Alcohol Withdrawal Seizure
nodes.body: Open Alcohol Withdrawal for the full CIWA / benzodiazepine / phenobarbital pathway. Typical pattern: generalized tonic-clonic seizure 6-48 h after the last drink, often in the first 24 h, usually 1-2 brief seizures (\u201crum fits\u201d). But do NOT reflexively attribute every seizure in a drinker to withdrawal. [9] Next 5 minutes: - Benzodiazepines are the treatment and prevent recurrence: loraze
nodes.recommendation: Benzos treat and prevent recurrence; thiamine before glucose; replace Mg/K. Phenytoin does not work here. Image if first-ever or focal. Watch for DTs.

nodes.title: Hyponatremic Seizure — Hypertonic Saline
nodes.body: Open Sodium Disorders for the full correction-rate and etiology pathway. A seizure from hyponatremia is a neurologic emergency and one of the few indications for rapid, deliberate sodium correction. [10] Next 5 minutes: - Hypertonic saline (3%): 100-150 mL IV bolus over 10 min, may repeat \u00d7 1-2 to raise sodium ~4-6 mmol/L acutely and stop the seizure. Do NOT give free water or hypotonic fluid
nodes.recommendation: 3% saline 100-150 mL bolus to break the seizure (may repeat), then cap correction at 6-8 mmol/L/24 h. Recheck Na q2h. Send osmolalities + urine Na. Admit.

nodes.title: Consider PNES — But Exclude Real Seizure First
nodes.body: Open Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizures for the differentiation and management pathway. PNES is a diagnosis of caution in the ED, not a snap judgment. Features that SUGGEST (but never prove) PNES: gradual onset/offset, side-to-side head shaking, forced eye closure with resistance to opening, pelvic thrusting, asynchronous limb movements, retained awareness during bilateral movements, prolonged dur
nodes.recommendation: Suggestive features only \u2014 confirm glucose and exclude true seizure/status first. Avoid escalating sedation. Non-confrontational communication; neurology for video-EEG.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Recovered or Breakthrough Seizure
nodes.summary: IV + glucose + focused labs (Na/Ca/Mg, hCG, lactate, AED levels) + ECG + thiamine + injury survey. Persistent altered = suspect non-convulsive status or structural cause.
nodes.body: No active seizing, no immediate life-threat hit. Standard ED bundle while you determine first-vs-breakthrough and hunt the trigger: [1,2] THE BUNDLE: - IV access, monitor, continuous SpO2. Position for airway protection until fully alert. - Point-of-care glucose (again, if not already) \u2014 the single most important test. - Focused labs: CMP (sodium, calcium, magnesium, BUN/Cr, glucose), CBC, \u

nodes.title: Reassess — Back to Baseline?
nodes.summary: Recovered known epileptic \u2192 discharge. First seizure \u2192 image + workup. Persistent altered/focal \u2192 STOP, re-enter exclusions (non-convulsive status).
nodes.body: Re-examine: mental status, focal deficit, vitals, lab results, whether this is a first or breakthrough seizure.

nodes.title: Imaging & Workup Decision
nodes.summary: Emergent CT for first seizure, focal deficit, persistent altered, trauma, anticoag, immunocompromised, age >40. Add CTV/CTA per suspicion. Outpatient MRI + EEG + neuro for a resolved first seizure.
nodes.body: Not every seizure needs a scan, but a first seizure and any red flag do. [1,2,12] Emergent non-contrast CT head in the ED if ANY of: - First-ever seizure (ACEP Level B \u2014 image first seizures) [1] - New focal deficit or failure to return to baseline - Persistent altered mentation - Head trauma / fall with the seizure - Anticoagulated or bleeding risk - Immunocompromised (HIV, transplant, malig

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge a recovered known epileptic; observe a resolved first seizure with pending workup; admit status / structural / infectious / refractory.
nodes.body: Match disposition to the cause and the recovery. Defer to the deep-dive consult when a specific diagnosis is committed.

nodes.title: Discharge — Known Epileptic / Provoked & Corrected
nodes.body: Safe discharge criteria: [1,2,12] 1. Returned fully to baseline mental status and neuro exam. 2. Known cause \u2014 subtherapeutic AED / missed dose, or a provoked seizure whose trigger is corrected (glucose, sodium, fever source treated). 3. Benign workup \u2014 normal glucose/electrolytes, no red flags, imaging (if indicated) unremarkable. 4. AED plan \u2014 restart / adjust dose; if new AED sta
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only if at baseline, cause known/corrected, workup benign, AED plan set, neurology follow-up arranged. Document driving/safety counseling and return precautions.

nodes.title: Observe — Resolved First Seizure / Pending Workup
nodes.body: ED observation / short-stay appropriate when: [2,12] - First unprovoked seizure, now at baseline, normal CT, but MRI/EEG/neurology not yet completed and same-day outpatient arrangement is not feasible - Provoked seizure whose cause needs a few hours of monitoring (electrolyte correction, resolving intoxication, fever workup) - Borderline social/safety situation preventing safe discharge - Recurren
nodes.recommendation: Obs/short-stay with seizure precautions + serial neuro exams; complete workup and arrange EEG/neurology. Escalate to admit for recurrence or persistent deficit.

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admit when: [2,3] - Status epilepticus (any) \u2014 ICU if refractory, intubated, or on anesthetic infusion; continuous EEG. - Structural cause \u2014 SAH, ICH, CVST, stroke, mass, abscess (neuro/neurosurgery service). - CNS infection \u2014 meningitis / encephalitis on antibiotics + acyclovir. - Eclampsia \u2014 OB service, magnesium infusion, delivery planning. - Refractory metabolic cause \u201
nodes.recommendation: Admit status, structural/infectious cause, eclampsia, refractory metabolic cause, or persistent altered/focal exam. ICU for status/airway; EEG to exclude non-convulsive status.

nodes.title: Sepsis — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Sepsis-3: suspected infection + SOFA increase >=2; septic shock: vasopressors + lactate >2 despite fluids; mortality >=40%
nodes.body: Sepsis Steps Summary Sepsis-3 Definition: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Clinically identified as suspected infection with SOFA score increase ≥2. [1] Septic Shock: Vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Mortality ≥40%. [1][3] Key Principle: Early recognition → aggressive

nodes.title: Source Evaluation
nodes.summary: Focused H&P for source — pneumonia 50%, urosepsis 20%, intra-abdominal 20%; do not anchor on minor findings
nodes.body: Systematic source identification — the most valuable method for source detection is a focused history and physical examination. [24][25] Common sources of sepsis: [23] • Pneumonia (~50%) — respiratory symptoms, CXR, lung POCUS • Urosepsis (~20%) — dysuria, flank pain, UA, urine culture • Intra-abdominal (~20%) — cholangitis, C. diff, appendicitis, perforation • Skin/soft tissue — cellulitis, necro

nodes.title: Lab Workup & Cultures
nodes.summary: Labs within 45min: 2 blood cultures from separate sites before abx, lactate, CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags, CXR, POCUS
nodes.body: Obtain within 45 minutes (do NOT delay fluids or antibiotics): [2][24] Routine labs: • CBC with differential, BMP, LFTs, coagulation studies (INR, PTT) • Serum lactate — elevated >2 mmol/L indicates severity [2] • Procalcitonin — useful for guiding antibiotic de-escalation, NOT for initial diagnosis (pooled sensitivity only 77%) [24] • ABG/VBG — assess acid-base status Microbiology (BEFORE antibio

nodes.title: Suspected Source of Infection
nodes.summary: Identify most likely source to guide empiric antibiotics — pulmonary, urinary, intra-abdominal, or skin/endovascular
nodes.body: Identify the most likely source based on history, exam, and initial workup to guide empiric antibiotic selection. Empiric Antibiotic Selection Table

nodes.title: Classify Severity
nodes.summary: Classify: sepsis (SOFA >=2 + infection) vs septic shock (vasopressor-dependent MAP >=65 + lactate >2)
nodes.body: Sepsis: Suspected infection + organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2 increase from baseline) [1] • Acute kidney injury, altered mentation, hypotension, tachypnea, coagulopathy, elevated lactate Septic Shock: Sepsis + vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg + lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation [1][3] • Mortality: sepsis ≥10%, septic shock ≥40% CMS SEP-1 differs: Defines septic shoc

nodes.title: Airway & Breathing Stabilization
nodes.summary: Optimize MAP before intubation — push-dose phenylephrine or start norepinephrine first; ketamine for induction
nodes.body: Supplemental O₂ for all patients with hypoxia. Target SpO₂ 90-96%. [24] Intubation indications: • Airway protection (encephalopathy, depressed consciousness) • Refractory hypoxemia despite high-flow O₂ • Respiratory failure / increased work of breathing • Facilitating procedures (source control) Peri-intubation risks in sepsis: • Hemodynamic collapse is common — optimize MAP before intubation • Pu

nodes.title: IV Fluid Resuscitation
nodes.summary: 30 mL/kg LR within 3hr in 500mL boluses — avoid HES (increased mortality); restrict fluids after initial resuscitation
nodes.body: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid — start within 1 hour, complete within 3 hours [2][24] Fluid choice: Balanced crystalloid preferred (Lactated Ringer's) [24] • SMART trial: lower composite of death, new RRT, and persistent renal dysfunction vs 0.9% NaCl [24][27] • Avoid HES — 6S trial: increased mortality (51 vs 43%) and RRT (22 vs 16%) [10] • No benefit to albumin vs crystalloid (SAFE trial) [24][28] Admi

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotic Selection
nodes.summary: Antibiotics within 1hr — beta-lactam FIRST before vancomycin; pip-tazo, cefepime, or meropenem as backbone
nodes.body: Administer within 1 hour of sepsis recognition. Each hour of delay increases mortality. [2][20] Beta-lactam FIRST when also giving vancomycin (improved survival). [24] Beta-lactam backbone (choose one): [23][24] • Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h (extended infusion 4h) — broadest anaerobic coverage • Cefepime 2g IV q8h — antipseudomonal, less anaerobic coverage • Meropenem 1g IV q8h — reserve f

nodes.title: MRSA Coverage
nodes.summary: Vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg load AFTER beta-lactam — discontinue if no MRSA cultured at 48hr
nodes.body: MRSA risk factors: [24] • Soft tissue infection (especially abscesses) • Central line infection / hemodialysis • Recent hospitalization or long-term care • IV drug use • Known MRSA colonization • Nosocomial / surgical site infection First-line: Vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg IV loading dose, then 15-20 mg/kg q8-12h [24][31] • Administer AFTER beta-lactam (beta-lactam first improves survival) [24] Alternat

nodes.title: Source Control
nodes.summary: Source control within 6-12hr — remove lines, drain abscesses, ERCP for cholangitis, surgical repair for perforation
nodes.body: Source control within 6-12 hours when feasible — undrained foci may not respond to antibiotics alone. [2][24] Interventions by source: • Intravascular catheter infection: Remove catheter after establishing alternative access • Abscess: Percutaneous or surgical drainage (including thoracic empyema, joint) • Ascending cholangitis: ERCP or percutaneous decompression • Nephrolithiasis with obstruction

nodes.title: 1-3 Hour Reassessment
nodes.summary: Reassess at 1-3hr: MAP, perfusion, UOP, repeat lactate — use dynamic fluid responsiveness measures
nodes.body: After initial fluid bolus and antibiotics, reassess: • MAP: Target ≥65 mmHg • Perfusion: Capillary refill time <3 seconds, skin color, mentation • Urine output: Target ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr • Lactate: Repeat if initial >2 mmol/L — trending toward normalization? Fluid responsive? Assess with dynamic measures: passive leg raise, IVC variability, pulse pressure variation [24] Is the patient responding to ini

nodes.title: Vasopressor Initiation — Norepinephrine
nodes.summary: Norepinephrine first-line vasopressor — start 0.05 mcg/kg/min, can start peripherally for <6hr; NOT dopamine (more arrhythmias)
nodes.body: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor for septic shock. [2][11][24] Dosing: Start 0.05 mcg/kg/min (4-6 mcg/min), titrate by 0.02-0.05 mcg/kg/min to MAP ≥65 mmHg [24] Mechanism: Predominantly alpha-1 agonist (vasoconstriction) with some beta-1 (supports cardiac function). Reduces endothelial permeability. [23] Can start peripherally for <6 hours while obtaining central access (SSC 2021). [2]

nodes.title: Second-Line Vasopressor Selection
nodes.summary: Add vasopressin 0.03-0.04 units/min early before escalating NE; epinephrine for low CO/bradycardia
nodes.body: If norepinephrine alone is insufficient, add a second agent: [2][24] Vasopressin 0.03-0.04 units/min (fixed dose, non-titratable) • Reduces NE requirement, lower AF risk (RR 0.77) [24] • VASST + VANISH trials: no mortality benefit but NE-sparing [12][13] • Best as early second agent — add before escalating NE to high doses [23] Epinephrine 0.01-0.5 mcg/kg/min • Alternative first-line for bradycard

nodes.title: MAP Targets & Personalization
nodes.summary: Default MAP >=65; personalize for chronic HTN (80-85) or normotensive elderly (60-65); CRT <3sec emerging target
nodes.body: Default MAP target: ≥65 mmHg (SSC 2021) [2] Personalized targets: [23] • Chronic hypertension: Consider MAP 80-85 mmHg (SEPSISPAM: improved renal outcomes but more AF) [19] • Younger / previously normotensive: MAP 60-65 may be sufficient (65-Trial) [18] • Elevated CVP or IAP: Higher MAP may be needed to maintain organ perfusion gradient [23] Capillary Refill Time (CRT) — emerging perfusion target:

nodes.title: Fluid Responsiveness Assessment
nodes.summary: RESTRICT fluids after initial 30mL/kg — use passive leg raise for assessment; fluid responsiveness is normal, not an indication
nodes.body: After initial resuscitation, RESTRICT further fluids — ongoing crystalloid is often harmful. [9][23] CLASSIC trial: Restrictive fluid strategy safe, trend toward less intubation [9] • CLASSIC criteria for additional fluid: lactate >4, MAP <50 despite vasopressors, mottling beyond kneecap, UOP <0.1 mL/kg/hr for 2h, or ongoing overt losses [23] Dynamic measures (preferred over static CVP): [24] • Pa

nodes.title: Inotrope Consideration
nodes.summary: Dobutamine 2-5 mcg/kg/min for septic cardiomyopathy — low pulse pressure, cool extremities despite adequate MAP
nodes.body: Consider inotropes for septic cardiomyopathy or low cardiac output despite adequate vasopressors. [24] POCUS assessment: Reduced LVEF, global hypokinesis, elevated E/e'. [23] Clues suggesting need for inotropy: [23] • Pulse pressure <40 mmHg (suggests low stroke volume) • Cool extremities despite adequate MAP • Heart rate inappropriately low (<80 bpm) for shock • Inappropriately normal lactate (su

nodes.title: Refractory Shock
nodes.summary: Reassess for missed source, wrong diagnosis, or inadequate antibiotics — methylene blue as salvage vasopressor
nodes.body: If shock persists despite fluids + norepinephrine + vasopressin +/- inotrope: [23] Reassess for: • Missed or inadequately treated source of infection • Incorrect diagnosis (sepsis mimics — adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, PE, hemorrhage) • Inadequate antibiotic coverage • Undrained abscess or infected hardware • Pneumothorax from central line placement • Septic cardiomyopathy Methylene Blue — salvag

nodes.title: Corticosteroid Therapy
nodes.summary: Hydrocortisone 50mg IV q6h for vasopressor-dependent shock — reduces shock duration; taper over 2-3 days when off pressors
nodes.body: For patients on vasopressors for septic shock: [2][14][15] Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h OR 200 mg/day continuous infusion [2] Evidence: • ADRENAL trial (n=3800): Steroids reduce time on vasopressors, ICU LOS, and duration of intubation. No increase in superinfection. [14] • APROCCHSS trial (n=1241): Hydrocortisone + Fludrocortisone 50 mcg PO daily × 7 days reduced 90-day mortality (43% vs 49.1%) [1

nodes.title: Septic Cardiomyopathy
nodes.summary: Reversible cardiomyopathy in up to 50% of septic shock — POCUS for LVEF <45%, treat with inotropy not more vasoconstrictors
nodes.body: Occurs in up to 50% of septic shock patients. [23] Features: • Acute, biventricular myocardial dysfunction • Reversible within 7-10 days • Systemic vasodilation may mask low EF (pseudo-normal LVEF) • Low cardiac output with vasopressor-refractory shock Diagnosis: [23] • POCUS: LVEF <45%, reduced GLS (<-17%), MAPSE reduction • Lateral e' <8 cm/s strongly predicts mortality • Lateral E/e' >13 cm/s s

nodes.title: Blood Transfusion Thresholds
nodes.summary: Transfuse only for Hgb <=7 g/dL (TRISS) — 50% fewer transfusions with no increased ischemic events
nodes.body: Restrictive transfusion strategy: Transfuse for Hgb ≤7 g/dL [2][22][24] Evidence: [22][24] • TRISS trial (n=998): No difference in 28-day mortality between restrictive (Hgb ≤7) vs liberal (Hgb ≤9) strategies in septic shock • Restrictive strategy resulted in 50% fewer transfusions with no increase in ischemic events [22] Exceptions (consider higher threshold): • Active hemorrhagic shock • Acute my

nodes.title: Sepsis Mimics
nodes.summary: If not responding, reconsider diagnosis — adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, PE, mesenteric ischemia, anaphylaxis, HLH
nodes.body: If the patient is not responding to treatment, reconsider the diagnosis. Suspect a mimic if: no clear infectious source, procalcitonin unexpectedly low, or atypical course. [23] Infectious mimics: • Endocarditis causing valve failure (check echo) • Tick-borne illness (anaplasmosis, babesiosis) • Invasive candidiasis / aspergillosis (beta-D-glucan, galactomannan) • PJP pneumonia (diffuse infiltrate

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Pregnancy, elderly, cirrhosis, ESRD, immunosuppressed — same principles with population-specific adjustments
nodes.body: Pregnancy: [24] • Same resuscitation principles apply • Physiologic changes (lower BP, higher HR, lower platelets) make recognition harder • Higher risk for pneumonia and genitourinary infections • Left lateral decubitus positioning after 20 weeks • Fetal monitoring when feasible Elderly / Frail: [24] • Higher mortality, impaired immune/cardiovascular response • 65-Trial: MAP target >60 mmHg safe

nodes.title: Resuscitation Endpoints
nodes.summary: CRT <3sec, MAP >=65, UOP >=0.5mL/kg/hr, lactate trending down — lactate is epinephrine index, not perfusion marker
nodes.body: Clinical targets (follow continuously): [2][24] • MAP ≥65 mmHg (individualize within 60-70 range) • Urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr — good UOP is reassuring; low UOP is nonspecific (may be ATN) • Capillary refill time <3 seconds (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2: improved composite outcome) [17] • Perfusion index >1.4-2% from pulse oximetry (emerging target) [23] • Mentation improving • Heart rate — mild tachycardia

nodes.title: Treatment Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Most respond within 6-24hr — improving MAP, declining lactate, adequate UOP signals de-escalation readiness
nodes.body: Most patients respond within 6-24 hours. Resolution may take days to weeks. [24] Signs of improvement: • MAP stable on stable or decreasing vasopressors • Lactate declining • Urine output adequate • Mentation improving • CRT normalizing (<3 seconds) Signs of failure: • Escalating vasopressor requirements • Rising lactate (reassess diagnosis, source control, antibiotic adequacy) • New organ dysfunc

nodes.title: Antibiotic De-escalation
nodes.summary: Narrow antibiotics at 48-72hr by cultures; typical course 5-7 days; D/C vancomycin if no MRSA at 48hr
nodes.body: Assess daily for de-escalation opportunity. [24] Narrowing (48-72 hours): [24] • When culture and susceptibility results return, narrow to pathogen-directed therapy • If no MRSA cultured within 48h → discontinue vancomycin • If no pathogen identified (~50% of cases) → use clinical judgment + fixed course of broad-spectrum (3-5 days) Duration: Typically 5-7 days [24] • Longer for: S. aureus bactere

nodes.title: Fluid & Vasopressor Weaning
nodes.summary: Reduce fluids and vasopressors as tolerated — wean NE first when on dual agents; taper steroids over 2-3 days
nodes.body: Once hemodynamic targets met (usually hours to 1-2 days): [24] Fluid de-escalation: • Reduce rate or stop IV fluids • Consider diuretics if fluid overloaded • Monitor for cardiogenic and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) • Restrictive approach decreases duration of mechanical ventilation and ICU stay [24] Vasopressor weaning: [23] • Down-titrate as tolerated — target lowest effective dose • If

nodes.title: ICU Admission Criteria
nodes.body: ICU admission indicated for: [24] • Vasopressor requirement • Mechanical ventilation • Multiple organ dysfunction • Lactate ≥4 mmol/L despite resuscitation • Escalating hemodynamic instability • Need for continuous renal replacement therapy • Anticipated source control requiring close monitoring Risk factors for progression to shock (consider ICU consultation): [24] • Intermittent hypotension • La
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU for vasopressor-dependent septic shock, mechanical ventilation, or multiorgan dysfunction. Low threshold for ICU consultation when risk factors for deterioration are present.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Floor admission appropriate when: • Sepsis without shock • Responding to initial fluid resuscitation • No vasopressor requirement • Source identified and controlled (or being addressed) • Stable on oral or IV antibiotics • Lactate trending toward normal • Adequate mentation and organ function Continue monitoring: • Vital signs q4-6h • Daily labs (CBC, BMP, lactate if indicated) • Antibiotic de-esc
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored floor bed for sepsis without shock that is responding to initial resuscitation. Continue antibiotics, monitor closely, and plan for de-escalation.

nodes.title: Observation / ED Observation
nodes.body: ED observation may be appropriate for: • Low-risk sepsis (e.g., young, no comorbidities, single organ involvement) • Rapid response to 1-2L IV fluids • Lactate normalizing (<2 mmol/L on repeat) • Source identified and treatable (e.g., uncomplicated pyelonephritis) • Reliable follow-up within 24-48 hours • Normal mentation • No vasopressor requirement at any point Ensure before discharge: • Source
nodes.recommendation: Consider ED observation for low-risk sepsis with rapid response to resuscitation, normalizing lactate, and reliable follow-up.

nodes.title: Post-Sepsis Care (PICS)
nodes.summary: PICS affects up to 50% of ICU survivors — physical, cognitive, psychological; sepsis is leading cause of 30-day readmission
nodes.body: Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS): Increasingly recognized health burden after sepsis. Significant overlap with "long COVID." [24] Domains affected: • Physical: Weakness, fatigue, reduced functional capacity • Cognitive: Memory impairment, difficulty concentrating, executive dysfunction • Psychological: Depression, anxiety, PTSD Incidence: Up to 50% of ICU sepsis survivors experience long-term i

nodes.title: Septic Arthritis
nodes.summary: Orthopedic emergency — irreversible cartilage destruction in 8hr; knee most common (50%), bimodal age distribution
nodes.body: Septic arthritis is a bacterial infection of a joint space and its synovial fluid. It is an orthopedic emergency because irreversible cartilage destruction develops within 8 hours through proteolytic enzyme release from neutrophils. [1,2] Epidemiology: - Knee most commonly affected (~50% of cases) - Bimodal age distribution (young children and adults >55 years) - Incidence: 2-10 per 100,000 person

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Joint pain + swelling + limited ROM; monoarticular 80%+; fever absent in up to 56% of elderly/immunocompromised
nodes.body: Classic presentation: - Joint pain (most sensitive symptom) - Swelling and effusion - Warmth and erythema - Limited range of motion (active AND passive) - Fever present in 44-97% (may be absent in elderly/immunocompromised) [1,4] Monoarticular in >80% of cases. [1] Physical examination: - Joint held in position of maximal comfort (maximizes joint volume) - Hip: flexed, abducted, externally rotated

nodes.title: Pediatric: Kocher Criteria
nodes.summary: Kocher criteria for pediatric HIP only: 0 predictors=0.2%, 4=99.6%; CRP is strongest independent factor
nodes.body: Kocher Criteria distinguishes septic arthritis from transient synovitis in children with inflamed hip. [5] Original 4 criteria: 1. Fever >38.5C (101.3F) 2. Inability to bear weight 3. ESR >40 mm/hr 4. WBC >12,000 cells/uL Probability of septic arthritis: - 0 predictors: 0.2% - 1 predictor: 3% - 2 predictors: 40% - 3 predictors: 93.1% - 4 predictors: 99.6% Modified Kocher (Caird) adds CRP as 5th cr

nodes.title: Adult Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: Kocher has LIMITED adult utility — crystals do NOT exclude infection (1-2% dual diagnosis); all acute monoarthritis is septic until proven otherwise
nodes.body: Kocher criteria have LIMITED utility in adults. [6] In the adult population, PMN percentage, ESR, serum WBC, fever, and weight-bearing status were not significant predictors of septic arthritis. What matters in adults: - Clinical suspicion based on risk factors - Synovial fluid analysis (most important) - Gram stain and culture Newman criteria for adult septic arthritis: [7] - Any synovial fluid w

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Distinguish native vs prosthetic joint, gout/pseudogout coexistence, and reactive arthritis in differential
nodes.body: Key differentials for acute monoarticular arthritis: Crystal arthropathies: Gout, pseudogout (CPPD) - Can coexist with infection - Presence of crystals does NOT rule out infection [8] Reactive arthritis: Post-infectious (GI, GU), usually days-weeks after infection Trauma: Hemarthrosis, internal derangement Inflammatory: RA flare, psoriatic arthritis Other infections: Lyme arthritis (endemic areas)

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup Overview
nodes.summary: Arthrocentesis is gold standard — do NOT delay for labs, imaging, or coagulopathy; serum markers unreliable for diagnosis
nodes.body: Arthrocentesis is the gold standard. [1] Do NOT delay arthrocentesis for: - Blood tests to return - Imaging to be performed - Coagulopathy (relative, not absolute contraindication) - Overlying cellulitis (approach from unaffected area) Labs to order: - CBC, CMP, ESR, CRP - Blood cultures (positive in up to 66% of bacterial septic arthritis) [4] - Procalcitonin if available Serum markers are NOT re

nodes.title: Synovial Fluid Analysis
nodes.summary: WBC >50K only 56% sensitive — 39% culture-positive have <50K; synovial lactate >10 mmol/L is best single test (86% sens, ~100% spec)
nodes.body: Collect for: [1,10] - Cell count with differential - Gram stain - Culture (aerobic and anaerobic) - Crystal analysis (polarized microscopy) - Consider: lactate, glucose Synovial WBC interpretation: [10,11] | WBC Count | +LR | Sensitivity | Specificity | |-----------|-----|-------------|-------------| | >25,000/mm3 | 3.2 | 73% | 77% | | >50,000/mm3 | 4.7 | 56% | 90% | | >100,000/mm3 | 13.2 | 19% |

nodes.title: Effect of Prior Antibiotics
nodes.summary: Prior antibiotics lower WBC cutoff to >16K (vs >33K without); culture sensitivity drops >30% if abx given >4hr before tap
nodes.body: Antibiotics before arthrocentesis alter synovial WBC thresholds. [12] Without prior antibiotics: - Optimal cutoff: >33,000 cells - Sensitivity 96%, Specificity 95% With prior antibiotics (within 24h): - Optimal cutoff: >16,000 cells - Sensitivity 82%, Specificity 76% Key implications: - Lower threshold if patient received antibiotics - Culture sensitivity reduced >30% if LP >4 hours after antibiot

nodes.title: Gram Stain & Culture
nodes.summary: Gram stain only 29-50% sensitive — negative does NOT rule out infection; S. aureus is most common organism (50-70%)
nodes.body: Gram stain: [1,4] - Sensitivity: only 29-50% (identifies organisms in only 1/3 of cases) - Specificity: >97% - Positive = treat - Negative = does NOT rule out infection Culture: [1] - Non-gonococcal: >90% positive - Gonococcal: only 25-70% positive (fastidious organism) - Request specifically if gonococcal suspected - Consider blood culture bottles for small volumes Microbiology by patient populat

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.summary: US guides aspiration and confirms effusion; MRI most sensitive for early detection; plain films have limited acute utility
nodes.body: Plain radiographs: [1] - Limited utility for acute septic arthritis - May show: soft tissue swelling, effusion, periarticular osteopenia - Useful for: baseline, excluding fracture, detecting osteomyelitis (late) - Changes take 10-14 days to appear Ultrasound: [1] - Excellent for confirming effusion - Guides arthrocentesis (improves success rate) - Can detect as little as 1-2 mL fluid - Preferred f

nodes.title: Suspected Pathogen Type
nodes.summary: Gonococcal clues: young, migratory polyarthritis, tenosynovitis, pustules; non-GC: monoarticular, toxic, purulent
nodes.body: Based on clinical presentation and risk factors, what is the most likely etiology? [1,2,14] Gonococcal clues: - Young, sexually active patient - Migratory polyarthralgia/polyarthritis - Tenosynovitis (especially wrists, fingers, ankles) - Dermatitis-arthritis syndrome (pustular/vesicular skin lesions) - 4:1 female predominance Non-gonococcal clues: - Monoarticular (large joint) - Risk factors: DM,

nodes.title: Empiric: Non-Gonococcal
nodes.summary: Vancomycin 15-20mg/kg IV for MRSA coverage; add ceftriaxone 2g for gram-neg risk (IVDU, immunocompromised, elderly)
nodes.body: Empiric regimen for non-gonococcal septic arthritis: [1,2,15] Standard coverage (gram-positive focus): - Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h - Covers MRSA (up to 50% of S. aureus in some regions) - Target trough 15-20 mcg/mL Add gram-negative coverage if: [1] - IVDU (Pseudomonas risk) - Immunocompromised - Elderly - Gram stain shows gram-negative rods - Neonates Gram-negative options: - Ceftriaxone 2

nodes.title: Gonococcal Septic Arthritis (DGI)
nodes.summary: Ceftriaxone 1g + doxycycline for chlamydia coverage; often managed WITHOUT surgery; culture positive only 25-70%
nodes.body: Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) presents as: [14,16] - Arthritis-dermatitis syndrome (60%): migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions - Localized septic arthritis (40%): monoarticular, purulent Treatment: [16] - Ceftriaxone 1g IV/IM q24h - Continue until 24-48h after clinical improvement - Transition to oral (total 7+ days): - Cefixime 400mg PO BID, OR - Fluoroquinolon

nodes.title: Empiric: Broad Coverage
nodes.summary: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + doxycycline covers MRSA, gram-neg, GC, and chlamydia — de-escalate by cultures
nodes.body: When uncertain between gonococcal and non-gonococcal: [1,2,16] Empiric regimen: - Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h PLUS - Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h PLUS - Empiric Chlamydia coverage: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 7 days This covers: - MRSA and MSSA - Streptococci - Most gram-negatives - N. gonorrhoeae - C. trachomatis (empiric PO) De-escalate based on: - Culture and sensitivity results - Clinical respon

nodes.title: Prosthetic Joint Infection (PJI)
nodes.summary: Prosthetic joint: synovial WBC >3000 (MUCH lower threshold); MSIS 2018 point-based criteria for diagnosis
nodes.body: Prosthetic joint infection requires different thresholds and approach. [17] MSIS 2018 Diagnostic Criteria: [17] Major Criteria (definitive): - Two positive cultures of same organism, OR - Sinus tract communicating with joint Minor Criteria (point-based): - Serum CRP >1 mg/dL (2 points) - Serum ESR >30 mm/hr (1 point) - D-dimer >860 ng/mL (2 points) - Synovial WBC >3,000/uL (3 points) - MUCH lower

nodes.title: PJI: ED Management
nodes.summary: Vancomycin + cefepime for PJI; ortho + ID consult; rifampin for biofilm penetration once sensitivities known
nodes.body: ED role in prosthetic joint infection: [17] Immediate actions: 1. Arthrocentesis (if safe and not planned for OR) 2. Blood cultures 3. Empiric antibiotics (after cultures obtained) 4. Orthopedic surgery consultation 5. Infectious disease consultation Empiric antibiotics: [17] - Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h PLUS - Cefepime 2g IV q8h (gram-negative coverage including Pseudomonas) Special conside

nodes.title: Joint Drainage
nodes.summary: Antibiotics alone insufficient — serial aspiration, arthroscopy, or arthrotomy; no significant outcome difference between approaches
nodes.body: Source control is essential. Antibiotics alone are insufficient. [1,18] Drainage options: [18] 1. Serial arthrocentesis (needle aspiration): - Minimally invasive - Can repeat daily until effusion resolves - Effective for accessible joints (knee, ankle, elbow, wrist) - May be sufficient for gonococcal and some streptococcal infections 2. Arthroscopic irrigation & debridement: - Breaks down loculati

nodes.title: Drainage Approach
nodes.summary: Choose serial aspiration for accessible joints vs surgical drainage for hip/shoulder/SI or failed aspiration
nodes.body: Select the appropriate drainage strategy based on joint and clinical factors: [18]

nodes.title: Serial Arthrocentesis Protocol
nodes.summary: Aspirate daily until effusion resolves; escalate to surgery if no improvement by 5-7 days or loculations found
nodes.body: Serial aspiration approach: [18] Technique: - Aspirate joint daily (or BID if rapidly reaccumulating) - Document volume removed - Send initial fluid for analysis; subsequent taps for culture only if deteriorating - Use ultrasound guidance for optimal drainage Success indicators: - Decreasing effusion volume - Improving synovial WBC count - Clinical improvement (pain, ROM, fever) When to escalate t

nodes.title: Surgical Drainage Indications
nodes.summary: Hip, shoulder, SI joint require surgical drainage — consult ortho EARLY; do not delay for serial aspiration
nodes.body: Indications for surgical irrigation & debridement: [1,18] Absolute: - Hip joint (difficult to aspirate, high complication rate) - Shoulder joint - Sternoclavicular/sacroiliac joints - Prosthetic joint infection - Osteomyelitis coexisting with septic arthritis - Failed serial aspiration (no improvement in 5-7 days) Relative: - Virulent organism (MRSA, Pseudomonas) - Immunocompromised patient - Locu

nodes.title: Gonococcal: Drainage Approach
nodes.summary: GC arthritis often managed without surgery — 1-3 aspirations usually sufficient; partner notification and STI screening required
nodes.body: Gonococcal septic arthritis often managed WITHOUT surgical drainage. [14,16] Typically adequate: - Serial arthrocentesis for initial drainage - May need 1-3 aspirations - Good response to antibiotics alone Consider surgical drainage if: [14] - Purulent effusion with large volume - No improvement after 3-4 days of antibiotics - Hip or shoulder involvement - Immunocompromised patient Key differences

nodes.title: Antibiotic Duration
nodes.summary: S. aureus 3-4wk, Strep 2-3wk, GC 7-14d, Pseudomonas 4-6wk; IV-to-oral when clinically improving with susceptible oral agent
nodes.body: Treatment duration by pathogen: [1,15] | Organism | Total Duration | IV Phase | |----------|---------------|----------| | S. aureus | 3-4 weeks | 2-3 weeks | | Streptococci | 2-3 weeks | 1-2 weeks | | N. gonorrhoeae | 7-14 days | Until improved | | Gram-negatives | 3-4 weeks | 2-3 weeks | | P. aeruginosa | 4-6 weeks | 3-4 weeks | IV to oral transition criteria: [15] - Clinical improvement (decreas

nodes.title: Treatment Monitoring
nodes.summary: CRP most useful trend marker — normalizes within 1 week; poor response: wrong antibiotic, inadequate drainage, or abscess
nodes.body: Response assessment: [1] Clinical: - Daily joint exam (effusion, warmth, ROM) - Fever curve - Pain level - Ability to bear weight Laboratory: - CRP most useful - rises within hours, normalizes within 1 week with effective treatment [1] - ESR slower to normalize (may remain elevated for weeks) - WBC less helpful - Repeat synovial fluid if poor response Expected timeline: - Fever: resolves 48-72h -

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ALL suspected septic arthritis requires admission — determine floor vs ICU based on hemodynamic status
nodes.body: All patients with suspected or confirmed septic arthritis require admission. [1] Determine appropriate level of care:

nodes.title: Medical Floor Admission
nodes.body: Admission orders: [1] Consultations: - Orthopedic surgery (all cases) - Infectious disease (recommended) Antibiotics: - Continue empiric IV antibiotics per earlier recommendations - De-escalate when culture and sensitivities available Monitoring: - Daily joint exam - Serial CRP (most useful for trend) - Repeat imaging if clinical concern for complications Activity: - Non-weight bearing initially -
nodes.recommendation: Admit to medical floor for IV antibiotics, serial drainage, and orthopedic consultation. ID consultation recommended.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: [1] Indications: - Sepsis or septic shock - Polyarticular septic arthritis with bacteremia - Endocarditis suspected (S. aureus bacteremia) - Necrotizing fasciitis or significant soft tissue involvement - Respiratory failure - Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors ICU management: - Aggressive fluid resuscitation - Vasopressors if needed - Broad-spectrum antibiotics
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for sepsis management, aggressive resuscitation, and emergent surgical consultation for source control.

nodes.title: Serotonin Syndrome
nodes.summary: Serotonergic excess causing AMS, autonomic dysfunction, neuromuscular excitation — onset within 24h of drug change, clonus is hallmark
nodes.body: Serotonin Syndrome Steps Summary Definition: Life-threatening condition caused by excessive serotonergic activity in the CNS. [1] Classic Triad: [1][2] • Altered mental status (agitation, confusion, anxiety) • Autonomic dysfunction (hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, mydriasis) • Neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, rigidity) Key Features: • Onset typically within 24 hours

nodes.title: Serotonergic Drug Exposure?
nodes.summary: Determine serotonergic drug exposure — required for Hunter Criteria diagnosis, check SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs/tramadol/MDMA/linezolid
nodes.body: Has the patient taken a serotonergic drug? Hunter Criteria REQUIRE exposure to a serotonergic agent for diagnosis. Serotonergic Drug List Common triggers: • SSRI/SNRI (most common) • MAOI combinations (most severe) • Tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine • MDMA/ecstasy, cocaine, amphetamines • Linezolid, methylene blue (MAOIs) • Drug interactions (SSRI + triptan, SSRI + MAOI)

nodes.title: Investigate Drug Exposure
nodes.summary: Complete medication history including Rx, OTC/supplements, and recreational drugs — check for new starts, dose changes, and interactions
nodes.body: Obtain Complete Medication History: [3] Prescription medications: • Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs) • Psychiatric medications (buspirone, lithium) • Pain medications (tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine) • Migraine medications (triptans) • Antibiotics (linezolid) • Antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide) OTC/Supplements: • Dextromethorphan (DXM in cough syrups) • St. John's Wort • SAMe, t

nodes.title: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria
nodes.summary: Hunter Criteria (84% sens, 97% spec) — serotonergic agent + clonus/tremor/hyperreflexia/hypertonia, check ankle clonus >3 beats
nodes.body: Hunter Criteria — More sensitive (84%) and specific (97%) than Sternbach criteria. [4] REQUIRES: 1. Exposure to serotonergic agent, AND 2. ONE of the following: Spontaneous clonus ✓ Inducible clonus + (agitation OR diaphoresis) ✓ Ocular clonus + (agitation OR diaphoresis) ✓ Tremor + hyperreflexia ✓ Hypertonia + temp >38°C + (ocular OR inducible clonus) ✓ Key exam findings: • Clonus — rhythmic, inv

nodes.title: Hunter Criteria Result
nodes.summary: Assess if patient meets Hunter Criteria — serotonergic exposure + one clinical finding cluster
nodes.body: Does the patient meet Hunter Criteria? Serotonergic agent exposure + ONE of: • Spontaneous clonus • Inducible clonus + agitation/diaphoresis • Ocular clonus + agitation/diaphoresis • Tremor + hyperreflexia • Hypertonia + temp >38°C + ocular/inducible clonus

nodes.title: Differential Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Differentiate SS from NMS, anticholinergic toxicity, malignant hyperthermia, sympathomimetics, sepsis, thyroid storm
nodes.body: Consider these mimics: [2][5] • Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) • Anticholinergic toxicity • Malignant hyperthermia • Sympathomimetic toxicity • Meningitis/encephalitis • Sepsis • Thyroid storm • Heat stroke SS vs NMS Differentiator Key differentiating features: • Onset timing (SS rapid, NMS slow) • Muscle tone (SS hyperkinetic/clonus, NMS rigid/bradyreflexic) • Drug class (serotonergic vs do

nodes.title: SS vs NMS Differentiation
nodes.summary: Compare SS vs NMS features — onset speed, drug class, muscle tone (hyperkinetic vs rigid), reflexes, pupils, CK level
nodes.body: Key differentiating features: [5][6] | Feature | Serotonin Syndrome | NMS | |---------|-------------------|-----| | Onset | Hours (within 24h) | Days to weeks | | Drug | Serotonergic | Dopamine antagonist | | Muscle | Hyperkinetic, clonus | "Lead-pipe" rigidity | | Reflexes | Hyperreflexia | Bradyreflexia | | Pupils | Dilated (mydriasis) | Normal | | Bowel sounds | Hyperactive | Normal/decreased |

nodes.title: NMS — Different Management
nodes.body: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome requires different treatment: [6] Immediate: • Stop offending antipsychotic • Aggressive cooling • IV fluids • Benzodiazepines for rigidity Specific therapy: • Dantrolene — muscle relaxant, first-line • Bromocriptine — dopamine agonist (contraindicated in SS!) Duration: • Resolution takes days to weeks • 2-week washout before restarting antipsychotics ICU admission f
nodes.recommendation: Consult toxicology and psychiatry. ICU admission for moderate-severe NMS.

nodes.title: Alternative Diagnosis
nodes.body: Serotonin syndrome unlikely — consider: [1][5][7] • Anticholinergic toxicity: Dry, hot, flushed, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds • Sympathomimetic: Cocaine, amphetamines — similar but no clonus • Sepsis: Fever, altered mental status — check source • Meningitis/Encephalitis: Meningismus, CSF analysis • Thyroid storm: History of hyperthyroidism, check TSH • Heat stroke: Environmental exposure
nodes.recommendation: Continue workup for alternative etiology.

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Classify severity: mild (tremor, alert), moderate (agitation, temp 38.5-40), severe (temp >40, rigidity, seizures, rhabdo)

nodes.title: Mild SS — Treatment
nodes.summary: Stop serotonergic agents, benzos for agitation/tremor, IV fluids, observe 6-12h — most resolve in 24-72h
nodes.body: Mild Serotonin Syndrome Management: [1][7] 1. STOP offending agent(s) • Identify and discontinue ALL serotonergic drugs • Review medication list thoroughly 2. Supportive care: • IV fluids • Cardiac monitoring • Observation for 6-12 hours 3. Symptom management: • Benzodiazepines for agitation/tremor - Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV or - Diazepam 5-10 mg IV 4. Cyproheptadine (optional for mild): • Generally no

nodes.title: Moderate SS — Treatment
nodes.summary: Stop agents, high-dose benzos, cyproheptadine 12mg load then 2mg q2h (max 32mg/day), cooling — avoid restraints and antipyretics
nodes.body: Moderate Serotonin Syndrome Management: [1][7][8] 1. STOP all serotonergic agents 2. Supportive care: • IV fluids (aggressive hydration) • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Cooling measures if temp >38.5°C 3. Sedation: • Benzodiazepines — first-line for agitation - Lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q15-30min PRN - Diazepam 5-10 mg IV q15min PRN • May require large doses • Also reduces muscle activity → decreases

nodes.title: Severe SS — Treatment
nodes.summary: Secure airway (avoid succinylcholine), aggressive cooling, high-dose benzos, paralysis if needed, cyproheptadine via NG
nodes.body: SEVERE Serotonin Syndrome — Life-Threatening Emergency [1][7][8] 1. ABC — Secure airway if needed • Consider early intubation if severely agitated/rigid • Avoid succinylcholine (hyperkalemia risk with rhabdo) • Use rocuronium or vecuronium 2. Aggressive cooling: • Target temp <38.5°C • Ice packs, cooling blankets, mist/fan • Consider ice water immersion if >41°C • Paralysis may be needed for intra

nodes.title: Disposition — Mild SS
nodes.summary: Discharge if resolving after 6-12h observation, stable vitals, tolerating PO — educate on drug interactions, psych follow-up
nodes.body: Discharge Considerations: [7] May discharge if: • Symptoms resolving after 6-12 hour observation • Vital signs stable and normalizing • Able to tolerate PO • No ongoing exposure risk • Reliable follow-up Before discharge: • Confirm offending agent discontinued • Educate on drug interactions • Provide return precautions • Psychiatry follow-up if on psychotropic medications Return precautions: • Fev

nodes.title: Disposition — Moderate SS
nodes.summary: Telemetry admission, continue benzos and cyproheptadine q6h for 24-48h, tox and psych consults — MAOIs may take up to 1 week
nodes.body: Admission Required: [7] Floor vs Telemetry: • Telemetry bed preferred • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Frequent neuro checks Monitoring: • Vital signs q2-4h • Neuro exam q4h (clonus, reflexes, mental status) • Temperature trending • CK levels if concern for rhabdomyolysis Treatment continuation: • Continue benzodiazepines PRN • Continue cyproheptadine q6h for 24-48h • IV fluids until PO tolerant

nodes.title: Disposition — Severe SS
nodes.summary: ICU for temp >40, intubation, paralysis, hemodynamic instability, rhabdo with renal failure, DIC — MAOI cases longest duration
nodes.body: ICU Admission Required: [7][8] ICU level care for: • Temp >40°C • Intubation needed • Paralysis required for hyperthermia control • Hemodynamic instability • Rhabdomyolysis with renal failure • Seizures • DIC ICU monitoring: • Continuous vital signs • Core temperature • Urine output • Serial CK, renal function, coags • Lactate trending Prolonged recovery: • Severe cases may take days to weeks • MA

nodes.recommendation: Management pathway complete. Ensure psychiatry follow-up for medication reconciliation.

nodes.title: Shoulder Dislocation
nodes.summary: Most common large joint dislocation — anterior 95-97%; posterior easily missed (seizure/electrocution); inferior is rare but high NV injury
nodes.body: Shoulder Reduction Summary — assessment, reduction, and disposition pathway. Most common large joint dislocation — comprising ~50% of all major joint dislocations seen in the ED. Anterior dislocation: 95-97% of all shoulder dislocations • Mechanism: abduction + external rotation + extension • Arm held in slight abduction, externally rotated • Loss of deltoid contour, prominent acromion Posterior d

nodes.title: Neurovascular Assessment
nodes.summary: MANDATORY pre-reduction exam — axillary nerve (regimental badge sensation), radial pulse, document ALL deficits
nodes.body: MANDATORY pre-reduction neurovascular exam: Axillary nerve (most commonly injured — 5-35%): • Sensation: "regimental badge" area (lateral deltoid) • Motor: deltoid contraction (difficult to test pre-reduction) • Document ANY sensory deficit before reduction Musculocutaneous nerve: • Sensation: lateral forearm • Motor: elbow flexion Vascular assessment: • Radial pulse — compare to unaffected side •

nodes.title: First-Time or Recurrent?
nodes.summary: First-time needs pre-reduction imaging and has higher injury risk; recurrent may reduce easily with less analgesia
nodes.body: Determine dislocation history: First-time dislocation: • Higher risk of associated injuries (Bankart, Hill-Sachs, GT fracture) • Pre-reduction imaging more important • Higher recurrence risk in young patients Recurrent dislocation: • Often requires less analgesia/sedation • May self-reduce or reduce easily • Known mechanism and anatomy • May defer pre-reduction imaging Is this a first-time or recu

nodes.title: Recurrent Dislocation Assessment
nodes.summary: Red flags in recurrent dislocators: new neurovascular deficit, unusual position, significantly more pain than usual
nodes.body: Recurrent dislocators often require: • Less or no sedation • Simpler reduction techniques • May self-reduce with coaching Consider pre-reduction imaging if: • Different mechanism than usual • Higher energy mechanism • More pain than prior episodes • Concern for new fracture Red flags in recurrent dislocator: • New neurovascular deficit • Unusual limb position • Significantly more pain than prior D

nodes.title: Pre-Reduction Imaging

nodes.title: FARES Method

Apply gentle longitudinal traction (along axis of arm) 3. Begin vertical oscillations (±5 cm up/down) at 2-3 cycles/second 4. Slowly abduct arm while maintaining traction and oscillations 5. Patient prone on stretcher, affected arm hanging off edge 2. Apply 5-10 lbs downward traction on arm 3. Push inferior tip of scapula medially (toward spine) 4. Slowly externally rotate forearm (moving hand away from body) 3. Rotate at ~1° per second — SLOW is key 4. Continue to maximum external rotation (~90°) 5. nodes.title: Stimson Technique (Prone)
nodes.summary: Prone with arm hanging + 5-10lb weight — wait 15-30 min for muscle fatigue; no assistant needed but time-intensive
