nodes.body: McRoberts maneuver + suprapubic pressure have been applied. Did the shoulder dystocia resolve? Expected success rate: 50–60% with both maneuvers combined. [5][6]

nodes.title: Wood's Screw & Rubin's Maneuver
nodes.summary: Corkscrew rotate posterior shoulder 180° (Wood) or flex shoulders across chest (Rubin) — try both directions
nodes.body: Rotational maneuvers use progressive corkscrew rotation of the posterior shoulder to release the impacted anterior shoulder. WOOD'S SCREW MANEUVER (1943) • Apply pressure on the anterior surface of the posterior shoulder • Progressively rotate the posterior shoulder 180° in a corkscrew fashion • This rotates the baby's shoulder girdle, freeing the anterior shoulder from behind the symphysis RUBIN'

nodes.title: Delivery of the Posterior Arm — MOST RELIABLE Maneuver
nodes.summary: MOST RELIABLE maneuver — 84% single-maneuver success (Hoffman 2011 NICHD). Flex elbow via antecubital pressure, grasp forearm/wrist only, sweep across fetal chest. Menticoglou axillary traction if arm cannot be reached.
nodes.body: ⭐ MOST RELIABLE MANEUVER FOR RESOLVING SHOULDER DYSTOCIA. In the NICHD Consortium on Safe Labor analysis (Hoffman 2011), delivery of the posterior arm had the highest single-maneuver success rate of ANY shoulder dystocia maneuver — 84.4% — far exceeding McRoberts (24.3%), suprapubic pressure (62.2%), or rotational maneuvers (66.0-72.0% — Rubin/Woods corkscrew). [9] Poggi (2003) and Chauhan (2010)

nodes.title: Second-Line Resolution Check
nodes.summary: Assess if rotational maneuvers or posterior arm resolved dystocia — if not, escalate to last resort
nodes.body: Rotational maneuvers and/or posterior arm delivery have been attempted. Did the shoulder dystocia resolve? McFarland (1996) found that McRoberts + suprapubic + Wood's screw + posterior arm delivery were sufficient to resolve all remaining cases in his series. [6]

nodes.title: Last Resort Maneuvers
nodes.summary: Zavanelli (push head back + emergency C-section), all-fours, deliberate clavicle fracture, symphysiotomy — all carry major risk
nodes.body: If all standard maneuvers have failed, consider these last-resort options. Each carries significant maternal and/or fetal risk. ZAVANELLI MANEUVER (Cephalic Replacement) First described by Dr. Zavanelli (1977, Pleasanton, CA). • Set up for emergency cesarean section first • Rotate fetal head to occiput anterior position • Flex the head and apply constant firm pressure to push it back into the vagi

nodes.title: Recommended Protocols — Summary
nodes.summary: ACOG sequence: McRoberts → suprapubic → rotational → posterior arm → Zavanelli. Posterior arm has highest single-maneuver success (84%) — prioritize if first-line fails.
nodes.body: The most important aspect of resolving shoulder dystocia is having a clear, well-rehearsed sequence of maneuvers in mind before it occurs. [1] ACOG PROTOCOL (Practice Bulletin No. 178, 2017) [1] 1. McRoberts maneuver + suprapubic pressure 2. Episiotomy (controversial) 3. Rotational maneuvers 4. Delivery of posterior arm 5. Zavanelli / symphysiotomy if all else fails GHERMAN USC PROTOCOL (1998) [11

nodes.title: Shoulder Dystocia — Resolved
nodes.body: POST-DELIVERY MANAGEMENT • Immediate neonatal assessment — Pediatrics/NICU should already be present • Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes • Evaluate for injury: - Brachial plexus palsy (Erb's) — asymmetric arm movement, "waiter's tip" posture - Clavicle fracture — crepitus, asymmetric Moro reflex - Humeral fracture — if posterior arm delivery was performed • Maternal assessment — check for vaginal/ce
nodes.recommendation: Shoulder dystocia resolved. Complete neonatal assessment, evaluate for brachial plexus injury and fractures, assess maternal status, and document all maneuvers and timing thoroughly.

nodes.title: Sickle Cell Disease — ED Management
nodes.summary: Obtain genotype, baseline Hgb, prior complications, individualized pain plan, immunization status, and hydroxyurea use
nodes.body: SCD Steps Summary Sickle cell disease (SCD) affects ~100,000 Americans. Occurs in ~1 of 365 Black/African American births and ~1 of 16,300 Hispanic American births. [1][2] Multiple acute complications can affect any organ system. Prompt recognition and management reduces morbidity and mortality. [1][3] SCD Genotypes & Severity Key History to Obtain: • SCD genotype (HbSS, HbSC, HbSβ0, HbSβ+) • Base

nodes.title: Key History & Baseline Assessment
nodes.summary: HbSS most severe (Hgb 6-8), HbSC moderate (Hgb 10-15); prior complications and pain plan guide ED management
nodes.body: SCD Genotype & Severity: • HbSS — most severe, baseline Hgb 6–8 g/dL • HbSβ0-thalassemia — similar severity to HbSS • HbSC — moderate severity, baseline Hgb 10–15 g/dL • HbSβ+-thalassemia — moderate, baseline Hgb 9–12 g/dL • HbAS (Sickle Cell Trait) — generally benign carrier state SCD Genotypes & Severity Critical History Elements: • Prior complications (ACS, stroke, splenic sequestration, priapi

nodes.title: Priapism in SCD
nodes.body: Priapism affects ~40% of males with SCD. [1] Intervention should occur within 4 hours of erection duration to prevent permanent scarring and erectile dysfunction. Initial Management: • IV hydration • Analgesia (per VOC pathway) • Supplemental oxygen • Oral pseudoephedrine 30–60 mg may be considered [1] • Ketamine at procedural sedation doses has been shown to assist with corporal detumescence [1]
nodes.recommendation: Initiate IV hydration, analgesia, and O2. If >4 hours duration, proceed to corporal aspiration per Priapism consult. Emergent urology consultation.

nodes.title: Vaso-Occlusive Crisis (VOC)
nodes.summary: Most common SCD complication — diagnosis is clinical, no biomarker validates severity; individualized pain plans reduce admissions 24%
nodes.body: VOC Pain Management Algorithm Differential Diagnosis VOC is the most common SCD complication and leading cause of ED visits (~40,000 annual pediatric ED visits in the US). [1][3] Pathophysiology: HbS polymerization → sickled RBC → microvascular occlusion → tissue ischemia and infarction. [1] Common Triggers: • Dehydration • Infection / fever • Cold exposure / weather changes • Hypoxia / acidosis •

nodes.title: Triage — Intranasal Fentanyl
nodes.summary: IN fentanyl 1-1.5 mcg/kg at triage BEFORE IV access — goal analgesia within 30min; heat packs, continuous SpO2
nodes.body: GOAL: Analgesia within 30 minutes of triage, 60 minutes of ED arrival. [4] Intranasal Fentanyl at Triage (before IV access): Fentanyl 1–1.5 mcg/kg IN via MAD atomizer (max 100 mcg) • Onset 5–10 min • Shortens ED length of stay [7] • Administer BEFORE establishing IV access Triage Actions: • Place PIV / access port • Obtain labs — SCD Lab Panel & Rationale • Urine HCG (females >10 years) • If ill-a

nodes.title: IV Analgesia & Fluids
nodes.summary: Ketorolac + opioid IV; NS 10mL/kg bolus; incentive spirometry q2h prevents ACS; AVOID corticosteroids — rebound pain and stroke risk
nodes.body: NSAID (administer with first opioid dose): Ketorolac 0.5 mg/kg IV • Max 15 mg if <16 years, max 30 mg if ≥16 years • Reduces opioid requirements [8] • Contraindications: pregnancy, renal impairment, ketorolac within 5 days, ibuprofen within 6 hours, bleeding concerns, history of renal impairment Opioid (choose one based on patient preference/pain plan): Morphine 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV (max 8 mg) OR Hydr

nodes.title: Reassess Pain (q30 min)
nodes.summary: Reassess pain q30min, up to 3 opioid doses — wake patient even if sleeping; watch for developing ACS symptoms
nodes.body: RN reassess pain 30 minutes after each opioid dose. [4][5] • May give up to 3 doses of opioid • Wake patient to reassess even if sleeping • Notify provider before each additional dose • Continue incentive spirometry Monitor for: • Respiratory depression (SpO2, respiratory rate) • Sedation level • Developing fever, chest pain, or dyspnea (→ ACS)

nodes.title: Refractory Pain
nodes.summary: Sub-dissociative ketamine 0.1-0.3 mg/kg IV (ASH-recommended); CXR if any respiratory symptoms develop — 10-20% VOC admissions develop ACS
nodes.body: Sub-dissociative Ketamine (ASH-recommended adjunct): [5] Ketamine 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV over 10–15 min • Reduces opioid consumption in pediatric SCD patients [10] • May repeat q15–20 min PRN • ACEP supports use for SCD pain Additional Steps: • Contact hematology for pain plan guidance • Consider patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) if admitting • Review for other diagnoses: osteomyelitis, avascular necro

nodes.title: VOC — Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge Criteria: • Pain controlled with oral medications • Tolerating oral fluids • Afebrile • Stable hemoglobin • Reliable caregivers Discharge Plan: • Continue home pain regimen (scheduled NSAID + PRN opioid) • Refill home pain medications for 2–3 day supply if needed • Hematology follow-up within 24–48 hours • Continue incentive spirometry at home Return Precautions: • Fever ≥ 38.5°C (101.3°
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with oral pain regimen. Hematology follow-up within 24–48 hours. Return for fever, worsening pain, SOB, or chest pain.

nodes.title: VOC — Admission
nodes.body: Admission Criteria: • Pain not controlled after 3 opioid doses in ED • New respiratory symptoms (evaluate for ACS) • Unable to tolerate oral fluids/medications • Hemodynamic instability • Significant hemoglobin decline from baseline Inpatient Management: • PCA morphine or hydromorphone • Scheduled NSAIDs + PRN opioids (multimodal) • Incentive spirometry q2h while awake • Maintenance IV fluids (avo
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV PCA, multimodal analgesia, incentive spirometry. Hematology consult. Monitor for ACS development.

nodes.title: Fever — Medical Emergency
nodes.summary: Fever >=38.5C is MEDICAL EMERGENCY — functional asplenia; ceftriaxone within 1hr; S. pneumoniae most common pathogen
nodes.body: Fever Evaluation Algorithm Fever ≥ 38.5°C (101.3°F) in SCD = MEDICAL EMERGENCY [4] Why fever is dangerous in SCD: • Functional asplenia develops by 3 months of age • Impaired clearance of encapsulated organisms • Risk for overwhelming sepsis and death Most Likely Pathogens: • Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common) • Haemophilus influenzae • Neisseria meningitidis • Salmonella species (osteomyeliti

nodes.title: Fever — Workup
nodes.summary: Blood culture ALWAYS before abx, CXR if any respiratory symptoms; positive viral test does NOT exclude bacteremia in SCD
nodes.body: Obtain BEFORE antibiotics: • Blood culture (ALWAYS — regardless of how well the patient appears) [1][4] Laboratory Studies: • CBC with differential + reticulocyte count • CMP (comprehensive metabolic panel) • Urinalysis if UTI concern Imaging: • CXR if ANY respiratory symptoms (cough, chest pain, hypoxia, tachypnea) — evaluate for ACS [1] Additional Assessment: • Vaccination status — PCV15/PCV20,

nodes.title: Empiric Antibiotics
nodes.summary: Ceftriaxone 50mg/kg IV (max 2g) immediately after blood cultures — assess for meningitis signs requiring expanded coverage
nodes.body: GIVE IMMEDIATELY after blood cultures: [4] Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) Covers: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, most Salmonella [1] Is there concern for meningitis?

nodes.title: Meningitis Coverage
nodes.summary: Meningitic dose ceftriaxone 100mg/kg + vancomycin 20mg/kg; parvovirus B19 causes aplastic crisis (retic <1% + Hgb drop >30%)
nodes.body: Meningitic Antibiotic Dosing: Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) — meningitic dose PLUS Vancomycin 20 mg/kg IV (max 1500 mg) The increased ceftriaxone dose ensures adequate CNS penetration. Vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcus and MRSA. [1][4] Age <60 Days: Full sepsis workup per AAP 2021 guidelines required: Peds Fever < 6 Months Parvovirus B19 / Aplastic Crisis: • 80% of SCD patients infecte

nodes.title: Fever — Disposition
nodes.body: Safe to Discharge: [4][12] • Well-appearing after observation • Reliable caregivers • Hematology follow-up confirmed within 24 hours • Completed pneumococcal vaccine series • No focal bacterial infection requiring IV antibiotics • Parenteral antibiotics given in ED Must Admit: [4] • Ill-appearing • WBC >30,000 or <5,000 /mcL [13] • Hypotensive for age • Continued fever despite antibiotics • CXR in
nodes.recommendation: Well-appearing, vaccinated patients may be discharged after parenteral antibiotics with confirmed 24-hour hematology follow-up. Admit ill-appearing patients, those with abnormal WBC, hemodynamic instability, or CXR infiltrate.

nodes.title: Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS)
nodes.summary: New infiltrate + fever/respiratory symptoms = ACS; accounts for 25% of SCD deaths; CXR may lag behind clinical symptoms
nodes.body: ACS Recognition & Management Definition: New radiodensity on chest imaging WITH fever and/or respiratory symptoms [1] ACS accounts for up to 25% of SCD-related deaths. [1] Common Triggers: • Infection — S. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, viral • Fat embolism from bone marrow infarction • In situ sickling • Pulmonary infarction from VOC Clinical Presentation: • Chest pain, cough, dyspnea, tachyp

nodes.title: ACS — Treatment
nodes.summary: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin; O2 ONLY for SpO2 <90%; incentive spirometry q2h; AVOID corticosteroids — stroke risk
nodes.body: Antibiotics (cover typical + atypical): Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV (max 2 g) PLUS Azithromycin 10 mg/kg IV (max 500 mg) Oxygen Management: • Supplemental O2 ONLY for SpO2 <90% [1] • Higher O2 in non-hypoxic patients blunts bone marrow response to RBC breakdown • Target SpO2 ≥ 92% Respiratory Support: • Incentive spirometry q2h while awake — proven to prevent ACS progression [1] • Bronchodilators PRN

nodes.title: ACS — Transfusion Decision
nodes.summary: Simple transfusion if Hgb drops >1g/dL below baseline; target HbS <30%, Hgb ~10; do NOT exceed Hgb 11 (hyperviscosity)
nodes.body: Transfusion Guidelines Simple Transfusion Indications: [4] • Hgb drops >1 g/dL below baseline • Goal: decrease HbS to <30% Transfusion Targets: • Hgb ~10 g/dL • HbS <30% • Do NOT exceed Hgb 11 g/dL (hyperviscosity risk) What is the patient's clinical trajectory?

nodes.title: ACS — Exchange Transfusion
nodes.summary: Exchange transfusion for worsening respiratory failure — target HbS <30%; contact blood bank early for extended antigen matching
nodes.body: Exchange Transfusion Indications: [4] • Worsening respiratory distress despite O2 • Worsening hypoxia while on supplemental oxygen • Progressive pulmonary infiltrates on CXR • Worsening anemia after simple transfusion • Multilobar disease • Rapid clinical deterioration Targets: • HbS <30% • Hgb ~10 g/dL (avoid >11 g/dL) Contact blood bank EARLY: • Extended antigen matching required (anti-C, E, Kel

nodes.title: ACS — Admission
nodes.body: Admit ALL patients with ACS. [4] ICU Criteria: • Exchange transfusion needed • FiO2 >40% to maintain SpO2 ≥ 92% • Worsening respiratory status • Hemodynamic instability • Rapidly progressive infiltrates • Multilobar disease Ongoing Management: • Continue antibiotics (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) • Incentive spirometry q2h while awake • Judicious IV fluids — avoid overhydration (worsens pulmonary ed
nodes.recommendation: Admit all ACS patients. ICU if exchange transfusion, FiO2 >40%, worsening status, or hemodynamic instability. Continue antibiotics + incentive spirometry.

nodes.title: SCD — Acute Stroke
nodes.summary: SCD children 33x more likely to have ischemic stroke — peak age 2-9yr; activate stroke alert and notify hematology immediately
nodes.body: A child with SCD is 33× more likely to have an ischemic stroke than an age-matched healthy counterpart. [1] Incidence: Highest between ages 2–9 years. Prior to stroke-reducing protocols, ischemic stroke affected 10% of children with SCD. [1][6] Pathophysiology: • Decreased cerebrovascular reserve • Increased baseline cerebral blood flow • Impaired cerebral autoregulatory function • Increased basel

nodes.title: Stroke — Workup & Imaging
nodes.summary: Emergent CT to rule out hemorrhage, then MRI/MRA; type and crossmatch for exchange transfusion; pediatric NIHSS
nodes.body: Imaging: • Emergent CT head — rule out hemorrhage (hemorrhagic stroke more common in adult SCD) • MRI/MRA if hemorrhage ruled out — define infarct, identify large vessel vasculopathy (stenosis/occlusion with or without moyamoya collaterals) [1][6] Laboratory: • CBC with reticulocyte count • Coagulation studies • Hemoglobin electrophoresis — determine HbS% [1] • Type and crossmatch — prepare for ex

nodes.title: Stroke — Transfusion
nodes.summary: Exchange transfusion within 2hr targeting HbS <30%; tPA NOT recommended for children <18yr; simple transfusion only if Hgb <8.5
nodes.body: Transfusion Guidelines ASH recommends transfusion within 2 hours of neurologic symptom onset. [6] Exchange transfusion is recommended over simple transfusion. [6] • Target: HbS <30%, HbA >70%, Hgb ~10 g/dL • Simple transfusion can be done first to avoid delays, followed by exchange transfusion Important Thresholds: • If HbS already <50% → exchange transfusion may not be indicated [6] • If Hgb >8.5

nodes.title: Stroke — Disposition
nodes.body: Admit to ICU. [1][6] • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Serial neurologic assessments • Neurology + hematology co-management Long-term Management: • Chronic transfusion program — monthly transfusions to maintain HbS <30% [6] • Stroke prevention protocols (transcranial Doppler screening) have led to 10-fold decrease in stroke over the last decade [1] • After ≥1 year of chronic transfusion with norma
nodes.recommendation: Admit ICU. Exchange transfusion targeting HbS <30%. Neurology + hematology co-management. Chronic transfusion program for secondary prevention.

nodes.title: Splenic Sequestration
nodes.summary: Life-threatening — can progress to shock in hours; tachycardia is often first sign; establish two large-bore IVs immediately
nodes.body: Life-threatening complication — can progress to shock and cardiac arrest within hours. [1] Pathophysiology: Sickling in the relatively hypoxic splenic environment → RBCs trapped → ongoing cycle of sequestration → acute splenomegaly + severe anemia + thrombocytopenia [1] Typical Age: • HbSS: 6 months – 5 years (median 1.4 years) — before autoinfarction of spleen [1] • HbSC / HbSβ+: can present late

nodes.title: Splenic Sequestration — Treatment
nodes.body: Transfusion — CRITICAL NUANCE: [4] • pRBC in 5 mL/kg aliquots, standard infusion rate (3–4 hours) • DO NOT transfuse past Hgb 8 g/dL Why the Hgb 8 ceiling matters: Sequestered RBCs eventually re-enter the bloodstream ("reverse sequestration" or "autotransfusion"). If over-transfused → severe hyperviscosity → hypertension, heart failure, intracerebral hemorrhage. [1][4] Fluid Resuscitation: • Cryst
nodes.recommendation: Emergent pRBC transfusion in 5 mL/kg aliquots. Do NOT exceed Hgb 8 g/dL. Admit all. Hematology consult. High recurrence rate — consider splenectomy.

nodes.title: Sickle Cell Trait (HbAS)
nodes.summary: SCT is generally benign but has specific risks under physiologic stress — ECAST, rhabdo, renal papillary necrosis, medullary carcinoma
nodes.body: SCT Complications Sickle cell trait (SCT) is NOT sickle cell disease. [1] • ~8% of African Americans carry HbAS • Generally a benign carrier condition • Red blood cells function normally under typical conditions However, specific risks exist under physiologic stress: • High altitude • Severe dehydration • High-intensity or prolonged physical exertion • These conditions can induce sickling and vaso

nodes.title: ECAST — Exertional Collapse
nodes.summary: ECAST: 28x death risk during intense exercise; stop activity, cool, aggressive IV fluids targeting UOP 200-300mL/hr
nodes.body: Exercise Collapse Associated with Sickle Cell Trait (ECAST) Associated with competitive athletes and military training. Kark et al (1987) found 28× increased risk of exercise-related death among recruits with SCT compared to those without. [19] Pathophysiology: Metabolic crisis from known sickling risk factors during intense exercise: • Dehydration + acidosis + hypoxia + hyperthermia → sickling in

nodes.title: SCT — Renal Complications
nodes.summary: Renal papillary necrosis most common hematuria cause in SCT; flank pain + hematuria = CT urography for medullary carcinoma (median survival 15wk)
nodes.body: Renal Papillary Necrosis (most common cause of hematuria in SCT) [1] • Painless gross hematuria • Microinfarctions in renal medulla from sickling in vasa recta capillaries • Hypoxic, acidotic environment promotes sickling Workup: Urinalysis, urine culture, BMP (renal function), renal ultrasound with bladder Management: • Mild: outpatient — bed rest, oral hydration, urine alkalinization • Severe: i

nodes.title: SCT — Disposition
nodes.body: ECAST: • Admit to ICU for aggressive fluid resuscitation • Serial CK, BMP, blood gas monitoring • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Watch for rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC Hematuria: • Mild painless hematuria: outpatient with urology referral • Flank pain + hematuria: CT urography to rule out renal medullary carcinoma • Severe hematuria: admit for urologic management Counseling: • Exertional risks — avoi
nodes.recommendation: ECAST: admit ICU with aggressive fluids and monitoring. Hematuria: urology referral, CT urography if flank pain. Counsel on exertional risks and hydration.

nodes.title: Special Populations & Considerations
nodes.summary: Opioid misuse rate in SCD is LOWER than general population — treat pain first; individualized pain plans reduce admissions 24%
nodes.body: Pregnant Patients: [1] • Increased risk for VOC, ACS, preeclampsia/eclampsia, stillbirth, cesarean delivery, low birth weight • Early multidisciplinary team: obstetrics + hematology • More aggressive monitoring and lower intervention thresholds Unvaccinated Children: [1] • PCV7 vaccine reduced pneumococcal infection by 90% • Unvaccinated children at dramatically higher risk even on penicillin prop

nodes.title: SJS / TEN: Recognition
nodes.summary: Drug-induced emergency — the rash that hurts; stop the culprit drug now
nodes.body: SJS/TEN Steps Summary — stepwise approach. SJS/TEN is a drug-induced dermatologic emergency — keratinocyte apoptosis with epidermal detachment, on a spectrum with toxic epidermal necrolysis. The earliest, highest-value intervention is stopping the culprit drug; delay correlates with mortality. 5 DO-NOT-MISS: • The rash that hurts. Skin pain out of proportion — often *preceding* the rash — is the b

nodes.title: Bedside Findings
nodes.summary: URI-like prodrome → painful truncal dusky macules; Nikolsky/Asboe-Hansen positive
nodes.body: Prodrome (1–3 days before rash): fever (often >39°C), malaise, sore throat, cough, conjunctivitis, myalgias — looks like a URI/flu. Skin: dusky/purpuric macules and flat atypical targets beginning truncally, coalescing → dusky skin → detachment. Maximum extent usually by ~4 days. Skin is painful and tender. Provocative signs: • Nikolsky sign — lateral shear on erythematous skin peels the epidermis

nodes.title: Classify the Eruption
nodes.summary: <10% = SJS · 10–30% = overlap · >30% = TEN · EM is a separate disease
nodes.body: Classification rests on maximal % BSA epidermal detachment plus lesion morphology. Erythema multiforme is a distinct entity, NOT mild SJS — it is infection-driven (HSV, Mycoplasma), with *typical* acral target lesions and is Nikolsky-negative. Which picture fits?

nodes.title: Erythema Multiforme (distinct entity)
nodes.summary: EM = HSV-driven acral typical targets, Nikolsky-neg, self-limiting — not SJS
nodes.body: EM is not on the SJS/TEN spectrum. It is driven by infection — HSV is the dominant trigger (also Mycoplasma) — not drugs. Recognize it: *typical* target lesions = 3 concentric zones (central dusky/bullous → pale edematous ring → outer erythema), <3 cm, well-defined, acral (dorsal hands/feet) spreading proximally. Nikolsky-negative. Self-limiting over 1–2 weeks. EM minor = no/minimal mucosa, no sys
nodes.recommendation: Erythema multiforme: infection-driven (HSV most common), acral typical targets, Nikolsky-negative, self-limiting. Treat trigger (e.g., aciclovir for HSV-associated/recurrent EM), supportive care. This is NOT SJS/TEN — different pathophysiol

nodes.title: MIRM / RIME
nodes.summary: Infection-triggered mucositis + minimal skin, no drug, good prognosis
nodes.body: Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM) — and the broader reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) — is a syndrome distinct from both SJS/TEN and EM (Canavan 2015). Picture: prominent mucositis (≥2 sites) with minimal/absent skin (<10% BSA, scattered atypical targets or vesiculobullous), in children/young adults, after Mycoplasma or another respiratory pathogen (C. pneumoniae, influe
nodes.recommendation: MIRM/RIME: infection-triggered (classically Mycoplasma), prominent mucositis with minimal skin, no culprit drug, good prognosis. Treat the infection + supportive mucosal care. Distinguish from SJS/TEN (drug-driven, skin-dominant).

nodes.title: Identify & Stop the Culprit
nodes.summary: Stop the drug now; review last 4–8 weeks; allopurinol/anticonvulsants/sulfa/NSAIDs
nodes.body: STOP the culprit drug immediately — earlier withdrawal of short-half-life culprits lowers mortality. Review all drugs started in the prior 4–8 weeks (typical latency 4–28 days; anticonvulsants up to ~8 weeks). High-risk culprit drugs — full list with notoriety. Highest-risk (RegiSCAR/EuroSCAR): allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfonamide antibiotics (TMP-SMX), su

nodes.title: Severity: SCORTEN
nodes.summary: 7 variables, day 1 + day 3; ≥3 → high mortality; low score ≠ under-treat
nodes.body: Calculate SCORTEN — 7 variables, 1 point each: age >40, malignancy, HR >120, BSA detachment >10%, BUN >28 mg/dL, glucose >252 mg/dL, bicarbonate <20 mEq/L. Mortality bands: 0–1 ≈3% · 2 ≈12% · 3 ≈35% · 4 ≈58% · ≥5 ≈90%. Score on day 1 AND day 3 — a single early score underestimates risk for scores ≥3 (BSA and HR are unstable early and it does not capture evolving sepsis). A low early score never ju

nodes.title: ED Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Stop drug · ⅔ Parkland to UOP 0.5–1 · urgent ophtho · no prophylactic abx
nodes.body: This is acute skin failure — manage like a burn, but with less fluid. • Fluids: estimate first-24h crystalloid at 2 mL/kg × %BSA (≈⅔ Parkland), then titrate to urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr. Over-resuscitation → pulmonary/intestinal edema. Cannulate through non-lesional skin where possible. • Temperature: warm ambient (30–32°C) — thermoregulation is lost. • Eyes: urgent ophthalmology — ocular diseas

nodes.title: Disease-Modifying Therapy
nodes.summary: Derm-guided, weak evidence; cyclosporine favored; etanercept emerging
nodes.body: Adjuvant therapy is dermatology-guided and the evidence base is weak (rare disease, mostly observational). None is mandated standard-of-care; supportive care + drug withdrawal remain the backbone. • Cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day — most-favored adjunct; meta-analyses show a mortality signal but data are observational with publication bias. • Etanercept / TNF-α inhibitors — emerging; one open-label RCT

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: >10% BSA → ICU; TEN → burn center; multidisciplinary, urgent ophthalmology
nodes.body: Any >10% BSA epidermal loss = ICU / specialist unit (acute skin failure: thermoregulatory dysfunction, insensible loss, hemodynamic instability, sepsis risk). Burn-center transfer for TEN (>30% BSA) and/or deterioration — extension of detachment, wound conversion, local sepsis, delayed healing. Multidisciplinary team: dermatology (lead + adjuvant decision), ophthalmology (urgent), urology/gynecolo
nodes.recommendation: Stop the culprit drug. >10% BSA → ICU/specialist unit; TEN → burn-center transfer. Engage dermatology, urgent ophthalmology, and burn surgery. Supportive care (⅔-Parkland fluids to UOP, no prophylactic antibiotics) is the backbone; adjuvant

nodes.title: Snake Bite: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Remove jewelry, immobilize, mark swelling edge with time, baseline labs — do NOT ice, tourniquet, or incise; 20-25% are dry bites
nodes.body: North American venomous snakes: - Pit vipers (Crotalinae) — 99% of US venomous bites - Rattlesnakes (50-55%) - Copperheads (30-45%) - Cottonmouths/water moccasins - Coral snakes (Elapidae) — ~1% of bites Immediate Actions: 1. Remove jewelry/constrictive items 2. Immobilize extremity at heart level 3. Mark leading edge of swelling with time 4. Large-bore IV access 5. Baseline labs: CBC, PT/INR, PTT

nodes.title: Snake Identification
nodes.summary: Pit vipers cause significant local swelling; coral snakes cause minimal local but delayed neurotoxicity — treat by presentation if unidentified
nodes.body: Can you identify the snake type? Pit Viper Features: - Triangular head - Elliptical (cat-like) pupils - Heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril - Retractable front fangs - Rattlesnakes have rattle (may be broken) Coral Snake Features: - Small, slender (40-70 cm) - Round pupils - Red, yellow, black bands - "Red touches yellow, kill a fellow" (US only) - ⚠️ Rhyme NOT reliable outside US Clinical Cl

nodes.title: Pit Viper: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Serial circumference measurements q30-60min; labs requiring antivenom: plt <100K, fibrinogen <100, INR >3, PTT >50
nodes.body: Perform serial assessments every 30-60 minutes: - Circumference measurements at consistent landmarks - Leading edge marking with time stamps - Pain assessment - Systemic symptoms review Snakebite Severity Score (SSS): 0-20 points - Change of 1 point = clinically significant worsening - Used to track progression and response to treatment Severity Score Calculator Initial Lab Thresholds Requiring An

nodes.title: Severity Grade
nodes.summary: Grade 0-3: dry (fang marks only) to severe (rapid progression, hypotension, coagulopathy); copperheads often mild
nodes.body: Grade the envenomation: | Grade | Local Signs | Systemic | Labs | |-------|------------|----------|------| | Dry (0) | Fang marks only | None | Normal | | Mild (1) | Local edema, not crossing joint | Minimal | Normal | | Moderate (2) | Entire extremity | Nausea, paresthesias | Minor abnl | | Severe (3) | Rapid progression, necrosis | Hypotension, AMS | Severe abnl | Copperhead bites are often mild

nodes.title: Dry Bite Management
nodes.summary: Observe minimum 8hr, repeat labs before discharge, tetanus prophylaxis — 20-25% of pit viper bites are dry
nodes.body: No envenomation detected — observation protocol: Observation Period: - Minimum 8 hours (some recommend 12-24h) - Serial exams every 2-4 hours - Repeat labs before discharge Tetanus prophylaxis if not current. Wound care: - Clean with soap and water - No prophylactic antibiotics (unless infection signs) Discharge criteria: - No progression of swelling - Normal repeat labs - No systemic symptoms - A

nodes.title: Mild Envenomation
nodes.summary: Copperhead bites often managed without antivenom; rattlesnake bites have lower threshold for antivenom; watch for progression
nodes.body: Mild envenomation — management decision: Current status: - Local edema not crossing a major joint - No systemic symptoms - Normal or near-normal labs Copperhead bites: - Often managed WITHOUT antivenom - Observation 12-24 hours - Antivenom if progression Rattlesnake bites: - Lower threshold for antivenom - Watch closely for progression Monitor for progression to moderate/severe: - Swelling crossin

nodes.title: Moderate Envenomation
nodes.summary: Antivenom indicated for progressive swelling, systemic toxicity, or lab abnormalities — antivenom treats swelling, NOT fasciotomy
nodes.body: Moderate envenomation — antivenom indicated: Indications for antivenom: - Progressive local swelling beyond bite site - Systemic toxicity (hypotension, airway swelling, neurotoxicity) - Hematologic abnormalities: - Platelets < 100,000 - Fibrinogen < 100 mg/dL - INR > 3.0 - PTT > 50 seconds Proceed to antivenom selection and dosing. Key Point: Swelling is typically subcutaneous. True compartment sy

nodes.title: Severe Envenomation
nodes.summary: High-dose antivenom (8-12 CroFab or 10+ Anavip); treat coagulopathy with antivenom FIRST, blood products only for active bleeding
nodes.body: Severe envenomation — aggressive management: Immediate priorities: 1. Airway assessment — early intubation for head/neck bites 2. Large-bore IV × 2 3. Aggressive fluid resuscitation 4. Blood products if active bleeding (see below) 5. HIGH-DOSE ANTIVENOM Antivenom dosing for severe: - CroFab: 8-12 vials initial (vs 4-6 for moderate) - Anavip: 10+ vials Coagulopathy management: ⚠️ Treat with ANTIVEN

nodes.title: Antivenom Selection
nodes.summary: CroFab (shorter half-life, needs maintenance) vs Anavip (longer half-life, no maintenance); pediatric dose = adult dose
nodes.body: Two FDA-approved pit viper antivenoms: CroFab (Fab - Ovine): - Shorter half-life - Requires maintenance dosing (2 vials at 6, 12, 18h) - Higher recurrence rates (32-50%) - More clinical experience Anavip (F(ab')₂ - Equine): - Longer half-life - No scheduled maintenance dosing - Lower recurrence rates - Newer, less clinical experience Both are effective — use what is available. Pediatric dose = Adu

nodes.title: CroFab Administration
nodes.summary: CroFab 4-6 vials (severe: 8-12) in 250mL NS; start slow 25-50mL/hr x10min then 250mL/hr; maintenance 2 vials at 6/12/18hr
nodes.body: CroFab Dosing Protocol: Reconstitution: 1. Reconstitute each vial with 18 mL NS 2. Mix by continuous manual inversion (1-2/sec) 3. DO NOT SHAKE (causes foaming) 4. Reconstitution should take < 7 min 5. Dilute total dose to 250 mL NS 6. Use within 4 hours Initial Dose: - Standard: 4-6 vials IV - Severe: 8-12 vials IV - Pediatric = Adult dose Administration: - Start slow: 25-50 mL/hr × 10 min - If n

nodes.title: Anavip Administration
nodes.summary: Anavip 10 vials over 60min; repeat hourly until control; no scheduled maintenance needed; 4 vials PRN for recurrence
nodes.body: Anavip Dosing Protocol: Reconstitution: 1. Reconstitute each vial with 10 mL NS 2. Dilute total dose to 250 mL NS Initial Dose: - 10 vials IV over 60 minutes - Pediatric = Adult dose Administration: - Infuse over 60 minutes - Monitor for anaphylaxis Repeat Dosing: - Repeat 10 vials every hour until initial control - No scheduled maintenance required - For recurrence: 4 vials as needed Advantages:

nodes.title: Response Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess 30-60min post-infusion: swelling halted, systemic symptoms improving, labs stabilizing = initial control
nodes.body: Assess response to antivenom: Initial control achieved if: - Swelling progression halted - Systemic symptoms improving - Labs stabilizing Reassess 30-60 minutes post-infusion. If inadequate response: - Repeat initial dose - Continue until control achieved Allergic reactions: - Stop infusion - IM epinephrine (preferred over SC) - IVF, supportive care - When stable: restart at slower rate Papain/pap

nodes.title: Initial Control Achieved
nodes.summary: CroFab: 32-50% late hematologic recurrence days 2-7; follow-up labs days 2-3 and 5-7 for all rattlesnake/antivenom cases
nodes.body: Envenomation controlled — ongoing management: If using CroFab: - Maintenance: 2 vials at 6, 12, and 18 hours - Controversial — consult poison center If using Anavip: - No scheduled maintenance - PRN dosing for recurrence Monitoring: - Serial exams q2-4h - Repeat labs at 6, 12, 24 hours - Watch for recurrence phenomenon Recurrence Risk (especially CroFab): - 32-50% develop late hematologic toxicity

nodes.title: Inadequate Response
nodes.summary: No maximum dose — repeat antivenom until control; persistent coagulopathy = more antivenom, NOT blood products alone
nodes.body: Continued progression despite antivenom: Repeat antivenom: - CroFab: Repeat 4-6 vials - Anavip: Repeat 10 vials - Continue hourly until control No maximum dose — give what is needed. Persistent coagulopathy without bleeding: - More antivenom (NOT blood products) - Antivenom addresses underlying cause - Blood products only temporarily effective Persistent coagulopathy WITH significant bleeding: - A

nodes.title: Antivenom Allergic Reaction
nodes.summary: Stop infusion, epinephrine 0.3-0.5mg IM; when stable restart at slower rate — antivenom benefit usually outweighs reaction risk
nodes.body: Anaphylaxis/Hypersensitivity Management: Immediate: 1. STOP infusion 2. Epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM (preferred over SC) 3. IVF bolus 4. Supportive care When stable: - Restart infusion at SLOWER rate - Antivenom benefit usually outweighs reaction risk - Premedicate if restarting (diphenhydramine, steroids) Risk factors for CroFab retext: - Papain, chymopapain, papaya extract allergy - Bromelain (pine

nodes.title: Observation Protocol
nodes.summary: Serial exams q30-60min x4hr then q2h; repeat labs at 6hr minimum; give antivenom if crosses joint or labs abnormal
nodes.body: Observation without antivenom: Monitoring: - Serial exams q30-60 min × 4h, then q2h - Mark swelling edge with time - Circumference measurements at fixed landmarks Repeat labs: - At 6 hours (minimum) - Before discharge Indications to give antivenom: - Swelling crosses major joint - Systemic symptoms develop - Lab abnormalities: - Platelets < 100,000 - Fibrinogen < 100 - INR > 3.0 - PTT > 50 Copperh

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Screen for pediatric, pregnant, or head/neck bite — each has specific management considerations
nodes.body: Does the patient fall into a special population? - Pediatric — dosing considerations - Pregnant — maternal/fetal considerations - Head/Neck bite — airway concerns - None — standard management

nodes.title: Pediatric Considerations
nodes.summary: SAME antivenom dose as adults — dosing based on venom amount, NOT weight; children may have more severe effects
nodes.body: Pediatric snake envenomation: Key Point: SAME ANTIVENOM DOSE AS ADULTS - Dosing is based on VENOM amount - NOT based on patient weight - Children may have more severe effects (smaller body mass dilutes venom less) Fluid Volume: - Adjust dilution volume for small children - Prevent fluid overload - Use smaller volume (100-150 mL) for infants Antivenom Safety: - Safe in pediatric and infant populati

nodes.title: Pregnancy Considerations
nodes.summary: Do NOT withhold antivenom in pregnancy — untreated envenomation poses greater fetal risk; monitor for placental abruption
nodes.body: Pregnant patient with snake envenomation: Key Point: DO NOT WITHHOLD ANTIVENOM - Maternal health and prognosis takes priority - Untreated envenomation poses greater fetal risk than antivenom - Standard dosing applies Fetal Monitoring: - Continuous fetal monitoring - OB consultation - Monitor for placental abruption (coagulopathy risk) Limited Data: - No RCTs in pregnancy (obviously) - Case reports

nodes.title: Head/Neck Bite — Airway Management
nodes.summary: Early intubation for progressive facial/oropharyngeal edema — do NOT wait for respiratory distress; aggressive antivenom 8-12 vials
nodes.body: Head, face, or neck bites — high airway risk: Early Intubation Considerations: - Progressive facial/oropharyngeal edema - Stridor or voice changes - Difficulty managing secretions - Concern for rapid progression Do NOT wait for respiratory distress — edema may make later intubation impossible. Approach: - Early airway assessment - Prepare for difficult airway - Have surgical airway available - Con

nodes.title: Coral Snake Envenomation
nodes.summary: Minimal local effects but delayed neurotoxicity (12+ hr) — presynaptic toxin may be irreversible; ALL bites need 24hr ICU
nodes.body: Coral snake (Elapidae) — DIFFERENT from pit vipers: Clinical Pattern: - Minimal local effects (unlike pit vipers) - Delayed neurotoxicity (may take 12+ hours) - Presynaptic neurotoxin → potentially irreversible Identification: - Red, yellow, black bands - "Red touches yellow, kill a fellow" (US only) - Small, slender snake - Round pupils ⚠️ DO NOT wait for symptoms to develop - Once neurotoxicity

nodes.title: Coral Snake Antivenom
nodes.summary: NACSA 3-5 vials at first neurotoxicity sign — availability crisis (production stopped 2003); Coralmyn via Poison Control if unavailable
nodes.body: North American Coral Snake Antivenin (NACSA): ⚠️ AVAILABILITY CRISIS: - Production stopped 2003 - FDA extending expiration on existing lots - Current lot (CL6814) extended through June 30, 2026 (FDA stability data) - No FDA-approved alternative in US Dosing: - 3-5 vials IV for adults/adolescents - Do NOT give empirically before symptoms - Give at first sign of neurotoxicity Alternative (Investigat

nodes.title: Coral Snake Monitoring
nodes.summary: ICU neuro checks q1-2h for ptosis (early sign), diplopia, dysarthria, limb weakness — early intubation for bulbar weakness
nodes.body: ICU monitoring for all suspected coral snake bites: Neurotoxicity Signs (may be delayed 12+ hours): - Ptosis (early sign) - Diplopia - Dysarthria, dysphagia - Limb weakness - Respiratory depression Monitoring: - Neuro checks q1-2h - Respiratory monitoring - Bedside spirometry if available - ABG if respiratory concerns Intubation Criteria: - Progressive bulbar weakness - Declining respiratory effor

nodes.title: Coral Snake Disposition
nodes.summary: All coral snake bites: ICU 24hr minimum; if no symptoms at 24hr may discharge with return precautions; full recovery possible with support
nodes.body: Coral snake disposition: All patients: - ICU admission for minimum 24 hours - Cannot be discharged from ED If no symptoms at 24 hours: - Discharge with close follow-up - Return precautions for delayed symptoms If symptoms develop: - Antivenom if available and early - Prolonged ICU stay - May require weeks of mechanical ventilation - Full recovery possible with support Poison Control: 1-800-222-122

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Disposition based on severity, antivenom given, lab trends, and social factors — dry/mild may discharge, moderate/severe admit
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition: Consider: - Severity grade - Antivenom given? - Response to treatment - Lab trends - Social factors (distance from hospital, reliability)

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Minimum 8hr dry bite, 12-24hr mild; normal repeat labs, no progression, no NSAIDs; 5% readmission rate
nodes.body: Safe for discharge if ALL criteria met: Clinical: - Minimum 8 hours observation (dry bite) - Minimum 12-24 hours (mild envenomation) - No progression of swelling - No systemic symptoms - Tolerating PO - Adequate pain control with oral medications Labs: - Normal or stable repeat labs - No unfavorable trends Social: - Reliable patient - Access to return if needed - Understands return precautions Dis

nodes.title: Observation Unit
nodes.summary: CDU 12-24hr for mild/copperhead without antivenom; serial exams q2-4h, repeat labs at 6 and 12hr
nodes.body: Observation unit admission: Appropriate for: - Mild envenomation without antivenom - Copperhead bites (often mild) - Stable after initial antivenom - Needs extended monitoring Monitoring: - Serial exams q2-4h - Repeat labs at 6, 12 hours - Circumference measurements - Pain assessment Escalation criteria: - Progression of swelling - New systemic symptoms - Lab abnormalities - Inadequate pain contro

nodes.title: Inpatient Admission
nodes.summary: Admit for moderate/severe or antivenom-treated; labs q6-12h; watch for late coagulopathy peak days 2-7
nodes.body: Inpatient admission indicated for: Clinical: - Moderate/severe envenomation - Antivenom administered - Ongoing swelling or symptoms - Significant pain requiring IV medications Lab abnormalities: - Persistent coagulopathy - Thrombocytopenia - Need for repeat antivenom Monitoring: - Serial exams q2-4h - Labs q6-12h until stable - Maintenance antivenom if CroFab (controversial) Recurrence monitoring:

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.summary: ICU for airway involvement, anaphylaxis, severe systemic toxicity, hemodynamic instability, or any coral snake bite
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: Mandatory ICU: - Airway involvement (head/neck/face bites with edema) - Anaphylaxis to antivenom - Severe systemic toxicity - Hemodynamic instability - Coral snake envenomation (any) Consider ICU: - Severe coagulopathy - Need for blood products - Multiple comorbidities - Uncertain trajectory ICU Management: - Airway monitoring/protection - Hemodynamic monitoring - Serial la

nodes.title: Recurrence Phenomenon
nodes.summary: CroFab recurrence 32-50% at days 2-7; follow-up labs days 2-3 and 5-7; retreat if INR >3, plt <25K, fibrinogen <50
nodes.body: Late Coagulopathy — Important Patient Counseling: CroFab-Specific Issue: - Half-life < 12 hours (shorter than venom persistence) - 32-50% develop late hematologic toxicity - Occurs days to weeks after treatment - Venom depots released after antivenom clears Peak Risk: - Days 2-7 post-treatment - Rattlesnake > copperhead - Can occur even after hospital discharge Follow-up Labs (Rattlesnake or antiv

nodes.title: Sodium Bicarbonate Drip Protocol
nodes.summary: Bicarbonate infusion is indication-specific; avoid routine use without severe acidemia, alkalinization target, or tox indication.
nodes.body: Bicarbonate Drip Steps This consult is for continuous sodium bicarbonate infusion, not reflex ampules during routine resuscitation. Common ED/ICU indications: - Severe metabolic acidemia, especially pH <=7.20 with moderate-severe AKI or bicarbonate loss - Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis when isotonic bicarbonate can be used as resuscitative fluid - Salicylate toxicity requiring serum/urine al

nodes.title: Indication
nodes.summary: The target and rate depend on whether the goal is pH correction, potassium shift, urine alkalinization, or sodium-channel rescue.
nodes.body: Why are you starting a bicarbonate drip?

nodes.title: Severe Metabolic Acidemia / AKI
nodes.summary: Best evidence is severe acidemia with AKI; bicarbonate is a bridge, not source control.
nodes.body: Consider bicarbonate infusion when severe metabolic acidemia is clinically important and reversible/supportable. Best-supported ICU phenotype: - pH <=7.20 with low bicarbonate and moderate-severe AKI - Uremic or non-anion-gap/bicarbonate-loss acidosis - Severe acidemia contributing to vasopressor resistance or cardiac dysfunction Recipe: - Sodium bicarbonate 150 mEq in 1 L D5W or sterile water per

nodes.title: Hyperkalemia + Metabolic Acidosis
nodes.summary: Isotonic bicarbonate can help acidotic hyperkalemia, but calcium/insulin/removal remain essential.
nodes.body: Bicarbonate is most useful for hyperkalemia when metabolic acidosis is present. Do first if ECG changes/severe K: - Calcium for membrane stabilization - Insulin/dextrose and albuterol for rapid intracellular shift - Dialysis/diuresis/potassium binders for removal when appropriate Bicarbonate strategy: - Use Sodium bicarbonate isotonic infusion as resuscitative fluid when hypovolemic/acidotic - Rec

nodes.title: Salicylate Toxicity
nodes.summary: Salicylate bicarbonate infusion targets urine pH and requires aggressive potassium support.
nodes.body: Goal is serum and urine alkalinization, not correction of a bicarbonate number. Initial sequence: - Call poison center/toxicology and nephrology early - Give Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus if severe toxicity, acidemia, altered mental status, or before unavoidable intubation - Start infusion: 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W, typically 150-250 mL/hr - Add Potassium chloride IV 20-40 mE

nodes.title: TCA / Sodium-Channel Blocker
nodes.summary: TCA/sodium-channel toxicity uses boluses first, then infusion to maintain pH/QRS targets.
nodes.body: Bicarbonate infusion is maintenance therapy after boluses when sodium-channel blockade persists. Initial therapy: - Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus - Repeat boluses q3-5 min until QRS narrows, hypotension improves, or pH target reached - Target serum pH 7.50-7.55 and QRS <100 ms when feasible Infusion: - 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr - Continue while QRS or hemodyna

nodes.title: Not Routine Bicarbonate Drip
nodes.summary: Bicarbonate infusion should not be reflexive for routine arrest, respiratory acidosis, DKA, or lactic acidosis.
nodes.body: Do not start bicarbonate infusion for: - Routine cardiac arrest/CPR without hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker toxicity - Isolated respiratory acidosis; improve ventilation instead - Routine lactic acidosis without severe acidemia/AKI or bicarbonate-loss physiology - Routine DKA; insulin/fluids/potassium are definitive. The 2024 ADA hyperglycemic crises consensus report recommends bicarbonate
nodes.recommendation: Hold bicarbonate drip and treat the underlying process unless a clear indication/target exists.

nodes.title: Recipe / Administration
nodes.summary: Standard drip recipe is 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W/sterile water, rate by indication.
nodes.body: Common isotonic bicarbonate recipe: - 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate = three 50 mEq ampules of 8.4% NaHCO3 - Add to 1 L D5W or sterile water per local pharmacy policy - Final solution is approximately isotonic bicarbonate, ~150 mEq/L sodium bicarbonate Rates: - Maintenance/metabolic acidosis: commonly 100-250 mL/hr - Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis with hypovolemia: may run 500-1000 mL/hr as resuscita

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.summary: Monitor pH, sodium, potassium, ionized calcium, volume, ECG, and ventilation.
nodes.body: Core monitoring: - VBG/ABG q2-4 hr during active titration; q1-2 hr if unstable or target-dependent tox case - BMP q2-4 hr: sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, creatinine - Ionized calcium q4-6 hr or sooner if symptomatic/hypocalcemia risk - Volume status, pulmonary edema, urine output - Continuous ECG for hyperkalemia, TCA/sodium-channel toxicity, severe acidemia, or rapid shifts Toxicology

nodes.title: Complications
nodes.summary: Major risks are sodium/volume load, hypokalemia, low ionized calcium, alkalemia, and CO2 generation.
nodes.body: Watch for: - Hypernatremia and hyperosmolality - Hypokalemia from intracellular shift - Lower ionized calcium with tetany, seizures, hypotension, or reduced contractility - Volume overload/pulmonary edema - Metabolic alkalosis - Increased CO2 load with worsening respiratory acidosis if ventilation is inadequate - Delayed dialysis when bicarbonate is used beyond its role as a bridge Stop or slow th

nodes.title: Disposition / Handoff
nodes.summary: Bicarbonate drips require monitored disposition and explicit stop criteria.
nodes.body: Most bicarbonate drip patients need ICU, stepdown, or close monitored care. Handoff must include: - Indication and target: pH, urine pH, QRS, potassium, or bridge to dialysis - Recipe and current rate - Total bicarbonate/sodium administered - Latest pH, Na, K, ionized Ca, creatinine, urine output - Ventilation status and CO2 clearance - Stop criteria and next lab time - Toxicology/nephrology/poiso
nodes.recommendation: Continue only with a clear endpoint, monitoring schedule, and definitive treatment plan.

nodes.title: Sodium Level
nodes.summary: Confirm sodium result with clinical context — repeat if unexpected or drawn from IV-containing arm
nodes.body: Sodium Disorders Steps Summary \u2014 stepwise management of hyponatremia and hypernatremia. What is the serum sodium level? Confirm result with clinical context. Consider repeating if unexpected or if sample was drawn from an IV-containing arm.

nodes.title: Symptom Severity
nodes.summary: Symptom severity determines urgency — seizures/coma need emergent 3% saline; incidental finding needs slow workup
nodes.body: Assess for neurological symptoms of hyponatremia. Symptom severity \u2014 not the sodium number alone \u2014 determines urgency of treatment. Severe symptoms: \u2022 Seizures \u2022 Obtundation or coma \u2022 Respiratory arrest Moderate symptoms: \u2022 Nausea and vomiting \u2022 Confusion or disorientation \u2022 Severe headache Mild or asymptomatic: \u2022 Subtle cognitive changes, gait instabil

nodes.summary: Order serum osm, urine osm, urine sodium simultaneously; give thiamine 100mg IV empirically; check and correct potassium
nodes.body: Order the diagnostic triad simultaneously: \u2022 Serum osmolality \u2014 distinguishes true hypotonic hyponatremia from non-hypotonic causes \u2022 Urine osmolality \u2014 determines if ADH is active (>100 mOsm/kg) or suppressed (<100) \u2022 Urine sodium \u2014 distinguishes renal from extrarenal sodium losses Hyponatremia Lab Interpretation \u2014 stepwise algorithm for interpreting results Add

nodes.title: Serum Osmolality Result
nodes.summary: Serum osm <275 = true hypotonic hyponatremia; >=275 = pseudohyponatremia or translocational (hyperglycemia, mannitol)
nodes.body: The serum osmolality determines whether this is true hypotonic hyponatremia or a non-hypotonic cause. Hypotonic (<275 mOsm/kg): True hyponatremia \u2014 excess water relative to sodium. Proceed to urine osmolality. Non-hypotonic (\u2265275 mOsm/kg): Pseudohyponatremia or translocational hyponatremia. The sodium is artifactually low or diluted by effective osmoles. nodes.title: Non-Hypotonic Hyponatremia
nodes.body: This is NOT true hyponatremia. The measured sodium is low but total body water and sodium balance may be normal. nodes.title: Urine Osmolality
nodes.summary: Urine osm <100 = ADH suppressed (water excess); >100 = ADH active (appropriate or inappropriate) — proceed to urine sodium
nodes.body: Urine osmolality determines whether ADH (vasopressin) is active. Urine Osm < 100 mOsm/kg \u2014 ADH is appropriately suppressed. The kidney is maximally diluting urine. The problem is excessive water intake or inadequate solute intake overwhelming the kidney\u2019s diluting capacity. Urine Osm > 100 mOsm/kg \u2014 ADH is active (either appropriately or inappropriately). The kidney is concentrating

nodes.title: Water Intake > Solute Intake
nodes.body: ADH is suppressed \u2014 the kidney is doing its job. The problem is excessive free water intake or severely low solute intake overwhelming diluting capacity (~20 L/day max). Causes: \u2022 Primary polydipsia \u2014 psychiatric patients, often on medications that cause dry mouth \u2022 Beer potomania \u2014 low-solute diet (beer has minimal protein/electrolytes, so minimal obligate solute excretio

nodes.title: Urine Sodium
nodes.summary: UNa <30 = kidney retaining sodium (hypovolemic or edematous); UNa >30 = kidney wasting (SIAD, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency)
nodes.body: Urine sodium differentiates renal sodium losses from extrarenal losses in the setting of ADH-mediated hyponatremia. Urine Na < 30 mEq/L \u2014 The kidney is retaining sodium. Volume depletion (hypovolemic) or edematous states (hypervolemic) with reduced effective arterial blood volume. Urine Na > 30 mEq/L \u2014 The kidney is wasting sodium. SIAD, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, cerebral salt wa

nodes.title: Low UNa \u2014 Volume Assessment
nodes.summary: Distinguish hypovolemic (dry: GI losses, third-spacing) from hypervolemic (edematous: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome)
nodes.body: The kidney is retaining sodium, indicating reduced effective circulating volume. The key distinction is between true hypovolemia and hypervolemic states with reduced effective arterial blood volume. Hypovolemic (dry): \u2022 GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea) \u2022 Third-spacing (pancreatitis, burns) \u2022 Diaphoresis, insensible losses \u2022 Clinical: tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, poor ski

nodes.title: Emergency Hypertonic Saline
nodes.summary: 3% NaCl 100-150mL bolus over 10-20min (repeat x2); target 4-6 mEq/L rise in 1-2hr; peripheral access OK; give thiamine
nodes.body: Immediate treatment for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma, respiratory distress). 3% Hypertonic Saline 100-150 mL IV bolus over 10-20 minutes. Repeat up to 2 additional times (total 3 boluses) if severe symptoms persist. Target: Raise Na+ by 4-6 mEq/L in the first 1-2 hours \u2014 this is sufficient to reverse cerebral edema and stop seizures. Each 100 mL bolus of 3% NaCl raises Na+

nodes.title: Correction Rate Limits
nodes.summary: Max 10 mEq/L in 24hr (8 for high-risk); overcorrection causes ODS; K+ repletion counts toward Na+ correction (40 mEq KCl ~= +1 Na)
nodes.body: Overcorrection causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) \u2014 a devastating and often irreversible pontine and extrapontine injury. Maximum correction rates: \u2022 Standard risk: \u226410 mEq/L in first 24 hours, \u226418 mEq/L in 48 hours \u2022 High risk for ODS: \u22648 mEq/L in first 24 hours ODS Risk Factors \u2014 high-risk populations include: Na+ \u2264105, alcohol use disorder, liver

nodes.title: DDAVP Clamp Strategy
nodes.summary: DDAVP clamp gives complete correction control — locks kidneys, Na+ rises only from administered 3% boluses
nodes.body: The DDAVP clamp (also called "proactive DDAVP" or "DDAVP clamp-and-bolus") is the safest approach to controlled sodium correction. How it works: DDAVP locks the kidneys in a maximally concentrating state (prevents free water excretion). This gives the clinician complete control over the correction rate \u2014 Na+ rises only from administered hypertonic saline boluses, not from unpredictable renal

nodes.title: DDAVP Clamp-Bolus Protocol
nodes.summary: DDAVP 2mcg IV q6-8h locks kidneys; 3% NaCl 100mL boluses q4-6h for controlled correction; Na+ q2h; taper DDAVP to q12h before stopping
nodes.body: Step 1 \u2014 Lock the kidneys: Desmopressin (DDAVP) 2 mcg IV q6-8h (schedule doses around the clock). This prevents all renal free water excretion. Step 2 \u2014 Controlled bolus correction: 3% Hypertonic Saline 100 mL IV bolus \u2014 each bolus raises Na+ approximately 2 mEq/L in a 70 kg adult. nodes.title: High UNa \u2014 Differential
nodes.summary: High UNa: SIAD (euvolemic, most common), diuretic-induced (thiazides >> loops), or adrenal insufficiency (check cortisol/ACTH)
nodes.body: Urine Na >30 mEq/L with ADH-mediated hyponatremia. The kidney is actively wasting sodium. The three main causes are: SIAD (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis): \u2022 Most common cause of euvolemic hyponatremia \u2022 Euvolemic on exam, urine Osm >100, urine Na >30, low uric acid \u2022 SIAD Causes & Diagnosis \u2014 medications, malignancy, neurologic, pulmonary Diuretic-induced: \u2022 Thiaz

nodes.title: SIAD Treatment
nodes.summary: Fluid restrict 800-1000mL/day; oral urea 15-30g if restriction fails; vaptans NOT recommended — overcorrection risk, hepatotoxicity
nodes.body: First-line: Fluid restriction \u2022 Restrict to 800-1000 mL/day total fluid intake \u2022 Effective only if urine Osm < 500 AND urine Osm/serum Osm ratio < 1.0 \u2022 If ratio >1.0, every mL of urine excretes more water than intake replaces \u2014 fluid restriction will fail Second-line: Oral urea Oral Urea 15-30g PO daily (titrate up to 60g/day). Creates obligate osmotic diuresis. Bitter taste \

nodes.title: Diuretic-Induced Hyponatremia
nodes.body: Thiazide diuretics are the most common medication cause of hyponatremia. Typically occurs within 2 weeks of initiation, especially in elderly women with low body mass. Mechanism: Thiazides impair the kidney\u2019s diluting segment (distal convoluted tubule) while preserving the concentrating segment. Loops do the opposite \u2014 they impair concentration, which is why loop diuretics rarely cause s
nodes.recommendation: Hold thiazide immediately and never rechallenge. Replace volume deficit with NS if hypovolemic. Correct K+ and Mg2+. HIGH overcorrection risk once diuretic held \u2014 consider proactive DDAVP clamp if Na+ <120. Monitor Na+ q2h for 24 hours

nodes.title: Adrenal Insufficiency
nodes.body: Cortisol deficiency causes hyponatremia through two mechanisms: \u2022 Cortisol tonically inhibits ADH \u2014 deficiency leads to unopposed ADH secretion \u2022 Reduced cardiac output and GFR \u2192 nonosmotic ADH release Diagnosis: \u2022 AM cortisol <3 mcg/dL \u2192 virtually diagnostic \u2022 AM cortisol 3-18 mcg/dL \u2192 cosyntropin stimulation test \u2022 AM cortisol >18 mcg/dL \u2192 AI unl
nodes.recommendation: Check AM cortisol and ACTH. If hemodynamically unstable, give stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat (do not wait for results), then 50 mg IV q8h. If stable, draw labs then start physiologic replacement (15 mg AM / 5 mg PM). Na+ corrects

nodes.title: Hypovolemic Hyponatremia
nodes.body: Volume depletion triggers nonosmotic ADH release \u2014 the body prioritizes volume over tonicity. ADH retains free water, diluting sodium. Common causes: \u2022 GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea, NG suction) \u2022 Third-spacing (pancreatitis, burns, bowel obstruction) \u2022 Diaphoresis, insensible losses in febrile patients \u2022 Cerebral salt wasting (post-neurosurgery) Management: \u2022 Normal
nodes.recommendation: Resuscitate with normal saline. HIGH overcorrection risk once euvolemia restored and ADH suppresses. If Na+ <120, start proactive DDAVP clamp before NS resuscitation. Monitor Na+ q2h. Watch for sudden urine output increase (signals ADH supp

nodes.title: Hypervolemic Hyponatremia
nodes.body: Edematous states with reduced effective arterial blood volume trigger ADH release despite total body water excess. Causes: \u2022 Heart failure \u2014 poor forward flow \u2192 baroreceptor-mediated ADH release \u2022 Cirrhosis \u2014 splanchnic vasodilation \u2192 reduced effective arterial volume \u2022 Nephrotic syndrome \u2014 hypoalbuminemia \u2192 reduced oncotic pressure Management: \u2022 F
nodes.recommendation: Fluid restriction 1-1.5 L/day. Loop diuretic (furosemide 20-40 mg IV) for diuresis. Sodium restriction <2g/day. Treat the underlying disease (GDMT for HF, TIPS for cirrhosis). Avoid NS, hypertonic saline (unless seizures/coma), and vaptans.

nodes.title: HypoNa Monitoring & Disposition
nodes.body: Ongoing monitoring during hyponatremia treatment. Active correction (Na+ <125 or symptomatic): \u2022 Check Na+ every 2 hours \u2022 Plot correction trajectory on flow sheet \u2022 Track all IV fluids, PO intake, and urine output \u2022 I&O catheter for accurate urine measurement Stable/improving (Na+ 125-130): \u2022 Check Na+ every 4-6 hours \u2022 Continue fluid restriction or treatment of unde
nodes.recommendation: Monitor Na+ q2h during active correction, q4-6h once stable. ICU for Na+ <120, DDAVP clamp, severe symptoms, or hypertonic saline infusion. Track correction trajectory on flow sheet. Correct concurrent K+ and Mg2+. Step down when Na+ >125 a

nodes.summary: Almost always free water deficit — inadequate intake, excessive loss, or rarely sodium gain; assess volume status and urine output
nodes.body: Hypernatremia (Na+ >145 mEq/L) is almost always a free water deficit \u2014 either inadequate intake or excessive loss. Rarely, it results from sodium gain. Assess volume status and urine output: Volume depleted (most common): \u2022 Inadequate water intake (altered mental status, intubated, elderly, infant) \u2022 GI losses + inadequate replacement \u2022 Insensible losses (fever, burns, mechanic

nodes.body: Polyuria with dilute urine (Urine Osm <300 mOsm/kg) suggests diabetes insipidus. Central DI \u2014 deficient ADH production: \u2022 Post-neurosurgery (pituitary), head trauma, brain death \u2022 Tumors (craniopharyngioma, metastases) \u2022 Autoimmune hypophysitis \u2022 Diagnostic clue: Urine Osm rises >50% after DDAVP 2 mcg IV trial Nephrogenic DI \u2014 kidney resistant to ADH: \u2022 Lithium (

nodes.title: Central DI Treatment
nodes.summary: DDAVP replacement + free water deficit correction; post-neurosurgical: watch for triphasic response (DI days 1-5, SIAD days 5-10)
nodes.body: Replace ADH with DDAVP + replace free water deficit. DDAVP replacement: Desmopressin (DDAVP) 2 mcg IV q8-12h (acute inpatient) OR 10 mcg intranasal BID (stable/outpatient) Free water replacement: Calculate deficit and replace (see next step). nodes.title: Nephrogenic DI Treatment
nodes.summary: DDAVP ineffective — remove offending agent; thiazide paradox for antidiuresis; may need 10-20 L/day free water intake
nodes.body: The kidney does not respond to ADH \u2014 DDAVP is ineffective. Treatment relies on reducing solute load and using pharmacologic tricks. Step 1 \u2014 Remove the offending agent: \u2022 Lithium \u2014 discuss with psychiatry before discontinuing. Amiloride 5-10 mg BID blocks lithium entry into collecting duct cells (partially protective even if lithium continued) \u2022 Hypercalcemia \u2014 treat

nodes.title: Free Water Deficit & Replacement
nodes.summary: FWD = TBW x (Na/140 - 1); add 1-1.5L/day for ongoing losses; correct chronic over 48-72hr, max 10-12 mEq/L per 24hr
nodes.body: Calculate the free water deficit (FWD) to guide replacement volume. Formula: FWD (liters) = TBW \u00d7 [(Na/140) - 1] \u2022 TBW = weight (kg) \u00d7 0.6 (men) or \u00d7 0.5 (women/elderly) \u2022 Example: 70 kg male, Na+ 160 \u2192 TBW = 42L, FWD = 42 \u00d7 (160/140 - 1) = 6.0 liters The FWD formula underestimates true deficit \u2014 it does not account for ongoing losses (insensible, urinary, G

nodes.title: Hypernatremia + Volume Overload
nodes.summary: Furosemide produces hypotonic urine (removes more Na than water); replace urine volume with D5W; switch maintenance from NS to D5W
nodes.body: Iatrogenic hypernatremia from excessive sodium administration is increasingly common in ICU patients receiving NS boluses, NaHCO\u2083, and high-sodium medications. Causes: \u2022 Large-volume NS resuscitation without free water \u2022 NaHCO\u2083 infusions (isotonic bicarb = 150 mEq Na/L) \u2022 High-sodium medications (piperacillin-tazobactam = 4.7 mEq Na per gram) \u2022 Hypertonic saline overc

nodes.title: Hypernatremia Monitoring & Disposition
nodes.body: Ongoing monitoring during hypernatremia treatment. Active correction: \u2022 Check Na+ every 4-6 hours \u2022 Strict intake and output (I&O catheter recommended) \u2022 Daily weights \u2022 Monitor for signs of cerebral edema during correction (headache, confusion, seizures) Correction targets: \u2022 Chronic: maximum 10-12 mEq/L decrease in 24 hours \u2022 Acute (<48h): can correct 1 mEq/L/hr \u2
nodes.recommendation: Monitor Na+ q4-6h during active correction. Correct chronic hypernatremia slowly (max 10-12 mEq/L/day). ICU for Na+ >160, hemodynamic instability, or active DI with massive polyuria. Overcorrection risk is low (unlike hyponatremia). Hospita

nodes.title: Hypernatremia in the Elderly
nodes.summary: Elderly hypernatremia almost always chronic from impaired thirst — correct slowly; ensure caregiver-driven water schedule on discharge
nodes.body: Hypernatremia in elderly patients is almost always chronic and related to impaired thirst or access to water. Why the elderly are vulnerable: \u2022 Diminished thirst \u2014 aging blunts the thirst response to hypertonicity \u2022 Reduced total body water \u2014 TBW factor ~0.45-0.50 (vs 0.60 in younger adults) \u2022 Impaired renal concentrating ability \u2014 maximum urine Osm declines with age

nodes.title: Severe Sore Throat Hub — Is the Airway Threatened?
nodes.summary: Screen for airway red flags FIRST (stridor, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, trismus, tongue elevation). If present: sit up, minimal stimulation, ENT + anesthesia early, do not force a throat exam or lie the patient flat.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Epiglottitis / supraglottitis \u2014 rapid airway obstruction; sitting-forward, drooling, muffled voice, stridor. Do NOT lie the patient down or examine the throat aggressively. 2. Ludwig angina \u2014 bilateral submandibular swelling, tongue elevation, floor-of-mouth induration; airway emergency. 3. Retropharyngeal / deep-neck abscess \u2014 neck stiffness, fever, d

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions — Pick the One That Fits
nodes.summary: Airway threats first (epiglottitis, Ludwig, deep-neck, angioedema), then PTA, then redirect ingestions. Each branch links to its deep-dive or airway plan.
nodes.body: Airway threats first. Each branch routes to a deep-dive (or an airway plan) and the next action. --- *Basis:* this is a routing node \u2014 each branch label is a recognition pattern, not a treatment recommendation, and the evidence for what to do sits in the destination node and its linked consult. The branch set and the airway-first ordering derive from emergency-medicine reviews of the sore thr

nodes.title: Epiglottitis / Supraglottitis — Airway Emergency
nodes.body: (No dedicated consult yet \u2014 airway pathways linked below.) Adult epiglottitis is easy to miss because the throat can look unremarkable; the tip-off is severe odynophagia/dysphagia out of proportion to the visible exam, plus a muffled voice, drooling, and a preference to sit forward. Progression to complete obstruction can be sudden. [4] The cardinal rule: minimize stimulation. Do NOT force a
nodes.recommendation: Minimal stimulation, sit up, oxygen, keep calm. ENT + anesthesia NOW for a controlled/awake airway with surgical backup. IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone \u00b1 vancomycin) + steroids. Do not force a throat exam or lie the patient flat.

nodes.title: Ludwig Angina — Floor-of-Mouth Airway Threat
nodes.body: (No dedicated consult yet \u2014 airway + antibiotic pathway below.) Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular/sublingual spaces, usually from a dental source. It elevates and displaces the tongue posteriorly and threatens the airway. [5] Recognize: bilateral submandibular swelling and induration, elevated/protruding tongue, floor-of-mouth swelling, drooling, t
nodes.recommendation: Sit up + oxygen + calm; ENT/OMFS + anesthesia early for a controlled/awake airway with surgical backup. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + steroids. CT neck once stable. Source control and admission.

nodes.title: Deep Neck / Retropharyngeal Abscess
nodes.body: Open Deep Neck Infection for the full imaging, antibiotic, and drainage pathway. Retropharyngeal and other deep-neck-space abscesses present with fever, severe sore throat, odynophagia, neck stiffness/pain, and an ill appearance; retropharyngeal abscess classically causes neck extension posturing and can descend into the mediastinum (mediastinitis) \u2014 a life-threatening complication. [6] Next
nodes.recommendation: CT neck with contrast to localize and find drainable collection/mediastinal spread. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + fluids. ENT for drainage; watch for descending mediastinitis. Airway first if red flags. Admit.

nodes.title: Angioedema — Sudden Airway Swelling
nodes.body: Open Angioedema for the allergic vs bradykinin-mediated pathway and airway management. Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat \u2014 especially in a patient on an ACE inhibitor or after an allergen exposure \u2014 can obstruct the airway. Distinguish histaminergic/allergic angioedema (urticaria, itching, responds to epinephrine/antihistamines/steroids) from bradykinin-mediated angioedema (
nodes.recommendation: Continuous airway assessment with early ENT/anesthesia if progressing. Treat allergic angioedema as anaphylaxis (epinephrine); for ACE-inhibitor/hereditary angioedema stop the drug and use targeted therapy \u2014 standard allergy meds often

nodes.title: Peritonsillar Abscess
nodes.body: Open Peritonsillar Abscess Drainage for the drainage technique and management pathway. Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is the most common deep infection of the head and neck: unilateral severe sore throat, trismus, a \u201chot potato\u201d/muffled voice, uvular deviation away from the affected side, and a bulging, fluctuant peritonsillar swelling. [8] Next 5 minutes: - Assess the airway (usually no
nodes.recommendation: Drain the abscess (needle aspiration or I&D; ENT if difficult), antibiotics (Strep + anaerobe cover), analgesia, IV fluids, and a dose of dexamethasone. Ultrasound distinguishes abscess from cellulitis. Escalate airway if red flags.

nodes.title: Ingestion / Post-Tonsillectomy — Redirect
nodes.body: Some \u201csore throats\u201d are really an ingestion or a post-procedure complication. Redirect to the correct pathway. [1] Choose the matching consult: - Esophageal food bolus (sudden dysphagia, drooling, chest/throat fullness after eating): Esophageal Food Bolus. - Caustic ingestion (acid/alkali, drooling, oral burns, odynophagia): Caustic Ingestion \u2014 do NOT induce vomiting or blindly pass
nodes.recommendation: Redirect to the specific pathway: esophageal food bolus, caustic ingestion, button battery (time-critical), or post-tonsillectomy bleed. Airway first, IV access, NPO, and the matching specialist.

nodes.title: Initial Bundle — Sore Throat Without Airway Threat
nodes.summary: Confirm airway safe; Centor/McIsaac + rapid strep for pharyngitis; analgesia (acetaminophen/NSAID) + a dose of dexamethasone + IV fluids if cannot swallow. Consider mono (avoid amoxicillin). Escalate if new airway signs.
nodes.body: No airway red flag and no deep-space infection. nodes.title: Reassess — Swallowing and Airway
nodes.summary: Improving + swallowing + safe airway \u2192 discharge. Cannot swallow/unclear \u2192 image/observe. New airway signs \u2192 STOP, return to exclusions.
nodes.body: Re-examine: airway status, ability to swallow, pain trend, and whether a specific diagnosis has declared itself.

nodes.title: Imaging Decision
nodes.summary: CT neck with contrast for deep-neck abscess/Ludwig (after airway secured); lateral neck X-ray only in a stable patient for epiglottitis/retropharyngeal; US to distinguish PTA from cellulitis; chest imaging if mediastinitis. Simple pharyngit
nodes.body: Most sore throats need no imaging; image when a deep-space infection, airway threat, or complication is suspected. [2,6] CT neck with IV contrast \u2014 the workhorse for deep-neck disease: - Suspected retropharyngeal / parapharyngeal / other deep-neck abscess (fever + neck pain/stiffness + dysphagia, ill appearance) - Peritonsillar swelling with concern for deeper extension or when drainage/diagn

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge safe-airway benign pharyngitis; observe/admit for cannot-swallow or IV-antibiotic infections; ICU/airway admit for epiglottitis, Ludwig, or airway-threatening deep-neck disease.
nodes.body: Disposition is driven by airway safety, ability to swallow, and the specific diagnosis. Defer to the deep-dive consult once committed.

nodes.title: Discharge — Benign Pharyngitis, Safe Airway
nodes.body: Safe discharge criteria: [3,9] 1. Airway is unequivocally safe \u2014 no stridor, no drooling, no muffled voice, no trismus, handling secretions. 2. Able to swallow fluids and saliva; adequately hydrated or hydrated in the ED. 3. Benign cause \u2014 viral pharyngitis, streptococcal pharyngitis (treated), or drained/uncomplicated PTA with reliable follow-up per that pathway. 4. Pain controlled on o
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only with an unequivocally safe airway, ability to swallow, controlled pain, correct treatment (antibiotics only for confirmed strep), airway-focused return precautions, and reliable follow-up.

nodes.title: Observe / Admit Ward — Cannot Swallow or IV Antibiotics
nodes.body: Monitored inpatient/observation bed appropriate when: [6,8] - Odynophagia severe enough to prevent oral intake \u2014 dehydration needing IV fluids and IV analgesia, but airway is safe - Peritonsillar or deep-neck infection requiring IV antibiotics and reassessment, without a threatened airway - Post-drainage observation (PTA) when oral intake is not yet adequate - Diagnostic uncertainty requiring
nodes.recommendation: Monitored ward/obs bed for cannot-swallow dehydration or IV-antibiotic deep-space infection with a safe airway. IV fluids/antibiotics/analgesia, ENT reachable, trial PO before discharge. Escalate if any airway red flag.

nodes.title: Admit — Airway-Threatening Infection
nodes.body: Airway-monitored / ICU admission for: [4,5] - Epiglottitis / supraglottitis with any airway compromise or high risk \u2014 airway-monitored bed, ENT/anesthesia immediately available, plan for controlled airway. - Ludwig angina \u2014 airway threat, IV antibiotics, ENT/OMFS, source control. - Deep-neck / retropharyngeal abscess with airway compromise, sepsis, or descending mediastinitis. - Angioede
