nodes.body: Lethal means restriction SAVES LIVES Most lethal methods: • Firearms (~90% case fatality) • Drowning (56%) • Hanging/suffocation (53%) • Poisoning/overdose (~2%) Key point: 90% who survive an attempt do NOT die by suicide later. Reducing access to lethal means prevents impulsive deaths. CALM approach: • Clarify if means are accessible • Ask about willingness to secure • Listen to barriers • Make a

nodes.title: Firearms Counseling
nodes.summary: Firearms = 50% of suicide deaths. Counsel on temporary storage outside home.
nodes.body: Firearms account for 50% of US suicide deaths Ask directly: "Do you have access to any guns?" Counseling (non-judgmental): "Many people in crisis find it helpful to temporarily store firearms outside the home." Options for temporary storage: • Trusted friend/family member • Gun shop or shooting range • Law enforcement (some jurisdictions) • Gun safe with trusted keyholder Document: Counseling prov

nodes.title: Medication Safety
nodes.summary: Limit med quantities, lock up pills, consider weekly dispensing for at-risk patients.
nodes.body: Medication overdose — most common attempt method High-risk medications: • Opioids • Benzodiazepines • TCAs (10-day supply can be lethal) • Tylenol (hepatotoxic) • Insulin • Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers Counseling: • Limit quantities prescribed • Lock up or store with trusted person • Consider dispensing weekly • Naloxone for opioid-prescribed patients If discharging a patient at risk: •

nodes.title: Safety Planning Intervention
nodes.summary: Stanley-Brown Safety Plan: warning signs, coping, contacts, professionals, means safety.
nodes.body: Stanley-Brown Safety Plan — 6 steps: 1. Warning signs — What tells you crisis is building? 2. Internal coping — What can you do alone? (walk, music, breathing) 3. Social contacts — Who can distract you? (friends, places) 4. Family/friends to contact — Who can you call for help? 5. Professionals to contact — Therapist, doctor, crisis line 6. Making environment safe — Means restriction plan Write it

nodes.title: Creating the Plan
nodes.summary: Collaborative safety planning — patient completes with provider, keeps copy.
nodes.body: Collaborative process: Step 1: Warning signs "What thoughts, feelings, or situations tell you that a crisis may be developing?" Step 2: Internal coping "What are things you can do on your own to take your mind off problems?" Step 3: Social settings/people "What places can you go or people you can be around that provide distraction?" Step 4: People to contact "Who are family or friends you can cont

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Disposition based on risk level, patient agreement, and available resources.
nodes.body: Based on risk level and clinical judgment:

nodes.title: Discharge with Safety Plan
nodes.summary: Discharge: safety plan, means restriction, 24-72h follow-up, crisis resources, caring contact.
nodes.body: Before discharge, ensure: ✓ Safety plan completed and reviewed ✓ Means restriction addressed and documented ✓ Follow-up appointment within 24-72 hours ✓ Crisis resources provided: • 988 — Suicide & Crisis Lifeline • 741741 — Crisis Text Line (text HOME) • Local crisis number ✓ Family/support notified (with patient consent) ✓ Prescriptions limited to safe quantities Caring Contacts: Brief follow-up
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with safety plan, means restriction, and follow-up within 24-72h.

nodes.title: Voluntary Psychiatric Admission
nodes.summary: Voluntary admission — preferred when patient agrees. Better therapeutic alliance.
nodes.body: Patient agrees to admission: • Explain treatment plan and expected duration • Complete medical clearance per facility requirements • Transfer to psychiatric facility or unit • Document patient's voluntary agreement • Notify family (with consent) Preferred over involuntary when patient willing — better therapeutic alliance.
nodes.recommendation: Voluntary psychiatric admission for high-risk patient who agrees to treatment.

nodes.title: Involuntary Hold
nodes.summary: Involuntary hold — state-specific criteria. Document specific risk behaviors.
nodes.body: State-specific criteria — generally: • Danger to self due to mental illness • Unable to care for self • Refuses voluntary treatment Documentation required: • Specific behaviors/statements demonstrating risk • Mental illness diagnosed or suspected • Less restrictive alternatives considered • Time-limited hold (typically 72 hours) Patient rights: • Right to hearing/review • Right to legal representa
nodes.recommendation: Involuntary hold for imminent risk when patient refuses voluntary admission.

nodes.title: Medical Admission
nodes.summary: Post-attempt — medical admission with 1:1, psych consult, transfer when stable.
nodes.body: Post-attempt requiring medical care: • Stabilize medical condition first • Continue 1:1 sitter observation • Psychiatry consult for ongoing assessment • Transfer to psychiatry when medically clear Common post-attempt presentations: • Overdose requiring monitoring/treatment • Self-inflicted wounds requiring surgery • Aspiration pneumonia • Rhabdomyolysis
nodes.recommendation: Medical admission with 1:1 sitter, psych consult, transfer when medically stable.

nodes.title: Crisis Stabilization Unit
nodes.summary: CSU — voluntary, 24-72h, less restrictive alternative to inpatient.
nodes.body: Alternative to inpatient admission: Criteria for CSU (if available): • Moderate-high risk but not imminent • Voluntary participation • No acute medical needs • Benefit from brief stabilization (24-72h) CSU provides: • Crisis intervention • Safety monitoring • Brief therapy • Connection to outpatient resources Advantages: Less restrictive, shorter stay, maintains community connections.
nodes.recommendation: Crisis stabilization unit as alternative to inpatient for moderate-high risk.

nodes.title: Assessment Complete
nodes.summary: Document all screening, risk assessment, safety plan, and disposition.
nodes.body: Documentation reminders: • Screening tool used and results • Risk level determination • Means restriction counseling provided • Safety plan (attach copy) • Disposition and rationale • Follow-up arranged • Crisis resources provided
nodes.recommendation: Document screening, risk level, means counseling, safety plan, and follow-up.

nodes.title: Suicide Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Universal screening is standard of care — ED-SAFE doubled detection, reduced attempts 30%; use C-SSRS
nodes.body: Universal screening is standard of care — Joint Commission requires validated screening for all behavioral health presentations. [1][2] ED-SAFE Study: Universal screening doubled detection (2.9% → 5.7%) and reduced subsequent attempts by 30%. [3] Key principles: • Ask directly — asking does NOT increase risk • Use validated tool (C-SSRS) • Obtain collateral from family/friends • Document thoroughl

nodes.title: C-SSRS Screening Questions
nodes.summary: C-SSRS Q1-Q6 in order — Q6 behavior or Q4-Q5 intent/plan = HIGH risk; Q2-Q3 ideation = MODERATE
nodes.body: Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale — ask in order: [1] Q1: Have you wished you were dead or wished you could go to sleep and not wake up? *(Past month)* Q2: Have you actually had any thoughts of killing yourself? *(Past month)* If NO to Q2 → skip to Q6 If YES to Q2 → ask Q3-Q5 Q3: Have you been thinking about how you might do this? *(Plan)* Q4: Have you had these thoughts and had some intentio

nodes.title: Negative Suicide Screen
nodes.body: No current suicidal ideation or recent behavior identified. Continue standard care for presenting complaint. Still consider: • Why did this patient present? Address underlying stressors • Provide 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline information • Brief supportive counseling if appropriate Document: • C-SSRS screening performed, negative • No current suicidal ideation • Crisis resources provided
nodes.recommendation: Negative suicide screen. Continue standard care. Provide crisis resources.

nodes.title: HIGH Risk — Active SI with Intent/Plan/Behavior
nodes.summary: HIGH risk — immediate 1:1 observation, remove means from room, psychiatric consult, assess lethality of plan
nodes.body: This patient is at HIGH risk for suicide. [5][6] Immediate actions: • 1:1 observation / suicide precautions • Remove all potential means from room (cords, sharps, medications) • Do NOT leave patient alone • Contact psychiatric consultation Assess for markers of serious intent: • High-lethality method planned (firearm, hanging, jumping) • Steps taken to avoid discovery • Final acts (note, giving aw

nodes.title: High-Risk Factor Assessment
nodes.summary: Weigh prior attempt (STRONGEST predictor), means access, support system, protective factors for disposition
nodes.body: Non-modifiable risk factors: • Prior suicide attempt (STRONGEST predictor) • Family history of suicide • Male sex, older age • Chronic pain or terminal illness Modifiable risk factors: • Access to lethal means (especially firearms) • Untreated psychiatric illness • Hopelessness • Substance use/intoxication • Social isolation • Recent loss or stressor • Sleep disturbance Protective factors: • Stron

nodes.title: MODERATE Risk — Ideation Without Clear Intent
nodes.summary: Ideation without clear intent — full assessment of duration, method, barriers, access, support, and psych history
nodes.body: Suicidal ideation present but no clear intent or recent behavior. Full assessment required: • Duration and frequency of thoughts • Specific method considered? • What has prevented acting? • Access to means? • Support system availability • Psychiatric history • Substance use Key question: *"What has kept you from acting on these thoughts?"* This identifies protective factors and reasons for living.

nodes.title: Moderate Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Balance risk vs protective factors — contract for safety alone has limited value; err toward psych consult if uncertain
nodes.body: Evaluate the balance of risk vs. protective factors. Questions to determine disposition: • Can patient contract for safety? (Limited value as sole criterion) • Is there a reliable support person who can supervise? • Can lethal means be restricted? • Is outpatient follow-up available within 24-72 hours? • Is patient sober and able to engage in safety planning? If uncertain: Err on the side of psych

nodes.title: LOWER Risk — Passive Ideation Only
nodes.summary: Passive ideation still requires full assessment, safety planning, lethal means counseling, and outpatient referral
nodes.body: Passive ideation (wishes to be dead) without active suicidal thoughts. Still requires: • Full assessment of risk/protective factors • Exploration of underlying causes • Safety planning • Lethal means counseling • Outpatient referral Consider hospitalization if: • Recent escalation • Poor insight • Severe depression or psychosis • No social support • History of rapid escalation in past

nodes.title: Stanley-Brown Safety Planning
nodes.summary: 6-step collaborative safety plan WITH patient — warning signs, coping, social contacts, professionals, 988, means restriction
nodes.body: Evidence-based 6-step collaborative safety plan [7] Create WITH the patient, not FOR them. Give copy to patient AND support person. Step 1: Warning Signs *"What thoughts, moods, or situations tell you a crisis is starting?"* Step 2: Internal Coping *"What can you do by yourself to take your mind off problems?"* (Exercise, music, journaling, deep breathing) Step 3: Social Distractions *"Who can you

nodes.title: Lethal Means Counseling (CALM)
nodes.summary: Firearms = 50% of suicides — temporary storage outside home; involve support person for means restriction
nodes.body: Reducing access to lethal means during crisis saves lives. [8] Firearms (50% of suicides): • Store outside home temporarily (trusted friend, family, gun range, police) • Lock in safe with ammunition stored separately • Cable lock through action • Remove firing pin Medications: • Give to family member to dispense • Lock in safe or lockbox • Dispose of unused medications • Limit quantities prescribe

nodes.title: Psychiatric Admission Indicated
nodes.body: This patient requires inpatient psychiatric admission. [5][6] Indications: • Active suicidal ideation with intent and plan • Recent serious attempt • Unable to contract for safety • No social support • Psychotic symptoms • Severe intoxication with persistent SI when sober • Unable to engage in safety planning Actions: • Maintain 1:1 observation • Medical clearance per local protocol • Contact inpa
nodes.recommendation: Psychiatric admission indicated. Maintain suicide precautions. Contact inpatient psychiatry.

nodes.title: Psychiatric Consultation Required
nodes.summary: Prepare C-SSRS results, risk/protective factors, collateral, and medical clearance for psychiatric consultant
nodes.body: Consult psychiatry for formal evaluation and disposition recommendation. Prepare for consultant: • C-SSRS results • Risk and protective factors identified • Collateral information obtained • Medical clearance completed • Patient's stated wishes While awaiting consult: • Maintain appropriate observation level • Continue supportive care • Avoid confrontational approach • Allow support person presenc

nodes.title: Psychiatry Recommendation
nodes.summary: Disposition based on psychiatry recommendation — admit, discharge with plan, or partial hospitalization/IOP
nodes.body: What did the psychiatric consultant recommend? Consultant should provide: • Risk level assessment • Specific disposition recommendation • Follow-up plan if discharging • Treatment recommendations

nodes.title: Partial Hospitalization / IOP
nodes.body: Intensive outpatient treatment recommended. Appropriate when: • Moderate risk but stable • Good support system at home • Able to contract for safety overnight • Can attend daily programming Discharge requirements: • Safety plan completed • Lethal means counseling done • Program intake scheduled for next business day • 24/7 crisis resources provided • Support person educated • Follow-up call planne
nodes.recommendation: Discharge to partial hospitalization or intensive outpatient. Safety plan and means restriction completed.

nodes.title: Safe Discharge Checklist
nodes.summary: ALL criteria must be met: safety plan, means restricted, support person present, follow-up within 72h, sober
nodes.body: ALL criteria must be met for safe ED discharge: [5][6] ☐ Low-to-moderate risk after full assessment ☐ Patient engaged in safety planning ☐ Written safety plan given to patient AND support person ☐ Lethal means counseling completed with specific plan ☐ Reliable support person present and educated ☐ Outpatient follow-up confirmed within 24-72 hours ☐ 988 and crisis resources provided ☐ Patient is so

nodes.title: Address Discharge Barriers
nodes.summary: Identify and address specific barriers — no support person, means access, no follow-up, or intoxication
nodes.body: What barrier(s) prevent safe discharge? Address each before discharging or escalate care level.

nodes.title: No Support Person Available
nodes.summary: Social work consult, crisis respite, extended observation — consider admission if truly no support available
nodes.body: Absence of support increases risk significantly. Options: • Social work consult to identify resources • Contact family/friends patient hasn't considered • Crisis respite programs if available locally • Extended ED observation with intensive safety planning • Consider admission if truly no support Document: • Efforts made to identify support • Resources offered • Rationale for final disposition

nodes.title: Lethal Means Restriction Barrier
nodes.summary: Refusal to restrict means may indicate higher risk — grounds for admission or extended observation
nodes.body: If patient or family refuses means restriction: For firearms: • Explain that temporary removal saves lives • Offer alternatives: gun safe with code held by friend, store at range or PD • If patient insists on keeping at home, strongly document counseling provided and refusal • Consider whether this refusal indicates higher risk → admission Involve family/support: • Can they secure means without pa

nodes.title: No Outpatient Follow-up Available
nodes.summary: FQHC, community mental health, telehealth options — highest risk is first 30 days post-discharge
nodes.body: Follow-up within 24-72 hours is critical — highest risk is first 30 days post-discharge. Options: • Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) — sliding scale • Community mental health center • Crisis stabilization unit • Hospital outpatient psychiatry clinic • ED-based case management to establish care • Telehealth psychiatry options If truly no options: • Schedule phone follow-up with ED • Longer

nodes.title: Patient Intoxicated
nodes.summary: Cannot assess while intoxicated — observe until sober, re-administer C-SSRS; chronic substance use is a risk factor
nodes.body: Patients cannot be accurately assessed for suicide risk while intoxicated. Management: • Observe until clinically sober • Re-administer C-SSRS when sober • Reassess risk level and protective factors • Many patients will have resolution of acute SI with sobriety Document: • Initial presentation and SI • Reassessment when sober • Change in risk level Note: Chronic alcohol or substance use is a risk

nodes.title: Safe Discharge with Follow-up
nodes.body: Patient meets criteria for safe ED discharge. [5][6] Discharge packet includes: • Written safety plan (patient copy + chart copy) • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline card • Local crisis line number • Appointment confirmation for outpatient follow-up • ED callback number Support person education: • Reviewed warning signs • Knows to call 911 or bring back if SI worsens • Has copy of safety plan • Unders
nodes.recommendation: Safe for discharge. Safety plan completed. Lethal means counseling done. Follow-up scheduled within 72 hours.

nodes.title: Documentation Requirements
nodes.summary: C-SSRS, risk/protective factors, means assessment, safety plan, disposition rationale — suicide within 7 days = sentinel event
nodes.body: Joint Commission (NPSG.15.01.01 — renumbered NPSG.08.01.01 in the 2026 standards) requirements: [2] Document all of: ☐ Validated screening tool used (C-SSRS) and results ☐ Risk factors identified (list specific ones) ☐ Protective factors identified ☐ Collateral obtained (family, records, outpatient providers) ☐ Mental status examination ☐ Lethal means assessment and counseling provided ☐ Risk stra

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Select population for modified assessment approach — pediatric, geriatric, or veteran
nodes.body: Some populations require modified approach. Select if applicable:

nodes.title: Pediatric/Adolescent Considerations
nodes.summary: Involve parents in ALL means counseling; assess social media/cyberbullying; LGBTQ+ youth at elevated risk
nodes.body: Mental health now 1 in 7 pediatric ED visits. [5] Key differences: • Involve parents/guardians in ALL lethal means counseling • Parents often unaware of access to means in home • Social media and cyberbullying assessment • School performance and peer relationships • LGBTQ+ youth at elevated risk — affirming approach essential Lethal means in homes with children: • 40% of US homes with children hav

nodes.title: Geriatric Considerations
nodes.summary: Highest completion rate — more lethal methods, less likely to disclose; lower threshold for admission
nodes.body: Elderly have highest suicide completion rate. [5][6] Key differences: • 81.9% hospitalization rate for suicidal ideation/self-harm • More likely to use highly lethal methods (firearms) • Less likely to disclose SI — actively screen • Physical illness and chronic pain major contributors • Social isolation and loss of independence • Cognitive impairment may limit insight Assessment: • Depression scr

nodes.title: Veteran/Military Considerations
nodes.summary: Veterans Crisis Line 988 press 1; high firearm ownership; combat exposure, PTSD, TBI as risk factors
nodes.body: Veterans have elevated suicide risk. [5] Risk factors: • Combat exposure and moral injury • PTSD and TBI • Military sexual trauma • Transition to civilian life • Loss of unit cohesion and identity • High firearm ownership Assessment: • C-SSRS with attention to PTSD symptoms • Lethal means counseling — veterans often own multiple firearms • VA connection status Resources: • Veterans Crisis Line: 98

nodes.title: Supraglottic Airway - ED Rescue Tool
nodes.summary: SGA restores oxygenation quickly but does not protect the trachea from aspiration.
nodes.body: Steps Summary Use case: rapidly restore oxygenation/ventilation when BVM is failing, intubation has failed, or cardiac arrest airway control must not interrupt compressions. Frame: SGA buys oxygenation and time. It does not seal the trachea or eliminate aspiration risk. Start by identifying the scenario.

nodes.title: Why Are You Placing the SGA?
nodes.body: Choose the clinical lane. This determines how aggressively you plan for intubation or cric after oxygenation is restored.

nodes.title: Plan B Rescue: Oxygenation First
nodes.summary: After failed intubation, declare failure, place SGA for oxygenation, and stop repeated laryngoscopy.
nodes.body: Declare failed intubation, call for help, oxygenate with SGA, and stop the spiral of repeated laryngoscopy. If RSI cricoid pressure is blocking placement, release it with suction ready. Once ventilation works, pause and choose: awaken if appropriate, intubate through/after SGA if stable, or continue to definitive rescue.

nodes.title: Cardiac Arrest: Low-Interruption Airway
nodes.summary: In arrest, SGA is acceptable based on system skill and should not interrupt compressions.
nodes.body: Do not let airway placement interrupt high-quality compressions. If an advanced airway is used, SGA is acceptable when ETI success is low, training opportunities are limited, or access is poor. After placement, ventilate about 10/min with continuous compressions. If ventilation fails, remove and return to BVM while preparing the next airway step.

nodes.title: Bridge: Buy Time for Definitive Airway
nodes.summary: Use SGA as a bridge when oxygenation is urgent and definitive airway setup needs time.
nodes.body: Place SGA when oxygenation is the immediate problem and intubation setup needs time. Best bridge examples: post-failed attempt desaturation, delayed expert arrival, difficult access, or short transport from prehospital bay to resus room. If there is airway obstruction below the glottis, SGA will not bypass it.

nodes.title: RODS: Will the SGA Fail?
nodes.body: RODS Tool Screen before relying on the device. In a crash airway, this screen should take seconds.

nodes.title: Reasonable SGA Candidate
nodes.summary: Proceed when anatomy and lung mechanics make SGA ventilation plausible.
nodes.body: Proceed if mouth opening is adequate, upper airway anatomy can accept the device, and expected ventilation pressure is within SGA seal capability. Prefer second-generation SGA with gastric drain when available.

nodes.title: Aspiration Risk Present?
nodes.body: SGA is not a cuffed tracheal tube. Use it if oxygenation requires it, but plan early conversion to a definitive airway when aspiration risk is high.

nodes.title: Choose Device
nodes.body: Sizing Guide If available, choose a second-generation device with a gastric drainage channel. Size by device instructions and patient anatomy.

nodes.title: Size Selection
nodes.summary: i-gel adult sizing: 3 for 30-60 kg, 4 for 50-90 kg, 5 for >90 kg.
nodes.body: Sizing Guide For i-gel adults: size 3 = 30-60 kg, size 4 = 50-90 kg, size 5 = >90 kg. Use anatomy and package guidance at weight overlaps. For cuffed LMA, follow the device package and avoid overinflation.

nodes.title: Prep: Suction, Lubrication, Backup
nodes.summary: Prep suction, EtCO2, oxygen, BVM/PEEP, securement, gastric tube if available, and definitive backup.
nodes.body: Insertion Guide Prepare suction, BVM/PEEP valve, EtCO2, oxygen source, securing tape, gastric tube if device supports it, and definitive airway backup. Lubricate the posterior surface only. Do not leave a bolus of lubricant in the bowl/cuff.

nodes.title: Insertion Attempt Result
nodes.body: Insert along the hard palate until seated. Avoid force. Optimize head/neck position if safe. Was ventilation achieved after placement?

nodes.title: Confirm Effective Ventilation
nodes.body: Confirm with visible chest rise, EtCO2 waveform or color change, improving SpO2, bilateral breath sounds, and acceptable leak. Remember: confirmation of ventilation is not the same as aspiration protection.

nodes.title: Troubleshoot: Leak / Poor Seal
nodes.summary: Fix seal quickly. Do not keep repeating attempts while oxygenation worsens.
nodes.body: Troubleshooting Tool Try: deeper seating, jaw thrust, head repositioning if safe, smaller/larger size, cuff pressure check if cuffed, and lowering inspiratory pressure. If this is attempt 3 or oxygenation is falling, stop and change plans.

nodes.title: Troubleshoot: Obstruction / High Pressure
nodes.summary: SGA will fail when resistance is distal or pressures exceed seal capability.
nodes.body: Check for biting, laryngospasm, kinked circuit, malposition, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, ARDS, or obstruction below the glottis. If lung mechanics require high pressures or obstruction is distal, SGA may not work. Move toward definitive airway or cric depending on BVM and oxygenation.

nodes.title: Regurgitation / Soiled Airway
nodes.summary: Suction first. SGA does not protect against aspiration.
nodes.body: Turn/suction aggressively, clear the pharynx, and reassess whether SGA can ventilate. If oxygenation is adequate, prepare definitive cuffed tracheal airway. If oxygenation is not adequate, remove/replace SGA only as part of an active rescue plan.

nodes.title: Now What?
nodes.body: Once oxygenation is restored, choose the endpoint. Avoid drifting with an SGA in place when a definitive airway is clearly needed.

nodes.title: Intubation Through SGA
nodes.summary: Intubate through SGA only with stable oxygenation, compatible device, and guided technique.
nodes.body: Only attempt if oxygenation is stable, the device is compatible, and the operator is trained. Use fiberoptic/video guidance when possible. Blind intubation through an SGA is not recommended. Limit attempts and keep oxygenation as the priority.

nodes.title: Convert to Definitive Airway
nodes.summary: Do not remove a working SGA until the next airway plan is fully ready.
nodes.body: Prepare suction, VL/DL, bougie, smaller ETT, backup SGA, and cric kit before removing a working device. If the SGA is working but the patient needs ICU ventilation or aspiration protection, coordinate the exchange rather than rushing it. Use Difficult Airway / Bougie-First or Awake Intubation when appropriate.

nodes.title: Failed SGA Ventilation
nodes.summary: After failed SGA, return to BVM if possible. If BVM fails too, declare CICO.
nodes.body: Declare failed SGA ventilation. Limit to 3 total attempts, changing something meaningful each time: size, device type, position, depth, or operator. If BVM works, oxygenate and choose intubation/awake/specialist plan. If BVM fails, this is CICO.

nodes.title: CICO: Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate
nodes.summary: Failed tube + failed SGA + failed BVM = CICO. Move to cricothyrotomy.
nodes.body: If intubation failed, SGA failed, and BVM cannot oxygenate: declare CICO and perform emergency front-of-neck access. Do not delay for more supraglottic attempts. Go to Emergency Cricothyrotomy.

nodes.title: Disposition / Handoff
nodes.summary: Document device/size/attempts/confirmation and whether the SGA is bridge or endpoint.
nodes.body: Document indication, device, size, attempts, EtCO2/ventilation evidence, complications, and definitive airway plan. Handoff must explicitly state whether the SGA is a bridge or the current airway plan.
nodes.recommendation: Secure device, monitor continuously, and communicate whether this is bridge oxygenation or definitive short-term airway management.

nodes.title: SVT Assessment
nodes.summary: SVT types: AVNRT (50-60%), AVRT (30%), atrial tach (10%), flutter; assess stability first
nodes.body: SVT Overview Supraventricular Tachycardia: Regular, narrow-complex tachycardia originating above the ventricles. Common Types: • AVNRT (50-60%): Dual AV nodal pathways, pseudo S-wave in II/III/aVF • AVRT (30%): Accessory pathway (includes WPW), short PR at baseline • Atrial tachycardia (10%): P-wave before/after QRS • Atrial flutter: Saw-tooth pattern, typically 150 bpm (2:1 block) Typical HR: 140

nodes.title: Vagal Maneuver Selection
nodes.summary: Vagal maneuvers first-line; modified Valsalva preferred (43% vs 17% conversion)
nodes.body: Modified Valsalva Technique Vagal maneuvers are first-line for stable SVT (Class I, ACC/AHA 2015). Modified Valsalva (REVERT Trial): • 43% conversion vs 17% standard Valsalva • NNT = 3.8 • Zero-cost, no adverse effects Carotid Sinus Massage: • 20-40% success for AVNRT • Risk: 1 in 1,000 stroke risk • Contraindicated: carotid bruits, recent TIA/stroke, MI <3 months Which maneuver?

nodes.title: Modified Valsalva Technique (REVERT)
nodes.summary: REVERT: blow into syringe 15s → immediately flat → legs up 15s; 43% success
nodes.body: REVERT Trial Technique (REVERT Trial): Step 1: Patient sitting upright at 45° Step 2: Blow into 10mL syringe (move plunger) for 15 seconds (~40 mmHg pressure) Step 3: IMMEDIATELY lie patient flat Step 4: Elevate legs to 45° for 15 seconds Step 5: Return to sitting, check rhythm Success Rate: 43% conversion to NSR Tips: • Can repeat 2-3 times • Works best for AVNRT and AVRT • Patient may feel brief

nodes.title: Carotid Sinus Massage
nodes.summary: CSM: firm pressure 5-10s at carotid bifurcation; 20-40% success; 1:1000 stroke risk
nodes.body: Technique: Positioning: Patient supine, neck extended, head turned away Location: Below angle of jaw, at level of thyroid cartilage (over carotid bifurcation) Pressure: Firm circular pressure for 5-10 seconds Sequence: Try RIGHT side first, wait 1 minute, then LEFT if needed ⚠️ NEVER bilateral simultaneous massage Success Rate: 20-40% for AVNRT Contraindications: • Carotid bruits • Recent TIA/stro

nodes.title: Adenosine Administration
nodes.summary: 6mg rapid IV push + 20mL flush; repeat 12mg if needed; reduce to 3mg for central line
nodes.body: Adenosine Dosing Dosing: • Initial: 6mg rapid IV push (1-2 seconds) • Repeat: 12mg if no response in 1-2 minutes • Max: 12mg × 2 (some sources allow 18mg) Administration Technique (Critical): 1. Use proximal IV (antecubital preferred) 2. Rapid bolus over 1-2 seconds (half-life ~10 seconds) 3. Immediately follow with 20mL NS flush 4. Optional: elevate arm to 90° for 10-20 seconds Single-Syringe Met

nodes.title: Adenosine Response
nodes.summary: Abrupt termination = reentrant (AVNRT/AVRT); slowing reveals flutter; no response = consider VT
nodes.body: Expected Effects (warn patient): • Transient asystole (1-3 seconds) — normal • Chest pressure, warmth, dyspnea (5-10 seconds) • Sensation of "impending doom" • ALL symptoms resolve within seconds Interpretation: Abrupt termination during push: → AVNRT or AVRT (reentrant mechanism) Slowing then revealing underlying rhythm: → Atrial tachycardia or flutter (transient AV block reveals atrial activity)

nodes.title: Atrial Flutter Identified
nodes.summary: Flutter revealed: saw-tooth waves, 150 bpm (2:1 block); rate control or cardiovert; anticoagulation needed
nodes.body: Adenosine revealed flutter waves — this is atrial flutter, not AVNRT/AVRT. Atrial Flutter Characteristics: • Saw-tooth pattern in II, III, aVF • Atrial rate typically 280-320 bpm • Ventricular rate typically 150 bpm (2:1 block) or irregular Management Differs from Other SVT: Rate Control: • Diltiazem or beta-blocker (same as other SVT) • Goal: ventricular rate <110 bpm Rhythm Control: • Cardiovers

nodes.title: Rate Control Options
nodes.summary: Diltiazem preferred (98% success, faster onset); metoprolol if hypotension concern; amiodarone if refractory
nodes.body: Rate Control Agents If adenosine fails or SVT recurs, rate control agents are next. Diltiazem (Preferred): • 15-20mg (0.25 mg/kg) IV over 2 minutes • Repeat 20-25mg (0.35 mg/kg) in 15 min if needed • Infusion: 5-15 mg/hr • 98% reach target HR; 50% at 5 min • Caution: more hypotension than metoprolol (39% vs 24%) Metoprolol: • 5mg IV every 5 minutes × 3 doses (max 15mg) • Slower onset but less hypo

nodes.title: Diltiazem for SVT
nodes.summary: Diltiazem 15-20mg IV bolus, repeat 20-25mg; infusion 5-15 mg/hr; 98% success, 50% at 5 min
nodes.body: Diltiazem Dosing Initial Bolus: • 15-20mg (0.25 mg/kg) IV over 2 minutes • Flush with saline Repeat Bolus (if needed): • 20-25mg (0.35 mg/kg) IV in 15 minutes Maintenance Infusion: • 5-15 mg/hr (titrate to HR <100) • Start at 5 mg/hr, increase as needed Response: • 50% reach HR <100 by 5 minutes • 95% reach target by 30 minutes • 98% overall success Monitor For: • Hypotension (39% experience drop)
nodes.recommendation: Diltiazem 15-20mg IV over 2 min, repeat 20-25mg if needed. Infusion 5-15 mg/hr. 98% success.

nodes.title: Metoprolol for SVT
nodes.summary: Metoprolol 5mg IV q5min × 3 doses (max 15mg); slower onset but less hypotension; avoid in asthma
nodes.body: Dosing: • 5mg IV over 2 minutes • Repeat every 5 minutes × 3 doses (max 15mg total) Onset: Slower than diltiazem (46% at target HR by 30 min vs 50% at 5 min) Advantages: • Less hypotension than diltiazem (24% vs 39%) • Better for patients with borderline BP Monitor For: • Bradycardia • Hypotension • Bronchospasm (avoid in asthma/COPD) Contraindications: • Decompensated heart failure • Severe asthm
nodes.recommendation: Metoprolol 5mg IV q5min × 3 doses. Slower onset but less hypotension than diltiazem.

nodes.title: Amiodarone for Refractory SVT
nodes.summary: Amiodarone 150mg IV load, 1 mg/min infusion; for refractory SVT; works with structural heart disease
nodes.body: Use when diltiazem/metoprolol fail or contraindicated. Loading Dose: • 150mg IV over 10-15 minutes • Mix in D5W (precipitates in NS at high concentrations) Maintenance Infusion: • 1 mg/min × 6 hours • Then 0.5 mg/min × 18 hours • Max 2.2g in 24 hours Advantages: • Works in structural heart disease • Less negative inotropy than other agents • Both rate and rhythm control Side Effects (Acute): • Hyp
nodes.recommendation: Amiodarone 150mg IV over 10-15 min, then 1 mg/min × 6h. Use for refractory SVT or structural heart disease.

nodes.title: Unstable SVT — Cardioversion
nodes.summary: Unstable = hypotension, AMS, chest pain, pulmonary edema; sedate → synchronized cardioversion 50-100J
nodes.body: Cardioversion Protocol Indications for Immediate Cardioversion: • Hypotension (SBP <90) • Altered mental status • Chest pain/ischemic ECG changes • Pulmonary edema • Signs of shock Do NOT delay for vagal maneuvers or adenosine if truly unstable. Synchronized Cardioversion Protocol: 1. Sedation (if time permits): • Propofol 0.5-1 mg/kg IV, OR • Etomidate 0.2-0.3 mg/kg IV, OR • Midazolam 0.05-0.1 mg

nodes.title: Post-Cardioversion
nodes.summary: Post-cardioversion: monitor for recurrence; if unsuccessful, increase energy and verify sync mode
nodes.body: Assess rhythm after cardioversion: If converted to NSR: • Monitor for recurrence • Consider rate control agent to prevent recurrence • Evaluate for underlying cause (electrolytes, thyroid, drugs) If unsuccessful: • Verify SYNC mode was ON • Increase energy and repeat • Consider adenosine between shocks • Rule out WPW if not responding What was the result?

nodes.title: WPW Assessment
nodes.summary: WPW: short PR, delta wave; orthodromic = narrow (safe for AV blockers); pre-excited AF = AVOID AV blockers
nodes.body: WPW Overview Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome: Accessory pathway bypasses AV node → risk of rapid conduction in AF/flutter. Baseline ECG Clues: • Short PR interval (<120ms) • Delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) • Wide QRS (>120ms) WPW + SVT Presentation: Orthodromic AVRT (90%): • Narrow complex (antegrade through AV node) • AV nodal blockers may be used cautiously Antidromic AVRT (10%): • Wide complex

nodes.title: WPW — Orthodromic AVRT
nodes.summary: Orthodromic AVRT: narrow complex, AV blockers generally safe; refer for EP study + ablation
nodes.body: Orthodromic AVRT (narrow complex): Conduction goes antegrade through AV node, retrograde through accessory pathway. Management: • Vagal maneuvers (safe, try first) • Adenosine (generally safe — blocks AV node) • Diltiazem/metoprolol (acceptable) • Cardioversion if unstable Why it's safer: • AV nodal blockers slow the normal pathway • Accessory pathway is only conducting retrograde • No risk of acc
nodes.recommendation: Orthodromic AVRT: vagal → adenosine → diltiazem acceptable. Monitor for AF after conversion.

nodes.title: WPW + Pre-excited AF — DANGER
nodes.summary: WPW + pre-excited AF: AVOID AV nodal blockers (causes VF); cardiovert or procainamide; admit for EP
nodes.body: WPW + AF Protocol ⚠️ THIS IS A CRITICAL DIAGNOSIS ECG Features: • Irregular rhythm (AF) • Very fast (often >200 bpm) • Wide QRS (pre-excited) • Variable QRS morphology 🚫 AVOID THESE DRUGS (can cause VF): • Adenosine • Diltiazem/Verapamil • Beta-blockers • Digoxin Why dangerous: AV nodal blockers remove the "brakes" — AF conducts rapidly down accessory pathway → VF ✅ SAFE TREATMENTS: 1. Synchroniz
nodes.recommendation: WPW + AF: AVOID adenosine/diltiazem/beta-blockers. Cardiovert if unstable. Procainamide if stable.

nodes.title: SVT Converted — Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if: known SVT history, stable, no ischemia, reliable follow-up; admit first episode or complications
nodes.body: SVT has converted to normal sinus rhythm. Evaluate for discharge criteria: Discharge Appropriate If: • Known SVT history with similar episodes • Hemodynamically stable throughout • No chest pain or ischemic ECG changes • No elevated troponin (or demand ischemia only) • Reliable follow-up available • No WPW identified Admit If: • First episode of SVT • Failed conversion (required multiple agents) •

nodes.title: SVT Discharge
nodes.summary: Discharge: teach Valsalva, avoid triggers, cardiology follow-up 1-2 weeks, consider EP referral for ablation
nodes.body: Discharge Instructions: Patient Education: • Teach modified Valsalva for home use • Avoid triggers: caffeine, alcohol, decongestants, stimulants • Return if: palpitations persist >30 min, chest pain, syncope, SOB Medications (optional, per cardiology preference): • Metoprolol 25-50mg PO BID, OR • Diltiazem ER 120-180mg PO daily • "Pill in pocket" approach for infrequent episodes Follow-up: • Cardi
nodes.recommendation: Teach modified Valsalva. Avoid triggers. Follow-up cardiology 1-2 weeks. Consider EP referral for ablation.

nodes.title: SVT Admission
nodes.summary: Admit: telemetry, check TSH/lytes, echo if needed, cardiology consult, EP referral for ablation
nodes.body: Admission Criteria Met: Monitoring: • Continuous telemetry • Serial ECGs • Electrolyte monitoring (K, Mg) • Consider echo if structural heart disease suspected Workup: • TSH (hyperthyroidism can cause SVT) • Electrolytes (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) • Drug screen if appropriate • Echo if first presentation or suspected structural disease Cardiology Consult For: • EP study and ablation considerati
nodes.recommendation: Admit for telemetry, workup (TSH, lytes, echo), cardiology consult, EP referral if WPW.

nodes.title: Transient Loss of Consciousness (TLOC)
nodes.summary: First priority: exclude life-threatening conditions — abnormal vitals, neuro deficit, chest pain, hemorrhage
nodes.body: Syncope Evaluation Steps Summary Patient presents with transient loss of consciousness. First priority: exclude immediately life-threatening conditions. Are any of the following present? • Persistent abnormal vital signs (hypotension, tachycardia, bradycardia, hypoxia, tachypnea) • Neurologic deficit or headache • Chest pain or dyspnea • Abdominal pain or pulsatile mass • Evidence of hemorrhage or

nodes.title: Evaluate for Life-Threatening Etiology
nodes.body: TLOC with persistent abnormalities is NOT simple syncope until serious diagnoses are excluded. [1,2] Evaluate based on clinical findings: • Hypotension + tachycardia → hemorrhage, PE, sepsis, AAA • Chest pain → ACS, aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax • Headache + neuro deficit → SAH, stroke, ICH • Abdominal pain → ruptured AAA, ectopic pregnancy • Hypoxia + tachypnea → PE, pneumothorax •
nodes.recommendation: Workup directed by presenting symptoms. Syncope is a diagnosis of exclusion when life-threatening features are present.

nodes.title: Seizure vs. Syncope
nodes.summary: Syncope commonly causes myoclonic jerks — lateral tongue laceration, >20 rhythmic jerks, prolonged postictal favor seizure
nodes.body: Bystanders often call any convulsive activity a "seizure." Syncope commonly causes myoclonic jerks (especially if patient cannot lie flat). [4,5] Features favoring seizure: • Prolonged postictal disorientation (>few seconds) • Tongue laceration (lateral) • Head-turning, unusual posturing • >20 rhythmic jerks Features favoring syncope: • Presyncope (lightheadedness, diaphoresis, palpitations) • Los

nodes.title: Seizure Suspected
nodes.body: Clinical features suggest seizure rather than syncope. Evaluate and manage per seizure pathway. Pearl: Elevated serum lactate within 2 hours of the event is superior to CK for distinguishing seizure from syncope (positive LR 5.8). [7] If seizure is excluded after further workup, return to syncope evaluation.
nodes.recommendation: Manage per seizure pathway. Consider serum lactate within 2 hours to help differentiate.

nodes.title: ECG Assessment
nodes.summary: ECG mandatory for ALL syncope — 50% arrhythmic causes detected within 2h; QTc >500 ms = high risk
nodes.body: ECG is mandatory for ALL syncope patients — even those with suspected vasovagal syncope. [1,2] Place on continuous telemetry. In low-risk patients, 50% of arrhythmic causes are detected within 2 hours; 6 hours for medium/high-risk. [8] Review ECG carefully for: • Nonsinus rhythm or significant ectopy • Conduction abnormalities (AV block, BBB, pre-excitation) • QTc prolongation (>460 ms concerning,

nodes.title: Abnormal ECG — High-Risk Feature
nodes.summary: Abnormal ECG = high-risk in ALL syncope tools — BBB, QTc >460, pre-excitation, Brugada, epsilon waves
nodes.body: Abnormal ECG is a high-risk feature in all syncope risk stratification tools. [1,2,10] ECG findings associated with serious cardiac arrhythmias within 30 days: [9] • Nonsinus rhythm • Mobitz II or third-degree AV block • Bundle branch block (especially new LBBB) • QTc >460 ms • Pre-excitation (WPW) • Brugada type 1 pattern • Epsilon waves (ARVC) • "Dagger" Q waves (HCM) • ST depression or T-wave i

nodes.title: Focused History
nodes.summary: History is the single most important tool — activity, prodrome, duration, medications, cardiac/family history
nodes.body: The history is the single most important tool in identifying the cause of syncope. [1,2] Historical Features by Etiology Assess: • Activity at onset: position, exertion, triggers (pain, blood, emotional) • Prodrome: nausea, sweating, lightheadedness, palpitations, tunnel vision • During event: duration, witnessed movements, skin color • After event: orientation, confusion duration, injuries • Prio

nodes.title: Laboratory Testing
nodes.summary: Labs low-yield unless directed — troponin predicts 30-day mortality; do NOT routinely D-dimer or head CT
nodes.body: Labs are low-yield unless directed by history/exam. [1,2] Consider in patients without clear benign diagnosis: • CBC — anemia (but initial Hgb may be normal in acute hemorrhage) • BMP — electrolytes, renal function, glucose • Pregnancy test — all women of childbearing age • Troponin (hs-cTnT) — elevated troponin is an independent predictor of 30-day mortality [13] • BNP/NT-proBNP — elevated BNP co

nodes.title: Neurally Mediated (Reflex) Syncope
nodes.body: Most common identified cause of syncope. Good long-term prognosis. [17,18] Subtypes: • Vasovagal — triggered by pain, blood, emotions, medical procedures; prodrome with nausea, sweating, warmth. More common age <40. • Situational — Valsalva, post-exercise, coughing, swallowing, defecation • Carotid sinus — head-turning, shaving (age >40) For unexplained syncope in patients >40 years, consider caro
nodes.recommendation: Low-risk. Discharge with reassurance and follow-up for recurrent episodes. Avoid known triggers. Counsel on counterpressure maneuvers.

nodes.title: Orthostatic Hypotension
nodes.body: Orthostatic hypotension = SBP drop >20 mmHg (or DBP drop >10 mmHg) within 3 minutes of standing, or symptoms with position change. [1] Most common cause: medications (~40% of cases). [22] Drug-related causes: • Antihypertensives (ACEi, ARBs, beta-blockers, CCBs) • Diuretics • Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, doxazosin) • Nitrates • Antidepressants (TCAs, MAOIs) • Antipsychotics Other causes: volume dep

nodes.title: Orthostatic Syncope — Modifiable Cause
nodes.summary: Medications cause ~40% of orthostatic syncope — normal orthostatics do NOT predict outcomes in elderly
nodes.body: Medication or volume-related orthostatic syncope with otherwise reassuring evaluation. Management: • IV fluids if volume-depleted • Review and adjust offending medications • Educate on slow position changes • Compression stockings and increased salt/fluid intake for recurrent episodes • PCP follow-up for medication adjustment Important: In elderly patients, identifying orthostasis allows modificat
nodes.recommendation: Low to intermediate risk. Treat volume depletion, adjust medications, PCP follow-up for med reconciliation. Review Discharge Instructions with patient.

nodes.title: Cardiac Syncope Suspected
nodes.summary: Cardiac syncope = highest morbidity — exertional, no prodrome, supine, palpitations, structural disease, abnormal ECG
nodes.body: Cardiac syncope carries the highest morbidity of all causes. Patients with underlying cardiac disease + syncope have higher all-cause mortality. [25] Features suggesting cardiac syncope: • Syncope during exertion • Palpitations immediately before syncope • Syncope while supine • Syncope without prodrome (abrupt) • History of structural heart disease (HF, CAD, valvular) • Family history of sudden c

nodes.title: Cardiac Syncope Workup
nodes.summary: Structural heart disease + syncope = HIGH RISK — troponin, BNP, echo if HF/CAD/abnormal ECG/elevated biomarkers
nodes.body: Structural heart disease + syncope = HIGH RISK. [1,2,25] Recommended ED workup: • Continuous telemetry monitoring (minimum 6 hours for high-risk) [8] • Troponin (hs-cTnT) — elevated is independent predictor of 30-day mortality [13] • BNP/NT-proBNP — aids in recognition of cardiac syncope [14,15] • Echocardiography — high yield when HF, CAD, abnormal ECG, or elevated biomarkers present [26] Conside

nodes.title: Arrhythmia Suspected
nodes.summary: Arrhythmias typically resolve before ED — telemetry 2-6h based on risk; ambulatory monitor within 15 days for higher yield
nodes.body: Arrhythmias are the most common cause of cardiac syncope — and typically resolve before ED arrival. [1,2] Clues to arrhythmic syncope: • Abrupt onset without prodrome • Syncope while sitting or supine • Palpitations preceding the event • Abnormal ECG (bundle branch block, prolonged QTc, pre-excitation, Brugada pattern) • Known cardiac device (pacemaker/ICD) ED monitoring: • Continuous telemetry —

nodes.title: Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: CSRS (best validated) and SFSR for risk stratification — tools do not outperform clinical judgment consistently
nodes.body: For patients with unexplained syncope after history, exam, and ECG — apply risk stratification. [1,2] Risk stratification tools do not consistently outperform clinical judgment, but help identify high-risk features. [29,30] Use the calculators below to aid disposition: • CSRS — Canadian Syncope Risk Score (best validated, multicenter) [31,32] • SFSR — San Francisco Syncope Rule (simple binary scre

nodes.title: Pediatric Syncope
nodes.summary: 80% pediatric syncope is neurally mediated — cardiac features rare; avoid excessive testing (58% get low-yield head CT)
nodes.body: Approach mirrors adults. History, exam, and ECG are the most useful components. [34] 80% of pediatric syncope is neurally mediated — vast majority have benign etiology. Most cardiac syncope can be diagnosed by history, exam, and ECG. [34] Features suggesting cardiac cause in children: • Exertional syncope • Syncope without prodrome • Syncope while supine • Family history of sudden cardiac death •

nodes.title: Elderly Syncope
nodes.summary: 25-50% of elderly falls may be syncope — hospitalization does not improve 30-day outcomes; mortality from comorbidities
nodes.body: Particularly challenging — many present with unexplained falls rather than syncope. [37,38] Key points: • 25-50% of unexplained falls in elderly may be syncope-related [37,39] • Almost half of elderly with dementia referred for unexplained falls receive a syncope diagnosis [39] • Neurally mediated syncope is still common in this age group [37] • QTc prolongation occurs in 25% of elderly — QTc >500

nodes.title: High-Risk — Admit
nodes.body: Hospital admission or observation unit recommended. [1,2] Indications for admission: • Sustained or symptomatic ventricular tachycardia • Symptomatic conduction system disease or high-grade AV block • Symptomatic bradycardia or sinus pauses (not reflex-mediated) • Symptomatic SVT • Pacemaker/ICD malfunction • Inheritable cardiovascular conditions predisposing to arrhythmias • Cardiac ischemia • Se
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored bed. Cardiology consult. Continuous telemetry. Echo if structural disease suspected.

nodes.title: Intermediate Risk — Observation vs. Outpatient
nodes.body: Shared decision-making recommended. [1,2] Intermediate-risk factors: [1] • Age ≥50 years • Prior history of cardiac disease • Cardiac device without dysfunction • Family history of early sudden cardiac death • Symptoms not consistent with reflex-mediated syncope Key point: Patients with risk factors by PMH (CAD, HF) but with a benign cause identified in the ED (e.g., dehydration) may be discharged
nodes.recommendation: Shared decision-making. Consider ED observation protocol. If discharge: close follow-up + ambulatory monitoring referral.

nodes.title: Low Risk — Discharge
nodes.body: Low-risk patients should generally be discharged, even with unexplained syncope. [1,2] Low-risk features (ESC): [2] • Young age with typical features of reflex syncope • No history of cardiac disease • Syncope only when standing • Identifiable trigger (pain, blood, prolonged standing) • Normal ECG • Normal vital signs Discharge counseling: • Explain diagnosis and expected benign prognosis • Counse
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with reassurance, trigger avoidance counseling, and PCP follow-up. Address driving restrictions if applicable. Review Discharge Instructions with patient.

nodes.title: Head CT Is NOT Indicated
nodes.summary: ACEP Choosing Wisely: no head CT without neuro deficit or head trauma — <0.1% yield for syncope cause
nodes.body: ACEP "Choosing Wisely" recommendation: Avoid head CT in asymptomatic patients with syncope, minimal trauma, and a normal neurologic examination. [16] Evidence: • Head CT has very low yield (<0.1%) in determining the cause of syncope [50] • Commonly ordered despite lack of utility — one study found 58% of pediatric syncope patients received head CT [36] • No neurological symptoms + no head trauma +

nodes.title: Pulmonary Embolism & Syncope
nodes.summary: Routine D-dimer NOT indicated — PE uncommon in syncope; apply standard PERC/Wells only when clinically suspected
nodes.body: PE is uncommon among syncope patients. [51,52] Existing clinical decision rules (PERC) adequately identify syncope patients with PE. [51] Routine D-dimer is NOT indicated in syncope patients without independent indications for PE evaluation. [53,54] When to consider PE: • Unexplained persistent tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, or hypoxia in ED • Recent surgery, immobilization, or other VTE ris

nodes.title: Carotid Sinus Massage
nodes.summary: Carotid sinus massage for undiagnosed syncope >40y — diagnostic in up to 60%; contraindicated if carotid bruit/stenosis
nodes.body: AHA and ESC recommend carotid sinus massage in patients >40 years with undiagnosed syncope after initial evaluation. [1,2] Diagnostic in up to 60% of patients (increasing with advanced age). [19] Positive result (carotid sinus hypersensitivity): • Syncope reproduced, OR • Asystole >3 seconds, OR • AV block, OR • SBP drop ≥50 mmHg Contraindications: • Carotid bruit • Known carotid stenosis >70% • H

nodes.title: Syphilis — ED Evaluation
nodes.summary: Syphilis 80% increase since 2018 — "the great imitator"; route by presentation: lesion, rash, screening, partner, neuro, pregnancy
nodes.body: Syphilis Steps Summary 207,255 total US cases in 2022 (80% increase since 2018). 59,233 primary/secondary cases. Congenital syphilis increased 755% from 2012-2022. Known as "the great imitator" — can mimic many conditions. [1][2][4]

nodes.title: Partner Notification Exposure
nodes.summary: Partner exposure <90 days: treat presumptively even if seronegative; contact tracing windows vary by stage
nodes.body: Exposed contacts of primary/secondary syphilis within the preceding 90 days should be treated presumptively, even if seronegative. [5][21] Contacts >90 days ago should be tested and treated based on results. Contact tracing windows by stage: • Primary syphilis: 3 months + symptom duration • Secondary syphilis: 6 months + symptom duration • Early latent: 1 year Partner Notification & Reporting

nodes.title: Neurological, Ocular, or Otic Symptoms
nodes.summary: Neurosyphilis can occur at ANY stage — ocular/otosyphilis are clinical diagnoses requiring neurosyphilis-level treatment
nodes.body: Neurosyphilis can occur at ANY stage of syphilis infection. Ocular and otosyphilis are clinical diagnoses that require neurosyphilis-level treatment regardless of CSF findings. [1][6] Key findings: • Ocular: uveitis (most common), vision loss, floaters, disc edema, retinitis • Otic: hearing loss (conductive or sensorineural), tinnitus, vertigo • Meningeal: headache, stiff neck, photophobia, CN VI/

nodes.title: Neurosyphilis Pathway
nodes.body: Patient has neurological, ocular, or otic symptoms with known or suspected syphilis. This requires the neurosyphilis evaluation pathway. Neurosyphilis Evaluation & Treatment — full CSF workup and IV Penicillin G protocol. Key principles: • Ocular/otosyphilis is treated as neurosyphilis regardless of CSF findings — do NOT delay treatment for LP results • Penicillin G (IV) 18-24 million units/day (3
nodes.recommendation: Route to Neurosyphilis consult for CSF evaluation and IV Penicillin G protocol.

nodes.title: Syphilis in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Pregnancy: PCN ONLY effective — desensitize if allergic; congenital syphilis up 755%; Jarisch-Herxheimer can cause preterm labor
nodes.body: Syphilis in pregnancy is a public health emergency. Congenital syphilis cases increased 755% from 2012-2022 (3,761 cases in 2022), with 282 stillbirths and infant deaths. [3][10][11] Critical rules: • ALL pregnant patients with syphilis must receive penicillin — there are NO adequate alternatives • If PCN-allergic: desensitization is MANDATORY (oral protocol preferred, can be done in ED/L&D with m

nodes.title: Syphilis Stage Classification
nodes.summary: Classification determines treatment — stage by clinical findings, serologic history, and time since acquisition
nodes.body: Classification determines treatment. Staging is based on clinical findings, serologic history, and time since acquisition. [1][2] Stage Classification Guide Syphilis progresses through defined stages. Previous infection does not confer immunity, and reinfected patients are less likely to be symptomatic.

nodes.title: Primary Syphilis
nodes.summary: Painless indurated chancre at inoculation site, 10-90 days post-exposure — heals spontaneously, often unnoticed
nodes.body: Classic chancre: painless, firm, round, indurated ulcer with clean base at the inoculation site. Appears 10-90 days after exposure (average 21 days). Heals spontaneously in 3-6 weeks even without treatment. [1][14][15] Characteristics: • Usually single, but can be multiple (especially in HIV+ patients or with high spirochete load) • Common sites: penis, vulva, cervix, anus, mouth (oral sexual cont

nodes.title: Secondary Syphilis
nodes.summary: Diffuse rash with palms/soles (50-80%), condylomata lata, mucous patches — hematogenous dissemination 4-10w after chancre
nodes.body: Occurs 4-10 weeks after chancre (which may still be present). Represents hematogenous dissemination of T. pallidum. [1][16][17] Rash: • Diffuse, symmetric, maculopapular • Classically involves palms and soles (50-80% of cases) • Non-pruritic, red to red-brown, flat and scaly • Can be more generalized — "the great imitator" can mimic virtually any dermatologic condition • May be difficult to identi

nodes.title: Early Latent Syphilis
nodes.summary: Early latent: <1 year, asymptomatic, still sexually transmissible — same treatment as primary/secondary
nodes.body: Acquired within the preceding year but no clinical signs or symptoms. [1][5] Diagnosed when: • Documented seroconversion or 4-fold titer rise within 12 months • History of primary/secondary symptoms within 12 months • Sex partner with primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis within 12 months • Reactive NTT and TT only in persons previously tested seronegative within 12 months Clinical signific

nodes.title: Late Latent / Unknown Duration
nodes.summary: Late latent >1 year or unknown — not sexually transmissible but can transmit vertically; 3 weekly PCN doses
nodes.body: Acquired > 1 year ago OR unknown duration of infection. [1][5] Key points: • Not sexually transmissible (except in pregnancy — can transmit vertically at any stage) • Can progress to tertiary syphilis (in ~30% of untreated patients) over years to decades • If no documentation of timing, classified as late latent (more conservative treatment — 3 weekly doses) Evaluate for neurosyphilis if: • Neurol

nodes.title: Tertiary Syphilis
nodes.summary: Tertiary in ~30% untreated: gummatous, cardiovascular (aortitis/aneurysm), or neurologic — must rule out neurosyphilis
nodes.body: Occurs in ~30% of untreated patients, 3-15+ years after initial infection. Now rare in developed countries. [1][19] Gummatous syphilis (~15%): • Granulomatous, nodular lesions with necrotic center surrounded by immune cells • Found in skin, bone, liver, testes, and other organs • Destructive but responds well to treatment Cardiovascular syphilis (~10%): • Aortitis, ascending aortic aneurysm, aorti

nodes.title: Risk Factor Assessment
nodes.summary: MSM 56% of primary/secondary cases; HIV co-infection 2-5x mutual facilitation; mandatory co-testing: HIV, GC/CT, HepB/C
nodes.body: Document risk factors to guide testing strategy and counseling. [1][2][14] High-risk populations: • MSM — highest incidence (56% of primary/secondary cases, rate 240× higher than women) • HIV co-infection — syphilis facilitates HIV acquisition 2-5× and vice versa • Persons on PrEP — test at initiation and at least every 6 months (every 3 months for high-risk MSM) • Multiple sexual partners, sex wo

nodes.title: Diagnostic Testing Strategy
nodes.summary: Two algorithms: traditional (NTT first) or reverse (TT first) — combination of NTT + TT + clinical context determines diagnosis
nodes.body: Two serologic algorithms exist. Most labs now use the reverse algorithm (start with treponemal test). No single test is definitive in all scenarios — the combination of NTT + TT + clinical context determines diagnosis. [6][22][23] Testing Algorithm Guide Nontreponemal tests (NTT): RPR, VDRL — detect antibodies to tissue damage, not T. pallidum itself. Quantitative titers correlate with disease act

nodes.title: ED Lab Orders for Syphilis
nodes.summary: Order RPR (quantitative) + treponemal test + HIV + GC/CT NAAT + HepB/C; very early primary can be seronegative
nodes.body: Standard ED workup: [22][23] Serologic testing: • RPR (quantitative) — nontreponemal test, reflects disease activity • Treponemal test (TP-PA or FTA-ABS) — if not already reflexed by lab Co-testing: • HIV Ag/Ab combo (4th generation) — mandatory • GC/CT NAAT (urine or swab) • Hepatitis B surface Ag/Ab/core Ab, Hepatitis C Ab If neurologic symptoms: • LP for CSF-VDRL, cell count, protein → Neurosyp

nodes.title: Point-of-Care Testing
nodes.summary: Rapid POC tests 85-98% sensitive — TT positive for life, still need NTT for staging; dark-field rarely available in EDs
nodes.body: Rapid treponemal POC tests are becoming available in the US (Syphilis Health Check™, DPP® HIV-syphilis assay). [26][27] Performance: • Sensitivity 85-98%, specificity 95-99% for treponemal antibodies • Comparable to laboratory-based treponemal testing Limitations: • TT positive for life — cannot distinguish active vs treated • Still require NTT (RPR) for staging/monitoring • Positive → confirm wit

nodes.title: Serologic Test Interpretation
nodes.summary: Interpret NTT + TT combination — both may be nonreactive in 30% of primary syphilis; 5 result patterns
nodes.body: Interpret the combination of nontreponemal test (NTT = RPR or VDRL) and treponemal test (TT = TP-PA, FTA-ABS, EIA, or CIA). Both tests may be nonreactive in up to 30% of patients with primary syphilis. [6][22][23] Testing Algorithm Guide

nodes.title: NTT Reactive + TT Reactive
nodes.summary: NTT+/TT+ = confirmed treponemal infection — compare titers to prior; 4-fold rise = reinfection/failure
nodes.body: Classic positive result — confirms treponemal infection. [6][22][23] No prior treatment: • New diagnosis — stage and treat accordingly • RPR ≥1:32 → higher neurosyphilis risk Prior treatment: • Compare current vs prior RPR titer • 4-fold rise (e.g., 1:4 → 1:16) = reinfection/failure → re-treat • Stable low titer = serofast state (~10% of treated patients) — may not need re-treatment

nodes.title: NTT Nonreactive + TT Reactive
nodes.summary: NTT-/TT+: most likely prior treated; may be very early primary or very late latent — clinical context determines
nodes.body: Clinical context determines interpretation. [6][22][23] Most common: Previously treated • Documented treatment + asymptomatic → no re-treatment Very early primary: • TT seroconverts before NTT • Chancre present → treat empirically, repeat RPR in 2-4 weeks Very late latent: • NTT reverts in ~25% of untreated late latent • No documented treatment → treat as late latent Reverse algorithm discordance:

nodes.title: NTT Reactive + TT Nonreactive
nodes.summary: NTT+/TT- = likely biologic false positive — no treatment; prozone phenomenon can cause false-negative in secondary
nodes.body: Most likely biologic false-positive (BFP) — no syphilis treatment. [6][22][30] BFP causes: Pregnancy, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, acute illness, vaccination, IVDU, liver disease, advanced age, HIV Action: No treatment. Consider repeat TT with different assay. Chronic BFP (>6 mo) → autoimmune workup. ⚠️ Prozone phenomenon: Very high titers in secondary syphilis can saturate assay → false-negati

nodes.title: Both Tests Nonreactive
nodes.summary: Both nonreactive: no syphilis or window period — treat empirically if high suspicion, repeat serology in 2-4 weeks
nodes.body: No serologic evidence of syphilis. [6][22][23] High suspicion (chancre present): May be in window period (1-4 wks post-exposure). Treat empirically, repeat serologies in 2-4 wks. Recent exposure (<90 days): Treat presumptively, repeat serologies in 2-4 wks. Low suspicion: Syphilis excluded.

nodes.title: Treatment by Stage
nodes.summary: PCN G is the only proven treatment — regimen determined by stage; Jarisch-Herxheimer is NOT an allergy
nodes.body: Penicillin G is the only proven treatment for syphilis. Treatment regimen is determined by disease stage. [1][5][31] Treatment Summary Table Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur within hours of treatment — counsel all patients. [32]

nodes.title: Early Syphilis Treatment
nodes.body: Primary / Secondary / Early Latent (<1 year): [1][5][31] Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4M units IM × 1 dose Jarisch-Herxheimer: [32] 10-35% primary, 75-90% secondary. Onset 2-8h, resolves <24h. Fever, rigors, myalgias — NOT an allergic reaction (dying spirochetes). Treat supportively. Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction Follow-up: RPR at 6 & 12 months. Expect 4-fold titer decline.
nodes.recommendation: Benzathine PCN-G 2.4M units IM × 1. Counsel on Jarisch-Herxheimer. RPR at 6 and 12 months.

nodes.title: Late Syphilis Treatment
nodes.body: Late Latent / Tertiary (non-neurologic): [1][5][31] Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4M units IM weekly × 3 weeks (total 7.2M units) Missed dose: >14 days between doses → restart series. Before treating: Rule out neurosyphilis (neuro exam; LP if RPR ≥1:32, HIV+, or neuro symptoms). CV syphilis: treatment doesn't reverse aortic damage. Follow-up: RPR at 6, 12, 24 months. No 4-fold decline → evaluate for f
nodes.recommendation: Benzathine PCN-G 2.4M units IM weekly × 3 weeks. Rule out neurosyphilis. RPR at 6, 12, 24 months.

nodes.title: Penicillin Allergy Alternatives
nodes.summary: Azithromycin NOT recommended — documented resistance and failures; desensitization preferred over alternatives
nodes.body: Desensitization preferred — PCN is the only proven curative therapy. [1][5][31][33] ⚠️ Azithromycin NOT recommended — macrolide resistance documented, treatment failures in US. [34][35][36]

nodes.title: PCN Allergy — Early Syphilis Alternatives
nodes.body: Non-pregnant, Primary / Secondary / Early Latent: [1][5][31] First: Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 14 days (contraindicated in pregnancy) Second: Ceftriaxone 1-2g IM/IV daily × 10-14 days (PCN cross-reactivity ~2-5%)
nodes.recommendation: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID × 14 days. RPR at 6 and 12 months.

nodes.title: PCN Allergy — Late Syphilis Alternatives
nodes.body: Non-pregnant, Late Latent / Tertiary: [1][5][31] Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 28 days ⚠️ Must rule out neurosyphilis first — doxy doesn't reach CSF. If neuro can't be excluded → Neurosyphilis PCN Allergy
nodes.recommendation: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID × 28 days. Rule out neurosyphilis first. RPR at 6, 12, 24 months.

nodes.title: Syphilis in Pregnancy — Treatment
nodes.body: Penicillin is the ONLY acceptable treatment. No alternatives prevent congenital syphilis. [3][10][11][12] PCN-allergic: Desensitization is MANDATORY (oral protocol preferred, can be done in ED/L&D). Treatment: Same as non-pregnant — Early: 2.4M units × 1; Late: 2.4M units weekly × 3 Jarisch-Herxheimer in pregnancy: Can precipitate preterm labor. Continuous fetal monitoring × 24h if viable GA. Do N
nodes.recommendation: PCN per stage. PCN-allergic: desensitize. Fetal monitoring if viable GA. OB involvement mandatory.

nodes.title: Neurosyphilis — PCN Allergy
nodes.body: Desensitization strongly preferred — PCN is the only proven neurosyphilis therapy. [1][7][8] Alternative: Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily × 10-14 days (PCN cross-reactivity ~2-5%) True IgE-mediated anaphylaxis → desensitization under allergist supervision. Neurosyphilis Evaluation
nodes.recommendation: Desensitize if possible. Alternative: Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily × 10-14 days.

nodes.title: Empiric Treatment
nodes.body: High clinical suspicion, results pending. [1][5] Indications: Partner exposure <90 days, classic chancre, palms/soles rash, high-risk with concerning lesion. Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4M units IM × 1 ⚠️ Draw RPR + TT BEFORE treatment to establish baseline. Follow up results — if late latent confirmed, add 2 more weekly doses.
nodes.recommendation: Draw RPR + TT first, then Benzathine PCN-G 2.4M IM × 1. Follow up results.

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Most patients discharged after ED treatment — mandatory public health reporting, partner notification, RPR monitoring
nodes.body: Most patients discharged after ED treatment. [1][5] All patients: Mandatory public health reporting (all 50 states), partner notification, RPR monitoring. Partner Notification & Reporting

nodes.title: Discharge Plan
nodes.body: Mandatory: File public health report, partner notification. [1][5][21] Counseling: No sex × 7 days + lesion resolution. Return for vision/hearing changes or neuro symptoms. Follow-up: STI clinic 1-2 wks. RPR at 6, 12, 24 months. HIV result if pending.
nodes.recommendation: File report. Partner notification. STI clinic follow-up. RPR monitoring.

nodes.title: Admission Criteria
nodes.body: Admit for: [1][6][7] • Neurosyphilis (IV PCN × 10-14 days) • Ocular syphilis (+ ophthalmology) • Otosyphilis (+ ENT/audiology) • PCN desensitization • Pregnant at viable GA (fetal monitoring) • CV syphilis with acute complications • Congenital syphilis in newborn All admissions: ID consult mandatory.
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV PCN. ID consult. Ophthalmology/ENT if ocular/otic.

nodes.title: Tar / Asphalt Burn — Dissolve, Don\u2019t Peel
nodes.summary: Cool, then dissolve adherent tar with petroleum emulsifier; never peel.
nodes.body: Adherent hot tar traps heat and hides burn depth. The core rule: never mechanically peel adherent tar — it strips viable skin. Cool first, then dissolve with a petroleum-based emulsifier. Tools (open first): - Procedure Steps Summary - Dissolution-Agent Ladder - Burn TBSA + Transfer Criteria - Analgesia Options - Do-NOT List

nodes.title: Airway / Inhalation First
nodes.summary: Screen inhalation injury first; airway/CO/CN supersede wound care.
nodes.body: Wound care never precedes airway. Hot-tar exposures (enclosed spaces, kettle flashes) can carry inhalation injury. Screen before focusing on the skin.

nodes.title: Airway Takes Priority
nodes.summary: Airway/CO/CN first; resume tar care after stabilization; transfer if airway + burn.
nodes.body: Manage the airway and systemic injury before tar: - Early intubation if progressive airway edema, stridor, or deep facial burns - 100% oxygen for suspected carbon monoxide; consider cyanide toxicity in enclosed-space fires - Then return to tar dissolution once the patient is stabilized Use the burn-center criteria in Burn TBSA + Transfer; significant burns with airway involvement warrant transfer.
nodes.recommendation: Stabilize airway, treat CO/CN, then resume tar dissolution.

nodes.title: Step 1 — Cool + Analgesia
nodes.summary: Cool ~20 min (no ice), analgesia early, do not peel.
nodes.body: 1. Cool the tar immediately with room-temperature water to stop ongoing thermal injury and harden the tar so it stops spreading. Cool ~20 minutes; avoid ice (worsens injury) and avoid hypothermia in large burns. 2. Provide analgesia early — tar burns are painful and dissolution takes time. See Analgesia Options. 3. Do NOT attempt to pick, peel, or scrub the tar off at this stage. Once cooled and t

nodes.title: Step 2 — Select Dissolution Agent
nodes.summary: Petroleum/surfactant emulsifier (bacitracin, Tween-80, mineral oil, vit E); never acetone/gasoline.
nodes.body: Tar is petroleum-based, so a petroleum/surfactant emulsifier dissolves it without harming skin. Pick what you have — full ladder in Dissolution-Agent Ladder. Never use organic solvents (acetone, gasoline) — they cause chemical injury.

nodes.title: Step 3 — Apply + Dwell
nodes.summary: Apply emulsifier thickly under dressing, reapply q1-2h, let tar release atraumatically.
nodes.body: 1. Apply the chosen emulsifier generously over ALL adherent tar. 2. Cover with a non-adherent dressing and a bulky outer wrap to hold the agent against the tar. 3. Let it dwell. Tar dissolves gradually — reapply the agent every 1-2 hours. As the tar softens it lifts off atraumatically with gentle wiping; let it release on its own. 4. Do NOT force, scrub, or peel any tar that is still adherent — re

nodes.title: Step 4 — Reassess Burn Depth
nodes.summary: Assess depth + TBSA only after tar cleared; tetanus; refer deep/large burns.
nodes.body: Burn depth CANNOT be judged while tar covers the skin. Only after the tar is cleared: - Estimate depth (superficial / partial / full thickness) and TBSA — use Burn TBSA + Transfer - Superficial and small partial-thickness burns → standard burn wound care, topical antibiotic, dressing, outpatient follow-up - Deep partial / full thickness, or large TBSA → burn-center referral - Update tetanus status

nodes.title: Disposition + Note
nodes.summary: Discharge small burns w/ emulsifier + follow-up; transfer if burn-center criteria.
nodes.body: Disposition: - Discharge: small superficial/partial-thickness burns once tar is substantially cleared and pain is controlled; ongoing emulsifier ointment + non-adherent dressing; burn-clinic or PCP follow-up in 24-48 h; clear return precautions (increasing pain, redness, fever, drainage). - Admit / transfer: burn-center criteria met (deep partial/full thickness, large TBSA, hands/face/feet/perineu
nodes.recommendation: Discharge small superficial burns with ongoing emulsifier + follow-up; transfer if burn-center criteria.

nodes.title: TCA Overdose — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Na channel blockade → QRS widening → VT/VF; lethal dose only 3-5x therapeutic; alert to arrest within 1 hour
nodes.body: TCA Overdose Steps Summary — quick reference. Tricyclic antidepressants remain a leading cause of death from prescription drug overdose. Narrow therapeutic index — lethal dose is only 3-5× the therapeutic dose [1][3]. Multiple mechanisms of toxicity: • Sodium channel blockade → QRS widening → ventricular arrhythmias (most dangerous) • Anticholinergic effects → tachycardia, mydriasis, AMS • Alpha-1

nodes.title: Anticholinergic Toxidrome
nodes.summary: Anticholinergic toxidrome — sinus tachycardia most common; do NOT be reassured, rapid deterioration possible
nodes.body: "Blind as a bat, dry as a bone, hot as a hare, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, full as a flask" [3][13] • Tachycardia (most common cardiac finding) • Mydriasis (dilated pupils) • Dry skin and mucous membranes • Urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds • Hyperthermia • Agitation → delirium → coma Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding and may be the only abnormality in mild toxicity [1].

nodes.title: Immediate Resuscitation
nodes.summary: ECG STAT, bicarb if QRS wide, TCA levels NOT useful — intubate if GCS ≤12
nodes.body: Initiate immediately: • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Two large-bore IVs • 12-lead ECG STAT — most important test [1][3] • BMP, blood gas (pH), lactate, glucose • Acetaminophen and salicylate levels (coingestion screening) • Urine drug screen (false positives common: diphenhydramine, cyclobenzaprine, carbamazepine) [3] ⚠️ TCA levels are NOT useful for acute management — do not correlate with tox

nodes.title: GI Decontamination
nodes.summary: Charcoal 1 g/kg if airway protected — anticholinergic delays gastric emptying so window may extend beyond 2h
nodes.body: Activated Charcoal — 1 g/kg PO (max 50g) [4][18] Anticholinergic effects delay gastric emptying → charcoal may be beneficial even beyond the typical 1-2 hour window [3][16]. ⚠️ Do NOT induce emesis — risk of rapid deterioration [4]. Is the airway protected?

nodes.title: Intubation Considerations
nodes.summary: CRITICAL: avoid hypoventilation post-intubation — respiratory acidosis worsens toxicity; hyperventilate to ETCO2 25-30
nodes.body: Indications: GCS ≤12, seizures, hypoventilation with respiratory acidosis [16]. ⚠️ CRITICAL: Avoid hypoventilation post-intubation — respiratory acidosis worsens TCA toxicity by increasing free (unbound) drug, creating a vicious spiral [16][17]. Before intubation: • Give Sodium Bicarbonate if QRS wide — allow minutes for CO₂ to blow off • Start vasopressor if hypotensive Post-intubation: • Immedia

nodes.title: ECG Assessment
nodes.summary: ECG is the single most important test — QRS >100 ms = seizure risk, >160 ms = VT/VF risk; R wave >3 mm aVR confirms blockade
nodes.body: The 12-lead ECG is the single most important test [1][3]. ECG Findings in TCA Toxicity — detailed reference. Critical ECG markers: • QRS >100 ms → increased seizure risk [1] • QRS >160 ms → increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias [1] • R wave >3 mm in aVR → sensitive marker of Na channel blockade [2] • R/S ratio >0.7 in aVR • Rightward axis of terminal 40 ms QRS • QT prolongation (K+ channel blo

nodes.title: Normal QRS — Monitor Closely
nodes.summary: QRS <100 ms low risk but can change rapidly — check R wave aVR >3 mm; serial ECGs q15-30 min for 2 hours
nodes.body: QRS < 100 ms suggests low risk, but do not be reassured — toxicity can develop rapidly [1]. Still check: • R wave in aVR >3 mm — may be positive even with normal QRS. Liebelt 1995 found aVR may be more sensitive than QRS for predicting seizures and arrhythmias [2]. • R/S ratio >0.7 in aVR • Brugada-like pattern (coved ST elevation V1-V3) Monitoring plan: • Serial ECGs q15-30 min for first 2 hours

nodes.title: R Wave in aVR
nodes.summary: aVR R wave >3 mm: 81% sensitivity for seizures/arrhythmias — may be positive even with normal QRS
nodes.body: R wave amplitude >3 mm in lead aVR is a sensitive marker of sodium channel blockade [2]. • R/S ratio >0.7 in aVR • Terminal 40 ms rightward axis deviation — the sodium channel blockade preferentially affects the right bundle, causing rightward shift of the terminal QRS vector • May be positive even when QRS <100 ms Liebelt et al (1995): In TCA overdose, aVR findings had sensitivity 81% for predict

nodes.title: Serial ECG Monitoring
nodes.summary: Serial ECGs q15-30 min for 2h, then q2h for 6h total — any QRS widening mandates reassessment
nodes.body: ECG monitoring protocol: • Serial 12-lead ECGs every 15-30 min for first 2 hours [3] • Continuous telemetry — minimum 6 hours after last ECG abnormality resolves [5] • QRS can widen rapidly — any change mandates reassessment QT prolongation: • Present due to K+ channel blockade • Less prognostically significant than QRS widening • Torsades de pointes is uncommon as long as the patient remains tach

nodes.title: Sodium Bicarbonate — Cornerstone of Treatment
nodes.summary: NaHCO3 1-2 mEq/kg IV push q3-5 min until QRS narrows — dual action: sodium loading + alkalosis; no ceiling dose
nodes.body: NaHCO₃ Protocol — detailed reference. Indications for bicarbonate [4][16]: • QRS >100 ms • Ventricular arrhythmias • Hypotension refractory to fluids • Seizures (adjunct) Bolus: Sodium Bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV push. Repeat every 3-5 minutes until QRS narrows [4][16]. Mechanism (dual action) [16]: 1. Sodium loading — high sodium content competes for cardiac sodium channels 2. Alkalosis — increases

nodes.title: QRS >160 ms — Aggressive Bicarbonate
nodes.summary: QRS >160 ms = high VT/VF risk — aggressive bicarb boluses + hyperventilate if intubated; consider lidocaine early
nodes.body: ⚠️ QRS >160 ms = high risk of ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Immediate actions: • Sodium Bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV push — repeat q3-5 min until QRS narrows [4] • If intubated: hyperventilate simultaneously (fastest way to alkalinize) [16] • Consider early Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV if QRS not responding [6][16] • Prepare for cardiovascular collapse — have vasopressors ready Severe cases may require ma

nodes.title: Treatment Goals & Monitoring
nodes.summary: Target QRS <100 ms, pH 7.50-7.55, Na ≤155 — replete K+ aggressively; excessive alkalinization (>7.55) increases risk
