nodes.body: Target goals [16][18]: • QRS < 100 ms (if possible — may not be achievable if severely prolonged) • Serum pH 7.50–7.55 — achieve via bicarb + hyperventilation if intubated [16] • Serum Na ≤ 155 mEq/L — bicarb amps are extremely hypertonic (1000 mOsm/L) [12] Monitor closely [16]: • ABG/VBG q30-60 min to guide therapy • Serum K+ — alkalosis causes acute hypokalemia (K+ shifts intracellularly). Reple

nodes.title: Bicarbonate Infusion
nodes.summary: Maintenance: 150 mEq in 1L D5W; continue until QRS <100 ms for ≥6h — TCA half-life 24-36h, toxicity prolonged
nodes.body: After initial boluses narrow QRS: Maintenance infusion: 150 mEq (3 amps) in 1L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr [4][16]. Isotonic bicarbonate is inferior to hypertonic boluses for acute QRS widening — it lacks the sodium-loading effect on cardiac channels. Use it for maintenance only [16]. Duration: • Continue until QRS normalizes AND remains <100 ms for ≥6 hours • Wean slowly while monitoring ECG — QRS widen

nodes.title: Bicarbonate-Refractory QRS Widening
nodes.summary: Bicarb-refractory: hypertonic saline 3%, hyperventilation, lidocaine — question diagnosis if no response
nodes.body: QRS not narrowing despite adequate bicarbonate dosing? Three additional strategies [12][16][18]: 1. Hypertonic saline 3% — additional sodium loading if Na <155 mEq/L [18] 2. Hyperventilation — if intubated, fastest way to achieve alkalosis. Target ETCO₂ ~25-30 mmHg [16] 3. Lidocaine — Class IB antiarrhythmic that competes for sodium channel binding sites. Paradoxically IMPROVES sodium channel func

nodes.title: Seizure Assessment
nodes.summary: Seizures cause acidosis → increases free TCA → worsens cardiac toxicity in lethal positive feedback loop
nodes.body: Seizures occur in 10-20% of significant TCA ingestions — usually brief but may be refractory [3]. 🛑 Seizures are EXTREMELY dangerous in TCA overdose — they cause lactic acidosis, which increases free (unbound) TCA → worsens cardiac toxicity in a lethal positive feedback loop [3][16][18]. Seizure Management Guide — detailed reference. Is the patient actively seizing?

nodes.title: First-Line: Benzodiazepines
nodes.summary: BZDs first-line (GABA-A agonist counters TCA GABA antagonism) + simultaneous bicarb for acidosis
nodes.body: First-line — choose one: • Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) — repeat q5 min [4][18] • Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM (max 10 mg) — when IV access unavailable [4] • Diazepam 0.15-0.2 mg/kg IV (max 10 mg) — alternative [18] Simultaneously give Sodium Bicarbonate — alkalinize to prevent TCA crossing the BBB and to counteract seizure-induced acidosis [16][18]. TCAs cause seizures via GABA-A receptor antagoni

nodes.title: Seizure Response
nodes.summary: Assess BZD response — controlled seizure allows hemodynamic assessment; refractory needs escalation
nodes.body: Did benzodiazepines terminate the seizure?

nodes.title: Refractory Seizures
nodes.summary: Propofol or phenobarbital for refractory seizures — do NOT use phenytoin/fosphenytoin (blocks Na channels, may cause arrest)
nodes.body: Second-line options: • Propofol — 1-2 mg/kg bolus, then 30-200 mcg/kg/min. Requires intubation. Caution: may worsen hypotension [16]. • Phenobarbital — 15-20 mg/kg IV at ≤50 mg/min. Acts on GABA-A differently than BZDs — effective when BZDs fail [16]. Maintenance antiepileptic: • Levetiracetam — preferred for recurrent seizures. No sodium channel effects, no drug interactions [16]. 🚫 Do NOT use p

nodes.title: Contraindicated Antiepileptics
nodes.summary: AVOID phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide — all Na channel blockers; safe: BZDs, phenobarbital, propofol, levetiracetam
nodes.body: 🚫 Do NOT use these agents in TCA overdose: • Phenytoin / Fosphenytoin — blocks sodium channels (Class IB), may worsen cardiac toxicity and precipitate arrhythmias [3][4][6] • Carbamazepine — sodium channel blocker • Lamotrigine — sodium channel blocker • Lacosamide — enhances slow inactivation of sodium channels Safe antiepileptics in TCA overdose: • Benzodiazepines (GABA-A agonists — directly co

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Assessment
nodes.summary: Three mechanisms of hypotension: alpha-1 blockade, Na channel impaired contractility, arrhythmias
nodes.body: ⚠️ Refractory hypotension may be the most common cause of death in TCA overdose [16]. Three mechanisms of hypotension [16]: 1. Alpha-1 receptor blockade → peripheral vasodilation 2. Sodium channel blockade → impaired myocardial contractility 3. Arrhythmias → reduced cardiac output Is the patient hypotensive (SBP <90 or MAP <65)?

nodes.title: Volume Resuscitation
nodes.summary: NS/LR 1-2L bolus — patients often refractory to fluids alone; do not delay vasopressors
nodes.body: Initial fluid bolus: • NS or LR 1-2L IV bolus [3] • If isotonic bicarbonate available (150 mEq in 1L D5W), use as the fluid — accomplishes two goals simultaneously [16] • Avoid NS in large volumes — may promote acidosis. Balanced crystalloid (LR, Plasmalyte) or isotonic bicarb preferred [16]. ⚠️ Patients are often refractory to fluids alone — most are not hypovolemic [16]. Do not delay vasopressor

nodes.title: Vasopressor Selection
nodes.summary: Norepinephrine first-line — alpha agonism counters TCA alpha-blockade; avoid pure beta-agonists
nodes.body: Choose vasopressor based on heart rate [16][17]: • Norepinephrine — first-line. Alpha agonism directly counters TCA alpha-receptor blockade [3][16]. • Epinephrine — if bradycardic or NE-refractory. Combined alpha + beta agonism [16]. • Phenylephrine — if markedly tachycardic (pure alpha, no beta stimulation) [16]. • Vasopressin — for refractory cases. Bypasses the alpha-adrenergic receptor entirel

nodes.title: Wide-Complex Tachycardia Management
nodes.summary: Wide QRS often sinus tachy NOT VT — bicarb first, lidocaine for Na channel; AVOID amiodarone/Class IA/IC
nodes.body: ⚠️ Wide-complex tachycardia in TCA often represents sinus tachycardia with a widened QRS from delayed conduction — NOT true ventricular tachycardia [16]. Treatment: 1. Sodium Bicarbonate — first-line for ALL wide-complex rhythms in TCA [3][16] 2. Lidocaine — 1-1.5 mg/kg IV push, then 1-4 mg/min infusion. Class IB antiarrhythmic that competes for sodium channel binding — paradoxically improves chan

nodes.title: Lipid Emulsion Therapy
nodes.summary: Lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus — rescue therapy for cardiac arrest or refractory toxicity only
nodes.body: Lipid Emulsion 20% — rescue therapy for cardiac arrest or refractory toxicity [14][16]. Dosing: • 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus over 1 minute • Then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion × 30-60 min • May repeat bolus ×2 at 5 min intervals if no ROSC [3] Evidence: • No high-quality human evidence [11][16] • Animal models show mixed results — one study showed ILE superior to bicarb in guinea pigs [14], another showed equiv

nodes.title: ECMO — Final Rescue
nodes.summary: VA-ECMO is last resort — TCA toxicity is REVERSIBLE; bridge therapy can lead to full neurologic recovery
nodes.body: VA-ECMO is the last resort for refractory TCA cardiac arrest or hemodynamic collapse [9][16][18]. Key principle: TCA toxicity is potentially REVERSIBLE — aggressive bridge therapy can lead to full neurologic recovery [9][10]. • Contact cardiac surgery/ECMO team EARLY if clinical trajectory suggests need • Case reports document full recovery after prolonged resuscitation with ECMO support [9] • Bri

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Psychiatric evaluation MANDATORY for intentional ingestions; disposition based on clinical status
nodes.body: Disposition Criteria — detailed reference. Psychiatric evaluation is MANDATORY for all intentional ingestions after medical clearance [3][5]. What is the patient's current clinical status?

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria [3][5]: • QRS widening (current or resolved within last 6h) • Ventricular arrhythmias • Seizures • Hypotension requiring vasopressors • Altered mental status • Requiring bicarbonate infusion In the ICU: • Continuous telemetry — minimum 6 hours after last ECG abnormality resolves [3][5] • Serial ABGs and electrolytes to guide bicarbonate therapy • Late deterioration possible
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous cardiac monitoring, bicarbonate infusion, and serial ECGs until QRS normalizes for ≥6 hours.

nodes.title: Monitored Bed — Observation
nodes.body: Monitored bed criteria: • Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic • Normal ECG (QRS <100 ms) at presentation • Reported ingestion requiring observation Monitoring protocol: • Serial ECGs q2h for minimum 6 hours [3][5] • Continuous telemetry • If ANY QRS widening develops → escalate to bicarbonate protocol immediately Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222
nodes.recommendation: Telemetry observation with serial ECGs q2h for minimum 6 hours. Escalate to ICU if any QRS widening or clinical deterioration.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.body: Safe for discharge ONLY if ALL criteria met [3][5]: • Asymptomatic for ≥6 hours • QRS persistently <100 ms on serial ECGs • Normal mental status • Normal hemodynamics • Psychiatric clearance obtained (MANDATORY for intentional ingestions) Before discharge: • Document lethal means counseling • Counsel family/caregivers to remove access to TCAs • Consider safer antidepressant alternatives (SSRIs, SN
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with psychiatric clearance after 6+ hours of observation with normal ECGs and mental status.

nodes.title: Thromboelastography (TEG) — Whole-Blood Viscoelastic Testing
nodes.body: TEG Basics: When to Use & Limits — read first. The 4 Trauma Parameters · Treatment Ladder · Do NOT TEG measures real-time clot formation → strengthening → lysis in whole blood, mapping the cell-based coagulation model at the point of care. Early values return in ~5–10 min — fast enough to direct goal-directed component therapy instead of fixed-ratio resuscitation. [1, 3] ⚠️ Assay matters. Cutoffs

nodes.title: What do you need from the TEG?
nodes.body: Pick your task. You can return here to address additional findings.

nodes.title: Which TEG 6s value is abnormal?
nodes.body: Read the live tracing — you can usually call a weak clot by ~10 min, before the full ~50-min trace completes. Tap the abnormal parameter to get its targeted treatment, then come back for the next one. Normal ranges (TEG 6s trauma cartridge): [6, 7] • CK-R 4.6–9.1 min — clotting factors • CFF-MA 15–32 mm — fibrinogen • CRT-MA 52–70 mm — overall strength (platelets + fibrinogen) • CK-LY30 0–2.6% — f

nodes.title: Prolonged CK-R → Replace Clotting Factors
nodes.body: A prolonged CK-R (>10 min) means delayed clot initiation — factor deficiency or a circulating anticoagulant. [6] Give: • Plasma / FFP 15–30 mL/kg IV (~4 units in a 70 kg adult). • Low-volume alternative: 4-factor PCC 25–50 IU/kg (off-label in trauma; thrombotic risk). Before blaming factors: • If on heparin, check the heparin effect (CK-R vs CKH-R) → protamine, not plasma. • Reassess CK-R on a rep
nodes.recommendation: Prolonged CK-R: give plasma 15–30 mL/kg (or 4F-PCC 25–50 IU/kg as a low-volume alternative); rule out a heparin effect first if on heparin.

nodes.title: Low CFF-MA → Replace Fibrinogen (FIRST)
nodes.body: A low CFF-MA (<14 mm) means inadequate fibrinogen contribution to the clot. Functional fibrinogen is the first deficit to correct — a low overall clot strength (CRT-MA) is frequently driven by low fibrinogen, and cryo also raises the CRT-MA. [6, 7] Give: • Cryoprecipitate 10 units (≈6 g) — or fibrinogen concentrate 4–6 g. • Each 10 U cryo raises fibrinogen ~50–100 mg/dL. Target: fibrinogen >150 mg
nodes.recommendation: Low CFF-MA: give cryoprecipitate 10 U (≈6 g fibrinogen) or fibrinogen concentrate 4–6 g, target fibrinogen >150 (>200 if TBI). Correct fibrinogen before platelets.

nodes.title: Low CRT-MA → Platelets (after fibrinogen is adequate)
nodes.body: A low CRT-MA (<52 mm) reflects weak overall clot strength. The MA is ~80% platelets, ~20% fibrinogen — so confirm CFF-MA is adequate (≥15 mm) first. If fibrinogen is low, correct it and recheck before giving platelets. [6, 7] If CFF-MA is adequate and CRT-MA is low: • CRT-MA <45 mm → Platelets 1–2 apheresis units. • CRT-MA 45–50 mm → Platelets 1 apheresis unit. ⚠️ Blind spot: standard TEG is throm
nodes.recommendation: Low CRT-MA with adequate fibrinogen: give 1 apheresis platelet unit (CRT-MA 45–50) or 1–2 units (<45). Correct fibrinogen first; TEG is blind to antiplatelet drugs.

nodes.title: Elevated CK-LY30 → Antifibrinolytic (TXA)
nodes.body: An elevated CK-LY30 (>2.6%) signals hyperfibrinolysis — the clot is being broken down faster than it forms. [10, 11] Give: • Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h (CRASH-2 regimen). [7, 8] Timing is critical: • Greatest mortality benefit when given ≤3 h from injury. • Given >3 h out, CRASH-2 showed TXA may increase bleeding death — weigh carefully. [8] Use the Fibrinolysis Pheno
nodes.recommendation: Elevated CK-LY30 (>2.6%) = hyperfibrinolysis: give TXA 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h, ideally ≤3 h from injury.

nodes.title: Fibrinolysis Phenotype & the TXA Decision
nodes.body: Post-injury fibrinolysis is a spectrum with U-shaped mortality — both extremes are worse than physiologic. Cut-points below are from the Denver rapid-TEG cohort (Moore 2016, n=2,540). [10, 11] • Shutdown — LY30 <0.8% (~46%): impaired clot clearance, increased mortality (~22%). • Physiologic — LY30 0.8–2.9% (~36%): lowest mortality (~14%) — the target. • Hyperfibrinolysis — LY30 ≥3% (~18%): highest
nodes.recommendation: Classify LY30: shutdown <0.8% / physiologic 0.8–2.9% / hyperfibrinolysis ≥3% (TEG 6s flags >2.6%). Give TXA for hyperfibrinolysis; the "TXA harms shutdown" idea is an unproven hypothesis.

nodes.title: Heparin Effect — CK-R vs CKH-R (Heparinase)
nodes.body: The TEG 6s runs a heparin-neutralized channel (CKH, kaolin + heparinase) alongside the standard CK channel. Comparing the two isolates a heparin effect. [15, 16] Interpretation: • CK-R prolonged + CKH-R normal (CK-R > ~1.5× CKH-R, or Δ >2 min) → circulating heparin → consider protamine 25–50 mg IV. • Both prolonged → factor deficiency/anticoagulant, not heparin → give plasma, not protamine. ⚠️ Cav
nodes.recommendation: CK-R prolonged but CKH-R (heparinase) normal = heparin effect → protamine 25–50 mg. Both prolonged = factor deficiency → plasma. Protamine logic is cardiac-derived, not trauma-validated.

nodes.title: TEG PlateletMapping — Antiplatelet Assessment
nodes.body: PlateletMapping quantifies platelet inhibition in the aspirin (AA / thromboxane) and P2Y12 (ADP) pathways. Standard TEG is thrombin-driven and overrides platelet inhibition, so PlateletMapping is required to see antiplatelet effect. [12, 13] Channels: MA-Thrombin (HKH, max function) · MA-ActF (fibrin-only floor) · MA-AA (aspirin) · MA-ADP (P2Y12). % Inhibition = 100 − [(MA_agonist − MA_ActF) / (MA
nodes.recommendation: PlateletMapping: aspirin effect if AA %inhibition ≥50% (or AA-MA <51 mm); P2Y12 effect if MA-ADP <~47–50 mm. Elective/peri-procedural use only — not the acute bleed.

nodes.title: Normal TEG but Still Bleeding
nodes.body: A normal TEG in a bleeding patient is a meaningful result: the clotting machinery is working. The bleeding is usually anatomic/surgical, or from something TEG cannot see. [1, 6] Think: • Surgical / structural bleed — TEG cannot detect anatomic bleeding. Pursue source control and transfuse 1:1:1 to replace ongoing losses evenly. • TEG blind spots: • Aspirin / P2Y12 platelet inhibition (thrombin-dri
nodes.recommendation: Normal TEG + ongoing bleeding = think surgical/structural bleed or a TEG blind spot (antiplatelet drugs, vWD, hypothermia, acidosis, low ionized Ca). Source control + 1:1:1; warm and correct Ca/pH.

nodes.title: Reassess & Targets
nodes.body: TEG-guided resuscitation is iterative — treat, then re-test. [1, 6] Reassess: • Repeat TEG every 30–60 min or with each MTP round / after each product given. • Re-test specifically after the intervention that targeted the abnormal channel. Targets (TEG 6s trauma cartridge): [6, 7] • CK-R ≤10 min (factors) • CFF-MA ≥15 mm / fibrinogen >150 mg/dL (>200 if TBI) • CRT-MA ≥52 mm (overall strength) • CK
nodes.recommendation: Re-test TEG q30–60 min / per MTP round. Targets: CK-R ≤10, CFF-MA ≥15, CRT-MA ≥52, CK-LY30 ≤2.6%. Maintain temperature, ionized calcium, and pH — the TEG cannot show these.

nodes.title: Tendon-Sheath Steroid Injection — de Quervain / Trigger Finger
nodes.summary: Single steroid injection is first-line for de Quervain + trigger finger; confirm sheath, avoid SC deposit.
nodes.body: A single corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath is first-line for de Quervain tenosynovitis and trigger finger, often giving same-visit relief. Tools (open first): - Procedure Steps Summary - Steroid Prep + Dose Card - Sheath-vs-Tendon Confirmation Checklist - Skin Atrophy / Depigmentation Caution - Hand-Surgery Referral Criteria

nodes.title: Which Condition?
nodes.summary: de Quervain (Finkelstein) vs trigger finger (A1 nodule/triggering); exclude infection.
nodes.body: Confirm the diagnosis clinically and exclude infection before injecting any steroid.

nodes.title: Do NOT Inject — Work Up First
nodes.summary: Rule out flexor tenosynovitis (Kanavel) / infection before injecting; surgical if present.
nodes.body: Steroid into an infected sheath is dangerous. Exclude flexor tenosynovitis (Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, finger held in flexion, tenderness along the flexor sheath, pain on passive extension) — this is a surgical emergency, not an injection. If infection or trauma is suspected: - Do NOT inject corticosteroid - Evaluate for septic flexor tenosynovitis → urgent hand surgery - Image / work up at
nodes.recommendation: Exclude flexor tenosynovitis and infection before any tendon-sheath steroid injection.

nodes.title: Contraindications + Consent
nodes.summary: No infection/septic sheath/allergy; counsel flare, fat atrophy/depigmentation, rupture, recurrence.
nodes.body: Before injecting: - Absolute: overlying skin infection, suspected septic tenosynovitis, known steroid/anesthetic allergy - Relative / counsel: poorly controlled diabetes (transient glucose rise), prior injections at the same site (limit repeats; diminishing returns and tissue effects), anticoagulation (superficial injection, low risk; hold pressure) - Consent points: transient post-injection flare

nodes.title: Proceed to Target
nodes.summary: Choose first dorsal compartment (de Quervain) or A1 pulley (trigger finger).
nodes.body: Pick the compartment to inject. Each uses the same principle: deposit steroid + anesthetic INTO the sheath (free flow, low resistance), not into the tendon.

nodes.title: de Quervain — Landmarks
nodes.summary: First dorsal compartment (APL/EPB) at radial styloid; avoid radial sensory nerve/artery; watch for septum.
nodes.body: Target: the first dorsal compartment sheath containing abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) at the radial styloid. 1. Identify the radial styloid; palpate the tender APL/EPB tendons as the patient extends/abducts the thumb. 2. Beware the radial sensory nerve branches and the radial artery in the anatomical snuffbox just distal/dorsal — avoid them. 3. Watch for a septum

nodes.title: Trigger Finger — Landmarks
nodes.summary: A1 pulley at distal palm over MCP nodule; palmar midline approach; avoid lateral digital bundles.
nodes.body: Target: the flexor tendon sheath at the A1 pulley, located over the metacarpal head / distal palmar crease region of the affected digit (palpable tender nodule that moves with the tendon). 1. Palpate the A1 pulley nodule at the distal palm over the MCP of the affected finger. 2. Approach from the palmar surface at a shallow angle aimed proximally/into the sheath; the digital neurovascular bundles

nodes.title: Injection Technique
nodes.summary: Steroid + lidocaine into sheath; low-resistance flow; back out if needle moves with tendon; avoid SC.
nodes.body: Same principle for both targets. Dose details in Steroid Prep + Dose Card. 1. Sterile prep. Draw corticosteroid + a small volume of Lidocaine 1% (e.g., ~1 mL total injectate). 2. Insert a 25-27 ga needle into the sheath at the landmark. 3. Confirm you are in the sheath, not the tendon \u2014 use the Sheath-vs-Tendon Confirmation Checklist: the injectate should flow with LOW resistance; if you meet

nodes.title: High Resistance on Injection?
nodes.summary: Low resistance → inject; high resistance → withdraw off the tendon before injecting.
nodes.body: Resistance is the key intra-procedural safety signal. High resistance = needle in the tendon \u2014 injecting risks rupture.

nodes.title: Aftercare + Counseling
nodes.summary: Counsel days-to-relief (~70% trigger finger), flare, atrophy/depigmentation, infection/rupture return.
nodes.body: 1. Apply a small dressing; brief pressure. 2. Counsel: - Relief typically over days; up to ~70% improve after a single injection for trigger finger; de Quervain also responds well, especially with a complete sheath block. - A transient post-injection pain flare in the first 24-48 h is common. - Watch the injection site for fat atrophy / skin depigmentation (usually months later, often reversible).

nodes.title: Procedure Note Template
nodes.summary: Note: target, diagnosis, infection excluded, agent/dose, sheath confirmation, dispo + referral.
nodes.body: Procedure: Tendon-sheath corticosteroid injection \u2014 [first dorsal compartment, de Quervain / A1 pulley, trigger finger], [right/left] [thumb/finger]. Indication: [de Quervain tenosynovitis (positive Finkelstein) / trigger finger (A1 nodule + triggering)]; infection/septic tenosynovitis excluded. Consent: Risks of flare, fat atrophy/depigmentation, tendon rupture, infection, and recurrence dis
nodes.recommendation: Document target, diagnosis, infection exclusion, agent/dose, sheath confirmation, dispo/referral.

nodes.title: Terrestrial Envenomations Overview
nodes.summary: Spider, scorpion, hymenoptera envenomations. Hymenoptera anaphylaxis kills most. Anascorp dramatically reduces peds scorpion ICU time. Loxoscelism <10% but deadly.
nodes.body: See Steps Summary for rapid-action checklist. Scope: Non-snake, non-marine envenomations seen in the US ED. [1,2] - Spiders: Black widow (*Latrodectus*), brown recluse (*Loxosceles*), hobo, tarantula - Scorpions: Bark scorpion (*Centruroides sculpturatus*, AZ/NM/southern CA) - Hymenoptera: Bees, wasps, hornets, fire ants — leading cause of envenomation deaths in US (anaphylaxis) - Other: Centipede

nodes.title: Steps Summary
nodes.body: Rapid-action checklist for terrestrial envenomations: [1,2,3] 1. ABCs + anaphylaxis screen — if systemic urticaria, hypotension, respiratory distress → IM epi 0.3-0.5 mg adult / 0.01 mg/kg peds 2. Identify organism — spider vs scorpion vs hymenoptera vs other (geography, exposure, lesion) 3. Local vs systemic — most are local, but ~10-15% develop systemic signs 4. Targeted workup: - Severe widow:

nodes.title: Initial Triage — Systemic Reaction?
nodes.body: Screen every patient for anaphylaxis and severe systemic envenomation before drilling down on the organism. [1,3] Anaphylaxis criteria (any of): - Skin/mucosa + respiratory compromise (wheezing, stridor, hypoxia) - Skin/mucosa + hypotension or end-organ dysfunction - Known exposure + 2 of: skin, GI, respiratory, cardiovascular Severe systemic envenomation (non-anaphylactic): - Hypertension >180/11

nodes.title: Identify the Organism
nodes.body: Geography, exposure, and lesion pattern usually pin the organism even if the patient never saw it. [1,2] Clues: - **Black widow (*Latrodectus*): dark spider with red hourglass; pain + abdominal rigidity + HTN + diaphoresis; bite mark may be invisible - Brown recluse (*Loxosceles*): South/Central US; "violin" marking; painless bite → necrotic ulcer over days; rare systemic loxoscelism (peds, hemoly

nodes.title: Which Spider?
nodes.body: Match the lesion and symptoms to the species. [2,4,5] | Feature | Black Widow | Brown Recluse | Hobo/Tarantula | |---------|-------------|---------------|----------------| | Geography | US-wide | South/Central US | NW US (hobo); SW US (tarantula) | | Bite pain | Sharp, then dull | Painless, late necrosis | Mild | | Systemic | HTN, abd rigidity, sweating, tremor | Rare loxoscelism (hemolysis, DIC)

nodes.title: Black Widow (Latrodectism)
nodes.summary: Black widow: opioids + benzos first-line; calcium gluconate NOT recommended; antivenom for refractory severe cases only (anaphylaxis risk).
nodes.body: Mechanism: alpha-latrotoxin → massive presynaptic neurotransmitter release (ACh, NE) → autonomic storm + muscle cramping. [2,4] Clinical features: [2,4] - Onset 30 min - 2 h post-bite - Severe muscle cramps (abdomen, back, thighs) — mimics acute abdomen - HTN, tachycardia, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia - "Facies latrodectismica" — sweating, grimacing, periorbital edema - Peaks at 12-24h, reso

nodes.title: Brown Recluse (Loxoscelism)
nodes.summary: Loxoscelism: wound care + observation; NO FDA antivenom in US; dapsone NOT recommended; systemic loxoscelism (<10%) in peds needs admission for hemolysis/DIC monitoring.
nodes.body: Mechanism: sphingomyelinase D → dermonecrosis + complement activation. [2,5] Local (cutaneous loxoscelism): [2,5] - Initial painless bite → 2-8 h erythema, blanching ("red-white-blue" sign), then central necrosis over 3-7 days - Final lesion: necrotic eschar with surrounding violaceous halo - Resolves over weeks to months; rarely requires surgery (avoid early debridement — delineate the lesion fir

nodes.title: Hobo, Tarantula, Other Spiders
nodes.summary: Hobo/tarantula/other spiders: mostly local; treat as routine wound; tarantula urticating hairs can cause keratitis if eye exposure.
nodes.body: Most non-medically-significant spider bites cause only local reactions. [2] **Hobo spider (*Eratigena agrestis*, NW US): [2] - Historically blamed for necrotic lesions, but CDC removed from list of medically significant spiders in 2017 - Treat as routine wound — soap and water, ice, NSAIDs, tetanus Tarantulas: [2] - Local pain, mild erythema; rarely systemic - Some species shed urticating hairs —

nodes.title: Bark Scorpion — Severity Grading
nodes.body: Centruroides Severity Grading (used to guide Anascorp antivenom use): [3,6] | Grade | Findings | |-------|----------| | I | Local pain, paresthesias at sting site only | | II | Pain + paresthesias remote from sting site | | III | Either: (a) cranial nerve dysfunction (roving eye movements, blurred vision, dysphagia, slurred speech, tongue fasciculations) OR (b) somatic skeletal neuromuscular dysfu

nodes.title: Grade I-II — Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Grade I-II scorpion: opioids + benzos + observation 4-6 h; no antivenom; watch for progression to grade III in peds.
nodes.body: Grade I-II envenomation (local pain or remote paresthesias only): [3,6] Treatment: - Analgesia — opioids (morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV or hydromorphone 0.015 mg/kg IV) titrated; NSAIDs adjunct - Benzodiazepines — lorazepam 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV for muscle spasm or anxiety - Cold compresses to sting site - Tetanus update if indicated - NO antivenom — Anascorp reserved for grade III-IV Observation: - Monitor 4

nodes.title: Grade III-IV — Anascorp Antivenom
nodes.summary: Anascorp 3 vials IV over 10 min for grade III-IV scorpion envenomation (especially peds). Resolution 1-4 h vs 10-15 h without (Boyer 2009 NEJM). Anaphylaxis rate <2.4%.
nodes.body: Anascorp (Centruroides immune F(ab')₂) — Level A evidence per ACMT, FDA-approved 2011. Dramatically reduces duration of symptoms and need for sedation/ICU in children with grade III-IV envenomation (Boyer 2009 NEJM RCT). [3,6] Indications: - Grade III or IV envenomation (any age, but especially children <10 yo) - Particularly indicated if respiratory compromise, severe agitation, or anticipated ne

nodes.title: Hymenoptera — Local vs Systemic vs Massive
nodes.body: Hymenoptera (bees, wasps, hornets, fire ants) — most common envenomation; leading cause of envenomation deaths in US via anaphylaxis. [1,7] Categories: - Local reaction: pain, erythema, swelling at sting site; large local reactions can be >10 cm but limited to one extremity - Systemic / anaphylaxis: urticaria distant from sting, respiratory compromise, hypotension, GI symptoms - Massive envenomati

nodes.title: Anaphylaxis Pathway
nodes.summary: IM epi 0.3-0.5 mg adult / 0.01 mg/kg peds q5-15 min — DO NOT delay for antihistamines/steroids. Observe 4-6 h, d/c with 2 epi-pens + allergist referral.
nodes.body: IM epinephrine is the only intervention proven to reduce mortality. Give it BEFORE labs, IV access, or imaging. [7,8] Epinephrine IM (anterolateral thigh): [7,8] | Patient | Dose | |---------|------| | Adult | 0.3-0.5 mg IM (0.3-0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) — repeat q5-15 min PRN | | Peds | 0.01 mg/kg IM (max 0.3 mg) — repeat q5-15 min PRN | | EpiPen | Adult 0.3 mg; Junior (15-30 kg) 0.15 mg | Refractory an

nodes.title: Local & Large Local Reactions
nodes.summary: Local/large local: scrape stinger, ice, NSAIDs, antihistamine, topical steroid; oral steroid for severe large local. NOT cellulitis early on. Discharge home.
nodes.body: Local reaction: [1,7] - Pain, erythema, swelling at sting site - Peaks at 24-48 h, resolves over 3-7 days Large local reaction: [1,7] - Contiguous swelling >10 cm, lasting >24 h - Can involve entire extremity - NOT anaphylaxis, NOT cellulitis - ~10% lifetime risk of progression to anaphylaxis on future stings (lower than systemic reaction history) Treatment: - Stinger removal — scrape with credit

nodes.title: Massive Envenomation Syndrome
nodes.summary: Massive stings (>50): rhabdo + AKI + hemolysis + hepatic injury + DIC. Aggressive IVF, monitor q6-8h labs, admit all, ICU for organ dysfunction.
nodes.body: >50 stings or Africanized ("killer bee") attacks → direct venom toxicity overwhelms. [7,9] Clinical features: [7,9] - Rhabdomyolysis — CK can exceed 100,000 - Hemolysis — anemia, jaundice, hemoglobinuria - AKI — multifactorial (rhabdo, hemoglobinuria, direct nephrotoxicity) - Hepatic injury — transaminitis - DIC — coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia - Cardiac toxicity — direct myocardial venom effects,

nodes.title: Centipedes, Millipedes, Kissing Bugs, Blister Beetles
nodes.summary: Centipede: hot water + analgesia; millipede: irrigate, watch eyes; kissing bug: consider Chagas if endemic; blister beetle: cool compress, no unroofing.
nodes.body: Less venomous arthropods rarely cause systemic toxicity. [1,2,10] Centipede bite: [1] - Severe, sharp local pain (worse than wasp) - Erythema, swelling, occasional lymphangitis - Treatment: hot water immersion (40-45°C), NSAIDs, opioids if needed, wound care, tetanus - Resolves over hours-days; rarely systemic Millipede contact: [1] - Defensive secretion = chemical irritant (benzoquinones) - Brown

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Select disposition based on severity, response to treatment, and need for ongoing monitoring: [1,3,7]

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admission criteria: [3,7,9] - Severe systemic envenomation requiring ongoing treatment - Antivenom administered (Anascorp, Merck widow antivenom) — observe for serum sickness, late reactions - Massive envenomation (>50 stings) — serial labs q6-8 h x 24-48 h - Suspected systemic loxoscelism (hemolysis, DIC, AKI) - Severe anaphylaxis with refractory symptoms or biphasic risk - Grade IV scorpion or g
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored bed (ICU if organ dysfunction, grade IV scorpion, or refractory anaphylaxis). Continue targeted antivenom/supportive therapy. Serial labs as indicated.

nodes.title: Observe 4-6 h Then Discharge
nodes.body: Observation criteria: [7,8] - Anaphylaxis treated with epi, asymptomatic, no biphasic risk factors - Scorpion grade III adult responding to Anascorp - Black widow with controlled symptoms after opioids/benzos - Large local reaction with severe pain controlled Observation period: - Minimum 4-6 h after symptom resolution - Monitor for biphasic anaphylaxis (occurs in 5-20% within 6-12 h) - Reassess v
nodes.recommendation: Observe 4-6 h after symptom resolution. Discharge with 2 epi-pens (if anaphylaxis), allergist referral, antihistamine + steroid course, return precautions, PCP follow-up.

nodes.title: Discharge Home
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: [1,2,7] - Local reaction only, no systemic signs - Mild scorpion grade I-II with symptoms controlled - Mild latrodectism with controlled pain on PO regimen - Brown recluse lesion without systemic signs - Centipede, millipede, blister beetle exposure with local symptoms only Discharge instructions: - Wound care: soap and water cleansing, dry dressing, elevation - Pain: ibuprofen
nodes.recommendation: Discharge home with wound care, NSAIDs, antihistamines as appropriate, tetanus update, PCP recheck 24-48 h, strict return precautions documented. Allergist referral for any systemic hymenoptera reaction.

nodes.title: Acute scrotal pain — could this be testicular torsion?
nodes.body: Surgical detorsion within 6 hours of pain onset preserves >90% testicular salvage. By 12 hours, salvage drops to ~50%; by 24 hours, near zero. Time is testicle.[1] First question: how long has the pain been there?

nodes.title: TWIST score — risk stratify before imaging
nodes.body: The TWIST (Testicular Workup for Ischemia and Suspected Torsion) score uses 5 findings to stratify torsion risk:[2] - Hard testis (2) - Swelling (2) - Nausea/vomiting (1) - Absent cremasteric reflex (1) - High-riding testis (1) Total score → low (0–2), intermediate (3–4), high (5–7). Use the TWIST Score calculator to score this patient.

nodes.title: High TWIST → straight to OR
nodes.body: TWIST 5–7 has PPV ~93–100% for torsion. Pediatric urology / urology consult NOW. Imaging delays salvage — do not wait for ultrasound if the surgeon is willing to operate on clinical findings.[2,3] While arranging OR: - IV access, NPO - Pain control: opioid (e.g. morphine 0.1 mg/kg IV) - Antiemetic - Consent / labs / type & screen per surgeon - Manual detorsion while waiting — see Module 3

nodes.title: Intermediate TWIST → Doppler ultrasound
nodes.body: TWIST 3–4 is the imaging zone. Order STAT Doppler ultrasound and call urology in parallel. Do not let imaging delay surgical consult.[2] Bedside POCUS by ED-trained sonographer can reduce time to diagnosis by ~30 minutes versus radiology US.[4]

nodes.title: Low TWIST → torsion unlikely, find alternative
nodes.body: TWIST 0–2 has NPV ~96%.[2] Consider epididymitis, orchitis, torsed appendix testis (blue dot sign), Henoch-Schönlein purpura, hernia, hydrocele, Fournier gangrene. Caveat: Low TWIST does NOT exclude torsion in classic clinical scenarios (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding testis on a cooperative exam). When in doubt, get imaging.

nodes.title: Doppler ultrasound results
nodes.body: Color Doppler ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice (sens 86–100%, spec 100% in experienced hands).[5] Look for: - Whirlpool sign of spermatic cord (pathognomonic) - Absent or markedly reduced intratesticular flow - Heterogeneous testicular parenchyma (later finding) - Reactive hydrocele

nodes.title: Torsion confirmed → OR
nodes.body: Page urology immediately, OR-bound. Continue analgesia. NPO confirmed. Consent process per surgeon. Manual detorsion can buy time if OR delay is anticipated — see Module 3. Document time of pain onset, time of presentation, time of imaging, and time of surgical contact in the chart — this is a high-litigation diagnosis.

nodes.title: Equivocal imaging → surgical exploration
nodes.body: Equivocal Doppler in a clinically suspicious patient is a surgical indication, not a discharge criterion. False-negative US occurs in spontaneous detorsion, partial torsion, and torsion of an appendix.[5,6] Call urology, plan exploration. Can repeat imaging only if surgeon explicitly requests it.

nodes.title: Alternative diagnosis identified
nodes.body: Common alternatives: - Epididymitis — increased flow, gradual onset, dysuria, +cremasteric → adult UTI tree for antibiotics - Torsed appendix testis — focal upper-pole tenderness, blue dot sign, supportive - Orchitis — viral (mumps), bacterial spread - Fournier gangrene — perineum erythema, crepitus, systemic toxicity → emergent surgical consult, broad antibiotics, debridement - Incarcerated herni
nodes.recommendation: Treat the alternative diagnosis and arrange follow-up.

nodes.title: Attempt manual detorsion?
nodes.body: Manual detorsion is a temporizing maneuver. It does not replace surgical exploration — even successful detorsion still requires bilateral orchidopexy.[3] Indications: confirmed or strongly suspected torsion with delayed OR access (>30 min), patient cooperative. Contraindications: patient unwilling, severe agitation/non-cooperation, surgeon already in OR or arriving in <15 min.

nodes.title: Open Book technique
nodes.body: Standard "open book" maneuver — patient supine, examiner at the foot of the bed: 1. Adequate analgesia (opioid + spermatic cord block with ~10 mL 1% lidocaine at the external ring). 2. Visualize as if reading a book — testicles are the pages. 3. Rotate the affected testicle outward (laterally) from the midline. Right testis → counterclockwise from your view; left testis → clockwise. 4. May require

nodes.title: Detorsion outcome
nodes.body: Did the maneuver work?

nodes.title: Successful detorsion — still go to OR
nodes.body: Even with full clinical and Doppler resolution, the patient still needs urgent bilateral orchidopexy. ~30% will retort.[3] Document: - Time of detorsion - Direction of rotation that worked - Number of turns - Doppler before/after - Pain score before/after Proceed to OR handoff.

nodes.title: Pain worsened — try reverse direction
nodes.body: Pain getting worse during the maneuver suggests you twisted the testicle further. Reverse the direction (medial rotation) for the same number of turns and reassess. If still worse, stop. Move to OR.

nodes.title: OR handoff checklist
nodes.body: - IV access ×2 - NPO confirmed (time of last PO) - Pain controlled - Antiemetic given - Consent process started - Type & screen, basic labs (CBC, BMP) per surgeon - Pediatric: parents in room, child-life if available - Documented: time of pain onset → time of presentation → time of US → time of surgical contact → time to OR Call surgeon at the door of the OR with vitals and any change.

nodes.title: Pediatric or neonatal patient
nodes.body: Age determines pathway:[7,8] - Neonate (<30 days): prenatal/perinatal extravaginal torsion; usually firm, painless mass with discoloration. Salvage rates near zero — but bilateral exploration is still standard to fix the contralateral side. - Pre-pubertal (1 month – 12 years): intravaginal torsion, classic presentation may be obscured (kids underreport pain). - Adolescent (12–18 years): peak incid

nodes.title: Neonatal torsion — bilateral exploration
nodes.body: Presentation: firm, non-tender, discolored hemiscrotum noted at birth or in first 30 days. Often missed at first newborn exam. Workup: scrotal Doppler US to confirm and rule out alternatives (incarcerated inguinal hernia, neonatal hydrocele, tumor). Action: immediate pediatric urology consult for bilateral exploration. Even though the affected side is rarely salvageable, contralateral orchidopexy

nodes.title: Pre-pubertal torsion — high index of suspicion
nodes.body: Pediatric red flags: - Sudden onset abdominal pain or vomiting without clear scrotal complaint — always check the testes. - Presentation often delayed because kids underreport. - Cremasteric reflex less reliable in young children. Workup: Doppler US AND parallel pediatric urology consult. Lower threshold for OR than adults.[8] Continue to TWIST scoring as a framework, but bias toward exploration.

nodes.title: Subacute or atypical presentation
nodes.body: Atypical presentations to consider:[6,9] - Intermittent torsion / detorsion — recurrent acute pain that resolves spontaneously within minutes to hours. Surgical fixation indicated. - Torsion of appendix testis — focal upper-pole tenderness, blue dot sign, supportive care. - Missed / late torsion (>24h) — necrotic testis, may need orchiectomy not orchidopexy. - Post-traumatic torsion — torsion can

nodes.title: Intermittent torsion-detorsion
nodes.body: Pattern: episodes of acute scrotal pain that resolve spontaneously within minutes to hours. May have a "bell clapper" deformity. Action: even if the patient is pain-free at presentation, refer urology for elective bilateral orchidopexy. Each episode risks transition to complete torsion.[9] Safety-net: return immediately for sustained severe pain.

nodes.title: Late torsion (>24h) — orchiectomy likely
nodes.body: After 24h the testicle is rarely salvageable. Doppler usually shows no flow with a heterogeneous, enlarged testis. Plan: still consult urology — necrotic testis is a source of infection and can autoimmunize the contralateral testis ("sympathetic orchitis"). Orchiectomy + contralateral orchidopexy is the standard.[3] Counsel family on fertility implications and high probability of orchiectomy.

nodes.title: Torsion of testicular / epididymal appendix
nodes.body: Findings: focal upper-pole tenderness, blue dot sign through scrotal skin, normal cremasteric reflex, normal Doppler flow. Treatment: supportive — NSAIDs, scrotal support, ice. Resolves in 5–10 days as the appendix necroses and resorbs. Caveat: if Doppler is at all equivocal or the exam is not classic, treat as torsion until proven otherwise.[6]
nodes.recommendation: Supportive care; close follow-up in 24–48h or sooner for worsening.

nodes.title: Post-traumatic scrotal pain
nodes.body: Trauma can trigger torsion. Do not assume scrotal pain after trauma is just hematoma. Doppler is essential to evaluate for: - Testicular rupture (loss of contour, intratesticular hematoma) — surgical emergency - Hematocele - Torsion (post-traumatic) If Doppler findings unclear or rupture suspected → urology now.[6]

nodes.title: Disposition and follow-up
nodes.body: OR-bound patients: admit to surgery; ED disposition complete. Discharged patients (alternative dx, intermittent torsion pending elective surgery): - Strict return precautions: any sudden severe pain → return to ED immediately. - Urology follow-up within 1–2 weeks for elective fixation if intermittent. - Pain control: NSAIDs ± short opioid course if severe. - Activity restrictions per urology prefe

nodes.title: Pitfalls & medicolegal pearls
nodes.body: Top pitfalls in testicular torsion: 1. Adolescent with abdominal pain alone — ALWAYS exam the testes. Torsion frequently presents as periumbilical or LLQ pain. 2. Assuming epididymitis in a young patient — sexual history negative, no dysuria, sudden onset → think torsion. 3. Trusting a normal Doppler in a high TWIST patient — false-negative US is real (spontaneous detorsion, partial torsion). Clin

nodes.title: Summary card
nodes.body: Acute scrotal pain — testicular torsion: - Time is testicle: <6h salvage >90%, <12h ~50%, >24h ~0%. - TWIST 5–7 → OR. TWIST 3–4 → US. TWIST 0–2 → search alternatives, but clinical concern still wins. - Doppler: absent flow / whirlpool = torsion. Equivocal in clinically suspicious patient = exploration. - Manual detorsion = "open book," outward rotation. Even if successful, still needs bilateral or

nodes.title: Tetanus — ED Approach
nodes.summary: Two scenarios: wound prophylaxis (Tdap/TIG decision) vs active tetanus (ICU); toxin binding is IRREVERSIBLE
nodes.body: Tetanus is caused by *Clostridium tetani* neurotoxin (tetanospasmin). The toxin irreversibly binds spinal cord inhibitory interneurons → unopposed muscle contraction. Why It Matters: • Mortality 10-20% even with modern ICU care • Higher mortality in elderly and neonates • Completely preventable with vaccination • Toxin binding is IRREVERSIBLE — recovery requires new synapse formation (weeks-months

nodes.title: Wound Classification
nodes.summary: Classify wound: clean/minor vs tetanus-prone (puncture, dirty, >6h, burns, crush, contaminated)
nodes.body: Tetanus-Prone Wounds: • Puncture wounds • Contaminated with dirt, feces, soil, saliva • Crush injuries, avulsions • Burns (any degree) • Frostbite • Wounds >6 hours old • Devitalized tissue • Missile injuries (gunshot, shrapnel) • Compound fractures • IVDU injection sites Clean, Minor Wounds: • Clean lacerations <6 hours old • Superficial abrasions • No devitalized tissue • No contamination Classi

nodes.title: Clean Wound — Vaccination History
nodes.summary: Clean wounds: TIG never needed; vaccine based on prior doses and time since booster (10-year interval)
nodes.body: For Clean, Minor Wounds: TIG is NOT indicated regardless of vaccination status. Vaccine (Td or Tdap) is indicated based on: • Number of prior doses • Time since last booster Tdap vs Td: • Tdap (with pertussis) preferred if never received Tdap as adult • Td acceptable if prior Tdap received What is the vaccination history?

nodes.title: Clean Wound — Incomplete Vaccination
nodes.summary: Clean wound + <3 doses: give Tdap today, no TIG needed; refer PCP for series completion
nodes.body: Clean wound + <3 prior doses or unknown: ✅ Give Tdap (or Td) today ❌ TIG NOT needed Important: • Patient needs to complete primary series (3-dose total) • Refer to PCP for remaining doses: - Dose 2: 4-8 weeks after dose 1 - Dose 3: 6-12 months after dose 2 Tdap Preference: • If never received Tdap as adult, give Tdap • Can use Td if Tdap unavailable Documentation: • Provide immunization record to

nodes.title: Clean Wound — Booster Needed
nodes.summary: Clean wound + ≥3 doses + >10 years: give Tdap booster, no TIG
nodes.body: Clean wound + ≥3 doses + last booster >10 years ago: ✅ Give Tdap (or Td) booster ❌ TIG NOT needed Rationale: • Protective antibodies decline over time • Booster restores immunity rapidly • 10-year interval standard for clean wounds Tdap vs Td: • Tdap preferred if never received as adult (pertussis protection) • Td acceptable if prior Tdap received [1][2]

nodes.title: Clean Wound — Protected
nodes.summary: Clean wound + ≥3 doses + ≤10 years: adequately protected, standard wound care only
nodes.body: Clean wound + ≥3 doses + last booster ≤10 years: ❌ No Tdap/Td needed ❌ No TIG needed Patient is adequately protected. Standard wound care only: • Clean and irrigate wound • Debride devitalized tissue if present • Primary closure if appropriate • Standard discharge instructions [1][2]

nodes.title: Tetanus-Prone Wound — Vaccination History
nodes.summary: Tetanus-prone: 5-year booster interval (vs 10 for clean); TIG if <3 doses or unknown vaccination
nodes.body: For Tetanus-Prone Wounds: Both vaccine AND TIG may be indicated. Key Decision Points: 1. Is primary series complete (≥3 doses)? 2. When was last booster? TIG Indications (tetanus-prone wounds): • <3 doses or unknown vaccination history • Some experts: immunocompromised patients regardless of history What is the vaccination history?

nodes.title: Tetanus-Prone — TIG + Vaccine Required
nodes.summary: Tetanus-prone + <3 doses: give BOTH TIG 250 units IM AND Tdap — DIFFERENT injection sites, NEVER mix
nodes.body: Tetanus-prone wound + <3 doses or unknown: ✅ Give BOTH: 1. Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) • TIG 250 units IM • Provides immediate passive immunity • Lasts ~4 weeks 2. Tdap (or Td) • 0.5 mL IM • Starts active immunity ⚠️ CRITICAL: Different Injection Sites • TIG and Tdap must be given at DIFFERENT anatomic sites • Use opposite deltoids, or deltoid + anterolateral thigh • NEVER mix in same syringe Wh

nodes.title: TIG Administration Details
nodes.summary: TIG 250 units IM at different site than Tdap — passive immunity lasts ~4 weeks; check pharmacy stock
nodes.body: Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) — Prophylaxis: Dose: 250 units IM (standard prophylaxis dose) Administration: • Deltoid or anterolateral thigh • DIFFERENT site than Td/Tdap • Some experts: infiltrate portion around wound edges For Large/Contaminated Wounds: • Some authorities recommend 500 units • Can infiltrate up to half the dose locally Do NOT Give TIG If: • History of severe allergic reaction to

nodes.title: Tetanus-Prone — Booster Needed
nodes.summary: Tetanus-prone + ≥3 doses + >5 years: Tdap booster only, no TIG needed
nodes.body: Tetanus-prone wound + ≥3 doses + last >5 years: ✅ Give Tdap (or Td) booster ❌ TIG NOT needed Note the 5-year interval: • Tetanus-PRONE wounds: booster if >5 years • CLEAN wounds: booster if >10 years • More aggressive threshold for dirty wounds Rationale: • Antibody levels may be suboptimal after 5 years • Higher-risk wound warrants earlier booster [1][2]

nodes.title: Tetanus-Prone — Protected
nodes.summary: Tetanus-prone + ≥3 doses + ≤5 years: adequately protected, focus on wound care
nodes.body: Tetanus-prone wound + ≥3 doses + last ≤5 years: ❌ No Tdap/Td needed ❌ No TIG needed Patient has adequate immunity from recent vaccination. Focus on Wound Care: • Thorough irrigation • Debridement of devitalized tissue (critical for tetanus prevention) • Consider delayed primary closure for contaminated wounds • Antibiotic prophylaxis per wound type Tetanus Spores: • Killed by debridement and oxyge

nodes.title: Bite Wounds — Tetanus Consideration
nodes.summary: Bite wounds are tetanus-prone — apply standard tetanus-prone guidelines; also consider rabies and antibiotics
nodes.body: Animal and Human Bites: Bite wounds are considered tetanus-prone due to: • Contamination with oral flora • Puncture component • Crush injury • Devitalized tissue Apply Standard Tetanus-Prone Guidelines: • <3 doses or unknown: TIG + Tdap • ≥3 doses, >5 years: Tdap booster • ≥3 doses, ≤5 years: No tetanus prophylaxis needed Remember Other Bite Considerations: • Rabies prophylaxis (animal bites) • An

nodes.title: Wound Care for Tetanus Prevention
nodes.summary: Debride ALL devitalized tissue — aerobic wound bed prevents spore germination; antibiotics do NOT replace TIG
nodes.body: Wound Care is Critical: Proper wound care is as important as prophylaxis. Debridement: • Remove ALL devitalized tissue • Spores survive in necrotic tissue • Aerobic wound bed prevents spore germination Irrigation: • Copious irrigation with saline or water • High pressure for contaminated wounds • Reduces bacterial/spore load Closure: • Clean wounds: primary closure OK • Contaminated wounds: consid

nodes.title: Suspected Active Tetanus — Assessment
nodes.summary: Clinical diagnosis — trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus; shorter incubation = worse prognosis
nodes.body: Clinical Tetanus is a CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS No confirmatory lab test. Culture rarely positive. Classic Presentation: • Trismus (lockjaw) — often first symptom • Risus sardonicus — sardonic smile from facial muscle spasm • Opisthotonus — arched back from paraspinal spasm • Dysphagia — difficulty swallowing • Muscle rigidity — diffuse, especially abdomen • Reflex spasms — triggered by stimuli Incubatio

nodes.title: Generalized Tetanus
nodes.summary: Generalized tetanus: spatula test 94%/100% sensitivity/specificity; progresses from trismus to opisthotonus to autonomic instability
nodes.body: Generalized Tetanus (80% of cases) Progression: 1. Trismus (lockjaw) — earliest sign 2. Neck stiffness and dysphagia 3. Risus sardonicus — facial muscle spasm 4. Opisthotonus — severe back arching 5. Board-like abdomen — can mimic acute abdomen 6. Reflex spasms — triggered by any stimuli (noise, light, touch) 7. Autonomic instability (later) — BP swings, tachycardia, arrhythmias Spatula Test: • To

nodes.title: Localized Tetanus
nodes.summary: Localized: rigidity near wound, 1% mortality — can rapidly progress to generalized, treat seriously
nodes.body: Localized Tetanus: Muscle rigidity confined to the region of the wound. Features: • Continuous muscle contraction near wound • May have local spasms • No trismus or generalized symptoms • Often seen in partially immune patients Prognosis: • Generally milder than generalized • Mortality ~1% (vs 10-20% generalized) • Can progress to generalized tetanus — requires close monitoring Management: • Same

nodes.title: Cephalic Tetanus
nodes.summary: Cephalic tetanus: CN palsies, 15-30% mortality, frequently progresses to generalized — ICU required
nodes.body: Cephalic Tetanus: Rare form following head/face wounds or otitis media. Features: • Cranial nerve palsies (especially VII) • Trismus common • Dysphagia • Facial weakness or spasm • Often follows otitis media or facial wounds Incubation: • Often shorter (1-2 days) • Shorter incubation = worse prognosis Danger: • High mortality (15-30%) • Frequently progresses to generalized tetanus • Airway at risk

nodes.title: Active Tetanus — Treatment Overview
nodes.summary: Priority: airway → TIG 3000-6000 units → metronidazole → BZDs for spasms → MgSO4 for autonomic instability
nodes.body: Treatment Priorities (in order): 1. AIRWAY — Early intubation for generalized tetanus 2. NEUTRALIZE UNBOUND TOXIN — TIG • TIG 3000-6000 units IM • Does NOT reverse bound toxin • Give ASAP — toxin binding is irreversible 3. ELIMINATE SOURCE — Antibiotics + Wound • Metronidazole preferred • Aggressive wound debridement 4. CONTROL SPASMS — Benzodiazepines • Diazepam or midazolam • May need MASSIVE do

nodes.title: Airway Management in Tetanus
nodes.summary: Intubate EARLY — laryngospasm can be sudden and fatal; trismus limits access, have surgical airway backup
nodes.body: Intubation in Tetanus: ⚠️ Intubate EARLY — do not wait for respiratory failure Indications for Immediate Intubation: • Generalized tetanus with severe spasms • Laryngospasm or stridor • Inability to handle secretions • Respiratory muscle involvement • Cephalic tetanus Challenges: • Trismus limits mouth opening • Spasms during intubation • Laryngospasm can be sudden and fatal Approach: • RSI with n

nodes.title: TIG — Therapeutic Dosing
nodes.summary: Therapeutic TIG 3000-6000 units IM (NOT 250 unit prophylaxis dose) — only neutralizes UNBOUND toxin, give ASAP
nodes.body: Tetanus Immune Globulin — Active Disease: Dose: TIG 3000-6000 units IM • Much higher than prophylaxis (250 units) • Some give 500 units intrathecally (controversial, not FDA approved) Timing: • Give immediately — don't delay for wound care • Only neutralizes UNBOUND toxin • Toxin already bound to neurons is irreversible Administration: • Large IM dose — may need to divide into multiple sites • Int

nodes.title: Antibiotics in Active Tetanus
nodes.summary: Metronidazole preferred — penicillin is a GABA antagonist and may worsen spasms; aggressive wound debridement
nodes.body: Antibiotic Choice: ✅ Metronidazole (PREFERRED) • Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6-8h × 7-10 days • Excellent anaerobic coverage • Achieves high tissue levels ⚠️ Penicillin (AVOID if possible) • Historically used but NOT preferred • Penicillin is a GABA antagonist → may worsen spasms • Use only if metronidazole unavailable Why Antibiotics? • Kills vegetative C. tetani at wound site • Stops further toxin

nodes.title: Spasm Control — Benzodiazepines
nodes.summary: BZDs first-line for spasms — may need MASSIVE doses (100s of mg diazepam/day); tolerance develops rapidly
nodes.body: Benzodiazepines are First-Line: Mechanism: Enhance GABA (counteracts toxin effect) Diazepam: • 10-40 mg IV q1-8h PRN (can titrate higher) • Severe cases: continuous infusion 5-15 mg/hr • May need 100s of mg per day in severe cases Midazolam: • 5-15 mg/hr infusion • Shorter acting, easier to titrate • Preferred for infusion Lorazepam: • 2-10 mg IV q2-6h or infusion • Alternative if propylene glycol

nodes.title: Autonomic Instability
nodes.summary: MgSO4 first-line for autonomic instability — AVOID beta-blockers (can cause asystole); target Mg 3.5-5.5
nodes.body: Autonomic Dysfunction: Major cause of death in ICU-managed tetanus. Manifestations: • Labile blood pressure (hypertensive crises → hypotension) • Tachycardia, bradycardia, arrhythmias • Diaphoresis • Hyperpyrexia • Cardiac arrest Management: ✅ Magnesium Sulfate (FIRST-LINE) • Loading: 5g IV over 20 min • Infusion: 1-3 g/hr (titrate to effect) • Target Mg level: 3.5-5.5 mEq/L • Also helps with spas

nodes.title: ICU Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Dark quiet room, minimize stimulation; early enteral nutrition; 3-6 week ICU course for generalized tetanus
nodes.body: Supportive Care in Tetanus: Environment: • Dark, quiet room • Minimize stimulation (triggers spasms) • Limit procedures, cluster care Nutrition: • Early enteral nutrition • High caloric needs (hypermetabolic state) • May need NG/PEG if prolonged DVT Prophylaxis: • LMWH or heparin • SCDs • High risk due to immobility Pressure Ulcer Prevention: • Frequent repositioning • Specialized mattress Duratio

nodes.title: Post-Recovery Vaccination
nodes.summary: Tetanus infection does NOT confer immunity — must complete full 3-dose vaccination series after recovery
nodes.body: Critical Point: ⚠️ Tetanus infection does NOT confer immunity The toxin dose causing disease is too small to trigger immune response. After Recovery from Tetanus: • Complete full 3-dose primary series • Start Td/Tdap before discharge or at first follow-up • Follow standard schedule: - Dose 1: Now - Dose 2: 4-8 weeks later - Dose 3: 6-12 months after dose 2 Document and Communicate: • Clear documen

nodes.title: Special Populations
nodes.summary: Select special population for modified tetanus management — pregnancy, neonate, IVDU, immunocompromised
nodes.body: Select the special population:

nodes.title: Tetanus in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: Tdap recommended 27-36 weeks all pregnancies — Tdap and TIG both safe in pregnancy; protects newborn passively
nodes.body: Tdap in Pregnancy: Routine Recommendation: • Tdap recommended for ALL pregnant women • Optimal timing: 27-36 weeks gestation • Protects newborn via passive antibody transfer Wound Prophylaxis in Pregnancy: • Same guidelines as non-pregnant • Tdap and TIG are both SAFE in pregnancy • Do not withhold due to pregnancy Maternal Tetanus: • Rare in developed countries • High mortality for mother and fet

nodes.title: Neonatal Tetanus
nodes.summary: Neonatal tetanus: 60-80% mortality — onset day 3-14, inability to suck first sign; maternal vaccination is key prevention
nodes.body: Neonatal Tetanus: Usually from contaminated umbilical stump. Risk Factors: • Unvaccinated mother • Unclean delivery conditions • Traditional umbilical stump treatments (ash, dung) • Home births without sterile technique Presentation: • Onset typically day 3-14 of life • Inability to suck (first sign) • Rigidity, opisthotonus • Spasms triggered by handling • High-pitched cry Prognosis: • Mortality

nodes.title: Tetanus in IVDU
nodes.summary: IVDU: lower threshold for TIG — even "clean" injection sites contaminated; assume incomplete vaccination
nodes.body: IV Drug Users — High Risk: Why IVDU are High Risk: • Contaminated drug supply (especially "black tar" heroin) • Non-sterile injection technique • Skin popping creates tetanus-prone wounds • Often undervaccinated • Delayed presentation "Wound" May Be Any Injection Site: • Even apparently clean sites can be contaminated • Subcutaneous abscesses common • Lower threshold for TIG Management: • Lower th

nodes.title: Immunocompromised Patients
nodes.summary: Lower threshold for TIG — may not respond to vaccine; consider TIG even with complete vaccination if active chemo/low CD4
nodes.body: Immunocompromised — Special Considerations: May Not Respond to Vaccine: • HIV (especially low CD4) • Transplant recipients • Chemotherapy • Chronic steroids • Congenital immunodeficiency Recommendations: • Lower threshold for TIG with tetanus-prone wounds • Some experts: TIG for ANY tetanus-prone wound regardless of vaccination history • Tdap still recommended (may have partial response) TIG Indic

nodes.title: Discharge — Wound Prophylaxis
nodes.summary: Verify wound care, vaccines/TIG given, series completion plan documented; provide immunization record
nodes.body: Discharge After Tetanus Prophylaxis: Before Discharge: ✓ Wound properly cleaned and managed ✓ Tdap given if indicated ✓ TIG given if indicated (at different site) ✓ Patient understands need for series completion (if applicable) ✓ Follow-up arranged Discharge Instructions: • Wound care instructions • Signs of wound infection • Complete vaccination series with PCP (if <3 doses) • Next booster in 10

nodes.title: Disposition — Active Tetanus
nodes.summary: Generalized: ICU mandatory, 3-6 weeks; localized: floor with close monitoring for progression
nodes.body: Disposition for Active Tetanus: Generalized Tetanus: • ICU admission mandatory • Intubation often required • Expected course: 3-6 weeks • Multi-disciplinary care Localized Tetanus: • Floor admission with close monitoring • May progress to generalized — ICU transfer PRN Cephalic Tetanus: • ICU admission • High risk of progression Prognosis Factors: • Shorter incubation = worse outcome • Older age =

nodes.title: Resuscitative Thoracotomy: 2-Minute Review
nodes.summary: Rapid review: incision, pericardium, hemorrhage control, massage, aortic clamp, OR.
nodes.body: Use this as a rapid procedural reminder for selected traumatic arrest. Open first: - 2-Minute Steps - Indications - Incision Landmarks Core sequence: 1. Left anterolateral thoracotomy 2. Enter pleura and spread ribs 3. Open pericardium anterior to phrenic nerve 4. Relieve tamponade/control cardiac wound 5. Open cardiac massage 6. Cross-clamp descending thoracic aorta when indicated 7. Move to OR f

nodes.title: Is Thoracotomy Indicated?
nodes.summary: Confirm indication before committing to an open thoracic resuscitation.
nodes.body: Proceed only for selected traumatic arrest or profound peri-arrest shock where thoracotomy can correct a survivable physiology.

nodes.title: Thoracotomy Not Indicated
nodes.summary: Avoid thoracotomy when objective survival predictors are absent.
nodes.body: Do not perform thoracotomy when the patient is outside survivable selection criteria. Continue or terminate based on local traumatic arrest policy after reversible causes are addressed: - Hemorrhage control/MTP - Oxygenation/airway - Bilateral chest decompression - Tamponade assessment when appropriate - POCUS cardiac motion when available
nodes.recommendation: Avoid nonbeneficial thoracotomy; document mechanism, signs of life, CPR time, rhythm, cardiac motion, and HOTT interventions.

nodes.title: Setup / Roles
nodes.summary: Assign roles and prepare thoracotomy instruments while MTP and airway continue.
nodes.body: Roles: - Operator at left chest - Assistant for exposure/suction - Airway/ventilation lead - Blood/MTP lead - Procedure nurse/tech for instruments - Trauma surgery/OR activation Equipment: - Large scalpel, heavy scissors, forceps, clamps - Finochietto/rib spreader if available - Suction x2 if possible - Vascular clamp for aorta - Satinsky/vascular clamps, needle driver, cardiac sutures/stapler/Fol

nodes.title: Position / Prep
nodes.summary: Supine, wide prep, left 4th/5th interspace, incision sternum to posterior axillary line.
nodes.body: Position: - Supine - Left arm abducted if feasible; do not delay if not feasible - Prep wide: neck to groin, bilateral chest, upper abdomen Landmark: - Left 4th or 5th intercostal space, usually inframammary fold/nipple line region - Incision from sternum toward posterior axillary line - Enter over the superior rib edge Have the team ready to extend to clamshell if exposure is inadequate or right-

nodes.title: Incision / Enter Chest
nodes.summary: Large left anterolateral incision, enter pleura, spread ribs, evacuate hemothorax.
nodes.body: Steps: 1. Make a large left anterolateral incision in the 4th/5th intercostal space. 2. Cut skin/subcutaneous tissue/muscle decisively; inadequate incision slows exposure. 3. Enter pleura over the superior rib edge. 4. Sweep finger to clear adhesions and confirm intrathoracic entry. 5. Insert rib spreader if available and open gradually. 6. Evacuate hemothorax and pack/suction as needed. If exposu

nodes.title: Open Pericardium
nodes.summary: Open pericardium anterior to phrenic nerve; evacuate tamponade and inspect heart.
nodes.body: Open the pericardium when tamponade or cardiac injury is possible. Steps: 1. Identify phrenic nerve running along the lateral pericardium. 2. Grasp/tent pericardium anterior to the phrenic nerve. 3. Make a small opening with scissors or scalpel. 4. Extend longitudinally from apex toward aortic root, staying anterior to phrenic nerve. 5. Evacuate clot and deliver heart only as needed for inspection

nodes.title: Cardiac Injury / Tamponade Control
nodes.summary: Control cardiac wound immediately, then restore perfusion and bridge to OR.
nodes.body: After pericardium is open, inspect rapidly for tamponade, cardiac wound, or empty heart from exsanguination.

nodes.title: Control Cardiac Wound
nodes.summary: Use digital pressure, Foley balloon, staples, or suture control as a bridge to OR.
nodes.body: Temporary options: - Direct digital pressure - Foley catheter through wound, balloon inflated gently, traction applied - Skin stapler for small linear ventricular wounds if appropriate - Horizontal mattress sutures with pledgets if available Avoid tying sutures through coronary arteries. Continue blood resuscitation and prepare immediate OR transfer.

nodes.title: Pulmonary Hilum Control
nodes.summary: Hilar control is temporary for massive lung bleeding or air embolism physiology.
nodes.body: For massive unilateral pulmonary hemorrhage or suspected air embolism, obtain temporary hilar control. Options: - Manual compression of hilum - Clamp pulmonary hilum en bloc if experienced and exposure is adequate - Consider right mainstem intubation to improve left chest exposure when appropriate This is temporizing. Definitive repair requires OR.

nodes.title: Cross-Clamp Descending Thoracic Aorta
nodes.summary: Clamp descending aorta above diaphragm for exsanguinating lower-body hemorrhage.
nodes.body: Indications: - Exsanguinating subdiaphragmatic hemorrhage - Empty heart despite blood resuscitation - Need to prioritize coronary/cerebral perfusion during open resuscitation Technique reminder: 1. Retract left lung superiorly/anteriorly. 2. Identify descending thoracic aorta just anterior/lateral to spine and above diaphragm. 3. Open pleura over aorta bluntly. 4. Place vascular clamp across aorta

nodes.title: Open Cardiac Massage
nodes.summary: Massage supports perfusion only if volume and obstruction are addressed.
nodes.body: Technique: - Use two hands when possible - Compress from apex toward base, avoiding ventricular twisting - Allow complete filling between compressions - Coordinate with blood resuscitation and definitive repair - Defibrillate internal paddles if available for VF/VT; external pads may still be used per local practice If the heart is empty, massage alone will not restore output; prioritize blood and

nodes.title: Response After Thoracotomy
nodes.summary: Thoracotomy must rapidly transition to OR or termination decision.
nodes.body: Reassess response after tamponade relief, hemorrhage control attempts, blood resuscitation, aortic clamp when indicated, and open cardiac massage.

nodes.title: Post-ROSC Thoracotomy Handoff
nodes.summary: ROSC after thoracotomy requires immediate OR/source-control handoff.
nodes.body: Immediate handoff: - Trauma surgeon assumes definitive operative plan - Maintain airway, oxygenation, normocapnia, warmth - Continue balanced blood products and calcium - Keep aortic clamp time visible - Control open chest bleeding and contamination - Expedite OR transfer; CT is rarely appropriate before definitive hemorrhage control Document indication, arrest time, CPR duration, incision time, p
nodes.recommendation: Move directly to OR with surgical team for definitive repair and damage control.

nodes.title: No Response / Stop Decision
nodes.summary: Stop when no survivable physiology remains after indicated correction attempts.
nodes.body: If there is no cardiac activity or perfusion after appropriate correction attempts, further resuscitation is unlikely to benefit. Before stopping, confirm: - HOTT causes addressed - Pericardium opened if tamponade suspected - Cardiac wound/hemorrhage control attempted if present - Blood resuscitation underway - Aortic clamp considered if indicated - Rhythm/cardiac motion reassessed Follow local po
nodes.recommendation: Terminate when thoracotomy does not reveal or correct a survivable cause and there is no physiologic response.

nodes.title: Thrombocytopenia - First Look
nodes.summary: Low platelets require bleeding assessment plus TTP/DIC/HIT/pregnancy/marrow failure screen before anchoring on ITP.
nodes.body: Thrombocytopenia steps | Differential guide | Platelet transfusion Definition: platelet count <150,000/microL. ED risk depends less on the number alone and more on bleeding, acuity, trajectory, smear findings, coagulopathy, pregnancy, heparin exposure, thrombosis, infection, and marrow failure clues.
