nodes.title: Confirm True Thrombocytopenia
nodes.summary: Repeat CBC/smear and rule out platelet clumping before treating a stable unexpected low platelet count.
nodes.body: Before escalating a stable patient, confirm the result is real. [1] Check immediately: - Prior platelet counts and rate of fall. - Repeat CBC if the result is unexpected or discordant with the patient. - Peripheral smear review for platelet clumping, giant platelets, schistocytes, blasts, dysplasia. - If clumping is reported or suspected, repeat platelet count in citrate or heparin tube. Pseudothr

nodes.title: Bleeding Severity and Platelet Threshold
nodes.summary: Bleeding site and urgency determine threshold; suspected TTP/HIT are platelet-transfusion exceptions.
nodes.body: Transfusion guide Critical bleeding: intracranial, airway, massive GI, hemoptysis with compromise, postpartum/obstetric hemorrhage, uncontrolled surgical/procedural bleeding, shock, or bleeding needing emergent intervention. Common ED platelet targets: [6] - Stable, no bleeding, marrow suppression: consider prophylaxis at <10k. - Fever/sepsis or additional bleeding risk: often <20k. - Active major

nodes.title: Critical Bleeding: Stabilize First
nodes.summary: Resuscitate and transfuse for critical bleeding, but keep the dangerous differential open.
nodes.body: Treat the bleeding patient while the differential runs. [6] Immediate actions: - ABCs, two large-bore IVs, type and cross, activate MTP if shock or massive bleeding. - Platelet transfusion if thrombocytopenic and bleeding is major, procedural, or critical site. - Send CBC with smear, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, CMP, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, retic, type/screen. - Correct fibrinogen with

nodes.title: Dangerous Syndrome Screen
nodes.summary: Screen TTP/TMA, DIC, HIT, pregnancy emergencies, and marrow failure before diagnosing ITP.
nodes.body: Labs guide Look for the patterns that change ED management now: TTP/TMA: thrombocytopenia + MAHA: schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin, renal injury, neuro symptoms. Coags often normal. [3,4] DIC/sepsis: thrombocytopenia + prolonged PT/aPTT, low or falling fibrinogen, high D-dimer, critical illness, shock, trauma, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe. [7] HIT: platelet fall usu

nodes.title: TTP/TMA Pattern
nodes.summary: MAHA + thrombocytopenia requires urgent hematology and TTP/TMA pathway; do not wait for ADAMTS13.
nodes.body: PLASMIC calculator | TTP consult Treat as TTP/TMA until proven otherwise when thrombocytopenia plus MAHA is present. [3,4] Send now: - CBC with smear, LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin, retic count. - Creatinine, UA, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen. - ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor before plasma exposure if feasible. - Pregnancy test when applicable. Actions: - Call hematology urgently. - Calculate PLASM

nodes.title: DIC / Sepsis / Consumption Pattern
nodes.summary: DIC requires trigger control plus targeted platelet/fibrinogen/coag support when bleeding or procedural.
nodes.body: ISTH DIC score | DIC consult DIC is always secondary. The primary treatment is source control and reversal of the trigger. [7] Pattern: thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/INR, prolonged aPTT, high D-dimer/FDPs, low or falling fibrinogen, bleeding and/or thrombosis. ED actions: - Treat sepsis, trauma, obstetric hemorrhage, malignancy/APL, liver failure, or other trigger immediately. - Send serial CBC,

nodes.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia
nodes.summary: 4Ts >=4 means stop all heparin and use non-heparin anticoagulation unless bleeding prohibits it.
nodes.body: 4Ts framework Think HIT when platelet fall follows heparin exposure and thrombosis risk is high. [5] 4Ts score: - Thrombocytopenia magnitude. - Timing of platelet fall. - Thrombosis or skin/systemic reaction. - Other causes of thrombocytopenia. Management by probability: [5] - Low 4Ts (0-3): HIT unlikely; do not reflexively test. - Intermediate/high 4Ts (>=4): stop all heparin, send PF4 immunoassa

nodes.title: HIT Action Bundle
nodes.summary: HIT action: stop every heparin exposure, test, anticoagulate with non-heparin agent, avoid early warfarin.
nodes.body: Intermediate/high probability HIT: [5] 1. Stop all heparin products: UFH, LMWH, flushes, heparin-coated lines when possible. 2. Send PF4/heparin immunoassay. Send functional assay if available or if immunoassay positive. 3. Start non-heparin anticoagulant unless major bleeding risk: argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or DOAC in selected stable patients per local protocol and specialist guidanc

nodes.title: Pregnancy or Postpartum Thrombocytopenia
nodes.summary: Pregnancy thrombocytopenia requires HELLP/preeclampsia, DIC, and TTP/HUS screen before benign labeling.
nodes.body: Do not assume gestational thrombocytopenia when the patient is sick or the count is very low. Danger patterns: - Preeclampsia/HELLP: hypertension, headache, RUQ/epigastric pain, elevated AST/ALT, hemolysis, renal injury. - DIC: abruption, fetal demise, sepsis, postpartum hemorrhage, amniotic fluid embolism. - TTP/HUS: MAHA, neuro symptoms, renal injury, often coags less abnormal than DIC. - ITP: i

nodes.title: Blasts, Pancytopenia, or Marrow Failure Pattern
nodes.summary: Blasts, pancytopenia, or severe unexplained cytopenias need urgent heme/onc evaluation.
nodes.body: Red flags for marrow disease: [1] - Blasts or promyelocytes on smear. - Pancytopenia or severe anemia/neutropenia with thrombocytopenia. - New bruising/bleeding with fatigue, fever, weight loss, night sweats, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly. - Chemotherapy/radiation, known cancer, marrow infiltration, aplastic anemia, MDS. ED actions: - Call hematology/oncology when blasts, pancytopeni

nodes.title: Isolated or Chronic Pattern
nodes.summary: After dangerous syndromes, classify isolated thrombocytopenia by ITP, drug, liver/spleen, infection, or unclear.
nodes.body: If the dangerous screen is negative, classify by mechanism. [1] Isolated thrombocytopenia: normal hemoglobin/WBC, no schistocytes/blasts, normal PT/aPTT/fibrinogen, no systemic illness. Common ED considerations: ITP, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, viral infection, alcohol, liver/splenic sequestration, chronic baseline. Pattern questions: - Any new medication within days to 2 weeks? - Any re

nodes.title: Likely Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
nodes.summary: ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia after exclusions; treat based on bleeding, count, risk, and follow-up reliability.
nodes.body: ITP guide ITP pattern: isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise reassuring smear and no alternative cause. [2] ED treatment frame: [2] - No or minor bleeding and platelets generally >=30k: often no emergent treatment; arrange close follow-up. - Platelets <30k, significant mucosal bleeding, high-risk patient, or unreliable follow-up: hematology discussion for corticosteroids. - Severe mucosal bleed

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Thrombocytopenia
nodes.summary: Stop likely culprit medications; distinguish immune abrupt isolated thrombocytopenia from marrow suppression.
nodes.body: Medication review is a core diagnostic test. [1] Common ED culprits: - Heparin/LMWH: consider HIT if timing and thrombosis fit. - Quinine/tonic water, TMP-SMX, vancomycin, beta-lactams, linezolid, rifampin, valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, thiazides, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors, chemotherapy, alcohol. - Herbal/supplement exposures and recent vaccines can be relevant but require context. Pattern: ab

nodes.title: Liver Disease, Alcohol, or Splenic Sequestration
nodes.summary: Chronic liver/spleen thrombocytopenia is baseline-driven; sudden drops need a new cause search.
nodes.body: Common chronic thrombocytopenia bucket: [1] - Cirrhosis/portal hypertension with splenic sequestration. - Alcohol-related marrow suppression and nutritional deficiency. - Chronic viral hepatitis. - Hypersplenism from hematologic or portal hypertensive causes. ED approach: - Compare with baseline; sudden large drops need another diagnosis. - Check INR/PT, fibrinogen when bleeding or ill. INR does n

nodes.title: Infection and Systemic Illness
nodes.summary: Infection-related thrombocytopenia ranges from benign viral suppression to DIC/sepsis; trend and coags matter.
nodes.body: Infection can cause thrombocytopenia by marrow suppression, immune destruction, consumption, splenic sequestration, or DIC. [1,7] High-yield ED checks: - Sepsis screen, cultures, lactate, source evaluation when ill. - HIV and hepatitis C testing when new isolated thrombocytopenia is unexplained or risk is present. - Tickborne disease, dengue, malaria, EBV/CMV, COVID/influenza, and travel-associate

nodes.title: Pseudothrombocytopenia
nodes.summary: Platelet clumping is a lab artifact, not a bleeding disorder.
nodes.body: Platelet clumping can falsely lower the automated platelet count. [1] Confirm: - Smear shows platelet clumps. - Repeat CBC in citrate or heparin tube normalizes or improves count. - Patient has no bleeding phenotype. Management: no platelet-directed treatment. Document the artifact clearly so future clinicians do not transfuse or cancel needed care based on a false count.
nodes.recommendation: Repeat platelet count in a non-EDTA tube and document pseudothrombocytopenia if confirmed.

nodes.title: Core ED Workup
nodes.summary: New thrombocytopenia needs repeat CBC, smear, coag/hemolysis labs when indicated, HIV/HCV, pregnancy test, and type/screen by risk.
nodes.body: Labs guide Core labs for new or unexplained thrombocytopenia: [1] - Repeat CBC with differential. - Peripheral smear review by lab/pathology. - PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer when bleeding, ill, pregnant/postpartum, or DIC/TMA concern. - CMP including creatinine and liver tests. - LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, reticulocyte count when hemolysis/TMA concern. - HIV and HCV when isolated/unexplained

nodes.title: Platelet Transfusion Decisions
nodes.summary: Transfusion thresholds depend on bleeding/procedure and diagnosis; avoid routine platelets in TTP/HIT/ITP.
nodes.body: Platelet transfusion guide Use platelets for a clinical target, not for cosmetic correction of the CBC. [6] Common targets: - <10k: prophylactic transfusion in stable hypoproliferative/marrow-suppression patients. - <20k: consider with fever, sepsis, rapid fall, or additional bleeding risk. - <50k: active major bleeding or most invasive procedures. - <100k: CNS bleeding, posterior eye bleeding, ne

nodes.title: Who to Call Now
nodes.summary: Call hematology for TTP/TMA, HIT, DIC, severe ITP/bleeding, blasts/pancytopenia, or pregnancy danger patterns.
nodes.body: Call hematology urgently for: - Suspected TTP/TMA or PLASMIC intermediate/high. - Suspected HIT with thrombosis or need for alternative anticoagulation. - DIC with bleeding/thrombosis, unclear trigger, or possible APL. - Platelets <10k, severe mucosal bleeding, wet purpura, critical bleeding, or urgent procedure. - Blasts, pancytopenia, suspected leukemia/marrow failure. - Severe thrombocytopenia

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition is driven by bleeding, diagnosis, platelet depth/trend, smear/coags, pregnancy, and follow-up reliability.
nodes.body: Disposition guide Admit or transfer when the diagnosis can deteriorate faster than outpatient follow-up can protect the patient. Usually admit: - Critical or recurrent bleeding. - Suspected TTP/TMA, DIC, HIT needing non-heparin anticoagulation, APL/leukemia/marrow failure. - Platelets <10k, or <20k with risk factors/bleeding concern. - Severe ITP needing IVIG, platelet support, or unreliable follo

nodes.title: Admit / Transfer / Observe
nodes.summary: Admit high-risk thrombocytopenia and document trend, smear, coags, hemolysis markers, heparin exposure, and pending tests.
nodes.body: Admission targets: - Telemetry/ICU if bleeding, TTP/TMA, DIC, severe sepsis, neurologic symptoms, severe renal injury, or transfusion need. - Hematology-capable center for TTP/TMA/plasma exchange, suspected acute leukemia/APL, severe refractory ITP, or complex HIT. - OB-capable setting for pregnancy/postpartum HELLP/TMA/DIC. Handoff must include: platelet count and trend, smear findings, coags/fib
nodes.recommendation: Admit or transfer when dangerous syndrome, critical bleeding risk, severe platelet depth, or follow-up uncertainty is present.

nodes.title: Discharge Safety Net
nodes.summary: Safe discharge requires no bleeding, reassuring smear/coags, noncritical stable count, no HIT/TMA/DIC/pregnancy danger, and reliable follow-up.
nodes.body: Discharge only if all are true: - No active bleeding, no wet purpura, no concerning neuro/renal/systemic symptoms. - Smear has no schistocytes or blasts. - Coagulation profile does not suggest DIC when clinically relevant. - Platelets are not in a critical range and are stable or have a clear benign/chronic explanation. - No intermediate/high probability HIT, no pregnancy danger pattern, no acute
nodes.recommendation: Discharge can be appropriate only after dangerous causes are reasonably excluded and near-term follow-up is reliable.

nodes.title: Thrombolytic Protocols
nodes.summary: Thrombolytic dosing and contraindications are indication-specific.
nodes.body: Thrombolytic Steps Systemic thrombolytics are high-risk, time-sensitive medications. The indication determines the drug, dose, contraindication framework, anticoagulation plan, and monitoring. Common ED use cases: - Acute ischemic stroke - STEMI when timely PCI is unavailable - Massive PE or PE arrest/peri-arrest - Selected catheter-directed or reduced-dose PE strategies with specialist input

nodes.title: Indication
nodes.summary: Choose indication before choosing drug/dose.
nodes.body: Which thrombolytic use case is being considered?

nodes.title: Universal Contraindication Screen
nodes.summary: Screen contraindications by indication; PE arrest can shift risk-benefit.
nodes.body: High-risk contraindication screen: - Any intracranial hemorrhage history or current hemorrhage on imaging - Known structural cerebral vascular lesion or malignant intracranial neoplasm - Ischemic stroke within 3 months (except current acute ischemic stroke pathway) - Suspected aortic dissection - Active internal bleeding or bleeding diathesis - Significant closed-head/facial trauma or intracranial

nodes.title: Acute Ischemic Stroke
nodes.summary: Stroke thrombolysis requires CT exclusion of hemorrhage, BP control, and strict post-lytic monitoring.
nodes.body: Core requirements: - Disabling neurologic deficit within protocol window - Noncontrast CT excludes hemorrhage - BP <185/110 before treatment and <180/105 for 24 hr after - Glucose and stroke mimic screen addressed without delaying eligible treatment Common regimens: - Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, max 25 mg, where adopted by local stroke protocol - Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV, max 90 mg; give 10% a

nodes.title: Post-Stroke Lytic Care
nodes.summary: Post-stroke thrombolysis care prioritizes BP control and hemorrhage monitoring.
nodes.body: After IV stroke thrombolysis: - Neuro checks and BP monitoring per stroke protocol - Maintain BP <180/105 - No antithrombotics for 24 hr unless specialist-directed - Repeat brain imaging at 24 hr or sooner for deterioration - Treat severe headache, vomiting, hypertension, or neurologic worsening as possible symptomatic ICH Do not place nonessential invasive lines for 24 hr.

nodes.title: STEMI Fibrinolysis
nodes.summary: STEMI lytics are for eligible STEMI when timely PCI is unavailable.
nodes.body: Use STEMI fibrinolysis when: - Diagnostic STEMI or STEMI-equivalent - Symptom onset generally <=12 hr - PCI cannot be achieved within guideline time targets, commonly FMC-to-device >120 min - No contraindications Regimens: - Tenecteplase weight-based single IV bolus; reduce dose by 50% if age >=75 per many protocols - Alteplase/reteplase per institutional STEMI lytic protocol if tenecteplase unava

nodes.title: Failed Reperfusion / Rescue PCI
nodes.summary: Failed reperfusion after STEMI lytic requires rescue PCI.
nodes.body: Assess 60-90 min after lytic: - ST resolution <50% - Persistent chest pain - Hemodynamic/electrical instability - Worsening heart failure Any of these should trigger urgent rescue PCI. Even successful lysis usually requires transfer for early angiography/pharmaco-invasive strategy.

nodes.title: PE Severity
nodes.summary: PE thrombolysis depends on shock/arrest versus intermediate-risk status.
nodes.body: Which PE lytic scenario is present?

nodes.title: Massive PE With Shock
nodes.summary: Massive PE shock generally warrants systemic alteplase unless contraindication dominates.
nodes.body: Massive/high-risk PE with shock is a systemic thrombolysis indication unless bleeding risk clearly outweighs imminent death risk. Common systemic regimen: - Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hr - Hold UFH during alteplase per many protocols; restart without bolus when aPTT/anti-Xa permits If lysis contraindicated or fails: activate PERT/ICU/interventional radiology/cardiothoracic surgery for catheter-dir

nodes.title: PE Arrest / Peri-Arrest
nodes.summary: PE arrest may require alteplase 50 mg push and prolonged CPR.
nodes.body: When PE is strongly suspected or confirmed in arrest/peri-arrest: - Continue high-quality CPR and treat reversible causes - Alteplase 50 mg IV push during arrest; consider repeat 50 mg if no ROSC and PE remains likely per local protocol - Continue CPR for an extended period after thrombolytic administration when feasible - Activate ECMO/PERT/thrombectomy pathway if available Evidence is limited, b

nodes.title: Intermediate-Risk / Submassive PE
nodes.summary: Intermediate-risk PE generally gets anticoagulation unless deteriorating or selected for specialist-directed reperfusion.
nodes.body: Normotensive PE with RV strain is not an automatic systemic lytic indication. Consider escalation when: - Clinical deterioration despite anticoagulation - Worsening shock index, lactate, oxygenation, RV failure - Low bleeding risk and high decompensation risk - PERT/specialist consensus favors catheter-directed or reduced-dose strategy Use Half-Dose Alteplase Calculator only when a reduced-dose st

nodes.title: After PE Lysis
nodes.summary: PE lysis requires ICU monitoring and a clear anticoagulation restart plan.
nodes.body: After PE thrombolysis: - ICU monitoring - Reassess shock, oxygenation, RV function, bleeding - Restart anticoagulation per protocol when safe, commonly UFH without bolus once aPTT/anti-Xa permits - Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures - Escalate to catheter/surgical/ECMO strategy if persistent shock or recurrent arrest Document indication, contraindication discussion, dose, CPR duration if arrest

nodes.title: Bleeding / Reversal Plan
nodes.summary: Major bleeding requires stopping lytics/anticoagulants and fibrinogen-focused resuscitation.
nodes.body: For serious bleeding after thrombolytic therapy: - Stop thrombolytic and anticoagulants - Activate massive transfusion/critical bleeding pathway if unstable - Check CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, type/cross - Replace fibrinogen with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate per protocol - Consider antifibrinolytic therapy such as TXA or aminocaproic acid with specialist input - Repeat neuroimaging

nodes.title: Disposition / Handoff
nodes.summary: Clear handoff and monitored disposition are mandatory after thrombolytics.
nodes.body: Every thrombolytic handoff must include: - Indication and time zero - Drug, exact dose, start/stop time - Contraindications reviewed and key risks accepted - BP target and monitoring frequency - Anticoagulant/antiplatelet hold or restart plan - Bleeding watch points and reversal plan - Destination: stroke unit/ICU/cath lab/PERT-capable ICU Do not send a post-lytic patient to an unmonitored setting
nodes.recommendation: Post-thrombolytic patients need monitored disposition and explicit bleeding/anticoagulation plan.

nodes.title: Thyroid Disorders — Presentation
nodes.summary: Thyroid emergencies are clinical diagnoses — do NOT delay treatment for labs; sepsis is #1 precipitant for both
nodes.body: Thyroid Disorders Steps Summary Thyroid emergencies are rare but lethal. Decompensated hypothyroidism mortality: 25-50%. Thyroid storm mortality: 8-25%. Both are clinical diagnoses — lab values reflect chronic state, not acute severity. Do NOT delay treatment for lab confirmation. [1][14] Sepsis is the most common precipitant for BOTH conditions and can occur concurrently. Always consider endocrin

nodes.title: Confirm Decompensated Hypothyroidism
nodes.summary: Decompensated hypothyroidism: AMS (~90%), hypothermia (70-90%), bradycardia (~70%) — 25-50% mortality
nodes.body: "Myxedema coma" is a misnomer — most patients are NOT comatose, and most do not have myxedema. Better termed decompensated hypothyroidism: hypothyroidism causing organ failure, with the brain typically failing first. [3][14] Core features (IBCC): • Altered mental status (~90%) — usually hypoactive delirium, rarely frank coma • Hypothermia (70-90%) — may be severe; concurrent infection can mask thi

nodes.title: Confirm Thyroid Storm
nodes.summary: Thyroid storm = thyrotoxicosis + end-organ dysfunction — Burch-Wartofsky helps frame but is NOT diagnostic
nodes.body: Thyroid storm = thyrotoxicosis causing end-organ dysfunction. No validated diagnostic test — diagnosis is clinical. The Burch-Wartofsky Score helps frame the assessment but is NOT diagnostic. [4][9] IBCC cognitive triggers to consider thyroid storm: 1. Known hyperthyroid + any acute deterioration 2. New-onset AFib and/or dilated cardiomyopathy 3. New delirium/psychosis + fever + tachycardia 4. Hyp

nodes.title: Mild Thyrotoxicosis — Outpatient Management
nodes.body: No features of thyroid storm or end-organ dysfunction. ED Workup: TSH, free T4, free T3 Symptomatic relief: Propranolol 10-40 mg PO TID for palpitations, tremor, anxiety (if no contraindications) Disposition: • Urgent endocrinology referral (1-2 weeks) • Return precautions: fever >38.5°C, confusion, persistent vomiting, palpitations at rest, inability to take fluids
nodes.recommendation: Endocrinology referral within 1-2 weeks. Return for worsening symptoms.

nodes.title: Airway Assessment & Supportive Care
nodes.summary: Difficult airway (macroglossia, goiter); passive rewarming ONLY — active rewarming causes cardiovascular collapse
nodes.body: Airway is the first priority — these patients have a physiologically AND anatomically difficult airway. Anatomic challenges: macroglossia, posterior pharyngeal myxedema, goiter (tracheal compression, laryngeal deviation), vocal cord edema, reduced neck mobility Physiologic challenges: severe respiratory muscle weakness, depressed central ventilatory drive (CO₂ narcosis), decreased lung elasticity,

nodes.title: Step 1 — Stress-Dose Steroids FIRST
nodes.summary: Give steroids BEFORE T4 — concomitant adrenal insufficiency in 5-10%; T4 without cortisol can precipitate adrenal crisis
nodes.body: CRITICAL SEQUENCE: Give steroids BEFORE thyroid hormone replacement. Concomitant adrenal insufficiency is present in ~5-10% of patients (autoimmune polyglandular syndrome or pituitary disease). Thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol metabolism — giving T4 without cortisol can precipitate adrenal crisis. [1][5][14] Adults: • Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, then 50 mg IV q8h • IBCC protocol: 50 mg IV

nodes.title: Step 2 — IV Levothyroxine (T4)
nodes.summary: Levothyroxine 200-400 mcg IV load — oral unreliable in decompensated state; safe to give empirically
nodes.body: Levothyroxine — mainstay of thyroid replacement: Loading dose: 200-400 mcg IV • IBCC: 200 mcg for most patients (lower end preferred) • ATA guidelines: 200-400 mcg based on severity, age, body weight, cardiac history [5] • Use lower end (200 mcg) for: elderly, low body weight, coronary artery disease, arrhythmias Maintenance: 50-100 mcg IV daily (or 1.2 mcg/kg/day IV) [5] Why IV? GI absorption is

nodes.title: Step 3 — Consider IV Liothyronine (T3)
nodes.summary: T3 is biologically active, faster onset but higher risk — reserve for critically ill; stop after 48h or if T3 elevated
nodes.body: T3 is the biologically active form — faster onset but higher risk. Rationale: In decompensated hypothyroidism, peripheral T4→T3 conversion may be impaired. T3 bypasses this step. However, older studies associated high-dose T3 (>75 mcg/day) with increased mortality. [5] IBCC recommendation: Reserve T3 for critically ill patients requiring hemodynamic or ventilatory support. Not mandatory. [3] If ad

nodes.title: Evaluation & Lab Workup
nodes.summary: TSH, fT4, random cortisol, BMP, ABG, CK; infection workup mandatory — sepsis is #1 precipitant
nodes.body: Core labs: • TSH — very high in primary hypothyroidism (most common), low/normal in central (pituitary) • Free T4 — should be low; low-normal does not exclude diagnosis [3] • Random cortisol — rule out concurrent adrenal insufficiency • BMP — hyponatremia (~50%), hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia (rare) • CBC — anemia common, leukopenia possible • Lactate • ABG/VBG — hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis (ev

nodes.title: Monitoring & Ongoing Care
nodes.summary: ICU monitoring mandatory — avoid sedatives/opioids (extreme sensitivity); vasopressors unlikely to work until T4 takes effect
nodes.body: ICU-level monitoring is mandatory for decompensated hypothyroidism. Monitoring parameters: • Core temperature q1h — goal: passive rewarming to normothermia • Continuous cardiac monitoring — bradycardia, QT prolongation, heart block • Glucose q2-4h — risk of recurrent hypoglycemia • Sodium q4-6h — hyponatremia corrects with T4 therapy; fluid restrict if Na <130 • Hemodynamics q1h — BP, HR, urine ou

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Follow clinical parameters (mental status, temperature, hemodynamics) — TSH/fT4 changes lag by days
nodes.body: Clinical improvement expected in 24-72h with appropriate treatment. TSH/fT4 are NOT useful for acute decision-making — changes lag by days. Follow clinical parameters: mental status, temperature, hemodynamics. [3][5] All patients with decompensated hypothyroidism require admission. The question is ICU vs monitored floor. [14]

nodes.title: ICU Admission — Decompensated Hypothyroidism
nodes.body: Continue: • IV Levothyroxine maintenance (50-100 mcg/day or 1.2 mcg/kg/day) • Stress-dose hydrocortisone until cortisol results available • IV liothyronine if started (reassess at 48h) • Aggressive treatment of precipitant (antibiotics if infection suspected) • Passive rewarming • Glucose + electrolyte monitoring Consults: • Endocrinology • Consider ENT/anesthesia if airway concerns Complications
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. Endocrinology consult. Continue IV T4 + steroids.

nodes.title: Monitored Floor Admission
nodes.body: Transition plan: • Switch to PO Levothyroxine (1.6 mcg/kg/day) when tolerating oral intake • Taper hydrocortisone over 2-3 days once cortisol results confirm adequate adrenal function • Aggressive bowel regimen (hypothyroid patients have severe constipation) • Telemetry monitoring for arrhythmias Follow-up: • TSH recheck in 6-8 weeks (adjustments in 12.5-25 mcg increments) • Endocrinology referral
nodes.recommendation: Monitored floor with telemetry. Transition to PO T4. Endocrinology follow-up.

nodes.title: Step 1 — Evaluation & Sepsis Workup
nodes.summary: ECHO BEFORE beta-blockers — 38% develop cardiogenic shock; full sepsis workup, empiric antibiotics if any concern
nodes.body: Thyroid storm mimics sepsis — and sepsis can trigger thyroid storm. Always perform full sepsis workup. [2][14] Labs: • TSH, free T4, free T3 (T3 often disproportionately elevated in storm) • BMP, CBC with differential, lactate • Blood cultures, UA/UCx • LFTs (hepatic dysfunction common — if severe, consider congestive hepatopathy from heart failure) [14] • Coags + fibrinogen (DIC can occur) [2] •

nodes.title: Step 2 — Steroids
nodes.summary: Steroids: dual benefit — blocks T4→T3 conversion and treats potential concurrent adrenal insufficiency
nodes.body: Give early — dual benefit: 1. Blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion (reduces active hormone) 2. Treats potential concurrent adrenal insufficiency IBCC protocol (preferred): • Hydrocortisone 300 mg IV loading dose, then 100 mg IV q8h [2] ATA protocol: • Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h (no separate load) [8] Alternative if HC unavailable: • Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV load, then 60 mg IV daily Duration:

nodes.title: Step 3 — Thionamide (Block Synthesis)
nodes.summary: Thionamide blocks new synthesis — give BEFORE iodine; PTU mandatory in 1st trimester pregnancy
nodes.body: Thionamides block new thyroid hormone synthesis by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase. They have NO effect on pre-formed hormone already released. Must give BEFORE iodine. [2][8] Thionamide Comparison — Methimazole vs PTU Methimazole (IBCC preferred — safer long-term): • Methimazole 40 mg PO load, then 20 mg PO q6h [2] • Longer duration of action, irreversible binding to thyroperoxidase • Lower risk of

nodes.title: Step 4 — Iodine (Block Release)
nodes.summary: Iodine MUST wait ≥1h after thionamide — given too early, iodine becomes substrate for MORE hormone synthesis
nodes.body: Iodine immediately suppresses thyroid hormone release via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect. [2] TIMING: Give ≥1 hour after thionamide. Without thionamide on board, iodine can be used as substrate for NEW hormone synthesis — potentially worsening thyrotoxicosis (especially with toxic multinodular goiter or toxic adenoma). [2][8] Dosing options: • SSKI 5 drops (250 mg) PO q6h • Lugol's 5% solution 8 drops

nodes.title: Step 5 — Cholestyramine (Block Recirculation)
nodes.summary: Cholestyramine 4g PO q6h — blocks enterohepatic recirculation, reduces T4 20-30%; separate oral meds by 1-2h
nodes.body: Cholestyramine 4 g PO q6h Binds thyroid hormone in the gut, preventing enterohepatic recirculation. Effective even in endogenous thyrotoxicosis (Graves, toxic adenoma) — not just exogenous overdose. Can reduce T4 levels by an additional 20-30%. [2][16] IBCC considers this an important adjunct that is often overlooked. Extremely safe (available OTC for diarrhea). [2] Drug interaction warning: Chole

nodes.title: Step 6 — Hyperthermia Management
nodes.summary: Acetaminophen for fever — AVOID aspirin/NSAIDs (displace T4 from binding protein, worsen thyrotoxicosis)
nodes.body: Acetaminophen 650-1000 mg PO/IV q6h (max 4g/day) Active cooling for temp >40°C: cooling blankets, ice packs to axillae/groin [2][12] AVOID aspirin and NSAIDs — they displace T4 from thyroxine-binding globulin, increasing free (active) T4 and T3 levels. This can worsen thyrotoxicosis. [14] Hyperthermia is harmful: increases myocardial oxygen demand and can cause rhabdomyolysis, delirium, and organ

nodes.title: Step 7 — Agitation Management
nodes.summary: Olanzapine preferred for agitation — avoid haloperidol (QT risk) and ketamine (sympathomimetic)
nodes.body: Agitation worsens hyperthermia and impedes care. IBCC preferred: Olanzapine 5-10 mg IM/PO [2] • Provides sedation without respiratory depression • May have direct antithyroid properties Alternatives: • Benzodiazepines (midazolam 2-5 mg IM) — avoid in elderly • Dexmedetomidine (ICU setting) — alpha-2 agonist, no respiratory depression • Phenobarbital — historical agent, enhances T4 hepatic metaboli

nodes.title: Step 8 — Cardiovascular Management
nodes.summary: ECHO FIRST before any cardiovascular intervention — up to 38% develop cardiogenic shock; beta-blockers in decompensated HF = arrest
nodes.body: THE most controversial topic in thyroid storm management. ECHO FIRST — this is the critical step before ANY cardiovascular intervention. [2] Thyroid storm causes complex hemodynamic derangements: 1. Hypovolemia (diaphoresis, vomiting, diarrhea) 2. Systolic heart failure (thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy — up to 38% of ICU patients) 3. Distributive shock (systemic vasodilation from tissue hypermetabolism)

nodes.title: Beta-Blocker Use — Preserved EF
nodes.summary: ONLY with preserved EF — esmolol preferred (ultra-short, titratable); start low, stop immediately if hypotension
nodes.body: ONLY if echo confirms preserved ejection fraction and no decompensated heart failure. Traditional ATA/EMP view: Beta-blockers are first-line for rate/symptom control. Propranolol preferred (also blocks T4→T3 conversion at high doses). [8][14] IBCC critical view: Beta-blockers may be harmful — use for standard accepted indications (hypertension, preserved-EF rate control) rather than reflexively in

nodes.title: Reduced EF / Heart Failure — Avoid Beta-Blockers
nodes.summary: Reduced EF: NO beta-blockers — treat the storm; digoxin for rate (no negative inotropy); permissive tachy HR <130
nodes.body: If EF is reduced or clinical signs of decompensated heart failure: do NOT give beta-blockers. [2] Manage tachycardia by treating the storm: 1. Aggressive multimodal thyroid storm treatment (steps 2-7) will reduce heart rate as thyroid hormone levels fall 2. Digoxin 0.25-0.5 mg IV — lacks negative inotropic properties. However, thyrotoxicosis increases renal clearance and Vd, so higher doses may be

nodes.title: AFib in Thyroid Storm
nodes.summary: AFib in 10-35% — usually resolves with storm treatment; cardioversion ineffective until hormones normalize
nodes.body: AFib occurs in 10-35% of thyroid storm. Usually resolves spontaneously once thyrotoxicosis is treated (within 8-10 weeks). [14] Rate control (depends on EF): • Preserved EF: Cautious beta-blocker (esmolol preferred — titratable) or diltiazem • Reduced EF: Digoxin (reduced effectiveness in thyrotoxicosis but no negative inotropy), amiodarone (contains iodine — give AFTER methimazole; reasonable sho

nodes.title: Thyroid Storm in Pregnancy
nodes.summary: PTU mandatory 1st trimester (methimazole teratogenic); iodine cautiously (fetal goiter risk); coordinate with OB/MFM
nodes.body: Treatment is similar to non-pregnant patients with key modifications: [15] Special Populations Guide Thionamide: • 1st trimester: PTU is MANDATORY — PTU methimazole is teratogenic (aplasia cutis, choanal/esophageal atresia, cardiac malformations) • 2nd/3rd trimester: Switch to methimazole (lower hepatotoxicity risk) • Use the lowest effective dose — both drugs cross the placenta and can cause feta

nodes.title: Thyroid Storm — Disposition
nodes.summary: ALL thyroid storm patients require ICU — mortality 8-25%; improvement expected 24-72h with aggressive multimodal therapy
nodes.body: All thyroid storm patients require ICU admission. Mortality 8-25%. [1][14] Monitor for complications: • Worsening hemodynamics / cardiogenic shock • Arrhythmias (AFib, VT) • Hepatic failure (elevated LFTs common — liver failure is a grave prognostic sign) • DIC • Rhabdomyolysis Clinical improvement expected in 24-72h with aggressive multimodal therapy. [2] Risk factors for mortality: Age >60, neur

nodes.title: ICU Admission — Thyroid Storm
nodes.body: Continue full multimodal regimen: • Steroids (taper as storm resolves) • Thionamide (transition to maintenance dosing — methimazole 10-20 mg daily preferred long-term) • Iodine (continue up to 10 days, then discontinue) • Cholestyramine (continue until improved) • Supportive care (temperature, agitation, hemodynamics) Consults: • Endocrinology • Consider cardiology if cardiomyopathy or persistent
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission. Multimodal thyroid storm treatment. Endocrinology consult.

nodes.title: Refractory Thyroid Storm
nodes.body: If no improvement after 24-48h of maximal medical therapy: [2] 1. Therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) — most effective short-term rescue. Removes circulating thyroid hormones, autoantibodies, catecholamines, cytokines. Can be a bridge to thyroidectomy. [13] 2. Emergency thyroidectomy — definitive treatment. Very high surgical risk in unstable patients. Typically done after plasmapheresis
nodes.recommendation: Multidisciplinary: endocrinology, surgery, critical care, nephrology (if plasmapheresis).

nodes.title: Incidental Thyroid Lab Abnormality
nodes.summary: Euthyroid sick syndrome in acute illness — do NOT treat; reassess after illness resolves
nodes.body: Incidental finding on ED labs. Most common: elevated TSH with normal free T4 (subclinical hypothyroidism). Prevalence: 4-10% of general population, higher in elderly and women. [14] Euthyroid sick syndrome: Acutely ill patients often have low T3 with low/normal TSH and free T4. This is NOT primary thyroid disease — do not treat. Reassess thyroid function after illness resolves. [14] Lab Interpreta

nodes.title: Subclinical Hypothyroidism — Initiate Treatment
nodes.body: TSH ≥10 mIU/L is associated with progression to overt hypothyroidism, increased risk of coronary heart disease, heart failure, and cardiovascular mortality. Treatment is recommended. [14][17] Start: Levothyroxine 25-50 mcg PO daily • Elderly or cardiac disease: start 12.5-25 mcg • Take on empty stomach, 30-60 min before breakfast • Separate from calcium, iron, antacids by 4 hours Follow-up: • TSH
nodes.recommendation: Start levothyroxine 25-50 mcg daily. PCP/endocrinology follow-up in 6-8 weeks.

nodes.title: Mild Subclinical Hypothyroidism — Observation
nodes.body: TSH 4.5-10 mIU/L with normal free T4 in an asymptomatic patient. No treatment in the ED. [14] Treatment may be considered if: • Symptomatic (fatigue, weight gain, cognitive changes) • Pregnant or planning pregnancy • Anti-TPO antibodies positive (higher progression risk — ~4.3%/year) • Significant cardiovascular risk factors Annual TSH monitoring recommended — progression to overt hypothyroidism o
nodes.recommendation: PCP follow-up within 1-2 months. Annual TSH monitoring.

nodes.title: Subclinical Hyperthyroidism — Urgent Referral
nodes.body: Suppressed TSH (<0.1 mIU/L) with normal free T4/T3. Risk depends on degree of TSH suppression and age. [14] Risks of untreated subclinical hyperthyroidism: • AFib (especially if TSH <0.1 and age >65) • Osteoporosis (accelerated bone turnover) • Progression to overt hyperthyroidism Common causes (check first): • Exogenous thyroid hormone (most common cause — is patient on levothyroxine?) • Amiodaro
nodes.recommendation: Urgent endocrinology referral within 1-2 weeks. Confirm with repeat labs.

nodes.title: TIA Workup: Overview
nodes.summary: Resolved focal neuro + negative DWI = true TIA; 90-day stroke risk up to 17.8%, 50% in first 2 days
nodes.body: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) is an acute neurovascular syndrome with transient focal neurologic dysfunction attributable to a specific vascular territory, with rapid resolution and no evidence of infarction on DWI-MRI. Critical points: - Resolved symptoms + Positive DWI = Ischemic Stroke (not TIA) - Resolved symptoms + Negative DWI = True TIA - 90-day stroke risk up to 17.8%, with ~50% in first

nodes.title: TIA Definition: Tissue vs Time
nodes.summary: Tissue-based definition: no infarct on DWI MRI — 30-50% of time-based "TIAs" are actually strokes
nodes.body: Modern Tissue-Based Definition (AHA 2009, reaffirmed 2023): - Acute focal neurologic dysfunction - Symptoms attributable to a single vascular territory - Rapid resolution - No infarction on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) Time-Based (Legacy): - Symptoms resolve within 24 hours - Limitation: ~30-50% of "TIAs" by time criteria have infarct on MRI Clinical Reality: - Most true TIAs last <1 hour (often <

nodes.title: Classic TIA Presentation
nodes.summary: Sudden onset, negative symptoms, focal deficit in single vascular territory, duration <1h, risk factors
nodes.body: Red Flags FOR TIA (Against Mimics): Symptom Quality: - Sudden onset (maximal at onset, "like a switch") - Negative symptoms (weakness, numbness, vision loss) - Definite focal deficits in single vascular territory Typical TIA Symptoms: - Unilateral motor weakness - Unilateral sensory loss - Speech disturbance (aphasia, dysarthria) - Monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) - Hemianopia - Ataxia, ver

nodes.title: Vascular Territory Patterns
nodes.summary: MCA (face/arm > leg), ACA (leg > arm), ophthalmic (amaurosis), posterior (crossed deficits, diplopia)
nodes.body: Anterior Circulation (Carotid): MCA Territory: - Contralateral face/arm > leg weakness - Contralateral sensory loss - Aphasia (dominant hemisphere) - Neglect (non-dominant hemisphere) ACA Territory: - Contralateral leg > arm weakness - Personality changes, abulia Ophthalmic Artery: - Amaurosis fugax (monocular vision loss) - "Curtain coming down" description Posterior Circulation (Vertebrobasilar)

nodes.title: TIA Mimics (Up to 60% of Referrals)
nodes.summary: Up to 60% of TIA referrals are mimics — migraine, seizure, hypoglycemia, syncope, vestibular, TGA
nodes.body: Common Mimics: | Mimic | Key Differentiating Features | |-------|------------------------------| | Migraine with aura | Gradual spread (5-20 min), positive phenomena (scintillations, tingling), headache follows | | Seizure/Todd's | Convulsive activity, tongue bite, postictal confusion, gradual recovery | | Hypoglycemia | Rapidly correctable, autonomic symptoms, altered consciousness | | Syncope |

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation Assessment
nodes.summary: Sudden onset + negative symptoms + single territory favors TIA; gradual/positive phenomena favors mimic
nodes.body: Assess the presentation: Does the history suggest true TIA or a potential mimic? Favors TIA: - Sudden onset, maximal immediately - Negative symptoms (weakness, numbness, vision loss) - Single vascular territory - Duration <1 hour - Vascular risk factors present Favors Mimic: - Gradual onset or spread - Positive phenomena - Non-anatomic distribution - Loss of consciousness - Preceding headache What

nodes.title: When TIA Mimic Suspected
nodes.summary: Even if mimic suspected, perform basic workup if any risk factors — consequences of missing TIA outweigh over-evaluation
nodes.body: Even if mimic suspected, consider: Still perform basic TIA workup if: - Any vascular risk factors present - Cannot definitively confirm mimic diagnosis - First episode (no prior similar events) - Patient/family concerned about stroke Minimum evaluation: - Fingerstick glucose - ECG (rule out afib) - Basic neuro exam - CT head if any red flags Specific mimic workups: - Migraine: History, triggers, p

nodes.title: Risk Stratification Overview
nodes.summary: Canadian TIA Score preferred (AUC 0.70 vs 0.60), but always identify high-risk features regardless of score
nodes.body: Goal: Identify patients at highest risk for early stroke. Available Tools: 1. ABCD2 Score (Classic but limited) - Simple 7-point scale - ACEP 2016: Do NOT use alone to identify safe discharges - Poor sensitivity for low-risk, poor specificity for high-risk 2. Canadian TIA Score (Preferred, validated 2021) - 13 variables including imaging findings - Superior discrimination (AUC 0.70 vs 0.60) - Bett

nodes.title: Tick Paralysis
nodes.summary: A neurotoxin-mediated GBS mimic reversed by removing the tick. Classic: young child, scalp tick attached 4-7 days.
nodes.body: Tick paralysis is an acute ascending flaccid paralysis caused by a neurotoxin in the saliva of an engorged feeding female tick. There is no pathogen — it is a toxin, not an infection (distinct from Lyme/RMSF). Why it matters: it is a near-perfect Guillain-Barré mimic that is reversed in hours by a 30-second physical act — pulling the tick. Miss it and you watch a curable patient progress to respir

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Ascending flaccid paralysis + areflexia + SPARED sensation + normal mentation + afebrile. Ataxia may come first in kids.
nodes.body: The syndrome (the GBS look-alike): - Prodrome: anorexia, lethargy, irritability (esp. children) - Ataxia frequently precedes weakness — consider tick paralysis in ANY child with acute ataxia - Acute symmetric ascending flaccid paralysis (legs → trunk → arms) over 24-48 h - Areflexia / hyporeflexia - Bulbar + respiratory involvement late — dysarthria, dysphagia, then respiratory failure The sparing

nodes.title: FIND THE TICK — Full Skin Search
nodes.summary: No lab confirms it — the diagnosis is finding the tick. Search scalp/hairline/ears/axillae/groin/perineum. Found on head/neck in ~60-70%. CSF normal.
nodes.body: Diagnosis is clinical and there is no confirmatory test — the diagnosis IS finding the tick. Patients rarely recall a bite, so a meticulous head-to-toe search is mandatory and is the single highest-yield action in this consult. Search every hidden, hairy, and intertriginous site: - Entire scalp and hairline (a fine-toothed comb helps) — most ticks hide here - Behind the ears, in the ear canal - Ax

nodes.title: Remove the Tick — Definitive Treatment
nodes.summary: Removal is curative (North American). Fine forceps at the skin, straight-up steady pull, no twist/crush/folklore. May progress up to ~2 days post-removal.
nodes.body: Removing the tick IS the treatment. North American (Dermacentor) tick paralysis reverses within hours to days of complete removal; supportive care alone is then curative. Proper removal (CDC technique): 1. Grasp with clean fine-tipped tweezers/forceps as close to the skin as possible. 2. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. Do NOT twist or jerk. 3. Do NOT crush or squeeze the tick body (av

nodes.title: Respiratory Monitoring
nodes.summary: Respiratory failure is the killer. Monitor bulbar function + ventilation; SpO2 is a late indicator. Support airway for impending failure.
nodes.body: Respiratory failure is the cause of death in untreated or severe tick paralysis — make monitoring the priority while you search for and remove the tick. Watch for: - Bulbar signs: weak cough, dysphagia, pooling secretions, dysarthria - Declining respiratory effort, rising CO2, fatigue on repeat exam - Single-breath count, vital capacity / bedside mechanics if available Pulse oximetry is a late, po

nodes.title: Geographic Risk: North American vs Australian
nodes.summary: North American = rapid recovery, supportive. Australian I. holocyclus = severe, can WORSEN post-removal, admit + toxicology for antitoxin.
nodes.body: The species changes everything. Risk-stratify by geography/tick type. North American (Dermacentor andersoni / variabilis): - Excellent prognosis — rapid reversal (hours-days) after removal - Supportive care is curative; antitoxin NOT used - Can still progress up to ~2 days post-removal — monitor Australian (Ixodes holocyclus — the paralysis tick): - Far more severe — higher rate of respiratory par

nodes.title: Differential & Mimics
nodes.summary: GBS (CSF/NCS/no tick), MFS (eyes), botulism (descending/pupils), MG (fatigable), TM (sensory level), hypoK (check K+). IVIG/PLEX do NOT work — remove the tick.
nodes.body: Tick paralysis sits in the acute-flaccid-paralysis differential — here is how it separates: - Guillain-Barré (AIDP) — also ascending + areflexic, but CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation, NCS is demyelinating, no tick, and it progresses slower. *Caveat: early GBS (≤4 days) may lack the CSF protein rise, so normal CSF supports but does not absolutely prove tick paralysis.* - Miller Fisher varia

Australian (I. holocyclus): guarded — admit for several days; paralysis can worsen post-removal; respiratory support may be needed for >1 week; death possible within 1-2 days if inadequately treated. nodes.title: Etiology Assessment
nodes.summary: Acquired (>95% ED) vs congenital LQTS — treatment is fundamentally different
nodes.body: What is the most likely etiology of the prolonged QT? Acquired causes (>95% in ED): medications, electrolyte abnormalities, structural heart disease, bradycardia. Congenital LQTS clues: young patient, family history of sudden death, prior syncopal events, no QT-prolonging drugs, baseline ECG with QTc >480 ms without medications.

nodes.body: Most common cause of TdP in the ED (>95%). Common triggers: • Medications — antiarrhythmics (sotalol, dofetilide), antibiotics (fluoroquinolones, macrolides), antipsychotics (haloperidol, ziprasidone), antiemetics (ondansetron IV), methadone, SSRIs (citalopram) • Electrolytes — hypokalemia (most important), hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia • Bradycardia — any cause (pause-dependent TdP) • Structural h

nodes.summary: Beta-blockers first-line, isoproterenol CONTRAINDICATED — opposite of acquired TdP treatment
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Treatment of congenital LQTS is fundamentally different from acquired. In congenital LQTS: • Beta-blockers are FIRST-LINE (nadolol, propranolol) — reduce adrenergic triggers • Isoproterenol is CONTRAINDICATED — paradoxically prolongs QT and increases TdP risk • Triggered by exercise, emotional stress, auditory stimuli (varies by LQTS type) Acute management: • IV Magnesium (same dosing as

nodes.title: Congenital LQTS — Management & Disposition
nodes.body: Acute stabilization: • Magnesium Sulfate 2 g IV bolus (repeat 2 g at 5–15 min if it persists) → infusion per the magnesium protocol • IV beta-blocker (esmolol drip or propranolol) • Transvenous pacing if bradycardic or refractory • Avoid: isoproterenol, all sympathomimetics, QT-prolonging drugs Disposition: • ICU admission with continuous telemetry • Emergent Cardiology/Electrophysiology consult •
nodes.recommendation: ICU + EP consult + genetics referral + ICD evaluation.

nodes.title: Unknown Etiology — Treat as Acquired
nodes.summary: When uncertain treat as acquired — Mg safe in both, gather history while treating
nodes.body: When uncertain, treat as acquired (safer default). Reasoning: • Acquired TdP is >95% of cases in the ED • Magnesium is beneficial in both acquired and congenital • Overdrive pacing is safe in both • Isoproterenol is safe in acquired but harmful in congenital — but you will only reach isoproterenol if refractory to Mg + pacing Gather history while treating: • Family history of sudden cardiac death
