nodes.summary: TdP terminated — continue Mg infusion protocol, address underlying cause
nodes.body: TdP has terminated. Continue magnesium infusion per protocol. • Continue Mg infusion: 1–4 g/hr titrated to target (EMCrit taper: 1 g/hr × 4h → 0.5 g/hr × 20h) • Target serum Mg 3.5–5.0 mg/dL • Monitor serum Mg q2–4h Now address the underlying cause: • Stop all QT-prolonging drugs • Correct electrolytes aggressively • Identify and treat precipitating factors Proceed to drug review and electrolyte c

nodes.title: Overdrive Pacing & Isoproterenol
nodes.summary: Transvenous pacing 90-110bpm preferred; isoproterenol 1-10mcg/min as bridge — acquired LQTS only
nodes.body: For TdP refractory to or recurrent despite magnesium. Overdrive Pacing (preferred): • Transvenous pacing at 90–110 bpm (up to 140 bpm if needed) • Eliminates the short-long-short sequences that trigger TdP • Preferred over pharmacologic approach when available Pharmacologic Overdrive (bridge to pacing): • Isoproterenol 1–10 mcg/min IV, titrate to HR 90–110 bpm • Start at 2 mcg/min, increase every

nodes.title: Lidocaine — Antiarrhythmic of Choice
nodes.summary: Lidocaine 1-1.5mg/kg IV — Class IB shortens QT, safe in TdP, use if refractory to Mg + pacing
nodes.body: Lidocaine is one of the few antiarrhythmics SAFE in TdP. Lidocaine • Loading: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV push over 2 min • Infusion: 1–4 mg/min continuous • May repeat bolus 0.5–0.75 mg/kg q5–10 min (max 3 mg/kg total) Why lidocaine works: • Class IB antiarrhythmic — shortens QT interval (unlike Class IA/III which prolong QT) • Suppresses triggered activity and early afterdepolarizations • Competes for sodium

nodes.title: 🚫 Drugs to AVOID in TdP
nodes.summary: Amiodarone prolongs QT and WILL worsen TdP — most common lethal error in TdP management
nodes.body: These drugs prolong QT and WILL worsen TdP: • Amiodarone — Class III, prolongs QT significantly. The most common error in TdP management. • Procainamide — Class IA, prolongs QT • Sotalol — Class III, prolongs QT • Beta-blockers — in acquired TdP, can worsen pause-dependent mechanism (appropriate in congenital LQTS) • Any Class IA or Class III antiarrhythmic • Ibutilide, dofetilide, dronedarone, fl

nodes.title: Response to Full Treatment
nodes.summary: Assess rhythm after full protocol — Mg + overdrive pacing/isoproterenol + lidocaine
nodes.body: After magnesium + overdrive pacing/isoproterenol + lidocaine, what is the rhythm status?

nodes.title: Stop All QT-Prolonging Drugs
nodes.summary: Review and stop ALL QT-prolonging meds — antiarrhythmics, FQs, macrolides, antipsychotics, methadone
nodes.body: Review and discontinue ALL medications that prolong QT. Use the QT Drug Checker tool in the toolbar to search specific medications. Most common ED culprits: • Antiarrhythmics: amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, procainamide • Antibiotics: fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin > levofloxacin), macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin), fluconazole • Antipsychotics: haloperidol (IV >> oral), droperidol, zipras

nodes.title: Aggressive Electrolyte Correction
nodes.summary: Target K >4.5, Mg 3.5-5.0, normalize Ca — correct Mg before K repletion will be effective
nodes.body: Target electrolyte levels for TdP management: Potassium: >4.5 mEq/L • KCl IV — most important modifiable risk factor • Hypokalemia prolongs QT and is refractory until Mg is corrected • Central line preferred for rapid repletion (20 mEq/hr via central, 10 mEq/hr peripheral) Magnesium: 3.5–5.0 mg/dL • Magnesium Sulfate — continue infusion per EMCrit protocol • Must correct Mg before K+ repletion wil

nodes.title: TdP Risk Factor Review
nodes.summary: Risk is multiplicative — drug + electrolyte + structural heart is classic scenario
nodes.body: Non-Modifiable Risk Factors: • Female sex (longer baseline QTc) • Age >65 years • Congenital LQTS (any type) • Structural heart disease (LVH, CHF) Modifiable/Treatable Risk Factors: • Hypokalemia (most important) • Hypomagnesemia • Hypocalcemia • Bradycardia (any cause) • QT-prolonging medications (especially multiple concurrent) • CYP3A4/2D6 inhibitors with QT substrate • Heart failure with reduc

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: All TdP patients require ICU — determine level of intervention needed
nodes.body: All TdP patients require ICU admission. The question is the level of intervention needed. What is the current clinical status?

nodes.title: Disposition — Resolved TdP
nodes.body: ICU admission with: • Continuous telemetry monitoring (minimum 48–72 hours) • Continue Mg infusion per EMCrit protocol (24h total) • Electrolyte monitoring q2–4h → q6h once stable • Cardiology consult for QTc monitoring and medication review • Complete medication reconciliation — identify and permanently discontinue QT-prolonging drugs • Evaluate need for alternative medications (e.g., non-QT anti
nodes.recommendation: ICU + telemetry + continue Mg infusion + cardiology consult + full medication review.

nodes.title: Disposition — Recurrent TdP
nodes.body: ICU admission with escalated care: • Overdrive pacing at 90–110 bpm (maintain until QT normalizes) • Continue isoproterenol if pacing not yet placed • Lidocaine infusion if contributing to rhythm control • Electrophysiology (EP) consult — may need long-term pacing or ICD • Continue aggressive Mg and electrolyte repletion • Serial QTc measurements q4–6h Consider: • Temporary transvenous pacemaker i
nodes.recommendation: ICU + overdrive pacing + EP consult. Extended monitoring until QT normalizes and trigger eliminated.

nodes.title: Disposition — Refractory TdP
nodes.body: Maximal escalation of care: • ECMO consideration — for hemodynamically unstable refractory TdP • Emergent EP consult — for catheter ablation or ICD placement • Continue all anti-TdP measures: Mg infusion, pacing, lidocaine • Evaluate for congenital LQTS — may benefit from IV beta-blocker trial • Consider stellate ganglion block (reduces sympathetic drive) Transfer considerations: • If no EP/ECMO c
nodes.recommendation: ECMO consideration + emergent EP + ICD evaluation. Transfer to tertiary center if needed.

nodes.title: Toxic Alcohols — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Parent compounds cause intoxication; metabolites cause organ damage — methanol→blindness, EG→renal failure
nodes.body: Toxic Alcohol Summary — quick reference. The toxic alcohols are: • Methanol — windshield washer fluid, paint thinner, moonshine • Ethylene glycol — antifreeze (sweet taste), brake fluid • Isopropyl alcohol — rubbing alcohol, hand sanitizer • Propylene glycol — IV drug diluent (lorazepam, phenytoin, esmolol) Key clinical concept: The parent compounds cause intoxication. The metabolites cause organ

nodes.title: Identify the Toxic Alcohol
nodes.summary: Visual symptoms→methanol; renal failure→EG; ketosis without acidosis→isopropanol; ICU drips+lactic→propylene glycol
nodes.body: Clinical clues to identify the toxic alcohol: | Feature | Methanol | Ethylene Glycol | Isopropanol | |---------|----------|-----------------|-------------| | Classic source | Windshield washer | Antifreeze | Rubbing alcohol | | Key finding | Visual symptoms | Renal failure | Ketosis w/o acidosis | | Anion gap | YES (severe) | YES (severe) | NO | | Osmolar gap | Elevated early | Elevated early | El

nodes.title: Methanol Toxicity
nodes.summary: Methanol→formic acid→retinal toxicity; visual symptoms pathognomonic; as little as 30mL can cause blindness
nodes.body: Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid (toxic metabolite) [1][3] Sources: Windshield washer fluid (30-50%), paint thinner, moonshine, industrial solvents Classic presentation: • Visual symptoms — blurred vision, "snowstorm" appearance, photophobia, blindness • Headache, dizziness, abdominal pain • Biphasic course: Early CNS depression, then delayed severe acidosis (12-24h) Examination findings: • O

nodes.title: Severe Methanol Toxicity — Emergent Treatment
nodes.summary: Vision changes = formic acid damage NOW; fomepizole + urgent HD + folic acid; dialysis if methanol >50-70 mg/dL or vision symptoms
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Vision changes indicate formic acid accumulation — irreversible damage occurring NOW Immediate actions (do all simultaneously): 1. Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading dose — blocks alcohol dehydrogenase [1][4] 2. Nephrology consult for urgent hemodialysis — removes methanol AND formic acid [1][4] 3. Folic acid 50 mg IV Q4-6H — enhances formic acid metabolism [1][3] 4. Sodium bicarbonate if pH

nodes.title: Ethylene Glycol Toxicity
nodes.summary: EG→glycolic/oxalic acid; three phases: CNS→cardiopulmonary→renal failure; hypocalcemia + Ca-oxalate crystals pathognomonic
nodes.body: Ethylene glycol → glycolaldehyde → glycolic acid → glyoxylic acid → oxalic acid [1][2] Sources: Antifreeze (95-100%, sweet taste), brake fluid, industrial coolants Classic three-phase presentation: Phase 1 (0.5-12h) — CNS: • Resembles ethanol intoxication • Ataxia, nausea, vomiting • May appear "drunk" without alcohol on breath Phase 2 (4-12h) — Cardiopulmonary: • Tachycardia, hypertension • Pulmo

nodes.title: Severe Ethylene Glycol Toxicity — Emergent Treatment
nodes.summary: Renal failure = oxalate precipitation; fomepizole + HD + thiamine/pyridoxine; check/replace calcium; HD if EG >310 or AKI
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Renal failure indicates oxalic acid precipitation — ongoing nephrotoxicity Immediate actions (do all simultaneously): 1. Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading dose — blocks alcohol dehydrogenase [1][4] 2. Nephrology consult for urgent hemodialysis — removes EG AND glycolic acid [1][4] 3. Thiamine 100 mg IV Q6H + Pyridoxine 100 mg IV Q6H — shunt glyoxylic acid away from oxalate [1][2] 4. Check i

nodes.title: Isopropyl Alcohol Toxicity
nodes.summary: Isopropanol→acetone (not toxic); KETOSIS WITHOUT ACIDOSIS; GI symptoms, CNS depression; rarely lethal, supportive care
nodes.body: Isopropyl alcohol → acetone (not highly toxic) [1][5] Sources: Rubbing alcohol (70%), hand sanitizer, nail polish remover Key differentiator: Ketosis WITHOUT acidosis [1][5] • Acetone produces ketonemia/ketonuria • But acetone is NOT an acid — no metabolic acidosis • If acidosis present, look for another cause (co-ingestion, lactate from shock) Clinical presentation: • 2-3× more potent CNS depress

nodes.title: Isopropanol Treatment
nodes.summary: Isopropanol: supportive care only; fomepizole NOT indicated (acetone not toxic); dialysis rarely needed
nodes.body: Isopropanol is the "benign" toxic alcohol — no toxic metabolites [1][5] Treatment is supportive: • IV fluids for hypotension • Antiemetics for GI symptoms • Glucose monitoring • Airway protection if severe CNS depression Fomepizole is NOT indicated [1][5] • Acetone is not toxic — no benefit to blocking ADH • Would just prolong isopropanol half-life Dialysis rarely indicated: • Consider only if: pe

nodes.title: Propylene Glycol Toxicity
nodes.summary: Propylene glycol: iatrogenic from IV drips (lorazepam); causes lactic acidosis, mimics sepsis; check osmolar gap in ICU patients
nodes.body: Propylene glycol → lactic acid (via alcohol dehydrogenase) [6] Sources: IV drug diluent — lorazepam, diazepam, phenytoin, esmolol, nitroglycerin Risk factors for accumulation: • High-dose continuous IV infusions (especially lorazepam >1 mg/kg/day) • Renal dysfunction • Children <4 years (immature metabolism) • Hepatic dysfunction • Disulfiram or metronidazole use (inhibit ADH) Clinical presentatio

nodes.title: Propylene Glycol Treatment
nodes.summary: Stop the drip (switch to midazolam); supportive care; fomepizole reasonable; dialysis for severe cases
nodes.body: Treatment for propylene glycol toxicity: 1. Stop the offending agent • Discontinue lorazepam/diazepam drip • Switch to non-propylene glycol alternatives: - Midazolam (no propylene glycol) - Dexmedetomidine - Propofol 2. Supportive care • IV fluids for hypotension • Bicarbonate for severe acidosis if needed 3. Fomepizole consideration • May block conversion to lactate [6] • Limited evidence, but re

nodes.title: Empiric Treatment — Unknown Toxic Alcohol
nodes.summary: Start fomepizole empirically for osmolar gap >10 + acidosis — differentiate later based on clinical findings and levels
nodes.body: When you suspect toxic alcohol but can't identify which: Start fomepizole empirically if [1][4]: • History of toxic alcohol ingestion • Osmolar gap >10 mOsm/kg without explanation • Anion gap metabolic acidosis without clear cause • Altered mental status + metabolic derangement Simultaneous workup: • Send serum methanol and ethylene glycol levels (if available) • Check lactate, ketones, glucose •

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Osmolar gap early (parent), anion gap late (metabolites) — get levels, VBG, BMP, lactate, ketones, UA for crystals
nodes.body: Order these labs immediately: Gap calculations: • Osmolar gap = Measured osmolality - Calculated osmolality • Calculated = 2[Na] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 + EtOH/4.6 • Normal <10 mOsm/kg; >10 suggests exogenous osmoles [1][2] • Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3); normal 8-12 Specific labs: • Serum methanol and ethylene glycol levels (if available) • Serum ethanol level (co-ingestion common, also therapeuti

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Severe = pH <7.3, visual symptoms, renal failure, AMS; treat methanol ≥20 mg/dL, EG ≥20-25 mg/dL
nodes.body: Assess severity to guide treatment intensity: Severe toxicity (any of): • pH <7.3 • Anion gap >20 • Visual symptoms (methanol) • Renal failure (ethylene glycol) • Altered mental status • Hemodynamic instability Moderate toxicity: • Osmolar gap >10 without significant acidosis • Normal vision and renal function • Alert mental status Treatment thresholds [AACT guidelines]: • Methanol ≥20 mg/dL — tre

nodes.title: Fomepizole — First-Line Antidote
nodes.summary: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg load, 10 mg/kg Q12H × 4, then 15 mg/kg Q12H — blocks ADH with 8000× affinity vs ethanol
nodes.body: Fomepizole (Antizol) — competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase [1][4] Mechanism: 8000× higher affinity for ADH than ethanol → prevents conversion of methanol/EG to toxic metabolites. Indications: • Documented methanol or EG ingestion • Osmolar gap >10 with metabolic acidosis • Suspected toxic alcohol pending confirmation Standard Dosing: • Loading dose: 15 mg/kg IV over 30 minutes • Mainten

nodes.title: Fomepizole During Hemodialysis
nodes.summary: During HD: fomepizole Q4H (auto-induces metabolism) or 1-1.5 mg/kg/hr infusion; HD cuts methanol half-life 71h→2.5h
nodes.body: Fomepizole is dialyzed — dosing changes during HD [1][4]: During hemodialysis: • Give doses Q4H instead of Q12H (fomepizole induces its own metabolism) • If last dose was >6 hours ago, give supplemental dose at HD start Alternative continuous infusion during HD: • 1-1.5 mg/kg/hr continuous IV infusion during dialysis • European protocol, simpler than intermittent dosing After dialysis ends: • If <

nodes.title: Ethanol — Alternative Antidote
nodes.summary: Ethanol alternative if fomepizole unavailable — 0.8 g/kg load, target 100-150 mg/dL; harder to manage, more adverse events
nodes.body: IV or oral ethanol — competitive substrate for alcohol dehydrogenase [1][4] Use when fomepizole unavailable or delayed. Target serum ethanol: 100-150 mg/dL [1] Dosing (IV preferred): • Loading: 0.8 g/kg ethanol (dilute 10% ethanol in D5W) • Maintenance: 66-130 mg/kg/hr (higher in chronic drinkers) • Titrate to ethanol level 100-150 mg/dL Oral dosing (emergency backup): • 80-proof liquor (40% ethan

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Indications
nodes.summary: HD for methanol >50-70 mg/dL or vision/coma; EG: glycolate/anion-gap or severe-feature criteria plus EG level; isopropanol rarely needs HD
nodes.body: EXTRIP guidelines for hemodialysis [1][4]: METHANOL — Dialysis recommended if: • Methanol >70 mg/dL (or >50 mg/dL with severe acidosis) • Vision changes • Coma or seizures • Renal dysfunction • Severe metabolic acidosis despite treatment ETHYLENE GLYCOL — use the newest EXTRIP criteria: • Recommend ECTR if glycolate >12 mmol/L or anion gap >27 mmol/L when there is credible EG exposure • Suggest EC

nodes.title: Hemodialysis Protocol
nodes.summary: High-flux HD 4-6+ hours until level undetectable; watch for post-HD rebound; check level 2-4h after completion
nodes.body: Dialysis setup: • High-flux dialyzer with surface area >2.1 m² • Blood flow 300-400 mL/min • Dialysate flow 500-800 mL/min • Bicarbonate dialysate for acidosis Duration: • Continue until toxic alcohol level undetectable • Minimum 4-6 hours typically needed • Methanol especially requires prolonged HD (formate removal) Monitoring during HD: • Toxic alcohol level Q2-4H during dialysis • pH/bicarbonat

nodes.title: Cofactor Therapy
nodes.summary: Methanol: folic acid 50mg IV Q4-6H; EG: thiamine 100mg + pyridoxine 100mg IV Q6H; alcoholics: high-dose thiamine 200-500mg Q8H
nodes.body: Cofactors enhance metabolism of toxic metabolites: METHANOL: • Folic acid 50 mg IV Q4-6H (max 50 mg/dose) • OR Folinic acid (leucovorin) 50-100 mg IV Q4H (preferred over folic acid when available; EMCrit IBCC 2025) • Mechanism: Enhances formate → CO₂ + H₂O conversion via tetrahydrofolate pathway [1][3] • Continue until methanol <20 mg/dL ETHYLENE GLYCOL: • Thiamine 100 mg IV Q6H • Pyridoxine (B6)

nodes.title: Sodium Bicarbonate Therapy
nodes.summary: Bicarbonate for pH <7.3; target pH >7.3-7.45; alkalinization reduces formic acid CNS penetration in methanol
nodes.body: Sodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis [1]: Indications: • pH <7.3 (especially <7.1) • Severe symptomatic acidosis • Bridging therapy while awaiting dialysis Rationale: • Formic acid (methanol metabolite) is more toxic in acidic environment • Alkalinization increases proportion of ionized formate (less CNS penetration) • May be neuroprotective in methanol toxicity [1][3] Dosing: • 1-2 mE

nodes.title: Ongoing Monitoring
nodes.summary: Levels Q4-6H, VBG Q4-6H, visual acuity Q4-6H for methanol; endpoints: level <20, pH normal, no symptoms
nodes.body: Monitoring during treatment: Labs: • Toxic alcohol levels Q4-6H (Q2H during dialysis) • ABG/VBG Q4-6H (Q2H if severely acidotic) • BMP Q4-6H (creatinine for EG, bicarbonate) • Ionized calcium Q6H (if EG) • Osmolality Q6H (track osmolar gap closure) Clinical monitoring: • Visual acuity Q4-6H if methanol • Fundoscopic exam Q12H if methanol • Urine output (AKI marker in EG) • Mental status • Hemodyna

nodes.title: Treatment Response
nodes.summary: Good response: pH improving, levels decreasing; poor response: persistent acidosis, new vision/renal symptoms
nodes.body: Assess response to treatment: Good response: • pH improving or normalized • Toxic alcohol level decreasing • No new or worsening symptoms • Osmolar gap closing Poor response / Complications: • Persistent or worsening acidosis • New vision changes (methanol) • Developing renal failure (EG) • Hemodynamic instability How is the patient responding?

nodes.title: Vision Changes — Emergent Ophthalmology
nodes.summary: Vision changes = active retinal toxicity; urgent ophthalmology, maximize HD, push pH >7.45, max folic acid
nodes.body: New or worsening vision changes indicate active formate toxicity to retina/optic nerve Immediate actions: 1. Urgent ophthalmology consult — document visual acuity, fundoscopic exam 2. Maximize dialysis — if not already on HD, start immediately 3. Confirm fomepizole dosing adequate (Q4H during HD) 4. Push pH >7.45 with bicarbonate — reduces formate toxicity 5. Maximize folic acid — ensure receiving

nodes.title: Escalation for Poor Response
nodes.summary: Check fomepizole dosing and dialysis adequacy; consider CRRT if unstable; call Poison Control 1-800-222-1222
nodes.body: If patient not responding to standard therapy: Check the basics: • Is fomepizole dosing adequate? (Q12H normally, Q4H during HD) • Is dialysis effective? (check clearance, blood flow) • Any co-ingestions? (check ethanol, aspirin, acetaminophen) Escalation options: 1. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) if hemodynamically unstable 2. Prolonged dialysis — some patients need 12+ hours 3. ICU

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Always admit methanol/EG (biphasic); isopropanol may observe 6h; psych eval mandatory for intentional
nodes.body: Psychiatric evaluation is MANDATORY for all intentional ingestions after medical clearance. Key considerations: • Methanol and EG: Always admit — even asymptomatic patients can deteriorate (biphasic toxicity) • Isopropanol: May observe and discharge if asymptomatic 6+ hours, mild ingestion • Propylene glycol: ICU admission typically (iatrogenic, already critical) What is the patient's disposition?

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU admission criteria: • Any hemodialysis requirement • Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.25) • Altered mental status • Hemodynamic instability • Visual symptoms (methanol) • Renal failure (ethylene glycol) • On fomepizole infusion ICU monitoring: • Continuous telemetry • Arterial line if hemodynamically unstable • Serial toxic alcohol levels Q4-6H • ABG/VBG Q4-6H until normalized • Visual acuity
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with continuous monitoring. Continue fomepizole ± dialysis until toxic alcohol undetectable and pH normal.

nodes.title: Monitored Bed — Observation
nodes.body: Monitored bed criteria: • Stable hemodynamics • Mild/moderate acidosis (pH >7.25) • On fomepizole but no dialysis needed • Improving trend Monitoring protocol: • Continuous telemetry • Vitals Q2H • Toxic alcohol levels Q6H • ABG/VBG Q6H • Visual acuity Q6H (if methanol) • BMP Q12H Escalate to ICU if: • Worsening acidosis • New visual symptoms • Developing renal failure • Hemodynamic instability Du
nodes.recommendation: Monitored bed with telemetry. Serial labs. Escalate to ICU if any deterioration.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria (Isopropanol Only)
nodes.body: Safe for discharge ONLY if ALL criteria met: Applies to ISOPROPANOL only — never discharge methanol or EG [1][5] • Confirmed isopropanol (not methanol/EG) • Asymptomatic for ≥6 hours • Normal vital signs • Normal mental status (back to baseline) • Normal anion gap (ketosis ok, acidosis not) • Tolerating PO • Safe social situation • Psychiatric clearance (if intentional ingestion) Before discharge:
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with psychiatric clearance after 6+ hours asymptomatic observation. Isopropanol ONLY — never discharge methanol/EG.

nodes.title: Tracheostomy Emergency
nodes.summary: Apply O2 to BOTH face AND stoma — tracheostomy has dual airway, laryngectomy stoma is ONLY airway
nodes.body: NTSP Emergency Algorithm: Tracheostomy patient in distress FIRST ACTIONS (simultaneous): 1. Call for expert airway help 2. Apply high-flow O2 to BOTH face AND stoma 3. Assess: Is this a tracheostomy or laryngectomy? Critical distinction: - Tracheostomy: Upper airway may be patent - can oxygenate from above - Laryngectomy: NO connection between mouth and lungs - stoma is ONLY airway Look for: - Red

nodes.title: Tracheostomy or Laryngectomy?
nodes.summary: Laryngectomy = NO oral airway possible; tracheostomy = dual airway — check bedside sign
nodes.body: Laryngectomy = Total surgical removal of larynx - NO connection between oropharynx and airway - CANNOT be intubated from above - Stoma is the ONLY airway Tracheostomy = Tube through trachea, larynx intact - Upper airway may be patent - Can potentially oxygenate/intubate from above - Dual oxygenation strategy possible If uncertain: Attempt to feel airflow from mouth during ventilation. No airflow =

nodes.title: Laryngectomy Emergency
nodes.summary: Stoma is ONLY airway — BVM over stoma, suction, replace with ETT 6.0 through stoma, no oral intubation
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Stoma is ONLY airway - cannot oxygenate from above Emergency management: 1. Apply O2 directly to stoma (pediatric face mask or trach collar) 2. If not breathing: BVM over stoma with pediatric face mask 3. Remove any devices/dressings from stoma 4. Suction stoma gently 5. If tube present: deflate cuff, remove inner cannula, attempt suction If tube removal needed: - Replace with tracheosto

nodes.title: Initial Assessment: Problem Type?
nodes.summary: Classify problem: obstruction, dislodgement, or bleeding — apply capnography to assess
nodes.body: Look, listen, feel at both mouth AND stoma Signs of OBSTRUCTION: - Unable to pass suction catheter - High resistance to BVM ventilation - Visible secretions/blood in tube Signs of DISLODGEMENT: - Tube appears malpositioned or loose - Subcutaneous emphysema - Unable to ventilate through tube despite clear lumen Signs of BLEEDING: - Blood from stoma or tube - Sentinel bleed (small bleed preceding ma

nodes.title: Tracheostomy Equipment Checklist
nodes.summary: Bedside equipment: spare tube (same + smaller), suction, syringe, stitch cutters, lubricant, BVM
nodes.body: Bedside equipment for EVERY trach patient: Immediate access: - Spare tracheostomy tube (same size + one size smaller) - Spare inner cannula (if applicable) - Suction equipment with appropriate catheters - 10 mL syringe for cuff deflation - Stitch cutters/scissors - Water-soluble lubricant - Tracheal dilators (for mature stomas) Nearby access: - Bag-valve-mask with pediatric face mask (for stoma ve

nodes.title: Tracheostomy Tube Types
nodes.summary: Cuffed vs uncuffed, inner cannula removal first for obstruction, deflate cuff before speaking valve
nodes.body: CUFFED vs UNCUFFED: - Cuffed: Inflatable balloon creates seal for mechanical ventilation - Uncuffed: For spontaneous breathers, allows speech with finger occlusion INNER CANNULA: - Removable inner tube for easy cleaning - ALWAYS remove inner cannula first when troubleshooting obstruction - Not all tubes have inner cannulas FENESTRATED: - Holes in outer cannula allow airflow through vocal cords - U

nodes.title: Tracheostomy Sizing & Replacement
nodes.summary: Size by ID/OD, ETT 6.0 fits most adult stomas, water-soluble lubricant only
nodes.body: Tracheostomy tube sizing: - ID (inner diameter): Corresponds roughly to ETT size (7.0, 8.0, etc.) - OD (outer diameter): Critical for stoma fit - Length: Standard vs extended length for obese patients Common adult sizes: - Female: 6.0-7.0 ID - Male: 7.0-8.0 ID - Shiley, Portex, Bivona are common brands (not interchangeable) Replacement strategy: - Use same brand/model if possible - If unavailable:

nodes.title: Obstruction: Sequential Algorithm
nodes.summary: Sequential: remove devices, remove inner cannula, pass suction, deflate cuff, remove tube — use capnography
nodes.body: NTSP Obstruction Algorithm - work through sequentially: Step 1: Remove any external devices - Speaking valve, cap, HME filter - Trach collar or humidity device Step 2: Remove inner cannula - Pull out and inspect - Reassess ventilation immediately Step 3: Pass suction catheter - If passes easily: suction and reassess - If cannot pass: complete obstruction present Step 4: Deflate cuff (if present) -

nodes.title: Obstruction: Response to Algorithm?
nodes.summary: Reassess after algorithm — capnography waveform present means improving
nodes.body: Reassess after working through algorithm: Improved: - Can now pass suction catheter - Capnography shows waveform - Patient oxygenating Not improved: - Still cannot ventilate - No capnography waveform - Patient deteriorating Common obstruction causes: - Mucus plug (most common) - Blood clot - Granulation tissue - False passage/displacement - Tracheal stenosis [1][2][4]

nodes.title: Post-Obstruction Care
nodes.summary: Replace inner cannula, confirm with capnography, humidify to prevent recurrence
nodes.body: Obstruction cleared - next steps: Immediate: - Replace inner cannula (cleaned or new) - Confirm ventilation with capnography - Humidification to prevent recurrence - Document intervention Prevention of recurrence: - Regular inner cannula cleaning/replacement - Adequate humidification - Regular suctioning PRN - Hydration If recurrent obstructions: - Consider bronchoscopy to evaluate for granulation

nodes.title: Refractory Obstruction: Rescue Airway
nodes.summary: Mature: dilators + smaller tube; fresh: oral intubation ONLY — do NOT blind replace fresh trach
nodes.body: Tube removed but still cannot ventilate - RESCUE AIRWAY If mature stoma (>7 days): 1. Insert tracheal dilators to maintain stoma patency 2. Replace with smaller trach tube or ETT through stoma 3. Consider fiberoptic guidance 4. If failure: oral intubation (advance cuff past stoma) If fresh stoma (<7 days) - HIGH RISK: 1. Do NOT attempt blind reinsertion 2. Oxygenate via face (BVM, oral intubation)

nodes.title: Dislodgement: Fresh or Mature Trach?
nodes.summary: Fresh <7d = high risk for false passage, do NOT blind replace; mature >7d = bedside replacement safe
nodes.body: CRITICAL DISTINCTION: Age of tracheostomy Fresh tracheostomy (<7 days): - Tract NOT fully epithelialized - HIGH RISK of false passage with blind reinsertion - Stoma may close rapidly - DO NOT attempt blind replacement Mature tracheostomy (>7 days): - Established epithelialized tract - Generally safe for bedside replacement - May still close over hours if left open Risk factors for difficult reinse

nodes.title: Fresh Trach (<7 days): DO NOT REPLACE
nodes.summary: Blind reinsertion contraindicated — oxygenate via face, occlude stoma, oral intubate past stoma, call surgeon
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Blind reinsertion contraindicated in fresh trach Risks of blind reinsertion: - False passage into pretracheal space - Subcutaneous emphysema - Pneumomediastinum - Complete loss of airway - Death Immediate management: 1. Call for help (anesthesia, ENT, surgery) 2. Oxygenate via FACE: BVM or oral intubation 3. Occlude stoma with gauze/finger during face ventilation 4. Advance ETT cuff PAST

nodes.title: Mature Trach (>7 days): Replacement
nodes.summary: Deflate cuff, lubricate, insert along tract, inflate, confirm with capnography — do NOT force
nodes.body: Mature stoma replacement - generally safe bedside procedure: Preparation: 1. Gather equipment: same size tube + one size smaller, lubricant, suction 2. Oxygenate patient well before attempt 3. Position: slight neck extension, shoulder roll 4. Deflate cuff completely Replacement technique: 1. Remove old tube gently along curve 2. Inspect stoma briefly 3. Lubricate new tube 4. Insert along natural t

nodes.title: Confirm Trach Placement
nodes.summary: Capnography is gold standard — do NOT rely on misting or SpO2 alone, fiberoptic if uncertain
nodes.body: ALWAYS confirm proper placement after replacement: Clinical confirmation: - Capnography waveform (GOLD STANDARD) - Suction catheter passes easily past tube tip - Bilateral chest rise with ventilation - Bilateral breath sounds DO NOT rely solely on: - Misting in tube (can occur with false passage) - Patient phonation - Oxygen saturation (delayed indicator) If uncertain placement: - Do NOT inflate c

nodes.title: Bleeding: Timing & Severity
nodes.summary: Late bleeding >72h = sentinel bleed for tracheo-innominate fistula until proven otherwise
nodes.body: Tracheostomy bleeding - assess timing and severity: Early bleeding (<48 hours post-op): - Usually minor: skin edges, granulation - Related to suctioning, manipulation - Rarely life-threatening Late bleeding (>72 hours, especially 7-14 days): - HIGH RISK for tracheo-innominate fistula (TIF) - Innominate artery erosion - mortality approaches 50% - Any late bleeding may be "sentinel bleed" before mas

nodes.title: Minor Bleeding Management
nodes.summary: Suction, direct pressure, topical epi, silver nitrate, TXA gauze — check coags
nodes.body: Minor trach site bleeding: Immediate actions: - Suction to clear blood from airway - Direct pressure to stoma site - Inspect for obvious source (granulation, skin edge) Local hemostasis: - Topical epinephrine (1:1000 on gauze) - Hemostatic agents (Surgicel, gelfoam) - Silver nitrate cautery for granulation tissue - Tranexamic acid-soaked gauze Systemic considerations: - Check coagulation (PT/INR,

nodes.title: Tracheo-Innominate Fistula Concern
nodes.summary: Any bleeding 7+ days post-trach = potential TIF sentinel bleed — call vascular/ENT, do NOT remove tube
nodes.body: Tracheo-innominate fistula (TIF) - LIFE-THREATENING Risk factors: - Trach placement 7-21 days ago (peak incidence) - Low stoma site (below 4th tracheal ring) - High cuff pressure - Excessive tube movement - Prior radiation ANY bleeding 7+ days post-trach = sentinel bleed until proven otherwise Immediate actions: 1. Call for HELP (vascular surgery, ENT, OR team) 2. Type and crossmatch, prepare for

nodes.title: Massive Trach Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Hyperinflate cuff 50mL, Utley maneuver if fails (finger compression against sternum), emergency sternotomy
nodes.body: MASSIVE HEMORRHAGE - TIF protocol: Step 1: Hyperinflate the cuff - Inject 50 mL air into cuff (adult) - Creates tamponade against innominate artery - If uncuffed tube: replace with cuffed ETT Step 2: If cuff hyperinflation fails - UTLEY MANEUVER - Insert finger into tracheostomy stoma - Apply digital compression of innominate artery against posterior sternum - Maintain pressure until OR Step 3: Re

nodes.title: Fresh vs Mature: Management Path
nodes.summary: Fresh <7d: stay sutures, not epithelialized; 7-14d: intermediate caution; percutaneous may take longer
nodes.body: Determining stoma maturity: Fresh (<7 days): - Recently placed - May have stay sutures - Tract not epithelialized - Document in chart: "FRESH TRACH - NO BLIND REINSERTION" Mature (>7 days): - Established tract - Healed stoma edges - Generally safe for bedside exchange Special cases: - 7-14 days: "Intermediate" - use caution, consider fiberoptic - Difficult anatomy: treat as fresh regardless of tim

nodes.title: Stable After Intervention
nodes.body: Patient stable after tracheostomy emergency: Documentation: - Detailed description of event and interventions - Current tube type, size, brand - Stoma age and maturity - Confirmation of placement (capnography) Orders: - Bedside emergency equipment check - Appropriate monitoring (SpO2, capnography if indicated) - Humidification - Suction PRN Consults: - ENT/surgery if any concerns - Respiratory the
nodes.recommendation: Stable after tracheostomy emergency. Ensure bedside equipment, appropriate monitoring, and document intervention thoroughly.

nodes.title: ENT/Surgical Consultation Required
nodes.body: Indications for urgent ENT/surgical consultation: Absolute: - Fresh trach dislodgement - Bleeding concerning for TIF - Failed bedside replacement - Suspected false passage - Laryngectomy emergency Relative: - Recurrent obstruction - Difficult anatomy - Need for trach change to different type/size - Granulation tissue causing symptoms Information for consultant: - Original indication for tracheosto
nodes.recommendation: ENT/surgical consultation required for specialist management. Stabilize airway while awaiting consultation.

nodes.title: Dual Oxygenation Strategy
nodes.summary: Apply O2 to both sites, occlude stoma for face ventilation, pediatric mask over stoma for stoma ventilation
nodes.body: EMCrit "Double-bagging" approach: Apply oxygen to BOTH sites simultaneously: 1. Non-rebreather or BVM to face 2. Tracheostomy collar or pediatric face mask to stoma When ventilating via face: - Occlude stoma with gauze or finger - Prevents air leak through stoma - May need to deflate trach cuff When ventilating via stoma: - Occlude nose and mouth - Or use tracheostomy BVM adapter - Pediatric face

nodes.title: Oral Intubation with Tracheostomy
nodes.summary: Uncut ETT, advance cuff past stoma level, occlude stoma, confirm with capnography
nodes.body: When to intubate orally: - Fresh trach dislodgement (< 7 days) - Failed stoma replacement - Cannot ventilate through stoma - Upper airway confirmed patent Technique: 1. Standard oral intubation approach 2. Use UNCUT endotracheal tube 3. Advance cuff PAST the tracheostomy stoma level 4. Confirm placement with capnography 5. Occlude stoma to prevent air leak Considerations: - May need to deflate tra

nodes.title: Granulation Tissue
nodes.summary: Fenestrated tubes and chronic irritation cause granulation — bronchoscopy for diagnosis and treatment
nodes.body: Granulation tissue formation: Causes: - Tube friction against tracheal wall - Fenestrated tubes (tissue grows through holes) - Chronic irritation - Infection - High cuff pressure Presentation: - Recurrent obstruction - Bleeding with suctioning - Difficulty passing suction catheter - Stridor after tube removal Management: - Bronchoscopy for diagnosis and treatment - Silver nitrate cautery - Laser a

nodes.title: Tracheal Stenosis
nodes.summary: 3-12% develop stenosis — high cuff pressure most common cause, bronchoscopy is gold standard diagnosis
nodes.body: Post-tracheostomy tracheal stenosis (PTTS): Incidence: 3-12% develop clinically significant stenosis Causes: - High cuff pressure (most common) - Infection - Excessive tube movement - Prolonged intubation before trach - Low trach placement Presentation: - Failure to wean from ventilator - High peak airway pressures - Difficulty passing suction catheter - Stridor after decannulation - Dyspnea on ex

nodes.title: Tracheo-Innominate Fistula
nodes.summary: TIF is near-100% fatal without surgery; sentinel bleed precedes massive hemorrhage by 24-48 hours
nodes.body: TIF Steps Summary Tracheo-Innominate Fistula (TIF) is a catastrophic complication of tracheostomy with near-100% mortality without intervention and 50-70% mortality even with surgery. [1][2] Key Principle: Massive hemorrhage occurring 3 days to 6 weeks after tracheostomy is TIF until proven otherwise. [1][3] Incidence: 0.1-1% of tracheostomies; accounts for ~10% of significant tracheostomy bleeds.

nodes.title: Timing of Bleeding
nodes.summary: Stratify by time since tracheostomy: 3d-6wk is TIF window, <72h usually benign, >6wk less likely
nodes.body: The timing of tracheostomy bleeding is critical for risk stratification. [1][2] TIF time window: 3 days to 6 weeks post-tracheostomy - Peak incidence: 7-14 days (first 3 weeks = 72% of cases) - Minimum development time: 48 hours post-procedure - Late presentations (>1 year) documented but rare Early bleeding (<72 hours): Usually benign [5] - Suctioning trauma - Manipulation injury - Surgical site

nodes.title: Early Bleeding (<72h)
nodes.summary: Early trach bleeding usually benign — suctioning, manipulation, coagulopathy; escalate if arterial or >50 mL
nodes.body: Early bleeding is usually benign but warrants evaluation. [5] Common causes: - Suctioning trauma - Manipulation/movement - Surgical site oozing - Coagulopathy - Granulation tissue (forming) Management: - Gentle suctioning to assess source - Check coagulation studies - Evaluate for proper tube positioning - Local hemostatic measures - Optimize cuff pressure (20-25 cm H2O) Red flags requiring escala

nodes.title: Late Bleeding (>6 Weeks)
nodes.summary: Late trach bleeding often granulation tissue; arterial/pulsatile features still warrant full TIF protocol
nodes.body: Late bleeding is less commonly TIF but still possible. [2] Common causes: - Granulation tissue (most common) - Stoma infection - Tracheitis - Mucosal erosion - Malignancy (rare) Late TIF still occurs: - Case reports of TIF >1 year post-tracheostomy - Risk factors: high cuff pressure, chronic inflammation Evaluate based on bleeding characteristics: Low concern (granulation tissue): - Small volume,

nodes.title: Sentinel Bleed Recognition
nodes.summary: 50% of TIF patients have sentinel bleed; pulsating trach tube + bleeding = pathognomonic triad; CTA only 20-30% sensitive
nodes.body: The sentinel bleed is your warning sign. [1][4] Definition: A brief, self-limited hemorrhage that spontaneously stops - preceding catastrophic massive hemorrhage by 24-48 hours. Key statistics: [4] - 50% of TIF patients have sentinel bleed before massive hemorrhage - Only 35% exhibit the "pathognomonic triad" Pathognomonic triad: [1] 1. Sentinel bleeding (small bleed that stops) 2. Pulsations of t

nodes.title: Sentinel Bleed Management
nodes.summary: Sentinel bleed = imminent hemorrhage; call surgery STAT, activate MTP, type & cross, NPO for OR
nodes.body: A sentinel bleed is NOT reassuring - it is a WARNING. [1][4] Sentinel bleed = imminent massive hemorrhage within 24-48 hours. [4] IMMEDIATE actions: 1. Call surgery STAT (CT surgery/vascular/trauma) 2. Activate MTP - have blood at bedside 3. Type and crossmatch - anticipate massive transfusion 4. Keep patient NPO - prepare for emergent OR 5. Do NOT send for imaging if it delays surgical consultati

nodes.title: Lower Risk Bleeding
nodes.body: If bleeding is truly low-risk, conservative management may be appropriate. [5] Low-risk features: - Small volume (<10 mL) - Venous-appearing (dark) - Associated with manipulation/suctioning - Self-limited and non-recurrent - No pulsatile component - Tube NOT pulsating with heartbeat Management: - Gentle suctioning - Check cuff pressure (20-25 cm H2O) - Humidification optimization - Evaluate for in
nodes.recommendation: Conservative management appropriate if truly low-risk. Monitor closely for 48 hours. Any recurrence or change in bleeding character warrants immediate TIF workup.

nodes.title: Hyperinflate Cuff - First Maneuver
nodes.summary: Hyperinflate trach cuff to ~50 mL as first maneuver — 85% success rate, temporizing only, prepare for OR
nodes.body: Cuff hyperinflation is the FIRST-LINE maneuver for TIF bleeding. [1][6] Technique: 1. Slowly add air to the tracheostomy cuff balloon 2. Target: ~50 mL total volume (much higher than normal) 3. Goal: Tamponade the bleeding vessel by compressing against tracheal wall Success rate: 85% [6] 2024 data: Cuff overinflation reduced mortality from 80% to 52.2% (p<0.001). [4] Critical points: - This is a t

nodes.title: Cuff Hyperinflation Result
nodes.summary: Assess cuff hyperinflation response; bleeding past cuff means fistula is proximal — proceed to Utley maneuver
nodes.body: Assess response to cuff hyperinflation. [1][6] Monitor for: - Cessation of bleeding - Reduction in bleeding volume - Blood in suction catheter If bleeding continues: - Fistula may be proximal to the cuff - Cuff may not be achieving adequate tamponade - Proceed to finger tamponade (Utley maneuver) If bleeding stops: - DO NOT relax vigilance - DO NOT move the tube - Maintain cuff inflation - Continu

nodes.title: Cuff Hyperinflation Successful
nodes.summary: Cuff tamponade successful but NOT definitive — do not move tube, suction, or deflate; continue to OR
nodes.body: Bleeding controlled - but this is NOT definitive treatment. [1][6] Maintain strict precautions: DO: - Keep cuff hyperinflated - Keep patient completely still - Continue surgical preparation - Maintain MTP activation - Have finger tamponade equipment ready - Keep oral ETT at bedside DO NOT: - Move the tracheostomy tube - Deflate the cuff - Suction through the trach - Send patient for imaging - Dela

nodes.title: Partial Bleeding Control
nodes.summary: Partial control: add oral ETT deep past stoma for additional tamponade, or replace trach with cuffed ETT
nodes.body: If bleeding is reduced but not stopped: [1][6] Option 1 - Add oral ETT: 1. Have assistant continue to add air to trach cuff 2. Perform oral intubation with DEEP advancement 3. ETT cuff should be 2 cm past the stoma site 4. Inflate ETT cuff for additional tamponade 5. This provides backup airway if trach fails Option 2 - Replace trach with cuffed ETT through stoma: 1. Remove tracheostomy tube 2. In

nodes.title: Finger Tamponade - Utley Maneuver
nodes.summary: Utley maneuver is the lifesaving bedside intervention — >80% success; provider stays attached to patient until OR
nodes.body: The Utley maneuver is THE lifesaving bedside intervention when cuff hyperinflation fails. [1][7] Success rate: >80% for controlling hemorrhage via direct tamponade. [7] CRITICAL RULE: The provider who performs this maneuver MUST NOT MOVE THEIR FINGER until the patient is in the OR under surgical care. [1][7] You will be physically attached to this patient during transport to OR. Before starting: 1

nodes.title: Utley Maneuver - Step by Step
nodes.summary: Secure oral ETT first, remove trach, finger through stoma into pretracheal space, compress artery vs sternum
nodes.body: Finger Tamponade Technique: [1][7] Step 1 - Secure Airway: - Deflate tracheostomy cuff - Insert cuffed oral ETT deep (cuff 2 cm past stoma) - Inflate ETT cuff - Confirm ventilation Step 2 - Remove Tracheostomy: - With airway secured, remove tracheostomy tube - May need to extend stoma incision vertically for access Step 3 - Insert Finger: - Insert index finger through stoma into pretracheal space

nodes.title: Utley Maneuver Considerations
nodes.summary: Extend stoma if too small; external sternal notch pressure as alternative; maintain pressure during OR transport
nodes.body: Practical considerations for finger tamponade: [1][7] Anatomic orientation: - Innominate artery crosses anterior to trachea - Usually at rings 6-9, but can be higher (high-riding variant) - Your finger compresses artery between itself and sternum Stoma too small? - Extend incision inferiorly with scalpel - Blunt dissection of pretracheal space - You need enough room to maneuver Alternative if cann

nodes.title: Surgical Activation
nodes.summary: Mortality without surgery ~100%, with surgery 50-70%; call CT surgery/vascular STAT, prepare sternotomy tray
nodes.body: TIF is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. [1][2][8] Mortality without surgery: ~100% [2] Mortality with surgery: 50-70% (but survival is possible) [4] Call IMMEDIATELY: - CT surgery / Cardiothoracic surgery - Vascular surgery - Trauma surgery (depending on institution) - Anesthesia - OR charge nurse Information for surgical team: - Time of tracheostomy placement - Current bleeding status - Interventions perfor

nodes.title: Surgical Management Options
nodes.summary: Ligate AND divide innominate artery; ligation alone risks re-fistulization; endovascular stent-graft emerging option
nodes.body: Definitive surgical management: [2][8] Standard approach - Median sternotomy: 1. Median sternotomy (or collar + partial upper sternotomy) 2. Identify innominate artery and fistula 3. Ligate AND divide innominate artery proximal and distal to fistula 4. Cover tracheal defect with muscle flap (usually pectoralis major) CRITICAL: Ligation WITHOUT division is contraindicated - artery can re-fistulize.

nodes.title: Stabilization
nodes.summary: Activate MTP with 1:1:1 ratio, large-bore IV x2, airway backup plan, TXA per protocol
nodes.body: Resuscitation while preparing for OR: [1][3] Massive Transfusion Protocol: - Activate immediately - Blood products at bedside - Anticipate massive blood loss (liters) - 1:1:1 ratio PRBCs:FFP:Platelets IV Access: - Large-bore IV x2 minimum - Consider central line if time permits - Rapid infuser ready Airway Management: - If trach in place with controlled bleeding: leave it - If finger tamponade: or

nodes.title: Critical DO NOTs
nodes.summary: Never remove trach unless doing Utley; never delay for imaging; never ligate without division; never release finger tamponade
nodes.body: Actions that can be FATAL in TIF: [1][3] DO NOT: 1. Remove the tracheostomy tube unless proceeding to finger tamponade - The tube provides tamponade and airway 2. Delay for imaging if clinical suspicion is high - CTA/bronchoscopy only 20-30% sensitive - Clinical diagnosis is sufficient 3. Attempt ligation without division - Artery can re-fistulize - Must ligate AND divide 4. Suction aggressively t

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: All TIF patients go directly to OR. [1][2] There is no observation period for suspected TIF. Disposition pathway: 1. ED/ICU recognition 2. Immediate hemorrhage control (cuff/finger tamponade) 3. Surgical activation 4. Direct transport to OR 5. Postoperative ICU Postoperative considerations: [8] - ICU admission mandatory - Vigilant neuro monitoring (right-sided deficits possible) - Airway managemen
nodes.recommendation: Direct transport to OR for definitive surgical management. Postoperative ICU admission. Monitor for neurological deficits and re-bleeding.

nodes.title: TGA — ED Evaluation
nodes.body: Steps Summary Classic Presentation: • Sudden onset anterograde amnesia • Repetitive questioning ("What day is it?" "Why am I here?") • Personal identity preserved • No focal neurologic deficits • Resolves within 24 hours Key History (from witness): • Exact onset time • Precipitating event (physical exertion, emotional stress, Valsalva, water immersion) • Witnessed seizure activity? • Recent head t

nodes.title: TGA — Diagnostic Criteria
nodes.body: Hodges & Warlow Diagnostic Criteria (1990): ALL must be present: 1. ✓ Attack witnessed by capable observer 2. ✓ Clear-cut anterograde amnesia during attack 3. ✓ No clouding of consciousness or loss of personal identity 4. ✓ No focal neurologic signs during or after attack 5. ✓ No epileptic features 6. ✓ No recent head injury 7. ✓ Resolution within 24 hours Supportive features: • Age typically 50-8

nodes.title: TGA Confirmed — Pathophysiology
nodes.body: Transient Global Amnesia — Confirmed: Epidemiology: • Incidence: 3-8 per 100,000/year • Peak age: 50-70 years • Rare <40 years (consider epilepsy) • Slight female predominance Proposed mechanisms: • Transient hippocampal dysfunction • Venous congestion (Valsalva, jugular reflux) • Cortical spreading depression • NOT ischemic stroke (despite DWI lesions) Common triggers: • Physical exertion • Emoti

nodes.title: Stroke Workup — TGA Mimic
nodes.body: Posterior Circulation Stroke vs TGA: Red flags for stroke: • Focal neurologic deficits (even transient) • Vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria • Visual field cut • Ataxia • Duration >24 hours • Vascular risk factors prominent Thalamic/PCA stroke can cause: • Anterograde amnesia (similar to TGA) • But usually has other posterior circulation signs Workup: • Non-contrast CT head (rule out hemorrhage) • MRI

nodes.title: Transient Epileptic Amnesia
nodes.body: Transient Epileptic Amnesia (TEA) vs TGA: Suspect TEA if: • Episodes <1 hour (TGA usually 4-8 hours) • Recurrent episodes (TGA rarely recurs) • Occurs upon waking • Subtle automatisms or lip smacking • History of epilepsy • Younger patient (<50) TEA features: • Brief episodes of isolated amnesia • May be only seizure manifestation • Often temporal lobe origin • Responds to antiepileptics Workup: •

nodes.title: Post-Traumatic Amnesia
nodes.body: Post-Traumatic Amnesia vs TGA: Key difference: Recent head injury Post-traumatic amnesia (PTA): • Occurs after head trauma • Duration correlates with injury severity • May have retrograde + anterograde components • Often associated with other TBI findings Assessment: • CT head per Canadian CT Head Rule or PECARN • GCS monitoring • Repeated neuro exams • Consider MRI if persistent deficits Manageme

nodes.title: Other TGA Mimics
nodes.body: Differential Diagnosis: Vascular: • Posterior circulation TIA/stroke • Thalamic infarct • Subarachnoid hemorrhage Epileptic: • Transient epileptic amnesia • Post-ictal confusion • Complex partial status Toxic/Metabolic: • Hypoglycemia • Wernicke encephalopathy • Drug intoxication (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics) • Carbon monoxide Psychiatric: • Dissociative amnesia (psychogenic) • Malingering I

nodes.title: TGA — Workup Strategy
nodes.body: ED Workup for TGA: Minimal workup (classic presentation): • Fingerstick glucose • Basic labs if indicated (CBC, BMP) • ECG (atrial fibrillation screening) Extended workup (atypical features): • CT head (rule out hemorrhage, mass) • MRI with DWI (posterior circulation stroke, hippocampal lesions) • EEG (if seizure suspected) • CTA (vascular risk factors) MRI findings in TGA: • Small punctate DWI le

nodes.title: TGA — Imaging
nodes.body: Imaging in TGA: CT Head: • Usually normal in TGA • Rules out hemorrhage, mass • Reasonable first-line for atypical cases MRI Brain (DWI): • Gold standard if obtained • Small hippocampal DWI lesions in 70-80% • Best seen 24-72 hours after symptom onset • CA1 region of hippocampus most affected • Lesions resolve without infarction Timing of MRI: • If needed, can do in ED or within 24-72h outpatient

nodes.title: TGA — Prognosis
nodes.body: Excellent Prognosis: Natural history: • Complete resolution within 24 hours (usually 4-8h) • Dense amnesia for the event itself persists • Retrograde amnesia for hours-days before event • Full cognitive recovery otherwise Recurrence: • Annual recurrence rate: 2-3% • Lifetime recurrence: 6-10% • If frequent recurrence: reconsider diagnosis (TEP?) Long-term outcomes: • NO increased stroke risk • NO

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition considerations: Admit if: • Persistent deficits >24 hours • Focal neurologic signs • Stroke on imaging • Recurrent episodes needing EEG • Diagnostic uncertainty Discharge if: • Classic TGA criteria met • Symptoms resolving or resolved • No focal deficits • Safe home environment • Reliable follow-up What is the clinical status? *Basis: the admit triggers listed (duration >24 hours, foca

nodes.title: TGA — Observation
nodes.body: Observation Protocol: If symptoms ongoing: • Serial neuro exams q1-2h • Monitor for resolution • Most resolve within 4-8 hours • Max duration by definition: 24 hours Reassess at 4-6 hours: • Improving → continue observation, plan discharge • Worsening or focal signs → CT/MRI, neuro consult Reassess at 24 hours: • Resolved → discharge with follow-up • NOT resolved → no longer TGA, admit for workup

nodes.title: Discharge — TGA Resolved
nodes.body: Discharge — Classic TGA: Criteria: • Symptoms fully resolved • No focal deficits • Normal mental status • Able to form new memories • Safe home environment with observer Instructions: • TGA is benign, NOT a stroke • Patient will NOT remember the episode • This is normal and expected • Low recurrence risk (2-3%/year) • No specific treatment needed Activity: • No driving for 24-48 hours (patient dis
nodes.recommendation: Discharge home. Classic TGA, benign prognosis. No driving 24-48h. PCP follow-up 1-2 weeks. Return for new symptoms.

nodes.title: Admit — Stroke Identified
nodes.body: Admission for Stroke: If stroke identified on workup: • This is NOT TGA • Follow standard stroke protocols • Admit to stroke service/neuro ICU Standard stroke workup: • MRI DWI if not done • CTA head/neck • Echo (TTE or TEE) • Telemetry • Lipids, A1c • Hypercoagulability workup if young Treatment: • Antiplatelet therapy • Statin • Risk factor modification • Consider thrombolysis if within window a
nodes.recommendation: Admit stroke service. This is NOT TGA. Follow stroke protocol.

nodes.title: Admit — Diagnostic Uncertainty
nodes.body: Admission for Workup: Indications: • Symptoms >24 hours • Recurrent episodes • Atypical features • Cannot rule out stroke/seizure • Young patient (<50) Workup: • MRI brain with DWI • EEG (routine or prolonged) • Continuous telemetry • Neurology consult If TEA suspected: • EEG (may need sleep-deprived) • Trial of antiepileptic If vascular concern: • Complete stroke workup • Echo, CTA Observation: •
nodes.recommendation: Admit for observation and workup. MRI, EEG, neuro consult. Monitor for resolution.

nodes.title: Acute Transverse Myelitis
nodes.summary: Acute cord inflammation: bilateral weakness + sensory level + sphincter dysfunction. ED job = exclude compression first.
nodes.body: Transverse myelitis (TM) is an acute inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord producing a band of motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below the lesion. "Transverse" = across the cord at one or more segments. The triad that says "this is the cord": - Bilateral motor weakness (para- or quadriparesis) - A sensory level — a horizontal line below which sensation changes - Sphincter/autonomic dysf

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation & Localization
nodes.summary: Establish sensory level + post-void residual. Any compression red flag → MRI now.
nodes.body: Map the deficit: - Sensory level — test pinprick/temperature ascending up the trunk until it normalizes; that dermatome localizes the lesion (thoracic most common). - Weakness — bilateral, often initially flaccid (spinal shock) then spastic with hyperreflexia + Babinski over days. - Bladder/bowel — urinary retention or incontinence; always check a post-void residual. - Back pain at the level in ~o

nodes.title: ROOT GATE: Emergent MRI to Exclude Compression
nodes.summary: MRI whole cord with + without gad BEFORE LP. Compression = surgery; intrinsic signal = inflammatory workup.
nodes.body: This is the decision the whole consult hinges on. Transverse myelitis is a diagnosis of exclusion — you cannot call cord dysfunction "inflammatory" until you have ruled out a surgically correctable compressive lesion. Order: MRI of the spinal cord, WITH and WITHOUT gadolinium. - Image the clinically suspected level plus the whole cord — multifocal disease and skip lesions are common, and a cervica

nodes.title: Compressive Myelopathy — Off-Ramp
nodes.summary: Compression = surgical emergency. Abscess → abx + decompress; hematoma → reverse + decompress; mets → dex + rad-onc.
nodes.body: This is not transverse myelitis. This is a surgical spinal emergency. Immediate actions by lesion: - Epidural abscess — blood cultures, broad-spectrum abx covering MRSA (vancomycin) + gram-negatives; emergent neurosurgery for decompression. Do NOT wait for cultures. - Epidural hematoma — reverse anticoagulation, emergent neurosurgery. - Metastatic cord compression — dexamethasone 10 mg IV then 4 m
nodes.recommendation: Compressive myelopathy is a neurosurgical emergency, not inflammatory myelitis. Consult neurosurgery immediately. For abscess: empiric vancomycin + gram-negative coverage and source control. For mets: high-dose dexamethasone + rad-onc. Do n

nodes.title: Inflammatory Workup (after compression excluded)
nodes.summary: LP (cells, protein, OCB) + serum AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG, B12/HIV/RPR, plus MRI brain. Antibody status changes therapy.
nodes.body: CSF (LP): - Cell count + differential (pleocytosis supports inflammation; >50 lymphocytes seen in MS/idiopathic, neutrophils suggest infection) - Protein (often elevated) - Oligoclonal bands + IgG index (positive favors MS) - Infectious studies as indicated: HSV/VZV PCR, enterovirus, VDRL Serum (the antibody triad reframes the disease): - AQP4-IgG (aquaporin-4) — neuromyelitis optica spectrum diso

nodes.title: Transverse Myelitis Consortium Criteria (2002)
nodes.summary: 2002 criteria: bilateral cord signs + sensory level + inflammation + nadir 4h-21d; exclude compression/infarct/AVM/radiation.
nodes.body: Transverse Myelitis Consortium Working Group (2002) — the operational standard for idiopathic ATM. INCLUSION (all required): 1. Bilateral (not necessarily symmetric) sensory, motor, or autonomic dysfunction attributable to the cord 2. A clearly defined sensory level 3. Inflammation: CSF pleocytosis or elevated IgG index, or gadolinium enhancement on MRI (if absent initially, repeat 2-7 days later)

nodes.title: Etiology Buckets
nodes.summary: Buckets: demyelinating (MS/NMOSD/MOGAD), para/post-infectious, direct infection, systemic autoimmune, paraneoplastic, idiopathic. Lesion length triages MS vs NMOSD.
nodes.body: Classify the cause — it drives long-term treatment: Demyelinating / autoimmune - Multiple sclerosis (usually short-segment, <2 segments, partial) - NMOSD (AQP4-IgG; longitudinally extensive, ≥3 segments) - MOGAD (MOG-IgG; often LETM, conus involvement, better recovery) Parainfectious / post-infectious (commonest in kids) - After viral illness or vaccination — immune-mediated Direct infection - HSV

nodes.title: Acute Treatment
nodes.summary: IV methylpred 1 g/day x3-5d first line; PLEX for refractory/severe NMOSD (start early if AQP4+). Cover infection before steroids if plausible.
nodes.body: First line — high-dose IV corticosteroids: - Methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily x 3-5 days (pediatric 30 mg/kg/day, max 1 g). - Start once compression is excluded and active untreated infection is reasonably considered/covered. Steroids-before-infection caveat (FLAGGED — confirm locally): if epidural abscess or active CNS infection (e.g., HSV myelitis) is plausible, treat/cover the infection and disc

nodes.title: Differential & Must-Not-Miss Mimics
nodes.summary: Mimics: compression (surgical), cord infarct (nadir <12h, no enhancement), GBS (no level), cauda equina, DAVF, B12. Tempo + MRI + CSF separate them.
nodes.body: 1. Compressive myelopathy (MUST NOT MISS — already gated above): abscess, hematoma, tumor, disc. MRI distinguishes. Surgical. 2. Spinal cord infarct (anterior spinal artery): - Hyperacute — maximal at onset / nadir <12 h (vs TM's 4h-21d climb) - Anterior cord syndrome: motor + spinothalamic loss, dorsal columns spared - Often painful at onset; risk factors = aortic disease/surgery, hypotension - M

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit all acute myelopathy. ICU for cervical/respiratory/autonomic risk. Neuro ± neurosurgery; bladder care, DVT ppx, rehab.
nodes.body: Admit every acute myelopathy. - Neurology consult for all suspected TM; neurosurgery if any compressive component. - ICU/step-down if: cervical lesion with respiratory compromise, rapid ascending progression, or autonomic instability. - High cervical lesions can impair the diaphragm (C3-5) — monitor respiratory function. In-hospital: - Continue IV steroids; arrange PLEX if refractory. - Bladder sc

nodes.title: Prognosis
nodes.summary: Rule of thirds for recovery; most gains by 3-6 months. LETM/AQP4+/complete syndromes do worse. Recurrence → hunt NMOSD/MOGAD/MS.
nodes.body: Rule of thirds (idiopathic ATM): - ~1/3 good/full recovery - ~1/3 moderate residual deficit - ~1/3 poor recovery / severe disability Recovery usually begins within 1-3 months; most gains by 3-6 months, continuing up to 2 years. Worse prognosis: - Rapid progression to nadir / hyperacute onset - Complete (vs partial) cord syndrome; spinal shock with flaccidity - Longitudinally extensive lesion (LETM
nodes.recommendation: Exclude compression with emergent MRI, establish a sensory level and post-void residual, send LP + serum AQP4-IgG/MOG-IgG, and start IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day x 3-5 days once compression is excluded and infection considered/covered. PLE

nodes.title: Traumatic Arrest
nodes.summary: Treat traumatic arrest by correcting reversible trauma physiology immediately.
nodes.body: Traumatic arrest is managed by rapidly correcting reversible trauma physiology rather than defaulting to a medical arrest algorithm. Immediate priorities: - Announce traumatic arrest and assign task leads - Treat HOTT causes: hypovolemia, oxygenation, tension pneumothorax, tamponade - Activate trauma surgery, MTP, airway, ultrasound, and OR/IR pathways - Decide early whether resuscitative thoracot

nodes.title: Confirm Scenario
nodes.summary: Separate true traumatic arrest from peri-arrest shock or primary medical arrest.
nodes.body: Which scenario best describes the patient right now?

nodes.title: Peri-Arrest Traumatic Shock
nodes.summary: Peri-arrest shock needs the same source-control urgency as pulseless arrest.
nodes.body: Treat as imminent traumatic arrest. Do now: - Activate trauma team, MTP, OR/IR, and massive hemorrhage resources - Place pelvic binder if pelvic injury possible - Control external hemorrhage with tourniquet/pressure/hemostatic packing - Bilateral chest decompression if severe chest trauma or obstructive physiology - Intubate only if it will not delay hemorrhage control, thoracostomy, or thoracotom

nodes.title: Consider Primary Medical Arrest
nodes.summary: Use medical ACLS if trauma is secondary, while actively excluding traumatic causes.
nodes.body: If trauma appears secondary to a medical collapse, use the standard cardiac arrest pathway while still screening for occult traumatic causes. Minimum trauma screen: - Bilateral breath sounds and chest exam - eFAST if available - Hemorrhage check, pelvis assessment, long-bone deformity - Temperature and tox/metabolic clues when relevant If major injury, hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, or tamponad
nodes.recommendation: Run medical ACLS when arrest is likely primary medical, but do not miss reversible traumatic causes.

nodes.title: Immediate HOTT Bundle
nodes.summary: Correct hemorrhage, oxygenation, tension pneumothorax, and tamponade in parallel.
nodes.body: Assign simultaneous tasks. Do not wait for serial completion. H - Hypovolemia / hemorrhage - Direct pressure, tourniquets, pelvic binder, MTP, rapid source control O - Oxygenation / airway - High-flow oxygen, airway control as needed, confirm ventilation with waveform ETCO2 T - Tension pneumothorax - Bilateral finger thoracostomies or chest tubes in traumatic arrest with chest trauma or suspected

nodes.title: Mechanism Drives Thoracotomy Threshold
nodes.summary: Penetrating thoracic arrest has the strongest thoracotomy indication.
nodes.body: What is the arrest mechanism?

nodes.title: Pregnant Traumatic Arrest
nodes.summary: Maternal resuscitation first; perform resuscitative hysterotomy when indicated.
nodes.body: Use standard traumatic arrest priorities plus pregnancy-specific actions. Do now: - Manual left uterine displacement - Resuscitate mother first - Activate OB, trauma, anesthesia, neonatology - If uterus is at/above umbilicus and no ROSC by 4 minutes, proceed to resuscitative hysterotomy pathway Continue HOTT treatment simultaneously. Thoracic indications do not disappear because the patient is pre

nodes.title: Penetrating Trauma: Signs of Life / CPR Time
nodes.summary: Penetrating arrest with signs of life and short CPR favors thoracotomy.
nodes.body: Assess signs of life and downtime immediately. Signs of life include pupillary response, spontaneous ventilation, palpable pulse/BP, organized cardiac electrical activity, cardiac motion on ultrasound, or extremity movement.

nodes.title: Blunt Trauma: Very Selective Thoracotomy
nodes.summary: Blunt arrest thoracotomy is exceptional and requires strict selection.
nodes.body: Survival after blunt traumatic arrest is low. Consider thoracotomy only for a highly selected patient with witnessed arrest, signs of life, short CPR interval, and a team capable of immediate definitive care.

nodes.title: Resuscitative Thoracotomy: Indicated / Strongly Consider
nodes.summary: Appropriate penetrating arrest should trigger rapid thoracotomy and OR mobilization.
nodes.body: Proceed if local skill, staffing, and surgical backup are available. Primary goals: - Relieve tamponade - Control cardiac or hilar hemorrhage - Perform open cardiac massage - Cross-clamp descending thoracic aorta when appropriate - Bridge to OR for definitive repair Open the dedicated 2-minute procedure review before or during setup if time allows. Thoracotomy Procedure
nodes.recommendation: Proceed with resuscitative thoracotomy for appropriate penetrating traumatic arrest while continuing blood resuscitation and source control.

nodes.title: Blunt Arrest: Consider Thoracotomy Only If Selected
nodes.summary: Blunt thoracotomy is selective; no signs of life generally argues against it.
nodes.body: Thoracotomy after blunt trauma is a narrow decision. Reasonable to consider when all are present: - Witnessed arrest or arrest immediately before ED arrival - Signs of life or cardiac motion - Short CPR interval, generally <10 minutes - Potentially correctable thoracic cause - Trauma surgeon/proceduralist and OR pathway immediately available Avoid thoracotomy for blunt arrest without signs of life
nodes.recommendation: Discuss immediately with trauma surgery. Proceed only for selected blunt arrest with signs of life and short CPR interval.

nodes.title: Airway / Oxygenation Priorities
nodes.summary: Airway matters, but source control should not wait for a prolonged airway attempt.
nodes.body: Oxygenation is a reversible cause, but airway procedures should not delay hemorrhage control, bilateral thoracostomy, or thoracotomy. Practical sequence: - BVM with high-flow oxygen while other tasks start - Intubate when it can be done rapidly with minimal interruption - Confirm with waveform capnography - Avoid hyperventilation unless herniation is suspected - Reassess chest rise after decompres

nodes.title: Bilateral Finger Thoracostomies / Chest Tubes
nodes.summary: Bilateral decompression rapidly treats occult tension physiology.
nodes.body: In traumatic arrest with chest trauma, positive pressure ventilation, or suspected obstructive physiology, decompress both chests early. Approach: - 4th/5th intercostal space, anterior-to-mid axillary line - Incise, blunt dissect over superior rib, enter pleura, finger sweep - Convert to chest tubes after immediate decompression when feasible - Large hemothorax or massive air leak should trigger o

nodes.title: Hemorrhage Control / MTP
nodes.summary: Control external bleeding and move rapidly to definitive hemorrhage control.
nodes.body: Exsanguination is the most common reversible cause of traumatic arrest. Do now: - Direct pressure, tourniquet, wound packing, junctional pressure device when available - Pelvic binder if pelvic injury is possible - Activate MTP with balanced RBC/plasma/platelets per local protocol - Calcium replacement during high-volume transfusion - TXA if major hemorrhage and within 3 hours of injury per local

nodes.title: Pelvis / Noncompressible Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: Binder, blood, and source control are time-critical for pelvic exsanguination.
nodes.body: If pelvic or junctional hemorrhage is possible, treat during arrest rather than after ROSC. Actions: - Pelvic binder at greater trochanters - Pack open pelvic/perineal wounds - Activate OR/IR early - Consider REBOA only where trained team, equipment, and definitive hemorrhage control are immediately available - Avoid crystalloid-heavy resuscitation Pelvic Fracture Management

nodes.title: POCUS During Traumatic Arrest
nodes.summary: Use POCUS for immediate decisions, not as a delay before life-saving interventions.
nodes.body: Use ultrasound only when it answers an immediate resuscitation question and does not delay procedures. Useful targets: - Cardiac motion vs standstill - Pericardial effusion/tamponade - Massive intraperitoneal fluid - Pneumothorax if thoracostomy has not already been performed Do not let ultrasound replace empiric bilateral decompression or indicated thoracotomy in an arresting trauma patient.

nodes.title: ROSC / Transient Response
nodes.summary: ROSC is a bridge to OR/IR/source control.
nodes.body: ROSC after traumatic arrest is a bridge to definitive source control, not the endpoint. Immediate post-ROSC priorities: - Maintain oxygenation and normocapnia - Continue balanced blood-product resuscitation - Correct calcium, temperature, acidosis, and coagulopathy - Repeat eFAST/CXR/pelvic assessment as needed - Move to OR/IR/CT only when hemodynamically appropriate - If thoracotomy performed, tr
nodes.recommendation: Treat ROSC as temporary until hemorrhage, tamponade, tension physiology, and contamination are definitively controlled.

nodes.title: Termination / Withholding Considerations
nodes.summary: Document reversible causes treated and objective futility markers.
nodes.body: Consider withholding or terminating resuscitation when survival is not physiologically plausible after reversible causes have been addressed. Factors supporting termination: - Injuries incompatible with life - No signs of life and prolonged downtime - Asystole with no cardiac motion after HOTT interventions - Blunt traumatic arrest without signs of life - No response after hemorrhage control, oxyg
nodes.recommendation: Terminate when reversible traumatic causes have been addressed and ongoing resuscitation is futile by mechanism, downtime, rhythm, and cardiac activity.

nodes.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia — ED Approach
nodes.summary: Unilateral V2/V3 electric-shock pain, seconds-min, triggered by light touch. ICHD-3 §13.1.1.
nodes.body: Paroxysmal, unilateral, electric-shock / stabbing facial pain confined to one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (V1/V2/V3 — most commonly V2 maxillary or V3 mandibular; pure V1 is rare and should prompt a hunt for secondary cause). Each paroxysm lasts seconds to <2 min; bouts of many paroxysms per day are typical. Triggered by innocuous stimuli to the face: chewing, talking, brushing teeth

nodes.title: Does this fit ICHD-3 §13.1.1 trigeminal neuralgia?
nodes.summary: ICHD-3 §13.1.1: paroxysmal unilateral V-distribution, seconds-2 min, innocuous trigger. Atypical → MRI first.
nodes.body: Required (all): - A. Recurrent paroxysms of unilateral facial pain in distribution of one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve, with no radiation beyond - B. Pain has all 3 of: • Lasts fraction of a second to 2 min • Severe intensity • Electric shock-like, shooting, stabbing, or sharp quality - C. Precipitated by innocuous stimuli within the affected trigeminal distribution - D. Not better ac

nodes.title: Secondary-Cause Screen — Who Needs an MRI?
nodes.summary: MRI (FIESTA/CISS) standard pre-Rx. Vascular loop (60-80%), MS (2-4%), structural lesion (5-10%). Refer accordingly.
nodes.body: MRI brain with contrast + dedicated FIESTA/CISS trigeminal sequences is the standard pre-treatment imaging in modern guidelines (AAN/EFNS Cruccu 2008, EAN 2019). High-yield in patients <40 yo, bilateral pain, sensory deficit, atypical phenotype, or any TN refractory to maximum-tolerated CBZ. Three imaging-defined etiologies — different management implications: 1. Vascular loop / neurovascular conf

nodes.title: Atypical TN — MRI Before Pharmacotherapy
nodes.body: Atypical features make secondary TN likely. Order MRI brain with contrast + FIESTA/CISS trigeminal sequences BEFORE starting carbamazepine. Findings and next steps: - MS plaque at trigeminal root → neurology referral; treat MS per disease-modifying protocol; symptomatic TN therapy follows the same ladder (CBZ → oxcarb → adjuncts) but expect lower MVD success if surgery considered later - Vestibula
nodes.recommendation: MRI first; bridge with IV phenytoin/fosphenytoin if severe; defer chronic CBZ until imaging and HLA cleared.

nodes.title: Burchiel Classification (TN1 vs TN2)
nodes.summary: TN1 = purely paroxysmal (best MVD candidate). TN2 = paroxysmal + constant baseline (lower MVD success, lower CBZ response).
nodes.body: The Burchiel classification (Neurosurgery 2003) refines ICHD-3 by the presence of constant baseline pain — useful for surgical prognostication. TN1 — Classical (purely paroxysmal): - >50% of pain is episodic, paroxysmal, electric shock-like - Pain-free or near-pain-free between paroxysms - Best response to CBZ - Best MVD surgical candidate — 90% immediate pain relief, ~70% sustained at 10 years (B

nodes.title: BEFORE Starting Carbamazepine — HLA-B*1502 Screen
nodes.summary: HLA-B*1502 screen BEFORE CBZ in Han Chinese / Thai / Vietnamese / Filipino / Malay / Indonesian ancestry. Positive → avoid BOTH CBZ + oxcarb. Counsel rash warning.
nodes.body: 🛑 FDA BOXED WARNING (2007). Before the first dose of carbamazepine OR oxcarbazepine in a patient with ancestry from a population where the HLA-B\\*1502 allele is prevalent, **screen for HLA-B\\*1502. At-risk ancestry (HLA-B\\*1502 prevalence ≥10%):** - Han Chinese (10-15%) - Thai (8-27%) - Filipino - Malay - Vietnamese - Indonesian - Southern Indian (variable) - Indigenous populations of Southeas

nodes.title: Carbamazepine — First-Line Dosing
nodes.summary: CBZ 100 mg BID → titrate q3d → 600-1200 mg/d (max 1600). NNT 2. Watch Na, CBC, LFTs, rash. Auto-inducer.
nodes.body: Carbamazepine 100 mg PO BID start. Titrate: increase by 100–200 mg every 3 days as tolerated → target 600–1200 mg/day divided BID or TID. Maximum 1600 mg/day. Efficacy (Wiffen Cochrane 2014): NNT ~2 for at least 50% pain reduction. ~70% achieve good initial control. Effect dampens over years in ~50% (escape phenomenon). Use IR (immediate-release) for ED initiation because it titrates faster; trans

nodes.title: CBZ Response After Adequate Trial
nodes.summary: Adequate trial = 600 mg/d × 3 wk OR max tolerated. Failure/intolerance → ladder.
nodes.body: Adequate trial = titrated to 600 mg/d or maximum tolerated for ≥3 weeks at the stable dose. Inadequate response or intolerance triggers the ladder.

nodes.title: Pharmacologic Ladder Beyond CBZ
nodes.summary: 2L oxcarb 150 BID → 1200/d. CBZ-induced hypoNa → do NOT switch to oxcarb. Adjuncts: baclofen, gabapentin, lamotrigine (slow titration!).
nodes.body: 2L Oxcarbazepine — Oxcarbazepine 150 mg PO BID start; titrate by 300 mg/week to 1200 mg/day (max 2400 mg/day). Similar efficacy to CBZ (Cruccu Neurology 2008); better tolerability for most patients; fewer drug interactions (weak CYP3A4 inducer). 🛑 CRITICAL — CBZ-induced HYPONATREMIA: do NOT switch to oxcarbazepine. Oxcarbazepine causes MORE frequent and MORE severe hyponatremia than CBZ — inciden

nodes.title: Refractory After Adequate Ladder Trial
nodes.summary: Refractory = ≥2 first-line failures at adequate dose/duration. Refer surgical — do not delay.
nodes.body: AAN/EFNS definition of medical refractoriness: failure of ≥2 first-line agents (typically CBZ + oxcarbazepine, or CBZ + a different mechanism agent) at adequate dose and duration with disabling pain. This triggers surgical referral — do not delay further medical trials at the cost of months of severe pain and weight loss.

nodes.title: Surgical Options for Refractory TN
nodes.summary: MVD = best for TN1 + vascular loop + fit. Glycerol/balloon/RF rhizotomy for poor surgical candidates. Gamma knife for elderly, MS-TN, refusers.
nodes.body: Four established procedures, each with a distinct trade-off. Refer to a neurosurgery service with TN experience — outcomes are operator-dependent. 1. Microvascular Decompression (MVD) — Jannetta procedure - Best long-term outcome for classical (TN1) primary TN with imaging-proven vascular loop - Initial pain relief: ~90% (Barker NEJM 1996) - Sustained at 10 years: ~70% - Definitive — does NOT inju

nodes.title: Patient Education — Triggers, Daily Function, ED Return
nodes.summary: Trigger avoidance, liquid nutrition during flare, rash → STOP + ED, no abrupt CBZ stop, pregnancy planning needs neuro input.
nodes.body: Trigger avoidance during a flare (most patients learn these intuitively): - Chew on the unaffected side - Soft foods (yogurt, smoothies, soup) until under control - Wear a scarf over the lower face in cold wind - Use lukewarm water for shaving / face washing - Electric toothbrush often better tolerated than manual - Avoid air conditioner vents blowing on the face Nutrition + hydration — under-reco

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Discharge if controlled + follow-up. Admit for crisis, dehydration, SI, or HLA-pending in at-risk.
nodes.body: Most TN patients go home with a titration plan + neurology follow-up. Admit thresholds are narrow but specific.

nodes.title: Discharge Plan
nodes.body: Confirm before discharge: - Ancestry / HLA-B\\*1502 question addressed — if at-risk and unknown, test ordered AND non-CBZ bridge (gabapentin / baclofen) prescribed - Initial pharmacologic plan documented with titration schedule: • Carbamazepine 100 mg BID → titrate q3d → 600 mg/d target (if HLA clear), OR • Oxcarbazepine 150 mg BID → titrate, OR • Gabapentin / Baclofen titration if CBZ/oxcarb cont
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with titration plan + safety counseling + neuro follow-up within 2 weeks.

nodes.title: Admit — TN Crisis / Safety / Refractory
nodes.body: Admit when: - Active TN crisis (paroxysms preventing all oral intake; severe dehydration; weight loss) - Suicidal ideation - HLA-B\\*1502 test pending in at-risk patient who cannot safely bridge as outpatient - New atypical features requiring expedited MRI + neuro consult that cannot be arranged outpatient - Severe medication adverse event (significant hyponatremia, rash, cytopenia) requiring IV c
