nodes.recommendation: Admit to medicine/neurology; IV bridge therapy + expedited workup + safety planning.

nodes.title: TTP — Recognition
nodes.summary: MAHA + thrombocytopenia = suspect TTP — >90% mortality without treatment, <10% with prompt TPE
nodes.body: TTP Steps Summary Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is a life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by ADAMTS13 deficiency causing microvascular platelet aggregation. [1][2] Mortality without treatment: >90% Mortality with prompt TPE: <10% [3] Key Principle: TTP is a clinical diagnosis requiring emergent plasma exchange (TPE). Do NOT wait for ADAMTS13 results to start treatm

nodes.title: MAHA + Thrombocytopenia Present?
nodes.summary: Schistocytes + low platelets + elevated LDH + undetectable haptoglobin + negative Coombs = MAHA
nodes.body: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) is defined by: [1][2] • Schistocytes on peripheral smear (fragmented RBCs) • Elevated LDH (often markedly elevated) • Undetectable haptoglobin • Elevated indirect bilirubin • Negative direct Coombs (not immune-mediated hemolysis) Thrombocytopenia in TTP: [4] • Usually severe (<30 × 10⁹/L) • May be moderate (30-100 × 10⁹/L) • NOT due to consumption by DIC (n

nodes.title: While Awaiting Labs
nodes.summary: If unstable: draw ADAMTS13 before plasma, call hematology, prepare emergent TPE or FFP bridge
nodes.body: Do not delay treatment in critically ill patients. [3][4] While awaiting smear and hemolysis markers: If hemodynamically unstable or neurological symptoms: • Draw ADAMTS13 before any plasma exposure • Call hematology emergently • Prepare for emergent TPE • Consider FFP infusion (30 mL/kg) as bridge if TPE delayed If stable: • Expedite peripheral smear review (call lab directly) • STAT LDH, haptogl

nodes.title: TTP Unlikely — Consider Alternatives
nodes.body: Without MAHA and thrombocytopenia, TTP is unlikely. [1][2] Alternative diagnoses to consider: If thrombocytopenia WITHOUT hemolysis: • ITP (immune thrombocytopenia) • Drug-induced thrombocytopenia • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) • Bone marrow failure • Splenic sequestration If hemolysis WITHOUT schistocytes: • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
nodes.recommendation: Without confirmed MAHA + thrombocytopenia, TTP is unlikely. Pursue alternative workup based on clinical picture.

nodes.title: PLASMIC Score
nodes.summary: PLASMIC 6-7 = 72% probability TTP; 5 = 24%; 0-4 = 5% with 98% NPV — guides urgency of TPE
nodes.body: PLASMIC score predicts probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (<10%). [5] PLASMIC Calculator | Parameter | Criteria | Points | |-----------|----------|--------| | Platelet count | <30 × 10⁹/L | 1 | | hemoLysis | Retic >2.5%, haptoglobin undetectable, OR indirect bili >2 mg/dL | 1 | | Absence of active cancer | No active malignancy | 1 | | Stem cell/solid organ transplant | No transplant history

nodes.title: Low PLASMIC — Consider Other TMAs
nodes.summary: Low PLASMIC (0-4) has 98% NPV — consider HUS, DIC, drug-induced TMA, HELLP, malignant HTN instead
nodes.body: PLASMIC 0-4 has 98% negative predictive value for TTP. [5] More likely diagnoses with low PLASMIC: [6] Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS): • STEC-HUS (Shiga toxin): bloody diarrhea, severe AKI • Atypical HUS (complement-mediated): recurrent, familial DIC: • Abnormal coags (prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen) • Underlying trigger (sepsis, trauma, malignancy, OB) Drug-Induced TMA: [7] • Quinine (most com

nodes.title: Differentiate TMA Causes
nodes.summary: Normal coags = TTP not DIC; mild Cr (<2) favors TTP over HUS; HELLP resolves with delivery but TTP does not
nodes.body: TMA Differential Table Key differentiating features: [6][7] | | TTP | HUS | DIC | HELLP | |---|---|---|---|---| | ADAMTS13 | <10% | Normal | Normal | Low (>10%) | | Coags | Normal | Normal | Abnormal | Normal | | Renal | Mild | Severe | Variable | Moderate | | Neuro | Prominent | Less common | Variable | Less common | | Trigger | Autoimmune | STEC/complement | Sepsis/trauma | Pregnancy | Red flags

nodes.title: DIC — Different Pathway
nodes.body: DIC is NOT treated with plasma exchange. [6] Key differences from TTP: • Coags: Prolonged PT/PTT, elevated D-dimer, low fibrinogen • Mechanism: Systemic activation of coagulation cascade • Treatment: Address underlying cause (sepsis, malignancy, OB emergency) DIC management: • Treat underlying cause (antibiotics, delivery, tumor) • Supportive care • Transfuse for bleeding only: - FFP if PT >1.5× n
nodes.recommendation: Abnormal coagulation studies indicate DIC rather than TTP. Treat underlying cause. TPE is not indicated for DIC.

nodes.title: HUS — Different Pathway
nodes.body: HUS is characterized by severe renal involvement. [6][9] STEC-HUS (typical HUS): • Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7) • Bloody diarrhea → MAHA/thrombocytopenia → severe AKI • Antibiotics may worsen (increase toxin release) • Supportive care: dialysis PRN, avoid platelets • Usually self-limited (2-3 weeks) Atypical HUS (aHUS): • Complement-mediated (genetic or acquired) • No diarrheal prodrome
nodes.recommendation: Severe AKI with diarrheal prodrome suggests STEC-HUS. Supportive care is mainstay. For aHUS, consider eculizumab. ADAMTS13 should be normal.

nodes.title: ADAMTS13 Testing
nodes.summary: ADAMTS13 <10% = TTP confirmed — draw BEFORE any plasma exposure to avoid false elevation
nodes.body: ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic of TTP. [2][4] Important: Draw ADAMTS13 BEFORE any plasma exposure (FFP or TPE). Plasma contains ADAMTS13 and will falsely elevate levels. [4] Interpretation: [2] • <10%: Severe deficiency = TTP confirmed • 10-20%: Possible TTP — repeat testing, treat if symptomatic • >20%: TTP unlikely — consider other TMA causes Turnaround time: [4] • Send-out test: 2-7 days

nodes.title: ⚠️ DO NOT Transfuse Platelets
nodes.summary: Platelet transfusion CONTRAINDICATED — "adding fuel to the fire", may cause sudden death/MI/stroke
nodes.body: Platelet transfusion is CONTRAINDICATED in TTP except for life-threatening bleeding. [4][11] "Adding fuel to the fire" [11] Rationale: • TTP is a prothrombotic state with microvascular platelet aggregation • Transfused platelets may worsen microvascular thrombosis • Historical reports of sudden death, MI, and stroke after platelet transfusion Only transfuse platelets if: [4] • CNS hemorrhage • Lif

nodes.title: Initiate Treatment
nodes.summary: Initiate TPE within 4-8 hours — reduces mortality from >90% to <10%; start steroids simultaneously
nodes.body: Treatment is a medical emergency. [3][4] Initiate TPE within 4-8 hours of suspected TTP. [3] TPE is the cornerstone of TTP treatment: [3][4] • Removes ultra-large vWF multimers • Removes anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies • Replaces functional ADAMTS13 • Reduces mortality from >90% to <10% While awaiting TPE: • Call hematology emergently • Arrange TPE (apheresis team, vascular access) • Start corticoste

nodes.title: FFP Bridge While Awaiting TPE
nodes.summary: FFP 30mL/kg as bridge if TPE delayed >4-6h — NOT a substitute for TPE, monitor for volume overload
nodes.body: If TPE will be delayed >4-6 hours: [3][4] FFP Infusion Protocol: • 30 mL/kg as temporizing measure • Provides exogenous ADAMTS13 • NOT a substitute for TPE — only a bridge • Monitor for volume overload Practical considerations: • 30 mL/kg ≈ 2.1 L for 70 kg patient • May need to give in divided doses • Consider diuretics if volume-sensitive • Cryo-poor plasma (CPP) is alternative if available While

nodes.title: Plasma Exchange (TPE) Protocol
nodes.summary: Daily TPE 1.0-1.5 plasma volumes until platelets >150k x2 consecutive days — median 7 sessions
nodes.body: TPE is EMERGENT — goal is initiation within 4-8 hours. [3][4] TPE Volume Calculator TPE Parameters: [3][4] • Volume: 1.0-1.5 plasma volumes (40-60 mL/kg) per session • Replacement fluid: FFP or cryo-poor plasma (CPP) • Frequency: Daily (including weekends) until remission • Vascular access: Large-bore central catheter (apheresis catheter) Monitoring during TPE: • Vital signs q15min • Citrate toxic

nodes.title: Corticosteroids
nodes.summary: Prednisone 1mg/kg/day or methylprednisolone pulse — suppresses autoantibody production, start with TPE
nodes.body: Start corticosteroids immediately with TPE. [3][4] Mechanism: Suppress autoantibody production. [4] Dosing options: [4][12] | Regimen | Dose | Notes | |---------|------|-------| | Standard | Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day | Most common, continue until remission | | High-dose pulse | Methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg/day × 3 days → 2.5 mg/kg/day | May improve remission rates | | Pulse (refractory) | Methylpredni

nodes.title: Adjunctive Therapy
nodes.summary: Caplacizumab now standard for acute iTTP; rituximab for refractory/relapsing cases
nodes.body: Modern TTP treatment includes adjunctive therapies beyond TPE + steroids. [3][4][13] Caplacizumab: [13] • Anti-vWF nanobody — blocks platelet aggregation • HERCULES trial: 74% reduction in composite outcome • Faster platelet normalization • Now standard of care for acute iTTP Rituximab: [14] • Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody • Depletes B cells producing anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies • Used for refractory

nodes.title: Caplacizumab (Cablivi)
nodes.summary: Anti-vWF nanobody 10mg IV before first TPE then 10mg SC daily — 74% reduction in composite outcome
nodes.body: Caplacizumab is an anti-vWF nanobody that prevents platelet aggregation. [13] HERCULES Trial Results: [13] • 74% reduction in composite outcome (death, recurrence, thromboembolism) • Faster platelet normalization • Lower recurrence during treatment Dosing: [13] • Loading: 11 mg IV before first TPE • Maintenance: 11 mg SC daily • Duration: Continue until 30 days after last TPE • Can extend up to 28

nodes.title: Refractory TTP
nodes.summary: No response by day 5-7: add rituximab 375mg/m2 weekly, escalate steroids, consider twice-daily TPE
nodes.body: Refractory TTP: No response to TPE + steroids by day 5-7. [4][14] Criteria for refractory: [4] • Persistent thrombocytopenia despite 5-7 daily TPE • No improvement in LDH • Clinical deterioration • Persistent neurological symptoms Escalation strategies: [4][14] 1. Add Rituximab: • 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 weeks • Alternative: 375 mg/m² × 2 doses within 4 days, + 3rd at day 15 • TPE timing: Hold TPE fo

nodes.title: Relapsing TTP
nodes.summary: 20-50% relapse risk within 2 years — ADAMTS13 <20% without symptoms can be treated preemptively with rituximab
nodes.body: Relapse risk: 20-50% of patients relapse, most within first 2 years. [15] Two types of relapse: [10][15] 1. Clinical relapse: • Return of thrombocytopenia + MAHA + ADAMTS13 <10% • Treat as acute episode (TPE + steroids + caplacizumab) 2. ADAMTS13 relapse (biochemical): • ADAMTS13 <20% without clinical symptoms • Can be treated preemptively to prevent clinical relapse • Rituximab 375 mg/m² × 4 week

nodes.title: Pregnancy-Associated TTP
nodes.summary: HELLP resolves with delivery in 2-3 days; TTP continues to deteriorate postpartum without TPE
nodes.body: TTP in pregnancy: Incidence 1 in 25,000-100,000 pregnancies. [8][16] Key differentiator from HELLP: [8] • HELLP resolves with delivery (improvement within 2-3 days) • TTP continues to deteriorate postpartum without TPE ADAMTS13 levels: [8] • HELLP: Low but >10% (average 31%) • TTP: <10% Treatment in pregnancy: [16] • TPE + steroids remain mainstay • Caplacizumab can be considered (limited data) •

nodes.title: HELLP — Monitor for TTP
nodes.body: HELLP should improve within 48-72 hours of delivery. [8] Monitor closely: • Daily CBC, LDH, haptoglobin • Renal function • Neurological status If NOT improving by 72 hours post-delivery: [8] • Suspect TTP rather than HELLP • Send/expedite ADAMTS13 • Initiate TPE + steroids • Hematology consultation Red flags for TTP during HELLP monitoring: • Worsening thrombocytopenia • Rising LDH • New neurologi
nodes.recommendation: Monitor post-delivery. HELLP should improve within 72 hours. If deterioration or no improvement, suspect TTP and initiate treatment.

nodes.title: Acute Monitoring
nodes.summary: ICU admission, daily CBC/LDH, neuro checks q4h — stop TPE when platelets >150k x2 consecutive days
nodes.body: TTP requires ICU admission. [4] Daily monitoring: [4] | Parameter | Target | |-----------|--------| | Platelet count | Normalization (>150k × 2 days) | | LDH | Trending toward normal | | Hemoglobin | Stabilization | | Creatinine | Stability or improvement | | Neuro checks | Q4h minimum — no deterioration | When to stop TPE: [4] • Platelet count >150 × 10⁹/L for 2 consecutive days • LDH normalizing

nodes.title: Disposition & Follow-Up
nodes.body: All TTP patients require ICU admission. [4] Rationale: • Can deteriorate rapidly and abruptly • Requires emergent TPE • High mortality without treatment • Neurological monitoring essential Hematology involvement: [4] • Emergent consultation at diagnosis • Daily follow-up during acute treatment • Arrange outpatient follow-up before discharge Long-term monitoring: [10] • ADAMTS13 every 3-6 months in
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission is mandatory. Arrange emergent hematology consultation and TPE. After recovery, establish close follow-up with hematology for ADAMTS13 monitoring every 3-6 months.

nodes.title: Call Hematology Emergently
nodes.body: TTP requires emergent hematology involvement. [4] When to call: • Immediately when TTP is suspected (PLASMIC ≥5) • Before initiating TPE if possible (but do NOT delay treatment) • Any neurological or cardiac deterioration • Refractory cases (no response by day 5-7) • Rituximab or caplacizumab decision-making Information for hematologist: • PLASMIC score • Current labs (CBC, smear, LDH, haptoglobin
nodes.recommendation: Emergent hematology consultation is essential. Provide PLASMIC score, current labs, ADAMTS13 status, and treatment plan. Do not delay treatment while awaiting consultation.

nodes.title: Tuberculosis
nodes.summary: 2 billion infected globally, 1.23 million deaths/yr — prompt diagnosis reduces transmission
nodes.body: TB Steps Summary — quick reference. Nearly 2 billion people (~25% of world population) are infected with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million became ill with TB (131/100,000 incidence), and 1.23 million died. [1] Prompt diagnosis facilitates timely treatment and minimizes community transmission. [1] This consult covers: • ED evaluation and isolation decisions • Diagnost

nodes.title: Clinical Suspicion
nodes.summary: Cough >2-3wk + epidemiologic risk factors — prior TB, endemic travel, incarceration, HIV, immunosuppression
nodes.body: Suspect pulmonary TB in patients with relevant clinical manifestations AND epidemiologic risk factors: [1] Symptoms: • Cough >2–3 weeks duration • Lymphadenopathy • Fevers, night sweats • Weight loss • Hemoptysis Epidemiologic factors: • History of prior TB infection or disease • Known or possible TB exposure • Past or present residence in / travel to TB-endemic area • Incarceration, homelessness,

nodes.title: Airborne Isolation Required?
nodes.summary: Airborne isolation (negative pressure, N95) for active cough + risk factors or positive AFB smear
nodes.body: Patients being evaluated for pulmonary TB who pose a public health risk for transmission should be admitted and isolated with airborne precautions (negative pressure room, N95 respirator). [1] Isolate if: • Active cough + risk factors for TB • Chest imaging consistent with active TB • Known TB exposure + symptoms • Sputum AFB smear positive

nodes.title: Specimen Collection
nodes.summary: Collect 3 sputum specimens 8+ hours apart (1 early morning) — induced sputum if cannot produce
nodes.body: The diagnosis of pulmonary TB is definitively established by isolation of M. tuberculosis from a bodily secretion, fluid, or tissue. [1] Collect 3 sputum specimens at least 8 hours apart (including one early morning specimen). [1] Specimen options:

nodes.title: Sputum Collection Technique
nodes.summary: Deep breaths + forceful cough into sterile container; hypertonic saline 3-5% nebulization if unable to produce
nodes.body: Expectorated sputum: • Patient takes deep breaths, coughs forcefully • Collect in sterile container • Early morning specimen has highest yield Induced sputum (preferred if patient cannot produce): • Nebulize with hypertonic saline (3–5%) • 15–20 minutes of inhalation • Yields specimens comparable to bronchoscopy in many studies [1] Collect 3 specimens at least 8 hours apart — sensitivity increases

nodes.title: Bronchoscopy Specimens
nodes.summary: BAL directed to affected lobe when sputum-negative — aerosol-generating, full airborne precautions required
nodes.body: Indications for bronchoscopy: [1] • Unable to produce sputum (even with induction) • Smear-negative sputum with high clinical suspicion • Need for tissue sampling Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): • Directed to affected lobe on imaging • Send for AFB smear, NAA testing, and mycobacterial culture • Higher yield than sputum in some smear-negative cases Post-bronchoscopy sputum — collect sputum specimen

nodes.title: Chest Radiography
nodes.summary: Upper lobe cavitation classic; HIV patients may have atypical/normal CXR — never treat based on CXR alone
nodes.body: CXR is an important supportive diagnostic tool but cannot confirm or exclude TB. [1] Classic findings (immunocompetent): • Upper lobe infiltrates or cavitation • Apical scarring • Hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy • Miliary pattern (diffuse small nodules) Atypical presentations (HIV/immunocompromised): • Lower lobe disease • Non-cavitary infiltrates • Isolated lymphadenopathy • Normal CXR (up to 1

nodes.title: AFB Smear & NAA Testing
nodes.summary: AFB smear rapid but 50-80% sensitive; NAA 95-98% in smear-positive — positive NAA sufficient for diagnosis
nodes.body: AFB/NAA Interpretation Algorithm — diagnostic decision aid. AFB Smear (Ziehl-Neelsen or Fluorochrome): • Rapid result (same day) • Sensitivity: 50–80% for pulmonary TB (higher with cavitary disease) • Specificity: limited — positive smear could be non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) • Fluorochrome staining is preferred (faster, more sensitive than Ziehl-Neelsen) [1] Nucleic Acid Amplification (NAA)

nodes.title: AFB Smear & NAA Results
nodes.summary: AFB+/NAA+ = treat; AFB-/NAA+ = treat (sufficient); AFB+/NAA- = consider NTM; AFB-/NAA- = clinical judgment
nodes.body: Interpretation of combined AFB smear and NAA results: [1] Note: Culture remains the gold standard — send all specimens for mycobacterial culture regardless of smear/NAA results.

nodes.title: AFB (+) / NAA (−) — Consider NTM
nodes.summary: AFB+/NAA- most likely NTM — repeat NAA, maintain isolation, treat empirically if high TB risk
nodes.body: When AFB smear is positive but NAA is negative: [1] • Most likely explanation: non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) rather than TB • Repeat NAA testing on a new specimen — false-negative NAA can occur • Clinical context matters — if TB risk is high, treat empirically while awaiting culture • If repeat NAA remains negative and clinical suspicion is low → likely NTM Do NOT delay isolation — maintain a

nodes.title: Smear-Negative TB
nodes.summary: Smear-negative TB not excluded — consider bronchoscopy, urine LAM in HIV+ with CD4 <200
nodes.body: When both AFB smear and NAA are negative: [1] • TB is less likely but not excluded — smear-negative TB accounts for a significant proportion of cases • Clinical judgment is essential — if suspicion remains high: → Continue isolation → Repeat sputum collection → Consider bronchoscopy for BAL → Await culture results (2–6 weeks) • If clinical suspicion is low and alternative diagnosis is likely → dis

nodes.title: Mycobacterial Culture
nodes.summary: Culture is gold standard — MGIT 960 detects in 1-3wk; DST on ALL isolates for INH and RIF resistance
nodes.body: Culture is the gold standard for TB diagnosis and is essential for drug susceptibility testing (DST). [1] Conventional culture (Löwenstein-Jensen solid media): • Growth in 3–6 weeks (slow but highly sensitive) • Allows full drug susceptibility testing Rapid liquid culture (BACTEC MGIT 960): • Growth detection in 1–3 weeks • Preferred method due to faster time to detection [1] Drug Susceptibility T

nodes.title: TB Diagnosis Confirmed
nodes.summary: Isolate, notify public health, baseline labs, HIV testing — assess for drug resistance risk factors
nodes.body: Active TB diagnosed or presumptive treatment initiated. Immediate actions: • Airborne isolation if not already in place • Notify public health department (TB is a reportable disease in all US states) [1] • Obtain baseline labs: LFTs, CBC, BMP, HIV testing, hepatitis B/C serologies [2] • Assess for drug-resistant TB risk factors Risk factors for drug-resistant TB: [1] • Prior TB treatment • Contact

nodes.title: RIPE Regimen — Standard Treatment
nodes.summary: INH+RIF+PZA+EMB x2mo then INH+RIF x4mo — add pyridoxine B6 25-50mg daily to prevent neuropathy
nodes.body: TB Treatment Regimens — full dosing tables. The ATS/CDC/IDSA standard regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: [2,8] Intensive Phase (2 months — daily): • Isoniazid 5 mg/kg PO daily (max 300 mg) • Rifampin 10 mg/kg PO daily (max 600 mg) • Pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg PO daily (max 2000 mg) • Ethambutol 15–20 mg/kg PO daily (max 1600 mg) Continuation Phase (4 months — daily or 3×/week): • Isoniazid + Ri

nodes.title: 2-Month Sputum Culture Check
nodes.summary: 2-month culture + cavitation determines continuation phase — positive culture or cavity = extend to 9 months
nodes.body: After completing the intensive phase (2 months), obtain sputum cultures to assess treatment response. [2] The combination of 2-month culture result and cavitary disease on initial CXR determines continuation phase duration:

nodes.title: Standard Continuation Phase
nodes.body: Continue INH + RIF for 4 additional months (6 months total). [2] Monitoring during continuation phase: • Monthly sputum cultures until conversion documented • Monthly clinical assessment (symptoms, weight, adherence) • LFTs if symptomatic hepatotoxicity suspected • Directly observed therapy (DOT) strongly recommended [2] Completion criteria: • Minimum 6 months of treatment AND • Minimum 4 months o
nodes.recommendation: Complete 6-month RIPE regimen with DOT. Monthly sputum cultures, clinical monitoring, and LFT surveillance.

nodes.title: Extended Continuation — Cavitary Disease
nodes.body: Cavitary disease on initial CXR with negative 2-month culture — consider extending continuation phase to 7 months (9 months total). [2] Rationale: Cavitary disease is associated with higher bacterial burden and increased risk of relapse with standard 6-month therapy. [2] Continued monitoring: • Monthly sputum cultures • Monthly clinical assessment • Complete minimum 9 months of treatment AND minim
nodes.recommendation: Extend to 9-month regimen (7-month continuation of INH + RIF) for cavitary disease.

nodes.title: Positive Culture at 2 Months
nodes.summary: Positive at 2mo = repeat DST, ensure DOT, extend to 9mo — never add single drug to failing regimen
nodes.body: Positive sputum culture at 2 months indicates higher risk of treatment failure and relapse. [2] Immediate actions: • Repeat drug susceptibility testing — rule out acquired resistance • Extend continuation phase to 7 months (9 months total minimum) • Ensure directly observed therapy — non-adherence is the most common cause • Assess for malabsorption, drug interactions, or incorrect dosing If cultur

nodes.title: 4-Month Rifapentine-Moxifloxacin Regimen
nodes.summary: INH+RPT+MOX+PZA x4mo — strict criteria: non-cavitary, HIV-negative (or CD4>100), no FQ resistance
nodes.body: TB Treatment Regimens — comparative dosing table. CDC 2022 interim guidance introduced a shortened 4-month regimen for selected patients: [2,9] Regimen (daily throughout): • Isoniazid 300 mg PO daily • Rifapentine 1200 mg PO daily • Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO daily • Pyrazinamide (weight-based, 2 months only) Patient selection (ALL criteria must be met): [2,9] • Age ≥12 years • Drug-susceptible, non-c

nodes.title: Drug-Induced Hepatotoxicity?
nodes.summary: AST/ALT >3x ULN with symptoms OR >5x without = hepatotoxicity — stop hepatotoxic drugs
nodes.body: Hepatotoxicity Management — stepwise protocol. Baseline LFTs should be obtained in all patients before starting TB treatment. [2] Monitor for hepatotoxicity if: • Baseline LFTs abnormal • HIV co-infection • Chronic hepatitis B or C • Alcohol use • Age >35 years • Pregnancy or immediate postpartum • Concurrent hepatotoxic medications [2] Definition of drug-induced hepatotoxicity: • AST/ALT >3× ULN

nodes.title: Hepatotoxicity Management
nodes.body: Step 1 — Stop ALL hepatotoxic TB drugs (INH, RIF, PZA). [2] • Continue ethambutol (not hepatotoxic) • Consider adding a fluoroquinolone (Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO daily) as bridge therapy Step 2 — Monitor LFTs weekly until AST/ALT <2× ULN [2] Step 3 — Stepwise rechallenge (one drug at a time, 1 week apart): [2] 1. Rifampin first (least hepatotoxic of the 3, most important for efficacy) 2. Isoniazid s
nodes.recommendation: Hold hepatotoxic TB drugs. Stepwise rechallenge: RIF → INH → PZA, one week apart. If PZA omitted permanently, extend to 9 months total.

nodes.title: Latent TB Infection
nodes.summary: Positive TST/IGRA with no active disease — treatment reduces reactivation risk by up to 90%
nodes.body: TB infection (latent TB) = positive TST or IGRA with no clinical, radiographic, or microbiologic evidence of active disease. [3] Treatment of latent TB reduces reactivation risk by up to 90%. [3] Who to treat: [3] • Positive TST or IGRA AND any of: → Close contacts of active TB case → HIV infection → Immunosuppression (TNF-α inhibitors, transplant, chronic steroids ≥15 mg/day prednisone) → Recent

nodes.title: Exclude Active TB Disease
nodes.summary: Must exclude active TB before treating latent — symptom screen, CXR, baseline LFTs if risk factors
nodes.body: Before starting latent TB treatment, MUST exclude active TB disease: [3] 1. Symptom screen: • Cough (any duration), fevers, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis • Any positive symptom → evaluate for active TB before treating latent 2. Chest radiography: • Normal CXR → proceed with latent TB treatment • Abnormal CXR → sputum for AFB/culture before starting therapy • Old fibrotic changes without sy

nodes.title: Latent TB Regimen Selection
nodes.summary: Rifamycin-based preferred (shorter, better adherence) — 3HP, 4R, 3HR, or 9H based on patient factors
nodes.body: TB Treatment Regimens — comparative latent TB dosing table. Rifamycin-based regimens are preferred over isoniazid monotherapy due to shorter duration, better adherence, and comparable efficacy. [3] Select regimen based on patient factors:

nodes.title: 3HP — Weekly INH + Rifapentine × 12 Weeks
nodes.body: Regimen: [3] • Isoniazid 15 mg/kg rounded to nearest 50/100 mg (max 900 mg) ONCE WEEKLY • Rifapentine 900 mg (weight >50 kg) ONCE WEEKLY • Pyridoxine (B6) 50 mg with each dose • 12 doses total — must complete all 12 within 16 weeks Administration: Directly observed therapy (DOT) recommended [3] Contraindications: • Age <2 years • Pregnancy or planning pregnancy during treatment • HIV on protease i
nodes.recommendation: Start 3HP regimen (12 weekly doses of INH + rifapentine by DOT). Complete within 16 weeks. Pyridoxine with each dose.

nodes.title: 4R — Rifampin Daily × 4 Months
nodes.body: Regimen: [3] • Rifampin 10 mg/kg PO daily (max 600 mg) × 4 months • Self-administered (DOT not required) Advantages: [3] • Shorter than INH monotherapy • Better tolerated (lower hepatotoxicity rate than INH) • Good for INH-resistant TB contacts • Self-administered — no DOT required Cautions: • Potent CYP3A4 inducer — extensive drug interactions • Cannot use with most HIV ARVs (protease inhibitors,
nodes.recommendation: Start rifampin 600 mg PO daily × 4 months. Monthly clinical assessment. Counsel about drug interactions and orange body fluids.

nodes.title: 3HR — INH + Rifampin Daily × 3 Months
nodes.body: Regimen: [3] • Isoniazid 5 mg/kg PO daily (max 300 mg) × 3 months • Rifampin 10 mg/kg PO daily (max 600 mg) × 3 months • Pyridoxine (B6) 25–50 mg PO daily Similar efficacy to 3HP — option when rifapentine is unavailable. [3] Same drug interaction profile as 4R (rifampin-based). Monitoring: Baseline LFTs if risk factors. Monthly clinical assessment. TB Patient Information — shareable patient educat
nodes.recommendation: Start 3HR regimen (daily INH + rifampin × 3 months). Pyridoxine supplementation. Monthly clinical assessment.

nodes.title: 9H — Isoniazid Daily × 9 Months
nodes.body: Regimen: [3] • Isoniazid 5 mg/kg PO daily (max 300 mg) × 9 months • Pyridoxine (B6) 25–50 mg PO daily • Alternative: 15 mg/kg PO twice weekly by DOT (max 900 mg) [3] Use when rifamycins are contraindicated: • HIV on protease inhibitors or certain ARVs • Drug interactions precluding rifampin/rifapentine • Known rifampin-resistant TB contact [3] Drawback: Lowest completion rates (~50%) due to 9-mont
nodes.recommendation: Start isoniazid 300 mg PO daily × 9 months with pyridoxine. Monthly LFTs if age >35. Monitor adherence closely.

nodes.title: Drug-Resistant TB Classification
nodes.summary: Monoresistant, MDR (INH+RIF), pre-XDR/XDR — resistance changes regimen entirely, expert consultation required
nodes.body: MDR-TB Drug Guide — regimen building reference. Resistance definitions: [4] • Monoresistant: Resistance to ONE first-line drug only • Polyresistant: Resistance to >1 first-line drug (but NOT both INH + RIF) • MDR-TB: Resistance to at least isoniazid AND rifampin • Pre-XDR-TB: MDR-TB + resistance to any fluoroquinolone • XDR-TB: MDR-TB + resistance to a fluoroquinolone AND at least one Group A drug

nodes.title: INH Monoresistance
nodes.body: INH monoresistance is the most common resistance pattern worldwide. [4] Recommended regimen: [4] • Discontinue isoniazid • Continue Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol • Add a fluoroquinolone (Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily preferred) • Duration: 6 months minimum (extend to 9 months if PZA not tolerated) [4] Monitoring: • Monthly sputum cultures • Drug susceptibility testing to confirm no additional res
nodes.recommendation: Discontinue INH. Continue RIF + PZA + EMB + add moxifloxacin. Minimum 6 months. Monthly sputum cultures.

nodes.title: MDR-TB — Initial Approach
nodes.summary: MDR-TB: 4-5 effective drugs, WHO Group A first (FQ, bedaquiline, linezolid) — never add single drug to failing regimen
nodes.body: MDR-TB = resistance to at least INH + RIF. [4] This requires expert consultation — management should be undertaken by individuals with TB expertise or in close consultation with such individuals. [4] Guiding principles: [4] • Never add a single drug to a failing regimen • Include at least 4–5 effective drugs in the regimen • Use DST results to guide drug selection • Prioritize WHO Group A drugs (f

nodes.title: BPaL / BPaLM Regimens
nodes.summary: BPaL x26wk: bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid — QTc monitoring monthly, weekly CBC for linezolid
nodes.body: MDR-TB Drug Guide — detailed drug dosing and monitoring. BPaL Regimen (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid): [4] • Bedaquiline 400 mg daily × 2 weeks, then 200 mg 3×/week × 24 weeks • Pretomanid 200 mg daily × 26 weeks • Linezolid 1200 mg daily × 26 weeks (reduce to 600 mg if toxicity) • Total duration: 26 weeks (6 months) BPaLM Regimen (add Moxifloxacin): [4] • Same as BPaL PLUS Moxifloxacin 400

nodes.title: MDR-TB Treatment Plan
nodes.body: Selected MDR-TB regimen initiated. [4] Ongoing management: • Monthly sputum cultures until conversion documented • DST-guided therapy — adjust regimen based on full susceptibility results • Monthly clinical assessment: weight, symptoms, adherence • Monthly labs: LFTs, CBC (weekly if on linezolid), BMP • ECG monitoring for QTc (monthly minimum if on bedaquiline/moxifloxacin) [4] Treatment completio
nodes.recommendation: MDR-TB regimen with expert consultation. Monthly cultures, QTc monitoring, CBC, LFTs. Minimum 6 months (BPaL) or 15-20 months (longer regimen).

nodes.title: HIV-TB Co-infection
nodes.summary: Start TB treatment immediately, ART within 2wk if CD4 <50 (8wk for CNS TB) — never delay TB treatment
nodes.body: HIV-TB Considerations — ARV interactions reference. TB treatment in HIV-positive patients requires simultaneous consideration of: [5] • Anti-TB regimen — same RIPE backbone, but drug interactions with ARVs • Antiretroviral therapy (ART) — timing, drug selection, interaction management • Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) — paradoxical worsening • Duration adjustments — may need ext

nodes.title: ARV Considerations with TB
nodes.summary: Rifampin = potent CYP3A4 inducer — dolutegravir 50mg BID, efavirenz standard dose; PIs incompatible
nodes.body: Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer — major drug interactions with ARVs: [5] Compatible ARV regimens: [5] • Efavirenz-based — standard dose, no adjustment needed • Dolutegravir-based — increase to DTG 50 mg BID (from daily) with rifampin • Raltegravir-based — increase to RAL 800 mg BID with rifampin Incompatible with rifampin: • Protease inhibitors (boosted or unboosted) • Cobicistat-boosted regim

nodes.title: Treatment Duration — HIV
nodes.summary: Assess clinical response — good = standard duration, poor = extend, paradoxical worsening = suspect IRIS
nodes.body: Standard RIPE regimen duration for HIV-TB: [5] Traditional regimen: Same as HIV-negative patients, but extend if: • Cavitary disease AND positive 2-month sputum culture → extend to 9 months total 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen: [5] • May be used in HIV+ patients with CD4 >100 who are on compatible ARVs • Not recommended if CD4 ≤100 Assess clinical response:

nodes.title: HIV-TB Monitoring & Follow-Up
nodes.body: Treatment monitoring for HIV-TB: [5] Sputum monitoring: • Monthly cultures until conversion documented • If positive at 2 months → extend therapy to 9 months total Drug-related side effects: [5] • Monitor for hepatotoxicity (INH, RIF, PZA — all hepatotoxic, HIV increases risk) • Peripheral neuropathy (INH — give pyridoxine B6) • Optic neuritis (EMB — monthly visual acuity) • GI intolerance, rash A
nodes.recommendation: Standard RIPE regimen with monthly sputum cultures. Monitor for hepatotoxicity, IRIS. ART timing per CD4 count. Pyridoxine B6 with INH.

nodes.title: Extended Therapy — HIV-TB
nodes.body: Extend continuation phase to 7 months (9 months total) if: [5] • Cavitary disease on initial CXR • Positive sputum culture at 2 months • Slow clinical response If cultures remain positive at 4 months: [5] • Consider treatment failure • Repeat DST — exclude acquired drug resistance • Consult TB specialist • Assess adherence, malabsorption, drug interactions • Consider TDM (therapeutic drug monitori
nodes.recommendation: Extend to 9-month regimen. Repeat DST if cultures positive at 4 months. Ensure ART adherence and compatibility.

nodes.title: IRIS — Immune Reconstitution
nodes.body: Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS): [5] Paradoxical clinical worsening after starting ART, caused by recovering immune system mounting an exaggerated inflammatory response to TB antigens. Timing: Typically 1–4 weeks after ART initiation, more common with: • Low baseline CD4 (<50) • High TB burden (cavitary, disseminated) • Early ART initiation [5] Clinical features: • New or worsen
nodes.recommendation: Continue both TB treatment and ART. Mild IRIS: NSAIDs. Moderate-severe: prednisone taper. Do NOT stop ART unless life-threatening.

nodes.title: Typhoid Fever — Recognition
nodes.summary: Travel history drives empiric therapy — Pakistan/Iraq = XDR risk; avoid fluoroquinolones (>70% resistant)
nodes.body: Typhoid Fever Steps Summary Typhoid fever is a systemic infection caused by *Salmonella enterica* serovar Typhi. Endemic in South Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean. [1][2] Key Principles: • Travel history is critical — 85% of US cases are travelers returning from endemic areas • Classic presentation (stepladder fever, rose spots, bradycardia) is rare now — present in <12% of contempor

nodes.title: XDR Typhoid Alert — Pakistan/Iraq
nodes.summary: XDR typhoid: ceftriaxone will fail — use azithromycin (uncomplicated) or meropenem (severe)
nodes.body: Extensively Drug-Resistant (XDR) Typhoid is endemic in Pakistan and Iraq since 2016 outbreak. [3][4] XDR Definition: Resistant to: • Ampicillin • Chloramphenicol • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole • Fluoroquinolones • Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone) Only effective agents: • Azithromycin — first-line for uncomplicated XDR • Meropenem — for complicated/severe XDR Clinical Outcomes: • Defe

nodes.title: No Travel History — Low Probability
nodes.summary: No travel: typhoid rare — consider malaria, dengue, rickettsial infections, or bacterial sepsis
nodes.body: Without endemic travel, typhoid is very rare in the US. [1][2] Rare exceptions: • Contact with a chronic carrier (1-4% of infected become carriers) • Consumption of contaminated food from endemic region • Laboratory exposure • Non-endemic traveler visiting friends/relatives who traveled Alternative diagnoses to consider: • Malaria (if mosquito-endemic area) • Dengue, Zika, chikungunya • Leptospiro

nodes.title: Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: Classic presentation rare now — fever + headache + abdominal pain in traveler = suspect typhoid
nodes.body: Classic presentation is now rare — maintain high index of suspicion in travelers with fever. [1][2][5] Timeline by Week: | Week | Findings | |------|----------| | Week 1 | Insidious fever (rises gradually), headache, profound fatigue, myalgias | | Week 2 | Persistent high fever (39-40°C), rose spots, relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly | | Week 3+ | Complications: perforation, hemorrhage, enc

nodes.title: Diagnostic Workup
nodes.summary: Blood culture BEFORE antibiotics — 60-80% sensitive week 1; repeat if negative + high suspicion
nodes.body: Blood culture is the gold standard — send BEFORE antibiotics. [1][2][6] Blood Culture: • Sensitivity 60-80% in week 1 of untreated illness • Sensitivity drops to 20-30% after week 1 • Takes 3-5 days for final result • Draw 2-3 sets before initiating antibiotics Bone Marrow Culture: • Sensitivity ~80% even in week 2+ of illness • Can remain positive despite antibiotic therapy • Rarely obtained in E

nodes.title: Widal Test — Do NOT Use
nodes.summary: Widal test is a trap — poor sensitivity/specificity; do NOT use for acute diagnosis
nodes.body: The Widal test is unreliable and should NOT be used for acute diagnosis. [6][7] Why Widal fails: • Poor sensitivity (63-82%) and specificity (18-73%) • Single positive test unreliable — especially in endemic areas (high baseline antibodies) • Takes 7-14 days for antibodies to rise (useless for acute decision-making) • Cross-reacts with non-typhoidal Salmonella, malaria, dengue • False positives fr

nodes.title: Severity Assessment
nodes.summary: Complicated = AMS, shock, GI bleeding, unable to take PO; uncomplicated = stable + tolerating oral
nodes.body: Assess severity to guide treatment intensity and disposition. [1][2][8] Complicated/Severe Typhoid: • Altered mental status (typhoid encephalopathy) • Hemodynamic instability (SBP <100 mmHg, tachycardia) • Signs of sepsis or septic shock • GI bleeding or suspected perforation • Unable to tolerate oral medications • Severe dehydration unresponsive to oral fluids • Immunocompromised patient • Age >5

nodes.title: Uncomplicated Typhoid — Treatment by Region
nodes.summary: Pakistan/Iraq = XDR (use azithromycin); other endemic = MDR (ceftriaxone or azithromycin)
nodes.body: Empiric antibiotic selection depends on travel region due to resistance patterns. [3][4][8] Key Resistance Patterns: | Region | Resistance | Empiric Therapy | |--------|------------|------------------| | Pakistan/Iraq | XDR (ceftriaxone-resistant) | Azithromycin | | India, Bangladesh | MDR + FQ-resistant | Ceftriaxone or Azithromycin | | Africa, Latin America | Variable MDR | Ceftriaxone or Azithr

nodes.title: XDR Typhoid Treatment — Azithromycin
nodes.summary: XDR: Azithromycin 1g day 1 → 500mg daily × 6 days; defervescence expected by day 5-7
nodes.body: For uncomplicated XDR typhoid (Pakistan/Iraq travelers): [3][4][8] First-Line: • Azithromycin 1g PO day 1, then 500mg PO daily × 6 days (7 days total) • Pediatric: 20mg/kg/day PO daily × 7 days Why azithromycin works: • Intracellular concentration exceeds MIC • Mean defervescence: 7.1 days • Oral bioavailability allows outpatient treatment If unable to take PO: • Azithromycin 500mg IV daily, trans

nodes.title: MDR Typhoid Treatment — Ceftriaxone or Azithromycin
nodes.summary: MDR: Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily OR Azithromycin PO; avoid fluoroquinolones
nodes.body: For uncomplicated MDR typhoid (India, Bangladesh, Africa, Latin America): [4][8][9] First-Line Options: Ceftriaxone: • Adults: 2g IV once daily × 5-7 days, then transition to oral azithromycin to complete 7-14 days • Pediatric: 50-100mg/kg/day IV (max 4g) • Mean defervescence: 5-7 days OR Azithromycin: • Adults: 1g PO day 1, then 500mg PO daily × 6 days (7 days total) • Pediatric: 20mg/kg/day PO d

nodes.title: Complicated/Severe Typhoid Treatment
nodes.summary: Severe XDR: Meropenem IV; severe non-XDR: Ceftriaxone IV; dexamethasone for encephalopathy
nodes.body: Complicated typhoid requires IV antibiotics, admission, and close monitoring. [4][8][9] For severe typhoid from Pakistan/Iraq (XDR risk): • Meropenem 1g IV q8h (or 20mg/kg IV q8h peds) • Duration: 10-14 days • Mean defervescence: 6.7 days • Consider adding azithromycin for dual coverage For severe typhoid from other endemic regions: • Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12-24h (total 2-4g/day) • Duration: 10-14 da

nodes.title: Complications — Week 2-3
nodes.summary: Complications week 2-3: perforation, hemorrhage, encephalopathy — each requires specific management
nodes.body: Complications occur in 10-15% of hospitalized patients, typically weeks 2-3. [1][2][11] Major Complications: Intestinal Perforation (TIP): • Occurs ~day 14 of untreated illness • Necrosis of Peyer's patches → ulceration → perforation • Sudden severe abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, rapid deterioration • Mortality: 5-20% GI Hemorrhage: • Source: Terminal ileum ulcers, ileocecal valve, colon • Mass

nodes.title: Intestinal Perforation
nodes.summary: Perforation = surgical emergency — NPO, fluids, anaerobic coverage, immediate OR consult
nodes.body: Typhoid intestinal perforation is a surgical emergency. [11][12] Pathophysiology: • Necrosis of Peyer's patches in terminal ileum • Ulceration progresses to full-thickness perforation • Typically occurs day 10-14 of untreated illness • Multiple perforations in 30% of cases Presentation: • Sudden severe abdominal pain (may initially localize to RLQ) • Abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness • Rapid
nodes.recommendation: Surgical emergency — NPO, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic coverage, immediate surgical consult.

nodes.title: GI Hemorrhage
nodes.summary: GI hemorrhage: IV access, transfuse, NPO, GI consult — most self-limited but can be massive
nodes.body: GI hemorrhage complicates ~12% of severe typhoid cases. [11][12] Source: • Terminal ileum ulcers (100%) • Ileocecal valve (57%) • Colon (29-43%) • Erosion of blood vessels adjacent to necrotic Peyer's patches Presentation: • Melena or bright red blood per rectum • Hemodynamic instability • Falling hemoglobin Management: 1. Two large-bore IVs, type and screen 2. IV fluid resuscitation 3. Transfusio
nodes.recommendation: Resuscitation, transfusion if needed, NPO, GI consult. Continue antibiotics. Surgery if uncontrolled.

nodes.title: Typhoid Encephalopathy
nodes.summary: Encephalopathy: Dexamethasone 3mg/kg load → 1mg/kg q6h × 48h reduces mortality; avoid if perforation suspected
nodes.body: Typhoid encephalopathy (typhoid state) occurs in ~25% of hospitalized cases. [10][11] Pathophysiology: • Blood-brain barrier disruption from typhoid toxin • Direct CNS invasion uncommon but can cause meningitis Risk Factors: • Age >50 years • Delayed treatment • Dehydration • High Widal titers (if obtained) • Elevated WBC (uncommon in typhoid) Presentation: • Muttering delirium (picking at bedclot

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Uncomplicated + stable + reliable follow-up = outpatient; otherwise admit
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition based on severity and reliability of follow-up. [1][2][8] Most uncomplicated typhoid can be managed as outpatient with oral azithromycin if: • Hemodynamically stable • Tolerating oral medications • No complications • Reliable follow-up available • Able to return if symptoms worsen

nodes.title: Discharge — Outpatient Management
nodes.summary: Azithromycin 1g then 500mg daily × 6d; follow-up 2-3 days; return for abdominal pain/bleeding/confusion
nodes.body: Discharge criteria met — outpatient treatment appropriate. [1][2][8] Discharge Medications: • Azithromycin 1g PO day 1 (taken in ED), then 500mg PO daily × 6 more days • Consider antiemetic if nausea • Encourage oral hydration Patient Instructions: • Complete full 7-day antibiotic course — do NOT stop early • Rest; avoid strenuous activity • Return for: high fever unresponsive to antipyretics, sev
nodes.recommendation: Discharge on azithromycin × 7 days. Follow-up in 2-3 days. Return precautions for severe abdominal pain, bleeding, or confusion.

nodes.title: Admit — Inpatient Management
nodes.summary: Admit: IV antibiotics, fluids, enteric precautions, ID consult; monitor for perforation/hemorrhage/encephalopathy
nodes.body: Admission criteria met — inpatient treatment required. [1][2][8] Admission Indications: • Altered mental status or encephalopathy • Hemodynamic instability • Signs of sepsis or septic shock • GI bleeding or suspected perforation • Unable to tolerate oral medications • Severe dehydration • Immunocompromised patient • Age >50 or very young children • Unreliable outpatient follow-up Inpatient Managem
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV antibiotics, hydration, and monitoring. ID consult recommended. Watch for complications weeks 2-3.

nodes.title: Prevention & Vaccination Counseling
nodes.summary: Vaccinate travelers to endemic areas (50-80% effective); food/water precautions essential — vaccination alone not sufficient
nodes.body: Counsel patients on prevention for future travel to endemic areas. [1][2][13] Vaccination: | Vaccine | Route | Age | Schedule | Booster | |---------|-------|-----|----------|----------| | Typhim Vi (ViCPS) | IM | ≥2 years | 1 dose ≥2 weeks before travel | Every 2 years | | Vivotif (Ty21a) | PO | ≥6 years | 4 capsules every other day | Every 5 years | Vaccine Effectiveness: • 50-80% protective (not

nodes.title: Relapse & Chronic Carriage
nodes.summary: 10% relapse if undertreated; 1-4% become chronic carriers; stool cultures × 3 to document clearance
nodes.body: Relapse and chronic carriage are important long-term considerations. [1][2] Relapse: • Occurs in ~10% of inadequately treated patients • Typically 1-3 weeks after apparent recovery • Usually milder than initial illness • Risk factors: short treatment course, poor compliance • Treatment: Repeat full antibiotic course Chronic Carriage: • 1-4% of infected persons become chronic carriers • Shed *S. Ty

nodes.title: Facial Pain-Unilateral - First Pass
nodes.summary: Facial Pain-Unilateral: dangerous exclusions first, then pattern recognition.
nodes.body: Open first: Steps | Differential | Red Flags Goal: decide whether this is dangerous eye/orbit, neurovascular, deep infection, GCA, zoster, cranial neuralgia, TAC/cluster, dental, sinus/ear, TMJ, or migraine/headache phenotype. First 60 seconds: - Vitals, fever, toxic appearance, immunocompromise. - Visual acuity, pupils, red eye, cornea/fluorescein, IOP when angle closure is plausible, EOM pain/re

nodes.title: Early Differential - Say It Before You Narrow
nodes.summary: Name dangerous and common buckets before anchoring on a benign cause.
nodes.body: Dangerous buckets: - Eye/orbit: acute angle closure, keratitis/uveitis, orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus process, HZO. - Neurovascular: carotid/vertebral dissection, stroke/TIA, SAH/ICH, cavernous sinus thrombosis. - Inflammatory: giant cell arteritis. - Infection: odontogenic abscess/cellulitis, deep neck infection, sinusitis with orbital/intracranial complication, mastoiditis. - Zoster: HZO,

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the First Hit
nodes.summary: Eye, neurovascular, infection, GCA, and zoster red flags come before benign pattern labels.
nodes.body: Choose the most dangerous active pattern. You can come back for phenotype sorting after urgent threats are addressed.

nodes.title: Eye / Orbit Emergency Lane
nodes.body: Open AACG, Orbital Cellulitis, or Monocular Vision Loss Hub based on the exam. Immediate exam: visual acuity, pupils, EOM, IOP when angle closure is plausible, fluorescein/slit lamp, lid/orbit exam, proptosis, fever, cranial nerves. High-risk patterns: - Mid-dilated pupil, corneal haze, halos, nausea/vomiting, very high IOP: AACG. - Painful/restricted EOM, diplopia, proptosis, fever, eyelid edema:
nodes.recommendation: Treat eye/orbit red flags as time-sensitive specialty problems. Do not discharge without visual acuity and ophthalmology plan when objective eye risk is present.

nodes.title: Neurovascular / Dissection Lane
nodes.body: Open Cervical Artery Dissection, Stroke, SAH, ICH, or Anisocoria based on the dominant finding. Dissection clues: unilateral face/head/neck pain, partial Horner syndrome, transient monocular vision loss, TIA/stroke symptoms, posterior headache/neck pain, recent neck trauma/manipulation, cough/vomiting/exertion trigger. Imaging: CTA head/neck is the practical ED first-line study when dissection, st
nodes.recommendation: CTA head/neck for dissection or neurovascular facial pain patterns. Use stroke/SAH/ICH workflows when neuro deficits or thunderclap are present.

nodes.title: Dental / Deep-Space Infection Lane
nodes.body: Open Dental Pain Hub, Deep Neck Infection, or Orbital Cellulitis. Airway and source screen: trismus, muffled voice, drooling, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth elevation, neck swelling, immunocompromise, diabetes, toxic appearance, odontogenic swelling, periorbital spread. Imaging: CT face/neck with IV contrast when deep-space infection, orbital extension, Ludwig angina, osteomyelitis, abscess, or complic
nodes.recommendation: Prioritize airway, CT with contrast for deep-space concern, and dental/OMFS/ENT source control.

nodes.title: Giant Cell Arteritis Lane
nodes.body: Consider in age >50 with new unilateral temple/scalp/facial pain, especially jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms, diplopia, PMR shoulder/hip symptoms, constitutional symptoms, abnormal temporal artery, or unexplained inflammatory syndrome. ED workup: ESR, CRP, CBC with platelets, CMP. Normal inflammatory markers reduce likelihood but do not fully exclude GCA when the clinical story
nodes.recommendation: Age >50 plus jaw/scalp/vision/PMR symptoms should trigger ESR/CRP/CBC and empiric steroids when suspicion is meaningful.

nodes.title: Zoster / Cranial Neuropathy Lane
nodes.body: Patterns: dermatomal burning or allodynia before rash, vesicles, V1 forehead/scalp involvement, nose-tip involvement, red eye/photophobia/vision change, ear vesicles, hearing symptoms, vertigo, or facial weakness. HZO eye risk: any V1 rash plus ocular symptoms, red eye, decreased vision, photophobia, dendritic/pseudodendritic lesions, or tip-of-nose involvement needs careful eye exam and ophthalmo
nodes.recommendation: Identify HZO eye risk early. Antivirals plus ophthalmology for eye involvement or uncertain ocular disease.

nodes.title: Pattern Recognition - What Does the Pain Behave Like?
nodes.summary: Use pain behavior and exam localization after dangerous lanes are addressed.
nodes.body: After danger signals are cleared or addressed, use behavior of pain plus exam localization. Choose the closest phenotype.

nodes.title: Trigeminal Neuralgia Pattern
nodes.body: Open Trigeminal Neuralgia. Classic phenotype: recurrent unilateral brief electric-shock pains in trigeminal distribution, abrupt onset/termination, severe intensity, triggerable by innocuous stimuli, no objective sensory loss. MRI / secondary cause triggers: sensory loss, bilateral symptoms, age <40, constant pain between paroxysms, hearing loss, brainstem signs, multiple sclerosis history, cancer
nodes.recommendation: Use TN consult for HLA screen, medication ladder, MRI triggers, and neurology referral.

nodes.title: Cluster / TAC Pattern
nodes.body: Open Cluster Headache. Cluster phenotype: strictly unilateral orbital/supraorbital/temporal severe attacks lasting 15-180 minutes, with ipsilateral autonomic signs or restlessness/agitation. Attacks often cluster by circadian/circannual pattern. ED treatment: high-flow 100% oxygen by non-rebreather and a triptan when not contraindicated. Treat pain while still screening first/atypical presentation
nodes.recommendation: Treat likely cluster promptly with oxygen/triptan and image atypical or first presentations.

nodes.title: Dental / Odontogenic Pattern
nodes.body: Open Dental Pain Hub. Look for: caries, cracked tooth, percussion sensitivity, focal gingival swelling, fluctuance, facial cellulitis, immunocompromise, fever, trismus, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth elevation, and airway symptoms. Antibiotics: uncomplicated pulpitis or localized apical periodontitis without systemic involvement generally needs dental treatment and analgesia, not antibiotics. Antibioti
nodes.recommendation: Dental source control is the definitive treatment. Use antibiotics for systemic/spreading/deep infection patterns.

nodes.title: Sinus / Ear Pattern
nodes.body: Bacterial rhinosinusitis criteria: persistent symptoms >10 days without improvement, severe fever with purulent nasal discharge or facial pain for at least 3-4 consecutive days, or double-worsening after initial improvement. Avoid the trap: unilateral facial pain alone is not enough to diagnose bacterial sinusitis. Dental, migraine, TN, cluster/TAC, HZO, and eye disease commonly masquerade as "sin
nodes.recommendation: Use bacterial sinusitis criteria. Image or consult when orbital, neurologic, toxic, or immunocompromised features are present.

nodes.title: TMJ / Myofascial Pattern
nodes.body: Typical: jaw clicking/locking, chewing-related pain, masseter/temporalis tenderness, bruxism, limited opening from pain rather than trismus, normal eye/neuro exam, no fever, no dental swelling. Do not overcall TMJ when: true trismus, fever, facial swelling, dental abscess, floor-of-mouth elevation, neurologic signs, temporal artery symptoms, vision change, or first severe headache is present. ED m
nodes.recommendation: TMJ is a diagnosis after eye, neurovascular, infection, GCA, dental, and zoster concerns are not present.

nodes.title: Migraine / Primary Headache Pattern
nodes.body: Open Headache Hub or Migraine. Migraine can present as unilateral face, jaw, sinus, dental, or orbital pain. Diagnosis is stronger with prior similar attacks, photophobia/phonophobia, nausea, movement sensitivity, aura history, family history, and normal eye/neuro/dental exam. Still image or escalate when: first/worst, thunderclap, neurologic deficit, pregnancy/postpartum, cancer/immunosuppression
nodes.recommendation: Use Headache Hub for red flags and Migraine for treatment when primary headache is likely.

nodes.title: Testing and Imaging - Match Study to Risk
nodes.summary: Image by red flag and anatomy, not by pain severity alone.
nodes.body: Open Testing Guide. Eye/orbit: visual acuity, fluorescein/slit lamp, IOP when angle closure plausible, CT orbit/sinuses with contrast for orbital cellulitis/extension. Neurovascular: non-contrast CT head for sudden severe/SAH/ICH concern; CTA head/neck for dissection, aneurysm, stroke/TIA pattern, Horner, or transient neurologic symptoms; MRI/MRA if CTA/CT unrevealing and suspicion remains. Deep i

nodes.title: Treatment Bridge While Diagnosis Firms Up
nodes.summary: Treat pain while protecting time-sensitive diagnoses.
nodes.body: Analgesia: acetaminophen, NSAID if safe, targeted nerve pain plan when TN/zoster likely, antiemetic/migraine regimen when migraine phenotype. Time-sensitive treatments: - AACG: IOP-lowering regimen and ophthalmology. - Cluster: high-flow oxygen and triptan if not contraindicated. - GCA: glucocorticoids when suspected, urgent ophtho/rheum for vision symptoms. - HZO: antiviral therapy and ophthalmol

nodes.title: Reassess and Disposition
nodes.summary: Disposition hinges on objective danger, diagnostic certainty, reassessment, and follow-up reliability.
nodes.body: After treatment and targeted workup, choose the safest disposition lane.

nodes.title: Admit / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit, transfer, or keep under specialty service when there is threatened vision, orbital cellulitis, AACG, neurovascular diagnosis, suspected CNS infection, SAH/ICH/stroke, GCA with visual symptoms, deep-space infection, airway concern, immunocompromised severe infection, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, unsafe ambulation/neurologic exam, or inability to obtain needed urgent follow-up. Use disease-spe
nodes.recommendation: Admit or transfer when objective risk, threatened vision, airway/deep infection, neurovascular disease, or unsafe follow-up exists.

nodes.title: Observation / Recheck Lane
nodes.body: Use observation when the initial red-flag screen is incomplete, pain is severe or atypical, consultant decision is pending, imaging/labs are pending, airway/eye/neuro exam needs serial reassessment, or social factors make immediate discharge risky. Good observation endpoints: stable vitals, documented repeat eye/neuro/mouth/neck exam, pain controlled with an outpatient plan, no progression of swel
nodes.recommendation: Observe when the diagnosis is not settled or the safety exam needs serial confirmation.

nodes.title: Discharge Criteria
nodes.body: Discharge is reasonable only when all are true: - Normal or explained eye exam: visual acuity addressed, no red painful eye/vision loss/proptosis/painful EOM. - No focal neuro deficit, AMS, thunderclap, Horner, meningismus, or dissection story. - No fever/toxic appearance, deep-space infection, trismus, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth swelling, or spreading cellulitis. - GCA and zoster eye risk consider
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only after documented negative danger screen, pain control, and a specific follow-up/safety-net plan.

nodes.title: Return Precautions
nodes.body: Return immediately for vision change, red eye, eye swelling, new rash near eye/nose/ear, facial weakness, weakness/numbness, speech trouble, confusion, severe sudden headache, neck pain with neurologic symptoms, fever, vomiting, worsening swelling, trouble swallowing, trouble opening mouth, drooling, shortness of breath, uncontrolled pain, or inability to obtain urgent dental/ophthalmology/neurolo
nodes.recommendation: Safety net should match the dangerous lanes, not just "return if worse."

nodes.title: Unilateral Leg Swelling — Sick Check First
nodes.body: A swollen leg is not just "DVT vs cellulitis." Before you settle on the common causes, exclude the limb- and life-threats that share the same presentation: a threatened limb (phlegmasia, acute ischemia, compartment syndrome), a necrotizing infection, and a systemic driver (right-heart failure, massive DVT with PE). ⚠️ 5 DO-NOT-MISS diagnoses 1. DVT with PE — a swollen calf plus pleuritic chest pai

nodes.title: Rule In / Rule Out — Pick the Thread
nodes.summary: Eight-branch triage: acute ischemia / phlegmasia / necrotizing infection / compartment syndrome / DVT\u00B1PE / right-heart failure / benign / undifferentiated.
nodes.body: Work the limb- and life-threats first, then DVT, then the benign mimics. Each branch runs a validated tool or a tight clinical gate to an explicit verdict; excluded branches return here for the next differential.

nodes.title: Acute Limb Ischemia — 6 Ps Gate
nodes.summary: 6 Ps + absent pulses = acute limb ischemia; sensorimotor deficit = threatened limb. Check both legs.
nodes.body: A cold, pulseless, painful limb is acute limb ischemia \u2014 time-critical. The classic 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia (cold), Paresthesia, Paralysis. Paresthesia and paralysis mark a threatened/immediately-threatened limb (Rutherford IIa/IIb). Swelling can coexist (reperfusion, coexisting venous disease). Check pulses / Doppler signals in BOTH legs.

nodes.title: Acute Limb Ischemia — Anticoagulate + Emergent Vascular
nodes.body: Open Acute Limb Ischemia for the full pathway. Next steps: - Emergent vascular surgery consult \u2014 revascularization (surgical embolectomy, thrombolysis, or endovascular) is time-critical; a sensorimotor deficit (Rutherford IIb) means hours, not days. - Immediate systemic anticoagulation with heparin (unless contraindicated) to prevent clot propagation. - Keep the limb dependent and warm; do NO
nodes.recommendation: Emergent vascular surgery + immediate heparin; keep limb warm/dependent; CTA if it won\u2019t delay revascularization. Salvage is time-dependent.

nodes.title: Acute Limb Ischemia — Excluded
nodes.body: A warm limb with palpable or Doppler-detectable pulses excludes acute arterial ischemia right now. Re-check pulses if the limb changes \u2014 pain out of proportion, worsening pallor, or a new sensorimotor deficit warrants immediate re-evaluation (a tense compartment can also abolish pulses late). Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Ischemia excluded with intact pulses; reassess immediately if pulses, color, or sensation change.

nodes.title: Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens — Threatened-Limb Gate
nodes.summary: Tense cyanotic whole-leg swelling + pain = phlegmasia (massive iliofemoral DVT); venous gangrene / limb loss without decompression.
nodes.body: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is a massive iliofemoral DVT that obstructs venous outflow \u2014 the limb becomes tensely swollen, painful, and dusky/cyanotic, and venous gangrene and limb loss follow. It is a limb-threatening emergency distinct from an ordinary DVT. Look for the whole-leg tense swelling, cyanotic mottling, and severe pain; a compromised limb may lose pulses secondarily from the massiv

nodes.title: Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens — Anticoagulate + Emergent Vascular
nodes.body: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here); it sits on the DVT spectrum as its most severe, limb-threatening form: - Immediate systemic anticoagulation with heparin \u2014 the cornerstone; start unless contraindicated. - Emergent vascular surgery / interventional radiology consult \u2014 catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy is often required to salvage the li
nodes.recommendation: Immediate heparin + emergent vascular/IR for catheter-directed thrombolysis/thrombectomy; elevate limb + fluids; watch for compartment syndrome.

nodes.title: Phlegmasia — Excluded
nodes.body: The limb is not tensely swollen or cyanotic and is not threatened \u2014 phlegmasia is not the picture. An ordinary DVT is still very much on the table. Return to the hub and run the DVT branch.
nodes.recommendation: Phlegmasia excluded; proceed to risk-stratify for ordinary DVT.

nodes.title: Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection — Toxicity Gate
nodes.summary: Pain out of proportion + toxicity + crepitus/skin necrosis = necrotizing infection; emergent surgery, do not wait for imaging.
nodes.body: "Cellulitis" that hurts far more than it looks is a necrotizing infection until proven otherwise. The alarm signs: pain out of proportion to exam, systemic toxicity, crepitus, dusky/bullous/necrotic skin, rapidly spreading erythema, or firm "woody" induration beyond the erythema. ⚠️ LRINEC IS NOT A RULE-OUT TEST. Pooled meta-analysis (23 studies, n=5,982): LRINEC ≥6 sensitivity only 68.2% (specifi

nodes.title: Necrotizing Infection — Resuscitate + Emergent Debridement
nodes.body: Open Necrotizing Fasciitis for the full pathway. Next steps: - Emergent surgical consult for operative debridement \u2014 do NOT wait for imaging. Source control is the definitive treatment; mortality rises with every hour of delay. - Broad-spectrum antibiotics: gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic cover (e.g., vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. -
nodes.recommendation: Emergent operative debridement (do not wait for imaging) + broad-spectrum abx with clindamycin + aggressive sepsis resuscitation.

nodes.title: Necrotizing Infection — Unlikely
nodes.body: Erythema and warmth proportional to the pain, no systemic toxicity, and no crepitus/skin necrosis make a necrotizing infection unlikely right now. It evolves fast \u2014 if pain out of proportion, toxicity, crepitus, or skin necrosis appears on reassessment, resuscitate and consult surgery immediately. (Ordinary cellulitis is handled in the benign branch.) ⚠️ "Unlikely" is a clinical judgment, not
nodes.recommendation: Necrotizing infection unlikely without toxicity/skin signs; re-examine and escalate immediately if it evolves. A low LRINEC or normal CT does NOT rule it out.

nodes.title: Compartment Syndrome — Pressure Gate
nodes.summary: Tense compartment + pain on passive stretch = compartment syndrome; pulselessness is LATE. Measure pressures if unsure; fasciotomy is definitive.
nodes.body: Acute compartment syndrome is rising pressure within a fascial compartment that strangles perfusion \u2014 it destroys muscle and nerve within hours. Suspect it with a tense, swollen compartment and pain out of proportion, especially pain on passive stretch of the muscles in that compartment; paresthesia is an early nerve sign. Classic after fracture, crush, reperfusion, or a tight cast, but also

nodes.title: Compartment Syndrome — Emergent Fasciotomy
nodes.body: Acute compartment syndrome (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - Emergent orthopedic / surgical consult for fasciotomy \u2014 the only definitive treatment. Time to decompression drives outcome; irreversible damage begins within hours. - Immediate first aid: remove all constricting casts/dressings, keep the limb at heart level (do NOT elevate above the heart \u2014 it lowers perfusion p
nodes.recommendation: Emergent fasciotomy; remove constricting dressings, keep limb at heart level, correct hypotension; check pressures if unsure; monitor for rhabdo.

nodes.title: Compartment Syndrome — Unlikely
nodes.body: Soft compartments, no pain on passive stretch, and normal sensation make acute compartment syndrome unlikely right now. Serial exams are essential in an at-risk limb (post-fracture, crush, reperfusion) \u2014 escalating analgesia requirements, increasing tension, or new paresthesia warrant repeat assessment \u00B1 pressure measurement. Return to the hub for the next differential.
nodes.recommendation: Compartment syndrome unlikely now; serial exams in at-risk limbs and re-check with any escalation of pain/tension/paresthesia.

nodes.title: DVT — Wells + Chest-Symptom Gate
nodes.summary: Wells \u22641 + neg D-dimer excludes; Wells \u22652 \u2192 US (D-dimer cannot exclude). Check FEU vs DDU units. Chest symptoms \u2192 screen PE.
nodes.body: Risk-stratify with the Wells DVT score (in the toolbar), then combine with D-dimer and ultrasound. Wells DVT \u2014 two-tier model (the one that pairs with D-dimer): - DVT UNLIKELY (Wells \u22641) + negative high-sensitivity D-dimer \u2192 DVT excluded, no imaging needed. - DVT LIKELY (Wells \u22652) \u2192 go straight to compression ultrasound. A negative D-dimer does NOT exclude DVT in this grou

nodes.title: Concurrent PE — Work It Up Now
nodes.body: A swollen leg with chest symptoms or hypoxia is a pulmonary embolism until excluded. Open PE Treatment for the full pathway. Next steps: - Assess hemodynamic stability; if unstable / massive PE, this is a resuscitation (consider thrombolysis). - CT pulmonary angiography (or V/Q) to confirm; ECG, troponin, and echo help risk-stratify (RV strain). - Start anticoagulation unless contraindicated while
nodes.recommendation: Screen/confirm PE (CTPA), assess stability (thrombolysis if unstable), start anticoagulation while working up; do not wait for leg US.

nodes.title: DVT — Anticoagulate + Risk-Stratify
nodes.body: Open DVT for the full pathway and dosing in special populations. Next steps: - Start anticoagulation (DOAC first-line for most; LMWH/heparin where a DOAC is unsuitable \u2014 pregnancy, severe renal disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, some active cancer per shared decision) unless a contraindication exists. Single-drug DOAC regimens for acute PROXIMAL DVT (no heparin lead-in required): [9] - Apixa
nodes.recommendation: Anticoagulate proximal DVT (apixaban 10 mg BID \u00D7 7d \u2192 5 mg BID, or rivaroxaban 15 mg BID \u00D7 21d \u2192 20 mg daily WITH FOOD; minimum 3 months) + risk-stratify for outpatient vs admission. Isolated distal DVT: serial imaging \

nodes.title: DVT — Excluded
nodes.body: Wells UNLIKELY (\u22641) + negative high-sensitivity D-dimer excludes DVT with a high negative predictive value (3-month VTE rate <1%). No imaging, no anticoagulation. ⚠️ A negative ultrasound does NOT automatically exclude DVT \u2014 it depends which study you got. [6] - Negative WHOLE-LEG (complete) compression US \u2192 DVT excluded; no repeat scan needed. - Negative PROXIMAL or 2-POINT compres
nodes.recommendation: DVT excluded by Wells \u22641 + negative D-dimer, or by a negative WHOLE-LEG US. A negative proximal/2-point US in a Wells-likely patient is NOT exclusion \u2014 repeat compression US at 5\u20137 days or get a whole-leg study.

nodes.title: Right-Heart Failure — Systemic Gate
nodes.summary: Asymmetric edema can still be cardiac (dyspnea, raised JVP, S3); do not miss a superimposed DVT.
nodes.body: Heart failure classically causes bilateral edema, but it can present asymmetrically (dependent positioning, prior DVT, venous insufficiency, or unilateral lymphatic disease). Suspect a cardiac driver with dyspnea, orthopnea, a raised JVP, an S3, hepatomegaly, or a known cardiac history. Do NOT anchor on "cardiac edema" and miss a superimposed DVT \u2014 they coexist, and stasis in the failing pati

nodes.title: Right-Heart Failure — Treat the Pump
nodes.body: Open Right-Heart Failure and CHF Exacerbation for the full pathways. Next steps: - Work up the cardiac cause: ECG, chest imaging, BNP/NT-proBNP, troponin, and bedside/formal echo (RV size/function, valvular disease, pulmonary hypertension). - Treat congestion (diuresis) while respecting preload-dependent RV physiology; treat the underlying driver (ischemia, PE, pulmonary hypertension, valvular dis
nodes.recommendation: Confirm and treat the cardiac cause (echo, diuresis, treat driver) while excluding a superimposed DVT in the asymmetric leg.

nodes.title: Right-Heart Failure — Unlikely
nodes.body: No dyspnea, no raised JVP, and no cardiac history \u2014 a cardiac driver is unlikely for this asymmetric swelling. Return to the hub for the benign mimics.
nodes.recommendation: Cardiac cause unlikely without cardiopulmonary signs; proceed to the benign mimics.

nodes.title: Benign Mimics — Characterize
nodes.summary: Sort benign mimics; ~30% of "cellulitis" is pseudocellulitis; measure SVT length and distance from the SFJ. Keep DVT and nec-fasc safety nets up.
nodes.body: Once the limb- and life-threats are excluded, sort the common causes \u2014 but keep the safety nets up (cellulitis can be early necrotizing infection; a "Baker cyst" swelling can hide a DVT). - Cellulitis: warm, tender, spreading erythema \u00B1 fever, often a portal of entry; usually unilateral \u2014 bilateral lower-leg "cellulitis" is more often venous stasis dermatitis. ⚠️ ~30% of patients ad

nodes.title: Cellulitis — Antibiotics + Reassess Safety Nets
nodes.body: Cellulitis (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here): - Empiric antibiotics covering streptococci \u00B1 staphylococci (add MRSA cover for purulence, penetrating trauma, or risk factors); mark the erythema border and reassess. - Re-confirm this is NOT a necrotizing infection \u2014 pain out of proportion, toxicity, crepitus, or rapid spread \u2192 back to the necrotizing branch and surgery. -
nodes.recommendation: Empiric strep\u00B1staph (MRSA if purulent) abx, mark and reassess; actively consider pseudocellulitis (bilateral/itchy/afebrile = stasis dermatitis, not infection); keep necrotizing-infection and DVT safety nets up; admit if toxic/failing.

nodes.title: Baker Cyst / Venous / Lymphedema — Symptomatic Care + Follow-Up
nodes.body: Ruptured Baker cyst, superficial thrombophlebitis, chronic venous insufficiency, or lymphedema (no dedicated consult yet \u2014 manage here) in a well patient with the emergencies excluded: - Ruptured Baker cyst: confirm with ultrasound (and exclude DVT), then symptomatic care \u2014 rest, ice, elevation, NSAIDs, compression; treat the underlying knee arthropathy. - Superficial vein thrombosis (SV
nodes.recommendation: Symptomatic care + compression + outpatient follow-up for Baker cyst / venous / lymphedema; US-confirm and exclude DVT. Superficial vein thrombosis: within 3 cm of the SFJ \u2192 therapeutic anticoagulation; \u22655 cm and >3 cm from the ju

nodes.title: Initial Bundle
nodes.body: The swollen-leg work-up bundle (scale to acuity): - Focused exam: pulses and skin color/temperature of BOTH legs, compartment tension, pain on passive stretch, calf circumference, portal of entry, and chest symptoms / hypoxia. - Wells DVT score + D-dimer + compression ultrasound \u2014 the DVT pathway (Wells in the toolbar). Check whether your D-dimer is reported in FEU (cutoff 500 ng/mL) or DDU (

nodes.title: Reassess After the Bundle
nodes.summary: Limb threat / necrotizing infection / PE / toxic → escalate; stable + diagnosed → disposition.
nodes.body: After the focused exam, ultrasound, and initial labs \u2014 where does the patient stand?

nodes.title: Imaging
nodes.body: Match the study to the question: - Compression ultrasound with Doppler \u2014 the primary test for DVT; also distinguishes a ruptured Baker cyst and assesses superficial veins. Specify what you want: WHOLE-LEG (complete) US needs no repeat if negative; a PROXIMAL or 2-point study in a Wells-LIKELY patient needs a repeat scan at 5\u20137 days if negative. For SVT, ask for thrombus length and distan

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: OR/admit the limb-threats; observe/anticoagulate the DVTs and borderlines; discharge benign/cellulitis with follow-up.
nodes.body: Where does this patient go?

nodes.title: Admit / OR
nodes.body: To the OR / admit the limb- or life-threat. - Acute limb ischemia \u2192 emergent revascularization (embolectomy / thrombolysis / bypass) + heparin. - Phlegmasia \u2192 heparin + catheter-directed thrombolysis/thrombectomy, limb elevation, resuscitation. - Necrotizing infection \u2192 emergent debridement + broad-spectrum abx + resuscitation. - Compartment syndrome \u2192 emergent fasciotomy. - Ma
nodes.recommendation: OR/emergent intervention for ischemia / phlegmasia / necrotizing infection / compartment syndrome; admit high-risk DVT-PE; ICU if unstable.

nodes.title: Observe / Short Stay
nodes.body: Observation / short stay for the borderline patient \u2014 e.g., a confirmed DVT started on anticoagulation who needs teaching and follow-up arranged, a limb where ischemia/compartment is not fully excluded and needs serial exams, or cellulitis borderline for outpatient failure. - Serial exams (pulses, compartments), repeat ultrasound if the picture changes, and specialist input before disposition
nodes.recommendation: Short observation + serial exams + specialist input; arrange anticoagulation follow-up, then admit or discharge with tight follow-up.

nodes.title: Discharge
nodes.body: Discharge the well patient with a clear plan. - Uncomplicated DVT: DOAC started (apixaban 10 mg BID \u00D7 7 d \u2192 5 mg BID, or rivaroxaban 15 mg BID \u00D7 21 d \u2192 20 mg daily, WITH FOOD), outpatient management confirmed, anticoagulation follow-up, and strict PE return precautions (chest pain, dyspnea, syncope). Confirm the patient can actually obtain and afford the drug before discharge.
nodes.recommendation: Discharge benign/uncomplicated patients with anticoagulation or antibiotics as indicated, compression, and explicit PE / limb-threat return precautions. Book the 5\u20137 day repeat US before discharge if the negative study was proximal/2-p

nodes.title: Unknown Ingestion Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Bedside glucose, naloxone trial, ECG, ABG, and the universal lab bundle (APAP + salicylate always).
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Acetaminophen \u2014 silent early; level on every unknown ingestion, start NAC by nomogram. 2. Salicylate \u2014 mixed acid-base, tinnitus, tachypnea; level + serial levels. 3. Sodium-channel blocker / TCA \u2014 wide QRS \u2192 sodium bicarbonate. 4. Toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol) \u2014 high osmolar/anion gap; fomepizole. 5. Cardiotoxins (beta-blocker,

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Match the Toxidrome
nodes.summary: 12 toxidrome buckets cover the high-mortality ingestions; default to the undifferentiated pathway when none fit.
nodes.body: Pick the closest pattern. When two fit, work the more time-critical first.

nodes.title: TCA / Sodium-Channel Blocker
nodes.body: Open TCA Toxidrome. Next 5 minutes: Sodium Bicarbonate Drip target serum pH 7.50-7.55, intubate if AMS/hypoventilation, treat seizures with lorazepam, norepi for hypotension (avoid pure-alpha unless markedly tachycardic).
nodes.recommendation: Wide QRS is the trigger - bicarb goes in before the level returns.

nodes.title: Salicylate Toxicity
nodes.body: Open Salicylate. Next 5 minutes: isotonic bicarbonate drip (target urine pH >7.5), serial levels q2h, EXTRIP-criteria hemodialysis \u2014 recommended: level >100 mg/dL, or >90 mg/dL with impaired kidney function, altered mental status, new hypoxemia requiring oxygen, or failure of standard therapy; suggested: level >90 mg/dL, or >80 mg/dL with impaired kidney function, or pH \u22647.20. (EXTRIP fr
nodes.recommendation: Bicarbonate + dialysis. Intubation is dangerous - the patient breathes off the acid.

nodes.title: Acetaminophen Toxicity
nodes.body: Open Acetaminophen and apply the Rumack-Matthew Nomogram. Next 5 minutes: start N-acetylcysteine if level above treatment line, unknown timing, staggered ingestion, or massive/concerning exposure. 4-hour level is the earliest interpretable value.
nodes.recommendation: When in doubt, start NAC. Risk of treatment is negligible vs cost of missed hepatotoxicity.

nodes.title: Opioid / Xylazine Toxidrome
nodes.body: Open Xylazine Toxicity. Next 5 minutes: Naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV titrated to respirations, NOT consciousness. Xylazine sedation does NOT reverse with naloxone - support ventilation, monitor for opioid recurrence as naloxone wears off. Xylazine is the top adulterant in the US fentanyl supply (~30% of DEA-seized fentanyl powder, ~6% of pills, 2023 NDTA; detected in 48 of 50 states) and exceeds 70-90%
nodes.recommendation: Titrate naloxone to breathing. Xylazine adds sedation that naloxone will not fix.

nodes.title: Sympathomimetic Crisis
nodes.body: Next 5 minutes: aggressive lorazepam or midazolam titration, active cooling (target <39C in <30 min if hyperthermic), IV fluids, ECG, CK/lactate/troponin. Avoid pure beta-blockers (unopposed alpha = HTN crisis). For severe HTN: nicardipine or phentolamine. Watch for rhabdo, seizures, ischemic chest pain.
nodes.recommendation: Benzos first. Cooling second. Beta-blockers last and never alone.

nodes.title: Cholinergic / Organophosphate
