nodes.body: Next 5 minutes: decontaminate (remove clothes, wash skin - protect yourself with PPE). Atropine 2-5 mg IV, DOUBLE every 5 min until tracheobronchial secretions dry (HR/BP secondary). Add pralidoxime 1-2 g IV over 30 min for organophosphate, then infusion. Seizures: lorazepam. Plan for prolonged ventilation; intermediate syndrome appears 24-96 h post-exposure.
nodes.recommendation: Atropine endpoint is dry secretions, not heart rate. Decontaminate the patient AND the staff.

nodes.title: Anticholinergic Toxidrome
nodes.body: Next 5 minutes: lorazepam for agitation, active cooling, IV fluids, ECG (check QRS - many anticholinergics also have Na-channel blockade). Physostigmine 1-2 mg IV slow push ONLY for pure anticholinergic toxicity with severe agitation/delirium - CONTRAINDICATED if any QRS prolongation, TCA, or unknown co-ingestion. Differential pitfall: dry/hot = anticholinergic; wet/hot = sympathomimetic or seroto
nodes.recommendation: Benzos and cooling for everyone. Physostigmine only when QRS is narrow and the toxidrome is pure.

nodes.title: Serotonin Syndrome
nodes.body: Open Serotonin Syndrome. Next 5 minutes: stop offending agents, lorazepam titration, active cooling, IV fluids. Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO/NGT then 2 mg q2h for moderate-severe cases. Intubate + paralyze if hyperthermia >41.5C unresponsive to sedation.
nodes.recommendation: Clonus + recent serotonergic agent is the recognition combo. Cooling beats meds.

nodes.title: CO +/- Cyanide
nodes.body: Open CO Toxicity. Next 5 minutes: 100% non-rebreather (or intubate), co-oximetry (standard SpO2 is unreliable), lactate (>10 raises cyanide suspicion in fire victims). Empiric hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV for closed-space fire with lactate >8-10 or AMS. Hyperbaric oxygen for severe CO (LOC, ischemia, pregnancy, persistent symptoms).
nodes.recommendation: Treat CO and cyanide simultaneously in fire victims. Do not wait for cyanide level.

nodes.title: Caustic Ingestion
nodes.body: Open Caustic Ingestion. Next 5 minutes: NPO, IV access, airway assessment (drooling, stridor, voice change = early intubation), CT neck/chest if perforation concern, GI consult for endoscopy within 24h. NO neutralization, NO charcoal, NO NG tube. Watch for mediastinitis with alkali, hemorrhage with acid.
nodes.recommendation: Airway first. Endoscopy is for staging, not therapy.

nodes.title: Toxic Alcohols
nodes.body: Open Toxic Alcohols. Next 5 minutes: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV loading dose if osm gap or AG acidosis with appropriate history. Bicarbonate drip for severe acidemia. Cofactors: folate (methanol), thiamine + pyridoxine (ethylene glycol). Dialysis for severe acidosis, end-organ damage, or level >50 mg/dL (where available).
nodes.recommendation: Empiric fomepizole pays for itself in saved retinas and kidneys.

nodes.title: Digoxin / Cardiac Glycoside
nodes.body: Open Digoxin Toxicity. Next 5 minutes: ECG (any rhythm except VT/VF), level, K+ (high K predicts mortality in acute, treat with Digibind NOT calcium first). Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV for symptomatic brady. Empiric 10-20 vials Digibind for life-threatening arrhythmia / cardiac arrest. Plant exposure (oleander, foxglove): assume worse, dose higher.
nodes.recommendation: Hyperkalemia + brady + GI + visual = call Digibind in. Calcium is debated.

nodes.title: Undifferentiated Ingestion - No Clean Toxidrome
nodes.summary: Drive workup with derangements (QRS, AG, osm gap, lactate, glucose, temperature). Poison Control 1-800-222-1222.
nodes.body: Many real ingestions present in the gaps between toxidromes. Drive workup with what is abnormal, not what was claimed. Sort by physiology: - Wide QRS, prolonged QT, conduction block: sodium channel blocker, K-channel blocker (citalopram/quetiapine), CCB/beta-blocker. Empiric bicarb if QRS >100, calcium + HDI for CCB/BB physiology. - AG metabolic acidosis with normal lactate: salicylate, toxic alco

nodes.title: Resus / Decon / Antidote - In That Order
nodes.summary: Stabilize physiology before decontamination. Charcoal is narrow. Lipid emulsion is the cardiac arrest rescue.
nodes.body: Resuscitation first: - Airway (RSI with ketamine/etomidate; succinylcholine OK except organophosphate/burn/hyperK). - Breathing (ventilate to match metabolic acidosis - salicylate, toxic alcohol patients need high minute ventilation). - Circulation (fluids, then norepi; calcium + HDI for CCB/BB; bicarb for Na-channel; lipid emulsion as rescue for severe lipophilic tox). Decontamination - narrow in

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Reassess physiology q15-30 min in any ingestion; deterioration triggers a return to exclusions.
nodes.body: Toxicology trajectories diverge fast - resolving sympathomimetics look like ventricular ectopy on the way down, salicylate looks great until the brain swells.

nodes.title: Imaging + Labs
nodes.summary: Trust the mandatory bundle. Add levels/imaging only when they will change the next 15 minutes of care.
nodes.body: Mandatory bundle (already sent at ui-start): glucose, electrolytes, BUN/Cr, lactate, AG, osmolar gap, APAP, salicylate, ABG/VBG, ECG. Add when indicated: - Urine drug screen: LOW yield, slow, full of false positives/negatives. Do not let it change management. Skip unless required for psych/disposition. - Specific levels: lithium, digoxin, valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine, iron, theophylline - a

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: ICU for instability/infusion; admit if half-life or sustained-release demands it; psych path for intentional; discharge only after clear observation.
nodes.body: Disposition follows trajectory + agent half-life + intentional vs unintentional.

nodes.title: ICU / Resus Admission
nodes.body: ICU for: intubation, vasopressor/inotrope requirement, dialysis, antidote infusion (fomepizole, NAC infusion, HDI, lipid emulsion), refractory acidosis, persistent QRS prolongation, ongoing seizures, hyperthermia, body packer with leak. Call regional Poison Control + medical toxicology for ALL ICU-level ingestions.
nodes.recommendation: Loop in toxicology. Specialty dosing and antidote logistics save lives in the second 24 hours.

nodes.title: Admit / Observation
nodes.body: Admit for: sustained-release agent (CCB, lithium, bupropion, salicylate), long half-life (digoxin, methadone, phenobarbital), staggered APAP, ongoing supportive care, persistent mild toxicity, social inability to manage. Observation period varies: 6h for most short-acting agents with normal repeat ECG and exam; 24h+ for sustained-release.
nodes.recommendation: When in doubt, observe one more half-life. Tox rebounds are real.

nodes.title: Medical Clearance + Psych Disposition
nodes.body: Medical clearance for psych pathway: vitals normal, exam normal, repeat ECG normal, mandatory labs back and reassuring, observation window appropriate for agent passed. Document: agent(s), dose, time, intent, medical clearance criteria met. Pitfall: APAP can be normal at 4h and lethal at 24h with staggered ingestion. Recheck level + LFTs at 24h if any doubt about timing.
nodes.recommendation: Do not psych-clear until APAP/salicylate trajectory is established.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when: asymptomatic through full observation window for the agent, normal repeat vitals/ECG, mandatory labs normal, accidental/exploratory ingestion in a competent adult or supervised child, reliable caregiver and follow-up. Return precautions: any new symptom, vomiting, drowsiness, behavior change, jaundice, dark urine, decreased urine output, palpitations, syncope. Call Poison Cont
nodes.recommendation: Document the observation window, agent half-life, and the precautions you gave.

nodes.title: Upper GI Bleed — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Hemorrhage proximal to Treitz — TXA NOT recommended (HALT-IT: no benefit, increased VTE/seizures)
nodes.body: UGIB Steps Summary Definition: Hemorrhage proximal to ligament of Treitz (esophagus, stomach, duodenum). [1][2] Presentation: • Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-ground) • Melena (black, tarry stool) • Hematochezia (if massive — brisk UGIB) • Syncope, lightheadedness, presyncope Critical History: • NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants • Alcohol use, known liver disease/cirrhosis • Prior GI bleeding, H.

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Status
nodes.summary: Assess SBP, HR, mental status, perfusion — hemodynamic instability triggers resuscitation pathway
nodes.body: Assess hemodynamic stability: [1][2] Signs of Shock: • SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 • HR >100 with hypotension • Altered mental status • Cool, clammy extremities • Weak/thready pulse High-Risk Features: • Hematemesis with active bleeding • Syncope at presentation • Age >65 with comorbidities What is the patient's hemodynamic status?

nodes.title: Risk Stratification
nodes.summary: GBS 0-1 = low risk (<1% need intervention), consider outpatient EGD; AIMS65 >=2 = 31% mortality

nodes.title: Cirrhosis or Liver Disease?
nodes.summary: Variceal bleeding = 59% of GI bleeds in cirrhotics — changes entire management pathway
nodes.body: Variceal bleeding accounts for 10-20% of UGIB [6] In cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding: • 59% variceal • 16% peptic ulcer disease • 25% other causes Signs suggesting cirrhosis: • Known liver disease history • Jaundice, ascites, spider angiomata • Thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy • Hepatomegaly/splenomegaly Does patient have known or suspected cirrhosis?

nodes.title: Unstable UGIB — Resuscitation
nodes.summary: 2 large-bore IVs, T&C, intubate if GCS <8 — restrictive transfusion Hgb <7 (Villanueva: 45% mortality reduction)
nodes.body: Immediate Actions: [1][2][7] Access & Labs: • 2 large-bore IVs (16-18G) or central line • Type and crossmatch (4+ units if massive) • CBC, BMP, PT/INR, fibrinogen, lactate • Consider MTP activation if exsanguinating Airway Protection: • Intubate if: GCS <8, massive hematemesis, inability to protect airway • Suction ready at bedside Blood Products — RESTRICTIVE Strategy: [8] • Transfuse when Hgb <7

nodes.title: Transfusion Strategy
nodes.summary: Restrictive: Hgb <7 threshold (except ACS >8) — excessive transfusion increases portal pressure/worsens varices
nodes.body: Restrictive Transfusion (Recommended): [8] | Threshold | Hgb <7 g/dL | |-----------|-------------| | Target | 7-8 g/dL | | Exception | ACS: target >8 g/dL | Why Restrictive? • Excessive transfusion increases portal pressure • Worsens variceal bleeding • Villanueva: 45% mortality reduction with restrictive approach Coagulation Targets: • Platelets >50,000 • Fibrinogen >150 mg/dL • INR: Consider rev

nodes.title: Non-Variceal UGIB — Causes
nodes.summary: Peptic ulcer 35-50%, erosive gastritis 8-15%, Mallory-Weiss 8-15% — BUN:Cr >30 suggests upper source
nodes.body: Differential Diagnosis: [1][2] | Cause | Frequency | Key Features | |-------|-----------|---------------| | Peptic Ulcer | 35-50% | NSAIDs, aspirin, H. pylori | | Erosive Gastritis | 8-15% | NSAIDs, alcohol, stress | | Mallory-Weiss | 8-15% | Retching/vomiting first | | Esophagitis | 5-15% | GERD history | | Dieulafoy Lesion | 1-2% | Large arteriole, intermittent massive bleed | | Malignancy | 1-4

nodes.title: PPI Therapy
nodes.summary: Pre-EGD: PPI 80mg IV; post-EGD high-risk: 8mg/hr infusion x72h or 40mg IV BID-QID x3 days
nodes.body: Pre-Endoscopy PPI: [1][9] • ACG 2021: No strong recommendation (limited evidence) • If used: Pantoprazole 80 mg IV or Esomeprazole 80 mg IV Post-Endoscopy PPI (High-Risk Ulcers): [9] • Bolus: 80 mg IV • Then: 8 mg/hr infusion x 72h OR 40 mg IV BID-QID x 3 days • Rationale: Raises gastric pH >6, stabilizes clot EMCrit/IBCC Approach: • PPI 40 mg IV Q12h (bolus dosing = infusion efficacy) Duration: •

nodes.title: Pre-Endoscopy Preparation
nodes.summary: Erythromycin 250mg IV 20-90min pre-EGD — improves visualization (OR 3.4), reduces repeat endoscopy
nodes.body: Erythromycin (Prokinetic): [1][10] • Dose: 250 mg IV over 10-30 min (or 3 mg/kg) • Timing: 20-90 minutes before EGD • Benefits: - Improves visualization (OR 3.4) - Reduces repeat endoscopy (OR 0.51) - Shorter hospital stay • Best for: Active hematemesis, blood on NG lavage Pre-EGD Checklist: 1. Hemodynamic stabilization 2. Airway protection (intubate if GCS <8) 3. Erythromycin 250 mg IV 4. PPI 40-

nodes.title: Endoscopy Timing
nodes.summary: Standard within 24h; urgent <12h if unstable despite resuscitation; emergent <6h for massive hemorrhage
nodes.body: Standard Timing: [1][11] • Within 24 hours for most patients (ACG 2021) • Earlier endoscopy (<12h) NOT shown to improve outcomes Urgent EGD (<12 hours): • Hemodynamic instability DESPITE resuscitation • Ongoing active bleeding • High-risk features Emergent EGD (<6 hours): • Massive hemorrhage with persistent shock • Suspected variceal bleeding with instability When to Skip EGD → Go to IR: • Suspec

nodes.title: Variceal Bleeding — Overview
nodes.summary: Start vasoactive therapy IMMEDIATELY, restrictive transfusion critical, antibiotics reduce mortality
nodes.body: Key Principles: [6][12] 1. Start vasoactive therapy IMMEDIATELY (even before EGD confirmation) 2. Restrictive transfusion critical — over-resuscitation increases portal pressure 3. Antibiotics reduce mortality in cirrhosis 4. Target mild hypotension rather than normotension Vasoactive Agents: • Octreotide (US standard) • Terlipressin (if available — only one with mortality benefit) Avoid: • Excess

nodes.title: Octreotide Protocol
nodes.body: Octreotide Dosing: [6][12] Loading dose: 50 mcg IV bolus Maintenance: 50 mcg/hr continuous infusion Duration: 2-5 days Mechanism: • Reduces splanchnic blood flow • Decreases portal pressure • Start immediately when varices suspected Side Effects: • QT prolongation • Bradycardia • Hyperglycemia • Gallbladder sludge (prolonged use) Terlipressin (if available): • 2 mg IV bolus, then 1 mg IV q4-6h • O
nodes.recommendation: Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hr x 2-5 days. Start BEFORE EGD.

nodes.title: Antibiotic Prophylaxis
nodes.body: MANDATORY for all cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding: [6][12][13][18][19] First-line: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily up to 7 days — AASLD 2024 allows discontinuation once hemostasis achieved and vasoactive drugs stopped Alternative: Norfloxacin 400 mg PO BID up to 7 days (avoid if high quinolone resistance) Evidence: • Reduces bacterial infections • Reduces rebleeding • May reduce mortality • Most infec
nodes.recommendation: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily up to 7 days for cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding. May discontinue once hemostasis achieved and vasoactives stopped (AASLD 2024).

nodes.title: Variceal Resuscitation Principles
nodes.summary: Avoid over-resuscitation — excessive fluids increase portal pressure, target SBP 90-100 acceptable
nodes.body: CRITICAL: Avoid Over-Resuscitation [6][8] Why less is more: • Excessive fluid increases portal pressure • Increased portal pressure worsens variceal bleeding • Dilutional coagulopathy • Pulmonary edema in cirrhosis Targets: • Permissive hypotension: SBP 90-100 mmHg acceptable • Hgb 7-8 g/dL (restrictive transfusion critical) • Avoid crystalloid boluses if possible Blood Products: • pRBCs when Hgb

nodes.title: Balloon Tamponade — Indications
nodes.summary: Last resort for exsanguinating variceal bleeding — 80-90% effective temporary control, bridge to TIPS
nodes.body: Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota Tube: [14][15] Indications: • Massive, exsanguinating variceal bleeding uncontrolled by medical/endoscopic therapy • Bridge to TIPS or definitive treatment • Last resort when endoscopy unavailable or failed • 80-90% effective for temporary control Minnesota Tube Preferred (has esophageal aspiration port) Contraindications (Relative): • Esophageal stricture • Recen

nodes.title: Balloon Tamponade — Preparation
nodes.summary: INTUBATE FIRST — test balloons underwater, CXR before inflation, airway protection is MANDATORY
nodes.body: Equipment: [14][15] • Sengstaken-Blakemore (3 lumen) or Minnesota tube (4 lumen) • 60 mL syringes (Luer-lock and slip-tip) • Three-way stopcocks • Manometer for pressure monitoring • 1000 mL IV bag for traction • Water basin for balloon testing • Water-soluble lubricant Pre-Procedure: 1. INTUBATE THE PATIENT — aspiration risk is high 2. Test both balloons underwater — inflate to max, check for lea

nodes.title: Balloon Tamponade — Technique
nodes.summary: CXR before inflation, gastric balloon to 250-500mL, traction 0.5-1kg, mark tube position at teeth
nodes.body: Insertion (from Roberts & Hedges): [14] 1. Insert deflated tube orally (preferred) or nasally 2. Advance to 50-cm mark (past GE junction) 3. Confirm gastric position: auscultate epigastrium + air injection STOP — Obtain CXR to confirm position BEFORE inflation Gastric Balloon Inflation: 1. Inflate with 50 mL air initially 2. Add 50 mL increments to 250-300 mL (SBT) or 450-500 mL (Minnesota) 3. If

nodes.title: Esophageal Balloon (If Needed)
nodes.summary: Only if gastric tamponade fails — target 30-40mmHg, NEVER exceed 45mmHg, deflate q6-8h, max 24h
nodes.body: Only inflate if gastric tamponade fails: [14][15] Technique: 1. Inflate esophageal balloon in 5-10 mmHg increments 2. Target pressure: 30-40 mmHg 3. NEVER exceed 45 mmHg (esophageal necrosis/rupture risk) 4. Monitor pressure continuously with manometer Post-Placement: • CXR to confirm final position • ICU admission mandatory • Continuous vital sign monitoring • Tube position checks Q1-2h • Deflate

nodes.title: Balloon Tamponade — Complications
nodes.summary: Esophageal rupture up to 6%; if airway obstruction from migration CUT ALL LUMENS and remove immediately
nodes.body: Complications: [14][15] Minor: • Nasal/pharyngeal irritation • Epistaxis • Hoarseness Major: • Aspiration pneumonia (most common) • Esophageal rupture (up to 6%, often fatal) • Esophageal/gastric necrosis • Airway obstruction from tube migration • Rebleeding on deflation (~50%) Catastrophic: • Tracheal compression • Tracheoesophageal fistula • Cardiopulmonary arrest EMERGENCY TUBE REMOVAL: If airw

nodes.title: TIPS Consultation
nodes.summary: AASLD 2024: evaluate ALL AVH patients for preemptive TIPS at index presentation; Child-Pugh C or B-with-active-bleeding = preemptive TIPS <72h (86% vs 61% 1-yr survival)
nodes.body: Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS): [6][16][18] AASLD 2024 Paradigm Shift: At initial presentation with acute variceal hemorrhage, evaluate ALL patients for preemptive TIPS candidacy — not just rescue. Six-week mortality for AVH is 10-15%; high-risk patients benefit most. [18] Preemptive (Early) TIPS — within 72h of admission: • Child-Pugh C (score 10-13) with acute variceal blee

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: GBS 0-1 = outpatient; GBS >=2 = floor; AIMS65 >=2 or unstable = ICU
nodes.body: Risk-Stratify for Disposition: [1][2][4] GBS 0-1 = Low Risk: • <1% need intervention • Consider outpatient EGD within 24-48h • Requires reliable follow-up Admission Criteria: • GBS ≥2 or any high-risk feature • Required transfusion • Hemodynamic instability • Active bleeding • Anticoagulation that needs management ICU Criteria: • AIMS65 ≥2 • Hemodynamic instability • Ongoing bleeding • Intubated •

nodes.title: Low-Risk UGIB — Outpatient
nodes.body: GBS 0-1 = Low Risk, Outpatient Candidate: [4][17] Criteria for Outpatient Management: • GBS 0-1 • Hemodynamically stable • No transfusion required • No high-risk comorbidities • Reliable follow-up available • Can tolerate PO Discharge Plan: • PPI: Omeprazole 40 mg PO BID until EGD • Outpatient EGD within 24-48 hours • Avoid NSAIDs, aspirin (discuss with PCP) • Clear liquid diet, advance as tolerat
nodes.recommendation: GBS 0-1: Outpatient PPI + EGD within 24-48h. Strict return precautions.

nodes.title: Floor Admission
nodes.body: Admission Orders: [1][2] Monitoring: • Vital signs Q4h • Serial hemoglobin Q6-8h • NPO until after EGD Medications: • PPI 40 mg IV Q12h (or 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hr if high-risk) • Consider erythromycin 250 mg IV pre-EGD Consults: • GI for EGD within 24 hours Blood Bank: • Type and screen on hold • Crossmatch if high-risk Post-EGD: • Risk-stratify based on endoscopic findings • High-risk ulcer (Forre
nodes.recommendation: Floor admission: IV PPI, EGD within 24h, serial Hgb. GI consult.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU Admission Criteria: [1][2][5] • AIMS65 ≥2 • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation • Ongoing active bleeding • Intubated for airway protection • Cirrhosis with variceal bleeding • Multiple vasopressor requirement • Balloon tamponade in place ICU Orders: • Continuous telemetry • Arterial line for BP monitoring • Central access for resuscitation • Ventilator management if intubated • Seri
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for high-risk UGIB. Urgent GI + consider IR for TIPS.

nodes.title: Post-Endoscopy Management
nodes.summary: Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa = PPI infusion x72h; IIc/III = PO PPI; all patients need H. pylori testing
nodes.body: Based on Endoscopic Findings: [1][9] Forrest Classification (Ulcers): | Class | Description | Rebleed Risk | |-------|-------------|--------------| | Ia | Spurting hemorrhage | 90% | | Ib | Oozing hemorrhage | 50% | | IIa | Visible vessel | 43% | | IIb | Adherent clot | 22% | | IIc | Flat pigmented spot | 7% | | III | Clean ulcer base | 3% | High-Risk (Ia, Ib, IIa): • PPI infusion x 72h • Second-l

nodes.title: Acute Urinary Retention
nodes.summary: Bladder scan >300mL confirms retention — assess structural, medication, neurogenic, infectious causes
nodes.body: Inability to voluntarily void urine. Most common urologic emergency in men. Immediate actions: \u2022 Bladder scan to confirm retention (>300 mL) \u2022 Assess for signs of infection (fever, dysuria, pyuria) \u2022 Review medication list for anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, opioids \u2022 Check for neurologic symptoms (saddle anesthesia, leg weakness, fecal incontinence) Four categories of caus

nodes.title: Red Flag Assessment
nodes.summary: Screen for cauda equina, urethral trauma, and urosepsis before catheterization
nodes.body: Screen for emergent etiologies that change management: Cauda equina syndrome signs: \u2022 Saddle anesthesia \u2022 Bilateral leg weakness \u2022 Fecal incontinence \u2022 Recent back pain with progressive symptoms Sepsis/Pyelonephritis: \u2022 Fever, tachycardia, hypotension \u2022 Costovertebral angle tenderness Trauma: \u2022 Blood at urethral meatus \u2022 Pelvic fracture \u2022 Perineal hemat

nodes.title: Neurologic Emergency
nodes.body: Cauda equina syndrome suspected. Immediate actions: \u2022 Place Foley catheter for bladder decompression \u2022 Emergent MRI lumbar spine \u2022 Neurosurgery consult STAT \u2022 Dexamethasone 10 mg IV if malignancy or epidural abscess suspected Cauda equina is a surgical emergency. Time to decompression correlates with neurologic recovery. Note: Women and children with AUR should have neurologic
nodes.recommendation: Emergent MRI and neurosurgery consult. Foley placement for decompression. Consider IV steroids if malignancy suspected.

nodes.title: Urethral Trauma
nodes.body: Do NOT attempt blind urethral catheterization. Signs of urethral injury: \u2022 Blood at urethral meatus \u2022 High-riding prostate on rectal exam \u2022 Perineal ecchymosis \u2022 Pelvic fracture mechanism Management: \u2022 Retrograde urethrogram (RUG) to assess integrity \u2022 If RUG shows disruption: suprapubic catheter by urology \u2022 If RUG normal: gentle Foley attempt may proceed Urolog
nodes.recommendation: Retrograde urethrogram before any catheter attempt. Urology consult for suprapubic catheter if urethral disruption confirmed.

nodes.title: Urosepsis
nodes.body: Obstructed infected system = emergent decompression. Immediate actions: \u2022 Place Foley catheter immediately \u2022 Blood cultures x 2 \u2022 Urinalysis and urine culture \u2022 IV fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid) \u2022 Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour Empiric antibiotics: \u2022 Ceftriaxone 2g IV OR \u2022 Piperacillin-Tazobactam 4.5g IV if high-risk Admit to ICU if persiste
nodes.recommendation: Immediate Foley catheter, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation. ICU admission if hemodynamically unstable.

nodes.title: Bladder Volume
nodes.summary: Bedside bladder US: <300mL = not retention, 300-1000mL = standard, >1000mL = high volume/POD risk
nodes.body: Perform bedside bladder ultrasound to assess volume. Bladder volume = (Height x Width x Depth) x 0.75 Most modern bladder scanners calculate this automatically. Interpretation: \u2022 <300 mL: Not true retention - consider other diagnoses \u2022 300-1000 mL: Typical acute retention \u2022 >1000 mL: High volume - increased risk of post-obstructive diuresis

nodes.title: Not True Retention
nodes.body: Bladder volume <300 mL suggests alternative diagnosis. Consider: \u2022 UTI/cystitis with urinary urgency \u2022 Prostatitis \u2022 Pelvic pain syndromes \u2022 Psychogenic urinary hesitancy Workup: \u2022 Urinalysis \u2022 Prostate exam \u2022 Abdominal/pelvic imaging if indicated Treat underlying cause.
nodes.recommendation: Not true urinary retention. Evaluate for alternative diagnoses (UTI, prostatitis, pelvic pathology).

nodes.title: High Volume Retention
nodes.summary: >1000mL increases POD risk — get BMP, UA; rapid drainage is safe, no need to clamp
nodes.body: Volume >1000 mL increases risk of: \u2022 Post-obstructive diuresis (POD) \u2022 Acute kidney injury (if chronic retention) \u2022 Hematuria ex vacuo Labs to obtain: \u2022 BMP (creatinine, electrolytes) \u2022 Urinalysis Note on drainage: Rapid vs gradual drainage is equivalent. Evidence does NOT support clamping at 200-500 mL intervals. Complete drainage is safe and does not increase complicatio

nodes.title: Catheter Selection
nodes.summary: 16-18Fr standard, coude first-line in older men with BPH, insert to hub before inflating balloon
nodes.body: Standard Foley catheter technique: 1. Position patient supine 2. Sterile prep and drape 3. Liberal lubrication (lidocaine jelly preferred) 4. In uncircumcised men: retract foreskin, replace AFTER insertion 5. Insert to hub before inflating balloon 6. Inflate balloon with 10 mL sterile water 7. Gently withdraw until resistance felt Catheter sizing: \u2022 Standard: 16-18 Fr (most adults) \u2022 Hem

nodes.title: Post-Catheterization
nodes.summary: Document initial volume, send UA/BMP, monitor output for POD (>200mL/hr x2h or >3L/24h)
nodes.body: Document initial drained volume. Assess for hematuria ex vacuo: Brief, self-limited hematuria after rapid decompression is common and benign. Usually resolves within hours. Labs to send: \u2022 Urinalysis and culture \u2022 BMP (especially if high volume or suspected chronic retention) Output monitoring: Post-obstructive diuresis = >200 mL/hr for 2+ consecutive hours OR >3000 mL in 24 hours.

nodes.title: Failed Catheterization
nodes.summary: Try coude tip (curve UP), extra lidocaine jelly, larger or smaller catheter, Seldinger technique
nodes.body: First attempt failed - troubleshooting: Try Coude catheter: Curved tip (15-30 degree angle) navigates elevated bladder neck in BPH. Ensure curve points UP (toward ceiling) during insertion. Other techniques: \u2022 Additional lubrication \u2022 Lidocaine jelly intraurethral (2% lidocaine, 10-20 mL, wait 5 min) \u2022 Larger catheter (sometimes passes easier) \u2022 Smaller catheter over guide wire

nodes.title: Urology Consult
nodes.summary: Urology for cystoscopy-guided placement or suprapubic catheter — avoid further blind attempts
nodes.body: Consult urology for: \u2022 Failed standard and coude catheter attempts \u2022 Suspected urethral stricture or false passage \u2022 Known complex urologic history Urology options: \u2022 Flexible cystoscopy with guidewire-assisted catheter placement \u2022 Suprapubic catheter if urethral route not possible Suprapubic catheter indications: \u2022 Urethral stricture not amenable to dilation \u2022 U

nodes.title: Suprapubic Catheter
nodes.body: Post-suprapubic catheter care: \u2022 Keep dressing clean and dry \u2022 May shower after 24-48 hours (no baths) \u2022 Monitor for signs of infection at insertion site \u2022 Urology follow-up in 1-2 weeks for evaluation of underlying cause Advantages of suprapubic route: \u2022 Avoids urethral trauma \u2022 Easier hygiene \u2022 Can trial voiding by clamping (while leaving catheter in place) Com
nodes.recommendation: Suprapubic catheter care instructions. Start tamsulosin for TWOC optimization. Urology follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

nodes.title: Post-Obstructive Diuresis
nodes.summary: UOP >200mL/hr x2h — physiologic (self-limited ~24h) vs pathologic (>48h); monitor BMP q12-24h
nodes.body: Definition: Urine output >200 mL/hr for 2+ consecutive hours OR >3 L in 24 hours. Types: \u2022 Physiologic POD: Self-limiting (~24 hours), excretion of retained fluid/solutes \u2022 Pathologic POD: Persists >48 hours, tubular dysfunction, requires intervention Risk factors: \u2022 Bilateral obstruction (or unilateral with solitary kidney) \u2022 Chronic retention with elevated creatinine \u2022 C

nodes.title: POD Fluid Management
nodes.body: Fluid replacement strategy: General principle: Replace 50-75% of prior hour urine output. \u2022 Do NOT match 100% - this perpetuates diuresis \u2022 Use 0.45% NS (half-normal saline) for IV replacement \u2022 Encourage oral fluids if patient can drink Example: If UOP was 400 mL in last hour, give 200-300 mL NS over next hour. When diuresis slows (<200 mL/hr): \u2022 Reduce replacement to 50% of o
nodes.recommendation: Admit for POD monitoring. Replace 50-75% of urine output. Check electrolytes q12-24h. Nephrology consult if refractory >48h.

nodes.title: BPH Medications
nodes.summary: Tamsulosin 0.4mg at catheterization — improves TWOC success from 26% to 48%, onset 4-8h
nodes.body: Alpha-blockers (first-line for AUR from BPH): Tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO daily \u2022 Onset: 4-8 hours (some immediate effect) \u2022 Selective for alpha-1A receptors (prostate-specific) \u2022 Less orthostatic hypotension than non-selective agents \u2022 Start AT TIME OF CATHETERIZATION - improves TWOC success \u2022 Continue for at least 3-7 days before TWOC attempt Evidence: Alpha-blockers increase T

nodes.title: Trial Without Catheter (TWOC)
nodes.summary: TWOC optimal after 3-7 days of alpha-blocker — success = void >150mL with PVR <100mL
nodes.body: TWOC = removing catheter and assessing ability to void Timing: \u2022 Optimal: After 3-7 days of alpha-blocker therapy \u2022 Early TWOC (3 days) has similar success to late (7 days) \u2022 Longer catheterization (7 days) has more complications (UTI, leakage) TWOC success factors: \u2022 Younger age (<70) \u2022 Lower retention volume (<1000 mL) \u2022 Identifiable precipitant (medication, constip

nodes.title: Etiology Assessment
nodes.summary: Determine BPH, medication-induced, neurogenic, infectious, or malignant cause for follow-up planning
nodes.body: Determine underlying cause for follow-up planning: BPH (most common in men >50): \u2022 Gradual onset of LUTS (frequency, weak stream, nocturia) \u2022 History of urinary hesitancy Medication-induced: \u2022 Recent start of anticholinergic, opioid, decongestant, antihistamine \u2022 Often precipitates in patient with underlying BPH Neurogenic: \u2022 Diabetic neuropathy \u2022 Multiple sclerosis \

nodes.title: Discharge - BPH / Medication-Induced
nodes.body: Discharge with Foley catheter in place: Medications: \u2022 Tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO daily (30 min after same meal daily) Catheter leg bag instructions: \u2022 Empty when half to two-thirds full \u2022 Keep bag below bladder level at all times \u2022 Night drainage bag for sleeping \u2022 Clean connection site with alcohol when switching bags \u2022 Increase fluid intake to prevent blockage Return pre
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with Foley. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. Urology follow-up in 3-7 days for TWOC. Return if fever, no drainage, or severe symptoms.

nodes.title: Complex / Neurogenic Etiology
nodes.body: Requires specialist evaluation: Neurogenic bladder workup: \u2022 Urology referral for urodynamic studies \u2022 Neurology evaluation if not already established \u2022 Consider EMG, MRI if etiology unclear Management: \u2022 May need long-term catheterization (indwelling or intermittent self-cath) \u2022 Anticholinergics for overactive bladder component (paradoxical - specialist decision) \u2022 B
nodes.recommendation: Foley placement, tamsulosin, urology referral for urodynamics. Neurology evaluation if not established.

nodes.title: Concern for Malignancy
nodes.body: Red flags suggesting malignancy: \u2022 Weight loss, night sweats, bone pain \u2022 Hard, nodular prostate on DRE \u2022 Gross hematuria (especially painless) \u2022 Rapidly progressive symptoms \u2022 Known history of GU malignancy ED workup: \u2022 BMP, CBC \u2022 PSA (if not recently checked - note: catheterization may falsely elevate) \u2022 CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast if gross hematuria o
nodes.recommendation: Foley placement. Labs including PSA. Imaging if indicated. URGENT urology referral. Consider admission for complications.

nodes.title: Urinary Sphincter Emergencies
nodes.summary: Bladder dysfunction + back pain + leg symptoms = cauda equina until proven otherwise
nodes.body: Urinary sphincter dysfunction presents as either retention or incontinence. Both can signal life-threatening neurologic emergencies. Key Principle: Bladder dysfunction + back pain + leg symptoms = cauda equina until proven otherwise. Normal voiding requires: - Intact detrusor muscle contraction (parasympathetic S2-S4) - Coordinated sphincter relaxation (somatic S2-S4) - Patent urethra - Intact cor

nodes.title: Chief Complaint
nodes.summary: Determine retention vs incontinence vs mixed — retention with overflow dribbling is common overlap
nodes.body: Determine the primary presentation: Retention (cannot void): - Suprapubic pain/fullness - Urge to void but unable - Dribbling without complete emptying - No urine output despite adequate intake Incontinence (loss of control): - Urge incontinence - sudden uncontrollable need - Overflow incontinence - constant dribbling - Functional incontinence - unable to reach toilet - Total incontinence - contin

nodes.title: Incontinence Classification
nodes.summary: Overflow (high PVR), urge (detrusor overactivity), neurogenic (back pain, weakness, bowel changes)
nodes.body: Types of urinary incontinence: Overflow incontinence: - Bladder overdistention with passive leakage - Often neurogenic or obstructive - Palpable bladder, high PVR Urge incontinence: - Sudden, intense urge followed by involuntary loss - Detrusor overactivity - Often idiopathic, UTI, or neurologic Stress incontinence: - Leakage with cough, sneeze, exertion - Pelvic floor weakness - NOT typically an

nodes.title: Neurologic Red Flags
nodes.summary: Saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, bowel incontinence, severe back pain = emergent MRI
nodes.body: Screen for emergent neurogenic causes FIRST: Cauda equina syndrome (CES): - Saddle anesthesia (perineum, inner thighs) - Bilateral leg weakness or numbness - New bowel incontinence or constipation - Back pain (often severe, recent onset) - Bilateral sciatica Spinal cord compression: - Sensory level on exam - Upper motor neuron signs below lesion - History of malignancy Conus medullaris syndrome: -

nodes.title: Non-Neurogenic Etiologies
nodes.summary: BPH most common in men >50; check medication list (anticholinergics, opioids); infectious and post-op causes
nodes.body: Common causes of acute urinary retention: Obstructive (most common in men): - BPH - gradual LUTS, nocturia, weak stream - Urethral stricture - history of STI, trauma, instrumentation - Prostate cancer - hard nodular prostate on DRE - Bladder neck obstruction Medication-induced: - Anticholinergics (antihistamines, TCAs, antipsychotics) - Opioids (common post-operative) - Alpha-agonists (decongestan

nodes.title: Infectious Causes
nodes.summary: Prostatitis: do NOT massage prostate (bacteremia); HSV sacral radiculitis causes retention in young patients
nodes.body: Acute bacterial prostatitis: - Fever, chills, perineal pain - Exquisitely tender, boggy prostate on DRE - Do NOT massage prostate (bacteremia risk) - UA: pyuria, bacteriuria - Treatment: fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX x 4-6 weeks Severe UTI with retention: - Inflammation may cause transient obstruction - Catheterize AND treat infection Genital herpes (HSV): - Sacral radiculitis causing urinary retenti

nodes.title: Post-Operative Retention
nodes.summary: 5-70% incidence post-op; single in-out cath often sufficient — worry if >48h or neurologic symptoms
nodes.body: Post-operative urinary retention (POUR): Incidence: 5-70% depending on procedure type. Risk factors: - Age >60 - Male sex - Pre-existing BPH/LUTS - Pelvic/anorectal surgery - Spinal anesthesia (especially with morphine) - Opioid use - Large volume IV fluids - Duration of surgery >2 hours Management: 1. Bladder scan - confirm >300-400 mL 2. Single in-out catheterization often sufficient 3. If persi

nodes.title: ED Evaluation
nodes.summary: Medication list, prostate exam, perineal sensation, anal wink — bladder US (PVR) is most important test
nodes.body: History: - Duration and onset of symptoms - Associated pain, fever, neurologic symptoms - Medication list (anticholinergics, opioids, alpha-agonists) - Surgical history (especially pelvic, spinal) - Prior episodes of retention - Baseline urinary function (LUTS, nocturia) Physical exam: - Abdomen: palpable bladder, suprapubic tenderness - GU: urethral meatus (blood, discharge), phimosis - Rectal: p

nodes.title: Neurologic Examination
nodes.summary: Absent bulbocavernosus + absent anal wink = sacral nerve dysfunction — any findings trigger emergent MRI
nodes.body: Focused neuro exam for bladder dysfunction: Sensory: - Perineal/saddle sensation (S2-S4) - Perianal sensation - Lower extremity dermatomes Motor: - Bilateral leg strength (hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion) - Toe walking and heel walking Reflexes: - Patellar (L3-L4) - Achilles (S1-S2) - Bulbocavernosus reflex (S2-S4): squeeze glans/clitoris, feel anal sphincter contract - Anal wink (

nodes.title: Post-Void Residual
nodes.summary: PVR <50mL normal; >300mL = catheterize; >1000mL = high volume with POD risk
nodes.body: Post-void residual (PVR) measurement: Perform bedside bladder ultrasound. Interpretation: - <50 mL: Normal - 50-100 mL: Equivocal, repeat if symptomatic - 100-200 mL: Elevated, suggests incomplete emptying - 200-300 mL: Significant retention, needs intervention - >300 mL: Definite retention, catheterize - >1000 mL: High volume, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis If unable to void at all: PVR =

nodes.title: Low PVR - Reassess
nodes.body: PVR <100 mL suggests adequate emptying. If patient still symptomatic, consider: Urinary urgency without retention: - UTI/cystitis - Overactive bladder - Interstitial cystitis - Bladder tumor (rare) Incomplete emptying sensation: - May be false sensation with prostatitis - Psychogenic Workup: - Urinalysis and culture - If hematuria: consider CT urogram, cystoscopy referral Disposition: - Treat unde
nodes.recommendation: PVR normal. Treat underlying cause. Urology follow-up if symptoms persist.

nodes.title: High-Volume Retention
nodes.summary: >1000mL: get BMP, monitor for POD (>200mL/hr); complete drainage is safe — clamping myth debunked
nodes.body: PVR >1000 mL - increased risk of complications: Obtain labs: - BMP (creatinine often elevated in chronic retention) - UA and culture Complications to monitor: Post-obstructive diuresis (POD): - Definition: >200 mL/hr x 2+ hours OR >3L in 24h - Risk factors: bilateral obstruction, AKI, CHF - Management: replace 50-75% of output (NOT 100%) Hematuria ex vacuo: - Brief bleeding after rapid decompressi

nodes.title: Catheterization Technique
nodes.summary: Coude first-line in older men (curve UP); 16-18Fr standard; lidocaine jelly 2% 10-20mL, wait 5min
nodes.body: Standard Foley catheter insertion: Sizing: - Standard adult: 16-18 Fr - Hematuria with clots: 20-22 Fr - Suspected stricture: 14 Fr Coude tip catheter: Curved tip (15-30 degrees) navigates elevated bladder neck. Recommended first-line in older men with suspected BPH. Ensure curve points UP (toward ceiling). Technique: 1. Sterile prep and drape 2. Liberal lubrication (lidocaine jelly 2%, 10-20 mL,

nodes.title: Catheterization Result
nodes.summary: Assess success: urine drains immediately with relief vs resistance/blood without urine (false passage)
nodes.body: Assess catheterization success: Successful catheterization: - Urine drains immediately - Patient experiences relief - Document initial volume Signs of difficulty: - Resistance at prostatic urethra (try Coude) - False passage (blood without urine) - Complete obstruction

nodes.title: Alpha-Blocker Therapy
nodes.summary: Tamsulosin 0.4mg at catheterization — improves TWOC success 26% to 48% (OR 2.47)
nodes.body: Start alpha-blocker AT TIME OF CATHETERIZATION Tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO daily Why start immediately? - Improves trial without catheter (TWOC) success - TWOC success: 26% without vs 48% with alpha-blocker (OR 2.47) [9] - Some effect within 4-8 hours - Optimal benefit after 3-7 days Mechanism: Relaxes smooth muscle at bladder neck and prostate (alpha-1A selective). Side effects: - Orthostatic hypotensio

nodes.title: 5-Alpha Reductase Inhibitors
nodes.summary: 5-ARIs take 3-6 months to work — not helpful acutely, typically started by urology for long-term management
nodes.body: 5-Alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs): Finasteride 5 mg daily Dutasteride 0.5 mg daily NOT helpful acutely - effect takes 3-6 months. Mechanism: Blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT, causing prostate shrinkage (20-30% reduction over 6-12 months). When to consider: - Large prostate (>40 mL) - Recurrent retention episodes - PSA >1.5 ng/mL Typically started by urology, not in ED. Side effects: -

nodes.title: Failed Catheterization
nodes.summary: Coude first, then urology for cystoscopy or suprapubic catheter — avoid further blind attempts
nodes.body: Standard catheter failed - escalation pathway: Step 1: Coude catheter - Curved tip navigates BPH - Ensure curve points UP Step 2: Additional techniques - More lubrication - Larger catheter (paradoxically easier sometimes) - Smaller catheter over guidewire (Seldinger) Step 3: Urology consult - Flexible cystoscopy with guidewire placement - Suprapubic catheter if urethral route impossible Suprapubic

nodes.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
nodes.summary: Emergent MRI + neurosurgery STAT — decompression <24h best outcomes; bladder function has worst recovery
nodes.body: SURGICAL EMERGENCY - Time to decompression matters Classic triad (often incomplete): 1. Saddle anesthesia 2. Bladder dysfunction (retention > incontinence) 3. Bilateral leg weakness/sciatica Additional features: - Severe low back pain - Decreased anal tone - Fecal incontinence - Sexual dysfunction Immediate actions: 1. Foley catheter for bladder decompression 2. EMERGENT MRI lumbar spine (gold sta

nodes.title: CES - Emergent MRI
nodes.body: MRI lumbar spine WITHOUT contrast (unless infection/tumor suspected) Findings in cauda equina: - Large central disc herniation (most common cause) - Spinal stenosis - Epidural abscess - Epidural hematoma - Tumor/metastasis If MRI unavailable: - CT myelogram (invasive but diagnostic) - Transfer to facility with MRI and neurosurgery Do NOT delay imaging for any other workup. Disposition: - Emergent
nodes.recommendation: Emergent MRI lumbar spine. Neurosurgery consult. Foley catheter. NPO for likely OR. Time-critical surgical decompression.

nodes.title: Spinal Cord Compression
nodes.summary: Malignant cord compression: dexamethasone 10mg IV then 4mg q6h + emergent radiation therapy
nodes.body: Upper motor neuron bladder (suprasacral lesion): Presentation: - Urinary urgency and frequency (early) - Urge incontinence - Retention (later, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia) - Associated sensory level, spasticity Causes: - Metastatic disease (most common) - Trauma - Epidural abscess - Demyelinating disease (MS, transverse myelitis) - Vascular (spinal cord infarct) Management: - MRI entire spine i

nodes.title: Urge Incontinence Workup
nodes.body: New urge incontinence without neurologic signs: Most common causes: - UTI (most common in ED) - Overactive bladder - Bladder irritation (tumor, stone, foreign body) - Diabetes (polyuria) - Medication effect ED workup: - Urinalysis and culture - Bladder scan (rule out overflow) - Glucose if diabetic symptoms If UTI confirmed: - Treat with appropriate antibiotics - Symptoms should resolve within 48-
nodes.recommendation: UA and culture. Treat UTI if present. PCP follow-up. Urology if persistent or red flags.

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Neuro emergency = admit; POD/AKI = admit for monitoring; stable with catheter = discharge with urology follow-up
nodes.body: Determine appropriate disposition: Admission criteria: - Neurologic emergency (CES, cord compression) - Post-obstructive diuresis with electrolyte abnormalities - AKI (elevated creatinine) - Sepsis/urosepsis - Failed catheterization requiring procedure - Unable to manage catheter at home Observation criteria: - High-volume retention monitoring for POD - Borderline renal function Discharge criteria

nodes.title: Admit - Neurologic Emergency
nodes.body: Neurologic emergency requiring admission: Cauda equina syndrome: - ICU or step-down for close monitoring - Foley catheter in place - Neurosurgery primary service - Serial neuro exams q2-4h - NPO for likely surgery Spinal cord compression: - Oncology, neurosurgery, radiation oncology involved - Continue dexamethasone - Arrange emergent radiation if indicated Prognostic discussion: - Bladder functio
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU/step-down. Neurosurgery primary. Emergent decompression. Serial neuro exams.

nodes.title: Admit - Medical Management
nodes.body: Admission for POD or AKI: Post-obstructive diuresis management: - I/O q2h - Replace 50-75% of hourly urine output with 0.45% NS - Do NOT replace 100% (perpetuates diuresis) - BMP q12-24h (monitor Na, K, Mg, Phos) - Nephrology consult if refractory >48h AKI management: - Serial creatinine monitoring - Avoid nephrotoxins - Adequate hydration - Urology involvement for etiology Expected course: - Phys
nodes.recommendation: Admit for monitoring. Replace 50-75% urine output. BMP q12-24h. Urology and nephrology as needed.

nodes.title: Discharge with Foley
nodes.body: Discharge instructions: Medications: - Tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO daily (30 min after same meal) - Continue any other prescribed medications Catheter care: - Keep drainage bag below bladder level - Empty bag when 2/3 full - Use leg bag during day, drainage bag at night - Clean connection with alcohol when switching - Increase fluid intake - Shower OK after 24h, no baths Return immediately if: - Fever or
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with Foley. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. Urology follow-up in 3-7 days for TWOC. Strict return precautions.

nodes.title: Patient Age
nodes.summary: Age-based triage for suspected pediatric UTI — defines UTI criteria and exclusion populations
nodes.body: Inclusion criteria: Pediatric patient with suspected urinary tract infection. UTI definition: >50,000 CFU/mL in catheter-obtained specimen OR ≥100,000 CFU/mL in clean catch specimen, with pyuria on urinalysis. Note — Exclusion criteria: Immunocompromised patients, indwelling urinary catheter, known complex urologic anatomy (unless first presentation), and patients <7 days of life should be managed

nodes.title: Neonatal UTI — Confirmed Diagnosis
nodes.summary: Neonatal UTI pathway for <48wk PMA — exclude Candida, bacteremia, meningitis; do NOT repeat culture for test of cure
nodes.body: This pathway applies to infants <48 weeks postmenstrual age and >7 days of life with UTI defined as >50,000 CFU/mL in catheter-obtained specimen. Exclusion criteria: • History of Candida infection (consult Infectious Disease) • Concomitant bacteremia or meningitis • >48 weeks PMA • <7 days of age Alter antibiotic therapy based on culture-specific antimicrobial susceptibility. DO NOT repeat urine c

nodes.title: UTI Risk Screening (2–24 months)
nodes.summary: Risk-stratify febrile infants 2-24mo for UTI >1% probability — screen all uncircumcised febrile males
nodes.body: Assess probability of UTI >1%: Females — 2 or more risk factors: • Non-Black race • Temperature ≥39°C • Fever ≥2 days duration • No apparent source of infection • Age <12 months Males (uncircumcised): Any febrile male — screen. Males (circumcised): 3 or more risk factors: • Non-Black race • Temperature ≥39°C • Fever ≥2 days duration • No apparent source of infection • Age <6 months Also screen if:

nodes.title: UTI Screening (>24 months / Toilet Trained)
nodes.summary: Screen toilet-trained children with urinary symptoms, prior UTI with fever, or prolonged fever >5 days
nodes.body: Screen all patients with: • Symptoms referable to the urinary tract (dysuria, frequency, urgency, abdominal/flank pain, new incontinence) • Prior history of UTI with fever ≥2 days • Prolonged fever (≥5 days) without identified source Collection method: Clean catch UA with micro. Include additional tests if STI is being considered.

nodes.title: Obtain UA (Catheter or SPA)
nodes.summary: Catheter or SPA specimen required — bag specimens NOT acceptable for culture
nodes.body: Order UA with Micro. Collection: OPTION 1: Catheter or suprapubic aspirate (preferred) OPTION 2: Bag specimen UTI Definitions & Urinalysis Positive UA: Leukocyte esterase OR nitrites OR microscopic WBC/bacteria.

nodes.title: Clean Catch UA
nodes.summary: Obtain clean catch UA with micro — must use catheter or clean catch for culture if positive
nodes.body: Obtain clean catch urine analysis with micro. Include additional tests if STI is being considered. If UA positive, must obtain catheter or clean catch specimen for culture — bag specimens are not acceptable for culture. UTI Definitions & Urinalysis

nodes.title: UA Results
nodes.summary: Assess UA for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, or microscopic WBC/bacteria
nodes.body: Assess urinalysis results. Positive UA: leukocyte esterase OR nitrites OR microscopic WBC/bacteria.

nodes.title: UA Negative — Discharge
nodes.body: Negative UA. Discharge with PCP or ED follow-up in 24–48 hours. Close clinical follow-up recommended. Consider alternative diagnoses for fever source.
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with PCP/ED follow-up in 24–48 hours.

nodes.title: Order Urine Culture
nodes.summary: Culture MUST come from catheter, SPA, or clean catch — never bag specimen
nodes.body: MUST be obtained from clean catch, catheter, or suprapubic aspirate. If bag sample was previously tested, another specimen must be obtained for culture. Case manager follow-up on culture results.

nodes.title: Disposition Assessment
nodes.summary: Admit if ill-appearing, dehydrated, vomiting, social concerns, or failed outpatient treatment
nodes.body: Assess for hospital admission criteria. Inpatient criteria: • Ill-appearing (SIRS/sepsis) • Dehydration requiring IV or NG fluids • Persistent vomiting / inability to tolerate PO antibiotics • Social indicators affecting compliance or follow-up • Failure of outpatient treatment

nodes.title: ED/Outpatient Antibiotic Management
nodes.summary: Cephalexin first-line PO; ceftriaxone IM if <6mo or compliance concern; 7-day course (10 if <6mo)
nodes.body: First Line: Cephalexin 50 mg/kg/day divided TID–QID | Max 1 g/dose Alternative: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate 20–40 mg/kg/day divided BID | Max 875 mg/dose If IgE-mediated allergy to penicillins AND cephalosporins: Ciprofloxacin 20 mg/kg/day divided BID | Max 750 mg/dose Medication intolerant, concern for compliance, or age <6 months: Consider single dose Ceftriaxone 75 mg/kg IV or IM prior to discharge

nodes.title: Inpatient Antibiotic Management
nodes.summary: IV cefazolin first-line; ceftriaxone if CNS concern; transition PO at 24-48h; total 7 days
nodes.body: First Line: Cefazolin 50 mg/kg/day divided q8h | Max 2 g/dose If IgE-mediated allergy to penicillins AND cephalosporins: Aztreonam 90 mg/kg/day divided q8h | Max 2 g/dose, plus Gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg/day q24h If concern for CNS involvement: Ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day divided q12h | Max 2 g/dose Transition criteria: 24–48 hours of IV therapy with clinical improvement. Assess susceptibility and narrow

nodes.title: Neonatal UTI — Antibiotic Selection
nodes.summary: Classify neonatal UTI as complicated vs uncomplicated based on anatomy, catheter, recent abx, immunosuppression
nodes.body: Treatment is based on whether UTI is complicated or uncomplicated. Complicated UTI criteria: • Functional or anatomic abnormality • Indwelling catheter • Recent instrumentation • Recent antibiotics • Immunosuppression

nodes.title: Neonatal UTI — Uncomplicated Treatment
nodes.summary: IV cefazolin then PO cephalexin for 7 days — do NOT repeat culture for test of cure unless Candida/ESBL
nodes.body: IV: Cefazolin 50 mg/kg/day divided q8h Transition to PO if term (by PMA), once sensitivities completed: Cephalexin • ≤28 days of life: 75 mg/kg/day divided q8h • ≥29 days of life: 100 mg/kg/day divided q6h Duration: 7 days Alter therapy based on culture susceptibility. DO NOT repeat urine culture for test of cure unless Candida or ESBL.

nodes.title: Neonatal UTI — Complicated Treatment
nodes.summary: Same regimen as uncomplicated but extended to 10-day total course for complicated neonatal UTI
nodes.body: Same antibiotic regimen as uncomplicated but Duration: 10 days. IV: Cefazolin 50 mg/kg/day divided q8h Transition to PO: Cephalexin • ≤28 days of life: 75 mg/kg/day divided q8h • ≥29 days of life: 100 mg/kg/day divided q6h Alter therapy based on culture susceptibility. DO NOT repeat urine culture unless Candida or ESBL.

nodes.title: Neonatal Post-Treatment Imaging
nodes.summary: Obtain RBUS after neonatal UTI treatment; sooner if fever persists >48h or unusually severe illness
nodes.body: Obtain renal and bladder ultrasound (RBUS) following UTI treatment completion. *If fever persists >48 hours after start of antibiotics or unusually severe clinical illness, obtain RBUS sooner.

nodes.title: Neonatal RBUS Risk Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess for atypical pathogen, VUR/CAKUT family history, complex course, or prior UTI
nodes.body: Are any of the following present? • Atypical pathogen (non-E. coli) • Family history of VUR or CAKUT • Complex clinical course • Any prior UTI

nodes.title: RBUS Results
nodes.summary: Assess RBUS for hydronephrosis, parenchymal abnormalities, or size discrepancies
nodes.body: Assess renal and bladder ultrasound findings.

nodes.title: Abnormal RBUS — Further Workup
nodes.body: Obtain VCUG. Obtain renal functional panel. Consult Urology. Consider Nephrology consult. Patients with grade IV or V VUR are at increased risk of future complications.
nodes.recommendation: Obtain VCUG, renal functional panel, Urology consult, consider Nephrology.

nodes.title: Neonatal UTI — Complete
nodes.body: RBUS normal, no risk factors. Complete antibiotic course. No further evaluation is necessary.
nodes.recommendation: Complete antibiotic course. No further imaging or evaluation needed.

nodes.title: ED Discharge & Culture Follow-up
nodes.summary: Discharge with PCP/ED follow-up in 24-48h; adjust antibiotics based on culture susceptibility
nodes.body: Discharge with PCP or ED follow-up in 24–48 hours. Case manager follow-up on urine culture. If culture positive: Assess antibiotic susceptibility and adjust as necessary with PCP involvement. If culture negative: Contact PCP with results.

nodes.title: Inpatient Discharge Criteria
nodes.summary: Discharge when non-toxic, hydrated, tolerating PO, normal anatomy, and quality follow-up arranged
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: • Non-toxic appearing • Well-hydrated • Can tolerate oral antibiotics and fluids • Normal genitourinary anatomy • RBUS reviewed if performed • Quality follow-up within 24–48 hours • Clinically stable for home

nodes.title: Imaging Recommendations
nodes.summary: RBUS for first febrile UTI 2-24mo; also if non-E. coli, family hx, or no improvement at 48h
nodes.body: RBUS criteria: • Age 2–24 months with first febrile UTI • Children >24 months: pathogen other than E. coli, family history of renal/urologic disease, hypertension, poor growth, no improvement after 48h empiric therapy Timing: • Outpatient: order RBUS >48h of antibiotics • Inpatient: order after 36h (no less than 24h)

nodes.title: RBUS Findings
nodes.summary: Assess RBUS for hydronephrosis, parenchymal loss, kidney size discrepancies, or radiologist concern
nodes.body: Assess for: • Hydronephrosis (pelvocaliectasis) • Renal parenchymal loss • Kidney size discrepancies independent of SFU grade • Radiologist recommendation for further imaging

nodes.title: VCUG Criteria
nodes.summary: VCUG criteria: hydronephrosis, scarring, dilated ureter, non-E. coli pathogen, ESBL, or radiologist recommendation
nodes.body: Criteria for obtaining VCUG: • Hydronephrosis • Scarring • Dilated pelvis • Dilated ureter • Recommended by reviewing pediatric radiologist • Chronic hypertension +/- poor growth • Urinary pathogen other than E. coli • ESBL-producing E. coli

nodes.title: VCUG — Urology Consult
nodes.body: Consider Urology consult if abnormal VCUG. Patients with grade IV or V VUR are at increased risk of future complications.
nodes.recommendation: Urology consult for abnormal VCUG. Grade IV–V VUR requires close follow-up.

nodes.title: UTI Management Complete
nodes.body: Antibiotic course complete. Ensure PCP follow-up within 24–48 hours. Monitor for recurrent UTI symptoms.
nodes.recommendation: Complete antibiotic course, ensure PCP follow-up in 24–48 hours.

nodes.title: Low Risk — Manage Off-Pathway
nodes.body: UTI likelihood ≤1% based on risk factor screening. Manage off-pathway with close clinical follow-up. Consider alternative diagnoses for fever source.
nodes.recommendation: Manage off-pathway with close clinical follow-up.

nodes.title: VAD Emergency Management
nodes.summary: No pulse is NORMAL in continuous-flow LVADs — use Doppler MAP, listen for pump hum, contact VAD coordinator
nodes.body: VAD Steps Summary Ventricular Assist Device (VAD/LVAD) patient presenting to the ED. Key principles: \u2022 No pulse is NORMAL \u2014 continuous-flow LVADs produce minimal/zero pulsatility \u2022 Contact VAD coordinator immediately \u2014 every ED visit \u2022 Listen for pump hum \u2014 absence = pump failure = emergency \u2022 MAP via Doppler \u2014 traditional BP cuffs are unreliable

nodes.title: Contact VAD Coordinator
nodes.summary: Call VAD center IMMEDIATELY — gather device type, baseline parameters, INR target, VAD center number
nodes.body: Call the VAD center IMMEDIATELY while beginning assessment. Information to gather from patient/family/wallet card: \u2022 Device type (HeartMate 3, HeartMate II, HVAD) \u2022 Baseline pump parameters (speed, power, flow, PI) \u2022 Current INR target and last INR \u2022 Recent device issues or hospitalizations \u2022 VAD center contact number \u2022 Transplant candidacy status The patient and fami

nodes.title: Auscultate for Pump Hum
nodes.summary: Auscultate for pump hum — absence means pump failure; SpO2 unreliable, use capnography and perfusion signs
nodes.body: Listen over the precordium/epigastrium for the pump hum. A steady high-pitched mechanical whirr confirms the pump is running. Absence of hum = pump failure. Simultaneous assessment: \u2022 Airway: Standard assessment \u2022 Breathing: SpO\u2082 may be unreliable (non-pulsatile flow) \u2014 use waveform capnography if available \u2022 Circulation: Assess perfusion by mental status, skin color/temp,

nodes.title: No Pump Hum \u2014 Device Failure
nodes.summary: No hum = pump failure — troubleshoot connections/batteries, do NOT clamp outflow graft, start inotropes
nodes.body: No hum = pump not running. This is a critical emergency. Immediate troubleshooting: 1. Check all connections \u2014 reseat driveline to controller 2. Swap to backup batteries or connect to AC power 3. Use patient's backup controller if available 4. If pump cannot be restarted \u2192 patient has native cardiac function only (severely impaired) Hemodynamic support: \u2022 Dobutamine 2.5-5 mcg/kg/min

nodes.title: MAP Assessment (Doppler)
nodes.summary: Doppler MAP: cuff + pencil Doppler over brachial; first flow signal = MAP; target 70-90 mmHg
nodes.body: Measure MAP using Doppler technique: 1. Place pencil Doppler probe over brachial artery 2. Inflate standard BP cuff proximally 3. Inflate >30 mmHg above last audible flow signal 4. Slowly deflate \u2014 pressure at first return of flow signal = MAP This single value approximates MAP, not systolic BP. Without Doppler: Use stethoscope \u2014 first Korotkoff sound = MAP. For critically ill patients:

nodes.title: Controller Parameter Check
nodes.summary: Read and compare controller parameters to baseline — speed, power, flow, PI; do NOT change speed
nodes.body: Read and record all controller parameters. Compare to patient's baseline values (from wallet card or family). Device Parameter Reference | Parameter | Normal | Significance | |-----------|--------|-------------| | Speed (RPM) | Device-specific | Set by VAD team \u2014 do NOT change | | Power (Watts) | 3-7 W | \u2191 = thrombus or \u2191 flow demand | | Flow (L/min) | 3-6 | \u2193 = hypovolemia, ob

nodes.title: VAD Hypertension (MAP > 90)
nodes.summary: MAP >90 increases stroke risk — hydralazine first-line, avoid IV beta-blockers in VAD patients
nodes.body: Hypertension in VAD patients increases hemorrhagic stroke risk and reduces pump efficiency. The LVAD pumps against systemic vascular resistance \u2014 higher afterload = lower flow. Goal MAP: 70-80 mmHg (never >90) Treatment: 1. Hydralazine 10-25 mg PO q6-8h (preferred first-line) 2. ACE inhibitor or ARB for chronic management 3. IV nicardipine or clevidipine for acute/severe hypertension 4. Avoid

nodes.title: Low Flow Evaluation
nodes.summary: Low flow differential: flat IVC = hypovolemia/bleeding; distended IVC = RV failure, PE, or tamponade
nodes.body: Low flow (<3 L/min) requires rapid differential diagnosis. The key discriminator is volume status \u2014 assess JVP and IVC on bedside ultrasound. VAD Echo Findings | JVP / IVC | Flow | Likely Cause | |-----------|------|--------------| | Low / Flat | \u2193 | Bleeding / Hypovolemia | | High / Distended | \u2193 | RV failure, PE, Tamponade | | Variable | \u2191 | Vasodilation (sepsis) |

nodes.title: Alarm Troubleshooting
nodes.summary: Check connections, batteries, pump hum; position flat before battery swap; red alarms = life-threatening
nodes.body: Systematic alarm response: 1. Check all connections \u2014 driveline to controller, controller to power source 2. Ensure batteries are charged \u2014 swap to backup battery or AC power 3. Auscultate \u2014 confirm pump hum is present 4. If controller fault \u2192 use patient's backup controller (they should carry one) 5. Position patient flat before any battery swap to prevent suction event 6. Cal

nodes.title: Complication Triage
nodes.summary: Select most acute VAD complication — GI bleed most common; pump thrombosis and stroke are emergencies
nodes.body: What is the primary presenting complaint? Select the most acute/urgent if multiple are present. Common VAD ED presentations by frequency: \u2022 GI bleeding (~30% of readmissions) \u2022 Infection (20-50%) \u2022 Arrhythmia (~50% lifetime) \u2022 Pump thrombosis (1.5-5%/year) \u2022 RV failure (9-40%) \u2022 Stroke (~10% by 2 years)

nodes.title: Suction Event
nodes.summary: LV too empty pulling septum against cannula — give 250-500mL NS, do NOT increase speed
nodes.body: The LV is too empty \u2014 the pump pulls the septum or ventricular wall against the inflow cannula. Causes: Hypovolemia, RV failure, tamponade, arrhythmia, excessive pump speed Controller signs: Low flow, power fluctuations, low PI Echo findings: Small LV cavity, septal deviation toward inflow cannula Management: 1. Volume challenge: 250-500 mL NS bolus \u2014 LVADs are preload dependent 2. Heart

nodes.title: Stroke in VAD Patient
nodes.summary: STAT CT head — systemic tPA contraindicated; hemorrhagic: reverse with VitK+PCC; MRI contraindicated
nodes.body: Both ischemic (6.8%) and hemorrhagic (8.4%) strokes are common in VAD patients. Immediate workup: 1. STAT CT head (non-contrast) \u2014 determine type 2. CTA head/neck if ischemic 3. Check INR \u2014 patients are on Warfarin 4. Full neurologic exam 5. Check pump parameters \u2014 high power may indicate underlying thrombosis Hemorrhagic stroke: \u2022 Hold all anticoagulation and antiplatelet ther

nodes.title: Bleeding Management
nodes.summary: GI bleed #1 cause of VAD ED visits — use ONLY leukoreduced irradiated blood to preserve transplant candidacy
nodes.body: GI bleeding is the #1 cause of ED visits for VAD patients. Mechanism: Continuous flow \u2192 acquired von Willebrand disease (shear forces destroy large VWF multimers) + intestinal AVMs from non-pulsatile flow + chronic anticoagulation. CRITICAL transfusion principle: \u2022 Use ONLY leukoreduced, irradiated blood products \u2022 Prevents HLA allosensitization that could preclude future heart tran

nodes.title: Active Bleeding Management
nodes.summary: Transfuse leukoreduced/irradiated pRBCs; DDAVP for acquired vWD; octreotide for GI AVMs; warfarin reversal safe
nodes.body: Resuscitation: 1. Large-bore IV access, type & crossmatch 2. Transfuse leukoreduced, irradiated pRBCs \u2014 target Hgb >7 g/dL 3. Hold Warfarin 4. Anticoagulation reversal (discuss target INR with VAD team): \u2022 Vitamin K 2.5-5 mg IV \u2022 4-factor PCC for life-threatening bleeding \u2022 Warfarin reversal carries LOW risk for acute pump thrombosis \u2014 do not withhold in life-threatening b

nodes.title: Minor / Controlled Bleeding
nodes.summary: Check INR, local hemostasis, consider DDAVP; monitor 4-6h — VAD bleeding can escalate rapidly
nodes.body: Minor bleeding (epistaxis, gingival, small-volume GI, bruising): 1. Check INR \u2014 often supratherapeutic 2. Local hemostatic measures (direct pressure, nasal packing) 3. Consider holding warfarin dose or reducing target INR (discuss with VAD team) 4. Desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg IV if continued oozing 5. Labs: CBC, INR, fibrinogen, type & screen 6. Monitor for 4-6 hours \u2014 VAD bleeding can escal

nodes.title: Pump Thrombosis
nodes.summary: High power + hemolysis = pump thrombosis — heparin drip, IV fluids, emergent VAD center transfer; 48% mortality
nodes.body: High power + hemolysis = pump thrombosis until proven otherwise. This is a surgical emergency \u2014 48% six-month mortality without intervention. Hemolysis Lab Panel Diagnosis: \u2022 Rising power trend or power >10 W (classic, but see caveat below) \u2022 LDH >2.5\u00D7 upper limit normal (>1,150 IU/L highly suggestive) \u2022 Haptoglobin undetectable \u2022 Plasma free hemoglobin >40 mg/dL \u20

nodes.title: Device Infection
nodes.summary: Classify infection: driveline exit site (most common), pump pocket, or bloodstream/endocarditis
nodes.body: 20% of VAD patients develop device-related infection within the first year. | Type | Location | Frequency | |------|----------|----------| | Driveline exit site | Skin around cable | Most common | | Pump pocket | Device housing | Serious | | Bloodstream / endocarditis | Pump surfaces | Life-threatening | Common organisms: Staph aureus, coag-negative Staph, Pseudomonas, Candida Initial workup: Bloo

nodes.title: Driveline Exit Site Infection
nodes.summary: Wound culture, blood cultures, local care; NEVER pull or rotate the driveline — surgically anchored
nodes.body: Most common VAD infection \u2014 accounts for ~50% of device infections. Assessment: \u2022 Erythema, warmth, tenderness around exit site \u2022 Purulent drainage \u2022 Exposed velour or cable \u2022 Granulation tissue breakdown Management: 1. Wound culture before antibiotics 2. Blood cultures \u00D72 (rule out bacteremia) 3. Local wound care \u2014 cleanse with chlorhexidine, dry dressing 4. Ant

nodes.title: Bloodstream / Deep Infection
nodes.summary: Broad-spectrum IV abx, TTE/TEE for vegetations, 6+ weeks therapy; device removal may be needed
nodes.body: VAD-related bloodstream infection carries high morbidity and mortality. Management: 1. Blood cultures \u00D72 (peripheral sites) 2. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics: \u2022 Vancomycin + cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam \u2022 Add antifungal coverage if prior Candida or prolonged antibiotics 3. TTE/TEE \u2014 evaluate for vegetations on pump components 4. CT chest/abdomen \u2014 driveline tract abs

nodes.title: RV Failure Management
nodes.summary: RV failure: milrinone for afterload, dobutamine for contractility, vasopressin for MAP; AVOID intubation if possible
nodes.body: RV failure is the Achilles heel of LVAD therapy. The LVAD only supports the left ventricle. When the LVAD increases LV output, the RV must handle the increased venous return \u2014 and it often cannot. VAD Echo Findings Signs: Elevated JVP, peripheral edema, ascites, hepatic congestion, low LVAD flow despite adequate speed. Management \u2014 optimize the RV triangle (preload, afterload, contractil

nodes.title: Arrhythmia in VAD Patient
nodes.summary: VAD patients may TOLERATE VT/VF — pump maintains flow; assess hemodynamic stability, not just rhythm
nodes.body: VAD patients may TOLERATE sustained VT/VF because the pump maintains forward flow independent of cardiac rhythm. However, prolonged ventricular arrhythmias \u2192 decreased RV filling \u2192 decreased LVAD preload \u2192 low flow \u2192 end-organ damage. Assessment: 1. Is the patient hemodynamically stable? (conscious, MAP >60, adequate LVAD flow) 2. Check electrolytes (K\u207A >4.0, Mg\u00B2\u207

nodes.title: Stable Arrhythmia Management
nodes.summary: Amiodarone for VT; avoid IV beta-blockers; AP pad placement away from device; all VAD arrhythmias admit
nodes.body: VT (hemodynamically tolerated): 1. Correct electrolytes: K\u207A >4.0, Mg\u00B2\u207A >2.0 2. Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min \u00D76h, then 0.5 mg/min \u00D718h 3. Alternative: Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV bolus, then 1-4 mg/min infusion 4. Interrogate/reprogram ICD if inappropriate shocks 5. Cardiology/EP consult 6. Evaluate for reversible causes: ischemia, electrolytes, suction even

nodes.title: VAD Cardiac Arrest Protocol
nodes.summary: Assess perfusion NOT pulse; check pump hum/controller; CPR if unresponsive + MAP <50 or ETCO2 <20
nodes.body: MODIFIED ACLS \u2014 Critical differences from standard resuscitation. VAD Cardiac Arrest Protocol Step 1 \u2014 Assess perfusion, NOT pulse: \u2022 Responsiveness / consciousness \u2022 MAP by Doppler (perfusion if >50) \u2022 ETCO\u2082 if intubated (perfusion if >20) \u2022 Skin perfusion \u2014 color, temperature, capillary refill Step 2 \u2014 Check the pump: \u2022 Auscultate for hum \u2022

nodes.title: Defibrillation & ACLS Medications
nodes.summary: Defibrillation safe — AP pads away from device; disconnect AC power; all standard ACLS meds permitted
nodes.body: Defibrillation is SAFE in VAD patients. Pad placement: Anterior-posterior preferred \u2022 Do NOT place pads directly over LVAD device or driveline \u2022 Standard biphasic energy (200J) \u2022 Disconnect from AC power during shock (run on batteries only) \u2022 Never disconnect LVAD controller during defibrillation ALL standard ACLS medications are permitted: \u2022 Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 mi

nodes.title: Arrest Echo & Reversible Causes
nodes.summary: Echo-guided differential: small RV+LV = hypovolemia; large RV = PE; large both = pump thrombus; effusion = tamponade
nodes.body: Bedside echo during arrest guides the differential: VAD Echo Findings | Finding | Diagnosis | Action | |---------|-----------|--------| | Small RV + Small LV | Hypovolemia | Volume resuscitation | | Large RV + Small LV | PE, RV infarct | Consider thrombolytics | | Large RV + Large LV | Pump thrombosis | Heparin, VAD team | | Pericardial effusion | Tamponade | Pericardiocentesis | | Small LV, septa

nodes.title: Post-Arrest Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess perfusion restoration: MAP >60, ETCO2 >20, improving consciousness and pump parameters
nodes.body: Assess for return of perfusion: \u2022 MAP >60 by Doppler \u2022 ETCO\u2082 >20 and rising \u2022 Return of consciousness \u2022 Improving pump parameters (flow, PI) \u2022 Improving skin perfusion If perfusion restored \u2192 post-arrest care with targeted temperature management, hemodynamic optimization, and identify the precipitating cause.

nodes.title: Refractory Arrest
nodes.body: When standard ACLS fails in a VAD patient: 1. Continue CPR and ACLS 2. Exhaust device troubleshooting \u2014 swap controller, check all connections 3. Consider VA-ECMO if available and patient is a candidate \u2022 Initiation within 60 minutes improves outcomes \u2022 Most feasible at VAD/transplant center 4. Address all reversible causes (Hs and Ts + device-specific) 5. Contact VAD center emergen
nodes.recommendation: Emergent contact with VAD center. Consider ECMO. If all measures exhausted, discuss goals of care with family and VAD team.

nodes.title: Disposition Decision
nodes.summary: Nearly ALL VAD ED visits require admission or transfer — discharge is rare and needs explicit VAD team approval
nodes.body: Nearly ALL VAD patients presenting to the ED require admission or transfer. Discharge is rare and requires explicit VAD team approval. Can this be managed at your facility?

nodes.title: Admit
nodes.body: Admission orders: 1. ICU/CCU or telemetry floor based on acuity 2. Continuous telemetry 3. Doppler MAP checks q4h (or continuous arterial line if critical) 4. Record pump parameters q shift (speed, power, flow, PI) 5. Anticoagulation management: \u2022 Heparin bridge if warfarin is held \u2022 Target PTT per VAD team guidance 6. Daily labs: CBC, BMP, coags, LDH, haptoglobin 7. Daily driveline site
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU/CCU with VAD team co-management. Record pump parameters every shift.

nodes.title: Transfer to VAD Center
nodes.body: Transfer is required for any of the following: \u2022 Pump malfunction or failure \u2022 Suspected pump thrombosis requiring exchange \u2022 Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) \u2022 Device infection requiring surgical management \u2022 Hemodynamic instability refractory to ED management \u2022 Driveline damage or electrical fault \u2022 Need for pump speed adjustment (only VAD team can do this) Tra
nodes.recommendation: Emergent transfer to VAD center. Stabilize before transport. Ensure pump power continuity during transport.

nodes.title: Discharge (Rare)
nodes.body: VAD patient discharge from the ED is RARE and requires VAD team clearance. May be appropriate for: \u2022 Minor driveline site issue managed with local wound care \u2022 INR check with therapeutic result and stable parameters \u2022 Resolved alarm with confirmed normal parameters \u2022 Medication refill with no acute complaints Discharge requirements: 1. VAD team contacted and explicitly approves
nodes.recommendation: Discharge only with explicit VAD team approval. Arrange follow-up within 24-48 hours.

nodes.title: Video-Assisted Flexible Endoscopic Intubation — Overview
nodes.summary: Video laryngoscopy + flexible endoscope combined; VL clears path, FE guides tube through cords; maintains breathing
nodes.body: Video-Assisted Flexible Endoscopic Intubation combines video laryngoscopy to expose the airway with flexible endoscopy to guide tube delivery. [1] WHY THIS TECHNIQUE? Combines the best of both: • VL clears path through mouth, lifts epiglottis • FE provides continuous visualization through cords • No nasal route needed (avoids epistaxis) • Allows awake/breathing approach KEY ADVANTAGES: • Maintains

nodes.title: Indications
nodes.summary: Angioedema, Ludwig, trauma, tumors, morbid obesity, failed VL, "scared to paralyze" patients
nodes.body: PRIMARY INDICATIONS: [2,6,7] Anatomically Difficult/Distorted Airways: • Angioedema (most common indication) • Ludwig angina / deep neck infection • Oropharyngeal abscess / hematoma • Laryngeal or orofacial trauma • Airway tumors / masses • Prior surgery or radiation to head/neck Intrinsic Difficult Airway Features: • Micrognathia / retrognathia • Limited mouth opening (trismus) • Morbid obesity •

nodes.title: Relative Contraindications
nodes.summary: Relative CIs: massive bleeding, complete obstruction, impending arrest, severely uncooperative
nodes.body: RELATIVE CONTRAINDICATIONS: [6,8] Visualization Barriers: • Massive upper airway bleeding (obscures scope) • Profuse secretions / vomiting • Complete upper airway obstruction Time Constraints: • Severely diminished ventilation / impending arrest • Cannot preoxygenate adequately • Rapidly deteriorating airway with no time Patient Factors: • Severely uncooperative / combative (for awake approach) •

nodes.title: Select Approach
nodes.summary: Awake = safest for distorted airways; RSI-then-flexible-endoscope for rescue; KOBI = ketamine-only breathing
nodes.body: Choose intubation approach based on patient status and airway assessment. *Basis:* These three approaches are NOT of equal measured performance. In the National Emergency Airway Registry analysis of 12,511 ED intubations, unadjusted first-attempt success was 61% for ketamine-only, 85% for topical anaesthesia (with or without low-dose sedation), and 90% for RSI; at least one adverse event occurred

nodes.title: Preparation — Awake Approach
nodes.summary: VL operator at left shoulder, FE operator at head; patient semi-Fowler; split-screen monitor
nodes.body: AWAKE PREPARATION: [1,3,7] Equipment Setup: • Video laryngoscope (hyperangulated preferred) • Flexible endoscope with ETT preloaded • Suction x2 (VL operator + backup) • Topical anesthetics (4% lidocaine) • Antisialagogue (glycopyrrolate) • Low-dose ketamine + midazolam drawn • Standard airway backup + cricothyrotomy kit Operator Positioning: • VL Operator: Behind patient's LEFT shoulder • FE Oper

nodes.title: Preparation — RSI Rescue
nodes.summary: For RSI rescue: VL maintains view, FE operator brings scope, proceed directly; have FE ready pre-RSI
nodes.body: RSI-THEN-FLEXIBLE-ENDOSCOPE (RESCUE SCENARIO): [1] When standard VL intubation fails but patient is oxygenating: Setup (should already be ready): • VL in place with view obtained • Flexible endoscope preloaded with ETT • Second operator available Transition to combined technique: 1. VL operator maintains laryngeal view 2. FE operator brings scope to bedside 3. No additional meds needed (already pa

nodes.title: Ketamine-Only Breathing Intubation (KOBI)
nodes.summary: Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg or 25mg aliquots; maintains breathing; MUST have paralytic ready for laryngospasm
nodes.body: KOBI APPROACH: [4,5] Dissociative-dose ketamine WITHOUT paralytic. Patient breathes throughout. INDICATIONS: • Distorted airway where paralysis is dangerous • Need to maintain spontaneous ventilation • Alternative to awake approach in uncooperative patient KETAMINE DOSING: • Dissociative: 1-2 mg/kg IV • Titration method: 25 mg aliquots q15 seconds until dissociated • Have RSI backup ready CRITICAL

nodes.title: Antisialagogue & Drying
nodes.summary: Glycopyrrolate 0.2mg IV or 0.4mg IM; give 10-20 min before; dry mucosa enhances lidocaine effect
nodes.body: DRY THE AIRWAY FIRST: [3,7,8] Topical anesthesia works better on dry mucosa.
