GLYCOPYRROLATE (preferred): • Dose: 0.2 mg IV or 0.4 mg IM • Give 10-20 minutes before procedure • Does not cross blood-brain barrier • Less tachycardia than atropine ATROPINE (alternative): • Dose: 0.5-1.0 mg IV or IM • Faster onset than glycopyrrolate • More tachycardia, can cause confusion MECHANICAL DRYING: • Gauze to

nodes.title: Topical Airway Anesthesia
nodes.summary: Max lidocaine 7 mg/kg; nebulize + atomize + viscous; spray cords through scope channel
nodes.body: TOPICALIZATION TECHNIQUE: [3,7,8] MAXIMUM LIDOCAINE DOSE: 7 mg/kg — calculate before starting! NEBULIZED LIDOCAINE: • 4% lidocaine via nebulizer • Low flow rate (4-8 L/min) • 4-5 mL over 10-15 minutes • Anesthetizes entire upper airway ATOMIZED LIDOCAINE: • MAD (Mucosal Atomization Device) or LMA MAD • 4% lidocaine in 10 mL syringe • Spray tonsillar pillars, posterior pharynx • Spray base of tongu

nodes.title: Lidocaine Dose Calculation
nodes.summary: 7 mg/kg max; 70kg patient = ~12 mL of 4% lidocaine total; watch for toxicity signs
nodes.body: LIDOCAINE TOXICITY PREVENTION: [3] MAXIMUM DOSE: 7 mg/kg QUICK CALCULATION: • 70 kg patient: max 490 mg • 4% lidocaine = 40 mg/mL • 490 mg ÷ 40 mg/mL = ~12 mL of 4% TYPICAL DISTRIBUTION: • Nebulizer: 4-5 mL (160-200 mg) • Atomizer to pharynx: 3-4 mL (120-160 mg) • Through scope to cords: 2-3 mL (80-120 mg) • Total: ~9-12 mL (360-480 mg) LIDOCAINE TOXICITY SIGNS: • Perioral numbness, metallic taste

nodes.title: Sedation for Awake Intubation
nodes.summary: Ketamine 10-30mg titrated preferred; midazolam 0.5-1mg adjunct; avoid over-sedation
nodes.body: SEDATION OPTIONS: [3,4] Goal: Anxiolysis and comfort while maintaining airway reflexes and breathing. KETAMINE (preferred): • Low-dose: 0.1-0.5 mg/kg IV (10-30 mg typical) • Titrate with 20 mg aliquots q2 minutes • Preserves respiratory drive and reflexes • Provides analgesia and amnesia MIDAZOLAM (adjunct): • 0.5-1 mg IV aliquots • Provides anxiolysis and amnesia • Use cautiously — can cause apne

nodes.title: Ketamine Specifics
nodes.summary: Low-dose 20-30mg titrated; KOBI 1-2 mg/kg; ALWAYS have paralytic ready for laryngospasm
nodes.body: KETAMINE FOR AWAKE INTUBATION: [4,5] LOW-DOSE (Procedural Sedation): • 0.3-0.5 mg/kg IV (20-30 mg typical) • Maintains protective reflexes • Patient arousable but comfortable • Can follow commands TITRATION METHOD: • Draw 100 mg ketamine in 10 mL syringe (10 mg/mL) • Give 20 mg (2 mL) every 2 minutes • Stop when patient appears relaxed but breathing DISSOCIATIVE DOSE (KOBI): • 1-2 mg/kg IV • Patie

nodes.title: Procedure — Step by Step
nodes.summary: VL obtains view → FE advances to blade tip → guides through cords on VL screen → carina → railroad ETT
nodes.body: THE TECHNIQUE: [1] STEP 1: VL INSERTION • VL operator inserts blade, obtains laryngeal view • Maintains position with LEFT hand • Keeps suction ready in RIGHT hand • "Sets the table" for FE operator STEP 2: FE INSERTION • FE operator looks INTO patient's mouth (direct vision) • Advances scope to tip of VL blade under direct view • Then looks at VL SCREEN to guide scope to cords STEP 3: CORD PASSAG

nodes.title: Railroading the ETT
nodes.summary: Pre-load ETT on scope; rotate 90° CCW if hang-up at cords; confirm position 2-3cm above carina
nodes.body: ETT DELIVERY OVER FLEXIBLE SCOPE: [1,8] PRE-LOADED SETUP: • ETT should be loaded on FE BEFORE starting • Standard 7.0-7.5 (women) or 7.5-8.0 (men) • Lubricate both scope and ETT RAILROADING TECHNIQUE: 1. FE operator holds scope steady at carina 2. Assistant advances ETT over scope 3. Rotate ETT 90° counterclockwise if resistance at cords 4. Advance until cuff passes cords (visible on FE screen) 5.

nodes.title: Confirmation & Securing
nodes.summary: Waveform capnography mandatory; ETT 2-3cm above carina; secure at 21-25cm at teeth
nodes.body: CONFIRM SUCCESSFUL INTUBATION: [1,9] PRIMARY CONFIRMATION: • Waveform capnography — MANDATORY • Sustained ETCO2 waveform for 5-6 breaths • No capnography = not confirmed SECONDARY CONFIRMATION: • Bilateral breath sounds • Chest rise • Misting in ETT • SpO2 maintained/improving DEPTH CONFIRMATION: • Visualize carina through scope before withdrawal • ETT tip 2-3 cm above carina • Typical depth: 21-2

nodes.title: Troubleshooting
nodes.body: Select the issue you are encountering:

nodes.title: Poor Visualization
nodes.summary: VL operator suctions aggressively; warm scope to prevent fog; reposition; BURP; clean lens
nodes.body: ADDRESSING VISUALIZATION PROBLEMS: [1] SOILED AIRWAY (blood/secretions): • VL operator MUST suction aggressively • Suction is in VL operator's right hand at all times • Clear pharynx before FE insertion • May need repeated suctioning FOGGING: • Warm scope in warm water before use • Anti-fog solution on lens • Wipe lens on mucosa gently POOR VL VIEW: • Reposition patient (more sniffing position) •

nodes.title: Cannot Advance Through Cords
nodes.summary: More lidocaine + wait; advance during inspiration; if laryngospasm → give paralytic
nodes.body: CORDS NOT OPENING: [1,3,4] AWAKE PATIENT: • More topical lidocaine to cords (via FE channel) • Wait 30-60 seconds for effect • Ask patient to take deep breath • Advance during inspiration when cords open LARYNGOSPASM: • STOP attempting to advance • Withdraw scope slightly • More lidocaine to cords if possible • If persistent: give paralytic (this is why it's drawn!) - Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg or - Suc

nodes.title: ETT Won't Pass Over Scope
nodes.summary: Rotate ETT 90° CCW; withdraw + re-advance; jaw thrust; try smaller tube; DO NOT FORCE
nodes.body: TUBE HANG-UP SOLUTIONS: [1,8] AT THE VOCAL CORDS: Most common - tube catches on right arytenoid. SOLUTIONS: 1. Rotate 90° counterclockwise — most effective - Turns bevel posteriorly - Slides past arytenoids 2. Withdraw and re-advance - Pull back 1-2 cm - Re-advance with rotation 3. Jaw thrust - VL operator lifts jaw - Opens glottic inlet 4. Smaller ETT - Try 6.5 or 6.0 tube - Easier passage, can u

nodes.title: Desaturation During Procedure
nodes.summary: STOP → remove equipment → BVM → if no improvement → SGA → if CICO → cricothyrotomy
nodes.body: MANAGING DESATURATION: [1,9] IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: 1. STOP procedure 2. Remove FE and VL 3. BVM ventilate with 100% O2 4. Reassess airway patency IF PATIENT OXYGENATING: • Allow recovery to SpO2 >95% • Consider apneic oxygenation (nasal cannula 15 L/min) • Reattempt when stable IF CANNOT VENTILATE: • Reposition airway (jaw thrust, head tilt) • Two-person BVM technique • PLACE SUPRAGLOTTIC AIRWAY (LMA

nodes.title: Intubation Successful
nodes.summary: Confirm with capnography, bilateral breath sounds; secure tube; sedate; CXR; document
nodes.body: Video-assisted flexible endoscopic intubation completed successfully.
nodes.recommendation: POST-INTUBATION CHECKLIST: CONFIRMATION: ☐ Waveform capnography confirmed ☐ Bilateral breath sounds ☐ ETT depth appropriate (21-25 cm) ☐ ETT secured IMMEDIATE CARE: ☐ Sedation/analgesia initiated ☐ Ventilator settings adjusted ☐ OG/NG tube

nodes.title: Vaginal Bleeding Hub - Sick Check First
nodes.summary: Vitals, bleeding volume, pregnancy test, pain, postpartum/late pregnancy, anticoag/coagulopathy, and malignancy-risk lanes first.
nodes.body: \u26A0\uFE0F 5 DO NOT MISS: 1. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy \u2014 positive \u03B2-hCG + bleeding/shock. 2. Hemorrhagic shock from any source \u2014 pads/hour, clots, shock index; resuscitate first. 3. Postpartum hemorrhage / retained products \u2014 recent delivery, boggy uterus. 4. Late-pregnancy bleeding (placenta previa/abruption) \u2014 do NOT do a digital/speculum exam until previa excluded. 5

nodes.title: Time-Critical Exclusions - Pick the Best Fit
nodes.summary: Unstable hemorrhage, pregnancy-related bleeding, postpartum/late pregnancy, coagulopathy, adolescent, postmenopausal, trauma, and stable AUB are separate lanes.
nodes.body: Choose the most dangerous lane first. You can return after the immediate action.

nodes.title: Unstable Bleeding / Hemorrhage
nodes.body: Open Massive Transfusion when hemorrhagic shock is possible. Immediate actions: two large-bore IVs or IO, type and cross, CBC/coags/fibrinogen if severe or obstetric, pregnancy test, bedside US when skilled, pelvic exam/speculum if it will identify a controllable source, OB/GYN early, and blood products for shock rather than crystalloid-heavy resuscitation. TXA \u2014 postpartum hemorrhage is the
nodes.recommendation: Treat unstable vaginal bleeding as hemorrhage first, diagnosis second. In PPH give TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth - there is no benefit after that.

nodes.title: Early Pregnancy Bleeding / Ectopic / Miscarriage
nodes.body: Open First Trimester Emergencies. Core workup: quantitative beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, CBC, type and screen when moderate bleeding or pain, OB/GYN for unstable, ectopic suspicion, concerning free fluid, or pregnancy of unknown location with high-risk features. \uD83D\uDED1 A single beta-hCG value does not exclude ectopic pregnancy. ACEP gives a Level B recommendation: do not use the beta-h
nodes.recommendation: Bleeding with positive pregnancy test requires ectopic-safe documentation and follow-up. Do not use a beta-hCG value to rule out ectopic.

nodes.title: Bleeding at >=20 Weeks Pregnancy
nodes.body: Open Pregnancy Trauma when trauma is involved, and involve OB urgently. Do not perform digital cervical exam until placenta previa is excluded. Priorities are maternal stabilization, fetal assessment when viable, Rh status, type and cross, CBC/coags/fibrinogen if significant bleeding, ultrasound for placental location, and OB/OR readiness. Consider placenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa
nodes.recommendation: Late-pregnancy bleeding is OB-led after maternal stabilization; avoid digital exam until previa excluded.

nodes.title: Postpartum / Post-Procedure Bleeding
nodes.body: Recent delivery, miscarriage management, abortion, D&C, IUD insertion/removal, or gynecologic procedure changes the risk. Think: uterine atony, retained products, laceration, uterine rupture/perforation, endometritis/sepsis, coagulopathy, secondary postpartum hemorrhage. Actions: resuscitate, uterine massage if postpartum atony suspected, OB/GYN early, type and cross, CBC/coags/fibrinogen when sig
nodes.recommendation: Postpartum or procedural bleeding deserves early OB/GYN involvement and hemorrhage/infection posture.

nodes.title: Adolescent Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
nodes.body: ACOG recommends considering an underlying bleeding disorder in adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding, especially anemia, flooding, bleeding through products quickly, easy bruising, epistaxis, surgical/dental bleeding, or family history. ED priorities: pregnancy test, CBC/ferritin when appropriate, hemodynamics, bleeding severity, medication safety, and gynecology/hematology involvement for sev
nodes.recommendation: Heavy adolescent bleeding is a bleeding-disorder screen, not only a period complaint.

nodes.title: Anticoagulant / Coagulopathy Bleeding
nodes.body: Identify DOAC/warfarin/heparin/antiplatelet exposure, last dose, renal/liver disease, thrombocytopenia, cancer therapy, inherited bleeding disorder, and anemia symptoms. Open Anticoagulation Reversal when bleeding is major, unstable, or reversal is being considered. Workup: CBC, type and screen, pregnancy test, PT/INR/aPTT when relevant, fibrinogen in severe obstetric bleeding, renal/liver functio
nodes.recommendation: Major vaginal bleeding on anticoagulants is major bleeding until proven otherwise.

nodes.title: Postmenopausal Bleeding / Malignancy-Risk Lane
nodes.body: Postmenopausal bleeding requires outpatient gynecology evaluation even if ED bleeding has stopped. The ED role is to stabilize, exclude severe anemia/hemorrhage, identify obvious non-uterine sources, and arrange timely follow-up. \uD83D\uDED1 Do not discharge on a "thin stripe." ACOG updated this in 2026: transvaginal ultrasound alone is no longer sufficient initial evaluation for most patients wi
nodes.recommendation: Do not label postmenopausal bleeding benign without gynecology follow-up.

nodes.title: Trauma / Laceration / Foreign Body / Assault
nodes.body: Open DFSA / SANE Workup when sexual assault or drug-facilitated assault is possible. Actions: trauma-informed consent, stabilize bleeding, inspect for laceration/foreign body only with consent and appropriate support, forensic/SANE pathway, STI/pregnancy prophylaxis when indicated, mandatory reporting rules for minors/vulnerable adults, and surgical/OB/GYN help for deep laceration, expanding hemat
nodes.recommendation: Use trauma-informed care and forensic preservation when assault is possible.

nodes.title: Stable Nonpregnant Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
nodes.body: Open Abnormal Uterine Bleeding. Stable AUB priorities: pregnancy excluded, anemia assessed, bleeding severity estimated, contraindications to estrogen/progestin/TXA considered, malignancy risk and follow-up arranged. ACOG frames acute AUB treatment around hemodynamic status, medical therapy when stable, and procedural/surgical management when unstable or refractory.
nodes.recommendation: Stable nonpregnant AUB can usually be medically managed, but pregnancy and instability must be excluded first.

nodes.title: Rescue / Initial Bundle + Reassess
nodes.summary: Pregnancy test, bleeding quantification, CBC/type and screen, targeted coags, pelvic exam when useful, and ultrasound by lane.
nodes.body: Default ED bundle: - Pregnancy test, vitals trend, orthostatics only if safe. - CBC; type and screen/cross when moderate/heavy bleeding, pregnancy, anemia symptoms, or instability. - Rh status when pregnant \u226512+0 weeks or pregnancy status uncertain. Below 12+0 weeks, ACOG 2024 suggests forgoing routine Rh testing/RhIg while SMFM dissents \u2014 follow local protocol and document it. [10] - Co

nodes.title: Reassess After Initial Bundle
nodes.summary: Ongoing bleeding or pregnancy-related concern should reset the pathway to high risk.
nodes.body: Recheck vitals, ongoing bleeding, pain, dizziness/syncope, Hgb risk, and imaging/workup results.

nodes.title: Imaging / Workup Strategy
nodes.summary: Image by pregnancy status, bleeding severity, and whether the result changes urgent management.
nodes.body: Positive pregnancy test: transvaginal ultrasound for IUP/ectopic/free fluid, with quantitative beta-hCG interpreted carefully. Pregnancy >=20 weeks: ultrasound for placental location/fetal status, OB-led pathway; avoid digital cervical exam until previa excluded. Nonpregnant AUB: ultrasound is helpful for structural causes when ED result changes disposition or urgent follow-up; many stable cases c

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit unstable or high-risk pregnancy/postpartum/coagulopathy bleeding. Discharge only controlled, explained, and followed.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on physiology, pregnancy/postpartum status, bleeding control, anemia symptoms, diagnosis, and follow-up.

nodes.title: Admit / Consult / Transfer
nodes.body: Admit, transfer, or urgently consult for hemorrhagic shock, ongoing heavy bleeding, severe symptomatic anemia, ectopic concern, pregnancy >=20 weeks bleeding, postpartum hemorrhage, suspected retained products with infection/hemorrhage, major anticoagulant/coagulopathy bleeding, unstable adolescent bleeding, or inability to ensure follow-up.
nodes.recommendation: High-risk vaginal bleeding needs specialty and hemorrhage support, not routine discharge.

nodes.title: Urgent Follow-Up / Observation
nodes.body: Use observation or urgent follow-up for pregnancy of unknown location, improving but still significant bleeding, anemia without instability, new heavy menstrual bleeding needing medication initiation, postmenopausal bleeding, or coagulopathy medication adjustment. Give exact repeat beta-hCG/US timing when early pregnancy is unresolved.
nodes.recommendation: The follow-up plan is part of the treatment, especially for pregnancy of unknown location.

nodes.title: Discharge Checklist
nodes.body: Discharge only when vitals are stable, bleeding is controlled, pregnancy status and ectopic risk have a written plan, Hgb risk is acceptable, pain is controlled, no late-pregnancy/postpartum/coagulopathy danger remains, and follow-up is realistic. Return now for: soaking pads rapidly, syncope, worsening pain, shoulder pain, dizziness, fever, pregnancy symptoms with bleeding, passing large clots, s
nodes.recommendation: Document pregnancy test result, bleeding control, anemia assessment, and follow-up timing.

nodes.title: Peripheral Vasopressor Extravasation Rescue
nodes.summary: Stop infusion, leave catheter, aspirate, do not flush, and assess ischemia immediately.
nodes.body: Extravasation Rescue Steps Use this pathway for suspected extravasation from peripheral norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, dopamine, vasopressin, or mixed vasopressor infusions. Immediate priorities: - Stop the infusion immediately - Leave the catheter in place initially - Disconnect tubing and aspirate residual drug through the catheter - Do not flush the line - Notify pharmacy/clinician

nodes.title: Recognition
nodes.summary: Severity is determined by perfusion, neurovascular findings, location, and progression.
nodes.body: What is present at the infusion site? Concerning findings include pain, blanching, cool skin, swelling, mottling, delayed capillary refill, numbness, paresthesia, tense compartments, blistering, or rapidly expanding discoloration.

nodes.title: Immediate Nonpharmacologic Rescue
nodes.summary: Stop, aspirate, avoid flushing, warm compress, elevate, document, and move pressor access.
nodes.body: Perform these steps before antidote infiltration. 1. Stop vasopressor infusion immediately. 2. Leave catheter in place initially. 3. Disconnect tubing and aspirate residual drug from the catheter. 4. Do not flush. 5. Remove catheter after aspiration unless pharmacy/toxicology directs otherwise. 6. Elevate the extremity. 7. Apply dry warm compresses for vasopressor extravasation. 8. Mark borders, p

nodes.title: Ischemia Present
nodes.summary: Ischemia requires antidote plus early surgery/plastics escalation when location or progression is concerning.
nodes.body: Treat as time-sensitive limb/skin ischemia. Do now: - Perform immediate rescue steps - Obtain Phentolamine if alpha-adrenergic vasopressor involved - Escalate early to pharmacy, toxicology/poison center, and surgery/plastics for hand, foot, large-volume, delayed, or progressive ischemia - Reassess pain, color, temperature, capillary refill, sensation, motor function, and pulses every 15-30 minutes

nodes.title: Surgical / Plastics Escalation
nodes.summary: Progressive ischemia or tissue injury is not a watch-and-wait problem.
nodes.body: Necrosis, blistering, tense compartments, progressive ischemia, or neurovascular deficit requires immediate specialist involvement. Parallel actions: - Continue local rescue and antidote steps when appropriate - Consult surgery/plastics/hand surgery based on location - Consider compartment pressure assessment if exam suggests compartment syndrome - Continue systemic resuscitation and alternative v
nodes.recommendation: Escalate immediately for necrosis, blistering, compartment concern, or progressive ischemia.

nodes.title: Which Vasopressor Extravasated?
nodes.summary: Alpha-adrenergic injury favors phentolamine; isolated vasopressin requires extra caution.
nodes.body: Choose the best match. If mixed infusion or uncertain, treat as alpha-adrenergic until clarified with pharmacy/toxicology.

nodes.title: Phentolamine Protocol
nodes.summary: Phentolamine 5-10 mg in 10 mL NS, infiltrated locally, is the main antidote for alpha-pressor extravasation.
nodes.body: Use for norepinephrine/epinephrine/phenylephrine/dopamine extravasation with ischemic risk. Dose: - Phentolamine 5-10 mg diluted in 10 mL normal saline - Infiltrate subcutaneously/intradermally throughout the affected area using small aliquots - Use a small-gauge needle and inject around the margins and through the ischemic field - Best as soon as possible; DailyMed labeling specifies treatment wi

nodes.title: If Phentolamine Is Unavailable
nodes.summary: If phentolamine is unavailable, terbutaline and topical nitroglycerin are reported alternatives with limited evidence.
nodes.body: Evidence is limited and largely case-based. Use local policy and pharmacy/toxicology guidance. Adult alternatives described in the literature: - Terbutaline 1 mg diluted in 10 mL normal saline, infiltrated subcutaneously around the affected area - Nitroglycerin 2% ointment topically over the ischemic area; avoid if hypotension or recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure - Continue warm compresses, elevatio

nodes.title: Vasopressin-Specific Nuance
nodes.summary: Isolated vasopressin injury is not alpha-mediated; use rescue steps and early expert escalation for ischemia.
nodes.body: Isolated vasopressin extravasation is V1-receptor mediated, not alpha-adrenergic. Phentolamine is not a direct reversal agent for vasopressin. Recommended approach: - Perform immediate nonpharmacologic rescue steps - Stop infusion, aspirate, do not flush, elevate, warm compress - Restart vasopressin/pressors through reliable alternate access - Consult pharmacy/toxicology early if ischemia is prese

nodes.title: Reassess After Rescue
nodes.summary: Response is judged by serial perfusion and neurovascular exams, not a single look.
nodes.body: Reassess after local treatment and warm compresses. Check: - Pain - Skin color and temperature - Capillary refill - Motor/sensory function - Pulses/Doppler when relevant - Borders of swelling/discoloration

nodes.title: Persistent Ischemia
nodes.summary: Persistent ischemia needs expert escalation and serial exams; avoid blind repeated infiltration.
nodes.body: If ischemia persists: - Confirm the vasopressor has been moved to reliable alternate access - Verify antidote reached the entire affected area - Continue dry warm compresses and elevation - Call poison center/toxicology and pharmacy if not already involved - Consult surgery/plastics/hand surgery early for distal extremity, large-volume, delayed presentation, or progression - Consider additional lo

nodes.title: Monitoring / Documentation
nodes.summary: Serial neurovascular exams and documentation are part of the treatment.
nodes.body: Document and trend: - Vasopressor, concentration, estimated volume, time of recognition - IV location, catheter size, ultrasound-guided or not - Symptoms and exam at recognition - Borders marked and photos per policy - Antidote dose, dilution, time, and infiltration field - Serial neurovascular exam every 15-30 minutes initially until clearly stable, then per local protocol - Pain control and woun

nodes.title: Disposition / Follow-Up
nodes.summary: Disposition depends on trajectory and neurovascular stability.
nodes.body: What is the current clinical course?

nodes.title: Improving After Rescue
nodes.summary: Improvement still requires observation and documented stability.
nodes.body: Continue observation until the site remains stable and perfusion is clearly normalizing. Before leaving ED/ICU handoff: - Document stable/improving exam - Ensure alternate vasopressor access is secure - Provide local wound instructions and escalation triggers - Arrange follow-up/wound check if any residual injury remains Escalation triggers after initial improvement: - Recurrent pain or blanching
nodes.recommendation: Observe until stable, document serial improvement, and arrange follow-up if residual injury remains.

nodes.title: Persistent Abnormal Exam
nodes.summary: Persistent abnormal perfusion or pain needs observation and specialist input.
nodes.body: Persistent pain, swelling, color change, or equivocal perfusion after rescue should not be discharged without a plan. Recommended actions: - Continue serial neurovascular checks - Involve pharmacy/toxicology and surgery/plastics/hand surgery based on site - Consider admission/observation for distal extremity involvement or unreliable follow-up - Provide wound care and clear return precautions - Re
nodes.recommendation: Observe or admit with specialist input when exam remains abnormal after initial rescue.

nodes.title: STOP: High-Risk Extravasation
nodes.summary: High-risk extravasation requires immediate escalation, not routine observation.
nodes.body: Stop and escalate immediately if any are present: - Hand, foot, genital/perineal, or large-volume extravasation - Blanching/coolness with poor capillary refill - Numbness, weakness, severe pain, or tense compartments - Blistering, necrosis, or rapidly expanding skin changes - Delayed recognition with ongoing ischemia - Need for ongoing high-dose peripheral vasopressors without reliable access Do n
nodes.recommendation: Escalate to pharmacy/toxicology and surgery/plastics/hand surgery immediately for high-risk features.

nodes.title: Ventricular Tachycardia
nodes.summary: Wide complex tachycardia >120ms, rate 150-250 bpm — check pulse immediately to determine protocol
nodes.body: VT Management Steps Summary VT confirmed: wide complex tachycardia, rate usually 150–250 bpm. Key Features: • QRS duration >120 ms • AV dissociation (if present, highly specific for VT) • Concordance across precordial leads • Fusion/capture beats ⚠️ Check pulse immediately — pulseless VT and VT with pulse have fundamentally different management protocols.

nodes.title: Pulse Check
nodes.summary: Pulseless VT = cardiac arrest protocol; pulse present = assess hemodynamic stability
nodes.body: Is a pulse present?

nodes.title: QRS Morphology
nodes.summary: Monomorphic vs polymorphic VT determines treatment pathway — check QTc for polymorphic
nodes.body: What is the QRS morphology?

nodes.title: Pulseless VT — Defibrillation
nodes.summary: Shock 200J biphasic immediately — resume CPR right after, do NOT pause for rhythm check
nodes.body: Shock immediately: 200J biphasic. Resume CPR immediately after shock — do NOT check pulse first. Same protocol as VF. Key Points: • Biphasic 200J (or manufacturer max if different device) • Resume chest compressions immediately — do not pause for rhythm analysis • 2-minute CPR cycles between rhythm checks • Minimize hands-off time (<10 sec for shock delivery)

nodes.title: CPR + Epinephrine + Antiarrhythmic
nodes.summary: Epi 1mg after 2nd shock q3-5min; amiodarone 300mg after 3rd shock; high-quality CPR 100-120/min
nodes.body: Epinephrine: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO after 2nd shock, repeat every 3–5 minutes. Antiarrhythmic after 3rd shock: • Amiodarone 300 mg IV push, then 150 mg IV push if still in VT/VF • OR Lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg IV, then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg q5–10 min (max 3 mg/kg) Continue: • High-quality CPR (100–120/min, ≥2 inches depth, full recoil) • Rhythm check every 2 minutes • Search for reversible causes (H's and T's

nodes.title: Rhythm Check After 2-min CPR Cycle
nodes.summary: After 2-min CPR: assess for ROSC, persistent pVT, or Torsades morphology
nodes.body: After 2-minute CPR cycle: what does the rhythm check show?

nodes.title: Refractory Pulseless VT
nodes.summary: Consider double sequential defib, esmolol, pad repositioning, ECPR; search reversible causes H/T
nodes.body: Refractory pulseless VT: follow VF/VT arrest escalation protocol. Consider: • Double sequential defibrillation (DSD) • Esmolol 500 mcg/kg IV bolus • Pad position change (anterolateral → anterior-posterior) • ECPR if available and criteria met • Reversible cause search (H's and T's) Refractory VF/VT Protocol

nodes.title: Polymorphic VT in Arrest — Check QTc
nodes.summary: If prolonged QTc: MgSO4 2g IV push, do NOT give amiodarone — it worsens Torsades; overdrive pace if available
nodes.body: Polymorphic VT in arrest → check baseline QTc if known. If prolonged QTc → Torsades protocol: • Magnesium Sulfate 2 g IV push (can give rapidly in arrest), repeat 2 g at 5–15 min if it persists, then start a continuous infusion • ⚠️ Do NOT give amiodarone — it prolongs QT and worsens Torsades • Overdrive pacing if available Torsades de Pointes Protocol

nodes.title: ROSC — Post-Cardiac Arrest Care
nodes.body: ROSC achieved → immediate post-cardiac arrest care. Priorities: • 12-lead ECG immediately — ischemia-driven VT may need emergent cath lab • Start antiarrhythmic maintenance infusion (amiodarone 1 mg/min × 6h → 0.5 mg/min or lidocaine 1–4 mg/min) • Targeted temperature management • Identify and treat VT trigger Post-Cardiac Arrest Care
nodes.recommendation: Post-ROSC: 12-lead ECG immediately, antiarrhythmic infusion, identify VT trigger.

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Stability
nodes.summary: Unstable if SBP <90, AMS, ischemic chest pain, or pulmonary edema — immediate cardioversion
nodes.body: Is the patient hemodynamically unstable? Unstable criteria: • SBP <90 mmHg • Altered mental status • Ischemic chest pain • Acute pulmonary edema

nodes.title: Unstable VT — Synchronized Cardioversion
nodes.summary: Synchronized cardioversion 100J-200J-360J; confirm sync mode; if deteriorates to pulseless, unsync 200J
nodes.body: Synchronized cardioversion: • Start 100J → 200J → 360J (biphasic) • Confirm synchronized mode — shock must land on R wave • If sync mode fails to track → switch to unsynchronized Sedation (if hemodynamics tolerate brief sedation): • Midazolam 2–5 mg IV • OR Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV ⚠️ If patient deteriorates to pulseless → unsynchronized shock 200J immediately.

nodes.title: Post-Cardioversion Management
nodes.summary: 12-lead ECG, start antiarrhythmic infusion, check K+ >4.0 and Mg2+ >2.0, identify trigger
nodes.body: Post-cardioversion checklist: • 12-lead ECG (compare to prior) • Start maintenance antiarrhythmic infusion • Check electrolytes (K+ target >4.0, Mg2+ target >2.0) • Identify trigger: ischemia, electrolyte abnormality, drug-induced • Cardiology consult If VT recurs → consider alternative antiarrhythmic or repeat cardioversion.

nodes.title: Stable Monomorphic VT — IV Antiarrhythmic
nodes.summary: Amiodarone 150mg/10min OR procainamide (preferred per 2025 AHA IIa vs IIb); avoid procainamide if prolonged QTc or CHF/impaired LV → use amiodarone
nodes.body: Monomorphic stable VT — IV antiarrhythmic. First-line options: • Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min → 1 mg/min × 6h → 0.5 mg/min • Procainamide 20–50 mg/min until arrhythmia suppresses, hypotension, QRS widens >50%, or max 17 mg/kg • Lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg → 0.5–0.75 mg/kg q5–10 min → infusion 1–4 mg/min Procainamide may be preferred (2025 AHA: procainamide Class IIa vs amiodarone Class IIb) — higher

nodes.title: Response to Antiarrhythmic
nodes.summary: Assess antiarrhythmic response: converted, persisting stable, or deteriorating to unstable
nodes.body: What is the response to antiarrhythmic therapy?

nodes.title: Refractory Stable Monomorphic VT
nodes.summary: Try alternative antiarrhythmic; consider cardioversion; do NOT combine amiodarone + procainamide (QT prolongation)
nodes.body: Refractory stable monomorphic VT: • Try alternative antiarrhythmic if first agent failed (e.g., procainamide after amiodarone) • Consider synchronized cardioversion even if "stable" — pharmacologic conversion has limitations • Electrophysiology consult for catheter ablation consideration • Continuous hemodynamic monitoring — stable VT can deteriorate without warning Do NOT combine amiodarone + pro

nodes.title: Polymorphic VT — Baseline QTc
nodes.summary: Prolonged QTc >480ms = Torsades (MgSO4, no amiodarone); normal QTc = likely ischemia-driven
nodes.body: What is the baseline QTc?

nodes.title: Polymorphic VT — Normal QTc (Ischemia)
nodes.summary: Normal QTc polymorphic VT = treat as ACS — emergent cath lab, beta-blockers, aggressive lyte correction
nodes.body: Polymorphic VT with normal QTc: treat like ischemia. Usually ischemia-driven. Treat as ACS: • Emergent cardiology consult + cath lab activation • Beta-blockers may help suppress catecholamine-driven VT • Amiodarone acceptable (QT not prolonged) • Aggressive electrolyte correction (K+ >4.0, Mg2+ >2.0) NSTEMI Management

nodes.title: Polymorphic VT + Prolonged QTc = Torsades
nodes.summary: Torsades: MgSO4 2g IV then infusion, overdrive pace 90-110bpm; do NOT give amiodarone or procainamide
nodes.body: Polymorphic VT with prolonged QTc = Torsades de Pointes. Treatment is OPPOSITE of standard VT. ⚠️ Do NOT give amiodarone or procainamide — they prolong QT and will worsen Torsades. Immediate treatment: • Magnesium Sulfate 2 g IV over 5–15 min, repeat 2 g at 5–15 min if it persists, then start a continuous infusion • Overdrive pacing to 90–110 bpm • Isoproterenol infusion if pacing unavailable • St

nodes.title: Post-Conversion Checklist
nodes.summary: 12-lead ECG, lytes K+ >4.0 Mg2+ >2.0, troponin, echo, identify cause, start maintenance antiarrhythmic
nodes.body: Post-conversion checklist: • 12-lead ECG (compare to prior) • Electrolytes: K+ target >4.0, Mg2+ target >2.0 • Troponin (ischemia trigger?) • Echo if not done (EF, wall motion abnormalities) • Identify and treat cause: ischemia, electrolyte, drug-induced, structural heart disease • Start maintenance antiarrhythmic infusion

nodes.title: Recurrent VT Management
nodes.summary: EP consult, ICD if EF <=35%, catheter ablation for recurrent monomorphic VT, beta-blocker therapy
nodes.body: Recurrent VT management: • Electrophysiology consult • ICD evaluation (EF ≤35%, or survived VT arrest) • Amiodarone maintenance (200–400 mg PO daily) as bridge to ICD • Catheter ablation for recurrent monomorphic VT [12] • Medication review — discontinue QT-prolonging agents • Beta-blocker therapy (reduces VT recurrence in structural heart disease)

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.body: Disposition: ICU with continuous telemetry. All VT patients require inpatient monitoring: • Continuous telemetry (minimum 48 hours) • Cardiology/EP consult • Echo if not done (assess EF, structural heart disease) • ICD evaluation if EF ≤35% or survived VT arrest • Complete medication reconciliation • Electrolyte monitoring q4–6h until stable
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission with telemetry, cardiology/EP consult, echo, ICD evaluation if EF ≤35%.

nodes.title: Vertigo: Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: TITRATE approach: classify dizziness by timing and triggers, not symptom quality — distinguish BPPV, vestibular neuritis, posterior stroke
nodes.body: Vertigo Steps Summary — timing-and-triggers approach (TITRATE), not quality of dizziness. Core principle: The word "dizzy" means different things. Focus on timing (constant vs episodic), triggers (spontaneous vs positional), and exam findings — NOT "is it vertigo or lightheadedness." Patients are unreliable on quality descriptors. First actions: • Full vitals including orthostatic BP — POTS and or

nodes.title: Characterize the Dizziness
nodes.summary: Differentiate true vertigo (illusory motion) from presyncope/disequilibrium — patient descriptors are unreliable
nodes.body: Ask: "Can you describe what you feel without using the word dizzy?" True vertigo = illusory sense of motion (spinning, tilting, rocking). Often with nausea, nystagmus, gait disturbance. Non-vertigo dizziness = lightheaded, presyncope, "about to pass out," faint, weak. Points to orthostatic, cardiac, metabolic, or anemia etiology. Disequilibrium = unsteadiness without illusory motion. Often multifa

nodes.title: Orthostatic Vital Signs
nodes.summary: Check orthostatic vitals before assuming vestibular cause — POTS and orthostatic hypotension masquerade as vertigo
nodes.body: Get orthostatic vitals BEFORE assuming peripheral vestibular cause. POTS and orthostatic hypotension frequently masquerade as vertigo — especially in young women and elderly. Orthostatic criteria: • Orthostatic hypotension: SBP drop ≥20 mmHg OR DBP drop ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing • POTS: HR increase ≥30 bpm (≥40 in adolescents) within 10 minutes of standing, without orthostatic hypotens

nodes.title: Non-Vestibular Dizziness
nodes.body: This is likely not peripheral or central vestibular disease. Consider alternate etiologies: Cardiovascular: • Orthostatic hypotension (volume, meds, autonomic) • POTS / dysautonomia • Arrhythmia — consider Syncope Evaluation • Aortic stenosis, HOCM Metabolic / Hematologic: • Hypoglycemia • Severe anemia / GI bleed • Electrolyte derangement • Thyroid disease Medication side effects — review med lis

nodes.title: Time Course & Triggers (TITRATE)
nodes.summary: Classify vertigo by timing/triggers: AVS (constant hours-days), t-EVS (brief positional), s-EVS (spontaneous episodic)
nodes.body: Classify the vertigo syndrome by timing and triggers — this drives the rest of the workup: Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS): • Constant vertigo lasting hours to days • Persistent nausea/vomiting, gait instability • Spontaneous nystagmus present • → HINTS exam pathway Triggered Episodic Vestibular Syndrome (t-EVS): • Brief episodes <1 minute • Triggered by head position change (rolling over, looking

nodes.title: Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS)
nodes.summary: AVS = constant vertigo >24h with spontaneous nystagmus — key DDx: vestibular neuritis vs cerebellar stroke, HINTS exam is next
nodes.body: Definition: Acute onset of continuous vertigo lasting >24 hours, with nausea/vomiting, head motion intolerance, unsteady gait, and spontaneous nystagmus on exam. Key differential: • Vestibular neuritis (peripheral) — viral inflammation of vestibular nerve • Labyrinthitis (peripheral) — vestibular neuritis + hearing loss • Posterior circulation stroke (central) — cerebellar or brainstem infarct • L

nodes.title: Triggered Episodic Vertigo (t-EVS)
nodes.summary: t-EVS = brief (<1min) positional episodes — most commonly BPPV, but central positional vertigo can mimic it
nodes.body: Definition: Brief episodes of vertigo (seconds to <1 minute) triggered by head position change — rolling over in bed, looking up ("top-shelf vertigo"), bending down. Classic features: • Episodes <1 minute, often seconds • No vertigo between episodes • Triggered reliably by specific head positions • No hearing loss, no tinnitus • No focal neurologic signs Most common cause: BPPV (Benign Paroxysmal

nodes.title: Spontaneous Episodic Vertigo (s-EVS)
nodes.summary: s-EVS = spontaneous episodes min-hours — vestibular migraine most common, distinguish from TIA in vascular risk patients
nodes.body: Definition: Episodes of vertigo lasting minutes to hours, occurring without a positional trigger. Patient is normal between episodes. Differential: • Vestibular migraine — most common cause; 50% have NO headache with vertigo • Ménière disease — vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness • TIA (posterior circulation) — especially in vascular risk patients • Panic attack / anxiet

nodes.title: Central Feature Screen (Deadly D's)
nodes.summary: Screen for Deadly Ds (dysarthria/dysphagia/diplopia/dysmetria) and red flags — ANY positive finding skips HINTS, goes to stroke workup
nodes.body: Before performing HINTS, screen for central red flags. ANY positive finding routes directly to stroke workup — HINTS is not needed and should not be used. The Deadly D's: • Dysarthria • Dysphagia • Diplopia • Dysmetria (finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin) • Dysphonia / hoarseness • Downbeat or direction-changing nystagmus Additional red flags: • New severe headache or neck pain (dissection risk) • Focal

nodes.title: Central Features Present — Stroke Pathway
nodes.summary: Central features present — activate stroke team, establish last known well. Posterior circulation strokes are misdiagnosed ~37% of the time vs ~16% anterior
nodes.body: STOP. Do not perform HINTS exam. Central features indicate posterior circulation stroke until proven otherwise. Immediate actions: • Activate stroke team / neurology consult • Last known well time — determines thrombolytic window • Continuous cardiac monitoring • IV access × 2 • NPO • BP management if >220/120 (permissive hypertension in acute stroke) • NIHSS — note: NIHSS underscores posterior ci

nodes.title: Posterior Circulation Stroke Workup
nodes.summary: CT ~42% sensitive for ischemic stroke and worse in the posterior fossa — MRI-DWI misses 12-20% at 24-48h and ~53% of strokes <=10mm; repeat at 48-72h if negative with high suspicion
nodes.body: Imaging Decision Guide CT head non-contrast is NOT adequate to rule out posterior circulation stroke. • CT sensitivity for acute *ischemic* stroke overall: ~42% (Hwang 2012, n=1,356) — and substantially worse in the posterior fossa, where beam-hardening artifact from the skull base obscures the brainstem and cerebellum • CT is useful only to exclude hemorrhage or mass effect before treatment. A ne

nodes.title: Posterior Circulation Stroke — Admit
nodes.body: Disposition: Stroke unit admission. Neurology consult. Continuous telemetry. If within thrombolytic window (<4.5h from last known well): • Follow Stroke Consult for IVT/EVT decisions • Posterior circulation strokes are eligible for tPA — do NOT withhold based on isolated vertigo presentation • EVT for large vessel occlusion (basilar, vertebral) — time-sensitive Ongoing workup: • Repeat MRI at 48-7

nodes.title: BPPV History Confirmation
nodes.summary: Classic BPPV: <1min episodes triggered by head position, no hearing loss — posterior canal 85%, confirm with Dix-Hallpike test
nodes.body: Classic BPPV features (all should be present): • Brief episodes <1 minute (often 5-30 seconds) • Triggered by head position change — rolling over, looking up, lying down • No vertigo at rest • No spontaneous nystagmus • No hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurologic signs • Onset often on waking or rolling in bed Epidemiology: • Most common peripheral vestibular disorder • Peak incidence 50-70 years old

nodes.title: Dix-Hallpike Test
nodes.summary: Dix-Hallpike technique and interpretation — upbeat-torsional = posterior BPPV, pure horizontal = horizontal canal, red flags: pure vertical nystagmus
nodes.body: Dix-Hallpike & Epley Technique Technique (right side): 1. Patient sits upright on exam table, legs extended 2. Turn head 45° to the right 3. Rapidly lay patient supine with head extending 20° off the end of the table 4. Observe for nystagmus for 30-45 seconds 5. Return to sitting, observe for reversal nystagmus 6. Repeat on left side Classic posterior canal BPPV response: • Upbeat-torsional nystag

nodes.title: Posterior Canal BPPV — Epley Maneuver
nodes.summary: Epley maneuver for posterior canal BPPV — Cochrane OR 4.42 vs sham (56% vs 21%, NNT~3), 80-95% single-maneuver success, no post-maneuver restrictions. AAO-HNS 2017 recommends AGAINST routine vestibular suppressants
nodes.body: Canalith Repositioning Procedure (Epley Maneuver): first-line treatment. Cochrane 2014: OR 4.42 for symptom resolution vs sham — 21% of sham-treated vs 56% of Epley-treated patients resolved, i.e. NNT ≈ 3. Technique (for right-sided BPPV): 1. Position 1: Start in Dix-Hallpike right (head 45° right, supine with head hanging). Hold 30-60 seconds or until nystagmus stops. 2. Position 2: Without lifti

nodes.title: Supine Roll Test — Horizontal Canal
nodes.summary: Supine roll test for horizontal canal BPPV — geotropic = canalithiasis (more intense side affected), apogeotropic = cupulolithiasis
nodes.body: Supine roll test (Pagnini-McClure): used to confirm and sub-type horizontal canal BPPV. Technique: 1. Patient supine with head flexed 30° (pillow under head) 2. Rapidly rotate head 90° to one side 3. Observe for nystagmus 30-60 seconds 4. Return head to midline 5. Rotate 90° to opposite side, observe Interpretation: Geotropic nystagmus (beats toward the ground on both sides): • Canalithiasis (part

nodes.title: Horizontal Canal BPPV — Treatment
nodes.summary: Do NOT use Epley for horizontal canal — use Gufoni or Barbecue Roll maneuver, 70-80% success for canalithiasis
nodes.body: Do NOT use Epley maneuver — Epley is specific to the posterior canal. Gufoni Maneuver (easier for ED): 1. Patient sits upright on exam table 2. Quickly lay patient on the UNAFFECTED side (for geotropic canalithiasis) 3. Hold for 1-2 minutes until nystagmus stops 4. Quickly rotate head 45° toward the floor (nose toward bed) 5. Hold 1-2 minutes 6. Return to sitting Barbecue Roll (Lempert) Maneuver —

nodes.title: Verify Cure — Repeat Dix-Hallpike
nodes.summary: Wait 15min post-maneuver then repeat Dix-Hallpike — may repeat maneuver 1-2 more times if still positive, 15-30% annual recurrence
nodes.body: Wait 15 minutes after the maneuver, then repeat Dix-Hallpike (or supine roll for horizontal canal) to verify. Resolved: • No nystagmus • No vertigo with positional testing • Patient can lie down and sit up without symptoms Still positive: • Persistent nystagmus on repeat test • May repeat maneuver 1-2 more times • Consider switching canals (posterior → horizontal conversion can occur) • Refer for

nodes.title: Failed Maneuver — Home Exercises
nodes.summary: Failed Epley: re-check the canal and the diagnosis first. Brandt-Daroff (5 reps x 3 sessions/day x 2 weeks) is rated INFERIOR to repositioning by AAO-HNS 2017 — adjunctive only; refer vestibular PT
nodes.body: ⚠️ First, reconsider the diagnosis. A posterior-canal Epley has an 80-95% single-maneuver success rate. If repeated correctly-performed maneuvers fail, the leading possibilities are wrong canal (horizontal/anterior — Epley will not treat these), cupulolithiasis rather than canalithiasis (responds better to Semont), or not BPPV at all. Re-examine before defaulting to home exercises. Brandt-Daroff E

nodes.title: BPPV — Discharge
nodes.body: Disposition: Discharge home with clear instructions. Medications: • Meclizine 25 mg PO q8h PRN — maximum 48-72 hours. Not curative. Can delay vestibular compensation if overused. • Antiemetics PRN: Ondansetron 4-8 mg ODT q8h PRN • Avoid Diazepam for BPPV — benzodiazepines delay recovery Patient education: • Movement does NOT cause harm — gradually return to activity • Expect mild symptoms for a fe

nodes.title: HINTS Exam — Patient Appropriate?
nodes.summary: HINTS only valid with continuous vertigo + spontaneous nystagmus. 100% sens is neuro-otologist data (Kattah 2009); untrained EPs achieve only 83% sens / 44% spec (Ohle 2020) — a peripheral HINTS in untrained hands is not a rule-out
nodes.body: HINTS Exam Technique HINTS is ONLY valid when ALL of the following are true: • Patient has continuous (AVS) vertigo, not episodic • Spontaneous nystagmus is present at rest • No central red flags (already screened) • Symptoms currently active (not between episodes) HINTS is INVALID and DANGEROUS when: • No spontaneous nystagmus → HIT will appear "normal" in healthy people, falsely suggesting centr

nodes.title: Step 1: Nystagmus Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess nystagmus: remove fixation first — unidirectional horizontal = peripheral, direction-changing/vertical/pure torsional = central
nodes.body: Nystagmus Interpretation Guide Critical technique: remove visual fixation. Peripheral nystagmus suppresses with fixation — you may miss it entirely unless you eliminate fixation. Three methods: • Frenzel goggles (ideal but rarely available in ED) • Ophthalmoscope trick — look at one fundus while asking patient to cover other eye. Nystagmus direction reverses what you see through the scope. • "Pape

nodes.title: Step 2: Head Impulse Test (HIT)
nodes.summary: COUNTERINTUITIVE: abnormal HIT (catch-up saccade) = peripheral/reassuring, normal HIT = central/worrisome for stroke
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Patient fixates on your nose 2. Hold head gently with both hands 3. Rapidly turn head ~20° to one side (high-velocity, small-amplitude thrust) 4. Watch the eyes — do they stay fixated on your nose, or do they drift and make a corrective saccade? 5. Repeat to the other side ⚠️ COUNTERINTUITIVE RULE ⚠️ Abnormal HIT (corrective saccade present) = REASSURING for peripheral cause. • Perip

nodes.title: Step 3: Test of Skew (Alternate Cover Test)
nodes.summary: Alternate cover test: vertical skew deviation = central lesion (98% specificity), most specific finding in HINTS exam
nodes.body: Technique: 1. Patient fixates on your nose with both eyes open 2. Cover one eye with your hand or occluder 3. Rapidly uncover and immediately cover the other eye 4. Watch the newly uncovered eye for vertical refixation movement 5. Repeat several times Interpretation: No skew deviation = peripheral (reassuring) • Eyes remain vertically aligned with cover-uncover Vertical skew deviation = CENTRAL (w

nodes.title: Step 4: Bedside Hearing (HINTS+)
nodes.summary: HINTS+: new unilateral hearing loss = AICA stroke until proven otherwise — labyrinthine artery involvement, NOT labyrinthitis
nodes.body: HINTS+ (HINTS plus hearing) extends sensitivity by detecting AICA (anterior inferior cerebellar artery) strokes, which can present with unilateral hearing loss due to labyrinthine artery involvement. Technique: 1. Rub fingers together 6 inches from each ear 2. Ask patient if they hear it equally on both sides 3. Whisper a word at each ear 4. Compare both sides If abnormal available: Weber and Rinn

nodes.title: Peripheral HINTS → Vestibular Neuritis
nodes.summary: All HINTS peripheral: unidirectional nystagmus + abnormal HIT + no skew + normal hearing = vestibular neuritis. 100% sens is specialist data; untrained EPs achieve 83%
nodes.body: HINTS "INFARCT" mnemonic — remember the CENTRAL (stroke) pattern: • Impulse Normal • Fast-phase Alternating (direction-changing nystagmus) • Refixation on Cover Test (skew) Any of these findings = think INFARCT (central stroke), not peripheral. Peripheral (reassuring) is the opposite pattern — the one this patient has: unidirectional nystagmus + abnormal HIT (catch-up saccade) + no skew + normal h

nodes.title: Central HINTS → Stroke Pathway
nodes.summary: ANY central HINTS finding = posterior circulation stroke — vertebral dissection possible even in young patients, do not be reassured by age
nodes.body: ANY central finding in HINTS → posterior circulation stroke until proven otherwise. Central HINTS findings (any one of): • Direction-changing, vertical, or pure torsional nystagmus • Normal HIT (no catch-up saccade) in a patient with AVS • Vertical skew deviation • New unilateral hearing loss (HINTS+) Do NOT be reassured by young age. • Vertebral artery dissection can cause cerebellar stroke in pa

nodes.title: Vestibular Neuritis — Treatment
nodes.summary: Ondansetron preferred antiemetic, meclizine/diazepam max 72h — suppressants delay compensation, steroids controversial, antivirals not indicated
nodes.body: Supportive care is the mainstay. Vestibular neuritis resolves spontaneously over 1-2 weeks as central compensation develops. Symptom control (short-term only): • Ondansetron 4 mg IV/ODT q6-8h PRN nausea — preferred antiemetic (does not suppress vestibular compensation) • Meclizine 25 mg PO q8h PRN — maximum 72 hours (suppressants delay compensation) • Diazepam 2-5 mg PO/IV q8-12h PRN for severe re

nodes.title: Vestibular Migraine Criteria
nodes.summary: Vestibular migraine: >=5 episodes + migraine history + migrainous features in >=50% — 50% occur WITHOUT headache, most common recurrent vertigo cause
nodes.body: Vestibular Migraine Criteria Bárány Society / International Headache Society Criteria (Lempert 2012; reaffirmed with minor revision, Lempert 2022): Definite Vestibular Migraine requires ALL: 1. ≥5 episodes of vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours 2. Current or past history of migraine with or without aura (ICHD-3 criteria) 3. ≥50% of vestibular episodes

nodes.title: Meets Vestibular Migraine Criteria?
nodes.summary: Apply Barany criteria checklist — if not met, consider Meniere (requires hearing loss), posterior circulation TIA, panic, or arrhythmia
nodes.body: Apply the Bárány criteria to this patient: Criteria checklist: • ≥5 prior episodes of vertigo lasting 5 min-72 h? ☐ • Current or past migraine headache history (or family history)? ☐ • ≥50% of episodes have migraine features (headache, photophobia/phonophobia, aura)? ☐ • No alternative vestibular or neurologic diagnosis? ☐ Additional supportive features: • Female preponderance • Menstrual relation

nodes.title: Vestibular Migraine — Acute Treatment
nodes.summary: Acute VM: metoclopramide 10mg IV + diphenhydramine 25mg IV + ketorolac + IV fluids — triptans controversial, magnesium if aura history
nodes.body: Acute treatment parallels standard migraine care, with dopamine antagonists particularly useful due to the dual antiemetic and antimigraine effect. First-line (combine): • Metoclopramide 10 mg IV over 15 min • Diphenhydramine 25 mg IV — ⚠️ note the reason. nodes.title: s-EVS Risk — TIA Workup Needed?
nodes.summary: Assess TIA risk: age >=60, vascular risk factors, focal neuro symptoms, hearing loss, neck pain — recurrent TIAs herald large vessel stroke
nodes.body: Spontaneous episodic vertigo without migraine features raises concern for posterior circulation TIA, especially in vascular risk populations. nodes.title: Transient Vertigo — Low Risk
nodes.body: Disposition: Discharge with outpatient follow-up. Most likely etiologies in young, low-risk patients: • Vestibular migraine (often undiagnosed) • Post-concussive vestibular dysfunction • Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) • Anxiety-related vertigo • Mild medication side effect • Early Ménière (should have hearing symptoms) Outpatient plan: • Neurology referral — vestibular specialist

nodes.summary: Admit if: unable to tolerate PO, intractable vomiting, severe gait instability, elderly with comorbidities, or diagnostic uncertainty

nodes.title: Vestibular Medication Principles
nodes.summary: 72-hour rule: limit suppressants to acute phase only — ondansetron is vestibular-neutral, benzos/antihistamines delay compensation
nodes.body: Core principle: vestibular suppressants impair central compensation. The brain recovers from peripheral vestibular injury by remapping its reference frame — a process called central compensation. This requires sensory input and active movement. nodes.title: Vestibular Rehabilitation Guidance
nodes.summary: Vestibular PT is the single most effective intervention — early initiation improves outcomes, superior to medication long-term
nodes.body: Vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) is the single most effective intervention for persistent peripheral vestibular symptoms. nodes.title: Viral Myositis Assessment
nodes.summary: Age-based triage: pediatric BACM has excellent prognosis; adults higher rhabdomyolysis and AKI risk
nodes.body: Viral Myositis is an acute inflammatory condition of skeletal muscle following viral infection. In children, it typically presents as Benign Acute Childhood Myositis (BACM) with excellent prognosis. In adults, it may progress to rhabdomyolysis with potential for acute kidney injury. Common causative viruses: \u2022 Influenza A and B (most common) \u2022 Parainfluenza, RSV \u2022 Enteroviruses, Cox

nodes.title: Toxic / Ill-Appearing Patient
nodes.body: Patient appears systemically ill, suggesting severe viral myositis with potential rhabdomyolysis or alternative diagnosis. IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: \u2022 IV access, cardiac monitor \u2022 Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (NS at 10-20 mL/kg bolus) \u2022 Labs: CBC, CMP, CK, UA, myoglobin, lactate \u2022 ECG (hyperkalemia screening) RED FLAGS for Alternative Diagnoses: \u2022 Focal neurologic deficits (
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV fluid resuscitation and close monitoring. Consider ICU if hemodynamic instability, severe hyperkalemia, or respiratory compromise. Consult nephrology early if AKI present.

nodes.title: BACM Clinical Presentation
nodes.summary: BACM: bilateral calf pain, refusal to walk, post-viral prodrome in boys 5-9yo; resolves 3-5 days
nodes.body: Benign Acute Childhood Myositis (BACM): Typical presentation: \u2022 Age: Peak 5-9 years (range 2-14) \u2022 Sex: Male predominance (3:1) \u2022 Timing: 1-7 days after viral prodrome (often influenza) Classic Symptoms: \u2022 Sudden-onset bilateral calf pain (90%) \u2022 Refusal to walk or "duck waddle" gait \u2022 Calf tenderness to palpation \u2022 May have resolving URI symptoms Key Features: \

nodes.title: Exclude Serious Conditions
nodes.summary: Exclude GBS (ascending weakness), DVT (asymmetric), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis before diagnosing BACM
nodes.body: Before diagnosing BACM, exclude conditions requiring emergent management. RED FLAGS: \u2022 Asymmetric leg pain/swelling (DVT, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis) \u2022 Focal tenderness over bone (fracture, osteomyelitis) \u2022 Joint effusion/erythema (septic arthritis) \u2022 Abdominal pain + leg pain (psoas abscess, appendicitis) \u2022 Ascending weakness (Guillain-Barre syndrome) \u2022 Petechia

nodes.title: Adult Viral Myositis
nodes.summary: Adults: diffuse myalgias, proximal weakness; dark urine = myoglobinuria; higher AKI risk than children
nodes.body: Adult Viral Myositis: Unlike pediatric BACM, adults have higher risk of rhabdomyolysis and AKI. Common Presentation: \u2022 Diffuse myalgias (not limited to calves) \u2022 Proximal weakness (thighs, shoulders) \u2022 Muscle tenderness \u2022 May have ongoing fever/constitutional symptoms Associated Features: \u2022 Dark urine (myoglobinuria) - concerning sign \u2022 Decreased urine output \u2022 F

nodes.title: Adult Myositis Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess for rhabdomyolysis progression: dark urine, decreased UOP, severe weakness, concurrent statin use
nodes.body: Assess for features suggesting progression to rhabdomyolysis. Concerning Features: \u2022 Tea-colored or dark urine \u2022 Decreased urine output \u2022 Severe muscle pain/weakness \u2022 Inability to ambulate \u2022 Fever persisting >5 days \u2022 Concurrent statin/fibrate use Select the clinical picture:

nodes.title: BACM Laboratory Workup
nodes.summary: CK + UA minimum; CK does NOT correlate with severity in BACM; even massive CK rarely causes AKI in children

nodes.title: BACM CK Results
nodes.summary: Risk-stratify by CK level and UA myoglobin — dipstick blood+ with <5 RBCs on micro = myoglobinuria
nodes.body: Review CK level and urinalysis results. nodes.title: Mild Adult Myositis Workup
nodes.summary: Mild symptoms: CK, BMP, UA; if normal renal and CK <5000, supportive care and PO hydration at home

nodes.summary: Interpret mild adult labs: CK <5000 + normal renal = low risk; CK >10000 or AKI = rhabdomyolysis

nodes.title: BACM - Low Risk
nodes.body: Benign Acute Childhood Myositis - Low Risk CK <5,000 U/L with no myoglobinuria indicates excellent prognosis. Management: \u2022 Oral hydration encouraged (2-3x normal intake) \u2022 Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO q6-8h PRN for pain (max 400 mg/dose) \u2022 OR Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg PO q4-6h PRN \u2022 Rest with gradual return to activity Expected Course: \u2022 Symptoms resolve in 3-5 days \u2022 CK norma
nodes.recommendation: Discharge home with supportive care. No routine CK recheck needed. Follow-up PRN or if symptoms worsen.

nodes.title: BACM - Moderate CK Elevation
nodes.body: BACM with CK 5,000-10,000 U/L While still likely benign, higher CK warrants closer monitoring. Management Options: Option A - ED Observation (Preferred if concerns): \u2022 IV NS 10-20 mL/kg bolus, then maintenance + deficit \u2022 Repeat CK, BMP in 4-6 hours \u2022 If CK trending down and normal renal function: discharge Option B - Discharge with Close Follow-up: \u2022 Aggressive PO hydration \u
nodes.recommendation: Consider ED observation with IV hydration and CK recheck. If stable, may discharge with next-day CK recheck and strict return precautions.

nodes.title: BACM - High CK or Myoglobinuria
nodes.body: BACM with CK >10,000 U/L or Myoglobinuria Risk of rhabdomyolysis complications requires admission. Management: IV Fluid Resuscitation: \u2022 NS 20 mL/kg bolus \u2022 Then 1.5-2x maintenance rate \u2022 Goal: UOP 2-3 mL/kg/hr Monitoring: \u2022 Strict I/Os \u2022 Foley catheter if needed for accurate UOP \u2022 Serial CK q6-12h until downtrending \u2022 BMP q8-12h (monitor K+, creatinine) Consults
nodes.recommendation: Admit for IV fluid hydration and monitoring. Goal UOP 2-3 mL/kg/hr. Serial CK until downtrending. Most children do well even with very high CK.

nodes.title: Adult Myositis - Low Risk
nodes.body: Adult Viral Myositis - Low Risk CK <5,000 U/L with normal renal function. Outpatient Management: \u2022 Aggressive oral hydration (2-3 L/day) \u2022 Acetaminophen 650-1000 mg PO q6h PRN \u2022 OR Ibuprofen 400-600 mg PO q6-8h PRN \u2022 Avoid strenuous activity until symptoms resolve \u2022 Hold statins/fibrates temporarily (if applicable) If Influenza Confirmed: \u2022 Consider Oseltamivir 75 mg
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with supportive care and hydration. Consider oseltamivir if confirmed influenza <48h from onset. Follow-up with PCP in 3-5 days or sooner if worsening.

nodes.title: Adult Myositis - Moderate Risk
nodes.body: Adult Viral Myositis - Moderate Risk CK 5,000-10,000 U/L or mild creatinine elevation. ED Observation Recommended: \u2022 IV NS 1-2 L bolus \u2022 Then 150-200 mL/hr maintenance \u2022 Goal UOP >100 mL/hr (2 mL/kg/hr) \u2022 Recheck CK, BMP in 4-6 hours Discharge if: \u2022 CK stable or downtrending \u2022 Creatinine stable or improving \u2022 Tolerating PO \u2022 UOP adequate Admit if: \u2022 Ris
nodes.recommendation: ED observation with IV fluids. If improving after 4-6 hours, may discharge with 24-hour CK recheck. If any concerning trends, admit.

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis Management
nodes.summary: Myoglobin causes direct tubular toxicity and renal vasoconstriction — 21% AKI incidence in rhabdomyolysis
nodes.body: Rhabdomyolysis from Viral Myositis CK >10,000 U/L OR evidence of AKI OR myoglobinuria requires aggressive management. Pathophysiology: \u2022 Muscle cell necrosis releases myoglobin \u2022 Myoglobin precipitates in renal tubules \u2022 Direct tubular toxicity \u2022 Renal vasoconstriction \u2022 AKI can occur rapidly Complications: \u2022 AKI (21% incidence in rhabdomyolysis) \u2022 Hyperkalemia (

nodes.title: Rhabdomyolysis Treatment Protocol
nodes.body: IV Fluid Resuscitation: \u2022 NS 1-2 L bolus (adults) or 20 mL/kg (peds) \u2022 Then 200-300 mL/hr (or 3-5 mL/kg/hr peds) \u2022 Goal UOP: 200-300 mL/hr (adults) or 2-3 mL/kg/hr (peds) \u2022 May require 10-12 L in first 24 hours Electrolyte Management: \u2022 Hyperkalemia: Treat if K+ >6.0 or ECG changes - Calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilization - Insulin + dextrose, albuterol - Avo
nodes.recommendation: Admit to ICU or step-down. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation targeting UOP 200-300 mL/hr. Serial CK, BMP, and UOP monitoring. Early nephrology consult if AKI progressing.

nodes.title: Influenza-Associated Myositis
nodes.summary: Oseltamivir within 48h of onset; influenza B more associated with BACM than A; vaccination reduces incidence

nodes.summary: If high clinical suspicion persists despite normal imaging, consult neurosurgery — exam may be more reliable

Imaging suggesting malfunction: - Ventricular enlargement compared to baseline - New periventricular edema/hypodensity - Discontinuity, fracture, or kinking on shunt series - Catheter migration (proximal or distal) - Distal catheter in unexpected location (bowel, liver, chest) Imaging may be normal despite malfunction: - Intermittent obs

nodes.title: Shunt Infection Evaluation
nodes.summary: 90% of infections within 6 months of surgery; S. epidermidis most common; malfunction can be caused by infection
nodes.body: Infection vs Malfunction - differentiate these overlapping presentations. Shunt infection basics: - 5-12% annual incidence - 90% occur within 6 months of surgery/revision - Most common organism: Staphylococcus epidermidis - Other: S. aureus, gram-negative rods, Propionibacterium Clinical features suggesting infection: - Fever (but may be absent) - Wound erythema, swelling, drainage - Abdominal pai

nodes.title: Laboratory Workup for Infection
nodes.summary: Serum CBC/CRP/cultures; half of infected shunts have negative CSF cultures but positive hardware cultures

nodes.title: Shunt Infection Treatment
nodes.summary: IDSA empiric: vancomycin + cefepime/ceftazidime/meropenem; source control is central when hardware infection is suspected
nodes.body: Empiric antibiotic selection: cover coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, and gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas when healthcare-associated risk is present. IDSA empiric regimen: - Vancomycin IV, dosed by weight/renal function; adult serious infection target trough 15-20 mcg/mL if trough-based monitoring is used - PLUS an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam: - Cefepime IV - OR ceftazidime

Breathing: Maintain SpO2 >94%, avoid hypoxia 3.
