ICU admission indications: - Signs of herniation or elevated ICP - Hemodynamic instability - Post-operative monitoring - EVD in place - Confirmed infection requiring IV antibiotics - Declining neurologic status Floor admission: - Confirmed malfunction awaiting OR - Stable with mild symptoms, normal ICP - Ob

nodes.title: Observation Protocol
nodes.summary: Neuro checks q2-4h; minimum 24h observation; clear neurosurgery follow-up 24-72h before any discharge
nodes.body: Observation for suspected intermittent malfunction or normal imaging with clinical concern: Monitoring: - Neurologic checks every 2-4 hours - Serial vital signs (watch for Cushing response) - Repeat imaging if symptoms recur or worsen - Pain assessment and treatment Nursing alerts: - Any change in mental status - New headache or worsening of existing headache - New vomiting - Vital sign changes (b

nodes.title: ICU Management
nodes.summary: ICU: continuous tele, arterial line if unstable, ICP via EVD, avoid high PEEP, NPO for surgery prep
nodes.body: ICU management of VP shunt malfunction: Monitoring: - Continuous telemetry - Arterial line if hemodynamically unstable - Frequent neuro checks (q1-2h or per protocol) - ICP monitoring if EVD in place ICP management: - HOB elevation 30 degrees - Normothermia (treat fever aggressively) - Seizure prophylaxis if indicated - Continued hyperosmolar therapy as needed - EVD drainage per neurosurgery proto

nodes.title: Transfer to Neurosurgical Center
nodes.summary: Secure airway, begin HTS, physician-to-physician handoff; send imaging, labs, and intervention details
nodes.body: Preparation for transfer: Before transfer: - Secure airway if GCS <8 or declining - Establish IV access (two large-bore) - Begin hyperosmolar therapy if elevated ICP - Stabilize hemodynamics Documentation to send: - Complete H&P with neuro exam - All imaging (CT, shunt series) - Prior imaging for comparison if available - Shunt tap results if performed - Labs (CBC, BMP, coags) - List of interventi

nodes.title: VP Shunt Complications Summary
nodes.body: Key Takeaways: 1. High index of suspicion: - Pediatric shunts have high early complication and revision burden - Symptoms may be subtle or intermittent - Caregiver concern for "acting like previous malfunction" is valuable 2. Normal imaging does NOT exclude malfunction: - Chronically shunted ventricles may not dilate - Clinical assessment may be more reliable than imaging - Consult neurosurgery if
nodes.recommendation: Maintain high suspicion for shunt malfunction in any patient with VP shunt presenting with headache, vomiting, or altered mental status. Normal imaging does not exclude obstruction. Consult neurosurgery early. Use hypertonic saline for ICP

nodes.title: Wellens Syndrome
nodes.summary: Pain may be gone, troponin may be low, but anterior T-wave pattern can signal critical LAD stenosis.
nodes.body: Wellens syndrome = a pre-infarction LAD warning pattern. Plain English: the ECG can look "not that bad" because the pain has improved, but the LAD is often critically narrowed and can close again. Classic context: - Recent anginal chest pain, now pain-free or improved - Little or no ST elevation - Normal or only mildly elevated troponin - Characteristic anterior T-wave changes in V2-V3, often exte

nodes.title: Presentation
nodes.summary: Active ischemia gets active ACS pathway; pain-free recent angina is the classic Wellens trap.
nodes.body: How is the patient presenting now? Wellens is usually recognized after chest pain improves. Active pain, shock, STEMI, or refractory ischemia should be treated as active ACS/OMI, not a calm observation case.

nodes.title: Active ACS / Possible OMI
nodes.summary: Active ischemia overrides pattern recognition: manage as high-risk ACS/OMI.
nodes.body: Do not anchor on Wellens if the patient is actively ischemic. Immediate actions: - Repeat ECG now and compare with prior - Activate ACS pathway if STEMI/OMI or refractory ischemia - Aspirin 162-325 mg chewed - Anticoagulation per ACS protocol - High-intensity statin - Nitroglycerin if no contraindication - Cardiology/cath lab discussion now High-risk features: refractory pain, hemodynamic instabil
nodes.recommendation: Treat as active high-risk ACS/OMI. Do not delay for Wellens classification.

nodes.title: History Check
nodes.summary: Resolved angina is easy to miss. Ask directly before downgrading the ECG.
nodes.body: Ask specifically about recent angina. Patients may not volunteer resolved pain. Ask: - Any chest pressure, tightness, burning, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, or arm/jaw discomfort in the last days to weeks? - Did symptoms resolve before the ECG? - Any exertional pattern or crescendo episodes? - Any cocaine/stimulant use? - Prior ECG for comparison?

nodes.title: ECG Pattern
nodes.summary: Type A = biphasic V2-V3. Type B = deep symmetric anterior T-wave inversion.
nodes.body: Wellens ECG patterns: Type A: - Biphasic T waves in V2-V3 - Usually begins with positive deflection then terminal negativity - Less common, can evolve into Type B Type B: - Deep, symmetric T-wave inversion in V2-V3 - Often extends into V1-V6, I, aVL - More common Supportive criteria: - Isoelectric or minimally elevated ST segment, usually <1 mm - No pathologic precordial Q waves - Preserved R-wave

nodes.title: Does This Fit Wellens?
nodes.summary: Wellens is ECG plus resolved angina. Troponin can be unimpressive.
nodes.body: Wellens pattern requires ECG + story. High suspicion if ALL are present: - Recent angina, now pain-free or improved - Biphasic or deep symmetric T-wave inversion in V2-V3 - Minimal ST elevation, usually <1 mm - No pathologic precordial Q waves - Preserved R-wave progression - Troponin normal or mildly elevated only Does the ECG/story fit?

nodes.title: High Suspicion Wellens
nodes.summary: High-risk NSTE-ACS equivalent: aspirin, anticoagulation, statin, telemetry, cardiology, no stress test.
nodes.body: Treat as high-risk NSTE-ACS / LAD reperfusion warning. Immediate actions: - Aspirin 162-325 mg chewed - Anticoagulation per NSTE-ACS protocol unless contraindicated - High-intensity statin - Nitroglycerin for recurrent pain if no contraindication - Continuous telemetry - Serial ECGs and troponins - Cardiology consultation for early invasive evaluation Do NOT: - Do NOT discharge because pain resolv
nodes.recommendation: Admit, monitor, and involve cardiology for invasive evaluation. Avoid stress testing.

nodes.title: No Stress Test
nodes.summary: Stress testing can convert a warning ECG into anterior MI.
nodes.body: Do NOT stress test suspected Wellens syndrome. Plain English: stress testing asks the heart to work harder when the LAD may already be barely open. Analogy: it is like flooring the gas pedal while a bridge ahead is cracked. Why: - The pattern suggests critical LAD stenosis or unstable reperfusion - Stress testing can precipitate MI, malignant arrhythmia, or death - The safer next test is coronary

nodes.title: Initial Management
nodes.summary: Treat as high-risk NSTE-ACS, but coordinate P2Y12 timing with cardiology.
nodes.body: Initial ED management mirrors high-risk NSTE-ACS. Core treatments: - Aspirin 162-325 mg chewed - Anticoagulation: UFH or enoxaparin per local ACS pathway - High-intensity statin, e.g. atorvastatin 80 mg PO - Nitroglycerin for recurrent pain if no hypotension, RV infarct, or recent PDE-5 inhibitor - Beta blocker only if appropriate and no acute HF/shock/bradycardia P2Y12 loading: - Follow local car

nodes.title: Cath Strategy
nodes.summary: Classic stable Wellens is not low risk. It still needs early invasive planning.
nodes.body: How urgent is the cath discussion? Wellens usually needs early invasive evaluation. Emergent cath depends on active ischemia or instability.

nodes.title: Urgent Cath Discussion
nodes.summary: Recurrent symptoms or instability turns Wellens into an immediate cath conversation.
nodes.body: Call cardiology/cath lab now. Triggers: - Recurrent or refractory ischemic pain - Hemodynamic instability - VT/VF or malignant arrhythmia - Acute heart failure/pulmonary edema - Dynamic ST elevation/depression - Concern for active LAD occlusion Continue: aspirin, anticoagulation, statin, telemetry, repeat ECGs.
nodes.recommendation: Immediate cardiology/cath lab discussion. Manage as active high-risk ACS.

nodes.title: Early Invasive Pathway
nodes.summary: Pain-free does not mean safe. Stable classic Wellens still needs monitored admission and early invasive evaluation.
nodes.body: Stable classic Wellens: admit for early invasive evaluation. Recommended approach: - Telemetry admission - Cardiology consult from ED - Coronary angiography planning, often within 24 hours depending on local pathway and risk features - Continue ACS medical therapy - No stress testing before coronary anatomy is addressed Why: a normal or low troponin does not make this low risk.
nodes.recommendation: Admit to monitored setting with cardiology-directed invasive evaluation. Do not stress test.

nodes.title: Serial ECG Strategy
nodes.summary: Wellens can be dynamic. Serial ECGs matter more than a single reassuring troponin.
nodes.body: Use serial ECGs to catch dynamic LAD reperfusion/re-occlusion. Do: - Repeat ECG with any symptom recurrence - Repeat ECG in 15-30 min if uncertain or evolving - Compare with old ECGs - Look for evolution from biphasic T waves to deep inversion - Look for conversion to anterior STEMI/OMI If ECG evolves or symptoms recur: - Upgrade to urgent cath discussion - Do not wait for the next troponin

nodes.title: Troponin Trap
nodes.summary: A low troponin does not clear a classic Wellens ECG.
nodes.body: Troponin may be normal or only mildly elevated. Plain English: the artery may have almost closed, then reopened before the blood test showed major damage. Analogy: the smoke alarm chirped before the house caught fire. Do not downgrade if: - Pain resolved - First troponin is negative - Vital signs are stable - ECG has classic Wellens pattern Use troponin for risk and trend, not to dismiss the ECG.

nodes.title: Mimics / Pseudo-Wellens
nodes.summary: Mimics exist, but diagnostic uncertainty should not create a low-risk discharge.
nodes.body: Anterior T-wave inversion is not always Wellens. Important mimics: - LVH/strain - PE or RV strain - CNS catastrophe - Takotsubo cardiomyopathy - Myocarditis/pericarditis - Cocaine/stimulant vasospasm - Electrolyte abnormalities - Persistent juvenile T-wave pattern - Post-tachycardia or memory T waves Pseudo-Wellens still may be dangerous. If the history is ischemic or ECG is dynamic, keep ACS/card

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Classic Wellens needs monitored admission and cardiology, not discharge.
nodes.body: Disposition depends on risk, but classic Wellens is not an outpatient diagnosis.

nodes.title: Admit: Monitored ACS Pathway
nodes.summary: Use explicit handoff language to prevent accidental stress testing or discharge.
nodes.body: Admit to telemetry/stepdown per local ACS pathway. Handoff language: "Concern for Wellens syndrome: recent angina with anterior biphasic/deep T-wave inversion. Pain improved and troponin may be low, but this is high-risk LAD disease. No stress test. Needs cardiology and invasive evaluation." Orders/plan: - Telemetry - Serial ECGs/troponins - ACS medical therapy - Cardiology consult - NPO if cath a
nodes.recommendation: Admit monitored. Cardiology consult. No stress testing.

nodes.title: Observation / Diagnostic Uncertainty
nodes.summary: Uncertain anterior T-wave inversion deserves observation and comparison, not reflex discharge.
nodes.body: If not classic but concerning, observe rather than discharge. Minimum: - Serial ECGs and troponins - Compare prior ECG - Consider echo for wall motion abnormality - Cardiology input if ECG remains concerning - Avoid stress test until Wellens is reasonably excluded Escalate immediately if: - Pain recurs - ECG evolves - Troponin rises - New wall motion abnormality - Hemodynamic instability
nodes.recommendation: Observe with serial ECGs/troponins and low threshold for cardiology. Avoid stress test until Wellens is excluded.

nodes.title: Wide Complex Tachycardia
nodes.summary: WCT = QRS >120ms + rate >100. 80% is VT baseline, 98% if prior MI. Stability does NOT differentiate.
nodes.body: WCT Decision Summary Definition: QRS >120ms + rate >100 bpm The Golden Rule: Wide + regular = VT until proven otherwise Pre-test probability of VT: • Baseline WCT: 80% VT • Age >35: 85% VT • Structural heart disease: >90% VT • History of MI: 98% VT ⚠️ Hemodynamic stability does NOT differentiate VT from SVT — stable VT is common and does NOT rule out VT.

nodes.title: Sodium Channel Blockade Screen
nodes.summary: Objective ECG screen for sodium channel blockade BEFORE any antiarrhythmic — wide-for-rate, wide+slow, aVR findings, P waves, tox context.
nodes.body: Look at the tracing before you decide what this is. This screen is intentionally placed ahead of everything else, because the single most dangerous error in wide complex tachycardia is giving procainamide to a patient who is already sodium-channel blocked by a drug. Procainamide is itself a sodium channel blocker. You do NOT need to suspect poisoning to answer this. Answer from the ECG in your han

nodes.title: Special Population Screen
nodes.summary: Screen for special populations: sodium channel blocker OD, hyperkalemia, WPW — different treatment
nodes.body: Is this a toxicologic or metabolic cause? Suspect if: • Known overdose (TCA, diphenhydramine, cocaine, flecainide) • Peaked T waves (hyperkalemia) • Known WPW + irregular rhythm • QRS widening from baseline

nodes.title: Which Special Population?
nodes.summary: Branch based on suspected special population: sodium channel blocker, hyperK, or WPW+AFib
nodes.body: Select the suspected etiology:

nodes.title: Sodium Channel Blockade — Diagnostic Criteria
nodes.summary: Criteria for drug-induced sodium channel blockade: aVR R ≥3mm (81%/73%), R/S >0.7 (NPV 95%), QRS change from baseline. Brugada/Vereckei never validated in poisoning.
nodes.body: What you are looking for: a wide complex tachycardia caused by a drug blocking the cardiac fast sodium channel, rather than by a ventricular focus. The distinction matters because it flips the treatment to its opposite. --- ### The drugs that do this The American Heart Association 2023 poisoning update names these sodium channel blockers: • Tricyclic and tetracyclic antidepressants (TCAs) — amitri

nodes.title: Sodium Channel Blockade — Your Read
nodes.summary: Break ties toward bicarbonate: bicarb in VT is reversible, procainamide in poisoning stacks a second blockade.
nodes.body: Having worked through the criteria, how does this rhythm read? If you are genuinely torn, choose "Cannot exclude it." The two errors are not equal: • Sodium bicarbonate given to a ventricular tachycardia patient — a monitored, reversible sodium and pH load. • Procainamide given to a poisoned patient — stacks a second sodium channel blockade onto a conduction system that is already failing. A QRS t

nodes.title: Sodium Channel Blockade — Treatment
nodes.summary: Bicarb 50-150 mEq IV push (1-3 mEq/kg peds), repeat q3-5min; infusion 150 mEq/L at 1-3 mL/kg/h. Hard stops pH 7.55, Na 155. NO procainamide or amiodarone.
nodes.body: 🛑 DO NOT GIVE PROCAINAMIDE. It is a Vaughan-Williams class Ia sodium channel blocker. Giving it here adds a second blockade to a conduction system already poisoned by the first. 🛑 DO NOT GIVE AMIODARONE. It carries sodium channel blocking activity alongside its other effects. --- ### Sodium bicarbonate — the treatment Bolus: Sodium Bicarbonate 50–150 mEq intravenous push in an adult; 1–3 mEq/kg

nodes.title: Response to Sodium Bicarbonate
nodes.summary: A QRS that narrows after bicarbonate is diagnostic. No response = escalate before hitting pH/sodium ceilings.
nodes.body: Re-read the ECG 3–5 minutes after each bolus. A QRS that narrows after bicarbonate is itself diagnostic — it confirms sodium channel blockade, and it is a much safer diagnostic test than committing to procainamide. What happened?

nodes.title: Refractory Sodium Channel Blockade
nodes.summary: Refractory: lidocaine (2a cocaine, 2b class Ia/Ic), lipid emulsion (1 for local anesthetic, 2b refractory SCB, 3 for BB/CCB), VA-ECMO 2a. Dialysis NOT recommended (EXTRIP 1D).
nodes.body: First, confirm this is genuinely refractory. Have you actually given adequate bicarbonate, and have the pH and sodium not yet reached the hard stops (pH 7.55, sodium 155 mEq/L)? Refractory means refractory to *adequate* therapy. --- ### Lidocaine — yes, genuinely, and this is a change from older teaching This is counterintuitive, so read it carefully. Lidocaine is a Vaughan-Williams class Ib sodiu

nodes.title: Three Mimics of Drug-Induced Sodium Channel Blockade
nodes.summary: Mimics: hyperkalemia (send a K+, ECG unreliable), hypothermia (core temp, Osborn wave), pre-excited AF (irregular + fast — procainamide IS correct there).
nodes.body: A wide, slow rhythm has three common non-toxicologic causes that look nearly identical on the tracing. Send the tests — the ECG cannot reliably sort them. --- ### 1. Hyperkalemia Peaked T waves, flattened or absent P waves, progressive QRS widening toward a sine wave. Think renal failure, a missed dialysis session, crush injury, or a potassium-sparing medication. ⚠️ Do not rely on the ECG to detec

nodes.title: After Bicarbonate — Monitoring and Disposition
nodes.summary: Bicarb competes, does not remove drug — QRS can rebound. Continue infusion, ICU admission, serial ECGs. One normal ECG is not a clearance.
nodes.body: The QRS narrowed. You are not finished. Sodium bicarbonate does not remove the drug — it competes with it at the channel. As the bolus wears off, or as more drug is absorbed from the gut, the QRS can widen again. ### Continue • Keep the bicarbonate infusion running (150 mEq/L at 1–3 mL/kg/h). Do not stop it because the QRS looks better. • Continuous cardiac monitoring, with a repeat 12-lead ECG at

nodes.title: Hyperkalemic WCT
nodes.summary: Hyperkalemic WCT: calcium first (membrane stabilization), then insulin/glucose + albuterol, HD if severe
nodes.body: Treatment priority: membrane stabilization Calcium (immediate): • Calcium gluconate 3g IV over 10 min • OR Calcium chloride 1g IV (central line preferred) • May repeat in 5 min if no ECG improvement Shift potassium: • Regular insulin IV — dose by hypoglycemia risk. Give WITH 25 g dextrose (D50 50 mL) unless glucose >250 mg/dL - 5 units (or 0.1 units/kg, max 10) — eGFR <60, dialysis-dependent, pre-

nodes.title: WPW + AFib (Pre-excited AFib)
nodes.summary: WPW+AFib: NO adenosine, CCB, BB, or digoxin (lethal). Treat with cardioversion or procainamide.
nodes.body: 🛑 AV nodal blockers ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED: • Adenosine • Diltiazem / Verapamil • Beta-blockers • Digoxin Why deadly: Block AV node → all conduction goes down accessory pathway → VF ECG Clues: • Irregular WCT • Very fast rate (often >200 bpm) • Varying QRS width • Delta waves visible in some beats Treatment: • Unstable: Synchronized cardioversion 200J • Stable: Procainamide 20-50 mg/min IV •

nodes.title: Hemodynamic Stability
nodes.summary: Unstable = SBP <90, AMS, ischemia, or shock → immediate cardioversion
nodes.body: Is the patient hemodynamically unstable? Unstable criteria (any): • SBP <90 mmHg • Altered mental status • Ischemic chest pain • Acute pulmonary edema / shock

nodes.title: Unstable WCT — Cardioversion
nodes.summary: Unstable WCT: synchronized cardioversion 100J → 200J → 360J. Sedate if time. If pulseless, unsync shock.
nodes.body: Immediate synchronized cardioversion: • 100J → 200J → 360J (biphasic) • Confirm sync mode enabled • If sync fails to track → unsync shock Sedation (if time permits): • Midazolam 2-5 mg IV, OR • Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV, OR • Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV ⚠️ If deteriorates to pulseless: → Unsynchronized shock 200J immediately → Begin ACLS arrest protocol Post-cardioversion: • 12-lead ECG • Electrolytes (K+,

nodes.title: Pre-test Probability
nodes.summary: Age >35, prior MI, structural heart disease = high probability VT (85-98%). Treat as VT.
nodes.body: Does the patient have high pre-test probability of VT? High probability (treat as VT): • Age >35 years (85% VT) • History of MI (98% VT) • Known structural heart disease • Prior VT or has ICD • New symptoms began post-MI

nodes.title: Treating as VT
nodes.summary: High pre-test probability: treat as VT. VT treatments safe for SVT; SVT treatments may kill VT patient.
nodes.body: High pre-test probability → treat as VT This is the safe approach: • VT treatments (procainamide, cardioversion) are safe for SVT • SVT treatments (adenosine, CCB) can be lethal for VT Proceed to VT treatment without diagnostic delay.

nodes.title: Prior ECG Comparison
nodes.summary: If prior ECG shows same wide QRS in sinus, suggests pre-existing BBB (SVT). Otherwise assume VT.
nodes.body: Is a prior ECG available showing the same QRS morphology in sinus rhythm?

nodes.title: QRS Match — Possible SVT
nodes.summary: Matching prior QRS suggests SVT+BBB, but VT still possible. Proceed with caution, treat as VT if doubt.
nodes.body: Prior ECG shows same wide QRS morphology in sinus rhythm This suggests SVT with pre-existing bundle branch block. However: • VT can still occur in patients with BBB • If ANY doubt, treat as VT • May consider diagnostic adenosine trial (with caution) Proceed to diagnostic algorithms or empiric VT treatment.

nodes.title: Pathognomonic VT Features
nodes.summary: Pathognomonic VT: AV dissociation, fusion beats, capture beats. If present = confirmed VT.
nodes.body: If ANY of these present → confirms VT: AV dissociation: • P waves at different rate than QRS • Classic finding, highly specific Fusion beats: • Hybrid complex (sinus + ventricular origin) • QRS morphology intermediate between normal and VT Capture beats: • Narrow QRS "captured" during wide complex tachycardia • Sinus impulse reaches ventricles between VT beats ⚠️ Absence of these does NOT rule out

nodes.title: High Specificity VT Features
nodes.summary: VT features: QRS >140-160ms, extreme axis, concordance across precordials, slurred QRS onset.
nodes.body: Features highly suggestive of VT: QRS duration: • >140ms (RBBB pattern) → favors VT • >160ms (LBBB pattern) → favors VT Axis: • Extreme axis deviation ("northwest axis") • Positive aVR, negative I and aVF Concordance: • ALL precordial leads positive (R waves), OR • ALL precordial leads negative (S waves) QRS onset: • >40ms to first peak • Slurred/notched initial deflection

nodes.title: Diagnostic Algorithm
nodes.summary: Choose Brugada (precordial) or Vereckei (aVR only) algorithm, or skip and treat as VT.
nodes.body: Which algorithm would you like to apply? Note: Algorithms help differentiate VT vs SVT but have imperfect accuracy. When in doubt, treat as VT.

nodes.title: Brugada Algorithm
nodes.summary: Brugada: 4 steps — no RS in precordials, RS >100ms, AV dissociation, morphology criteria. Any YES = VT.
nodes.body: Step-by-step (stop if YES at any step = VT): Step 1: Absence of RS complex in ALL precordial leads (V1-V6)? • All monophasic = VT Step 2: RS interval >100ms in any precordial lead? • Measure R onset to S nadir • >100ms = VT Step 3: AV dissociation present? • P waves at different rate = VT Step 4: Morphology criteria (V1 and V6): • RBBB pattern: Tall left rabbit ear in V1, or QS/rS in V6 = VT • LBB

nodes.title: Brugada Result
nodes.summary: Any Brugada step positive = VT. All negative suggests SVT. Uncertain = treat as VT.
nodes.body: What was the Brugada algorithm result?

nodes.title: Vereckei aVR Algorithm
nodes.summary: Vereckei: aVR only — initial R, initial r/q >40ms, notched downstroke, Vi/Vt ≤1. Any YES = VT.
nodes.body: Analyze lead aVR only (faster than Brugada): Step 1: Initial dominant R wave in aVR? • YES = VT Step 2: Initial r or q wave width >40ms? • YES = VT Step 3: Notching on initial downstroke of predominantly negative QRS? • YES = VT Step 4: Vi/Vt ratio ≤1? • Vi = vertical excursion in initial 40ms • Vt = vertical excursion in terminal 40ms • Ratio ≤1 = VT If all 4 steps NO → suggests SVT ⏱️ Faster tha

nodes.title: Vereckei Result
nodes.summary: Any Vereckei step positive = VT. All negative suggests SVT. Uncertain = treat as VT.
nodes.body: What was the Vereckei aVR algorithm result?

nodes.title: VT Morphology
nodes.summary: Monomorphic = stable QRS; polymorphic = varying. Polymorphic requires QTc check for Torsades.
nodes.body: Is the VT monomorphic or polymorphic? Monomorphic: Same QRS shape beat-to-beat Polymorphic: Varying QRS shape/axis

nodes.title: Before Procainamide — Sodium Channel Blockade Check
nodes.summary: Hard gate before procainamide: exposure history, QRS ≥160 at rate <130, aVR findings, QRS widening from baseline, tox context. Any hit = bicarbonate instead.
nodes.body: 🛑 Stop for ten seconds before you push this drug. Procainamide is itself a Vaughan-Williams class Ia sodium channel blocker. If this wide QRS is caused by a drug blocking that same channel, procainamide stacks a second blockade onto a conduction system that is already failing, and can precipitate asystole. This is the single most dangerous error available in wide complex tachycardia. Re-check all

nodes.title: Stable Monomorphic VT Treatment
nodes.summary: Stable monomorphic VT: procainamide 20-50 mg/min (PROCAMIO superior to amio). Stop if QRS widens >50%.
nodes.body: First-line: Procainamide (PROCAMIO trial — superior to amiodarone) • Procainamide 20-50 mg/min IV • OR 10 mg/kg over 20 min • Max: 17 mg/kg total 🛑 STOP infusion if: • QRS widens >50% from baseline • Hypotension develops • Arrhythmia terminates PROCAMIO results: 67% termination vs 38% amiodarone, fewer adverse events (9% vs 41%) Alternative: Amiodarone • Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min • Then 1

nodes.title: Response to Treatment
nodes.summary: If VT converts with antiarrhythmic, proceed to post-conversion care. If refractory, cardiovert.
nodes.body: Did the VT convert with antiarrhythmic therapy?

nodes.title: Cardioversion for Refractory VT
nodes.summary: Refractory VT: synchronized cardioversion 100J → 200J → 360J. Sedate. Confirm sync mode.
nodes.body: Synchronized cardioversion: • 100J → 200J → 360J (biphasic) • Sedate if patient conscious Sedation options: • Midazolam 2-5 mg IV • Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV • Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV ⚠️ Confirm sync mode — unsynchronized shock may land on T wave and induce VF If still refractory: • Consider overdrive pacing • EP consult urgently • Search for reversible triggers (ischemia, electrolytes)

nodes.title: Polymorphic VT — QTc Check
nodes.summary: Polymorphic VT: check QTc. Prolonged = Torsades (magnesium). Normal = ischemia (treat ACS).
nodes.body: What is the baseline QTc (from prior ECG or post-conversion)? Prolonged QTc: >480-500ms Normal QTc: <460ms (men), <470ms (women)

nodes.title: Torsades de Pointes
nodes.summary: Torsades: magnesium 2g IV then infusion. NO amiodarone/procainamide (prolong QT). Overdrive pace if recurrent.
nodes.body: 🛑 DO NOT give amiodarone or procainamide — They prolong QT → worsen Torsades → may be lethal Treatment: • Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 5-15 min, repeat 2 g at 5-15 min if it persists • Can push over 1-2 min in arrest • Then start a continuous infusion — a bolus alone wears off and TdP recurs If recurrent: • Overdrive pacing to 90-110 bpm (shortens QT) • Isoproterenol if pacing unavailable (2-10

nodes.title: Polymorphic VT — Normal QTc
nodes.summary: Polymorphic VT + normal QT = likely ischemia. Treat as ACS, cath lab. Amiodarone OK here.
nodes.body: Polymorphic VT with normal QT = likely ischemia Treatment: • Treat as acute coronary syndrome • Emergent cardiology consult • Cath lab activation Antiarrhythmic: • Beta-blockers may suppress catecholamine-driven VT • Amiodarone acceptable (QT not prolonged) • Lidocaine alternative Supportive: • Aggressive electrolyte correction (K+ >4.0, Mg2+ >2.0) • Continuous telemetry • Prepare for cardioversio

nodes.title: Possible SVT with Aberrancy
nodes.summary: If algorithm suggests SVT and regular rhythm: adenosine 6mg → 12mg → 12mg. Any doubt = treat as VT.
nodes.body: Algorithm suggests SVT — but proceed with caution Before adenosine, confirm: • Regular rhythm (NOT irregular) • No pre-excitation / WPW suspected • Not polymorphic WCT ⚠️ If ANY doubt → treat as VT Adenosine trial: • Adenosine 6 mg IV rapid push → 12 mg → 12 mg • Follow with 20 mL NS flush • Record continuous rhythm strip Outcomes: • Converts → confirms SVT • Unmasks underlying rhythm → treat acco

nodes.title: Adenosine Response
nodes.summary: Adenosine converts = SVT. Unmasks AFib/flutter = underlying atrial arrhythmia. No effect = likely VT.
nodes.body: What was the response to adenosine?

nodes.title: Confirmed SVT
nodes.summary: Confirmed SVT: rate/rhythm control, workup, may discharge if stable with cardiology follow-up.
nodes.body: Rhythm confirmed as SVT with aberrancy For recurrence prevention: • Rate control: diltiazem, metoprolol • Rhythm control: discuss with cardiology Workup: • 12-lead ECG in sinus • Echocardiogram • Electrolytes • TSH Disposition: • May discharge if first episode, hemodynamically stable • Cardiology follow-up within 1-2 weeks • Return precautions for recurrence, syncope, chest pain

nodes.title: Post-Conversion Care
nodes.summary: Post-conversion: 12-lead, lytes (K >4, Mg >2), troponin, maintenance antiarrhythmic, identify trigger.
nodes.body: Immediate post-conversion checklist: • 12-lead ECG (compare to prior) • Electrolytes: K+ target >4.0, Mg2+ target >2.0 • Troponin (ischemic trigger?) • BNP if heart failure suspected Maintenance antiarrhythmic: • Continue amiodarone infusion if used • OR procainamide infusion 1-4 mg/min Identify trigger: • Ischemia (most common) • Electrolyte abnormality • Drug-induced (cocaine, digoxin, QT-prolon

nodes.title: Disposition
nodes.summary: Admit ALL VT to ICU/tele. EP consult if EF ≤35%, arrest survivor, recurrent. Echo required.
nodes.body: Admit ALL VT patients • ICU or telemetry with continuous monitoring • Minimum 48 hours observation • Cardiology consult EP consultation for: • EF ≤35% (ICD candidate) • Survived VT arrest • Recurrent VT • Consider catheter ablation for monomorphic VT Echo required for: • All new VT • Assess EF, wall motion, structural disease 🛑 DO NOT discharge first-episode VT from ED

nodes.title: Rare Discharge Exceptions
nodes.summary: Discharge rare: functioning ICD with device interrogation OR known benign idiopathic VT + EP approval.
nodes.body: May consider discharge ONLY if ALL criteria met: • Properly functioning AICD with appropriate therapy • Device interrogation completed • Cardiology/EP discussion and approval • Patient has close follow-up arranged OR: • Known idiopathic VT (e.g., RVOT VT) • Prior documentation of benign pattern • Cardiologist approval for outpatient management • Reliable patient with clear return precautions ⚠️ Wh

nodes.title: WCT Management Complete

nodes.title: Xylazine Toxicity — Initial Assessment
nodes.summary: Alpha-2 agonist NOT reversed by naloxone — medetomidine now 72% of Philly supply (10x more potent than xylazine)
nodes.body: Xylazine Quick Reference — key facts at a glance. What is Xylazine ("Tranq")? • Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (same class as clonidine, dexmedetomidine) • FDA-approved for veterinary use ONLY — not approved for humans The epidemic (2025 update): • MEDETOMIDINE now dominant in some markets — detected in 72% of Philadelphia samples (Oct-Dec 2024), while xylazine dropped from 98% to 31% [8] • Medetomidi

nodes.title: Xylazine Quick Reference
nodes.summary: Half-life 23-50min; not detected on standard UDS; no antidote exists; prolonged sedation despite naloxone
nodes.body: Mechanism: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (central sympatholysis) Street names: Tranq, Tranq dope, Sleep cut, Zombie drug NOT detected by: Standard urine drug screen Detected by: GC-MS, LC-MS (7-8 day turnaround), lateral flow test strips Half-life: 23-50 minutes IV, longer with IM/SC Key clinical features: • Prolonged sedation DESPITE naloxone • Bradycardia + hypotension • Hypothermia • Hyperglycemia

nodes.title: OA2A Toxidrome
nodes.summary: OA2A: naloxone improves respirations BUT patient stays sedated — bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia common
nodes.body: OA2A = Opioid + Alpha-2 Agonist — the combined toxidrome of fentanyl + xylazine [1]. Tranq vs Opioid Withdrawal | Finding | Pure Opioid | OA2A (Xylazine + Opioid) | |---------|-------------|---------------------------| | Miosis | ✓ | ✓ | | Sedation | ✓ | ✓ (prolonged) | | Respiratory depression | ✓ | ✓ | | Naloxone response | Full arousal | Respirations improve, stays sedated | | Bradycardia | Rar

nodes.title: Respiratory Assessment
nodes.summary: Xylazine + opioid = synergistic respiratory depression — assess airway/breathing first priority
nodes.body: First priority: Assess airway and breathing. Xylazine + opioid = synergistic respiratory depression • Both cause CNS depression • Xylazine alone rarely causes apnea • Combined with fentanyl → profound respiratory failure [1] What is the respiratory status?

nodes.title: Naloxone Administration
nodes.summary: Titrate naloxone to RR >12, NOT wakefulness — excess naloxone risks withdrawal with aspiration in sedated patient
nodes.body: STILL GIVE NALOXONE — 95% of xylazine ODs involve fentanyl [1][2] Naloxone Dosing Reference Critical difference from pure opioid OD: > Titrate to adequate respiratory rate, NOT wakefulness EMCrit warning [1]: > "Avoid excessive naloxone dosing. High naloxone could provoke opioid withdrawal in a patient who remains sedated by alpha-2 agonists, leading to emesis with aspiration." Dosing: | Route | D

nodes.title: Naloxone Response
nodes.summary: Full arousal = pure opioid; improved breathing but sedated = OA2A; no response to 10mg = non-opioid cause
nodes.body: Assessing response to naloxone: Pure opioid OD: Respirations improve AND patient wakes up OA2A toxidrome: Respirations improve BUT patient stays sedated If no response to 10mg total naloxone: • Consider non-opioid cause • May need airway protection regardless [1] How did the patient respond?

nodes.title: Airway Management
nodes.summary: Recovery position if breathing; BVM for rescue breaths; intubate if persistent apnea, GCS <8, or refractory hypoxia
nodes.body: Indications for intubation: • Persistent apnea despite naloxone • GCS <8 with aspiration risk • Copious secretions/emesis • Refractory hypoxia [1] Airway approach: 1. Position in recovery position if spontaneous respirations 2. Bag-valve mask — rescue breaths especially helpful 3. Supplemental O₂ via NC or NRB 4. Intubation if above criteria met Post-intubation considerations: • Continue supportiv

nodes.title: Cardiovascular Assessment
nodes.summary: Initial peripheral vasoconstriction then central sympatholysis — expect bradycardia + hypotension
nodes.body: Xylazine cardiovascular effects [1][2]: Mechanism: 1. Initial: Peripheral alpha-2B activation → vasoconstriction → transient hypertension 2. Then: Central alpha-2A activation → reduced NE release → bradycardia + hypotension Expected findings: • HR 40-60 bpm (bradycardia) • SBP 80-100 (hypotension) • Possible QTc prolongation What cardiovascular findings are present?

nodes.title: Hypotension Management
nodes.summary: NS/LR bolus first-line; NE for refractory hypotension; avoid pure alpha agonists — worsen tissue perfusion
nodes.body: First-line: Volume resuscitation [1] • Normal saline or Lactated Ringer's • 500-1000 mL bolus • Often sufficient for mild-moderate hypotension Refractory hypotension: • Norepinephrine 0.1-0.3 mcg/kg/min • Start low — underlying vasoconstriction may be present Caution: Alpha-2 agonism causes vasoconstriction peripherally — pure alpha agonists may worsen tissue perfusion. NE preferred over phenyleph

nodes.title: Bradycardia Management
nodes.summary: Avoid atropine — risk of hypertensive crisis from unopposed vasoconstriction; dobutamine preferred if treatment needed
nodes.body: EMCrit approach (preferred) [1]: • Bradycardia often does NOT require treatment • Avoid atropine — difficult to titrate, risk of hypertensive crisis from unopposed vasoconstriction If symptomatic (hypotension, AMS, chest pain): | Option | Dose | Notes | |--------|------|-------| | Observation | — | Preferred if stable | | Dobutamine | 2.5-10 mcg/kg/min | Inodilator, titratable | | Isoproterenol |

nodes.title: Monitoring Parameters
nodes.summary: Monitor SpO2, telemetry, temperature, glucose; minimum 4-6h post-naloxone; no antidote exists for xylazine
nodes.body: Standard monitoring: • Continuous pulse oximetry • Cardiac telemetry • Temperature (hypothermia common) • Glucose (hyperglycemia common) • ECG at baseline (QTc) Labs: • BMP (glucose, renal function) • VBG/ABG if concern for hypoperfusion • Lactate • Consider troponin if chest pain Duration: • Minimum 4-6 hours post-naloxone • Longer if xylazine confirmed/suspected • Watch for delayed wound complic

nodes.title: Xylazine Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Symptoms begin 4-6h after last use (faster than opioids); no GI symptoms; buprenorphine does NOT treat it
nodes.body: Timeline: Symptoms begin 4-6 hours after last use (faster than opioid withdrawal) Tranq vs Opioid Withdrawal Comparison Xylazine/medetomidine withdrawal symptoms (NOT reversed by opioids): • Anxiety, irritability, restlessness, dysphoria • Tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension • No GI symptoms (unlike opioid withdrawal) Key difference from opioid withdrawal: • Buprenorphine/methadone do NOT treat

nodes.title: Xylazine vs Opioid Withdrawal
nodes.summary: Key difference: opioid withdrawal has GI symptoms and mydriasis; xylazine does not; clonidine treats both
nodes.body: Comparison Table: | Symptom | Opioid Withdrawal | Xylazine Withdrawal | |---------|-------------------|---------------------| | Onset | 8-24h (short-acting) | 8-24h | | Duration | 5-7 days | 3-5 days | | Anxiety/Restlessness | ✓ | ✓ | | Tachycardia | ✓ | ✓ | | Hypertension | ✓ | ✓ | | Diaphoresis | ✓ | ✓ | | Nausea/Vomiting | ✓ | ✗ | | Diarrhea | ✓ | ✗ | | Piloerection | ✓ | ✗ | | Yawning/Lacrimat

nodes.title: Xylazine Withdrawal Treatment
nodes.summary: Clonidine 0.1-0.3mg PO q4-6h first-line; hold if SBP <90 or HR <50; dex for severe ICU cases
nodes.body: No FDA-approved medications — alpha-2 agonists are first-line empirically [1][5] Treatment Protocol: | Medication | Dose | Notes | |------------|------|-------| | Clonidine | 0.1-0.3 mg PO q4-6h | First-line. Hold if SBP <90, HR <50 | | Dexmedetomidine | 0.2-1.4 mcg/kg/hr IV | ICU only. Severe withdrawal | | Tizanidine | 2-4 mg PO q6-8h | Alternative alpha-2 agonist | | Gabapentin | 300-600 mg PO

nodes.title: MOUD Considerations
nodes.summary: Xylazine does NOT block buprenorphine — MOUD still works for opioid component; start both simultaneously
nodes.body: MOUD = Medications for Opioid Use Disorder Key point: Xylazine does NOT block buprenorphine binding — MOUD still works for the opioid component [1][5] Buprenorphine initiation: • Standard COWS-based protocol • Wait for COWS ≥8-12 before dosing • Start 2-4 mg SL, titrate up Methadone: • Can be started in ED under federal exemption (72-hour rule) • Refer to OTP for continuation Counseling points: •

nodes.title: Disposition Assessment
nodes.summary: Discharge if stable 4-6h post-naloxone, HR >50, SBP >90, RR >12; admit if persistent depression or infected wounds
nodes.body: Discharge criteria: • Hemodynamically stable (HR >50, SBP >90) • Adequate respirations (RR >12, SpO₂ >92%) • Ambulatory • Tolerating PO • Wound care plan in place (if applicable) • 4-6 hours post-naloxone without re-sedation Admit criteria: • Persistent respiratory depression • Hemodynamic instability requiring pressors • Stage 2-3 wounds with infection • Severe withdrawal requiring dex infusion •

nodes.title: ED Observation
nodes.summary: Observe 4-6h post-naloxone; continuous SpO2 and vitals q1h; re-dose naloxone if RR <12 or SpO2 <92%
nodes.body: Observation period: 4-6 hours post-naloxone Rationale: • Fentanyl half-life can outlast naloxone • Xylazine effects persist longer • Watch for recurrent respiratory depression Monitoring during observation: • Pulse oximetry continuous • Vitals q1h • LOC checks • Aspiration precautions (elevate HOB) Re-dose naloxone if: • RR <12 • SpO₂ <92% • Increasing sedation

nodes.title: Discharge Planning
nodes.body: Discharge supplies — "Harm Reduction Kit": • Narcan nasal spray (2 doses) • Fentanyl test strips • Xylazine test strips (if available) • Sterile injection supplies • Wound dressings and ointments (if applicable) Resources: • Never Use Alone: 1-800-484-3731 (call before using) • SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 • Local syringe service programs • Low-barrier wound care clinics Follow-up: • W
nodes.recommendation: Discharge with harm reduction supplies, wound care if needed, MOUD referral, and clear return precautions.

nodes.title: Admit — Observation/Telemetry
nodes.body: Admission indications: • Persistent sedation >6 hours • Wound requiring IV antibiotics or serial debridement • Withdrawal management with clonidine (close monitoring needed) • Social concerns (no safe discharge environment) Monitoring: • Telemetry • Vitals q2-4h • Serial wound exams • Symptom reassessment (COWS if opioid component, clinical assessment for xylazine) Consults: • Addiction medicine •
nodes.recommendation: Telemetry admission for observation, wound care, and/or withdrawal management.

nodes.title: ICU Admission
nodes.body: ICU criteria: • Intubated for airway protection • Vasopressor requirement • Dexmedetomidine infusion for severe withdrawal • Stage 3 wounds with sepsis/bacteremia • End-organ dysfunction Emerging concern — Medetomidine: • 100-200x more potent than xylazine • Being detected in some drug supplies • 77.5% of medetomidine withdrawal cases require ICU [5] • Higher sedation, longer recovery, more severe
nodes.recommendation: ICU admission for ongoing hemodynamic support, airway management, or severe xylazine/medetomidine withdrawal.
